question: The device to convert alternating current into direct current is
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Rectification is the process of converting AC to pulsating DC using diodes, which conduct only in forward bias. A half-wave rectifier uses one diode and passes only one half-cycle. A full-wave rectifier uses two diodes with a centre-tapped transformer, or four diodes in a bridge, and passes both half-cycles with the same polarity. The output is still pulsating, so a filter (usually a capacitor) smooths it into steady DC. The reverse conversion, DC to AC, is done by an inverter. Elimination: a transformer works on mutual induction and changes the AC voltage level (step-up or step-down) without changing AC to DC, and it does not work on DC. An alternator is an AC generator that converts mechanical energy into AC. A condenser is an old name for a capacitor, which stores charge, blocks DC and passes AC. Only the rectifier performs AC to DC conversion. Rectifiers are used in battery chargers, power supplies, radio and TV circuits, and electroplating.
explanations: (a) Wrong: a transformer changes the voltage and current of an AC supply by mutual induction. It does not change AC to DC and cannot work on DC.
(b) Correct: a rectifier, made of diodes, allows current in one direction only and so converts AC to DC.
(c) Wrong: an alternator is a generator that produces AC from mechanical energy, which is the opposite of the required conversion.
(d) Wrong: a condenser (capacitor) stores charge and blocks DC. It is used only as a filter to smooth rectifier output.
keyfact: Rectifier converts AC to DC; inverter converts DC to AC; transformer changes AC voltage only.
option_notes: Transformer: a static device working on Faraday's law of mutual induction. It steps AC voltage up or down, with power nearly constant (V1/V2 = N1/N2). It is used in power transmission and has high efficiency of about 95-99%. Losses are copper, iron (eddy current and hysteresis) and flux leakage. It does not work on DC.

Rectifier: a circuit that converts AC to pulsating DC using p-n junction diodes. Types are half-wave, full-wave centre-tap and bridge rectifiers. The ripple is smoothed by a capacitor or LC filter. Full-wave output frequency is twice the input frequency. Used in chargers, adapters and power supplies. The reverse device is an inverter.

Alternator: an AC generator based on electromagnetic induction. Mechanical energy rotates a rotor (field) inside a stator (armature) and produces AC. Power stations use synchronous alternators driven by turbines. India's mains frequency is 50 Hz. Car alternators produce AC, which is then rectified to charge the battery. A dynamo produces DC.

Condenser: the older name for a capacitor, a device that stores electric charge and energy in an electric field between two plates separated by a dielectric. Capacitance is measured in farads (C = Q/V). It blocks DC and passes AC. It is used in filters, tuning circuits and power factor correction. 'Condenser' also means a heat-exchanger that turns vapour into liquid.
related: Inverter converts DC to AC.
Transformer works only on AC, by mutual induction.
Dynamo produces DC; alternator produces AC.
Full-wave rectifier output frequency is twice the input frequency.
India's AC supply is 50 Hz, 230 V.
RMS value of AC = peak value/√2.
A capacitor is used to filter the ripple in rectifier output.
Fleming's right-hand rule applies to generators.
summary: The answer is (b) Rectifier. A rectifier uses unidirectional conducting devices such as diodes to convert alternating current (AC), which periodically reverses direction, into direct current (DC), which flows in one direction only.
topic_notes: Current electricity can be direct (DC) or alternating (AC). DC flows in a constant direction, as from cells and batteries. AC reverses direction periodically, and India's supply is 230 V at 50 Hz, so the direction changes 100 times per second. AC is preferred for long-distance transmission because transformers can easily step its voltage up and down, which reduces I²R losses. Key devices: the rectifier (AC to DC), the inverter (DC to AC), the transformer (changes AC voltage), the dynamo (DC generator), the alternator (AC generator), the capacitor (stores charge), the diode (one-way conductor) and the choke or inductor (opposes AC changes). Rectifier types: half-wave (one diode, ripple frequency equal to input), full-wave (ripple frequency twice the input), and bridge (four diodes). The p-n junction diode is the basis of rectification. Other diodes: Zener (voltage regulation), LED (light emission), photodiode (light detection) and solar cell (photovoltaic). RMS value of AC = peak value/√2, about 0.707 times the peak. An AC ammeter measures the RMS value. A moving-coil galvanometer detects DC, a hot-wire instrument measures AC, and a UPS contains both a rectifier and an inverter. Generators and motors: a motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy, while a generator does the reverse. Fleming's right-hand rule gives generator current direction and the left-hand rule gives motor force direction. Transformer types: step-up (more secondary turns) and step-down (fewer secondary turns).

question: Combustion of a candle is a
subject: General Science
detail: Combustion is a rapid oxidation reaction between a fuel and oxygen that releases energy as heat and usually light. Candle wax is paraffin, a mixture of long-chain alkanes (roughly C20H42 to C40H82). When the wick is lit, heat melts the wax, the molten wax rises up the wick by capillary action, vaporises, and the vapour burns in the flame. The approximate reaction is C25H52 + 38 O2 -> 25 CO2 + 26 H2O + heat. Since the products have lower enthalpy than the reactants, delta H is negative, which is the mark of an exothermic reaction. Melting and vaporising the wax are physical changes, and they happen alongside the chemical change of burning. Burning itself is chemical and irreversible because new substances form. Elimination: (c) is wrong because new substances form. (d) is wrong because heat is released, not absorbed. (a) is wrong because a photochemical reaction needs light to start it, whereas here light is a product. All combustion reactions are exothermic.
explanations: Incorrect: a photochemical reaction is driven by absorbing light, as in photosynthesis or silver bromide decomposing. In a candle, light is emitted, not required.
Correct: burning wax gives CO2 and water and releases heat and light, so delta H is negative.
Incorrect: the burning is a chemical change because new substances form irreversibly. Only the melting of wax is a physical change.
Incorrect: an endothermic reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings, but a burning candle gives heat out.
keyfact: Burning of a candle is a chemical, exothermic (combustion) reaction; only the melting of the wax is a physical change.
option_notes: A photochemical reaction is one that is initiated or driven by absorbing light energy. Examples are photosynthesis, photography (AgBr decomposing), the formation of ozone from oxygen, and the reaction of H2 with Cl2 in sunlight. Light is a reactant or energy source here, unlike in combustion, where it is a product.

An exothermic reaction releases energy, usually as heat, to the surroundings, and has a negative delta H. Examples are combustion, respiration, neutralisation, the slaking of quicklime and rusting. Burning of fuels such as LPG, coal and wax is always exothermic. The reaction mixture feels hot, and the products have lower enthalpy than the reactants.

A physical change alters form, state or appearance, with no new substance formed, and is usually reversible. Examples are melting of ice, boiling of water, dissolving sugar and the melting of wax. In a candle, melting is physical, but burning of the vapour is chemical.

An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings and has a positive delta H. Examples are photosynthesis, thermal decomposition of limestone (CaCO3), dissolving ammonium chloride in water, electrolysis of water and the melting of ice. The surroundings become cooler.
related: All combustion reactions are exothermic.
Hydrogen has the highest calorific value among common fuels.
The outermost zone of a flame is the hottest, being non-luminous with complete combustion.
A yellow, luminous flame is due to incandescent unburnt carbon particles.
Photosynthesis is an endothermic photochemical reaction.
Rusting of iron is a slow exothermic oxidation reaction.
Quicklime reacting with water (slaking) is exothermic.
Candle wax is paraffin, a mixture of higher alkanes.
summary: The answer is (b) Exothermic reaction. Burning a candle oxidises the paraffin wax vapour with oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water, releasing heat and light. Heat is given out to the surroundings, so the reaction is exothermic.
topic_notes: Chemical vs physical changes: a chemical change forms new substances with different properties, is generally irreversible, and involves energy change. A physical change affects only state or shape. In a burning candle both occur: the wax melts and vaporises (physical) and the vapour burns (chemical). Combustion needs three things: fuel, oxygen (a supporter of combustion) and the ignition temperature. Ignition temperature is the minimum temperature at which a substance catches fire. Fire extinguishing works by removing one of these three components. The structure of a flame has three zones: the innermost dark zone of unburnt vapour (coolest), the middle luminous zone with partial combustion (yellow, from glowing unburnt carbon particles), and the outermost non-luminous zone with complete combustion (hottest, blue). Complete combustion gives CO2 and H2O, and incomplete combustion gives CO and soot. Types of combustion: rapid, spontaneous (white phosphorus) and explosive (firecrackers). Calorific value is the heat released on burning 1 kg of fuel, in kJ/kg. Hydrogen has the highest calorific value, about 150000 kJ/kg, and is used as rocket fuel. Other exothermic processes: respiration, neutralisation, dissolving NaOH or conc. H2SO4 in water, and the setting of cement. Endothermic examples: photosynthesis, thermal decomposition and dissolving NH4NO3. Other reaction types: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, and redox, where oxidation means gain of oxygen or loss of electrons.

question: Which of the following is a chemical compound?
subject: General Science
detail: A chemical compound is a pure substance formed when two or more different elements combine chemically in a fixed mass ratio. Its properties differ from those of its constituents, and it can be split only by chemical means. An element consists of one kind of atom only, such as O2 (molecular oxygen) or Hg (mercury, the only metal liquid at room temperature). A mixture, such as air, contains substances physically combined in variable proportions, which can be separated by physical methods like fractional distillation of liquid air. Ammonia (NH3) is formed from nitrogen and hydrogen in the Haber-Bosch process (about 200 atm, 450 C, iron catalyst), giving a fixed N:H mass ratio of 14:3. Elimination: air is a mixture (about 78% N2, 21% O2, 0.9% Ar, 0.04% CO2). Oxygen is a diatomic element. Mercury is a metallic element with symbol Hg. Only ammonia fits the definition of a compound.
explanations: Wrong: air is a homogeneous mixture of gases (N2, O2, Ar, CO2 and others) in variable proportions, not a compound.
Wrong: oxygen is an element (O2, atomic number 8), made of one kind of atom, so it is not a compound.
Correct: ammonia (NH3) is a compound of nitrogen and hydrogen combined chemically in a fixed ratio of 1:3 by atoms.
Wrong: mercury (Hg, atomic number 80) is a metallic element and the only common liquid metal at room temperature.
keyfact: Ammonia (NH3) is a compound; air is a mixture; oxygen and mercury are elements.
option_notes: Air is a homogeneous mixture of gases: about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.93% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide, plus traces of neon, helium, methane and water vapour. Its composition varies with place and conditions. Its components can be separated physically, for example by fractional distillation of liquid air. It is not a pure substance, so it is not a compound.

Oxygen is a non-metallic element with symbol O and atomic number 8. It exists as diatomic O2 and as ozone (O3), its allotrope. It was discovered by Priestley and Scheele, and Lavoisier named it. It supports combustion and respiration, and makes up about 21% of air by volume and about 46% of the Earth's crust by mass.

Ammonia is NH3, a colourless gas with a pungent smell, very soluble in water, and its solution is basic. It is made industrially by the Haber-Bosch process from N2 and H2 at about 450 C and 200 atm with an iron catalyst. It is used for fertilisers such as urea, for refrigeration, and for making nitric acid. Its molecule is pyramidal.

Mercury is a metallic element with symbol Hg (from Latin hydrargyrum) and atomic number 80. It is the only metal liquid at room temperature, has high density (13.6 g/cm3), and is toxic. It is used in thermometers, barometers and amalgams. The Minamata disease in Japan was caused by mercury poisoning, and the Minamata Convention (2013) regulates it.
related: Air is a mixture, not a compound, with nitrogen at about 78%.
Water (H2O) is a compound: hydrogen and oxygen combine in a mass ratio of 1:8.
Mercury and bromine are the only two elements liquid at room temperature.
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, and bronze of copper and tin.
Haber process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst.
Law of definite proportions was given by Proust.
Ozone (O3) is an allotrope of oxygen.
summary: The answer is (c) Ammonia. Ammonia (NH3) is a chemical compound made of nitrogen and hydrogen chemically combined in a fixed 1:3 ratio, whereas air is a mixture and oxygen and mercury are elements.
topic_notes: Classification of matter: matter divides into pure substances and mixtures. Pure substances are elements (one kind of atom, such as H2, O2, Fe, Hg) and compounds (two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, such as H2O, NH3, CO2, NaCl). Mixtures may be homogeneous (solutions, air, brass, alloys) or heterogeneous (soil, smoke, milk as a colloid). Key differences: compounds have properties unlike their constituents, a fixed composition (law of definite proportions, Proust), and need chemical methods to separate them. Mixtures keep the properties of their components, have variable composition and can be separated physically (filtration, distillation, evaporation, magnetic separation, chromatography). Common examples: air is a mixture, water is a compound (H2O, with H:O mass ratio 1:8), and brass (Cu and Zn), bronze (Cu and Sn) and steel (Fe and C) are alloys, i.e. homogeneous mixtures. Common gases: nitrogen makes up 78% of air, and carbon dioxide is a compound used in fire extinguishers. Other angles: allotropes (diamond, graphite and fullerene are forms of carbon, and ozone is an allotrope of oxygen), liquid elements (mercury and bromine), and the number of known elements (118). Compound names and formulae: common salt NaCl, baking soda NaHCO3, washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O, quicklime CaO, slaked lime Ca(OH)2, bleaching powder CaOCl2, marble CaCO3.

detail: Distance-time graph questions are answered by reading the graph. The slope of a distance-time line equals speed, so a steeper line means a faster runner. topic_notes: Distance-time graphs plot time on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis. Slope equals speed (distance divided by time). A straight line means uniform speed. A horizontal segment means the object is stationary. A steeper line means higher speed. A curve that steepens means acceleration, and a curve that flattens means deceleration. Where two lines intersect, both objects are at the same position at the same time. If both lines begin at the origin, both start from the same place. If one line begins above the origin, that runner has a head start. If a line begins later on the time axis, that runner has a late start. Average speed equals total distance divided by total time, which is the slope of the line joining the start and end points. The winner is the runner who reaches the finish distance in the least time. Typical exam questions ask for the speed from a given graph, who is ahead at a particular time, when and where one overtakes the other, and how far apart the runners are at a stated time. For relative speed, subtract the speeds when the runners move in the same direction and add them when they move in opposite directions. Always read the axis scales carefully, because unequal units can mislead. Practise converting km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18.

question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Nuclear Power Programme of India :
1. Pressurised heavy water reactors have been set up at Kaiga (Karnataka) and Rawatbhata (Rajasthan).
2. Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre, Kolkata is one of the ﬁve Research Centres under the Department of Science and Technology.
3. India has a vast resource of Thorium and the third stage of Indian Nuclear Power Programme envisages the use of Thorium for power genera on. Which of these statements is/are correct?
subject: General Science
detail: India's three-stage nuclear programme was conceived by Homi J. Bhabha. Stage I uses Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) fuelled by natural uranium, with heavy water as moderator and coolant. Kaiga (Karnataka), Rawatbhata/RAPS (Rajasthan), Narora, Kakrapar, Tarapur and Madras are PHWR sites. Stage II uses Fast Breeder Reactors, with plutonium-239 recovered from Stage I spent fuel; the PFBR at Kalpakkam is the flagship. Stage III uses thorium-232 and U-233 in advanced reactors, for example the AHWR, to exploit India's large thorium reserves in the monazite sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Odisha. India holds roughly a quarter or more of the world's thorium reserves. The Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC), Kolkata, is a constituent unit of the DAE, along with BARC, IGCAR, RRCAT and others. The DST has different institutes, such as the Bose Institute, IIA, and the Birbal Sahni Institute. So statement 2 fails, which eliminates (a), (b) and (d). Only (c) remains.
explanations: Wrong. It says only statement 2 is correct, but 2 is false because VECC is under the DAE, and 1 and 3 are true.
Wrong. It includes statement 2, which is false because VECC is not a DST centre.
Right. Statements 1 and 3 are accurate and statement 2 is inaccurate.
Wrong. It treats all three as correct, but statement 2 wrongly places VECC under the DST.
keyfact: VECC Kolkata is a Department of Atomic Energy unit; PHWRs are Stage I and thorium is Stage III of India's nuclear programme.
option_notes: Statement 2 alone. VECC Kolkata is a DAE unit that runs cyclotrons for nuclear physics research and for producing medical isotopes. It is not part of the DST. DST institutes include the Bose Institute, IIA Bengaluru, the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology, BSIP Lucknow and the S.N. Bose National Centre. This option fails because it omits true statements and relies on a false one.

Statements 1 and 2. Statement 1 is true: PHWRs run at Kaiga and Rawatbhata. Statement 2 is false because VECC belongs to the DAE. India's PHWR fleet is operated by NPCIL, and the standard indigenous designs are 220, 540 and 700 MWe. This option is wrong because it includes statement 2.

Statements 1 and 3. This is the correct combination. PHWRs at Kaiga and Rawatbhata form Stage I, and thorium use in Stage III is the long-term goal of Bhabha's three-stage plan. Stage II is the fast breeder programme at Kalpakkam, using the 500 MWe PFBR operated by BHAVINI.

Statements 1, 2 and 3. It would be right only if VECC were under the DST. VECC is actually one of the DAE's research centres, along with BARC, IGCAR and RRCAT. DAE reports directly to the Prime Minister, and its 'Atomic Energy Commission' is chaired by the DAE Secretary.
related: Bhabha's three-stage nuclear programme was formulated in 1954.
The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (500 MWe) is at Kalpakkam, developed by BHAVINI.
Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu) uses Russian VVER pressurised water reactors.
Tarapur was India's first nuclear power station (BWR, 1969).
KAMINI at Kalpakkam is a U-233 fuelled research reactor.
Uranium is mined at Jaduguda (Jharkhand) by UCIL.
VECC is in Kolkata and belongs to the DAE.
The Atomic Energy Commission was established in 1948.
statements: 1 — Correct: PHWRs operate at Kaiga and Rawatbhata. PHWRs are the backbone of Stage I and use natural uranium with heavy water as moderator and coolant. Rawatbhata (RAPS) in Rajasthan started with the Canadian-assisted CANDU-type RAPS-1 in 1973. Kaiga in Karnataka has four 220 MWe units, and Kaiga-1 and Kaiga-2 became operational around 2000. Other PHWR sites are Narora, Kakrapar, Madras (Kalpakkam) and Tarapur. The newer 700 MWe indigenous PHWRs are at Kakrapar and Rawatbhata. The Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd (NPCIL) operates them.

2 — Incorrect: VECC Kolkata is a unit of the Department of Atomic Energy, not the DST. VECC at Bidhannagar, Kolkata, was set up in the 1970s and built a K-130 variable energy cyclotron, and later a superconducting cyclotron. It does research in nuclear physics, accelerator technology and radiopharmaceuticals (medical cyclotron). It also helped with the ALICE experiment at CERN. DAE research units include BARC, IGCAR, RRCAT, VECC and the Atomic Minerals Directorate (AMD). DST instead runs bodies like SERB, the Bose Institute and the Indian Institute of Astrophysics.

3 — Correct: India has vast thorium resources and Stage III envisages thorium-based power. Thorium-232 is fertile and converts to fissile U-233 through neutron capture. Monazite sands on the coasts of Kerala (Chavara), Tamil Nadu and Odisha, and in Andhra Pradesh, hold very large reserves. The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is being developed at BARC as a thorium-fuelled design. The KAMINI reactor at Kalpakkam uses U-233 fuel. IREL (India) Ltd handles processing of monazite. Bhabha's 1954 plan set out this three-stage sequence.
summary: The answer is (c), 1 and 3. Statements 1 and 3 are correct: PHWRs operate at Kaiga and Rawatbhata, and Stage III of India's programme is built around thorium. Statement 2 is wrong because VECC Kolkata is a unit of the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), not the Department of Science and Technology.
topic_notes: India's nuclear programme follows Homi Bhabha's three-stage plan (1954), designed to use limited uranium and large thorium reserves. Stage I: PHWRs, natural uranium fuel, heavy water as moderator and coolant, producing plutonium as by-product. Stage II: Fast Breeder Reactors using Pu-239 and U-238, with a blanket of thorium to produce U-233. The 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor is at Kalpakkam, built by BHAVINI. Stage III: thorium/U-233 reactors, including the AHWR. Institutions: the Department of Atomic Energy (set up 1954) and the Atomic Energy Commission (1948). BARC at Trombay; IGCAR at Kalpakkam; RRCAT at Indore; VECC at Kolkata; NPCIL builds and operates power reactors; the Uranium Corporation of India Ltd (UCIL) mines uranium at Jaduguda; IREL handles rare earths and monazite; and the Heavy Water Board produces heavy water. The first reactor was Apsara (1956), then CIRUS (1960) and Dhruva. Tarapur (1969) was India's first commercial plant and uses BWRs. Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu has Russian VVER-1000 reactors (PWR type). India's 123 Agreement with the US was signed in 2007-08, the NSG waiver came in 2008, and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act is from 2010. India has a 'no first use' policy and the Nuclear Doctrine from 2003. Thorium is found mainly in monazite sands along the coasts of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. Potential angles: the Kakrapar and Rawatbhata 700 MWe fleet-mode reactors, plans for Small Modular Reactors, and the Atomic Energy Act of 1962.

question: Carbohydrates are stored in the body as
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Carbohydrates in food (starch, sucrose, lactose) are digested to monosaccharides, chiefly glucose, which is absorbed in the small intestine. Glucose is used for immediate energy through glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. Surplus glucose is converted into glycogen by glycogenesis (enzyme glycogen synthase, stimulated by insulin). Glycogen is a highly branched polymer of alpha-D-glucose with alpha-1,4 and alpha-1,6 linkages, often called animal starch. The liver holds about 100-120 g and uses it to maintain blood glucose through glycogenolysis (stimulated by glucagon and adrenaline). Muscle holds about 300-400 g and uses it locally for contraction, because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. When glycogen stores are full, excess glucose is converted to fat (triglycerides) in adipose tissue. Elimination: starch is the plant reserve, so (b) is wrong. Glucose circulates in the blood as a transport and fuel molecule and is not the storage form, so (c) is wrong. 'Sugars' is a general term for the small soluble carbohydrates and these are not stored as such, so (a) is wrong. Only glycogen fits the question.
explanations: Wrong: 'sugars' are simple soluble carbohydrates such as glucose, fructose and sucrose. They are absorbed, circulated and used, not stored as such in the body.
Wrong: starch is the reserve carbohydrate of plants, stored in seeds, roots and tubers. Humans eat and digest it, but do not store it.
Wrong: glucose is the blood sugar and the immediate fuel. Only small amounts remain free in blood, normally about 70-110 mg/dL fasting. The stored form is its polymer.
Correct: glycogen is the storage polysaccharide of animals, held mainly in the liver and muscles, and made from surplus glucose by glycogenesis.
keyfact: Carbohydrates are stored in the body as glycogen (liver and muscles); plants store starch.
option_notes: Sugars are the sweet, water-soluble carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose) and disaccharides (sucrose, lactose, maltose). They give quick energy. Table sugar is sucrose, milk sugar is lactose, and fruit sugar is fructose. They are not the body's long-term carbohydrate store.

Starch is a polysaccharide of alpha-glucose made of amylose (unbranched) and amylopectin (branched). It is the plant reserve food, made in photosynthesis and stored in cereals, potatoes and legumes. It gives a blue-black colour with iodine. It is digested by salivary and pancreatic amylase.

Glucose is a monosaccharide (C6H12O6), also called dextrose or blood sugar. It is the main cell fuel and the only fuel the brain normally uses. Blood level is regulated by insulin, which lowers it, and by glucagon, which raises it. Diabetes mellitus is the disorder of its regulation.

Glycogen is a highly branched glucose polymer, called animal starch. It is stored in the liver (about 6-8% of liver weight) and in muscles. It is made by glycogenesis and broken down by glycogenolysis. Liver glycogen maintains blood sugar. Muscle glycogen fuels exercise. It was discovered by Claude Bernard in 1857.
related: Glycogen is the animal reserve carbohydrate; starch is the plant reserve.
Glycogenesis forms glycogen from glucose; glycogenolysis breaks it down.
Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.
Liver glycogen maintains blood sugar; muscle glycogen serves the muscle itself.
Cellulose is the most abundant organic compound on Earth, and humans cannot digest it.
Carbohydrates and proteins give 4 kcal/g; fats give 9 kcal/g.
Starch gives a blue-black colour with iodine.
summary: The answer is (d) Glycogen. In humans and other animals, excess glucose from digested carbohydrates is polymerised into glycogen and stored mainly in the liver and skeletal muscles. Starch is the storage form in plants, not in the body.
topic_notes: Carbohydrates are compounds of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, usually in the ratio Cn(H2O)n. They are classified into monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose), disaccharides (sucrose = glucose + fructose, lactose = glucose + galactose, maltose = glucose + glucose) and polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin). Energy value is about 4 kcal per gram, against 9 kcal for fat and 4 kcal for protein. Carbohydrates should supply about 55-60% of daily energy. Digestion starts in the mouth with salivary amylase, continues with pancreatic amylase, and is completed by brush-border enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase). Absorbed glucose goes through the hepatic portal vein to the liver. Insulin from the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans promotes glucose uptake and glycogenesis. Glucagon from the alpha cells promotes glycogenolysis. Gluconeogenesis is the making of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources such as amino acids and glycerol. Cellulose is the structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls, and humans cannot digest it, but it acts as dietary fibre. Chitin forms the exoskeleton of arthropods and fungal cell walls. Lactose intolerance is due to lactase deficiency. Deficiency of carbohydrate and protein together causes marasmus, and protein deficiency with adequate calories causes kwashiorkor. Excess carbohydrate is converted to fat. Glycogen storage diseases include Von Gierke disease (type I) and Pompe disease (type II).

question:
Bacteria and viruses cause
(a) Allergies
(b) Non-communicable diseases
(c) Degenerative diseases
(d) Infectious diseases
Consider the following statements:
1. A ran throughout the given period of me with
uniform velocity.
2. A ran throughout the given period of me with
uniform accelera on.
3. B stopped running a er 2 hours.
4. A ran faster than B near the 2-hr stage.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
(a) 2 and 3
(b) 1, 3 and 4
(c) 4 only
(d) 1, 2, 3 and 4
subject: General Science
detail: Infectious (communicable) diseases are caused by pathogens: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and helminths. Bacterial diseases include tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, diphtheria, pertussis, plague, leprosy and anthrax. Viral diseases include polio, measles, mumps, rabies, dengue, hepatitis A/B, influenza, COVID-19, HIV/AIDS, chickenpox and smallpox (eradicated 1980). Allergies are hypersensitive immune reactions to harmless substances such as pollen or dust, and are not caused by pathogens. Non-communicable diseases (diabetes, cancer, hypertension, heart disease) do not spread from person to person. Degenerative diseases (osteoarthritis, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's) result from progressive wear or loss of function of tissues, ageing and genetics. Elimination: the question asks about pathogens, so only 'infectious' fits. Antibiotics act on bacteria but not on viruses; viral infections are prevented mainly by vaccines and treated with antivirals.
explanations: Wrong: allergies are immune over-reactions to allergens such as pollen, dust or certain foods, and are not caused by bacteria or viruses.
Wrong: non-communicable diseases do not spread from person to person, whereas bacterial and viral diseases are transmissible.
Wrong: degenerative diseases come from progressive deterioration of tissues, ageing or genetics, not from pathogens.
Correct: bacteria and viruses are pathogens, and the diseases they cause are infectious (communicable).
keyfact: Bacteria and viruses are pathogens that cause infectious (communicable) diseases.
option_notes: Allergy is a hypersensitivity reaction of the immune system to a normally harmless antigen (allergen). It involves IgE antibodies, mast cells and histamine release. Examples are hay fever, asthma, food allergy, urticaria and anaphylaxis. Treatment uses antihistamines, steroids and adrenaline for severe cases. It is not infectious.

Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are chronic conditions that do not pass from person to person. They include cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes and chronic respiratory disease. Main risk factors are tobacco, alcohol, poor diet and inactivity. India runs the NP-NCD programme (NPCDCS), and NCDs are the leading cause of death globally.

Degenerative diseases involve progressive loss of structure or function of cells, tissues or organs, usually with age. Examples are osteoarthritis, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, macular degeneration and atherosclerosis. Causes include ageing, genetics and lifestyle. They are non-infectious and generally have no cure, only management.

Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, worms) and may be transmitted by air, water, food, contact, vectors or body fluids. Control relies on sanitation, vaccination, vector control, antibiotics and antivirals. They are the same as communicable diseases, and their outbreaks can be epidemics or pandemics.
related: Polio is a viral disease; India was certified polio-free in 2014.
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium and transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito.
Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses.
Smallpox was declared eradicated by WHO in 1980.
Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Dengue is a viral disease spread by Aedes aegypti.
Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine (smallpox, 1796).
summary: The question asked is 'Bacteria and viruses cause ...'. The answer is (d) Infectious diseases, because bacteria and viruses are pathogens that invade the body, multiply and spread from person to person or via vectors, water, food and air. The statements about runners A and B depend on a distance-time graph that is missing from the OCR, so they cannot be evaluated and have been left out.
topic_notes: Diseases are classed as communicable (infectious) or non-communicable. Pathogens: bacteria are prokaryotes treated with antibiotics; viruses are acellular, need a host cell and are not affected by antibiotics. Bacterial diseases: TB (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), cholera (Vibrio cholerae), typhoid (Salmonella typhi), leprosy (M. leprae), plague (Yersinia pestis), tetanus, diphtheria, whooping cough, anthrax, syphilis, gonorrhoea. Viral diseases: polio, measles, mumps, rubella, rabies, dengue, chikungunya, hepatitis, influenza, HIV, COVID-19, smallpox. Protozoan diseases: malaria (Plasmodium, female Anopheles), amoebiasis, sleeping sickness, kala-azar. Fungal: ringworm, athlete's foot. Helminth: filariasis, ascariasis. Vaccines: Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine (1796), Louis Pasteur the rabies vaccine, and Salk and Sabin the polio vaccines. India was declared polio-free in 2014. Smallpox was eradicated in 1980. Deficiency diseases (scurvy, rickets, beriberi) come from lack of nutrients. Genetic diseases include haemophilia, sickle-cell anaemia and thalassemia. Lifestyle diseases include diabetes and hypertension. The Universal Immunization Programme in India began in 1985. Antibiotics: Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.

question:
Substances which are obtained from micro
organisms but used to destroy micro organisms
are
(a) Antigens
(b) An bio cs
(c) An bodies
(d) An sep cs
Directions: The following Two (8 & 9) items consist
of two statements, one labelled the 'Assertion (A)
and the other labelled the 'Reason (R)'. You are to
examine these two statements carefully and
decide if the Assertion (A) and the Reason (R) are
individually true and if so, whether the Reason (R)
is a correct explana on of the Assertion (A). Select
your answers to these items using the Codes given.
below and mark your answer-sheet accordingly
Codes:
(a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct
explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct
explanation of A
(c) A is true but R is false
(d) A is false but R
subject: Computers
detail: An antibiotic is a metabolite made by one microorganism that, at low concentration, kills or stops the growth of other microorganisms. The term 'antibiosis' was coined by Vuillemin, and Selman Waksman later popularised the word 'antibiotic'. Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 from the mold Penicillium notatum. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain developed it for clinical use around 1940, and the three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize. Streptomycin, from Streptomyces griseus, was discovered by Waksman in 1943 and was the first effective drug against tuberculosis. Other examples are tetracycline, chloramphenicol, erythromycin and gentamicin. Antibiotics act on bacteria and are not effective against viruses. Overuse leads to antimicrobial resistance. Elimination: antigens are foreign substances that trigger an immune response. Antibodies are proteins made by the host's B-lymphocytes (plasma cells), not by microorganisms. Antiseptics are chemicals applied to living tissue to prevent infection, and they are usually synthetic and not obtained from microbes. Only antibiotics are both microbial in origin and used to destroy microbes.
explanations: Wrong: antigens are substances, often parts of pathogens, that provoke antibody production. They do not destroy microorganisms.
Correct: antibiotics are made by microorganisms (fungi, bacteria, actinomycetes) and used to kill or inhibit other microorganisms.
Wrong: antibodies are immunoglobulin proteins produced by the host's plasma cells, not obtained from microorganisms.
Wrong: antiseptics are chemicals applied to skin or tissue to stop microbial growth. They are generally not derived from microorganisms.
keyfact: Antibiotics are made by microbes and used to kill other microbes; penicillin (Fleming, 1928) was the first.
option_notes: Antigens are molecules, usually proteins or polysaccharides on pathogens, pollen or transplanted cells, that the immune system recognises as foreign. They stimulate B and T cells to respond. Vaccines contain antigens, in the form of weakened or killed pathogens or their parts, to build immunity. They do not kill microbes themselves.

Antibiotics are microbial metabolites that kill (bactericidal) or inhibit (bacteriostatic) other microbes. Penicillin was discovered by Fleming in 1928, and streptomycin by Waksman in 1943. They are ineffective against viruses, and misuse causes resistant strains such as MRSA. Broad-spectrum examples are tetracycline and chloramphenicol.

Antibodies, or immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD), are Y-shaped proteins made by plasma cells derived from B-lymphocytes. They bind specific antigens and neutralise or mark them for destruction. IgG is the most abundant and crosses the placenta. IgA is found in milk and mucosal secretions. They are produced by the host, not by microbes.

Antiseptics are chemicals that prevent the growth of microbes on living tissue, such as skin, wounds and mucous membranes. Examples are dettol, tincture of iodine, boric acid, hydrogen peroxide and povidone-iodine. Disinfectants are stronger and are used on non-living surfaces. Phenol was introduced as an antiseptic by Joseph Lister.
related: Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 from Penicillium notatum.
Streptomycin, from Streptomyces griseus, was discovered by Selman Waksman in 1943 and is used against TB.
Antibiotics do not work against viruses.
Antibodies are proteins made by plasma cells (B-lymphocytes).
Antiseptics are used on living tissue; disinfectants on non-living objects.
Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796.
Salvarsan, made by Paul Ehrlich, was a synthetic drug against syphilis.
Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for penicillin.
summary: The answer is (b) Antibiotics. Antibiotics are chemical substances produced by microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi and actinomycetes, and they kill or inhibit other microorganisms. Antigens, antibodies and antiseptics do not fit this description.
topic_notes: Antibiotics are secondary metabolites of microorganisms that act against other microorganisms. Fleming noticed in 1928 that Penicillium notatum inhibited Staphylococcus colonies. Florey and Chain purified penicillin in 1940, and all three received the 1945 Nobel Prize. Waksman discovered streptomycin in 1943 and received the 1952 Nobel Prize. Sources: Penicillium (penicillin), Streptomyces (streptomycin, tetracycline, erythromycin), Bacillus (bacitracin, polymyxin), Cephalosporium (cephalosporins). Penicillin acts by inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis. Tetracyclines and aminoglycosides inhibit protein synthesis. Antibiotics do not work against viruses, so colds and flu are not treated by them. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) comes from overuse and incomplete courses, and India's National Action Plan on AMR was launched in 2017. Related terms: antiseptic (applied to living tissue), disinfectant (applied to inanimate objects), antigen (immune trigger), antibody (host protein), vaccine (prepared antigen), antitoxin (antibody that neutralises toxin), and antipyretic (reduces fever). Interferons are proteins released by virus-infected cells that give resistance to other cells. Paul Ehrlich developed Salvarsan (arsphenamine) in 1909 against syphilis, an early chemotherapeutic, but it is synthetic and not a true antibiotic. Sulpha drugs are synthetic antibacterials, discovered by Domagk (Prontosil, 1930s). Vaccination was pioneered by Edward Jenner (smallpox, 1796) and Louis Pasteur (rabies, anthrax).

question:
Assertion (A): A bus and a car (with lower
weight than that of the bus) moving at the same
velocity, are brought to rest on a level road by
applying brakes which exert same retarding force.
The car will travel lesser distance before coming to
rest.
Reason (R): The kine c energy to be destroyed is
equal to the work done by the retarding force.
subject: General Science
detail: This is the work-energy theorem applied to braking. Work done by the retarding force (F × d) equals the kinetic energy lost (½mv²). So d = mv²/(2F). With v and F equal for both vehicles, d is directly proportional to mass m. The car has less mass, hence less kinetic energy to be destroyed, hence a shorter stopping distance. Assertion A is therefore true. Reason R states the work-energy principle, which is true and is exactly the step that gives the result, so it is the correct explanation. Equivalent kinematic approach: deceleration a = F/m is larger for the car, and d = v²/(2a) is smaller. Note that in real life brake force often scales with weight through friction (F = μmg), in which case stopping distance becomes v²/(2μg), independent of mass; but the question explicitly fixes the same retarding force, so mass matters. Elimination: option (b) would require R not to explain A, (c) would need A false, (d) would need A to be true and R false or both false. None applies because both statements are true and linked. The options in the OCR are the standard A/R choices, with (a) meaning both true and R the correct explanation.
explanations: Correct: A is true (d = mv²/2F, smaller m gives smaller d) and R is the work-energy relation that directly explains it.
Wrong: this would hold only if R were true but not the explanation; here R is exactly the reason for A.
Wrong: this would need A true and R false, but R is a true statement of the work-energy theorem.
Wrong: this would need A false, but the car does stop in a shorter distance under equal force and speed.
keyfact: Stopping distance d = mv²/(2F): for equal speed and braking force, the lighter vehicle stops sooner.
option_notes: Option (a) in an Assertion-Reason item means both A and R are individually true and R is the correct explanation of A. This is the standard first choice in UPSC-style A/R questions, and the pattern appears often in physics questions on mechanics and energy.

Option (b) in an Assertion-Reason item means both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. It is chosen when the two statements are both facts but are logically unrelated or only loosely related.
Option (c) in an Assertion-Reason item usually means A is true but R is false. It is chosen when the main claim is correct but the supporting reason contains an error.

Option (d) in an Assertion-Reason item usually means A is false but R is true. It is chosen when the main claim is wrong though the reason stated is a valid fact. Check the exact wording in the paper, as the order can vary.
related: Work-energy theorem: net work equals change in kinetic energy.
Kinetic energy = ½mv²; doubling velocity quadruples KE.
Stopping distance d = v²/(2a) for uniform deceleration.
SI unit of work and energy is joule; of power is watt.
KE in terms of momentum: p²/2m.
With friction braking F = μmg, stopping distance is independent of mass.
1 horsepower ≈ 746 watts.
summary: The answer is (a): both A and R are true and R explains A. Same retarding force F and same initial speed mean stopping distance d = KE/F = mv²/(2F), so the lighter car, with less kinetic energy, stops in a shorter distance than the bus.
topic_notes: Work, energy and power form a core part of the physics syllabus. Work W = F·d·cosθ, measured in joules (1 J = 1 N·m). Kinetic energy = ½mv². Potential energy near Earth = mgh. The work-energy theorem says that the net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy. For braking: F·d = ½mv², so d = mv²/(2F). Stopping distance is proportional to mass for a fixed force and to the square of velocity: doubling speed quadruples the stopping distance. Using kinematics, a = F/m and v² = 2ad give the same result. In practice friction braking force is μmg, so stopping distance is v²/(2μg), independent of mass. This is why the same road conditions give the same stopping distance for heavy and light vehicles if tyres grip equally. Momentum p = mv; for the same stopping force, stopping time t = mv/F is also proportional to mass. Kinetic energy is converted into heat in the brake pads, and regenerative braking recovers part of it as electrical energy. Related ideas include the law of conservation of energy, power P = W/t (watt, 1 horsepower ≈ 746 W), and the relationship between kinetic energy and momentum: KE = p²/2m. Common numerical questions ask for the ratio of stopping distances for different masses or speeds, and the effect of a changed velocity on KE.

question:
Assertion (A): A train has come out of the
platform and is accelera ng. If a person si ng in
the train and facing engine, throws up a coin, it will
fall ahead of him.
Reason (R): A force acts on the coin whose
magnitude is equal to the product of the mass of
the coin and accelera on of the train.
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a question on inertia and non-inertial frames. When the person throws the coin straight up, the coin already has the train's forward velocity. Once it leaves the hand, the only real force on it is gravity, which is vertical. There is no horizontal force, so its horizontal velocity stays constant (Newton's first law). The train, however, keeps accelerating forward, so during the coin's flight the train moves farther forward than the coin. The coin therefore lands behind the thrower, which makes A false. In the train's own frame, which is non-inertial, an observer explains this by a pseudo (fictitious) force of magnitude m×a acting backward on the coin. R says a force equal to mass times the train's acceleration acts on the coin. This is true as a description of the pseudo force, though it is not a real force and it acts backward, not forward. R is therefore accepted as true, and it explains why the coin falls behind, which contradicts A. If the train moved at uniform velocity, the coin would land back in the thrower's hand. If the train were decelerating, the coin would land ahead.
explanations: Wrong: this option needs A to be true, but the coin falls behind, not ahead.
Wrong: A is false, so 'both true' cannot hold, whether or not R explains A.
Wrong: A is not true; the coin lands behind the person. This option says A is true and R is false, which is the reverse of the actual position.
Correct: A is false because the coin lands behind the person. R is true as the pseudo force m×a in the train's frame.
keyfact: In an accelerating train a coin tossed up lands behind the thrower, because a pseudo force of magnitude m×a acts backward in the train's frame.
option_notes: Option (a) means both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. It is chosen when the reason actually explains the assertion. Here it fails because A itself is false.
Option (b) means both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. It is used when the two statements are independently true but unrelated in cause.
Option (c) means A is true but R is false. It is chosen when the assertion holds and the reason is wrong.

Option (d) means A is false but R is true. It is chosen when the assertion is incorrect while the reason is a valid statement. This matches the question: the coin lands behind the person, and the force m×a is a valid description of the pseudo force.
related: Inertia is the property of a body to resist change in its state of rest or uniform motion; mass is its measure.
Pseudo force = −m×a, acting opposite to the frame's acceleration, and appears only in non-inertial frames.
In uniform motion a coin tossed up in a train falls back into the thrower's hand.
In a lift accelerating upward the apparent weight is m(g+a); in free fall it is zero.
Newton's first law is also called the law of inertia, and the second law gives F = ma.
Centrifugal force is a pseudo force seen in a rotating frame.
The SI unit of force is the newton, 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
statements: A — Incorrect: the coin falls behind the person, not ahead. In the ground frame the coin keeps its horizontal velocity while the train gains speed. This is the same effect as passengers being pushed backward when a bus starts suddenly, which is inertia of motion. For uniform motion the coin returns to the hand. For a decelerating or braking train the coin would land ahead of the thrower. Galileo's relativity principle says that experiments in uniformly moving frames give the same results as at rest.

R — Correct (as a statement of the pseudo force): in the accelerating train's frame, an observer feels a fictitious force F = m×a directed opposite to the train's acceleration. It is not a real force because it has no physical agent. It arises only because the frame is non-inertial. Other examples are the centrifugal force and the Coriolis force. In an inertial (ground) frame this force does not exist. The direction is backward, which is why the coin lands behind the person.
summary: The answer is (d): A is false and R is true. The coin keeps the train's horizontal velocity from the moment it is thrown, while the train speeds up beneath it. So the coin lands behind the person, not ahead. R describes the pseudo force m×a seen from the accelerating train.
topic_notes: Newton's first law (inertia) says a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless an external force acts on it. Inertia has three kinds: inertia of rest, of motion and of direction. Passengers lurch backward when a bus starts, forward when it brakes, and outward on a sharp turn. Newton's second law gives F = ma, and momentum is p = mv. An inertial frame is one that is unaccelerated, and Newton's laws hold in it directly. A non-inertial frame is accelerated. To apply Newton's laws there, a pseudo force of magnitude m×a is added, directed opposite to the frame's acceleration. Examples are the backward push felt in an accelerating car, the apparent weight change in a lift, and the centrifugal force in a rotating frame. Lift cases: accelerating upward gives apparent weight m(g+a); accelerating downward gives m(g−a); free fall gives zero apparent weight. For a ball thrown up in a train moving at uniform velocity, it returns to the thrower's hand because the horizontal velocity is shared. For an accelerating train it lands behind; for a retarding train it lands ahead. For projectile motion, the horizontal velocity is constant and the vertical motion has acceleration g. For a train taking a curve, the ball deviates toward the outer side of the curve. Related future questions could cover Newton's third law, the impulse–momentum theorem, friction, circular motion and centripetal force.

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. Intel's Pen um IV is an opera ng system used
in PCs.
2. During boo ng period of a PC, the opera ng
system is ﬁrst loaded.
3. Analogue computers are useful only in
scien ﬁc ﬁeld while digital computers have
application in scien ﬁc as well as in business,
administrative functions.
4. Micro-computer is another name for microprocessor.
Which of these statements are correct?
(a) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(b) 2 and 3

(a) Median

subject: Computers
detail: Booting is the start-up process in which the BIOS/firmware runs POST (power-on self test) and then the bootstrap loader loads the operating system kernel from disk into RAM. So the OS is the first major software loaded, which makes statement 2 acceptable as framed for this exam. Intel's Pentium IV (launched November 2000, NetBurst architecture) is a CPU chip, so statement 1 confuses hardware with system software such as Windows, Linux or Unix. A microprocessor is a single-chip CPU; a microcomputer is a complete small computer (microprocessor plus memory plus I/O), such as a PC, so statement 4 is wrong. Analogue computers process continuous physical quantities (voltage, pressure, temperature) and were used mainly in scientific, engineering and process-control work. Digital computers process discrete binary data and serve scientific, business and administrative uses, so statement 3 matches the standard textbook view. Elimination: 1 is clearly false, which removes (a), (c) and (d), leaving (b). The question paper also carries stray OCR text of an unrelated statistics question (median, second quartile, 5th decile, all equal), which is ignored here.
explanations: Wrong: statements 1 and 4 are false, so not all four can be correct.
Right: only statements 2 and 3 are correct.
Wrong: Pentium IV is not an operating system, and a microcomputer is not the same as a microprocessor.
Wrong: statement 1 and statement 4 are false, even though statement 2 is correct.
keyfact: Pentium IV is a CPU (microprocessor), not an OS; a microcomputer is a complete computer built around a microprocessor.
option_notes: Option (a), all four statements, would need Pentium IV to be an OS and a microcomputer to equal a microprocessor, which is wrong. The Pentium IV was introduced by Intel in 2000 and is a CPU on the NetBurst architecture. Microprocessors such as the Intel 4004 (1971) and 8086 (1978) are single-chip CPUs. Operating systems manage hardware and software resources. Examples include Windows, Linux and macOS.

Option (b), statements 2 and 3, is the correct choice. It reflects that booting loads the OS first, and that analogue computers were mainly scientific while digital computers have broad application. Booting uses the BIOS and POST. Analogue computers handle continuous data and digital ones handle discrete binary data. Hybrid computers combine the two. Digital computers are general purpose and are the dominant type in use today.

Option (c), statements 1 and 4, combines two false claims. Pentium IV is a processor, not an OS. A microcomputer is a complete computer, whereas a microprocessor is the CPU chip inside it. Microprocessors are built using VLSI technology, and the fourth generation of computers is based on them. Intel, AMD and ARM are major processor makers. Popular microcomputers include the PC, laptop and tablet.

Option (d), statements 1, 2 and 4, wrongly includes the two false statements 1 and 4 and omits the true statement 3. The ideas involved are processor versus OS and microprocessor versus microcomputer. The CPU has an ALU, a control unit and registers. A microprocessor is the CPU on one integrated circuit. System software includes the OS, compilers and utilities, while application software includes MS Office and similar tools.
related: Intel 4004 (1971) was the first commercial microprocessor.
Pentium IV was launched by Intel in 2000.
BIOS is stored in ROM and starts the POST at power on.
Cold boot is a start from power off, and warm boot is a restart without power off.
Analogue computers handle continuous data, and digital computers handle binary data.
Hybrid computers combine analogue and digital features, as in ICU monitors.
PARAM is India's series of supercomputers developed by C-DAC.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Pentium IV is a microprocessor, not an operating system. Pentium IV is Intel's seventh-generation x86 CPU, released in 2000 with the NetBurst architecture and clock speeds from 1.3 GHz upward. It succeeded the Pentium III. Operating systems such as Windows XP, Linux and Unix run on it. Intel later replaced the line with Pentium D and Core series processors. Intel's first microprocessor was the 4004 (1971).

2 — Correct: During booting, the bootstrap loader loads the operating system into RAM. When the power is switched on, the BIOS in ROM performs POST, finds the boot device and loads the bootstrap program, which loads the OS kernel into main memory. A cold boot is a start from power off, while a warm boot is a restart using Ctrl+Alt+Del. Booting is the process of starting a computer and getting the OS ready for use. Windows uses the boot sector or MBR.

3 — Correct: Analogue machines were limited mainly to scientific and engineering work, while digital computers are general purpose. Analogue computers measure continuous physical quantities, as in speedometers, thermometers and the old differential analysers, and have limited accuracy. Digital computers count discrete binary digits, have high accuracy and storage, and are used in science, business, banking and administration. Hybrid computers combine both and are used in hospitals (ICU monitors) and in industrial process control.

4 — Incorrect: A microprocessor is only the CPU on a single chip, while a microcomputer is the whole system. A microcomputer contains a microprocessor along with memory (RAM and ROM), input/output units and storage, as in a desktop, laptop or PC. The first microcomputers appeared in the mid-1970s, such as the Altair 8800 (1975). The classes of computer by size are micro, mini, mainframe and supercomputer. India's PARAM is a well-known supercomputer.
summary: The correct option is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct. Pentium IV is a microprocessor (not an operating system), and a microcomputer is a complete computer built around a microprocessor, so statements 1 and 4 are wrong.
topic_notes: Computer basics frequently appear in the EPFO General Awareness and Computers section. Generations: first generation used vacuum tubes (1940-56), second used transistors (1956-63), third used ICs (1964-71), fourth used microprocessors/VLSI (1971 onward), and fifth is based on AI and ULSI. Types by data: analogue (continuous data), digital (discrete data) and hybrid. Types by size: supercomputer (PARAM, Cray), mainframe, minicomputer and microcomputer. Hardware means the physical parts, namely the CPU (ALU, CU, registers), memory (RAM is volatile, ROM is non-volatile), and input/output devices. Software means system software (OS, compilers, assemblers, device drivers, utilities) and application software. The OS manages memory, processes, files and devices. Booting: POST, then the bootstrap loader, then the kernel is loaded into RAM. A cold boot is a start from power off, and a warm boot is a restart. Processors: Intel 4004 (1971) was the first microprocessor, then 8086, 80386, Pentium (1993), Pentium IV (2000), then Core series. Clock speed is measured in Hz (MHz/GHz). Memory units: 1 byte is 8 bits, then KB, MB, GB, TB. Related ideas include the stored-program concept (von Neumann), the BIOS and firmware, and cache memory. Number systems such as binary, octal and hexadecimal are also commonly asked.

question:
Which positional value divides the series
into equal parts?
(d) (ABC/3) + (XYZ/4)
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Positional averages are measures of central tendency defined by position in an ordered series rather than by calculation over all values. The Median divides an ordered series into two equal halves, with 50% of observations on each side. For n observations, the median is the ((n+1)/2)th item when the data are ungrouped. For a continuous series it is L + [(N/2 - cf)/f] x h. Quartiles divide the series into four equal parts (Q1, Q2 = median, Q3). Deciles divide it into ten parts, and percentiles into one hundred. The Mode is the most frequent value and is also a positional average, but it does not split the series. The Mean is a calculated average. The median is not affected by extreme values and can be found graphically from the ogive, where the less-than and more-than curves intersect at the median. In this question the options are corrupted. The only readable fragment, (ABC/3)+(XYZ/4), is a meaningless expression, so the mapping of the correct term to a letter cannot be verified. Elimination by concept leaves the median as the answer.
explanations: Chosen as the best guess: if option (a) holds 'Median', it is correct. The option text is missing from the OCR, so this cannot be confirmed.
Probably wrong if (b) is quartile, mode, mean or similar. Quartiles split into four parts, and the mode and mean do not split the series.
Probably wrong for the same reason. The text is not available to confirm it.
Option (d) reads (ABC/3)+(XYZ/4), which is a formula-like fragment, not a positional value, so it is not the answer.
keyfact: The Median is the positional value that divides an ordered series into two equal parts (Q2 = D5 = P50).
option_notes: Option (a): its text is lost in the OCR. If it is the Median, it is the middle value of an ordered series. It divides the data into two equal halves, is not affected by extreme values, and is found as the ((n+1)/2)th item. It is located graphically from the intersection of the less-than and more-than ogives.

Option (b): its text is lost in the OCR. Possible candidates are the quartile, mode or mean. Quartiles divide the data into four equal parts. The mode is the most frequent value, with the empirical relation Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean. The mean is the arithmetic average.

Option (c): its text is lost in the OCR. Candidates include deciles (ten equal parts) and percentiles (one hundred equal parts). Both are partition values related to the median, since D5 = P50 = Q2 = Median.

Option (d): the text reads (ABC/3)+(XYZ/4), which is not a recognised statistical measure. It appears to be OCR debris from another question or a corrupted option, and it does not represent any positional value.
related: Median divides an ordered series into two equal parts.
Q2 = D5 = P50 = Median.
Empirical relation: Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean.
Quartiles divide data into 4 equal parts; deciles into 10; percentiles into 100.
Median is the best average for open-ended distributions.
Median is found graphically from the intersection of the less-than and more-than ogives.
