summary: The question is garbled by OCR: the positional value that divides a series into two equal parts is the Median, but the option texts are lost and cannot be matched to letters. The most defensible pick is (a), but this is a low-confidence guess and should be checked against the original paper.
topic_notes: Measures of central tendency are the mean (arithmetic, geometric, harmonic), the median and the mode. Positional averages are the median and the mode, and partition values (quartiles, deciles, percentiles) are related to them. The median is the middle value when data are arranged in ascending or descending order. For odd n it is the ((n+1)/2)th item. For even n it is the average of the (n/2)th and (n/2+1)th items. For grouped data, Median = L + [(N/2 - cf)/f] x h. Quartiles Q1, Q2 and Q3 divide the data into four parts, with Q2 equal to the median. Deciles D1 to D9 divide it into ten parts, and percentiles P1 to P99 into one hundred. The median is best for open-ended classes and skewed data, and it is not affected by extreme values. The mean is the most affected by outliers. The mode is the most frequent value and may be unimodal or bimodal. In a symmetric distribution Mean = Median = Mode. For a moderately skewed distribution, Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean (Karl Pearson's empirical relation). Quartile deviation = (Q3 - Q1)/2. Bowley's coefficient of skewness = (Q3 + Q1 - 2 Median)/(Q3 - Q1). Graphically, the median is found from the ogives and the mode from the histogram.

question: A town 'P' is located in a particular district. The town 'A' is west of 'P'. Town 'T' is east of 'P'. Town 'K' is east of 'B' but west of 'T' and 'A'. They are all in the same district. Which town is the farthest west?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a linear direction-ordering (east-west line) reasoning question. Put all towns on a single west-to-east line and place them using each clue. Clue 1: A is west of P, so A < P (taking west as smaller). Clue 2: T is east of P, so P < T. Combined, A < P < T. Clue 3: K is east of B, so B < K. K is west of T and A, so K < A and K < T. Combining everything gives B < K < A < P < T. B is therefore the farthest west, and T the farthest east. Note the OCR'd clue 'west of T and A' is read as K being west of both. Elimination: P is east of A, so it cannot be farthest west. K is east of B, so it is out. A is east of K, so it is out. Only B has no town to its west. Tip: for such questions, draw the line, place the chain of relations step by step, and check which element has nothing before it. Always check whether the clues are consistent before choosing.
explanations: Wrong: P is east of A, and A is east of K and B, so P is near the east end.
Wrong: K is east of B (given), so K cannot be the farthest west.
Correct: the order is B, K, A, P, T from west to east, so B is the westernmost.
Wrong: A is west of P but east of K, and K is east of B, so A is third from the west.
keyfact: Order from west to east is B, K, A, P, T, so B is the farthest west.
option_notes: P is the town given as the reference point. A lies to its west and T to its east. In the final order it is fourth from the west, so only T is further east.
K is east of B but west of A, P and T. It is second from the west, a middle-west position that works as a distractor.
B is the town with no town to its west, since K is east of B and K is west of every other town. It is the westernmost point in the arrangement.
A is west of P but east of K. It is third in the west-to-east order B, K, A, P, T.
related: Sun rises in the east, so morning shadows fall toward the west.
A 90 degree clockwise turn from north faces east.
The north-east direction lies midway between north and east.
In a 3-4-5 walk, the shortest distance from start is 5 units.
Linear order chains: if A<B and B<C then A<C (transitivity).
The four cardinal directions are north, east, south and west; intercardinal ones are NE, SE, SW and NW.
summary: The answer is (c) B. Taking the statements as given, B is the westernmost town, because K lies east of B and K is itself west of A, P and T. The question has a minor inconsistency that is explained below.
topic_notes: Direction sense and linear arrangement questions are a regular feature of the reasoning section. Key method: fix a reference line (west to east on a horizontal line, or north to south on a vertical line), then convert each clue into an inequality such as X < Y meaning X is west of Y. Chain the inequalities to get a full order, and look for the element with no predecessor (farthest in that direction) or no successor (farthest in the opposite direction). Related types UPSC and other exams ask: (1) Distance and direction problems, where a person walks in various directions and you need the final displacement using Pythagoras (for example 3-4-5 triangles). (2) Shadow problems: in the morning the shadow falls to the west, and in the evening to the east, because the sun rises in the east. (3) Turns: a right turn from north faces east, and a left turn from north faces west. A 90 degree clockwise turn goes N to E to S to W. (4) Relative direction such as north-east, which lies between north and east. (5) Ranking and ordering puzzles, where the same inequality-chain method applies. Common pitfalls: misreading 'east of' as 'west of', ignoring that a clue applies to two towns at once ('west of T and A'), and not testing the clues for consistency. Practice drawing the number line and writing the final order, then verifying each clue against it.

question: A factory has three belt conveyors ﬁ ed in its loading sta on. Conveyors 'A' and 'B' opera ng simultaneously li all the goods in the same me during which the goods can be li ed by the conveyor 'C' opera ng alone. Conveyor 'B' li s all the goods five hours faster than conveyor 'A' but four hours slower than the conveyor 'C' The dura ons of me required to li all the goods, individually by the conveyors 'A', 'B' and 'C' are
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a time-and-work question on combined rates. Work rate is the reciprocal of time taken, and rates add when workers operate together. Let B take x hours. The question says B is 5 hours faster than A, so A = x + 5. It also says B is 4 hours slower than C, so C = x − 4. A and B together take the same time as C alone, so 1/(x+5) + 1/x = 1/(x−4). Simplifying gives (2x+5)(x−4) = x(x+5), then 2x² − 3x − 20 = x² + 5x, then x² − 8x − 20 = 0, so (x−10)(x+2) = 0. Time cannot be negative, so x = 10. Hence A = 15, B = 10, C = 6. Check: 1/15 + 1/10 = 2/30 + 3/30 = 5/30 = 1/6, which matches C. In an exam, plug the options in rather than solving the quadratic. Only option (b) has the right differences (15−10 = 5 and 10−6 = 4) and also satisfies the rate equation. The other options fail either the differences or the rate sum, so (b) is the only one that works.
explanations: (a) Wrong. The differences are 17−12 = 5 and 12−8 = 4, which fit, but 1/17 + 1/12 = 29/204 ≈ 0.142, not 1/8 = 0.125.
(b) Correct. The differences are 15−10 = 5 and 10−6 = 4. Also 1/15 + 1/10 = 1/6, so A and B together take exactly C's time.
(c) Wrong. The differences are 5 and 4, which fit, but 1/16 + 1/11 = 27/176 ≈ 0.153, not 1/7 ≈ 0.143.
(d) Wrong. The differences are 5 and 4, which fit, but 1/14 + 1/9 = 23/126 ≈ 0.183, not 1/5 = 0.2.
keyfact: Rates add: 1/A + 1/B = 1/C gives B = 10, so A, B, C = 15, 10, 6 hours.
option_notes: Option (a) gives A = 17, B = 12, C = 8 hours. It has the correct time gaps of 5 and 4 hours, so it is a deliberate distractor. Combined rate of A and B is 29/204 per hour, so they would take about 7.03 hours, not 8 hours. Always test the rate-sum condition and not only the differences. The correct triple is shifted down by 2 hours from this one.

Option (b) gives A = 15, B = 10, C = 6 hours, and it is the correct triple. The quadratic x² − 8x − 20 = 0 has the roots 10 and −2, and only 10 is valid. Combined rate of A and B is 1/15 + 1/10 = 1/6, equal to C's rate. The gaps are 5 hours (A to B) and 4 hours (B to C). Rate is the reciprocal of time, and rates add for simultaneous work.

Option (c) gives A = 16, B = 11, C = 7 hours. The gaps of 5 and 4 hours match the question, but the rate condition fails. 1/16 + 1/11 = 27/176, so A and B together would need about 6.52 hours, while C alone needs 7. It is a near-miss distractor, one hour above the correct triple. Elimination by checking the sum of rates removes it.

Option (d) gives A = 14, B = 9, C = 5 hours. The gaps of 5 and 4 hours match, but 1/14 + 1/9 = 23/126, so A and B together need about 5.48 hours, not 5. The combined rate is lower than C's rate of 1/5. Compare this with the correct triple, which is 1 hour longer for each conveyor. Such shifted series are a common design in these options.
related: Rate of work = 1/time; combined rate = sum of individual rates.
Two workers taking a and b hours together take ab/(a+b) hours.
If A is n times as efficient as B, A takes 1/n of B's time.
In pipes and cisterns, outlet pipes carry a negative rate.
Wages are shared in the ratio of work done by each worker.
If 1/c = 1/a + 1/b, then c is smaller than both a and b.
summary: The answer is (b) 15, 10, 6 hrs. Setting B = x gives A = x + 5 and C = x − 4, and the condition 1/A + 1/B = 1/C reduces to x² − 8x − 20 = 0, so x = 10. That makes A = 15, B = 10 and C = 6.
topic_notes: Time and work rests on a few ideas. Work done = rate × time. Rate = 1/time taken to finish the whole job. Rates of workers operating together add up. If A takes a hours and B takes b hours, together they take ab/(a+b) hours. Efficiency is inversely proportional to time taken, so if A is twice as efficient as B, A takes half the time. Pipes and cisterns follow the same rules: inlet pipes add to the rate and outlet pipes subtract from it. For wages, work is shared in proportion to the work done, which is each person's rate × days worked. Related types are alternate-day work, where you compute the work done in one cycle, and leaving or joining midway, where you compute the work completed in each stage. For problems with 'faster by' and 'slower by' relations, set one unknown x, express the others in terms of x, and form an equation in reciprocals. This usually gives a quadratic, and you reject the negative root. In multiple-choice papers, test the options directly: check the time gaps first, then the reciprocal sum. A useful shortcut is that if two workers together match a third, then 1/c = 1/a + 1/b. Other angles UPSC could ask are two workers finishing in a and b days and the time when one leaves early, the ratio of efficiencies, and the cost sharing of a job. Also revise the time-speed-distance relation of speed = distance/time, where relative speed works like combined rate.

question:
According to a certain code
*
means 'greater than'
+
means 'less than'
÷
means 'equal to'
% means 'plus'
If A * X, B ÷ Z, Y + C; then the relation. between
ABC and XYZ is
(a) ABC + XYZ
(b) (ABC % XYZ) * (2XYZ)
(c) (2XYZ) * (ABC % XYZ)
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a symbol-substitution (coding-decoding of inequalities) question. First replace each symbol with its meaning. '*' is greater than, '+' is less than, '÷' is equal to, and '%' is plus. 'A * X' becomes A > X. 'B ÷ Z' becomes B = Z. 'Y + C' becomes Y < C, which is the same as C > Y. Treat ABC as the sum A+B+C and XYZ as X+Y+Z. When inequalities point the same way, or are equalities, they can be added. So A+B+C > X+Z+Y, which means ABC > XYZ. Now test the options. (a) 'ABC + XYZ' decodes to ABC < XYZ, which is wrong. (b) '(ABC % XYZ) * (2XYZ)' decodes to (ABC + XYZ) > 2XYZ. Subtracting XYZ from both sides gives ABC > XYZ, which is true. (c) '(2XYZ) * (ABC % XYZ)' decodes to 2XYZ > ABC + XYZ, which gives XYZ > ABC and is false. Option (d) is garbled in the OCR, and it would presumably be 'none of these', which is not needed because (b) holds. Always decode first, then simplify. This reading assumes ABC and XYZ denote sums, which is the only reading that lets the options be evaluated.
explanations: (a) is wrong. 'ABC + XYZ' decodes to ABC < XYZ, the opposite of the derived ABC > XYZ.
(b) is right. It decodes to (ABC + XYZ) > 2XYZ, which simplifies to ABC > XYZ, matching the derived relation.
(c) is wrong. It decodes to 2XYZ > ABC + XYZ, which gives XYZ > ABC, the reverse of the true relation.
(d) is wrong. The option text is garbled and appears to be a repeat of the label 'a'. It is not needed because (b) is exactly correct.
keyfact: Decode first: A>X, B=Z, C>Y, so A+B+C > X+Y+Z, which is option (b).
option_notes: Option (a) 'ABC + XYZ' uses the '+' symbol, which in this code means 'less than'. It states ABC < XYZ. In coding-decoding questions the trap is reading the symbols with their usual arithmetic meaning. Always substitute the given meanings before judging. Here it contradicts A>X, B=Z, C>Y, which together force ABC to be greater.

Option (b) '(ABC % XYZ) * (2XYZ)' uses '%' as plus and '*' as greater than. It reads (ABC + XYZ) > 2XYZ. Subtracting XYZ from both sides gives ABC > XYZ, which is what the three given relations imply. The option is a disguised form of the basic conclusion, and such rewriting is a common UPSC device.

Option (c) '(2XYZ) * (ABC % XYZ)' reads 2XYZ > ABC + XYZ. It simplifies to XYZ > ABC. This is the mirror image of option (b) and is the standard distractor, where the two sides of the inequality are swapped. It is false because ABC is actually greater than XYZ.

Option (d) is garbled by OCR, showing '(a) (a)' and appearing to be a repeat of the label. In the original paper it was most likely 'none of these'. Since (b) holds exactly, 'none of these' would be wrong. In such questions, check every option before choosing 'none of these'.
related: Inequalities pointing the same way can be added: a>b, c>d gives a+c>b+d.
If a>b and b=c then a>c (transitivity with equality).
In a chain like P>Q<R, no relation between P and R can be concluded.
Multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses its sign.
'Either/or' conclusions occur when two conclusions are complementary, such as X>Y and X≤Y.
In coding-decoding questions, always replace the symbols with their assigned meanings before judging the options.
summary: The answer is (b). Decoding the symbols gives A > X, B = Z and Y < C (so C > Y). Adding these, A+B+C > X+Y+Z, so ABC > XYZ. Option (b), (ABC + XYZ) > 2XYZ, reduces to exactly this relation.
topic_notes: Topic: coding-decoding of mathematical symbols (inequality substitution), a recurring Quantitative Aptitude and Reasoning item in the EPFO papers. Method: (1) write each symbol's assigned meaning in a table; (2) rewrite every given statement in ordinary signs; (3) simplify. Inequalities pointing the same way can be added: if a>b and c>d then a+c>b+d. If one is an equality (b=z), it can still be added. Opposite-direction inequalities cannot be combined, as nothing can be concluded. Reverse the direction when an inequality is multiplied by a negative number. Treat grouped letters such as ABC as a sum only when the question's logic requires it. Here the options are consistent only with the sum reading. Check each option by decoding it and simplifying algebraically, not by guessing. Common traps: reading '+' as plus, swapping the two sides of an inequality, and an option that is the correct statement written in a different form. Related question types include 'statements and conclusions' with symbols like @, #, $, where A@B means A≥B. In those, a conclusion is 'definitely true' only if it follows from the chain of relations, and 'either/or' arises when two conclusions are complementary (> and ≤, or < and ≥). Practise chains: P>Q=R<S gives no definite relation between P and S. Speed tip: decode only the relations needed and eliminate options whose direction clearly contradicts the derived relation.

question:
What is the maximum number of pieces 1
cm in diameter and 20 cm long that can be
cut out of a cylindrical wooden block 20 cm
in length and 3 cm in diameter?
(a) 4
(a) Pune
(c) 6
(b) Warangal
(d) 7
(c) Bangalore
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Because the pieces are as long as the block (20 cm), they must run parallel to its axis, and no length is left over to stack a second layer. The cross-section of the block is a circle of diameter 3 cm (radius 1.5 cm), and each piece has a cross-section of diameter 1 cm (radius 0.5 cm). The question is therefore the classic packing of n equal circles in a larger circle. Place one circle at the centre. Six more circles can touch it, because six equal circles around a central one form a regular hexagon whose side equals the circle diameter. The centres of the outer six lie at distance 1 cm from the centre (twice the radius), so their outer edges reach 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 cm, which is exactly the block's radius. So 7 pieces fit exactly. Eight would need the container radius to be about 3.30 times the small radius, but here the ratio is exactly 3, so 8 is impossible. Area gives only a loose upper bound of 9 (9/1), which is why the geometry matters. Option (a) 4 and option (c) 6 are below the achievable number. The option (b) text is garbled in the OCR.
explanations: (a) 4 is wrong. Four pieces fit easily but are not the maximum; the central-plus-six arrangement gives more.
(b) The text of this option is garbled in the OCR, apparently mixed with another question. It cannot be the answer, since 7 is the true maximum and the readable option (d) states it.
(c) 6 is wrong. Six pieces fit in a ring around the centre, but the empty centre can hold a seventh piece of the same size.
(d) 7 is correct. One central piece plus six around it fills the 3 cm diameter exactly, and 8 would need a larger block.

question:
A group of boys decided to buy a few
cassettes whose price was between Rs.200/and Rs.250/-. But at the me of purchase,
two of the boys declined to contribute as a
result of which the remaining boys had to
pay Rs. 1/- more than they had originally
planned. What was the price of the cassettes
if the boys contributed equally and in whole
number of rupees?
(a) Rs. 220/(b) Rs. 210/(c) Rs. 230/(d) Rs. 240/Directions (for next Five items): Sumeet, Philips,
Wasim, Bishan and Chetan are ﬁve players of
the College Cricket team and their home
towns are Surat, Pune, Warangal, Bangalore
and Chandigarh but not in that order. The
ﬁve specialist slots of spinner, pace bowler,
wicket-keeper, batsman and the captain are
held by them, again not in the order of their
names stated above.
(i) Their names, home towns and the specialities
do not start with the same le er.
(ii) Neither Philips nor Wasim is the captain and
they do not belong to either Surat or
Bangalore.
(iv)
(vi) The captain's hometown is Pune while the

subject: Computers
detail: This is a standard 'dropout contribution' problem. Let n be the original number of boys, x the original share per boy, and P the total price. Then P = n·x. After two boys drop out, P = (n−2)(x+1). Expanding gives nx = nx + n − 2x − 2, so n = 2x + 2 and x = (n−2)/2. Because each share is a whole number of rupees, n must be even. Substituting, P = n(n−2)/2. Trying even values: n=20 gives 180, n=22 gives 220, n=24 gives 264. Only 220 lies between 200 and 250. Check: 22 boys pay Rs.10 each, and 20 boys pay Rs.11 each, which is Rs.1 more, and both come to Rs.220. Elimination also works by testing the options. 210 = 21×10 would need 19 boys to pay 11.05, which is not a whole number. 230 and 240 fail the same test with the relevant factor pairs. The key shortcut is that the two totals must differ by exactly 2 in the number of payers and 1 in the share, so look for factor pairs of P that differ by 2.
explanations: Correct. 220 = 22×10 = 20×11. The share rises by exactly Rs.1 when two boys leave, and 220 lies in the 200–250 range.

Incorrect. 210 would need two factors that differ by 2 and whose paired shares differ by 1. 210 = 15×14 gives shares differing by 1, but the payer counts differ by only 1, not 2. No valid pair exists.
Incorrect. 230 = 2×5×23. No pair of divisors differs by 2 with shares differing by 1, so no valid pair exists.

Incorrect. 240 = 16×15 gives payer counts differing by 1, not 2. For 2 fewer payers the shares would differ by more than Rs.1 (e.g. 20 and 12 payers differ by 8 and shares 12 and 20 differ by 8). So it fails.
keyfact: 2 boys drop out, share rises Re.1: P = n(n−2)/2, so n=22 and price Rs.220 (22×10 = 20×11).
option_notes: Rs. 220: the only price in the range 200–250 that equals n(n−2)/2 for a whole-number n (n=22). Originally 22 boys pay Rs.10 each, and after two drop out, 20 boys pay Rs.11 each. Its factorisation is 2²×5×11, and the divisor pair 22 and 20 is what makes the problem work.

Rs. 210: equals 2×3×5×7. It has divisor pairs like 21×10, 15×14 and 14×15, but none has payer counts differing by 2 with shares differing by 1. For example, 21 boys pay 10 each, and 19 boys cannot split 210 into whole rupees. It is a distractor.
Rs. 230: equals 2×5×23, so its divisors are only 1, 2, 5, 10, 23, 46, 115 and 230. No two divisors differ by 2 within a sensible group size, so it cannot satisfy the condition. It is a distractor.

Rs. 240: a highly composite number, 2⁴×3×5, with many divisors. Pairs like 16 and 15 or 24 and 10 exist. But no pair of divisors differs by 2 while the corresponding shares differ by 1. For example, 24 and 22 payers do not both divide 240. It is a distractor.
related: If k boys leave and the share rises by d, the original group size n = k(x+d)/d.
Here n = 22 boys, original share Rs.10, new share Rs.11 with 20 boys.
Total price P = n(n−2)/2 when 2 boys drop out and the share rises by Re.1.
Share increased by 10 percent (10 to 11).
Always check that the share is an integer and the total lies within the stated range.
Option testing by factor pairs is the fastest exam method for such problems.
summary: The answer is (a) Rs. 220. If n boys planned to share the cost, then P = n·x = (n−2)(x+1), which gives n = 2x+2 and P = n(n−2)/2. Only n = 22 puts P between 200 and 250, so P = 220.
topic_notes: This question belongs to Algebra and Number Systems, specifically time-and-share word problems about partners, friends or contributors who drop out. The general method is to define n as the original group size, x as the original share, and P as the total, and then form two equations: P = n·x and P = (n−k)(x+d), where k is the number of dropouts and d is the increase in share. Solving gives n·d = k·x + k·d, so n = k(x+d)/d. Here k=2 and d=1, so n = 2(x+1) = 2x+2. Always apply the conditions given: whole-number share, the price range and integer headcount. Quick checks: P must equal the product of two integers that differ by 2 (the two group sizes) only when the share changes by exactly 1, so P = n(n−2)/2 for k=2, d=1. Related variants: a bill split among friends where some leave, and the increase in share is different (e.g. Rs.2 or Rs.5). In that case use n = k(x+d)/d and test integers. Another variant asks for the number of boys, which here is 22. Other common angles: the shares in each case (Rs.10 and Rs.11), the difference between the two totals paid per head, and the percentage increase in the share, which is 10%. Practise testing options by factor pairs, which is the fastest method in the exam.

question: A and B stand in a circular ring with 10 other persons. If the arrangement of 12 persons is randomly done, the chance, that there are exactly 3 persons between A and B is
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a circular-arrangement probability question. In a circle of n = 12 people, only relative positions matter. Fix A at one seat. B can then be in any of the remaining 11 seats, each equally likely, so the sample space is 11. 'Exactly 3 persons between A and B' means that, counting along one arc, there are 3 people strictly between them. B is therefore 4 seats away from A. Going clockwise, B sits at position +4. Going anticlockwise, B sits at position -4 (equivalent to +8). These are two distinct seats because 12 is not equal to 8, so they do not coincide. The favourable cases are 2. Probability = 2/11. Check by counting arrangements: total circular arrangements = 11!. Favourable = 2 choices for B's seat x 10! for the others = 2 x 10!. Ratio = 2 x 10!/11! = 2/11. A common trap is to say 3/12 or to divide by 12 instead of 11, forgetting that A's seat is fixed. Another trap is to count only one direction. Option (c) 2/13 is impossible because the denominator must be 11 here. Note that if 'exactly 5 persons between them' were asked, the answer would be 1/11, because the two seats coincide (the opposite seat).
explanations: (a) 3/12 is wrong. It wrongly uses 12 seats as the denominator and 3 as the count, ignoring that A's seat is fixed and B has only 11 choices.
(b) 2/11 is correct. B has 11 equally likely seats, and exactly 2 of them (4 places clockwise or anticlockwise from A) leave 3 persons between them.
(c) 2/13 is wrong. The denominator 13 has no basis, as only 11 other seats exist for B.
(d) 3/11 is wrong. The denominator is right but the numerator is wrong, since only 2 seats satisfy the condition, not 3.
keyfact: Fix A's seat, then B has n-1 = 11 equally likely seats and 2 of them have exactly 3 persons between, giving 2/11.
option_notes: 3/12 = 1/4 = 0.25. It would be the answer only if a person had 12 equally likely seats and 3 were favourable. In a circle of 12, after fixing one person, only 11 seats remain, so this value does not arise here.

2/11 is about 0.1818. It is the probability that two specified people in a circle of 12 have exactly 3 people between them on one side. The general rule for n people is 2/(n-1) when the seats are not diametrically opposite.
2/13 is about 0.1538. It would correspond to a circle of 14 people (n-1 = 13). Here the circle has 12 people (A, B and 10 others), so it does not apply.
3/11 is about 0.2727. It would arise if 3 distinct seats qualified. Only 2 seats are exactly 4 places away from A, so it is not correct.
related: Circular permutations of n distinct objects = (n-1)!
Necklace or garland arrangements = (n-1)!/2
Two specified persons adjacent in a circle of n: probability 2/(n-1)
Two specified persons together in a circle: 2 x (n-2)! arrangements
In a circle of 12, probability of exactly 5 between A and B = 1/11
Linear arrangement with A and B adjacent: 2 x (n-1)! arrangements
summary: The answer is (b) 2/11. Fix A's position; B can occupy any of the 11 other positions equally likely, and exactly 3 persons lie between them in the two positions 4 places away, one in each direction, so the probability is 2/11.
topic_notes: Probability in circular arrangements: In a circular permutation of n distinct objects, the number of arrangements is (n-1)!, because rotations are identical. To find probabilities involving two named people, fix one person's seat and treat the other's seat as uniformly random among n-1 seats. If exactly k persons lie between them on one side, then B is (k+1) seats away. This gives 2 favourable seats if k+1 differs from n-(k+1), and 1 favourable seat if they are equal, which happens when the two are diametrically opposite (n even, k = n/2 - 1). Probability that A and B are adjacent = 2/(n-1). For n = 12 that is 2/11, which is the same as the answer here, because adjacent means k = 0 and the 2 seats are +1 and -1. Probability that they are opposite (n = 12, k = 5) = 1/11. Counting method: favourable arrangements = 2 x (n-2)!, total = (n-1)!. For linear arrangements the counting differs: the number of positions for A and B with exactly k people between them is 2(n-k-1) of n(n-1) ordered pairs. Related areas include necklace and garland problems, where reflection symmetry halves the count to (n-1)!/2, and problems with people sitting at a round table with restrictions such as two people always together (treated as one unit, giving 2 x (n-2)!). EPFO papers often test these basic permutation and probability ideas, so memorise the fix-one-person technique.

question: 15 men can complete a work in 280 days. They started the work and a er every 10 days, 15 additional men were employed. In how many days the work was completed?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a man-days problem with a changing workforce. First convert the job to a fixed quantity: 15 men × 280 days = 4200 man-days. The workforce grows in steps. Days 1-10 have 15 men and give 150 man-days. Days 11-20 have 30 men and give 300. Days 21-30 have 45 men and give 450. Block k has 15k men working 10 days, giving 150k man-days. The cumulative total after k blocks is 150 × k(k+1)/2 = 75k(k+1). Setting 75k(k+1) = 4200 gives k(k+1) = 56, so k = 7, since 7 × 8 = 56. The cumulative sums are 150, 450, 900, 1500, 2250, 3150 and 4200. The work therefore ends exactly at the end of the 7th block, which is day 70, with no fractional block. Elimination: 50 days (5 blocks) gives only 75 × 30 = 2250, which is about half the work. 55 days would end mid-block, but the total only becomes exactly 4200 at day 70. 60 days (6 blocks) gives 75 × 42 = 3150, still short. Always check that the sum lands exactly on the total, and use the triangular-number pattern to speed up the calculation.
explanations: Correct. Seven blocks of 10 days give 150 + 300 + 450 + 600 + 750 + 900 + 1050 = 4200 man-days, which equals the total work. So 70 days.
Incorrect. At 60 days, six blocks give 75 × 6 × 7 = 3150 man-days. That is only 75% of the work, so 750 man-days remain.
Incorrect. At 55 days, five full blocks give 2250 and half of the sixth block adds 450, for 2700 man-days. This is well short of 4200.
Incorrect. At 50 days, five blocks give 75 × 5 × 6 = 2250 man-days. That is about 54% of the work, so the job is far from done.
keyfact: 4200 man-days = 75k(k+1) gives k = 7 blocks, so the work is done in 70 days.
option_notes: 70 days equals 7 blocks of 10 days. It is the correct answer because 75 × 7 × 8 = 4200. By then the workforce has grown from 15 to 105 men. The final block has 105 men, who do 1050 man-days of work. The last block ends exactly as the work completes.

60 days equals 6 blocks of 10 days, with the workforce reaching 90 men in the last block. Cumulative work is 3150 man-days, which is 75% of the total. It is a tempting wrong option for students who stop one block early.

55 days is a mid-block value, with 5 full blocks plus 5 days at 90 men. Work done is 2250 + 450 = 2700 man-days. It would only be right if the total were 2700 man-days, for example a work that 15 men finish in 180 days.

50 days equals 5 blocks of 10 days, with the workforce reaching 75 men in the last block. Cumulative work is 2250 man-days. This is the answer to a different problem in which the total work is 2250 man-days, i.e. 15 men finishing in 150 days.
related: Work = Men × Days × Hours/day × Efficiency.
If A and B take a and b days alone, together they take ab/(a+b) days.
Sum of first n natural numbers = n(n+1)/2.
Total work in this question = 15 × 280 = 4200 man-days.
Cumulative work after k blocks = 75k(k+1) man-days, equal to 4200 at k = 7.
If men are removed midway, remaining work is computed in man-days and divided by the new strength.
Wages are shared in proportion to work done (man-days contributed).
summary: The work took 70 days (option a). Total work is 15 × 280 = 4200 man-days, and with 15 extra men added every 10 days the cumulative work after k blocks is 150(1+2+...+k) = 75k(k+1). This equals 4200 exactly at k = 7, so the work finished in 7 blocks of 10 days.
topic_notes: Time and Work: the basic idea is that Work = Men × Days (× hours per day × efficiency). Total work is treated as a fixed pool of man-days, here 4200. Key relations: M1·D1 = M2·D2 when efficiency is equal. If A does a job in a days and B in b days, together they take ab/(a+b) days. Pipes and cisterns follow the same logic, with inlets adding and outlets subtracting. Workforce-change problems: when the workforce changes in regular steps, the work forms an arithmetic progression, and the cumulative work is a triangular-number pattern. The sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n+1)/2. Useful triangular numbers: 28 (n=7), 36 (n=8), 45 (n=9), 55 (n=10). Such problems usually need a perfect-square-like factorisation, for example k(k+1) = 56. Other variants UPSC and EPFO ask: men leaving midway, which delays completion; work done in fractions (for example 1/3 done in 10 days, then men added); wages divided in proportion to work done; and efficiency ratios, where one man equals two women or similar. Exam approach: 1) compute total man-days, 2) write the cumulative series, 3) match it to the total, 4) check for a partial block. Always verify by summing the series.

question:
Bag 'A' contains 5 white and 2 black balls.
Bag 'B' contains 2 white and 3 black balls. If
any one bag is chosen and a ball is taken out
of it at random, what is the probability that
the ball is black?
(d) 4:1
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a total probability (law of total probability) problem. When an experiment has two stages, first choosing a bag and then drawing a ball, we add the probabilities of each path leading to the required event. Bag A holds 7 balls (5 white, 2 black), so P(black | A) = 2/7. Bag B holds 5 balls (2 white, 3 black), so P(black | B) = 3/5. Each bag is equally likely to be chosen, so P(A) = P(B) = 1/2. Therefore P(black) = (1/2)(2/7) + (1/2)(3/5) = 1/7 + 3/10 = 10/70 + 21/70 = 31/70, about 0.443. A common mistake is to pool all the balls (5 black out of 12 gives 5/12), which is wrong because the bags have different sizes and the bag is chosen first. Another mistake is to add 2/7 and 3/5 without weighting by 1/2. The options in the OCR are garbled (only '4:1' is visible, which is an odds ratio and does not match 31/70, whose odds are 31:39). I have assumed option (a) is 31/70, since the source options are not readable. Verify this against the original paper.
explanations: (a) Assumed to be 31/70, the value computed from the total probability theorem. The option text is unreadable in the OCR, so this is an inference.
(b) Not supported: the option text is unreadable, and the computed value 31/70 is assumed to sit elsewhere.
(c) Not supported: the option text is unreadable. Pooling the balls would give 5/12, which is a wrong method.
(d) The visible text '4:1' is an odds ratio and does not equal 31/70 (odds of 31:39), so it is incorrect.
keyfact: P(black) = ½·(2/7) + ½·(3/5) = 31/70 (total probability theorem).
option_notes: Option (a): assumed to be 31/70, the probability of drawing a black ball from a randomly chosen bag. It comes from P(A)P(B|A)+P(B)P(B|B) where each bag has probability 1/2. Its decimal value is about 0.443. The original text is not legible in the OCR.

Option (b): the text is not legible in the OCR. A likely distractor would be 5/12, the answer from pooling all balls (5 black out of 12 total), which ignores that the bag is chosen first with equal probability.

Option (c): the text is not legible in the OCR. Another likely distractor is 2/7 + 3/5 = 31/35, which forgets to weight each bag by 1/2. A probability must also not exceed 1, so check the result for sense.
Option (d): reads '4:1', an odds-style ratio. Odds of 4:1 would mean a probability of 4/5 = 0.8, which is far too high here. The correct odds in favour of black are 31:39, so this option is wrong.
related: Total probability theorem: P(E)=ΣP(Bi)P(E|Bi).
Bayes' theorem gives the reverse (posterior) probability.
Here P(black)=31/70 and P(white)=39/70.
Given black, P(it came from Bag A)=10/31.
Odds in favour = P/(1−P).
For independent events P(A∩B)=P(A)·P(B).
summary: The answer is (a), which the OCR'd options leave unreadable, but the computed probability is 31/70. Choosing a bag at random (1/2 each) and applying the total probability theorem gives P(black) = 1/2 × 2/7 + 1/2 × 3/5 = 31/70.
topic_notes: Probability basics: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total equally likely outcomes, and 0 ≤ P ≤ 1. For mutually exclusive events P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B). For independent events P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B). Conditional probability is P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B). Total probability theorem: if B1, B2, ..., Bn partition the sample space, then P(E) = ΣP(Bi)P(E|Bi). Bayes' theorem reverses this: P(Bi|E) = P(Bi)P(E|Bi)/P(E). In this problem, the Bayes follow-up would ask: given the ball is black, what is the probability it came from Bag A? That is (1/7)/(31/70) = 10/31, and from Bag B it is 21/31. Typical UPSC EPFO variants include: drawing balls with or without replacement, choosing among urns, dice and coin problems, and odds. Odds in favour = P/(1−P); odds against = (1−P)/P. Common traps: pooling all the balls when the container is chosen first, forgetting to weight by the selection probability, and confusing odds with probability. Permutation and combination counting is used when several balls are drawn: P = C(favourable)/C(total).

question:
Three containers have their volumes in the ra o 3: 4:
5. They are full of mixtures of milk and water. The mixtures contain milk and water in the ra o of 4:1, 3:1 and 5:2 respectively. The contents of all these three containers are poured into a fourth container. The ra o of milk and water in the fourth container is
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a mixture-of-mixtures problem, so the safe method is to convert each ratio into the fraction of milk in that container and weight it by volume. Container 1 is milk:water = 4:1, so milk is 4/5 of its volume. Container 2 is 3:1, so milk is 3/4. Container 3 is 5:2, so milk is 5/7. Let the volumes be 3k, 4k and 5k, with total 12k. Milk is 3k(4/5) + 4k(3/4) + 5k(5/7) = k(12/5 + 3 + 25/7). The LCM of the denominators is 35, so this is k(84 + 105 + 125)/35 = 314k/35. Water is 12k - 314k/35 = (420 - 314)k/35 = 106k/35. The ratio is 314:106 = 157:53, since both divide by 2 and 157 is prime. Check: 157/210 is about 0.7476, the overall milk fraction, which lies between 5/7 (0.714) and 4/5 (0.8), as a weighted average must. Elimination: 5:2 is just container 3's ratio and would need the whole mix to match it. 151:48 gives a milk fraction of 151/199 = 0.7588, which does not match 0.7476. Option (a) is garbled and is not a ratio.
explanations: Wrong. 'Y is wise' is an OCR corruption and is not a ratio. It cannot be the milk-to-water ratio.

Wrong. 5:2 is the ratio in the third container only. The first two containers are richer in milk (4/5 = 0.8 and 3/4 = 0.75), so the blend has a milk fraction of 157/210 = 0.7476, which is above 5/7 = 0.714. The ratio is therefore not 5:2.
Correct. Milk = 314k/35 and water = 106k/35, so the ratio is 314:106 = 157:53.
Wrong. 151:48 corresponds to a milk fraction of 151/199 = 0.7588, whereas the correct value is 157/210 = 0.7476. It looks like a near-miss from an arithmetic slip.
option_notes: This option is garbled OCR text ('Y is wise') and has no mathematical meaning. In the original paper it was probably a numeric ratio. For such questions, ignore a corrupted option and solve independently. The correct answer is a ratio in lowest terms, here 157:53. Always reduce a final ratio by the common factor, which is 2 here.

5:2 is the milk-to-water ratio of the third container. It means 5/7 (about 71.4%) of that mixture is milk and 2/7 (about 28.6%) is water. A blend of mixtures always has a milk fraction between the smallest and largest component fractions. Here these are 5/7 and 4/5, so the blend equals 5:2 only if all parts were identical to it.

157:53 is the correct final ratio of milk to water. It means milk is 157/210, about 74.8%, and water is 53/210, about 25.2%. The ratio comes from weighting each container's milk fraction by its volume (3:4:5) and adding. It lies between 5/7 and 4/5 as it must, and it is in lowest terms since 157 is prime and does not divide 53.

151:48 is a plausible-looking distractor that is not the answer. It implies milk is 151/199, about 75.9%, of the mixture. This is higher than the true 74.8%. It would arise from a small error in adding the fractions 12/5, 3 and 25/7, for example a wrong conversion to the common denominator 35.
related: Ratio a:b means the first component's fraction is a/(a+b).
Never add ratios directly. Weight each by its volume first.
Alligation: ratio of quantities = (c2 - c)/(c - c1).
After n replacements of x from V, remaining quantity = V(1 - x/V)^n.
A blend's concentration always lies between its component concentrations.
157 is a prime number, so 157:53 cannot be reduced further.
Mixture of milk and water in 4:1 contains 80% milk.
summary: The answer is (c) 157:53. Take the volumes as 3, 4 and 5 units, find the milk in each (12/5, 3 and 25/7), add them to get 314/35 of the 12 units, and the water is 106/35. The ratio of milk to water is 314:106, which reduces to 157:53.
topic_notes: Mixtures and alligation is a staple of the quantitative aptitude section in EPFO exams. Key methods: (1) Fraction method. Convert each ratio a:b to the fraction a/(a+b), multiply by the volume, and sum the milk and water separately. (2) Alligation rule. When two mixtures of concentrations c1 and c2 are mixed to get c, the ratio of quantities is (c2 - c)/(c - c1). It handles two components quickly, but with three containers the fraction method is cleaner. (3) Replacement problems. If a container of volume V has x units removed and replaced with water n times, the final milk is V(1 - x/V)^n. (4) Profit-based mixture questions involve cost price of the mixture and the selling price per unit. Useful checks: the blend's fraction must lie between the minimum and maximum component fractions, and the total of the ratio parts should equal the total volume. For this problem the volumes are 3:4:5 with fractions 4/5, 3/4 and 5/7. The common denominator is 35, so milk is (84 + 105 + 125)/35 = 314/35 and water is 106/35. Dividing by 2 gives 157:53. Typical traps include forgetting that a ratio like 4:1 means 4/5 milk rather than 4/1, adding ratios directly without weighting by volume, and failing to reduce the final ratio. Related question types: finding the ratio of one liquid in the final mixture, finding the volume of water to add to reach a target ratio, and finding the quantity of milk in the final mixture.

question: Two dice are thrown simultaneously. The probability that the product of the two numbers on the two dice is an even number is
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Two dice give 6 x 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. A product is even if at least one factor is even, so the quickest route is the complement rule: P(even) = 1 - P(odd). A product is odd only if both numbers are odd. Each die has 3 odd faces (1, 3, 5) out of 6, so P(odd on one die) = 1/2. The two dice are independent, so P(both odd) = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4, or 9 favourable outcomes out of 36. Hence P(product even) = 1 - 9/36 = 27/36 = 3/4. Elimination: 1/2 is the probability that the SUM is odd, or that one die is even, and is not the answer here. 5/16 and 3/8 are not multiples of 1/36, so they cannot be probabilities for this sample space of 36 outcomes (5/16 = 11.25/36 and 3/8 = 13.5/36). Only 3/4 = 27/36 fits. The complement method saves time in the exam.
explanations: Incorrect: 1/2 would be 18 outcomes out of 36. The actual count of even-product outcomes is 27. 1/2 is the probability that the sum is odd, or that a single die shows an even number.
Correct: 27 of the 36 outcomes give an even product (36 - 9 both-odd outcomes), so the probability is 27/36 = 3/4.
Incorrect: 5/16 is not a multiple of 1/36, so it cannot be a probability in a 36-outcome sample space. It is also far too low, because the probability that at least one die is even is high.
Incorrect: 3/8 is not a multiple of 1/36, so it is impossible for this sample space. It is also less than 1/2, whereas the true value is 3/4.
keyfact: Product of two dice is odd only if both are odd (1/4), so P(even) = 3/4.
option_notes: 1/2: this is the probability of getting an even number on a single die, or an odd sum on two dice (18 of 36 outcomes). It is also the chance of heads on a fair coin. It is a common distractor because the symmetry of odd and even numbers suggests 1/2.

3/4: this equals 27/36. It is the probability that at least one of two dice shows an even number, and also the probability of at least one head in two coin tosses. It is the complement of P(both odd) = 1/4.

5/16: a fraction with denominator 16, which is not possible for two dice. It would arise in other contexts, such as 5 favourable cases out of 4 binary trials (2^4 = 16 outcomes). It is useful to remember that two-dice denominators divide 36.

3/8: this equals 3 out of 8 outcomes. It is the probability of exactly 2 heads in 3 coin tosses is 3/8, and of exactly 1 head in 3 tosses is also 3/8. It cannot arise with two dice because 36 is not divisible by 8.
related: Two dice have 36 equally likely outcomes.
P(sum = 7) = 1/6, the most probable sum.
P(product odd) = 1/4 and P(product even) = 3/4.
P(at least one six in two dice) = 11/36.
P(doublet) = 1/6.
Complement rule: P(A) = 1 - P(A').
summary: The answer is (b) 3/4. The product of two dice numbers is odd only when both numbers are odd, which has probability 1/4, so the product is even with probability 1 - 1/4 = 3/4.
topic_notes: Probability with dice is a regular topic in APFC quantitative aptitude. The sample space for one die is 6 outcomes, for two dice 36, and for three dice 216. Probability = favourable outcomes / total outcomes, and it always lies between 0 and 1. The complement rule P(A) = 1 - P(not A) is the fastest route for 'at least one' type questions. For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Key two-dice facts: sum of 7 is the most likely (6/36 = 1/6); sums of 2 and 12 have 1/36 each; the sum is even with probability 1/2; doubles occur with probability 1/6; the product is odd with probability 1/4; the product is even with probability 3/4. P(sum = 9 or more) = 10/36. P(at least one six) = 11/36. P(both numbers are the same) = 6/36. P(product is 12) = 4/36 (2x6, 6x2, 3x4, 4x3). For coins: n tosses give 2^n outcomes; P(at least one head) = 1 - 1/2^n. For cards: 52 cards, 26 red, 26 black, 12 face cards, 4 aces. Addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). Mutually exclusive events have P(A and B) = 0. Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B). Quick check: any answer must be a multiple of 1/36 when two dice are used.

question: The ﬂowers in a basket become double every minute and the basket gets full in one hour. In how much me, the basket was 1/32 full?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: This is a classic exponential growth (doubling) problem. If the quantity doubles every minute and reaches full capacity (1) at t = 60 minutes, then at time t the fraction filled is 2^(t-60). To find when the basket is 1/32 = 2^(-5) full, set t - 60 = -5, so t = 55 minutes. The trap is to think linearly: a linear thinker would say 1/32 of 60 minutes is about 1.9 minutes, or pick 12 or 32 by guesswork. Doubling processes spend most of their time at tiny quantities and fill up in the last few steps. Each step back in time halves the content: 59 min = 1/2, 58 = 1/4, 57 = 1/8, 56 = 1/16, 55 = 1/32. Elimination: 12 and 32 minutes are far too early, since the basket would be 2^-48 and 2^-28 full, essentially empty. 45 minutes gives 2^-15 = 1/32768, still far too small. Only 55 minutes matches 1/32. The same logic applies to lily-pond, bacteria-culture and similar questions, where the answer is always the full time minus the number of doublings.
explanations: (a) 12 minutes is wrong: the basket would be 2^(12-60) = 2^-48 full, which is practically empty, not 1/32.
(b) 32 minutes is wrong: the fraction would be 2^-28, far smaller than 1/32.
(c) 45 minutes is wrong: the fraction would be 2^-15 = 1/32768, still much smaller than 1/32.
(d) 55 minutes is correct: 5 minutes before full, the content has been halved five times, giving 1/2^5 = 1/32.
keyfact: Doubling process: quantity is 1/2^k of full k periods before it is full, so 1/32 full is 5 minutes earlier, at 55 minutes.
option_notes: 12 minutes: at this time the basket holds 2^-48 of its capacity, a negligible amount. It would be the answer only if growth were roughly linear, which it is not. A common wrong guess from intuition.
32 minutes: it coincides numerically with the denominator 32, which is the trap. The fill at 32 minutes would be 2^-28, about 3.7 x 10^-9 of the basket. Do not confuse the denominator with time.
45 minutes: fraction is 2^-15 = 1/32768. It is 15 minutes before full. It would be correct only for a question asking for 1/32768 full.
55 minutes: 5 minutes before full. With doubling each minute, the fill is 2^-5 = 1/32. Related values: 59 min = 1/2, 58 = 1/4, 57 = 1/8, 56 = 1/16. This is the correct answer.
related: Doubling each minute and full at T: half full at T-1 minutes.
Fraction filled at k periods before full = 1/2^k.
If growth triples each period, k periods before full the fraction is 1/3^k.
Starting with two baskets of doubling flowers, the time to fill is one minute less.
Rule of 72: doubling time is approximately 72 divided by the percentage growth rate.
summary: The answer is (d) 55 minutes. The flowers double every minute and the basket is full at 60 minutes, so working backwards, it was 1/2 full at 59, 1/4 at 58, 1/8 at 57, 1/16 at 56 and 1/32 at 55 minutes.
topic_notes: This question tests exponential (geometric) growth, a staple of the Quantitative Aptitude and Reasoning section in EPFO papers. The key idea is that if a quantity doubles in each period and is full at time T, then at time T - k it is 1/2^k full. Equivalent forms: fraction at time t = 2^(t-T). Variants often asked: (1) If the basket is full in 60 minutes and the flowers double every minute, when was it half full? Answer: 59 minutes. (2) If two baskets of flowers start together, when do they fill together? If you start with two identical baskets, the quantity is doubled from the start, so the time to fill one basket is one minute less, giving 59 minutes. (3) Lily pond problems: a pond is fully covered on day 48 and the lily doubles daily, so it was half covered on day 47. (4) If the growth triples every period, then k periods earlier the fraction is 1/3^k. (5) Bacteria that double every 20 minutes, so count doublings as time divided by 20. Related concepts include compound growth, population growth, and the compound interest formula A = P(1 + r/100)^n, where doubling corresponds to r = 100 percent per period. The rule of 72 gives the approximate doubling time as 72 divided by the percent rate. Always work backwards from the known full state to avoid algebra, and check by repeated doubling: 1/32, 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1.

question:
If X is mortal, Y is wise. If Z is not good, A
will suﬀer. Y is not wise, if A suﬀers. If B is a
slave, X is immortal. If A suﬀers, what
follows?
(b) 1/2
(a) X is mortal
(c) 5/12
(b) B is a slave
(d) 3/5
(c) Z is good
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a conditional-logic (syllogism) question. Premises: (1) X mortal → Y wise. (2) Z not good → A suffers. (3) A suffers → Y not wise. (4) B slave → X immortal. Given: A suffers. From (3), Y is not wise. By contraposition of (1), Y not wise → X is not mortal, so X is immortal. Statement (4) says B slave → X immortal; X being immortal is the consequent, and affirming the consequent proves nothing, so we cannot conclude whether B is a slave. Statement (2) is Z not good → A suffers; A suffering is the consequent, so affirming it does not prove Z is not good, and it also does not prove Z is good. Hence: 'X is mortal' is false, 'B is a slave' is undetermined, 'Z is good' is undetermined. Only 'X is immortal' follows, and it is not among the options as read, so the answer is 'none of these'. Key rules: contraposition is valid; converse and affirming the consequent are fallacies.
explanations: Wrong: A suffers gives Y not wise, which by contraposition gives X not mortal. So X being mortal contradicts the premises.
Wrong: B slave → X immortal. X immortal is true, but that is the consequent, so it does not establish that B is a slave.
Wrong: A suffering does not tell us whether Z is good or not good, since the rule only runs from Z not good to A suffers.
Correct: only 'X is immortal' follows, which is not listed, so none of the stated conclusions follows.
keyfact: From 'If P then Q' only modus ponens and contraposition are valid; the converse is not.
option_notes: X is mortal: this is the antecedent of premise 1. It is false here because Y is not wise.
B is a slave: this is the antecedent of premise 4. It cannot be deduced, because the consequent is true but is not enough.
Z is good: this is the negation of the antecedent of premise 2. It cannot be deduced either, since denying the antecedent is a fallacy.
None of these (the OCR-garbled option d): this is the correct choice, because the only valid inference, 'X is immortal', is not offered.
related: Contrapositive of 'If P then Q' is 'If not Q then not P'.
Affirming the consequent is a logical fallacy.
Denying the antecedent is a logical fallacy.
'P only if Q' means P → Q.
'Unless P, Q' is equivalent to 'if not P then Q'.
Chain rule: P → Q and Q → R give P → R.
summary: The answer is (d), which is the option 'Z is good'? No: the options are garbled by OCR. The sensible reading of the options is (a) X is mortal, (b) B is a slave, (c) Z is good, (d) none of these. Given A suffers, Y is not wise, so X is not mortal (X is immortal), so B is not a slave. Whether Z is good cannot be concluded, because 'If Z is not good, A will suffer' does not reverse. So none of the listed conclusions follows, and the answer is (d).
topic_notes: Conditional reasoning questions use statements of the form 'If P then Q'. Valid inferences: modus ponens (P true, so Q true) and modus tollens (Q false, so P false). Equivalent form: contrapositive (not Q → not P). Invalid inferences: affirming the consequent (Q true, so P true) and denying the antecedent (P false, so Q false). The converse and inverse of a conditional are not logically equivalent to it. Method for exam: write each premise symbolically, chain implications from the given fact, then test each option against the derived set of truths. Options that are consistent with the premises but not forced by them are 'cannot be determined' and should not be chosen. Related reasoning topics: syllogisms with Venn diagrams, 'only if' statements (P only if Q means P → Q), 'unless' statements (unless P, Q means not P → Q), and chain implications such as P → Q, Q → R, so P → R. Always check whether the question asks what 'must follow', 'may follow', or 'cannot follow'. Mistakes typically come from reversing the direction of an arrow. Note that OCR garbling of options in this question means the options have to be reconstructed carefully, so this key is an inference.

question: In a group of 36 persons, a total of 16 take tea while 9 take tea but not coﬀee. How many persons in this group take coﬀee but not tea?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a two-set Venn diagram problem using n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). Let T = tea drinkers and C = coffee drinkers. Given n(T) = 16 and n(T only) = 9, so n(T ∩ C) = 16 − 9 = 7. The total group is 36. The question does not state that everyone takes at least one drink, but the only way to get an answer from the data is to assume the group is T ∪ C, so nobody takes neither. Then persons who do not take tea are all coffee-only, so coffee-only = 36 − 16 = 20. Check: tea only 9 + both 7 + coffee only 20 = 36. Elimination: 27 = 36 − 9 would count the both-group as coffee-only (wrong, since it removes only tea-only). 25 and 11 do not come from any consistent region of the diagram: 11 = 36 − 25 and 25 = 9 + 16 are arbitrary sums. Remember the standard technique: draw two circles, fill the intersection first, then the exclusive regions, and check that the regions sum to the total.
explanations: Incorrect for 27: this is 36 − 9, which wrongly treats everyone except tea-only drinkers as coffee-only. It ignores the 7 who take both.
Correct: both = 16 − 9 = 7; coffee only = total 36 − tea drinkers 16 = 20 (check 9 + 7 + 20 = 36).
Incorrect for 25: this equals 9 + 16 and has no meaning in the Venn regions; it would make the total exceed 36 when added to the other regions.
Incorrect for 11: this has no valid derivation. Adding tea only 9 + both 7 + 11 gives 27, not 36, so the total is not satisfied.
keyfact: Coffee only = total − all tea drinkers = 36 − 16 = 20 (both = 16 − 9 = 7), assuming everyone takes at least one drink.
option_notes: 27 is the number of people who do not belong to the tea-only region (36 − 9). It is a common distractor, formed by subtracting only the tea-only count from the total. In Venn terms it equals both (7) plus coffee only (20), which is the total number of coffee drinkers.

20 is the number in the coffee-only region. It equals the total minus all tea drinkers (36 − 16). With tea only = 9 and both = 7, the diagram is complete: 9 + 7 + 20 = 36. This assumes every person takes at least one of tea or coffee.

25 is 9 + 16, a meaningless sum of the given numbers. It does not match any region of the diagram. Such distractors come from adding data without a sound set relationship. It is not equal to total coffee drinkers (27) or coffee only (20).

11 is a distractor with no basis in the regions. It might come from careless arithmetic such as 36 − 25. The true values are tea only 9, both 7, coffee only 20. Always verify that the region counts add up to the stated total.
related: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
A only = n(A) − n(A ∩ B).
Neither = Total − n(A ∪ B).
Minimum overlap of two sets = n(A) + n(B) − Total (if positive).
Maximum overlap of two sets = smaller of n(A) and n(B).
Three-set formula adds back the triple intersection n(A∩B∩C).
summary: The answer is (b) 20 only if every person takes tea or coffee; the question's wording is ambiguous, but the intended reading gives 20. Tea drinkers total 16 and 9 take tea only, so 7 take both. Coffee-only = 36 − 16 = 20, assuming everyone takes at least one beverage.
topic_notes: Set theory and Venn diagram problems are regular in the Quantitative Aptitude and Reasoning section of the EPFO exams. The core formula is n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). Related identities: n(A only) = n(A) − n(A ∩ B); n(neither) = total − n(A ∪ B). For three sets: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A∩B) − n(B∩C) − n(A∩C) + n(A∩B∩C). Method: first fill the innermost region (intersection), then the exclusive regions, then the outside region, and check that all regions sum to the total. Watch the wording: 'tea but not coffee' means tea only; 'tea' alone means all tea drinkers including those taking both; 'either ... or' can be inclusive; 'exactly one' means the sum of the two exclusive regions. When the question does not state that everyone drinks something, check whether the data forces the assumption, and use the answer options to confirm. In this problem tea total 16 and tea only 9 give both 7. Coffee only = total − tea total = 20 when no one takes neither. Coffee total would then be 27. Other likely angles: finding the number who take neither when a coffee total is given; the maximum and minimum overlap of two sets (the minimum overlap is n(A) + n(B) − total, the maximum is the smaller set); and percentage-based Venn problems that convert percentages to numbers on a base of 100.

question:
Two pipes 'A' and 'B' can ﬁll a tank in 15
minutes and 20 minutes respec vely. Both
the pipes are opened together but a er 4
minutes, pipe 'A' is turned oﬀ. What is the
total time required to ﬁll the tank?
(a) 12 mt 30 sec
(b) 14 mt 40 sec
(c) 10 mt 20 sec
(d) 11 mt 45 sec
Directions (For next Two items): A cube has six
faces, each of a diﬀerent colour. The red face
is opposite to black. The green face is
between red and black. The blue face is
adjacent to white. The brown face is
adjacent to blue. The red face is the bo om
most face.
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a standard 'pipes and cisterns' problem. Treat the whole tank as 1 unit and find each pipe's rate as 1/time. Pipe A fills 1/15 per minute and pipe B fills 1/20 per minute. Together they fill 1/15 + 1/20 = 4/60 + 3/60 = 7/60 per minute. In the first 4 minutes both pipes work, so the filled part is 4 x 7/60 = 28/60 = 7/15. The remaining part is 1 - 7/15 = 8/15. Pipe B alone fills 1/20 per minute, so the time needed is (8/15) / (1/20) = (8 x 20)/15 = 160/15 = 10 2/3 minutes = 10 min 40 sec. Total time = 4 min + 10 min 40 sec = 14 min 40 sec. Elimination: the total must exceed 4 + (8/15 of 20) and cannot be below about 14 minutes, because B alone needs 20 minutes for the whole tank and A's help for 4 minutes saves only a little. That rules out 10:20, 11:45 and 12:30. A quick check is that the total must be more than 4 plus the time B needs for the part A did not fill, and only 14:40 satisfies this.
explanations: Incorrect: 12 min 30 sec is too short. It would imply B alone fills the remaining part in 8.5 minutes, which does not match 8/15 of the tank.
Correct: 4 min together fill 7/15 of the tank. B fills the other 8/15 in 10 min 40 sec, so the total is 14 min 40 sec.
Incorrect: 10 min 20 sec is too short. Even both pipes working together all the time would need 60/7, about 8 min 34 sec, and A is switched off after 4 minutes, so the total must be well above that.
Incorrect: 11 min 45 sec does not match the calculation. It would need B to fill 8/15 of the tank in 7 min 45 sec, but B needs 10 min 40 sec.
keyfact: A+B fill 7/60 per minute; after 4 min 8/15 remains, B alone needs 10 min 40 sec, so total 14 min 40 sec.
option_notes: 12 min 30 sec is a distractor value. In pipes problems, such wrong options often come from mistakes like adding the rates wrongly or forgetting that only B works after A is turned off. Always verify by recomputing the filled fraction.

14 min 40 sec = 14 2/3 minutes = 44/3 minutes. It is the correct total here: 4 min with both pipes plus 10 2/3 min with B alone. Remember to convert fractions of a minute into seconds by multiplying by 60 (2/3 x 60 = 40 sec).
10 min 20 sec is a distractor. It is below the time needed even if only part of the tank were left for B, so it cannot be right. Quick sanity bounds help rule out such options.
11 min 45 sec is a distractor value. It may tempt students who average the times or mishandle the 4-minute period. The correct approach is to use fractions of the tank filled.
related: Combined time of two pipes = ab/(a+b).
Use LCM of times as tank capacity to avoid fractions.
Outlet pipe or leak has a negative rate in the net-rate calculation.
Net rate with a leak = 1/a - 1/c.
In a cube, each face has exactly one opposite face and four adjacent faces.
Convert 2/3 minute to 40 seconds by multiplying by 60.
summary: The answer is (b) 14 min 40 sec. Pipes A and B together fill 7/60 of the tank per minute. In 4 minutes they fill 28/60 = 7/15, and pipe B alone then fills the remaining 8/15 in 10 min 40 sec.
topic_notes: Pipes and cisterns is the same as time and work, where the tank is the work and pipes are workers. An inlet pipe fills the tank and an outlet pipe (leak) empties it. Rate = 1/time. If A fills in a minutes and B in b minutes, together they take ab/(a+b) minutes. Here 15 x 20/35 = 60/7 min, about 8 min 34 sec, if both ran throughout. If an outlet empties in c minutes, the net rate is 1/a - 1/c, and the tank fills only if a < c. Method for partial-operation questions: (1) compute the rates, (2) compute the part filled in the first stage, (3) subtract from 1, (4) divide the remainder by the rate of the pipe still working, (5) add the times. Use LCM of the times (here 60) as the tank capacity to avoid fractions: A fills 4 units per minute and B fills 3 units per minute, so together 7 units per minute. In 4 minutes they fill 28 units, leaving 32 units, which B fills in 32/3 = 10 min 40 sec. Other likely angles are a pipe closed midway, a leak that empties the tank in a given time, and alternate opening of pipes, where each pair of minutes fills the combined rate for one cycle.
