question: Which of the following statements is not correct?
options: The 42nd Amendment extended the term of Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies from 5 years to 6 years
The President can dissolve the Lok Sabha on the advice of the Prime Minister
Money Bills cannot be introduced in the Rajya Sabha
One third members of the Rajya Sabha re re on the expiry of every third year
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is not subject to dissolution. Under Article 83(1), one third of its members retire on the expiry of every second year, and each member serves a six-year term. This staggering is why the House never dissolves. Statement (d) says 'third year', so it is wrong. Statement (a) is correct: the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 (during the Emergency) extended the term of the Lok Sabha (Art. 83(2)) and State Assemblies (Art. 172) from five to six years. The 44th Amendment, 1978 restored the five-year term. Statement (b) is correct in practice. Under Article 85(2)(b) the President dissolves the Lok Sabha, and by convention he acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister (Art. 74). Statement (c) is correct under Article 109 and Article 110: a Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations within 14 days. For 'not correct' questions, test each statement against a specific number or article. Here the error is a single changed number, 'third' instead of 'second'.
explanations: Correct statement. The 42nd Amendment (1976) raised the term to 6 years, and the 44th Amendment (1978) reverted it to 5. Since the question asks for the incorrect statement, this is not the answer.
Correct statement. Art. 85(2)(b) gives the President the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha, and by convention he acts on ministerial advice. This is not the answer.
Correct statement. Art. 109 and Art. 110 require a Money Bill to originate only in the Lok Sabha. This is not the answer.
Incorrect statement. One third of members retire every second year, not every third year. This is therefore the answer.
keyfact: Rajya Sabha is permanent: one third of its members retire every SECOND year (6-year term).
option_notes: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, known as the 'Mini Constitution', was passed during the Emergency under Indira Gandhi. It added the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity to the Preamble, inserted the Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Art. 51A), and extended the Lok Sabha's term to 6 years. The 44th Amendment, 1978, restored the 5-year term. In an Emergency the term can be extended by Parliament by law for one year at a time.

The President summons, prorogues and dissolves the Lok Sabha under Art. 85. He acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers under Art. 74, as the 42nd and 44th Amendments made binding. Dissolution ends the House's life, and a Lok Sabha dissolved before its term ends means fresh general elections. Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved. A Prime Minister who has lost majority support may still advise dissolution, but the President may use discretion in a hung House.

A Money Bill is defined in Art. 110 and covers taxation, borrowing, the Consolidated Fund, and similar matters. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation. The Rajya Sabha has 14 days to return it with recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject. The Speaker certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill, and that decision is final. If the Rajya Sabha does not return it in 14 days, it is deemed passed.

The Rajya Sabha is the Council of States, with a maximum strength of 250 (238 elected and 12 nominated). It is a permanent House. Members serve six years and one third retire every second year, under Art. 83(1) and the Representation of the People Act. Members are elected by the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies by single transferable vote. The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman. A member needs to be at least 30 years old.
related: Art. 83(1): Rajya Sabha is not subject to dissolution; one third retire every second year.
Art. 83(2): Lok Sabha term is 5 years, extendable by 1 year at a time during Emergency.
Art. 110 defines a Money Bill; the Speaker certifies it.
42nd Amendment (1976) added Fundamental Duties and the words Socialist, Secular, Integrity.
44th Amendment (1978) restored the 5-year Lok Sabha term and deleted the right to property as a Fundamental Right.
Art. 108: joint sitting is presided over by the Speaker.
Rajya Sabha has 14 days to return a Money Bill.
Maximum strength: Lok Sabha 552, Rajya Sabha 250.
summary: The answer is (d). One third of Rajya Sabha members retire every second year, not every third year, because members have a six-year term and the House is a permanent body. The other three statements are correct (the 42nd Amendment did extend the term to six years, and it was later reversed).
topic_notes: Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha (Art. 79). The Lok Sabha has a maximum of 552 members (530 from States, 20 from Union Territories and, until the 104th Amendment, 2 Anglo-Indians), and the present strength is 543. Its normal term is 5 years from its first sitting (Art. 83(2)). In a National Emergency the term can be extended by one year at a time, but not beyond six months after the Emergency ends. The Rajya Sabha has a maximum of 250 members, of whom 12 are nominated for expertise in literature, science, art and social service, and it is never dissolved. One third retire every second year. Money Bills: Art. 110 defines them, they originate only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha has 14 days to make recommendations. Financial Bills fall under Art. 117. In a deadlock over an ordinary Bill, the President summons a joint sitting under Art. 108, presided over by the Speaker. Joint sittings do not apply to Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills. Joint sittings have occurred in 1961 (Dowry Prohibition Bill), 1978 (Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill) and 2002 (POTA). Other points: the Lok Sabha Speaker is elected by its members, and the Vice-President chairs the Rajya Sabha. The Rajya Sabha has special powers under Art. 249 (legislating on a State subject in the national interest) and Art. 312 (creating All-India Services), which need a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. The 42nd Amendment's other changes were reversed or modified by the 43rd and 44th Amendments, which restored the 5-year term, among other things.

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. For the three All-India Services, there are 24 State cadres including three joint cadres.
2. Union Public Service Commission is the cadre controlling authority for Indian Administrative Service.
3. Staﬀ Selection Commission is entrusted with the task of making recruitment to all the Group 'B' and Group 'C' posts under the Government. Which of these statements is/are correct?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The three All-India Services are the IAS, IPS and Indian Forest Service. They are created under Article 312 and are governed by the All India Services Act, 1951. Each service is organised into State cadres, and some States share a joint cadre: Assam-Meghalaya, Manipur-Tripura and, for the IAS/IPS, the Arunachal Pradesh-Goa-Mizoram-Union Territories (AGMUT) cadre. The UPSC conducts the Civil Services Examination and recommends candidates, but it does not control cadres. The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions is the cadre controlling authority for the IAS, through the DoPT. The Ministry of Home Affairs controls the IPS cadre, and the Ministry of Environment and Forests controls the IFS cadre. The Staff Selection Commission was set up in 1975 as the Subordinate Services Commission. It recruits to non-technical Group B (non-gazetted) and Group C posts in central ministries, but many posts are outside its scope. Examples are posts filled by the Railway Recruitment Boards, the IBPS for banks, and department-specific recruitment. Statements 2 and 3 are therefore wrong, so only statement 1 is correct.
explanations: Correct. Only statement 1 is true: it matches the cadre structure, while statements 2 and 3 are false.
Incorrect. It treats statement 2 as true, but the cadre controlling authority for the IAS is the DoPT, not the UPSC.
Incorrect. It treats statements 2 and 3 as true. Statement 2 is false because the DoPT controls the IAS cadre. Statement 3 is false because the SSC does not recruit for all Group B and C posts.
Incorrect. It treats statements 2 and 3 as true along with statement 1, but both of them are false.
keyfact: DoPT, not UPSC, controls the IAS cadre; the SSC does not recruit for all Group B and C posts.
option_notes: Option (a) says only statement 1 is correct. This is the right answer. It reflects the fact that the All-India Services are organised into State cadres, some of them joint. The IAS, IPS and IFS are the three All-India Services. They were created under Article 312 and the All India Services Act, 1951. Officers are recruited by the Centre through the UPSC but serve in the States, and cadre allocation is handled by the central government.

Option (b) combines statements 1 and 2. Statement 1 is true but statement 2 is false. The UPSC conducts the Civil Services Examination but does not control the IAS cadre. Cadre control for the IAS lies with the DoPT. The UPSC is a constitutional body under Articles 315 to 323, with a Chairman and members appointed by the President, and its role is recruitment and advice.

Option (c) combines statements 2 and 3, both of which are false. The UPSC is not the IAS cadre controller, which is the DoPT. The SSC does not handle all Group B and C recruitment. The SSC is an attached office of the DoPT. It was created in 1975 and is headquartered in New Delhi, with regional offices across the country.

Option (d) says all three statements are correct, which is wrong. Only statement 1 holds. Statement 2 wrongly assigns cadre control of the IAS to the UPSC. Statement 3 wrongly says the SSC recruits for every Group B and C post. Absolute words like 'all' in such statements often signal an incorrect claim.
related: Article 312 empowers Parliament to create All-India Services by Rajya Sabha resolution (two-thirds majority).
The All India Services Act was passed in 1951.
The UPSC is a constitutional body under Article 315.
The SSC was established in 1975 as the Subordinate Services Commission.
The DoPT is the cadre controlling authority for the IAS.
The Home Ministry is the cadre controlling authority for the IPS.
The Indian Forest Service was created in 1966.
Joint cadres: Assam-Meghalaya, Manipur-Tripura and AGMUT.
statements: 1 — Correct: As of the paper's date, the three All-India Services had 24 State cadres including three joint cadres. Joint cadres exist for several small States. The All India Services Act, 1951 provides for cadre allocation. Article 312 allows Parliament to create All-India Services if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. The IAS, IPS and IFS are the three existing services. Their officers are recruited by the Centre and serve under both Union and State governments. Cadre strength is fixed under the cadre rules, and the allocation of officers is done by the DoPT. The number of cadres has changed since, for example after the formation of new States such as Telangana, so a student should check the current figure.

2 — Incorrect: The UPSC is a constitutional body under Article 315 that conducts recruitment examinations and advises on service matters. It is not the cadre controlling authority. For the IAS, that authority is the DoPT in the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. The Home Ministry controls the IPS, and the Environment Ministry controls the IFS. Cadre control covers cadre review, allocation of officers to States, deputation and inter-cadre transfers. The UPSC's role ends with the recommendation of candidates for appointment, after which the government allocates them.

3 — Incorrect: The SSC began in 1975 as the Subordinate Services Commission and was renamed the Staff Selection Commission in 1977. It is an attached office of the DoPT. It conducts examinations such as the CGL, CHSL and MTS for various non-technical Group B (non-gazetted) and Group C posts. It does not recruit for all such posts, because railways, banks, defence civilian posts and many departments use their own recruitment agencies. Gazetted Group B posts are generally filled through the UPSC, so the word 'all' makes the statement false.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Statement 1 matches the cadre structure of the All-India Services as it stood around 2002. Statement 2 is wrong because the cadre controlling authority for the IAS is the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), not the UPSC. Statement 3 is wrong because the SSC does not recruit for all Group B and C posts.
topic_notes: All-India Services are the IAS, IPS and Indian Forest Service. Article 312 allows Parliament to create new All-India Services if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting. The All India Services Act, 1951 governs them. The IAS and IPS were successors of the ICS and IP. The IFS was created in 1966. Officers are recruited by the Centre, allotted to State cadres, and can serve on central deputation. They are subject to dual control: the State government uses them day to day, but the Centre controls discipline and dismissal. Cadre controlling authorities are the DoPT for the IAS, the Ministry of Home Affairs for the IPS, and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for the IFS. Joint cadres exist: Assam-Meghalaya, Manipur-Tripura, and AGMUT for the IAS and IPS. The UPSC is a constitutional body under Articles 315 to 323. Its members hold office for six years or until age 65, whichever is earlier. It conducts examinations and advises on recruitment rules, promotions, transfers and disciplinary matters. The SSC began in 1975 as the Subordinate Services Commission, was renamed the Staff Selection Commission in 1977, and is an attached office of the DoPT. It recruits for non-technical Group B (non-gazetted) and Group C posts through the CGL, CHSL, MTS and stenographer examinations. The Railway Recruitment Boards, the IBPS and the State Public Service Commissions handle other recruitment. Possible future questions could cover Article 312, the creation of a new All-India Service such as the Indian Judicial Service, the removal of UPSC members under Article 317, and the difference between a constitutional body and a statutory body.

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. Part 'B' of the Budget speech of the ﬁnance minister includes description of the ini a ves on economic front to be taken up by the Government for the coming year in addition to direct and indirect tax proposals.
2. The receipts on account of the par al disinvestment of Central Government's holdings in the equity capital of public sector enterprises are revenue receipts. Which of these statements is/are correct?
subject: Indian Economy
detail: The Union Budget speech of the Finance Minister has two parts. Part A deals with the general economic survey of the country, the policy initiatives and the programmes and schemes the Government will take up in the coming year. Part B deals with the tax proposals, both direct taxes (income tax, corporation tax) and indirect taxes (customs, excise, and now GST changes), and the Finance Bill measures. Statement 1 puts the initiatives in Part B 'in addition to' tax proposals, which is wrong because initiatives are in Part A. On receipts, revenue receipts are those that neither create a liability nor reduce an asset of the Government, such as tax revenue and non-tax revenue like interest, dividends, profits and fees. Capital receipts either create a liability (borrowings) or reduce an asset (recovery of loans, disinvestment or sale of PSU equity). Selling equity reduces the Government's assets, so partial disinvestment proceeds are capital receipts. Hence both statements fail and option (d) is correct. Options (a), (b) and (c) each accept at least one false statement.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is false: initiatives on the economic front are in Part A, not Part B.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is false: disinvestment receipts are capital receipts, not revenue receipts.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct, so they cannot both be right.
(d) is correct because statement 1 swaps Part A and Part B, and statement 2 misclassifies disinvestment proceeds as revenue receipts.
keyfact: Budget speech: Part A = economy and initiatives; Part B = tax proposals. Disinvestment receipts = capital receipts.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only. This would be right only if Part B carried policy initiatives. In fact Part A of the Budget speech covers the economic situation, policy and schemes, while Part B covers the tax proposals. The Budget is presented under Article 112 as the Annual Financial Statement, and the Finance Bill enacts the tax changes. The Budget is introduced in the Lok Sabha, usually on 1 February.

Option (b), statement 2 only. This would mean disinvestment is a revenue receipt. Revenue receipts are tax revenue (income tax, corporation tax, GST, customs) and non-tax revenue (interest, dividends, profits, fees, grants). They do not create a liability or reduce an asset. Disinvestment reduces the Government's asset holding, so it is a capital receipt, recorded under miscellaneous capital receipts.

Option (c), both statements. This would require Part B to hold initiatives and disinvestment to be revenue. Both are wrong. Part A deals with the economy and initiatives, Part B with taxes. Disinvestment is a capital receipt. Capital receipts include borrowings, recoveries of loans and disinvestment, and they feed into the financing of the fiscal deficit.

Option (d), neither statement. This is the correct answer. Part A covers the economic survey and policy initiatives, Part B covers the direct and indirect tax proposals. Disinvestment proceeds are capital receipts, along with borrowings and loan recoveries. Revenue receipts comprise tax and non-tax revenue. Knowing this classification is essential for deficit concepts such as revenue deficit and fiscal deficit.
related: Article 112 requires the Annual Financial Statement (Budget) to be laid before Parliament.
Part A of the Budget speech: economy and policy; Part B: tax proposals.
Disinvestment proceeds are capital receipts.
Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings.
Railway Budget merged with the General Budget in 2017.
The Budget has been presented on 1 February since 2017.
DIPAM under the Ministry of Finance handles disinvestment.
Appropriation Bill is under Article 114.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Initiatives on the economic front are in Part A; Part B holds the tax proposals. Part A of the Budget speech reviews the state of the economy and sets out the Government's policy direction, sector-wise priorities and new schemes for the coming year. Part B presents the revenue side, covering the changes in direct taxes (income tax slabs, corporate tax, surcharge) and indirect taxes (customs duty changes, and earlier excise and service tax). The Finance Bill gives legal effect to Part B. The Budget is presented under Article 112 as the Annual Financial Statement. Since 2017 it is presented on 1 February, and the Railway Budget was merged with the General Budget that year.

2 — Incorrect: Partial disinvestment proceeds are capital receipts because they reduce the Government's asset holding. Disinvestment means selling part or all of the Government's equity in public sector enterprises. Receipts from it are shown under 'Miscellaneous Capital Receipts' in the Budget. Capital receipts also include market borrowings, external loans, small savings, provident funds and loan recoveries. Revenue receipts include tax revenue and non-tax revenue like dividends and interest. The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) handles disinvestment. Disinvestment proceeds reduce the fiscal deficit financing need but do not count as revenue.
summary: The answer is (d), neither statement is correct. Statement 1 reverses the structure of the Budget speech: Part A covers the economic situation and policy initiatives, while Part B contains the tax proposals. Statement 2 is wrong because disinvestment proceeds are capital receipts, not revenue receipts.
topic_notes: The Union Budget is the Annual Financial Statement under Article 112. It shows estimated receipts and expenditure for the financial year (1 April to 31 March). It is presented in the Lok Sabha by the Finance Minister, and since 2017 on 1 February. The Railway Budget was merged with the General Budget in 2017, and the plan and non-plan distinction was removed in 2017-18. The Budget speech has two parts: Part A covers the state of the economy, policy and programme announcements, and Part B covers tax proposals. The Finance Bill gives effect to tax proposals. The Appropriation Bill authorises withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 114). Receipts divide into revenue receipts and capital receipts. Revenue receipts: tax revenue (income tax, corporation tax, GST, customs, union excise) and non-tax revenue (interest receipts, dividends and profits, fees, grants). Capital receipts: borrowings, recoveries of loans, disinvestment and other receipts. Test: does it create a liability or reduce an asset? If so, it is a capital receipt. Deficit concepts: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments. Effective revenue deficit excludes grants for creation of capital assets. The FRBM Act 2003 set deficit targets. Funds: Consolidated Fund (Article 266), Contingency Fund (Article 267), Public Account (Article 266(2)). Vote on account is under Article 116. Disinvestment is handled by DIPAM under the Ministry of Finance. A first major disinvestment push came after the 1991 reforms. A Disinvestment Ministry was created in 1999 and later became a department.

question:
The Comptroller and Auditor General of
India is appointed by the
(a) Prime Minister
(b) President
(c) Finance Minister
(d) Finance Minister
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 148 provides for the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Clause (1) says he shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal, and can be removed only in the like manner and on the like grounds as a Supreme Court judge, i.e. by the President on an address by both Houses of Parliament, supported by a special majority, for proved misbehaviour or incapacity. In practice the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister, but formally the appointing authority is the President, so (a) is not correct. The oath is taken before the President (Third Schedule). The term is 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier. Salary is equal to that of a Supreme Court judge and is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. After office, the CAG is ineligible for any further office under the Union or a State Government. His duties and powers are governed by the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. He audits accounts of the Union and States and submits reports to the President (Union) or Governor (State) under Articles 151. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called him potentially the most important officer under the Constitution. Elimination: the Finance Minister has no appointing role, and the Prime Minister only advises.
explanations: Incorrect: the Prime Minister only advises; the constitutional appointing authority under Art. 148(1) is the President.
Correct: Article 148(1) says the CAG is appointed by the President by warrant under hand and seal.
Incorrect: the Finance Minister has no role in appointing the CAG, whose independence from the executive is deliberately protected.
Incorrect: it repeats option (c), apparently an OCR duplication, and is wrong for the same reason.
keyfact: CAG: appointed by the President (Art. 148), removable like a Supreme Court judge, 6 years or 65 years of age.
option_notes: The Prime Minister is head of the Council of Ministers (Art. 74) and the real executive head of the Union government. He advises the President on key appointments, including the CAG, but does not formally appoint. He is appointed by the President (Art. 75), is generally the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha, and is the link between the President and the Council of Ministers.

The President is the constitutional head of the Union (Art. 52) and executive power is vested in him (Art. 53). He appoints the CAG, Supreme Court and High Court judges, the Attorney General, the Chief Election Commissioner and the UPSC chairman, acting on ministerial advice (Art. 74). Election is by an Electoral College under Art. 54, with a 5-year term.

The Finance Minister heads the Ministry of Finance and presents the Union Budget under Art. 112. The Minister is responsible for the Department of Economic Affairs, Revenue and Expenditure. He is accountable to Parliament for public finance, and the CAG audits the spending of his ministry like any other, so he cannot appoint the auditor.

This is a duplicate of option (c), the Finance Minister, apparently an OCR error. The Finance Minister is a Union Cabinet minister who manages taxation, expenditure and budget policy, and is subject to CAG audit. He has no power to appoint or remove the CAG, so this option is wrong.
related: Article 148 deals with the CAG; Article 149 with his duties and powers.
The CAG's term is 6 years or up to age 65, whichever is earlier.
He is removed like a Supreme Court judge, by Parliament's address with special majority.
CAG reports on the Union go to the President, and on States to the Governor (Art. 151).
The Public Accounts Committee works with the CAG, who acts as its friend, philosopher and guide.
The CAG (DPC) Act, 1971 governs his duties, powers and service conditions.
The CAG is ineligible for any further office under the Government of India or a State after retirement.
The CAG's salary is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
summary: The correct answer is (b) President. Under Article 148(1) of the Constitution, the CAG of India is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. Options (c) and (d) appear to be an OCR duplicate and are in any case wrong, as is the Prime Minister in (a).
topic_notes: The CAG is an independent constitutional authority under Articles 148 to 151 in Part V, Chapter V. Article 148 covers appointment, oath, salary and service conditions. Article 149 covers duties and powers. Article 150 says the accounts of the Union and States are kept in the form prescribed by the President on the advice of the CAG. Article 151 requires the CAG's reports on Union accounts to go to the President, who lays them before Parliament, and reports on State accounts to go to the Governor, who lays them before the State Legislature. The CAG is often called the guardian of the public purse. He is not a member of the Indian Audit and Accounts Service by right, but heads it. He audits receipts and expenditure of the Consolidated Funds, Contingency Funds and Public Accounts, and also audits government companies and corporations as provided by law. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) examines CAG reports and is helped by the CAG, who is described as its friend, philosopher and guide. The CAG can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge. His salary and conditions cannot be changed to his disadvantage after appointment. The first CAG of independent India was V. Narahari Rao (1948). The CAG Act, 1971 was amended in 1976 to separate accounts from audit. Other angles: the CAG has no power over the audit of the Supreme Court's or defence intelligence funds beyond the legal limits; Girish Chandra Murmu was CAG from 2020 and K. Sanjay Murthy from 2024.

question: Assertion (A): Point of order is raised to criticize a policy of the government. Reason (R): It is an important tool of legislative control. Codes:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
subject: Computers
detail: A point of order (Rule 376 of Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure) is a procedural device. A member raises it when he believes the proceedings of the House, or a matter before it, violate the Rules, the Constitution (for example Articles 105, 118, 121) or the Directions of the Speaker. It must relate to a matter within the cognizance of the House, must pose a question the Chair can decide, and must be raised at the moment the alleged irregularity occurs. It cannot be raised on a hypothetical issue, cannot be used to make a speech or to debate policy, and a member raising it cannot interrupt a speaker unless it is a genuine procedural breach. The Speaker's ruling on it is final. Because it is not meant to attack policy, A is false. R, saying it is an important tool of legislative control, is generally a true proposition about parliamentary devices, as questions, calling attention, adjournment motions and no-confidence motions are the actual means of controlling the executive. Hence the combination is A false, R true, and option (d) is correct. Options (a), (b) and (c) all treat A as true, so they fail.
explanations: Wrong: A is false because a point of order concerns procedure, not criticism of policy, so R cannot explain it.
Wrong: A is not true. A point of order is not used to criticize government policy, so the pairing 'both true' fails.
Wrong: A is false, and (c) wrongly takes A as true and R as false.
Correct: A is false, since a point of order only raises a breach of rules or the Constitution. R, as a general statement about parliamentary tools of control, is true.
keyfact: A point of order concerns breach of rules or the Constitution, never policy criticism; no debate is allowed on it and the Speaker's ruling is final.
option_notes: Both true with R explaining A. This would be correct only if a point of order were a policy-criticism device. It is not, as it deals with the rules of procedure and conduct of business in the House.
Both true but R not explaining A. This is rejected because A itself is untrue. Parliamentary devices like questions and motions are policy-oriented, whereas a point of order is purely procedural.

A true, R false. This reverses the real position, since A is false. Instruments of legislative control such as the Question Hour, Zero Hour, discussion motions and the no-confidence motion do exist, so R is not false.

A false, R true. This matches the position. A point of order draws attention to a violation of rules, the Speaker decides on it, and no debate is allowed on it. Control over the executive works through other devices.
related: Rule 376 of Lok Sabha Rules deals with points of order.
Zero Hour is not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure; it began in 1962.
Adjournment motion needs the support of 50 members in Lok Sabha.
No-confidence motion can be moved only in Lok Sabha, under Rule 198.
Article 118 empowers each House to make its own rules of procedure.
Article 75(3): Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to Lok Sabha.
Calling attention notice is Rule 197; it is a procedural device of Indian origin.
summary: The correct answer is (d): Assertion A is false and Reason R is true. A point of order is raised to draw the Presiding Officer's attention to a breach of the rules of procedure or the Constitution, not to criticize government policy. Legislative control over the executive is exercised through tools such as questions, motions, and debates, so R is a true statement in a general sense.
topic_notes:
Parliamentary procedure and devices. Point of order: Rule 376 in Lok Sabha and Rule 258 in Rajya Sabha. It takes precedence over other business as it concerns the regularity of proceedings. The Speaker or Chairman decides it, and the ruling is final. No debate on it is permitted, and it cannot be raised on a matter outside the House's cognizance.

Devices for controlling the executive: Question Hour (starred, unstarred, short notice questions, and questions to private members), Zero Hour (an Indian innovation, started in 1962, not in the Rules), half-an-hour discussion, short duration discussion (Rule 193), calling attention notice (Rule 197), adjournment motion (Rule 56, needs 50 members' support, involves censure of government), no-confidence motion (Rule 198, needs 50 members' support, only in Lok Sabha), censure motion, cut motions on demands for grants (policy cut, economy cut, token cut), motion of thanks to the President's address, and committees such as the Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee and Committee on Public Undertakings. Article 75(3) establishes the collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to Lok Sabha. Other features: privilege motion, closure motion, guillotine, and the Speaker's casting vote (Article 100). Rules of Procedure derive from Article 118.

question: Who of the following is the Chairman of Planning Commission in India?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The Planning Commission was established on 15 March 1950 by an executive (Cabinet) resolution of the Government of India. It was a non-constitutional and non-statutory body. It was formed on the recommendation of the Advisory Planning Board (K.C. Neogy, 1946), and its first Deputy Chairman was Gulzarilal Nanda. The Prime Minister was always the ex officio Chairman, with Jawaharlal Nehru the first. The Deputy Chairman, with the rank of Cabinet Minister, ran the Commission's work. Members included some Union ministers (such as Finance and Planning) and full-time expert members, and the Member Secretary was usually a senior civil servant. Its role was to assess resources, formulate Five-Year Plans, and advise on priorities. The National Development Council (NDC), also chaired by the PM, approved the Plans. The Commission was replaced on 1 January 2015 by NITI Aayog, which is also chaired by the PM. Elimination: the President is only the nominal executive head and holds no chair in planning bodies. The Finance and Home Ministers may be members or attendees but never the Chairman. Only the PM fits.
explanations: Incorrect: The Finance Minister was at most a member or special invitee of the Commission, not its Chairman.
Correct: The Prime Minister was the ex officio Chairman of the Planning Commission from 1950 until it was replaced in 2015.
Incorrect: The President is the constitutional head of state and had no role in chairing the Commission.
Incorrect: The Home Minister was never the Chairman; the Home Ministry deals with internal security and Centre-State relations.
keyfact: The Prime Minister is ex officio Chairman of the Planning Commission (1950) and of its successor NITI Aayog (2015).
option_notes: The Finance Minister heads the Ministry of Finance and presents the Union Budget under Article 112. He or she was sometimes a member of the Planning Commission, and is an ex officio member of the NITI Aayog Governing Council. The Finance Minister is not a chair of planning bodies.

The Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers under Article 74 and is the real executive head. The PM chaired the Planning Commission, the National Development Council and now NITI Aayog. Nehru was the first to chair the Planning Commission (1950), and Manmohan Singh the last (2014).

The President is the constitutional head of state under Article 52, elected indirectly under Article 54, and acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers under Article 74. The President has no role in the working of the Planning Commission. The first President was Dr. Rajendra Prasad.

The Home Minister heads the Ministry of Home Affairs, which handles internal security, the police, the Central Armed Police Forces, disaster management and Centre-State relations. Sardar Patel was the first Home Minister. The Home Minister had no chairing role in planning.
related: Planning Commission was set up on 15 March 1950 by a Cabinet resolution.
It was a non-constitutional and non-statutory body.
The first Deputy Chairman was Gulzarilal Nanda.
NITI Aayog replaced it on 1 January 2015.
The Prime Minister chairs both the National Development Council and NITI Aayog.
The first Five-Year Plan (1951-56) was based on the Harrod-Domar model.
Montek Singh Ahluwalia was the longest-serving Deputy Chairman.
The first Vice-Chairman of NITI Aayog was Arvind Panagariya.
summary: The answer is (b) Prime Minister of India. The Planning Commission, set up in 1950 by a Cabinet resolution, was chaired ex officio by the Prime Minister, while the Deputy Chairman handled day-to-day work.
topic_notes: Planning in India: The idea goes back to the 1934 Visvesvaraya plan 'Planned Economy for India', the 1938 National Planning Committee under Nehru, the 1944 Bombay Plan, and the Gandhian and People's Plans. The Planning Commission was set up on 15 March 1950 by a Cabinet resolution. It was neither constitutional nor statutory. The Prime Minister was Chairman. The Deputy Chairman was the effective full-time head, with Cabinet rank. Montek Singh Ahluwalia held the post longest (2004-2014). The first Five-Year Plan (1951-56) was based on the Harrod-Domar model. The second Plan (1956-61) was the Mahalanobis model, which stressed heavy industry. The twelfth Plan (2012-17) was the last. The National Development Council, formed in 1952, approved Plans and included the PM, Union Cabinet ministers and Chief Ministers. In 2015 NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission by a Cabinet resolution dated 1 January 2015. Its Chairperson is the PM, with a Vice-Chairperson (first Arvind Panagariya), a CEO, a Governing Council of Chief Ministers and Lieutenant Governors, and regional councils. It is a think tank and promotes cooperative federalism, with a bottom-up approach, unlike the top-down Planning Commission. Other points: Plan Holidays (1966-69) came after the third Plan; Rolling Plan (1978-80) was under the Janata Government; and the 2015 shift ended the formal Five-Year Plans.

Who among the following became the
President of India without having been the Vice –
President?
(a) Shri V. V. Giri
(b) Shri Venkataraman
(c) Shri N. Sanjeeva Reddy
(d) Shri Zakir Hussain
(b) Yuan Chwang
(c) Fa Hien

subject: Computers
detail: The Vice-President of India is elected under Article 66 and is ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64). Several Presidents moved up from the Vice-President's office: S. Radhakrishnan (VP 1952-62, President 1962-67), Zakir Hussain (VP 1962-67, President 1967-69), V. V. Giri (VP 1967-69, President 1969-74), R. Venkataraman (VP 1984-87, President 1987-92), Shankar Dayal Sharma (VP 1987-92, President 1992-97) and K. R. Narayanan (VP 1992-97, President 1997-2002). Presidents who were not Vice-Presidents include Rajendra Prasad, Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed, N. Sanjiva Reddy, Giani Zail Singh, A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, Pratibha Patil, Pranab Mukherjee, Ram Nath Kovind and Droupadi Murmu. Sanjiva Reddy was elected unopposed in July 1977 after the Janata Party came to power, and he was the sixth President. He had been Lok Sabha Speaker (1967-69, and again in 1977), and had lost to V. V. Giri in 1969 as the official Congress candidate. Elimination: Giri, Venkataraman and Zakir Hussain were all Vice-Presidents first, so only Reddy fits.
explanations: Incorrect: V. V. Giri was Vice-President (1967-69) before becoming President in 1969.
Incorrect: R. Venkataraman was Vice-President (1984-87) before becoming President (1987-92).
Correct: N. Sanjiva Reddy became President in 1977 directly, without holding the Vice-President's office.
Incorrect: Zakir Hussain was Vice-President (1962-67) before becoming President in 1967.
keyfact: N. Sanjiva Reddy (President 1977-82) is the one among the options who became President without being Vice-President.
option_notes: V. V. Giri (1894-1980) was the 4th President, 1969-74. He was earlier Vice-President, Governor of UP, Kerala and Mysore, and Union Labour Minister. He won the 1969 election as an independent candidate, backed by Indira Gandhi, in the only presidential election decided on second-preference votes. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1975.

R. Venkataraman (1910-2009) was the 8th President, 1987-92. He had been Vice-President (1984-87), Finance and Defence Minister, and Tamil Nadu politician. He was a Constituent Assembly member and a Supreme Court-level lawyer. During his term there were four Prime Ministers: Rajiv Gandhi, V. P. Singh, Chandra Shekhar and Narasimha Rao.

N. Sanjiva Reddy (1913-1996) was the 6th President, 1977-82, and the only President elected unopposed. He was the first Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, a Lok Sabha Speaker, and a Union Minister. He is the only person to hold the offices of Speaker and President. He was a Janata Party-era choice, having contested and lost in 1969.

Zakir Hussain (1897-1969) was the 3rd President, 1967-69, and the first to die in office. He was Vice-President (1962-67), Governor of Bihar, and Vice-Chancellor of Aligarh Muslim University. He co-founded Jamia Millia Islamia and received the Bharat Ratna in 1963. He was the first Muslim President of India.

summary: The answer is (c) Shri N. Sanjeeva Reddy. He was elected President in 1977 without ever having served as Vice-President. He had earlier been Lok Sabha Speaker. V. V. Giri, R. Venkataraman and Zakir Hussain all served as Vice-President before becoming President.
topic_notes: The President is elected by an electoral college of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the State Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry) under Article 54, using proportional representation by single transferable vote with secret ballot (Article 55). Qualifications (Article 58) are Indian citizenship, age 35 or above, eligibility for the Lok Sabha, and no office of profit. The term is five years (Article 56), and the President can be removed by impeachment under Article 61, which needs a two-thirds majority in both Houses. The Vice-President is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament only (Article 66), must be at least 35, and holds a five-year term. The Vice-President acts as President during a vacancy for up to six months, until a new President is elected (Article 65). Order of Presidents: Rajendra Prasad (1950-62), Radhakrishnan, Zakir Hussain, V. V. Giri, F. A. Ahmed (died in office, 1977), N. S. Reddy, Zail Singh, Venkataraman, S. D. Sharma, K. R. Narayanan, A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, Pratibha Patil (first woman), Pranab Mukherjee, Ram Nath Kovind and Droupadi Murmu. Acting Presidents: V. V. Giri (1969), M. Hidayatullah (1969) and B. D. Jatti (1977). Only Rajendra Prasad served two terms. Disputes over the election are decided by the Supreme Court (Article 71).

question: Nalanda University ﬂourished during the reign of which of the following rulers?
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: Nalanda Mahavihara, in Bihar near Rajgir, was established under Gupta patronage, traditionally by Kumaragupta I (c. 427 CE). The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) visited India in Harsha's reign, stayed at Nalanda about 5 years (c. 637-642 CE), studied Yogachara under the head Silabhadra, and described its large body of students and teachers, its libraries and its rigorous entry tests. Harsha of Pushyabhuti dynasty (capital Kannauj) endowed it with the revenue of about 100 villages and built a copper-plated monastery there. Later I-Tsing visited too (c. 673-695). The Palas (Dharmapala, Devapala) continued patronage, and Bakhtiyar Khilji destroyed it around 1193 CE. Elimination: Chandragupta Maurya (c. 321-297 BCE) and Ashoka (268-232 BCE) preceded Nalanda's founding by centuries; Ashoka is linked with Sanchi, Sarnath and the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra. Kanishka (Kushana, c. 78-101 CE) is linked with the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir and Gandhara art, not Nalanda. Hence Harsha.
explanations: Incorrect: Chandragupta Maurya ruled around 321-297 BCE, some 700 years before Nalanda was founded; he is associated with Jainism and Megasthenes' visit.
Incorrect: Ashoka (268-232 BCE) predates Nalanda; his Buddhist links are Kalinga, edicts, stupas and the Third Council at Pataliputra.
Incorrect: Kanishka was a Kushana ruler (c. 78 CE onward) with a Peshawar/Mathura base; he convened the Fourth Council and patronised Mahayana, not Nalanda.
Correct: Harsha (606-647 CE) patronised Nalanda; Xuanzang studied there in his reign, and Nalanda then flourished as a major centre.
keyfact: Nalanda: founded by Kumaragupta I (Gupta), flourished under Harsha (Xuanzang's visit), destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji c. 1193.
option_notes: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire c. 321 BCE with Chanakya's help, defeated the Nandas and Seleucus Nicator (305 BCE), and ruled from Pataliputra. Megasthenes wrote Indica at his court. Tradition says he became a Jain and died at Shravanabelagola.

Ashoka, the Mauryan emperor (268-232 BCE), fought the Kalinga war (261 BCE), embraced Buddhism, promoted dhamma, issued rock and pillar edicts in Brahmi, Kharosthi and Greek/Aramaic, and sent missionaries including Mahendra and Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka. Edicts were deciphered by James Prinsep.

Kanishka was the greatest Kushana king, whose era is often linked with the Saka era (78 CE). He had capitals at Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura, patronised Mahayana Buddhism, and convened the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir under Vasumitra. Ashvaghosha, Charaka and Nagarjuna are linked to his court.

Harsha Vardhana (606-647 CE) of Thanesar and Kannauj was the last great Hindu emperor of north India. He was defeated by Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas on the Narmada. Banabhatta wrote the Harshacharita; Harsha wrote Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda. He held quinquennial assemblies at Prayag and hosted Xuanzang.
related: Xuanzang visited India during Harsha's reign and wrote Si-Yu-Ki.
Vikramashila University was founded by the Pala king Dharmapala.
Bakhtiyar Khilji destroyed Nalanda around 1193 CE.
Nalanda became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.
Faxian visited India during Chandragupta II's reign.
Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha on the Narmada.
Kumaragupta I is traditionally credited with founding Nalanda.
summary: The answer is (d) Harsha. Nalanda was founded in the Gupta period (c. 5th century CE, by Kumaragupta I) but it flourished as the great international Buddhist centre of learning under Harsha (606-647 CE), when Xuanzang studied and taught there. Harsha patronised it generously, so among the given options he is the best fit.
topic_notes: Nalanda Mahavihara (Bihar) was a leading Buddhist monastic university from the 5th to 12th centuries CE. Founded under the Guptas, traditionally by Kumaragupta I, it received later support from Harsha and the Palas. Xuanzang called it Nalanda Mahavihara and recorded that admission was very difficult, with a gatekeeper-scholar testing applicants. Silabhadra was its head in his time. Subjects included Buddhist philosophy (Mahayana, Yogachara, Madhyamaka), logic, grammar, medicine, Vedas and mathematics. Famous scholars include Nagarjuna, Aryadeva, Dharmapala, Dignaga, Dharmakirti and Santarakshita. The great library complex was called Dharmaganja, with the buildings Ratnasagara, Ratnodadhi and Ratnaranjaka. It was sacked by Bakhtiyar Khilji around 1193 CE. The ruins were identified by Francis Buchanan-Hamilton and excavated by the ASI, and the site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016. A modern Nalanda University was established by an Act of Parliament in 2010 near Rajgir and linked with the East Asia Summit. Other ancient universities: Takshashila (Taxila, now Pakistan), Vikramashila (founded by Dharmapala, Pala king, near Bhagalpur), Odantapuri (Bihar Sharif), Somapura (Paharpur, now Bangladesh) and Vallabhi (Gujarat, under the Maitrakas). Other Chinese travellers are Faxian (Chandragupta II) and I-Tsing (late 7th century).

question:
The foreign traveller who visited India
during Vijayanagar period was?

subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Vijayanagara Empire (1336-1646 CE) was founded by Harihara I and Bukka Raya of the Sangama dynasty. Foreign visitors left detailed accounts of the capital Hampi. Nicolo de Conti, an Italian, came in about 1420 under Deva Raya I. Abdur Razzak, a Persian ambassador of the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh, came in 1443 under Deva Raya II. Domingo Paes, a Portuguese, visited around 1515 under Krishnadevaraya. Fernao Nuniz, also Portuguese, was in Vijayanagara around 1535-37 under Achyuta Raya. Afanasy Nikitin, a Russian merchant, visited the Bahmani kingdom around 1470 but not Vijayanagara. Megasthenes was the Seleucid envoy to Chandragupta Maurya and wrote Indica. Fa-Hien (Gupta period, Chandragupta II), Hiuen Tsang (Harsha), Al-Biruni (Mahmud of Ghazni) and Ibn Battuta (Muhammad bin Tughluq) belong to other periods. The elimination logic is therefore to reject anyone tied to the Mauryan, Gupta, Harsha or Delhi Sultanate courts, which rules out option (a) at once.
explanations: Incorrect: Megasthenes visited the Mauryan court of Chandragupta around 302-298 BCE, about 1,600 years before Vijayanagara.
Option (b) is blank in the OCR, so it cannot be assessed. It would be right only if it names Abdur Razzak, Conti, Paes or Nuniz.

option_notes: Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador of Seleucus I Nicator at Chandragupta Maurya's court in Pataliputra. He wrote Indica, which survives only in fragments quoted by later authors such as Arrian and Strabo. It describes Mauryan administration, the seven-caste classification, and the city of Pataliputra.

Not legible in the OCR. If it names Domingo Paes or Fernao Nuniz, they were Portuguese chroniclers. Paes visited under Krishnadevaraya and Nuniz under Achyuta Raya, and their accounts are compiled in Sewell's A Forgotten Empire.

Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador to Chandragupta Maurya's court around 300 BCE, so he cannot be the Vijayanagara-period traveller. The usual options in this question are Abdur Razzak, Nicolo Conti, Domingo Paes, Fernao Nuniz and Ibn Battuta, but since none of them is visible, 'a' is the only letter that can be eliminated. The answer letter in ans_ai is a best guess, not a confirmed one.
topic_notes: Vijayanagara, founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka with the help of the sage Vidyaranya, had four dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu. Its best-known ruler was Krishnadevaraya (1509-29) of the Tuluva dynasty, who wrote the Telugu work Amuktamalyada and had Ashtadiggajas at his court. The empire fell after the Battle of Talikota (Rakshasa-Tangadi) in 1565, when the Deccan sultanates defeated Rama Raya. Its capital Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its monuments include the Virupaksha temple, the Vittala temple with its stone chariot, and the Hazara Rama temple. Foreign accounts matter for the period's history. Conti and Abdur Razzak described the city's size and wealth. Paes and Nuniz described the Mahanavami festival, taxes, and the army. Barbosa was another Portuguese visitor. Other travellers by era: Megasthenes (Mauryan), Fa-Hien (Gupta), Hiuen Tsang and I-Tsing (Harsha and later), Al-Biruni (Ghaznavid), Ibn Battuta (Tughluq), Marco Polo (Pandya and Kakatiya coast, c. 1288-93), Nikitin (Bahmani), Bernier, Tavernier and Manucci (Mughal), and Thevenot.

question: Who among the following was a great protagonist of the 'Doctrine of Lapse'?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Doctrine of Lapse was an annexation policy of the British East India Company. Under it, a dependent princely state would 'lapse' to the Company if its ruler died without a natural-born male heir, and the Company would not recognise an adopted son as successor. Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General from 1848 to 1856, applied it most vigorously. States annexed by lapse: Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854), and Karauli (1855, later reversed). Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of misgovernment, not lapse. The policy caused deep resentment among Indian rulers and is counted among the causes of the Revolt of 1857. Elimination: Wellesley (1798-1805) is linked with the Subsidiary Alliance, not lapse. Minto (Minto II, 1905-10) is linked with the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 and separate electorates. Curzon (1899-1905) is linked with the Partition of Bengal, the Universities Act and the Ancient Monuments Act. So only Dalhousie fits.
explanations: Correct: Dalhousie was the chief architect and most active user of the Doctrine of Lapse, annexing Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur and other states.
Wrong: Lord Minto is associated with the Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms), which introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
Wrong: Lord Curzon is associated with the Partition of Bengal (1905), the Indian Universities Act (1904) and the Archaeological Survey reforms.
Wrong: Lord Wellesley used the Subsidiary Alliance system to extend British control, not the Doctrine of Lapse.
keyfact: Doctrine of Lapse = Lord Dalhousie (1848-56); first state annexed was Satara in 1848.
option_notes: Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General 1848-56) was a great moderniser. He introduced railways (first line Bombay-Thane, 1853), the telegraph, the Post Office Act of 1854, Wood's Despatch (1854), the PWD, and the Widow Remarriage Act (1856, passed under Canning). He annexed Punjab in 1849 after the Second Anglo-Sikh War and Lower Burma in 1852. He is best known for the Doctrine of Lapse.

Lord Minto II (Viceroy 1905-10) oversaw the Indian Councils Act 1909, called the Morley-Minto Reforms, which expanded the legislative councils and gave Muslims separate electorates. His term saw the Swadeshi movement, the Surat split of 1907 and the founding of the Muslim League in 1906. The Press Act of 1910 was also passed in this period.

Lord Curzon (Viceroy 1899-1905) set up the Police Commission under Andrew Fraser, the Universities Commission (1902) and the Indian Universities Act (1904). He passed the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act (1904), created the North-West Frontier Province (1901), held the Delhi Durbar of 1903 and partitioned Bengal in 1905. He resigned in 1905 after a dispute with Kitchener.

Lord Wellesley (Governor-General 1798-1805) pursued an aggressive expansion policy. He introduced the Subsidiary Alliance, first accepted by Hyderabad (1798), and defeated Tipu Sultan in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799). He also fought the Second Anglo-Maratha War and founded Fort William College in 1800 in Calcutta.
related: Satara was the first state annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse (1848).

summary: The answer is (a) Lord Dalhousie. As Governor-General of India (1848-56), he applied the Doctrine of Lapse to annex Indian princely states whose rulers died without a natural male heir, and he refused to recognise adopted heirs.
topic_notes: The Doctrine of Lapse was the policy by which the East India Company annexed a dependent Indian state if its ruler died without a natural heir. It was used mainly by Lord Dalhousie, though the principle had earlier precedents. Dalhousie distinguished three classes of states: independent states, states that were tributary to the Company, and states created or restored by the British, to which the doctrine applied. States annexed by lapse include Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854), Karauli (1855) and Awadh (1856, by misgovernment). Nana Sahib, the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, was denied his pension, and Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi was denied her adopted heir. Both became leaders in the Revolt of 1857. After the Revolt, Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 ended the doctrine, and the right of adoption was recognised. Other Dalhousie reforms: the Railways Minute of 1853, the Telegraph (1852-53), the Postal reforms of 1854, the Engineering College at Roorkee, Wood's Despatch of 1854 (the 'Magna Carta of English Education in India'), the Public Works Department and the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act of 1856 (passed under Canning). Comparable policies by other Governors-General: Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance, Cornwallis's Permanent Settlement, and Bentinck's abolition of sati (1829).

question: Chauri Chaura is known in the history of India's struggle for freedom because
options: Gandhiji launched his ﬁrst Satyagraha in India from this place
Gandhiji withdrew his Satyagraha movement when an irate mob set ﬁre to a police sta on and burnt some policemen
Hundreds of freedom ﬁghters were shot dead at this place by the police
Gandhiji sat on a hunger strike
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: Chauri Chaura is remembered for the violent incident of 4 February 1922. A procession of Non-Cooperation volunteers and local peasants was fired on by police, or provoked by them, after which the mob chased the police into the thana and set it on fire. About 22 or 23 policemen died. Gandhiji believed the country was not yet prepared for non-violent mass action and held that violence violated the principle of ahimsa. He suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement, which began in 1920 after the Calcutta and Nagpur sessions of Congress, and announced this at Bardoli (the Bardoli resolution of 12 February 1922). Many leaders, including Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, Subhas Bose and Jawaharlal Nehru, were dismayed by the suspension. Gandhi was arrested in March 1922 and sentenced to six years for sedition. 172 villagers were sentenced to death by the Gorakhpur sessions court, and the High Court later reduced this to 19 executions. Elimination: Gandhi's first Satyagraha in India was Champaran (1917), so (a) is wrong. Mass shootings of freedom fighters describe Jallianwala Bagh (1919), so (c) is wrong. Chauri Chaura was not a hunger strike, so (d) is wrong.
explanations: Incorrect. Gandhi's first Satyagraha in India was at Champaran in 1917 (indigo). Ahmedabad mill strike and Kheda followed in 1918. Chauri Chaura was not the site of a Gandhian launch.
Correct. The mob burned the Chauri Chaura police station on 4 Feb 1922, killing policemen, and Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement.
Incorrect. Mass shooting of unarmed people describes Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, on 13 April 1919 under General Dyer. At Chauri Chaura the policemen were the ones killed.

Incorrect. Gandhi did not fast at Chauri Chaura. After the incident he did a five-day penance fast at Bardoli, but that is not why the place is known. His other famous fasts include the Poona Pact fast (1932) and the Calcutta fast (1947).
keyfact: Chauri Chaura (4 Feb 1922, Gorakhpur): mob burnt police station, policemen killed, Gandhi withdrew Non-Cooperation Movement.
option_notes: Champaran Satyagraha (1917) in Bihar was Gandhi's first satyagraha in India. It was against the tinkathia system of compulsory indigo cultivation. Rajkumar Shukla invited him. Associates included Rajendra Prasad, J.B. Kripalani and Mahadev Desai. The Champaran Agrarian Act 1918 ended the system.

This is the correct event. Chauri Chaura is in Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh. The incident took place on 4 Feb 1922. About 22 or 23 policemen died when the thana was set on fire. Gandhi suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement on 12 Feb 1922. The incident is part of the history of the 1920-22 mass movement. Gandhi was arrested in March 1922.

This describes the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 13 April 1919 in Amritsar. General Dyer ordered firing on a crowd gathered on Baisakhi, protesting the Rowlatt Act and the arrest of Kitchlew and Satyapal. The Hunter Committee investigated. Tagore renounced his knighthood. Udham Singh killed Michael O'Dwyer in 1940.

Gandhi undertook many fasts. The 1932 Yerwada fast against the Communal Award led to the Poona Pact between Gandhi and Ambedkar. The 1933 fast was for Harijan welfare. The 1943 fast was in detention. The 1947 Calcutta fast stopped communal riots. His final fast was in January 1948 in Delhi.
related: Chauri Chaura incident: 4 February 1922, Gorakhpur, UP
Non-Cooperation Movement suspended on 12 February 1922 (Bardoli resolution)
Gandhi's first satyagraha in India: Champaran 1917
Jallianwala Bagh massacre: 13 April 1919, General Dyer
Swaraj Party was founded in 1923 by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru
Gandhi was sentenced to six years in March 1922 by Judge Broomfield
Civil Disobedience Movement began with the Dandi March on 12 March 1930
summary: The answer is (b). At Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh) on 4 February 1922, an angry mob set fire to a police station and 22 or 23 policemen died. Gandhiji then withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement on 12 February 1922.
topic_notes: The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) was the first mass movement under Gandhi. It was launched after the Khilafat issue, the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. Congress endorsed it at the Calcutta special session (September 1920), and the Nagpur session (December 1920) confirmed it. The programme included boycott of councils, courts, schools and foreign cloth, and promotion of khadi and national institutions. Gandhi returned titles such as the Kaisar-i-Hind medal. The movement saw the Prince of Wales visit boycotted in November 1921. Chauri Chaura on 4 February 1922 led to its suspension. The Bardoli resolution of 12 February 1922 withdrew it, and a constructive programme was adopted instead. The Congress Working Committee ratified this. Gandhi was tried in March 1922, and Judge Broomfield sentenced him to six years. He was released in 1924 on health grounds. Afterward the Swaraj Party was formed by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru in 1923 to enter the councils. Later movements: Civil Disobedience (1930, Dandi March 12 March, Salt Satyagraha), Quit India (8 August 1942). Earlier Gandhian satyagrahas: Champaran 1917, Ahmedabad 1918, Kheda 1918. Rowlatt Satyagraha in 1919 was also called off after violence, which Gandhi called a Himalayan blunder. Important fact: Chauri Chaura centenary was observed in 2022, and the Gorakhpur site has a memorial.

question: The 'Grand Trunk Road' connects
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Grand Trunk Road traces back to the ancient Uttarapatha of the Mauryan period (Chandragupta Maurya). Sher Shah Suri (1540-45) rebuilt and extended it as the Sadak-e-Azam from Sonargaon (Bengal) to Peshawar and beyond to Kabul, adding sarais, wells, trees, mosques and the dak-chowki postal system. The Mughals maintained it and the British renamed it the Grand Trunk Road, improving it and metalling it in the 1830s-1860s under Lord Auckland and Lord Dalhousie. Today it passes through West Bengal, Jharkhand, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Haryana and Punjab, via cities such as Asansol, Dhanbad, Varanasi, Kanpur, Delhi, Ambala, Ludhiana and Amritsar, and runs on to Lahore and Peshawar in Pakistan. Hence option (c) is the best fit. Option (a) Kolkata-Mumbai is the NH 6 corridor (Golden Quadrilateral east-west link), option (b) Delhi-Chennai is the NH 44 north-south corridor (formerly NH 7 and others), and option (d) is a made-up combination, since Tirupati lies in Andhra Pradesh, far from the GT Road.
explanations: Incorrect: Kolkata-Mumbai is served by the NH 6 and the Golden Quadrilateral, not the GT Road, which runs north-west from Kolkata.
Incorrect: Delhi-Chennai is a north-south route (NH 44 and the Golden Quadrilateral); the GT Road runs east-west across the Indo-Gangetic plain.
Correct: The GT Road links Kolkata with Amritsar (and onward to the Wagah-Attari border), passing through Delhi.
Incorrect: Tirupati (Andhra Pradesh) is in the south and has no connection to the GT Road; the pairing is nonsensical.
keyfact: Grand Trunk Road = Sher Shah Suri's Sadak-e-Azam, linking Kolkata to Amritsar (and on to Peshawar/Kabul); now NH 19 and NH 44.
option_notes: Kolkata-Mumbai: linked by NH 6 (Kolkata-Dhule via Raipur, Nagpur, Surat in the older numbering), a part of the Golden Quadrilateral and the east-west corridor. The Golden Quadrilateral, launched in 2001 under NHDP, connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, with a total length of about 5,846 km. It is different from the GT Road.

Delhi-Chennai: the Golden Quadrilateral's diagonal link and the long NH 44 (earlier NH 7, Srinagar-Kanyakumari) form north-south connections. NH 44 at about 3,745 km is India's longest national highway. The Delhi-Chennai route runs via Agra, Jhansi, Nagpur, Hyderabad and Bengaluru in different segments.

Kolkata-Amritsar: the Grand Trunk Road on the Indian side, historically from Sonargaon to Kabul, about 2,500 km in total. Built by Sher Shah Suri as the Sadak-e-Azam, it was named Grand Trunk Road by the British. It is today designated NH 19 (Kolkata-Delhi) and NH 44 (Delhi-Amritsar section), and the Delhi-Kolkata part is formerly NH 2.

Tirupati-Ludhiana: not a recognised route. Tirupati is a pilgrimage city in Andhra Pradesh, famous for the Venkateswara temple at Tirumala. Ludhiana is a Punjab industrial city on the GT Road (NH 44). The option is a distractor combining a southern and a northern city.
related: Sher Shah Suri built the Sadak-e-Azam, later called the Grand Trunk Road.
