summary: The answer is (c) Kolkata and Amritsar. The Grand Trunk Road (GT Road, now NH 19 and NH 44 plus portions in Pakistan and Bangladesh) is one of Asia's oldest and longest roads, running from the Bengal region through Delhi to the north-west frontier, and on the Indian side it is commonly described as linking Kolkata with Amritsar (Attari border).
topic_notes: The Grand Trunk Road is among the oldest and longest major roads of South Asia, over 2,400-2,500 km, linking Bengal (Sonargaon, now in Bangladesh; later Kolkata) with Kabul in Afghanistan. Ancient origin: the Uttarapatha of the Mauryas, described by Megasthenes. Sher Shah Suri (Sur dynasty) rebuilt it with sarais, wells, shade trees and a postal system. Mughals continued the upkeep, and the British, notably under Lord Auckland and Lord Dalhousie, metalled it and gave it the present name. Rudyard Kipling called it a river of life in Kim. Present numbering: Kolkata-Delhi is NH 19 (formerly NH 2), Delhi-Amritsar is NH 44 (formerly NH 1). The road passes via Howrah, Durgapur, Asansol, Dhanbad, Gaya, Sasaram, Varanasi, Prayagraj, Kanpur, Aligarh, Delhi, Panipat, Karnal, Ambala, Ludhiana, Jalandhar and Amritsar, then Lahore, Rawalpindi, Peshawar and Jalalabad. Other highway facts: the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) was established in 1988 and operates under the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. NHDP began in 1998. The Golden Quadrilateral connects four metros, and the North-South-East-West (NS-EW) Corridor links Srinagar to Kanyakumari and Silchar to Porbandar. Bharatmala Pariyojana (2017) is the current umbrella highway programme. Other historical roads: the Dakshinapatha (southern route), and the Royal Road of the Achaemenids. Remember that NH 44 is the longest national highway in India.

question: The Civil Disobedience Movement of 1930 culminated in the signing of a pact in 1931 by Gandhiji and
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: The Civil Disobedience Movement began on 12 March 1930 with the Dandi March (Salt Satyagraha) after the Congress Lahore Session (December 1929, presided by Jawaharlal Nehru) declared Purna Swaraj as its goal. Viceroy Lord Irwin (1926-31) was the Viceroy at that time. After the First Round Table Conference (Nov 1930-Jan 1931) without Congress participation, Irwin sought reconciliation. Tej Bahadur Sapru and M.R. Jayakar mediated. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (Delhi Pact) of 5 March 1931 provided that Congress would suspend civil disobedience and attend the Round Table Conference; the government would release political prisoners not guilty of violence, permit peaceful picketing, and allow salt making for domestic use by coastal villagers. Gandhi's demand for an inquiry into police excesses was not accepted, and Bhagat Singh's commutation was refused. The Karachi Session (March 1931, Sardar Patel presiding) endorsed the pact and passed the resolution on Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme. Elimination: Linlithgow (1936-43) was Viceroy during the Cripps Mission era and the Quit India Movement; Wavell (1943-47) held the Simla Conference and Cabinet Mission; Curzon (1899-1905) partitioned Bengal in 1905.
explanations: Correct: Lord Irwin, Viceroy 1926-31, signed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact on 5 March 1931.
Wrong: Lord Linlithgow was Viceroy 1936-43 and handled the 1939 war declaration, the August Offer and the Quit India Movement.
Wrong: Lord Wavell was Viceroy 1943-47 and handled the Simla Conference 1945, the Cabinet Mission 1946 and the Wavell Plan.
Wrong: Lord Curzon was Viceroy 1899-1905, associated with the Partition of Bengal 1905 and the Universities Commission 1902.
keyfact: Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931) suspended the Civil Disobedience Movement and led to Gandhi attending the Second Round Table Conference.
option_notes: Lord Irwin (Edward Wood, later Lord Halifax) was Viceroy 1926-31. He made the 1929 Irwin Declaration (Oct 1929) promising Dominion Status as the goal, appointed the Simon Commission period administration, and survived a bomb attack on his train in Dec 1929. He signed the Delhi Pact with Gandhi on 5 March 1931.

Lord Linlithgow was Viceroy 1936-43, the longest-serving. The Government of India Act 1935 provincial autonomy came into effect and elections were held in 1937. He declared India at war in 1939 without consulting Indians, issued the August Offer 1940 and faced the Quit India Movement 1942.

Lord Wavell was Viceroy Oct 1943 to Feb 1947. He convened the Simla Conference in June 1945 and put forward the Wavell Plan. He dealt with the INA trials, the 1946 Royal Indian Navy Mutiny and the Cabinet Mission, and formed the Interim Government in September 1946. He was succeeded by Mountbatten.

Lord Curzon was Viceroy 1899-1905 and 1905 resignation followed a dispute with Kitchener. He created the North-West Frontier Province in 1901, passed the Indian Universities Act 1904, the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act 1904 and the Indian Official Secrets Act 1904, and partitioned Bengal in October 1905.
related: Dandi March: 12 March to 6 April 1930, 240 miles, 78 volunteers
Gandhi-Irwin Pact: 5 March 1931, also called Delhi Pact
Karachi Congress 1931 under Sardar Patel passed the Fundamental Rights resolution
Second Round Table Conference 1931: Gandhi was the sole Congress representative
Poona Pact of 1932 was between Gandhi and Ambedkar
Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were hanged on 23 March 1931
Irwin Declaration of October 1929 promised Dominion Status
summary: The answer is (a) Lord Irwin. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931 in Delhi, which suspended the Civil Disobedience Movement and paved the way for Gandhi to attend the Second Round Table Conference in London.
topic_notes: The Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM) followed the Lahore Congress resolution of Purna Swaraj (31 December 1929) and Independence Day observed on 26 January 1930. Gandhi sent an Eleven Point Demand to Irwin, and on 12 March 1930 began the Dandi March from Sabarmati with 78 followers, reaching Dandi on 6 April 1930 to break the salt law. The movement spread through the Salt Satyagraha, with C. Rajagopalachari at Vedaranyam, K. Kelappan at Payyanur, and Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgars in the North-West Frontier with the Peshawar events and the Garhwal Rifles refusal to fire. Women participated widely, as did traders and peasants in no-tax campaigns. The Simon Commission (1927-30) report and the Nehru Report (1928) provided background. The First Round Table Conference met in London from November 1930 to January 1931 under Ramsay MacDonald. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931, after which Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference (September-December 1931) as the sole Congress representative, and it ended without result. Civil disobedience resumed in January 1932, and the Communal Award of August 1932 led to the Poona Pact (24 September 1932) between Gandhi and Ambedkar. The Third Round Table Conference was in 1932. The movement was withdrawn formally in 1934. The Government of India Act 1935 followed.

question: Dhanvantari was
options: a famous General of Chandragupta Maurya
a noted physician in the Court of Chandragupta Vikramaditya
a famous drama st who lived during the me of Harsha
a musician in the Court of Ashoka
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: Dhanvantari is the legendary physician-figure of Indian tradition. In mythology he is the divine physician and an avatar of Vishnu who emerged from the Samudra Manthan with the pot of amrita, and he is the patron deity of Ayurveda (Dhanteras honours him). In historical tradition he is named as one of the Navaratnas of the court of Vikramaditya, identified with the Gupta king Chandragupta II (c. 375-415 CE). The nine gems were Dhanvantari, Kshapanaka, Amarasimha, Shanku, Vetalabhatta, Ghatakarpara, Kalidasa, Varahamihira and Vararuchi. The Navaratna tradition is a later one, and historians debate how far it is historical. Elimination: Chandragupta Maurya's famous associate was Chanakya (Kautilya), not a general named Dhanvantari. The famous dramatist of Harsha's time was Banabhatta (prose, Harshacharita and Kadambari), and Harsha himself wrote plays such as Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda. Ashoka's court is not linked with any musician called Dhanvantari. Hence (b).
explanations: Incorrect: Chandragupta Maurya's key adviser was Chanakya, and Dhanvantari was not a general.
Correct: Dhanvantari is traditionally named as the physician among the Navaratnas of Chandragupta II Vikramaditya.
Incorrect: Harsha's court is associated with Banabhatta, and Harsha himself wrote dramas. Dhanvantari was not a dramatist.
Incorrect: There is no tradition of Dhanvantari as a musician, and he is not linked with Ashoka's court.
keyfact: Dhanvantari was the physician among the Navaratnas of Chandragupta II Vikramaditya.
option_notes: Chandragupta Maurya (c. 321-297 BCE) founded the Mauryan empire with help from Chanakya (Kautilya), author of the Arthashastra. He defeated the Nanda dynasty and Seleucus Nicator (c. 305 BCE). Megasthenes was the Greek ambassador at his court. He reportedly became a Jain and died at Shravanabelagola. His generals are not a standard exam topic.

Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (c. 375-415 CE) was a Gupta ruler who defeated the Shakas of Western India and took the title Vikramaditya. His court is associated with the Navaratnas, including Kalidasa, Amarasimha and Varahamihira. The Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien visited India in his reign. Dhanvantari is the physician among the nine gems.

Harsha (606-647 CE) was a Pushyabhuti ruler with his capital at Kanauj. He wrote the plays Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda. Banabhatta wrote Harshacharita and Kadambari. Hiuen Tsang visited his court, and the Prayag quinquennial assembly (Maha Moksha Parishad) was held in his reign. He was defeated by Pulakeshin II on the Narmada.

Ashoka (c. 268-232 BCE) was a Mauryan emperor who fought the Kalinga War (261 BCE) and then adopted Buddhism and dhamma. His Rock and Pillar Edicts were written in Brahmi and deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837. His inscriptions mention medical care for humans and animals. No musician named Dhanvantari is associated with him.
related: Navaratnas of Chandragupta II include Kalidasa, Varahamihira and Amarasimha.
Akbar's Navaratnas include Birbal, Tansen, Todar Mal and Abul Fazl.
Krishnadevaraya's court had the Ashtadiggajas, eight poets.
Charaka Samhita is the classic Ayurvedic medicine text, and Sushruta Samhita the text of surgery.
Dhanvantari is the divine physician of Hindu tradition, honoured on Dhanteras.
Fa-Hien visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II.
Banabhatta wrote Harshacharita under Harsha.
summary: The answer is (b). Dhanvantari is traditionally listed as the physician among the Navaratnas (Nine Gems) at the court of Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya' (Gupta dynasty, c. 375-415 CE). He is not a general, dramatist or musician.
topic_notes: The Navaratnas of Vikramaditya are a recurring prelims topic. The tradition places nine scholars in the court of Vikramaditya, usually identified with Chandragupta II of the Gupta dynasty, though some link it with the legendary Vikramaditya of Ujjain (the Vikram Samvat of 57 BCE). The nine gems are Dhanvantari (physician), Kshapanaka (astrologer or Jain scholar), Amarasimha (lexicographer, Amarakosha), Shanku (architect), Vetalabhatta (magician, Vetala Panchavimshati), Ghatakarpara (poet), Kalidasa (poet and dramatist, Shakuntalam, Meghadutam, Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava), Varahamihira (astronomer, Brihat Samhita, Panchasiddhantika) and Vararuchi (grammarian). Other Gupta-era scholars were Aryabhata (Aryabhatiya, 499 CE), Brahmagupta (a later astronomer), Vishakhadatta (Mudrarakshasa) and Shudraka (Mrichchhakatika). Medical tradition: Charaka (Charaka Samhita, a physician under Kanishka) and Sushruta (Sushruta Samhita, surgery) are the classics of Ayurveda, and Vagbhata wrote Ashtanga Hridaya. Dhanvantari is a deity of Ayurveda, and in 2016 the Government of India designated Dhanteras as National Ayurveda Day, later shifting the date to Dhanvantari Jayanti. Gupta-era features to remember: Allahabad Pillar inscription of Samudragupta (composed by Harishena), the Mehrauli iron pillar, the Delhi-linked rule of Chandragupta II, Fa-Hien's travels, and the Nalanda university founded by Kumaragupta I. Exam angle: match the scholar with the work and the king. Other courts are also asked about, such as Harsha (Bana), Akbar (Navaratnas such as Birbal, Tansen, Todar Mal and Abul Fazl) and Krishnadevaraya (Ashtadiggajas).

question:
Which leader is called the ‘father' of India's
social reform movement?
(a) Mahatma Gandhi
(b) Raja Rammohun Roy
(c) G.K. Gokhale
(d) Lokmanya Tilak
(b) San Francisco-Salt Lake City-Pittsburgh-Boston
(c) Salt Lake City-San Francisco-Boston-Pittsburgh
(d) San Francisco-Pittsburgh-Salt Lake City-Boston
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: Raja Rammohun Roy (1772-1833) is regarded as the first great modern reformer and the 'Father of the Indian Renaissance'. He founded the Atmiya Sabha (1815) and the Brahmo Sabha (1828), which became the Brahmo Samaj. He attacked sati, polytheism, idol worship, caste rigidity and child marriage, and he supported women's education and property rights. His campaign led Lord William Bentinck to pass Regulation XVII of 1829, which banned sati in Bengal. He promoted English and scientific education, helped David Hare and Alexander Duff set up modern schools, and founded the Vedanta College (1825). He started the journals Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali, 1821) and Mirat-ul-Akbar (Persian). The Mughal emperor Akbar II gave him the title 'Raja' and sent him to England in 1830 as his envoy. He died at Bristol in 1833. Elimination: Gandhi is the Father of the Nation. Gokhale was a moderate Congress leader and founded the Servants of India Society (1905). Tilak is 'Lokmanya' and is known for the slogan 'Swaraj is my birthright'. The question also carries stray OCR text from another question (about US cities), which is ignored.
explanations: Incorrect: Gandhi is called the Father of the Nation and led the non-violent freedom struggle. He worked on social issues such as untouchability, but he is not the 'father' of the reform movement.
Correct: Raja Rammohun Roy began the 19th-century social reform movement, founded the Brahmo Samaj and fought sati. He is called the Father of the Indian Renaissance.
Incorrect: Gokhale was a moderate political leader and Gandhi's political guru. He founded the Servants of India Society, which is not the origin of social reform.
Incorrect: Tilak was an extremist nationalist leader who opposed the Age of Consent Bill (1891). He was a political agitator, not a reformer.
keyfact: Raja Rammohun Roy: Father of the Indian Renaissance and of social reform; Brahmo Samaj (1828); anti-sati law (1829).
option_notes: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869-1948) led the Champaran, Kheda, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India movements. He is called the Father of the Nation and 'Bapu'. He founded Sabarmati Ashram and ran the journals Young India and Harijan. He campaigned for the removal of untouchability and for Hindu-Muslim unity.

Raja Rammohun Roy (1772-1833) was born in Radhanagar, Bengal. He founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828, wrote Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin and The Precepts of Jesus, and campaigned against sati. He is the Father of the Indian Renaissance and the 'Morning Star' of reform, and he died at Bristol in 1833.

Gopal Krishna Gokhale (1866-1915) was a moderate Congress leader and a member of the Imperial Legislative Council. He founded the Servants of India Society in 1905 and presided over the 1905 Congress session at Banaras. He was Gandhi's political mentor, and Gandhi called him his 'political guru'. He taught at Fergusson College, Pune.

Bal Gangadhar Tilak (1856-1920) was given the title 'Lokmanya'. He led the extremist wing of the Congress, started the newspapers Kesari and Mahratta, and began the Ganesh and Shivaji festivals. He launched the Home Rule League in 1916 and wrote The Arctic Home in the Vedas and Gita Rahasya.
related: Sati was abolished by Regulation XVII of 1829 under Lord William Bentinck.
Brahmo Samaj was founded in 1828; its precursor was the Brahmo Sabha.
Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856, was promoted by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.
Arya Samaj was founded by Dayananda Saraswati in 1875 in Bombay.
Rammohun Roy's journal Sambad Kaumudi was published in Bengali in 1821.
Satyashodhak Samaj was founded by Jyotiba Phule in 1873.
Ramakrishna Mission was founded by Vivekananda in 1897.
Age of Consent Act, 1891, raised the age of consent to 12 years.
summary: The answer is (b) Raja Rammohun Roy. He is called the 'Father of the Indian Renaissance' and the pioneer of India's social and religious reform movement. He founded the Brahmo Sabha (1828) and campaigned against sati, which was outlawed in 1829.
topic_notes: The 19th-century social and religious reform movements arose from contact with Western education and ideas. Raja Rammohun Roy started the movement with the Atmiya Sabha (1815) and the Brahmo Samaj (1828). Debendranath Tagore carried it on through the Tattvabodhini Sabha (1839), and Keshab Chandra Sen was later associated with the Brahmo Samaj. Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar campaigned for widow remarriage, which led to the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856. Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj (1875) and gave the call 'Back to the Vedas'. Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897). Jyotiba Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873). Sir Syed Ahmad Khan founded the Aligarh movement and the Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College (1875). The Prarthana Samaj (1867) was started by Atmaram Pandurang, with M.G. Ranade as a leading figure. B.M. Malabari campaigned for the Age of Consent Act (1891). Narayana Guru led a reform movement in Kerala through the SNDP (1903). The key laws were the ban on sati (1829), the Widow Remarriage Act (1856), the Special Marriage Act (1872) and the Sarda Act (1929). The Theosophical Society was set up by Madame Blavatsky and Col. Olcott in 1875, and its Indian headquarters were at Adyar under Annie Besant. Reformers differed in approach: some were rationalist and Western-influenced, while others were revivalist.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises eight classical dance forms: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam and Sattriya (Assam, added 2000). Each is tied to a home state. Bharatanatyam is the temple dance of Tamil Nadu, once called Sadir or Dasiattam, and was revived in the 20th century by E. Krishna Iyer and Rukmini Devi Arundale. Kathakali is the dance-drama of Kerala, known for elaborate make-up, costumes and stories from the epics. Kuchipudi comes from Kuchipudi village in Andhra Pradesh and is linked to Siddhendra Yogi. For elimination, Odisha means Odissi and Manipur means Manipuri, so neither belongs with these three dances. Options (a) and (c) pair Bharatanatyam with Andhra Pradesh, which is wrong. Option (d) pairs Kathakali with Manipur, which is wrong. Only (b) gives Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Andhra Pradesh in the right order. Note that the printed lists are garbled, so the match was reconstructed from the option codes and the geography.
explanations: Wrong. It pairs Bharatanatyam with Andhra Pradesh and Kathakali with Manipur, which is incorrect.
Correct. Bharatanatyam is matched with Tamil Nadu (2), Kathakali with Kerala (5) and Kuchipudi with Andhra Pradesh (4).
Wrong. It pairs Bharatanatyam with Andhra Pradesh and Kathakali with Kerala. Kathakali is right but Bharatanatyam is not.
Wrong. Bharatanatyam is correct with Tamil Nadu, but Kathakali is paired with Manipur instead of Kerala.
keyfact: Bharatanatyam = Tamil Nadu, Kathakali = Kerala, Kuchipudi = Andhra Pradesh; the answer is (b).
option_notes: Code 4-3-1 as read here would give Andhra Pradesh, Manipur and Odisha. Those states correspond to Kuchipudi, Manipuri and Odissi, so the code is a mismatch for this list. Odissi is the Odisha dance with the Tribhangi posture, linked to the Jagannath temple and the Mahari tradition. Manipuri is the Raslila dance of Manipur, with soft, graceful movements.

Code 2-5-4 gives Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Andhra Pradesh. This is the correct code. Bharatanatyam is the Tamil Nadu dance, Kathakali the Kerala dance and Kuchipudi the Andhra Pradesh dance. All three are among the eight forms recognised by Sangeet Natak Akademi.

Code 4-5-1 gives Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Odisha. Only the Kerala match for Kathakali is right. Kuchipudi belongs to Andhra Pradesh, not Odisha, and Bharatanatyam belongs to Tamil Nadu. Odisha's classical dance is Odissi, which has Tribhangi and Chauka postures.

Code 2-3-4 gives Tamil Nadu, Manipur and Andhra Pradesh. Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi are right, but Kathakali is wrongly matched with Manipur. Manipur's classical form is Manipuri, associated with Vaishnava Raslila themes, the Pung drum and the Kumil costume.
related: Eight classical dances are recognised by Sangeet Natak Akademi.
Sattriya of Assam got classical status in 2000.
Rukmini Devi Arundale founded Kalakshetra in 1936.
Kathakali make-up types include Pacha, Kathi and Thadi.

statements: E (Bharatanatyam) — Correct: it belongs to Tamil Nadu (code 2). It is the oldest classical dance of Tamil Nadu, performed in temples by devadasis as Sadir. It was revived by E. Krishna Iyer and Rukmini Devi Arundale, who founded Kalakshetra in 1936. The Tanjore Quartet systematised its repertoire. Its stages are Alarippu, Jatiswaram, Shabdam, Varnam, Padam and Tillana. It is known for the Araimandi (half-sitting) posture and sharp, geometric movements.

F (Kathakali) — Correct: it belongs to Kerala (code 5). It is a classical dance-drama that grew from Ramanattam and Krishnanattam and from folk forms such as Kalaripayattu. Performers wear elaborate make-up in green, red and black (types such as Pacha, Kathi and Thadi), with huge headgear. They use mudras and facial expression and do not speak. Stories come from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas. Vallathol founded Kerala Kalamandalam in 1930 to revive it.

G (Kuchipudi) — Correct: it belongs to Andhra Pradesh (code 4). It is named after Kuchipudi village in Krishna district and was systematised by Siddhendra Yogi in the 15th century. It began as a male Brahmin dance-drama tradition. It is known for the Tarangam, where the dancer performs on the rim of a brass plate while balancing a pot of water on the head. Vempati Chinna Satyam and Yamini Krishnamurthy popularised it.
summary: The answer is (b): Bharatanatyam is from Tamil Nadu, Kathakali from Kerala and Kuchipudi from Andhra Pradesh. The OCR has scrambled the numbering. Read the lists as 1 Odisha, 2 Tamil Nadu, 3 Manipur, 4 Andhra Pradesh, 5 Kerala. The code 2-5-4 then matches the correct pairs.
topic_notes: Sangeet Natak Akademi, set up in 1952, recognises eight classical dances. Bharatanatyam is from Tamil Nadu, with Nattuvanar and Tanjore Quartet traditions, and its stages are Alarippu, Jatiswaram, Shabdam, Varnam, Padam and Tillana. Kathak is from North India (Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan), with Jaipur, Lucknow and Banaras gharanas. It shows Persian influence and has Hindustani music, tatkar and chakkars. Kathakali is from Kerala and is a dance-drama with heavy make-up. Mohiniyattam is also from Kerala, a graceful women's dance, with Swathi Thirunal as a patron. Kuchipudi is from Andhra Pradesh and is known for the Tarangam. Odissi is from Odisha and is known for Tribhangi, the Konark and Jagannath temple links, and Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra. Manipuri is from Manipur and centres on Raslila, with the Pung and Kartal. Sattriya is from Assam, was created by Sankaradeva in the 15th century and is performed in Sattras (monasteries). It received classical status in 2000. Related folk and other dances: Garba (Gujarat), Bihu (Assam), Chhau (Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal), Yakshagana (Karnataka), Bhangra (Punjab), Lavani (Maharashtra), Ghoomar (Rajasthan). Mudras come from the Natya Shastra of Bharata Muni and the Abhinaya Darpana of Nandikeshwara. Rasa theory has nine rasas (Navarasa). Prominent exponents: Birju Maharaj (Kathak), Sonal Mansingh (Odissi and Bharatanatyam), Padma Subrahmanyam (Bharatanatyam), Kalamandalam Gopi (Kathakali), Guru Bipin Singh (Manipuri).

detail: Statement 1 is correct: Bermuda lies in the western North Atlantic Ocean, about 1,000 km east of North Carolina, and is a self-governing British Overseas Territory. Its capital is Hamilton. Statement 2 is wrong because it mixes up two Asian partition lines. The 38th Parallel divided North and South Korea in 1945 after World War II, with the Soviet Union and the USA occupying the two zones. Vietnam was divided at the 17th Parallel by the 1954 Geneva Accords, along the Ben Hai River. Vietnam was reunified in 1976 after the fall of Saigon in 1975. Statement 3 is wrong because the Bahamas, an archipelago east of Florida, is a sovereign Commonwealth realm. It became independent from Britain on 10 July 1973. Its capital is Nassau, and its head of state is the British monarch, represented by a Governor-General. Elimination: since statement 3 is false, options (b) and (c) go. Since statement 2 is false, option (d) goes. Only (a) remains.
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is true and statements 2 and 3 are false, so only 1 is correct.
Wrong: statement 3 is false because the Bahamas is a sovereign country, and statement 2 is false because the 38th Parallel divided Korea.
Wrong: statement 3 is false, as the Bahamas is not a US state.

keyfact: Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory; Vietnam was divided at the 17th Parallel (38th was Korea); the Bahamas is an independent country.

Statements 1 and 3: statement 3 is false. The Bahamas lies about 80 km east of Florida at its nearest point. It is a parliamentary democracy under the Westminster system. It is not a US territory, unlike Puerto Rico, Guam or the US Virgin Islands. It uses the Bahamian dollar.

Statements 1 and 2: statement 2 is false. The 17th Parallel divided North and South Vietnam from 1954, along the Ben Hai River with a demilitarised zone. The 38th Parallel divided Korea. statements: 1 — Correct: Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory in the western North Atlantic. Bermuda is a self-governing territory with its own premier and parliament, while the UK handles defence and foreign affairs. Its capital is Hamilton. It is famous for the Bermuda Triangle legend and is a major offshore financial and insurance centre. It is not part of the Caribbean, and its people are British Overseas Territories citizens. Its currency, the Bermudian dollar, is pegged to the US dollar.

2 — Incorrect: The 38th Parallel divided Korea, not Vietnam. The Korean division was made in 1945 and led to the Korean War (1950-53). The armistice line is now the Demilitarised Zone, near the 38th Parallel. Vietnam was divided at the 17th Parallel by the 1954 Geneva Conference after the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu. summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory in the western North Atlantic. The 17th Parallel (not the 38th) divided North and South Vietnam, and the Bahamas is an independent country, not a US state.
topic_notes: This question tests world geography on territories and dividing lines. Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory in the North Atlantic. Other UK Overseas Territories include Gibraltar, the Falkland Islands, the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Anguilla, Montserrat, Turks and Caicos, St Helena, the Pitcairn Islands and the British Indian Ocean Territory (Chagos). Remember the major boundary lines. The 38th Parallel divided Korea, and the Korean Demilitarised Zone follows the 1953 armistice line. The 17th Parallel divided Vietnam (1954-76). The 49th Parallel is the US-Canada boundary. The 24th Parallel was a proposed boundary in the Sir Creek and Indo-Pak context. The Mannerheim Line was a Finnish defence line. The Siegfried Line was a German defence line, and the Maginot Line was French. The Hindenburg Line was German in WWI. The McMahon Line separates India and China in the east, and the Durand Line (1893) separates Afghanistan and Pakistan. The Radcliffe Line (1947) separates India and Pakistan. The Oder-Neisse Line is the Germany-Poland boundary. The Bahamas, Jamaica, Cuba, Haiti, the Dominican Republic and Barbados are independent Caribbean or Atlantic island states, while Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands are US territories. Hawaii is the only US state that is an island group.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. Falkland Islands are situated in Paciﬁc Ocean.
2. Red Sea separates Sudan from Egypt.
3. England, Norway, Denmark surround North Sea. Which of these statements is/are correct?
subject: Computers
detail: This question tests basic world geography of oceans, seas and boundaries. The Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas) are a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean, about 480 km east of the southern tip of Patagonia, Argentina. Argentina and Britain fought the Falklands War over them in 1982. Sudan and Egypt share a land boundary along roughly the 22°N parallel, which includes the disputed Halaib Triangle. The Red Sea lies to the east of both countries, so it does not lie between them. The Red Sea separates northeast Africa (Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea) from Arabia (Saudi Arabia, Yemen). The North Sea is an arm of the Atlantic Ocean bordered by the UK (Great Britain/England and Scotland), Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Elimination logic: statements 1 and 2 are false, so options (a), (b) and (c) fail, leaving (d). When statement 3 is verified as true, the answer is confirmed.
explanations: Wrong: statement 2 is false, so '2 only' cannot be correct. Egypt and Sudan are separated by a land border, not by the Red Sea.
Wrong: statement 1 is false because the Falklands are in the South Atlantic, so '1 and 3' is incorrect even though statement 3 is true.
Wrong: statement 2 is false because Egypt and Sudan share a land border, so '2 and 3' fails.
Correct: only statement 3 is true. England, Norway and Denmark all have North Sea coasts.
keyfact: The Falklands are in the South Atlantic, Egypt and Sudan share a land border, and the North Sea borders England, Norway and Denmark.
option_notes: Option (a), '2 only', is the choice that treats the Red Sea as a divider between Sudan and Egypt. In fact the Red Sea separates Africa (Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea) from Arabia (Saudi Arabia, Yemen). It is about 2,250 km long and up to about 355 km wide. It is linked to the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal (opened 1869) and to the Gulf of Aden via the Bab-el-Mandeb strait. Its maximum depth is about 3,000 m. It is among the saltiest seas and is known for coral reefs.

Option (b), '1 and 3', combines a false statement with a true one. The Falklands are in the South Atlantic, in the Patagonian shelf region east of Argentina. Their capital is Stanley, and they have been under British administration since 1833. The 1982 war ended with an Argentine surrender. They are known for wildlife such as penguins and sea lions. The North Sea part of this option is correct.

Option (c), '2 and 3', pairs the false Red Sea claim with the true North Sea claim. Egypt and Sudan are neighbours on land. Egypt is in the northeast of Africa and spans Africa and Asia through Sinai. Sudan lies to its south, and its Red Sea coast of about 750 km lies near Port Sudan. The Nile flows north from Sudan into Egypt, and Lake Nasser straddles the border.

Option (d), '3 only', is the correct choice. The North Sea is an epicontinental sea of the Atlantic, about 575,000 sq km in area, with an average depth of about 95 m. The Norwegian Trench is its deepest part, at about 700 m. England, Scotland, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France have coasts on it. Rotterdam is a major port on the North Sea.
related: The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic, and the 1982 war was fought over them.
The Red Sea connects to the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal, which opened in 1869.
The Bab-el-Mandeb strait links the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
The North Sea borders the UK, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France.
The Dogger Bank in the North Sea is a major fishing ground.
The Dead Sea is the lowest land point on Earth, at about 430 m below sea level.
The Caspian Sea is the world's largest inland water body.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Falklands are in the South Atlantic, not the Pacific. They are a British Overseas Territory of about 12,000 sq km, made up of East Falkland and West Falkland plus hundreds of small islands. The capital is Stanley. Argentina claims them as the Malvinas. Argentina invaded in April 1982, and Britain retook the islands in June 1982 after a war of about 74 days. A 2013 referendum showed about 99.8% of voters wanted to remain British. The economy rests on fishing, sheep farming and tourism.

2 — Incorrect: Egypt and Sudan share a land border of about 1,275 km. The Red Sea lies east of both and does not run between them. The Halaib Triangle and the Bir Tawil area are disputed or unclaimed border zones. The Red Sea itself is about 2,250 km long and connects to the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal in the north and to the Indian Ocean through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait in the south. It separates Africa from Asia (Arabia).

3 — Correct: The North Sea borders Britain (England and Scotland), Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France. It connects to the Atlantic through the English Channel in the south and the Norwegian Sea in the north, and to the Baltic Sea through the Skagerrak and Kattegat. It is shallow, and the Dogger Bank is a famous fishing ground. It holds major oil and gas fields such as Brent and Ekofisk, and it is one of the busiest shipping areas in the world.
summary: The answer is (d) 3 only. The Falkland Islands lie in the South Atlantic Ocean, not the Pacific, and the Red Sea does not separate Sudan from Egypt because the two share a land border. England, Norway and Denmark do border the North Sea, so only statement 3 is correct.
topic_notes: World geography questions on oceans, seas, straits and island locations are a regular feature of general studies papers. Key points on islands: the Falklands are in the South Atlantic, and South Georgia lies to their southeast. Easter Island (Chile), the Galápagos (Ecuador) and Hawaii (USA) are in the Pacific. Madagascar, Mauritius, Maldives and Seychelles are in the Indian Ocean. Key points on seas: the Red Sea separates Africa from Arabia and connects the Mediterranean with the Indian Ocean via the Suez Canal. The Dead Sea is an inland salt lake on the Jordan and Israel border, and it is the lowest land point on Earth. The Black Sea connects to the Mediterranean through the Bosporus, the Sea of Marmara and the Dardanelles. The Baltic Sea connects to the North Sea through the Danish straits. The Caspian Sea is the largest inland water body, with five littoral states: Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan. Key straits: Gibraltar (Atlantic and Mediterranean), Bab-el-Mandeb (Red Sea and Gulf of Aden), Hormuz (Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman), Malacca (Andaman Sea and South China Sea), Bering (Arctic and Pacific), and Palk (India and Sri Lanka). Remember the countries that border the Red Sea: Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti (near the strait), Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Jordan and Israel (at the Gulf of Aqaba).

question: Latitude of a place is indicative of its
subject: General Science
detail: Latitude is the angular distance of a place north or south of the Equator (0°), measured from 0° to 90°N or S. It determines the angle of incidence of the sun's rays and the length of day. Near the Equator the rays are almost vertical and concentrate heat over a small area, giving high temperatures. Towards the poles the rays are oblique and spread over a larger area, and they also pass through more atmosphere, so temperatures fall. This is why the world is divided into the Torrid Zone (between 23½°N and 23½°S), the Temperate Zones (23½° to 66½°) and the Frigid Zones (66½° to 90°). The temperature falls by about 0.5°C for each degree of latitude moving poleward. Altitude is not indicated by latitude: it is measured above mean sea level, and temperature falls about 6.5°C per 1,000 m (the normal lapse rate). Rainfall depends on winds, distance from the sea, relief and ocean currents, so latitude is only an indirect factor. Local time is linked to longitude (15° equals 1 hour). Elimination: (a) is a garbled option and probably refers to time, which longitude governs; (b) and (c) are not directly fixed by latitude; (d) is the primary effect.
explanations: Incorrect: the option is garbled by OCR. If it meant 'time', time is determined by longitude, not latitude.
Incorrect: altitude is height above sea level. Places at the same latitude can have very different altitudes, such as Quito and the Amazon lowlands.
Incorrect: rainfall depends on winds, relief, distance from the sea and ocean currents. Places at the same latitude can be desert or rainforest, so latitude does not indicate rainfall.
Correct: latitude governs the angle of the sun's rays and the length of day, so it indicates the temperature a place receives, hot in the tropics and cold at the poles.
keyfact: Latitude controls the sun's angle and hence temperature; longitude controls time.
option_notes: Option (a) is garbled ('me'), probably 'time'. Local time is based on longitude: the Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so 15° of longitude equals 1 hour, or 1° equals 4 minutes. Indian Standard Time uses 82½°E, near Mirzapur, and is 5½ hours ahead of GMT. The Prime Meridian passes through Greenwich.

Altitude is the elevation of a place above mean sea level and is measured in metres. Temperature falls about 6.5°C per 1,000 m (the normal lapse rate). Mount Everest, at 8,849 m (8,848.86 m by the 2020 survey), is the highest peak. Contour lines on maps show altitude. Altitude is independent of latitude.

Rainfall is measured with a rain gauge in mm or cm. It is controlled by prevailing winds, relief (orographic rain), distance from the sea, ocean currents and pressure belts. Mawsynram in Meghalaya is among the wettest places on Earth. Equatorial regions receive heavy convectional rain, while the 20°–30° belts are generally dry.

Temperature is the degree of hotness of the air. Latitude is its main control, along with altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, winds and cloud cover. Heat zones: Torrid between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, Temperate from 23½° to 66½°, Frigid beyond 66½°. Isotherms are lines joining places of equal temperature.
related: Latitude determines the heat zones: Torrid, Temperate and Frigid.
Longitude determines local time: 1° equals 4 minutes.
Indian Standard Time is based on 82½°E and is 5½ hours ahead of GMT.
The Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 Indian states.
The normal lapse rate is about 6.5°C per 1,000 m.
The Equator is 0° latitude; the Prime Meridian is 0° longitude.

summary: The answer is (d) temperature. Latitude fixes the angle at which the sun's rays strike a place, and this largely decides how much solar heat it receives, so latitude indicates its temperature. Option (a) is garbled by OCR; it most likely read 'time' (local time is tied to longitude, not latitude).
topic_notes: Latitudes are imaginary parallel circles running east-west around the Earth. The Equator (0°) is the longest, and the poles are at 90°N and 90°S. Important parallels: Tropic of Cancer 23½°N, which passes through 8 Indian states; Tropic of Capricorn 23½°S; Arctic Circle 66½°N; Antarctic Circle 66½°S. One degree of latitude is about 111 km. India lies between 8°4'N and 37°6'N, and the mainland's southern tip is Kanyakumari, at about 8°4'N. Longitudes are meridians from pole to pole, with the Prime Meridian at 0° through Greenwich. There are 360 meridians, and the International Date Line follows roughly 180°. The Earth's tilt of 23½° and its revolution cause the seasons. At the equinoxes, 21 March and 23 September, day and night are equal. At the June solstice (21 June) the sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, giving the longest day in the Northern Hemisphere. At the December solstice (22 December) it is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn. Factors controlling temperature are latitude, altitude, distance from the sea (continentality), ocean currents, prevailing winds, slope and aspect, and cloud cover. Annual range of temperature is lowest at the equator and increases with latitude inland. Typical UPSC angles are latitude versus longitude, standard time, the heat zones, the lapse rate and temperature inversion.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. Alluvial soil is rich in chemical proper es and is capable of yielding Rabi and Kharif crops.
2. Black soil is suitable for co on, groundnut.
3. Rabi crops are reaped in autumn after sowing in June. Which of these statements are correct?
subject: General Science
detail: Indian soils are classified by ICAR into alluvial, black, red, laterite, arid/desert, forest/mountain and saline/alkaline types. Alluvial soil, the most widespread (about 40% of the land area), is deposited by the Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra rivers and is rich in potash, lime and humus-forming organic matter, though often poor in nitrogen and phosphorus. It supports wheat, rice, sugarcane, jute and pulses, so it yields both Rabi and Kharif crops. Black soil (regur), formed from Deccan basalt, is rich in iron, lime, calcium, magnesium and alumina, retains moisture and is ideal for cotton, so it is also called black cotton soil. It also suits groundnut, sorghum (jowar), soybean, sunflower and tobacco. Crop seasons: Kharif is sown with the monsoon in June-July and harvested in September-October; Rabi is sown in October-November and harvested in March-April; Zaid is the summer crop between the two. Statement 3 reverses the Rabi pattern, since it describes a Kharif-like sowing in June. Elimination: because 3 is wrong, options (a), (c) and (d) all fall, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 3, which wrongly describes the Rabi season.
Correct: statements 1 and 2 are accurate and statement 3 is false.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, and it excludes statement 1, which is true.
Wrong: it includes statement 3 and excludes statement 2, which is true.
keyfact: Alluvial soil supports both Rabi and Kharif crops; black soil suits cotton and groundnut; Rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in spring, not sown in June.
option_notes: 1, 2 and 3: this would require all three statements to be true. Statement 3 fails because Rabi crops are winter-sown, so this option is wrong. Remember the season framework: Kharif (June-July sowing, autumn harvest), Rabi (October-November sowing, March-April harvest) and Zaid (summer).

1 and 2 only: alluvial soil is the most fertile and widespread soil in India (about 40% of the area), covering the Indo-Gangetic plain and the coastal deltas. Black soil (regur) is formed from basalt, holds moisture and suits cotton. Both statements match standard soil geography, which makes this the correct answer.

2 and 3: pairs the true black-soil statement with the false Rabi statement. Rabi crops such as wheat, gram, mustard and barley are sown in October-December with the withdrawal of the monsoon and need cool weather. They are harvested in spring. Because statement 1 is also true, this option is incomplete as well as wrong.

1 and 3: pairs the true alluvial statement with the false Rabi statement. Alluvial soil is correctly described as supporting both Rabi and Kharif crops, but statement 3 is wrong because Rabi sowing is in winter, not June. It also wrongly leaves out the true statement 2 on black soil.
related: Black soil is also called regur or black cotton soil and is formed from Deccan basalt.
Alluvial soil is divided into Bhangar (old) and Khadar (new).
Kharif crops are sown in June-July and harvested in September-October.
Rabi crops such as wheat, gram and mustard are sown in October-November.
Zaid crops are grown between Rabi and Kharif, in March-June.
Laterite soil suits tea, coffee, rubber and cashew.
The Soil Health Card scheme was launched in 2015.
Red soil owes its colour to iron oxide.
statements: 1 — Correct: Alluvial soil is fertile and supports both Rabi and Kharif crops. It covers the northern plains, the eastern coastal plains and the river deltas. It is classified as Khadar (new alluvium) and Bhangar (old alluvium). It is rich in potash and lime and poor in phosphorus and nitrogen. Its crops include wheat, rice, sugarcane, jute, maize and pulses. Irrigation and fertilisers make it highly productive. It supports the densest agricultural populations in India, in Punjab, Haryana, UP, Bihar and West Bengal.

2 — Correct: Black soil is suitable for cotton and groundnut. It is formed from volcanic basalt (Deccan Trap) in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. It is clayey, retains moisture, swells when wet and develops deep cracks when dry. Its colour comes from titaniferous magnetite. It is rich in iron, lime, calcium, magnesium and aluminium but poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter. It suits cotton, sorghum, groundnut, soybean, sugarcane, citrus fruits and tobacco.

3 — Incorrect: Rabi crops are sown in winter (October-December) and harvested in spring (March-April), not reaped in autumn after June sowing. Examples are wheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas and linseed. They need cool weather for growth and warm weather for ripening. Crops sown in June-July with the monsoon are Kharif crops (rice, maize, cotton, jowar, bajra, groundnut, soybean), harvested in September-October. Zaid crops (watermelon, cucumber, fodder) are grown in March-June.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is wrong. Alluvial soil is fertile and supports both Rabi and Kharif crops, and black (regur) soil suits cotton and groundnut. Rabi crops are sown in October-November (winter) and harvested in March-April (spring), not reaped in autumn after June sowing.
topic_notes: Soils of India (ICAR classification): alluvial, black, red, laterite, arid, saline, peaty/marshy and forest soils. Alluvial soil covers about 40% of the area, is transported by rivers, is divided into Bhangar and Khadar, and is rich in potash but deficient in nitrogen and phosphorus. Black soil (regur) is found in the Deccan Trap region, is the typical soil for cotton, and has high clay content and high moisture retention. Red soil gets its colour from iron oxide and suits millets, groundnut and pulses; it is poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus. Laterite soil forms under heavy rainfall with leaching and suits tea, coffee, rubber, cashew and tapioca. Desert soil is sandy and low in humus, and suits bajra and drought-resistant crops with irrigation. Cropping seasons: Kharif is sown with the southwest monsoon (June-July) and harvested in September-October, with rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, jute, groundnut and soybean. Rabi is sown in October-November and harvested in March-April, with wheat, barley, gram, peas, mustard and linseed; Rabi in the north-west benefits from western disturbances. Zaid is grown in March-June, with watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber and fodder. Related institutions: ICAR, the National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (Nagpur), and the Soil Health Card scheme (2015). Other angles UPSC asks about: soil-crop matching, soil erosion types, the minimum support price for Rabi and Kharif crops, and the major crops and leading states.

question: Consider the following statements : While it is 6:30 AM (Sunday) in London, it is around 1. 2.30 AM (Sunday) in Honolulu (Hawaii) 2. 8.30 PM (Saturday) in Honolulu (Hawaii) 3. 3.30 PM (Sunday) in Tokyo 4. 1:30 AM (Sunday) in Tokyo Which of these statements is/are correct?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Time zones are fixed by longitude: the Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so 15° of longitude equals 1 hour, or 1° equals 4 minutes. London lies on the Prime Meridian (0°), and Greenwich Mean Time (GMT/UTC) is the reference. Places east of Greenwich are ahead of GMT; places west are behind. Tokyo is near 135°E (Japan Standard Time, UTC+9), so it is 9 hours ahead: 6:30 AM + 9 h = 3:30 PM Sunday. Honolulu, Hawaii, is near 157.5°W (Hawaii Standard Time, UTC-10), so it is 10 hours behind: 6:30 AM - 10 h = 8:30 PM Saturday, the previous day. Crossing westward toward the International Date Line (180°) makes the date earlier. Elimination: statement 1 (2:30 AM) would imply a 4-hour difference, which is wrong; statement 4 (1:30 AM Sunday) would imply Tokyo is behind London, but Tokyo is east and so ahead. Only 2 and 3 are consistent. Note that London is on BST (UTC+1) in summer, but the question assumes GMT; Japan and Hawaii do not use daylight saving.
explanations: Wrong: (a) says only 4 is correct, but 4 is wrong since Tokyo is ahead of London, not behind it.
Correct: (b) statements 2 and 3 match the offsets of UTC-10 for Honolulu and UTC+9 for Tokyo.
Wrong: (c) statements 1 and 4 both use incorrect offsets of -4 h and -5 h.
Wrong: (d) statement 2 is correct, but 4 is incorrect, as Tokyo cannot be behind London.
keyfact: East of Greenwich gains time, west loses; London 6:30 AM Sunday = Tokyo 3:30 PM Sunday (UTC+9) = Honolulu 8:30 PM Saturday (UTC-10).
option_notes: Statement 4 alone: it claims Tokyo shows 1:30 AM Sunday. That is wrong because Tokyo at 135°E is 9 hours ahead of Greenwich. Eastern longitudes are always ahead of GMT, so the time there must be later than London's, not earlier. Japan Standard Time is UTC+9 all year, with no daylight saving.

Statements 2 and 3: Honolulu at UTC-10 shows 8:30 PM Saturday and Tokyo at UTC+9 shows 3:30 PM Sunday. This is correct. The gap between Honolulu and Tokyo is 19 hours, and the International Date Line at 180° lies between them, which explains the date difference.

Statements 1 and 4: both are incorrect. Statement 1 gives Honolulu a 4-hour lag rather than 10 hours, and statement 4 makes Tokyo behind London. Such options test whether you know the direction of the time difference as well as its size.

Statements 2 and 4: statement 2 is right but statement 4 is wrong. This option tests whether you know that Tokyo is ahead of London by 9 hours. Remember the calculation: 15° of longitude equals 1 hour, 1° equals 4 minutes.
related: 15° of longitude equals 1 hour; 1° equals 4 minutes.
IST is based on 82°30'E and is UTC+5:30, ahead of GMT by 5.5 hours.
The Prime Meridian passes through Greenwich, adopted in 1884.
The International Date Line runs near 180°, crossing the Pacific Ocean.
Japan Standard Time is UTC+9, based on 135°E.
Hawaii is UTC-10 and does not observe daylight saving time.
Russia has 11 time zones; China uses only one (UTC+8).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Honolulu is 10 hours behind London, so the time is 8:30 PM Saturday, not 2:30 AM Sunday. Honolulu uses Hawaii Standard Time (UTC-10), based on about 157.5°W, and Hawaii does not observe daylight saving time. It is one of the westernmost US states and is far from the Greenwich meridian. Because it lies west of the Prime Meridian, its clocks run behind GMT, and it is a day behind for part of every day.

2 — Correct: 6:30 AM minus 10 hours gives 8:30 PM of the previous day, Saturday. Hawaii lies in the Hawaii-Aleutian time zone (UTC-10). The Hawaiian islands lie in the central Pacific at around 19°-22°N latitude, and Honolulu is on Oahu island. Its standard meridian is 150°W, but the legal offset is UTC-10. Because Hawaii does not use daylight saving time, the offset stays constant all year.

3 — Correct: Tokyo is on Japan Standard Time (UTC+9), based on the 135°E meridian, which passes through Akashi. 6:30 AM + 9 hours = 3:30 PM Sunday. Japan does not observe daylight saving time. The country is a single time zone even though it spans a considerable range of longitude. Japan is called the Land of the Rising Sun because it is among the first places to see the sunrise, being far east of Greenwich.

4 — Incorrect: Tokyo is east of London, so it is ahead and not behind. 1:30 AM Sunday would be 5 hours behind, which is impossible. India (IST, UTC+5:30, 82.5°E meridian through Mirzapur) is 3.5 hours behind Tokyo, which helps a quick check. Places east of Greenwich gain time, while places west lose time, the rule behind the saying 'east gain, west lose'.
summary: The correct answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct. Honolulu is at UTC-10, so 6:30 AM Sunday in London (GMT) is 8:30 PM Saturday there, and Tokyo is at UTC+9, so it is 3:30 PM Sunday there.
topic_notes: Time and longitude: the Earth rotates west to east once in 24 hours, covering 360°, so 15° equals 1 hour and 1° equals 4 minutes. The Prime Meridian (0°) passes through Greenwich, London, and was adopted at the International Meridian Conference in Washington in 1884. GMT/UTC is the global reference. Places east of Greenwich are ahead in time; places west are behind. Local time is the time based on a place's own meridian, while standard time is the uniform time adopted for a country or zone. India's Standard Time is based on 82°30'E, passing near Mirzapur (Uttar Pradesh), and is 5 h 30 min ahead of GMT. India has a single time zone though it spans nearly 30° of longitude, about two hours of local time. The International Date Line follows roughly 180° with deviations; crossing it westward adds a day, and crossing it eastward subtracts a day. Countries with many time zones: Russia has 11, France (with overseas territories) has the most overall, and the USA mainland has four (Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific), with Alaska and Hawaii additional. China uses one time zone (UTC+8) despite its width. Daylight saving time moves clocks forward by an hour in summer in many countries, but not in India, Japan, or Hawaii. Key reference offsets: New York UTC-5, Los Angeles UTC-8, Honolulu UTC-10, Tokyo UTC+9, Sydney UTC+10, Dubai UTC+4, Beijing UTC+8. Frequently asked angles are conversions between cities, the date at the International Date Line, why India's time zone proposals (such as a separate time for the North-East) are discussed, and the Greenwich meridian's role.

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. Prime Meridian passes through Greenwich and is at 0° Longitude.
2. International Date Line, on the map appears as a straight line along 180° Longitude.
3. While crossing International Date Line from east to west, one gains a day.
4. Tropic of Cancer lies at 23½° Latitude S. Which of these statements are correct?
subject: Computers
detail: Longitude is measured east and west from the Prime Meridian, which passes through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, London. It was fixed at the International Meridian Conference in Washington in 1884. The 180° meridian is its antimeridian. The International Date Line (IDL) roughly follows 180° but deviates to avoid splitting countries and island groups. It bends around Russia's Chukotka, the Aleutians (Alaska), Fiji, Tonga, Kiribati and Samoa. So it is not a straight line. Crossing the IDL from east to west (for example, America to Asia) moves the date forward by one day, so the calendar date gains a day. Crossing from west to east moves the date back by one day, which is a loss. The Tropic of Cancer is 23½° N (23°26′ N) and passes through eight Indian states. The Tropic of Capricorn is 23½° S. Eliminating: statement 4 is wrong, which rules out (a). Statement 2 is wrong, which rules out (b) and (d). That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statements 2 and 4, which are both incorrect.
Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is false because the IDL zigzags, and omits statement 3, which is true.
Correct: statements 1 and 3 are true. Statements 2 and 4 are false.
Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is false, and omits statement 1, which is true.
keyfact: Prime Meridian at Greenwich is 0°; the IDL zigzags near 180°; crossing it east to west gains a day; Tropic of Cancer is 23½° N.
option_notes: All four statements together. This would require the IDL to be straight and the Tropic of Cancer to be in the southern hemisphere. Neither holds. The Tropic of Cancer is 23½° N, and the IDL is irregular and deviates from 180° in several places to avoid splitting territories.

Statements 1 and 2 only. It correctly includes the Prime Meridian but wrongly takes the IDL as straight. The IDL deviates around Russia's Chukotka, the Aleutians, Fiji, Tonga and Kiribati. It also omits the true rule about gaining a day when crossing from east to west.

Statements 1 and 3 only. This is the correct choice. The Prime Meridian at Greenwich is 0° and was fixed in 1884. Crossing the IDL east to west advances the date by a day. The other two statements fail on the IDL's irregular path and the Tropic of Cancer's northern location.

Statements 2 and 3 only. It correctly identifies the date rule but wrongly asserts the IDL is straight. It also omits the true statement about the Prime Meridian at Greenwich, which is basic geographical knowledge.
related: Prime Meridian: 0° at Greenwich, fixed in 1884 at the Washington conference.
IDL: approximately 180°, zigzag, in the Pacific Ocean.
East to west across the IDL: gain a day. West to east: lose a day.
Tropic of Cancer: 23½° N, passes through 8 Indian states.
India's Standard Meridian: 82½° E, near Mirzapur.
IST is GMT + 5:30.
1° of longitude equals 4 minutes of time.
Indira Point at 6°45′ N is India's southernmost point.
statements: 1 — Correct: Greenwich is on the Prime Meridian at 0° longitude. The Prime Meridian passes through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, London, and divides the Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. It was adopted at the 1884 International Meridian Conference. GMT/UTC is based on it. It passes through Britain, France, Spain, Algeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Togo and Ghana. Its antimeridian is 180°.

2 — Incorrect: The IDL is not a straight line. It follows 180° only approximately and zigzags to keep countries and island groups on the same date. It bends east near the Aleutian Islands, around Chukotka in Russia, and around Fiji, Tonga and Kiribati. Kiribati moved its portion in 1995, and Samoa shifted to the west side in 2011. The IDL is a convention, not a legally defined line. The date changes by one day when crossing it.

3 — Correct: Going east to west across the IDL, the traveller moves from the Western Hemisphere to the Eastern Hemisphere and advances the calendar by one day, for example Sunday becomes Monday. This is called gaining a day. Going west to east, one repeats the same day, which is a loss of a day. Each 15° of longitude corresponds to one hour of time, so 180° corresponds to 12 hours either side of Greenwich, and the two sides differ by 24 hours.

4 — Incorrect: The Tropic of Cancer lies at 23½° N, not S. It is the northernmost latitude where the sun can be directly overhead, which happens at the summer solstice on 21 June. The Tropic of Capricorn lies at 23½° S, with overhead sun on 22 December. India's Tropic of Cancer passes through Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3. The Prime Meridian passes through Greenwich at 0° longitude, and crossing the International Date Line from east to west makes you skip a day, which is a gain in calendar date. Statement 2 is wrong because the IDL zigzags and is not a straight line, and statement 4 is wrong because the Tropic of Cancer is 23½° N.
topic_notes: Latitudes and longitudes form the Earth's coordinate grid. Latitudes are parallels, and the equator is 0°. The poles are at 90° N and 90° S. Important parallels are the Tropic of Cancer (23½° N), the Tropic of Capricorn (23½° S), the Arctic Circle (66½° N) and the Antarctic Circle (66½° S). The distance between two latitude degrees is about 111 km. Longitudes are meridians, which are half great circles joining the poles. The Prime Meridian is 0° and passes through Greenwich. There are 360 meridians at 1° intervals. The Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so 15° equals 1 hour and 1° equals 4 minutes. India's standard meridian is 82½° E, which passes near Mirzapur (Naini, Prayagraj) in Uttar Pradesh. IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT. The longitudinal extent of India is about 68°7′ E to 97°25′ E, and the latitudinal extent is 8°4′ N to 37°6′ N, excluding Andaman and Nicobar. The mainland extends to 6°45′ N (Indira Point) including Andaman and Nicobar. The IDL lies mostly in the Pacific, roughly along 180°. The Tropic of Cancer passes through 17 countries. The Arctic Circle region has the midnight sun. Equinoxes fall on 21 March and 23 September. The solstices fall on 21 June and 22 December. Local time differs from standard time by longitude. Time zones: Russia has 11, France has the most overall including overseas territories, and the USA has several. Related topics are Earth's rotation and revolution, seasons, and the inclination of the axis at 23½° from the perpendicular to the orbital plane, which is 66½° to the plane.

question:
Consider the following statements : According to Census 2001
1. The literacy rate increase for males is more than that of the females during last one decade.
2. Amongst the States and Union Territories, Delhi has the highest population density while Sikkim has the lowest.
3. The correct sequence of population in descending order of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka is Tamil Nadu-Madhya Pradesh-Rajasthan-Karnataka. Which of these statements is/are correct?
subject: General Science
detail: Census 2001 recorded India's population at 1,028 million (1.028 billion). Literacy was 64.84% overall, up from 52.21% in 1991. Male literacy rose from 64.13% to 75.26%, a gain of about 11.1 points. Female literacy rose from 39.29% to 53.67%, a gain of about 14.4 points. So the female gain was larger and the gap narrowed, which makes statement 1 wrong. For density, India's figure was 324 persons per sq km. Delhi was the highest among States and UTs at about 9,294 per sq km, followed by Chandigarh at about 7,900. The lowest was Arunachal Pradesh at about 13 per sq km, while Sikkim had about 76, so statement 2 fails on its second half. After Chhattisgarh was carved out of it in 2000, Madhya Pradesh had about 60.3 million people, which is below Tamil Nadu's 62.4 million but above Rajasthan's 56.5 million. Karnataka had about 52.8 million. Statement 3 is therefore right. Elimination: statements 1 and 2 are both wrong, so only (d) survives.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect: the female literacy increase was larger than the male increase, and statement 2 is also incorrect because Sikkim does not have the lowest density.
(b) is wrong because it includes statement 2, which fails: Arunachal Pradesh, not Sikkim, has the lowest density, even though Delhi is the densest.
(c) is wrong because it includes both statement 1 and statement 2, and both are factually incorrect.
(d) is correct because only statement 3 is correct: the population order Tamil Nadu > Madhya Pradesh > Rajasthan > Karnataka matches Census 2001.
keyfact: Census 2001: female literacy rose faster than male, Delhi is the densest, Arunachal Pradesh the sparsest, and the population order is TN > MP > Rajasthan > Karnataka.
related: Census 2001 India population: about 1,028 million; the decadal growth rate was 21.54%.
Census 2001 literacy: total 64.84%, male 75.26%, female 53.67%.
Kerala has the highest literacy (90.86%) and Bihar the lowest (47.00%) in Census 2001.
Delhi had the highest density (about 9,294 per sq km) and Arunachal Pradesh the lowest (about 13).
Census 2001 sex ratio was 933, with Kerala highest (1,058) and Haryana lowest (861).
Uttar Pradesh was the most populous State in 2001 (about 166 million), and Sikkim the least populous State.
Census 2011: population 1,210 million, literacy 74.04%, sex ratio 943, density 382.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the female literacy gain (about 14.4 points) exceeded the male gain (about 11.1 points) between 1991 and 2001. Census 2001 literacy figures: male 75.26%, female 53.67%, total 64.84%. Kerala was the most literate State at about 90.9%, and Bihar was the least at about 47.5%. The male-female literacy gap fell from about 24.8 to about 21.6 points. Literacy counts people aged 7 and above who can read and write with understanding. The 2001 Census was the first to treat literacy as a rate for the population aged 7+ in all States, and it saw a rise in absolute numbers of illiterates falling for the first time.

2 — Incorrect: Delhi is the densest at about 9,294 per sq km, but the lowest density is in Arunachal Pradesh at about 13 per sq km, not Sikkim. Among the larger States, Bihar was the densest at about 880 per sq km, followed by West Bengal. Sikkim's density was about 76, and Mizoram's was about 42. All-India density was 324 per sq km, up from 267 in 1991. Among the Union Territories, Chandigarh and Delhi were the densest, while Andaman and Nicobar Islands were the sparsest at about 43 per sq km.

3 — Correct: the 2001 populations were Tamil Nadu about 62.4 million, Madhya Pradesh about 60.3 million, Rajasthan about 56.5 million and Karnataka about 52.8 million. The largest States in 2001 were Uttar Pradesh (166 million), Maharashtra (97 million), Bihar (83 million), West Bengal (80 million), Andhra Pradesh (76 million) and Tamil Nadu (62 million). Madhya Pradesh dropped in rank after Chhattisgarh was formed in November 2000. Rajasthan overtook Karnataka. Rajasthan is the largest State by area, at about 342,000 sq km.
summary: The answer is (d): only statement 3 is correct. In Census 2001 the order of population was Tamil Nadu (about 62.4 million), Madhya Pradesh (about 60.3 million), Rajasthan (about 56.5 million) and Karnataka (about 52.8 million). Female literacy rose faster than male literacy, and Arunachal Pradesh, not Sikkim, has the lowest density.
topic_notes: Census 2001 was the 14th census since 1872 and the 6th since independence, with 1 March 2001 as the reference date. The Census Commissioner was J. K. Banthia. Total population was 1,028.7 million, of which males were 532.2 million and females 496.5 million. The decadal growth rate was 21.54%, down from 23.87% in the 1991 decade. The sex ratio was 933 females per 1,000 males, up from 927 in 1991. Kerala had the best sex ratio at 1,058, while Haryana had the worst among States at 861 (Daman and Diu was lowest among UTs at 710). The child sex ratio (0-6 years) was 927. Literacy was 64.84%, with male 75.26% and female 53.67%. The most literate State was Kerala at 90.86%, followed by Mizoram and Goa, and the least literate was Bihar at 47.00%. Among UTs, Lakshadweep (87.52%) and Chandigarh were high. Density was 324 per sq km. Delhi (9,294) was the highest and Arunachal Pradesh (13) the lowest. Uttar Pradesh was the most populous State at about 166 million, and Sikkim the least populous State at about 0.54 million. Lakshadweep was the least populous UT. Nagaland had the lowest population growth in the 1991-2001 decade in the sense of negative growth (-0.47%) per the 2001 provisional data, while Dadra and Nagar Haveli had the highest growth among UTs. Related angles are the Census 2011 comparisons (population 1,210 million, literacy 74.04%, sex ratio 943, density 382) and Article 246 (Census is a Union subject, Seventh Schedule Entry 69).

question:
Match List-I (Park/Sanctuary) with List-II (State) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: List-I (Park/Sanctuary) List-II (State) A. Keoladeo National
1. Assam Park B. Corbe National Park
2. Kerala C. Kaziranga Sanctuary
3. Uttar Pradesh D. Periyar Sanctuary
4. Rajasthan
5. U aranchal Code: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a standard national parks and sanctuaries matching question. Keoladeo Ghana National Park (Bharatpur, Rajasthan) is a Ramsar site and UNESCO World Heritage Site, famous for migratory birds and the Siberian crane. Corbett, India's oldest national park (1936, originally Hailey National Park), lies in Uttarakhand, which was called Uttaranchal from 2000 to 2007 and was part of Uttar Pradesh before that. Project Tiger began there in 1973. Kaziranga in Assam is known for the one-horned rhinoceros and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Periyar in Kerala (Idukki and Pathanamthitta districts) is a tiger reserve around the Periyar lake, known for elephants. Elimination: Corbett's list entry must be 5 (Uttaranchal) because the paper was set in 2002, after the state's creation, which rules out options (b) and (c), where B is 3. Keoladeo is in Rajasthan, which rules out (a) and (c), where A is 2. Only (d) remains, and it is consistent with Kaziranga-Assam and Periyar-Kerala.
explanations: Wrong: it puts Keoladeo in Kerala and Corbett in Uttaranchal while giving Kaziranga to Rajasthan, which is incorrect.
Wrong: it matches Corbett with Uttar Pradesh. The paper was set after Uttaranchal was created, and Corbett lies in that state, so this is wrong.
Wrong: it puts Keoladeo in Kerala and Kaziranga in Rajasthan, both incorrect.
Correct: A-4 Rajasthan, B-5 Uttaranchal, C-1 Assam, D-2 Kerala. All four pairs are right.
keyfact: Keoladeo-Rajasthan, Corbett-Uttarakhand, Kaziranga-Assam, Periyar-Kerala.
option_notes: Combination A-2, B-5, C-4, D-1: incorrect. It would place Keoladeo in Kerala, Kaziranga in Rajasthan and Periyar in Assam. Real locations: Keoladeo in Rajasthan (Bharatpur, bird sanctuary, Ramsar site), Kaziranga in Assam (rhino), Periyar in Kerala (elephant and tiger).

Combination A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2: nearly right, but Corbett is wrongly placed in Uttar Pradesh. Corbett, founded in 1936, is in Uttarakhand. Uttar Pradesh has Dudhwa National Park (Lakhimpur Kheri) and Chandraprabha sanctuary.
Combination A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1: wrong on all four pairs. The correct locations are Rajasthan, Uttarakhand, Assam and Kerala respectively.

Combination A-4, B-5, C-1, D-2: the correct answer. Keoladeo (Rajasthan), Corbett (Uttarakhand), Kaziranga (Assam), Periyar (Kerala). All are well known for birds, tigers, rhinos and elephants respectively.
related: Corbett is India's oldest national park (1936) and the first Project Tiger site (1973).
Kaziranga is in Assam and is known for the one-horned rhinoceros.
Keoladeo (Bharatpur) is a Ramsar site and World Heritage Site in Rajasthan.
Periyar Tiger Reserve is in Kerala, near the Mullaperiyar Dam.
Gir National Park in Gujarat is the only home of the Asiatic lion.
Uttaranchal was renamed Uttarakhand in 2007.
Wildlife (Protection) Act was enacted in 1972.
Sundarbans in West Bengal is a mangrove tiger reserve and World Heritage Site.
statements: A — Correct: Keoladeo National Park matches 4, Rajasthan. Located in Bharatpur, it was a duck-shooting reserve of the Maharajas, became a sanctuary in 1971 and a national park in 1981. It is a Ramsar site (1981) and World Heritage Site (1985), and a wetland habitat for migratory waterfowl.

B — Correct: Corbett National Park matches 5, Uttaranchal (now Uttarakhand). Established in 1936 as Hailey National Park, it was renamed in 1956 after Jim Corbett. It lies in Nainital and Pauri Garhwal districts on the Ramganga river, and was the first Project Tiger reserve in 1973.

C — Correct: Kaziranga matches 1, Assam. It is a national park (1974) and was a sanctuary earlier. It lies on the Brahmaputra floodplain in Golaghat and Nagaon districts, holds about two-thirds of the world's one-horned rhinos, and has been a World Heritage Site since 1985.

D — Correct: Periyar matches 2, Kerala. It was declared a sanctuary in 1950 and a tiger reserve in 1978, and became a national park in 1982. It surrounds the Periyar lake formed by the Mullaperiyar Dam (1895), and Thekkady is its main tourist centre.
summary: The correct answer is (d): A-4, B-5, C-1, D-2. Keoladeo National Park is in Rajasthan, Corbett National Park is in Uttaranchal (now Uttarakhand), Kaziranga is in Assam and Periyar is in Kerala.
topic_notes: National parks and sanctuaries are a staple of the geography and environment questions in the EPFO exam. India has over 100 national parks, and protected areas are governed by the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Project Tiger started in 1973, with Corbett as the first reserve. Key parks by state: Assam has Kaziranga (rhino), Manas (tiger reserve and World Heritage Site) and Nameri. Rajasthan has Keoladeo (Bharatpur), Ranthambore (tiger) and Sariska. Uttarakhand has Corbett, Rajaji and Nanda Devi (World Heritage Site). Uttar Pradesh has Dudhwa. Madhya Pradesh has Kanha, Bandhavgarh, Pench and Satpura. Gujarat has Gir (Asiatic lion). West Bengal has Sundarbans (mangrove, tiger, World Heritage Site). Kerala has Periyar, Silent Valley (saved from a hydro project in the 1980s) and Eravikulam (Nilgiri tahr). Karnataka has Bandipur and Nagarhole. Tamil Nadu has Mudumalai and Indira Gandhi (Anamalai). Odisha has Bhitarkanika (saltwater crocodile) and Simlipal. Also remember Uttaranchal was renamed Uttarakhand in 2007, and that national parks give stronger protection than sanctuaries because no human activity such as grazing is allowed. Ramsar sites such as Chilika and Keoladeo are frequently asked, as are biosphere reserves such as Nilgiri (the first, in 1986) and Nanda Devi.

detail: This question tests the location of multi-purpose river valley projects. The Purna project is on the Purna river, a tributary of the Godavari, in Maharashtra (Purna in Hingoli/Parbhani region). The Bhima project (Ujjani dam on the Bhima river, a tributary of the Krishna) is in Maharashtra, but Bhima flows through Karnataka too, and the Bhima project listed here is matched with Karnataka (5) because Maharashtra is already used for Purna. The Kakrapara project is on the Tapi river in Gujarat (Surat district). The Tehri Dam is on the Bhagirathi river at Tehri in Uttarakhand (formerly Uttaranchal), the tallest dam in India at 260.5 m. Elimination: Tehri = Uttaranchal (3) removes option (d). Kakrapara = Gujarat (1) removes (a) and leaves (b) and (c). Purna = Maharashtra (2) removes (c), leaving (b). The key traps are Bhima's dual-state character and Tehri's wrongly placed Uttar Pradesh option, since Uttaranchal was carved from UP in 2000.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it pairs Purna with Gujarat and Bhima with Maharashtra, which does not fit the Purna project's location.
(b) Right: Purna - Maharashtra, Bhima - Karnataka, Kakrapara - Gujarat, Tehri - Uttaranchal.
