(d) Wrong: it places Kakrapara in Uttar Pradesh, but Kakrapara is in Gujarat.
keyfact: Purna-Maharashtra, Bhima-Karnataka, Kakrapara (Tapi)-Gujarat, Tehri (Bhagirathi)-Uttarakhand: option (b).
option_notes: Option (a) assigns Purna to Gujarat, Bhima to Maharashtra, Kakrapara to Karnataka and Tehri to Uttaranchal. The Gujarat Purna is a different small river in Navsari, and the real Purna project is in Maharashtra, so the pairing fails. Kakrapara is on the Tapi in Gujarat, not Karnataka. Only the Tehri pairing is right. Remember that same-named rivers in different states are a common trap.

Option (b) gives Purna-Maharashtra, Bhima-Karnataka, Kakrapara-Gujarat and Tehri-Uttaranchal. All four pairs are acceptable. Purna is a Godavari tributary; the Bhima, a Krishna tributary, runs through Maharashtra, Karnataka and Telangana; Kakrapara is on the Tapi near Surat; Tehri is on the Bhagirathi, the tallest Indian dam at 260.5 m, commissioned around 2006.

Option (c) gives Purna-Gujarat, Bhima-Uttaranchal, Kakrapara-Karnataka and Tehri-Uttar Pradesh. It is wrong on almost every pair. Uttaranchal, now Uttarakhand, was created from Uttar Pradesh on 9 Nov 2000 (named Uttaranchal until 2007), so Tehri is no longer in UP. Bhima never flows in Uttarakhand. It serves as a distractor.

Option (d) gives Purna-Maharashtra, Bhima-Uttar Pradesh, Kakrapara-Gujarat... as coded, but Tehri is misplaced. Its pairs include Bhima with UP and Kakrapara with Karnataka, both wrong. Bhima belongs to the Deccan, not UP. UP projects include Rihand (Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar), Matatila and Ramganga.
related: Tehri Dam (260.5 m) on Bhagirathi is India's tallest dam.
Hirakud on the Mahanadi is the longest dam in India.
Kakrapara is on the Tapi river in Gujarat; Ukai is upstream.
Bhima is a Krishna tributary that rises near Bhimashankar.
Purna is a Godavari tributary; Yeldari dam is on it.
Damodar Valley Corporation was India's first multipurpose river valley project (1948).
Uttaranchal was created on 9 Nov 2000 and renamed Uttarakhand in 2007.
Sardar Sarovar is on the Narmada in Gujarat.
statements: A (Purna) — Correct match with Maharashtra (2): the Purna is a Godavari tributary; the project lies in Marathwada (Parbhani/Hingoli, Yeldari dam on Purna). Yeldari and Siddheshwar dams are on this river. The Purna rises in the Ajanta range and flows through Maharashtra before joining the Godavari near Purna town. It supports irrigation and drinking water in Marathwada. Do not confuse it with the Purna of Gujarat (Navsari) or the Purna in Vidarbha (a Tapi tributary).

B (Bhima) — Correct match with Karnataka (5) in this list: the Bhima rises in the Western Ghats near Bhimashankar in Maharashtra and joins the Krishna near Raichur in Karnataka. Ujjani dam (Maharashtra, Solapur) and Bhima Lift Irrigation/Sonna barrage (Karnataka) exist. It is a major Krishna tributary, about 861 km long. The listed pairing uses Karnataka because Maharashtra is taken by Purna.

C (Kakrapara) — Correct match with Gujarat (1): the Kakrapara weir/dam is on the Tapi river in Surat district, Gujarat, with canals for irrigation in south Gujarat. Ukai dam is upstream on the same river and is the larger multi-purpose project. The Tapi (Tapti) rises at Multai in Madhya Pradesh and drains into the Gulf of Khambhat. Kakrapara also hosts the Kakrapara Atomic Power Station nearby.

D (Tehri) — Correct match with Uttaranchal (3): the Tehri Dam is on the Bhagirathi at its confluence with the Bhilangana, in Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand. At 260.5 m it is India's highest dam and among the tallest in the world. Its capacity is 1000 MW, with the Koteshwar dam downstream, and the project is run by THDC India Ltd. It was affected by the long Tehri Bachao Andolan led by Sunderlal Bahuguna.
summary: The correct option is (b): Purna - Maharashtra, Bhima - Karnataka, Kakrapara - Gujarat, Tehri - Uttaranchal. This matches the codes 2, 5, 1, 3, which appear only in option (b).
topic_notes: Multi-purpose river valley projects were central to Nehru's idea of 'temples of modern India'. Key projects by state: Bhakra-Nangal (Sutlej, Punjab/Himachal; Gobind Sagar, 226 m high), Hirakud (Mahanadi, Odisha, longest earthen dam about 25.8 km), Damodar Valley (Jharkhand/West Bengal; modelled on the TVA; the first multipurpose project), Nagarjuna Sagar (Krishna, Telangana/Andhra), Tungabhadra (Karnataka/Andhra), Koyna (Maharashtra), Sardar Sarovar (Narmada, Gujarat), Ukai and Kakrapara (Tapi, Gujarat), Rihand (UP), Chambal projects (Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar, Jawahar Sagar in MP/Rajasthan), Mettur (Cauvery, Tamil Nadu), Idukki (Kerala, arch dam), Tehri (Uttarakhand), Indira Gandhi Canal (Rajasthan), Farakka Barrage (Ganga, West Bengal), Kosi (Bihar, Nepal-linked). Peninsular rivers: Godavari tributaries include Purna, Manjra, Pranhita, Indravati; Krishna tributaries include Bhima, Tungabhadra, Koyna, Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, Musi. Tapi flows west from Multai (MP) through Maharashtra and Gujarat. Tallest dam in India: Tehri (260.5 m); longest: Hirakud. Himalayan rivers give perennial water while peninsular ones are seasonal, which makes storage dams important. Related: Polavaram (Godavari, Andhra Pradesh) is a national project; Mullaperiyar is a Kerala-Tamil Nadu dispute; Cauvery tribunal; Narmada Bachao Andolan led by Medha Patkar against Sardar Sarovar; Tehri Bachao Andolan led by Sunderlal Bahuguna.

question:
Match List-I (City) with List-II (River Passing through the city) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: List-I (City) List-II (River passing through the city) A. Nasik
1. Krishna B. Surat
2. Cauvery C. Ujjain
3. Godawari D. Vijayawada
4. Shipra
5. Tap Code: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a standard river-city geography question. Nasik (Nashik, Maharashtra) lies on the Godavari near its origin at Trimbakeshwar, and hosts the Simhastha Kumbh Mela. Surat (Gujarat) lies on the Tapi (Tapti) near its mouth in the Gulf of Khambhat. Ujjain (Madhya Pradesh) lies on the Shipra (Kshipra) and is one of the seven sacred cities (Saptapuri); it also hosts the Simhastha Kumbh Mela and has the Mahakaleshwar Jyotirlinga. Vijayawada (Andhra Pradesh) lies on the Krishna, below the Prakasam Barrage. Elimination: Nasik-Godavari (3) rules out b and d, which give Nasik as 4. Surat-Tapi (5) then rules out c, which gives Surat as 1. Only (a) is consistent with all four matches. Remember that the Cauvery flows through Srirangapatna, Tiruchirappalli and Thanjavur, and Srirangam is an island formed by the Cauvery and Kollidam. The Tapi and Narmada are west-flowing rivers that drain into the Arabian Sea through rift valleys.
explanations: Correct: all four matches (Nasik–Godavari, Surat–Tapi, Ujjain–Shipra, Vijayawada–Krishna) are right.
Wrong: it pairs Nasik with the Shipra and Surat with the Krishna, and both are incorrect.
Wrong: it pairs Surat with the Krishna and Vijayawada with the Cauvery, and both are incorrect.
Wrong: it pairs Nasik with the Shipra and Ujjain with the Godavari, and both are incorrect.
keyfact: Nasik–Godavari, Surat–Tapi, Ujjain–Shipra, Vijayawada–Krishna.
option_notes: Code 3-5-4-1: the Godavari, Tapi, Shipra and Krishna match Nasik, Surat, Ujjain and Vijayawada respectively. This is the correct combination. The Godavari is the longest peninsular river, the Tapi is a west-flowing river, the Shipra is a Chambal tributary, and the Krishna rises in Mahabaleshwar and ends in the Bay of Bengal.

Code 4-1-3-2 is wrong. The Shipra is a Malwa river that flows through Ujjain, not Nasik. The Krishna flows through Sangli and Vijayawada, not Surat. The Godavari flows through Nasik, Nanded and Rajahmundry. The Cauvery flows through Srirangapatna, Tiruchirappalli and Thanjavur and enters the Bay of Bengal.

Code 3-1-4-2 is wrong. It gets Nasik and Ujjain right but errs on Surat and Vijayawada. Surat is on the Tapi. Vijayawada is on the Krishna, not the Cauvery. The Cauvery is a Deccan river rising at Talakaveri in Karnataka and flowing through Tamil Nadu, about 800 km long.

Code 4-5-3-1 is wrong. It gets Surat and Vijayawada right but swaps Nasik and Ujjain. Nasik is on the Godavari, and Ujjain is on the Shipra. The Shipra joins the Chambal, which in turn joins the Yamuna, a tributary of the Ganga.
related: Kumbh Mela is held at Haridwar (Ganga), Prayagraj (Ganga-Yamuna-Saraswati), Ujjain (Shipra) and Nashik (Godavari).
The Godavari is the longest peninsular river and is called Dakshin Ganga.
The Tapi and Narmada are the main west-flowing rivers draining into the Arabian Sea.
Prakasam Barrage at Vijayawada is built across the Krishna.
The Shipra is a tributary of the Chambal.
Srirangam island is formed by the Cauvery and the Kollidam.
Hyderabad stands on the Musi, a tributary of the Krishna.
statements: A. Nasik — Correct: it is on the Godavari. Nashik is in Maharashtra, close to the Godavari's source at Trimbakeshwar in the Brahmagiri hills of the Western Ghats. Ramkund is a bathing ghat on the river here. The city hosts the Kumbh Mela every 12 years and is also known for grapes and wine, the Currency Note Press and HAL. The Godavari is the longest peninsular river, called Dakshin Ganga, about 1,465 km long, and ends in the Bay of Bengal.

B. Surat — Correct: it is on the Tapi (Tapti). Surat in Gujarat stands on the Tapi, close to its mouth at the Gulf of Khambhat. Historically it was a major Mughal-era port and a centre for textiles and diamonds. The Tapi rises near Multai in the Betul district of Madhya Pradesh and is about 724 km long. It flows west through a rift valley south of the Narmada, and the Ukai Dam is built on it.

C. Ujjain — Correct: it is on the Shipra (Kshipra). Ujjain in Madhya Pradesh is an ancient city, once called Avanti or Ujjayini, and the capital of the Avanti mahajanapada. It is one of the Saptapuri and has the Mahakaleshwar Jyotirlinga. The Simhastha Kumbh is held every 12 years on the Shipra. The Shipra is a tributary of the Chambal and rises near Indore. Ujjain was long a reference point for Indian prime meridian calculations in astronomy.

D. Vijayawada — Correct: it is on the Krishna. Vijayawada in Andhra Pradesh lies on the Krishna and is flanked by the Indrakeeladri hills, with the Kanaka Durga temple. The Prakasam Barrage across the river feeds canals. It is an important rail and road junction. The Krishna rises near Mahabaleshwar in the Western Ghats, is about 1,400 km long, and enters the Bay of Bengal near Hamsaladeevi. The Nagarjuna Sagar and Srisailam dams are on it.
summary: The correct answer is (a): Nasik–Godavari (3), Surat–Tapi (5), Ujjain–Shipra (4), Vijayawada–Krishna (1). Each city is matched to the river on whose banks it stands. Cauvery (2) is the extra, unused item in List-II.
topic_notes: Matching cities with rivers is a classic geography staple. Key pairs: Delhi–Yamuna; Agra and Mathura–Yamuna; Varanasi, Kanpur, Prayagraj (Allahabad), Patna and Haridwar–Ganga; Lucknow–Gomti; Ahmedabad–Sabarmati; Vadodara–Vishwamitri; Surat–Tapi; Bharuch–Narmada; Jabalpur–Narmada; Nasik, Nanded and Rajahmundry–Godavari; Pune–Mula-Mutha; Hyderabad–Musi; Vijayawada–Krishna; Kurnool–Tungabhadra; Tiruchirappalli–Cauvery; Madurai–Vaigai; Cuttack–Mahanadi; Kolkata–Hooghly; Guwahati–Brahmaputra; Srinagar–Jhelum; Ludhiana–Sutlej; Ayodhya–Saryu; Ujjain–Shipra; Kota–Chambal; Jaunpur–Gomti; Ferozepur–Sutlej; Bareilly–Ramganga; Gorakhpur–Rapti; Mumbai–Mithi; Bhopal has lakes rather than a major river. Peninsular rivers: east-flowing (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery) form deltas; west-flowing (Narmada, Tapi) form estuaries. Godavari: about 1,465 km, rising at Trimbakeshwar. Krishna: about 1,400 km, with tributaries Bhima, Tungabhadra, Koyna and Musi. Tapi: about 724 km. Narmada: about 1,312 km, rising at Amarkantak. Cauvery: about 800 km, rising at Talakaveri. Kumbh sites are Haridwar, Prayagraj, Ujjain and Nashik. Ujjain also has a link with the Tropic of Cancer, which passes close to it.

question: Recently, Cannes Film Festival was held in
subject: Computers
detail: Cannes is a resort city in southeastern France in the Alpes-Maritimes department, on the Mediterranean coast. The Festival de Cannes was conceived in 1939 as a French answer to the Venice festival, which was seen as politically influenced by Fascist Italy. The first planned edition was cancelled because of the outbreak of World War II, and the first full festival took place in 1946. It is now held annually in May at the Palais des Festivals. The top award was the Grand Prix until 1955, when it became the Palme d'Or. It is one of the 'Big Three' European festivals, along with Venice (Italy, Golden Lion) and Berlin (Germany, Golden Bear). Elimination: Switzerland hosts the Locarno festival (Golden Leopard). Italy hosts Venice, the oldest film festival, founded in 1932. England has no festival of this rank; the BAFTA awards and the London Film Festival are its main events. A question that links a festival to a country can be answered once you know these pairings.
explanations: Incorrect. Switzerland hosts the Locarno Film Festival, not Cannes. Locarno's top award is the Golden Leopard.
Correct. Cannes is a city on the French Riviera, and the Cannes Film Festival is held there every May.
Incorrect. Italy hosts the Venice Film Festival, which gives the Golden Lion. Venice is the oldest film festival in the world.
Incorrect. England hosts the BAFTA awards and the London Film Festival, not Cannes.
keyfact: Cannes Film Festival: France, every May, Palme d'Or.
option_notes: Switzerland: its main film festival is Locarno, held in August since 1946, with the Golden Leopard as its top prize. Switzerland also hosts the Montreux Jazz Festival and the World Economic Forum at Davos. Its capital is Bern, and Geneva hosts many UN bodies.

France: the capital is Paris and the currency is the euro. The Cannes Film Festival has been held since 1946 and gives the Palme d'Or. France is also the home of the Césars, the French national film awards. Indian films that have won at Cannes include Neecha Nagar (1946, Grand Prix) and, in 2024, All We Imagine as Light, which won the Grand Prix.

Italy: Venice hosts the oldest film festival, founded in 1932, with the Golden Lion as its top prize. Italy's national film awards are the David di Donatello. Rome is the capital. The Rome Film Festival began in 2006.

England: its main film awards are the BAFTAs, given by the British Academy of Film and Television Arts. The BFI London Film Festival is held every October. England is part of the United Kingdom, and its capital is London.
related: Cannes top award: Palme d'Or, introduced in 1955.
Venice Film Festival (Italy), founded 1932, is the oldest film festival in the world.
Berlin International Film Festival gives the Golden Bear.
IFFI is held in Goa, with the first edition in 1952.
Neecha Nagar (1946) won the Grand Prix at the first Cannes festival.
Payal Kapadia's All We Imagine as Light won the Grand Prix at Cannes in 2024.
Locarno Festival in Switzerland gives the Golden Leopard.
Dadasaheb Phalke Award is India's highest honour in cinema.
summary: The answer is (b) France. The Cannes Film Festival is held every year in the city of Cannes on the French Riviera (Côte d'Azur), usually in May. Its top prize is the Palme d'Or.
topic_notes: Major international film festivals: Cannes (France, May, Palme d'Or), Venice (Italy, August-September, Golden Lion, founded 1932, oldest), Berlin or Berlinale (Germany, February, Golden Bear), Locarno (Switzerland, Golden Leopard), Toronto (Canada, People's Choice Award), Sundance (USA, Utah, independent films), Busan (South Korea), Tokyo, Karlovy Vary (Czech Republic), and Moscow. The Cannes festival began in 1946 and the Palme d'Or was introduced in 1955. India has taken part since the beginning. Neecha Nagar by Chetan Anand won the Grand Prix at the first festival in 1946. Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali won 'Best Human Document' in 1956. Other Indian films that have competed include Do Bigha Zamin and Garm Hava. Shaji N. Karun's Piravi and Swaham were also in competition. Payal Kapadia's All We Imagine as Light won the Grand Prix in 2024, the first Indian film to be in competition for the Palme d'Or in thirty years. Other awards: the Oscars (Academy Awards, USA), the Golden Globes, BAFTA (UK), and the César (France). In India, the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) is held in Goa every November and was first held in 1952. The Dadasaheb Phalke Award is India's highest film honour, and the National Film Awards are given by the Directorate of Film Festivals.

question: Shri Kiran Karnik is the
options: Chairman of the Board of Control of Cricket for India
Chairman of Maharashtra State Public Service Commission
Managing Director of Engineers India Ltd
subject: Insurance
detail: Kiran Karnik (born 1948) is an Indian management professional and IT industry leader. He began his career at the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and worked with Vikram Sarabhai. He was among the first employees of ISRO's Development and Educational Communication Unit and helped plan SITE (Satellite Instructional Television Experiment, 1975-76). He became the founding Managing Director of Discovery Networks India, then Managing Director of Doordarshan's early commercial arm, and later President of NASSCOM (2001-2008), succeeding Dewang Mehta, who died in 2001. At NASSCOM he promoted India as a global IT and BPO destination, worked on IT-ITeS export growth, data security and IPR issues, and championed the IT industry. He later served on the board of several companies and was a member of the Prime Minister's Council on Trade and Industry. He also wrote 'The Creative Society' (2012). Elimination: the BCCI chairman post does not exist in that form (BCCI has a President), the Maharashtra PSC and Engineers India Ltd are unrelated to his career, which was in space, media and IT. So (a) is the only fit.
explanations: Correct: Kiran Karnik was President of NASSCOM from 2001 to 2008, the period covering this 2002 question.
Incorrect: BCCI is led by a President, and Karnik has no connection with cricket administration. Jagmohan Dalmiya and Sharad Pawar are names associated with it around then.
Incorrect: He never headed the Maharashtra Public Service Commission. His career was in ISRO, media and the IT industry.
Incorrect: Engineers India Ltd is a public sector engineering consultancy. Karnik was never its Managing Director.
keyfact: Kiran Karnik = ISRO alumnus, Discovery India MD, NASSCOM President 2001-08.
option_notes: NASSCOM is the apex trade body and chamber of commerce for the Indian IT-BPM industry, founded in 1988 and headquartered in New Delhi. It is a non-profit body. Presidents include Dewang Mehta (the founding-era head), Kiran Karnik (2001-08), Som Mittal (2009-15), R. Chandrashekhar (2015-18) and Debjani Ghosh (2018-22). Its role is advocacy, policy input and promoting exports and standards.

BCCI, the Board of Control for Cricket in India, was founded in 1928 and is registered under the Tamil Nadu Societies Registration Act. It is headed by a President. Past presidents include Jagmohan Dalmiya, Sharad Pawar, N. Srinivasan and Sourav Ganguly (2019-22). The Lodha Committee reforms of 2016 and the Supreme Court shaped its governance.

The Maharashtra Public Service Commission (MPSC) is a state commission under Article 315 of the Constitution, headquartered in Mumbai. It recruits for state government services. Members are appointed by the Governor, and the term is six years or until age 62, whichever is earlier. It is headed by a Chairman.

Engineers India Limited (EIL) is a Government of India public sector enterprise, set up in 1965. It is headquartered in New Delhi and provides engineering consultancy and EPC services, mainly for the oil, gas and petrochemical sectors. It is a Miniratna (Category I) company, and the top executive is the Chairman and Managing Director.
related: NASSCOM was founded in 1988 and is based in New Delhi.
Kiran Karnik was NASSCOM President from 2001 to 2008.
Dewang Mehta was an early and influential NASSCOM head, who died in 2001.
SITE (1975-76) was a satellite television experiment in which ISRO worked with NASA's ATS-6.
STPI was established in 1991 to promote software exports.
The IT Act 2000 gave legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures.
Debjani Ghosh was NASSCOM President from 2018 to 2022.
summary: The answer is (a). Kiran Karnik was President of NASSCOM (National Association of Software and Services Companies) from 2001 to 2008, so he held that post when the 2002 paper was set. He is known as a leading figure of the Indian IT industry.
topic_notes: Kiran Karnik is an ISRO alumnus who worked under Vikram Sarabhai and helped plan SITE in the 1970s, an early satellite-based education television experiment. He led Discovery Networks India as Managing Director, and he was President of NASSCOM from 2001 to 2008. He also served as a member of the National Knowledge Commission-related advisory forums and wrote 'Crafting Strategy' type management work and 'The Creative Society'. NASSCOM was founded in 1988 and is the main industry body for software and services. Key NASSCOM themes are IT-ITeS exports, BPO growth, the India brand in IT, intellectual property protection and the IT Act 2000. Related people: Dewang Mehta, the early NASSCOM leader who died in 2001, N. R. Narayana Murthy (Infosys founder), Azim Premji (Wipro) and Nandan Nilekani (Infosys, later UIDAI chairman). Related ideas for exams: the IT Act 2000 was India's first law on electronic commerce and cybercrime, Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) was set up in 1991, and Bangalore became known as India's Silicon Valley. Exams often ask who heads which body, such as the NASSCOM president, the BCCI president, the ISRO chairman or the chairman of a commission.

question: Knesset is the name of the Parliament of
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The Knesset (Hebrew for 'assembly') is the unicameral legislature of Israel and has 120 members. It is modelled on the Great Assembly (Knesset HaGedolah) of the Second Temple period. It was established in 1949 after the Constituent Assembly elected in January 1949 renamed itself the First Knesset. It sits in Jerusalem, in a building opened in 1966. Members are elected by nationwide proportional representation using closed party lists, with an electoral threshold (currently 3.25%). The usual term is four years, though early dissolution is common. The Knesset enacts laws, elects the President of the State (a largely ceremonial post, seven-year single term), approves the government, and supervises the executive. Israel has no single written constitution, only Basic Laws. For elimination, remember the parliament names of the other countries: Norway has the Storting, Sweden the Riksdag, and Spain the Cortes Generales with its Congress of Deputies and Senate. Each of these names is distinct from the Knesset, so only Israel fits.
explanations: Norway: wrong. Its parliament is the Storting, not the Knesset.
Sweden: wrong. Its parliament is the Riksdag, a unicameral body of 349 members.
Israel: correct. The Knesset is Israel's 120-member unicameral parliament in Jerusalem.
Spain: wrong. Its parliament is the Cortes Generales, which has two houses.
keyfact: Knesset = Israel's 120-member unicameral parliament in Jerusalem.
option_notes: Norway is a Scandinavian constitutional monarchy. Its parliament is the Storting, with 169 members. It was established under the 1814 Constitution, and Oslo is the capital. Norway has a long tradition of parliamentary democracy. The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo by a committee appointed by the Storting. It is not an EU member but is part of the European Economic Area.

Sweden is a constitutional monarchy with its parliament, the Riksdag, in Stockholm. The Riksdag is unicameral and has 349 seats. It has existed in its modern unicameral form since 1971. Members are elected by proportional representation every four years, with a 4% threshold. Sweden joined the EU in 1995 and NATO in 2024. The Nobel Prizes, except the Peace Prize, are awarded in Stockholm.

Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948. Its parliament, the Knesset, has 120 members and sits in Jerusalem. It is elected by proportional representation with party lists. The Knesset elects the President, who serves a single seven-year term. The Prime Minister heads the government. Israel has no single codified constitution but is governed by Basic Laws passed by the Knesset.

Spain is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy under the 1978 Constitution. Its parliament is the Cortes Generales, made up of the Congress of Deputies (350 members, lower house) and the Senate (upper house). Madrid is the capital. The monarch is King Felipe VI, and the head of government is the President of the Government (Prime Minister). Spain joined the EU in 1986.
related: Storting is the parliament of Norway.
Riksdag is the parliament of Sweden.
Folketing is the parliament of Denmark.
Cortes Generales is the parliament of Spain.
Bundestag is Germany's lower house.
Diet is the parliament of Japan.
Duma is the lower house of Russia's parliament.
Jatiya Sangsad is the parliament of Bangladesh.
summary: The answer is (c) Israel. The Knesset is Israel's unicameral national legislature, with 120 members. Norway's parliament is the Storting, Sweden's is the Riksdag, and Spain's is the Cortes Generales.
topic_notes: Parliament names of countries are a frequent static-GK topic. Israel: Knesset (120 members, unicameral). Norway: Storting. Sweden: Riksdag. Denmark: Folketing. Finland: Eduskunta. Iceland: Althing, among the oldest parliaments in the world. Spain: Cortes Generales. Germany: Bundestag (lower house) and Bundesrat (upper house). Switzerland: Federal Assembly. Netherlands: States General. Russia: Federal Assembly, consisting of the State Duma and the Federation Council. Japan: Diet. China: National People's Congress. Iran: Majlis. Afghanistan: Shora. Nepal: Federal Parliament (Sansad). Bhutan: Tshogdu. Bangladesh: Jatiya Sangsad. Pakistan: Majlis-e-Shoora, with the National Assembly and the Senate. Sri Lanka: Parliament. Mongolia: State Great Khural. Poland: Sejm (lower house) and Senate. Ireland: Oireachtas, with the Dáil Éireann. Libya: General National Congress. USA: Congress, made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives. UK: Parliament, with the House of Commons and the House of Lords. Israel specifics: Knesset elections use a single nationwide constituency and proportional representation. The President is elected by the Knesset. The Supreme Court operates without a single written constitution, relying on Basic Laws. The first Knesset met in 1949, with Chaim Weizmann as the first President and David Ben-Gurion as the first Prime Minister. Similar names are frequently confused in exams, so learn them in pairs of country and legislature.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a current-affairs matching question from the 2001-02 period. Dennis Tito, an American millionaire and former NASA engineer, became the first paying space tourist in April-May 2001. He flew on a Russian Soyuz TM-32 to the International Space Station, and the trip cost about 20 million US dollars. Colin Powell served as US Secretary of State from January 2001 to January 2005 under President George W. Bush. He was the first African-American to hold that post. Jacques Chirac was President of France from 1995 to 2007, and earlier served as Prime Minister and Mayor of Paris. Donald Rumsfeld was US Secretary of Defense in 2001-2006, and also held the post in 1975-77 under Ford. Elimination: Tito is the only item that matches 'first space tourist', so options (a) and (c) with A-1 are out. Powell is Secretary of State (3), which removes (b), where B is 2. Only (d) remains, and it is consistent with C-1 and D-2. Note that the question text is garbled by OCR, since a second matching table has leaked into it, but the valid table here is unambiguous.
explanations: Wrong: it pairs Tito with President of France and Powell with Secretary of State, but Tito is the space tourist.
Wrong: it gives Powell as Defence Secretary and Rumsfeld as Secretary of State, which reverses their roles.
Wrong: it pairs Tito with President of France and Chirac with space tourist, which is incorrect.
Correct: A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2 matches every person with the right role.
keyfact: Tito = first space tourist (2001); Powell = US Secretary of State; Chirac = French President; Rumsfeld = US Defence Secretary.
option_notes: Option (a) 1-3-4-2 would make Tito the French President and Chirac the space tourist, so it is wrong. It does get Powell as Secretary of State and Rumsfeld as Defence Secretary right. The real holders were: France's President Chirac (1995-2007) and the first space tourist Tito (2001). Always anchor on the unique item, the space tourist, to eliminate.

Option (b) 4-2-1-3 correctly links Tito to space tourist and Chirac to French President. However, it reverses Powell and Rumsfeld. Powell was Secretary of State (the foreign minister equivalent, 2001-05), and Rumsfeld was Defence Secretary (the Pentagon head, 2001-06). Know the cabinet portfolios of the Bush administration: Cheney as VP, Ashcroft as Attorney General, and Rice as National Security Adviser.

Option (c) 1-2-4-3 gets nearly everything wrong. Tito was not a politician, and Chirac was not a space tourist. Only the pairing of Powell with Defence Secretary is wrongly offered. Remember that Tito flew on a Russian Soyuz in 2001, and that Chirac, a Gaullist and founder of the RPR, led France through 2007 before Nicolas Sarkozy.

Option (d) 4-3-1-2 is the correct key. Tito is the first space tourist, Powell is Secretary of State, Chirac is President of France, and Rumsfeld is Defence Secretary. These were all prominent news figures in 2001-02, following the 9/11 attacks and the Afghan war. Questions of this type test current-affairs personalities and their offices.
related: Dennis Tito flew to the ISS in 2001 aboard Soyuz TM-32.
Mark Shuttleworth was the second space tourist (2002) and the first from Africa.
Anousheh Ansari was the first woman space tourist (2006).
Colin Powell was the first African-American US Secretary of State.
Condoleezza Rice succeeded Powell in 2005.
Jacques Chirac was France's President from 1995 to 2007.

statements: A — Correct: Dennis Tito matches 4, first space tourist. He was an American businessman and former NASA JPL engineer who flew to the ISS in 2001 on Soyuz TM-32 as a paying passenger. He spent about 8 days in space, reportedly paying around 20 million US dollars. Russia's space agency and the company Space Adventures arranged the flight. Mark Shuttleworth of South Africa followed in 2002 as the second space tourist. NASA initially objected to his visit to the ISS.

B — Correct: Colin Powell matches 3, Secretary of State of the USA. He served from 2001 to 2005 under George W. Bush. He was a retired four-star general and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff during the Gulf War of 1991. He was the first African-American Secretary of State. He presented the US case on Iraq's weapons to the UN in February 2003. Condoleezza Rice succeeded him.

C — Correct: Jacques Chirac matches 1, President of France. He was President from 1995 to 2007 and was re-elected in 2002 after defeating Jean-Marie Le Pen. He served twice as Prime Minister and was Mayor of Paris from 1977 to 1995. He opposed the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq. He was the Chief Guest at India's Republic Day in 1998 and 2008 (Sarkozy). The presidential term was cut from seven to five years in 2002.

D — Correct: Donald Rumsfeld matches 2, US Defence Secretary. He served from 2001 to 2006 under George W. Bush, and earlier from 1975 to 1977 under Gerald Ford, when he was the youngest Defense Secretary. He was a key architect of the Afghanistan war (2001) and the Iraq war (2003). He resigned in November 2006 after the Republican defeat in the midterms. Robert Gates succeeded him.
summary: The correct answer is (d): A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2. Dennis Tito was the first space tourist, Colin Powell was US Secretary of State, Jacques Chirac was President of France, and Donald Rumsfeld was US Defence Secretary.
topic_notes: Personalities in the news in 2001-02. Space tourism: Dennis Tito (April 28, 2001) was the first, and Mark Shuttleworth (2002) was the second. Later tourists include Gregory Olsen (2005), Anousheh Ansari (2006, first woman space tourist) and Charles Simonyi. Space Adventures arranged these flights. In 2021, Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic began suborbital tourism. The Bush administration (2001-09) included Dick Cheney as Vice President, Colin Powell as Secretary of State, Donald Rumsfeld as Defense Secretary, John Ashcroft as Attorney General, and Condoleezza Rice as National Security Adviser, who later became Secretary of State (2005-09). France: the President is the head of state, elected directly for five years since 2002. Chirac (1995-2007) was followed by Sarkozy (2007-12), Hollande (2012-17), Macron (2017 onward). The French Prime Minister is head of government. UK Prime Minister in 2001 was Tony Blair (1997-2007). Russia's President was Vladimir Putin from 2000. UN Secretary-General was Kofi Annan (1997-2006). Other 2001 events: the 9/11 attacks, Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan, and the attack on the Indian Parliament on December 13, 2001. Pakistan's leader was Pervez Musharraf. For revision, make a table of office-holders with their terms, and learn the first-of-its-kind records in space.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The FIFA World Cup is held every four years, and the host country changes each time. The four editions in this question are 1986 (Mexico), 1990 (Italy), 1994 (USA) and 1998 (France). Mexico was the first country to host the tournament twice (1970 and 1986), and the 1986 final was won by Argentina, led by Maradona, who beat West Germany. Italy hosted in 1990 (its second time, after 1934), and West Germany beat Argentina in the final. The USA hosted in 1994, and Brazil beat Italy on penalties in the final. France hosted in 1998 and won its first title by beating Brazil 3-0. Spain hosted in 1982 and Italy won that edition, so Spain (5) is a distractor and does not match any of the four years. Elimination: A must be 2 (Mexico), which rules out options (a) and (c), which both start with 5. Then B must be 1 (Italy), which rules out (d), whose second entry is 3. Only (b) remains.
explanations: Wrong: it pairs 1986 with Spain, but Spain hosted in 1982. It also pairs 1990 with France and 1994 with Mexico, which are both wrong.
Correct: 1986 – Mexico, 1990 – Italy, 1994 – USA, 1998 – France, which is the code 2 1 4 3.
Wrong: it pairs 1986 with Spain (the 1982 host) and 1994 with Mexico (1986 and 1970 host). Only B matches.
Wrong: A (Mexico) and C (USA) are right, but 1990 was hosted by Italy, not France, and 1998 by France, not Italy.
keyfact: World Cup hosts: 1982 Spain, 1986 Mexico, 1990 Italy, 1994 USA, 1998 France.
option_notes: Code 5 3 2 1 pairs 1986 with Spain, 1990 with France, 1994 with Mexico and 1998 with Italy. Spain hosted in 1982 (Italy won). France hosted in 1938 and 1998. Mexico hosted in 1970 and 1986. Italy hosted in 1934 and 1990. None of these pairings is correct.

Code 2 1 4 3 gives Mexico 1986, Italy 1990, USA 1994 and France 1998, which is correct. Argentina won in 1986, West Germany in 1990, Brazil in 1994 and France in 1998. The 1994 final was the first to be decided on penalties, and the USA set attendance records.

Code 5 1 2 3 gives Spain 1986, Italy 1990, Mexico 1994 and France 1998. Only 1990 and 1998 are right. Spain hosted in 1982 and Mexico in 1970 and 1986. Spain has not hosted since 1982, though it is a joint host for 2030.
Code 2 3 4 1 gives Mexico 1986, France 1990, USA 1994 and Italy 1998. Only 1986 and 1994 are right. France hosted in 1998 and Italy in 1990. The swap of France and Italy is the trap in this option.
related: Mexico was the first country to host the World Cup twice (1970 and 1986).
Italy hosted the World Cup in 1934 and 1990.
1994 USA final: Brazil beat Italy on penalties.
1998: France won its first title, beating Brazil 3-0.
2002 was the first World Cup in Asia and the first with joint hosts (South Korea and Japan).
Spain hosted in 1982; Italy won.
Qatar hosted in 2022 and Argentina won.
summary: The correct answer is (b): 1986 – Mexico (2), 1990 – Italy (1), 1994 – USA (4), 1998 – France (3). This gives the code 2 1 4 3.
topic_notes: The FIFA World Cup began in 1930 in Uruguay, which also won the first title. It is held every four years, apart from 1942 and 1946, when it was cancelled because of World War II. The trophy was the Jules Rimet Trophy until 1970. Brazil kept it permanently after its third win that year, and the FIFA World Cup Trophy has been used since 1974. Hosts by year: 1930 Uruguay, 1934 Italy, 1938 France, 1950 Brazil, 1954 Switzerland, 1958 Sweden, 1962 Chile, 1966 England, 1970 Mexico, 1974 West Germany, 1978 Argentina, 1982 Spain, 1986 Mexico, 1990 Italy, 1994 USA, 1998 France, 2002 South Korea/Japan (the first joint hosts and the first in Asia), 2006 Germany, 2010 South Africa (the first in Africa), 2014 Brazil, 2018 Russia, 2022 Qatar (the first in the Arab world), 2026 USA/Canada/Mexico. Winners: Brazil has 5 titles (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002), Germany has 4 (West Germany 1954, 1974, 1990, and Germany 2014), Italy has 4 (1934, 1938, 1982, 2006), Argentina has 3 (1978, 1986, 2022), France has 2 (1998, 2018), and Uruguay has 2 (1930, 1950). England (1966), Spain (2010) and 1998 France complete the list of winners. Golden Boot and Golden Ball awards are also commonly asked. Maradona's 'Hand of God' goal came in 1986. Zinedine Zidane scored twice in the 1998 final. In 2026 the tournament expands to 48 teams.

question: Raksha Kavach' is
options: a new safety equipment designed for the soldiers of Indian Army
an an -collision device to prevent collision between trains designed by the Konkan Railway Corporation
a new design for earthquake resistant buildings
a new device for the Indian airports for the safe landing of aircrafts
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Raksha Kavach was the name of the Anti-Collision Device (ACD) developed by Konkan Railway Corporation Ltd (KRCL) in the late 1990s, after the collision-related accidents of that period. The ACD was a self-acting, microprocessor-based system that did not need human input. It warned drivers and applied brakes automatically when two trains were on the same track within a danger distance. It also helped with unmanned level-crossing alerts and signal-passing alerts, and it was trialled on Northeast Frontier Railway. Later, Indian Railways developed its own indigenous Automatic Train Protection system, 'Kavach', through RDSO with Indian industry. This is a later and separate system, but it is often confused with Raksha Kavach. Elimination: the name is not associated with army soldier equipment (option a), with earthquake-resistant building design (option c), or with aircraft landing aids such as ILS at airports (option d). Railway safety and 'Kavach' words always point to train protection systems.
explanations: Incorrect: Raksha Kavach was not army equipment. Army protective items include bulletproof jackets and helmets, and have different names.
Correct: Raksha Kavach was the ACD developed by Konkan Railway Corporation to prevent train collisions.
Incorrect: Earthquake-resistant building designs are covered by BIS codes (IS 1893) and not by a scheme called Raksha Kavach.
Incorrect: Safe landing at airports uses ILS, DVOR and similar systems, not Raksha Kavach.
keyfact: Raksha Kavach = Konkan Railway's anti-collision device (ACD) for trains.
option_notes: Army soldier safety equipment includes ballistic helmets, bulletproof jackets (such as the Bhabha Kavach, developed by BARC and DRDO) and similar items. The Army is not the user of Raksha Kavach. The DRDO and the Defence Ministry oversee such gear, and procurement is carried out through the Ordnance Factory Board and private vendors.

This is the correct option. Konkan Railway Corporation Ltd was set up in 1990 to build the Konkan Railway (Roha to Mangalore, 741 km), opened in 1998. KRCL developed the Anti-Collision Device, called Raksha Kavach, which could automatically brake trains approaching each other on the same track. KRCL has headquarters in Navi Mumbai.

Earthquake-resistant design in India follows BIS codes such as IS 1893 (seismic design), IS 4326 and IS 13920 (ductile detailing). India is divided into seismic zones II to V. The National Disaster Management Authority and the Building Materials and Technology Promotion Council (BMTPC) publish guidelines. None of these is called Raksha Kavach.

Safe landing at airports relies on Instrument Landing Systems (ILS), VOR, DME, and GPS-aided GAGAN, which was developed by ISRO and the Airports Authority of India. The Airports Authority of India, formed in 1995, manages airport navigation systems. The DGCA regulates safety. These are not called Raksha Kavach.
related: Raksha Kavach was the Anti-Collision Device of Konkan Railway.
Konkan Railway runs from Roha (Maharashtra) to Mangalore (Karnataka), 741 km.
KRCL was incorporated in 1990 and the line was fully opened in 1998.
Kavach is the indigenous Automatic Train Protection system developed by RDSO.
Bhabha Kavach is a lightweight bulletproof jacket developed by BARC.
The Commissioner of Railway Safety works under the Ministry of Civil Aviation.
GAGAN is a GPS-aided navigation system by ISRO and AAI for aviation.
summary: The answer is (b). 'Raksha Kavach' was the name given to the anti-collision device (ACD) developed by Konkan Railway Corporation Ltd (KRCL) to prevent head-on and rear-end train collisions. It was a GPS-free, network-based system that acted automatically when trains were on the same track.
topic_notes: Railway safety technology is a recurring topic in current affairs and general awareness. Konkan Railway Corporation Ltd (KRCL) was incorporated in 1990 and built the 741 km Roha-Mangalore line, which opened fully in January 1998. It is a Public Sector Undertaking under the Ministry of Railways. It used the BOOT-like model of state-sharing, with Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka and Kerala holding stakes. The Anti-Collision Device (ACD), branded as Raksha Kavach, was developed by KRCL and used a GPS-independent communication network to detect trains on the same track and to apply brakes automatically. It was tested on the Northeast Frontier Railway in 2000-2002. Later, the Research Designs and Standards Organisation (RDSO) developed the indigenous Automatic Train Protection system called Kavach, which uses RFID tags on tracks and UHF radio, and is aligned to SIL-4 safety level. Kavach was trialled in 2016 and officially adopted as the National ATP system in 2020. Related items: TCAS (Train Collision Avoidance System), Train Protection and Warning System (TPWS), and the Automatic Block Signalling system. Other safety concepts include the Interlocking system, Axle Counters and Track circuits. Indian Railways has zones and headquarters, and the Commissioner of Railway Safety (CRS) works under the Ministry of Civil Aviation, not the Railways, for independence in accident inquiries.

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of Soccer World Cup :
1. Prior to FIFA-2002 Cup, Brazil had won the World Cup four mes.
2. Indomitable Lions' is the nickname for Cameroon team. 3. 'Azzurri' is the nickname for the Italian team.
4. Senegal, Slovenia and Ecuador participating in FIFA-2002 are the only teams par cipa ng in the World Cup for the first me. Which of these statements are correct?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The 2002 FIFA World Cup was co-hosted by South Korea and Japan, the first in Asia and the first with joint hosts. Brazil won it, beating Germany 2-0 in the final, which gave them a fifth title. Before 2002, Brazil's four wins were 1958 (Sweden), 1962 (Chile), 1970 (Mexico) and 1994 (USA), so statement 1 is correct. National team nicknames are a standard quiz area: Cameroon are the Indomitable Lions and Italy are the Azzurri (the Blues, from the colour of the Savoy royal house). Statement 4 is a trap because it uses the word 'only'. In 2002 the debutants were China, Ecuador, Senegal and Slovenia. Because China is missing from the list, statement 4 is false. Elimination: statements 1, 2 and 3 are all true, so only option (a) fits. Options (c) and (d) contain statement 4, and option (b) leaves out statement 1.
explanations: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 3 are all true and statement 4 is false, which matches this option exactly.
Wrong: statements 2 and 3 are correct, but this option leaves out statement 1, which is also correct (Brazil had four titles before 2002).
Wrong: it includes statement 4, which is false because China was also a debutant, and it omits statement 2, which is correct.
Wrong: it includes statement 4, which is false because of China's debut, and it omits statement 3, which is correct.
keyfact: Before FIFA 2002 Brazil had four titles; Cameroon are the Indomitable Lions; Italy are the Azzurri; 2002 had four debutants (China, Ecuador, Senegal, Slovenia).
option_notes: Statements 1, 2 and 3: Brazil with four earlier titles, Cameroon as the Indomitable Lions and Italy as the Azzurri. This is the right combination. Brazil beat Germany 2-0 in the 2002 final in Yokohama, and Ronaldo scored both goals. The tournament was co-hosted by Japan and South Korea, the first held in Asia. South Korea reached the semi-finals, which is the best Asian result so far. Turkey finished third.

Statements 2 and 3 only: both are correct facts, but the combination is incomplete. Cameroon, the Indomitable Lions, were the first African quarter-finalists, in 1990. Italy, the Azzurri, have four World Cups, tied with Germany for second place behind Brazil's five. The combination wrongly excludes the true Brazil statement. Argentina and France have won more recently, in 2022 and 2018 respectively.

Statements 1, 3 and 4: it pairs two true statements with the false statement 4, which wrongly claims the three named teams were the only debutants. The 2002 debutants were actually four: China, Ecuador, Senegal and Slovenia. The 2002 tournament had 32 teams, the format used from 1998 to 2022. The 2026 tournament expands to 48 teams, hosted by the USA, Canada and Mexico.

Statements 1, 2 and 4: it combines true statements 1 and 2 with false statement 4 and leaves out the true statement 3. The 2002 tournament's debutants included China, which is the key fact that refutes statement 4. Senegal, Slovenia and Ecuador were also first-timers. Note that exam-style statements using 'only' are often false for this reason.
related: Brazil has won the World Cup five times (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002) and is the only nation to play in every edition.
The 2002 World Cup was co-hosted by Japan and South Korea, the first in Asia and the first with joint hosts.
2002 debutants: China, Ecuador, Senegal and Slovenia.
Italy are the Azzurri and have won four World Cups (1934, 1938, 1982, 2006).
Cameroon were the first African quarter-finalists, at Italy 1990.
Miroslav Klose (Germany) is the top World Cup scorer, with 16 goals.
Senegal beat defending champions France 1-0 in the 2002 opener.
The 2026 World Cup will have 48 teams, hosted by the USA, Canada and Mexico.
statements: 1 — Correct: Brazil had won in 1958, 1962, 1970 and 1994, so four titles before 2002. Brazil is the only team to have played in every World Cup. They added titles in 2002, making five. They also lost the 1950 final round decider to Uruguay (the Maracanazo) and the 1998 final to France. Pelé won three World Cups (1958, 1962, 1970). The Jules Rimet Trophy was kept permanently by Brazil after the 1970 win, and the current FIFA World Cup Trophy was introduced in 1974.

2 — Correct: Cameroon's national team is called the Indomitable Lions (Les Lions Indomptables). They were the first African team to reach a World Cup quarter-final, in Italy 1990, led by Roger Milla. They have qualified for the World Cup many times, more than any other African nation along with a few others, and won the Africa Cup of Nations five times. Other African nicknames: Nigeria are the Super Eagles, Senegal the Lions of Teranga, Ghana the Black Stars, and Egypt the Pharaohs.

3 — Correct: Italy's national team is called the Azzurri, meaning 'the Blues', after the blue shirts derived from the royal House of Savoy colours. Italy have won four World Cups (1934, 1938, 1982, 2006). Vittorio Pozzo coached them to the first two titles. They lost the 1970 and 1994 finals to Brazil, the latter on penalties, and lost the 2000 European Championship final to France. They failed to qualify for the 2018 and 2022 World Cups. Other nicknames: Argentina are La Albiceleste, Netherlands are Oranje, and Germany are Die Mannschaft.

4 — Incorrect: Senegal, Slovenia and Ecuador were debutants in 2002, but China also made its first appearance, so they were not the only first-timers. China, coached by Bora Milutinović, lost all three group games and scored no goals. Senegal famously beat defending champions France 1-0 in the opening match and reached the quarter-finals, losing to Turkey. Slovenia and Ecuador went out in the group stage. The 2002 tournament also saw Turkey finish third and Ronaldo win the Golden Boot with 8 goals.
summary: Answer is (a): statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct, while statement 4 is wrong. Brazil had four titles before 2002 (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994), Cameroon are the 'Indomitable Lions' and Italy are the 'Azzurri'. Statement 4 fails because China also made its World Cup debut in 2002.
topic_notes: The FIFA World Cup began in 1930 in Uruguay, who won it. It is held every four years, with breaks in 1942 and 1946 because of World War II. The governing body is FIFA, founded in 1904 and headquartered in Zurich. Winners: Brazil 5 (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002), Germany 4 (1954, 1974, 1990, 2014), Italy 4 (1934, 1938, 1982, 2006), Argentina 3 (1978, 1986, 2022), France 2 (1998, 2018), Uruguay 2 (1930, 1950), England 1 (1966) and Spain 1 (2010). Qatar 2022 was the first World Cup in the Middle East. Russia 2018 was the first in Eastern Europe. The 2026 tournament will be in the USA, Canada and Mexico and will feature 48 teams. Miroslav Klose of Germany is the all-time top scorer with 16 goals. Just Fontaine scored 13 goals in the 1958 tournament, the record for a single edition. Pelé is the only player to have won three World Cups. Maradona's 'Hand of God' goal came in 1986. In 2002, Brazil's captain Cafu lifted the trophy, Oliver Kahn won the Golden Ball, Ronaldo took the Golden Boot, and the mascots were Ato, Kaz and Nik. Many nicknames are asked in quizzes: Brazil are the Seleção, Argentina the Albiceleste, France Les Bleus, Germany Die Mannschaft, Netherlands Oranje, Spain La Roja, and Cameroon the Indomitable Lions.

question: Recently, Government disinvested stake in VSNL, IBP and IPCL to
options: Bhar Telesonic, Reliance and GAIL, respectively
Tata Group of Industries, Indian Oil Corporation and Reliance, respectively
Bhar Telesonic, Royal Dutch Shell and Pﬁzer, respectively
Motorala, Kuwait Petroleum Ranbaxy, respectively and
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: India's disinvestment programme moved from minority share sales to strategic sales in 1999-2000, under the Department of Disinvestment (created 1999, made a Ministry in 2001, headed by Arun Shourie). Strategic sale means transfer of management control to a private or other buyer. VSNL (Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd, international telecom monopoly until 2002): Panatone Finvest (Tata group) bought 25% for about Rs 1,439 crore in February 2002, and the government kept about 26% then. IPCL (Indian Petrochemicals Corporation Ltd, Vadodara, Gujarat): Reliance Industries bought the government's 26% in May 2002 for about Rs 1,490 crore, then made an open offer. IBP Co. Ltd (formerly Indo-Burma Petroleum): IOC acquired the government's 33.58% stake in 2002 and later merged IBP into itself in 2007-08. Elimination: Bharti Telesonic was not the VSNL buyer (it only joined the earlier bids), Royal Dutch Shell and Pfizer did not take these stakes, Motorola, Kuwait Petroleum and Ranbaxy did not either, and GAIL did not acquire IPCL (it was only a bidder, as was IOC). Hence only (b) fits.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Bharti Telesonic did not acquire VSNL and Reliance did not buy IBP. GAIL was a bidder for IPCL but lost to Reliance.
(b) Correct: Tata took VSNL, IOC took IBP and Reliance took IPCL, all in 2002.
(c) Wrong: Bharti Telesonic did not take VSNL, Royal Dutch Shell did not buy IBP (it was a bidder) and Pfizer has no link to IPCL, a petrochemical firm.
(d) Wrong: Motorola, Kuwait Petroleum and Ranbaxy were not the buyers of these companies.
keyfact: 2002 strategic sales: VSNL to Tata, IBP to IOC, IPCL to Reliance.
option_notes: Bharti Telesonic was part of Bharti Enterprises, a telecom firm run by Sunil Bharti Mittal, which later became Bharti Airtel. GAIL (Gas Authority of India Ltd, 1984) is a Navratna PSU in natural gas transmission. Reliance Industries is Mukesh Ambani's company, founded by Dhirubhai Ambani. This combination is not what happened.

The Tata group is a conglomerate founded by Jamsetji Tata. Indian Oil Corporation (formed 1964) is India's largest oil company and a Maharatna PSU. Reliance Industries is a private conglomerate with refineries at Jamnagar. This is the true set of 2002 buyers for VSNL, IBP and IPCL.

Royal Dutch Shell is an Anglo-Dutch oil major, now Shell plc. Pfizer is a US pharmaceutical company, with no link to petrochemicals. Bharti Telesonic was a telecom entity. None of them took these stakes.

Motorola is a US telecom equipment maker. Kuwait Petroleum Corporation is a state oil company of Kuwait. Ranbaxy is an Indian pharma company, later bought by Sun Pharma in 2014-15 after Daiichi Sankyo's acquisition in 2008. None of them acquired the PSUs.
related: VSNL was renamed Tata Communications in 2008.
Modern Foods was the first PSU strategically sold, in 2000, to Hindustan Lever.
BALCO was sold to Sterlite in 2001.
Air India was sold to Talace (Tata) in 2021-22.
DIPAM was created in 2016 under the Finance Ministry.
The National Investment Fund was set up in 2005.
IBP was merged with IOC in 2007-08.
summary: The correct option is (b). In the 2002 disinvestments, the Tata Group acquired a 25% strategic stake in VSNL (Feb 2002), Indian Oil Corporation bought IBP (strategic sale, 2002), and Reliance Industries acquired IPCL (May 2002). The other options pair the companies with wrong buyers.
topic_notes: Disinvestment is the sale of government equity in PSUs. The 1991 reforms began minority sales to mutual funds and financial institutions. The Disinvestment Commission (1996, chaired by G.V. Ramakrishna) advised on selling PSUs. Strategic sales began in 1999-2000 with Modern Foods India (sold to Hindustan Lever), the first strategic sale. The Department of Disinvestment was set up in December 1999 and became a full Ministry in September 2001 (Arun Shourie as minister). Major 2000-2004 deals: BALCO (Sterlite/Vedanta, 2001), Hindustan Zinc (Sterlite, 2002), CMC (TCS, 2001), HTL, IBP (IOC, 2002), IPCL (Reliance, 2002), VSNL (Tata, 2002), Maruti Suzuki share sales, Hotel Corporation of India and Centaur Hotel properties. Maruti Udyog was another important case, where Suzuki increased its stake. In 2004 the ministry was converted back into a Department under the Finance Ministry. Later, the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) was formed in 2016. Air India was sold to the Tata group in 2021-22 (Talace Pvt Ltd, Rs 18,000 crore). Other later events: the 2017 ONGC-HPCL deal, the BPCL privatisation plan, the LIC IPO (May 2022), and the NITI Aayog role in identifying PSUs. Policy now stresses the 2021 Public Sector Enterprise Policy with strategic and non-strategic sectors. Disinvestment proceeds go to the National Investment Fund (set up in 2005).

question: Stockholm Syndrome is a mental condition experienced by
options: the young persons who take up jobs in the industry a er passing out from the Management Schools
persons who migrate from rural areas to urban ci es, during the earlier stages of their stay
hostages and kidnap vic ms in which positive feelings develop towards their captors
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Stockholm Syndrome is a coping mechanism or trauma response seen in captive or abused people. Over time, the victim bonds with the captor and may defend the captor or resist rescue. The name comes from the August 1973 robbery of Kreditbanken at Norrmalmstorg, Stockholm. Hostages were held for about six days, and afterwards some defended their captors and refused to testify against them. The criminologist and psychiatrist Nils Bejerot coined the term. Related factors are perceived threat to survival, small acts of kindness from the captor, isolation from outside views, and a perceived lack of escape. It is not a formal diagnosis in DSM-5 or ICD, but it is widely discussed in psychology. Similar phenomena include the Patty Hearst case (1974) and, in the opposite direction, Lima Syndrome, where captors develop sympathy for hostages. Elimination: (a) describes the transition or reality shock of new management graduates, (b) describes culture shock or adjustment stress of migrants, and (c) describes withdrawal or rehabilitation issues. None of these involves bonding with a captor, so only (d) fits.
explanations: Wrong: new management graduates entering industry experience reality shock or adjustment stress, not captor bonding.
Wrong: rural-to-urban migrants experience culture shock or acculturative stress, which is unrelated to Stockholm Syndrome.
Wrong: drug addicts in rehabilitation face withdrawal, craving and relapse issues, not captor bonding.
Correct: hostages and kidnap victims develop positive feelings towards their captors, as in the 1973 Stockholm bank robbery.
keyfact: Stockholm Syndrome: hostages bond with captors, named after the 1973 Stockholm bank robbery.
option_notes: Young management graduates joining industry often face 'reality shock', a gap between classroom theory and workplace practice. Organisations handle it through induction, mentoring and management trainee programmes. The term 'reality shock' was popularised by Kramer in nursing studies. It is an organisational behaviour concept and is not called Stockholm Syndrome.

Migrants moving from villages to cities commonly experience culture shock, a term introduced by anthropologist Kalervo Oberg in 1954. Its stages are honeymoon, frustration or crisis, adjustment and acceptance. Urban stressors include housing, language, anonymity and job insecurity. This is acculturative stress, not Stockholm Syndrome.

Drug addicts in rehabilitation centres go through detoxification, withdrawal symptoms, counselling and relapse prevention. In India the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction and NDPS Act, 1985 are relevant. The key concepts are dependence, tolerance and withdrawal, not captor bonding.

Stockholm Syndrome is a psychological response in which captives bond with their captors. It was named after the Norrmalmstorg robbery of 1973 in Stockholm, and Nils Bejerot coined the term. The Patty Hearst case of 1974 is a famous example. It is not an official DSM diagnosis. Lima Syndrome is the reverse, with captors sympathising with hostages.
related: Stockholm Syndrome originated from the 1973 Norrmalmstorg bank robbery in Sweden.
Nils Bejerot coined the term.
Lima Syndrome is the reverse, in which captors sympathise with hostages.
Munchausen Syndrome is faking illness to gain attention.
Paris Syndrome affects tourists whose expectations of Paris are not met.
Culture shock was a term popularised by Kalervo Oberg in 1954.
Patty Hearst (1974) is a famous Stockholm Syndrome case in the US.
summary: The correct answer is (d). Stockholm Syndrome is a psychological response in which hostages or kidnap victims develop positive feelings, such as trust, sympathy or affection, towards their captors. It is named after the 1973 Norrmalmstorg bank robbery in Stockholm, Sweden.
topic_notes: Stockholm Syndrome belongs to general psychology and current-affairs vocabulary. It was named after the 23-28 August 1973 hostage crisis at Kreditbanken, Norrmalmstorg, Stockholm. Jan-Erik Olsson held four employees hostage. Afterwards the hostages defended their captors. The criminologist and psychiatrist Nils Bejerot coined the term 'Norrmalmstorg syndrome', later called Stockholm Syndrome. Typical conditions are a perceived threat to life, small kindnesses from the captor, isolation from other perspectives, and a perceived inability to escape. It is a coping or survival strategy, and it is not a formal diagnosis in DSM-5. Related ideas include the Patty Hearst case (1974), Lima Syndrome (Lima, Peru, 1996-97, Japanese embassy hostage crisis, where captors softened towards hostages), and Helsinki Syndrome as a term in some contexts. Other named syndromes UPSC likes to ask about include Munchausen Syndrome (faking illness for attention), Down Syndrome (trisomy 21), Imposter Syndrome (feeling like a fraud despite success), Peter Pan Syndrome (refusal to grow up), Jerusalem Syndrome (religious delusions during a visit to Jerusalem), Paris Syndrome (shock of Japanese tourists at Paris not matching expectations), Stendhal Syndrome (overwhelmed by art), and Diogenes Syndrome (extreme self-neglect and hoarding). Also remember culture shock (Oberg), reality shock, burnout (Freudenberger) and Hawthorne effect in organisational behaviour. In exams, match the syndrome with its definition, the person or place behind the name, and its year.

question:
Match List-I (Football World Cup/Year) with List-II (Host Country) and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists: List-I (Prominent Football Player) A. Michael Owen B. Luis Figo C. Gabriel Batistuta D. Raul Gonzalez List-II (Country)
1. Italy
2. Spain
3. Portugal
4. Argentina
5. England
6. Brazil Code: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a 'player and country' matching question. The heading mentions World Cup hosts, but the lists actually pair prominent footballers with their national teams, so the match is by nationality. Michael Owen was a Liverpool striker who scored a famous goal for England against Argentina at France 1998, and he later played for Real Madrid and Newcastle. Luis Figo was a Portuguese winger from the 'Golden Generation'. He won the FIFA World Player of the Year award in 2001 and the Ballon d'Or in 2000, and he moved from Barcelona to Real Madrid in 2000. Gabriel Batistuta ('Batigol') was Argentina's all-time leading scorer until Messi passed him. He scored in the 1994 and 1998 World Cups and starred for Fiorentina. Raul Gonzalez was Real Madrid's long-time captain and striker and played for Spain. Elimination: Owen as England (5) rules out (b) and (d), which give Brazil. Figo as Portugal (3) rules out (a). That leaves (c). Italy and Brazil are distractors, since none of the four players is from those countries.
explanations: Wrong: it pairs Figo with Spain (2) and Raul with Portugal (3). Figo is Portuguese and Raul is Spanish, so the two are swapped.
Wrong: it gives Owen as Brazil (6) and Batistuta as Italy (1). Owen is English and Batistuta is Argentine.
Right: Owen is England (5), Figo is Portugal (3), Batistuta is Argentina (4) and Raul is Spain (2).
Wrong: it gives Owen as Brazil (6), Figo as Spain (2), Batistuta as Italy (1) and Raul as Portugal (3). Every pairing is wrong.
keyfact: Owen is English, Figo is Portuguese, Batistuta is Argentine and Raul is Spanish, so the code is 5 3 4 2.
option_notes: Option (a) 5 2 4 3 gets Owen and Batistuta right but swaps Figo and Raul. It is a typical swap trap built on the fact that Portugal and Spain are neighbours on the Iberian Peninsula. Figo and Raul were rivals-turned-teammates at Real Madrid, which is why they are easily confused. Spain won the World Cup in 2010 and Portugal won Euro 2016.

Option (b) 6 3 1 2 pairs Owen with Brazil and Batistuta with Italy. Brazil has won 5 World Cups (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002). Italy has won 4 (1934, 1938, 1982, 2006). Batistuta played club football in Italy for Fiorentina and Roma but was never Italian. Owen is English.

Option (c) 5 3 4 2 is the correct code: England, Portugal, Argentina, Spain. England's only World Cup win was in 1966 on home soil. Argentina won in 1978, 1986 and 2022. Spain won in 2010. Portugal has never won the World Cup.

Option (d) 6 2 1 3 is wrong on all four pairings. It uses Brazil and Italy as distractors, since none of these four players is from either country. Brazil and Italy are the two most successful World Cup nations after Germany, which has 4 titles.
related: Luis Figo won the Ballon d'Or in 2000.
Brazil won the 2002 World Cup, hosted by Japan and South Korea.
Spain won the 2010 World Cup in South Africa.
Argentina won the World Cup in 1978, 1986 and 2022.
England's only World Cup win was in 1966.
FIFA is headquartered in Zurich and was founded in 1904.
The first World Cup was in 1930 in Uruguay.
statements: A — Correct: Michael Owen matches 5 (England). He was born in 1979 and came through at Liverpool. He burst onto the scene at the 1998 World Cup with a solo goal against Argentina. He won the Ballon d'Or in 2001 and later played for Real Madrid, Newcastle, Manchester United and Stoke. He scored 40 goals in 89 England appearances.

B — Correct: Luis Figo matches 3 (Portugal). Born in 1972, he played for Sporting CP, Barcelona, Real Madrid and Inter Milan. He won the Ballon d'Or in 2000 and FIFA World Player of the Year in 2001. His transfer from Barcelona to Real Madrid in 2000 was controversial. He captained Portugal at Euro 2004, where Portugal were runners-up.

C — Correct: Gabriel Batistuta matches 4 (Argentina). Born in 1969, he was nicknamed 'Batigol'. He starred for Fiorentina, then Roma, with whom he won Serie A in 2001. He scored 10 World Cup goals across 1994, 1998 and 2002 and was a Copa América winner in 1991 and 1993. He scored 54 goals for Argentina.

D — Correct: Raul Gonzalez matches 2 (Spain). Born in 1977, he was Real Madrid's captain and a one-club icon until 2010. He won several La Liga titles and three Champions League titles (1998, 2000, 2002). He scored 44 goals for Spain. He later played for Schalke 04, Al-Sadd and the New York Cosmos.
summary: The correct answer is (c). Michael Owen is English (5), Luis Figo is Portuguese (3), Gabriel Batistuta is Argentine (4) and Raul Gonzalez is Spanish (2), which gives the code 5 3 4 2.
topic_notes: This is a sports general-awareness question about players and nationalities. UPSC often asks about football stars, World Cup hosts and winners, and trophies. Key World Cup facts: the first tournament was in 1930 in Uruguay, which also won it. Brazil has 5 titles. Germany and Italy have 4 each. Argentina has 3 (1978, 1986, 2022). France has 2 (1998, 2018). Uruguay has 2 (1930, 1950). England (1966) and Spain (2010) have 1 each. The 2002 World Cup was co-hosted by Japan and South Korea and won by Brazil, with Ronaldo as top scorer. 2006 was in Germany, won by Italy. 2010 was in South Africa, the first in Africa, won by Spain. 2014 was in Brazil, won by Germany. 2018 was in Russia, won by France. 2022 was in Qatar, won by Argentina. 2026 will be hosted by the USA, Canada and Mexico. Other awards: the Golden Ball goes to the best player, the Golden Boot to the top scorer, and the Golden Glove to the best goalkeeper. Related players: Pele (Brazil), Maradona (Argentina), Zidane (France), Ronaldo Nazario (Brazil), Beckham (England), Messi (Argentina), Cristiano Ronaldo (Portugal). The Ballon d'Or was started in 1956 by France Football. FIFA was founded in 1904 and is headquartered in Zurich.

question:
Match List-I (City) with List-II (Establishment) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: List-I (City) A. Arkonnam B. Allahabad C. Kamptee D. Mhow List-II (Establishment)
1. Central Air Command HQ
2. Naval Air Base
3. Institute of Military Law
4. Coast Guard District HQ
5. College of Combat Code: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This question tests the locations of key defence establishments. Arakkonam in Tamil Nadu hosts INS Rajali, the Indian Navy's largest air station, commissioned in 1992. Allahabad (now Prayagraj) hosted the HQ of the IAF Central Air Command, which was set up in 1962 and moved there from Calcutta. Kamptee, near Nagpur, houses the Institute of Military Law, which trains Army, Navy and Air Force officers in military law. Mhow (Dr Ambedkar Nagar), Madhya Pradesh, is home to the Army War College, the College of Combat (now the Army War College), the Infantry School and the Military College of Telecommunication Engineering. Elimination: A is the Naval Air Base, so only (a) and (c) remain, since (b) and (d) give A as 3. B is Central Air Command HQ, which gives (c) and eliminates (a), where B is 5. Coast Guard District HQs are not at any of these cities in the list, so option 4 is a distractor. The answer is (c).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it matches Allahabad with College of Combat, but Allahabad hosts the Central Air Command HQ.
(b) Wrong: it matches Arakkonam with the Institute of Military Law, but Arakkonam is a Naval Air Base. It also gives Kamptee as Coast Guard HQ.
(c) Correct: Arakkonam-Naval Air Base, Allahabad-Central Air Command HQ, Kamptee-Institute of Military Law, Mhow-College of Combat.
(d) Wrong: A is not the Institute of Military Law, B is not the College of Combat, and C is not Coast Guard HQ.
keyfact: Arakkonam = Naval Air Base; Allahabad = Central Air Command; Kamptee = Institute of Military Law; Mhow = College of Combat.
option_notes: Matches A-2, B-5, C-3, D-1. It treats Allahabad as the College of Combat and Mhow as Central Air Command, both wrong. Central Air Command HQ is at Allahabad (Prayagraj), and the College of Combat is at Mhow. Remember the pairings by city, not by order.

Matches A-3, B-1, C-4, D-5. It makes Kamptee a Coast Guard district HQ, which is wrong. Coast Guard regional HQs are at Mumbai, Chennai, Gandhinagar, Kolkata and Port Blair, and the Coast Guard HQ is in New Delhi. Kamptee is a cantonment near Nagpur and houses the Institute of Military Law.

Matches A-2, B-1, C-3, D-5. It is the correct matching. INS Rajali is at Arakkonam, Central Air Command is at Allahabad, the Institute of Military Law is at Kamptee, and the College of Combat is at Mhow. All four pairings are consistent with the establishments' locations.
Matches A-3, B-5, C-4, D-1. All four pairings are wrong. Arakkonam is not the Institute of Military Law, and Mhow is not Central Air Command. It is a distractor built by shuffling the lists.
related: INS Rajali, Arakkonam, is the Navy's largest air station.
IAF Central Air Command HQ is at Prayagraj (Allahabad).
Institute of Military Law is at Kamptee near Nagpur.
Army War College is at Mhow (Dr Ambedkar Nagar).
NDA is at Khadakwasla, Pune; IMA is at Dehradun.
Indian Coast Guard HQ is in New Delhi; it was established in 1978.
IAF Maintenance Command HQ is at Nagpur.
summary: The correct option is (c): Arakkonam – Naval Air Base (INS Rajali); Allahabad – Central Air Command HQ (Indian Air Force); Kamptee – Institute of Military Law; Mhow – College of Combat. The matching is A-2, B-1, C-3, D-5.
topic_notes: Indian defence establishments are often asked as city-institution matches. Air Force commands: Western (New Delhi), Eastern (Shillong), Central (Allahabad/Prayagraj), Southern (Thiruvananthapuram), South Western (Gandhinagar), Training (Bengaluru), Maintenance (Nagpur). Navy commands: Western (Mumbai), Eastern (Visakhapatnam), Southern (Kochi, training). Army commands: Northern (Udhampur), Western (Chandimandir), South Western (Jaipur), Southern (Pune), Eastern (Kolkata), Central (Lucknow), ARTRAC (Shimla). Key institutions: National Defence Academy (Khadakwasla, Pune), Indian Military Academy (Dehradun), Officers Training Academy (Chennai), Defence Services Staff College (Wellington), National Defence College (New Delhi), Indian Naval Academy (Ezhimala), Air Force Academy (Dundigal, Hyderabad). Mhow hosts the Army War College, the Infantry School and the MCTE, and is the birthplace of Dr B R Ambedkar, hence its renamed form. Kamptee has a cantonment and the Institute of Military Law. INS Rajali at Arakkonam is the base for P-8I aircraft. Coast Guard was set up in 1978 and became statutory under the Coast Guard Act, 1978; its HQ is in New Delhi.

question:
Match List-I (Library) with List-II (City) and select the correct answer List-I (Library) A. National Library B. State Central Library C. Connemara Public Library List-II (City)
1. New Delhi
2. Kolkata
3. Mumbai
4. Chennai Code: A B C
subject: Insurance
detail: This is a simple fact-matching question on Indian libraries. The National Library of India is at Belvedere House, Alipore, Kolkata. It descends from the Imperial Library (1903), which grew out of the Calcutta Public Library (1836), and it was opened to the public in 1953 under the Imperial Library (Change of Name) Act. It is the largest library in India and a depository under the Delivery of Books and Newspapers (Public Libraries) Act, 1954. The Connemara Public Library, Egmore, Chennai, was founded in 1896 and named after Lord Connemara, the Governor of Madras. It is a repository of all books and periodicals published in India. The State Central Library in Mumbai is the Maharashtra State Central Library at Asiatic Society area (Town Hall/Fort), and the question treats it as Mumbai. Elimination logic: Connemara is certainly in Chennai, so options (a) and (b) are the only ones that pair C with 4, and the National Library being in Kolkata, not New Delhi, rules out (a). Only (b) fits. Options (c) and (d) pair Connemara with Mumbai, which is wrong.
explanations: Wrong: places the National Library in New Delhi. It is in Kolkata, although Delhi has the Delhi Public Library and other libraries.
Correct: A-2 Kolkata, B-3 Mumbai, C-4 Chennai. All three matches are right.
Wrong: puts the National Library in New Delhi and the State Central Library in Chennai and Connemara in Mumbai, so all three matches are wrong.
Wrong: the National Library match is right, but Connemara is in Chennai, not Mumbai, and the State Central Library is paired with Chennai instead of Mumbai.
keyfact: National Library - Kolkata; Connemara Library - Chennai; State Central Library - Mumbai (answer b: 2-3-4).
option_notes: Option (a) 1-3-4 pairs the National Library with New Delhi. The Delhi Public Library, started in 1951 as a UNESCO pilot project, is in Delhi, but the National Library is not. The other two matches (Mumbai for the State Central Library and Chennai for Connemara) are right, which makes this a tempting but wrong option.

Option (b) 2-3-4 is the correct combination. Kolkata houses the National Library of India at Belvedere Estate. Mumbai houses the Maharashtra State Central Library, and Chennai houses the Connemara Public Library, founded in 1896. Connemara became a National Depository Library in 1955.

Option (c) 1-4-3 is wrong on all counts. New Delhi does not house the National Library, which is in Kolkata. Chennai has the Connemara Library, not a State Central Library, in this question's matching. Mumbai is where the State Central Library is located.
Option (d) 2-4-3 gets Kolkata right for the National Library but swaps Mumbai and Chennai. Connemara is in Chennai, the capital of Tamil Nadu, and the library at Mumbai is the State Central Library.
related: National Library of India is at Belvedere Estate, Alipore, Kolkata.
Connemara Public Library (1896), Chennai, is a National Depository Library.
Delhi Public Library was set up in 1951 as a UNESCO pilot project.
S. R. Ranganathan is the Father of Library Science in India; his birthday, 12 August, is National Librarian's Day.
Raja Rammohun Roy Library Foundation was set up in 1972 in Kolkata.
Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Library is in Patna; Rampur Raza Library is in Rampur.
The Delivery of Books and Newspapers (Public Libraries) Act was passed in 1954.
summary: The correct answer is (b): National Library - Kolkata (2), State Central Library - Mumbai (3), Connemara Public Library - Chennai (4). The National Library of India is at Belvedere Estate, Kolkata, and the Connemara Public Library is one of the four National Depository Libraries, located in Chennai (Egmore).
topic_notes: Libraries in India: The National Library of India, Kolkata, is the largest library by volume. It was formed by merging the Imperial Library with the Calcutta Public Library (founded 1836 by Dwarkanath Tagore and others). Its first Librarian was Harinath De in the Imperial Library era. It operates under the Ministry of Culture. The Delivery of Books and Newspapers (Public Libraries) Act, 1954, requires publishers to deposit copies in four libraries: the National Library (Kolkata), the Connemara Public Library (Chennai), the Asiatic Society Library (Mumbai) and the Delhi Public Library. The Raja Rammohun Roy Library Foundation (RRRLF), Kolkata, was set up in 1972 to promote the public library movement. Other notable libraries: Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Public Library, Patna; Rampur Raza Library, Rampur; Saraswati Mahal Library, Thanjavur; Asiatic Society Library, Mumbai (Town Hall); Delhi Public Library, started in 1951 with UNESCO's help; Parliament Library, New Delhi; and Theosophical Society's Adyar Library, Chennai. The Library of Congress, Washington, D.C., is the largest library in the world, and the British Library in London is the national library of the UK. Ranganathan, the Father of Library Science in India, developed the Colon Classification and the Five Laws of Library Science (1931). National Library Day is observed on 12 August, on his birthday.

question: Crop Yield Formula on Unit which has developed sta s cal models to forecast crop yield works under the control of
options: Department of Agriculture and Co operation
Department of Food and Public Distribution
subject: Insurance
detail: Crop yield forecasting in India has two strands. The first is the statistical-weather model approach: regression and agro-meteorological models relate yield to weather parameters such as rainfall, temperature and humidity at different crop stages. This work is done by agrometeorology bodies, chiefly the India Meteorological Department (Ministry of Earth Sciences) through its Agricultural Meteorology Division at Pune, along with agricultural universities and ICAR institutes. The second strand is the official crop estimates compiled by the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES) in the Department of Agriculture and Cooperation, which depend on crop-cutting experiments, general crop estimation surveys and area statistics. Related bodies are FASAL (Forecasting Agricultural output using Space, Agro-meteorology and Land based observations), the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre, and CAPE. Elimination: the Ministry of Water Resources deals with irrigation and water, not forecasting yields. The Department of Food and Public Distribution handles procurement, storage and PDS. The Department of Agriculture and Cooperation produces estimates through sample surveys, not weather-based statistical models. That leaves the IMD as the best fit.
