explanations: Wrong: the Ministry of Water Resources handles water resources, irrigation and river management, and does not build crop yield models.
Wrong: this Department compiles crop estimates through crop-cutting surveys and area statistics. It is the user of forecasts, not the developer of weather-based statistical models.
Correct: the IMD's Agricultural Meteorology Division develops statistical crop-weather models used for yield forecasting.
Wrong: this Department deals with food grain procurement, storage, distribution and sugar and edible oil policy, and has no forecasting role.
keyfact: Weather-based statistical crop yield forecasting models are developed by the IMD's Agricultural Meteorology Division, Pune.
option_notes: The Ministry of Water Resources (now merged into the Ministry of Jal Shakti, 2019) covers irrigation policy, river basin management, the Central Water Commission and the Central Ground Water Board. It deals with water resource planning and disputes, not crop forecasting.

The Department of Agriculture and Cooperation (now the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare) in the Ministry of Agriculture runs crop schemes and policy. Its Directorate of Economics and Statistics releases advance and final crop estimates based on crop-cutting experiments.

The India Meteorological Department, founded in 1875 and headquartered in Delhi, is the national weather service. It now functions under the Ministry of Earth Sciences. Its Agrometeorology Division at Pune issues agromet advisories and develops crop-weather models.

The Department of Food and Public Distribution, under the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, manages the Food Corporation of India, the Public Distribution System, minimum support price procurement, and food storage and warehousing.
related: IMD was established in 1875 and is now under the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
IMD's agromet advisory service is Gramin Krishi Mausam Sewa (GKMS).
FASAL stands for Forecasting Agricultural output using Space, Agro-meteorology and Land based observations.
Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (MNCFC) is under the Ministry of Agriculture.
Crop-cutting experiments are the basis of official yield estimates and of PMFBY claims.
The Directorate of Economics and Statistics releases advance estimates of foodgrain production.
The Agriculture Census is conducted every five years.
summary: The answer is (c) India Meteorological Department. The Agricultural Meteorology Division of the IMD, Pune, has developed statistical crop-weather models and a crop yield forecasting approach. The 'Crop Yield Formula on Unit' is not an official key-verified name, so this answer is my best reasoning rather than a confirmed fact.
topic_notes: Agricultural statistics in India come from several sources. The Directorate of Economics and Statistics (Ministry of Agriculture) publishes land use statistics and crop estimates, and its reporting chain runs from states to the centre. Crop-cutting experiments under the General Crop Estimation Surveys (GCES) are the standard way to estimate yield. The National Sample Survey Office, now part of the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, supports the sample design. Weather-based forecasting uses regression of yield on weather variables, such as rainfall and temperature in critical crop stages. The IMD, set up in 1875, has its Agricultural Meteorology Division at Pune. It issues Gramin Krishi Mausam Sewa (GKMS) agromet advisories through Agromet Field Units. Remote sensing is used through the FASAL programme, and the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (MNCFC) uses satellite data. The Space Applications Centre (ISRO) developed the CAPE project (Crop Acreage and Production Estimation) and later projects. Other areas UPSC could ask about include the three advance estimates of foodgrain production, the Agricultural Census conducted every five years, the Price Policy role of CACP, the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, which uses crop-cutting experiments to assess yield losses, and the Kharif and Rabi crop seasons. The 2002 question wording is garbled, so treat the IMD answer as best-judgement.

question: East Timor, the latest independent na on in the world was ruled by
subject: Current Affairs
detail: East Timor occupies the eastern half of Timor island in Southeast Asia. It was a Portuguese colony for about 400 years. After Portugal's Carnation Revolution (1974) it withdrew, and Fretilin declared independence on 28 November 1975. Indonesia invaded on 7 December 1975 and formally annexed the territory in 1976 as its 27th province, a claim the UN never recognised. In the UN-organised referendum of 30 August 1999, about 78.5% voted against autonomy within Indonesia, which triggered violence by pro-Indonesia militias. The UN Security Council authorised the Australian-led INTERFET force, and UNTAET governed the territory from 1999 to 2002. Independence was restored on 20 May 2002, with Xanana Gusmao as the first President. The country is officially Timor-Leste, with Dili as its capital. It became the 191st UN member in 2002 and joined ASEAN as the 11th member in October 2025. Elimination: Australia, Malaysia and the Philippines never ruled East Timor. Australia only led the peacekeeping force in 1999.
explanations: Correct: Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975, annexed it in 1976 and ruled it until the 1999 referendum and the UN transition.
Wrong: Australia led the INTERFET peacekeeping force in 1999 but never ruled East Timor. It is also a party to the Timor Sea maritime dispute.
Wrong: Malaysia had no colonial or administrative control over East Timor.
Wrong: The Philippines never ruled East Timor. It was a Spanish and then US colony, and later a sovereign state.
keyfact: East Timor: Portuguese colony, annexed by Indonesia 1975-99, independent on 20 May 2002.
option_notes: Indonesia is the world's largest archipelagic state, with its capital at Jakarta (Nusantara is the planned new capital). It was a Dutch colony and became independent in 1945, with recognition in 1949. It annexed East Timor from 1975 to 1999. It is a member of ASEAN, the G20 and BRICS (since 2025).

Australia is a Commonwealth country and a continent-nation, with Canberra as its capital. It led the INTERFET force into East Timor in September 1999. It is a member of Quad, AUKUS and the Commonwealth. It has had a maritime boundary dispute with Timor-Leste over Timor Sea oil and gas, settled by a 2018 treaty.

Malaysia is a federal constitutional monarchy in Southeast Asia, with Kuala Lumpur as its capital. It was formed in 1963 and became independent from Britain in 1957 (Malaya). It is a founding member of ASEAN (1967). It has no historical link to East Timor's rule.

The Philippines is an archipelagic republic with Manila as its capital. It was a Spanish colony until 1898 and then a US colony, and became independent in 1946. It is a founding member of ASEAN (1967). It has never governed East Timor.
related: Timor-Leste became independent on 20 May 2002.
Indonesia invaded East Timor on 7 December 1975.
Referendum held 30 August 1999 with about 78.5% voting for independence.
UNTAET administered East Timor from 1999 to 2002.
Dili is the capital of Timor-Leste.
South Sudan (2011) is the newest UN member state.
Timor-Leste became ASEAN's 11th member in October 2025.
summary: The answer is (a) Indonesia. East Timor (Timor-Leste) was a Portuguese colony until 1975, was then invaded and annexed by Indonesia, and became independent on 20 May 2002 after a UN-supervised transition.
topic_notes: Timor-Leste is a small Southeast Asian nation on the eastern half of Timor island, plus the Oecusse enclave and the islands of Atauro and Jaco. The capital is Dili. Official languages are Tetum and Portuguese. Its currency is the US dollar. Portugal colonised it from the 16th century, while the western half went to the Dutch and later to Indonesia. After Portugal left in 1975, Indonesia invaded and annexed it in 1976, and the resistance was led by Fretilin and Falintil. The 1991 Santa Cruz massacre in Dili drew international attention. Bishop Carlos Belo and Jose Ramos-Horta won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1996. In 1999 the UN-run referendum (UNAMET) favoured independence. Violence followed, INTERFET intervened, and UNTAET administered the territory until 20 May 2002. Xanana Gusmao became the first President and Mari Alkatiri the first Prime Minister. It joined the UN in September 2002 and became ASEAN's 11th member in October 2025. Its economy depends on Timor Sea petroleum revenues held in a sovereign Petroleum Fund. Note that South Sudan (2011) is the world's newest country, so Timor-Leste was the newest only in 2002. Other UPSC angles include Kosovo (2008, partially recognised), Montenegro (2006) and Eritrea (1993).

question: What is the chronological sequence of the following developments?
options: National Film Archives of India : Pune
National Archives of India : New Delhi
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The four options are institution:headquarters pairs, so the only workable reading is to find the pair that is wrongly matched. The Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) was set up in 1948 under the Ministry of Mines and has its headquarters in Nagpur, Maharashtra, with regional offices in places such as Bangalore, Ajmer, Hyderabad, Kolkata and Dhanbad. Dhanbad is better known for the Indian School of Mines (now IIT-ISM), the Central Institute of Mining and Fuel Research (CIMFR) and the Bharat Coking Coal Ltd HQ, which is why it works as a trap. NALCO, a Navratna PSU founded in 1981, has its registered office in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, with its mines at Damanjodi and its smelter at Angul. The National Film Archive of India was set up in 1964 in Pune under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The National Archives of India is in New Delhi at Janpath, and it began in 1891 as the Imperial Record Department in Calcutta. Elimination: (a), (c) and (d) are all correct, which leaves (b) as the only wrong match. If the question really wanted a chronology, the order would be NAI (1891), IBM (1948), NFAI (1964), NALCO (1981), but this does not fit the four options.
explanations: (a) is wrong as the answer because NALCO really is headquartered at Bhubaneswar, so this is a correct pair.
(b) is the answer because the Indian Bureau of Mines is headquartered in Nagpur; Dhanbad is only the site of a regional office and of other mining institutions.
(c) is wrong as the answer because the National Film Archive of India is correctly placed at Pune.
(d) is wrong as the answer because the National Archives of India is correctly placed at New Delhi.
keyfact: Indian Bureau of Mines is at Nagpur (not Dhanbad); NALCO-Bhubaneswar, NFAI-Pune and NAI-New Delhi are correct.
option_notes: NALCO (National Aluminium Company Ltd) was established in 1981 and is a Navratna PSU under the Ministry of Mines. Its registered office is in Bhubaneswar, Odisha. Its bauxite mine and alumina refinery are at Damanjodi (Koraput), and its smelter and captive power plant are at Angul. It exports alumina and aluminium and sells in domestic markets. It is one of the largest integrated bauxite-alumina-aluminium complexes in Asia.

The Indian Bureau of Mines was set up in 1948 and is a subordinate office of the Ministry of Mines. It is headquartered in Nagpur, Maharashtra. Its role is to promote systematic and scientific mining, conserve minerals, and protect the mining environment. It keeps the National Mineral Inventory and mineral statistics and enforces the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules. Dhanbad hosts the Indian School of Mines (IIT-ISM) and CIMFR instead.

The National Film Archive of India was founded in 1964 in Pune under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. It stands near the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII). P.K. Nair was its celebrated curator and founder-director. It acquires, preserves and restores films, scripts, posters and songbooks. It has been part of the National Film Heritage Mission since 2016 and has been merged into NFDC.

The National Archives of India was founded on 11 March 1891 as the Imperial Record Department in Calcutta. It moved to New Delhi in the 1920s-30s after the capital shifted, and its Janpath building was designed by Lutyens. It holds public records, private papers, maps and treaties. It works under the Ministry of Culture and the Public Records Act, 1993, and its head is the Director General of Archives (also called Archivist of India).
related: IBM headquarters: Nagpur; established 1948.
Geological Survey of India: HQ Kolkata, established 1851.
Bharat Coking Coal Ltd HQ: Dhanbad.
NALCO: Navratna PSU, HQ Bhubaneswar, smelter at Angul.
NFAI (1964) and FTII are both in Pune.
National Archives of India: founded 1891 in Calcutta as the Imperial Record Department.
Hindustan Copper Ltd HQ: Kolkata.
Coal India Ltd HQ: Kolkata.
statements: a — Correct: NALCO is headquartered at Bhubaneswar. NALCO, the National Aluminium Company Ltd, was incorporated in 1981 as a PSU under the Ministry of Mines. It runs the Damanjodi bauxite mine in Koraput, an alumina refinery at Damanjodi, a smelter and captive power plant at Angul, and ports facilities at Visakhapatnam. It is a Navratna company and one of Asia's large integrated aluminium complexes, and it exports alumina and aluminium.

b — Incorrect: the Indian Bureau of Mines is headquartered in Nagpur, not Dhanbad. The IBM was established in 1948 and is a subordinate office of the Ministry of Mines. It promotes scientific mining and conservation of minerals and enforces the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules. It maintains the National Mineral Inventory and prepares mineral statistics. It has regional offices across India. Dhanbad is known for the ISM/IIT-ISM, CIMFR and BCCL, which causes the confusion.

c — Correct: the National Film Archive of India (NFAI) is in Pune. It was established in February 1964 under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and is on the Law College Road campus, adjacent to FTII. P.K. Nair was its famous curator and founder-director. It collects, preserves and restores Indian and foreign films, and its holdings include the surviving Raja Harishchandra fragments. It is now part of the National Film Heritage Mission.

d — Correct: the National Archives of India is in New Delhi. It was founded as the Imperial Record Department on 11 March 1891 in Calcutta and shifted to New Delhi after the capital moved in 1911. The present building at Janpath, designed by Edwin Lutyens, was completed in the late 1920s and early 1930s. It is the custodian of non-current government records, falls under the Ministry of Culture, and works under the Public Records Act, 1993.
summary: The stem as printed asks for a 'chronological sequence', but the options are institution:location pairs, so the OCR has probably garbled an 'incorrectly matched pair' question. Read that way, the answer is (b). The Indian Bureau of Mines is headquartered in Nagpur, not Dhanbad. The other three pairs are correct.
topic_notes: This is a 'location of institution' question, a common static-GK type. UPSC repeatedly asks for headquarters of national bodies, so the usual traps are cities that are famous for a related sector. The Ministry of Mines is the parent of NALCO, the Indian Bureau of Mines (Nagpur), the Geological Survey of India (Kolkata, founded 1851), Hindustan Copper (Kolkata) and the National Institute of Rock Mechanics (Bengaluru). Coal bodies include Coal India Ltd (Kolkata), Bharat Coking Coal Ltd (Dhanbad), Central Coalfields Ltd (Ranchi), Northern Coalfields Ltd (Singrauli) and Singareni Collieries (Kothagudum). Dhanbad also has IIT (ISM), CIMFR and the Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS). The cultural bodies fall under different ministries. The National Archives (New Delhi, 1891) and the Archaeological Survey of India (1861, Alexander Cunningham) fall under Culture. NFAI (Pune, 1964), FTII (Pune), Films Division (Mumbai), CBFC (Mumbai) and Doordarshan sit under I&B. Other institutions worth remembering are the National Museum (New Delhi), the Indian Museum (Kolkata, 1814), the National Library (Kolkata), Sangeet Natak Akademi, Sahitya Akademi and Lalit Kala Akademi (all New Delhi). Chronology matters too: IBM 1948, NFAI 1964, NALCO 1981 and NAI 1891.

question: Sagar Samrat' is the name of
options: a drilling ship in Bombay High
name of a 5-star hotel in Goa
subject: Computers
detail: Sagar Samrat is a self-propelled mobile offshore drilling unit owned by the Oil and Natural Gas Commission (now ONGC). It was built by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Japan, and commissioned in 1973. It drilled the discovery well in the Bombay High (Mumbai High) field, which lies about 160 km off the Mumbai coast in the Arabian Sea. Bombay High was discovered in 1974 and is India's most productive offshore field. Sagar Samrat is therefore an oil exploration platform, not a geographical place or a hotel. Elimination: Port Blair is in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and no island with this name is near it. The Maldives is an independent island nation southwest of India; Sagar Samrat is not an island there. 'Sagar Samrat' literally means 'Emperor of the Sea', which fits an offshore rig. A 5-star hotel in Goa is a distractor with no basis. Related ONGC assets worth knowing are Sagar Vikas, Sagar Bhushan, Sagar Pragati and Neelam. Also note ONGC was founded in 1956, and Bombay High was operated through platforms like Bombay High North and South.
explanations: Incorrect: No island near Port Blair is named Sagar Samrat. Islands there include Ross, Neil and Havelock.
Correct: Sagar Samrat is the ONGC offshore drilling rig used in the Bombay High field.
Incorrect: It is not an island, and the Maldives has no island by this name that is relevant here.
Incorrect: It is not a hotel in Goa; the name belongs to a drilling unit.
keyfact: Sagar Samrat = ONGC's offshore drilling rig at Bombay High.
option_notes: Port Blair is the capital of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, located on South Andaman Island. Nearby islands include Ross Island (now Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep), Viper Island, Neil (Shaheed Dweep) and Havelock (Swaraj Dweep). The Cellular Jail, built by the British in 1906, stands there. Sagar Samrat is not connected with this area.

Bombay High is an offshore oil and gas field in the Arabian Sea about 160 km west of Mumbai, discovered in 1974 and operated by ONGC. Sagar Samrat was the drilling unit used there, built in Japan and commissioned in 1973. It is the correct answer. Bombay High has long been India's largest oil-producing field, though its output has declined with age.

The Maldives is an island republic in the Indian Ocean southwest of India, with capital Malé. It consists of about 26 atolls and over 1,000 islands. It became independent from Britain in 1965. It is separated from India's Minicoy by the Eight Degree Channel. No island called Sagar Samrat is associated with it.

Goa is a state on India's west coast, with capital Panaji. It was liberated from Portuguese rule in December 1961 through Operation Vijay. It is known for tourism, with many luxury hotels and resorts at places like Calangute and Baga. Sagar Samrat is not a hotel name in this context and has no known link to Goa's tourism.
related: Sagar Samrat is an ONGC offshore drilling rig built in Japan.
Bombay High was discovered in 1974 and lies about 160 km off Mumbai.
ONGC was founded in 1956.
Digboi in Assam is India's oldest oil field, with oil found in 1889.
NELP was launched in 1999; HELP replaced it in 2016.
The Krishna-Godavari basin is a major east-coast hydrocarbon area.
Sagar Samrat means 'Emperor of the Sea'.
Oil India Limited was founded in 1959.
summary: The answer is (b). 'Sagar Samrat' is an ONGC offshore drilling rig (jack-up/drill ship) in the Bombay High oil field, off Mumbai's coast. It was India's first mobile offshore drilling unit, built in Japan, and began work in 1970s.
topic_notes: Offshore oil exploration in India is led by ONGC, established in 1956 as a commission and converted to a corporation in 1994. The Bombay High (Mumbai High) field was discovered in 1974 after seismic surveys, and Sagar Samrat was the pioneering drilling unit. Production began in 1976. It lies in the Arabian Sea on the continental shelf off Maharashtra and is India's biggest offshore field, with platforms such as Bombay High North and South. Other important areas are the Krishna-Godavari basin on the east coast, where Reliance's KG-D6 block is located. Cauvery basin, Cambay basin, Assam (Digboi, discovered 1889, India's oldest oil field) and Rajasthan's Barmer are also key. Drilling vessels and rigs are named with 'Sagar': Sagar Bhushan, Sagar Vikas, Sagar Gaurav, Sagar Kiran. The Neelam and Heera fields are also offshore, near Bombay High. Related institutions are Oil India Limited (founded 1959), GAIL, IOC (established 1959, Indian Oil), Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (1993), and the New Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP, 1999) and its successor HELP (2016). Terms to know: jack-up rig, semi-submersible, drill ship, FPSO. India's petroleum refining capacity and import dependence of over 80% are common questions. Also note the Mumbai High North platform fire in 2005, a major accident.

question: Which tourist des na on from amongst the following will be developed as an international des na on for tourism according to the Budget 2002-03?
subject: Computers
detail: The Union Budget 2002-03, presented by Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha on 28 February 2002, included tourism promotion measures. My recollection is that it named Hampi as a destination to be developed to international standards. I could not verify the exact budget wording from a source, so treat this as the best-supported choice rather than a certainty. Hampi in Karnataka was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire (14th-16th century) and sits on the Tungabhadra river. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986, and its main monuments are the Virupaksha Temple, Vittala Temple with its stone chariot, and the Lotus Mahal. Elimination logic: Port Blair is a gateway to the Andaman Islands and is mainly promoted for island and beach tourism. Pushkar in Rajasthan is known for its Brahma temple and the annual camel fair. Nalanda in Bihar is a Buddhist university site, part of the Buddhist circuit, and was inscribed as a World Heritage Site only in 2016. Among the options, Hampi is the one with the strongest international heritage profile at that time.
explanations: Port Blair: not the destination named in the budget for development as an international site; the Andamans are promoted under island tourism.
Hampi: correct. The Budget 2002-03 named Hampi for development as an international tourist destination, consistent with its World Heritage status.
Pushkar: a pilgrimage and fair town in Rajasthan, not the budget's named international destination.
Nalanda: an ancient Buddhist university site in Bihar, part of the Buddhist circuit, but not the one named in the budget.
keyfact: Budget 2002-03 named Hampi (Karnataka, UNESCO site since 1986) for development as an international tourist destination.
option_notes: Port Blair is the capital of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, on South Andaman. It has the Cellular Jail, built by the British between 1896 and 1906 and now a national memorial, and Veer Savarkar International Airport. It is also the base for Ross Island, Havelock and Neil Island. The city is named after Lt Archibald Blair, who surveyed the islands in 1789. Port Blair was renamed Sri Vijaya Puram in 2024.

Hampi is in Vijayanagara district, Karnataka, on the Tungabhadra river. It was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, founded in 1336 by Harihara I and Bukka I. Its monuments include the Virupaksha Temple, Vittala Temple, Hazara Rama Temple and Lotus Mahal. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986 and is also known as the Group of Monuments at Hampi. The Archaeological Survey of India and the Hampi World Heritage Area Management Authority manage the site.

Pushkar is in Ajmer district, Rajasthan, and has the Pushkar Lake and the rare Brahma Temple. The Pushkar Camel Fair is held every year around Kartik Purnima in October-November. It is one of the oldest Hindu pilgrimage towns and is among the five sacred dhams called Pancha Sarovar. The town draws many domestic and foreign tourists.

Nalanda is in Bihar, near Rajgir. It was a major Buddhist monastic university from the 5th century CE under the Gupta ruler Kumaragupta I, and it was destroyed around 1193 by Bakhtiyar Khilji. Xuanzang and Yijing studied there. The Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016. A new Nalanda University was established near the site under a 2010 Act.
related: Union Budget 2002-03 was presented by Yashwant Sinha on 28 February 2002.
Hampi became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
Hampi was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire on the Tungabhadra river.
ITDC was established in 1966.
The Incredible India campaign was launched in 2002.
Nalanda was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2016.
Port Blair was renamed Sri Vijaya Puram in 2024.
Swadesh Darshan scheme was launched in 2014-15.
summary: The answer is (b) Hampi. The Union Budget 2002-03 (presented by Yashwant Sinha) announced that Hampi, along with a few other sites, would be developed as an international tourist destination. The reason is Hampi's UNESCO World Heritage status and the Vijayanagara heritage that gives it global appeal.
topic_notes: Tourism in India has been supported through budget announcements, the Ministry of Tourism (formed as a separate ministry in 1999 from the earlier combined portfolio) and the India Tourism Development Corporation (ITDC, set up in 1966). The National Tourism Policy was announced in 2002, and the Incredible India campaign was launched in 2002. Tourism budgets often single out heritage sites, circuits and infrastructure such as airports and roads. Karnataka's Hampi is a World Heritage Site (1986), with the Group of Monuments at Pattadakal (1987) as another in the state. Related schemes include Swadesh Darshan (2014-15, theme-based circuits), PRASHAD (pilgrimage rejuvenation) and the Adarsh Smarak scheme. Key heritage tourism categories include Buddhist, Jain, Ramayana and Spiritual circuits. UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India number over 40, and recent additions include Dholavira (2021) and Santiniketan (2023). Other angles UPSC could ask: the difference between pilgrimage sites and heritage sites; the ASI and its role (founded 1861 by Alexander Cunningham); the Ministry of Tourism's rankings and the Travel & Tourism Development Index; visa facilitation such as e-Visa (launched in 2014); and the contribution of tourism to GDP and foreign exchange earnings. For budget-based questions, remember that the 2002-03 Budget was presented by Yashwant Sinha, who held the Finance portfolio in the NDA government under Atal Bihari Vajpayee.

question: Shri Rajender Singh won the Ramon Magsaysay Award for
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Rajendra Singh (born 1959, Uttar Pradesh) is an Ayurveda-trained activist who moved to Alwar district, Rajasthan, in 1975 and joined Tarun Bharat Sangh (TBS), founded in 1975. From the mid-1980s he promoted johads (earthen check dams) and other traditional rainwater-harvesting structures in villages, which recharged groundwater and revived dry rivers such as the Arvari, and later Ruparel, Sarsa, Bhagani and Jahajwali. He received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2001 in the category of Community Leadership, and later the Stockholm Water Prize in 2015. The Ramon Magsaysay Award, set up in 1957 in memory of the Philippine President Ramon Magsaysay, is often called Asia's Nobel Prize. Categories (until 2008) were Government Service; Public Service; Community Leadership; Journalism, Literature and Creative Communication Arts; Peace and International Understanding; and Emergent Leadership (added 2001). Elimination: Emergent Leadership is for younger leaders (40 or under) and was new in 2001, illiteracy eradication and biotechnology are not award categories and not connected with his work. Hence (b).
explanations: Incorrect: Emergent Leadership was introduced in 2001 for leaders aged 40 or under, but it was not Rajendra Singh's category; he received Community Leadership.
Correct: Rajendra Singh won the 2001 Ramon Magsaysay Award for Community Leadership, for water harvesting and community-based revival of rivers and groundwater in Alwar.
Incorrect: His work was about water conservation, not literacy. Illiteracy eradication is not a Magsaysay category.
Incorrect: Biotechnology is not a Magsaysay category and has no link to his work.
keyfact: Rajendra Singh, Waterman of India (Tarun Bharat Sangh, Alwar), won the 2001 Magsaysay Award for Community Leadership.
option_notes: Emergent Leadership: a Ramon Magsaysay Award category created in 2001 to recognise individuals aged 40 or under who are leading to address social issues in their communities. It was later discontinued as a separate category, as the award was restructured after 2008. It is distinct from Community Leadership, which Rajendra Singh won.

Community Leadership: a Ramon Magsaysay Award category honouring grassroots, community-based initiatives for social good. Indian winners include Rajendra Singh (2001), Arvind Kejriwal (2006, Emergent Leadership), and Pradip Kumar Tamta, among others in similar fields. Rajendra Singh's johad-based water conservation in Alwar through Tarun Bharat Sangh earned him this award in 2001.

Illiteracy eradication: not an award category. Literacy work is generally honoured under categories such as Public Service or Community Leadership. In India, literacy is promoted through the National Literacy Mission (1988) and Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (2001). It has no link with Rajendra Singh.

Biotechnology: not a Magsaysay category. Science honours in India include the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize, and biotechnology is overseen by the Department of Biotechnology (set up 1986) under the Ministry of Science and Technology. It is unrelated to Rajendra Singh's work.
related: Ramon Magsaysay Award was established in 1957 and is called Asia's Nobel Prize.
Rajendra Singh is called the Waterman of India and heads Tarun Bharat Sangh, Alwar.
Rajendra Singh won the Stockholm Water Prize in 2015.
Arvind Kejriwal won the 2006 Magsaysay Award for Emergent Leadership.
Johads are small earthen check dams used for rainwater harvesting in Rajasthan.
Vinoba Bhave was the first Indian Magsaysay awardee, in 1958.
Ravish Kumar won the 2019 Magsaysay Award for journalism.
summary: The answer is (b) Community leadership. Rajendra Singh, the 'Waterman of India', won the 2001 Ramon Magsaysay Award for Community Leadership for reviving traditional water-harvesting structures (johads) in Alwar, Rajasthan, through Tarun Bharat Sangh.
topic_notes: The Ramon Magsaysay Award was established in 1957 by the Rockefeller Brothers Fund and the Philippine government in memory of President Ramon Magsaysay, who died in a plane crash in 1957. It is given to Asians for outstanding service and is often called the Nobel Prize of Asia. It is administered by the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation in Manila. Before 2009 its categories were Government Service; Public Service; Community Leadership; Journalism, Literature and Creative Communication Arts; Peace and International Understanding; and Emergent Leadership (from 2001). Since 2009, awards have been given without fixed categories. Rajendra Singh (b. 1959) was trained in Ayurveda, joined Tarun Bharat Sangh in Alwar, and promoted johads, small earthen check dams, that recharge groundwater. His work revived the Arvari river and others, and the Arvari River Parliament was set up for community governance of water. He is known as the Waterman of India and received the Stockholm Water Prize in 2015. Other Indian awardees: Vinoba Bhave (1958), Mother Teresa (1962, Peace and International Understanding), Verghese Kurien (1963), Satyajit Ray (1967), M.S. Subbulakshmi (1974), Baba Amte (1985), Kiran Bedi (1994), Arvind Kejriwal (2006), Ravish Kumar (2019), Bezwada Wilson (2016), T.M. Krishna (2016), and Sonam Wangchuk (2018). Related water ideas include the Jal Shakti Abhiyan, Atal Bhujal Yojana, and Jal Jeevan Mission.

question: Which among the following became the ﬁrst woman Prime Minister in the world?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Sirimavo Ratwatte Dias Bandaranaike took office on 21 July 1960 after her husband, S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike, was assassinated in 1959. She led the Sri Lanka Freedom Party (SLFP) to victory in the July 1960 general election. She served three terms: 1960-65, 1970-77 and 1994-2000. Her first term made her the world's first woman Prime Minister. Indira Gandhi became India's PM in January 1966, which is six years later. Margaret Thatcher became UK PM in May 1979 and was the first woman PM of the UK and of any major Western democracy. Kim Campbell became Canada's first woman PM in June 1993 and held office only a few months. Elimination is by date: 1960 comes before 1966, 1979 and 1993. In 1972 she also oversaw the change of the country's name from Ceylon to Sri Lanka, with a republican constitution. Her daughter Chandrika Kumaratunga later became President (1994-2005).
explanations: Incorrect: Indira Gandhi became India's PM in January 1966, after Sirimavo Bandaranaike's 1960 start. She was India's first and so far only woman PM.
Incorrect: Kim Campbell became Canada's first woman PM in June 1993, which is far later. She served only until November 1993.
Incorrect: Thatcher became PM of the UK in 1979, nearly two decades after 1960. She was the first woman PM of the UK.
Correct: Sirimavo Bandaranaike became PM of Ceylon on 21 July 1960, the first woman anywhere to head a government.
keyfact: World's first woman PM: Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Ceylon, 21 July 1960.
option_notes: Indira Gandhi (1917-1984) was India's PM in 1966-77 and 1980-84. She was daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru. Key events include bank nationalisation (1969), the 1971 Bangladesh war, the Emergency (1975-77) and Operation Blue Star (1984). She was assassinated on 31 October 1984 and awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1971.

Kim Campbell (born 1947) was Canada's 19th PM from June to November 1993. She led the Progressive Conservative Party and succeeded Brian Mulroney. Her party was heavily defeated in the 1993 election, and she lost her own seat. She was Canada's first woman PM and first woman Minister of Defence.

Margaret Thatcher (1925-2013), the 'Iron Lady', was UK PM from 1979 to 1990, the longest continuous tenure in the 20th century. She led the Conservative Party. Her tenure saw the Falklands War (1982), privatisation, and conflict with trade unions. She resigned in November 1990 after a leadership challenge.

Sirimavo Bandaranaike (1916-2000) was PM of Ceylon/Sri Lanka in 1960-65, 1970-77 and 1994-2000. She was the world's first woman PM. Her party was the SLFP. She nationalised key sectors and introduced the 1972 republican constitution, renaming the country Sri Lanka. Her daughter Chandrika Kumaratunga later became President.
related: Sirimavo Bandaranaike became PM on 21 July 1960.
Indira Gandhi became India's first woman PM in January 1966.
Golda Meir was Israel's PM from 1969 to 1974.
Margaret Thatcher was UK PM from 1979 to 1990.
Benazir Bhutto was the first woman PM of a Muslim-majority country (1988).
Sucheta Kripalani was India's first woman Chief Minister (UP, 1963).
Pratibha Patil was India's first woman President (2007).
summary: The answer is (d) Sirimavo Bandaranaike. She became Prime Minister of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) on 21 July 1960, making her the world's first elected woman head of government.
topic_notes: Women heads of government and state are a recurring topic in general awareness. The first woman PM in the world was Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Ceylon in 1960. Indira Gandhi followed in India in 1966, and Golda Meir became Israel's PM in 1969. Isabel Perón of Argentina was the first woman President, in 1974, though she came to office as vice-president. Vigdís Finnbogadóttir of Iceland was the first woman directly elected president in 1980. Margaret Thatcher served as UK PM in 1979-90, and Theresa May and Liz Truss later held the office. Benazir Bhutto became the first woman PM of a Muslim-majority country (Pakistan) in 1988. Other notable leaders include Angela Merkel, German Chancellor in 2005-2021, and Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, who became Africa's first elected woman head of state (Liberia) in 2006. Jacinda Ardern of New Zealand (2017-2023) gave birth while in office. In India, Pratibha Patil was the first woman President (2007-12), Droupadi Murmu is the second (2022), and Sarojini Naidu was the first woman Governor. Sucheta Kripalani was India's first woman Chief Minister (Uttar Pradesh, 1963). Sri Lanka also had the world's first mother-daughter pair of heads of government and state, Sirimavo and Chandrika.

question: Who among the following wrote the book Algebra of Inﬁnite Jus ce?
subject: Computers
detail: Arundhati Roy, born 1961 in Shillong, won the Booker Prize in 1997 for her debut novel 'The God of Small Things'. After that she turned largely to non-fiction and activism. 'The Algebra of Infinite Justice' (2001) gathers essays including 'The End of Imagination' (on India's 1998 nuclear tests), 'The Greater Common Good' (on the Narmada dams) and the title essay, first published in The Guardian after the 11 September 2001 attacks. The title refers to the US operation originally called 'Infinite Justice', later renamed 'Enduring Freedom'. Elimination: Anita Desai is known for 'Clear Light of Day', 'In Custody' and 'Fire on the Mountain'. Vikram Seth wrote 'A Suitable Boy', 'The Golden Gate' and 'An Equal Music'. Rohinton Mistry, an Indian-born Canadian, wrote 'Such a Long Journey', 'A Fine Balance' and 'Family Matters'. None of these three wrote this essay collection, so only Roy fits.
explanations: Anita Desai is wrong: she is a novelist known for 'Clear Light of Day', 'In Custody' and 'The Village by the Sea', not this essay collection.
Vikram Seth is wrong: he is known for 'A Suitable Boy' and 'The Golden Gate', and has no link to this book.
Arundhati Roy is correct: she wrote 'The Algebra of Infinite Justice' (2001), a collection of political essays.
Rohinton Mistry is wrong: he wrote 'A Fine Balance' and 'Such a Long Journey', which are novels.
keyfact: 'The Algebra of Infinite Justice' (2001) is a collection of essays by Arundhati Roy.
option_notes: Anita Desai (b. 1937) is an Indian novelist and a Sahitya Akademi winner for 'Fire on the Mountain' (1978). She was shortlisted for the Booker three times, for 'Clear Light of Day', 'In Custody' and 'Fasting, Feasting'. Her daughter Kiran Desai won the Booker in 2006 for 'The Inheritance of Loss'. She received the Padma Bhushan in 2014.

Vikram Seth (b. 1952) is an Indian poet and novelist. His works include 'The Golden Gate' (a verse novel, 1986), 'A Suitable Boy' (1993), 'An Equal Music' (1999) and 'Two Lives'. He also wrote the travel book 'From Heaven Lake'. He received the Padma Shri in 2007 and the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1994.

Arundhati Roy (b. 1961) is an author and activist. She won the Booker Prize in 1997 for 'The God of Small Things'. Her later works include 'The Algebra of Infinite Justice' (2001), 'Listening to Grasshoppers', 'Walking with the Comrades' and the novel 'The Ministry of Utmost Happiness' (2017). She is associated with the Narmada Bachao Andolan. She earlier won the National Film Award for the screenplay of 'In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones'.

Rohinton Mistry (b. 1952) is an Indian-born Canadian writer of Parsi origin. His works include 'Tales from Firozsha Baag', 'Such a Long Journey' (1991, which won the Commonwealth Writers' Prize), 'A Fine Balance' (1995) and 'Family Matters' (2002). He was shortlisted for the Booker Prize three times. He lives in Canada.

summary: The answer is (c). 'Algebra of Infinite Justice' (2001) is a collection of essays by Arundhati Roy (the option's 'Arundha' is an OCR slip), written on politics, globalisation, dams, nuclear weapons and the post-9/11 world.
topic_notes:
Arundhati Roy won the 1997 Booker Prize for 'The God of Small Things', set in Ayemenem, Kerala; she was the first Indian woman to win it. Her non-fiction includes 'The Algebra of Infinite Justice' (2001), 'The Cost of Living' (1999, on dams and nuclear tests), 'Power Politics', 'An Ordinary Person's Guide to Empire', 'Broken Republic', 'Capitalism: A Ghost Story' and 'Azadi'. She won the Sydney Peace Prize in 2004 and returned her Sahitya Akademi Award in 2015, which she had received for 'In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones'. She is a prominent critic of large dams, the nuclear programme and US foreign policy.

Other Indian Booker winners: Salman Rushdie ('Midnight's Children', 1981), Arundhati Roy (1997), Kiran Desai (2006), Aravind Adiga ('The White Tiger', 2008) and V. S. Naipaul (Indian-origin, 1971). Geetanjali Shree won the International Booker in 2022 for 'Tomb of Sand'. Related Indian writers and works: Amitav Ghosh ('The Shadow Lines', Jnanpith 2018), Jhumpa Lahiri ('Interpreter of Maladies', Pulitzer 2000) and Vikram Seth ('A Suitable Boy'). In exams, questions are usually of the form 'author and book' pairs, so learn the notable works of each major author together with the awards they won.

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. The demand for commodi es having a large number of close subs tutes is less elas c than the commodi es having a smaller number of substitutes
2. Luxury items have a highly elas c demand
3. The commodi es whose consumption cannot easily be postponed have less elas c demand Which of these statements is/are correct?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. Its main determinants are: (1) availability of substitutes, where more and closer substitutes make demand more elastic because consumers switch easily when the price rises (e.g. one brand of tea versus tea in general); (2) nature of the good, where necessities (salt, medicines, food grains) are inelastic and luxuries (cars, jewellery, air-conditioners) are elastic; (3) postponability, where goods whose consumption can be delayed have elastic demand and urgent goods that cannot be delayed have inelastic demand; (4) proportion of income spent, where a larger share makes demand more elastic; (5) time period, where demand is more elastic in the long run; (6) habits, where addictive goods are inelastic; and (7) the breadth of the definition of the good, where a narrowly defined good is more elastic. Elimination: statement 1 reverses the substitute rule, so any option containing 1 (a, c, d) is wrong. Only (b) is left, and it agrees with statements 2 and 3.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect: many close substitutes make demand more elastic, and statements 2 and 3 are also correct, so 1 alone cannot be the answer.
(b) is right because statement 2 (luxuries are elastic) and statement 3 (non-postponable goods are inelastic) are both correct, and statement 1 is wrong.
(c) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is false, and leaves out statement 3, which is true.
(d) is wrong because statement 1 is false, so not all three can be correct.
keyfact: More substitutes, luxuries and postponable goods mean elastic demand; necessities and urgent goods mean inelastic demand.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would be right only if substitutes lowered elasticity. In fact more substitutes raise elasticity. Remember that substitute availability is the most important determinant of PED. Perfect substitutes give infinitely elastic demand for a single seller's product under perfect competition, so the firm's demand curve is horizontal.

Option (b), '2 and 3 only', is the correct choice. Luxuries are elastic, and urgent, non-postponable goods are inelastic. Other factors that affect PED are the share of income spent, the time horizon, habit and the width of the good's definition.

Option (c), '1 and 2', pairs a wrong statement with a right one. Its error is the claim about substitutes. It also omits the postponability rule, which is a standard determinant of PED in Indian textbooks.

Option (d), 'all three', is a trap for students who accept every statement. Check each carefully. Statement 1 has the relationship reversed: the substitutes rule is a direct relationship with elasticity, not an inverse one.
related: Necessities have inelastic demand (PED < 1); luxuries have elastic demand (PED > 1).
More close substitutes means more elastic demand.
Demand for salt is highly inelastic because it is a small share of income and has no close substitute.
Cross elasticity is positive for substitutes and negative for complements.
Alfred Marshall introduced the concept of price elasticity of demand.
Perfectly inelastic demand has a vertical demand curve, with Ed = 0.
Governments levy heavy taxes on inelastic goods such as petrol and tobacco to raise revenue.
Straight-line demand curve: elasticity is 1 at the midpoint.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: a large number of close substitutes makes demand MORE elastic, not less. Substitutes are goods that satisfy the same want, such as tea and coffee or Pepsi and Coke. If a good's price rises, buyers shift to the substitute, so quantity demanded falls sharply. A good with few or no substitutes (salt, life-saving drugs) has inelastic demand. Cross elasticity of demand is positive for substitutes. A narrowly defined product (a particular brand) has more substitutes than a broad category (cold drinks) and so is more elastic.

2 — Correct: luxury items have highly elastic demand. They are not essential, so consumers can cut consumption or do without them when prices rise. Their income elasticity is also greater than 1. Examples are cars, jewellery, foreign holidays and air-conditioners. Necessities have PED below 1, and comforts are in between. Giffen goods and some prestige or Veblen goods are exceptions to the usual downward-sloping demand pattern.

3 — Correct: goods whose consumption cannot easily be postponed, such as urgent medicines, food and fuel for daily needs, have less elastic (inelastic) demand. The consumer must buy them whatever the price. Goods that can be deferred, such as furniture, clothes and consumer durables, have more elastic demand because purchase can wait for a price fall. Urgency and necessity are therefore linked to low elasticity.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is wrong. Demand is MORE elastic when a commodity has many close substitutes, luxuries have elastic demand, and goods whose consumption cannot be postponed (necessities) have inelastic demand.
topic_notes: Price elasticity of demand is defined as Ed = (%ΔQ)/(%ΔP). Its types are perfectly elastic (infinity), elastic (>1), unitary (=1), inelastic (<1) and perfectly inelastic (=0). The total expenditure method says that when demand is elastic, a price fall raises total expenditure. When demand is inelastic, a price fall lowers total expenditure. Measurement methods are the total outlay method, the proportionate or percentage method, and the point and arc methods. For a straight-line demand curve, elasticity is higher at the upper points and lower at the lower points, and it equals 1 at the midpoint. The determinants are: availability of substitutes, nature of the good (necessity, comfort or luxury), postponability, proportion of income spent, time period, habit, number of uses, and the price level. Other related concepts are income elasticity (positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods, above 1 for luxuries), cross elasticity (positive for substitutes, negative for complements, zero for unrelated goods) and advertising elasticity. Taxation links to elasticity because governments earn more revenue by taxing goods with inelastic demand, such as petrol, tobacco and liquor. The incidence of a tax falls more on the side of the market that is less elastic. Farmers' income can fall in a bumper harvest because demand for food grains is inelastic. Giffen goods are inferior goods for which demand rises as price rises. Sir Robert Giffen was linked to the observation, and Alfred Marshall popularised the elasticity concept.

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. Launching of Fourth ﬁve-year plan was postponed and three annual plans had to be resorted to between 1966 to 1969.
2. Fi h ﬁve-year plan was terminated a year earlier.
3. Eighth ﬁve-year plan commenced in 1992 instead of 1990. Which of these statements is/are correct?
subject: Computers
detail: Indian planning began in 1951. The Third Plan (1961-66) failed due to the 1962 Sino-Indian war, the 1965 Indo-Pak war and two severe droughts in 1965-66. The Fourth Plan was postponed, and three Annual Plans (1966-67, 1967-68, 1968-69) were run during the 'Plan Holiday'. The Fourth Plan then ran from 1969 to 1974 under Gandhian-style stress on growth with stability and 'growth with justice'. The Fifth Plan (1974-79), with 'Garibi Hatao' and Removal of Poverty as objectives, was terminated in March 1978, a year early, by the Janata Party Government, which introduced the Rolling Plan (1978-83) under the Sixth Plan. The Rolling Plan was itself discarded in 1980 and the Sixth Plan ran 1980-85. The Seventh Plan ended in March 1990. Because of rapid changes at the Centre (the V.P. Singh and Chandra Shekhar governments), the Eighth Plan could not start on 1 April 1990. Annual Plans were followed for 1990-91 and 1991-92, and the Eighth Plan ran 1992-97 under P.V. Narasimha Rao, with the new economic policy and human development as the central focus. Since all three statements match this record, option (d) is right and the others fail by wrongly excluding a true statement.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it leaves out statement 1, which is true: the Plan Holiday of 1966-69 is well established.
(b) is wrong because it leaves out statement 3, which is also true: the Eighth Plan began in 1992.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out statement 2: the Fifth Plan was terminated in 1978, a year early.
(d) is right because all three statements match the planning history of India.
keyfact: Plan Holiday 1966-69; Fifth Plan ended 1978; Eighth Plan began 1992 after Annual Plans 1990-92.
option_notes: Options 2 and 3: Fifth Plan terminated early in 1978 and Eighth Plan delayed to 1992. Both are true, but this option wrongly omits the Plan Holiday of 1966-69. The Fifth Plan (1974-79) was ended by the Janata Government. The Eighth Plan (1992-97) was launched under Narasimha Rao, with the new economic policy at its core.

Options 1 and 2: Plan Holiday (1966-69) and early end of the Fifth Plan (1978). Both are true, but the option omits the delayed Eighth Plan. The Plan Holiday followed the wars and droughts, with three Annual Plans. The Fifth Plan was cut short by the Janata Government, which brought in the Rolling Plan.

Options 1 and 3: Plan Holiday and the delayed Eighth Plan. Both are true, but the option leaves out the early termination of the Fifth Plan. The Third Plan failed in 1966, which led to three Annual Plans, and political uncertainty led to Annual Plans in 1990-92 before the Eighth Plan began in 1992.

Options 1, 2 and 3: all statements are true. This reflects the main disruptions to India's Five-Year Plan sequence: the Plan Holiday 1966-69, the early end of the Fifth Plan in 1978, and the Annual Plans of 1990-92. It is the correct answer and a standard fact for planning questions.
related: Plan Holiday: 1966-69 with three Annual Plans
Fourth Plan ran 1969-74
Fifth Plan was terminated in 1978 by the Janata Government
Rolling Plan concept was supported by Gunnar Myrdal
Eighth Plan covered 1992-97 under P.V. Narasimha Rao
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015
Twelfth Plan (2012-17) was the last Five-Year Plan
statements: 1 — Correct: The Fourth Plan was delayed and Annual Plans were run from 1966 to 1969. The Plan Holiday followed the wars of 1962 and 1965, the droughts of 1965-66, rupee devaluation in June 1966, and inflation. The three Annual Plans maintained continuity of schemes, with agriculture and the Green Revolution strategy given priority. The Fourth Plan began on 1 April 1969, drafted by Ashok Mehta and later D.R. Gadgil, and ran to 1974. Its two main aims were growth with stability and progressive self-reliance. Its targets were missed because of the Bangladesh war and refugee burden in 1971.

2 — Correct: The Fifth Plan was meant to run from 1974 to 1979 and was terminated in 1978. The Janata Party Government under Morarji Desai came to power in 1977 and ended the plan a year early. It was replaced by the Rolling Plan (1978-80), whose idea was proposed by Gunnar Myrdal. The Fifth Plan was drafted by D.P. Dhar and stressed removal of poverty (Garibi Hatao) and self-reliance. The Minimum Needs Programme was introduced in this plan. It was also the first plan with a major emphasis on the poor.

3 — Correct: The Eighth Plan started in 1992 instead of 1990. The Seventh Plan ended in 1990, but political instability at the Centre and the economic crisis of 1991 meant that two Annual Plans (1990-91 and 1991-92) were run. The Eighth Plan ran 1992-97 and was launched under P.V. Narasimha Rao, with Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister. Its focus was human development, employment, population control, literacy and infrastructure. It marked the shift to indicative planning and market-oriented reforms. Targeted growth was 5.6 percent, and the actual achieved was about 6.8 percent.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. The Fourth Plan was delayed to 1969 after the 1962 China war, 1965 Pakistan war, droughts and devaluation, so three Annual Plans covered 1966-69. The Fifth Plan (1974-79) was ended in 1978 by the Janata Government, and the Eighth Plan began in 1992 because of political instability and the 1990-92 Annual Plans.
topic_notes: Planning in India began in 1951 with the First Plan (1951-56), based on the Harrod-Domar model and focused on agriculture and irrigation. The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950 by a Cabinet resolution, and the National Development Council in 1952. The Second Plan (1956-61), the Mahalanobis model, stressed heavy industry. The Third Plan (1961-66) aimed at a self-reliant, self-generating economy but failed. The Plan Holiday (1966-69) had three Annual Plans. The Fourth Plan (1969-74) targeted growth with stability. The Fifth Plan (1974-79) was cut short in 1978. The Rolling Plan ran 1978-80. The Sixth Plan (1980-85) targeted poverty alleviation, and IRDP and NREP were launched. The Seventh Plan (1985-90) emphasised food, work and productivity. Annual Plans ran 1990-92. The Eighth Plan (1992-97) was the first in the liberalisation era, and growth was 6.8 percent. The Ninth (1997-2002) was growth with social justice and equity. The Tenth (2002-07) aimed at 8 percent growth. The Eleventh (2007-12) stressed inclusive growth, and the Twelfth (2012-17) targeted faster, more inclusive and sustainable growth. The NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015. The Twelfth Plan was the last. Related angles: the Bombay Plan of 1944, the People's Plan by M.N. Roy, the Gandhian Plan by S.N. Agarwal, and the Sarvodaya Plan by Jayaprakash Narayan. Plan Holiday periods and early terminations are frequently tested.

question: Assertion (A): Macro-economic deals with the study of aggregates and averages. Reason (R): Central problem of macro-economics is the determination of income and employment Codes:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Macroeconomics (the term was popularised by Ragnar Frisch in 1933) studies the economy as a whole. It deals with aggregates such as national income, total savings and investment, aggregate demand and supply, total employment, and with averages such as the general price level, the interest rate and the average wage. Keynes's General Theory (1936) made income and employment determination the core of macroeconomics, built on the principle of effective demand, which is why it is called the theory of income and employment. Microeconomics, in contrast, deals with individual units: consumer, firm, a single price, and the central problem there is price determination (hence 'price theory'). For Assertion-Reason questions, first test A and R separately, then ask whether R causes or explains A. A describes the method and scope (aggregation). R describes the central problem or subject matter. Both are valid descriptions of macroeconomics, but R is not the reason A holds. Aggregates are studied because macro looks at the economy as a whole, not because income and employment are the central problem. Hence (b). Option (a) is the tempting trap. Options (c) and (d) fail because both statements are true.
explanations: Wrong: both statements are true, but R does not explain why macroeconomics deals with aggregates and averages. R states the central problem, which is a separate fact.
Right: A is true because macroeconomics studies aggregates and averages. R is true because income and employment determination is its central problem. R is not the explanation of A.
Wrong: R is not false. The Keynesian theory of income and employment is central to macroeconomics.
Wrong: A is not false. Aggregates (national income, total output) and averages (price level) are the subject matter of macroeconomics.
keyfact: Macroeconomics studies aggregates and averages, and its central problem is the determination of income and employment (Keynes, 1936).
option_notes: Option (a) is the 'both true and R explains A' pattern. It is correct only when R is the actual cause or justification of A. Here that link is missing. Such a pairing would apply to a case like 'Demand curves slope downward because of diminishing marginal utility'.

Option (b) is the 'both true but R is not the correct explanation' pattern. It applies when the two statements are each valid but are independent facts, as in this question: scope of macro (aggregates) versus its central problem (income and employment).

Option (c) is the 'A true, R false' pattern. It would apply if R were incorrect, for example if it named price determination as the central problem of macroeconomics, which is actually the central problem of microeconomics.

Option (d) is the 'A false, R true' pattern. It would apply if A were wrong, for example if it said macroeconomics studies individual units like a single firm. That description fits microeconomics, not macroeconomics.
related: Ragnar Frisch coined the terms 'micro' and 'macro' economics in 1933.
Keynes's General Theory was published in 1936.
The central problem of microeconomics is price determination.
Say's Law: supply creates its own demand (classical view).
Paradox of thrift is a macroeconomic concept.
Macroeconomics is also called income and employment theory.
summary: The answer is (b). Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. Macroeconomics does study aggregates and averages (total output, general price level, total employment), and its central problem is the determination of national income and employment. R describes the main problem studied, not the reason the subject deals with aggregates.
topic_notes: Economics is divided into microeconomics and macroeconomics, terms popularised by Ragnar Frisch (1933). Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, including national income, aggregate demand and supply, general price level, inflation, unemployment, money supply, interest rates, the balance of payments, economic growth and fiscal and monetary policy. Its central problem is the determination of the level of national income and employment. Keynes's General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936) founded modern macroeconomics, emphasising effective demand, the multiplier, the consumption function, the marginal efficiency of capital and liquidity preference. The classical school, with Say's Law ('supply creates its own demand'), assumed full employment; Keynes rejected this and advocated government intervention during depressions. Microeconomics studies individual consumers, firms and markets; its central problem is price determination and resource allocation (price theory). Related concepts: the paradox of thrift (a macro phenomenon, where saving is a virtue for the individual but a vice for the economy), the fallacy of composition, and the interdependence of micro and macro. Macro tools include GDP, GNP, NNP and the price indices WPI and CPI. Schools beyond Keynes: monetarism (Milton Friedman), new classical economics (Lucas), and new Keynesian thought. Common exam angles include identifying whether an issue is micro or macro, such as inflation (macro) versus the price of wheat (micro), and the Keynesian versus classical views on employment and the role of the state.

question: S₁: We Indians by nature are extremely emotional. S6: What must be appreciated is that none of the members of the Indian team has reacted to this mind game u erance of Hayden. P: Had the political par es in India not been busy in ﬁgh ng among themselves, they would have asked the Central Government to refuse visa to Hayden. Q: Sta s cians are working over me to prove how our players have not been selﬁsh. R: Suddenly Hayden has become a villain. S: Without realizing Hayden's intent in calling subcontinent players selﬁsh, we have reacted angrily. The correct sequence should be:
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a sentence-rearrangement (para-jumble) item. The method is to find the opening link, then the logical chain, then the link into the closing sentence. S1 says Indians are extremely emotional, so the next sentence should give an example of emotional behaviour. S fits: 'we have reacted angrily' without understanding Hayden's intent in calling subcontinent players selfish. Q follows, because it explains the hidden intent: statisticians are working to disprove the selfishness charge. R then shows the result, that 'suddenly' Hayden has become a villain. P extends the over-reaction: even political parties would have demanded that his visa be refused had they not been squabbling. S6 then contrasts with all of this, saying 'What must be appreciated is that none of the team reacted'. Elimination: R cannot come first because 'suddenly' needs prior context and S1 is about emotion. In (a), P comes before R, but P ('would have asked to refuse visa') presupposes that Hayden is already seen as a villain. In (d), R opens the passage and breaks the link with S1.
explanations: Wrong. P (political parties wanting a visa refusal) presupposes Hayden is already a villain, which R establishes later. Ending on Q also fits S6 poorly.
Wrong. R, with 'Suddenly', cannot directly follow S1, which is about emotional nature. It needs the angry reaction (S) as context first.
Correct. S gives the emotional reaction, Q the statisticians' defence, R the sudden villain image, and P the political over-reaction. S6 then contrasts with these by praising the team's restraint.
Wrong. R cannot open after S1, and P before S breaks the cause-effect order. S, which explains the angry reaction, should come first.
keyfact: Correct sequence is S-Q-R-P: angry reaction, statisticians' defence, sudden villain image, political over-reaction, then S6.
option_notes: S-P-R-Q: this ordering places the political parties' hypothetical demand for a visa refusal before Hayden is called a villain. That inverts cause and effect. It does begin correctly with S, but the middle and end are illogical. It is a typical distractor that gets the first sentence right and the rest wrong.

R-Q-S-P: this starts with 'Suddenly Hayden has become a villain', which has no antecedent. S1's emotional theme is not picked up, and Q before S puts the defence before the accusation. Para-jumble distractors often start with a sentence containing a sudden-change word, so check that such a sentence has context before it.

S-Q-R-P: this is the correct chain. The angry reaction (S) leads to the statisticians' counter-evidence (Q). The sudden villain image (R) follows, then the political parties' hypothetical demand (P). The passage closes with S6, which contrasts the team's restraint with that over-reaction. The chain moves from the general emotional nature to specific examples, then to the contrast.

R-P-S-Q: this opens with R, which lacks context after S1. P follows R plausibly, but S, which explains the origin of the angry reaction, then arrives late. Q ends the chain, but the link to S6 ('none of the team reacted') is weaker than from P. It is a plausible-looking but incorrect arrangement.
related: Para-jumble: first find the opening sentence, then the connectors.
'Suddenly' and 'however' need prior context, so they rarely open a sequence.
Pronouns like 'this' and 'they' point back to an antecedent in an earlier sentence.
Sledging means verbally pressuring opponents in cricket, also called a 'mind game'.
'Had + subject + past participle... would have' is an inverted third conditional.
Contrast or appreciation statements often close a para-jumble.
Option elimination on the first two sentences saves time.
summary: The correct sequence is S-Q-R-P, option (c). S continues the idea of Indians being emotional, with an angry reaction to Hayden. Q, R and P then build up the over-reaction, and P leads naturally into S6, which says the Indian team did not react.
topic_notes: Sentence rearrangement (para-jumble) questions in UPSC EPFO English test coherence. Steps: (1) Find the opening sentence, one that introduces the topic and has no pronouns or connectors needing a prior reference. When S1 is fixed, find what naturally follows it. (2) Look for the closing sentence, which is often a conclusion or contrast; here S6 is given. (3) Identify pronoun-antecedent links such as 'this', 'they', 'it'. (4) Watch for connectors: 'suddenly', 'however', 'therefore', 'but', 'also', 'had... would have'. (5) Follow chronological or cause-and-effect order. (6) Use elimination: test the options' first or last pairs rather than every permutation. Here the first pair after S1 is the key. The theme is the Matthew Hayden remark calling subcontinent players selfish, to which Indians reacted emotionally, while the team itself stayed calm. The 'mind games' idea comes from sledging in cricket, where psychological pressure is used on opponents. The same skills help in related English questions such as error spotting, sentence improvement, one-word substitution, idioms and phrases, and comprehension passages. Practice tip: read the sentences aloud in the proposed order; if a connector like 'suddenly' appears without prior context, the sequence is wrong. Conditional sentences ('Had... would have') usually come after the situation they refer to has been set up. Contrast markers like 'What must be appreciated is that...' usually conclude a passage after a negative picture.

question: S1: In the roll call of human history, the sleepy capital town of Madhya Pradesh is indelibly linked with one of the world's worst man-made catastrophes. S6: Industries across the globe became less complacent and began ghtening their safety protocols. P: More than 2, 000 died instantly. Q: On the night of December 3, 1984, a poisonous grey cloud spread out from the Union Carbide Plant in Bhopal, suﬀoca ng more than three lakhs of its unsuspecting residents. R: The disaster shook the world, especially when hindsight revealed that almost all safety regulations had been ﬂouted by the plant. S: The rest were doomed to wheeze, hobble and gasp their way through life, their organs "eaten up by the deadly combina on of gases that leaked out of the plant. The correct sequence should be
subject: Computers
detail: This is a para-jumble (sentence rearrangement) question with fixed first and last sentences. S1 introduces Bhopal as linked to a man-made catastrophe. The next sentence must name the event, and Q does this: it gives the date, the Union Carbide plant and the gas cloud affecting three lakh people. P follows naturally because 'More than 2,000 died instantly' refers to the people suffocated in Q. S then says 'The rest were doomed...', which only makes sense after P, since 'the rest' means the survivors not counted among the 2,000 dead. R comes last before S6: the disaster 'shook the world' and hindsight showed safety rules were flouted, which leads to S6, where industries became less complacent and tightened safety protocols. Elimination: options (b) and (d) begin with S, but 'The rest' cannot open the sequence. Option (a) puts S after R and leaves P last, which separates 'the rest' from the deaths it refers to and breaks the link to S6. Key tools are chronology, pronoun and reference words ('the rest', 'the disaster'), and the cause-then-effect flow.
explanations: Wrong: Q-R-S-P places P, the 2,000 deaths, at the end, so 'the rest' in S has no antecedent, and the closing sentence does not lead into S6.
Wrong: S cannot come first because 'The rest' needs an earlier mention of the dead. It also leaves Q, the event itself, until after the deaths.
Correct: Q names the event, P gives the immediate deaths, S covers the survivors ('the rest'), and R gives the world's reaction that leads into S6.
Wrong: S opens the sequence without any antecedent, and R ('the disaster') appears before the disaster is described in Q.
keyfact: Para-jumble: event (Q) then immediate deaths (P) then 'the rest' (S) then world reaction (R): Q-P-S-R.
option_notes: Q-R-S-P: This order would start with the gas leak and then move to the global reaction. It fails because P (the instant deaths) must come directly before S (the rest). Remember that 'the rest' needs a prior number or group to refer to. The Bhopal gas tragedy occurred on the night of 2-3 December 1984, with the leak of methyl isocyanate (MIC) from the Union Carbide India Limited pesticide plant.

S-P-Q-R: This order begins with the survivors and then gives the deaths and the event. It is illogical because the event (Q) has to be introduced first. Bhopal is the capital of Madhya Pradesh. The plant was owned by Union Carbide India Ltd, a subsidiary of the US firm Union Carbide Corporation. Warren Anderson was its chairman at the time.

Q-P-S-R: This is the correct order. It runs from event to immediate deaths, then survivors' suffering, then the global reaction. The tragedy led to the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and the Public Liability Insurance Act 1991. The 1989 settlement with Union Carbide was for 470 million US dollars.

S-R-Q-P: This order begins with the survivors and the reaction before the event is described. It is wrong because Q must precede both. The Bhopal tragedy is often cited as the world's worst industrial disaster, and it prompted worldwide reviews of chemical plant safety and community right-to-know laws.

Bhopal gas tragedy facts: it occurred on the night of 2-3 December 1984 at the Union Carbide India Limited pesticide plant in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. The gas was methyl isocyanate (MIC). Official immediate deaths were about 2,000-3,800, and later estimates run much higher, with hundreds of thousands affected. Legal and policy aftermath: the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act 1985; the 1989 settlement of 470 million US dollars between the Government of India and Union Carbide; the Environment (Protection) Act 1986; the Public Liability Insurance Act 1991; the National Environment Tribunal Act 1995; the National Green Tribunal Act 2010; and the Factories Act amendment of 1987, which added provisions on hazardous processes. Para-jumble (sentence rearrangement) questions are common in the APFC English section. A reliable method has five steps. First, identify the opening sentence, which is usually a general statement or the one that introduces the subject. Second, look for pronouns, connectors such as 'And', 'But' and 'Thus', and repeated phrases such as 'From...to', which tie sentences together. The passage here is about Operation Flood, also called the White Revolution, which has several facts worth knowing. It was launched on 13 January 1970 by the NDDB, which was set up in 1965 and is headquartered at Anand, Gujarat. Verghese Kurien was its architect, and the Amul cooperative, founded in 1946 at Anand, was its model. The programme was funded through food aid from the EEC and the World Bank. detail: This is a sentence-rearrangement question. The fixed frame is 'revealed that the Government would initiate a dialogue...', so the fragment that completes 'initiate a dialogue' must come first. That fragment is R. Next, 'dialogue' takes the preposition 'with', so Q ('with political parties, industry and other bodies') follows directly. The clause 'on how best the private sector could fulfil' (S) comes after the dialogue's participants. It needs an object, and the only fragment that can serve as one is P ('Tribes'). Strategy: find the sentence's fixed start, match verb-preposition pairs ('dialogue with', 'fulfil' plus object), and place the object or noun at the end.

Option (b) R-Q-S-P gives 'would initiate a dialogue with political parties, industry and other bodies on how best the private sector could fulfil ... Tribes'. It is the correct sequence. It follows the pattern verb + object + 'with' + participants + 'on' + topic. The verb 'fulfil' takes the final fragment as its object.

Option (c) S-Q-R-P begins with S, 'on how best the private sector could fulfil', then runs 'with political parties...' and 'initiate a dialogue' before ending on 'Tribes'. 'Tribes' is wrongly placed after 'dialogue', and 'fulfil' is followed by a preposition phrase instead of an object. detail: This is a sentence-rearrangement (para-jumble) item. The parts are P 'War minus shooting but there was nothing to suggest any', Q 'was how cricket between India and Pakistan', R 'increase of animosity between the players or the spectators', and S 'was visualised before the first ball was bowled'. The method is to find the opening part, then link the parts by grammar. P ends with the word 'any', which must be followed by a noun phrase. R, 'increase of animosity...', is the only part that completes 'any increase of animosity between the players or the spectators', so P-R must be adjacent. That removes (b) and (d), which do not begin with P. Q 'was how cricket between India and Pakistan' needs a subject before it, and R's phrase can serve as that link. S 'was visualised before the first ball was bowled' then completes the passive 'cricket... was visualised'. Option (c) has P-S-Q-R, which breaks 'any' from 'increase' and places 'was visualised' before the noun it describes. Option (a) therefore gives the intended sense: before the match the contest was imagined as war without shooting, yet nothing suggested a rise in hostility. Always look for fixed collocations such as 'any + increase' and for verb-subject links.
explanations: Correct. P-R-Q-S keeps 'any increase of animosity' together and ends with 'was visualised before the first ball was bowled', so the sentence is coherent.
Wrong. It begins with R, 'increase of animosity...', which has no opening clause to attach to, and the 'any... increase' link is broken.
Wrong. P-S-Q-R separates 'any' from 'increase of animosity', and 'was visualised' would come right after a clause that cannot take it. The result is ungrammatical.
Wrong. It starts with Q, 'was how cricket...', which has no subject, and it places R after R-less P in an illogical way, so the sentence does not hold together.
keyfact: In a para-jumble, 'any' must be followed by its noun phrase: any + increase of animosity (P-R-Q-S).
option_notes: P-R-Q-S: This is the sequence that forms a complete, meaningful sentence. 'any' leads into 'increase of animosity', and 'was how cricket... was visualised' ends the thought. In para-jumble questions, the correct option is the one whose adjacent pairs are linked by grammar.
Q-S-P-R: This order starts with a predicate fragment and has no subject. It would also place 'was visualised' ahead of the clause it should follow. It is wrong.
P-S-Q-R: This order starts correctly with P but then jumps to S, so 'any' is left without its noun. 'Increase of animosity' ends up as a dangling phrase at the finish. It is wrong.
Q-R-P-S: This order starts with Q, a verb phrase, and has no subject. It breaks the P-R link needed for 'any increase', so it is wrong.

topic_notes: Sentence rearrangement (para-jumble) is a regular part of the General English section of the EPFO papers. A reliable approach has five steps. First, identify the opening sentence or clause. It usually introduces the subject and does not begin with a pronoun, a conjunction, or a verb fragment. Second, look for fixed pairs: determiner plus noun ('any' plus 'increase'), preposition plus object, or a verb that needs its subject. Third, find the closing part, which often completes the main verb or carries a concluding phrase. Fourth, use the options to eliminate. Check each option's first part against your opening and discard the ones that fail, then test the remaining orders by reading them aloud. Fifth, check logic and tense consistency. A pronoun must follow the noun it replaces, and a time marker such as 'before the first ball was bowled' qualifies the verb 'visualised'. Typical traps are options that differ only in the order of the middle parts, so always test the adjacency of the middle parts. The same passage-based set also appeared with comprehension questions. detail: This is a sentence-rearrangement question. The opening phrase 'The advent' needs 'of satellite television was a silent' (Q) to complete the subject and verb. question: What is the reason that ﬁsh can survive in the oceans?
options: Ice ﬂoats on the surface of the oceans
Evaporation and condensa on create a water cycle
