Members are chosen from territorial constituencies, which are delimited by the Delimitation Commission. The 42nd and 84th Amendments froze the seat allocation based on the 1971 Census until after the first Census following 2026. Smaller States such as Sikkim, Mizoram and Goa have fewer than 60 members under special provisions. Uttar Pradesh has the highest strength at 403, and Puducherry and Delhi have Assemblies under separate provisions.

2 — Correct: Article 171(1) limits the Legislative Council to one-third of the Assembly's total strength and sets a floor of 40 members. Councils are indirectly elected and partly nominated: one-third by local bodies, one-third by MLAs, one-twelfth by graduates, one-twelfth by teachers, and one-sixth nominated by the Governor. Article 169 lets Parliament create or abolish a Council if the Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority. The Council is a permanent house, and one-third of its members retire every two years. Currently Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh have Councils. Jammu and Kashmir's Council was abolished in 2019.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Article 170 fixes the Legislative Assembly strength at not more than 500 and not less than 60 members, and Article 171 caps the Council at one-third of the Assembly strength with a minimum of 40.
topic_notes: State legislatures are covered in Part VI of the Constitution, Articles 168 to 212. Article 168 provides that every State has a Legislature consisting of the Governor and the Assembly, plus a Council in some States. Article 169 allows creation or abolition of a Council: the Assembly passes a resolution by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting, and Parliament then passes a law by simple majority. This is not treated as a constitutional amendment under Article 368. Article 170 sets Assembly strength at 60 to 500, with one member nominated by the Governor from the Anglo-Indian community (this was removed by the 104th Amendment in 2020). Article 171 sets the Council's size and composition. Article 172 gives the Assembly a five-year term, which can be extended during a national emergency by Parliament for one year at a time. The Council is not subject to dissolution. Article 173 covers qualifications: Indian citizen, minimum age 25 for Assembly and 30 for Council. Articles 174 to 177 deal with sessions, dissolution and the Governor's address. Article 178 provides for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, and Article 182 for the Council's Chairman and Deputy Chairman. The Council can only delay a Money Bill for 14 days, and for ordinary bills it can delay by three months the first time and one month the second time. Under the 7th Amendment, the Council's size was fixed, with a floor of 40. States with Councils: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra and Karnataka. Related issues: delimitation under Article 82 and 170, and the 2002 Delimitation Act.

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are two States with maximum popula on of the Scheduled Castes.
2. Punjab has the highest ra o of the Scheduled Caste popula on to its total population.
3. There was a provision for set ng up a National Commission for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes under the Article 338 of the Cons tu on of India. However, by a Cons tu onal Amendment Act, separate National Commission for the Scheduled Castes and National Commission for the Scheduled Tribes have been set up. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Scheduled Caste data comes from the Census. By absolute SC population, Uttar Pradesh is first (about 35.1 million in 2001 and 41.4 million in 2011). West Bengal is second (18.4 million in 2001 and 21.5 million in 2011). Bihar is third in 2001 (13.0 million), and in 2011 it is third (16.5 million) with Tamil Nadu close behind (14.4 million). So 'UP and Bihar' is not the correct pair. By proportion, Punjab leads with 28.9% in 2001 and 31.9% in 2011, followed by Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal. Constitutionally, the original Article 338 provided a Special Officer for SCs and STs. The 65th Amendment (1990) created a joint National Commission for SCs and STs under Article 338. The 89th Amendment Act, 2003 (in force 2004) split it: Article 338 now covers the National Commission for Scheduled Castes, and the new Article 338A covers the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes. Elimination: statement 1 is false, which removes (b) and (d). Statements 2 and 3 are both true, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong: statement 2 is correct, but statement 3 is also correct, so '2 only' is incomplete.
Wrong: statement 1 is false because West Bengal, not Bihar, has the second-largest SC population.
Right: statements 2 (Punjab has the highest SC ratio) and 3 (the 89th Amendment created separate commissions) are both correct.
Wrong: statement 1 is false, so this pairing fails even though statement 3 is correct.
keyfact: Punjab has the highest SC share; UP is first and West Bengal second by SC numbers; the 89th Amendment (2003) split the SC/ST commission into Article 338 (NCSC) and Article 338A (NCST).
option_notes: Option (a), '2 only', is the statement that Punjab has the highest SC share (28.9% in 2001, 31.9% in 2011). That claim is true, but the option leaves out the true statement 3 on the commissions. Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal are the next highest by share. Uttar Pradesh is highest by absolute number. This option is a partial-truth distractor.

Option (b), '1 and 2', would require UP and Bihar to be the top two by SC population, which is false. West Bengal ranks second, and Bihar ranks third. The option does pair this with the correct claim about Punjab. UP has about 41.4 million SCs and West Bengal about 21.5 million (Census 2011). The all-India SC population is about 201 million, or 16.6%.

Option (c), '2 and 3', is the correct answer. Punjab has the highest SC proportion, and the 89th Amendment Act (2003) split the joint SC/ST commission. Article 338 now covers the NCSC, and Article 338A covers the NCST. The separate commissions started functioning in 2004. Their members are appointed by the President under warrant and seal.

Option (d), '1 and 3', correctly includes the true statement on the commissions but wrongly includes statement 1. Bihar is not among the top two states by SC population. West Bengal is second. Tamil Nadu overtook it in some rankings for 2011 and stands close to Bihar. The 89th Amendment is the correct basis for statement 3.
related: Article 341 deals with the list of Scheduled Castes; Article 342 with Scheduled Tribes.
The 89th Amendment Act, 2003 split the joint commission into the NCSC and NCST.
Article 338 covers the NCSC; Article 338A covers the NCST; Article 338B covers the NCBC.
The 102nd Amendment (2018) gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes.
Punjab has the highest percentage of SCs (31.9% in 2011); Uttar Pradesh has the highest number.
The SC population was 16.6% of India in Census 2011, about 201 million.
The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was enacted in 1989.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability; the Protection of Civil Rights Act came in 1955.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Uttar Pradesh is first, but the second-largest SC population is in West Bengal, not Bihar. Census 2011 figures are UP 41.4 million, West Bengal 21.5 million, Bihar 16.5 million and Tamil Nadu 14.4 million. Together UP and West Bengal hold a large share of India's roughly 201 million SCs, who are 16.6% of the population in 2011. Bihar ranks third in 2001 and 2011, with Tamil Nadu close behind in 2011. Lists of SCs are notified by the President under Article 341.

2 — Correct: Punjab has the highest proportion of SCs in its population, 28.9% in 2001 and 31.9% in 2011. Himachal Pradesh (about 25%) and West Bengal (about 23.5%) come next. Some states and UTs, such as Nagaland, Mizoram, Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar, and Meghalaya, have no notified SC population. The SC share is lowest in the north-eastern states. Punjab's SCs include communities such as Mazhabi Sikhs, Ravidasias and Balmikis.

3 — Correct: Article 338 originally provided for a Special Officer for SCs and STs. The 65th Amendment (1990) replaced this with a joint National Commission for SCs and STs. The 89th Amendment Act, 2003 split it into the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (Article 338) and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A). The separate commissions took effect in 2004. Each has a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson and three members, appointed by the President. They investigate safeguards, inquire into complaints and advise on planning. The 2018 102nd Amendment gave constitutional status to the NCBC (Article 338B).
summary: The answer is (c), statements 2 and 3 only. Punjab has the highest share of Scheduled Castes in its population, and the 89th Constitutional Amendment (2003) split the joint commission into separate SC and ST commissions. Statement 1 is wrong because West Bengal, not Bihar, has the second-largest SC population.
topic_notes: Scheduled Castes are communities notified under Article 341 by the President (and by Parliament for changes). Article 342 does the same for Scheduled Tribes. The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950 is the first notification. Census 2011 counts about 201.4 million SCs, which is 16.6% of the population. The largest SC populations are in Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Bihar, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. The highest SC shares are in Punjab (31.9%), Himachal Pradesh (25.2%), West Bengal (23.5%) and Uttar Pradesh (20.7%). Constitutional safeguards include Article 15(4) on special provisions, Article 16(4) and 16(4A) on reservation in jobs and promotion, Article 17 abolishing untouchability, Article 46 as a Directive Principle, Articles 330 and 332 on reserved seats in the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabhas, and Article 243D on Panchayats. The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 provide legal protection. The commission history is as follows. Under the original Article 338 there was a Special Officer (the Commissioner for SCs and STs). The 65th Amendment (1990) created a joint National Commission. The 89th Amendment (2003) split it into the NCSC (Article 338) and the NCST (Article 338A). The 102nd Amendment (2018) gave the NCBC constitutional status under Article 338B. The 123rd Bill had been proposed for this. The NCSC has a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson and three members, with a three-year term under the rules. The commissions have the powers of a civil court when inquiring into complaints. The reports of the commissions are laid before Parliament and the State Legislatures. Other related bodies include the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis and the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. An amendment of the Cons tu on of India can be initiated by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in Lok Sabha only.
2. A Bill providing for the formation of new States and for the altera on of boundaries or names of exis ng States in India can be introduced in the Parliament only on the recommendation of the President of India.
3. In India, a Bill seeking to amend the representation of States in Parliament has to be passed by a simple majority of both Houses of Parliament. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 368 lets a constitutional amendment Bill be introduced in either House of Parliament, not Lok Sabha only, and no prior presidential permission is needed. Article 3 says a Bill for forming new States or altering areas, boundaries or names of States can be introduced only on the President's recommendation, and the President must refer it to the concerned State Legislature for its views, which are not binding. Under Article 4, such laws are not treated as amendments under Article 368 and need only a simple majority. The representation of States in Parliament is different: it falls under Article 368(2) proviso (d), which needs a special majority (majority of the total membership plus two-thirds of members present and voting) in each House, plus ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures. So statement 3 is false. Elimination: statement 1 is false, which removes (a), (c) and (d), leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is false because an amendment Bill can start in either House, and statement 3 is also false.
Correct: only statement 2 is true, as Article 3 requires the President's recommendation for such a Bill.
Wrong: statements 1 and 3 are both false. Statement 1 ignores Rajya Sabha, and statement 3 ignores the special majority and State ratification needed.
Wrong: statements 1 and 3 are false, so the combination fails.
keyfact: Article 3 Bills need the President's recommendation and a simple majority, while changes to State representation in Parliament need a special majority plus ratification by half the States.
option_notes: Option (a), statements 1 and 2: it pairs the false Lok Sabha-only claim with the true Article 3 statement. A constitutional amendment Bill can be introduced in either House. A candidate who recalls the Article 3 rule but confuses the Article 368 procedure would choose this.

Option (b), 2 only: this is the correct answer. Article 3 requires the President's recommendation, and the State Legislature's views are only advisory. A simple majority passes the Bill under Article 4, and it is not treated as an Article 368 amendment. Such Bills can start in either House, and only the President's recommendation is mandatory.

Option (c), statements 1 and 3: it combines two false statements. Statement 3 wrongly assumes simple-majority passage for changes to State representation in Parliament, which actually needs a special majority plus ratification by half the States. It does not match any true reading of Article 368.

Option (d), all three: it would hold only if the amendment procedure were Lok Sabha-only and simple-majority. Article 368 contradicts both claims. The Constitution has three types of amendment: simple majority, special majority, and special majority with ratification by half the States.
related: Article 368 gives Parliament power to amend the Constitution; Part XX is titled 'Amendment of the Constitution'.
Article 3 Bills need the President's recommendation, and the State Legislature's views are not binding.
Under Article 4, laws under Articles 2 and 3 are not Article 368 amendments.
Ratification by half the State Legislatures is required for federal provisions.
The 24th Amendment (1971) made presidential assent compulsory for amendment Bills.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic structure doctrine.
The Constitution has no provision for a joint sitting on a constitutional amendment Bill.
The 7th Amendment (1956) implemented the States Reorganisation Act.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Article 368 allows an amendment Bill to be introduced in either House. Facts: the procedure is in Part XX. The Bill needs a special majority in each House, and ratification by half the States for federal provisions. The President must give assent and has no veto after the 24th Amendment (1971). There is no joint sitting for a constitutional amendment Bill, so a deadlock means the Bill fails. Prior permission of the President is not required, and a State Legislature cannot initiate an amendment, except that Article 169 or 171 legislation involves a resolution of the Legislative Assembly.

2 — Correct: Article 3 requires the President's recommendation for introducing the Bill. Facts: Parliament can form a new State, increase or diminish a State's area, or alter its boundaries or name. The President refers the Bill to the State Legislature concerned to express its views within a stipulated period, but Parliament is not bound by them. Article 4 says such laws are not amendments under Article 368, so a simple majority suffices. Examples: the States Reorganisation Act 1956, Telangana in 2014 through the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, and Uttarakhand, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh in 2000. Berubari (1960) held that ceding territory to another country needs an Article 368 amendment.

3 — Incorrect: this needs a special majority and State ratification, not a simple majority. Facts: Article 368(2) proviso lists the federal provisions needing ratification by at least half the State Legislatures. These are the election of the President (Arts 54, 55), the extent of executive and legislative power of the Union and States, the Supreme Court and High Courts, the Union Territories High Courts, legislative relations (Part XI), the Seventh Schedule lists, representation of States in Parliament, and Article 368 itself. Ratification must happen before the Bill goes to the President. No time limit is fixed for ratification.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. Article 3 requires the President's recommendation before a Bill for new States or altering boundaries or names of States is introduced, but statements 1 and 3 are wrong on the amendment procedure.
topic_notes: Article 368 (Part XX) sets out Parliament's power to amend the Constitution and the procedure. There are three categories. First, amendment by simple majority, outside Article 368: this covers the admission or formation of new States (Arts 2, 3, 4), the Second Schedule, Citizenship, Fifth and Sixth Schedules, and the creation or abolition of Legislative Councils (Art 169). Second, amendment by special majority: most provisions, including Fundamental Rights and DPSPs. This means a majority of the total membership of each House plus two-thirds of members present and voting. Third, special majority plus ratification by at least half the States: the federal provisions. The Bill may be introduced in either House and needs no prior permission. There is no joint sitting for deadlock. The President must give assent, as made compulsory by the 24th Amendment (1971). Key cases: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) held Fundamental Rights could be amended. Golak Nath (1967) held they could not. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) laid down the basic structure doctrine. Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Art 368(4) and (5), which the 42nd Amendment had added. The 42nd Amendment (1976) is called the mini-Constitution. The 44th Amendment (1978) restored balance and removed the right to property from Fundamental Rights. The 101st Amendment introduced GST and needed ratification. The 103rd Amendment gave 10% EWS reservation. The 106th Amendment is the Women's Reservation Act 2023. The 7th Amendment (1956) reorganised States. Berubari Union case (1960) held that Article 3 does not cover ceding territory to a foreign country.

question: Which one of the following is the correct statement? The term of Lok Sabha can be extended by the Parliament for a period
options: not exceeding six months at a me during proclamation of emergency but not exceeding in any case a period of three months a er the proclamation of emergency has ceased to operate
not exceeding one year at a me during proclamation of emergency but not exceeding in any case a period of six months a er the proclamation of emergency has ceased to operate
not exceeding one year at a me during proclamation of emergency but not exceeding in any case a period of three months a er the proclamation of emergency has ceased to operate
not exceeding six months at a me during proclamation of emergency but not exceeding in any case a period of one month a er the proclamation of emergency has ceased to operate
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 83(2) fixes the normal term of the Lok Sabha at five years from the date of its first meeting. The same clause allows Parliament to extend this term by law during a Proclamation of Emergency. Each extension can be for up to one year at a time, and there is no limit on how many times it can be repeated while the Emergency lasts. After the Proclamation ceases to operate, the extension cannot go beyond six months. The 42nd Amendment (1976) first raised the term to six years, and the 44th Amendment (1978) restored five years. The same limits apply to State Legislative Assemblies under Article 172(1). Precedent: the 5th Lok Sabha, elected in 1971, had its term extended in 1976 and 1977 during the Emergency, and it was dissolved in January 1977. The Emergency ended in March 1977. Elimination: options (a) and (d) give only six months at a time, which is too short, and options (c) and (a) give three months or less after the Emergency, which is too short. Only (b) combines one year at a time with six months after the Emergency.
explanations: Incorrect: six months at a time and three months afterwards are both wrong. The correct figures are one year and six months.
Correct: Article 83(2) allows extension for one year at a time during a national Emergency, and not beyond six months after the Emergency ceases.
Incorrect: the one-year extension is right, but the three-month limit after the Emergency is wrong. It should be six months.
Incorrect: six months at a time and one month afterwards are both wrong.
keyfact: Article 83(2): during a national Emergency the Lok Sabha's term can be extended one year at a time, and not beyond six months after the Emergency ends.
option_notes: Six months at a time with a three-month tail does not match any constitutional provision for the Lok Sabha. Six months is the maximum gap between two sessions of Parliament under Article 85. It is also the period within which Parliament must approve a Proclamation of Emergency under Article 352 if it is not dissolved. Do not confuse these figures with the term extension.

This is the correct provision under Article 83(2). Extension is by law of Parliament, in one-year steps, only while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation. It must end within six months of the Emergency ceasing. The same rule applies to State Assemblies under Article 172(1). The 5th Lok Sabha's term was extended in 1976 under this provision.

One year at a time is right, but the three-month tail is wrong. Three months is the period after which a Proclamation of Emergency lapses if it is not approved by Parliament under the older rule. The 44th Amendment changed this to one month, and the approval period is now one month.

Six months at a time with a one-month tail is also wrong. One month is the period within which Parliament must approve a Proclamation of Emergency after the 44th Amendment (1978). It is a different rule and is often confused with the term extension.
related: Article 83(2): Lok Sabha's normal term is five years from its first sitting.
Article 172(1): the State Assembly's term is five years, extendable in an Emergency in the same way.
Article 352 Emergency must be approved by Parliament within one month.
The 44th Amendment (1978) restored the five-year term of Lok Sabha after the 42nd Amendment had made it six.
The 5th Lok Sabha's term was extended in 1976 and 1977.
Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is not subject to dissolution; members serve six-year terms.
Article 85: the gap between two sessions of Parliament cannot exceed six months.
summary: The correct answer is (b). Under Article 83(2), while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, Parliament may by law extend the Lok Sabha's term for up to one year at a time. The extension cannot continue beyond six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate.
topic_notes: Lok Sabha term: Article 83(2) gives five years from the first meeting. The term can be cut short by dissolution by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers. It can be extended only during a national Emergency under Article 352, by a law of Parliament, for one year at a time. The extension cannot go beyond six months after the Emergency ends. Rajya Sabha under Article 83(1) is a permanent House and is not subject to dissolution. One-third of its members retire every second year. Its members serve six-year terms. Related periods: a Proclamation of Emergency must be approved by both Houses within one month, by a special majority (a majority of the total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting). Once approved it lasts six months and can be renewed for further six-month periods by simple majority. A resolution to revoke it can be passed by simple majority in Lok Sabha. Ten percent of Lok Sabha members can requisition a special sitting to consider revocation. The 42nd Amendment (1976) raised the Lok Sabha term to six years, and the 44th Amendment (1978) reversed this. History: the 5th Lok Sabha ran from 1971 to 1977, and its term was extended twice, in 1976 and 1977. The Emergency was in force from June 1975 to March 1977. Assemblies: Article 172 gives State Legislative Assemblies a five-year term, extendable in the same manner. Under President's Rule, Article 356, Parliament can keep a State Assembly in suspended animation, but it does not extend its term.

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Indian Parliament is not sovereign, and the legislation passed by it is subject to judicial review.
2. In India, the Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy are enforceable by the courts. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: India follows constitutional supremacy, not parliamentary sovereignty as in the UK. Parliament's powers are limited by the distribution of powers between Union and States (Seventh Schedule), by Fundamental Rights (Part III) and by the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973). Judicial review is derived from Articles 13, 32, 131, 136, 226 and 246, and the Supreme Court and High Courts can declare laws void if they are unconstitutional. The Supreme Court has held that judicial review is part of the basic structure (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997; Minerva Mills, 1980). Statement 1 is therefore correct. Statement 2 is wrong because Article 37 says the Directive Principles in Part IV are not enforceable by any court, even though they are fundamental in the governance of the country. Fundamental Rights can be enforced directly through writs under Articles 32 and 226. Courts have, however, used Directive Principles to interpret Fundamental Rights, and Article 31C gives some of them primacy over Articles 14 and 19. Because statement 2 lumps the two together, options (b) and (c) are eliminated, and (d) is eliminated because statement 1 is true.
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is true and statement 2 is false, so only 1 is correct.
Wrong: statement 2 is false because Directive Principles are non-justiciable under Article 37.
Wrong: this would require statement 2 to be true, but DPSPs cannot be enforced by courts.
Wrong: statement 1 is true because Parliament is not sovereign and its laws are subject to judicial review.
keyfact: India has constitutional supremacy with judicial review, and only Fundamental Rights, not DPSPs, are justiciable (Article 37).
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: this is the correct choice. It reflects constitutional supremacy and judicial review in India, where Parliament's laws can be struck down by the Supreme Court and High Courts if they violate the Constitution or its basic structure, while DPSPs remain non-justiciable.

Option (b) 2 only: this would mean Parliament is sovereign and DPSPs are enforceable. Both ideas are incorrect. Parliamentary sovereignty is the British model, and DPSPs are non-justiciable under Article 37, unlike Fundamental Rights, which are enforceable under Articles 32 and 226.

Option (c) Both 1 and 2: this wrongly treats DPSPs as enforceable. Only Fundamental Rights carry a direct judicial remedy. DPSPs are guidelines for the State, though courts may use them to interpret Fundamental Rights and to uphold laws made to give effect to them under Article 31C.

Option (d) Neither 1 nor 2: this would deny judicial review of Parliament's laws, which is wrong. Judicial review is a basic structure feature, recognised in Kesavananda Bharati and later cases, and gives the courts power over legislative acts.
related: Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void.
Article 37 says DPSPs are not enforceable by any court.
Article 32 gives the right to constitutional remedies and was called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution by Dr Ambedkar.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic structure doctrine.
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down parts of the 42nd Amendment and balanced FRs with DPSPs.
I.R. Coelho (2007) held that Ninth Schedule laws are subject to basic structure review.
The 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A, the right to education.
DPSPs were borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
statements: 1 — Correct: Parliament is bound by the Constitution and its laws can be reviewed by the judiciary. Judicial review means courts examine whether legislative and executive acts conform to the Constitution. Its sources are Articles 13, 32, 226, 131 and 246. Key cases: Golak Nath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973) which laid down the basic structure doctrine, Minerva Mills (1980) and L. Chandra Kumar (1997). The Ninth Schedule laws are also reviewable after I.R. Coelho (2007). The UK, by contrast, has parliamentary sovereignty. India has a blend of parliamentary supremacy and judicial review.

2 — Incorrect: Only Fundamental Rights are justiciable. Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36-51) are non-justiciable under Article 37, though they are fundamental in governance and the State should apply them in making laws. They were borrowed from the Irish Constitution. Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12-35) are enforceable through Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Courts). In Champakam Dorairajan (1951) Fundamental Rights prevailed over DPSPs, but later cases such as Minerva Mills (1980) sought harmony between the two. Article 31C and the 42nd Amendment (1976) strengthened DPSPs.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. India's Parliament is not sovereign because the written Constitution is supreme and courts can strike down laws that violate it, but only Fundamental Rights are justiciable, while Directive Principles are expressly non-enforceable by courts (Article 37).
topic_notes: India has a written Constitution that is supreme, with a federal structure and an independent judiciary. Parliament has wide powers but they are limited. Parliament can amend the Constitution under Article 368, but not its basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, by 7:6). Judicial review covers legislative acts, executive actions and, in some cases, constitutional amendments. Article 13 declares void any law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights, and the Supreme Court has described judicial review as the basic feature of the Constitution. Article 32 is the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution according to Dr Ambedkar. Writs available: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. The High Courts' writ power under Article 226 is wider because it also covers 'any other purpose'. Directive Principles come from the Irish Constitution, and are classified as socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual. Key articles: 39(b) and (c), 40 (village panchayats), 44 (Uniform Civil Code), 45 (early childhood care), 48 (cattle and agriculture), 48A (environment) and 50 (separation of judiciary from executive). The 42nd Amendment added Articles 39A, 43A and 48A. The 86th Amendment (2002) made education a Fundamental Right under Article 21A and changed Article 45. Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A) were added by the 42nd Amendment on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation and are also non-justiciable. In Minerva Mills the Court held that the Constitution rests on a balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs. The Ninth Schedule, added by the First Amendment, protects laws from review only if they do not violate the basic structure.

question:
Consider the following statements related to the World War II:
1. Germany a acked the US naval base at Pearl Harbour.
2. Winston Churchill was the British Prime Minister during the World War II.
3. The Versailles Treaty which is generally cited as one of the main causes of the World War II was signed just before the World War II in 1939.
4. Franklin Roosevelt was the President of the United States were dropped over the Japanese ci es of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Which of the statement given above is/are correct?
subject: General Science
detail: This question tests basic WWII chronology. The war began on 1 September 1939 with Germany's invasion of Poland. Winston Churchill became PM on 10 May 1940, replacing Neville Chamberlain, and led Britain until July 1945, when Clement Attlee succeeded him after the general election. Japan attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on 7 December 1941, bringing the US into the war; Germany only declared war on the US a few days later. The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919, ending WWI. Its harsh terms (war guilt clause, reparations, territorial losses and disarmament) fed German resentment and are cited as a cause of WWII. So signing it in 1939 is wrong. The atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima (6 August 1945) and Nagasaki (9 August 1945) on the orders of President Harry Truman, because Roosevelt had died on 12 April 1945. Statement 4 is also garbled by OCR, but its content is wrong either way. Only statement 2 survives, so (c) is correct. Options (a), (b) and (d) each include a false statement (1, 3 or 4).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 3, both false. Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, and Versailles was signed in 1919.
Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 4, both false. Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, and the atomic bombs were dropped under Truman.
Correct: only statement 2, about Churchill, is true.
Wrong: it includes statements 3 and 4, both false, and omits the true statement 2.
keyfact: Japan hit Pearl Harbor (1941); Versailles was 1919; Churchill was WWII PM; Truman ordered the atomic bombs.
option_notes: Statements 1, 2 and 3 combined. It wrongly makes Germany the attacker at Pearl Harbor (it was Japan, 7 Dec 1941) and dates Versailles to 1939 (actually 1919). Only the Churchill statement in this set is true. Pearl Harbor drew the US into WWII, and Versailles ended WWI formally with Germany.

Statements 1, 2 and 4 combined. It wrongly blames Germany for Pearl Harbor and gives a garbled claim about Roosevelt and the atomic bombs. Roosevelt died in April 1945, and Truman authorised the bombings in August 1945. Roosevelt led the US through the New Deal and most of WWII, and was elected four times.

Statement 2 only: Churchill as British PM in WWII. He took office on 10 May 1940 and led the wartime coalition until July 1945. He was a key member of the Allied 'Big Three' with Roosevelt and Stalin, and he signed the Atlantic Charter with Roosevelt in August 1941. This is the correct answer.

Statements 3 and 4 combined. Both are false: Versailles dates from 1919, and the atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki under Truman, not Roosevelt. The Potsdam Declaration of July 1945 demanded Japan's surrender. Japan's refusal was followed by the bombings and then its surrender.
related: Pearl Harbor attack: 7 December 1941 by Japan.
Treaty of Versailles: signed 28 June 1919.
WWII began 1 September 1939 with Germany's invasion of Poland.
Atomic bombs: Hiroshima 6 Aug 1945, Nagasaki 9 Aug 1945, under President Truman.
Roosevelt died 12 April 1945; Truman succeeded him.
Churchill was PM 1940-45 and 1951-55; Attlee took over in July 1945.
UN founded 24 October 1945.
Yalta Conference, February 1945: Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Japan, not Germany, attacked Pearl Harbor. Pearl Harbor is a US naval base on Oahu, Hawaii. The surprise Japanese air raid came on 7 December 1941 and was led by Admiral Yamamoto's plan, with Admiral Nagumo commanding the carrier strike force. It sank or damaged many battleships and killed about 2,400 Americans. The next day the US declared war on Japan. Germany and Italy, as Japan's Axis partners under the Tripartite Pact (1940), declared war on the US on 11 December 1941.

2 — Correct: Winston Churchill was British PM during WWII. He served 1940-45 and again 1951-55. He led a coalition government after Chamberlain resigned, was known for his 'blood, toil, tears and sweat' speech and for the Battle of Britain in 1940, and attended the Atlantic Charter (1941), Tehran, Yalta and Potsdam conferences. He lost the July 1945 election to Clement Attlee and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953.

3 — Incorrect: the Versailles Treaty was signed on 28 June 1919, not 1939. It was imposed on Germany after WWI at the Paris Peace Conference by the 'Big Three' (Wilson, Lloyd George, Clemenceau). It included the war guilt clause (Article 231), heavy reparations, loss of territory such as Alsace-Lorraine, a 100,000-man army limit, demilitarisation of the Rhineland and the creation of the League of Nations. The resentment it caused helped Hitler rise to power.

4 — Incorrect: the statement is garbled and wrong. Franklin D. Roosevelt was US President from 1933 until his death on 12 April 1945. The atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima ('Little Boy', 6 August 1945) and Nagasaki ('Fat Man', 9 August 1945) under President Harry S. Truman. The Manhattan Project, begun under Roosevelt, developed the bombs. Japan announced surrender on 15 August 1945 and signed the instrument on 2 September 1945.
summary: The answer is (c): only statement 2 is correct. Churchill was British Prime Minister for most of WWII (1940-45). Japan, not Germany, attacked Pearl Harbor; the Versailles Treaty was signed in 1919; and the statement about Roosevelt is garbled and wrong, since the atomic bombs were dropped under Truman.
topic_notes: World War II ran from 1 September 1939 (German invasion of Poland) to 2 September 1945 (Japanese surrender). The main Allied powers were Britain, the USSR, the USA, France and China. The Axis powers were Germany, Italy and Japan, linked by the Tripartite Pact of 1940. Causes include the harsh Treaty of Versailles (1919), the Great Depression, the rise of fascism and Nazism, appeasement (the Munich Agreement of 1938) and the League of Nations' failure. Key events: fall of France (June 1940), Battle of Britain (1940), Operation Barbarossa (June 1941), Pearl Harbor (7 Dec 1941), Stalingrad (1942-43), D-Day (6 June 1944), VE Day (8 May 1945) and the atomic bombs (6 and 9 August 1945). Leaders: Churchill and Attlee (UK), Roosevelt and Truman (USA), Stalin (USSR), Hitler (Germany), Mussolini (Italy), Hirohito and Tojo (Japan), and De Gaulle (Free France). Wartime conferences: Atlantic Charter (1941), Casablanca (1943), Tehran (1943), Yalta (Feb 1945) and Potsdam (July-Aug 1945). Post-war outcomes: the United Nations (founded 24 October 1945), the Bretton Woods institutions, the Nuremberg trials, the start of the Cold War and decolonisation, including Indian independence in 1947. India's link: about 2.5 million Indian soldiers served in the British Indian Army. The Cripps Mission (1942) and the Quit India Movement (1942) came during the war, and Subhas Chandra Bose formed the INA with Japanese support.

question: Assertion (A): During the British rule, the Congress Ministers resigned in 1939 in all the provinces where they were in oﬃce. Reason (R): Congress wanted fresh elec ons as it was frustrated with Jinnah’s campaign of twonation theory. Codes:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
subject: Computers
detail: Under the Government of India Act 1935, provincial autonomy began in 1937. Congress won majorities in 5 provinces (Madras, Bihar, Orissa, UP, Central Provinces) and formed ministries in 7 (adding Bombay) and later 8 with the NWFP and a coalition in Assam, so it held office in 8 or 11 provinces depending on the count. When war broke out on 3 September 1939, Linlithgow announced India's involvement without consulting the central legislature or provincial governments. The Congress Working Committee, at Wardha, demanded a clear statement of war aims and a promise of independence. The Viceroy's August Offer of 1940 came later. The government's reply was unsatisfactory, so Congress ministries resigned in late October 1939. Jinnah observed 22 December 1939 as a Day of Deliverance. The two-nation idea was formalised in the Lahore Resolution of March 1940, after the resignations, so R is chronologically and causally wrong. Congress never demanded fresh elections as the reason. Hence A is true, R is false, and option (c) is correct. Option (a) and (b) fail because R is false. Option (d) fails because A is true.
explanations: Wrong: R is false, because the resignations were a protest against India being dragged into the war without consent, not a response to Jinnah's two-nation campaign.
Wrong: R is not a true statement at all, so the question of whether it explains A does not arise.
Correct: Congress ministries did resign in 1939 in the provinces where they held office, while R gives a wrong cause and a wrong chronology.
Wrong: A is true, since Congress ministries resigned in October-November 1939, so the claim that A is false cannot hold.
keyfact: Congress ministries resigned in 1939 against the Viceroy's unilateral declaration of war, not over the two-nation theory, which came in 1940.
option_notes: Option (a) says both A and R are true and R explains A. It would apply only if the resignations had been caused by the Jinnah campaign. The true cause was the unilateral declaration of war by Viceroy Linlithgow on 3 September 1939. Congress demanded clarity on war aims and a promise of independence. The Lahore Resolution came in March 1940.

Option (b) says both are true but R does not explain A. It is wrong because R is false. Congress did not seek fresh elections. Its stated objection was the lack of consultation over India's entry into the war and the vague British statements on post-war freedom.

Option (c) says A is true and R is false. It is correct. Congress ministries resigned in October-November 1939 on the Working Committee's instruction. Muslim League leaders celebrated 22 December 1939 as the Day of Deliverance. Linlithgow's later offers included the August Offer of 1940 with the promise of dominion status after the war.

Option (d) says A is false and R is true. This is wrong on both counts. A is accurate, and R is a fabricated reason. The two-nation theory was formally adopted by the Muslim League at Lahore in March 1940 and not as a cause of the 1939 resignations.
related: Provincial autonomy began under the Government of India Act 1935 in April 1937.
Congress ministries resigned in October-November 1939 over India's forced entry into World War II.
Jinnah observed 22 December 1939 as the Day of Deliverance.
Lahore Resolution was adopted in March 1940.
August Offer was made in 1940 by Linlithgow.
Vinoba Bhave was the first Individual Satyagrahi in 1940.
Congress won a majority in 5 of 11 provinces in the 1937 elections.
summary: The answer is (c): A is true, R is false. The Congress ministries resigned in October-November 1939 because the Viceroy Linlithgow unilaterally declared India a belligerent in World War II without consulting Indian leaders. They did not resign to force fresh elections or because of Jinnah's two-nation theory.
topic_notes: The Government of India Act 1935 introduced provincial autonomy, effective April 1937. The 1937 elections saw Congress win a majority in 5 of 11 provinces: Madras, Bihar, Orissa, UP and Central Provinces. It later formed ministries in Bombay, NWFP and Assam, so it governed 8 provinces. The Muslim League did poorly, and Jinnah rejected a coalition in UP, which hardened League attitudes. Congress rule saw some reforms, but the League alleged oppression in the Pirpur Report and the Shareef Report. When World War II began, Linlithgow declared India at war without consulting Indians. The Congress Working Committee demanded a declaration of war aims and independence. After an unsatisfactory reply the ministries resigned around 22-29 October 1939. Jinnah called for a Day of Deliverance on 22 December 1939. In March 1940 the Lahore Resolution demanded autonomous Muslim-majority areas, later called the Pakistan Resolution. The August Offer of 1940 promised dominion status after the war and an expanded Executive Council, but Congress rejected it and launched the Individual Satyagraha in October 1940 with Vinoba Bhave as the first satyagrahi. Subsequent events were the Cripps Mission of 1942, the Quit India Movement of August 1942 and the Cabinet Mission of 1946. Learn this sequence in order, as UPSC often asks about it.

question: Assertion (A): Aurangzeb released Shahu from the prison shortly before Aurangzeb died in 1707. Reason (R): Zulfiqar pointed that Shahu’s return to his Kingdom would cause a division among the Marathas who would thus be disabled from plundering the imperial territories. Codes:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
subject: Computers
detail: Shahu (Shivaji II), son of Sambhaji, was captured at Raigad in 1689 as a child and brought up in the Mughal camp. Aurangzeb treated him with kindness and gave him a mansab, but never released him. He kept Shahu as a bargaining chip against the Marathas. Aurangzeb died on 3 March 1707 at Ahmednagar. The Mughal throne was then contested, and Azam Shah, who held Shahu, was defeated and killed at Jajau in 1707. Azam Shah had released Shahu in May 1707 on his march north, because he wanted to cause trouble for the Marathas. Zulfiqar Khan, the Mughal noble, advocated this policy. Azam Shah then released him, and Shahu returned to Maharashtra. It is commonly stated that Azam Shah released him on Zulfiqar Khan's advice. This is the version in many textbooks. Either way, Aurangzeb did not release Shahu, so A is false. R states the logic of the release (divide the Marathas, and Tarabai's faction would be pitted against Shahu), so R is true. Shahu defeated Tarabai's forces at Khed in 1707. Elimination: (a) and (b) need A to be true. (c) is wrong because R is true.
explanations: Wrong: A is false, since Aurangzeb never released Shahu. He died in March 1707 with Shahu still in Mughal custody.
Wrong: A is false, so the pair cannot both be true.
Wrong: A is false, and R is true rather than false.
Correct: A is false, because the release came after Aurangzeb's death. R is true, because Zulfiqar Khan's advice was that Shahu's return would divide the Marathas.
keyfact: Shahu was freed in 1707 after Aurangzeb's death, on Zulfiqar Khan's advice to divide the Marathas; Aurangzeb never released him.
option_notes: Option (a) would require A to be true and R to explain it. R does explain why Shahu was released, but the release was not by Aurangzeb. Such options are used where the reason is valid but is attached to a wrong assertion.
Option (b) says both are true but R does not explain A. It fails because A is false. Aurangzeb held Shahu captive from 1689 to 1707, treating him as a hostage and giving him a mansab.
Option (c) says A is true and R is false. This is the reverse of the real position. The Mughal policy of dividing the Marathas by releasing Shahu is a well-documented fact.

Option (d) is correct. Shahu was released in 1707 and returned to Maharashtra. He claimed the Maratha throne against Tarabai, the regent of her son Shivaji II, defeated her at Khed in October 1707, and was crowned at Satara in 1708.
related: Aurangzeb died on 3 March 1707 at Ahmednagar.
Shahu was captured at Raigad in 1689 along with his mother Yesubai.
Battle of Khed (1707): Shahu defeated Tarabai.
Shahu was crowned at Satara in 1708.
Balaji Vishwanath became Peshwa in 1713.
Treaty of Warna (1731) recognised the Kolhapur and Satara gaddis.
Tarabai ruled as regent for her son Shivaji II.
summary: The answer is (d): A is false and R is true. Shahu was released in 1707 by Bahadur Shah I (Muazzam) after Aurangzeb's death, not by Aurangzeb himself. The release was advised by Zulfiqar Khan, who argued that it would split the Marathas.
topic_notes: Shahu (1682-1749) was the son of Sambhaji and grandson of Shivaji. He was captured by the Mughals at Raigad in 1689 when Sambhaji was executed, and he grew up in Mughal custody. On Aurangzeb's death (3 March 1707, Ahmednagar), Azam Shah freed him, and Zulfiqar Khan is associated with the advice to divide the Marathas. Shahu's return caused a civil war with Tarabai, who ruled in the name of her son Shivaji II from Kolhapur. Shahu won at Khed (1707) and was crowned at Satara in 1708. The Maratha state then split into the Satara and Kolhapur gaddis (Treaty of Warna, 1731). Shahu appointed Balaji Vishwanath as Peshwa in 1713. Balaji secured the Mughal grant of chauth and sardeshmukhi from the Sayyid brothers in 1719 (a Mughal-Maratha treaty under Emperor Farrukhsiyar). The Peshwa gradually became the real power while Shahu remained a figurehead after his death in 1749. Related topics: Aurangzeb's Deccan wars, Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687), Sambhaji's execution (1689), Rajaram's escape to Jinji, Tarabai's resistance, Bahadur Shah I (1707-12), and the later Peshwas: Baji Rao I, Balaji Baji Rao, and the Third Battle of Panipat (1761).

question:
Match List-I with List-II and select the
correct answer using the code given below the
lists:
List-I (Indian Kings)
E. Karikala
F. Rudradaman
G. Milinda
H. Kanishka
List-II (Dynasty)
5. Bacteria Greek
6. Chola
7. Chalukya
8. Kushanas
9. Shakas
Codes:
A B C D
(e) 2 4 1 5
(f) 1 5 3 4
(g) 2 5 1 4
(h) 1 4 3 5
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The question tests ancient Indian rulers and their dynasties. Karikala was the greatest early Chola king of the Sangam age, known for the battle of Venni and for building the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) on the Kaveri. Rudradaman I (c. 130-150 AD) was the Shaka Western Kshatrapa ruler of Ujjain; his Junagadh rock inscription is the earliest long inscription in classical Sanskrit and records repairs to the Sudarshana lake. Milinda, or Menander, was an Indo-Greek (Bactrian Greek) king with his capital at Sakala (Sialkot), and he was converted to Buddhism by Nagasena (Milindapanho). Kanishka was the Kushana emperor who started the Saka era in 78 AD, held the Fourth Buddhist Council and had his capital at Purushapura (Peshawar). The Chalukya option is the distractor: the Chalukyas (Pulakeshin II) are a much later dynasty, and no king in List-I belongs to it. In the list as printed, the numbering is garbled by OCR: List-II is read as 1 Bactrian Greek, 2 Chola, 3 Chalukya, 4 Kushanas, 5 Shakas. The correct sequence is then Karikala 2, Rudradaman 5, Milinda 1, Kanishka 4, so the code 2 5 1 4 is right.
explanations: Option (a), code 2 4 1 5, wrongly gives Rudradaman as Kushana and Kanishka as Shaka, so it is incorrect.
Option (b), code 1 5 3 4, makes Karikala a Bactrian Greek and Milinda a Chalukya, so it is wrong.
Option (c), code 2 5 1 4, gives Karikala Chola, Rudradaman Shakas, Milinda Bactrian Greek and Kanishka Kushanas, so it is correct.
Option (d), code 1 4 3 5, makes Karikala a Bactrian Greek and Milinda a Chalukya, so it is wrong.
keyfact: Karikala-Chola, Rudradaman-Shaka, Milinda (Menander)-Bactrian Greek, Kanishka-Kushana.
option_notes: Code 2 4 1 5 is a mixed pairing that confuses the Kushanas and Shakas. The Kushanas were Central Asian Yuezhi people, while the Shakas were Scythians who ruled the western Indian Kshatrapa kingdoms.

Code 1 5 3 4 pairs the kings with the wrong dynasties. It involves the Chalukyas, a dynasty of Badami founded by Pulakeshin I in the 6th century AD, whose Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha around 618-619 AD.
Code 2 5 1 4 gives the correct matching. The Cholas, Shakas, Bactrian Greeks and Kushanas are the early dynasties of Sangam Tamil Nadu, western India, the north-west, and the Kushana empire.

Code 1 4 3 5 is also incorrect. It confuses the Bactrian Greeks, who were the first foreign rulers to issue gold coins in India (the Kushanas later issued the main gold coinage), with the other dynasties.
related: Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradaman (150 AD) is in Sanskrit
Kanishka's Saka era began in 78 AD
Milindapanho records the dialogue of Menander with Nagasena
Karikala built the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) on the Kaveri
Kanishka's Fourth Buddhist Council was held in Kashmir
Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated the Shakas
Chalukya Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha
statements: E. Karikala — Correct: Chola. He was the early Chola king of the Sangam age, with his capital at Uraiyur and later Puhar (Kaveripattinam). He won the battle of Venni against the Cheras and Pandyas, and built embankments on the Kaveri. He is praised in Pattinappalai and Porunararruppadai.

F. Rudradaman — Correct: Shakas. He was the most famous Western Kshatrapa ruler, c. 130-150 AD, and he ruled Gujarat, Malwa and Konkan. His Junagadh inscription of 150 AD records the repair of the Sudarshana lake, built by the Mauryas and repaired under Pushyagupta and Tushaspa. He defeated the Satavahanas but did not destroy them.

G. Milinda — Correct: Bactrian Greek. Menander ruled c. 165-145 BC from Sakala. The Milindapanho records his dialogues with the Buddhist monk Nagasena. His coins carry the Greek title Soter, and he is the best known Indo-Greek ruler. He invaded the Ganga valley.

H. Kanishka — Correct: Kushanas. He ruled c. 78-101 AD, with capitals at Purushapura and Mathura, and patronised Mahayana Buddhism. The Fourth Buddhist Council was held in Kashmir under Vasumitra and Ashvaghosha. Court figures included Charaka, Nagarjuna and Ashvaghosha. Gandhara and Mathura art flourished.
summary: Karikala was a Chola king, Rudradaman a Shaka (Western Kshatrapa) ruler, Milinda (Menander) a Bactrian Greek, and Kanishka a Kushana. This gives the matching Chola, Shakas, Bactrian Greek, Kushanas, which corresponds to the option that pairs the four kings with these dynasties in that order (the code 2 5 1 4, option c).
topic_notes: The post-Mauryan period (200 BC to 300 AD) saw a succession of foreign dynasties in north and north-west India: the Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians (Pahlavas) and Kushanas. The Indo-Greeks came first and issued the first coins that carried the king's name and image. Demetrius and Menander were the best known. The Shakas followed, and their branches ruled in Taxila, Mathura, Ujjain and elsewhere. Rudradaman was the greatest of the Western Kshatrapas. Vikramaditya's victory over the Shakas is traditionally linked with the Vikrama era of 58 BC. The Kushanas came from the Yuezhi tribe; Kujula Kadphises founded the dynasty, and Kanishka was the most famous. His Saka era began in 78 AD. The Kushana gold coins were widely issued. Gandhara art, with Greco-Roman influence, and Mathura art flourished. In the south, the Sangam age saw the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas. Karikala of the Cholas won the battle of Venni and built the Kallanai. The Satavahanas of the Deccan, with Gautamiputra Satakarni, defeated the Shakas, Pahlavas and Yavanas. Possible questions include the Junagadh inscription, the Fourth Buddhist Council, the Milindapanho, the Saka era, and the Gandhara and Mathura schools.

question: During the World War II, Indian soldiers fought heroically in the Ba le at Monte Cassino. Where is Monte Cassino located?
subject: Computers
detail: Monte Cassino is a rocky hill near the town of Cassino in Lazio, central Italy, overlooking the Liri valley and Route 6 to Rome. It anchored the German Gustav Line, which blocked the Allied advance from southern Italy to Rome after the 1943 landings at Salerno. Four battles were fought between January and May 1944. The Allied side included American, British, New Zealand, Indian, Polish, French, Canadian and other forces. The Allies bombed the 6th-century abbey, founded by St Benedict around 529 AD, on 15 February 1944. Indian divisions (4th, 8th and 10th) took part in the second and later battles, and many Indian soldiers earned gallantry awards, including Victoria Crosses at nearby Italian fronts. The Polish II Corps finally captured the ruins on 18 May 1944, which causes confusion with option (a). Germany and Greece were fronts for other campaigns, not this one. To eliminate, remember that Monte Cassino belongs to the Italian Campaign, which includes Sicily, Salerno, Anzio, Cassino and the Gothic Line.
explanations: Wrong: Poland is linked to the battle only because the Polish II Corps under General Anders captured the abbey ruins, but the location is Italy.
Correct: Monte Cassino is in Lazio, central Italy, on the Gustav Line south of Rome, and Indian divisions fought there in 1944.
Wrong: Germany was the enemy homeland, but the battle was fought in Italy, where German forces defended the Gustav Line.
Wrong: Greece saw Axis occupation and the 1941 campaign, but Monte Cassino has no connection to it.
keyfact: Monte Cassino is in central Italy (Lazio) on the Gustav Line, where Indian divisions fought in 1944.
option_notes: Poland: Invaded on 1 September 1939 by Germany, which began WWII in Europe, and then by the USSR on 17 September. Its capital is Warsaw. The Polish II Corps fought at Monte Cassino in May 1944 and planted the Polish flag on the ruins. Poland is not where the battle took place.

Italy: Mussolini's Fascist state joined the Axis in 1940. Allied forces invaded Sicily in July 1943, and Italy surrendered in September 1943. Germany then held the Gustav Line until 1944. Rome fell on 4 June 1944. Monte Cassino abbey was rebuilt after the war and reconsecrated in 1964.

Germany: Hitler's Nazi state was the main Axis power and surrendered on 8 May 1945. German paratroopers (Fallschirmjäger) defended Monte Cassino. Berlin fell in May 1945, and Germany was divided into four occupation zones afterward.

Greece: Italy attacked Greece in October 1940, and Germany conquered it in April 1941. The Axis occupation lasted until 1944. Crete fell in May 1941 to German airborne landings. Greece was not the site of the Monte Cassino battle.
related: Monte Cassino abbey was founded by St Benedict around 529 AD.
The abbey was bombed by the Allies on 15 February 1944.
The Polish II Corps under General Anders captured Monte Cassino on 18 May 1944.
4th, 8th and 10th Indian Divisions fought in the Italian Campaign.
Sepoy Kamal Ram won the Victoria Cross in Italy in 1944.
The Gustav Line was the German defensive line across Italy.
Rome fell to the Allies on 4 June 1944.
summary: The answer is (b) Italy. Monte Cassino is a hill about 130 km southeast of Rome, crowned by a Benedictine abbey, and it was the site of the 1944 Battle of Monte Cassino, where the 4th, 8th and 10th Indian Divisions fought as part of the Allied forces.
topic_notes: The Italian Campaign (1943-45) followed the Allied victory in North Africa. Sicily was invaded in Operation Husky (July 1943), and Mussolini was deposed on 25 July 1943. Italy signed an armistice on 8 September 1943. The Allies landed at Salerno and Taranto, and Germany occupied the north and built defensive lines, including the Winter Line, Gustav Line and Gothic Line. The Anzio landings (January 1944) were meant to bypass the Gustav Line. Monte Cassino saw four battles from January to May 1944. The abbey was bombed on 15 February 1944. The Indian Army contributed heavily: the 4th Indian Division fought at Cassino, the 8th Indian Division crossed the Gari and Rapido, and the 10th Indian Division fought in the Apennines. India sent over 2.5 million volunteers in WWII, the largest volunteer army in history. Indian soldiers won 31 Victoria Crosses and George Crosses in the war, including Sepoy Kamal Ram (8th Indian Division) at the Gari river in May 1944, and Sepoy Ali Haidar and Naik Yeshwant Ghadge in Italy. Commonwealth war cemeteries in Cassino contain Indian graves. UPSC may also ask about other WWII sites such as El Alamein, Imphal-Kohima, Burma, Singapore and Tobruk, and about Subhas Bose's INA.

question:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists: List-I (Ba les) A. Battle of Chausa B. Battle of Ghagra C. Battle of Kanwah D. Battle of Talikota List-II (Fought between)
1. Babar and Rajputs
2. Humayun and Sher Khan
3. Babar and Afghans of Bihar & Bengal
4. Vijayanagar ruler and the Decca Sultanates Codes: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This question tests four battles that shaped the Mughal-Afghan-Rajput-Deccan power struggle in 16th-century India. Babur founded the Mughal empire at Panipat (1526) by defeating Ibrahim Lodi. He then defeated the Rajput confederacy led by Rana Sanga of Mewar at Khanwa/Kanwah (1527), and the Afghan chiefs of Bihar and Bengal (led by Mahmud Lodi, with the Bengal Sultan's support) at Ghagra (1529). Humayun was defeated by Sher Khan (Sher Shah Suri) at Chausa (June 1539) and again at Bilgram/Kannauj (1540), which forced him into exile. Talikota (Rakshasa-Tangadi), 1565, saw the Deccan Sultanates of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar defeat Rama Raya of Vijayanagar, leading to the sacking of Hampi. Elimination: Chausa is clearly Humayun vs Sher Khan, which gives A-2 and rules out (b) and (d). Kanwah is the Rajput battle (C-1), which rules out (a), leaving (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it pairs Ghagra with Rajputs and Kanwah with the Afghans, which reverses the two Babur battles.
(b) is wrong because it pairs Chausa with the Deccan Sultanates and Talikota with Humayun and Sher Khan, which is chronologically and geographically impossible.
(c) is correct: Chausa is Humayun vs Sher Khan, Ghagra is Babur vs the Afghans, Kanwah is Babur vs the Rajputs, and Talikota is Vijayanagar vs the Deccan Sultanates.
(d) is wrong because it pairs Chausa with the Deccan Sultanates and Talikota with Humayun and Sher Khan, and it also swaps Ghagra and Kanwah.
keyfact: Chausa 1539 = Humayun vs Sher Khan; Ghagra 1529 = Babur vs Afghans; Kanwah 1527 = Babur vs Rajputs; Talikota 1565 = Vijayanagar vs Deccan Sultanates.
option_notes: Option (a) pairs A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4. Only Chausa and Talikota are right. It swaps Ghagra (1529, vs the Afghans) and Kanwah (1527, vs the Rajputs). Rana Sanga of Mewar led the Rajputs at Kanwah and was defeated, which made Babur's hold on north India secure.

Option (b) pairs A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2. Only Ghagra and Kanwah are right. Chausa (1539) was fought on the Ganga in Bihar, not in the Deccan. Talikota (1565) was fought in the Deccan, decades after Humayun's defeats, and Sher Shah died in 1545.

Option (c) pairs A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4, and all four pairs are right. Chausa (1539) was Sher Khan's victory over Humayun. Ghagra (1529) and Kanwah (1527) were Babur's victories. Talikota (1565) was the Deccan Sultanates' victory over Vijayanagar.

Option (d) pairs A-4, B-1, C-3, D-2, and all four pairs are wrong. It mixes the Deccan battle with the Bihar battle, and the Rajput battle with the Afghan battle. Neither Ghagra nor Kanwah involved the Vijayanagar ruler or Humayun.
related: First Battle of Panipat (1526): Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi.
Rana Sanga was the Mewar ruler defeated at Khanwa (1527).
Babur took the title Ghazi after Khanwa.
Sher Shah defeated Humayun at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540).
Second Battle of Panipat (1556): Akbar's forces defeated Hemu.
Talikota (1565) led to the fall of Hampi and the decline of Vijayanagar.
Battle of Haldighati (1576): Akbar's forces vs Maharana Pratap.
statements: A — Correct match with 2: Chausa (26 June 1539), on the Ganga near Buxar in Bihar. Sher Khan surprised Humayun's army, and Humayun nearly drowned, saved by a water-carrier (Nizam). Sher Khan then took the title Sher Shah and had the khutba read in his name.

B — Correct match with 3: Ghagra (6 May 1529), near the Ghaghara-Ganga confluence in Bihar. Babur defeated the Afghans of Bihar and Bengal, and Mahmud Lodi was routed. It was Babur's last major battle and ended the Afghan threat to his rule in the east.

C — Correct match with 1: Kanwah/Khanwa (16 March 1527), near Agra. Babur defeated Rana Sanga of Mewar and the Rajput confederacy, using artillery and the tulughma tactic. He declared jihad and took the title Ghazi. Rajput power in north India was broken.

D — Correct match with 4: Talikota (23 January 1565), also called Rakshasa-Tangadi. The Deccan Sultanates' alliance defeated Rama Raya (Aliya Rama Raya) of the Aravidu dynasty of Vijayanagar, and the capital Hampi was plundered. The empire declined thereafter.
summary: The correct option is (c): A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4. Chausa (1539) was Humayun vs Sher Khan; Ghagra (1529) was Babur vs the Afghans of Bihar and Bengal; Kanwah (1527) was Babur vs the Rajputs under Rana Sanga; Talikota (1565) was Vijayanagar vs the Deccan Sultanates.
topic_notes:
Early Mughal and contemporary battles, in chronological order:
- First Battle of Panipat (21 April 1526): Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, ended the Delhi Sultanate and founded the Mughal empire. He used gunpowder artillery and the tulughma and araba tactics, with Ustad Ali Quli and Mustafa as gunners.
- Khanwa (1527): Babur defeated Rana Sanga, ending Rajput hopes of dominating north India.
- Chanderi (1528): Babur defeated Medini Rai.
- Ghagra (1529): Babur defeated the Afghans of Bihar and Bengal.
- Babur died in 1530 and Humayun succeeded him.
- Chausa (1539) and Bilgram/Kannauj (1540): Sher Shah defeated Humayun, who fled to Persia. Sher Shah's Sur rule lasted 1540-55, and he introduced the rupee, the Grand Trunk Road and land revenue reforms. Humayun regained Delhi in 1555 after Sirhind.
- Second Panipat (1556): Akbar's general Bairam Khan defeated Hemu.
- Haldighati (1576): Akbar's forces under Man Singh defeated Maharana Pratap.
- Talikota (1565): the Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar) defeated Vijayanagar under Rama Raya. The Bahmani successor states were involved, and Hampi was sacked.
- Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) belong to the later British period.
UPSC often asks about the commanders, the tactics, the places and the effects of these battles.

question: When Akbar besieged the Fort of Chi oor, who among the following defended it for four months?
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: Akbar marched against Chittor in 1567 because Mewar's Rana Udai Singh II refused to submit and Chittor commanded the route to Gujarat. Udai Singh left the fort for the Aravalli hills (later founding Udaipur) and put Jaimal, a Rathore chieftain of Merta, in charge along with Patta of Kailwa. Akbar's engineers dug sabats (covered approaches) and mines. Akbar is said to have shot Jaimal with his gun Sangram. After Jaimal's death, the Rajputs performed jauhar and fought to the last. The fort fell on 23 February 1568, and about 30,000 civilians were massacred. Akbar later put up statues of Jaimal and Patta at Agra Fort as a tribute. Elimination: Udai Singh fled, so (a) is wrong. Rana Pratap, his son, fought at Haldighati in 1576, so (b) is wrong. Bahman Shah is unrelated, being the founder of the Bahmani kingdom, so (c) is wrong. Only Jaimal fits.
explanations: Wrong: Udai Singh II left Chittor for the hills before the siege became severe and did not defend the fort.
Wrong: Rana Pratap was Udai Singh's son. He became Rana in 1572 and fought Akbar's forces at Haldighati in 1576, not at the 1567-68 siege.
Wrong: Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu, Alauddin Bahman Shah) founded the Bahmani Sultanate in the Deccan in 1347, which has no connection to Chittor.
Correct: Jaimal (Jaimal Rathore of Merta) commanded the garrison, with Patta of Kailwa, and defended Chittor until he was killed in the final phase of the siege.
keyfact: Chittor siege 1567-68: Jaimal and Patta defended; Udai Singh II had fled to the hills; fort fell on 23 Feb 1568.
option_notes: Udai Singh II (r. 1537-72) was a Sisodia ruler of Mewar and the father of Rana Pratap. He succeeded after Banbir's usurpation ended. He founded Udaipur around 1559 and moved his capital there. He refused to accept Akbar's suzerainty and abandoned Chittor in 1567 when it was besieged. He died at Gogunda in 1572.

Rana Pratap (1540-97) was the Sisodia ruler of Mewar from 1572. He refused to submit to Akbar and fought the Mughals under Man Singh at the Battle of Haldighati on 18 June 1576. His horse was Chetak. He later recovered much of Mewar except Chittor. He died at Chavand, which he had made his capital.

Bahman Shah, also called Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah or Hasan Gangu, founded the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347 after revolting against Muhammad bin Tughlaq. His capital was first Gulbarga, later moved to Bidar. The dynasty broke up into the five Deccan sultanates by about 1518. He has no link to Akbar or Chittor.

Jaimal (Jaimal Rathore) was a Rathore chieftain of Merta and a commander under Udai Singh II. He led Chittor's defence in 1567-68 with Patta of Kailwa. He was shot dead by Akbar, reportedly with the musket Sangram. His bravery was honoured when Akbar set up stone statues of Jaimal and Patta on elephants at the gate of Agra Fort.
related: Siege of Chittor: October 1567 to 23 February 1568.
Akbar's Chittor victory was commemorated with statues of Jaimal and Patta at Agra Fort.
Udai Singh II founded Udaipur and lived there after leaving Chittor.
Battle of Haldighati was fought on 18 June 1576 between Rana Pratap and Man Singh.
Ranthambhor fell to Akbar in 1569 and Rai Surjan Hada surrendered.
Alauddin Khalji captured Chittor in 1303 from Rana Ratan Singh.
Rani Karnavati performed jauhar at Chittor in 1535 during Bahadur Shah's attack.
Chittorgarh is part of the UNESCO Hill Forts of Rajasthan (2013).
summary: The answer is (d) Jaimal. In the siege of Chittor (October 1567 to February 1568), Akbar's army besieged the fort for about four months, and the Sisodia commander Jaimal (Jaimal Rathore of Merta), together with Patta (Fatta) of Kailwa, led the defence after Rana Udai Singh II had withdrawn to the hills.
topic_notes: Akbar's conquest of Rajasthan was a key part of Mughal expansion. Chittor, the Sisodia capital of Mewar, was the main obstacle. Akbar began the siege in October 1567 and the fort fell on 23 February 1568 after about four months. Udai Singh II had left for the hills, so Jaimal and Patta defended the fort. Akbar's sappers dug mines and sabats, and when Jaimal was killed, the Rajput women performed jauhar and the men rode out to die. Akbar ordered a massacre of about 30,000 people because the peasants had helped in the defence. Ranthambhor fell in 1569 to Akbar's forces, with Rai Surjan Hada surrendering, and Kalinjar fell in the same year. Marwar was taken in 1570 and Bikaner and Jaisalmer accepted Mughal overlordship, with marriage alliances. Amber's Bharmal was the first major Rajput ruler to ally with Akbar (1562), and his son Bhagwan Das and grandson Man Singh became top mansabdars. Mewar resisted under Rana Pratap, who fought at Haldighati (1576), and Rana Amar Singh finally made peace with Jahangir in 1615. Earlier sieges of Chittor: Alauddin Khalji in 1303 (Rani Padmini legend, Rana Ratan Singh) and Bahadur Shah of Gujarat in 1535 (Rani Karnavati's jauhar). The Chittor Fort is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2013, Hill Forts of Rajasthan). Other landmarks: Vijay Stambh by Rana Kumbha and Kirti Stambh.

question: Which one of the following statements is not correct?
options: Lord Wellesley set up the ﬁrst three Indian Universities
Lord Dalhousie introduced telegraph in India
Lord Ripon introduced a system of local selfgovernment both for towns and country-side areas
Lord Curzon presided over the Delhi Durbar of 1903
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The question asks for the statement that is NOT correct. Wellesley (Governor-General 1798-1805) is known for the Subsidiary Alliance, the Fort William College (1800) for training civil servants, and the wars against Tipu Sultan and the Marathas. He had nothing to do with universities. The modern university system came from Wood's Despatch (1854), called the 'Magna Carta of English Education in India', which recommended universities modelled on London University at the three presidency towns. Under Lord Canning, the University of Calcutta was founded on 24 January 1857, followed by Bombay and Madras the same year. Option (b) is correct: Dalhousie (1848-56) introduced the telegraph (first line 1851 Calcutta-Diamond Harbour, O'Shaughnessy), railways (1853 Bombay-Thane), and the postal reforms of 1854. Option (c) is correct: Ripon's Resolution of 1882 on local self-government earned him the title 'Father of Local Self-Government' in India. Option (d) is correct: Curzon presided over the Delhi Durbar of 1 January 1903 for Edward VII's coronation. Elimination: b, c, d are factually right, leaving a.
explanations: Incorrect statement, so it is the answer. The universities were established in 1857 under Canning following Wood's Despatch, not by Wellesley.
Correct statement. Dalhousie introduced the telegraph (1851 onwards) and a network linking major cities, so it is not the answer.
Correct statement. Ripon's 1882 resolution promoted elected local bodies in both urban (municipal) and rural (local boards) areas, so it is not the answer.
Correct statement. Curzon presided over the 1903 Delhi Durbar marking Edward VII's accession, so it is not the answer.
keyfact: Calcutta, Bombay and Madras universities (1857) came under Canning after Wood's Despatch 1854, not under Wellesley.
option_notes: Wellesley was Governor-General 1798-1805, known for the Subsidiary Alliance system, the defeat of Tipu Sultan in 1799 (Fourth Anglo-Mysore War), and the Second Anglo-Maratha War. He founded Fort William College in Calcutta in 1800. He did not found universities; Calcutta, Bombay and Madras universities date to 1857 under Canning.

Dalhousie was Governor-General 1848-56. He introduced the Doctrine of Lapse, the first railway line (Bombay-Thane, 1853), the telegraph (1851, W. B. O'Shaughnessy), the Post Office Act of 1854 with uniform postage, the Public Works Department, and endorsed Wood's Despatch. He annexed Punjab in 1849 and Awadh in 1856.

Ripon was Viceroy 1880-84. He repealed Lytton's Vernacular Press Act (1882), passed the Local Self-Government Resolution (1882), the first Factory Act (1881), the Hunter Commission on education (1882), and the Ilbert Bill controversy (1883). He is regarded as the Father of Local Self-Government in India.

Curzon was Viceroy 1899-1905. He held the 1903 Delhi Durbar, partitioned Bengal in 1905, passed the Indian Universities Act (1904), the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act (1904), set up the Archaeological Survey reforms under John Marshall, and the Police Commission under Fraser. He resigned in 1905 after a dispute with Kitchener.
related: Wood's Despatch 1854 is called the Magna Carta of English Education in India.
Calcutta, Bombay and Madras universities were founded in 1857.
Ripon is called the Father of Local Self-Government in India (Resolution 1882).
Delhi Durbars were held in 1877 (Lytton), 1903 (Curzon), 1911 (Hardinge, George V).
First railway in India ran from Bombay to Thane on 16 April 1853 under Dalhousie.
Indian Universities Act 1904 was passed under Curzon.
Fort William College was founded in 1800 by Wellesley.
summary: The incorrect statement is (a). The first three Indian universities (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras) were set up in 1857, after Wood's Despatch of 1854, during Lord Canning's tenure as Governor-General, not by Lord Wellesley, who ruled 1798-1805.
topic_notes: Governors-General and Viceroys are a favourite UPSC topic. Wellesley (1798-1805): Subsidiary Alliance, Fort William College. Cornwallis: Permanent Settlement (1793), civil service reform. William Bentinck (1828-35): abolition of Sati (1829), English as the medium via Macaulay's Minute (1835). Dalhousie (1848-56): Doctrine of Lapse, railways, telegraph, postal reform, Wood's Despatch (1854), Engineering college at Roorkee. Canning (1856-62): Revolt of 1857, last Governor-General and first Viceroy after the Government of India Act 1858; universities of Calcutta, Bombay, Madras founded 1857; Indian Councils Act 1861. Lytton (1876-80): Vernacular Press Act, Delhi Durbar 1877 (Queen Victoria proclaimed Empress), Arms Act. Ripon (1880-84): local self-government, Ilbert Bill, Hunter Commission. Dufferin: INC founded 1885. Lansdowne: Age of Consent Act 1891, Indian Councils Act 1892. Curzon (1899-1905): Delhi Durbar 1903, Partition of Bengal, Universities Act 1904, Imperial Cadet Corps. Minto (1905-10): Morley-Minto reforms 1909. Hardinge II: capital shifted to Delhi in 1911 (Delhi Durbar of George V, 1911), Bengal partition annulled. Chelmsford: Montagu-Chelmsford reforms 1919, Jallianwala Bagh. Irwin: Simon Commission, Gandhi-Irwin Pact. Delhi Durbars: 1877, 1903, 1911. Later universities: Allahabad, Punjab (1882), etc.

question: Which one of the following is the correct chronological sequence of the given dynas es of Delhi Sultanate?
options: Khaljis – Sayyids – Lodis – Tughlaqs (d) Tughlaqs – Khaljis – Sayyids – Lodis
subject: Computers
detail: The Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) was ruled by five dynasties in this order: Mamluk/Slave (1206–1290), Khalji (1290–1320), Tughlaq (1320–1414), Sayyid (1414–1451) and Lodi (1451–1526). The Khaljis began with Jalaluddin Khalji after the fall of the last Slave ruler, Kaikhusrau/Kayumars. Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) is the best-known Khalji ruler, noted for his market reforms and Deccan campaigns. Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founded the Tughlaq dynasty in 1320, and Muhammad bin Tughlaq shifted the capital to Daulatabad and introduced token currency. Timur's invasion of 1398 weakened the Tughlaqs. Khizr Khan, who claimed to be a Sayyid, founded the Sayyid dynasty in 1414. Bahlul Lodi founded the Lodi dynasty in 1451, and Ibrahim Lodi lost to Babur at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. Elimination: (a) puts Sayyids first, which is wrong. (c) puts Sayyids before Tughlaqs and Lodis before Tughlaqs, which is wrong. (d) puts Tughlaqs before Khaljis, which is wrong. Only (b) is correct. Note that the fourth line of the question text, 'Tulsidas-Guru Nanak Ramdas-Tukaram', is stray OCR text from another question and is not a valid option.
explanations: Incorrect: it places the Sayyids first, but they ruled from 1414, after the Khaljis and Tughlaqs.
Correct: Khaljis (1290–1320), Tughlaqs (1320–1414), Sayyids (1414–1451), Lodis (1451–1526) is the true order.
Incorrect: the Tughlaqs came before the Sayyids and Lodis, not after them.
Incorrect: the Khaljis preceded the Tughlaqs, so this order is reversed at the start.
keyfact: Delhi Sultanate order: Slave – Khalji – Tughlaq – Sayyid – Lodi (1206–1526).
option_notes: Sayyid dynasty (1414–1451): founded by Khizr Khan, who ruled as a deputy of Timur and never took the title of Sultan. Its rulers were Khizr Khan, Mubarak Shah, Muhammad Shah and Alauddin Alam Shah. The dynasty was weak and its territory was limited to Delhi and its surroundings. Alam Shah voluntarily handed power to Bahlul Lodi.

Khalji dynasty (1290–1320): founded by Jalaluddin Khalji, whose rise is called the 'Khalji Revolution'. Alauddin Khalji introduced price controls and market regulation, a standing army with the dagh (branding) and chehra (descriptive roll) systems, and conquered Gujarat, Chittor and Ranthambore.
