Malik Kafur led the southern campaigns. The last ruler was Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah, killed by Khusrau Khan.

Lodi dynasty (1451–1526): the first Afghan dynasty of Delhi, founded by Bahlul Lodi. Sikandar Lodi founded Agra in 1504 and introduced the gaz-i-Sikandari. Ibrahim Lodi was defeated and killed by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, ending the Sultanate and beginning Mughal rule.

Tughlaq dynasty (1320–1414): founded by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, who built Tughlaqabad. Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced token currency and moved the capital to Daulatabad. Firoz Shah Tughlaq built canals and the town of Firozabad. Timur sacked Delhi in 1398 during the reign of Nasiruddin Mahmud. Ibn Battuta visited India during this period.
related: Delhi Sultanate ran from 1206 (Aibak) to 1526 (First Battle of Panipat).
Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid dynasty in 1414 and nominally ruled for Timur.
Bahlul Lodi founded the Lodi dynasty in 1451 and Ibrahim Lodi was its last ruler.
Timur invaded Delhi in 1398 during the Tughlaq period.
Alauddin Khalji introduced price control and the dagh and chehra systems.
Sikandar Lodi founded Agra in 1504.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced token currency and shifted the capital to Daulatabad.
summary: The correct sequence is Khaljis (1290) – Tughlaqs (1320) – Sayyids (1414) – Lodis (1451), which is option (b). The Slave dynasty came before the Khaljis, and the Mughals replaced the Lodis in 1526.
topic_notes: The Delhi Sultanate lasted from 1206 to 1526 and had five dynasties. Slave/Mamluk (1206–1290): Qutbuddin Aibak, Iltutmish, Razia, Balban. Aibak began the Qutub Minar. Iltutmish introduced the silver tanka and the iqta system and organised the Chihalgani. Balban propounded the theory of kingship and introduced Sijda and Paibos. Khalji (1290–1320): Jalaluddin, Alauddin, Mubarak Shah. Alauddin's market reforms were described by Barani, and Amir Khusrau was a poet of this period. Tughlaq (1320–1414): Ghiyasuddin, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Firoz Shah. Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiments included the capital shift, token currency and the Doab tax. Firoz Shah founded Jaunpur, Hissar and Firozabad and introduced the Diwan-i-Khairat. Vijayanagara (1336) and the Bahmani kingdom (1347) arose during this period. Sayyid (1414–1451): Khizr Khan, Mubarak Shah, Muhammad Shah, Alam Shah. Lodi (1451–1526): Bahlul, Sikandar, Ibrahim. Key sources include Barani's Tarikh-i-Firozshahi, Minhaj-us-Siraj's Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, Ibn Battuta's Rihla and Amir Khusrau's works. Administration: the Sultan, with ministers such as the Wazir (Diwan-i-Wizarat), Ariz-i-Mumalik (military), Diwan-i-Risalat and Diwan-i-Insha. Architecture: Qutub Minar, Alai Darwaza, Tughlaqabad and the Lodi Gardens tombs. Currency: tanka (silver) and jital (copper).

question:
Consider the following statements: According to the Mountbatten Plan
1. The Union of India and Pakistan were to be granted freedom not later than June 1948.
2. The Legislative Assembly of Sindh was to decide whether it wanted to join the Constituent Assembly of India or not.
3. Baluchistan was to decide whether it wanted to stay with the Indian Union or become separate. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Computers
detail: The Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947) accepted the principle of Partition. It replaced the Cabinet Mission's June 1948 deadline, set in Attlee's statement of 20 February 1947, with an early transfer of power. The Indian Independence Act 1947 fixed the date as 15 August 1947. The plan said that Bengal and Punjab legislators would meet in two groups (Hindu-majority and Muslim-majority districts) to vote on partition. Sindh's Legislative Assembly would decide its own course. NWFP would hold a referendum. The Muslim-majority district of Sylhet in Assam would also hold a referendum. In Baluchistan, the Quetta Shahi Jirga and the non-official members of the Quetta Municipality were to decide whether to join India's or Pakistan's Constituent Assembly, so a separate option was not offered. The plan also proposed a Boundary Commission, chaired by Cyril Radcliffe, for Punjab and Bengal. Princely states were not covered by the plan; paramountcy would lapse. Elimination: statement 1 is wrong because of the 1948 date, which rules out (a) and (d). Statement 3 is wrong, which rules out (b). That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false because power was transferred in August 1947, not June 1948.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is false because Baluchistan had no option of separate status under the plan.
Right: only statement 2 matches the plan, since Sindh's Legislative Assembly was to decide its constituent assembly.
Wrong: it combines statements 1 and 3, and both are false.
keyfact: Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947): freedom on 15 Aug 1947, Sindh's assembly decided itself, Baluchistan's jirga chose between India and Pakistan.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2: this pairing is wrong because statement 1 is false. The June 1948 deadline came from Attlee's announcement of 20 February 1947. Mountbatten, who arrived as Viceroy on 22 March 1947, advanced the date to 15 August 1947, which was symbolically the anniversary of Japan's surrender in 1945. The Indian Independence Act was passed in July 1947.

Statements 2 and 3: this pairing is wrong because statement 3 is false. Baluchistan's decision was left to the Quetta Shahi Jirga and non-official members of the Quetta Municipality, who chose Pakistan on 29 June 1947. Kalat remained a separate princely state until 1948, when it acceded to Pakistan.

Statement 2 only: this is the correct option. The Sindh Legislative Assembly was to decide at a special session which Constituent Assembly to join. Sindh joined Pakistan. The plan also provided for referenda in NWFP and Sylhet, and for separate votes by the Bengal and Punjab legislatures on partition.

Statements 1 and 3: this pairing is wrong because both statements are false. The transfer of power took place in 1947, not 1948, and Baluchistan's decision rested with the Quetta Shahi Jirga and the municipality's non-official members, with options of joining India or Pakistan only.
related: Mountbatten became Viceroy on 22 March 1947 and was the last Viceroy and first Governor-General of independent India.
The 3 June 1947 Plan advanced the transfer of power to 15 August 1947.
The Radcliffe Boundary Commission award was announced on 17 August 1947.
NWFP and Sylhet held referenda in July 1947.
The Indian Independence Act 1947 received royal assent on 18 July 1947.
Attlee's 20 February 1947 statement fixed June 1948 as the deadline for the transfer of power.
Baluchistan's choice was made by the Quetta Shahi Jirga on 29 June 1947.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Mountbatten Plan advanced independence to 15 August 1947. The June 1948 date came from Attlee's statement of 20 February 1947. The Indian Independence Act received royal assent on 18 July 1947. It created the two dominions of India and Pakistan from 15 August 1947 and ended British paramountcy over the princely states. Both dominions initially had Mountbatten and then Jinnah as Governor-General, with Mountbatten staying in India. The speed of the transfer was widely criticised for the violence that accompanied Partition.

2 — Correct: The plan provided that the Sindh Legislative Assembly would meet and decide, at a special session, whether to join the existing Constituent Assembly or a new one. Sindh opted for Pakistan in June 1947. Its legislators had already shown strong Muslim League leanings, and the province later became part of Pakistan. NWFP was handled differently, with a referendum in July 1947 in which the Pathans voted for Pakistan, although the Congress-led Khan Brothers boycotted it.

3 — Incorrect: Baluchistan was not given a free choice to stay with India or become separate. The plan said the Quetta Shahi Jirga and the non-official members of the Quetta Municipality would decide on joining India's or Pakistan's Constituent Assembly. On 29 June 1947 they chose Pakistan. The Kalat princely state, under the Khan of Kalat, briefly declared independence on 15 August 1947 but was annexed by Pakistan in March 1948. British Baluchistan was a Chief Commissioner's province.
summary: The answer is (c) 2 only. Under the Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947), the Sindh Legislative Assembly was to decide at a special session whether to join the existing Constituent Assembly of India or a new one. Statements 1 and 3 are wrong: power was transferred on 15 August 1947, not June 1948, and Baluchistan's fate was not left to a free choice between staying in India or becoming separate.
topic_notes: The Mountbatten Plan, also called the 3 June Plan or the Dickie Bird Plan, was announced on 3 June 1947 by Viceroy Lord Mountbatten after consultation with Congress and League leaders. Mountbatten had replaced Wavell in March 1947. Earlier, Attlee's statement of 20 February 1947 had promised a transfer of power by June 1948. The main provisions were as follows. India would be partitioned into India and Pakistan. The legislative assemblies of Bengal and Punjab would meet in two sections to vote on partition, and if either section voted for it, the province would be divided. Sindh's assembly would decide for itself. NWFP and the Sylhet district of Assam would hold referenda. Baluchistan's decision would be made by the Quetta Shahi Jirga and the non-official members of the Quetta Municipality. A Boundary Commission would demarcate borders, and the Radcliffe Award was announced on 17 August 1947. Princely states would become free of paramountcy and could join either dominion, and Britain would not recognise their independence. The Indian Independence Act 1947 received royal assent on 18 July 1947 and took effect on 15 August 1947. The Congress accepted the plan at the AICC meeting of 14-15 June 1947, and the Muslim League also accepted it. Related events include the Cabinet Mission (1946), Direct Action Day (16 August 1946), the Interim Government (September 1946), and the Simla Conference (1945). Likely exam angles are dates, personalities and the provisions on provinces and princely states. The Partition Council and the Punjab Boundary Force are also worth knowing.

question: In the year 1919, what was the reason for Mahatma Gandhi to warn the Viceroy that a countrywide Satyagraha would be launched?
options: He wanted the Government to withdraw the Rowla Act immediately
He was forcing the British rulers to be sensi ve to the Khilafat Movement
He wanted the Government to abolish the Zamindari System to alleviate the miseries of peasants
He was forcing the British rulers to give at least the dominion status to India to make Home Rule possible
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: The Rowlatt Act was passed on 18 March 1919 by the Imperial Legislative Council, despite unanimous opposition from the Indian members. It followed the recommendations of the Sedition Committee chaired by Justice Sidney Rowlatt (1918). It allowed arrest without warrant, detention without trial for up to two years, in-camera trials and no appeal. Gandhi called it a 'black act'. He had formed the Satyagraha Sabha in Bombay in February 1919 and pledged resistance. He appealed to the Viceroy to withdraw the Bill and, when this failed, launched a nationwide hartal on 6 April 1919. Protests followed, and Punjab saw the arrest of Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal. This led to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on 13 April 1919 under General Dyer. Elimination: the Khilafat Movement began in 1919-20 and Gandhi's non-cooperation came in 1920, so (b) is wrong. Zamindari abolition was not a 1919 Gandhian demand (Champaran 1917 dealt with indigo, tinkathia system), so (c) is wrong. Dominion status and Home Rule was not the 1919 trigger, so (d) is wrong.
explanations: Correct: Gandhi's Satyagraha threat in 1919 was directed against the Rowlatt Act, which he wanted withdrawn.

Wrong: the Khilafat issue gained momentum after the war and the Treaty of Sevres (1920). Gandhi took up the cause with the All India Khilafat Conference in November 1919 and non-cooperation in 1920, but it was not the trigger for the Satyagraha warning.
Wrong: Gandhi did not demand abolition of the Zamindari system in 1919. His peasant campaigns were Champaran (1917) and Kheda (1918), which dealt with specific grievances.
Wrong: Dominion status and Home Rule were the focus of the Home Rule Leagues (1916) and the Montagu Declaration (1917), not of Gandhi's 1919 Satyagraha warning.
keyfact: Gandhi's 1919 Satyagraha threat was against the Rowlatt Act (the 'Black Act'), his first all-India mass agitation.
option_notes: The Rowlatt Act (Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, 1919) was passed on 18 March 1919 on the basis of the Rowlatt Committee report. It allowed detention without trial and trial without a jury. It was called the 'Black Act' and 'No dalil, no vakil, no appeal'. It led to the Rowlatt Satyagraha and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. It was repealed in 1922.

The Khilafat Movement (1919-24) was led by Muslims, mainly Ali brothers Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, and Maulana Azad, to protect the Ottoman Caliph's position after World War I. Gandhi joined it and linked it with non-cooperation in 1920. The movement ended when Turkey's Kemal Ataturk abolished the Caliphate in 1924.

The Zamindari system was introduced by the Permanent Settlement of 1793 under Cornwallis in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Zamindars were hereditary revenue collectors and owners of the land. It was abolished after independence by state laws in the 1950s. Gandhi's earlier peasant movements were Champaran in 1917 and Kheda in 1918.

Dominion status means self-governing status within the British Empire. The Home Rule Leagues were founded in 1916 by Tilak (April, Poona) and Annie Besant (September, Madras). The August Declaration of 1917 by Montagu promised 'responsible government'. The Nehru Report of 1928 demanded dominion status, and the Lahore Congress of 1929 demanded Purna Swaraj.
related: Rowlatt Act passed on 18 March 1919.
Rowlatt Committee was headed by Justice Sidney Rowlatt.
Satyagraha Sabha was formed by Gandhi on 24 February 1919.
Hartal against the Rowlatt Act took place on 6 April 1919.
Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar.
Hunter Committee was set up to investigate the Punjab disturbances.
Gandhi called off the Rowlatt Satyagraha, calling it a 'Himalayan blunder'.
Chauri Chaura incident of February 1922 led to withdrawal of non-cooperation.
summary: The answer is (a). In 1919 Gandhi warned the Viceroy (Lord Chelmsford) that a countrywide Satyagraha would be launched if the Rowlatt Act (Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, 1919) was not withdrawn. The Act allowed detention without trial and curbs on the press.
topic_notes: The Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919) was Gandhi's first all-India mass movement. Background: WWI ended, and Indians expected reforms. Instead, the Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford reforms) and repressive laws came. The Rowlatt Committee (1917-18) recommended extension of wartime emergency powers. The Act was passed on 18 March 1919 despite opposition by Jinnah, Madan Mohan Malaviya and Mazhar-ul-Haq, who resigned from the Council. Gandhi launched the Satyagraha Sabha on 24 February 1919, and a hartal was called on 6 April and later extended. Violence broke out in Delhi, Punjab, Ahmedabad and Bombay, and Gandhi called off the movement, calling it a 'Himalayan blunder'. In Amritsar, the arrest of Kitchlew and Satyapal on 10 April led to riots. On 13 April 1919, General Reginald Dyer fired on a crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, killing hundreds. The Hunter Committee (1919) was set up to inquire, and Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood in protest. Gandhi returned his Kaiser-i-Hind medal. The Congress held its Amritsar session in December 1919 under Motilal Nehru. The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) followed, which ended after the Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922). Earlier Gandhi movements: Champaran (1917), Ahmedabad mill strike (1918), Kheda (1918).

question: Who among the following introduced the celebration of Ganesh Chaturthi and Shivaji Festivals to bring the Indian society together and inspire patriotic feelings among the people?
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: Bal Gangadhar Tilak (1856-1920), called 'Lokmanya' and the 'Father of Indian Unrest' by Valentine Chirol, was the leading Extremist (Garam Dal) leader of the Indian National Congress. Political meetings were restricted under colonial law, so he used religious and cultural occasions as platforms for mass mobilisation. In 1893 he started public Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations in Pune (Ganesh Utsav), and in 1895 the Shivaji Festival, to invoke the memory of Chhatrapati Shivaji as a symbol of resistance to foreign rule. He edited the newspapers Kesari (Marathi) and Mahratta (English), and gave the slogan 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it'. He founded the Home Rule League in 1916 and was a signatory to the Lucknow Pact of 1916. Elimination: Gokhale and Ranade were Moderates who favoured constitutional, reformist methods; Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society (1905), and Ranade was a social reformer associated with the Prarthana Samaj. Phule led the anti-caste Satyashodhak Samaj (1873), and he opposed Brahmanical dominance, so he is not linked to these festivals.
explanations: Correct. Tilak launched public Ganesh Utsav (1893) and the Shivaji festival (1895) in Maharashtra to build unity and nationalism.
Wrong. Gokhale was a Moderate, Tilak's rival at the 1907 Surat split, and he founded the Servants of India Society in 1905. He did not start these festivals.
Wrong. Jyotirao Phule was a social reformer who founded the Satyashodhak Samaj and fought caste discrimination. He criticised Brahmin-dominated politics and was not behind these festivals.
Wrong. Ranade was a judge and social reformer who co-founded the Prarthana Samaj and wrote on Indian economics. He is not linked with these festivals.
keyfact: Tilak: Ganesh Utsav 1893, Shivaji festival 1895, Kesari and Mahratta, Home Rule League 1916.
option_notes: Bal Gangadhar Tilak (1856-1920) was born in Ratnagiri and led the Extremists in the Congress. He edited Kesari and Mahratta and wrote The Arctic Home in the Vedas and Gita Rahasya. He founded the Home Rule League (April 1916, Pune) and was jailed for sedition in 1897 and 1908 (Mandalay). He died on 1 August 1920.

Gopal Krishna Gokhale (1866-1915) was a Moderate Congress leader and the political guru of Gandhi. He founded the Servants of India Society in 1905, presided over the Congress at Banaras in 1905, and was a member of the Imperial Legislative Council. He was associated with Ranade and with the Deccan Education Society, and he opposed the 1907 split of the Congress.

Jyotirao Govind Rao Phule (1827-1890) was a social reformer from Maharashtra. He opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848 with his wife Savitribai, and founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873. He wrote Gulamgiri and Sarvajanik Satyadharma, and he campaigned for lower-caste and women's education and for widow remarriage.

Mahadev Govind Ranade (1842-1901) was a judge, scholar and social reformer, called the 'Maharashtra Socrates'. He co-founded the Prarthana Samaj (1867) with Atmaram Pandurang, started the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha and the Deccan Education Society, and founded the Widow Remarriage Association. He is known for his work on Indian economics and the 'Indian Economic Thought' school, and he promoted the National Social Conference (1887).
related: Tilak started Ganesh Utsav in 1893 and the Shivaji festival in 1895.
Tilak's newspapers: Kesari (Marathi) and Mahratta (English).
Tilak's slogan: 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it'.
Tilak founded the Home Rule League in April 1916 at Pune.
Lucknow Pact 1916: Congress-Muslim League agreement, with Tilak's role.
Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in 1905.
Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873.
Ranade co-founded the Prarthana Samaj in 1867.
summary: The answer is (a) Bal Gangadhar Tilak. In 1893 he transformed the private household Ganesh Chaturthi into a large public festival, and in 1895 he began the Shivaji festival at Raigad, to unite people across castes and spread nationalist feeling against British rule.
topic_notes: Tilak and the Extremist phase: After the Partition of Bengal (1905), the Swadeshi movement and Boycott brought Extremists (Lal-Bal-Pal: Lala Lajpat Rai, Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal) to the fore. The Surat session of 1907 split the Congress between Moderates and Extremists; the two sides reunited only at Lucknow in 1916. Tilak was tried for sedition in 1897 for speeches on Shivaji and the Afzal Khan killing, and again in 1908 for writings praising the Muzaffarpur bomb attack, which led to six years of imprisonment in Mandalay. He established the Home Rule League in April 1916, and Annie Besant launched hers in Madras in September 1916. His books include The Arctic Home in the Vedas and Gita Rahasya, which he wrote in Mandalay. He died on 1 August 1920, the day the Non-Cooperation Movement began. Gandhi called him the 'Maker of Modern India'. Other related points: the Deccan Education Society was founded in 1884 by Tilak, Agarkar and Chiplunkar, and Fergusson College was set up in Pune. Tilak also used festivals as political platforms: the Ganapati festival in 1893 and the Shivaji festival in 1895 with the aim of mass mobilisation. Moderates such as Dadabhai Naoroji, Gokhale, Ranade and Pherozeshah Mehta believed in the 'Prayer, Petition and Protest' method and in British justice, whereas Extremists wanted Swaraj and direct action. Reformers like Phule worked on caste and women's emancipation, and Ranade worked on widow remarriage and other social reform through the Prarthana Samaj.

question:
Which one of the following is the correct
chronological sequence of the given Bhak
Saints?
(a) Guru Nanak-Tulsidas Ramdas Tukaram
(b) Tulsidas-Guru Nanak Tukaram-Ramdas
(c) Guru Nanak-Tulsidas Tukaram-Ramdas
subject: Computers
detail: The question tests the order of Bhakti saints by lifetime. Guru Nanak, founder of Sikhism, was born in 1469 at Talwandi (Nankana Sahib) and died in 1539 at Kartarpur. Tulsidas, author of Ramcharitmanas (written in Awadhi, begun 1574), lived c.1532-1623 and belonged to the Ram-bhakti saguna tradition. The two Maharashtra saints were contemporaries of Shivaji's era. Tukaram (c.1608-1650) was a Varkari saint of Dehu who composed abhangas devoted to Vithoba of Pandharpur. Samarth Ramdas (1608-1681), author of Dasbodh, was associated with Shivaji as his spiritual guide. Elimination: Tulsidas cannot come before Guru Nanak, which rules out (b). The only difference between (a) and (c) is the order of Ramdas and Tukaram. Tukaram died in 1650 and Ramdas in 1681, and Tukaram is conventionally placed first, so (c) is correct. Option (d) simply repeats the label form and is not a valid sequence. Note that the OCR'd options show hyphens separating pairs, so each option reads as a four-name sequence.
explanations: Wrong: places Ramdas before Tukaram. Tukaram's life and death (1650) precede Ramdas (1681), so the order is reversed.
Wrong: puts Tulsidas before Guru Nanak, but Nanak was born in 1469, about six decades before Tulsidas.
Correct: Guru Nanak, Tulsidas, Tukaram, Ramdas follows the order of birth and death dates.
Wrong: (d) is not a distinct sequence in the question; it is an OCR artefact and gives no valid order.
keyfact: Order: Guru Nanak (1469) < Tulsidas (c.1532) < Tukaram (1608-50) < Ramdas (1608-81).
option_notes: Sequence Nanak-Tulsidas-Ramdas-Tukaram. Ramdas (1608-1681) wrote Dasbodh and Manache Shlok, founded the Samarth sampradaya and had Chaphal as a base. He is linked with Shivaji. This order is wrong only because Tukaram died earlier (1650).

Sequence Tulsidas-Nanak-Tukaram-Ramdas. Tulsidas (c.1532-1623) wrote Ramcharitmanas, Vinaya Patrika and Kavitavali, and lived during Akbar's reign in Varanasi. Putting him before Nanak (1469-1539) is wrong, so this option fails.

Sequence Nanak-Tulsidas-Tukaram-Ramdas. Guru Nanak taught Ik Onkar, Nam japna, Kirat karni and Vand chhakna, and started langar. Tukaram (Dehu, Pune) was a Varkari poet whose abhangas are in Marathi. This is the correct order.
Option (d) is an OCR repeat of the option labels and has no sequence of its own. It should not be selected. The real options are (a) to (c), and the correct one is (c).
related: Guru Nanak: born 1469 at Talwandi, died 1539 at Kartarpur.
Tulsidas wrote Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi.
Tukaram was a Varkari saint who composed abhangas in praise of Vithoba.
Ramdas wrote Dasbodh and was Shivaji's spiritual guide.
Ramanuja propounded Vishishtadvaita; Madhva propounded Dvaita.
Chaitanya (1486-1534) was a saint of Bengal who popularised Krishna bhakti.
Jnaneshwar wrote the Jnaneshwari, a Marathi commentary on the Gita.
summary: The correct chronological order is Guru Nanak (1469-1539), Tulsidas (c.1532-1623), Tukaram (c.1608-1650), Ramdas (1608-1681). This is option (c). Tukaram is placed before Ramdas because he died earlier (1650 against 1681), and both were born around 1608.
topic_notes: The Bhakti movement was a medieval devotional movement that stressed personal devotion to God over ritual, and it rejected caste hierarchy to varying degrees. It began in the Tamil country with the Alvars (Vishnu) and Nayanars (Shiva), and moved north from the 13th-15th centuries. Key saints and dates: Ramanuja (c.1017-1137, Vishishtadvaita), Madhva (1238-1317, Dvaita), Ramananda (14th-15th century, a disciple of Ramanuja's line who taught in Hindi), Kabir (c.1440-1518, nirguna), Ravidas, Chaitanya (1486-1534, Bengal, Gaudiya Vaishnavism), Vallabhacharya (1479-1531, Pushtimarga), Mirabai (c.1498-1546, devoted to Krishna), Surdas (Sur Sagar), Guru Nanak (1469-1539), Tulsidas (c.1532-1623), Eknath (1533-1599), Tukaram (c.1608-1650), Ramdas (1608-1681), Namdev (c.1270-1350), Jnaneshwar (1275-1296, Jnaneshwari, a commentary on the Gita), and Shankaradeva (1449-1568, Assam). Maharashtra's Varkari tradition centres on Pandharpur and Vithoba. Sufi movements ran in parallel: Chishti (Moinuddin Chishti, Nizamuddin Auliya) and Suhrawardi orders. Distinguish saguna bhakti (Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai) from nirguna bhakti (Kabir, Nanak, Dadu). Likely questions: authorship of works, language used, and the philosophical school associated with each saint.

question:
Match List-I. (Persons) with List-II (Writings) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: LIST I (Persons) LIST II (Wri ngs) A. Asvaghosha
1. Buddha Charita B. Nagarjuna
2. Madhyamika Sutra C. Patanjali
3. Vedanta Sangraha D. Ramanuja
4. Yogasutra Code: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a straightforward author-work matching question from ancient Indian literature and philosophy. Asvaghosha, a court poet-philosopher at the time of Kanishka (Kushana period, 1st-2nd century CE), wrote the Sanskrit epic poem Buddha Charita, as well as Saundarananda and the play Sariputraprakarana. Nagarjuna (c. 2nd century CE), a Mahayana Buddhist from the Satavahana region, founded the Madhyamika (Shunyavada) school and is credited with the Madhyamaka Karika, here called Madhyamika Sutra. Patanjali compiled the Yogasutra, the foundation of the Yoga school, and also wrote the Mahabhashya commentary on Panini. Ramanuja (11th-12th century), the exponent of Vishishtadvaita, wrote Sri Bhashya, Vedartha Sangraha, Vedanta Sara and Vedanta Dipa; the Vedanta Sangraha is associated with him in this question. Elimination: Buddha Charita clearly goes with Asvaghosha, which removes (a) and (c). Yogasutra with Patanjali then leaves only (b) rather than (d), where Nagarjuna and Ramanuja are swapped.
explanations: Wrong: it gives Asvaghosha the Yogasutra and Patanjali the Buddha Charita, which is a reversal.
Correct: it matches all four pairs, A-1, B-2, C-4, D-3.
Wrong: it gives Asvaghosha the Yogasutra and Patanjali the Buddha Charita, which is incorrect.
Wrong: A-1 and C-4 are right, but B-3 and D-2 swap Nagarjuna's and Ramanuja's works.
keyfact: Asvaghosha: Buddha Charita; Nagarjuna: Madhyamika; Patanjali: Yogasutra; Ramanuja: Vedanta Sangraha.
option_notes: Option (a) 4-3-1-2 would give Asvaghosha the Yogasutra, which is wrong. The Yogasutra is Patanjali's text on the Yoga school, with 195 sutras and the eight limbs of yoga, namely yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana and samadhi. The Buddha Charita is Asvaghosha's life of the Buddha in Sanskrit verse, written in the Kushana period.

Option (b) 1-2-4-3 is correct. Asvaghosha wrote the Buddha Charita, Nagarjuna the Madhyamika work on Shunyavada, Patanjali the Yogasutra, and Ramanuja the Vedanta Sangraha. Together these represent Buddhist poetry, Mahayana philosophy, the Yoga school and Vishishtadvaita Vedanta.

Option (c) 4-2-1-3 is wrong because it gives Asvaghosha the Yogasutra and Patanjali the Buddha Charita. Only B-2 and D-3 are right. Patanjali's Yogasutra and the Mahabhashya are distinct works, and neither concerns the Buddha's life, which is Asvaghosha's subject.

Option (d) 1-3-4-2 is wrong. Asvaghosha and Patanjali are correct, but Nagarjuna did not write the Vedanta Sangraha, since he was a Buddhist Madhyamika. Ramanuja was a Vaishnava Vedantin and is not credited with the Madhyamika Sutra. Such swaps between Buddhist and Vedantic authors are a common UPSC trap.
related: Fourth Buddhist Council was held under Kanishka in Kashmir, presided over by Vasumitra with Asvaghosha as deputy.
Charaka was the court physician of Kanishka and wrote the Charaka Samhita.
Ramanuja propounded Vishishtadvaita; Shankara propounded Advaita; Madhva propounded Dvaita.
Patanjali's Mahabhashya is a commentary on Panini's Ashtadhyayi.
Kalhana's Rajatarangini is a chronicle of Kashmir kings.
Buddhaghosha wrote Visuddhimagga in Pali.
Nagarjuna's Madhyamika school is called Shunyavada.
statements: A-1 — Correct: Asvaghosha composed the Buddha Charita. He was a Brahmin convert to Buddhism and a contemporary of the Kushana king Kanishka. The Buddha Charita is an epic (mahakavya) on the life of the Buddha in Sanskrit, and was later translated into Chinese and Tibetan. He also wrote Saundarananda and the Sariputraprakarana drama, and is often called the first Sanskrit dramatist.

B-2 — Correct: Nagarjuna is linked with the Madhyamika school, whose doctrine is Shunyata (emptiness) and which is often described as a middle path. His chief work is the Madhyamaka Karika (Mulamadhyamakakarika). He is believed to have lived near Nagarjunakonda in Andhra, during Satavahana times. He is also said to have written the Suhrllekha, a letter to a king.

C-4 — Correct: Patanjali compiled the Yogasutra, the base text of the Yoga darshana, which has 195 sutras in four padas (Samadhi, Sadhana, Vibhuti, Kaivalya) and describes the eight-limbed (Ashtanga) yoga. A grammarian of the same name wrote the Mahabhashya on Panini's Ashtadhyayi in the Shunga period, under Pushyamitra.

D-3 — Correct: Ramanuja (c. 1017-1137) was a Vaishnava acharya from Sriperumbudur in Tamil Nadu who taught Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism). His works include Sri Bhashya, a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, Vedartha Sangraha, Vedanta Sara, Vedanta Dipa and a commentary on the Gita. He spent his later life at Srirangam and opposed Shankara's Advaita.
summary: The correct answer is (b): A-1, B-2, C-4, D-3. Asvaghosha wrote the Buddha Charita, Nagarjuna propounded the Madhyamika (Madhyamaka) philosophy in the Madhyamaka Karika/Sutra, Patanjali compiled the Yogasutra, and Ramanuja wrote the Vedanta Sangraha.
topic_notes: Ancient Indian authors and works are a frequent matching topic. Buddhist: Asvaghosha (Buddha Charita, Saundarananda), Nagarjuna (Madhyamaka Karika, Shunyavada), Vasubandhu (Abhidharmakosha, Yogachara), Dignaga (Pramanasamuccaya), Buddhaghosha (Visuddhimagga, Pali commentator), Dharmakirti. Philosophy: Shankara (Advaita, Brahma Sutra Bhashya), Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita, Sri Bhashya), Madhva (Dvaita), Nimbarka (Dvaitadvaita), Vallabha (Shuddhadvaita). Six darshanas and their founders: Nyaya (Gautama), Vaisheshika (Kanada), Sankhya (Kapila), Yoga (Patanjali), Purva Mimamsa (Jaimini), Uttara Mimamsa/Vedanta (Badarayana). Grammar: Panini (Ashtadhyayi), Patanjali (Mahabhashya), Katyayana (Varttika). Classical Sanskrit: Kalidasa (Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha), Shudraka (Mricchakatika), Vishakhadatta (Mudrarakshasa), Bana (Harshacharita, Kadambari), Bhasa (Svapnavasavadatta), Kalhana (Rajatarangini), Jayadeva (Gita Govinda), Dandin (Dashakumaracharita), Amarasimha (Amarakosha). Science: Aryabhata (Aryabhatiya), Varahamihira (Brihat Samhita, Panchasiddhantika), Brahmagupta (Brahmasphutasiddhanta), Charaka (Charaka Samhita), Sushruta (Sushruta Samhita). Kushana-era patrons: Kanishka sponsored the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir under Vasumitra and Asvaghosha, and Charaka was his court physician. Remember who belongs to which tradition and period, since exams swap authors between Buddhist, Vedantic and literary categories.

question:
Match List-I. (Historical Sites) with List-II (State) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: LIST I (Historical Site) LIST II (State) A. Shore Temple
1. Karnataka B. Bhimbetka
2. Tamil Nadu C. Kesava Temple
3. Kerala (Hoysala Monument) D. Hampi
4. Madhya Pradesh
5. Rajasthan Code: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This question tests the location of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India. The Shore Temple at Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram) was built by the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) in the early 8th century CE. It is part of the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, inscribed in 1984. Bhimbetka rock shelters lie near Bhopal (Raisen district), Madhya Pradesh, and were inscribed in 2003. They hold Mesolithic and earlier paintings. The Kesava Temple at Somanathapura (Mysuru district, Karnataka) was built around 1268 CE by Somanatha, a general of the Hoysala king Narasimha III. It is a star-shaped trikuta temple, and the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas were inscribed in 2023. Hampi, the Vijayanagara capital on the Tungabhadra, is in Karnataka and was inscribed in 1986. Elimination: Hampi is Karnataka (1) and the Hoysala temple is Karnataka (1), so any option giving Hampi a different state, or the Hoysala temple a state other than Karnataka, fails. Options (a), (c) and (d) all do this or place the Shore Temple in Kerala or Bhimbetka in Rajasthan, so only (b) works.
explanations: Wrong: it places the Shore Temple in Kerala (3) and Bhimbetka in Rajasthan (5). The Shore Temple is in Tamil Nadu and Bhimbetka is in Madhya Pradesh.
Correct: A-2 (Tamil Nadu), B-4 (Madhya Pradesh), C-1 (Karnataka), D-1 (Karnataka). Every pairing matches.
Wrong: it places the Shore Temple in Kerala (3) and the Hoysala Kesava Temple in Tamil Nadu (2). The Shore Temple is in Tamil Nadu and the Hoysala temple is in Karnataka.
Wrong: it places Bhimbetka in Rajasthan (5) and Hampi in Madhya Pradesh (4). Bhimbetka is in Madhya Pradesh and Hampi is in Karnataka.
keyfact: Shore Temple - Tamil Nadu; Bhimbetka - Madhya Pradesh; Hoysala Kesava Temple (Somanathapura) and Hampi - Karnataka.
option_notes: Code 3-5-2-1 would give Shore Temple-Kerala, Bhimbetka-Rajasthan, Kesava Temple-Tamil Nadu, Hampi-Karnataka. Only the last pair is right. Kerala's heritage is mostly temples and palaces such as Padmanabhaswamy, plus Mattancherry and the Jew Town. Rajasthan's UNESCO sites include Jantar Mantar (Jaipur), Amber and the other hill forts, Keoladeo, and Kalbeliya-related heritage. The Kesava Temple is not in Tamil Nadu.

Code 2-4-1-1 is the correct combination. The Shore Temple (Tamil Nadu), Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh), Kesava Temple at Somanathapura (Karnataka) and Hampi (Karnataka) are all matched correctly. All four sites are UNESCO World Heritage Sites or part of one: Mahabalipuram (1984), Hampi (1986), Bhimbetka (2003), Hoysala ensembles (2023).

Code 3-4-2-2 would give Shore Temple-Kerala, Bhimbetka-Madhya Pradesh, Kesava Temple-Tamil Nadu, Hampi-Tamil Nadu. Only Bhimbetka is right. Tamil Nadu's real sites include the Great Living Chola Temples (Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram, Darasuram), Mahabalipuram and the Nilgiri Mountain Railway. Hampi is in Karnataka, not Tamil Nadu.

Code 2-5-1-4 would give Shore Temple-Tamil Nadu, Bhimbetka-Rajasthan, Kesava Temple-Karnataka, Hampi-Madhya Pradesh. Only the first and third pairs are right. Madhya Pradesh's UNESCO sites are Sanchi, Khajuraho, Bhimbetka, and the Archaeological Park of Champaner is in Gujarat, not MP. Hampi is not in MP. Bhimbetka is not in Rajasthan.
related: Shore Temple, Mamallapuram: Pallava king Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), 8th century, Tamil Nadu.
Bhimbetka rock shelters: Madhya Pradesh, UNESCO site since 2003.
Kesava Temple, Somanathapura: Hoysala, c. 1268 CE, Karnataka.
Hampi: Vijayanagara capital, UNESCO site since 1986, on the Tungabhadra.
Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (Belur, Halebidu, Somanathapura) inscribed by UNESCO in 2023.
Sanchi Stupa, Madhya Pradesh: UNESCO site since 1989.
Pancha Rathas at Mamallapuram are monolithic Pallava rock-cut structures.
Battle of Talikota (1565) ended Vijayanagara power.
statements: A — Correct match with 2 (Tamil Nadu): The Shore Temple stands on the Bay of Bengal coast at Mamallapuram. It was built by the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) in the 8th century CE. It is a structural granite temple with two Shiva shrines and one Vishnu shrine. It is part of the UNESCO Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram (1984), which also has the Pancha Rathas and Arjuna's Penance.

B — Correct match with 4 (Madhya Pradesh): Bhimbetka rock shelters are in the Vindhya foothills near Bhopal, in Raisen district. They contain over 700 shelters with paintings from the Mesolithic period and later. The site is linked with Palaeolithic occupation. It was discovered by V.S. Wakankar in 1957 and inscribed as a UNESCO site in 2003.

C — Correct match with 1 (Karnataka): The Kesava Temple at Somanathapura was built around 1268 CE under the Hoysala king Narasimha III. It is a triple-shrined (trikuta) temple on a star-shaped platform and is dedicated to Vishnu. Other Hoysala masterpieces are the Chennakesava temple at Belur and the Hoysaleswara temple at Halebidu. The Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas were inscribed by UNESCO in 2023.

D — Correct match with 1 (Karnataka): Hampi is in Vijayanagara (formerly Bellary) district on the Tungabhadra river. It was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka. Its monuments include the Virupaksha temple, the Vitthala temple with its stone chariot, and the Lotus Mahal. The empire fell after the Battle of Talikota (1565). Hampi was inscribed by UNESCO in 1986.
summary: The correct answer is (b): A-2, B-4, C-1, D-1. The Shore Temple is at Mamallapuram in Tamil Nadu, Bhimbetka is in Madhya Pradesh, and the Hoysala Kesava Temple (Somanathapura) and Hampi are both in Karnataka.
topic_notes: Indian World Heritage Sites are a staple of the General Awareness section. Tamil Nadu has Mahabalipuram (1984), the Great Living Chola Temples (1987, 2004), and the Mountain Railways of India (Nilgiri). Karnataka has Hampi (1986), Pattadakal (1987) and the Western Ghats (shared with others, 2012). The Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (Belur, Halebidu, Somanathapura) were inscribed in 2023. Madhya Pradesh has Sanchi Stupa (1989), Khajuraho (1986), Bhimbetka (2003), and the Chandela Khajuraho temples. Hoysala architecture uses soapstone and stellate (star-shaped) platforms, and the dynasty was founded by Sala (capital Belur, later Halebidu). The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka, and its famous ruler was Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva dynasty (1509-1529). Pallava art includes rock-cut mandapas, monolithic rathas (Pancha Rathas) and structural temples (Shore Temple, Kailasanatha at Kanchipuram). Bhimbetka contains paintings in red and white pigments showing hunting, dancing and animals, with the oldest dating to the Mesolithic. Other inscriptions to remember: Ajanta and Ellora (1983, Maharashtra), Agra Fort and Taj Mahal (1983), Konark Sun Temple (1984, Odisha), Elephanta Caves (1987, Maharashtra), Qutub Minar (1993), Humayun's Tomb (1993), and Dholavira (2021, Gujarat). UNESCO inscription criteria are cultural (i-vi) and natural (vii-x). The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) manages most protected monuments under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958.

question: Which country among the following is the biggest producer of co on?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Cotton (Gossypium) is the most important natural fibre crop and a major kharif cash crop in India. World production is concentrated in a few countries. China is the top producer, mainly in Xinjiang, which now supplies about 85-90% of Chinese output. India ranks second and has the largest area under cotton, about 120-130 lakh hectares, but its yield per hectare is lower than China's, Brazil's or Australia's. The USA ranks third and is the largest exporter of raw cotton, with Brazil also a major exporter. Other producers are Brazil, Pakistan, Uzbekistan, Australia and Turkey. Indonesia grows very little cotton and imports most of what its textile industry needs. To answer: China leads in production. India leads in area, which is a common trap behind option (b). The USA leads in exports, which is the trap behind (d). Indonesia is a textile importer, so (c) is wrong. Ranks shift slightly between years, but China has been first for decades. India's main cotton states are Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Haryana, Punjab and Rajasthan. Cotton needs black (regur) soil, 21°C or more of temperature, a frost-free period of about 210 days and moderate rainfall.
explanations: Correct. China is the world's largest cotton producer, with output concentrated in Xinjiang.
Wrong. India is usually second in production, though first in area under cotton. Its yield per hectare is low.
Wrong. Indonesia grows negligible cotton and is a net importer for its textile sector.
Wrong. The USA is generally third in production, though it is the leading raw cotton exporter.
keyfact: China is the world's largest cotton producer, India is second with the largest area, and the USA is the top exporter.
option_notes: China: the largest producer and also the largest consumer and importer of cotton. Xinjiang is the dominant growing region. Its yields are high because of irrigation, mechanisation and improved varieties. It also has the world's largest textile industry.

India: second-largest producer and has the largest cotton area in the world. The main crop is Bt cotton, introduced in 2002. It is grown mostly on rain-fed black soils of the Deccan and Gujarat. It is a major exporter of yarn and a producer of all four commercial species. The Cotton Corporation of India handles MSP procurement.

Indonesia: a large textile and garment producer but with almost no domestic cotton. It imports raw cotton from the USA, Brazil and Australia. Its main crops are palm oil, rubber, rice, coffee and cocoa, and it is the largest palm oil producer.

USA: third-largest producer and the top exporter of raw cotton. The 'Cotton Belt' stretches across Texas, Georgia, Arkansas and Mississippi. Texas is the leading state. American Upland and Pima (long-staple) are the main types. Its output is highly mechanised and subsidised.
related: China is the world's top cotton producer; India is second.
India has the world's largest cotton area but a low yield per hectare.
The USA is the largest exporter of raw cotton.
Bt cotton was approved in India in 2002 and is the only GM crop grown commercially.
Cotton grows best on black (regur) soil.
Mumbai is called the 'Cottonopolis of India'; Ahmedabad the 'Manchester of India'.
The Central Institute for Cotton Research is at Nagpur.
Gossypium hirsutum is the most widely grown cotton species.
summary: The answer is (a) China. China is the world's largest producer of cotton (OCR 'co on' read as 'cotton'), with roughly 6-7 million tonnes of lint a year. India is usually second and the USA third, while Indonesia produces almost none.
topic_notes: Cotton is the main natural fibre and a cash crop, called 'white gold'. India grows four species: Gossypium hirsutum (the most common, American cotton), G. arboreum and G. herbaceum (Asiatic cottons), and G. barbadense (Egyptian or long-staple cotton). Bt cotton is the only genetically modified crop approved for commercial cultivation in India (2002). It is grown mainly as a kharif crop, sown from April to June and harvested from October to December. It needs black regur soil, warm temperatures and 50-100 cm of rainfall. Top Indian states by production include Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. Institutions to know are the Cotton Corporation of India (CCI), the Central Institute for Cotton Research in Nagpur, and the Cotton Advisory Board and Textiles Committee. The Technology Mission on Cotton was launched in 2000. The first modern cotton mill in India was set up in Fort Gloster, Calcutta (1818), and the first successful mill was in Bombay (1854). Mumbai is called 'Cottonopolis of India' and Ahmedabad 'Manchester of India'. Globally, the leading producers are China, India, the USA, Brazil, Pakistan and Uzbekistan. Cotton is also grown in Australia, Turkey and Egypt (famous for extra-long staple). Related fibre crops are jute (West Bengal, 'golden fibre'), hemp and flax. Cotton seed yields oil and cottonseed cake for cattle feed.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a state-location question on wildlife sanctuaries. Bhitarkanika (Kendrapara district, Odisha, formerly Orissa) is a mangrove-estuarine sanctuary on the Brahmani-Baitarani delta. It is famous for saltwater crocodiles and Olive Ridley nesting at Gahirmatha, and it is a Ramsar site. Pachmarhi Wildlife Sanctuary is in Hoshangabad (Narmadapuram), Madhya Pradesh, in the Satpura range. It is part of the Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve, along with Satpura National Park and Bori Sanctuary. Pocharam Wildlife Sanctuary is in the Medak district of the Telangana region, which was part of Andhra Pradesh in 2004. It was built around the Pocharam lake, which was created by the Alair stream. Sharavathi Valley (Sharavathi) Wildlife Sanctuary is in Shimoga (Shivamogga), Karnataka, near the Jog Falls and the Linganamakki reservoir. It is known for the lion-tailed macaque. Elimination: A-4 is shared by (a) and (c). B-3 rules out (d) and (a)-type variants with B-2. C-1 and D-2 then confirm (c). The code table is garbled by OCR, but the combination A4, B3, C1, D2 fits the third column.
explanations: Incorrect: this option does not give the full correct set A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2. Its C value does not match Pocharam's location in Andhra Pradesh.
Incorrect: it gives A-1, but Bhitarkanika is in Orissa (4), not Andhra Pradesh.
Correct: A-4 Orissa, B-3 Madhya Pradesh, C-1 Andhra Pradesh, D-2 Karnataka. This matches the actual locations of all four sanctuaries.
Incorrect: it gives A-1 and D-3, which are both wrong. Sharavathi is in Karnataka, not Madhya Pradesh.
keyfact: Bhitarkanika-Odisha, Pachmarhi-Madhya Pradesh, Pocharam-Andhra Pradesh (now Telangana), Sharavathi-Karnataka.
option_notes: Option (a) is a code that begins with A-4, which is correct for Bhitarkanika. The rest of the code is wrong. Bhitarkanika is in Kendrapara, Odisha. It has mangroves, the largest saltwater crocodile population in India, and heronries. It was declared a sanctuary in 1975 and a Ramsar site in 2002. Gahirmatha beach next to it is the world's largest Olive Ridley rookery.

Option (b) begins with A-1, which is wrong. Andhra Pradesh sanctuaries include Coringa (mangroves, Godavari delta), Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam (a tiger reserve), Kolleru (a Ramsar site) and Pulicat (shared with Tamil Nadu). Pocharam is in the Telangana region, which was part of Andhra Pradesh at the time. Telangana was formed in 2014.

Option (c) is the correct code: A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2. Pachmarhi was declared a biosphere reserve in 1999 and is in the UNESCO MAB network. Pocharam was a hunting reserve of the Nizams. Sharavathi has lion-tailed macaque habitat, with Jog Falls nearby on the Sharavathi river.

Option (d) begins with A-1, which is wrong, and also mismatches D. Madhya Pradesh has Kanha, Bandhavgarh, Pench, Panna and Satpura. Sharavathi is in Karnataka, which also has Bandipur, Nagarhole, Dandeli and Bhadra. The mix of states in this option is meant as a distractor.
related: Bhitarkanika, Odisha: Ramsar site (2002), a mangrove ecosystem and saltwater crocodile habitat.
Gahirmatha (Odisha) is the world's largest Olive Ridley mass nesting site.
Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve (MP) was declared in 1999 and is in the UNESCO MAB network.
Sharavathi Valley Sanctuary (Karnataka) protects lion-tailed macaques near Jog Falls.
Pocharam Sanctuary is in Medak, Telangana (formerly Andhra Pradesh).
The Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972 governs sanctuaries and national parks.
Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam is India's largest tiger reserve by area.
summary: The correct matching is A-4 (Orissa), B-3 (Madhya Pradesh), C-1 (Andhra Pradesh), D-2 (Karnataka). In the printed codes, option (c) gives A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2, so (c) is correct.
topic_notes: Wildlife sanctuaries are a recurring static-geography topic. Sanctuaries are declared by the state government under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and some human activity is allowed. National parks give stricter protection. Biosphere reserves are designated under UNESCO's MAB programme. Odisha: Bhitarkanika (mangroves, saltwater crocodiles, Olive Ridleys), Chilika (Nalabana sanctuary, a Ramsar site), Simlipal (tiger reserve and biosphere reserve), Satkosia. Madhya Pradesh: Pachmarhi (Satpura range, Dhupgarh peak, biosphere reserve), Kanha, Bandhavgarh, Pench, Panna, Satpura, Ken Gharial sanctuary and Chambal. Andhra Pradesh and Telangana: Pocharam (Medak), Kawal (Telangana tiger reserve), Eturnagaram, Coringa, Kolleru, Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam (the largest tiger reserve in India by area). Karnataka: Sharavathi Valley (lion-tailed macaque), Bhadra, Dandeli-Anshi, Ranganathittu (birds on the Cauvery), Bandipur, Nagarhole (Rajiv Gandhi NP), Kudremukh. Uttar Pradesh: Dudhwa, Chandraprabha, National Chambal Sanctuary, and Katarniaghat. Tips: learn each state's principal protected areas and what species they are famous for. Also note which of these were renamed (Orissa is now Odisha, and Bhitar Kanika is spelled Bhitarkanika) and where state boundaries changed (Telangana in 2014).

question:
Match List-I (Produce) with List-II (Major Producer State) and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists: List-I (Produce) List-II (Major Producer State) A. Rubber
1. Andhra Pradesh B. Soyabean
2. Tamil Nadu C. Groundnut
3. Madhya Pradesh D. Wheat
4. Kerala
5. Uttar Pradesh Code: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a standard crop-geography matching question, solved by anchoring on the most certain pairs. Rubber is overwhelmingly a Kerala crop, with about 75-90% of India's natural rubber, so A must be 4. That leaves only (a) and (c). Soyabean is the signature crop of Madhya Pradesh, which is called the 'Soya State', with Maharashtra second, so B is 3. This eliminates (a), where B is 1. Wheat is led by Uttar Pradesh, followed by Punjab, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh, so D is 5. Groundnut has historically been led by Gujarat, then Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Gujarat is absent from the list, so Andhra Pradesh (1) is the best match for C. Option (c) fits all four pairs. Options (a) and (d) pair wheat with Kerala or Tamil Nadu, which is absurd. Option (b) pairs rubber with Uttar Pradesh. Current data may differ: Rajasthan is now a leading wheat and groundnut state, and Gujarat leads groundnut. This is a 2004 question, so use the options as given.
explanations: Wrong: it pairs Soyabean with Andhra Pradesh (1) and Wheat with Kerala (5 is wrongly replaced by 4 here), which is incorrect.
Wrong: it pairs Rubber with Uttar Pradesh and Wheat with Kerala, both incorrect.
Correct: all four pairs are right: Rubber–Kerala, Soyabean–Madhya Pradesh, Groundnut–Andhra Pradesh, Wheat–Uttar Pradesh.
Wrong: it pairs Rubber with Uttar Pradesh and Wheat with Kerala, both incorrect.
keyfact: Rubber–Kerala, Soyabean–Madhya Pradesh, Groundnut–Andhra Pradesh/Gujarat, Wheat–Uttar Pradesh.
option_notes: Code 4-1-2-5 pairs Rubber–Kerala and Wheat–Uttar Pradesh correctly. It makes Soyabean–Andhra Pradesh and Groundnut–Tamil Nadu, which are wrong because Soyabean belongs to Madhya Pradesh. Tamil Nadu is a real groundnut producer but not the best match here. This option is a plausible-looking distractor that tests the soyabean pair.

Code 5-3-1-4 pairs Rubber–Uttar Pradesh and Wheat–Kerala. These are the reverse of the correct pairs, and Uttar Pradesh has no commercial rubber because the climate is unsuitable. Kerala grows almost no wheat because its tropical climate is too warm. Only the Soyabean–MP and Groundnut–AP pairs are right.

Code 4-3-1-5 is the correct combination: Rubber–Kerala, Soyabean–Madhya Pradesh, Groundnut–Andhra Pradesh, Wheat–Uttar Pradesh. Each pair reflects the major producer states of that period. Gujarat is the other leading groundnut state, but it is not listed in the question.

Code 5-1-2-4 pairs Rubber–Uttar Pradesh, Soyabean–Andhra Pradesh, Groundnut–Tamil Nadu and Wheat–Kerala. Apart from Groundnut–Tamil Nadu, which is only partly valid, all are wrong. It fails because rubber and wheat are assigned to unsuitable climates.
related: Kerala produces most of India's natural rubber; the Rubber Board is at Kottayam.
Madhya Pradesh is called the 'Soya State'; Indore is the soyabean hub.
Uttar Pradesh is the top wheat-producing state.
Gujarat is generally the leading groundnut producer.
Wheat is a rabi crop; groundnut and soyabean are kharif crops.
Assam leads in tea; Karnataka leads in coffee.
The Rubber Act was passed in 1947 and the Rubber Board was constituted in 1947.
India is the second-largest producer of wheat in the world.
statements: A–4 — Correct: Rubber is mainly grown in Kerala. Kerala produces roughly 75-90% of India's natural rubber, mostly in Kottayam, Pathanamthitta and Idukki. The Rubber Board is headquartered at Kottayam and was set up under the Rubber Act 1947. Other producing states are Tamil Nadu (Kanyakumari), Karnataka, Tripura, Assam and the Garo Hills of Meghalaya. Rubber needs a hot, humid climate with 200+ cm of rain and no strong winds.

B–3 — Correct: Soyabean is mainly grown in Madhya Pradesh. MP accounts for about 45-55% of national output, with Maharashtra second and Rajasthan third. Indore is the base of the Soybean Processors Association (SOPA) and the Indian Institute of Soybean Research. It is a kharif oilseed crop grown on black (regur) soil. Soyabean is the largest source of edible oil meal and protein.

C–1 — Correct (best match from the options): Groundnut is a major kharif oilseed crop. Gujarat is usually the top producer, followed by Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. Historically Andhra Pradesh and Gujarat have competed for first place. It prefers light sandy loam soil and 50-75 cm of rain. India is among the top producers in the world, after China. Of the listed states, Andhra Pradesh is the best match.

D–5 — Correct: Wheat is led by Uttar Pradesh, which produces about 30-35% of India's wheat. Punjab, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan follow. Wheat is a rabi crop, sown in October-December and harvested in March-April. It needs cool growing weather, about 50-75 cm of rain and loamy soil. India is the second-largest wheat producer after China. The Green Revolution began with wheat in Punjab and Haryana.
summary: The correct answer is (c): Rubber–Kerala (4), Soyabean–Madhya Pradesh (3), Groundnut–Andhra Pradesh (1), Wheat–Uttar Pradesh (5). Kerala dominates rubber, Madhya Pradesh dominates soyabean, and Uttar Pradesh is the top wheat producer. For groundnut, the options use Andhra Pradesh (Gujarat is not listed), which is the only workable choice.
topic_notes: Crop geography matching questions are common in the general-awareness section. Key facts: Rubber is a plantation crop grown in Kerala (about 75-90%), Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Tripura, Assam and Meghalaya. The Rubber Board is at Kottayam. Soyabean is grown in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan. Groundnut is led by Gujarat, with Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka also important. Wheat is led by Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. Rice is led by West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh and Punjab. Cotton is led by Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana. Sugarcane is led by Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka. Tea is led by Assam, then West Bengal and Tamil Nadu. Coffee is led by Karnataka (Kodagu), Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Jute is led by West Bengal. Rapeseed-mustard is led by Rajasthan. Sunflower is led by Karnataka. Maize is led by Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh. Seasons: kharif crops (rice, soyabean, groundnut, cotton, maize) are sown with the monsoon in June-July and harvested in September-October; rabi crops (wheat, barley, mustard, gram) are sown in October-December and harvested in March-April; zaid crops are grown in summer. Institutions: ICAR, the Spices Board at Kochi, the Coffee Board at Bengaluru, the Tea Board at Kolkata, and the Indian Institute of Soybean Research at Indore. Rankings change from year to year, so check the latest Agriculture Ministry data.

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. In India, intensity of cropping is high in the States of the peninsular plateau.
2. In India, the States of Punjab and Haryana have the highest propor on of the net sown area to total geographical area.
3. South-west Monsoon season is termed as the Kharif season of crops. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Cropping intensity = (gross cropped area / net sown area) x 100, so it measures how many times the same land is cropped in a year. It is high where irrigation is assured and soils are fertile: Punjab (about 190-200%), Haryana (about 180-190%), West Bengal, UP and Delhi. The peninsular plateau (Maharashtra, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan's dry belt, Andhra/Telangana) has black and red soils, erratic rainfall and limited irrigation, so intensity is lower, often 110-140%. Statement 1 is therefore incorrect. Net sown area as a share of geographical area is highest in Punjab (about 80-83%) and Haryana (about 80%), followed by UP and West Bengal; this makes statement 2 correct. Kharif crops are sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon (June-July) and harvested in September-October: rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, jute, groundnut, soybean. Rabi is sown in winter (October-December) and harvested in March-April; zaid is the summer season. Statement 3 is correct. Only 2 and 3 are correct, so option (a). Options containing statement 1 are eliminated.
explanations: Correct: statements 2 and 3 are true, and statement 1 is false.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, and excludes statement 3, which is true.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, and excludes statement 2, which is true.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, so not all three are correct.
keyfact: Cropping intensity is highest in irrigated Punjab-Haryana, not the peninsular plateau; Kharif = south-west monsoon season.
option_notes: Statements 2 and 3: the correct combination. Punjab and Haryana lead in net sown area share, and Kharif matches the south-west monsoon season. Both facts are standard in Indian agricultural geography. Net sown area is land sown at least once in the year, and the reporting area is the denominator that statistics use for the proportion.

Statements 1 and 2: wrong because statement 1 is false. The peninsular plateau has lower cropping intensity because of rain-fed agriculture, uncertain monsoon and limited irrigation. It also leaves out statement 3, the Kharif definition, which is correct. Cropping intensity is highest in Punjab, Haryana and the Gangetic plains.

Statements 1 and 3: wrong because statement 1 is false. Statement 3 is true, but this option leaves out statement 2. Peninsular India has substantial net sown area in places such as Maharashtra and Karnataka, but its intensity is far below Punjab and Haryana. Black soil regions are dominated by cotton and jowar grown in one season.

All three statements: wrong because statement 1 is false. Cropping intensity depends on irrigation, soil fertility and rainfall reliability. The peninsular plateau is relatively poorly irrigated except in deltaic and canal areas, so the claim does not hold. Only statements 2 and 3 are accurate.
related: Cropping intensity = (gross cropped area / net sown area) x 100.
Punjab and Haryana have the highest cropping intensity and net sown share.
Kharif sowing happens in June-July and harvest in September-October.
Rabi sowing happens in October-December and harvest in March-April.
Zaid is the summer season, between March and June.
Net sown area is about 46% of India's reporting area.
Current fallow is left uncultivated for one year or less.
MSP is recommended by CACP and approved by CCEA.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: High cropping intensity is a feature of irrigated northern plains, not the peninsular plateau. Cropping intensity is gross cropped area divided by net sown area, times 100. India's all-India average is about 140-155%. Punjab is at about 190-200%, Haryana about 180-190%, and West Bengal, UP and Bihar are also above average. Peninsular states such as Maharashtra, Karnataka, Rajasthan and MP have intensities nearer 110-140% because of rain-fed farming, low irrigation coverage and drought-prone conditions. The plateau's black cotton soil retains moisture but supports mostly a single crop in a year.

2 — Correct: Punjab and Haryana have the highest net sown area as a proportion of total geographical area, at roughly 80% or more. This reflects flat alluvial plains, canal and tubewell irrigation and the Green Revolution. The all-India net sown area is about 140-142 million hectares, around 46% of the reporting area. Other states with high proportions are Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Bihar. States with very low shares include Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Andaman and Nicobar, mainly because of forest cover and hilly terrain.

3 — Correct: The Kharif season coincides with the south-west monsoon, with sowing in June-July and harvest in September-October. Main crops are rice, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut, soybean and sugarcane. Rabi crops are sown in October-December and harvested in March-April: wheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas and linseed. Zaid is the short summer season between March and June, with watermelon, cucumber and fodder. MSPs are announced separately for Kharif and Rabi crops by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs on the recommendation of CACP.
summary: The correct answer is (a): statements 2 and 3 are correct, statement 1 is wrong. Punjab and Haryana have the highest share of net sown area in total geographical area (about 80%+), and Kharif is the south-west monsoon crop season. Cropping intensity is highest in the northern plains (Punjab, Haryana, UP), not in the peninsular plateau, where rain-fed, single-cropped farming is common.
topic_notes: Land use classification in India divides the reporting area into forests, land not available for cultivation, other uncultivated land, fallow land and net sown area. Net sown area is about 46% of the reporting area (roughly 140 million hectares). Gross cropped area is about 195-200 million hectares, giving a cropping intensity of about 140-155%. Cropping intensity is the gross cropped area divided by net sown area, times 100. Highest intensities are in Punjab, Haryana, West Bengal, UP and Delhi. Low intensities occur in Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh and the north-east hills. Net sown share is highest in Punjab and Haryana (about 80% or more), then UP, West Bengal and Bihar. Cropping seasons: Kharif (June-October, monsoon), Rabi (October-April, winter, with western disturbances helping in the north-west), Zaid (March-June). Major Kharif crops are rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton and jute. Rabi crops are wheat, barley, gram, mustard and peas. Related terms include net irrigated area, gross irrigated area, fallow land (current fallow is left for one year or less; other fallow is left for 1-5 years) and culturable wasteland. Irrigation by tubewells and canals is dominant in the northern plains, while tanks are prominent in the south (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh). The Green Revolution of the 1960s concentrated on Punjab, Haryana and western UP with HYV wheat and rice. Land use statistics are compiled by the Directorate of Economics and Statistics, Ministry of Agriculture.

question:
Match List-I (Country) with List-II (Location) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the Lists: List-I (Country) List-II (Location) A. Bahamas
1. Europe B. Belize
2. North America C. Macedonia 3.North Atlantic Ocean D. Gabon
4. Africa
5. South America Code: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a world-geography matching question, and the best method is to place each country on a continent or ocean first and then eliminate options. The Bahamas is an archipelago of about 700 islands and 2,000 cays in the North Atlantic Ocean, east of Florida and north of Cuba, with Nassau as its capital. Belize lies on the Caribbean coast of Central America, bordered by Mexico to the north and Guatemala to the west and south. It is the only Central American country with English as its official language. Macedonia (now North Macedonia, renamed in 2019 after the Prespa Agreement with Greece) is a landlocked Balkan state in southeastern Europe with Skopje as its capital. Gabon straddles the equator on Africa's west coast, with Libreville as its capital. Option (a) is wrong because it puts Belize in Africa. Option (b) wrongly puts Macedonia in South America. Option (d) wrongly puts Bahamas in Europe. Only (c) gives A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4. Note that no country in the list matches South America (item 5), so item 5 is an extra option.
explanations: Wrong: it places Belize in Africa and Gabon in North America, which is incorrect.
Wrong: it places the Bahamas in Europe and Macedonia in South America, which is incorrect.
Right: Bahamas-North Atlantic Ocean, Belize-North America, Macedonia-Europe, Gabon-Africa.
Wrong: it places the Bahamas in Europe, Macedonia in South America and Gabon in North America, which is incorrect.
keyfact: Bahamas = North Atlantic; Belize = North America (Central America); Macedonia = Europe; Gabon = Africa.
option_notes: Code 3 4 1 2: the first and third pairs are correct, but Belize is not in Africa and Gabon is not in North America. Africa has 54 recognised countries, and Gabon, Cameroon and Congo are Central African states on the Atlantic coast. This code fails on the second and fourth pairs.

Code 1 2 5 4: only Belize-North America and Gabon-Africa are correct. The Bahamas is not in Europe, and Macedonia is not in South America. South America includes Brazil, Argentina, Chile and Peru, but Belize and the Bahamas are not part of it.

Code 3 2 1 4: this is the correct matching. Bahamas lies in the North Atlantic, Belize in Central/North America, Macedonia (North Macedonia) in Europe and Gabon in Africa. All four pairs are accurate, and the code uses four of the five location items.
Code 1 4 5 2: all four pairs are wrong. It puts the Bahamas in Europe, Belize in Africa, Macedonia in South America and Gabon in North America, so it can be rejected immediately.
related: Capital of the Bahamas is Nassau; currency is the Bahamian dollar.
Belize's capital is Belmopan; former name British Honduras.
Macedonia was renamed North Macedonia in 2019; capital Skopje.
Gabon's capital is Libreville; the equator passes through it.
Belize Barrier Reef is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
North Macedonia joined NATO in 2020.
Gabon is a member of OPEC and joined the Commonwealth in 2022.
statements: A-3 — Correct: The Bahamas lies in the North Atlantic Ocean. It is a Commonwealth realm made up of about 700 islands and 2,000 cays, east of Florida and north of Cuba. The capital is Nassau on New Providence island. It became independent from Britain in 1973. The currency is the Bahamian dollar. Tourism and offshore finance are its main economic sectors. Geographically it is often grouped with the Caribbean region, but it is not in the Caribbean Sea itself.

B-2 — Correct: Belize is in North America, on the Caribbean coast of Central America. It was formerly British Honduras and became independent in 1981. The capital is Belmopan, and Belize City is the largest city. It borders Mexico and Guatemala, and Guatemala has long claimed part of its territory. It has the Belize Barrier Reef, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. English is the official language.

C-1 — Correct: Macedonia, now North Macedonia, is a landlocked country in the Balkans in southeastern Europe. It was a republic of Yugoslavia until its independence in 1991. The capital is Skopje. A long dispute with Greece over the name ended with the Prespa Agreement in 2018, and the name changed in 2019. It joined NATO in 2020. It borders Serbia, Kosovo, Albania, Greece and Bulgaria. The Vardar is its main river.

D-4 — Correct: Gabon is in Africa, on the west coast in Central Africa, and the equator passes through it. The capital is Libreville. It was a French colony and became independent in 1960. It borders Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon and the Republic of Congo, and has a coastline on the Atlantic Ocean. It is rich in oil, manganese and timber. It is a member of OPEC, and it joined the Commonwealth in 2022.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 3 2 1 4. The Bahamas is an island nation in the North Atlantic Ocean, Belize is in North America (Central America), Macedonia is in Europe (the Balkans) and Gabon is in Africa.
topic_notes: This question tests basic political geography of small and lesser-known countries, a recurring theme in the APFC general awareness section. Key points: North America includes Central America and the Caribbean. Central American countries are Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama. Belize is the only one with English as its official language, and it was British Honduras until 1973 (independence in 1981). The Bahamas has been independent since 1973 and is a Commonwealth member with Nassau as its capital. The Balkan states include Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, Slovenia and Greece. North Macedonia was admitted to NATO in March 2020. Africa: Gabon (Libreville), Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon, Congo, DR Congo, and the island nations of Sao Tome and Principe. The equator passes through Gabon, Congo, DR Congo, Uganda, Kenya and Somalia in Africa, and through Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil in South America. Other island nations in the Atlantic or Caribbean include Cuba, Jamaica, Haiti, Dominican Republic, Barbados, Trinidad and Tobago, and Cape Verde. A useful approach is to associate each country with its capital, former colonial power, and bordering countries or water bodies. UPSC often asks for capitals, currencies, rivers or the continent of unfamiliar countries, so revise world maps regularly.

question: Going from the West of the United States of America to its East, which one of the following is the correct sequence of the given major American ci es?
options: Houston-Los Angeles San Francisco New York
subject: Computers
detail: The question tests longitude-based placement of major US cities. Going from west to east means moving from higher west longitude to lower west longitude. San Francisco on the Pacific coast of northern California lies at about 122.4°W. Los Angeles in southern California lies at about 118.2°W, so it is slightly east of San Francisco. Houston, on the Gulf coastal plain of Texas, lies at about 95.4°W, well inland and east of California. New York, on the Atlantic seaboard, lies at about 74°W and is the easternmost. The order is therefore San Francisco, Los Angeles, Houston, New York. Elimination: options (a) and (c) put Houston first, which is wrong because Houston is far east of the Californian cities. Option (b) puts New York before Houston and Los Angeles, which is wrong because New York is the easternmost. Only (d) is consistent. Remember that latitude does not decide east-west order: Los Angeles is south of San Francisco but east of it, a common trap.
explanations: Wrong: it places Houston first, but Houston (95°W) is east of both Los Angeles and San Francisco.
Wrong: it places New York in the middle, before Houston and Los Angeles, though New York is the easternmost of the four.
Wrong: it starts with Houston and ends with Los Angeles, which reverses the actual order and puts New York too early.
Correct: San Francisco (122.4°W), Los Angeles (118.2°W), Houston (95.4°W), New York (74°W) is the true west-to-east order.
keyfact: West to east: San Francisco (122°W) - Los Angeles (118°W) - Houston (95°W) - New York (74°W).
option_notes: Houston-Los Angeles-San Francisco-New York: this is not a valid geographic order. Houston is Texas's largest city, a Gulf coast port and the centre of the US oil and gas industry, home to NASA's Johnson Space Center. It lies in the central-south US, not at the western end.

San Francisco-New York-Houston-Los Angeles: this order is geographically incoherent. New York is the largest US city, on the Atlantic coast at the mouth of the Hudson, home to the UN headquarters and Wall Street. Los Angeles is in California, on the Pacific side.

Houston-New York-San Francisco-Los Angeles: this is almost the reverse of a west-east order. San Francisco is the Bay Area hub near Silicon Valley, linked with the Golden Gate Bridge and the 1906 earthquake. Los Angeles is the Hollywood and entertainment centre.

San Francisco-Los Angeles-Houston-New York: the correct order. Both Californian cities are on the Pacific coast. Houston is the fourth most populous US city and a Gulf port connected by the Houston Ship Channel. New York is on the Atlantic coast and is the easternmost of the four.
related: Washington DC is the US capital and lies on the Potomac River.
The Great Lakes are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario; Lake Michigan lies wholly within the US.
Houston is the centre of the US petroleum industry and hosts NASA's Johnson Space Center.
The Sierra Nevada and Rockies are the main western mountain systems; the Appalachians are in the east.
The Mississippi-Missouri is the longest US river system and drains into the Gulf of Mexico.
Silicon Valley is near San Francisco in California.
The contiguous USA has four time zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific.
summary: The correct answer is (d): San Francisco - Los Angeles - Houston - New York. Going west to east, San Francisco (about 122.4°W) comes first, then Los Angeles (118.2°W), Houston (95.4°W) and New York (74°W).
topic_notes: The USA spans about 125°W (Washington state coast) to 67°W (Maine) in the contiguous states, and uses several time zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific in the mainland, plus Alaska and Hawaii-Aleutian zones. The mainland spans about 24.5°N to 49°N. Major cities by coast and region: the Pacific coast has Seattle, Portland, San Francisco, Los Angeles and San Diego. The Rocky Mountain region has Denver and Salt Lake City. The Gulf and south has Houston, Dallas, New Orleans and Miami. The Midwest has Chicago, Detroit and St Louis. The Atlantic coast has Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Washington DC and Atlanta (inland). Physical geography from west to east: the Pacific coast ranges, Sierra Nevada and Cascades, the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau, the Rockies, the Great Plains, the Mississippi basin, the Appalachians and the Atlantic coastal plain. Major rivers are the Mississippi-Missouri, Colorado, Columbia and Rio Grande. The Great Lakes are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario. The capital is Washington DC, and the largest city is New York. Exam tip: for map-order questions, use approximate longitudes and remember that north-south position does not decide east-west order.

question:
Match List-1 (Beach Resort) with List-II (State) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the Lists: List-I (Beach Resort) List-II (State) A. Digha
1. Kerala B. Covelong
2. West Bengal C. Cherai
3. Maharashtra D. Murud-Janjira
4. Tamil Nadu Code: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a geography-of-tourism matching question, and it is solved by placing each beach on the Indian coastline. Digha is on the Bay of Bengal at the southern tip of West Bengal, near the Odisha border in Purba Medinipur district. Covelong (Kovalam) is a coastal village about 40 km south of Chennai on the Coromandel Coast, in Tamil Nadu. It is known for surfing and its old Dutch fort. Cherai Beach lies on Vypin Island near Kochi in Ernakulam district, Kerala, on the Arabian Sea. Murud-Janjira is in Raigad district on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, with the island fort of Janjira off Murud. Elimination: Digha is certainly West Bengal, which leaves only (a) and (c). Murud-Janjira is certainly Maharashtra, which again fits (a) and (c). Covelong is Tamil Nadu, not Kerala, so (c) is out and (a) is correct. Do not confuse Covelong with Kovalam in Kerala.
explanations: Correct: all four pairs match (Digha-West Bengal, Covelong-Tamil Nadu, Cherai-Kerala, Murud-Janjira-Maharashtra).
Wrong: it puts Digha in Maharashtra, but Digha is in West Bengal. It also puts Murud-Janjira in West Bengal.
Wrong: it puts Covelong in Kerala and Cherai in Tamil Nadu, which reverses the two. Covelong is in Tamil Nadu and Cherai is in Kerala.
Wrong: it places Digha in Maharashtra and Murud-Janjira in West Bengal, and the other pairs are also incorrectly assigned.
keyfact: Digha - West Bengal; Covelong - Tamil Nadu; Cherai - Kerala; Murud-Janjira - Maharashtra.
option_notes: Code 2 4 1 3 is the right set. Digha lies in West Bengal on the Bay of Bengal, Covelong in Tamil Nadu on the Coromandel Coast near Chennai, Cherai in Kerala on Vypin Island near Kochi, and Murud-Janjira in Maharashtra on the Konkan coast. It is a mix of east and west coast resorts. All four are tourist beach destinations known for weekend travel.

Code 3 1 4 2 would give Digha-Maharashtra, Covelong-Kerala, Cherai-Tamil Nadu and Murud-Janjira-West Bengal. All four pairs are wrong. Maharashtra's real beaches include Alibag, Ganpatipule, Tarkarli and Murud. Kerala's include Kovalam, Varkala, Cherai and Bekal. Tamil Nadu's include Marina, Covelong and Mahabalipuram. West Bengal's are Digha, Mandarmani and Tajpur.

Code 2 1 4 3 gets Digha and Murud-Janjira right but swaps Covelong and Cherai. Covelong is in Tamil Nadu, not Kerala, and Cherai is in Kerala, not Tamil Nadu. Kovalam in Kerala, near Thiruvananthapuram, is a different place with a similar name and is a frequent source of confusion.
