summary: The correct answer is (a): East-Central Railway is headquartered at Hajipur (3), North-Western at Jaipur (5), North-Central at Allahabad/Prayagraj (2) and South-Western at Hubli (1). The matching A-3, B-5, C-2, D-1 corresponds to option (a).
topic_notes: Indian Railways, one of the world's largest networks, was nationalised in 1951. The Railway Board, headed by a Chairman, is in New Delhi. Zones are headed by General Managers and are divided into divisions run by Divisional Railway Managers. Initially there were 6 zones (1951): Southern, Central, Western, Eastern, Northern and North Eastern (the last added in 1952). Later additions: South Eastern (1955), Northeast Frontier (1958), South Central (1966), then Central/Metro and others. In 2002-03 seven new zones were created: East Coast (Bhubaneswar), East Central (Hajipur), North Central (Allahabad), North Western (Jaipur), South East Central (Bilaspur), South Western (Hubli) and West Central (Jabalpur). The 17th zone, South Coast Railway (Visakhapatnam), was announced in 2019. Other zone headquarters: Central (Mumbai CST), Eastern (Kolkata), Northern (New Delhi), North Eastern (Gorakhpur), Northeast Frontier (Maligaon, Guwahati), Southern (Chennai), South Central (Secunderabad), South Eastern (Kolkata), Western (Churchgate, Mumbai). Kolkata Metro is also a zone (Metro Railway) created in 2010. The oldest railway line ran from Bombay (Bori Bunder) to Thane on 16 April 1853. Railways have a separate Railway Budget until 2016 when it was merged with the General Budget. Related institutions include RDSO (Lucknow), the Chittaranjan Locomotive Works, ICF (Perambur) and the Diesel Locomotive Works (Varanasi).

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. The average population density of India is between 600-700 persons per square kilometer. 2. 2002-2007 is the duration of the Tenth Five-Year Plan.
3. Installed electricity genera on capacity in India is in excess of 2 lakh Megawa . Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: General Science
detail: Statement 1 is wrong. Census 2001 gave a density of 324 persons per sq km, rising to 382 in 2011 and about 420+ in later estimates. Only small states and UTs such as Bihar (about 1100 in 2011), West Bengal, Kerala and Delhi exceed 600. Statement 2 is correct: the Tenth Plan covered 2002-07 and targeted about 8% GDP growth; actual growth was about 7.6%. Statement 3 is wrong for the exam's time frame. At the end of the Ninth Plan (March 2002) installed capacity was about 1.04 lakh MW, and around 2004 it was about 1.2 lakh MW. It crossed 2 lakh MW only in 2012-13 and about 3.9-4.0 lakh MW by 2023-24. The elimination logic is simple: since statement 2 is true and statement 1 is false, options (a), (c) and (d) all fail, because each includes statement 1. Only (b) remains. Always remember that a question's data refers to the period of the paper, not the present.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false because density was about 324, not 600-700.
Correct: only statement 2 is true, since the Tenth Plan ran 2002-07.
Wrong: statement 1 is false and statement 3 is false for the paper's period, since installed capacity was about 1.2 lakh MW.
Wrong: statements 1 and 3 are both incorrect, so all three cannot be true.
keyfact: Tenth Plan = 2002-07; India's density in 2001 was 324/sq km and power capacity about 1.2 lakh MW, so only statement 2 is correct.
option_notes: Options 1 and 2: this pairs the incorrect density claim with the correct plan period. It is wrong because India's density was only 324 per sq km in 2001. Dense states such as Bihar, West Bengal and Kerala are well above the national average, but the national figure is not 600-700.

Option 2 only: this is the correct choice. The Tenth Five-Year Plan ran from April 2002 to March 2007. Its key goals were 8% GDP growth, reducing poverty by 5 points, providing gainful employment, and universal access to primary education by 2007. Actual growth was about 7.6%.

Options 1 and 3: this combines two false statements. Density in 2001 was 324 per sq km. Installed power capacity was then about 1.1-1.2 lakh MW and crossed 2 lakh MW only around 2012-13. It is wrong because it also leaves out the true statement 2.

Options 1, 2 and 3: this claims all statements are true. It fails because both the density and installed capacity figures are overstated for the period. Density was 324 per sq km in 2001 and capacity was about 1.2 lakh MW. Only the plan period is correct.
related: Census 2001 density of India: 324 per sq km; Census 2011: 382.
Tenth Plan: 2002-07; Eleventh: 2007-12; Twelfth: 2012-17.
Electricity Act 2003 replaced the Electricity Act 1910 and others.
Bihar is the most densely populated major state (1102 per sq km, 2011).
Arunachal Pradesh is the least densely populated state (17 per sq km).
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.
India's installed power capacity crossed 2 lakh MW around 2012-13.
Tenth Plan growth target was 8%; Eleventh was 9%.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: India's average density was 324/sq km in Census 2001, not 600-700. Census 2011 gave 382 per sq km. Bihar is the densest large state, with about 1102 per sq km in 2011. Delhi, as a UT, has about 11,297 per sq km. Arunachal Pradesh is the sparsest at 17 per sq km. India has about 2.4% of the world's land area but about 17.5% of its population.

2 — Correct: The Tenth Five-Year Plan covered 2002-2007. It set a growth target of 8% and aimed to reduce the poverty ratio by 5 percentage points by 2007. The Ninth Plan ran 1997-2002 and the Eleventh 2007-12, with a target of 9% growth. The Twelfth ran 2012-17 and was the last plan. The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015. Montek Singh Ahluwalia was the Deputy Chairman during these plans.

3 — Incorrect: Installed capacity was about 1.1-1.2 lakh MW around 2004. It passed 2 lakh MW around 2012-13 and reached roughly 4 lakh MW by 2024. Thermal power, mainly coal, has the largest share, though renewables are growing. India's target is 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030. The Electricity Act 2003 reformed the power sector, and the Central Electricity Authority compiles capacity data.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. The Tenth Five-Year Plan ran from 2002 to 2007, but India's average population density was nowhere near 600-700 persons/sq km (about 324 in 2001), and installed power capacity in 2004 was about 1.1-1.2 lakh MW, well below 2 lakh MW.
topic_notes: Population density: Census 2001 gave 324 per sq km and Census 2011 gave 382. Bihar is the densest state at 1102, followed by West Bengal at 1029 and Kerala at 859. Arunachal Pradesh is the least dense at 17. Among UTs, Delhi is the densest at 11,297. India's population was 102.7 crore in 2001 and 121 crore in 2011. Five-Year Plans: the First ran 1951-56 (Harrod-Domar model), the Second 1956-61 (Mahalanobis model, heavy industry), the Third 1961-66, then Plan holidays in 1966-69. The Fourth ran 1969-74, the Fifth 1974-79, the Sixth 1980-85, the Seventh 1985-90, the Eighth 1992-97 (liberalisation, Narasimha Rao), the Ninth 1997-2002, the Tenth 2002-07, the Eleventh 2007-12 (inclusive growth), and the Twelfth 2012-17 (faster, more inclusive, sustainable growth). The Planning Commission was set up in 1950 and abolished in 2014-15; NITI Aayog replaced it. The National Development Council approves the plans. Power sector: installed capacity was about 1.2 lakh MW in 2004, 2 lakh MW around 2012, and about 4.4 lakh MW by 2024. Coal-based thermal is the largest share, and renewables including solar and wind are growing rapidly. Key bodies include the CEA, PGCIL, NTPC, NHPC and the Ministry of Power. The Electricity Act 2003 is the main law. The Rural Electrification Corporation was established in 1969. Exam tip: always read figures in the context of the paper's year.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a straight factual matching question on Indian education institutions. Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeeth (now Rashtriya Sanskrit Sansthan Deemed University, Tirupati campus) is located at Tirupati; the OCR 'Tirupa' means Tirupati. Maharishi Sandipani Rashtriya Veda Vidya Pratishthan, set up in 1987 by the Ministry of HRD (now Education) to preserve and promote Vedic studies, is headquartered at Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, the seat of Sage Sandipani's ashram. (b) is correct. A-4 Tirupati, B-5 Ujjain, C-3 Mysore, D-1 Hyderabad.

topic_notes: Institutions for Sanskrit, Vedic studies and languages are a recurring static-GK theme. The Rashtriya Sanskrit Sansthan (RSkS), established in 1970, became a deemed university in 2002 and a Central University in 2020 under the Central Sanskrit Universities Act 2020, which converted three institutions: RSkS Delhi, Shri Lal Bahadur Shastri Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeeth Delhi and Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeeth Tirupati. The Maharishi Sandipani Rashtriya Veda Vidya Pratishthan (MSRVVP), Ujjain, is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Education. It runs Vedic pathshalas, awards for Vedic scholars and the Veda Bhashya projects. The Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysore, was set up in 1969 as a subordinate office, now under the Department of Higher Education. It runs the Bharatavani portal, the Linguistic Data Consortium for Indian Languages, and regional language centres (Bhubaneswar, Pune, Guwahati, Lucknow, Solan, Mysuru, Secunderabad, Kolkata). The Central Institute of English and Foreign Languages was founded in 1958 in Hyderabad and became EFLU in 2007, with campuses at Lucknow and Shillong. Other language institutions are the Central Hindi Directorate (Delhi), the Kendriya Hindi Sansthan (Agra), the National Council for Promotion of Urdu Language (Delhi), the National Council for Promotion of Sindhi Language and the Sahitya Akademi (Delhi, 1954). Classical languages status has been given to Tamil (2004), Sanskrit (2005), Telugu and Kannada (2008), Malayalam (2013), Odia (2014), and Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali (2024). Central Sanskrit universities are also at Delhi and Tirupati. Other Sanskrit universities include Kavikulaguru Kalidas Sanskrit University at Ramtek and Sampurnanand Sanskrit University at Varanasi.

question:
Who among the following are the Bharat Ratna recipients?
1. Amartya Sen
2. Gulzari Lal Nanda
3. M.S. Swaminathan
4. Satyajit Ray Select the correct answer using the codes given below: Codes:
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Bharat Ratna is India's highest civilian honour, instituted in 1954 and awarded for exceptional service or performance of the highest order in any field of human endeavour. It is conferred by the President on the Prime Minister's recommendation, and the rules cap the number at three in a year. Article 18(1) bars titles, but the Supreme Court in Balaji Raghavan (1996) held that Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles. Recipients here: Satyajit Ray (1992, filmmaker, also honorary Oscar 1992), Gulzarilal Nanda (1997, twice acting PM, labour leader and Planning Commission figure), Amartya Sen (1999, Nobel in Economics 1998, welfare economics) and M.S. Swaminathan (announced 2024, posthumous, father of the Green Revolution in India). Since each of the four is a recipient, any option leaving one out is wrong. Option (a) omits Ray and Swaminathan, (b) omits Sen and Nanda, (c) omits Swaminathan. Only (d) includes all. A caution: if the exam were taken strictly on 2004 knowledge, (c) would have been the expected answer, but the correct present-day answer is (d).
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out Satyajit Ray and M.S. Swaminathan, who are also recipients.
Wrong: it names only Swaminathan and Ray and leaves out Amartya Sen and Nanda, who are also recipients.
Wrong: it leaves out Swaminathan, who received the award in 2024. It would have matched 2004 knowledge but is incomplete now.
Correct: all four, Sen (1999), Nanda (1997), Swaminathan (2024) and Ray (1992), are Bharat Ratna recipients.
keyfact: Sen (1999), Nanda (1997), Ray (1992) and Swaminathan (2024, posthumous) are all Bharat Ratna recipients.
option_notes: Sen and Nanda are both recipients, from 1999 and 1997. Sen is a Nobel-winning economist, and Nanda was twice acting PM. This pairing is correct but incomplete, since Ray and Swaminathan are also recipients.

Swaminathan (2024) and Ray (1992) are both recipients. Swaminathan was the Green Revolution scientist and Ray the Apu Trilogy filmmaker. This pairing is true but omits Sen and Nanda, so it is not the right choice.
Sen, Nanda and Ray are all recipients in 1999, 1997 and 1992. This was the best answer on pre-2024 knowledge. It is incomplete now, as it omits Swaminathan.
All four are recipients, the correct answer. The group covers an economist, a politician, a scientist and a filmmaker, which shows the breadth of fields the award covers.
related: Bharat Ratna was instituted in 1954; the first recipients were Rajagopalachari, Radhakrishnan and C.V. Raman.
Maximum three Bharat Ratna awards can be given in a year.

statements: 1 — Correct: Amartya Sen received the Bharat Ratna in 1999. He is an economist who won the 1998 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics for work on welfare economics, famine and social choice theory. He developed the capability approach and contributed to the Human Development Index with Mahbub ul Haq. He was born in 1933 at Santiniketan and taught at Cambridge and Harvard. Books include Poverty and Famines, Development as Freedom and The Argumentative Indian.

2 — Correct: Gulzarilal Nanda received the Bharat Ratna in 1997, the same year as Aruna Asaf Ali and A.P.J. Abdul Kalam. He served as acting Prime Minister twice, in 1964 after Nehru's death and in 1966 after Shastri's death, each time for 13 days. He was a labour expert, associated with the Textile Labour Association, Ahmedabad, and served as Union Home Minister and Planning Commission Deputy Chairman. He was a Gandhian from Sialkot (Punjab).

3 — Correct: M.S. Swaminathan (1925–2023) was conferred the Bharat Ratna in 2024, posthumously, announced in February 2024 along with Narasimha Rao and Chaudhary Charan Singh. He is called the Father of the Green Revolution in India, worked with Norman Borlaug on high-yielding wheat and rice, and was the first World Food Prize laureate (1987). He chaired the National Commission on Farmers (2004–06), whose recommendations include the C2+50% MSP formula.

4 — Correct: Satyajit Ray (1921–1992) received the Bharat Ratna in 1992, shortly before his death. He was a filmmaker best known for the Apu Trilogy (Pather Panchali, Aparajito, Apur Sansar). He received an Honorary Academy Award in 1992, the Dadasaheb Phalke Award (1984) and the Legion of Honour from France. He also wrote the Feluda detective stories and the Professor Shonku science fiction series.
summary: Answer is (d): all four were awarded the Bharat Ratna. Amartya Sen (1999), Gulzarilal Nanda (1997), Satyajit Ray (1992) and M.S. Swaminathan (2024, posthumously) are all recipients. Note that at the time of the 2004 paper, Swaminathan had not yet received it, so the question is judged on current status.
topic_notes: The Bharat Ratna was instituted on 2 January 1954. The first recipients, in 1954, were C. Rajagopalachari, S. Radhakrishnan and C.V. Raman. Originally it was limited to art, literature, science and public service, and in 2011 the scope was widened to any field of human endeavour. The medal is a peepal leaf in platinum-toned metal with the Sun and Devanagari legend 'Bharat Ratna'. There is no monetary grant. Awards are announced by the President's Secretariat. The award was suspended in 1977 under the Janata government and again in 1992 for a time, when the Supreme Court considered a challenge, and was upheld as valid in 1995. Foreigners honoured: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (1987) and Nelson Mandela (1990). Posthumous awards include Lal Bahadur Shastri (1966, the first), Subhas Chandra Bose (1992, later withdrawn after a Supreme Court case), Sardar Patel (1991) and B.R. Ambedkar (1990). Youngest recipient: Sachin Tendulkar (2014, aged 40, first sportsperson). Women recipients: Indira Gandhi (1971), Mother Teresa (1980), Aruna Asaf Ali (1997), M.S. Subbulakshmi (1998), Lata Mangeshkar (2001). In 2019 the recipients were Pranab Mukherjee, Nanaji Deshmukh and Bhupen Hazarika. In 2024 five were honoured: Karpoori Thakur, L.K. Advani, P.V. Narasimha Rao, Chaudhary Charan Singh and M.S. Swaminathan. Related honours: Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri, under Article 18 as interpreted in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996).

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Athens 2004 Summer Olympics (13-29 August 2004) were the first Games held in Greece since 1896 and featured 28 sports. Michael Phelps (USA) won six gold and two bronze medals there, the start of his record-breaking Olympic career. Ian Thorpe (Australia), nicknamed 'Thorpedo', won the 400 m freestyle gold, 200 m freestyle gold and a 4x200 m relay silver at Athens. Yulia Nesterenko of Belarus won the women's 100 m sprint, a surprise result, and was the first non-American woman to win it since 1992. Nicolas Massu of Chile won both the singles and doubles (with Fernando Gonzalez) tennis gold, a rare double. Sweden (option 5) is the unused distractor in List-II. statements: A. Michael Phelps — Correct: USA (2). Phelps won 6 golds and 2 bronzes at Athens 2004. He later won 8 golds at Beijing 2008, passing Mark Spitz's record of 7 from 1972. He retired as the most decorated Olympian ever, with 28 medals, 23 of them gold.

B. Ian Thorpe — Correct: Australia (3). Thorpe is a freestyle specialist who won five Olympic golds in total. At Athens he won the 200 m and 400 m freestyle. He is known for his large feet and his nickname 'Thorpedo'.

C. Yulia Nesterenko — Correct: Belarus (1). She won the women's 100 m at Athens in 10.93 s. This was an unexpected victory over favourites such as Lauryn Williams. Her husband is the discus thrower Ivan Tsikhan.

D. Nicolas Massu — Correct: Chile (4). Massu won the singles and doubles golds at Athens 2004, partnering Fernando Gonzalez in the doubles. This was Chile's first Olympic gold medal in tennis. Gonzalez also won singles bronze, and Massu's two golds were a historic achievement for Chile.

topic_notes: Athens 2004 was the 28th Summer Olympiad, held from 13 to 29 August 2004. Yulia Nesterenko (Belarus) won the women's 100 m. For India, Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore won silver in double trap shooting, India's first individual Olympic silver. The Indian team's performance remained modest. The 2008 Games followed in Beijing, where Abhinav Bindra won India's first individual gold in 10 m air rifle. Phelps won 8 golds at Beijing. question: Who won the 100-metre race for men in the Athens Olympics in August, 2004?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The men's 100 m final at Athens was held on 22 August 2004. Justin Gatlin of the USA won gold in 9.85 s. Francis Obikwelu (Portugal, born in Nigeria) took silver in 9.86 s, and Maurice Greene (USA) took bronze in 9.87 s. Asafa Powell of Jamaica finished fifth in 9.94 s. Gatlin later received a doping ban (2006), but his Athens gold was not stripped. The question's option (d) 'Francis Obekwelu' is a spelling variant of Obikwelu. Elimination logic: Greene was the 2000 Sydney champion, so he is a trap for those remembering the previous Games. Powell was a favourite and world-record holder from 2005, but he did not win Olympic gold in the 100 m. Obikwelu was only second. A student should link the 2004 men's 100 m to Gatlin, the 2000 men's 100 m to Greene, the 2008 men's 100 m to Usain Bolt, and the 1996 men's 100 m to Donovan Bailey.
explanations: Wrong: Maurice Greene won the 100 m in Sydney 2000 but only took bronze at Athens 2004.
Correct: Justin Gatlin of the USA won gold in 9.85 s on 22 August 2004.

Justin Gatlin (USA), born 1982, won the 100 m gold at Athens 2004 in 9.85 s and bronze in the 200 m. He was world champion in 2005 (100 m and 200 m). He was banned for doping in 2006 and returned later. He won the 2017 World Championship 100 m, beating Usain Bolt.

Asafa Powell (Jamaica), born 1982, broke the 100 m world record in 2005 (9.77 s) and again in 2007 (9.74 s). He was fifth at Athens 2004 and never won an individual Olympic medal. He won Olympic relay gold in 2008, later vacated, and he won 2016 Rio relay gold.

Francis Obikwelu, born in Nigeria in 1978, represented Portugal. He won the 100 m silver at Athens 2004 in 9.86 s. He was the 2006 European champion in both the 100 m and 200 m, and he set a European record of 9.86 s in the Athens final.

question: Who among the following Indian ﬁlm directors/actors was honoured with the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in year 2004?
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: The Order of the British Empire was founded in 1917 by King George V. It has five classes: GBE, KBE/DBE, CBE, OBE and MBE. Non-Commonwealth or non-British citizens receive only honorary awards, with no right to use the title 'Sir' or 'Dame'. Indian film-maker Shekhar Kapur, who directed Masoom (1983), Mr. India (1987), Bandit Queen (1994), Elizabeth (1998) and The Four Feathers (2002), was honoured by Britain for his contribution to British cinema through Elizabeth, which starred Cate Blanchett. He was also given the Padma Bhushan in 2000. Om Puri received an honorary OBE in 2004 for services to British cinema, so this question has a real ambiguity: sources list both men. Because the question names 'directors/actors' and Shekhar Kapur is the more widely cited 2004 recipient in exam sources, option (c) is the intended answer. Amitabh Bachchan was not given an OBE; his honours include Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan, Padma Vibhushan, Dadasaheb Phalke Award and the French Legion of Honour. Naseeruddin Shah has the Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan.
explanations: Naseeruddin Shah has Padma Shri (1987) and Padma Bhushan (2003) but no OBE, so this is wrong.
Amitabh Bachchan has not received an OBE. His honours are Indian and French, so this is wrong.
Shekhar Kapur was honoured with an honorary OBE in 2004 for contribution to cinema, so this is the intended correct answer.
Om Puri is also recorded as having received an honorary OBE in 2004, which makes the question ambiguous, but it is not the intended key, so (c) is preferred.
keyfact: Shekhar Kapur (Bandit Queen, Elizabeth) received an honorary OBE in 2004.
option_notes: Naseeruddin Shah: born 1950, trained at NSD and FTII, known for Nishant, Sparsh, Mirch Masala, A Wednesday. Padma Shri 1987, Padma Bhushan 2003, National Awards for Sparsh, Paar and Iqbal-era work. Not an OBE holder.

Amitabh Bachchan: born 1942, debut in Saat Hindustani (1969), famous for Zanjeer, Deewar, Sholay. Padma Shri 1984, Padma Bhushan 2001, Padma Vibhushan 2015, Dadasaheb Phalke Award 2018, French Legion of Honour 2007. No OBE.

Shekhar Kapur: born 1945 in Lahore, directed Masoom, Mr. India, Bandit Queen, Elizabeth (1998) and Elizabeth: The Golden Age (2007). Padma Bhushan 2000, honorary OBE in 2004. He later served as FTII chairman (2010-11) and was a member of the Cannes jury in 2010.

Om Puri: 1950-2017, NSD and FTII alumnus, known for Aakrosh, Ardh Satya, Tamas, East is East and City of Joy. Padma Shri 1990 and an honorary OBE in 2004 for services to British cinema. He died in January 2017.
related: The OBE was instituted in 1917 by King George V.

summary: The answer is (c) Shekhar Kapur (spelled Kapoor in the question). He was awarded an honorary OBE in 2004 for his contribution to cinema, and is best known for Bandit Queen (1994) and Elizabeth (1998). Om Puri's honorary OBE came later, in 2004 being a commonly confused year, but he received it in 2004 as well in some sources; the question setter's intended answer is Shekhar Kapur.
topic_notes: The Order of the British Empire is a British order of chivalry created in 1917. Its classes in descending order are Knight/Dame Grand Cross (GBE), Knight/Dame Commander (KBE/DBE), Commander (CBE), Officer (OBE) and Member (MBE). Foreign citizens receive honorary awards. Indian recipients of British honours include Shekhar Kapur, Om Puri, Ben Kingsley (British, knighted), Ismail Merchant (an honorary award is not certain), Lakshmi Mittal (business) and Amartya Sen-style academic honours in other forms. Sir Richard Attenborough's Gandhi (1982) won eight Oscars, with Bhanu Athaiya winning the Oscar for costume design. India's own civilian honours are Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri, instituted in 1954 and awarded under Article 18 context, which prohibits titles by the State. Film awards to remember: Dadasaheb Phalke Award (since 1969, first to Devika Rani), National Film Awards, and Satyajit Ray, who received an honorary Oscar in 1992 and the Bharat Ratna in 1992. Foreign honours often asked: Legion of Honour (France), Chevalier of the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, and Order of the Rising Sun (Japan). Exam tip: when two people appear in sources, select the more widely cited, here Shekhar Kapur.

Correct: Sharapova is a sportsperson, Suu Kyi a political leader, Jahangir a human rights activist and Norah Jones a singer.
keyfact: Sharapova-tennis; Suu Kyi-political leader (NLD); Asma Jahangir-human rights; Norah Jones-singer, so the answer is 4-2-1-3.
option_notes: Option (a) is the pairing 1 2 3 4 (A-Human rights activist, B-Political leader, C-Singer, D-Sportsperson). It is the same order as List-II, so it is a typical distractor. Only the Suu Kyi match is right. The correct key is the pairing 4 2 1 3.

Option (b) is the pairing 4 3 2 1. Only Sharapova as sportsperson is right. Suu Kyi is not a singer, Jahangir is not a political leader and Jones is not a human rights activist. It is a distractor built from a scrambled order.

Option (c) is the pairing 1 3 2 4. All four matches are wrong. Sharapova is not a human rights activist, Suu Kyi is not a singer, Jahangir is not mainly a political leader and Jones is not a sportsperson.
Option (d) is the pairing 4 2 1 3: Sharapova-sportsperson, Suu Kyi-political leader, Jahangir-human rights activist, Jones-singer. All four are correct, so this is the answer.
related: Aung San Suu Kyi won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991.
Asma Jahangir co-founded the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan in 1987.
Norah Jones is the daughter of sitar maestro Ravi Shankar.
Maria Sharapova won Wimbledon in 2004 at age 17.
Shirin Ebadi won the 2003 Nobel Peace Prize.
Wangari Maathai won the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize.
Malala Yousafzai is the youngest Nobel laureate, in 2014.
statements: A — Maria Sharapova = Sportsperson (4): Russian-born tennis player, born 1987 in Nyagan and trained in Florida. She won Wimbledon 2004, the US Open 2006, the Australian Open 2008 and the French Open 2012, completing a career Grand Slam. She reached world No. 1 and was banned for doping (meldonium) in 2016, and she retired in 2020.

B — Aung San Suu Kyi = Political leader (2): Daughter of Aung San, the architect of Burmese independence. She co-founded the NLD in 1988, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991 and the Jawaharlal Nehru Award for International Understanding in 1993. She became State Counsellor in 2016. She was removed in the February 2021 military coup and detained.

C — Asma Jahangir = Human rights activist (1): Pakistani lawyer who co-founded the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (1987) and the Women's Action Forum. She served as UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief and was the first woman president of the Supreme Court Bar Association. She won the Right Livelihood Award in 2014 and died in 2018.

D — Norah Jones = Singer (3): American singer-songwriter and pianist, daughter of Ravi Shankar and sister of Anoushka Shankar. Her 2002 debut album Come Away With Me won eight Grammys in total, five of them in 2003, including Album of the Year. She is known for jazz, pop and country-influenced music.
summary: The correct answer is (d): A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3. Maria Sharapova is a sportsperson (tennis), Aung San Suu Kyi a political leader, Asma Jahangir a human rights activist, and Norah Jones a singer.
topic_notes: This question tests recognition of newsmakers in sports, politics, human rights and the arts, as the EPFO exam often asks. Maria Sharapova won Wimbledon 2004 and was a Grand Slam champion. Aung San Suu Kyi, Nobel Peace laureate 1991, leads the NLD in Myanmar, was State Counsellor 2016-21 and was detained after the 2021 coup. Asma Jahangir was a Pakistani lawyer who co-founded the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, received the UN Human Rights Prize in 2018 and died in 2018. Norah Jones is an American singer and the daughter of Ravi Shankar. Related personalities likely to be asked: Malala Yousafzai (Nobel Peace Prize 2014, education activist, shared with Kailash Satyarthi), Shirin Ebadi (Iran, Nobel Peace Prize 2003, human rights lawyer), Wangari Maathai (Kenya, Nobel Peace Prize 2004, environmentalist), Serena Williams and Sania Mirza (tennis), Lata Mangeshkar (singer, Bharat Ratna 2001), and Benazir Bhutto (Pakistani political leader). Strategy: for matching questions, fix the one or two items you are sure of and eliminate the options that contradict them.

question:
Match List-I (Author) with List-II (Book) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the Lists: List-I (Author) A. Bill Clinton B. Henry Kissinger C. Nelson Mandela D. Hillary Clinton List-II (Book)
1. Between Hope and History
2. Living History
3. Diplomacy
4. Long Walk to Freedom Codes: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a straightforward author-book matching question, so the approach is to anchor on the most certain pairs and eliminate. Nelson Mandela's autobiography is 'Long Walk to Freedom' (1994), so C-4. Hillary Clinton's memoir of her White House years is 'Living History' (2003), so D-2. Henry Kissinger, the US Secretary of State and National Security Adviser under Nixon and Ford, wrote 'Diplomacy' (1994), so B-3. That leaves 'Between Hope and History: Meeting America's Challenges for the 21st Century' (1996), which is Bill Clinton's book, so A-1. Checking the codes: option (a) gives A-2 and D-1, a swap of the Clintons' books. Option (c) also has A-2. Option (d) pairs Mandela with Diplomacy-type mismatches (C-3, B-4). Only (b) satisfies all four pairs. Keep in mind that 'My Life' (2004) is Bill Clinton's autobiography, which is a common trap, as is Hillary's later 'Hard Choices' (2014).
explanations: Wrong: it gives Bill Clinton 'Living History' and Hillary 'Between Hope and History', which reverses the two Clinton books, and also gives Mandela 'Diplomacy'.
Correct: all four pairs match: A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2.
Wrong: it matches A-2 (incorrect) and D-1 (incorrect), although B-3 and C-4 are right.
Wrong: it gives Mandela 'Diplomacy' and Kissinger 'Long Walk to Freedom', and also swaps the Clintons' books in part.
keyfact: Bill Clinton – Between Hope and History; Kissinger – Diplomacy; Mandela – Long Walk to Freedom; Hillary Clinton – Living History.
option_notes: Option (a) 2-4-3-1 is incorrect. It would make Bill Clinton the author of 'Living History' and Kissinger the author of 'Long Walk to Freedom'. In fact 'Living History' is Hillary Clinton's 2003 memoir and 'Long Walk to Freedom' is Mandela's 1994 autobiography. It is a distractor built on mixing the two Clintons.

Option (b) 1-3-4-2 is correct. Bill Clinton: 'Between Hope and History' (1996). Kissinger: 'Diplomacy' (1994). Mandela: 'Long Walk to Freedom' (1994). Hillary Clinton: 'Living History' (2003). All four pairings are factually accurate, which makes this the only option that matches the lists.

Option (c) 2-3-4-1 is incorrect. B-3 and C-4 are correct, but it assigns Bill Clinton 'Living History' and Hillary Clinton 'Between Hope and History'. The two spouses' books were swapped to create a trap. Remember that Hillary wrote 'Living History' in 2003 and Bill wrote 'My Life' in 2004.

Option (d) 1-4-3-2 is incorrect. A-1 and D-2 are right, but it gives Kissinger 'Long Walk to Freedom' and Mandela 'Diplomacy'. Mandela's autobiography is 'Long Walk to Freedom' (1994), and Kissinger's 'Diplomacy' (1994) examines statecraft and the balance of power.
related: Mandela's 'Long Walk to Freedom' was published in 1994, the year he became President.
Hillary Clinton's 'Living History' appeared in 2003; Bill Clinton's 'My Life' in 2004.
Kissinger won the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize (shared with Le Duc Tho, who declined).
Mandela and F. W. de Klerk shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize.
Barack Obama wrote 'The Audacity of Hope' (2006).
Mandela received India's Bharat Ratna in 1990.
statements: A-1 — Correct: Bill Clinton wrote 'Between Hope and History'. It was published in 1996 during his presidency, setting out his vision for America's challenges in the 21st century, and was written ahead of the 1996 re-election campaign. His full autobiography is 'My Life' (2004). He was the 42nd US President (1993-2001), a Democrat from Arkansas.

B-3 — Correct: Henry Kissinger wrote 'Diplomacy' (1994), a history of international relations and the balance-of-power tradition from Richelieu to the post-Cold War era. Kissinger was US Secretary of State (1973-77), won the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize for the Vietnam ceasefire talks, and also wrote 'White House Years', 'On China' (2011) and 'World Order' (2014).

C-4 — Correct: Nelson Mandela wrote 'Long Walk to Freedom' (1994), an autobiography partly drafted secretly in prison on Robben Island. He was jailed for 27 years, became South Africa's first democratic, Black President (1994-99), shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk, and received the Bharat Ratna in 1990.

D-2 — Correct: Hillary Clinton wrote 'Living History' (2003), a memoir of her years as First Lady (1993-2001). She was later US Senator from New York, Secretary of State (2009-13) and the 2016 Democratic presidential nominee. Her other books include 'It Takes a Village' (1996) and 'Hard Choices' (2014).
summary: The correct option is (b): A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2. Bill Clinton wrote 'Between Hope and History', Kissinger wrote 'Diplomacy', Mandela wrote 'Long Walk to Freedom', and Hillary Clinton wrote 'Living History'.
topic_notes: Books and authors is a recurring static GK topic in EPFO papers. Group the material by person. Nelson Mandela: 'Long Walk to Freedom' (1994), plus 'Conversations with Myself' (2010). Bill Clinton: 'Between Hope and History' (1996), 'My Life' (2004), 'Giving' (2007). Hillary Clinton: 'It Takes a Village' (1996), 'Living History' (2003), 'Hard Choices' (2014), 'What Happened' (2017). Henry Kissinger: 'A World Restored' (1957), 'White House Years' (1979), 'Diplomacy' (1994), 'On China' (2011), 'World Order' (2014), 'Leadership' (2022). Other political autobiographies often asked: Barack Obama, 'Dreams from My Father' (1995), 'The Audacity of Hope' (2006) and 'A Promised Land' (2020); Michelle Obama, 'Becoming' (2018); Mikhail Gorbachev, 'Perestroika'; Benazir Bhutto, 'Daughter of the East'; Pervez Musharraf, 'In the Line of Fire' (2006); Aung San Suu Kyi, 'Freedom from Fear'; Margaret Thatcher, 'The Downing Street Years'. Indian counterparts: Nehru, 'Discovery of India' and 'Glimpses of World History'; Gandhi, 'My Experiments with Truth'; A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, 'Wings of Fire' and 'India 2020'; Manmohan Singh, 'Strictly Personal'; Atal Bihari Vajpayee, 'Kaidi Kavirai ki Kundalian'; Jaswant Singh, 'Jinnah: India-Partition-Independence'. Tip: when two options differ only by a swap, verify the pair you are most sure about, then follow through the rest.

question:
Match List-1 (Distinguished Women) with List-II (Known As/Area) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the Lists: List-I (Distinguished Women) A. Shanta Sinha B. Kalpana Lajmi C. Romila Thapar D. Radha Reddy List-II (Known As/Area)
1. Film Direction
2. Community Leadership
3. Dancer
4. Historian
5. Business-woman Codes: A B C D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a straight factual matching question on distinguished Indian women. Shanta Sinha founded the MV Foundation in Andhra Pradesh, which works to abolish child labour and put children in school. She was the first Chairperson of the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR, 2007-2013) and received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2003. Kalpana Lajmi (1954-2018) directed Ek Pal, Rudaali, Darmiyaan and Daman. Romila Thapar is an eminent historian of ancient India, author of 'Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas' and 'A History of India Vol. 1'. Radha Reddy, with her husband Raja Reddy, is a well-known Kuchipudi dancer and Padma Bhushan awardee. Elimination: Romila Thapar is a historian (4), so options (b) and (d) can be dropped only if C=4 holds, and (c) fails because it pairs Radha Reddy with film direction and Kalpana Lajmi with dance. Only (a) fits all four matches. No item matches the business-woman category (5), which is a distractor.
explanations: Correct: it gives A-Community Leadership, B-Film Direction, C-Historian, D-Dancer, and all four pairs are accurate.
Wrong: it makes Shanta Sinha a historian and Kalpana Lajmi a dancer, and Radha Reddy is not a film director.
Wrong: Kalpana Lajmi is a film director, not a dancer, and Radha Reddy is a dancer, not a film director. Only A and C are right.
Wrong: Shanta Sinha is not a historian, and neither Romila Thapar nor Radha Reddy fits the business-woman category.
keyfact: Shanta Sinha = child rights leader (MV Foundation); Lajmi = films; Thapar = historian; Radha Reddy = Kuchipudi dancer.
option_notes: Code 2-1-4-3: Community Leadership, Film Direction, Historian, Dancer. This is the right combination. Shanta Sinha is a child-rights activist, Kalpana Lajmi directed Rudaali, Romila Thapar is a historian of ancient India, and Radha Reddy is a Kuchipudi dancer.

Code 4-3-5-1 is wrong. It would make Shanta Sinha a historian, Kalpana Lajmi a dancer, Romila Thapar a business-woman and Radha Reddy a film director. Business-woman examples from India include Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw of Biocon, a biotechnology entrepreneur, and Indra Nooyi, the former PepsiCo CEO.

Code 2-3-4-1 is partly right: A and C are correct. B and D are swapped, since Lajmi directed films and Radha Reddy dances. Kuchipudi is a classical dance form from Andhra Pradesh, and Bharatanatyam is a classical dance of Tamil Nadu.

Code 4-1-5-3 is wrong. Only B is correct. Romila Thapar is a historian, not a business-woman, and Shanta Sinha is a community and child-rights leader. Radha Reddy is a dancer, a match which this code gets right only by chance.
related: Shanta Sinha was the first Chairperson of the NCPCR (2007-2013).
Shanta Sinha received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2003.
Kalpana Lajmi directed Rudaali (1993), starring Dimple Kapadia.
Romila Thapar wrote 'Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas'.
Radha Reddy and Raja Reddy are Kuchipudi exponents.
Ela Bhatt founded SEWA, the Self Employed Women's Association.
Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw founded Biocon.
Kuchipudi is a classical dance form of Andhra Pradesh.
statements: A. Shanta Sinha — Correct: she is matched with Community Leadership (2). She founded the MV Foundation (Mamidipudi Venkatarangaiya Foundation) in 1991, which campaigns against child labour and for the right to education. She was the first Chairperson of the NCPCR from 2007 to 2013 and won the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2003. She was awarded the Padma Shri in 1998. She is an academic by training, having been a professor at the University of Hyderabad.

B. Kalpana Lajmi — Correct: she is matched with Film Direction (1). She was a filmmaker and the niece of Guru Dutt. She directed Ek Pal (1986), Rudaali (1993), Darmiyaan (1997), Daman (2001) and Chingari (2006). She won a National Award for Daman, and she collaborated closely with Bhupen Hazarika. She died in 2018.

C. Romila Thapar — Correct: she is matched with Historian (4). She is a professor emerita of ancient Indian history at JNU. Her works include 'Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas' (1961), 'Ancient Indian Social History: Some Interpretations' and 'The Penguin History of Early India'. She declined the Padma Bhushan and received the Kluge Prize in 2008.

D. Radha Reddy — Correct: she is matched with Dancer (3). She is a Kuchipudi exponent who performs with her husband Raja Reddy, and they run the Kuchipudi Art Academy in Delhi. They were jointly awarded the Padma Shri (1984) and the Padma Bhushan (2000). Her daughters Yamini Reddy and Bhavana Reddy are also dancers, and Yamini is a Kuchipudi dancer.
summary: The correct option is (a): A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3. Shanta Sinha is a child-rights and community leader, Kalpana Lajmi was a film director, Romila Thapar is a historian, and Radha Reddy is a Kuchipudi dancer.
topic_notes: This question tests recognition of distinguished Indian women and their fields, a recurring area in the General Awareness section. Shanta Sinha: MV Foundation, NCPCR first chair, Magsaysay 2003, Padma Shri 1998. Kalpana Lajmi: director of Ek Pal, Rudaali, Darmiyaan, Daman and Chingari. Romila Thapar: ancient Indian historian, emerita professor at JNU, Kluge Prize 2008, refused the Padma Bhushan. Radha Reddy: Kuchipudi dancer, Padma Bhushan 2000. Related figures that UPSC often asks about: Medha Patkar (Narmada Bachao Andolan), Ela Bhatt (SEWA founder, Magsaysay 1977), Aruna Roy (RTI activist, MKSS), Kiran Bedi (first woman IPS), Mary Kom (boxer), Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw (Biocon), Mrinal Sen and Mira Nair (film directors), Sonal Mansingh (Odissi and Bharatanatyam), Mallika Sarabhai (Kuchipudi and Bharatanatyam), Bharati Mukherjee and Arundhati Roy (writers; Roy won the Booker Prize in 1997), Amrita Pritam (Punjabi poet, Jnanpith 1981), Mahasweta Devi (Bengali writer and activist), and Anita Desai (novelist). Questions in this format usually ask for matching of persons with fields, so link each name to one iconic work, institution or award. Ramon Magsaysay Award winners from India are another common theme.

question: Assertion (A): In its Global Development Finance Report 2004, the World Bank has categorised India as a less indebted country for the year 2002. Reason (R): During the last decade, India’s outstanding external debt has considerable reduced
options: Both A and R are individually true and R is the correct explana on of A
Both A and R are individually true and R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
subject: Computers
detail: The World Bank's Global Development Finance (GDF) classifies developing countries as severely indebted, moderately indebted or less indebted. The classification uses ratios such as present value of debt to GNI and to exports, and debt service to exports. After the 1991 balance of payments crisis India cut short-term debt and relied more on long-term, concessional borrowing. By 2002 its debt ratios were low: debt-to-GDP was about 21-22%, down from about 38% in 1991-92, and the debt-service ratio was about 13-14%. Foreign exchange reserves were large, at about 75% of total debt. India therefore moved into the less indebted group. The improvement came from falling ratios, not from a falling stock. Total external debt rose from roughly US$ 83-85 billion in 1991 to about US$ 98-100 billion in 2002, after peaking near US$ 100 billion in 1998-99. So R is false because debt did not 'considerably reduce' in absolute terms. Elimination: (a) and (b) need R true, and (d) needs A false, but A is true. That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong. R is false because India's external debt stock increased over the decade. The improvement came through better ratios, so R cannot explain A.
Wrong. A is true, but R is false because the absolute outstanding external debt did not fall considerably.
Correct. A is true because the World Bank classed India as less indebted in 2002. R is false because the debt stock rose; only the ratios improved.
Wrong. A is not false, since India was categorised as less indebted in GDF 2004.
keyfact: India was 'less indebted' in 2002 because its debt ratios fell, even though the absolute debt stock rose to about US$ 100 billion.
option_notes: Option (a) would require both statements to be true with R explaining A. It fails here because R is factually incorrect. India's improved debt indicators came from a high reserves cover, a lower debt-GDP ratio, a lower debt-service ratio and a higher share of long-term and concessional debt, not from a fall in the absolute debt stock.

Option (b) would apply if both A and R were true but unconnected. R is false, so it does not apply. In Assertion-Reason questions, always check the truth of each statement first and then test whether R explains A.

Option (c) says A is true and R is false. It is the correct choice. India was called less indebted in 2002 on the strength of its ratios. Its external debt in absolute terms grew from about US$ 83 billion in 1991 to about US$ 100 billion by 2002, so R fails.
Option (d) says A is false and R is true. It is wrong on both counts: the World Bank did classify India as less indebted, and the debt stock did not fall considerably.
related: GDF is the World Bank's annual report on external debt; it is now called International Debt Statistics.
Debt-service ratio equals debt service payments divided by current receipts.
India's debt-GDP ratio fell from about 38% in 1991-92 to about 21% in 2002.
The 1991 crisis forced India to pledge gold with the Bank of England and Union Bank of Switzerland.
Reserves exceeded 70% of external debt in 2002.
The HIPC initiative was launched in 1996 by the IMF and World Bank.
summary: The best answer is (c): A is true and R is false. The World Bank's Global Development Finance 2004 classed India as a 'less indebted' country for 2002. India's outstanding external debt did not fall over the decade; it rose in absolute terms, so the reason offered is wrong.
topic_notes:
External debt is the part of a country's debt owed to non-residents and repayable in foreign currency or goods. India's external debt rose sharply in the 1980s through commercial borrowing and NRI deposits. This led to the 1991 crisis, when reserves covered only about 2-3 weeks of imports. Reforms then restricted short-term borrowing and favoured long-term and concessional loans. They also built up forex reserves and promoted equity-type flows such as FDI and FPI.

Key indicators:
- Debt-GDP ratio: about 38% in 1991-92 and about 21-22% in 2002.
- Debt-service ratio: about 35% in 1990-91 and about 13-14% in 2002.
- Reserves to debt: about 7% in 1990-91 and above 70% in 2002.
- Short-term debt share: fell sharply after 1991.
- Multilateral and bilateral debt are the largest components, along with commercial borrowings, NRI deposits and rupee debt.

The World Bank's Global Development Finance (now International Debt Statistics) classifies countries as severely indebted, moderately indebted or less indebted. In India, the Ministry of Finance publishes 'India's External Debt: A Status Report', and the RBI publishes data on external debt. Related policy points: the Rangarajan Committee on the balance of payments (1993) and the Committee on External Debt (Reddy Committee, 1993) advised a conservative approach to external debt. More recently, India's external debt stood at about US$ 620-650 billion with a debt-GDP ratio of roughly 18-19%, and its debt remains mostly long-term. Later exam questions could ask about the components of external debt, the debt-service ratio, the Bretton Woods institutions or the HIPC initiative.

question:
Consider the following statements: India had plan holiday during 1966-69 due to
1. Indo-Pakistan conﬂict in 1965.
2. Severe drought for two successive years. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Computers
detail: After the Third Five-Year Plan (1961-66) ended, the Fourth Plan could not start on schedule. The Third Plan had already been hurt by the 1962 Sino-Indian war. The 1965 Indo-Pakistan war then diverted resources to defence and led the US to suspend aid. Two successive severe droughts (1965-66 and 1966-67) cut foodgrain output sharply, pushed up inflation and forced food imports under PL-480. Foreign exchange was scarce, and the rupee was devalued in June 1966 (from Rs 4.76 to Rs 7.50 per US dollar). The Planning Commission therefore shelved the draft Fourth Plan and ran three Annual Plans (1966-67, 1967-68, 1968-69), which are called the Plan Holiday. During this period the Green Revolution strategy (HYV seeds, fertilisers, the Agricultural Prices Commission, the Food Corporation of India, both set up in 1965) took shape. The Fourth Plan began in 1969 under Gadgil's strategy, with the aims of growth with stability and self-reliance. Both statements give genuine causes, so (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out the droughts, which were an equally important cause.
Wrong: it leaves out the 1965 war, which was also a cause.
Correct: both the war and the successive droughts, along with devaluation and the resource crunch, caused the plan holiday.
Wrong: both statements are factually valid causes.
keyfact: Plan holiday 1966-69: war (1965), two successive droughts, and devaluation led to three Annual Plans before the Fourth Plan.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only, would credit only the 1965 war. The war began in August 1965 over Kashmir, with Operation Gibraltar and Operation Grand Slam, and ended with the Tashkent Agreement in January 1966. It raised defence spending and cut foreign aid, but it was not the only cause of the plan holiday.

Option (b), 2 only, would credit only the drought. The droughts of 1965-66 and 1966-67 sharply cut foodgrain output and forced PL-480 imports. They were a major cause, but the war and the foreign-exchange crisis also contributed to the plan holiday.

Option (c), both 1 and 2, is correct. The plan holiday ran from 1966 to 1969 as three Annual Plans, replacing the Fourth Plan, which was then launched in 1969-74. It was caused by the war, the droughts, inflation, the rupee devaluation of 1966 and the loss of foreign aid. Plan outlays were kept modest during this period.

Option (d), neither, is wrong because both factors are well documented causes. It would have been right only if the plan holiday had other, unrelated causes. Note that the Third Plan failed partly because of the 1962 China war, and the plan holiday followed that failure.
related: Plan holiday: 1966-67, 1967-68 and 1968-69, three Annual Plans.
Rupee devalued in June 1966, from Rs 4.76 to Rs 7.50 per US dollar.
Fourth Plan ran 1969-74; its stated aim was growth with stability.
Annual Plans were also run in 1990-92, before the Eighth Plan.
Rolling Plan: 1978-80, introduced by the Janata government.
Tashkent Declaration: January 1966, Shastri and Ayub Khan.
FCI and Agricultural Prices Commission were set up in 1965.
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.
statements: 1 — Correct: The 1965 war with Pakistan strained resources and disrupted aid. The war took place in Aug-Sept 1965 and ended with the Tashkent Declaration on 10 January 1966, signed by Lal Bahadur Shastri and Ayub Khan. Defence spending rose, and the US and other donors suspended or reduced aid, which worsened the external payments position. This delayed finalising the Fourth Plan. The Third Plan's targets had already been missed after the 1962 China war. Together these shifted national priorities to defence and short-term stabilisation.

2 — Correct: Two consecutive droughts hit in 1965-66 and 1966-67. Foodgrain output fell from about 89 million tonnes in 1964-65 to about 72 million tonnes in 1965-66. Prices rose and India became dependent on US PL-480 wheat imports, the 'ship-to-mouth' situation. The droughts weakened agriculture, which was the base of the economy, and cut government revenue. They also pushed policymakers to the Green Revolution strategy, using HYV seeds from 1966-67, with M.S. Swaminathan and Norman Borlaug among its key figures, and C. Subramaniam as Agriculture Minister.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. India took a 'plan holiday' from 1966 to 1969, with three Annual Plans in place of the Fourth Five-Year Plan. The causes were the 1965 Indo-Pakistan war, the severe droughts of 1965-66 and 1966-67, resource strain, and the devaluation of the rupee in 1966.
topic_notes: Indian planning began in 1951 with the First Plan (1951-56, Harrod-Domar model). The Second Plan (1956-61) followed the Mahalanobis model, stressing heavy industry. The Third Plan (1961-66) aimed at a self-reliant, self-generating economy but failed because of the 1962 China war, the 1965 Pakistan war and the droughts. The plan holiday of 1966-69 consisted of three Annual Plans. Key events of the period were the devaluation of the rupee in June 1966, the launch of the HYV seed programme (the Green Revolution), the creation of the Agricultural Prices Commission (1965) and the Food Corporation of India (1965), and the nationalisation of 14 banks in 1969. The Fourth Plan (1969-74), under D.R. Gadgil, aimed at growth with stability and progressive achievement of self-reliance. It also missed its targets. Later plans: Fifth (1974-78, ended early by the Janata government; Garibi Hatao), Rolling Plan (1978-80), Sixth (1980-85), Seventh (1985-90), Annual Plans (1990-92) because of the political instability and BoP crisis, Eighth (1992-97, liberalisation), Ninth (1997-2002), Tenth (2002-07), Eleventh (2007-12), Twelfth (2012-17). The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015. The National Development Council approves plans. Possible questions concern the plan models, the periods of annual plans, the chairs and the Green Revolution.

question:
Consider the following statements:
1. The members of the Employees' Provident
Fund and exempted Provident Funds are
eligible for the Employees' Deposit-Linked
Insurance Scheme.
2. Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 was
introduced for the industrial workers.
3. Coverage under the Employees' Provident
Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act is
restricted to establishments employing 20 or
more persons.
Which of the statements given above is/are
correct?
a) 1 and 2
b) 1, 2 and 3
c) 1 and 3
d) 3 only
subject: Social Security
detail: The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 provides three schemes: the Employees' Provident Fund Scheme, 1952, the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 (which replaced the Family Pension Scheme, 1971, with effect from 16 November 1995) and the Employees' Deposit-Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976. The Act applies to factories engaged in notified industries and to other establishments notified by the Central Government. The general threshold is 20 or more employees, and the Central Government can lower it to 10 for notified classes. The same threshold is the basis of statement 3 being treated as correct in the exam context. Strictly the Act can also cover establishments with fewer than 20 employees by voluntary extension under Section 1(4). EDLI covers all members of the EPF and of exempted establishments, because exempted establishments contribute to EDLI. The EPS covers employees of all covered establishments with pay up to the wage ceiling. It is not restricted to industrial workers, so statement 2 is wrong. Eliminating statement 2 removes options (a) and (b). Of the remaining options, (c) fits because statements 1 and 3 are both correct.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 2 and leaves out statement 3. The EPS, 1995 is not limited to industrial workers.
(b) is wrong because it includes statement 2, which wrongly limits the EPS, 1995 to industrial workers.
(c) is right because statements 1 and 3 are correct and statement 2 is incorrect.
(d) is wrong because it ignores statement 1. EDLI covers members of both the EPF and exempted funds.
keyfact: EDLI, 1976 covers EPF and exempted fund members; the EPS, 1995 covers all employees, not only industrial workers.
option_notes: Option (a), statements 1 and 2: it pairs the EDLI coverage with the EPS, 1995. The EPS replaced the Family Pension Scheme, 1971, from 16 November 1995. It covers all employees of covered establishments, not only industrial workers. It is funded by 8.33% of the employer's contribution and a Central Government share. The wage ceiling is Rs 15,000.

Option (b), statements 1, 2 and 3: it would be right only if the EPS were limited to industrial workers. In fact the three schemes under the 1952 Act are the EPF, the EPS and EDLI. The Central Board of Trustees administers them, with the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation as the executive body. The EPFO is under the Ministry of Labour and Employment.

Option (c), statements 1 and 3: this is the correct combination. EDLI, 1976 covers EPF and exempted fund members. The Act applies to establishments with 20 or more employees. The coverage threshold can be lowered to 10 by the Central Government, and voluntary coverage is possible under Section 1(4).

Option (d), statement 3 only: it recognises only the 20-employee coverage rule. It wrongly drops statement 1. EDLI, 1976 covers all members of both the EPF and exempted funds. The employer alone contributes 0.5% of wages up to the ceiling. The benefit is paid to the nominee on the member's death in service.
related: EPF & MP Act was enacted in 1952.
EDLI Scheme started on 1 August 1976.
EPS, 1995 came into effect on 16 November 1995.
EPS employer's share is 8.33% of wages.
The Central Government contributes 1.16% to the EPS.
UAN was launched in 2014.
Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the EPF Act.
The EPFO is under the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
statements: 1 — Correct: EDLI Scheme, 1976 covers members of the EPF and of exempted provident funds, since exempted establishments must also contribute to EDLI. The scheme is mandatory for all covered employees. The employer pays 0.5% of wages (up to the ceiling) and the employee pays nothing. On the death of a member in service, the nominee or heir receives an insurance benefit linked to the average PF balance and wages. The scheme began on 1 August 1976. The Central Board of Trustees administers it, and the benefit has been revised several times.

2 — Incorrect: The Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 was introduced with effect from 16 November 1995, replacing the Employees' Family Pension Scheme, 1971. It covers all employees who are members of the EPF or exempted funds, not only industrial workers. It provides superannuation, retirement, widow, children, orphan and disability pensions. The employer's share of 8.33% of wages funds it, together with a Central Government contribution of 1.16%. The wage ceiling was raised to Rs 15,000 in 2014. Pensionable service is at least 10 years.

3 — Correct: The EPF & MP Act, 1952 applies to establishments employing 20 or more persons. The Act extends to the whole of India, except Jammu and Kashmir at that time. Under Section 1(3)(a) it applies to factories in scheduled industries employing 20 or more persons. Under 1(3)(b) the Central Government may apply it to other establishments. Under Section 1(4) establishments may be brought in voluntarily by agreement. Under Section 1(5) the Act can be extended to establishments with fewer than 20 persons. The Central Government may also reduce the threshold to 10 for notified classes.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. EDLI Scheme, 1976 covers members of both the EPF and exempted provident funds, and the EPF & MP Act, 1952 applies to establishments employing 20 or more persons. Statement 2 is wrong because the EPS, 1995 covers all EPF members in covered establishments, not only industrial workers.
topic_notes: The EPF & MP Act, 1952 is the main social security law for organised-sector workers in India. It provides for three schemes: the Employees' Provident Fund Scheme, 1952, the Employees' Deposit-Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976 and the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995. The Central Board of Trustees (EPF) administers them, and the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) is the executive arm. The EPFO is under the Ministry of Labour and Employment and has its headquarters in New Delhi. It is among the world's largest social security organisations. Coverage applies to scheduled industries and to other classes of establishments notified by the Government. The base threshold is 20 or more employees, which can be reduced to 10 for notified classes. Voluntary coverage is possible under Section 1(4). The employee contributes 12% of basic wages plus dearness allowance, and the employer contributes 12% (10% in certain cases). Of the employer's 12%, 8.33% goes to the EPS and the remaining 3.67% goes to the EPF. The Central Government pays 1.16% towards the EPS. The EDLI employer contribution is 0.5%. Administration charges are levied from the employer. Exempted establishments run their own provident fund trusts but still contribute to the EPS and EDLI. The statutory wage ceiling is Rs 15,000 per month. Settlement of claims uses the UAN (Universal Account Number), which was launched in 2014. Other angles UPSC could ask are the Family Pension Scheme, 1971, the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995, the 2014 pension reforms, the minimum pension of Rs 1,000, the interest rate declared by the CBT, and the Employees' Enrolment Campaign. The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the EPF Act.

question:
Which one of the following statements is
not correct?
a) The Special Marriage Act, 1954 extends to all
the States and Union Territories of India
b) The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 applies to
Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs in addition to Hindus
c) The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 recognizes the
right of women to inherit property of an
intestate equally with men
d) Muslims, Chris ans and Parsis in India have no
adoption laws and can take a child under the
Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 only under
foster care
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: The Special Marriage Act, 1954 provides a civil form of marriage for any two persons, irrespective of religion. Section 1 originally said it extended to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir, and it also applied to Indian citizens domiciled abroad. Only after the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 did it extend fully to all States and Union Territories. This is why (a) was the incorrect statement in 2004. Under Section 2 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, it applies to Hindus in the broad sense, including Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs, as well as Virashaivas, Lingayats and followers of the Brahmo, Prarthana and Arya Samaj. Under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Class I heirs of an intestate male Hindu include the widow, sons and daughters, who take equal shares. The 2005 amendment made daughters coparceners by birth. Muslims, Christians and Parsis have no codified adoption law. They use the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, which gives only guardianship, not full adoption. Elimination: (b), (c) and (d) are accurate, which leaves (a).
explanations: Correct choice. In 2004 the Special Marriage Act, 1954 did not extend to Jammu and Kashmir, so saying it applied to all States and UTs was incorrect. It was extended only after 2019.
Not the answer, because the statement is correct. Section 2 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 applies it to Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs as well as Hindus.

Not the answer, because the statement is broadly correct. Class I heirs of an intestate Hindu male, including daughters and the widow, share equally with sons. The 2005 amendment strengthened this further.

Not the answer, because the statement is correct. Muslims, Christians and Parsis have no adoption law of their own. The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 gives only guardianship or foster care, with no change of legal parentage.
keyfact: Before 2019 the Special Marriage Act, 1954 excluded Jammu and Kashmir; the Hindu Marriage Act covers Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs, and Muslims, Christians and Parsis have only guardianship under the 1890 Act.
option_notes: The Special Marriage Act, 1954 is a secular law for civil marriage between any two persons, whatever their religion, and for inter-faith marriages. It requires a 30-day notice to the Marriage Officer. It originally excluded J&K and covered Indian nationals abroad. It replaced the 1872 Act. It also governs divorce for marriages solemnised under it, and it extends to all of India since 2019.

The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 codified Hindu marriage law. It applies to Hindus in the wide sense, including Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs, Virashaivas, Lingayats and followers of the Brahmo, Prarthana and Arya Samaj. It does not apply to Scheduled Tribes unless the Centre notifies otherwise. It prescribes monogamy, the age of marriage (18 for the bride, 21 for the groom), and grounds for divorce, and it was amended in 1976.

The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 governs intestate succession among Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs. Class I heirs, namely sons, daughters, the widow and the mother, inherit simultaneously and equally. The 2005 amendment made daughters coparceners by birth with the same rights as sons. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) held that this applies even if the father died before 2005.

Muslims, Christians, Parsis and Jews have no secular adoption law. They can take a child only as a guardian under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, which gives no inheritance rights. The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 covers Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs. The Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 allows anyone to adopt, regardless of religion, through CARA.
related: Article 44 (Directive Principle) calls for a Uniform Civil Code.
The Special Marriage Act, 1954 requires 30 days' public notice of intended marriage.
Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 made daughters coparceners by birth.
The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 covers Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs.
Shayara Bano (2017) struck down instant triple talaq.
CARA is the statutory body for adoption under the Ministry of Women and Child Development.
Goa follows a common Portuguese-origin Civil Code.
Parsi marriage law is the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936.
summary: The answer is (a). When this paper was set in 2004, the Special Marriage Act, 1954 extended to all of India except Jammu and Kashmir, so the claim that it covered all States and Union Territories was wrong. The other three statements were accurate.
topic_notes: Personal laws in India differ by religion, while some laws are secular and apply to everyone. The Hindu code bills of the 1950s produced four Acts: the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, and the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. 'Hindu' in these Acts includes Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs. Muslims follow the Shariat Application Act, 1937, the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939, and the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986. The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 criminalised instant triple talaq after Shayara Bano (2017). Christians are governed by the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872 and the Indian Divorce Act, 1869. Parsis are governed by the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936. The Special Marriage Act, 1954 gives a secular civil marriage route, and the Foreign Marriage Act, 1969 covers marriages involving Indian citizens abroad. Adoption outside Hindu law is possible under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, administered through CARA. The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 deals with guardianship only. Article 44 of the Directive Principles calls for a Uniform Civil Code. Key cases are Shah Bano (1985), Sarla Mudgal (1995) and Shayara Bano (2017). The Child Marriage Restraint Act of 1929 was replaced by the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006. Possible future questions include the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, the grounds for divorce under each Act, the marriage age, the Goa Civil Code and the Law Commission's views on the UCC.

question:
Why did Mo lal Nehru and Chi aranjan
Das form a separate group known as Swaraj Party
within the Congress?
a) They were not sa sﬁed with the progress
made by the Congress in achieving Swaraj
b) It was their reac on to Mahatma Gandhi's
sudden decision to suspend the NonCooperation Movement
c) They were interested in forming more ac ve
party with revolutionary ideas
d) They felt that their opinions and views were
not given due importance in the Congress
Sessions
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: After the violence at Chauri Chaura (5 February 1922), Gandhi suspended Non-Cooperation, and he was jailed in March 1922. This left nationalists demoralised and without a programme. Congress then split into two camps. The Pro-Changers (Swarajists) were Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das and later Vithalbhai Patel. They wanted to enter the Legislative Councils and obstruct the government from within. The No-Changers were Rajagopalachari, Vallabhbhai Patel and Rajendra Prasad. They wanted to stay with constructive work and boycott the councils. The Gaya session of Congress (December 1922, presided over by C.R. Das) rejected council entry. Das and Motilal then resigned their posts and announced the Swaraj Party on 1 January 1923. The Delhi special session (September 1923, under Maulana Azad) allowed Swarajists to contest elections. In the 1923 elections they won 42 of 101 elected seats in the Central Legislative Assembly. Option (b) is the direct trigger. Option (a) is too vague. Option (c) is wrong because the Swarajists were not revolutionaries and used constitutional means. Option (d) is not the reason, since the dispute was over strategy.
explanations: Wrong as the main cause: dissatisfaction with progress was general, and the specific trigger was the suspension of the movement.
Correct: the sudden withdrawal after Chauri Chaura left a political vacuum, and the Swarajists responded with a council-entry strategy.
Wrong: the Swarajists were not revolutionary. They wanted to use the councils to obstruct the government by constitutional means.
Wrong: this was a disagreement over strategy, not a complaint about neglect at Congress sessions.
keyfact: Swaraj Party (1 Jan 1923, Das and Motilal) was formed in reaction to Gandhi's suspension of Non-Cooperation after Chauri Chaura, to pursue council entry.
option_notes: Dissatisfaction with Congress progress was a general sentiment of the time. It was not the founding cause of the Swaraj Party, which grew out of the post-1922 debate on council entry versus constructive work.

Gandhi suspended Non-Cooperation on 12 February 1922 at Bardoli, after Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur, UP, 5 February 1922), where a mob burned a police station and killed 22 policemen. This is the immediate cause of the split among Congress leaders.

The Swarajists favoured parliamentary obstruction, not revolution. Revolutionary groups of the period included the HRA (1924) and Anushilan Samiti. The Swarajists aimed to expose the sham of the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms.

The Swarajists did not form the party because they were ignored. The Gaya session did reject their proposal, but the real disagreement was ideological, over council entry versus the No-Changers' programme of constructive work.
related: Chauri Chaura incident took place on 5 February 1922 in Gorakhpur district.
Swaraj Party was founded on 1 January 1923 with C.R. Das as president and Motilal Nehru as secretary.
No-Changers included C. Rajagopalachari, Vallabhbhai Patel and Rajendra Prasad.
Swarajists won 42 of 101 elected seats in the Central Legislative Assembly in 1923.
Vithalbhai Patel became Speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly in 1925.
The Delhi special session in September 1923 permitted Congressmen to contest council elections.
C.R. Das died in June 1925.
summary: The answer is (b). Motilal Nehru and C.R. Das formed the Congress-Khilafat Swaraj Party in January 1923 mainly as a reaction to Gandhi's sudden suspension of the Non-Cooperation Movement after the Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922). They wanted to carry the struggle forward by another route, namely council entry.
topic_notes: The Swaraj Party was formally the Congress-Khilafat Swaraj Party. It was founded on 1 January 1923 at Allahabad, with C.R. Das as president and Motilal Nehru as secretary. Other prominent members were Vithalbhai Patel, N.C. Kelkar, Hakim Ajmal Khan and Madan Mohan Malaviya (who supported them). Their aims were to end the dyarchy system, demand self-government, and obstruct the government through walkouts and by rejecting budgets. Achievements: in the 1923 elections they won 42 seats in the Central Legislative Assembly, and they also did well in the Central Provinces and Bengal. In 1925 Vithalbhai Patel became Speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly. In 1925 the Swarajists defeated the Finance Bill, which was later certified by the Viceroy. They also supported the Public Safety Bill debate, and in 1928 they backed the Nehru Report. Decline: C.R. Das died in June 1925, internal differences grew (the Responsivists wanted to cooperate with the government), and the Swarajists walked out of the Assembly in 1926. They returned to Congress in 1930 when the Civil Disobedience Movement began. Related background: the Muddiman Committee (1924) reviewed the working of the 1919 Act, and the Bardoli resolution (1922) suspended the movement. Gandhi was released in February 1924. The Swarajists influenced the later Congress approach towards legislatures, as seen in the 1937 elections.

question:
Which of the following is detected and
estimated by the Pollution Check' carried out on
motor cars at service sta ons?
a) Lead and carbon particles
b) Oxides of nitrogen and sulphur
c) Carbon monoxide
d) Carbon dioxide
subject: General Science
detail: The PUC test is mandated under Rule 115 of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 (Motor Vehicles Act, 1988). For petrol (and CNG/LPG) vehicles, an exhaust gas analyser measures carbon monoxide as a percentage by volume at idling, and hydrocarbons in ppm. Diesel vehicles are tested for smoke density using the Hartridge Smoke Unit or the light-absorption coefficient, with a free acceleration test. Bharat Stage norms set the limits. For BS-IV and BS-VI petrol cars, the idling CO limit is 0.3% and HC is 200 ppm. For older vehicles, such as those registered before 2000, the CO limit is 3-4.5%. Oxides of nitrogen and sulphur are regulated in type-approval and certification tests (NOx) and by fuel quality (sulphur), not by the routine roadside PUC test. Lead was removed from petrol in India in 2000, so it is not tested. CO2 is a greenhouse gas, not a regulated pollutant in the PUC test, although analysers may display it for diagnostic reasons. The best answer is therefore CO. Elimination: (a) and (b) are not measured routinely, and (d) is not the pollutant checked.
explanations: Wrong: Lead was phased out of petrol in India (unleaded petrol from 1995 in metros, nationwide by Feb 2000). The PUC test does not measure lead, and carbon particles are measured only indirectly as diesel smoke opacity.
Wrong: NOx is controlled in type-approval testing on a chassis dynamometer, and sulphur is controlled through fuel specifications. The routine service-station PUC does not estimate them.
Correct: CO is measured as % volume in petrol vehicle exhaust by a gas analyser, and it is the main parameter of the PUC check.
Wrong: CO2 is not a limit parameter in the PUC certificate. It is a greenhouse gas and is sometimes shown by the analyser, but it is not what the check is meant to detect.
keyfact: The PUC test for petrol vehicles measures carbon monoxide (and hydrocarbons), while diesel vehicles are tested for smoke density.
option_notes: Lead: Tetraethyl lead was an anti-knock additive in petrol. It damages the nervous system and affects children's IQ. India banned leaded petrol fully from 1 Feb 2000. Carbon particles (soot) come from diesel engines and are measured as smoke opacity and particulate matter.

NOx (NO and NO2) forms at high combustion temperatures and causes smog, acid rain and respiratory harm. SO2 comes from sulphur in fuel. India reduced sulphur in fuel through the Bharat Stage norms, with BS-VI at 10 ppm from April 2020. These are controlled at the type-approval and fuel-specification level.

Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas formed by incomplete combustion. It binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, which reduces oxygen transport. It is the key PUC parameter for petrol vehicles, measured at idle by a non-dispersive infrared analyser. The BS-IV idling limit is 0.3% for petrol cars.

Carbon dioxide is the main greenhouse gas produced by complete combustion. Vehicle CO2 is controlled through fuel economy and CO2 norms (India's CAFE norms from 2017), not through the PUC test. It is not toxic at normal exhaust levels, but it drives global warming.
related: PUC test is conducted under Rule 115 of the CMVR, 1989.
India moved directly from BS-IV to BS-VI on 1 April 2020.
Leaded petrol was completely banned in India from 1 February 2000.
Catalytic converters use Pt, Pd and Rh to reduce CO, HC and NOx.
Diesel vehicles are tested for smoke opacity, not CO.
CO binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin.
CPCB was established in 1974 under the Water Act.
summary: The answer is (c) Carbon monoxide. The 'Pollution Under Control' (PUC) check at service stations measures CO (% by volume) in petrol vehicle exhaust, and smoke density/opacity for diesel vehicles. Of the options given, CO is the one the test measures.
topic_notes: Vehicle pollution control in India rests on the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 (Rule 115 sets emission standards). The Pollution Under Control (PUC) certificate is mandatory, and its validity is 1 year for BS-IV and newer vehicles and 3 months for others in many states. In Delhi, the Supreme Court in M.C. Mehta cases pushed CNG for public transport (2001) and phased out older vehicles. Bharat Stage norms are based on the Euro norms. BS-I came in 2000, BS-II in 2001-2003, BS-III in 2005-2010, and BS-IV in 2010 (nationwide from April 2017). India skipped BS-V and moved to BS-VI from 1 April 2020. BS-VI cut sulphur to 10 ppm and sharply reduced NOx and PM. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways (MoRTH) set the standards. The Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI) and ICAT certify vehicles. Petrol vehicles are tested for CO and HC at idle. Diesel vehicles are tested for smoke opacity (light absorption coefficient, m^-1). Other related points are the National Air Quality Index (launched 2014), the National Clean Air Programme (2019), and the Graded Response Action Plan in Delhi-NCR. Catalytic converters use platinum, palladium and rhodium to convert CO, HC and NOx to CO2, N2 and water. Common pollutants and their effects are CO (poisoning), NOx and SO2 (acid rain), ozone (smog), PM2.5 (lung disease), and lead (neurotoxin).

question:
Directions: The following items consist of
two statements, one labelled the 'Assertion (A)
and the other labelled the 'Reason (R)'. You are to
examine these two statements carefully and
decide if the Assertion (A) and the Reason (R) are
individually true and if so, whether the Reason (R)
is a correct explana on of the Assertion (A).
Select your answers to these items using the
Codes given. below and mark your answer-sheet
accordingly
Assertion (A): The salinity of the open seas is very
high compared to that of inland seas.
Reason (R): The water of rivers ﬂowing into open
seas contains dissolved salts.
Codes:
(a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct
explanation of A
