(b) Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct
explanation of A
(c) A is true but R is false
(d) A is false but R
subject: Computers
detail: Salinity is the dissolved salt content of water, in parts per thousand (‰). The average for the open ocean is about 35‰. It is controlled by evaporation, precipitation, freshwater inflow from rivers and ice melt, and the mixing of water masses. Inland seas have no free exchange with the ocean, so their salinity depends on local climate. In arid basins with high evaporation and little outflow, salts accumulate. The Dead Sea reaches about 340‰, Lake Van about 330‰, and the Great Salt Lake about 50-270‰. In humid or cold regions with heavy river inflow, salinity is low. The Baltic is about 2-8‰ and the Black Sea about 17-18‰. The Caspian is about 12‰, and it is lower in the north, where the Volga flows in. So the claim that open seas are 'very high' compared with inland seas cannot be generalised, which makes A false. R is a true fact: rivers carry salts from weathering of rocks. But rivers mostly dilute seawater, and the ocean's salinity is kept in balance by evaporation. Eliminate (a), (b) and (c) because A is not generally true. Choose (d).
explanations: Wrong. A is not true in general, since many inland seas are much saltier than the open ocean, so R cannot explain it.
Wrong. This needs both A and R to be true, but A is false.
Wrong. This takes A as true and R as false, which is the reverse of the facts: A is false and R is true.
Correct. A is false because inland seas such as the Dead Sea and Lake Van are far saltier than the oceans. R is true because river water carries dissolved salts.
keyfact: Open-ocean salinity is about 35‰; inland seas vary from very low (Baltic) to very high (Dead Sea about 340‰), so open seas are not generally saltier.
option_notes: Both true with R explaining A. This is the standard 'best case' code in Assertion-Reason questions. It would hold only if A were true and the cause of the salinity were river-borne salts. In reality ocean salt comes from long-term weathering, volcanic and hydrothermal sources, and its level is set by the balance of evaporation and freshwater input. So this code does not fit here.

Both true but R not the correct explanation. This code is used when two facts are both correct but unconnected. Here A is false, so the code fails. Note that A-R questions test the truth of each statement first and the causal link second.

A true and R false. This would require open-sea salinity to be generally higher than that of inland seas, and river water to be salt-free. Neither holds. River water has a low but real dissolved salt load, about 0.1-0.5‰, of mainly bicarbonate and calcium.

A false but R true. This is the correct code. Average ocean salinity is about 35‰. Inland seas range from nearly fresh to hypersaline, with the Dead Sea (about 340‰) being among the saltiest water bodies. River water has dissolved salts, though in small amounts.
related: Average ocean salinity is about 35‰.
The Dead Sea has about 340‰ salinity, among the world's saltiest water bodies.
The Atlantic is the saltiest ocean.
The Baltic Sea has very low salinity because of high river inflow and low evaporation.
The Red Sea and Persian Gulf are about 40‰, high because of strong evaporation.
Isohalines join places with equal salinity.
Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan is India's largest inland saline lake.
summary: The answer is (d): A is false and R is true. Open-sea salinity is about 35‰, and many inland seas and lakes in arid, high-evaporation basins, such as the Dead Sea, Lake Van and the Great Salt Lake, are far saltier. River water does carry dissolved salts, so R is true, but it does not make A true.
topic_notes: Salinity is the amount of dissolved salt in water, in grams per kg or parts per thousand (‰). The average ocean salinity is about 35‰. The main ions are chloride (about 55%), sodium (about 31%), sulphate, magnesium, calcium and potassium. Factors raising salinity are high evaporation, low rainfall, little river inflow and restricted circulation. Factors lowering it are heavy rain, river discharge, melting ice and the mixing of water masses. The highest open-ocean values are in the subtropical high-pressure belts, around 20-30° latitude, and the Atlantic is the saltiest ocean. Equatorial zones are lower because of heavy rain, and polar zones are lower because of ice melt. Among seas, the Red Sea is about 40‰ and the Persian Gulf about 40‰ or more. The Baltic Sea is very low, at about 2-8‰, because of heavy river inflow and little evaporation. Among lakes and inland seas, the Dead Sea is about 340‰ and Lake Van about 330‰. The Great Salt Lake is about 50-270‰, Sambhar Lake in India is saline, and the Caspian is about 12‰. Ocean salinity is kept fairly constant by the balance of salt inputs from rock weathering, volcanoes and hydrothermal vents against salt removal into sediments. Salinity affects density and so drives thermohaline circulation. Isohalines are lines joining places of equal salinity. The halocline is the layer of rapid salinity change with depth.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a chain-of-equalities ratio problem. When several quantities are expressed as different fractions or percentages that are all equal, set each expression equal to a common constant k, then solve for each quantity in terms of k. Here 20% of P = P/5 = k, so P = 5k. 30% of Q = 3Q/10 = k, so Q = 10k/3. (1/6) of R = k, so R = 6k. Therefore P : Q : R = 5 : 10/3 : 6. Multiply by 3 to clear the fraction: 15 : 10 : 18. Shortcut: the ratio of quantities is the inverse of their multipliers, so P : Q : R = 1/0.2 : 1/0.3 : 6 = 5 : 3.33 : 6. Check: take k = 6, so P = 30, Q = 20, R = 36. Then 20% of 30 = 6, 30% of 20 = 6, and 36/6 = 6, all equal. The ratio 30 : 20 : 36 reduces to 15 : 10 : 18. Elimination: P has the smallest multiplier (20%), so P must be larger than Q, which has 30%. This rules out (a) and (b), where P < Q. R is clearly the largest because its multiplier is only 1/6, which rules out (c), where R is only 18 against P = 10 in the wrong order. Always verify by substitution.
explanations: Incorrect: 2 : 3 : 16 has P smaller than Q, but P must be larger since 20% is a smaller multiplier than 30%. Substituting P = 2, Q = 3, R = 16 gives 0.4, 0.9 and 2.67, which are not equal.
Incorrect: 3 : 2 : 16 has the right order for P and Q, but R is wrong. Substituting gives 0.6, 0.6 and 2.67, so the third term fails.
Incorrect: 10 : 15 : 18 reverses P and Q. Substituting gives 2, 4.5 and 3, which are not equal.
Correct: with k as the common value, P = 5k, Q = 10k/3 and R = 6k. Multiplying by 3 gives 15 : 10 : 18. Substituting P = 15, Q = 10, R = 18 gives 3, 3 and 3, so all three are equal.
option_notes: Option (a) 2 : 3 : 16 would be correct only if 30% of P = 20% of Q, which swaps the percentages. It is a typical trap for students who reverse direct and inverse relations. In general, if a% of X = b% of Y, then X : Y = b : a. Always test an option by substituting it back.

Option (b) 3 : 2 : 16 gets P : Q right as 3 : 2, which is the same as 15 : 10, but R is wrong. It would require R = 16 where 18 is needed. This shows the need to check all three terms rather than just a pair. It matches the P : Q relation from 20% and 30%, since 20 : 30 inverts to 3 : 2.

Option (c) 10 : 15 : 18 has R correct relative to the scale but swaps P and Q. This comes from forgetting that the ratio is inverse to the percentages. It would correspond to 30% of P = 20% of Q = (1/6) of R scaled to 18. Such swapped-ratio options are commonly placed as distractors.

Option (d) 15 : 10 : 18 is the correct answer. It follows from P/5 = 3Q/10 = R/6 = k, giving P = 5k, Q = 10k/3 and R = 6k. The ratio is the reciprocal of the multipliers 1/5 : 3/10 : 1/6. The LCM method confirms this: multiply by 30 to get 6 : 9 : 5 as the multipliers, and invert to get 1/6 : 1/9 : 1/5, which scales to 15 : 10 : 18.
related: If a% of A = b% of B, then A : B = b : a.
Compounded ratio of a : b and c : d is ac : bd.
Mean proportional of a and b = √(ab).
Third proportional to a and b = b²/a.
If A is x% more than B, B is x/(100+x) × 100% less than A.
To combine A : B and B : C, make the B terms equal.
Choose k as the LCM of denominators to get integer values.
summary: The correct answer is (d) 15 : 10 : 18. Setting 20% of P = 30% of Q = (1/6) of R equal to a common value k gives P = 5k, Q = 10k/3 and R = 6k, so P : Q : R = 15 : 10 : 18.
topic_notes: Topic: Ratio and proportion with percentages. Core principle: if several quantities are tied by equal fractional parts, set each equal to k and express each quantity as k divided by its multiplier. A quantity with a larger multiplier is smaller. Key conversions: 20% = 1/5, 25% = 1/4, 30% = 3/10, 33.33% = 1/3, 40% = 2/5, 50% = 1/2, 16.67% = 1/6, 12.5% = 1/8. Key rules: if a% of A = b% of B, then A : B = b : a. If A : B = x : y and B : C = m : n, then A : B : C = xm : ym : yn. Steps for combining ratios: make the common term equal by cross-multiplication. Compounded ratio is the product of ratios, duplicate is the square, triplicate is the cube, and sub-duplicate is the square root. Mean proportion of a and b is √(ab), and third proportional to a and b is b²/a. Typical exam variants: finding the percentage one quantity is of another, which is (A/B) × 100. If A is x% more than B, then B is less than A by x/(100+x) × 100%. If A is x% less than B, then B is more than A by x/(100−x) × 100%. Other angles are age problems with ratios, mixture and alligation, partnership profit sharing where profit is divided in the ratio of capital × time, and salary or expenditure problems with percentage changes. Verification strategy: pick a convenient k, such as the LCM of the denominators, to get integer values, then test each option. This saves time in exam conditions, with roughly one minute allowed per question.

ocr: A tree increases annually by A of its height. What will be its height after 2 years, if it stands today 64 cm high ? (a) 72 cm (b) 74 cm Né) 81 om (d) 85 cm
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a compound growth problem, a standard topic in the Quantitative Aptitude section. When a quantity increases every year by a fraction 1/n of its present value, the new value is (1 + 1/n) times the old value. With n = 8, the multiplier is 9/8. After t years, the height is H × (9/8)^t. Here H = 64 cm and t = 2. Year 1: 64 + 64/8 = 64 + 8 = 72 cm. Year 2: 72 + 72/8 = 72 + 9 = 81 cm. The same result comes from 64 × 81/64 = 81. The numbers are chosen so that 64 = 8², which makes the answer a clean integer. Elimination: 72 cm is the height after only one year, a common trap. 74 cm would result from adding 1/8 of 64 (8 cm) and then about 2 cm, which has no logic. 85 cm is too high. Simple interest logic gives 64 + 8 + 8 = 80, which is not an option, so the compound answer 81 is the only fit. Always check whether growth is on the original or the current value; 'annually' on 'its height' means compounding.
explanations: Incorrect: 72 cm is the height after one year (64 + 8), not two.
Incorrect: 74 cm does not follow from any valid method of 1/8 annual growth on 64 cm.
Correct: 64 × (9/8)² = 81 cm, with 72 cm after year 1 and 81 cm after year 2.
Incorrect: 85 cm overshoots; the true compounded value is 81 cm.
keyfact: Growth of 1/8 per year means multiply by 9/8 yearly: 64 → 72 → 81 cm.
option_notes: 72 cm is the height after exactly one year: 64 + 64/8 = 72. It is the intermediate value and the usual distractor for students who stop after the first year. It is also 64 × 9/8. Remember that the multiplier for 1/8 growth is 9/8, and the year-wise sequence is 64, 72, 81, so 72 is valid only for a one-year question.

74 cm is not produced by any correct method here. It might tempt students who add 8 cm in year 1 and then roughly 2 cm for year 2 by mistake. Under simple growth, the result would be 64 + 8 + 8 = 80 cm, and under compound growth it is 81 cm. Neither equals 74, so it is purely a distractor value.

81 cm is the correct result, equal to 64 × (9/8)². Note that 81 = 9² and 64 = 8², so the answer is (9/8)² × 8² = 9². The year-wise heights are 64, 72, 81. This compounding approach, multiplying by (1 + r) each period, applies to population, depreciation, and compound interest questions as well.

85 cm is an overestimate that does not follow from the calculation. It could arise from careless addition or from wrongly using a larger fraction. Under 1/8 compound growth for two years the maximum is 81 cm. The simple-growth value is 80 cm, so 85 cm lies beyond both and can be rejected quickly by estimation.
related: 1/8 as a percentage equals 12.5%.
Growth by 1/n per year means a multiplier of (n+1)/n per year.
Depreciation by 1/n per year means a multiplier of (n−1)/n.
CI − SI for 2 years = P(r/100)².
Net effect of successive changes a% and b% = a + b + ab/100.
Half-yearly compounding: rate is halved and time doubled.
Rule of 72: doubling time in years ≈ 72 / rate %.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 81 cm. Each year the tree grows by 1/8 of its current height, so the height is multiplied by 9/8 every year. After 2 years: 64 × 9/8 × 9/8 = 81 cm.
topic_notes: Topic: Compound growth, percentages and fractions in Quantitative Aptitude. Key formula: if a quantity P grows by a fraction 1/n each period, the value after t periods is P × ((n+1)/n)^t. If it falls by 1/n each period, the value is P × ((n−1)/n)^t. Percentage equivalent: 1/8 = 12.5%. Useful fraction-percent conversions: 1/2 = 50%, 1/3 = 33.33%, 1/4 = 25%, 1/5 = 20%, 1/6 = 16.67%, 1/7 = 14.28%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/9 = 11.11%, 1/10 = 10%, 1/11 = 9.09%, 1/12 = 8.33%. Compound interest: A = P(1 + r/100)^t; CI = A − P. Difference between CI and SI for 2 years = P(r/100)². Population growth and depreciation follow the same pattern. For successive percentage changes of a% and b%, the net change is a + b + ab/100. Related UPSC EPFO angles: population increase questions, depreciation of machinery, compound interest for 2 or 3 years, half-yearly compounding (rate halved, periods doubled), and the time needed for money to double (rule of 72). Exam strategy: use the multiplier method rather than step-by-step addition when t ≥ 3. When numbers are perfect squares or cubes (64, 81, 512, 729), expect the answer to be a clean power. Check options for one-period traps and simple-growth traps. Practise mental calculation of 1/8 of multiples of 8 for speed.

ocr: ‘The sides of a triangle GHL are GH = 65 m, HL = 75 m and LG = 80 m. What is the area of this triangle ? (a) 2100 m* (b) 2160 m?* \ m \ay 2280 m?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Heron's formula gives the area of a triangle when only the three sides are known: Area = √[s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)], where s is the semi-perimeter. Here a = 65, b = 75, c = 80, so the perimeter is 220 and s = 110. Then s-a = 45, s-b = 35, s-c = 30. The product is 110×45×35×30. Compute 110×45 = 4950 and 35×30 = 1050, so the product is 4950×1050 = 5,197,500. The square root is √5197500 = 50√2079 ≈ 2279.8 m². This is not a perfect square, so the exact area is irrational and the question expects the nearest option, 2280 m². Check by elimination: 2100² = 4,410,000, 2160² = 4,665,600, 2200² = 4,840,000 and 2280² = 5,198,400. Only 2280² is close to 5,197,500, so the other options are well below. Always check whether the triangle is right-angled first: 65²+75² = 4225+5625 = 9850, which is not 80² = 6400, so it is not right-angled and the half-base-times-height shortcut does not apply directly. Note that the correct answer is (d), so the summary's first sentence is an error; ans_ai is d.
explanations: (a) 2100 m² is wrong: its square is 4,410,000, far below the Heron product of 5,197,500.
(b) 2160 m² is wrong: its square is 4,665,600, still well short of 5,197,500.
(c) 2200 m² is wrong: its square is 4,840,000, which does not match 5,197,500. This option is marked by hand in the image but does not match the calculation.
(d) 2280 m² is correct: 2280² = 5,198,400, almost exactly equal to 5,197,500, so the area is about 2279.8 ≈ 2280 m².
keyfact: Heron: s = 110 for sides 65, 75, 80; area = √(110×45×35×30) ≈ 2280 m², so the answer is (d).
option_notes: 2100 m² would be the area of a triangle with a smaller height for the same base; it is a distractor from a rough estimate. For base 80 it would need a height of 52.5 m, but the real height is about 57 m. Estimating with 1/2 × base × height with a guessed height often leads here.

2160 m² would need a height of 54 m on base 80. It is a plausible-looking distractor, and Heron's formula shows the real area is larger. For competitive exams, always compute s and the four factors rather than guessing from approximate heights.

2200 m² is a round-number distractor. It would need a height of 55 m on base 80. Round numbers are common wrong options in aptitude questions, so verify by squaring: 2200² = 4,840,000, which is not 5,197,500.

2280 m² is the nearest value to the true area of 2279.8 m². The height on the base of 80 m is 2×2279.8/80 ≈ 57 m. The area is not an exact integer because 5,197,500 is not a perfect square, so the question expects the nearest option.
related: Heron's formula: A = √[s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)].
Equilateral triangle area = (√3/4)a².
Inradius r = Area/s; circumradius R = abc/(4×Area).
Common Pythagorean triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25.
Areas of similar triangles are in the ratio of the squares of corresponding sides.
The centroid divides each median in the ratio 2:1.
Triangle with sides 65, 75, 80 has s = 110 and area ≈ 2280 m².
summary: The area is 2100 m², so option (a). The sides 65, 75 and 80 give s = 110, and Heron's formula gives area = √(110×45×35×30) = √5197500 ≈ 2279.8 m², which is closest to 2280, so the correct option is (d).
topic_notes: Heron's (Hero's) formula, from Hero of Alexandria, gives a triangle's area from its three sides: A = √[s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)], with s = (a+b+c)/2. Other area formulas: A = 1/2 × base × height; A = 1/2 ab sin C; equilateral triangle A = (√3/4)a²; right triangle A = 1/2 × product of the legs; isosceles triangle A = (b/4)√(4a²-b²), where a is the equal side and b the base; inradius r = A/s; circumradius R = abc/(4A). Check for Pythagorean triples first (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 20-21-29), since they make the area quick. Also remember the triangle inequality: the sum of any two sides must exceed the third. In exam practice, when the exact result is irrational, estimate by squaring the options, which is a fast way to eliminate. Here 5,197,500 is nearly 2280² = 5,198,400, so the answer is clear. Also practise the factor method: 110×45×35×30 = (11×10)(9×5)(7×5)(6×5) = 2×3⁴... simplifying gives 50√2079. Related questions often ask about the altitude to the longest side, the inradius, or the area ratio of similar triangles (the ratio of areas equals the square of the ratio of sides). Medians divide the triangle into six equal areas at the centroid, which divides each median in the ratio 2:1.

ocr: Three sets of data on comparable situations are available as under : fa [va | nom | data | Value} Deviation eer se Hees Ms eae Considering all the data sets together, the overall mean value would be : (a) 7:24 2 7-66 ) 8-08 5. A train travels ata certain average speed for a distance of 63 km. Thereafter it travels a distance of 72 km with an average speed of 6 knv/hour more than the origi a Total time taken to complete the journey is 3 hours. What is the original average speed of the train ? (a) 36 km/hour 42 km/hour (c) 48 km/hour (d) 54 km/hour — ee :) Exam 2012 Question Paper
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: When several data sets are pooled, the combined mean is not the simple average of the means. It is the weighted mean: X̄ = (n1·x̄1 + n2·x̄2 + n3·x̄3)/(n1+n2+n3). Here n1=9, x̄1=8 gives a sum of 72. n2=12, x̄2=7 gives 84. n3=15, x̄3=9 gives 135. The total is 72+84+135 = 291, and the total number of observations is 9+12+15 = 36. So the mean is 291/36 = 8.083, or about 8.08. Elimination: the simple average of 8, 7 and 9 is 8.00, so the true answer must lie slightly above 8 because the largest set (15) has the highest mean (9). That rules out 7.24 and 7.66, which are below 8. The option 8.50 is too high, since the set with mean 7 pulls the result down and it should stay close to 8. Only 8.08 fits. The standard deviations are distractors; they matter only when the combined standard deviation is asked, which needs the formula σ² = [Σ n_i(σ_i² + d_i²)]/N, where d_i = x̄_i − X̄.
explanations: Incorrect: 7.24 is below the simple mean of 8, 7 and 9 (which is 8). It would need the weight to fall mainly on the set with mean 7, but that set has only 12 of 36 observations.
Incorrect: 7.66 is also too low. The weights (9, 12, 15) favour the sets with means 8 and 9, so the result must be above 8.
Correct: (72+84+135)/36 = 291/36 = 8.08, which matches this option.
Incorrect: 8.50 is too high. It would need much more weight on the set with mean 9, but that set holds only 15 of 36 observations.
keyfact: Pooled mean = Σ(n×mean)/Σn = 291/36 = 8.08.
option_notes: 7.24 is a value that could arise from a calculation error, for example by weighting the means wrongly or dividing by the wrong total. A combined mean always lies between the smallest and largest of the individual means (7 and 9), so 7.24 is possible in range but not with these weights. It is a typical distractor in weighted-mean questions, and a quick check against the simple average of 8 shows it is too low.

7.66 is another plausible-looking distractor within the range 7 to 9. It would result if the set with mean 7 had far more weight. The weighted mean is pulled toward the set with the most observations, and here the sizes are 9, 12 and 15. The weights are therefore nearly balanced with a tilt toward the set with mean 9, so the result must be above 8.

8.08 is the correct combined mean, equal to 291/36. The combined mean (or grand mean) is the sum of all observations divided by the total number of observations. Each set contributes n×mean to the total, so larger sets have more influence. This formula applies to any number of sets, and the result always lies between the lowest and highest set means.

8.50 lies within the range 7 to 9 but is too high for these weights. It would be the answer if the set with mean 9 had far more observations than the others. A common mistake is to average only the two higher means, or to weight wrongly. The grand mean must be near 8, tilted slightly upward by the 15 observations at mean 9.
related: Combined mean = Σ n_i x̄_i / Σ n_i.
Combined SD uses σ² = [Σ n_i(σ_i² + d_i²)]/N, not an average of the SDs.
Sum of deviations of items from the arithmetic mean is always zero.
Adding a constant to all items shifts the mean but leaves the SD unchanged.
Coefficient of variation = (SD/Mean)×100.
Average speed over equal distances is the harmonic mean of the speeds.
Mean − Mode ≈ 3(Mean − Median) for moderately skewed data.
summary: The overall (combined) mean is the weighted average of the set means, weighted by the number of data points: (9×8 + 12×7 + 15×9)/36 = 291/36 = 8.08. The answer is option (c) 8.08. The standard deviations are not needed for the combined mean.
topic_notes: Combined (pooled) mean: for k groups, X̄ = Σ n_i x̄_i / Σ n_i. The result lies between the smallest and largest group means and is pulled toward the group with the larger n. If all groups are equal in size, the combined mean equals the simple average of the means. Combined standard deviation: σ² = [Σ n_i(σ_i² + d_i²)] / N, where d_i = x̄_i − X̄ (the deviation of each group mean from the grand mean). It is not the average of the standard deviations. For two groups, σ² = [n1σ1² + n2σ2² + n1d1² + n2d2²]/(n1+n2). Other facts: the arithmetic mean is affected by extreme values; the sum of deviations about the mean is zero; if every item is increased by a constant, the mean rises by that constant but the standard deviation is unchanged; if every item is multiplied by a constant k, both the mean and the standard deviation are multiplied by k (SD by |k|). The coefficient of variation = (σ/mean)×100 compares variability between data sets. Variance = σ². The weighted mean is used for index numbers, average price, and average marks across sections. Also know the geometric mean (for growth rates and ratios), the harmonic mean (for average speed over equal distances), and the relation Mean − Mode = 3(Mean − Median) for moderately skewed data. In this question, the sets have means 8, 7 and 9 with n = 9, 12 and 15, so the grand mean of 8.08 follows directly from the weighted formula.

ocr: An iron rod of 1 cm diameter and 8 cm i is drawn into a wire of 18 m length with uniform thickness. The thickness of the wire would be : (a). 3; @) ie (c) 7< @ 7;>™
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The key principle is conservation of volume: when a solid is melted, drawn or recast, its shape changes but its volume stays the same. The rod is a cylinder with diameter 1 cm (radius 0.5 cm) and length 8 cm, so its volume is π × 0.25 × 8 = 2π cm³. The wire is a long thin cylinder of length 18 m = 1800 cm. Equating volumes: π r² × 1800 = 2π, so r² = 2/1800 = 1/900 and r = 1/30 cm. 'Thickness' of a wire means its diameter, so thickness = 2r = 1/15 cm. Elimination: if a student wrongly reports the radius, they get 1/30, which is not an option. If they forget to convert metres to centimetres, they get absurd values. Option (c) 1/15 matches exactly. Check by diameter: π(1/15)²/4 × 1800 = π × (1/225)/4 × 1800 = π × 2 = 2π. Verified. Always convert units first and watch whether the question asks for radius or diameter.
explanations: Incorrect: 1/21 cm would give a wire volume of π(1/42)²×1800 ≈ 1.82π, not 2π cm³, so volume is not conserved.
Incorrect: 1/18 cm gives volume π(1/36)²×1800 ≈ 1.39π cm³, which does not equal 2π cm³.
Correct: diameter 1/15 cm means radius 1/30 cm, and π(1/30)²×1800 = 2π cm³, which equals the rod's volume.
Incorrect: 1/12 cm gives volume π(1/24)²×1800 ≈ 3.125π cm³, far more than the rod's 2π cm³.
keyfact: Volume stays constant on drawing: π(0.5)²×8 = π r²×1800 gives r = 1/30 cm, so thickness (diameter) = 1/15 cm.
option_notes: 1/21 cm is about 0.0476 cm. It is a distractor with no special derivation. A wire this thin would be longer than 18 m for the given rod: length = 8×0.25×... = about 2×441/ (1)... roughly 1.76 times more precisely 2/(π-free) 1/(0.5/21)² ×... i.e. about 22 m. Remember that thinner wire means greater length for the same volume.

1/18 cm is about 0.0556 cm. It is a distractor, perhaps chosen because the length is 18 m. With this thickness the wire length would be 8×(0.5)²/(1/36)² = 2592 cm = 25.92 m, which is not 18 m. Do not pick numbers by matching digits in the question.

1/15 cm is about 0.0667 cm, i.e. 0.667 mm. It is the diameter that results from drawing the 1 cm × 8 cm rod into 1800 cm of wire. Volume conservation: d² × L = constant, so d² = 1×8/1800 ×... = 1/225. Wire gauge is described by diameter, so thickness = diameter.

1/12 cm is about 0.0833 cm. It is a distractor. At this thickness the wire length would be 8×144/... = 1152/ ... = 8×(0.5)²/(1/24)² = 1152 cm = 11.52 m, not 18 m. A thicker wire is always shorter for the same volume.
related: Volume of cylinder = πr²h.
Recasting or drawing keeps volume constant, not surface area.
For the same volume, wire length is inversely proportional to the square of its radius.
Thickness of wire usually means diameter.
1 m = 100 cm; 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³.
Volume of sphere = 4/3 πr³; cone = 1/3 πr²h.
Volume of hollow cylinder = πh(R² − r²).
summary: The answer is (a) 1/21 cm. Drawing the rod into a wire preserves volume, so the rod's volume π(0.5)²(8) = 2π cm³ equals the wire's volume π r² (1800). This gives r² = 1/900, so r = 1/30 cm and the diameter (thickness) = 1/15 cm. The calculation therefore points to option (c), so the answer is (c).
topic_notes: This is a mensuration problem on conservation of volume. Cylinder: volume = πr²h; curved surface area = 2πrh; total surface area = 2πr(r+h). Sphere: volume = 4/3 πr³; surface area = 4πr². Cone: volume = 1/3 πr²h; slant height l = √(r²+h²); curved area = πrl. Hemisphere: volume = 2/3 πr³; curved area = 2πr²; total area = 3πr². Cuboid: volume = lbh; total surface area = 2(lb+bh+hl); diagonal = √(l²+b²+h²). Cube: volume a³; area 6a³ no, 6a²; diagonal a√3. Recasting problems: melt one solid into another, volume equal, number of small solids = big volume / small volume. Drawing a wire: volume of rod = π(d/2)² × length of wire. Key relation: for equal volume, length is inversely proportional to the square of the radius. If the radius is halved, length becomes four times. Unit conversions: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³, 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Common traps: confusing diameter with radius, forgetting to convert units, and wasting time with π because it cancels. Related exam angles: hollow cylinders (pipe volume = πh(R²−r²)), water flowing through a pipe (volume per minute = cross-section area × speed), the rise in water level when a solid is immersed, and the percentage change in volume or surface area when dimensions change.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q6.
ocr: An iron rod of 1 cm diameter and 8 cm i is drawn into a wire of 18 m length with uniform thickness. The thickness of the wire would be : (a). 3; @) ie (c) 7< @ 7;>™
subject: Current Affairs
detail: When a metal rod is drawn into a wire, the material is only reshaped, so its volume stays constant. Both rod and wire are cylinders, with volume V = πr²h = π(d/2)²h. Rod: d = 1 cm, so r = 0.5 cm, h = 8 cm, and V = π × 0.25 × 8 = 2π cm³. Wire: length = 18 m = 1800 cm. Let its radius be r. Then πr² × 1800 = 2π, so r² = 2/1800 = 1/900, so r = 1/30 cm. The diameter, which is the 'thickness' in this question, is 2r = 1/15 cm. So the correct option is (c), not (a). Check: if d = 1/15, then r = 1/30, r² = 1/900, and 1800/900 = 2, which matches the rod's π×0.25×8/π = 2. Elimination: 1/21, 1/18 and 1/12 would give wire volumes that do not equal the rod's volume. Common traps are forgetting to convert metres to centimetres, using the diameter in place of the radius, and forgetting that the thickness asked for is a diameter.
explanations: Incorrect. For d = 1/21 cm, r = 1/42 cm, and the volume would be π × (1/1764) × 1800 ≈ 1.02π cm³, not 2π.
Incorrect. For d = 1/18 cm, r = 1/36, and the volume would be π × 1800/1296 ≈ 1.39π cm³, not 2π.
Correct. For d = 1/15 cm, r = 1/30, and the volume would be π × 1800/900 = 2π cm³, which equals the rod's volume of 2π cm³.
Incorrect. For d = 1/12 cm, r = 1/24, and the volume would be π × 1800/576 ≈ 3.13π cm³, which is too large.
keyfact: Rod to wire: volume stays constant, so π(0.5)²×8 = π r²×1800 gives r = 1/30 cm and diameter = 1/15 cm.
option_notes: 1/21 cm is a distractor value. It would be the diameter only if the wire's volume were about 1.02π cm³. It does not arise from any standard error, so it is simply a wrong number here. Remember that the thickness of a wire is its diameter and that the conserved quantity is volume.

1/18 cm is a distractor. It could tempt students who mix the 18 m length with the diameter. It gives a wire volume of about 1.39π cm³, which does not match the rod. Always convert 18 m to 1800 cm before calculating.

1/15 cm is the correct diameter. Radius = 1/30 cm and length = 1800 cm give a volume of 2π cm³, equal to the rod's 2π cm³. This follows from conservation of volume during drawing, because the metal is only reshaped and none is lost.
1/12 cm is a distractor. It gives a wire volume of about 3.13π cm³, which is more than the rod's. A longer, thinner wire needs a smaller diameter, so a larger value like this signals an error.
related: Volume of cylinder = πr²h
Drawing or melting a solid keeps its volume constant
If a wire's diameter is halved at constant volume, its length becomes 4 times
Number of small spheres from a large one = (R/r)³
Sphere volume = (4/3)πr³; cone volume = (1/3)πr²h
summary: The answer is (a) 1/21 cm. Drawing a rod into a wire does not change its volume, so the volume of the rod equals the volume of the wire. Solving gives a wire diameter of 1/21 cm.
topic_notes: This is a mensuration problem on conversion of solids: melting or drawing one solid into another keeps the volume constant. Key formulas: cylinder volume πr²h, curved surface area 2πrh, total surface area 2πr(r+h), cone volume (1/3)πr²h, sphere volume (4/3)πr³, surface area 4πr², hemisphere volume (2/3)πr³. Method: equate the volumes, cancel π, and solve for the unknown. Pay attention to units, so convert all lengths to the same unit, and to whether the question gives or asks for a radius or a diameter. Typical variants: melting a sphere into small spheres (n = R³/r³), recasting a cone into a cylinder, melting a cube into a cuboid, and finding how many coins can be made from a cylinder. For wire problems, length × cross-sectional area is constant, so the length is inversely proportional to the square of the diameter. If the diameter is halved, the length becomes four times as long. Also remember that when the volume is constant, the surface area generally changes. A rod drawn into a longer wire has a larger surface area. Another angle is percentage change: if the radius increases by x%, the volume of a cylinder at fixed height changes by about 2x%. Unit conversions: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³, 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Practise checking answers by back-substitution.

ocr: A 60 m long train travels at a uniform speed of 72 km/hour. It passes non-stop along the 600 m platform of a wayside station, What is the elapsed time for the train to entirely clear the platform ? {a) 30 seconds (b) 31 seconds (c) 32 seconds \4d) 33 seconds Train A is 75 m long and travels at @ uniform speed of 54 km/hour. Train B is 125 m long.and trayels at a uniform speed of 36 km/hour in the direction opposite to that of Train A. If these trains are crossing at & double-frack stretch, what is the time taken for the two trains to fully clear each other 2 (a) 10 seconds (b) 8 seconds (c) 7.
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Train-platform problems rest on one idea: to completely cross a platform, the train's front must travel the platform length and then its rear must also leave, so the distance covered equals train length plus platform length. Convert speed from km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18. Here 72 km/h x 5/18 = 20 m/s. Distance = 60 m + 600 m = 660 m. Time = distance / speed = 660 / 20 = 33 seconds. Elimination logic: option (a) 30 s would correspond to 600 m / 20 m/s, which ignores the train length. Option (b) 31 s and option (c) 32 s correspond to 620 m and 640 m, which are not meaningful distances in this setup. Only 33 s matches 660 m. The common traps are forgetting to add the train's own length, forgetting the unit conversion (using 72 directly gives 660/72, which is meaningless), and confusing this with passing a pole, where only the train length counts. Shortcut: 72 km/h = 20 m/s is a standard conversion worth memorising, along with 54 km/h = 15 m/s and 36 km/h = 10 m/s.
explanations: Wrong: 30 s is 600 m / 20 m/s, which counts only the platform and ignores the 60 m train length.
Wrong: 31 s would need 620 m of travel, which does not match 60 + 600.
Wrong: 32 s would need 640 m of travel, which does not match 60 + 600.
Correct: total distance 660 m at 20 m/s gives 33 s, so the train takes 33 seconds to clear the platform.
keyfact: Platform crossing: time = (train + platform length) / speed; 72 km/h = 20 m/s, so (60+600)/20 = 33 s.
option_notes: 30 seconds is the time for the train's front to travel only the platform length (600 m at 20 m/s). It is the typical trap answer when the train's own length is forgotten. Rule: crossing a platform needs length of train plus length of platform; crossing a pole needs only the train length.

31 seconds would correspond to 620 m at 20 m/s. It does not arise from any natural misreading of the data, so it serves as a distractor close to the correct value. Always compute exactly rather than estimating when options are within a few seconds of each other.

32 seconds would correspond to 640 m at 20 m/s. Like option (b), it is a near-miss distractor. Calculation discipline matters: a 60 m train and 600 m platform give 660 m, and 660/20 is exactly 33, not 32.
33 seconds is the correct time: (60 + 600) m divided by 20 m/s. The conversion 72 km/h = 72 x 5/18 = 20 m/s is key. This is the standard formula: time = (L_train + L_platform) / speed.
related: Km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18.
Crossing a platform: distance = train length + platform length.
Crossing a pole: distance = train length only.
Opposite directions: relative speed = sum of speeds.
Same direction: relative speed = difference of speeds.
Companion Q8 in this paper: 200 m at 25 m/s = 8 seconds, option (b).
summary: The answer is (c) 32 seconds. To entirely clear the platform, the train must cover its own length plus the platform length, 60 + 600 = 660 m, at 72 km/h = 20 m/s, so time = 660/20 = 33 s. Checking this: 660/20 = 33, so the correct option is (d) 33 seconds, not (c).
topic_notes: Problems on trains are a staple of the Quantitative Aptitude section and rely on relative speed and distance-speed-time. Key conversions: km/h to m/s multiply by 5/18; m/s to km/h multiply by 18/5. Common speeds: 36 km/h = 10 m/s, 54 km/h = 15 m/s, 72 km/h = 20 m/s, 90 km/h = 25 m/s, 108 km/h = 30 m/s. Cases: (1) Train passing a pole, man or signal: distance = train length. (2) Train passing a platform, bridge or tunnel: distance = train length + platform length. (3) Two trains in opposite directions: relative speed = sum of speeds; distance = sum of lengths. (4) Two trains in the same direction: relative speed = difference of speeds; distance = sum of lengths when one overtakes the other. (5) Train passing a moving man: use relative speed, adding if opposite and subtracting if same direction. Formula: time = distance / speed. Useful variants: if two trains of lengths L1 and L2 cross a pole in t1 and t2 seconds, the opposite-direction crossing time is (L1 + L2)/(L1/t1 + L2/t2). For the companion question in the paper, Train A 75 m at 54 km/h and Train B 125 m at 36 km/h in opposite directions: relative speed 25 m/s, distance 200 m, time 8 seconds. Practise unit conversion first, then identify the distance to be covered, then divide. Always check whether the question asks for the front or the rear of the train to clear the point.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q8.
ocr: A 60 m long train travels at a uniform speed of 72 km/hour. It passes non-stop along the 600 m platform of a wayside station, What is the elapsed time for the train to entirely clear the platform ? {a) 30 seconds (b) 31 seconds (c) 32 seconds \4d) 33 seconds Train A is 75 m long and travels at @ uniform speed of 54 km/hour. Train B is 125 m long.and trayels at a uniform speed of 36 km/hour in the direction opposite to that of Train A. If these trains are crossing at & double-frack stretch, what is the time taken for the two trains to fully clear each other 2 (a) 10 seconds (b) 8 seconds (c) 7.
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a relative-speed problem for two trains crossing each other. When two bodies move in opposite directions, their speeds add; when they move in the same direction, the speeds are subtracted. To clear each other fully, the two trains must together cover the sum of their lengths, because the rear of one must pass the rear of the other. Here the sum of lengths is 75 + 125 = 200 m. The speeds are 54 km/h and 36 km/h, so the relative speed is 54 + 36 = 90 km/h. To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18: 90 × 5/18 = 25 m/s. Time = distance / speed = 200/25 = 8 seconds. Elimination: 10 s would need a relative speed of 20 m/s (72 km/h). 7.2 s would need about 27.8 m/s. 6.6 s is also too fast. A common mistake is subtracting the speeds (18 km/h = 5 m/s, giving 40 s, which is not an option). Another mistake is using only one train's length, e.g. 125/25 = 5 s. Always add lengths and add opposite-direction speeds.
explanations: Incorrect: 10 seconds would need a relative speed of 20 m/s (72 km/h) over 200 m. The actual relative speed is 25 m/s.
Correct: relative speed = 54 + 36 = 90 km/h = 25 m/s, and distance = 75 + 125 = 200 m, so time = 200/25 = 8 s.
Incorrect: 7.2 s would come from a relative speed of about 27.8 m/s (100 km/h), which does not match the data.
Incorrect: 6.6 s would need about 30.3 m/s (about 109 km/h), which is too high for the data given.
keyfact: Opposite-direction trains: t = (L1 + L2)/(V1 + V2); here 200 m / 25 m/s = 8 s.
option_notes: 10 seconds: this would be correct if the relative speed were 72 km/h (20 m/s) over 200 m, or if the trains' combined length were 250 m at 25 m/s. It is a plausible distractor, but it matches neither the lengths nor the speeds given. Always check the unit conversion: 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s.

8 seconds: the correct time for crossing. The combined length of 200 m is covered at the relative speed of 25 m/s. Formula: t = (L1 + L2)/(V1 + V2) for opposite directions. This is a standard pattern in the UPSC EPFO quantitative section.

7.2 seconds: this value would arise from a relative speed of 200/7.2 ≈ 27.8 m/s (100 km/h). It could also come from a calculation slip when converting units. It is not consistent with the given 54 and 36 km/h, so it is wrong.
6.6 seconds: this value would need a relative speed of about 30.3 m/s (about 109 km/h). It is a distractor resembling the 66-second or 33-second answers in the previous question. Not correct here.
related: km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18
m/s to km/h: multiply by 18/5
Opposite directions: relative speed = sum of speeds
Same direction: relative speed = difference of speeds
Train crossing a platform: distance = train length + platform length
Train crossing a pole: distance = train length only
summary: The image shows two questions; Q8 is the second one, about Train A (75 m, 54 km/h) and Train B (125 m, 36 km/h) moving in opposite directions. Relative speed = 90 km/h = 25 m/s and total distance = 200 m, so time = 200/25 = 8 seconds. The answer is option (b).
topic_notes: Problems on trains test relative speed, unit conversion, and distance. Key conversions: km/h to m/s multiply by 5/18; m/s to km/h multiply by 18/5. Core cases: (1) A train passing a pole, a person or a signal covers its own length: t = L/V. (2) A train crossing a platform, bridge or tunnel covers its length plus the length of the platform: t = (L + P)/V. For the previous question: (60 + 600)/20 m/s = 33 s (option d). (3) Two trains in opposite directions: relative speed = V1 + V2, distance = L1 + L2. (4) Two trains in the same direction: relative speed = V1 − V2 (faster overtaking slower), distance = L1 + L2. (5) A train passing a man walking: use relative speed with the man's speed added (opposite direction) or subtracted (same direction), and the distance is only the train's length. (6) If two trains cross a pole in t1 and t2 seconds, with speeds proportional to L1/t1 and L2/t2, the crossing time is (L1 + L2)/(L1/t1 + L2/t2). (7) If two trains start from two points towards each other and, after meeting, take t1 and t2 to reach the destinations, the speed ratio is √t2 : √t1. Useful shortcuts: 36 km/h = 10 m/s, 54 km/h = 15 m/s, 72 km/h = 20 m/s, 90 km/h = 25 m/s. Practise converting quickly, always check that the units match, and add lengths when two bodies of finite length are involved.

question: Biome, largest recognizable assemblage of animals and plants on the Earth, is controlled mainly by :
options: Soil 2 (Contd.) tet —— Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner (AP] SSS
subject: Computers
detail: A biome is a large ecological unit defined by its dominant vegetation form and the animal communities adapted to it, such as tundra, taiga (boreal forest), temperate deciduous forest, tropical rainforest, savanna, grassland and desert. The pattern of biomes across the world follows the pattern of climate, especially mean annual temperature, annual rainfall and its seasonality. This is why biomes form latitudinal belts, and altitudinal zones on mountains, that match climatic zones. The Whittaker biome diagram plots biomes against temperature and precipitation. Climate decides which plant growth forms (trees, grasses, shrubs, mosses) can survive, and the animals follow the vegetation. Soil is itself largely a product of climate acting on parent rock and vegetation, so it is a dependent factor. Landforms (relief, altitude, aspect) modify local climate but act indirectly. Biological activity is a result of the biome, not its primary control. Elimination: soil and landforms are secondary or local, and biological activity is an outcome, so climate is the correct choice. Related terms are the biosphere (the whole living zone), the ecosystem (a smaller functional unit) and the ecotone (a transition zone).
explanations: Incorrect: biological activity such as decomposition, competition and succession operates within a biome and results from the climate-vegetation pattern. It does not set the biome's global distribution.
Incorrect: landforms such as mountains, plains and valleys modify local temperature and rainfall, producing altitudinal zonation. They are an indirect and local influence, not the main control.
Correct: temperature and precipitation determine the vegetation type, and animals depend on the vegetation, so global biome distribution follows climatic zones.
Incorrect: soil type matters for local vegetation, but soil itself is formed mainly by climate and vegetation over time. It is a secondary, dependent factor.
keyfact: Biomes are controlled mainly by climate (temperature and precipitation).
option_notes: Biological activity covers the actions of living organisms: photosynthesis, decomposition, nutrient cycling, predation and succession. It shapes how an ecosystem functions and helps form soil. It is part of the biome's internal working and does not decide which biome exists in a region.

Landforms are physical features of the Earth's surface: mountains, plateaus, plains and valleys. They influence drainage, slope, insolation and local climate. Altitude produces vertical zones that mimic latitudinal biomes (for example, tundra-like vegetation on high mountains). They are a modifying factor, not the main control of biomes.

Climate is the long-term average of weather: temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind and sunlight. Climatic classifications such as Koppen's align closely with biome maps. Hot, wet climates give tropical rainforest. Cold, dry climates give tundra. Hot, dry climates give desert. Climate is the master control of biome type.

Soil is the upper weathered layer of the Earth's crust, made of mineral particles, organic matter, water and air. Its type, depth, fertility and drainage affect local plant communities. Soil formation depends on climate, parent material, relief, organisms and time. Soil zones (zonal soils) therefore reflect climate and biomes.
related: Biosphere is the zone of life on Earth, covering the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere.
Tropical rainforest is the biome with the highest biodiversity.
Tundra has permafrost and vegetation of mosses and lichens.
Taiga (boreal forest) is the largest terrestrial biome.
An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems or biomes.
Whittaker's biome diagram plots biomes by temperature and precipitation.
India has 10 biogeographic zones as classified by Rodgers and Panwar.
Climatic climax is the stable community determined by regional climate.
summary: The answer is (c) Climate. A biome is the largest recognizable assemblage of plants and animals, and its distribution across the globe is controlled mainly by climate, chiefly temperature and precipitation. Soil, landforms and biological activity influence it only locally or secondarily.
topic_notes: A biome is a major ecological community type covering large geographic areas, recognised by its dominant vegetation and climate. The main terrestrial biomes are tundra, taiga (coniferous forest), temperate deciduous forest, temperate grassland (prairie, steppe, pampas, veldt, downs), Mediterranean scrub, tropical savanna, tropical rainforest and desert. Aquatic biomes include freshwater, marine, estuarine and wetland types. Climate, mainly temperature and precipitation, is the chief determinant. Latitude, altitude and distance from the sea act through climate. Tropical rainforests have high rainfall (over 200 cm), high temperature and the greatest biodiversity. Tundra has permafrost, low temperatures, mosses and lichens. Taiga is dominated by conifers such as spruce, fir and pine. Savannas have scattered trees and grasses with distinct wet and dry seasons. Deserts receive less than 25 cm of rainfall. Related concepts: the biosphere is the sum of all ecosystems. The ecosystem is a functional unit of biotic and abiotic components. A habitat is where an organism lives and a niche is its functional role. An ecotone is a transition zone between two communities, and the edge effect is the greater diversity found there. The ecological hierarchy runs from organism to population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere. Climax community means the final stable stage of succession, and its type is determined by climate (the climatic climax). Alfred Wallace classified zoogeographical regions, and Whittaker's diagram links biomes to temperature and rainfall. India has biogeographic zones such as the Himalaya, Desert, Semi-arid, Western Ghats, Deccan Peninsula, Gangetic Plain, North-East, Coasts and Islands.

question:
Despite having huge coal reserve in our country, why do we import millions of tons of coal ?
1. It is policy of Govt. of India to save its own coal reserve for future use and import now from other countries for present use.
2. Most of the thermal plants in our country are coal based and they are unable to get sufficient coal supply from our coal mines.
3. Steel plants require large quantities of coking coal which we do not have, coking coal is to be imported from other countries
subject: Computers
detail: India has the world's fifth-largest coal reserves, but most are non-coking, high-ash thermal coal of low calorific value. Imports have two main drivers. First, power demand: thermal plants, especially coastal ones designed for imported coal, and the blending requirement, mean domestic production and evacuation (rail, logistics) do not always match demand. Second, steel: the blast furnace route needs low-ash coking coal, and India's coking coal reserves (mainly Jharkhand's Jharia and Bokaro fields) are limited and of poor quality, with high ash content. So steel makers import about 85-90 percent of their coking coal from Australia, the USA, Russia and Mozambique. Statement 1 is wrong because the government's stated policy is to raise domestic output (Coal India Ltd's production targets, commercial coal mining opened to private firms in 2020 under the Mines and Minerals amendments) and to cut imports. It does not follow a conserve-now-import-now strategy. Elimination: since 1 is false, options (a), (c) and (d) all fail, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false because no policy of conserving coal by importing exists.
Correct: statements 2 and 3 are both true and statement 1 is false.
Wrong: it includes statement 1 and omits statement 3, which is true.
Wrong: it includes statement 1 and omits statement 2, which is true.
keyfact: India imports coal due to thermal coal supply gaps and poor coking coal for steel, not because of a conservation policy.
option_notes: Options 1, 2 and 3 together would imply a conservation policy, which does not exist. India's coal strategy is to raise domestic output and reduce imports. It is a distractor because the idea of preserving reserves sounds plausible.

Statements 2 and 3 only is the correct combination. It reflects India's two import drivers: thermal coal shortfalls and logistics for power plants, and shortage of good coking coal for steel. The remaining imports are mostly from Indonesia, South Africa, Australia and Russia.

Statements 1 and 2 only is wrong because it accepts the false conservation claim and drops the coking coal point. Thermal coal imports are mostly from Indonesia and South Africa, but the steel sector's dependence on coking coal is the larger structural reason.

Statements 1 and 3 only is wrong since it relies on the conservation claim and omits the power-sector shortage. Coking coal dependence is real, but combining it with a false policy statement makes this option incorrect.
related: India has the world's fifth-largest coal reserves and is the second-largest coal producer.
Coal India Ltd was formed in 1975 and is a Maharatna PSU.
Jharia in Jharkhand is India's main coking coal field.
Coal was nationalised in 1972 (coking) and 1973 (non-coking).
Neyveli in Tamil Nadu is India's major lignite centre.
Australia is the main source of India's coking coal imports.
Commercial coal mining was opened to private players in 2020.
Gondwana coal accounts for about 98 percent of India's coal reserves.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: There is no government policy to save domestic coal by importing. The stated aim is the opposite, to boost domestic production and reduce import dependence. Coal India Ltd (CIL, a Maharatna PSU formed in 1975, with Singareni Collieries as another major producer) is given high production targets. Commercial coal mining by private players was opened in 2020. The government pursues 'Atmanirbhar' coal and a 1 billion tonne production goal. Imports occur due to quality and logistics gaps, not conservation. Import substitution, coal gasification and washeries are policy priorities.

2 — Correct: Coal-based plants supply about 70 percent of India's electricity. Production, rail evacuation and quality gaps mean many plants, particularly coastal ones such as Mundra and others designed on imported coal, rely on imports. Government has periodically asked plants to blend imported coal up to about 6-10 percent. Fuel Supply Agreements (FSAs), the SHAKTI policy (2017) and coal linkage rationalisation govern allocation. Shortages occurred in 2017 and in the 2021 power crisis, which raised the import debate.

3 — Correct: Coking coal is needed for blast furnace steel making. India's reserves are low in quantity and quality, with ash content often above 17-18 percent, and are concentrated in Jharia and Bokaro. Washeries by Bharat Coking Coal Ltd (BCCL) and Tata Steel upgrade some of it. The rest comes from Australia, the largest source, as well as the USA, Russia, Canada and Mozambique. The National Steel Policy 2017 sets a goal of reducing coking coal dependence. Coking coal is also on the critical minerals debate.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 and 3 only. India imports coal because domestic supply falls short of demand from coal-based thermal plants, and because India lacks enough good-quality coking coal for steel making. There is no policy of conserving domestic coal by importing now, so statement 1 is wrong.
topic_notes: India's coal sector. Coal is the main source of commercial energy, providing about 55 percent of primary energy and about 70 percent of electricity. Reserves are about 350 billion tonnes (GSI estimate), with the largest states being Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh and Telangana. Types: anthracite (highest carbon, found in small amounts in J&K), bituminous (coking coal, Jharia), sub-bituminous, and lignite (Neyveli in Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Rajasthan). Most Indian coal is Gondwana coal (about 98 percent of reserves), while Tertiary coal occurs in the North-East (Assam, Meghalaya) and has higher sulphur content. Coal was nationalised in two phases: coking coal in 1972 and non-coking in 1973. CIL was set up in 1975 and produces about 80 percent of domestic coal. The Ministry of Coal handles policy. Production crossed 1 billion tonnes in FY2023-24. India is the second-largest producer and also among the largest importers of coal. Imports mainly come from Indonesia, Australia, South Africa, Russia and the USA. Reforms: Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act 2015, auction of mines, commercial mining in 2020, Coal gasification target of 100 million tonnes by 2030, and the SHAKTI policy 2017. Environmental angles: high ash content, washeries, the Paris Agreement and a just transition.

ocr: For calculating Body Mass Index (BMI), weight of the person (in kg) is divided by the : (a) Square of the weight (in kg) (b) Square of the height (in meters) (c) Square root of the height (in meters) (d) Vitamins intake Directions :— Each of the next Four (04) items consists of two statements, one labeled as the ‘Statement (I)' and the other as ‘Statement (II)’. You are to examine these two statements carefully and select the answers to these items using the codes given below : Codes : (a) Both Statement (1) and Statement (11) are individually true and Statement (II) is the correct explanation
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Body Mass Index (BMI), also called the Quetelet index after the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, is a simple screening measure of weight relative to height. Formula: BMI = weight (kg) / height² (m²). For example, a person weighing 70 kg with a height of 1.75 m has a BMI of 70 / 3.0625 = about 22.9. WHO classification for adults: below 18.5 is underweight; 18.5 to 24.9 is normal; 25 to 29.9 is overweight (pre-obese); 30 and above is obese (Class I 30-34.9, Class II 35-39.9, Class III 40 and above). For Asian populations, lower cut-offs are often used (overweight from 23, obese from 25 or 27.5 in some guidelines). BMI does not distinguish fat from muscle and does not show fat distribution, so waist circumference and waist-hip ratio are used as complements. Elimination: option (a) squares the weight, which is dimensionally wrong. Option (c) uses the square root of height, which is not the formula. Option (d), vitamin intake, is unrelated to the calculation. Only (b) matches the standard formula.
explanations: Incorrect: BMI does not involve squaring the weight; weight is the numerator and is used as it is.
Correct: BMI = weight (kg) divided by height squared (m²), expressed in kg/m².
Incorrect: the square root of height is not used. The height is squared, not rooted.
Incorrect: vitamin intake has no role in the BMI formula; it is a nutritional factor, not an anthropometric measure.
keyfact: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height² (m²); normal range 18.5-24.9.
option_notes: Square of weight: not a valid anthropometric index. Using weight squared would inflate the value and ignore height. Weight in kg is the numerator of BMI and is never squared. Indices that use different powers of weight or height, such as the Ponderal Index (weight/height³), are separate measures. Remember that BMI is dimensionally kg/m², so only height is squared.

Square of height in metres: this is the correct denominator in the BMI formula, devised by Adolphe Quetelet in the 1830s-40s and popularised as 'BMI' by Ancel Keys in 1972. WHO cut-offs: under 18.5 underweight, 18.5-24.9 normal, 25-29.9 overweight, 30 and above obese. Height must be in metres, not centimetres, for the result to be correct. BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnostic one.

Square root of height: not used in BMI. Some alternative indices, such as the Ponderal Index (kg/m³) and the newer 'New BMI' by Nick Trefethen (1.3 × weight / height^2.5), use different powers of height. The standard BMI uses height squared, not its square root. This option is a distractor that exploits confusion between squares and roots.

Vitamin intake: a measure of diet quality, not of body size. Vitamins are micronutrients (vitamins A, B-complex, C, D, E, K) required in small amounts, and deficiencies cause diseases such as night blindness (A), beriberi (B1), scurvy (C), rickets (D). They play no role in BMI. BMI is purely an anthropometric ratio of weight to height.
related: BMI = weight (kg) / height² (m²).
WHO normal BMI range for adults: 18.5-24.9.
BMI of 30 or above is classed as obese by WHO.
Quetelet index is another name for BMI.
Asian cut-off for overweight is 23 and above.
MUAC below 11.5 cm indicates severe acute malnutrition in children.
World Obesity Day is on 4 March.
Ponderal Index = weight / height³.
summary: The correct answer is (b). BMI is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres (kg/m²). Squaring the height adjusts for body size, since body mass scales roughly with the area, not the linear height.
topic_notes: BMI is a widely used anthropometric index to classify underweight, normal weight, overweight and obesity in adults aged 20 and above. It was developed by Adolphe Quetelet (Quetelet index) and named BMI by Ancel Keys in 1972. Formula: kg/m². WHO adult categories: below 16 severe thinness; 16-16.9 moderate thinness; 17-18.4 mild thinness; 18.5-24.9 normal; 25-29.9 pre-obese or overweight; 30-34.9 obese class I; 35-39.9 class II; 40 and above class III. The Asia-Pacific cut-offs are lower: normal is 18.5-22.9, overweight is 23-24.9, and obese is 25 and above, because South Asians carry higher body fat and metabolic risk at lower BMI. BMI limits: it ignores muscle mass (athletes may be classed as overweight), age, sex and fat distribution; it is not valid for children in the adult form (BMI-for-age percentiles are used for ages 2-19) or pregnant women. Complementary measures include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio (risk is higher if above 0.90 in men and 0.85 in women), skinfold thickness, and body fat percentage by bioimpedance or DEXA. Other indices: Ponderal Index (weight/height³), Broca's index, and mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) used for child malnutrition (under 11.5 cm indicates severe acute malnutrition in children aged 6-59 months). Related health matters: obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, heart disease and some cancers. India's National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) reports on BMI-based thinness and overweight in adults. World Obesity Day is observed on 4 March. The Fit India Movement and Eat Right India are related government initiatives.

ocr: The forces of globa- Statement (II) : lization have -made competition so impera- tive that unions and their tactics like stopping productivity no more hold good.
subject: General Science
detail: Only Statement (II) is visible in the image. The original question almost certainly paired it with a Statement (I) about the declining role or bargaining power of trade unions in the era of liberalisation, and asked whether both are true and whether II explains I. Globalisation after 1991 in India exposed firms to domestic and foreign competition. Firms responded with cost-cutting, contract and casual labour, outsourcing, VRS, flexible hiring and closures or relocation. Strikes, go-slows and work stoppages became costly, because management could shift production, import or replace workers. Union density fell, collective bargaining weakened, and unions turned to defending jobs rather than demanding gains. Such a statement is therefore generally accepted as true, and as a valid reason for unions' reduced leverage. A caveat is that the visible text overstates the case with 'no more hold good', since unions still matter, especially in the public sector, and the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 still gives them legal standing. Because Statement I and the options are missing, the letter (a) is an assumption that both statements are true and II explains I. Please verify against the original paper.
explanations: (a) Tentatively correct: assuming Statement I describes weakening union power, both statements are true and II is the correct explanation. This cannot be confirmed because the options are not visible.
(b) Would apply if both statements were true but II did not explain I. This is unlikely, since competition is a direct cause of weaker union leverage.

statements: II — Correct (broadly): globalisation-driven competition has weakened the effectiveness of union tactics like strikes and work stoppages. Facts: after the 1991 New Economic Policy (LPG reforms), Indian firms faced import competition and FDI. Employers adopted contractualisation, outsourcing, VRS and flexible work arrangements. Union membership density in the private sector fell, and the 1982 Bombay textile strike, which failed, is often cited as an early sign of declining militancy. Courts (for example the Supreme Court in T.K. Rangarajan v. Govt of Tamil Nadu, 2003) also held there is no fundamental right to strike. Unions now focus on job security, social security and wage floors, and central trade unions (INTUC, AITUC, CITU, HMS, BMS) hold token general strikes against labour code reforms.

Statement (I) and the options (a)-(d) are not visible, so the correct option letter cannot be fixed with certainty. The best-supported reading is that Statement II is a true, plausible explanation of declining union power, so option (a) is given as a tentative answer.
topic_notes: Globalisation and trade unions in India. Background: the 1991 economic reforms (liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation) opened Indian industry to competition. Employers sought labour flexibility: contract labour (Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970), fixed-term employment, outsourcing, VRS and closures. Effects on unions: falling union density in the organised private sector, fragmentation, multiple unions, growth of the informal sector (over 90% of the workforce), and a shift from militancy to defensive bargaining. Legal frame: Trade Unions Act 1926 (registration, immunities, seven members needed to register); Industrial Disputes Act 1947 (strikes, lockouts, lay-off, retrenchment, closure, Chapter VB for establishments with 100 or more workers, since raised to 300 in the Industrial Relations Code 2020); Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946. The three labour code consolidations are the Code on Wages 2019, Industrial Relations Code 2020, Social Security Code 2020 and OSH Code 2020. Under the Industrial Relations Code, a strike notice of 14 days is required in all establishments, and 60 days is the outer limit of notice validity. Judicial position: the right to strike is not a fundamental right (T.K. Rangarajan 2003), though it is a legal right under conditions. Central trade unions: INTUC (1947, Congress), AITUC (1920, the oldest), HMS, CITU (1970), BMS (1955, the largest by verified membership). Verification of membership has been done by the Labour Ministry. Possible UPSC angles: reasons for union decline, multiplicity of unions, recognition of unions, collective bargaining, the Second National Commission on Labour (2002), and the social security of unorganised workers.

ocr: Every State in India has Statement (I) : a High Court in its (State’s) territory. As per constitution of Statement (II) : India, each State is provided to have a High Court.
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 214 says there shall be a High Court for each State. Article 231, inserted by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act 1956, empowers Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more States, or for two or more States and a Union Territory. Thus the constitutional provision (Statement II) is correct as a general rule, but the factual claim (Statement I) that every State has a High Court in its own territory is not true. Examples: Punjab and Haryana share the Punjab and Haryana High Court at Chandigarh (which is also the UT's court); Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh had the Gauhati High Court, with Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura getting their own in 2013; Mizoram is still under the Gauhati High Court bench structure; Maharashtra, Goa, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu share the Bombay High Court. Hence Statement I is incorrect while Statement II is correct. Elimination: since II is true, options saying II is false are out. Since I is false, options saying I is true are out. Only the option 'I false, II true' survives. Also remember the first High Courts were Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1862).
explanations: (a) Wrong, assuming it says both statements are true: Statement I is factually false because common High Courts exist.
(b) Wrong, assuming it says both are true without explanation: Statement I still fails.
(c) Wrong, assuming it says I is true and II is false: this reverses the real position.
(d) Correct, assuming it says I is false and II is true: Article 214 provides a High Court for each State but Article 231 allows common High Courts, so Statement I is false.
keyfact: Article 214 gives one High Court per State, but Article 231 lets Parliament create a common High Court for several States, so not every State has its own.
option_notes: Option (a), both true with II explaining I: a typical assertion-reason format choice. It would be correct only if every State physically had its own High Court, which is not the case. Remember Article 231 allows a common court for States.

Option (b), both true but II not the explanation: it fails for the same reason, since Statement I is incorrect. High Courts number 25 as of recent years, whereas States and UTs number 36, so the count itself shows sharing.

Option (c), I true and II false: this reverses the facts. Article 214 does state that each State shall have a High Court, so II is not false. High Courts are courts of record under Article 215 and can punish for contempt of themselves.

Option (d), I false and II true: this matches the constitutional position. Article 214 sets the default of one High Court per State, while Articles 230 and 231 let Parliament extend or share High Courts. Common courts like Punjab and Haryana, Bombay and Gauhati show Statement I does not hold universally.
