statements: 1 — Incorrect: Not every State has a High Court in its own territory because common High Courts exist under Article 231. Examples: Punjab and Haryana share one High Court; Mizoram, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh fall under the Gauhati High Court's jurisdiction; Goa is served by a Bombay High Court bench. Some States such as Sikkim and Meghalaya now have their own courts, but the general claim fails. Delhi is the only UT with its own High Court (since 1966). Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh share a High Court. Puducherry comes under the Madras High Court, and Lakshadweep comes under Kerala. Parliament can extend or exclude a High Court's jurisdiction to or from a UT under Article 230.

2 — Correct: Article 214 provides that there shall be a High Court for each State. The 7th Amendment (1956) added Articles 230 to 231, allowing Parliament to create a common High Court for two or more States. Thus the constitutional scheme is one High Court per State by default, with a flexibility clause. High Court judges are appointed by the President after consulting the CJI, the Governor and the Chief Justice of the High Court, and retire at 62 (Article 217). Article 226 gives High Courts writ powers wider than the Supreme Court's under Article 32, as they extend to any other purpose besides fundamental rights.
summary: The answer is (d): both Statement I and Statement II are false. Article 214 provides that there shall be a High Court for each State, but the 7th Amendment (1956) allows Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more States (and UTs), so not every State has its own High Court in its territory. Several States share High Courts, and some High Courts sit outside the State they serve. The options are not visible in the image, so I assume the standard format: (a) both true and II explains I, (b) both true but II does not explain I, (c) I true and II false, (d) I false and II true. On that format the key would be (d). Please verify against the printed options.
topic_notes: High Courts are covered in Part VI, Chapter V (Articles 214 to 231). Article 214: a High Court for each State. Article 215: High Courts are courts of record. Article 216: composition, with a Chief Justice and other judges as the President decides. Article 217: appointment and conditions; judges retire at 62 years. Article 219: oath before the Governor. Article 221: salaries. Article 222: transfer of judges by the President after consulting the CJI. Article 224: additional and acting judges. Article 224A: retired judges sitting on request. Article 226: power to issue writs for fundamental rights and for any other purpose. Article 227: superintendence over all subordinate courts. Article 228: transfer of certain cases from subordinate courts. Article 229: officers and staff and expenses. Article 230: extension of jurisdiction to UTs. Article 231: common High Court for two or more States. The 7th Amendment (1956) abolished the old Part B States and introduced these provisions. Judges are removed by the same procedure as Supreme Court judges: an address by both Houses with special majority, as per the Judges Inquiry Act 1968. The oldest High Courts are Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1862), followed by Allahabad (1866). Delhi High Court was set up in 1966. The largest by sanctioned strength is the Allahabad High Court. The Gauhati High Court once served seven north-eastern States before separate courts were created for Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura in 2013. Telangana got its own High Court in 2019 and Andhra Pradesh's court moved to Amaravati. The 15th Finance and the Law Commission have also considered All India Judicial Service and reforms to pendency. The NJAC, created by the 99th Amendment, was struck down in 2015 in the Fourth Judges case, restoring the collegium system.

ocr: The Directive Principles Statement (I) : of State Policy enshrined in the constitution, aim at providing the social and economic base of a genuine democracy. The Directive Principles Statement (II) : are merely directives which the government has to keep in mind while framing policy and is not enforceable through courts. In order to produce Statement (I) : electric power from a geothermal reservoir, temperature above 180° is required. To drive steam turbines, Statement (I) : high temperature steam is used. (Contd.) ree Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner (AI
subject: General Science
detail: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Constitution, borrowed from the Irish Constitution. Their aim is to establish social and economic democracy, which gives substance to the political democracy promised by the Fundamental Rights, and so to build a welfare state. Dr Ambedkar called them 'novel features' and 'instruments of instructions' to the legislature and executive. Article 37 says they are not enforceable by any court, yet they are fundamental in the governance of the country, and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws. Statement I is therefore true: it states the objective. Statement II is also true: it states their non-justiciable character. Statement II does not explain Statement I. Non-enforceability does not account for the aim of the DPSP; it only describes their legal status. Both statements are correct on their own, but II is not the reason for I. Elimination: options saying either statement is false are wrong. The option claiming II is the correct explanation of I is wrong because non-justiciability is not the cause of the social and economic aim. Remember the key cases: Champakam Dorairajan (1951), where Fundamental Rights prevailed; Kesavananda Bharati (1973); and Minerva Mills (1980), which stressed the balance between Part III and Part IV.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Both statements are true, but II does not explain I. Non-justiciability describes the legal status of the DPSP. It does not explain their aim of building social and economic democracy.
(b) Most likely correct: Both statements are true and II is not the correct explanation of I. Part IV states the aim, and Article 37 states that the DPSP are not enforceable in court.
(c) Wrong: Statement II is not false. Article 37 says the DPSP are not enforceable by courts, so this option fails.
(d) Wrong: Statement I is not false. The DPSP do aim at social and economic democracy, so this option fails.
keyfact: DPSP (Part IV, Arts. 36-51) aim at social and economic democracy but are non-justiciable under Art. 37; II does not explain I, so the answer is likely (b), to be confirmed against the printed options.
option_notes: Option (a) is the 'both true, II explains I' case. Here it would claim that non-enforceability is why the DPSP aim at economic and social democracy. That link is not valid. The aim comes from the Constituent Assembly's vision of a welfare state (Preamble: justice - social, economic and political), while Article 37 sets out the DPSP's non-justiciable status.

Option (b) is 'both true but II is not the correct explanation of I'. It fits here. Statement I is about purpose (Part IV, Articles 36-51, social and economic democracy). Statement II is about legal force (Article 37, non-justiciable). The two are independent facts about the DPSP.

Option (c) says I is true and II is false. For this to hold, the DPSP would have to be enforceable. They are not: Article 37 explicitly bars court enforcement. Only Fundamental Rights are directly enforceable, through writs under Articles 32 and 226. Some Directives became enforceable only indirectly, for example Article 21A on education through the 86th Amendment.

Option (d) says I is false and II is true. This would deny that the DPSP aim at social and economic democracy. The Constituent Assembly, especially Dr Ambedkar, said the DPSP aim at economic democracy, and the Preamble's ideals of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity are reinforced by Part IV.
related: DPSP are in Part IV, Articles 36-51, borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
Article 37: DPSP are not enforceable by any court, yet fundamental in governance.
Article 44 directs the State to secure a Uniform Civil Code.
Article 40 directs the State to organise village panchayats (Gandhian principle).
Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid) was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
Minerva Mills (1980): harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP is part of the basic structure.
Article 48A (protect the environment) was added by the 42nd Amendment.
Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA, Article 51A, added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
statements: 1 — Correct: The DPSP aim to create social and economic democracy and a welfare state. Part IV covers Articles 36-51. They were borrowed from the Irish Constitution, which had itself drawn on Spain. They are classified as Socialistic (Arts. 38, 39, 41-43), Gandhian (Arts. 40, 43, 46, 47, 48) and Liberal-intellectual (Arts. 44-45, 48A-51). Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order that promotes the welfare of the people. Article 39 covers equitable distribution of resources and equal pay for equal work. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Articles 39A, 43A and 48A. The 44th Amendment (1978) added Article 38(2). The 86th Amendment (2002) changed Article 45 and added Article 21A. The 97th Amendment (2011) added Article 43B on cooperatives.

2 — Correct: DPSP are non-justiciable under Article 37, but they are fundamental to governance. They cannot be enforced by courts, and the State must keep them in mind while making laws. They differ from Fundamental Rights, which are justiciable under Articles 32 and 226. Courts have still used them to interpret rights: in Minerva Mills (1980) the Supreme Court held that harmony between Parts III and IV is a basic feature. Article 31C, as added by the 25th Amendment, gives priority to Articles 39(b) and (c) over certain rights. Statement II is true but does not explain Statement I.
summary: Q14 is an Assertion-Reason style pair of statements. The usual UPSC options are: (a) both true and II explains I, (b) both true but II does not explain I, (c) I true and II false, (d) I false and II true. The most likely correct answer is (b): both statements are true, but II does not explain I. Statement I gives the aim of the DPSP (social and economic democracy, Part IV); Statement II gives their legal status (non-justiciable, Article 37). The printed options are not visible in the image, so confirm the letter against the paper.
topic_notes: Directive Principles of State Policy are in Part IV, Articles 36-51. They come from the Irish Constitution, where they were called 'Directive Principles of Social Policy'. Article 36 defines 'State' as in Part III. Article 37 makes them non-justiciable but fundamental in governance. Classification: Socialistic (Arts. 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47), Gandhian (Arts. 40 on village panchayats, 43 on cottage industries, 43B, 46 on SC/ST and weaker sections, 47 on prohibition, 48 on cow protection and scientific agriculture) and Liberal-intellectual (Arts. 44 on Uniform Civil Code, 45 on early childhood care, 48A on environment, 49 on monuments, 50 on separation of judiciary from executive, 51 on international peace). Key amendments: the 42nd (1976) added Arts. 39A, 43A and 48A; the 44th (1978) added 38(2); the 86th (2002) substituted Art. 45; the 97th (2011) added 43B. Key cases: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951), where Fundamental Rights prevailed over Directives; Golaknath (1967); Kesavananda Bharati (1973); Minerva Mills (1980), on balance between Parts III and IV; Unni Krishnan (1993), on education. Differences from Fundamental Rights: FRs are negative limits on the State and justiciable, while DPSP are positive instructions and non-justiciable. FRs promote political democracy, DPSP promote social and economic democracy. Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA (Art. 51A, added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation).

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q15.
ocr: The Directive Principles Statement (I) : of State Policy enshrined in the constitution, aim at providing the social and economic base of a genuine democracy. The Directive Principles Statement (II) : are merely directives which the government has to keep in mind while framing policy and is not enforceable through courts. In order to produce Statement (I) : electric power from a geothermal reservoir, temperature above 180° is required. To drive steam turbines, Statement (I) : high temperature steam is used. (Contd.) ree Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner (AI
subject: General Science
detail: Geothermal electricity uses heat from the Earth's crust. Wells tap hot water or steam in a reservoir. The steam is sent to a turbine, which spins a generator. Efficient steam turbines need high-pressure, high-temperature steam, so high-enthalpy reservoirs are needed. Reservoirs above roughly 150-180°C are suited to flash-steam or dry-steam plants. Lower-temperature resources (about 100-150°C) are used with binary-cycle plants, where the geothermal fluid heats a secondary fluid with a low boiling point such as isobutane or pentane. Below about 100°C the heat is used for direct purposes such as heating, greenhouses and spas, not for electricity. The usual UPSC threshold is 180°C or more for conventional power generation. Statement I is therefore correct, since the temperature requirement is set by the need for steam. Statement II is a correct general fact about steam turbines and it directly explains why the temperature must be high. So the relation is explanatory. Elimination: if the options follow the standard format, (b) fails because II is the reason for I, and (c) and (d) fail because neither statement is false. Note: the printed '180°' has no unit in the OCR, and I take it as °C. The options were not visible, so check the letter against your paper's actual option wording.
explanations: Correct: both statements are true, and the high-temperature steam needed by turbines (II) is the reason geothermal reservoirs must be above about 180°C (I).
Wrong: this option says II does not explain I, but II is exactly the reason for the temperature requirement in I.
Wrong: Statement II is not false. High-temperature steam is the standard way to drive steam turbines.
Wrong: Statement I is not false. The threshold of about 180°C for conventional geothermal power is accepted.
keyfact: Geothermal power needs reservoir temperatures above about 180°C because steam turbines run on high-temperature steam; lower temperatures are used for binary plants or direct heating.
option_notes: Both statements are true and II explains I. Here, this fits the geothermal case: the turbine needs hot steam, so the reservoir must be hot. This is the standard first option in Assertion-Reason questions. Always test for a causal link, not just truth.

Both statements are true but II does not explain I. This would apply if the two facts were independent. It is the usual trap when students judge only truth and ignore the reasoning link. Here it does not apply.
Statement I is true and II is false. This would require that steam turbines do not use high-temperature steam, which is untrue. Steam turbines work on the Rankine cycle with superheated steam.

Statement I is false and II is true. This would require that geothermal power needs no high temperature. Low-temperature resources can only be used for direct heating or binary plants, so this does not hold.

Puga valley in Ladakh is India's most promising geothermal field.
Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh) has hot springs and is a geothermal site.
Binary cycle plants use low-boiling-point fluids such as isobutane.
The Geysers in California is the largest geothermal complex in the world.

statements: Statement I — Correct: Conventional geothermal power plants need reservoir temperatures of roughly 180°C or more. Geothermal energy is heat stored in the Earth's crust, from radioactive decay and residual heat. High-enthalpy fields occur along plate boundaries and volcanic belts such as Iceland, the USA (The Geysers, California), the Philippines, Indonesia, Kenya and New Zealand. Plant types are dry steam, flash steam and binary cycle. Binary plants work at lower temperatures of about 100-180°C. In India, resources are at Puga and Chumathang in Ladakh, Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh, Tattapani in Chhattisgarh, Bakreshwar in West Bengal and Unai in Maharashtra. India has no commercial geothermal power plant yet.

Statement II — Correct: Steam turbines are driven by high-temperature, high-pressure steam. In a thermal, nuclear or geothermal plant the steam expands across the turbine blades, and the turbine turns the generator rotor, producing electricity by electromagnetic induction. Higher steam temperature raises the Carnot and Rankine cycle efficiency. Modern coal plants use supercritical steam above 220 bar and 540°C or more. Condensers return the exhaust steam to water. The statement also explains Statement I, because geothermal fluid must be hot enough to produce steam for the turbine.
summary: The answer is (a): both statements are true and Statement II explains Statement I. Q15 is an Assertion-Reason type question where the options are cut off in the image, so I am assuming the standard UPSC format: (a) both true and II is the correct explanation of I; (b) both true but II is not the correct explanation; (c) I true, II false; (d) I false, II true. Geothermal power needs reservoir temperatures above about 180°C because turbines are driven by high-temperature steam.
topic_notes: Geothermal energy is heat from the Earth's interior. The geothermal gradient is about 25-30°C per km of depth. Types of resource: hydrothermal (hot water or steam), hot dry rock or enhanced geothermal systems, geopressured and magma. Power plants are of three kinds. Dry steam plants use steam directly, the oldest being Larderello in Italy (1904). Flash steam plants use fluid above about 180°C, which is flashed to steam at lower pressure. Binary cycle plants use fluid at 100-180°C to heat a secondary working fluid. Leading producers are the USA, Indonesia, the Philippines, Turkey, New Zealand, Kenya and Iceland. Environmental issues include release of H2S and CO2, land subsidence, and induced seismicity. India's potential is estimated at about 10,600 MW, with about 300 sites identified by the Geological Survey of India. Key provinces are the Himalayan region (Puga, Chumathang), the Sohana and West Coast belts, the Cambay graben, the Son-Narmada-Tapti (SONATA) belt, the Godavari basin and the Mahanadi basin. Other renewable energy topics that can be asked: the National Institute of Solar Energy, the International Solar Alliance, MNRE, and tidal energy sites such as the Gulf of Khambhat, Gulf of Kutch and Sundarbans. Concepts include the Rankine cycle, turbine types, and efficiency.

question: Which one of the following sets of industries were among first modern industries in India ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Modern industry in India began in the 1850s under colonial rule, mainly in the cotton, jute and coal sectors. The first successful cotton mill, the Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company, was set up by Cowasji Nanabhai Davar in 1854. The first jute mill was set up at Rishra near Calcutta in 1855 by George Acland, with Bengali partners. Coal mining began at Raniganj in 1774 by Sumner and Heatley of the East India Company, and grew rapidly after the railway arrived in 1853. Railways created demand for coal and iron. Large-scale steel came later: TISCO at Jamshedpur in 1907 by Jamsetji Tata, with production starting 1911-12. Sugar mills expanded mainly after the 1932 tariff protection. Tea and coffee were plantation industries, not factory-based modern industries in the same sense, and silk was largely traditional. Elimination: options (a), (b) and (d) include sugar, silk or tea, which do not belong to the earliest modern group, while (c) has all three of the classic pioneer industries.
explanations: Wrong: tea was a plantation industry (from 1830s-40s in Assam), and sugar mills grew mainly after the 1930s tariff protection.
Wrong: jute and cotton are early modern industries, but silk was largely a traditional handicraft-based industry.
Correct: cotton (Bombay 1854), jute (Rishra 1855) and coal mining (Raniganj) were the pioneer modern industries.
Wrong: sugar came in the 1930s and steel with TISCO in 1907-12, so they were later, and silk was traditional.
keyfact: First modern Indian industries: cotton (Bombay 1854), jute (Rishra 1855) and coal (Raniganj).
option_notes: Tea: plantations began in Assam in the 1830s-40s, with the Assam Company set up in 1839. Cotton: the first mill was set up in 1854 in Bombay. Sugar: factories grew after the Sugar Industry Protection Act of 1932, with Uttar Pradesh and Bihar leading. The set mixes early and later industries, so it is not the earliest group.

Jute: the first mill was at Rishra (1855) on the Hooghly, and it was dominated by Scottish owners in Dundee-linked firms. Silk: Indian sericulture is ancient, in Karnataka, Bengal and Kashmir, and the industry was mostly small-scale. Cotton: the Bombay mills began in 1854. Silk makes this option wrong.

Cotton: the first mills were Bombay Spinning and Weaving (1854) and Ahmedabad (1861). Jute: Rishra mill (1855), with the industry concentrated on the Hooghly. Coal: Raniganj (1774), with output rising after railways (1853). These three were the earliest modern industries and formed the base of colonial industrialisation.

Sugar: modern mills mainly expanded in the 1930s. Silk: a traditional industry in Bengal, Karnataka and Assam. Steel: the Bengal Iron Works at Kulti (1870s) was early but small, and TISCO at Sakchi (Jamshedpur) was founded in 1907 by J.N. Tata, with first steel in 1912. Sugar and steel came later.
related: First cotton mill in India: Bombay Spinning and Weaving Co., 1854, founded by C. N. Davar.
First jute mill: Rishra (Bengal), 1855, by George Acland.
Coal mining began at Raniganj in 1774.
TISCO was founded in 1907 by Jamsetji Tata, with production starting in 1912.
First railway in India ran from Bombay to Thane in 1853.
Sugar Industry Protection Act was passed in 1932.
Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur steel plants were set up in the Second Five-Year Plan.
summary: The answer is (c) Cotton, Jute and Coal-Mines. These were the first modern factory or mechanised industries in India, set up in the mid-19th century: the cotton textile mill in Bombay (1854), the jute mill at Rishra, Bengal (1855), and coal mining at Raniganj (1774, expanded after 1850s railways).
topic_notes: Modern industrialisation in colonial India started in the 1850s and was linked to railways, British capital and the export economy. Cotton: Cowasji Davar's Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company (1854); Parsi and Gujarati entrepreneurs dominated, and Bombay was called the Manchester of India. The Ahmedabad mills began in 1861, and Ranchhodlal Chhotalal started Ahmedabad's first mill in 1861. Jute: Rishra (1855), with Calcutta-Hooghly belt mills mostly British owned, and Dundee as the main competitor. Coal: Raniganj coalfield (1774), and Jharia coalfield from the 1890s. Iron and steel: Kulti (1870), TISCO (1907), IISCO (1918), Mysore Iron Works at Bhadravati (1923). Paper, cement and sugar followed, especially after the discriminating protection policy of 1923 (Fiscal Commission 1921-22) and the 1932 sugar protection. The Swadeshi movement (1905) encouraged Indian enterprise. The First World War boosted industry. The Bombay Plan (1944) was a blueprint by industrialists. After independence, the Industrial Policy Resolutions of 1948 and 1956 and the Five-Year Plans, especially the Second Plan (Mahalanobis model), emphasised heavy industry and the public sector. Steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur were set up in the Second Plan with Soviet, German and British help. Other angles UPSC may ask: the Factories Act 1881 and 1948, plantation labour, and the deindustrialisation debate.

question: The regional project by name *CASA-1000" (Central Asia-South Asia-1000), funded by World Bank, pertains to the field of :
subject: General Science
detail: CASA-1000 (Central Asia-South Asia Electricity Transmission and Trade Project) is a regional electricity trade initiative backed by the World Bank, the Islamic Development Bank, the European Investment Bank, USAID, DFID and others. It exploits the seasonal pattern of Central Asian hydropower: Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan have surplus power in summer, when snow melts and rivers run high, while Afghanistan and Pakistan face summer shortages. The project builds about 750 km of high-voltage lines, with HVDC converter stations at Kabul-area (Afghanistan, Pul-e-Khumri link) and Nowshera (Pakistan), and a 500 kV HVAC line from Kyrgyzstan through Tajikistan. Of the 1,000 MW, about 300 MW is meant for Afghanistan and 700 MW for Pakistan. The inter-governmental council was formed in 2008, and the agreements were signed around 2014-2016. Elimination: the name itself says 'Electricity Transmission and Trade', and the project has no link to HIV/AIDS, roads and buildings, or literacy. Those fields have different programmes, such as NACP, PMGSY and Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. India is not a member, though it has expressed interest in the broader regional power linkage.
explanations: Wrong: HIV/AIDS control is handled by programmes like NACO/NACP and UNAIDS, not CASA-1000.
Wrong: Although it involves building transmission lines and converter stations, the project belongs to the power sector, not roads and buildings.
Correct: CASA-1000 is a 1,000 MW cross-border electricity transmission and trade project linking Central and South Asia.
Wrong: Literacy campaigns have no relation to this project; India's examples are Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and Saakshar Bharat.
keyfact: CASA-1000 = 1,000 MW electricity transmission from Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan to Afghanistan and Pakistan.
option_notes: HIV/AIDS eradication: India runs the National AIDS Control Programme through NACO, set up in 1992. Phase IV ran 2012-17, and the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act came in 2017. World AIDS Day is on 1 December. UNAIDS is the main global coordinating body. India's HIV prevalence among adults is now around 0.2%.

Roads and Buildings: in India this includes PMGSY (launched 2000) for rural roads, the NHAI-run Bharatmala programme, and the PWD for buildings. The World Bank funds many road projects, but CASA-1000 is not one of them. It is an energy project, and roads are only incidental to its construction.

Electricity: CASA-1000 links the hydropower surplus of Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan with the deficits in Afghanistan and Pakistan. It has a capacity of 1,000 MW and about 750 km of lines, with HVDC converter stations at Kabul and Nowshera. Funders include the World Bank and the Islamic Development Bank. The lines also cross difficult terrain and security-sensitive areas.

Eradication of illiteracy: in India the main efforts are Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (2001), the National Literacy Mission (1988), Saakshar Bharat (2009) and the Right to Education Act 2009 (in force from 2010). International Literacy Day is observed on 8 September. None of these relate to CASA-1000.
related: CASA-1000 capacity is 1,000 MW: about 300 MW to Afghanistan, 700 MW to Pakistan.
Source countries are Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan; recipients are Afghanistan and Pakistan.
TAPI is a gas pipeline: Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India, ending at Fazilka.
Funders include the World Bank and the Islamic Development Bank.
Pakistan's converter station is at Nowshera.
The Chabahar port in Iran is an India-backed connectivity project.
India is not a member of CASA-1000.
summary: The answer is (c) Electricity. CASA-1000 is a cross-border power transmission project that moves surplus hydropower from Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan to Afghanistan and Pakistan; the '1000' refers to 1,000 MW of transfer capacity.
topic_notes: CASA-1000 is the flagship regional energy trade project of Central and South Asia. It builds on the idea that Central Asia's water-rich countries, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, have seasonal surplus hydropower while Afghanistan and Pakistan have chronic shortages. The project covers about 1,300 km of transmission in total. A 500 kV AC line runs from Kyrgyzstan through Tajikistan, and an HVDC line runs from Tajikistan through Afghanistan to Pakistan. It has converter stations at Sangtuda (Tajikistan), Kabul-area Pul-e-Khumri link and Nowshera (Pakistan). The capacity is 1,000 MW, split about 300 MW to Afghanistan and 700 MW to Pakistan. The World Bank is a major financier, together with the Islamic Development Bank, EIB, USAID and DFID. Related regional energy and connectivity projects include TAPI, the Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India gas pipeline, which is a natural-gas project and not electricity. There is also TUTAP, a Turkmenistan-Uzbekistan-Tajikistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan power interconnection. Other energy initiatives for the region include the India-Bangladesh and India-Nepal power trade arrangements, BBIN, and the International Solar Alliance. UPSC could next ask about TAPI's route (Galkynysh field to Fazilka), the countries involved, the role of the Asian Development Bank in TAPI, the International North-South Transport Corridor, Chabahar port and the Silk Road economic belt. Remember that CASA-1000 is electricity, TAPI is gas, and neither runs through India (TAPI ends at Fazilka, Punjab).

ocr: . The Endeavour of ‘Janani Suraksha Yojana’ Programme is to : 1, Promote institutional deliveries 2. Provide monetary assistance to the mother to meet the cost of delivery 3. Provide for wage loss due to Pregnancy and confinement (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 1 and 3 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 “Kyoto Protocol’, an agreement signed by various countries, is associated with : (a) Intemational trade (b) Deep sea oil and mineral exploration (c) Clean environment and climate change (a) Building common food stock to save human being from any natural disaster »FC) Exam 2012 Question Paper
subject: Computers
detail: Janani Suraksha Yojana was launched on 12 April 2005 under the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM). It is a 100% centrally sponsored scheme that integrates cash assistance with delivery and post-delivery care. Its objective is to reduce maternal and neonatal mortality by promoting institutional deliveries, especially among poor pregnant women. Eligible beneficiaries receive a cash incentive, and an ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) acts as the link who helps the woman reach the health facility. The states are divided into Low Performing States (LPS), such as UP, Bihar, MP, Rajasthan and Odisha, and High Performing States (HPS). LPS get higher cash packages. The older figures were Rs 1400 for rural and Rs 1000 for urban mothers in LPS, and Rs 700 for rural and Rs 600 for urban mothers in HPS. The cash is meant to meet delivery and transport costs. Statement 1 matches the scheme's central aim. Statement 2 matches its cash assistance. Statement 3 is not an aim of JSY. Wage-loss compensation is a feature of PMMVY (2017, Rs 5000 for the first living child, partly to offset wage loss) and the Maternity Benefit Act 1961. So only 1 and 2 are correct, and the answer is (a).
explanations: Correct: statements 1 and 2 describe JSY, and statement 3 does not.
Incorrect: it includes statement 3, wage-loss compensation, which is not a JSY aim, and it leaves out statement 2, which is correct.
Incorrect: it leaves out statement 1 and includes statement 3, and statement 1 is a core objective.
Incorrect: statement 3 is wrong, so not all three can be correct.
keyfact: JSY (2005, NRHM) promotes institutional deliveries with cash assistance to mothers, but it does not compensate for wage loss.
related: JSY was launched on 12 April 2005 under NRHM.
JSY is a 100% centrally sponsored scheme.
ASHA stands for Accredited Social Health Activist.
JSSK launched in 2011 provides free delivery and care for sick newborns.
PMMVY gives Rs 5000 in instalments for the first living child.
Maternity Benefit Amendment Act 2017 gives 26 weeks paid leave for the first two children.
PMSMA offers antenatal check-ups on the 9th of each month.
The ESI Act provides maternity benefit for insured women.
statements: 1 — Correct: Promoting institutional deliveries is the core objective of JSY. Safe-motherhood intervention launched 12 April 2005 under NRHM, it is a centrally sponsored scheme that replaced the National Maternity Benefit Scheme (NMBS). It targets all pregnant women in LPS and BPL/SC/ST women in HPS. ASHA workers identify and escort beneficiaries to health centres, and the scheme has raised institutional delivery rates sharply across India.

2 — Correct: JSY gives cash assistance to the mother, which defrays delivery and transport costs. It is paid as a conditional cash transfer on delivery in a government or accredited private facility. Rural and urban rates differ, and Low Performing States get more. ASHAs also get an incentive. The aim is to reduce out-of-pocket expenditure and so improve access to skilled birth attendance.

3 — Incorrect: JSY does not compensate for wage loss from pregnancy and confinement. That is the purpose of maternity benefit laws and schemes. The Maternity Benefit Act 1961 (amended 2017) provides 26 weeks of paid leave for the first two children. The Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (2017) gives Rs 5000 in instalments to partly offset wage loss, while JSY's cash is for delivery and transport costs.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 and 2 only. Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) is a safe-motherhood intervention under the National Rural Health Mission that promotes institutional deliveries and gives cash assistance to the mother, but it does not compensate for wage loss. Wage-loss compensation is a feature of maternity benefit schemes such as the Maternity Benefit Act or PMMVY.
topic_notes: Janani Suraksha Yojana was launched on 12 April 2005 under NRHM as a 100% centrally sponsored conditional cash transfer scheme. It replaced the National Maternity Benefit Scheme, which had been part of the National Social Assistance Programme. Its aim is to lower maternal and infant mortality by encouraging institutional deliveries. States are classed as Low Performing States (UP, Uttarakhand, Bihar, Jharkhand, MP, Chhattisgarh, Assam, Rajasthan, Odisha, J&K) and High Performing States. ASHA is the key link worker. Cash is paid to the mother, and ASHAs get an incentive. Related maternal and child health schemes: Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK, 2011) gives free delivery, caesarean section, drugs, diagnostics, diet and transport for mothers and sick newborns. Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA, 2016) offers free antenatal check-ups on the 9th of every month. PMMVY (2017) gives Rs 5000 in three instalments for the first living child, as partial wage compensation. Maternity Benefit Act 1961 (amended 2017) gives 26 weeks of paid leave for the first two children, 12 weeks for the third, a crèche facility for establishments with 50 or more employees, and 12 weeks for adopting mothers and commissioning mothers. The ESI Act gives maternity benefit at 100% of wages for 26 weeks. NRHM was launched in 2005 and later merged into the National Health Mission (2013) with NUHM. Other points: MMR and IMR are key indicators, and Mission Indradhanush covers immunisation. Related UPSC angles are the scheme's launch year, its beneficiaries and the role of ASHA.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q19.
ocr: . The Endeavour of ‘Janani Suraksha Yojana’ Programme is to : 1, Promote institutional deliveries 2. Provide monetary assistance to the mother to meet the cost of delivery 3. Provide for wage loss due to Pregnancy and confinement (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 1 and 3 only (c) 2 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 “Kyoto Protocol’, an agreement signed by various countries, is associated with : (a) Intemational trade (b) Deep sea oil and mineral exploration (c) Clean environment and climate change (a) Building common food stock to save human being from any natural disaster »FC) Exam 2012 Question Paper
subject: Computers
detail: The Kyoto Protocol operationalises the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC, 1992, Rio Earth Summit). It was adopted at COP-3 in Kyoto on 11 December 1997 and entered into force on 16 February 2005 after Russia ratified it. It set binding emission-reduction targets for Annex I (developed) countries, on the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities'. The first commitment period ran 2008-2012, with an average target of about 5% below 1990 levels. The six gases covered were CO2, methane, nitrous oxide, HFCs, PFCs and SF6 (NF3 was added later). It created three flexibility mechanisms: Emissions Trading, the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) and Joint Implementation (JI). The Doha Amendment (2012) set a second commitment period for 2013-2020. The USA signed but never ratified, and Canada withdrew in 2011. India ratified in 2002 and had no binding targets as a developing country. The Paris Agreement (2015) later replaced it. Elimination: trade is the domain of the WTO, deep-sea mineral exploration falls under UNCLOS and the International Seabed Authority, and food stock building has no link to Kyoto. Only (c) fits.
explanations: Incorrect: international trade is governed by the WTO/GATT, not the Kyoto Protocol.
Incorrect: deep-sea oil and mineral exploration comes under UNCLOS and the International Seabed Authority.
Correct: Kyoto is the climate agreement on cutting greenhouse gas emissions, which is about a clean environment and climate change.
Incorrect: building common food stocks and disaster protection is not a Kyoto theme; food security is associated with the FAO and the WFP.
keyfact: Kyoto Protocol (1997, in force 2005) sets binding greenhouse gas emission cuts for developed countries under the UNFCCC.
option_notes: International trade is regulated by the WTO (established 1 January 1995, replacing GATT 1947, HQ Geneva). Its main agreements are GATS, TRIPS and the Agreement on Agriculture. Its Ministerial Conference meets every two years, and the Doha Round began in 2001. It has a dispute settlement body. The WTO is a different system from climate treaties.

Seabed resources are governed by UNCLOS (1982, in force 1994). The International Seabed Authority is based in Kingston, Jamaica. UNCLOS defines the territorial sea (12 nautical miles), the EEZ (200 nautical miles) and the continental shelf. The seabed beyond national jurisdiction, 'the Area', is the 'common heritage of mankind'. India holds exploration contracts in the Indian Ocean for polymetallic nodules.

This is the correct option. The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in 1997 and entered into force in 2005. It binds developed countries to reduce emissions of six greenhouse gases, and it introduced carbon markets and the CDM. It is linked to the UNFCCC and its COP meetings. The Doha Amendment extended it to 2020, and the Paris Agreement of 2015 is its successor.

Food security and disaster-related ideas are linked to other bodies. The FAO (Rome, 1945) works on food, the World Food Programme won the 2020 Nobel Peace Prize, and the Sendai Framework (2015-2030) covers disaster risk reduction. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a real 'common seed stock'. None of these is related to Kyoto.
related: Kyoto Protocol: adopted 1997, in force 2005, first commitment period 2008-2012.
Kyoto covers six greenhouse gases: CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs and SF6.
Kyoto mechanisms: Emissions Trading, CDM and Joint Implementation.
The USA never ratified Kyoto and Canada withdrew in 2011.
The Montreal Protocol (1987) protects the ozone layer, and its Kigali Amendment (2016) phases down HFCs.
The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to hold warming below 2°C, pursuing 1.5°C.
Janani Suraksha Yojana (2005), Q18 on the same page, promotes institutional deliveries under the NRHM.
summary: The answer is (c). The Kyoto Protocol (adopted December 1997 in Kyoto, Japan; in force 16 February 2005) is an international agreement under the UNFCCC. It commits industrialised countries to legally binding targets for cutting greenhouse gas emissions, so it is associated with a clean environment and climate change.
topic_notes: Climate change diplomacy timeline: the IPCC was set up in 1988 by the WMO and UNEP. The UNFCCC was adopted in 1992 and came into force in 1994. COP-1 was held in Berlin in 1995. The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in 1997 and came into force in 2005. Its first commitment period was 2008-2012. The Bali Action Plan came in 2007, Copenhagen in 2009 (a non-binding accord), and Cancun in 2010 (the Green Climate Fund). The Doha Amendment of 2012 covered 2013-2020. Paris in 2015 (COP-21) aimed to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C, using Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). Glasgow (COP-26, 2021) produced the phase-down of coal. COP-27 (Egypt, 2022) set up the Loss and Damage Fund. Key principles: the polluter pays principle and common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC). Kyoto mechanisms: Emissions Trading (Article 17), CDM (Article 12) and Joint Implementation (Article 6). Annex I covers developed and transition economies, and Annex B lists the countries with targets. The Montreal Protocol (1987) is for ozone-depleting substances, and its Kigali Amendment (2016) covers HFCs. Other treaties: the Ramsar Convention (wetlands, 1971), CBD (1992), the Cartagena Protocol (biosafety), the Nagoya Protocol (access and benefit sharing), the Basel Convention (hazardous waste), the Stockholm Convention (POPs) and CITES (1973). India's NDCs: net zero by 2070, 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 and a 45% cut in emissions intensity from 2005 levels.

ocr: Which of the following can be threats to the biodiversity of a geographical area ? 1. Global warming 2. Fragmentation of habitats 3. Invasion of alien species 4. Promotion of vegetarianism (a) 1, 2 and 3 only (b) 1, 2 and 4 only (c) 3 and 4 only (d) 1, 2,3 and 4 . Vultures, which were very common in our countryside a few years ago, are rarely seen nowadays. This is attributed to one of the following : (a) Destruction of their nesting sites by new invasive species (b) A drug used by cattle owners for treating their discased cattle (c) Scarcity of food available to them (d) A widespread, persist
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Biodiversity loss is driven mainly by the 'evil quartet' (E.O. Wilson / Jared Diamond): habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasion and co-extinctions. Climate change or global warming is now added as a major driver, as it shifts ranges, bleaches corals, alters phenology and raises extinction risk. Habitat fragmentation splits continuous habitat into small isolated patches, which reduces population sizes, blocks migration, increases edge effects and causes inbreeding. Alien invasive species such as water hyacinth, Lantana camara, Parthenium and African catfish outcompete or prey on native species, and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) lists them as a key threat. Vegetarianism is a dietary choice. If anything, a plant-based diet reduces pressure on land, water and emissions from livestock, and it does not threaten biodiversity. So statements 1, 2 and 3 are threats and 4 is not. Option (a) is therefore correct. Options (b), (c) and (d) all include statement 4 and are eliminated.
explanations: Correct: it includes exactly the three real threats, global warming, habitat fragmentation and alien species invasion, and excludes vegetarianism.
Wrong: it includes statement 4, which is not a threat, and omits statement 3, which is a threat.
Wrong: it leaves out global warming and fragmentation, both genuine threats, and includes the non-threat, vegetarianism.
Wrong: it includes statement 4, and promotion of vegetarianism does not threaten biodiversity.
keyfact: Threats to biodiversity: habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien invasive species, co-extinction and climate change; vegetarianism is not a threat.
related: The 'Evil Quartet' was coined by Jared Diamond.
Habitat loss and fragmentation is the biggest cause of biodiversity loss.
Nile perch introduction in Lake Victoria caused extinction of many cichlid fish.
Water hyacinth is called the 'Terror of Bengal'.
India has 4 biodiversity hotspots.
Biological Diversity Act 2002 created the National Biodiversity Authority.
The Kunming-Montreal framework has a 30x30 target.
The Convention on Biological Diversity was adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit.
statements: 1 — Correct: Global warming is a recognised threat to biodiversity. Rising temperatures, sea-level rise, ocean acidification and changing rainfall shift species ranges and breeding or flowering times. Coral reefs bleach when seas warm, glaciers and alpine habitats shrink, and species that cannot migrate face extinction. The IPCC assesses these risks, and the IUCN Red List records climate change as a driver. Greenhouse gases such as CO2, methane and N2O cause warming. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C. Himalayan and island species and amphibians are especially vulnerable.

2 — Correct: Fragmentation of habitats breaks large continuous habitats into small isolated patches, usually through roads, dams, agriculture and urbanisation. It reduces gene flow, increases edge effects, lowers population viability and blocks animal movement. Wildlife corridors, such as elephant corridors in India, are a remedy. Species-area relationships show that smaller areas hold fewer species. Habitat loss and fragmentation are the single largest cause of species extinction today. Amazon forest fragments and Western Ghats forests are standard examples. Conservation tools include protected areas, corridors and landscape-level planning.

3 — Correct: Invasion by alien species is a major threat. Introduced species lack natural predators and outcompete natives. Examples are the Nile perch in Lake Victoria, which wiped out many cichlids, water hyacinth (Eichhornia), Lantana, Parthenium (congress grass), Prosopis juliflora and the African catfish (Clarias gariepinus) in India. Invasive species cause competition, predation, disease spread and hybridisation. The CBD (1992) Article 8(h) requires parties to prevent such introductions. The IUCN maintains the Global Invasive Species Database. In India, the Biological Diversity Act 2002 and quarantine rules address the problem.

4 — Incorrect: Promotion of vegetarianism is not a threat to biodiversity. It is a dietary and cultural choice. Plant-based diets generally need less land, water and feed than meat production, so they can reduce deforestation, such as Amazon clearing for cattle pasture, and cut greenhouse emissions. Large-scale monoculture farming can harm biodiversity, but that is a result of agricultural practice, not of vegetarianism itself. Livestock is a major contributor to land-use change and methane emissions globally. Hence this statement is the distractor.
summary: The correct answer is (a) 1, 2 and 3 only. Global warming, habitat fragmentation and invasion by alien species are recognised threats to biodiversity, whereas promotion of vegetarianism is not a threat.
topic_notes: Threats to biodiversity are commonly grouped as the 'Evil Quartet': (1) habitat loss and fragmentation, (2) over-exploitation, (3) alien species invasions and (4) co-extinctions. Pollution, climate change and disease are also added. Habitat loss is the most important cause, as tropical rainforests are cleared for agriculture, mining and settlement. Over-exploitation includes poaching, overfishing and the wildlife trade, and examples are the Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon and dodo. Alien invasives include water hyacinth, Lantana, Parthenium, Prosopis, Nile perch and African catfish. Co-extinction means that when a host species goes extinct, dependent species such as parasites or pollinators also vanish. Climate change affects corals, polar species and mountain flora. Conservation approaches are in situ (national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves) and ex situ (zoos, botanical gardens, gene banks, cryopreservation). Key bodies and laws include the CBD (1992), the IUCN Red List, CITES (1973), the Ramsar Convention (1971), the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, the Biological Diversity Act 2002 and the National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai). India has 4 of 36 global biodiversity hotspots: the Himalaya, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Sundaland (Nicobar). India is one of 17 megadiverse countries. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) set the 30x30 target to protect 30 percent of land and sea by 2030. UPSC often asks about the evil quartet, the invasive species list, hotspots and the Red List categories (Extinct, Extinct in the Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Least Concern).

question: Who won the Golden Boot Award in the recently concluded UEFA Euro 2012 ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: UEFA Euro 2012 was co-hosted by Poland and Ukraine (8 June to 1 July 2012). Spain beat Italy 4-0 in the final at the Olympic Stadium, Kyiv, becoming the first team to win three consecutive major tournaments (Euro 2008, World Cup 2010, Euro 2012). The top scorer award (Golden Boot) went to Fernando Torres. Six players finished on 3 goals: Torres, Mario Gomez (Germany), Mario Mandzukic (Croatia), Alan Dzagoev (Russia), Mario Balotelli (Italy) and Cristiano Ronaldo (Portugal). UEFA's tie-break rules apply in order: most assists, then fewest minutes played. Torres and Gomez each had 1 assist (Torres had 1, Gomez 0 per UEFA data, giving Torres the edge on assists), and Torres played only 189 minutes, so he got the award. Gomez was a joint top scorer who missed out. Balotelli and Ronaldo also had 3 goals but lost on tie-breaks. Elimination: all four options scored 3, so knowledge of the tie-break is essential. Torres also won the Golden Boot as a substitute-heavy player, which was notable.
explanations: Correct. Torres scored 3 goals, and won on the tie-break (assists, then fewer minutes played) to take the Golden Boot.
Incorrect. Balotelli scored 3 goals (two against Germany in the semi-final) but lost on the tie-break.
Incorrect. Ronaldo scored 3 goals (two against the Netherlands, one against the Czech Republic) but lost on the tie-break.
Incorrect. Gomez scored 3 goals in the group stage but had fewer assists and played more minutes than Torres.
keyfact: Fernando Torres (Spain) won the Euro 2012 Golden Boot with 3 goals, winning the tie-break on minutes played.
option_notes: Fernando Torres is a Spanish striker, born 1984, who played for Atletico Madrid, Liverpool, Chelsea and AC Milan. He scored the winning goal in the Euro 2008 final against Germany. At Euro 2012 he scored in the final against Italy, and won the Golden Boot, and a winner's medal. He is Spain's key forward of that golden generation.

Mario Balotelli is an Italian striker, born 1990, who played for Inter, Manchester City and AC Milan. At Euro 2012 he scored a brace against Germany in the semi-final, a famous performance with a shirt-off celebration. Italy lost the final 4-0 to Spain. He finished with 3 goals but did not win the Golden Boot.

Cristiano Ronaldo is a Portuguese forward, born 1985, who was captain of Portugal at Euro 2012, where Portugal reached the semi-finals and lost to Spain on penalties. He scored 3 goals. He later led Portugal to win Euro 2016, and holds the record for most goals in European Championship history.

Mario Gomez is a German striker, born 1985, who played for Bayern Munich at the time. He scored 3 goals at Euro 2012, all in the group stage (two against the Netherlands, one against Denmark). Germany lost the semi-final to Italy 2-1. He was joint top scorer but lost the tie-break.
related: Euro 2012 hosts: Poland and Ukraine.
Euro 2012 final: Spain 4-0 Italy at Kyiv.
Spain became the first team to win Euro, World Cup, Euro in a row (2008-2012).
Andres Iniesta was Player of the Tournament at Euro 2012.
Michel Platini scored 9 goals at Euro 1984, the record for a single tournament.
Euro 2016 winner: Portugal; Euro 2020 winner: Italy; Euro 2024 winner: Spain.
Euro trophy is called the Henri Delaunay Cup.
summary: The answer is (a) Fernando Torres of Spain. He won the Golden Boot at UEFA Euro 2012 with 3 goals, tied with several players on goals and assists, and won on fewest minutes played.
topic_notes: UEFA Euro 2012 was the 14th European Championship, held in Poland and Ukraine, with 16 teams. Spain won, beating Italy 4-0 in the final in Kyiv; goals came from David Silva, Jordi Alba, Fernando Torres and Juan Mata. Spain's Iker Casillas was captain. Andres Iniesta was named Player of the Tournament. The official awards: Golden Boot (top scorer) Fernando Torres, with 3 goals, based on tie-breaks of assists and minutes. Spain kept the trophy, the Henri Delaunay Cup. Tournament mascots were Slavek and Slavko. Spain's win was the first time a national team won back-to-back European titles, and with the 2010 World Cup, three straight major tournaments. The next editions: Euro 2016 in France (Portugal won, beating France 1-0 after extra time, with Eder scoring), Euro 2020 (held in 2021, Italy won against England on penalties), and Euro 2024 in Germany (Spain won, beating England 2-1). Other football awards to remember: the FIFA World Cup Golden Boot, the Ballon d'Or and the Golden Ball. At the 2010 World Cup, Thomas Muller won the Golden Boot. At the 2014 World Cup, James Rodriguez won it with 6 goals. Michel Platini holds the record for most goals at a single Euro (9 in 1984).

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q22.
ocr: . Who won the Golden Boot Award in the recently concluded UEFA Euro 2012 ? (a) Fernando Torres (Spain) (b) Mario Balotelli (Italy) (c) Cristiano Ronaldo (Portugal) (d) Mario Gomez (Germany)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The UEFA Euro 2012 was co-hosted by Poland and Ukraine from 8 June to 1 July 2012. Spain won the final 4-0 against Italy in Kyiv, becoming the first team to win three consecutive major tournaments (Euro 2008, World Cup 2010, Euro 2012). The top-scorer award (Golden Boot) is decided by goals scored, then assists, then fewest minutes played. Six players finished on three goals: Mario Gomez (Germany), Mario Mandzukic (Croatia), Fernando Torres (Spain), Alan Dzagoev (Russia), Mario Balotelli (Italy) and Cristiano Ronaldo (Portugal). Gomez, Mandzukic, Torres and Ronaldo etc. were compared on assists; Gomez and Torres: Torres had 1 assist and Gomez had 0 under the official count, so the official tiebreak needs care. UEFA's official outcome: Torres received the Golden Boot, having 3 goals, 1 assist and fewer minutes (only 189 minutes played). Gomez had 3 goals, 0 assists, 3 starts. Therefore the correct answer is (a) Fernando Torres.
explanations: Placeholder
Placeholder
Placeholder
Placeholder
summary: The correct answer is (d) Mario Gomez (Germany). Euro 2012 had a six-way tie on 3 goals each, and the Golden Boot went to Gomez, who had the fewest minutes played and no further tie-breaker advantage was needed beyond that. The tie-break order was goals, then assists, then fewest minutes played, with Gomez ranking first among the tied players on that basis.

question: Which of the following sets of countries has only federations ?
options: New Zealand, India, Zimbabwe and Argentina
India, Nepal, Sri Lanka and South Africa
France, Germany, Sweden and Switzerland (Contd.) Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner (APFC) —
subject: Computers
detail: A federation has a written constitution that divides powers between a national government and constituent units, with both levels constitutionally protected, usually with an independent judiciary arbitrating disputes. Option (b) fits: Malaysia (13 states plus federal territories, a constitutional monarchy with a rotating Yang di-Pertuan Agong), Australia (6 states, federated 1901), Nigeria (36 states plus the FCT, Abuja) and Brazil (26 states plus the Federal District, a federal republic). Elimination: New Zealand is a unitary parliamentary state with no provinces holding constitutional power, so (a) is out. Nepal adopted federalism in 2015 with 7 provinces, but Sri Lanka is unitary, though it has provincial councils created by the 13th Amendment, so (c) is out. France and Sweden are unitary, which rules out (d), even though Germany and Switzerland are federal. In (a), Zimbabwe is unitary and Argentina is federal. India is described in Article 1 as a 'Union of States', which is quasi-federal, with a strong centre.
explanations: Incorrect: New Zealand is unitary and Zimbabwe is unitary, so the set is not made up only of federations. Argentina is federal and India is a quasi-federal Union.
Correct: Malaysia, Australia, Nigeria and Brazil are all federal states with constitutional division of powers between the centre and the states.

Incorrect: Sri Lanka is a unitary state, and South Africa is a decentralised unitary state with nine provinces (it is often called quasi-federal). Nepal has been federal since 2015. India is quasi-federal.

keyfact: Malaysia, Australia, Nigeria and Brazil are all federations; New Zealand, France, Sweden, Sri Lanka and Zimbabwe are unitary.
option_notes: New Zealand is a unitary parliamentary monarchy with a single-chamber Parliament (since 1951) and local governments created by statute. India is a Union of States (Article 1) with a federal structure and unitary bias. Zimbabwe is a unitary presidential republic. Argentina is a federal republic with 23 provinces and the autonomous city of Buenos Aires. Only two of the four are federal.

Malaysia was formed in 1963 and is a federation of 13 states and 3 federal territories, with a rotating monarch elected by the Conference of Rulers. Australia is a federation under the 1901 Commonwealth Constitution with 6 states. Nigeria has 36 states plus the FCT, and Brazil has 26 states plus the Federal District. All four are federal.

India is a Union of States with a strong centre. Nepal's 2015 Constitution created a federal democratic republic with 7 provinces. Sri Lanka is unitary under the 1978 Constitution, with provincial councils introduced by the 13th Amendment in 1987. South Africa's 1996 Constitution creates 9 provinces under a largely unitary system with some federal features.

France is a unitary republic with departments and regions under the Fifth Republic (1958). Germany is a federation of 16 Länder under the 1949 Basic Law. Sweden is a unitary parliamentary monarchy with municipalities and counties. Switzerland is a confederation in name but a federation in practice, with 26 cantons under the 1848 and 1999 Constitutions.

The USA was the first modern federation (1787).
Canada has a federation with a strong centre (British North America Act, 1867).

summary: The answer is (b). Malaysia, Australia, Nigeria and Brazil are all federations. Each other set includes at least one unitary or non-federal state.
topic_notes: Federalism divides sovereignty between a national government and regional units. K.C. Wheare called the Indian system 'quasi-federal'. The classic features of a federation are a written constitution, division of powers, constitutional supremacy, a rigid amendment procedure, an independent judiciary and usually a bicameral legislature. The USA (1787) was the first modern federation. Canada (1867) is a federation with a strong centre, and the Canadian model influenced India's. Australia's federation dates from 1901, and Switzerland's from 1848. Germany's Basic Law dates from 1949. Federations can be 'coming together' (USA, Australia, Switzerland), where previously independent units join, or 'holding together' (India, Spain, Belgium), where power is devolved to keep a diverse country united. Unitary states include the UK (with devolution to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland), France, Japan, China, Sweden, Italy, New Zealand and Sri Lanka. Belgium became federal in 1993. Some countries sit in between: South Africa is often called quasi-federal, and Spain is a quasi-federal state of autonomous communities. India's federal features include the Seventh Schedule with its Union, State and Concurrent Lists, an independent judiciary, and a written constitution. Its unitary features include a single citizenship, a strong centre, the Governor, emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356 and 360), and All-India Services. The Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai (1994) held federalism to be part of the basic structure.

detail: Dalveer Bhandari was a judge of the Supreme Court of India and earlier Chief Justice of the Bombay High Court. In November 2012 he was elected to the International Court of Justice, the principal judicial organ of the United Nations. The ICJ sits at the Peace Palace in The Hague and was established under the UN Charter in 1945; it began work in 1946. It has 15 judges, each serving a nine-year term, with one-third retiring every three years. A candidate needs an absolute majority in both the UN General Assembly (97 of 193 votes) and the Security Council (8 of 15 votes), voting independently and at the same time. No two judges may be of the same nationality. He was re-elected in November 2017 after the UK withdrew its candidate, Christopher Greenwood, before a Security Council vote. Elimination: the UN Human Rights Council has 47 elected member states, not individuals. The WTO Director-General in 2012 was Pascal Lamy, followed by Roberto Azevedo in 2013. Correct: Bhandari was elected a judge of the ICJ in 2012, which is why he was in the news.

option_notes: UN Human Rights Council: a 47-member intergovernmental body of the UN, based in Geneva. It replaced the Commission on Human Rights in 2006. Members are elected by the General Assembly for three-year terms and cannot serve more than two consecutive terms. Seats are distributed by region. India has been a member several times, including 2019-21 and 2022-24. It runs the Universal Periodic Review.

International Court of Justice: the principal judicial organ of the UN, seated at The Hague. It has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms by the UNGA and UNSC together. It decides disputes between states (contentious jurisdiction) and gives advisory opinions. Its Statute is annexed to the UN Charter. Indian judges have included Nagendra Singh, R.S. Pathak and Bhandari. The Kulbhushan Jadhav case (2019) was heard here.

World Trade Organization: set up on 1 January 1995 after the Uruguay Round, replacing GATT, and headquartered in Geneva. It has 164 members. Its Director-General is appointed by consensus for a four-year term. Pascal Lamy served 2005-13 and Roberto Azevedo 2013-20. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala has been DG since March 2021, the first woman and first African in the role.

SAARC Secretary-General: SAARC was founded in 1985 at Dhaka and its secretariat is in Kathmandu. The Secretary-General is appointed by the Council of Ministers for a three-year term, rotating alphabetically among member states. Ahmed Saleem of the Maldives held the post in 2012. The organisation has eight members, including Afghanistan since 2007.

topic_notes: The International Court of Justice is one of the six principal organs of the UN, the others being the General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, Trusteeship Council and Secretariat. It is the only one not located in New York. Its predecessor was the Permanent Court of International Justice (1922) under the League of Nations. Only states may be parties in contentious cases. Its judgments are binding and final, with no appeal, but enforcement depends on the Security Council under Article 94 of the UN Charter. Judges are elected on merit, not as representatives of their countries, and an ad hoc judge may be appointed by a party that has no national on the bench. The Court is separate from the International Criminal Court (ICC), which is based in The Hague under the 2002 Rome Statute and tries individuals; India is not a party to it. Other bodies include the Permanent Court of Arbitration (The Hague) and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (Hamburg). topic_notes: International organisations and their heads are a regular source of Current Affairs questions in EPFO exams. The World Bank Group has five institutions (IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID). detail: Rain-fed (dryland) agriculture depends wholly on monsoon rainfall, so the crop must tolerate moisture stress and need little assured water. Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi, and pulses such as arhar, gram and moong, are the classic dryland crops. Jowar grows in 40-100 cm rainfall, mostly on black and red soils in Maharashtra, Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh, and is a kharif and rabi crop. Arhar is a deep-rooted kharif pulse that fixes nitrogen and is often intercropped with jowar or cotton. Potato is a cool-season rabi crop that needs frequent, assured irrigation, and cannot be grown dependably without it. Cotton is traditionally grown rain-fed on black soil in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Telangana, but its demand is high (50-100 cm rainfall, with an ideal of about 210 frost-free days). The question asks what a cultivator without irrigation facilities would like to grow. The safest and most expected choice is the hardy jowar and arhar pair. Potato is clearly wrong, which eliminates (a), (b) and (c), since each includes either potato or cotton, leaving (d).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes cotton and potatoes, which need assured water, especially potatoes.
(b) Wrong: it drops potato but still includes cotton, which is risky without irrigation and is a cash crop with high water needs.
(c) Wrong: cotton and potatoes are the two least suited crops here, so this is the opposite of the right answer.
(d) Correct: jowar and arhar are hardy, low-water crops typical of rain-fed dryland farming and are often intercropped.
keyfact: Jowar and arhar are the classic hardy rain-fed crops; potato needs irrigation and cotton is riskier without it, so the answer is (d).
option_notes: Option (a) all four crops: Jowar and arhar are dryland crops, cotton is partly rain-fed black-soil crop, potato is an irrigated rabi tuber. No crop set mixing all four fits unirrigated land. Such 'all of the above' options are common distractors, and the crops differ greatly in season and water needs.

Option (b) 1, 2 and 3: Jowar, cotton and arhar are all kharif crops commonly grown in rain-fed black-soil tracts of the Deccan, and are often intercropped. Cotton is grown rain-fed on a large area in Maharashtra and Telangana, yet it is more risk-prone and water-sensitive than millets and pulses, so the examiner excludes it.

Option (c) 2 and 4: Cotton is a kharif fibre crop needing a long warm season, while potato is a rabi tuber needing cool weather and irrigation. They differ in season and region. Neither is a typical low-input dryland crop, so this pair is a poor choice for a rain-fed farmer.

Option (d) 1 and 3: Jowar (sorghum) and arhar (pigeon pea) are classic rain-fed crops of the semi-arid tropics, used in intercropping systems such as jowar+arhar. They tolerate drought, grow on poor soils, and give food, fodder and pulses, with arhar also improving soil nitrogen. They suit a farmer with no irrigation.

statements: 1 — Correct: Jowar is a drought-hardy rain-fed millet. Sorghum is India's major coarse cereal, also called 'jawar' or 'cholam'. Maharashtra is the largest producer, followed by Karnataka, and it is grown in both kharif and rabi seasons. It grows on black, red and light soils, needs 30-100 cm rainfall, and is used for food, fodder and ethanol. It is a nutri-cereal (millet) and was prominent in the 2023 International Year of Millets.

2 — Incorrect: Cotton is a kharif cash crop that needs a long frost-free period, warm temperatures and 50-100 cm rainfall. It is usually grown on black (regur) soil in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Telangana and Rajasthan, with a large irrigated share. Although much of it is rain-fed, it is risky without irrigation and is a commercial rather than a safe dryland crop. India is a leading producer; Bt cotton was introduced in 2002. Pink bollworm is a major pest.

3 — Correct: Arhar (tur, red gram, pigeon pea) is a main kharif pulse. India is the largest producer and consumer. It is deep-rooted, drought-tolerant and fixes atmospheric nitrogen. Maharashtra, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh are leading states. It is commonly intercropped with jowar, bajra, cotton or groundnut in rain-fed areas. It is a rich protein source, used as dal, and the MSP is announced yearly by the CACP.

4 — Incorrect: Potato is a cool-season rabi tuber crop, sown in Oct-Nov in the plains and requiring frequent irrigation. Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Bihar are the leading producers. It grows best at 15-25°C on loamy soil. It originated in South America and was introduced to India by the Portuguese. The Central Potato Research Institute is at Shimla. It is unsuitable for unirrigated land.

The answer is (d) 1 and 3 only: Jowar (sorghum) and Arhar (pigeon pea/tur) are hardy, drought-tolerant dryland crops suited to rain-fed conditions. Cotton and potatoes need more water or irrigation.
topic_notes: Rain-fed (dryland) agriculture covers about 51-55% of India's net sown area and produces roughly 40% of food grains. It depends on monsoon rainfall, so soil moisture conservation is key. Areas getting under 75 cm are dryland; 75-115 cm are rain-fed. Typical dryland crops are the coarse cereals/millets (jowar, bajra, ragi), pulses (arhar, gram, moong, urad), oilseeds (groundnut, castor, sunflower) and cotton. Techniques include contour bunding, mulching, farm ponds, watershed management, crop rotation and intercropping (e.g. jowar+arhar, bajra+moong), plus drought-resistant varieties. Institutions: CRIDA (Central Research Institute for Dryland Agriculture), Hyderabad; ICRISAT, Patancheru, Hyderabad; and the National Rainfed Area Authority (NRAA, set up 2006). Schemes: Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY, 2015) with the slogan 'Per drop more crop', and the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture, which has a Rainfed Area Development component. Kharif crops are sown with the onset of monsoon in June-July and harvested in Sept-Oct (rice, jowar, bajra, maize, cotton, arhar, groundnut, soybean). Rabi crops are sown in Oct-Dec and harvested in Mar-Apr (wheat, barley, gram, mustard, potato, peas). Zaid crops come in between (watermelon, cucumber, fodder). Black soil suits cotton, jowar and pulses because it retains moisture. India is the largest producer of pulses, and the 2023 International Year of Millets was proposed by India. Millets are called Shree Anna.

statements: 1 — Correct: Jowar is a classic rain-fed millet. Jowar (Sorghum bicolor) is the third most important food grain after rice and wheat in many dry regions, and India is among the top producers. Maharashtra is the leading state. It is grown as kharif (monsoon) and rabi crops, tolerates drought and waterlogging better than maize, and needs about 25-35 degrees C. It is used for food (roti), fodder and ethanol. Bt cotton was approved in 2002. The Cotton Corporation of India handles MSP operations.

3 — Correct: Arhar (tur, red gram) is a drought-hardy pulse. Arhar, Cajanus cajan, is the second most important pulse in India after gram. It is a deep-rooted legume that fixes nitrogen and survives dry spells, so it is usually intercropped with jowar, bajra or cotton in rain-fed areas. Maharashtra, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh are the main producers. It is a kharif crop sown in June-July and harvested in December-January, and it needs 60-65 cm rainfall.

4 — Incorrect: Potato needs assured irrigation. Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is a rabi crop in the plains, planted in October-November. It is shallow-rooted, so it needs frequent light irrigation, cool nights and well-drained loam. It was introduced to India by the Portuguese. Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Bihar produce the most, and India is the second-largest producer after China. The Central Potato Research Institute is at Shimla. Rain-fed cultivation would give poor yields.
summary: The answer is (b), 1, 2 and 3 only. Jowar, cotton and arhar (pigeon pea) are hardy crops suited to rain-fed, unirrigated land. Potato needs a cool climate and assured, repeated irrigation, so it is unsuitable. (The image shows two questions, and I have taken the cultivator question as Q27.)
topic_notes: Rain-fed (dryland) agriculture covers about 51-55 percent of India's net sown area and produces roughly 40 percent of food grain output. It is practised in regions with less than about 75-100 cm annual rainfall or erratic monsoons: the Deccan plateau, parts of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and the semi-arid peninsula. Typical dryland crops are the coarse cereals or millets (jowar, bajra, ragi), pulses (arhar, gram, moong, urad), oilseeds (groundnut, castor, sesame) and cotton. The main practices are mixed and inter-cropping (for example jowar + arhar), contour bunding, watershed management, farm ponds, mulching, and the use of short-duration, drought-resistant varieties. The Central Research Institute for Dryland Agriculture (CRIDA) is at Hyderabad, and ICRISAT, also near Hyderabad, works on semi-arid tropics crops. The National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture and the Rainfed Area Development programme promote dryland farming, and the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana and the watershed programmes aim at 'more crop per drop'. Irrigation-intensive crops include rice, wheat, sugarcane, potato, jute and vegetables. Black (regur) soil is ideal for cotton, with high moisture retention, while red and laterite soils suit millets and groundnut. Crop seasons: kharif is sown June-July and harvested September-October. Rabi is sown October-November and harvested March-April. Zaid is the summer crop season between rabi and kharif.
