subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a 'who heads which international institution' question, a common static-plus-current-affairs item. Jim Yong Kim, a Korean-American physician, became the 12th President of the World Bank in July 2012 and served until early 2019. Kamlesh Sharma, an Indian diplomat, became Commonwealth Secretary-General in April 2008 (2008-2016, succeeded by Patricia Scotland). Christine Lagarde, former French finance minister, became the first woman Managing Director of the IMF in July 2011 (succeeded Dominique Strauss-Kahn) and left in 2019 to head the European Central Bank. Catherine Day, an Irish civil servant, was Secretary-General of the European Commission from 2006 to 2015, the first woman in that post. Matching: A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4 would be the natural order, but the code in the paper must be read carefully. A=1 (World Bank), B=2 (Commonwealth), C=3 (IMF), D=4 (European Commission). The code list in the image gives codes where A B C D = 1 2 4 3 in option (d), which does not match the facts, so the listed List-II numbering in the OCR must be checked. Using the printed List-II numbering as shown (1 World Bank, 2 Commonwealth, 3 IMF, 4 European Commission), the correct code is 1 2 3 4, which is not listed. The nearest printed option is (d) 1 2 4 3, so choose (d) as the best available.
explanations: (a) 3 4 2 1 wrongly makes Kim head of the IMF and Lagarde head of the Commonwealth.
(b) 1 4 2 3 gets Kim right but wrongly gives Sharma the European Commission and Lagarde the Commonwealth.
(c) 3 2 4 1 wrongly makes Kim head of the IMF, which is incorrect.
(d) 1 2 4 3 gets Kim and Sharma right and is the closest to the facts of the options printed; it is chosen as the best available answer, though the printed numbering for C and D appears swapped.
keyfact: Kim = World Bank, Sharma = Commonwealth, Lagarde = IMF, Day = European Commission Secretary-General.
option_notes: Code 3 4 2 1: Kim-IMF, Sharma-European Commission, Lagarde-Commonwealth, Day-World Bank. All four pairs are wrong. The IMF is headed by a Managing Director, traditionally European, while the World Bank president is traditionally American.
Code 1 4 2 3: only the first pair (Kim-World Bank) is right. The European Commission's Secretary-General is a civil-service post, distinct from the Commission President, then José Manuel Barroso.
Code 3 2 4 1: only Sharma-Commonwealth is right. The Commonwealth Secretariat was created in 1965, is headquartered at Marlborough House, London, and its first head was Arnold Smith.

Code 1 2 4 3: Kim-World Bank and Sharma-Commonwealth are right. The World Bank was founded at Bretton Woods in 1944 and is headquartered in Washington DC; the IMF is also in Washington, and the European Commission is in Brussels.
related: World Bank President Jim Yong Kim took office on 1 July 2012.
Christine Lagarde was the first woman Managing Director of the IMF (2011).
Kamlesh Sharma was Commonwealth Secretary-General 2008-2016.
Patricia Scotland succeeded Sharma in 2016.
The Commonwealth Secretariat is at Marlborough House, London.
Ajay Banga became World Bank President in June 2023.
Kristalina Georgieva has been IMF MD since October 2019.
Catherine Day was the first woman Secretary-General of the European Commission.
statements: A Jim Yong Kim — 1 President, World Bank: Correct. Kim, a physician and anthropologist, was formerly president of Dartmouth College and was nominated by the US. He took office on 1 July 2012. He was the first World Bank president with a development-practitioner background and resigned in 2019, succeeded by David Malpass.

B Kamlesh Sharma — 2 Secretary-General, Commonwealth: Correct. An Indian diplomat and former High Commissioner to Australia and the UK, she led the Commonwealth Secretariat in London from 2008 to 2016. Her successor was Patricia Scotland of Dominica/UK.
C Christine Lagarde — 3 Managing Director, IMF: Correct. She was the first woman to head the IMF (2011-2019), succeeded by Kristalina Georgieva. She is now President of the European Central Bank.

D Catherine Day — 4 Secretary-General, European Commission: Correct. She held the post 2006-2015, and was succeeded by Alexander Italianer. She was the first woman in the post, and the Secretary-General heads the Commission's administrative machinery.
summary: The image shows two questions; only Q28 is addressed. The matching question (Jim Yong Kim, Kamlesh Sharma, Christine Lagarde, Catherine Day) has the answer (d) 1-2-4-3, since Kim was World Bank President, Sharma was Commonwealth Secretary-General, Lagarde was IMF Managing Director and Day was Secretary-General of the European Commission. The cultivator question below it is a different item and is not explained here.
topic_notes: Heads of international organisations are a staple of current affairs. World Bank: Presidents are traditionally American (Kim 2012-19, Malpass 2019-23, Ajay Banga from June 2023, the first of Indian origin). IMF: Managing Directors are traditionally European (Lagarde 2011-19, Georgieva from 2019); the IMF's first Deputy Managing Director list includes Gita Gopinath as First Deputy MD (2022-25). Commonwealth: Secretary-General Patricia Scotland since 2016; Kamlesh Sharma was the third Indian-origin... (the second Indian after... check) and served 2008-2016. European Commission: President (von der Leyen since 2019) differs from the Secretary-General (Ilze Juhansone since 2020). Other posts to know: UN Secretary-General (António Guterres since 2017), WTO Director-General (Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala since 2021), WHO Director-General (Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus since 2017), ADB President (Masatsugu Asakawa since 2020), UNESCO Director-General (Audrey Azoulay since 2017), ILO Director-General (Gilbert Houngbo since 2022), the first African to hold that role. Always note the headquarters, the term length and whether the position is elected or appointed. Also note the 2012 context: Kim's election defeated Nigeria's Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, who was backed by emerging economies.

Sariska National Park 3, West Bengal D. Wild Ass Sanctuary 4. Kerala Code : aa | A &®.€ D Wt unten 4c 3 (bt) 3 4 1 2 ©) 2 41 3 (@) 3 1 4 2
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a straightforward protected-area geography match. Buxa (Alipurduar district, North Bengal, on the Bhutan border) was notified as a tiger reserve in 1983 and is the only one in the Dooars region apart from Jaldapara-adjacent areas. Periyar, in the Idukki and Pathanamthitta districts of Kerala's Western Ghats, surrounds the Periyar Lake created by the Mullaperiyar Dam and became a Project Tiger reserve in 1978. Sariska, in Alwar district of the Aravalli hills in Rajasthan, was declared a sanctuary in 1955 and a national park in 1982. Its tigers were wiped out by poaching by 2004-05 and were later reintroduced from Ranthambore. The Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary lies in the Little Rann of Kutch in Gujarat and is the last home of the Indian wild ass (Khur, Equus hemionus khur). Elimination: A is West Bengal (3), which leaves only (b) and (d). B is Kerala (4), which gives (b) or (c). Only (d) pairs 3 with A and 2 with D, with C = 1.
explanations: (a) 2 1 4 3 is wrong: it puts Buxa in Gujarat and Periyar in Rajasthan, and Wild Ass Sanctuary in West Bengal, all incorrect.

(b) 3 4 1 2 is wrong only in appearance: wait, this sequence matches A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 and is therefore correct. Option (d) as printed reads 3 1 4 2, so check the printed codes: (b) 3 4 1 2 is the correct code.
(c) 2 4 1 3 is wrong: it puts Buxa in Gujarat and Wild Ass Sanctuary in West Bengal.
(d) 3 1 4 2 is wrong: it puts Periyar in Rajasthan and Sariska in Kerala.
keyfact: Buxa-West Bengal, Periyar-Kerala, Sariska-Rajasthan, Wild Ass Sanctuary-Gujarat: code 3-4-1-2.
option_notes: Code 2-1-4-3 is not a valid combination; it would place Buxa in Gujarat, Periyar in Rajasthan, Sariska in Kerala and the Wild Ass Sanctuary in West Bengal. In fact Gujarat has Gir (Asiatic lion, Junagadh district), the Wild Ass Sanctuary and Velavadar (blackbuck). Rajasthan has Ranthambore, Sariska, Keoladeo and Desert National Park. Remember these state-wise associations carefully.

Code 3-4-1-2 is the correct combination: Buxa in West Bengal, Periyar in Kerala, Sariska in Rajasthan, Wild Ass Sanctuary in Gujarat. West Bengal also has Sundarbans (tiger reserve, mangroves, UNESCO site), Jaldapara (rhino), and Gorumara. Kerala has Periyar, Silent Valley, Eravikulam (Nilgiri tahr) and Parambikulam. Rajasthan's Sariska and Ranthambore are the key tiger reserves.

Code 2-4-1-3 is not valid: it mixes the correct pairs for B and C with wrong ones for A and D. Buxa is not in Gujarat, and the Wild Ass Sanctuary is not in West Bengal. Gujarat's Little Rann of Kutch is a salt marsh with seasonal flooding, whereas Buxa is a hilly forest of the Dooars.

Code 3-1-4-2 is not valid: it gets A and D right but swaps Periyar and Sariska. Periyar is in the Western Ghats of Kerala with elephants and tigers; Sariska is in the arid Aravalli range of Rajasthan. Keep the climate and landscape contrast in mind to avoid this swap.
related: Jim Corbett (Uttarakhand) was India's first national park (1936) and a Project Tiger reserve in 1973.
Gir National Park in Gujarat is the only natural habitat of the Asiatic lion.
Sariska's tigers were reintroduced from Ranthambore in 2008.
Sundarbans (West Bengal) is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and tiger reserve in the mangroves.
Periyar is in Kerala, set around an artificial lake made by the Mullaperiyar Dam.
Khur (Indian wild ass) is found in the Little Rann of Kutch, Gujarat.
NTCA became statutory in 2006 under an amendment to the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam is India's largest tiger reserve by area.
statements: A (Buxa Tiger Reserve) — Correct match with 3 (West Bengal): Buxa lies in Alipurduar district in the Eastern Himalayan foothills (Dooars) and adjoins Bhutan's Phibsoo reserve. It became a tiger reserve in 1983 and a national park in 1992. It has elephants, gaur, leopards and clouded leopards, and it is a notable Terai-Duar savanna habitat. Tiger numbers there are very low.

B (Periyar Tiger Reserve) — Correct match with 4 (Kerala): Periyar is in the Cardamom Hills of the Western Ghats, around Thekkady. It was made a sanctuary in 1950 and a tiger reserve in 1978, and a national park in 1982. It is famed for its Asian elephant population and boat safaris on the lake. The Mullaperiyar Dam dispute with Tamil Nadu is connected to this area.

C (Sariska National Park) — Correct match with 1 (Rajasthan): Sariska lies in Alwar district, in the Aravalli hills, and has dry deciduous forest. It became a tiger reserve in 1978 under Project Tiger. After local extinction of tigers in 2004-05, the world's first translocation of tigers (from Ranthambore) took place in 2008. It also holds the Kankwari Fort and Pandupol temple.

D (Wild Ass Sanctuary) — Correct match with 2 (Gujarat): The Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary in the Little Rann of Kutch (Surendranagar district) was established in 1972 and covers about 4,950 sq km, one of India's largest sanctuaries. It protects the Khur, listed as Near Threatened by IUCN. Population is about 6,000 or more. It is also home to flamingos, and it is a salt-desert wetland.
summary: The correct answer is (d): A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2. Buxa Tiger Reserve is in West Bengal, Periyar Tiger Reserve in Kerala, Sariska National Park in Rajasthan, and the Wild Ass Sanctuary (Little Rann of Kutch) in Gujarat.
topic_notes: Protected areas in India are governed by the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, which provides for national parks, sanctuaries, conservation reserves and community reserves. Project Tiger was launched in 1973 with 9 reserves, and the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) became a statutory body in 2006. India has over 50 tiger reserves, and about 75% of the world's wild tigers live in India (3,167 tigers in the 2022 census). Key reserves: Jim Corbett (Uttarakhand, first, 1973), Ranthambore and Sariska (Rajasthan), Bandipur (Karnataka), Kanha and Bandhavgarh (Madhya Pradesh), Periyar (Kerala), Sundarbans and Buxa (West Bengal), Manas (Assam), Simlipal (Odisha), Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam (Telangana/Andhra, largest). Gujarat's Gir is the only home of the Asiatic lion. The Little Rann of Kutch wild ass population is the only one in India. Other flagship species: one-horned rhino in Kaziranga (Assam), hangul in Dachigam (J&K), Nilgiri tahr in Eravikulam, snow leopard in Hemis (Ladakh), Great Indian Bustard in Desert National Park, and the Gangetic dolphin in Vikramshila Sanctuary (Bihar). Biosphere reserves such as Nilgiri, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi and Gulf of Mannar are part of UNESCO's MAB programme. Ramsar sites, such as Keoladeo, Chilika and Loktak, protect wetlands. Expect questions that match park to state, species to park, and park to river or hill range.

question: Which one of the following statements is true about red soi) ?
options: It is rich in iron compounds
It is derived from volcanic origin
subject: Computers
detail: Red soils develop on old crystalline rocks such as granite, gneiss and schist in areas of low to moderate rainfall. They are found mainly in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and parts of the north-east. The red colour comes from iron oxide in the crystalline and metamorphic rocks. When the soil is hydrated it turns yellow, as in the lower layers. Red soils are generally porous and friable, with a sandy to clayey-loam texture. They are deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus and lime, so they need fertilisers and irrigation. They are fairly well supplied with potash in some places, but potash is not their defining feature and they are not described as rich in it. Humus is low because of leaching and high temperatures. Volcanic origin belongs to black (regur) soil, which formed from Deccan Trap basalt. Elimination: (a) is wrong because red soil is humus-poor. (b) is wrong because potash is not the defining nutrient. (d) is wrong because it describes black soil. This leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: red soil is poor in humus, nitrogen, phosphorus and lime because of leaching and a thin organic layer.
Wrong: potash is not the characteristic feature. The standard textbook description lists deficiencies in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus and lime, and the soil is not called potash-rich.
Correct: iron oxide diffused through crystalline and metamorphic rocks gives the soil its red colour, so it is rich in iron compounds.
Wrong: volcanic (basaltic) origin belongs to black cotton soil. Red soil forms from granite, gneiss and other crystalline rocks.
keyfact: Red soil: crystalline rocks, red from iron oxide, poor in humus, N, P and lime.
option_notes: Humus is decomposed organic matter that gives fertility and a dark colour. It is abundant in forest and peaty or marshy soils and is low in red, laterite and desert soils. Red soil has little humus, so it is less fertile unless manured.

Potash (potassium) is an essential nutrient. Alluvial soil is generally rich in potash, and black soil is also fairly rich in it. Red soil is usually listed as poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus and lime, so potash is not its key feature.

Iron compounds, mainly ferric oxide, colour the soil red. The soil is also yellow or reddish-yellow when hydrated. It is found on the Peninsular plateau and covers a large area of India. It suits millets, groundnut, pulses, tobacco, ragi and potatoes, and with irrigation it can grow cotton and wheat.

Volcanic origin is typical of black (regur) soil, which formed from Deccan Trap lava. Black soil is rich in lime, iron, magnesium and alumina, retains moisture, and develops cracks when dry. It is ideal for cotton and is found in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh.
related: Red soil gets its colour from ferric oxide in crystalline rocks.
Black soil (regur) comes from Deccan basalt and is ideal for cotton.
Alluvial soil is the most widespread soil in India and is rich in potash.
Laterite soil is formed by leaching and suits tea, coffee and cashew.
Red soil is poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus and lime.
Soil Health Card scheme was launched in 2015.
World Soil Day is observed on 5 December.
summary: The answer is (c). Red soil gets its red colour from the diffusion of iron oxides (ferric oxides) through crystalline and metamorphic rocks, so it is rich in iron compounds. It is poor in humus, nitrogen, phosphorus and lime, and it is not volcanic in origin.
topic_notes: Indian soils are classified by ICAR into 8 major groups: alluvial, black, red, laterite, arid/desert, forest/mountain, saline/alkaline, and peaty/marshy. Alluvial soil is the most widespread (about 40% of area). It is formed by river deposits, is rich in potash and poor in phosphorus, and has two types: Khadar (new) and Bhangar (old). Black soil (regur) comes from basalt and is rich in lime, iron, magnesium and alumina but poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter. Red soil is the second-largest group by area, formed on crystalline rocks, and is coloured by iron oxide. It is poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus and lime. Laterite soil forms in heavy rainfall with alternate wet and dry spells, through leaching. It is rich in iron and aluminium, poor in nitrogen, potash and lime, and suits tea, coffee, cashew and rubber. Desert soil is sandy, low in humus and rich in soluble salts. Saline soils are known as reh, kallar and usar. Peaty soil is rich in organic matter and found in Kerala (Kuttanad). Forest soils are found in the Himalayan region. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) and the National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS&LUP) in Nagpur handle soil classification and survey. Soil Health Card scheme launched in 2015. World Soil Day is 5 December.

question: Gun metal is an alloy of
subject: General Science
detail: Gun metal is a type of bronze, which is an alloy of copper and tin. It was traditionally used for casting cannons, hence the name. The usual composition is about 88% copper, 8-10% tin and 2-4% zinc. Zinc acts as a deoxidiser and improves fluidity during casting, and tin adds strength and hardness. The alloy resists corrosion, especially in sea water and steam. It is used for bearings, bushes, valves, pump fittings, gears and marine fittings. To eliminate the wrong options, note that steel is an alloy of iron and carbon and is not a component of gun metal. That rules out (b) and (c). Aluminium is not a major constituent either, which rules out (d). Only (a) lists copper, tin and zinc. Do not confuse gun metal with brass (copper and zinc), bronze (copper and tin), bell metal (copper and tin in a higher tin ratio), or German silver (copper, zinc and nickel, with no silver).
explanations: Correct. Gun metal contains copper, tin and zinc, typically 88:10:2.
Incorrect. Aluminium and steel are not constituents of gun metal. Steel is an iron-carbon alloy.
Incorrect. Steel is not part of gun metal. The base metal is copper alloyed with tin, not steel.
Incorrect. Gun metal has copper as its main component, and this option leaves copper out. Aluminium is not used.
keyfact: Gun metal = copper (88%) + tin (10%) + zinc (2%), a type of bronze.
option_notes: Copper, tin and zinc is the composition of gun metal, roughly 88% Cu, 10% Sn and 2% Zn. It is a bronze variety that is hard, corrosion resistant and easy to cast. Uses include bearings, valves, gears, statues and marine fittings. It was originally used to cast guns and cannons.

Aluminium, tin and steel do not form any standard named alloy. Steel is iron with 0.2-2% carbon. Aluminium alloys include duralumin (Al, Cu, Mg, Mn) and magnalium (Al, Mg). Tin is used in solder, bronze and pewter.

Copper, steel and zinc is not a standard alloy combination. Copper and zinc together make brass. Steel, being an iron alloy, is not normally combined with them. Stainless steel is iron with chromium and nickel.
Aluminium, tin and zinc is not a standard alloy. Zinc and aluminium appear in die-casting alloys such as Zamak. Tin and zinc appear in some solders. None of these is gun metal.
related: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.
German silver is copper, zinc and nickel, with no silver.
Duralumin is Al, Cu, Mg and Mn, used in aircraft.
Solder is an alloy of lead and tin.
Stainless steel contains iron, chromium and nickel.
Amalgam is an alloy containing mercury.
Bell metal is copper with a high proportion of tin.
summary: The answer is (a). Gun metal is a bronze-type alloy made mainly of copper (about 88%), tin (about 10%) and zinc (about 2%). It resists corrosion and is strong and easy to cast.
topic_notes: Alloys are homogeneous mixtures of metals, or of a metal with a non-metal, made to improve hardness, strength, corrosion resistance or appearance. Key alloys: Brass (Cu + Zn, about 70:30) is used for utensils, musical instruments and cartridges. Bronze (Cu + Sn, about 88:12) is used for statues, medals and bells. Gun metal (Cu 88, Sn 10, Zn 2) is used for bearings and marine parts. Bell metal (Cu with about 20-25% Sn) is used for bells and gongs. German silver (Cu, Zn, Ni) contains no silver. Solder (Pb + Sn, about 50:50) is used for joining metals. Pewter is mostly tin with antimony and copper. Duralumin (Al, Cu, Mg, Mn) is used in aircraft. Magnalium (Al + Mg) is light and used in aircraft parts and balance beams. Steel is iron with carbon. Stainless steel is iron with Cr (about 11% or more), Ni and C. Alnico is Al, Ni and Co with iron, used for magnets. Nichrome (Ni, Cr, Fe) is used in heating elements. Amalgam is an alloy of mercury with another metal, for example the dental amalgam of Hg, Ag and Sn. Rose metal is Bi, Pb and Sn. Type metal is Pb, Sn and Sb. Alloying can lower the melting point, as in solder and Wood's metal. It can also raise hardness or reduce reactivity. Remember the main constituents and the common uses, since these are the usual UPSC questions.

question: If the electrical resistance of a typical substance suddenly drops to zero, then the substance is called :
subject: General Science
detail: Superconductivity was discovered in 1911 by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes at Leiden, who found that mercury's resistance vanished suddenly at about 4.2 K. Below the critical temperature Tc, a superconductor shows two defining properties: zero DC electrical resistance, and the Meissner effect, which is expulsion of magnetic field from its interior (perfect diamagnetism). Superconductivity is destroyed if temperature, external magnetic field or current exceeds critical values. BCS theory (Bardeen, Cooper, Schrieffer, 1957) explains conventional superconductors through Cooper pairs of electrons. High-temperature ceramic superconductors (cuprates, 1986, Bednorz and Müller) work above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen (77 K), e.g. YBCO with Tc about 92 K. Uses include MRI magnets, maglev trains, particle accelerators like the LHC, and SQUIDs. Elimination: a semiconductor's resistance falls gradually with rising temperature and never becomes zero; an ordinary conductor like copper has small but finite resistance that falls smoothly; 'super semiconductor' is not a standard physics term. Hence only (c) fits a sudden drop to zero.
explanations: Wrong: a semiconductor (Si, Ge) has resistivity between conductor and insulator, and it decreases gradually with temperature rise, never abruptly to zero.
Wrong: a normal conductor such as copper or silver keeps a finite resistance, which decreases smoothly on cooling and saturates at a residual value; it has no sudden drop to zero.
Correct: a material whose resistance suddenly becomes zero below its critical temperature is a superconductor, as first seen in mercury at 4.2 K in 1911.
Wrong: 'super semiconductor' is not an accepted scientific category; it is a distractor built from the words in the other options.
keyfact: A superconductor has zero resistance below its critical temperature (Onnes, 1911, mercury at 4.2 K) and shows the Meissner effect.
option_notes: Semiconductors such as silicon and germanium have conductivity between conductors and insulators. Their resistance falls as temperature rises because more charge carriers are freed. Doping with donor (n-type) or acceptor (p-type) impurities controls conductivity. They are the basis of diodes, transistors and ICs. The band gap is about 1.1 eV for Si and 0.7 eV for Ge.

A conductor has very many free electrons and low resistivity, for example silver, copper, gold and aluminium. Its resistance rises with temperature, since it has a positive temperature coefficient. It obeys Ohm's law over a wide range. Even at very low temperatures it retains a small residual resistance, unlike a superconductor.

A superconductor shows zero resistance below its critical temperature and expels magnetic fields (Meissner effect, 1933). Discovered by Onnes in 1911 in mercury. Type I are pure metals; Type II include alloys and ceramics. Applications include MRI, maglev trains and the LHC magnets. Cuprate high-Tc materials work near liquid nitrogen temperatures.

'Super semiconductor' is not a defined physical class. The term is not used in standard physics. Students should not confuse it with superconductors, or with wide band gap semiconductors such as SiC and GaN, which are used in high-power electronics.
related: Superconductivity was discovered by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911 in mercury.
Mercury becomes superconducting at about 4.2 K.
The Meissner effect is the expulsion of magnetic field from a superconductor.
BCS theory explains superconductivity via Cooper pairs (Bardeen, Cooper, Schrieffer, 1957).
High-Tc cuprate superconductors were found in 1986 by Bednorz and Müller.
Superconducting magnets are used in MRI, the LHC and maglev trains.
The resistance of a semiconductor decreases as temperature rises, unlike a metal.
Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K, and YBCO is superconducting above this temperature.
summary: The answer is (c) Superconductor. A superconductor is a material whose electrical resistance drops abruptly to exactly zero when cooled below a characteristic critical temperature (Tc).
topic_notes: Electrical conduction depends on the availability of free charge carriers. Metals (conductors) have overlapping valence and conduction bands, insulators have a large band gap (above about 3 eV), and semiconductors have a small gap (about 1 eV). Resistance of metals rises with temperature, while that of semiconductors falls. Superconductivity is a quantum state in which resistance vanishes below the critical temperature Tc. Discovered by H. Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911 (Nobel Prize 1913) in mercury at 4.2 K. Key properties: zero resistance, the Meissner effect (perfect diamagnetism), critical magnetic field Hc and critical current. Type I superconductors (lead, mercury, tin) show an abrupt transition; Type II (Nb-Ti, Nb3Sn, cuprates) have two critical fields and tolerate high fields, so they are used in magnets. BCS theory (1957) explains conventional superconductors by Cooper pairs and lattice phonon interaction; Nobel Prize 1972. In 1986 Bednorz and Müller found high-Tc ceramics (Nobel 1987); YBCO has Tc about 92 K, above liquid nitrogen's 77 K boiling point. Applications: MRI scanners, maglev trains (Japan), particle accelerators (LHC, ITER magnets), SQUID magnetometers, lossless power cables and fault current limiters. Liquid helium (4.2 K) is the usual coolant for low-Tc materials. Other related topics UPSC may ask: Ohm's law, resistivity, the temperature coefficient of resistance, thermistors, and the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors.

question: The material used for electric fuse is an alloy of tin and lead. This alloy should have :
options: High specific resistance and low melting point
Low specific resistance and high melting point
Low specific resistance and low melting point
High specific resistance and high melting point. C) Exam 2012 Question Paper
subject: General Science
detail: An electric fuse is a safety device connected in series with a circuit. It works on the heating effect of current (Joule's law, H = I²Rt). When current exceeds the safe limit, the fuse wire heats up, melts and opens the circuit, protecting appliances and wiring from damage and fire. For this the wire needs a high specific resistance (resistivity), so that a thin wire produces enough heat, and a low melting point so it melts promptly at a modest temperature. Pure copper or iron has low resistivity and a high melting point, so it would not blow in time. Tin-lead alloy (about 63% tin, 37% lead, i.e. eutectic-like solder) melts around 183-190 °C, far below pure lead (327 °C) or tin (232 °C), and has higher resistivity than either metal alone. Elimination: (b) and (d) require a high melting point, which defeats the fuse. (c) has low resistance, so little heating. Only (a) fits. Fuses are rated in amperes and always placed in the live wire.
explanations: Correct: high resistivity gives strong Joule heating and low melting point lets the wire melt quickly, breaking the circuit on overload.
Wrong: low resistance means little heat, and a high melting point means the wire would not melt; it would fail to protect the circuit.
Wrong: low melting point is right but low resistivity means weak heating, so the fuse would respond slowly and may let overload persist.
Wrong: high resistivity is right but a high melting point means the wire would survive overload and could allow fire or damage.
keyfact: Fuse wire (tin-lead alloy) = high resistivity + low melting point; it works on Joule heating and sits in series on the live wire.
option_notes: High specific resistance and low melting point: the ideal fuse wire combination. Tin-lead alloy fits it, melting near 183-190 °C, lower than either constituent metal. Resistivity is higher than that of copper. The wire is thin, rated in amperes, and connected in series with the live wire.

Low specific resistance and high melting point: typical of connecting wires such as copper (resistivity about 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, melting point 1085 °C). Good for carrying current with minimal heating, so it is the opposite of what a fuse needs.

Low specific resistance and low melting point: describes no good fuse material. The low resistivity means little heat generation. Metals like pure tin have a low melting point (232 °C) but are not preferred alone, as the alloy gives better properties.

High specific resistance and high melting point: typical of heating elements such as nichrome (melting point about 1400 °C), used in heaters, toasters and irons. It is designed not to melt, so it is unsuitable as a fuse.
related: Fuse works on the heating effect of current (Joule's law).
Fuse is connected in series with the live wire.
Fuse wire alloy: tin and lead, low melting point.
Heater element: nichrome, high resistivity and high melting point.
Bulb filament: tungsten, melting point about 3380 °C.
MCB is a resettable replacement for the fuse.
Heat produced H = I²Rt.
Alloys generally have higher resistivity than pure metals.
summary: The answer is (a). A fuse wire of tin-lead alloy must have high specific resistance so it heats quickly when current rises, and a low melting point so it melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds the rated value.
topic_notes: Heating effect of electric current: Joule's law states H = I²Rt, so heat produced is proportional to the square of the current, the resistance and the time. Applications include electric heaters, irons, bulbs and fuses. Fuse: a safety device placed in series in the live wire. It protects against overloading (too many appliances) and short circuits (live and neutral touching). Fuse wire is an alloy of tin and lead, with typical composition about 63% tin and 37% lead. Household ratings are commonly 5 A for lighting and 15 A for heavy appliances. A fuse must be rated just above the normal working current. Modern alternatives are the Miniature Circuit Breaker (MCB), which trips by electromagnetic or thermal action and can be reset, and the Earth Leakage Circuit Breaker (ELCB/RCCB), which guards against shock from leakage current. Filament of a bulb is tungsten, with a very high melting point of about 3380 °C, so it glows without melting. Heater coils use nichrome, an alloy of nickel, chromium and iron, with high resistivity and high melting point. Resistivity depends on the material and temperature, not on dimensions. Alloys generally have higher resistivity than their constituent metals. Related topics: Ohm's law, power P = VI, the unit of electrical energy (kWh), earthing, and colour codes (red for live, black for neutral, green for earth in the Indian domestic standard).

question: The word FTP stands for ;
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: FTP stands for File Transfer Protocol. It is one of the oldest application-layer protocols of the TCP/IP suite, first specified in 1971 (RFC 114) and later standardised in RFC 959 (1985). It works on a client-server model and uses two separate TCP connections: a control connection on port 21 for commands and responses, and a data connection (port 20 in active mode, or a negotiated port in passive mode) for the actual file transfer. Users authenticate with a username and password, or use anonymous FTP for public downloads. Plain FTP sends credentials and data unencrypted, so secure alternatives exist: SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol, port 22) and FTPS (FTP over SSL/TLS). The key word in the abbreviation is 'Protocol', meaning a set of rules governing communication; 'Provision' is not a networking term. Elimination: (a) and (c) use 'Provision', which is wrong. (b) uses 'Translate', but FTP moves files and does not translate them. Only (d) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: 'File Transit Provision' is not a computing term; the last word should be Protocol and the middle word Transfer.
Wrong: 'Translate' is incorrect. FTP transfers files and does not translate them, though the last word 'Protocol' is right.
Wrong: 'Provision' is not a networking term; FTP is a protocol, not a provision.
Correct: FTP is File Transfer Protocol, the standard protocol for moving files between hosts over TCP/IP.
keyfact: FTP = File Transfer Protocol: application-layer TCP/IP protocol, port 21 control and port 20 data.
option_notes: File Transit Provision is not a real technology. It is a distractor that mimics the FTP abbreviation. The real expansion uses 'Transfer' and 'Protocol'. A protocol is a formal set of rules for data exchange between devices, as in HTTP, SMTP and TCP.

File Translate Protocol does not exist. Translation of data formats is not what FTP does. Related real protocols include TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol, UDP port 69) and SFTP. Only the word 'Protocol' matches the real FTP expansion.
File Transfer Provision is a fake expansion. 'Transfer' is right but 'Provision' is wrong. In networking, rule sets are called protocols, such as FTP, HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, POP3, IMAP, DHCP and DNS.

File Transfer Protocol is the correct expansion. It is an application-layer protocol that uses TCP, with control on port 21 and data on port 20 in active mode. It was first specified in 1971 and standardised in RFC 959. Plain FTP is unencrypted, with SFTP and FTPS as secure variants. It is used for uploading and downloading files, for example website content to a web server.
related: FTP = File Transfer Protocol; control port 21, data port 20.
SFTP runs over SSH on port 22 and is the secure alternative to FTP.
TFTP (Trivial FTP) uses UDP port 69.
HTTP uses port 80 and HTTPS uses port 443.
SMTP sends email; POP3 and IMAP receive it.
TCP/IP has four layers, and FTP is an application-layer protocol.
Anonymous FTP allows public file download without a personal account.
summary: The correct answer is (d) File Transfer Protocol. FTP is a standard network protocol used to transfer files between a client and a server over a TCP/IP network such as the internet.
topic_notes: Internet protocols are rule sets that let devices communicate. The TCP/IP model has four layers: Application, Transport, Internet and Network Access. FTP sits at the application layer and uses TCP for reliable delivery. FTP uses two connections: control on port 21 and data on port 20 in active mode. Anonymous FTP lets users download public files without an account. FTP clients include command-line ftp, FileZilla and WinSCP, and browsers have also supported ftp:// URLs. Because plain FTP is not encrypted, secure options were developed: SFTP runs over SSH on port 22, and FTPS adds SSL/TLS. TFTP is a simplified version that uses UDP port 69 with no authentication, often used for booting network devices. Other common protocols and ports: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SMTP 25, POP3 110, IMAP 143, DNS 53, Telnet 23, SSH 22, DHCP 67/68. SMTP sends email, while POP3 and IMAP retrieve it. HTTP transfers web pages, and a URL such as ftp://example.com shows the protocol in use. Other frequently tested abbreviations: URL (Uniform Resource Locator), HTML (HyperText Markup Language), IP (Internet Protocol), ISP (Internet Service Provider), WWW (World Wide Web, created by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989-91), VPN (Virtual Private Network), and LAN, MAN and WAN for network scope.

question: RAM stands for :
subject: Computers
detail: RAM stands for Random Access Memory. 'Random access' means the CPU can reach any memory cell directly, in about the same time, without reading through the cells before it. Tapes and similar media work sequentially and do not have this property. RAM is the primary (main) memory and holds the operating system, running programs and the data currently in use. It is volatile, so its contents are lost when power is switched off. It is read-write memory, unlike ROM, which is non-volatile and mostly read-only. The two main types are DRAM, which is cheap, needs periodic refreshing and is used as main memory, and SRAM, which is faster, costlier, needs no refresh and is used for cache. RAM is measured in MB, GB and so on. Elimination: 'Read Access Memory', 'Random Attribute Memory' and 'Random Applicable Memory' are not standard computing terms. The phrase 'Read Access' also wrongly suggests read-only behaviour, whereas RAM supports both reading and writing.
explanations: Correct: RAM expands to Random Access Memory, meaning any location can be accessed directly in near-constant time.
Wrong: 'Read Access Memory' is not a standard term. RAM is read-write, and read-only memory is ROM.
Wrong: 'Random Attribute Memory' is a made-up expansion with no technical meaning.
Wrong: 'Random Applicable Memory' is also invented and not used in computing.
keyfact: RAM = Random Access Memory: volatile, read-write main memory of a computer.
option_notes: Random Access Memory is the main, volatile, read-write memory of a computer. It stores the programs and data in current use and gives the CPU fast direct access to any location. Its main types are DRAM and SRAM. Its contents are lost on power-off, and its capacity affects multitasking performance.

Read Access Memory is not a recognised computer term. It may be confused with ROM (Read Only Memory), which is non-volatile and holds firmware such as the BIOS or bootstrap program. RAM is not read-only, because the CPU both reads from and writes to it.

Random Attribute Memory is a fabricated expansion. Memory is described by access method (random or sequential), volatility, speed and capacity, and 'attribute' is not part of any standard memory name.

Random Applicable Memory is also a fabricated term. The correct expansion uses 'Access' because the key property is direct, random access to any address, unlike sequential-access devices such as magnetic tape.
related: RAM is volatile; ROM is non-volatile.
DRAM needs periodic refreshing; SRAM does not.
Cache memory sits between the CPU and RAM and is faster than RAM.
ROM stands for Read Only Memory; EPROM is erased using UV light.
1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KB = 1024 bytes.
Virtual memory uses hard disk space as an extension of RAM.
Registers are the fastest memory inside the CPU.
summary: The correct answer is (a) Random Access Memory. RAM is the computer's main volatile working memory, in which any location can be read or written directly in roughly the same time, whatever its address.
topic_notes: Computer memory is divided into primary and secondary memory. Primary memory is directly accessed by the CPU and includes RAM, ROM and cache. RAM is volatile read-write memory. DRAM (Dynamic RAM) uses capacitors, needs periodic refreshing, is cheaper and is used as main memory. SRAM (Static RAM) uses flip-flops, is faster and costlier, needs no refresh and is used for cache memory. ROM is non-volatile and holds firmware. Its types are PROM (programmable once), EPROM (erasable with UV light), EEPROM (electrically erasable) and flash memory. Cache memory is a small, very fast memory between the CPU and RAM that holds frequently used data. Virtual memory uses part of the hard disk as an extension of RAM. Secondary memory includes hard disks, SSDs, CDs, DVDs and pen drives, and is non-volatile with larger capacity but slower speed. The memory hierarchy, from fastest and smallest to slowest and largest, is registers, cache, RAM, then secondary storage. Units of memory: 1 byte = 8 bits, 1 KB = 1024 bytes, then MB, GB, TB, PB. Other frequently asked abbreviations: CPU, ALU, CU, BIOS, USB, BIT, ROM.

ocr: Which of the following is also known as brain of computer ? (2) Monitor (b) Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) (c) Control Unit (d) Central Processing Unit (CPU)
subject: Computers
detail: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the main processing component of a computer and is popularly called its 'brain'. It fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, executes them and stores the results (the fetch-decode-execute cycle). It has three main parts: the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), which performs arithmetic (add, subtract, multiply, divide) and logical operations (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons); the Control Unit (CU), which directs and coordinates the flow of data and instructions among the CPU, memory and I/O devices; and registers, which are small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU. On a PC the CPU is built as a single chip called a microprocessor. Its speed is measured in Hertz (MHz/GHz). Elimination: the Monitor is only an output device. The ALU and the Control Unit are sub-components of the CPU, so each is only part of the brain, not the whole. The CU is sometimes called the 'nerve centre' of the computer. The complete unit that matches 'brain of computer' is the CPU.
explanations: Incorrect: the Monitor is an output device (VDU) that displays information; it does no processing.
Incorrect: the ALU only performs arithmetic and logical operations. It is one component inside the CPU, not the whole brain.
Incorrect: the Control Unit only directs and coordinates operations. It is a part of the CPU, not the whole, though it is sometimes called the nerve centre.
Correct: the CPU is the processor that executes instructions and controls the computer, so it is universally called the brain of the computer.
keyfact: CPU = brain of the computer (ALU + Control Unit + registers); the Control Unit is the nerve centre.
option_notes: Monitor: also called the Visual Display Unit (VDU), it is an output device that shows text, images and video. Types include CRT, LCD, LED and OLED. Screen quality is described by resolution (pixels), size (diagonal in inches) and refresh rate. It connects through VGA, HDMI or DisplayPort. A touchscreen monitor also works as an input device. It has no role in processing data.

Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): the part of the CPU that carries out arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and logical operations (comparisons such as greater than, equal to, and AND/OR/NOT). It takes operands from registers and returns results to them, with the accumulator holding intermediate results. It is described as the 'mathematical brain' of the CPU, but it works under the direction of the Control Unit.

Control Unit (CU): the part of the CPU that fetches instructions from memory, decodes them and issues control signals to the ALU, memory and I/O devices. It does not process or store data itself but manages the sequence of operations. It uses the program counter and instruction register. It is often described as the 'nerve centre' of the computer system.

Central Processing Unit (CPU): the processor that executes program instructions; the main chip is called a microprocessor. It consists of the ALU, the CU and registers. The first commercial microprocessor was the Intel 4004 (1971). Speed is measured in MHz or GHz, and modern CPUs have multiple cores. Cache memory (L1, L2, L3) sits close to the CPU to speed up access.
related: The CPU consists of the ALU, the Control Unit and registers.
The ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations.
The Control Unit is called the nerve centre of the computer.
A microprocessor is a CPU on a single integrated circuit chip.
Registers are the fastest and smallest memory in a computer.
The Intel 4004 (1971) was the first commercial microprocessor.
The monitor is an output device, and the keyboard and mouse are input devices.
CPU speed is measured in Hertz (MHz/GHz).
summary: The correct answer is (d) Central Processing Unit (CPU). The CPU is called the 'brain of the computer' because it interprets instructions, performs calculations and controls all other components of the system.
topic_notes: The CPU is the core of the computer's hardware. It has the ALU, the Control Unit and registers (the accumulator, program counter, instruction register, memory address register and memory data register). The machine cycle is fetch, decode, execute and store. The CPU communicates with other parts through buses: the data bus, the address bus and the control bus. Cache memory (L1, L2, L3) is fast memory that reduces the time taken to access main memory. Clock speed is measured in Hz, and performance also depends on the number of cores, word length and cache size. The computer's components are classified as input devices (keyboard, mouse, scanner, light pen, OMR, OCR, MICR, barcode reader), output devices (monitor, printer, plotter, speakers) and memory. Primary memory includes RAM (volatile) and ROM (non-volatile), while secondary memory includes hard disks, CDs, DVDs and flash drives. Memory units: 1 byte = 8 bits, 1 KB = 1024 bytes, then MB, GB and TB. Generations of computers: first used vacuum tubes, second transistors, third integrated circuits, fourth microprocessors (VLSI) and fifth uses AI. The von Neumann architecture is the stored-program concept. Software is classified as system software (operating system, compilers, utilities) and application software. Related nicknames to remember: the Control Unit is the 'nerve centre', the motherboard is the main circuit board, and the CPU is the 'brain'. Other angles UPSC could ask: the full forms of CPU, ALU, CU, RAM, ROM, BIOS and VDU, which unit performs comparison operations, and which memory is fastest (registers).

question: A technique in which data is written to two duplicate disks simultaneously, is called :
subject: General Science
detail: Disk mirroring is a fault-tolerance technique, standardised as RAID 1 (Redundant Array of Independent/Inexpensive Disks). Every write is sent simultaneously to two disks (a mirrored pair), so the two disks always hold identical data. If one disk fails, the system keeps running from the surviving disk, and the failed disk is replaced and resynchronised. Reads can be faster because either disk can serve them. The costs are 50% usable capacity and no protection against accidental deletion, virus damage or corruption, because those are mirrored too, so mirroring is not a substitute for backup. Related terms: disk duplexing is mirroring where each disk has its own controller, which also protects against controller failure. RAID 0 is striping with no redundancy. RAID 5 is striping with distributed parity and needs at least 3 disks. RAID 10 combines mirroring and striping. Elimination: multiplexing means combining several signals over one channel in communications. Duplicating and copying are generic words and not standard technical terms for this simultaneous dual-disk write technique. Hence (a).
explanations: Correct: mirroring is the standard term for writing identical data to two disks at the same time (RAID 1).
Wrong: multiplexing combines multiple signals or data streams over a single channel or medium. It is not about disk redundancy.
Wrong: duplicating is a general word, not the standard term for simultaneous dual-disk writing.
Wrong: copying is a general operation, usually done at a point in time, not simultaneous real-time writing to two disks.
keyfact: Mirroring = RAID 1: identical data written simultaneously to two disks for fault tolerance.
option_notes: Mirroring: RAID 1. Data is written identically to two or more disks in real time. It gives high availability and fast reads, and usable capacity is 50% for a pair. It protects against disk failure but not against deletion, corruption or malware. Disk duplexing is a variant with separate controllers.

Multiplexing: a communications technique that combines several signals into one shared channel or medium. Types include FDM (frequency division), TDM (time division) and WDM (wavelength division, used in fibre). A multiplexer (MUX) combines signals and a demultiplexer (DEMUX) separates them. It is unrelated to disk storage redundancy.

Duplicating: a general word meaning making an identical copy. It is not a recognised RAID or storage-fault-tolerance term. Duplication of files is usually a manual or scheduled operation and does not give real-time simultaneous writing to paired disks.

Copying: the ordinary operation of reproducing files or data from one location to another, such as the copy command or Ctrl+C. It happens at a point in time and is not continuous. Backups use copying, but they are not real-time mirroring.
related: Disk mirroring is RAID 1; striping is RAID 0.
RAID 5 uses distributed parity and needs a minimum of 3 disks.
Disk duplexing is mirroring with separate controllers for each disk.
RAID 10 combines mirroring and striping and needs at least 4 disks.
RAID is not a substitute for backup.
Multiplexing (TDM, FDM, WDM) combines signals over one channel.
A hot spare is a standby disk that takes over when a disk fails.
summary: The answer is (a) Mirroring. Disk mirroring (RAID 1) writes the same data to two identical disks at the same time, so if one disk fails the other still holds a complete copy.
topic_notes: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) was proposed in 1987 by Patterson, Gibson and Katz at UC Berkeley. It combines several physical disks into one logical unit for performance, redundancy or both. Key levels: RAID 0 is striping, which splits data across disks for speed, needs at least 2 disks and has no fault tolerance. RAID 1 is mirroring with 2 disks, tolerating one failure with 50% capacity efficiency. RAID 2, 3 and 4 are rarely used and rely on bit-level or byte-level striping with dedicated parity. RAID 5 is block-level striping with distributed parity, needs at least 3 disks and survives one disk failure. RAID 6 uses double parity, needs at least 4 disks and survives two failures. RAID 10 (1+0) is a stripe of mirrors, needs at least 4 disks and gives both speed and redundancy. Other storage terms: a hot spare is a standby disk that automatically replaces a failed one. Hot swapping means replacing a disk without shutting the system down. Backup differs from RAID: a backup is a separate, usually offline or offsite copy, while RAID is for availability. Types of backup are full, incremental and differential. Other terms: SAN (storage area network), NAS (network attached storage), a disk controller, and disk striping with parity. Likely questions ask which RAID level is mirroring, which is striping, and which uses parity.

question: The term ‘e-Waste’ refers to :
options: The files that are deleted and enter the *Waste-bin’ folder in a computer,
The temporary files, folders, links etc, that are rarely used in a computer
The electronic products such as mobiles, PCs etc. that are disposed off after their useful life
A portal that offers services for collecting houschold waste
subject: Computers
detail: e-Waste (electronic waste) covers end-of-life or discarded electrical and electronic equipment (EEE), including computers, mobile phones, printers, TVs, refrigerators, batteries and CFL lamps. It contains valuable metals (gold, copper, silver) and also hazardous substances such as lead, mercury, cadmium, brominated flame retardants and beryllium, so unscientific recycling harms health and the environment. In India it is governed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The E-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011, in force from 1 May 2012, introduced Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR). They were replaced by the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016 and later by the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, effective 1 April 2023, which have EPR certificates and a mandatory registration regime. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards oversee implementation. The Basel Convention governs transboundary movement of hazardous wastes. Elimination: (a) and (b) are about digital files and are not e-waste. (d) describes a waste-collection portal, a service, not the waste itself. Only (c) gives the correct definition.
explanations: Wrong: files in the Recycle Bin are digital data, not physical electronic waste.
Wrong: temporary or rarely used files are software clutter, not e-waste.
Correct: e-waste is discarded electronic products such as mobiles and PCs at the end of their useful life.
Wrong: a portal for household waste collection is a service, not what the term e-waste means.
keyfact: e-Waste = discarded electrical and electronic equipment (mobiles, PCs, TVs etc.) at end of life, regulated in India by the E-Waste Rules built on EPR.
option_notes: The Recycle/Waste-bin folder temporarily holds deleted files so they can be restored. It is a software feature in Windows (Recycle Bin) and has no connection to hazardous physical waste. Files are permanently removed only when the bin is emptied or Shift+Delete is used.

Temporary files (such as .tmp files, cache and browser cookies) are created by the OS or applications for short-term use. Cleaning them frees disk space. Disk Cleanup tools remove them. They are digital clutter, not environmental waste.

This is the correct definition. e-Waste includes discarded computers, phones, TVs, fridges, chargers and batteries. It holds recoverable metals and toxic materials (lead, mercury, cadmium). India regulates it through the E-Waste Rules 2011, 2016 and 2022, which use Extended Producer Responsibility. Informal recycling is a major problem in India.

A waste-collection portal is an online service, which may be municipal or private, that arranges pickup of household waste. It is not a definition of e-waste. Examples of related efforts include Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) digital tools and various e-waste pickup apps.
related: E-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011 came into force on 1 May 2012.
E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 took effect on 1 April 2023.
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is the core principle of India's e-waste rules.
CPCB is the main monitoring agency for e-waste rules in India.
Basel Convention regulates transboundary movement of hazardous wastes.
Lead, mercury and cadmium are key toxic components of e-waste.
Urban mining means recovering metals like gold and copper from e-waste.
summary: The answer is (c). e-Waste means discarded electrical and electronic equipment such as mobiles, PCs, TVs and refrigerators that are disposed of after their useful life. It is a physical waste category, not a computer file or a web portal.
topic_notes: e-Waste is among the fastest-growing solid waste streams. India is one of the top e-waste generators after China, the USA and Japan, with Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and Chennai being major hubs. Key legal framework: the E-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011 (effective 1 May 2012) were the first to bring in Extended Producer Responsibility. The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016 added PROs (Producer Responsibility Organisations), dismantlers and recyclers, collection targets and authorisation. The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 took effect on 1 April 2023, with EPR certificates, an online registration portal, and a ban on unregistered operators. They also cover refurbishers. The 2016 rules also covered CFL and other mercury-containing lamps. The Central Pollution Control Board monitors compliance. Hazardous constituents: lead (CRT monitors, solder), mercury (lamps, switches), cadmium (batteries), arsenic, and PBDEs (flame retardants). Valuable materials: gold, silver, copper, palladium, which supports urban mining. Global context: the Basel Convention (1989, in force 1992) regulates hazardous waste movement. The Basel Ban Amendment prohibits export from OECD to non-OECD countries. The Global E-waste Monitor is published by the UN University, ITU and ISWA. The StEP (Solving the E-waste Problem) initiative and the Bamako Convention (Africa) are also relevant. Related concepts: Extended Producer Responsibility, the polluter pays principle, 3Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle), circular economy, and the Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 and Plastic Waste Rules. Possible future questions concern toxic metals, rule years, EPR, and the agencies involved.

question: CAD stands for :
options: Coded Addressable Design (Contd.) Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner (APF(
subject: Computers
detail: CAD stands for Computer Aided Design (often also expanded as Computer-Aided Drafting). It is software-based design in which the computer helps the designer create 2D drawings and 3D models, modify them quickly, analyse them and produce documentation. The pioneering work was Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad (1963) at MIT. Commercial packages include AutoCAD (Autodesk, first released 1982), SolidWorks, CATIA, Pro/ENGINEER and Revit. CAD is used in mechanical, civil, electrical and architectural design, and in aerospace and automobile design. Its output often feeds CAM (Computer Aided Manufacturing), together called CAD/CAM. Typical advantages are accuracy, easy editing, reusable libraries, simulation, and lower design time and cost. Elimination logic: the standard industry expansion uses the word 'Aided', so 'Computer Application in Design' is a plausible-sounding distractor but not the accepted expansion. 'Coded Algorithm in Design' and 'Coded Addressable Design' are invented phrases with no standard meaning in computing. Hence only (a) is correct.
explanations: Correct: CAD is universally expanded as Computer Aided Design.
Wrong: 'Computer Application in Design' is not the standard expansion, though it sounds similar.
Wrong: 'Coded Algorithm in Design' is a made-up phrase with no technical meaning.
Wrong: 'Coded Addressable Design' is also invented and not a recognised term.
keyfact: CAD = Computer Aided Design (Sketchpad 1963; AutoCAD 1982).
option_notes: Computer Aided Design: use of computer software to create, edit, analyse and document designs in 2D or 3D. Origins in Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad (1963). Popular tools: AutoCAD (1982), SolidWorks, CATIA, Revit. Used in engineering, architecture, automobile and aerospace design, and often linked to CAM for manufacturing.

Computer Application in Design: not an accepted expansion of CAD. It merely describes the general idea of applying computers to design. Standard terminology uses 'Aided'. It is a typical distractor in competitive exams, so do not confuse it with the official term.

Coded Algorithm in Design: not a real computing term. Algorithms are step-by-step procedures, and while CAD software uses algorithms internally (geometric modelling, rendering), this phrase is not any recognised acronym expansion.
Coded Addressable Design: not a real term. 'Addressable' appears in other contexts, such as addressable memory or addressable fire alarm systems, but has nothing to do with CAD.
related: CAM = Computer Aided Manufacturing
CAE = Computer Aided Engineering
Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad (1963) is regarded as the ancestor of CAD
AutoCAD was first released by Autodesk in 1982
DWG and DXF are AutoCAD file formats
CIM = Computer Integrated Manufacturing
CAI = Computer Assisted Instruction
A plotter is a typical output device for CAD drawings
summary: The correct answer is (a) Computer Aided Design. CAD means using computer systems to create, modify, analyse and optimise engineering and architectural designs and drawings.
topic_notes: CAD (Computer Aided Design) uses computers to assist in creating, modifying, analysing and optimising a design. Early history: Patrick Hanratty developed PRONTO (1957) and Ivan Sutherland created Sketchpad (1963), often called the ancestor of modern CAD and of graphical user interfaces. AutoCAD by Autodesk was released in December 1982 for microcomputers and made CAD widely affordable. Types: 2D drafting (vector drawings of plans) and 3D modelling (wireframe, surface, solid modelling, parametric modelling). Common file formats: DWG, DXF (AutoCAD), STEP and IGES (exchange formats), STL (3D printing). Related terms: CAM (Computer Aided Manufacturing) controls machine tools using CNC; CAE (Computer Aided Engineering) covers simulation such as finite element analysis; CIM (Computer Integrated Manufacturing) integrates design and production; CAI (Computer Assisted Instruction) is used in education; CAT (Computer Aided Translation/Testing) is used in other fields. Hardware often used with CAD: high-resolution monitors, plotters, light pens, digitisers/graphic tablets, graphics cards. Applications: architecture (building plans), civil engineering, mechanical parts, electronics (PCB layout), fashion, animation and 3D printing. Advantages: high accuracy, faster revisions, easy storage and sharing, simulation before production, standardisation. UPSC-style questions on computers often test full forms of acronyms such as CAD, CAM, CAI, CIM, ASCII, BIOS, so memorise them.

ocr: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists : List-I List-IT (Contribution) (Contributor) A. Industrial Welfare 1, Charles A Myers Movement B. Human Relations 2. A.K. Rice Thought C. Concept of Third 3, Robert Owen Force D. Ahmedabad 4, Elton Mayo Experiment Code : A BC D 1G) Goel A) 3 (bo) 3 1 4 2 Cite + Awd @) 3 4 1 2
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Working through the list as printed: A. Industrial Welfare Movement is associated with Robert Owen (3). B. Human Relations Thought is associated with Elton Mayo (4). C. The concept of Third Force is associated with A.K. Rice (2). D. The Ahmedabad Experiment is associated with A.K. Rice of the Tavistock Institute (Rice's 1950s study at Calico Mills, Ahmedabad on autonomous work groups). The correct pairing under the standard textbook view is therefore A-3, B-4, C-?, D-2. The printed options do not cleanly contain A-3, B-4. Option (d) has A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2, which matches A, B and D with the standard facts. Charles A. Myers is the author of 'Industrial Relations in India' and the 'Third Force' idea in industrial relations (the state/community as a third party alongside labour and management) is a concept sometimes credited to him in Indian IR texts, so C-1 fits. Hence the answer is (d), and the summary above should be read as (d), not (b). Elimination: A-3 rules out (a) and (c); B-4 rules out (b); only (d) remains.
explanations: Wrong: gives A-2 and B-1, but Industrial Welfare is Owen (3) and Human Relations is Mayo (4).
Wrong: A-3 is right, but B-1 is wrong, since Human Relations belongs to Elton Mayo (4).
Wrong: A-2 is wrong, since Industrial Welfare belongs to Robert Owen (3).
Correct: A-3 Owen, B-4 Mayo, C-1 Myers, D-2 Rice, matching the standard facts.
keyfact: Owen: welfare; Mayo: human relations; Myers: Third Force (Indian IR); Rice: Ahmedabad Experiment.
option_notes: Option (a) 2-1-4-3: pairs Industrial Welfare with A.K. Rice and Human Relations with Myers. Rice is a Tavistock socio-technical systems scholar. Myers wrote on Indian industrial relations. Both pairings are wrong; Owen is the welfare pioneer and Mayo the Hawthorne researcher.

Option (b) 3-1-4-2: gets Owen for welfare and Rice for Ahmedabad right but misplaces Myers and Mayo. Myers is not the Human Relations thinker; Mayo's Hawthorne experiments at Western Electric (1924-32) founded that school.

Option (c) 2-4-1-3: Mayo for Human Relations is correct, but welfare is Owen's work, not Rice's, and the Ahmedabad Experiment was Rice's, not Owen's. Owen's New Lanark mills were in the early 1800s, long before the 1950s Ahmedabad study.

Option (d) 3-4-1-2: the correct code. Owen (welfare movement, New Lanark), Mayo (Hawthorne, human relations), Myers (Indian IR, Third Force) and Rice (Ahmedabad Experiment, Tavistock Institute, autonomous work groups).
related: Robert Owen ran the New Lanark mills in Scotland.
Elton Mayo conducted the Hawthorne Studies at Western Electric, 1924-32.
A.K. Rice of the Tavistock Institute conducted the Ahmedabad Experiment.
Dunlop's systems approach views IR as a system of actors, contexts and ideology.
Taylor wrote Principles of Scientific Management in 1911.
The Industrial Disputes Act was enacted in 1947.
Socio-technical systems theory came from the Tavistock Institute.
statements: A — Correct (3): Robert Owen (1771-1858), Welsh social reformer and mill owner at New Lanark, Scotland, pioneered industrial welfare. He improved housing, reduced hours, set up schools and banned child labour under age 10, and is called the father of the cooperative and welfare movement and of modern personnel management.

B — Correct (4): Elton Mayo led the Hawthorne Studies (1924-32) at Western Electric's Hawthorne Works, Chicago. They showed social relations, group norms, attention and informal organisation affect productivity. This founded the Human Relations school, stressing the 'social man' and morale over purely economic incentives.

C — Correct (1): Charles A. Myers, an MIT scholar, studied Indian industrial relations (Industrial Relations in India, 1958). The Third Force concept is the role of the state or community as an additional actor beside management and labour, via tripartism, adjudication and conciliation, and is credited to him in Indian IR texts.

D — Correct (2): The Ahmedabad Experiment (1953-56) by A.K. Rice of the Tavistock Institute at the Calico Mills, Ahmedabad, a weaving shed study, introduced autonomous work groups and a socio-technical systems approach, showing improved efficiency and morale when work was reorganised around group tasks.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 3-1-4-2. The Industrial Welfare Movement is linked to Robert Owen (3), Human Relations Thought to Elton Mayo (4), the Third Force concept to A.K. Rice (2), and the Ahmedabad Experiment to Charles A. Myers (1) as listed in the question. Matching code A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 does not follow from the list as printed, so see the detail note below.
topic_notes: Industrial welfare began with Robert Owen at New Lanark in the early 19th century. Scientific management by F.W. Taylor (1911) emphasised time and motion study, and Henri Fayol gave 14 principles of management. The Human Relations school grew from Elton Mayo's Hawthorne Studies, including the Relay Assembly Test Room and the Bank Wiring Room, and showed the importance of informal groups. Later came behavioural science (Maslow, McGregor's Theory X and Y, Herzberg). The Tavistock Institute of Human Relations in London developed the socio-technical systems approach, with Trist, Bamforth, Emery and A.K. Rice. Rice's Ahmedabad Experiment at the Calico Mills (Ahmedabad Manufacturing and Calico Printing Company) was sponsored by the Ahmedabad Textile Industry's Research Association (ATIRA) and tested autonomous groups in weaving. Charles A. Myers wrote Labor Problems in the Industrialisation of India (1958) and Industrial Relations in India. In Indian IR the state is regarded as a third party through tripartite bodies such as the Indian Labour Conference and Standing Labour Committee, and mechanisms such as conciliation, arbitration and adjudication under the Industrial Disputes Act 1947. Other angles include Dunlop's systems approach to IR, the Marxist and pluralist approaches, the Gandhian trusteeship approach and the Whitley Committee.

ocr: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists : List-I List-I (Board/Committee) (Chairperson) A. First National Com- 1. GK. Chadha mission on Labour, 1969 B. Wage Board for 2. Ravindra Working Journalists, Verma 2009 C. Second National 3, P.B, Gajendra- Commission on gadkar Labour, 2002 D.Index Review 4. GR. Majithia Committee, 2009 Code : A B SENNA weweg (a) 3 4 (b) 1 4 (oe) 2 2 (@) 1 :) Exam 2012 Question Paper
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: This question tests the chairpersons of major labour-related commissions and committees in India. The First National Commission on Labour was set up in 1966 and submitted its report in 1969 under Justice P.B. Gajendragadkar, a former Chief Justice of India. It reviewed the whole range of labour issues after Independence. The Second National Commission on Labour was constituted in October 1999 and reported in 2002 under Ravindra Verma, a former Union Labour Minister. It recommended consolidating the central labour laws into broad groups, and this later fed into the idea of labour codes. The Wage Board for Working Journalists and Non-Journalist Newspaper Employees was set up in 2007 under Justice G.R. Majithia, and it reported in 2010. The Index Review Committee on the Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) was headed by G.K. Chadha, an economist and former Vice-Chancellor of South Asian University. Elimination: Gajendragadkar is definitely tied to the 1969 commission, so A-3 is fixed. Only option (a) has A-3 together with B-4, which also matches Majithia with the Wage Board. Options (b) and (d) give A=1, and options (b) and (d) are therefore wrong. Option (c) gives B=2, which is wrong.
explanations: Correct. A-3, B-4, C-2 and D-1 is the right combination: Gajendragadkar, Majithia, Verma and Chadha.
Wrong. It gives A=1 (Chadha) for the 1969 commission, which is incorrect. The 1969 commission was headed by Gajendragadkar.
Wrong. It gives B=2 (Verma) for the journalists' wage board, which is incorrect. Verma headed the Second Labour Commission, and the wage board was headed by Majithia.
Wrong. It gives A=1 and B=2, and both are incorrect.
keyfact: 1st NCL 1969: Gajendragadkar; 2nd NCL 2002: Ravindra Verma; Wage Board for Journalists: Majithia; Index Review Committee: G.K. Chadha.
option_notes: Option (a): A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1. This is the correct set. Gajendragadkar chaired the First Labour Commission, Majithia the Wage Board, Verma the Second Labour Commission and Chadha the Index Review Committee. Justice Gajendragadkar was also a Chief Justice of India (1964-66) and headed other notable commissions.

Option (b): A-1, B-4, C-2, D-3. This is incorrect because it swaps Gajendragadkar and Chadha. Chadha, an economist, headed the CPI-IW review, not the 1969 commission. Gajendragadkar was a jurist who led the First Labour Commission and also the Gajendragadkar Committee on Bonus.

Option (c): A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1. This is incorrect because it swaps Verma and Majithia. Ravindra Verma was Labour Minister in the Janata government and later chaired the Second Labour Commission. Majithia, a retired Supreme Court judge, chaired the wage boards for journalists.

Option (d): A-1, B-2, C-4, D-3. This is incorrect because it gets all four wrong. In this arrangement every pairing is wrong, so the option can be eliminated at once. The actual pairings are A-3, B-4, C-2 and D-1.
related: The First National Commission on Labour (1969) was chaired by P.B. Gajendragadkar.
The Second National Commission on Labour (2002) was chaired by Ravindra Verma.
The Majithia Wage Board dealt with working journalists and non-journalist newspaper employees.
The Labour Bureau compiles the CPI-IW; its current base year is 2016.
The Whitley Commission (Royal Commission on Labour) was appointed in 1929.
The Gajendragadkar Committee on Bonus reported in 1961, leading to the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965.
The Working Journalists Act was passed in 1955.
The four labour codes consolidated 29 central labour laws.
statements: A — First National Commission on Labour, 1969: Correct match with 3 (P.B. Gajendragadkar). The commission was appointed in December 1966 and reported in August 1969. It was the first comprehensive review of labour conditions, wages, industrial relations and social security after Independence. Its recommendations influenced the Industrial Relations Bill proposals, wage policy and the need for a national labour policy.

B — Wage Board for Working Journalists, 2009: Correct match with 4 (G.R. Majithia). Justice Majithia headed the Wage Board constituted under the Working Journalists Act, 1955. It was set up in 2007 and made recommendations in 2010. The Supreme Court upheld them in 2014 in the Dainik Bhaskar case, and they were made binding on newspaper establishments.

C — Second National Commission on Labour, 2002: Correct match with 2 (Ravindra Verma). It was set up in 1999 and submitted its report in June 2002. It recommended grouping the 44 central labour laws into broad groups, such as industrial relations, wages, social security, safety and welfare. It also proposed an umbrella law for the unorganised sector.

D — Index Review Committee, 2009: Correct match with 1 (G.K. Chadha). The committee reviewed the base year and methodology of the Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW), which is compiled by the Labour Bureau. The base year was revised from 1982 to 2001 on its lines, and later to 2016.
summary: The correct answer is (a) A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1. The First National Commission on Labour (1969) was chaired by P.B. Gajendragadkar, the Wage Board for Working Journalists (2009) by Justice G.R. Majithia, the Second National Commission on Labour (2002) by Ravindra Verma, and the Index Review Committee (2009) by G.K. Chadha.
topic_notes: Labour commissions and committees are a standard topic in the Industrial Relations and Labour Laws section. The Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley Commission, 1929-31) was the first major inquiry, under J.H. Whitley. After Independence, the First National Commission on Labour (1966-69) under P.B. Gajendragadkar reviewed all aspects of labour. The Second National Commission on Labour (1999-2002) was chaired by Ravindra Verma. It recommended consolidating the central labour laws into broad groups, an umbrella legislation for the unorganised sector and a review of the laws on retrenchment. These ideas led to the four labour codes: the Code on Wages 2019, the Industrial Relations Code 2020, the Code on Social Security 2020 and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020. Other bodies worth remembering: the Gajendragadkar Committee on Bonus (1961), the Payment of Bonus Act 1965, the Kothari Committee, the Dutt Committee on licensing, the Bhagwati Committee on minimum wages and the Rege Committee on labour welfare. Wage boards for working journalists are set up under the Working Journalists and Other Newspaper Employees (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955. The Palekar wage board (1980s) and the Manisana wage boards are earlier examples. The Labour Bureau, headquartered at Chandigarh/Shimla, compiles the CPI-IW, with a current base year of 2016=100. The Index Review Committee under G.K. Chadha dealt with base-year revisions and methodology. UPSC often asks which person chaired which commission, so remember the matches and the years.

question: Which of the following is NOT covered by the Employees Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 ?
subject: Social Security
detail: The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 is a social security statute administered by the EPFO under the Ministry of Labour and Employment. Its 'miscellaneous provisions' are three schemes framed under Section 5, 6 and 6A, 6C: the Employees' Provident Fund Scheme, 1952 (Section 5), the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 (Section 6A, replacing the Family Pension Scheme 1971) and the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976 (Section 6C). Together they give old-age savings, pension (superannuation, disablement, widow, children and orphan pension) and life insurance cover to the family on the death of a member in service. Employment injury benefits are a different branch of social security. They are provided by the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 (formerly the Workmen's Compensation Act), which places a liability on the employer, and by the ESI Act, 1948, which gives employment injury benefit through the ESIC. Elimination: (a), (b) and (c) are each a scheme under the EPF Act, so the only item outside its scope is (d).
explanations: Pension is covered: the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 is framed under Section 6A of the EPF Act, so this is not the answer.
Provident Fund is the core subject of the Act, through the EPF Scheme 1952, so this is not the answer.
Deposit Linked Insurance is covered by the EDLI Scheme 1976 under Section 6C, so this is not the answer.
Injury compensation is governed by the Employees' Compensation Act 1923 and the ESI Act 1948, not the EPF Act, so this is the correct answer.
keyfact: EPF Act = PF + Pension (EPS 1995) + EDLI (1976); injury compensation belongs to the Employees' Compensation Act 1923 and ESI Act 1948.
option_notes: Pension: the Employees' Pension Scheme 1995 (EPS-95) came into force on 16 Nov 1995 and replaced the Family Pension Scheme 1971. It is funded by 8.33% of wages from the employer's share plus a government contribution of 1.16%. It provides superannuation, early, disablement, widow, children and orphan pensions.

Provident Fund: the EPF Scheme 1952 is a contributory savings scheme. The employee and employer each contribute 12% of basic wages plus DA (10% in some establishments). The wage ceiling for compulsory coverage is Rs 15,000 per month. Interest is declared yearly by the CBT and the amount is withdrawable on retirement or in specified situations.

Deposit Linked Insurance: the EDLI Scheme 1976 is funded by an employer contribution of 0.5% of wages, with no employee contribution. It pays a lump sum to the nominee or family on the death of a member while in service. The maximum benefit was raised to Rs 7 lakh in 2021, and the scheme is linked to the PF balance.

Injury compensation: the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 makes the employer liable to pay compensation for injury, disease or death arising out of and in the course of employment. The ESI Act 1948 gives employment injury benefit, including disablement and dependants' benefit. Neither Act is part of the EPF framework.
related: EPF Scheme 1952 is framed under Section 5 of the EPF & MP Act.
EPS 1995 is framed under Section 6A; EDLI 1976 under Section 6C.
The Employees' Compensation Act 1923 was earlier called the Workmen's Compensation Act.
ESI Act 1948 provides employment injury benefit through the ESIC.
The EPF Act applies to establishments with 20 or more employees.
The EPFO's apex body is the Central Board of Trustees, chaired by the Union Labour Minister.
