topic_notes: The Mid-Day Meal Scheme is the world's largest school feeding programme. Tamil Nadu started a noon meal scheme in the 1960s under Kamaraj, and MGR expanded it in 1982. The national programme (NP-NSPE) began on 15 August 1995 for classes I-V in 2,408 blocks, covering all blocks by 1997-98. It initially gave 3 kg foodgrains per child per month with 80% attendance. In November 2001 the Supreme Court (PUCL v. Union of India, right to food case) directed states to provide cooked meals; the Centre made this compulsory. In October 2007 it was extended to classes VI-VIII in educationally backward blocks and universalised for upper primary in 2008. Nutritional norms are 450 kcal and 12 g protein (primary) and 700 kcal and 20 g protein (upper primary). The National Food Security Act 2013 (Section 4) made meals a legal entitlement for children aged 6-14. The scheme is centrally sponsored, with the Centre providing foodgrains free and sharing cooking costs with states. Management is done by self-help groups, local bodies or NGOs such as Akshaya Patra and ISKCON's Food for Life. In 2021 the scheme was renamed PM POSHAN (Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman) and extended to pre-primary (Bal Vatika) children, with a five-year outlay till 2025-26. Related programmes: ICDS (1975), Integrated Child Development Services for under-six children, the Anganwadi system, Poshan Abhiyaan (2018), Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (2001) and the Right to Education Act 2009 (Article 21A). Social audits, kitchen gardens and the use of fortified rice are recent features.

question:
The President of India is elected by the 59, members of an electoral college consisting of elected members of :
1. Both Houses of Parliament
2. The Legislative Assemblies of the States
3. Union Council of Ministers
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 54 provides that the President is elected by an electoral college consisting of (a) the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and (b) the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States. The 70th Amendment Act, 1992 clarified that 'States' includes the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry. Nominated members of Parliament and of State Assemblies, and members of State Legislative Councils (Vidhan Parishads), do not vote. Article 55 prescribes the manner of election: uniformity of representation among the States, and parity between the States as a whole and the Union. The election uses the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, with a secret ballot. Value of an MLA's vote = State population (1971 census) / (elected MLAs x 1000). Value of an MP's vote = total value of all MLAs' votes / elected MPs. The 84th Amendment freezes the 1971 census base until after the first census following 2026. Item 3 fails because the Council of Ministers is not an electoral constituency. Ministers vote only if they are elected MPs or MLAs, and then in that capacity. Hence only 1 and 2 are correct.
explanations: Incorrect: it omits the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies, who are also in the electoral college.
Incorrect: it omits the elected members of both Houses of Parliament, who are also in the electoral college.
Correct: Article 54 names exactly these two groups, the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies.
Incorrect: it includes the Union Council of Ministers, which is not a separate electoral group.
keyfact: Article 54: the President is elected by elected members of both Houses of Parliament and State Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry) by STV; nominated members and Council members do not vote.
option_notes: Parliament-only option: Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. The Lok Sabha has up to 552 members and the Rajya Sabha up to 250. The Vice-President, in contrast, is elected by all members of both Houses, including nominated members, under Article 66. The President's electors also include State members, which is why this option is incomplete.

State-only option: State Legislative Assemblies have 60 to 500 members (Article 170), with exceptions for smaller States such as Sikkim, Goa and Mizoram. Elected MLAs count in the Presidential electoral college, but they do not make up the whole of it. The State Legislative Councils, which exist in only some States, have no role in the election.

Correct option: the electoral college under Article 54 has elected MPs of both Houses and elected MLAs of States, plus Delhi and Puducherry. It numbers about 4,800 electors. The vote is by single transferable vote under proportional representation (Article 55). The election is conducted by the ECI. Disputes go to the Supreme Court under Article 71.

Option of State Assemblies plus the Council of Ministers: the Union Council of Ministers does not vote as a body, and its inclusion would also leave out Parliament. Ministers can vote only if they are elected members. Article 74 provides for the Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President, and Article 75 deals with its appointment and responsibility.
related: Article 54 gives the electoral college; Article 55 gives the manner of election.
The 70th Amendment (1992) brought Delhi and Puducherry into the electoral college.
Nominated members and Legislative Council members do not vote in the Presidential election.
The Vice-President is elected by all members of both Houses of Parliament (Article 66), including nominated members.
The 84th Amendment (2001) freezes the 1971 census for vote values until after the first census after 2026.
Disputes about the Presidential election are decided by the Supreme Court (Article 71).
The President can be impeached under Article 61 by a two-thirds majority of each House.
V.V. Giri (1969) was elected through the second-preference count.
statements: 1 — Correct: Elected members of both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha are part of the electoral college under Article 54. Nominated members (12 in Rajya Sabha, up to 2 Anglo-Indian members in the Lok Sabha before 2020) cannot vote. Each MP's vote value is calculated by dividing the total value of all MLAs' votes by the number of elected MPs. The total is 776 MPs (543 + 233 elected). The Returning Officer is usually the Secretary-General of a House of Parliament, appointed by rotation. Elections are conducted by the Election Commission of India under Article 324.

2 — Correct: Elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (Vidhan Sabhas) are part of the college. Delhi and Puducherry were included by the 70th Amendment (1992). Members of Legislative Councils are excluded. An MLA's vote value depends on State population (1971 census) divided by the number of elected MLAs times 1000, so Uttar Pradesh has the highest value (208) and Sikkim the lowest (7). The total number of MLAs is 4,033 (4,120 minus the nominated and Jammu and Kashmir seats at present). The election is held by secret ballot.

3 — Incorrect: The Union Council of Ministers is not a constituency of the electoral college. It is the executive body headed by the Prime Minister that aids and advises the President under Article 74. Ministers can vote only as elected members of Parliament or Assemblies. The Council has Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers, and is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha under Article 75(3). Its size is capped at 15% of the Lok Sabha's strength, by the 91st Amendment (2003).
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 2. Under Article 54, the President is elected by an electoral college made up of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States (and, since 1992, of the NCT of Delhi and Puducherry). The Union Council of Ministers is not a separate constituency.
topic_notes: Election of the President: Articles 52 to 62 deal with the office. The President must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old and qualified to be a member of the Lok Sabha. The candidate must not hold an office of profit. The nomination needs 50 electors as proposers and 50 as seconders, and the security deposit is Rs 15,000. The term is five years (Article 56), though the President continues in office until a successor takes over, and is eligible for re-election with no limit on terms. Impeachment is under Article 61 for violation of the Constitution, requiring a two-thirds majority in each House, with at least 14 days' notice signed by one-fourth of the members of the House that initiates the charge. Both Houses, including nominated members, participate in impeachment. A vacancy must be filled within six months. The Vice-President acts as President (Article 65) in the interim, and if that office is vacant the Chief Justice of India acts under the 1969 Act. Value of votes: MLA vote value = population of State (1971 census) / (total elected MLAs x 1000), with fractions above one-half rounded up. MP vote value = total value of all MLAs' votes / total elected MPs. A candidate must secure a quota, which is (total valid votes / 2) + 1. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the only President elected twice. Neelam Sanjiva Reddy was the only one elected unopposed. V.V. Giri won in 1969 on second-preference votes, the only such case. Droupadi Murmu (2022) is the 15th President and the first tribal woman holder. Dr. Zakir Husain was the first Muslim President and K.R. Narayanan the first Dalit President.

question: The responsibility of preparation of electoral rolls in India rests with :
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Article 324(1) of the Constitution states that the superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to Parliament and State Legislatures and to the offices of President and Vice-President shall be vested in the Election Commission. Article 325 provides that there shall be one general electoral roll for every territorial constituency, with no exclusion on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex. Article 326 provides for adult suffrage, with the voting age lowered from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment (1988). Parliament has power under Article 327 to make laws on elections, and it did so through the Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951. The RP Act 1950 deals with the allocation of seats, delimitation and the preparation of rolls. The 1951 Act deals with the conduct of elections and disputes. In practice, the Chief Electoral Officer of each State and the District Election Officer, along with the Electoral Registration Officer, do the field work, but they act under the superintendence of the ECI. Parliament only legislates, the local administration only assists, and the Returning Officer conducts the election in a constituency. Hence (c) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: Parliament makes laws on elections under Article 327 but does not prepare the rolls.
Wrong: Local officials may assist, but they work under the ECI's control and do not hold the constitutional responsibility.
Correct: Article 324(1) gives the ECI superintendence, direction and control over the preparation of electoral rolls.
Wrong: The Returning Officer conducts the election in a constituency and handles nominations and counting. The Electoral Registration Officer prepares the roll.
keyfact: Article 324(1): the Election Commission of India controls the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections.
option_notes: Parliament is the legislature of the Union, made up of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. Under Article 327 it can make provision for elections, including electoral rolls and delimitation. It has done so through the RP Acts of 1950 and 1951 and the Delimitation Acts. It legislates on these matters but does not administer them.

The local administration means the district and State machinery, such as the District Magistrate, who often acts as the District Election Officer. These officials are placed at the ECI's disposal during elections under Article 324(6). They carry out field work such as house-to-house verification. They do not hold independent responsibility for the rolls.

The Election Commission of India is a permanent constitutional body set up under Article 324 on 25 January 1950. It consists of the CEC and other Election Commissioners, and since 1993 it has been a multi-member body. It oversees rolls, the conduct of elections, and the registration and symbol allotment of parties. It is not responsible for State local body elections, which are handled by State Election Commissions.

The Returning Officer is appointed under the RP Act 1951 for each constituency. His duties include accepting nominations, scrutiny, conducting the poll, counting and declaring the result. He is usually a government or local authority officer nominated by the ECI in consultation with the State government. He is separate from the Electoral Registration Officer, who prepares the roll.
related: Article 324 creates the Election Commission of India.
Article 326 provides adult suffrage, with the voting age lowered to 18 by the 61st Amendment in 1988.
Article 329 bars court interference in electoral matters.
The Election Commission was set up on 25 January 1950, and 25 January is National Voters' Day.
State Election Commissions handle panchayat and municipal polls under Articles 243K and 243ZA.
RP Act 1950 deals with electoral rolls and RP Act 1951 with the conduct of elections.
The ECI became a multi-member body in 1993.
Article 327 lets Parliament make laws on elections.
summary: The correct answer is (c) The Election Commission. Article 324(1) vests the superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls, and the conduct of all elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President, in the Election Commission of India.
topic_notes: The Election Commission of India was established on 25 January 1950, which is celebrated as National Voters' Day. Article 324 gives it superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, the President and the Vice-President. It does not cover panchayat and municipal elections, which are conducted by State Election Commissions under Articles 243K and 243ZA. The CEC and Election Commissioners are appointed by the President. The CEC can be removed in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge. The tenure is six years or until age 65, whichever is earlier. A multi-member Commission has existed since the Election Commissioner Amendment Act 1993. Article 325 provides for a single general electoral roll with no discrimination, and Article 326 provides for universal adult suffrage at age 18, following the 61st Amendment in 1988. Article 327 allows Parliament to make election laws, and Article 328 lets State Legislatures do so in the absence of parliamentary provision. Article 329 bars courts from interfering in electoral matters, so election disputes go to election petitions in High Courts. The RP Act 1950 covers seat allocation, constituency delimitation, qualifications of voters and preparation of rolls. The RP Act 1951 covers the conduct of elections, qualifications and disqualifications of members, corrupt practices and election disputes. The ECI also enforces the Model Code of Conduct, recognises parties, allots symbols under the Symbols Order 1968, and has used EVMs and VVPAT. Delimitation is done by the Delimitation Commission, whose orders cannot be questioned in court. Related institutions include the CEO of a State and the Electoral Registration Officer.

question: At the time of becoming the Prime Minister of our country one :
options: Must be a member of one of the Houses of the Parliament. If not, must become a member of one of the Houses within Six months. 60
Need not necessarily be a member of one of the Houses of Parliament but must get elected as a member of Lok Sabha within Six months
Must be a member of one of the Houses of Parliament prior to appointment
Must be a member of Rajya Sabha. PFC) Exam 2012 Question Paper
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The Constitution does not explicitly prescribe qualifications for the Prime Minister. Article 75(1) says the PM is appointed by the President, and Article 75(5) says a Minister who is not a member of either House for six consecutive months ceases to be a Minister. Since the PM is the head of the Council of Ministers, the same rule applies to the PM. So a non-member can be appointed PM but must get elected to the Lok Sabha or be elected or nominated to the Rajya Sabha within six months. The Supreme Court in S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001) held that a non-legislator cannot be repeatedly re-appointed as minister for successive six-month terms without being elected. Examples: H.D. Deve Gowda (1996) and I.K. Gujral (1997) were Rajya Sabha members, and Manmohan Singh (2004 to 2014) was a Rajya Sabha member throughout. P.V. Narasimha Rao in 1991 was not an MP at appointment and later won a Lok Sabha by-election from Nandyal. Eliminate (b) because it demands only the Lok Sabha. Eliminate (c) because it makes prior membership mandatory. Eliminate (d) because it limits the PM to the Rajya Sabha.
explanations: Correct: Article 75(5) allows a non-member to be PM for up to six months, within which he or she must become a member of either House.
Incorrect: Election need not be to the Lok Sabha only. Membership of the Rajya Sabha, by election or nomination, also satisfies the requirement.
Incorrect: Prior membership is not compulsory. Narasimha Rao in 1991 was appointed PM without being an MP.
Incorrect: The PM may belong to either House, and Lok Sabha members such as Indira Gandhi (from 1967), Rajiv Gandhi and Narendra Modi have held the office.
keyfact: A non-MP can be PM for six months under Article 75(5), but must then become a member of either House.
option_notes: This is the actual constitutional position: the PM must be a member of Parliament or become one within six months. It follows from Article 75(5), which covers all ministers including the PM. Narasimha Rao (1991) is the classic case. The Supreme Court in S.R. Chaudhuri (2001) barred repeated six-month appointments of a non-member.

This is wrong because it demands election to the Lok Sabha only. In practice a PM can be a Rajya Sabha member, as Indira Gandhi was in 1966, when she was elected to the Rajya Sabha before moving to the Lok Sabha in 1967. Manmohan Singh was PM for ten years as a Rajya Sabha member from Assam.

This describes the rule in some other systems, such as the UK, where the PM is an MP. India does not require prior membership. Narasimha Rao in 1991 and H.D. Deve Gowda in 1996, who was then Karnataka Chief Minister, are examples of PMs who were not sitting MPs when appointed.

This is wrong because there is no rule restricting the PM to the Rajya Sabha. The constitutional convention is that the PM usually belongs to the Lok Sabha, which is the House that holds the Council of Ministers collectively responsible under Article 75(3). Most PMs have been Lok Sabha members.
related: Article 75(5): a minister who is not a member of Parliament for six consecutive months ceases to be a minister.
Article 75(1): the PM is appointed by the President.
S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001): non-legislator cannot be repeatedly re-appointed as minister.
91st Amendment (2003) caps the council of ministers at 15 percent of the Lok Sabha strength.
Manmohan Singh was PM for ten years as a Rajya Sabha member.
Article 78 lists the PM's duties to the President.
Article 74 provides for the Council of Ministers headed by the PM.
summary: The correct answer is (a). The Prime Minister must be a member of either House of Parliament, but a non-member can be appointed on the condition that he or she becomes a member of either House within six months. This follows from Article 75(5) as interpreted in practice, and it is not restricted to the Lok Sabha.
topic_notes: The Prime Minister is the real executive head under the Westminster-style parliamentary system. Article 74 provides for a Council of Ministers with the PM at its head to aid and advise the President. Article 75 covers appointment, tenure, and responsibilities: the PM is appointed by the President, other ministers on the PM's advice, and the council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)). The total strength of the council is limited to 15 percent of the Lok Sabha strength by the 91st Amendment (2003), with a minimum of 12 ministers in a state. Article 75(5) allows a non-member minister for six months. Article 78 imposes on the PM the duty to communicate to the President all council decisions on administration and legislative proposals. The PM leads the Lok Sabha majority party or coalition, chairs the NITI Aayog, heads the Cabinet Secretariat and the Atomic Energy and Space departments, and chairs committees like the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet. The PM's oath of office is administered by the President under the Third Schedule. The PM's salary is set by Parliament under Article 75(6). The tenure is at the pleasure of the President, but in practice depends on the Lok Sabha majority. Rajya Sabha PMs include Indira Gandhi (1966), Deve Gowda (1996, he was not an MP and later entered the Rajya Sabha), I.K. Gujral and Manmohan Singh. Nehru was the first PM, from 1947 to 1964. A PM may be a member of either House, but can vote only in the House of which he or she is a member.

ocr: Match List-1 with List-I] and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists : List-1 List-ll (Commission) (Chairperson) A. Second Adminis- 1. Vijay Kelkar trative Reforms Commission B. Second Commis- 2. Justice M.N. sion on Centre- Venkatachaliah State relations C. Thirteenth Finance 3. Justice Madan Commission Mohan Punchi D. National Com- 4. M.Vecrappa mission for the Moily Review of the working of the Constitution Code : A (a) 4 (b) 2 (c) vs (d)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a straightforward 'commission and chairperson' matching question, and all four pairings are well-established facts. The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (set up August 2005) was headed first by Veerappa Moily and submitted 15 reports. The Second Commission on Centre-State Relations (constituted 2007) was chaired by Justice Madan Mohan Punchhi, a former Chief Justice of India, and reported in 2010. The Thirteenth Finance Commission (constituted 2007, under Article 280, covering 2010-15) was chaired by Dr. Vijay Kelkar. The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (NCRWC) was set up in 2000 under Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah, a former CJI, and reported in 2002. Elimination: once A = Moily (4) is fixed, only (a) and (c) remain. Then B = Punchhi (3) eliminates (c), which gives B = 1. Equally, D = Venkatachaliah (2) confirms (a). Option (b) wrongly gives A = 2 and (d) wrongly gives B = 1.
explanations: Correct: A-4 (Moily), B-3 (Punchhi), C-1 (Kelkar), D-2 (Venkatachaliah) is the right matching.
Wrong: it gives A = Venkatachaliah, but the Second ARC was chaired by Moily, not Venkatachaliah.
Wrong: although A = 4 is right, B = 1 and C = 3 swap Kelkar and Punchhi, so it fails.
Wrong: it gives A = 2 and swaps B and C, so the first three pairs are all wrong.
keyfact: Second ARC – Veerappa Moily; Punchhi – Centre-State relations; 13th FC – Vijay Kelkar; NCRWC – Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah.
option_notes: Option (a) 4-3-1-2: the correct combination. It shows Moily heading the Second ARC, Punchhi the Centre-State Commission, Kelkar the 13th Finance Commission and Venkatachaliah the NCRWC. These four commissions are frequently asked about in UPSC papers, along with their chairpersons, years and main recommendations.

Option (b) 2-3-1-4: wrongly puts Venkatachaliah at the Second ARC and Moily at the NCRWC. Only B and C are right in this option. Moily headed the Second ARC, not the NCRWC. Venkatachaliah headed the NCRWC (2000-02) and was also the CJI who chaired the NHRC in the 1990s.

Option (c) 4-1-3-2: gets A and D right but swaps B and C. Vijay Kelkar chaired the Thirteenth Finance Commission and not the Centre-State Commission, while Justice Punchhi chaired the Centre-State Commission and not the Finance Commission. The Sarkaria Commission (1983) was the first commission on Centre-State relations.

Option (d) 2-1-3-4: all four pairings are wrong. It reverses the correct pairs for A and D and for B and C. It is useful to remember that the Second ARC was Moily's, the Punchhi Commission was on Centre-State relations, the Kelkar-led body was the 13th FC and the NCRWC was Venkatachaliah's.
related: First ARC (1966) was chaired by Morarji Desai, later K. Hanumanthaiya.
Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State relations was set up in 1983 and reported in 1988.
Finance Commission is a constitutional body under Article 280.
14th Finance Commission (Y.V. Reddy) recommended 42% devolution of the divisible pool.
15th Finance Commission was chaired by N.K. Singh.
Inter-State Council is provided under Article 263 and was set up in 1990.
Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended Fundamental Duties.
NCRWC was also known as the Venkatachaliah Commission.
statements: A — Correct: Second ARC matches 4 (M. Veerappa Moily). The Second ARC was constituted in August 2005 and submitted 15 reports by 2009, covering topics such as ethics in governance, e-governance, citizen-centric administration, and local governance. Moily, a Union Law Minister and former Karnataka CM, chaired it. The First ARC (1966) was chaired by Morarji Desai and then K. Hanumanthaiya. The Second ARC's recommendations were taken up by the government in stages.

B — Correct: Second Commission on Centre-State Relations matches 3 (Justice Madan Mohan Punchhi). It was set up in April 2007 and submitted its report in March 2010. It examined the working of Centre-State relations since the Sarkaria Commission (1983-88), with recommendations on the role of Governors, Article 356, and inter-state councils. Punchhi was CJI from 1998 to 1998. Its seven volumes covered federalism, finance and security issues.

C — Correct: Thirteenth Finance Commission matches 1 (Vijay Kelkar). Constituted in November 2007 under Article 280, it covered the 2010-15 period. Kelkar is an economist who also chaired the Kelkar Committee on fiscal consolidation and the committee on PPP. It recommended a 32% share of central taxes for states and proposed a Goods and Services Tax framework. The Fourteenth FC was chaired by Y.V. Reddy (raised the share to 42%), and the Fifteenth by N.K. Singh.

D — Correct: NCRWC matches 2 (Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah). The commission was set up in February 2000 by the NDA government and submitted its report in March 2002. It examined the Constitution's working without altering its basic structure and recommended, among other things, constitutional status for the Inter-State Council, a National Judicial Commission and the right to work. Venkatachaliah was CJI from 1993 to 1994 and also chaired the National Human Rights Commission.
summary: The correct answer is (a) 4-3-1-2. The Second ARC was chaired by M. Veerappa Moily, the Second Commission on Centre-State Relations by Justice Madan Mohan Punchhi, the Thirteenth Finance Commission by Vijay Kelkar, and the NCRWC by Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah.
topic_notes: Commissions and committees on administration, federalism and the Constitution are a staple of the polity section. The First ARC (1966) was chaired by Morarji Desai (later K. Hanumanthaiya) and recommended Lokpal and Lokayukta institutions. The Second ARC (2005) was chaired by M. Veerappa Moily, with 15 reports, among them 'Ethics in Governance', 'Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance' and 'Local Governance'. Centre-State relations have been reviewed by the Sarkaria Commission (1983, report 1988), the Punchhi Commission (2007, report 2010) and the Rajamannar Committee (Tamil Nadu, 1969). The Sarkaria report favoured a permanent Inter-State Council (set up under Article 263 in 1990). Finance Commissions are constituted under Article 280 every five years: 12th (C. Rangarajan), 13th (Vijay Kelkar), 14th (Y.V. Reddy), 15th (N.K. Singh), 16th (Arvind Panagariya). The 14th raised states' share in the divisible pool to 42%, and the 15th set it at 41% after the creation of the UT of Jammu and Kashmir. The NCRWC (2000-02), chaired by Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah, reviewed the Constitution without changing its basic structure. Other relevant bodies include the Swaran Singh Committee (1976, on Fundamental Duties), the Dinesh Goswami Committee (electoral reforms), the Vohra Committee (criminalisation of politics) and the Santhanam Committee (corruption). Questions often pair the commission with the chairperson or with the year of constitution.

question: What is common to Sardar Hukum Singh, Jagjivan Ram, Inderjit Gupta, Somnath Chatterjee and Seth Govind Das ?
options: They were Speakers of the Lok Sabha
They were Deputy Speakers of the Lok Sabha
They were Pro-tem Speakers of the Lok Sabha
None of the Above (Contd.) Assistant Provident Fund Commission
subject: Indian Polity
detail: A Pro-tem Speaker is a temporary presiding officer. Under Article 95(1), the President appoints one, usually the senior-most member, after a general election. The Pro-tem Speaker administers the oath to new members and conducts the election of the regular Speaker, and the office ends once the Speaker is elected. This is not a post for life. Several veteran MPs held it, including Hukam Singh, Seth Govind Das, Jagjivan Ram (1977) and Inderjit Gupta (1999). Somnath Chatterjee also held it, and later served as the regular Speaker from 2004 to 2009. Elimination logic: Jagjivan Ram, Inderjit Gupta and Seth Govind Das were never elected Speaker, so (a) fails. Jagjivan Ram, Gupta and Seth Govind Das were also not Deputy Speakers, so (b) fails. Since the Pro-tem role is the common thread, (d) fails. Note that the Pro-tem role is a one-off duty and is separate from the elected Speaker and Deputy Speaker posts under Article 93. I am working from memory on the exact years of each person's appointment, so verify those before relying on them.
explanations: Incorrect: Only Hukam Singh and Somnath Chatterjee were elected Speakers. Jagjivan Ram, Inderjit Gupta and Seth Govind Das never held that office.
Incorrect: Only Hukam Singh was a Deputy Speaker (1956-62). The others never held that post.
Correct: Each of the five was appointed Pro-tem Speaker at the start of a Lok Sabha, to administer oaths and conduct the Speaker's election.
Incorrect: A common link exists, namely the Pro-tem Speaker role.
keyfact: The Pro-tem Speaker is appointed by the President under Article 95(1) to administer oaths and conduct the Speaker's election; the five named persons were all Pro-tem Speakers.
option_notes: Speaker of the Lok Sabha: the presiding officer elected by members under Article 93. G.V. Mavalankar was the first Speaker (1952-56). Hukam Singh (1962-67) and Somnath Chatterjee (2004-09) were also Speakers. The Speaker decides on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, certifies Money Bills and presides over joint sittings.

Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha: elected by the House under Article 93 and presides in the Speaker's absence. M.A. Ayyangar was the first Deputy Speaker (1952-56), followed by Hukam Singh (1956-62). By convention the post goes to the opposition, though this is not always followed. The Deputy Speaker is not subordinate to the Speaker and answers directly to the House.

Pro-tem Speaker: a temporary presiding officer appointed by the President under Article 95(1). The post is held by a senior member who administers the oath to new MPs and oversees the election of the Speaker. The office ends once the regular Speaker is elected. It is not a post for life.
None of the above: this would be correct only if no common link existed. Here the common link is the Pro-tem Speaker role, so this option is wrong.
related: Article 93: election of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Article 94: vacation, resignation and removal of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker
Article 95: duties of the Speaker's office when it is vacant, and the basis for the Pro-tem Speaker
G.V. Mavalankar was the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Meira Kumar was the first woman Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Article 108: the Speaker presides over joint sittings
Tenth Schedule (anti-defection): the Speaker decides on disqualification
Balram Jakhar was the longest-serving Lok Sabha Speaker, with two full terms
summary: The answer is (c). All five were appointed Pro-tem Speaker of the Lok Sabha at the start of a new House. Jagjivan Ram and Inderjit Gupta never became Speaker, which rules out (a), and not all of them were Deputy Speakers.
topic_notes: The presiding officers of the Lok Sabha are the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker, elected by members under Article 93. The Speaker's resignation is addressed to the Deputy Speaker (Article 94). A Speaker can be removed by a resolution passed by an effective majority, with 14 days' notice. Article 95 provides for the Deputy Speaker or another person to perform the Speaker's duties when the office is vacant, and it is also the basis for appointing a Pro-tem Speaker. The Speaker does not vote except to break a tie. The Speaker presides over joint sittings of both Houses (Article 108), decides whether a bill is a Money Bill, and decides disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (Kihoto Hollohan case, 1992, made this decision subject to judicial review). Key office holders: G.V. Mavalankar (first Speaker), M.A. Ayyangar (second Speaker, 1956-62), Hukam Singh (1962-67), Neelam Sanjiva Reddy (1967-69; he resigned from his party on becoming Speaker), G.S. Dhillon, Bali Ram Bhagat, Balram Jakhar (served two full terms), P.A. Sangma, G.M.C. Balayogi, Manohar Joshi, Somnath Chatterjee, Meira Kumar (first woman Speaker, 2009-14), Sumitra Mahajan and Om Birla (17th Lok Sabha, re-elected in the 18th). The Pro-tem Speaker is temporary: the President appoints the senior-most member under Article 95(1), and the office lapses when the Speaker is elected. The Rajya Sabha has a Chairman (the Vice-President, ex officio) and a Deputy Chairman, who is elected by members.

question: The purpose of Adjournment motion in our Parliament is :
options: To allow a discussion on a definite matter of urgent public importance
To let opposition members collect information from concerned Ministers
To allow a reduction of specific amount in the demand of grant
To postpone the proceedings to check the inappropriate or the violent behavior on the part of some members
subject: Insurance
detail: The Adjournment Motion is a parliamentary device for interrupting the normal business of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance. It is not mentioned in the Constitution; it derives from the Rules of Procedure (Lok Sabha Rule 56). In India it is available only in the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha. Conditions: it must concern a specific, recent matter of fact; it must be urgent and of public importance; it must not raise more than one issue; it must not relate to a matter that is sub judice; and it must not raise a question of privilege. It requires the support of at least 50 members (leave granted by rising in their seats). The discussion lasts not less than 2.5 hours. Because it interrupts business and implies censure of the government, it is considered extraordinary. The Speaker decides on admissibility. Option (b) describes questions and calling attention notices. Option (c) describes a cut motion (policy cut, economy cut, token cut). Option (d) confuses the motion with the Speaker's power to adjourn the House under disorder.
explanations: Correct: the Adjournment Motion allows discussion of a definite matter of urgent public importance.
Wrong: collecting information from Ministers is the purpose of questions, calling attention notices and short-duration discussions, not adjournment motions.
Wrong: reducing the amount in a demand for grant is done through cut motions (policy cut, economy cut, token cut).
Wrong: postponing proceedings because of disorder is the Presiding Officer's power to adjourn the House, not an adjournment motion.
keyfact: Adjournment motion: Lok Sabha only, 50 members, 2.5 hours, definite matter of urgent public importance, implies censure of government.
option_notes: Adjournment Motion: introduced to draw the attention of the House to a definite matter of urgent public importance. It needs the support of 50 members and its discussion lasts at least 2.5 hours. It is available only in the Lok Sabha and is governed by Rule 56. It is considered an extraordinary device because it interrupts regular business and carries an element of censure of the government. The Speaker decides its admissibility.

Obtaining information from Ministers is done through Question Hour (starred, unstarred, short notice questions), calling attention motions and zero hour mentions. Question Hour is normally the first hour of a sitting. Its purpose is to elicit information and hold the executive accountable. It does not interrupt regular business and does not involve a vote.

A cut motion is moved to reduce the amount of a demand for grant. It is of three types: a policy cut (reduced to Re 1), an economy cut (reduced by a specified amount), and a token cut (reduced by Rs 100). Cut motions can be moved only in the Lok Sabha, because demands for grants are voted only there. They are intended to draw attention to specific grievances, and they must be passed to be effective.

Maintaining order in the House is the duty of the Speaker or Chairman. The Presiding Officer can direct a member to withdraw, name the member, suspend the member, or adjourn the House when there is grave disorder (Rules 373, 374 and 374A of the Lok Sabha Rules). These powers are different from an adjournment motion, which is a tool for the members, not for the Chair.
related: Adjournment motion is available only in the Lok Sabha, not in the Rajya Sabha.
It requires the support of 50 members and discussion of at least 2.5 hours.
Rule 56 of the Lok Sabha Rules covers adjournment motion.
No-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha (Rule 198).
Calling Attention Notice was introduced in India in 1954 and is governed by Rule 197.
Cut motions are of three types: policy cut, economy cut and token cut.
Zero Hour is an Indian innovation and not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure.
Adjournment sine die is done by the Presiding Officer, while prorogation is by the President.
summary: The answer is (a). An Adjournment Motion is introduced in Parliament to draw the attention of the House to a definite matter of urgent public importance, and it is discussed for not less than two and a half hours. It is an extraordinary device, and its admission is treated as a censure of the government.
topic_notes: Parliamentary devices fall into several groups. Question Hour (first hour of a sitting) includes starred questions (oral answer, supplementaries allowed), unstarred (written answer), short notice questions (less than ten days' notice), and questions to private members. Zero Hour is an Indian innovation, not in the Rules, starting at about 12 noon. Motions include: Adjournment Motion (Lok Sabha only, 50 members, 2.5 hours); Calling Attention Notice (a Minister is called on to make a statement on an urgent matter; it is borrowed from India's own practice, not from Britain); No-Confidence Motion (Lok Sabha only, under Rule 198, needs 50 members' support, no reasons need to be stated); Censure Motion (against a Minister or the Council of Ministers for specific policies, with reasons stated); Motion of Thanks on the President's Address; Cut Motions (policy cut, economy cut, token cut); Privilege Motion; Closure Motion (guillotine, kangaroo, closure by compartments); Short Duration Discussion (Rule 193 in Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha Rule 176), with no formal motion or voting; Half-an-Hour Discussion. Resolutions can be private members', government, or statutory. Adjournment sine die is done by the Presiding Officer; prorogation is done by the President. Dissolution only applies to the Lok Sabha. Mention in the Constitution: Article 85 (sessions, prorogation, dissolution), Article 105 (privileges), Article 118 (rules of procedure).

question:
Consider the following statements regarding limitations on the authority of the Indian Parliament :
1. Most of the important laws can be introduced in the Parliament with the prior consent of the President.
2. Parliament has to operate within the jurisdiction earmarked by the Constitution. Which of these statements is/are correct ?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Parliament in India is not sovereign in the British sense. Its authority is limited by a written Constitution with a federal division of powers (Seventh Schedule: Union, State and Concurrent Lists, Art. 246), by Fundamental Rights (Art. 13 bars laws that take away or abridge them), and by judicial review. The basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) also limits the amending power. Other limits include the President's veto and the requirement of special procedures for certain bills. Statement 1 is wrong because prior recommendation or sanction of the President is needed only for specific bills. These include a Money Bill (Art. 117(1)), a bill affecting taxation in which States are interested (Art. 274), bills altering State boundaries or names (Art. 3), and bills involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund (Art. 117(3), recommendation needed for consideration). Under Art. 304(b), a State bill restricting trade needs prior sanction of the President. Most ordinary bills are introduced without any prior consent. So the claim that 'most important laws' need it is an overgeneralisation, and only statement 2 stands.
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect, because only certain categories of bills need prior Presidential consent.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' cannot be right.
Wrong: this picks statement 1, which wrongly says most important laws need prior consent.
Correct: statement 2 states a genuine limitation, and statement 1 is false.
keyfact: Parliament is not sovereign: it must act within the Seventh Schedule and other constitutional limits, and prior Presidential consent applies only to specific bills.
option_notes: Both 1 and 2: it would be right only if prior Presidential consent were needed for most important laws. In fact it applies only to Money Bills, Art. 3 bills, Art. 274 bills and a few others, so this option fails.

Neither 1 nor 2: it would imply Parliament has no constitutional limits. In reality Parliament is bound by the federal division of powers, Fundamental Rights, judicial review and the basic structure doctrine, so this option is wrong.

1 only: this option takes the overgeneralised claim as true. Prior consent is needed for specific bills such as Money Bills (Art. 117), Art. 3 bills and Art. 274 bills, not for most important laws, so it is wrong.

2 only: this is the correct option. Parliament works within its constitutionally earmarked jurisdiction (Art. 245-246, Seventh Schedule), and is also limited by Fundamental Rights, judicial review and the basic structure doctrine.
related: Art. 246 distributes legislative powers between the Union and the States via the Seventh Schedule.
Art. 249 lets Parliament legislate on a State List subject if the Rajya Sabha passes a two-thirds resolution.
Money Bills need the President's recommendation and can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha (Art. 117).
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic structure doctrine.
Art. 3 bills on States' boundaries need the President's recommendation.
Art. 253 empowers Parliament to legislate to implement international treaties.
Art. 13 makes laws that violate Fundamental Rights void.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Prior Presidential recommendation is required only for particular categories of bills, not for most important laws. Facts: Money Bills (Art. 110 and 117(1)) can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation. Bills for the formation of new States or the alteration of boundaries and names (Art. 3) need the President's recommendation. Financial Bills Category I (Art. 117(1)) also need his recommendation for introduction. Bills affecting taxation in which States are interested (Art. 274) need it, and Art. 117(3) requires it for consideration of bills involving expenditure. Ordinary bills such as those on criminal law, labour or education do not need prior consent to be introduced.

2 — Correct: Parliament must legislate within the jurisdiction given by the Constitution. Facts: Art. 246 and the Seventh Schedule divide subjects into the Union List (originally 97, now 98 subjects), the State List (originally 66, now 59) and the Concurrent List (47, now 52). Parliament can legislate on State subjects only in exceptional cases: Art. 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds in the national interest), Art. 250 (Emergency), Art. 252 (States' consent) and Art. 253 (international treaties). Its power is also limited by Fundamental Rights (Art. 13), the basic structure doctrine and judicial review, so it is not a sovereign body.
summary: The answer is (d): only statement 2 is correct. Parliament is a body of limited powers and must work within the legislative lists and other limits set by the Constitution, but most important laws do not need the President's prior consent for introduction, since only specific categories do.
topic_notes: Parliament of India consists of the President, Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha (Art. 79). Its powers are wide but limited. Main limitations: (1) Federal distribution of powers under the Seventh Schedule, with the Union List (98 subjects), State List (59) and Concurrent List (52). (2) Fundamental Rights: Art. 13(2) bars laws that take away or abridge them. (3) Judicial review by the Supreme Court and High Courts (Arts. 32, 226). (4) Basic structure doctrine from Kesavananda Bharati (1973), reaffirmed in Minerva Mills (1980). (5) Presidential veto and the requirement of assent (Art. 111). (6) Special procedure for certain bills, such as the President's prior recommendation for Money Bills, Art. 3 bills and Art. 274 bills. (7) Constitutional provisions such as the need for a special majority and State ratification for some amendments (Art. 368). Parliament can legislate on State subjects only under Art. 249, 250, 252, 253, 356 and 357. Residuary powers rest with Parliament (Art. 248). Money Bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha may only recommend changes within 14 days. Art. 368 empowers Parliament to amend the Constitution, but not its basic structure. Parliamentary privileges (Arts. 105, 194) and the anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule) are other topics worth revising.

question: anenee” studies suggest the theory le
options: All the continents were settled with human societies at about the same time
Farming societies developed before bunting and gathering
The earliest human evolved in the Rift valley in East Africa
The wheel was in use in all ancient societies er (APFC) Exam 2012 Question Paper
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: The question text is partly garbled by OCR. It appears to ask what archaeological or genetic studies suggest, and the only option consistent with accepted evidence is (c). Fossils of early hominins such as Australopithecus afarensis ('Lucy', Hadar, Ethiopia, about 3.2 million years ago), the Turkana Boy (Homo erectus, Kenya) and Olduvai Gorge (Tanzania, the Leakeys' finds) all come from the East African Rift Valley. Genetic studies of mitochondrial DNA ('Mitochondrial Eve') and Y-chromosome data show the greatest human genetic diversity in Africa. This points to an African origin of Homo sapiens roughly 300,000 years ago (Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, is the oldest known site), followed by migration out of Africa about 70,000-60,000 years ago. Option (a) is wrong because continents were settled at very different times: Australia about 50,000 years ago, the Americas about 15,000-20,000 years ago, and Pacific islands only in recent millennia. Option (b) is wrong because hunting-gathering was the original mode of subsistence, and farming began only in the Neolithic, about 10,000 years ago. Option (d) is wrong because the wheel was not universal; the pre-Columbian Americas and Australia lacked it for practical use.
explanations: Correct. Fossil evidence (Lucy, Turkana Boy, Olduvai) and genetic diversity data point to an African origin of humans, with the East African Rift Valley a key site, supporting the Out of Africa theory.
Incorrect. Hunting and gathering was the earliest subsistence pattern, lasting for hundreds of thousands of years. Farming began only with the Neolithic revolution, about 10,000 years ago.
Incorrect as a universal claim. Settlement times differ greatly: Africa and Eurasia are far older than the Americas, Australia and Oceania.
Incorrect. The wheel appeared about 3500 BCE in Mesopotamia. Many ancient societies, such as the pre-Columbian Americas and Aboriginal Australia, did not use it.
keyfact: Out of Africa: the earliest humans evolved in Africa (East African Rift Valley) and later spread worldwide; hunting-gathering preceded farming.
option_notes: Settlement of all continents at about the same time did not happen. Humans moved out of Africa into Asia and Europe by about 1.8 million years ago (Homo erectus), and Homo sapiens reached Australia about 50,000 years ago and the Americas about 15,000-20,000 years ago. Antarctica was never settled until modern times, and islands such as New Zealand were settled only about 1300 CE.

Farming societies came after hunting and gathering. The Neolithic revolution began about 10,000 BCE in the Fertile Crescent, with wheat and barley and sheep and goat domestication. In India, Mehrgarh (Baluchistan, about 7000 BCE) is an early farming site. The term 'Neolithic Revolution' was coined by V. Gordon Childe. Before that, Palaeolithic and Mesolithic people lived by hunting, fishing and gathering.

The Rift Valley is the Great Rift Valley of East Africa, formed by tectonic plate divergence. It holds key hominin sites: Olduvai Gorge (Tanzania), Koobi Fora and Lake Turkana (Kenya) and Hadar and Afar (Ethiopia). Fossils include Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis, 3.2 mya), Homo habilis and Homo erectus. This supports the Out of Africa model of human origins.

The wheel was first used for pottery and then for transport in Mesopotamia (Sumer), about 3500 BCE. The Indus Valley people used wheeled carts and toy models. Pre-Columbian American civilisations such as the Maya and Inca knew the wheel only in toys and had no draught animals to pull carts. Aboriginal Australians had no wheel, so it was not universal.
related: Out of Africa theory: Homo sapiens originated in Africa about 300,000 years ago.
Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) was found at Hadar, Ethiopia, in 1974.
Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, was explored by Louis and Mary Leakey.
Neolithic revolution began about 10,000 BCE in the Fertile Crescent; term coined by V. Gordon Childe.
Mehrgarh (Baluchistan) is the earliest known farming site in the Indian subcontinent, about 7000 BCE.
Bhimbetka rock shelters (Madhya Pradesh) are a UNESCO World Heritage Site with Palaeolithic to Mesolithic paintings.
Homo erectus was the first hominin to use fire and migrate out of Africa.
Svante Pääbo received the 2022 Nobel Prize in Medicine for work on Neanderthal genomes.
summary: The answer is (c). Fossil and genetic studies support the 'Out of Africa' theory, which holds that the earliest humans evolved in Africa, with the East African Rift Valley as a key region, and later spread to other continents. The other options contradict well-established archaeological evidence.
topic_notes: Human origins and prehistory form a recurring theme. The dominant model is 'Out of Africa' (Recent African Origin), which says anatomically modern Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago (Jebel Irhoud, Morocco; Omo Kibish and Herto, Ethiopia) and dispersed across the world from about 70,000 years ago. The rival 'Multiregional' hypothesis says archaic populations evolved in parallel across regions, but genetic data favour Out of Africa. Hominin sequence: Australopithecus (about 4-2 mya), Homo habilis (the 'handy man', stone tools, about 2.4 mya), Homo erectus (used fire, first to leave Africa, about 1.9 mya), Homo neanderthalensis (Europe and West Asia, interbred with Homo sapiens, so non-Africans carry 1-2% Neanderthal DNA) and Homo sapiens. Denisovans were identified from a Siberian cave. Stone Age phases: Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age; hunting-gathering, chipped tools, fire), Mesolithic (microliths, bow and arrow, early domestication of the dog) and Neolithic (farming, pottery, polished tools, settled life). Indian sites: Bhimbetka (rock shelters, Madhya Pradesh), Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu, Middle Palaeolithic tools about 385,000 years old), Mehrgarh (early Neolithic), Burzahom (Kashmir; pit dwellings), Chirand (Bihar) and Koldihwa (Uttar Pradesh; early rice). The Bronze Age and the Chalcolithic followed, then the Iron Age. Key features of civilisation include writing, cities, the wheel (Sumer, about 3500 BCE) and metallurgy. Related concepts include Mitochondrial Eve and Y-chromosomal Adam, and the use of radiocarbon dating (up to about 50,000 years), potassium-argon dating (for older sites) and DNA analysis. Svante Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Medicine for work on ancient genomes.

question: Which term is used to describe the spread of Buddhism from India through Southeast Asia ?
subject: Computers
detail: Cultural diffusion means the spread of cultural elements such as religion, language, technology, art and architecture between societies, through trade, missions, migration, conquest or travel. Buddhism spread from the Gangetic plains through several routes. Emperor Ashoka (3rd century BCE) sent missions after the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra. His son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitta carried Buddhism to Sri Lanka, and Sona and Uttara were sent to Suvarnabhumi (Southeast Asia, probably Lower Burma). Indian merchants and Brahmin and Buddhist monks later carried Buddhist and Hindu culture to Funan, Champa, Srivijaya, Angkor and Java. Borobudur in Java (8th-9th c.) and Angkor Wat in Cambodia (Hindu, later Buddhist) show this influence. Theravada became dominant in Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Sri Lanka. Elimination: social mobility is movement between social strata; ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own standards; interdependence is mutual reliance among nations or groups. None of these describes the spread of a religion, so only cultural diffusion fits.
explanations: Incorrect: social mobility refers to movement of individuals or groups between social classes or statuses, not to the spread of a religion.
Correct: cultural diffusion is the spread of religion, ideas and customs from one culture to another, as Buddhism spread from India to Southeast Asia.
Incorrect: ethnocentrism is the belief in the superiority of one's own culture and judging others by its standards; it is an attitude, not a process of spread.
Incorrect: interdependence means mutual dependence among countries or groups, usually economic or political, and does not describe the transmission of a religion.
keyfact: Spread of a religion or culture from one society to another = cultural diffusion; Ashoka's missions spread Buddhism to Sri Lanka and Suvarnabhumi.
option_notes: Social mobility is the movement of individuals or families up or down a society's social or economic hierarchy. It can be vertical (change of class) or horizontal (change of job at the same level), and intergenerational or intragenerational. Open systems such as class societies have high mobility, while closed systems such as caste in its rigid form have low mobility. Sociologists such as Pitirim Sorokin studied it.

Cultural diffusion is the spread of cultural items such as ideas, styles, religions and technologies between individuals or societies. Its forms include direct contact (trade, war, migration), indirect diffusion through intermediaries, and stimulus diffusion. Examples: Buddhism to East and Southeast Asia, the Silk Road exchanges, Indian numerals reaching Europe via the Arabs, and the Columbian Exchange. The term comes from anthropology and sociology.

Ethnocentrism is evaluating other cultures by the standards of one's own and regarding one's own group as superior. The term was popularised by William Graham Sumner in 1906. It is contrasted with cultural relativism, which judges a culture by its own values. It can lead to stereotyping, prejudice and discrimination, and is a standard concept in sociology and anthropology.

Interdependence is the mutual reliance of states, economies or people on one another. In international relations, Keohane and Nye developed 'complex interdependence' (1977), in which trade, institutions and transnational links reduce the use of force. Globalisation increases economic interdependence through supply chains and trade, as in the WTO system and regional blocs.
related: Ashoka sent his son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitta to Sri Lanka.
Third Buddhist Council was held at Pataliputra under Ashoka, presided by Moggaliputta Tissa.
Borobudur in Java was built by the Sailendra dynasty.
Theravada Buddhism dominates Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia.
Ethnocentrism was popularised by William Graham Sumner.
Sanskritisation is a term coined by M.N. Srinivas.
Fa-Hien, Xuanzang and I-tsing were Chinese pilgrims to India.
summary: The answer is (b) Cultural diffusion. It is the term for the spread of beliefs, practices, art and ideas from one society to another, and Buddhism's transmission from India to Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Indonesia and beyond is a standard example.
topic_notes: Spread of Buddhism: The Buddha (c. 563-483 BCE; some date later) gave his first sermon at Sarnath (Dhammachakkapravartana). The Buddhist councils were: First at Rajagriha (Ajatashatru, Mahakassapa presiding), Second at Vaishali (Kalashoka), Third at Pataliputra (Ashoka, Moggaliputta Tissa), and Fourth at Kashmir (Kanishka, Vasumitra/Ashvaghosha; Mahayana split). Ashoka's Dhamma missionaries went to Sri Lanka (Mahinda, Sanghamitta), Suvarnabhumi (Sona and Uttara), Gandhara, Kashmir, Mahisamandala, Yavana lands and others. Sri Lanka became the centre of Theravada (Pali canon written down at Aluvihara in the 1st c. BCE). Southeast Asia: Theravada in Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia; Mahayana and Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms in Srivijaya (Sumatra), the Sailendras of Java (Borobudur), Champa and Khmer (Angkor, Bayon of Jayavarman VII). East Asia: Buddhism entered China around the 1st c. CE through the Silk Road; Fa-Hien (Gupta period), Xuanzang (Harsha) and I-tsing came to India. Korea and Japan received it from China (Japan c. 6th c.). Tibet received Vajrayana through Padmasambhava and Atisha. Nalanda, Vikramashila and Odantapuri were main learning centres. Related sociology terms: acculturation (adopting traits through contact), assimilation, syncretism, cultural lag (Ogburn), cultural relativism, and Sanskritisation (M.N. Srinivas), which is internal diffusion within India.

question: The main objective of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 is to safeguard the interests of the workers engaged in :
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 was enacted to prevent exploitation of labour in employments where workers are unorganised, have little collective bargaining strength and are paid very low wages. It applies to the 'scheduled employments' listed in the Schedule to the Act. Both the Centre and the States are 'appropriate governments' and may add employments to the Schedule. The Act empowers the appropriate government to fix and revise minimum wages, with a revision at intervals not exceeding five years. It works through advisory boards, a Central Advisory Board and committees or sub-committees. It follows Article 43 (living wage) of the Directive Principles. The Act came out of the ILO Minimum Wage-Fixing Machinery Convention, 1928 (No. 26). Elimination: (b) is opposite, since organised-sector workers are protected by collective bargaining and industrial laws. (c) is too narrow, because the Act covers many non-industrial employments. (d) is also too narrow, because agriculture is only one scheduled employment. The broad purpose is to protect unorganised and sweated labour, so (a) is the best answer. The Act is now subsumed in the Code on Wages, 2019.
explanations: Correct: the Act's core objective is to protect unorganised, sweated and low-bargaining-power workers by statutory minimum wages.
Incorrect: organised-sector workers have unions, collective bargaining and other protective laws, so they are not the main target.
Incorrect: too narrow, as the Act covers scheduled employments beyond industry, such as agriculture, construction and stone breaking.
Incorrect: agriculture is just one scheduled employment, not the Act's overall focus; the question asks for the broad category.
keyfact: Minimum Wages Act, 1948 protects unorganised, sweated labour by statutory wage fixation; revision within five years.
option_notes: The unorganised sector comprises enterprises and workers without formal job security, social security or collective bargaining. It makes up over 90% of India's workforce. It is covered by laws such as the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 and the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. Examples include agricultural labour, construction workers, domestic workers and street vendors.

The organised sector consists of registered enterprises with regular, formal employment, with job security, fixed wages and social security (EPF, ESI, gratuity). Workers are usually unionised and are covered by the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and factory laws. It employs under 10% of India's workforce. It is not the main target of minimum wage law.

The industrial sector covers manufacturing, mining, construction and utilities. Industrial workers are covered by the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Factories Act, 1948 and related laws. Minimum wages extend beyond industry, so this option is too restrictive as the Act's main objective.

Agricultural employment was added to the Schedule of the Minimum Wages Act, which covers farm labour in cultivation and allied work. Minimum wages here are fixed by State governments. Agriculture is a major unorganised employment, but it is only one part of the Act's coverage.
related: Minimum Wages Act, 1948 was enacted under Article 43 (DPSP) spirit.
Minimum wages must be revised at intervals not exceeding five years.
Both Centre and State are appropriate governments for fixing minimum wages.
Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) upheld the Act's validity.
Code on Wages, 2019 subsumed four wage-related laws including this Act.
The Code on Wages, 2019 introduced a national floor wage.
Fair Wages Committee (1948) defined minimum, fair and living wage.
ILO Convention No. 26 (1928) relates to minimum wage-fixing machinery.
summary: The answer is (a) Unorganized sector. The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 aims to protect workers in sweated and unorganised employments, where bargaining power is weak and exploitation is common, by letting the appropriate government fix statutory minimum wage rates.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 received assent on 15 March 1948. It originally covered employments such as woollen carpet-making, rice, flour and dal mills, tobacco manufacture, plantations, oil mills, stone breaking, road building, mica works and public motor transport. Agriculture was added in 1950s. It extends to the whole of India. The appropriate government (Centre or State) fixes minimum wages for scheduled employments, with different rates for different zones, occupations, age groups and sizes of establishment. Wages may be fixed by the time rate, piece rate, guaranteed time rate or overtime rate. Two methods are used: the committee method and the notification method. Revision must be done at intervals of not more than five years. The Central Advisory Board coordinates advice between Centre and States and is tripartite. Concepts to know: Minimum wage (covers basic needs of the worker), fair wage (between minimum and living wage), and living wage (a decent standard of living including education, health and comfort). The Fair Wages Committee, 1948 defined these. The Supreme Court in Raptakos Brett (1992) listed components of a need-based minimum wage, and in Workmen v. Reptakos Brett it added 25% for children's education, medical needs and recreation. In Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955), the Court upheld the Act as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(6). The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumed four laws: the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. It introduced a floor wage set by the Centre.

question: Which one of the following expresses the relation between normal price and market price ?
options: Market price is greater than normal price
Market price is equal to normal price
Market price tends to be equal to normal price
Market price is lesser than normal price
subject: Current Affairs
detail: In Marshallian economics, market price is the price that prevails at a given moment in a market, determined by the demand and supply of that time (very short run, where supply is nearly fixed). Normal price, also called long-run equilibrium price, is the price at which supply fully adjusts to demand, so that the firm earns only normal profit and has no incentive to enter or exit. Marshall compared the two to a ball in a bowl: it oscillates, but gravitates to the bottom. Market price can be above normal price when demand rises or supply falls, drawing in new supply and pushing price down. It can be below normal price when there is a glut, causing supply to contract and price to rise. So the relationship is one of a tendency toward equality over time, not a fixed inequality. Options (a) and (d) state a permanent inequality, which is wrong because market price fluctuates on both sides. Option (b) states exact equality, which holds only at the moment of long-run equilibrium. Hence (c) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: market price is above normal price only temporarily, such as when demand surges; it is not always greater.
Wrong: the two are equal only at the instant of long-run equilibrium; in general market price fluctuates around normal price.
Correct: market price fluctuates but gravitates toward normal price as supply adjusts to demand over time.
Wrong: market price is below normal price only during gluts or demand slumps, and it is not always lesser.
keyfact: Market price fluctuates around and tends toward normal (long-run equilibrium) price.
option_notes: Market price above normal price occurs when demand exceeds supply in the short run. Abnormal profits attract new supply, which pushes price back down toward normal price. Market price is a short-period concept, determined by the demand and supply prevailing at the time. In the very short period supply is fixed, so demand dominates price determination, as with perishable goods such as fish or vegetables.

Exact equality of market price and normal price holds only at long-run equilibrium, where firms earn normal profit and there is no entry or exit. Marshall treated normal price as a centre of gravity. Perfect equality is an ideal, not a continuous reality, because demand and supply conditions keep changing.

Market price tends toward normal price. This is Marshall's idea of a stable equilibrium: deviations set up forces that restore the long-run price. Marshall introduced the time-period classification of market period, short run and long run, in Principles of Economics (1890). Normal price is the long-run supply price, which covers cost of production including normal profit.

Market price below normal price arises in a glut, when supply exceeds demand, giving losses. Firms then reduce output or exit, supply falls, and price rises back toward normal price. Perishable goods sold at the end of the day are a typical example. It is a temporary deviation, not a permanent rule.
related: Normal price is the long-run equilibrium price at which firms earn only normal profit.
Market price is a very short-run price determined by the demand and supply of the moment.
Marshall's Principles of Economics was published in 1890.
Marshall likened demand and supply to the two blades of a pair of scissors.
In the market period, the supply of perishable goods is perfectly inelastic.
In long-run perfect competition, price equals minimum average cost.
Quasi-rent is the short-run surplus over variable cost earned by fixed factors.
summary: The answer is (c). Normal price is the long-run equilibrium price set by demand and supply (Marshall), and the market price, which fluctuates day to day, gravitates toward it. The market price tends to equal the normal price but is rarely exactly equal at any given time.
topic_notes: Price determination under Marshall depends on the time period. In the market period (very short run) supply is fixed, so price is demand-determined; the supply curve is vertical for perishables, or limited by stock for durables. In the short run, supply can be changed only by varying variable inputs, and the plant is fixed. Firms may earn super-normal profit or incur losses. In the long run all factors are variable and firms can enter or exit. Price equals minimum average cost in perfect competition, and firms earn only normal profit. This long-run equilibrium price is the normal price. Marshall's analogy: demand and supply are the two blades of a pair of scissors; time is the key to the analysis. Marshall's Principles of Economics was published in 1890. Normal profit is the minimum reward to the entrepreneur and is counted as a cost; super-normal (abnormal) profit is the surplus above it. Quasi-rent is the short-run surplus over variable cost to fixed factors. Related angles: equilibrium price is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; a rise in demand raises price and quantity; a rise in supply lowers price and raises quantity. Stable equilibrium restores itself after a disturbance, whereas unstable equilibrium does not. The cobweb theorem deals with lagged supply adjustments in agriculture. Market price for perishables is determined mostly by demand; for durables the seller can withhold stock.

question:
Consider the following statements about heritage :
1. Heritage is that which has been or may be inherited.
2. Heritage is anything given or received to be a proper possession. Which of these statements is/are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The word heritage comes from the idea of inheritance: what is passed from past generations to the present and then handed on to the future. Dictionary definitions match both statements. Heritage is 'that which has been or may be inherited' (property, traditions, qualities), and also 'anything given or received to be a proper possession', that is a legacy or birthright. UNESCO divides heritage into cultural (monuments, groups of buildings, sites), natural (physical, biological and geological formations) and mixed. Cultural heritage can be tangible (movable or immovable) or intangible (oral traditions, performing arts, rituals, festivals, traditional crafts). The World Heritage Convention was adopted in 1972 and came into force in 1975; India ratified it in 1977. The Convention on Intangible Cultural Heritage dates from 2003. Elimination logic: option (a) is garbled by OCR and must mean '1 only', which wrongly rejects statement 2. Option (b) wrongly rejects statement 1. Option (d) rejects both and is clearly wrong. Because both statements are standard definitions, (c) is correct.
explanations: (a) Wrong: the option text is garbled, but it would mean statement 1 only. That leaves out statement 2, which is also a valid definition.
(b) Wrong: statement 1 is also correct, since heritage is what is or may be inherited, so '2 only' is incomplete.
(c) Correct: both statements are accepted definitions of heritage as inheritance and as a proper possession received.
(d) Wrong: both statements are correct, so rejecting both is false.
keyfact: Heritage is what is inherited and received as a proper possession; both statements are correct, so the answer is (c).
option_notes: Option (a), read as 'statement 1 only', would hold that heritage is just what is inherited. That is only part of the definition, because heritage is also a legacy received as one's own. The concept spans cultural heritage (monuments, art, traditions), natural heritage (landscapes, ecosystems) and mixed heritage. UNESCO's 1972 World Heritage Convention governs sites of outstanding universal value. India has over 40 inscribed sites, including the Taj Mahal and Kaziranga.

Option (b), '2 only', would hold that heritage is just a proper possession given or received. It is true but incomplete, since it omits the notion of inheritance across generations. Heritage law in India includes the AMASR Act 1958 (amended 2010) and the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972. The Archaeological Survey of India, founded in 1861 by Alexander Cunningham, protects centrally protected monuments. INTACH, founded in 1984, works on conserving built and living heritage.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is correct. Heritage is inherited legacy and a rightful possession handed down. It includes tangible heritage (monuments, artefacts, sites) and intangible heritage (oral traditions, performing arts, festivals, crafts), as the UNESCO 2003 convention recognises. Examples from India on the intangible list include Kutiyattam, Vedic chanting, Ramlila, Yoga, Kumbh Mela, Durga Puja in Kolkata and Garba of Gujarat. Heritage is meant to be preserved for future generations.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', is wrong because both statements are valid definitions. It would deny that heritage has anything to do with inheritance or possession. The term derives from Old French 'heritage', from 'heriter' (to inherit), and the concept underpins heritage conservation policy worldwide. National heritage bodies include the ASI, the National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities, and the Ministry of Culture. UNESCO's World Heritage Committee decides on inscriptions each year.
related: UNESCO World Heritage Convention adopted in 1972; India ratified it in 1977.
ASI was founded in 1861 by Alexander Cunningham.
AMASR Act 1958 was amended in 2010 to create the National Monuments Authority.
INTACH was established in 1984.
Convention on Intangible Cultural Heritage dates from 2003.
Ajanta, Ellora, Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal were India's first World Heritage Sites (1983).
HRIDAY scheme (2015) focused on heritage city development.
statements: 1 — Correct: This is the standard dictionary definition of heritage as inheritance. Heritage covers what earlier generations leave to later ones, including property, traditions, values, monuments and natural features. It is passed down, preserved and transmitted onward. UNESCO's framework treats heritage as a legacy from the past, held in the present and kept for the benefit of future generations. It includes cultural, natural and mixed heritage. India has 40+ World Heritage Sites, and heritage can be tangible or intangible.

2 — Correct: This is the second dictionary sense of heritage, a thing given or received as a proper possession, such as a legacy, birthright or portion. It stresses that heritage belongs to a community or person by right of descent. The idea underlies laws such as the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, and the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972, which treat heritage as a national possession to be protected. Heritage here includes monuments, art, crafts, language and customs.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. Heritage is whatever has been or may be inherited, and also whatever is given or received as a proper possession, covering both tangible and intangible legacies passed between generations.
topic_notes: Heritage means the legacy of physical artefacts and intangible attributes that a society inherits from past generations, maintains in the present and bestows for the benefit of future generations. Types: (1) Cultural heritage, tangible (movable such as paintings, manuscripts and coins; immovable such as monuments and archaeological sites) and intangible (oral traditions, performing arts, social practices, rituals, festive events, traditional craftsmanship). (2) Natural heritage: natural features, geological formations and habitats of threatened species. (3) Mixed heritage, with both cultural and natural values. International framework: the UNESCO Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage was adopted in 1972, and the World Heritage List is maintained by the World Heritage Committee. The Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage was adopted in 2003. India ratified the 1972 convention in 1977. The first Indian sites inscribed (1983) were Ajanta Caves, Ellora Caves, Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal. India's first natural site was Kaziranga (1985). Dholavira and Ramappa Temple were inscribed in 2021, and Santiniketan in 2023. Indian laws and bodies: the ASI (1861), the AMASR Act 1958 with its 2010 amendment creating the National Monuments Authority, the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, INTACH (1984) and the National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities (2007). The Ministry of Culture handles heritage policy. Related schemes include HRIDAY (heritage city development, 2015) and the Adopt a Heritage scheme (2017), now called Apni Dharohar Apni Pehchaan.

question: Bancassurance is :
options: An insurance scheme to insure bank deposits
An insurance scheme exclusively for bank employees
Acomposite financial service offering both bank and insurance products
A bank deposit scheme exclusively for employees of insurance companies 18 (Contd.) rte tet ——— Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner
subject: Insurance
detail: Bancassurance (bank + assurance, a term from France in the 1980s) is a distribution partnership under which an insurer uses a bank's branch network, customer base and relationship managers to sell life, general and health insurance. The bank earns commission or fee income, the insurer gains reach, and the customer gets one-stop financial services. In India, IRDA (Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority, now IRDAI) allowed banks to enter insurance in 2000 after the IRDA Act, 1999. Banks can act as corporate agents (the earlier cap was 1 insurer per category, relaxed in 2024 to allow up to 9 tie-ups in each of life, general and health), or set up insurance subsidiaries or joint ventures with RBI approval. Examples include SBI Life, HDFC Life, ICICI Prudential and Canara HSBC OBC Life. Elimination: (a) confuses it with deposit insurance, which is the job of DICGC. (b) and (d) wrongly restrict the scheme to employees; bancassurance is aimed at the general public.
explanations: Wrong: insuring bank deposits is deposit insurance, provided by DICGC (a subsidiary of RBI), not bancassurance.
Wrong: bancassurance is for bank customers at large, not a scheme limited to bank employees.
