subject: Social Security
detail: The question is about human development, the idea that development means expanding people's capabilities and choices, not just raising income. The UNDP Human Development Report (first published 1990, based on Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen) introduced the Human Development Index (HDI), which combines health (life expectancy), education (mean and expected years of schooling) and standard of living (GNI per capita). Delivering human development needs partnership between the State, the market and civil society. NGOs have grassroots reach, flexible structures and specialised skills, so they are used in literacy, health, microfinance, SHGs and disaster relief. Their skills can therefore be put to work in society, which makes statement 1 correct. Statement 2 is also sound. Periodic review of policies and programmes exposes gaps in the delivery system, such as regional, gender and social disparities, and learning from international experience (for example Kerala-style models, Scandinavian social security, Brazil's Bolsa Familia, Bangladesh's Grameen model) helps fix those gaps. Both statements are positive, non-extreme and consistent with the human-development framework, so option (d) is correct. Options (a), (b) and (c) wrongly reject at least one valid statement.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 2 is also correct; review and international experience do help fill internal gaps.
(b) is wrong because statement 1 is also correct; NGO skills can be used in society.
(c) is wrong because both statements are correct, so rejecting both is incorrect.
(d) is correct: both NGO participation and review combined with international experience support human development.
keyfact: Human development = expanding capabilities (UNDP, 1990); NGO partnership plus review and international learning both support it.
option_notes: Only statement 1: this would mean NGO skills are useful but system review and international learning are not. That is wrong. NGOs are important partners in development delivery, such as SEWA in livelihoods and Pratham in education, but they are one among several tools. Government reviews, such as NITI Aayog evaluations, and international comparisons are equally part of the policy cycle.

Only statement 2: this would imply reviews and international experience help but NGOs do not. That is wrong. NGOs are regarded as vital in participatory development, and the 12th Plan and NITI Aayog's NGO-Darpan portal promote voluntary-sector partnership in service delivery.

Neither 1 nor 2: this would reject both approaches. It contradicts the standard human development approach of UNDP, which stresses participation, partnerships, capacity building and cross-country learning. UNDP's Human Development Reports regularly highlight civil society and shared global experience as drivers of progress.

Both 1 and 2: the correct option. Human development is a people-centred approach introduced by UNDP in 1990, measured with the HDI. Achieving it needs the State, markets and civil society (including NGOs) to work together, with regular review of programmes and use of best practices from other countries to remove gaps in delivery.
related: The first Human Development Report was published by UNDP in 1990.
HDI dimensions: health, education and standard of living.
Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen are the architects of the human development concept.
MPI was introduced in 2010 by UNDP and OPHI.
CAPART was set up in 1986 to fund rural voluntary organisations.
FCRA 2010 regulates foreign contributions to NGOs in India.
The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) decentralised planning and development.
NGO-Darpan is the NITI Aayog portal for NGO registration.
statements: 1 — Correct: NGOs bring grassroots reach and specialised skills that can be used in service delivery and in building capabilities. NGOs are non-profit, voluntary, citizen-based organisations. In India they work in education, health, microfinance, environment and rights, and are registered under the Societies Registration Act 1860, Indian Trusts Act or Section 8 of the Companies Act 2013. CAPART, set up in 1986, funds rural NGOs. The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA) 2010 regulates their foreign funding. The Planning Commission set up a Voluntary Action Cell and the NGO-Partnership System (NGO-PS, NITI Aayog portal). Examples include Pratham, SEWA, Goonj and Akshaya Patra. The 12th Five-Year Plan stressed partnerships with the voluntary sector.

2 — Correct: Reviewing systems and borrowing from international experience helps identify and fill internal gaps. Human development is measured by the HDI, with the Human Development Report published yearly by UNDP since 1990. Related indices are IHDI (inequality-adjusted), GDI (gender development), GII (gender inequality) and MPI (multidimensional poverty, 2010, with OPHI). Mahbub ul Haq (Pakistan) and Amartya Sen developed the concept, which is based on Sen's capability approach. India ranks in the medium human development group (about 134th in 2023-24). Cross-country learning has shaped schemes such as MGNREGA, the mid-day meal and the Right to Education Act 2009.
summary: The answer is (d) – both statements are correct. NGO participation helps bring skills into the service of society, and review and international experience can help fill internal gaps in the system, so both support human development.
topic_notes: Human development means widening people's choices and building capabilities so they can lead long, healthy and creative lives. The concept was developed by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen, building on Sen's capability approach, and the first UNDP Human Development Report appeared in 1990. The HDI has three dimensions: health (life expectancy at birth), education (mean years and expected years of schooling) and standard of living (GNI per capita, PPP). It is the geometric mean of the three normalised indices (since 2010). Related indices are IHDI, GDI, GII and MPI. The HDI groups countries as very high, high, medium and low. India is in the medium category, and Switzerland, Norway and Iceland are typically at the top. Human development differs from human capital, which treats people as a means of production, and from welfare approaches, which treat them as passive recipients. Key India links include the Kerala model, the National Human Development Reports (Planning Commission), the Right to Education Act 2009, the National Health Mission, MGNREGA 2005 and the Public Distribution System. Partnerships with NGOs and civil society, decentralisation through Panchayati Raj (73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992) and participatory planning are major tools. NGOs can fill gaps in delivery, advocacy, monitoring and social audit. Regular review and evaluation (for example by the Independent Evaluation Office, established 2013) and borrowing international experience help correct internal gaps. UNDP's Sustainable Development Goals (2015) have taken the human development agenda forward through the 2030 Agenda.

question:
Which of the following are the main causes of the slow rate of growth of per capita income in India ?
1. High rate of capital formation
2. High level of fiscal deficits 3... High rate of growth of population
subject: Indian Economy
detail: Per capita income is national income divided by population, so it grows only when national income grows faster than population. Slow growth results from two broad factors. The first is a fast-growing population, which inflates the denominator, absorbs savings in consumption and social needs, and lowers savings and investment per head. The second is persistent high fiscal deficits, which raise government borrowing, crowd out private investment, raise interest costs and debt-servicing burdens, squeeze productive public capital spending, and can feed inflation. These are listed as structural weaknesses in standard textbooks. Capital formation (investment) is the engine of growth in Harrod-Domar and similar models, so a high rate raises output and per capita income. Indeed, India's problem has historically been low capital formation and low savings, especially in the early planning period. Statement 1 therefore reverses the logic. Elimination: statement 1 is wrong, so options (a), (b) and (c) fall away, which leaves (d). The question is a conceptual one and not a statistical one. For reference, India's gross capital formation is about 30-33 percent of GDP in recent years, and the population growth rate has fallen to roughly 1 percent a year or lower.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, and a high rate of capital formation is a growth-enhancing factor, not a cause of slow growth.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is incorrect, even though statement 2 is correct.
Wrong: it includes statement 1 and omits fiscal deficits, which is a genuine cause of slow growth.
Correct: high fiscal deficits and a high population growth rate both depress per capita income growth, and capital formation is not a drag.
keyfact: Capital formation raises growth; high fiscal deficits and rapid population growth depress per capita income growth.
option_notes: Option (a) claims that capital formation, fiscal deficits and population growth are all causes. It is wrong because capital formation is a driver of growth. Capital formation means net additions to the stock of capital goods and is funded by savings. The Harrod-Domar model gives growth = savings rate divided by the capital-output ratio. India's investment rate peaked at about 38 percent of GDP in 2007-08. Only two of the three listed factors are true drags on growth.

Option (b) pairs capital formation with fiscal deficits. It is wrong because it includes capital formation and leaves out population growth. The fiscal deficit is the gap between total expenditure and total receipts excluding borrowing. Under the FRBM Act 2003 the target was 3 percent of GDP, and revised roadmaps have set fresh glide paths since then. High deficits crowd out private investment, but population growth is also a key cause, so this pairing is incomplete and wrong.

Option (c) pairs capital formation with population growth. It is wrong because capital formation is not a cause of slow growth. Population growth is a true cause: India had about 121 crore people at the 2011 Census, with a decadal growth of 17.7 percent. This option also omits the fiscal deficit, which is a recognised constraint on public investment, so it is incorrect.

Option (d) is the correct one. It names high fiscal deficits and high population growth as the causes of slow per capita income growth. Fiscal deficits reduce public savings and investment, and population growth reduces income per head. Per capita income is NNP or GDP divided by population. India's per capita net national income at current prices was about Rs 1.85 lakh in 2022-23. Capital formation itself is not a drag, so statement 1 is excluded.
related: Per capita income = National income divided by total population.
Hindu rate of growth (about 3.5 percent) was a term coined by Prof. Raj Krishna.
The FRBM Act was enacted in 2003 and targets a fiscal deficit of 3 percent of GDP.
The Harrod-Domar model stresses the savings rate and capital-output ratio in growth.
India's population as per Census 2011 was 121.09 crore, with a decadal growth of 17.64 percent.
National accounts in India are compiled by the NSO under MoSPI, with base year 2011-12.
Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: High capital formation promotes growth and raises per capita income; low capital formation is the real constraint. Capital formation means additions to the stock of physical capital (machinery, buildings, infrastructure, inventories), funded by domestic savings and foreign capital. It is measured as Gross Capital Formation or Gross Fixed Capital Formation as a percentage of GDP. In India it rose from about 10-12 percent in 1950-51 to about 35-38 percent at its 2007-08 peak, and has been around 30-33 percent recently. The incremental capital-output ratio (ICOR) links investment to growth, and the Harrod-Domar model stresses the savings rate. Higher capital formation therefore means faster growth.

2 — Correct: Large fiscal deficits crowd out private investment, raise interest and debt burdens and reduce public capital spending, so growth slows. The fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowing. The FRBM Act 2003 set targets to reduce it, aiming at 3 percent of GDP, and the N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP anchor of 60 percent for general government. It rose sharply to 9.2 percent in 2020-21 because of COVID-19, and the Centre targets about 4.5 percent by 2025-26. Persistent deficits cause revenue deficits and inflationary pressure, which hurt growth.

3 — Correct: Rapid population growth raises the denominator in per capita income and diverts resources into consumption, so it holds down per capita income growth. India's population grew at about 2.2 percent a year in the 1960s-70s, and the decadal growth rate fell to 17.7 percent in 2001-2011. The 2011 Census population was 121 crore, and the UN estimates say India overtook China in 2023 as the most populous country. The total fertility rate is about 2.0 (NFHS-5), which is below the replacement level of 2.1. The National Population Policy 2000 sought to stabilise the population.
summary: The answer is (d) 2 and 3 only. A high level of fiscal deficits and a high rate of population growth hold back per capita income growth. A high rate of capital formation speeds up growth, so it cannot be a cause of slow growth.
topic_notes: Per capita income is national income divided by mid-year population, so it grows only when output grows faster than population. India's per capita income was stagnant under colonial rule, and the 'Hindu rate of growth' of about 3.5 percent (a term coined by Raj Krishna) described 1950-80, which gave only about 1.2-1.5 percent growth in per capita income. Growth accelerated after the 1980s and especially after the 1991 reforms, reaching 8-9 percent in 2003-08. Causes of slow growth in per capita income include rapid population growth, low savings and investment, low productivity in agriculture, which employs a large share of the workforce, large fiscal deficits, weak infrastructure, inequality, unemployment and underemployment, and technological backwardness. Demographic ideas include the demographic transition and the demographic dividend, since India has a large working-age share. Key population facts: the 2011 Census counted 121.09 crore people, the sex ratio was 943, literacy was 74.04 percent, and the decadal growth rate was 17.64 percent. Key fiscal facts: the FRBM Act 2003 was amended in 2018 to set a debt target, and the Centre's fiscal deficit was 5.8 percent of GDP in 2023-24 (revised), against 9.2 percent in 2020-21. Measures of income include GDP, GNP, NNP at factor cost, and per capita NNI. The base year for national accounts is 2011-12, and the CSO/NSO (MoSPI) compiles the data. Related angles UPSC could ask are the vicious circle of poverty (Nurkse), the Lewis model, ICOR, savings and investment rates, the Human Development Index and the Kuznets curve.

question: If the RBI adopts an expansionist open market operations policy, this means it will :
options: Sell securities in the open market
Openly announce to the market that it intends to expand credit
Offer commercial banks more credit in the open market
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Open Market Operations (OMO) are outright purchases or sales of government securities by the central bank to regulate liquidity. When the RBI buys securities, it pays by crediting banks' reserve accounts or issuing cheques to the public, which are deposited in banks. This raises bank reserves and the monetary base, allowing banks to lend more through the money multiplier, and it tends to lower interest rates. This is the expansionary or easy money stance. When the RBI sells securities, it absorbs liquidity, reduces reserves and contracts credit, which is the contractionary or tight money stance. OMO is a quantitative, market-based tool, unlike the repo/reverse repo (LAF), which is a temporary repurchase arrangement. Elimination: (a) is the contractionary action. (c) confuses OMO with announcement or moral suasion, and OMO works through actual transactions. (d) describes lending or refinance facilities such as LAF, MSF or bank rate, not OMO, which is a purchase or sale of securities. Hence (b) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: selling securities withdraws money from the system and is a contractionary OMO.
Correct: buying securities from non-government holders (banks, institutions, public) injects reserves and liquidity and expands credit capacity.
Wrong: OMO is an actual market transaction, not a mere announcement. Announcements fall under moral suasion or forward guidance.
Wrong: offering banks credit is done through LAF, MSF, bank rate or refinance windows, not OMO, which deals in securities.
keyfact: RBI buys securities = expansionary OMO (liquidity injected); RBI sells securities = contractionary OMO (liquidity absorbed).
option_notes: Selling securities: the RBI sells G-secs or T-bills to mop up excess liquidity during inflation. Bank reserves fall, lending capacity shrinks, and yields rise. It is the tight money or contractionary OMO. Related sterilisation tools include the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) bonds, introduced in 2004.

Buying securities: the RBI purchases G-secs from banks and the public, releasing primary money into the system. It is used when liquidity is tight or growth needs support. Purchases raise bond prices and lower yields. Recent examples include OMO purchases and the Operation Twist (simultaneous buying and selling of long- and short-dated securities).

Announcing intent to expand credit: this is closer to moral suasion or forward guidance, a qualitative tool of persuasion with no direct transaction. Qualitative tools also include credit rationing, margin requirements, direct action and selective credit control. Such announcements are not what OMO means.

Offering banks more credit: this is done through the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (repo, since 2000), Marginal Standing Facility (2011-12), bank rate or refinance. These are lending or repo facilities against collateral, and they are not outright sale or purchase of securities in the open market.
related: Expansionary OMO = RBI buys securities; contractionary OMO = RBI sells securities.
Repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against securities; reverse repo absorbs liquidity.
LAF was introduced in June 2000 on the Narasimham Committee recommendation.
MSF was introduced in May 2011 and is priced at repo + 25 bps today.
MSS bonds (2004) were used to sterilise capital inflows.
Moral suasion, credit rationing and margin requirements are qualitative tools.
The Monetary Policy Committee (six members) was set up in 2016 under the RBI Act amendment.
Bank rate is aligned with the MSF rate.
summary: The answer is (b). An expansionist (easy money) open market operation means the RBI buys government securities from banks and the public (non-government holders), which injects liquidity and expands the money supply and credit.
topic_notes: Monetary policy tools of the RBI are of two types. Quantitative (general) tools: CRR, SLR, bank rate, repo and reverse repo, MSF, and OMO. Qualitative (selective) tools: margin requirements, moral suasion, credit rationing, direct action and selective credit control. Open market operations are outright buying or selling of government securities. Buying is expansionary, as it raises reserves and the money supply. Selling is contractionary, as it reduces reserves. The money multiplier is 1/reserve ratio, and the monetary base (reserve money) is currency plus bank reserves plus other deposits with the RBI. The LAF was introduced in June 2000 after the Narasimham Committee recommendations. Repo injects liquidity, while reverse repo absorbs it. The MSF was introduced in May 2011 with a rate of repo + 100 bps (now repo + 25 bps), and the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) was introduced in 2022. The MSS was introduced in 2004 to sterilise capital inflows. Under the Monetary Policy Committee (2016, six members), the inflation target is 4% with a ±2% band. The policy repo rate is the main operating target. CRR is the share of NDTL kept with the RBI, with no interest paid. SLR is held in liquid assets such as gold, cash and G-secs, and the statutory limit under Sec 24 of the Banking Regulation Act is a maximum of 40% (the SLR is currently 18%). Dear money means a tight policy and cheap money means an easy policy.

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommendation of the National Cooperative Farming Advisory Board for putting cooperative farming on a sounder footing ?
options: Every Society should have a definite programme for total pooling of lands
Financial assistance should be given only for purchase of new land
State Governments should give priority to revitalization of the existing socicties
Joint farming must be practiced with respect to all lands of the society. APFC) Exam 2012 Question Paper
subject: Computers
detail: Cooperative farming was promoted in India after the First Five Year Plan, and the Planning Commission's Working Group and the National Cooperative Farming Advisory Board reviewed its progress. By the early 1960s many societies were weak, with poor management, little land pooling and heavy dependence on government aid. The Board's suggestions to put the movement on a sounder footing stressed consolidation over expansion. Societies should have a definite programme for total pooling of land and should practise joint farming on all the society's land, not just part of it. State Governments should give priority to revitalizing existing societies instead of forming new ones carelessly. Aid should go to viable societies for working capital, improvements and managerial support. Option (b) is out of line because restricting aid to the purchase of new land would encourage expansion and would not strengthen the societies already functioning. Elimination logic: (a), (c) and (d) all reflect pooling, joint farming and revival, which are the consistent themes. I am working from general knowledge of the Board's themes and have not checked the original report text, so this answer is an inference from those themes.
explanations: Incorrect as the answer: total pooling of land was a recommended goal, so this is a genuine recommendation.
Correct answer: restricting financial aid only to purchase of new land is not a recommendation. Aid was meant to strengthen existing, viable societies.
Incorrect as the answer: priority to revitalization of existing societies matches the consolidation approach.
Incorrect as the answer: joint farming on all the society's lands is consistent with the push for real collective operation.
keyfact: The Board stressed consolidation: revive existing societies and pool all land. It did not limit aid to new land purchase.
option_notes: Total pooling of land means members surrender land to be farmed jointly as one unit, with returns paid for labour and for land. It is the defining feature of genuine cooperative joint farming and was urged for societies that only pooled part of their land.

Financial aid for new land purchase: cooperative farming societies, especially tenant and collective types, did receive aid for land, but this was not the Board's sole recommended channel. Aid was meant for working capital, improvements and managerial staff in viable societies.

Revitalization of existing societies means reviving dormant or weak farming societies through better management, finance, and supervision. It was preferred over starting many new societies, which often failed in the early 1960s.

Joint farming means members cultivate land as a single unit under common management. The Board wanted it practised over all of a society's land, since partial pooling defeated the purpose of cooperative farming.
related: Nagpur Resolution of Congress (1959) endorsed cooperative joint farming
Four types: better farming, joint farming, tenant farming, collective farming
97th Constitutional Amendment (2011) added Article 43B on cooperatives
Right to form cooperative societies is in Article 19(1)(c)
NCDC was set up in 1963
Cooperative Societies Act of 1904 started the formal cooperative movement; the 1912 Act broadened it
NABARD was established in 1982
summary: The answer is (b). The National Cooperative Farming Advisory Board did not recommend restricting financial assistance to the purchase of new land. Its recommendations focused on reviving existing societies, pooling land, and improving the management and working of cooperative farming societies.
topic_notes: Cooperative farming in India was encouraged from the First Five Year Plan (1951-56), which saw it as a way to overcome the problems of small, fragmented holdings. The Nagpur Congress Resolution (1959) pushed for service cooperatives first and joint farming later, with the aim of reorganising agriculture on cooperative lines within a few years. Four types are usually recognised: better farming societies, joint farming societies, tenant farming societies and collective farming societies. Better farming societies are the loosest form, where members keep their own land but adopt improved practices jointly. Joint farming societies pool land and manage it as a unit. Tenant farming societies hold land on lease, often from the state, and sublet or farm it jointly. Collective farming societies are the most integrated type, with owned land and common management. The Planning Commission and the National Cooperative Farming Advisory Board reviewed progress and found that many societies were poorly managed, had weak finances, and relied on government aid. Policy therefore shifted to consolidating existing societies rather than expanding. Related institutions include the National Cooperative Union of India (NCUI), NABARD (1982), the National Cooperative Development Corporation (1963), and the Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS). Possible future questions concern the types of cooperative farming, the Nagpur Resolution, the Cooperative Societies Act 1912, Article 43B (added by the 97th Amendment, 2011) and Article 19(1)(c).

question: Structural Planning refers to :
options: Laying down broad goals and strategies
Changing existing institutions or creating new ones
subject: Computers
detail: In planning theory, a distinction is drawn between functional planning and structural (institutional) planning. Functional planning takes the existing institutional and socio-economic framework as given and tries to achieve targets (output, investment, employment) within it. Structural planning seeks to change the framework itself: reforming or abolishing old institutions, creating new ones and altering property relations, so that growth and social justice become possible. Indian examples are zamindari abolition and tenancy reform, nationalisation of banks (1969), creation of the Planning Commission (1950), NITI Aayog (2015), cooperatives, Panchayati Raj (73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992) and agencies such as NABARD (1982). Mahalanobis-type heavy industry strategy and public sector expansion also had structural elements. Elimination: (a) centralized planning concerns who decides, not what is changed; (b) laying down broad goals and strategies describes perspective or indicative planning; (d) flexible targets describes rolling or indicative planning. Only (c) matches the definition of institutional change.
explanations: Wrong: centralized planning refers to decision-making concentrated in a central authority. It is not the meaning of structural planning.
Wrong: laying down broad goals and strategies is perspective or strategic planning, a long-term vision such as the 15-20 year perspective plan.
Correct: structural planning means changing existing institutions or creating new ones to remove structural obstacles to development.
Wrong: fixing flexible targets relates to rolling or indicative planning, where targets are revised periodically.
keyfact: Structural (institutional) planning means changing existing institutions or creating new ones, unlike functional planning, which works within them.
option_notes: Centralized planning: planning where a central authority sets targets and allocates resources for the whole economy, as in the Soviet Gosplan model. India followed a mixed form: the Planning Commission (1950-2014) was central, but states prepared their own plans under the National Development Council. Its opposite is decentralized planning, linked to Panchayati Raj and the District Planning Committees (Art. 243ZD).

Laying down broad goals and strategies describes perspective planning, a long-term plan covering 10-20 years that sets the overall direction. India's perspective planning was influenced by P.C. Mahalanobis, and the Planning Commission prepared long-term perspective documents. It is distinct from the five-year plan, which is the medium-term operational plan. Strategic goals guide the plan but do not themselves change institutions.

Changing existing institutions or creating new ones is the definition of structural or institutional planning. It aims to alter the socio-economic structure through measures such as land reforms, nationalisation, cooperative formation, and creating bodies like NABARD, SEBI or NITI Aayog. It is the counterpart of functional planning, which operates within the existing framework.

Fixing flexible targets refers to indicative or rolling plan ideas. Rolling plans were introduced by the Janata government (1978-83), with annual revision of targets, and Gunnar Myrdal's ideas about flexible planning are related. Indicative planning, as in France, gives guidance to the private sector rather than binding targets. India moved towards indicative planning from the 8th Plan (1992-97).
related: Planning Commission was set up in March 1950; replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 Jan 2015.
Functional planning works within the existing institutional framework.
Rolling plan was introduced by the Janata government (1978-83).
Eighth Plan (1992-97) adopted indicative planning.
Second Plan followed the Mahalanobis heavy industry model.
The Bombay Plan of 1944 was drawn up by leading industrialists.
The National Development Council was formed in 1952.
summary: The answer is (c). Structural planning (institutional planning) means changing existing institutions or creating new ones, such as land reforms, banking reforms and new administrative bodies, so that the socio-economic structure supports development goals. It contrasts with functional planning, which works within existing institutions.
topic_notes: Types of planning: (1) Functional vs structural planning: functional works within existing institutions; structural changes institutions. (2) Centralized vs decentralized planning. (3) Imperative (command) vs indicative planning: the 8th Plan (1992-97) under P.V. Narasimha Rao adopted indicative planning. (4) Physical vs financial planning. (5) Perspective, medium-term (five-year) and annual plans. (6) Rolling plan: proposed by Gunnar Myrdal and implemented by the Janata government for 1978-83 and again as annual plans 1990-92. Indian planning background: Planning Commission set up in March 1950 by a Cabinet resolution (an extra-constitutional, non-statutory body), with the Prime Minister as chairman. The National Development Council was set up in 1952. The First Plan (1951-56) used the Harrod-Domar model and focused on agriculture; the Second Plan (1956-61) used the Mahalanobis model and emphasised heavy industry. Plan holidays occurred in 1966-69, with annual plans. The Twelfth Plan (2012-17) was the last. NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015. Structural reforms in India include zamindari abolition, bank nationalisation (1969 and 1980), the Panchayati Raj amendments, and the 1991 liberalisation reforms. Other angles UPSC may ask: models of planning, the Bombay Plan (1944), the People's Plan, the Gandhian Plan, the Sarvodaya Plan (Jayaprakash Narayan, 1950), and the Planning Commission's functions.

question: Three States which have Human Development Index (HDI) higher than China are :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Human Development Index (HDI) is published by UNDP in the Human Development Report. It is a geometric mean of three dimensions: health (life expectancy at birth), education (mean and expected years of schooling) and standard of living (GNI per capita, PPP). China's national HDI was roughly 0.70 around 2012, which put it in the 'high' or upper-medium group, while India as a whole was about 0.59 and in the 'medium' group. Sub-national HDIs for Indian states come from the India Human Development Reports (Planning Commission / IAMR), and the figures are not strictly comparable with UNDP's national figures. Even so, Kerala consistently ranks first among large states, with an HDI of about 0.79. Punjab and Maharashtra consistently sit in the upper tier, above the all-India average. Madhya Pradesh, along with Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha and Chhattisgarh, sits at the bottom, below the national average and far below China. Elimination: options (a), (c) and (d) all include Madhya Pradesh, so they are wrong. That leaves option (b). Caveat: a strict numerical match with China's HDI may not hold for every state named, so the question is best treated as a relative-ranking question.
explanations: Wrong: it includes Madhya Pradesh, a consistently low-HDI state that is well below China and below the national average.
Correct: Kerala, Punjab and Maharashtra are all high-ranking states on human development and contain no laggard state. This is the only option without Madhya Pradesh.
Wrong: it includes Madhya Pradesh and also omits Kerala, the top-ranked state.
Wrong: it includes Madhya Pradesh, which is a low-HDI state, so the combination fails even though Kerala and Gujarat are comparatively better.
keyfact: Kerala tops Indian states on HDI, and Madhya Pradesh is among the lowest, so the right option is the one with Kerala, Punjab and Maharashtra.
option_notes: Kerala, Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh: Kerala leads the states with an HDI of about 0.79, driven by high literacy, a high life expectancy of around 75 years and low infant mortality. Maharashtra is an industrialised, urbanised state in the upper tier. Madhya Pradesh is a large central state with high poverty and malnutrition, and its HDI is among the lowest of the major states, near 0.4 on the Planning Commission 2011 scale.

Kerala, Punjab and Maharashtra: three states that rank above the all-India average on HDI. Kerala is the best performer on health and education. Punjab has high per-capita income and strong agriculture and was a leader in the 1990s. Maharashtra has the highest state GDP and strong urban services. Together they are the best fit for the 'higher than China' claim.

Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Punjab: this combination mixes two relatively well-developed states with Madhya Pradesh. Punjab ranks high in income and health outcomes. Madhya Pradesh has historically had high infant and maternal mortality, low female literacy and a large tribal population. It is part of the 'BIMARU' group of states (Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh).

Kerala, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat: Gujarat is a high-growth state with strong industry, but its human development ranking is only middling because of weaker health and nutrition indicators. This contrasts with its economic performance and is often used as an example of growth not translating into human development. Madhya Pradesh again drags the combination down.
related: HDI was developed by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen in 1990.
HDI dimensions: health, education and standard of living.
Since 2010 HDI uses the geometric mean of its three dimension indices.
Kerala ranks first among large Indian states on HDI.
Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh are among the lowest-ranked states on HDI.
The Multidimensional Poverty Index was introduced by UNDP and OPHI in 2010.
The Human Development Report is published annually by UNDP.
summary: The best answer is (b) Kerala, Punjab and Maharashtra. These are among India's better-performing states on human development, and they are the only trio that leaves out Madhya Pradesh, which has long been one of the lowest-ranked large states. The question is dated and the comparison with China depends on the data series used, so this is the most defensible choice by elimination.
topic_notes: HDI was introduced by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen in 1990 for UNDP's Human Development Reports. Since 2010 it has used three dimensions: a long and healthy life (life expectancy at birth), knowledge (mean years of schooling for adults and expected years of schooling for children) and a decent standard of living (GNI per capita in PPP US$). Dimension indices are combined by a geometric mean. Countries are grouped as very high, high, medium and low human development. Related indices include the Inequality-adjusted HDI, Gender Development Index, Gender Inequality Index and Multidimensional Poverty Index (introduced in 2010). India's national HDI has risen over time: roughly 0.58 in 2012 and about 0.64 in recent reports, keeping it in the medium category. Sub-national HDIs come from the India Human Development Reports (2001 by Planning Commission, 2011 by IAMR and Planning Commission), and state-level rankings are based on different data, so they cannot be compared directly with UNDP country values. Kerala is first among large states, with Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Goa and Punjab also ranking high. Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and Chhattisgarh rank at the bottom. China's HDI placed it in the 'high' group by 2012, well ahead of India, mainly on income, health and schooling. India also has its own state-level and national indicators such as the NITI Aayog's National Multidimensional Poverty Index (first released in 2021, using health, education and standard of living), the SDG India Index and Human Development reports from individual states. Likely exam angles are the dimensions of HDI, who created it, the Kerala model of development, and comparisons of India with neighbours such as China, Sri Lanka and Pakistan.

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) : 1, Reports on the accounts of the States are submitted to the President who shall cause these to be placed before the Parliament.
2. CAG is appointed by the President of India and can be removed only on grounds and procedure similar to those of a Supreme Court Judge.
3. The form in which accounts of the Centre and States are to be kept is prescribed by CAG Which of these statements are correct ?
options: 1 and 3 only 26 (Contd.) fiche Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner (/
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Part V, Chapter V of the Constitution (Articles 148-151) deals with the CAG. Article 148 provides that the CAG is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. He can be removed only in the manner and on the grounds applicable to a Supreme Court Judge, that is, by an address of both Houses supported by a special majority on proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Article 150 says the accounts of the Union and the States are kept in the form the President prescribes on the advice of the CAG. In practice the CAG prescribes the form for States, and for the Union the President acts on his advice. Article 151(1) says the CAG's reports on Union accounts go to the President, who places them before Parliament. Article 151(2) says reports on State accounts go to the Governor, who places them before the State Legislature. Statement 1 therefore fails because it names the President. Statement 3 is accepted as correct in the traditional reading, since the form of State accounts is set on the CAG's advice. Elimination: rejecting 1 leaves only option (c).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because State reports go to the Governor, so not all three statements are correct.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and leaves out statement 3, which is correct.
Right: statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is incorrect.
Wrong: it includes statement 1 and leaves out statement 2, which is correct.
keyfact: CAG reports: Union to the President (Art. 151(1)), States to the Governor (Art. 151(2)); removal as for a Supreme Court Judge.
option_notes: Option (a) says all three statements are correct. It would be true only if State reports went to the President. Art. 151(2) sends them to the Governor, who places them before the State Legislature. The CAG's Union audit reports are the ones laid before Parliament by the President. The reports are of three kinds: Appropriation Accounts, Finance Accounts, and audit reports on commercial and other accounts.

Option (b) says 1 and 2 only. It gets the removal point right but wrongly accepts the President for State reports and rejects Art. 150. The CAG is independent, and removal needs an address by both Houses passed by a special majority. The office is modelled on the British Comptroller and Auditor General. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the CAG as possibly the most important officer under the Constitution.

Option (c) says 2 and 3 only. This is the correct option. The CAG is appointed by the President and removed as a Supreme Court Judge is. The form of accounts is prescribed on the CAG's advice under Art. 150. The first CAG of independent India was V. Narahari Rao (1948). Reports go to the Governor for the States. The CAG audits only on the basis of the PAC process, and his role is audit, not control.

Option (d) says 1 and 3 only. It wrongly accepts statement 1 and wrongly rejects statement 2. Statement 2 reflects Arts. 148(1) and (2). The CAG holds office for 6 years or until age 65. He may resign by writing to the President. He is not a member of the executive, and he is not eligible for further government office after retirement.
related: Art. 148 creates the office of the CAG.
Art. 150: form of accounts is prescribed by the President on the CAG's advice.
Art. 151: CAG reports go to the President (Union) or the Governor (States).
The CAG's tenure is 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier.
The CAG is removed like a Supreme Court Judge.
The CAG (DPC) Act of 1971 governs his duties and powers.
The CAG is the guide of the Public Accounts Committee.
The CAG's salary is charged to the Consolidated Fund of India.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: State account reports go to the Governor under Art. 151(2), not to the President. The Governor lays them before the State Legislature, where the Public Accounts Committee examines them. Union reports go to the President under Art. 151(1) and are laid before Parliament, where the PAC examines them. The CAG is called the guardian of the public purse. He audits the Consolidated Fund, the Contingency Fund and the Public Account, and also audits government companies and bodies substantially financed by the government. He acts as the PAC's friend, philosopher and guide.

2 — Correct: Art. 148(1) provides for appointment by the President by warrant. Art. 148(2) requires an oath before the President. Removal is the same as for a Supreme Court Judge under Art. 124(4). The CAG's salary is equal to that of a Supreme Court Judge. After retirement he cannot hold any further office under the Government of India or a State. His term is 6 years or age 65, whichever comes first. His conditions of service cannot be changed to his disadvantage after appointment. His office expenses are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India.

3 — Correct: Art. 150 says the accounts of the Union and the States are kept in the form the President prescribes on the advice of the CAG. The CAG's duties, powers and conditions of service are governed by the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. The 1976 amendment to that Act separated accounts from audit at the Union level, and departmental accounting passed to the ministries. The CAG still compiles State accounts in many States and prepares the Appropriation Accounts and Finance Accounts. The CAG is also the external auditor of the UN and its agencies at times.
summary: The correct answer is (c): statements 2 and 3 are correct, and statement 1 is wrong. The CAG's reports on State accounts go to the Governor of the State, who places them before the State Legislature, not to the President. Only the Union accounts reports go to the President (Art. 151(1)).
topic_notes: The CAG is an independent constitutional authority under Articles 148-151. He is appointed by the President by warrant and takes an oath before the President. His term is 6 years or until age 65, whichever is earlier. He can be removed only in the manner of a Supreme Court Judge, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by an address of both Houses with a special majority. His salary is equal to that of a Supreme Court Judge and is charged to the Consolidated Fund of India, as are his office expenses. His service conditions cannot be varied to his disadvantage after appointment. After retirement he is barred from further office under the Union or any State. Art. 149 empowers Parliament to prescribe his duties and powers, which is done through the CAG (DPC) Act, 1971. He audits the Consolidated Funds of India and the States, the Contingency Funds, and the Public Accounts. He also audits the accounts of government companies and of bodies substantially financed by the government. He audits only on the legality, regularity and propriety of spending, and some audits cover economy, efficiency and effectiveness (the performance audit). He does not control the issue of money from the Consolidated Fund; that is a difference from the British position. Under Art. 151, reports on the Union go to the President, who places them before Parliament. Reports on the States go to the Governor, who lays them before the State Legislature. The Public Accounts Committee examines the reports, and the CAG acts as its guide. Committees on Public Undertakings also use CAG reports. Reports are prepared on revenue, expenditure, and commercial matters. Other angles UPSC may ask are the CAG's relationship with the Estimates Committee, the 1976 separation of accounts from audit, and the status of the CAG's Department as the Indian Audit and Accounts Department.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the features of the Special Economic Zones (SEZ) being set up for promoting exports ?
options: Foreign workers will be allowed free entry without Visa restrictions
The SEZ area will be treated as foreign territory for trade operations, duties and tariff
There will be no routine examination by customs authorities of import/export cargo,
No license is required for import into the zone
subject: Indian Economy
detail: Special Economic Zones are geographically demarcated enclaves given liberal economic laws to boost exports, investment and employment. The policy was announced in April 2000 as an extension of the EPZ regime, replacing the earlier Export Processing Zones (Kandla, 1965, was Asia's first EPZ). The SEZ Act, 2005 and SEZ Rules came into force on 10 February 2006. Core features: the SEZ is deemed foreign territory for trade operations, duties and tariffs; duty-free import/domestic procurement of goods for authorised operations; no licence requirement for imports; self-certification and no routine customs examination; exemption from income tax for units (Section 10AA of the Income Tax Act, 100% for 5 years, 50% for the next 5 years); exemption from Central Sales Tax, service tax and often state levies; single-window clearance; and external commercial borrowing freedom. Labour laws are largely administered by the Development Commissioner. Entry of foreign nationals remains governed by the Indian visa regime: foreigners need valid visas, and employment visas are required for work. Hence (a) is the exception, while (b), (c), (d) are standard SEZ features.
explanations: Correct choice (NOT a feature): foreign workers do not get visa-free entry into SEZs; normal visa and employment-permit rules apply.
Incorrect choice: this is a genuine feature; the SEZ is deemed foreign territory for trade operations, duties and tariffs.
Incorrect choice: this is a genuine feature; SEZ units operate on self-certification and there is no routine customs examination of cargo.
Incorrect choice: this is a genuine feature; imports into the zone for authorised operations need no licence.
keyfact: SEZ = deemed foreign territory with duty-free imports, no licence and self-certification, but foreign workers still need visas.
option_notes: Visa-free entry for foreign workers: not provided by the SEZ regime. Foreign nationals visiting or working in SEZs need valid Indian visas and, for employment, an employment visa. The Ministry of Home Affairs controls visa policy, though SEZ authorities may facilitate processing. Any claim of free entry is therefore wrong, which makes this the correct answer to a NOT question.

Foreign territory treatment: SEZs are deemed to be outside the customs territory of India for authorised operations. Goods moving from the DTA into an SEZ are treated as exports, and SEZ-to-DTA sales are treated as imports with duty payable. This concept dates to the 2000 SEZ policy and the SEZ Act 2005, effective February 2006.

No routine customs examination: SEZ units rely on self-certification, and customs checks are minimal and based on risk. Cargo moves under simplified procedures, with the Development Commissioner and Customs officers at the zone. This reduces transaction costs and speeds up exports, and it is a key incentive of the SEZ regime.

No import licence: SEZ units may import capital goods, raw materials and consumables for authorised operations without a licence, and duty-free. Exceptions are a few prohibited or restricted items under the Foreign Trade Policy. The units must be net foreign exchange earners over the five-year period from commencement of production.
related: SEZ Act came into force on 10 February 2006.
Kandla (1965) was Asia's first Export Processing Zone.
SEZ policy was announced in April 2000 in the EXIM Policy.
Board of Approval for SEZs is chaired by the Commerce Secretary.
Section 10AA of the Income Tax Act governs SEZ unit tax holidays.
Baba Kalyani Committee (2018) reviewed SEZ policy.
Proposed DESH Bill is meant to replace the SEZ Act.
summary: The answer is (a). SEZs are treated as foreign territory for trade operations, duties and tariffs, with no licence needed for imports and no routine customs examination of cargo. However, foreign nationals working in an SEZ still need valid visas and employment permits; there is no free, visa-free entry.
topic_notes: SEZ policy was introduced in the Export-Import Policy of 1 April 2000 to give a globally competitive environment for exports. The SEZ Act, 2005 and SEZ Rules, 2006 came into effect on 10 February 2006. Earlier zones: Kandla EPZ (1965), the first in Asia, followed by Santacruz (SEEPZ, Mumbai) and others; EPZs were converted into SEZs. Administration: Board of Approval chaired by the Commerce Secretary; Unit Approval Committee at the zone level; Development Commissioner heads each SEZ. Incentives: duty-free import and procurement, 100% FDI under the automatic route in manufacturing, income-tax holiday under Section 10AA (units commencing from 2006 to 2020), exemption from service tax, CST and stamp duty, and external commercial borrowing up to USD 500 million a year. The Minimum Alternate Tax and Dividend Distribution Tax were imposed on SEZs in 2011, and the Section 10AA benefit lapsed for units beginning after 31 March 2020. Minimum land requirements vary by type: multi-product SEZs 1,000 hectares (reduced later), sector-specific smaller, with relaxed norms for IT/ITES and for certain states. SEZs are also subject to the Baba Kalyani Committee (2018) review of the SEZ policy; the government is reworking SEZs into 'DESH' (Development of Enterprise and Service Hubs) through a bill proposed in the 2022-23 Budget. Related institutions: National Investment and Manufacturing Zones (NIMZ) under the 2011 National Manufacturing Policy; Export Oriented Units (EOUs, 1981); Software Technology Parks (STPI, 1991). Typical exam angles are the year of the Act, the authority, the tax exemptions and the difference between SEZ and EPZ.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a recall question on committees and commissions and their chairpersons. The key is to anchor on the names you are sure of. B.N. Srikrishna, a retired Supreme Court judge, headed the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission (FSLRC, set up in 2011, report in 2013), which proposed an Indian Financial Code and a unified financial regulator. Anil Kakodkar, former Atomic Energy Commission chairman, headed the High Level Safety Review Committee on Indian Railways (2011), which recommended a Railway Safety Authority and a large safety investment. Adi Godrej chaired the committee on the Air India and Indian Airlines merger (2007), which was one of several corporate-sector committees he led. D.M. Dharmadhikari, a retired judge, chaired the 2000 Corporate Governance committee under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs and later worked on the National Corporate Governance policy. Elimination: fixing B=3 removes options (b) and (d)? B=3 appears in (a) and (b). Fixing C=4 appears in (a) and (b). Fixing A=1 leaves only (a), because options (b) and (d) put A=2. Option (c) has B=4, which is wrong. So the answer is (a).
explanations: Correct: A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2 matches all four pairs correctly.
Wrong: it gives A-2 and D-1, which reverses Dharmadhikari and Godrej.
Wrong: it gives B-4 and C-3, which reverses Kakodkar and Srikrishna.
Wrong: it gives A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1, so all four pairings are wrong.
keyfact: Srikrishna chaired FSLRC; Kakodkar chaired the Railway Safety Review Committee; Godrej chaired the Air India-Indian Airlines merger committee; Dharmadhikari was linked to corporate governance (answer: a).
option_notes: Code 1-3-4-2: Dharmadhikari for corporate governance, Kakodkar for railway safety, Srikrishna for financial sector reforms, Godrej for the Air India merger. This is the correct set, each backed by a separate committee. Kakodkar's railway safety report came out in 2012, and the FSLRC's in 2013. Both are well known for their recommendations of statutory bodies, the Railway Safety Authority and the Indian Financial Code.

Code 2-3-4-1: it swaps the Dharmadhikari and Godrej issues. Dharmadhikari did not chair a merger committee, and Godrej was not linked to the National Corporate Governance Policy. It is a partly right distractor, as B and C are matched correctly. Remember that the Air India-Indian Airlines merger formed NACIL in 2007, later renamed Air India Ltd.

Code 1-4-3-2: it swaps Kakodkar and Srikrishna. Kakodkar is a nuclear scientist and would not chair a financial sector commission, while Srikrishna is a judge who chaired FSLRC. The FSLRC report in 2013 proposed a unified Indian Financial Code, and Kakodkar's report in 2012 sought a Railway Safety Authority.
Code 2-4-3-1: every pair is wrong. It is a complete distractor meant to catch students who guess without anchoring on any known pair. Anchoring on Srikrishna with FSLRC alone rules this option out.
related: FSLRC (2011-2013), chaired by Justice B.N. Srikrishna, proposed the Indian Financial Code.

statements: A — Correct: D.M. Dharmadhikari is matched with 1, the National Corporate Governance Policy. He was a retired Supreme Court judge who chaired the 2000 Ministry of Corporate Affairs committee on corporate governance. His work fed into corporate governance guidelines issued in the 2000s, including voluntary guidelines for companies. Corporate governance in India was shaped by the Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee (SEBI, 1999), Clause 49 of the listing agreement, Narayana Murthy Committee (2003), and the Companies Act 2013. Note that this matching is the least well known of the four, so use elimination.

B — Correct: Anil Kakodkar is matched with 3, the High Level Safety Review Committee on Indian Railways. The committee was formed in 2011 after a series of railway accidents and reported in February 2012. It recommended a statutory Railway Safety Authority, eliminating level crossings in five years, and an investment of about Rs 1 lakh crore for safety. Kakodkar is a nuclear scientist who headed the Atomic Energy Commission (2000-2009), and was awarded the Padma Vibhushan.

C — Correct: B.N. Srikrishna is matched with 4, the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission. FSLRC was set up in March 2011 by the Ministry of Finance and submitted its report in March 2013. It proposed a unified Indian Financial Code, a Unified Financial Agency, and a Financial Sector Appellate Tribunal. Srikrishna also headed the Commission on the Telangana issue in 2010 and the Data Protection committee in 2017, and he investigated the 1992-93 Mumbai riots.

D — Correct: Adi Godrej is matched with 2, the Air India and Indian Airlines merger. The merger was approved in 2007 and the new entity was named National Aviation Company of India Ltd (NACIL), which later became Air India Ltd. Godrej, chairman of the Godrej Group, chaired a committee on aspects of the merger. Air India was privatised in January 2022 when the Tata Group took it over, and Vistara later merged with Air India in 2024.
summary: The correct code is (a) A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2. D.M. Dharmadhikari chaired the National Corporate Governance committee, Anil Kakodkar chaired the Railway Safety Review Committee, B.N. Srikrishna chaired the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission, and Adi Godrej chaired the committee on the Air India-Indian Airlines merger.
topic_notes: This question tests knowledge of committees and commissions and their chairpersons, a recurring theme in current affairs and economy. The four items cover corporate governance, railway safety, financial sector reform and civil aviation. Corporate governance: the Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee (1999) led to Clause 49; the Naresh Chandra Committee (2002) dealt with audit and auditor independence; the Narayana Murthy Committee (2003) reviewed Clause 49; the J.J. Irani Committee (2005) reformed company law, leading to the Companies Act 2013; Uday Kotak Committee (2017) reformed SEBI listing governance. Railways: the Kakodkar Committee (2012) on safety, the Bibek Debroy Committee (2014-15) on restructuring, the Sam Pitroda committee on modernisation (2012), and the Rakesh Mohan Committee (2001) on railway reforms. Financial sector: the Narasimham Committee (1991, 1998) on banking reform, the Raghuram Rajan Committee (2008) on financial sector reforms, the FSLRC under Srikrishna (2013), the P.J. Nayak Committee (2014) on bank governance, and the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) on monetary policy framework. Aviation: Air India and Indian Airlines merged in 2007 as NACIL, then Air India Ltd; privatised to the Tata Group in January 2022; Vistara merged with it in 2024. Strategy for these questions: remember one or two certain pairs and eliminate the options that contradict them, because matching tables are usually built to differ in pairs.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The National Rural Livelihoods Mission (NRLM), launched in June 2011 by the Ministry of Rural Development and renamed DAY-NRLM (Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana-NRLM) in 2015, is a poverty alleviation programme. It restructured the earlier Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY). Its core strategy is social mobilisation: organising poor women into SHGs, then into village organisations and cluster-level federations. These bodies get capacity building, a revolving fund and community investment support, and access to bank credit at subsidised interest (interest subvention). Skill development comes through DDU-GKY (placement-linked training for rural youth) and RSETIs (Rural Self Employment Training Institutes). The mission is supported by the World Bank, and its aim is to reach about 7 crore rural poor households. Elimination: statement 1 is wrong because NRLM promotes self-employment and micro-enterprises, not large factories. Statement 3 is wrong because free supply of seeds, fertilisers, pump-sets and irrigation equipment is not an NRLM feature; such inputs come from agriculture schemes and are subsidised, not free. Only statement 2 is correct, so (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 3, which describe industries and free inputs that NRLM does not provide.
Correct: only statement 2 (SHG strengthening and skill development) describes NRLM.
Wrong: free supply of agricultural inputs is not an NRLM feature, and statement 2 is correct but is left out.
Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect, and statement 2 is correct but is left out.
keyfact: NRLM (2011, renamed DAY-NRLM in 2015) builds SHG federations of the rural poor and gives skills and credit, not free farm inputs or big industries.
option_notes: The option '1, 2 and 3' combines all the statements. It is wrong because two of them do not describe NRLM.
The option '2 only' is the correct choice. It captures NRLM's two main tools, SHG-based institution building and skill development.
The option '3 only' is wrong. Free inputs are not provided by NRLM, whose support is credit, capacity building and institutions.
The option '1 only' is wrong. NRLM promotes micro-enterprises and self-employment, not big manufacturing industries.
related: NRLM was launched in June 2011 by the Ministry of Rural Development.
NRLM replaced the Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY).
NRLM was renamed DAY-NRLM in 2015.
DDU-GKY is the placement-linked skill programme for rural youth aged 15-35.
RSETIs are Rural Self Employment Training Institutes run with banks' support.
NULM is the urban counterpart of NRLM, launched in 2013.
Kudumbashree (Kerala) and Jeevika (Bihar) are State Rural Livelihood Missions.
MKSP under NRLM aims to empower women farmers.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: NRLM does not aim to set up a large number of manufacturing industries or agribusiness centres. It builds institutions of the poor and promotes micro-enterprises. Facts: NRLM was launched on 3 June 2011 under the Ministry of Rural Development, and the Mission is a demand-driven, community-led programme. It targets about 7 crore rural poor households across the country. Its strategy covers social mobilisation, financial inclusion, sustainable livelihoods (farm and non-farm) and convergence with other schemes. Large-scale industry promotion belongs to industrial policy, not NRLM.

2 — Correct: Strengthening SHGs and providing skill development are central to NRLM. Facts: Poor women are organised into SHGs, then into village organisations and cluster-level federations. The Mission gives a revolving fund and a community investment fund, and bank credit linkage with interest subvention. Skills training runs through DDU-GKY, launched in 2014 for rural youth aged 15-35, and through RSETIs. In 2015 NRLM was renamed DAY-NRLM. The Mission has been supported by the World Bank, and its predecessor was SGSY, launched in 1999.

3 — Incorrect: NRLM does not supply seeds, fertilisers, diesel pump-sets and micro-irrigation equipment free of cost to farmers. Facts: Inputs of this kind are supported through agriculture schemes such as the National Food Security Mission, the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana and Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana, which provide subsidies rather than free supply. NRLM's agriculture work is the Mahila Kisan Sashaktikaran Pariyojana (MKSP), which builds the capacity of women farmers in sustainable practices.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. NRLM (Aajeevika, launched June 2011) works by mobilising rural poor households into Self Help Groups and federations and by providing skill development and credit linkages. It does not set up large manufacturing industries or give free inputs to farmers.
topic_notes: NRLM (Aajeevika) was launched in June 2011 by the Ministry of Rural Development and restructured SGSY. It was renamed DAY-NRLM in 2015. Its goal is to reduce rural poverty by enabling poor households to access gainful self-employment and skilled wage employment. The strategy is a three-tier set of institutions: SHGs, village organisations and cluster-level federations. It is a demand-driven mission and gives states the flexibility to design their own programmes through State Rural Livelihood Missions (for example Kudumbashree in Kerala and Jeevika in Bihar). Key components include social mobilisation, financial inclusion (revolving fund, community investment fund, interest subvention, bank linkage), livelihood promotion (MKSP, Start-up Village Entrepreneurship Programme), skills (DDU-GKY, RSETIs) and convergence with other schemes. The World Bank has supported it. NRLM focuses on women, with the aim of covering at least one woman from each poor household in SHGs. Related schemes UPSC may ask about: MGNREGA (2005, 100 days of guaranteed wage employment), PMAY-G, DDU-GKY, NULM (urban counterpart, 2013), PMGSY and the Lakhpati Didi initiative. Also remember that SGSY (1999) was an earlier self-employment scheme and that IRDP was merged into it. Rural development subject areas include panchayati raj (73rd Amendment, 1992), the Eleventh Schedule and the SECC 2011 data used to identify beneficiaries.

question: Which one of the following explanations is indicated by the term ‘welfare’ as a total concept?
options: It is a desirable state of existence involving physical, mental, moral and emotional well-being
It is the welfare of man, his family and community
It is contingent upon time and space
It demands certain minimum acceptable conditions of existence, biologically and socially
subject: Computers
detail: Labour welfare is a standard topic in the Industrial Relations and Social Security syllabus. The classic exposition (Labour Welfare textbooks such as Moorthy's and the Report of the Labour Investigation Committee, 1946) describes welfare as a 'total concept' in the sense of a desirable state of existence involving the physical, mental, moral and emotional well-being of the individual. It has several features. It is relative: it depends on time and space, so it varies by country, era and social context. It is dynamic. It has a social dimension, covering the welfare of man, his family and community. It also has a minimum-standards aspect, since it needs certain acceptable conditions of existence, both biological and social. Option (a) is the only one that defines the concept itself in terms of all dimensions of human well-being, so it matches the phrase 'total concept'. Options (b), (c) and (d) each state one feature of welfare: its scope, its relativity, and its minimum requirements. Elimination logic: when a question asks what the 'total concept' indicates, choose the option that is holistic and multi-dimensional, which is (a).
explanations: Correct: it gives the holistic definition of welfare, covering physical, mental, moral and emotional well-being.
Incorrect: it describes the scope or beneficiaries of welfare (individual, family, community), not the total concept itself.
Incorrect: it states the relativity of welfare, which changes with time and place. This is a feature, not the definition.
Incorrect: it states the minimum-conditions aspect of welfare. This is a requirement, not the holistic meaning.
keyfact: Welfare as a total concept means a desirable state of existence covering physical, mental, moral and emotional well-being.
option_notes: This is the holistic definition of welfare. It treats the person as a whole being, with body, mind, morals and emotions, and it underlies labour welfare thinking in India and ILO approaches.

This points to the social scope of welfare. Welfare is not limited to the worker but extends to the family and the wider community. Many Indian labour welfare measures, such as housing, education and recreation, reach workers' families.
This is the relativity feature. Welfare standards differ between countries and change over time with economic development and social values. Therefore no universal fixed standard exists.

This is the minimum-standards feature. Welfare requires basic conditions such as food, shelter, clothing, health and social security for biological survival and social participation. These are the floor, not the whole concept.
related: Factories Act 1948 requires a welfare officer where 500 or more workers are employed.
Crèche is mandatory in factories with more than 30 women workers.
Canteen is mandatory in factories with more than 250 workers.
Intramural welfare is inside the workplace and extramural welfare is outside it.
The Whitley Commission (1931) is the Royal Commission on Labour.
The Rege Committee (1946) is the Labour Investigation Committee.
The ILO defined labour welfare in 1963 as services, facilities and amenities for workers.
summary: The answer is (a). In labour welfare literature, 'welfare' as a total concept means a desirable state of existence that covers physical, mental, moral and emotional well-being. The other options describe scope, relativity or minimum conditions, which are different features of the concept.
topic_notes: Labour welfare covers facilities and services that employers, government or other agencies provide to improve workers' working and living conditions beyond wages. The ILO (1963) described it as services, facilities and amenities that enable workers to perform their work in healthy, congenial surroundings and to have facilities for health and good living conditions. Key features: it is relative, dynamic, adaptive and multi-dimensional, and it aims to improve the worker's efficiency and morale. Classification of welfare activities: intramural (inside the workplace, such as canteens, crèches, washing facilities, rest rooms) and extramural (outside, such as housing, education, recreation, medical care). Approaches or theories of labour welfare include the policing theory, the religious theory, the philanthropic theory, the paternalistic theory, the placating theory, the public relations theory, the functional theory and the social theory. Statutory welfare provisions in India: the Factories Act 1948 (Chapter V, with canteens, crèches, welfare officers and shelters), the Mines Act 1952, the Plantations Labour Act 1951, the Contract Labour Act 1970, the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979, and the Beedi and Cigar Workers Act 1966. The Labour Welfare Funds Acts of various states, and the welfare funds for mica, coal, iron ore and beedi workers, are also relevant. The Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley Commission, 1931) and the Labour Investigation Committee (Rege Committee, 1946) gave important recommendations. The Factories Act requires a welfare officer where 500 or more workers are employed. A crèche is required where more than 30 women are employed, and a canteen where more than 250 workers are employed.

question: Atonement’ and ‘Investment’ are two co-equal aspects of which one of the following labour welfare theory?
subject: Insurance
detail: Theories of labour welfare explain why welfare work is undertaken. The Religious (Theological) theory holds that welfare is driven by religious feeling. It has two aspects: Atonement, where the employer does good work to atone for the sins of exploitation or wrongdoing, and Investment, where welfare is seen as a spiritual investment that earns merit and reward in the next world. The Philanthropic theory rests on love of fellow human beings and charity, so the employer acts out of humanitarian impulse and a sense of duty toward the weak. The Placating (Appeasement) theory says welfare is used to pacify militant workers and to forestall unrest and unionisation, as a sop to the growing consciousness of labour. The Public Relations theory says welfare is meant to build a good image of the employer among workers, the public and the government. Others include the Policy theory (welfare as a business policy to get work done), the Paternalistic theory, the Functional theory (efficiency), and the Social/Trusteeship theory (Gandhian). Elimination: the terms atonement and investment point to religion and sin, not charity, appeasement or image.
explanations: Incorrect: the Philanthropic theory is based on humanitarian love and charity, not atonement or spiritual investment.
Incorrect: the Placating theory is about pacifying militant labour and preventing unrest, not about religious motives.
Incorrect: the Public Relations theory aims at building a favourable image of the employer, not at atonement or spiritual investment.
Correct: the Religious theory has atonement for sins and investment for spiritual reward as two co-equal aspects.
keyfact: Religious theory of labour welfare = atonement for sins plus investment for spiritual reward.
option_notes: Philanthropic theory: welfare is provided out of love for fellow human beings, charity and a sense of duty. The employer is seen as a benefactor helping the weak. It is criticised for being paternalistic, unsystematic and dependent on the employer's whims. It is one of the classic theories alongside the Policy, Paternalistic and Placating theories.

Placating (Appeasement) theory: employers offer welfare to appease or pacify workers, especially as labour becomes more conscious and organised. The aim is to reduce unrest, blunt the appeal of trade unions and prevent strikes. Welfare is thus a defensive measure and a sop. It is sometimes called the appeasement theory.

Public Relations theory: welfare is undertaken to create goodwill and a positive image of the employer among workers, the community and the government. It is akin to a publicity tool and aims at better industrial relations and a favourable public opinion. It is also known as the Public Relations or image-building theory.

Religious (Theological) theory: welfare is motivated by religious feelings. It has two co-equal aspects: atonement for sins and exploitation, and investment, which means earning spiritual merit and reward after death. Many early Indian and Western employers built temples, dharamshalas and charities under this impulse.
related: Religious theory: atonement and investment.
Placating theory: welfare to pacify militant labour.
Trusteeship theory: Gandhian idea of employer as trustee.
Factories Act Section 49: Welfare Officers where 500 or more workers.
Section 46: canteen where 250 or more workers.
Section 48: creche where more than 30 women workers.
Rege Committee 1946 is the Labour Investigation Committee.
summary: The answer is (d), the Religious theory. Under this theory of labour welfare, employers do welfare work to atone for their sins or exploitation (atonement) and to earn spiritual merit or a reward in the afterlife (investment). The two are treated as co-equal aspects.
topic_notes: Labour welfare covers services, facilities and amenities that improve workers' working and living conditions beyond wages. The ILO defines it as services, facilities and amenities such as canteens, rest and recreation, sanitation, medical aid, housing and transport that enable workers to perform their work in healthy, congenial surroundings. Welfare work is classed as statutory (required by laws such as the Factories Act 1948, Mines Act 1952 and Plantations Labour Act 1951), voluntary (by employers) and mutual (by unions). Intra-mural facilities are within the establishment; extra-mural ones are outside, such as housing and education. The Royal Commission on Labour (1931) and the Labour Investigation Committee (Rege Committee, 1946) studied welfare in India. The Labour Welfare Funds Acts of states and the Central Labour Welfare Funds for mines (coal, mica, iron ore, limestone and dolomite) and for beedi workers finance welfare. Theories include Policy (welfare as sound business policy, to secure a reward), Philanthropic, Paternalistic (employer as father), Placating, Public Relations, Religious, Functional (efficiency and productivity) and the Social or Trusteeship theory (employer as trustee of workers' interests, a Gandhian idea). Other angles for exams are principles of welfare (adequacy, totality, responsiveness), Welfare Officers under Section 49 of the Factories Act (500 or more workers), and canteens under Section 46 (250 or more workers) and creches under Section 48 (30 or more women workers).

question: The first Factories Act for India was enacted in the year:
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Indian Factories Act, 1881 was the first legislation regulating factory conditions in British India. It was driven partly by Lancashire mill-owners, who wanted to curb Indian competition, and partly by humanitarian concern over working conditions. It applied to factories using mechanical power and employing 100 or more workers. It prohibited employment of children under 7, limited the working hours of children aged 7-12 to 9 per day, required four holidays a month for children, and required fencing of dangerous machinery. It had no provisions for women's hours and no effective inspection. The Factories Act of 1891 followed, after the Bombay Factory Commission of 1884 and the Berne Conference (1890). It covered factories with 50 or more workers, fixed 7 hours for children (9-14 years), limited women to 11 hours, and gave women a break. The 1911 Act dealt with working hours for adult men in textile factories (12 hours). The 1922 Act was passed after India joined the ILO. The 1934 Act was based on the Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley, 1929-31) recommendations. The 1948 Act is the current law, post-independence. Elimination: 1948 is the current Act, 1911 and 1891 are later amendments or replacements, and 1881 is the first.
explanations: Incorrect: 1948 is the year of the present Factories Act, which came into force on 1 April 1949, not the first Act.
Correct: The Indian Factories Act of 1881 was the first factory legislation in India.
Incorrect: 1911 was the third Act, which introduced a 12-hour daily limit for adult males in textile factories.
Incorrect: 1891 was the second Act, which replaced the 1881 Act and extended coverage to factories with 50 or more workers.
keyfact: First Factories Act in India: 1881 (Lord Ripon); then 1891, 1911, 1922, 1934, and the present Act of 1948.
option_notes: The Factories Act, 1948 is the current principal law on health, safety, welfare, working hours, and employment of young persons and women in factories. It came into force on 1 April 1949, was enacted following the Rege Committee recommendations, and applies to factories with 10 or more workers using power or 20 or more without power. It is administered by the state governments and was amended in 1976 and 1987 (after the Bhopal gas tragedy).

The Indian Factories Act, 1881 was the first factory law in British India, enacted under Viceroy Lord Ripon. It applied to mechanically powered factories with 100 or more workers. It banned child employment under 7, limited children aged 7-12 to 9 hours a day, and required machinery to be fenced. It lacked proper inspection and did not cover women's hours.

The Factories Act, 1911 was the third Act and came into force on 1 July 1912. It restricted adult male workers in textile factories to 12 hours a day and limited children's hours to 6.
