It also dealt with health, sanitation, and ventilation. It was followed by the 1922 Act, which was passed after India joined the ILO and lowered the weekly limit to 60 hours.

The Factories Act, 1891 was the second Act, enacted after the Bombay Factory Commission (1884) and influenced by the Berne Conference (1890). It applied to factories with 50 or more workers, raised the minimum age for children to 9, limited children to 7 hours a day, restricted women to 11 hours a day with a rest interval, and gave a weekly holiday to all workers. It was the first Act to include women.
related: The first Indian Factories Act was passed in 1881 under Lord Ripon.
The 1891 Act first included provisions on women's working hours.
The 1948 Act came into force on 1 April 1949.
The Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley) was set up in 1929 and reported in 1931.
The 1987 amendment to the Factories Act followed the Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984.
The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 subsumes the Factories Act, 1948.
The Factories Act 1948 defines a factory as having 10 or more workers with power, or 20 or more without power.
summary: The first Factories Act for India was enacted in 1881 (option b). It was a modest law, passed under Lord Ripon's viceroyalty, mainly to regulate child labour and basic safety in textile factories. It was later replaced by the Acts of 1891, 1911, 1922, 1934 and finally 1948.
topic_notes: Factory legislation in India evolved gradually through colonial and post-independence stages. Before 1881, working conditions in cotton and jute mills were unregulated. The 1881 Act was the first law, and it was limited in scope. The 1891 Act followed after the Bombay Factory Commission of 1884 and the Berne Conference of 1890, and it protected women and children more. The 1911 Act regulated adult male hours in textile mills. The 1922 Act, passed after India's ILO membership in 1919, reduced the daily limit to 10 hours and applied to factories with 20 or more workers. The 1934 Act was based on the Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley Commission, 1929-31) and introduced a distinction between seasonal and perennial factories and a 54-hour week. The Factories Act, 1948 is the current law, covering health, safety, welfare, working hours, annual leave with wages, and employment of young persons and women. Key features of the 1948 Act: a 48-hour week, a 9-hour day, spread-over of 10.5 hours, a weekly holiday, overtime at double the wage rate, and safety officers in factories with 1,000 or more workers. The Act defines 'factory' under Section 2(m) and 'occupier' under Section 2(n), and a 'worker' under Section 2(l). The 1987 amendment, passed after the Bhopal gas tragedy, added provisions on hazardous processes and the 'right to know' for workers. Other related laws: the Mines Act 1952, the Plantation Labour Act 1951, and the new Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which subsumes the Factories Act.

question: Which one of the following statements with regard to the provision for ‘Welfare Officer’ is NOT correct?
options: This provision is given in the Factories Act 1948
This provision, in case of Mines and Plantations, is given in the central rules of these two Acts but not in the main Acts
For factories and plantations this provision is applicable when 500 or more workers are employed
In mines this provision is made applicable when 500 or more workers are employed
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Welfare Officers are a statutory welfare measure for large workplaces. Sec 49 of the Factories Act 1948 requires every factory employing 500 or more workers to appoint Welfare Officers, and the State Government prescribes their number, qualifications, duties and conditions of service. Sec 58 of the Mines Act 1952 requires a Welfare Officer in every mine where 500 or more persons are ordinarily employed. Sec 18 of the Plantations Labour Act 1951 requires one in every plantation employing 300 or more workers. Option (a) is correct because the Factories Act 1948 contains the provision. Option (d) is correct for mines. Option (c) lumps plantations with factories at 500, which is wrong because the plantation threshold is 300. Option (b) is also inaccurate, since the provision sits in the main Acts, with the central rules and state rules only prescribing qualifications and duties. Because (c) contains the well-known numerical error, it is the intended answer. Remember the thresholds as factories 500, mines 500 and plantations 300. Note that the Factories Act threshold for a Safety Officer is 1000 workers, and the threshold for a canteen is 250.
explanations: (a) is a correct statement: Sec 49 of the Factories Act 1948 provides for Welfare Officers, so it is not the answer.

(b) is not accurate, because Sec 58 of the Mines Act and Sec 18 of the Plantations Labour Act are in the main Acts. It is flawed, but (c) is the clearer and more deliberate error, so it is chosen as the intended answer.
(c) is incorrect because the plantation threshold is 300 or more workers, not 500, so this is the statement that is NOT correct.
(d) is correct: Sec 58 of the Mines Act 1952 applies when 500 or more persons are employed in a mine.
keyfact: Welfare Officer threshold: factories 500, mines 500, plantations 300.
option_notes: Factories Act 1948, Sec 49: every factory with 500 or more workers must appoint Welfare Officers. The State Government prescribes their number, qualifications, duties and service conditions. The Act's welfare chapter (Sec 42-50) also covers washing facilities, first aid, canteens (250 workers), shelters and rest rooms, and creches (30 women workers).

The Mines Act 1952 and Plantations Labour Act 1951 both contain the Welfare Officer provision in the main Act (Sec 58 and Sec 18 respectively). The rules framed under them, such as the Mines Rules 1955 and state plantation rules, deal with qualifications, duties and conditions of service. Mines are regulated by the DGMS, and plantations by state governments.

The Plantations Labour Act 1951 covers tea, coffee, rubber, cinchona, cardamom and similar plantations of 5 hectares or more with 15 or more workers. Sec 18 requires a Welfare Officer at 300 or more workers. The Factories Act figure is 500. The statement is wrong because it assigns 500 to plantations.

Mines Act 1952, Sec 58: a Welfare Officer is required in every mine where 500 or more persons are ordinarily employed. The Act is administered by the DGMS under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, and Sec 58 also lets the Government prescribe the officer's qualifications and duties. The statement is correct.
related: Factories Act 1948 Sec 49: Welfare Officer at 500 or more workers.
Mines Act 1952 Sec 58: Welfare Officer at 500 or more persons.
Plantations Labour Act 1951 Sec 18: Welfare Officer at 300 or more workers.
Factories Act: Safety Officer at 1000 or more workers.
Factories Act: canteen required above 250 workers; creche above 30 women workers.
Plantations Labour Act applies to plantations of 5 hectares or more with 15 or more workers.
The OSH Code 2020 subsumes the Factories Act, Mines Act and several other labour laws.
summary: The answer is (c). Under the Plantations Labour Act 1951 (Sec 18), a Welfare Officer is required when 300 or more workers are employed, not 500. Factories (Sec 49, Factories Act 1948) and mines (Sec 58, Mines Act 1952) use the 500 threshold. Option (b) is also factually doubtful, so (c) is chosen as the intended best answer.
topic_notes: Welfare Officers are a statutory feature of three major Indian labour laws. Factories Act 1948, Sec 49: 500 or more workers. Mines Act 1952, Sec 58: 500 or more persons. Plantations Labour Act 1951, Sec 18: 300 or more workers. The State Government under the Factories Act, or the Central/State Government under the other two, frames rules on qualifications, duties and conditions of service. The role is to look after workers' welfare, such as canteens, creches, housing, recreation and grievances, and to liaise between management and labour. Other related thresholds under the Factories Act: Safety Officer at 1000 or more workers (or where hazardous processes occur), canteen at more than 250 workers, creche at more than 30 women workers, and lunch/rest rooms at more than 150 workers. The Act applies to premises with 10 or more workers using power or 20 or more without power. The Plantations Labour Act 1951 also covers housing, medical facilities, educational facilities for children (when there are more than 25 children between 6 and 12), and creches. Other labour welfare institutions include the Labour Welfare Funds for mines (coal, mica, iron ore, limestone and dolomite, and others), administered by the Labour Welfare Organisation. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020 subsumes these Acts, though the older Acts are the basis for this exam question. The Code was enacted in 2020, but its implementation has been awaited.

question: Which one of the following is NOT a ‘welfare measure’ under the Factories Act 1948?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Factories Act 1948 Chapter III (ss.11-20) covers Health: cleanliness (s.11), disposal of wastes (s.12), ventilation and temperature (s.13), dust and fume (s.14), artificial humidification (s.15), overcrowding (s.16), lighting (s.17), drinking water (s.18), latrines and urinals (s.19), spittoons (s.20). Chapter IV (ss.21-41) covers Safety. Chapter V (ss.42-50) covers Welfare: washing facilities (s.42), facilities for storing and drying clothes (s.43), sitting facilities (s.44), first-aid appliances (s.45), canteens (s.46), shelters, rest rooms and lunch rooms (s.47), crèches (s.48), welfare officers (s.49), power to make rules to supplement this chapter (s.50). So first aid, canteen and crèche are all welfare measures in the Welfare chapter, while drinking water is a health provision. Elimination: b, c and d are all in Chapter V; only a is in Chapter III. Note that in a broad sense drinking water is a welfare amenity, but the Act's classification decides UPSC-style questions. Thresholds: first-aid box per 150 workers; canteen if over 250 workers; crèche if over 30 women workers; shelters if over 150 workers; welfare officer if 500 or more workers.
explanations: Correct answer: drinking water is under s.18 in Chapter III (Health), not in the Welfare chapter, so it is the one that is not a welfare measure.
Crèches are under s.48 in Chapter V (Welfare), required where more than 30 women are employed, so this is a welfare measure and not the answer.
First-aid appliances are under s.45 in Chapter V (Welfare), one box per 150 workers, so this is a welfare measure and not the answer.
Canteens are under s.46 in Chapter V (Welfare), required where more than 250 workers are employed, so this is a welfare measure and not the answer.
keyfact: Drinking water is s.18 (Health chapter); first aid s.45, canteen s.46, crèche s.48 are Welfare chapter (Ch. V).
option_notes: Drinking water (s.18): occupiers must provide a sufficient supply of wholesome drinking water at suitable points, marked 'drinking water' in a language understood by most workers. In factories with over 250 workers in hot weather, cool drinking water must be provided. Water points must be 6 metres from latrines, urinals and similar places. It lies in Chapter III on Health.

Crèches (s.48): factories with more than 30 women workers must provide a suitable room for children under 6 years. The room must be adequately lit and ventilated, kept clean, and supervised by women trained in child care. State rules prescribe standards. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 also mandates crèches in establishments with 50 or more employees.

First aid (s.45): first-aid boxes or cupboards, equipped with prescribed contents, must be provided at the rate of one for every 150 workers. They must be in the charge of a trained person who is always available during working hours. Where over 500 workers are employed, an ambulance room with prescribed facilities and medical and nursing staff is needed.

Canteen (s.46): the State Government may require a canteen in factories with more than 250 workers. State rules cover the building, accommodation, furniture, food items and prices (on a non-profit basis), and a managing committee representing the workers. It is part of Chapter V on Welfare.
related: Welfare officer under s.49 is required where 500 or more workers are employed.
Canteen under s.46 is required where more than 250 workers are employed.
Crèche under s.48 is required where more than 30 women workers are employed.
First-aid box under s.45: one per 150 workers; ambulance room if over 500 workers.
Shelters, rest rooms and lunch rooms under s.47 apply where more than 150 workers are employed.
Chapter IVA on hazardous processes was added in 1987 after the Bhopal gas disaster.
Adult weekly working limit under the Factories Act is 48 hours.
summary: The answer is (c) First aid. Under the Factories Act 1948, drinking water falls under Chapter III (Health, s.18), while crèches (s.48), canteens (s.46) and first-aid appliances (s.45) sit in Chapter V (Welfare). However, the strict textual answer is tricky: first aid (s.45) is in the Welfare chapter, so drinking water (s.18, Health chapter) is the item that is NOT a 'welfare measure' in the statutory chapter sense. Correction: the correct option is (a) Drinking water.
topic_notes: The Factories Act 1948 came into force on 1 April 1949, replacing the 1934 Act. It applies to premises with 10 or more workers using power, or 20 or more workers without power. Chapters: I Preliminary; II Inspecting Staff; III Health (ss.11-20); IV Safety (ss.21-41); IVA Hazardous Processes (ss.41A-41H, added after the Bhopal gas tragedy in 1987); V Welfare (ss.42-50); VI Working Hours of Adults (ss.51-66); VII Employment of Young Persons (ss.67-77); VIII Annual Leave with Wages (ss.78-84); IX Special Provisions; X Penalties and Procedure. Key numbers: adult weekly limit 48 hours, daily 9 hours, spread-over 10.5 hours, rest interval after 5 hours of work for at least half an hour, overtime wages at twice the ordinary rate. Child under 14 cannot be employed, and adolescents aged 15-18 need a certificate of fitness. Annual leave is 1 day for every 20 days worked by adults and 1 for every 15 by children. Welfare officers are required where 500 or more workers are employed. Safety officers are required where 1000 or more workers are employed or where hazardous processes are carried out. Women may work only between 6 am and 7 pm unless the State permits otherwise. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020 will subsume this Act.

question: Under the provisions of the Maternity Benefit Act 1961, what is the amount of medical bonus paid?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Section 8 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 entitles every woman to a medical bonus if her employer does not provide free medical care (prenatal confinement and postnatal care) at no charge. The original amount was Rs. 25, later Rs. 250, then raised to Rs. 1,000 (1995 amendment era) and Rs. 2,500 by notification. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2008 empowered the Central Government to raise the amount, and the amount was fixed at Rs. 3,500 (notification of 2011, effective 1 January 2011). The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 retained the provision, with Section 8 allowing the Centre to revise the amount every three years, up to Rs. 20,000. A related provision is that the 2017 amendment raised paid maternity leave from 12 to 26 weeks for the first two children. Elimination: Rs. 1,000 and Rs. 2,500 are older, superseded figures, and Rs. 3,000 was never a statutory figure. Rs. 3,500 is the figure used in the examination context for this question. Note that the ESI Act maternity benefit and the Maternity Benefit Act do not apply together to the same woman, as ESI covered women get benefit under ESI.
explanations: Incorrect: Rs. 1,000 was an earlier figure and has been superseded by later revisions.
Incorrect: Rs. 2,500 was the amount after the 1995 revision, later raised further.
Incorrect: Rs. 3,000 was never the prescribed medical bonus amount.
Correct: Rs. 3,500 is the medical bonus under Section 8 as revised by the Central Government.
keyfact: Medical bonus under Section 8 of the Maternity Benefit Act 1961 is Rs. 3,500.
option_notes: Rs. 1,000: an earlier medical bonus figure under Section 8, replaced by subsequent revisions. It was paid when the employer provided no free prenatal and postnatal care.
Rs. 2,500: the medical bonus figure fixed by the 1995 revision, later superseded. Students often confuse it with the current amount.
Rs. 3,000: not a prescribed statutory amount for the medical bonus. It acts as a distractor between the older and the current figures.

Rs. 3,500: the medical bonus fixed by the Central Government under Section 8 (2011 notification). It is payable if the employer does not provide free medical care to the woman. The Act permits the Centre to revise the amount.
related: Maternity leave under the 2017 amendment is 26 weeks for the first two children.
Qualifying service is 80 days in the preceding 12 months.
Creche facility is mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees.
Miscarriage leave is 6 weeks under Section 9.
Tubectomy leave is 2 weeks under Section 9A.
Nursing breaks continue until the child is 15 months old.
summary: The answer is (d) Rs. 3,500. Section 8 of the Maternity Benefit Act 1961 provides a medical bonus when the employer does not provide free prenatal confinement and postnatal care. The amount was Rs. 250 originally, raised to Rs. 1,000 and then Rs. 2,500 (1995), and was revised to Rs. 3,500 by the Central Government notification of 2011 (effective 2008 revision per Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2008).
topic_notes: The Maternity Benefit Act 1961 regulates employment of women in certain establishments for a fixed period before and after childbirth and provides maternity benefit. It applies to factories, mines, plantations, shops and establishments with ten or more persons, and the circus industry. Key sections: Section 5 gives the right to payment of maternity benefit at the average daily wage; Section 5(3) as amended in 2017 gives 26 weeks for the first two children (8 weeks before delivery at most) and 12 weeks for a third child onward. Adopting mothers (child below three months) and commissioning mothers get 12 weeks. Section 5A allows work from home after the leave period by mutual agreement. Section 8 gives the medical bonus. Section 9 gives leave for miscarriage (6 weeks) and Section 9A gives leave for tubectomy (2 weeks). Section 10 gives leave for illness arising out of pregnancy (one month). Section 11 provides nursing breaks (two breaks daily until the child is 15 months). Section 11A requires a creche for establishments with 50 or more employees, with four visits a day permitted. Section 12 protects against dismissal during pregnancy. To qualify, a woman must have worked at least 80 days in the 12 months preceding the expected delivery. Inspectors enforce the Act. Women covered under the ESI Act receive maternity benefit under ESI instead. The Act is now subsumed in the Code on Social Security 2020.

question: Under the Maternity Benefit Act 1961, what is the minimum number of days a woman employee must have worked under an employer in the twelve months preceding the date of expected delivery for becoming eligible for maternity benefit?
subject: Social Security
detail: Section 5(2) of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 sets the eligibility condition: a woman is entitled to maternity benefit only if she has actually worked in an establishment of the employer for not less than 80 days in the 12 months immediately preceding the date of her expected delivery. Days on which she was laid off or held holidays with wages count as days worked. The rate of benefit is the average daily wage for the days of actual absence. The 2017 Amendment (in force from 1 April 2017) raised paid leave from 12 to 26 weeks for the first two children, and 12 weeks for a third child or more. Of the 26 weeks, no more than 8 can be taken before the expected delivery. It also gave 12 weeks to adopting mothers (child under 3 months) and commissioning mothers, made a creche mandatory in establishments with 50 or more employees, and allowed work from home. Elimination: 90 days is a distractor, 180 days and 240 days resemble thresholds in other laws, such as 240 days for continuous service under the Industrial Disputes Act and 190/240 days under the Factories Act. Only 80 days matches the Maternity Benefit Act.
explanations: Incorrect: 90 days is not the statutory threshold in the Act. The Act specifies 80 days.
Correct: Section 5(2) requires at least 80 days of actual work in the 12 months preceding the expected delivery.
Incorrect: 180 days is not the requirement. It is a distractor, possibly confused with the 26 weeks (182 days) of leave under the 2017 amendment.
Incorrect: 240 days relates to continuous service under the Industrial Disputes Act (Section 25B) for retrenchment, not to maternity benefit.
keyfact: Maternity Benefit Act, 1961: 80 days of actual work in the 12 months before expected delivery; 26 weeks of leave for the first two children.
option_notes: 90 days is not a threshold in the Maternity Benefit Act. It is sometimes confused with the 3-month age limit of a child for adoption or commissioning mothers to claim leave. Several labour laws use 90-day-type periods for other purposes, such as notice or qualifying periods, but not here.

80 days is the qualifying period under Section 5(2) of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961. The woman must have actually worked for at least 80 days in the 12 months before the expected delivery date. Days of lay-off and paid holidays count as worked. The ESI Act has a separate scheme for insured women with its own contribution conditions.

180 days is not the qualifying period for maternity benefit. The nearest figure is 26 weeks, which is about 182 days, the maximum paid maternity leave since the 2017 amendment for the first two children. It is a leave duration, not an eligibility criterion.

240 days is the working period that defines continuous service of one year under Section 25B of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (and in some contexts for underground mines or other establishments). It is used for retrenchment compensation eligibility, not for maternity benefit.
related: Section 5(2) of the MB Act requires 80 days of work in the 12 months before delivery.
The 2017 Amendment raised maternity leave from 12 to 26 weeks.
Third child onwards gets 12 weeks of maternity leave.
A creche is mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees (Section 11A).
Adopting or commissioning mothers get 12 weeks of leave.
Miscarriage or MTP leave is 6 weeks; tubectomy leave is 2 weeks.
Medical bonus under the Act is Rs 3,500.
Dismissal on account of pregnancy is prohibited under Section 12.
summary: The answer is (b) 80 days. Section 5(2) of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 entitles a woman to maternity benefit only if she has actually worked for at least 80 days in the 12 months immediately preceding the date of her expected delivery.
topic_notes: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 regulates the employment of women in certain establishments for a fixed period before and after childbirth and provides maternity benefit. It applies to factories, mines, plantations, shops and establishments, and to establishments employing 10 or more persons. The Act is anchored in the Directive Principles (Article 42, just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief). Key points: eligibility is 80 days of actual work in the 12 months before expected delivery (Section 5). The 2017 Amendment raised leave to 26 weeks for the first two surviving children (8 weeks pre-delivery at most) and 12 weeks for a third child onwards. Adopting mothers of a child under 3 months and commissioning mothers (surrogacy) get 12 weeks. Section 11A makes a creche mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees, with four visits a day permitted including the rest interval. Employers must inform women of their benefits in writing or electronically at the time of appointment. Work from home may be allowed after the leave period by mutual agreement where the nature of work permits. Medical bonus is payable if the employer provides no pre-natal or post-natal care (Rs 3,500, which the Centre may revise). Leave for miscarriage or medical termination is 6 weeks, for tubectomy 2 weeks, and up to 1 month for illness arising from pregnancy, delivery, premature birth or miscarriage. Dismissal during pregnancy is prohibited (Section 12). Inspectors enforce the Act, and the penalty for contravention is imprisonment of 3 months to 1 year and a fine of Rs 2,000 to Rs 5,000. For insured women, maternity benefit under the ESI Act, 1948 is similar. The 2017 amendment also aligned ESI maternity benefit to 26 weeks.

question: Under the provisions of the Employees’ Compensation Act 1923, what will be the amount of compensation payable to an employee suffering from permanent total disability with his monthly salary drawn Rs. 15, 800 and the relevant factor 181.37?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Under Section 4 and Schedule IV of the Employees' Compensation Act 1923, compensation for permanent total disability equals 60% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor. The relevant factor depends on the employee's age at the last birthday, and 181.37 corresponds to age 20-21 or thereabouts. For death, the percentage is 50%. The Employees' Compensation (Amendment) Act 2009, effective from 18 January 2010, fixed the ceiling on monthly wages for computation at Rs. 8,000. The Central Government can revise this ceiling by notification. Actual wages of Rs. 15,800 therefore do not matter, because only Rs. 8,000 is counted. Calculation: 60% of 8,000 = 4,800, and 4,800 × 181.37 = 8,70,576. Minimum compensation is Rs. 1,40,000 for permanent total disability and Rs. 1,20,000 for death. Elimination: (d) is the statutory minimum, which applies only when the formula gives less. (b) is not derived from the formula. (a) matches no correct step. Using the uncapped wage of 15,800 would give about Rs. 17.19 lakh, which is not offered. Only (c) matches the capped-wage computation.
explanations: Correct. 60% × Rs. 8,000 (the wage ceiling) × 181.37 = Rs. 8,70,576.
Wrong. Rs. 5,40,000 does not come from the formula with any valid wage or factor in this question.
Wrong. Rs. 7,75,376 does not match the capped-wage computation. It would need a different wage base or percentage.
Wrong. Rs. 1,40,000 is only the statutory minimum for permanent total disability. The formula result is higher, so the minimum does not apply.
keyfact: Permanent total disability compensation = 60% × monthly wages (capped at Rs. 8,000) × relevant factor, so 4,800 × 181.37 = Rs. 8,70,576.
option_notes: Rs. 7,75,376 is a distractor. It does not correspond to a valid calculation under Schedule IV. The correct formula is 60% of capped monthly wages × relevant factor for permanent total disability. Students should not use any other percentage, such as 50%, which applies to death cases.

Rs. 5,40,000 is a distractor with no basis in the Act. Compensation always follows the Schedule IV factor tables, which are linked to the age of the employee, and the wage ceiling set by notification. It is not a statutory fixed sum.

Rs. 8,70,576 is the correct result: 60% × 8,000 × 181.37. The Rs. 8,000 monthly wage ceiling came with the 2009 amendment, effective 18 January 2010. The relevant factor is read from Schedule IV according to the employee's age at the last birthday, and it declines as age rises.

Rs. 1,40,000 is the minimum compensation for permanent total disability under Section 4, as amended in 2010. The minimum for death is Rs. 1,20,000. Where the formula gives a smaller sum, the minimum is payable. Here the formula gives much more, so this option is wrong.
related: Death compensation under the Act = 50% of monthly wages × relevant factor, minimum Rs. 1,20,000.
Permanent total disability minimum compensation = Rs. 1,40,000.
The wage ceiling for computing compensation is Rs. 8,000 per month under the 2010 notification.
Temporary disablement: half-monthly payment of 25% of wages from the 11th day.
The Workmen's Compensation Act was renamed the Employees' Compensation Act with effect from 18 January 2010.
Interest on delayed compensation is 12% per annum after one month of falling due.
Claims are to be filed before the Commissioner for Employees' Compensation within 2 years.
Schedule IV gives the relevant factors according to the employee's age.
summary: The answer is (c) Rs. 8,70,576. For permanent total disability, compensation is 60% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor. Monthly wages are capped at Rs. 8,000 for this calculation, so the figure is 0.60 × 8,000 × 181.37 = Rs. 8,70,576.
topic_notes: The Employees' Compensation Act 1923 (formerly the Workmen's Compensation Act) provides compensation to employees and their dependants for injury by accident arising out of and in the course of employment, and for occupational diseases listed in Schedule III. It was renamed by the 2009 amendment, effective 18 January 2010. The employer is liable under Section 3, subject to exceptions: disablement lasting under 3 days (except in the case of permanent disablement), or injury caused by intoxication, wilful disobedience of safety rules, or removal of safety devices. Compensation formulas: death = 50% of monthly wages × relevant factor, with a minimum of Rs. 1,20,000. Permanent total disability = 60% of monthly wages × relevant factor, with a minimum of Rs. 1,40,000. Partial permanent disability = the percentage loss of earning capacity (Schedule I lists specific injuries) × the permanent total disability compensation. Temporary disability = a half-monthly payment of 25% of monthly wages, beginning from the 11th day after the disablement. Wage ceiling for calculation: Rs. 8,000 per month (2010 notification), which the Government may revise. Interest and penalty: interest at 12% per annum if compensation is not paid within one month of falling due, and the Commissioner may impose a penalty of up to 50% of the compensation for delay without reasonable cause. Employers must notify the Commissioner of fatal accidents. Commissioners for Employees' Compensation decide claims. Claims must be made within 2 years of the accident or death. Appeals go to the High Court on a substantial question of law, and only where the amount is not less than Rs. 10,000 in the case of some orders. Also remember Schedule II (persons treated as employees), Schedule III (occupational diseases), and Schedule IV (relevant factors by age).

question: Who among the following is NOT a dependent under the provisions of the Employees’ Compensation Act 1923?
options: A parent other than a widowed mother
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Section 2(1)(d) of the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 defines 'dependant' in two tiers. The first tier is covered whether or not the person depended on the employee's earnings. It includes a widow, a minor legitimate son, an unmarried legitimate daughter, and a widowed mother. The second tier covers relatives who must be wholly or partly dependent on the employee's earnings at the time of death. It includes a widower, a parent other than a widowed mother, a minor illegitimate son or unmarried illegitimate daughter, and a married or widowed minor daughter. It also includes a minor brother, an unmarried sister, or a widowed sister if a minor, and a widowed daughter-in-law. Further members are a minor child of a pre-deceased son, a minor child of a pre-deceased daughter where no parent of the child is alive, and a paternal grandparent if no parent of the employee is alive. An infirm son or daughter aged 18 or more is a dependant only if wholly dependent. The widowed sister qualifies only while a minor, so an adult widowed sister is outside the definition. The other three options appear expressly in the list. The Act was renamed from the Workmen's Compensation Act in 2009. Dependants claim compensation in case of the employee's death, and the Commissioner for Employees' Compensation decides disputes.
explanations: Wrong: a widower is a listed dependant, provided he was wholly or partly dependent on the deceased employee's earnings.
Correct: the Act includes a widowed sister only if she is a minor, so an adult widowed sister is not a dependant.
Wrong: a parent other than a widowed mother (for example, a father) is a dependant if wholly or partly dependent on the employee's earnings.
Wrong: a widowed daughter-in-law is expressly listed as a dependant if wholly or partly dependent on the employee's earnings.
keyfact: Under Section 2(1)(d), a widowed sister counts as a dependant only if she is a minor, so an adult widowed sister is not a dependant.
option_notes: A widower is the surviving husband of a deceased female employee. Under Section 2(1)(d)(ii), he is a dependant only if wholly or partly dependent on her earnings at the time of death. A widow, by contrast, is a dependant without any proof of dependency. This asymmetry is a common exam point. The dependant's share of compensation is decided by the Commissioner for Employees' Compensation.

A widowed sister is a dependant only if she is a minor, and she must be wholly or partly dependent on the employee. An adult widowed sister has no standing as a dependant. The same clause includes a minor brother and an unmarried sister. An unmarried sister is covered regardless of age, whereas a widowed sister is covered only while a minor.

A parent other than a widowed mother means the father, or a mother who is not widowed. Such a parent is a dependant only if wholly or partly dependent on the employee's earnings. A widowed mother is in the unconditional first tier and needs no proof of dependency. This distinction between the two tiers is often tested.

A widowed daughter-in-law is expressly listed in the second tier of Section 2(1)(d). She qualifies if wholly or partly dependent on the earnings of the deceased employee. There is no age restriction. Daughters-in-law who are not widowed, and sons-in-law, are not listed as dependants.
related: Section 2(1)(d) of the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 defines 'dependant'.
Widow, minor legitimate son, unmarried legitimate daughter and widowed mother are dependants without proof of dependency.
A widowed sister is a dependant only if a minor.
An unmarried sister is a dependant if wholly or partly dependent on the employee.
The Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 was renamed the Employees' Compensation Act by the 2009 amendment.
Claims for compensation are decided by the Commissioner for Employees' Compensation.
An infirm son or daughter aged 18 or more is a dependant only if wholly dependent.
A paternal grandparent is a dependant if no parent of the employee is alive.
summary: The answer is (b), an adult widowed sister. Section 2(1)(d) of the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 lists a widowed sister as a dependant only if she is a minor, so an adult widowed sister is excluded. A widower, a parent other than a widowed mother, and a widowed daughter-in-law are all listed dependants.
topic_notes: The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 (earlier the Workmen's Compensation Act, renamed by the 2009 amendment) provides compensation to employees or their dependants for injury or death arising out of and in the course of employment, including occupational diseases. The employer is liable to pay. There is no liability if the injury results in disablement for fewer than 3 days, or if the employee was under the influence of drink or drugs, wilfully disobeyed a safety rule, or removed a safety guard. Compensation is paid through the Commissioner for Employees' Compensation, who also adjudicates disputes. Key sections: Section 2(1)(d) defines dependant; Section 3 deals with the employer's liability; Section 4 deals with the amount of compensation and the definition of partial and total disablement; Section 4A covers payment and penalty for delay; Section 5 sets out the method of calculating wages; Section 8 provides that death compensation is deposited with the Commissioner; Section 10 sets a 2-year limitation for claims, with notice to be given; Section 22 deals with applications; and Section 30 deals with appeals to the High Court on a substantial question of law. The Act applies to employees not covered by the ESI Act, since the ESI Act provides its own benefits and bars double claims. Compensation for death is 50% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor, or a fixed minimum amount. Disability compensation depends on percentage of loss of earning capacity; Schedule I lists injuries and loss percentages, Schedule II lists persons treated as employees, and Schedule III lists occupational diseases. Interest on delayed payment and penalty are also provided. The first-tier dependants (widow, minor legitimate son, unmarried legitimate daughter, widowed mother) need no proof of dependency; the second tier needs wholly or partial dependency. Related ideas for exams: definitions of 'wages', 'employer', 'partial disablement' and 'total disablement'; the Wages Ceiling, which was removed by the 2009 amendment; and the Act's relationship to the ESI Act and the Social Security Code 2020.

question: Who among the following is the ex-officio Chairman of the Medical Benefit Council constituted under the Employees’ Insurance Act 1948?
options: The Director General, Health Services, Government of India
The Medical Commissioner of the Employees State Insurance Corporation
The Director General, Employees State Insurance Corporation
subject: Insurance
detail: Section 10 of the ESI Act 1948 provides for the Medical Benefit Council. Its members are: the Director General, ESIC, as ex-officio Chairman; the Medical Commissioner of the ESIC (Deputy Chairman in some versions of the provision, whose role should be checked against the bare Act); the Director General of Health Services (Government of India) or his nominee; one member each representing the medical profession, employers and employees; and representatives of State governments. The Council advises the Corporation and the Standing Committee on administering medical benefit, on the certification for entitlement to benefit, on the standard of medical care, and on other matters referred to it. The Corporation is the apex body (Section 3), the Standing Committee is its executive body (Section 8), and the Medical Benefit Council is an advisory body (Section 10). Elimination: the Director General of Health Services and the Chairman of the Medical Council of India are members at most, not the Chair. The Medical Commissioner is a member, not the Chairman. The Director General of the ESIC is the chief executive officer of the Corporation and holds the chair.
explanations: Wrong: the DGHS (Government of India) is a member of the Council, not its Chairman.
Wrong: the Medical Commissioner of the ESIC is a member (the Council's senior medical officer), not the ex-officio Chairman.
Correct: the Director General, ESIC, is the ex-officio Chairman under Section 10.
Wrong: the Chairman of the Medical Council of India (now the National Medical Commission) is not the chair of the ESI Medical Benefit Council.
keyfact: Medical Benefit Council (Section 10, ESI Act): Director General, ESIC, is ex-officio Chairman.
option_notes: The Director General of Health Services (DGHS) is the principal medical adviser to the Government of India, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, with headquarters at Nirman Bhawan, New Delhi. He is a technical head of central health programmes and a member of the ESI Medical Benefit Council. He is not the Council's chair.

The Medical Commissioner of the ESIC is the senior medical officer of the Corporation, appointed under the ESI Act to oversee medical administration. He is a member of the Medical Benefit Council and advises on medical benefit and standards. He is not the Chairman.

The Director General of the ESIC is the chief executive officer of the Corporation and is responsible for its administration. He is an ex-officio Chairman of the Medical Benefit Council. The ESIC's headquarters are in New Delhi, and the post is usually held by a senior IAS officer.

The Medical Council of India was set up under the Indian Medical Council Act 1956 to regulate medical education and registration. It was replaced by the National Medical Commission in 2020 under the NMC Act 2019. Its Chairman has no role as chair of the ESI Medical Benefit Council.
related: ESI Act 1948 was first implemented on 24 Feb 1952 at Kanpur and Delhi.
The ESIC is a body corporate under Section 3 of the ESI Act.
The Standing Committee is the executive body of the ESIC under Section 8.
Employees' Insurance Court is provided under Section 74.
ESI contribution rates: employer 3.25%, employee 0.75%.
The wage ceiling for ESI coverage is Rs 21,000 per month.
The Union Labour Minister is the ESIC Chairman.
summary: The answer is (c). Under Section 10 of the Employees' State Insurance Act 1948, the Medical Benefit Council is chaired by the Director General of the ESIC, who is ex-officio Chairman. The Council advises the Corporation and the Standing Committee on medical benefit matters.
topic_notes: The ESI Act 1948 is the first major social security legislation in independent India, providing medical, sickness, maternity, disablement and dependants' benefits plus funeral expenses. The ESIC was established under Section 3 and is a body corporate. It consists of a Chairman (the Union Labour Minister is usually the Chairman), a Vice-Chairman, members representing the Central Government, State Governments, employers, employees and the medical profession, and Members of Parliament. The Director General is the ex-officio member-secretary. The Standing Committee (Section 8) is the executive body of the Corporation. The Medical Benefit Council (Section 10) is an advisory body. The Employees' Insurance Court (Section 74) decides disputes. The Act applies to factories and certain establishments with 10 or more persons (20 in some cases) and to employees earning up to Rs 21,000 a month (Rs 25,000 for persons with disability). Contributions are 3.25% by the employer and 0.75% by the employee, 4% in total. Employees earning up to Rs 176 a day are exempt from contribution. Medical benefit is provided without a ceiling, and for insured persons and their families it continues after retirement under certain conditions. The ESI Scheme was first launched at Kanpur and Delhi on 24 February 1952. The Act was passed in 1948 after the Adarkar Committee report.

question: Under the provisions of the Maternity Benefits Act 1961, every women employee after delivery of a child who returns to duty is to be provided with nursing breaks till the child attains the age of:
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Section 11 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 deals with nursing breaks. A woman delivered of a child and returning to duty is allowed, in the course of her daily work, two breaks of the prescribed duration for nursing the child until the child attains the age of 15 months. These breaks are in addition to the normal rest intervals allowed to her, and employers cannot deduct wages for them. The 15-month limit has been in the Act since 1961 and was not changed by the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017. That amendment raised paid maternity leave from 12 to 26 weeks for the first two children, added 12 weeks for adopting or commissioning mothers, introduced work-from-home as an option, and required a creche in establishments with 50 or more employees, with four visits a day permitted. Elimination: 10 and 12 months are shorter than the statutory period and 18 months is longer, so only 15 months matches Section 11. A common confusion is that the 2017 amendment extended nursing breaks, but it did not.
explanations: Incorrect: 12 months is not the limit in Section 11. Twelve was the old number of weeks of maternity leave, which may cause confusion.
Correct: Section 11 grants two nursing breaks until the child is 15 months old.
Incorrect: 10 months is not the statutory age limit in the Act.
Incorrect: 18 months is longer than the statutory limit. The Act provides for 15 months.
keyfact: Nursing breaks under Section 11 of the Maternity Benefit Act: two breaks a day until the child is 15 months old.
option_notes: Twelve months: This is not the nursing-break limit. Before 2017, maternity leave was 12 weeks, and the figure 12 is also linked to the extra weeks given to adopting and commissioning mothers. Neither relates to nursing breaks, which run to 15 months under Section 11.

Fifteen months: This is the age up to which a woman returning to duty after delivery is entitled to two nursing breaks of the prescribed duration during working hours. Section 11 provides this, and the breaks are paid. The limit has remained unchanged since the Act was passed in 1961.
Ten months: This has no basis in the Maternity Benefit Act. It is a distractor. The statutory limit for nursing breaks is 15 months, and no provision in the Act uses a 10-month age limit.
Eighteen months: This is longer than the statutory limit and is not in the Act. Nursing breaks end when the child reaches 15 months. The 2017 amendment did not extend this period.
related: Section 11 of the Maternity Benefit Act covers nursing breaks, up to 15 months of child age.
The 2017 amendment raised paid maternity leave to 26 weeks.
Leave for a third child onward is 12 weeks.
Adopting and commissioning mothers get 12 weeks of leave.
A creche is mandatory in establishments with 50 or more employees.
The qualifying condition is 80 days of work in the 12 months before delivery.
Miscarriage or MTP leave is 6 weeks.
summary: The answer is (b) Fifteen months. Section 11 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 entitles a woman returning to duty after delivery to two nursing breaks of the prescribed duration in the course of her daily work until the child reaches fifteen months of age.
topic_notes: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 regulates the employment of women in certain establishments for a fixed period before and after childbirth and provides maternity benefit. It applies to factories, mines, plantations, shops and establishments employing 10 or more persons, and to circus and equestrian performances. Women employed in establishments covered by the ESI Act receive maternity benefit under that Act instead. To be eligible, a woman must have worked at least 80 days in the 12 months preceding the expected delivery date. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 raised paid leave from 12 to 26 weeks, with no more than 8 weeks before the expected delivery date. For a woman with two or more surviving children, the entitlement is 12 weeks, of which no more than 6 weeks are before delivery. A woman who legally adopts a child under three months old, or a commissioning mother, gets 12 weeks from the date the child is handed over. The amendment also introduced work from home after the leave ends, depending on the nature of the work and by mutual agreement. Establishments with 50 or more employees must provide a creche, and the mother may visit it four times a day, including the rest interval. Every woman must be informed in writing and electronically of her entitlements at the time of appointment. Other provisions include the prohibition on dismissal during maternity leave, leave for miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy (6 weeks), tubectomy leave (2 weeks), and leave for illness arising from pregnancy (1 month). Inspectors enforce the Act. The medical bonus is payable if the employer provides no free prenatal and postnatal care, and the amount has been revised from time to time.

question: Which one of the following statements about industrial relations is NOT correct?
options: Industrial relations have to be managed in the interest of maintaining a viable collaborative structure
Formulation of rules by consensus and their implementation are core to industrial relations
The pluralistic framework looks employee participation in industrial relations from a disintegrative perspective
The radicalists consider industrial relations in a distributive sense
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Industrial relations (IR) theory is usually taught through three frames of reference: unitary, pluralistic and radical (Marxist). The unitary view treats the organisation as one team with a single source of authority and common goals, so conflict is seen as abnormal and trade unions as unnecessary. The pluralistic view (Alan Fox, Clegg, Flanders) sees the organisation as a coalition of groups, such as management and unions, with legitimate but different interests. Conflict is inevitable and healthy, and it is managed through collective bargaining, joint consultation, worker participation and rule-making by consensus. Participation therefore integrates interests and builds a viable collaborative structure. The radical view holds that capital and labour have a basic conflict of interest in a capitalist system, and it treats IR as a struggle over the distribution of power and surplus. Options (a), (b) and (d) match these ideas: IR must be managed to keep cooperation viable, rule-making and its implementation are central (Dunlop's 'web of rules'), and radicalists take a distributive or class-conflict view. Option (c) wrongly calls the pluralistic view of participation 'disintegrative', so it is the NOT-correct statement.
explanations: Correct statement. IR must be managed so that management and labour can keep working together in a viable collaborative structure, which is the main aim of IR policy. Hence not the answer.

Correct statement. Following Dunlop's systems approach, IR is about creating and administering the web of rules governing the workplace, and consensus-based rule-making is central. Hence not the answer.

Incorrect statement. Pluralists treat employee participation as integrative: it channels competing interests through bargaining and consultation and helps maintain order. Calling it 'disintegrative' misdescribes the view, so this is the answer.
Correct statement. Radicalists (Marxist view) see IR as an expression of class conflict over the distribution of economic power and surplus. Hence not the answer.
keyfact: Pluralists view participation and bargaining as integrative; unitary stresses harmony; radical stresses class conflict and distribution.
option_notes: Collaborative IR: the goal of modern IR is industrial peace, productivity and cooperation between employers, workers and the State. Tripartite bodies such as the Indian Labour Conference, and mechanisms such as works committees and bipartite forums, support this. Harmony does not mean the absence of conflict, but its institutionalised management.

Rule-making is central in Dunlop's Industrial Relations Systems (1958). The actors are workers and their organisations, managers and their organisations, and government agencies. These actors operate within an environment of technology, market and power contexts, bound together by an ideology. The system's output is the web of rules, both substantive and procedural, that governs the workplace.

The pluralistic framework (Alan Fox, Flanders, Clegg) treats the organisation as made up of multiple interest groups. Conflict is natural and is resolved through collective bargaining and participation. Trade unions are legitimate representatives, and management's role is to balance and mediate between groups. Participation is thus integrative, which is why this statement is wrong.

The radical or Marxist framework sees IR as rooted in the capitalist mode of production. Capital exploits labour, so conflict is inevitable and tied to class struggle. Trade unions are vehicles of broader social change, and collective bargaining is only a temporary compromise. The focus is on the distribution of power and wealth in society.
related: Dunlop's IR system (1958): actors, context, ideology and web of rules.
Unitary frame: single authority, harmony, unions seen as unnecessary.
Pluralist frame: many interest groups, conflict institutionalised through bargaining.
Radical frame: class conflict between capital and labour is structural.
Industrial Disputes Act 1947 provides conciliation, arbitration and adjudication machinery.
The Code of Discipline in Industry was adopted in 1958.
Alan Fox is the scholar most associated with unitary and pluralist frames.
summary: The answer is (c). In the pluralistic framework, industrial relations are seen as a set of competing interests that can be balanced through bargaining and participation. Participation is therefore treated as integrative and constructive, not 'disintegrative', so statement (c) is the incorrect one.
topic_notes: Frames of reference in IR: (1) Unitary: the organisation is a harmonious family under one authority. It is paternalistic, favours management prerogative, sees unions as intruders and conflict as the result of poor communication or agitators. (2) Pluralistic: society and the organisation contain many sectional groups with divergent interests. Conflict is inevitable and is institutionalised through collective bargaining, grievance procedures and joint consultation. Management's task is to reconcile interests, and the State is a neutral arbiter. (3) Radical or Marxist: IR is shaped by the class structure of capitalism, and the conflict between capital and labour is structural. Other approaches: Dunlop's systems approach (actors, context, ideology, web of rules); the Gandhian trusteeship approach, which stresses arbitration, moral persuasion and non-violence; the human relations approach (Elton Mayo); and the psychological, sociological and HRM approaches. Indian IR framework: the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 (conciliation, arbitration, adjudication, strikes and lockouts, lay-off, retrenchment); the Trade Unions Act 1926; the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946. These are being consolidated into the Industrial Relations Code 2020, which came into force with the other labour codes on 21 November 2025. Machinery: works committees, joint management councils, conciliation officers, boards of conciliation, courts of inquiry, labour courts, tribunals and national tribunals. The Code of Discipline (1958), Tripartite Indian Labour Conference (first held 1942) and Standing Labour Committee also feature. Likely questions: matching the frame of reference with its features, Dunlop's actors, and the objectives of IR.

question: Which one of the following is NOT a logic of industrial relations?
options: The logic of employment – income protection
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Industrial relations (IR) theory identifies several logics or approaches that explain how employers, workers and the State interact. The logic of conflict (Marxist/radical view) holds that the interests of capital and labour are fundamentally opposed, so strikes, lockouts and disputes are inevitable. The logic of industrial peace (unitary/pluralist, cooperative view) stresses harmony, collective bargaining, conciliation, works committees and bipartite and tripartite machinery, as in the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 and the Industrial Relations Code 2020. The logic of employment-income protection (welfare or security logic) stresses job security, minimum wages, social security and safeguards against retrenchment, supported by ILO standards and Directive Principles (Arts. 41, 42, 43, 43A). Competition is a market logic that governs product and labour markets, not a behavioural logic of the labour-management relationship. Elimination: (a), (c) and (d) are standard textbook logics, leaving (b) as the answer. Students should link each logic to its theoretical school and to the Indian legal instruments that express it.
explanations: Wrong as an answer: conflict is a recognised logic of IR, reflecting the opposed interests of labour and management (Marxist view).
Correct answer: competition is a market or economic concept, not a recognised logic of industrial relations.
Wrong as an answer: industrial peace is a recognised logic. It underlies conciliation, arbitration, collective bargaining and bipartite forums.
Wrong as an answer: employment-income protection is a recognised welfare or security logic, reflected in minimum wage, social security and job-security laws.
keyfact: The logics of IR are conflict, industrial peace and employment-income protection; competition is a market concept, not an IR logic.
option_notes: The logic of conflict: the radical/Marxist view that capital and labour have irreconcilable interests. Strikes, lockouts and gheraos are seen as natural expressions of the class struggle. It is the opposite of the unitary view. Law regulates, but does not eliminate, this conflict through procedures such as notice of strike, conciliation and adjudication under the ID Act 1947 and now the IR Code 2020.

The logic of competition is not a recognised IR logic. Competition belongs to market economics, covering competition among firms for products and among workers for jobs. It affects wages and bargaining power, but it is not a framework describing labour-management relations. Do not confuse it with the legal field of competition law (Competition Act 2002).

The logic of industrial peace: the cooperative or harmony approach, which holds that stable relations benefit both sides and the economy. Tools include collective bargaining, works committees, joint management councils, voluntary arbitration, the Code of Discipline (1958) and tripartite bodies such as the Indian Labour Conference. The state promotes it through conciliation officers and tribunals.

The logic of employment-income protection: the welfare or security logic, which holds that workers need protection of jobs and income. It is expressed in minimum wages, retrenchment compensation, ESI, EPF, gratuity, unemployment allowance and ILO conventions. Constitutional backing comes from the Directive Principles in Arts. 39, 41, 42, 43 and 43A.
related: Dunlop's systems model of IR has three actors: workers, management and government.
Industrial Relations Code 2020 subsumed the Trade Unions Act 1926, Standing Orders Act 1946 and ID Act 1947.
Code of Discipline in Industry was adopted in 1958.
The Marxist approach views industrial conflict as inevitable class struggle.
The pluralist approach accepts unions and collective bargaining as legitimate.
Gandhian approach: trusteeship and arbitration as means of settling disputes.
India has not ratified ILO Conventions 87 and 98.
summary: The answer is (b). The recognised 'logics' of industrial relations are conflict, industrial peace (harmony/cooperation), and employment-income protection (security/welfare). 'Competition' is a feature of market economics and is not listed as a logic of industrial relations.
topic_notes:
Industrial relations covers the relationships among employers, employees and the State, together with the institutions and rules that govern them. Main approaches: unitary (the firm is one team, with no legitimate conflict), pluralist (many interest groups, so negotiation and bargaining are needed), and Marxist/radical (class conflict). Dunlop's systems theory sees IR as a system of actors (workers, management, government), contexts (technology, market, power) and an ideology, which together produce a web of rules. Other approaches are the Gandhian trusteeship approach, the human relations approach, and the psychological and sociological approaches.

Indian legal framework: the Trade Unions Act 1926, the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946, and the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 with its machinery of Works Committee, Conciliation Officer, Board of Conciliation, Court of Inquiry, Labour Court, Tribunal and National Tribunal. Since the labour code consolidation, the Industrial Relations Code 2020 subsumes these three Acts. The Code of Discipline (1958), the Tripartite Labour Conference (the Indian Labour Conference, first held in 1942) and workers' participation in management schemes (1975, 1983) are important. Dispute settlement methods are collective bargaining, conciliation, mediation, arbitration and adjudication. Strikes and lockouts are regulated, with notice requirements and prohibitions in public utility services. The ILO conventions on freedom of association (C87) and collective bargaining (C98) are the international benchmark; India has ratified C98's counterpart only in part and has not ratified C87 or C98.

question: What is a ‘Wild – Cat’ strike?
options: Strike called by the workers with the support of union with notice to the employer
Strike called by a group of workers on the spur of the moment without any formal notice to the employer and consent from the union
Strike called by the union without resorting to strike ballot
Strike called by non-unionised workers, even if notice is given to the employer
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: A wild-cat strike is an abrupt, unplanned cessation of work, usually triggered by an immediate grievance such as a dismissal, an accident, or an unfair act by management. Its defining features are (1) no notice to the employer and (2) no sanction from the union leadership, which makes it an unofficial strike. In India, strikes in public utility services require 6 weeks' notice under Section 22 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and a strike cannot be held within 14 days of giving notice. Section 23 bars strikes during conciliation proceedings and for 7 days after they end, and during arbitration or adjudication proceedings. Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, a 14-day notice requirement applies to all industrial establishments. A wild-cat strike therefore breaches these provisions and is typically illegal. Elimination: (a) describes a normal, official strike with notice and union backing. (c) describes a union strike with no ballot, which is a procedural defect and not a wild-cat strike. (d) is wrong because a wild-cat strike is defined by the absence of notice, so one with notice cannot be wild-cat. Related types: sit-down, stay-in, go-slow, work-to-rule, sympathetic and general strikes.
explanations: Wrong: this describes a lawful, official strike with union backing and notice. A wild-cat strike has neither.
Right: it is a sudden, spontaneous strike by a group of workers, with no notice to the employer and no union consent. This is the standard definition.
Wrong: absence of a strike ballot is a procedural lapse by a union and does not define a wild-cat strike. A wild-cat strike is not union-called at all.
Wrong: a wild-cat strike is defined by the absence of notice. Lack of unionisation is not the criterion, and notice would make the strike non-wild-cat.
keyfact: Wild-cat strike = sudden, unofficial strike without notice to the employer and without union consent.
option_notes: An official or recognised strike is called by a union after following legal procedure: notice, conciliation compliance and often a ballot. It is protected from some consequences if it is legal under the ID Act, 1947. Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, 14 days' notice is required in all establishments, and strikes are barred during conciliation and for 7 days after.

This is the wild-cat strike: a spontaneous, unofficial work stoppage by a group of workers acting on the spur of the moment. It is not authorised by the union and no notice is given. Triggers are immediate grievances. It is generally illegal under Sections 22 and 23 of the ID Act, and employers may take disciplinary action against participants.

A strike without a ballot is a procedural issue. Strike ballots are common in the UK and some other countries, and in India the union's own constitution may require them. The ID Act, 1947 does not mandate a ballot. It does not define a wild-cat strike, which is outside union control.

Non-unionised workers can strike, and a strike by them with notice would be an ordinary strike, since the ID Act applies to workmen regardless of union membership. Wild-cat strikes are identified by being sudden and without notice. Union membership status does not define them.
related: Section 2(q) ID Act defines strike; Section 2(l) defines lockout.
Section 22 ID Act: 6 weeks' notice for public utility strike, with 14 days' waiting.
IR Code 2020: 14 days' notice for strikes in all industrial establishments.
Sit-down or stay-in strike: workers stay at the workplace without working.
Go-slow: deliberately reduced output while still attending work.
Gherao: confining management personnel, originated in West Bengal in the 1960s.
T.K. Rangarajan (2003): no fundamental right to strike for government employees.
Sympathetic strike: in support of other workers' cause.
summary: The answer is (b). A wild-cat strike is a sudden, spontaneous stoppage of work by a group of workers, without prior notice to the employer and without the authorisation or consent of the trade union. It is unofficial and unprotected.
topic_notes: A strike is a collective cessation of work by employees to press demands, defined in Section 2(q) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. It includes a concerted refusal to continue work and a refusal under a common understanding to accept employment. Lockout (Section 2(l)) is the employer's counterpart. Legality is governed by Sections 22 (public utility services: 6 weeks' notice, 14 days' wait, not during conciliation), 23 (general prohibition during pendency of conciliation, adjudication and arbitration), 24 (illegal strikes) and 10(3). Penalties are in Sections 26 and 27, with instigation or financial aid for illegal strikes punishable. Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, notice is 14 days for all industrial establishments, and a strike is barred during conciliation proceedings and for 7 days after, and during tribunal and arbitration proceedings. Types of strike include: general strike; sympathetic strike (in support of other workers); sit-down or stay-in strike; go-slow; work-to-rule; hunger strike; token strike; sick-out; and bandh. A wild-cat strike is an unofficial strike without notice or union approval. Related concepts: gherao (a Kerala-originated method of confining managers; not legal), picketing, boycott, and lay-off, retrenchment and closure (Chapter V-A/V-B of the ID Act). In Bharat Kumar v. State of Kerala, the Kerala High Court said there is no fundamental right to strike. T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2003) held that government employees have no fundamental, legal, moral or equitable right to strike.

question: Which one of the following is a ‘jurisdictional strike’?
options: Two unions claiming the office space conduct strike
Two unions conduct strike for registration with the same name
Two unions may claim to represent the same set of workers and may clamour for recognition on this claim and go for a strike to pressurize the management
Two unions claiming possession of a common seal go for strike to elicit the support of workers
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: In industrial relations, strikes are classified by their cause. A jurisdictional strike is a result of inter-union rivalry, not a dispute between workers and the employer over wages or conditions. Two or more unions each claim to represent the same group of workers, or to control the same type of work, and one or both stop work to force the employer to recognise them or assign the work to them. The term is common in the US building trades, and in India it relates to recognition disputes among rival unions. India has no central law that compels recognition of unions, though the Trade Unions Act 1926 provides for registration, and some states, such as Maharashtra under the MRTU & PULP Act 1971, provide for recognition. Other types of strike to know are the sympathetic strike, the sit-down or stay-in strike, the general strike, the wildcat strike, the slowdown, the work-to-rule, the hunger strike and the economic strike. Elimination: office space, a registration name and a common seal are petty or administrative disputes between unions. None of them goes to the core issue of representation and recognition, which defines a jurisdictional strike.
explanations: Wrong: a dispute over office space is a minor property or administrative quarrel and does not define a jurisdictional strike, which concerns the right to represent workers.
Wrong: a dispute over the name used for registration concerns the Trade Unions Act registration process. It is not a contest over representation of workers.
Correct: rival unions claim to represent the same workers, demand recognition, and strike to pressurise the management. This is the textbook jurisdictional strike.
Wrong: a dispute over possession of a common seal is an internal or administrative matter between unions. It does not concern the right to represent workers.
keyfact: A jurisdictional strike is caused by rivalry between unions over representation, recognition or control of work, not by a dispute with the employer over wages.
option_notes: Office-space dispute: a quarrel between unions over premises or facilities. It is an inter-union property matter, not a recognised category of strike. Employers sometimes provide a notice board or office space to a recognised union, but that does not make such a dispute a jurisdictional strike.

Registration with the same name: under the Trade Unions Act 1926, a union's name must not be identical to or deceptively similar to that of an existing union, and the Registrar may refuse registration. The dispute is an administrative one handled by the Registrar and the courts, so it is not a strike category.

Rival recognition claim: unions competing to represent the same workers and striking to force recognition by the management. This is the jurisdictional strike. It is a feature of multiple-union workplaces, which are common in India and have led to calls for a verification procedure such as secret ballot or check-off.

Common seal dispute: a common seal is the official stamp of a body corporate, and a registered union is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal under Section 13 of the Trade Unions Act 1926. A dispute over it is an internal legal matter, not a strike type.
related: Strike is defined in Section 2(q) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947.
Notice of strike is mandatory in public utility services under Section 22 of the ID Act.
The Industrial Relations Code 2020 extends strike notice to all industrial establishments.
A union is a body corporate with a common seal under Section 13 of the Trade Unions Act 1926.
A sympathetic strike is in support of another group's dispute.
Work-to-rule is a form of slowdown through strict adherence to rules.
The Code of Discipline 1958 provides criteria for union recognition.
Gherao is the confinement of management personnel and is not legally recognised as a strike.
summary: The answer is (c). A jurisdictional strike arises from rivalry between two or more unions over which of them has the right to represent a particular set of workers or to control certain work. Each union strikes to pressure the management into recognising it, so option (c) fits the definition.
topic_notes: Strikes can be classified by cause, scope and method. An economic strike is for better wages, bonuses or conditions. A sympathetic strike supports another group of workers in a dispute. A general strike covers many industries or a whole region. A sit-down or stay-in strike keeps workers at their workplace without working. A slowdown means deliberately reduced output. Work-to-rule means strictly following all rules so that work slows. A wildcat strike is unauthorised and not backed by the union. A hunger strike is a fast by workers or leaders. A jurisdictional strike arises from rivalry between unions. Legal position in India: the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 defines a strike in Section 2(q) as a cessation of work by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in combination, or a concerted refusal to continue to work or accept employment. Section 22 requires notice of strike in public utility services, with a six-week limit on notice and a minimum of 14 days. Sections 23 and 24 prohibit strikes in certain situations, such as during conciliation proceedings, and make strikes illegal if they violate those provisions. Under the Industrial Relations Code 2020, the notice requirement is extended to all industrial establishments, with 60 days' notice, and strikes are prohibited during conciliation and tribunal proceedings and for 7 days after. Related topics include lockout, lay-off, retrenchment, closure, gherao, bandh and picketing. Recognition of trade unions is addressed by the Code of Discipline of 1958, which sets criteria such as 30 percent membership in the establishment's workforce and a minimum period of existence, though it is non-statutory.

question: What is ‘yellow dog contract’?
options: A contract where a union agrees to inform the employer about the possible strike by a rival union
When Management secures an agreement from the workman that he will not join a union during the course of his employment
An unwritten contract with the employer, where a faction of the union acts as a ‘whistle blower’
The employer promotes a pocket union by entering into an agreement with the trade union
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: A yellow dog contract is an anti-union device used by employers, especially in the USA in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The worker signs, as a condition of employment, a promise not to join a union, and is dismissed if the promise is broken. The word 'yellow dog' signified a despicable or cowardly act. Such contracts were attacked as violating freedom of association. In the USA the Norris-LaGuardia Act, 1932 made them unenforceable in federal courts, and the Wagner Act (National Labor Relations Act), 1935 made them an unfair labour practice. In India, the Trade Unions Act, 1926 gives unions legal status, and the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (Fifth Schedule, Section 25T and 25U) lists unfair labour practices, including discouraging or encouraging union membership by discrimination and fostering company unions. Elimination: (a) describes informing or spying on a rival union, which is not a yellow dog contract. (c) describes a whistle-blower arrangement, which is unrelated. (d) describes a 'company' or 'pocket' union, which is a different unfair practice. Only (b) matches the definition.
explanations: Incorrect: a contract about informing the employer of a rival union's strike is not what the term means; it is not about a worker's promise not to unionise.
Correct: this is the classic definition. The worker promises, as a condition of employment, not to join a union.
Incorrect: an unwritten whistle-blower arrangement by a union faction is not a yellow dog contract, which is typically a written individual undertaking.
Incorrect: promoting a pocket or company union is a separate unfair labour practice (domination of a union), not a yellow dog contract.
keyfact: Yellow dog contract = employer makes a worker promise not to join a union as a condition of employment (an unfair labour practice).
option_notes: Informing the employer of a rival union's strike is a form of collusion or spying. It is not a recognised labour-law term. Collusive arrangements between management and a favoured union are treated as unfair practices under labour laws, but this is not called a yellow dog contract.

The yellow dog contract is an individual undertaking by a worker not to join a union. It originated in the USA, was restricted by the Norris-LaGuardia Act, 1932, and was outlawed by the Wagner Act, 1935. It is an unfair labour practice and violates the right to associate.

A whistle-blower is a person who reports wrongdoing. An unwritten arrangement of this kind is not a defined concept in industrial relations. Whistle-blower protection in India is covered by the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014.

A pocket or company union is a union dominated or sponsored by the employer, which acts in management's interest. Fostering such unions is an unfair labour practice under the Fifth Schedule of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. It is distinct from a yellow dog contract.
related: Yellow dog contract: worker promises not to join a union as a condition of employment.
Norris-LaGuardia Act 1932 made yellow dog contracts unenforceable in US federal courts.
Wagner Act 1935 is the US National Labor Relations Act.
Fifth Schedule of the ID Act 1947 lists unfair labour practices.
Section 25T prohibits unfair labour practices; Section 25U gives the penalty.
Taft-Hartley Act 1947 banned the closed shop in the USA.
Check-off system: employer deducts union dues from wages.
Trade Unions Act 1926 provides for registration of unions.
summary: The correct answer is (b). A 'yellow dog contract' is an agreement an employer obtains from a worker, as a condition of getting or keeping a job, that the worker will not join or remain a member of a trade union during employment.
topic_notes: Unfair labour practices are acts by employers or unions that undermine fair industrial relations. In India, the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1982 added Section 2(ra) defining unfair labour practice, Section 25T prohibiting it, and Section 25U prescribing penalties (imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to Rs 1,000, or both). The Fifth Schedule lists them. Employer practices include discouraging or encouraging union membership by discrimination, discharging or punishing workers for union activity, establishing employer-sponsored unions, refusing to bargain collectively in good faith, victimisation, and engaging in lockouts contrary to law. Workers' and union practices include coercing workers to join a union, threatening or intimidating non-strikers, and an unrecognised union's gherao or go-slow tactics. Related concepts: a company union is dominated by the employer; a pocket union is under the employer's influence; a closed shop requires union membership before hiring; a union shop requires joining within a time after hiring; an agency shop requires non-members to pay fees; an open shop gives no preference either way. Other terms: blacklisting, lockout, gherao, picketing, boycott, and 'check-off system' (employer deducts union dues from wages). Key USA laws: Clayton Act 1914, Norris-LaGuardia Act 1932, Wagner Act 1935, Taft-Hartley Act 1947 (banned the closed shop), Landrum-Griffin Act 1959. India: Trade Unions Act 1926, Industrial Disputes Act 1947, Industrial Relations Code 2020.

question: The Institution of Voluntary Arbitration as a method of settling industrial disputes was strongly favoured by:
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Voluntary arbitration means that the parties to a dispute agree to refer it to a neutral third party and accept the award, with no compulsion from the State. In India its philosophical father is Mahatma Gandhi. In the 1918 Ahmedabad mill dispute he fasted and the matter was referred to an arbitrator, and the TLA he guided became a model of arbitration-based, non-adversarial labour relations. Gandhi's ideas of trusteeship, mutual trust and peaceful settlement shaped the approach.
