After Independence the idea was institutionalised: V V Giri, as Labour Minister and later President, promoted it through the 'Giri Approach' (emphasising bipartite settlement, voluntary arbitration and collective bargaining), and the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 (Section 10A, added in 1956) gave voluntary arbitration legal recognition. The Indian Labour Conference 1957 adopted the Code of Discipline (1958). The Second Five Year Plan and the Code of Discipline also stressed voluntary arbitration. Elimination: Giri is linked to the approach but the question asks who strongly favoured the institution as a method historically, which is Gandhi. Nanda is associated with the Code of Conduct and the Code of Discipline. Lala Lajpat Rai was the first AITUC president (1920) and had no link with arbitration.
explanations: Incorrect: Nanda, as Labour Minister, is linked with the Code of Discipline, the Code of Conduct and tripartite consensus, not with originating arbitration.
Incorrect: V V Giri did advocate voluntary settlement (the Giri Approach), but the founding and strongest champion of the arbitration institution was Gandhi, so he is not the best answer.
Incorrect: Lala Lajpat Rai was the first AITUC president (1920) and a nationalist leader, not an arbitration proponent.
Correct: Gandhi used and promoted arbitration at Ahmedabad (1918) and through the TLA, preferring it to strikes and State intervention.
keyfact: Voluntary arbitration in Indian labour relations traces back to Gandhi and the Ahmedabad TLA; ID Act Sec 10A gives it a legal basis.
option_notes: Gulzari Lal Nanda (1898-1998) was twice acting Prime Minister and Union Labour Minister. He was associated with the Code of Discipline in Industry (1958) and the Indian Labour Conference. He was a Gandhian trade unionist and a founder of INTUC. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1997.

V V Giri (1894-1980) was Labour Minister (1952-54) and later the fourth President of India (1969-74). He was a trade unionist who headed the All India Railwaymen's Federation. The Giri Approach favours bipartite negotiation, voluntary arbitration and minimal State intervention in disputes.

Lala Lajpat Rai (1865-1928), known as Punjab Kesari, was the first president of AITUC at its Bombay session in 1920. He was an Arya Samaj leader and founder of the Servants of the People Society, and he died after the Simon Commission protest lathi charge.

Mahatma Gandhi (1869-1948) founded the Textile Labour Association in Ahmedabad in 1920 (the Ahmedabad dispute dated from 1918). He championed arbitration, trusteeship and non-violent settlement, and his labour philosophy shaped INTUC and Indian labour policy.
related: Section 10A of the ID Act 1947 provides for voluntary reference of disputes to arbitration.
Section 10A was inserted by the 1956 amendment.
The Code of Discipline was adopted in 1958.
Gandhi founded the Textile Labour Association, Ahmedabad (1920).
The Giri Approach favours bipartite settlement and voluntary arbitration.
Lala Lajpat Rai was the first AITUC president (1920).
An arbitration award is binding on the parties.
summary: The answer is (d) Mahatma Gandhi. Gandhi's Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (TLA, 1918) practised voluntary arbitration, and he strongly advocated it as the best way to settle industrial disputes without strikes or State compulsion.
topic_notes: Methods of settling industrial disputes in India fall into bipartite (collective bargaining, works committees, grievance procedure) and tripartite or State machinery (conciliation, Boards of Conciliation, Courts of Inquiry, Labour Courts, Tribunals, National Tribunal). Voluntary arbitration sits between them: the parties choose the arbitrator and are bound by the award. Section 10A of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 was inserted in 1956 and lets parties refer a dispute to an arbitrator by a written agreement before it goes to a Labour Court or Tribunal. The award is published by the government and is binding. Gandhi's Ahmedabad experiment and the TLA are the classic examples. The Giri Approach holds that disputes are best settled by mutual negotiation. The Code of Discipline was adopted in 1958 at the 16th Indian Labour Conference. The Second Five Year Plan stressed voluntary arbitration. The National Commission on Labour (1969) also encouraged it. The Industrial Disputes Act 1947 also provides for Works Committees (Sec 3), Conciliation Officers and Boards (Secs 4 and 5), Courts of Inquiry (Sec 6), Labour Courts, Tribunals and National Tribunals (Secs 7, 7A and 7B), and strike and lockout provisions (Sec 22 onwards). The Industrial Relations Code 2020 consolidates these laws and envisages Industrial Tribunals and tripartite bodies, with provisions for conciliation and arbitration.

question: The Industrial Disputes Bill 1947 observed that ‘industrial peace will be most enduring where it is founded on voluntary settlement’. Which one of the following machineries under the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 was created for this purpose?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Industrial Disputes Bill 1947 stressed that peace is most lasting when based on voluntary settlement, so the Act first provides for conciliation, and only then for adjudication. Under Section 4 the appropriate Government appoints Conciliation Officers, and under Section 5 it constitutes Boards of Conciliation, each with a chairman (independent person) and two or four members representing the parties in equal numbers. Their duty under Section 12 is to mediate and promote a settlement; if a settlement is reached, a memorandum is signed and the report is sent to the Government. If it fails, a failure report is sent, and the Government may refer the dispute to adjudication. The Works Committee (Section 3) is a preventive body for day-to-day cooperation in establishments with 100 or more workmen. A Court of Enquiry (Section 6) only investigates matters and reports, usually within six months. Labour Courts (Section 7) and Tribunals (Sections 7A, 7B) adjudicate and give binding awards, so they are compulsory, not voluntary. Hence only (b) fits the question's purpose of voluntary settlement through conciliation.
explanations: (a) Incorrect: the Works Committee under Section 3 is a preventive forum for ongoing cooperation, not the machinery for settling an existing dispute by conciliation.
(b) Correct: the Board of Conciliation under Section 5 mediates and promotes voluntary settlement between the parties, which is the Bill's stated aim.
(c) Incorrect: a Court of Enquiry under Section 6 only investigates and reports on a matter. It does not try to bring about a settlement.
(d) Incorrect: a Labour Court under Section 7 adjudicates and gives a binding award. This is compulsory adjudication, not voluntary settlement.
keyfact: Voluntary settlement under the ID Act 1947 is promoted through conciliation: Conciliation Officers and Boards of Conciliation (Sections 4, 5 and 12).
option_notes: Works Committee: under Section 3 of the ID Act, the appropriate Government may require an employer with 100 or more workmen to constitute one. It has equal numbers of employer and workmen representatives, and the workmen's representatives are chosen in consultation with the trade union. Its role is to promote measures for amity and good relations and to resolve common-interest differences. It is a preventive machinery.

Board of Conciliation: constituted ad hoc under Section 5 by the appropriate Government for a particular dispute. It has a chairman who is an independent person, plus two or four other members nominated in equal numbers by the parties. It mediates and promotes settlement under Section 12, and its report is due within two months of the dispute being referred to it. It is used far less often than Conciliation Officers.

Court of Enquiry: under Section 6, the Government constitutes one to inquire into any matter connected with or relevant to an industrial dispute. It can have one or more independent persons, and the chairman is usually a High Court judge. It submits its report within six months. It is a fact-finding body, and its report is not binding.

Labour Court: under Section 7, it adjudicates disputes on matters in the Second Schedule, such as the propriety of dismissal, discharge or suspension and the legality of strikes. It is headed by a person who is or has been a High Court judge, a district judge, or an equivalent. Its award is binding once published. It is a compulsory adjudication body.
related: Section 2(k) defines 'industrial dispute'.
Section 2(s) defines 'workman'.
A Conciliation Officer must submit a report within 14 days of the commencement of conciliation proceedings.
A Court of Enquiry must submit its report within six months.
Section 25F: one month's notice and 15 days' average pay per completed year of service for retrenchment.
Chapter VB requires Government permission for lay-off, retrenchment and closure in establishments with 100 or more workmen.
The Industrial Relations Code 2020 subsumes the ID Act, the Trade Unions Act and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act.
summary: The answer is (b) Board of Conciliation. The Industrial Disputes Act 1947 provides conciliation machinery (Conciliation Officers and Boards of Conciliation) to promote voluntary settlement of disputes, in line with the Bill's observation that industrial peace is most enduring when founded on voluntary settlement.
topic_notes: The Industrial Disputes Act 1947 came into force on 1 April 1947. It replaced the Trade Disputes Act 1929 and the Defence of India Rules (Rule 81A). Its main objectives are investigating and settling industrial disputes and securing industrial peace. The Act has a graded structure of authorities. Preventive: the Works Committee (Section 3). Conciliation: Conciliation Officers (Section 4) and Boards of Conciliation (Section 5). Investigative: Courts of Enquiry (Section 6). Adjudication: Labour Courts (Section 7), Industrial Tribunals (Section 7A), and the National Tribunal (Section 7B), which handles national-importance disputes. Conciliation proceedings are deemed to begin when a strike or lockout notice is received by the Conciliation Officer, and the officer must submit a report within 14 days. Section 10 empowers the Government to refer disputes. Section 11A gives wide powers to adjudicators to set aside discharge or dismissal and grant lesser punishment. Section 22 and Section 23 restrict strikes and lockouts in public utility services. Section 25F governs retrenchment conditions: one month's notice and compensation of 15 days' average pay for each completed year of service. Chapter VB (Sections 25K to 25R) applies to establishments with 100 or more workmen and requires prior permission for lay-off, retrenchment and closure. The Industrial Relations Code 2020 will subsume this Act. It replaces Conciliation Boards and Labour Courts with Industrial Tribunals and requires 300 workers as the threshold for prior permission.

question: In India, which one of the following systems prevails in respect of adjudication in industrial disputes?
options: Voluntary reference and voluntary acceptance of the award
Voluntary reference but compulsory acceptance of the award
Compulsory reference but voluntary acceptance of the award
Discretionary reference and compulsory acceptance of the award
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Indian adjudication under the ID Act, 1947 is a mix of state control and binding outcomes. Neither party has a right to take a dispute directly to adjudication. The appropriate Government decides under Section 10(1) whether to refer it to a Labour Court, Industrial Tribunal or National Tribunal. It may also decline to refer, and the Supreme Court has held that the decision is administrative and not judicial, though a refusal must record reasons (Section 12(5)) and is open to judicial review. Since the 2010 amendment, an individual dismissal dispute can go directly to the Labour Court under Section 2A(2) and (3) after 45 days of conciliation. Once adjudicated, the award is published within 30 days (Section 17) and becomes final. It is binding under Section 18(3) on the parties, on those who were summoned, and on successors and workers. It comes into force 30 days after publication (Section 17A), and the Government may prohibit strikes during proceedings (Section 10(3)). Violating it is penalised under Section 29. Option (a) describes voluntary arbitration, as in the Gandhian Ahmedabad model. Options (b) and (c) are incorrect because the reference is not voluntary for parties and not compulsory for the Government. Compulsory reference was the Australian and New Zealand model.
explanations: Wrong: this is voluntary arbitration, where both parties agree to refer and to abide by the outcome. It is not the general Indian system of adjudication.
Wrong: the reference is not left to the parties' will. The Government decides it, though acceptance is indeed compulsory.
Wrong: reference is not compulsory, since the Government can refuse under Section 10. Acceptance is binding, not voluntary.
Correct: the Government has discretion to refer under Section 10, and the published award is binding under Sections 17 and 18.
keyfact: In India, reference to adjudication is at the Government's discretion (Section 10), but the award, once published, is binding (Section 18).
option_notes: Voluntary reference with voluntary acceptance is how voluntary arbitration works in principle. Section 10A of the ID Act lets employer and workers refer a dispute to an arbitrator by written agreement. The Gandhian Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association approach and the Second Plan and Code of Discipline (1958) promoted it. The arbitrator's award is nonetheless binding once published, and it is encouraged as an alternative to adjudication.

Voluntary reference with compulsory acceptance describes something close to Section 10A arbitration, where parties choose to refer and the award then binds them. It is not how Government-driven adjudication in India works. Under Section 10(1) the Government alone makes the reference to Labour Courts or Tribunals, and the parties cannot demand it.

Compulsory reference with voluntary acceptance is not a recognised Indian system. Compulsory arbitration, as in Australia and New Zealand, makes the reference mandatory and the award binding. In India, compulsory adjudication applied only in wartime under the Defence of India Rules, notably Rule 81A (1942) during the Second World War.

Discretionary reference means the appropriate Government may or may not refer a dispute (Section 10). Compulsory acceptance means the award binds the parties (Section 18). Other points: Labour Courts, Tribunals and National Tribunals are the three adjudication bodies, and National Tribunals handle matters of national importance. Awards can be challenged by writ under Articles 226 and 32.
related: Section 10 of the ID Act governs reference of disputes by the appropriate Government.
Section 10A deals with voluntary reference to arbitration.
Section 2A covers individual disputes of discharge, dismissal, retrenchment and termination.
Section 18 provides that settlements and awards are binding.
Section 22 requires a 6-week strike notice in public utility services.
Section 25F lays down the conditions for valid retrenchment: 1 month's notice and 15 days' average pay per completed year.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes the ID Act, 1947.
Under the Code of Discipline (1958), parties pledged to use voluntary arbitration.
summary: The answer is (d). Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the appropriate Government has discretion to refer a dispute to a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal (Section 10), but once an award is made and published it is binding on the parties (Sections 17 and 18). So reference is discretionary and acceptance is compulsory.
topic_notes: The ID Act, 1947 provides a graded machinery for preventing and settling disputes. Its main elements are: Works Committees (Section 3), Conciliation Officers and Boards of Conciliation (Sections 4 and 5), Courts of Inquiry (Section 6), Voluntary arbitration (Section 10A), and then adjudication by Labour Courts, Industrial Tribunals and National Tribunals (Section 7, 7A, 7B). The Act's key features are as follows. Conciliation is mandatory in public utility services, and strikes and lockouts there require a 6-week notice (Section 22). Section 23 bars strikes and lockouts during pending proceedings. The Act defines lay-off, retrenchment and closure, and Chapter VA covers lay-off and retrenchment compensation. Chapter VB (Sections 25K to 25S) requires prior government permission for lay-off, retrenchment and closure in establishments with 100 or more workers (the 1976 amendment applied the threshold of 300 to Chapter VB; check current status). The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 will replace the ID Act, the Trade Unions Act 1926 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946. It sets up Industrial Tribunals with two members and abolishes Labour Courts, and raises the Chapter X (lay-off, retrenchment and closure) threshold to 300 workers. The Code was passed in 2020 and was brought into force on 21 November 2025, so verify its status for current questions. Related ideas include collective bargaining under the Code of Discipline, the Industrial Truce Resolution (1947) and the Whitley Commission.

question: In India which one of the following bodies was created particularly to focus on social and labour issues arising out of economic reforms in 1991?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: After the 1991 New Economic Policy (liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation), trade unions raised concerns about job losses, disinvestment, exit policy and the social safety net. To bring government, employers and workers together on these concerns, the Government of India constituted a Special Tripartite Committee (1992). It discussed the social and labour dimensions of structural adjustment, including labour law reform, a National Renewal Fund and workers' retraining. This is distinct from permanent tripartite machinery. The Indian Labour Conference (ILC, first held 1942) and the Standing Labour Committee (1943) are the apex and subsidiary tripartite consultative bodies for general labour matters, not created for the 1991 reforms. Joint Consultation Boards belong to the Central Government's Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM, 1966) for employer-employee relations among government staff. The National Apex Body was formed in 1975 under the workers' participation scheme to promote participation in management, not to handle reform issues. Elimination: match each body to its purpose and date, and the one tied to the post-1991 reform era is the Special Tripartite Committee.
explanations: Correct. The Special Tripartite Committee was formed specifically to discuss the social and labour implications of the 1991 economic reforms.
Incorrect. The National Apex Body (1975) deals with workers' participation in management and is unrelated to the reforms.
Correct as the answer choice: this is the body constituted to address social and labour issues arising from the reforms.
Incorrect. The Standing Labour Committee is a long-standing tripartite body (1943) that handles general labour matters and advises the Indian Labour Conference.
keyfact: Special Tripartite Committee (early 1990s) was formed to address social and labour issues arising from the 1991 economic reforms.
option_notes: Joint Consultation Boards: bodies used for consultation between employers and workers, notably in the Joint Consultative Machinery for central government employees (1966). They cover service conditions and promote cooperation, with a National Council, Departmental Councils and Regional or Office Councils. They are not linked to the 1991 reforms.

National Apex Body: set up in 1975 as part of the Workers' Participation in Management scheme, with tripartite representation, to review and promote participation in management in industry. It is a workers' participation forum, not a response to economic reforms.

Special Tripartite Committee: constituted by the Government of India in the early 1990s with representatives of government, employers and trade unions. Its purpose was to consider the social and labour impact of structural adjustment and economic reforms, including issues such as retrenchment, retraining and the safety net.

Standing Labour Committee: a tripartite body formed in 1943 that works as a subcommittee of the Indian Labour Conference. It meets more often, examines labour issues and prepares the agenda for the ILC. It is a permanent body and not specific to the 1991 reforms.
related: The Indian Labour Conference first met in 1942.
The Standing Labour Committee was constituted in 1943.
Article 43A (inserted by the 42nd Amendment) deals with workers' participation in management.
The National Renewal Fund was set up in 1992 to help workers displaced by restructuring.
The Joint Consultative Machinery for central government employees dates from 1966.
The Second National Commission on Labour reported in 2002.
The National Apex Body was set up in 1975 under the workers' participation scheme.
summary: The answer is (c) Special Tripartite Committee. It was set up by the Government of India in the early 1990s (around 1992) to examine social and labour issues arising from the economic reforms and structural adjustment begun in 1991. The other bodies are older, general consultative forums.
topic_notes: Tripartism is a basic feature of Indian industrial relations, drawn from ILO principles (India is a founding ILO member, 1919). The apex tripartite forum is the Indian Labour Conference (first session 1942, in New Delhi), advised by the Standing Labour Committee (1943). Industrial Committees cover specific industries (for example plantations, coal mining, textiles, jute), and the Central Board for Workers' Education works on workers' education. Workers' participation in management has a long history: the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 created Works Committees; the 1956 Industrial Policy Resolution and the 1958 scheme of Joint Management Councils followed; the 1975 scheme in the 20-point programme set up shop councils and joint councils; the 1977 Constitution (42nd Amendment) inserted Article 43A on participation of workers in management. The National Apex Body was formed in 1975 on the same theme. The 1991 reforms brought concerns over exit policy, closures and retrenchment (Chapter V-B of the Industrial Disputes Act, a long-debated issue), contract labour and unorganised-sector workers. Responses included the National Renewal Fund (1992) for retraining and compensating displaced workers, and the Second National Commission on Labour (2002), which recommended consolidating labour laws. Later, the four labour codes were enacted in 2019-2020: Wages, Industrial Relations, Social Security, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions. The Joint Consultative Machinery (1966) handles central government staff relations, and Joint Consultation Boards are part of that approach to consultation.

question: Which one of the following was NOT recommended by the Second National Commission on Labour?
options: Labour Management Relations Law consolidating the relevant laws be enacted
Go Slow’ and ‘Work to Rule’ be regarded as misconducts
Strike Ballot’ for public utility services
All the three methods of union recognition namely Membership verification, Secret Ballot, and Check-Off be the basis for choosing a bargaining agent
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Second NCL was set up in 1999 and reported in June 2002. It argued for simplifying and consolidating labour laws and for a minimum protective floor for workers, especially in the unorganised sector. On industrial relations it proposed a single Labour Management Relations Law, merging the Trade Unions Act 1926, the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946. It also dealt with strikes. It wanted a strike ballot before a strike in public utility services and wanted go-slow and work-to-rule treated as misconduct. On recognition, it favoured a union with majority support (about 66% for sole bargaining agent status) or, failing that, a bargaining council proportionate to union strength. Membership was to be verified through check-off, with a secret ballot used when check-off could not settle the matter. So the idea that all three methods together form the basis is the odd one out. Elimination: (a), (b) and (c) are specific, well-known proposals, so (d) is left.
explanations: (a) was recommended: the Commission proposed one consolidated Labour Management Relations Law covering trade unions, industrial disputes and standing orders, so it is not the answer.
(b) was recommended: go-slow and work-to-rule were to be treated as misconduct, so it is not the answer.
(c) was recommended: a strike ballot before strikes in public utility services, so it is not the answer.
(d) is the answer: the Commission preferred check-off based verification, with a secret ballot where verification is disputed or not feasible, and did not endorse all three methods as joint bases.
keyfact: Second NCL (2002, Ravindra Varma) recommended one Labour Management Relations Law and check-off based union verification with a secret ballot as backup, not all three methods together.
option_notes: Labour Management Relations Law: the Second NCL's proposal to merge the Trade Unions Act 1926, the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946 into one code. It aimed to simplify the industrial relations framework. The idea was later pursued in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which replaced these three Acts.

Go-slow and work-to-rule are forms of industrial action short of a strike. Go-slow means deliberately reducing output while remaining at work. Work-to-rule means following every rule so strictly that work slows. The Second NCL wanted them treated as misconduct, and courts have also treated go-slow as misconduct. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020, widened the definition of strike to cover mass casual leave.

A strike ballot is a vote of workers on whether to strike. The Second NCL proposed it for public utility services, where strikes affect the community. Public utility services under the ID Act include railways, posts, water, power and similar services. Strike notice of 14 days and a 6-week notice period are required there. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020, extended notice requirements to all establishments.

Union recognition methods: membership verification, secret ballot and check-off. Check-off means the employer deducts union dues from wages and pays them to the union, so the dues records show membership. A secret ballot is a vote among workers. The Second NCL favoured check-off verification with a secret ballot when needed. The Code on Industrial Relations 2020 provides for a sole negotiating union with 51% membership, or a negotiating council otherwise.
related: Second NCL was chaired by Ravindra Varma and reported in 2002.
First NCL was chaired by P.B. Gajendragadkar and reported in 1969.
The Second NCL recommended an umbrella legislation for the unorganised sector.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 replaced the Trade Unions Act 1926, the ID Act 1947 and the Standing Orders Act 1946.
Section 2(q) of the ID Act defines strike.
Check-off means employer deduction of union dues from wages.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 provides a sole negotiating union with 51% membership.
summary: The answer is (d). The Second National Commission on Labour (2002, chaired by Ravindra Varma) did not recommend all three methods (membership verification, secret ballot and check-off) as the joint basis for choosing a bargaining agent. It preferred a single route: check-off based membership verification, with a secret ballot only where that is disputed or not feasible. The other three options match its recommendations, as far as I recall them. There is no official key, so the answer rests on that recollection.
topic_notes: The Second National Commission on Labour was constituted in October 1999 under Ravindra Varma and submitted its report in June 2002. The First NCL was set up in 1966 under P.B. Gajendragadkar and reported in 1969. The Second NCL's main concerns were the protection of workers in the unorganised sector and a simpler legal framework. It proposed an Umbrella Legislation on a minimum level of protection for all workers, including the self-employed. It also proposed consolidating the 44 central labour laws into broad groups, such as industrial relations, wages, social security, safety and welfare, and working conditions. On industrial relations it recommended a single Labour Management Relations Law. It wanted the right to strike retained, but subject to notice and a ballot, and it wanted go-slow and work-to-rule treated as misconduct. It proposed a Labour Relations Commission-style machinery and a bargaining council. It recommended raising the threshold for compulsory retrenchment permission under Chapter VB of the ID Act, while also suggesting a more flexible approach to hiring and firing in small units. It suggested that trade unions be required to have a minimum membership and that outsiders in union office be limited. The Government later enacted the four Labour Codes: Code on Wages 2019, Industrial Relations Code 2020, Social Security Code 2020, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020. UPSC may ask about the recommendations, the codes, the 1966 and 1999 commissions, and the definition of strike under the Industrial Disputes Act (Section 2(q)).

question: The view that people can learn through observation and direct experience is associated with which one of the following theories of learning?
subject: General Science
detail: Social Learning Theory, developed by Albert Bandura (1960s-70s, later renamed Social Cognitive Theory), says that learning is not only the result of direct reinforcement. People also learn by watching the behaviour of models and noting its consequences. His 1961 Bobo doll experiment showed that children imitated aggression they had seen adults display. Four processes govern observational learning: attention, retention, motor reproduction and motivation (reinforcement or punishment, including vicarious reinforcement). In organisational behaviour, this theory explains how employees learn from role models, mentors and supervisors. Classical conditioning (Pavlov) is about learning through association between stimuli, so it is passive and involuntary. Operant conditioning (Skinner) is about learning through consequences of voluntary behaviour, and it leaves out observation of others. Reinforcement is a concept within operant conditioning, not a theory in itself. Only social learning explicitly combines observation with direct experience, so (a) is correct. Elimination logic: the key phrase 'observation' points to Bandura and rules out the stimulus-response and consequence-based theories.
explanations: Correct. Bandura's Social Learning Theory says people learn through observing models and through direct experience.
Incorrect. Skinner's operant conditioning explains learning through the consequences (reward or punishment) of one's own behaviour, not observing others.
Incorrect. Reinforcement is a mechanism used in operant conditioning to strengthen behaviour. It is not a distinct theory about observational learning.
Incorrect. Pavlov's classical conditioning is learning by associating a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus, not by observation.
keyfact: Observational learning or modelling = Bandura's Social Learning Theory.
option_notes: Social learning: proposed by Albert Bandura. Learning occurs in a social context through observation, imitation and modelling. Its processes are attention, retention, reproduction and motivation. The 1961 Bobo doll study is the classic evidence. It was later extended into Social Cognitive Theory, which adds self-efficacy (1977, 1986). It is widely applied in training, mentoring and leadership.

Operant conditioning: B.F. Skinner's theory (also called instrumental conditioning, linked to Thorndike's Law of Effect). Voluntary behaviour is shaped by its consequences: positive and negative reinforcement increase behaviour, while punishment and extinction decrease it. Skinner used the 'Skinner box'. Reinforcement schedules include fixed or variable ratio and fixed or variable interval. It is applied in organisational behaviour modification.

Reinforcement: a concept, not a standalone theory. It means any consequence that strengthens a behaviour. Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus, and negative reinforcement removes an aversive one. It is distinct from punishment. It is central to Skinner's operant conditioning and also appears in Hull's drive reduction theory and in Bandura's idea of vicarious reinforcement.

Classical conditioning: Ivan Pavlov's theory, from experiments with dogs and salivation in the 1890s-1900s. A neutral stimulus (bell) is paired with an unconditioned stimulus (food) until it becomes a conditioned stimulus eliciting a conditioned response. Key terms are acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation and discrimination. John B. Watson applied it to humans in the Little Albert experiment (1920).
related: Bandura proposed Social Learning Theory; the Bobo doll experiment was in 1961.
Pavlov's classical conditioning used dogs and salivation.
Skinner's operant conditioning used the Skinner box and reinforcement schedules.
Thorndike's Law of Effect came from the cat puzzle box experiment.
Kohler's insight learning used the chimpanzee Sultan.
Tolman is associated with latent learning and cognitive maps.
Variable ratio schedule produces the highest and most persistent response rates.
Bandura's four processes: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation.
summary: The answer is (a) Social learning. Albert Bandura's Social Learning Theory holds that people learn by observing others (modelling) as well as through direct experience, with attention, retention, reproduction and motivation as the key processes.
topic_notes: Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour resulting from experience. The major theories are: (1) Classical conditioning, by Ivan Pavlov, based on stimulus-stimulus association (UCS, UCR, CS, CR). Watson founded behaviourism and ran the Little Albert experiment. (2) Operant conditioning, by B.F. Skinner, building on Thorndike's Law of Effect (trial and error with a cat puzzle box). Behaviour depends on its consequences: positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, punishment and extinction. Schedules of reinforcement are continuous or intermittent (fixed ratio, variable ratio, fixed interval, variable interval); variable ratio produces the strongest and most persistent response. (3) Social learning (Social Cognitive) theory, by Albert Bandura, with observation, modelling, vicarious reinforcement and self-efficacy. (4) Cognitive learning, covering Kohler's insight learning with the chimpanzee Sultan, and Tolman's latent learning and cognitive maps. (5) Other learning theories include Gestalt, Hull's drive reduction, Bruner's discovery learning, Piaget's cognitive development and Vygotsky's sociocultural theory with the zone of proximal development. In organisational behaviour, learning links to behaviour modification (OB Mod), training, mentoring and shaping. Remember the contrasts: classical conditioning is involuntary or respondent behaviour, operant is voluntary behaviour, and social learning needs no direct reinforcement for the learner. Typical UPSC questions match a theorist to a theory, or a key term to its concept.

question: Employees’ belief in the degree to which they affect their work environment, their competence, the meaningfulness of their job and their perceived autonomy in their work indicates:
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Psychological empowerment is an intrinsic motivational state. Thomas and Velthouse (1990) proposed it, and Spreitzer (1995) developed a measurement scale with four dimensions. Impact is the belief that one can influence work outcomes and the work environment. Competence (self-efficacy) is the belief in one's capability to perform the job well. Meaning is the value of the work goal in relation to one's own ideals. Self-determination (autonomy) is the sense of choice in starting and regulating one's actions. The question lists exactly these four: 'degree to which they affect their work environment' (impact), 'competence', 'meaningfulness' and 'perceived autonomy'. Organisational commitment is an attitude of attachment to the organisation, covered by Meyer and Allen's three-component model (affective, continuance and normative). Affective commitment is only one component of that model, an emotional attachment. Job satisfaction is a positive feeling or evaluation about one's job, such as pay, supervision and the work itself. None of these three captures the cognitions of impact, competence, meaning and autonomy, so they are eliminated.
explanations: Incorrect: organisational commitment is the strength of an employee's identification with and attachment to the organisation, not beliefs about impact, competence, meaning and autonomy.
Correct: impact, competence, meaning and self-determination are the four dimensions of psychological empowerment (Spreitzer 1995).
Incorrect: affective commitment is the emotional attachment and desire to stay with the organisation, one part of Meyer and Allen's model; it does not cover the four cognitions.
Incorrect: job satisfaction is an affective evaluation of the job (pay, work, supervision, colleagues, promotion), as measured by the JDI or MSQ, not a set of empowerment beliefs.
keyfact: Psychological empowerment = meaning + competence + self-determination (autonomy) + impact (Spreitzer).
option_notes: Organisational commitment is an employee's psychological attachment to and identification with the organisation. Meyer and Allen (1991) split it into affective (want to stay), continuance (need to stay) and normative (ought to stay) commitment. It is linked to lower turnover and absenteeism. Porter's Organisational Commitment Questionnaire (OCQ) is a well-known measure.

Psychological empowerment is an intrinsic task motivation made up of four cognitions: meaning, competence, self-determination and impact. It was proposed by Thomas and Velthouse (1990) and measured by Spreitzer (1995). It differs from structural empowerment, which concerns delegation of power and resources. It is linked to job performance, innovation and lower strain.

Affective commitment is the emotional attachment, identification and involvement an employee feels toward the organisation; employees stay because they want to. It is one of the three components in Meyer and Allen's model and is generally the strongest predictor of positive outcomes such as performance and citizenship behaviour.

Job satisfaction is the positive emotional state resulting from appraisal of one's job. It is measured by the Job Descriptive Index (Smith, Kendall and Hulin), the Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire and the Job in General scale. Herzberg's two-factor theory and Locke's value-discrepancy theory explain it. Its facets include pay, promotion, supervision, co-workers and the work itself.
related: Spreitzer (1995) defined four dimensions of psychological empowerment: meaning, competence, self-determination, impact.
Meyer and Allen's three-component model: affective, continuance, normative commitment.
Hackman and Oldham's Job Characteristics Model has five core job dimensions.
Job Descriptive Index (JDI) measures job satisfaction facets.
Bandura's self-efficacy corresponds to the competence dimension of empowerment.
Herzberg's two-factor theory separates hygiene factors from motivators.
Kanter's structural empowerment stresses access to information, resources, support and opportunity.
summary: The answer is (b) Psychological empowerment. Employees' beliefs about their impact, competence, meaningfulness of work and autonomy (self-determination) are the four cognitions that define psychological empowerment, as set out by Spreitzer and by Thomas and Velthouse.
topic_notes:
Psychological empowerment belongs to organisational behaviour and is a core idea in modern HRM. Conger and Kanungo (1988) first described empowerment as enhancing self-efficacy. Thomas and Velthouse (1990) built a cognitive model of intrinsic task motivation. Spreitzer (1995) validated a 12-item scale with 4 dimensions: meaning, competence, self-determination and impact. Structural empowerment (Kanter) is about access to information, support, resources and opportunity. Psychological empowerment is the employee's perception of that empowerment.

Related attitudes and concepts:
- Job satisfaction: an evaluation of the job. Theories include Herzberg, Maslow and Locke. Measures include JDI and MSQ.
- Job involvement: the degree to which a person identifies psychologically with the job.
- Organisational commitment: Meyer and Allen's three components (affective, continuance, normative).
- Organisational citizenship behaviour (Organ): voluntary behaviour beyond role requirements.
- Job characteristics model (Hackman and Oldham): five core dimensions (skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, feedback), three psychological states (experienced meaningfulness, responsibility, knowledge of results), and the Motivating Potential Score.
- Self-efficacy (Bandura): belief in one's ability to succeed, which maps to the competence dimension.
- Locus of control (Rotter) and self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan: autonomy, competence, relatedness).

UPSC often tests the difference between attitudes (satisfaction, commitment, involvement, empowerment) and the theories behind them. Remember that the job characteristics model produces meaningfulness and responsibility, while empowerment adds impact and competence.

question: The tendency of individuals to attribute their own success to internal factors and put the blame for failures on external factors indicates:
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Attribution theory (Fritz Heider, later developed by Harold Kelley) explains how people infer the causes of behaviour. Causes are either internal (dispositional: ability, effort, personality) or external (situational: luck, task difficulty, other people). Kelley's covariation model uses three cues: distinctiveness, consensus and consistency. Two classic distortions are asked in exams. The fundamental attribution error is the tendency, when judging OTHER people, to overestimate dispositional factors and underestimate situational ones. The self-serving bias is the tendency to take credit for one's own successes (internal) and blame failures on external causes. The question describes the person's own success and failure, so it is self-serving bias. Selective perception is the tendency to interpret what we see based on our interests, background and attitudes, so we notice only certain information. Contrast effect is the evaluation of a person's characteristics being affected by comparison with others recently encountered who rank higher or lower on the same traits. Elimination: (a) concerns judgments of others, (c) concerns filtering of information, (d) concerns comparison, and none of these involve self-protective explanations of one's own outcomes.
explanations: Wrong: fundamental attribution error concerns how we judge other people's behaviour, overweighting internal causes. It does not describe explaining one's own success and failure differently.
Correct: self-serving bias means attributing one's own successes to internal factors and failures to external factors, which is exactly what the question describes.
Wrong: selective perception is about filtering and interpreting information according to one's interests, experience and attitudes. It is not about attributing causes of success or failure.
Wrong: contrast effect is the distortion in evaluating someone because of comparison with other people recently assessed, for example an average candidate looking poor after a very strong one.
keyfact: Self-serving bias = my success is due to me (internal), my failure is due to others or luck (external).
option_notes: Fundamental attribution error: the tendency to underestimate situational factors and overestimate dispositional factors when explaining the behaviour of others. Example: a manager assumes a late employee is lazy and ignores a traffic jam. It is also called correspondence bias. It is a core concept of attribution theory in organisational behaviour and is often paired in questions with self-serving bias.

Self-serving bias: the tendency of individuals to attribute their own successes to internal factors (ability, effort) and their failures to external factors (luck, others, difficulty). It protects self-esteem and is a major attribution distortion in organisational behaviour. Example: a student who passes credits hard work, but one who fails blames an unfair paper.

Selective perception: people selectively interpret what they see based on their own interests, background, experience and attitudes. Because we cannot assimilate everything, we pick out information that fits our views. Example: a manager from the sales department sees problems mainly as sales issues. It is one of the common shortcuts in judging others, along with the halo effect, contrast effect and stereotyping.

Contrast effect: an evaluation of a person's characteristics is affected by comparisons with other people recently encountered who rank higher or lower on the same characteristics. Example: an interviewer rates an average candidate lower after interviewing a brilliant one. It is a perceptual error that distorts judgment of others, and is treated as a shortcut in judging people in organisational behaviour texts.
related: Heider (1958) is the father of attribution theory.
Kelley's covariation model uses distinctiveness, consensus and consistency.
Fundamental attribution error applies to judging others, self-serving bias to judging oneself.
Halo effect: forming a general impression of a person from a single characteristic.
Projection: attributing one's own traits to other people.
Pygmalion effect (Rosenthal) is a self-fulfilling prophecy of expectations.
Stereotyping: judging someone by the group they belong to.
summary: The answer is (b) Self-serving bias. It is the tendency to credit one's own successes to internal factors such as ability and effort, and to blame failures on external factors such as bad luck or other people, which protects self-esteem.
topic_notes:
Perception is the process by which individuals organise and interpret sensory impressions to give meaning to their environment. Behaviour is based on perceived, not actual, reality. Factors influencing perception lie in the perceiver (attitudes, motives, interests, experience, expectations), the target (novelty, motion, sounds, size, background, proximity, similarity) and the situation (time, work setting, social setting).

Attribution theory (Heider, 1958) deals with how we explain behaviour by attributing it to internal or external causes. Kelley's three determinants are distinctiveness (different behaviour in different situations), consensus (everyone responds the same way) and consistency (the person responds the same way over time). High distinctiveness, high consensus and low consistency point to an external cause; low distinctiveness, low consensus and high consistency point to an internal cause.

Attribution errors and biases: fundamental attribution error (judging others) and self-serving bias (judging oneself).

Shortcuts in judging others: selective perception, halo effect (general impression from one trait), contrast effect, projection (attributing one's own characteristics to others), stereotyping (judging someone based on the group they belong to), and the Pygmalion or self-fulfilling prophecy effect (expectations shape performance; Rosenthal).

Other related concepts: perceptual defence, first-impression error, and the primacy and recency effects. Applications of perception in organisations include employment interviews, performance expectations, performance evaluation and employee effort. Likely future questions ask for the term matching a given definition, so learn each definition precisely.

question: Intuitive decision making means:
options: a non-conscious process created out of distilled experience
making decisions by constructing simplified models without capturing complexity
behaving in such a way so as to maximize output
subject: Current Affairs
detail: In organisational behaviour (Stephen Robbins), decision making is described through three models: the rational model, bounded rationality and intuition. Intuitive decision making is defined as 'a non-conscious process created out of distilled experience'. It does not work independently of rational analysis; the two complement each other. It is typically used when there is a high level of uncertainty, little precedent, variables are less scientifically predictable, facts are limited, facts do not clearly point the way, analytical data are of little use, there are several plausible alternatives, and time is limited with pressure to be right. Experienced managers rely on pattern recognition and 'gut feel'. Elimination: (b) describes bounded rationality, where people build simplified models that extract the essential features of problems without capturing all their complexity (Herbert Simon). (c) describes the rational or economic assumption of maximising outcomes, which is not intuition. (d) describes conscious development of alternatives, which is part of the rational decision-making model. Only (a) matches the definition of intuition.
explanations: Correct. This is the standard textbook definition of intuitive decision making: a non-conscious process created out of distilled experience.
Incorrect. This describes bounded rationality, where decision makers use simplified models of complex problems and accept a satisficing solution.
Incorrect. Maximising output or value is the aim of the rational, economic-man model, not a definition of intuition.
Incorrect. Consciously developing alternatives is a step of the rational decision-making process, the opposite of a non-conscious intuitive process.
keyfact: Intuition = non-conscious process created out of distilled experience; bounded rationality = simplified models; rational = maximise.
option_notes: Intuitive decision making is a subconscious process based on accumulated experience, pattern recognition and feelings. Robbins calls it 'distilled experience'. It is fast, works best under uncertainty and time pressure, and is used alongside rational analysis. Related concepts include gut feeling, hunches and experiential judgement. Research shows that experienced managers use it effectively, but it can suffer from biases.

This describes bounded rationality, proposed by Herbert Simon, who won the Nobel Prize in 1978. Because human cognitive capacity is limited, individuals build simplified models that capture the essential features of a problem. They then look for a satisfactory ('satisficing') solution rather than the optimal one. It is the most common alternative to the rational model in organisational settings.

Maximising output or value is the assumption of the rational decision-making model, or 'economic man'. The rational model assumes a clear problem, known options, clear preferences, constant preferences, no time or cost constraints, and a final choice that maximises economic payoff. In practice these assumptions seldom hold, which is why bounded rationality and intuition are used instead.

Consciously developing alternatives is a step in the rational decision-making model. The steps are: define the problem, identify decision criteria, allocate weights to criteria, develop alternatives, evaluate alternatives, and select the best one. It is a deliberate, analytical process, the opposite of the non-conscious nature of intuition.
related: Bounded rationality was proposed by Herbert Simon.
Satisficing means choosing the first acceptable solution, not the optimal one.
The rational model assumes complete information and maximising outcomes.
Escalation of commitment means continuing a failing course of action.
Simon's decision phases are intelligence, design and choice.
Nominal group technique restricts discussion during decision making.
The Delphi technique uses written expert opinions in several rounds.
summary: The answer is (a). Intuitive decision making is a non-conscious process created out of distilled experience. Decision makers draw on accumulated experience and pattern recognition to reach a quick judgment, without step-by-step analysis.
topic_notes: Decision making is a core topic of organisational behaviour and management. Robbins describes three main approaches. (1) Rational model: a six-step process of defining the problem, identifying criteria, weighting criteria, generating alternatives, rating alternatives and computing the optimal decision. It assumes problem clarity, known options, clear and constant preferences, no constraints and maximum payoff. (2) Bounded rationality (Herbert Simon): people have limited information-processing capacity, so they construct simplified models and settle for satisficing, meaning the first acceptable solution. (3) Intuitive decision making: a non-conscious process created out of distilled experience. It is fast and affect-driven, and it complements rational analysis. Robbins lists conditions favouring intuition: high uncertainty, little precedent, unpredictable variables, limited facts, unhelpful analytical data, several plausible solutions, and time pressure. Other related ideas: escalation of commitment, which is increasing commitment to a previous decision despite negative information; common biases such as overconfidence, anchoring, confirmation, availability, representation, hindsight and randomness errors; programmed decisions, which are routine and rule-based, versus non-programmed decisions, which are novel; and group decision making techniques such as brainstorming, nominal group technique, the Delphi technique and electronic meetings. Also remember Vroom-Yetton's normative leadership-decision model, Simon's three phases of intelligence, design and choice, and the garbage can model of Cohen, March and Olsen. Future questions may ask for the definition of satisficing, the distinction between programmed and non-programmed decisions, or the biases.

question: A group, whose efforts result in performance that is greater than the sum of the individual inputs, is called:
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a standard organisational behaviour distinction, drawn from Stephen Robbins. A work group interacts mainly to share information and make decisions that help each member perform within their own area of responsibility. It has no need or opportunity to engage in collective work, so its performance is merely the sum of individual contributions, which gives neutral or sometimes negative synergy. A work team generates positive synergy through coordinated effort. Its members have individual and mutual accountability, complementary skills and a shared purpose, so its performance is greater than the sum of individual inputs. Team types include problem-solving teams, self-managed (self-directed) work teams, cross-functional teams and virtual teams. Elimination: (a) is wrong because a work group produces only an additive result. (c) A virtual team is a team type defined by its use of technology to link dispersed members, and the term does not describe the synergy concept. (d) A self-managed group is a team type defined by its autonomy and does not define synergy. The general concept asked about is therefore the work team.
explanations: Incorrect: a work group shares information, has individual accountability only, and its output equals the sum of individual efforts, with no positive synergy.
Correct: a work team creates positive synergy through coordinated effort, mutual accountability and complementary skills, so output exceeds the sum of individual inputs.
Incorrect: a virtual team is a type of team that uses computer technology to unite physically dispersed members. It is defined by the medium, not by synergy.
Incorrect: a self-managed group is a team type that operates without a manager and takes over supervisory duties. It is defined by autonomy, not by the synergy concept.
keyfact: Work team = positive synergy (output greater than the sum of individual inputs); work group = merely the sum of individual inputs.
option_notes: Work group: a group that interacts primarily to share information and make decisions to help members perform in their own areas. It has no joint work, individual accountability and neutral or negative synergy. Examples are a department of employees reporting to one manager. Robbins contrasts it directly with the work team.

Work team: a group whose individual efforts produce performance greater than the sum of inputs (positive synergy). Features include shared goals, complementary skills, mutual accountability and coordinated effort. Robbins lists the main types as problem-solving, self-managed, cross-functional and virtual teams.

Virtual team: a team that uses computer technology to tie together physically dispersed members to achieve a common goal. Members collaborate online through email, video conferencing and shared platforms. It became common with globalisation and remote work. Its challenges include weaker social rapport and less direct interaction.

Self-managed (self-directed) work team: a group of about 10 to 15 people who take on the responsibilities of their former supervisors, such as planning and scheduling work, controlling pace, assigning tasks and choosing members. It is associated with empowerment and the sociotechnical approach, and it often reduces the need for supervisors.
related: Synergy: the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.
Work group output = sum of individual contributions; work team output exceeds it.
Tuckman's stages: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning (adjourning added later).
Quality circles are a form of problem-solving team.
Social loafing is the tendency to put in less effort when working collectively.
Groupthink was described by Irving Janis.
Cross-functional teams bring together members from different areas at the same hierarchical level.
summary: The answer is (b) Work Team. A work team generates positive synergy through coordinated effort, so its collective performance exceeds the sum of its members' individual inputs. A work group only shares information and its output is just the sum of individual contributions.
topic_notes: Groups versus teams is a core topic in organisational behaviour. A group is two or more interacting and interdependent individuals who come together to achieve particular objectives. Groups may be formal (command and task groups set by the organisation) or informal (friendship and interest groups arising naturally). Tuckman's stages of group development are forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. Work groups share information, with individual accountability, random or varying skills, and a neutral or negative synergy. Work teams show positive synergy, with both individual and mutual accountability and complementary skills. Types of teams (Robbins): problem-solving teams (for example quality circles, of 5 to 12 members who discuss quality improvement but lack authority to implement), self-managed work teams, cross-functional teams (members from different departments, such as task forces and committees) and virtual teams. Belbin described nine team roles, including plant, resource investigator, coordinator, shaper, monitor-evaluator, teamworker, implementer, completer-finisher and specialist. Other related concepts are social loafing (individuals exert less effort in a group), groupthink (Irving Janis), group cohesiveness, norms, roles and the Hawthorne studies on informal groups. Synergy means the whole is greater than the sum of the parts. UPSC may also ask about types of groups, Tuckman's stages, or the definition of each team type.

question: The concept that a subordinate should have only one superior to whom he or she is directly responsible is known as:
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Unity of command is one of Henri Fayol's 14 principles of management, set out in 'Administration Industrielle et Générale' (1916). It means a subordinate has one and only one boss for any given action. Dual command causes conflicting orders, divided loyalty, weakened discipline and difficulty in fixing responsibility. It is closely linked to, but distinct from, 'unity of direction' (one head and one plan for a group of activities with the same objective). Span of control (also called span of management) is the number of subordinates a manager can effectively supervise. Chain of command (scalar chain) is the formal line of authority running from top to bottom of an organisation, along which communication flows. 'Authority control' is not a standard management term, so option (d) is a distractor. Elimination: the question asks about ONE superior, which points to unity of command. Span of control concerns a count of subordinates, and chain of command concerns the hierarchy or line of authority, not exclusivity of the superior.
explanations: Incorrect: span of control is the number of subordinates reporting to one manager, not the one-boss rule.
Correct: unity of command means a subordinate reports to and takes orders from only one superior.
Incorrect: chain of command is the hierarchical line of authority from top to bottom, not the single-superior principle itself.
Incorrect: 'authority control' is not an established management concept, so it is a distractor.
keyfact: Unity of command = one subordinate, one superior (Fayol's principle); span of control = number of subordinates; chain of command = line of authority.
option_notes: Span of control (span of management) is the number of subordinates a manager can effectively supervise. A narrow span gives a tall structure with many levels, and a wide span gives a flat structure. V.A. Graicunas studied the mathematical relationships among superiors and subordinates. The ideal span depends on task complexity, subordinate skill and the manager's capacity. Classical writers often suggested about 6 to 8 subordinates, though there is no fixed rule.

Unity of command is Fayol's principle that an employee receives orders from only one superior. It ensures clear accountability, discipline and order, and avoids conflict from dual instructions. It is one of Fayol's 14 principles and was widely accepted in classical organisation theory. Matrix organisations deliberately violate it by giving employees two bosses. Do not confuse it with unity of direction.

Chain of command, or scalar chain, is the formal line of authority and communication from the top of an organisation to the lowest level. Fayol called it the scalar chain and also allowed a 'gang plank' (Fayol's bridge) for direct cross-communication between peers at the same level. It defines who reports to whom and the route for passing orders and escalating issues.

Authority control is not a recognised principle in management theory. Related genuine concepts include authority and responsibility (Fayol's 2nd principle), delegation of authority, centralisation and decentralisation, and span of control. It appears here only as a plausible-sounding distractor.
related: Fayol's 14 principles were published in 1916 in Administration Industrielle et Générale.
Unity of direction means one head and one plan for a group of activities with the same objective.
Scalar chain is Fayol's term for the chain of command; the gang plank allows direct lateral contact.
Graicunas is associated with the mathematics of span of control.
Matrix organisations breach unity of command through dual reporting.
POSDCORB was coined by Luther Gulick in 1937.
Taylor's functional foremanship contradicts unity of command.
summary: The answer is (b) Unity of command. It is Henri Fayol's 5th principle of management: each employee should receive orders from, and be answerable to, only one superior, which avoids conflicting instructions and confusion over accountability.
topic_notes: Henri Fayol (1841-1925), a French mining engineer, is regarded as the father of modern (general) management theory. His 1916 book identified five functions of management: planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling. Later writers recast them as POSDCORB (Luther Gulick): Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting, Budgeting. His 14 principles are: division of work, authority and responsibility, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, subordination of individual interest to general interest, remuneration, centralisation, scalar chain, order, equity, stability of tenure, initiative and esprit de corps. Related organisation concepts are hierarchy, span of control, delegation, line and staff authority, functional authority, and centralisation versus decentralisation. Other thinkers: F.W. Taylor (scientific management, functional foremanship, which violates unity of command), Max Weber (bureaucracy, ideal type with hierarchy and rules), Mary Parker Follett (coordination, power-with), Elton Mayo (Hawthorne experiments, human relations), Chester Barnard (The Functions of the Executive, acceptance theory of authority), and Herbert Simon (administrative behaviour, bounded rationality). Taylor's functional foremanship gave each worker eight bosses, which Fayol's unity of command opposes. Modern matrix structures and project teams use dual reporting. Remember the distinction: unity of command is about one boss per person, and unity of direction is about one plan and one head per group of activities.

question: Which one of the following appraisal methods combines the benefits of narratives, critical incidents and quantified scales by assigning scale points with specific examples of good or poor performance?
subject: General Science
detail: BARS was developed by Smith and Kendall in 1963 and is described by Dessler as combining the benefits of narratives, critical incidents and quantified ratings. It is built in steps. First, experts and job holders generate critical incidents that show effective and ineffective behaviour. Next, the incidents are grouped into performance dimensions such as customer handling or planning. A second group then retranslates the incidents, and only those that are consistently assigned to the same dimension are kept. Each retained incident is rated for effectiveness, and these ratings place it on a scale, typically of 7 or 9 points. The result is a scale in which every point is tied to a concrete behavioural example. Its strengths are clearer standards, less rater bias, and useful feedback. Its weaknesses are high cost and time to develop, and the need for a separate scale for each job. Elimination: forced distribution forces ratings into a fixed curve and uses no behavioural anchors. Alternation ranking orders employees from best to worst. A graphic rating scale lists traits with a scale but gives no behavioural examples.
explanations: Incorrect: forced distribution places fixed percentages of employees into performance categories. It uses no narratives, incidents or behavioural anchors.
Incorrect: alternation ranking is a ranking method. The rater alternately picks the best and worst employee. It has no scale points or examples.

Correct: BARS ties each scale point to a specific behavioural example drawn from critical incidents. This is exactly the combination of narrative, critical incident and quantified scale that the question describes.
Incorrect: a graphic rating scale rates traits such as quality or dependability on a continuum. Its points are not anchored to specific behavioural examples, and it is subjective.
keyfact: BARS = critical incidents + quantified scale, with behavioural anchors (Smith and Kendall, 1963).
option_notes: Forced distribution is a comparative method, like grading on a curve. Raters assign employees to categories in predetermined proportions, for example 10% top, 20% high, 40% average, 20% low and 10% poor. It prevents leniency and central tendency, but it is unfair to teams that are uniformly strong or weak. General Electric made it well known as 'rank and yank'.

Alternation ranking is a ranking method. The rater lists all employees, picks the best and the worst, then alternately picks the next best and next worst until all are placed. It is simple and cheap and cuts down on rating inflation. However, it shows only relative position, not the size of the performance gap, and it gives poor feedback.

The Behaviourally anchored rating scale was developed by Smith and Kendall in 1963. It places critical-incident-based behavioural examples along a vertical scale of 7 to 9 points for each performance dimension. It is more objective and gives better feedback, but it is costly and job-specific to develop. It is a hybrid of the critical incident method and the rating scale method.

The graphic rating scale is the oldest and most common appraisal method. It lists traits such as quality, quantity, initiative and reliability, and the rater marks a point on a scale for each. It is quick and standardised. Its weaknesses are halo effect, leniency, central tendency and subjective trait definitions.
related: BARS was developed by Smith and Kendall in 1963.
BARS combines critical incidents with a quantified rating scale.
MBO was propounded by Peter Drucker in 1954 in The Practice of Management.
The critical incident technique is associated with Flanagan.
Forced distribution forces rating onto a normal curve, causing 'rank and yank'.
Halo effect means one trait influences the rating of all other traits.
360-degree feedback uses ratings from multiple sources.
Paired comparison involves n(n-1)/2 comparisons.
summary: The answer is (c) Behaviourally anchored rating scale (BARS). BARS anchors each point on a quantified rating scale to specific, observed examples of good or poor job behaviour. In this way it combines narratives, critical incidents and numerical scaling.
topic_notes: Performance appraisal methods fall into two groups, traditional and modern. Traditional methods include the graphic rating scale, ranking (straight and alternation), paired comparison, forced distribution, forced choice, checklists, critical incident, essay or narrative, field review and confidential report. Modern methods include MBO (Management by Objectives, Peter Drucker, 1954), BARS, assessment centres, 360-degree feedback, the balanced scorecard, human resource accounting and 720-degree appraisal. Paired comparison compares each employee with every other, giving n(n-1)/2 comparisons. The critical incident method, associated with Flanagan in 1954, records specific incidents of effective and ineffective behaviour. BARS builds on this method. The assessment centre method originated with the German military and was used by AT&T in the US. It uses in-basket exercises, group discussion and role plays. 360-degree feedback gathers ratings from superiors, peers, subordinates, customers and self. Common rating errors include halo effect, horn effect, leniency, strictness, central tendency, recency bias, similar-to-me bias and the contrast effect. Behavioural observation scales (BOS) are a related variant of BARS. They use frequency ratings of behaviours. For exams, remember the one-line association for each method: BARS is behavioural anchors, forced distribution is a bell curve, MBO is goal-based, and 360-degree is multi-rater.

question: Which one of the following demographic characteristics reflects surface-level diversity?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: In organisational behaviour (Robbins; Harrison, Price and Bell), workforce diversity is divided into two levels. Surface-level diversity consists of observable, mostly demographic differences: age, gender, race, ethnicity, physical abilities and disabilities. These are easy to see, are often immutable, and may trigger stereotypes and bias early in a working relationship. Deep-level diversity consists of differences in values, attitudes, personality, beliefs, work preferences, knowledge and skills. These become apparent only after people interact and learn about one another. Research suggests surface-level differences have a stronger effect on team dynamics in the early stages, while deep-level differences matter more as team members get to know one another over time. Applying this to the question, ethnicity is a visible demographic characteristic and so is surface-level. Values, personality and work preferences are psychological, internal traits that cannot be seen directly, so they are deep-level. The elimination logic is to ask whether the trait can be perceived at first sight; only ethnicity passes this test.
explanations: Wrong: differences in values are internal and learned through interaction, so they are deep-level diversity.
Correct: ethnicity is an observable demographic trait and a classic example of surface-level diversity.
Wrong: personality is a psychological, deep-level trait that is not visible at first sight.
Wrong: work preferences are attitudinal and revealed only over time, so they are deep-level diversity.
keyfact: Surface-level diversity = visible demographics (age, gender, race, ethnicity, disability); deep-level = values, personality, work preferences.
option_notes: Values are enduring beliefs about what is right, important or desirable (Rokeach's terminal and instrumental values). They shape attitudes and behaviour, and differences in values are a key deep-level diversity dimension. They are not visible and are discovered through communication and experience. Value differences between people can cause conflict or enrich decision-making depending on how they are managed.

Ethnicity refers to a shared cultural identity based on common ancestry, language, religion, customs or nationality. It is related to, but distinct from, race, which is based on physical traits. Along with age, sex, race and disability, ethnicity is a standard surface-level demographic characteristic. It is often visible and can lead to stereotyping and discrimination at work, and the Indian Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth under Articles 15 and 16.

Personality is the stable set of psychological traits that determine how a person reacts to and interacts with others. The Big Five model (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, emotional stability, openness to experience) and the MBTI are widely used frameworks. Personality is a deep-level diversity attribute that is not visible at first sight and is revealed only through behaviour over time.

Work preferences are individual choices about how, when and where people prefer to work, such as autonomy versus structure, team versus solo work, flexible hours and preferred tasks. They are attitudinal in nature and are known only through interaction. They count as deep-level diversity and are important for job design, motivation and the management of diverse teams.
related: Surface-level diversity: age, gender, race, ethnicity, disability.
Deep-level diversity: values, personality, work preferences, attitudes.
Over time, deep-level diversity becomes more important than surface-level diversity in teams.
Similarity-attraction paradigm explains preference for similar colleagues.
Glass ceiling is an invisible barrier to promotion of women and minorities.
Big Five traits: extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, emotional stability, openness.
Biographical characteristics: age, sex, race, tenure, marital status.
summary: The answer is (b) Ethnicity. Surface-level diversity covers visible, readily observable demographic traits such as ethnicity, race, age, sex and physical disability. Values, personality and work preferences are deep-level, underlying attributes that emerge only through interaction.
topic_notes: Workforce diversity means that organisations are becoming more heterogeneous in terms of gender, age, race, ethnicity, sexual orientation and other characteristics. Robbins and Judge classify diversity into two layers. Surface-level diversity covers easily perceived characteristics such as age, gender, race, ethnicity and disability. These characteristics do not necessarily reflect how people think or feel, but they can lead to stereotyping. Deep-level diversity covers differences in values, personality and work preferences. These become more important in determining similarity as people get to know one another. Social identity theory and the similarity-attraction paradigm help explain why people prefer working with similar others. Research (Harrison, Price and Bell, 1998) found that the effects of surface-level diversity on group cohesion weaken over time, while the effects of deep-level diversity strengthen. Other related ideas include demographic characteristics (biographical characteristics such as age, sex, tenure and marital status), the glass ceiling, discrimination, stereotype threat, and diversity management programmes such as mentoring, diversity training and inclusive policies. Ability is also classified into intellectual and physical ability, which Robbins treats as a further diversity dimension. Related Indian legislation includes the Equal Remuneration Act 1976, the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 and the Maternity Benefit Act 1961. UPSC could next ask for examples of deep-level diversity, the definition of workforce diversity, the effects of diversity on team performance, or the biographical characteristics that affect organisational behaviour.

question: A ‘SMART’ mnemomic criterion is used in:
subject: Current Affairs
detail: SMART is a goal-setting criterion associated with George T. Doran (1981, 'There's a S.M.A.R.T. way to write management's goals and objectives') and widely used in Management by Objectives (MBO), popularised by Peter Drucker. In performance management, the manager and employee agree on objectives at the start of the cycle, monitor progress, review and appraise results at the end, and link them to rewards, training and development. SMART ensures objectives are Specific (clear, unambiguous), Measurable (quantifiable indicators), Achievable (within the employee's capacity and resources), Relevant or Realistic (aligned to organisational goals) and Time-bound (with a deadline). Variants expand the letters differently, e.g. Assignable, Agreed, Attainable, Results-oriented. Elimination: selection uses tests, interviews and screening; job rotation is a training and development technique that moves employees across jobs; compensation management deals with job evaluation, pay structure and incentives. None of these is defined by the SMART mnemonic. Though compensation may be linked to performance outcomes, SMART itself belongs to performance planning and appraisal.
explanations: Incorrect: selection relies on screening, tests, interviews and reference checks, not SMART goals.
Incorrect: job rotation is a training and development method of moving employees between jobs to broaden skills.
