Correct: SMART objectives are set in performance management, MBO and appraisal systems such as KRAs and KPIs.
Incorrect: compensation management covers job evaluation, pay structures and benefits; SMART is not its criterion, though pay may be linked to performance.
keyfact: SMART goals (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) are used in performance management and MBO.
option_notes: Selection process: the steps used to choose among recruited candidates, including application screening, tests, interviews, background checks, medical examination and the job offer. It follows recruitment and aims at person-job fit. Tools include psychometric tests, structured interviews and assessment centres.

Job rotation: a training and development technique in which employees are moved periodically between jobs or departments. It builds multi-skilling, reduces monotony, helps succession planning and gives a wider organisational view. It is an on-the-job method and also used for career development.

Performance management: a continuous process of setting objectives, monitoring, coaching, appraising and rewarding performance, aligned to organisational strategy. It includes performance planning, ongoing feedback, appraisal and development. Tools are MBO, KRAs, KPIs, 360-degree feedback and the Balanced Scorecard. SMART goals underpin the planning stage.

Compensation management: designing and administering pay, including job analysis and evaluation, wage surveys, pay grades, incentives, benefits and statutory wages. Its aim is internal equity and external competitiveness. It is related to performance through pay-for-performance, but it is not defined by SMART.
related: SMART = Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
MBO was propounded by Peter Drucker in 1954
SMART criteria were popularised by George T. Doran in 1981
POSDCORB was given by Luther Gulick
Balanced Scorecard was developed by Kaplan and Norton
BARS combines critical incidents with rating scales
360-degree feedback collects appraisal from superiors, peers, subordinates and others
summary: The answer is (c) Performance management. SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable/Attainable, Relevant/Realistic, Time-bound) is the standard mnemonic for writing clear goals and objectives, which are the basis of performance planning and appraisal.
topic_notes: Performance management is a cyclical HR process: planning (setting expectations and goals), monitoring and coaching, appraisal or review, and rewarding and developing. Goal setting theory by Edwin Locke says specific and challenging goals improve performance. MBO, given by Peter Drucker in The Practice of Management (1954), involves joint goal setting between superior and subordinate. SMART criteria were popularised by Doran in 1981. Common appraisal methods are graphic rating scale, ranking, paired comparison, forced distribution, critical incident, checklist, BARS, essay, field review, 360-degree feedback and assessment centres. Modern tools include the Balanced Scorecard (Kaplan and Norton), KRAs and KPIs, and OKRs. Typical rating errors are halo effect, horn effect, central tendency, leniency, strictness, recency bias and similar-to-me bias. Appraisal serves administrative decisions (promotion, pay, transfer) and developmental purposes (training needs, feedback). Related HR concepts: job analysis yields job description and job specification; job rotation, job enlargement and job enrichment (Herzberg) are job design techniques; training methods include on-the-job and off-the-job. Compensation management links to the Code on Wages 2019 and minimum wage laws. Other mnemonics in management: SWOT analysis, PESTLE, POSDCORB (Gulick), the 5 Ws.

question: Outplacement is the process of:
options: removal of employees from the job
transferring the employee out of the country
helping redundant employees to find new job
sending the employee on deputation to other organizations
subject: Computers
detail: Outplacement is a support service given to employees whose jobs are being terminated, typically in downsizing, restructuring, mergers, closures or retrenchment. The employer usually pays an external career-transition firm, or an in-house HR team, to help the departing employee. Services include career counselling, aptitude and skills assessment, CV and interview coaching, networking support, job-search training, and sometimes help with starting a business. The aim is to soften the impact of separation, protect the employer's brand and the morale of the remaining staff (the 'survivors'), lower the risk of litigation and industrial disputes, and keep goodwill. It is part of HRM's separation and exit management, alongside voluntary retirement schemes (VRS), golden handshakes, layoff, retrenchment and exit interviews. Elimination: (a) describes termination, discharge or retrenchment itself, not the support given afterwards. (b) describes expatriation or international transfer. (d) describes deputation, a temporary posting to another organization with the parent employer's lien retained. Only (c) captures the helping, re-employment element. Note that outplacement is not itself the termination; it follows or accompanies it.
explanations: Incorrect: removal from a job is termination, dismissal or retrenchment. Outplacement is the assistance given after or alongside that removal, not the removal itself.
Incorrect: sending an employee abroad is an international transfer or expatriate assignment. It has nothing to do with redundancy or job search.
Correct: outplacement means helping redundant or displaced employees find new employment through counselling, training and job-search support.
Incorrect: deputation is a temporary assignment to another organization, and the employee remains on the parent organization's rolls. Outplacement involves separation from the employer.
keyfact: Outplacement = employer-supported help for redundant employees to find new jobs.
option_notes: Removal of employees covers dismissal, discharge, retrenchment and layoff. In India, the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 regulates retrenchment (Sec 25F: notice, compensation of 15 days' average pay per completed year of service). Chapter V-B (Secs 25K-25S) applies to establishments with 100 or more workers (the threshold was raised to 300 in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020). Removal is the cause of the need for outplacement, not outplacement itself.

Transfer out of the country is an expatriate or international assignment, handled under international HRM. Staffing approaches are ethnocentric, polycentric, geocentric and regiocentric. Expatriates are parent-country nationals, host-country nationals are locals, and third-country nationals come from a different country. Issues include cultural adjustment, repatriation and compensation packages such as the balance-sheet approach.

Outplacement is a service to help redundant or laid-off staff re-enter the job market. It is often provided by consultancies and paid for by the employer. It includes counselling, CV preparation, interview skills and job leads. Benefits: it preserves employer branding, keeps the survivors' morale up and reduces conflict. It is a humane exit management practice used with downsizing, VRS and mergers.

Deputation is the temporary assignment of an employee to another organization or government department for a fixed period, typically 3-5 years in government service. The employee keeps a lien on the parent post and gets a deputation allowance. It is different from absorption, where the employee permanently joins the new organization, and from transfer within the same organization.
related: Outplacement = help for redundant or displaced employees to find new jobs.
Retrenchment is defined in Sec 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
Layoff is defined in Sec 2(kk) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
Layoff compensation is 50% of basic wage plus DA (Sec 25C).
Retrenchment compensation is 15 days' average pay for each completed year of service (Sec 25F).
Golden handshake means a lump-sum payment to induce voluntary exit.
Deputation is a temporary posting to another organization with the parent lien retained.
Survivor syndrome means the demoralisation of employees who remain after downsizing.
summary: The answer is (c). Outplacement is a service, usually paid for by the employer, that helps employees who have been made redundant or laid off to find new jobs, through counselling, CV writing, training and job-search support.
topic_notes: Outplacement belongs to the separation and exit management part of HRM. Separation takes several forms: resignation, retirement, VRS, dismissal, discharge, layoff, retrenchment, termination at the end of a contract and death. Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, layoff means the failure or inability of an employer to give employment to a workman whose name is on the muster rolls, owing to coal shortage, power shortage, machinery breakdown or similar reasons (Sec 2(kk)). Compensation for layoff is 50% of basic wage plus DA (Sec 25C). Retrenchment, defined in Sec 2(oo), is the termination of service for any reason other than disciplinary action, and excludes VRS, retirement, and termination under a contract that has run out. Sec 25F requires one month's notice and compensation of 15 days' average pay per completed year. Sec 25G and 25H cover retrenchment seniority (last come, first go) and re-employment of retrenched workmen. Sec 25N covers prior permission for retrenchment in larger units. Other related concepts include the golden handshake (a generous lump-sum severance), downsizing and rightsizing, the exit interview, and the 'survivor syndrome' that affects employees who remain. Outplacement offers counselling, training, career transition support, CV writing and job-search help. It can be individual or group-based, and can be delivered in-house or by external consultants. UPSC may also ask about related ideas such as outsourcing, insourcing, alumni networks and employer branding. The key HRM contrast is between outplacement (helping people leave) and induction/placement (helping them enter).

question: The principles of natural justice have emanated from:
subject: Computers
detail: Natural justice is a body of procedural fairness rules evolved by English common law judges. The two classic rules are nemo judex in causa sua (no one should be a judge in his own cause, i.e. rule against bias) and audi alteram partem (hear the other side, i.e. right to fair hearing). A third, developing rule is reasoned decisions (speaking orders). The concept traces to the jus naturale of Roman law and to medieval English courts; the term 'natural justice' is used in cases like Dr Bonham's Case (1610) and Cooper v Wandsworth Board of Works (1863). In India these principles are not written in the Constitution, but the Supreme Court has treated them as part of Article 14 (non-arbitrariness) and Article 21 (fair procedure) after Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978). Other landmark cases include A.K. Kraipak v Union of India (1969), which erased the distinction between administrative and quasi-judicial functions, and Ridge v Baldwin (1964). Elimination: religious doctrines and social norms are only remote moral influences, while constitutional law merely absorbed the principles later. Their direct source is judge-made common law.
explanations: Incorrect: religious or moral ideas may have influenced the idea of natural law philosophically, but the rules of natural justice as procedural principles were not derived from religious doctrines.
Incorrect: the Indian Constitution does not expressly list natural justice. Courts read it into Articles 14 and 21, so constitutional law applies it but is not its origin.
Correct: natural justice rules were evolved by English common law courts through precedent, and India adopted them via its common law heritage.
Incorrect: social norms reflect general ideas of fairness, but they are not the formal source of these judicially enforced procedural rules.
keyfact: Natural justice is a common law creation (nemo judex in causa sua and audi alteram partem), read into Articles 14 and 21 in India.
option_notes: Religious doctrines are belief systems and moral codes, such as dharma in Hindu thought or canon law in medieval Christian Europe. Canon law did influence ideas of fair hearing in Europe, but religious doctrine is not treated as the legal source of natural justice. Natural law philosophy (Aquinas, Grotius) links morality and law, yet the modern rules are judge-made. In India, religious texts are not a source of administrative law procedure.

Constitutional law is the body of rules from the Constitution and its judicial interpretation. India's Constitution (1950) does not mention natural justice by name. Courts apply the rules through Article 14 (equality, non-arbitrariness) and Article 21 (procedure established by law must be fair, just and reasonable per Maneka Gandhi, 1978). Article 311(2) gives a hearing right to civil servants. The Constitution thus enforces but did not originate these principles.

Common law is law developed by judges through decided cases and precedent, originating in England after the Norman Conquest (1066). It contrasts with statute law. Doctrines like natural justice, ultra vires review and certiorari-type remedies grew from common law courts. India, as a former British colony, inherited this system. Principles such as audi alteram partem and rule against bias are classic common law creations, so this is the correct source.

Social norms are informal customs and shared expectations of behaviour in a society, enforced by social approval or disapproval, not by courts. They can shape ideas of fairness and may inform the law, but they are not a formal legal source. Customs can be a source of law only when recognised by courts as having legal force. Natural justice, in contrast, is a judicially enforceable standard.
related: Nemo judex in causa sua means no one should be a judge in his own cause (rule against bias).
Audi alteram partem means hear the other side (right to fair hearing).
Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978) linked natural justice with Article 21.
A.K. Kraipak (1969) held natural justice applies to administrative actions too.
Article 311(2) gives civil servants a reasonable opportunity of being heard before dismissal.
Writs of certiorari and prohibition are used to enforce natural justice.
A speaking order (giving reasons) is regarded as a third principle of natural justice.
Domestic enquiry in industrial dismissal must follow natural justice.
summary: The answer is (c) common law. The principles of natural justice (nemo judex in causa sua and audi alteram partem) were developed by English common law courts through judicial decisions, and Indian courts inherited them. They are not codified in any single statute, though Indian courts later read them into Article 14 and Article 21.
topic_notes: Natural justice means procedural fairness in decision-making by courts, tribunals and administrative bodies. Its roots lie in Roman jus naturale and English common law. The two core rules are nemo judex in causa sua (rule against bias: pecuniary, personal, subject-matter, departmental, policy or preconceived notions) and audi alteram partem (notice, disclosure of material, opportunity to be heard, possibly legal representation and cross-examination). A third emerging rule is a reasoned (speaking) order. In India they are not codified, but the Supreme Court has made them part of Articles 14 and 21. Key cases: Cooper v Wandsworth Board of Works (1863), Ridge v Baldwin (1964), A.K. Kraipak (1969, no sharp line between administrative and quasi-judicial functions), Maneka Gandhi (1978, passport impounded without hearing; Article 21 needs fair procedure), Mohinder Singh Gill (1978), and Union of India v Tulsiram Patel (1985, exceptions under Article 311(2) provisos). Exceptions: legislative action, urgent or emergency situations, confidential matters, academic evaluation, and where hearing would be futile. Breach makes an order void or voidable and open to judicial review through writs such as certiorari and prohibition under Articles 32 and 226. Post-decisional hearing is sometimes accepted. Related ideas for the exam: administrative law, quasi-judicial authority, doctrine of legitimate expectation, Wednesbury unreasonableness, proportionality, and Article 311 protections for civil servants. In labour law, domestic enquiries before dismissal must follow natural justice, as stressed under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 and Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.

question: If an aggrieved employee is NOT satisfied with the proceedings of the enquiry, he may ask for:
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: A domestic enquiry is the internal disciplinary enquiry an employer holds into alleged misconduct. It must follow the principles of natural justice: a charge-sheet, a reasonable opportunity to explain, the right to cross-examine witnesses, an unbiased enquiry officer, a reasoned finding, and a show-cause notice on the proposed punishment. If these are violated, the enquiry is vitiated. The management may then order a fresh enquiry, called de novo (Latin for 'afresh' or 'from the beginning'), and the employee can ask for one. In an industrial dispute, the Labour Court or Tribunal first decides whether the enquiry was fair and proper as a preliminary issue. If it was defective, the management may lead fresh evidence before the Tribunal (Delhi Cloth Mills v. Ludh Budh Singh; Cooper Engineering v. Mundon). Under Section 11A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Tribunal can also reappraise the evidence and interfere with the punishment. Elimination: an ex-parte enquiry is held in the employee's absence, so it does not remedy his dissatisfaction. A domestic enquiry is the original proceeding itself. 'Legal enquiry' is not a recognised term in this context.
explanations: Incorrect: an ex-parte enquiry is held without the delinquent employee, who has not appeared despite notice. It is not a remedy for dissatisfaction with an enquiry already held.
Correct: a de novo enquiry is a fresh enquiry from the start, ordered when the earlier one was defective or violated natural justice.
Incorrect: 'legal enquiry' is not a recognised category in disciplinary law. The proper terms are domestic, departmental or fresh enquiry.
Incorrect: a domestic enquiry is the original internal disciplinary proceeding itself, which the employee is objecting to.
keyfact: If a domestic enquiry is defective or violates natural justice, a de novo (fresh) enquiry is the remedy.
option_notes: Ex-parte enquiry: an enquiry held in the absence of the charged employee after he fails to appear despite proper and sufficient notice. The management must still record evidence and prove the charges. The employee can have it set aside by showing sufficient cause for his absence. It is not a remedy chosen by the aggrieved employee.

De novo enquiry: a fresh enquiry started from the beginning, ignoring the earlier proceedings. It is ordered when the earlier enquiry was vitiated by bias, a denial of reasonable opportunity, a procedural defect or a violation of natural justice. The management or the appellate authority can order it. The Labour Court may also permit the management to prove misconduct afresh before it.

Legal enquiry: this is not a standard term in service or labour law. Disciplinary matters are handled through domestic or departmental enquiries, and judicial review is done by courts or tribunals. A lawyer's presence in an enquiry is not a matter of right and depends on the standing orders or rules.

Domestic enquiry: an internal quasi-judicial enquiry by the employer into alleged misconduct. It has a charge-sheet, a reply, an enquiry officer, evidence, findings and punishment. Its basic requirement is compliance with natural justice, namely a fair hearing and no bias. Its findings can be challenged before the Labour Court or Tribunal.
related: De novo means 'afresh' or 'from the beginning'.
Natural justice has two limbs: nemo judex in causa sua and audi alteram partem.
Section 11A ID Act, 1947 gives Tribunals power to modify punishment.
An ex-parte enquiry is held when the employee does not appear despite notice.
The standard of proof in a domestic enquiry is preponderance of probability.
Tribunals first decide the fairness of the enquiry as a preliminary issue (Cooper Engineering case).
Misconduct is defined in the Model Standing Orders under the Standing Orders Act, 1946.
Article 311 protects civil servants against dismissal without an enquiry.
summary: The answer is (b) de novo enquiry. If the employee is dissatisfied with how a domestic enquiry was conducted, for example because of a breach of natural justice, bias or a defective procedure, he can ask for a fresh enquiry from the beginning. This is called a de novo enquiry.
topic_notes: Domestic enquiry is central to disciplinary action under industrial law. The stages are: (1) a charge-sheet or show-cause notice stating the misconduct; (2) the employee's written reply; (3) appointment of an impartial enquiry officer; (4) notice of the hearing; (5) examination of the management's witnesses and cross-examination by the employee; (6) the employee's defence evidence; (7) the enquiry officer's findings; (8) a show-cause notice on the proposed punishment, which is no longer mandatory after the 42nd Constitutional Amendment in government service but remains relevant in industry; (9) the order of punishment. Natural justice principles are: nemo judex in causa sua (no one should be a judge in his own cause) and audi alteram partem (hear the other side). Misconduct is defined in the Model Standing Orders under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. Under Section 11A of the ID Act, 1947 (added in 1971), the Labour Court or Tribunal can set aside a discharge or dismissal and order reinstatement or a lesser punishment. If the enquiry is held defective, the management gets an opportunity to prove misconduct before the Tribunal. Related cases: Workmen of Motipur Sugar Factory v. Motipur Sugar Factory (1965); Khem Chand v. Union of India (1958); Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel (1985, Article 311 exceptions). Other terms are suspension (subsistence allowance), preliminary enquiry, and a fact-finding enquiry. The standard of proof in a domestic enquiry is preponderance of probability, not proof beyond reasonable doubt.

question: In case of disciplinary action, the principles of natural justice have given rise to which one of the following procedural safeguards?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Natural justice rests on two principal rules: nemo judex in causa sua (no one should be a judge in his own cause, so the adjudicator must be unbiased) and audi alteram partem (no one should be condemned unheard). In disciplinary proceedings, audi alteram partem produces concrete procedural safeguards: a written charge-sheet or memorandum of charges with a statement of allegations, a reasonable opportunity to submit a written defence, inspection of documents, an oral enquiry by an impartial enquiry officer, cross-examination of witnesses, a personal hearing, a copy of the enquiry report, and a reasoned order. Article 311(2) of the Constitution protects civil servants from dismissal, removal or reduction in rank without an enquiry in which they are informed of the charges and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Other relevant rules include CCS (CCA) Rules 1965, Rule 14 (major penalty procedure) and Rule 16 (minor penalty). Elimination: punishment without enquiry violates natural justice, so (b) is wrong. Disproportionate punishment is a ground for judicial review under proportionality or Wednesbury unreasonableness, not a safeguard, so (c) is wrong. An FIR is a criminal-law step under Section 154 CrPC, so (d) is wrong.
explanations: Correct. The charge-sheet is the direct outcome of the audi alteram partem rule: it gives the employee notice of the allegations so that he can defend himself.
Wrong. Punishment without enquiry is the very thing natural justice forbids. It is a violation, not a safeguard, and it contravenes Article 311(2) for civil servants.
Wrong. Disproportionate punishment is a defect which courts can correct through judicial review under the doctrine of proportionality. It is not a procedural safeguard.
Wrong. An FIR is the first step in a criminal investigation of a cognizable offence under Section 154 CrPC. It is not a departmental disciplinary safeguard.
keyfact: Audi alteram partem leads to the charge-sheet and a reasonable opportunity of defence, as under Article 311(2).
option_notes: A charge-sheet (memorandum of charges) is a formal written document that states the articles of charge, the statement of imputations, and the lists of documents and witnesses. It is issued under Rule 14 of the CCS (CCA) Rules 1965 for a major penalty. It gives the employee a fair chance to reply, and a defective or vague charge-sheet can vitiate the whole proceeding.

Punishment without enquiry means penalising an employee without hearing him. It is generally illegal for permanent employees under Article 311(2). The only exceptions are the three provisos to Article 311(2): conviction on a criminal charge, impracticability of holding an enquiry, and security of the State. Courts strike down such orders for breach of natural justice.

Disproportionate punishment is a penalty that is shockingly excessive for the misconduct proved. Courts apply proportionality, as in Ranjit Thakur v. Union of India (1987), and the Wednesbury principle. Ordinarily they remand the matter to the disciplinary authority and do not substitute their own punishment, except in rare cases.

A First Information Report is the information about a cognizable offence recorded by the police under Section 154 CrPC (now Section 173 of BNSS 2023). It sets the criminal law in motion. It belongs to criminal procedure and is distinct from departmental charge-sheets, though both proceedings can run in parallel.
related: Audi alteram partem means 'hear the other side'.
Nemo judex in causa sua means no one should be a judge in his own cause (rule against bias).
Article 311 protects civil servants from arbitrary dismissal, removal or reduction in rank.
The 42nd Amendment removed the second show-cause notice on the proposed penalty.
ECIL v. B. Karunakar (1993) requires the enquiry report to be furnished to the delinquent.
Rule 14 of the CCS (CCA) Rules 1965 governs the major penalty procedure.
Maneka Gandhi (1978) brought natural justice within Article 14 and Article 21.
Departmental enquiries are decided on preponderance of probability.
summary: The answer is (a) Charge-sheet. Natural justice (audi alteram partem, 'hear the other side') requires that a delinquent employee be told the specific allegations against him in writing, which is done through a charge-sheet or memorandum of charges. Options (b), (c) and (d) are either violations of natural justice or belong to criminal procedure.
topic_notes: Natural justice is a body of common-law principles of fairness that Indian courts treat as part of Article 14 and Article 21 (Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, 1978). Its three pillars are: (1) the rule against bias (nemo judex in causa sua), (2) the rule of fair hearing (audi alteram partem), and (3) reasoned decisions. In service law, Article 311 gives civil servants protection against dismissal, removal or reduction in rank by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority, and requires an enquiry with a reasonable opportunity of hearing. The Constitution (42nd Amendment) removed the requirement of a second show-cause notice on the proposed penalty. The three exceptions in the second proviso are conviction on a criminal charge, impracticability of an enquiry (the reasons must be recorded in writing), and the interest of State security. Procedure under CCS (CCA) Rules 1965: Rule 11 lists the penalties (minor and major), Rule 14 sets the procedure for a major penalty (charge-sheet, written statement of defence, enquiry officer, presenting officer, report), and Rule 16 covers a minor penalty. Key cases: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel (1985) on the exceptions to Article 311; State of Orissa v. Binapani Dei (1967) on natural justice in administrative action; A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India (1969) on bias and the blurring of the administrative/quasi-judicial distinction; Ridge v. Baldwin (UK). Other points UPSC may ask: suspension is not a punishment, the departmental enquiry standard is preponderance of probabilities and not proof beyond reasonable doubt, the enquiry officer's report must be supplied to the delinquent (ECIL v. B. Karunakar, 1993), and departmental and criminal proceedings can run together.

question: Audi alteram partem’ is associated with:
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Audi alteram partem is a Latin maxim meaning 'let the other side be heard'. It is one of the two pillars of natural justice, the other being nemo judex in causa sua (no one should be a judge in his own cause). In labour law it applies chiefly to disciplinary proceedings and domestic enquiries. The employer must issue a charge-sheet or show-cause notice, give the workman a reasonable opportunity to reply, allow him to produce evidence and cross-examine witnesses, and then pass a reasoned order. Key cases include Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978), which read natural justice into Article 21, and Delhi Transport Corporation v DTC Mazdoor Congress (1991). Under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946, the model standing orders require an inquiry before dismissal. Section 33 of the ID Act and Section 11A (power of the Tribunal to reduce punishment) also bear on this. Elimination: strikes, trade unions and closure are matters of collective action, registration or retrenchment procedure, and are not directly linked to the hearing rule. A violation of the rule can be cured by a fresh inquiry or by leading evidence before the Labour Court.
explanations: Wrong: strikes are governed by Sections 22-24 of the ID Act (notice for public utility services, illegal strikes) and have no direct link to the hearing rule.
Correct: the maxim requires a fair hearing, a charge-sheet and an opportunity to defend before punishment in a domestic enquiry.
Wrong: trade unions are governed by the Trade Unions Act 1926 (registration, immunities), not by this maxim.
Wrong: closure is governed by Sections 25FFA and 25O of the ID Act (notice and permission). It is a procedural matter, not the classic area for this maxim.
keyfact: Audi alteram partem means 'hear the other side', which is the core of fair disciplinary enquiry.
option_notes: Strike: a cessation of work by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in combination, or a concerted refusal to continue work (Section 2(q) of the ID Act). Public utility services require 6 weeks' notice, and a strike is illegal if it breaches Sections 22-23. Wages for the strike period depend on whether it was legal and justified.

Disciplinary action: punishment for misconduct, imposed after a charge-sheet, an enquiry and a finding. The principles of natural justice apply: notice, a fair hearing, an unbiased enquiry officer and a reasoned order. Punishments include warning, suspension, demotion and dismissal. Section 11A allows the Tribunal to interfere with the punishment.

Trade Union: an association of workers or employers formed to regulate relations, registered under the Trade Unions Act 1926. Seven members are needed to apply for registration. A registered union is a body corporate, with immunity from criminal conspiracy and civil suits for trade disputes. The Industrial Relations Code 2020 replaces this Act.

Closure: the permanent shutting down of a place of employment (Section 2(cc) of the ID Act). Under Section 25FFA, 60 days' notice is required. Section 25O requires government permission in establishments with 100 or more workers (the Code raises this to 300). Compensation is payable under Section 25FFF.
related: Nemo judex in causa sua means no one should be a judge in his own cause (rule against bias).
Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978) read natural justice into Article 21.
Article 311 gives civil servants an opportunity to be heard before dismissal.
Section 11A of the ID Act empowers Labour Courts and Tribunals to modify punishment.
Subsistence allowance during suspension is 50% for the first 90 days under the Standing Orders.
Section 33 ID Act requires permission or approval for action during the pendency of proceedings.
A domestic enquiry defect can be cured by leading evidence before the Labour Court.
summary: The answer is (b) Disciplinary action. 'Audi alteram partem' means 'hear the other side', the second rule of natural justice, which requires that a person be given a fair hearing before any adverse action such as a domestic or disciplinary inquiry.
topic_notes: Natural justice has two basic rules. Nemo judex in causa sua means no bias. Audi alteram partem means a fair hearing. Later additions are the duty to give reasons and the rule against arbitrary action. In India, the principles flow from Articles 14 and 21 (Maneka Gandhi, 1978) and Article 311 for civil servants. In industrial law they govern domestic enquiries. The steps are a charge-sheet, a reply, an impartial enquiry officer, evidence and cross-examination, findings, and a show-cause notice on the proposed punishment. Where the enquiry is defective, the employer may lead evidence before the Labour Court (Shankar Chakravarti v Britannia Biscuit, Cooper Engineering). Other angles include the Standing Orders Act 1946 (misconduct and procedure), Section 11A ID Act (Tribunal power over punishment), Section 33 (conditions of service during pendency of proceedings, requiring approval for dismissal), suspension and subsistence allowance (50% for the first 90 days, then 75%), and the ruling that the principles may be excluded only by statute or in emergencies. Related maxims are: res ipsa loquitur, ultra vires, ex parte, and quasi-judicial.

question: Under the provisions of the Trade Union Act 1926, what is the maximum time period for which the members of the executive and other office bearers of a trade union shall be elected?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 6 of the Indian Trade Unions Act 1926 lists the matters that must be provided for in a registered union's rules. Section 6(e) requires the rules to provide for the admission of ordinary members and of honorary or temporary members as office-bearers. It also requires the members of the executive and other office-bearers to be elected. Regulations made under the Act (Central Trade Union Regulations 1938) and the common exam formulation state that the executive and office bearers are elected for a term of not more than one year. In practice, many unions hold annual elections at the general body meeting. The Act's other key provisions include: registration needs at least 7 members (Section 4), and the minimum is also 10% or 100 workmen, whichever is less, after the 2001 Amendment. Section 22 requires that at least half the office-bearers are actually engaged in the industry, and the 2001 Amendment limited outsiders to one-third or five, whichever is less. Section 28 requires an annual return to the Registrar. Section 13 gives registered unions corporate status. Sections 17 and 18 give immunity from criminal conspiracy and civil suits. The options two, three and four years are therefore wrong, because the maximum is one year.
explanations: Correct: office bearers are elected for a period not exceeding one year, per the regulations under the Trade Unions Act 1926 (Section 6(e) requires the rules to provide for election of the executive).
Incorrect: two years is longer than the maximum permitted term.
Incorrect: four years is not any term specified for trade union office bearers.
Incorrect: three years is often confused with other terms, but it is not the maximum for union office bearers.
keyfact: Trade union office bearers are elected for a maximum of one year.
option_notes: One year: the maximum term for elected union executive members and office bearers. Elections are therefore annual, usually at the general body meeting, which keeps the leadership accountable to members. Unions must also submit an annual return to the Registrar under Section 28.
Two years: this is not the term for union office bearers under the Trade Unions Act 1926. A two-year term appears in other bodies, but not in this Act or its regulations.
Four years: this is not a term specified for trade union executives. It is a distractor, and it resembles terms in other institutions rather than the 1926 Act.
Three years: this is not the maximum term for union office bearers. Some other bodies use three-year terms, so it is a common distractor, but it does not apply here.
related: Trade Unions Act 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927.
Minimum 7 members are required to register a trade union.
Section 22: outsiders limited to one-third of office-bearers or five, whichever is less.
Section 13: a registered union is a body corporate.
Section 28: an annual return must be submitted to the Registrar.
Section 17 gives immunity from criminal conspiracy; Section 18 gives immunity from civil suits.
The Industrial Relations Code 2020 subsumes the Trade Unions Act 1926.
Section 16 allows a separate political fund.
summary: The answer is (a) One year. The Trade Unions Act 1926 does not fix an election term for office bearers in its main body. The point comes from Section 6(e), read with the Indian Trade Unions Regulations. The Central Government's regulations require office bearers to be elected for a period not exceeding one year. This is the standard exam answer.
topic_notes: The Trade Unions Act 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927. It provides for the registration of trade unions and defines their legal status. The Act is administered by the appropriate government through the Registrar of Trade Unions. Its key provisions are as follows. Section 2(h) defines a trade union as a combination, temporary or permanent, formed to regulate relations between workmen and employers, between workmen and workmen, or between employers and employers. Section 4 allows any 7 or more members to apply for registration. The 2001 Amendment added a requirement of at least 10% of the workmen or 100 workmen, whichever is less, subject to a minimum of 7. Section 6 lists the matters the rules must cover, including the name, objects, funds, and election of the executive. Section 8 deals with the registration certificate. Section 9 covers cancellation. Section 13 makes a registered union a body corporate with perpetual succession. Section 15 lists the objects on which general funds may be spent. Section 16 allows a separate political fund. Section 17 gives immunity from criminal conspiracy. Section 18 gives immunity from civil suits. Section 22 requires that at least half the office-bearers be persons actually engaged or employed in the industry. The 2001 Amendment capped outsiders at one-third of the total office-bearers or five, whichever is less. Section 28 requires an annual return. The Act has been replaced in substance by the Industrial Relations Code 2020, which has not yet been fully brought into force. Appeals against the Registrar's decisions go to the Labour Court or Industrial Court.

question: Under the provisions of the Trade Union Act 1926, what is the minimum amount of subscription that can be fixed for the members of a trade union of rural workers?
subject: Indian Economy
detail: Section 6 of the Trade Unions Act 1926 lists what the rules of a registered trade union must provide. Clause (c) requires the rules to fix the admission of ordinary members, who must be persons actually engaged or employed in the industry the union represents. Clause (d) deals with the payment of a subscription by members, and it was amended in 2001 to fix minimum subscription rates: Rs 1 per annum for rural workers, Rs 3 per annum for workers in other unorganised sectors, and Rs 12 per annum for all other cases. These figures follow the Trade Unions (Amendment) Act 2001. The minimum for rural workers is therefore Rs 1 a year. Elimination: (b) One rupee per month is wrong because the minimum is annual, not monthly. (a) Three rupees per annum is the figure for the unorganised sector other than rural workers. (d) Six rupees per annum is not a statutory figure. So (c) is correct. Students should remember the three-tier structure of Re 1, Rs 3 and Rs 12 per annum.
explanations: Wrong: Rs 3 per annum is the minimum subscription for workers in the unorganised sector other than rural workers, not for rural workers.
Wrong: the subscription is fixed per annum, not per month, and One rupee per month would be Rs 12 per year, which is the minimum for the general category.
Correct: the Trade Unions (Amendment) Act 2001 provides a minimum subscription of Re 1 per annum for rural workers under Section 6.
Wrong: Rs 6 per annum is not the minimum for any category under the Act.
keyfact: Minimum trade union subscription: Re 1 per annum for rural workers, Rs 3 for other unorganised sector, Rs 12 for others.
option_notes: Rs 3 per annum is the minimum membership subscription for members of unions in the unorganised sector, other than rural workers. The 2001 amendment to Section 6 introduced it so that unions of low-income workers can collect modest dues and still be registered.

Re 1 per month works out to Rs 12 per annum, which matches the minimum subscription for all other trade union members in the organised sector. The Act states the minimum in annual terms, so the monthly form is a distractor.

Re 1 per annum is the minimum subscription for rural workers. The 2001 amendment brought it in to encourage unionisation among agricultural and other rural labourers. It is the lowest of the three rates, and rural workers' unions are exempted from the higher rates.
Rs 6 per annum is not specified in the Act. It is a distractor that sits between the Rs 3 and Rs 12 figures and has no statutory basis.

summary: The answer is (c) One rupee per annum. Section 6(c) of the Trade Unions Act 1926 sets the minimum membership subscription at 25 paise per month for ordinary members and 12 paise per month for workers in the rural areas. Twelve paise per month comes to about Re 1.44 a year. The 1926 Act as amended in 2001 states that the minimum rate is 'one rupee per annum' for rural workers.
topic_notes: The Trade Unions Act 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927 and provides for registration of trade unions and for their rights, liabilities and immunities. It is administered by the Registrar of Trade Unions of each State, and the Central Government appoints the Registrar for unions whose objects extend beyond one State. Any seven or more members can apply to register a union (Section 4). The 2001 amendment requires that at least 10% or 100 workers, whichever is less, subject to a minimum of seven, must be connected with the establishment. It also requires that not less than half of the office bearers be persons actually engaged in the industry, except for outsiders. The limit on outsiders is that no more than one-third of the office-bearers, or five, whichever is less, may be outsiders. Section 6 lists the rules a union must contain, including its name, objects, fund purposes, membership and subscription. Section 15 lists the objects on which general funds may be spent. Section 16 permits a separate political fund, to which contributions are voluntary. Section 17 gives immunity from criminal conspiracy and Section 18 from civil suits, while Section 19 protects the union's agreements. Section 28 requires the annual returns to be sent to the Registrar. The Act's main weakness is that it contains no provision for compulsory recognition of unions; this is left to the Code of Discipline and some State laws. Related items are the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 and the Industrial Relations Code 2020, which will subsume the Trade Unions Act when brought into force.

question: Under the provisions of the Trade Union Act 1926, ordinarily what is the minimum age a person should have attained to become a member of a registered trade union?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 21 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 deals with the rights of minors to membership. It says any person who has attained the age of fifteen years may be a member of a registered trade union, subject to anything contained in the rules of the union. Such a minor may enjoy all the rights of a member and may execute a valid instrument of agreement in respect of the union's membership, but cannot be an office-bearer. Under Section 21A (inserted in 1960), a person must be at least eighteen years old to be a member of the executive or an office-bearer. The 2001 Amendment also requires that not less than one-half of the office-bearers (or a minimum of the executive) be persons actually engaged in the industry, with outsiders limited to a maximum of one-third of total office-bearers or five, whichever is less. Elimination: 14 was the age in the Child Labour norms and Apprentices contexts, not for trade union membership; 16 is not used; 18 applies to office-bearers, not to ordinary membership. Hence 15 years is the answer.
explanations: Incorrect: 14 years is not the age in Section 21; the Act fixes 15 years for membership.
Correct: Section 21 allows a person who has attained 15 years to be a member of a registered trade union, subject to the union's rules.
Incorrect: 16 years has no basis in the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
Incorrect: 18 years is the minimum age for being an office-bearer or executive member under Section 21A, not for ordinary membership.
keyfact: Trade Unions Act 1926, Section 21: membership at 15 years; office-bearer at 18 years (Section 21A).
option_notes: Fourteen years: this is the age below which children cannot be employed in hazardous occupations and was the threshold in the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, and later the 2016 amendment. It is not the minimum age for trade union membership.

Fifteen years: the minimum age for membership of a registered trade union under Section 21 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926, subject to the union's rules. A minor member has full membership rights but cannot hold office. It is also the age in the Factories Act's adolescent definition (15 to 18 years).

Sixteen years: it has no specific role in the Trade Unions Act, 1926. Other contexts include the age at which some statutes treat a person as a young person, but it is not relevant to union membership.

Eighteen years: the minimum age for being an office-bearer or committee member of a registered trade union under Section 21A, inserted in 1960. It is also the age of majority under the Indian Majority Act, 1875.
related: Trade Unions Act came into force on 1 June 1927.
Seven members are the minimum needed to register a trade union.
Section 21A: office-bearers must be at least 18 years old.
Section 16 provides for a separate political fund.
Outsiders in a union's executive are limited to one-third or five, whichever is less (2001 amendment).
Registered union is a body corporate with perpetual succession (Section 13).
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
summary: The answer is (a) Fourteen years. Section 21 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 says a person who has attained the age of 15 years may be a member of a registered trade union, subject to any rules of the union. The option set shows 15 as (b). The correct answer is therefore (b) Fifteen years.
topic_notes: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927 and is the central law on registration and regulation of trade unions in India. It has since been subsumed in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which is not yet fully in force. Key features: any seven or more members can apply for registration (Section 4), and a registered union is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal (Section 13). Registration is done by the Registrar of Trade Unions appointed by the appropriate government. Section 15 lists the objects on which general funds may be spent, and Section 16 allows a separate political fund, with the contribution voluntary and members free to opt out. Sections 17 and 18 give immunity from criminal conspiracy and civil suits for acts done in furtherance of a trade dispute. Section 21 sets the 15-year membership age, and Section 21A sets the 18-year minimum for office-bearers, with disqualifications for persons convicted of offences involving moral turpitude. Amendment of 2001 requires that at least 10% or 100 workmen, whichever is less, are needed to apply for registration, subject to a minimum of seven. It also limits outsiders in the executive to one-third of the total or five, whichever is less. Section 28 requires an annual return. Cancellation of registration is under Section 10. Related laws are the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. The Central Government is the appropriate government for unions whose objects are not confined to one state.

question: Under the provisions of the Trade Union Act 1926, what is the minimum number of members engaged in the establishment as workmen required for registration of a trade union?
options: Ten percent of the total employees
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 4(1) of the Trade Unions Act 1926 says any seven or more members of a trade union may, by subscribing their names to the rules of the union and by otherwise complying with the Act, apply for registration. The 2001 Amendment added a proviso: the registration application is not valid unless at the date of making it the union has as members at least 10% or 100 of the workmen engaged or employed in the establishment or industry, whichever is less. It also provides that the applicant union must have at least seven workmen as members, and that the number of members should not fall below 7 for registration to continue. Section 4(1) proviso also sets that the number should not be less than seven. The 2001 Amendment also required that no less than half of the office-bearers of unions in unorganised sectors be persons actually engaged in the industry. Elimination: (b) 100 and (c) 10% are the upper-cap proviso, not the minimum number of applicants. (d) 21 has no basis in the Act. Hence the minimum number of members needed to apply is seven.
explanations: Correct: Section 4 allows any seven or more members to apply for registration of a trade union.
Wrong: 100 is only the ceiling in the '10% or 100, whichever is less' membership proviso, not the minimum number of applicants.
Wrong: 10% of employees is part of the proviso (inserted in 2001), and it is capped at 100 members. It is not the minimum number asked here.
Wrong: Twenty-one has no basis in the Trade Unions Act 1926.
keyfact: Seven members can apply for registration of a trade union under Section 4 of the Trade Unions Act 1926.
option_notes: Seven: the minimum number of members who must subscribe their names to the rules to apply for registration under Section 4. A registered union must also keep at least seven members, and the Registrar can cancel registration if membership falls below seven (Section 10).

One hundred: the cap in the 2001 proviso to Section 4. A union needs 10% of workmen or 100 workmen, whichever is less, as members at the time of applying. So a large establishment never needs more than 100 members.
Ten percent of total employees: the percentage limb of the 2001 proviso. It applies together with the 100-member cap and is the lesser of the two. It is not a stand-alone requirement.
Twenty-one: a distractor. No provision of the Trade Unions Act 1926 sets 21 as a membership requirement. Do not confuse it with other statutory thresholds in labour law.
related: Trade Unions Act 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927.
Section 4: seven or more members can apply for registration.
Section 13: registered union is a body corporate.
Section 28: annual returns are submitted to the Registrar.
Section 10: cancellation of registration by the Registrar.
The Trade Unions (Amendment) Act 2001 limited outsiders among office-bearers.
The Industrial Relations Code 2020 subsumes the Trade Unions Act 1926.
summary: The answer is (a) Seven. Under Section 4 of the Trade Unions Act 1926, any seven or more members of a trade union may subscribe their names to its rules and apply for registration. The Act also requires at least 10% or 100 of the workmen (whichever is less) to be members, but the figure the question asks for is seven.
topic_notes: The Trade Unions Act 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927 and was the first law on registration of trade unions in India. It was amended in 2001. Section 2(h) defines a trade union as a combination, temporary or permanent, formed mainly to regulate relations between workmen and employers, between workmen and workmen, or between employers and employers. Registration is voluntary. The Registrar of Trade Unions is appointed by the appropriate government. Section 4 covers registration by seven or more members, and the Registrar cancels or withdraws registration under Section 10. Section 6 lists the matters that must be provided in the rules. Section 9A, inserted in 2001, covers the minimum membership requirement. Section 13 makes a registered union a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal. Sections 15 and 16 cover the objects on which the general funds may be spent and the political fund. Sections 17 and 18 give immunity from criminal conspiracy and civil suits for trade disputes. The 2001 amendment also limited the number of outsiders among office-bearers: not more than one-third of office-bearers, or five, whichever is less, may be outsiders. Office-bearers of unorganised-sector unions are the exception, as described above. Unions must submit annual returns (Section 28). The Act is expected to be replaced by the Industrial Relations Code 2020, which sets out its own registration requirements and the recognition of a sole negotiating union.

question: Which one of the following can be considered a precursor of the Trade Union Movement in India?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Early labour organisation in India went through phases. Before 1918 there were welfare and philanthropic associations led by social reformers and the educated middle class, not true unions. Examples are the Sasipada Banerjee's Working Men's Club (1870) and Sorabjee Shapurji Bengalee's efforts (1870s-80s) for factory legislation. The Bombay Millhands' Association (1890), led by Narayan Meghaji Lokhande, was the first organised body of workers. It had no formal membership or funds, but it published the newspaper Dinabandhu and secured a weekly Sunday holiday in 1890. The Factory Commission of 1875 and the Factories Acts of 1881 and 1891 were part of this background. Genuine trade unions began in 1918 with the Madras Labour Union (B. P. Wadia) and the Textile Labour Association, Ahmedabad (1918, Anusuya Sarabhai and Gandhi). The AITUC followed in 1920 and the Trade Unions Act in 1926. Options (a) and (b) are real unions of 1918, not precursors. Option (d), the Kamgar Hitvardhak Sabha (1909), was a later welfare body, so (c) is the best answer.
explanations: (a) Wrong: the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (1918) was a true trade union, based on Gandhian principles of arbitration, so it is not a precursor.
(b) Wrong: the Madras Labour Union (April 1918) is considered the first modern trade union in India, not a precursor.
(c) Correct: the Bombay Millhands' Association (1890) was the earliest organised labour body and the usual precursor of trade unionism.
(d) Wrong: the Kamgar Hitvardhak Sabha (1909) was a smaller, later welfare-type body and is not the standard answer.
keyfact: Bombay Millhands' Association (1890, N. M. Lokhande) is the precursor of Indian trade unionism, while the Madras Labour Union (1918) is the first real trade union.
option_notes: The Textile Labour Association (TLA) of Ahmedabad was formed in 1918 after the textile strike, and Gandhi guided it. Anusuya Sarabhai and Shankarlal Banker were prominent. It followed the principles of trusteeship, arbitration and non-violence. It was organised as a federation of craft unions and later affiliated with INTUC. It was among the largest and most stable unions in India.

The Madras Labour Union was founded in April 1918 by B. P. Wadia with the help of Thiru Vi. Kalyanasundara Mudaliar and others, among the workers of the Buckingham and Carnatic Mills. It is often called the first trade union in India in the modern sense, with regular membership, subscriptions and an organised structure.

The Bombay Millhands' Association was founded in 1890 by Narayan Meghaji Lokhande, a former mill hand and Jyotiba Phule's Satyashodhak associate. It had no formal membership or funds. It published the Dinabandhu newspaper and petitioned for a weekly holiday, which was granted in 1890. It is considered the first labour organisation in India.

The Kamgar Hitvardhak Sabha was formed in Bombay in 1909, a labour welfare association. It sought to improve conditions for workers, but it was weak and not a union with real bargaining power. The period also saw the Social Service League (1911) formed by N. M. Joshi and the Printers' Union of Calcutta (1905).
related: Bombay Millhands' Association (1890) was founded by N. M. Lokhande.
Madras Labour Union (1918) was founded by B. P. Wadia and is often called India's first trade union.
AITUC was formed in 1920 and its first president was Lala Lajpat Rai.
The Trade Unions Act of 1926 provided for registration of unions.
INTUC was formed in 1947 and BMS in 1955.
The Factories Act of 1881 was the first factory legislation in India.
Lokhande's newspaper was Dinabandhu.
summary: The answer is (c) Bombay Millhands' Association, founded in 1890 by N. M. Lokhande. It is widely regarded as the first organised labour body in India and a precursor of the trade union movement, though it was not a trade union in the modern sense. Note that the Kamgar Hitbardhak Sabha (1909) is a rival candidate in some sources, but the standard textbook answer is the Bombay Millhands' Association.
topic_notes: Phases of the labour movement: (1) 1850-1917, philanthropic and welfare activity led by reformers, including Sorabjee Shapurji Bengalee, Sasipada Banerjee (Working Men's Club, 1870, and the paper Bharat Sramajibi), and N. M. Lokhande (Bombay Millhands' Association, 1890). The Amrita Bazar Patrika and Bombay's Dinabandhu supported workers. (2) 1918-1923, rise of real unions, such as the Madras Labour Union (1918), the TLA (1918) and the Bombay Textile Labour Union (1919), under the influence of World War I inflation, the Russian Revolution and the ILO (1919). (3) 1920, AITUC founded in Bombay, with Lala Lajpat Rai as first president and Dewan Chaman Lall as general secretary. (4) Legislation: the Trade Unions Act, 1926 gave legal recognition, registration and immunity, and the Trade Disputes Act, 1929 restricted strikes. (5) Splits and rival bodies: the All India Trade Union Federation (1929, N. M. Joshi), the Red Trade Union Congress (1931), and later INTUC (1947, Congress), HMS (1948, socialists), UTUC (1949) and BMS (1955, Sangh-linked). Early factory laws: the Factories Acts of 1881, 1891, 1911 and 1922, and the Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley, 1929-31). Early strikes: the 1862 Howrah railway strike and the 1882-84 Bombay mill strikes. The 1908 Bombay strike after Tilak's conviction was the first political strike.

question: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of establishment of trade union federations in India starting with the earliest?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Indian trade union federations grew out of political currents. AITUC was founded on 31 October 1920 in Bombay, with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first president and Joseph Baptista as vice-president. INTUC was formed on 3 May 1947 under the Congress, after the communists dominated AITUC. HMS was founded in December 1948 at Howrah by socialists, with Ashok Mehta, R.S. Ruikar and others. BMS was founded on 23 July 1955 in Bhopal by Dattopant Thengdi, linked to the RSS ideology. CITU was founded in May 1970 at Kolkata after the 1964 CPI split, when the CPI(M) leaders left AITUC, with B.T. Ranadive as first president. The elimination logic is simple. AITUC must come first because it is the oldest, which rules out (a) and (d), where INTUC is placed first. Between (b) and (c), HMS (1948) precedes BMS (1955) and CITU (1970), so (c), which puts HMS last, is wrong. That leaves (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it puts INTUC first and AITUC third, but AITUC (1920) is the oldest federation, and CITU (1970) cannot come before BMS (1955).
(b) is correct because it gives the sequence AITUC 1920, INTUC 1947, HMS 1948, BMS 1955, CITU 1970.
(c) is wrong because it places HMS (1948) last, after BMS (1955) and CITU (1970).
(d) is wrong because it places INTUC before AITUC and puts HMS after BMS.
keyfact: Order of founding: AITUC 1920, INTUC 1947, HMS 1948, BMS 1955, CITU 1970.
option_notes: (a) INTUC, HMS, AITUC, CITU, BMS: this is a wrong order. INTUC was founded in 1947 and is the Congress-affiliated federation. It was formed after the communist influence in AITUC grew, and it favours conciliation and arbitration. It is among the largest central trade unions, and its first president was Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's associate, with Gulzarilal Nanda also prominent in the movement.

(b) AITUC, INTUC, HMS, BMS, CITU: this is the correct order. AITUC is the oldest central union, founded in 1920 and now linked to the CPI. INTUC (1947) is Congress-linked, and HMS (1948) is socialist. BMS (1955) is linked to the RSS and has been the largest in membership by verification. CITU (1970) is linked to the CPI(M).

(c) AITUC, INTUC, BMS, CITU, HMS: this is a wrong order. It starts correctly with AITUC and INTUC but misplaces HMS, which was formed in 1948 at Howrah by socialists. HMS is not tied to any single party in the same way as the others, and it was formed after the Praja Socialist and Socialist Party currents broke away.

(d) INTUC, AITUC, BMS, HMS, CITU: this is a wrong order. AITUC came before INTUC, so INTUC cannot be first. BMS was set up on 23 July 1955 in Bhopal by Dattopant Thengdi. Its slogan stresses nationalism and the idea of the nation first, then industry, then labour.
related: First modern trade union in India: Madras Labour Union (1918), B.P. Wadia.

Trade Unions Act 1926 provides registration of unions.
INTUC founded 3 May 1947, Congress-linked.
HMS founded 1948 at Howrah, socialist-linked.
BMS founded 1955, linked to the RSS; Dattopant Thengdi.
CITU founded 1970 at Kolkata, CPI(M)-linked.
Indian Labour Conference first held in 1942.
summary: The correct answer is (b): AITUC (1920), INTUC (1947), HMS (1948), BMS (1955), CITU (1970). The order follows the founding dates of the federations, which are tied to the political currents behind each one.
topic_notes: Trade unionism in India began with early welfare bodies such as the Bombay Mill Hands Association (1890, N.M. Lokhanday). The Madras Labour Union (1918, B.P. Wadia) is generally regarded as the first modern trade union. AITUC was formed in 1920, and Lala Lajpat Rai was its first president. The Trade Unions Act 1926 gave legal recognition and registration to unions. It was later amended, and it is now subsumed under the Industrial Relations Code 2020. Splits followed political lines. In 1929 the moderates left AITUC and formed the Indian Trade Union Federation. The communists later gained influence in AITUC. INTUC was set up in 1947 as the Congress-backed federation, and HMS was founded in 1948. UTUC was founded in 1949 by the left parties. BMS followed in 1955. CITU was formed in 1970 after the CPI split. Later bodies include NFITU, SEWA (a union founded by Ela Bhatt in 1972), and TUCC. Union recognition is determined by membership verification. Central trade unions are consulted by the government, and they take part in the Indian Labour Conference, which was first held in 1942. Related topics are the tripartite structure of the ILO, which India joined in 1919, and the labour codes.

question: Who among the following was the first President of the All India Trade Union Congress?
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: The AITUC was the first national-level central trade union organisation of India. It was founded on 31 October 1920 at Bombay (Empire Theatre). The background was the growth of industrial unrest after World War I, the formation of the ILO in 1919 and the need to nominate Indian workers' delegates to the ILO's International Labour Conference. Lala Lajpat Rai, the Punjab nationalist leader known as 'Punjab Kesari' and 'Sher-e-Punjab', was elected the first President. Joseph Baptista, associated with the Home Rule movement, was a Vice-President. Dewan Chaman Lall was prominent in the early years, and N M Joshi served as General Secretary. Lajpat Rai is credited with linking capitalism with imperialism in his presidential address. Elimination: Gandhi founded the Textile Labour Association (Majur Mahajan Sangh) in Ahmedabad in 1918 and was never AITUC's first president. N M Joshi later split from AITUC and formed the All India Trade Union Federation (1929) and was a Servants of India Society member. Subhas Chandra Bose presided over AITUC in 1931 and 1938 but not as the first president.
explanations: Wrong: Gandhi led the Ahmedabad textile workers' union (TLA, 1918) but did not preside over AITUC's foundation.
Wrong: N M Joshi was a General Secretary of AITUC and later led the moderate split, forming the AITUF in 1929, but he was not its first President.
Wrong: Bose was AITUC President in later years (1931 and 1938), not the first.
Correct: Lala Lajpat Rai presided over the first AITUC session at Bombay on 31 October 1920.
keyfact: AITUC: founded 31 Oct 1920 in Bombay; first President Lala Lajpat Rai.
option_notes: Mahatma Gandhi (1869-1948) led Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad mill workers' struggles in 1917-18. He founded the Textile Labour Association (TLA) in Ahmedabad in 1918, which was based on arbitration and trusteeship. He stressed non-violent, conciliatory labour relations. He was not connected with the founding presidency of AITUC.

N M Joshi (Narayan Malhar Joshi, 1879-1955) was a Servants of India Society member and a moderate trade unionist. He was an AITUC General Secretary and nominated workers' delegate to the ILO. He founded the All India Trade Union Federation in 1929 after the split. He was also a founder of the Social Service League in 1911, and was a nominated member of the Central Legislative Assembly.

Subhas Chandra Bose (1897-1945) was President of AITUC in 1931 and 1938. He was Congress President in 1938 (Haripura) and 1939 (Tripuri), after which he formed the Forward Bloc. He founded the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj) in 1943. He was involved in the Tata Steel labour union in Jamshedpur.

Lala Lajpat Rai (1865-1928) was the 'Lion of Punjab' and one of the Lal-Bal-Pal trio. He was President of AITUC at its first session in 1920 and was a Congress President in the Calcutta special session of 1920. He founded Punjab National Bank in 1894 and was associated with the Arya Samaj and DAV institutions. He died after being injured in the lathi-charge against the Simon Commission protest in Lahore in 1928.

summary: The answer is (d) Lala Lajpat Rai. He presided over the inaugural session of the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) in Bombay on 31 October 1920. Joseph Baptista was elected Vice-President, and Dewan Chaman Lall and N M Joshi were among the early leaders (Joshi was a General Secretary).
topic_notes: AITUC was formed on 31 October 1920 in Bombay. Lala Lajpat Rai was the first President and Dewan Chaman Lall was the General Secretary in the early period. Its formation was prompted by the establishment of the ILO in 1919 and the need for a representative body to select Indian workers' delegates. Early leaders included B P Wadia, who formed the Madras Labour Union in 1918 (often called the first modern trade union in India), and C F Andrews, who was a president in the 1920s. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 gave legal recognition to unions and allowed registration. Splits occurred in 1929 (moderates formed the AITUF under N M Joshi, and the communists later gained dominance) and again in 1931. Post-independence unions include INTUC (1947, Congress), HMS (1948, socialists), UTUC (1949) and later CITU (1970, after the CPI(M) split from AITUC), BMS (1955, RSS-linked), and others. Key labour laws: the Workmen's Compensation Act 1923, the Trade Disputes Act 1929, and the Industrial Disputes Act 1947. The 2020 labour codes consolidated 29 laws into four codes: Code on Wages, Industrial Relations Code, Social Security Code, and OSH Code. Other items to remember: the Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley, 1929-31) and the first factory legislation, the Factories Act of 1881.

question: Which one of the following statements with regard to the Council of Indian Employers (CIE) is NOT true?
options: It was formed in the year 1956
It unified the All India Organisation of Employers (AIOE) and the Employers Federation of India (EFI)
The Standing Conference on Public Enterprises has not joined the CIE
The AIOE and EFI still retain their identity while sending equal number of representatives to the CIE
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Council of Indian Employers (CIE) is the apex, non-statutory joint forum of Indian employers' organisations. It was set up in 1956 by the All India Organisation of Employers (AIOE, founded 1932) and the Employers' Federation of India (EFI, founded 1933), so that India could speak with one voice on labour matters. The CIE nominates the employers' delegation to the International Labour Conference (ILO) and the employers' representatives on tripartite bodies such as the Indian Labour Conference and the Standing Labour Committee. The AIOE and EFI did not merge. Each keeps its own identity and sends an equal number of representatives to the CIE. Later, the Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE), the apex body of public sector employers, also joined, so the CIE now represents both private and public sector employers. Elimination: (a), (b) and (d) match the standard description of the CIE's origin and structure. Statement (c) contradicts the fact that SCOPE is a constituent, so it is the NOT true statement. Note that (b) uses 'unified' loosely, meaning a joint body rather than a merger, and (d) confirms the two bodies were not dissolved.
explanations: (a) is true: the CIE was formed in 1956 as a joint body of the AIOE and EFI, so it cannot be the NOT-true statement.
(b) is true in the loose sense the question intends: the CIE brought the two main employers' bodies, AIOE and EFI, onto one common platform. It is a joint forum, not a merger.
(c) is NOT true: SCOPE, the apex body of public sector enterprises, has joined the CIE. The statement says the opposite, so it is the correct answer.
(d) is true: the AIOE and EFI remain separate organisations and send an equal number of representatives to the CIE.
keyfact: The CIE was formed in 1956 by the AIOE and EFI, which keep their identities, and SCOPE has joined it.
option_notes: Formation year 1956: the CIE was constituted in 1956 as the common national platform of Indian employers. It is non-statutory and has no legal powers of its own. Its main roles are to nominate employers' delegates to the ILO's International Labour Conference and to name employers' representatives to national tripartite forums, which gives employers one voice in labour policy.

AIOE and EFI: the All India Organisation of Employers was founded in 1932 and mainly represents large industrial and trading interests. The Employers' Federation of India was founded in 1933 and is based in Mumbai. Both are voluntary associations of employers. They came together in the CIE for joint representation, but each remains an independent body with its own membership.

SCOPE: the Standing Conference of Public Enterprises is the apex association of central public sector enterprises, formed in 1973 and based in New Delhi. It represents public sector employers on labour and industrial relations matters. It has joined the CIE, so the CIE covers both private and public sector employers. This is why option (c), which says it has not joined, is false.

Equal representation: the AIOE and EFI keep their separate identities and send equal numbers of representatives to the CIE. The CIE is therefore a federation-like joint forum rather than a single merged organisation. This arrangement lets each body preserve its own membership while the CIE speaks for all employers at the national and international level.
related: The CIE was formed in 1956 by the AIOE and the EFI.
SCOPE has joined the CIE.
The AIOE was founded in 1932 and the EFI in 1933.
The CIE nominates the employers' delegation to the International Labour Conference.
The ILO has a tripartite structure of governments, employers and workers, and was founded in 1919.
The Indian Labour Conference is a tripartite consultative body first held in 1942.
The CIE is a non-statutory voluntary body.
summary: The answer is (c). The Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE) has joined the Council of Indian Employers, so saying it has not joined is the false statement. The CIE was formed in 1956 by the AIOE and EFI acting together, and the two bodies keep their separate identities.
topic_notes:
The Council of Indian Employers (CIE) is the apex employers' body for labour and industrial relations matters in India. It was formed in 1956 by the AIOE (1932) and the EFI (1933). It is non-statutory and has no legal authority of its own. Its constituents keep their separate identities and send equal numbers of representatives. SCOPE, the apex body of public sector enterprises, has also joined, so the CIE represents both private and public sector employers.

Functions: the CIE nominates the employers' delegation to the International Labour Conference at the ILO, along with employers' advisers. It also names employers' representatives to the Indian Labour Conference (ILC), the Standing Labour Committee, and other tripartite committees and boards. Employers' views on labour legislation, wages, social security and industrial relations reach the government through the CIE. India is a founder member of the ILO (1919), and the tripartite principle of government, employers and workers is central to ILO structure.

Other employers' bodies worth knowing: FICCI (1927), ASSOCHAM (1920) and CII (1895 origins). The main central trade unions are INTUC, AITUC, HMS, CITU, BMS and UTUC. The Indian Labour Conference was first held in 1942 and is the main tripartite consultative body. Related questions could ask about the ILO (HQ Geneva, 1919, tripartite structure), the composition of the ILC, or the difference between employers' and workers' organisations, as well as which bodies are tripartite. Remember that the CIE, like trade union centres, is a voluntary and non-statutory body.

question: Under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, the average pay for a monthly paid workman means the average of the:
options: wages payable in six completed calendar months preceding the date on which the average pay becomes payable
wages payable in three completed calendar months preceding the date on which the average pay becomes payable
wages payable in four completed calendar months preceding the date on which the average pay becomes payable
wages payable in twelve completed calendar months preceding the date on which the average pay becomes payable
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Section 2(aa) of the ID Act defines 'average pay' by reference to the type of workman, and the rule is used to compute lay-off compensation, retrenchment compensation and closure compensation (Sections 25C, 25F, 25FFF, 25-O). The Act gives three formulae. (i) Monthly paid workman: average of wages payable for the three completed calendar months preceding the date. (ii) Weekly paid workman: average of the wages payable for the preceding four completed weeks. (iii) Daily paid workman: average of the wages payable for the twelve full working days preceding the date, calculated as wages for the days actually worked. Remember the pattern 3 months / 4 weeks / 12 days. Elimination: six months and twelve months do not appear in the definition for monthly workers. Four relates to weeks, not months, and twelve relates to working days for daily-rated workers. Retrenchment compensation under Section 25F(b) is 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service. Lay-off compensation under Section 25C is 50 percent of the total of basic wages and dearness allowance.
explanations: Incorrect: six months is not the period prescribed in the definition of average pay in the ID Act.
Correct: Section 2(aa) specifies the average of wages payable for the three completed calendar months preceding the date for a monthly paid workman.
Incorrect: four is the number of completed weeks for a weekly paid workman, not months for a monthly paid one.
Incorrect: twelve is the number of full working days for a daily paid workman, not twelve months. Some other labour statutes use a twelve-month wage period, which may cause confusion.
keyfact: Average pay: monthly paid = 3 completed calendar months; weekly paid = 4 weeks; daily paid = 12 working days.
option_notes: Six months: not used in the ID Act's average pay definition. Six months does appear in other contexts, for example a 6-month limit in some wage or contribution periods, but it is not relevant to average pay under Section 2(aa).

Three completed calendar months: the correct period for a monthly paid workman under Section 2(aa). The average is taken of wages payable for the three completed calendar months preceding the date on which the average pay becomes payable. It is used to calculate retrenchment, lay-off and closure compensation.
Four: the preceding four completed weeks form the basis for a weekly paid workman. It is not a months-based period. The basis is the average of wages payable for those four weeks.

Twelve: for a daily paid workman, average pay is computed on the wages for the twelve full working days preceding the date. It is not a twelve-month period. Twelve months or a year is relevant elsewhere, for instance in measuring continuous service of 240 days in a year under Section 25B.
related: Average pay for a monthly paid workman: average of wages of three completed calendar months.
Weekly paid workman: average of four completed weeks.
Daily paid workman: wages for twelve full working days.
Section 25F: retrenchment compensation is 15 days' average pay per completed year of service.
Section 25C: lay-off compensation is 50 percent of basic wages plus DA.
Section 25B: continuous service means 240 days in a year.
Chapter VB applies to industrial establishments with 100 or more workmen.
Section 2(s) defines 'workman'; Section 2(j) defines 'industry'.
