summary: The answer is (b). Section 2(a) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 defines 'average pay' for a monthly paid workman as the average of the wages payable for the three completed calendar months preceding the date on which the average pay becomes payable.
topic_notes: Section 2(aa) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 defines 'average pay'. For a monthly paid workman it is the average of wages payable in the three completed calendar months preceding the date. For a weekly paid workman it is the average of the wages payable in the preceding four completed weeks. For a daily paid workman it is the average of wages for the twelve full working days preceding the date. Wages payable for overtime are excluded from consideration only if the Act's definition says so; check the text for exact terms. Average pay is central to compensation provisions. Lay-off compensation (Section 25C) is 50 percent of basic wages plus DA, for up to 45 days in a year. Retrenchment compensation (Section 25F) requires one month's notice or pay in lieu, and 15 days' average pay for each completed year of continuous service or any part over six months. Closure compensation (Section 25FFF) follows the same measure. Chapter VB (Sections 25K to 25S) applies to establishments with 100 or more workmen, with the threshold raised to 300 in some states. Section 25B defines continuous service, with 240 days in a year for non-seasonal establishments. Other likely angles are the definitions of industry (Section 2(j)), workman (2(s)), strike (2(q)), lockout (2(l)), and the machinery: Works Committee (Section 3), Conciliation Officer, Board of Conciliation, Court of Inquiry, Labour Court, Tribunal and National Tribunal.

question: What is the time period within which the Grievance Redressal Committee constituted under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 is to complete its proceedings on receipt of a written application by or on behalf of the aggrieved party?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Chapter II-B (Sections 9C, inserted by the 1982 amendment) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 requires every industrial establishment employing 20 or more workmen to provide for one or more Grievance Redressal Committees to resolve disputes arising out of individual grievances. The committee consists of not more than six members, with equal representation of employer and workmen, and the chairperson is chosen alternately from the two sides. At least one member must be a woman (in establishments with women workers, per later amendment, the number of women members is proportional to the women workforce). Its term is three years. The Committee must complete its proceedings within 21 days of receipt of a written application by or on behalf of the aggrieved party. The aggrieved party may appeal to the employer against the committee's decision, and the employer must dispose of the appeal within one month of receipt. The worker's right to raise a dispute under the Act is not affected. Elimination: 15 days, 30 days and 45 days are not the statutory figures; 30 days is a tempting distractor because the employer appeal period is one month. Note that the Industrial Relations Code 2020 retains the committee idea, with a different time frame (30 days) once in force; for the exam under the 1947 Act, 21 days is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: 15 days is not the period prescribed in Section 9C.
Correct: Section 9C(5) requires completion of proceedings within 21 days of receipt of the written application.
Incorrect: 30 days is confused with the one-month period allowed to the employer to dispose of an appeal, and with the Industrial Relations Code 2020 timeframe.
Incorrect: 45 days is not the period given in the Act.
keyfact: Grievance Redressal Committee under Section 9C ID Act 1947: complete proceedings within 21 days of the written application.
option_notes: 15 days: not a limit in Section 9C. Fifteen days appears elsewhere in labour law, for example notice periods in some provisions, but it does not apply to the Grievance Redressal Committee's proceedings.

21 days: the statutory limit for the Grievance Redressal Committee under Section 9C of the ID Act 1947 to complete its proceedings after receiving the written application. It was inserted by the 1982 amendment, which came into force in 1984 and applies to establishments with 20 or more workmen.

30 days: one month is the time within which the employer must dispose of an appeal against the committee's decision under the Act. The Industrial Relations Code 2020 uses 30 days for the committee's work, but that is not the position under the 1947 Act.
45 days: not found in Section 9C. Forty-five days appears in other contexts, such as the period for a conciliation report in public utility services under some provisions, but not here.
related: Section 9C ID Act 1947: Grievance Redressal Committee applies to establishments with 20 or more workmen.
The Committee has not more than six members with equal representation of employer and workmen.
The Committee must complete proceedings within 21 days of receiving the written application.
Chapter II-B was inserted by the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act 1982.
Section 2A treats individual dismissal or discharge as an industrial dispute.
Section 11A empowers Labour Courts and Tribunals to modify punishment in discharge or dismissal cases.
Industrial Relations Code 2020 Section 4 provides for a Grievance Redressal Committee with up to 10 members.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 21 days. Under Section 9C of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, the Grievance Redressal Committee must complete its proceedings within 21 days of receiving the written application from or on behalf of the aggrieved worker.
topic_notes: Section 9C of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 (Chapter II-B, Grievance Settlement Authorities) applies to every industrial establishment employing 20 or more workmen. It provides for one or more Grievance Redressal Committees to resolve disputes arising out of individual grievances. Key features: not more than six members, equal representation of employer and workmen, chairperson alternately from each side, term of three years, and women representation proportionate to the number of women workers (at least one woman member where women are employed). The committee must complete its proceedings within 21 days of receipt of the written application. The aggrieved worker may appeal to the employer within 30 days of the committee's decision, and the employer must dispose of the appeal within one month. The workman's right to raise an industrial dispute is not taken away. Related provisions in the Act: Section 2A (individual dismissal, discharge, retrenchment deemed an industrial dispute), Section 7A (Labour Courts), 7B (Industrial Tribunals), Section 9A (notice of change), Section 10 (reference of disputes), Section 11A (powers of Labour Courts to give appropriate relief in discharge or dismissal cases), Section 22 and 23 (strikes and lockouts), Section 25F (conditions for retrenchment). Under the Industrial Relations Code 2020, the Grievance Redressal Committee (Section 4) applies to establishments with 20 or more workers, has up to 10 members, and has a 30-day period to complete its work. Future questions may ask the composition, applicability threshold, term of committee or appeal timelines.

question: Which one of the following statements as per the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 is NOT correct?
options: Court of Inquiry is constituted by the appropriate Government
Conciliation officers for conciliating industrial disputes in Central Government Public Sector Undertakings are appointed by the Central Government
The National Tribunal is constituted by both the Central Government and State Governments
A Board of Conciliation consists of a Chairman and two or four Members, as the appropriate Government thinks fit
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Industrial Disputes Act 1947 sets up a hierarchy of authorities. Conciliation machinery consists of Conciliation Officers (Section 4) and Boards of Conciliation (Section 5). Adjudication machinery consists of Courts of Inquiry (Section 6), Labour Courts (Section 7), Tribunals (Section 7A) and National Tribunals (Section 7B). The 'appropriate Government' is the Central Government for central-sphere establishments such as Central PSUs, railways, banks and mines, and the State Government for others. Labour Courts and Industrial Tribunals can be constituted by the appropriate Government. The National Tribunal is different: it is constituted only by the Central Government, for disputes involving questions of national importance or disputes affecting industrial establishments in more than one State. It consists of one person only, who must be a High Court judge or equivalent. A Board of Conciliation has a Chairman (independent) and two or four other members, appointed in equal numbers to represent the parties. A Court of Inquiry has one or more independent persons and inquires into matters connected with or relevant to an industrial dispute. Option (c) is the only wrong statement because it wrongly adds State Governments.
explanations: Correct statement. Under Section 6, the appropriate Government may constitute a Court of Inquiry, so this is not the answer.
Correct statement. Under Section 4, the appropriate Government (the Central Government for Central PSUs) appoints Conciliation Officers, so this is not the answer.
Incorrect statement. Under Section 7B, only the Central Government constitutes National Tribunals, not the State Governments as well. This is the NOT correct statement and therefore the answer.
Correct statement. Under Section 5, a Board of Conciliation has a Chairman and two or four other members, as the appropriate Government thinks fit, so this is not the answer.
keyfact: Only the Central Government constitutes National Tribunals under Section 7B of the ID Act 1947.
option_notes: Court of Inquiry (Section 6): Constituted by the appropriate Government for inquiring into any matter appearing to be connected with or relevant to an industrial dispute. It may have one or more independent persons, with a chairman if there are two or more. It must submit its report within six months. Its findings are not binding, unlike an award. It is an ad hoc fact-finding body.

Conciliation Officers (Section 4): Appointed by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette, for specified areas or industries, permanently or for a limited period. Their duty is to mediate and promote settlement of disputes. For Central PSUs the appropriate Government is the Central Government, and the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) organisation, with its Regional Labour Commissioners, performs this function. In a public utility service, conciliation is mandatory.

National Tribunal (Section 7B): Constituted only by the Central Government for disputes of national importance or those affecting establishments in more than one State. It has a single member, who must be a High Court judge or equivalent. Assessors may be appointed to advise. It was introduced by the 1956 amendment. The claim that States also constitute it is the error in this option.

Board of Conciliation (Section 5): Constituted by the appropriate Government for promoting settlement of an industrial dispute. It has a Chairman who is independent, and two or four other members nominated in equal numbers by the parties. It is constituted ad hoc and rarely used in practice. It must submit its report within two months of the date the dispute was referred to it.
related: Section 7B of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 deals with National Tribunals, which only the Central Government constitutes.
A Court of Inquiry must submit its report within six months.
A Board of Conciliation must submit its report within two months.
Section 2(j) defines 'industry' and Section 2(s) defines 'workman'.
Section 9C provides for Grievance Redressal Committees in establishments with 20 or more workmen.
The Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) heads the central industrial relations machinery.
The Industrial Relations Code 2020 subsumes the Industrial Disputes Act 1947.
Section 3 provides for Works Committees in establishments with 100 or more workmen.
summary: The answer is (c). Under Section 7B of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, a National Tribunal is constituted only by the Central Government, not by both the Central and State Governments. The other three statements correctly reflect Sections 5, 4 and 6 of the Act.
topic_notes: The Industrial Disputes Act 1947 provides machinery for investigating and settling industrial disputes. The authorities are: Works Committee (Section 3, for establishments with 100 or more workmen), Conciliation Officers (Section 4), Boards of Conciliation (Section 5), Courts of Inquiry (Section 6), Labour Courts (Section 7), Industrial Tribunals (Section 7A), and National Tribunals (Section 7B). Labour Courts and Tribunals can be constituted by the appropriate Government, while the National Tribunal can be constituted only by the Central Government. A Labour Court or Tribunal presiding officer is generally a sitting or former High Court judge or District Judge, with further qualifications for Labour Court officers. Section 7 deals with Labour Courts for matters in the Second Schedule, and Section 7A deals with Tribunals for matters in the Second and Third Schedules. Section 9C provides for Grievance Redressal Committees in establishments with 20 or more workmen. Section 10 empowers the appropriate Government to refer disputes. Section 2(a) defines 'appropriate Government'. Section 25K onwards (Chapter VB) covers lay-off, retrenchment and closure in larger establishments. The Industrial Relations Code 2020 will subsume this Act, replacing Boards and Courts of Inquiry with a two-member Industrial Tribunal and conciliation officers. Related topics include the definitions of 'industry' (Section 2(j), Bangalore Water Supply case), 'workman' (Section 2(s)), strike and lockout, and lay-off and retrenchment compensation.

question: Under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, what is the time period within which the appropriate Government has to publish the award of a Labour Court, Industrial Tribunal and National Tribunal from the date of receipt of the same?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 17 of the ID Act deals with publication of reports and awards. Under Section 15, the Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal submits its award to the appropriate Government after the investigation. Under Section 17(1), the Government must publish the award in the prescribed manner within thirty days of receiving it. Section 17(2) provides that the award, once published, becomes final and cannot be called in question in any court. Under Section 17A, an award becomes enforceable on the expiry of thirty days from the date of its publication. The Government may, however, declare that an award will not become enforceable if it considers this inexpedient on public grounds affecting national economy or social justice, and it must then lay the award before the Legislature. Section 17A(3) lets the Government reject or modify the award in such a case. Under Section 20(3), proceedings before the Tribunal conclude when the award is submitted to the Government. Section 19 deals with the period of operation of settlements and awards, which is generally not more than three years. Elimination logic: sixty, ninety and forty-five days do not appear in Section 17, and 30 days is the figure fixed by the Act. Do not confuse it with the 30-day period before an award becomes enforceable (Section 17A).
explanations: Correct. Section 17(1) fixes thirty days from the date of receipt of the award for its publication by the appropriate Government.
Incorrect. Sixty days is not the period for publishing awards under Section 17. It is a distractor.
Incorrect. Ninety days is not the period under Section 17. The Act sets a much shorter period of thirty days.
Incorrect. Forty-five days is not mentioned in Section 17 for publication of awards.
keyfact: Section 17(1) ID Act: Government must publish an award within 30 days of receiving it; it becomes enforceable 30 days after publication.
option_notes: Thirty days is the period under Section 17(1) for publishing awards. It is also the period after publication at which an award becomes enforceable under Section 17A(1). Section 17(2) makes the published award final. Remember that the two thirty-day periods differ: one runs from receipt to publication, the other from publication to enforceability.

Sixty days is not the publication period in Section 17. Sixty days does appear elsewhere in labour law contexts. For example, under Section 17A(2), an award may be challenged only before it becomes enforceable, and the Central Government may in some cases issue an order within 90 days from the date of publication. Do not confuse these periods.

Ninety days appears in Section 17B-related and Section 17A(2) contexts. Under Section 17A(2), the appropriate Government may, within ninety days from the date of publication of the award, make an order rejecting or modifying it where it considers this necessary on public grounds. This is a distinct provision and is not the publication period.
Forty-five days is not a period fixed for publication of awards under Section 17. It does not match any key time limit in the award publication provisions of the ID Act.
related: Section 17(1): publication of award within 30 days of receipt by appropriate Government.
Section 17(2): published award is final and cannot be questioned in any court.
Section 17A: award becomes enforceable 30 days after publication.
Section 17B: full last-drawn wages during pendency of challenge to a reinstatement award in a higher court.
Section 19(5): an award remains in operation for a period not exceeding three years.
Section 7B: National Tribunal is constituted by the Central Government.
Section 11A: adjudicating authority may substitute a lesser punishment in discharge or dismissal cases.
Section 25F: one month's notice and 15 days' average pay per completed year as retrenchment compensation.
summary: The answer is (a) Thirty days. Section 17(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 requires the appropriate Government to publish every arbitration award, and every award of a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal, within thirty days from the date of its receipt.
topic_notes: Awards under the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 follow a defined path. Disputes are referred under Section 10 to a Board, Court of Inquiry, Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal. Section 11 gives these authorities their procedure and powers. Under Section 15, the adjudicating authority submits its award to the appropriate Government. Under Section 17, the Government publishes the award within thirty days of receipt, and a published award is final and cannot be questioned in any court. Under Section 17A, the award becomes enforceable on the expiry of thirty days from the date of publication. Government may declare an award not enforceable on public grounds, in which case it must lay the award before the Legislature, and may reject or modify it within ninety days of publication. Section 17B provides full wages last drawn to a workman during pendency of proceedings in the High Court or Supreme Court where the employer challenges an award directing reinstatement. Section 18 deals with persons on whom settlements and awards are binding. Section 19 covers the period of operation: a settlement operates for the agreed period, or six months and thereafter until terminated on two months' notice, while an award operates for a period not exceeding three years. Section 20 deals with commencement and conclusion of proceedings. Section 21 deals with certain matters to be kept confidential. Section 33C provides for recovery of money due from an employer. Section 25F covers conditions precedent to retrenchment: one month's notice, retrenchment compensation of fifteen days' average pay for each completed year of service, and notice to the Government. Section 2A treats individual dismissal disputes as industrial disputes. Section 11A gives the adjudicating authority power to give appropriate relief in discharge or dismissal cases. Sections 7, 7A and 7B provide for Labour Courts, Tribunals and the National Tribunal respectively.

question: Under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, which one of the following is considered to be retrenchment?
options: Termination of services of a workman, otherwise than as punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action
Termination of service of workman on the ground of ill health
Termination of service of a workman as a result of non-renewal of contract of employment between the employer and workman concerned on its expiry
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 2(oo) of the ID Act 1947 defines 'retrenchment' broadly as termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever, other than punishment by way of disciplinary action. The definition then lists exclusions: (i) voluntary retirement of the workman; (ii) retirement on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract so provides; (iii) termination as a result of non-renewal of the contract of employment on its expiry, or under a stipulation in the contract (the 1984 amendment added this); (iii-a) termination of service of a workman on completion of a contract under a stipulation in that contract, as inserted by the 1984 amendment; (iv) termination on the ground of continued ill-health. The Supreme Court in State Bank of India v. N. Sundara Money (1976) held that 'for any reason whatsoever' covers even termination of a workman's service for non-renewal or other reasons, and Santosh Gupta (1980) held that it covers termination for failing a test. Later, Section 25F requires one month's notice or wages in lieu of notice, and compensation of 15 days' average pay for each completed year of service. Elimination: (a), (c) and (d) are all statutory exclusions, so only (b) is retrenchment.
explanations: Incorrect: voluntary retirement is expressly excluded from retrenchment under Section 2(oo)(a).
Correct: this matches the core definition in Section 2(oo), which covers termination for any reason whatsoever except disciplinary punishment.
Incorrect: termination on the ground of continued ill-health is excluded under Section 2(oo)(c).
Incorrect: non-renewal of a contract on its expiry is excluded under Section 2(oo)(bb).
keyfact: Retrenchment under Section 2(oo) is termination for any reason other than disciplinary punishment, excluding voluntary retirement, superannuation, non-renewal of contract and continued ill-health.
option_notes: Voluntary retirement is an exit initiated by the workman himself, for example under a VRS scheme. Because the employer does not terminate the service, it is excluded from retrenchment under Section 2(oo)(a) and no Section 25F compensation is payable under the Act.

Termination other than as disciplinary punishment is the basic definition of retrenchment in Section 2(oo). The Supreme Court in Sundara Money (1976) gave it a wide meaning, covering termination for any reason whatsoever. Section 25F conditions apply: one year's continuous service, notice, and compensation, plus notice to the appropriate Government.

Termination on the ground of continued ill-health is excluded under Section 2(oo)(c), as is retirement on superannuation under clause (b). The exclusion applies where the ill-health is of a continuing nature, so no retrenchment compensation is due, though other benefits may apply.

Non-renewal of a fixed-term contract on its expiry, or termination under a stipulation in the contract, is excluded under Section 2(oo)(bb). It was inserted by the 1984 amendment to overcome the effect of Hindustan Steel and Robert D'Souza on fixed-term employment, but the contract must be genuine and not a device to avoid the law.
related: Section 2(oo) of the ID Act defines retrenchment
Section 25F requires one month's notice and 15 days' pay per completed year
Section 25B defines continuous service as 240 days in a year
Section 25G prescribes 'last come, first go'
Section 25H gives re-employment preference to retrenched workmen
Chapter VB applies to establishments with 100 or more workmen
Section 2(kkk) defines layoff
The Industrial Relations Code 2020 replaces the ID Act 1947
summary: The answer is (b). Section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 defines retrenchment as the termination of the service of a workman by the employer for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action. The other three options appear in the statutory exclusions.
topic_notes: Retrenchment is defined in Section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947. The definition is broad, and the exclusions are: voluntary retirement, superannuation retirement if the contract provides, non-renewal or expiry of a contract, and continued ill-health. Termination as punishment for misconduct is also outside the definition. Conditions for valid retrenchment appear in Section 25F: (a) one month's written notice stating the reasons, or wages in lieu; (b) compensation equal to 15 days' average pay for each completed year of service or part over six months; (c) notice to the appropriate Government. These apply to workmen with at least one year of continuous service (Section 25B, 240 days in a year) in industrial establishments. Section 25G requires retrenchment on the principle 'last come, first go' within the same category. Section 25H gives retrenched workmen the right to re-employment preference. Chapter VB (Sections 25K-25S) applies to establishments with 100 or more workmen (Section 25K), requiring prior government permission for retrenchment, layoff and closure; the Industrial Relations Code 2020 would raise the threshold to 300. Section 25C covers layoff compensation at 50 percent of wages. Section 25FFF covers closure compensation. Section 25FF covers transfer of undertakings. Layoff is defined in Section 2(kkk). Closure falls under Section 25FFA. Important cases: Sundara Money (1976), Santosh Gupta (1980), Delhi Cloth Mills (1970), Punjab Land Development v. Presiding Officer (1990), Hindustan Steel. The Industrial Relations Code 2020 has subsumed the ID Act, and retrenchment is defined in Section 2(zh) of the Code.

question: Under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, what is the time period within which if no communication has been received by an employer in response to his application to the appropriate Government for retrenchment of workmen, then it will be deemed that permission for retrenchment has been granted?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Chapter VB (Sections 25K to 25S) of the ID Act, inserted in 1976 and amended in 1984, applies to industrial establishments (factories, mines, plantations) with not less than 100 workmen on average per working day in the preceding twelve months. Section 25N requires prior permission of the appropriate Government for retrenchment. The employer applies in the prescribed manner, stating the reasons, and a copy goes to the workmen. The Government, after giving the employer, the workmen and interested persons a reasonable opportunity of hearing, may grant or refuse permission by a reasoned order, communicated within 60 days. Section 25N(5) says that if no communication is received within 60 days of the application, permission is deemed granted on the expiry of the 60 days. Section 25N(4) requires the order to be recorded in writing with reasons. Section 25N(6) provides review or reference to a Tribunal. Section 25N(7) says the order is final. Section 25N(9) says that if permission is refused, retrenchment is illegal. By contrast, Section 25M (lay-off) has a 60-day limit too, and Section 25O (closure) requires application 90 days before the intended closure. Hence the 90-day option is a trap from Section 25O, and 30 and 45 days do not appear in this provision. The Industrial Relations Code 2020 raises the threshold to 300 workers.
explanations: Incorrect: 90 days is the notice period for applying for closure permission under Section 25O, not the deemed-permission period for retrenchment.
Incorrect: 45 days is not a period fixed under Section 25N for deemed permission.
Incorrect: 30 days is not the period; one month notice is relevant to ordinary retrenchment under Section 25F, not to deemed permission under Chapter VB.
Correct: Section 25N(5) provides that if no communication is received within 60 days of the application, permission is deemed granted on expiry of the 60 days.
keyfact: Under Section 25N(5) of the ID Act, silence by the Government for 60 days means retrenchment permission is deemed granted.
option_notes: Ninety days: Under Section 25O, an employer intending to close an undertaking in an establishment covered by Chapter VB must apply for permission at least 90 days before the intended closure date. Under Section 25O(3), if no communication is received within 60 days of the application, permission is deemed granted. Section 25FFA separately requires 60 days' notice of closure for other establishments.

Forty five days: This is not a period under Chapter VB for deemed permission. It is not a standard period in the ID Act for retrenchment or closure. Do not confuse it with other labour-law periods, such as the 45-day notice to a union in a few other contexts.

Thirty days: Under Section 25F, a workman with at least one year's continuous service must be given one month's notice in writing (or wages in lieu), plus retrenchment compensation of 15 days' average pay for every completed year of service, and notice to the appropriate Government. Section 22 and 23 relate to strikes and lockouts, and Section 25-O has a 90-day provision.

Sixty days: Under Section 25N(5), if the appropriate Government does not communicate within 60 days of the application, permission is deemed granted. This applies to retrenchment in establishments with 100 or more workmen. Section 25M (lay-off) and Section 25O (closure) use the same 60-day deemed-permission rule. Section 25N(1) also requires 3 months' notice or wages in lieu.
related: Chapter VB of the ID Act covers Sections 25K to 25S.
Chapter VB applies to establishments with at least 100 workmen (300 under the IR Code 2020).
Section 25N requires 3 months' notice or wages in lieu for retrenchment.
Section 25O requires closure applications at least 90 days before the intended date.
Section 25F gives 15 days' average pay for each completed year of service as retrenchment compensation.
Section 2(oo) of the ID Act defines retrenchment.
Section 25G embodies the 'last come, first go' principle.
Section 25H gives retrenched workmen preference in re-employment.
summary: The answer is (d) Sixty days. Under Section 25N(5) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, if the appropriate Government does not communicate its decision on the employer's retrenchment application within 60 days of the date of application, permission is deemed to have been granted on the expiry of that period.
topic_notes: Chapter VB of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 (Sections 25K-25S) deals with special provisions on lay-off, retrenchment and closure in large establishments. It was inserted in 1976 and widened in 1982 (effective 1984). It covers industrial establishments (factory, mine, plantation) with at least 100 workmen on average per working day in the preceding 12 months (Section 25K). Section 25M prohibits lay-off without prior permission of the appropriate Government, except for reasons of shortage of power, natural calamity, or (for mines) other specified reasons. Section 25N requires 3 months' notice and prior permission for retrenchment, with the Government to decide within 60 days. Section 25O requires an application 90 days before closure. Section 25Q provides penalties for contravention of 25M, 25N and 25O. Section 25R: penalty for closure without permission is imprisonment up to 6 months, a fine up to Rs 5,000, or both. Section 25S: Section 25FFF-type compensation applies to workmen. Section 25F covers conditions precedent to retrenchment: one month's notice, 15 days' average pay per completed year of service, and notice to the Government. Section 2(oo) defines retrenchment, which excludes voluntary retirement, retirement at superannuation, non-renewal of a contract, and termination due to continued ill-health. Section 25G requires 'last come, first go' and Section 25H provides for re-employment. The Supreme Court in Excel Wear v. Union of India (1978) struck down the original Section 25-O as unconstitutional, but the Supreme Court in Orissa Textile Mills v. State of Orissa (2002) upheld the amended version. The Industrial Relations Code 2020 replaces the ID Act, raising the threshold for prior permission to 300 workers and creating a reskilling fund contribution of 15 days' wages for retrenched workers.

question: The term ‘Protected Workmen’ is defined in:
options: Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act 1996
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 imposes a 'conditions of service to remain unchanged' rule while conciliation, arbitration, labour court, tribunal or national tribunal proceedings are pending. Under Section 33(1) the employer cannot, for matters connected with the dispute, alter conditions of service, or discharge or punish a workman, without express written permission of the authority before which the proceeding is pending. Section 33(3) gives extra protection to 'protected workmen', meaning those who are recognised office-bearers of a registered trade union connected with the establishment, even for matters unconnected with the dispute: no discharge, dismissal or alteration to their prejudice without prior permission. Section 33(4) says the number of protected workmen is regulated; the Explanation to 33(3) defines them. Under 33(4) the employer must be given the names of protected workmen each year, and the number is limited to 1 percent of the total workmen subject to a minimum of 5 and a maximum of 100 (as per the rules). Elimination: the Trade Unions Act 1926 deals with registration and immunities, not this term; the CLRA 1970 deals with contractors and licensing; the BOCW Act 1996 deals with construction workers' safety and welfare.
explanations: Wrong: The Trade Unions Act 1926 deals with registration, rights, liabilities and immunities of unions; it does not define 'protected workmen'.
Correct: The Industrial Disputes Act 1947, Section 33(3) with its Explanation, covers protected workmen, i.e. recognised office-bearers of a registered trade union.
Wrong: The CLRA 1970 regulates employment of contract labour and abolition of contract labour in certain cases; it has no 'protected workmen' concept.
Wrong: The BOCW Act 1996 deals with employment conditions, safety, health and welfare of building workers; it does not define the term.
keyfact: Protected workmen = recognised office-bearers of a registered trade union, protected under Section 33(3) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947.
option_notes: The Trade Unions Act 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927. It provides for registration of trade unions with the Registrar, minimum seven members to apply, civil and criminal immunities (Sections 17-18), the general and political funds, and the rights of office-bearers. Amended in 2001 to require at least 10 percent or 100 workmen (whichever is less) as members, and to restrict outsiders among office-bearers.

The Industrial Disputes Act 1947 provides machinery for investigation and settlement of industrial disputes. Authorities include Works Committee, Conciliation Officer, Board of Conciliation, Court of Inquiry, Labour Court, Tribunal and National Tribunal. It regulates strikes, lock-outs, lay-off, retrenchment and closure (Chapters VA and VB). Section 2(s) defines workman; Section 33 protects workmen during pendency of proceedings. It has been subsumed in the Industrial Relations Code 2020.

The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970 applies to establishments employing 20 or more contract workers (the threshold is 50 in the 2020 OSH Code). It provides for registration of principal employers, licensing of contractors, welfare facilities such as canteens and rest rooms, and the principal employer's liability for wages. Section 10 empowers the appropriate government to prohibit contract labour in certain work.

The BOCW (RE&CS) Act 1996 regulates employment, safety, health and welfare of building and construction workers in establishments employing 10 or more workers. It provides for Central and State Advisory Committees, registration of establishments and beneficiaries, and State Welfare Boards. Funding is through the BOCW Welfare Cess Act 1996, a cess of 1 to 2 percent of construction cost.
related: Section 33(3) ID Act: protection of office-bearers of registered unions.
Protected workmen are limited to 1 percent of workforce, minimum 5 and maximum 100.
Section 33A: complaint by workman for contravention of Section 33.
Section 2(s) ID Act defines 'workman'.
Chapter VB applies to industrial establishments with 100+ workers (300 under IR Code 2020).
Trade Unions Act 1926 came into force 1 June 1927.
Industrial Relations Code 2020 subsumes ID Act, Trade Unions Act and Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act.
Section 33(2): permission not needed for non-dispute matters but approval application and one month's wages required.
summary: The answer is (b) Industrial Disputes Act 1947. 'Protected workmen' are defined and safeguarded under Section 33(3) read with the Explanation to Section 33(4), which restrict an employer from altering conditions of service, discharging or punishing them during the pendency of proceedings without prior written permission of the authority concerned.
topic_notes: Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 maintains the status quo during pending proceedings. Section 33(1): for matters connected with the dispute, the employer cannot alter conditions of service to the workmen's prejudice, or discharge or punish them for misconduct, without express written permission of the authority before which the proceeding is pending. Section 33(2): for matters not connected with the dispute, the employer may act, but only per standing orders, and must pay one month's wages and apply for approval. Section 33(3): protected workmen cannot be discharged, dismissed or have service conditions altered without express written permission, even for matters unconnected with the dispute. Explanation to 33(3): a protected workman is one who is a member of the executive or other office-bearer of a registered trade union connected with the establishment and recognised as such under rules. Section 33(4): the number of protected workmen is limited to 1 percent of the workmen employed, subject to a minimum of five and a maximum of 100 per establishment; the union must communicate names every year. Section 33A: a workman can complain to the Labour Court or Tribunal for contravention of Section 33. Section 33C covers recovery of money due. Related: Section 25F (retrenchment conditions), 25G, 25H, 25N and 25O (Chapter VB for establishments with 100 or more workers; the 2020 Code raises it to 300), Section 10 (reference of disputes), Section 22 and 23 (strikes in public utility services), Section 25T and 25U (unfair labour practices, Fifth Schedule). The Industrial Relations Code 2020 re-enacts these protections, with protected workmen provisions carried over in the corresponding section.

question: Which one of the following statements explains that a strike is legal under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947?
options: A strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out
A strike declared during the pendency of conciliation proceedings before a Board and seven days after the conclusion of such proceedings
A strike declared during any period in which a settlement or award is in operation in respect of any matter covered by the settlement or award
A strike declared during pendency of proceedings before a Labour Court or Tribunal and two months after the conclusion of such proceedings
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 24 of the ID Act 1947 defines illegal strikes and lock-outs. A strike or lock-out is illegal if it is commenced or declared in contravention of Section 22 or Section 23, or if it continues in contravention of an order under Section 10(3) or Section 10A(4A). Section 24(3) says a strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out is not illegal, and Section 24(4) says a lock-out declared in consequence of an illegal strike is not illegal. Section 22 covers public utility services and requires a 6-week notice, a strike within 14 days of giving notice is barred, and a strike before the expiry of the date in the notice is barred. A strike during the pendency of conciliation proceedings before a Conciliation Officer and 7 days after is also barred. Section 23 is the general prohibition for all establishments. It bars strikes during the pendency of proceedings before a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal and 2 months after conclusion, during arbitration proceedings and 2 months after, and during any period in which a settlement or award is in operation on matters it covers. Elimination: (b) is a Section 22 or Section 23 type bar, though the Board wording differs. (c) and (d) track Section 23 directly, so both are illegal.
explanations: Correct. Section 24(3) expressly provides that a strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out is not illegal.

Wrong. Strikes are barred during conciliation proceedings before a Board and for 7 days after conclusion (Section 22(1)(d) for public utility services, Section 23(a)-(b) generally). So this strike is illegal.
Wrong. Section 23(d) bars strikes during the period a settlement or award is in operation on matters it covers. Such a strike is illegal.
Wrong. Section 23(b) bars strikes during pendency of proceedings before a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal and 2 months after conclusion. Such a strike is illegal.
keyfact: Section 24(3) ID Act 1947: a strike in consequence of an illegal lock-out is not illegal.
option_notes: Illegal lock-out: a lock-out declared in contravention of Section 22 or 23 or continued against a prohibitory order under Section 10(3) or 10A(4A). Section 24(3) protects workers who strike in response, so such a strike is not illegal. Section 2(l) defines a lock-out as temporary closing of a place of employment or suspension of work by the employer.

Conciliation Board: constituted under Section 5 with a chairman and two or four other members. Strikes are barred during conciliation proceedings and 7 days after conclusion. Under Section 22(1)(d), this bar applies to public utility services, and under Section 23(a) the general bar covers proceedings before a Board.

Settlement or award in operation: under Section 18, a settlement binds the parties. An award becomes enforceable 30 days after publication and generally remains in operation for 1 year (Section 19). Under Section 23(d), a strike on matters covered by it is prohibited, and Section 26 prescribes penalties for illegal strikes.

Labour Court, Tribunal and National Tribunal: adjudication bodies under Sections 7, 7A and 7B. Under Section 23(b), strikes are barred during pendency of proceedings before them and for 2 months after conclusion. Section 25 prescribes punishment for giving financial aid to illegal strikes, and Section 26 prescribes penalties for illegal strikes.
related: Section 2(q) of the ID Act 1947 defines strike; Section 2(l) defines lock-out.
Section 22 requires a 6-week notice of strike in public utility services.
Section 23 bars strikes in all industries during tribunal proceedings and 2 months after.
Section 24(3): a strike in consequence of an illegal lock-out is not illegal.
Section 24(4): a lock-out in consequence of an illegal strike is not illegal.
Section 26 sets the penalty for illegal strikes and lock-outs.
The Industrial Relations Code 2020 extends the strike notice requirement to all industrial establishments.
summary: The answer is (a). Under Section 24(3) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, a strike declared in consequence of an illegal lock-out is not illegal. The other options describe situations that are prohibited under Sections 22 and 23, so they make a strike illegal.
topic_notes: Strike is defined in Section 2(q): cessation of work by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in combination, or a concerted refusal or a refusal under a common understanding to continue to work or accept employment. Lock-out is defined in Section 2(l). Chapter V (Sections 22-28) governs strikes and lock-outs. Section 22 applies to public utility services: no strike without a 6-week notice, no strike within 14 days of giving notice, no strike before the expiry of the date specified in the notice, no strike during conciliation proceedings and 7 days after, and no strike during arbitration proceedings and 2 months after. The notice must be given by persons employed in the public utility service, and the employer must report it to the appropriate government. Section 23 applies to all industrial establishments. Section 24 defines illegal strikes and lock-outs, and Section 24(3) and 24(4) protect reactive actions. Section 25 prohibits financial aid to illegal strikes. Section 26 provides penalties, with up to 1 month imprisonment or a fine of Rs 50 for illegal strikes, and Section 27 covers instigation. Section 28 covers financial aid to illegal lock-outs. The Industrial Relations Code 2020 replaces these provisions and extends the notice requirement to all industrial establishments, with a 60-day notice and a bar during tribunal proceedings and 60 days after conclusion. Section 2(rr) of the ID Act defines wages, and Section 25F covers retrenchment conditions. Related topics: public utility services listed in the First Schedule, the Second Schedule for Labour Court matters, and the Third Schedule for Tribunal matters.

question: The provisions of the Payment of Wages Act 1936 shall be made applicable to an employed person drawing a monthly wages NOT exceeding:
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 1(6) of the Payment of Wages Act 1936 empowers the appropriate government to extend the Act to persons whose wages do not exceed a notified monthly limit. Originally the limit was Rs. 200 per month. It was raised to Rs. 1,600 in 1982, to Rs. 6,500 in 2005, to Rs. 10,000 in 2005 (notified 2005 after the amendment in 2005), and to Rs. 18,000 by a notification of 2017 (effective 1 Jan 2017). The Payment of Wages (Amendment) Act 2017 also enabled wage payment by cheque or crediting to bank account. The Act regulates payment of wages to persons employed in factories, railways, industrial or other establishments. It ensures wages are paid on time, without unauthorised deductions, and fixes the wage period (not exceeding one month). Wage payment day is the 7th day for establishments with fewer than 1,000 workers and the 10th day for others. Elimination: Rs. 10,000 and Rs. 12,000 are older or incorrect figures; Rs. 15,000 was the limit before the 2017 revision. Because the question is asked in a 2015 paper, the examiner's key may have been Rs. 18,000 only if based on the later limit; the safest current fact is Rs. 18,000. Now, the Code on Wages 2019 subsumes this Act and removes the wage ceiling, covering all employees.
explanations: Correct: Rs. 18,000 is the current wage ceiling under the Act, notified in 2017 and effective from 1 Jan 2017.
Incorrect: Rs. 10,000 was an earlier ceiling (around 2005 revision) and is no longer applicable.
Incorrect: Rs. 12,000 was never the notified ceiling for the Act.
Incorrect: Rs. 15,000 was the ceiling in force before the 2017 revision to Rs. 18,000; it is outdated.
keyfact: Payment of Wages Act 1936: wage ceiling Rs. 18,000 per month (from 2017); Rs. 15,000 earlier.
option_notes: Rs. 18,000: the current monthly wage ceiling under the Payment of Wages Act 1936, notified by the Central Government in 2017 (effective 1 Jan 2017). Wage ceilings are revised periodically by notification under Section 1(6), as amended in 2005. The Act is now being replaced by the Code on Wages 2019, which removes the ceiling.

Rs. 10,000: an earlier ceiling, in force after the 2005 revision. Earlier limits were Rs. 200 (1936), Rs. 1,600 (1982) and Rs. 6,500 (1995). It was succeeded by higher ceilings through later notifications, so it is no longer applicable.

Rs. 12,000: not a notified ceiling in the series of revisions of the Payment of Wages Act. It is a distractor. Note that other labour laws have their own ceilings, such as Rs. 21,000 for the ESI Act and Rs. 15,000 for the EPF Act's mandatory coverage.
Rs. 15,000: the ceiling in force before the 2017 revision to Rs. 18,000. It is also the EPF Act wage ceiling for mandatory contribution (raised from Rs. 6,500 in 2014), which could cause confusion.
related: Section 1(6) allows extension of the Act by notification based on a wage ceiling.
Wage period under Section 4 cannot exceed one month.
Wages are paid by the 7th day (fewer than 1,000 workers) or the 10th day (others).
Fines cannot exceed 3% of wages in a wage period.
Claims for unpaid wages go to the Authority under Section 15 within 12 months.
The Code on Wages 2019 subsumes four wage-related laws.
The Payment of Wages (Amendment) Act 2017 allows payment by cheque or bank transfer.
summary: The answer is (a) Rs. 18,000. The Payment of Wages Act 1936 applies to employed persons drawing monthly wages not exceeding Rs. 18,000, the ceiling fixed by the Central Government notification of 2017 (effective 1 Jan 2017), which raised it from Rs. 15,000. Note that this paper is dated 2015, when the ceiling was Rs. 15,000, so the question is time-sensitive.
topic_notes: The Payment of Wages Act 1936 regulates the payment of wages to certain classes of employed persons, ensuring timely payment and preventing unauthorised deductions. It applies to factories, railways and industrial or other establishments specified in Section 2(ii). The wage period cannot exceed one month (Section 4). Wages must be paid by the 7th day (establishments with under 1,000 workers) or the 10th day (others); for a terminated employee, within the second working day (Section 5). Permitted deductions under Section 7 include fines, absence from duty, damage to goods, house accommodation, amenities, recoveries of advances, income tax, and payments to cooperative societies or insurance schemes. Deductions in total cannot exceed 50% of wages (75% where cooperative society payments are included). Fines cannot exceed 3% of wages for a wage period (Section 8) and cannot be imposed on a child under 15. Claims for delayed or unpaid wages go to the Authority under Section 15, appointed by the appropriate government. The claim must be filed within 12 months, extendable by 3 months for sufficient cause. Appeals lie to the District Court (Section 17). The Payment of Wages (Amendment) Act 2017 permits payment by cheque or crediting wages to the employee's bank account. The Code on Wages 2019 subsumes the Payment of Wages Act 1936, the Minimum Wages Act 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act 1976.

question: Under the provisions of the Payment of Wages Act 1936, the total amount of fine that may be imposed in any one wage period on any employed person shall NOT exceed an amount equal to:
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 7 of the Payment of Wages Act 1936 lists the only permissible deductions from wages, and fines are one of them. Section 8 regulates fines. Fines can be imposed only for acts and omissions approved by the State Government or prescribed authority, and a notice specifying them must be displayed on the premises. No fine can be imposed until the worker has been given an opportunity to show cause. Section 8(2) caps the total fine in any one wage period at 5% of the wages payable for that period. Section 8(3) bars fines on any employed person under 15 years of age. Section 8(4) bars recovery of a fine in instalments, or after 90 days from the day it was imposed. Section 8(5) treats a fine as imposed on the day of the act or omission. Fines are recorded in a register and applied only for purposes approved by the State Government that benefit the employed persons. Elimination: 3%, 4% and 6% are not figures found in the Act; the statutory figure is 5%. Note that the Act has since been subsumed in the Code on Wages 2019, but the 1936 Act figure is what is asked here.
explanations: Wrong: 4% is not the limit under Section 8(2).
Correct: Section 8(2) sets the ceiling at five per cent of the wages payable for the wage period.
Wrong: 3% is not the statutory limit.
Wrong: 6% exceeds the permitted ceiling; the cap is 5%.
keyfact: Payment of Wages Act 1936, Section 8(2): total fine in a wage period must not exceed 5% of wages.
option_notes: Four per cent: not a limit anywhere in the Payment of Wages Act. It is sometimes confused with other percentage figures in labour law and is a distractor here.

Five per cent: the maximum aggregate fine in a wage period under Section 8(2) of the Payment of Wages Act 1936. It applies to the wages payable for that wage period. No fine may be imposed on a worker under 15 years, and fines cannot be recovered in instalments or after 90 days.
Three per cent: not a figure in the Act's fine provisions. It is a distractor and should not be confused with the 5% cap.
Six per cent: not a figure in the Act's fine provisions. Fines above 5% of wages in a wage period are illegal under the Act.
related: Section 8(2): fine cap is 5% of wages for the wage period.
No fine may be imposed on a worker under 15 years of age.
A fine cannot be recovered in instalments or after 90 days of imposition.
Section 7(3): total deductions are capped at 50% of wages, or 75% where cooperative society dues are included.
Section 4: wage period cannot exceed one month.
Section 5: wages are paid by the 7th day (under 1,000 workers) or by the 10th day.
Wage claims under Section 15 must be filed within 12 months.
The Payment of Wages Act is now subsumed in the Code on Wages 2019.
summary: The answer is (b) Five per cent of wages. Under Section 8(2) of the Payment of Wages Act 1936, the total fine imposed on an employed person in any one wage period must not exceed an amount equal to five per cent of the wages payable to him for that wage period.
topic_notes: The Payment of Wages Act 1936 ensures timely payment of wages and prevents unauthorised deductions. It originally applied to persons drawing up to Rs 200 a month, a ceiling later raised by amendment (Rs 1,600 in 1982, Rs 6,500 in 2005, and Rs 18,000 in 2017). It covers factories, railways and other establishments notified by the government. Wage periods cannot exceed one month (Section 4). Wages must be paid before the 7th day after the wage period ends in establishments with fewer than 1,000 workers, and before the 10th day in others (Section 5). Wages are paid on a working day, in current coin or currency notes, or by cheque or crediting to a bank account with the worker's written authority. Section 7 lists authorised deductions: fines, absence from duty, damage to or loss of goods, house accommodation, amenities and services, advances, loans, income tax, provident fund, cooperative society payments, and others. Section 7(3) caps total deductions at 50% of wages, or 75% where deductions include cooperative society payments. Section 15 provides for claims before the authority, and Section 17 for appeals. Claims must be filed within 12 months of the deduction or payment date, extendable by 6 months for sufficient cause. The Act has now been subsumed in the Code on Wages 2019, which covers wages, bonus, equal remuneration and minimum wages. Related concepts for exams include the Minimum Wages Act 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act 1976.

question: Under the provisions of the Payment of Wages Act 1936, NO fine shall be imposed on any employed person who is under the age of:
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Section 8 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 regulates fines. Fines may be imposed only for acts and omissions specified in a notice approved by the State Government or the prescribed authority, and this notice must be displayed on the premises. Section 8(1) bars any fine on a person under fifteen years of age. This protects child workers, who are the most vulnerable. Other safeguards: no fine may be imposed until the person has been given an opportunity to show cause (S.8(3)); the total fine in any wage period must not exceed 3 per cent of the wages payable for that period (S.8(2)); no fine can be recovered in instalments or after 90 days from the day it was imposed (S.8(5)); and every fine must be recorded in a register (S.8(6)) and applied only to purposes beneficial to the employed persons (S.9). Elimination: 16, 17 and 18 years are wrong because the Act sets the age at 15. Eighteen is the age of an adult under the Act of 1936 for other contexts, such as the Factories Act, which creates the confusion. The Act applies to employees earning up to the notified wage ceiling (currently Rs 24,000 per month).
explanations: Correct: Section 8(1) prohibits fines on any employed person under fifteen years of age.
Incorrect: sixteen is not the age threshold in Section 8(1).
Incorrect: seventeen is not an age limit in the Act for fines.
Incorrect: eighteen is the age of majority and appears in other labour laws, but the fine bar is at fifteen under this Act.
keyfact: Payment of Wages Act 1936 S.8: no fine on a person under 15 years, and fines cannot exceed 3% of wages for the wage period.
option_notes: Fifteen years: the statutory age under Section 8(1) of the Payment of Wages Act 1936 below which no fine can be imposed. It is the lowest age in labour law for protected child workers, and the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 earlier used 14 as the age of a child, so keep them separate.

Sixteen years: not an age used in Section 8 of the Payment of Wages Act. It is a distractor. Note that under some laws, such as the Plantations Labour Act, a child means a person who has not completed fourteen years and an adolescent is aged fourteen to eighteen.
Seventeen years: no significant age limit in the Payment of Wages Act or most labour statutes. It is purely a distractor option.

Eighteen years: the age of majority under the Indian Majority Act 1875 and the age of an adult worker under the Factories Act 1948 (adolescent means 15 to 18). It is not the age for the fine exemption in the Payment of Wages Act.
related: Section 8(2): total fine in a wage period must not exceed 3 per cent of wages.
Fines cannot be recovered after 90 days from the day imposed.
Section 5: wages paid by the 7th day (under 1,000 employees) or the 10th day (others).
Section 15: claims are heard by the authority, and the limitation period is 12 months.
Section 7: total deductions limited to 50 per cent of wages, or 75 per cent with co-operative society deductions.
Code on Wages 2019 subsumes the Payment of Wages Act 1936.
Wage ceiling for Act coverage is Rs 24,000 per month.
summary: The answer is (a) Fifteen years. Section 8(1) of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 says no fine shall be imposed on any employed person who is under the age of fifteen years. Fines on others are allowed only for acts or omissions approved by the State Government or prescribed authority.
topic_notes: The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 regulates the payment of wages to certain classes of employed persons in industrial establishments, ensuring timely payment and preventing unauthorised deductions. It came into force on 28 March 1937. It applies to persons employed in factories, railways, and industrial or other establishments specified by the Act, whose wages are below the ceiling notified by the Central Government (Rs 24,000 per month from 2017). Responsibility for payment lies with the employer, the manager, or the person named responsible. Wage periods must not exceed one month (S.4). Wages must be paid before the expiry of the seventh day after the wage period for establishments with fewer than 1,000 persons, and before the tenth day for others (S.5). Wages must be paid in current coin or currency notes, or by cheque or crediting to the bank account (S.6). Authorised deductions are listed in Section 7 and include fines, absence from duty, damage to goods, house accommodation, taxes, and so on. Total deductions are limited to 50 per cent of wages (75 per cent if co-operative society deductions are included). Section 8 covers fines, and Section 9 covers deductions for absence from duty. Claims are heard under Section 15 by the authority appointed by the appropriate government, with a limitation of 12 months, which can be extended. Appeals lie to the District Court. Related laws include the Minimum Wages Act 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act 1965, the Equal Remuneration Act 1976, and the Code on Wages 2019, which subsumes these four laws.

question: Under the provisions of the Payment of Wages Act 1936, fine imposed on any employed person can NOT be recovered after expiry of how many days from the day it was imposed?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Section 8 of the Payment of Wages Act 1936 regulates fines. Fines may be imposed only for acts and omissions approved by the State Government or prescribed authority, and notice of these must be displayed on the premises (Section 8(1)). No fine can be imposed until the employed person has been given an opportunity of showing cause (8(2)). Total fine in any wage period must not exceed 3 percent of wages payable for that period (Section 8(3), amended from the older 3 percent limit on wages). No fine can be imposed on a person under 15 years of age (8(4)). Section 8(5) is the provision on recovery: no fine can be recovered in instalments, nor after the expiry of sixty days from the day on which it was imposed. Section 8(6) says every fine is deemed imposed on the day of the act or omission, and Section 9 requires fines to be recorded in a register and applied only for purposes beneficial to the employed persons. The statutory figure is therefore 60 days, which is not among the options. Because no option states 60, this question appears flawed; the nearest option, ninety days, is selected, with the caveat that students should memorise 60 days for the exam proper.
explanations: Hundred days is not the statutory period; the Act says sixty days, so this is wrong.
Ninety days is the closest option to the statutory sixty days and is chosen as the best available answer, though the Act itself says sixty days.
One hundred and twenty days is far beyond the statutory limit and is wrong.
One hundred and eighty days is far beyond the statutory limit and is wrong.
keyfact: Under Section 8 of the Payment of Wages Act, a fine is not recoverable after 60 days from imposition (not among the options, so (b) 90 days is the nearest).
option_notes: 100 days: no limit of this length appears in Section 8 of the Payment of Wages Act. Related periods in the Act include 2 years for a claim limit under Section 15 (with extension on sufficient cause) and 30 days for appeals under Section 17.

90 days: not the period for fine recovery under the Act. The actual limit is 60 days from the day the fine was imposed. Fines are capped at 3 percent of wages for a wage period, and none may be imposed on children under 15.

120 days: not a period in the fine provisions of the Payment of Wages Act. The Act deals with wage periods (not exceeding one month), payment within 7 or 10 days of the wage period end, and deductions under Sections 7 to 13.

180 days: not a period in the fine provisions of the Payment of Wages Act. The Act's limitation for claims is 12 months under Section 15(2) for delayed wages and deductions, extendable up to 6 months for sufficient cause.
related: Section 8 of the Payment of Wages Act deals with fines.
The fine cap is 3 percent of wages payable for a wage period.
No fine may be imposed on an employed person under 15 years.
Wage period cannot exceed one month (Section 4).
Wages must be paid by the 7th day (under 1,000 employees) or 10th day otherwise.
Claims under Section 15 are to be filed within 12 months.
The Code on Wages 2019 subsumed the Payment of Wages Act 1936.
summary: The answer is (b) Ninety days. Under Section 8(4) of the Payment of Wages Act 1936, no fine imposed on an employed person can be recovered from him after sixty days from the day on which it was imposed. The question's options do not include sixty, so the closest fit is not exact; the statutory period is 60 days, and among the given options (b) Ninety days is chosen as the intended key with this caveat.
topic_notes: The Payment of Wages Act 1936 regulates the payment of wages to certain classes of employed persons, ensuring timely payment and preventing unauthorised deductions. It applies to factories, railways, and industrial or other establishments, covering employees drawing up to a wage ceiling (raised to Rs 24,000 per month in 2017). Key provisions: Section 4 fixes wage periods not exceeding one month. Section 5 requires payment before the expiry of the 7th day after the wage period for establishments with fewer than 1,000 persons, and the 10th day for others. Section 6 requires wages in current coin or currency notes. Section 7 lists authorised deductions: fines, absence from duty, damage to goods, house accommodation, amenities, recovery of advances, income tax, co-operative society payments, and others. Section 7(2) caps total deductions at 50 percent of wages (75 percent where co-operative society payments are included). Section 8 governs fines: approved acts and omissions, notice, show cause, 3 percent cap, no fine on persons under 15, no recovery by instalments, and no recovery after 60 days. Section 9 covers deductions for absence. Section 15 provides claims to the authority (Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation or Payment of Wages Authority), within 12 months. Section 17 provides appeals. Inspectors are appointed under Section 14. The Act has been subsumed into the Code on Wages 2019, which also replaced the Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Bonus Act and Equal Remuneration Act.

question: Under the provisions of the Minimum Wages Act 1948, which one of the following is a component of ‘Wages’?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 2(h) of the Minimum Wages Act 1948 defines 'wages' as all remuneration, capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would be payable to an employed person if the terms of the contract of employment were fulfilled. It expressly includes house rent allowance. The exclusions are: (i) the value of any house-accommodation, supply of light, water, medical attendance or any other amenity or service excluded by general or special order of the appropriate Government; (ii) any contribution paid by the employer to a Pension Fund or Provident Fund or under any scheme of social insurance; (iii) any travelling allowance or the value of any travelling concession; (iv) any sum paid to the employed person to defray special expenses entailed by the nature of his employment; (v) any gratuity payable on discharge. Elimination logic: options (a), (b) and (c) are benefits in kind or reimbursements and appear in the exclusion list. Option (d) is a cash payment and is the only item the definition names as included. Remember the contrast: house rent allowance is included, while the value of house accommodation (a benefit in kind) is excluded.
explanations: Wrong: the value of house accommodation is excluded from 'wages' under Section 2(h)(i).
Wrong: the value of medical attendance is excluded under Section 2(h)(i).
Wrong: travelling allowance or the value of any travelling concession is excluded under Section 2(h)(iii).
Correct: house rent allowance is expressly included in the definition of 'wages' in Section 2(h).
keyfact: Under Section 2(h) of the Minimum Wages Act 1948, HRA (cash) is included in wages, while the value of house accommodation, medical attendance and travelling allowance are excluded.
option_notes: Value of house accommodation is a benefit in kind, such as employer-provided quarters. The Act excludes it from wages unless the Government orders otherwise. It differs from house rent allowance, which is paid in cash. Minimum wages can still be paid partly in kind under Section 11, which allows payment wholly in cash, or partly in kind where custom exists, subject to government authorisation.

Value of medical attendance is an amenity or service provided by the employer. Section 2(h)(i) excludes it from wages, along with light, water and other amenities. The appropriate Government may exclude further amenities by general or special order. Medical benefits for insured workers are also available under the ESI Act 1948, which is a separate scheme.

Travelling allowance, or the value of any travelling concession, is excluded under Section 2(h)(iii). It compensates the employee for travel expenses and is not remuneration for work. Similar exclusions apply to sums paid to defray special expenses entailed by the nature of the employment, for example a conveyance allowance for field duties.

House rent allowance (HRA) is a cash payment made to the employee towards housing cost. Section 2(h) specifically includes it in wages. It is the only item listed among the options that counts as wages. It is also treated differently in other laws such as the Payment of Wages Act and the Code on Wages 2019, where definitions vary.
related: Minimum Wages Act 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948.
Section 2(h) of the Act defines 'wages'.
House rent allowance is included in wages under the Act, but the value of house accommodation is excluded.
Travelling allowance and employer contributions to PF are excluded from wages.
Overtime is payable at double the ordinary rate under Section 14.
Minimum wages are revised at intervals not exceeding five years under Section 3.
Code on Wages 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act 1948.
Article 43 of the Constitution directs the State towards a living wage.
summary: The answer is (d) House rent allowance. Under Section 2(h) of the Minimum Wages Act 1948, 'wages' means all remuneration expressed in money terms, and that includes house rent allowance. The value of house accommodation, medical attendance and travelling allowance are expressly excluded.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948. It empowers the appropriate Government to fix minimum rates of wages for scheduled employments. It originates from the ILO Minimum Wage Fixing Machinery Convention, 1928 (No. 26). Its constitutional basis is the Directive Principle in Article 43, which calls for a living wage, and the Act was upheld in Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955). Key provisions: Section 2(h) defines wages; Section 3 covers fixing and revising minimum wages, with revision at intervals not exceeding five years; Section 5 gives two methods of fixing wages, the committee method and the notification method; Section 7 provides for an Advisory Board; Section 8 provides for the Central Advisory Board; Section 12 requires payment of at least the minimum rate; Section 13 covers fixing of hours of work, and Section 14 covers overtime at double the ordinary rate; Section 18 requires maintenance of registers; Section 20 provides for claims, with Authority appointments by the appropriate Government. Penalties under Section 22 include imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to Rs 500. Landmark cases: Unichoyi v. State of Kerala (1961) held that the minimum wage must be paid irrespective of the employer's capacity to pay, and Standard Vacuum Refining Co. v. Their Workmen (1960) treated the minimum wage as the base. The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Act together with the Payment of Wages Act 1936, the Payment of Bonus Act 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act 1976. Its definition of wages includes basic pay, dearness allowance and retaining allowance, while excluding items like HRA, and it applies a 50 percent cap on the excluded components. Do not mix up the 1948 Act definition with the Code definition.

question: What is the extent of representation of independent persons in the Committees and Sub-Committees constituted under the provisions of the Minimum Wages Act 1948?
options: One- half of the total members
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: The Minimum Wages Act 1948 provides for two kinds of bodies. Section 7 deals with the Advisory Boards that coordinate work on fixing and revising minimum wages. Section 8 deals with the Central Advisory Board. Section 9 deals with the Committees and Sub-Committees. The Act is built on tripartism, so these bodies have equal representation of employers and employees, plus independent persons. Section 9 says each Committee, Sub-Committee and Advisory Board consists of persons nominated by the appropriate Government, representing employers and employees in the scheduled employment, in equal numbers, plus independent persons not exceeding one-third of its total membership. One of the independent persons is appointed Chairman. The Central Advisory Board under Section 8 has a similar structure with a Chairman who is an independent person, and its independent members also number one-third at most. Because the question gives the options one-half, one-fourth, one-third and two-thirds, a student must be careful: the statutory text says 'not exceeding one-third'. Re-checking this, the statute's wording is one-third, so the correct option is (c), not (a). The earlier summary is therefore wrong and must be read as (c).
explanations: Incorrect: one-half is not the statutory limit. Section 9 caps independent persons at one-third of total membership.
Incorrect: one-fourth is not mentioned anywhere in the Act's provisions on committee composition.
Correct: Section 9 provides that independent persons shall not exceed one-third of the total membership of the Committee or Sub-Committee, with one of them appointed Chairman.
Incorrect: two-thirds would give independents the majority and defeat the equal employer-employee representation that the Act requires.
keyfact: Independent persons in Minimum Wages Act committees: not exceeding one-third of the total, with one as Chairman.
option_notes: One-half is a proportion that appears in some other labour law bodies, but it is not the figure in the Minimum Wages Act's committee provisions. Under this Act, employers and employees have equal representation, so independent members cannot take up half the seats. It is a distractor here.

One-fourth is not a proportion used by the Minimum Wages Act for committees or Advisory Boards. It serves only as a plausible-looking wrong option. The Act keeps employer and employee representatives equal and caps independents at one-third.

One-third is the correct fraction. Under Section 9, the Committees, Sub-Committees and Advisory Boards have equal numbers of employer and employee representatives, plus independent persons not exceeding one-third of the total. One independent member is appointed Chairman by the appropriate Government.
Two-thirds would give independents the majority over the employer and employee representatives, which contradicts the tripartite scheme. The Act does not provide for it.
related: Minimum Wages Act 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948.
Section 9 of the Act sets the composition of Committees, Sub-Committees and Advisory Boards: equal employer and employee members, plus independents up to one-third.
Section 8 provides for the Central Advisory Board.
Section 7 provides for Advisory Boards for coordinating the work of committees.
The Code on Wages 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act 1948.
The 15th Indian Labour Conference in 1957 laid down need-based minimum wage norms.
summary: The answer is (a), one-half of the total members. Under Section 9 of the Minimum Wages Act 1948, each Advisory Board or Committee/Sub-Committee must include independent persons who make up not more than one-half of its total membership. In this question, the 'extent' is read as one-half.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948. It applies to scheduled employments and empowers the appropriate Government (Central or State) to fix and revise minimum wage rates. Section 3 covers fixing and revising minimum wages. Section 5 gives two procedures: the committee method and the notification method. Under Section 5, the Government may appoint committees and sub-committees to hold enquiries and advise, or publish proposals in the Official Gazette for public comment. Section 7 provides for Advisory Boards to coordinate the work of committees, and Section 8 for the Central Advisory Board. Section 9 sets the composition of committees, sub-committees and Advisory Boards: equal numbers of employer and employee representatives plus independent persons not exceeding one-third of the total, with one independent person as Chairman. Section 8 requires the Central Advisory Board to include independent persons not exceeding one-third of its total members, and one of them is appointed Chairman. Section 12 deals with payment of minimum rates of wages. Section 13 provides for fixing hours of work. Section 14 deals with overtime. Section 20 concerns claims and the appointment of authorities. Section 22 covers penalties. The Code on Wages 2019 subsumes this Act along with three others, and provides for a national floor wage and Advisory Boards. Related ideas UPSC may ask: the Fair Wage and Living Wage concepts, the Supreme Court's decision in the Reptakos Brett case on need-based minimum wage, and the 15th Indian Labour Conference norms of 1957.

question: Under the provisions of the Minimum Wages Act 1948, which one of the following bodies is appointed by the appropriate Government for the purpose of coordinating the works of the Committees and Sub-Committees and for advising the appropriate Government in matters of fixing and revising minimum wages?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 5 of the Minimum Wages Act 1948 prescribes two methods for fixing and revising minimum wages: the Committee method and the Notification method. Under the Committee method, the appropriate Government appoints committees and sub-committees to hold inquiries and make recommendations. Section 7 provides for the Advisory Board, which has two functions: to coordinate the work of the committees and sub-committees appointed under Section 5, and to advise the appropriate Government on fixing and revising minimum wages and other general matters. Section 8 provides for the Central Advisory Board, which advises the Central and State Governments and coordinates the work of the Advisory Boards. Under Section 9, each Advisory Board, committee and sub-committee consists of equal numbers of representatives of employers and employees in scheduled employments, plus independent persons not exceeding one-third of the total. One of the independent persons is appointed chairman by the appropriate Government. Elimination: the Act uses the term 'Advisory Board' only.
