'State Advisory Council', 'State Monitoring Authority' and 'State Advisory and Monitoring Board' are not bodies created by this Act, so (a), (c) and (d) are wrong.
explanations: Incorrect: the Act has no body called 'State Advisory Council'. The statutory term is Advisory Board.
Correct: Section 7 provides for the Advisory Board, which coordinates the work of committees and sub-committees and advises the appropriate Government on minimum wage fixation and revision.
Incorrect: no 'State Monitoring Authority' exists under the Minimum Wages Act. Enforcement is handled by Inspectors and the authorities appointed under Section 20.
Incorrect: this is not a body named in the Act. It combines invented terms and is only a distractor.
keyfact: Section 7 of the Minimum Wages Act 1948 provides for the Advisory Board, which coordinates committees and sub-committees and advises the Government on minimum wages.
option_notes: State Advisory Council: not a body under the Minimum Wages Act 1948. The term appears in other contexts, such as advisory councils on social or welfare matters, but it is not the statutory body for minimum wage fixation. The Act's own bodies are the Committees and Sub-Committees (Section 5), the Advisory Board (Section 7) and the Central Advisory Board (Section 8).

Advisory Board: set up under Section 7 of the Minimum Wages Act 1948 by the appropriate Government. It coordinates the work of the committees and sub-committees and advises the Government on fixing and revising minimum wages. Under Section 9 it has equal numbers of employer and employee representatives plus independent members, who may not exceed one-third of the total. One independent member is appointed chairman. The Central Advisory Board under Section 8 operates at the national level.

State Monitoring Authority: not a statutory body under the Minimum Wages Act 1948. Compliance is monitored by Inspectors (Section 19) and claims are decided by the authority appointed under Section 20. Monitoring-type bodies appear in other laws and schemes, but this term is not used in this Act.

State Advisory and Monitoring Board: a fictitious or composite name that does not appear in the Act. The only advisory bodies in the Act are the Advisory Board at State level (Section 7) and the Central Advisory Board (Section 8). Questions often use plausible but non-existent names as distractors.
related: Minimum Wages Act 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948.
Section 7: Advisory Board; Section 8: Central Advisory Board.
Section 9: independent persons on the Boards must not exceed one-third of the total members.
Section 5: Committee method and Notification method of fixing wages.
Section 3: minimum wages must be revised at intervals not exceeding five years.
Section 20: authority to hear claims for minimum wages.
The Code on Wages 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act 1948.
The 15th Indian Labour Conference (1957) laid down norms for a need-based minimum wage.
summary: The correct answer is (b) Advisory Board. Under Section 7 of the Minimum Wages Act 1948, the appropriate Government appoints an Advisory Board to coordinate the work of the committees and sub-committees and to advise it on fixing and revising minimum wages.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act 1948 is a core law in the Labour Laws syllabus. It came into force on 15 March 1948. It empowers the appropriate Government to fix minimum wage rates for scheduled employments and to review and revise them at intervals not exceeding five years (Section 3). Section 3 also allows a minimum wage to be fixed on a time-work, piece-work or guaranteed time-rate basis. Section 4 covers the components of a minimum rate of wages, including a basic rate and a cost-of-living allowance. Section 5 sets out the two procedures for fixing wages: the Committee method (committees and sub-committees hold inquiries and advise) and the Notification method (proposals published for representations, with a minimum period of two months). Section 7 provides for the Advisory Board. Section 8 provides for the Central Advisory Board, which coordinates the work of the Advisory Boards and advises on matters under the Act. Section 9 sets the composition: equal numbers of employer and employee representatives plus independent persons not exceeding one-third, with one independent person as chairman. Section 12 requires employers to pay at least the minimum wage. Section 13 covers fixing of hours of work, a weekly day of rest and overtime. Section 14 provides for overtime at the prescribed rate. Section 18 covers registers and records. Section 19 deals with Inspectors. Section 20 covers claims and the authority to decide them. Section 22 provides for penalties. The Act applies to employments listed in the Schedule, and the appropriate Government may add to the Schedule. Related concepts are the Fair Wages Committee 1948, the 15th Indian Labour Conference 1957 norms on need-based minimum wage, the Supreme Court's Reptakos Brett judgment (1992), and the Code on Wages 2019, which subsumes this Act.

question: Under the provisions of the Minimum Wages Act 1948, who among the following can NOT be appointed as the Authority by the appropriate Government to hear and decide any claims arising out of payment of less wages than the minimum rates of wage?
options: Labour Commissioner of a State Government
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 20 deals with claims arising out of payment of less than the minimum rates of wages or of remuneration for overtime. It lets the appropriate Government appoint an Authority by notification. For scheduled employments carried on by or under the authority of the Central Government, a railway administration, a mine, oil field, major port or a Central corporation, the Authority may be a Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation, or an officer of the Central Government exercising functions as a Regional Labour Commissioner, or another officer with judicial experience (civil court judge or stipendiary magistrate). For other scheduled employments, the State Government may appoint a Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation, an officer with judicial experience, or any State officer not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Labour (the exact State-officer rank is recalled from memory, so verify it against the bare Act). The application must normally be made within six months of the date the wages became payable. The Authority can direct payment of the shortfall plus compensation up to ten times the amount. Elimination: the Labour Commissioner (State), the Regional Labour Commissioner (Central) and the Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation are all expressly eligible. The Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central) is the only one not expressly named in the Central clause, so (d) is the answer.
explanations: Wrong option for this question: a State Labour Commissioner is above the minimum rank of State officer who can be appointed under the State clause of Section 20(1), so he can be appointed.
Wrong option for this question: an officer of the Central Government exercising functions as Regional Labour Commissioner is expressly named in Section 20(1) for Central-sphere employments.
Wrong option for this question: a Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation is expressly named in Section 20(1) for both Central and State appointments.

Correct: an Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central) is not listed in the Central-sphere clause, which names only the Regional Labour Commissioner, the Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation and judicially experienced officers. He therefore cannot be appointed as the Authority on that basis.
keyfact: Under Section 20 of the Minimum Wages Act, the Central-sphere Authority can be a Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation or a Regional Labour Commissioner (Central), but an Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central) is not named.
option_notes: The Labour Commissioner is the head of a State labour department and enforces State and Central labour laws within the State. He is typically appointed as an Authority under the Minimum Wages Act, the Payment of Wages Act and similar laws. He ranks above Assistant Labour Commissioners and Deputy Labour Commissioners in the State hierarchy.

The Regional Labour Commissioner (Central) is an officer in the Central Industrial Relations Machinery (CIRM) under the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), headquartered in New Delhi. He is the Central Government's enforcement officer in a region. He is the named Authority under Section 20 for Central-sphere scheduled employments, and also handles conciliation and inspection.

The Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation is appointed under the Workmen's Compensation Act 1923 (now the Employees' Compensation Act 1923) to settle compensation claims for workplace injury or death. He is often a State Labour Department officer or a judicial officer. He is also commonly the Authority under the Minimum Wages Act and the Payment of Wages Act.

The Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central) is a junior gazetted officer in the Central Industrial Relations Machinery. He serves as a conciliation officer under the Industrial Disputes Act and as an inspector under Central labour laws. Unlike the Regional Labour Commissioner, he is not named in the Central clause of Section 20 of the Minimum Wages Act.
related: Section 20 of the Minimum Wages Act 1948 provides for claims and the appointment of the Authority.
A claim must normally be filed within six months of the date the minimum wage became payable.
Compensation on a successful claim can be up to ten times the shortfall.
Overtime under the Act is paid at double the ordinary rate (Section 14).
Minimum wages must be reviewed at intervals not exceeding five years (Section 3).
The Central Advisory Board is constituted under Section 8.
The 15th Indian Labour Conference (1957) laid down the need-based minimum wage norms.
The Code on Wages 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act 1948.
summary: The answer is (d). Under Section 20(1) of the Minimum Wages Act 1948, for Central-sphere scheduled employments the Authority can be a Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation, a Regional Labour Commissioner (Central), or another officer with experience as a civil court judge or stipendiary magistrate. An Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central) is not listed in that clause. A State officer of Labour Commissioner rank is eligible under the State clause.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948. It gives the appropriate Government the power to fix minimum wage rates for scheduled employments, and its constitutional basis lies in the Directive Principles (Art. 43). Fixation and revision procedure is in Section 5: the committee method and the notification method. Section 3 covers fixation and revision, and rates must be reviewed at intervals not exceeding five years. Section 4 sets out the components of the minimum wage rate, which may be a basic rate plus a cost of living allowance, or an all-inclusive rate. Section 13 deals with fixing hours of work. Section 14 provides for overtime at double the ordinary rate. Section 17 deals with claims and Section 20 with the Authority. Section 18 covers maintenance of registers and records, and Section 19 covers inspectors. Section 22 sets penalties: imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to Rs 500, or both, for paying less than the minimum wage. The Act has been subsumed into the Code on Wages 2019, which also merges the Payment of Wages Act, the Payment of Bonus Act and the Equal Remuneration Act. The Central Advisory Board (Section 8) advises on minimum wages and coordinates State Advisory Boards. The Central Government is the appropriate Government for Central-sphere establishments such as railways, mines and major ports. The National Floor Level Minimum Wage was recommended on the basis of the Labour Ministry's norms, and the 15th Indian Labour Conference in 1957 laid down the need-based minimum wage norms. UPSC may also ask about the Authority's powers: directing payment of the shortfall plus compensation up to ten times, and penalising a vexatious claimant up to Rs 50.

question: Under the provisions of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970, how many members may be nominated by the Central Government while constituting the Central Advisory Board?
options: Not exceeding seventeen but not less than eleven
Not exceeding fifteen but not less than ten
Not exceeding twenty but not less than fifteen
Not exceeding twelve but not less than seven
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Section 3 of the CLRA Act 1970 requires the Central Government to constitute the Central Advisory Contract Labour Board. Its job is to advise the Central Government on matters arising from administration of the Act that are referred to it, and to carry out other assigned functions. Composition under Section 3(2): (a) a Chairman appointed by the Central Government; (b) the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), ex officio, who is a member; (c) such number of members, not exceeding seventeen but not less than eleven, nominated by the Central Government to represent the Government, railways, coal industry, mining industry, contractors, workmen and any other interests the Government thinks should be represented. The Board is a purely advisory body. The State equivalent under Section 4 is the State Advisory Contract Labour Board, with the Labour Commissioner (or equivalent) as a member and nominated members numbering not more than eleven and not less than nine. The Act also provides for committees and sub-committees (Section 5) and terms of office and allowances (Section 3(4) and 3(5)). Elimination: the range 'seventeen and eleven' is the specific statutory range. Options (b), (c) and (d) use plausible but incorrect ranges, and the 9-11 range belongs to the State Board.
explanations: Correct: Section 3 provides for not exceeding seventeen but not less than eleven nominated members on the Central Board.
Incorrect: 10 to 15 is not the statutory range for the Central Board; it matches neither the Central nor the State Board.
Incorrect: 15 to 20 overstates both limits. The upper limit is seventeen and the lower limit is eleven.
Incorrect: 7 to 12 is too small for the Central Board. A 9 to 11 range applies to the State Board.
keyfact: CLRA Act 1970, Section 3: Central Advisory Contract Labour Board has 11 to 17 nominated members, in addition to the Chairman and the Chief Labour Commissioner.
option_notes: Not exceeding 17 but not less than 11: this is the nominated-member range for the Central Advisory Contract Labour Board under Section 3 of the CLRA Act 1970. Nominees represent the Central Government, railways, coal and mining industries, contractors, workmen and other interests. They are in addition to the Chairman and the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), who is a member ex officio. The Board advises the Central Government on administration of the Act.

Not exceeding 15 but not less than 10: this range does not appear in the CLRA Act for any Board. The Act fixes 11 to 17 for the Central Board and 9 to 11 for the State Board. It is a distractor with plausible-sounding numbers. Remember that nominated members, not the total, are counted within the statutory limits.

Not exceeding 20 but not less than 15: this range is not in the CLRA Act. It inflates the Central Board limits, which are 11 to 17. The Central Board's membership has to include representatives of the Government, railways, coal, mining, contractors and workmen, and the Act caps it at seventeen nominated members.

Not exceeding 12 but not less than 7: this range does not match the CLRA Act. The State Advisory Contract Labour Board under Section 4 has not more than 11 and not less than 9 nominated members, so this option is wrong for both Boards. The State Board includes the Labour Commissioner and a Chairman appointed by the State Government.
related: CLRA Act 1970 applies to establishments and contractors with 20 or more contract workmen.
Central Advisory Contract Labour Board: Chairman, Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) ex officio, plus 11 to 17 nominated members.
State Advisory Contract Labour Board: nominated members not more than 11 and not less than 9.
Section 10 allows the appropriate Government to prohibit contract labour after consulting the Board.
Under Section 21, the principal employer is liable to pay wages if the contractor fails.
Under Section 12, every contractor must hold a licence.
The OSH Code 2020 subsumes the CLRA Act and sets the threshold at 50 workers.
summary: The answer is (a). Section 3(3)(c) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 says the Central Government nominates not more than seventeen and not less than eleven members to the Central Advisory Contract Labour Board. These members represent the Government, railways, coal and mining industries, contractors, workmen and other interests.
topic_notes: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 regulates employment of contract labour in establishments and provides for abolition of contract labour in certain circumstances. It came into force in 1970-71 and applies to establishments employing 20 or more workmen as contract labour (the State may extend it to establishments with fewer) and to contractors who employ or employed 20 or more workmen on any day of the preceding 12 months. It does not apply to establishments where work is of intermittent or casual nature. Key features: Section 3 Central Advisory Contract Labour Board; Section 4 State Advisory Board; Section 5 committees; Sections 7 and 12 registration of principal employers and licensing of contractors; Section 10 prohibition of employment of contract labour by the appropriate Government after consulting the Board; Sections 16 to 20 welfare and health provisions, including canteens, rest rooms, drinking water and first aid; Section 21 responsibility for payment of wages, with the principal employer liable if the contractor fails; Section 25 and later sections cover offences and penalties. Inspectors are appointed under Section 28. Related Boards and bodies: the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) heads the Central Industrial Relations Machinery. The Act is among the laws merged into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which raises the threshold for contract labour to 50 workers. Exam angles include Board compositions, the thresholds of 20 and 50, definitions of 'contractor' and 'principal employer', licence fees and validity, and the penalties.

question: Under the provisions of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970, a contractor has to provide and maintain a canteen wherein ordinarily a minimum of:
options: 50 contract workers are employed by a contractor
100 contract workers are employed by a contractor
20 contract workers are employed by a contractor
70 contract workers are employed by a contractor
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970 regulates contract labour in establishments employing 20 or more workmen as contract labour (the Act's applicability threshold), and it prohibits contract labour in core or perennial work through Section 10. Welfare amenities are in Chapter V, Sections 16 to 20. Section 16 covers canteens (the heading under it is actually in the Act as 'Canteens'), Section 17 rest rooms, Section 18 drinking water, latrines and urinals, Section 19 first aid, and Section 20 the principal employer's liability when the contractor fails to provide them. Note that the central rules (Rule 40 to 42) lay out the details. The canteen provision applies where contract labour of 100 or more is ordinarily employed in work of a continuing nature expected to last at least 6 months. Rest rooms are required where contract labour is required to halt at night, and a contractor is also required to provide creches where 20 or more women are ordinarily employed. Options 50, 70 and 20 are wrong numbers: 20 is the applicability threshold for the Act itself and for creches (women), not for canteens. If the contractor fails, the principal employer must provide the amenities and may recover the cost from the contractor.
explanations: Incorrect: 50 is not the threshold for a canteen under the Act or the Rules.
Correct: the canteen requirement applies where 100 or more contract workers are ordinarily employed (Rule 41 of the Central Rules, read with the welfare provisions of Chapter V).
Incorrect: 20 is the threshold for applicability of the Act to an establishment or contractor, and for creches under the rules, not for canteens.
Incorrect: 70 is not a threshold in the Act or Rules for canteens.
keyfact: CLRA Act 1970: canteen where 100 or more contract workers are ordinarily employed; the Act applies from 20 workers.
option_notes: 50 workers: not a statutory threshold for any welfare amenity under the CLRA Act. The 50 figure appears in other labour laws, for example the Factories Act canteen threshold is 250 workers and the Industrial Disputes Act chapter V-B uses 100. The number 50 is also used in the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act context in some states.

100 workers: this is the canteen threshold. A canteen is required in an establishment where contract labour of 100 or more is ordinarily employed in work of a continuing nature, and where the work is likely to last for six months or more. The principal employer provides it if the contractor fails and recovers the cost from the contractor.

20 workers: this is the basic applicability threshold of the CLRA Act, which applies to every establishment and contractor employing 20 or more workmen as contract labour on any day of the preceding 12 months. Creches are required where 20 or more women are ordinarily employed. It is not the canteen threshold.

70 workers: not a statutory threshold in the CLRA Act or the Central Rules for any welfare amenity. It is a distractor, and students should not confuse it with the figures 20, 50 or 100 that do appear in labour legislation.
related: CLRA Act 1970 applies to establishments with 20 or more contract workers.
Canteen under CLRA: 100 or more contract workers ordinarily employed.
Section 10 CLRA empowers the government to prohibit contract labour.
Section 21 CLRA: the principal employer is liable for wages if the contractor fails to pay.
Factories Act 1948 canteen: more than 250 workers.
Factories Act creche: more than 30 women workers.
OSH Code 2020 raises the contract labour threshold to 50 workers.
Central Advisory Contract Labour Board is constituted under Section 3.
summary: The answer is (b) 100 contract workers. Under Section 18 of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970 read with Rule 41 of the Central Rules 1971, a canteen must be provided where the contract labour employed is ordinarily 100 or more.
topic_notes: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970 came into force in 1971 to regulate the employment of contract labour and to abolish it in certain circumstances. It applies to every establishment employing 20 or more workmen as contract labour on any day of the preceding 12 months, and to every contractor employing 20 or more workmen. It does not apply to establishments where work is of an intermittent or casual nature. The principal employer must register the establishment (Section 7), and the contractor must obtain a licence (Section 12). Central and State Advisory Boards are constituted under Sections 3 and 4. Section 10 allows the appropriate government to prohibit contract labour in any process, operation or work after consultation with the Boards, considering factors such as whether the work is perennial, incidental or necessary to the industry. Welfare provisions are in Chapter V: canteens, rest rooms, drinking water, latrines and urinals, washing facilities and first aid. Section 21 deals with responsibility for payment of wages: the contractor pays, and the principal employer must nominate a representative to be present at disbursement, and pays if the contractor fails. Section 25 deals with the effect of laws and agreements inconsistent with the Act. Penalties include imprisonment up to three months or a fine up to Rs 1,000 for contravention. The Act has been subsumed into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020, which raises the applicability threshold to 50 workers. Other related thresholds include the canteen requirement in the Factories Act (250 workers) and creche (30 women).

question: Which one of the following provisions is NOT covered under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970?
options: Sufficient supply of wholesome drinking water
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Chapter V of the CLRA Act 1970 (Sections 16-20) deals with the welfare and health of contract labour. Section 16 requires canteens where the work is likely to continue for at least six months and 100 or more contract workers are employed. Section 17 requires rest-rooms or alternative accommodation where workers must stay at night or halt during working hours. Section 18 covers other facilities: (a) sufficient supply of wholesome drinking water at convenient places, (b) a sufficient number of latrines and urinals, and (c) washing facilities. Section 19 requires first-aid facilities. Section 20 makes the principal employer liable to provide these amenities if the contractor fails to, and he can recover the cost from the contractor. The Act has no crèche provision. Crèches are statutory under the Factories Act 1948 (Sec 48, where more than 30 women are employed), the Plantations Labour Act 1951, the Mines Act 1952, the Building and Other Construction Workers Act 1996, and the Maternity Benefit Act as amended in 2017 (50 or more employees). Elimination: options a, b and c are expressly named in the CLRA Act, so only crèches remain. The Act is now subsumed in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.
explanations: Wrong choice: sufficient supply of wholesome drinking water is expressly required by Section 18(a) of the CLRA Act, so it is covered.
Wrong choice: rest-rooms are provided for by Section 17, so they are covered.
Wrong choice: first-aid facilities are provided for by Section 19, so they are covered.
Correct choice: the CLRA Act contains no provision for crèches, so this is the one NOT covered. Crèches are required under the Factories Act, Plantations Labour Act, BOCW Act and others.
keyfact: CLRA Act 1970 (Ch. V) covers canteen, rest-rooms, drinking water, latrines, washing and first-aid, but not crèches.
option_notes: Drinking water: under Section 18(a) the contractor must provide sufficient wholesome drinking water at convenient places. Sections 18(b) and 18(c) add latrines and urinals, and washing facilities. If the contractor fails, the principal employer must provide them under Section 20 and recover the cost from the contractor. The detailed standards are in the Central Rules 1971.

Rest-rooms: Section 17 requires the contractor to provide suitable rest-rooms or other suitable alternative accommodation where contract labour is required to halt at night in connection with the work. The rooms must be sufficiently lighted and ventilated and maintained in a clean and comfortable condition. The Rules prescribe the detailed standards. The principal employer is liable under Section 20 if the contractor defaults.

First aid: Section 19 requires one or more first-aid boxes, equipped with the prescribed contents, at the work place of contract labour. The boxes must be readily accessible during working hours. The Rules also require them to be kept in the charge of a person trained in first-aid. Under Section 20 the principal employer is liable if the contractor fails to provide them.

Crèches: facilities for the care of young children of women workers, provided under the Factories Act 1948 (Sec 48, more than 30 women workers), the Plantations Labour Act 1951, the Mines Act 1952 and the BOCW Act 1996. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 requires them in establishments with 50 or more employees. The CLRA Act 1970 itself does not provide for crèches, so this is the answer.
related: CLRA Act 1970 applies to establishments with 20 or more contract workers; the 2020 Code raises this to 50.
Section 10 CLRA allows prohibition of contract labour; SAIL (2001) held there is no automatic absorption.
Section 16: canteens; Section 17: rest-rooms; Section 18: drinking water, latrines, urinals, washing; Section 19: first-aid.
Section 20: the principal employer is liable for amenities if the contractor fails.
Factories Act Sec 48: a crèche is required where more than 30 women are employed.
Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017: a crèche is required in establishments with 50 or more employees.
The CLRA Act is subsumed in the OSH & Working Conditions Code 2020.
Contractor licensing is under Section 12; registration of the principal employer is under Section 7.
summary: The answer is (d) Crèches. Chapter V of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 covers canteens, rest-rooms, drinking water, latrines and urinals, washing facilities and first-aid, but it has no provision for crèches. Crèches appear in other labour laws such as the Factories Act, the Plantations Labour Act and the BOCW Act.
topic_notes: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970 came into force in 1971. It applies to establishments and contractors employing 20 or more workmen (the threshold is 50 in the 2020 Code). It provides for Central and State Advisory Boards, registration of principal employers, and licensing of contractors. Section 10 allows the appropriate government to prohibit contract labour in certain processes, operations or work, after consulting the Advisory Board. It looks at whether the work is perennial, whether it is incidental to the main work, and whether regular workmen are employed for it. Chapter V (Sections 16-20) covers welfare and health: canteens, rest-rooms, drinking water, latrines and urinals, washing facilities, first-aid, and the principal employer's liability under Section 20. Chapter VI covers payment of wages. The contractor must pay wages, and a representative of the principal employer must be present at disbursement. If the contractor fails, the principal employer pays and recovers the amount. Section 25 provides that the Act overrides inconsistent provisions of other laws. Penalties are in Sections 23-25. Key case law is Air India Statutory Corporation v. United Labour Union (1996), which held that abolition of contract labour leads to automatic absorption, and SAIL v. National Union Waterfront Workers (2001), which overruled it. That later ruling held there is no automatic absorption, and that Section 10 has no such effect. The Act is now subsumed in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. Related statutes that can be asked about include the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979 and the Factories Act 1948.

question: Under the provisions of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970, which one of the following statements is true relating to the appointment of the Chairman of the State Advisory Board?
options: The Chairman is to be appointed by the State Government
The Labour Commissioner of the State shall be the ex-officio Chairman
The Chairman is to be appointed by the State Government in consultation with the Central Government
Labour Minister of the State shall be the ex-officio Chairman
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 3 of the CLRA Act 1970 provides for the Central Advisory Contract Labour Board, and Section 4 provides for the State Advisory Contract Labour Board. Section 4 says the State Government shall constitute the Board to advise it on matters arising out of the administration of the Act, as it may refer. The Board consists of a Chairman to be appointed by the State Government, the Chief Labour Commissioner-type officer is not relevant at the state level, and other members are nominated by the State Government. The members include the Labour Commissioner, if any, as an ex-officio member, other members representing the State Government, an equal number of representatives of the employers (principal employers and contractors) and of the workmen, and (as per the Act) persons representing any other interests the State Government thinks fit. The Central Board, by contrast, has the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) as ex-officio Chairman. The Central Government is not consulted on the State Chairman's appointment. Elimination: (b) and (d) wrongly make the post ex-officio, and (c) invents a requirement of consultation with the Centre.
explanations: Correct. Section 4(2) says the Chairman of the State Board is appointed by the State Government, which is the appointing authority for the whole Board.

Incorrect. The Labour Commissioner is at most a member of the State Board; the Chairman is not ex-officio. The ex-officio Chairman pattern applies to the Central Board (Chief Labour Commissioner (Central)).
Incorrect. The Act has no requirement of consulting the Central Government for the State Chairman's appointment; the State Government acts on its own.
Incorrect. The Act does not make the State Labour Minister the ex-officio Chairman; the State Government appoints the Chairman by nomination.
keyfact: State Advisory Contract Labour Board (Section 4, CLRA 1970): Chairman is appointed by the State Government, not ex-officio.
option_notes: The State Government appoints the Chairman of the State Advisory Contract Labour Board under Section 4 of the CLRA Act 1970. The Board advises the State Government on matters arising from the administration of the Act. It includes representatives of the State Government, principal employers, contractors and workmen, and the Chairman is a nominated person, not an ex-officio holder.

The Labour Commissioner is the senior state official administering labour laws. Under the CLRA Act he may sit on the State Board, but as a member, not as Chairman. The idea of an ex-officio Chairman resembles the Central Board, where the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) is the Chairman. Hence this option is wrong.

This option is a distractor. Under Sections 3 and 4, the Central Government constitutes the Central Board and the State Government constitutes the State Board, each acting in its own sphere. The Act does not require consulting the Centre for the State Chairman. Consultation provisions in the Act exist elsewhere, such as the Central Government acting in consultation with Boards when making rules.

The Labour Minister is a political head of the department and is not named in the Act as the Chairman. The State Government nominates the Chairman, who need not be a Minister. Ex-officio Chairman provisions are found for the Central Board, held by the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central).
related: CLRA Act 1970 applies to establishments and contractors with 20 or more workmen.
Section 3 provides for the Central Advisory Contract Labour Board; Section 4 for the State Board.
The Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) is the Chairman of the Central Board.
Section 10 deals with prohibition of contract labour.
Section 12 requires contractors to hold a licence.
Section 21 makes the principal employer liable for wages if the contractor defaults.
The CLRA Act is subsumed in the OSH Code 2020.
summary: The correct answer is (a). Under Section 4 of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970, the State Government constitutes the State Advisory Contract Labour Board and appoints a person to be its Chairman. The Act does not make the Labour Commissioner or the Labour Minister ex-officio Chairman.
topic_notes: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970 regulates the employment of contract labour in certain establishments and provides for its abolition in certain circumstances. It came into force on 10 February 1971 (some provisions from later notified dates). It applies to every establishment in which twenty or more workmen are employed, or were employed on any day of the preceding twelve months, as contract labour, and to every contractor who employs or employed twenty or more workmen. The appropriate Government may extend it to establishments with a smaller number. It does not apply to establishments where work is of an intermittent or casual nature. Advisory Boards: Section 3 covers the Central Advisory Contract Labour Board, chaired by the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), and Section 4 covers the State Advisory Contract Labour Board, whose Chairman is appointed by the State Government. Both Boards have equal representation of employers and workmen, plus members for other interests. Other key provisions are: Section 7 registration of principal employers; Section 10 prohibition of employment of contract labour by the appropriate Government after consulting the Boards; Section 12 licensing of contractors; Sections 16 to 19 welfare and health facilities such as canteens, rest rooms, drinking water, latrines and first aid; Section 21 responsibility for payment of wages, with the principal employer liable if the contractor fails; Section 23 onward on penalties. Inspectors are appointed under Section 28. The Act was amended in 2016 for certain rules, and the Code on Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions 2020 subsumes it. Likely future questions include the threshold of 20 workmen, the license provisions, and the Central Board's composition.

question: Under the provisions of the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, the Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee consists of a Chairman and such other members NOT exceeding:
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 5 of the 1986 Act empowers the Central Government to constitute, by notification in the Official Gazette, the Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee (CLTAC). Its job is to advise the Centre on adding occupations and processes to the Schedule in Part A (occupations) and Part B (processes) of the Act. The Committee consists of a Chairman and such other members, not exceeding ten, as the Central Government appoints. Under the original 1986 Act, Part A lists occupations in which children (below 14) are prohibited from working, and Part B lists hazardous processes. The Act banned child employment in these and regulated working conditions elsewhere. The Committee regulates its own procedure, including quorum. The 2016 Amendment (in force 1 September 2016) renamed the Act the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, banned employment of children below 14 in all occupations except family enterprises and audio-visual entertainment outside school hours, and prohibited adolescents (14-18) from hazardous work. Eliminating options: five is too small, while fifteen and twenty are numbers the Act never uses for this Committee. Remember the figure 'ten' for the CLTAC.
explanations: Incorrect: the ceiling is ten, not five.
Correct: Section 5(2) says the Committee has a Chairman and members not exceeding ten.
Incorrect: fifteen exceeds the statutory limit.
Incorrect: twenty exceeds the statutory limit.
keyfact: CLTAC under the Child Labour Act 1986 (Section 5) = Chairman + not more than ten members.
option_notes: Five: no link to the CLTAC's strength. Five is a distractor. Small bodies of about five members exist in other labour laws, but the Child Labour Act does not fix the Committee at this number.

Ten: the statutory maximum number of members, besides the Chairman, of the Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee under Section 5 of the 1986 Act. The Central Government appoints them by notification. The Committee advises on adding occupations and processes to the Schedule.

Fifteen: not the figure in Section 5. Fifteen appears in other contexts, such as the age at which the Factories Act bars young children and older limits in some bodies, but it is not the CLTAC's ceiling. It is a distractor.
Twenty: exceeds the limit set by the Act. Larger advisory boards, such as the Central Board of Trustees of EPFO, have bigger memberships, but the CLTAC is limited to ten members besides the Chairman.
related: CLTAC: Chairman plus not more than ten members (Section 5).
The CLTAC advises on adding occupations and processes to the Schedule.
The 1986 Act defined a child as below 14 years.
The 2016 amendment introduced the category of adolescent (14-18) and banned them from hazardous work.
Article 24 bans employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.
The National Child Labour Project began in 1988.
India ratified ILO Conventions 138 and 182 in 2017.
The PENCIL portal is for tracking and eliminating child labour.
summary: The correct answer is (b) Ten. Section 5 of the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 provides for a Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee made up of a Chairman and other members not exceeding ten, appointed by the Central Government.
topic_notes: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 was enacted after the Gurupadaswamy Committee (1979) recommended regulating child labour and banning it in hazardous work. It defined a child as a person below 14. Part A of the Schedule lists prohibited occupations, and Part B lists prohibited processes. Section 5 creates the Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee, with a Chairman and members not exceeding ten, to advise on additions to the Schedule. Section 3 prohibits employment in scheduled occupations and processes. Part III regulates conditions of work in non-prohibited establishments, with limits such as six hours of work per day including a one-hour interval, no work between 7 pm and 8 am, and a weekly holiday. Section 14 provides penalties. The 2016 Amendment renamed it the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act. It prohibits children below 14 from all work except helping family enterprises after school hours and working as child artists. It defines an adolescent as aged 14-18 and bars adolescents from hazardous occupations, and it raised penalties: imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years and a fine of Rs 20,000-50,000. Related constitutional provisions are Article 24 (no child below 14 in a factory, mine or hazardous employment), Article 21A (free and compulsory education for ages 6-14), Article 39(e) and 39(f), and Article 45. Other items are the National Child Labour Project (NCLP, 1988), the Right to Education Act 2009, the ILO Conventions 138 (minimum age) and 182 (worst forms), both ratified by India in 2017, and the PENCIL portal.

question: Under the provisions of the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, the list of occupations in which children are prohibited to be employed is provided in :
options: Part B of the Schedule under the Act
Part A of the Schedule under the Act
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The 1986 Act, in its original form, was divided into Part I (preliminary, Sections 1-2), Part II (prohibition of employment of children in certain occupations and processes, Sections 3-5), Part III (regulation of conditions of work of children in employments not prohibited, Sections 6-13) and Part IV (miscellaneous, Sections 14-release). A 'child' was a person who had not completed 14 years. Section 3 is the key prohibition: no child shall be employed or permitted to work in any occupation listed in Part A of the Schedule, or in any workshop where a process listed in Part B is carried on. Part A covers occupations such as transport of passengers by railways, cinder picking, handling of ash pits, catering at railway establishments, construction work on railways, and work in ports. Part B covers processes such as bidi-making, carpet weaving, cement manufacture, cloth printing, dyeing and weaving, and manufacture of matches, explosives and fireworks. Section 4 gives the Central Government power to amend the Schedule. Section 5 provides for the Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee. Section 6 only deals with the application of Part III. Elimination: Sections 4 and 6 do not contain the list, and Part B lists processes, not occupations, so only Part A remains. The 2016 Amendment later banned all work for children under 14 and restricted adolescents (14-18) from hazardous work, and the old Schedule was replaced.
explanations: Wrong. Part B of the Schedule lists prohibited processes (for example bidi-making, carpet weaving, and manufacture of matches and fireworks), not occupations.
Wrong. Section 4 empowers the Central Government to amend the Schedule by notification. It does not contain the list.
Wrong. Section 6 deals with the application of Part III, which regulates conditions of work in non-prohibited employments. It has no list.
Correct. Part A of the Schedule lists the occupations in which children are prohibited from employment under Section 3.
keyfact: Under the 1986 Act, Section 3 prohibits child employment: Part A of the Schedule lists occupations and Part B lists processes; Section 4 allows the Schedule to be amended.
option_notes: Part B of the Schedule lists the prohibited processes. Examples are bidi-making, carpet weaving, cement manufacture, cloth printing, dyeing and weaving, manufacture of matches, explosives and fireworks, mica cutting and splitting, shellac manufacture, soap manufacture, tanning, wool cleaning, and building and construction. Under Section 3, a child cannot work in a workshop where these processes are carried on. Exceptions applied to a workshop run by a family or a government-recognised school.

Section 4 gives the Central Government the power to add to the Schedule, that is, to amend Part A or Part B by notification in the Official Gazette. Its purpose is to keep the lists of hazardous occupations and processes up to date. The Schedule was expanded several times, for example in 2006 to add domestic work and dhabas and in 2008 for further processes.

Section 6 begins Part III of the Act, which regulates conditions of work for children in employments not prohibited. It states which establishments the Part applies to, namely those not covered by the Schedule. Sections 7 to 13 then cover hours of work (not more than 3 hours at a stretch, 6 hours a day), a weekly holiday, a notice to the Inspector, a health register and penalties.

Part A of the Schedule lists the prohibited occupations. Examples are transport of passengers, goods or mails by railway, cinder picking or clearing of ash pits, catering at railway stations, construction of a railway station, work in a port, work relating to selling of crackers and fireworks in temporary licensed shops, abattoirs and slaughterhouses, automobile workshops and garages, and hazardous work such as handloom and powerloom industry. Section 3 prohibits children from working in these.
related: Article 24 prohibits employing children below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous employment.
Section 3 of the 1986 Act is the prohibition section; Part A of the Schedule lists occupations and Part B lists processes.
The 2016 Amendment bans employment of all children below 14, and bars adolescents of 14-18 from hazardous work.
The National Child Labour Project (NCLP) was launched in 1988.
The Gurupadswamy Committee (1979) led to the 1986 Act.
The PENCIL portal (2017) is used to monitor child labour.
Article 21A ensures free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14.
The ILO Minimum Age Convention 138 and Worst Forms of Child Labour Convention 182 were ratified by India in 2017.
summary: The answer is (d). Section 3 of the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 prohibits employment of children in the occupations and processes listed in the Schedule, and Part A of the Schedule lists the prohibited occupations. Part B lists the prohibited processes.
topic_notes: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 followed the Gurupadswamy Committee (1979) recommendations. It defined a child as a person below 14 years. Part II (Sections 3-5) prohibits child employment in hazardous occupations and processes. Part III (Sections 6-13) regulates working conditions in other employments: a maximum of 6 hours a day including 1 hour of rest, work only between 8 am and 7 pm, no overtime, a weekly holiday, and a notice to the Inspector within 30 days of employing a child. Section 14 contains penalties: imprisonment of 3 months to 1 year, or a fine of Rs 10,000 to 20,000, or both. The Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee under Section 5 advises on additions to the Schedule. The Act was amended in 2016 as the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act. It prohibits employment of children below 14 in all occupations and processes, except helping family or family enterprises after school hours, or working as child artists in audio-visual entertainment. Adolescents aged 14-18 are barred from hazardous occupations. The Schedule was reduced to three hazardous processes: mines, inflammable substances and explosives, and hazardous processes under the Factories Act. Penalties were raised to imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years, or a fine of Rs 20,000 to 50,000, or both. Related provisions: Article 24 of the Constitution bans employment of children below 14 in factories, mines or other hazardous work. Article 21A gives free and compulsory education for ages 6-14. Article 39(e)-(f) is a Directive Principle. The National Child Labour Project (NCLP, 1988) and the PENCIL portal (2017) are related schemes. Other related laws are the Factories Act 1948, the Mines Act 1952 and the Right to Education Act 2009.

question: Which one of the following is to be constituted under the provisions of the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Correction to the summary: the answer is (b) Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee. Section 5 of the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 empowers the Central Government to constitute, by notification, a Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee (CLTAC) to advise it on adding occupations and processes to the Schedule (Part A occupations and Part B processes) in Section 3 where employment of children is prohibited. The Committee consists of a Chairman and not more than ten other members appointed by the Central Government. It regulates its own procedure. Section 4 deals with the Schedule's amendment by notification; Section 3 prohibits employment of children (below 14 years) in hazardous occupations; Section 14 gives penalties. The 2016 Amendment Act renamed the law as the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, prohibiting employment of children below 14 in all occupations, and adolescents (14-18) in hazardous ones. Elimination: 'Advisory Board', 'Regulating Machinery' and 'Regulating Advisory Board' are not statutory bodies under the 1986 Act. Only the Technical Advisory Committee is mentioned by name.
explanations: Incorrect: no body called 'Child Labour Advisory Board' exists under the 1986 Act; the Act provides for a Technical Advisory Committee.
Correct: Section 5 provides for the Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee, constituted by the Central Government to advise on additions to the Schedule of banned occupations and processes.
Incorrect: 'Regulating Machinery' is not a body in the Act; it is a made-up phrase. Enforcement is by inspectors appointed under Section 17.
Incorrect: 'Child Labour Regulating Advisory Board' is not provided for in the Act.
keyfact: Section 5 of the Child Labour Act 1986 creates the Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee, which advises on the Schedule of banned occupations.
option_notes: Child Labour Advisory Board: not a statutory body under the 1986 Act. It is easily confused with the Technical Advisory Committee. Advisory boards of similar kind exist in other labour laws, such as the Central Advisory Board under the Contract Labour Act, 1970 and the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, but not here.

Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee (CLTAC): constituted under Section 5 of the 1986 Act by the Central Government through notification. It has a Chairman and up to ten other members. Its function is to advise the Government on adding occupations and processes to the Schedule of Part A and Part B. It was constituted following the Gurupadswamy Committee (1979) and M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996) recommendations.

Child Labour Regulating Machinery: no such body exists in the Act. Enforcement is carried out by Inspectors appointed by the appropriate government under Section 17. The term is a distractor and has no legal standing.

Child Labour Regulating Advisory Board: not a body in the Act. It is a distractor combining words from the Act's title and advisory bodies in other labour laws. The Act's only constituted body is the Technical Advisory Committee.
related: Section 5 of the 1986 Act provides for the Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee.
Article 24 of the Constitution bans employment of children below 14 in hazardous work.
The 2016 Amendment renamed the law as the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act.
Adolescent under the 2016 Amendment is a person aged 14 to 18.
National Child Labour Project (NCLP) started in 1988.
India ratified ILO Conventions 138 and 182 in 2017.
The PENCIL portal is used for the elimination of child labour.
Gurupadswamy Committee (1979) preceded the 1986 Act.
summary: The correct answer is (a) Child Labour Advisory Board. Under the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, the Central Government constitutes the Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee under Section 5. The Act has no 'Child Labour Advisory Board', so I need to correct this: the right option is (b).
topic_notes: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 was enacted following the Gurupadswamy Committee (1979) report. It prohibited employment of children (below 14 years) in hazardous occupations and processes listed in Part A (occupations) and Part B (processes) of the Schedule, and regulated work conditions in other employments. Section 2 defines child as a person who has not completed 14 years. Section 3 contains the prohibition. Section 5 provides for the Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee. Section 6-13 relate to regulation of conditions of work (hours of work of not more than 6 hours with an interval after 3 hours, no work between 7 pm and 8 am, weekly holiday, notice to the Inspector, health and safety). Section 14 sets penalties: originally imprisonment 3 months to 1 year or fine Rs 10,000 to Rs 20,000, or both. The 2016 Amendment (effective 1 September 2016) renamed the Act as the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, banned employment of children below 14 in all occupations, except in family enterprises or as child artist in audio-visual entertainment (outside school hours), and prohibited adolescents (14-18) from hazardous occupations. It also increased penalties: 6 months to 2 years imprisonment or fine Rs 20,000-50,000. Related: Article 24 of the Constitution prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work; Article 21A gives right to education; Article 39(e),(f) as DPSPs; National Child Labour Project (NCLP) scheme 1988; Right to Education Act 2009; ILO Conventions 138 (minimum age) and 182 (worst forms of child labour), both ratified by India in 2017; PENCIL portal.

question: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct under the provisions of the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986?
options: No child shall be permitted to work between 7 pm and 8 am
The total period of work including interval for rest shall not spread over more than six hours
A child may be permitted to work overtime maximum for two hours in a day
No child shall work for more than three hours before he has had an interval for rest for at least one hour
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Section 7 of the 1986 Act governs hours and period of work for children in the occupations and processes where they could still be employed (the regulated part of the Act). Its main rules are: (i) the work period on any day must not exceed three hours at a stretch, and a child must get a rest interval of at least one hour before working more than three hours; (ii) including the rest interval and waiting time, the work must not spread over more than six hours a day; (iii) no child may work between 7 pm and 8 am; (iv) no child may be required or permitted to work overtime; (v) no child may work in an establishment on a day on which he has already worked in another establishment; (vi) every child is entitled to a weekly holiday of one whole day (Section 8). Options (a), (b) and (d) restate Section 7 almost word for word, so they are correct. Option (c) invents an overtime allowance of two hours, which the Act does not give, so it is the statement that is NOT correct. Note that the 2016 Amendment Act changed the title to the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act and banned work by children below 14 in all occupations, except helping family enterprises or working as child artists after school hours.
explanations: Correct as a statement of the law: Section 7(4) bars work between 7 pm and 8 am. It is therefore not the answer.
Correct as a statement of the law: Section 7(3) limits the spread-over, including rest and waiting time, to six hours. It is therefore not the answer.
Incorrect as a statement of the law: Section 7(5) prohibits overtime for children altogether, and no two-hour allowance exists. This is the NOT-correct statement, so it is the answer.
Correct as a statement of the law: Section 7(2) says no more than three hours of work before a rest interval of at least one hour. It is therefore not the answer.
keyfact: Under Section 7 of the Child Labour Act 1986: 3 hours work then 1 hour rest, 6-hour spread-over, no work 7 pm-8 am, and NO overtime.
option_notes: Night-work ban: under Section 7(4), the permitted working window for a child is 8 am to 7 pm. Combined with the six-hour spread-over, this prevents night work. Adolescents aged 14-18 are covered separately after the 2016 Amendment, which bars them from hazardous occupations.

Six-hour spread-over: Section 7(3) says the child's work, inclusive of the rest interval and time spent waiting for work, shall not spread over more than six hours in a day. Effective work is therefore limited to about three to five hours depending on the interval. The Act also gives a weekly holiday under Section 8.

Overtime: Section 7(5) says no child shall be required or permitted to work overtime. This is a flat ban. The two-hour limit in the option is a distractor, resembling overtime limits for adult workers under the Factories Act 1948 (which sets a 9-hour day and 48-hour week).

Rest interval: Section 7(2) says each work period shall not exceed three hours, and a child shall not work more than three hours before an interval of at least one hour for rest. This is a correct statement of the Act.

summary: The answer is (c). Section 7 of the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 says no child shall be required or permitted to work overtime. The law allows no overtime at all, so a maximum of two hours is wrong.
topic_notes: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 came into force on 23 December 1986, following the Gurupadswamy Committee (1979) recommendations. It banned employment of children below 14 in listed hazardous occupations and processes (Part A and Part B of the Schedule) and regulated conditions of work in other employments. Key provisions: Section 3 prohibits employment in scheduled occupations; Section 7 covers hours of work; Section 8 gives a weekly holiday; Section 9 requires a notice of employment to the Inspector; Section 11 provides for maintaining a register; Section 14 sets penalties. The Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee advises on additions to the Schedule. The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act 2016, in force from 1 September 2016, renamed the Act, prohibited work by children below 14 in all occupations and processes, and allowed exceptions for family enterprises (after school hours or in vacations) and for child artists in audio-visual entertainment (not circus). It created the category of adolescent (14-18) and barred them from hazardous work. Penalties were raised, with imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years and/or a fine of Rs 20,000 to Rs 50,000 for a first offence, and offences made cognizable. Related law and policy: Article 24 of the Constitution (no child below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work); Article 21A (free and compulsory education, ages 6-14); the Right to Education Act 2009; the National Child Labour Project (NCLP, 1988); the ILO Conventions 138 (minimum age) and 182 (worst forms), both ratified by India in 2017; the Factories Act 1948 and Mines Act 1952 (adolescent provisions); and the PENCIL portal for tracking child labour.

question: Under the provisions of the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, an employer is liable to pay the amount of gratuity within:
subject: Social Security
detail: Section 7 of the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 governs the determination and payment of gratuity. Once gratuity becomes payable, the employer must determine the amount and give written notice to the employee (and to the nominee or legal heir if the employee has died) and to the controlling authority within 15 days (Section 7(2)). Under Section 7(3), the employer must pay the gratuity within 30 days from the date it becomes payable. Section 7(3A) says that if payment is delayed beyond 30 days, the employer must pay simple interest at the rate notified by the Central Government, unless the delay is due to the employee's fault and the controlling authority has granted exemption. Any dispute about the amount, or about who is entitled, is referred to the controlling authority under Section 7(4). The appeal lies within 60 days to the appropriate government or appellate authority. Elimination: 15 days is the period for the employer's notice under Section 7(2), not for payment, which is a common trap. 45 days is not found in Section 7. 60 days is the appeal period. So 30 days is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: 15 days is the period for the employer to issue the notice determining the gratuity amount (Section 7(2)), not the payment period.
Correct: Section 7(3) requires payment within 30 days of the gratuity becoming payable, with simple interest on delay under Section 7(3A).
Incorrect: 45 days has no relevance in Section 7 of the Act.
Incorrect: 60 days is the appeal period under Section 7(7), not the payment period.
keyfact: Gratuity must be paid within 30 days of becoming payable (Section 7(3)), with simple interest on delay.
option_notes: 15 days: the time within which the employer must determine the gratuity amount and give written notice to the person entitled and to the controlling authority under Section 7(2). This is also the period for an application for gratuity to be dealt with in some contexts. It is a notice period and does not govern payment.

30 days: the statutory limit for the employer to pay gratuity from the date it becomes payable (Section 7(3)). After this, simple interest accrues at the notified rate (Section 7(3A)). A failure to pay can lead to recovery as arrears of land revenue by the Collector (Section 8) and to penalty under Section 9.

45 days: not a period prescribed in Section 7 of the Act for payment or notice. It works as a distractor. Remember the key periods in the Act instead: 15 days for notice, 30 days for payment, 60 days for appeal, and 30 days for the nomination or other time-bound steps.

60 days: the period within which an appeal may be filed against the controlling authority's order under Section 7(7), extendable by a further 60 days for sufficient cause. It is also the time limit before which the appellate authority hears the appeal. It is not the limit for payment.
related: Section 7(2): the employer's notice determining gratuity within 15 days.
Section 7(3): payment within 30 days; Section 7(3A): simple interest on delay.
Section 7(7): appeal within 60 days.
Gratuity ceiling is Rs 20 lakh since 29 March 2018.
Formula: last drawn wages x 15/26 x completed years of service.
Minimum five years of continuous service, except on death or disablement.

summary: The correct answer is (b) 30 days. Under Section 7(3) of the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, the employer must pay the gratuity within 30 days of it becoming payable, and simple interest is due on any delay.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972 and extends to the whole of India. It applies to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and establishments, and other establishments employing 10 or more persons on any day of the preceding 12 months. Gratuity is a lump-sum retirement benefit for service. It is payable on superannuation, retirement or resignation, death or disablement due to accident or disease. A minimum of five years of continuous service is required, but this condition is relaxed for death or disablement. Calculation for most employees is 15 days' wages for each completed year of service or part exceeding six months, based on the last drawn wages. The formula is last drawn monthly wages x 15/26 x years of service. The ceiling was raised to Rs 20 lakh by the 2018 amendment, effective 29 March 2018. Under Section 4(6), gratuity can be forfeited to the extent of damage if the employee's services were terminated for causing damage to property, and wholly forfeited if terminated for violent or riotous conduct or an offence involving moral turpitude in the course of employment. Section 5 empowers the appropriate government to exempt establishments. Section 6 covers nomination, Section 7 covers payment, Section 8 covers recovery, Section 9 covers penalties, and Section 13 gives protection against attachment. The controlling authority is appointed by the appropriate government, and the appellate authority hears appeals. Employer contributions are not required from employees, and the employer bears the entire cost. The Code on Social Security 2020 subsumes this Act, and it provides for gratuity to fixed-term employees after one year of service.

question: Under the provisions of the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, what is the maximum amount of gratuity payable?
subject: Social Security
detail: Section 4(3) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 caps the gratuity payable to an employee. The ceiling was originally Rs. 10,000. It was raised to Rs. 20,000 in 1984, to Rs. 3.5 lakh in 1994, and to Rs. 10 lakh by the 2010 Amendment (effective 24 May 2010). The 2010 Amendment also widened the definition of 'employee' and made other changes. Gratuity is payable after 5 years of continuous service, on superannuation, retirement, resignation, death or disablement. The 5-year condition is waived in cases of death or disablement. The formula is 15 days' wages x years of service / 26 for establishments covered by the Act, with wages meaning last drawn basic plus dearness allowance. Service of more than 6 months in the final year is rounded up to a full year. Elimination: Rs. 3.5 lakh is the pre-2010 figure, so (a) is outdated. Rs. 7.5 lakh and Rs. 5 lakh were never statutory ceilings, so (b) and (d) are wrong. The 2018 Amendment (effective 29 March 2018) allowed the Central Government to notify the ceiling, but the Rs. 10 lakh ceiling is still in force. It also increased maternity leave from 12 to 26 weeks for the purposes of continuous service.
explanations: Wrong: Rs. 3,50,000 was the ceiling from 1994 until the 2010 Amendment raised it.
Wrong: Rs. 7,50,000 has never been a statutory ceiling under the Act.
Correct: The 2010 Amendment (effective 24 May 2010) fixed the ceiling at Rs. 10,00,000 under Section 4(3).
Wrong: Rs. 5,00,000 has never been a ceiling under the Act.
keyfact: Maximum gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 is Rs. 10 lakh (since 24 May 2010).
option_notes: Rs. 3.5 lakh was the ceiling fixed by the 1994 amendment, which was in force until 2010. It is a favourite distractor in questions on this topic because it is the old figure. The ceiling was raised after that, so this figure is no longer valid.

Rs. 7.5 lakh is not a gratuity ceiling under the Payment of Gratuity Act. It is a distractor with no statutory basis. Do not confuse it with other thresholds such as tax-exemption limits, which have been revised separately over the years.

Rs. 10 lakh is the maximum gratuity under Section 4(3) after the 2010 Amendment, effective 24 May 2010. It applies to employees covered by the Act. The Central Government may notify a higher ceiling under the 2018 Amendment. Gratuity above the ceiling may still be paid under the contract or employer policy.
Rs. 5 lakh is not a ceiling under the Act at any point in its history. It is a distractor. The ceiling moved from Rs. 3.5 lakh directly to Rs. 10 lakh.
related: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972.
The gratuity ceiling was raised to Rs. 10 lakh by the 2010 Amendment, effective 24 May 2010.
Gratuity formula: last drawn wages x 15/26 x completed years of service.
Five years of continuous service is required, except in cases of death or disablement.
Employees make no contribution to gratuity; it is paid by the employer alone.
The Act applies to establishments with 10 or more employees.
Gratuity must be paid within 30 days of it becoming payable.
The 2018 Amendment allows the Central Government to notify the ceiling.
summary: The answer is (c) Rs. 10,00,000. The Payment of Gratuity (Amendment) Act, 2010 raised the ceiling in Section 4(3) from Rs. 3,50,000 to Rs. 10,00,000, with effect from 24 May 2010. This was the ceiling in force when the 2015 paper was set.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972. It extends to the whole of India. It applies to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and establishments, and to other establishments with 10 or more employees on any day of the preceding 12 months. Once covered, an establishment remains covered even if numbers fall below 10. Gratuity is a statutory retirement benefit, funded entirely by the employer, with no employee contribution. Eligibility generally requires 5 years of continuous service, which is waived on death or disablement. Calculation is 15 days' wages for each completed year of service, using the formula last drawn wages x 15/26 x years of service. For seasonal establishments, 7 days' wages per season is payable. Under Section 4, gratuity may be forfeited in whole or in part for damage or loss caused by the employee's wilful act, or for misconduct amounting to an offence involving moral turpitude. Section 7 requires the employer to pay within 30 days of it becoming due, failing which simple interest is payable. The employee or nominee applies in Form I, and the controlling authority decides disputes, with appeal to the appropriate government or appellate authority. Section 5 allows exemption. Section 6 deals with nomination. Section 13 protects gratuity from attachment. Penalties are in Sections 9 and 10. Key amendments came in 1984, 1987, 1994, 2010 and 2018. The 2010 Amendment included teachers in the definition of 'employee' retrospectively from 3 April 1997, following the Supreme Court decision in Birla Institute of Technology. The 2018 Amendment extended the maternity leave provisions for purposes of continuous service.

question: Under the provisions of the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, who among the following is NOT part of the ‘family’ of a male employee?
options: His children whether married or unmarried
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Section 2(h) of the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 defines 'family'. For a male employee it comprises: (i) his wife, (ii) his children, whether married or unmarried, (iii) his dependent parents, and (iv) the widow and children of his predeceased son, together with the children of a predeceased son's widow where applicable. For a female employee it comprises: her husband, her children (married or unmarried), her dependent parents OR the dependent parents of her husband, and the widow and children of her predeceased son. The definition matters for nomination under Section 6 and for payment on the employee's death under Section 4(1). A nomination made by an employee with a family is valid only in favour of family members, and if the employee later acquires a family, the earlier nomination becomes invalid. Key trap: for a male employee only HIS own parents count; the wife's parents are excluded. In the question, children of a predeceased SON are covered, but the statutory text does not name children of a predeceased daughter. Option (b) is therefore a distractor that sounds plausible, yet option (d) is the clearly excluded category and the intended answer. Note that after the 2018 amendment the definition was widened for female employees, who may choose either her own or her husband's parents.
explanations: Incorrect as the answer: children, married or unmarried, are expressly included in 'family' under Section 2(h).
Not the best answer: the Act names the widow and children of a predeceased son, not of a daughter. Even so, the examiner's intended exclusion is the wife's parents, so this is not the key.
Incorrect as the answer: the employee's own dependent parents are expressly included in the family of a male employee.
Correct: the wife's parents are not part of a male employee's family. Only a female employee can include her husband's dependent parents, as an alternative to her own.
keyfact: A male employee's family excludes his wife's parents, while a female employee's family may include her husband's parents (Section 2(h), Gratuity Act 1972).
option_notes: Children of the employee, married or unmarried, are part of the family under Section 2(h). This includes sons and daughters regardless of marital status. Their inclusion matters for nomination and for distributing gratuity on the employee's death under Section 4(1) and Section 6.

Children of a predeceased daughter are not named in Section 2(h). The Act covers the widow and children of a predeceased son. This is a common trap, since a candidate may assume that all grandchildren are included. Grandchildren through a daughter are not listed.

Dependent parents of the employee are included in the family of a male employee. For a female employee, the Act allows either her own dependent parents or her husband's dependent parents. Dependency on the employee is the key condition.

Dependent parents of the wife (the in-laws) are not included in a male employee's family. This is the standard exclusion in Section 2(h), and it is the answer to this question. The in-law provision applies only to female employees, for whom the husband's parents may be nominated.
related: Section 2(h) defines 'family' under the Payment of Gratuity Act.
Gratuity ceiling is Rs 20 lakh after the 2018 amendment.
Gratuity is calculated as 15 days' wages for each completed year of service.
Five years' continuous service is not required in case of death or disablement.
Section 4(6) provides for forfeiture of gratuity for wilful damage or moral turpitude.
Nomination is made under Section 6 using Form F.
Section 13 protects gratuity from attachment.
A female employee's family may include either her own or her husband's dependent parents.
summary: The answer is (d). Under Section 2(h) of the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, the 'family' of a male employee means his wife, his children (whether married or unmarried), his dependent parents and the widow and children of his predeceased son. The dependent parents of his wife are not included, so (d) is the one that is NOT part of the family.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972. It applies to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railway companies, shops and establishments with 10 or more employees, and to other notified establishments. Gratuity is payable on superannuation, retirement or resignation, and on death or disablement due to accident or disease. The five-year continuous service requirement does not apply to death or disablement. Continuous service means 240 days in a year (or 190 days for mines), and 120 days for an establishment with a 6-day week. The 5-year minimum was relevant in the Mettur Chemical case and other cases. The formula for gratuity is 15 days' wages for each completed year of service or part thereof exceeding 6 months. For establishments not covered by seasonal work, wages are last drawn basic plus DA, with 15 days computed as (last drawn wages × 15 / 26). Seasonal establishments pay 7 days per season. The maximum gratuity is Rs 20 lakh, raised from Rs 10 lakh by the 2018 amendment. The controlling authority is appointed under Section 3 and the appropriate government may notify it. The employer must pay within 30 days of it becoming payable, and simple interest is due on delay. The appellate authority hears appeals within 60 days. Nomination is under Section 6 using Form F. Forfeiture of gratuity is allowed under Section 4(6) for damage to property caused by wilful act, and for moral turpitude offences. Gratuity is exempt from attachment under Section 13. Penalties for offences are in Section 9. The 2018 amendment also allowed the government to notify the ceiling and extended maternity provisions. Other angles: the definitions of 'employee', 'wages' and 'continuous service', the role of the controlling authority, and the exemptions under Section 5.

question: Under the provisions of the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, what is the minimum period of service an employee must have served to make him eligible for gratuity on his retirement or resignation?
subject: Social Security
detail: Section 4(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 says gratuity is payable to an employee on termination of employment after he has rendered continuous service of not less than five years: (a) on superannuation, (b) on retirement or resignation, or (c) on death or disablement due to accident or disease. The five-year condition does not apply where termination is due to death or disablement; in that case gratuity is payable to the employee or his nominee/legal heir regardless of length of service. Judicial interpretation (and Section 2A) treats 'continuous service' as uninterrupted service, including periods of absence due to sickness, accident, leave, lay-off, strike or lock-out that is not illegal. Completing 240 days in a year counts as a year for establishments working 6 days a week (190 days for mines and seasonal establishments; 120 days for seasonal establishments is separate). The rate is 15 days' wages for every completed year of service or part thereof exceeding six months, computed on last drawn wages (basic plus DA) divided by 26 days; the ceiling is Rs 20 lakh (since 2018). Options of ten, seven and six years do not match any provision of the Act, so they are wrong.
explanations: Incorrect: Ten years is not a threshold in the Act. It has no bearing on eligibility for gratuity.
Correct: Section 4(1) requires at least five years of continuous service for gratuity on retirement or resignation.
Incorrect: Seven years is not prescribed anywhere in the Act.
Incorrect: Six years is not the qualifying period. Six months is relevant only for rounding up a part-year of service when calculating the amount.
