keyfact: Gratuity on retirement or resignation needs 5 years of continuous service (Sec 4(1)); no minimum on death or disablement.
option_notes: Ten years: There is no ten-year rule in the Payment of Gratuity Act. Ten or more employees on any day of the preceding 12 months is the coverage threshold for establishments (factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and establishments), not a service period. Once covered, an establishment stays covered even if employee numbers later fall below ten.

Five years: This is the minimum continuous service under Section 4(1) for gratuity on superannuation, retirement or resignation. It is waived on death or disablement. Courts have held that the figure means five years of continuous service, so a person who has completed 4 years and 240 days is treated as having completed five years in some interpretations of the Act. Gratuity is 15 days' wages per completed year, with a ceiling of Rs 20 lakh.

Seven years: The Act has no seven-year provision. Do not confuse it with other labour-law periods, such as the seven-year limit that features in some pension or service contexts. Gratuity eligibility is fixed at five years.

Six years: Not a qualifying period. The figure 'six months' is used in the gratuity formula: a part of a year exceeding six months is counted as a full year. For example, 7 years and 8 months of service is counted as 8 years for calculating the amount.
related: Payment of Gratuity Act came into force on 16 September 1972.
Gratuity ceiling is Rs 20 lakh since the 2018 amendment.
Gratuity formula: last drawn wages x 15/26 x completed years of service.
Five-year minimum is waived on death or disablement of the employee.
Act applies to establishments with ten or more employees.
Employer must pay gratuity within 30 days of it becoming payable.
The Code on Social Security 2020 allows fixed-term employees gratuity after one year.
Controlling Authority under Section 3 decides gratuity disputes.
summary: The answer is (b) Five years. Under Section 4(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, gratuity becomes payable on superannuation, retirement or resignation only after the employee has completed five years of continuous service.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972 and extends to the whole of India. It applies to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railway companies, shops and establishments with ten or more employees, and to other establishments notified by the Central Government. Gratuity is a statutory retirement benefit, a recognition of long service, and is not a gift. Eligibility under Section 4: five years of continuous service on superannuation, retirement, resignation, or death or disablement (no minimum for death or disablement). Formula: (last drawn monthly wages x 15 x years of service) / 26. Wages mean basic plus dearness allowance. A part of a year exceeding six months counts as a full year. Maximum gratuity is Rs 20 lakh (raised from Rs 10 lakh by the 2018 amendment). Employers must pay within 30 days of it becoming payable, otherwise simple interest is due. The employee or nominee applies on Form I (nomination Form F). Gratuity can be forfeited wholly or partly for damage or loss caused by the employee's wilful act or negligence, or for termination due to riotous or violent conduct or an offence involving moral turpitude committed in the course of employment. Gratuity is exempt from tax up to the statutory limit for covered employees. Controlling Authority is appointed under Section 3, and appeals go to the appropriate Government or appellate authority within 60 days. Disputes about the amount are decided by the Controlling Authority. The Code on Social Security 2020 subsumes this Act and allows fixed-term employees gratuity after one year of service. Other angles: Section 2A continuous service, Section 5 exemptions, Section 13 protection of gratuity from attachment, Section 14 overriding effect, and penalties under Section 9.

question: Under the provisions of the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act 1996, employment of how many female construction workers make it mandatory for providing crèche facilities?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The BOCW Act, 1996 (central Act; commenced 1996 along with the BOCW Welfare Cess Act, 1996) regulates employment and safety, health and welfare in building and other construction work. It applies to establishments employing ten or more workers. Section 36 of the Act requires the employer to provide crèches, and the details are in the BOCW Central Rules, 1998. Rule 243 says that where more than fifty female building workers are ordinarily employed, there must be a suitable room or rooms for the use of children under six years. The rules also deal with the room's size, lighting, ventilation, cleanliness, and the staff to be provided. Students often mix this up with the thresholds in other labour laws. The Factories Act, 1948 (Sec 48) uses more than thirty women workers. The Contract Labour Act, 1970 uses twenty or more women. The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 uses fifty or more women. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 requires a crèche in establishments with fifty or more employees, counting all employees. Elimination: twenty, thirty and forty are not BOCW thresholds, which leaves fifty. Note that the 'forty' option has no statutory use in any of these Acts.
explanations: Incorrect: 'More than twenty' is not the BOCW threshold. Twenty is the number of women in the Contract Labour Act (Rule 43) for crèche provision.
Incorrect: 'More than thirty' is the Factories Act, 1948 (Sec 48) threshold for women workers, not the BOCW threshold.
Incorrect: 'More than forty' is not a crèche threshold in any major labour law, so it is a distractor.
Correct: BOCW Central Rules, 1998 (Rule 243) require a crèche where more than fifty female building workers are ordinarily employed.
keyfact: BOCW crèche: more than 50 female workers, children under 6 years; Factories Act 30; Contract Labour 20.
option_notes: Twenty: the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and its Central Rules require a crèche where twenty or more women are ordinarily employed by a contractor. The Act applies to establishments with twenty or more contract workers. It is a frequent confusion with the BOCW rule. Wrong here because BOCW uses fifty.

Thirty: Section 48 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires a crèche in every factory where more than thirty women workers are ordinarily employed. The room is for children under six years. State rules prescribe standards. The Factories Act applies to premises with ten or more workers using power, or twenty or more without power. Wrong here because BOCW uses fifty.

Forty: this is not a statutory crèche threshold under the Factories Act, the Contract Labour Act, the Plantations Labour Act or the BOCW Act. It appears only as a distractor. Do not confuse it with any thresholds for canteens, welfare officers or safety committees, which have their own numbers. Wrong here.

Fifty: the BOCW Central Rules, 1998 (Rule 243) require a crèche where more than fifty women are ordinarily employed as building workers. It is for children under six years. The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 uses fifty or more women. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 uses fifty or more employees. This is the correct option.
related: BOCW Act, 1996 applies to establishments employing ten or more building workers.
The BOCW Welfare Cess Act, 1996 levies a cess of 1 percent of the cost of construction.
BOCW Central Rules, 1998 (Rule 243) require a crèche where more than fifty women are employed.
Factories Act, 1948 requires a crèche where more than thirty women are employed.
Contract Labour Act, 1970 requires a crèche where twenty or more women are employed.
Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 requires a crèche in establishments with fifty or more employees.
BOCW workers must be aged 18 to 60 and have worked 90 days in the preceding twelve months to register as beneficiaries.
The BOCW Act is subsumed in the OSH and Working Conditions Code, 2020.
summary: The answer is (d), more than fifty. Under the BOCW Act, 1996 and the BOCW Central Rules, 1998 (Rule 243), a crèche must be provided where more than fifty female building workers are ordinarily employed. The crèche is for children below six years of age.
topic_notes: The Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 was enacted after the Supreme Court and the National Commission on Labour stressed the need for a law for this sector. It applies to every establishment employing ten or more building workers, and to building or other construction work in which the project cost exceeds a prescribed amount in some cases. Its companion law is the BOCW Welfare Cess Act, 1996, which levies a cess of 1 to 2 percent of the cost of construction, with 1 percent now notified. State Welfare Boards use the cess to fund benefits. The Central Rules, 1998 prescribe the detailed standards. The Act provides for Advisory Committees (central and state), registration of establishments, registration of beneficiaries aged 18 to 60 who have worked 90 days in the preceding twelve months, and Welfare Boards. It also covers safety committees, safety officers, canteens, drinking water, urinals, latrines and first aid, accommodation, and a crèche where more than fifty women are employed. Inspectors are appointed for enforcement. Cess collected is deposited with the state boards. The Act was repealed and subsumed in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, though the older Act is the basis of exam questions. Other crèche thresholds: Factories Act 30 women, Contract Labour 20 women, Plantations Labour Act 50 women, Mines Act 50 women (for the crèche), Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 50 employees, with four visits a day allowed to the mother. Also recall that the Interstate Migrant Workmen Act, 1979 is another law frequently confused with this one.

question: Which one of the following is NOT a statutory provision under the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act 1996?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: The BOCW (RE&CS) Act 1996 has a chapter on welfare measures and on safety and health. Its welfare provisions require the employer to provide basic facilities at the building or construction site. These include drinking water, latrines and urinals, temporary living accommodation near the site, canteens where the number of workers is large, and crèches where women are employed. First-aid facilities are also required. The Building and Other Construction Workers Central Rules 1998 detail these facilities, for example standards for water points, the number of latrines per workers, and accommodation. The phrase 'shelters, rest rooms and lunch rooms' comes from Section 47 of the Factories Act 1948, which is for factories with more than 150 workers. It is not the wording used in the BOCW Act. Elimination: drinking water, latrines and urinals, and accommodation are standard BOCW welfare items, so they cannot be the 'NOT' answer. Rest rooms and lunch rooms is the factory-law phrase, so (d) is the odd one out. A companion law is the BOCW Welfare Cess Act 1996, which funds the Welfare Boards.
explanations: Incorrect as the answer: drinking water is a welfare facility the employer must provide under the BOCW Act and Rules, so it is a statutory provision.
Incorrect as the answer: temporary living accommodation near the site is a statutory welfare provision for building workers, who are often migrants.
Incorrect as the answer: sanitary latrines and urinals are statutory welfare and sanitation provisions under the Act and Rules.
Correct answer: 'Rest rooms and lunch rooms' is the Factories Act Sec 47 phrase and is not the BOCW Act's wording, so it is the item that is NOT a statutory provision here.
keyfact: Rest rooms and lunch rooms are a Factories Act (Sec 47) provision, not a BOCW Act 1996 provision.
option_notes: Drinking water: a basic welfare facility at construction sites. The BOCW Central Rules 1998 require a sufficient supply of wholesome drinking water, and the Factories Act 1948 also requires it (Sec 18). It is among the first facilities listed in welfare chapters of labour laws.

Accommodation: the BOCW Act requires the employer to provide temporary living accommodation, with cooking and sanitary facilities, to workers at or near the site. This suits construction workers, who are often migrants. The Rules set standards for space and facilities.
Latrines and urinals: sanitation facilities required at sites. The Rules specify separate facilities for men and women and ratios per number of workers. The Factories Act also requires them (Sec 19).

Rest rooms and lunch rooms: the phrase comes from Sec 47 of the Factories Act 1948, which requires shelters, rest rooms and lunch rooms in factories with more than 150 workers. The BOCW Act does not use this wording. It applies to factories and is not a BOCW provision.
related: BOCW Act 1996 applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers.
The BOCW Welfare Cess Act 1996 levies cess of 1 to 2 percent of construction cost.
The BOCW Act came into force on 19 March 1996.
Factories Act Sec 47: shelters, rest rooms and lunch rooms for factories with more than 150 workers.
Factories Act Sec 48: crèche where more than 30 women are employed.
The OSH Code 2020 subsumes the BOCW Act and the Cess Act.
State Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Boards administer the cess funds.
summary: The answer is (d). Rest rooms and lunch rooms are a Factories Act 1948 provision (Sec 47, shelters, rest rooms and lunch rooms). The BOCW Act 1996 lists drinking water, latrines and urinals, and temporary accommodation among its welfare facilities, but not 'rest rooms and lunch rooms'. This answer rests on my recollection of the Act's section numbering, not a re-check against the text.
topic_notes: The Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act 1996 came into force on 19 March 1996. It followed a Supreme Court direction and the long-standing demand for protecting construction workers. It applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers. The Act regulates employment and conditions of service, and provides for safety, health and welfare measures. It covers working hours, weekly rest, overtime, wages, safety committees and the appointment of safety officers. It also provides for registration of establishments and of beneficiaries. State Welfare Boards are constituted under it. The companion Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Cess Act 1996 levies a cess of 1 to 2 percent of the cost of construction, collected from employers, to finance the Welfare Boards. Welfare measures include drinking water, latrines and urinals, accommodation, canteens, crèches and first aid. Benefits through the Boards include pension, accident and medical assistance, and education help for children. The Central Rules were made in 1998. Related labour laws a student should compare are the Factories Act 1948, the Mines Act 1952 and the Contract Labour Act 1970. Under the Code on Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions 2020, the BOCW Act is subsumed along with 12 other central laws. The Factories Act Sec 46 deals with canteens, Sec 47 with shelters and rest rooms, and Sec 48 with crèches.

question: Under the provisions of the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act 1996, the employer of an establishment has to appoint a Safety Officer if there are:
options: five hundred or more building workers
two hundred and fifty or more building workers
three hundred or more building workers
one hundred or more building workers
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The BOCW (RE&CS) Act 1996 and the BOCW Central Rules 1998 together regulate safety, health and welfare of construction workers. The Act is applicable to every establishment employing 10 or more building workers. Safety provisions: Section 40 requires safety committees where 500 or more workers are ordinarily employed (this is a statutory provision of the Act, Section 40, covering constitution of Safety Committees by employers). Section 40(2) provides for appointment of safety officers by employers, the qualifications and duties of whom are prescribed by rules. The Central Rules 1998 (Rule 209) lay down that an employer ordinarily employing 500 or more workers must appoint a Safety Officer, and Rule 210 describes duties. Safety committee provisions (Rule 38 of the rules) also relate to 500 or more workers. The 500 figure is the standard threshold; 250, 300 and 100 are distractors with no basis in the safety officer provision. Elimination: pick the highest, round threshold familiar from the safety committee rule (500), and remember that 100 workers is not a threshold here, and 250/300 do not appear in this context. Related thresholds in other statutes: Factories Act requires a Welfare Officer at 500 workers and a Safety Officer at 1000 workers.
explanations: Correct: the Safety Officer requirement applies where 500 or more building workers are ordinarily employed in an establishment.
Incorrect: 250 is not a threshold for a Safety Officer under the Act or Rules.
Incorrect: 300 is not the threshold; the requirement starts at 500 workers.
Incorrect: 100 is too low; the Safety Officer requirement does not apply at this level.
keyfact: BOCW: Safety Officer is required where 500 or more building workers are employed.
option_notes: 500 or more workers: the threshold at which a construction employer must appoint a Safety Officer and also constitute a Safety Committee under the BOCW law. The Safety Officer must have prescribed qualifications (e.g. a degree/diploma in engineering plus a safety qualification) and duties such as advising on safety, inspecting sites and investigating accidents. This is the correct option.

250 workers: not a recognised threshold in the BOCW Act or Rules for Safety Officers. It is a plausible distractor. In the BOCW framework, the key worker-number thresholds are 10 (applicability of the Act), 50 (some welfare facilities) and 500 (Safety Officer/Committee). Do not confuse it with other labour laws.

300 workers: not a recognised threshold for Safety Officers under the BOCW Act. Thresholds of 300 appear elsewhere, such as the Industrial Disputes Act (Chapter V-B, earlier 100, with proposals to raise it to 300 in labour codes) and Standing Orders. It does not apply here.

100 workers: not the Safety Officer threshold under the BOCW Act. 100 appears in other laws, such as the Industrial Disputes Act (Chapter V-B applies to establishments with 100 or more workers) and the Contract Labour Act (applicable to 20 or more workers). It is a distractor in this question.
related: The BOCW Act 1996 applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers.
The BOCW Welfare Cess Act 1996 levies a cess of 1 to 2 percent of construction cost.
BOCW Central Rules were framed in 1998.
Beneficiaries must be aged 18 to 60 and have worked at least 90 days in the preceding 12 months.
State Building Workers Welfare Boards are constituted under Section 18.
The BOCW Act is subsumed under the OSH and Working Conditions Code 2020.
Safety Committee is required where 500 or more workers are employed.
summary: The answer is (a): five hundred or more building workers. Under the BOCW Central Rules 1998 (Rule 209), made under the 1996 Act, every employer who ordinarily employs 500 or more building workers must appoint a Safety Officer. This threshold is the one to memorise.
topic_notes: The BOCW (RE&CS) Act 1996 was enacted to regulate employment and conditions of service, safety, health and welfare measures of building workers. It was passed along with the BOCW Welfare Cess Act 1996, under which a cess of 1 to 2 percent of construction cost is levied to fund Welfare Boards. The Act applies to every establishment which employs, or employed on any day of the preceding twelve months, ten or more building workers. The Central Rules 1998 were framed under the Act. Key features: registration of establishments (Section 7), Central and State Advisory Committees, State Building Workers Welfare Boards (Section 18), registration of beneficiaries (workers aged 18 to 60 with at least 90 days of work in the preceding year), and safety provisions in Chapter VII. Chapter VI deals with hours of work, welfare measures and other conditions. Inspectors are appointed under Section 39. Penalties are prescribed in Chapter X. The Act was enacted following the Supreme Court's concern, as in the case of the construction workers, and it implements Articles 39, 42 and 43 of the Directive Principles. The Act is being subsumed into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020. Other angles: the Safety Committee (Section 40), the requirement of a safety policy, the appointment of Safety Officers, the cess rate, and the number of workers for which welfare facilities such as canteens are required.

question: Under the provisions of the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act 1996, a building worker who has been registered as a beneficiary can contribute to the Fund created under the Act till he attains the age of:
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 regulates employment, safety, health and welfare in construction. It came into force on 19 March 1996 and applies to establishments employing 10 or more workers. It was passed after the Supreme Court's directions in the Public Union for Civil Liberties case and the 1996 Cess Act. Section 12 covers registration of building workers as beneficiaries. The worker must be at least 18 and under 60 years of age, and must have done at least 90 days of construction work in the preceding 12 months. A registered beneficiary contributes to the Welfare Fund at the rate set by the State Welfare Board's rules, and stays a beneficiary until he reaches 60. State Building Workers Welfare Boards (Section 18) administer the Fund, financed mainly by the cess of 1 to 2 percent of construction cost under the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996. Options 62 and 65 are wrong because they exceed the statutory age limit. Option 58 is wrong because it is the age used in some other schemes, not this Act. Hence 60 years.
explanations: Wrong: 62 years is not the age limit in the Act. It is a distractor.
Correct: Section 12 sets the eligible age at 18 to 60 years, and the beneficiary contributes and remains registered until 60.
Wrong: 58 years is the retirement or pension age in some other schemes, such as the old EPS retirement age, not in the BOCW Act.
Wrong: 65 years is too high. It is not the BOCW age limit, though 65 appears in some other welfare contexts.
keyfact: BOCW Act Section 12: workers aged 18 to under 60 with at least 90 days of work in the past 12 months can register, and remain beneficiaries until 60.
option_notes: Sixty-two years is not the age limit under the BOCW Act. Some service rules and a few state schemes use retirement or pension ages around 62 (for example, certain university and judicial posts). The BOCW Act sets no such age. Eligibility to register as a beneficiary is 18 to under 60 years.

Sixty years is the upper age limit for registration and contribution as a beneficiary under Section 12 of the BOCW Act 1996. The lower limit is 18 years. The worker must also have done at least 90 days of construction work in the preceding 12 months. Many state welfare boards pay pension to registered workers on reaching 60.

Fifty-eight years was the age for EPF/EPS pension entitlement (the EPS 1995 pension starts at 58 years). It is a well-known EPFO figure but unrelated to BOCW registration. EPS allows early pension from 50 years with reduction. It is a frequent distractor.

Sixty-five years is not specified for BOCW registration. It appears in other contexts, such as the eligibility age for old age benefit in some schemes and the retirement age of certain constitutional posts like the High Court judges, who retire at 62, and Supreme Court judges at 65. It is not the BOCW limit.
related: BOCW Act 1996 came into force on 19 March 1996.
It applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers.
Eligible beneficiary age is 18 to under 60 years, with at least 90 days of work in the preceding 12 months.
Welfare cess under the Cess Act 1996 is 1 to 2 percent of the cost of construction.
State Building Workers Welfare Boards are constituted under Section 18.
Registering Officers are appointed under Section 7 for establishments.
The Act is being subsumed into the OSH Code 2020.
summary: The answer is (b) Sixty years. Under Section 12 of the BOCW Act 1996, a building worker aged 18 to 60 who has worked at least 90 days in the preceding 12 months can register as a beneficiary. The beneficiary contributes to the Welfare Fund and remains a member until he attains 60 years.
topic_notes: The BOCW (RE&CS) Act, 1996 was enacted to regulate the employment and conditions of service of building and other construction workers and to provide for their safety, health and welfare. It came into force on 19 March 1996 and applies to every establishment employing 10 or more building workers. It is supported by the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996, which levies a cess of 1 to 2 percent of the cost of construction, and the central and state rules of 1998. Key structures: the Central Advisory Committee (Section 3), State Advisory Committees, and State Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Boards (Section 18), which administer the Welfare Fund and registered beneficiaries. Under Section 12, a building worker aged 18 to 60 years with at least 90 days of work in the preceding 12 months can be registered as a beneficiary. Employers must register their establishments with the Registering Officer (Section 7). Welfare Boards provide benefits such as pension, accident assistance, medical aid, maternity benefit, education aid for children and housing loans. Safety provisions cover Chapter VI, with Safety Committees (Section 40) required in establishments with 500 or more workers, and Safety Officers where 500 or more are employed. Inspectors are appointed under Section 39, and penalties are in Chapter X. The Act is now being subsumed into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. Related angles for future questions are the cess rate, the number of workers that triggers applicability, the age limits, the Fund contribution, and the Supreme Court's role in implementing the cess collection.

question: Under the Fundamental Rights in the Constitution of India, Right to religion is NOT restricted by:
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 25(1) guarantees every person freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion, 'subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part'. These are the grounds on which the State may restrict the right. Article 25(2) also lets the State regulate economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religious practice, provide for social welfare and reform, and throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus. The definition of Hindus in the Explanation includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists. Article 26 gives religious denominations the right to establish and maintain institutions (a), manage their own affairs in religion (b), own and acquire movable and immovable property (c), and administer such property in accordance with law (d). Articles 26(a) and (b) are also subject to public order, morality and health. The right to acquire and administer property is therefore a component of the religious freedom of denominations, not a limit on it. Elimination: public order, morality and health are the three textual limits in Articles 25 and 26, so (a), (b) and (c) are wrong. That leaves (d) as the answer. Note that the property right in Article 26 is itself subject to 'in accordance with law'. Property in general ceased to be a Fundamental Right through the 44th Amendment in 1978, which made it a legal right under Article 300A.
explanations: Wrong: public order is an express restriction in Article 25(1), and also in Article 26 for the denominational rights.
Wrong: morality is an express restriction in Article 25(1), and also in Article 26 for the denominational rights.
Wrong: health is an express restriction in Article 25(1), and also in Article 26 for the denominational rights.
Correct: acquiring and administering property is a right of religious denominations under Article 26(c)-(d). It is not a ground that restricts the right to religion.
keyfact: Articles 25-26 are limited by public order, morality and health; the right to own and administer property is a positive right of denominations under Article 26(c)-(d).
option_notes: Public order: a ground for restricting fundamental freedoms. It appears in Article 19(2)-(4) and in Articles 25 and 26. It is wider than law and order, and courts distinguish public order from the narrower law and order and from the wider security of the State. It was added to Article 19(2) by the First Amendment in 1951.

Morality: a restriction on religious freedom in Articles 25(1) and 26. Practices judged immoral, for example certain forms of devadasi dedication or human sacrifice, can be regulated or prohibited. In the Sabarimala judgment (2018) the Supreme Court read it as constitutional morality, not popular or social morality.

Health: a restriction in Articles 25(1) and 26. The State may regulate religious practices that endanger public health, for example sanitation at pilgrimages or animal sacrifice. It is one of the three textual grounds, along with public order and morality.

Acquiring and administering property: this is the content of Article 26(c) and (d), the right of religious denominations to own and acquire movable and immovable property and to administer it in accordance with law. The Shirur Mutt case (1954) established the 'essential religious practices' doctrine. The Supreme Court held that the State cannot take away a denomination's right to administer property, although it can regulate the administration.
related: Article 25 applies to all persons, including non-citizens; Article 26 applies to religious denominations.
Article 27: no compulsion to pay taxes for promoting a particular religion.
Article 28: regulates religious instruction in educational institutions.
The Explanation to Article 25 treats the wearing and carrying of kirpans as part of the Sikh religion.
The 'essential religious practices' test originated in the Shirur Mutt case (1954).
The 44th Amendment (1978) removed property from Fundamental Rights and added Article 300A.
'Secular' was inserted in the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976).
Article 25(2)(b) allows the opening of Hindu religious institutions to all Hindus, including Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists.
summary: The answer is (d). Article 25(1) makes the freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion subject to public order, morality, health and other Fundamental Rights. The right to acquire and administer property is not a restriction on this right. It is an affirmative right of religious denominations under Article 26(c) and (d).
topic_notes: Articles 25-28 make up the Right to Freedom of Religion. Article 25 gives all persons, citizens and non-citizens alike, freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion. It is subject to public order, morality, health and the other Fundamental Rights. The State may regulate secular activities and provide for social reform. Wearing and carrying kirpans is deemed part of the Sikh profession of religion. Article 26 gives religious denominations the rights to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes, to manage their affairs in matters of religion, to own and acquire property, and to administer it according to law. Article 27 says no person shall be compelled to pay taxes for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion. Article 28 deals with religious instruction in educational institutions. There is none in institutions wholly maintained by the State. Institutions recognised or aided by the State cannot compel attendance at religious instruction without consent. Key cases: Shirur Mutt (1954) on essential religious practices; Ratilal Panachand Gandhi (1954); Bijoe Emmanuel (1986) on the national anthem; S.R. Bommai (1994) on secularism as part of the basic structure; Sabarimala (2018); Hijab case (Karnataka, 2022, a split verdict). The word 'secular' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. Fundamental Rights are in Part III, Articles 12-35. Article 25 applies to individuals, while Article 26 applies to denominations. Property is now a legal right under Article 300A.

question: Right to Privacy is an implied Fundamental Right traceable to:
options: Right to Life and Personal Liberty
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Privacy is not expressly mentioned in the Constitution; it is an implied right read into Part III by judicial interpretation. Article 21 says no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Through Maneka Gandhi (1978), 'life' and 'liberty' were given a wide meaning, and procedure must be fair, just and reasonable. Earlier cases such as M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) had denied a general fundamental right to privacy; Gobind v. State of M.P. (1975) and R. Rajagopal (1994), PUCL v. Union of India (1997) recognised it in part. The nine-judge bench in Puttaswamy (24 August 2017) unanimously overruled M.P. Sharma and the Kharak Singh portion denying privacy, and held privacy to be protected under Article 21 as part of the dignity of the individual, along with Articles 19 and the freedoms in Part III. Elimination: Equality (Arts 14-18), Exploitation (Arts 23-24) and Religion (Arts 25-28) deal with different subjects. Hence (d). Note: the 2015 exam predates Puttaswamy but the Article 21 link was already established in case law.
explanations: Incorrect: Right to Equality (Arts 14-18) covers equality before law, non-discrimination and equality of opportunity, not privacy.
Incorrect: Right against Exploitation (Arts 23-24) bans trafficking, forced labour and child labour in hazardous work; unrelated to privacy.
Incorrect: Freedom of Religion (Arts 25-28) protects conscience, practice and propagation of religion and management of religious affairs; privacy is not derived from it.
Correct: Privacy flows from Article 21 (life and personal liberty), as held in Puttaswamy (2017) and earlier cases like Gobind and PUCL.
keyfact: Privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21 (and Part III) per Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2017.
option_notes: Right to Equality: Articles 14-18 guarantee equality before law and equal protection of laws (14), prohibition of discrimination (15), equality in public employment (16), abolition of untouchability (17) and abolition of titles (18). Article 14 has been used for the doctrine of arbitrariness, reasonable classification and the rule of law. It is not the source of privacy, though Puttaswamy noted overlap among Articles 14, 19 and 21 (golden triangle).

Right against Exploitation: Articles 23 and 24. Article 23 prohibits human trafficking, begar and other forced labour; it applies against private persons too. Article 24 prohibits employing children below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous jobs. Key cases include PUDR v. Union of India (Asiad workers, 1982) and Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984). Not linked to privacy.

Right to Freedom of Religion: Articles 25-28. Article 25 gives freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion, subject to public order, morality and health. Article 26 allows religious denominations to manage their affairs; Article 27 bars compulsory taxes for promoting a religion; Article 28 concerns religious instruction in educational institutions. Not the source of privacy.

Right to Life and Personal Liberty: Article 21, which cannot be suspended even during Emergency (44th Amendment, Art 359). Maneka Gandhi (1978) expanded it. It now includes privacy, dignity, livelihood, speedy trial, clean environment, health and education (Art 21A added by the 86th Amendment, 2002). Puttaswamy (2017) located privacy here.
related: Puttaswamy case decided 24 August 2017 by a nine-judge bench.
Puttaswamy overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) on privacy.
ADM Jabalpur (1976) was also held wrongly decided in Puttaswamy.
Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Article 21: procedure must be just, fair and reasonable.
Article 21A (education 6-14 years) was inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002.
Digital Personal Data Protection Act was enacted in 2023.
B.N. Srikrishna Committee drafted the data protection framework in 2018.
Article 21 cannot be suspended during Emergency (44th Amendment).
summary: The correct answer is (d) Right to Life and Personal Liberty. The Supreme Court in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) held that privacy is a fundamental right intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21, and also part of the freedoms in Part III.
topic_notes: Right to privacy timeline: M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra (1954, 8 judges) held no privacy right against search and seizure. Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1962, 6 judges) struck down night domiciliary visits but held privacy not a fundamental right (Justice Subba Rao dissented). Gobind v. State of M.P. (1975) accepted a limited privacy right subject to compelling state interest. R. Rajagopal v. State of T.N. (1994) recognised privacy in the context of publication of personal life, the 'Auto Shankar' case. PUCL v. Union of India (1997) held phone tapping violates privacy and laid down safeguards. Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) addressed mental privacy and narco-analysis. Puttaswamy (2017): nine-judge bench, led by CJI J.S. Khehar, unanimously held privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21 and the freedoms of Part III; Justice D.Y. Chandrachud wrote the lead opinion overruling ADM Jabalpur (1976) as well. The case arose from challenges to Aadhaar. Puttaswamy II (2018) upheld Aadhaar with limits (struck down Section 57, restricted private use). Related legislation: Information Technology Act 2000 (Sections 43A, 72), Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, and the B.N. Srikrishna Committee (2017-18) on data protection. Privacy is subject to reasonable restrictions: legality, legitimate aim and proportionality. Other angles: Article 21 expansions, the golden triangle of Articles 14, 19 and 21, and the right to be forgotten.

question: Who appoints the Judges of High Court of a State?
options: The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
The Governor of the concerned State
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Appointment of High Court judges is governed by Article 217. The formal appointing authority is the President, acting on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister (Art. 74). In practice the Collegium system, evolved through the Three Judges Cases (S.P. Gupta 1981, Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association 1993, Special Reference 1998), gives primacy to the judiciary. The Collegium for High Court appointments consists of the CJI and the two senior-most Supreme Court judges, and the proposal is initiated by the High Court Chief Justice with his two senior-most colleagues. The NJAC (99th Amendment, 2014) was struck down in October 2015 in the Fourth Judges Case. Qualifications under Art. 217(2): Indian citizen, and either 10 years as a judicial officer or 10 years as a High Court advocate. Retirement age is 62 years (Art. 217(1), 15th Amendment 1963). Removal is the same as for Supreme Court judges, by Parliament through impeachment (Art. 124(4)). Elimination: the CJI only recommends and consults, the Governor is merely consulted, and the PM only advises. None of them is the appointing authority.
explanations: Incorrect: the Chief Justice of India is only consulted, and heads the Collegium that recommends names; he does not issue the appointment.
Correct: Art. 217(1) vests the power in the President, who appoints by warrant under his hand and seal.
Incorrect: the Governor is consulted in the process and appoints no High Court judges. He does appoint district judges under Art. 233, after consulting the High Court.
Incorrect: the Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers that advises the President, but the formal appointment is made by the President.
keyfact: High Court judges are appointed by the President (Art. 217) after consulting the CJI, the Governor and the High Court Chief Justice.
option_notes: The Chief Justice of India heads the Supreme Court and the Collegium, which consists of the CJI and the four senior-most judges for Supreme Court appointments and the CJI and two senior-most judges for High Court matters. Appointed by the President under Art. 124. Retirement age is 65. The CJI is consulted on High Court appointments and transfers (Art. 222), but the formal power rests with the President.

The President of India is the head of State, elected indirectly under Art. 54 for a 5-year term. Under Art. 74 he acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers. He appoints Supreme Court and High Court judges (Arts. 124 and 217), the Governors (Art. 155), the CAG, the Attorney General and others. The power to appoint judges is exercised in line with the Collegium's recommendations.

The Governor is the nominal executive head of a State (Art. 153), appointed by the President for 5 years (Art. 155-156). He is consulted in High Court judge appointments and appoints district judges (Art. 233) in consultation with the High Court. He appoints the Advocate General (Art. 165) and the State Public Service Commission members (Art. 316).

The Prime Minister is head of the Council of Ministers (Art. 74 and 75), appointed by the President. He is the link between the President and the Cabinet (Art. 78). He advises on appointments, but the Constitution does not make him the appointing authority for judges. Under the Collegium system the executive's role is limited to processing and returning names.
related: Art. 217: appointment and conditions of a High Court judge's office.
Retirement age: High Court judges 62 years; Supreme Court judges 65 years.
Art. 124: appointment of Supreme Court judges by the President.
NJAC was struck down by the Supreme Court in October 2015.
Art. 233: district judges are appointed by the Governor after consulting the High Court.
Art. 222: the President transfers judges after consulting the CJI.
Art. 226: High Court power to issue writs.
Art. 231: common High Court for two or more States.
summary: The correct answer is (b) The President of India. Under Article 217(1) of the Constitution, a High Court Judge is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal, after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State and, for judges other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of the High Court.
topic_notes: Judges of the High Courts are covered in Chapter V, Part VI of the Constitution (Arts. 214-231). Art. 214 provides for a High Court in each State, and Art. 231 allows Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more States. There are 25 High Courts in India; the Calcutta High Court (1862) is the oldest, and the Delhi High Court is the only UT with its own High Court besides J&K-Ladakh, Bombay and Madras. The Chief Justice is appointed by the President after consultation with the CJI and the Governor. Judges' salaries are charged to the Consolidated Fund of the State. Additional and acting judges are covered by Arts. 224 and 224A, which also allow the appointment of retired judges as ad hoc judges. Judges are transferred under Art. 222. The High Courts have writ jurisdiction under Art. 226, wider than the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction under Art. 32, and superintendence over subordinate courts under Art. 227. A judge resigns by writing to the President (Art. 217(1)(a)). Removal needs a special majority in both Houses under the Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968. Past exam angles: the age of retirement (62 for High Court, 65 for Supreme Court), the NJAC (99th Amendment and 121st Bill, struck down on 16 October 2015), the Second Judges Case (1993, primacy of CJI), the Third Judges Case (1998, Collegium of five) and the Memorandum of Procedure.

question: The Concurrent List to the Constitution of India was first introduced by:
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Before 1935, India had no Concurrent List. The Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford reforms) separated subjects into Central and Provincial lists, and it also split provincial subjects into Reserved and Transferred (dyarchy). The Government of India Act, 1935 proposed an All-India Federation and distributed legislative powers through the Seventh Schedule, which had three lists: the Federal Legislative List (59 items), the Provincial Legislative List (54 items) and the Concurrent List (36 items). Residuary powers were not given to either the federal or provincial legislatures but to the Governor-General. The Constitution of India, 1950 borrowed this three-list scheme, but it was not the first to introduce it. It also placed residuary powers with Parliament (Article 248), and it was influenced by the Canadian model on this point. The Constitution's Seventh Schedule (Article 246) now has the Union List (originally 97, now 98 items), the State List (originally 66, now 59) and the Concurrent List (originally 47, now 52). The Indian Independence Act, 1947 created the two dominions and did not create a Concurrent List. Eliminating (a), (c) and (d) leaves (b).
explanations: Incorrect: the 1919 Act had only Central and Provincial lists, plus the Reserved/Transferred division of provincial subjects, and no Concurrent List.
Correct: the 1935 Act first introduced the Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists in its Seventh Schedule.
Incorrect: the Constitution of 1950 adopted and continued the Concurrent List, but it was not the first to introduce it.
Incorrect: the Indian Independence Act, 1947 partitioned India and ended British paramountcy. It did not create any legislative list.
keyfact: The Concurrent List was first introduced by the Government of India Act, 1935, and the Constitution later adopted it.
option_notes: The Government of India Act, 1919 implemented the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms. It introduced dyarchy in the provinces, a bicameral central legislature (Council of State and Legislative Assembly), a separation of central and provincial subjects, and communal electorates for Sikhs and others. It also provided for a statutory commission after 10 years, and the Simon Commission followed in 1927. It set up the Public Service Commission, with the Lee Commission recommending the creation of the Federal Public Service Commission in 1926.

The Government of India Act, 1935 was the longest British-era Act, with 321 sections and 10 schedules. It provided for an All-India Federation, which never materialised, provincial autonomy, and dyarchy at the Centre. It created the Federal Court (1937), the Reserve Bank of India (1935), and the Federal, Provincial and Joint Public Service Commissions. It abolished dyarchy in the provinces, and it extended separate electorates to depressed classes, women and labour. Burma was separated and Sindh and Orissa were created as new provinces.

The Constitution of India came into force on 26 January 1950. The Seventh Schedule has the Union List, State List and Concurrent List. Article 246 distributes legislative powers, and Article 254 provides that on the Concurrent List, a Union law prevails in a conflict. Residuary powers rest with Parliament under Article 248. The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved five subjects to the Concurrent List: education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice.

The Indian Independence Act, 1947 was passed by the British Parliament on 18 July 1947 and came into effect on 15 August 1947. It created two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, and ended British suzerainty over the princely states. It also gave the Constituent Assemblies the power to frame constitutions and made the Governor-General a constitutional head. The Secretary of State for India's office was abolished. Until new constitutions were framed, the dominions were governed under the 1935 Act as adapted.
related: The Government of India Act, 1935 had a Federal List of 59 items, a Provincial List of 54 items and a Concurrent List of 36 items.
The Constitution's Concurrent List originally had 47 items and now has 52.
Article 254 provides that Union law prevails over State law on a Concurrent List conflict.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved education, forests, weights and measures, wild animals protection and administration of justice to the Concurrent List.
Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List give residuary powers to Parliament.
The Government of India Act, 1935 created the Federal Court (1937) and the RBI (1935).
Labour welfare and social security are in the Concurrent List, which is why both Parliament and States can legislate on them.
summary: The correct answer is (b) The Government of India Act, 1935. This Act introduced a three-fold division of legislative powers, with the Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists, for the first time. The Constitution of India, 1950 later adopted this scheme, with its Seventh Schedule containing the Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
topic_notes: Distribution of legislative powers in India follows a long history. The Government of India Act, 1919 divided subjects into Central and Provincial lists. The Government of India Act, 1935 introduced the three-fold list system in its Seventh Schedule: the Federal List (59 items), the Provincial List (54 items) and the Concurrent List (36 items). The Constitution of India continues this in its own Seventh Schedule under Article 246. The Union List has 98 items, the State List has 59 items and the Concurrent List has 52 items. On the Concurrent List, both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate, but under Article 254, if the two conflict, the Union law prevails. A State law can prevail only if it has received the President's assent (Article 254(2)). The idea of a Concurrent List was borrowed from the Government of India Act, 1935, and the concept of the Concurrent List was also influenced by the Australian Constitution. Residuary powers were given to the Centre, following the Canadian model. The 42nd Amendment (1976) transferred five subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List, namely education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice. Criminal law, marriage and divorce, bankruptcy, trade unions, labour welfare, social security and social insurance, and economic and social planning are also in the Concurrent List. Under Article 249, Parliament can legislate on a State List subject in the national interest if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a two-thirds majority. The Sarkaria Commission (1983) examined Centre-State relations, and the Punchhi Commission followed in 2007.

question: The Constituent Assembly which drafted the Constitution of India was set up under the:
options: Joint Resolution of Provincial Legislatures and Princely States, 1946
subject: Computers
detail: The Constituent Assembly of India was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan of May 1946. The Mission had three members: Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander. Its scheme provided for a 389-member Assembly: 296 seats for British India (292 from the Governor's provinces and 4 from Chief Commissioner's provinces) and 93 for princely states. Provincial seats were allotted in proportion to population (roughly one per million) among Muslims, Sikhs and General communities, and were filled by indirect election by the provincial legislative assemblies using the single transferable vote. Elections were held in July-August 1946 and the Congress won 208 seats and the Muslim League 73. The first meeting was on 9 December 1946, with Sachchidananda Sinha as temporary president; Rajendra Prasad became permanent president on 11 December 1946. The Objectives Resolution was moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946. The Indian Independence Act 1947 did not create the Assembly; it only made it a fully sovereign body, and after partition the membership fell to about 299. Option (a) is a non-existent instrument, and (d), the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947, dealt with partition.
explanations: Incorrect: there was no such 'Joint Resolution'. The Assembly was not created by a resolution of the provincial legislatures and princely states; the provincial legislatures only elected the members.
Correct: the Cabinet Mission Plan of 16 May 1946 laid down the composition, the method of election and the working procedure of the Constituent Assembly.
Incorrect: the Indian Independence Act 1947 came later. It made the Assembly sovereign and a dominion legislature, but did not set it up.
Incorrect: the Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947) provided for the partition of India and the transfer of power, not for the creation of the Constituent Assembly.
keyfact: The Constituent Assembly (389 members, indirectly elected) was set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 and first met on 9 December 1946.
option_notes: No such formal instrument exists. Provincial legislatures did elect the British Indian members indirectly, and the princely states were to negotiate their representation through a negotiating committee. Students should not confuse this with any statutory basis; the legal basis was the Cabinet Mission's statement of 16 May 1946, accepted by the Congress and (initially) the Muslim League.

The Cabinet Mission (March-June 1946) comprised Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State for India), Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander, and was sent by the Attlee government. It rejected the demand for a separate Pakistan and proposed a three-tier federal union with Groups A, B and C. It also provided for an interim government and for the Constituent Assembly of 389 members, elected indirectly.

The Indian Independence Act 1947 received royal assent on 18 July 1947 and came into force on 15 August 1947. It created the two dominions of India and Pakistan, ended British paramountcy over the princely states, and made the Constituent Assembly a sovereign body that could also act as the dominion legislature. It abolished the office of Secretary of State for India.

The Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947 (also called the 3 June Plan or Dickie Bird Plan) accepted the partition of India. It provided for referendums or votes in the NWFP, Sylhet, Punjab and Bengal, and for dominion status for both countries. It led to the Indian Independence Act 1947, and Mountbatten was the last Viceroy and then the first Governor-General of independent India.
related: Cabinet Mission members: Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps, A.V. Alexander.
First meeting of the Constituent Assembly: 9 December 1946; permanent president Rajendra Prasad.
Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947 with Ambedkar as chairman.
Objectives Resolution was moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947.
Constitution adopted on 26 November 1949; enforced on 26 January 1950.
Original Constituent Assembly strength was 389, reduced to 299 after partition.
M.N. Roy first proposed the idea of a Constituent Assembly in 1934.
B.N. Rau was the constitutional adviser to the Assembly.
summary: The correct answer is (b) Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946. The Constituent Assembly was constituted in 1946 under the scheme proposed by the Cabinet Mission (announced 16 May 1946), with members indirectly elected by provincial legislatures plus nominees of princely states.
topic_notes: Demand for a Constituent Assembly: M.N. Roy first proposed it in 1934; the Congress formally demanded it in 1935; the British accepted it in principle in the August Offer 1940, and the Cripps Mission 1942 repeated this. The Cabinet Mission 1946 finally gave the scheme. Composition: 389 members (296 British India, 93 princely states). After partition the membership fell to 299 (229 from provinces and 70 from princely states). Meetings: first on 9 December 1946 (the Muslim League boycotted it); Sachchidananda Sinha was interim chairman; Rajendra Prasad was elected president on 11 December 1946; H.C. Mukherjee was vice-president; B.N. Rau was constitutional adviser. Objectives Resolution: moved on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947. Drafting Committee: set up on 29 August 1947 with B.R. Ambedkar as chairman and seven members. Time taken: 2 years, 11 months and 18 days; there were 11 sessions. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. The national flag was adopted on 22 July 1947. The National Song and Anthem were accepted on 24 January 1950, when members signed the document, 284 members signing in all. The Assembly became a sovereign body and also acted as the Dominion Legislature from 14 August 1947, with G.V. Mavalankar as Speaker of the legislative body. Other angles include the committees (Union Powers under Nehru, Provincial Constitution under Patel, Rules of Procedure under Rajendra Prasad, Steering Committee), and the original Constitution, which had 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules.

question: The Proclamation, under Article 356 of the Constitution of India, imposing President’s Rule in a State, has to be approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament before the expiration of:
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 356 allows the President, on the Governor's report or otherwise, to proclaim President's Rule if the constitutional machinery in a State has failed. Article 356(3) says the Proclamation must be laid before each House of Parliament and ceases to operate at the expiry of two months unless approved by resolutions of both Houses before then. If the Lok Sabha is dissolved during the two months, or dissolves without approving, the Proclamation survives until 30 days after the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha, provided the Rajya Sabha has approved it meanwhile. Once approved, it lasts six months from the date of the Proclamation and can be extended by six months at a time, up to a maximum of three years. Approval and each extension need only a simple majority of members present and voting. Extension beyond one year needs both a national Emergency in force (or in the whole of India or any part of the State) and an Election Commission certificate that elections cannot be held (Article 356(5), 44th Amendment 1978). Option (a) is the duration of one approval, not the deadline for approval. Options (b) and (d) are not constitutional periods for this purpose.
explanations: Incorrect: six months is the period for which an approved Proclamation continues (and each extension), not the deadline for Parliamentary approval.
Incorrect: six weeks is not a period prescribed anywhere in Article 356.
Correct: Article 356(3) requires approval by both Houses within two months of the Proclamation, failing which it lapses.
Incorrect: two weeks is not the period under Article 356; it is too short compared with the constitutional two months.
keyfact: President's Rule under Art. 356 must be approved by both Houses within two months; it lasts six months at a time, up to three years.
option_notes: Six months: the duration of President's Rule after Parliamentary approval, and of each extension (Art. 356(4)). The maximum is three years in total. Beyond one year, extension needs a national Emergency in force or an Election Commission certificate that elections cannot be held (44th Amendment, 1978). The 42nd Amendment (1976) had earlier raised the term from six months to one year.

Six weeks: no constitutional relevance to Article 356. Note that for Parliament, a gap of more than six months between two sessions is barred (Art. 85). Also, the 44th Amendment fixed one month for approval of a national Emergency, while the Proclamation under Art. 356 gets two months. Six weeks is a distractor.

Two months: the period within which Parliament must approve a Proclamation under Art. 356(3). If it is not approved, the Proclamation lapses and the State government is restored. Approval needs a simple majority in each House. The same two-month period applies to Proclamations of financial emergency under Art. 360(2).
Two weeks: not a period in Art. 356. Fourteen days appears elsewhere, for example the notice period for a no-confidence motion, but not here. It is a distractor, as the actual window is two months.
related: Art. 356(3): approval by both Houses within two months or the Proclamation lapses.
Maximum duration of President's Rule is three years, with extensions every six months.
Extension beyond one year requires a national Emergency or an EC certificate (44th Amendment).
S.R. Bommai case (1994) made the Proclamation subject to judicial review.
Art. 352 national Emergency: approval within one month (after the 44th Amendment).
Art. 360 financial emergency: approval within two months.
Art. 365: failure to comply with Union directions can be treated as a breakdown of constitutional machinery.
Art. 357 deals with the exercise of legislative powers under the Proclamation.
summary: The correct answer is (c) Two months. Under Article 356(3), a Proclamation of President's Rule must be approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament within two months of its issue, or it ceases to operate at the end of that period.
topic_notes: Article 356 deals with failure of constitutional machinery in a State (President's Rule, State Emergency). Article 365 says that if a State fails to comply with Union directions, the President may hold that the constitutional machinery has failed. On a Proclamation, the President can assume the functions of the State government, and the powers of the State Legislature become exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament. The State Legislative Assembly is either suspended or dissolved. The President can also authorise expenditure from the State Consolidated Fund pending Parliamentary sanction. Laws made by Parliament or the President during the Proclamation continue after it ends, until altered by the State Legislature. The High Court's powers cannot be taken over. Approval needs only a simple majority, unlike a national Emergency, which needs a special majority for continuation. Key cases: State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977); S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), which made the Proclamation judicially reviewable, held that the floor of the House is the test of majority, and said that Parliament must approve before the Assembly can be dissolved (until then it is only suspended). Sarkaria Commission (1988) said Art. 356 should be used sparingly and as a last resort. Punchhi Commission (2010) also recommended safeguards. Proclamation under Art. 356 was first used in Punjab (PEPSU) in 1951. Under Art. 357, legislative powers are conferred on the President or Parliament. Art. 239AB covers failure in Delhi. Under Art. 356(5), the 44th Amendment added the one-year limit and the Election Commission certificate requirement. Art. 356 is derived from the Government of India Act, 1935 (Section 93).

question: The President of India has the power to nominate two members to the Lok Sabha from:
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 331 allowed the President to nominate not more than two Anglo-Indians to the House of the People if he was of the opinion that the community was not adequately represented. Article 333 gave the Governor a similar power for State Legislative Assemblies, with one member. These were originally to lapse after 10 years but were extended repeatedly by amendments (8th, 23rd, 45th, 62nd, 79th, 95th). The 95th Amendment (2009) extended them to 25 January 2020. The 104th Amendment (2019) discontinued Anglo-Indian nomination in both the Lok Sabha and Assemblies, while extending SC/ST reservation of seats by 10 more years to 2030. Elimination logic: SC/ST members are elected from reserved constituencies under Article 330, not nominated. There is no constitutional reservation or nomination for OBCs in legislatures. Persons of eminence (art, literature, science, social service) are nominated by the President only to the Rajya Sabha, up to 12 members, under Article 80. So only Anglo-Indian fits Lok Sabha nomination, and this is the answer as per the law at the time of the 2015 exam.
explanations: Wrong: SC/ST seats are reserved and filled by election from reserved constituencies (Article 330), not by presidential nomination.
Wrong: The Constitution provides no reservation or nomination of OBCs in Parliament or State Legislatures.
Wrong: Persons with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service are nominated to the Rajya Sabha (12 members), not the Lok Sabha.
Correct: Article 331 empowered the President to nominate up to two Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha. The power ended with the 104th Amendment, effective 25 January 2020.
keyfact: Before 25 Jan 2020, the President nominated up to 2 Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha under Article 331; the 104th Amendment ended this.
option_notes: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes: Article 330 reserves Lok Sabha seats for SCs and STs in proportion to their population, and Article 332 does the same for State Assemblies. Members are elected by all voters in reserved constituencies. The reservation was introduced in 1950 and extended by successive amendments. The 104th Amendment (2019) extended it to 25 January 2030. Articles 341 and 342 define SCs and STs.

Other Backward Classes: OBCs have no reservation in legislatures. They have 27% reservation in central government jobs and education, following the Mandal Commission (1979, report 1980) and the Indra Sawhney case (1992). Article 340 provides for a commission on backward classes. The National Commission for Backward Classes got constitutional status through the 102nd Amendment (2018), Article 338B.

Persons of eminence: Article 80(1)(a) allows the President to nominate 12 members to the Rajya Sabha with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service. Nominated members can't vote in Presidential elections but can vote in Vice-Presidential elections. The idea came from the Irish Constitution. Examples include Sachin Tendulkar, Rekha and Lata Mangeshkar's era nominations.

Anglo-Indian community: Article 366(2) defines an Anglo-Indian as a person whose father or male-line ancestor was European but who is domiciled in India. Article 331 gave 2 Lok Sabha nominees and Article 333 gave 1 Assembly nominee per state. Frank Anthony was a prominent nominated member. The 104th Amendment Act, 2019 ended these nominations from 25 January 2020.
related: Article 331: Anglo-Indian nomination to the Lok Sabha, ended in 2020.
Article 333: Governor's Anglo-Indian nominee to Assemblies, ended in 2020.
104th Amendment 2019: ended Anglo-Indian nomination and extended SC/ST reservation to 2030.
Rajya Sabha has 12 nominated members under Article 80.
Nominated Rajya Sabha members cannot vote in the Presidential election.
Article 330 reserves Lok Sabha seats for SC/ST.
Frank Anthony was a long-time nominated Anglo-Indian leader.
Article 366(2) defines Anglo-Indian.
summary: The correct answer is (d) Anglo-Indian community. Under Article 331 of the Constitution, the President could nominate not more than two members of the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha if the community was not adequately represented. The provision was in force in 2015 and was later removed by the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019, effective 25 January 2020.
topic_notes: Nominated members in Indian legislatures. Lok Sabha: the maximum strength is 550 (530 from states and 20 from Union Territories, Article 81), now 543 elected members. Before 2020, Article 331 allowed 2 Anglo-Indian nominees, making the strength 545. Rajya Sabha: the maximum strength is 250, of which 238 are elected and 12 nominated by the President under Article 80 for their expertise in literature, science, art and social service. State Legislative Assemblies: Article 333 allowed the Governor to nominate 1 Anglo-Indian, and this too was abolished in 2020. Legislative Councils: Article 171 provides that one-sixth of the members are nominated by the Governor from literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service. Reservations: Articles 330 and 332 reserve seats for SC/ST, and Article 334 sets the time limit of the reservation, which has been extended every 10 years. The original limit was 10 years, i.e. 1960. Extensions came through the 8th (1960), 23rd (1969), 45th (1980), 62nd (1989), 79th (1999), 95th (2009) and 104th (2019) Amendments. The 104th Amendment extended SC/ST reservation but removed the Anglo-Indian provision. The Delimitation Act and the 84th and 87th Amendments cover the freeze on seats until after the first census after 2026. Related questions could ask the number of nominated members, who nominates them, whether nominated members can vote in Presidential elections (they cannot), and whether they can become ministers (they can, within 6 months of joining).

question: Which one of the following Constitutional Amendments accorded position of primacy to Directive Principles of State Policy over Fundamental Rights?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The conflict between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) ran through Champakam Dorairajan (1951, FRs prevail), Golaknath (1967) and Kesavananda Bharati (1973). The 25th Amendment (1971) first inserted Article 31C, which protected laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31. The 42nd Amendment (1976, Swaran Singh Committee, Indira Gandhi government) widened Article 31C to cover all Directive Principles in Part IV, so a law implementing any DPSP could not be invalidated for violating Articles 14, 19 or 31. This is the amendment that accorded primacy to DPSP. It also added the Preamble words Socialist, Secular and Integrity, added Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Art. 51A) and new DPSPs (Arts. 39A, 43A, 48A). In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) the Supreme Court held the extended Art. 31C invalid as it violated the basic structure, restoring the balance between Parts III and IV. Elimination: the 16th (1963) dealt with sovereignty and integrity oaths; the 25th gave only limited primacy (Art. 39(b),(c)); the 44th (1978) removed the right to property from Part III and reversed several 42nd changes.
explanations: Incorrect: The 16th Amendment (1963) required oaths to uphold sovereignty and integrity of India and allowed restrictions on freedoms under Art. 19; it did not give DPSP primacy.

Incorrect: The 25th Amendment (1971) gave only partial primacy, protecting laws under Art. 39(b) and (c) via Art. 31C. It did not extend to all DPSPs, and it also curtailed the right to property compensation.
Correct: The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended Art. 31C to all Directive Principles, placing them above Arts. 14, 19 and 31. This was later struck down in Minerva Mills (1980).

Incorrect: The 44th Amendment (1978) deleted the right to property as a Fundamental Right (Art. 19(1)(f), Art. 31) and made it a legal right under Art. 300A. It restricted emergency powers and did not give DPSP primacy.
keyfact: The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended Art. 31C to all DPSPs, giving them primacy over FRs, but Minerva Mills (1980) struck it down.
option_notes: Sixteenth Amendment (1963): passed after the Chinese war and secessionist concerns. It added the ground of sovereignty and integrity of India to the restrictions in Art. 19(2), (3) and (4). It also changed the oaths and affirmations for legislators, ministers, judges and others to include upholding sovereignty and integrity.

Twenty-Fifth Amendment (1971): replaced the word compensation with amount in Art. 31(2), reducing the property right. It inserted Art. 31C, which protected laws implementing Art. 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Arts. 14, 19 and 31. The part barring judicial review was struck down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

Forty-Second Amendment (1976): called the mini-Constitution, passed during the Emergency on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendations. It added Socialist, Secular and Integrity to the Preamble, added Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A) and extended Art. 31C to all DPSPs. It also extended the Lok Sabha term to six years and made the President bound by Cabinet advice. Many provisions were later reversed by the 43rd and 44th Amendments.

Forty-Fourth Amendment (1978): passed by the Janata government to undo Emergency excesses. It removed the right to property from Part III and added Art. 300A. It restored the Lok Sabha term to five years and substituted internal disturbance with armed rebellion in Art. 352. It protected Art. 20 and Art. 21 from suspension during an Emergency and required written Cabinet advice for proclaiming one.
related: Art. 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) and extended by the 42nd Amendment (1976).
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Art. 31C.
Art. 39(b) and (c) deal with distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth.
The 44th Amendment (1978) made property a legal right under Art. 300A.
Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A) came via the 42nd Amendment on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.
Art. 37 states that DPSPs are not enforceable by courts.
The 42nd Amendment added the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity to the Preamble.
The 86th Amendment (2002) added Art. 21A and the 11th Fundamental Duty.
summary: The answer is (c) Forty-Second Amendment. The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted a new Article 31C provision extending protection to all Directive Principles (not only Art. 39(b) and (c)) against challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31, giving DPSP primacy over Fundamental Rights. The Supreme Court struck down this extension in Minerva Mills (1980).
topic_notes: The relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles has evolved through court judgments and amendments. State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951): FRs are sacrosanct and prevail over DPSP. Golaknath (1967): Parliament cannot amend FRs. The 24th and 25th Amendments (1971) responded to this; the 25th inserted Art. 31C. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic structure doctrine and upheld the first part of Art. 31C but struck down the clause barring judicial review. The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended Art. 31C to all DPSPs. Minerva Mills (1980) struck down this extension and the clauses (4) and (5) added to Art. 368, declaring that harmony and balance between Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure. Later, in Waman Rao (1981), the Court held that Art. 31C as it stood before the 42nd Amendment is valid, and that the Ninth Schedule rules apply only to laws placed after 24 April 1973. Other key points: Part IV covers Arts. 36-51; DPSP are non-justiciable (Art. 37); the Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation (10 duties originally, 11th added by the 86th Amendment, 2002). The 42nd Amendment also added Arts. 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), 43A (worker participation in management) and 48A (environment) to the DPSPs, and moved subjects such as education and forests to the Concurrent List. The 44th Amendment removed Art. 31 and Art. 19(1)(f). Upcoming questions could ask about Art. 31C, Minerva Mills, Kesavananda or the 86th Amendment.

question: Articles 155-156 of the Constitution of India deal with:
options: The power of President to appoint and dismiss State Governors
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Part VI, Chapter II of the Constitution deals with the State Executive and begins with the Governor. Article 153 says there shall be a Governor for each State (the 7th Amendment, 1956, allowed one Governor for two or more States). Article 154 vests the executive power of the State in the Governor. Article 155 says the Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal; there is no election, unlike in the USA. Article 156 provides that the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President, normally for a term of five years, and may resign by writing to the President. Article 157 gives the qualifications (citizen of India, at least 35 years old), Article 158 the conditions of office, Article 159 the oath, and Article 161 the pardoning power. Elimination: the Election Commission is under Article 324 (Part XV); the Inter-State Council is under Article 263 (Part XI); the Inter-State Trade and Commerce Commission is under Article 307 (Part XIII). None of these is in Articles 155-156, so only (d) fits. Note that the Governor is not dismissed by a fixed procedure; removal is at the President's pleasure, acting on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers.
explanations: Wrong: the Inter-State Commerce Commission is linked to Article 307 (Part XIII, Trade, Commerce and Intercourse), not Articles 155-156.
Wrong: the Election Commission is provided for in Article 324 (Part XV, Elections), not Articles 155-156.
Wrong: the Inter-State Council is provided for in Article 263 (Part XI, Centre-State relations), not Articles 155-156.

Correct: Article 155 provides for appointment of the Governor by the President, and Article 156 provides that the Governor holds office during the President's pleasure (term of five years, resignation to the President).
keyfact: Article 155 = Governor appointed by the President; Article 156 = Governor holds office during the President's pleasure (five-year term).
option_notes: Inter-State Commerce Commission: Article 307 empowers Parliament to appoint an authority to carry out the functions under Articles 301-304 (freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse). Article 301 declares trade, commerce and intercourse free throughout India. No such commission has actually been set up. It is in Part XIII (Articles 301-307).

Election Commission: a constitutional body under Article 324, which vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President in it. It consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners, appointed by the President. It was set up on 25 January 1950 (National Voters' Day). Since 1993 it has been a multi-member body.

Inter-State Council: Article 263 allows the President to establish it to investigate and discuss subjects of common interest between States, or between the Union and States. It was set up in 1990 on the recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission. The Prime Minister is its chairman. It is a recommendatory body and is not permanent.
