Appointment and tenure of Governor: appointed by the President under Article 155, and holds office at the President's pleasure under Article 156. The normal term is five years, but it is not a fixed tenure. The Governor must be an Indian citizen and at least 35 years old (Article 157). Governors have been removed or transferred before completing their terms. The Supreme Court in B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010) held that removal must not be arbitrary or capricious.
related: Article 153: there shall be a Governor for each State.
Article 154: the executive power of the State is vested in the Governor.
Article 157: a Governor must be a citizen of India and at least 35 years old.
Article 159: the Governor's oath is administered by the Chief Justice of the High Court.
Article 161: the Governor's power to pardon, though not in respect of death sentences.
Article 163: Council of Ministers aids and advises the Governor.
Article 213: the Governor's ordinance-making power.
B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010): the pleasure doctrine is not absolute; removal must not be arbitrary.
summary: The answer is (d). Articles 155 and 156 fall in Part VI (The States), Chapter II (The Executive), and deal with the Governor: Article 155 provides for appointment by the President, and Article 156 provides that the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President.
topic_notes: The Governor is the constitutional head of the State executive (Articles 153-167 cover the State executive generally). Article 153: a Governor for each State, and one person may serve as Governor of two or more States (7th Amendment, 1956). Article 154: the executive power of the State is vested in the Governor. Article 155: appointment by the President by warrant under hand and seal. Article 156: office held during the President's pleasure, five-year term, resignation to the President; the Governor continues in office until the successor takes over. Article 157: qualifications (citizen of India, 35 years of age). Article 158: conditions of the office; the Governor must not be a member of Parliament or a State Legislature and gets emoluments and allowances without rent for the official residence. Article 159: oath or affirmation, administered by the Chief Justice of the High Court. Article 160: the President may make provisions for discharge of the Governor's functions in contingencies. Article 161: power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of sentences (but not the death sentence pardon, which only the President can grant). Article 163: Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor, except in matters where the Governor acts in his discretion. Article 164: appointment of the Chief Minister and other ministers by the Governor. Article 165: Advocate General. Article 166: conduct of government business. Article 167: the Chief Minister's duties to furnish information to the Governor. Article 174: summoning and proroguing the House and dissolving the Assembly. Article 200: assent to Bills, reservation for the President. Article 213: ordinance-making power. Article 356: the Governor's report is a basis for President's Rule. The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2010) made recommendations on Governors. Related cases: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), Nabam Rebia (2016).

question: The President of India has been empowered to return a Bill, as soon as possible, on presentation to him after its having been passed by the Houses of Parliament for assent, except in the case of:
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 111 deals with the President's assent to Bills. When a Bill passed by both Houses is presented to the President, he may declare that he assents, withholds assent, or, in the case of a Bill other than a Money Bill, return it as soon as possible with a message requesting reconsideration of the Bill or of specified provisions, or suggesting amendments. This return is the suspensive veto. If Parliament passes the Bill again, with or without amendments, and presents it again, the President cannot withhold assent. The Money Bill exception exists because Money Bills (Article 110) are the Lok Sabha's financial preserve, and the Rajya Sabha has only recommendatory powers over them. A Money Bill also requires the President's prior recommendation for introduction under Article 117(1), so he cannot send it back. The President may also withhold assent altogether, which is the absolute veto, and may let a Bill lapse without acting, which is the pocket veto. Neither is limited by the Money Bill exception. Elimination: an Ordinary Bill can be returned, so (a) is wrong. An Ordinance (Article 123) is issued by the President himself and is not a Bill passed by Parliament. A Statute is an Act already enacted. So (c) and (d) do not fit the question. Only (b) matches the Article 111 exception.
explanations: Incorrect: an Ordinary Bill can be returned by the President for reconsideration under Article 111, so it is not the exception.
Correct: Article 111 expressly excludes Money Bills from the President's power to return a Bill. He can only assent or withhold assent.
Incorrect: an Ordinance is promulgated by the President under Article 123 when Parliament is not in session. It is not a Bill passed by Parliament and has no return procedure.
Incorrect: a Statute is an Act that has already received assent. It is not a Bill awaiting assent, so the return power does not apply to it.
keyfact: Under Article 111, the President can return any Bill for reconsideration except a Money Bill, and also except a Constitution Amendment Bill.
option_notes: Ordinary Bill: a Bill on any subject other than money or financial matters. It can be introduced in either House, must be passed by both, and is resolved by a joint sitting under Article 108 if the Houses disagree. The President can assent, withhold assent, or return it once for reconsideration.

Money Bill: defined in Article 110 and concerns taxation, borrowing, the Consolidated Fund and similar matters. It can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha, with the President's recommendation. The Rajya Sabha has 14 days to make recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject. The Speaker certifies a Bill as a Money Bill, and that decision is final. The President cannot return it.

Ordinance: a law made by the President under Article 123 when Parliament is not in session, with the same force as an Act. It must be laid before Parliament and ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles, unless approved earlier. The Governor has a similar power under Article 213. Its validity can be challenged in court, as in the D.C. Wadhwa case.

Statute: an Act of the legislature that has been passed by Parliament and has received the President's assent. It is a written law, also called an enactment. Once enacted, it becomes part of the law of the land and can be amended or repealed only by the legislature or struck down by courts if unconstitutional.
related: Article 111: the President's assent to Bills and the return of Bills other than Money Bills.
Article 110 defines a Money Bill, and the Lok Sabha Speaker certifies it.
Article 109: Rajya Sabha has 14 days to return a Money Bill with recommendations.
Article 123: the President's Ordinance-making power, limited to six weeks after Parliament reassembles.
Pocket veto: used by President Zail Singh in 1986 on the Indian Post Office Bill.
Constitutional Amendment Bills cannot be returned by the President (24th Amendment).
Article 108: Joint sitting, not applicable to Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills.
Article 117: Financial Bills; the President's recommendation is required for introduction.
summary: The answer is (b) Money Bill. Under Article 111, the President may return a Bill (other than a Money Bill) with a message asking Parliament to reconsider it. A Money Bill cannot be returned, so the President must either give assent or withhold it.
topic_notes: Article 111 gives the President three choices on a Bill presented to him: assent, withhold assent, or return it for reconsideration (not for Money Bills). If Parliament re-passes the Bill, the President must assent. This is a suspensive veto. The absolute veto means withholding assent. The pocket veto means taking no action, and the Constitution sets no time limit. The pocket veto was used in 1986 on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill by President Zail Singh. For Constitution Amendment Bills (Article 368), the President must give assent and cannot return them, as the 24th Amendment made explicit. For Money Bills, the President may assent or withhold assent only. For State Bills, Article 200 allows the Governor to reserve a Bill for the President, and Article 201 covers the President's action on it. The President can return a non-Money Bill reserved by the Governor, and the State legislature must reconsider it within six months. Money Bills are defined in Article 110, and Financial Bills fall under Article 117. A Financial Bill under Article 117(1) or 117(3) can be returned, unlike a Money Bill. Article 109 sets out the special Rajya Sabha procedure for Money Bills, with a 14-day limit. Article 108 provides for a joint sitting, which is not available for Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills. Joint sittings have been held in 1961 (Dowry Prohibition Bill), 1978 (Banking Services Commission Repeal Bill) and 2002 (POTA).

question: Which one of the following is NOT covered under the Seventy Third Amendment of the Constitution of India?
options: Provision for the State Finance Commission
Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Women
Provision for the State Planning Commission
Provision for the State Election Commission
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 came into force on 24 April 1993 and gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj. It inserted Part IX (Arts. 243-243O) and the Eleventh Schedule, which lists 29 subjects. Its main features are the Gram Sabha (Art. 243A), a three-tier structure (Art. 243B), direct elections to all seats (Art. 243C), reservation for SCs and STs in proportion to population and not less than one-third of seats for women (Art. 243D), a five-year term with fresh elections within six months of dissolution (Art. 243E), the State Election Commission for superintending elections (Art. 243K), and the State Finance Commission, constituted every five years, to review the finances of Panchayats (Art. 243I). Art. 243ZD, inserted by the 74th Amendment, provides for the District Planning Committee. The Constitution has no article creating a State Planning Commission, and any such body is an administrative creation of the state government. Options (a), (b) and (d) are all explicit 73rd Amendment provisions. Option (c) is the only one that is not, so it is the answer.
explanations: Incorrect choice: Art. 243I provides for the State Finance Commission, so it is covered by the 73rd Amendment.
Incorrect choice: Art. 243D reserves seats for SCs, STs and women, so it is covered.
Correct choice: the 73rd Amendment has no provision for a State Planning Commission. The only planning provision is the District Planning Committee (Art. 243ZD), which came from the 74th Amendment.
Incorrect choice: Art. 243K provides for the State Election Commission, so it is covered.
keyfact: The 73rd Amendment (Part IX) covers the State Election Commission, the State Finance Commission and reservation for SCs, STs and women, but not a State Planning Commission.
option_notes: The State Finance Commission is constituted by the Governor under Art. 243I, within a year of the Amendment's commencement and then every five years. It recommends how tax proceeds are shared between the state and the Panchayats, which grants-in-aid they receive, and how their finances can be improved. Art. 243Y applies the same arrangement to Municipalities. The Governor lays its report before the state legislature.

Art. 243D reserves seats in Panchayats for SCs and STs in proportion to their population, and reserves not less than one-third of seats for women, including those reserved for SCs and STs. The same applies to chairperson posts. States may reserve seats for backward classes. Many states have raised women's reservation to 50 per cent. The Constitution (110th Amendment) Bill, 2009 was introduced to raise it to 50 per cent but was not enacted.

The State Planning Commission or Board is not a constitutional body. It is set up by the executive decision of a state government and advises it on planning. The Planning Commission at the Centre was created in 1950 by a Cabinet resolution and replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015. Constitutional planning machinery below the state level consists of the District Planning Committee under Art. 243ZD and, in metropolitan areas, the Metropolitan Planning Committee under Art. 243ZE.

The State Election Commission is provided for in Art. 243K for Panchayats and Art. 243ZA for Municipalities. It consists of a State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor. The Commissioner can be removed only in the way a High Court judge is removed, and his conditions of service cannot be changed to his disadvantage after appointment. It conducts local body elections independently of the Election Commission of India.
related: 73rd Amendment came into force on 24 April 1993
Part IX covers Arts. 243 to 243O; Eleventh Schedule has 29 subjects
Art. 243K is the State Election Commission; Art. 243I is the State Finance Commission
Art. 243D reserves at least one-third of seats for women
74th Amendment added Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule with 18 subjects
Art. 243ZD provides for the District Planning Committee
PESA Act 1996 extended Panchayat provisions to Scheduled Areas
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended the three-tier system
summary: The answer is (c). The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 added Part IX (Articles 243 to 243O) on Panchayats. It provides for the State Finance Commission (Art. 243I), reservation of seats for SCs, STs and women (Art. 243D) and the State Election Commission (Art. 243K). It has no provision for a State Planning Commission.
topic_notes:
The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj. It was enacted under P.V. Narasimha Rao's government and came into force on 24 April 1993, which is observed as National Panchayati Raj Day. Part IX has Arts. 243 to 243O, and the Eleventh Schedule lists 29 functional subjects. Art. 243G gives Panchayats powers and responsibilities for economic development and social justice.

Background: the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended the three-tier system. The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) recommended a two-tier system. The G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985) and the L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) preceded the amendment, and Singhvi recommended constitutional recognition. Rajasthan (Nagaur, 2 October 1959) was the first state to introduce Panchayati Raj.

Key provisions: the Gram Sabha; a three-tier system, with states of population under 20 lakh exempt from the intermediate tier; direct elections to all seats; reservation for SCs, STs and women; a five-year term; disqualification rules; the State Election Commission; the State Finance Commission; and audit of accounts. Part IX does not apply to Scheduled Areas (Art. 243M), which are covered by the PESA Act, 1996. It also does not apply to Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and certain hill areas of Manipur and West Bengal.

The 74th Amendment Act, 1992 is the counterpart for urban local bodies. It inserted Part IXA (Arts. 243P to 243ZG) and the Twelfth Schedule, which has 18 subjects. Art. 243ZD provides for the District Planning Committee and Art. 243ZE for the Metropolitan Planning Committee. The 73rd Amendment's Panchayat provisions are partly mandatory and partly voluntary. Common exam angles are article numbers, committees, the number of Schedule subjects, and the bodies that are not constitutional.

question: The Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India contains:
options: Salaries of the President and Vice-President
Union List, State List and Concurrent List
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The Seventh Schedule is linked to Article 246, which divides legislative powers between Parliament and State Legislatures. It originally had three lists: the Union List (97 subjects at commencement, now 98 after later changes), the State List (66 originally, now 59 after items were removed or moved), and the Concurrent List (47 originally, now 52). Parliament has exclusive power over the Union List, States over the State List, and both can legislate on the Concurrent List, where the Union law prevails in a conflict (Article 254). Residuary powers lie with Parliament (Article 248, Entry 97 of the Union List). The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved five subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List: education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and administration of justice. The 7th Amendment (1956) reorganised the lists after the States Reorganisation. Elimination: the salaries of the President and Vice-President are in the Second Schedule, tribal and Scheduled areas are in the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, and languages are in the Eighth Schedule.
explanations: Wrong: salaries and emoluments of the President, Governors, Speakers, judges, CAG and others are in the Second Schedule. The Vice-President is not listed there as such; the Vice-President draws salary as ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha under a Parliamentary law.
Wrong: administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes is in the Fifth Schedule, and of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram is in the Sixth Schedule.
Correct: the Seventh Schedule contains the Union List, State List and Concurrent List, the basis of the Centre-State legislative distribution.
Wrong: the 22 recognised languages are in the Eighth Schedule, which originally had 14 and now has 22 languages.
keyfact: Seventh Schedule = Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Article 246).
option_notes: The Second Schedule lists the emoluments, allowances and privileges of the President, Governors of States, Speakers and Deputy Speakers, Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the Comptroller and Auditor General. It is linked to Articles 59, 65, 75, 97, 125, 148, 158, 164, 186 and 221.

The Fifth Schedule covers the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram (Article 244(1)). The Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas of those four states (Article 244(2)) and provides for Autonomous District Councils and Regional Councils. The Governor and the Tribes Advisory Council play key roles in the Fifth Schedule areas.

The Seventh Schedule has the Union List (Parliament has exclusive power), the State List (States have exclusive power) and the Concurrent List (both can legislate). It comes under Article 246. The idea of the Concurrent List was borrowed from Australia, and the scheme of division follows the Government of India Act, 1935.

The Eighth Schedule lists the recognised languages, with 22 now. Originally there were 14. Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment (1967), Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali by the 71st (1992), and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali by the 92nd (2003). Odia replaced Oriya by the 96th Amendment (2011). It relates to Articles 344(1) and 351.
related: Article 246 divides legislative subjects through the Seventh Schedule.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved five State List subjects to the Concurrent List.
Residuary legislative power lies with Parliament (Article 248).
The Eighth Schedule has 22 languages.
The Ninth Schedule was added by the 1st Amendment (1951).
The Tenth Schedule is the anti-defection law (52nd Amendment).
The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 Panchayat subjects and the Twelfth lists 18 Municipality subjects.
Under Article 254, a Union law prevails over a State law in the Concurrent List, subject to Presidential assent for a State law.
summary: The correct answer is (c). The Seventh Schedule of the Constitution contains the Union List, State List and Concurrent List, which distribute legislative subjects between the Union and the States under Article 246.
topic_notes: The Constitution has 12 Schedules, with 395 Articles at commencement and 8 Schedules, then 12 now. First Schedule: States and Union Territories. Second: emoluments of high officials. Third: forms of oaths and affirmations. Fourth: allocation of Rajya Sabha seats. Fifth: Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes. Sixth: tribal areas in the four northeastern states. Seventh: the three legislative lists. Eighth: languages. Ninth: validation of laws, added by the 1st Amendment (1951), to protect land reform laws from judicial review. Tenth: anti-defection law, added by the 52nd Amendment (1985). Eleventh: Panchayati Raj, 29 subjects, added by the 73rd Amendment (1992). Twelfth: Municipalities, 18 subjects, added by the 74th Amendment (1992). Seventh Schedule points: Article 246 governs the distribution, Article 248 the residuary powers, Article 249 allows Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest by a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by two-thirds of those present and voting, Article 250 covers legislation during an Emergency, and Article 252 covers legislation by consent of States. Article 254 resolves conflicts in the Concurrent List. The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) examined Centre-State relations. Entry 97 is the residuary entry in the Union List. GST (101st Amendment, 2016) modified the lists, adding Article 246A and omitting Entry 92 and some others. Future questions may ask which schedule covers a given topic, the number of subjects in each list, and which subjects moved to the Concurrent List.

question: Who among the following is the ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 63 provides for a Vice President of India, and Article 64 makes him the ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States. Article 89 repeats this and also provides for a Deputy Chairman, who is elected by Rajya Sabha members from among themselves. The Vice President is elected under Article 66 by an electoral college of members of both Houses of Parliament, including nominated members, through proportional representation by single transferable vote with secret ballot. His term is five years (Article 67), but he continues until his successor takes office. He can be removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by an effective majority (a majority of all the then members) and agreed to by the Lok Sabha by a simple majority, with 14 days' notice. He has only a casting vote in case of a tie. When he acts as President (Article 65) during a vacancy, he does not perform the duties of Chairman. Elimination: the President is part of Parliament (Article 79) but not a member of either House. The Prime Minister is the leader of the Lok Sabha, usually. The Deputy Speaker assists the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, a different House.
explanations: Incorrect: The President is a constituent part of Parliament under Article 79 but presides over neither House.
Correct: Article 64 and Article 89(1) make the Vice President ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
Incorrect: The Prime Minister is head of the Council of Ministers and a member of either House, but holds no presiding role in the Rajya Sabha.
Incorrect: The Deputy Speaker is the Lok Sabha's deputy presiding officer and has no role in the Rajya Sabha.
keyfact: The Vice President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha under Articles 64 and 89.
option_notes: The President of India is the constitutional head of state under Article 52. He is elected under Article 54 by an electoral college of elected members of Parliament and State Legislative Assemblies, with a five-year term. He summons, prorogues and addresses Parliament, can dissolve the Lok Sabha, and gives assent to Bills. He is not a member of either House.

The Vice President is the second-highest constitutional office (Article 63). He is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament under Article 66 and must be at least 35 years old and eligible for election as a Rajya Sabha member. His term is five years. He acts as President for up to six months in a vacancy and is ex-officio Rajya Sabha Chairman. He receives a salary in that capacity.

The Prime Minister (Article 74-75) is the head of the Council of Ministers and is appointed by the President. He is the real executive head, a member of either House, and the leader of the House he belongs to. He is not an ex-officio presiding officer of any House of Parliament.

The Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by Lok Sabha members from among themselves (Article 93). He presides in the Speaker's absence and, once elected, is not subordinate to the Speaker, because he is directly responsible to the House. By convention he belongs to the opposition, and the post was vacant for the whole of the 17th Lok Sabha.
related: Article 64: Vice President is ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States.
Article 66: Vice President is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament.
Article 67: the Vice President's term is five years, and he can be removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution agreed to by the Lok Sabha.
Article 89: Rajya Sabha Chairman and Deputy Chairman.
Article 93: Lok Sabha Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
The Rajya Sabha has a maximum strength of 250, including 12 nominated members.
The Vice President must be at least 35 years old.
Article 65: the Vice President acts as President during a vacancy.
summary: The correct answer is (b) Vice President. Under Article 89(1) of the Constitution, the Vice President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Council of States). He does not become a member of the House by virtue of this office.
topic_notes: Parliament of India consists of the President, the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) and the Lok Sabha (House of the People) under Article 79. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House that cannot be dissolved, with one-third of its members retiring every two years. Its maximum strength is 250: 238 representatives of States and Union Territories, plus 12 nominated members with expertise in literature, science, art and social service. The current strength is 245. Members serve six-year terms and must be at least 30 years old. The Chairman is the Vice President (Art. 89), and the Deputy Chairman is elected from among the members. The Chairman's powers are given in the Rajya Sabha Rules of Procedure. He cannot vote in the first instance but has a casting vote on a tie. When he is acting as President or discharging the President's functions, he does not perform the Chairman's duties. Money Bills can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha has to return them within 14 days. Under Article 249 the Rajya Sabha can empower Parliament to legislate on State List subjects by a two-thirds special majority, and under Article 312 it can authorise the creation of All-India Services. The Lok Sabha's presiding officers are the Speaker and Deputy Speaker (Articles 93-96). The Speaker is the final authority on interpreting the Rules of the House and on deciding whether a Bill is a Money Bill. The Speaker can also vote only in case of a tie.

question: Which one of the following Articles of the Constitution of India empowers the Parliament to create one or more All India Services?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 312 in Part XIV (Services under the Union and the States) deals with All India Services. Under Article 312(1), if the Rajya Sabha declares by a resolution supported by at least two-thirds of members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest, Parliament may by law create one or more All India Services common to the Union and the States, and regulate the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to them. The Rajya Sabha is given this special role because it represents the States. The three services recognised are the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), the Indian Police Service (IPS) and the Indian Forest Service (IFoS). Article 312(2) states that the IAS and IPS, existing at the commencement of the Constitution, are deemed to be services created by Parliament under this article. The All India Services Act, 1951 governs them. The Indian Forest Service was created in 1966. Elimination: Article 300 concerns suits and proceedings against the Union or States; Articles 301 and 304 are in Part XIII on trade, commerce and intercourse, so they are unrelated to services.
explanations: Incorrect: Article 300 deals with the legal personality of the Union and States, i.e. suits and proceedings by or against the Government, not services.
Incorrect: Article 304 deals with restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse among States, which States may impose in the public interest. It has nothing to do with services.
Incorrect: Article 301 declares that trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free. It is unrelated to services.
Correct: Article 312(1) empowers Parliament to create All India Services after a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
keyfact: Article 312(1): Parliament can create All India Services after a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
option_notes: Article 300 provides that the Government of India may sue or be sued in the name of the Union of India, and a State Government in the name of the State. Liability is the same as that of the Dominion of India and the Provinces before the Constitution. It lies in Part XII. Article 300A, inserted by the 44th Amendment in 1978, makes the right to property a constitutional right: no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law.

Article 304 permits States to impose restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse. Under it a State may tax goods imported from other States at the same rate as local goods, and may impose reasonable restrictions in the public interest. A Bill or amendment for this purpose needs the President's previous sanction. It forms part of Part XIII (Articles 301-307), which governs trade, commerce and intercourse within India.

Article 301 states that, subject to the other provisions of Part XIII, trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free. It protects the freedom of inter-State trade and aims at a common national market. Article 302 allows Parliament to impose restrictions in the public interest. Article 303 limits legislative power to discriminate between States, and Article 305 saves existing laws and State monopolies.

Article 312 empowers Parliament to create All India Services. Clause (1) requires a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, stating that it is in the national interest. Clause (2) deems the IAS and IPS to be services created under it. Clause (3) covers the All India Judicial Service. The 42nd Amendment of 1976 widened this provision. The Indian Forest Service was created in 1966.
related: Article 312: All India Services, requires a Rajya Sabha resolution by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
The three All India Services are IAS, IPS and Indian Forest Service (1966).
Article 311: protection against dismissal, removal or reduction in rank.
Article 315: Union and State Public Service Commissions.
Article 324: Election Commission.
Article 310: civil servants hold office during the pleasure of the President or Governor.
Article 320: functions of the UPSC.
The All India Services Act was passed in 1951.
summary: The correct answer is (d) Article 312(1). It empowers Parliament to create one or more All India Services common to the Union and the States, provided the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of members present and voting, declaring that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest.
topic_notes: Part XIV (Articles 308-323) covers services and Public Service Commissions. Article 308 is the interpretation clause, Article 309 empowers recruitment and conditions of service regulation, Article 310 states the doctrine of pleasure, Article 311 gives protection against dismissal, removal or reduction in rank without a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and Article 312 deals with All India Services. Article 312A covers the power of Parliament to vary or revoke conditions of service of officers of certain services. Article 313 is on transitional provisions. Article 314 was repealed. Articles 315-323 deal with the UPSC and State PSCs: Article 315 establishes them, Article 316 covers appointment and term, Article 317 removal and suspension, Article 320 their functions and Article 323 their reports. The UPSC has a Chairman and members appointed by the President, with a six-year term or age 65, whichever is earlier. The three All India Services are the IAS, IPS and IFoS. They are recruited by the Union, but the officers are allotted to State cadres and serve both the Union and the States. Disciplinary control rests with the Centre. The All India Services Act, 1951 and the rules made under it govern them. The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted a provision for the All India Judicial Service, which has not yet been created. Compare with the 'Central Services' (such as IFS, IRS), which are under the Union, and the State Services, which are under the States.

question: How many members are nominated by the President to the Rajya Sabha?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 80 fixes the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha at 250, of whom 238 are representatives of the States and Union Territories and 12 are nominated by the President under Article 80(3). The nominated members must have special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service (the mnemonic is LSAS). The 12 figure comes from the original Constitution, and the Fourth Schedule allocates seats among States and UTs. Elected members are chosen indirectly: State members by the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies through the single transferable vote under proportional representation, and UT members by an electoral college specified by Parliament. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House that is not subject to dissolution, and one-third of its members retire every second year. Each member serves a six-year term. Nominated members may join a political party within six months of taking their seats; otherwise they are treated as unattached under the Tenth Schedule. Nominated members can vote in the election of the Vice-President but not in the election of the President. The Lok Sabha, by comparison, has up to 2 Anglo-Indian nominees (Art. 331), a provision removed by the 104th Amendment in 2020. Options 14, 20 and 15 do not match any constitutional figure for nominations.
explanations: Incorrect: 14 is not the number of Presidential nominees to the Rajya Sabha. The Constitution provides for 12.
Incorrect: 20 has no basis in Article 80. It is not the number of nominees.
Correct: Article 80(1)(a) and 80(3) provide for 12 members nominated by the President for expertise in literature, science, art and social service.
Incorrect: 15 is not the number of nominees. The figure is 12.
keyfact: The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha (Art. 80(3)), from literature, science, art and social service.
option_notes: 14: This is not a constitutional number for Rajya Sabha nominations. Nominated seats are 12 out of a maximum of 250. Students may confuse it with other figures, such as the 14 seats in some State Council contexts, so memorise 12 for the Rajya Sabha.

20: This figure has no link to Article 80. The Rajya Sabha has 238 elected and 12 nominated members, with a maximum strength of 250. The current actual strength is 245, of which 233 are elected and 12 are nominated.

12: This is the correct figure. Article 80(3) lists the fields of literature, science, art and social service. Nominated members are chosen by the President on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers. They cannot vote in the Presidential election, but they can vote in the Vice-Presidential election. Examples include Sachin Tendulkar, Rekha, Lata Mangeshkar's era-appointed artists, and scholars such as Dr. Karan Singh in earlier terms.

15: This is not the number of Rajya Sabha nominees. Do not confuse it with other numbers in the Constitution, such as the 15 members-style provisions in other bodies. For the Rajya Sabha the number is 12, and the maximum strength is 250.
related: Article 80: composition of the Rajya Sabha, with a maximum of 250 members
12 nominated members are drawn from literature, science, art and social service
Rajya Sabha members serve a six-year term, with one-third retiring every two years
The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
Nominated members cannot vote in the Presidential election
The Fourth Schedule allocates Rajya Sabha seats among States and UTs
The 104th Amendment (2020) ended the Anglo-Indian nomination to the Lok Sabha
Minimum age for Rajya Sabha membership is 30 years
summary: The answer is (c) 12. Under Article 80(1)(a) of the Constitution, the President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha from persons with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service.
topic_notes: The Rajya Sabha (Council of States) is the Upper House of Parliament, with a maximum strength of 250 under Article 80. Of these, 238 represent States and UTs and 12 are nominated by the President. The present strength is 245 (233 elected and 12 nominated). Nominated members come from literature, science, art and social service. They enjoy the same rights as elected members, except that they cannot vote in the Presidential election. They can vote in the Vice-President's election, because that electorate includes all members of both Houses. Under the Tenth Schedule, a nominated member can join a party within six months of taking a seat, and after that is subject to anti-defection law. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House: one-third of members retire every two years, and each member serves six years. The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman, and the House elects a Deputy Chairman. The qualifications for membership under Article 84 are citizenship, a minimum age of 30, and any other qualifications prescribed by Parliament. Article 249 empowers the Rajya Sabha to authorise Parliament to legislate on State List subjects in the national interest by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. Article 312 allows it to create All-India Services in the same way. Money Bills can only be recommended for return, not amended, by the Rajya Sabha, which has 14 days to return them. UPSC may also ask about the Lok Sabha's maximum strength of 550 (currently 543 elected), the Fourth Schedule's seat allocation, the single transferable vote system, and the 104th Amendment ending Anglo-Indian nomination.

question: The One Hundred and Sixth Constitutional Amendment Bill relates to:
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Constitutional Amendment Bills are numbered in advance, and many lapse, so a Bill number can differ from the number of the Act that is eventually passed. That is the trap in this question. Article 311 protects civil servants of the Union and the States: a person cannot be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to the one that appointed them, and cannot be dismissed, removed or reduced in rank without an inquiry in which they are told the charges and given a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Clause (2) has exceptions: conviction on a criminal charge, impracticability of holding an inquiry, and security of the State. Proposals to amend Article 311 have aimed at easing action against corrupt officials. The other options are easy to eliminate. Co-operative societies were dealt with by the 97th Amendment, 2011 (Part IXB, Article 243ZH to 243ZT, and the right to form co-operatives under Article 19(1)(c)). Tribal governance relates to the Fifth and Sixth Schedules and PESA 1996. Office of profit relates to Articles 102(1)(a) and 191(1)(a). I could not verify the Bill's number from a source, so treat this as the best-supported option.
explanations: Incorrect: tribal governance is dealt with under the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, Article 244 and PESA 1996, and is not linked to this Bill.
Incorrect: co-operative societies were covered by the 97th Amendment Act, 2011, which inserted Part IXB and made the right to form co-operatives a fundamental right.
Correct (best available answer): the 106th Amendment Bill is recalled as concerning Article 311, which governs dismissal, removal or reduction in rank of civil servants.
Incorrect: office of profit is governed by Articles 102 and 191 and the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959, amended in 2006, and is not the subject of this Bill.
keyfact: Article 311 gives civil servants safeguards against dismissal, removal or reduction in rank; the 106th Amendment Bill is recalled as relating to it (not the 2023 Act on women's reservation).
option_notes: Tribal governance: Article 244 applies the Fifth Schedule to Scheduled Areas and the Sixth Schedule to tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. The Sixth Schedule provides Autonomous District Councils with legislative, judicial and executive powers. PESA 1996 extends Panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas and gives Gram Sabhas central powers. The 73rd Amendment's Part IX excludes Scheduled Areas unless Parliament extends it. The 2003 amendment created the Bodoland Territorial Council. The 5th Schedule falls under the Governor's control.

Co-operative societies: the 97th Amendment Act, 2011 made forming co-operative societies a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(c), added the Directive Principle Article 43B, and inserted Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT). It fixed a maximum of 21 directors, a five-year term and professional directors. In Union of India v. Rajendra Shah (2021) the Supreme Court struck down Part IXB for State co-operatives because it lacked ratification by half the States, but upheld it for multi-state co-operatives. The Ministry of Co-operation was created in 2021.

Amendment of Article 311: Article 311 gives civil servants safeguards against arbitrary dismissal, removal or reduction in rank. Clause (1) requires that the dismissing authority be not subordinate to the appointing authority. Clause (2) requires an inquiry with a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Exceptions are in the second proviso: conviction on a criminal charge, impracticability of holding an inquiry, and security of the State. The 42nd Amendment, 1976 removed the requirement of a second show-cause notice on the proposed punishment. Article 311 does not apply to defence personnel in the same way as to civil servants. Article 310 states the doctrine of pleasure.

Office of profit: Articles 102(1)(a) and 191(1)(a) disqualify an MP or MLA who holds an office of profit under the Union or State government, unless Parliament or the State legislature has exempted that office by law. The Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959 lists exempted offices. The 2006 amendment, after the Jaya Bachchan case, was passed to protect several offices. The Election Commission advises the President or Governor on disqualification. The Supreme Court in Jaya Bachchan v. Union of India (2006) held that what matters is the capacity to hold the office, not actual receipt of benefits. Article 103 and 192 settle disputes on disqualification.
related: Article 311 protects civil servants from dismissal by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority.
Article 310 states the doctrine of pleasure; Article 311 limits it.
The 97th Amendment, 2011 added Part IXB on co-operative societies.
The 106th Amendment Act, 2023 is the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam on women's reservation.
Articles 102(1)(a) and 191(1)(a) cover disqualification for holding an office of profit.
Article 312 provides for All India Services.
The 42nd Amendment, 1976 removed the second show-cause notice under Article 311(2).
The Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
summary: The best answer is (c), Amendment of Article 311, though there is no official key and I am working from memory. The 106th Amendment Bill is recalled as a pending private or government Bill from the 2000s on the protection given to civil servants under Article 311. Note that the 106th Amendment Act, 2023 (women's reservation) is a different matter and could not have been intended in a 2015 paper.
topic_notes: Article 311 and the protection of civil servants. Part XIV, Chapter I, deals with services under the Union and the States. Article 308 defines 'State' for this chapter. Article 309 empowers Parliament and State legislatures to regulate recruitment and conditions of service, and the executive may do so until a law is made. Article 310 states that civil servants hold office during the pleasure of the President or Governor. Article 311 limits that pleasure by giving procedural safeguards. Dismissal and removal differ: dismissal disqualifies the person from future public employment, but removal does not. Reduction in rank is also covered. The safeguards do not apply to defence personnel and are subject to the exceptions in the second proviso to clause (2). Courts have held that these safeguards apply to punishments, not to termination of a temporary employee's service simply by notice. Related ideas: All India Services under Article 312 are created by Parliament with a Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds majority. The UPSC under Articles 315 to 323 is consulted on disciplinary matters under Article 320(3)(c). Bill numbering note: the 106th Amendment Act, 2023 is the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, which reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies. A Bill's number and the numbering of the Act that finally gets passed can differ, since many Bills lapse or are withdrawn. Other amendments to remember: 97th (co-operatives, 2011), 101st (GST, 2016), 102nd (NCBC, 2018), 103rd (EWS 10% quota, 2019), 104th (ends SC/ST reservation in legislatures from 2030 extension, removes Anglo-Indian nomination, 2020), 105th (2021, States' power to identify SEBCs).

question: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of India?
options: It contains the scheme of the distribution of powers between the Union and the States
It contains the languages listed in the Constitution
It contains the provisions regarding the administration of tribal areas
It allocates seats in the Council of States
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Fourth Schedule contains the table showing how many Rajya Sabha seats each State and Union Territory gets. It is linked to Article 80 (composition of the Council of States: maximum 250 members, of whom 238 represent States and UTs and 12 are nominated by the President for expertise in literature, science, art and social service) and Article 4 (laws made for admission or formation of new States, which may amend the First and Fourth Schedules without being treated as constitutional amendments under Article 368). The allocation is based broadly on population, so it changes when States are reorganised, for example after the creation of Telangana in 2014 (Andhra Pradesh and Telangana seats were divided) and of Jammu and Kashmir as a UT in 2019. Elimination: the distribution of powers between the Union and States is the Seventh Schedule (Union, State and Concurrent Lists); the languages are in the Eighth Schedule (originally 14, now 22); tribal area administration is in the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes) and the Sixth Schedule (tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram). Only option (d) matches the Fourth Schedule.
explanations: Wrong: the division of powers between the Union and States is in the Seventh Schedule, under Article 246, with the Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
Wrong: the languages recognised by the Constitution are in the Eighth Schedule, which has 22 languages after the 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali.

Wrong: administration of tribal areas is in the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas in States other than the four northeastern States) and the Sixth Schedule (tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram).
Correct: the Fourth Schedule lays down the allocation of Rajya Sabha (Council of States) seats to States and UTs, under Articles 4 and 80.
keyfact: Fourth Schedule = allocation of Rajya Sabha seats (Articles 4 and 80); Seventh = lists, Eighth = languages, Fifth/Sixth = tribal areas.
option_notes: The Seventh Schedule (Article 246) contains the Union List (originally 97 subjects, now 100), State List (originally 66, now 61) and Concurrent List (originally 47, now 52). The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved five subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List: education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice. Residuary powers lie with the Union (Article 248).

The Eighth Schedule lists the official languages recognised by the Constitution. It originally had 14 languages. Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment (1967). Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali were added by the 71st Amendment (1992). Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali were added by the 92nd Amendment (2003), bringing the total to 22. Articles 344(1) and 351 refer to it.

The Fifth Schedule (Article 244(1)) governs the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. The Sixth Schedule (Articles 244(2) and 275(1)) provides for Autonomous District Councils and Regional Councils in those four northeastern States. The Governor plays the central role in the Fifth Schedule, and a Tribes Advisory Council is set up.

The Fourth Schedule allocates seats in the Council of States to States and UTs. Article 80 fixes the maximum strength at 250 (238 elected plus 12 nominated); the present actual strength is 245 (233 elected plus 12 nominated). Uttar Pradesh has the most seats (31), followed by Maharashtra (19). Members serve six-year terms, with one-third retiring every two years. Rajya Sabha is a permanent house and is not subject to dissolution.
related: First Schedule lists States and UTs; Second covers emoluments of constitutional office-holders.
Third Schedule has the forms of oaths and affirmations.
Ninth Schedule was added by the First Amendment, 1951.
Tenth Schedule (anti-defection) was added by the 52nd Amendment, 1985.
Eleventh Schedule (Panchayats) was added by the 73rd Amendment; Twelfth (Municipalities) by the 74th.
Rajya Sabha has a maximum of 250 members: 238 representatives plus 12 nominated.
The Eighth Schedule has 22 languages; Sindhi was added in 1967.
Article 4 laws amending the First and Fourth Schedules are not constitutional amendments under Article 368.
summary: The correct answer is (d). The Fourth Schedule of the Constitution allocates seats in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) to the States and Union Territories, as provided under Articles 4(1) and 80(2).
topic_notes: The Constitution has 12 Schedules (originally 8). First: names of States and UTs and their territories (Article 1 and Article 4). Second: emoluments and salaries of the President, Governors, Speakers, Judges and the CAG. Third: forms of oaths and affirmations. Fourth: allocation of Rajya Sabha seats. Fifth: administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes. Sixth: administration of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Seventh: Union, State and Concurrent Lists. Eighth: languages (22). Ninth: added by the First Amendment (1951) to protect land reform laws from judicial review; after I.R. Coelho (2007), laws placed in it after 24 April 1973 are open to review on the basis of the basic structure. Tenth: anti-defection provisions, added by the 52nd Amendment (1985). Eleventh: Panchayat powers (29 subjects), added by the 73rd Amendment (1992). Twelfth: Municipality powers (18 subjects), added by the 74th Amendment (1992). Rajya Sabha facts: Vice President is the ex officio Chairman; the Deputy Chairman is elected by members; election is by the single transferable vote through proportional representation by MLAs (Article 80(4)); there is no residence requirement after the 2003 amendment, and the open ballot was introduced in 2003; the minimum age is 30. Rajya Sabha has special powers under Article 249 (Parliament legislating on a State List subject in the national interest) and Article 312 (creation of All India Services), each by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. Typical UPSC angles: matching Schedules to their contents, the amendments that added Schedules, and the number of seats per State.

question: Adjudication of disputes relating to the inter-state river water are made by:
options: Tribunals set up by the Union Government
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 262 has two clauses. Clause (1) says Parliament may by law provide for the adjudication of any dispute or complaint about the use, distribution or control of the waters of any inter-state river or river valley. Clause (2) says Parliament may by law provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in such a dispute. Parliament used this power in the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 (River Boards Act, 1956 is a separate Act). Under the 1956 Act, a State government first asks the Centre; if negotiation fails, the Centre constitutes an ad hoc Tribunal. The Tribunal's award is final and binding, and Section 11 bars court jurisdiction. The Supreme Court can still hear writs on other grounds, such as Article 32 and Article 136 (special leave), because constitutional remedies are not wholly excluded. The 2002 amendment set time limits: 1 year to report, extendable up to 3 years, and 5 years for a final award. Elimination: Parliament only legislates and does not adjudicate (a); High Courts and the Supreme Court are barred by Section 11 (b, c). Article 131, the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction, does not cover these disputes when the Act applies.
explanations: Wrong: Parliament only makes the law under Article 262. It does not decide the disputes itself.
Wrong: High Courts are excluded by Section 11 of the 1956 Act, and in any case a dispute between States is not a High Court matter.
Wrong: The Supreme Court's jurisdiction is barred under Article 262(2) and the 1956 Act. Its original jurisdiction under Article 131 does not apply to these disputes.
Correct: The Centre constitutes ad hoc Tribunals under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, and their awards are final and binding.
keyfact: Article 262 plus the 1956 Act: inter-state river disputes go to ad hoc Tribunals set up by the Centre, and courts are barred.
option_notes: Parliament is the Union legislature, made up of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. Under Article 262 it may legislate on inter-state river disputes and, under Entry 56 of the Union List, on regulation and development of inter-state rivers in the public interest. It passed the River Boards Act, 1956 and the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956. It does not adjudicate disputes itself.

High Courts are constitutional courts under Articles 214-231, with writ jurisdiction under Article 226. They have territorial jurisdiction only within their State or States. Section 11 of the 1956 Act bars every court, including High Courts, from deciding river water disputes referred to a Tribunal. A dispute between two States cannot be decided by one State's High Court.

The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction under Article 131 for disputes between the Centre and States, or between States. Article 131 begins 'Subject to the other provisions of this Constitution', so Article 262 overrides it. It is barred from water disputes under Article 262(2) and the 1956 Act. It does hear related matters, such as the Cauvery Tribunal award appeals via SLP, and in 2018 it modified the Cauvery award.

Ad hoc Tribunals are constituted by the Union Government on a State's request when negotiation fails. Examples are Krishna, Godavari, Narmada, Cauvery, Ravi-Beas, Mahadayi and Vansadhara. Each has a Chairman and two members, who are Supreme Court or High Court judges. Awards are final and binding. Under the 2002 amendment, a Tribunal must report within 3 years, and the final award is due within 5 years.
related: Article 262: adjudication of inter-state river and valley disputes.
Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 creates ad hoc Tribunals.
Entry 56, Union List: regulation of inter-state rivers; Entry 17, State List: water.
River Boards Act, 1956: advisory River Boards for inter-state rivers.
Article 263: Inter-State Council, for coordination and recommendations.
Article 131: Supreme Court's original jurisdiction in disputes between States.
Cauvery Tribunal final award 2007; Supreme Court modified it in 2018.
2002 amendment: Tribunal must give its report within 3 years, and the final award within 5 years.
summary: The correct answer is (d): disputes relating to inter-state rivers are adjudicated by ad hoc Tribunals set up by the Union Government under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, enacted under Article 262. Article 262(2) lets Parliament bar the Supreme Court and other courts from exercising jurisdiction over such disputes, and the 1956 Act does exactly that.
topic_notes: Water is a State subject under Entry 17 of the State List, but it is subject to Entry 56 of the Union List, which covers regulation and development of inter-state rivers and river valleys to the extent Parliament declares it expedient in the public interest. Article 262 provides for adjudication of inter-state river disputes. Parliament enacted the River Boards Act, 1956, for advisory River Boards, which have never actually been constituted. It also enacted the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, for adjudication by ad hoc Tribunals. The 2002 amendment fixed time limits and allowed the Tribunal's report to be treated like a Supreme Court decree. A permanent Disputes Resolution Committee and a single standing Tribunal were proposed in the Inter-State River Water Disputes (Amendment) Bill, 2017 and 2019, with a Bench structure. The Sarkaria Commission and the Punchhi Commission also discussed these issues. Key Tribunals: Krishna (1969, 2004 Brijesh Kumar), Godavari (1969), Narmada (1969, award 1979), Cauvery (1990, final award 2007; Supreme Court modified it in Feb 2018), Ravi-Beas (1986), Mahadayi (2010, award 2018), Vansadhara (2010). Related: the Inter-State Council under Article 263 is a recommendatory body for coordination, and the Zonal Councils were created by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. Inter-state water issues also arise under the Indus Waters Treaty, 1960 with Pakistan, and under the Ganga Water Treaty, 1996 with Bangladesh.

question: The Reports of the State Public Service Commissions are presented annually to the:
options: President of India directly to be laid before each House of Parliament
respective Governors of States, who then forward the Reports to the Government of India
respective Governors who then forward the Reports to the State Legislatures concerned
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 323 deals with the reports of the Public Service Commissions. For the UPSC, Article 323(1) requires the Commission to present an annual report to the President, who lays it before each House of Parliament with a memorandum explaining the cases where the Commission's advice was not accepted and why. For a State PSC, Article 323(2) requires the report to go to the Governor, who lays it before the State Legislature, with a similar memorandum. For a Joint State PSC, the report goes to each Governor concerned, and each lays it before the Legislature of his own State. The reports do not go to the Centre, and they do not go to legislative committees as the first step. Related facts: members of a State PSC are appointed by the Governor but can be removed only by the President (Art. 317) on grounds of misbehaviour after a Supreme Court inquiry, or on certain other grounds without an inquiry. The tenure is 6 years or age 62, whichever is earlier. The UPSC tenure is 6 years or age 65. Elimination: (a) describes the UPSC procedure, (b) wrongly routes the report to the Centre, and (d) names the wrong recipient. Only (c) matches Art. 323(2).
explanations: Incorrect: this is the procedure for the UPSC under Art. 323(1), not for State PSCs. State PSC reports go to the Governor.
Incorrect: the Governor does not forward State PSC reports to the Government of India. He lays them before the State Legislature.
Correct: under Art. 323(2) the State PSC reports to the Governor, who lays the report before the State Legislature with a memorandum on non-accepted advice.
Incorrect: the report is presented to the Governor, not to legislative committees. Committees such as the Committee on Public Undertakings or the Public Accounts Committee do not receive it directly.
keyfact: Art. 323: the UPSC reports to the President, and State PSCs report to the Governor, who lays the report before the State Legislature.
option_notes: The UPSC reports to the President under Art. 323(1). The President lays the report before both Houses of Parliament with a memorandum explaining any cases where advice was not accepted. The UPSC is a constitutional body under Art. 315, and its Chairman and members are appointed by the President. Tenure is 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier. After their term, the Chairman and members are barred from further government employment, with limited exceptions.

The Governor does not forward State PSC reports to the Union Government. Under the federal scheme, State PSCs are answerable to the State executive and Legislature. The Governor appoints State PSC members (Art. 316), but only the President can remove them (Art. 317). The Governor determines their conditions of service, which cannot be varied to their disadvantage after appointment.

This is the correct constitutional procedure under Art. 323(2). The State PSC presents an annual report to the Governor. The Governor causes it to be laid before the State Legislature with a memorandum explaining the cases where the Commission's advice was not accepted and the reasons. Joint State PSCs report to each Governor concerned, and each lays it before his own State Legislature. This parallels the UPSC arrangement, with the Governor in place of the President.

Legislative committees do not receive the report directly. The report goes to the Governor, who places it before the whole Legislature. Committees such as the Public Accounts Committee or the Estimates Committee are parliamentary or legislative financial committees with different functions. Parliament does have a Committee on Subordinate Legislation and other committees, but none is the formal recipient of PSC reports.
related: Art. 323(1): UPSC annual report goes to the President, who lays it before Parliament.
Art. 323(2): State PSC annual report goes to the Governor, who lays it before the State Legislature.
Art. 316: the Governor appoints State PSC members, and the President appoints UPSC members.
Art. 317: State PSC members can be removed only by the President.
Art. 322: PSC expenses are charged to the Consolidated Fund.
The State PSC tenure is 6 years or age 62, and the UPSC tenure is 6 years or age 65.
Art. 315(2): a Joint State PSC can be created by Parliament law on the request of the State Legislatures.
The advice of a PSC is advisory and not binding on the government.
summary: The correct answer is (c). Under Article 323(2), the State Public Service Commission presents an annual report to the Governor, who causes it to be laid before the State Legislature along with a memorandum explaining any non-acceptance of the Commission's advice and the reasons for it.
topic_notes: Part XIV, Chapter II (Arts. 315-323) covers Public Service Commissions. Art. 315 provides for the PSCs of the Union and the States, and for Joint State PSCs, which Parliament may create at the request of the State Legislatures concerned. The UPSC Chairman and members are appointed by the President. State PSC members are appointed by the Governor. Art. 316 sets out the appointment and term: 6 years or age 65 for the UPSC, and 6 years or age 62 for a State PSC. One-half of the members must have held office for at least ten years under the Government of India or a State. Art. 317 provides that removal and suspension are by the President only. The President can remove for misbehaviour after a Supreme Court inquiry, or without an inquiry for insolvency, engaging in paid employment outside duties, or unfitness by infirmity of mind or body. Art. 318 empowers the President (UPSC) or the Governor (State PSC) to make regulations on staff and conditions of service. Art. 319 bars the Chairman and members from further employment after ceasing to hold office. The UPSC Chairman is ineligible for further employment under the Government of India or a State. A State PSC Chairman can become Chairman or member of the UPSC or another State PSC, but not otherwise be employed. Other members can become Chairman of their own PSC or the UPSC. Art. 320 lists the functions: conducting recruitment examinations, advising on recruitment rules, promotions, transfers, and disciplinary matters. Art. 321 allows extension of functions by Act. Art. 322 provides that expenses are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India (UPSC) or of the State (State PSC). Art. 323 deals with the annual reports. The advisory nature of the PSCs means their advice is not binding on the government, which is why a memorandum explaining non-acceptance is required.

question: Which one of the following is NOT correct with regard to Article 243 ZD of the Constitution of India?
options: In every State at the district level, there shall be a District Planning Committee to prepare a draft development plan for the district
The draft development plan must have regard to matters of common interest between the Panchayats and the Municipalities in the district
The Legislature of a State may make provision for the composition of the District Planning Committee
The development plans are forwarded to the State Planning Commissions for mandatory consideration
subject: Computers
detail: Article 243ZD, inserted by the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 (Part IXA, The Municipalities), provides for a District Planning Committee (DPC) in every State at the district level. Its job is to consolidate the plans prepared by the Panchayats and the Municipalities in the district and to prepare a draft development plan for the district as a whole. Clause (1) creates the DPC. Clause (2) lets the State Legislature make law on its composition, on how seats are filled, and on the functions and the chairperson's selection. At least four-fifths of the members must be elected by and from the elected members of the district panchayat and the municipalities in the district, in proportion to the rural and urban population. Clause (3) requires the DPC to have regard to matters of common interest between the Panchayats and Municipalities, such as spatial planning, sharing of water and other physical and natural resources, integrated development of infrastructure and environmental conservation. It must also have regard to the extent and type of available resources, financial or otherwise, and to consult institutions and organisations as the Governor may specify. Clause (4) says the Chairperson of the DPC forwards the development plan to the State Government. Options (a), (b) and (c) match this text. Option (d) is the odd one out: the Constitution has no State Planning Commission step, and the plan goes to the State Government.
explanations: Correct statement: Art. 243ZD(1) requires a DPC in every State at the district level to consolidate the plans of Panchayats and Municipalities and prepare a draft development plan for the whole district. So this is not the answer.

Correct statement: Art. 243ZD(3)(a) requires the DPC to have regard to matters of common interest between the Panchayats and Municipalities, including spatial planning, shared resources, infrastructure integration and environmental conservation. So this is not the answer.

Correct statement: Art. 243ZD(2) empowers the State Legislature to make provisions by law for the composition of the DPC and the manner of filling its seats, subject to the four-fifths elected-members rule. So this is not the answer.

Incorrect statement and hence the answer: under Art. 243ZD(4) the DPC Chairperson forwards the development plan to the State Government. The article does not mention State Planning Commissions or any mandatory consideration by them.
keyfact: Art. 243ZD: the DPC consolidates Panchayat and Municipal plans, and its Chairperson forwards the draft district plan to the State Government, not to a State Planning Commission.
option_notes: The District Planning Committee is the constitutional body under Art. 243ZD, created by the 74th Amendment (1992, in force 1 June 1993). It operates at district level in every State. It consolidates rural and urban local body plans into one draft district development plan. Art. 243ZD(2) says four-fifths of its members are elected from the district panchayat and municipalities, in proportion to rural and urban population.

Art. 243ZD(3) requires the DPC to have regard to matters of common interest between the Panchayats and Municipalities. These include spatial planning, sharing of water and other physical and natural resources, integrated development of infrastructure, and environmental conservation. It must also consider the available financial and other resources. This clause aims to integrate rural and urban planning in the district.

Art. 243ZD(2) lets the State Legislature, by law, make provisions regarding the composition of the DPC. This covers how its seats are filled and its functions relating to district planning. It also covers how the chairperson is chosen. The only fixed condition is that not less than four-fifths of the members are elected by and from the elected members of the district panchayat and municipalities in the district.

This option describes a step that does not exist. Under Art. 243ZD(4), the Chairperson of each DPC forwards the development plan to the State Government. The State Planning Board or Commission is an administrative body set up by State governments, not a constitutional body. It has no constitutional role in the DPC process. The NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission at Union level in 2015.
related: Art. 243ZD: District Planning Committee; Art. 243ZE: Metropolitan Planning Committee.
The 74th Amendment Act, 1992 added Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule (18 functions).
The DPC has at least four-fifths elected members; the MPC has at least two-thirds elected members.
A metropolitan area has a population of 10 lakh or more.
Wards Committees (Art. 243S) are mandatory for municipalities with a population of 3 lakh or more.
The DPC Chairperson forwards the development plan to the State Government.
The 73rd Amendment added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects).
Art. 243Q: Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council and Municipal Corporation.
summary: The answer is (d). Article 243ZD requires the District Planning Committee (DPC) to consolidate the plans prepared by Panchayats and Municipalities into a draft development plan for the whole district. The Chairperson of the DPC forwards that plan to the State Government, not to a State Planning Commission, and the article has no provision for 'mandatory consideration' by a State Planning Commission.
topic_notes: Part IX (Panchayats, Arts. 243 to 243O) came from the 73rd Amendment, and Part IXA (Municipalities, Arts. 243P to 243ZG) came from the 74th Amendment. Both were passed in 1992 and came into force in 1993. The 74th Amendment added the Twelfth Schedule, which lists 18 functions for urban local bodies. The 73rd Amendment added the Eleventh Schedule, which lists 29 functions for Panchayats. Art. 243ZD provides for the District Planning Committee. Art. 243ZE provides for the Metropolitan Planning Committee (MPC) in every metropolitan area, i.e. one with a population of 10 lakh or more. At least two-thirds of an MPC's members are elected by and from the elected members of the municipalities and the chairpersons of the Panchayats in the metropolitan area. Art. 243ZD(4)(b) says the DPC Chairperson forwards the plan to the State Government. Related provisions: Art. 243I and Art. 243Y provide for State Finance Commissions, constituted every five years. Art. 243K and Art. 243ZA provide for State Election Commissions. Art. 243ZF deals with continuance of existing laws. Art. 243ZG bars courts from interfering in electoral matters of municipalities. Art. 243Q provides for three types of municipalities: Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council and Municipal Corporation. Art. 243R covers the composition of municipalities. Art. 243S covers Wards Committees, for municipalities with a population of three lakh or more. Art. 243U fixes a five-year term and requires an election within six months of dissolution. Art. 243W covers the powers, authority and responsibilities of municipalities. Art. 243X covers the power to levy taxes. Art. 243P(e) defines a Metropolitan Area as one with a population of ten lakh or more. Possible future questions include the composition of the DPC, the MPC's two-thirds rule, the Twelfth Schedule functions, and the differences between DPC and MPC.

question: In 1947, India had municipal corporations at:
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Urban local government in India began in the Presidency towns under the East India Company. The Madras Municipal Corporation was set up in 1688 by a royal charter, making it the oldest in India. In 1726 a charter established mayor's courts and corporations in Bombay and Calcutta. Over time these were reorganised: the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act 1888 and the Calcutta Municipal Act 1923 (earlier 1899) gave them their later form. Lord Ripon's 1882 Resolution on local self-government is called the 'Magna Carta' of local government, and Ripon is the 'Father of Local Self-Government in India'. The Government of India Act 1919 made local government a transferred subject; the 1935 Act continued it as a provincial subject. After 1947 municipal corporations spread to other cities, and the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act 1992 (Part IXA, Articles 243P-243ZG, 12th Schedule) gave them constitutional status. Elimination: Delhi and Lucknow were not corporations in 1947 (Delhi's MCD came in 1957, Lucknow's corporation later), so options (a), (b) and (d) fail.
explanations: Wrong: Delhi had no municipal corporation in 1947; the Municipal Corporation of Delhi was created in 1957 under the DMC Act 1957.
Wrong: Lucknow had a municipality (board), not a corporation, in 1947; Lucknow Nagar Nigam came later (1959 in UP).
Correct: Madras (1688), Bombay and Calcutta (1726) were the Presidency-town corporations existing in 1947.
Wrong: Lucknow did not have a corporation in 1947, so this pairing is incorrect even though Calcutta and Madras were right.
keyfact: In 1947 the corporations were the Presidency towns: Madras (1688), Bombay and Calcutta (1726).
option_notes: Madras, Calcutta, Delhi: Madras (1688) and Calcutta (1726) were old corporations. Delhi was governed by a municipal committee and NDMC arrangements; the Municipal Corporation of Delhi was established in 1957 and was trifurcated into North, South and East MCDs in 2012, then unified in 2022.

Lucknow, Calcutta, Bombay: Calcutta and Bombay were Presidency corporations. Lucknow was a municipal board under the UP Municipalities Act 1916; it became a municipal corporation only after independence (Nagar Nigam, 1960s).

Madras, Calcutta, Bombay: the three Presidency towns of British India. Madras Corporation (1688) is the oldest in India; Bombay Municipal Corporation (BMC) was governed by the 1888 Act and Calcutta by the Calcutta Municipal Act. They were the model for later corporations.
Lucknow, Calcutta, Madras: Calcutta and Madras were corporations, but Lucknow was not one in 1947. Lucknow was the capital of the United Provinces and had a municipal board only.
related: Madras Corporation (1688) is the oldest municipal corporation in India.
Lord Ripon is the Father of Local Self-Government in India (1882 Resolution).
74th Amendment (1992) added Part IXA and the 12th Schedule (18 functions).
Articles 243P-243ZG deal with municipalities.
Municipal Corporation of Delhi was established in 1957.
Balwantrai Mehta Committee (1957) dealt with rural panchayati raj.
State Election Commission conducts municipal elections (Article 243ZA).
Central Council of Local Government was set up in 1954.
summary: The answer is (c) Madras, Calcutta and Bombay. These three Presidency towns were the first to get municipal corporations: Madras in 1688, Bombay in 1726 and Calcutta in 1726 (a corporation with a mayor's court). They were the only corporations at independence in the classical sense of the colonial Presidency towns.
topic_notes: Evolution of urban local government in India: 1687-88 Madras Municipal Corporation by charter; 1726 corporations at Bombay and Calcutta; 1793 Charter Act extended municipal powers in Presidency towns; 1870 Lord Mayo's Resolution on financial decentralisation; 1882 Lord Ripon's Resolution, the 'Magna Carta' of local self-government, which promoted elected non-official majorities and chairmen; 1907 Royal Commission on Decentralisation (Hobhouse); 1909 its recommendations; 1919 Government of India Act, dyarchy, local self-government a transferred subject under Indian ministers; 1924 Cantonment Act; 1935 Act, provincial subject. Post-independence: Article 40 (DPSP) directs states to organise village panchayats; 1957 Balwantrai Mehta Committee (panchayats); 1978 Ashok Mehta Committee; 1989 Thungon Committee; 1989 the 65th Amendment Bill failed in Rajya Sabha; 1992 the 74th Amendment (in force 1 June 1993) added Part IXA, Articles 243P-243ZG and the 12th Schedule with 18 functions. Types of urban bodies: municipal corporation, municipality, notified area committee, town area committee, cantonment board, township, port trust, special purpose agency. Central Council of Local Government (1954) is an advisory body. Corporations are headed by a mayor; commissioner is the executive head. Wards committees are required for populations of 3 lakh or more (Article 243S). Municipal elections are conducted by State Election Commissions (Article 243ZA).

question: Which one of the following is NOT an objective of Non-Aligned Movement?
options: To contribute to the game of power politics
To play a role in the process of decolonization of the slave countries
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: NAM grew out of the 1955 Bandung Asian-African Conference and the Panchsheel principles (1954). It was formally launched at the Belgrade Summit in September 1961 by Nehru (India), Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Nkrumah (Ghana).
