The BIOS or UEFI handles the initial hardware check at startup (POST). Interfaces to know are USB, which was designed to replace serial and parallel ports and has speeds of 480 Mbps (USB 2.0) and 5 Gbps (USB 3.0), plus HDMI, VGA, SATA, FireWire (IEEE 1394) and Bluetooth. Peripherals are classed as input, output and storage devices. Possible next questions are the difference between plug and play and hot swap, the meaning of a device driver, and the full forms of USB, BIOS and POST.

question: Which one of the following software applications would be the most appropriate for performing numerical and_ statistical calculations ?
subject: Computers
detail: A spreadsheet (Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc, Google Sheets) is application software built around a grid of cells identified by column letter and row number, e.g. A1. Cells hold numbers, text or formulas, and a change in one value automatically recalculates every dependent cell. Built-in functions include SUM, AVERAGE, MEDIAN, MODE, STDEV, VAR, CORREL, COUNT, IF and VLOOKUP. Spreadsheets also offer pivot tables, what-if analysis, goal seek, solver, the Data Analysis ToolPak (regression, t-test, ANOVA) and charts. VisiCalc (1979) was the first spreadsheet program. Elimination: a database (MS Access, Oracle, MySQL) is meant to store, retrieve and manage large structured records with queries; it is not meant for general calculation. A graphics package (Paint, CorelDRAW, Photoshop) creates or edits images. A document processor (word processor such as MS Word) prepares text documents, and although it has tables, its calculation ability is minimal. So the spreadsheet is the best fit.
explanations: Incorrect: a database stores and queries structured records. Its calculation ability is limited and secondary.
Correct: a spreadsheet has formulas, statistical functions and automatic recalculation, so it is designed for numerical and statistical work.
Incorrect: a graphics package is for drawing, designing and editing images, not for calculation.
Incorrect: a document processor is for creating and formatting text. It has only basic table arithmetic.
keyfact: Spreadsheets (Excel/Calc) are the tool for numerical and statistical calculation using cell formulas and functions.
option_notes: A database is an organised collection of related data managed by a DBMS (MS Access, Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server). Data is stored in tables of records and fields, with primary keys and relationships. It is queried with SQL. Its strengths are storage, retrieval, integrity and multi-user access, and it can do aggregate calculations, but it is not a general calculation tool.

A spreadsheet is an electronic worksheet of rows and columns, and its intersections are cells. Examples are MS Excel (file extension .xlsx), LibreOffice Calc and Google Sheets. It has formulas that begin with =, functions, charts, pivot tables, sorting and filtering. VisiCalc (1979) was the first, followed by Lotus 1-2-3. A workbook contains multiple worksheets.

A graphics package is software for creating, editing and manipulating images. Examples are MS Paint, Adobe Photoshop (raster), CorelDRAW and Illustrator (vector), and GIMP. Common formats are JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP and SVG. It is used for design, illustration and photo editing, not for calculation.

A document processor, or word processor, creates, edits, formats and prints text documents. Examples are MS Word (.docx), LibreOffice Writer and Google Docs. Features include fonts, styles, spell check, mail merge, headers and footers, and tables. It is used for letters, reports and books. Its calculation ability is minimal.
related: VisiCalc (1979) was the first electronic spreadsheet program.
Excel formulas begin with the equals sign (=).
Modern Excel has 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns (A to XFD).
The default Excel workbook extension is .xlsx.
Absolute cell reference uses the $ sign, e.g. $A$1.
Open-source spreadsheet: LibreOffice Calc; cloud spreadsheet: Google Sheets.
Pivot tables summarise large datasets in a spreadsheet.
MS Access is a desktop database application.
summary: The answer is (b) Spreadsheet. A spreadsheet organises data in rows and columns of cells and has built-in formulas and statistical functions, so it is the most suitable tool for numerical and statistical calculations.
topic_notes: Application software is used for specific user tasks, as opposed to system software such as the operating system. Main categories: word processors (MS Word, Writer), spreadsheets (Excel, Calc), presentation software (PowerPoint, Impress), database software (Access, MySQL), graphics software (Photoshop, CorelDRAW), web browsers and email clients. Spreadsheet basics: a cell address like B3 is a relative reference, $B$3 is an absolute reference and $B3 is a mixed reference. A formula starts with =. Common functions include SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT, COUNTA, IF, VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, ROUND, STDEV and CORREL. Excel 2007 and later has 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns (XFD), while Excel 2003 had 65,536 rows and 256 columns (IV). The default file extension is .xlsx, and .xls was used earlier. Other features are the active cell, formula bar, name box, fill handle, sorting, filtering, conditional formatting, pivot tables, charts, macros and the Data Analysis ToolPak. Other angles UPSC could ask: the full forms and uses of DBMS, RDBMS and SQL; the difference between a workbook and a worksheet; typical extensions (.docx, .pptx, .accdb); and software types such as freeware, shareware and open source. Also remember MS Office as a suite, the idea of integrated software, and basic keyboard shortcuts such as Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Z and F2 for editing a cell.

question: Consider the following statements on Global Positioning System (GPS) : i GPS allows accurate time-stamping on ATM transactions. 2: GPS relies on a set of satellites for transferring signals worldwide. Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
subject: General Science
detail: The Global Positioning System is a satellite-based radionavigation system owned by the US government and operated by the US Space Force. It has a nominal constellation of 24 operational satellites (currently about 31) in Medium Earth Orbit at roughly 20,200 km, in six orbital planes with an inclination of 55 degrees. Each satellite carries atomic clocks (rubidium and caesium) and continuously broadcasts its position and the precise time. A receiver needs signals from at least four satellites to compute latitude, longitude, altitude and the time correction (trilateration). Besides navigation, GPS is a major source of precise timing. Banks, telecom networks, power grids and stock exchanges use GPS time to synchronise systems and to time-stamp transactions, including ATM and card transactions, so that records are accurate and ordered. Statement 1 is therefore correct. Statement 2 is correct because the system works by sending signals from a set of satellites that cover the whole globe. Elimination: since both statements describe real, standard features of GPS, options (a), (b) and (d) fail and only (c) holds.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 2 is also correct, so 'statement 1 only' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong because statement 1 is also correct: GPS timing is used for time-stamping ATM transactions.
(c) is right because GPS gives accurate timing for transaction time-stamping and works through a global satellite constellation.
(d) is wrong because both statements are factually correct.
keyfact: GPS is a satellite constellation (about 24+ satellites at 20,200 km) that gives position and precise atomic-clock time, which is used for time-stamping transactions.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would mean GPS timing is useful but that the satellite statement is false. In fact GPS is by definition a satellite-based system. The timing statement is true, as GPS supplies precise time for banking and telecom, but it is not the only true statement.

Option (b), '2 only', would accept that GPS uses satellites but deny its timing role. In reality GPS is one of the main sources of precise time. Its satellites carry atomic clocks, and timing is one of the three core services: positioning, navigation and timing (PNT).

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is correct. GPS is a global navigation satellite system (GNSS) that provides positioning, navigation and timing. It is used for aviation, shipping, mapping, agriculture, disaster management, and for financial and telecom time synchronisation.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', would deny both the timing use and the satellite basis of GPS, which is contrary to the facts. GPS is fundamentally a satellite constellation and a time-distribution system.
related: GPS was developed by the US Department of Defense and became fully operational in 1995.
A GPS receiver needs signals from at least 4 satellites for a 3D fix plus time.
GPS satellites orbit at about 20,200 km in Medium Earth Orbit.
NavIC (IRNSS) is India's regional navigation system, with 7 satellites.
GAGAN is the ISRO-AAI GPS-augmentation system for civil aviation.
Russia's GNSS is GLONASS, Europe's is Galileo, and China's is BeiDou.
GPS satellites carry atomic clocks (rubidium and caesium).
statements: 1 — Correct: GPS provides very accurate time (nanosecond-level) that financial networks use for time-stamping ATM transactions. GPS satellites carry atomic clocks synchronised to UTC through ground control. Receivers derive time from the signals, and it is used widely in banking, stock exchanges, telecom base stations and power grids for synchronisation, audit trails and dispute resolution. Time-stamping gives each transaction a verifiable sequence and prevents disputes over when it occurred.

2 — Correct: GPS depends on a constellation of satellites that transmit signals covering the entire globe. The constellation has at least 24 satellites in MEO at about 20,200 km, with an orbital period of about 12 hours. At least four satellites are visible from almost anywhere on Earth. It was developed by the US Department of Defense, started in the 1970s, and was declared fully operational in 1995. It is free for civilian use worldwide.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. GPS time signals from atomic clocks on satellites are used to time-stamp financial transactions such as ATM transactions, and GPS works through a constellation of satellites that broadcast signals worldwide.
topic_notes: GPS is a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) developed by the US Department of Defense. Work began in the 1970s, the first satellite was launched in 1978, and the system became fully operational in 1995. The nominal constellation is 24 satellites in six orbital planes at about 20,200 km altitude, inclined at 55 degrees, with an orbital period of about 11 hr 58 min. The system has three segments: space (satellites), control (ground stations, with the master control station at Schriever Space Force Base) and user (receivers). A receiver calculates position by trilateration using the travel time of signals from at least four satellites: three for position and one for correcting the receiver clock. Satellites carry atomic clocks, and relativistic corrections are applied. Other GNSS systems include Russia's GLONASS, the EU's Galileo, China's BeiDou, Japan's QZSS (regional) and India's NavIC. NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), formerly IRNSS, is run by ISRO. It is a regional system with 7 satellites, covers India and up to about 1,500 km beyond its borders, and offers the Standard Positioning Service and a restricted service. GAGAN is India's GPS-Aided GEO Augmented Navigation system, built by ISRO and the Airports Authority of India for aviation. Applications of GPS include navigation, surveying, precision agriculture, disaster management, fleet tracking, and timing for banking, power grids and telecom networks. Limitations include signal blockage indoors, urban canyons and jamming or spoofing.

question:
Consider the following statements : Cellular technology evolves in stages called Generation (G), where
1. A Generation represents the number of subscribers; higher Generation has more subscribers. 2. 2G technology has two standards CDMA and GSM. 8. 2G technology has CDMA standard and 3G has GSM standard. Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Mobile generations (1G to 5G) mark major changes in radio technology, data speed, spectrum use and services, not the number of subscribers. 1G (1980s) was analogue voice (AMPS). 2G (1990s) went digital, with voice, SMS and low-speed data. Its main standards were GSM (TDMA based, Europe, SIM card) and CDMA (IS-95, developed by Qualcomm). 2.5G/2.75G added GPRS and EDGE. 3G (2000s) brought mobile broadband, with UMTS/WCDMA (the GSM evolution) and CDMA2000 (the CDMA evolution), so 3G was not tied to GSM alone. 4G (LTE, LTE-Advanced) is all-IP packet switched; VoLTE carries voice. 5G uses NR with enhanced mobile broadband, URLLC and massive IoT. Elimination: statement 1 is wrong because generation does not mean subscriber count. Statement 3 is wrong because it assigns CDMA exclusively to 2G and GSM exclusively to 3G. Statement 3 appears as '8' in the OCR, which is clearly a typo for 3. So only statement 2 survives, giving (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statements 1 and 3 are both incorrect: generation is not about subscriber numbers, and CDMA and GSM are not split between 2G and 3G.
(b) is wrong because statement 1 confuses a technology generation with subscriber count.
(c) is wrong because statement 3 wrongly limits CDMA to 2G and GSM to 3G; the option itself is also a mis-OCR of 3.
(d) is correct because statement 2 is accurate: 2G had the two standards GSM and CDMA.
keyfact: 2G = digital, with two standards GSM and CDMA; generations mark technology, not subscriber numbers.
option_notes: Option (a) combines statements 1 and 3. Statement 1 defines generation by subscriber count, which is wrong. Statement 3 mixes up standards by generation. Real definition: generations are set by technology, spectrum, speed and services, with ITU IMT specifications for 3G, 4G and 5G. Both statements fail, so the option is wrong.

Option (b) says statement 1 only. It claims that a higher generation has more subscribers. In reality, 2G and even 3G often had more subscribers than newer generations early in the new generation's rollout. Generations are classed by the technology used. The option is wrong.

Option (c) says statement 3 only. It claims that 2G is CDMA and 3G is GSM. In reality, GSM was the dominant 2G standard, and 3G had UMTS/WCDMA (the GSM family) and CDMA2000. Hence the claim is wrong. The '8' in the OCR stands for 3.

Option (d) says statement 2 only. It is correct: 2G had two standards, GSM (TDMA based, SIM cards, Europe) and CDMA (IS-95, Qualcomm, spread spectrum). Both were digital, offering voice, SMS and low-rate data (GPRS/EDGE).
related: GSM uses SIM cards; CDMA phones were often locked to the network without SIMs.
First commercial GSM network launched in 1991 in Finland.
CDMA was developed by Qualcomm (IS-95, cdmaOne).
3G standards: UMTS/WCDMA and CDMA2000.
4G LTE is all-IP, with VoLTE for voice.
5G was launched in India in October 2022.
ITU standards: IMT-2000 (3G), IMT-Advanced (4G), IMT-2020 (5G).
TRAI was established in 1997.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: A generation denotes a technological stage (air interface, speed, services), not subscriber numbers. Higher generations do not necessarily have more subscribers; 2G still had huge user bases after 3G arrived. Facts: 1G was analogue (AMPS, NMT). 2G was digital (GSM, CDMA). 3G offered data at 384 kbps to several Mbps. 4G LTE targets 100 Mbps or more. 5G targets up to 20 Gbps peak under ITU IMT-2020. ITU defines generation standards under IMT-2000 (3G), IMT-Advanced (4G) and IMT-2020 (5G).

2 — Correct: 2G had two main standards, GSM and CDMA. GSM, from the Groupe Spécial Mobile in Europe, was commercially launched in 1991 in Finland, uses TDMA/FDMA and SIM cards, and is the most widely used. CDMA (IS-95, cdmaOne) was developed by Qualcomm and used spread spectrum. In India, GSM operators were Airtel, Vodafone and Idea; CDMA operators were Reliance, Tata Indicom and MTS. Mobile services in India began in 1995 (Kolkata, Jyoti Basu to Sukh Ram call). 2G data used GPRS and EDGE.

3 — Incorrect: CDMA is not exclusive to 2G and GSM is not exclusive to 3G. Both families evolved: GSM went to GPRS, EDGE, then UMTS/WCDMA (3G) and HSPA. CDMA went from IS-95 to CDMA2000 and EV-DO (3G). 3G in India was launched by BSNL in 2008 and spectrum auctioned in 2010. 3GPP standardises the GSM, UMTS, LTE and 5G family, while 3GPP2 handled CDMA2000. LTE ended the split, as CDMA operators moved to LTE.
summary: The correct answer is (d): only statement 2 is correct. 2G technology had two main standards, GSM and CDMA (IS-95/cdmaOne). A generation reflects a technology leap, not subscriber numbers, and both CDMA and GSM existed in 2G (and 3G also had both families), so statement 3 is wrong.
topic_notes: Mobile generations: 1G (1980s) analogue voice using FDMA, with AMPS in the US, NMT in the Nordic countries and TACS in the UK. 2G (1990s) digital using GSM (TDMA) and CDMA IS-95; services included SMS, MMS and encrypted voice; GPRS (2.5G) and EDGE (2.75G) added packet data. 3G (2000s) is defined by IMT-2000 with at least 144 kbps to 2 Mbps; main systems were UMTS/WCDMA, HSPA, CDMA2000 and EV-DO, enabling video calling and mobile internet. 4G is defined by IMT-Advanced, with peak speeds of 100 Mbps (mobile) and 1 Gbps (stationary); LTE and WiMAX; all-IP, with VoLTE for voice. 5G (IMT-2020) offers up to 20 Gbps peak, latency of about 1 ms, and massive IoT; it uses sub-6 GHz and mmWave bands. India: mobile services began in 1995; NTP 1999 introduced revenue share; 3G launched in 2008 by MTNL and BSNL; 3G auction in 2010; 4G in 2012 (Airtel in Kolkata) and Jio in 2016; 5G launched in October 2022 at the India Mobile Congress, with auctions in 2022. Key bodies: TRAI (1997), DoT, ITU, 3GPP. Other angles: Bluetooth, Wi-Fi standards (IEEE 802.11), NFC, SIM and IMEI, roaming, MNP (Mobile Number Portability, 2011), and spectrum bands (700 MHz, 800, 900, 1800, 2100, 2300, 2500, 3300 MHz, 26 GHz).

question: LAN, WAN and MAN are computer networks 84. covering different areas. Their first alphabets L, W and M respectively stand for
subject: Computers
detail: Computer networks are classified by geographical coverage. A LAN (Local Area Network) connects devices within a limited area such as a room, office, building or campus. It typically uses Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) or Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11), offers high speed and is privately owned. A MAN (Metropolitan Area Network) spans a city or large campus, roughly 5-50 km, and is used for cable TV networks, city-wide broadband or linking bank branches within a city. A WAN (Wide Area Network) spans countries or continents and uses leased lines, satellites or public carriers. The Internet is the largest WAN. Related types are PAN (Personal Area Network, a few metres, e.g. Bluetooth), CAN (Campus Area Network) and SAN (Storage Area Network). Elimination: 'World' in (a) is wrong because WAN means Wide, and 'Middle' is not a network term. 'Long' and 'Wireless' in (b) are wrong. 'Least' and 'Maximum' in (d) are meaningless. Only (c) gives Local, Wide and Metropolitan.
explanations: Wrong: W in WAN stands for Wide, not World, and M in MAN stands for Metropolitan, not Middle.
Wrong: L is Local, not Long, and W is Wide, not Wireless. Only M for Metropolitan is correct.
Correct: Local Area Network, Wide Area Network and Metropolitan Area Network.
Wrong: Least, Wireless and Maximum are not the expansions of any of these abbreviations.
keyfact: LAN = Local, MAN = Metropolitan, WAN = Wide Area Network, in increasing order of coverage.
option_notes: Local, World, Middle: this is a made-up combination. 'World Area Network' is not a standard term, although WANs can be global, and 'Middle Area Network' does not exist. The correct terms are Wide and Metropolitan.
Long, Wireless, Metropolitan: only Metropolitan is valid. WLAN means Wireless LAN, a different term. 'Long' is not used, although long-haul links are a feature of WANs.
Local, Wide, Metropolitan: the standard expansions. LAN covers a small area at high speed. MAN covers a city. WAN covers countries or continents, with the Internet as the best-known example.
Least, Wireless, Maximum: these are invented and have no networking meaning. They only mimic the idea of small and large coverage.
related: LAN is limited to a building or campus and is usually privately owned.
MAN covers a city, roughly 5-50 km.
The Internet is the largest WAN.
PAN covers a few metres, e.g. Bluetooth.
WLAN means Wireless Local Area Network (Wi-Fi, IEEE 802.11).
Ethernet is standardised as IEEE 802.3.
A router connects different networks and works at the network layer.
IPv4 is 32-bit and IPv6 is 128-bit.
summary: The correct answer is (c). LAN stands for Local Area Network, WAN for Wide Area Network and MAN for Metropolitan Area Network. The three differ in the geographical area they cover: a building or campus, a city, or a country or the globe.
topic_notes: Networks are classified by scale. PAN (Personal Area Network) covers about 1-10 m, for example Bluetooth or USB tethering. LAN covers up to a few km, usually one building or campus. It is high speed (100 Mbps to 10 Gbps), uses Ethernet or Wi-Fi, and is built with switches, hubs and routers. CAN is a campus network linking several LANs. MAN covers a city, about 5-50 km. It uses fibre or microwave links, and standards include DQDB (IEEE 802.6) and FDDI. WAN covers countries or the globe. It uses routers, leased lines, MPLS, satellite and undersea cables, and has lower speed and higher cost than a LAN. The Internet is the largest WAN. Other related terms: VPN (Virtual Private Network, a secure tunnel over a public network), Intranet (private network within an organisation), Extranet (an intranet shared with trusted outsiders), and SAN (Storage Area Network). Topologies include bus, star, ring, mesh and tree. Devices: a hub works at the physical layer, a switch at the data link layer, a router at the network layer, and a gateway connects different protocols. The OSI model has 7 layers and TCP/IP has 4. Protocols: HTTP, FTP, SMTP and TCP/IP. IP addresses: IPv4 is 32-bit and IPv6 is 128-bit.

question: A rectangular garden is to be twice as long as its width. If 360 m of fencing including gates will totally enclose this garden, what is the length of the garden ? 85
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a basic perimeter problem on rectangles. The perimeter of a rectangle is P = 2(l + w). The question gives the relation l = 2w, and says the fencing, including gates, totally encloses the garden, so the whole 360 m is the perimeter (gates do not change the length of the boundary). Substituting gives 2(2w + w) = 6w = 360, so w = 60 m and l = 120 m. Check: 2(120 + 60) = 360 m, which matches. Area = 120 × 60 = 7200 sq m. Elimination: if l = 180, then w = 90 and perimeter = 540, too large. If l = 140, then w = 70 and perimeter = 420, too large. If l = 150, then w = 75 and perimeter = 450, too large. Only 120 gives 360. A quick shortcut: with a ratio of 2:1, the perimeter is 6 parts, so one part is 360/6 = 60 and the length is 2 parts = 120. Watch for the trap word 'gates': it is a distractor, not a deduction. Always check for the phrase 'including' or 'excluding' in such questions.
explanations: Correct. w = 60 m, l = 120 m, perimeter = 2(120 + 60) = 360 m.
Incorrect. l = 180 gives w = 90 and perimeter 540 m, not 360 m.
Incorrect. l = 140 gives w = 70 and perimeter 420 m, not 360 m.
Incorrect. l = 150 gives w = 75 and perimeter 450 m, not 360 m.
keyfact: 2:1 rectangle with perimeter 360 m: perimeter = 6 × width, so width = 60 m and length = 120 m.
option_notes: 120 m is the length of a rectangle of width 60 m. It has perimeter 360 m, area 7200 sq m and diagonal about 134.2 m (60√5). Its length-to-width ratio is 2:1, so the perimeter is 6 times the width.

180 m would be the length if the width were 90 m in a 2:1 rectangle. The perimeter would be 540 m and the area 16200 sq m. It is what you get if you wrongly take 360 as half the perimeter (the semi-perimeter l + w = 270 is a different quantity), or if you take 3w = 360 and then misassign terms.

140 m would be the length if the width were 70 m in a 2:1 rectangle. The perimeter would be 420 m and the area 9800 sq m. It is a plausible-looking distractor close to the correct value but does not satisfy the perimeter condition.

150 m would be the length if the width were 75 m in a 2:1 rectangle. The perimeter would be 450 m and the area 11250 sq m. It is a distractor; 150 is a round number that tempts guessers but fails the 360 m check.
related: Rectangle perimeter = 2(l + w); area = l × w.
Rectangle diagonal = √(l² + w²).
For a given perimeter, a square encloses the maximum area among rectangles.
If one side is a wall, fencing = 2w + l.
1 hectare = 10,000 sq m.
Square diagonal = side × √2.
Circle circumference = 2πr, area = πr².
summary: The answer is (a) 120 m. The perimeter is 360 m and length = 2 × width, so 2(2w + w) = 6w = 360, giving w = 60 m and length = 120 m.
topic_notes: Mensuration of 2D figures is a regular topic in the Quantitative Aptitude section. Key formulas: rectangle perimeter = 2(l + w), area = l × w, diagonal = √(l² + w²). Square perimeter = 4a, area = a², diagonal = a√2. Circle circumference = 2πr, area = πr². Triangle area = ½ × base × height, and Heron's formula = √[s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)] where s is the semi-perimeter. Equilateral triangle area = (√3/4)a². Trapezium area = ½ (a + b) h. Rhombus area = ½ d1 d2. Parallelogram area = base × height. For a fixed perimeter, the square has the maximum area among rectangles. Ratio problems: if sides are in the ratio a:b, then perimeter = 2(a + b) parts. Fencing problems: check whether gates, or one side (such as a wall), are excluded. If one side lies along a wall, then fencing = 2w + l. Path-around-garden problems: area of path = outer area minus inner area. Cost of fencing = perimeter × rate per metre. Cost of carpeting or turfing = area × rate. Unit conversions: 1 hectare = 10,000 sq m, 1 acre ≈ 4047 sq m. Practise setting variables, writing the equation, solving and verifying against the options.

question: The ‘Cloud Computing’ technology refers to
options: Aset of algorithms that solves problems using fuzzy logic
Many computers that are interconnected through wireless networks and satellites
A distributed computer architecture wae that provides software, infrastructure and platforms just as required by applications/users
A futuristic technology that will use clouds to perform computing B-CRHE-O-PAPA (28-A)
subject: Computers
detail: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of computing resources (servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics) over the internet, usually with pay-as-you-go pricing. NIST (SP 800-145) defines five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. It has three service models: IaaS (e.g., Amazon EC2), PaaS (e.g., Google App Engine, Azure App Service) and SaaS (e.g., Gmail, Salesforce). It has four deployment models: public, private, hybrid and community. Option (c) captures the core idea of software, infrastructure and platforms provided as required. Option (a) describes fuzzy-logic or soft-computing techniques, which are unrelated to service delivery. Option (b) describes only a networking arrangement, and cloud computing does not depend on wireless links or satellites. Option (d) is wrong because the technology is not futuristic and does not use atmospheric clouds. The word 'cloud' comes from the cloud symbol used in network diagrams to represent the internet. In India, MeghRaj is the government's cloud initiative under MeitY.
explanations: Wrong: fuzzy logic is a soft-computing technique for reasoning with degrees of truth. It is not cloud computing.
Wrong: interconnected computers describe a network or grid. Cloud computing does not require wireless or satellite links and is defined by on-demand service delivery.
Correct: this matches the NIST-style definition. It is a distributed architecture that provides software (SaaS), platforms (PaaS) and infrastructure (IaaS) on demand.
Wrong: the technology is already widely used, and the 'cloud' is a metaphor for the internet, not real clouds.
keyfact: Cloud computing = on-demand delivery of software (SaaS), platforms (PaaS) and infrastructure (IaaS) over a network.
option_notes: Fuzzy logic was introduced by Lotfi Zadeh in 1965. It handles partial truth values between 0 and 1 instead of strict true/false. It is used in control systems such as washing machines, ACs and automotive systems. It is part of soft computing, alongside neural networks and genetic algorithms. It has no link to cloud service delivery.

This describes a computer network, such as a WAN or the internet, that may use Wi-Fi, microwave or satellite links. Networking is only a basis for cloud services. Grid computing also links many computers, but its purpose is pooling resources for large tasks, not offering on-demand services to users.

Cloud computing is defined by NIST SP 800-145. Its service models are IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. Its deployment models are public, private, hybrid and community. Its key features are elasticity, resource pooling, measured service and pay-per-use. Major providers are AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. In India, MeghRaj is the government cloud initiative launched in 2014.

This is a distractor. Cloud computing is a current technology, in use since the mid-2000s (AWS launched in 2006). The word 'cloud' is a metaphor taken from network diagrams, where a cloud shape stands for the internet. It has nothing to do with weather clouds.
related: NIST SP 800-145 gives the standard definition of cloud computing.
The three service models are IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Virtualization via a hypervisor is the key enabling technology of the cloud.
MeghRaj is the Government of India's cloud initiative, launched in 2014.
The four deployment models are public, private, hybrid and community cloud.
AWS launched EC2 in 2006 and is the largest public cloud provider.
Gmail and Google Docs are examples of SaaS.
Elasticity and pay-per-use (measured service) are core cloud features.
summary: The answer is (c). Cloud computing is a distributed model that delivers software (SaaS), platforms (PaaS) and infrastructure (IaaS) over a network on demand, as users or applications need them. The other options describe fuzzy logic, wireless networks or a made-up idea.
topic_notes: Cloud computing delivers IT resources over the internet on demand. The term was popularised around 2006, when Amazon launched EC2 and S3 and Google's CEO Eric Schmidt used the phrase. The NIST definition lists five characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling (multi-tenancy), rapid elasticity and measured service. Service models: IaaS gives virtual machines, storage and networks (AWS EC2, Azure VMs). PaaS gives a platform for developing and deploying applications (Google App Engine, Heroku). SaaS gives ready-made software through a browser (Gmail, Office 365, Salesforce). Deployment models: public cloud (shared, run by a provider), private cloud (a single organisation), hybrid cloud (a mix of the two) and community cloud (shared by organisations with common concerns). Related concepts: virtualization (the enabling technology, using a hypervisor), data centres, edge computing, fog computing, serverless computing (FaaS) and containers (Docker, Kubernetes). Benefits are lower capital expenditure, scalability, flexibility and disaster recovery. Risks are data security, privacy, vendor lock-in and dependence on connectivity. Indian context: MeghRaj (GI Cloud) was launched by MeitY in 2014, and the Government e-Marketplace and DigiLocker use cloud infrastructure. MeitY's empanelment of cloud service providers requires data localisation and security audits (STQC). Other computing paradigms UPSC may ask about: grid, cluster, utility, mobile and quantum computing, as well as the Internet of Things and big data.

question:
Consider the following statements for Nano-technology :
1. It is the technology of creating materials and devices atom-by-atom.
2. Physical properties change at the nanometer scale.
3. Chemical properties change at the nanometer scale. Which of the above statements are correct ?
subject: General Science
detail: Nanotechnology deals with structures of roughly 1-100 nanometres (1 nm = 10^-9 m). Its defining idea is control over matter at the atomic and molecular level. This is done by the bottom-up approach (assembling atom by atom or molecule by molecule, for example with self-assembly or chemical vapour deposition) and the top-down approach (carving nanostructures from bulk material, for example by lithography or milling). Richard Feynman's 1959 talk 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom' anticipated the field, and Norio Taniguchi coined the term in 1974. At the nanoscale the surface-area-to-volume ratio rises sharply and quantum effects begin to dominate. Physical properties therefore change: gold nanoparticles look red or purple instead of yellow, melting points fall, and optical, electrical and magnetic behaviour shifts. Chemical properties change too, because reactivity and catalytic activity increase; nano-platinum and nano-gold are good catalysts, although bulk gold is inert. Since all three statements match standard definitions, (a), (b) and (c) are each eliminated for wrongly dropping a correct statement.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statement 3, which is correct, because chemical properties do change at the nanoscale.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 2, which is correct, because physical properties such as colour and melting point change at the nanoscale.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 1, which is correct, because nanotechnology is the engineering of matter atom by atom or molecule by molecule.
Correct: all three statements are accurate, so the answer is 1, 2 and 3.
keyfact: Nanotechnology works at 1-100 nm by atom-level assembly, and both physical and chemical properties change at this scale.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 and 2 only', would mean that chemical properties stay constant at the nanoscale. They do not. Reactivity and catalytic behaviour change greatly because of the large surface-area-to-volume ratio. This option mixes up the fact that nanomaterials show altered physical properties with the idea that chemistry is unaffected.

Option (b), '1 and 3 only', would mean that physical properties do not change at the nanoscale. They do: optical colour, melting point, electrical conductivity, magnetism and mechanical strength all shift. For example, gold nanoparticles are red and quantum dots emit size-dependent colours.

Option (c), '2 and 3 only', would deny that nanotechnology is about atom-by-atom construction. Atomic-scale manipulation is central to the field, as in bottom-up assembly, molecular self-assembly and scanning probe microscopy. Feynman's 1959 vision described exactly this.

Option (d), '1, 2 and 3', is correct. Nanotechnology works at 1-100 nm, builds structures from atoms or molecules, and exploits changed physical properties (optical, electrical, magnetic, mechanical) and changed chemical properties (reactivity, catalysis). Applications include medicine (drug delivery), electronics, energy, water purification and materials.
related: Nanometre = 10^-9 metre; the nanoscale ranges from 1 to 100 nm.
Richard Feynman's 1959 lecture 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom' is regarded as the conceptual birth of nanotechnology.
Norio Taniguchi coined the term 'nanotechnology' in 1974.
India's Nano Mission was launched in 2007 under the Department of Science and Technology.
Carbon nanotubes were discovered by Sumio Iijima in 1991.
Graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms, won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics for Geim and Novoselov.
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2023 was awarded for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots.
The scanning tunnelling microscope, invented in 1981, allows imaging and manipulation of single atoms.
statements: 1 — Correct: Nanotechnology is defined as creating and manipulating materials and devices at the atomic or molecular scale, including atom-by-atom assembly. Facts: the bottom-up method builds structures from atoms and molecules, and the scanning tunnelling microscope (1981, Binnig and Rohrer) and the atomic force microscope let scientists see and move single atoms. In 1989 IBM researchers spelled 'IBM' with 35 xenon atoms. The National Nanotechnology Initiative (USA, 2000) defines the field as work at 1-100 nm. India launched the Nano Mission in 2007 under the Department of Science and Technology.

2 — Correct: Physical properties such as colour, melting point, conductivity, strength and magnetism change at the nanoscale. Facts: gold nanoparticles appear red or purple because of surface plasmon resonance, and the melting point of gold nanoparticles falls well below that of bulk gold (1064 °C). Quantum dots change their emission colour with particle size. Carbon nanotubes are about 100 times stronger than steel at a sixth of its weight. Opaque copper becomes transparent, and ordinarily non-magnetic materials can turn magnetic or superparamagnetic.

3 — Correct: Chemical properties such as reactivity, catalytic activity and solubility also change at the nanoscale. Facts: a high surface-area-to-volume ratio exposes more atoms on the surface and makes particles more reactive. Bulk gold is chemically inert, but nano-gold is an effective catalyst, for example in CO oxidation. Nano-platinum is used in catalytic converters, and nano-titanium dioxide acts as a photocatalyst. Aluminium nanoparticles can burn explosively, so they are used in rocket propellants. This reactivity also raises toxicity and safety concerns.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. Nanotechnology builds and manipulates materials and devices at the atomic or molecular scale (about 1-100 nm), and at that scale both physical and chemical properties differ from those of the bulk material.
topic_notes:
Nanotechnology is the science and engineering of matter at 1-100 nm. One nanometre is one-billionth of a metre; a human hair is about 80,000 nm wide and a DNA strand about 2 nm. Two approaches exist. Top-down shapes bulk material into nanostructures, for example by lithography, and bottom-up builds from atoms and molecules, for example by self-assembly. Properties change because the surface-area-to-volume ratio rises and quantum confinement effects appear.

Key nanomaterials: fullerenes (C60, buckyballs, discovered 1985 by Kroto, Curl and Smalley, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1996), carbon nanotubes (Iijima, 1991), graphene (Geim and Novoselov, Nobel Prize in Physics 2010), quantum dots (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2023 to Bawendi, Brus and Ekimov), nanowires and nanoparticles of silver, gold and titanium dioxide.

Applications: targeted drug delivery and cancer therapy, nano-sensors, water purification, nano-silver antimicrobials, sunscreens (ZnO, TiO2), stronger lightweight composites, solar cells, batteries and electronics, and agriculture (nano-fertilisers such as IFFCO's nano urea).

Tools: the scanning tunnelling microscope (1981), the atomic force microscope (1986) and the transmission electron microscope.

India: the Nano Mission was launched in 2007 by the Department of Science and Technology with an outlay of Rs 1000 crore. Nano science institutes include the INST in Mohali.

Risks: toxicity, bioaccumulation, environmental release, and the unknown health effects of inhaled nanoparticles.

question: The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) used in the CERN project is a particle accelerator located on the border between
subject: Computers
detail: CERN (European Organization for Nuclear Research, from the French Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire) was founded in 1954 and has its headquarters at Meyrin, near Geneva, Switzerland. The LHC is the world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator. It lies in a circular tunnel of 26.7 km circumference, about 50 to 175 m underground, crossing the border between Switzerland (canton of Geneva) and France (departments of Ain and Haute-Savoie). It was built between 1998 and 2008 and first beam circulated on 10 September 2008. It collides protons (and heavy ions such as lead) at energies up to 13-13.6 TeV. In July 2012 the ATLAS and CMS experiments announced discovery of the Higgs boson, and Higgs and Englert received the 2013 Physics Nobel. Other experiments are ALICE, LHCb, TOTEM and LHCf. Elimination: Spain and Germany have no part of CERN's site, so options (a), (b) and (c) are wrong. Only France and Switzerland share the site. India became an Associate Member State of CERN in January 2017.
explanations: Wrong: Spain has no border site of CERN. Spain is a member state but the LHC is not located there.
Wrong: Germany is a member state and a major funder, but the LHC does not lie on the France-Germany border.
Wrong: Spain does not border Switzerland, so the LHC cannot straddle that line.
Correct: the LHC ring lies under the France-Switzerland border near Geneva.
keyfact: The LHC at CERN is a 27-km ring under the France-Switzerland border near Geneva.
option_notes: Spain and France share the Pyrenees border and the small enclave of Llivia. Spain is a CERN member (since 1961, left 1969, rejoined 1983), but no CERN accelerator is located on that border. The Canfranc underground laboratory in the Spanish Pyrenees is a separate dark matter and neutrino facility.

France and Germany border along the Rhine and Alsace. Germany is one of CERN's largest contributors. Germany hosts DESY in Hamburg, which runs the PETRA and former HERA accelerators, and GSI/FAIR in Darmstadt, which are not CERN's LHC.
Spain and Switzerland do not share a border, since France and Italy lie between them. This pairing is geographically impossible for the LHC. Both are, however, CERN member states.

France and Switzerland share a border of about 573 km. The CERN campus at Meyrin lies in Switzerland, with the Prévessin site in France. The LHC tunnel, formerly used by the LEP collider (1989-2000), passes under both countries, so the correct pairing is this one.
related: LHC circumference is about 27 km (26.7 km).
Higgs boson discovery was announced on 4 July 2012 at CERN.
The World Wide Web was invented at CERN by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989.
CERN was founded in 1954 and is headquartered in Geneva.
India became an Associate Member of CERN in January 2017.
The LHC's magnets operate at about 1.9 K using liquid helium.
The 2013 Physics Nobel went to Peter Higgs and François Englert.
summary: The answer is (d) France and Switzerland. CERN's Large Hadron Collider is a 27-km circular tunnel buried near Geneva that straddles the Franco-Swiss border.
topic_notes: CERN was established on 29 September 1954 with 12 founding members. It is based in Geneva and is the world's largest particle physics laboratory. Its member states number about 23, and India has been an Associate Member since 2017. The LHC is a 26.7 km ring with superconducting magnets cooled to 1.9 K (about -271.3 °C) by liquid helium, and the beams travel in ultra-high vacuum. It is a proton-proton collider at 13.6 TeV (Run 3 began in 2022). The main detectors are ATLAS, CMS, ALICE and LHCb. The Higgs boson, the particle associated with the Higgs field that gives mass to elementary particles, was announced on 4 July 2012. It is sometimes called the 'God particle', a nickname that physicists dislike. The World Wide Web was invented at CERN by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989. CERN also hosts the Antiproton Decelerator and the Proton Synchrotron (1959) and Super Proton Synchrotron (1976). The Future Circular Collider, about 91 km in circumference, is being studied as a successor. Indian institutions such as TIFR and BARC have contributed to CMS, ALICE and magnet development. Other major facilities include Fermilab (USA, Tevatron, closed 2011), KEK (Japan), and the India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO), which is planned in Tamil Nadu. Related concepts include quarks, leptons, bosons, the Standard Model, dark matter and antimatter.

question: The method of communication in which transmission can take place in _ both directions, but happens only in one direction at a time, is called
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Data communication modes are classified by the direction and simultaneity of signal flow. Simplex is strictly one-way (the receiver can never reply), as in keyboard to computer, radio or TV broadcast, and a monitor display. Half duplex is two-way but alternating: a single channel is shared, so when one device transmits, the other must listen. Examples are walkie-talkies, CB radio and older Ethernet using hubs with CSMA/CD. Full duplex is two-way and simultaneous, using separate channels or paths (or separate wire pairs), as in a telephone call, mobile networks and modern switched Ethernet. The term 'duplex' alone is generic and means two-way capability; it does not specify whether simultaneity exists, so it is not the best answer here. Elimination: the phrase 'only in one direction at a time' excludes full duplex (simultaneous) and simplex (one direction only). 'Duplex' is vague, leaving half duplex as the specific term. Remember the walkie-talkie 'over' protocol as a memory aid. Also note that bandwidth use is more efficient in full duplex, while half duplex is cheaper because it needs only one channel.
explanations: Wrong: 'Duplex' is a generic term for two-way communication and does not by itself convey the one-direction-at-a-time restriction; the precise term is half duplex.
Correct: Half duplex allows transmission in both directions but only one direction at any moment, e.g. walkie-talkie.
Wrong: Full duplex permits simultaneous two-way transmission, like a telephone conversation, which contradicts 'one direction at a time'.
Wrong: Simplex permits transmission in only one fixed direction, never both, like radio or TV broadcasting.
keyfact: Half duplex = two-way but one direction at a time (walkie-talkie); full duplex = simultaneous (telephone); simplex = one-way (TV).
option_notes: Duplex is the general term for a communication system in which two connected parties can communicate with each other in both directions. It is subdivided into half duplex (alternating) and full duplex (simultaneous). Telephones and most computer networks are duplex systems. In exams, 'duplex' without a qualifier usually refers to two-way capability, and the specific variants are asked for by name.

Half duplex is a two-way mode in which signals travel in both directions but not at the same time; the devices share one channel and take turns. Examples: walkie-talkies, CB radio, early Ethernet hubs using CSMA/CD, and some serial links. It is cheaper than full duplex since it needs only one channel, but throughput is lower because of turn-taking delays and possible collisions.

Full duplex lets both ends transmit and receive simultaneously, usually via separate channels or separate wire pairs. Examples: telephone calls, mobile phone networks, and modern switched Ethernet. It doubles effective throughput compared with half duplex and eliminates collisions on a link. Full duplex is often described as two simplex channels operating in opposite directions together.

Simplex is a one-way communication mode in which data flows in a single fixed direction only, and the receiver cannot send anything back. Examples: keyboard to computer, computer to printer or monitor, radio and television broadcasting, and a loudspeaker system. It uses the entire channel capacity for one direction and is the simplest and cheapest mode.
related: Simplex: one-way only, e.g. keyboard, TV broadcast.
Half duplex: two-way alternately, e.g. walkie-talkie.
Full duplex: two-way simultaneously, e.g. telephone.
Hubs operate in half duplex; switches support full duplex.
CSMA/CD is used for collision handling in half duplex Ethernet.
Asynchronous serial transmission uses start and stop bits.
The OSI physical layer deals with transmission mode and bit transfer.
summary: The answer is (b) Half Duplex. In half duplex communication data can travel in both directions, but only one direction at a time, so the two ends must take turns.
topic_notes: Transmission modes describe the direction of signal flow between two devices. Three standard modes: Simplex (unidirectional), Half duplex (bidirectional, alternate) and Full duplex (bidirectional, simultaneous). Simplex examples: keyboard, monitor, TV and radio broadcast, public address systems. Half duplex examples: walkie-talkie, CB radio, legacy hub-based Ethernet where CSMA/CD manages collisions. Full duplex examples: telephone, mobile networks, switched Ethernet, video conferencing. Related networking concepts: parallel versus serial transmission (parallel sends multiple bits at once over multiple lines, over short distances; serial sends bit by bit over a single line, used for long distances); synchronous versus asynchronous transmission (asynchronous uses start and stop bits, synchronous uses clock timing and sends blocks); unicast, multicast and broadcast; and the OSI model, where the physical layer defines the transmission mode. Network topologies include bus, star, ring, mesh and tree. Network types by size are PAN, LAN, MAN and WAN. Devices include hubs (half duplex, layer 1), switches (layer 2, full duplex capable), routers (layer 3) and gateways. Bandwidth is measured in bits per second, and the Shannon and Nyquist theorems give channel capacity limits. In exams, key discriminators are: 'one direction only' means simplex, 'both but alternately' means half duplex, and 'both simultaneously' means full duplex. Modems can operate in either half or full duplex mode, and Ethernet auto-negotiation chooses the mode between devices.

question: A collection of programs that controls how th: computer system runs and __ processe: information is called
subject: Computers
detail: An Operating System (OS) is system software that acts as an interface between the user/application programs and computer hardware. It manages the CPU (process scheduling), main memory (allocation, virtual memory), file systems, and input/output devices, and provides security and a user interface (CLI or GUI). Examples: Windows, Linux, UNIX, macOS, Android, iOS, MS-DOS. Types include batch, time-sharing, multiprogramming, multitasking, real-time, distributed and network OS. The kernel is the core part of the OS. By contrast, compilers, assemblers, interpreters and linkers are language processors or utility programs: they translate or combine code but do not control the overall running of the system. A compiler converts a whole high-level program into machine code; an assembler converts assembly language into machine code; a linker joins object modules and libraries into one executable. Elimination logic: the phrase 'controls how the computer system runs and processes information' describes overall resource management, which is the function of the OS alone, so a, c and d are wrong.
explanations: Wrong: A compiler only translates high-level source code into machine code; it does not control system operation.
Correct: The operating system is the set of programs that controls how the computer runs and processes information, managing all resources.
Wrong: A linker combines object files and libraries into an executable; it is a utility and not a system controller.
Wrong: An assembler translates assembly language into machine language; it does not manage system resources.
keyfact: The Operating System is the system software that controls and manages computer hardware, resources and program execution.
option_notes: Compiler: a language translator that converts the entire high-level source program (C, C++, Java) into object or machine code before execution, reporting errors for the whole program. It is faster in execution than an interpreter. Examples are GCC and javac. It is system software but a language processor, not a system controller.

Operating System: system software that manages hardware and software resources and provides common services to programs. Functions: process, memory, file, device and security management. Examples: Windows, Linux, UNIX, Android. The kernel is its core. Types: batch, multitasking, real-time, distributed. It is loaded into memory by the bootstrap loader at startup.

Linker: a utility program that combines one or more object files produced by compilers or assemblers, along with library routines, into a single executable file. It resolves symbolic references between modules. A loader then places the executable into memory for running. It is system software but does not control the computer's overall operation.

Assembler: a language processor that converts assembly language programs (mnemonics such as ADD, MOV) into machine language (binary). It performs a one-to-one translation of instructions, unlike compilers. Assembly is a low-level language specific to a processor architecture. It is a translator, not the controller of the system.
related: Linux was created by Linus Torvalds in 1991 and is open source.
Compiler translates the whole program at once; interpreter translates line by line.
Assembler converts assembly language into machine code.
The kernel is the core part of an operating system.
Booting loads the OS into RAM; the bootstrap program resides in ROM.
MS-DOS is a command-line, single-user OS.
Android is based on the Linux kernel.
summary: The answer is (b) Operating System. An operating system is the collection of programs (system software) that controls how a computer system runs and processes information, managing hardware, memory, processes, files and user interaction.
topic_notes: System software vs application software is a frequent topic. System software includes operating systems, device drivers, utility programs and language translators (compiler, interpreter, assembler). Application software performs user tasks, such as MS Word, Excel and Tally. The OS manages the processor (scheduling), memory (paging, segmentation, virtual memory), files, devices (via drivers) and security. Types of OS: batch, time-sharing, multiprogramming, multitasking, multiprocessing, real-time (hard and soft) and distributed. The kernel is the core; the shell is the interface between user and kernel. Booting is the process of loading the OS into RAM from secondary storage, and the bootstrap loader is stored in ROM or BIOS. Popular OSes: Windows (Microsoft), UNIX (Bell Labs, 1969), Linux (Linus Torvalds, 1991, open source), macOS (Apple), Android (Google, Linux-based). Language translators: assembler (assembly to machine code), compiler (whole program translation), interpreter (line-by-line translation). Other utilities: linker, loader, debugger, editor. Deadlock, thrashing, spooling and the GUI versus CLI distinction are also common exam angles. BIOS and firmware are also related concepts.

question: SMPS is the acronym for 92
subject: Statistics
detail: SMPS stands for Switch Mode Power Supply (also called Switched-Mode Power Supply). It is the power unit inside desktop computers (the ATX power supply), chargers, TVs and many other electronic devices. Operation: incoming AC mains is rectified and filtered into high-voltage DC. A switching transistor (MOSFET) then chops this DC at high frequency, typically tens to hundreds of kHz. The chopped signal goes through a small, light high-frequency transformer, which steps the voltage down and provides isolation. It is then rectified and filtered again to give a stable low-voltage DC output. A feedback loop adjusts the pulse width (PWM) to keep the output regulated. Advantages over a linear power supply are high efficiency (about 70-90%), small size, light weight and low heat. Disadvantages are electrical noise (EMI/RFI), a more complex circuit and some ripple. A computer SMPS gives outputs of +3.3 V, +5 V, +12 V, -12 V and a +5 V standby. Elimination: 'Store', 'Single' and 'Start' mode are not standard terms in power electronics, so only (c) is valid.
explanations: Incorrect: 'Store Mode Power Supply' is not a real technical term; SMPS does not refer to storing power.
Incorrect: 'Single Mode' is used for optical fibre (single-mode fibre), not for power supplies.
Correct: SMPS is Switch Mode Power Supply, which regulates output by high-frequency switching.
Incorrect: 'Start Mode Power Supply' is not a standard term; the 'S' stands for Switch.
keyfact: SMPS = Switch Mode Power Supply: high-frequency switching and PWM give efficient, compact regulated DC.
option_notes: Store Mode Power Supply: a made-up expression. Energy storage in power supplies is done by capacitors and inductors, and backup is done by UPS or batteries. It is not a recognised category of power supply.

Single Mode Power Supply: also invalid. 'Single-mode' appears in single-mode optical fibre, which carries one light mode over long distances with a thin core of about 9 micrometres. It has no link to power supplies.

Switch Mode Power Supply: a power converter that uses a switching regulator (MOSFET) at high frequency with PWM control, a ferrite-core transformer and feedback. It is highly efficient and compact, and it is used in PCs, mobile chargers, LED drivers and TVs.
Start Mode Power Supply: not a real term. Soft-start and standby circuits exist inside power supplies, but they do not give SMPS its name.
related: SMPS = Switch Mode Power Supply; its switching element is usually a MOSFET.
SMPS is more efficient (about 70-90%) than a linear power supply.
SMPS uses a small high-frequency transformer, unlike the heavy 50 Hz transformer of a linear supply.
Output regulation in an SMPS is done by PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) with feedback.
A PC SMPS gives +3.3 V, +5 V, +12 V, -12 V and +5 V standby.
UPS stands for Uninterruptible Power Supply and provides battery backup.
A major drawback of SMPS is electrical noise (EMI/RFI).
summary: The correct answer is (c) Switch Mode Power Supply. SMPS is an electronic power supply that uses a switching regulator, with transistors turned rapidly on and off, to convert and regulate voltage efficiently.
topic_notes: A power supply unit (PSU) converts mains AC into the regulated DC that electronic components need. There are two main types. A linear power supply uses a heavy 50/60 Hz transformer followed by a rectifier, filter and linear regulator. It is simple and low-noise, but bulky and inefficient (about 40-60%) because excess voltage is lost as heat. An SMPS rectifies the mains first, switches the DC at high frequency, uses a small transformer and regulates by PWM, which gives high efficiency, compactness and light weight. Common SMPS topologies are buck (step-down), boost (step-up), buck-boost, flyback and forward. Main SMPS blocks: input rectifier and filter, switching transistor, high-frequency transformer, output rectifier and filter, and feedback/control circuit. In computers, ATX PSUs give +3.3 V, +5 V, +12 V, -12 V and +5 V standby (5VSB). The 20/24-pin connector goes to the motherboard, Molex connectors power drives, and SATA power connectors serve modern drives. Related power devices: a UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) gives battery backup during outages, an online UPS gives continuous isolation, and a voltage stabiliser regulates mains voltage. Other common computing acronyms: PSU is Power Supply Unit, AVR is Automatic Voltage Regulator, and PWM is Pulse Width Modulation. Exam angles: full forms, the efficiency comparison of SMPS and linear supplies, which component is the switching element, and the voltages a PC SMPS produces.

question: USB is the acronym for
subject: Current Affairs
detail: USB stands for Universal Serial Bus. It is a standard developed in the mid-1990s (USB 1.0 released in January 1996) by a consortium including Intel, Microsoft, IBM, Compaq, DEC, NEC and Nortel. It replaced a variety of older serial and parallel ports (RS-232, PS/2, parallel printer ports) with a single universal connector. 'Universal' means one standard for many device types (keyboards, mice, printers, storage, phones); 'Serial' means data is sent bit by bit over a serial line; 'Bus' means a shared communication pathway. Speeds have grown: USB 1.1 (12 Mbps), USB 2.0 (480 Mbps, 2000), USB 3.0 (5 Gbps, 2008), USB 3.1 (10 Gbps), USB 3.2 (20 Gbps), USB4 (up to 40 Gbps). Connector types include Type-A, Type-B, Mini, Micro and Type-C (reversible). USB supports hot-swapping and plug-and-play, and also provides power. Options (a), (b) and (d) are invented expansions; 'Broadcasting' has no relation to a hardware interface, and 'Unique Solution Bus' is not a real term.
explanations: Wrong: 'Uniform Service Broadcasting' is not a computing term; USB is a hardware interface, not a broadcast service.
Wrong: 'Unique Solution Bus' is a made-up expansion; the first word is Universal, not Unique, and the second is Serial.
Correct: USB = Universal Serial Bus, the standard port and cable interface for connecting peripherals.
Wrong: 'Universal Service Broadcasting' is fictitious; it confuses USB with telecom/broadcast terms such as Universal Service Obligation.
keyfact: USB = Universal Serial Bus, a plug-and-play, hot-swappable standard (1996) for connecting peripherals and supplying power.
option_notes: Uniform Service Broadcasting is not a recognised technology or body. Broadcasting refers to sending radio or TV signals to many receivers, handled in India by Prasar Bharati and regulated by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. It has no link to USB, which is a wired computer interface standard for peripherals.

Unique Solution Bus is not a real standard. A bus in computing is a communication pathway carrying data between components, for example the system bus, address bus, data bus and control bus. Real bus standards include PCI, SATA, I2C and USB, but none is named 'Unique Solution'.

Universal Serial Bus is the standard connecting peripherals to computers, introduced in 1996 by Intel, Microsoft, IBM and others. It supports plug-and-play, hot swapping and power delivery. Versions run from USB 1.x to USB4, and connectors include Type-A, Type-B, Micro and Type-C, which is reversible and now common on phones and laptops.

Universal Service Broadcasting is not a real term. It sounds like 'Universal Service Obligation' (USO), the telecom policy in India that funds rural connectivity through the Universal Service Obligation Fund (USOF), now called Digital Bharat Nidhi. It is unrelated to the USB hardware interface.
related: USB was first released as version 1.0 in January 1996.
USB Type-C is a reversible connector and supports power delivery and video.
USB 2.0 has a maximum speed of 480 Mbps; USB 3.0 has 5 Gbps.
USB standards are maintained by the USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF).
A single USB host controller can support up to 127 devices.
USB supports hot swapping and plug-and-play.
HDMI stands for High-Definition Multimedia Interface.
PS/2 ports were used for keyboards and mice before USB.
summary: The correct answer is (c) Universal Serial Bus. USB is an industry-standard interface for connecting peripherals and devices to a computer for data transfer and power supply.
topic_notes: Computer ports and buses are a frequent source of UPSC EPFO acronym questions. A bus is a set of wires or paths carrying data, addresses or control signals between components. Internal buses: data bus (carries data, bidirectional), address bus (unidirectional, carries memory addresses) and control bus (carries control signals). USB is an external serial interface launched in 1996 by a group of companies led by Intel; the standards are managed by the USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF). Key features: plug-and-play, hot-swappable, supplies power (5 V in the basic standard), and can connect up to 127 devices via hubs. Speeds: USB 1.0 at 1.5 Mbps (Low Speed) and 12 Mbps (Full Speed); USB 2.0 at 480 Mbps (High Speed); USB 3.0 at 5 Gbps (SuperSpeed); USB 3.1 at 10 Gbps; USB 3.2 at 20 Gbps; USB4 at up to 40 Gbps. Connectors: Type-A (flat rectangular, host side), Type-B (printers), Mini and Micro (older mobiles) and Type-C (small, reversible, supports power delivery and video). Other ports and acronyms often asked: HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface), VGA (Video Graphics Array), PS/2 (keyboard and mouse), SATA (Serial Advanced Technology Attachment), PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect), Thunderbolt (Intel and Apple), FireWire (IEEE 1394), Bluetooth and Wi-Fi (wireless). Related acronyms: BIOS, CMOS, RAM, ROM, CPU, ALU, OCR, MICR, LCD, LED, DVD.

question: Ina chess tournament, each of the six players will play with every other player exactly once. What is the number of matches that will be played during the tournament ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a basic combinations (handshake) problem. When every player in a group of n plays every other player exactly once, each match corresponds to an unordered pair, so the total is nC2 = n(n-1)/2. For n = 6 this gives 6×5/2 = 15. An alternative check is to add up the matches player by player: the first player plays 5 others, the second plays 4 new opponents, then 3, 2 and 1, so the total is 5+4+3+2+1 = 15. The same formula is called the sum of the first (n-1) natural numbers. Order does not matter because A vs B is the same match as B vs A. Elimination: 10 is 5C2 (what you would get with 5 players), 20 is 6C3 (choosing 3 of 6, not 2), and 25 has no basis in the formula. If the matches were played twice (home and away), the answer would be doubled to 30, which is n(n-1). The trailing '93' in the OCR text is stray page text and is ignored.
explanations: (a) 10 is wrong: it equals 5C2, the number of matches for 5 players, not 6.
(b) 15 is correct: 6C2 = 6×5/2 = 15, also equal to 5+4+3+2+1.
(c) 20 is wrong: it equals 6C3, which counts groups of 3 players, not pairs.
(d) 25 is wrong: it does not match any valid counting formula for this situation.
keyfact: Matches in a single round-robin of n players = nC2 = n(n-1)/2; for 6 players it is 15.
option_notes: 10 is the value of 5C2 = 5×4/2, the number of matches in a 5-player round robin. It is also the 4th triangular number (1+2+3+4). It is the typical trap if a student uses n-1 = 5 in place of n = 6 in the formula.

15 is 6C2, the 5th triangular number (1+2+3+4+5). It is the number of matches in a 6-player single round-robin tournament and of handshakes among 6 people. It is also the number of lines joining 6 points, no three collinear, and the number of edges in the complete graph K6.

20 is the value of 6C3 = 6×5×4/6, the number of ways to choose 3 from 6. It is also 5×4 = 20, the number of ordered pairs from 5 items (5P2). It is not the answer here because matches are unordered pairs.

25 is 5², a perfect square and not a combination value for n=6. It might be chosen by mistake from approximate multiplication. For reference, the single round-robin counts are 3 players: 3, 4: 6, 5: 10, 6: 15, 7: 21, 8: 28.
related: Round-robin with n teams: nC2 = n(n-1)/2 matches.
Knockout tournament with n teams: n-1 matches.
Double round-robin (home and away): n(n-1) matches.
Diagonals of an n-sided polygon: n(n-3)/2.
nCr = nC(n-r); nC0 = nCn = 1.
Handshakes among 10 people: 45.
summary: The answer is (b) 15. Each match is a unique pair of players, so the number of matches is 6C2 = (6×5)/2 = 15.
topic_notes: Topic: Permutations and combinations, specifically round-robin and handshake problems. Key formulas: nPr = n!/(n-r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!), and nCr = nC(n-r). The number of matches in a single round-robin with n teams is nC2 = n(n-1)/2. If each pair plays twice (home and away), the total is n(n-1). In a knockout tournament with n teams, the number of matches is n-1, because each match eliminates exactly one team. Handshake problem: n people each shaking hands once gives nC2 handshakes. Geometry applications: the number of lines through n points with no three collinear is nC2; the number of diagonals of an n-sided polygon is nC2 - n = n(n-3)/2; the number of triangles from n points is nC3. Group formation: choosing a committee of r from n is nCr, and arrangements in a row use nPr. Triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36 give the round-robin counts for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 players. Exam tip: first decide whether order matters. If A-B is the same as B-A, use combinations; if the roles differ (e.g., a president and a secretary), use permutations. Another frequent variant is to give the total number of matches and ask for the number of players: solve n(n-1)/2 = M, e.g., 28 matches means 8 players.

question: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (M.B. Act) provides for how many weeks’ wages during the maternity period ?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 regulates the employment of women in certain establishments (factories, mines, plantations, shops and establishments, and others) for a fixed period before and after childbirth, and provides maternity benefit and other benefits. Under the original Section 5, a woman was entitled to payment of maternity benefit at the rate of the average daily wage for the period of her actual absence, with a maximum of 12 weeks: up to 6 weeks before the expected date of delivery and 6 weeks immediately after. Since the question is from APFC 2016, it was set before the 2017 amendment (in force from 1 April 2017), so 12 weeks is the expected answer. The 2017 amendment raised the benefit to 26 weeks for the first two children (8 weeks pre-delivery, 18 weeks post), and 12 weeks (6 + 6) for a third child onwards. It also provides 12 weeks for adopting mothers (child under 3 months) and commissioning mothers, a work-from-home option, and a creche requirement for establishments with 50 or more employees. Eliminate 11, 13 and 14 weeks because these figures never appeared in the Act. The woman must have worked at least 80 days in the 12 months preceding the expected delivery.
explanations: Incorrect: 11 weeks was never the statutory period under the Act.
Correct: the Act as originally enacted gave a maximum of 12 weeks (6 before and 6 after delivery), which applied at the time of the 2016 paper.
Incorrect: 13 weeks was not the period under the Act. Some other laws use similar figures, but this one does not.
Incorrect: 14 weeks is the ILO Convention 183 minimum, not the Indian Act's figure. India's Act gave 12 weeks until 2017, then 26 weeks.
keyfact: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 originally gave 12 weeks (6 + 6), raised to 26 weeks in 2017 for the first two children.
option_notes: 11 weeks is not a period in the Maternity Benefit Act. It is a distractor figure close to the actual 12 weeks. The Act's periods have been 12 weeks (original), 26 weeks (after 2017 for the first two children), 12 weeks (third child onwards), and 6 weeks for miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy.

12 weeks was the original maximum maternity benefit under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, with no more than 6 weeks before the expected delivery. It is the correct answer for 2016. The Act applies to establishments employing 10 or more persons. Under the 2017 amendment, 12 weeks still applies to a woman with two or more surviving children, and to adopting and commissioning mothers.

13 weeks is not the statutory maternity period in India. Beware of confusing it with other figures in labour law. The ESI Act gave 12 weeks of maternity benefit, extended to 26 weeks in 2017, in line with the Maternity Benefit Act. The Act's leave for illness arising from pregnancy is one month.

14 weeks is the minimum maternity leave recommended by ILO Convention No. 183 (2000), and Recommendation 191 suggests 18 weeks. India has not ratified C183. The Indian Act provided 12 weeks until 2017, after which it went to 26 weeks, exceeding the ILO standard.
related: The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 raised paid leave to 26 weeks.
For a third child onwards, maternity benefit is 12 weeks (6 before delivery).
Eligibility: at least 80 days worked in the preceding 12 months.
Miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy: 6 weeks of leave with wages.
The creche facility is mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees.
The Act is now subsumed in the Code on Social Security, 2020.
ILO Convention 183 sets 14 weeks as the minimum maternity leave.
summary: The answer is (b) 12 weeks. As originally enacted in 1961 and as it stood for the 2016 paper, the Maternity Benefit Act provided maternity benefit for a maximum of 12 weeks, of which not more than 6 weeks could precede the expected delivery date. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 later raised this to 26 weeks.
topic_notes: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 applies to factories, mines, plantations, the equestrian, acrobatic and circus establishments, shops and establishments with 10 or more employees, and other establishments the government notifies. It is administered by the Ministry of Labour and Employment. Eligibility requires the woman to have actually worked for at least 80 days in the 12 months preceding the expected delivery date. Payment is at the average daily wage rate. Original provisions: a maximum of 12 weeks (6 before delivery), 6 weeks for miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy, 1 month for illness arising from pregnancy, delivery, premature birth or miscarriage, and 2 weeks for tubectomy. Medical bonus: Rs 3,500 originally, later raised to Rs 3,500 and then Rs 20,000 by notification. Dismissal during maternity absence is prohibited, and two nursing breaks per day are allowed until the child is 15 months old. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 (effective 1 April 2017): 26 weeks for the first two children (maximum 8 pre-delivery), 12 weeks for the third child onwards, 12 weeks for adopting mothers (child under 3 months) and commissioning mothers, a work-from-home option for suitable work after the leave period, a mandatory creche for establishments with 50 or more employees with four visits a day permitted, and a requirement to inform the woman of her entitlements in writing and electronically at the time of appointment. Related: the ESI Act 1948 gives maternity benefit to insured women at 100% of wages. The PMMVY gives Rs 5,000 for the first living child. The Code on Social Security 2020 subsumes the Maternity Benefit Act.

question:
Which of the following are the instruments of providing social security in India ?
1. Income Tax
2. Employees’ Provident Fund
3. General Sales Tax
4. LIC
5. National Pension Scheme
6. Postal Provident Fund Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
subject: Social Security
detail: Social security means protection against contingencies such as old age, sickness, death, disability, maternity and unemployment. Instruments are of three broad types: social insurance (contributory, e.g., EPF, ESI, LIC policies), social assistance (non-contributory, tax-funded, e.g., NSAP/IGNOAPS pensions) and provident or savings-based schemes (EPF, PPF, NPS). Here, EPF (under the EPF & MP Act 1952, run by EPFO) gives retirement savings, pension (EPS) and insurance (EDLI). LIC, set up in 1956 by nationalisation of life insurance, provides life cover and annuities. NPS, launched in 2004 for new central government entrants (voluntary for all citizens since 2009) and regulated by PFRDA, is a defined-contribution pension. Postal Provident Fund (the Public Provident Fund is run through post offices and banks) is a long-term savings instrument. Income tax and sales tax (GST today) are fiscal tools for raising government revenue; they may finance social security, but they are not instruments that deliver benefits. Elimination: options (a), (b) and (d) each contain tax items 1 or 3, so only (c) is clean.
explanations: Wrong: it includes Income Tax (1) and General Sales Tax (3), which are taxes rather than social security instruments.
Wrong: it includes General Sales Tax (3), a revenue tax, and leaves out the Postal Provident Fund (6).
Correct: EPF, LIC, NPS and Postal Provident Fund are all schemes that give old-age, pension or insurance protection.
Wrong: it includes General Sales Tax (3) and omits EPF (2), which is the main contributory scheme.
keyfact: Social security instruments pay benefits (EPF, LIC, NPS, PPF); taxes like income tax and sales tax only raise revenue.
option_notes: Options 1, 2, 3 and 4: this mixes two taxes (Income Tax and Sales Tax) with EPF and LIC. Income tax is a direct tax under the Income-tax Act 1961. Sales tax was an indirect state tax, now replaced by GST from 2017. Taxes raise public revenue and only indirectly finance welfare, so the set is wrong because of 1 and 3.

Options 2, 3, 4 and 5: this pairs EPF, LIC and NPS with General Sales Tax. EPF is run by EPFO, LIC is the public life insurer, and NPS is overseen by PFRDA. GST is a destination-based indirect tax on supply of goods and services, administered by the GST Council under Article 279A. It is not a benefit instrument.

Options 2, 4, 5 and 6: these are EPF (1952 Act, EPFO), LIC (1956), NPS (2004, PFRDA) and Postal/Public Provident Fund (1968). All four give contributors protection against old age, death or loss of income. This is the correct combination.

Options 3, 4, 5 and 6: this includes General Sales Tax (3) together with LIC, NPS and PPF. Sales tax is a state indirect levy replaced by GST in July 2017 under the 101st Amendment. It is a revenue measure, so the set is incorrect, and it also omits EPF.
related: EPF and MP Act was enacted in 1952; EPFO is under the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
Employees' Pension Scheme (EPS) began in 1995; EDLI scheme in 1976.
NPS started 1 January 2004; PFRDA became statutory in 2013.
Atal Pension Yojana launched 2015 for unorganised workers aged 18-40.
ESI Act 1948 provides sickness, maternity, disablement and dependants' benefits.
Code on Social Security 2020 subsumes nine labour laws and covers gig workers.
LIC was formed on 1 September 1956 by nationalising life insurance.
Article 41 of the DPSP deals with public assistance in old age, sickness and disablement.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Income Tax is a revenue source, not a benefit-delivering instrument. Income tax is a direct tax levied on income under the Income-tax Act, 1961, with the Centre collecting it (Union List, Entry 82, agricultural income excepted). It funds public expenditure including welfare, and gives rebates for contributions such as EPF, PPF and life insurance premiums under Section 80C. The tax itself offers no protection against contingencies, so it is classed as a fiscal measure.

2 — Correct: EPF is a core social security instrument. The Employees' Provident Fund is governed by the EPF & Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, and administered by EPFO under the Ministry of Labour and Employment. It has three schemes: EPF Scheme 1952, Employees' Pension Scheme 1995 and EDLI Scheme 1976. Both employer and employee contribute 12 percent of basic wages plus DA. It covers establishments with 20 or more employees.

3 — Incorrect: General Sales Tax is an indirect tax on goods and not a social security measure. Sales tax was a state levy on sale of goods, now subsumed in GST since 1 July 2017 (101st Constitutional Amendment). It raises revenue for governments and gives individuals no protection. Any link to social security is only through general budgetary financing of welfare schemes.
