In the given sentence, 'soul' signals a moral or spiritual quality, so purity and flawlessness are intended. Elimination: 'Excited' describes an emotional state of enthusiasm and has no link to purity. 'Extraordinary' means beyond the ordinary and describes unusualness, not cleanliness or faultlessness. 'Unparalleled' means having no equal; it measures superiority, not purity. Only 'spotless' carries the core idea of being free from blemish. Related vocabulary students should know: pristine, unblemished, flawless, impeccable, unsullied, pure. Antonyms: tainted, stained, sullied, blemished, defiled, flawed. A useful exam tip is to break the word into its root (macula = spot) to decode similar words such as 'maculate' and 'immaculate'.
explanations: Correct: 'Spotless' means free from any spot or stain, the exact sense of immaculate, here applied figuratively to a pure soul.
Wrong: 'Excited' means feeling enthusiastic or stirred up; it has no connection with purity or flawlessness.
Wrong: 'Extraordinary' means remarkable or beyond the usual; it describes rarity, not freedom from blemish.
Wrong: 'Unparalleled' means without equal or peer; it indicates superiority in comparison, not cleanliness or purity.
keyfact: IMMACULATE = spotless, pure, without blemish (Latin in- + macula, 'spot').
option_notes: Spotless: adjective meaning absolutely clean, without any spot or stain; figuratively, without moral blemish (a spotless reputation or record). Synonyms include immaculate, pristine, unblemished, impeccable and unsullied. Antonyms are dirty, stained and tarnished. It is formed from 'spot' + the suffix '-less' (without).

Excited: adjective meaning feeling or showing enthusiasm, eagerness or agitation; from the verb 'excite' (Latin excitare, to rouse). Synonyms include thrilled, eager, animated and elated. Antonyms include bored, calm and apathetic. It describes an emotion and is often confused with 'exciting', which describes what causes the emotion.

Extraordinary: adjective meaning very unusual, remarkable or beyond what is ordinary; from Latin 'extraordinarius' (outside the usual order). Synonyms include remarkable, exceptional, phenomenal and singular. Antonyms include ordinary, common and mundane. It is often paired with 'extraordinary session' or 'extraordinary powers' in formal and legal usage.

Unparalleled: adjective meaning having no equal or match; unrivalled, unmatched, peerless, supreme. It is formed from 'un-' + 'parallel' (alongside, equal). Antonyms include ordinary, comparable and mediocre. It is used for achievements, beauty, success or scale (for example, unparalleled success) and not for cleanliness or purity.
related: Immaculate comes from Latin in- (not) + macula (spot).
Antonyms of immaculate: tainted, sullied, blemished, stained, flawed.
Synonyms of immaculate: pristine, impeccable, unblemished, flawless, spotless.
Unparalleled means without equal; synonyms include peerless, unrivalled and matchless.
Eminent (famous) and imminent (about to happen) are commonly confused.
Impeccable means faultless; from Latin in- + peccare (to sin).
Pristine means in original, unspoiled condition.
summary: The answer is (a) Spotless. IMMACULATE means perfectly clean, pure and free from any stain or fault, and 'spotless' is its closest synonym in this context of a pure soul.
topic_notes: This question tests vocabulary, specifically synonyms inferred from context. UPSC EPFO English papers regularly include synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutions, idioms and phrases, spotting errors, sentence improvement, fill in the blanks and comprehension. For synonym questions, first read the sentence to determine the sense of the word (literal or figurative), then eliminate options belonging to a different semantic field. Word roots help: 'macula' (spot) gives immaculate and maculate; 'mal-' means bad (malevolent, malice); 'bene-' means good (benevolent, benefactor); 'omni-' means all (omniscient, omnipotent). Common near-meaning clusters: pure (immaculate, pristine, unsullied, spotless, chaste); excellent (impeccable, flawless, exemplary, superb); unique (unparalleled, unmatched, peerless, unrivalled, incomparable). Beware of traps where an option is positive in tone but not the same in meaning, as 'extraordinary' and 'unparalleled' are here. Also know the Immaculate Conception, a Christian doctrine regarding Mary, which is the best-known use of the word in culture. Prepare by keeping a notebook of 10 new words daily with synonym, antonym, root and a sentence. Practise previous-year papers, because words often repeat as options or answers in later years. Also revise commonly confused pairs such as eminent/imminent, immanent/imminent, and elicit/illicit.

question: Which one of the following is the antonym of the word written in capital letters in the sentence, “There is a great deal of ENMITY”?
subject: General English
detail: Enmity (noun) is a state of mutual hostility, hatred or active opposition, from Old French 'enemistie', ultimately from Latin 'inimicus' (enemy, not-friend). Its true antonym is 'amity', from Latin 'amicitia' (friendship), meaning a friendly relationship, especially between states, as in 'treaty of peace and amity'. Both words are formed on the same root pair, amicus (friend) and inimicus (enemy), which is why they are exact opposites. For antonym questions, first identify the exact part of speech and meaning of the capitalised word, then discard synonyms, and finally choose between true opposites and loosely related words. Here, Hostility is a synonym of enmity, so (d) is eliminated at once. Dispute (a quarrel or argument) is related in sense and also not an opposite, so (c) is out. Cooperation means working together; it is a plausible opposite of conflict or rivalry, but it describes action, not the feeling or state of friendliness. Amity matches enmity as a noun denoting a state of relations, so it is the best answer.
explanations: Correct: Amity means friendship and goodwill, the direct opposite of enmity (hatred, ill will).
Wrong: Cooperation is joint action; it is a loose contrast with conflict but not the exact opposite of the state of enmity.
Wrong: Dispute means a quarrel or disagreement, which is related to enmity in sense, not opposite.
Wrong: Hostility is a synonym of enmity, so it cannot be the antonym.
keyfact: Enmity (hatred, hostility) is opposite to Amity (friendship); Hostility is a synonym, not an antonym.
option_notes: Amity: a noun meaning friendly relations, especially between nations or groups; from Latin amicitia via Old French amitie. Commonly seen in the phrase 'peace and amity'. Synonyms: friendship, harmony, goodwill, concord, cordiality. Antonyms: enmity, hostility, animosity, discord. Often confused with 'amnesty' (pardon) in exams, so watch the spelling and meaning.

Cooperation: the act of working together towards a common goal or of assisting willingly. Synonyms: collaboration, teamwork, assistance, partnership. Antonyms: competition, opposition, non-cooperation, obstruction. Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement (1920) is its famous contrast. It is an action noun, unlike enmity, which is a feeling or state.

Dispute: a noun and verb meaning a disagreement, argument or debate, or to question the truth of something. Synonyms: quarrel, altercation, controversy, row, contest. Antonyms: agreement, accord, concord. In labour law, an 'industrial dispute' is defined in Section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, a useful link for EPFO aspirants.

Hostility: a noun meaning unfriendly or aggressive behaviour or strong opposition, from Latin hostilis (of an enemy). Synonyms: enmity, animosity, antagonism, malice, ill will, aggression. Antonyms: friendliness, amity, goodwill, warmth. The plural 'hostilities' refers to acts of war.
related: Amity is the antonym of enmity; hostility, animosity and rancour are its synonyms.
Amicus means friend and inimicus means enemy in Latin, the roots of amity and enmity.
Inimical means hostile or harmful; amicable means friendly.
Benevolent is the opposite of malevolent.
Concord is the opposite of discord.
Amnesty means a pardon and is not related to amity.
In antonym questions, always eliminate synonyms first.
summary: The answer is (a) Amity. Enmity means deep-rooted hostility or ill will, and its direct opposite is amity, meaning friendly relations and goodwill between people or nations.
topic_notes: Antonym questions in the UPSC EPFO English section test vocabulary, usually with a single word in capitals inside a sentence. Strategy: identify the part of speech, recall the root meaning, eliminate synonyms (a frequent trap, as hostility here), then eliminate loosely related words. Useful pairs built on Latin roots: amity-enmity (amicus-inimicus); benevolent-malevolent (bene-male); concord-discord; amicable-inimical; philanthropy-misanthropy; amateur from amare (to love). Common antonym pairs to revise: prodigal-frugal, candid-evasive, verbose-concise, zenith-nadir, ephemeral-permanent, benign-malignant, lenient-strict, obstinate-flexible, transparent-opaque, aggravate-alleviate, hamper-facilitate, scarce-abundant, vindicate-accuse, ostentatious-modest. Synonyms of enmity: animosity, rancour, antipathy, antagonism, acrimony, malice, hatred. Related word forms: enemy, inimical (hostile, harmful), amicable (friendly), amiable (pleasant). Exam tips: when two options both seem opposite, choose the one that matches the grammatical category and the sense (state versus action). Practise with root-word families, because UPSC repeatedly uses words of Latin and Greek origin, and often reuses wrong options as correct answers in later papers. Also revise one-word substitutions, idioms, and spot-the-error rules, which appear in the same section.

question: Which one of the following is the antonym of the word written in capital letters in the sentence, “She was RELUCTANT to sell her car”?
subject: General English
detail: Reluctant (adjective) means unwilling, disinclined or hesitant to act; the noun is reluctance and the adverb is reluctantly. In antonym questions, first fix the exact meaning of the capitalised word in the sentence's context, then look for the opposite and discard words that are synonyms or only loosely related. Here the context is a person hesitant to sell her car, so the opposite is a person keen or willing to sell. 'Eager' (keen, enthusiastic, ready) fits exactly. 'Unwilling' is a synonym of reluctant, so it cannot be the antonym, even though it looks like a negative word; students often wrongly pick it because of the negative prefix. 'Anxious' means worried or uneasy, and can also mean eagerly desiring (as in 'anxious to please'), but it does not directly oppose reluctance. 'Happy' describes a feeling of pleasure, not readiness to act. Other antonyms of reluctant include willing, keen, enthusiastic, ready, and zealous. Synonyms include loath, averse, hesitant, disinclined, and unwilling. Always check whether the question asks for synonym or antonym, because UPSC places the synonym among the options as a trap.
explanations: (a) Anxious means worried, nervous or uneasy; it is not the opposite of reluctant, so it is wrong.
(b) Happy refers to a feeling of joy or contentment; it does not express willingness to act, so it is wrong.
(c) Eager means keen, enthusiastic and ready to do something. It is the direct opposite of reluctant, so it is correct.
(d) Unwilling is a synonym of reluctant, not an antonym, so it is wrong.
keyfact: Reluctant = unwilling; its antonym is eager (willing, keen).
option_notes: Anxious (adjective): feeling worried, nervous or uneasy about something uncertain; noun: anxiety. It can also mean eagerly desirous, as in 'anxious to succeed'. Synonyms: worried, apprehensive, uneasy, fearful. Antonyms: calm, relaxed, unconcerned, composed. In this question it is a distractor because it describes an emotional state, not readiness to act.

Happy (adjective): feeling or showing pleasure, contentment or joy; also fortunate or apt, as in 'a happy coincidence'. Noun: happiness. Synonyms: glad, cheerful, delighted, joyful, content. Antonyms: sad, unhappy, miserable, sorrowful. It is not an opposite of reluctant, because one can be happy yet still hesitant to act.

Eager (adjective): strongly wanting to do or have something; keen, enthusiastic and impatient to begin. Noun: eagerness; adverb: eagerly. Synonyms: keen, avid, enthusiastic, zealous, ardent, willing. Antonyms: reluctant, unenthusiastic, indifferent, apathetic, loath. It is the correct antonym here and a frequent pair in UPSC vocabulary questions.

Unwilling (adjective): not ready, eager or prepared to do something; opposed or averse. Noun: unwillingness; adverb: unwillingly. Synonyms: reluctant, loath, disinclined, averse, hesitant, resistant. Antonyms: willing, eager, ready, agreeable, keen. It is a synonym of the given word, hence the classic trap option in antonym questions.
related: Antonym of reluctant: eager, willing, keen.
Synonyms of reluctant: loath, averse, hesitant, unwilling.
Reluctance is the noun form; reluctantly is the adverb.
Antonym of benevolent is malevolent.
Antonym of frugal is extravagant or wasteful.
Antonym of transient is permanent or lasting.
In antonym questions, a synonym of the given word is often placed as a distractor option.
summary: The answer is (c) Eager. 'Reluctant' means unwilling or hesitant to do something, so its antonym is a word meaning keen or willing, which is 'eager'.
topic_notes: Antonym and synonym questions form the vocabulary part of the General English section in the EPFO (APFC and EO/AO) paper, usually with several questions a year. UPSC tests common but nuanced words, and the options often contain a synonym of the given word as a trap. Strategy: (1) read the sentence to determine the sense in which the word is used, since many words have multiple meanings; (2) decide whether the question wants a synonym or an antonym; (3) eliminate synonyms and unrelated words; (4) use prefixes and suffixes (un-, in-, dis-, -less) as clues but do not rely on them blindly. Reluctant belongs to a group of words describing willingness: willing, eager, keen, enthusiastic, ready (positive) versus reluctant, loath, averse, hesitant, unwilling, disinclined (negative). Related word families to revise: abundant/scarce, benevolent/malevolent, candid/evasive, diligent/lazy, frugal/extravagant, hostile/friendly, obscure/clear, prudent/reckless, transient/permanent, verbose/concise. Also revise one-word substitutions, idioms and phrases, spelling errors, sentence correction, and comprehension, which are the other recurring English areas. Build a habit of learning words in pairs of synonyms and antonyms, and revise root words from Latin and Greek, because they help decode unfamiliar words quickly. Practise past papers of UPSC, as repeated words and their opposites often reappear across years.

question: Which one of the following is the antonym of the word written in capital letters in the sentence, “I cannot comply with the QUEER regulations of your land”?
subject: General English
detail: The question asks for the antonym of QUEER used as an adjective in the sentence 'I cannot comply with the QUEER regulations of your land'. In this sense queer means odd, peculiar, unconventional or out of the ordinary (an older, general usage, not related to its modern identity-related meaning). Its synonyms are strange, weird, eccentric, bizarre, curious and abnormal. Its antonyms are usual, normal, common, customary, conventional and ordinary. Elimination: (a) Strange is a synonym, so it is the opposite of what is asked. (b) Nimble means quick and light in movement and has no semantic link to queer. (c) Everyday means ordinary or routine and is close, but it mostly describes daily occurrence (everyday clothes, everyday life) and is a weaker fit for 'regulations'. (d) Customary means according to custom or usual practice, and it collocates naturally with rules and regulations. UPSC's official key is (d). Exam tip: first find the synonym among the options and discard it, then pick the option whose meaning is the true opposite in context. 'Comply' means to obey or conform, which also hints that the regulations are unusual.
explanations: Incorrect: Strange is a synonym of queer, not an antonym.
Incorrect: Nimble means agile or quick and is unrelated to the meaning of queer.
Incorrect: Everyday means ordinary or routine and is loosely opposite, but it is less apt for regulations than customary, and the official key does not choose it.
Correct: Customary means usual, conventional or according to established practice, which is the direct opposite of queer (odd, unusual).
keyfact: Queer = odd or unusual; its antonym is customary (usual, conventional).
option_notes: Strange: an adjective meaning unusual, unfamiliar or hard to explain. Synonyms include odd, peculiar, weird and curious. Antonyms include familiar, normal and usual. It also describes something not previously known or experienced (a strange city). In antonym questions it is typically the synonym trap.

Nimble: an adjective meaning quick, light and agile in movement or thought (nimble fingers, a nimble mind). Synonyms: agile, spry, lithe, deft, sprightly. Antonyms: clumsy, awkward, sluggish, slow, lumbering. It is often asked in synonym and antonym sets, and it is derived from Old English 'numol', meaning quick to seize.

Everyday: an adjective meaning happening or used daily, or ordinary and commonplace (everyday life, everyday objects). Synonyms: routine, daily, usual, commonplace, mundane. Antonyms: unusual, exceptional, extraordinary, rare. Do not confuse it with the two-word phrase 'every day', which is an adverbial expression of time.

Customary: an adjective meaning in accordance with custom or usual practice (customary greeting, customary law). Synonyms: usual, habitual, traditional, conventional, accustomed, routine. Antonyms: unusual, uncommon, unconventional, odd, queer. It derives from 'custom', and customary law is a recognised source of law in many legal systems.
related: Queer means odd or strange; its antonyms include normal, usual and customary.
Comply means to obey; its antonyms include defy, disobey and violate.
Nimble means agile; its antonyms include clumsy and sluggish.
In antonym questions, always eliminate the synonym option first.
Eccentric is a synonym of queer; conventional is its antonym.
Everyday means routine; its antonyms include unusual and exceptional.
summary: The answer is (d) Customary. 'Queer' here means odd, strange or unusual, so its antonym is a word meaning usual or conventional, and 'customary' fits best.
topic_notes: Antonyms (opposites) form a regular part of the General English section in EPFO papers, together with synonyms, idioms, one-word substitution, error spotting and cloze tests. Method: (1) read the sentence to fix the sense of the word, because many words have multiple meanings; (2) identify and discard any synonym among the options, since examiners plant it as a trap; (3) choose the option giving the clearest opposite in that context. Queer (adjective): odd, strange, unconventional; also in older English, slightly ill or faint ('feeling queer'), and in informal use, suspicious or questionable (as in 'queer fish'). Synonyms: odd, peculiar, eccentric, weird, bizarre, offbeat, curious. Antonyms: normal, usual, ordinary, conventional, customary, common, regular, standard. Comply (verb): to act in accordance with a rule or request; synonyms obey, conform, abide by, adhere to; antonyms defy, disobey, resist, violate. Regulation (noun): an official rule or directive. Other frequent word pairs: conventional versus unorthodox, eccentric versus normal, bizarre versus ordinary, abnormal versus typical, peculiar versus common. Vocabulary strategy: learn words in groups of synonyms and antonyms, note multiple meanings, and read editorials from newspapers to meet words in context. Also revise prefixes such as un-, in-, dis-, mis-, non-, which often form antonyms, though not every word follows the pattern (customary is not made opposite by simple prefixing; 'uncustomary' is rarely used).

ocr: Which one of the following parts of the sentence, “As you know that the ignorant are easily duped”, has an error? (a) As you know (b) that the ignorant (c) are easily duped (ad) No error
subject: General English
detail: This is a spot-the-error question on conjunctions and clause structure. 'As' here works as a conjunction or relative-type connector meaning 'in the way that / since', and 'As you know' is a complete parenthetical clause. Once 'As' has joined this clause to the main clause, a second conjunction 'that' cannot be added. Compare 'As you know, he is honest' (correct) with 'You know that he is honest' (correct, since 'that' is the only link). Using both, as in 'As you know that...', doubles the conjunctions and is an error. The idiom 'the + adjective' for a class of people (the ignorant, the poor, the rich) takes a plural verb, so 'are easily duped' is correct. 'Duped' is the right past participle of 'dupe' (to deceive), and the passive construction is fine. Elimination: (a) is a correct introductory clause. (c) is correct in agreement and voice. (d) is wrong because the redundant 'that' is a clear error. So the faulty part is (b), where 'that' should be deleted.
explanations: (a) 'As you know' is a correct introductory clause and is grammatically fine by itself, so the error does not lie here.
(b) Correct answer. The part 'that the ignorant' contains the redundant conjunction 'that'. 'As you know' already links the clauses, so 'that' must be dropped.
(c) 'are easily duped' is correct: 'the ignorant' is a plural noun phrase, so 'are' agrees, and the passive voice with the adverb 'easily' is properly formed.
(d) 'No error' is wrong because the extra 'that' after 'As you know' is an error, as the official answer confirms.
keyfact: 'As you know' already links the clause, so adding 'that' is a redundant conjunction: say 'As you know, the ignorant are easily duped.'
option_notes: 'As you know' is a parenthetical or introductory clause used to remind the listener of a known fact. It is normally set off by a comma: 'As you know, the meeting is cancelled.' 'As' here acts as a conjunction meaning 'in the way that'. The clause is complete in itself and needs no further conjunction after it. Similar forms are 'As I said', 'As we all know', and 'As is well known'.

'that the ignorant' is the faulty part. 'That' is a subordinating conjunction that introduces noun clauses after verbs such as know, say or think. It cannot follow 'As you know' because 'As' already performs the linking. Also note that 'the + adjective' (the ignorant, the poor) denotes a whole class of people and takes a plural verb.

'are easily duped' is a passive verb phrase made of 'are' plus the past participle 'duped'. 'Dupe' means to deceive or trick someone, and it can also be a noun for a person who is deceived. Synonyms include cheat, hoodwink, gull and delude. The adverb 'easily' correctly modifies the participle.

'No error' is the standard final option in spot-the-error questions. It is chosen only if all parts are grammatically right. Examiners usually include it as a distractor, and it is correct in a minority of questions. Always check conjunction duplication, subject-verb agreement, tense, prepositions and articles before choosing it.
The four options are the three sentence segments and 'No error', so no extra option facts are needed beyond those above.
related: 'As you know' is an introductory clause and takes no additional 'that'.
'The + adjective' (the poor, the ignorant) denotes a class and takes a plural verb.
Do not use double conjunctions: 'Although... but' and 'Because... so' are wrong.
'Dupe' means to deceive or trick; synonyms are hoodwink, cheat and gull.
'Prefer' is followed by 'to', not 'than': 'I prefer tea to coffee'.
'No sooner... than' and 'hardly... when' are the correct correlative pairs.
'Each' and 'every' are followed by singular verbs.
A comma normally follows an introductory clause such as 'As you know'.
summary: The answer is (b) 'that the ignorant'. The sentence 'As you know that the ignorant are easily duped' wrongly uses the conjunction 'that' right after 'As you know'. 'As you know' already introduces the clause, so 'that' is redundant and makes the sentence ungrammatical. The correct form is 'As you know, the ignorant are easily duped.'
topic_notes: Spot-the-error questions test grammar rules in context. For this question, the key area is conjunctions and redundancy. Common patterns UPSC uses: (1) Double conjunctions, such as 'Although he is poor, but he is honest' (wrong; drop 'but'), 'As you know that...' (wrong), and 'Because... therefore...' (wrong). (2) Correlative pairs: either-or, neither-nor, not only-but also, both-and, whether-or, no sooner-than, hardly-when, scarcely-when. (3) 'The + adjective' used for a class takes a plural verb: the poor are, the rich are, the young are. (4) Subject-verb agreement: each, every, either, neither take singular verbs; a collective noun takes a singular verb when it acts as one unit; 'one of the' takes a plural noun plus a singular verb. (5) Redundancy and pleonasm: 'return back', 'repeat again', 'reason is because', 'more better'. (6) Prepositions: prefer to, different from, superior to, inferior to, senior to, junior to, and similar fixed pairs. (7) Tense sequence and conditionals. (8) Articles: use 'an' before a vowel sound (an hour, an honest man, a university, a European). Strategy: read each segment, ask whether it duplicates a function already performed, then check agreement, tense, and idiom. Mark 'No error' only after checking every part. Related ideas that may be asked next time are the use of 'as' versus 'like', 'that' as a relative pronoun, and the omission of 'that' in reported speech. Note that 'as' can mean because, while, when or in the way that, depending on context.

question: Which one of the following parts of the sentence, “After a lot of argument I brought him forward to my point of view”, has an error?
subject: General English
detail: This is a spotting-the-error question that tests phrasal verbs and idioms. The sentence means the speaker persuaded the other person to agree after much argument. The standard idiom for this sense is 'bring someone round (to)', i.e. win them over to one's opinion. 'Bring forward' has different meanings: to propose or table an idea for discussion, to advance a meeting or event to an earlier date, or to carry a figure forward in accounts. None of these means persuade, so 'brought him forward' is the faulty segment. Elimination logic: (a) 'After a lot of argument' is grammatical and idiomatic, since 'a lot of' is acceptable in standard usage and 'after' correctly takes the noun phrase. (c) 'to my point of view' is correct, because the idiom 'bring round to' takes the preposition 'to'. (d) is ruled out because a genuine error exists in (b). Corrected sentence: 'After a lot of argument I brought him round to my point of view.' In such questions, check idiomatic phrasal verbs first, since the error is often a wrong particle.
explanations: Incorrect: 'After a lot of argument' is a grammatically sound introductory phrase, and 'a lot of' is acceptable in standard usage.
Correct: 'brought him forward' is the erroneous part. The idiom meaning to persuade is 'brought him round', whereas 'bring forward' means to propose or advance.
Incorrect: 'to my point of view' is correct, since 'round to' takes the preposition 'to' before the viewpoint.
Incorrect: There is an error in part (b), so 'No error' cannot be right.
keyfact: Persuading someone to your view is 'bring round (to)', not 'bring forward'; 'bring forward' means to propose or advance a date.
option_notes: 'After a lot of argument' is an adverbial prepositional phrase of time or circumstance. 'A lot of' is informal-standard and works with both countable and uncountable nouns. 'Argument' here means a discussion involving disagreement, with reasons offered. The phrase is a correct opening and has no fault, so it is not the answer.

'Brought him forward' is a misuse of the phrasal verb 'bring forward'. Bring forward means to introduce a topic or proposal for discussion, to move an event to an earlier time, or to carry a total to the next page or column in book-keeping. It never means to persuade someone. The correct idiom is 'bring round'. This is the error segment.

'To my point of view' is a prepositional phrase meaning 'to my opinion or perspective'. The related fixed expressions are 'from my point of view' (my perspective) and 'bring round to' (convert to an opinion). The preposition 'to' is correct after 'brought him round', so this part is not erroneous.

'No error' is the standard fourth option in spot-the-error questions. It is correct only when all the parts are grammatical and idiomatic. Here the phrasal verb in part (b) is misused, so this option is wrong. In UPSC papers, 'No error' is right in only a minority of such questions.
related: 'Bring round' means to persuade someone or to revive someone from unconsciousness.
'Bring forward' means to propose a matter or advance an event to an earlier date.
'Bring about' means to cause something to happen.
'Come round to' means to change one's opinion and accept another's view.
'Prefer X to Y' is correct; 'prefer X than Y' is wrong.
'Discuss' is transitive and takes no preposition: 'discuss the matter', not 'discuss about the matter'.
'Win over' means to gain someone's support by persuasion.
'Bring up' means to rear a child or raise a topic.
summary: The answer is (b): the phrase 'brought him forward' is wrongly used. The correct idiom is 'brought him round' (or 'around') to my point of view, meaning to persuade someone to change their opinion.
topic_notes: This question belongs to the spotting-the-error section of General English, where UPSC EPFO tests idioms, phrasal verbs, prepositions, tenses, subject-verb agreement, articles and word order. Phrasal verbs are a favourite area because a wrong particle changes the meaning entirely. Key points on 'bring': bring about (cause to happen), bring up (raise a child or a topic), bring out (publish or reveal), bring down (reduce or topple), bring in (introduce, earn), bring off (accomplish), bring round or around (persuade, or revive from unconsciousness), bring forward (propose, advance a date, carry over in accounts), bring back (return, recall) and bring on (cause an illness or progress). Related persuasion idioms: win over, talk into, talk round, prevail upon, carry conviction. Strategy for error-spotting: read each segment for grammatical form first, then for idiomatic correctness. Check prepositions that follow verbs or adjectives, for example 'prefer X to Y', 'different from', 'comprise of' (wrong), 'discuss about' (wrong) and 'despite of' (wrong). Remember that 'No error' is a legitimate answer, but it should be chosen only after all segments are verified. Revise common confusions such as bring/take, rise/raise, lay/lie, and affect/effect. Also revise the idioms 'come round to' (change one's mind) and 'come around', which are the intransitive counterparts of 'bring round'.

question: Which one of the following parts of the sentence, “Don’t ask him how he is because if he starts talking about his health you'll never get off from him”, has an error?
options: Don’t ask him how he is because
if he starts talking about his health you'll never
subject: General English
detail: This is a spotting-the-error question that tests prepositional usage with phrasal verbs. The sentence means that if you ask the man about his health, he will talk so long that you cannot escape from him. 'Get off' means to leave a vehicle, to escape punishment, or to stop using something, and it is normally followed by an object directly ('get off the bus', 'get off my back') or by 'with' ('get off with a warning'). It is not followed by 'from' in the sense of escaping a person. The natural correction is 'you'll never get away from him' or 'you'll never get rid of him'. Part (a) is correct: 'how he is' is a proper indirect question with normal word order, and 'because' correctly introduces the reason. Part (b) is correct: the conditional 'if he starts ... you'll never' uses the present tense in the if-clause and the future in the main clause (first conditional), and 'talking about his health' uses the right preposition. Since part (c) alone is faulty, 'No error' is eliminated. In such questions, check the prepositions attached to verbs first.
explanations: Wrong: 'Don't ask him how he is because' is a correct imperative with an indirect question in normal word order, and the conjunction fits.
Wrong: 'if he starts talking about his health you'll never' is a correct first conditional, and 'talk about' takes the right preposition.
Correct: 'get off from him' is an error. The usage should be 'get away from him' or 'get rid of him'; 'get off' does not take 'from' here.
Wrong: There is an error, in part (c), so 'No error' cannot be the answer.
keyfact: 'Get off from him' is wrong; use 'get away from him' or 'get rid of him'.
option_notes: This part is an imperative negative followed by an indirect question. In reported questions, the word order is subject then verb ('how he is'), not 'how is he'. 'Because' introduces a clause of reason. Ending with a conjunction is acceptable in these split-sentence formats, since the next part continues the clause.

This part is the first conditional: 'if' plus the simple present in the condition, and the simple future ('will') in the result. 'Start' can take a gerund or an infinitive ('start talking' or 'start to talk'). 'Talk about' is the standard collocation for a topic. 'You'll never' leads into the verb in part (c).

'Get off' is a phrasal verb meaning to leave a bus, train or horse, to escape punishment ('get off lightly'), or to begin ('get off to a good start'). 'Get off with' means to be let off with a lesser penalty. 'Get away from' means to escape someone, and 'get rid of' means to be freed of a nuisance. Neither takes 'from' after 'get off' in this sense.

'No error' is the option for a sentence that has no mistake. In UPSC EPFO papers it is correct only when every part passes the checks on tense, agreement, prepositions, articles and word order. Choose it only after testing each segment, because it is often a distractor.
related: 'Get away from' means to escape someone or something; 'get rid of' means to be freed of it.
'Get off with' means to escape with a light punishment.
'Get along with' means to have a good relationship with someone.
First conditional: if + simple present, will + base verb.
Indirect questions use statement word order: 'asked how he is'.
'Despite' is never followed by 'of'; 'in spite of' is correct.
'Comprise' is used without 'of'; 'consist of' takes 'of'.
'Each' and 'every' take singular verbs.
summary: The answer is (c). The phrasal verb 'get off' is wrongly followed by 'from'; the idiomatic form in the sense of escaping or getting rid of someone is 'get away from him' or 'get rid of him'. The other parts are grammatically correct.
topic_notes: Spotting-the-error questions in the EPFO papers regularly test the following areas. First, prepositions that go with verbs, adjectives and nouns: 'get away from', 'get rid of', 'prefer X to Y', 'despite' (not 'despite of'), 'comprise' (not 'comprise of'), 'discuss' (no preposition), 'married to', 'good at', 'afraid of', 'accuse of', 'consists of'. Second, subject-verb agreement: 'each', 'every', 'neither' and 'either' take a singular verb, and 'one of the' takes a plural noun with a singular verb. Third, tense sequence in conditionals: first conditional (if + present, will), second conditional (if + past, would), third conditional (if + past perfect, would have). Fourth, articles ('a university', 'an hour'), pronoun case ('between you and me'), and comparatives ('more better' is wrong). Fifth, word order in indirect questions ('I asked where he lived', not 'where did he live'). Sixth, confusing word pairs such as 'lie/lay', 'affect/effect', 'principal/principle'. Strategy: read each segment on its own, find the verb and check what preposition it takes, then check agreement and tense. If everything is fine, choose 'No error', but only after careful checking. Phrasal verbs are a favourite area: 'get off', 'get over', 'get along with', 'get through', 'get by', 'get at', each with a distinct meaning and preposition.

ocr: Which one of the following words can be used as a substitute for the phrase, “A nursery where children of working parents are cared for while their parents are at work”? (a) Sculler (b) Créche (c) Dormitory (ad) Refectory [P.T. 0.
subject: General English
detail: This is a one-word-substitution question, a regular feature of the General English section in UPSC EPFO papers. The phrase to be replaced is 'a nursery where children of working parents are cared for while their parents are at work'. The word that matches is 'crèche' (pronounced 'kresh'), which comes from French and originally meant a manger or crib. It now means a day-care centre for infants and young children. It also has a legal side that is relevant for labour-law aspirants. Section 11A of the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 requires every establishment with 50 or more employees to provide a crèche facility within a prescribed distance. The mother is allowed four visits a day to the crèche, including her rest interval. Elimination logic: a sculler is a person who rows a light boat with a pair of sculls, or the boat itself, so it has nothing to do with child care. A dormitory is a large sleeping room with several beds, as in hostels or schools. A refectory is a dining hall in a school, college, monastery or similar institution. Only 'crèche' relates to child care.
explanations: Incorrect: a sculler is a rower or a small racing boat, and has nothing to do with child care.
Correct: a crèche is a day nursery where children of working parents are looked after during working hours.
Incorrect: a dormitory is a large communal sleeping room, for example in a hostel, and does not provide child care.
Incorrect: a refectory is a dining hall in a school, college or monastery, so it does not match the phrase.
keyfact: Crèche = a day nursery for children of working parents; dormitory = sleeping hall; refectory = dining hall; sculler = rower.
option_notes: Sculler: a person who rows a boat using sculls, which are a pair of short oars with one held in each hand. The word also refers to the light racing boat itself. Sculling is an Olympic rowing discipline, with events such as single sculls, double sculls and quadruple sculls. It differs from sweep rowing, in which each rower handles one oar. The word is often confused with 'sculptor', a person who makes sculptures.

Crèche: a French loanword meaning a day nursery for babies and young children. It originally meant a manger or crib, and it can also mean a nativity scene at Christmas. In India the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 makes a crèche mandatory in establishments with 50 or more employees. The Rajiv Gandhi National Crèche Scheme also supports day care for children of working mothers.

Dormitory: a large room with many beds, or a building providing sleeping accommodation for a group of people such as students, soldiers or workers. It comes from the Latin 'dormitorium', from 'dormire', to sleep. It is often shortened to 'dorm'. A 'dormitory town' is a residential area from which people commute to work elsewhere.

Refectory: a room used for communal meals in an institution such as a monastery, convent, school or college. It comes from the Latin 'reficere', to remake or refresh. Monastic refectories were often large halls where monks ate in silence while a reading was given. The related word 'refection' means refreshment by food and drink.
related: Crèche = a day nursery for children of working parents.
Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017: a crèche is mandatory in establishments with 50 or more employees.
The 2017 amendment gives 26 weeks of paid maternity leave for the first two children.
Dormitory = a large sleeping room with many beds.
Refectory = a dining hall in a school, college or monastery.
Sculler = a rower using two sculls (short oars).
Orphanage = a place for the care of orphans.
Sanatorium = a place for the treatment and recuperation of patients with chronic illness.
summary: The answer is (b) Crèche. A crèche is a nursery or day-care facility where babies and young children are looked after while their parents are at work. The other options name a rower, a sleeping hall and a dining hall, so none fits the definition.
topic_notes: This question belongs to the 'one-word substitution' topic of General English. In it, a descriptive phrase has to be replaced by a single precise word. UPSC EPFO papers regularly carry 2-3 such questions, usually with everyday and institutional vocabulary. Related words for places: crèche (day nursery), dormitory (sleeping hall), refectory (dining hall), orphanage (home for orphans), sanatorium (a place for recuperation or treatment of chronic illness), aviary (a place for birds), apiary (a place for bees), arsenal (a place for storing weapons), mortuary (a place for dead bodies), nursery (a place where plants are grown, or a place for young children), gymnasium (a place for exercise), granary (a place for storing grain), menagerie (a collection of wild animals), asylum (an institution for care, once used for the mentally ill), armoury, laboratory, observatory and cloister. Exam tips: learn the Latin and French roots, because 'crèche' (French), 'refectory' (Latin 'reficere') and 'dormitory' (Latin 'dormire') have patterns that help recall. Also practise the reverse type, where the word is given and the meaning must be chosen. Other types include synonyms, antonyms, idioms and phrases, spelling errors and sentence improvement. Link to labour law: the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 raised paid maternity leave to 26 weeks for the first two children and made crèches mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees. This overlap with Industrial Relations and Labour Laws shows why the word is worth knowing.

question: Which one of the following words can be used as a substitute for the phrase, “That which cannot be taken by force”?
subject: General English
detail: This is a one-word-substitution question from General English. 'Impregnable' (adjective) comes from Old French 'imprenable', from 'prendre' (to take), and so literally means 'not able to be taken'. It is typically used for fortresses, castles, defences, positions or arguments that cannot be conquered, captured or defeated by force. Examples: an impregnable fortress, an impregnable defence, an impregnable lead. Elimination logic: 'Impossible' refers to something that cannot happen or be done, with no link to force or capture. 'Improbable' means unlikely to happen or be true, a matter of probability. 'Impeccable' means faultless or flawless, usually of conduct, taste or performance. Only 'impregnable' relates to resisting capture or seizure. Students should note that 'impregnable' has a second sense in its verb family: 'impregnate' means to make pregnant or to saturate, but the adjective 'impregnable' is unrelated to pregnancy. Beware of confusion with 'inviolable' (cannot be violated), 'invincible' (cannot be conquered, said of persons or armies) and 'unassailable' (cannot be attacked). Learn these as a cluster, since UPSC often tests near-synonyms as distractors.
explanations: Wrong: 'Impossible' means unable to occur or be done. It says nothing about force or capture, so it does not fit the phrase.
Wrong: 'Improbable' means not likely to happen or be true. It deals with likelihood, not with resisting force.
Wrong: 'Impeccable' means without fault or flaw, as in impeccable manners. It has no connection to being taken by force.
Correct: 'Impregnable' means incapable of being captured or entered by force, such as a fortress. It exactly matches the phrase, and the official answer is (d).
keyfact: Impregnable = that which cannot be taken by force (from Old French prendre, 'to take').
option_notes: Impossible: adjective meaning not able to exist, happen or be done. From Latin 'impossibilis'. Example: an impossible task. Related terms: infeasible, unattainable. It describes impracticability in general and carries no sense of force or siege, so it is a common general distractor in one-word-substitution questions.

Improbable: adjective meaning not likely to be true or to happen. From the Latin 'improbabilis'. Example: an improbable story. It is a matter of low probability, not impossibility. Related terms: unlikely, doubtful, far-fetched. Do not confuse it with 'impossible', which means that something cannot happen at all.

Impeccable: adjective from Latin 'impeccabilis', meaning incapable of sin, and now meaning faultless or perfect. Example: impeccable manners, an impeccable record. It is a term of praise for conduct, taste or appearance. Do not confuse it with 'impregnable' because the two sound alike and begin with 'imp'.

Impregnable: adjective meaning unable to be captured or broken into by force. From Old French 'imprenable' (prendre, to take). Used for forts, defences and positions, and figuratively for arguments or leads. Synonyms: unconquerable, invulnerable, unassailable, secure. Do not confuse it with 'impregnate', which means to make pregnant or to saturate.
related: Inviolable means that cannot be violated or dishonoured.
Invincible means that cannot be conquered or defeated.
Indelible means that cannot be erased or removed.
Infallible means incapable of making mistakes.
Incorrigible means that cannot be corrected or reformed.
Indefatigable means one who never gets tired.
Unassailable means that cannot be attacked or questioned.
Impeccable means faultless or flawless.
summary: The answer is (d) Impregnable. 'Impregnable' means incapable of being captured or broken into by force, which matches the phrase 'that which cannot be taken by force'. The other options mean something different (not possible, unlikely, flawless).
topic_notes: This question belongs to the vocabulary section of EPFO General English, where one-word substitution, synonyms, antonyms and idioms appear regularly. The most efficient method is to break a word into prefix, root and suffix. 'Im-' or 'in-' means not, and 'prendre' (to take) gives 'impregnable'. Other frequently tested substitutions: 'inviolable' (that which cannot be violated), 'invincible' (that cannot be defeated), 'indelible' (that cannot be erased or removed), 'inevitable' (that cannot be avoided), 'incorrigible' (that cannot be corrected), 'inaudible' (that cannot be heard), 'illegible' (that cannot be read), 'indefatigable' (that does not tire), 'infallible' (that cannot make mistakes), 'insurmountable' (that cannot be overcome), 'inexorable' (that cannot be persuaded or stopped), 'impregnable' (that cannot be captured), 'irreparable' (that cannot be repaired), and 'unassailable' (that cannot be attacked). Compare also words for people: 'philanthropist' (lover of mankind), 'misanthrope' (hater of mankind), 'altruist' (selfless), 'egoist' (self-centred), 'cynic' (distrusts human motives), 'pedant' (shows off learning). In exams, always eliminate options by checking whether their meaning fits the whole phrase, not just the sound. Keep a running list of confusable pairs such as impregnable/impeccable, imminent/eminent, and ingenious/ingenuous, because UPSC uses look-alike distractors.

ocr: Which one of the following is the appropriate question tag in the sentence, “Take a seat, a (a) shall you? (b) can’t you? (ec) won't you? (a) would you?
subject: General English
detail: Question tags are short questions added to the end of a statement to seek confirmation or to soften a command. For most statements the tag reverses polarity: a positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag. Imperative sentences (commands, requests, invitations) are special. A positive imperative such as "Take a seat" or "Open the door" is commonly followed by "won't you?" when it is an invitation or offer, and by "will you?" or "can you?" when it is a request or command. A negative imperative such as "Don't be late" takes "will you?". "Let's ..." takes "shall we?". "Let us/me ..." in the sense of permission takes "will you?". Elimination: "shall you?" is wrong because "shall" is used in tags only with first-person subjects (I/we), as in "Let's go, shall we?". "Can't you?" suggests surprise or irritation about ability, not an invitation, and is not the standard imperative tag. "Would you?" is possible for polite requests but is not the standard tag for an invitation. "Won't you?" is the standard tag for a positive invitation, hence option (c), which is also the official answer.
explanations: Wrong: "shall" is used in tags only with I/we ("Let's go, shall we?"). It cannot pair with the subject "you" in this way.
Wrong: "can't you?" implies a challenge about ability or irritation. It is not the standard tag for the invitation "Take a seat".
Correct: A positive imperative expressing an invitation or offer takes "won't you?". This matches the official key.
Wrong: "would you?" is used for polite requests such as "Pass the salt, would you?". It is not the standard invitation tag and is not the official answer.
keyfact: Positive imperative invitation: "Take a seat, won't you?"; "Let's..." takes "shall we?"; "I am" takes "aren't I?".
option_notes: "Shall you?" is not a normal tag. "Shall" appears in tags with first-person subjects, such as "I shall go, shall I?", and in suggestions like "Let's begin, shall we?". Traditionally "shall" with I/we expresses future, offers or suggestions, while "will" is used with other subjects. Used with "you", it is archaic or formal, as in legal texts where "shall" imposes duty.

"Can't you?" is a negative tag built on the modal "can". It follows positive statements with "can", for example "You can swim, can't you?". With imperatives it can express impatience or complaint, like "Do be quiet, can't you?". Modal tags repeat the modal from the main clause, so it fits statements, not the invitation "Take a seat".

"Won't you?" is the negative tag from "will". It follows positive statements with "will", as in "You will come, won't you?". With positive imperatives it makes an invitation or offer sound warm and persuasive: "Have some tea, won't you?" and "Take a seat, won't you?". With commands, "will you?" is more usual.

"Would you?" is the past or polite form of "will". It is used in tags to make requests more polite, for example "Close the window, would you?". It is an acceptable alternative for requests, but for invitations the standard tag is "won't you?". Also used in tags after statements with "would", such as "He would come, wouldn't he?".
related: "Let's go, ___?" takes "shall we?".
"I am late, ___?" takes "aren't I?".
Negative imperative "Don't be late, ___?" takes "will you?".
"Nobody came, ___?" takes "did they?".
"He used to smoke, ___?" takes "didn't he?".
"There is a problem, ___?" takes "isn't there?".
"Everyone is present, ___?" takes "aren't they?".
"She hardly speaks, ___?" takes "does she?".
summary: The answer is (c) won't you?. The sentence "Take a seat" is an imperative, and imperatives take the tag "won't you?" (or "will you?" / "would you?" in some usages). UPSC's official key accepts (c).
topic_notes: Question tags are a regular topic in the General English section of the EPFO exam. A question tag is a short interrogative clause added after a statement. The main rules are as follows. First, polarity: a positive statement takes a negative tag ("She is here, isn't she?") and a negative statement takes a positive tag ("She isn't here, is she?"). Second, the tag repeats the auxiliary verb of the main clause; if there is none, use do/does/did ("He works hard, doesn't he?"). Third, the tag subject is a pronoun matching the main subject. Fourth, special cases: "I am" takes "aren't I?"; "Let's" takes "shall we?"; positive imperatives take "will you?", "won't you?" (invitation), "can you?" or "would you?"; negative imperatives take "will you?"; "There is/are" keeps "there" in the tag ("There is a problem, isn't there?"); "Nobody, nothing, none, never, hardly, seldom, rarely, scarcely" make the statement negative, so the tag is positive ("Nobody came, did they?"); "everyone, someone, anybody" take "they" in the tag; "this/that" take "it"; "these/those" take "they". "Used to" takes "didn't" ("He used to smoke, didn't he?"). "Had better" takes "hadn't" and "ought to" takes "shouldn't" or "oughtn't". "Must" for necessity takes "needn't" or "mustn't", while "must" for deduction takes the tag of the following verb. "I wish" takes "may I?". Intonation matters too: a rising tone is a real question, a falling tone seeks confirmation. UPSC often tests these exceptional patterns, so memorise them.

question: Which one of the following is the appropriate question tag in the sentence, “Anyone can make mistakes, "9
subject: General English
detail: Question tags are short questions added to the end of a statement. The basic rule is that a positive statement takes a negative tag and a negative statement takes a positive tag. The tag repeats the auxiliary or modal verb of the main clause. If there is no auxiliary, the tag uses do/does/did. The pronoun in the tag must match the subject. Indefinite pronouns such as anyone, everyone, someone, no one, somebody and nobody take "they" in the tag, as in "Everyone loves music, don't they?". Here the statement "Anyone can make mistakes" is positive and its modal is "can", so the tag is "can't they?". Elimination: (a) "isn't it?" uses the wrong auxiliary and the singular pronoun "it", which does not refer to a person. (b) "shall they?" is a positive tag after a positive statement and uses the wrong modal. (d) "is it?" is positive and uses the wrong verb and pronoun. Only (c) matches polarity, modal and pronoun. Remember the special cases: "I am" takes "aren't I?", "Let's" takes "shall we?", an imperative takes "will you?", and sentences with never, hardly, scarcely, seldom or nobody count as negative and take positive tags.
explanations: Wrong: "isn't it?" uses the auxiliary "is", which does not match the modal "can". The pronoun "it" also cannot refer to "anyone", which means a person.
Wrong: "shall they?" is a positive tag after a positive statement, and "shall" does not repeat the modal "can".
Correct: "can't they?" is negative to balance the positive statement, repeats the modal "can", and uses "they" for the indefinite pronoun "anyone".
Wrong: "is it?" is positive, so it does not reverse the polarity. It also uses the wrong verb and the wrong pronoun.
keyfact: For a positive statement with a modal and "anyone", the tag is the negative of the same modal plus "they", so "Anyone can make mistakes, can't they?".
option_notes: "Isn't it?" is the negative tag for statements whose verb is "is" and whose subject is a singular non-person noun or "it" or "this" or "that". Example: "It is a fine day, isn't it?". It is not used with "can" or with people-related indefinite pronouns. Contracted negative tags are standard in spoken English, and the full form "is it not?" is more formal.

"Shall they?" is a positive tag with the modal "shall". It would follow a negative statement containing "shall", such as "They shall not go, shall they?". "Shall we?" is the fixed tag after "Let's", as in "Let's go, shall we?". Shall is used mostly with I and we for suggestions, offers and formal rules or promises.

"Can't they?" is the negative tag for a positive statement with the modal "can" and a plural or indefinite subject. Example: "Anyone can join, can't they?". The spelling is always "can't" in the tag, and the full form "can they not?" is rare and formal. "Can't I?" is used for "I can", while "aren't I?" is used only for "I am".

"Is it?" is a positive tag used after negative statements with "is", such as "It isn't raining, is it?". It can also express surprise when it is used as a reply. It is not suitable here because the statement is positive and its verb is the modal "can".
related: Positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag.
Anyone, everyone, someone and nobody take the tag pronoun "they".
"I am" takes the tag "aren't I?".
"Let's" takes the tag "shall we?".
An imperative sentence usually takes "will you?" as the tag.
Hardly, never, seldom and scarcely make a statement negative, so the tag is positive.
"Everything" and "nothing" take the tag pronoun "it".
"Ought to" takes "shouldn't" or "oughtn't" as the tag.
summary: The answer is (c) can't they? The main clause "Anyone can make mistakes" is positive and uses the modal verb "can", so the tag must be negative, reuse the same modal, and take the plural pronoun "they" (which is conventionally used for "anyone").
topic_notes: Question tags are a standard topic in the General English section of UPSC EPFO papers. The central rule is opposite polarity. A positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag. The tag must repeat the auxiliary or modal of the statement. If the statement has no auxiliary, use do, does or did according to tense. The pronoun must agree with the subject. Key special cases to memorise: (1) Everyone, anyone, someone, no one, everybody, nobody and somebody take "they". (2) Nothing, everything and something take "it". (3) "I am" takes "aren't I?". (4) "Let's" takes "shall we?". (5) An imperative takes "will you?", "won't you?" or "can you?". (6) "There is" takes "isn't there?". (7) Negative words such as never, hardly, rarely, seldom, barely, scarcely, little and few make the statement negative, so the tag is positive. Example: "He hardly speaks, does he?". (8) "Used to" takes "didn't" or "usedn't". (9) "Have" as a main verb of possession can take "haven't" or "don't". (10) "Must" takes "mustn't" for obligation, or the tag follows the sense when it expresses a deduction. (11) "Ought to" takes "shouldn't" or "oughtn't". (12) "Had better" takes "hadn't". (13) "I wish" and similar forms take "may I?". Related areas that UPSC tests alongside tags are subject-verb agreement, modals, indefinite pronouns and sentence correction. In a tag question, a rising intonation asks a real question, while a falling intonation seeks confirmation.

question: Which one of the following phrasal verbs may be used in the blank space in the sentence, “He is fond of art and seems (suited) to be an artist”?
subject: General English
detail: This question tests idiomatic phrasal verbs. 'Be cut out for something' or 'be cut out to be something' is an informal idiom meaning to have the natural qualities or ability needed for a role or job. It is nearly always used in the passive form ('is/seems cut out'), and it is often used in negatives such as 'He is not cut out to be a teacher'. The sentence gives a clue: fondness for art leads to the inference that he has the natural aptitude to be an artist, so the blank needs a word meaning 'naturally suited'. Elimination: 'fit out' means to equip or supply with necessary items (fit out a ship, fit out an expedition), not to be suited. 'Bring out' means to publish, release, or reveal a quality (bring out a book, bring out the best in someone), and does not fit grammatically with 'to be an artist'. 'Suit out' is not a standard English phrasal verb at all; it is a distractor built on the word 'suited' in the stem. Hence (c). Tip for exams: learn common 'cut' phrasal verbs such as cut down, cut off, cut out, cut in, cut back, cut up, and cut across.
explanations: (a) Wrong: 'fit out' means to equip or furnish something with the needed fittings; it does not describe personal aptitude.
(b) Wrong: 'bring out' means to publish, launch, or make a quality more noticeable; it cannot be followed by 'to be an artist' to express suitability.
(c) Correct: 'cut out' (be cut out to be) means naturally suited or qualified, matching the sense of the sentence.
(d) Wrong: 'suit out' is not a recognised English phrasal verb; it is a distractor derived from the word 'suited' in the stem.
keyfact: 'Be cut out to be/for' = naturally suited to; 'suit out' is not a real phrasal verb.
option_notes: Fit out: to supply a person, ship, or building with the equipment or clothing needed for a purpose. Examples: 'The company fitted out the office with new computers'; 'They fitted out an expedition'. The related noun is 'outfit'. It is a transitive phrasal verb, commonly used in naval, military, and business contexts. It is different from 'fit in' (belong or be accepted) and 'fit into'.

Bring out: has several meanings: to publish or release a product or book ('bring out a new edition'), to reveal or emphasise a quality ('bring out the best in him'), and to help someone become less shy. It is a transitive phrasal verb. It is often confused with 'bring up' (raise a child or mention a topic) and 'bring about' (cause to happen).

Cut out: has multiple meanings: to remove by cutting; to stop doing or eating something ('cut out sugar'); to stop working suddenly, as with an engine; and, in the passive 'be cut out for/to be', to be naturally suited. Related idioms: 'have your work cut out' (face a difficult task) and 'cut it out' (stop it). It is a frequently tested phrasal verb in competitive exams.

Suit out: not a standard phrasal verb in English. It is a made-up distractor. The genuine words around it are 'suit' (be appropriate or acceptable, as in 'This job suits him') and 'suit up' (put on special clothing, as in 'astronauts suit up'). The adjective 'suited' means right for a purpose, as in 'suited to the role'. Students should not form phrasal verbs by guesswork.
related: 'Be cut out for' means to have natural ability for something.
'Have your work cut out' means to face a very difficult task.
'Fit out' means to equip; 'fit in' means to belong.
'Bring about' means to cause; 'bring up' means to raise or mention.
'Put off' means to postpone; 'put up with' means to tolerate.
'Call off' means to cancel; 'turn down' means to reject.
'Fond of' takes the preposition 'of'; 'suited to' or 'suited for' takes 'to' or 'for'.
summary: The correct answer is (c) cut out. The phrasal verb 'be cut out (to be / for)' means to be naturally suited or having the right qualities for something, which fits the sentence 'He is fond of art and seems cut out to be an artist'.
topic_notes: Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle (adverb or preposition) to form a meaning that is often idiomatic and cannot be guessed from the parts. Types: transitive and intransitive; separable (cut the tree down / cut down the tree) and inseparable (look after the child); and three-word phrasal verbs (put up with, look forward to, run out of). In UPSC EPFO English papers, questions usually give a sentence with a blank, or an underlined phrase to be replaced, and ask for the correct phrasal verb or the meaning of an idiom. The best strategy is to read the context for the sense, then eliminate options that are not real phrasal verbs or have the wrong meaning. Common groups to revise: 'cut' (cut down = reduce, cut off = disconnect, cut in = interrupt, cut back = reduce expenditure, cut out = stop or be suited); 'bring' (bring about, bring up, bring down, bring in, bring out); 'put' (put off = postpone, put up with = tolerate, put out = extinguish); 'turn' (turn down = reject, turn up = arrive, turn out = prove to be); 'give' (give in = surrender, give up = quit, give away = reveal or donate); 'call' (call off = cancel, call on = visit); 'look' (look into = investigate, look down on = despise, look up to = admire); 'break' (break down, break out, break in). Related idioms include 'be cut out for', 'have one's work cut out', and 'cut corners'. Also revise prepositions that usually accompany adjectives such as 'fond of', 'suited to', and 'capable of'.

question: Which one of the following phrasal verbs may be used in the blank space in the sentence, “We were happy in the beginning, but now all the troubles have ____. (appeared)”?
subject: General English
detail: Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle (adverb or preposition) to give an idiomatic meaning, and the question tests whether the candidate can match the meaning 'appeared' to the right one. 'Crop up' means to occur or appear unexpectedly, and it is used for problems, issues, difficulties and questions: 'Problems cropped up during the project.' In the sentence, troubles emerge after a happy start, which is exactly this sense. 'Come about' means to happen or take place, usually used to explain how something occurred ('How did this come about?'), and it does not mean 'appear'. 'Come out' means to be published, to become known, to emerge from a place, or to bloom, and it does not suit troubles. 'Rushed in' means to enter hurriedly or to act hastily, and it does not fit the meaning or grammar here ('have rushed in' would be an odd collocation for troubles). Elimination: test each option by substituting the given meaning and checking idiomatic collocation. Only 'cropped up' collocates naturally with 'troubles', 'problems' and 'issues' in the sense of appearing unexpectedly.
explanations: Correct: 'cropped up' means appeared or arose unexpectedly, which fits troubles appearing after a happy beginning.
Wrong: 'come about' means to happen or take place and explains how something occurred. It does not carry the meaning 'appear'.
Wrong: 'come out' means to be published, become known, emerge or bloom. It is not the idiomatic choice for troubles appearing.
Wrong: 'rushed in' means to enter hurriedly or act hastily. It does not convey appearing unexpectedly and is awkward here.
keyfact: Crop up = appear or arise unexpectedly, as with troubles, problems or issues.
option_notes: Crop up: to appear or occur unexpectedly, especially of problems, issues, questions or difficulties. It is intransitive and cannot be used in the passive. Example: 'A new issue cropped up at the meeting.' It is informal to neutral in register, and the past form is 'cropped up'. Related phrases: turn up, pop up, arise, surface.

Come about: to happen, take place or occur, often by chance or gradually, and often used to ask or explain how an event happened. Example: 'How did the change come about?' It is also used in nautical language, meaning to change tack. It is intransitive and has no passive form. Related: take place, occur, transpire.

Come out: has many senses. It can mean to be published or released (a book comes out), to become known (the truth came out), to emerge from a place, to bloom (flowers come out), to appear (the sun came out), or to openly declare something about oneself. The sense depends on context, and it is not idiomatic for troubles arising.

Rush in: to enter a place hurriedly, or to act without proper thought, as in the proverb 'Fools rush in where angels fear to tread'. It can also describe something flowing in quickly. It suggests haste and does not mean appearing unexpectedly. Related: rush into, hurry in, barge in.
related: Crop up = appear or arise unexpectedly.
Come across = meet or find by chance.
Come about = happen or take place.
Put off = postpone.
Call off = cancel.
Put up with = tolerate.
Look into = investigate.
Fall through = fail to happen.
summary: The answer is (a) cropped up. The phrasal verb 'crop up' means to appear or arise unexpectedly, which matches the given meaning 'appeared' for troubles surfacing after a happy beginning.
topic_notes: Phrasal verbs are a regular feature of the General English section in EPFO papers, usually as fill-in-the-blank questions or as questions asking for the meaning of a given phrasal verb. A phrasal verb is a verb plus an adverb or preposition (or both) whose meaning is often different from the individual words. They can be transitive (take a clause down) or intransitive (the plan fell through), separable (switch the light on / switch on the light) or inseparable (look after the child). Useful groups to revise: Appear or happen: crop up, turn up, come up, show up, pop up, come about, take place. Postpone or cancel: put off, call off, hold off, put back. Tolerate or endure: put up with, bear with, live with. Discover or investigate: find out, look into, dig up, make out. Fail or succeed: fall through, break down, pull off, come off. Reduce or end: cut down, cut off, wind up, wear off, die out. Exam strategy: substitute the meaning given in brackets into the sentence, check the collocation (what kind of noun usually goes with the verb), and eliminate options that are literal or have a different sense. Also learn whether the verb is separable, because that can matter for correct usage. Questions are often built on pairs that look similar, such as come about, come across, come out, come up, and come along, so learn the distinct meaning of each.

question: Which one of the following phrasal verbs may be used in the blank space in the sentence, “No one knows how it all (happened)”?
subject: General English
detail: This question tests phrasal verbs built on 'come'. 'Come about' is intransitive and means to happen, occur, or take place, usually with a sense of how or why a situation arose. It is therefore the natural phrasal verb after 'how it all ...' when the idea is the origin or occurrence of events. Related meanings: 'come about' can also be used of a ship changing direction (nautical use). 'Come across' means to find or meet by chance, or to give a certain impression (he comes across as shy). 'Come into' needs an object and usually means to inherit (come into money) or to enter a state (come into force, come into being). 'Come forward' means to volunteer, offer help or information, or present oneself (witnesses came forward). Elimination logic: the sentence has no object and no sense of chance discovery, inheritance or volunteering. Only 'came about' conveys 'how the events happened'. Similar synonyms for 'happen' are 'take place', 'occur', 'come off' (succeed), and 'crop up' (appear unexpectedly). Remember to check whether the verb needs an object.
explanations: Incorrect: 'came across' means found by chance or gave an impression, so 'how it all came across' does not mean 'how it happened'.
Correct: 'came about' means happened or took place, which is the official answer and fits the sentence in sense and grammar.
Incorrect: 'came into' is transitive and needs an object (came into money, came into force), but the sentence has none and the sense is wrong.
Incorrect: 'came forward' means volunteered or stepped up to offer help or information, which does not suit 'how it all happened'.
keyfact: 'Come about' = happen or take place; 'come across' = find by chance; 'come into' = inherit or enter a state; 'come forward' = volunteer.
option_notes: 'Come across' means (1) to find or meet by chance (came across an old friend) or (2) to be perceived in a certain way (comes across as arrogant). It can also mean to be understood, as in 'his message came across clearly'. It is a separable-meaning phrasal verb commonly tested alongside 'run across' and 'stumble upon'.

'Come about' means to happen or take place, often explaining how a situation arose (How did this come about?). It is intransitive and cannot take a direct object. In nautical English it also means a sailing ship changes tack. Synonyms: occur, arise, transpire, take place. Commonly tested in competitive exams.

'Come into' is a transitive phrasal verb used in set expressions: come into money (inherit), come into force (become effective, as with laws), come into being (begin to exist), come into play (become active), and come into view (become visible). It always needs an object, which is why it fails here.

'Come forward' means to present oneself voluntarily, especially to offer help, evidence or information, or to be a candidate (witnesses were asked to come forward). Related verbs: step forward, volunteer. It describes a deliberate human action, not the occurrence of events, so it is wrong here.
related: Come about = happen or take place.
Come across = find by chance or give an impression.
Come up with = think of or produce an idea or plan.
Come down with = become ill with a disease.
Come into force = begin to operate (laws).
Come round = regain consciousness or change one's opinion.
Come by = obtain or acquire.
Come off = succeed or take place as planned.
summary: The answer is (b) 'came about'. The phrasal verb 'come about' means 'to happen' or 'to take place', which fits the sentence 'No one knows how it all came about'.
topic_notes: Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle (preposition or adverb) to create a meaning that is often not obvious from the parts. UPSC EPFO English papers regularly test them through fill-in-the-blank sentences, so learn them by meaning and by whether they take an object. Key 'come' phrasal verbs: come about (happen), come across (find by chance or seem), come along (accompany or progress), come around/round (regain consciousness, change one's opinion, or visit), come down with (fall ill with), come up with (think of an idea or plan), come off (succeed, or become detached), come out (be published or revealed), come through (survive or succeed), come by (obtain), come over (visit), come to (regain consciousness or amount to), come upon (discover by chance), come into (inherit or enter a state), come forward (volunteer), come back (return), come apart (break into pieces), come down (fall or decrease), come up (arise or be mentioned), come at (attack), come under (be subject to). Tips: (1) identify the sentence meaning first; (2) check whether an object follows; (3) distinguish transitive from intransitive; (4) look at collocations like 'come into force', 'come to light', 'come to terms'. Related exam topics: idioms and phrases, one-word substitution, prepositions, and synonyms. Practise grouping phrasal verbs by base verb (get, take, put, look, run, turn, break, call, bring, make, give, set) because the same particles change meaning across verbs.

question: Which one of the following phrasal verbs may be used in the blank space in the sentence, “I have to (finish) this work before I leave tomorrow morning”?
subject: General English
detail: This is a General English question on phrasal verbs, where the meaning depends on the verb plus particle, and on the object that follows. 'Clear up' has several senses: to tidy a place, to explain or resolve a doubt or problem, to improve (weather, illness), and to finish off outstanding or pending work. 'I have to clear up this work before I leave' uses the last sense, in which work is a pile of pending tasks to be dealt with. 'Clean up' means to remove dirt or make a place or person clean, and it is also used figuratively for cleaning up an image or a city, but it does not naturally take 'work' as an object. 'Finish up' does mean to complete, and in everyday usage it is often interchangeable with 'finish', so many students will argue for it. The question setter, however, treats (a) as the intended answer, so accept the official key. 'Do away with' means to abolish or get rid of, so it changes the sense completely and is wrong. For elimination: reject (d) first on meaning, then (b) on collocation with dirt or mess, and then pick between (a) and (c). Follow the official key, (a).
explanations: Correct: 'clear up' can mean to deal with and finish pending work, which suits 'finish this work before I leave', and it is the official answer.
Incorrect: 'clean up' refers to removing dirt or mess, or figuratively to reforming something. It is not the normal phrasal verb for completing pending work.
Incorrect as per the official key: 'finish up' means to complete and is close in meaning, but the key does not accept it. It is the closest distractor, so be careful with it.
Incorrect: 'do away with' means to abolish or discard. It would mean getting rid of the work, not completing it.
keyfact: Clear up = resolve or finish off pending matters; do away with = abolish; clean up = remove dirt; finish up = complete, but the official key here is (a) clear up.
option_notes: Clear up: a phrasal verb meaning (1) to tidy a place, (2) to resolve a misunderstanding or mystery, (3) to improve, as weather or a rash does, and (4) to finish off pending tasks or a backlog. Examples: 'clear up the confusion', 'The sky cleared up', 'clear up the paperwork'. It is transitive and separable: 'clear the matter up'.

Clean up: a phrasal verb meaning to make a place or person clean, or to remove dirt or mess. It is also used figuratively, for example 'clean up politics' or 'clean up one's act'. In slang it can mean to win a lot of money. It is transitive and separable: 'clean the room up'.

Finish up: a phrasal verb meaning to complete something, or to consume the last of something, as in 'finish up the food'. It can also mean to end up in a certain place or state, as in 'finished up in Delhi' (British usage). It is usually interchangeable with 'finish', and the 'up' only adds emphasis.

Do away with: an inseparable three-word phrasal verb meaning to abolish, discard or eliminate something, for example 'The government did away with the old tax'. In informal usage it can also mean to kill someone, as in 'do away with oneself'. It is not used for completing work.
related: 'Clear up' can mean to resolve a doubt, as in 'clear up the confusion', or to finish pending work.
'Do away with' means to abolish or get rid of.
'Put up with' means to tolerate.
'Call off' means to cancel and 'put off' means to postpone.
'Look into' means to investigate.
'Carry out' means to execute or perform.
'Take after' means to resemble a family member.
'Up' in phrasal verbs often shows completion, as in finish up, use up and eat up.
summary: The answer is (a) clear up. In this sentence the phrasal verb must mean to complete or dispose of pending work, and 'clear up' is the one that fits, as in clearing up a backlog of work before leaving. The official UPSC key treats (a) as correct.
topic_notes: Phrasal verbs combine a verb with an adverb or preposition, or both, to create a meaning that often differs from the literal sense of the verb. They are a regular feature of the General English section of the EPFO papers. There are four broad types. Transitive separable verbs allow the object between the verb and particle, as in 'clear the work up' or 'clean it up'. Transitive inseparable verbs, such as 'do away with', 'look after' and 'run into', do not allow this. Intransitive verbs take no object, for example 'The weather cleared up' and 'He showed up'. Three-word phrasal verbs include 'put up with', 'look forward to', 'run out of' and 'get along with'. The particle 'up' often adds the idea of completion, as in eat up, finish up, use up, drink up, write up and clear up. For exam strategy, first fix the meaning the sentence needs, then check collocation with the object, then eliminate options that change the sense, and finally choose between near-synonyms using the official key or the most idiomatic usage. Frequently tested phrasal verbs include: call off (cancel), put off (postpone), carry out (execute), bring up (raise a child or topic), turn down (reject), look into (investigate), give up (quit), break down (fail), set up (establish), take after (resemble), and run out of (exhaust).
