Policymakers, including the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee, watch it to judge whether price pressures are generalised. The RBI's inflation target is 4% CPI with a band of +/-2%, under the 2016 amended RBI Act. Elimination: (b) is the exact opposite of the definition. (c) is wrong because core inflation is still derived from a commodity price index such as CPI or WPI. (d) is misleading, since core inflation does not 'consider only core items of consumption'; it is defined by what it excludes, namely volatile items, not by a notion of core consumption. So (a) is correct.
explanations: Correct: core inflation leaves out volatile items such as food and fuel from the price index, while headline inflation includes them.
Incorrect: including volatile articles is what characterises headline inflation, not core inflation.
Incorrect: core inflation is computed from the same commodity price indices (CPI or WPI) after excluding volatile items.
Incorrect: this is a loose, circular description. Core inflation is defined by excluding volatile components, not by selecting 'core consumption' items.
keyfact: Core inflation = headline inflation minus volatile items (food and fuel).
option_notes: Ignoring volatile items: this is the standard definition. Core inflation removes food and fuel (sometimes energy) from CPI or WPI. It is used to gauge underlying inflation and is less affected by temporary supply shocks. In India, CPI excluding food and fuel is the common proxy, and RBI analyses it in its Monetary Policy Reports.

Considering volatile items: this describes headline inflation, which covers all commodities in the basket, including food, fuel and primary articles. Headline inflation is the official measure. India's CPI-Combined, compiled by the NSO under MoSPI, is the basis of the RBI's inflation targeting, while WPI is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT.

Not based on a commodity price index: wrong, since core inflation is derived from CPI or WPI. India has no separate core price index. Core is calculated by excluding components. Price indices track the cost of a basket of goods and services, and CPI base year is 2012 while WPI base year is 2011-12.

Only core items of consumption: this is not the accepted definition. Core inflation does not select a special set of core goods. It is obtained by removing items with high price volatility, chiefly food and fuel. Some analysts also strip out administered prices or energy, but the principle remains exclusion of volatile components.
related: Headline inflation includes all items; core inflation excludes food and fuel.
RBI inflation target: 4% CPI with +/-2% band, set under the 2016 amendment to the RBI Act.
The Monetary Policy Committee has six members: three from the RBI and three appointed by the Government.
WPI base year is 2011-12; CPI base year is 2012.
CPI-IW is compiled by the Labour Bureau and used for dearness allowance.
CPI is compiled by the NSO (MoSPI); WPI by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT.
WPI does not include services; CPI does.
summary: The answer is (a). Core inflation is headline inflation with volatile components, mainly food and fuel (and sometimes energy), stripped out, so it shows the underlying, persistent price trend.
topic_notes: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. Headline inflation is the total inflation measured by the full price index. In India the main indices are the Wholesale Price Index (WPI), compiled monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (base year 2011-12), and the Consumer Price Index (CPI), compiled by the National Statistical Office under MoSPI (base year 2012). CPI-Combined (rural + urban) has been the key measure for monetary policy since the 2014 Urjit Patel Committee, and the RBI Act was amended in 2016 to set up a six-member Monetary Policy Committee and a flexible inflation targeting framework: 4% target, tolerance band 2-6%. If inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must report to the government. Core inflation removes volatile food and fuel components and reflects demand-side, structural pressures. Food has a large weight in CPI (about 45.86% for CPI-Combined, including food and beverages), so headline inflation is highly sensitive to vegetable and pulses prices. Types of inflation: demand-pull, cost-push, structural; related terms: disinflation, deflation, reflation, stagflation, and skewflation. Tools to control inflation: repo rate, CRR, SLR, open market operations, and fiscal measures such as taxes and subsidies. WPI excludes services, while CPI includes them. Other related measures: GDP deflator, CPI-IW (Labour Bureau, base 2016), CPI-AL and CPI-RL for agricultural and rural labourers.

question: Who among the following is the author of the book, Choice of Techniques?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Choice of Techniques (first published 1960 by Basil Blackwell, Oxford; later editions in 1962 and 1968) was Amartya Sen's early major work, based on his Cambridge research under Joan Robinson and Maurice Dobb. It belongs to development economics and planning theory. Sen analysed how a labour-surplus, capital-scarce economy should choose between labour-intensive and capital-intensive techniques. He examined the trade-off between present employment/consumption and future growth through reinvestment of surplus, and discussed the criteria proposed by Dobb, Kahn and others (such as the marginal reinvestment quotient). The work is linked to debates around India's Second Five Year Plan (Mahalanobis model, heavy industry emphasis). Elimination logic: K. N. Raj is associated with planning, public finance and the Kerala model, and with the Raj-Sen model of the 1960s with Sen; V. K. R. V. Rao is known for national income estimation in India and founding the Delhi School of Economics; Sukhamoy Chakravarty is known for 'Capital and Development Planning' and 'Development Planning: The Indian Experience' and for chairing the 1985 monetary policy review committee. Remember Sen: Nobel 1998, Bharat Ratna 1999.
explanations: Correct: A. K. Sen wrote Choice of Techniques (1960).
Incorrect: K. N. Raj wrote on Indian planning and public finance, not this book.
Incorrect: V. K. R. V. Rao is known for national income work and 'The National Income of British India, 1931-41', not this book.
Incorrect: Sukhamoy Chakravarty wrote 'Capital and Development Planning' (1969) and 'Development Planning: The Indian Experience', not this book.
keyfact: Choice of Techniques (1960) was written by Amartya Sen.
option_notes: A. K. Sen (born 1933, Santiniketan) is an economist and philosopher, Nobel laureate in Economics 1998 for welfare economics, and Bharat Ratna 1999. Major works: Collective Choice and Social Welfare (1970), Poverty and Famines (1981), Development as Freedom (1999), The Argumentative Indian (2005), The Idea of Justice (2009). He developed the capability approach and contributed to the Human Development Index with Mahbub ul Haq.

K. N. Raj (1924-2010) was an Indian economist who helped draft the Second Five Year Plan and was a founder of the Centre for Development Studies, Thiruvananthapuram. He is linked to the Kerala development model, and to the Raj-Sen model of the 1960s. He also served as Vice-Chancellor of Delhi University. Works include 'Indian Economic Growth: Performance and Prospects' and writings on public finance and agriculture.

V. K. R. V. Rao (1908-1991) was a pioneering Indian economist who first estimated India's national income scientifically. He founded the Delhi School of Economics (1949) and the Institute for Social and Economic Change, Bangalore. He was a Union Minister for Education and Planning member. Known for work on national income, the multiplier theory in underdeveloped economies, and 'The National Income of British India 1931-41'.

Sukhamoy Chakravarty (1934-1990) was an Indian economist and planner, a member of the Planning Commission and Chairman of the Committee to Review the Working of the Monetary System (1985), the Chakravarty Committee. He was an adviser to Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi. He wrote 'Capital and Development Planning' (1969), 'Development Planning: The Indian Experience' (1987) and worked on optimal growth theory.
related: Amartya Sen won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1998 and the Bharat Ratna in 1999.
Sen's 'Poverty and Famines' (1981) argued famines result from entitlement failure, not just food shortage.
'Development as Freedom' (1999) is by Amartya Sen.
Mahalanobis model underpinned India's Second Five Year Plan (1956-61).
V. K. R. V. Rao founded the Delhi School of Economics in 1949.
The Chakravarty Committee (1985) reviewed India's monetary system.
Sen's capability approach influenced the Human Development Index.
summary: The answer is (a) A. K. Sen. 'Choice of Techniques: An Aspect of the Theory of Planned Economic Development' (1960) was written by Amartya Sen. It examines which production techniques (labour-intensive or capital-intensive) a developing economy should choose to balance employment, savings and growth.
topic_notes: Choice of techniques is a core theme in development economics. A labour-surplus, capital-scarce economy faces a trade-off: labour-intensive methods create more jobs and use abundant labour, while capital-intensive methods give higher output per worker and a larger surplus for reinvestment, so faster future growth. Sen's 1960 work analysed this trade-off, including criteria like the marginal per capita reinvestment quotient. Maurice Dobb argued for capital-intensive techniques for long-run growth, whereas others stressed employment. The debate shaped India's planning. The First Plan (1951-56) followed the Harrod-Domar model. The Second Plan (1956-61) used the Mahalanobis two-sector/four-sector model, emphasising heavy industry and capital goods, with P. C. Mahalanobis founding the Indian Statistical Institute (1931). Gandhian thinking favoured small-scale and village industries and labour-intensive methods. E. F. Schumacher's 'Small is Beautiful' (1973) promoted intermediate technology. Other Indian economists and works: D. R. Gadgil, C. N. Vakil and P. R. Brahmananda (wage-goods model), Jagdish Bhagwati and Padma Desai ('India: Planning for Industrialization'), Manmohan Singh ('India's Export Trends', Oxford DPhil), and Amartya Sen's later works on famine and capability. Sen's other honours include the Bharat Ratna (1999), and the Nobel (1998) for contributions to welfare economics, social choice theory and the study of famines and poverty. UPSC often asks author-book matching in this area.

question: Which one of the following bodies has formulated the ‘National Student Startup Policy’, launched by _ the President of India in November 2016?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The National Student Startup Policy (NSSP) 2016 was drafted by AICTE, the statutory body for planning and coordinating technical education in India, set up in 1945 as an advisory body and given statutory status by the AICTE Act, 1987. The policy was released by President Pranab Mukherjee at the Rashtrapati Bhavan in November 2016, and it was aligned with the Startup India Action Plan (January 2016). It encourages institutions to build an entrepreneurial ecosystem: creating Institution Innovation Councils, setting up incubation centres, allowing students to take a break or earn credit for startup work, and giving faculty and students flexibility to run ventures. It also envisaged an Institute-level startup policy, mentoring, seed funding access, and intellectual property support. Elimination logic: UGC regulates university education and deals with higher education grants; NCERT prepares school curriculum and textbooks; AIU is an association of universities that acts as an inter-university body and recognises degree equivalence. None of these is the technical education regulator linked to engineering and management institutions. Hence AICTE is the correct answer. Remember the link: technical education plus startups equals AICTE.
explanations: Incorrect: UGC regulates standards and funding of universities; it did not draft the National Student Startup Policy.
Incorrect: NCERT is a school-education body for curriculum and textbooks, not involved in this policy.
Incorrect: AIU is an association of Indian universities handling equivalence and sports and research coordination, not policy formulation on startups.
Correct: AICTE formulated the National Student Startup Policy 2016, which was launched by the President in November 2016.
keyfact: National Student Startup Policy 2016 was formulated by AICTE and launched by President Pranab Mukherjee in November 2016.
option_notes: UGC, the University Grants Commission, was set up in 1956 under the UGC Act as a statutory body. It coordinates, determines and maintains standards of university education and gives grants to universities. It has its headquarters in New Delhi, and it also runs the NET exam for eligibility for assistant professor roles. The government proposed replacing it with the Higher Education Commission of India (HECI), which was later folded into the NEP 2020 framework.

NCERT, the National Council of Educational Research and Training, was established in 1961 in New Delhi as an autonomous organisation under the Ministry of Education. It prepares the National Curriculum Framework, publishes school textbooks used by CBSE schools, and conducts research and training in school education. It also runs the National Talent Search Examination (NTSE), and it advises the central and state governments on school education policy.

AIU, the Association of Indian Universities, was founded in 1925 as the Inter-University Board of India. Based in New Delhi, it acts as a representative body of universities, grants equivalence to degrees, publishes the University News journal, and promotes inter-university sports and cultural activities. It is a membership association, not a statutory regulator, and it has no role in formulating national startup policies for students.

AICTE, the All India Council for Technical Education, was established in 1945 as an advisory body and became statutory through the AICTE Act, 1987. It is headquartered in New Delhi, approves technical institutions in engineering, management, pharmacy, architecture and hotel management, and sets norms and standards. It formulated the National Student Startup Policy 2016 and also runs initiatives such as the Smart India Hackathon, and it works under the Ministry of Education.
related: AICTE was set up in 1945 and given statutory status by the AICTE Act, 1987.
Startup India Action Plan was announced on 16 January 2016.
The Atal Innovation Mission was launched by NITI Aayog in 2016.
Stand-Up India was launched in April 2016 to support SC/ST and women entrepreneurs.
The Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell was established in 2018.
UGC was established in 1956 under the UGC Act.
NCERT was established in 1961.
Pranab Mukherjee was India's President from 2012 to 2017.
summary: The answer is (d) AICTE. The National Student Startup Policy 2016 was formulated by the All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) and launched by President Pranab Mukherjee in November 2016 to promote student entrepreneurship in technical institutions.
topic_notes: The National Student Startup Policy 2016 was prepared by AICTE after the Startup India Action Plan was announced on 16 January 2016, and the policy was launched by President Pranab Mukherjee in November 2016. Its goal was to turn technical institutions into hubs of innovation and entrepreneurship, so that students become job creators rather than job seekers. Main features included setting up Institution Innovation Councils and incubation facilities, giving students and faculty flexibility to work on ventures with academic credit or leave, mentoring support, IP facilitation, and a target that institutions should create startup-friendly policies. Related institutions: AICTE regulates technical education, UGC regulates universities, NCERT handles school curriculum, AIU coordinates universities, and the NITI Aayog runs the Atal Innovation Mission (AIM), launched in 2016, including Atal Tinkering Labs and Atal Incubation Centres. The Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell (MIC), established in 2018, works with AICTE and launched the Institution's Innovation Council (IIC) programme. Other startup-related schemes include Startup India (2016), Stand-Up India (April 2016), MUDRA Yojana (2015), and the Fund of Funds for Startups managed by SIDBI with a corpus of Rs 10,000 crore. DPIIT (formerly DIPP) recognises startups and gives tax benefits under Section 80-IAC of the Income Tax Act for eligible startups. Skill India Mission was launched in 2015. Possible future questions may ask about who launched a policy, which body drafted it, or the ministry linked with these bodies, so remember that AICTE handles technical education and was behind NSSP.

question: Who among the following was the Chairman of the Working Group for determining the methodology for construction of Producer Price Index (PPI) in India (2014)?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: India has long used the Wholesale Price Index (WPI), compiled monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser (OEA), DIPP, Ministry of Commerce and Industry. WPI has conceptual weaknesses: it includes taxes, it mixes prices at different stages of production, and it can double-count. The Kelkar Committee on Wholesale Price Index revision (2010-11) and the Abhijit Sen Committee (2010) on the new WPI series (base 2004-05) had already pointed towards a PPI. In 2014 the government constituted a Working Group on Producer Price Index under Prof. B. N. Goldar, with the aim of recommending a methodology for a PPI that measures the average change in prices received by domestic producers, excluding indirect taxes and trade margins. Its work was a step towards the eventual replacement of WPI by PPI. The WPI base was later revised to 2011-12 (released in 2017). Elimination: Saumitra Chaudhuri was a Planning Commission/CEA-related economist and a member of the Prime Minister's Economic Advisory Council, Subbarao was RBI Governor (2008-13), and Abhijit Sen chaired the 2010 WPI committee, so only Goldar fits the PPI working group.
explanations: Incorrect: Saumitra Chaudhuri was an economist and member of the Prime Minister's Economic Advisory Council (as well as a former Planning Commission member), not the chairman of the PPI Working Group.
Incorrect: D. Subbarao was RBI Governor from 2008 to 2013 and was not associated with chairing the PPI group.
Incorrect: Abhijit Sen chaired the 2010 Working Group for the revision of WPI (base 2004-05), but not the 2014 PPI Working Group.
Correct: Prof. B. N. Goldar chaired the 2014 Working Group on the methodology for constructing a PPI in India.
keyfact: B. N. Goldar chaired the 2014 Working Group on the Producer Price Index (PPI) methodology in India.
option_notes: Saumitra Chaudhuri: an economist, formerly a member of the Prime Minister's Economic Advisory Council, and a former member of the Planning Commission, known for his work on macroeconomic analysis and credit rating. He is not linked to the PPI group.

D. Subbarao: Duvvuri Subbarao was the 22nd RBI Governor (Sept 2008 to Sept 2013), a former Finance Secretary, who led the RBI through the global financial crisis and wrote 'Who Moved My Interest Rate?'. He is not connected with the PPI group.

Abhijit Sen: Planning Commission member (2004-14), an agricultural economist and chairman of the Committee on Long-Term Grain Policy (2002). He chaired the 2010 Working Group on WPI revision to the 2004-05 base, but not the PPI group.

B. N. Goldar: a professor at the Institute of Economic Growth, Delhi, and a specialist in industrial economics, productivity and trade. He headed the 2014 Working Group on the PPI and also worked on the WPI revision.
related: WPI is compiled monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
The current WPI base year is 2011-12, introduced in 2017.
CPI-Combined is compiled by NSO, MoSPI, with base 2012.
RBI uses CPI-Combined as the nominal anchor for inflation targeting (4% ±2%).
Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended CPI as the key inflation measure.
PPI excludes indirect taxes and trade margins, unlike WPI.
CPI-IW is compiled by the Labour Bureau, Shimla/Chandigarh.
The Index of Industrial Production has base year 2011-12.
summary: The answer is (d) B. N. Goldar. The Working Group set up in 2014 by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DIPP, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, to recommend a methodology for moving from the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) to a Producer Price Index (PPI) was chaired by Prof. B. N. Goldar, an economist at the Institute of Economic Growth.
topic_notes: A Producer Price Index measures the average change over time in the selling prices received by domestic producers for their output. It differs from the WPI in three ways: it excludes taxes, trade and transport margins, and it avoids multiple counting by using a stage-of-production classification. The international standard is the PPI Manual of the IMF, ILO, OECD, Eurostat, UNECE and World Bank. India's present price indices: WPI, compiled by OEA, DPIIT (earlier DIPP) with base 2011-12 (revised in 2017 from 2004-05), covering about 697 items at launch; CPI (Combined), compiled by NSO under MoSPI, with base 2012 (to be revised to 2024); CPI-IW, compiled by the Labour Bureau; CPI-AL and CPI-RL, also by the Labour Bureau. The RBI shifted to CPI-Combined for inflation targeting under the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommendations, with a 4% target and a ±2% band under the 2016 amendment to the RBI Act. The Abhijit Sen Committee (2010) recommended WPI revision. The Kelkar Committee reviewed the WPI. The Goldar working group (2014) laid the ground for PPI, and a further working group under Ramesh Chand (NITI Aayog member) was set up in 2017 to revise WPI to the 2011-12 base. The NSO now also compiles a trial PPI series. Related areas UPSC could ask: GDP deflator, base-year revisions, the Index of Industrial Production (base 2011-12), and the difference between wholesale and retail inflation.

question: Which one of the following schemes is aimed at all-round development of adolescent girls in the age group of 11-18 years and making them selfreliant?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: RGSEAG (SABLA) was launched in 2010-11 by the Ministry of Women and Child Development. It was run through the ICDS platform and Anganwadi Centres, initially in 200 selected districts. Its objectives are to enable adolescent girls to become self-reliant and aware, improve their nutritional and health status, promote awareness of health, hygiene, nutrition, adolescent reproductive and sexual health and family and child care, upgrade home-based and vocational skills, and provide information on existing public services. Girls aged 11-18 are covered. Out-of-school girls aged 11-14 receive nutrition, and girls aged 14-18 get nutrition plus vocational training. The scheme has a nutrition component and a non-nutrition component. In 2017 it was later merged into the Scheme for Adolescent Girls (SAG) and the focus shifted to out-of-school girls aged 11-14. Elimination: IGMSY is a maternity benefit scheme for pregnant and lactating women. NMEW is a mission for the empowerment of women. RMK is a micro-finance institution for poor women. None of these is specific to adolescent girls aged 11-18.
explanations: Correct. RGSEAG (SABLA) is meant for the all-round development and self-reliance of adolescent girls aged 11-18.
Incorrect. IGMSY (Indira Gandhi Matritva Sahyog Yojana) provides conditional cash transfers to pregnant and lactating women, not adolescent girls.
Incorrect. NMEW (National Mission for Empowerment of Women) is an umbrella mission for convergence of women's schemes, not specific to adolescent girls.
Incorrect. RMK (Rashtriya Mahila Kosh) gives micro-credit to poor women through intermediary organisations, not an adolescent girl development scheme.
keyfact: RGSEAG (SABLA), 2010-11: scheme for adolescent girls aged 11-18, run via Anganwadi Centres under the Ministry of Women and Child Development.
option_notes: RGSEAG, or SABLA, is the Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for Empowerment of Adolescent Girls, launched in 2010-11 by the Ministry of Women and Child Development. It covers girls aged 11-18 through Anganwadi Centres, offering nutrition, health education, life-skills and vocational training. It was initially piloted in 200 districts and was later merged into the Scheme for Adolescent Girls in 2017, with a focus on out-of-school girls.

IGMSY is the Indira Gandhi Matritva Sahyog Yojana, a conditional maternity benefit scheme begun in 2010 as a pilot in 52 districts. It gave Rs 4,000 in installments to pregnant and lactating women aged 19 and above for the first two live births. It was later subsumed in the Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY), launched in 2017 with Rs 5,000 for the first living child.

NMEW is the National Mission for Empowerment of Women, launched on International Women's Day, 8 March 2010, by the Ministry of Women and Child Development. It ensures inter-sectoral convergence of schemes for women and economic and social empowerment. It is implemented via a National Mission Authority headed by the Prime Minister and State Mission Authorities. Its logo and a dedicated Mission Directorate support coordination.

RMK is the Rashtriya Mahila Kosh, set up in 1993 as a national-level society under the Ministry of Women and Child Development. It provides micro-finance to poor women through NGOs and self-help groups as intermediary organisations, at concessional rates, for income-generating activities. It aims at socio-economic upliftment and promotes thrift and credit. It is not meant specifically for adolescent girls.
related: SABLA was launched in 2010-11 for girls aged 11-18.
The Scheme for Adolescent Girls (2017) focuses on out-of-school girls aged 11-14.
Kishori Shakti Yojana was merged into SABLA.
IGMSY was succeeded by PMMVY (Rs 5,000 in installments).
Rashtriya Mahila Kosh was set up in 1993 for micro-credit to poor women.
NMEW was launched on 8 March 2010.
Beti Bachao Beti Padhao was launched in 2015 from Panipat.
Mission Poshan 2.0 includes the Scheme for Adolescent Girls.
summary: The answer is (a) RGSEAG, the Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for Empowerment of Adolescent Girls, better known as SABLA. It targets adolescent girls aged 11-18 for all-round development and self-reliance through nutrition, health, life-skills and vocational training.
topic_notes: Women and child development schemes are a frequent source of questions. Adolescent girls' schemes: SABLA (RGSEAG) from 2010-11 covered girls aged 11-18 via Anganwadi Centres. It was restructured in 2017 as the Scheme for Adolescent Girls, which targets out-of-school girls aged 11-14 and places the focus on nutrition, health and life skills. Kishori Shakti Yojana (KSY) was an earlier ICDS-based scheme for adolescent girls, begun in 2000, and was merged with SABLA. Nutrition programmes for the age group include the Nutrition Programme for Adolescent Girls (NPAG). Maternity schemes: IGMSY, then PMMVY (2017), which gives Rs 5,000 in three installments for the first living child, and Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) under the National Health Mission to promote institutional delivery. Empowerment institutions: NMEW (2010), Rashtriya Mahila Kosh (1993), the National Commission for Women (1992), Mahila Samakhya (1988), STEP (Support to Training and Employment Programme for Women), and Swadhar Greh and Ujjawala for protection and rehabilitation. Girl child schemes: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015, Panipat, Haryana), Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (2015) for savings, and CBSE's Udaan. Mission Shakti (2022) and Poshan Abhiyaan (2018) are the umbrella programmes now in force. Mission Poshan 2.0 combined Anganwadi Services, Poshan Abhiyaan and the Scheme for Adolescent Girls. Another angle UPSC may ask is the ministry in charge, the target age, and which scheme merged into which.

question: Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 permits _ selfgovernance of natural resources by
options: the Chairman of Gram Panchayat forest dwellers of a village situated
in the areas mentioned in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution of India
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) extends Part IX of the Constitution (Articles 243-243O) to the Fifth Schedule areas, with modifications. This was done to give tribal communities self-rule based on their customs. It was enacted on the basis of the Bhuria Committee (1995) recommendations. Section 4(d) says every Gram Sabha is competent to safeguard and preserve the traditions and customs of the people, their cultural identity, community resources and the customary mode of dispute resolution. Section 4(m) gives Gram Sabhas and Panchayats powers over minor forest produce, minor water bodies, minor minerals, village markets, land alienation, and control over money lending and local plans. Section 4(i) requires Gram Sabha or Panchayat consultation before land acquisition and resettlement. Elimination: the Gram Panchayat is the elected executive body and works under or alongside the Gram Sabha, so it is not the primary holder of power under PESA. The Chairman (Sarpanch) of the Gram Panchayat is an individual office-holder with no independent authority over resources. Options (c) and (d) are OCR fragments, and the phrase 'forest dwellers of a village situated in the areas mentioned in the Fifth Schedule' only describes the context. The ten states with Fifth Schedule areas are the ones PESA covers.
explanations: Correct: PESA vests natural resource management, including minor forest produce, in the Gram Sabha, which is the primary body for self-governance.
Incorrect: The Gram Panchayat is the elected executive body. PESA requires it to work with and under the Gram Sabha, which holds the central role.
Incorrect: The Chairman or Sarpanch is only an office-bearer. PESA gives no individual authority over natural resources.
Incorrect: This is a fragment describing the area of application (Fifth Schedule areas). It does not name the body that exercises self-governance.
keyfact: PESA 1996 makes the Gram Sabha the centre of self-governance of natural resources in Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas.
option_notes: Gram Sabha: the body of all persons on the electoral rolls of a village (Article 243(b)). Under PESA it approves plans and programmes, identifies beneficiaries, and issues utilisation certificates. It safeguards community resources and customs, and its consent is needed before land acquisition. It is the foundation of village democracy, and the 73rd Amendment (1992) gave it constitutional recognition.

Gram Panchayat: the elected village-level executive body of the three-tier Panchayati Raj system under Part IX. Members are elected directly for five years and are headed by a Sarpanch or Pradhan. It implements schemes, collects local taxes and prepares plans, and it is accountable to the Gram Sabha. Under PESA at least half of the seats are reserved for Scheduled Tribes, and all Chairpersons' posts at every level are reserved for STs.

Chairman (Sarpanch) of Gram Panchayat: the elected head of the Gram Panchayat, who presides over its meetings and supervises its administration. The post has no independent power over natural resources. In Scheduled Areas, PESA reserves the office of Chairperson of Panchayats at all levels for Scheduled Tribes.

Fifth Schedule areas: Article 244(1) and the Fifth Schedule govern the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. These four are covered by the Sixth Schedule. The Governor can declare Scheduled Areas, and the President notifies them. A Tribes Advisory Council exists in each state. Ten states have Fifth Schedule areas: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha and Rajasthan.
related: PESA was enacted in 1996 on the Bhuria Committee recommendations.
Article 243M exempts Scheduled Areas from Part IX unless Parliament extends it.
Fifth Schedule: ten states; Sixth Schedule: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.
Under PESA, ownership of minor forest produce rests with Panchayats at the appropriate level and Gram Sabha.
Forest Rights Act 2006 gives the Gram Sabha power to initiate recognition of forest rights.
Niyamgiri hills case (2013): Supreme Court directed Gram Sabhas to decide on Vedanta bauxite mining.
Article 243(b) defines Gram Sabha as a body of persons registered in the electoral rolls of a village.
All Panchayat Chairperson posts in Scheduled Areas are reserved for Scheduled Tribes.
summary: The answer is (a) Gram Sabha. PESA 1996 makes the Gram Sabha, the general body of all adult voters in a village, the central body for self-governance and management of natural resources in Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas.
topic_notes: PESA 1996 was enacted on 24 December 1996 to extend Part IX provisions to Fifth Schedule areas, following the Bhuria Committee report. Article 243M exempted Scheduled Areas from Part IX, and Parliament could extend it with exceptions and modifications. Key features: the state legislation must follow the customary law, social and religious practices, and traditional management practices of community resources. A village is usually a habitation or group of habitations comprising a community and managing its affairs by traditions and customs. Every village has a Gram Sabha. Gram Sabha powers include: approving plans and programmes before the Panchayat implements them; identifying beneficiaries; certifying fund use; being consulted before land acquisition for development projects and resettlement; planning and managing minor water bodies; granting prospecting licences or mining leases for minor minerals; ownership of minor forest produce; power to prevent alienation of tribal land and restore unlawfully alienated land; regulating sale and consumption of intoxicants; managing village markets; controlling money lending; and controlling institutions and functionaries in social sectors and tribal sub-plans. Reservation: seats in every Panchayat are reserved for Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population, with at least half of the seats for STs, and all Chairperson posts reserved for STs. The state Governor can nominate persons of tribes lacking representation in intermediate or district Panchayats, up to one-tenth of the total. Related laws: Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises forest dwellers' rights with the Gram Sabha as the initiating authority, and the Samatha judgment (1997) concerned mining in Scheduled Areas. The Niyamgiri case (2013) upheld Gram Sabha consent in the Vedanta bauxite matter. Related questions could ask about Sixth Schedule autonomous councils, the Bhuria Committee and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.

question: Which one of the following countries is not a member of WTO?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The World Trade Organization (WTO) came into being on 1 January 1995 as the successor to GATT (1947), following the Uruguay Round (1986-94) and the Marrakesh Agreement (15 April 1994). It is headquartered in Geneva and has about 164-166 members (Liberia and Yemen joined in 2016; Comoros and Timor-Leste in 2024). Japan was a founding member in 1995. China joined on 11 December 2001 after about 15 years of negotiation. Russia became the 156th member on 22 August 2012 after 18 years of talks. Iran applied to join GATT in 1996, and its accession working party was only established in 2005. Because of political objections, mainly from the US, it is still an observer and not a full member. Observer governments must begin accession talks within five years of getting observer status. Elimination logic: the three major economies Japan, China and Russia are well-known members, so the remaining country, Iran, must be the non-member. Decisions in the WTO are generally taken by consensus, which is why the accession of politically sensitive countries is slow.
explanations: Incorrect: Japan is a founding member of the WTO (since 1 January 1995) and had been a GATT member since 1955.
Incorrect: China is a WTO member, having joined on 11 December 2001 as the 143rd member.
Correct: Iran is not a WTO member. It holds observer status and its accession is still pending.
Incorrect: Russia has been a WTO member since 22 August 2012, after 18 years of negotiations.
keyfact: Iran is not a WTO member (observer only), while Japan (1995), China (2001) and Russia (2012) are.
option_notes: Japan: the world's third or fourth largest economy, a GATT member from 1955 and a WTO founding member from 1995. It is a key participant in the trade rules system and in regional pacts such as CPTPP and RCEP.

China: became the 143rd WTO member on 11 December 2001 after a protocol of accession that required major tariff cuts and market opening. It is the largest merchandise exporter and often appears in WTO disputes both as complainant and respondent.

Iran: it applied for GATT membership in 1996. A WTO working party was set up in 2005 after repeated US blocking. It has observer status and is not a member. Sanctions and political issues complicate its accession.
Russia: it joined as the 156th member on 22 August 2012 after the longest negotiation of any major economy. It has since faced trade restrictions and disputes, but remains a WTO member.
related: WTO came into existence on 1 January 1995 and replaced GATT.
The WTO is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland.
The Director-General is Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, in office since March 2021.
The Trade Facilitation Agreement came out of the Bali Ministerial (2013) and entered into force in February 2017.
China joined the WTO in 2001; Russia in 2012.
The WTO Appellate Body has been non-functional since December 2019.
Iran, Iraq and Ethiopia have been observers seeking accession.
summary: The answer is (c) Iran (OCR'd as 'Tran'). Iran is not a WTO member; it has only observer status and its accession application has been pending for decades. Japan (WTO founding member, 1 Jan 1995), China (11 Dec 2001) and Russia (22 Aug 2012) are all members.
topic_notes: The WTO is the only global international organisation dealing with the rules of trade between nations. It was established under the Marrakesh Agreement, signed 15 April 1994, and began operating on 1 January 1995. It replaced GATT, which had operated since 1948 as a provisional agreement. Its headquarters are in Geneva, Switzerland. The highest decision-making body is the Ministerial Conference, which meets at least once every two years. The General Council runs the WTO day to day. The WTO's main agreements are GATT (goods), GATS (services) and TRIPS (intellectual property). It also has the Agreement on Agriculture, TRIMS, SPS, TBT and the Anti-dumping agreement. The Dispute Settlement Body administers disputes, and its Appellate Body has been non-functional since December 2019 because the US has blocked appointments. The Director-General is Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala of Nigeria, the first woman and first African in the role, who has served since 1 March 2021. India is a founding member of both GATT and the WTO. Ministerial conferences: Singapore 1996, Doha 2001 (Doha Development Agenda), Cancun 2003, Hong Kong 2005, Bali 2013 (Trade Facilitation Agreement), Nairobi 2015, Buenos Aires 2017, Geneva 2022, Abu Dhabi 2024 (MC13). Other states with observer status include Iraq, Ethiopia, Libya and Turkmenistan, though some have since progressed. Decisions are taken by consensus. Concepts to remember are most-favoured-nation (MFN), national treatment, the Green Box, Amber Box and Blue Box subsidies, and the Peace Clause.

ocr: A StandUp enterprise can be established in farming sector se 2 manufacturing sector 3. service sector 4 trading sector Select the correct answer using the code given below. 1, 2 and 4 (a) 1, 3 and 4 (b) 1, 2 and 3 (c) (a) 2,3 and 4
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Stand-Up India was launched on 5 April 2016 to promote entrepreneurship among Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST) and women. It facilitates bank loans between Rs 10 lakh and Rs 1 crore per bank branch to at least one SC/ST borrower and at least one woman borrower, for setting up a greenfield enterprise. Greenfield means the first-time venture of the beneficiary. The enterprise may be in manufacturing, services or the trading sector, and later the activities allied to agriculture were also brought in (fisheries, poultry, dairy, agri-allied activities), but plain farming/crop cultivation is not covered. In a non-individual enterprise, at least 51% of shareholding and controlling stake must be held by an SC/ST or woman entrepreneur. Loan tenure is up to 7 years with a moratorium of up to 18 months; it comprises a composite loan (term loan plus working capital) with up to 75% of project cost covered. It is implemented by SIDBI with a Stand-Up India portal and through Scheduled Commercial Banks. Elimination logic: the original scheme excluded 'farming', so any option containing 1 (a, b, c) fails. Only (d) lists manufacturing, services and trading.
explanations: (a) Wrong: includes farming (1), which is not covered, though 2 and 4 are right.
(b) Wrong: includes farming (1), even though 3 and 4 are valid sectors.
(c) Wrong: includes farming (1) and omits trading (4), so it is doubly incorrect.
(d) Correct: manufacturing, services and trading are the three eligible sectors; farming is excluded.
keyfact: Stand-Up India (5 April 2016): Rs 10 lakh–1 crore loans for SC/ST and women greenfield enterprises in manufacturing, services and trading; not farming.
option_notes: Option (a), 1, 2 and 4: the combination would include farming, manufacturing and trading. Farming is outside Stand-Up India, which targets non-farm greenfield enterprises. Manufacturing and trading are valid. Farm support is delivered instead through schemes like Kisan Credit Card (introduced 1998), PM-KISAN (2019, Rs 6,000 a year in three installments) and NABARD refinance. Agri-allied activities such as dairy and poultry were later brought under Stand-Up India, but not crop farming.

Option (b), 1, 3 and 4: it pairs farming with services and trading. Services (salons, repair shops, clinics) and trading (retail and wholesale) are valid sectors under Stand-Up India, but farming is not. The scheme provides Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore loans, for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs. It was launched on 5 April 2016 by PM Narendra Modi and implemented with SIDBI as the main agency, covering all Scheduled Commercial Bank branches.

Option (c), 1, 2 and 3: it includes farming, manufacturing and services but leaves out trading. Trading is actually an eligible sector, and farming is not. Stand-Up India focuses on first-time (greenfield) entrepreneurs, with composite loans covering term loan and working capital. Up to 75% of project cost is covered by the loan, and borrowers contribute at least 10% as their own share, with the remainder possible from other schemes.

Option (d), 2, 3 and 4: manufacturing, services and trading, the correct answer. Stand-Up India (5 April 2016) funds greenfield enterprises by SC/ST and women entrepreneurs with loans of Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore. Tenure is up to 7 years with up to 18 months moratorium. The Stand-Up India portal (standupmitra.in) provides handholding support, and credit is backed by the CGFSI managed by NCGTC.
related: Stand-Up India was launched on 5 April 2016.
Loan range under Stand-Up India: Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore.
Target group: SC/ST and women entrepreneurs.
Greenfield means the first-time venture of the beneficiary in manufacturing, services or trading.
SIDBI is the main implementing agency of the scheme.
Credit Guarantee Fund for Stand-Up India (CGFSI) is managed by NCGTC.
Start-up India was launched on 16 January 2016.
PM Mudra Yojana loan categories are Shishu, Kishor and Tarun.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Farming/crop cultivation is not an eligible activity under Stand-Up India. Stand-Up India is aimed at non-farm enterprises; later extension covered only agri-allied activities such as fisheries, poultry, dairy and not primary farming. Related farm credit comes via Kisan Credit Card, PM-KISAN and NABARD schemes rather than this scheme. The scheme itself was announced in Budget 2015-16 and launched on 5 April 2016, with its portal managed by SIDBI.

2 — Correct: Manufacturing is an eligible sector. Stand-Up India supports greenfield manufacturing units, such as small factories, food processing and textile units, owned by SC/ST or women entrepreneurs. Loans range from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore, with repayment up to 7 years. Bank branches must lend to at least one SC/ST and one woman borrower. Refinance is provided by SIDBI, with Rs 10,000 crore initial refinance window.

3 — Correct: The service sector is eligible. Service ventures such as salons, clinics, repair shops, transport services, and IT or consultancy units can be financed under the scheme. The borrower must be above 18 years, and in the case of non-individual enterprises 51% shareholding and controlling stake must be held by SC/ST or women. Borrowers should not be defaulters to any bank or financial institution. Credit guarantee is available via the Credit Guarantee Fund for Stand-Up India (CGFSI) managed by NCGTC.

4 — Correct: The trading sector was added when the scheme was finalised, so retail and wholesale trading enterprises are eligible. This differs from some other schemes like PM Mudra, which cover non-farm business activities broadly. The scheme operates through all Scheduled Commercial Bank branches, and applications may be made via the Stand-Up Mitra portal, directly at branches, or through the Lead District Manager. Margin money is 25% of the project cost, which can be combined with central or state schemes.
summary: The answer is (d) 2, 3 and 4. Under the Stand-Up India scheme (launched 5 April 2016), loans are for greenfield enterprises in manufacturing, services or the trading sector. Farming (agriculture) is not covered, so statement 1 is wrong.
topic_notes: Stand-Up India Scheme: announced in Budget 2015-16, launched on 5 April 2016 (Noida) by PM Narendra Modi, with the aim of promoting entrepreneurship among SC/ST and women. It offers bank loans between Rs 10 lakh and Rs 1 crore for setting up greenfield enterprises in manufacturing, services or the trading sector. Activities allied to agriculture were later added (such as fisheries, poultry, dairy, agro-processing), but not plain crop farming. Eligibility: SC/ST and/or women entrepreneurs above 18 years; in non-individual enterprises at least 51% shareholding and controlling stake must be held by SC/ST or women; the borrower must not be in default to any bank or financial institution. Loan structure: composite loan covering term loan and working capital, up to 75% of project cost, repayment up to 7 years with a moratorium of up to 18 months, and the borrower contributes at least 10% of project cost. Institutions: SIDBI is the main implementing agency and operates the Stand-Up India portal (Stand-Up Mitra); refinance window of Rs 10,000 crore initially; Credit Guarantee Fund for Stand-Up India (CGFSI) is managed by NCGTC; Department of Financial Services in the Ministry of Finance oversees it. Each bank branch is expected to give at least one loan to an SC/ST borrower and one to a woman borrower. The scheme was extended up to 2025. Related schemes UPSC may ask: Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana (April 2015; Shishu up to Rs 50,000, Kishor Rs 50,000 to 5 lakh, Tarun Rs 5 lakh to 10 lakh), Start-up India (16 January 2016), Make in India (2014), PMEGP (2008), and Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme. Possible angles: the target beneficiaries, loan limits, the definition of greenfield, and the agencies involved.

question:
Who among the following were conferred with Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna Award for the year 2016?
1. Jitu Rai
2. Dipa Karmakar
3. P.
V. Sindhu
4. Sakshi Malik Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna, instituted in 1991-92, is India's highest sporting honour, given by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports for the most spectacular and outstanding performance in the field of sports over a four-year period, usually at international level. The first recipient was chess player Viswanathan Anand (1991-92). For 2016, the awards were announced in August 2016 after the Rio Olympics: Sindhu won badminton silver, Sakshi Malik won wrestling bronze (57 kg), Dipa Karmakar finished fourth in vaulting after being the first Indian woman gymnast to qualify for the Olympics, and Jitu Rai was the shooter who won medals at the Commonwealth Games and Asian Games and the 2014 World Cup. The award was presented on 29 August 2016 (National Sports Day) by President Pranab Mukherjee. Elimination logic: once a student knows that Sindhu and Sakshi are certain, and that Dipa and Jitu were also named, only option (d) fits. The award carried Rs 7.5 lakh cash at that time, later raised to Rs 25 lakh. It was renamed Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna in August 2021.
explanations: Incorrect: it leaves out Jitu Rai and Sakshi Malik, both of whom were awarded the Khel Ratna in 2016.
Incorrect: it leaves out Jitu Rai, who also received the award in 2016 along with the other three.
Incorrect: it names only Jitu Rai and Sakshi Malik and omits Dipa Karmakar and P. V. Sindhu, who also got the award.
Correct: all four, Jitu Rai, Dipa Karmakar, P. V. Sindhu and Sakshi Malik, were conferred the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna for 2016.
keyfact: Khel Ratna 2016: Sindhu, Sakshi Malik, Dipa Karmakar and Jitu Rai, all four jointly honoured after Rio 2016.
option_notes: Dipa Karmakar and P. V. Sindhu: Dipa is a gymnast from Tripura who finished fourth in vault at Rio 2016 with the Produnova vault. Sindhu is a badminton player who won Olympic silver at Rio 2016 and the World Championship gold in 2019. Both were Khel Ratna recipients in 2016, but this option is incomplete because it omits two other awardees.

Dipa Karmakar, Sindhu and Sakshi Malik: these three were the Rio 2016 women stars. Dipa was fourth in vault, Sindhu won silver, and Sakshi won bronze in wrestling, the first Indian woman wrestler to win an Olympic medal. All three received the Khel Ratna, but the option omits shooter Jitu Rai, who also got it.

Jitu Rai and Sakshi Malik: Jitu Rai is an Army shooter with Commonwealth and Asian Games gold in 2014, and Sakshi Malik is a wrestler from Haryana who won Rio 2016 bronze. Both were awardees in 2016, but the option wrongly excludes Dipa Karmakar and P. V. Sindhu.

All four: Jitu Rai, Dipa Karmakar, P. V. Sindhu and Sakshi Malik were jointly honoured. The announcement came in August 2016 and the awards were presented on 29 August 2016, National Sports Day, which is the birthday of hockey legend Major Dhyan Chand. This is the official correct answer.
related: Khel Ratna was instituted in 1991-92; first recipient was Viswanathan Anand.
Renamed Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna in August 2021.
Sakshi Malik was the first Indian woman wrestler to win an Olympic medal (Rio 2016 bronze).
Dipa Karmakar was the first Indian woman gymnast to compete at the Olympics.
Sindhu won the 2019 BWF World Championship, the first Indian to do so.
National Sports Day is on 29 August, the birthday of Major Dhyan Chand.
Arjuna Award was instituted in 1961; Dronacharya Award in 1985.
Sachin Tendulkar was the first cricketer to receive the Khel Ratna (1997-98).
statements: 1 — Correct: Jitu Rai was among the four 2016 Khel Ratna recipients. Jitu Rai is a shooter in the 10m air pistol and 50m pistol events, born in Nepal and serving in the Indian Army (Gorkha Rifles). He won gold at the 2014 Commonwealth Games (Glasgow) in 50m pistol, gold at the 2014 Asian Games (Incheon) and 2014 World Cup gold in Changwon. He competed at Rio 2016 without a medal. He later won gold in the 2018 Commonwealth Games and 2018 Asian Games, and also received the Arjuna Award (2014).

2 — Correct: Dipa Karmakar received the Khel Ratna for 2016. She is a gymnast from Tripura, the first Indian woman gymnast to qualify for and compete in the Olympics (Rio 2016). She finished fourth in the vault final, missing a bronze by 0.15 points. She performed the Produnova vault, called the 'vault of death'. She won bronze at the 2014 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, the first Indian woman gymnast to win a medal there, and received the Arjuna Award in 2015 and Padma Shri in 2017.

3 — Correct: P. V. Sindhu was a 2016 Khel Ratna recipient. Pusarla Venkata Sindhu, a badminton player from Hyderabad, won silver at Rio 2016 in women's singles, losing to Carolina Marin of Spain. She became the youngest Indian Olympic medallist in an individual event at that time. She won the 2019 BWF World Championships gold in Basel, the first Indian to do so, and bronze at Tokyo 2020. She received the Arjuna Award (2013), Padma Shri (2015), and Padma Bhushan (2020).

4 — Correct: Sakshi Malik was a 2016 Khel Ratna recipient. A wrestler from Rohtak, Haryana, she won bronze in the 58 kg freestyle category at Rio 2016, becoming the first Indian woman wrestler to win an Olympic medal. She also won bronze at the 2014 Commonwealth Games and silver at the 2014 Dave Schultz Memorial International. She received the Padma Shri in 2017 and later won gold at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham.
summary: The answer is (d): all four, Jitu Rai, Dipa Karmakar, P. V. Sindhu and Sakshi Malik, received the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna for 2016. It was a rare year in which four sportspersons shared the award after the Rio Olympics 2016.
topic_notes: The Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna was instituted in 1991-92 and is India's highest sporting honour. Viswanathan Anand was the first recipient. It is given by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports for spectacular and outstanding performance over the preceding four-year Olympic cycle. The award consists of a medal, a certificate and a cash prize, which was Rs 7.5 lakh in 2016 and raised to Rs 25 lakh in 2018. It was renamed Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna in August 2021. Sachin Tendulkar was the first cricketer to receive it (1997-98), and Dhyan Chand's birthday, 29 August, is observed as National Sports Day. Awards are presented by the President at Rashtrapati Bhavan, though in some years virtually. Other national sports awards include the Arjuna Award (instituted 1961, for consistent outstanding performance over four years), Dronacharya Award (1985, for coaches), Dhyan Chand Award (2002, for lifetime achievement), and the Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (MAKA) Trophy for the overall best-performing university. The Rashtriya Khel Protsahan Puruskar recognises corporate and NGO support for sport. In 2016 Rio produced two medals for India: Sindhu silver and Sakshi bronze. Other Khel Ratna winners include Leander Paes, Karnam Malleswari, Abhinav Bindra, Mary Kom, Sushil Kumar, Vijender Singh, Saina Nehwal, Mariyappan Thangavelu and Devendra Jhajharia (2017), Virat Kohli and Mirabai Chanu (2018), Neeraj Chopra (2021). Mithali Raj and Ravichandran Ashwin were honoured in 2021. Questions often ask about the first recipient, instituting year, sports of awardees and the renaming.

question:
ISRO in August 2016 successfully test launched Supersonic Combustion Ramjet (Scramjet) Engine. Which of the following statements with regard to Scramjet Engine is/are correct?
1. It can efficiently operate both in subsonic and_— supersonic combustor modes.
2. India is the first country to demonstrate the flight testing of a Scramjet Engine. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Computers
detail: A scramjet (Supersonic Combustion Ramjet) is an air-breathing engine that burns fuel in a supersonic airflow. It has no moving compressor parts, because the vehicle's high speed compresses the intake air. Unlike a rocket, it takes oxygen from the atmosphere and does not carry an oxidiser, which lowers lift-off mass and cost. ISRO's Scramjet Engine Technology Demonstrator was launched on August 28, 2016 from Sriharikota, riding on a two-stage solid rocket booster, the Advanced Technology Vehicle (ATV), which is based on the RH-560 sounding rocket. It was flown to about 20 km altitude, where the scramjet ignited for about 5 seconds at roughly Mach 6. ISRO's design used hydrogen fuel and atmospheric oxygen, and its engine could operate in both subsonic and supersonic combustion modes. Elimination logic: statement 2 is a trap, because ISRO claimed to be the fourth country to demonstrate flight testing of a scramjet engine (after the USA, Russia and the EU), not the first. Since statement 2 fails, options (b), (c) and (d) are eliminated, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is true, since the engine is designed for both subsonic and supersonic combustion modes, and statement 2 is false, so only 1 is correct.
Wrong: statement 2 is false because India was not the first country to flight-test a scramjet; the USA, Russia and the EU had done so earlier.
Wrong: this would need statement 2 to be true, but it is not the case that India was first.
Wrong: statement 1 is correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: ISRO's scramjet test (28 Aug 2016, ATV, ~Mach 6, ~20 km) was dual-mode, but India was the fourth country to do it, not the first.
option_notes: Statement 1 only: the official answer. It reflects ISRO's dual-mode scramjet, which can burn fuel in both subsonic and supersonic combustion modes. The August 2016 test from Sriharikota used the ATV booster, based on the RH-560 sounding rocket. The engine burned hydrogen using atmospheric oxygen for about 5 seconds at Mach 6, at an altitude of about 20 km. It is a step towards reusable launch vehicles and cheaper access to space.

Statement 2 only: this would mean India was the first to flight-test a scramjet, which is false. The US (NASA X-43A reached about Mach 9.6 in 2004), Russia and the EU carried out earlier tests. ISRO said India was fourth. The claim is a typical 'first in the world' trap in UPSC current affairs questions, and ISRO's actual achievement is a successful first flight of its own design.

Both 1 and 2: this is incorrect because statement 2 is false. Statement 1 on dual-mode combustion is accurate, but India's claim was to be the fourth country, not the first, to demonstrate scramjet flight testing. Students should check superlatives such as 'first' and 'only' carefully in science and technology questions.

Neither 1 nor 2: this is incorrect because statement 1 is accurate. ISRO's scramjet engine was described as capable of operating in both subsonic and supersonic combustion modes. Rejecting both statements would require statement 1 to be false, which contradicts ISRO's technical description of the engine.
related: ISRO's scramjet test took place on August 28, 2016 from Sriharikota using the ATV (RH-560 based).
India described itself as the fourth country to demonstrate scramjet flight testing, after the USA, Russia and the EU.
Scramjet burns hydrogen with atmospheric oxygen, so no onboard oxidiser is needed.
RLV-TD HEX flight took place on May 23, 2016.
DRDO tested the HSTDV scramjet demonstrator in September 2020 at Mach 6.
Hypersonic speed means above Mach 5.
Scramjets cannot start from rest and need a booster to reach operating speed.
statements: 1 — Correct: ISRO's scramjet design supports both subsonic and supersonic combustion modes. A scramjet is an air-breathing engine that burns hydrogen with atmospheric oxygen, so it carries no oxidiser. The test flew on the ATV, a solid booster derived from the RH-560 sounding rocket. Ignition occurred at about 20 km altitude and Mach 6 for roughly 5 seconds. The engine is meant to cut launch costs and later support reusable launch vehicles (RLV-TD) and hypersonic flight.

2 — Incorrect: India was not the first country to flight-test a scramjet. ISRO described itself as the fourth country to do so, after the USA (NASA X-43A, 2004), Russia and the European Union. The August 28, 2016 test from Sriharikota was the first-ever flight test of ISRO's own scramjet engine. The ATV-D01 mission lasted about 300 seconds in total. ISRO's later scramjet work in 2016 sat alongside the RLV-TD test in May 2016. A second ATV scramjet test was planned later.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. ISRO's August 28, 2016 scramjet test used an engine designed to operate in both subsonic and supersonic combustion modes, but India was not the first country to flight-test a scramjet, as the USA, Russia and others had done so earlier.
topic_notes: Scramjet technology is central to hypersonic flight, which means speeds above Mach 5. A ramjet compresses incoming air using the vehicle's forward speed and burns fuel in subsonic airflow. A scramjet extends this by burning fuel in supersonic airflow and works at higher Mach numbers. Neither works from a standstill, so both need a booster to reach operating speed. ISRO's test on August 28, 2016 used the Advanced Technology Vehicle (ATV), a two-stage solid rocket based on the RH-560 sounding rocket, launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota. The scramjet engines sat on the second stage. The vehicle flew to about 20 km, and the engine fired for about 5 seconds at Mach 6. ISRO used hydrogen as fuel and atmospheric oxygen as the oxidiser, so no oxidiser is carried, which cuts lift-off mass and cost. ISRO's scramjet work also uses a titanium alloy and special heat-resistant materials. ISRO says the technology could contribute to low-cost reusable launch vehicles, including the Reusable Launch Vehicle Technology Demonstrator (RLV-TD), which had its first hypersonic flight experiment (HEX) on May 23, 2016. Countries active in scramjet research include the USA (NASA X-43A, X-51A), Russia, China, Japan, Australia (HIFiRE) and the EU. India's DRDO also developed a Hypersonic Technology Demonstrator Vehicle (HSTDV), tested in September 2020 at Mach 6 using a scramjet. Related UPSC angles include the differences between ramjet, scramjet, turbojet, cryogenic and semi-cryogenic engines, as well as ISRO's launch vehicles PSLV, GSLV and GSLV Mk III (LVM3).

question:
Startup Hubs are agreed to be set up in
1. ITs
2. IISERs
3. NITs
4. Central Universities Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Startup India Action Plan, launched by PM Narendra Modi on 16 January 2016, had three pillars: Simplification and Handholding, Funding Support and Incentives, and Industry-Academia Partnership and Incubation. Under the third pillar, the plan announced the setting up of 35 new incubators/Atal Incubation Centres in institutions, 31 innovation centres at national institutes, 7 new research parks (modelled on the IIT Madras Research Park) and 5 new Bio-clusters. It also stated that Startup hubs/centres would be set up in premier institutions such as IITs, IISERs and NITs, with the aim of nurturing innovation. The question's list draws on this. The question therefore tests whether you recall the institutions named: IITs, IISERs, NITs. Elimination logic: since the official answer includes 1, 2 and 3, options (b), (c) and (d) are wrong because each either omits IISERs or includes Central Universities. Statement 2 (IISERs) is the key discriminator: only option (a) includes it, so a student sure about IISERs can select (a) directly.
explanations: Correct: it lists IITs, IISERs and NITs, the three institution types in the Startup India plan for hubs.
Wrong: it omits NITs and IISERs and wrongly includes Central Universities.
Wrong: it excludes IITs and IISERs, and includes Central Universities, which are not in the official list.
Wrong: it leaves out IISERs and adds Central Universities, so it does not match the official key.
keyfact: Startup India Action Plan (16 Jan 2016): startup hubs in IITs, IISERs and NITs, not Central Universities.
option_notes: Option (a) 1, 2 and 3: IITs, IISERs and NITs are the premier technical and science institutions named for Startup Hubs under the Startup India Action Plan of 16 January 2016. Together they have strong research ecosystems. IITs number 23, NITs 31, and there are seven IISERs. They are institutes of national importance, so the plan used their infrastructure for incubation, research parks and mentoring of young entrepreneurs.

Option (b) 1 and 4 only: This combines IITs with Central Universities. IITs are valid, but Central Universities are not named, and it leaves out IISERs and NITs. Central Universities are created through Acts of Parliament; there are over 50, and the UGC acts as the main funding body. They are generally not the target institutions for the hubs mentioned here.

Option (c) 3 and 4 only: This pairs NITs with Central Universities. NITs are 31 institutes of national importance under the NIT Act 2007, but the option omits IITs and IISERs, so it is incomplete. Central Universities are not included, so the option is wrong. Remember that the NITs were formerly Regional Engineering Colleges, converted in stages from 2002 onwards.

Option (d) 1, 3 and 4: This takes IITs and NITs, both correct, but wrongly adds Central Universities and omits IISERs. The IISERs, at Pune, Kolkata, Mohali, Bhopal, Thiruvananthapuram, Tirupati and Berhampur, are science research institutions and were named in the plan. Hence the option fails because of both an omission and an inclusion.
related: Startup India Action Plan was launched on 16 January 2016.
Fund of Funds for Startups has a corpus of Rs 10,000 crore, managed by SIDBI.
Atal Innovation Mission is under NITI Aayog.
Stand-Up India was launched in April 2016 for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs.
DPIIT under the Commerce Ministry is the nodal body for Startup India.
National Startup Day is observed on 16 January.
Section 80-IAC gives income tax exemption to eligible startups for three consecutive years.
statements: 1 — Correct: IITs were named among the premier institutions for Startup Hubs under the Startup India Action Plan. The Indian Institutes of Technology are institutes of national importance under the IIT Act 1961 (as amended). There are now 23 IITs. Several, such as IIT Madras, with its Research Park and incubation cell, and IIT Bombay (SINE), are leading incubators in India. They are central to the industry-academia pillar of Startup India.

2 — Correct: IISERs were included in the institutions chosen for hubs. The Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research are autonomous institutes for science education and research, set up from 2006 with the first at Pune and Kolkata, and later Mohali, Bhopal, Thiruvananthapuram, Tirupati and Berhampur. They were declared institutes of national importance in 2012 and are funded by the Ministry of Education.

3 — Correct: NITs were named in the action plan for startup hubs. The National Institutes of Technology number 31, and are institutes of national importance under the NIT Act 2007. The former Regional Engineering Colleges were upgraded to NITs. They include Tiruchirappalli, Warangal, Surathkal, Rourkela and others. Many now host technology business incubators supported by the Department of Science and Technology.

4 — Incorrect: Central Universities were not listed as host institutions for the hubs in the official keyed answer. Central Universities are established by Acts of Parliament and funded by the UGC and the Ministry of Education, for example Delhi University, BHU and JNU. Their role in startup promotion is general and not part of this specific list.
summary: The official answer is (a) 1, 2 and 3. Under the Startup India Action Plan (January 2016), Startup India Hubs/incubators were to be set up in the IITs, IISERs and NITs (and similar premier institutions), not in Central Universities as such. Hence statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct and 4 is left out.
topic_notes: Startup India was announced by PM Modi on 15 August 2015 and the Action Plan was launched on 16 January 2016. It is run by DPIIT (Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, formerly DIPP) under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The plan rests on three pillars: simplification and handholding; funding support and incentives; and industry-academia partnership and incubation. Key features: self-certification compliance for labour and environmental laws for three to five years; a startup helpline and mobile app; a single-window clearance portal; a 80% rebate on patent filing fees; faster exit within 90 days under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code; and a Fund of Funds for Startups with a corpus of Rs 10,000 crore, managed by SIDBI. Tax benefits include a three-year income tax holiday out of ten years for eligible startups (Section 80-IAC), and exemption from capital gains on investment in a fund of funds. DPIIT recognition requires the entity to be incorporated as a private limited company, a registered partnership or an LLP, less than ten years old (extended later), with turnover not above Rs 100 crore in any financial year, and working on innovation. Other related initiatives: Atal Innovation Mission (NITI Aayog) with Atal Incubation Centres and Atal Tinkering Labs; Stand-Up India (April 2016) for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs, with bank loans of Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore; MUDRA Yojana (April 2015); Make in India (September 2014); and the Credit Guarantee Fund for Startups. National Startup Day is observed on 16 January. Likely UPSC angles: the ministry responsible, the fund corpus, definition criteria, tax benefits and the names of the pillars.

question: StandUp India Programme envisages each bank branch to give loan between * 10 lakh to * 100 lakh 1. to at least one SC/ST borrower 2. to at least one woman borrower 3. to at least one rural unemployed youth borrower Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Stand-Up India was announced in the Budget speech of 2015-16 and launched on 5 April 2016 by PM Narendra Modi at Noida. Its aim is to promote entrepreneurship among Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women. It facilitates bank loans between Rs 10 lakh and Rs 1 crore for setting up a greenfield enterprise in manufacturing, services, the trading sector (added later) or agri-allied activities. Every bank branch (scheduled commercial bank) must lend to at least one SC or ST borrower and at least one woman borrower. For non-individual enterprises, at least 51% of shareholding and controlling stake must be held by an SC/ST or woman entrepreneur. The borrower must be 18 or above and must not be in default to any bank or financial institution. The loan is a composite loan (term loan plus working capital) covering 75% of the project cost, repayable up to 7 years with a maximum moratorium of 18 months. The scheme is run through SIDBI, with a portal (standupmitra.in) and a Credit Guarantee Fund (CGFSIL, via NCGTC). Elimination: statement 3 is not a target category, so (b) and (c) go out. Statement 2 is correct, so (a) goes out, leaving (d).
explanations: Wrong: statement 2 is also correct, so 'statement 1 only' is incomplete.
Wrong: statement 3 (rural unemployed youth) is not a Stand-Up India target, and statement 1 is correct but missing from this option.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is not part of the scheme, and omits statement 2, which is correct.
Correct: the scheme covers at least one SC/ST borrower and one woman borrower per bank branch, as per the official answer.
keyfact: Stand-Up India (5 April 2016): Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore loan per bank branch to at least one SC/ST and one woman borrower for greenfield enterprises.
option_notes: Statement 1 only: SC/ST borrowers are indeed one of the scheme's two target groups, but the option leaves out women. Stand-Up India (April 2016) lends Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore for greenfield enterprises and is administered via SIDBI. It is not the right answer because it omits a valid statement.

Statements 2 and 3: women borrowers are valid, but 'rural unemployed youth' is not a category. Rural youth are served by PMEGP, DDU-GKY (skilling) and RSETIs. Mixing in statement 3 makes this option wrong, and it omits the SC/ST group.

Statements 1 and 3: SC/ST is a valid category, but rural unemployed youth is not a Stand-Up India target. Related youth-focused schemes include PMEGP (KVIC, subsidy 15-35%), Skill India and Mudra Yojana (Shishu, Kishor, Tarun loans up to Rs 10 lakh).

Statements 1 and 2: the official answer. Stand-Up India requires each scheduled commercial bank branch to lend to at least one SC/ST borrower and one woman borrower. The loan size is Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore for a first-time venture in manufacturing, services, trading or agri-allied activities, with the scheme administered through SIDBI and NCGTC credit guarantee.
related: Stand-Up India was launched on 5 April 2016 at Noida.
Loan range under Stand-Up India: Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore.
Stand-Up India is implemented through SIDBI; the credit guarantee is via NCGTC (CGFSIL).
Start-up India was launched on 16 January 2016.
Mudra Yojana (PMMY) was launched on 8 April 2015, with Shishu, Kishor and Tarun categories.
PMEGP is implemented by KVIC under the Ministry of MSME.
Stand-Up India requires 51% SC/ST or women stake in non-individual enterprises.
statements: 1 — Correct: Each bank branch is expected to lend to at least one SC/ST borrower. Stand-Up India was launched on 5 April 2016 and targets loans of Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore for greenfield enterprises. Eligible sectors are manufacturing, services, trading and agri-allied activities. Borrowers must be 18 or above and not in default to any bank. For non-individual units, 51% of shareholding and control must rest with SC/ST or women. The loan covers up to 75% of project cost, with repayment up to 7 years and an 18-month moratorium. SIDBI is the lead agency, and the scheme was extended to 2025.

2 — Correct: Each bank branch is also expected to lend to at least one woman borrower. Women entrepreneurs are the second target group of the scheme, along with SC/ST. The loan is for a first-time (greenfield) venture. It can be applied for through the Stand-Up Mitra portal, a bank branch, or the Lead District Manager. Refinance support comes from SIDBI, with a Credit Guarantee Fund Trust (CGFSIL) managed by NCGTC providing a guarantee cover. Interest rates are capped at the lowest applicable rate of the bank for that category. Banks are expected to support roughly 2.5 lakh borrowers across about 1.25 lakh branches.

3 — Incorrect: Rural unemployed youth are not a separate Stand-Up India category. That focus belongs to other schemes such as PMEGP (Prime Minister's Employment Generation Programme), run through KVIC, and earlier schemes like SGSY and the Rural Self Employment Training Institutes (RSETIs). PMEGP offers a credit-linked subsidy of 15-35% for micro-enterprises and is aimed at traditional artisans and unemployed youth. Stand-Up India's focus is SC/ST/women irrespective of rural or urban location. Mixing up these schemes is a common UPSC trap.
summary: The correct answer is (d) 1 and 2. Under the Stand-Up India scheme (launched 5 April 2016), each bank branch is expected to give a loan of Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore to at least one SC/ST borrower and at least one woman borrower. Rural unemployed youth are not a targeted category, so statement 3 is wrong.
topic_notes: Stand-Up India was announced in the Union Budget 2015-16 and launched on 5 April 2016 by PM Modi. Its objective is to promote entrepreneurship among SC, ST and women through bank loans. Loan range is Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore for greenfield enterprises in manufacturing, services, trading and agri-allied activities. Each bank branch is expected to give at least one loan to an SC/ST borrower and one to a woman borrower. Non-individual enterprises must have at least 51% stake held by SC/ST or women. The borrower must be 18 or above and not a defaulter. The composite loan (term plus working capital) covers up to 75% of project cost, with repayment up to 7 years and a moratorium of up to 18 months. SIDBI is the principal agency and runs the Stand-Up Mitra portal. A Credit Guarantee Fund (CGFSIL) is managed by NCGTC. The scheme was extended up to 2025. Related schemes: PMMY (Mudra, April 2015) offers loans up to Rs 10 lakh under Shishu (up to 50,000), Kishor (50,000 to 5 lakh) and Tarun (5 to 10 lakh). Start-up India (January 2016) supports innovative start-ups with tax benefits and a Fund of Funds (Rs 10,000 crore) managed by SIDBI. PMEGP (2008) is a credit-linked subsidy scheme under the Ministry of MSME, implemented via KVIC. Other angles: Mahila Udyam Nidhi, Annapurna Scheme, Trade Related Entrepreneurship Assistance and Development (TREAD) for women, and NSFDC and NSTFDC for SC/ST finance.

question: In case of gold, revenue is recognized in the accounting period in which the gold is
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Under the general realisation principle, revenue is recognised when the risks and rewards of ownership pass to the buyer, normally at sale or delivery (AS-9 / Ind AS 18, now Ind AS 115). Exceptions exist for items such as precious metals and certain agricultural produce, where there is an immediate marketability at a quoted or fixed price, the selling effort is negligible, and the market is assured. In such cases revenue is recognised at the point of completion of production, i.e. when the gold is mined (or produced), under the 'production basis' or 'completion of production method'. Other exceptions to the point-of-sale rule include long-term construction contracts (percentage of completion method), instalment sales, hire purchase, and by-products. Elimination: (a) delivered and (b) sold apply to ordinary goods; (d) identified to be mined is mere discovery or exploration, with no production and no realisable asset, so no revenue can arise. Hence (c) is correct, as official answer confirms.
explanations: Incorrect: Delivery is the normal point for ordinary goods, but gold is an exception due to assured market and price.
Incorrect: Sale is the general rule, but for gold revenue is recognised on production, before any sale.
Correct: Gold has a ready market at an assured price, so revenue is recognised when it is mined (production basis).
Incorrect: Merely identifying or discovering a deposit gives no produced, marketable asset, so no revenue is recognised.
keyfact: Gold and precious metals: revenue is recognised at production (mining), not at sale or delivery.
option_notes: Delivery: the point at which possession and control pass to the buyer. Under AS-9 and Ind AS 18, revenue from sale of goods is generally recognised when significant risks and rewards of ownership transfer, usually on delivery. It applies to most manufactured and traded goods, but not to precious metals with assured markets, where earlier recognition is permitted.

Sale: the transfer of property in goods from seller to buyer for a price (Sale of Goods Act, 1930). Revenue on sale is the general realisation principle in accounting, recognised when the sale is complete and the amount is measurable and reasonably certain. Gold is an exception because recognition happens earlier, at production.

Mined: the point at which gold ore is extracted and produced.
