Independent directors must hold a maximum of two terms of five consecutive years each, with a cooling-off period of three years.
related: Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires financial statements to follow Schedule III.
Schedule II deals with the useful life of assets for depreciation (Section 123).
Schedule IV is the Code for Independent Directors.
Schedule V deals with managerial remuneration (Sections 196 and 197).
Schedule VII lists the CSR activities (Section 135).
Section 133 deals with notification of accounting standards; Section 132 constitutes NFRA.
Schedule III Division II applies to Ind AS companies; Division III applies to NBFCs under Ind AS.
Section 2(40) defines financial statement, and Section 2(41) defines financial year.
summary: The answer is (c) Schedule III. Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes the format (Division I, II and III) of the Balance Sheet and the Statement of Profit and Loss, as required by Section 129.
topic_notes: Financial statements under the Companies Act, 2013: Section 2(40) defines financial statement to include the balance sheet, the statement of profit and loss (income and expenditure for non-profit), the cash flow statement, the statement of changes in equity where applicable, and explanatory notes. Section 129 requires that statements give a true and fair view, comply with accounting standards notified under Section 133, and follow Schedule III. Section 129(3) requires consolidated financial statements if the company has subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures. Section 134 deals with the Board's report and approval of financial statements. Section 137 requires filing with the Registrar within 30 days of the AGM. Section 138 covers internal audit. Section 139 deals with the appointment of auditors. Section 143 covers auditor powers and duties. Section 133 empowers the Central Government to notify accounting standards in consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) (under Section 132). Ind AS were notified in 2015 and apply on a phased basis by net worth thresholds, such as 500 crore and above from 1 April 2016, and listed companies from 2017. Financial year is defined in Section 2(41) as the period ending 31 March, with the exceptions allowed by the Tribunal. The Schedule III general instructions provide that the rounding off of figures depends on turnover: below 100 crore (nearest hundreds, thousands, lakhs or millions, or decimals thereof), and 100 crore or more (nearest lakhs, millions, crores or decimals thereof). Other schedules often asked: Schedule V (managerial remuneration), Schedule VI (the 2013 Act: land for relevant provisions), Schedule VII (CSR activities), Schedule VIII (omitted in 2013 Act?), and Schedule XI (omitted).

question: In the absence of any provision in the partnership agreement, profits and losses are shared by the partners
options: in the ratio of the capital of partners
in the ratio of loans given by them to the partnership firm
in the ratio of the initial capital introduced by the partners
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 (in force from 1 October 1932) defines partnership in Section 4 as the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. Section 13 lays down the mutual rights and liabilities of partners subject to contract between them. Section 13(b) says a partner is entitled to share equally in the profits earned and shall contribute equally to the losses sustained by the firm. This default rule holds even if capital contributions are unequal, or if partners devote unequal time and skill. Hence the capital ratio (a) and initial capital ratio (d) are wrong, as the Act does not link profit sharing to capital. Loans given by partners (c) are not a basis either; under Section 13(d), a partner who advances money beyond his agreed capital for the firm's business is entitled to interest at 6 percent per annum, which is separate from profit sharing. Also remember: no interest on capital is payable unless agreed (Section 13(c)), and no remuneration is payable for taking part in the business unless agreed (Section 13(a)). Elimination logic: only equal sharing is the statutory default.
explanations: Incorrect: the Act does not tie default profit sharing to capital ratios; that applies only if the partners agree so (in the deed).
Correct: Section 13(b) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 provides for equal sharing of profits and losses when there is no agreement.
Incorrect: loans by partners earn interest at 6 percent p.a. under Section 13(d); they do not determine profit shares.
Incorrect: initial capital is not the default basis; the statutory rule is equality, not proportion to initial capital.
keyfact: Without agreement, partners share profits and losses equally (Section 13(b), Indian Partnership Act, 1932), regardless of capital.
option_notes: Capital ratio: A method of sharing profits in proportion to each partner's capital, used when partners agree to it in the deed. Common in firms where capital is the main contribution. It is not the legal default under the Indian Partnership Act. Under the Act, capital contributions do not alter the equal-sharing presumption. Capital may be fixed or fluctuating; fixed capital stays unchanged, while fluctuating capital changes with profits, drawings and losses.

Equally: This is the default rule under Section 13(b) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. Partners share profits equally and bear losses equally unless the partnership deed or a contract says otherwise. It applies irrespective of unequal capital, skill or time. The same default is applied in the dissolution context and under Section 48 for losses, which are met first from profits, then capital, then by partners in their profit-sharing ratio.

Ratio of loans: Partner loans are advances beyond agreed capital. Under Section 13(d), a partner who advances money for the firm's business is entitled to interest at 6 percent per annum. On dissolution (Section 48), partner loans are repaid before partner capital, after outside creditors. Loans never determine profit shares and the loan ratio is not a statutory basis for sharing.

Initial capital ratio: A basis some firms may agree upon, but not a statutory default. The Act is silent on any link between initial capital and profit shares. Initial capital is the amount contributed at the firm's formation; subsequent additions or withdrawals are separate. Only an express or implied agreement can make profits follow initial capital proportions.
related: Section 13(b) Partnership Act: equal sharing of profits and losses by default.
Section 13(d): 6 percent interest on partner's advances beyond capital.
No interest on capital is allowed unless agreed (Section 13(c)).
Section 4 defines partnership; Section 5 says it arises from contract, not status.
Registration of firm is optional under Section 58; unregistered firm faces Section 69 disabilities.
Section 48: losses on dissolution are paid first from profits, then capital, then by partners in profit-sharing ratio.
Maximum partners: 50 under Companies Act, 2013 (Section 464).
LLP Act, 2008 created Limited Liability Partnerships as separate legal entities.
summary: The answer is (b) equally. Under Section 13(b) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, in the absence of any contract to the contrary, partners share profits equally and must also bear losses equally, irrespective of the capital each has contributed.
topic_notes: The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 governs partnerships in India, previously part of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Chapter XI, repealed). Section 4 defines partnership; Section 5 says partnership arises from contract, not status; Section 6 explains the mode of determining existence of partnership. Maximum partners: 50 under Section 464 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014 (earlier 10 for banking and 20 for other business). Minimum is 2. Registration of a firm is optional (Section 58), but an unregistered firm suffers disabilities under Section 69, such as inability to sue third parties or to enforce rights from the contract. Section 9 imposes the duty of utmost good faith; Section 10 duty to render true accounts; Section 11 sets out the extent of the contract. Section 12 covers conduct of the business. Section 13 lists mutual rights: no remuneration, equal profit and loss sharing, 6 percent interest on advances, no interest on capital unless agreed, indemnity of the firm by the partner for willful neglect (Section 13(f)), and indemnity to partners for expenses (Section 13(e)). Section 18: partner is agent of the firm. Section 19: implied authority. Section 25: joint and several liability of partners for firm's acts. Section 30: minor admitted to the benefits of partnership. Section 32: retirement. Section 39: dissolution of the firm. Section 48: settlement of accounts on dissolution. Types: partnership at will (Section 7) and particular partnership (Section 8). A partnership firm is not a separate legal entity from its partners, unlike a company or an LLP (Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008).

question: Works Committee, Safety Committee and Canteen Management Committee are the examples of
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Workers' participation in management (WPM) means involving employees in the decision-making of an enterprise at different levels. In India it takes several forms: Works Committees (Industrial Disputes Act 1947, Sec 3, for establishments with 100 or more workmen, with equal representation of employer and workers), Joint Management Councils (1958), Safety Committees (Factories Act 1948, Sec 41G, for factories with 250 or more workers, with equal representation), Canteen Committees (Factories Act Sec 46 and State Rules, for 250 or more workers), Shop Councils and Joint Councils (1975), Worker Directors (Sec 4 of the Companies Act in PSUs from 1970s), and the 1983 Scheme for Participation. Elimination: workers' education is the Central Board for Workers Education (1958), which trains workers in trade union and labour matters. Cooperatives are economic enterprises owned by members. Suggestion schemes are individual channels of ideas with rewards, not representative bodies. Committees with joint worker-management membership are clearly participative bodies, so (a) is correct.
explanations: Correct: all three committees have joint representation of workers and management and deal with welfare, safety and working conditions, which is participation in management.
Wrong: workers' education schemes are run by the Central Board for Workers Education to train workers, not by joint committees.
Wrong: cooperatives are member-owned business organisations, not joint consultative committees within an employer's establishment.
Wrong: suggestion schemes let individual workers submit ideas for rewards. They involve no representative committee structure.
keyfact: Works, Safety and Canteen Committees are joint worker-employer bodies and are forms of workers' participation in management (Article 43A).
option_notes: Workers' participation in management is the involvement of workers in an enterprise's decision-making. The forms are Works Committees, Joint Management Councils, Shop and Joint Councils, worker directors, and the 1983 and 1975 schemes. The Directive Principle in Article 43A (42nd Amendment, 1976) directs the State to secure workers' participation in management of industries. The ILO has also promoted it through its Recommendations on consultation and cooperation at the workplace. The levels are informational, consultative, associative, administrative and decisive participation.

Workers' education aims to make workers aware of their rights, responsibilities and union organisation. The Central Board for Workers Education (CBWE) was set up in 1958 under the Ministry of Labour and Employment. It runs a three-tier scheme: training of worker-teachers, then education officers, then workers. The Kothari-era Indian Labour Conference discussions led to its creation. It operates through regional and sub-regional centres and trains workers in rural, unorganised and organised sectors. Its work is educational rather than managerial.

Workers' cooperatives are enterprises owned and democratically controlled by the workers themselves, who are both members and employees. Examples include labour contract societies, industrial cooperatives and the Indian Coffee House societies. They follow cooperative principles such as open membership and one member one vote. In India, cooperatives are governed by state cooperative acts and the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act 2002. Article 43B, added by the 97th Amendment in 2011, promotes cooperatives. They are ownership structures and not joint committees.

A suggestion scheme invites employees to give ideas for improving productivity, safety, quality or cost, with rewards for accepted ideas. It is a one-way channel of communication, usually through suggestion boxes or committees that evaluate ideas. It is common in industrial undertakings such as railways, steel plants and public sector units. It is regarded as a minimal and informal form of involvement. It does not give workers an institutional role in decisions, so it differs from statutory joint committees.
related: Article 43A: participation of workers in management of industries (42nd Amendment, 1976).
Works Committee: Sec 3, Industrial Disputes Act 1947, for 100 or more workmen.
Safety Committee: Sec 41G, Factories Act 1948, for factories with 250 or more workers.
Joint Management Councils were introduced in 1958.
Shop Councils and Joint Councils were introduced in 1975.
Central Board for Workers Education was established in 1958.
Participation of Workers in Management Bill 1990 was never enacted.
Industrial Relations Code 2020 provides for Grievance Redressal Committees and Works Committees.
summary: The answer is (a) workers' participation in management. Works Committees, Safety Committees and Canteen Management Committees are statutory or quasi-statutory bodies in which workers' representatives sit with the employer's representatives and share in decisions on workplace matters.
topic_notes: Workers' participation in management (WPM) is a core topic in industrial relations. Constitutional basis: Article 43A (Directive Principle, added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976). Forms in India: (1) Works Committees under Sec 3 of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, for establishments with 100 or more workmen, with equal representation and a consultative role. (2) Joint Management Councils from 1958, following the Second Five Year Plan, for establishments with 500 or more workers. (3) Workers' representatives on Safety Committees (Factories Act Sec 41G) and Canteen Committees. (4) Shop Councils and Joint Councils, introduced in 1975. (5) Worker directors on boards of public sector enterprises such as Hindustan Machine Tools, and the 1983 scheme for PSUs. (6) The 1990 Participation of Workers in Management Bill was introduced but never enacted. The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956, along with the Labour Policy of the Second Plan, encouraged participation. Levels of participation: information sharing, consultation, association, administrative and decisive. Related institutions: the Central Board for Workers Education (1958), which promotes worker education, and the Indian Labour Conference, the tripartite body that guides policy. Related concepts: collective bargaining, bipartite and tripartite bodies, and the Industrial Relations Code 2020, which replaced the Industrial Disputes Act, the Trade Unions Act and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, providing for Works Committees to be replaced by Grievance Redressal Committees and Worker Re-skilling Fund. UPSC may ask which Act mandates which committee, the employee strength thresholds, or the form of participation represented by an example.

question: Which one of the following is not part of the aims and purposes of the ILO as per Philadelphia Declaration?
options: Freedom of expression and of association are essential to sustained progress
Poverty anywhere constitutes danger to prosperity everywhere
The war against want requires to be carried on with unrelenting vigour within each nation and is solely the responsibility of the government. 22 GRS-A-TNS/68-A
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Declaration concerning the aims and purposes of the International Labour Organisation was adopted at the 26th Session of the International Labour Conference in Philadelphia on 10 May 1944. It was annexed to the ILO Constitution in 1946. It restated the ILO's mission and rests on four fundamental principles: (a) labour is not a commodity; (b) freedom of expression and of association are essential to sustained progress; (c) poverty anywhere constitutes a danger to prosperity everywhere; (d) the war against want requires to be carried on with unrelenting vigour within each nation, and by continuous and concerted international effort in which representatives of workers and employers, enjoying equal status with those of governments, join with them in free discussion and democratic decision. This fourth principle embodies ILO tripartism. Options (a), (b) and (c) are verbatim principles. Option (d) is wrong because of the word 'solely' and the phrase 'responsibility of the government', which contradict the tripartite and international character of the principle. For elimination, whenever a statement adds absolutes like 'solely' that exclude workers, employers or international cooperation, suspect it is a distortion.
explanations: Incorrect as an answer: 'Labour is not a commodity' is the first principle of the Declaration, so it is part of the aims.
Incorrect as an answer: freedom of expression and association being essential to sustained progress is the second principle, so it is part of the aims.
Incorrect as an answer: 'Poverty anywhere constitutes a danger to prosperity everywhere' is the third principle, so it is part of the aims.

Correct answer: the actual fourth principle calls for national and international effort with workers and employers having equal status with governments. Saying it is 'solely the responsibility of the government' distorts it.
keyfact: Philadelphia Declaration (1944): four principles, and the war against want is fought nationally and internationally with tripartite participation, not solely by governments.
option_notes: 'Labour is not a commodity' is the first principle of the Philadelphia Declaration (1944). It asserts that work is not merely an item of trade to be priced by market forces, and that workers have dignity and rights. It echoes the 1919 ILO Constitution's principle that labour should not be regarded merely as a commodity or article of commerce. It underpins labour standards on wages, hours and conditions, and is a basis of social justice. The ILO was created in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles.

Freedom of expression and of association are essential to sustained progress is the second principle of the Declaration. It links to later ILO Conventions: C87 (Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise, 1948) and C98 (Right to Organise and Collective Bargaining, 1949). Both are among the fundamental conventions. India has ratified C98 only, not C87. This principle supports trade unions, employer organisations and social dialogue, and underlies the ILO tripartite structure.

'Poverty anywhere constitutes a danger to prosperity everywhere' is the third principle of the Declaration. It reflects the ILO's belief that universal and lasting peace depends on social justice, as stated in the 1919 Preamble. It treats poverty as a global concern, which justifies international cooperation, labour standards and development assistance. It is often quoted in discussions on global inequality, decent work and the Sustainable Development Goals.

This option is the distorted version of the fourth principle. The real text says the war against want must be waged with unrelenting vigour within each nation and by continuous and concerted international effort. Representatives of workers and employers, with equal status with governments, join in free discussion and democratic decision to promote the common welfare. It is the foundation of ILO tripartism. The word 'solely' makes this option false.
related: Philadelphia Declaration adopted 10 May 1944 at the 26th ILC session
It was annexed to the ILO Constitution in 1946
ILO founded in 1919, HQ Geneva, and the first UN specialised agency from 1946
ILO Governing Body has 56 members: 28 government, 14 employers, 14 workers
1998 Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work identified four categories, with a fifth added in 2022
ILO received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969
India has not ratified C87 but has ratified C98
summary: The answer is (d). The Philadelphia Declaration (1944) says the war against want must be carried on with unrelenting vigour within each nation, and also through continuous and concerted international effort in which workers and employers, enjoying equal status with governments, join in free discussion and democratic decision. It does not make this solely the government's responsibility.
topic_notes: The ILO was founded in 1919 by the Treaty of Versailles (Part XIII) as part of the League of Nations. It became the first specialised agency of the UN in 1946. It is headquartered in Geneva. It is unique in being tripartite: each member state sends four delegates, two government, one employer and one worker, to the International Labour Conference. Its main organs are the International Labour Conference (the annual general assembly), the Governing Body (the executive council, 56 members: 28 government, 14 employer, 14 worker) and the International Labour Office (the secretariat). The first Director-General was Albert Thomas (France); Gilbert Houngbo (Togo) took office in 2022. The ILO won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969 on its 50th anniversary. The Philadelphia Declaration was adopted on 10 May 1944 and annexed to the Constitution in 1946. It extended the ILO's remit to economic and financial policy matters affecting social welfare. The 1998 Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work covers four categories: freedom of association and collective bargaining; elimination of forced labour; abolition of child labour; and elimination of discrimination in employment. In 2022, a safe and healthy working environment was added as a fifth category. There are 10 fundamental conventions, now including C155 and C187. The 2008 Declaration on Social Justice for a Fair Globalization and the 2019 Centenary Declaration for the Future of Work are other key texts. India is a founding member of the ILO. Related angles: the ILO's flagship reports, the Decent Work Agenda, and the Maternity Protection Convention.

question: Which one of the following is an exception from the five functional types of unionism identified by Robert Hoxie?
subject: Computers
detail: Robert Franklin Hoxie (1868-1916), an American economist at the University of Chicago, studied American trade unions empirically and argued that unions differ in their psychology and functions, so no single theory fits all. His classification, published posthumously in 'Trade Unionism in the United States' (1917), has five types. (1) Business unionism: bread-and-butter aims, higher wages, shorter hours, job control, and collective bargaining within the existing system (Gompers-style AFL). (2) Uplift (friendly) unionism: aims at the moral and social betterment of workers and society, with idealistic aims beyond economics. (3) Revolutionary unionism: seeks to overthrow capitalism and replace the existing order (IWW, syndicalists, socialists). (4) Predatory unionism: uses force, racketeering and collusion with employers for narrow gain. (5) Dependent (or 'hold-up') unionism: has no independent strength, relies on employers' or other unions' support, and is found in subordinate trades. Elimination: business, predatory and revolutionary all appear on the list, so the term outside it, evolutionary, is the exception. Note that 'evolutionary' is sometimes used in other contexts, such as Fabian or reformist socialism, but it is not Hoxie's category.
explanations: Wrong: business unionism is one of Hoxie's five types, focusing on wages, hours and conditions through collective bargaining.
Wrong: predatory unionism is one of Hoxie's five types, using coercion or collusion for narrow gain.
Wrong: revolutionary unionism is one of Hoxie's five types, aiming to overthrow the capitalist order.
Correct: evolutionary unionism is not in Hoxie's classification, whose five types are business, uplift, revolutionary, predatory and dependent unionism.
keyfact: Hoxie's five types are business, uplift, revolutionary, predatory and dependent unionism, and evolutionary unionism is not among them.
option_notes: Business unionism is the pragmatic form of unionism focused on 'bread and butter' issues: wages, hours, job security and working conditions. It accepts the capitalist system and works through collective bargaining. It is associated with Samuel Gompers and the American Federation of Labor, and it is the dominant model in the US. Hoxie counted it as a distinct functional type.

Predatory unionism, in Hoxie's scheme, covers unions that use their power for narrow, often illegitimate gain, through coercion, racketeering, strike threats or collusion with employers against consumers and rivals. Such unions act like a monopoly in a limited field and are indifferent to the wider working class. It is one of the five types he identified.

Revolutionary unionism seeks to abolish the capitalist wage system through class struggle and direct action rather than gradual bargaining. Examples are the Industrial Workers of the World (the 'Wobblies', founded 1905), syndicalism and Marxist-influenced unions. Hoxie included it among his five functional types, alongside business, uplift, predatory and dependent unionism.

Evolutionary unionism is not a Hoxie type. The term loosely describes gradual, reformist change, as in Fabian socialism and the Webbs' view of unions evolving into democratic institutions. Hoxie's own list is business, uplift, revolutionary, predatory and dependent unionism, so this option is the exception and the correct answer.
related: Hoxie's five types: business, uplift, revolutionary, predatory and dependent unionism.
Hoxie's book: Trade Unionism in the United States (1917).
Sidney and Beatrice Webb wrote Industrial Democracy (1897).
Selig Perlman proposed the job-consciousness theory of the labour movement.
Trade Unions Act 1926 requires at least 7 members to register a union.
Gompers led the AFL and championed pure and simple (business) unionism.
The IWW (1905) is the classic example of revolutionary unionism.
summary: The answer is (d) Evolutionary Unionism. Robert Hoxie, in 'Trade Unionism in the United States' (1917), identified five functional types: business, uplift, revolutionary, predatory and dependent unionism. 'Evolutionary unionism' is not among them.
topic_notes: Robert F. Hoxie (1868-1916) was a labour economist at the University of Chicago and a member of the US Commission on Industrial Relations. His book 'Trade Unionism in the United States' was published in 1917, after his death. His method was to classify unions by function and by the psychology of their members, not to propose one universal theory. His five types are: business unionism, which seeks better wages and conditions through bargaining; uplift or friendly unionism, which pursues moral and social betterment and mutual aid; revolutionary unionism, which seeks to overthrow capitalism; predatory unionism, which uses coercion or collusion for narrow gain; and dependent unionism, which survives only on the support of others and has little independent power. Other theories of trade unionism that UPSC may ask about: the Webbs' theory (Industrial Democracy, 1897), under which unions work through mutual insurance, collective bargaining and legal enactment; Selig Perlman's theory of job-consciousness (A Theory of the Labor Movement, 1928); Marx's revolutionary theory; Tannenbaum's theory of the 'man against the machine'; Mitchell's and Commons' theories; and Gompers' pure and simple unionism. Indian context: Trade Unions Act 1926 (registration, with a minimum of 7 members); the Gandhian model (trusteeship, arbitration, as in the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association); and the central unions INTUC, AITUC, HMS, CITU and BMS, with their different political affiliations.

question: Which one of the following is the process in which representatives of workmen and employer involved in an industrial dispute are brought together before a third person or group of persons who facilitates/facilitate through mediation to reach a mutually _ satisfactory agreement?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Conciliation is the main machinery for settling industrial disputes under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (now subsumed in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020). The appropriate government appoints Conciliation Officers (Section 4) and Boards of Conciliation (Section 5). The conciliator's role is to mediate, persuade and assist the parties, not to decide. If settlement is reached, a memorandum of settlement is signed (Section 12(3)) and is binding under Section 18(3). If it fails, the officer sends a failure report to the government, which may refer the dispute to adjudication. Conciliation is mandatory in public utility services before a strike or lockout. Elimination: Arbitration (Section 10A) means the parties voluntarily submit the dispute to an arbitrator who gives a binding award, so the third party decides. Adjudication is compulsory decision-making by a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal. Collective negotiation or bargaining is direct talks between the parties with no third party. The key phrase 'facilitates through mediation to reach mutually satisfactory agreement' therefore points to conciliation.
explanations: Incorrect: in arbitration the third party hears both sides and gives a binding award; it does not merely facilitate agreement.
Incorrect: adjudication is a quasi-judicial process in which a Labour Court or Tribunal decides the dispute and issues a binding award.
Correct: conciliation involves a neutral third party who mediates between workmen and employer to help them reach a mutually acceptable settlement.
Incorrect: collective negotiation or bargaining is a bipartite process directly between employer and workers' representatives, with no third party.
keyfact: Conciliation = a neutral third party mediates to help the disputing parties reach agreement, without imposing a decision (ID Act 1947, Sections 4, 5, 12).
option_notes: Arbitration is a voluntary process under Section 10A of the ID Act, 1947. The parties agree in writing to refer the dispute to an arbitrator before it goes to a Labour Court or Tribunal. The arbitrator's award is binding, and the agreement is published by the government. It is quicker and cheaper than adjudication. The Code on Industrial Relations, 2020 retains it in modified form. It differs from conciliation because the arbitrator decides.

Adjudication is compulsory settlement of a dispute by the state's judicial machinery: Labour Court (Section 7), Industrial Tribunal (Section 7A) and National Tribunal (Section 7B). The government refers the dispute under Section 10, and the body gives a legally binding award. Labour Courts handle matters in the Second Schedule, such as dismissal, and Tribunals handle wider issues such as wages. It is used when conciliation fails. Under the 2020 Code, Tribunals replace Labour Courts.

Conciliation is a method of dispute settlement in which a neutral third party, a Conciliation Officer or Board, helps the parties reach agreement. It has no power to impose a decision. Under the ID Act, officers are appointed under Section 4 and Boards under Section 5. A settlement is binding under Section 18(3). Failure leads to a report under Section 12(4), after which the government may refer the dispute to adjudication. In public utility services, conciliation is compulsory before a strike or lockout.

Collective bargaining or negotiation is a bipartite process in which employer and trade union representatives negotiate wages, working conditions and related matters directly. ILO Convention 98 (1949) protects the right to organise and bargain collectively. India ratified it in 1949. In India, trade unions registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 conduct bargaining. It ends in a bipartite settlement, which is binding under Section 18(1) of the ID Act. There is no third party.
related: Conciliation Officers are appointed under Section 4 of the ID Act, 1947; Boards of Conciliation under Section 5.
Arbitration is under Section 10A; the arbitrator's award is binding.
Courts of Inquiry are under Section 6 and only investigate and report; they do not decide.
Labour Court is Section 7, Industrial Tribunal Section 7A, National Tribunal Section 7B.
A settlement reached in conciliation is binding on all parties under Section 18(3).
Works Committees under Section 3 are required in establishments with 100 or more workers.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 replaces the ID Act 1947, Trade Unions Act 1926 and Standing Orders Act 1946.
Strikes are prohibited during conciliation proceedings and for 7 days after they conclude.
summary: The answer is (c) Conciliation. It is the process in which a neutral third party (a conciliation officer or Board) brings the disputing workmen and employer together and mediates to help them reach a mutually satisfactory settlement, without imposing a decision.
topic_notes: Industrial disputes in India are governed by the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which is being replaced by the Industrial Relations Code, 2020. A dispute is any disagreement between employers and workmen, or between workmen, concerning employment, non-employment or conditions of labour (Section 2(k)). The machinery has several tiers. Bipartite machinery includes collective bargaining, Works Committees (Section 3, for 100 or more workers) and Grievance Redressal Committees. Tripartite machinery includes Conciliation Officers, Boards of Conciliation, and Courts of Inquiry (Section 6), which investigate and report in six months. Adjudication includes Labour Courts, Industrial Tribunals and National Tribunals. Voluntary arbitration is under Section 10A. Conciliation Officers are expected to complete proceedings within 14 days, and Boards within two months. Public utility services require 6 weeks' strike notice, and strikes are barred during conciliation proceedings and for 7 days after. Section 22 governs strikes and lockouts in public utility services, and Section 23 covers general prohibitions. Section 25F requires conditions such as one month's notice and compensation for retrenchment. Section 25N requires government permission for retrenchment in establishments with 100 or more workers; the 2020 Code raises this threshold to 300. Section 33 protects workmen during pendency of proceedings. A Labour Court award becomes enforceable 30 days after publication. Other angles UPSC may ask: the Code of Discipline (1958), the Tripartite Indian Labour Conference, the Whitley Commission (1931), the Royal Commission on Labour, and the Second National Commission on Labour (2002). Related ideas include Trade Unions Act 1926, Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946, and the 2020 Code's provisions, such as the two-member Industrial Tribunal and the 14-day strike notice for all establishments.

question: Questions relating to the application or interpretation of a _ standing order certified under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 may be referred to
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 requires employers of industrial establishments with 100 or more workers (the threshold in the Central Act; many states apply lower limits) to define the conditions of employment in standing orders and get them certified. The Certifying Officer, who is usually the Labour Commissioner or a Regional Labour Commissioner, certifies the draft after hearing objections. Appeal against his order lies to the Appellate Authority. Section 13-A was inserted by the 1956 amendment. It provides that if any question arises about the application or interpretation of a certified standing order, any employer or workman may refer it to any Labour Court constituted under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, whether or not it is specified in the Second Schedule of that Act. The Labour Court decides the question and its decision is final and binding. Elimination: the Industrial Tribunal handles Third Schedule matters and adjudicates disputes of wider scope. The Labour Commissioner acts as the Certifying Officer, not as an interpreter of standing orders. An 'Industrial Employment Court' does not exist under any statute.
explanations: Incorrect: the Industrial Tribunal adjudicates disputes on Second Schedule matters (those of wider impact) and Third Schedule matters. Section 13-A of the Standing Orders Act does not assign interpretation questions to it.
Incorrect: the Labour Commissioner usually acts as the Certifying Officer who certifies standing orders. He does not decide questions of their interpretation or application.
Correct: Section 13-A allows an employer or workman to refer questions about the application or interpretation of a certified standing order to the Labour Court.
Incorrect: there is no court called the Industrial Employment Court under Indian labour law. It is a distractor built from the Act's name.
keyfact: Section 13-A of the Standing Orders Act, 1946: questions on application or interpretation of certified standing orders go to the Labour Court.
option_notes: Industrial Tribunal: a adjudicating body under Section 7-A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, with one member who is or was a High Court judge, or a District Judge. It handles Second and Third Schedule matters such as wages, bonus, retrenchment, working hours and rationalisation. National Tribunals under Section 7-B deal with national-importance disputes. Its award is binding once published.

Labour Commissioner: a state or central officer who enforces labour laws, conciliates disputes and promotes industrial harmony. Labour Commissioners and Regional Labour Commissioners (Central) are usually appointed as Certifying Officers under the Standing Orders Act, 1946. They have conciliation powers but no adjudicating powers over standing-order interpretation.

Labour Court: constituted under Section 7 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and presided over by a person who is or was a High Court judge or District Judge, or who has held a judicial office for at least seven years. It adjudicates Second Schedule matters, including the propriety of discharge or dismissal and the interpretation of standing orders. Section 13-A of the Standing Orders Act refers such questions to it.

Industrial Employment Court: not a real forum. The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 is the statute's name, and it sets up no court of this kind. The Act provides for Certifying Officers and Appellate Authorities only. The option is a distractor and carries no legal weight.
related: Section 13-A of the Standing Orders Act deals with the interpretation of standing orders and was added in 1956.
Certifying Officers are usually Labour Commissioners or Regional Labour Commissioners.
Appeals against certification go to the Appellate Authority, whose decision is final.
Industrial Relations Code, 2020 raises the standing orders threshold to 300 workers.
Labour Courts are constituted under Section 7 and Industrial Tribunals under Section 7-A of the ID Act, 1947.
The Standing Orders Act, 1946 originally applied to establishments with 100 or more workmen.
summary: The answer is (c) Labour Court. Under Section 13-A of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, any question about the application or interpretation of a certified standing order may be referred by an employer or workman to the Labour Court constituted under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
topic_notes: The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 came into force on 23 April 1946. It applies to industrial establishments with 100 or more workmen, and appropriate governments may extend it to smaller units. Its aim is to require employers to define conditions of employment in writing, such as classification of workmen, shift hours, attendance, leave, holidays, termination, disciplinary action and grievance redress. Procedure: the employer submits draft standing orders to the Certifying Officer, who sends copies to the trade union or workers' representatives and invites objections. After hearing both sides he decides whether the draft is fair and reasonable and then certifies it. An appeal against his decision goes to the Appellate Authority, within 30 days. Certified standing orders come into operation after 30 days from authentication, or after the appeal is decided. Modification of the standing orders requires an application and is allowed only after six months from the last modification, except by agreement. Section 13-A (added in 1956) gives the Labour Court jurisdiction over application or interpretation questions. Section 13-B excludes industrial establishments covered by the Model Standing Orders from some requirements (the Act exempts those to which the Model Standing Orders apply). Section 14 empowers the government to exempt establishments. Penalties under Sections 12 and 13 cover failure to submit draft standing orders and contravention of them. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes this Act along with the Industrial Disputes Act and the Trade Unions Act, and makes standing orders mandatory for establishments with 300 or more workers.

question: A union whose membership may cover workers employed in many industries, employment and crafts is known as
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Trade unions are classified by the basis on which they organise members. A craft (horizontal) union organises workers of one skill or craft, such as carpenters or printers, across different employers and industries. An industrial (vertical) union organises all workers, skilled and unskilled, in one industry or establishment, for example railways, coal mining or textiles. A general union cuts across industries, crafts and employments, taking in any worker who wishes to join. Its strengths are a large membership, strong bargaining power and a large funds base. Its weaknesses are diverse interests among members, weak occupational identity and less focused bargaining. UK examples are the Transport and General Workers' Union and the GMB. Indian federations such as INTUC, AITUC, HMS and CITU are central organisations, not general unions in the strict sense. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 governs registration and the rights of unions in India. Elimination: option (a) is limited to one industry, (c) to one craft or skill, and (d) to a region and an industry combined. Only (b) matches the wording 'many industries, employment and crafts'.
explanations: Incorrect: an industrial union is confined to workers of a single industry, regardless of their craft or skill, so it does not span many industries.
Correct: a general union admits workers from many industries, occupations and crafts. That matches the definition in the question exactly.
Incorrect: a craft union is limited to workers of one skill or trade, so it is the opposite of a union covering many crafts.
Incorrect: a region-cum-industry union is limited to one industry within a geographical area, so it is not open to many industries.
keyfact: General union = open to workers of many industries and crafts; craft union = one skill; industrial union = one industry.
option_notes: An industrial or vertical union organises all workers in one industry or establishment, whatever their craft, grade or skill. Examples are railway, mining, textile and plantation unions. It gives strong unity within the industry and strong bargaining power against employers. Its drawback is that it cannot cover workers across industries. Many Indian unions follow this model, such as the National Federation of Indian Railwaymen.

A general union recruits workers from many industries, trades and crafts without limits on occupation. It emerged in nineteenth-century Britain to organise unskilled workers, who were excluded from craft unions. It has large membership and funds but diverse member interests. The UK's Transport and General Workers' Union and the GMB are classic examples. It is also called a 'general workers union'.

A craft or horizontal union organises workers of one skill, craft or occupation across employers and industries. It is the oldest form of trade union, arising from medieval craft guilds and early British unions such as the Amalgamated Society of Engineers. Members share occupational interests and can control the labour supply for their craft. Its weakness is that it divides the workforce along trade lines.

A region-cum-industry level union organises workers of a particular industry within a defined geographical region, for example cotton textile workers in Ahmedabad (the Textile Labour Association) or in Mumbai. It combines a territorial basis with an industrial one. It is a local or regional federation form that gives focused bargaining in a regional industry. It is not open to workers across industries.
related: Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927.
A minimum of seven members is needed to register a trade union.
Madras Labour Union (1918), founded by B.P. Wadia, was the first modern Indian trade union.
AITUC was founded in 1920 with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first president.
BMS, founded in 1955, is the largest central trade union organisation by verified membership.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumed the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
Craft unions are horizontal; industrial unions are vertical.
summary: The answer is (b) general union. A general union is open to workers from many industries, occupations and crafts, and is not restricted to one trade or sector. It recruits across the whole labour market, unlike craft or industrial unions.
topic_notes: Trade unions can be classified in several ways. By membership basis there are craft (horizontal), industrial (vertical) and general unions. Other forms include staff or white-collar unions, associations of professionals, and federations. By level there are plant or enterprise unions, local unions, regional or state unions, industry-wise federations and national centres. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 defines a trade union under Section 2(h) as a combination formed mainly to regulate relations between workmen and employers, between workmen and workmen, or between employers and employers. Registration requires at least seven members, and a union with membership of more than 100 workers or 10 percent of the workforce, whichever is less, needs a minimum number of members. Registration gives corporate status, with a common seal and perpetual succession, and immunity from criminal conspiracy and civil suits for legitimate trade dispute activities (Sections 17 and 18). Unions may maintain a general fund and a political fund, the latter requiring separate contributions. The first Indian union was formed in 1918 by B.P. Wadia in Madras (Madras Labour Union). The Textile Labour Association (1920, Ahmedabad) was a Gandhian model. AITUC was formed in 1920, INTUC in 1947, HMS in 1948, UTUC in 1949 and CITU in 1970. BMS (1955) is the largest central union by verified membership. Union recognition is not mandatory under central law, though some states have provisions, such as Maharashtra's MRTU and PULP Act, 1971. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 has subsumed the 1926 Act and provides for a negotiating union or council at enterprise level.

question: Which one of the following perspectives of industrial relations is based on the assumption that both the parties strive (and have opportunity) to exercise economic (wages and benefits) as well as political (control) power?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Perspectives (frames of reference) on industrial relations were popularised by Alan Fox (1966) and applied to industrial relations by Flanders and Clegg, with Fox's 1974 work extending them. The unitary view sees the enterprise as one team with a single authority and shared goals. It treats conflict as abnormal, caused by poor communication or troublemakers, and regards unions as unnecessary intruders. The pluralist view sees the enterprise as made up of sub-groups with different interests, such as management and labour. Conflict is normal and even healthy, and is managed by collective bargaining, joint consultation and state machinery. Power is dispersed, and both sides seek economic power (wages, benefits) and political power (control over decisions). The radical (Marxist or conflict) view sees conflict as arising from the capitalist structure, with capital dominating labour. It holds that power is unequally distributed, so it does not assume that both parties have equal opportunity. The trusteeship view is Gandhian: the employer holds wealth in trust for society and workers, with cooperation rather than conflict. Elimination: (b) and (d) assume harmony, and (c) assumes an imbalance of power. That leaves (a).
explanations: Correct: pluralism assumes both management and unions are legitimate interest groups that compete for and share economic and political power, and conflict is settled by bargaining.
Incorrect: the unitary view assumes one source of authority and common interests, so there is no legitimate rival power centre such as a union.
Incorrect: the radical view treats power as concentrated in capital and sees class conflict as inherent. Labour does not have an equal opportunity to wield power.
Incorrect: trusteeship is a Gandhian ethical doctrine of employer stewardship and harmony. It is not a power-sharing model.
keyfact: Pluralistic perspective: multiple legitimate interest groups, both sides wield economic and political power, conflict is resolved through bargaining.
option_notes: Pluralistic perspective: associated with Alan Fox, Flanders and Clegg. The organisation is a coalition of interest groups, and conflict is inevitable and manageable. Trade unions are legitimate representatives of labour. It favours collective bargaining, conciliation and a state role as rule-maker and arbiter. Management's task is to balance competing interests. Most modern democratic IR systems, including India's statutory machinery, reflect this view.

Unitary perspective: the organisation is seen as an integrated, harmonious team, like a family or sports team, with one authority and one set of goals. Conflict is pathological and blamed on agitators or poor communication. Unions are seen as unnecessary and disloyal. It is paternalistic and typical of non-union or HRM-style firms, and Fox criticised it as an ideology that serves management.

Radical (Marxist/conflict) perspective: sees industrial conflict as rooted in the capitalist system's class struggle between capital and labour. Employment relations reflect broader inequalities of power and property. Unions are a response to exploitation, and strikes are political as well as economic. Marx and Engels are the sources. Real change needs structural transformation, not just bargaining.

Trusteeship perspective: the Gandhian approach holds that owners are trustees of wealth for society and for workers. It stresses moral duty, non-violence, arbitration and cooperation. It is reflected in the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (1918) and in India's tripartite voluntary arbitration. Gandhi opposed class war and favoured voluntary renunciation by the owners.
related: Alan Fox (1966) gave the unitary and pluralist frames of reference.
Dunlop's systems model (1958) has actors, contexts and an ideology binding the system.
Unitary view treats conflict as abnormal and unions as unnecessary.
Pluralism accepts conflict as inevitable and settles it by collective bargaining.
Radical view regards conflict as arising from capitalist class structure.
Gandhian trusteeship was practised in the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (1918).
The Industrial Relations Code 2020 subsumes the ID Act 1947, Trade Unions Act 1926 and Standing Orders Act 1946.
summary: The answer is (a) Pluralistic perspective. It treats the organisation as a coalition of groups with distinct, legitimate interests. Employers and unions both have the opportunity and the aim to exercise economic power (wages, benefits) and political power (control, voice), so conflict is resolved through bargaining.
topic_notes: Frames of reference in industrial relations: Alan Fox (1966, Royal Commission research paper on Industrial Sociology and Industrial Relations) identified the unitary and pluralist frames. In 1974 he added the radical frame, and later work also noted the Marxist view. Key contrasts are conflict (abnormal in the unitary view, normal in the pluralist view, structural in the radical view), power (single authority, dispersed, concentrated in capital), role of unions (unnecessary, legitimate, a vehicle of class struggle) and role of the state (minimal, neutral arbiter, instrument of the ruling class). Other approaches to IR include the Gandhian approach (trusteeship, arbitration, non-violence), the systems approach of John Dunlop (1958: actors, contexts, ideology that binds the system and rules), the human relations approach (Elton Mayo, Hawthorne studies), the psychological approach, the sociocultural approach and the Marxist approach. Indian legislation includes the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 (conciliation, adjudication, strikes and lockouts), the Trade Unions Act 1926 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946. These are being merged into the Industrial Relations Code 2020. Machinery includes works committees, conciliation officers, boards, courts of inquiry, labour courts and tribunals. Likely future angles: matching perspectives with their features, the founder of each frame, the Dunlop systems model and the Gandhian trusteeship doctrine.

question: The provision of workers’ participation in management of industries is provided under
options: Article 39A of the Constitution of India
Article 43A of the Constitution of India
Article 42 of the Constitution of India
Article 43B of the Constitution of India
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 43A, in Part IV (DPSP), says the State shall take steps, by suitable legislation or in any other way, to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations engaged in any industry. It was added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, and reflects the Gandhian and socialist strands of the DPSPs. Being a directive, it is non-justiciable under Article 37. Elimination: Article 39A (added by the same amendment) deals with equal justice and free legal aid. Article 42 provides for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Article 43B was inserted by the 97th Amendment (2011) and promotes cooperative societies. Only Article 43A therefore matches workers' participation in management. Related institutional forms include Works Committees under the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 (Sec 3), Joint Management Councils (1958), and the 1975 Scheme of Workers' Participation in Management. Article 43 covers living wage and cottage industries.
explanations: Incorrect: Article 39A concerns equal justice and free legal aid, not workers' participation.
Correct: Article 43A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, directs the State to secure workers' participation in management of industrial undertakings.
Incorrect: Article 42 deals with just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
Incorrect: Article 43B, added by the 97th Amendment in 2011, deals with the promotion of cooperative societies.
keyfact: Article 43A (42nd Amendment, 1976) = workers' participation in management; 43B = cooperatives; 39A = free legal aid; 42 = humane work conditions and maternity relief.
option_notes: Article 39A: inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. It directs the State to ensure that the legal system promotes justice on the basis of equal opportunity and to provide free legal aid. It led to the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 and NALSA. It is a DPSP and is non-justiciable, though the courts read it with Article 21.

Article 43A: a DPSP inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. It directs the State to take steps to secure workers' participation in the management of industrial undertakings and establishments. It is non-justiciable. It is linked to Joint Management Councils and Works Committees, and to the 1975 participation scheme for industry.

Article 42: a DPSP that directs the State to make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief. It is the constitutional basis of the Maternity Benefit Act 1961. It is a Gandhian-socialist directive and is non-justiciable under Article 37.

Article 43B: inserted by the 97th Amendment Act, 2011. It directs the State to promote the voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of cooperative societies. The same amendment added the right to form cooperatives to Article 19(1)(c) and added Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT).
related: Article 43A was added by the 42nd Amendment Act 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.
Article 39A provides equal justice and free legal aid.
Article 43B (97th Amendment 2011) deals with cooperative societies.
Article 42 provides for humane work conditions and maternity relief.
Article 43 covers a living wage and the promotion of cottage industries.
Joint Management Councils were introduced in 1958 following the 1957 Indian Labour Conference.
Works Committees come under Section 3 of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947.
Directive Principles are non-justiciable under Article 37.
summary: The correct answer is (b) Article 43A. It is a Directive Principle of State Policy, inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, directing the State to take steps to secure workers' participation in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations engaged in industry.
topic_notes: Workers' participation in management (WPM) combines constitutional, statutory and policy elements. Article 43A (42nd Amendment, 1976) is the constitutional anchor. It is a DPSP in Part IV, so it is not enforceable by courts, though the State is expected to apply it in making laws. The 42nd Amendment, often called the Mini-Constitution, also added Article 39A, Article 48A and Article 51A (Fundamental Duties), and it moved the subjects of education and forests to the Concurrent List. Other labour-related DPSPs are Article 39(a), (d) and (e) (livelihood, equal pay for equal work, protection of workers' health), Article 41 (right to work and public assistance), Article 42 (humane conditions of work and maternity relief), Article 43 (living wage, decent standard of life, and cottage industries) and Article 43B (cooperatives). Forms of WPM in India include Works Committees under Section 3 of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, Joint Management Councils (recommended in 1957 and introduced from 1958), Shop Councils and Joint Councils under the 1975 scheme, workers' directors on boards of public sector undertakings (1970s), and the 1983 scheme for participation in public sector undertakings. The Industrial Relations Code 2020 retains the Works Committee concept and adds a Grievance Redressal Committee. The ILO also promotes participation through collective bargaining and cooperation conventions. Possible future questions: which amendment added a given article, which DPSPs are Gandhian, socialist or liberal, and which articles relate to labour rights such as Article 23 (forced labour) and Article 24 (child labour in hazardous employment).

question: Which one of the following is not a trade union security measure?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Union security measures are arrangements, usually negotiated in a collective agreement, that protect a trade union's membership and finances by linking employment to union membership or financial support. The main types are: (1) Closed shop, where only existing union members can be hired. (2) Union shop, where anyone can be hired but must join the union within a stated period, usually 30 days. (3) Agency shop, where a worker need not join the union but must pay it a service fee equal to dues, because the union bargains for all. (4) Maintenance of membership, where members who have joined must remain members during the agreement. (5) Preferential shop, where union members get hiring preference. (6) Check-off, where the employer deducts dues from wages. An open shop is the opposite: employment does not depend on union membership, and non-members get the same terms. It therefore weakens union security and is favoured by employers. The elimination logic is to check which option does not compel membership or fees. Only the open shop fails that test. In the USA, the Taft-Hartley Act 1947 banned closed shops, and right-to-work states ban union and agency shops. In India, the Trade Unions Act 1926 does not mandate any of these, though some forms exist by agreement.
explanations: Wrong as an answer: a closed shop is a union security measure because only union members may be hired.
Wrong as an answer: an agency shop is a union security measure because non-members must pay the union a service fee.
Correct answer: an open shop makes union membership and dues voluntary, so it gives the union no security.
Wrong as an answer: a union shop is a union security measure because new employees must join the union within a fixed period after hiring.
keyfact: Open shop = no compulsion to join or pay the union, so it is not a union security measure; closed, union and agency shops are.
option_notes: Closed shop: the employer may recruit only people who are already union members, so the union effectively controls the labour supply. It is common in industries such as printing, construction and docks. It was made illegal in the USA by the Taft-Hartley Act 1947. In India it is not statutorily recognised, though the practice has existed informally in some industries. It gives the union the strongest security of any arrangement.

Agency shop: employees need not join the union, but all must pay it a fee, usually equal to dues, as a condition of employment. The reasoning is that all workers benefit from collective bargaining and so should share its cost. It addresses the free-rider problem. It is allowed in many places but banned in right-to-work US states. It is a middle path between union shop and open shop.

Open shop: employment does not depend on union membership or paying dues. Workers may join or not, and union and non-union workers are treated equally. It is preferred by employers and is promoted by right-to-work laws in the USA. Because it leaves the union without guaranteed members or income, it is the opposite of a union security measure.

Union shop: the employer may hire anyone, but new employees must join the union within a stated time, typically 30 days, and stay members to keep the job. It was permitted under the US Taft-Hartley Act 1947, subject to conditions and state right-to-work laws. It differs from a closed shop because union membership is required after hiring, not before.
related: Closed shop means union membership before employment.
Union shop means membership within a fixed period after employment.
Agency shop requires non-members to pay a service fee to the union.
Check-off means the employer deducts union dues from wages.
Taft-Hartley Act 1947 (USA) banned closed shops.
Trade Unions Act 1926 Sec 16 allows a separate political fund.
Rand formula is the Canadian form of agency shop.
summary: The answer is (c) Open shop system. An open shop does not require workers to join or pay dues to a union, so it gives the union no security. Closed shop, union shop and agency shop are all union security arrangements that make membership or fee payment compulsory in some form.
topic_notes: Union security means protecting a union's survival, membership and funds. Employers often resist unions, and workers can free-ride on benefits won by collective bargaining, so unions seek clauses that guarantee membership or income. The common forms run from strongest to weakest. Closed shop: membership is required before hiring. Union shop: membership is required after hiring, within a period. Agency shop: no membership is needed, but a fee must be paid. Maintenance of membership: workers who join must stay members for the agreement's term. Preferential shop: the employer gives union members hiring preference. Check-off: the employer deducts dues from wages and remits them to the union. The open shop is the absence of security: no membership or fee is compelled. In India the Trade Unions Act 1926 provides registration, immunity from criminal conspiracy (Sec 17) and civil suits (Sec 18), and separate funds for political purposes (Sec 16). Recognition of unions is not compulsory under central law, though the Code of Discipline 1958 and the Industrial Relations Code 2020 deal with recognition. The Industrial Relations Code 2020 introduces the idea of a sole negotiating union (51 percent membership) and a negotiating council. Related topics UPSC may ask about include collective bargaining, the Code of Discipline, the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, the Taft-Hartley Act 1947, the Wagner Act 1935, and the Rand formula, a Canadian agency-shop arrangement.

question: Which one of the following is statutory machinery functioning at the central level?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: A statutory body derives its existence, powers and functions from an Act of Parliament or a state legislature. A non-statutory (executive) body is created by a government resolution or an administrative order. The ESIC was established under Section 3 of the ESI Act, 1948, as a corporate body with perpetual succession and a common seal. It administers the ESI Scheme through the Corporation, the Standing Committee and the Medical Benefit Council. The Corporation is headed by the Union Labour Minister as Chairman, with representatives of employers, employees, the Centre, states, Parliament and the medical profession. The Central Board for Workers' Education was set up in 1958 as a society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, following a Ministry of Labour initiative, so it is not created by a labour-law statute. The Standing Labour Committee is a tripartite advisory body, and the Central Implementation and Evaluation Committee is a tripartite monitoring body. Both came out of Labour Conferences and not out of any Act. Elimination: pick the only body that has an Act as its source, which is the ESIC.
explanations: Wrong. The Central Implementation and Evaluation Committee is a tripartite, non-statutory body formed to monitor the implementation of labour laws and agreements, and no Act creates it.

Wrong. The Central Board for Workers' Education is an autonomous society under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, registered under the Societies Registration Act, so it is not established by a labour statute.
Wrong. The Standing Labour Committee is a tripartite advisory committee of the Indian Labour Conference that was created by executive decision and has no statutory basis.
Correct. The ESIC is constituted under the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948, and is a statutory corporation functioning at the central level.
keyfact: ESIC is a statutory body under the ESI Act, 1948, while the Standing Labour Committee, CIEC and CBWE are non-statutory.
option_notes: The Central Implementation and Evaluation Committee is a tripartite body of the Ministry of Labour that reviews the implementation of labour laws, awards, agreements and the Code of Discipline. Its members are drawn from the Centre, the states, employers and workers. It came out of tripartite consensus in the 1950s and has an advisory and monitoring role without statutory powers.

The Central Board for Workers' Education (CBWE) was set up in 1958 under the Ministry of Labour and Employment. It runs programmes to make workers aware of their rights and duties, to build up trade union leadership and to promote education. It works through regional and sub-regional centres across India and is a registered society.

The Standing Labour Committee is a tripartite committee that assists the Indian Labour Conference (ILC). The ILC was first convened in 1942 and is the apex consultative forum on labour policy. The Standing Labour Committee meets between ILC sessions to screen agenda items and review decisions. It has no statutory status, and its members represent government, employers and workers.

The Employees' State Insurance Corporation is the statutory body that administers the ESI Scheme under the ESI Act, 1948. The scheme gives medical, sickness, maternity, disability and dependants' benefits to workers in covered establishments. The Corporation has its headquarters in New Delhi, and the Union Labour Minister serves as its Chairman. It is funded by employer and employee contributions, which are currently 3.25% and 0.75% of wages.
related: ESIC was constituted under Section 3 of the ESI Act, 1948.
The Union Labour Minister is the Chairman of ESIC.
The Indian Labour Conference was first held in 1942.
The CBWE was set up in 1958 as a society.
The EPFO Central Board of Trustees is statutory under the EPF & MP Act, 1952.
The ESI contribution rates are 3.25% from the employer and 0.75% from the employee.
The ESI wage ceiling for coverage is Rs 21,000 per month.
summary: The answer is (d) Employees' State Insurance Corporation. The ESIC is a statutory body created by the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948, and works at the central level. The other three are tripartite or administrative bodies set up by executive decision, not by a statute.
topic_notes: Statutory and non-statutory bodies in labour administration: Statutory bodies owe their existence to an Act. The key examples are the ESIC (ESI Act, 1948), the EPFO's Central Board of Trustees (EPF & MP Act, 1952), the Central Board of Trustees' Employees' Provident Fund, the Central Advisory Board and the Industrial Tribunals and Labour Courts under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and the Boards for Beedi and Cine Workers' welfare under their respective welfare fund Acts. The Contract Labour Advisory Boards derive from the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. Non-statutory bodies include the Indian Labour Conference (first held 1942), the Standing Labour Committee, the Central Implementation and Evaluation Committee and the Industrial Committees. The CBWE is a society. ESIC's structure comprises the Corporation, the Standing Committee and the Medical Benefit Council, and the Director General is its chief executive. The ESI Act applies to establishments with 10 or more employees, with a wage ceiling of Rs 21,000 per month for coverage. The EPF Act, 1952 has a Central Board of Trustees, an Executive Committee and the State Boards. The tripartite principle comes from the ILO, which India joined as a founding member in 1919. Questions often ask which body is statutory, who chairs it, which year it was set up and which Act governs it, so memorise the parent Act for each organisation.

question: Which one of the following explains the ‘citizen concept’ of labour?
options: Labour is largely regarded by the employers as _ operating organizations in industry
Labour is affected by the law of demand and supply
Labour has a right to be consulted in regard to the terms and conditions under which they are supposed to work
Labour is a cog in the machine
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Industrial relations thinking has passed through several concepts of labour. In the early phase, labour was a commodity, bought and sold in the market and governed by demand and supply, so wages were set by market forces. Next came the 'factor of production' view, in which labour was one input like land and capital, and the 'cog in the machine' view, in which the worker was only a mechanical part of production. Later came the humanitarian and welfare views, then the 'human resource' and 'partner' ideas. The citizen concept, tied to industrial democracy, holds that a worker is a citizen of the industrial society. The worker has a say in decisions that affect his working life, through collective bargaining, joint consultation, works committees and workers' participation in management. Article 43A of the Constitution (42nd Amendment, 1976) directs the State to secure workers' participation in management. Elimination: (b) describes the commodity concept, (d) the mechanical or factor-of-production view, and (a) is a vague employer-centric statement that does not state a rights-based position. Only (c) reflects consultation and rights.
explanations: Wrong: this reflects an employer-centred, managerial view of labour as something that runs the organisation. It says nothing about workers' rights or participation.
Wrong: this is the commodity concept. Labour is treated as a market good whose price (the wage) is set by supply and demand.

Correct: the citizen concept gives workers the status of citizens in industry, including the right to be consulted on the terms and conditions of their work, which is the basis of industrial democracy.
Wrong: this is the mechanical or 'factor of production' view, in which the worker is a replaceable part of the machine with no voice or dignity.
keyfact: Citizen concept of labour = worker as a citizen of industry with rights, dignity and consultation (industrial democracy), unlike commodity or cog-in-the-machine views.
option_notes: This option reflects a managerial or employer-centred view. Employers see labour as an operating resource that runs the organisation and serves production goals. It is not a recognised, rights-based concept in industrial relations theory. Such views underlie the unitary frame of reference, in which management expects loyalty and authority is not shared. It contrasts with pluralist and democratic views, which accept that workers have separate interests and a legitimate voice in decisions.

The commodity concept treats labour as a good bought and sold in the market, with wages fixed by demand and supply. It was dominant in the classical economic period and the early Industrial Revolution. The ILO's Philadelphia Declaration (1944) rejected it, stating that 'labour is not a commodity'. It underlies laissez-faire approaches. Labour legislation, minimum wages and collective bargaining developed in reaction to it.

This is the citizen concept of labour, linked to industrial democracy. Workers are regarded as citizens of the industrial society, with rights to dignity, fair treatment and a voice in decisions about work. It is realised through collective bargaining, works committees, joint management councils and workers' participation in management. Article 43A (42nd Amendment, 1976) is a Directive Principle on workers' participation in management. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provides for Works Committees under Section 3.

The 'cog in the machine' view treats the worker as a replaceable mechanical part of production, with no personal identity or voice. It is associated with early factory systems and, later, with Taylor's scientific management, which stressed efficiency and standardised tasks. It was criticised by the Human Relations school (Elton Mayo, Hawthorne experiments, 1924-32), which showed the importance of social and psychological factors at work.
related: ILO Philadelphia Declaration (1944): 'Labour is not a commodity'.
Article 43A (inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976): workers' participation in management.
Works Committees are provided for under Section 3 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
The Hawthorne experiments (Elton Mayo) led to the Human Relations approach.
Joint Management Councils were introduced in India in 1958.
Workers' participation in management scheme was introduced in 1975 and extended in 1977.
The Trade Unions Act, 1926 gave legal status to registered unions.
Industrial democracy means workers have a voice in decisions affecting them.
summary: The answer is (c). The 'citizen concept' of labour treats workers as citizens of the industrial community with rights, dignity and a voice, including the right to be consulted on the terms and conditions of their work. It contrasts with older views that treated labour as a commodity or a mere part of the machine.
topic_notes: Concepts of labour in industrial relations evolved in stages. (1) Commodity concept: labour is bought and sold in the market and wages follow demand and supply. The ILO's Philadelphia Declaration (1944) states that labour is not a commodity. (2) Factor of production concept: labour is one input along with land, capital and enterprise. (3) Goodwill concept: labour is a source of goodwill and productivity, so good treatment pays. (4) Human concept: workers are human beings with needs, emotions and aspirations, which was the emphasis of the Human Relations school (Elton Mayo). (5) Social asset or welfare concept: labour is a social asset, to be protected by welfare measures and State intervention. (6) Partnership concept: labour and management are partners sharing in production and profit. (7) Citizen concept: the worker is a citizen of industrial society, entitled to rights, dignity and consultation, which is the foundation of industrial democracy. Related Indian provisions include Article 43 (living wage and decent conditions of work), Article 43A (participation of workers in management of industries), Article 19(1)(c) (right to form associations and unions), and Article 23 (prohibition of forced labour). Mechanisms of participation include works committees (Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Section 3), joint management councils (1958), the Workers' Participation in Management Scheme (1975-77), and bipartite and tripartite bodies such as the Indian Labour Conference. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 gave legal recognition to unions. Frames of reference (unitary, pluralist, Marxist) are another exam angle. Dunlop's systems approach and Gandhian trusteeship are also commonly asked. UPSC often asks to match each concept with its description.

question: Who among the following can _ be appointed as the Chairman of the Central Advisory Board constituted by the Central Government under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948?
options: One of the independent members of the Board
One of the employers’ representatives of the Board
One of the employees’ representatives of the Board
A functionary of the Central Government nominated by the Government
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 sets up a tripartite structure for advising on wage fixation. Section 7 provides for Advisory Boards.
