Section 8 provides for the Central Advisory Board, which advises the Central and State Governments on fixing and revising minimum wages and on other matters under the Act, and coordinates the work of the Advisory Boards. Its members are nominated by the Central Government. They represent employers and employees in scheduled employments in equal numbers, plus independent persons not exceeding one-third of the total strength. The Act says that one of these independent persons shall be appointed Chairman by the Central Government. The Chairman is therefore neutral, neither employer nor employee nor a government official. Section 9 applies the same pattern to committees and sub-committees (equal representation, independent members up to one-third, and an independent Chairman). Elimination: options (b) and (c) are partisan representatives, which defeats the neutrality principle. Option (d) is not allowed because the Chairman must come from the independent category, not be a departmental official. Only (a) matches the statutory text.
explanations: Correct: Section 8 requires that one of the independent persons on the Board be appointed Chairman by the Central Government.
Incorrect: Employers' representatives are one of the two equal interest groups, and the Chairman must be independent of both.
Incorrect: Employees' representatives are the other interest group and cannot chair the Board, which must be neutral.
Incorrect: The Act does not provide for a government functionary to be nominated as Chairman. The Chairman comes from the independent members.
keyfact: Under Section 8, Minimum Wages Act 1948, the Central Government appoints one of the independent members as Chairman of the Central Advisory Board.
option_notes: Independent members are persons not representing employers or employees. Under Sections 8 and 9 they may not exceed one-third of the Board's or committee's strength. They bring neutral expertise, such as economists, academics or social workers. One of them is appointed Chairman by the appropriate Government, which makes the Chair impartial between the two sides.

Employers' representatives are nominated by the Government to speak for employers in scheduled employments. They must equal the number of employees' representatives. They bring industry views on the capacity to pay and on wage costs. The Act does not allow them to chair the Board because of the conflict of interest.

Employees' representatives are nominated to represent workers in scheduled employments, usually from trade unions. Their number equals that of the employers' representatives. They bring views on living wage and cost of living. They cannot be the Chairman, since the Chair has to be above the two interest groups.

A government functionary is an official of the Central Government. Under the Minimum Wages Act, officials are not a separate category for the Central Advisory Board's Chair. The Act names only independent persons for that role. Officials may serve as secretariat or in other capacities, but the statute does not make them Chairman.
related: Minimum Wages Act, 1948 was enacted on 15 March 1948 and is based on Article 43.
Section 8 provides for the Central Advisory Board and Section 7 for Advisory Boards.
Section 9 covers the composition of committees and sub-committees, with independent members up to one-third.
Section 5 gives two methods of fixing wages: the committee method and the notification method.
Section 22 provides penalties for offences under the Act.
Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) upheld the constitutional validity of the Act.
The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act, the Payment of Wages Act, the Payment of Bonus Act and the Equal Remuneration Act.
summary: The answer is (a). Section 8 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 says the Central Advisory Board has equal numbers of employers' and employees' representatives plus independent persons. The Central Government appoints one of the independent persons as Chairman.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 was enacted on 15 March 1948 and applies to scheduled employments. It rests on Article 43 (living wage) of the Directive Principles. Its main aim is to prevent exploitation of workers in sweated and unorganised industries. Section 3 empowers the appropriate Government to fix minimum rates of wages, and Section 4 describes what a minimum wage may consist of, including the basic rate and cost of living allowance. Section 5 lays down two methods of fixing wages: the committee method and the notification (public notice) method. Section 7 provides for Advisory Boards, and Section 8 for the Central Advisory Board. Section 9 provides for committees and sub-committees. The tripartite principle runs through all of these: equal employer and employee representatives, plus independent persons up to one-third, with an independent Chairman. Section 11 deals with wages in kind, Section 12 with payment of minimum rates, Section 13 with fixing hours of work, Section 14 with overtime, and Section 18 with registers. Section 19 deals with claims, and Section 20 with the authority that hears them. Section 22 provides penalties for offences, and Section 22A is a general provision for punishment of other offences. The Central Government is the appropriate Government for the Railways, mines, oilfields, major ports and other central spheres. The Supreme Court in Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) upheld the Act as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(6). In Crown Aluminium Works v. Workmen (1958), the Court held that no employer can carry on business without paying the minimum wage. The Act is being replaced by the Code on Wages, 2019, which also provides for a Central Advisory Board with an independent Chairman, among other changes.

ocr: Which one of the following comes under the ‘State List’ under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India? (a) Relief of the disabled and unemployable (b) Regulation of labour and safety in mines (c) Regulation and control of manufacture, supply and distribution of salt (ad) Social security and social insurance
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 246 divides legislative powers between Parliament and State legislatures through three lists in the Seventh Schedule: Union List (originally 97 entries, now 100), State List (originally 66, now 61 after deletions) and Concurrent List (originally 47, now 52). The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved five subjects to the Concurrent List: education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and administration of justice. The 7th Amendment (1956) abolished the old Part A/B/C/D classification of lists. Entry 9 of the State List covers relief of the disabled and unemployable. Regulation of labour and safety in mines is Union List Entry 55. Regulation and control of manufacture, supply and distribution of salt is Union List Entry 58, where salt is a Union subject covering the Central salt monopoly. Social security and social insurance is Concurrent List Entry 23. Labour welfare (Entry 24) and trade unions and industrial disputes (Entry 22) are also Concurrent. Elimination: mines and salt are central subjects, and social security is a shared subject. Only (a) is left for the States. In a conflict on a Concurrent subject, the Union law prevails under Article 254.
explanations: Correct. Relief of the disabled and unemployable is State List Entry 9, so only State legislatures can make laws on it.
Incorrect. Regulation of labour and safety in mines and oilfields is Union List Entry 55, so only Parliament can legislate on it.
Incorrect. Regulation and control of the manufacture, supply and distribution of salt is Union List Entry 58, so it is a Union subject.
Incorrect. Social security and social insurance is Concurrent List Entry 23, so both Parliament and the States can legislate, with the Union law prevailing in a conflict.
keyfact: Relief of the disabled and unemployable is State List Entry 9, while mines labour and salt are Union subjects and social security is Concurrent.
option_notes: Relief of the disabled and unemployable is State List Entry 9. It reflects the States' responsibility for public welfare and poverty relief. Related State List items include public health and sanitation (Entry 6), and poor relief is linked to the Directive Principle in Article 41, which covers the right to public assistance in unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement.

Regulation of labour and safety in mines and oilfields is Union List Entry 55. It underlies central laws such as the Mines Act 1952, and the DGMS (Directorate General of Mines Safety) enforces safety standards. Mines and mineral development is also Union List Entry 54, to the extent the Union takes control by law, while the States hold the subject under State List Entry 23 subject to Entry 54.

Regulation and control of the manufacture, supply and distribution of salt by Union agencies is Union List Entry 58. The Salt Commissioner's organisation is based in Jaipur. Salt carries historical weight in the Dandi March of 1930, when Gandhi protested the British salt monopoly and the salt tax.

Social security and social insurance is Concurrent List Entry 23, covering employment and unemployment. Central laws include the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 1952, the ESI Act 1948 and the Code on Social Security 2020. This is the central area for EPFO exams.
related: Article 246 distributes legislative powers through the Seventh Schedule.
Police and public order are State List subjects.
Education was moved from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment (1976).
Article 249 lets Parliament legislate on a State subject if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by two-thirds majority.
Trade unions and industrial disputes are Concurrent List Entries 22 and 23 and 24 range subjects.
Residuary powers lie with Parliament under Article 248.
Article 246A, inserted by the 101st Amendment, gives special provisions on GST.
Article 254 resolves conflicts between Union and State laws on Concurrent subjects.
summary: The answer is (a): 'Relief of the disabled and unemployable' is State List Entry 9 of the Seventh Schedule. The other three items sit in the Union List or the Concurrent List.
topic_notes: Article 246 gives the Seventh Schedule its structure. Parliament has exclusive power over the Union List (Entries 1-100), State legislatures over the State List (Entries 1-66, with several now omitted), and both over the Concurrent List (Entries 1-52). Residuary powers lie with Parliament under Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List. This differs from the USA and Australia, where residuary powers lie with the States. The Government of India Act 1935 provided the three-fold division of Federal, Provincial and Concurrent lists. Parliament can legislate on State List subjects only in special cases: Article 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds in the national interest), Article 250 (Emergency), Article 252 (consent of two or more States), Article 253 (international agreements) and Article 356 (President's Rule). Under Article 254, a Union law prevails over a State law on a Concurrent subject, but a State law with Presidential assent can prevail in that State. The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2010) examined Centre-State relations. The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced GST, with Article 246A giving Parliament and States concurrent power on GST and omitting State List Entry 54 and some others. Labour matters, such as trade unions, industrial disputes, labour welfare, social security and employment, are Concurrent, which is why both central and state labour laws exist. Other State List subjects include public order, police, agriculture, land, local government, liquor, and public health.

ocr: The assumption that “man is selfish and self-centered, and always tries to achieve his own ends even at the cost of others” explains which theory of labour welfare? (a) Placating theory (b) Police theory (c) Religious theory (ad) Philanthropic theory
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Theories of labour welfare try to explain why welfare measures exist and who drives them. The Police theory rests on a pessimistic view of human nature: man is selfish, self-centred and always seeks his own ends even at others' expense. Employers will therefore not voluntarily provide decent conditions, and the State must step in with compulsory legislation, inspection and penalties. This is why the theory is called the 'Police' theory: minimum standards are enforced by authority, as in the Factories Act 1948, which provides for inspectors, prosecution and penalties. Related theories include the Paternalistic (Trusteeship) theory, where employers act as guardians of workers; the Placating theory, where welfare is given to appease unrest or pre-empt unions; the Philanthropic theory, based on charity and humanitarian motives; the Religious theory, based on duty, charity and the desire for merit; the Functional (Efficiency) theory, where welfare raises productivity; and the Social theory and Public relations theory. Elimination: placating means appeasement, religious means spiritual merit, and philanthropic means goodwill. None of these starts from the assumption that man is selfish, so only the Police theory fits.
explanations: Incorrect: the Placating theory holds that welfare is granted to pacify workers, reduce discontent and forestall unions. It is about appeasement, not human selfishness.
Correct: the Police theory assumes man is selfish and self-centred, so compulsion through State law and enforcement is needed to protect workers' interests.
Incorrect: the Religious theory holds that welfare is a charitable act, a duty prompted by religious feeling or the wish to earn spiritual merit. It does not assume selfishness.
Incorrect: the Philanthropic theory holds that employers provide welfare out of humanitarian and charitable motives. This is the opposite of the selfishness assumption.
keyfact: Police theory = man is selfish, so welfare must be enforced by State compulsion and law.
option_notes: The Placating theory (also called the appeasement theory) says employers provide welfare facilities to placate or pacify workers and keep them from becoming militant. It aims to prevent unrest, reduce the appeal of trade unions and win loyalty. Welfare is a tool of industrial peace and is given in anticipation of or in response to labour agitation. It is a managerial strategy and is not driven by legal compulsion or charity.

The Police theory holds that man is selfish and will not look after others' interests voluntarily, so the State must compel employers through law to provide minimum welfare standards. It relies on inspection, enforcement and penalties. Factory legislation such as the Factories Act 1948 and the Mines Act 1952 reflects it. Its criticism is that it depends on coercion and ignores goodwill and cooperation.

The Religious theory holds that welfare work stems from religious feeling. Employers provide facilities such as temples, dharmashalas and charity out of duty, to gain spiritual merit or to atone for sins. It is rooted in the idea of charity and dharma. Welfare under it is voluntary and personal, and depends on individual employers' beliefs.

The Philanthropic theory holds that welfare is based on humanitarian and charitable motives. Employers and reformers help workers out of compassion, to relieve their suffering and improve their lot. Early welfare in India, such as the work of social reformers and Indian industrialists, is linked to it. Its weaknesses are that it is paternalistic, voluntary and uneven.
related: Factories Act 1948 requires a welfare officer where 500 or more workers are employed.
Creche is mandatory under the Factories Act where more than 30 women workers are employed.
Canteen is mandatory under the Factories Act where more than 250 workers are employed.
Placating theory means welfare given to appease workers and avoid unrest.
Trusteeship (Paternalistic) theory treats the employer as a trustee or guardian of workers.
Functional theory sees welfare as a way to increase efficiency and productivity.
Intramural welfare is inside the establishment; extramural is outside it.
The Rege Committee (1946) was the Labour Investigation Committee.
summary: The answer is (b) Police theory. This theory assumes that man is selfish and self-centred and will pursue his own ends at others' cost, so the State must use compulsion and legislation to force employers to protect workers.
topic_notes:
Labour welfare covers services, facilities and amenities provided in or near the workplace to improve workers' working and living conditions. The ILO defines it as services, facilities and amenities established in or near undertakings so that workers can perform their work in healthy, congenial surroundings. The Royal Commission on Labour (1931) and the Labour Investigation Committee (Rege Committee, 1946) studied welfare in India.

Main theories:
1. Police theory: it assumes man is selfish, so the State compels employers by law.
2. Religious theory: welfare is charity for spiritual merit.
3. Philanthropic theory: welfare comes from humanitarian motives.
4. Paternalistic or Trusteeship theory: the employer is a trustee and guardian of workers.
5. Placating theory: welfare appeases workers and forestalls unrest.
6. Public relations theory: welfare builds the employer's good image.
7. Functional or Efficiency theory: welfare raises productivity and efficiency.
8. Social theory: industry owes responsibility to society and its workers.

The Indian legal framework includes the Factories Act 1948 (chapter on welfare covering canteens, creches, washing facilities, first aid and welfare officers), the Mines Act 1952, the Plantations Labour Act 1951 and the Beedi and Cigar Workers Act 1966. Statutory welfare is compulsory, voluntary welfare is by employers, and mutual welfare comes from unions. Welfare covers intramural activities inside the workplace and extramural ones outside it. Central welfare funds exist for mine workers (coal, mica, iron ore, limestone and dolomite) and beedi workers, and are administered by the Labour Welfare Organisation. Likely questions include matching theories to their features, welfare officer thresholds (500 or more workers under the Factories Act), and the principles of labour welfare.

ocr: Dr. Aykroyd’s formula is associated with determination of (a) fair wage (b) minimum wage (c) living wage (ad) real wage
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Dr. W. R. Aykroyd, a nutrition expert, gave the nutritional yardstick used for fixing the need-based minimum wage in India. The 15th Indian Labour Conference (1957) set out norms for the need-based minimum wage: a standard working-class family of 3 consumption units (husband, wife and two children counted as one unit); minimum food requirement of 2,700 calories per adult consumption unit, following Dr. Aykroyd's recommendation; 72 yards of cloth per family per year (18 yards per capita); rent corresponding to the minimum area provided under the government's Industrial Housing Scheme; and fuel, lighting and other items at 20% of total minimum wage expenditure. The Supreme Court in Raptakos Brett & Co. v. Workmen (1992) added a 25% component for children's education, medical needs, minimum recreation, marriage and old age. Elimination: a fair wage lies between the minimum wage and the living wage, and the Committee on Fair Wages (1948) defined it. A living wage is the ideal level, higher than the fair wage. A real wage is the purchasing power of money wages. Only the minimum wage is tied to Aykroyd's calorie norm.
explanations: Incorrect: fair wage was conceptualised by the Committee on Fair Wages (1948), not by Aykroyd's nutrition formula.
Correct: Aykroyd's 2,700-calorie norm is a component of the need-based minimum wage fixed by the 15th ILC (1957).
Incorrect: a living wage is a higher, ideal standard that includes comforts and security. It is not what Aykroyd's formula determines.
Incorrect: real wage means the goods and services that money wages can buy. It has nothing to do with the formula.
keyfact: Aykroyd's 2,700-calorie norm is part of the need-based minimum wage fixed by the 15th Indian Labour Conference (1957).
option_notes: Fair wage: the wage between the minimum wage and the living wage. The Committee on Fair Wages (1948) under Justice Gajendragadkar's predecessor-era framework defined it. It depends on labour productivity, the prevailing rates of pay, the employer's capacity to pay and the national income level. Its three levels are the minimum wage as the floor, the living wage as the ceiling, and the fair wage in between.

Minimum wage: the lowest wage that must be paid to sustain the worker and the worker's family and preserve efficiency. The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 provides for fixing it, and the Code on Wages, 2019 now subsumes the Act. Need-based norms were set by the 15th ILC (1957) and supplemented by the Raptakos Brett case (1992). Both the Centre and the states can fix it for scheduled employments.

Living wage: a wage that gives the worker and the family a decent standard of living, including good food, housing, education, medical care and some insurance against old age. It is the upper limit in the wage hierarchy, and the Constitution's Article 43 directs the State to secure a living wage for workers. It is not yet legally enforceable.

Real wage: the purchasing power of the money wage, meaning the quantity of goods and services a worker can buy with it after adjusting for price changes. It is calculated by deflating the nominal wage with a price index such as the CPI-IW. It differs from the nominal (money) wage, which is the amount actually paid in currency.
related: The 15th ILC (1957) fixed need-based minimum wage norms.
Aykroyd's norm is 2,700 calories per adult consumption unit.
The standard family has 3 consumption units.
Raptakos Brett case (1992) added 25% for education, medical needs, recreation and old age.
Fair wage lies between the minimum wage and the living wage.
Article 43 directs the State to secure a living wage.
The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumed the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 and three other laws.
The Labour Bureau compiles the CPI-IW used for dearness allowance.
summary: The answer is (b) minimum wage. Dr. Wallace Aykroyd's formula links the minimum wage to a nutritional requirement, namely the minimum food (calorie) need of a worker. This was the basis used by the 15th Indian Labour Conference (1957) in its norms.
topic_notes: Wage concepts in India form a hierarchy: minimum wage at the bottom, then fair wage, then living wage at the top. The minimum wage covers bare subsistence, efficiency and some provision for education and medical needs. The fair wage depends on productivity, prevailing rates, capacity to pay and the national income level. The living wage ensures a decent life. Key sources: the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 (now merged in the Code on Wages, 2019, along with the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976). The Committee on Fair Wages (1948) classified wages into the three levels. The 15th Indian Labour Conference (1957) laid down the need-based minimum wage norms: 3 consumption units per family, 2,700 calories per unit (Aykroyd), 72 yards of cloth per year per family, housing rent as per the subsidised industrial housing scheme, and 20% for fuel, lighting and miscellaneous items. Raptakos Brett (1992) added 25% for children's education, medical needs, recreation and contingencies. Constitutional provisions: Article 43 (living wage, a DPSP), Article 39(d) (equal pay for equal work), Article 23 (forced labour prohibited), and Article 24 (child labour). The Code on Wages, 2019 introduces a statutory national floor wage, which the Centre fixes and below which states cannot set minimum wages. The Dearness Allowance (VDA) is linked to the CPI-IW, which is compiled by the Labour Bureau. Other related bodies: the Central Advisory Board on minimum wages, the Pay Commissions for government employees, and the Wage Boards for specific industries such as journalists.

question: “Everyone as a member of the society has the right to social security, and is entitled to realization through national efforts and international cooperation and in accordance with the organization and resources of each state of economic, social and cultural rights indispensable for his dignity and free development of his personality.” This statement which is emphasizing the importance of social * security has been expressed in which of the following?
options: Report of the First National Commission on Labour
Directive Principles of State Policy of the Indian Constitution
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Article 22 of the UDHR, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948 in Paris, states: 'Everyone, as a member of society, has the right to social security and is entitled to realization, through national effort and international co-operation and in accordance with the organization and resources of each State, of the economic, social and cultural rights indispensable for his dignity and the free development of his personality.' Article 25 adds the right to a standard of living adequate for health and well-being, including security in unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood and old age. Key cues in the quote are 'right', 'international cooperation' and 'resources of each state', which mark a universal human-rights text, not a labour-body or domestic document. The Philadelphia Declaration (1944) is an ILO aims-and-purposes statement that speaks of extending social security measures to provide a basic income and comprehensive medical care, and it does not use this wording. The First National Commission on Labour (1969, Chairman P.B. Gajendragadkar) reviewed Indian labour conditions and social security schemes. DPSPs (Articles 38, 39, 41, 42, 43, 47) direct the State and do not create an international 'right' in this phrasing.
explanations: Correct: the quotation is Article 22 of the UDHR (1948), which declares the right to social security.
Wrong: the Philadelphia Declaration (1944) is an ILO charter annex that sets out the organisation's aims and calls for extending social security measures. It does not contain this wording.
Wrong: the First National Commission on Labour (1969) was a domestic review body and did not originate this international-rights text.
Wrong: the DPSPs (Articles 41, 42, 43 and others) are non-justiciable state directives and do not use the phrases 'international cooperation' or 'free development of personality'.
keyfact: Article 22 of the UDHR (1948) declares that everyone, as a member of society, has the right to social security.
option_notes: The UDHR was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948 (observed as Human Rights Day), with Eleanor Roosevelt chairing the drafting committee. It has 30 articles covering civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights. It is not legally binding in itself, but it is the basis of the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966). Articles 22 and 25 deal with social security and an adequate standard of living.

The Declaration of Philadelphia was adopted in May 1944 at the 26th ILO Conference and later annexed to the ILO Constitution. It reaffirms that labour is not a commodity, that freedom of expression and association are essential, and that poverty anywhere endangers prosperity everywhere. It also commits the ILO to extending social security measures and comprehensive medical care.

The First National Commission on Labour was set up in 1966 under Justice P.B. Gajendragadkar and submitted its report in 1969. It reviewed wages, industrial relations, social security, and the working conditions of women and child labour. It recommended an integrated approach to social security. The Second National Commission on Labour, under Ravindra Varma, reported in 2002.

The Directive Principles in Part IV (Articles 36-51) are non-justiciable but fundamental to governance. Article 41 covers the right to work, education and public assistance in unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement. Article 42 covers just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Article 43 covers a living wage. Article 47 covers nutrition and public health. They were inspired by the Irish Constitution.
related: UDHR was adopted on 10 December 1948; Article 22 covers social security and Article 25 covers an adequate standard of living.
ILO Convention No. 102 (1952) sets minimum standards across nine branches of social security.
The Declaration of Philadelphia (1944) states that labour is not a commodity.
Article 9 of the ICESCR recognises the right to social security.
Entry 24 of the Concurrent List covers welfare of labour, including provident funds and pensions.
The Code on Social Security 2020 subsumes nine labour laws, including the EPF Act 1952 and the ESI Act 1948.
The Beveridge Report (1942) was the basis of the UK welfare state.
ILO Recommendation 202 (2012) concerns national social protection floors.
summary: The answer is (a) Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), 1948. The quoted words come almost verbatim from Article 22 of the UDHR, which recognises social security as a right of everyone as a member of society and links its realisation to national effort, international cooperation and each state's resources.
topic_notes: Social security has both an international and an Indian framework. Internationally, the key texts are the UDHR 1948 (Articles 22 and 25), the ILO Philadelphia Declaration 1944, ILO Convention No. 102 (Social Security, Minimum Standards, 1952), and the ICESCR 1966 (Article 9, the right to social security). The ILO also adopted Recommendation No. 202 (2012) on national social protection floors. Its conventions cover maternity protection (C103 and C183), employment injury (C121), invalidity, old age and survivors' benefits (C128), and medical care (C130). The Beveridge Report (1942) in the UK was a landmark that shaped the modern welfare state, and the US Social Security Act of 1935 was an early comprehensive law. In India, social security rests on the DPSPs (Articles 41, 42, 43, 47) and on Entry 24 of the Concurrent List (welfare of labour, including provident funds, employment injury, invalidity and old-age pensions, and maternity benefits). Main statutes are the Workmen's Compensation Act 1923 (now the Employees' Compensation Act), the ESI Act 1948, the EPF and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 1952, the Maternity Benefit Act 1961, and the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972. The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act 2008 covers informal workers. The Code on Social Security 2020 consolidates nine central laws. Schemes include the National Pension System, Atal Pension Yojana, PM-SYM, PMJJBY and PMSBY. The EPFO administers the EPF Scheme 1952, the EPS 1995 and the EDLI Scheme 1976.

question: For the first time in India, medical benefit as a non-cash benefit was provided under
subject: Social Security
detail: The Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 is India's first major social insurance legislation. It was enacted on 19 April 1948 and implemented first at Kanpur and Delhi on 24 February 1952. It covers factories and other establishments, now with 10 or more employees (20 in some states), where wages are within the prescribed ceiling (Rs 21,000 per month from 2017). It provides six benefits: sickness, maternity, disability (temporary and permanent), dependants' benefit, funeral expenses and medical benefit. Medical benefit is the in-kind benefit, covering full medical care for the insured person and, in the ESI scheme, his family, from the first day of employment. The ESI Corporation (ESIC) runs the scheme. It is financed by employer and employee contributions, and the state governments share the cost of medical care. The Factories Act, 1948 is a regulatory and welfare law that requires measures such as a first-aid box and an ambulance room, but it is not an insurance scheme. The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 gives paid leave, which is a cash benefit, plus a medical bonus. The Mines Act, 1952 regulates safety and health in mines. Eliminate (b), (c) and (d) as regulatory or cash-oriented laws.
explanations: Correct: the ESI Act, 1948 created the first statutory scheme giving insured workers medical care in kind, such as treatment, hospitalisation and medicines.
Incorrect: the Factories Act, 1948 regulates health, safety, working hours and welfare in factories. It is not an insurance scheme with medical benefits.
Incorrect: the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 mainly gives cash benefit as paid maternity leave, plus a small medical bonus. It was not the first Act to provide medical benefit.
Incorrect: the Mines Act, 1952 deals with safety, health, working hours and welfare in mines. It is not a social insurance law.
keyfact: ESI Act, 1948 was the first Indian law to give medical benefit in kind, and it was implemented from 1952.
option_notes: The Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 was enacted on 19 April 1948 and first implemented at Kanpur and Delhi on 24 February 1952. It is a contributory social insurance scheme run by the ESIC. It gives sickness, maternity, disability, dependants', funeral and medical benefits. The wage ceiling is Rs 21,000 per month (Rs 25,000 for persons with disability). It was inspired by the Beveridge report, and the ESIC is a statutory body.

The Factories Act, 1948 is a labour welfare and safety law that replaced the 1934 Act. It applies to premises with 10 or more workers using power, or 20 or more without power. It covers health, safety, welfare (canteen, crèche, first aid), working hours (48 per week, 9 per day), leave with wages and the employment of young persons and women. It is enforced by factory inspectors. The Chief Inspector of Factories heads enforcement in each state.

The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 regulates the employment of women in establishments for a period before and after childbirth. It provides paid maternity leave, raised from 12 to 26 weeks by the 2017 Amendment for the first two children. It also provides a medical bonus, a crèche facility for establishments with 50 or more employees, and work from home where possible. It is a cash-oriented benefit, and dismissal during maternity leave is prohibited.

The Mines Act, 1952 regulates the working conditions, health, safety and welfare of workers in mines. It replaced the Mines Act of 1923. It prescribes working hours (48 per week), the appointment of mine managers, inspectors and committees, and welfare measures such as drinking water, first aid and canteens. It is administered by the Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS) under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, and it is a regulatory law rather than an insurance scheme.
related: ESI Act was passed in 1948 and first implemented at Kanpur and Delhi in 1952.
The Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 was India's first social security law and gave cash compensation.
The Adarkar Plan (1944) proposed health insurance for industrial workers.
The ESI wage ceiling is Rs 21,000 per month.
The ESIC contribution rate is 3.25% from the employer and 0.75% from the employee.
The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 raised paid leave to 26 weeks.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes nine laws including the ESI and EPF Acts.
The EPF Act was passed in 1952.
summary: The answer is (a) the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948. It was the first Indian law to provide medical benefit as a non-cash (in-kind) benefit, meaning medical treatment and care for insured workers and their families. The other Acts deal mainly with safety, welfare or cash maternity benefit.
topic_notes: Social security in India developed gradually. The Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 was the first law on employer liability for injury at work, and it gave cash compensation. The ESI Act, 1948 was the first comprehensive social insurance law, covering medical care and cash benefits. It followed the Adarkar Plan (1944), prepared by Prof. B.P. Adarkar, which recommended health insurance for industrial workers. The ESI Corporation is the apex body, and the Union Labour Minister is its chairman. The Standing Committee is its executive body, and the Medical Benefit Council advises it. Contributions: the employer pays 3.25% and the employee 0.75% of wages (a total of 4%, as revised in 2019). Employees earning up to Rs 176 per day are exempt from the employee share. Benefits: sickness benefit is about 70% of wages for up to 91 days a year; maternity benefit is 100% of wages for 26 weeks; disability benefit is 90% of wages; dependants' benefit is 90% of wages; and funeral expenses are up to Rs 15,000. Other major social security laws include the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 (EPFO), the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 and the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 (renamed from the Workmen's Compensation Act in 2009). The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes nine Acts, including the ESI and EPF Acts. UPSC often asks about the first Act of its type, coverage thresholds, the benefit types and the ESIC's structure.

question: Which one of the following is the correct set of contingencies identified by William Beveridge in his comprehensive social security scheme?
options: Want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness
Want, sickness, disability, squalor and idleness
Want, disease, old age, squalor and unemployment
Disease, invalidity, old age, unemployment and ignorance
subject: Social Security
detail: Sir William Beveridge chaired the inter-departmental Committee on Social Insurance and Allied Services, and its report was published in November 1942 in Britain during the Second World War. The report named five Giant Evils on the road to reconstruction: Want (poverty), Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness (unemployment). Each was matched with a remedy: Want by social insurance and national assistance; Disease by a National Health Service; Ignorance by education reform; Squalor by housing and town planning; Idleness by full employment policy. The report rested on three assumptions: a children's allowance, comprehensive health and rehabilitation services, and maintenance of employment. Its principles were universality, uniform flat-rate contributions and benefits, unification of administration, adequacy of benefits, comprehensiveness and classification. It shaped the post-war Labour government's welfare state, including the National Insurance Act 1946, the National Health Service Act 1946 (NHS began in 1948) and the National Assistance Act 1948. Elimination: option (a) is the only one with all five evils in their exact form. (b), (c) and (d) mix in terms like sickness, disability, old age or invalidity, which are social security branches, not Beveridge's five evils.
explanations: Correct: it lists exactly the five Giant Evils named by Beveridge: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness.
Incorrect: 'sickness' and 'disability' are risks covered by social insurance, not Beveridge's named evils; Ignorance is missing.
Incorrect: 'old age' and 'unemployment' are contingencies covered by insurance benefits, and Ignorance and Idleness as named evils are missing.
Incorrect: invalidity, old age and unemployment are insurance contingencies; Want, Squalor and Idleness as evils are missing from this set.
keyfact: Beveridge Report (1942): five Giant Evils = Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor, Idleness.
option_notes: Beveridge's Five Giant Evils from the 1942 report: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor, Idleness. Each was to be tackled by a particular policy: social insurance, health service, education, housing and employment policy. The report is the foundation of the British welfare state and is also called the Beveridge Report.

'Want, sickness, disability, squalor and idleness' is a distractor mixing the evils with insurance risks. Sickness and disability are covered by benefits in the Beveridge scheme, such as sickness and disability benefit, but they are not the named evils. The correct term is Disease, and Ignorance is omitted here.

'Want, disease, old age, squalor and unemployment' is a distractor. Old age is covered by retirement pensions under the Beveridge scheme, and unemployment is the same as Idleness in meaning but not in his wording. Ignorance, one of the five evils, is missing.

'Disease, invalidity, old age, unemployment and ignorance' combines insurance contingencies, similar to those in ILO Convention 102 (1952), with one evil. ILO Convention 102 lists nine branches of social security, including medical care, sickness, unemployment, old age, employment injury, family, maternity, invalidity and survivors' benefits.
related: Beveridge Report 1942 is titled 'Social Insurance and Allied Services'.
The Five Giant Evils are Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness.
Beveridge's report led to the NHS in Britain in 1948.
ILO Convention 102 (1952) sets minimum standards for nine branches of social security.
Bismarck introduced the first social insurance in Germany in 1883.
The US Social Security Act was passed in 1935.
The ESI Act 1948 was influenced by Adarkar's 1944 report on health insurance.
Code on Social Security 2020 subsumes nine labour laws including the EPF Act and ESI Act.
summary: The correct answer is (a): Want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. These are the 'Five Giant Evils' that the Beveridge Report (Social Insurance and Allied Services, 1942) proposed to attack through a comprehensive, universal social security system.
topic_notes: The Beveridge Report, officially 'Social Insurance and Allied Services', was published in December 1942 (some sources say November) under Sir William Beveridge, an economist and Liberal. It proposed a comprehensive scheme of social insurance 'from the cradle to the grave', financed by flat-rate contributions from workers, employers and the state. Its three assumptions were children's allowances, a national health service and full employment. Its six principles were flat-rate subsistence benefit, flat-rate contribution, unification of administrative responsibility, adequacy of benefit, comprehensiveness and classification. The report led to the post-war Labour government under Clement Attlee passing the Family Allowances Act 1945, the National Insurance (Industrial Injuries) Act 1946, the National Insurance Act 1946, the National Health Service Act 1946 and the National Assistance Act 1948. Other related landmarks in social security history: Germany under Bismarck introduced the first modern social insurance (Sickness Insurance 1883, Accident Insurance 1884, Old Age and Invalidity 1889); the US Social Security Act of 1935; the New Zealand Social Security Act 1938; the ILO Philadelphia Declaration 1944; the Universal Declaration of Human Rights 1948 (Article 22 and 25); and ILO Convention 102, the Social Security (Minimum Standards) Convention, 1952. In India, relevant laws include the Workmen's Compensation Act 1923, the ESI Act 1948, the EPF & MP Act 1952, the Maternity Benefit Act 1961, the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 and the Code on Social Security 2020. The Bhore Committee (1946) and the Adarkar Report (1944) were Indian parallels to the Beveridge approach.

question: Which one of the following statements is not correct for Atal Pension Yojana?
options: There is guaranteed minimum monthly pension for the subscribers ranging between * 1, 000 and * 5, 000 per month
The benefit of minimum pension would be guaranteed by the Government of India
Government of India co-contributes 50% of the subscriber’s contribution or *1, 000 per annum, whichever is lower
It is applicable to all citizens of India aged above 40 years
subject: Social Security
detail: Atal Pension Yojana was launched on 9 May 2015 (announced in the Budget 2015-16 speech) and is administered by PFRDA through the National Pension System architecture. It targets workers in the unorganised sector. Eligibility: Indian citizen aged 18-40 years, holding a savings bank or post office account, with a mobile number (Aadhaar was the preferred identifier). The subscriber chooses a fixed monthly pension of Rs 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 or 5,000, payable from age 60. The contribution depends on the entry age and the chosen pension, so a younger entrant pays less. The Government guarantees the minimum pension; if returns fall short, it funds the gap, and if returns are higher the subscriber gets the higher benefit. Government co-contribution was 50% of the subscriber's contribution or Rs 1,000 per year, whichever is lower, for those who joined between 1 June 2015 and 31 March 2016 and were not income-tax payers or members of any statutory social security scheme, for five years. After the subscriber's death the spouse receives the pension, and then the nominee receives the accumulated corpus. Since 1 October 2022, income-tax payers are not eligible. Option (d) is wrong because it sets a lower age limit of 40 instead of an upper limit of 40.
explanations: Correct statement, so not the answer: APY offers guaranteed monthly pensions of Rs 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 or 5,000 from age 60.
Correct statement, so not the answer: the Government of India guarantees the minimum pension amount, covering any shortfall in returns.
Correct statement, so not the answer: the co-contribution was 50% of the subscriber's contribution or Rs 1,000 per year, whichever is lower, for the first five years for eligible early joiners.
Incorrect statement, so it is the answer: APY is for citizens aged 18-40 years, not those above 40, and it is not available to all citizens without conditions.
keyfact: APY: ages 18-40 only, pension Rs 1,000-5,000 from age 60, government-guaranteed, run by PFRDA; 'above 40' is wrong.
option_notes: Guaranteed pension slabs: the subscriber picks Rs 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 or 5,000 per month, payable from age 60. The contribution depends on entry age and chosen slab. The minimum contribution period is 20 years, so someone joining at 40 pays for 20 years. The amount is fixed at the time of joining, though the subscriber can later move to a higher or lower slab.

The Government of India guarantees the minimum pension. If the corpus built from contributions cannot sustain the promised pension, the government funds the gap. If returns are higher, the subscriber gets the higher pension. PFRDA runs the scheme, and the Pension Fund Managers invest the corpus under NPS norms. On the subscriber's death the spouse continues to get the pension, and the nominee receives the corpus after both have died.

Government co-contribution: 50% of the subscriber's contribution or Rs 1,000 per year, whichever is lower. It applied for five years to subscribers who joined between 1 June 2015 and 31 March 2016. They had to be non-members of any statutory social security scheme and not income-tax payers. The co-contribution has since ended for new joiners, so the scheme now runs on subscriber contributions with the government guarantee.

This is the incorrect statement. The eligibility age is 18-40 years, so people above 40 cannot join. The applicant must be an Indian citizen with a savings bank or post office account and a mobile number. Since 1 October 2022, income-tax payers cannot join. The scheme replaced the Swavalamban Yojana and targets unorganised-sector workers.
related: APY was launched on 9 May 2015 and is administered by PFRDA.
APY eligibility: Indian citizens aged 18-40 with a bank or post office savings account.
APY pension slabs: Rs 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 or 5,000 per month from age 60.
Minimum contribution period under APY is 20 years.
PMSBY: Rs 2 lakh accident cover at Rs 12 a year, ages 18-70.
PMJJBY: Rs 2 lakh life cover at Rs 330 a year, ages 18-50.
Income-tax payers are ineligible for APY from 1 October 2022.
PM Shram Yogi Maandhan offers Rs 3,000 monthly pension, entry age 18-40.
summary: The answer is (d). Atal Pension Yojana (APY) is open to Indian citizens aged 18 to 40 years, not to everyone above 40. The other three statements match the scheme's design: guaranteed pension of Rs 1,000-5,000, a government guarantee, and 50% co-contribution capped at Rs 1,000 per year.
topic_notes: Atal Pension Yojana is a defined-benefit-style, government-guaranteed pension scheme for unorganised-sector workers, launched on 9 May 2015 in Kolkata by the Prime Minister. It is run by PFRDA (Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority) under the NPS framework and replaced the Swavalamban Yojana. Key features: entry age 18-40; exit at 60; minimum 20 years of contribution; pension slabs of Rs 1,000 to 5,000 per month; contributions are auto-debited from the savings account, monthly, quarterly or half-yearly; a late-payment penalty applies (Rs 1 per Rs 100 per month contribution, varying by amount). Government co-contribution of 50% or Rs 1,000 a year applied for five years to early joiners. Death benefits: the spouse gets the same pension, and after both die the nominee gets the accumulated corpus. Premature exit is allowed only in exceptional cases such as terminal illness or death. Since 1 October 2022, income-tax payers are not eligible. Related schemes announced in Budget 2015-16: Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (accident insurance, Rs 2 lakh cover, premium Rs 12 a year for ages 18-70) and Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (life cover of Rs 2 lakh, premium Rs 330 a year, ages 18-50). Other pension schemes: NPS (launched 2004 for government employees and opened to all citizens in 2009), PM Shram Yogi Maandhan (2019, Rs 3,000 pension for unorganised workers aged 18-40) and the Employees' Pension Scheme 1995 under EPFO. UPSC may ask about the eligibility age, the administering body, the pension slabs, the nature of the guarantee, or comparisons with other schemes.

ocr: Which one of the following is the amount of annual premium of the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY) for accident and disability cover up to ¥ 2,00,000? (a) * 100 (b) ® 50 (c) ® 20 (da) #12 28 GRS-A-TNS/68-A Directions : The following two (2) items consist of two statements, Statement I and Statement II. Examine these two statements carefully and select the correct answer using the code given below. Code : (a) Both the statements are individually true and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I (b) Both the statements are individually true but Statement II is not the co
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: PMSBY is a government-backed pure accident insurance scheme announced in the Union Budget 2015-16 and launched on 9 May 2015 at Kolkata, along with the Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) and the Atal Pension Yojana (APY). It is open to bank account holders aged 18 to 70 years, and enrolment needs an Aadhaar-linked savings account with auto-debit consent. It is a one-year renewable cover running from 1 June to 31 May. The benefit is ₹2 lakh for accidental death or total permanent disability (loss of both eyes, both hands or feet, or one eye and one hand/foot), and ₹1 lakh for partial permanent disability (loss of one eye, one hand or one foot). The premium was ₹12 per year at launch, auto-debited in one instalment from the account, and was raised to ₹20 per year with effect from 1 June 2022. The scheme is offered through banks and public/private general insurers. In the exam, the options ₹100 and ₹50 are too high for this scheme, and ₹20 is the later revised figure and not the one applicable at the time of the 2017 paper. So ₹12 is the answer.
explanations: Incorrect: ₹100 is far above the PMSBY premium. It is not the premium of any of the three 2015 social security schemes.
Incorrect: ₹50 was never the PMSBY premium. It does not match the original or the revised figure.
Incorrect as per the 2017 key: ₹20 is the premium after the revision effective 1 June 2022. At the time of the paper, and per the official answer, the premium was ₹12.
Correct: ₹12 per annum was the PMSBY premium from launch in 2015, giving ₹2 lakh cover for accidental death or total disability.
keyfact: PMSBY: ₹12 a year at launch (2015), later ₹20 from June 2022; ₹2 lakh cover for death/total disability, ₹1 lakh for partial; age 18-70.
option_notes: ₹100: Not linked to PMSBY. For comparison, PMJJBY (life cover of ₹2 lakh) cost ₹330 a year at launch, later ₹436, and APY has contribution slabs by age and pension amount. A ₹100 premium matches no major 2015 scheme premium, so treat it as a distractor.

₹50: Not a premium in the Jan Suraksha family. The Jan Suraksha schemes were designed with very low premiums so that poor households could afford them, with auto-debit from savings accounts. ₹50 is a distractor figure and does not represent PMSBY at any point.

₹20: This is the revised PMSBY premium, effective 1 June 2022, raised from ₹12 for the first time since 2015. Note that PMJJBY was revised from ₹330 to ₹436 at the same time. The cover amounts stayed unchanged: ₹2 lakh for death or total disability and ₹1 lakh for partial disability.

₹12: The original PMSBY premium from 9 May 2015 until May 2022. It is auto-debited annually from the subscriber's bank account, about ₹1 a month. The cover is ₹2 lakh for accidental death or total permanent disability and ₹1 lakh for partial permanent disability, for ages 18-70.
related: PMSBY launched 9 May 2015 at Kolkata along with PMJJBY and APY.
PMSBY eligibility: age 18-70 with a bank account.
PMSBY partial permanent disability cover: ₹1 lakh.
PMSBY premium raised from ₹12 to ₹20 from 1 June 2022.
PMJJBY premium revised from ₹330 to ₹436 in 2022; cover ₹2 lakh.
APY is administered by PFRDA and offers pension of ₹1,000-₹5,000 per month.
Cover year for PMSBY and PMJJBY: 1 June to 31 May.
summary: The answer is (d) ₹12. Under the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY), launched in 2015, the annual premium is ₹12 per subscriber for accidental death and disability cover up to ₹2,00,000. (As of 2022 the premium was revised to ₹20, but the 2017 paper's official answer is ₹12.)
topic_notes: PMSBY belongs to the Jan Suraksha group of schemes announced in Budget 2015-16 by Finance Minister Arun Jaitley and launched by PM Narendra Modi on 9 May 2015 in Kolkata. The three schemes are PMSBY (accident insurance), PMJJBY (life insurance) and Atal Pension Yojana (pension). PMSBY: eligible age 18-70, requires a bank or post office savings account, with Aadhaar as the primary KYC. Cover period is 1 June to 31 May and renews annually; premium is auto-debited around May. Benefits: ₹2 lakh for death, total loss of both eyes, or loss of use of both hands or feet, or loss of one eye and one hand/foot; ₹1 lakh for loss of one eye, one hand or one foot. Premium was ₹12 until 2022, then ₹20. Cover ceases at age 70, if the account is closed, or if the person holds multiple accounts with insufficient funds (a person can be covered by only one account). Administered through public sector general insurers and other insurers tied up with banks. PMJJBY: ages 18-50 (cover continues to 55 if continued), ₹2 lakh on death from any cause, premium ₹330 initially and ₹436 now. APY: ages 18-40, guaranteed pension of ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 per month from age 60, administered by PFRDA; the government co-contribution was for those who joined before 31 March 2016 (and not in a statutory social security scheme) for five years. Related: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (August 2014) provided the base of bank accounts. Other angles UPSC may test: launch date and place, age limits, the cover amounts for partial disability, the premium revision, the administering bodies, and the nodal ministry (Ministry of Finance, Department of Financial Services).

ocr: Statement I: The force on Moon due to Earth is the action, while the force on Earth due to Moon is the reaction. Statement II : To every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
subject: General Science
detail: Statement I applies Newton's third law to the Earth-Moon system. The Earth pulls the Moon with a gravitational force, and the Moon pulls the Earth with a force of equal magnitude in the opposite direction, F = GMm/r². Statement II is the third law itself: forces always occur in pairs, acting on two different bodies, equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and of the same type (here both gravitational). Statement I is therefore a direct instance of Statement II, so II explains I. Two points are worth noting. First, which force is called 'action' and which 'reaction' is arbitrary, because neither comes first in time; they act simultaneously. Second, the forces are equal, but the accelerations are not, because a = F/m. The Moon's acceleration is large and the Earth's is tiny, so the Earth looks almost stationary. Action and reaction never cancel each other because they act on different bodies. The usual pattern for Assertion-Reason questions applies: check each statement for truth, then check whether the second is the correct explanation of the first. Here both checks pass.
explanations: Correct. Both statements are true, and the third law in Statement II is exactly what explains the Earth-Moon force pair in Statement I.
Wrong. This option says both are true but II is not the explanation of I. In fact II is the general law and I is its specific example, so II does explain I.
Wrong. This option says I is true and II is false. Statement II is a true statement of Newton's third law.
Wrong. This option says I is false and II is true. Statement I is true, since the Earth-Moon gravitational forces are an action-reaction pair.
keyfact: Newton's third law: action and reaction are equal, opposite, act on different bodies, and the Earth-Moon gravitational pair is an example.
option_notes: Both statements are true and II is the correct explanation of I. This is the standard first option in Assertion-Reason questions. To choose it, verify each statement independently, then confirm that the second gives the reason for the first. Here Newton's third law (II) gives the reason for the equal and opposite Earth-Moon forces (I). It is the official answer.

Both statements are true but II is not the correct explanation of I. This option applies when two true facts are only loosely related, for example 'the Moon has no atmosphere' and 'the Moon's gravity is one-sixth of the Earth's'. It is wrong here because the third law directly accounts for the Earth-Moon force pair.

Statement I is true and II is false. This option suits a case where a correct observation is paired with a wrong principle. It is wrong here because Statement II is a true statement of Newton's third law, so it cannot be called false.

Statement I is false and II is true. This suits a case where a general law is true but the example given breaks it. It is wrong here because the example is valid: the Earth and Moon do exert equal and opposite gravitational forces on each other.
related: Newton's third law: forces are equal and opposite and act on different bodies.
Action and reaction never cancel because they act on different bodies.
Gravitational force F = GMm/r²; G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg².
Newton's second law: F = dp/dt = ma for constant mass.
Rocket propulsion and gun recoil follow the third law and momentum conservation.
Escape velocity of the Earth is 11.2 km/s.
Moon's surface gravity is about one-sixth of the Earth's.
SI unit of force is the newton; the CGS unit is the dyne.
statements: Statement I — Correct: the Earth's pull on the Moon and the Moon's pull on the Earth form an action-reaction pair. Gravitation is a mutual attraction between two masses, given by F = GMm/r², with G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg². The pair acts along the line joining the centres, with equal magnitude and opposite direction, and each force acts on a different body. Tides arise from the Moon's pull on the Earth. The Earth-Moon distance is about 3.84 lakh km. Which force is the action and which the reaction is only a matter of naming.

Statement II — Correct: this is Newton's third law of motion, published in the Principia (1687). Forces come in pairs that act on different bodies, are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, simultaneous, and of the same nature. Because they act on different bodies, they do not cancel. Examples are a rocket's thrust, a gun's recoil, walking (the ground pushes us forward), and a swimmer pushing water back. Momentum conservation follows from the third law. Newton's first law defines inertia, and the second law gives F = ma.
summary: Option (a) is the official answer: both statements are true and Statement II correctly explains Statement I. The Earth-Moon gravitational pair is an action-reaction pair under Newton's third law, which says every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
topic_notes: Newton's laws of motion (Principia, 1687) are a core part of General Science. The first law, the law of inertia, says a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless an external force acts on it. The second law says force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = dp/dt, which reduces to F = ma for constant mass. The SI unit of force is the newton (kg m/s²). The third law says forces occur in equal and opposite pairs acting on different bodies. Key points: action and reaction are simultaneous, of the same type, and do not cancel because they act on different bodies. Applications include rocket propulsion, gun recoil, jet engines, walking, rowing a boat, and a balloon releasing air. Conservation of linear momentum follows from the second and third laws: in the absence of external force, total momentum stays constant. Universal gravitation: F = GMm/r². G was measured by Cavendish (1798). g = 9.8 m/s² on Earth, and the Moon's gravity is about 1/6 of the Earth's. Weight changes with location, while mass does not. Impulse equals force times time and equals the change in momentum. Common confusions UPSC may test: equal forces do not mean equal accelerations, since a = F/m. A horse-cart paradox arises because the pairs act on different bodies. Normal force and weight on a table are not a third-law pair; the pair for weight is the body's pull on the Earth. Other angles: friction, centripetal force, circular motion, Kepler's laws, escape velocity (11.2 km/s for the Earth), and satellite orbital velocity (about 7.9 km/s near the surface).

ocr: Statement I : It is a common observation that if we place a glass of ice-water on a table at room temperature, the ice-water will get warmer. Statement II : Heat is energy that flows between a system and its environment because of temperature difference between them.
subject: General Science
detail: Heat is energy in transit that flows spontaneously from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature. It is not a property stored in a body; what a body holds is internal (thermal) energy. A glass of ice-water on a table at room temperature (about 25-30 °C) is colder than the air, so the surroundings transfer heat to it by conduction through the glass, convection in the air and radiation. The ice absorbs this heat first as latent heat of fusion (about 334 J/g), so the mixture stays near 0 °C while ice remains. Once all the ice has melted, the water's temperature rises until it reaches room temperature, i.e. thermal equilibrium, when net heat flow stops. This is consistent with the Zeroth Law (thermal equilibrium) and the Second Law (Clausius statement: heat does not flow spontaneously from cold to hot). Elimination logic: Statement I is an everyday observation and is true. Statement II is the standard definition of heat and is true. The reason the ice-water warms is precisely the temperature difference driving heat flow, so II explains I. Hence option (a), not (b), which applies when II is true but is not the explanation.
explanations: Correct: both statements are true, and II (heat flows due to temperature difference) is the exact reason the cold ice-water warms in a warmer room.
Wrong: this option applies when both are true but II does not explain I. Here II does explain I.
Wrong: Statement I is true, since it is a common observation that ice-water warms up at room temperature.
Wrong: Statement II is true, as it is the standard definition of heat, so the option claiming it is false is incorrect.
keyfact: Heat is energy that flows because of a temperature difference, so cold ice-water in a warm room absorbs heat and warms up until equilibrium.
option_notes: Option (a): both statements are individually true and II is the correct explanation of I. This is the standard assertion-reason (statement-based) format in UPSC papers. Here the causal link is temperature difference driving heat flow, as in Newton's law of cooling, where the rate of heat exchange is proportional to the temperature difference with the surroundings.

Option (b): both statements are true but II is not the correct explanation of I. This is the choice used when the two are independently valid but unrelated causally, for example if II talked about specific heat while I talked about melting. It does not apply here because the temperature difference is the cause.

Option (c): Statement I is true and Statement II is false. This would be correct only if the definition of heat given were wrong, for example if heat were described as a property stored in a body or as flowing from cold to hot. The definition here is correct.

Option (d): Statement I is false and Statement II is true. This would require that ice-water does not warm in a warm room, which contradicts experience and the Second Law. Ice-water always moves toward equilibrium with its surroundings.
related: Heat flows spontaneously from higher to lower temperature (Clausius statement).
Zeroth Law of thermodynamics defines thermal equilibrium and temperature.
Latent heat of fusion of ice is about 334 J/g (80 cal/g).
Water has maximum density at 4 °C.
1 calorie = 4.186 joule.
Radiation is the only mode of heat transfer that needs no medium.
Newton's law of cooling: cooling rate is proportional to temperature difference with surroundings.
Specific heat of water (4.186 J/g·K) is unusually high.
statements: Statement I — Correct: ice-water at a lower temperature than its surroundings absorbs heat and warms up. Facts: the temperature of an ice-water mixture stays near 0 °C until all the ice melts, because the heat absorbed goes into latent heat of fusion (about 334 J/g or 80 cal/g). After that the water warms toward room temperature. Final state is thermal equilibrium, with no net heat flow. Heat transfer happens by conduction, convection and radiation.

Statement II — Correct: heat is energy that flows between a system and its environment because of a temperature difference. Facts: heat is energy in transit, not a stored quantity, and is a path function. SI unit is the joule (1 cal = 4.186 J). Direction of flow is from hot to cold (Clausius statement of the Second Law). Heat is distinct from temperature, which measures average kinetic energy of particles, and from internal energy. It explains Statement I directly.
summary: The official answer is (a): both statements are true and Statement II correctly explains Statement I. Ice-water at a temperature lower than the room's gains heat from the surroundings because of the temperature difference, so it warms up.
topic_notes: Heat and temperature are core thermodynamics topics. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; its SI unit is the joule, with the calorie as a common unit (1 cal = 4.186 J). Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules; SI unit is the kelvin (K = °C + 273.15). Modes of transfer: conduction (solids, needs contact, e.g. metal rod), convection (fluids, bulk movement, e.g. sea breeze), radiation (electromagnetic waves, needs no medium, e.g. sunlight). Laws: Zeroth Law defines thermal equilibrium and temperature; First Law is conservation of energy (ΔU = Q − W); Second Law (Kelvin-Planck and Clausius) gives the direction of heat flow and entropy increase; Third Law says entropy tends to a constant as T approaches absolute zero. Latent heat: fusion of ice about 334 J/g (80 cal/g); vaporisation of water about 2260 J/g (540 cal/g). Specific heat of water is 4.186 J/g·K, which is high and moderates coastal climates. Newton's law of cooling: the rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference. Black bodies are ideal absorbers and emitters; Stefan-Boltzmann law says E is proportional to T⁴; Wien's law says λmax·T is constant. Water has maximum density at 4 °C. Thermos flask minimises all three modes of transfer. Likely UPSC angles: difference between heat and temperature, heat flow direction, latent heat, thermal equilibrium, and calorimetry.

question: Which one of the following materials is mot diamagnetic at Standard Temperature and Pressure (STP)?
subject: General Science
detail: Diamagnetism is a universal, weak property of all matter. When an external magnetic field is applied, it induces a magnetic moment that opposes the field (Lenz's law), so the material is weakly repelled. Substances whose atoms, ions or molecules have all electrons paired show only diamagnetism. Paramagnetic materials have unpaired electrons and are weakly attracted to a field. Their susceptibility is small and positive, and it falls as temperature rises (Curie's law). Ferromagnetic materials (iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium at low temperature) have strongly interacting unpaired spins that line up in domains, giving very large positive susceptibility and permanent magnetism. Ferromagnetism disappears above the Curie temperature, which is 770 °C for iron. At STP (0 °C, 1 atm) iron is well below this, so it is ferromagnetic. Elimination logic: N2 has a triple bond with all electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic. NaCl consists of Na+ and Cl- ions with closed shells, so it is diamagnetic. H2O has all electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic. Only iron is not diamagnetic. Note that O2 is a common trap, because it is paramagnetic.
explanations: Wrong: N2 has all electrons paired in its molecular orbitals (bond order 3), so it is diamagnetic.
Wrong: NaCl contains Na+ and Cl- ions with closed noble-gas shells, so it is diamagnetic.
Wrong: Water has all electrons paired and is diamagnetic; this is why a strong magnet can slightly repel water and even levitate a frog.
Correct: Iron has unpaired 3d electrons and forms magnetic domains, so it is ferromagnetic, which is not diamagnetic, at STP.
keyfact: Iron is ferromagnetic (Curie temperature 770 °C), while N2, NaCl and H2O, with all electrons paired, are diamagnetic.
option_notes: Nitrogen (N2) is a colourless, odourless diatomic gas that makes up about 78% of air. It has a triple bond and all its electrons are paired, so it is diamagnetic. Liquid nitrogen boils at -196 °C. It is used in cryogenics and fertilisers (Haber process for ammonia) and as an inert atmosphere.

Sodium chloride (NaCl) is common salt, an ionic compound with an fcc rock-salt structure (6:6 coordination). Both Na+ and Cl- have closed-shell configurations, so it is diamagnetic. Its melting point is about 801 °C. It is also the raw material for the chlor-alkali industry, which makes NaOH, Cl2 and H2.

Water (H2O) is a bent polar molecule with an H-O-H angle of about 104.5°. All its electrons are paired, so it is weakly diamagnetic, with a susceptibility of about -9×10^-6. It has maximum density at 4 °C and a high specific heat. Strong magnetic fields can make water levitate, as in Geim's frog experiment (Nobel Prize 2010 for graphene).

Iron (Fe, atomic number 26, configuration [Ar]3d6 4s2) has four unpaired electrons. It is ferromagnetic below its Curie temperature of 770 °C (1043 K) and becomes paramagnetic above it. Its main ores are haematite and magnetite. Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon. Iron is the basis of electromagnets, transformer cores and permanent magnets.
related: Bismuth is the most strongly diamagnetic of the common metals.
Oxygen is paramagnetic because it has two unpaired electrons in its π* orbitals.
Curie temperature of iron is 770 °C.
Superconductors are perfect diamagnets (Meissner effect).
Ferromagnetic materials: Fe, Co, Ni, Gd.
Soft iron is used for electromagnets and transformer cores because of low retentivity.
Paramagnetic susceptibility varies inversely with temperature (Curie's law).
Diamagnetism is present in all materials.
summary: The answer is (d) Iron. Iron is ferromagnetic at STP because of unpaired 3d electrons that form aligned magnetic domains, whereas nitrogen, sodium chloride and water have all electrons paired and are diamagnetic. (The question's 'mot' is an OCR typo for 'not'.)
topic_notes: Magnetic materials are classified by their response to an applied field. Diamagnetic: all electrons paired, weakly repelled, small negative susceptibility, independent of temperature. Examples: water, copper, gold, silver, bismuth (strongest), NaCl, N2, diamond, graphite and superconductors (perfect diamagnets, which show the Meissner effect). Paramagnetic: unpaired electrons, weakly attracted, small positive susceptibility inversely proportional to temperature (Curie's law). Examples: aluminium, sodium, platinum, O2, Cu2+ and Fe3+ ions, liquid oxygen (attracted to a magnet). Ferromagnetic: strong attraction, domains, hysteresis, retains magnetism, and turns paramagnetic above the Curie temperature. Examples: Fe, Co, Ni, Gd and alloys such as alnico. Ferromagnets with high retentivity and coercivity (steel) make permanent magnets. Soft iron has low retentivity and coercivity, so it suits electromagnets and transformer cores. Antiferromagnetic: spins aligned oppositely and cancelling, for example MnO. Ferrimagnetic: unequal opposite moments, for example Fe3O4 (magnetite) and ferrites. Related ideas: magnetic susceptibility (χ) and permeability (μr = 1+χ). Curie's law gives χ ∝ 1/T, and the Curie-Weiss law applies above the Curie point. The Curie temperatures are Fe 770 °C, Ni 358 °C and Co 1115 °C. Earth's magnetism arises from the liquid outer core, not from permanent ferromagnetism, because the core is above the Curie temperature. UPSC may ask which gas is paramagnetic (O2, NO) or which metal is diamagnetic (Cu, Zn, Bi).

question: Which one of the following gases has the highest solubility in water?
subject: General Science
detail: Gas solubility in water depends on polarity, hydrogen bonding, chemical reaction with water, temperature and pressure (Henry's law: solubility is proportional to partial pressure; solubility falls as temperature rises). Ammonia (NH3) is polar, has a lone pair on nitrogen and forms hydrogen bonds with water. It also reacts reversibly: NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-. At 0 degrees C about 90 g of NH3 dissolves in 100 g of water, and about 700 volumes of gas dissolve in 1 volume of water at 20 degrees C. Chlorine is non-polar but reacts partly with water to give HCl and HOCl, so it dissolves only about 0.7 g per 100 mL (roughly 2-3 volumes per volume). CO2 is non-polar, dissolves about 1 volume per volume at 20 degrees C and forms a little carbonic acid. Nitrogen is non-polar, inert and has very low solubility (about 0.02 volume per volume). Elimination: pick the polar, hydrogen-bonding gas, which is ammonia. Nitrogen is the least soluble, with chlorine and CO2 in between.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Chlorine is non-polar and only partly reacts with water to form chlorine water, so its solubility is modest, about 2-3 volumes per volume of water.
(b) Correct: Ammonia is polar, hydrogen-bonds with water and ionises to NH4+ and OH-, giving about 700 volumes per volume of water, the highest of the four.
(c) Wrong: CO2 is non-polar and dissolves only about 1 volume per volume at ordinary temperature and pressure. Only a small fraction forms carbonic acid.
(d) Wrong: Nitrogen is non-polar and chemically inert, so it is very sparingly soluble, about 0.02 volume per volume. It is the least soluble of the four.
keyfact: Ammonia is the most soluble common gas in water, about 700 volumes per volume, because of hydrogen bonding and reaction with water.
option_notes: Chlorine (Cl2) is a greenish-yellow, poisonous gas and a halogen. Atomic number 17. It is prepared by the electrolysis of brine (the chlor-alkali process). It is used in water disinfection, bleaching powder and PVC. It dissolves in water to give chlorine water containing HCl and HOCl, and it is a strong oxidising and bleaching agent. It was used as a chemical weapon in World War I.

Ammonia (NH3) is a colourless gas with a pungent smell and a pyramidal shape, and it acts as a Lewis base. It is manufactured by the Haber-Bosch process: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, with an iron catalyst and molybdenum promoter, at about 200 atm and 450-500 degrees C. It is used for urea, fertilisers and refrigeration. Its aqueous solution is called liquor ammonia and is weakly basic.

Carbon dioxide (CO2) is a linear, non-polar gas and the main greenhouse gas. It makes up about 0.04% of the atmosphere. Solid CO2 is called dry ice, which sublimes at -78 degrees C. It is used in fire extinguishers, aerated drinks (under pressure), and photosynthesis uses it. It turns lime water milky because it forms CaCO3. It forms weak carbonic acid in water.

Nitrogen (N2) makes up about 78% of air by volume. It is a colourless, odourless, inert gas because of the strong N≡N triple bond. It is used in ammonia manufacture, as liquid nitrogen for cryogenics, and for inert packaging. It is fixed by Rhizobium in legume root nodules and by lightning. It has very low solubility in water. Decompression sickness (the bends) in divers is caused by dissolved nitrogen.
related: Henry's law: gas solubility is proportional to its partial pressure at constant temperature.
Gas solubility in water decreases as temperature rises.
Haber process makes NH3 from N2 and H2 with an iron catalyst.
NH3 is dried with quicklime (CaO), not with conc. H2SO4 or CaCl2.
Ammonia fountain experiment demonstrates its very high solubility in water.
Dry ice is solid CO2 and sublimes at -78 degrees C.
Divers get the bends from dissolved nitrogen coming out of blood on fast ascent.
Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, which is why thermal pollution harms fish.
summary: The answer is (b) Ammonia. Ammonia is a highly polar molecule that forms strong hydrogen bonds with water and also reacts with it to form NH4+ and OH- ions, so it is by far the most soluble of the four gases.
topic_notes: Solubility of gases in liquids is governed by Henry's law (William Henry, 1803): the mass of gas dissolved per unit volume of solvent at constant temperature is directly proportional to the gas's partial pressure. The constant KH is higher for less soluble gases. Solubility generally decreases with rising temperature because dissolution is exothermic, which is why warm water holds less dissolved oxygen and aquatic life suffers in thermal pollution. Applications: soda water and soft drinks are carbonated under high pressure, and opening the bottle releases CO2 as pressure falls. Scuba divers breathe helium-oxygen mixtures at depth to avoid nitrogen narcosis and the bends. Low oxygen at high altitude causes anoxia or altitude sickness. Ranking of common gases by solubility in water at about 20 degrees C: NH3 (about 700 volumes) > HCl (about 440 volumes) > SO2 (about 40) > Cl2 (about 2-3) > CO2 (about 1) > O2 (about 0.03) > N2 (about 0.02) > H2 and He (lowest). HCl and NH3 are used in the fountain experiment because of their extreme solubility. Reaction with water raises solubility: NH3, HCl, SO2 and CO2 all do so to different extents.
