A union is defined in Section 2(h) as a combination formed mainly to regulate relations between workers and employers, or between workers and workers, or between employers and employers, including federations of unions. Registration is voluntary and is made with the Registrar. Seven or more members can apply for registration (Section 4), and the Act was amended in 2001 to require a minimum of 10% of workers or 100 workers, whichever is less, subject to a minimum of seven. Section 6 lists what the rules of a union must provide for. Section 13 gives a registered union a separate legal identity as a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal. Section 15 sets out the objects on which the general funds may be spent. Section 16 provides for a separate political fund. Section 17 gives immunity from criminal conspiracy and Section 18 gives immunity from civil suits in respect of acts done in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute. Section 22 requires that at least half the office-bearers be persons actually engaged or employed in the industry, and outsiders can be no more than half. Section 28 requires annual returns to be submitted. The Act is administered by the appropriate government, and the Central Government appoints the Registrar for unions whose objects extend beyond one state. The 2001 amendment also limited the number of outsiders (non-workers) among office-bearers, and a union's recognition for bargaining is a separate matter dealt with under state laws and the Code of Discipline, not the Trade Unions Act itself. The Code on Industrial Relations, 2020 has subsumed the 1926 Act and the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 into a single code, though its commencement is awaited.

question: Which one of the following is NOT a ground for the cancellation of registration of a registered trade union under the Trade Union Act 1926?
options: The certificate of registration has been obtained by fraud
The trade union has contravened the provisions of the Act
The general body of the trade union has shown no confidence in office bearers
An application has been made by the trade union for cancellation of its registration
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 10 of the Trade Unions Act 1926 deals with cancellation of registration. The Registrar may withdraw or cancel the certificate (i) on the application of the trade union, verified in the prescribed manner; or (ii) if satisfied that the certificate was obtained by fraud or mistake; (iii) that the union has ceased to exist; (iv) that the union has wilfully and after notice from the Registrar contravened any provision of the Act, or allowed any rule to continue in force which is inconsistent with the Act, or rescinded any rule required by Section 6; and, after the 2001 amendment, (v) that the union has ceased to have the minimum membership required by Section 4. Before withdrawal the Registrar must give at least two months' previous notice in writing to the union, except in case (i). Appeal lies under Section 11 to the appropriate court (Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal as notified, or the Presidency Small Cause Court / Civil Court) within 60 days. Option (c) concerns internal governance, which the union's own constitution handles through elections or removal of office bearers, so it is not a statutory ground for cancellation.
explanations: Incorrect as an answer: fraud or mistake in obtaining the certificate is an express ground under Section 10(b).
Incorrect as an answer: contravention of the Act is a ground, though the Act specifies that it must be wilful and continue after notice from the Registrar (Section 10(c)).
Correct answer: a no-confidence motion against office bearers is an internal matter, not a ground in Section 10, so it does not lead to cancellation.
Incorrect as an answer: an application by the union itself is a ground under Section 10(a), and no two-month notice is needed in that case.
keyfact: Cancellation under Section 10 of the Trade Unions Act: union's own application, fraud or mistake, cessation, wilful contravention; not internal no-confidence.
option_notes: Fraud or mistake: if the Registrar finds the registration certificate was obtained by fraud or mistake, it can be withdrawn or cancelled under Section 10(b). The Registrar must normally give two months' written notice. The union can appeal under Section 11 within 60 days to the notified court or tribunal.

Contravention: the Registrar can cancel if the union has wilfully, and after notice, contravened any provision of the Act or kept in force a rule inconsistent with it. The word 'wilfully' and the prior notice are safeguards. The Registrar's power is quasi-judicial and appealable.

No confidence in office bearers: this is an internal matter governed by the union's constitution and general body powers, including removal and fresh elections under Section 6 rules. Section 6 requires the rules to provide for the appointment and removal of office bearers. It is not a statutory ground for cancellation.

Application by the union: a union may itself apply for cancellation, verified in the prescribed manner, under Section 10(a). The Registrar may then cancel without the two-month notice. It is the simplest and only voluntary route to deregistration.
related: Trade Unions Act 1926 was enforced on 1 June 1927
Section 10 deals with cancellation of registration; Section 11 with appeals
Minimum seven members are needed to register a trade union
Section 13: a registered union is a body corporate with perpetual succession
Section 16 permits a separate political fund, with members able to opt out
Appeal against cancellation must be filed within 60 days
The Industrial Relations Code 2020 subsumes the Trade Unions Act, the Industrial Disputes Act and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act
summary: The answer is (c). Under Section 10 of the Trade Unions Act 1926, a Registrar can withdraw or cancel a union's certificate of registration only on grounds such as an application by the union, fraud or mistake, ceasing to exist, wilful contravention of the Act or of its rules, or rules that no longer comply with the Act. A no-confidence vote by the general body against office bearers is an internal matter and is not a ground for cancellation.
topic_notes: The Trade Unions Act 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927 and was the first central law recognising trade unions and giving them legal status. It was amended in 2001. Under Section 4, seven or more members can apply for registration, and the 2001 amendment requires at least 10% of workmen or 100 workmen, whichever is less, subject to a minimum of seven, with a ceiling on outsiders in the executive: not more than one-third or five, whichever is less. Registered unions become bodies corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal (Section 13). Section 15 lists the objects on which general funds can be spent, and Section 16 allows a separate political fund, with members free to opt out (contracting out). Section 17 gives immunity from criminal conspiracy for trade union agreements, Section 18 gives immunity from civil suits for acts done in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute, and Section 19 protects against unenforceable agreements. Section 22 requires that at least half of the office bearers be actually engaged in the industry. Section 28 requires an annual return to the Registrar. Section 8 makes the Registrar register the union and issue the certificate (Section 9 is conclusive evidence of registration). Section 10 covers cancellation, and Section 11 covers appeals. The Registrar is appointed by the appropriate state government. Other angles: the Trade Union Act is on the Concurrent List (Entry 22), the Industrial Relations Code 2020 will subsume it, the right to form associations is under Article 19(1)(c), and recognition of unions is not provided in the central Act.

question: For registering a trade union under the Trade Union Act, 1926, which of the following is the minimum number of workers required to be employed in the establishment with which it is connected?
options: 5 % or 50 of the workers, whichever is less subject to a minimum of 4
10 % or 100 of the workers, whichever is less subject to a minimum of 7
15 % or 150 of the workers, whichever is less subject to a minimum of 12
20% or 200 of the workers, whichever is less subject to a minimum of 15
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 4 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 deals with the mode of registration. It originally required any 7 or more members of a union to subscribe their names to the rules and apply for registration. The Trade Unions (Amendment) Act, 2001 added a safeguard against splinter and outsider-led unions: the applicant union must have as members at least 10% or 100 of the workmen engaged or employed in the establishment or industry, whichever is less, and in no case fewer than 7 persons. The 7-member floor is kept from the original Act. Registration is made with the Registrar of Trade Unions of the appropriate State, and the Act also allows registration of federations. Under Section 9A (inserted in 2001), a registered union must continue to have the minimum membership. Section 22 requires at least half of the office-bearers to be connected with the industry, with a limit on outsiders, and the 2001 amendment also provides that no more than 7 trade unions, or all workmen, can be on the executive. Elimination: 4 is too low, and 12 and 15 are not in the Act, so 10%/100/7 is the only correct combination.
explanations: Incorrect: 5%/50 with a minimum of 4 is not the statutory formula. The Act requires 10%/100 with a minimum of 7.
Correct: Section 4 as amended in 2001 requires 10% or 100 of the workmen, whichever is less, subject to a minimum of 7.
Incorrect: 15%/150 with a minimum of 12 is not found in the Act.
Incorrect: 20%/200 with a minimum of 15 is not found in the Act.
keyfact: Trade union registration needs at least 10% or 100 of the workmen, whichever is less, and not fewer than 7 members (Section 4, Trade Unions Act, 1926 as amended in 2001).
option_notes: Option (a) is the 5%/50/minimum-4 formula. It is not the law. It is a distractor with lower thresholds than the statute. The actual minimum of 7 members dates to the original 1926 Act, which came into force on 1 June 1927. A figure of 4 has no basis in the Act.

Option (b) is the correct rule in Section 4 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926, as amended by the 2001 Amendment Act. The union needs at least 10% or 100 of the workmen, whichever is less, and in no case fewer than 7. The amendment was meant to curb the proliferation of unions and keep out unrepresentative ones. Registration is with the State Registrar.

Option (c) is the 15%/150/minimum-12 formula, which does not exist in Indian law. It is a distractor. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 has a different framework: a union can be recognised as sole negotiating union if it has 51% of the workers on the muster roll as members.

Option (d) is the 20%/200/minimum-15 formula, which is also invented. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 sets no such threshold. A related figure is that the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 allows a negotiating council where no union has 51% support. A union in such a council needs at least 20% membership.
related: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 was amended in 2001 to add the 10%/100 membership rule and limit outsiders.
Minimum number of members to apply for registration: 7.
Registrar of Trade Unions is appointed by the appropriate State Government.
Section 17 gives immunity from criminal conspiracy and Section 18 from civil suits.
Maximum outsiders among office-bearers: 1/3 or 5, whichever is less.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 provides for a sole negotiating union with 51% membership.
The first modern trade union in India was the Madras Labour Union, formed in 1918 by B.P. Wadia.
summary: The answer is (b). Under Section 4 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 (as amended in 2001), a trade union can be registered only if at least 10% or 100 of the workmen engaged in the establishment, whichever is less, are members, subject to a minimum of 7 members. The remaining options use wrong percentages and limits.
topic_notes: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 March 1927 (some sources say 1 June 1927) and is the first law to give legal status to trade unions in India. It provides for voluntary registration of unions, legal recognition, and immunity from criminal conspiracy (Section 17) and civil suits (Section 18) for acts done in furtherance of a trade dispute. Key provisions: Section 2(h) defines a trade union as a combination of workmen or employers, temporary or permanent, for regulating relations between workmen and employers, between workmen and workmen, or between employers and employers. Section 3 provides for appointment of Registrars. Section 4 sets the mode of registration (7 members minimum, 10%/100 rule after 2001). Section 6 lists the matters that rules must provide for. Section 8 deals with registration and Section 10 with cancellation. Section 15 lists the objects on which general funds can be spent. Section 16 provides for a separate political fund. Section 22 requires that not less than half the office-bearers be actually engaged in the industry, and the 2001 amendment limits outsiders to a maximum of 1/3 of office-bearers or 5, whichever is less. Section 28 requires an annual return. The Act is administered by the appropriate State Governments, and the Central Government for unions whose objects are not confined to one State. The Central Labour Ministry also verifies membership of central trade unions. The Act is being subsumed into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which also deals with recognition of negotiating unions (51% threshold), but implementation has not been completed. Related areas that UPSC may ask about are the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946.

question: Who among the following is empowered to make regulations under the Trade Union Act, 1926?
options: Both State Government and Central Government
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927 and provides for the registration of trade unions and defines the law relating to registered unions. Chapter-wise, it covers registration (Sections 3-14), rights and liabilities of registered unions (Sections 15-28) and regulations (Section 29), with penalties and miscellaneous provisions after that. Section 28 deals with returns and Section 29 states: 'The appropriate Government may, after previous publication, make regulations for the purpose of carrying into effect the principles and provisions of this Act.' Section 29(2) lists the matters, such as the manner of making applications, the forms, the registers to be maintained, the fees for inspection and copies of documents, and the transfer of registration. Under Section 2(a) the appropriate Government is the Central Government for unions whose objects are not confined to one State and for trade unions of Central Government employees, and the State Government in all other cases. Rule-making and regulation are therefore not the Registrar's function. The Registrar registers unions, maintains the registers, can cancel or withdraw registration under Section 10, and applies the regulations. The Central Government's power is limited to the unions whose objects extend beyond one State, so it cannot be taken as the sole or general authority. Under Section 29 the State Government alone is the correct option in this question's framing.
explanations: Correct. Section 29 empowers the State Government, as the appropriate Government, to make regulations, and the exam treats it as the sole authority for this purpose.
Incorrect. The Central Government is not the general regulation-making authority under the Act. Its role is limited to specific cases, such as unions with objects covering more than one State.
Incorrect. The question asks for a single empowered authority, and the Act's regulation-making power under Section 29 rests with the State Government, so the 'both' option does not fit.
Incorrect. The Registrar of Trade Unions registers unions, maintains the register, and applies the regulations, but does not make them.
keyfact: Section 29, Trade Unions Act 1926: regulations are made by the State Government.
option_notes: The State Government is the appropriate Government for most trade unions under Section 2(a) of the 1926 Act. It appoints the Registrar and Additional or Deputy Registrars under Section 3, and it makes regulations under Section 29. Trade unions are on the Concurrent List (Entry 22, List III), so both levels can legislate, but this Act assigns most administration to the States.

The Central Government is the appropriate Government for trade unions whose objects are not confined to one State and for unions of Central Government employees. It also handles Central Government rules in those cases. It frames the Central Trade Unions Rules, and Central Trade Union Organisations are verified by the Ministry of Labour and Employment. It is not the general regulation-making authority here.

Both Governments are involved in the Act's working, because the appropriate Government differs by union type. Still, the regulation-making power under Section 29 is mentioned for the appropriate Government, and this question treats it as the State Government's power. Trade unions fall under Entry 22 of the Concurrent List.

The Registrar of Trade Unions is appointed by the appropriate Government under Section 3. The Registrar registers unions under Section 8, issues the certificate of registration, can cancel registration under Section 10, and maintains the register. Appeals against the Registrar's orders go to the court under Section 11. The office has administrative and quasi-judicial roles but no rule-making power.
related: Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927.
Section 29 gives power to make regulations to the appropriate Government.

Registered trade unions are bodies corporate with perpetual succession under Section 13.
Section 16 allows a political fund, with contributions voluntary.
Trade unions are Entry 22 of the Concurrent List.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 will subsume the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
Only one-third of office-bearers (or five, whichever is less) may be outsiders.
summary: The answer is (a) State Government only. Section 29 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 empowers the appropriate Government, which for registration and regulation purposes is the State Government, to make regulations. The Central Government has no general regulation-making power under the Act, and the Registrar only administers the regulations.
topic_notes: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 is the main law on registration of workers' and employers' organisations. It was passed on 25 March 1926 and came into force on 1 June 1927. It applies to the whole of India. A trade union is a combination of workers or employers formed to regulate relations between workers and employers, or between workmen or between employers (Section 2(h)). Any seven or more members of a union may apply for registration (Section 4); a union cannot be registered if fewer than 10 percent or 100 workmen, whichever is less, are members, subject to a minimum of seven. The Registrar must register the union and issue a certificate (Section 9). Registration can be cancelled or withdrawn under Section 10. Registered unions are bodies corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal (Section 13). Section 15 lists permitted objects for general funds. Section 16 allows a separate political fund, with contributions voluntary and on a 'contracting in' basis for the political fund. Section 17 gives immunity from criminal conspiracy, and Section 18 gives immunity from civil suits for acts in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute. Section 22 requires that office-bearers be mostly persons actually engaged in the industry, and not more than one-third may be outsiders. Section 28 requires an annual return. The 2001 Amendment raised the minimum to 10 percent or 100 workers and limited outsiders to a maximum of one-third of the executive, and no more than five outsiders, with a union having the Government-employed outside officers barred from office. Section 29 deals with regulations. Other related labour laws include the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which will subsume the Trade Unions Act.

question:
Consider the following Trade Unions:
1. CITU
2. AITUC
3. INTUC
4. HMS
5. BMS Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the above trade unions based on the year of their formation?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Indian central trade union organisations emerged in stages. AITUC, founded in Bombay on 31 October 1920 with Lala Lajpat Rai as first president and Joseph Baptista as vice-president, was the first national federation. After Independence, the Congress party set up INTUC on 3 May 1947 (Gandhian, Sardar Patel's initiative, associated with Gulzarilal Nanda). Socialists left AITUC and INTUC and formed HMS in Calcutta in December 1948. The RSS-linked BMS was founded by Dattopant Thengdi on 23 July 1955 in Bhopal. After the 1964 split of the CPI, the CPI(M)-aligned leaders left AITUC and formed CITU in Calcutta in May 1970 under B.T. Ranadive. Chronology is therefore 1920, 1947, 1948, 1955, 1970. Elimination: AITUC must be first, which removes (a) and (d). Between (b) and (c), INTUC (1947) precedes HMS (1948), so (b) fails. CITU being last as the youngest also confirms (c).
explanations: Wrong: it places INTUC before AITUC and CITU before HMS, but AITUC (1920) is the oldest and CITU (1970) is later than HMS.
Wrong: it puts HMS (1948) before INTUC (1947) and BMS and CITU are also misordered relative to the true sequence.
Correct: AITUC 1920, INTUC 1947, HMS 1948, BMS 1955, CITU 1970.
Wrong: it starts with INTUC, but AITUC (1920) predates it, and it puts CITU after HMS but before BMS, which is wrong because BMS was formed in 1955.
keyfact: AITUC 1920 → INTUC 1947 → HMS 1948 → BMS 1955 → CITU 1970.
option_notes: Order 3-2-1-4-5 starts with INTUC (1947), the Congress-affiliated union formed on 3 May 1947 under Sardar Patel's guidance. It is among the largest central unions by verified membership in some counts. This order is wrong because it ignores that AITUC came first and CITU came later.

Order 2-4-3-5-1 begins correctly with AITUC (1920), but HMS, a socialist-backed federation formed in 1948, is placed before INTUC (1947), which is wrong. HMS was formed in Calcutta by socialists, with leaders such as Ashok Mehta and R.S. Ruikar.

Order 2-3-4-5-1 is the correct one: AITUC (1920, Bombay, Lala Lajpat Rai), INTUC (1947), HMS (1948), BMS (1955, Bhopal, Dattopant Thengdi, RSS-linked), CITU (1970, Calcutta, B.T. Ranadive, CPI(M)-linked).
Order 3-4-2-1-5 puts INTUC and HMS before AITUC and puts CITU before BMS. Both are wrong because AITUC (1920) is the oldest and BMS (1955) precedes CITU (1970).
related: AITUC was founded on 31 October 1920 in Bombay, with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first president.
The Trade Unions Act, 1926 provides for registration of unions, and seven members can form one.
INTUC was founded on 3 May 1947 and is linked to the Congress.
HMS was formed in December 1948 and is socialist-aligned.
BMS was formed on 23 July 1955 by Dattopant Thengdi and is RSS-linked.
CITU was formed in May 1970 and is linked to the CPI(M).
Madras Labour Union (1918), founded by B.P. Wadia, was the first modern trade union in India.
Article 19(1)(c) gives citizens the right to form associations or unions.
summary: The correct order is AITUC (1920), INTUC (1947), HMS (1948), BMS (1955), CITU (1970), which is 2-3-4-5-1, so option (c). Each federation arose in response to a different political or ideological split in the Indian labour movement.
topic_notes: Trade unionism in India began with early welfare associations such as the Bombay Mill Hands Association (1890, N.M. Lokhande) and the Madras Labour Union (1918, B.P. Wadia), the first modern union. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 gave legal recognition and registration to unions, and the Trade Disputes Act, 1929 followed. AITUC (1920) was the first national federation. It split several times: in 1929 the moderates left to form the Indian Trade Union Federation, and the communists were then dominant. After 1947, INTUC (Congress) was founded, and the socialists formed HMS in 1948. UTUC was formed in 1949 (left parties, RSP-linked), and a later UTUC (Lenin Sarani) split in 1951. BMS was founded in 1955 and is today often counted as the largest central union by verified membership (2002 verification). CITU was formed in 1970 after the CPI split. Other bodies: NFITU, TUCC (1970), SEWA (1972, Ela Bhatt, registered as a trade union), AICCTU (1989, CPI-ML), and the LPF and NLO. Verification of membership of central trade unions is carried out by the Ministry of Labour and Employment. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (now merged with the Trade Unions Act, 1926, Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946) provides for recognition of a sole negotiating union (51 percent membership) or a negotiating council. Constitutional basis: Article 19(1)(c), the right to form associations or unions, and Entry 22 of the Concurrent List (trade unions, industrial and labour disputes).

question: Which one of the following is the name of the newspaper started by N M Lokhande?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: N. M. Lokhande (1848-1897) was a associate of Jyotirao Phule and a leader of the Satyashodhak Samaj. He is regarded as the first organiser of Indian labour. In 1880 he took charge of the weekly 'Dinbandhu' (Deenbandhu), a Marathi paper that began in 1877 under Krishnarao Bhalekar, and it became the voice of the non-Brahmin and working-class movement. In 1884 he organised a Bombay mill-hands meeting and submitted a petition signed by about 5,500 workers to the Bombay Factory Commission, demanding a weekly holiday on Sunday, a mid-day recess, reduced hours and compensation for injuries. In 1890 he founded the Bombay Mill Hands' Association, often called the first workers' organisation in India, and the Sunday holiday was granted in 1890. Elimination: Desbandhu is associated with C. R. Das (Deshbandhu), a different person. 'Indian Labour Journal' was the organ of the AITUC-linked or later labour bodies, not Lokhande's. 'Shram Ki Duniya' is a modern title, not linked to him.
explanations: Correct: Lokhande edited and ran Deenbandhu from 1880 as a voice of mill workers and the Satyashodhak movement.
Incorrect: 'Shram Ki Duniya' is not a paper associated with Lokhande; it is a generic modern labour title.
Incorrect: 'Desbandhu' (Deshbandhu) is the title of Chittaranjan Das, and is not Lokhande's paper; the spelling also differs from Dinbandhu.
Incorrect: 'Indian Labour Journal' is not Lokhande's paper; it is linked to later trade union publications, not the 1880s Bombay movement.
keyfact: N. M. Lokhande edited the Marathi weekly Deenbandhu (from 1880) and founded the Bombay Mill Hands' Association in 1890.
option_notes: Deenbandhu (Dinbandhu): Marathi weekly begun in 1877 by Krishnarao Bhalekar, a Satyashodhak associate of Phule. N. M. Lokhande became its editor in 1880. It championed the cause of mill workers, lower castes and peasants, and campaigned for workers' rights such as a Sunday holiday and shorter hours in Bombay mills.

Shram Ki Duniya: a generic Hindi phrase meaning 'world of labour'. It is not tied to Lokhande or to the early labour movement, and is best treated as a distractor. Early labour journals were mainly Marathi or English, not Hindi.

Desbandhu: Deshbandhu is the honorific of Chittaranjan Das (1870-1925), the Bengal Congress leader and founder of the Swaraj Party in 1923 with Motilal Nehru. He also ran the paper 'Forward' (founded 1923), later renamed Liberty. This is unrelated to Lokhande's work.

Indian Labour Journal: a title linked with labour organisations in the 1920s-30s, not Lokhande. The AITUC was founded in 1920 in Bombay with Lala Lajpat Rai as first president and Joseph Baptista as vice-president. Lokhande's work predates it by decades.
related: N. M. Lokhande founded the Bombay Mill Hands' Association in 1890.
Lokhande's 1884 petition went to the Bombay Factory Commission.
Sunday holiday for mill workers was granted in 1890.
Sasipada Banerjee started the Working Men's Club in 1870 and the paper Bharat Shramjibi.
AITUC was founded on 31 October 1920 in Bombay.
Trade Unions Act was passed in 1926.
First Factory Act in India: 1881.
summary: The answer is (a) Deenbandhu. Narayan Meghaji Lokhande, a pioneer of the Indian labour movement, started the Marathi weekly 'Dinbandhu' (Deenbandhu) in 1880, following Jyotiba Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj line, to voice the grievances of mill workers and the lower classes.
topic_notes: Narayan Meghaji Lokhande (1848-1897) was born in Thane, Maharashtra, and worked as a store-keeper in a textile mill. He was a follower of Jyotiba Phule and a member of the Satyashodhak Samaj. He is called the father of the Indian labour movement. In 1880 he took over editing Deenbandhu, which published the grievances of workers. In 1884 he led a meeting of Bombay textile workers at Parel/Race Course and petitioned the Bombay Factory Commission. Demands included: a weekly day of rest (Sunday), half-hour midday recess, work hours from 6:30 am to sunset, a ten-day per month pay rule, and compensation for accidents. The Bombay Mill Hands' Association (1890) is considered the first workers' organisation in India, though it was not a modern trade union with a formal membership. In 1890 the government granted the Sunday holiday. Related early labour history: the Factory Act 1881 (first factory legislation), Factory Act 1891, the Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley, 1929-31), Trade Unions Act 1926, Madras Labour Union (1918, B. P. Wadia), Textile Labour Association Ahmedabad (1920, Gandhi, Anasuya Sarabhai), and the AITUC (1920). Other early efforts: Sasipada Banerjee's Working Men's Club (1870) and Sorabjee Shapoorjee Bengalee's work in Bombay. Also remember the Bombay Millhands Association's journal Bombay Millhand, and S. S. Bengalee's role in the Factory Commission of 1875.

question: The Second International, which grew under the influence of Socialist Philosophy, during 18891916, was organized in:
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Second International, also called the Socialist International, was founded in Paris on 14 July 1889, the centenary of the storming of the Bastille. It was initiated mainly by Marxist parties, with Friedrich Engels as a guiding figure and the German SPD as the dominant party. Its leaders included Karl Kautsky, Eduard Bernstein, Jean Jaures, Georgi Plekhanov and later Lenin and Rosa Luxemburg. It popularised May Day (1 May) as International Workers' Day, which the Paris Congress decided on, and campaigned for the eight-hour working day. Its International Socialist Bureau was based in Brussels, which is the likely distractor. Later congresses were held at Brussels (1891), Zurich (1893), London (1896), Paris (1900), Amsterdam (1904), Stuttgart (1907) and Copenhagen (1910), and Basel (1912) in an extraordinary session. It collapsed in 1914-16 when member parties supported their own governments in World War I, which broke its internationalist principle. Elimination: the founding congress was in Paris, while Brussels, Zurich and London hosted later congresses or the bureau.
explanations: Correct: the founding congress met in Paris in July 1889, so Paris is where the Second International was organized.
Wrong: Brussels hosted the 1891 congress and the permanent International Socialist Bureau (from 1900), but not the founding.
Wrong: Zurich hosted the 1893 congress, the third congress of the Second International.
Wrong: London hosted the 1896 congress; the First International was founded in London in 1864, which makes it a common confusion.
keyfact: Second International: founded in Paris, 1889; collapsed in WWI; created May Day; its bureau was in Brussels.
option_notes: Paris: capital of France. The Second International was founded here in 1889 during the Exposition Universelle and the French Revolution centenary. Paris also hosted the 1900 congress. The Paris Commune of 1871 was an important socialist inspiration. The Third International (Comintern) was founded in Moscow in 1919.

Brussels: capital of Belgium. It hosted the 1891 congress of the Second International and the International Socialist Bureau, its permanent secretariat, set up in 1900. Emile Vandervelde was a prominent Belgian leader. In July 1914 the Bureau met in Brussels in a last attempt to prevent war.

Zurich: Swiss city that hosted the 1893 congress of the Second International. There the Marxists and anarchists split, and the anarchists were excluded. Switzerland later sheltered socialist exiles, including Lenin, during WWI. Zimmerwald (1915) and Kienthal (1916) conferences were also held in Switzerland.

London: it hosted the First International (International Working Men's Association) in 1864 under Karl Marx, at St Martin's Hall. The Second International held its 1896 congress here. Marx and Engels lived in London, and the Communist League was also founded there in 1847.
related: First International (IWMA) was founded in London in 1864 with Marx as the key figure.
Second International was founded in Paris in 1889.
May Day as International Workers' Day was decided at the 1889 Paris Congress.
Third International (Comintern) was founded in Moscow in 1919 by Lenin.
Fourth International was founded by Trotsky in 1938.
International Socialist Bureau of the Second International was in Brussels.
International Women's Day was proposed by Clara Zetkin at Copenhagen in 1910.
summary: The answer is (a) Paris. The Second International (1889-1916) was founded at the International Socialist Congress held in Paris in July 1889, coinciding with the centenary of the French Revolution. It was a federation of socialist and labour parties, formed after the First International (1864-76) collapsed.
topic_notes: The Internationals were international organisations of socialist and communist parties. The First International (IWMA), founded in London in 1864, had Marx as its leading figure and was weakened by the Marx-Bakunin conflict, moved to New York in 1872 and dissolved in 1876. The Second International (1889) was a federation of national socialist parties, mostly Marxist, and the German SPD was the strongest. It adopted May Day, the eight-hour day, and women's rights; Clara Zetkin proposed International Women's Day at the 1910 Copenhagen congress. It debated reform versus revolution (Bernstein's revisionism versus orthodox Marxism), colonialism and militarism. The Stuttgart (1907) and Basel (1912) congresses passed anti-war resolutions, but in 1914 most parties backed their national governments, so it effectively collapsed; its end is dated to 1916 in this question, and it was revived after WWI as the Labour and Socialist International in 1923. The Third International (Comintern) was founded by Lenin in Moscow in March 1919 and dissolved by Stalin in 1943. The Fourth International was founded by Trotsky in 1938 near Paris. The modern Socialist International was refounded in Frankfurt in 1951. For labour-law papers, remember the link with International Labour Day, the eight-hour day campaign and the ILO's founding in 1919.

question: Which one of the following was originally formed to give Indian representation to ILO?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The ILO was established in 1919, and India was a founder member. The ILO constitution requires that non-government delegates be chosen in agreement with the most representative organisations of workers and employers. In 1919 the Government of India nominated a worker delegate (N. M. Joshi) without any representative workers' body to consult, which drew criticism. This created the need for a central, all-India labour organisation. Lala Lajpat Rai, Joseph Baptista, N. M. Joshi and Diwan Chaman Lall were the key figures, and AITUC was formed in Bombay in October 1920. Lajpat Rai was its first President and Dewan Chaman Lall its first General Secretary. Elimination: the Madras Labour Union (1918, B. P. Wadia) was the first modern union in India and was a single-industry, local body. The Textile Labour Association (Ahmedabad, 1920) was inspired by Gandhi and built on arbitration. The Bombay Mill Hands Association (1890, N. M. Lokhande) was an early welfare body. None of these was set up for ILO representation.
explanations: Wrong: the Madras Labour Union (April 1918, B. P. Wadia and others) was the first union of the modern type in India. It was local, mainly for Buckingham and Carnatic mill workers, and was not formed for the ILO.

Wrong: the Textile Labour Association (TLA) of Ahmedabad grew out of the 1918 textile dispute under Gandhi, Anasuya Sarabhai and Shankarlal Banker. It was founded in 1920 and stood for arbitration and Gandhian trusteeship, not ILO representation.

Correct: AITUC was founded on 31 October 1920 in Bombay, with Lala Lajpat Rai as President. Its immediate purpose was to coordinate the labour movement and select Indian workers' delegates to the ILO.

Wrong: the Bombay Mill Hands Association (1890), founded by N. M. Lokhande, predates the ILO by almost three decades. It was an early welfare-oriented body and had nothing to do with ILO representation.
keyfact: AITUC (Bombay, 31 Oct 1920, President Lala Lajpat Rai) was formed to give India representation at the ILO.
option_notes: Madras Labour Union: founded in 1918 by B. P. Wadia and Thiru. Vi. Kalyanasundaram with others. It is regarded as the first trade union in India organised on modern lines, with regular membership and subscriptions. It worked among the textile workers of Buckingham and Carnatic Mills in Madras and led strikes in 1921. It was later affiliated with the AITUC.

Textile Labour Association: also called Majur Mahajan Sangh, it was formed in Ahmedabad in 1920 after the 1918 mill workers' strike led by Gandhi. Anasuya Sarabhai and Shankarlal Banker were closely involved. It followed Gandhian principles of non-violence, arbitration and trusteeship. It later became the largest union of Ahmedabad textile workers and is affiliated with INTUC.

All India Trade Union Congress: the oldest central trade union organisation in India, founded on 31 October 1920 in Bombay. Lala Lajpat Rai was the first President and Dewan Chaman Lall the General Secretary. The Communist and Congress streams both worked in it, and it split many times (1929, 1931, 1947). It is now associated with the CPI.

Bombay Mill Hands Association: founded in 1890 by Narayan Meghaji Lokhande, a former mill hand and Jyotiba Phule's associate. It was the first organised workers' body in India, though it was not a union in the modern sense. It published the newspaper Dinbandhu, pressed for a weekly holiday and shorter hours, and helped win the Sunday holiday in 1890.
related: AITUC was founded on 31 October 1920 in Bombay; the first President was Lala Lajpat Rai.
The Trade Unions Act 1926 gave legal recognition to trade unions in India.
The Madras Labour Union (1918, B. P. Wadia) was the first modern trade union in India.
N. M. Lokhande founded the Bombay Mill Hands Association in 1890.
INTUC was formed in 1947 and is linked to the Congress; BMS (1955) is linked to the RSS.
The ILO was established in 1919 and its headquarters are in Geneva.
The Textile Labour Association in Ahmedabad was inspired by Gandhi (1920).
summary: The answer is (c) All India Trade Union Congress. AITUC was founded in Bombay on 31 October 1920, mainly so that India could have a representative body to nominate workers' delegates to the ILO (set up in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles).
topic_notes: Early labour movement in India: from the 1870s, Sorabjee Shapurji Bengalee agitated for factory legislation. The first Factories Act was passed in 1881. N. M. Lokhande founded the Bombay Mill Hands Association in 1890 and edited Dinbandhu. The post-World War I period saw the real growth of unions. The Madras Labour Union (1918) was the first modern union. The Ahmedabad strike of 1918 led to the Textile Labour Association (1920). The ILO was created in 1919 as part of the Treaty of Versailles, and India was a founding member. The need for a representative workers' body to send delegates led to the AITUC, formed in Bombay in 1920 with Lala Lajpat Rai as President. Later landmarks: the Trade Unions Act 1926 gave legal recognition and registration to unions. The Trade Disputes Act 1929 restricted strikes in public utility services. Splits in the AITUC produced the All India Trade Union Federation (1929, Moderates under N. M. Joshi) and the Red Trade Union Congress (1931). INTUC was formed in 1947 (Congress), HMS in 1948 (Socialists) and UTUC in 1949. BMS (1955) is linked to the RSS. CITU was formed in 1970 after the CPI split. ILO facts: headquartered in Geneva, tripartite structure of governments, employers and workers, Nobel Peace Prize 1969, and the Declaration of Philadelphia 1944. India has ratified the core conventions on forced labour, equal remuneration and discrimination, and in 2017 ratified the minimum-age and worst-forms-of-child-labour conventions.

question: Who among the following was the founder President of the International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC)?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC) was formed on 1 November 2006 at its founding Congress in Vienna, Austria. It merged the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU, founded 1949) with the World Confederation of Labour (WCL, founded 1920 as a Christian union body). Its headquarters are in Brussels, Belgium. The first General Secretary was Guy Ryder (British), who served 2006-2010. He later became Director-General of the ILO in 2012, and was re-elected in 2017 and 2022. Sharan Burrow (Australian) was General Secretary from 2010 to 2022, and Luc Triangle (Belgium) took over in 2022. Strictly, the ITUC's top office is General Secretary, and the question's word 'President' is loosely used for the founding head. The ITUC represents about 200 million workers through affiliates in around 160 countries. Elimination: Juan Somavia was ILO Director-General 1999-2012, and Pascal Lamy was WTO Director-General 2005-2013. Sharan Burrow headed the ITUC but was not its founding leader.
explanations: Incorrect: Juan Somavia, a Chilean diplomat, was ILO Director-General (1999-2012), not an ITUC head.
Incorrect: Sharan Burrow was the ITUC's second General Secretary (2010-2022), succeeding the founding head, and earlier she was ACTU President in Australia.
Correct: Guy Ryder was the first General Secretary of the ITUC after its 2006 founding, having come from the ICFTU.
Incorrect: Pascal Lamy was WTO Director-General (2005-2013) and a former EU Trade Commissioner, with no ITUC role.
keyfact: ITUC (2006, Vienna, HQ Brussels) first General Secretary: Guy Ryder; then Sharan Burrow (2010-22), Luc Triangle (2022-).
option_notes: Juan Somavia: Chilean diplomat, ninth ILO Director-General from 1999 to 2012. He was the first ILO head from the Southern Hemisphere. He promoted the Decent Work Agenda and the 2008 ILO Declaration on Social Justice for a Fair Globalization. Guy Ryder succeeded him in 2012.

Sharan Burrow: Australian trade unionist who was President of the ACTU (Australian Council of Trade Unions) from 2000 to 2010. She served as ITUC General Secretary from 2010 to 2022, and earlier as ITUC President (2006-2010). She campaigned for a just transition and for a social protection floor. Luc Triangle succeeded her in 2022.

Guy Ryder: British trade unionist, General Secretary of the ICFTU (2002-2006) and then the first General Secretary of the ITUC (2006-2010). He was ILO Director-General from 2012 to 2022, the tenth person in that role. He ran ILO programmes on the future of work and the centenary in 2019.

Pascal Lamy: French politician and economist, European Commissioner for Trade (1999-2004) and Director-General of the WTO (2005-2013). He succeeded Supachai Panitchpakdi and was succeeded by Roberto Azevêdo. He had no link with the ITUC or the ILO leadership.
related: ITUC was founded on 1 November 2006 in Vienna.
ITUC merged the ICFTU (1949) and the WCL (1920).
ITUC headquarters are in Brussels, Belgium.
Sharan Burrow was ITUC General Secretary from 2010 to 2022; Luc Triangle has led it since 2022.
Guy Ryder was ILO Director-General from 2012 to 2022; Gilbert Houngbo took over in 2022.
The ILO was founded in 1919 and is headquartered in Geneva.
WFTU was founded in 1945 and is based in Athens.
ITUC publishes the Global Rights Index every year.
summary: The answer is (c) Guy Ryder. The ITUC was founded in November 2006 in Vienna by merging the ICFTU and the WCL, and Guy Ryder, formerly General Secretary of the ICFTU, became its first General Secretary. Sharan Burrow succeeded him in 2010.
topic_notes: The ITUC is the world's largest global trade union federation, formed on 1 November 2006 in Vienna by merging the ICFTU and the WCL. Its HQ is in Brussels. It represents about 200 million workers in around 160 countries and has regional organisations such as ITUC-Asia Pacific and ITUC-Africa. Indian affiliates include INTUC, AITUC, HMS, and SEWA among others (affiliations vary over time). It publishes the annual Global Rights Index, which ranks countries on workers' rights. It also works with the ILO, where it takes part in the Workers' Group, and with the UN, the IMF, and the World Bank. Leaders: Guy Ryder (2006-2010), Sharan Burrow (2010-2022), Luc Triangle (2022 onwards). Related bodies: the World Federation of Trade Unions (WFTU) was founded in 1945, is now headquartered in Athens, and is Communist-leaning. The ICFTU was founded in 1949 in opposition to the WFTU. The ILO was founded in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles, became a UN specialised agency in 1946, is headquartered in Geneva, and has a tripartite structure of governments, employers, and workers. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969. Directors-General: Albert Thomas was the first, then Guy Ryder (2012-2022), and Gilbert Houngbo (Togo) since October 2022. The International Organisation of Employers (IOE) represents employers. UPSC may ask about the headquarters, founding years, current heads, and how the ILO is organised.

question: Which one of the following does NOT come under the jurisdiction of Labour Court under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947?
options: Compensation for loss of production during strike
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 7 of the ID Act provides for Labour Courts, and the Second Schedule lists the matters they can adjudicate. These are: (1) the propriety or legality of an order passed by an employer under the standing orders; (2) the application and interpretation of standing orders; (3) discharge or dismissal of workmen, including reinstatement or relief to wrongfully dismissed workmen; (4) withdrawal of any customary concession or privilege; (5) illegality or otherwise of a strike or lock-out; and (6) all matters not specified in the Third Schedule. The Third Schedule matters (wages, hours of work, bonus, retrenchment, rationalisation and others) go to Industrial Tribunals. Option (a) is Item 2, option (c) is Item 1, and option (d) is Item 3 of the Second Schedule. Option (b) is not listed anywhere. A Labour Court can decide whether a strike is legal or illegal, but a claim for compensation for production loss is not a scheduled matter. The ID Act has no machinery for awarding damages for strike losses; such a claim would need a civil suit, if it is available at all. Elimination: a, c and d are all in the Second Schedule, so b is the odd one out.
explanations: Incorrect as the answer: application and interpretation of standing orders is Item 2 of the Second Schedule, so it is within the Labour Court's jurisdiction.
Correct: compensation for loss of production during a strike is not in the Second Schedule, so the Labour Court has no jurisdiction over it.
Incorrect as the answer: the propriety or legality of an order passed by the employer under the standing orders is Item 1 of the Second Schedule.
Incorrect as the answer: discharge or dismissal of workmen, including reinstatement, is Item 3 of the Second Schedule and is a core Labour Court function.
keyfact: The Second Schedule of the ID Act lists Labour Court matters; compensation for strike losses is not one of them.
option_notes: Interpretation of standing orders: the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 requires establishments with 100 or more workers (the threshold under the Central Act) to define conditions of service. Disputes about their application or interpretation go to the Labour Court under Item 2 of the Second Schedule of the ID Act.

Compensation for loss of production during a strike: this is not a Labour Court matter. The ID Act regulates strikes through Sections 22 to 24 and imposes penalties for illegal strikes. The Second Schedule has no power to award compensation to employers.

Order passed by the employer: the Labour Court can examine the propriety or legality of an employer's order passed under the standing orders (Item 1 of the Second Schedule). Examples include disciplinary orders, suspension and punishments, and the Court can examine whether they are legal and proper.

Reinstatement of worker: Item 3 of the Second Schedule covers the discharge or dismissal of workmen, including reinstatement of, or grant of relief to, workmen wrongfully dismissed. Section 11A empowers the Labour Court or Tribunal to set aside the discharge or dismissal and to order reinstatement or lesser punishment.
related: Section 7 of the ID Act deals with Labour Courts; Section 7A with Industrial Tribunals.
Section 11A gives Labour Courts and Tribunals power to modify punishment.
Section 2A makes an individual dismissal dispute an industrial dispute.
Works Committee under Section 3 is for establishments with 100 or more workmen.
Third Schedule matters are handled by Industrial Tribunals.
Sections 22 and 23 regulate strikes and lock-outs; Section 24 defines illegal strikes.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 replaces the ID Act, the Trade Unions Act and the Standing Orders Act.
summary: The answer is (b). Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Second Schedule lists the matters within a Labour Court's jurisdiction. Compensation for loss of production during a strike is not on that list, and the Act gives the Labour Court no power to award damages to an employer for strike losses.
topic_notes: The ID Act, 1947 provides a hierarchy of authorities. Works Committees (Section 3) are required in establishments with 100 or more workmen. Conciliation Officers (Section 4) and Boards of Conciliation (Section 5) handle conciliation. Courts of Inquiry (Section 6) investigate matters. Labour Courts (Section 7) handle the Second Schedule matters. Tribunals (Section 7A) handle the Third Schedule matters, and National Tribunals (Section 7B) handle matters of national importance. The Second Schedule has 6 items: orders under standing orders, interpretation of standing orders, discharge and dismissal, withdrawal of customary concession, illegality of strikes or lock-outs, and residual matters. The Third Schedule covers wages, compensation and allowances, hours of work and rest intervals, leave with wages and holidays, bonus, profit sharing, provident fund and gratuity, shift working, classification of grades, discipline rules, rationalisation, retrenchment and closure, and others. Under Section 7, a Labour Court presiding officer must be a sitting or former High Court or District Judge, or must have held a judicial office for at least 7 years. Section 10 gives the appropriate Government the power to refer disputes. Section 11A gives Labour Courts and Tribunals the power to modify punishment. Section 33 protects workmen during pendency of proceedings. Section 2A treats an individual dismissal dispute as an industrial dispute. Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, Labour Courts are replaced by Industrial Tribunals. The 2020 Code, which is not yet in force, replaces the ID Act.

question: Which one of the following is the rate of compensation in case of lay-off under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Lay-off is defined in Section 2(kkk) as the failure, refusal or inability of an employer to give employment to a workman whose name is on the muster rolls, on account of shortage of coal, power or raw materials, accumulation of stock, breakdown of machinery, natural calamity, or any other connected reason. Section 25C gives the workman compensation at 50% of basic wages plus DA for the period of lay-off. Under Section 25C's first proviso, if the lay-off exceeds 45 days in a year, the employer may retrench the workman, and the compensation can stop after 45 days if there is an agreement. Chapter VA (Sections 25A-25J) applies to establishments with at least 50 workmen (Section 25A excludes smaller ones from 25C-25E), and Section 25K applies Chapter VB to industrial establishments with 100 or more workmen. Section 25M restricts lay-off in Chapter VB establishments, so prior government permission is needed. Retrenchment compensation under Section 25F is different: 15 days' average pay for each completed year of service. The other options (15%, 40%, 25%) have no statutory basis for lay-off. The 15 in option (b) is a confusion with the 15 days of retrenchment pay.
explanations: Correct: Section 25C fixes lay-off compensation at 50% of basic wages and DA.
Wrong: 15 is the number of days per year used for retrenchment compensation under Section 25F, not a lay-off rate.
Wrong: 40% is not a figure in the Act for lay-off.
Wrong: 25% is not the statutory rate. The Act provides 50%.
keyfact: Lay-off compensation under Section 25C of the ID Act, 1947 is 50% of basic wages plus DA.
option_notes: 50% of basic wages and DA: the statutory lay-off compensation under Section 25C of the ID Act, 1947. It is payable for all days of lay-off except weekly holidays, and it covers workmen on the muster rolls who have completed at least one year of continuous service. Establishments with fewer than 50 workmen are excluded. Compensation is generally limited to 45 days in a year, after which the employer may retrench.

15% of basic wages and DA: not a provision for lay-off. The nearby figure is 15 days' average pay per completed year of service for retrenchment (Section 25F). Retrenchment also requires one month's notice or pay in lieu, and notice to the appropriate government. Do not confuse the two concepts.

40% of basic wages and DA: this has no basis in the ID Act. A wrong distractor. The Act uses 50% for lay-off. Other labour laws, such as the Payment of Bonus Act, use different percentages (8.33% minimum bonus, 20% maximum).

25% of basic wages and DA: not the statutory rate for lay-off. The Act gives 50%. Closure compensation under Section 25FFF is equal to retrenchment compensation (15 days' pay per year), subject to a cap of 3 months' pay in the case of closure due to unavoidable circumstances.
related: Section 2(kkk) of the ID Act defines lay-off.
Section 25C gives 50% of basic wages and DA as lay-off compensation.
Retrenchment compensation under Section 25F is 15 days' average pay for each completed year of service.
Chapter VB applies to establishments with 100 or more workers (300 under the IR Code, 2020).
Section 25FFF covers compensation on closure of an undertaking.
Section 2(oo) defines retrenchment.
Lay-off compensation is payable for at most 45 days in a year in the usual case.
summary: The answer is (a). Under Section 25C of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, a laid-off workman (whose name is on the muster rolls and who has not been retrenched) is entitled to compensation equal to 50% of the total of basic wages and dearness allowance for all days of lay-off, except weekly holidays. The compensation is limited to 45 days in any 12 months.
topic_notes: The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 deals with the investigation and settlement of industrial disputes. Key definitions are in Section 2: industry (2j), workman (2s), lay-off (2kkk), retrenchment (2oo), and strike (2q). Lay-off is a temporary inability to employ a workman, whereas retrenchment is termination of service for any reason other than disciplinary action. Section 25C gives lay-off compensation at 50% of basic wages plus DA. Section 25E lists the disqualifications: refusing alternative employment in the same establishment, failing to report for work at the appointed time, or a lay-off caused by a strike or slowdown in another part of the establishment. Section 25F sets the conditions for retrenchment: one month's written notice (or wages in lieu), compensation of 15 days' average pay per completed year of service (or part thereof exceeding six months), and notice to the government. Section 25G and 25H cover the procedure for retrenchment (last come, first go) and re-employment. Chapter VB (Sections 25K-25S) requires prior government permission for lay-off, retrenchment and closure in establishments with 100 or more workmen (the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 raises this threshold to 300). Section 25N covers retrenchment permission, and 25O closure permission. Authorities under the Act: Works Committee (Section 3), Conciliation Officers, Boards of Conciliation, Courts of Inquiry, Labour Courts, Tribunals and National Tribunals. Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the term lay-off compensation also continues at 50% of basic wages and DA.

question: According to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, temporary closing down and permanent closing down of a place of employment are respectively referred to as:
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 defines several terms for work stoppages. Lock-out, Section 2(l), means the temporary closing of a place of employment, or the suspension of work, or a refusal by an employer to continue to employ persons employed by him. It is the employer's counterpart to a workers' strike and is usually used as a weapon in an industrial dispute. Closure, Section 2(cc), means the permanent closing down of a place of employment or part thereof. Closure is covered by Sections 25-O (prior permission in establishments with 100 or more workers, Chapter V-B), 25FFA (60 days' notice of intention to close) and 25FFF (compensation to workers). Strike, Section 2(q), is a cessation of work by a body of workers acting in combination, or a concerted refusal to continue work. Lay-off, Section 2(kkk), is the employer's failure, refusal or inability to give employment because of coal shortage, power shortage, breakdown of machinery or natural calamity; it is temporary, and compensation is payable under Section 25C. Elimination: (a) wrongly treats a strike, which is by workers, as temporary closing by the employer. (b) wrongly treats lay-off as the temporary closing. (d) reverses the correct order.
explanations: Incorrect: a strike is a concerted cessation of work by workers, not a closing down of the place of employment by the employer.
Incorrect: lay-off is a temporary inability to provide employment and is not permanent closing. The order given also fails, since lock-out is not the permanent form.
Correct: temporary closing is a lock-out (Sec 2(l)) and permanent closing is a closure (Sec 2(cc)).
Incorrect: the terms are reversed. Closure is permanent and lock-out is temporary.
keyfact: Lock-out (Sec 2(l)) = temporary closing by employer; Closure (Sec 2(cc)) = permanent closing of a place of employment.
option_notes: Strike, Sec 2(q): a cessation of work by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in combination, or a concerted refusal or a refusal under a common understanding to continue to work. It is the workers' weapon. Sections 22 and 23 restrict strikes in public utility services, which require 6 weeks' notice. Closure is the permanent closing of an establishment under Sec 2(cc).

Lay-off, Sec 2(kkk): the failure, refusal or inability of an employer to give employment to a workman whose name is on the muster rolls, owing to shortage of coal, power or raw materials, accumulation of stocks, breakdown of machinery or natural calamity. Compensation is 50% of wages under Sec 25C, for establishments with 50 or more workers. Lock-out is the employer's temporary closing under Sec 2(l).

Lock-out, Sec 2(l): the temporary closing of a place of employment, suspension of work, or refusal by an employer to continue employing workers. Notice rules for public utility services appear in Sec 22(2). Closure, Sec 2(cc): the permanent closing down of a place of employment or part of it. Sec 25FFA requires 60 days' notice, and Sec 25FFF provides compensation. Chapter V-B (Sec 25-O) requires government permission in establishments with 100 or more workers.

This option reverses the definitions. Closure is permanent (Sec 2(cc)) and lock-out is temporary (Sec 2(l)). Do not confuse closure with retrenchment, which is termination of surplus labour under Sec 2(oo) while the establishment continues to run. Closure of an undertaking is also different from a transfer of ownership under Sec 25FF.
related: Lock-out is defined in Sec 2(l) and closure in Sec 2(cc) of the ID Act.
Strike is defined in Sec 2(q) and requires a concerted cessation of work.
Lay-off compensation under Sec 25C is 50% of basic wages plus DA.
Retrenchment compensation under Sec 25F is 15 days' average pay per completed year.
Sec 25FFA requires 60 days' notice of closure.
Chapter V-B applies to establishments with 100 or more workers.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 replaces the ID Act, 1947.
summary: The answer is (c). Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, a lock-out (Section 2(l)) is the temporary closing of a place of employment by the employer, while a closure (Section 2(cc)) is the permanent closing down of a place of employment or part of it.
topic_notes: The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provides machinery for investigating and settling industrial disputes. It came into force on 1 April 1947. Key definitions: industry (Sec 2(j)), workman (Sec 2(s)), industrial dispute (Sec 2(k)), strike (2(q)), lock-out (2(l)), lay-off (2(kkk)), retrenchment (2(oo)) and closure (2(cc)). Authorities under the Act are Works Committee (Sec 3), Conciliation Officers (Sec 4), Boards of Conciliation (Sec 5), Courts of Inquiry (Sec 6), Labour Courts (Sec 7), Tribunals (Sec 7A) and the National Tribunal (Sec 7B). Chapter V-A (Sec 25A-25J) covers lay-off and retrenchment. Sec 25C gives lay-off compensation of 50% of basic wages plus DA. Sec 25F requires one month's notice and retrenchment compensation of 15 days' average pay per completed year of service. Chapter V-B applies special provisions to establishments with 100 or more workers (raised to 300 by the Industrial Relations Code, 2020). Sec 25N requires prior permission for retrenchment, 25-O for closure, and 25M for lay-off. Public utility services require a 6-week strike notice under Sec 22. Illegal strikes and lock-outs are covered by Sec 23-24. Unfair labour practices are in the Fifth Schedule, and Sec 25T and 25U provide penalties. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes this Act along with the Trade Unions Act, 1926 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946.

question: To which one of the following types of establishments, the provisions of Lay-off under Chapter VB of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, are NOT applicable?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Chapter VB was inserted in 1976 and amended in 1982. It imposes special provisions on lay-off, retrenchment and closure: Section 25M requires prior permission of the appropriate Government for lay-off, Section 25N for retrenchment, and Section 25O for closure. Section 25K defines the scope. It applies to an industrial establishment (factory, mine or plantation) in which not less than 100 workmen on average per working day were employed in the preceding 12 months. 'Industrial establishment' for this chapter is defined by reference to Section 25L: a factory as defined in the Factories Act 1948 s.2(m), a mine as defined in the Mines Act 1952 s.2(1)(j), or a plantation as defined in the Plantations Labour Act 1951 s.2(f). Ordinary lay-off under Chapter VA (Sections 25C-25E) covers a wider range of establishments, including hotels, but Chapter VB's stricter regime does not. Since factories, mines and plantations are all expressly named, only hotels are left out. Remember that Section 25M does not apply to seasonal industrial establishments in the way it applies to others, and that lay-off compensation is 50 percent of basic wages plus DA.
explanations: Incorrect: plantations are expressly included in the definition of industrial establishment in Section 25L, so Chapter VB applies to them.
Incorrect: mines are expressly included in Section 25L, so Chapter VB applies to them.
Correct: hotels are not factories, mines or plantations, so Chapter VB lay-off provisions do not apply to them.
Incorrect: factories are the first category covered by Section 25L, so Chapter VB applies.
keyfact: Chapter VB covers only factories, mines and plantations with 100 or more workmen; hotels are outside it.
option_notes: Plantations: defined in the Plantations Labour Act 1951 as a place for growing tea, coffee, rubber, cinchona, cardamom etc., with a minimum area (originally 5 hectares) and a minimum number of workers (originally 15). They are included in Chapter VB when they employ 100 or more workmen.

Mines: defined under the Mines Act 1952 as any excavation where operations for searching for or obtaining minerals are carried on. Mines with 100 or more workmen fall under Chapter VB, so lay-off, retrenchment and closure need government permission.

Hotels: a hotel is an industry under the ID Act, as shown by the Bangalore Water Supply case (1978) test, so Chapter VA may apply. It is not an 'industrial establishment' for Chapter VB, which covers only factories, mines and plantations.

Factories: defined in the Factories Act 1948 as premises with 10 or more workers using power, or 20 or more without power, engaged in manufacturing. A factory with 100 or more workmen is covered by Chapter VB.
related: Chapter VB applies to factories, mines and plantations with 100 or more workmen.
Section 25M requires prior permission for lay-off, 25N for retrenchment, 25O for closure.
Lay-off compensation is 50 percent of basic wages plus DA.
Section 2(kkk) of the ID Act defines lay-off.
Industrial Relations Code 2020 raises the permission threshold to 300 workers.
Section 25F sets the conditions precedent to retrenchment.
Section 25FFA requires 60 days' notice of closure.
summary: The answer is (c) Hotels. Chapter VB (Sections 25K-25S) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 applies to industrial establishments, defined as factories, mines and plantations, with 100 or more workmen. Hotels are not covered by this definition.
topic_notes: Chapter VA (Sections 25A-25J) deals with lay-off and retrenchment generally. Section 25C gives lay-off compensation of 50 percent of basic wages and DA to workmen with at least one year of continuous service. Section 25F sets the conditions for retrenchment: one month's notice or pay in lieu, and compensation of 15 days' average pay for each completed year of service. Section 25FFA requires 60 days' notice of closure for establishments with 50 or more workmen, and Section 25FFF gives compensation on closure. Chapter VB (Sections 25K-25S) was inserted in 1976 for establishments with 50 or more workmen, and the threshold was raised to 100 in 1982. It requires prior government permission for lay-off (25M), retrenchment (25N) and closure (25O). The Section 25-O closure provision was upheld in the Orissa Textile Mills case. Section 25Q provides penalties for contravention. Definitions: lay-off is in Section 2(kkk), retrenchment in 2(oo), and industry in 2(j). The Industrial Relations Code 2020 raises the threshold for prior permission to 300 workers and replaces the ID Act once it comes into force.

question: As per the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, an employer can NOT change the conditions of service specified in Fourth Schedule of the Act without giving notice and within:
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 9A (inserted in 1950) bars an employer from changing conditions of service applicable to a workman in respect of any matter in the Fourth Schedule unless (a) he has given the workmen likely to be affected notice of the proposed change in the prescribed manner, and (b) 21 days have elapsed since the notice was given. The notice must state the nature of the change and be served individually or displayed on notice boards at the establishment. The Fourth Schedule lists matters such as wages (including the period and mode of payment), contribution paid or payable by the employer to any provident fund or pension fund or for the benefit of workmen under any law, compensatory and other allowances, hours of work and rest intervals, leave with wages and holidays, starting/alteration/discontinuance of shift working otherwise than in accordance with standing orders, classification of workmen by grades, withdrawal of customary concessions or privileges or change in usage, introduction of new rules of discipline, rationalisation/standardisation/improvement of plant that may lead to retrenchment, and increase or reduction (other than casual) in the number of persons employed. Section 9A does not apply where the change is effected in pursuance of a settlement or award, or where workmen are governed by Central or State Government service rules. Section 9A is a notice of change, whereas Section 22 and 23 deal with strike/lockout notices (14 days and 6 weeks). Hence 21 days is correct; 15, 30 and 60 days are not the statutory period.
explanations: Incorrect: 15 days is not the period in Section 9A. It is sometimes confused with other notice periods, such as the 15-day notice under Section 33 or other provisions.
Correct: Section 9A requires 21 days' notice before changing Fourth Schedule conditions of service.
Incorrect: 30 days is not the Section 9A period. It is not the statutory period here, though 30 days features elsewhere in labour law notices.
Incorrect: 60 days is not the Section 9A period. Closure notice under Section 25FFA is 60 days, which is a different provision.
keyfact: Section 9A, ID Act 1947: Fourth Schedule changes need 21 days' notice to workmen.
option_notes: 15 days: not the Section 9A period. Fifteen days appears elsewhere in labour law, for example in some payment and notice provisions. It is a distractor here and must not be confused with the 21-day notice of change.

21 days: the statutory period under Section 9A of the ID Act, 1947 for notice of change in conditions of service on Fourth Schedule matters. The notice goes to the affected workmen in the prescribed manner. It was inserted in 1950 to protect workmen from unilateral changes.

30 days: not the Section 9A period. Thirty days appears in other labour statutes, such as notice periods under certain service rules or payment provisions, but it is not the notice of change period under the ID Act.

60 days: not the Section 9A period. Sixty days is the notice for closure of an undertaking under Section 25FFA, where the employer employs 50 or more workmen, and is also relevant to the notice of retrenchment/closure provisions in Chapter VB contexts.
related: Section 9A: 21 days' notice of change in conditions of service
Fourth Schedule lists matters requiring notice of change
Section 22: strike notice, 6 weeks maximum before and not within 14 days
Section 25F: retrenchment needs one month's notice and 15 days' pay per year
Section 25FFA: 60 days' notice for closure
Fifth Schedule lists unfair labour practices
Section 9A does not apply to changes under settlement or award
summary: The answer is (b) 21 days. Under Section 9A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, an employer cannot change conditions of service listed in the Fourth Schedule without giving each affected workman 21 days' notice, and cannot effect the change within 21 days of giving that notice.
topic_notes: Section 9A of the ID Act, 1947 deals with notice of change. Its purpose is to prevent employers from unilaterally altering service conditions to the detriment of workmen without giving them an opportunity to object or raise a dispute. Notice must be given to workmen likely to be affected, in the prescribed manner, and the change cannot take effect before 21 days have passed. Exceptions: changes under a settlement or award, and workmen covered by Central or State Government rules of service (for example, Civil Service rules). The Fourth Schedule lists the matters; the Third Schedule lists the matters within the jurisdiction of Industrial Tribunals; the Second Schedule lists matters for Labour Courts; the First Schedule lists industries which may be declared public utility services. The Fifth Schedule lists unfair labour practices (Section 25T and 25U penalise them). Related notice periods: strike or lockout in public utility services requires 6 weeks' notice, and the strike or lockout cannot occur within 14 days of giving notice (Section 22). Retrenchment under Section 25F requires one month's notice and compensation of 15 days' average pay per completed year of service. Layoff compensation under Section 25C is 50 percent of basic wages and DA. Closure notice under Section 25FFA is 60 days. Chapter VB applies to establishments with 100 or more workmen (the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 raises the threshold to 300). Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 the notice of change provisions are in Section 40, with the same 14-day notice concept in the Code's version, so students should watch which statute the question cites.

question: According to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which one of the following can NOT be raised as an industrial dispute by a trade union of workers?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 2(k) of the ID Act defines an industrial dispute as any dispute or difference between employers and employers, employers and workmen, or workmen and workmen, connected with the employment or non-employment, the terms of employment or the conditions of labour of any person. The Second Schedule lists matters within the jurisdiction of Labour Courts, such as discharge or dismissal, withdrawal of a customary concession, and illegality of strikes. The Third Schedule lists matters within the jurisdiction of Industrial Tribunals, such as wages, bonus, hours of work, leave, and rationalisation. Stoppage of an annual increment is a wage matter. Denial of promotion is a condition of service and employment. Discharge of a probationer is a question of non-employment, so it can be referred, even though termination of a probationer's services under the contract may not count as retrenchment under Section 2(oo). Recognition of a trade union is a matter between the union and the employer about the union's status. It is not a dispute over the employment terms of workmen as such, and it appears in neither Schedule. It is governed by the Trade Unions Act (which has no compulsory recognition provision), the Code of Discipline, and state laws like the Bombay IR Act or the Maharashtra MRTU and PULP Act. Hence (c) is the odd one out.
explanations: (a) is wrong as the answer: stoppage of an increment is a wage or terms-of-employment matter, listed in the Third Schedule, and can be raised as an industrial dispute.
(b) is wrong as the answer: denial of promotion concerns conditions of service, so it falls within the Section 2(k) definition and can be raised and referred for adjudication.

(c) is correct: recognition of a union is not within the ID Act's Schedules and does not concern the employment terms of workmen. It is governed by state laws and the Code of Discipline, so it cannot be raised as an industrial dispute under this Act.
(d) is wrong as the answer: discharge of a probationer concerns non-employment and can be raised and referred, particularly where it is alleged to be punitive, mala fide or victimisation.
keyfact: Increments, promotion and discharge are industrial disputes under the ID Act; recognition of a trade union is not covered by the Act's Schedules and is left to state laws and the Code of Discipline.
option_notes: Stoppage of annual increment: an increment is a periodic rise in pay within a scale. Stopping it, especially as a penalty, affects wages and terms of employment. Wages, allowances and the classification of grades are in the Third Schedule, which covers matters for Industrial Tribunals. A union can therefore raise this as an industrial dispute. The ID Act's definition of 'wages' follows Section 2(rr).

Denial of promotion: promotion is a condition of service. Courts have held that disputes over promotion policy, seniority and denial of promotion are 'conditions of employment' and so are industrial disputes if raised by a union or a substantial body of workmen. An individual dispute needs support under Section 2A or union backing. Promotion by merit-cum-seniority is a management function, but its application can still be challenged.

Recognition of trade union: recognition means the employer's acceptance of a union as the bargaining representative of workers. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 has no compulsory recognition provision. Recognition is regulated by the Code of Discipline (1958), state laws such as the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, the Maharashtra MRTU and PULP Act, 1971, and the Kerala and West Bengal rules. Refusing recognition is an unfair labour practice only in some state laws. The ID Act does not provide a remedy for it.

Discharge of a probationer: a probationer is employed on trial before confirmation. Discharge simpliciter under the contract is not retrenchment under Section 2(oo)(bb) in the case of contract expiry, but where it is punitive, stigmatic or mala fide it can be challenged. Discharge, dismissal and termination are Second Schedule matters for Labour Courts. Sections 2A and 10 allow the dispute to be raised and referred. Cases such as Dhingra's and Gujarat Steel Tubes deal with it.
related: Section 2(k) of the ID Act defines 'industrial dispute'.
Section 2A lets an individual workman raise a dispute over discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination.
Second Schedule: matters for Labour Courts; Third Schedule: matters for Industrial Tribunals.
Fifth Schedule lists unfair labour practices.
Section 25F: conditions precedent to retrenchment, including one month's notice and compensation.
Bangalore Water Supply (1978) laid down the triple test for 'industry'.
Chapter VB (Sec 25K onwards) applies to establishments with 100 or more workmen.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 will replace the ID Act, 1947, the Trade Unions Act and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act.
summary: The answer is (c) Recognition of trade union. Under Section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, an industrial dispute must relate to employment, non-employment, terms of employment or conditions of labour. Increments, promotion and discharge all fall within these heads.
