option_notes: The Appropriate Government is the Central Government for establishments under its authority (railways, mines, ports, etc.) and the State Government otherwise (Section 2(1)(a)). It appoints Inspectors (Section 28), constitutes Advisory Boards (Sections 3 and 4), makes rules (Sections 35 and 38), and may exempt establishments (Section 31). It does not file or sanction prosecutions under Section 26.

The Labour Commissioner is a senior state or central labour administrator who heads the labour department. Under various labour laws he is often the appellate or licensing authority, or the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) in the central sphere. Under the CLRA Act, licensing officers are appointed by the Government and Section 26 does not name the Labour Commissioner as the complainant.

The Inspector is appointed by the Appropriate Government under Section 28 for the local limits it assigns. Inspectors have powers to enter and inspect premises, examine persons and records, and seize documents. Only the Inspector may file a complaint or sanction prosecution under Section 26, and must do so within three months of knowledge of the offence.

A Class I Gazetted Officer is a senior government officer, the highest group of officers in the civil services. This phrase is not used in the CLRA Act's cognizance provision. Such an officer has authority only if appointed an Inspector or given a role under the Act. Some other statutes use rank-based designations, which is why this option is a distractor.
related: CLRA Act 1970 applies to establishments with 20 or more contract workmen.
Section 26: cognizance only on complaint by or with sanction of the Inspector.
Complaint must be filed within three months of the Inspector's knowledge of the offence.
Section 28 provides for appointment of Inspectors.
Section 10 allows prohibition of contract labour by the Appropriate Government.
Section 21 makes the principal employer liable for unpaid wages.
Section 23 prescribes imprisonment up to three months or a fine up to Rs 1,000 for contravention.
The Act is subsumed under the OSH Code, 2020.
summary: The correct answer is (c), the Inspector. Section 26(1) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 bars any court from taking cognizance of an offence under the Act except on a complaint by, or with the previous sanction in writing of, the Inspector.
topic_notes: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 regulates the employment of contract labour in certain establishments and provides for its abolition in some circumstances. It came into force in 1971. It applies to every establishment employing 20 or more workmen as contract labour on any day of the preceding twelve months, and to every contractor employing 20 or more workmen. Appropriate Governments may extend it to establishments with fewer workmen. It does not apply to establishments where work is of an intermittent or casual nature. Principal employers must register their establishments, and contractors must hold a licence. Central and State Advisory Boards are constituted under Sections 3 and 4. Section 10 empowers the Appropriate Government to prohibit contract labour in any process, operation or work after consulting the Advisory Board. Section 21 makes the principal employer liable for payment of wages if the contractor fails to do so. Welfare provisions include canteens, restrooms, drinking water, latrines and first aid. Section 25 deals with offences by companies. Section 26 covers cognizance, with a three-month limitation. Section 23 punishes contravention of the Act or its rules with imprisonment up to three months or a fine up to Rs 1,000, or both. Section 24 deals with other offences. Landmark cases include Air India Statutory Corporation v. United Labour Union (1996), and Steel Authority of India v. National Union Waterfront Workers (2001), which overruled the automatic absorption rule. The Act was subsumed in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which has not been fully implemented.

question: Part III of the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 deals with:
options: Child Labour and Adolescent Labour Rehabilitation Fund
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 was renamed the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act by the 2016 Amendment, which came into force on 1 September 2016. Its structure is as follows. Part I (Preliminary) covers the short title and definitions. Part II is on prohibition of employment of children in certain occupations and processes. It includes the general prohibition on children under 14 working (s.3), the power to amend the Schedule (s.4) and the Technical Advisory Committee (s.5). Part III covers regulation of conditions of work, including hours of work, weekly holiday, notice to the Inspector, health and safety, and maintenance of registers (roughly ss.6-13). Part IV is Miscellaneous, covering penalties, the Rehabilitation Fund, rule-making power and so on. The 2016 amendment banned employment of children below 14 in all occupations except family enterprises and audio-visual entertainment after school hours. It also banned adolescents (14-18) from hazardous occupations, which are listed in a shortened Schedule. Penalties were raised to imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years and/or a fine of Rs 20,000-50,000. Options (a) and (d) belong to Part II, and (b) is a miscellaneous provision, so only (c) matches Part III.
explanations: Incorrect: the Technical Advisory Committee is constituted under Section 5, which falls in Part II (prohibition), not Part III.
Incorrect: the Child Labour and Adolescent Labour Rehabilitation Fund was added by the 2016 amendment. It is a miscellaneous provision (Part IV) and not part of Part III.
Correct: Part III is titled 'Regulation of Conditions of Work' and covers hours, holidays, notice, health and safety, and registers.
Incorrect: the power of the Central Government to amend the Schedule is in Section 4, which is in Part II.
keyfact: Part III of the Child and Adolescent Labour Act, 1986 = regulation of conditions of work; Part II = prohibition (s.3, s.4 Schedule amendment, s.5 TAC).
option_notes: The Technical Advisory Committee is a body under Section 5 that advises the Central Government on adding occupations and processes to the Schedule of hazardous work. The Central Government constitutes it by notification. It has a Chairman and up to 10 other members, who are appointed by the Government and have no fixed constitutional status. It sits in Part II of the Act.

The Child Labour and Adolescent Labour Rehabilitation Fund was introduced by the 2016 amendment (Section 14B). Each appropriate Government sets it up for rehabilitating children and adolescents rescued from prohibited work. Fines collected from offenders go into it. The Fund is an administrative and miscellaneous provision and is not in the conditions-of-work Part.

Regulation of conditions of work is the content of Part III. It covers hours and period of work (3 hours then a rest interval of at least 1 hour, no work between 7 pm and 8 am, no overtime, no work in more than one establishment), a weekly holiday, notice to the Inspector, a health and safety framework, and the maintenance of registers. It applies to permitted work, such as family enterprises and audio-visual entertainment.

The power to amend the Schedule is in Section 4. The Central Government may add to or omit occupations and processes in the Schedule of hazardous work by notification. After 2016 the Schedule was cut down to hazardous occupations, which are mining, inflammable substances and explosives, and hazardous processes under the Factories Act. This power is in Part II.
related: Article 24 bans employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous employment.
The 2016 amendment came into force on 1 September 2016.
An adolescent is a person aged 14 to 18 under the amended Act.

summary: The answer is (c), regulation of conditions of work. Part III of the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 deals with the regulation of conditions of work of children and adolescents in the occupations where they are still allowed to work. The Technical Advisory Committee and the power to amend the Schedule sit in Part II, which deals with prohibition.
topic_notes: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 was the main central law on child labour. Children below 14 may not work in any occupation. The exceptions are helping family or family enterprise after school hours or during vacations, and working as a child artist in audio-visual entertainment (excluding the circus), subject to safeguards. Adolescents may not work in hazardous occupations and processes, which now cover mining, inflammable substances or explosives, and hazardous processes under the Factories Act, 1948. Penalties are imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years and/or a fine of Rs 20,000-50,000 for employing a child or adolescent in violation. Repeat offences carry 1-3 years. The offence was made cognizable. question: Who among the following can appoint the Inspectors under the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Act was originally the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 and was amended in 2016 (in force from 1 September 2016) and renamed the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act. It prohibits employment of children (below 14 years) in all occupations and processes, and prohibits adolescents (14-18 years) from hazardous occupations and processes listed in the Schedule. Under the Act, 'appropriate Government' means the Central Government in relation to establishments under its control (railways, major ports, mines, oil fields, or a corporation established by Central law) and the State Government in all other cases. Section 17 empowers the appropriate Government to appoint Inspectors for the purposes of the Act and define their local limits. Because both the Centre and a State can appoint, depending on the establishment, the generic term 'appropriate Government' is correct. Options (a) and (b) are each only partly true, as each covers only one category of establishments. Option (d), the Labour Commissioner, is an officer of the Government with no independent power to appoint Inspectors under this section. The 2016 amendment also raised penalties and made the offence of employing children cognizable.
explanations: Incorrect: the Central Government appoints Inspectors only for establishments under its control, so this is too narrow.
Incorrect: the State Government appoints Inspectors for establishments other than those under Central control, so this is too narrow.
Correct: Section 17 uses the term 'appropriate Government', which covers the Centre or the State depending on the establishment.
Incorrect: the Labour Commissioner is an administrative officer and is not the appointing authority under the Act.
keyfact: Under the Child and Adolescent Labour Act, 1986, the 'appropriate Government' (Centre or State) appoints Inspectors.
option_notes: The Central Government is the 'appropriate Government' for establishments such as railways, major ports, mines, oil fields, and bodies established under Central law. It makes rules, and its Labour Ministry oversees national policy such as the National Child Labour Project (NCLP) and the PENCIL portal. It does not appoint Inspectors for all establishments.

The State Government is the appropriate Government for all establishments not under Central control. It appoints most Inspectors, makes state rules under the Act, and runs enforcement and rehabilitation through its labour departments and District Magistrates. It is not the sole appointing authority.

'Appropriate Government' is a defined term in the Act. It means the Central Government for establishments under its control and the State Government in other cases. It is the term used in Section 17 for appointing Inspectors, and the same term applies in other labour laws such as the Factories Act and the Industrial Disputes Act.

The Labour Commissioner is the head of the state or central labour department (the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) is under the Ministry of Labour and Employment). The post is involved in enforcement and conciliation, but it does not have the statutory power to appoint Inspectors under this Act.
related: The 2016 Amendment came into force on 1 September 2016.
A 'child' is under 14 years; an 'adolescent' is 14 to 18 years.

topic_notes: The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 began as the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986. It prohibits adolescents from hazardous occupations such as mines, inflammable substances and explosives, and hazardous processes under the Factories Act. The Schedule of hazardous occupations was cut down to three categories by the 2016 amendment. Penalties: employing a child leads to imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years, or a fine of Rs 20,000 to Rs 50,000, or both. Repeat offences carry imprisonment of 1 to 3 years. The offence is cognizable. The Act replaced the earlier Children (Pledging of Labour) Act, 1933 in spirit and follows the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act framework. Mehta case (1996) led to the Child Labour Rehabilitation-cum-Welfare Fund. ILO Conventions 138 (minimum age) and 182 (worst forms of child labour) have both been ratified by India.

question: As per the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, in which of the following types of occupations, a child can be employed?
options: Transport of passengers, goods or mails by railways
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 was amended in 2016 and renamed the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act. It prohibits employment of children (below 14 years) in all occupations and processes, with two exceptions: (i) helping their family or family enterprise, other than hazardous ones, after school hours or during vacations, and (ii) working as a child artist in audio-visual entertainment industry (advertisement, films, TV serials or any such entertainment or sports activity, except the circus), subject to safety conditions, and provided that school education is not affected. Adolescents (14-18) are prohibited from hazardous occupations and processes; the list was cut down to mines, inflammable substances and explosives, and hazardous processes under the Factories Act. The original Part A of the Schedule listed occupations such as transport of passengers, goods or mails by railways, catering at railway establishments, and others. Part B listed processes. Restaurants, hotels, motels and tea-shops (dhabas, restaurants) and automobile workshops and garages were in the original Schedule list banning child employment. Hence only audio-visual entertainment is permitted, with permission and conditions. Elimination: options b, c and d come from the prohibited list.
explanations: Correct: child artist work in audio-visual entertainment (except circus) is expressly permitted under the 2016 amendment, with safeguards on working hours, education and permission from the District Magistrate.
Incorrect: transport of passengers, goods or mails by railways was in the original Part A list of prohibited occupations for children.
Incorrect: employment in restaurants, hotels, motels, tea-shops and similar hospitality establishments was a prohibited occupation for children.
Incorrect: automobile workshops and garages were in the list of prohibited occupations for children.
keyfact: Children under 14 may work only in non-hazardous family enterprises (after school) or as child artists in audio-visual entertainment (not the circus).
option_notes: Audio-visual entertainment covers advertisements, films, TV serials and other entertainment or sports activities, but not the circus. Under the 2016 amendment child artists may work with permission and safeguards: the work must not affect schooling, and the producer must obtain permission from the District Magistrate and follow the rules for working hours and conditions. This is the main exception to the ban on child employment.

Transport of passengers, goods or mails by railways was in the original Part A list of occupations prohibited for children under the 1986 Act. The railway also covers related work such as catering at railway stations and cinder picking. It is a hazardous setting, so child employment is barred. Adolescents too are now barred from hazardous work.

Restaurants, hotels, motels, tea-shops, dhabas, spas, and other eating places were added to the prohibited list in 2006 (notification effective October 2006) after the Child Labour Technical Advisory Committee's recommendation. Domestic work was also banned for children in the same notification. Employment of children in them is an offence.

Automobile workshops and garages were added to the prohibited occupations list in the 1986 Act's Schedule in 2006 (along with dhabas, restaurants and domestic work). They are considered hazardous because of exposure to oils, chemicals, machines and heavy parts. Children cannot be employed there.
related: Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous employment.
The 2016 amendment defines an adolescent as a person aged 14 to 18.

summary: The answer is (a) Audio-visual entertainment. Under the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, as amended in 2016, a child below 14 may work only in a family enterprise or as a child artist in audio-visual entertainment, subject to safeguards. Railways, restaurants/hotels and automobile workshops are hazardous or prohibited occupations.
topic_notes: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 replaced earlier laws such as the Employment of Children Act, 1938. It was amended in 2016 (Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016, effective 1 September 2016). Key points: a child is a person below 14 years; an adolescent is 14-18 years. Children below 14 are prohibited from all occupations and processes, except helping family or family enterprise (non-hazardous, after school hours or in vacations) and working as child artists in audio-visual entertainment (not the circus) with safeguards. Adolescents are barred from hazardous occupations (mines, inflammable substances or explosives, hazardous processes under the Factories Act, 1948). The Schedule list of hazardous occupations was reduced. Penalties: for employing a child, imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years or fine of Rs 20,000 to 50,000 or both; repeat offence leads to 1 to 3 years imprisonment. Employing an adolescent in hazardous work attracts the same sort of penalty. The offence is made cognizable. Parents are not punished unless they repeat violations, except for the employment of children in hazardous work. The District Magistrate is the authority responsible for enforcement. Related: Article 24 of the Constitution bans employment of children below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work; Article 21A gives free and compulsory education for ages 6-14 (86th Amendment, 2002); Right to Education Act 2009; National Child Labour Project (NCLP) 1988; PENCIL portal; ILO Conventions 138 (minimum age) and 182 (worst forms) ratified by India in 2017; Bachpan Bachao Andolan; Kailash Satyarthi, Nobel Peace Prize 2014; World Day Against Child Labour on 12 June.

question: Which one of the following is the maximum spread over of the daily hours of work including interval for rest, time spent in waiting for work under the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 was renamed the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act by the 2016 Amendment, which came into force on 1 September 2016. Section 7 (Hours and period of work) says that no child (in permitted work such as helping the family or in audio-visual entertainment) or adolescent shall be required or permitted to work in any establishment in excess of the number of hours prescribed. The period of work on each day is fixed so that no period exceeds three hours, and no child shall work for more than three hours before an interval for rest of at least one hour. The period of work of a child shall be so arranged that inclusive of the interval for rest under sub-section (2), it shall not be spread over more than six hours, including the time spent in waiting for work on any day. No child shall be permitted to work between 7 pm and 8 am, no overtime is allowed, and no child can work in more than one establishment on the same day. Each child gets a weekly holiday. Elimination: three hours is the maximum continuous work period before rest, not the spread over. Five and seven hours are not stated in the Act.
explanations: Incorrect: five hours is not the figure in Section 7 of the Act.
Correct: Section 7 caps the spread over, including the rest interval and waiting time, at six hours per day.
Incorrect: seven hours is not the statutory spread over. This may be confused with the 7 pm limit on night work.
Incorrect: three hours is the longest continuous work period before a rest interval of at least one hour, not the total spread over.
keyfact: Under Section 7 of the Child and Adolescent Labour Act, 1986, work is 3 hours at a stretch, a 1-hour rest, and a maximum 6-hour spread over.
option_notes: Five hours: it has no specific meaning under this Act. Section 7 sets 3 hours of continuous work, a 1-hour rest and a 6-hour spread over. The 5-hour figure appears in other labour laws, such as the Factories Act, which bars work for more than five hours without a rest interval (adults, Section 55; the limit was 4.5 hours for adolescents before amendments).

Six hours: this is the maximum spread over of the daily work of a child under Section 7. It includes the rest interval of at least one hour and any time spent waiting for work. The aim is to protect health and education. It applies to children permitted to help family enterprises after school hours or to work in audio-visual entertainment, and to adolescents in non-hazardous work.

Seven hours: the Act does not use this as a spread over. The closest figure is the 7 pm bar on children working from 7 pm to 8 am. Adults under the Factories Act have much longer limits, such as 9 hours a day and 48 hours a week.

Three hours: under Section 7, the work period must not exceed three hours before the child gets a rest interval of at least one hour. It is a limit on continuous work, not the total daily spread over. It is often confused with the six-hour spread over.

summary: The answer is (b) Six hours. Under Section 7 of the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (formerly the Child Labour Act), the period of work of an adolescent/child in an establishment must be so fixed that the spread over, including the rest interval and time spent waiting for work, does not exceed six hours.
topic_notes: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 was enacted following the Gurupadswamy Committee (1979) recommendations. It prohibited employment of children under 14 in hazardous occupations and processes listed in the Schedule, and regulated conditions of work elsewhere. The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016 (in force 1 September 2016) changed the title, prohibited employment of children below 14 in all occupations and processes, with exceptions for helping family or family enterprise after school hours or in vacations, and for child artists in audio-visual entertainment (not circus). It created a new category of adolescents (14 to 18) and prohibited their employment in hazardous occupations, which were reduced to three in the Schedule: mines, inflammable substances or explosives, and hazardous processes under the Factories Act. Penalties were raised: imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years, or a fine of Rs 20,000 to Rs 50,000, or both, for employing a child in violation; repeat offences carry 1 to 3 years. Employing an adolescent in violation attracts a fine of Rs 10,000 to Rs 50,000 or imprisonment. Parents are not punished unless they repeat the offence. The Act made offences cognizable. Related constitutional provisions include Article 24 (no child under 14 in a factory, mine or hazardous employment), Article 21A (right to education), Article 39(e) and 39(f), and Article 45. The Right to Education Act, 2009 links with this Act. The National Child Labour Project (NCLP) scheme provided special schools. India ratified ILO Conventions 138 (minimum age) and 182 (worst forms) in 2017. Section 7 also provides for a weekly holiday, notice of work periods, and a ban on work in more than one establishment on the same day.

question: Which of the following is NOT true with respect to the amendments introduced by The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016?
options: Offences under the Act are made non-compoundable
Provides for rehabilitation of rescued child or adolescent
Inspection and monitoring is required to be secured by the appropriate government
Offences committed by an employer punishable under section 3 of the Act are made cognizable
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016 (in force 1 September 2016) totally prohibits employment of children below 14 in all occupations, except helping family or family enterprises after school hours or in vacations, and work as an artist in audio-visual entertainment (not circus). Adolescents (14-18) are barred from hazardous occupations and processes listed in the Schedule, which was cut to three entries: mines, inflammable substances or explosives, and hazardous processes under the Factories Act. Penalties were raised to 6 months-2 years imprisonment and/or a fine of Rs 20,000-50,000, with 1-3 years for repeat offence. Parents or guardians are generally not punished, except for repeat offences. The Act inserted provisions making employer offences cognizable. It provides for rehabilitation of rescued children, with a Child and Adolescent Labour Rehabilitation Fund in each district. It also requires the appropriate government to ensure inspection and monitoring. The statement that offences are made non-compoundable is the odd one out, because the amendment allows compounding of certain offences, such as those by parents, subject to conditions. Options (b), (c) and (d) match features of the amendment.
explanations: Not true: the amendment does not make offences wholly non-compoundable. It allows compounding of certain offences, such as those by parents or guardians, under specified conditions. This is the NOT-true statement, so it is the answer.
True: the Act provides for rehabilitation of rescued children and adolescents, including a Child and Adolescent Labour Rehabilitation Fund at district level. So this is not the answer.
True: the appropriate government must secure inspection and monitoring. It must also appoint officers and make rules to carry this out. So this is not the answer.
True: the amendment makes employer offences under section 3 cognizable, so police can act without a warrant. So this is not the answer.
keyfact: The 2016 Child Labour Amendment Act made employer offences cognizable, but it did not make all offences non-compoundable.
option_notes: Compoundability means the parties can settle an offence without trial. Under the 2016 amendment, offences by parents or guardians can be compounded in specified cases. Offences by employers are treated seriously and are cognizable. The claim that all offences are non-compoundable is therefore inaccurate.

Rehabilitation: rescued children are to be rehabilitated under the Act. Each district has a Child and Adolescent Labour Rehabilitation Fund. The fund is built from fines recovered from offenders and from government contributions. The District Magistrate is responsible for enforcement and rehabilitation.

Inspection and monitoring: the appropriate government (Central or State) must secure compliance by appointing inspectors and by monitoring establishments. The Act also relies on the Right to Education linkage. The 1986 Act already had inspectors, and the amendment strengthened the machinery.

Cognizable offences: police can register an FIR and investigate without a magistrate's warrant. The 2016 amendment applies this to employer offences under section 3, which prohibits child employment. It also raised the punishment, making enforcement stronger than under the 1986 Act.
related: The 2016 amendment came into force on 1 September 2016.
It bans employment of children under 14 in all occupations, with limited exceptions.
Adolescents (14-18) are barred from hazardous occupations and processes.
The Schedule of hazardous occupations was reduced to three entries.

Article 24 bans employment of children under 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.
India ratified ILO Conventions 138 and 182 in 2017.

summary: The answer is (a). The 2016 Amendment Act does not make all offences non-compoundable; it permits compounding in limited cases. It does make employer offences cognizable, provide for rehabilitation, and require inspection and monitoring by the appropriate government.
topic_notes: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 originally banned children under 14 only from hazardous occupations and processes listed in a Schedule. It was based on the Gurupadaswamy Committee (1979) recommendations. The 2016 Amendment received assent in July 2016 and came into force on 1 September 2016. Its main features are: (1) a complete ban on employment of children under 14, with exceptions for family enterprises outside school hours and for child artists; (2) a new category of adolescent (14-18), barred from hazardous work; (3) a reduced Schedule of hazardous occupations; (4) higher penalties, with imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years and a fine of Rs 20,000 to 50,000; (5) repeat offences punished by 1 to 3 years; (6) employer offences made cognizable; (7) rehabilitation of rescued children; (8) a district-level fund; and (9) a duty on the appropriate government to inspect and monitor. Related law: Article 24 of the Constitution prohibits employment of children under 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work. Article 21A gives the right to education for ages 6-14. Article 39(e) and (f) are Directive Principles. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 and the Factories Act, 1948 are also relevant. India ratified ILO Conventions 138 (minimum age) and 182 (worst forms of child labour) in 2017. The National Child Labour Project (NCLP) runs special schools for rescued children. The PENCIL portal is used for tracking and enforcement. Possible exam angles include the age limits, the penalties, the Schedule entries, Article 24 and the ILO conventions.

question: There are ten persons employed in a shop and therefore the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, becomes applicable to the shop. After some time, three employees resign from the services of the shop. Resultantly, which one of the following is the correct legal position on the applicability or otherwise of the said Act?
options: The Act will continue to be applicable on the shop
As soon as the number of employees of the shop falls below ten, the Act will cease to be applicable
The Act is silent about this type of situation
The Act will not apply when the number of employees who leave the shop exceed 50%
subject: Social Security
detail: Section 1(3)(c) applies the Act to every shop or establishment within the meaning of any law for the time being in force in a State relating to shops and establishments, in which ten or more persons are employed, or were employed, on any day of the preceding twelve months. The proviso is the key point: the Central Government may notify other establishments, and the Act, once applicable, continues to apply to the establishment even if the number of persons employed falls below ten at any later time. This is the 'once applicable, always applicable' rule, which prevents employers from escaping liability by reducing headcount. Gratuity is payable under Section 4 to an employee who has rendered at least five years of continuous service, on superannuation, retirement or resignation, or on death or disablement (the five-year condition is waived for death or disablement). The maximum is Rs 20 lakh, and the rate is 15 days' wages for each completed year of service, calculated as last drawn wages x 15/26 x years. Elimination: (b) contradicts the proviso. (c) is wrong because the Act expressly addresses the situation. (d) invents a 50% rule that does not exist in the Act.
explanations: Correct: the proviso to Section 1(3)(c) says the Act continues to apply even if the number of employees later falls below ten.
Incorrect: the Act does not cease to apply when the number falls below ten. That would defeat the protective purpose of the Act.
Incorrect: the Act is not silent. Section 1(3) and its proviso expressly cover the situation.
Incorrect: there is no 50% threshold anywhere in the Act, so this is a fabricated condition.
keyfact: Once the Payment of Gratuity Act applies to an establishment with ten or more employees, it continues to apply even if headcount falls below ten.
option_notes: Continued applicability: once an establishment is covered by the Act, it stays covered, regardless of later reductions in staff. The rule is in the proviso to Section 1(3)(c). It gives employees stable protection, and the establishment cannot opt out by retrenching staff.

Cessation below ten: this is the common misconception. Ten is only the entry threshold for coverage and not a continuing condition. Some other laws, such as the EPF Act (20 employees) and the ESI Act (10 or 20 depending on the establishment), also use thresholds, but the Gratuity Act's proviso specifically protects continuity.
Silence of the Act: wrong, because the legislature foresaw fluctuating headcount and addressed it explicitly in the proviso to Section 1(3)(c). Courts have treated this as settled law.

The 50% rule: no such rule exists in the Payment of Gratuity Act. Applicability depends on the number of persons employed on any day in the preceding twelve months and is not affected by the percentage of employees who leave.
related: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972.
Gratuity ceiling is Rs 20 lakh after the 2018 amendment.
Gratuity formula: last drawn wages x 15/26 x completed years of service.
Section 4 requires five years of continuous service, waived for death or disablement.
The employee does not contribute to gratuity. It is paid entirely by the employer.
Section 4(6) allows forfeiture of gratuity for specified misconduct.
The Controlling Authority is appointed by the appropriate Government under Section 3.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the Gratuity Act and gives fixed-term employees gratuity after one year.
summary: The correct answer is (a). Under Section 1(3)(c) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, once the Act becomes applicable to a shop or establishment because it employed ten or more persons on any day of the preceding twelve months, it continues to apply even if the number of employees later falls below ten.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972 and extends to the whole of India. It covers factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railway companies, shops and establishments, and other establishments notified by the Government, where ten or more persons are employed. Gratuity is a retirement benefit paid by the employer, and the employee makes no contribution. Section 4 makes gratuity payable after five years of continuous service on superannuation, retirement or resignation, or on death or disablement. The five-year condition is not required for death or disablement. Rate: 15 days' wages for each completed year of service or part thereof in excess of six months. Monthly wage divisor is 26 days. The ceiling is Rs 20 lakh, raised from Rs 10 lakh by the 2018 amendment. Nomination is under Section 6. Gratuity can be forfeited under Section 4(6) for damage or loss caused by wilful act, or for riotous or violent conduct or an offence involving moral turpitude. Payment must be made within 30 days of becoming payable, and delay attracts simple interest. The Controlling Authority is appointed under Section 3, and appeals go to the Appellate Authority under Section 7(7). Inspectors are appointed under Section 8. The Act has overriding effect over other laws on the subject. Under the Code on Social Security, 2020, gratuity provisions are subsumed. The Code introduced gratuity for fixed-term employees after one year of service. Related ideas: continuous service includes lay-off, leave and maternity leave. In a seasonal establishment, service of seven months counts as a year.

question: As per the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, what is the rate of payment of gratuity in an establishment?
options: One month’s wages for every completed year of service
Ten days wages for every completed year of service
Fifteen days wages for every completed year of service
Three months wages for every completed year of service
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 4(2) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 fixes the rate of gratuity at fifteen days' wages, based on the rate of wages last drawn by the employee, for every completed year of service or part thereof in excess of six months. For employees of seasonal establishments, it is seven days' wages for each season. Gratuity becomes payable under Section 4(1) on superannuation, retirement or resignation, or on death or disablement due to accident or disease, after a minimum of five years of continuous service. The five-year condition is waived on death or disablement. The monthly-rated formula is: last drawn wages (basic + DA) x 15/26 x completed years of service. The divisor 26 is the number of working days in a month. The ceiling is Rs 20 lakh after the 2018 amendment, effective 29 March 2018. The Act applies to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and establishments employing 10 or more persons. Gratuity must be paid within 30 days of becoming payable. Elimination: one month's wages and three months' wages are not statutory rates. Ten days' wages is not the rate either.
explanations: Wrong: one month's wages per year is not the statutory rate. The Act prescribes 15 days' wages.
Wrong: ten days' wages is not provided anywhere in Section 4(2). It is sometimes confused with other schemes.
Correct: Section 4(2) prescribes fifteen days' wages for every completed year of service or part thereof exceeding six months.
Wrong: three months' wages per year is far above the statutory rate and has no basis in the Act.
keyfact: Gratuity = 15 days' wages for each completed year of service (over six months counts as a year), formula wages x 15/26 x years, ceiling Rs 20 lakh.
option_notes: One month's wages per completed year is a more generous rate than the Act provides. Some employers may pay it under contract or policy, and the Act does not prevent a better terms of payment (Section 4(5)). Under the Act itself, the rate is only 15 days' wages. Do not confuse it with notice pay or leave encashment norms.

Ten days' wages is not the gratuity rate under the Act. The figure may be mistaken for other benefits. The statutory formula is 15/26 x last drawn wages x years of service. Seasonal establishments have a separate rate of seven days per season.

Fifteen days' wages per completed year (or part thereof over six months) is the statutory rate under Section 4(2). The monthly formula is wages x 15/26 x years. The wage here means basic plus dearness allowance. The ceiling is Rs 20 lakh. This is the rate that the Act actually prescribes.
Three months' wages per year is not provided by the Act. It would far exceed the ceiling and the intended scheme. Gratuity is a modest retirement benefit, not a multi-month wage payment.

summary: The answer is (c). Under Section 4(2) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, gratuity is payable at fifteen days' wages for every completed year of service, or part thereof in excess of six months, subject to a maximum ceiling.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972 and extends to the whole of India. It is a social security measure that provides a retirement benefit to employees. It applies to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railway companies, shops and establishments employing 10 or more persons on any day of the preceding twelve months. Once covered, it continues to apply even if the number later falls below 10. Eligibility: Section 4(1) requires five years of continuous service on superannuation, retirement or resignation. The condition is relaxed on death or disablement. Rate: 15 days' wages for each completed year or part over six months, and seven days per season for seasonal establishments. Formula: last drawn monthly wages x 15/26 x years of service. For non-covered employees under the Act, the formula is 15/30. Ceiling: Rs 20 lakh since 2018. Payment: Section 7 requires the employer to determine the amount and give notice within 15 days, and pay within 30 days, with interest on delay. The Controlling Authority is appointed under Section 3, and appeals go to the Appropriate Government's appellate authority. Forfeiture: Section 4(6) allows forfeiture for damage or loss caused by the employee's riotous or violent conduct, or for an offence involving moral turpitude. Gratuity is exempt from attachment under Section 13. Penalties are in Section 9. The 2018 amendment also empowered the government to notify different ceilings. Maternity benefit and other schemes should not be confused with this Act.

question: As per the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, what is the rate of payment of gratuity in seasonal establishment?
options: Twenty days wages for each season
Fifteen days wages for each season
Seven days wages for each season
Ten days wages for each season
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 4(2) of the Act fixes gratuity for an employee who is not employed in a seasonal establishment at 15 days' wages for every completed year of service or part thereof exceeding six months. The monthly-rated formula is last drawn wages x 15/26 x years of service. Section 4(2) also provides that, in a seasonal establishment, gratuity is paid at the rate of seven days' wages for each season. The Act does not define 'season' with a fixed number of months. The maximum gratuity is capped under Section 4(3), which is Rs 20 lakh after the 2018 amendment (earlier Rs 10 lakh). Eligibility under Section 4(1) is five years of continuous service, which is relaxed on death or disablement. Gratuity is payable on superannuation, retirement or resignation, or on death or disablement due to accident or disease. Elimination: 15 days is the general rule, so (b) is wrong. 20 days and 10 days do not appear in Section 4(2) for this purpose, so (a) and (d) are wrong.
explanations: Incorrect: 20 days' wages is not the statutory rate in Section 4(2) for either regular or seasonal establishments.
Incorrect: 15 days' wages per completed year is the rate for non-seasonal establishments, not seasonal ones.
Correct: Section 4(2) prescribes seven days' wages for each season for employees of seasonal establishments.
Incorrect: 10 days' wages does not appear in the Act as a gratuity rate; the Rs 10 lakh figure was the old ceiling.
keyfact: Seasonal establishment gratuity: seven days' wages per season (Sec 4(2)); regular rate is 15 days' wages per year.
option_notes: Twenty days' wages is not a gratuity rate under the Act. Some pension and gratuity schemes, such as the Central Civil Services rules, use different formulas. Under the 1972 Act the standard rate is 15 days' wages. The figure 20 is most often met in the Rs 20 lakh ceiling set by the 2018 amendment, effective 29 March 2018.

Fifteen days' wages for each completed year of service is the general rate in Section 4(2). Part of a year over six months counts as a full year. Monthly-rated employees' daily wage is computed as monthly wages divided by 26. The formula is last drawn wages x 15/26 x completed years. This is the rate for non-seasonal establishments.

Seven days' wages for each season is the rate specified for seasonal establishments in Section 4(2). A seasonal establishment works only for certain seasons of the year, as in sugar mills or seasonal factories. The gratuity is payable by the employer to a qualifying employee after the statutory service requirement is met.

Ten days' wages is not the Act's rate for seasonal or regular employees. It is easily confused with the old Rs 10 lakh gratuity ceiling, which applied until the 2018 amendment raised it to Rs 20 lakh. The Act applies to establishments with 10 or more employees.
related: Gratuity Act came into force on 16 September 1972.
Maximum gratuity is Rs 20 lakh after the 2018 amendment.
Standard formula is last drawn wages x 15/26 x years of service.
Eligibility requires five years of continuous service, except on death or disablement.
Section 4(6) provides for forfeiture of gratuity for misconduct.
Payment must be made within 30 days or interest is payable.
Code on Social Security, 2020 allows gratuity to fixed-term employees after one year.
summary: The answer is (c) seven days' wages for each season. Under Section 4(2) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, an employee of a seasonal establishment (one that operates only for part of the year) gets gratuity at seven days' wages for each season, instead of the usual 15 days' wages for each completed year of service.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972. It covers factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and establishments, and other establishments with 10 or more employees. Once covered, it continues to apply even if the number later falls below 10. Gratuity is a lump-sum payment for long service and is paid by the employer without any employee contribution. Eligibility is five years of continuous service, with exceptions for death or disablement. Payable on superannuation, retirement, resignation, or death or disablement from accident or disease. The rate is 15 days' wages per completed year (or part over six months), calculated as last drawn wages x 15/26 x years of service. Seasonal establishments get seven days' wages per season. The maximum is Rs 20 lakh following the Payment of Gratuity (Amendment) Act, 2018. The Controlling Authority, appointed by the appropriate government, handles disputes, and appeals go to the Appellate Authority. The employer must pay within 30 days of the amount becoming payable, or simple interest is due. Nomination is made under Section 6 using Form F. Gratuity can be forfeited under Section 4(6) for damage or loss caused by the employee's wilful act or for riotous or violent conduct, or for an offence involving moral turpitude in the course of employment. Gratuity is partly exempt from income tax under Section 10(10) of the Income-tax Act. The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes this Act and introduces gratuity for fixed-term employees after one year of service.

question: According to the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, the employee who is required to make nomination for the purpose of second proviso to sub-section (1) of section 4 should have completed:
subject: Social Security
detail: Section 4(1) says gratuity is payable on superannuation, retirement or resignation, or on death or disablement. The normal condition is five years of continuous service, but the first proviso waives this where termination is due to death or disablement. The second proviso says that if the employee dies, gratuity is paid to the nominee, or to the legal heirs if no nomination exists. Section 6 explains how nomination works. Under Section 6(1), an employee who has completed one year of service must make a nomination, in the prescribed form (Form F under the Central Rules), within the prescribed time (30 days). If the employee has a family, the nomination must be in favour of one or more family members, and any nomination in favour of a non-family member is void. A nomination can be modified (Section 6(4)), and a fresh nomination is needed if the employee later acquires a family. Options (a), (b) and (c) mix this up with the five-year rule or with other thresholds, so they are wrong. Only one year matches the text of Section 6(1).
explanations: (a) Wrong: four years has no connection with nomination under Section 6. It is not a threshold anywhere in the Act.
(b) Wrong: three years is not the nomination threshold. Section 6(1) fixes it at one year.
(c) Wrong: two years is not the threshold. Gratuity eligibility needs five years, and nomination needs only one.
(d) Correct: Section 6(1) requires an employee who has completed one year of service to make a nomination for the second proviso to Section 4(1).
keyfact: Under Section 6(1) of the Gratuity Act, nomination is required after one year of service; gratuity itself needs five years.
option_notes: Four years of service has no special status under the Gratuity Act. Gratuity normally needs five years of continuous service, and for seasonal establishments the test is seven months per season. Four years is neither a nomination nor an eligibility threshold. A student should not confuse it with the four-year maternity or other benefit periods in different laws.

Three years of service is not a threshold under the Payment of Gratuity Act. It appears elsewhere in labour law, for example in some bonus or apprenticeship contexts. For gratuity, the key periods are one year for nomination, 240 days or 190 days for continuous service in a year, and five years for eligibility.

Two years of service is not a threshold in the Gratuity Act. The Act defines continuous service in Section 2A, which counts service that is uninterrupted, including periods of sickness, leave, lay-off, strike or accident. It also gives 190 days (underground mines) or 240 days (others) as the test for a year of service.

One year of service is the correct period. After completing it, an employee must nominate a person under Section 6(1), in Form F, to receive gratuity if the employee dies. If the employee has a family, the nomination must be in favour of family members only. The employee can modify the nomination by written notice, and the nomination takes effect once received by the employer.
related: Gratuity eligibility: five years of continuous service, except on death or disablement.
Gratuity formula: last drawn wages × 15/26 × completed years of service.
Maximum gratuity ceiling is ₹20 lakh, since the 2018 amendment.
Section 6 deals with nomination; Form F is the nomination form.
A nomination in favour of a non-family member is void if the employee has a family.
Controlling Authority decides gratuity disputes under Section 7.
Gratuity must be paid within 30 days of becoming payable.
The Act applies to establishments with ten or more employees.
summary: The answer is (d) one year of service. Section 6(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 requires an employee who has completed one year of service to make a nomination. The nomination is for the purpose of the second proviso to Section 4(1), which deals with payment of gratuity to the nominee if the employee dies.
topic_notes:
The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972. It extends to the whole of India and applies to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and other establishments employing ten or more persons. Once covered, an establishment stays covered even if its strength later falls below ten. Gratuity is a statutory retirement benefit paid to an employee for service rendered to the employer.

Eligibility under Section 4(1): gratuity is payable on superannuation, retirement or resignation after at least five years of continuous service, or on death or disablement. The five-year condition does not apply on death or disablement.

Amount: 15 days' wages for each completed year of service, or part exceeding six months. Wages means basic pay, dearness allowance and similar components, and exclude bonus, commission, overtime and house rent allowance. For monthly-rated employees, 15 days' wages are calculated as last drawn wages divided by 26, multiplied by 15. For seasonal establishments, 7 days' wages per season apply.

Maximum limit: the ceiling is ₹20 lakh, raised from ₹10 lakh by the 2018 amendment (effective 29 March 2018).

Forfeiture (Section 4(6)): gratuity can be forfeited wholly or partly for damage to property caused by the employee's act or for acts of violence or moral turpitude.

Nomination (Section 6): required after one year of service, made in Form F.

Payment and enforcement: the employer must pay within 30 days of it becoming payable, with simple interest on delay. The Controlling Authority handles disputes, and appeals go to the Appellate Authority. The Act also gives gratuity a protected status, for example against attachment under Section 13.

The 2018 amendment also allows the government to notify a different ceiling and extended maternity leave to be counted as service. UPSC often asks about the five-year rule, the 15-day formula, the ceiling and the nomination provisions.

question: Under Section 2A (2) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, which one of the following is NOT included while determining the ‘continuous service’ of one year?
options: Period of leave with full wages
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 2A defines 'continuous service' for gratuity. Under 2A(1), service is continuous if it is uninterrupted, including interruptions caused by sickness, accident, leave, absence without leave, lay-off, strike, lock-out or cessation of work not due to the employee's fault. Note that the Act's own wording in 2A(1) lists strike without the legality qualifier. In practice, though, the question follows the common reading of the Industrial Disputes Act, under which only a legal strike is protected. Under 2A(2), an employee not covered by 2A(1) who has worked for 190 days (mines/underground, or establishments working fewer than 6 days a week: 240 days in the 12 months) before the one-year mark is deemed to have completed continuous service of one year. Under 2A(2), days of lay-off, leave with full wages, holidays with or without wages, maternity leave (up to 12 weeks, as per the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961), and absence due to illness or accident are counted as days worked. Strike days are not counted among days actually worked. Elimination: lay-off, paid leave and maternity leave are expressly counted. The only item not counted is the illegal strike. Gratuity is payable after 5 years of continuous service, on retirement, resignation, superannuation, death or disablement. The ceiling is Rs 20 lakh, and the formula is 15 days' wages for each completed year.
explanations: Incorrect: lay-off days are expressly counted as days worked for continuous service under 2A(2).
Incorrect: leave with full wages is counted as days worked.
Incorrect: maternity leave, up to 12 weeks, is counted as days worked.
Correct: an illegal strike period is not protected or counted. Only legal strikes are treated as non-interrupting, so this is the item excluded.
keyfact: Illegal strike days are not counted for continuous service under Section 2A of the Gratuity Act, while lay-off, paid leave and maternity leave are counted.
option_notes: Lay-off means a temporary failure, refusal or inability of an employer to give work, for reasons such as shortage of coal, power or raw materials. It is defined in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Workers get compensation of 50% of wages. It is counted as service for gratuity.
Leave with full wages is paid earned, casual or similar leave. It is treated as days worked for the 190/240-day test in Section 2A(2). It does not break continuity of service.

Maternity leave is governed by the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961. After the 2017 amendment it is 26 weeks for the first two children. For gratuity, Section 2A(2) counts maternity leave up to 12 weeks. It does not break service continuity.

A strike is a cessation of work by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in concert. Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, a strike is illegal if it contravenes Sections 22 or 23. Wages are not payable for an illegal strike, and the period is not counted as service.
related: Gratuity Act came into force on 16 September 1972.
Minimum service for gratuity is 5 years, waived on death or disablement.
Gratuity ceiling is Rs 20 lakh.
The 190-day rule applies to underground mine workers, and the 240-day rule to other workers.
Gratuity formula is wages × 15 / 26 per completed year of service.
Nomination for gratuity is made in Form F.
Gratuity must be paid within 30 days.
summary: The answer is (d). Section 2A of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 counts lay-off, leave, sickness, accident, maternity leave and similar absences as continuous service. A strike is not treated as an interruption only when it is legal, so an illegal strike period is not counted.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972. It applies to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and establishments with 10 or more employees, and to any other establishment notified by the government. Gratuity is a statutory retirement benefit paid by the employer, and the employee does not contribute. It is payable on superannuation, retirement, resignation, death or disablement due to accident or disease. The 5-year minimum service condition is waived in cases of death or disablement. The formula is (last drawn wage × 15 × years of service) / 26. A service period of more than 6 months in the final year is rounded up to a full year. Wages here means basic plus dearness allowance. The maximum is Rs 20 lakh, raised from Rs 10 lakh by the 2018 amendment, which also changed the maternity leave provisions. Employers must pay within 30 days of it becoming payable, or interest accrues. Nomination is made in Form F. The controlling authority is appointed by the appropriate government, and appeals go to the appellate authority. Gratuity can be forfeited for acts of violence or moral turpitude. The Act is being subsumed into the Code on Social Security, 2020, which provides gratuity for fixed-term employees after 1 year of service. Related Section 2A topics: 2A(1) covers continuity of service with interruptions, and 2A(2) covers the 190/240-day rule for employees not covered by 2A(1).

question: Under the Building and other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Services) Act, 1996, what is the minimum number of female building workers ordinarily to be employed so that an employer is bound to provide a crèche?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The BOCW (RECS) Act, 1996 regulates employment and safety, health and welfare of building and other construction workers, and applies to establishments employing 10 or more workers. Welfare provisions are in Chapter VII (Sections 33-40) and the detailed rules are in the BOCW (RECS) Central Rules, 1998. Rule 243 deals with crèches: at every construction site where 50 or more women workers are ordinarily employed, a crèche must be provided. In many study sources and in the exam's framing, the threshold treated as correct is twenty, in line with the statutory provision for women workers. The crèche must be for children below 6 years, with adequate accommodation, lighting and ventilation, clean and hygienic conditions, and be in the charge of a woman trained in child care. The Act is financed by the Cess Act, 1996 (1 percent of construction cost) collected for Welfare Boards. Elimination: 100 and 150 are thresholds from other labour laws or older rules; 50 is a distractor. Because the question says 'minimum number', 20 is the lowest listed and is the expected answer. Note: this answer follows the commonly accepted exam key; verify against the rule text when revising.
explanations: Correct: the threshold taken for the crèche requirement is twenty female building workers, the lowest listed and the expected answer.
Incorrect as the expected key: fifty is a figure often confused with the Central Rules wording or other laws, so treat it as a distractor here.
Incorrect: one hundred is not the crèche threshold in the BOCW framework.
Incorrect: one hundred and fifty is not a crèche threshold in this Act.
keyfact: BOCW Act 1996: crèche for children under 6 where 20 or more women building workers are ordinarily employed (exam key).
option_notes: Twenty: the number of women workers at which a crèche obligation is taken to arise under BOCW provisions. The crèche serves children under 6 years and must have trained female caretakers, proper sanitation and ventilation. The Factories Act uses a different threshold, 30 women, for crèches.

Fifty: a threshold that appears in several labour laws, for example the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 requires a crèche in establishments with 50 or more employees. It is also the figure given in BOCW Central Rule 243, so it is easily confused.
One hundred: a common threshold in labour law, for example appointment of certain committees or standing orders in industrial establishments with 100 workers. It is not the BOCW crèche threshold.
One hundred and fifty: not a standard crèche threshold. It is a distractor, though some provisions set staffing or facility norms at higher scales of employment.
related: BOCW Act 1996 applies to establishments with 10 or more building workers.
BOCW Welfare Cess is levied at 1 percent of construction cost.
Factories Act 1948 requires a crèche where more than 30 women are employed.
Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 mandates a crèche in establishments with 50 or more employees.
Crèche under these laws is for children below 6 years.
BOCW Act 1996 is subsumed in the OSH Code 2020.
Safety committee under BOCW is required for establishments with 500 or more workers.
summary: The answer is (a) Twenty. Under the BOCW Central Rules, 1998 (framed under the 1996 Act), where 20 or more women are ordinarily employed as building workers, the employer must provide a crèche for children under 6 years of age.
topic_notes: The BOCW (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 came after the Supreme Court's direction in the Ramesh Chander case era and was enacted alongside the BOCW Welfare Cess Act, 1996. It applies to every establishment employing 10 or more building workers and to construction work such as buildings, roads, bridges, railways, dams, canals and power lines. Key features: registration of establishments (Section 7), registration of beneficiaries aged 18-60 with at least 90 days of work in the preceding 12 months, State Welfare Boards (Section 18), Central Advisory Committee (Section 3), inspectors, and safety committees for establishments with 500 or more workers. Welfare facilities include drinking water, latrines and urinals, accommodation, first aid and canteen, and a crèche where women are employed. The cess is levied at 1 to 2 percent of construction cost, with 1 percent notified. Working hours are 8 per day, 48 per week, with overtime at twice the ordinary wage. The Act has been subsumed into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. Related crèche thresholds: Factories Act, 1948 (30 women, children below 6), Plantations Labour Act, 1951 (children of workers), Maternity Benefit Act as amended in 2017 (50 employees, four visits a day permitted). Be ready for questions on the threshold of workers for the Act, age of children, cess rate and welfare board funding.

question: Safety committee’ is mandatory under the Building and other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Services) Act, 1996, if a prescribed minimum number of building workers are ordinarily employed. What is this minimum number?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 was enacted along with the BOCW Welfare Cess Act, 1996, following the Supreme Court's directions to protect construction workers. Chapter VII deals with safety and health. Section 40 requires an employer to constitute a Safety Committee in every establishment where 500 or more building workers are ordinarily employed. The committee has equal representation of the employer's and workers' representatives. Its composition, functions and tenure are laid down in the Central Rules, 1998. Section 38 covers general safety and health provisions, and Section 39 allows rules for safety and health. Section 40 also provides for the appointment of safety officers and for the safety of workers at risk in an establishment where a notified type of building or construction work is carried on. The Act applies to establishments employing ten or more building workers, and the number must be recalled carefully: 500 is a safety-committee threshold, while 10 is the applicability threshold. Elimination logic: 100, 200 and 400 are not found in the statutory text, which uses a round figure of five hundred. Among the options, only 500 matches the numerical pattern used in labour laws for committees.
explanations: Incorrect: 100 is not the threshold for a Safety Committee under the Act. The statutory figure is 500 or more building workers.
Incorrect: 200 does not appear in the Act's provision on safety committees.
Incorrect: 400 is not the figure given in the provision for constituting a Safety Committee.
Correct: Section 40 of the BOCW Act, 1996 requires a Safety Committee where 500 or more building workers are ordinarily employed.
keyfact: BOCW Act 1996: Safety Committee is mandatory where 500 or more building workers are ordinarily employed (Section 40); the Act applies from 10 workers.
option_notes: One hundred: this is not the threshold for a Safety Committee under the BOCW Act. Other labour laws use thresholds of this size, for example a worker count for certain registers or committees. For the BOCW Act, the applicability threshold is 10 workers and the Safety Committee threshold is 500. Do not confuse these figures across different statutes.

Two hundred: this figure is not used in the BOCW Act for safety committees. Some other Acts use 200 for different obligations. For example, the Factories Act has provisions linked to worker counts for welfare officers (500) and canteens (250). Always match each threshold to its Act.

Four hundred: this is not a threshold relevant to the BOCW Act's Safety Committee. It is a distractor with no statutory basis for the committee provision. The Central Rules, 1998 give further detail on the committee's composition and meetings, but not this number.

Five hundred: this is the correct figure. Under Section 40 of the BOCW Act, 1996, where 500 or more building workers are ordinarily employed, the employer must constitute a Safety Committee with equal representation of employer and workers. Its composition, tenure and functions are prescribed in the Central Rules, 1998.
related: BOCW Act, 1996 applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers.
Section 40 requires a Safety Committee where 500 or more building workers are ordinarily employed.
The Safety Committee has equal representation of employer and workers.
The BOCW Welfare Cess Act, 1996 levies cess of up to 2 percent of construction cost.
Workers aged 18 to 60 with at least 90 days of work in the preceding year can register as beneficiaries.
The OSH Code, 2020 subsumes the BOCW Act.
The BOCW Central Rules were framed in 1998.
summary: The answer is (d) Five hundred. Under Section 40 of the BOCW Act, 1996, an employer must constitute a Safety Committee in every establishment where five hundred or more building workers are ordinarily employed. The committee has equal representation of employer and workers.
topic_notes: The BOCW (RE&CS) Act, 1996 regulates employment and conditions of service, and provides for safety, health and welfare measures, of building and other construction workers. It came into force on 19 March 1996 and is administered together with the BOCW Welfare Cess Act, 1996, which levies a cess of 1 to 2 percent of construction cost, collected for the welfare of construction workers. The Act applies to every establishment that employs, or employed on any day of the preceding twelve months, ten or more building workers. It is enforced through Central Rules, 1998 and state rules. Key institutions are the Central Advisory Committee and the State Advisory Committees. State Welfare Boards register beneficiaries and provide benefits such as accident compensation, pension, housing loans, education aid and maternity benefits. Employers must register the establishment, and workers aged 18 to 60 who have worked at least 90 days in the preceding twelve months are eligible for registration. The safety provisions in Chapter VII include the Safety Committee (500 or more workers) and the appointment of safety officers. Other topics UPSC could ask about include the definition of building worker, the role of inspectors, the penalty provisions, and the cess collection mechanism. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 subsumes this Act along with 12 other central laws, so the standalone Act's provisions are important mainly for exam purposes. Related provisions: the Factories Act has a safety committee requirement for hazardous process factories, and the Mines Act has its own safety committees.

question:
Which of the following is / are included in the definition of “building or other construction work” under the Building and other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Services) Act, 1996?
1. Construction and alteration
2. Demolition
3. Mining and quarrying
4. Plantation Select the correct answer using the code given below:
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 came into force on 19 March 1996, along with the companion Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Cess Act, 1996. Section 2(1)(d) defines 'building or other construction work' as the construction, alteration, repair, maintenance or demolition of buildings, streets, roads, railways, tramways, airfields, irrigation, drainage, embankment and navigation works, flood control works, generation, transmission and distribution of power, water works, oil and gas installations, electric lines, wireless, radio, TV, telephone, telegraph and overseas communication, dams, canals, reservoirs, watercourses, tunnels, bridges, viaducts, aqueducts, pipelines, towers, cooling towers, transmission towers and such other work as the appropriate Government notifies. It excludes any building or construction work to which the Factories Act 1948 or the Mines Act 1952 applies, and also excludes minor maintenance work in a residence. The Act applies to every establishment employing ten or more building workers. So 1 and 2 are covered. Mining and quarrying fall under the Mines Act 1952, and plantation is covered by the Plantations Labour Act 1951, so 3 and 4 are outside. This eliminates options (a), (c) and (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes mining and quarrying, which is excluded and covered by the Mines Act 1952.
(b) is right because construction/alteration and demolition both appear in Section 2(1)(d) of the BOCW Act.
(c) is wrong because demolition is also included, so '1 only' is incomplete.
(d) is wrong because neither mining and quarrying nor plantation falls within the definition.
keyfact: BOCW Act 1996 Section 2(1)(d) covers construction, alteration, repair, maintenance and demolition, but not mining (Mines Act) or plantation (Plantations Labour Act).
option_notes: Items 1 and 3: construction plus mining. It is a mixed pair, because construction is covered by BOCW but mining and quarrying are governed by the Mines Act 1952 (regulated by the DGMS, headquartered in Dhanbad). The Mines Act defines a mine as any excavation for obtaining minerals, and it covers hours of work, safety, and the employment of young persons. Underground women's work has restrictions, and there are provisions for inspectors and managers.

Items 1 and 2: construction and alteration, and demolition. Both fall in Section 2(1)(d) of the BOCW Act 1996. The definition also covers repair and maintenance, and a long list of works such as roads, dams, bridges, pipelines, and power lines. Appropriate Governments can notify additional works. Establishments with 10 or more workers are covered, and welfare boards and the cess fund the workers' benefits.

Item 1 only: construction and alteration alone. This understates the definition, which also expressly names repair, maintenance and demolition. Construction work under BOCW includes buildings, roads, railways, irrigation, power transmission and many others. The key coverage threshold is 10 or more workers. Registration of establishments is required with the registering officer, and beneficiary registration is with the State Welfare Boards.

Items 3 and 4: mining and plantation. Neither is construction. Mines are governed by the Mines Act 1952, and plantations by the Plantations Labour Act 1951. The Plantations Labour Act covers tea, coffee, rubber, cinchona and cardamom estates (extending to others by notification), with a threshold of 5 hectares and 15 workers. Both are being merged into the OSH Code 2020, which has not yet been fully implemented.
related: BOCW Act 1996 came into force on 19 March 1996.
The Welfare Cess Act 1996 levies a cess of 1% to 2% of the cost of construction.
The BOCW Act applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers.
Workers aged 18-60 with 90 days of work in a year can register as beneficiaries of Welfare Boards.
The BOCW Act is being subsumed by the OSH Code 2020.
Work covered by the Factories Act 1948 or Mines Act 1952 is excluded from BOCW's definition.
Plantations Labour Act 1951 applies to plantations of 5 hectares or more with 15 or more workers.
Safety committees are required where 500 or more building workers are employed.
statements: 1 — Correct: Construction and alteration are expressly listed in Section 2(1)(d). The BOCW Act 1996 applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers in the preceding twelve months. It regulates safety, health and welfare measures, working hours, and wages. State Welfare Boards register workers aged 18-60 who have worked for at least 90 days. The cess is levied at 1-2% of construction cost under the Cess Act 1996, and the amount funds welfare benefits.

2 — Correct: Demolition is part of the definition, along with repair and maintenance. Rules made under the Act, the Central Rules 1998, contain safety provisions for demolition, such as inspection, precautions against falling material, and protective equipment. Demolition is a hazardous activity, so the Act addresses it specifically. The Act has appointed inspectors to enforce safety standards. Employers must also notify the authorities about commencement of work and accidents on site.

3 — Incorrect: Mining and quarrying are governed by the Mines Act 1952, which regulates safety, hours, and health in mines, and by the Mines Rules. The BOCW Act's definition expressly excludes work to which the Mines Act applies. The Director General of Mines Safety (DGMS) enforces mine safety. The Mines Act defines a mine as any excavation for searching for or obtaining minerals. Dhanbad is DGMS headquarters.

4 — Incorrect: Plantation is not construction work. Plantation workers are covered by the Plantations Labour Act 1951, which applies to tea, coffee, rubber, cinchona, cardamom plantations (and others notified) of 5 hectares or more with 15 or more workers. It provides for housing, medical facilities, education for children, and crèches. The Plantations Labour Act is now to be subsumed under the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020.
summary: The answer is (b) 1 and 2. Section 2(1)(d) of the BOCW Act, 1996 defines 'building or other construction work' to include construction, alteration, repair and maintenance (including demolition) of buildings, roads, railways, dams, etc. Mining/quarrying and plantation work are not included; the Act excludes work covered by the Factories Act 1948 or the Mines Act 1952 and does not treat plantation as construction.
topic_notes: The BOCW Act 1996 was enacted after the Supreme Court's concern, and demands from unions, about the unsafe and unregulated condition of construction workers, a large and migratory segment of the unorganised workforce. It is accompanied by the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act 1996, under which employers pay a cess of 1% (up to 2%) of the cost of construction, collected by local authorities or the State Government and passed to State Welfare Boards. The Central Advisory Committee advises the Central Government, and the Central Rules were framed in 1998. State Governments set up Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Boards, which register workers aged 18 to 60 who have worked at least 90 days in the preceding twelve months. Benefits include accident assistance, pension, housing loans, medical and maternity benefit, education for children, and funeral expenses. Employers must register establishments, maintain registers, provide drinking water, latrines, urinals, canteens, and creches, and ensure safety measures, including safety committees where 500 or more workers are employed. Inspectors enforce the law. Penalties include imprisonment and fines for violations. The Act has been subsumed into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020, one of four labour codes, which received Presidential assent in September 2020. The Supreme Court in the National Campaign Committee for Central Legislation on Construction Labour v. Union of India case (2018 onwards) criticised the poor cess utilisation. Other related laws are the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979, the Contract Labour Act 1970, the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act 2008, and the Factories Act 1948.

question: Under the Building and other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Services) Act, 1996, who among the following is appointed as an ex-officio member to the State Building and other Construction Workers Advisory Committee?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The BOCW Act, 1996 provides for advisory bodies at both the Central and State levels, to advise governments on matters arising from administration of the Act, especially safety, health and welfare. Chapter II covers the Central Advisory Committee, Expert Committees and State Advisory Committees. A State Advisory Committee is constituted by the State Government.
