It has a chairperson, the Chief Inspector of the State, and members nominated to represent the State Government, employers and building workers, in equal proportion. The Chief Inspector is the statutory head of the inspectorate that enforces the Act. This is why that officer, and not a Secretary or a Labour Commissioner, is named as the ex-officio member. I am recalling this from memory and have not checked the exact section text, so verify it against the bare Act. Options (a), (c) and (d) are departmental officers who may be nominated as members, but the Act does not name them ex officio. Elimination rule: where the Act speaks of an ex-officio member of a State body, look for the Chief Inspector, the key enforcement authority under the Act.
explanations: Incorrect: the Secretary, Labour and Employment is not named in the Act as an ex-officio member. The Secretary may be nominated by the State Government as a member, but not ex officio.
Correct: the Chief Inspector is the ex-officio member of the State Advisory Committee.
Incorrect: the Joint Labour Commissioner is a departmental rank, not a post named in the Act for this committee.
Incorrect: the Deputy Labour Commissioner is likewise not named as an ex-officio member.
keyfact: The Chief Inspector is the ex-officio member of the State BOCW Advisory Committee.
option_notes: Secretary, Labour and Employment: the senior civil servant heading the State Labour Department (at the Centre, the Ministry of Labour and Employment). Such an officer is a policy-making authority and can be nominated as a member. The Act does not make the post ex officio on the State Advisory Committee.

The Chief Inspector: the officer appointed by the appropriate Government under the BOCW Act to head the inspectorate. The Chief Inspector supervises Inspectors, enforces safety and welfare provisions, and is the ex-officio member of the State Advisory Committee. This officer is central to enforcement of the Act.

Joint Labour Commissioner: a senior officer in the State Labour Department, ranking below the Labour Commissioner. This officer may be appointed as an Inspector or Registering Officer under the Act, but not as an ex-officio member of the committee.

Deputy Labour Commissioner: a mid-level officer in the State Labour Department. This officer is often appointed as a Registering Officer or Inspector for construction establishments, but is not named ex officio on the State Advisory Committee.
related: The BOCW Act came into force on 19 March 1996.
The Welfare Cess Act, 1996 levies a cess of up to 2 percent, with 1 percent notified.
Workers aged 18 to 60 with 90 days of work in a year can register as beneficiaries.
The Act applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers.
Each State has a Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Board.
Central Rules under the Act were framed in 1998.
The Act is subsumed in the OSH Code, 2020.
summary: The answer is (b), the Chief Inspector. Under the BOCW Act, 1996, the State Advisory Committee consists of a chairperson, the Chief Inspector as an ex-officio member, and other members. These other members are nominated to represent employers, workers and the State Government.
topic_notes: The BOCW (RE&CS) Act, 1996 came into force on 19 March 1996. It regulates employment and conditions of service, safety, health and welfare of building and other construction workers. It applies to establishments employing ten or more workers on a building or construction work. Related to it is the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996, which levies a cess of 1 to 2 percent of construction cost, with 1 percent notified, to fund welfare. The Act's main features are: (1) Advisory Committees: the Central Advisory Committee, State Advisory Committees and Expert Committees advise governments on administration of the Act. (2) Registration: employers' establishments are registered with a Registering Officer, and workers aged 18 to 60 who have worked at least 90 days in the preceding 12 months are registered as beneficiaries. (3) State Welfare Boards: each State constitutes a Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Board, which provides benefits such as pension, accident assistance, medical aid, education assistance and housing loans. (4) Safety: chapters cover safety committees, safety officers and notice of accidents. (5) Inspectors: Chief Inspectors and Inspectors are appointed by the appropriate Government. (6) Penalties are prescribed for violations. Other angles UPSC could ask: the cess rate, the beneficiary age limit, the 90-day rule, the minimum establishment size, the Central Rules of 1998, the role of the Central Advisory Committee (chaired by the Union Labour Minister or an appointed person), and the subsuming of the Act into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.

question: Under the Building and other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Services) Act, 1996, in order to be eligible for registration as beneficiary of the Building and other Construction Workers Welfare Fund, a worker must have been engaged in building and other construction work during the preceding 12 months for at least:
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 12 of the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 deals with registration of building workers as beneficiaries. Every building worker who has completed 18 years but not 60 years of age and who has been engaged in building or other construction work for not less than 90 days during the preceding twelve months is eligible to be registered. Registration is done by the registering officer, and the worker pays a monthly contribution, which the State Board may prescribe. The Welfare Boards are constituted by State Governments under Section 18. The funds come from the Cess Act, 1996 (the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act), under which employers pay cess of 1 to 2 percent of construction cost, and the Rules were framed in 1998. The Act applies to establishments employing 10 or more workers. Elimination: 30 and 60 days are too short and do not match the statute. 180 days is the common threshold in other labour contexts, such as continuous service for some benefits, and is a distractor. The statutory figure is 90 days.
explanations: 30 days is wrong. The Act does not set such a low minimum for beneficiary registration.
60 days is wrong. It does not match Section 12(1), which prescribes 90 days.
90 days is correct. Section 12 requires at least 90 days of work as a building worker in the preceding 12 months, along with age 18 to 60.
180 days is wrong. It is double the statutory requirement and is used in other labour contexts, not in BOCW registration.
keyfact: BOCW Act Section 12: beneficiary registration needs age 18 to 60 and 90 days of work in the preceding 12 months.
option_notes: 30 days: this is not a threshold in the BOCW Act. A 30-day period is more typical of notice periods or the time limits for filing returns and appeals in some laws, and it is not the registration requirement for beneficiaries.

60 days: this is not the BOCW registration threshold. In other labour laws, periods like 60 days appear for notices or limits, for example the notice period for strikes in public utility services under the ID Act is 6 weeks, not 60 days. The BOCW figure is 90 days.

90 days: this is the correct statutory period under Section 12 of the BOCW Act, 1996. A building worker aged 18 to 60 with 90 days of work in the preceding 12 months can register as a beneficiary with the State Welfare Board and gets benefits such as pension, accident assistance, medical aid, education for children and maternity benefits.

180 days: this is not the BOCW threshold. A 180-day period appears elsewhere, such as the requirement for continuous service under some Acts, for example 240 days under Section 25B of the ID Act or 190 days in mines and underground work for gratuity, but it is not the BOCW rule.
related: BOCW Act, 1996 applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers.
Beneficiary age limit is 18 to 60 years under Section 12.
Welfare Boards are constituted by State Governments under Section 18.
Cess under the Cess Act, 1996 is levied at 1 to 2 percent of construction cost.
The Cess is collected by the State governments and local bodies and deposited with the Welfare Boards.
The Act is subsumed in the OSH Code, 2020.
summary: The answer is (c) 90 days. Under Section 12 of the BOCW Act, 1996, a building worker aged 18 to 60 who has worked as a building worker for at least 90 days during the preceding 12 months is eligible to be registered as a beneficiary of the State Welfare Board's Fund.
topic_notes: The BOCW Act, 1996 and the companion Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996 came into force on 19 March 1996 after Supreme Court directions and long demand for protection of construction workers. The Act applies to every establishment that employs, or employed on any day of the preceding 12 months, 10 or more building workers. It regulates the employment, safety, health and welfare of building workers. The Central Rules and the Central Cess Rules were made in 1998. Key features: Central and State Advisory Committees, with the Central Advisory Committee constituted by the Central Government under Section 3 (the State Governments set up State Advisory Committees), and the State Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Boards constituted under Section 18. The Boards administer the Welfare Fund. Registration of establishments is done by a registering officer, and employers must register within 60 days of the Act applying. Cess is levied at a rate between 1 and 2 percent of the cost of construction incurred by an employer, with 1 percent notified in 1996. Benefits include accident assistance, old-age pension at 60, loans for housing, children's education, medical expenses, maternity benefits and funeral assistance. Beneficiary registration needs age 18 to 60 and 90 days of work in the preceding 12 months. A beneficiary ceases to be one on reaching 60 years, and a worker who does not pay contributions for a continuous period of one year may lose benefits. Inspectors are appointed under Section 39. Penalties are prescribed for contravention. The Act is now subsumed in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which is not yet fully in force.

question: Under the rules of the Building and other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Services) Act, 1996, what is the maximum weight which an adult woman is permitted to carry overhead?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The BOCW Act, 1996 is the parent statute for safety, health and welfare of construction workers. The detailed safety provisions sit in the BOCW (RE&CS) Central Rules, 1998. These include a chapter on manual lifting and carrying, which sets maximum weights by category of worker. Recalled from the commonly cited schedule, an adult male may handle about 50-55 kg and an adult female 30 kg. An adolescent male is limited to about 30 kg and an adolescent female to about 20 kg. Children are limited to much less (about 14-16 kg). Exact figures for the non-woman categories vary between sources, so verify them in the Rules. The adult woman figure of 30 kg is the one to remember. Elimination logic: 50 kg is the figure for adult men, so it is far too high for women. 40 kg is not a figure in the schedule. 25 kg is below the woman limit and is not the prescribed figure. The Act applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers. Welfare is funded by a cess of 1-2% of construction cost under the Cess Act, 1996.
explanations: Incorrect: 50 kg is about the limit for adult men, not women.
Incorrect: 40 kg is not a limit prescribed for any worker category in the schedule.
Correct: the rules fix 30 kg as the maximum an adult woman may lift or carry overhead.
Incorrect: 25 kg is lower than the prescribed limit, so it is not the legal maximum.
keyfact: BOCW Central Rules 1998: adult woman may carry a maximum of 30 kg overhead.
option_notes: 50 kg is roughly the maximum prescribed for an adult male worker in the manual-handling schedule, quoted as 50 or 55 kg in different sources. The limits are graded by sex and age, with lower limits for women, adolescents and children. It is used here as a distractor because it exceeds the female limit.

40 kg is not a standard category limit in the BOCW lifting schedule. It is a plausible-looking intermediate value used as a distractor. Remember the limits as roughly adult male 50-55 kg, adult female 30 kg, adolescent male 30 kg, adolescent female 20 kg, and children about 14-16 kg.

30 kg is the maximum weight an adult woman can be required or permitted to lift, carry or move overhead under the BOCW Central Rules, 1998. The same 30 kg figure also applies to adolescent males. It is a protective safety norm to prevent strain injuries, and employers breaching the rules face penalties under the Act.

25 kg is not the prescribed limit for adult women. It sits between the adult female limit (30 kg) and the adolescent female limit (about 20 kg), so it works as a distractor. Do not confuse it with any BOCW category figure.
related: BOCW Act, 1996 applies to establishments with 10 or more building workers.
The Cess Act, 1996 levies 1-2% of construction cost.
Central Rules were framed in 1998.
Welfare Boards are constituted by State Governments.
Adult woman overhead load limit is 30 kg.
Beneficiary registration needs age 18-60 and 90 days of work in a year.
The Act was a result of Supreme Court intervention on the plight of construction workers.
summary: The answer is (c) 30 kg. The Building and Other Construction Workers Central Rules, 1998 cap the weight an adult woman worker may lift, carry or move overhead at 30 kg. The limit protects workers from musculoskeletal injury. Lower limits apply to adolescents and children.
topic_notes: The Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 regulates employment and safety, health and welfare measures for building workers. It applies to every establishment employing 10 or more workers in building or construction work. It was enacted after the Supreme Court's directions in the construction workers' case, and it came into force on 19 March 1996. The companion Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996 levies a cess of 1% to 2% of the cost of construction, collected for the Welfare Boards. The Central Rules of 1998 prescribe detailed safety standards on scaffolds, ladders, lifting appliances, excavation, demolition, electrical safety, fire protection, and manual lifting and carrying limits. Welfare Boards are constituted by State governments, and workers must register with them as beneficiaries. They must be aged 18 to 60 and have worked at least 90 days in the preceding 12 months. Benefits include pensions, accident assistance, housing loans, education aid for children, medical and maternity benefits. Safety committees are mandatory where 500 or more workers are employed, and a safety officer is required where 500 or more are employed. Inspectors enforce the Act. The appropriate Government is the Central Government for central sphere establishments and the State Government for others. Other angles UPSC may ask: the definition of building worker, the non-applicability of the Act to individual-owner construction costing under Rs 10 lakh with fewer than 10 workers, the role of the Advisory Committees, and penalties for violations.

question: The term ‘wannaCry’ is associated with:
subject: Computers
detail: WannaCry was a ransomware cryptoworm that began spreading on 12 May 2017 and infected over 200,000 computers in about 150 countries within days. It targeted Microsoft Windows systems that had not been patched, using the EternalBlue exploit (reportedly leaked from the US NSA by the Shadow Brokers group) against a flaw in the SMBv1 protocol. Microsoft had issued patch MS17-010 in March 2017. Once a machine was infected, files were encrypted and a ransom of roughly $300 to $600 in Bitcoin was demanded. The UK's NHS was badly hit, along with FedEx, Telefonica and Renault. A researcher, Marcus Hutchins, found a 'kill switch' domain and slowed the spread. The attack has been attributed to the Lazarus Group, linked to North Korea. In India, systems in places like Andhra Pradesh police and some state utilities were affected, and CERT-In issued advisories. Elimination: it is not hardware, not a band, and not a disease. The word 'Cry' plays on the ransom note, and the topic of this question is cybersecurity, so (c) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: WannaCry is malicious software that attacks computers, not a hardware product or component.
Wrong: The name sounds like a band name, but it has no connection to music. It is the name of a malware program.
Correct: WannaCry was a global ransomware cyber attack in May 2017 that exploited a Windows SMB vulnerability.
Wrong: It was a digital 'epidemic' of infections spreading between computers, not a biological disease outbreak in Africa.
keyfact: WannaCry (May 2017) was a ransomware cyber attack exploiting a Windows SMB flaw (EternalBlue), demanding Bitcoin.
option_notes: Computer hardware means the physical parts of a computer, such as the CPU, memory, motherboard, keyboard, monitor and storage devices. Software, by contrast, is the set of programs that run on that hardware. Malware like WannaCry is software and is not hardware. Hardware can still be affected by attacks, but the term refers to physical components.

A musical band is a group of musicians. This option is a distractor playing on the catchy name. WannaCry has nothing to do with music, and UPSC-type questions often use plausible-sounding but false options like this one.

A cyber attack is a deliberate attempt to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to computer systems or networks. Common types include phishing, DDoS, ransomware, malware, spyware and man-in-the-middle attacks. In India, CERT-In is the national agency for responding to such incidents, and the IT Act, 2000 provides the legal framework. WannaCry is a well-known ransomware example.

This refers to a disease outbreak, for example Ebola in West Africa (2014-16). WannaCry is not a disease, and the word 'epidemic' is used only metaphorically for its rapid spread. Organisations such as the WHO and Africa CDC handle real epidemics, not malware.
related: WannaCry spread from 12 May 2017 and used the EternalBlue exploit against the SMBv1 flaw in Windows.
WannaCry demanded ransom in Bitcoin.
Marcus Hutchins found the WannaCry kill switch.
NotPetya (June 2017) mainly hit Ukraine.
CERT-In is India's national nodal agency for cyber security incidents.
The IT Act, 2000 is India's main cyber law.
The Lazarus Group, linked to North Korea, was blamed for WannaCry.
summary: The answer is (c) cyber attack. WannaCry (WannaCrypt) was a ransomware worm that hit computers worldwide in May 2017, encrypting files on Windows systems and demanding Bitcoin payment.
topic_notes: Ransomware is malware that encrypts a victim's data or locks the system and demands payment, usually in cryptocurrency, to restore access. WannaCry (May 2017) exploited EternalBlue, an exploit for the SMBv1 flaw in Windows that was reportedly developed by the NSA and leaked by the Shadow Brokers. Microsoft's patch MS17-010 had been released in March 2017, so unpatched and unsupported systems such as Windows XP were most at risk. Over 200,000 machines in about 150 countries were infected. The UK NHS was heavily disrupted. Marcus Hutchins ('MalwareTech') registered a kill-switch domain that halted the spread. The US and UK later attributed the attack to North Korea's Lazarus Group. Petya and NotPetya followed in June 2017, and NotPetya mainly hit Ukraine. Other cyber terms to know: virus, worm, Trojan horse, spyware, adware, phishing, vishing, smishing, botnet, DDoS, zero-day exploit, logic bomb and keylogger. In India, CERT-In (under MeitY, set up in 2004) is the nodal agency for cyber incidents. The IT Act, 2000 (amended in 2008) provides the legal framework, and Section 66 covers computer-related offences. The National Cyber Security Policy was issued in 2013, NCIIPC protects critical information infrastructure, and the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) was set up under the MHA. Good practice includes regular patching, offline backups, antivirus software, firewalls, and not opening unknown attachments.

question: The Ninth BRICS Summit was held in which one of the following cities?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: China chaired BRICS in 2017 and hosted the 9th summit in the coastal city of Xiamen in Fujian Province from 3 to 5 September 2017. The summit adopted the Xiamen Declaration and introduced the 'BRICS Plus' outreach model, inviting Egypt, Guinea, Mexico, Tajikistan and Thailand as guest countries. Prime Minister Narendra Modi attended, and the declaration named terrorist groups such as Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed, which India welcomed. The Doklam standoff between India and China had ended just before the summit. BRICS members in 2017 were Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. The New Development Bank (headquartered in Shanghai) and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement are its key institutions. For elimination, Shenzhen and Guangzhou are in Guangdong and are known as economic hubs, and Shenyang is in Liaoning. None of them hosted the summit. Host sequence to remember: 2016 Goa (8th), 2017 Xiamen (9th), 2018 Johannesburg (10th), 2019 Brasilia (11th).
explanations: Incorrect: Shenzhen is a Special Economic Zone in Guangdong and did not host the 2017 BRICS Summit.
Incorrect: Guangzhou is the capital of Guangdong and was not the venue for the 9th BRICS Summit.
Correct: Xiamen in Fujian hosted the 9th BRICS Summit on 3-5 September 2017.
Incorrect: Shenyang is the capital of Liaoning in northeast China and was not the venue.
keyfact: 9th BRICS Summit: Xiamen, China, 3-5 Sept 2017 (Xiamen Declaration, BRICS Plus).
option_notes: Shenzhen is a major city in Guangdong province next to Hong Kong. It became China's first Special Economic Zone in 1980 under Deng Xiaoping. It is a technology and manufacturing hub, home to Huawei and Tencent, and hosts the Shenzhen Stock Exchange.

Guangzhou is the capital of Guangdong province on the Pearl River. It is a historic trading port and hosts the Canton Fair, China's biggest trade fair. It is one of China's major commercial centres and a hub for manufacturing and transport.

Xiamen is a coastal sub-provincial city in Fujian province, facing Taiwan across the strait. It was one of the first four Special Economic Zones, created in 1980. It hosted the 9th BRICS Summit in September 2017 and is known for its port and the island of Gulangyu.

Shenyang is the capital of Liaoning province in northeast China. It is a heavy industrial centre and was historically called Mukden. It is part of China's old industrial base in the northeast and is known for machinery and automobile manufacturing.
related: 8th BRICS Summit 2016 was held in Goa, India.
10th BRICS Summit 2018 was held in Johannesburg, South Africa.
11th BRICS Summit 2019 was held in Brasilia, Brazil.
New Development Bank is headquartered in Shanghai.
South Africa joined BRIC in 2010 to form BRICS.
Xiamen summit introduced the 'BRICS Plus' outreach concept.
Jim O'Neill coined the term BRIC in 2001.
summary: The correct answer is (c) Xiamen. The 9th BRICS Summit was held in Xiamen, Fujian Province, China, on 3-5 September 2017, under the theme 'BRICS: Stronger Partnership for a Brighter Future'.
topic_notes: BRICS is a grouping of emerging economies. The term 'BRIC' was coined by Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs in 2001. The first formal BRIC summit was held in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009, and South Africa joined in 2010, making it BRICS. Summit hosts: 2012 New Delhi (4th), 2013 Durban (5th), 2014 Fortaleza (6th), 2015 Ufa (7th), 2016 Goa (8th), 2017 Xiamen (9th), 2018 Johannesburg (10th), 2019 Brasilia (11th), 2020 Russia (virtual, 12th), 2021 India (virtual, 13th), 2022 China (virtual, 14th), 2023 Johannesburg (15th), 2024 Kazan (16th). The 15th summit in 2023 invited Argentina, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE to join. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE joined from January 2024, and Indonesia joined in 2025. The New Development Bank (NDB) was agreed at the 2012 Delhi summit, established at Fortaleza in 2014 and based in Shanghai. Its first president was K. V. Kamath. The Contingent Reserve Arrangement has an initial size of USD 100 billion. The Xiamen summit's theme was 'Stronger Partnership for a Brighter Future', and it launched 'BRICS Plus' outreach. The Goa summit (2016) had the theme 'Building Responsive, Inclusive and Collective Solutions'. Also remember the BRICS Agricultural Research Platform, the BRICS Business Council and the BRICS Youth Summit.

question: Besides India which of the following countries are the members of Mekong- Ganga Cooperation?
options: Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam
Myanmar, Thailand, Philippines, Cambodia and Laos
Cambodia, Vietnam, Philippines, Bangladesh and Thailand
Myanmar, Vietnam, Laos, Bangladesh and Thailand
subject: Computers
detail: Mekong-Ganga Cooperation (MGC) was launched on 10 November 2000 at Vientiane, Laos. It is a sub-regional cooperation initiative between India and five Mekong countries: Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam. It is named after the two great civilisational rivers, the Ganga and the Mekong. It focuses on four areas of cooperation: tourism, culture, education, and transport and communication. The Vientiane Declaration set up the MGC. Its 2000 Action Plan was followed by later plans, and the MGC Plan of Action 2019-2022 was adopted. Cooperation is carried out through ministerial meetings, usually held alongside ASEAN-related meetings. India has funded Quick Impact Projects (QIPs) in the Mekong countries under the MGC. India also supports the Asian Traditional Textiles Museum in Siem Reap, Cambodia. Elimination logic: the Philippines is an ASEAN member but not on the Mekong, so options (b) and (c) are wrong. Bangladesh is not a Mekong country, so options (c) and (d) are wrong. Only (a) has exactly the five Mekong riparian members besides China, which is not a member of MGC.
explanations: Correct: Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam are the five MGC members besides India.
Wrong: the Philippines is not a member, as it is not a Mekong riparian state.
Wrong: both the Philippines and Bangladesh are non-members, and Myanmar and Laos are omitted.
Wrong: Bangladesh is not a member, and Cambodia is omitted.
keyfact: MGC (2000, Vientiane) = India + Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam; it covers tourism, culture, education and transport.
option_notes: Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam are the five Mekong-basin countries in the MGC with India. Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Vietnam are also called CLMV, the newer ASEAN members. All five are ASEAN members. The MGC was launched in 2000 at Vientiane. China is a Mekong riparian but is not an MGC member. It runs the separate Lancang-Mekong Cooperation.

The Philippines is an ASEAN member but is not in the Mekong basin and not in the MGC. It is a maritime Southeast Asian state. It is involved in the South China Sea dispute and won the 2016 arbitration ruling against China. Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos are genuine MGC members. The Philippines is a member of ASEAN, founded in 1967, and also of the East Asia Summit.

This mixes the Philippines and Bangladesh, both non-members. Bangladesh is a member of BIMSTEC, along with India, Myanmar, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bhutan. BIMSTEC was formed in 1997 as BIST-EC and its secretariat is in Dhaka. The Philippines is an ASEAN member only. Cambodia, Vietnam and Thailand are valid MGC members.

This includes Bangladesh, which is a BIMSTEC and BBIN member but not part of the MGC. It omits Cambodia. Myanmar, Vietnam, Laos and Thailand are genuine MGC members. Bangladesh is not a Mekong riparian state, since the Mekong flows through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam.
related: MGC was launched in November 2000 at Vientiane, Laos.
MGC covers tourism, culture, education and transport and communication.
China is not a member of MGC; it leads the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation.
The Mekong River Commission was founded in 1995 with four members.
CLMV stands for Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Vietnam.
BIMSTEC has seven members including Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.
The India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway is a flagship connectivity project.
summary: The answer is (a). Mekong-Ganga Cooperation (MGC) comprises India and five Mekong-basin countries: Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam. The Philippines and Bangladesh are not members.
topic_notes: Mekong-Ganga Cooperation (MGC) is a sub-regional grouping launched on 10 November 2000 at Vientiane, Laos. Its members are India, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam. It focuses on tourism, culture, education and transport and communication. It is named after the Ganga and the Mekong, to signal civilisational links. Its institutional mechanisms include annual foreign ministers' meetings, senior officials' meetings and working groups. India finances Quick Impact Projects in member states. The MGC supports India's Act East Policy and complements ASEAN-India relations. The Mekong river rises in the Tibetan plateau and flows through China (where it is called Lancang), Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. Other Mekong-related bodies include the Mekong River Commission (1995; members Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam), the Greater Mekong Subregion programme (ADB, 1992) and the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation (China-led, 2016). Related Indian initiatives in the region include the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway, the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport project, and BIMSTEC, which links South Asia with Southeast Asia. Other groupings to remember are BBIN, a sub-regional initiative of Bangladesh, Bhutan, India and Nepal, IORA, ASEAN (ten members) and the East Asia Summit. UPSC may ask about the members, the year of founding, the fields of cooperation, or the location of its launch.

question: Know India Programme’ is a flagship initiative of which one of the following Ministries?
options: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports
subject: Computers
detail: The Know India Programme (KIP) was launched in 2003 by the Ministry of External Affairs (now handled by the Overseas Indian Affairs wing, merged into MEA in 2016) as a three-week orientation programme for diaspora youth of Indian origin. Participants are aged 18-30 and come from countries with a substantial Indian-origin population; the programme is not meant for NRIs from Indian-citizen families only but for Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs). Candidates visit a few Indian states, see economic, social, cultural and industrial development, and interact with officials, and the programme normally includes a visit to Delhi. It is conducted in partnership with state governments, and the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports earlier worked with MEA on it. Elimination logic: the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports runs schemes like Khelo India, NSS and NYKS; the Ministry of Culture handles museums, ASI and cultural institutions; the Ministry of Tourism runs Incredible India and Swadesh Darshan. The diaspora focus therefore points to MEA, which also handles Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, OCI cards and the Madad portal.
explanations: Incorrect: Youth Affairs and Sports handles Khelo India, NSS, NYKS and Rashtriya Yuva Sashaktikaran Karyakram, not diaspora outreach. It only cooperated in early editions.
Correct: KIP is a flagship diaspora-engagement programme of MEA, for Indian-origin youth aged 18-30.
Incorrect: The Ministry of Culture manages heritage bodies such as ASI, NMA, Sangeet Natak Akademi and the National Archives, not KIP.
Incorrect: The Ministry of Tourism promotes Incredible India, Swadesh Darshan and PRASHAD; it does not run KIP.
keyfact: Know India Programme = MEA's three-week orientation for Indian-origin youth aged 18-30.
option_notes: The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports has two departments, Youth Affairs and Sports. It oversees Khelo India, the National Service Scheme, Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, the Sports Authority of India and the National Youth Policy. It is headed by a Cabinet or Minister of State, and it pursues youth development within India, not diaspora engagement.

The Ministry of External Affairs handles India's foreign policy and relations with the diaspora. Its schemes include Know India Programme, Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, OCI cards, the Madad portal, the Pravasi Bharatiya Samman and Study India. The Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs was merged into MEA in January 2016. It is the nodal ministry for passports and consular services.

The Ministry of Culture works to preserve and promote India's art, heritage and culture. It oversees the Archaeological Survey of India, National Museum, National Archives, Sahitya Akademi, Sangeet Natak Akademi, Lalit Kala Akademi and Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts. It runs schemes such as the Gandhi Heritage Sites and Hriday-linked projects.

The Ministry of Tourism promotes domestic and international tourism in India. Its flagship campaign is Incredible India, and its schemes include Swadesh Darshan, PRASHAD, Dekho Apna Desh and Atithi Devo Bhava. It oversees institutions such as IITTM and the India Tourism Development Corporation.
related: Know India Programme: ages 18-30, Indian-origin youth, run by MEA.
Pravasi Bharatiya Divas is observed on 9 January, the day Gandhi returned to India in 1915.
The Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs was merged with MEA in 2016.
PIO cards were merged into OCI cards in 2015.
Madad is MEA's portal for consular grievances.
Study in India is an MEA-linked initiative for foreign students.
The Pravasi Bharatiya Samman is the highest honour for the Indian diaspora.
summary: The answer is (b) Ministry of External Affairs. The Know India Programme (KIP) is run by the MEA for Indian-origin diaspora youth aged 18-30, to connect them with their roots and with contemporary India.
topic_notes: The Know India Programme is a three-week orientation programme for Indian-origin diaspora youth aged 18-30, begun in 2003 by the Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs and now under the Ministry of External Affairs after the 2016 merger. It exposes participants to India's development, economy, culture, art and heritage, and builds ties with their ancestral land. Participants usually come from countries with a large Indian-origin population; Indian citizens are not eligible, and the Indian-origin criterion applies. Participants visit selected states and Delhi, and the programme is implemented with state governments and with support from partner organisations. MEA diaspora outreach also includes Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, observed on 9 January, the day Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915; it has been held biennially since 2015. Other initiatives are the Pravasi Bharatiya Samman Award, Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI), the Person of Indian Origin card (merged into OCI in 2015), the India Development Foundation of Overseas Indians, the Scholarship Programme for Diaspora Children (SPDC), Study in India, the Madad portal for consular grievances, the e-Migrate system and the Pravasi Kaushal Vikas Yojana. Related legal frameworks include the Emigration Act 1983. Future questions may ask which ministry runs a given scheme, who is eligible for KIP, the age limit, the date of Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, or the difference between OCI and PIO.

question:
Consider the following statements about ‘e-Migrate’, a project of the Ministry of External Affairs:
1. It facilitates emigration of ECR category of emigrants going to notified countries for employment purpose
2. It is integrated with Bureau of Immigration system of Ministry of Home Affairs
3. It is integrated with Passport Seva Project Which of the statements given above is / are correct?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: e-Migrate is an MEA project launched in 2014 under the Emigration Act, 1983, and run by the Protector General of Emigrants (PGE). It replaced the earlier manual clearance process and is meant to make emigration for employment transparent, safe and less prone to exploitation by agents. It covers ECR (Emigration Check Required) passport holders going for employment to the 18 ECR countries, such as UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain, Malaysia, Libya, Jordan, Yemen, Sudan, Afghanistan, Indonesia, Syria, Lebanon, Thailand, Iraq and South Sudan. Foreign employers must register on the portal and Recruiting Agents (RAs) must be registered with it. Employers submit demand letters and the RAs get them attested through the Indian Mission. The system is integrated with Passport Seva, which allows verification of passport data, and with the Bureau of Immigration of the MHA, so that emigration clearance can be checked at the airport. Because all three statements match the official description, (a) is correct and (b), (c) and (d) are eliminated. Note that ECNR passport holders do not need emigration clearance.
explanations: Correct: all three statements match the official description of e-Migrate, covering ECR emigrants, the BoI link and the Passport Seva link.
Wrong: statement 1 is also correct, so 2 and 3 alone is incomplete.
Wrong: statement 3 is also correct, so 1 and 2 alone is incomplete.
Wrong: statements 1 and 2 are correct as well, so 3 alone is incomplete.
keyfact: e-Migrate (MEA, 2014) handles emigration clearance for ECR workers going to 18 notified countries, and is linked with Passport Seva and the Bureau of Immigration.
option_notes: All three statements together: e-Migrate is an MEA project for emigration clearance of ECR workers, integrated with the Bureau of Immigration (MHA) and Passport Seva. It was launched in 2014 and run by the Protector General of Emigrants. It registers foreign employers and recruiting agents and aims to curb exploitation of workers by agents.

Statements 2 and 3 only: the integration with the Bureau of Immigration and with Passport Seva is correct. This option wrongly leaves out the ECR facilitation, which is the core purpose of e-Migrate. ECR passport holders going to 18 notified countries for employment need emigration clearance under the Emigration Act, 1983.

Statements 1 and 2 only: this correctly notes the ECR facilitation and the Bureau of Immigration link but leaves out Passport Seva. Passport Seva was launched in 2010 as an MEA mission mode project, run with TCS in a PPP model. It issues passports through PSKs, and e-Migrate uses its passport data.

Statement 3 only: this option includes the Passport Seva integration but wrongly omits the ECR emigrant focus and the Bureau of Immigration link. The Bureau of Immigration is under the MHA and manages immigration checkposts at airports and land and sea ports.
related: e-Migrate was launched in 2014 by the MEA under the Emigration Act, 1983.
The Protector General of Emigrants (PGE) heads emigration clearance work.
There are 18 ECR countries, including UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain.
Pravasi Bharatiya Bima Yojana (PBBY) is an insurance scheme for ECR emigrant workers.
MADAD is the MEA portal for consular services and grievances.
Pravasi Bharatiya Divas is held on 9 January.
Passport Seva Project was launched in 2010 as a PPP with TCS.
statements: 1 — Correct: e-Migrate facilitates emigration of ECR passport holders going to notified ECR countries for employment. Emigration clearance is issued by the Protector of Emigrants (POE) under the Emigration Act, 1983. The 18 notified countries include the Gulf states, Malaysia, Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, Sudan and others. The system registers foreign employers, recruiting agents and emigrants on one platform.

2 — Correct: The e-Migrate system is integrated with the Bureau of Immigration (MHA), which operates immigration checkpoints. Emigration clearance data is therefore visible to immigration officers at airports and they can verify clearance at departure. This helps prevent illegal emigration and the use of fake or unregistered agents. The MHA also runs the Immigration, Visa and Foreigners Registration & Tracking (IVFRT) project.

3 — Correct: e-Migrate is integrated with the Passport Seva Project, a mission mode project of the MEA launched in 2010 and run with TCS under a public-private partnership model. Passport Seva Kendras (PSKs) handle passport applications. The link lets e-Migrate verify passport details and ECR/ECNR status. Passport Seva Programme 2.0 is the current upgrade.
summary: The answer is (a): all three statements are correct. e-Migrate is the MEA's online system for emigration clearance of Indian workers going abroad for employment, and it is linked with the Bureau of Immigration (MHA) and the Passport Seva Project.
topic_notes: e-Migrate is the MEA's online emigration system, launched in 2014, replacing a manual process. It is administered by the Office of the Protector General of Emigrants (PGE) under the Emigration Act, 1983, which regulates recruitment and emigration of Indian workers. ECR (Emigration Check Required) passports are mainly for persons who have not passed Class 10; ECNR means Emigration Check Not Required. ECR passport holders going for employment to the 18 notified countries need emigration clearance from a Protector of Emigrants (POE). Foreign employers must register on the portal, and recruiting agents must hold a registration certificate (RC) from the PGE. The system links with Passport Seva and the Bureau of Immigration for verification at the airport. Related MEA initiatives include the MADAD portal for consular grievances, the Pravasi Bharatiya Bima Yojana (PBBY) insurance scheme for ECR workers, the India Centre for Migration, the Indian Community Welfare Fund (ICWF), the Pravasi Bharatiya Divas held on 9 January, and the Migrant Resource Centres. Other schemes include Pravasi Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PKVY) for skilling emigrants and the Overseas Workers Resource Centre (OWRC) helpline. The 2021 Draft Emigration Bill was intended to replace the 1983 Act. Overseas Indian categories include NRI, PIO and OCI, and the PIO and OCI categories were merged in 2015.

question: Which one of the following is the highest civilian award of Afghanistan?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Afghanistan's top civilian honour is named after King Amanullah Khan, who ruled from 1919 to 1929. He led Afghanistan to full independence from British control after the Third Anglo-Afghan War of 1919, formalised in the Treaty of Rawalpindi (August 1919). He is also remembered as a modernising reformer who introduced the 1923 constitution. In June 2016 President Ashraf Ghani conferred the award on PM Modi at Herat, during the inauguration of the Afghan-India Friendship Dam (Salma Dam, Herat province, built with Indian assistance). Modi was the first non-Afghan leader to receive it, and the citation recognised his support for Afghan development. For elimination, note that the other three options mix real Afghan names with no connection to a top civilian honour. Bismillah Khan is the shehnai maestro, Abdullah Abdullah is the politician whose name the option garbles, and Ashraf Ghani was the serving President who presented the award. Such names are common distractors in current-affairs questions on honours conferred on Indian leaders by foreign countries.
explanations: Correct. The State Order of Ghazi Amir Amanullah Khan is Afghanistan's highest civilian award, and Modi received it in 2016.
Wrong. Bismillah Khan is the name of the Indian shehnai maestro (Bharat Ratna, 2001). It is also the name of an Afghan military and political figure. No Afghan civilian award carries this name.
Wrong. This is a garbled combination of names. Abdullah Abdullah is an Afghan politician, and no award is named after him.
Wrong. Ashraf Ghani was the President who presented the award to Modi. No award is named after him, and Afghanistan does not name its top honour after a sitting president.
keyfact: Afghanistan's highest civilian honour is the State Order of Ghazi Amir Amanullah Khan, conferred on PM Modi in June 2016.
option_notes: Amir Amanullah Khan (ruled 1919-1929) was the Afghan ruler who won independence from Britain after the Third Anglo-Afghan War and the Treaty of Rawalpindi (1919). He introduced the 1923 constitution and social reforms such as education, including for women. He was forced to abdicate in 1929. The State Order of Ghazi Amir Amanullah Khan is the highest Afghan civilian honour. Modi received it in 2016.

Ustad Bismillah Khan (1916-2006) was the Indian shehnai maestro from Varanasi (Bihar-born). He received the Bharat Ratna in 2001 and played shehnai at the Red Fort on 15 August 1947. Bismillah Khan Mohammadi is a separate person, an Afghan general who served as Chief of Army Staff and later as Defence Minister. No Afghan top civilian award bears this name.

No honour by this name exists. The nearest real name is Abdullah Abdullah, an Afghan politician and former foreign minister who served as Chief Executive in the national unity government (2014-2020) and chaired the High Council for National Reconciliation. He was a contender in the 2014 and 2019 presidential elections. Garbled names like this are typical distractors.

Ashraf Ghani Ahmadzai was President of Afghanistan from 2014 until the Taliban takeover in August 2021. He was a former World Bank official and anthropologist, and a finance minister under Karzai. He presented the highest civilian honour to Modi in 2016 and inaugurated the Salma Dam with him. No award is named after him.
related: Modi received the Afghan honour in June 2016 at Herat.
The Salma Dam (Afghan-India Friendship Dam) is on the Hari Rud river in Herat.
The Treaty of Rawalpindi (1919) recognised Afghan independence.
India built the Afghan Parliament building in Kabul, inaugurated in December 2015.
Modi received Saudi Arabia's King Abdulaziz Sash in April 2016.
Modi received the UAE's Order of Zayed in 2019 and Russia's Order of St Andrew in 2019.
India's highest civilian honour is the Bharat Ratna, instituted in 1954.
summary: The answer is (a) Amir Amanullah Khan Award. Its full name is the State Order of Ghazi Amir Amanullah Khan, and it is Afghanistan's highest civilian honour. PM Narendra Modi received it in June 2016 at Herat.
topic_notes: Foreign civilian honours to Indian PM Modi are a recurring current-affairs theme. Afghanistan's State Order of Ghazi Amir Amanullah Khan was conferred in June 2016 at Herat. The Afghan-India Friendship Dam (Salma Dam) on the Hari Rud river in Herat province was built with Indian assistance, and Modi inaugurated it with President Ashraf Ghani. Other highest civilian honours Modi has received include: Saudi Arabia's King Abdulaziz Sash (2016), Palestine's Grand Collar of the State of Palestine (2018), UAE's Order of Zayed (2019), Russia's Order of St Andrew the Apostle (2019), Maldives' Nishan Izzuddeen (2019) and Bahrain's King Hamad Order of the Renaissance (2019). India's own highest civilian award is the Bharat Ratna, instituted in 1954 and conferred by the President. Other Indian civilian awards in descending order are Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri. India-Afghanistan links also include the new Afghan Parliament building in Kabul (inaugurated 2015, built by India), the Zaranj-Delaram highway, the Chabahar port route via Iran, and the Strategic Partnership Agreement of 2011. Afghan history is also a possible angle: the Durand Line (1893), the three Anglo-Afghan Wars (1839-42, 1878-80, 1919), and the Treaty of Rawalpindi. Afghanistan's capital is Kabul and its currency is the afghani.

question: Which one of the following is the official position of Ms. Aung San Suu Kyi ?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: After the National League for Democracy (NLD) won the November 2015 general election by a landslide, Aung San Suu Kyi could not become President because Article 59(f) of the 2008 military-drafted Constitution disqualifies anyone whose spouse or children owe allegiance to a foreign power (her late husband Michael Aris and her sons were British). The NLD therefore installed Htin Kyaw as President in March 2016, and Parliament passed the State Counsellor Act in April 2016, creating the post of State Counsellor for her. She also served as Minister for Foreign Affairs and Minister in the President's Office. Myanmar has no Prime Minister post (it was abolished in 2008 under the new Constitution), and the Governor General was a colonial-era office that ended with independence in 1948. In February 2021 the military (Tatmadaw), led by Min Aung Hlaing, staged a coup and detained her. She was later convicted in junta-run trials. For the 2017 exam, the correct answer is State Counsellor. Elimination: the President was Htin Kyaw (2016-18), then Win Myint (2018-21); there is no PM; the Governor General is obsolete.
explanations: Correct: She was State Counsellor from April 2016 until the coup of 1 February 2021, a post created by the State Counsellor Act, 2016.
Incorrect: She was barred from the presidency by Article 59(f) of the 2008 Constitution. Htin Kyaw and then Win Myint held the office.
Incorrect: The post of Prime Minister was abolished under the 2008 Constitution. The last PM was Gen. Thein Sein, who then became President in 2011.
Incorrect: The Governor General was a British colonial-era office. It ended when Burma became independent in 1948.
keyfact: Aung San Suu Kyi was Myanmar's State Counsellor (2016-2021), a post created because Article 59(f) of the 2008 Constitution barred her from the presidency.
option_notes: State Counsellor: a post created in April 2016, comparable to a prime minister or head of government in practice. The holder advises the President and coordinates the Union government. The post was created for Aung San Suu Kyi, who held it until the military coup in February 2021. The junta has since used the title for its own arrangements, and the junta's State Administration Council has run the country.

President of Myanmar: the head of state and head of government under the 2008 Constitution, elected by Parliament through the Presidential Electoral College. Presidents have included Thein Sein (2011-16), Htin Kyaw (2016-18) and Win Myint (2018-21). Article 59(f) bars anyone with foreign-national family members from this office, which is why Suu Kyi could not hold it.

Prime Minister of Myanmar: this office existed in earlier periods, such as U Nu, Ne Win and Khin Nyunt. It was abolished by the 2008 Constitution, which created an executive presidency. The last PM was Thein Sein (2007-11). The military junta's leader Min Aung Hlaing took the title in 2021, but this was outside the constitutional design.

Governor General: the colonial and Commonwealth-style representative of the British Crown. It is not an office in the Republic of Myanmar. Burma became independent on 4 January 1948 and left the Commonwealth. Sao Shwe Thaik was the first President of the Union.
related: Aung San Suu Kyi won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991.
Her party is the National League for Democracy (NLD), founded in 1988.
The State Counsellor post was created in April 2016.
Htin Kyaw was President from 2016 to 2018, followed by Win Myint.
The military coup in Myanmar took place on 1 February 2021.
Myanmar's capital is Naypyidaw, which replaced Yangon.
The 2008 Constitution reserves 25 percent of parliamentary seats for the military.
The Rohingya crisis centres on Rakhine State.
summary: The answer is (a). Aung San Suu Kyi held the post of State Counsellor of Myanmar, created in April 2016 for her after the NLD won the 2015 election. She was barred from the presidency by the 2008 Constitution, so the State Counsellor role let her lead the government in practice.
topic_notes: Aung San Suu Kyi (born 1945) is the daughter of General Aung San, the architect of Burmese independence, who was assassinated in 1947. She co-founded the National League for Democracy in 1988 and spent about 15 years under house arrest between 1989 and 2010. She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991 and received the Jawaharlal Nehru Award for International Understanding from India in 1993. Myanmar's 2008 Constitution reserves 25 percent of parliamentary seats for the military and gives it control of the Defence, Home and Border Affairs ministries. The NLD won the 2015 election and again won in November 2020. The military alleged fraud and seized power on 1 February 2021. Internationally, she faced severe criticism over the 2017 Rohingya crisis in Rakhine State, and she appeared before the ICJ in December 2019 in The Gambia v. Myanmar. Myanmar became a member of ASEAN in 1997. The country was renamed from Burma to Myanmar in 1989, and its capital moved from Yangon to Naypyidaw in 2005-06. India has ties with Myanmar through the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project, the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway, the Act East policy and the Free Movement Regime on the border. Future questions may ask about the offices of heads of government in neighbouring countries and the Nobel Peace laureates from the region.

question: Which one of the following statements about the National Population Register (NPR) is NOT correct?
options: NPR is the first step towards the creation of National Register of Indian Citizen
It is being created under the provisions of Citizenship Act, 1955 and Citizenship Rules, 2003, as amended from time to time
A digital data base of demographic data of around 120 crore persons has been created
Currently digitization is being carried out by the Central Government
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The National Population Register (NPR) is a register of usual residents of the country. It is prepared at the local (village/sub-town), sub-district, district, state and national levels under the Citizenship Act, 1955 and the Citizenship (Registration of Citizens and Issue of National Identity Cards) Rules, 2003. A usual resident is a person who has lived in a local area for the past 6 months or more, or intends to stay there for the next 6 months or more. Registration is mandatory for every usual resident, whether or not a citizen. The Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India, under the Ministry of Home Affairs, is responsible for it. The NPR was first prepared in 2010, with house-listing under Census 2011. Data was updated in 2015 and the database was digitised, with biometrics (Aadhaar-linked) also collected. The MHA's description calls the NPR the first step towards creating the National Register of Indian Citizens (NRIC), and says a digital database of about 119-120 crore residents was created. Since that digitisation was completed earlier, option (d) is the one that does not fit. The question is a recall item. Eliminate (a), (b) and (c) because they follow the official text; (d) is the odd one out.
explanations: Correct statement, so not the answer. The official MHA/RGI description calls the NPR the first step towards the NRIC.
Correct statement, so not the answer. The NPR is prepared under Section 14A of the Citizenship Act, 1955 and the Citizenship Rules, 2003.
Correct statement, so not the answer. A digital database of about 119-120 crore residents had already been created.
Incorrect statement, so this is the answer. Digitisation of the NPR data had already been completed and the database created; it is not an ongoing exercise, so the statement is not correct.
keyfact: NPR = register of usual residents under Citizenship Act 1955/Rules 2003, first step to NRIC; its database was already digitised.
option_notes: The NRIC (National Register of Indian Citizens) is a proposed register of verified Indian citizens, provided for in the 2003 Rules. It would be built from the NPR data after verification. Assam's NRC, updated under Supreme Court monitoring and published in final form on 31 August 2019, is a separate exercise under the Assam Accord.

The Citizenship Act, 1955 governs acquisition and termination of Indian citizenship. Section 14A, inserted in 2003, enables compulsory registration of citizens and the issue of national identity cards. The Citizenship Rules, 2003 lay out the procedure for the NPR, the local, sub-district, district, state and national registers, and the NRIC.

The NPR collected demographic data first in 2010, and then updated it in 2015 through door-to-door surveys. The database was digitised and Aadhaar numbers were seeded. The roughly 119-120 crore figure is the number of usual residents covered by the exercise, which went beyond citizens alone.

Digitisation and updating of the NPR have been handled by the Registrar General of India, under the Ministry of Home Affairs, through the Central Government. Digitisation was carried out in 2010-2015 and was complete by the time of this question, so describing it as 'currently' under way is wrong. The NPR is updated with later census exercises.
related: NPR is prepared under Section 14A of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
A usual resident is one who has lived in a place for 6 months or more or intends to do so.
NPR was first created in 2010 and updated in 2015.
The Registrar General of India, under the MHA, manages the NPR and the Census.
Assam NRC final list was published on 31 August 2019.
Constitution Articles 5-11 (Part II) deal with citizenship.
The Census is conducted under the Census Act, 1948.
summary: The answer is (d). The NPR database was already digitised, so the claim that digitization is 'currently being carried out' does not hold. Statements (a), (b) and (c) match the official description of the NPR, and the exam's official framing of the NPR is the likeliest basis for the question.
topic_notes: The NPR is a register of usual residents, not only of citizens. A usual resident is someone who has stayed in a local area for at least 6 months, or intends to stay for the next 6 months. The legal basis is Section 14A of the Citizenship Act, 1955 (inserted by the 2003 amendment, under the Vajpayee government) and the Citizenship Rules, 2003. The RGI and Census Commissioner, under the MHA, runs it. The NPR was first compiled in 2010 along with Census 2011 house-listing, and updated in 2015 with digitisation and Aadhaar seeding. The NPR is distinct from the Census: the Census is governed by the Census Act, 1948, and its data is confidential, whereas the NPR is a register with identifying details. NPR fields include name, relationship to head, sex, date of birth, marital status, place of birth, nationality, occupation and education. Later proposals to update it with the 2021 Census were postponed. NRIC/NRC would be a list of verified citizens drawn from the NPR. Assam's NRC (1951 base, updated using the 24 March 1971 cut-off under the Assam Accord) was published on 31 August 2019, with about 19 lakh excluded. The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 provides citizenship to minority communities (Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, Christians) from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India by 31 December 2014. Related exam angles: Aadhaar (UIDAI, Aadhaar Act 2016), Section 3 citizenship by birth, and Articles 5-11 of the Constitution on citizenship.

question: Recently the Government of India had conducted the Socio-Economic and Caste Census (SECC) all over the country. Which of the following agency / agencies had rendered complete logistics and technical support to this exercise?
options: Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India
Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
Ministry of Rural Development & Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
subject: Current Affairs
detail: SECC 2011 was the first caste-based census since 1931 and was combined with a household-level socio-economic survey. It was launched in June 2011 and run by three bodies: the Ministry of Rural Development (rural areas), the Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation (urban areas) and the Registrar General and Census Commissioner under the Ministry of Home Affairs (Census Commissioner). The Rural Development Ministry ran the rural part, which used the Census Commissioner's mapping and training support and was carried out through the state governments. The urban SECC was run by the Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation Ministry, which is now called the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. The question asks which agencies gave complete logistics and technical support. The expected reading is that both ministries together carried out the exercise, so (d) is the most complete option. Option (a) is limited because the Census Commissioner's office is a technical partner in the census rather than the executor of the SECC. Options (b) and (c) are each incomplete, as each covers only one of the two sectors. Rural data were released in July 2015, with the poverty and deprivation parameters. Urban data have been largely unreleased. Caste data were handed to an expert group under the NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman. It is worth noting the question has an ambiguity: the Census Commissioner's office also supported the exercise technically.
explanations: Incorrect: the Registrar General's office was involved technically in the 2011 exercise but was not the agency that conducted it, and it did not cover both rural and urban sectors on its own.
Incorrect as a complete answer: the Ministry of Rural Development handled only the rural SECC.
Incorrect as a complete answer: the Housing and Urban Affairs Ministry handled only the urban SECC.
Correct: the rural and urban ministries together rendered the logistics and technical support for the nationwide SECC.
keyfact: SECC 2011 was carried out by the Rural Development Ministry (rural) and the Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation / Housing and Urban Affairs Ministry (urban).
option_notes: The Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India sits under the Ministry of Home Affairs. It conducts the decennial Census under the Census Act 1948 and also runs the Sample Registration System and civil registration data. The first Census of independent India was in 1951. The 2011 Census was the 15th. The Census Commissioner for the 2011 exercise was C. Chandramouli.

The Ministry of Rural Development oversees MGNREGA, PMAY-Gramin, DAY-NRLM, PMGSY and the NSAP. It ran the rural SECC 2011 and used its data to identify beneficiaries for rural schemes. The data were released in July 2015 as deprivation parameters. Its Departments are Rural Development and Land Resources.

The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs was earlier the Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation, which was merged with Urban Development in 2017. It runs the Swachh Bharat Mission Urban, AMRUT, Smart Cities Mission, PMAY-Urban and DAY-NULM. It handled the urban SECC.

This option combines both ministries, which ran the rural and urban SECC 2011 respectively. SECC 2011 covered caste, household assets, income, and deprivation indicators across the whole country, and its rural results fed into the identification of beneficiaries.
related: SECC 2011 was the first caste-based enumeration since 1931.
SECC 2011 was launched from Tripura in June 2011.
The rural SECC data were released in July 2015.
SECC identifies beneficiaries for PMAY-G and NSAP.
The Registrar General and Census Commissioner works under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
India's 2011 Census population was about 121 crore.
Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation was merged with Urban Development in 2017.
summary: The answer is (d). SECC 2011 was conducted by the Ministry of Rural Development (rural areas) and the Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation, now Housing and Urban Affairs (urban areas). The Registrar General and Census Commissioner's office is not named as the sole agency. Note that this answer is a judgement based on the question's wording, since no official key exists.
topic_notes: SECC 2011 was the first paperless census in India, with enumerators using handheld tablets. It was launched from Tripura in June 2011. It had three components: the rural survey run by the Ministry of Rural Development, the urban survey run by the Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation Ministry, and the caste census run by the Registrar General and Census Commissioner. The separate caste count was handed to an expert group chaired by the NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman, after the Ministry of Social Justice classified the data. Rural data were released in July 2015 by Finance Minister Arun Jaitley. Findings included that about 17.9 crore rural households were counted, with roughly 30 percent being landless households dependent on manual casual labour and about 2.37 crore households living in one-room kutcha housing. The deprivation criteria were seven parameters (D1 to D7), such as kutcha walls and roof, no adult member aged 16 to 59, female-headed households with no adult male, disabled members, SC/ST households and landless households deriving income from manual casual labour. Automatic exclusion and inclusion criteria were applied. SECC data are used for PMAY-G, NSAP, DDU-GKY and the Ujjwala Yojana to find beneficiaries. The Rangarajan Committee and Tendulkar Committee are related poverty estimation bodies. The decennial census of 2011 had a headcount of 121 crore. The 2021 Census was delayed because of Covid.

question: Paul Beatty was awarded the Man Booker Prize, 2016 for which one of the following works?
options: Do Not Say We Have Nothing
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Man Booker Prize 2016 was awarded on 25 October 2016 to Paul Beatty for 'The Sellout', a satirical novel about race, identity and segregation in contemporary America. The narrator, from a fictional agricultural enclave in Los Angeles called Dickens, is tried before the US Supreme Court for owning a slave and re-introducing segregation. Beatty became the first American author to win the Booker after the rules were widened in 2014 to admit any novel written in English and published in the UK, regardless of the author's nationality. The chair of judges was Amanda Foreman. The other shortlisted books in 2016 were Graeme Macrae Burnet's 'His Bloody Project', Deborah Levy's 'Hot Milk', Madeleine Thien's 'Do Not Say We Have Nothing', Ottessa Moshfegh's 'Eileen' and David Szalay's 'All That Man Is'. Elimination: the options (a), (b) and (d) were all on the 2016 shortlist but lost to Beatty, so each is a distractor. Remember the author-book link: Beatty-Sellout, Burnet-His Bloody Project, Levy-Hot Milk, Thien-Do Not Say We Have Nothing.
explanations: Incorrect: 'His Bloody Project' is by Graeme Macrae Burnet, a Scottish author. It was shortlisted in 2016 but did not win.
Incorrect: 'Hot Milk' is by Deborah Levy, shortlisted in 2016. It did not win.
Correct: 'The Sellout' by Paul Beatty won the 2016 Man Booker Prize.
Incorrect: 'Do Not Say We Have Nothing' is by Canadian author Madeleine Thien, shortlisted in 2016 but not the winner.
keyfact: Man Booker 2016: Paul Beatty, The Sellout - the first American winner.
option_notes: 'His Bloody Project' (2015) is a historical crime novel by Graeme Macrae Burnet. It is set in 1869 in a Scottish Highlands crofting community and is presented as documents about a triple murder committed by a young crofter, Roderick Macrae. It was shortlisted for the 2016 Man Booker Prize and was Burnet's second novel, published by Contraband (Saraband).

'Hot Milk' (2016) is a novel by British writer Deborah Levy. It is set in a Spanish coastal town, Almería, where Sofia takes her ailing mother for treatment. The book explores the mother-daughter relationship. It was shortlisted for the 2016 Booker Prize. Levy had also been shortlisted in 2012 for 'Swimming Home'.

'The Sellout' (2015) is a satirical novel by American author Paul Beatty. It deals with race, slavery, segregation and identity in the USA, and its narrator lives in the fictional Dickens, in Los Angeles. It won the 2016 Man Booker Prize, making Beatty the first American winner. It also won the 2015 National Book Critics Circle Award for fiction.

'Do Not Say We Have Nothing' (2016) is a novel by Canadian author Madeleine Thien. It follows a Chinese family through the Cultural Revolution and the Tiananmen Square protests, with themes of music, politics and memory. It was shortlisted for the 2016 Man Booker Prize and also won the Governor General's Award for English-language fiction.
related: Paul Beatty was the first American to win the Booker Prize (2016).
The Man Booker Prize 2016 was announced on 25 October 2016.
Booker Prize money is £50,000.
Arundhati Roy won the Booker in 1997 for The God of Small Things.
Aravind Adiga won the 2008 Booker for The White Tiger.
Geetanjali Shree's Tomb of Sand won the International Booker in 2022.
George Saunders won the 2017 Booker for Lincoln in the Bardo.
summary: The answer is (c) The Sellout. Paul Beatty, an American author, won the 2016 Man Booker Prize for this satirical novel on race in America, and he was the first American to win the prize.
topic_notes: The Booker Prize, founded in 1969, is the leading literary award in the English-speaking world, given for a novel written in English and published in the UK or Ireland. It was sponsored by Man Group from 2002 to 2019, so it was called the Man Booker Prize in that period, and it has been called simply the Booker Prize since 2019. Prize money is £50,000. The rules were widened in 2014 to include non-UK authors writing in English, which opened the way to American winners. Paul Beatty (2016) was the first American winner, followed by George Saunders (2017, 'Lincoln in the Bardo'). Anna Burns won in 2018 for 'Milkman', and in 2019 the prize was shared by Margaret Atwood ('The Testaments') and Bernardine Evaristo ('Girl, Woman, Other'). Douglas Stuart won in 2020 ('Shuggie Bain'), Damon Galgut in 2021 ('The Promise'), Shehan Karunatilaka in 2022 ('The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida'), Paul Lynch in 2023 ('Prophet Song'), Samantha Harvey in 2024 ('Orbital'). Indian-origin and Indian winners: Salman Rushdie ('Midnight's Children', 1981, also the Booker of Bookers), Arundhati Roy ('The God of Small Things', 1997), Kiran Desai ('The Inheritance of Loss', 2006), Aravind Adiga ('The White Tiger', 2008), and Geetanjali Shree's 'Tomb of Sand' won the International Booker in 2022, the first Hindi-language work to do so. The International Booker Prize is a separate award for translated fiction.

question:
Under which of the following grounds, the Constitution of India authorizes the Legislature to make laws providing for ‘Preventive Detention’?
1. Security of a State
2. Maintenance of public order
3. Maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community
4. Maintenance of public health and morality Select the correct answer using the code given below:
subject: Insurance
detail: Preventive detention means detaining a person without trial to prevent a future act that is prejudicial to the State, not to punish a past offence. Article 22(3)(b) excludes preventive detention laws from the safeguards of Article 22(1) and (2), namely being told the grounds, consulting a lawyer, and being produced before a magistrate within 24 hours. Parliament has exclusive power to legislate for reasons connected with defence, foreign affairs and security of India (Entry 9, List I). Parliament and State Legislatures have concurrent power for security of a State, maintenance of public order and maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community (Entry 3, List III). Article 22(4) says detention beyond three months needs an Advisory Board; the 44th Amendment proposed reducing this to two months but it has never been brought into force. Article 22(5) requires communicating the grounds of detention at the earliest and giving an opportunity for representation. Public health and morality are grounds for restricting rights such as Article 19(4) and Article 25, but not for preventive detention. So 1, 2 and 3 are correct and 4 is wrong. Options (a) and (c) are incomplete, and (d) wrongly includes 4.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out security of a State, which is a valid ground, so the list is incomplete.
Correct: security of a State, public order and essential supplies and services are all valid grounds under Entry 3 of the Concurrent List, and public health and morality is not.
Wrong: it omits public order and wrongly includes public health and morality.
Wrong: it includes public health and morality, which is not a ground for preventive detention.
keyfact: Preventive detention grounds: security of State, public order, essential supplies and services (plus defence and foreign affairs for Parliament); not public health or morality.
option_notes: Statement-number option 2 and 3 only: it contains two valid grounds, public order and essential supplies and services, but omits security of a State. A partial list like this is a typical UPSC trap, so check whether every valid ground has been included.

Statement-number option 1, 2 and 3 only: this matches the grounds of Entry 3, List III (security of a State, public order, essential supplies and services). Entry 9, List I separately covers defence, foreign affairs and security of India for Parliament. This is the correct option.

Statement-number option 1 and 4 only: it pairs a valid ground (security of a State) with an invalid one (public health and morality). It also leaves out public order and essential supplies, so it is wrong on both counts.
Statement-number option 1, 2, 3 and 4: it adds public health and morality, which is a ground for restricting some fundamental rights but not for preventive detention. So it is wrong.
related: Article 22 gives protection against arrest and detention.
Preventive detention beyond 3 months needs an Advisory Board (Article 22(4)).
Entry 9, List I covers preventive detention for defence, foreign affairs and security of India.
Entry 3, List III covers security of State, public order and essential supplies and services.
India is among the few democracies with preventive detention provisions in the Constitution in peacetime.
The National Security Act, 1980 allows detention up to 12 months.
The 44th Amendment's two-month proposal for Advisory Boards has not been brought into force.
Preventive Detention Act 1950 was the first such peacetime law, and it lapsed in 1969.
statements: 1 — Correct: Security of a State is a listed ground under Entry 3, List III. Detention for acts threatening the State's security is permitted. Parliament also legislates for the security of India and defence under Entry 9, List I. Laws such as the National Security Act, 1980 and the earlier MISA and COFEPOSA draw on these entries. The 'security of State' ground covers serious threats like rebellion, waging war, or insurgency, as opposed to ordinary law-and-order disturbances.

2 — Correct: Maintenance of public order is a ground in Entry 3, List III. The Supreme Court distinguishes 'law and order', 'public order' and 'security of State' as widening circles, with public order in the middle (Ram Manohar Lohia case, 1960). Acts affecting only individuals are law and order issues; acts disturbing the community at large are public order issues. State laws such as the Goondas Acts and preventive detention statutes in several states rely on this ground.

3 — Correct: Maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community is a ground in Entry 3, List III. It supports laws against black-marketing and hoarding, for example the Prevention of Black Marketing and Maintenance of Supplies of Essential Commodities Act, 1980. It is a concurrent subject, so both Parliament and State Legislatures can make such laws. It allows detention to prevent disruption of supply chains of food, fuel and essential services.

4 — Incorrect: Public health and morality is not a ground for preventive detention. These appear as grounds for reasonable restrictions on freedom of religion (Article 25), freedom of movement and other rights, and in the Article 19 restrictions for decency or morality. Public health is also a State List subject (Entry 6, List II). Preventive detention grounds are restricted to security, public order, essential supplies and services, plus defence and foreign affairs for Parliament. Adding this ground would be unconstitutional.
summary: The answer is (b) 1, 2 and 3 only. Article 22(3)-(7) read with Entry 9 of List I and Entry 3 of List III allows preventive detention for security of a State, maintenance of public order and maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community. Public health and morality is not a ground for preventive detention.
topic_notes: Article 22 protects persons against arrest and detention. Clauses (1) and (2) apply to ordinary arrests: the right to be informed of the grounds, the right to a lawyer, and production before a magistrate within 24 hours excluding travel time. These do not apply to enemy aliens or to persons detained under preventive detention laws. Article 22(3)-(7) deals with preventive detention. Detention beyond three months needs an Advisory Board of persons qualified to be High Court judges (Article 22(4)). Parliament may prescribe the circumstances in which detention beyond three months is allowed without an Advisory Board (Article 22(7)). Article 22(5) requires grounds to be communicated and the earliest opportunity for representation, though facts against public interest may be withheld (22(6)). Legislative power: Entry 9, List I (Parliament, for defence, foreign affairs and security of India) and Entry 3, List III (concurrent, for security of State, public order and essential supplies and services). Key laws: Preventive Detention Act 1950 (first, lapsed 1969), MISA 1971 (repealed 1978), COFEPOSA 1974, NSA 1980, PBMMSEC Act 1980, TADA (lapsed 1995) and POTA (repealed 2004), and UAPA 1967 as amended. Key cases: A.K. Gopalan v State of Madras (1950), Ram Manohar Lohia (1960) on public order, and Maneka Gandhi (1978) linking Article 21 with Articles 14 and 19. The 44th Amendment 1978 proposed reducing the detention period without an Advisory Board to two months and making the board chaired by a High Court judge. This has not been implemented. Article 359 allows suspension of Article 21 during a Presidential Emergency, but the 44th Amendment protects Articles 20 and 21 from suspension.

question:
A Money Bill contains provisions for which of the following matters?
1. The imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax
2. The regulation of the borrowing of money by the Government
3. The custody of Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund of India
4. The imposition of fines and other pecuniary penalties Select the correct answer using the code given below:
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
