He was inducted into the ICC Hall of Fame in 2016. His bowling action drew controversy but was cleared by the ICC. He took 67 five-wicket hauls and 22 ten-wicket matches in Tests, both records.

James Anderson is the English swing bowler who debuted in Tests in 2003 and became the first fast bowler to pass 600 wickets in 2020. He went on to pass 700 wickets in 2024, finishing his Test career in July 2024 at Lord's with 704 wickets. He is England's leading Test wicket-taker and the third-highest overall behind Muralitharan and Shane Warne.

Stuart Broad is an English fast-medium bowler who debuted in Tests in 2007. He took a hat-trick against India in 2011 and 8 for 15 against Australia at Trent Bridge in 2015. He passed 500 Test wickets in 2016 and retired after the 2023 Ashes with 604 wickets. He is also known for scoring 169 against Pakistan in 2010 as a tailender.

Ravichandran Ashwin is an Indian off-spinner who debuted in Tests in 2011 against the West Indies. He was ICC Cricketer of the Year in 2016, and reached 300 wickets in 54 Tests, then 400 in 2021 and 500 in 2024. He took 8 Test wickets in his debut Test in Delhi. He is also a useful lower-order batsman with Test centuries. He retired from international cricket in December 2024.
related: Muralitharan holds the record for most Test wickets: 800.
Anil Kumble is India's leading Test wicket-taker with 619 wickets.
Ashwin took 400 Test wickets in 2021 and 500 in 2024.
Anderson retired from Test cricket in July 2024 with 704 wickets.
Broad retired in 2023 with 604 Test wickets.
Sachin Tendulkar holds 15,921 Test runs and 100 international centuries.
The first ICC World Test Championship final in 2021 was won by New Zealand against India.
Ashwin won the ICC Cricketer of the Year (Sir Garfield Sobers Trophy) in 2016.
summary: The answer is (d) Ravichandran Ashwin. He became the first bowler in Test history to take 200 wickets against left-handed batsmen, reaching the milestone in early 2021 during the India v England series in Chennai/Ahmedabad. His off-spin, which turns the ball away from left-handers, is the core reason.
topic_notes: This question belongs to the sports section of Current Affairs, where UPSC EPFO often asks about records, awards and tournament winners. Ravichandran Ashwin (born 1986, Chennai) has played for Tamil Nadu, Chennai Super Kings, Rajasthan Royals and Delhi Capitals in the IPL. He was a key player in India's 2011 World Cup win and the 2013 Champions Trophy. His Test career began in November 2011. He reached 200 wickets in 37 Tests (fastest by an Indian at that time bar none for the milestone, behind Dennis Lillee's mark for fewest matches by some measures) and 300 in 54 Tests, then 400 in 77 Tests, and 500 in 98 Tests in 2024 at Rajkot. He passed Anil Kumble's 619 as India's highest wicket-taker only in the sense of becoming second behind Kumble, who holds 619 Test wickets. In 2021 Ashwin was part of the team that won the series against England 3-1 and played in the first ICC World Test Championship final, lost to New Zealand at Southampton. The ICC World Test Championship began in 2019. Other angles: leading Test wicket-takers in order are Muralitharan (800), Shane Warne (708), James Anderson (704), Anil Kumble (619), Stuart Broad (604), Glenn McGrath (563). Leading Test run-scorers are Joe Root and Sachin Tendulkar (15,921 runs). Questions may also ask about Man of the Series, ICC awards such as the Sir Garfield Sobers Trophy, and the Border-Gavaskar Trophy.

question: Who among the following Speakers of Lok Sabha formally disassociated from the political party after his election as the Speaker ?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by the House (Article 93) and holds a office that must be impartial. In India the Speaker is not required by the Constitution to resign from their party, and the Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985) treats the Speaker's case specially (Paragraph 5, added by the 1985 amendment), allowing a Speaker to give up party membership without disqualification and rejoin later. Neelam Sanjiva Reddy, a senior Congress leader, was elected Speaker on 17 March 1967 and resigned from the Congress party, declaring that he was above party politics. He later contested the 1969 presidential election as the Congress official candidate in 1969 and lost to V.V. Giri, and he became President in 1977 (unopposed). Elimination: Mavalankar (first Speaker, 1952-56) and Hukam Singh (1962-67) remained party members; Sangma (1996-98) also stayed with the Congress. Hence only Reddy matches. Note that Reddy was the first Speaker to formally sever party ties. Somnath Chatterjee, by contrast, was expelled by the CPI(M) in 2008 while Speaker.
explanations: Incorrect: G.V. Mavalankar, the first Speaker (1952-56), did not leave the Congress party formally, though he was known for impartiality and set many conventions.
Incorrect: Sardar Hukam Singh, Speaker 1962-67, was elected as a Congress member and did not formally disassociate from the party.
Correct: Neelam Sanjiva Reddy resigned from the Congress party after being elected Speaker in 1967, the first to formally do so, to mark impartiality.
Incorrect: P.A. Sangma, Speaker 1996-98, was a Congress member elected as a consensus Speaker of the United Front era and did not formally leave the party.
keyfact: Neelam Sanjiva Reddy (Speaker 1967) was the first Speaker to formally resign from his party after election.
option_notes: G.V. Mavalankar (1888-1956) was the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha, serving 1952 until his death in February 1956. Known as the 'Father of the Lok Sabha', he established the Speaker's conventions and committee system, and was earlier Speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly (1946-47). His son, Purushottam Mavalankar, also became an MP. The Mavalankar Hall in Delhi is named after him.

Sardar Hukam Singh (1895-1983) was Speaker of the Lok Sabha from 1962 to 1967, after serving as Deputy Speaker (1956-62). He was a Akali Dal leader who later joined Congress. He later served as Governor of Rajasthan (1967-72). He was a member of the Constituent Assembly and well known as an advocate of Sikh interests and parliamentary procedure.

Neelam Sanjiva Reddy (1913-1996) was Speaker of the 4th Lok Sabha (1967-69) and the 6th Lok Sabha (1977), and the sixth President of India (1977-82), elected unopposed as the youngest President. He was the first Chief Minister of united Andhra Pradesh (1956-60). He resigned from Congress on becoming Speaker in 1967 and joined the Janata Party later in 1977.

P.A. Sangma (1947-2016) was Speaker of the 11th Lok Sabha (1996-98), from Meghalaya, and Chief Minister of Meghalaya (1988-90, 1990-91). He was a Congress leader who left with Sharad Pawar and Tariq Anwar in 1999 to form the NCP, later the National People's Party (2013). He contested the 2012 presidential election against Pranab Mukherjee and lost.
related: Article 93: Lok Sabha elects its Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
Article 94: Vacation, resignation and removal of Speaker; removal needs 14 days' notice.
Article 96: Speaker does not preside when their removal is under consideration.
Tenth Schedule Paragraph 5 gives an exemption to the Speaker/Chairman who give up party membership.
Meira Kumar was the first woman Speaker of Lok Sabha (2009-14).
G.V. Mavalankar was the first Lok Sabha Speaker (1952-56).
Somnath Chatterjee was expelled from the CPI(M) in 2008 while Speaker.
Kihoto Hollohan case (1992) held the Speaker's disqualification decision is judicially reviewable.
summary: The answer is (c) Neelam Sanjiva Reddy. He was elected Speaker of the 4th Lok Sabha in 1967 and resigned from the Congress party membership after his election, setting a precedent for the Speaker's impartiality and non-partisanship.
topic_notes: The Speaker's office is governed by Articles 93 to 97 and 100-and the Rules of Procedure. The Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its members soon after its first sitting. The Speaker holds office until just before the first meeting of the next Lok Sabha, and may be removed by a resolution passed by an effective majority (majority of all the then members) with 14 days' notice (Article 94, 96). During such a resolution the Speaker cannot preside but can speak and vote only in the first instance (not in a tie). The Speaker decides on money bill certification (Article 110), presides over joint sittings (Article 108), and decides disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (Kihoto Hollohan case, 1992: decisions are subject to judicial review). The Speaker has a casting vote only in a tie. The Speaker's salary is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. The Deputy Speaker is elected under Article 93 too; by convention, the post is offered to the Opposition. The first Speaker was G.V. Mavalankar, and the first Deputy Speaker was M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar. Madhav Shrikrishna? No: the first woman Speaker was Meira Kumar (2009-14), followed by Sumitra Mahajan (2014-19), Om Birla (2019 onwards). G.M.C. Balayogi was the first Speaker to die in office in an air crash (2002), and Balram Jakhar served the longest (two full terms, 1980-89). Practice in the UK: the Speaker gives up party affiliation and is returned unopposed; in India, the Speaker's Conference has long urged adopting this. Somnath Chatterjee was expelled by his party in 2008 for refusing to resign after the Left withdrew support to the government.

question: UNESCO has been observing February 21 as} 101. the International Mother Language Day since 2000. The idea to celebrate the International Mother Language Day was the initiative of which of the following nations ?
subject: Computers
detail: International Mother Language Day (IMLD) is observed every year on 21 February. The initiative came from Bangladesh (then East Pakistan's Bengali-language movement is the root). On 21 February 1952, students and activists in Dhaka protesting against Urdu being made the sole state language of Pakistan were fired upon by police; Salam, Barkat, Rafiq, Jabbar and others were killed. The day is commemorated as Shaheed Day (Language Martyrs' Day) in Bangladesh, with the Shaheed Minar in Dhaka as its memorial. Bangladesh, backed by a proposal from Rafiqul Islam (a Bangladeshi expatriate in Vancouver) and supported by many member states, moved the proposal at UNESCO; the General Conference approved it on 17 November 1999, and the UN General Assembly later (2002) welcomed it and, in 2008, declared 2008 the International Year of Languages. Elimination: Sri Lanka, India and Nepal had no such historical language-martyrdom movement that led to a UNESCO proposal. Bangladesh is the only country with a direct link between the date and its history.
explanations: Sri Lanka did not propose IMLD; its language politics (Sinhala Only Act 1956) is unrelated to the 21 February origin.
Correct. Bangladesh proposed the day, commemorating the 1952 Bengali Language Movement martyrs in Dhaka.
India did not initiate the proposal; the Indian linguistic issues (e.g., States Reorganisation) are different, and the date is tied to events in East Pakistan.
Nepal did not initiate the proposal; it has no connection to the 21 February 1952 events.
keyfact: Bangladesh proposed International Mother Language Day (21 February), commemorating the 1952 Dhaka Language Movement martyrs; UNESCO adopted it in 1999.
option_notes: Sri Lanka: island nation in South Asia with Sinhala and Tamil as official languages (Sinhala Only Act 1956, Thirteenth Amendment 1987 made Tamil official). Capital Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, commercial capital Colombo. Its language disputes contributed to ethnic conflict and the civil war (1983-2009). It did not initiate IMLD.

Bangladesh: formed in 1971 from East Pakistan after the Liberation War. Its identity is rooted in the Bengali Language Movement of 1952. 21 February is Ekushey February and Shaheed Dibas, a national holiday. Shaheed Minar in Dhaka commemorates the martyrs. Bangladesh proposed IMLD to UNESCO, adopted in 1999.

India: has 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, Hindi in Devanagari as the official language under Article 343, and English as an associate official language. Article 350A provides for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage. India did not initiate IMLD.

Nepal: Himalayan country, Nepali (Khas Kura) is the official language under its 2015 Constitution, with many other mother tongues recognised as national languages. Capital Kathmandu. Nepal did not originate the IMLD proposal.
related: IMLD is observed on 21 February; UNESCO proclaimed it on 17 November 1999.
First observed in 2000.
Bangladesh marks 21 February as Shaheed Dibas, with the Shaheed Minar in Dhaka.
Hindi Diwas in India is 14 September; World Hindi Day is 10 January.
Article 350A: facilities for instruction in mother tongue at primary stage.
Article 343: Hindi in Devanagari script is the Union's official language.
International Decade of Indigenous Languages: 2022-2032.
Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution lists 22 languages.
summary: The answer is (b) Bangladesh. The idea of International Mother Language Day was proposed by Bangladesh, in memory of the 21 February 1952 Language Movement in Dhaka, and UNESCO proclaimed the day in November 1999 (first observed in 2000).
topic_notes: International Mother Language Day is observed on 21 February to promote linguistic and cultural diversity and multilingualism. Background: after the 1947 Partition, Pakistan's leaders declared Urdu the sole national language in 1948 despite Bengali being spoken by a majority of the population. The Bhasha Andolan (Language Movement) culminated on 21 February 1952 when police fired on protesters at Dhaka University, killing several. Bengali was recognised as an official language of Pakistan in 1956. The Shaheed Minar, built in memory, is the focal point of commemoration. UNESCO's General Conference proclaimed the day on 17 November 1999; it has been observed since 21 February 2000. The UN General Assembly in its 2002 resolution encouraged member states to protect all languages, and 2008 was declared the International Year of Languages, with UNESCO as lead agency. Themes change each year, usually on multilingual education and technology. UNESCO also runs the Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger. The UN declared 2022-2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages. In India, the Constitution protects language rights through Articles 29, 30, 345-347, 350A and 351, and classical language status has been given to Tamil, Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, and more recently Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali (2024). Other UN days: World Hindi Day (10 January) is distinct from World Hindi Day, and Hindi Diwas is on 14 September.

question: Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala was recently selected as the first woman Director-General of WTO. She hails from which one of the following countries ?
subject: Computers
detail: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala was appointed the 7th Director-General of the WTO, with her term beginning on 1 March 2021 after General Council consensus in February 2021. She is the first woman and the first African to hold the post. She succeeded Roberto Azevêdo of Brazil, who resigned a year before his term ended. Her competitor in the final round was Yoo Myung-hee of South Korea, and the US under the Trump administration had earlier blocked consensus. She was reappointed for a second term from September 2025 to August 2029. A development economist trained at Harvard and MIT, she served twice as Nigeria's Finance Minister (2003-06 and 2011-15), was briefly Foreign Minister, and worked at the World Bank as Managing Director. She also chaired Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. Elimination: Japan, Ethiopia and Egypt are not her country. Ethiopia is linked with Tedros Adhanom, the WHO Director-General, which is a common distractor. The WTO is headquartered in Geneva and was established on 1 January 1995.
explanations: Incorrect: Japan has no connection to Okonjo-Iweala. Japan's Yasuhisa Shiozawa and others have headed other bodies, but no Japanese national has been WTO chief.
Incorrect: Ethiopia is the home of Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, so it is a distractor. Okonjo-Iweala is not Ethiopian.
Correct: She is Nigerian, born in Ogwashi-Ukwu, Delta State, and served as Nigeria's Finance Minister. She became the first woman and first African WTO Director-General.
Incorrect: Egypt is not her country. Egypt's connections to international bodies include former UN Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, but not the WTO chief.
keyfact: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala (Nigeria) became the first woman and first African WTO Director-General on 1 March 2021.
option_notes: Japan is an East Asian island nation with its capital in Tokyo. It is a G7 member and one of the world's largest economies. It has not produced a WTO Director-General. The WTO chiefs have come from Ireland, Italy, New Zealand, Thailand, France, Brazil and Nigeria.

Ethiopia is a landlocked East African country with its capital at Addis Ababa, which hosts the African Union headquarters. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, an Ethiopian, has been WHO Director-General since 2017, the first African to hold that post. It is Africa's second most populous country.

Nigeria is West Africa's largest country and Africa's most populous, with its capital at Abuja and its largest city at Lagos. It is a major oil producer and an OPEC member. Okonjo-Iweala served as its Finance Minister twice and is the first woman and first African WTO Director-General.

Egypt is a North African country with its capital at Cairo, controlling the Suez Canal. It is a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement and the Arab League. Egyptian Boutros Boutros-Ghali was UN Secretary-General from 1992 to 1996. No Egyptian has led the WTO.
related: Okonjo-Iweala is the 7th WTO Director-General and took office on 1 March 2021.
She is the first woman and first African to head the WTO.
Her predecessor was Roberto Azevêdo of Brazil.
WTO was established on 1 January 1995 and is headquartered in Geneva.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is from Ethiopia.
The WTO Appellate Body has been non-functional since December 2019.
MC13 of the WTO was held in Abu Dhabi in 2024.
WTO's Trade Facilitation Agreement came into force in February 2017.
summary: The answer is (c) Nigeria. Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala is a Nigerian economist and former Finance Minister of Nigeria who became the first woman and first African Director-General of the World Trade Organization in 2021.
topic_notes: The World Trade Organization is the global body that deals with the rules of trade between nations. It was established on 1 January 1995 following the Uruguay Round, replacing GATT of 1947, and has its headquarters at Centre William Rappard, Geneva. It has 166 members and the highest decision-making body is the Ministerial Conference, which meets at least every two years. The General Council acts between conferences. The Director-General is appointed by consensus for a four-year renewable term. Past Director-Generals: Peter Sutherland (Ireland, GATT/WTO 1993-95), Renato Ruggiero (Italy, 1995-99), Mike Moore (New Zealand, 1999-2002), Supachai Panitchpakdi (Thailand, 2002-05), Pascal Lamy (France, 2005-13), Roberto Azevêdo (Brazil, 2013-20) and Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala (Nigeria, from 2021). Key agreements include GATS (services), TRIPS (intellectual property), the Agreement on Agriculture, TRIMS, SPS and the Trade Facilitation Agreement, which came into force in 2017. The Dispute Settlement Body is hampered because the US blocks appointments to the Appellate Body, which has been non-functional since December 2019. Ministerial Conferences: MC12 was held in Geneva in 2022, MC13 in Abu Dhabi in 2024 and MC14 is scheduled for Cameroon in 2026. India joined the WTO on 1 January 1995 and was a GATT founding member. Other international heads often asked: WHO's Tedros (Ethiopia), IMF's Kristalina Georgieva (Bulgaria), World Bank's Ajay Banga (India-born American), and UN Secretary-General António Guterres (Portugal).

question: The Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project will connect India with which one of the following countries ? 104
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project (KMMTTP) is an India-funded connectivity project signed with Myanmar in 2008. Its purpose is to give landlocked Northeast India an alternative route to the sea, reducing dependence on the narrow Siliguri Corridor (Chicken's Neck). The route has four parts: (1) Kolkata to Sittwe port in Rakhine State by sea (about 539 km); (2) Sittwe to Paletwa in Chin State via the Kaladan river (about 158 km) by inland waterway; (3) Paletwa to Zorinpui on the Mizoram border by road (about 110 km); (4) Zorinpui to Lawngtlai and on to Aizawl, Mizoram, via NH-502A. The Ministry of External Affairs funds it, and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (through IPGL) executes the port and waterway parts. It is a key element of the Act East Policy. Elimination: Nepal, Bhutan and Afghanistan have no link with the Kaladan river or Sittwe port. Afghanistan is tied to Chabahar and INSTC, Nepal and Bhutan to land and rail links, so only Myanmar fits.
explanations: Incorrect: Nepal is linked to India by roads, rail and the Raxaul-Kathmandu pipeline and rail plans. It has no connection with the Kaladan river or Sittwe.
Correct: the project connects Kolkata with Sittwe in Myanmar, and then Mizoram via the Kaladan river and road.
Incorrect: Bhutan's connectivity with India runs through West Bengal and Assam, with hydropower and road projects. It has no link to Kaladan.
Incorrect: Afghanistan is connected through the Chabahar port in Iran and the International North-South Transport Corridor, not Kaladan.
keyfact: Kaladan Multi-Modal Project = India (Kolkata) to Myanmar (Sittwe port, Kaladan river, Paletwa) to Mizoram.
option_notes: Nepal is a landlocked Himalayan country that shares a long open border with India (about 1,751 km) under the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship. Connectivity includes the Raxaul-Kathmandu rail line, the Motihari-Amlekhgunj petroleum pipeline (South Asia's first cross-border pipeline), and Integrated Check Posts such as Birgunj and Biratnagar. Nepal is a member of BIMSTEC and SAARC.

Myanmar shares a roughly 1,643 km border with the Indian states of Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram. It is India's gateway to ASEAN under the Act East Policy. Projects include the Kaladan project, the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway (Moreh-Mae Sot), and the Sittwe port. Myanmar is a member of BIMSTEC and the Mekong-Ganga Cooperation.

Bhutan is a landlocked Himalayan kingdom that shares a border of about 699 km with India. The 2007 India-Bhutan Friendship Treaty replaced the 1949 treaty. India supports Bhutan's hydropower projects such as Chukha, Tala, Punatsangchhu and Mangdechhu. The two countries have a rail link plan (Kokrajhar-Gelephu), and Bhutan is in SAARC and BIMSTEC.

Afghanistan is a landlocked country with no common land border with India, though India claims territory touching it in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. India built the Zaranj-Delaram highway, the Salma Dam (Afghan-India Friendship Dam), and the Afghan Parliament building. It uses the Chabahar port in Iran as a trade route and is a member of SAARC.
related: Kaladan project: Kolkata-Sittwe-Paletwa-Zorinpui (Mizoram).
The Kaladan river flows through Myanmar's Chin and Rakhine states and enters the sea at Sittwe.
Sittwe port in Rakhine State is operated by India Ports Global Ltd.
The Trilateral Highway links Moreh (Manipur) to Mae Sot (Thailand).
Act East Policy was launched in 2014, replacing the Look East Policy of 1991.
Chabahar port (Iran) gives India access to Afghanistan and Central Asia.
The Siliguri Corridor (Chicken's Neck) is about 20-22 km wide at its narrowest.
BIMSTEC has seven members, including Myanmar and Thailand.
summary: The correct answer is (b) Myanmar. The Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project links Kolkata (India) port to Sittwe port in Myanmar by sea, then via the Kaladan river to Paletwa, and then by road to Mizoram in India's Northeast.
topic_notes: Connectivity projects are a recurring UPSC theme. The Kaladan project (agreement 2008, India-Myanmar) was meant to connect Kolkata, Sittwe, Paletwa and Mizoram, and the Sittwe port was operationalised in 2017 and is run by India Ports Global Ltd. The Paletwa-Zorinpui road section has been delayed by security issues in Rakhine and Chin states. The India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway (about 1,360 km) runs Moreh (Manipur) to Mae Sot (Thailand), and its extension to Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam is proposed. The Act East Policy (2014) replaced the Look East Policy (1991). Other regional connectivity items: BBIN Motor Vehicles Agreement (Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, 2015), where Bhutan did not ratify it; Chabahar port in Iran (India Ports Global); International North-South Transport Corridor (India, Iran, Russia, 2000) linking Mumbai to St Petersburg; and the Agartala-Akhaura rail link with Bangladesh. The Siliguri Corridor, also called the Chicken's Neck, is only about 20-22 km wide at its narrowest and connects the Northeast with the rest of India. BIMSTEC has seven members: India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand. The Mekong-Ganga Cooperation (2000) includes India, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam. Possible future questions include the states touched by the Kaladan route, the river it uses, the ministries involved, and comparisons with the Trilateral Highway and Chabahar.

question: What is the maximum amount of gratuity payable to the employees under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 ?
subject: Social Security
detail: Gratuity is a lump-sum retirement and terminal benefit under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, which came into force on 16 September 1972. It applies to establishments such as factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and establishments employing 10 or more persons. Under Section 4, gratuity is payable on superannuation, retirement, resignation, death or disablement due to accident or disease, after at least 5 years of continuous service. The 5-year condition is relaxed in cases of death or disablement. The formula is 15 days' wages for each completed year of service (or part exceeding 6 months), computed as last drawn wages x 15/26 x years of service. The ceiling was Rs 3.5 lakh (1994), Rs 10 lakh (2010) and Rs 20 lakh (Amendment Act 2018, notified 29 March 2018). Elimination logic: Rs 10 lakh is the old 2010 limit and a common trap, while Rs 5 lakh and Rs 15 lakh were never statutory ceilings. Hence only (d) is correct. Note that the Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes this Act, but the formula and ceiling concept continue.
explanations: Incorrect: Rs 5 lakh was never the statutory maximum; the ceiling was Rs 3.5 lakh before 2010.
Incorrect: Rs 10 lakh was the ceiling from 2010 until the 2018 amendment and is no longer valid.
Incorrect: Rs 15 lakh has never been a statutory ceiling under the Act.
Correct: the 2018 amendment raised the maximum gratuity to Rs 20 lakh, in line with the official answer.
keyfact: Maximum gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 is Rs 20 lakh (since 29 March 2018); earlier Rs 10 lakh.
option_notes: Rs 5,00,000: not a ceiling ever fixed under the Act. Ceilings were Rs 1,000 (1972), Rs 30,000 (1980), Rs 50,000 (1987), Rs 1 lakh (1994), Rs 3.5 lakh (1997), Rs 10 lakh (2010) and Rs 20 lakh (2018). It is a distractor and should not be confused with these.

Rs 10,00,000: the ceiling introduced by the Payment of Gratuity (Amendment) Act, 2009, effective 24 May 2010. It remained in force until 28 March 2018 and was superseded by the Rs 20 lakh limit. Questions often use it as the outdated option.

Rs 15,00,000: not a statutory gratuity limit under the 1972 Act. It is a distractor lying between the 2010 and 2018 ceilings. Do not confuse it with any figure from the Income-tax exemption limits, which also moved to Rs 20 lakh.

Rs 20,00,000: the present ceiling under Section 4(3), introduced by the Payment of Gratuity (Amendment) Act, 2018 with effect from 29 March 2018. It was also later fixed for tax exemption on gratuity for non-government employees. The Central Government can notify revisions in the ceiling.
related: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972.
The Act applies to establishments with 10 or more employees.
The minimum service for gratuity is 5 years, except in case of death or disablement.
Gratuity formula: last drawn wages x 15/26 x completed years of service.
The 2018 Amendment raised the ceiling to Rs 20 lakh with effect from 29 March 2018.
Gratuity must be paid within 30 days of becoming payable.
Nomination for gratuity is made in Form F.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the Gratuity Act and allows gratuity for fixed-term employees after 1 year.
summary: The answer is (d) Rs 20,00,000. The Payment of Gratuity (Amendment) Act, 2018 raised the ceiling on gratuity under Section 4(3) of the 1972 Act from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 20 lakh, effective 29 March 2018.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 provides for a scheme of compulsory gratuity as a measure of social security for workers in establishments with 10 or more employees. It extends to the whole of India, and an establishment once covered remains covered even if its strength later falls below 10. Eligibility requires 5 years of continuous service, except on death or disablement. Continuous service includes periods of lay-off, strike (not illegal), leave, accident and so on. Gratuity formula: (last drawn wage x 15 x years of service)/26 for employees under the Act, and 15/30 for seasonal establishments (7 days per season). Wages mean basic pay plus dearness allowance. The employer must pay within 30 days of it becoming payable, failing which simple interest is due. The Controlling Authority, appointed by the appropriate Government, decides disputes, and appeals go to the Appellate Authority within 60 days. Nomination is made in Form F. Gratuity can be forfeited wholly or partly for damage or loss caused by wilful act or riotous or violent conduct, or for an offence involving moral turpitude. Employers must obtain insurance for their liability for gratuity from LIC or an approved insurer, unless exempted. The 2018 amendment also empowered the Central Government to notify the ceiling, and a 2018 amendment extended maternity-related provisions in the gratuity context by enabling an increase in the ceiling without legislation. Under the Code on Social Security, 2020, gratuity eligibility for fixed-term employees is proportionately available after 1 year of service. Related areas include EPF Act 1952, ESI Act 1948 and the Maternity Benefit Act 1961.

question: What is the maximum number of hours in a week that an adult worker is allowed to work for ?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Weekly hours of work for adults are regulated mainly by Section 51 of the Factories Act, 1948: no adult worker shall be required or allowed to work in a factory for more than 48 hours in any week. Section 52 gives a weekly holiday (normally Sunday), with compensatory holidays where it is withheld. Section 54 caps daily hours at 9. Section 55 requires a rest interval of at least half an hour after 5 hours of work, and Section 56 fixes the spread-over at 10.5 hours, extendable to 12 with approval. Section 59 requires overtime to be paid at twice the ordinary rate of wages. Section 64 and the rules made under it allow the State Government to set limits on total overtime hours in a quarter. The 48-hour week follows ILO Convention No. 1 (1919), which set 8 hours a day and 48 hours a week. The ILO's later Forty-Hour Week Convention, 1935 (No. 47), was not ratified by India. Elimination logic: 35 and 40 hours are not statutory limits under the Factories Act, and 45 hours is not a standard ceiling in any major Indian labour law. Only 48 matches Section 51. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 also keeps 48 hours per week as the upper limit.
explanations: Incorrect: 35 hours is not the statutory weekly ceiling for adult workers. The Factories Act allows up to 48 hours.
Incorrect: 40 hours is the ILO's 1935 Convention No. 47 standard, which India has not ratified, and it is not the Indian legal maximum.
Incorrect: 45 hours does not correspond to any limit in Section 51 of the Factories Act or the OSH Code.
Correct: Section 51 of the Factories Act, 1948 limits adult workers to 48 hours per week, and the OSH Code, 2020 retains this limit.
keyfact: Adult workers: maximum 48 hours a week (Section 51, Factories Act, 1948), 9 hours a day, double-rate overtime.
option_notes: 35 hours: this is not a statutory figure for adult work in India. Some countries, such as France, have a 35-hour statutory working week, and it is sometimes mentioned as a benchmark. In India, no central labour law fixes 35 hours as the normal weekly limit for adults.

40 hours: this is the ILO Forty-Hour Week Convention, 1935 (No. 47) standard, a reduction from the 48-hour norm. India has not ratified it. Many countries and Indian government offices use a 5-day, roughly 40-hour week as practice, but it is not the Factories Act limit.

45 hours: this is not an established limit in Indian labour law. The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 sets 48 hours for adults, and the Mines Act, 1952 sets 48 hours per week above ground. Some private policies use 45 hours, but it has no statutory basis here.

48 hours: this is the maximum weekly hours for adult workers under Section 51 of the Factories Act, 1948. It is derived from ILO Convention No. 1 (1919), which set 8 hours a day and 48 a week. It is retained in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.
related: Section 51 of the Factories Act, 1948: weekly hours limit of 48.
Section 54: daily hours limit of 9 for adults.
Section 59: overtime wages at twice the ordinary rate.
Section 55: rest interval of at least half an hour after 5 hours.
Section 56: spread-over limited to 10.5 hours.
ILO Convention No. 1 (1919) set the 48-hour week; No. 47 (1935) set 40 hours.
Young persons (children 14 to 15) may work at most 4.5 hours a day under the Factories Act.
The OSH Code, 2020 retains 48 hours a week and 8 hours normal daily limit.
summary: The answer is (d) 48 hours. Under the Factories Act, 1948 (Section 51), an adult worker cannot be required or allowed to work in a factory for more than 48 hours in any week. The same ceiling is used in the Shops and Establishments Acts and the ILO's Hours of Work (Industry) Convention, 1919 (No. 1).
topic_notes: The Factories Act, 1948 is the main law for working conditions in factories, applying to premises with 10 or more workers using power or 20 or more without power. Chapter VI deals with working hours of adults. Section 51 sets weekly hours at 48. Section 52 gives a weekly holiday. Section 53 covers compensatory holidays. Section 54 sets daily hours at 9. Section 55 requires intervals of rest. Section 56 sets the spread-over at 10.5 hours. Section 57 prohibits overlapping shifts. Section 59 requires double-rate overtime wages. Section 61 requires a notice of periods of work. Section 66 restricts the employment of women, generally permitting work between 6 am and 7 pm unless conditions are met. Section 67 prohibits employment of children below 14. Adolescents (15 to 18) need a fitness certificate. Young persons may work only 4.5 hours a day under Section 71. Related laws: the Mines Act, 1952 allows 48 hours a week above ground and 8 hours a day below ground. The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 allows 48 hours for adults. The Motor Transport Workers Act, 1961 allows 48 hours a week and 8 hours a day. The Beedi and Cigar Workers Act, 1966 allows 9 hours a day and 48 hours a week. The four labour codes, including the OSH Code 2020, subsume many of these laws. The ILO's 1919 Convention No. 1 introduced the 8-hour day and 48-hour week for industry. Convention No. 30 (1930) extended it to commerce and offices.

question: What is the maximum period in which the appropriate government shall review and revise the minimum rates of wages under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 ?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 3 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 deals with fixation and revision of minimum rates of wages. Section 3(1)(a) requires the appropriate government to fix minimum rates of wages for scheduled employments. Section 3(1)(b) requires it to review at intervals not exceeding five years the minimum rates so fixed and revise them if necessary. So five years is the statutory maximum, and revision can happen earlier. The 'appropriate government' is the Central Government for scheduled employments under its authority (railways, mines, oil fields, major ports, central corporations) and the State Government for all other scheduled employments. Minimum wages can be fixed by the committee method or the notification method (Section 5), with advisory committees and an Advisory Board (Sections 7-9). Elimination: 2, 3 and 4 years are not the statutory period. Students often confuse the five-year review with the Code on Wages, 2019, which subsumes the Act and also provides for review and revision at intervals not exceeding five years (Section 8). The Code introduces a national floor wage, which the Central Government fixes, and states cannot set minimum wages below it.
explanations: Incorrect: 2 years is not the statutory review period. Section 3(1)(b) sets a maximum of five years.
Incorrect: 3 years is not the period prescribed in the Act. It is a distractor.
Incorrect: 4 years has no basis in the Act. The ceiling is five years.
Correct: Section 3(1)(b) says review at intervals not exceeding five years, and revision if necessary.
keyfact: Minimum wages must be reviewed and revised, if necessary, at intervals not exceeding 5 years (Section 3(1)(b), Minimum Wages Act, 1948).
option_notes: 2 years: no provision of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 uses this interval for wage review. Two years is a distractor. Under the Payment of Bonus Act and other laws, different periods apply to other matters. The Act's review interval is up to five years, though the government may revise earlier if needed.

3 years: this is not the review interval under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. Three years appears in other contexts, such as the term of the Central Advisory Board in some labour statutes or wage board tenures, but here it is a distractor. The statutory ceiling for wage review is five years.

4 years: the Act does not prescribe a four-year cycle. Some Pay Commission or wage-settlement cycles are longer or shorter, but minimum wage review under Section 3(1)(b) is at most five years. Treat this as a distractor with no statutory basis.

5 years: the maximum interval for reviewing and revising minimum wages under Section 3(1)(b) of the 1948 Act. The Code on Wages, 2019 (Section 8) retains the five-year ceiling. The Act applies to scheduled employments, and the appropriate government is either the Centre or the State depending on the employment.
related: Section 3(1)(b) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948: review at intervals not exceeding five years.
Minimum Wages Act, 1948 derives from Article 43 (living wage) of the DPSPs.
Section 5 provides the committee method and the notification method for fixing wages.
Section 14 provides for overtime at twice the ordinary rate.
Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes four laws, including the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.
Code on Wages, 2019 Section 8 retains the five-year review ceiling and sets a floor wage.
15th Indian Labour Conference (1957) set the need-based minimum wage norms.
Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) upheld the Act's constitutionality.
summary: The answer is (d) 5 years. Section 3(1)(b) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 requires the appropriate government to review and, if necessary, revise minimum wages at intervals not exceeding five years.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 is a core labour law enacted under the Directive Principles (Article 43, living wage) and the concurrent list. It empowers governments to fix minimum wages for employments listed in its Schedule. Section 3 covers fixing and revising wages. Section 4 states what minimum wages may consist of: a basic rate and cost-of-living allowance, or an all-inclusive rate. Section 5 gives two procedures: the committee method and the notification (public notice) method. Sections 7-9 provide for advisory committees, sub-committees and the Central Advisory Board, which coordinates advice. Section 12 requires payment of at least the minimum rate. Section 13 covers hours of work, weekly rest day and overtime (Section 14 gives overtime at double rate). Section 22 provides penalties. Sections 18-19 cover records and inspectors. Claims are heard under Section 20 by the authority appointed by the government. The Act was upheld in Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) as a reasonable restriction on the freedom to carry on a trade. In Workmen v. Reptakos Brett (1991), the Supreme Court discussed the components of need-based minimum wages, which stem from the 15th Indian Labour Conference (1957) norms. The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act, the Payment of Wages Act, the Payment of Bonus Act and the Equal Remuneration Act. It also introduces a floor wage and extends minimum wages to all employees. It is key for exam purposes. The National Floor Level Minimum Wage was introduced administratively in 1996.

question: Under Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana, what is the maximum amount that can be deposited during a financial year ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana was launched on 22 January 2015 at Panipat, Haryana, under the Beti Bachao Beti Padhao campaign. It is a small savings scheme for the girl child. An account can be opened in the name of a girl below 10 years of age by her natural or legal guardian, at a post office or an authorised bank branch. Only one account is allowed per girl, and a family can open accounts for at most two girls (a third is allowed only in cases of twins or triplets). The minimum annual deposit is Rs 250 and the maximum is Rs 1.5 lakh per financial year, in multiples of Rs 50. Deposits must be made for 15 years from the account opening date. The account matures 21 years after opening. Partial withdrawal of up to 50% of the balance is allowed after the girl turns 18 or passes Class 10, for higher education or marriage. The interest rate is set quarterly by the Government (about 8.2% in 2023-24 and 8.2% in early 2024-25) and compounded annually. The scheme has EEE tax status under Section 80C. The Rs 1.5 lakh cap matches the 80C limit, so options (b) and (c) are wrong, and Rs 2.5 lakh is not any SSY limit.
explanations: Correct: the maximum deposit allowed in a financial year is Rs 1.5 lakh, the same as the Section 80C ceiling.
Incorrect: Rs 1 lakh was never the SSY ceiling. It is not the maximum.
Incorrect: Rs 2 lakh is above the permitted limit. Deposits beyond Rs 1.5 lakh are not accepted.
Incorrect: Rs 2.5 lakh is not an SSY limit. It resembles the old basic income tax exemption limit.
keyfact: SSY: girl below 10, Rs 250 minimum to Rs 1.5 lakh maximum per year, 15 years of deposits, maturity at 21 years.
option_notes: Rs 1.5 lakh: the annual maximum for SSY, and also the overall Section 80C deduction ceiling. Deposits can be made in any number of instalments, in multiples of Rs 50, within the financial year. The minimum is Rs 250. If the minimum is not deposited, the account becomes defaulted and can be revived with a Rs 50 penalty per year of default.

Rs 1 lakh: not an SSY limit. It is sometimes confused with older limits on other small savings schemes. The PPF limit was Rs 70,000 until 2014 and then Rs 1.5 lakh. The SSY maximum has been Rs 1.5 lakh since the scheme began (it was Rs 1.5 lakh from its 2014 announcement).

Rs 2 lakh: not an SSY limit. No mainstream small savings scheme (PPF, SSY, NSC) has a Rs 2 lakh annual deposit cap. Rs 2 lakh was once the home loan interest deduction ceiling under Section 24(b) for a self-occupied house.
Rs 2.5 lakh: not an SSY limit. Rs 2.5 lakh was the basic income tax exemption limit for individuals (below 60 years) for many years until 2019-20. It is a distractor for SSY.
related: SSY was launched on 22 January 2015 at Panipat, Haryana.
Girl must be below 10 years of age to open an SSY account.
Minimum SSY deposit is Rs 250 per year; maximum is Rs 1.5 lakh.
SSY account matures 21 years after opening; deposits are made for 15 years.
Partial withdrawal of up to 50% is allowed after the girl turns 18 or passes Class 10.
SSY has EEE tax status under Section 80C (old regime).
Mahila Samman Savings Certificate allows up to Rs 2 lakh for 2 years at 7.5%.
PPF has a 15-year lock-in and a Rs 1.5 lakh annual limit.
summary: The answer is (a) Rs 1.5 lakh. Under the Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY), the maximum deposit in a financial year is Rs 1,50,000, and the minimum is Rs 250 (Rs 1,000 before 2018).
topic_notes: Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY) was launched on 22 January 2015 by PM Narendra Modi at Panipat as part of Beti Bachao Beti Padhao. Eligibility: a girl child below 10 years, with one account per girl and at most two accounts per family (exception for twins/triplets). Accounts can be opened at India Post offices and authorised commercial banks. Deposits: minimum Rs 250 a year (reduced from Rs 1,000 in 2018), maximum Rs 1.5 lakh a year. Deposits are made for 15 years, and the account matures after 21 years from opening, or on the girl's marriage after she turns 18. Partial withdrawal of up to 50% of the balance at the end of the preceding financial year is allowed after age 18 or Class 10 for education. Interest: notified quarterly by the Ministry of Finance, compounded annually, and higher than PPF. Tax: EEE (exempt on deposit under 80C, on interest and on maturity) under the old regime. Premature closure is allowed on the death of the account holder, on extreme medical grounds, or if the guardian dies. The account can be transferred anywhere in India. From 2019, interest is paid on the account until maturity, and in 2023 rules were clarified that only natural or legal guardians can operate accounts for girls. Related schemes: PPF (15-year tenure, Rs 500 minimum, Rs 1.5 lakh maximum), NSC (5-year), Senior Citizens Savings Scheme (Rs 30 lakh limit from 2023), and the Mahila Samman Savings Certificate (Rs 2 lakh, 2 years, 7.5%).

ocr: What is the minimum and maximum age at | 109. which a subscriber can join the Atal Pension Yojana ? (a) 21 years and 58 years respectively (b) 18 years and 40 years respectively C3 ame) pends and 50 years respectively (d) 21 years and 60 years respectively
subject: Social Security
detail: Atal Pension Yojana was announced in the Union Budget 2015-16 and launched on 9 May 2015 from Kolkata. It is administered by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) through the National Pension System (NPS) architecture. It is aimed mainly at workers in the unorganised sector and replaced the Swavalamban Scheme. Entry age is 18-40 years. Contributions must continue until age 60, so the minimum contribution period is 20 years for a person joining at 40. The subscriber receives a guaranteed minimum monthly pension of Rs 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 or 5,000 from age 60, depending on the contribution. The contribution rises the later a person joins. The subscriber needs a savings bank or post office account, and contributions are auto-debited. After the subscriber's death the spouse receives the same pension, and the nominee receives the accumulated corpus after both have died. Since October 2022, income-tax payers are not eligible to join. Elimination: 21 years is not the entry age, so (a) and (d) are wrong. The upper limit is 40, not 50, so (c) is wrong. Only (b) matches the scheme.
explanations: Incorrect: the minimum entry age is 18, not 21, and 58 is not the upper limit. 58 is not an APY age at all.
Correct: APY entry age is 18 to 40 years, which is the official UPSC answer.
Incorrect: 18 is the right minimum but the maximum entry age is 40, not 50.
Incorrect: 21 is not the minimum entry age. 60 is the age when the pension starts, not the last age at which one can join.
keyfact: Atal Pension Yojana: entry age 18-40, pension from age 60 (Rs 1,000-5,000/month), run by PFRDA, launched 9 May 2015.
option_notes: 21 and 58 years: this does not correspond to APY. 58 was the traditional superannuation or pension age under some schemes, such as the old EPS pension age, which is 58 for the regular pension. EPS-95 gives a monthly pension from age 58. This option mixes up that scheme with APY.

18 and 40 years: this is the APY eligibility range. The scheme was launched on 9 May 2015 and is run by PFRDA. It is meant for unorganised sector workers, offers guaranteed pensions of Rs 1,000 to 5,000 a month from age 60, and the government co-contributed 50% (up to Rs 1,000 a year) for eligible subscribers who joined before 31 March 2016 and were not covered by a statutory social security scheme.

18 and 50 years: the lower limit is right, but 50 is not the upper limit for APY. The NPS general entry age is 18-70 years (raised from 65 in 2022). The option may confuse APY with NPS or with other social security schemes.

21 and 60 years: 21 is not the APY minimum and 60 is the vesting age for APY pension. PM Shram Yogi Maan-dhan has an entry range of 18-40 and also pays a pension at 60, while PM Kisan Maan-dhan has a similar entry range. Some state employee schemes use 21 as a minimum age.
related: APY was launched on 9 May 2015 at Kolkata.
The regulator is PFRDA, which was given statutory status by the PFRDA Act 2013.
APY replaced the Swavalamban Scheme.
The guaranteed pension amounts under APY range from Rs 1,000 to Rs 5,000 per month.
The pension starts at age 60, so the minimum contribution period is 20 years.
Income-tax payers have been ineligible to join since 1 October 2022.
On the subscriber's death the spouse continues to receive the pension.
PM Shram Yogi Maan-dhan (2019) gives Rs 3,000 a month at age 60, with entry at 18-40.
summary: The answer is (b): 18 years and 40 years. Atal Pension Yojana (APY) is open to Indian citizens aged 18 to 40, so a subscriber must join within that window and then contribute until age 60 to receive the guaranteed pension.
topic_notes: Atal Pension Yojana is a government-backed pension scheme for citizens, especially unorganised sector workers. It was announced in Budget 2015-16, launched on 9 May 2015 and is administered by PFRDA under the NPS framework, with banks and post offices as points of presence. It replaced the Swavalamban Scheme. Eligibility: Indian citizen aged 18-40 with a savings bank or post office account, Aadhaar and mobile number (these are preferred, not mandatory in every case). Since 1 October 2022, income-tax payers cannot join. Benefits: a guaranteed fixed minimum monthly pension of Rs 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 or 5,000 from age 60, based on contribution and joining age. Contributions are monthly, quarterly or half-yearly, through auto-debit. A late payment attracts a penalty, from Rs 1 per Rs 100 per month, and accounts can be frozen and later closed for prolonged non-payment. Death benefit: the spouse gets the same pension after the subscriber's death; after both die, the nominee gets the corpus accumulated up to age 60. Exit before 60 is allowed only in exceptional cases such as death or terminal illness. The government co-contribution was available for 5 years to those who joined between 1 June 2015 and 31 December 2015, and was later extended to 31 March 2016. Related schemes: PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana, PM Suraksha Bima Yojana and PM Shram Yogi Maan-dhan, PM Kisan Maan-dhan, and NPS (regulated by PFRDA, set up under the PFRDA Act 2013). Likely exam angles are the launch date, the regulator, pension slabs, contribution period, the replaced scheme and the tax-payer exclusion.

question: Which one of the following denotes Gross Profit ? 110
options: Cost of goods sold + Opening stock
Sales less Cost of goods sold
Net profit less Expenses of the period
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Gross profit is the excess of net sales (sales minus sales returns) over the cost of goods sold (COGS). It is the balance of the Trading Account, which is the first part of the final accounts. COGS = Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses (carriage inwards, wages, freight, etc.) - Closing stock. Gross Profit = Net Sales - COGS. If COGS exceeds sales, the balance is a gross loss. Gross profit is then carried to the Profit and Loss Account, where indirect expenses (administrative, selling and distribution, finance costs) are deducted and indirect incomes added to arrive at Net Profit. The Gross Profit Ratio = (Gross Profit / Net Sales) x 100. Elimination: option (a) adds opening stock to COGS, which does not correspond to any profit measure. Option (c) ignores opening and closing stock and direct expenses, so it is incorrect unless there is no stock. Option (d) reverses the logic: net profit PLUS indirect expenses (less indirect incomes) gives gross profit, not net profit LESS expenses. Hence only (b) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: Adding opening stock to cost of goods sold gives no recognised profit measure. Opening stock is a component of the COGS calculation, not something added to it.
Correct: Gross profit = Net sales - Cost of goods sold. This is the standard definition and the balancing figure of the Trading Account.

Incorrect: Sales less purchases ignores opening and closing stock and direct expenses, so it does not give the true margin on goods sold. It would be right only if there were no stock changes and no direct expenses.
Incorrect: Subtracting expenses from net profit would give a figure lower than net profit. Gross profit is higher than net profit; it equals net profit plus indirect expenses minus indirect incomes.
keyfact: Gross Profit = Net Sales - Cost of Goods Sold (COGS = Opening stock + Purchases + Direct expenses - Closing stock).
option_notes: Cost of goods sold + opening stock is not a standard accounting term. COGS itself is Opening stock + Purchases + Direct expenses - Closing stock. It is a cost figure shown on the debit side of the Trading Account, used to compute gross profit, not a profit figure.

Sales less COGS is gross profit, the trading margin. Net sales are sales less returns. Gross profit measures production or purchase efficiency before indirect expenses. The Gross Profit Ratio is its percentage of net sales. A negative result is a gross loss.

Sales less purchases is a crude measure, sometimes called the trading margin on purchases, and ignores stock adjustments. Purchases means goods bought for resale, net of purchase returns. Purchases are only one component of COGS, along with opening and closing stock and direct expenses.

Net profit less expenses is not a standard measure. Net profit is already stated after deducting all expenses. The correct relationship is Net Profit = Gross Profit + Indirect incomes - Indirect expenses. Operating profit = Gross profit - operating expenses.
related: COGS = Opening stock + Purchases + Direct expenses - Closing stock.
Gross profit is the balancing figure of the Trading Account.
Net Profit = Gross Profit + Indirect incomes - Indirect expenses.
Carriage inwards is a direct expense (debited to Trading Account); carriage outwards is an indirect expense.
Closing stock is valued at cost or NRV, whichever is lower (AS-2).
Gross Profit Ratio = Gross profit / Net sales x 100.
Non-profit organisations prepare an Income and Expenditure Account, not a Trading Account.
Schedule III of the Companies Act 2013 prescribes the format of financial statements.
summary: The answer is (b): Gross Profit = Sales less Cost of Goods Sold. Gross profit is the margin earned on trading activity before deducting indirect operating expenses, so it is found by subtracting the cost of the goods actually sold from net sales revenue.
topic_notes: Final accounts of a trading concern have these components: Trading Account, Profit and Loss Account, and Balance Sheet. The Trading Account shows the result of buying and selling. Debit side: opening stock, purchases (less returns), direct expenses (wages, carriage inwards, freight, import duty, power and fuel, factory expenses). Credit side: sales (less returns) and closing stock. The balancing figure is gross profit (credit balance) or gross loss (debit balance). The Profit and Loss Account starts with gross profit on the credit side, then indirect incomes (interest received, discount received, commission) are added. Indirect expenses are on the debit side: office and administration, selling and distribution, financial expenses, depreciation, bad debts. The balance is net profit or net loss, transferred to the capital account (proprietorship or partnership) or retained earnings (company). Important concepts: matching principle, accrual basis, and the distinction between direct and indirect expenses. Closing stock is valued at the lower of cost or net realisable value (AS-2 / Ind AS 2). Related ratios: Gross Profit Ratio = GP / Net sales x 100; Net Profit Ratio = NP / Net sales x 100; Operating Ratio = (COGS + operating expenses) / Net sales x 100; Stock turnover = COGS / Average stock. Under the Companies Act 2013, Schedule III prescribes the format for the Balance Sheet and the Statement of Profit and Loss. A non-trading concern (club, hospital) prepares an Income and Expenditure Account instead.

question: What is the underlying accounting concept that supports no anticipation of profits but provision for all possible losses ?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Conservatism, also called the principle of prudence, is a basic accounting convention. Its guiding maxim is 'anticipate no profits, but provide for all possible losses.' Revenue and gains are recognised only when realised or reasonably certain, whereas expenses and losses are recognised as soon as they are probable. Practical applications include valuing closing stock at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower, creating provision for doubtful debts, creating provision for discount on debtors, not recognising unrealised appreciation in asset value, and writing down obsolete assets. Under Indian GAAP (AS 1, Disclosure of Accounting Policies), prudence is one of the three major considerations in selecting accounting policies, along with substance over form and materiality. Elimination logic: Matching concerns setting expenses against the revenues of the same period; Materiality concerns disclosing only items significant enough to influence decisions; Consistency requires applying the same accounting policies from period to period. None of these deals with the asymmetric treatment of profits and losses, so only Conservatism fits. Caution: excessive conservatism can create secret reserves and distort true and fair view.
explanations: Wrong. The matching concept requires expenses of a period to be matched against the revenues earned in that period; it does not address the asymmetric treatment of gains and losses. (The OCR'd option text is garbled but refers to matching.)
Wrong. Materiality means only information that could influence users' decisions need be separately disclosed; insignificant items may be ignored or aggregated.
Wrong. Consistency means following the same accounting methods and policies year after year so that results are comparable; it does not deal with anticipating profits or losses.
Correct. Conservatism or prudence says do not anticipate profits but provide for all probable losses, exactly as the question describes. This is the official answer.
keyfact: Conservatism (prudence) = anticipate no profits but provide for all possible losses.
option_notes: Matching concept: costs incurred in earning revenue are charged against that revenue in the same accounting period. It follows from the accrual basis and the periodicity assumption. Examples are adjusting for outstanding and prepaid expenses, accrued income, and depreciation allocation. It underlies the preparation of the profit and loss account and is closely linked to the revenue recognition principle.

Materiality: an item is material if its omission or misstatement could influence the economic decisions of users of financial statements. It is judged by its nature and size. AS 1 lists materiality as a key consideration in policy selection. Immaterial items, such as small stationery stock, may be written off as expenses immediately rather than capitalised.

Consistency: accounting policies and practices once adopted should be applied uniformly from one period to the next, enabling inter-period comparison. A change is permitted only if required by law, by an accounting standard, or if it gives a better presentation, and the effect must be disclosed. Consistency is one of the fundamental assumptions in AS 1, along with going concern and accrual.

Conservatism (prudence): a convention that avoids overstating assets and profits and understating liabilities and losses. Provisions for bad debts, lower of cost or net realisable value for inventory, and non-recognition of unrealised gains are applications. It is one of the three considerations in AS 1 (prudence, substance over form, materiality). Overuse can create hidden reserves and violate the true and fair view.
related: Conservatism maxim: anticipate no profits, provide for all possible losses.
Stock is valued at lower of cost or net realisable value, an application of conservatism.
AS 1 considerations: prudence, substance over form, materiality.
AS 1 fundamental assumptions: going concern, consistency, accrual.
Provision for doubtful debts is created on the basis of prudence.
Matching concept links expenses to the revenues of the same period.
Dual aspect concept underlies the accounting equation and double entry.
summary: The answer is (d) Conservatism. The concept of conservatism (prudence) says an accountant should not anticipate or record profits until they are realised, but should provide for all probable losses and liabilities as soon as they are foreseen.
topic_notes: Accounting concepts and conventions form the theoretical base of financial accounting. Fundamental assumptions under AS 1 (Disclosure of Accounting Policies) are going concern, consistency and accrual; if they are followed, no disclosure is needed, and if not followed, the fact must be disclosed. Major considerations in selecting policies are prudence, substance over form and materiality. Key concepts: business entity (the business is separate from its owner), money measurement, going concern (business will continue), cost concept (assets recorded at historical cost), dual aspect (Assets = Capital + Liabilities, the basis of double entry), accounting period (usually 12 months), realisation (revenue recognised when earned, e.g. on sale or delivery), matching, accrual, and full disclosure. Conventions include consistency, conservatism, materiality and full disclosure. Conservatism is applied in valuing stock at lower of cost and NRV, creating provisions for doubtful debts and discount, and treating contingent liabilities cautiously. Related ideas: the Conceptual Framework of the ICAI, Ind AS converged with IFRS, and the IFRS Conceptual Framework, which now treats prudence as supporting neutrality. UPSC often asks the concept behind a practical example, for example: stock at lower of cost or market is Conservatism; depreciation and outstanding expenses are Matching; same method of depreciation every year is Consistency; ignoring small items is Materiality; separate personal and business transactions is Business Entity; recording assets at purchase price is Cost concept.

question: Which one of the following accounting concepts is applied by an entity, when events such as new competitor entering in the market and rift between production and marketing 112. departments are not disclosed in the books of accounts ?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: The money measurement concept states that accounting records only those transactions and events that can be expressed in terms of money. This is why the books show assets like cash, stock and machinery, but not the skill of employees, managerial efficiency, brand loyalty, team morale, internal conflicts or competitive threats. The limitation is that the financial statements give an incomplete picture of the enterprise, and the changing purchasing power of money is ignored (the value of the rupee changes over time but records stay at historical figures). Elimination logic: Matching concept requires expenses of a period to be set against revenues of the same period, and it deals with timing, not with non-quantifiable events. Revenue Recognition decides when revenue is treated as earned (usually at the time of sale or delivery, or as per Ind AS 115 / AS 9), and it does not deal with qualitative events. The Cost concept says assets are recorded at their acquisition cost, not at market value. None of these explains the non-disclosure of qualitative events. The only concept that excludes non-monetary facts is money measurement, so (b) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: the Matching concept links expenses to the revenues of the same accounting period. It concerns the timing of expenses, not the exclusion of non-monetary events.
Correct: a new competitor and an internal departmental rift cannot be expressed in money, so under the money measurement concept they are not recorded in the books.
Incorrect: Revenue Recognition determines when revenue is considered earned and recorded. It has no bearing on qualitative events like competition or internal disputes.
Incorrect: the Cost concept requires assets to be recorded at their original acquisition cost. It does not explain why non-quantifiable events are omitted.
keyfact: Money Measurement: only events that can be expressed in money are recorded, so qualitative events such as competition or departmental rifts are left out of the books.
option_notes: Matching concept: expenses incurred in an accounting period are matched against the revenues earned in that period to determine profit or loss. It is the basis of accrual accounting and of adjustments such as outstanding and prepaid expenses, depreciation and provisions. It is closely related to the accrual and periodicity concepts. Without matching, profit would be distorted because costs and revenues of different periods would be mixed.

Money Measurement concept: only transactions that can be measured in monetary terms are recorded in the books. Money serves as the common unit for adding up different assets. Its limitations are the exclusion of qualitative factors (human resources, management quality, goodwill not purchased, competition), and it ignores the changing value of money over time. It is a fundamental accounting assumption in basic accounting theory.

Revenue Recognition (Realisation) concept: revenue is recognised when it is earned, normally when goods are sold or services rendered and the right to receive payment is established, not when cash is received. It is covered by AS 9 and Ind AS 115 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers), which follows a five-step model. Advance receipts are not revenue until the goods or services are delivered.

Cost concept (historical cost): assets are recorded at the price actually paid to acquire them, and this becomes the basis for later accounting, including depreciation. Market value changes are generally ignored. It gives objectivity and verifiability, but it may not show the current worth of assets during inflation. It is related to the going concern concept, since assets are held for use and not for sale.
related: Money measurement excludes qualitative factors such as employee skill, management quality and competition from the books.
Business Entity concept: the owner's drawings are treated as a reduction of capital, not as a business expense.
Going Concern, Consistency and Accrual are the three fundamental accounting assumptions under AS 1.
Conservatism: provide for all probable losses but do not anticipate profits.
Revenue recognition is covered by Ind AS 115; AS 9 is the older standard.
Historical cost concept: assets are recorded at acquisition cost, not market value.
Dual Aspect concept: Assets = Capital + Liabilities, the basis of double-entry bookkeeping.
Materiality convention: insignificant items may be ignored in financial statements.
summary: The answer is (b) Money Measurement. Only transactions and events that can be expressed in monetary terms are recorded in the books of accounts. Qualitative events such as a new competitor entering the market or a rift between the production and marketing departments cannot be quantified in money, so they are not disclosed.
topic_notes: Accounting concepts and conventions are the foundation of financial accounting. Accounting concepts (or assumptions) include: Business Entity (the business is separate from its owner), Money Measurement, Going Concern, Accounting Period (periodicity), Cost (historical cost), Dual Aspect (Assets = Liabilities + Capital), Revenue Recognition (realisation), Matching, and Accrual. AS 1 (Disclosure of Accounting Policies) recognises three fundamental accounting assumptions: Going Concern, Consistency and Accrual. Accounting conventions include Consistency, Full Disclosure, Materiality and Conservatism (prudence: anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses). Key points about each: Business Entity explains why the owner's drawings reduce capital. Going Concern assumes the business will continue, so fixed assets are depreciated and not valued at liquidation value. The Dual Aspect concept underlies double-entry bookkeeping. The Accounting Period is usually 12 months, and in India the financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March. Materiality means that insignificant items may be ignored. Full Disclosure requires all material information to be disclosed in the financial statements. Conservatism leads to valuing stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Ind AS are converged with IFRS and apply to companies above specified net-worth thresholds, while the ICAI issues Accounting Standards. UPSC often frames questions as scenarios (for example, rent due but unpaid points to accrual or matching; goodwill not recorded points to money measurement or cost; stock valued at the lower of cost or market points to conservatism), so students should link each concept to a typical example.

question: Which one of the following concerns prepares Receipts and Payments Account ?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: A Receipts and Payments Account is the real account of a non-trading (not-for-profit) entity. It is a summary of the cash book. It starts with opening cash and bank balances and records all actual receipts on the debit side and all actual payments on the credit side, ending with closing balances. Its key features are: (1) it records cash and bank items only, with no accruals or outstanding items; (2) it includes both capital and revenue items; (3) it is not restricted to the current period, so it also records receipts and payments relating to past or future periods; (4) it does not show non-cash items such as depreciation or bad debts. Non-trading concerns also prepare an Income and Expenditure Account, which is a nominal account and the counterpart of the Profit & Loss Account, together with a Balance Sheet. Trading, manufacturing and company entities follow the accrual (mercantile) system and prepare the Trading Account, Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet. Companies must comply with Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013. Elimination: (a), (c) and (d) are all profit-oriented entities, so only (b) fits.
explanations: Incorrect: trading concerns prepare a Trading Account, a Profit & Loss Account and a Balance Sheet on the accrual basis, not a Receipts and Payments Account.
Correct: non-trading concerns such as clubs, societies, charitable trusts and hospitals prepare the Receipts and Payments Account as a summary of their cash book.
Incorrect: manufacturing concerns prepare Manufacturing, Trading and Profit & Loss Accounts to compute the cost of production and profit.
Incorrect: companies under the Companies Act, 2013 must prepare a Balance Sheet and a Statement of Profit & Loss in Schedule III format, plus a cash flow statement where applicable.
keyfact: Receipts and Payments Account = summarised cash book of non-trading (not-for-profit) concerns; it is a real account on a cash basis.
option_notes: Trading concerns buy and sell goods to earn profit. They keep books on the mercantile system and prepare a Trading Account for gross profit, a Profit & Loss Account for net profit, and a Balance Sheet for financial position. Examples are wholesalers and retailers. They do not use a Receipts and Payments Account as a final account.

Non-trading concerns are organisations whose main aim is service, not profit, such as clubs, charitable institutions, hospitals, schools, libraries and trade associations. Their final accounts are the Receipts and Payments Account, the Income and Expenditure Account and the Balance Sheet. Any surplus is called surplus of income over expenditure and is added to the capital fund.

Manufacturing concerns convert raw materials into finished goods. They prepare a Manufacturing Account showing prime cost, factory overheads and cost of goods produced. The Trading Account, Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet follow. They work on the accrual basis and are profit-oriented, so they do not rely on a Receipts and Payments Account.

Companies registered under the Companies Act, 2013 are separate legal entities. They prepare financial statements in the format of Schedule III: Balance Sheet, Statement of Profit and Loss, Cash Flow Statement and notes. These are audited and approved by the board and the members. Section 129 requires a true and fair view. They use accrual accounting and do not prepare a Receipts and Payments Account.
related: Receipts and Payments Account is a real account; Income and Expenditure Account is a nominal account.
Surplus of Income and Expenditure Account is added to the Capital (General) Fund.
Receipts and Payments Account does not record non-cash items such as depreciation.
Life membership fees are usually capitalised.
Capital Fund = Assets − Liabilities in a non-profit organisation.
Specific donations are credited to a specific fund, not to income.
Subscriptions in Income and Expenditure Account = received + outstanding at end − outstanding at start − advance at end + advance at start.
Companies prepare financial statements in Schedule III format under the Companies Act, 2013.
summary: The answer is (b) Non-trading concerns. A Receipts and Payments Account is a summary of the cash and bank transactions of a non-profit organisation such as a club, society, trust, hospital or school. These bodies do not trade for profit, so they do not prepare Trading and Profit & Loss Accounts.
topic_notes:
Accounts of non-profit organisations (NPOs) are a regular UPSC EPFO topic. NPOs such as clubs, societies, trusts, charitable hospitals and educational institutions generally lack a profit motive. Their records are usually a cash book, with final accounts prepared at year end.

Receipts and Payments Account: a summary of the cash book and a real account. Receipts are on the debit side and payments on the credit side. It opens with cash and bank balances and closes with the balance carried forward. It includes capital and revenue items of any period, and it excludes non-cash items such as depreciation, outstanding and prepaid items, and accrued income.

Income and Expenditure Account: a nominal account prepared on the accrual basis. Revenue incomes are on the credit side and revenue expenses on the debit side. Capital items are excluded. The balancing figure is either a surplus or a deficit. The surplus or deficit is transferred to the Capital Fund (the accumulated fund).

Key adjustments: subscriptions are adjusted for arrears and advance amounts. Life membership fees and entrance fees are normally capitalised, though some bodies treat entrance fees as revenue. Legacies and general donations are capitalised, and specific donations go to a specific fund. The sale of old newspapers is an income. Stock of stationery used is calculated as opening stock plus purchases minus closing stock. Sports material is treated similarly. Profit on sale of an asset is an income, and a loss on it is an expense.

Balance Sheet: it shows assets, liabilities and the Capital Fund.

Other angles UPSC may ask: differences between the Receipts and Payments Account and the Income and Expenditure Account, treatment of special funds, the Capital Fund formula (assets minus liabilities), and the basis of accounting (cash versus accrual).

question: Which one of the following statements is correct about Income and _ Expenditure Account ?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Under the traditional (British) classification, accounts are Personal, Real or Nominal. Personal accounts relate to persons (natural, artificial or representative). Real accounts relate to assets and properties. Nominal accounts relate to expenses, losses, incomes and gains. The golden rule for nominal accounts is: debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains. The Income and Expenditure Account is prepared by non-profit organisations such as clubs, societies, trusts, hospitals and educational institutions. It is the nominal-account equivalent of the Profit and Loss Account of a trading concern. It follows the accrual basis, includes only revenue items of the current period, and excludes capital items. It starts with no cash or bank balance, and its balancing figure is a surplus (excess of income over expenditure) or a deficit. Capital items such as life membership fees, legacies, specific donations and the sale of assets go to the Balance Sheet. Elimination logic: it has no physical or tangible asset (so it is not Real), and it does not represent a person or group of persons (so it is neither Personal nor Representative Personal). That leaves Nominal.
explanations: Wrong: a Real Account deals with assets such as land, building or cash. The Income and Expenditure Account deals with revenue items, not assets.
Wrong: a Personal Account relates to individuals, firms, companies or institutions. This account is not in anyone's name.
Correct: it records expenses and incomes of a period, which is exactly what a Nominal Account does. Its surplus or deficit is transferred to the Capital Fund.

Wrong: Representative Personal Accounts are outstanding or prepaid expense and income accounts, such as outstanding salary, that represent a person. The Income and Expenditure Account is not of this type.
keyfact: Income and Expenditure Account = Nominal Account, the NPO's equivalent of the Profit and Loss Account, prepared on the accrual basis.
option_notes: Real Account: relates to assets and properties, both tangible (machinery, cash) and intangible (goodwill, patents). The rule is: debit what comes in, credit what goes out. Its balances are carried forward to the next year and are shown in the Balance Sheet. It is not closed at year end.
