explanations: Correct: SEBI is the statutory regulator of the securities market, and investor protection is its core mandate under the SEBI Act, 1992.
Incorrect: RBI is the central bank. It regulates banks, NBFCs, money markets, government securities and forex, but not the equity and corporate securities market.
Incorrect: IRDAI protects policyholders' interests and regulates the insurance sector, not securities investors.
Incorrect: TRAI regulates telecommunications and tariffs. It has no role in the securities market.
keyfact: SEBI (SEBI Act 1992, Mumbai) regulates the securities market and protects investors; the current ratio is current assets to current liabilities.
option_notes: SEBI: Securities and Exchange Board of India, established in 1988 and given statutory powers by the SEBI Act, 1992. Headquartered in Mumbai, with regional offices in Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Ahmedabad. It is headed by a Chairman and has board members from the Finance Ministry, the RBI and other nominated members. It has quasi-legislative, quasi-judicial and executive powers. Appeals against its orders go to the SAT.

RBI: Reserve Bank of India, established on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, and nationalised on 1 January 1949. Headquartered in Mumbai. It is the central bank, issues currency notes (other than one-rupee notes and coins), conducts monetary policy, regulates banks and NBFCs, manages forex under FEMA, and acts as banker to the government.

IRDAI: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, a statutory body under the IRDA Act, 1999. Headquartered in Hyderabad (earlier Delhi). It regulates and develops the insurance and reinsurance industry, licenses insurers and intermediaries, and protects policyholders' interests. Its predecessor was the Insurance Act, 1938 regime under the Controller of Insurance.

TRAI: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India, established in 1997 under the TRAI Act. Headquartered in New Delhi. It regulates telecom services, tariffs and interconnection, and has also covered broadcasting and cable services. Disputes go to TDSAT, set up in 2000 by an amendment to the TRAI Act. Its recommendations are largely advisory in licensing matters.

summary: The answer is (a) SEBI. The Securities and Exchange Board of India is the statutory regulator of the securities market and its main duty is to protect investor interests, promote market development and regulate market intermediaries.
topic_notes: SEBI is the key regulator of India's capital market. It began in 1988 as a non-statutory body under the Finance Ministry, and was given statutory powers by the SEBI Act, 1992 after the Harshad Mehta scam of 1992. Its objectives are investor protection, orderly development of the market and regulation. It regulates stock exchanges (BSE, NSE), brokers, depositories (NSDL, CDSL), mutual funds, FPIs, merchant bankers, venture capital funds, AIFs, REITs and InvITs, credit rating agencies and others. Its board has a Chairman, members nominated by the Union Finance Ministry and the RBI, and other members appointed by the Centre. SEBI has three kinds of powers: quasi-legislative (making regulations), quasi-judicial (adjudication, penalties, orders) and executive (inspection, investigation, search and seizure). The Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) hears appeals against its orders, and further appeals lie to the Supreme Court. Other relevant laws are the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, the Depositories Act, 1996, and the Companies Act, 2013, together with SEBI's regulations on insider trading, takeovers, and listing obligations (LODR). Other financial regulators: RBI (banking, money market), IRDAI (insurance), PFRDA (pensions, NPS), IFSCA (International Financial Services Centres, GIFT City), and the Forward Markets Commission, which was merged into SEBI in 2015 to regulate commodity derivatives. Investor education is carried out through the Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority (under MCA) and SEBI's SCORES grievance platform. The second question on the page covers the current ratio: current assets divided by current liabilities, with 2:1 as the traditional benchmark.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q63.
ocr: Which Regulatory body protects the interest of investors in the Securities Market ? (a) SEBI (b) RBI (c) IRDAI (dq) TRAI Current ratio is the ratio of : (a) Current assets to Sales (b) Current assets to Debtors (c) Current assets to Current liabilities (d) Current assets to Inventories
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Current ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities. It is the main measure of short-term solvency, or liquidity, and shows how many rupees of current assets are available for every rupee of current liability. The conventional benchmark is 2:1, which is often called the 'rule of thumb' or 'banker's ratio'. A ratio far below 1 signals liquidity stress. A very high ratio can mean idle cash, excess stock or poor use of funds. Current assets include cash, bank balances, marketable securities, debtors (receivables), bills receivable, inventories (stock) and prepaid expenses. Current liabilities include creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, short-term borrowings and the provision for tax. The stricter test is the Quick (Acid-test or Liquid) ratio = (Current assets - Inventories - Prepaid expenses) / Current liabilities, with a benchmark of 1:1. Elimination: Current assets to Sales relates to turnover, not liquidity. Current assets to Debtors is not a standard ratio, since debtors are only a part of current assets. Current assets to Inventories is also not a standard ratio, and the stock-related measure is inventory turnover. Only current assets to current liabilities is the definition of the current ratio.
explanations: Incorrect. Current assets to Sales is not a liquidity ratio. Sales are compared with assets in turnover ratios, such as current asset turnover = Sales / Current assets, and that is the inverse of this option.
Incorrect. Debtors are a component of current assets. Comparing current assets with debtors is not a standard ratio. The debtors turnover ratio uses credit sales divided by average debtors.
Correct. Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities. It measures the ability to pay short-term obligations out of short-term resources.

Incorrect. Inventory is a component of current assets. Excluding it from current assets gives the quick ratio, which divides by current liabilities. Current assets to inventories is not the current ratio.
keyfact: Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities (ideal 2:1); quick ratio excludes inventory.
option_notes: Current assets to Sales: no standard liquidity ratio uses this pairing. The related measure is working capital turnover or current asset turnover, which is Sales / Current assets. It is an activity (efficiency) ratio showing how well current assets generate sales. Activity ratios also include inventory turnover, debtors turnover and creditors turnover. A higher turnover generally means efficient use of assets.

Current assets to Debtors: this is not a recognised ratio. Debtors (accounts receivable) are money owed by customers for credit sales, and they form part of current assets. Related ratios are the debtors turnover ratio = net credit sales / average debtors, and the average collection period = 365 / debtors turnover. Provision for doubtful debts is deducted from debtors to show the net figure.

Current assets to Current liabilities: this is the current ratio, also called the working capital ratio. Current liabilities are obligations due within 12 months or one operating cycle. The ideal ratio is about 2:1. The ratio is a liquidity (short-term solvency) measure. Its limitation is that it includes inventory, which may not be quickly convertible to cash. Window dressing can distort it.

Current assets to Inventories: this is not a standard ratio. Inventories (stock) are the least liquid current asset. They are excluded when the quick ratio is calculated. Inventory turnover = Cost of goods sold / Average inventory. Inventory valuation follows the lower of cost or net realisable value under AS-2 (Ind AS 2).
related: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities; ideal 2:1.
Quick ratio = (Current assets - Inventory - Prepaid expenses) / Current liabilities; ideal 1:1.
Absolute (cash) ratio = (Cash + marketable securities) / Current liabilities; ideal 0.5:1.
Working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities.
Inventory turnover = COGS / Average inventory.
Debt-equity ratio is a solvency ratio; the usual benchmark is 2:1.
Q62 (Securities market investor protection): SEBI, statutory since 1992.
Bank overdraft is a current liability and is excluded from liquid liabilities in some quick ratio treatments.
summary: The image shows two questions. Q63 is the second one: 'Current ratio is the ratio of:'. The official answer is (c), Current assets to Current liabilities. The current ratio is a liquidity ratio that measures whether a firm can meet its short-term obligations from its short-term assets.
topic_notes: Ratio analysis is the interpretation of financial statements through numerical relationships. Ratios are grouped into four families. Liquidity ratios cover the current ratio (ideal 2:1), the quick or acid-test ratio (ideal 1:1) and the absolute or cash ratio (ideal 0.5:1). Solvency or leverage ratios cover debt-equity (Total debt / Shareholders' funds), proprietary ratio, interest coverage (EBIT / Interest) and debt service coverage. Activity or turnover ratios cover inventory turnover, debtors turnover, creditors turnover, fixed asset turnover and working capital turnover. Profitability ratios cover gross profit ratio, net profit ratio, operating ratio, return on investment or capital employed (ROCE), return on equity, earnings per share (EPS), price-earnings ratio and dividend payout. Working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities. Net working capital is the same figure, while gross working capital is the total of current assets. Liquid assets = Current assets - Inventories - Prepaid expenses. Common exam traps are these. Bank overdraft is a current liability. Prepaid expenses are a current asset but are excluded from liquid assets. Bills receivable are a current asset. Proposed dividend is a current liability. Debentures and long-term loans are non-current. Raising the current ratio when it is above 1 by paying a current liability reduces both sides equally, which raises the ratio if it was already above 1. A ratio below 1 means negative working capital. Ratios help in trend, inter-firm and inter-industry comparison. Their limitations include dependence on historical cost, window dressing, and differing accounting policies. Related investor-protection regulator for the first question on the image is SEBI, a statutory body since 1992 under the SEBI Act.

ocr: Which Regulatory body protects the interest of investors in the Securities Market ? (a) SEBI (b) RBI (c) IRDAI (dq) TRAI Current ratio is the ratio of : (a) Current assets to Sales (b) Current assets to Debtors (c) Current assets to Current liabilities (d) Current assets to Inventories
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: SEBI was set up on 12 April 1988 as a non-statutory body and was given statutory powers by the SEBI Act, 1992. Its headquarters are at Bandra Kurla Complex, Mumbai, with regional offices in Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Ahmedabad. The Preamble of the Act states its aim: to protect the interests of investors in securities and to promote the development of, and regulate, the securities market. It performs three kinds of functions. Protective functions include checking insider trading, fraudulent and unfair trade practices, and mis-selling. Developmental functions include investor education, training of intermediaries and promoting self-regulatory organisations. Regulatory functions include registering and regulating stock exchanges, brokers, mutual funds, FPIs, credit rating agencies and depositories, and regulating takeovers. SEBI has quasi-legislative, quasi-judicial and quasi-executive powers. Appeals against its orders go to the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT), then to the Supreme Court. Elimination: RBI regulates banks, money and forex markets, and monetary policy. IRDAI regulates insurance. TRAI regulates telecom and broadcasting tariffs. None of these has investor protection in securities as its core mandate, so only SEBI fits.
explanations: Correct. SEBI is the statutory regulator whose stated mandate is to protect investors in the securities market, to develop that market and to regulate it. The official answer is (a).

Incorrect. RBI is the central bank. It handles monetary policy, bank regulation, currency issue and forex management under the RBI Act, 1934 and the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. It does not regulate the securities market, though it does regulate the money and government securities markets.
Incorrect. IRDAI regulates and develops the insurance sector and protects policyholders, not investors in securities.
Incorrect. TRAI regulates telecommunication and broadcasting services and tariffs. It has no role in the securities market.
keyfact: SEBI (SEBI Act, 1992) is the securities market regulator that protects investors' interests.
option_notes: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) was formed in 1988 and made statutory by the SEBI Act, 1992. It is headquartered in Mumbai. Its board has a Chairman, two members from the Union Finance Ministry, one member from RBI and five other members, of whom three are whole-time. It regulates stock exchanges, brokers, mutual funds, FPIs, depositories and takeovers. Appeals against its orders go to SAT. It is the regulator for the capital market.

RBI (Reserve Bank of India) was established on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934 and was nationalised on 1 January 1949. Its headquarters are in Mumbai. It issues currency (except one-rupee notes and coins), acts as banker to the government and to banks, formulates monetary policy, manages forex under FEMA, and supervises banks and NBFCs. It regulates the money market, not the equity market.

IRDAI (Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India) was set up under the IRDA Act, 1999 and became statutory in April 2000. It is headquartered in Hyderabad. It licenses insurers and intermediaries, protects policyholders' interests and promotes orderly growth of the insurance industry. Its orders can be appealed to SAT. It is relevant to the insurance paper.

TRAI (Telecom Regulatory Authority of India) was established in 1997 under the TRAI Act, 1997 and is based in New Delhi. It regulates telecom and broadcasting tariffs, ensures quality of service and promotes fair competition. Appeals against its decisions go to TDSAT (Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal). It has no role in securities or investor protection.

summary: The answer is (a) SEBI. The Securities and Exchange Board of India is the statutory regulator of the securities market. Its legal mandate under the SEBI Act, 1992 is to protect the interests of investors in securities, to promote the development of the market and to regulate it.
topic_notes: Financial sector regulators in India each have their own domain. RBI regulates banks, NBFCs, payment systems and the money and forex markets. SEBI regulates the securities market (equity, debt, mutual funds, derivatives, commodity derivatives since 2015, when FMC was merged into it). IRDAI regulates insurance. PFRDA regulates pensions, specifically the NPS and APY, under the PFRDA Act, 2013. IFSCA regulates the GIFT City International Financial Services Centre. NABARD regulates rural credit and cooperative banks' refinance. SEBI's key laws are the SEBI Act, 1992, the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and the Depositories Act, 1996. Key regulations include the Insider Trading Regulations (2015), the Takeover Code (2011), the ICDR rules for IPOs and the LODR rules for listed companies. It has had several chairmen: Ajay Tyagi, Madhabi Puri Buch (the first woman chair, March 2022 to February 2025) and Tuhin Kanta Pandey (from March 2025). SEBI can impose penalties, ban entities, impound assets and issue directions. Appeals go to the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT), established in 1995. Investors can raise complaints through the SCORES portal and the Online Dispute Resolution mechanism. The Investor Protection and Education Fund is maintained by SEBI, and the IEPF Authority under the MCA handles unclaimed dividends. The market has a primary segment (IPOs, FPOs, rights issues) and a secondary segment (BSE, established 1875, and NSE, established 1992 and operational from 1994). The depositories are NSDL and CDSL. Related concepts include the Sensex and Nifty indices, T+1 settlement (fully implemented in January 2023), and the Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC), which coordinates the regulators.

ocr: Which Regulatory body protects the interest of investors in the Securities Market ? (a) SEBI (b) RBI (c) IRDAI (dq) TRAI Current ratio is the ratio of : (a) Current assets to Sales (b) Current assets to Debtors (c) Current assets to Current liabilities (d) Current assets to Inventories
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The current ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities. It is the most widely used liquidity (short-term solvency) ratio and shows how many rupees of current assets are available for each rupee of current liabilities. Current assets include cash, bank balances, marketable securities, debtors (receivables), bills receivable, inventories (stock), prepaid expenses and short-term loans and advances. Current liabilities include creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, short-term borrowings, bank overdraft, provision for tax and proposed dividend. The traditional ideal or rule-of-thumb standard is 2:1, which gives a margin of safety to short-term creditors. A very high ratio may signal idle funds or excess inventory, while a low ratio signals liquidity stress. Elimination logic: Sales is an income statement item, so a ratio of current assets to sales is not a liquidity ratio (it resembles a turnover measure). Current assets to debtors has no standard meaning. Current assets to inventories is not a standard ratio either. Only the pairing of current assets with current liabilities measures short-term solvency. The quick (acid-test) ratio excludes inventories and prepaid expenses from current assets, so it is a stricter test.
explanations: Incorrect: Sales is a flow item from the profit and loss account. Comparing it with current assets does not measure liquidity.
Incorrect: Debtors are only one component of current assets. Current assets to debtors is not a recognised ratio. The related ratios are the debtors turnover ratio and the average collection period.
Correct: Current ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities. It measures the ability to pay short-term obligations out of short-term resources.

Incorrect: Inventories are a part of current assets. Current assets to inventories is not the current ratio. Removing inventories from the numerator gives the quick ratio, whose denominator is still current liabilities.
keyfact: Current ratio = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities (norm 2:1); it is a liquidity ratio.
option_notes: Sales is the revenue from the sale of goods or services, shown at the top of the profit and loss statement. Sales is used in turnover and profitability ratios such as the gross profit ratio, net profit ratio, debtors turnover, inventory turnover and working capital turnover. Net sales = gross sales minus returns. Current assets to sales is not a standard ratio, although current assets turnover is sales divided by current assets.

Debtors (sundry debtors or accounts receivable) are amounts owed to the firm by customers for credit sales. They are a current asset and are usually shown net of a provision for doubtful debts. Related ratios are the debtors turnover ratio (net credit sales / average debtors) and the average collection period (365 / turnover). Together with bills receivable, debtors form the trade receivables.

Current assets are cash and other assets expected to be converted to cash or consumed within 12 months or one operating cycle. Current liabilities are obligations due within the same period. Current ratio = CA / CL, with a norm of 2:1. Working capital = CA minus CL. The ratio measures short-term solvency and the margin of safety for creditors. It can be window-dressed, which is a limitation.

Inventories (stock) are raw materials, work in progress and finished goods, valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. They are the least liquid current asset after prepaid expenses. Inventory turnover = cost of goods sold / average inventory. The quick ratio excludes inventory from the numerator. Valuation methods include FIFO and weighted average. LIFO is not permitted under AS 2 or Ind AS 2.
related: Current ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities; ideal norm 2:1.
Quick ratio = (CA minus inventory minus prepaid expenses) / CL; norm 1:1.
Absolute liquid ratio (cash ratio) norm is 0.5:1.
Working capital = Current Assets minus Current Liabilities.
Debt-equity ratio norm is 2:1.
Inventory turnover = COGS / average inventory.
Interest coverage ratio = EBIT / interest.

summary: The image shows two questions; Q65 is the one on the current ratio, which is the ratio of current assets to current liabilities, so the answer is (c). This is the standard liquidity ratio that tests whether a firm can meet its short-term obligations.
topic_notes: Ratio analysis is the study of relationships between items in financial statements. Ratios are grouped into four classes. Liquidity ratios include the current ratio (norm 2:1), the quick or acid-test ratio (norm 1:1, using liquid assets = CA minus inventory minus prepaid expenses) and the absolute liquid or cash ratio (norm 0.5:1). Solvency or leverage ratios include debt-equity (norm 2:1), proprietary ratio, total assets to debt, and interest coverage (EBIT / interest). Activity or turnover ratios include inventory turnover, debtors turnover, creditors turnover, fixed assets turnover and working capital turnover. Profitability ratios include gross profit, net profit, operating ratio, return on investment or capital employed, return on equity and earnings per share. Key formulas: working capital = CA minus CL. Operating cycle = inventory holding period + debtors collection period. Capital employed = fixed assets + working capital. Limitations of ratio analysis: it relies on historical data, ignores price-level changes, is affected by differing accounting policies, and is open to window dressing. A high current ratio is not always good, since it can mean idle cash or overstocking. Trend analysis, common-size statements and comparative statements are related techniques. The first question in the image, on SEBI, is about the securities market regulator, established in 1988 and given statutory status by the SEBI Act, 1992, which protects investors. UPSC may next ask for the formula or norm of the quick ratio, which items count as current assets or current liabilities, or the classification of a given ratio as liquidity, solvency, activity or profitability.

question: Which one among the following is the primary 70. objective of financial management ?
options: Minimization of cost of the firm
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Financial management covers the procurement, allocation and control of funds through three core decisions: investment (capital budgeting), financing (capital structure) and dividend policy. The traditional objective was profit maximization, which has well-known flaws: it is ambiguous (accounting profit vs economic profit), ignores the time value of money, ignores risk and uncertainty, and ignores the quality and timing of benefits. The modern objective, associated with Ezra Solomon, is wealth maximization, also called value maximization. It is measured as the net present value of the firm's future cash flows (discounted at a risk-adjusted rate) and is reflected in the market price per equity share. It addresses time value, risk, and the interests of shareholders as the residual owners. Other goals are secondary or are means to this end. Fixed asset management is part of the investment decision. Risk minimization is a constraint, not the aim, since higher risk can justify higher return. Cost minimization is a part of operational efficiency, and an overly low cost can reduce quality or sales. Hence (a) is correct, and (b), (c) and (d) are eliminated as partial or subordinate goals.
explanations: Correct: wealth maximization is the accepted primary objective of financial management. It considers risk, timing and the size of cash flows, and it is reflected in the share price.
Wrong: managing fixed assets is only part of the investment (capital budgeting) decision and of working capital/asset management. It is a function, not the overriding objective.
Wrong: risk is balanced against return. Minimizing risk alone would mean avoiding profitable projects, so it is a constraint and not the primary goal.
Wrong: cost minimization is an operational goal. Cutting costs without regard to revenue, quality or value may reduce the firm's worth, so it is not the ultimate objective.
keyfact: Primary objective of financial management = maximization of shareholders' wealth (market value of equity shares), not profit maximization.
option_notes: Maximization of shareholders' wealth means increasing the market value of the firm's equity shares, which is the present value of expected future cash flows discounted at a risk-adjusted rate. It is also called value maximization and net present value maximization. It is the normative goal in modern corporate finance, and it is superior to profit maximization because it covers time value and risk.

Management of fixed assets is the capital budgeting or investment function. It involves evaluating long-term projects using NPV, IRR, payback and profitability index, and it is about long-term asset allocation. Fixed assets are land, buildings and machinery. It is one of the key decision areas, along with financing, dividend and working capital management, but it is not the overall objective.

Minimization of risk is a risk management goal. In finance there is a risk-return trade-off: higher expected return usually needs higher risk. Tools include diversification, hedging and insurance. Risk is a constraint in the decision process and a factor in the discount rate, but eliminating it is neither feasible nor the main objective of the firm.

Minimization of cost of the firm refers to cost control and cost of capital. Cost of capital is the minimum return required by investors, and a lower weighted average cost of capital (WACC) raises firm value. Reducing costs is a useful operating strategy, but it is a means to improve profit and value, not the primary objective of financial management.
related: Wealth maximization is measured by the market price of equity shares.
Profit maximization ignores time value of money and risk.
Three major finance decisions: investment, financing and dividend.
Ezra Solomon is associated with the wealth maximization concept.
Agency problem arises from a conflict between managers and shareholders (Jensen and Meckling, 1976).
Capital budgeting deals with long-term investment decisions.
WACC is the weighted average cost of capital of a firm.
Modigliani-Miller propositions deal with capital structure irrelevance.
summary: The answer is (a) Maximization of shareholders' wealth. Modern financial management treats wealth maximization, reflected in the market value of the firm's equity shares, as the primary objective, because it accounts for the size, timing and risk of cash flows.
topic_notes: Financial management is the planning, organizing, directing and controlling of financial activities such as procuring and using funds. Its scope covers three major decisions. The investment decision includes capital budgeting and working capital management. The financing decision concerns capital structure, the debt-equity mix, and the cost of capital. The dividend decision concerns how much profit to pay out and how much to retain. Objectives are classified as profit maximization (the traditional approach) and wealth maximization (the modern approach). Criticisms of profit maximization: it ignores time value, risk, quality of earnings and the timing of benefits, and it is vague about which profit is meant. Wealth maximization is measured by NPV, with share price as the market's indicator. Ezra Solomon is associated with the wealth maximization concept. Agency theory (Jensen and Meckling, 1976) explains conflicts between managers and shareholders, and the agency cost of that conflict. Stakeholder theory is a broader view that also considers employees, creditors, customers and society. Related areas include the time value of money, the CAPM, the Modigliani-Miller theorems on capital structure and dividends, the theories of Gordon and Walter on dividends, and the liquidity-profitability trade-off in working capital. Finance functions are also split into the treasury function (raising funds, cash management, banking) and the controller function (accounting, audit, budgeting, taxes). A related concept is Economic Value Added (EVA), which is net operating profit after tax less a capital charge. Sound financial management requires balancing liquidity, profitability and solvency in the interest of owners.

question: How many constituents are there in BSE Sensex Index ? 71
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The BSE SENSEX (Sensitive Index) was launched on 1 January 1986, with base year 1978-79 and base value 100. It tracks 30 of the largest and most actively traded stocks on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE), the oldest stock exchange in Asia, established in 1875 and headquartered at Dalal Street, Mumbai. Since September 2003 it has been computed on the free-float market capitalisation method (earlier full market capitalisation). The index is reviewed semi-annually (June and December) by the index committee, and constituents must meet criteria such as listing history, trading frequency, and market cap rank. The index is maintained by Asia Index Pvt Ltd (a BSE and S&P Dow Jones Indices joint venture), now branded BSE SENSEX. Elimination logic: the NSE Nifty 50 has 50 stocks, which makes (d) the trap for the rival index; 35 and 40 are not the constituent count of any major headline Indian index. BSE 100 has 100, BSE 500 has 500. Hence 30 is correct.
explanations: Correct: the BSE Sensex has 30 constituent companies, a fixed count since its inception.
Incorrect: 35 is not the constituent count of the Sensex or of any major headline Indian index.
Incorrect: 40 does not match the Sensex; it is simply a distractor number.
Incorrect: 50 is the number of stocks in the NSE Nifty 50, a different index.
keyfact: BSE SENSEX = 30 stocks (free-float market cap, base 1978-79 = 100); NSE Nifty = 50 stocks.
option_notes: 30: the number of constituents in the BSE SENSEX, which represents the large-cap segment of the Indian market across sectors such as financials, IT, energy, FMCG, automobiles and telecom. Launched 1986 with base year 1978-79 = 100, calculated by the free-float market capitalisation method and reviewed twice a year (June and December).

35: not the size of any major Indian benchmark index. BSE and NSE headline indices use 30, 50, 100, 200 or 500 constituents. Selecting 35 would be a guess with no basis in index composition; it serves only as a distractor in this question.

40: not the constituent count of the Sensex. It has no standing as a major benchmark index size in India. Related sector and thematic indices have varying numbers of stocks, but the flagship Sensex has a fixed 30.

50: the number of stocks in the NSE Nifty 50, India's other leading benchmark index, launched in April 1996 by the National Stock Exchange (founded 1992, Mumbai) with base year 1995 = 1000, using free-float market capitalisation and managed by NSE Indices Ltd.

Nifty Bank index has 12 constituents.
Market-wide circuit breakers apply at 10%, 15% and 20% movements.
summary: The answer is (a) 30. The BSE Sensex (S&P BSE Sensex, now BSE SENSEX) is the benchmark index of the Bombay Stock Exchange and comprises 30 large, well-established, financially sound companies from key sectors, selected by free-float market capitalisation.
topic_notes: Stock market indices in India: the two headline indices are the BSE SENSEX (30 stocks) and the NSE Nifty 50 (50 stocks). BSE was established in 1875 as the Native Share and Stock Brokers Association and is the oldest exchange in Asia; it is located at Dalal Street, Mumbai, and became the first Indian exchange to be recognised permanently by the government under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956. The Sensex was launched on 1 January 1986 with base year 1978-79 = 100, and is calculated using the free-float market capitalisation method since 2003. Formula: Index = (Free-float market cap of constituents / Base market cap) x base value. NSE was incorporated in 1992, recognised as a stock exchange in 1993, and began trading in 1994; Nifty began in 1996. Other indices: BSE 100, BSE 200, BSE 500, BSE MidCap, BSE SmallCap, Nifty Next 50, Nifty Bank (12 stocks), Nifty 500. SEBI, the securities market regulator, was established in 1988 and given statutory status by the SEBI Act, 1992. Bull market: rising prices; bear market: falling prices. Circuit breakers (market-wide) are triggered at 10%, 15% and 20% index movements. Sensex milestones: crossed 1,000 in 1990, 10,000 in 2006, 50,000 in 2021 and 60,000 in 2021, and 70,000 in December 2023, with later highs above 80,000 in 2024. UPSC may ask about base year, method, the number of constituents, who computes the index, or which exchange hosts which index.

question: Which one of the following about financing through debentures is correct ?
options: The debentures carry a fixed rate of|72. interest
The rate of interest on debentures varies with the profit of the company
The debenture holders have the voting rights
The debentures carry a fixed rate of dividend
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: A debenture is a written acknowledgement of debt issued by a company under its common seal (Companies Act, 2013, Section 2(30)); it is a form of borrowed capital. The company promises to pay a fixed rate of interest at stated intervals and to repay the principal on maturity. The interest is a charge against profit, so it is paid even when the company makes a loss, and it is tax-deductible, which makes debentures a cheap source of finance. Debenture holders are creditors, not owners of the company. They therefore have no voting rights in general meetings, and they receive interest, not dividend. Debentures may be secured (with a charge on assets) or unsecured, and convertible or non-convertible, redeemable or irredeemable. Under Section 71, a debenture trustee must be appointed and a debenture redemption reserve may be required. Elimination: (b) is wrong because the interest is fixed and does not vary with profit. (c) is wrong because creditors have no vote. (d) is wrong because dividend is the return on shares, not on debentures. Only (a) fits.
explanations: Correct: debentures carry a fixed, pre-agreed rate of interest that must be paid regardless of the company's profit or loss.
Incorrect: the interest rate on debentures is fixed by contract and does not vary with profit. Variable returns, such as dividends on equity shares, depend on profit.
Incorrect: debenture holders are creditors, not members of the company, so they have no voting rights. Equity shareholders hold the voting rights.
Incorrect: dividend is a return on share capital, whereas debentures earn interest. Preference shares carry a fixed rate of dividend.
keyfact: Debentures = debt capital with a fixed rate of interest, no voting rights, and interest payable even in a loss.
option_notes: Fixed rate of interest: this is the defining feature of a debenture. The coupon rate is stated on the certificate and paid periodically (half-yearly or yearly), irrespective of profit. The interest is a charge on profit, is tax-deductible, and ranks ahead of dividends. If the company defaults, debenture holders can sue for recovery, and holders of secured debentures can enforce the charge on assets.

Interest varying with profit: this describes returns on equity capital (dividend), or on special instruments such as income bonds or participating debentures. Ordinary debentures carry fixed interest. Floating-rate debentures vary with a benchmark rate such as MIBOR or the repo rate, not with company profit.

Voting rights: these belong to equity shareholders, and in limited cases to preference shareholders (Section 47 of the Companies Act, 2013). Debenture holders are lenders and have no say in management. They are protected through the trust deed and the debenture trustee, who acts on their behalf.

Fixed rate of dividend: this is a feature of preference shares, for example 8% cumulative preference shares. Debentures pay interest, not dividend. Dividend is paid out of profit after tax, while debenture interest is paid before tax. Preference shareholders are owners, though they have preferential claims.
related: Debenture holders are creditors; shareholders are owners of the company.
Debenture interest is paid out of profit before tax and is tax-deductible; dividend is paid after tax.
Section 2(30) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines debenture; Section 71 governs its issue.
Preference shares carry a fixed rate of dividend; equity dividends vary with profit.
A debenture trustee protects the interests of debenture holders.
NCDs cannot be converted into equity; FCDs convert entirely into shares.
Trading on equity means using fixed-cost debt to raise returns for equity holders.
Zero-coupon bonds are issued at a discount and redeemed at face value, with no periodic interest.
summary: The correct answer is (a). Debentures are debt instruments that carry a fixed rate of interest, payable whether or not the company earns a profit. Debenture holders are creditors, not owners, so they have no voting rights, and the return they get is interest, not dividend.
topic_notes: Sources of corporate finance are split into owned capital (equity and preference shares, retained earnings) and borrowed capital (debentures, bonds, term loans, public deposits). A debenture is a debt instrument, defined in Section 2(30) of the Companies Act, 2013, and it includes debenture stock, bonds and other securities of a company. Key features: fixed interest, a maturity date, no ownership or voting rights, a priority claim over shareholders on winding up, and tax-deductible interest, which gives trading-on-equity benefits and leverage. Types by security: secured (mortgage debentures) and unsecured (naked). By tenure: redeemable and irredeemable (perpetual). By convertibility: non-convertible (NCD), partly convertible (PCD) and fully convertible (FCD). By registration: registered and bearer. Section 71 governs the issue of debentures. A debenture trustee must be appointed for a public issue, and the trust deed must be executed within the prescribed period. Debenture redemption reserve (DRR) rules were relaxed over time, and listed companies are now generally exempt. SEBI regulates listed debt through the SEBI (Issue and Listing of Non-Convertible Securities) Regulations, 2021. Advantages are no dilution of control, a lower cost than equity, and a tax shield. Disadvantages are a fixed burden that must be paid even in a loss, and the risk of insolvency on default. Debentures differ from shares in that they give creditorship, not ownership, and pay interest, not dividend. Related instruments include zero-coupon bonds, deep-discount bonds, floating-rate bonds and convertible bonds.

question: ABC Analysis is used in :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: ABC Analysis is a selective inventory control technique based on the Pareto principle (80:20 rule), which Vilfredo Pareto formulated in the 1890s. Items are ranked by annual consumption value (annual usage x unit cost). Category A holds about 10-20% of items but about 70-80% of total value, so it gets tight control, frequent review, accurate records, low safety stock and close supplier follow-up. Category B is the middle group, about 30% of items and about 15-20% of value, and gets moderate control. Category C holds about 50-60% of items but only about 5-10% of value, so it gets simple controls, bulk ordering and larger buffer stocks. The aim is to cut carrying and ordering costs without risking stock-outs of critical items. Related inventory tools include EOQ, VED (Vital-Essential-Desirable), FSN (Fast-Slow-Non-moving), HML (High-Medium-Low price), JIT and the two-bin system. Elimination: cash management uses models such as Baumol and Miller-Orr; receivables management uses credit policy and ageing schedules; corporate governance deals with boards, Clause 49/SEBI LODR and the Companies Act. None of these uses ABC classification, so only (b) fits.
explanations: Wrong: cash management uses models such as the Baumol model, the Miller-Orr model and cash budgets, not ABC classification.
Correct: ABC Analysis is a classic inventory control technique that groups items into A, B and C by consumption value.
Wrong: corporate governance concerns board structure, disclosure, ethics and shareholder rights, and has no ABC classification.
Wrong: receivables management uses credit terms, ageing schedules and collection policy. An ageing analysis is a different tool, although some texts apply a similar ABC idea to debtors.
keyfact: ABC Analysis is an inventory control technique based on the Pareto 80:20 rule: A items are few but high in value and get the tightest control.
option_notes: Cash Management: the planning and control of cash balances to maintain liquidity while avoiding idle cash. The motives are transaction, precautionary and speculative. The main models are the Baumol EOQ-type model (1952) and the Miller-Orr stochastic model (1966). Tools include cash budgets, float management and lockbox systems.

Inventory Management: the control of raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods to minimise total cost. Techniques are ABC, VED, FSN, EOQ, reorder level, safety stock, JIT and the Kanban system. Ind AS 2 (AS 2) governs inventory valuation at the lower of cost and net realisable value.

Corporate Governance: the system by which companies are directed and controlled. India's key sources are the Cadbury Report (UK, 1992), SEBI Clause 49 (2000), the Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee (1999), Companies Act 2013 and SEBI LODR 2015. Topics include independent directors, audit committees and disclosure.

Receivables Management: the management of credit sales and debtors. It covers credit policy, credit terms (for example 2/10 net 30), credit analysis through the 5 Cs, collection policy, ageing schedules, factoring and forfaiting. The aim is to balance sales growth against bad debts and the cost of funds tied up.
related: ABC Analysis follows the Pareto 80:20 principle.
Category A: few items, high value, tight control.
VED analysis classifies items by criticality: Vital, Essential, Desirable.
FSN analysis classifies items by movement rate: Fast, Slow, Non-moving.
EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C).
Baumol and Miller-Orr are cash management models.
AS 2 / Ind AS 2 values inventory at the lower of cost and NRV.
JIT originated at Toyota.
summary: The answer is (b) Inventory Management. ABC Analysis classifies inventory items into A, B and C categories by their value and consumption, so that the tightest control goes to the few items that account for most of the money.
topic_notes: ABC Analysis belongs to materials and inventory management within working capital management. It is a selective control method: the effort spent on an item is proportional to its value. Steps: list items, compute annual usage value, rank in descending order, compute cumulative percentages, then set the A, B and C cut-offs. A typical split is A at about 70-80% of value (10-20% of items), B at about 15-20% (about 30% of items) and C at about 5-10% (50-60% of items). Other classification systems appear often in exams. VED classifies by criticality (Vital, Essential, Desirable) and suits spare parts. FSN classifies by movement (Fast, Slow, Non-moving). HML classifies by unit price (High, Medium, Low). SDE classifies by availability (Scarce, Difficult, Easy). GOLF classifies by source (Government, Ordinary, Local, Foreign). XYZ classifies by closing stock value. Inventory costs are ordering costs, carrying costs and stock-out costs. EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), where A is annual demand, O is ordering cost per order and C is carrying cost per unit. Reorder level = maximum consumption x maximum lead time. Minimum level = ROL - (normal consumption x normal lead time). Maximum level = ROL + ROQ - (minimum consumption x minimum lead time). Valuation methods are FIFO, LIFO (not permitted under AS 2) and weighted average. Perpetual inventory and continuous stock-taking support ABC control. JIT, developed by Toyota (Taiichi Ohno), aims at near-zero inventory.

question: Which one of the following is the minimum rate of return that a firm must earn in order to satisfy the expectations of its investors ?
options: Cost of capital of the firm
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Cost of capital is the required rate of return on the firm's investments. It is the minimum acceptable return, also called the hurdle rate, cut-off rate or required rate of return. It reflects the opportunity cost of funds supplied by investors, who could earn similar returns elsewhere at similar risk. Normally it is expressed as the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC), i.e. the sum of each source's cost multiplied by its weight in the capital structure. The components are cost of debt (after tax: Kd(1-t)), cost of preference capital, cost of equity (estimated by CAPM, dividend growth model or earnings yield) and cost of retained earnings. In capital budgeting, a project is accepted if its IRR exceeds the cost of capital, or if its NPV, computed by discounting at that rate, is positive. If a firm earns exactly its cost of capital, the market price of its shares stays unchanged. Elimination logic: gross and net profit margins are profitability ratios computed as a percentage of sales, and say nothing about investor expectations. Cost of borrowing is only one component (debt) and ignores equity holders' expectations. Only (d) covers all investors.
explanations: Incorrect: Gross profit margin = (Sales - Cost of goods sold)/Sales. It is an operating performance ratio, not a required return for investors.
Incorrect: Net profit margin = Net profit/Sales. It measures overall profitability on sales and is not the minimum return investors expect.
Incorrect: Cost of borrowing (cost of debt) covers only lenders' interest. It ignores equity shareholders' required return, so it is not the firm's overall minimum return.
Correct: Cost of capital is the minimum rate of return a firm must earn on its investments to satisfy all its capital providers and keep share value unchanged. It is the hurdle rate for projects.
keyfact: Cost of capital = minimum required return (hurdle rate) a firm must earn to satisfy all investors; computed as WACC.
option_notes: Gross profit margin is a profitability ratio: (Sales - Cost of goods sold) / Sales x 100. It shows how efficiently a firm produces or buys goods before deducting operating expenses, interest and tax. A higher margin means better pricing or cost control. It is a margin on sales, so it is unrelated to investors' required return. It is used for comparing firms in the same industry and for trend analysis over time.

Net profit margin = Net profit after interest and tax / Net sales x 100. It shows how much of each rupee of sales remains as profit for shareholders. It is affected by operating efficiency, financing structure and tax. It is a performance measure of the firm. It is not the benchmark of the minimum return required by investors, and it is often compared with the industry average.

Cost of borrowing, or cost of debt, is the effective interest rate a firm pays on its loans, debentures and bonds. Because interest is tax-deductible, the after-tax cost is Kd(1-t). It is usually the cheapest source of finance because lenders bear lower risk and have a prior claim. It is only one component of WACC, and it covers only lenders' expectations, not equity holders'.

Cost of capital is the minimum rate of return a firm must earn on investments to keep the market value of its shares unchanged. It is the weighted average cost of debt, preference capital, equity and retained earnings (WACC). It serves as the discount rate in NPV and the benchmark for IRR in capital budgeting. It depends on business risk, financial risk and market interest rates. It is also called the hurdle rate or cut-off rate.
related: Cost of capital is also called the hurdle rate, cut-off rate or required rate of return.
Project acceptance rule: accept if IRR > cost of capital, or NPV > 0 when discounted at the cost of capital.
Debt is the cheapest source of finance because of the interest tax shield.
CAPM formula: Ke = Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf).
WACC = sum of (weight x cost) for each capital source, and market value weights are preferred.
Gordon model: Ke = D1/P0 + g.
The Modigliani-Miller theory (1958) says capital structure is irrelevant in a perfect market without taxes.
After-tax cost of debt = Interest rate x (1 - tax rate).
summary: The answer is (d) Cost of capital of the firm. It is the minimum rate of return a firm must earn on its investments so that the expectations of all its capital providers (equity holders and lenders) are satisfied and the market value of the firm is maintained.
topic_notes: Cost of capital is a core topic of financial management. It is the return required by the providers of long-term funds, and it is the opportunity cost of funds. Its uses: capital budgeting (the discount rate for NPV, the hurdle for IRR), capital structure decisions (the optimal structure minimises WACC), and evaluating the firm's financial performance. Components: (1) Cost of debt: Kd = I/NP before tax; after tax Kd(1-t). For redeemable debt, the yield-to-maturity approach is used. (2) Cost of preference capital: Kp = PD/NP. Dividends are not tax-deductible. (3) Cost of equity: the dividend yield method (D1/P0), the dividend growth model Ke = D1/P0 + g (Gordon), the earnings yield method (E/P), and CAPM Ke = Rf + beta(Rm - Rf). (4) Cost of retained earnings is akin to the cost of equity, with adjustments for taxes and brokerage. WACC = sum of Wi x Ki. Weights can be book value or market value (market value is preferred, and target weights are also used). Marginal cost of capital is the cost of raising an additional rupee. Specific cost is the cost of each individual source. Explicit cost is the discount rate that equates the present value of cash inflows with outflows. Implicit cost is the opportunity cost of funds that are retained. Other angles UPSC may ask: the order of costs is generally debt < preference < equity. Debt is cheapest due to the tax shield and lower risk. Modigliani-Miller propositions state that, without taxes, the capital structure does not affect the firm's value. The Net Income approach says that increased debt lowers WACC. The traditional approach says WACC has a U shape. Floatation costs raise the effective cost of new issues. Financial leverage and operating leverage influence risk.

question: An organization forecasts the requirement of IT enabled employees 10 years from now. This is an example of :
subject: Computers
detail: Manpower planning (Human Resource Planning, HRP) is the process of estimating the organization's future demand for human resources, comparing it with the expected supply, and acting on the gap so that the right number of people with the right skills are available at the right time. Its main steps are: analysing organizational objectives, forecasting demand (techniques include managerial judgment, Delphi technique, trend analysis, ratio analysis, regression and workload analysis), forecasting supply (internal through skills inventories, succession charts and Markov analysis; external through labour market studies), identifying the gap, and preparing action plans for recruitment, training or redeployment. Planning can be short term (up to 1 year), medium term (1-3 years) or long term (5 years or more). A 10-year forecast of IT-enabled staff is a long-term demand forecast within HRP. Elimination: HR audit is a review of existing HR policies and practices; 'job forecasting' is not a standard HRM term; personnel management is the broad function covering all people-related activities, not the specific act of forecasting requirements.
explanations: Correct: estimating future requirements of employees with specific skills (IT-enabled) over a 10-year horizon is the demand-forecasting part of manpower planning.
Wrong: a human resource audit examines and evaluates existing HR functions, policies and effectiveness; it is a review, not a forecast of future staffing.
Wrong: 'job forecasting' is not an established HRM concept; the recognised term for forecasting staffing needs is manpower or HR planning.
Wrong: personnel management is the overall management of the workforce (recruitment, training, pay, welfare, relations); it is too broad and does not describe this specific activity.
keyfact: Forecasting future staff requirements (demand and supply) = Manpower / Human Resource Planning.
option_notes: Manpower planning (HR planning) is the process of ensuring the right number and kind of people are in the right jobs at the right time. It involves demand forecasting, supply forecasting, gap analysis and action plans. It can be short, medium or long term, and links organizational strategy to staffing. Techniques include Delphi, trend analysis, ratio analysis, skills inventory and Markov analysis.

Human resource audit is a systematic review and evaluation of an organization's HR policies, practices, systems and functions to assess their effectiveness and compliance and to find areas for improvement. It looks at the present and past performance of HR, covering areas such as recruitment, training, compensation, and records. It is a control and diagnostic tool, not a forecasting tool.

Job forecasting is not a standard term in HRM literature. Related real concepts are job analysis (studying the duties and requirements of a job), job description and job specification, and job evaluation (determining the relative worth of jobs). Forecasting of staff needs falls under human resource planning, so this option is a distractor.

Personnel management is the traditional term for managing an organization's workforce: recruitment, selection, training, wages, discipline, welfare and industrial relations. It is more administrative and operational than the modern, strategic Human Resource Management. Manpower planning is one function within it, but the term itself is too general for this question.
related: HRP's first step is analysing organizational objectives and plans, followed by demand forecasting.
Delphi technique uses anonymous expert opinions over repeated rounds to forecast manpower demand.
Markov analysis predicts internal supply by tracking movement probabilities between job levels.
Job description states duties of a job; job specification states the qualifications needed in the person.
Job evaluation determines the relative worth of jobs for wage fixation.
HR audit evaluates existing HR practices and effectiveness.
Succession planning identifies and develops future leaders for key positions.
Long-term manpower plans generally cover 3 to 5 years or more.
summary: The answer is (a) Manpower planning. Forecasting the number and type of employees (here, IT-enabled staff) needed at a future date is the core activity of manpower or human resource planning.
topic_notes: Human Resource Planning (HRP) is the starting point of the staffing function. Definition: the process of forecasting an organization's future demand for and supply of the right type of people in the right number. Objectives: avoid both surplus and shortage of staff, support expansion and technological change, control labour cost, and prepare for succession. Process: (1) environmental scanning and objectives; (2) inventory of current human resources (skills inventory, HR information system); (3) demand forecasting; (4) supply forecasting; (5) gap analysis (surplus or deficit); (6) action plans such as recruitment, training, redeployment, VRS or retrenchment; (7) monitoring and control. Demand forecasting methods: expert or managerial judgment, Delphi technique, nominal group technique, trend analysis, ratio analysis, regression analysis, workload analysis, work-study techniques. Supply forecasting tools: staffing tables, Markov analysis (transition matrix), replacement and succession charts, and analysis of turnover and absenteeism. Time horizon: short term (up to 1 year), medium term (1-3 years), long term (3-5 years or more). Related concepts: job analysis, job description, job specification, job evaluation, human resource audit, human resource accounting, human resource information system (HRIS), and strategic HRM. Differences: personnel management is administrative and short-term; HRM is strategic and integrates people with business goals. UPSC-type questions often ask for the first step in HRP, the techniques of forecasting, the difference between job description and job specification, and the meaning of terms such as downsizing, outsourcing and succession planning.

question: The long-term direction and strategic intent of an organization is known as :
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: In strategic management, the hierarchy runs Vision, then Mission, then Objectives/Goals (targets), then Strategies, then Plans/Policies/Programmes, then Procedures. Vision is a forward-looking, aspirational statement of the desired future position of the organization, typically 10 to 20 years ahead. It gives long-term direction and strategic intent. Hamel and Prahalad popularised the term 'strategic intent' for an ambitious long-term goal that guides resource allocation. Mission states the present purpose: why the organization exists, whom it serves and what it does. Targets are specific, measurable, time-bound results, such as achieving 100 percent claim settlement within 30 days. Plans are detailed courses of action, with resources and schedules, for achieving objectives. Elimination logic: 'Target' is too narrow and short-term, so it is out. 'Plan' is operational and tactical, so it is out. 'Mission' is the most tempting distractor, but it answers 'what do we do now and why', not 'where do we want to be'. The words 'long-term direction' and 'strategic intent' therefore point to Vision.
explanations: Incorrect: a target is a specific, quantified, time-bound result, a short- or medium-term yardstick and not the overall long-term direction.
Correct: vision is the aspirational long-term picture of the organization's future and expresses its strategic intent and direction.
Incorrect: mission states the organization's present purpose, its business, its customers and its reason for existence. It is not the future-oriented direction.
Incorrect: a plan is an operational blueprint of actions, resources and timelines to achieve objectives, not the strategic intent.
keyfact: Vision = long-term aspiration and strategic intent (where we want to be); Mission = present purpose (why we exist).
option_notes: Target: a specific, measurable, time-bound level of performance that an organization aims to reach, for example collecting a given amount of contributions in a year. Targets derive from objectives and are used for monitoring and control. They are short- or medium-term and quantitative, sitting below vision and mission in the strategy hierarchy and giving a benchmark for evaluating performance.

Vision: an aspirational statement of what the organization wants to become or achieve in the long run. It is inspirational, concise and future-focused, and it gives direction and strategic intent. Example: 'To be the world's most customer-centric company'. It guides the mission, objectives and strategy, is reviewed rarely, and is normally set by top management or the board.

Mission: a statement of an organization's fundamental purpose and reason for existence, covering its business scope, its customers, its products or services and its values. It answers 'What business are we in and why?'. It is present-oriented and more concrete than vision. Vision is the destination, while mission is the road and purpose for travelling.

Plan: a predetermined course of action, specifying what is to be done, when, how and by whom, to achieve objectives. Plans include policies, procedures, rules, programmes, budgets and projects. They form the operational and tactical level of planning, with a defined time frame and resources, and are derived from strategy.
related: Vision is long-term and aspirational, while mission is the present purpose.
Hamel and Prahalad introduced the term 'strategic intent' in 1989.
Peter Drucker propounded Management by Objectives in 1954.
SWOT analysis covers internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats.
The BCG matrix classifies businesses as stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs.
Planning is the first function of management and is a primary, pervasive function.
A policy is a general guide to decision-making, a procedure is a chronological sequence of steps, and a rule is a specific mandatory action.
SMART objectives are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
summary: The answer is (b) Vision. A vision is the long-term direction and strategic intent of an organization, describing what it aspires to become or achieve in the future. Mission, target and plan deal with present purpose, specific goals and action steps respectively.
topic_notes: Strategic management follows a hierarchy. 1) Vision: the long-term aspiration or strategic intent, the 'where we want to be'. 2) Mission: the present purpose, the 'why we exist and what we do'. 3) Values or core beliefs: the principles that guide behaviour. 4) Objectives and goals: broad, desired end results. Objectives are usually qualitative or broad, while goals and targets are specific and quantified. 5) Strategy: the long-term course of action and resource allocation to achieve objectives, with levels at corporate, business and functional. 6) Plans: policies, procedures, rules, programmes, projects and budgets. 7) Control and feedback: monitoring against targets and taking corrective action. Related concepts: SWOT analysis (internal strengths and weaknesses, external opportunities and threats), PESTLE analysis of the environment, the BCG matrix (stars, cash cows, question marks, dogs), Porter's Five Forces and generic strategies (cost leadership, differentiation, focus), and the Ansoff matrix for growth strategies. Management by Objectives (MBO) was given by Peter Drucker in 1954 in 'The Practice of Management'. Planning is the primary function of management, followed by organizing, staffing, directing and controlling (Koontz and O'Donnell's POSDCORB is Gulick's list). A good vision statement is clear, inspiring, realistic, concise and future-oriented, and a mission statement identifies the customers, products, markets and philosophy. UPSC often tests the distinctions among vision, mission, goal, objective, policy, procedure and rule, so learn to tell each by its time horizon and its level of specificity.

ocr: An organization has uploaded new job openings on its website. This is an example of : Internal recruitment (a) (b) External recruitment (c) Social media campaign (d) Public relations
subject: Insurance
detail: Recruitment is the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs. Sources are classified as internal (promotions, transfers, job posting within the firm, employee referrals, recall from layoff) and external (direct recruitment, campus recruitment, advertisements, employment exchanges, placement agencies, walk-ins, e-recruitment or web publishing, labour contractors, and recommendations). When an organization uploads vacancies on its own website or on job portals, the notice is open to anyone, so it draws candidates from outside, and it is called external recruitment through e-recruitment. Internal recruitment would limit the notice to current employees, for example through an intranet or internal circular. Elimination: (a) is wrong because the website is publicly accessible and not restricted to staff. (c) A social media campaign would need platforms such as LinkedIn, Facebook or X, and the question mentions only the organization's own website. (d) Public relations is about building the organization's image and has nothing to do with filling vacancies. Hence (b). Note that recruitment is a positive process (attracting candidates), while selection is a negative process (rejecting unsuitable ones).
explanations: Incorrect: internal recruitment fills posts from existing employees through promotion, transfer or internal job posting. A public website is open to outsiders, so it does not qualify.
Correct: an open website posting reaches the general public and attracts outside candidates. This is external recruitment, specifically e-recruitment or direct advertisement.
Incorrect: a social media campaign uses platforms such as LinkedIn or Facebook. The question refers only to the organization's own website, which is a different channel, though both are external.
Incorrect: public relations manages the organization's image and its communication with the public. It is not a method of recruitment.
keyfact: Vacancies posted on a public website are external recruitment (e-recruitment), because they attract candidates from outside the organization.
option_notes: Internal recruitment means filling vacancies from within the existing workforce. Methods include promotions, transfers, internal job posting, employee referrals, and recall of former or laid-off employees. Advantages: it is cheap, quick, boosts morale and the candidates are already known. Disadvantages: it limits fresh talent and can cause internal politics and inbreeding of ideas. It is often governed by seniority or merit policy.

External recruitment means attracting candidates from outside the organization. Sources include newspaper advertisements, campus placements, employment exchanges, private placement agencies, walk-ins, e-recruitment through websites and job portals, and recommendations. Advantages: fresh ideas, a wider talent pool and new skills. Disadvantages: higher cost, longer time and a risk of lower morale among existing staff, who may feel passed over.

A social media campaign uses platforms such as LinkedIn, Facebook, X (Twitter) and Instagram to promote the brand or recruit, with targeted posts and ads. It is a modern, low-cost external recruitment and marketing tool and is popular for reaching younger and passive candidates. It is not the same as posting a vacancy on the organization's own website.

Public relations (PR) is the management function of building and maintaining a favourable public image and relationships with stakeholders such as media, customers, investors and government. Tools include press releases, events, CSR and publicity. It supports employer branding indirectly but is not a recruitment source. Practitioners are sometimes called PROs. The PR function is distinct from advertising, which is paid promotion.
related: Recruitment is a positive process; selection is a negative process.
Job analysis produces the job description and the job specification.
E-recruitment uses company websites and job portals and is an external source.
Promotions and transfers are internal sources of recruitment.
Campus recruitment is an external source targeting educational institutions.
Employment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification of Vacancies) Act, 1959 requires notifying vacancies to exchanges.
Article 320 of the Constitution lists the functions of the UPSC and the State PSCs, including advice on recruitment.
Headhunting means recruiting senior executives through specialised agencies.
summary: The answer is (b) External recruitment. Posting job openings on the organization's website invites applicants from outside the organization (the general public), which is an external source of recruitment, specifically the e-recruitment or direct-advertising route.
topic_notes:
Recruitment is the second step in the staffing and HR cycle after human resource planning and before selection. Edwin Flippo defined it as the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating and encouraging them to apply for jobs in the organization. It is called a positive process because it attracts as many candidates as possible, while selection is negative because it screens out unsuitable ones.

Sources of recruitment are classed as internal and external. Internal: promotions, transfers, job rotation, internal job posting, employee referrals, and re-employment of ex-employees. External: direct recruitment such as notice boards and walk-ins; indirect recruitment through advertisements; campus recruitment; employment exchanges, which under the Employment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification of Vacancies) Act, 1959 require notification of vacancies; private placement agencies and headhunters; labour contractors; casual callers; unsolicited applications; and e-recruitment through company websites, job portals such as Naukri, Monster and LinkedIn, and social media.

Other concepts: outsourcing, poaching or raiding (hiring from competitors), E-recruitment, Realistic Job Preview (RJP), and employer branding. Recruitment is followed by selection (screening, tests, interviews, reference checks, medical examination), then placement, induction and training. The relevant documents are the job description (what the job involves) and the job specification (the qualifications the person needs), which come from job analysis. Government recruitment in India takes place through the UPSC, SSC and State PSCs under Article 315 and Article 320 of the Constitution, which provide for the UPSC and the State PSCs. Reservation in recruitment is under Articles 15(4), 16(4) and 335.

question: The process of choosing individuals who have 78. relevant qualifications to fill existing or projected job openings is known as :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: In human resource management, staffing has two linked stages. Recruitment is the positive, search-oriented process of identifying sources and attracting a pool of potential candidates to apply for vacancies. Selection comes after it and is the negative or screening process, in which unsuitable candidates are filtered out and the most suitable are chosen and offered the job. The typical sequence is: manpower planning, job analysis, recruitment, application screening, tests, interviews, reference and background checks, medical examination, selection decision, job offer, placement and induction. Edwin Flippo defined recruitment as the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs. Selection is often described as a process of picking individuals with the qualifications needed to fill job vacancies in the organisation, so the wording of this question matches the standard definition of selection. Elimination logic: Recruitment (a) only attracts applicants and does not choose among them. Fitment (b) is not a standard HR process term; it is used loosely for person-job fit or pay fitment. Matching (c) is a general idea behind selection but not the formal name of the process. Hence (d).
explanations: Incorrect: recruitment is the process of searching for and attracting candidates to build an applicant pool. It does not choose among them.
Incorrect: fitment is not the standard HR term for choosing candidates. It is used for person-job fit or for pay fixation (pay fitment) in service matters.
Incorrect: matching describes the aim of selection (matching person to job), but it is not the formal name of the process.
Correct: selection is the process of choosing, from the available applicants, those with the relevant qualifications to fill current or projected vacancies.
keyfact: Recruitment attracts applicants; selection chooses the qualified ones from the pool for existing or projected vacancies.
option_notes: Recruitment is the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply. Sources are internal (promotions, transfers, job posting) and external (advertisements, campus hiring, employment exchanges, agencies, e-recruitment). It is called a positive process because it increases the number of applicants. In the Flippo definition it comes before selection and ends when applications are received.

Fitment usually means the fixing of an employee's pay or grade in a new pay structure, for example the fitment factor of 2.57 used by the 7th Pay Commission to convert old basic pay into new pay. In HR it may also loosely mean person-job fit. It is not the formal name for the choosing of candidates.

Matching refers to aligning an individual's skills, abilities and preferences with job requirements, the person-job fit idea. It is the principle behind selection and placement, not the formal stage name. In other contexts it is used for matching grants, matching principle in accounting and so on.

Selection is the process of differentiating between applicants and choosing those most likely to succeed in the job. Steps include screening, tests, interviews, reference checks, medical examination and the final decision, followed by the job offer, placement and induction. It is called a negative process because it rejects unsuitable candidates. It follows recruitment and precedes placement.
related: Recruitment is a positive process; selection is a negative (screening) process.
Job description lists duties; job specification lists the qualifications needed.
Recruitment comes before selection in the staffing process.
Placement and induction follow selection.
Article 315 provides for the Union and State Public Service Commissions.
Halo effect is an interview rating error caused by one favourable trait.
Fitment factor under the 7th Pay Commission was 2.57.
summary: The correct answer is (d) Selection. Selection is the process of choosing, from among the pool of applicants, those individuals who have the relevant qualifications to fill existing or projected job openings. Recruitment only creates the pool of candidates.
topic_notes: Staffing or acquisition is a core function of human resource management. It begins with human resource planning, which forecasts demand and supply of manpower, followed by job analysis, which produces the job description (duties, responsibilities) and the job specification (qualifications, skills required). Recruitment then builds the pool of applicants. Internal sources include promotions, transfers and job posting, while external sources include advertisements, campus recruitment, employment exchanges, private agencies, walk-ins, referrals and e-recruitment. Selection follows: preliminary screening, application blank, employment tests (aptitude, intelligence, personality, trade or proficiency tests), interviews (structured, unstructured, panel, stress), reference and background verification, medical examination, final decision and job offer. Placement assigns the person to the job, and induction or orientation introduces the person to the organisation. Key distinctions: recruitment is positive and aims to attract many applicants; selection is negative and aims to reject unsuitable ones. Recruitment is not a contract of employment, while selection leads to a contract. Related concepts include validity and reliability of selection tests, the halo effect and the horn effect as interview errors, realistic job preview, and the Public Service system in India where UPSC and SSC conduct recruitment under Article 315 and Article 320. Training and development, performance appraisal, compensation and separation follow in the HR cycle. In ESIC and EPFO papers, questions often ask for definitions, order of steps and differences between recruitment and selection.

question: The interview situation, where a candidate is given the maximum freedom in determining] 79. the course of the discussion is known as :
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: Interviews used in selection are classified by the degree of structure and by the type of question. In a non-directive (unstructured) interview, the interviewer asks few, broad, open-ended questions such as 'Tell me about yourself' and listens, letting the candidate lead the flow. It rests on the client-centred approach associated with Carl Rogers. Its strengths are that it reveals the candidate's attitudes, values and communication style and builds rapport. Its weaknesses are low reliability, interviewer bias, poor comparability between candidates and low predictive validity. A structured interview is the opposite: the same pre-set questions in the same order, with standard scoring, so the interviewer controls the course. Situational interviews pose hypothetical future scenarios ('What would you do if...'). Behavioural description interviews (BDI) ask about actual past behaviour, on the premise that past behaviour predicts future behaviour. Both are structured methods. Elimination: (a), (b) and (c) are all planned and interviewer-driven, so only (d) gives the candidate freedom to direct the discussion. Other types to remember are the patterned/semi-structured, stress, panel, group and depth interviews.
explanations: Incorrect: a structured interview uses predetermined questions in a fixed sequence, so the interviewer, not the candidate, controls the course.
Incorrect: a behavioural description interview asks set questions about specific past behaviour and is interviewer-directed and structured.
Incorrect: a situational interview presents hypothetical job-related scenarios chosen by the interviewer, so the candidate's freedom is limited.
Correct: a non-directive interview uses open-ended prompts and lets the candidate decide the direction and content of the discussion.
keyfact: Non-directive (unstructured) interview = open-ended questions, the candidate steers the discussion, maximum freedom.
option_notes: Structured interview: all candidates get the same standardised, job-related questions in the same order, and answers are scored against a rating scale. It is high in reliability, validity and legal defensibility, and it reduces interviewer bias. Its drawbacks are rigidity and little scope to probe. It is also called a directive or patterned interview, and it is the most recommended format in modern selection practice.

Behavioural description interview (BDI): developed by Tom Janz in the 1980s. The candidate is asked to describe actual past incidents, such as 'Tell me about a time you handled conflict', often in STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result). The premise is that past behaviour is the best predictor of future behaviour. It is structured and has good predictive validity.
