Situational interview: developed by Gary Latham and colleagues, and based on goal-setting theory. The candidate is given hypothetical job-related dilemmas and says what they would do. Answers are scored against pre-set benchmark answers. It is structured, future-oriented and has good validity, and it contrasts with the past-oriented behavioural interview.

Non-directive interview: unstructured and conversational, with broad open-ended questions and minimal interviewer control. The candidate chooses the topics and the pace. It is based on Carl Rogers's non-directive counselling. It is useful for probing attitudes and personality and for counselling or exit interviews, but it has low reliability and a high risk of bias.
related: Non-directive interview: the candidate has maximum freedom, and the format is based on Carl Rogers's approach.
Structured interview: highest reliability and validity among interview types.
Situational interview is linked to Latham and goal-setting theory; behavioural interview uses past behaviour.
STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Stress interview: deliberately creates pressure to test composure.
Halo effect: one good trait colours the whole evaluation.
Exit interview: held when an employee leaves, to learn why.
summary: The answer is (d) Non-directive interview. In this format the interviewer asks broad, open-ended questions and lets the candidate steer the discussion, so the candidate has maximum freedom in deciding its course.
topic_notes: Selection interviews are classified by structure, content and format. By structure there are four types. Unstructured or non-directive: free flow, open-ended questions, the candidate leads. Structured or directive: standard questions, fixed order, scoring guide. Semi-structured or patterned: a core set of questions plus freedom to probe. Mixed: a combination of both. By content there are two types. Situational: hypothetical future scenarios, based on Latham's goal-setting theory. Behavioural or job-related: past-behaviour questions, with the STAR method used for answers. Other formats include the stress interview, which deliberately creates pressure to test composure. A panel or board interview has several interviewers, as in UPSC's Personality Test. A group interview has several candidates together. A depth interview probes deeply into specific areas. A telephonic or video interview is used for screening. An exit interview is held when an employee leaves. Research consistently shows that structured interviews have higher reliability and validity than unstructured ones. Common interviewer errors are the halo effect, horn effect, similarity bias, first-impression bias, contrast effect, leniency and central tendency. Remember the ordering of freedom for the candidate: non-directive is highest, structured is lowest. Interviews fall under the selection stage of the HRM process, which also includes screening, tests, reference checks, medical examination and the job offer.

question: The process of systematically socializing new employees to become a part of the organization is known as:
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Onboarding (organizational socialization) is the comprehensive process by which a new hire acquires the knowledge, skills, behaviours, culture and values needed to become an effective insider. It typically begins at the offer or pre-joining stage and may continue for 3 to 12 months. It covers paperwork, orientation, training, mentoring or buddy systems, role clarity, feedback and cultural assimilation. Orientation is a short, formal, mostly one-time event (day 1 or week 1) that covers the company profile, policies, facilities, introductions and safety. Induction is a similar early-stage process of introducing the new employee to the job, the people and the organization, and is often used interchangeably with orientation in Indian textbooks. It is usually shorter and more procedural than onboarding. Familiarization is a general word for getting acquainted and is not a standard HR term for the whole process. Elimination logic: the keyword 'systematically socializing' signals a long-term, structured process. That points to onboarding, not to the one-off events of orientation or induction. The official key accepts (b).
explanations: Incorrect: orientation is a short initial event (introductions, policies, facilities), only one component of the socialization process.
Correct: onboarding is the systematic, extended process of socializing new employees into the organization, as the official answer holds.
Incorrect: induction is the early-stage introduction to the job and organization. It is narrower and shorter than full onboarding, though often used loosely as a synonym.
Incorrect: familiarization is a general term for becoming acquainted and is not the standard HR term for systematic socialization.
keyfact: Onboarding = the whole systematic, long-term socialization of a new hire; orientation/induction = the short initial introduction.
option_notes: Orientation: a formal, usually one-time programme (a day to a week) that introduces new hires to the company's history, mission, rules, benefits, safety norms, facilities and colleagues. It reduces anxiety and gives basic information. It is a part of onboarding, not the whole process. It is often delivered by HR using presentations, tours and handbooks.

Onboarding: the comprehensive, structured process of integrating new employees, from pre-joining (offer acceptance) through orientation, training, mentoring and feedback, until they are fully productive. It lasts months. It aims to improve retention, engagement, cultural fit and speed to productivity. It is also called organizational socialization. Typical tools are buddy systems, 30-60-90 day plans and check-ins.

Induction: the process of welcoming and introducing a new employee to the job, the work group and the organization's policies, so that he or she settles in quickly. It is usually shorter and more formal than onboarding. Indian HRM texts often treat it as a synonym for orientation. It covers the company background, rules, the job and the people.

Familiarization: the general act of making someone acquainted with something new, such as the workplace, tools or procedures. It is a loose, non-technical word and not a defined HR process. It may occur during induction or training, but it does not denote the systematic socialization of new employees.
related: Onboarding = organizational socialization, a long-term process lasting months.
Orientation/induction is a short initial introduction to the company and the job.
Placement means assigning the selected employee to a specific job.
Kirkpatrick's four levels: reaction, learning, behaviour, results.
Vestibule training uses a simulated job environment away from the actual workplace.
Training is job-specific and short-term, while development is career-oriented and long-term.
Hawthorne studies were conducted by Elton Mayo at Western Electric.
summary: The answer is (b) Onboarding. Onboarding is the broad, systematic, ongoing process of socializing new employees so they become integrated, productive members of the organization, whereas orientation and induction are shorter, initial events within it.
topic_notes: Staffing and HRM sequence: manpower planning, recruitment, selection, placement, induction/orientation, training, development, performance appraisal, compensation, and separation. Placement means assigning the selected candidate to a suitable job. Induction or orientation is the first step after placement and introduces the employee to the organization. Onboarding is the broader term. Its stages are often described as pre-boarding, orientation, role training, integration and follow-up. Researchers such as Bauer and Feldman link effective onboarding to higher job satisfaction, commitment and lower turnover. Van Maanen and Schein described organizational socialization tactics. These are collective vs individual, formal vs informal, sequential vs random, fixed vs variable, serial vs disjunctive, and investiture vs divestiture. Training types: on-the-job (coaching, mentoring, job rotation, understudy) and off-the-job (lectures, case study, role play, simulation, sensitivity training, vestibule training). Development is long-term and future-oriented, while training is short-term and job-specific. Related concepts: Kirkpatrick's four levels of training evaluation (reaction, learning, behaviour, results), the Hawthorne studies (Elton Mayo), and Maslow's and Herzberg's theories. Be careful with the exam's keywords: 'systematic and long-term socialization' means onboarding. 'Short initial introduction to the organization' means orientation or induction. 'Assigning a job to a selected employee' means placement.

question: Knowledge, skills and ability together are known as:
subject: Current Affairs
detail: In HRM, a competency is an underlying characteristic of a person, usually described as KSA (Knowledge, Skills, Abilities), sometimes KSAO (with Other characteristics such as attitude, motivation and personality). The concept was popularised by David McClelland (1973, 'Testing for Competence rather than Intelligence') and Richard Boyatzis (The Competent Manager, 1982). Competency mapping is used in recruitment, training needs analysis, performance appraisal, succession planning and career development. Knowledge is what a person knows (theory, facts); skill is the learned capacity to do a task (technical, human, conceptual, per Robert Katz); ability is the inherent or developed capacity to perform. Competency is a broader input concept; performance is the output or result when competencies are applied. Elimination: (b) attitude is only a mental disposition or feeling towards persons or things, so it is one component and not the KSA bundle. (c) Talent means innate natural aptitude, only part of ability. (d) Performance is the outcome or achievement measured against standards, not the bundle of inputs. Hence (a) is correct.
explanations: Correct: Competency is the combination of knowledge, skills and abilities needed for effective job performance, as in the KSA framework.
Wrong: Attitude is a predisposition, feeling or evaluative stance towards people, objects or situations. It is not the knowledge-skills-ability bundle.
Wrong: Talent is a natural, innate aptitude or gift. It is narrower than the combination of acquired knowledge, skills and abilities.
Wrong: Performance is the output or result of work measured against standards. It is the outcome of competencies, not the competencies themselves.
keyfact: Knowledge + Skills + Abilities (KSA) = Competency; performance is the outcome.
option_notes: Competency: a measurable cluster of knowledge, skills, abilities and behaviours that distinguishes effective performers. Popularised by David McClelland (1973) and Boyatzis (1982). Used in competency mapping, selection, training and appraisal. Types include core, functional/technical and behavioural competencies. Often expressed as KSA or KSAO. Iceberg model: knowledge and skills are visible, while traits, motives and self-concept lie hidden.

Attitude: a learned predisposition to respond favourably or unfavourably towards an object, person or situation. It has three components: cognitive (beliefs), affective (feelings) and behavioural (intention to act). Job satisfaction and organisational commitment are key work attitudes. Cognitive dissonance (Festinger) explains attitude-behaviour inconsistency. Attitudes can be changed through persuasion, training and experience.

Talent: an innate natural aptitude or gift for a particular activity, which can be developed through training. In HR, talent management covers attracting, developing, retaining and deploying high-potential employees. It is often called the 'war for talent', a term coined by McKinsey in 1997. Talent differs from skill, which is learned through practice.

Performance: the actual result or output of work compared with set standards or goals. It is measured through performance appraisal methods such as MBO (Peter Drucker, 1954), 360-degree feedback, BARS and the graphic rating scale. Performance is often modelled as function of ability, motivation and opportunity. It is an outcome, not an input.
related: KSA stands for Knowledge, Skills and Abilities.
David McClelland introduced competency thinking in 1973.
Job specification lists the qualifications and competencies a jobholder needs.
Katz's managerial skills are technical, human and conceptual.
Kirkpatrick's model has four levels: reaction, learning, behaviour and results.
Iceberg model: knowledge and skills are visible, while traits and motives are hidden.
Competency mapping identifies the competencies needed for a role.
MBO was proposed by Peter Drucker in 1954.
summary: The answer is (a) Competency. Competency is the combination of knowledge, skills and abilities (often with attitudes/behaviours) that enables a person to perform a job effectively. Attitude, talent and performance each describe only a part or an outcome, not the whole combination.
topic_notes: Competency and HRM basics. Competency is the combination of knowledge, skills, abilities and often attitudes or behaviours (KSAO) that lead to superior job performance. McClelland (Harvard, 1973) pioneered the idea, arguing that competence predicts job success better than IQ tests. Boyatzis (1982) developed the competency model for managers. The Iceberg model places knowledge and skills above the waterline, while self-concept, traits and motives sit below. Types: threshold competencies (minimum required) and differentiating competencies (separate superior from average performers); also core, functional and leadership competencies. Applications: job analysis, job description and job specification (the specification lists the KSAs required of the jobholder), recruitment, selection, training needs analysis, performance appraisal, career planning, succession planning and compensation. Competency mapping identifies the competencies needed for a role and assesses gaps. Related HR concepts: Katz's three managerial skills (technical, human, conceptual); Bloom's taxonomy of learning domains (cognitive/knowledge, psychomotor/skills, affective/attitude); Kirkpatrick's four levels of training evaluation (reaction, learning, behaviour, results); Maslow, Herzberg and Vroom motivation theories; Human Resource Development (HRD) concept introduced by Leonard Nadler in 1969. Performance = f(ability × motivation × opportunity). Distinguish: aptitude (potential to learn), skill (learned proficiency), ability (current capacity to perform), attitude (disposition), talent (innate gift), competency (integrated bundle), performance (outcome). UPSC often asks such definitional HRM questions, so know the distinctions precisely.

question: An organization outlines the academic qualifications required for a position of Deputy Director. This outlining of qualifications is technically known as :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: In HRM, job analysis is the systematic study of a job and yields two outputs: the job description and the job specification. The job description is job-oriented. It covers the job title, location, duties, tasks, responsibilities, reporting relationships, working conditions and tools used. The job specification, also called the person or employee specification, is person-oriented. It sets out the minimum acceptable human qualities: education, academic qualifications, experience, skills, knowledge, physical and mental abilities, and personality traits. Recruitment and selection advertisements use it to screen candidates. The question asks about the academic qualifications required of the incumbent, so it is a job specification. Elimination: job design (b) is about structuring tasks to improve motivation and efficiency, through job enlargement, enrichment, rotation or simplification. Job description (c) states what the job involves, not who should hold it. Job knowledge (d) is the understanding an employee has of the job, not a formal document. Hence (a).
explanations: Correct. Job specification lists the qualifications, education, experience and skills required of the jobholder, which is what the question describes.
Incorrect. Job design is the arrangement of tasks, duties and responsibilities to improve productivity and satisfaction. It does not list qualifications.
Incorrect. Job description lists the duties, tasks, responsibilities and conditions of the job, not the qualifications of the person.
Incorrect. Job knowledge is an employee's understanding of the work and is not a document outlining qualifications.
keyfact: Job description = duties of the job; job specification = qualifications of the person.
option_notes: Job specification is a written statement of the minimum qualifications, education, experience, skills, abilities and traits needed to perform a job successfully. It is a product of job analysis and is person-oriented. It is used in recruitment, selection and placement, and in advertisements for posts. It is often split into essential and desirable qualifications.

Job design is the process of deciding the content, methods and relationships of jobs to meet organizational and individual needs. Techniques include job simplification, job rotation, job enlargement (horizontal loading) and job enrichment (vertical loading, associated with Herzberg). It also covers the Hackman-Oldham job characteristics model and ergonomics-based design.

Job description is a written statement of what the jobholder actually does, how, and why. It includes the job title, summary, duties, responsibilities, authority, reporting lines, working conditions and equipment. It is job-oriented and is prepared from job analysis data. It is used for orientation, performance appraisal and job evaluation.

Job knowledge refers to the technical and practical understanding an employee has of the duties, procedures, tools and rules of their role. It is a performance appraisal factor and a component of competence (KSA: knowledge, skills, abilities). It is not a formal document that outlines qualifications.
related: Job analysis produces the job description and the job specification.
Job description is job-oriented, while job specification is person-oriented.
Job enrichment (vertical loading) is linked to Herzberg's two-factor theory.
Job enlargement means adding more tasks of a similar level (horizontal loading).
Job rotation moves employees across jobs to reduce monotony and build skills.
Job evaluation determines the relative worth of jobs for pay structures.
KSA stands for Knowledge, Skills and Abilities.
PAQ (Position Analysis Questionnaire) is a quantitative job analysis tool developed by McCormick.
summary: The answer is (a) Job specification. A job specification lists the qualifications, education, skills, experience and personal traits a person needs to perform a job, so outlining the academic qualifications for Deputy Director is a job specification.
topic_notes: Job analysis is the starting point of human resource planning, recruitment, selection, training, appraisal and compensation. It is the systematic process of collecting information on a job's duties, responsibilities, working conditions and the human requirements for it. Methods of data collection include observation, interview, questionnaire, the diary or log method, the critical incident technique, the technical conference method and work sampling. Formal tools include the Position Analysis Questionnaire (PAQ, McCormick), Functional Job Analysis (FJA) and the Management Position Description Questionnaire (MPDQ). The outputs are the job description (what the job is), the job specification (who can do it) and sometimes a job evaluation or job classification. Related ideas are job design (enlargement, enrichment, rotation, simplification), job evaluation (ranking, classification, point and factor comparison methods, which determine the relative worth of jobs for pay) and role analysis. Some texts add a third output, the job standard or performance standard, which sets the expected level of performance. Recruitment follows with sources such as internal promotions and transfers, and external advertisements, campus hiring and employment exchanges. Selection tools include tests, interviews and reference checks. UPSC often tests distinctions: description is job-oriented, specification is person-oriented, and design is about structuring work. Also remember the terms KSA and KSAO (knowledge, skills, abilities and other characteristics), which are the contents of a specification.

question:
Which among the following are parts of on-the-job training ? 1 Role play 2 Multimedia simulation
3. Apprenticeship 4 Internship 5 Job rotation Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Training methods in HRM are classified by where learning takes place. On-the-job (OJT) training happens at the actual workplace, during real work, usually under a supervisor, mentor or senior. Typical OJT methods are coaching, mentoring, job rotation, job instruction training (JIT), understudy or assistantship, apprenticeship, internship, committee assignments and temporary promotions. Off-the-job training takes place away from the immediate work setting, in classrooms or simulated environments. Typical methods are lectures, conferences, seminars, case studies, role play, simulation (including multimedia/computer simulation), vestibule training, sensitivity training, programmed instruction, business games and in-basket exercises. Applying this to the question: Role play (1) is a behavioural, off-the-job method in which participants act out situations. Multimedia simulation (2) imitates real work conditions with technology and is off-the-job. Apprenticeship (3), internship (4) and job rotation (5) all involve working in real jobs while learning. So the items 3, 4 and 5 form the correct set. Option (a) is wrong because role play is off-the-job. Options (b) and (d) are wrong because (b) omits job rotation and (d) includes multimedia simulation.
explanations: Wrong: it includes role play (1), which is an off-the-job method, and omits apprenticeship and internship.
Wrong: apprenticeship and internship are on-the-job, but job rotation (5) is also an on-the-job method and is missing from this option.
Correct: apprenticeship, internship and job rotation all involve learning while performing real work at the workplace.
Wrong: multimedia simulation (2) is an off-the-job method, and job rotation is left out.
keyfact: On-the-job: apprenticeship, internship, job rotation, coaching, mentoring. Off-the-job: role play, simulation, lectures, case study.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 and 5 only, pairs role play with job rotation. Role play is an off-the-job behavioural technique in which participants act out situations to build interpersonal skills; it comes from psychodrama (Moreno). Job rotation is on-the-job. Because the pair mixes the two categories, this option is wrong.

Option (b), 3 and 4 only, lists apprenticeship (Apprentices Act, 1961) and internship. Both are valid on-the-job methods, but the set is incomplete because job rotation is also on-the-job. Apprenticeship is statutory and stipend-based; internship is short-term practical exposure, usually for students.

Option (c), 3, 4 and 5, is the correct answer. It lists apprenticeship, internship and job rotation, all of which involve learning while working in the real workplace. Other on-the-job methods are coaching, mentoring, understudy, job instruction training and temporary assignments.

Option (d), 2, 3 and 4, includes multimedia simulation, which is off-the-job because it uses a simulated environment such as software, video or simulators. It resembles vestibule training. Apprenticeship and internship are on-the-job, but job rotation is missing, so the option is wrong.
related: Apprentices Act, 1961 governs apprenticeship training in India.
NAPS (National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme) was launched in 2016.
Vestibule training uses a replica of the workplace, and it is off-the-job.
Case study, lecture and sensitivity training are off-the-job methods.
Coaching, mentoring and understudy are on-the-job methods.
Kirkpatrick's four levels: reaction, learning, behaviour, results.
Job rotation helps with cross-training and succession planning.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Role play is an off-the-job method. Role play is a training technique in which trainees act out assigned roles in a hypothetical situation, such as a manager-subordinate conversation, a customer complaint or a negotiation. It was developed from psychodrama (J. L. Moreno) and is used to build interpersonal, communication, leadership and counselling skills. Trainers and peers give feedback afterwards. It is done in a classroom-like setting, away from actual work, and is classed as a behaviour-modelling or experiential method. It is common in sales, customer service and supervisory training.

2 — Incorrect: Multimedia simulation is an off-the-job method. Simulation training reproduces real work conditions in an artificial environment so trainees can practise without risk or cost to the organisation. Multimedia or computer-based simulation uses software, video, VR or simulators, such as flight simulators for pilots or machine-operation simulators. It is related to vestibule training. It is useful where errors on the real job would be dangerous or costly, as in aviation, defence, medicine and heavy industry. Trainees learn away from the actual workplace.

3 — Correct: Apprenticeship is an on-the-job method. Apprenticeship combines paid work with structured learning, usually under a skilled craftsperson, for skilled trades. In India it is governed by the Apprentices Act, 1961, amended in 1973, 1986 and 2014, with the aim of training in designated trades. Duration ranges from six months to four years depending on the trade. The apprentice receives a stipend, not a wage, and has no guarantee of employment. The scheme is run by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship. NAPS (National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme) was launched in 2016, and NATS covers graduate and diploma apprentices. Learning takes place at the real workplace.

4 — Correct: Internship is an on-the-job method. An internship is a short-term practical placement, typically for students or fresh graduates, in which they work in an organisation to gain exposure and experience. Interns work on real tasks under supervision, and the period is often tied to a degree or diploma requirement. It may be paid or unpaid. It differs from apprenticeship because it has no formal trade-based statutory framework and no guarantee of a job. The government's PM Internship Scheme was announced in the Budget of 2024-25. Learning occurs in the actual work setting.

5 — Correct: Job rotation is an on-the-job method. Job rotation moves employees systematically from one job or department to another over a set period so they acquire varied skills, broader perspective and an understanding of interdependence between functions. It is used in management development and for succession planning, and it reduces boredom and monotony. It can lower the depth of specialisation if overdone, and it needs planning to avoid disrupting work. It is also called cross-training. Learning happens through actual work, so it is classed as on-the-job.
summary: The answer is (c) 3, 4 and 5. Apprenticeship, internship and job rotation are on-the-job methods because the trainee learns while working in the real workplace. Role play and multimedia simulation are off-the-job methods, since they take place in a simulated setting away from actual work.
topic_notes: Training is a planned effort to improve the knowledge, skills and attitudes of employees for their present job. Development prepares them for future roles. Methods are divided into on-the-job and off-the-job. On-the-job training (OJT) takes place at the workplace during actual work. Its advantages are low cost, immediate relevance, learning by doing and no transfer-of-training problem. Its disadvantages are disruption of work, poor teaching skill in some supervisors and the risk of damage or errors. Main OJT methods are coaching, mentoring, job instruction training (JIT, with four steps: prepare, present, try-out, follow-up), job rotation, understudy, apprenticeship, internship and committee assignments. Off-the-job training takes place away from the work setting. Its methods include lectures, conferences, seminars, case study, role play, simulation, vestibule training, sensitivity (T-group) training, programmed instruction, business games, in-basket exercise and e-learning. It allows focused learning without work pressure but is costlier and has transfer-of-learning issues. Vestibule training uses a replica of the work area, with equipment, for example in training of machine operators or typists. The Kirkpatrick model evaluates training at four levels: reaction, learning, behaviour and results. Phillips added a fifth level, ROI. The training process steps are needs assessment (organisational, task and person analysis), design, delivery and evaluation. Related Indian provisions are the Apprentices Act, 1961; NAPS; Skill India Mission (2015); and the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC). UPSC may ask the classification of a method, the definition of a specific method, or the evaluation models.

question: When an organization has a policy to declare ‘Employee of the Month’, it is trying to motivate the employees by trying to fulfil their :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Maslow's hierarchy of needs (A.H. Maslow, 1943, 'A Theory of Human Motivation') arranges human needs in five levels: physiological, safety, social (belongingness/love), esteem and self-actualization. A lower need must be reasonably satisfied before the next level motivates behaviour, and a satisfied need no longer motivates. Esteem needs have two parts: internal (self-respect, autonomy, achievement, competence) and external (status, recognition, attention, prestige, appreciation from others). An 'Employee of the Month' award publicly acknowledges performance, confers status and boosts self-worth, so it directly serves esteem needs. Other tools that serve esteem needs are promotions, titles, awards, certificates and recognition programmes. Elimination: safety needs concern job security, pay stability, safe working conditions and pensions, which are not touched by an award. Social needs concern friendship, teamwork, belonging and group acceptance. Self-actualization concerns realising one's full potential, creativity and growth, which is addressed by challenging assignments and development opportunities rather than by a monthly recognition. Hence (c).
explanations: Wrong: safety needs relate to job security, stable income, benefits and a safe workplace; an award does not address these.
Wrong: social needs relate to belonging, friendship and team acceptance; the award singles out an individual for recognition rather than building affiliation.
Correct: the award gives recognition, status and respect, which are the external esteem needs, and it also raises self-respect.
Wrong: self-actualization is the highest need, met by personal growth, creativity and fulfilling one's potential; recognition awards are not primarily aimed at it.
keyfact: Employee of the Month = recognition and status = Maslow's esteem needs (fourth level).
option_notes: Safety needs are the second level of Maslow's hierarchy. They cover protection from physical harm, economic security, job security, health and insurance, and pensions. In organisations they are met by permanent employment, social security schemes (such as ESI and EPF), safe working conditions and fair pay.

Social needs (belongingness and love) form the third level. They cover affection, friendship, acceptance and being part of a group. Organisations satisfy them through teamwork, social events, good supervisor relations, informal groups and a cordial workplace culture.

Esteem needs form the fourth level. They are of two types: internal (self-respect, achievement, autonomy) and external (status, recognition, prestige, attention). Organisations meet them through awards, titles, promotions, praise, responsibility and public recognition such as Employee of the Month.

Self-actualization is the top level of Maslow's hierarchy. It is the drive to become all one is capable of: realising potential, creativity, self-fulfilment and growth. It is met by challenging work, autonomy, learning opportunities and creative tasks. Maslow held that it is never fully satisfied.
related: Maslow published his hierarchy in 1943 in Psychological Review.
Esteem needs include both self-respect and recognition from others.
Alderfer's ERG theory compresses Maslow's five needs into three: existence, relatedness and growth.
Herzberg's two-factor theory separates hygiene factors from motivators; recognition is a motivator.
McClelland's theory covers the needs for achievement, power and affiliation.
Vroom's expectancy theory is a process theory built on valence, instrumentality and expectancy.
Self-actualization is the highest level of Maslow's hierarchy.
summary: The answer is (c) Esteem needs. 'Employee of the Month' gives public recognition, status and respect, which are the core of esteem needs in Maslow's hierarchy.
topic_notes: Maslow's need hierarchy (1943) is the best-known content theory of motivation. The five levels, from lowest to highest, are physiological (food, water, shelter, rest), safety (security, stability), social/belonging, esteem and self-actualization. The first two are often called lower-order needs and the rest higher-order needs. Key assumptions are that behaviour is motivated by unsatisfied needs, that needs are satisfied in a rising order of priority, and that a satisfied need stops motivating. Criticisms are that the order is not rigid, that it lacks strong empirical support, and that it is culture-bound. Related theories UPSC may ask about: Alderfer's ERG theory (Existence, Relatedness, Growth), which allows frustration-regression and several needs at once; Herzberg's two-factor theory (hygiene factors versus motivators); McClelland's need for achievement, power and affiliation; McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y; Vroom's expectancy theory (process theory); Adams' equity theory; Skinner's reinforcement theory; and Locke's goal-setting theory. Mapping to workplace practice: physiological needs are met by wages and canteens; safety needs by job security and social security; social needs by teams and social events; esteem needs by recognition, awards and titles; self-actualization by challenging work and growth. In Herzberg's terms, recognition and achievement are motivators, while salary and working conditions are hygiene factors.

ocr: A person who desires to obtain any/84. information under the RTI Act, 2005 has to make an application accompanied by a prescribed fee. What is the fee prescribed under Rule 3 of the RTI Rules, 2012 ? (a) =10 (b) = 20 (oc). S25 (d) 50 85.
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Section 6(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 requires a person who wants information to apply in writing or electronically, with the prescribed fee, to the Public Information Officer (PIO) of the public authority. The Right to Information Rules, 2012 were notified by the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) and replaced the earlier 2005 Fee Rules. Rule 3 fixes the application fee at ₹10. Rule 4 sets the fee for providing information: ₹2 per page (A4 or A3 size) created or copied, actual cost for larger sizes, actual cost or price for samples and models, and, for inspection of records, no fee for the first hour and ₹5 for each subsequent hour or fraction of it. Information on a floppy or diskette costs ₹50. Printed publications are charged at their price, or ₹2 per page for photocopies of extracts. Applicants below the poverty line (BPL) pay no fee, provided they attach proof. Payment can be made in cash against a receipt, by demand draft, banker's cheque or Indian Postal Order, or online through the RTI portal. Elimination: ₹20, ₹25 and ₹50 are not the application fee under the Rules. ₹50 is the fee for information supplied on a floppy or diskette, a distractor taken from the same Rules.
explanations: Correct. Rule 3 of the RTI Rules, 2012 prescribes ₹10 as the application fee, as the official answer confirms.
Incorrect. ₹20 is not the fee prescribed under Rule 3. Some state RTI rules and old fee structures used different amounts, but the Central Rules say ₹10.
Incorrect. ₹25 is not the fee prescribed under Rule 3 of the Central RTI Rules, 2012.
Incorrect. ₹50 is the fee for information supplied on a floppy or diskette under Rule 4, not the application fee under Rule 3.
keyfact: RTI Rules, 2012, Rule 3: application fee is ₹10; copies cost ₹2 per page; BPL applicants pay nothing.
option_notes: ₹10 is the application fee for a request to a Central Public Authority under Rule 3 of the RTI Rules, 2012. It is paid in cash, by DD, banker's cheque or IPO, or online through the RTI portal (rtionline.gov.in). BPL applicants are exempt if they provide proof. State governments frame their own rules and fees, which vary: for example, ₹10 in many states and different amounts in others.

₹20 is not a fee under the Central RTI Rules, 2012. It is a plausible distractor, and some state rules or other fee schedules may use similar amounts. Do not confuse it with the Central application fee, which is ₹10. The per-page copy charge under Rule 4 is ₹2, not ₹20.

₹25 is not a prescribed fee in the Central RTI Rules, 2012. It serves only as a distractor. Remember the Central fee structure: ₹10 application fee, ₹2 per page copy, ₹50 for a diskette or floppy, and ₹5 per hour of inspection after the first free hour.

₹50 is the fee prescribed under Rule 4 of the RTI Rules, 2012 for providing information on a floppy or diskette. It is not the application fee. Candidates often mix it up with the application fee, which is ₹10. Larger-size paper, samples and models are charged at actual cost.
related: Application fee under the Central RTI Rules, 2012: ₹10.
Copy fee: ₹2 per page (A4 or A3 size).
Inspection of records: first hour free, then ₹5 per hour or fraction.
Floppy or diskette: ₹50.
BPL applicants are exempt from fees if they provide proof.
Normal time limit for a reply: 30 days; for life or liberty matters: 48 hours.
First appeal within 30 days; second appeal to the Information Commission within 90 days.
Penalty on PIO: ₹250 per day, up to a maximum of ₹25,000 (Section 20).
summary: The correct answer is (a) ₹10. Rule 3 of the RTI Rules, 2012 (Right to Information Rules, 2012, framed by the Central Government under Section 27) prescribes an application fee of ₹10 for requesting information from a Central Public Authority.
topic_notes: The Right to Information Act, 2005 came into force fully on 12 October 2005. It gives citizens the right to access information held by public authorities, promoting transparency and accountability. Key sections: Section 4 (proactive disclosure); Section 5 (designation of PIOs and APIOs); Section 6 (request for information); Section 7 (disposal of requests: 30 days normally, 48 hours for life or liberty matters); Section 8 (exemptions); Section 9 (grounds for rejection); Section 10 (severability); Section 11 (third-party information); Sections 12-14 (Central Information Commission, its constitution and removal of members); Sections 15-17 (State Information Commissions); Section 18 (powers and functions of the Commissions); Section 19 (first appeal within 30 days to an officer senior to the PIO, second appeal to the Information Commission within 90 days); Section 20 (penalty of ₹250 per day up to ₹25,000 on the PIO); Section 22 (overriding effect over the Official Secrets Act); Section 24 (exempt organisations, such as intelligence and security bodies in the Second Schedule, except for corruption and human rights violations); Section 27 (appropriate Government's rule-making power); Section 28 (competent authority's rule-making power). Under Section 8(2), information may be disclosed if the public interest outweighs the harm. Under the Right to Information (Amendment) Act, 2019, the tenure, salary and service conditions of Information Commissioners are decided by the Central Government. The Chief Information Commissioner is appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee of the PM, the Leader of Opposition and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM. The RTI Rules, 2012 replaced the earlier 2005 Fee Rules. Rule 3 sets the application fee, and Rule 4 sets the fees for further information, including ₹2 per page and the inspection charges.

question: What is the total amount of penalty that the Central or a State Information Commission can impose on any Central or State Public Information Officer for refusing to receive an application or not furnishing information within the specified time without any reasonable cause ?
options: There is no specific upper limit 86
subject: Insurance
detail: Section 20(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 empowers the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission, while deciding a complaint or appeal, to penalise a Central or State Public Information Officer. Grounds: refusing to receive an application, not furnishing information within the time specified in Section 7(1) (30 days), malafide denial of a request, knowingly giving incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, destroying information that was the subject of the request, or obstructing the furnishing of information. The penalty is Rs 250 per day until the application is received or the information is furnished, and the total cannot exceed Rs 25,000. The PIO must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and the burden of proving that he acted reasonably and diligently lies on the PIO. Section 20(2) is separate: for persistent default the Commission recommends disciplinary action under the service rules against the PIO. Elimination: Rs 5,000 and Rs 50,000 are not the statutory ceiling, and the claim of no upper limit is wrong because the Act expressly caps the penalty at Rs 25,000. Penalty is imposed by the Commission, not by the appellate authority under Section 19(1) or 19(2).
explanations: Incorrect: Rs 5,000 is not the cap in Section 20(1). The cap is Rs 25,000.
Correct: Rs 250 per day of delay, up to a maximum of Rs 25,000, is the penalty under Section 20(1) of the RTI Act.
Incorrect: Rs 50,000 exceeds the statutory ceiling. The Act does not provide for this amount.
Incorrect: The Act expressly specifies an upper limit of Rs 25,000, so there is a specific limit.
keyfact: RTI Section 20(1): Rs 250 per day of default, capped at Rs 25,000 total.
option_notes: Rs 5,000 is not a figure prescribed for PIO penalty under the RTI Act. It is a distractor. Some other statutes use different small penalty ceilings, but under Section 20(1) the cap is Rs 25,000. Do not confuse it with the daily rate of Rs 250, which is the base for the calculation.

Rs 25,000 is the maximum total penalty under Section 20(1) of the RTI Act, 2005. It accrues at Rs 250 per day, so the cap is reached after 100 days of default. The Central or State Information Commission imposes it after hearing the PIO, who bears the burden of proving reasonable cause.

Rs 50,000 is not provided in the RTI Act as the penalty ceiling. It is a distractor with double the real cap. Penalties under the Act are fixed at Rs 250 per day with a Rs 25,000 limit, and the Commission has no power to go beyond that figure.

This option is wrong because Section 20(1) contains a proviso-based cap of Rs 25,000. In practice the Commission can also recommend disciplinary action under Section 20(2), but that is separate from the monetary penalty and does not remove the cap on the fine.
related: Penalty under RTI Section 20(1): Rs 250 per day, maximum Rs 25,000.
Section 20(2) allows the Commission to recommend disciplinary action against a persistent defaulter PIO.
Standard time to supply information: 30 days; 48 hours for matters of life or liberty.
First appeal within 30 days; second appeal to the Commission within 90 days.
RTI Act enacted 15 June 2005 and fully effective 12 October 2005.
Section 24 exempts intelligence and security organisations, except for corruption and human rights violation allegations.
CIC appointment committee: Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM.
The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 gave the Centre power to fix the tenure and salary of Information Commissioners.
summary: The answer is (b) Rs 25,000. Under Section 20(1) of the RTI Act, 2005, the Information Commission can impose a penalty of Rs 250 per day of delay on the PIO, subject to a maximum total of Rs 25,000.
topic_notes: The Right to Information Act, 2005 came into force fully on 12 October 2005. It gives citizens a right to access information held by public authorities. Key structure: Section 4 (proactive disclosure), Section 5 (designation of PIOs and APIOs), Section 6 (request for information), Section 7 (disposal: 30 days; 48 hours if life or liberty is concerned), Section 8 (exemptions), Section 9 (copyright), Section 10 (severability), Section 11 (third-party information), Section 12 (Central Information Commission constitution), Section 13 (term and service conditions), Section 15 (State Information Commissions), Section 18 (powers and functions of Commissions, complaints), Section 19 (appeals: first appeal to the senior officer within 30 days, second appeal to the Commission within 90 days), Section 20 (penalties), Section 22 (overriding effect), Section 23 (bar on court jurisdiction), and Section 24 (exempt organisations, such as intelligence and security bodies, though corruption and human rights violation information must still be given). The application fee under the Central rules is Rs 10. No reasons need to be given for seeking information. BPL applicants pay no fee. Section 8(2) permits disclosure where public interest outweighs harm. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed the tenure, salary and service conditions of Information Commissioners, giving the Centre the power to prescribe them. Previously the term was five years or up to age 65, with salary equal to Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 amended Section 8(1)(j) on personal information. Future questions may test time limits, exemptions, the appointment committee (PM, Leader of Opposition, a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM) and the first Chief Information Commissioner, Wajahat Habibullah.

question: The Chief Information Commissioner and the Information Commissioners are appointed by the President of India on the recommendations of a Committee. Who is the Chairperson of that Committee ?
options: The Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Section 12 of the RTI Act, 2005 provides for the Central Information Commission (CIC), constituted by the Central Government through a gazette notification (the CIC was set up on 12 October 2005). Section 12(3) says the President appoints the Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioners on the recommendation of a Committee consisting of (i) the Prime Minister, who is the Chairperson, (ii) the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and (iii) a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister. If there is no recognised Leader of Opposition, the leader of the single largest opposition group in the Lok Sabha acts as the member. Candidates must be persons of eminence in public life with wide knowledge and experience in law, science and technology, social service, management, journalism, mass media, or administration and governance, and must not be MPs, MLAs or hold any office of profit. The Chief Justice of India and the Speaker are not on this committee; the CJI is part of the committees for the CBI Director and Lokpal selection. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed the tenure, salary and service conditions, which are now decided by the Central Government (earlier a 5-year term, or up to age 65, and status equal to the Election Commissioners). Elimination: (b) and (d) are not members at all, and (c) is only a member, not the chair. So (a) is correct.
explanations: Correct: Section 12(3) of the RTI Act makes the Prime Minister the Chairperson of the selection committee for the CIC and Information Commissioners.
Wrong: The Chief Justice of India is not a member of the CIC selection committee. The CJI sits on committees for the CBI Director, the Lokpal and others.
Wrong: The Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha is a committee member, but not its Chairperson.
Wrong: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha has no role in this committee. The Speaker is involved in Lokpal selection and other bodies, not the CIC.
keyfact: CIC and Information Commissioners are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee chaired by the Prime Minister (Section 12(3), RTI Act, 2005).
option_notes: The Prime Minister is the head of the Union Council of Ministers under Article 74 and is appointed by the President under Article 75. The PM chairs the CIC selection committee under Section 12(3) of the RTI Act, 2005. The PM also chairs the selection committees for the Lokpal, the CBI Director (with the CJI and the Leader of Opposition), and the CVC and Vigilance Commissioners. The PM heads the NITI Aayog and the Cabinet.

The Chief Justice of India heads the Supreme Court of India (Article 124) and is appointed by the President. The CJI is a member of the selection committees for the CBI Director, the Lokpal, and (since 2023) the Election Commissioners, but not of the CIC committee. The CJI administers the oath to the Chief Justices of High Courts and is the master of the roster. The retirement age is 65 years.

The Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha is a statutory post under the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977. The party must hold at least 10 percent of the seats (the convention based on the Mavalankar rule). The Leader is a member of the committees for the CIC, CVC, Lokpal, CBI Director and NHRC. The post has Cabinet-rank status and is a shadow-cabinet-type role.

The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by the members of the House from among themselves (Article 93). The Speaker presides over sittings, decides on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, certifies Money Bills, and chairs the Business Advisory Committee and the Rules Committee. The Speaker has a casting vote only in case of a tie. The Speaker is not part of the CIC selection committee but is a member of the NHRC selection committee.
related: Section 12(3) of the RTI Act, 2005 governs the appointment of the CIC and Information Commissioners.
The selection committee has three members: the PM (Chair), the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM.
The RTI Act was passed in 2005 and came into full force on 12 October 2005.
The first Chief Information Commissioner was Wajahat Habibullah.
The Central Information Commission can have up to 10 Information Commissioners besides the Chief.
The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 gave the Centre the power to decide the tenure and salaries of Information Commissioners.
State Information Commissioners are appointed by the Governor on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Chief Minister.
The penalty under RTI is Rs 250 per day, up to a maximum of Rs 25,000.
summary: The correct answer is (a) The Prime Minister. Under Section 12(3) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, the CIC and Information Commissioners are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee chaired by the Prime Minister.
topic_notes: The Right to Information Act, 2005 was enacted on 15 June 2005 and came into full force on 12 October 2005. It gives citizens the right to access information held by public authorities. The Central Information Commission (CIC) is a statutory body, not a constitutional one. Its headquarters are in New Delhi. It consists of a Chief Information Commissioner and up to 10 Information Commissioners. The State Information Commissions are set up under Section 15. The State Chief Information Commissioner and State Information Commissioners are appointed by the Governor on the recommendation of a committee comprising the Chief Minister (Chairperson), the Leader of Opposition in the Legislative Assembly, and a Cabinet Minister nominated by the Chief Minister. Important features: Public Information Officers (PIOs) must reply within 30 days (48 hours for matters of life and liberty). The first appeal goes to a senior officer in the department, and the second appeal goes to the CIC or SIC within 90 days. The penalty for delay or refusal is Rs 250 per day, up to a maximum of Rs 25,000. Section 8 lists the exemptions (national security, Cabinet papers, etc.) and Section 24 exempts certain intelligence and security organisations, though information on corruption and human rights violations must still be given. The Act does not apply to Jammu and Kashmir in its original form, which was changed after the Reorganisation Act, 2019. The 2019 Amendment gave the Centre control over the tenure and salaries of information commissioners. A CIC or commissioner can be removed by the President on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity after a Supreme Court inquiry (Section 14). Notable cases include CPIO v. Subhash Chandra Agrawal (2019), which held that the CJI's office comes under the RTI Act, and Anjali Bhardwaj v. Union of India (2019), on filling vacancies in the information commissions. The first CIC was Wajahat Habibullah.

question: In case the information sought for under the RTI Act, 2005 concerns the life or liberty of a person, the same shall ordinarily be provided within how many hours of the receipt of the request ?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Section 7(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 requires the Public Information Officer (PIO) to dispose of a request as expeditiously as possible, and in any case within 30 days of receipt. The proviso carves out an exception: where the information sought concerns the life or liberty of a person, it shall be provided within forty-eight hours. Since this is a statutory time limit, the figure of 48 hours is fixed by law and cannot be varied by the authority. Related timelines a student must know: 35 days if the request is received through the Assistant PIO (Section 5(2)); 30 days for a request transferred to another authority under Section 6(3), counted from the transfer; 40 days for third-party information under Section 7(1) read with Section 11, where the third party has been given notice; and 45 days for information relating to allegations of corruption and human rights violations by the security and intelligence organisations in the Second Schedule, which is provided only with the approval of the Central or State Information Commission (Section 24). The first appeal lies within 30 days. Elimination: 24 hours and 12 hours are shorter than the statute provides, and 72 hours is longer. Only 48 hours matches the proviso.
explanations: 72 hours is incorrect. The statute does not prescribe 72 hours for any RTI timeline, and it exceeds the 48-hour limit set for life or liberty cases.

48 hours is correct. The proviso to Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 requires information concerning the life or liberty of a person to be provided within forty-eight hours of receipt of the request.
24 hours is incorrect. It is shorter than the statutory limit, and the Act does not prescribe it for any RTI request.
12 hours is incorrect. The Act does not prescribe it, and the life or liberty limit is 48 hours.
keyfact: RTI life or liberty information: 48 hours (Section 7(1) proviso); normal limit is 30 days.
option_notes: 72 hours is not a timeline under the RTI Act. It is often confused with other legal periods, such as the 72-hour window for reporting certain data breaches under foreign laws. Under the RTI Act the main limits are 48 hours, 30 days, 35 days, 40 days and 45 days.

48 hours is the period within which a PIO must provide information concerning the life or liberty of a person, under the proviso to Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005. The Act came into force fully on 12 October 2005. Examples include information on a person's arrest, detention or imminent threat to life.

24 hours is not a statutory time limit under the RTI Act. It is sometimes confused with the arrest rule in Article 22(2), which requires an arrested person to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours, excluding travel time.
12 hours is not a time limit under the RTI Act. No provision of the Act sets such a short period. The shortest statutory period is 48 hours for life or liberty cases.
related: Section 7(1) proviso: 48 hours for life or liberty information
General RTI reply time: 30 days
Request through an Assistant PIO: 35 days
Second appeal to the Information Commission: within 90 days
Penalty under Section 20: Rs 250 per day, maximum Rs 25,000
Section 24 exempts the Second Schedule organisations, except on corruption and human rights violations
RTI Act came into full force on 12 October 2005
summary: The answer is (b) 48 hours. Under the proviso to Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005, where the information sought concerns the life or liberty of a person, it must be provided within 48 hours of receipt of the request. The normal limit is 30 days.
topic_notes: The Right to Information Act, 2005 was enacted on 15 June 2005 and came into full force on 12 October 2005. It gives citizens a statutory right to access information held by public authorities, and it is derived from Article 19(1)(a), as the Supreme Court recognised in cases such as Raj Narain and S.P. Gupta. Key machinery: each public authority designates Public Information Officers (PIOs) and Assistant PIOs (Section 5). A request is made under Section 6, with a prescribed fee (Rs 10 for central authorities); persons below the poverty line are exempt. Time limits under Section 7: 30 days in general; 48 hours for life or liberty; 35 days if the request is received through an APIO; 40 days where third-party information is involved. Section 8 lists exemptions, for example information affecting sovereignty and integrity, security, or Cabinet papers, and Section 8(2) allows disclosure where public interest outweighs the harm. Section 9 covers copyright, and Section 10 severability. Section 11 covers third-party information. Section 24 exempts the intelligence and security organisations listed in the Second Schedule, but not information on corruption or human rights violations. Appeals: the first appeal goes to a senior officer within 30 days, and the second appeal to the Information Commission within 90 days. Section 20 provides a penalty of Rs 250 per day, up to a maximum of Rs 25,000, for delay or refusal. The Central Information Commission (Section 12) consists of the Chief Information Commissioner and up to 10 Information Commissioners. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed their tenure and service conditions, which are now fixed by the Central Government. Section 4 requires proactive disclosure. Section 6(3) deals with transfer of requests.

ocr: Under the RTI Act, 2005, an applicant making request for information shall be required to give: 1. His contact details 2. His personal details 3. Reasons for requesting the information Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2and 3 only (c) land 2 only (d) 1,2and3 Every public authority under the RTI Act, 2005, shall designate as many officers as Central Public Information Officers or State Public Information Officers, as the case may be, in all administrative units or offices under it as may be necessary to provide information to persons requesting for information
subject: Insurance
detail: Section 6(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 lets a person request information in writing or by electronic means, in English, Hindi or the official language of the area, to the Public Information Officer (PIO), with the prescribed fee. Section 6(2) is the key provision: the applicant shall not be required to give any reason for requesting the information or any other personal details except those that may be necessary for contacting him. The Act is built on transparency and citizen empowerment, so the applicant's motive is irrelevant. Only a postal address, e-mail or phone number is needed so the PIO can reply. This rules out statement 3 (reasons) and statement 2 (wider personal details such as caste, occupation, ID or income). Any option containing 2 or 3, namely (b), (c) and (d), is therefore wrong. Only 1 is correct, which gives (a). Related points: if the request cannot be made in writing, the PIO must help the person reduce it to writing (Section 6(1) proviso). A request sent to the wrong authority must be transferred within 5 days (Section 6(3)). The usual time limit for a reply is 30 days (Section 7(1)), or 48 hours where life or liberty is involved.
explanations: Correct. Only contact details are mandatory under Section 6(2), so 1 only is right and it matches the official answer.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, and reasons for the request are not required. It also leaves out statement 1, which is required.
Wrong. Statement 2 (general personal details) is not required beyond contact particulars, and it omits nothing correct except 1 itself, so it is not the best answer.
Wrong. It includes both 2 and 3, and neither is required. Only 1 holds.
keyfact: RTI Section 6(2): no reasons and no personal details are needed, only contact details to receive the reply.
related: Section 6(2): no reason or personal details needed except contact details.
Section 5: PIOs to be designated within 100 days of enactment.
Section 7(1): reply within 30 days; 48 hours for life or liberty.
Section 19: first appeal within 30 days; second appeal within 90 days.

Section 24 and the Second Schedule exempt security and intelligence organisations.

statements: 1 — Correct: Contact details are the only particulars the applicant must give, because the PIO needs them to send the reply, fee demand or rejection order. Section 6(2) expressly permits 'such personal details as may be necessary for contacting him'. Facts: the RTI Act was enacted on 15 June 2005 and came fully into force on 12 October 2005. It applies to all of India except Jammu & Kashmir, which had its own Act until 2019 and is now covered by the central Act. The application fee is Rs 10 under the Central RTI Rules, 2012. A person below the poverty line (BPL) is exempt from the fee. The Act also provides for online filing through the RTI portal for central public authorities.

2 — Incorrect: The applicant need not give 'personal details' beyond what is needed for contact. Details such as caste, religion, occupation, income or ID proof cannot be demanded as a condition for accepting a request. Facts: Section 6(2) bars demands for anything except contact particulars. A PIO who refuses to accept an application may face a penalty under Section 20 of Rs 250 per day, up to a maximum of Rs 25,000. Some states have rules asking for ID, but the central framework does not require it. Personal information about third parties, however, is protected under Section 8(1)(j) if it has no public interest and would invade privacy. The 2023 Digital Personal Data Protection Act amended Section 8(1)(j).

3 — Incorrect: The applicant does not have to state why the information is wanted. The right to information is not linked to the applicant's motive. Facts: Section 6(2) says 'shall not be required to give any reason for requesting the information'. This distinguishes RTI from many foreign laws that demand purpose. Section 8 lists the exemptions from disclosure, and Section 9 allows refusal in case of copyright infringement. Section 24 exempts the intelligence and security organisations listed in the Second Schedule, except in cases of corruption and human rights violations. The appeal system is a first appeal to a senior officer within 30 days (Section 19(1)) and a second appeal to the Information Commission within 90 days (Section 19(3)).
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Under Section 6(2) of the RTI Act, 2005, an applicant need not give any reason for seeking information or any personal details, other than what is necessary to contact him or her. Only contact details are therefore required.
topic_notes: The Right to Information Act, 2005 gives citizens a legal right to access information held by public authorities. It was enacted on 15 June 2005 and came fully into force on 12 October 2005. It grew out of the MKSS movement in Rajasthan, the Tamil Nadu and Goa state laws, and the Freedom of Information Act, 2002, which was never notified. Section 2(h) defines 'public authority'. Section 2(f) defines 'information'. Section 2(j) defines the 'right to information'. Section 4 requires proactive disclosure. Section 5 requires every public authority to designate PIOs and APIOs within 100 days of enactment. Section 6 covers the request. Section 7 sets a 30-day reply limit, or 48 hours for matters of life and liberty. Section 8 lists the exemptions, including those affecting sovereignty, security, Cabinet papers, and information held in a fiduciary relationship. Section 8(2) provides that disclosure can be allowed where public interest outweighs the harm. Section 8(3) lifts the exemption for information more than 20 years old. Section 11 deals with third-party information. Section 12 governs the Central Information Commission (CIC), which has a Chief Information Commissioner and up to 10 Information Commissioners. Section 15 governs State Information Commissions. Section 18 covers complaints, and Section 19 covers appeals. Section 20 provides penalties. Section 22 gives the Act overriding effect. Section 23 bars the jurisdiction of courts, though the writ jurisdiction of the High Courts and Supreme Court remains. Section 24 exempts the intelligence and security organisations in the Second Schedule. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed the tenure and salaries of Information Commissioners, which are now set by the Centre. The Supreme Court has held RTI to be part of Article 19(1)(a) (Raj Narain case, S.P. Gupta case).

Reasons for requesting the information Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2and 3 only (c) land 2 only (d) 1,2and3 Every public authority under the RTI Act, 2005, shall designate as many officers as Central Public Information Officers or State Public Information Officers, as the case may be, in all administrative units or offices under it as may be necessary to provide information to persons requesting for information
subject: Insurance
detail: Section 5(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 says that every public authority shall, within one hundred days of the enactment of the Act, designate as many officers as Central Public Information Officers (CPIOs) or State Public Information Officers (SPIOs) in all administrative units or offices under it as may be necessary to provide information to persons requesting it. Section 5(2) requires every public authority to designate a Central or State Assistant Public Information Officer at each sub-divisional or sub-district level within the same 100 days. The APIO only receives applications and appeals and forwards them to the PIO or the appellate authority. The Act received Presidential assent on 15 June 2005, and most provisions came into force on 12 October 2005, the 120th day. Section 4(1)(b) proactive disclosure and Section 5 designation are both tied to this timeline, but Section 5 uses 100 days and Section 4 uses 120 days. Elimination: one month and forty-five days are far too short and appear nowhere in the Act. One year is far too long. Only 100 days matches Section 5(1). Remember the numbers 100 (PIO designation), 120 (Section 4 publication and commencement), 30 (reply) and 90 (second appeal).
explanations: Incorrect: one month is not the period in the Act. Section 5(1) gives 100 days. One month does appear elsewhere, in the 30-day reply time under Section 7(1).
Correct: Section 5(1) requires designation of CPIOs or SPIOs, and Section 5(2) requires APIOs, within one hundred days of the enactment of the Act.
Incorrect: one year is far longer than the statutory period. The Act was meant to be operational within about four months.

Incorrect: forty-five days is not used for designating officers. 45 days is the time for the Information Commission to decide a complaint under some rules, and the Act itself uses 30 and 45 days only in the appeal provisions of Section 19.
keyfact: RTI Act Section 5(1): PIOs/APIOs must be designated within 100 days of enactment, while Section 6(2) says no reason need be given for requesting information.
option_notes: One month (30 days) is the standard time for a PIO to reply to an RTI request under Section 7(1). It drops to 48 hours where the information concerns the life or liberty of a person. The first appeal under Section 19(1) must also be filed within 30 days of the decision or of the deadline for it. If the request goes through an APIO, 5 days are added to the reply period.

One hundred days is the period in Section 5(1) for designating PIOs and in Section 5(2) for APIOs. Under Section 5(1), each public authority designates PIOs in all administrative units or offices. Under Section 5(2), an APIO is designated at each sub-divisional or sub-district level. Section 5(3) says that APIOs receive applications or appeals and forward them to the PIO or the appellate authority. This period ran from the Act's enactment in June 2005.

One year is not a time limit set by the RTI Act for designation. A year does appear in Section 4(1)(b)-type discussions of implementation only loosely, and the Act sets no such deadline for officers. It is also the length of the Information Commission annual report cycle under Section 25, where the Commission reports each year to the government on the Act's implementation.

Forty-five days appears in Section 19(6), which says that the appeal shall be disposed of within 30 days, extendable to a maximum of 45 days, with written reasons. It is also the usual period within which a first appellate authority must dispose of an appeal. It has no role in designating officers, which is governed by 100 days under Section 5.

summary: The answer is (b), one hundred days. Section 5(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 requires every public authority to designate Central or State Public Information Officers in all its administrative units or offices within 100 days of the Act's enactment. The image shows two questions, and this note covers only the second, on designation of officers, which is the one the official answer (b) fits.
topic_notes: The Right to Information Act, 2005 is a central statute that gives citizens a legal right to information held by public authorities, in order to promote transparency and accountability. It received Presidential assent on 15 June 2005 and came fully into force on 12 October 2005. It replaced the Freedom of Information Act, 2002. It extends to the whole of India, and Jammu and Kashmir came under it after 2019 when the J&K Reorganisation Act extended central laws. Key sections: Section 2(h) defines a public authority, 2(j) defines the right to information, Section 3 gives the right to all citizens, Section 4 requires proactive disclosure and records management, Section 5 covers designation of PIOs and APIOs, and Section 6 governs the request. Under Section 6(2) the applicant need not give any reason for requesting the information or any personal details beyond what is necessary to contact him. Section 7 sets the reply time of 30 days, or 48 hours for matters of life and liberty. Section 8 lists exemptions such as national security, and Section 9 allows rejection on copyright grounds. Section 10 covers severability, Section 11 third-party information, Section 12 constitution of the Central Information Commission, and Section 15 the State Information Commissions. Section 18 covers complaints, Section 19 first and second appeals (the second appeal within 90 days), Section 20 penalties of Rs 250 per day up to Rs 25,000, Section 22 the overriding effect over the Official Secrets Act, and Section 24 exempts organisations listed in the Second Schedule, such as intelligence and security bodies, although they must still give information on corruption and human rights violations. The CIC consists of a Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 gave the Centre power to set the tenure, salaries and allowances of Information Commissioners. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 amended Section 8(1)(j) on personal information. The application fee under the central rules is Rs 10, and applicants below the poverty line pay no fee.

question:
The Right to Information, under the RTI Act, 90. 2005, includes the right to take : 8 Certified copies of documents ry Certified copies of records
3. Certified samples of materials Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Statistics
detail: Section 2(j) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 defines 'right to information' as the right to information accessible under the Act which is held by or under the control of any public authority. It includes the right to: (i) inspect work, documents and records; (ii) take notes, extracts or certified copies of documents or records; (iii) take certified samples of material; and (iv) obtain information in the form of diskettes, floppies, tapes, video cassettes or any other electronic mode, or through printouts where the information is stored in a computer or other device. The question's statements 1 (certified copies of documents), 2 (certified copies of records) and 3 (certified samples of material) match clause (ii) and clause (iii) of Section 2(j) word for word. Because every statement is supported by the statute, the combination containing all three is right. Options (a), (b) and (d) each leave out one valid item, so they are wrong. Related points: the Act came into force fully on 12 October 2005, Section 6 governs requests, Section 7 the time limit (30 days; 48 hours for life or liberty), and Section 8 the exemptions.
explanations: Wrong: it omits certified copies of records and certified samples of material, both of which Section 2(j) includes.
Wrong: it omits certified samples of material, which Section 2(j)(iii) expressly includes.
Correct: Section 2(j) covers certified copies of documents and records and certified samples of material, so all three statements are right.
Wrong: it leaves out certified copies of documents, which are expressly covered by Section 2(j)(ii).
keyfact: Section 2(j) of the RTI Act, 2005 covers inspection, notes, extracts, certified copies of documents and records, certified samples of material, and electronic-mode information.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: this would limit the right to certified copies of documents. The RTI Act is wider, because Section 2(j) lists inspection of work, documents and records; notes, extracts or certified copies; certified samples; and electronic-mode information. It is wrong because it treats the right as one narrow facility. Section 2(j) applies to information held by or under the control of any public authority, and Section 3 gives all citizens the right to information, not non-citizens or corporations as such.

Option (b) 1 and 2 only: this would recognise certified copies of documents and records but omit samples. The omission is the trap, since samples are in Section 2(j)(iii). Documents and records are closely linked: Section 2(i) defines a record broadly, including files, manuscripts, microfilm and computer-produced material. The statement is incomplete rather than false, which makes it the wrong choice here because the question asks for all that are included.

Option (c) 1, 2 and 3: this is the official answer. It matches Section 2(j) of the RTI Act, 2005, which lists inspection of work, documents and records; taking notes, extracts or certified copies; taking certified samples of material; and obtaining information via diskettes, floppies, tapes, video cassettes or other electronic modes or printouts. The Act was passed on 15 June 2005 and came into full force on 12 October 2005, replacing the Freedom of Information Act, 2002.

Option (d) 2 and 3 only: this would exclude certified copies of documents. It is wrong because Section 2(j)(ii) expressly names documents along with records. Students may be misled by the overlap between 'document' and 'record', but the statute lists both. Remember that Section 2(j) also gives the right to inspect work, documents and records, and to obtain information in electronic form, such as printouts, diskettes and tapes.
related: RTI Act, 2005 came into full force on 12 October 2005.
Section 2(j) defines 'right to information'.
Section 7: reply within 30 days; 48 hours for life or liberty.
Section 19 gives first and second appeals; the second appeal to the Information Commission is within 90 days.
Section 20 penalty: Rs 250 per day, maximum Rs 25,000.
Section 24 excludes the organisations in the Second Schedule, but not for corruption or human rights violation allegations.
The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed tenure and service conditions of Information Commissioners.
The RTI Act replaced the Freedom of Information Act, 2002.
statements: 1 — Correct: Section 2(j)(ii) allows certified copies of documents. A 'document' is anything recorded in writing, and certified copies are authenticated by the public authority. Under Section 2(f), 'information' means any material in any form, including records, documents, memos, emails, opinions, advices, press releases, circulars, orders, logbooks, contracts, reports, papers, samples, models and data held in electronic form. Applicants pay the prescribed fee for copies under the RTI Rules, and Central Government rules fix the application fee at Rs 10 and copy charges at Rs 2 per page. The Act applies to all public authorities across India except Jammu and Kashmir under the older law, though the J&K RTI Act was repealed after 2019 and the central Act now applies there.

2 — Correct: Section 2(j)(ii) also covers certified copies of records. Section 2(i) defines 'record' to include any document, manuscript and file; any microfilm, microfiche and facsimile copy of a document; any reproduction of image or images embodied in such microfilm; and any other material produced by a computer or any other device. So records of files, notings and registers are accessible, subject to the exemptions in Section 8 and the exclusion of certain organisations under Section 24 (such as intelligence and security agencies in the Second Schedule), though even they must disclose information on corruption and human rights violations.

3 — Correct: Section 2(j)(iii) grants the right to take certified samples of material. This is useful in matters such as quality of construction material, food grains in the public distribution system, or road works, where a physical sample is evidence. 'Information' under Section 2(f) expressly includes samples and models.
