The sample must be certified by the public authority, and access is subject to Section 8 exemptions and Section 9, which allows rejection where access would involve infringement of copyright held by a person other than the State.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1, 2 and 3. Section 2(j) of the RTI Act, 2005 defines 'right to information' to include taking notes, extracts or certified copies of documents or records, and taking certified samples of material. All three listed items are therefore covered.
topic_notes: The Right to Information Act, 2005 gives citizens a statutory right to access information held by public authorities, promoting transparency and accountability. It was passed by Parliament on 15 June 2005 and came into full force on 12 October 2005. It replaced the Freedom of Information Act, 2002. The Supreme Court had earlier read the right into Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech and expression) in cases such as State of UP v. Raj Narain (1975) and S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1982). Key sections: Section 2(h) defines a public authority; 2(f) information; 2(i) record; 2(j) right to information. Section 3 gives the right to all citizens. Section 4 imposes proactive disclosure duties. Section 5 requires appointment of Public Information Officers (PIOs) and Assistant PIOs. Section 6 covers requests, and no reason need be given. Section 7 sets the 30-day limit, or 48 hours where life or liberty is concerned. Section 8 lists exemptions, including national security, Cabinet papers, and personal information with no public interest, and Section 8(2) allows disclosure where public interest outweighs harm. Section 11 covers third-party information. Section 18 gives the Information Commission powers to inquire into complaints. Section 19 provides first appeal to a senior officer within the public authority and second appeal to the Information Commission within 90 days. Section 20 provides penalties of Rs 250 per day up to Rs 25,000. Section 22 gives the Act overriding effect. Section 24 excludes the organisations in the Second Schedule, except for corruption and human rights allegations. The Central Information Commission was constituted in 2005 and is headed by the Chief Information Commissioner. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed the tenure and service conditions of Information Commissioners, making them determined by the Central Government instead of a fixed five-year term. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 amended Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act.

question: Which one of the following is not covered under the definition of ‘Public authority’ under the RTI Act, 2005 ?
options: A body established by any law made by |?2" State Legislatures
A Non-Government Organization substantially financed by the Government
A family trust owned, controlled and financed by joint family property
An institution of self-government constituted under the Constitution of India
subject: Insurance
detail: Section 2(h) of the RTI Act, 2005 defines 'public authority' as any authority, body or institution of self-government established or constituted (a) by or under the Constitution; (b) by any other law made by Parliament; (c) by any other law made by a State Legislature; (d) by notification or order of the appropriate Government, which includes any body owned, controlled or substantially financed by the appropriate Government, and any non-Government organisation substantially financed, directly or indirectly, by funds provided by the appropriate Government. The test is therefore either statutory or constitutional origin, or government ownership, control or substantial finance. Option (a) matches clause (c) of the definition. Option (b) matches the explicit inclusion of NGOs. Option (d) matches clause (a), which covers bodies of self-government such as Panchayats and Municipalities under Articles 243 and 243P onwards. Option (c) is a private family trust whose funds are the family's own, with no government establishment, control or finance, so it falls outside the definition. Private bodies can still be reached indirectly under Section 2(f), which defines 'information' to include information about a private body that a public authority can access under any other law. Elimination: look for the option with no government or statutory link.
explanations: Wrong: a body created by a State Legislature law is expressly covered by Section 2(h)(c), so it is a public authority.
Wrong: an NGO substantially financed directly or indirectly by the appropriate Government is expressly included in Section 2(h)(d)(ii).
Correct: a family trust owned, controlled and financed by joint family property is private and has no government establishment or substantial funding, so it is not a public authority.
Wrong: an institution of self-government established under the Constitution, such as a Panchayat or Municipality, is covered by Section 2(h)(a).
keyfact: Public authority under RTI Section 2(h) requires constitutional or statutory origin, government notification, or government ownership, control or substantial finance; a purely private family trust is excluded.
option_notes: Bodies created by State Legislature Acts, such as State Electricity Boards, State Universities, State Public Service Commissions and State Information Commissions, are public authorities under Section 2(h)(c). They are covered because of their statutory origin, whatever their funding. Their Public Information Officers must answer RTI applications under Section 5 of the Act.

An NGO is covered if it is substantially financed, directly or indirectly, by the appropriate Government. The Act does not define 'substantial', so it is decided case by case. In DAV College Trust v. Director of Public Instruction (2019) and Thalappalam Service Cooperative Bank v. State of Kerala (2013), the Supreme Court held that financing must be substantial, not merely marginal. Such NGOs must appoint PIOs and respond to RTI applications.

A family trust owned, controlled and financed by joint family property is a private entity. It is not established by law or by government order, and it receives no government finance or control. It is therefore outside Section 2(h). Information about private bodies can still be sought only through a public authority, under Section 2(f), if that authority can legally access it.

Institutions of self-government constituted under the Constitution include Panchayats (Part IX, Article 243) and Municipalities (Part IXA, Article 243P onwards). The 73rd and 74th Amendments of 1992 created them. They fall under Section 2(h)(a) and are public authorities under the RTI Act.
related: RTI Act 2005 came into force fully on 12 October 2005.
Section 2(h) defines public authority.
Time limit for a PIO to reply is 30 days; 48 hours for life or liberty matters.
Section 8 lists exemptions; Section 24 and the Second Schedule exempt certain security organisations.
Second appeal lies to the Information Commission within 90 days.
Penalty on a PIO is Rs 250 per day up to Rs 25,000 under Section 20.
The CJI office was held a public authority in CPIO v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019).
The RTI Amendment Act 2019 let the Centre fix tenure and salaries of Information Commissioners.
summary: The answer is (c). Under Section 2(h) of the RTI Act, 2005, a 'public authority' is a body established or constituted by the Constitution, by Parliament or a State Legislature law, or by government notification or order, or a body owned, controlled or substantially financed by the government, including NGOs substantially financed by it. A private family trust funded from joint family property has no such government link.
topic_notes: The RTI Act, 2005 received assent on 15 June 2005 and came fully into force on 12 October 2005. It extends to the whole of India; Jammu and Kashmir was brought under it in 2019 after the repeal of Article 370 and its own State RTI Act. The Act gives citizens a right to information held by or under the control of public authorities. It derives from Article 19(1)(a), and the Supreme Court recognised the right in State of UP v. Raj Narain (1975) and S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1982). Key provisions: Section 2(h) defines public authority; Section 2(f) defines information; Section 4 requires proactive disclosure; Section 5 requires PIOs and APIOs; Section 6 deals with applications; Section 7 sets the time limit of 30 days, or 48 hours for matters of life and liberty; Section 8 lists exemptions; Section 9 allows refusal on copyright grounds; Section 10 provides severability; Section 11 covers third-party information; Section 18 covers complaints; Section 19 covers appeals to the first appellate authority and then to the Information Commission within 90 days; Section 20 provides penalties of Rs 250 per day up to Rs 25,000; Section 22 gives the Act overriding effect; Section 24 and the Second Schedule exempt certain intelligence and security organisations, though they must still disclose corruption and human rights violation information. The Central Information Commission is established under Section 12 and State Information Commissions under Section 15. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed the tenure, salaries and service conditions of Information Commissioners, leaving them to be prescribed by the Central Government. The Supreme Court held in CPIO v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019) that the office of the Chief Justice of India is a public authority. Political parties were declared public authorities by the CIC in 2013, but the matter is disputed.

question: Whenever an Information Commissioner is appointed as the Chief Information Commissioner under the Right to Information Act, 2005, his term of office shall not exceed :
options: Four years in aggregate as the|92. Information Commissioner and _ the Chief Information Commissioner
Five years in aggregate as the Information Commissioner and _ the Chief Information Commissioner
Six years in aggregate as the Information Commissioner and _ the Chief Information Commissioner
Seven years in aggregate as the Information Commissioner and _ the Chief Information Commissioner
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Section 13 of the RTI Act, 2005 dealt with the term of office and conditions of service of the CIC. Originally the CIC held office for a term prescribed by the Central Government, or until the age of 65 years, whichever was earlier, and was not eligible for reappointment. Section 13(1) proviso said that when an Information Commissioner is appointed as CIC, his term of office shall not exceed five years in aggregate as Information Commissioner and CIC. Information Commissioners likewise served five years or until 65 years, whichever was earlier, and were not eligible for reappointment as Information Commissioner, but could be appointed CIC (once) with the aggregate five-year cap. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed this: terms are now as prescribed by the Central Government, not a fixed five years, and salaries and allowances are also prescribed by the Centre, not equated to the Election Commissioner/CEC. The question is based on the original Act. Elimination: four, six and seven years do not match any statutory figure. Five years is the standard CIC tenure in the original Act.
explanations: Four years is not mentioned in the original Section 13 and is wrong.
Correct. The original Act caps the aggregate term as Information Commissioner and CIC at five years.
Six years does not appear in the Act, so it is wrong.
Seven years does not appear in the Act, so it is wrong.
keyfact: Original RTI Act Section 13: an IC who becomes CIC serves at most five years in aggregate in both posts (changed by the 2019 Amendment, which leaves tenure to be prescribed by the Centre).
option_notes: Four years: not a term specified for Information Commissioners or the CIC under the RTI Act. Four-year terms are not associated with this body. Remember that the original Act used five years or age 65, whichever was earlier. The 2019 Amendment later left the tenure to be prescribed by the Central Government.

Five years in aggregate: the original Section 13 tenure limit. The CIC and Information Commissioners held office for five years or until 65 years of age, whichever was earlier. They were ineligible for reappointment as CIC or IC, except that an IC could become CIC, with the aggregate not exceeding five years. The 2019 Amendment replaced the fixed term with a term to be prescribed by the Centre.

Six years: not a term under the RTI Act. Six years is the term of the Election Commissioners and the CEC (or until age 65), to whom the CIC and ICs were equated in salary and status under the original Act. The 2019 Amendment removed this equation, which is why it is a tempting distractor.
Seven years: not a term under the RTI Act. It does not match any CIC or IC tenure, and the UPSC Chairman holds office for six years or until age 65. It is a plain distractor.
related: The RTI Act was enacted on 15 June 2005 and came fully into force on 12 October 2005.
The CIC is a statutory body set up under Section 12 of the RTI Act.
The CIC comprises the CIC and up to 10 Information Commissioners.
The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 empowered the Centre to fix the tenure and salaries of the CIC and ICs.
The appointment committee consists of the PM, the Leader of Opposition and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM.
The Information Commissioners' retirement age under the original Act was 65 years.
The CIC and ICs are removed by the President after a Supreme Court inquiry on proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
The RTI Act's reply time limit is 30 days, or 48 hours where life and liberty are involved.
summary: The answer is (b). Under the original Section 13 of the RTI Act, 2005, an Information Commissioner who is appointed Chief Information Commissioner serves a term that must not exceed five years in aggregate as Information Commissioner and as CIC. This reflects the five-year cap on a CIC's term, which also applies to the combined service.
topic_notes: The Right to Information Act, 2005 was enacted on 15 June 2005 and came into full force on 12 October 2005. It gives citizens access to information held by public authorities, and it applies to the whole of India except Jammu and Kashmir, which had its own RTI Act until 2019. The Central Information Commission (CIC) is a statutory body set up under Section 12, consisting of the Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners. The President appoints them on the recommendation of a committee comprising the Prime Minister (chair), the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM. Candidates must be persons of eminence in public life, with wide knowledge and experience in law, science and technology, social service, management, journalism, mass media or administration and governance, and must not be MPs, MLAs or hold any office of profit. The original Act set the tenure at five years or until age 65, whichever was earlier, with no reappointment. Salaries were equal to those of the CEC (CIC) and an Election Commissioner (ICs). The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 gave the Central Government the power to prescribe tenure, salaries, allowances and service conditions through rules, and the 2019 Rules fixed a three-year term. Removal is by the President on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, after an inquiry by the Supreme Court, or on grounds such as insolvency or conviction. The 30-day time limit for a reply (48 hours for matters of life and liberty), the first appeal to a senior officer and the second appeal to the Commission are the other key provisions. Section 8 lists the exemptions, and Section 24 exempts security and intelligence organisations listed in the Second Schedule. The application fee is Rs 10 and the penalty is Rs 250 per day up to Rs 25,000. State Information Commissions are covered by Section 15. The DPDP Act, 2023 amended Section 8(1)(j) on personal information.

question: Where a request for information is rejected, the Central or State Public Information Officer is not required to communicate which one of the following to the person making the request ?
options: The penalty for seeking frivolous information
The period within which appeal against such rejection may be preferred
subject: Insurance
detail: Section 7(8) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 governs what the Public Information Officer must do when a request for information is rejected. The PIO must communicate to the requester: (i) the reasons for such rejection, (ii) the period within which an appeal against the rejection may be preferred (30 days under Section 19(1)), and (iii) the particulars of the appellate authority. The first appeal lies to an officer senior in rank to the PIO within the public authority; the second appeal lies to the Central or State Information Commission within 90 days under Section 19(3). Rejection can only be on grounds in Sections 8 and 9 (exemptions) or Section 24 (exempted organisations). The Act contains penalty provisions (Section 20), but these apply to PIOs who refuse requests without reasonable cause, delay, give incorrect or misleading information, or destroy information. The penalty is Rs 250 per day up to a maximum of Rs 25,000. The Act has no penalty for applicants seeking 'frivolous' information, and nothing requires the PIO to mention such a penalty. Elimination: options (a), (c) and (d) are the three express duties in Section 7(8), so (b) is the one not required.
explanations: Wrong: communicating the reasons for rejection is a mandatory duty under Section 7(8)(i).
Correct: no provision requires the PIO to inform the applicant of a penalty for seeking frivolous information, and the RTI Act prescribes no such penalty on applicants.
Wrong: Section 7(8)(ii) requires the PIO to state the period within which an appeal may be preferred.
Wrong: Section 7(8)(iii) requires the PIO to give the particulars of the appellate authority.
keyfact: Section 7(8) RTI Act: on rejection the PIO must give reasons, the appeal period and the appellate authority's particulars. No penalty on applicants for frivolous requests is mentioned.
option_notes: Reasons for rejection: Section 7(8)(i) requires the PIO to give specific reasons for refusal, which must be based on the exemptions in Section 8 or 9, or on Section 24. A bare refusal without reasons is a ground for complaint to the Information Commission under Section 18 and for penalty under Section 20.

Penalty for seeking frivolous information: this is not part of the RTI Act. Penalties under Section 20 apply only to PIOs, at Rs 250 per day up to Rs 25,000, plus possible disciplinary action recommended by the Commission. Frivolous or vexatious requests are dealt with by the Commissions' discretion, not by a statutory penalty on applicants.

Period for appeal: Section 7(8)(ii) requires the PIO to state the appeal period. The first appeal under Section 19(1) must be filed within 30 days of the decision, though the appellate authority may admit a late appeal if there is sufficient cause. The second appeal lies within 90 days.

Particulars of appellate authority: Section 7(8)(iii) requires the PIO to give the name and details of the first appellate authority, an officer senior in rank to the PIO in the same public authority. The applicant can then file the first appeal there under Section 19(1).
related: Section 7(1): 30 days to reply, 48 hours for life and liberty matters.
Section 19(1): first appeal within 30 days; Section 19(3): second appeal within 90 days.
Section 20: penalty Rs 250 per day, maximum Rs 25,000, on the PIO.
Section 8(2): public interest can override exemptions.
Section 24: exempted organisations (intelligence agencies), except corruption and human rights allegations.
RTI Act came fully into force on 12 October 2005.
Section 12 covers the CIC; Section 15 covers SICs.
The 2019 Amendment altered Information Commissioners' tenure and salary.
summary: The answer is (b). Under Section 7(8) of the RTI Act 2005, when a request is rejected the CPIO/SPIO must communicate the reasons for rejection, the period within which an appeal may be preferred, and the particulars of the appellate authority. There is no requirement to inform the applicant of any 'penalty for seeking frivolous information'.
topic_notes: The Right to Information Act, 2005 received assent on 15 June 2005 and came fully into force on 12 October 2005. It applies to all of India, with Jammu and Kashmir now covered by the central Act after 2019. Its purpose is to promote transparency and accountability in public authorities. Key points: Section 2(h) defines 'public authority'. Section 4 requires proactive disclosure. Section 5 requires every public authority to designate PIOs and APIOs. Section 6 covers the request, made in writing or electronically, with a fee (Rs 10 under the Central rules). No reason need be given for seeking information. Section 7 sets the time limit: 30 days in general, 48 hours for matters concerning life and liberty, and 35 days where the request goes through an APIO. Under Section 7(1), if the information concerns life or liberty, it must be provided within 48 hours. Deemed refusal applies if the time limit is breached. Section 8 lists exemptions, including national security, Cabinet papers and personal information, but Section 8(2) permits disclosure where public interest outweighs harm, and Section 8(3) limits the exemptions for information older than 20 years. Section 9 allows rejection where the request involves infringement of copyright. Section 11 covers third-party information. Section 12 provides for the Central Information Commission (CIC), and Section 15 for State Information Commissions. Section 18 covers complaints. Section 19 covers appeals. Section 20 covers penalties. Section 22 gives the Act overriding effect. Section 24 covers exempted organisations such as intelligence and security bodies, though allegations of corruption and human rights violations are not exempt. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed the tenure and service conditions of Information Commissioners, giving the Centre the power to prescribe them. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 amended Section 8(1)(j).

ocr: Which one of the following statements is not true ? (a) The Chief Secretary is the Residuary Legatee at the State level. (b) The Cabinet Secretary is the Primus Inter Pares among Secretaries. (c) The Cabinet Secretary has no ministerial responsibilities. (d)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests administrative-structure terms from Indian public administration (the Cabinet Secretariat and the State Secretariat). The Cabinet Secretary is the senior-most civil servant. He is ex-officio Chairman of the Civil Services Board, head of the Indian Administrative Service and the Secretary to the Cabinet. He is also called 'Primus Inter Pares' (first among equals) among Secretaries to the Government of India. The post has no ministerial responsibility because he is a permanent civil servant who works under the Prime Minister, who is in charge of the Cabinet Secretariat. The Cabinet Secretariat functions under the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961. The Chief Secretary is the administrative head of the State government, secretary to the State Cabinet, and ex-officio head of the State Civil Services Board and of the State Secretariat. Because the Chief Secretary does not hold ministerial office, he is not a minister. The phrase 'residuary legatee' is used for the Cabinet Secretary in some texts (e.g., he performs residual functions not assigned to others). Option (a) therefore appears to borrow the Cabinet Secretary's description and apply it at the State level, which makes it the odd one out. The text of option (d) is cut off in the image, so it cannot be fully verified.
explanations: Likely the 'not true' statement: the 'residuary legatee' role is associated with the Cabinet Secretary (Union level) or the Union under Art. 248. The Chief Secretary is the State's administrative head, though some texts also apply the analogy to the State level, which creates ambiguity.
True: the Cabinet Secretary is described as Primus Inter Pares (first among equals) among Secretaries to the Government of India.
True: the Cabinet Secretary is a permanent civil servant, not a minister, and has no ministerial responsibility; he works under the Prime Minister.
Truncated in the image; the Chief Secretary being ex-officio head of the State Civil Services Board or of the Secretariat is generally true, so it is unlikely to be the 'not true' statement.
keyfact: Cabinet Secretary = Primus Inter Pares, a non-minister civil servant; the 'residuary' label belongs to Union-level roles, not the Chief Secretary.
option_notes: Residuary Legatee: a person who receives what remains of an estate after specific bequests. In administration, the term is applied to the Cabinet Secretary, who takes on residual tasks not assigned to others, and in a constitutional sense to the Union (Art. 248, residuary legislative powers). Some texts also describe the Chief Secretary as the State's residuary functionary, since he handles matters that fall to no other department. This overlap is the likely reason the question was disputed.

Primus Inter Pares is Latin for 'first among equals'. The Cabinet Secretary is the senior-most civil servant, with rank first among Secretaries to the Government of India. He heads the Cabinet Secretariat, is the ex-officio Chairman of the Civil Services Board, and serves as the chief coordinator of the ministries. The Prime Minister is also often called first among equals in the Council of Ministers.

The Cabinet Secretary heads the Cabinet Secretariat, under the direct charge of the Prime Minister. He is a civil servant and has no ministerial portfolio or responsibility. He is appointed by the Government, usually from the IAS, and is placed first in the Warrant of Precedence among civil servants. He ensures the smooth transaction of business under the Allocation of Business Rules and the Transaction of Business Rules, 1961.

The Chief Secretary is the head of the State's civil service and secretariat. He is secretary to the State Cabinet and ex-officio head of the State Civil Services Board. He coordinates the State departments, acts as the principal adviser to the Chief Minister, and represents the State in matters involving the Centre. The option text is cut off in the image.
related: Cabinet Secretary is ex-officio Chairman of the Civil Services Board.
The Cabinet Secretariat is under the direct charge of the Prime Minister.
The Allocation of Business Rules and the Transaction of Business Rules were framed in 1961.
Art. 248 gives residuary legislative powers to the Union Parliament.
The Chief Secretary is the head of the State's administrative machinery and secretary to the State Cabinet.
Primus inter pares means 'first among equals'.
The Principal Secretary to the PM heads the PMO.
The Central Staffing Scheme governs central deputation of officers.
summary: The most defensible answer is (a). The Chief Secretary is not called the 'Residuary Legatee' at State level; that phrase is conventionally applied to the Cabinet Secretary at the Union level, or to the Union Home Ministry, or to the Union in the Constitution (Art. 248). The Chief Secretary is better described as the head of the State administration and ex-officio head of the Civil Services Board.
topic_notes: The Cabinet Secretariat is part of the Union administrative structure. It operates under the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961 and the Allocation of Business Rules, 1961. It is under the Prime Minister's direct charge. The Cabinet Secretary is the senior-most civil servant and the ex-officio head of the Civil Services Board and of the IAS. He is the chief coordinator of ministries and organises the Cabinet and its committees. He prepares agendas and keeps the minutes of Cabinet meetings. He is appointed for a fixed tenure (two years, extendable up to four years under the 1960s-era rules as amended). The Secretary to the Government of India heads a department and is the principal adviser to the Minister on policy and administration. At the State level the Chief Secretary heads the State administration, acts as secretary to the State Cabinet, and is the chief adviser to the Chief Minister. The Chief Secretary is also the ex-officio head of the State Civil Services Board. The Cabinet Secretary's relations with the PM and the Cabinet are governed by convention, neutrality and anonymity. Similar bodies include the Prime Minister's Office (PMO), which is a staff agency that assists the PM, with a Principal Secretary who is a key adviser. Other related topics include the Central Secretariat Service, the Allocation of Business Rules, the generalist versus specialist debate, the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966, chair Morarji Desai, then K. Hanumanthaiya), the role of Joint Secretaries, and the Central Staffing Scheme.
why_dropped: The 'residuary legatee' description is used loosely for both Cabinet Secretary and Chief Secretary in textbooks, and option (d) is cut off, so more than one statement could be argued to be not true, which probably led UPSC to drop it.

question: The Chief Secretary is the ex-officio Chairman of the Civil Service Board. Which one of the following statements is true ? National AYUSH Mission was launched
options: Sowa-Rigpa is one of the health traditions under AYUSH. AYUSH functions under the
administrative control of the Indian Drug Control Cell
States are authorized to mobilize their resources under the AYUSH Mission
subject: Current Affairs
detail: AYUSH stands for Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy. Sowa-Rigpa is the traditional Tibetan or Himalayan system of medicine, practised in Ladakh, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Darjeeling, and was formally recognised in India in 2010. The Department of AYUSH was set up in 2003 as the Department of Indian Systems of Medicine & Homoeopathy (ISM&H), renamed AYUSH in 2003, and upgraded to the Ministry of AYUSH in November 2014. The National AYUSH Mission was launched in September 2014 and approved to continue to 2026. It is a centrally sponsored scheme, so states implement it through State Annual Action Plans, with funding shared between Centre and states. The Chief Secretary being ex-officio Chairman of the Civil Service Board is an unrelated opening sentence and should be ignored. Elimination: (a) gives the wrong year, 2014 is correct. (c) names a non-existent controlling body, because AYUSH has its own Ministry. (d) is not the best choice because states get funds under a centrally sponsored scheme and are not given an independent authority to mobilise resources. (b) is the safest and factually correct statement.
explanations: (a) Incorrect: the National AYUSH Mission was launched in 2014 (approved September 2014), not 2010. 2010 is when Sowa-Rigpa was recognised.
(b) Correct: Sowa-Rigpa is one of the six systems under AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa, Homoeopathy). This matches the official answer.
(c) Incorrect: AYUSH works under the Ministry of AYUSH, not any 'Indian Drug Control Cell'. No such body controls it.

(d) Incorrect: NAM is a centrally sponsored scheme with funds shared between Centre and states through State Annual Action Plans. The statement overstates state authority to mobilise resources independently.
keyfact: Sowa-Rigpa (Tibetan medicine) is one of the six AYUSH systems; the National AYUSH Mission began in 2014 and the Ministry of AYUSH in 2014.
option_notes: 2010: the year Sowa-Rigpa gained formal recognition in India, with the Central Council of Indian Medicine Act amended to include it later. The National AYUSH Mission itself was launched in 2014. The National Rural Health Mission began in 2005, so students should not confuse these dates.

Sowa-Rigpa, or Tibetan medicine, is one of the oldest living medical traditions. It is practised in Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh and Darjeeling. The National Institute of Sowa-Rigpa is in Leh. It is based on the theory of three humours: rLung, mKhris-pa and Bad-kan.

The Ministry of AYUSH, not any drug control cell, administers the systems. The Ministry was formed in November 2014 from the Department of AYUSH, which was created in 2003. Drug regulation falls under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) under the Health Ministry.

The National AYUSH Mission is a centrally sponsored scheme that supports states through State Annual Action Plans. Its aims are to improve AYUSH services, education, quality of drugs and availability of raw materials. Funding is shared between Centre and states, with higher Centre share for the North-East and Himalayan states.
related: The Ministry of AYUSH was created in November 2014.
The National AYUSH Mission was launched in 2014 as a centrally sponsored scheme.
International Day of Yoga is observed on 21 June, since 2015.
The WHO Global Centre for Traditional Medicine is at Jamnagar, Gujarat (2022).
The National Medicinal Plants Board was set up in 2000.
The National Institute of Sowa-Rigpa is located in Leh.
The Chief Secretary is the ex-officio Chairman of the State Civil Services Board.
summary: The official answer is (b): Sowa-Rigpa is one of the traditional health systems recognised under AYUSH. The other options are wrong because the National AYUSH Mission (NAM) was launched in 2014, not 2010, and AYUSH is administered by its own Ministry, not a drug control cell. The question text is garbled by OCR, but the answer key points to the Sowa-Rigpa statement.
topic_notes: AYUSH covers six systems: Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy. The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy was set up in 1995, renamed AYUSH in 2003, and made a full Ministry in November 2014. The first Minister of State (Independent Charge) was Shripad Naik. The National AYUSH Mission was launched in 2014 as a centrally sponsored scheme to provide cost-effective AYUSH services, strengthen education, support quality control of ASU&H drugs and promote cultivation of medicinal plants. Key institutions include the All India Institute of Ayurveda (Delhi), the Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences, the Central Council of Indian Medicine (CCIM), the Central Council of Homoeopathy (CCH), and the National Medicinal Plants Board (2000). Related legal framework: the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and Rules cover ASU drugs, and the National Commission for Indian System of Medicine Act 2020 and the National Commission for Homoeopathy Act 2020 replaced the earlier councils. The WHO Global Centre for Traditional Medicine was set up in Jamnagar, Gujarat, in 2022. International Day of Yoga is observed on 21 June, since 2015, after a UN resolution in December 2014. The AYUSH Grid is an IT project, and the AYUSH Visa was introduced in 2022 for foreign nationals seeking AYUSH treatment. Possible future questions concern the six systems, their regional bases, institutions and dates.

question: Which one of the following is not a level in the 96. Panchayati Raj structure in India ?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 (in force from 24 April 1993; celebrated as National Panchayati Raj Day) added Part IX (Articles 243 to 243-O) and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects) to the Constitution. It created a uniform three-tier system: village level (Gram Panchayat), intermediate level (Panchayat Samiti, also called Block Samiti, Mandal Parishad or Taluka Panchayat depending on the state) and district level (Zila Parishad). States with a population under 20 lakh may skip the intermediate tier (Article 243B). Article 243A empowers the Gram Sabha. Article 243C covers composition, 243D reservation of seats for SC/ST and not less than one-third for women, 243E a five-year term, 243I the State Finance Commission and 243K the State Election Commission. Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended the three-tier model, and Rajasthan (Nagaur, 2 October 1959) was the first state to adopt it. Elimination: Gram Panchayat, Block Samiti and Zila Parishad are standard tiers, so (a), (b) and (d) are ruled out. 'Mandal Committee' is not a tier name in the constitutional scheme, which leaves (c).
explanations: Incorrect choice: Gram Panchayat is the village-level, lowest tier of the three-tier structure, so it is a level.
Incorrect choice: Block Samiti (Panchayat Samiti) is the intermediate tier at block level, so it is a level.
Correct choice: Mandal Committee is not a tier in the Panchayati Raj structure. The intermediate tier is called Panchayat Samiti/Block Samiti (Mandal Parishad in some states).
Incorrect choice: Zila Parishad is the district-level, topmost tier, so it is a level.
keyfact: Panchayati Raj has three tiers (Gram Panchayat, Panchayat/Block Samiti, Zila Parishad) under the 73rd Amendment; 'Mandal Committee' is not a tier.
option_notes: Gram Panchayat is the village-level body, elected directly by the people of a village or group of villages. It is accountable to the Gram Sabha, which consists of all registered voters of the village (Article 243A). It is headed by the Sarpanch/Pradhan. It carries out local development, sanitation, water supply and the preparation of village plans. Article 40 (a Directive Principle) directs the state to organise village panchayats.

Block Samiti, also called Panchayat Samiti, Mandal Parishad or Taluka Panchayat, is the intermediate tier between the Gram Panchayat and the Zila Parishad. It is generally headed by a Pradhan or Chairman and works through the Block Development Officer. Members are usually elected from territorial constituencies. It coordinates village plans and implements block-level development schemes. States with population below 20 lakh need not constitute it.

Mandal Committee is not a Panchayati Raj tier. The nearest concept is Mandal Praja Parishad, the name for the intermediate tier in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, which replaced the earlier Panchayat Samiti. The 1985 Asoka Mehta Committee (1977) had recommended a two-tier system with Mandal Panchayat. The name is also confused with the Mandal Commission (1979, B. P. Mandal) on backward classes.

Zila Parishad is the district-level, topmost tier of Panchayati Raj. It is headed by a Chairperson (Adhyaksha), and the CEO or District Collector assists in many states. It supervises Panchayat Samitis, approves their budgets and prepares district plans, which are consolidated by the District Planning Committee (Article 243ZD). It is composed of elected members, MPs/MLAs and ex-officio members in many states.
related: 73rd Amendment Act 1992 came into force on 24 April 1993; National Panchayati Raj Day is 24 April.
Part IX of the Constitution covers Panchayats (Articles 243 to 243-O); the Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects.
Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended the three-tier system; Rajasthan was the first state to adopt it (Nagaur, 1959).
Article 243K provides for the State Election Commission for Panchayat elections.
Article 40 (DPSP) directs the state to organise village panchayats.
PESA Act 1996 extends Panchayat provisions to Fifth Schedule areas.
Panchayats with population below 20 lakh need not have the intermediate tier.
The 74th Amendment (Part IXA) covers urban local bodies with the Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects).
summary: The answer is (c) Mandal Committee. The Panchayati Raj structure in India is three-tier: Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti / Block Samiti (intermediate) and Zila Parishad (district). 'Mandal Committee' is not a constitutionally recognised tier, although Mandal Praja Parishad existed in Andhra Pradesh under older state law.
topic_notes: Panchayati Raj is local self-government in rural India. Key milestones: Community Development Programme (1952) and National Extension Service (1953) led to the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957), which recommended a three-tier structure. Rajasthan (Nagaur, 2 Oct 1959) was first, followed by Andhra Pradesh. The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) proposed a two-tier system (Zila Parishad and Mandal Panchayat). The G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985) and L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) recommended constitutional status. The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 came into force on 24 April 1993 and added Part IX (Articles 243 to 243-O) and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects). Features: Gram Sabha; three tiers (optional intermediate tier for population under 20 lakh); direct elections for all seats; reservation for SC/ST in proportion to population; at least one-third for women (many states now give 50%); five-year term, with fresh elections within six months of dissolution; State Election Commission (Article 243K) for conducting elections; State Finance Commission (Article 243I) reviewed every five years; District Planning Committee (Article 243ZD). Exempted areas: Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram and some hill areas, though PESA 1996 extended the provisions to Fifth Schedule areas. Ministry: Ministry of Panchayati Raj (created 2004). Related: Gram Swaraj, e-Gram Swaraj, SVAMITVA scheme, Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan. The urban counterpart is the 74th Amendment (Part IXA, Articles 243P to 243ZG, Twelfth Schedule with 18 subjects).

question: Which one of the following Commissions laid down the qualifications and eligibility criteria for the appointment to the post of Governor ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Articles 153-162 of the Constitution deal with the Governor. Article 157 sets the only formal qualifications: the person must be an Indian citizen and at least 35 years old. Article 158 adds that the Governor must not be a member of Parliament or a state legislature and must not hold any office of profit. The Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State Relations was set up in 1983 under Justice R.S. Sarkaria and submitted its report in 1988. It made 247 recommendations and laid down additional criteria for the Governor: (1) eminent in some walk of life, (2) from outside the state, (3) a detached figure without intense involvement in local politics, (4) not having been active in politics, particularly in the recent past, and (5) not a member of the ruling party. It also recommended consulting the state Chief Minister, the Vice-President and the Lok Sabha Speaker before appointment, and a five-year tenure that should not be cut short except for the reasons that justify removal. The Punchhi Commission (2007-2010) revisited Centre-State relations and recommended that Governors have a fixed tenure of five years. Eliminate (c) and (d), because there is no Verghese or Chandrachud Commission on this subject. Between (a) and (b), Sarkaria is the classic source of the eligibility criteria.
explanations: Correct. The Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) laid down the qualifications and eligibility criteria for Governors: an eminent person from outside the state, detached from local politics and not recently active in politics.

Wrong. The Punchhi Commission (2007-10) reviewed Centre-State relations afresh. It recommended a five-year tenure and removal only by impeachment-like process, rather than first laying down the criteria.
Wrong. The Verghese Commission is not connected with the appointment of Governors. The name is associated with the Verghese Committee on Prasar Bharati (autonomy of broadcasting).
Wrong. No 'Chandrachud Commission' dealt with Governors' eligibility. Justice Chandrachud is known as a judge and Chief Justice, not for a Centre-State commission.
keyfact: Sarkaria Commission (1988): the Governor should be an eminent person from outside the state, detached from local politics and not recently active in politics.
option_notes: The Sarkaria Commission was appointed in June 1983 under Justice R.S. Sarkaria, a retired Supreme Court judge. It submitted its report in 1988 with 247 recommendations on Centre-State relations. It recommended the Inter-State Council (set up in 1990), caution in using Article 356, and criteria for Governors. It had two other members, B. Sivaraman and S.R. Sen.

The Punchhi Commission was set up in 2007 under Justice Madan Mohan Punchhi, a former Chief Justice of India. It reported in 2010. It recommended that a Governor's tenure be fixed at five years, that removal be only by the same process as the President's removal, and that Article 356 be used as a last resort. It also supported 'localising' emergency provisions under Articles 355 and 356.

Verghese refers to the Verghese Committee, chaired by B.G. Verghese in 1977-78, on autonomy for All India Radio and Doordarshan. It recommended an autonomous National Broadcast Trust called 'Akash Bharati'. It was not about Governors or Centre-State relations. This is the usual trap for confusing the name.

There is no known 'Chandrachud Commission' for Governors. Y.V. Chandrachud was the longest-serving Chief Justice of India (1978-85), and D.Y. Chandrachud was CJI from November 2022 to November 2024. The name is used here as a distractor and has no link to Centre-State relations.
related: Article 153: There shall be a Governor for each state.
Article 157: Governor must be a citizen of India and at least 35 years old.
Article 158: Governor cannot be a member of Parliament or a state legislature and cannot hold an office of profit.
Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) made 247 recommendations on Centre-State relations.
Punchhi Commission (2007-10) recommended a fixed five-year tenure for Governors.
B.P. Singhal case (2010): Governors cannot be removed arbitrarily.
Article 161: Governor's pardoning power, which does not extend to court-martial sentences or death sentences.
Inter-State Council (Article 263) was set up in 1990 on the Sarkaria recommendation.
summary: The answer is (a) Sarkaria Commission. It recommended that a Governor should be an eminent person from outside the state, detached from local politics, and not recently active in politics. These are the eligibility and qualification criteria for appointing a Governor.
topic_notes: The Governor is the nominal head of the state executive under Article 153, and one Governor can be appointed for two or more states. He is appointed by the President under Article 155 and holds office during the President's pleasure under Article 156, normally for five years. Article 157 requires Indian citizenship and a minimum age of 35. Article 158 bars membership of the legislature and any office of profit, and provides for emoluments and allowances. Article 159 prescribes the oath. Article 161 gives the Governor power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions. Article 163 provides for a council of ministers to aid and advise, with discretion in some cases. Article 200 covers the Governor's assent to Bills and Article 213 covers ordinance-making power. Article 356 deals with the report on breakdown of constitutional machinery. Commissions and cases to know: the Sarkaria Commission (1983-88), the Punchhi Commission (2007-10), the Rajamannar Committee (1969, Tamil Nadu), the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966-70) and the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (Venkatachaliah, 2000-02). Key cases: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) on Article 356 and floor tests; Rameshwar Prasad (2006) on dissolution of the Bihar Assembly; Nabam Rebia (2016) on the Governor's discretion; B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010) on removal of Governors without cause, held to be arbitrary. The Sarkaria Commission also recommended an Inter-State Council (Article 263), which was set up in 1990, and an all-India judicial service.

question: Which one of the following statements is not true of the National Education Policy (NEP) of India, 2020 ?
options: NEP recognizes 6 — 8 years of age as the crucial age for mental development of a child. 98
NEP emphasizes empowering students through flexibility in course choices
NEP aims at 100 percent Gross Enrolment Ratio in school education
In NEP, the teaching up to at least grade 5 will be in mother tongue or regional language
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: NEP 2020 was approved by the Union Cabinet on 29 July 2020. It was drafted by a committee chaired by K. Kasturirangan and replaced the NPE 1986 (modified in 1992). It replaces the 10+2 structure with 5+3+3+4: Foundational (ages 3-8, i.e. 3 years of preschool plus Grades 1-2), Preparatory (8-11, Grades 3-5), Middle (11-14, Grades 6-8) and Secondary (14-18, Grades 9-12). The policy's emphasis on early childhood care and education (ECCE) rests on the finding that over 85% of a child's cumulative brain development occurs before age 6. It therefore treats ages 0-6, and the wider 0-8 span, as critical, not 6-8 specifically. Statement (a) is therefore the false one. Statement (b) is true: the policy offers flexibility and choice of subjects, with no hard separation between arts, science and vocational streams. Statement (c) is true: it targets 100% GER in school education by 2030 and 50% GER in higher education by 2035. Statement (d) is true: the medium of instruction up to at least Grade 5, preferably Grade 8 and beyond, should be the home language, mother tongue, local language or regional language. Eliminate (b), (c) and (d) as well-known features, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct choice: NEP does not name 6-8 years as the crucial age. It stresses early childhood (0-6 years, with 85% of brain development by age 6) and the Foundational Stage of 3-8 years, so the statement is not true.
Incorrect choice: this statement is true. NEP stresses flexibility and choice of subjects, multidisciplinary learning and no rigid separation of streams.
Incorrect choice: this statement is true. NEP aims at universal access and 100% GER in school education (pre-school to secondary) by 2030.
Incorrect choice: this statement is true. NEP says the medium of instruction up to at least Grade 5, preferably Grade 8 and beyond, will be the mother tongue, home language or regional language.
keyfact: NEP 2020 stresses ECCE (85% of brain development before age 6) and a 3-8 Foundational Stage, not '6-8 years' as the crucial age.
option_notes: Statement (a) is a distorted claim. NEP 2020 highlights ECCE for ages 3-6 and the Foundational Stage of ages 3-8. It cites research that 85% of brain development occurs before age 6. The policy does not name 6-8 years as the single crucial age. The 5+3+3+4 structure replaces 10+2. The National Curriculum Framework for Foundation Stage was released in 2022, and NIPUN Bharat (2021) targets foundational literacy and numeracy by Grade 3.

Flexibility in course choices is a core principle of NEP 2020. School students can mix subjects across arts, science and vocational streams. In higher education it brings multiple entry and exit points, a four-year multidisciplinary UG programme, and the Academic Bank of Credits. Board exams are to be made low-stakes, with flexible choices at the secondary stage, and vocational education is integrated from Grade 6.

NEP 2020 targets 100% GER in school education (pre-school to secondary) by 2030 and 50% GER in higher education by 2035. It also aims to bring back about 2 crore out-of-school children. The earlier NPE 1986 had no comparable target. Universal access is meant to be supported by the RTE Act, which covers ages 6-14. NEP extends its scope to ages 3-18.

The three-language formula continues under NEP 2020, with greater flexibility and no imposition of any language on any state. The policy recommends the mother tongue, home language, local language or regional language as the medium of instruction up to at least Grade 5, preferably Grade 8 and beyond. It also promotes Sanskrit and other classical languages, and the Indian Institute of Translation and Interpretation (IITI) is proposed.
related: NEP 2020 was approved by the Union Cabinet on 29 July 2020.
The drafting committee was chaired by K. Kasturirangan.
School structure is 5+3+3+4, replacing 10+2.
GER targets: 100% school education by 2030, 50% higher education by 2035.
The policy proposes spending 6% of GDP on education.
HECI is the proposed single regulator for higher education, excluding medical and legal education.
PARAKH is the national assessment centre under NEP.
NIPUN Bharat targets foundational literacy and numeracy by Grade 3.
summary: The answer is (a). NEP 2020 does not single out 6-8 years as the crucial age for mental development. It stresses ages 0-8, with about 85% of a child's brain development occurring by age 6, and it created a 5+3+3+4 structure whose Foundational Stage covers ages 3-8. The other three statements are true of the policy.
topic_notes: NEP 2020 is India's third major education policy, after 1968 and 1986 (revised 1992). A committee led by K. Kasturirangan (former ISRO chief) drafted it, and the Cabinet approved it on 29 July 2020. The Ministry of Education name was restored in place of MHRD. Structure: 5+3+3+4 (Foundational 3-8, Preparatory 8-11, Middle 11-14, Secondary 14-18). School education: ECCE, NIPUN Bharat (foundational literacy and numeracy by Grade 3), a holistic progress card (HPC), PARAKH as the national assessment centre, vocational education and internships from Grade 6, and Board exams made low-stakes, with possibly two attempts. Language: three-language formula, mother tongue as medium up to at least Grade 5, and Sanskrit and Indian languages promoted. Higher education: GER target of 50% by 2035, a four-year multidisciplinary UG programme with multiple exits (certificate after 1 year, diploma after 2, degree after 3 or 4), the Academic Bank of Credits, a single regulator in the Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) with four verticals (NHERC, NAC, HEGC, GEC), the National Research Foundation, and MERUs (multidisciplinary universities). Others: public spending on education should reach 6% of GDP, the National Testing Agency conducts common entrance tests (CUET), the National Mission on Teachers and Mentoring, and the NCTE four-year integrated B.Ed. as the minimum qualification by 2030. Related schemes: PM SHRI schools, DIKSHA, SWAYAM, and the National Educational Technology Forum (NETF). UPSC often asks about these numbers, targets and body names.

question: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission suggested the establishment of a National Judicial Council under the Chairmanship of the :
options: Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The Second ARC (constituted 2005, chair Veerappa Moily) submitted 15 reports, including 'Ethics in Governance' (4th report, 2007). It noted that removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges under Articles 124(4) and 217(1)(b), via the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, requires a parliamentary address, which makes the process cumbersome and rarely used (e.g., Justice V. Ramaswami 1993, Justice Soumitra Sen 2011, Justice P.D. Dinakaran who resigned). The Commission therefore suggested a National Judicial Council to inquire into complaints of misconduct against judges, headed by the Vice President of India, who is ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Members were to include the Chief Justice of India, and others. Elimination logic: the Prime Minister is part of the executive, so heading a body overseeing judges would offend judicial independence. The Speaker and the Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha are partisan or House-specific figures and were not proposed. The Vice President is a neutral constitutional authority, so (b) fits. The related National Judicial Appointments Commission (99th Amendment, 2014) was struck down in 2015 in the Fourth Judges case.
explanations: Incorrect: the Prime Minister heads the executive, and having him chair a body to discipline judges would compromise judicial independence; the ARC did not recommend this.
Correct: the Second ARC suggested a National Judicial Council chaired by the Vice President of India to inquire into the conduct of higher judiciary members.
Incorrect: the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over one House and is not proposed to head the Council; the Speaker only takes part in the impeachment process in the Lok Sabha.
Incorrect: the Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha is a political position with no such role in the ARC's proposal.
keyfact: Second ARC proposed a National Judicial Council chaired by the Vice President of India.
option_notes: The Prime Minister of India is the head of the Council of Ministers under Article 74 and the real executive head. The PM is appointed by the President (Article 75), is the leader of the Lok Sabha majority, and advises the President on appointments, including those of judges in consultation with the judiciary. The PM chairs NITI Aayog and the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet, but no judicial discipline body.

The Vice President of India is elected under Article 66 by an electoral college of members of both Houses of Parliament, holds office for five years, and is ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64). The VP acts as President during a vacancy for up to six months. The VP's neutrality is why the Second ARC proposed the VP as Chairman of the National Judicial Council.

The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by the members of the House from among themselves (Article 93). The Speaker presides over joint sittings, certifies Money Bills, decides disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, and has only a casting vote. The Speaker receives and may admit a judge-removal motion in the Lok Sabha under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.

The Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha is the head of the largest opposition party in the House, recognised with a statutory salary and allowances under the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977. The LoP sits on selection committees for the CBI Director, Lokpal, CVC and NHRC. The LoP is not a constitutional office.
related: Second ARC was set up in 2005 under Veerappa Moily, with 15 reports.
Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 governs the removal procedure for SC/HC judges.
Article 124(4) provides for removal of Supreme Court judges.
99th Amendment (2014) created the NJAC, struck down in 2015.
No Indian judge has yet been removed by impeachment.
Vice President is ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 89).
First ARC (1966) was chaired by Morarji Desai.
summary: The answer is (b) Vice President of India. The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (chaired by M. Veerappa Moily) recommended a National Judicial Council headed by the Vice President to inquire into misconduct by higher judiciary members, as an alternative to the cumbersome impeachment process.
topic_notes: Judicial accountability in India rests on constitutional provisions plus statute. Judges of the Supreme Court are removed under Article 124(4), and High Court judges under Article 217 read with 124. Grounds are proved misbehaviour or incapacity. The process requires a motion signed by at least 100 Lok Sabha members or 50 Rajya Sabha members, a three-member inquiry committee under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, and a special majority in each House (majority of total membership plus two-thirds of those present and voting) in the same session, followed by a Presidential order. No judge has ever been removed. Justice V. Ramaswami's motion failed in 1993 in the Lok Sabha, Justice Soumitra Sen resigned in 2011 after the Rajya Sabha vote, and Justice P.D. Dinakaran resigned in 2011. Reform proposals include the Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill, 2010 (lapsed), which sought to create the National Judicial Oversight Committee, and the Second ARC's National Judicial Council headed by the Vice President. The Second ARC (2005-2009) was chaired first by Veerappa Moily, then by M. Veerappa Moily after Hanumantha Rao's earlier role. It produced 15 reports, including Right to Information, Ethics in Governance, Local Governance and Public Order. The First ARC (1966) was chaired by Morarji Desai, then K. Hanumanthaiya. The NJAC through the 99th Amendment and NJAC Act, 2014 was struck down in the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association case (2015), restoring the Collegium. Also note Article 124(2) (appointments), Article 50 (separation of judiciary from executive), and the 'in-house procedure' of 1999 for complaints against judges.

question: Which one of the following statements is not correct ?
options: Poshan Abhiyaan is a flagship programme of the Ministry of Agriculture
Mahila Shakti Kendra Scheme aims to empower women through community participation
Village Convergence and Facilitation Service aims to create awareness through community engagement
Ujjwala Scheme aims to combat trafficking of women and children
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Poshan Abhiyaan, also called National Nutrition Mission, was launched by PM Narendra Modi on 8 March 2018 at Jhunjhunu, Rajasthan. It is run by the Ministry of Women and Child Development (MoWCD). It targets stunting, undernutrition, anaemia and low birth weight, with goals such as reducing stunting by 2% per year and anaemia by 3% per year. It relies on convergence across ministries, technology (ICDS-CAS app), Jan Andolan and community mobilisation, so Agriculture is only one partner, not the owner. Mahila Shakti Kendra (MSK), launched 2017 under MoWCD, empowers rural women through community participation and provides convergence of schemes at village, block and district levels, using student volunteers. Village Convergence and Facilitation Service (VCFS) is a component of MSK/ Mission Shakti-linked structures at village level that spreads awareness through community engagement. Ujjwala (MoWCD, 2007) is a comprehensive scheme for prevention of trafficking and for rescue, rehabilitation, reintegration and repatriation of victims. Do not confuse it with Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (LPG, Petroleum Ministry, 2016). Since (b), (c), (d) match their schemes' objectives, only (a) is wrong.
explanations: Incorrect statement, hence the answer. Poshan Abhiyaan belongs to the Ministry of Women and Child Development, not Agriculture.
Correct statement. Mahila Shakti Kendra empowers rural women through community participation, so it is not the answer.
Correct statement. VCFS works at village level to create awareness and facilitate access to services through community engagement, so it is not the answer.
Correct statement. The Ujjwala scheme of MoWCD is aimed at preventing trafficking of women and children and rehabilitating victims, so it is not the answer.
keyfact: Poshan Abhiyaan (2018) belongs to the Ministry of Women and Child Development, not the Ministry of Agriculture.
option_notes: Poshan Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission) was launched on 8 March 2018 from Jhunjhunu, Rajasthan, by PM Modi. It is under the Ministry of Women and Child Development. It aims to reduce stunting, undernutrition, anaemia and low birth weight through convergence, technology (ICDS-CAS), and Jan Andolan. Poshan Maah is observed every September. In 2021 it was subsumed with others into Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0.

Mahila Shakti Kendra (MSK) was approved in 2017 under MoWCD as a centrally sponsored scheme. It provides an interface for rural women to access opportunities in skill development, employment, digital literacy, health and nutrition. It operates through community engagement via student volunteers and is set up at village, block and district levels, covering 115 most backward districts initially. It is now part of Mission Shakti.

Village Convergence and Facilitation Service (VCFS) is the village-level service under the Mahila Shakti Kendra framework. Community-level volunteers (such as Mahila Shakti Kendra workers and student volunteers) raise awareness, and help women access government schemes and entitlements. It uses community engagement and convergence of services at the grassroots, supporting the Block-level and District-level Centres for Women.

Ujjwala (2007) is a Ministry of Women and Child Development scheme, a comprehensive scheme for prevention of trafficking, and rescue, rehabilitation, reintegration and repatriation of victims of trafficking for commercial sexual exploitation. It is implemented mainly through NGOs. It is distinct from Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana, launched 1 May 2016 from Ballia, UP, giving free LPG connections to BPL women households.
related: Poshan Abhiyaan was launched on 8 March 2018 at Jhunjhunu, Rajasthan.
Poshan Abhiyaan is run by the Ministry of Women and Child Development.
Poshan Maah is celebrated every September; Poshan Pakhwada in March-April.
PM Ujjwala Yojana (LPG, 2016) is under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
Ujjwala (2007) is MoWCD's anti-trafficking scheme.
PM POSHAN is the renamed Mid-Day Meal scheme under the Education Ministry.
Mission Shakti, Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, and Mission Vatsalya are MoWCD umbrella schemes.
Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana gives Rs 5,000 in instalments for the first living child.
summary: The answer is (a). Poshan Abhiyaan (POSHAN = Prime Minister's Overarching Scheme for Holistic Nourishment) is a flagship programme of the Ministry of Women and Child Development, not the Ministry of Agriculture, so statement (a) is the incorrect one.
topic_notes: Women and child welfare schemes are a regular theme. The Ministry of Women and Child Development (MoWCD) was created as a separate ministry in 2006 (earlier a department under HRD). Its umbrella schemes: Mission Shakti (for safety and empowerment of women, 2021-22 onward, with Sambal and Samarthya verticals), Mission Poshan 2.0 (Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0), and Mission Vatsalya (child protection). Poshan Abhiyaan was launched on 8 March 2018 (International Women's Day) at Jhunjhunu, Rajasthan, with a three-year budget of about Rs 9,000 crore, partly funded by World Bank and bilateral support. Its targets: reduce stunting, undernutrition and low birth weight by 2% per year each, and anaemia by 3% per year; the goal was to achieve a Malnutrition-Free India by 2022. Key schemes: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015, Panipat, Haryana), One Stop Centre (Sakhi, 2015), Women Helpline 181, Swadhar Greh, Ujjwala (anti-trafficking), Working Women Hostel, Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (2017, Rs 5,000 maternity benefit), Mahila Shakti Kendra (2017), and NARI portal. Do not confuse similarly named programmes: PM Ujjwala Yojana (LPG, Petroleum Ministry), PM POSHAN (formerly Mid-Day Meal, Education Ministry, renamed 2021), and Ujjawala. Ministries: Agriculture handles PM-KISAN, PMFBY; Health handles Anaemia Mukt Bharat and Mission Indradhanush; Education handles PM POSHAN. UPSC often tests ministry-scheme matching and the launch details.

question: The Lokayukta Institution in India is based on: :
options: Its long tradition of vigilance commissions in the country
The recommendations of the First Administrative Reforms Commission
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Ombudsman is an official appointed by the legislature to investigate citizens' complaints against maladministration and corruption. Sweden created it in 1809, and Finland, Denmark, Norway and New Zealand followed. In India, the First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966-70, chaired first by Morarji Desai and then by K. Hanumanthaiya) recommended a two-tier machinery: Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayukta in the states. This idea was inspired by the Ombudsman and by New Zealand's Parliamentary Commissioner. Maharashtra was the first state to create a Lokayukta, in 1971 (Act of 1971, operational 1972). Odisha passed an Act earlier, in 1970, but it came into force only in 1983. The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 requires every state to establish a Lokayukta. Option (c) is tempting, but it names only the recommending body, whereas the question asks what the institution is based on, which is the Ombudsman model. Option (a) is wrong because vigilance commissions (CVC, 1964) are a separate Indian body. Option (b) is wrong because the Koban is a Japanese community policing system.
explanations: Incorrect: vigilance commissions such as the CVC (1964, Santhanam Committee) deal with administrative vigilance in the central government. They are not the basis of the Lokayukta.
Incorrect: Koban is a Japanese neighbourhood police-box system with no link to the Lokayukta.
Incorrect as the intended answer: the ARC did recommend Lokpal and Lokayukta, but the institution's conceptual basis is the Ombudsman. UPSC marks (d) as correct.
Correct: the Lokayukta is modelled on the Scandinavian Ombudsman system, which originated in Sweden in 1809.
keyfact: The Lokayukta is modelled on the Swedish (Scandinavian) Ombudsman, and the First ARC recommended it.
option_notes: Vigilance commissions: the Central Vigilance Commission was set up in 1964 on the Santhanam Committee's recommendation. It became statutory under the CVC Act, 2003. It advises on corruption in central government bodies and is headed by the Central Vigilance Commissioner. It is distinct from the Lokpal and Lokayukta.

Koban is a Japanese community policing system of small neighbourhood police boxes staffed by officers who patrol locally and help residents. It dates from the Meiji era. It has been studied by other countries as a model of community policing and has nothing to do with anti-corruption ombudsmen.

The First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966-70) was first chaired by Morarji Desai and then by K. Hanumanthaiya. It submitted a report on the Problems of Redress of Citizens' Grievances (1966) recommending Lokpal and Lokayukta. It also drew on the Ombudsman concept. The Lokpal Bill was first introduced in 1968 and finally became law in 2013.

The Ombudsman is a legislature-appointed officer who investigates complaints against public administration. Sweden established the office in 1809 (Justitieombudsmannen). Denmark adopted it in 1955 and New Zealand in 1962. Many countries have since copied it, and India's Lokpal and Lokayukta are its equivalents.
related: Sweden created the first Ombudsman in 1809.
The First ARC (1966-70) recommended Lokpal and Lokayukta.
Maharashtra established the first Lokayukta in 1971.
The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 came into force on 16 January 2014.
Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose was India's first Lokpal chairperson, appointed in 2019.
The CVC was set up in 1964 on the Santhanam Committee's recommendation.
The Lokpal Bill was first introduced in 1968 in the Lok Sabha.
summary: The answer is (d). The Lokayukta is modelled on the Scandinavian Ombudsman system, which began in Sweden in 1809. It is a grievance-redressal and anti-corruption institution at the state level.
topic_notes: The Lokpal and Lokayukta are India's anti-corruption ombudsman institutions. The First ARC (1966-70) recommended them, drawing on the Scandinavian Ombudsman and New Zealand's Parliamentary Commissioner. The Lokpal Bill was first introduced in the Lok Sabha in 1968 and lapsed repeatedly. After the Anna Hazare movement of 2011, the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 was passed, and it came into force on 16 January 2014. The first Lokpal chairperson, Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose, was appointed in March 2019. The Lokpal has a chairperson and up to 8 members, of whom 50% are judicial members, and 50% of all members belong to SC, ST, OBC, minorities and women. The Act requires states to set up a Lokayukta within one year. The Prime Minister falls within the Lokpal's ambit, with safeguards covering international relations, security, public order, atomic energy and space. Maharashtra was the first state to establish a Lokayukta, in 1971. Odisha passed its Act in 1970, but it came into force only in 1983. Other early states include Bihar (1973), Uttar Pradesh (1975), Madhya Pradesh (1981), Andhra Pradesh (1983), Himachal Pradesh (1983), Karnataka (1984) and Gujarat (1986). Structures differ by state, including the Lokayukta's qualifications, tenure and jurisdiction over the Chief Minister. Related bodies include the CVC (1964), the CBI (1963 resolution; DSPE Act 1946) and the Santhanam Committee (1962-64). The Lokpal also has an inquiry wing and a prosecution wing.

ocr: Match List I with List II and select the correct | 101. answer using the code given below the Lists : List I List IT (Programme | Institute) (Feature) A. Pradhan Mantri 1.. Public- Kaushal Vikas Yojana Private partnership firm B. National Skill 2. Outcome- 102. Development based skill Corporation training scheme C. Udaan 3. Special industry initiative D. National Policy on 4. Skilling Skill Development ecosystem in India 108. Code: A B Cc D (a) 2 1 3 4 (b) 2 3 af 4 () 4 3 t 2 (dd) 4 uf 3 2
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The question tests India's skill development architecture. The Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY), launched in 2015 under the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE), is the flagship short-term, outcome-based skill training scheme: training partners are paid on assessment and certification, with monetary rewards for certified candidates. The National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC), set up in 2008-09 under the Companies Act as a not-for-profit company, is a public-private partnership: the Government holds 49% and the private sector 51%. Udaan is a special industry initiative for Jammu and Kashmir youth, implemented by NSDC with the Ministry of Home Affairs, giving skill training and placement with corporates. The National Policy on Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (2015, replacing the 2009 policy) lays out the framework for the skilling ecosystem. Elimination: once PMKVY is matched to 2 (outcome-based), only option (a) or (b) remain; NSDC as PPP (1) then picks (a), because (b) gives NSDC the special industry initiative, which is Udaan's feature.
explanations: Correct: A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4 matches all four items with the right features, as per the official answer.
Incorrect: it matches B with 3 and C with 1, which is wrong because NSDC is the PPP firm and Udaan is the special industry initiative.
Incorrect: it matches A with 4 and D with 2, which swaps the scheme and the policy, so both are wrong.
Incorrect: A-4 and D-2 swap the scheme with the policy; PMKVY is the outcome-based scheme and the policy shapes the ecosystem.
keyfact: PMKVY = outcome-based training scheme; NSDC = PPP company (49:51); Udaan = J&K industry initiative; National Policy = skilling ecosystem.
option_notes: Option (a) A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4 is the correct combination. It pairs PMKVY with the outcome-based scheme, NSDC with the PPP company (49:51 Government and private), Udaan with the J&K special industry initiative, and the National Policy on Skill Development with the overall skilling ecosystem. All four institutions fall under or are linked with MSDE, formed in November 2014.

Option (b) A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4 is wrong because it gives NSDC the feature of a special industry initiative and Udaan the PPP firm feature. Udaan is a 2011 programme for J&K youth, run by NSDC with the Home Ministry, offering corporate training and placement. It is not a company; NSDC is the PPP company.

Option (c) A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2 is wrong on all four pairings. PMKVY (2015) is a scheme, not a policy or ecosystem. NSDC (2008) is a company with 49% government and 51% private ownership. Udaan is the J&K industry initiative, and the National Policy (2009, revised 2015) is a policy document, not an outcome-based training scheme.

Option (d) A-4, B-1, C-3, D-2 is wrong because it swaps PMKVY and the policy. B and C are right in this option, but A and D are not. PMKVY is the flagship outcome-based training scheme under Skill India, with versions 1.0 to 4.0, whereas the National Policy provides the overarching framework, not a training scheme.
related: MSDE was created in November 2014.
Skill India Mission was launched on 15 July 2015, World Youth Skills Day.
NSDC: 49% Government, 51% private shareholding.
NSQF has 10 levels.
Udaan (2011) is for J&K youth, run with the Home Ministry.
NAPS was launched in 2016 for apprenticeship promotion.
NCVET was set up in 2018 as the regulator for vocational education and training.
PMKVY 4.0 was launched in 2022-23.
statements: A — Correct: PMKVY matches 2 (outcome-based skill training scheme). PMKVY was launched on 15 July 2015 (World Youth Skills Day) by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship. It offers short-term training, recognition of prior learning (RPL) and special projects. Versions: PMKVY 1.0 (2015-16), 2.0 (2016-20), 3.0 (2021), and 4.0 (2022-23 onwards). NSDC implements the Short Term Training component. Candidates receive Skill India certification, and payment to training providers is linked to outcomes such as assessment, certification and placement.

B — Correct: NSDC matches 1 (public-private partnership firm). NSDC was incorporated in 2008 and is a not-for-profit public limited company under Section 25 of the Companies Act 1956 (now Section 8 of the 2013 Act). The Government of India, through MSDE, holds 49% and the private sector holds 51%. It funds private vocational training institutions and promotes Sector Skill Councils. The first chairman was Mr. Pratap Pawar. It is a key body in the Skill India Mission, launched in 2015.

C — Correct: Udaan matches 3 (special industry initiative). Udaan, launched in 2011, is a special industry initiative for Jammu and Kashmir, run by NSDC with funding from the Ministry of Home Affairs. It aims to give graduates, postgraduates and diploma holders from J&K exposure to corporate India through training of 3 to 12 months with leading corporates, providing employability skills and placement opportunities. It is part of efforts to integrate J&K youth into mainstream employment and reduce unemployment.

D — Correct: National Policy on Skill Development matches 4 (skilling ecosystem in India). The first policy came in 2009; the National Policy for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship was released in 2015 on World Youth Skills Day. It targets skilling at scale with speed and standards, aims to reach 400 million skilled persons by 2022 (an original target), and promotes entrepreneurship, the National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF), and links with Sector Skill Councils. MSDE was created in November 2014.
summary: The correct answer is (a): A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4. PMKVY is an outcome-based skill training scheme, NSDC is a public-private partnership company, Udaan is a special industry initiative for J&K youth, and the National Policy on Skill Development shapes the skilling ecosystem in India.
topic_notes: Skill development in India is coordinated by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE), created in November 2014; the first minister was Rajiv Pratap Rudy. The Skill India Mission was launched on 15 July 2015, which is also observed as World Youth Skills Day. The Mission has the National Policy for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship 2015, PMKVY, the National Skill Development Mission, and the Skill Loan scheme. Institutions include NSDC (2008, PPP), the National Skill Development Agency (NSDA), the National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET, 2018, which replaced NCVT and NSDA functions), the Directorate General of Training (DGT), which runs ITIs and apprenticeship, Sector Skill Councils (SSCs), and the Sector Skill Councils' National Occupational Standards. The National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF) has levels 1 to 10.
