The official key lists (b) 2060, and for the exam the key is to be treated as the accepted answer, while remembering the 2070 fact for other questions.
explanations: Factually, 2070 is the year India announced at COP26 and later submitted in its LT-LEDS. This conflicts with the official key, which marks (b), so this option should be remembered as India's actual target.
Per the official key, this is the accepted answer. 2060 is the net zero year of China, Russia, Saudi Arabia and others, and not what India announced at Glasgow.
2050 is the target of the US, EU, UK and Japan. It is not India's target.
2040 is not a net zero target India announced. Some countries, such as Finland (2035) and Austria (2040), have earlier dates.
keyfact: India announced net zero by 2070 at COP26 (Glasgow, 2021); the official key here marks 2060, which is China's target year.
option_notes: 2070: India's net zero target announced by PM Modi at COP26 in Glasgow on 1 Nov 2021. It was formalised in the updated NDC (Aug 2022) and the LT-LEDS submitted at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh. It is part of the 'Panchamrit' commitments, alongside 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.

2060: the net zero target year of China (announced in 2020), Russia, Saudi Arabia (2060) and Indonesia (2060). It is the answer in the official key for this question, though India's own announced target is 2070.

2050: the net zero year targeted by the EU (European Green Deal), the UK (legally binding since 2019), the US, Japan and Canada. Many developed countries chose this date in line with the IPCC 1.5 degree C pathway.
2040: not a common net zero target for large economies. Austria aims for 2040 and Finland for 2035. India has not announced this year; its 2030 goals are interim targets, not net zero.
related: COP26 was held in Glasgow, UK in 2021.
India's net zero target year is 2070, announced by PM Modi at COP26.
Panchamrit: five climate commitments announced by India at COP26.
Glasgow Climate Pact calls for a 'phase down' of unabated coal power.
India's LT-LEDS was submitted at COP27 in 2022.
COP28 was held in Dubai in 2023; COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt.
China's net zero target year is 2060; the EU, UK and US target 2050.
summary: The answer is (b) 2060 per the official key, though the facts say otherwise. At COP26 in Glasgow (November 2021), PM Narendra Modi announced that India would reach net zero emissions by 2070, and the 2070 target is the one India submitted to the UNFCCC. The official key marks 2060, which conflicts with this record, so the note flags the discrepancy.
topic_notes: COP26 was held in Glasgow, UK, 31 Oct to 13 Nov 2021, under the UK presidency (Alok Sharma as president), in partnership with Italy. It was the first COP to follow the Paris Agreement's five-year ratchet for updated NDCs. The Glasgow Climate Pact was the first climate agreement to explicitly mention coal: it called for a 'phase down' of unabated coal power after India and China's last-minute change from 'phase out'. It also asked countries to revisit their 2030 targets by end-2022, urged developed countries to double adaptation finance by 2025, and finalised Paris Agreement Article 6 rules on carbon markets. India's 'Panchamrit': 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030; 50% renewable energy share in energy needs by 2030; 1 billion tonne reduction in projected emissions by 2030; 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP by 2030 against 2005; net zero by 2070. Modi also launched the 'One Sun One World One Grid' initiative (Green Grids Initiative) with the UK, and 'LiFE' (Lifestyle for Environment) as a mass movement. India's updated NDC (2022) set a 45% emissions intensity cut and 50% cumulative non-fossil electric power capacity by 2030. COP27: Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt (2022), with the Loss and Damage fund. COP28: Dubai (2023), with the first 'global stocktake' and a call for transitioning away from fossil fuels. COP29: Baku (2024), focused on the climate finance goal.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q115.
ocr: The ‘Glasgow Climate Pact’ made during the COP26 Climate Summit emphasized: on India’s announcement of the target of becoming ‘Net Zero’ carbon emitter by : (a) 2070 (b) 2060 (c) 2050 (d) 2040
subject: General Science
detail: At COP26 (Glasgow, 31 Oct to 13 Nov 2021, UK presidency under Alok Sharma), PM Modi presented the 'Panchamrit' at the World Leaders' Summit on 1 Nov 2021. Its five elements are: (1) 500 GW non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030; (2) 50% of energy requirements from renewables by 2030; (3) a reduction of 1 billion tonnes of projected carbon emissions by 2030; (4) a reduction of the carbon intensity of the economy by 45% by 2030 over 2005 levels; (5) Net Zero by 2070. India later submitted an updated NDC in August 2022 (45% emissions-intensity cut and 50% non-fossil power capacity by 2030) and its Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy (LT-LEDS) at COP27 in 2022. The Glasgow Climate Pact called for a 'phase-down' of unabated coal power, after India pushed for it to replace 'phase-out'. It also asked countries to revisit their 2030 targets and to double adaptation finance. Elimination: 2050 is the date for the EU, USA and UK. 2060 is the date for China (and Russia, Saudi Arabia). 2040 is not an Indian target; Finland aims for 2035. So 2070 is the only date matching India's pledge.
explanations: Correct. India announced Net Zero by 2070 at COP26 in Glasgow in November 2021.
Incorrect. 2060 is China's carbon neutrality target (announced 2020), not India's.
Incorrect. 2050 is the Net Zero year for the EU, the UK, the USA and Japan, among others. India's target is two decades later.
Incorrect. 2040 is not India's target. Only a few countries set dates this early, and India has never announced it.
keyfact: India's COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) pledge: Net Zero by 2070, part of the five-point 'Panchamrit'.
option_notes: 2070: India's Net Zero target, announced by PM Modi at COP26 in Glasgow on 1 Nov 2021 as part of the 'Panchamrit'. It is later than the 2050 to 2060 dates of the major emitters, which India justifies by citing climate justice, common but differentiated responsibilities and its low per-capita emissions. India's LT-LEDS (2022) builds on this goal.

2060: The Net Zero or carbon neutrality year announced by China (President Xi, UN General Assembly, Sept 2020, with a peak before 2030). Russia, Saudi Arabia (2060) and Indonesia (about 2060) have similar dates. China is the world's largest emitter, so this is often confused with India's 2070.

2050: The common Net Zero year for developed economies: the EU (European Green Deal, 2050 climate neutrality), the USA, the UK (legally binding in 2019), Japan, Canada and South Korea. It is also the Paris Agreement-aligned global benchmark, with a 1.5°C pathway needing global Net Zero near 2050.

2040: Not India's target. Few countries aim this early; Iceland and Austria have set 2040 as a target, and Finland aims for 2035. India has no 2040 milestone under its NDCs or LT-LEDS. It is a distractor.
related: Panchamrit was announced by PM Modi at COP26, Glasgow, in Nov 2021.
India's target is 500 GW of non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030.
India's updated NDC (Aug 2022) targets a 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP by 2030 against 2005 levels.
The Glasgow Climate Pact changed 'phase-out' of coal to 'phase-down' at India's insistence.
Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) was launched by India at COP26.
China's carbon neutrality target is 2060, and the EU, US and UK aim for 2050.
COP28 (Dubai, 2023) operationalised the Loss and Damage Fund.
The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to keep warming well below 2°C and to pursue 1.5°C.
summary: The answer is (a) 2070. At COP26 in Glasgow (November 2021), PM Narendra Modi announced that India would reach Net Zero emissions by 2070, and the Glasgow Climate Pact took note of the pledges made by countries, including this one.
topic_notes: COP26, the 26th Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC, was held in Glasgow, UK, in Nov 2021 (delayed from 2020 by COVID-19). The UK held the presidency in partnership with Italy. The outcome, the Glasgow Climate Pact, was the first UN climate decision to explicitly mention coal: it called for a phase-down of unabated coal power and a phase-out of inefficient fossil-fuel subsidies. Following India's intervention, the final text changed 'phase-out' to 'phase-down'. The Pact urged countries to revisit and strengthen their 2030 targets by end-2022, and finalised the Paris Agreement rulebook, including Article 6 on carbon markets. Developed countries were urged to double adaptation finance by 2025, and the unmet $100 billion per year pledge was noted with regret. India's 'Panchamrit' pledges: 500 GW non-fossil capacity, 50% renewable energy share, 1 billion tonnes less emissions, 45% lower carbon intensity (by 2030, against 2005), and Net Zero by 2070. Modi also launched 'LiFE' (Lifestyle for Environment) and announced the Infrastructure for Resilient Island States (IRIS) initiative along with the International Solar Alliance and the Green Grids Initiative (One Sun One World One Grid). India's earlier NDC (2015) promised a 33 to 35% intensity cut and 40% non-fossil capacity by 2030. Later COPs: COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh (2022, Loss and Damage Fund), COP28 in Dubai (2023, 'transition away from fossil fuels'), COP29 in Baku (2024, new finance goal), and COP30 in Belém, Brazil (2025).

question: Which one of the following is the theme of} 119. International Women’s Day, 2022 observed by the United Nations ?
options: Gender equality today for a sustainable tomorrow
Time is Now: Rural and Urban Activists Transforming Women’s Lives
Think Equal, Build Smart, Innovate for Change
Women in Leadership : Achieving an equal future in a COVID-19 world
subject: Current Affairs
detail: International Women's Day (IWD) is observed every year on 8 March. The UN first celebrated it in 1975 (International Women's Year) and formally adopted a General Assembly resolution in 1977 inviting states to proclaim a day for women's rights and world peace. The UN theme for 2022 was 'Gender equality today for a sustainable tomorrow', recognising the contribution of women and girls around the world who are leading the charge on climate adaptation, mitigation and response to build a more sustainable future. It is linked to SDG 5 (gender equality) and SDG 13 (climate action). Note that the UN theme differs from the separate campaign theme of the IWD organisation, which in 2022 was '#BreakTheBias'. Elimination: (b) is the UN Women theme for 2018 ('Time is now: rural and urban activists transforming women's lives'); (c) 'Think equal, build smart, innovate for change' was the 2019 theme; (d) 'Women in leadership: Achieving an equal future in a COVID-19 world' was the 2021 theme. Students should memorise the year-wise themes since UPSC reuses them as distractors.
explanations: Correct: this is the official UN theme for IWD 2022, centred on gender equality and climate sustainability.
Wrong: this was the 2018 UN Women theme, which focused on rural and urban activists transforming women's lives.
Wrong: this was the 2019 theme, which focused on social protection, public services and sustainable infrastructure for gender equality.
Wrong: this was the 2021 theme, which highlighted women's leadership in the COVID-19 pandemic response.
keyfact: IWD 2022 UN theme: 'Gender equality today for a sustainable tomorrow' (2021 = Women in leadership; 2019 = Think equal, build smart; 2018 = Time is Now).
option_notes: 'Gender equality today for a sustainable tomorrow' is the UN theme for IWD 2022 (8 March 2022). It recognised women and girls leading climate change adaptation, mitigation and response. It ties into SDG 5 (gender equality) and SDG 13 (climate action) and drew on the Commission on the Status of Women's 66th session priority theme on achieving gender equality in the context of climate change and disaster risk reduction policies.

'Time is Now: Rural and Urban Activists Transforming Women's Lives' was the UN theme for 2018. It was set against the backdrop of the #MeToo and #TimesUp movements and highlighted activists, along with rural women whose rights and lives faced particular challenges. The 2018 CSW62 priority theme was on challenges and opportunities in achieving gender equality and empowering rural women and girls.

'Think equal, build smart, innovate for change' was the UN theme for 2019. It focused on innovative ways to advance gender equality, especially in social protection systems, access to public services and sustainable infrastructure. It aligned with CSW63's priority theme and stressed designing systems and technology that meet the needs of women and girls.

'Women in leadership: Achieving an equal future in a COVID-19 world' was the UN theme for 2021. It celebrated the efforts of women and girls around the world in shaping a more equal future and recovering from the pandemic. It aligned with CSW65's priority theme on women's full and effective participation and decision-making in public life.
related: IWD is observed every year on 8 March.
UN began observing IWD in 1975; General Assembly resolution adopted in 1977.
UN Women was created in 2010 and became operational in 2011.
Commission on the Status of Women was established in 1946 under ECOSOC.
IWD 2023 UN theme: 'DigitALL: Innovation and technology for gender equality'.
IWD 2021 UN theme: 'Women in leadership: Achieving an equal future in a COVID-19 world'.
IWD 2019 UN theme: 'Think equal, build smart, innovate for change'.
SDG 5 is gender equality; SDG 13 is climate action.
summary: The answer is (a): the UN theme for International Women's Day 2022 (8 March 2022) was 'Gender equality today for a sustainable tomorrow'. It focused on women and girls leading adaptation, mitigation and response to climate change and disaster risk reduction.
topic_notes: International Women's Day is observed on 8 March. Its roots lie in early 20th-century labour movements: the first National Woman's Day was held in the US in 1909, and Clara Zetkin proposed an international day at the 1910 Second International Conference of Working Women in Copenhagen. It was first celebrated on 19 March 1911 in several European countries, and 8 March became standard after the 1917 women's protests in Russia. The UN began observing it in 1975 and adopted the General Assembly resolution in December 1977. UN Women, created in 2010 and operational from 2011, is the UN entity for gender equality and women's empowerment; its Executive Director from 2021 is Sima Bahous. The Commission on the Status of Women (CSW), a functional commission of ECOSOC established in 1946, meets annually in March in New York; CSW66 in 2022 had the priority theme of gender equality and empowerment in the context of climate change, environmental and disaster risk reduction policies. Recent UN themes: 2020 'I am Generation Equality: Realizing Women's Rights'; 2021 'Women in leadership: Achieving an equal future in a COVID-19 world'; 2022 'Gender equality today for a sustainable tomorrow'; 2023 'DigitALL: Innovation and technology for gender equality'; 2024 'Invest in women: Accelerate progress'. The IWD campaign theme for 2022 was #BreakTheBias. The international colour symbols are purple, green and white. Related Indian items: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015), Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 giving 26 weeks leave, Women's Reservation Act 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), and the Global Gender Gap Index by the World Economic Forum.

question:
The National Education Policy, 2020 proposed a new curriculum structure 5 + 3 + 3+
4. The first 5 year period refers to :
options: Two years of early childhood care and education and classes 1, 2 and 3
Three years of early childhood care and education and classes 1 and 2 120
subject: Current Affairs
detail: NEP 2020 replaced the old 10+2 structure with a 5+3+3+4 design covering ages 3 to 18. The Foundational Stage (5 years, ages 3-8) combines three years of early childhood care and education (ECCE) in Anganwadi or pre-school with Classes 1 and 2 in primary school. It stresses play-based, activity-based and discovery-based learning, and the national mission on foundational literacy and numeracy (NIPUN Bharat, launched July 2021) targets universal basic skills by Grade 3. The Preparatory Stage (3 years, ages 8-11) covers Classes 3 to 5. The Middle Stage (3 years, ages 11-14) covers Classes 6 to 8. The Secondary Stage (4 years, ages 14-18) covers Classes 9 to 12 and is multidisciplinary, with semester options and flexibility of subject choice. Elimination: option (a) treats the first 5 years as Classes 1-5, which ignores ECCE and is the old structure. Option (b) gives only 2 years of ECCE and 3 years of school, which is wrong. Option (d), Classes 6-10, matches no stage. Only (c) matches the policy text. The policy was approved by the Union Cabinet on 29 July 2020 and was based on the Kasturirangan Committee report.
explanations: Incorrect: Classes 1 to 5 would leave out ECCE. In NEP 2020, Classes 3-5 belong to the Preparatory Stage, not the Foundational Stage.
Incorrect: the Foundational Stage has 3 years of ECCE, not 2, and only Classes 1 and 2, not Classes 1-3.
Correct: the Foundational Stage is 3 years of pre-school/Anganwadi (ages 3-6) plus Classes 1-2 (ages 6-8), totalling 5 years.
Incorrect: Classes 6-10 do not form any NEP stage. Classes 6-8 are the Middle Stage and Classes 9-12 the Secondary Stage.
keyfact: NEP 2020 5+3+3+4: the first 5 years (ages 3-8) = 3 years of pre-school/ECCE + Classes 1-2 (Foundational Stage).
option_notes: Classes 1 to 5 were the primary stage under the old 10+2 system. NEP 2020 splits these years: Classes 1-2 go into the Foundational Stage and Classes 3-5 into the Preparatory Stage. The Right to Education Act, 2009 covers ages 6-14 and does not include pre-school. NEP proposes extending the RTE framework to ages 3-18.

This option is a distractor with 2 years of ECCE plus Classes 1-3. NEP 2020 prescribes 3 years of ECCE (ages 3-6), and Class 3 starts the Preparatory Stage. The ECCE curriculum is built around the National Curricular Framework for Foundational Stage (NCF-FS 2022), with play-based learning and mother-tongue instruction.

This is the correct option. The Foundational Stage lasts 5 years across ages 3-8: 3 years of Anganwadi/pre-school plus Classes 1-2. Learning is play-based and activity-based, with stress on foundational literacy and numeracy. The Ministry of Women and Child Development and the Ministry of Education jointly oversee ECCE delivery.

Classes 6-10 do not correspond to any NEP stage. Classes 6-8 form the Middle Stage (ages 11-14), with subject-teachers, experiential learning and vocational exposure from Class 6, including internships. Classes 9-12 form the Secondary Stage (ages 14-18). The Board exams are retained but redesigned to test core competencies, and NEP 2020 proposes the option of taking them twice a year.
related: NEP 2020 was approved by the Union Cabinet on 29 July 2020, with K. Kasturirangan as the committee chair.
Foundational Stage: ages 3-8, with 3 years of ECCE plus Classes 1-2.
Preparatory Stage: ages 8-11, Classes 3-5.
Middle Stage: ages 11-14, Classes 6-8; Secondary Stage: ages 14-18, Classes 9-12.
NEP 2020 targets 100% GER in school education by 2030 and 50% GER in higher education by 2035.
NEP recommends 6% of GDP for public spending on education.
NIPUN Bharat Mission (2021) targets foundational literacy and numeracy by Grade 3.
PARAKH is the national assessment centre proposed under NEP 2020.
summary: The answer is (c). Under NEP 2020, the 5+3+3+4 structure begins with a 5-year Foundational Stage: 3 years of pre-primary (Anganwadi/pre-school, ages 3-6) plus Classes 1 and 2 (ages 6-8).
topic_notes: NEP 2020 is India's third national education policy, after 1968 (Kothari Commission) and 1986 (modified 1992). The Union Cabinet approved it on 29 July 2020, and a committee headed by K. Kasturirangan drafted it. It replaces the 10+2 system with 5+3+3+4: Foundational (ages 3-8, 5 years), Preparatory (8-11, Classes 3-5), Middle (11-14, Classes 6-8) and Secondary (14-18, Classes 9-12). Key features: the Ministry of Human Resource Development is renamed the Ministry of Education; the policy sets a 100% Gross Enrolment Ratio in school education by 2030 and 50% GER in higher education by 2035; it recommends public spending on education of 6% of GDP; and it promotes mother tongue or regional language as the medium of instruction at least until Grade 5, preferably Grade 8. It also recommends the three-language formula with flexibility and no imposition of any language. In higher education it proposes a single regulator, the Higher Education Commission of India (HECI), with four verticals: NHERC (regulation), NAC (accreditation), HEGC (funding) and GEC (standards). It also proposes the Academic Bank of Credits, multiple entry and exit in undergraduate degrees (4-year UG programme), the phasing out of MPhil, a National Research Foundation, PARAKH as a national assessment centre, and the National Testing Agency for common entrance exams. Related initiatives: NIPUN Bharat Mission, PM SHRI Schools, Vidya Pravesh, and DIKSHA.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) : 1 It was established in the year 1989 in Tokyo. 2: Initially its mandate was to examine and develop measures to combat money laundering.
3. The objectives of the FATF are to set standards and _ promote _ effective implementation of legal, regulatory and operational measures for combating money laundering, terrorist financing and other related threats to the integrity of the international financial system. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) is an inter-governmental policy-making body created in July 1989 by the G7 Summit held in Paris (the Arche Summit). The place of establishment is therefore Paris, not Tokyo, which makes statement 1 the trap. Its original mandate was to examine and develop measures to combat money laundering, mainly arising from drug trafficking. In 1990 it issued the 40 Recommendations. After 2001 its mandate expanded to terrorist financing (9 Special Recommendations), and in 2012 to proliferation financing. The objectives in statement 3 match the FATF's official description: setting standards and promoting effective implementation of legal, regulatory and operational measures against money laundering, terrorist financing and other threats to the integrity of the international financial system. Elimination logic: once statement 1 is recognised as wrong (Paris, not Tokyo), options (a) and (c) fall away. Statement 3 is correct, which eliminates nothing further by itself, but statement 2 is also correct, so (d) is out. That leaves (b). The FATF has its secretariat at the OECD headquarters in Paris. India became a member in 2010. The FATF maintains the grey list (jurisdictions under increased monitoring) and the black list (call for action).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which gives the wrong place of establishment (Tokyo instead of Paris).
Right: statements 2 and 3 are correct, and statement 1 is incorrect because the FATF was created in Paris in 1989.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and it leaves out statement 3, which is correct.
Wrong: statement 3 is correct, but statement 2 is also correct, so 3 alone is incomplete.
keyfact: The FATF was set up by the G7 in Paris in 1989 (not Tokyo) to fight money laundering, and now also covers terrorist and proliferation financing.
option_notes: Option (a), 1, 2 and 3: this would be correct only if the FATF had been established in Tokyo. The FATF was actually set up at the G7 Paris Summit in 1989. It began with 16 members and now has about 39 members, including the European Commission and the Gulf Cooperation Council. The secretariat is hosted by the OECD in Paris. Statements 2 and 3 are accurate, so only the Tokyo detail breaks this option.

Option (b), 2 and 3 only: this is the official answer. The FATF's initial mandate concerned money laundering, and its objectives are standard-setting and effective implementation of measures against money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing. It was founded by the G7 in 1989 in Paris. Its key output is the 40 Recommendations, enforced through peer-review mutual evaluations. India became a full member in 2010 and was evaluated in 2010 and again in 2023-24.

Option (c), 1 and 2 only: this combines the wrong statement 1 with the correct statement 2 and omits statement 3. It is wrong because the place is Paris and not Tokyo. Tokyo is sometimes confused with other G7 summits, for example the 1986 Tokyo Summit, but the FATF was not created there. The FATF's rotating presidency lasts two years. T. Raja Kumar of Singapore has been president since July 2022.

Option (d), 3 only: statement 3 is correct, as it states the FATF's objectives, but this option wrongly rejects statement 2. The money-laundering mandate was indeed the first one, and it was later broadened to terrorist financing after 2001 and proliferation financing in 2008. The FATF is a policy-making body and not a treaty-based organisation. It has no direct power to impose legal sanctions, but its listings carry strong economic pressure.
related: The FATF was set up in 1989 by the G7 at the Paris Summit; its secretariat is at the OECD in Paris.
The FATF's 40 Recommendations were first issued in 1990 and fully revised in 2012.
India became a full FATF member in 2010.
The FATF Black List is called 'High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action'; the Grey List is 'Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring'.
The FATF mandate was extended to terrorist financing after 2001 and to proliferation financing in 2008.
FIU-IND was set up in 2004 and receives suspicious transaction reports under the PMLA, 2002.
Pakistan was removed from the FATF grey list in October 2022.
The FATF presidency has a two-year term.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The FATF was set up in 1989 at the G7 Summit in Paris, not Tokyo. The G7 Summit of July 1989 (Arche de la Défense, Paris) created the FATF as a temporary body, initially with 16 members. Its mandate was later made open-ended and has been renewed periodically. The secretariat sits at the OECD headquarters in Paris. Its plenary meets three times a year, and the presidency rotates every two years. Because the body started as a G7 initiative, many students wrongly link it to other cities, which is why UPSC uses place-based traps.

2 — Correct: The original mandate was to examine and develop measures to combat money laundering. At that time the main concern was laundering of drug trafficking proceeds. In 1990 the FATF published its 40 Recommendations as the first global anti-money-laundering standard, revised in 1996, 2003 and 2012. After the 9/11 attacks in 2001 the mandate was extended to terrorist financing with 8 (later 9) Special Recommendations. In 2008 it added proliferation financing of weapons of mass destruction, and the 2012 revision merged everything into 40 Recommendations.

3 — Correct: This statement reflects the FATF's official objectives. It sets international standards (the 40 Recommendations) and promotes effective implementation of legal, regulatory and operational measures against money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing. It does this through mutual evaluations of member countries, followed by follow-up reports. It publishes two lists: the 'High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action' (black list, e.g. North Korea, Iran, Myanmar) and 'Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring' (grey list). It has about 39 members, including India (since 2010), and works with FATF-style regional bodies such as the APG.
summary: The correct answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct, statement 1 is incorrect. The FATF was established in 1989 by the G7 at the Paris Summit, not in Tokyo, and its secretariat is based at the OECD in Paris.
topic_notes: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) is an inter-governmental body established in 1989 by the G7 in Paris to combat money laundering. Its secretariat is hosted at the OECD headquarters in Paris. Its mandate has widened in stages: money laundering (1989), terrorist financing (2001), and proliferation financing (2008 onwards). The 40 Recommendations were first issued in 1990 and revised in 1996, 2003 and 2012, with later updates. They are the global standard for anti-money-laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CFT) systems. The FATF assesses countries through mutual evaluations, and the assessment also covers the effectiveness of the measures, not only their legal framework. Its lists are the Black List (High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action), which has included North Korea, Iran and Myanmar, and the Grey List (Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring). Being listed can restrict a country's access to funding from the IMF, World Bank and ADB, and can lower its credit ratings. Pakistan was on the grey list from 2018 to October 2022. India joined the FATF as a member in 2010. It is also a member of the Asia/Pacific Group on Money Laundering (APG) and the Eurasian Group (EAG) as an observer. India's relevant laws include the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), whose enforcement lies with the Enforcement Directorate, and the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 (UAPA). The Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND), set up in 2004, is the national agency that receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports. Related angles that UPSC may ask include the Egmont Group (association of FIUs), the Wolfsberg Group, the Basel AML Index, and the FATF plenary schedule. The FATF presidency rotates every two years.

question: In March 2022, which of the following Ministries of the Government of India launched two special initiatives — ‘Sambhav’ and ‘Svavlamban’ to promote entrepreneurship amongst youth, especially in aspirational districts all across the country ?
options: Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises
Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports
subject: Indian Economy
detail: The MSME Ministry is the nodal ministry for promoting entrepreneurship, startups and small businesses through bodies such as KVIC, NSIC, the MSME Development Institutes and the Office of the Development Commissioner (MSME). In March 2022 it announced two outreach initiatives, Sambhav and Svavlamban, to build an entrepreneurial culture among young people, with a focus on the 112 aspirational districts identified by NITI Aayog. Sambhav was a 100-day nationwide awareness campaign, and Svavlamban was an entrepreneurship development programme aimed at helping aspiring entrepreneurs start enterprises. Both were linked to the Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav celebrations. For elimination, the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) runs Skill India, PMKVY and NSDC, so it is a tempting distractor. The Ministry of Food Processing Industries runs PMKSY and PLISFPI and is not concerned with general youth entrepreneurship. The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports handles NYKS, NSS and Khelo India. Since the question asks about an entrepreneurship drive tied to enterprises, MSME is the logical choice.
explanations: Wrong: The Ministry of Food Processing Industries deals with food processing schemes such as PMKSY, PMFME and PLI for the food sector, not these initiatives.
Wrong: MSDE is responsible for skilling schemes like PMKVY, Skill India and NSDC. Its mandate overlaps with entrepreneurship in name, but it did not launch Sambhav and Svavlamban.
Correct: The Ministry of MSME launched Sambhav and Svavlamban in March 2022 to promote youth entrepreneurship, especially in aspirational districts.
Wrong: The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports runs youth programmes such as NYKS, NSS and Khelo India, but it did not launch these entrepreneurship initiatives.
keyfact: Sambhav and Svavlamban (March 2022) = Ministry of MSME initiatives for youth entrepreneurship in aspirational districts.
option_notes: The Ministry of Food Processing Industries was set up as a separate ministry in 1988. It implements the Pradhan Mantri Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (PMKSY), the PM Formalisation of Micro Food Processing Enterprises scheme (PMFME, launched 2020) and the PLI scheme for the food processing industry. It also oversees institutions such as NIFTEM. It is headed by a Union Cabinet Minister.

MSDE was created in November 2014 to coordinate skilling efforts. It runs Skill India (launched 15 July 2015), Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY), the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC), the National Skill Development Agency and the Sector Skill Councils. It also oversees ITIs through the DGT and runs the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme.

The Ministry of MSME is the nodal ministry for micro, small and medium enterprises under the MSMED Act 2006. Its bodies include KVIC, Coir Board, NSIC and the MSME-DIs. It runs PMEGP, the CGTMSE credit guarantee scheme, MSME Champions and the Udyam registration portal (from 1 July 2020). MSME classification was revised in 2020, with investment limits of ₹1 crore, ₹10 crore and ₹50 crore for micro, small and medium enterprises respectively.

The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports oversees Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, NSS, the Sports Authority of India, Khelo India and the Rajiv Gandhi National Institute of Youth Development. It also runs the National Youth Policy and the Fit India Movement (launched 29 August 2019). It is split into the Department of Youth Affairs and the Department of Sports.
related: Sambhav and Svavlamban were launched in March 2022 by the Ministry of MSME.
The Aspirational Districts Programme was launched in January 2018 and covers 112 districts.
Udyam Registration came into effect on 1 July 2020.
PMEGP is implemented by KVIC as the nodal agency at the national level.
Startup India was launched on 16 January 2016 by DPIIT.
MUDRA loans are offered in Shishu, Kishore and Tarun categories.
MSDE was formed in November 2014.
SIDBI was established in 1990 as the principal financial institution for MSMEs.
summary: The answer is (c) Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. In March 2022 the MSME Ministry launched 'Sambhav' (a nationwide awareness programme) and 'Svavlamban' (an entrepreneurship programme) to promote entrepreneurship among youth, especially in aspirational districts.
topic_notes: Entrepreneurship promotion in India is led mainly by the Ministry of MSME, with support from MSDE, DPIIT (Startup India), NITI Aayog (Atal Innovation Mission) and the Ministry of Finance. Sambhav and Svavlamban were March 2022 MSME initiatives meant to spread entrepreneurial awareness among youth, particularly in the 112 aspirational districts that NITI Aayog selected in 2018 under the Aspirational Districts Programme. The MSME Ministry's key schemes include PMEGP (credit-linked subsidy for new enterprises), the CGTMSE (collateral-free credit), the Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme, SFURTI (cluster development for traditional industries), the Entrepreneurship Skill Development Programme, and the MSME Champions scheme. The Udyam Registration portal replaced Udyog Aadhaar in 2020. The MSME definition changed in 2020 and again in 2025 with higher limits. Under the Atmanirbhar Bharat package of 2020 there was an emergency credit line guarantee scheme (ECLGS) for MSMEs. Related institutions include SIDBI, set up in 1990 to finance MSMEs, and NSIC, set up in 1955. Startup India was launched on 16 January 2016 by DPIIT, and 16 January is celebrated as National Startup Day. Stand-Up India (2016) gives bank loans to SC/ST and women entrepreneurs. The Atal Innovation Mission (2016) promotes Atal Tinkering Labs and incubators. MUDRA Yojana (2015) offers Shishu, Kishore and Tarun loans up to ₹10 lakh. Students should link each scheme to its nodal ministry because UPSC often tests this mapping.

question: Consider the following statements about a famous music composer of India : He composed the background music for one of the scenes in the 1956 film ‘Jhanak Jhanak Payal Baaje’. Later he collaborated with flutist Hariprasad Chaurasia and guitarist Brij Bhushan Kabra to produce the acclaimed concept album ‘Call of the Valley’. Along with Hariprasad Chatirasia, he composed music for many famous Hindi films like Silsila, Chandni and Darr. He was conferred with Padma Shri and Padma Vibhushan awards. Identify the person from the following :
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: Pandit Shivkumar Sharma (1938-2022) from Jammu was the musician who brought the santoor, a Kashmiri folk instrument with roughly 100 strings, into Hindustani classical music. His father, Uma Dutt Sharma, trained him in vocals and tabla before santoor. He played background music for a scene in V. Shantaram's 'Jhanak Jhanak Payal Baaje' (1956). His 1967 concept album 'Call of the Valley', with flautist Hariprasad Chaurasia and guitarist Brij Bhushan Kabra, became a classic of Indian instrumental music. As the duo Shiv-Hari, he and Chaurasia scored Faasle, Vijay, Lamhe, Chandni, Parampara, Darr and Silsila, which was the first of these films and came out in 1981. He got the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1986), the Padma Shri (1991) and Padma Vibhushan (2001). He died in May 2022. Elimination: O.P. Nayyar was a rhythm-driven Hindi film composer who never worked with Chaurasia. Salil Chowdhury was a Bengali-Hindi film composer and Ilaiyaraaja a South Indian composer. None of them was part of Shiv-Hari or played the santoor.
explanations: Wrong. O.P. Nayyar was a Punjabi-style film composer of the 1950s-70s (Naya Daur, Tumsa Nahin Dekha) and received no Padma award. He did not make 'Call of the Valley' or the Shiv-Hari scores.
Correct. Shivkumar Sharma fits every clue: the 1956 film, the 1967 album, the Shiv-Hari film scores, and the Padma Shri and Padma Vibhushan.
Wrong. Salil Chowdhury composed for Do Bigha Zamin, Madhumati and Anand and was known for blending folk and Western classical styles. He was not connected with Shiv-Hari or 'Call of the Valley'.
Wrong. Ilaiyaraaja is a Tamil film composer (Annakili, 1976) and a Padma Bhushan (2010) and Padma Vibhushan (2018) awardee. He is not associated with Silsila, Chandni or Darr.
keyfact: Shivkumar Sharma: santoor maestro, 'Call of the Valley' (1967), Shiv-Hari duo with Hariprasad Chaurasia (Silsila, Chandni, Darr), Padma Shri and Padma Vibhushan.
option_notes: O.P. Nayyar (1926-2007) was a Hindi film composer born in Lahore. He was known for a lively tonga-beat rhythm and for his work with Asha Bhosle and Mohammed Rafi, and he avoided using Lata Mangeshkar. His films include Aar Paar, Mr. & Mrs. 55, CID, Naya Daur and Kashmir Ki Kali. He won the Filmfare Award for Phir Wohi Dil Laya Hoon (1958 film Naya Daur, 1958). He received no Padma honour.

Shivkumar Sharma (1938-2022) was an Indian santoor player born in Jammu. He popularised the santoor in classical music. With Hariprasad Chaurasia he formed Shiv-Hari, which scored Silsila (1981), Chandni (1989) and Darr (1993). His awards included the Padma Shri and Padma Vibhushan. His son Rahul Sharma is also a santoor player.

Salil Chowdhury (1925-1995) was a Bengali composer, poet and lyricist. He composed for Hindi, Bengali and Malayalam films, including Do Bigha Zamin (1953), Madhumati (1958) and Anand (1971), and for Chemmeen (1965). He was associated with the IPTA movement and was known for songs of social protest. He received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award.

Ilaiyaraaja (born 1943) is a Tamil composer from Pannaipuram, Theni. He debuted with Annakili (1976) and has scored over 1,000 films. He was the first Asian to compose a full symphony, 'Valiant', in 1993. He received the Padma Bhushan (2010), the Padma Vibhushan (2018) and the National Film Awards. He was nominated to the Rajya Sabha in 2022.
related: Shivkumar Sharma died on 10 May 2022 in Mumbai after a cardiac arrest.
'Call of the Valley' was released in 1967 on HMV.
The santoor is a Kashmiri instrument with about 100 strings.
Shiv-Hari scored Silsila (1981), Lamhe (1991), Chandni (1989) and Darr (1993).
Hariprasad Chaurasia is a bansuri (flute) exponent and Padma Vibhushan awardee.
Brij Bhushan Kabra popularised Hindustani music on guitar.
The Sangeet Natak Akademi was established in 1952 as the national academy for music, dance and drama.
Ravi Shankar received the Bharat Ratna in 1999.
summary: The answer is (b) Shivkumar Sharma, the santoor maestro. He played the santoor in 'Jhanak Jhanak Payal Baaje' (1956), made 'Call of the Valley' (1967) with Hariprasad Chaurasia and Brij Bhushan Kabra, and formed the Shiv-Hari duo that scored Silsila, Chandni and Darr. He received the Padma Shri (1986) and Padma Vibhushan (2001).
topic_notes: The santoor is a hammered dulcimer of Kashmir, once called Shatatantri Veena, with about 100 strings and a trapezoid body. It was used in Sufiana Kalam. Shivkumar Sharma adapted it to the full range of Hindustani raga music by redesigning it with 31 bridges and a new playing technique. He first played in Mumbai in 1955 and then entered films, doing a stint with V. Shantaram. His 1967 album 'Call of the Valley' sold millions of copies. The Shiv-Hari duo scored eight films between 1981 and 1993. They won a Filmfare nomination for Chandni and Lamhe. Hariprasad Chaurasia, born in 1938 in Allahabad, is a bansuri maestro, who got the Padma Bhushan (1992) and Padma Vibhushan (2000). He was trained by Annapurna Devi. Brij Bhushan Kabra (1937-2021) was a pioneer of Hindustani classical music on the Hawaiian guitar. Other instruments and exponents to know: Ravi Shankar (sitar, Bharat Ratna 1999), Ali Akbar Khan (sarod), Amjad Ali Khan (sarod), Bismillah Khan (shehnai, Bharat Ratna 2001), Zakir Hussain (tabla), Vishwa Mohan Bhatt (Mohan veena, Grammy 1994), and Ustad Allah Rakha (tabla). UPSC often asks about Padma awardees, Sangeet Natak Akademi, instruments, gharanas and film music composers.

ocr: before the judge given that he was clearly P Q his decision to plead guilty S) (a) SQRP (b) QPSR (c) QSPR (ad) SRQP
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a sentence rearrangement (para-jumble) question where the parts P, Q, R and S must be arranged into a meaningful sentence. In the image only P ('before the judge'), Q ('given that he was clearly') and S ('his decision to plead guilty') are visible; R is cut off, so it likely sits in the opening or closing slot, probably a stem like 'The lawyer defended' or an ending such as 'repentant'. The official key QSPR places Q first, so the sentence opens with 'given that he was clearly ...', and R closes the sentence. The visible parts show the logic. 'Given that he was clearly' is a subordinate-clause starter and needs a complement. 'his decision to plead guilty' is a noun phrase, and 'before the judge' is an adverbial phrase that normally follows the verb or noun phrase it modifies. So Q to S to P is a natural chain, and R completes it. Strategy: find the opening part, link phrases by grammar (prepositions, conjunctions, noun phrases), and test each option. Options (a) SQRP, (b) QPSR and (d) SRQP break the Q-S-P chain, so they are eliminated. Because part R is missing from the image, the full sentence cannot be verified here, so rely on the official key.
explanations: (a) SQRP is wrong: it starts with S ('his decision to plead guilty'), which would leave the Q clause ('given that he was clearly') with no logical link and does not match the official key.

(b) QPSR is wrong: it places P ('before the judge') right after Q, so 'given that he was clearly before the judge' reads awkwardly and separates S from the phrase it should follow. It does not match the official key.
(c) QSPR is correct: it is the official answer. Q opens with 'given that he was clearly', S supplies 'his decision to plead guilty', P adds 'before the judge', and R completes the sentence.
(d) SRQP is wrong: it opens with S and ends with P, which breaks the Q-S-P sequence and does not match the official key.
keyfact: In para-jumble, chain parts by grammar: clause starter (Q) then noun phrase (S) then adverbial phrase (P) gives QSPR.
option_notes: SQRP is an arrangement beginning with the noun phrase S, 'his decision to plead guilty'. Such an order works only when a verb or a link follows immediately. Here Q ('given that he was clearly') would come second, which leaves the sentence without a stable subject-verb frame. It is a distractor that tests whether you notice the opening phrase.

QPSR begins with the subordinate clause Q and then places P ('before the judge'). The adverbial P normally modifies a verb or noun just before it, so putting it directly after 'clearly' creates the misleading reading 'clearly before the judge'. It is a typical para-jumble trap that swaps the order of two adjacent parts (P and S).

QSPR is the official answer. It starts with Q ('given that he was clearly'), links to S ('his decision to plead guilty'), then P ('before the judge'), with R finishing. The key lesson is to chain phrases by grammar: a clause starter, then its noun-phrase complement, then an adverbial phrase, then the closing part.

SRQP begins with S and ends with P, placing R and Q in the middle. Because Q ('given that he was clearly') is a subordinating clause starter, it must come before the idea it qualifies, not after R. This option breaks that logic and also leaves 'before the judge' stranded at the end. It is a distractor built by reversing the part order.
related: Para-jumble: first find the part that can start the sentence.
'Given that' introduces a subordinate clause meaning 'considering that'.
Plead guilty means to formally admit guilt in court.
A prepositional phrase like 'before the judge' modifies a nearby verb or noun.
Plea bargain: an agreement where the accused pleads guilty for a lighter sentence.
Eliminate options that split a phrase from the word it modifies.
summary: The answer is (c) QSPR. The sentence parts form a coherent order: 'given that he was clearly' (Q) + 'his decision to plead guilty' (S) + 'before the judge' (P) + R. Since R is not visible in the image, the order is based on the logic of the visible parts and the official key.
topic_notes: Sentence rearrangement (para-jumble) questions appear regularly in the General English section of the EPFO (APFC and EO/AO) exam. A sentence is split into parts labelled P, Q, R and S, and the candidate must arrange them into the most meaningful order. Useful steps: (1) Identify the opening part. It usually starts with a capital letter, a subject, an introductory clause, or a conjunction such as 'given that', 'although' or 'since'. (2) Look for the closing part, which usually ends with a full stop or completes the thought. (3) Find mandatory pairs, such as a noun phrase followed by its modifier, a preposition followed by its object, or a verb followed by its object. (4) Check connectors (however, therefore, thus) and pronouns (he, it, they), which refer back to something earlier. (5) Test each option and eliminate those that break grammar or logic. Common grammar areas linked to this topic: subordinate clauses, phrases (noun, prepositional, adverbial), subject-verb agreement, tenses and sequence of events. Legal vocabulary also appears: plead guilty, plead not guilty, before the judge, in the dock, plea bargain, verdict, acquittal and conviction. UPSC could also ask on sentence improvement, error spotting, fill in the blanks, one-word substitution, idioms and phrases, synonyms and antonyms, and reading comprehension. Practise with timed sets and always check the full sentence for meaning, since a part that looks right locally can fail in the whole.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a sentence rearrangement (para-jumbling) question in which the parts P, Q, S are given and the part R is not shown in the image (the stem reads 'when your stated principles' = P, 'it is difficult' = Q, 'to practise what you preach' = S). The visible parts are fragments of one sentence, and the official answer QSPR tells us the structure: 'It is difficult (Q) to practise what you preach (S) when your stated principles (P) [R: the missing ending, e.g. are not consistent with your actions or are at odds with your interests].' Key strategy: identify the opening segment. P begins with the conjunction 'when', so it cannot open the sentence; this eliminates (a) PRSQ. Q, 'it is difficult', is a dummy-subject construction that needs an infinitive complement, 'to practise...' (S), so S must follow Q directly. That supports QSPR and eliminates (b) SPRQ, which starts with an infinitive phrase lacking its main verb, and (c) QPRS, which separates 'it is difficult' from its infinitive. Look for connectors, dummy 'it', infinitive pairs and subordinate conjunctions. Note that the proverb 'practise what you preach' is a fixed collocation. Also note that 'practise' is the verb in British spelling, 'practice' the noun.
explanations: (a) PRSQ is wrong: it begins with the subordinate conjunction 'when' and ends with 'it is difficult', which leaves the infinitive phrase S stranded before the main clause Q, so the sentence is illogical.

(b) SPRQ is wrong: it opens with 'to practise what you preach', an infinitive with no governing 'it is difficult' before it, and it then places the 'when' clause in the middle, which breaks the grammar.

(c) QPRS is wrong: 'it is difficult when your stated principles ... to practise what you preach' separates 'difficult' from its infinitive complement and leaves the construction awkward and incomplete in meaning.

(d) QSPR is correct: 'It is difficult (Q) to practise what you preach (S) when your stated principles (P) ...(R)'. The main clause is complete first, then the 'when' clause supplies the condition, with R as its ending.
keyfact: It is difficult (Q) to practise what you preach (S) when your stated principles (P) ... (R) — a 'when' clause cannot open, and 'it is difficult' must be followed by its infinitive.
option_notes: PRSQ: this order starts with the 'when' clause (P, then R) and then puts S and Q at the end. It is a typical distractor that starts with a subordinating conjunction. A sentence can start with a 'when' clause, but then the main clause must follow in normal order (it is difficult to practise...), and here Q comes after S, which is ungrammatical.

SPRQ: this starts with the infinitive phrase S, 'to practise what you preach'. An infinitive phrase can be a subject (To err is human), but here the dummy-subject 'it is difficult' (Q) is placed at the end, which does not work. Remember that the 'it ... to' structure needs the adjective before the infinitive.

QPRS: this option keeps Q first, which is correct, but it inserts the 'when' clause (P, R) before S. The result splits 'it is difficult' from 'to practise what you preach'. The dummy 'it' construction normally keeps the adjective and its infinitive together.

QSPR: this is the official answer. It reads: it is difficult to practise what you preach when your stated principles... It follows the standard English pattern: main clause with dummy subject 'it', the infinitive complement, and then the adverbial 'when' clause giving the circumstance. The idiom 'practise what you preach' means to behave as you tell others to behave.
related: 'Practise what you preach' means to behave in the way you advise others to behave.
In British English, 'practise' is a verb and 'practice' is a noun.
A sentence starting with 'when' is a subordinate clause and needs a main clause.
The dummy-subject structure is 'It + be + adjective + to-infinitive'.
Correlatives such as 'not only... but also' must be kept together in rearrangement.
A hypocrite is a person who does not follow his or her stated principles.
Parajumble tip: find the opening sentence first, then link pairs.
The opposite of practising what you preach is hypocrisy.
summary: The correct answer is (d) QSPR, which forms 'it is difficult to practise what you preach when your stated principles ...'. The sentence needs the main clause Q + S first, and the subordinate clause starting with 'when' (P) must be completed by R.
topic_notes: Sentence rearrangement (para-jumbling) is a regular part of the General English section of the EPFO (APFC and EO/AO) paper. The questions give parts of a sentence labelled P, Q, R, S and ask for the correct sequence. Key techniques: (1) Find the opening part: one that is a self-contained subject or main clause, not starting with a conjunction (when, because, although, which), a pronoun with no antecedent, or a preposition that needs a prior noun. (2) Find mandatory pairs: dummy 'it' + adjective + infinitive (it is difficult to...), 'not only... but also', 'either... or', 'neither... nor', 'so... that', 'such... that', 'no sooner... than', 'hardly... when'. (3) Check grammar agreement of tense and number. (4) Look at the closing part: usually it completes a thought and often carries a full stop, a conclusion or a result. (5) Test the options by elimination: eliminate those starting with an impossible part first. Related idioms: practise what you preach; walk the talk; actions speak louder than words; hypocrisy. Spelling: in British English practise is the verb and practice is the noun; American English uses practice for both. Other angles UPSC could ask: idioms and phrases, one-word substitution, spot-the-error, active/passive voice, direct/indirect speech, fill in the blanks with prepositions, synonyms and antonyms, and comprehension passages. Practise at least 10 rearrangement questions daily and always read the final sentence aloud for flow.

Key strategy: (1) Identify the opener: a part that begins with a subordinating conjunction (when, if, although, because), or with a capitalised noun or proper name, or one that introduces the topic. (2) Spot parts that cannot start: those beginning with pronouns without antecedents, connectors like 'but', 'and', 'therefore', or with a verb or infinitive that depends on something earlier. (3) Look for fixed pairs: a clause and its completion, article and noun, preposition and object, subject and verb. (4) Check the final part: it often ends with a full stop and carries the conclusion. (5) Use elimination: if two options differ only in the first letter, decide the opener and you are done. Q, 'it is difficult', has the dummy subject 'it' and needs a complement, 'to practise what you preach'. So Q is followed by S. 'When your stated principles R' then forms the closing subordinate clause. The sentence reads: 'It is difficult to practise what you preach when your stated principles [R].' Elimination: (a) PRSQ and (c) QPRS break the Q-S link, and (a) and (b) begin with P or S, which cannot open the sentence. Remember that an opener cannot be a subordinate clause starting with when/if/although, and that 'it is + adjective' is followed by a to-infinitive.
explanations: (a) PRSQ is wrong: it starts with the dependent clause 'when your stated principles', and Q 'it is difficult' at the end is left without its infinitive complement.
(b) SPRQ is wrong: it starts with the infinitive 'to practise what you preach', which has no subject. The ending in Q also leaves 'it is difficult' dangling.
(c) QPRS is wrong: Q is correctly first, but P R then interrupts the link between 'it is difficult' and 'to practise what you preach'. The result is clumsy and illogical.
(d) QSPR is correct: 'It is difficult to practise what you preach when your stated principles [R]'. The main clause is complete first, and the 'when' clause follows.
keyfact: In para-jumble, 'It is difficult' (dummy subject) is followed by its infinitive 'to practise what you preach', and the 'when' clause comes last: QSPR.
option_notes: PRSQ: a sequence that begins with a subordinate 'when' clause. Such an order is valid only if the main clause follows directly; here Q, the main clause, comes last and has no complement. It tests the rule that dependent clauses can come first only when followed by their main clause.

SPRQ: starts with the infinitive phrase 'to practise what you preach'. An infinitive phrase can act as a subject, but only when the verb is next, such as 'is difficult'. Here P and R intervene, so the sentence is broken. It tests whether you can spot an unattached infinitive.

QPRS: begins correctly with 'it is difficult', but the next part is the 'when' clause, which pushes the infinitive S to the end. This reads awkwardly and R, the end of the P clause, is separated from its meaning. It tests how closely the dummy-subject 'it' is tied to its infinitive.

QSPR: the correct order. The dummy 'it' subject is followed by the adjective 'difficult' and then the infinitive 'to practise what you preach'. Next comes the temporal or conditional clause 'when your stated principles...', and R completes it. This is the standard pattern 'It is + adjective + to-infinitive + clause'.

topic_notes: Sentence rearrangement (para-jumble) appears in the General English section of the EPFO papers, usually as five items with parts P, Q, R, S. Strategy: (1) Find the opening part. It must be a self-contained start and not begin with a conjunction (when, but, and, because), a pronoun without an antecedent, or a bare infinitive. (2) Find mandatory pairs. A dummy 'it' goes with its to-infinitive or that-clause. An article or adjective goes with its noun. A subject goes with its verb. A conjunction goes with the clause it introduces. (3) Check logical flow and linking words such as however, therefore, thus, this, these. (4) Test the remaining options by reading them aloud. (5) Eliminate by the opening part: if only one option starts with the right part, you may not need to read the rest. question: The essay was badly researched and contained several platitudes and generalizations
subject: General Science
detail: The question tests vocabulary in context: the word 'platitudes' is paired with 'generalizations' in a sentence criticising a poorly researched essay. A platitude (noun, from French 'plat', flat) is a trite, commonplace statement, often a moral one, e.g. 'Honesty is the best policy' or 'Time heals all wounds' used as if profound. Its defining features are overuse and lack of originality, not falseness. Elimination logic: (a) 'Incorrect statements' confuses platitude with falsehood; platitudes are usually true but banal. (b) 'Imprecise comments' and (d) 'Vague, subjective statements' describe generalizations, which is the other word in the sentence, so they are tempting distractors but do not capture the stale, clichéd quality. (c) 'Often used and unoriginal ideas' matches the dictionary meaning exactly. Related words: cliché (overused phrase), truism (obvious truth), bromide (trite remark meant to soothe), banality, commonplace. Tip: in synonym questions, find the core defining feature of the word (here overuse and staleness) rather than being drawn to options matching nearby words.
explanations: Wrong: platitudes are not necessarily incorrect; they are often true but stale and obvious.
Wrong: imprecision describes vague or inexact remarks and fits 'generalizations' more than 'platitudes'.
Correct: a platitude is a trite, overused remark lacking originality, which is exactly this option.
Wrong: vagueness and subjectivity are not the defining traits of a platitude; a platitude can be clear and widely accepted.
keyfact: Platitude = a flat, overused, unoriginal remark (cliché), not a false or merely vague one.
option_notes: Incorrect statements are claims that are factually wrong or false. They are about accuracy, unlike platitudes, which are usually true but dull. Related words: fallacy, misstatement, error, falsehood. In exams, a statement can be incorrect without being a cliché, and a cliché can be correct. Do not confuse truth value with originality or freshness of expression.

Imprecise comments are remarks lacking exactness or specific detail, such as 'many people came' instead of giving a number. Synonyms: inexact, loose, approximate, ambiguous. Imprecision relates to the quality of detail, so it partly fits generalizations, but it does not convey the overused, stale quality that defines a platitude.

Often used and unoriginal ideas is the correct meaning of platitudes. A platitude is a flat, commonplace remark, often moral, delivered as though it were profound. Examples: 'Every cloud has a silver lining', 'Boys will be boys'. Related: cliché, truism, bromide, banality, hackneyed expression. The word comes from French 'plat' meaning flat, and entered English in the 19th century.

Vague, subjective statements are remarks that are unclear and based on personal opinion rather than fact, such as 'This is a nice place'. Synonyms: nebulous, hazy, opinionated, biased. Vagueness and subjectivity are separate faults from staleness. A platitude can be perfectly clear and widely shared, so this option does not capture its essence.
related: Platitude = trite, overused remark presented as significant.
Cliché = overused phrase or idea that has lost its force.
Truism = a statement that is obviously true and needs no saying.
Bromide = a trite remark meant to calm or soothe.
Aphorism = a short, pithy statement of a general truth.
Epigram = a concise, witty saying; an antonym-like contrast to platitude.
Banality = lack of originality that makes something boring.
Hackneyed = made commonplace by overuse.
summary: The answer is (c) Often used and unoriginal ideas. A platitude is a remark that has been used so often that it is dull, stale and lacks originality, though it is presented as if it were fresh or significant.
topic_notes: This question belongs to the General English vocabulary section of the EPFO exam, where synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutions, idioms and word meanings in context are tested regularly. Platitude is a noun meaning a remark or statement, especially a moral one, that has been used too often to be interesting or thoughtful. It comes from French 'plat' (flat), and the adjective is 'platitudinous'. Closely related words are cliché (an overused phrase or idea), truism (a statement so obviously true it needs no saying), bromide (a trite, unoriginal remark intended to soothe), banality (the quality of being boring through lack of originality), commonplace, and hackneyed or trite as adjectives. Words commonly confused with platitude include platitude vs. plethora (a large excess), plaudit (praise or applause), and attitude. Antonyms: originality, novelty, insight, epigram (a witty, memorable saying), or an incisive remark. Strategy for such questions: identify the core idea of the word (here, overuse and staleness), eliminate options that describe a different fault (falsehood, imprecision, subjectivity), and use the context. Also note that 'generalization' means a broad statement drawn from limited cases, so the sentence criticises both stale ideas and sweeping claims. UPSC may ask the same word in a synonym format, e.g. 'Platitude: (a) Banality (b) Wisdom (c) Novelty (d) Lie', so learn the synonym cluster rather than a single definition. Revise similar word clusters: aphorism, adage, maxim, proverb, axiom, and epigram, each of which has a distinct shade of meaning.

question: The judgment of beauty is based on the human capacity for disinterested pleasure in the natural world
options: Extremely focused ng sentences in which one word has been ch is closest to the meaning of the underlined accordingly
subject: General English
detail: The question is a synonym-in-context item on the word 'disinterested', one of the most frequently tested confusables in English. 'Disinterested' means impartial, neutral, and not influenced by personal advantage or self-interest. 'Uninterested' means bored, indifferent, or not curious. The sentence echoes Kant's aesthetics (Critique of Judgment, 1790), where the judgment of beauty is 'disinterested': pleasure in beauty is not tied to desire, utility, or ownership of the object. So 'disinterested pleasure' means pleasure free of any self-serving motive. Elimination: (a) Indifference and (c) Not caring for something both capture the 'uninterested' sense, so they are the trap options. Indifference would make 'pleasure' contradictory, since one cannot take pleasure in something while being indifferent to it. (d) Extremely focused is almost the opposite idea of detachment from self-interest and does not match either sense of the word. Only (b) correctly gives the sense of absence of selfish motive. Typical usage: a judge should be disinterested, meaning impartial, with no stake in the case.
explanations: Incorrect: Indifference matches 'uninterested', not 'disinterested', and it clashes with the idea of taking pleasure in beauty.
Correct: 'Disinterested' means free of self-interest or personal motive, which is exactly the Kantian sense of aesthetic pleasure.
Incorrect: Not caring for something is again the 'uninterested' meaning, which is the usual misuse of the word.
Incorrect: Extremely focused has no link to the lack of selfish motive; it suggests intense involvement.
keyfact: Disinterested = impartial, free of self-interest; uninterested = not interested.
option_notes: Indifference means lack of interest, concern, or sympathy toward something. It is the sense of 'uninterested' or 'apathetic'. Synonyms include apathy, unconcern, and detachment in the sense of not caring. It is a common distractor for 'disinterested' because the two words are often confused. Antonyms are concern, enthusiasm, and eagerness.

Free of all self-interest describes impartiality or objectivity: having no personal stake or selfish motive. This is the correct meaning of 'disinterested'. Related words are impartial, neutral, unbiased, objective, and dispassionate. A disinterested judge or referee is one who has no personal gain at stake in the outcome. The Kantian notion of aesthetic judgment uses this sense.

Not caring for something means lack of concern or attention. It corresponds to 'uninterested', 'unconcerned', or 'apathetic'. Many speakers use 'disinterested' this way, but standard usage reserves that for 'uninterested'. In exams it is a trap option that tests whether you know the distinction between the two words.

Extremely focused means deeply concentrated or absorbed in something. Related words are intent, engrossed, and rapt. It is nearly the opposite of the bored sense of 'uninterested' and unrelated to the impartial sense of 'disinterested'. It is included as an unrelated distractor.
related: Disinterested means impartial; uninterested means not interested.
Kant's Critique of Judgment (1790) calls aesthetic judgment disinterested.
Synonyms of disinterested: impartial, neutral, unbiased, dispassionate.
Antonyms of disinterested: biased, partial, partisan, self-serving.
Affect is usually a verb; effect is usually a noun.
Imply means to suggest; infer means to deduce.
Stationary means still; stationery means writing materials.
summary: The answer is (b) Free of all self-interest. In the phrase 'disinterested pleasure', 'disinterested' means impartial and free of personal or selfish motive. It does not mean 'uninterested', which is the common misuse.
topic_notes: This question tests commonly confused word pairs and vocabulary in context, a regular feature of the General English section. Disinterested means impartial and unbiased; uninterested means not interested. Other pairs often asked: affect/effect (affect is usually a verb, effect usually a noun); principal/principle; stationary/stationery; complement/compliment; continual/continuous; imply/infer; council/counsel; elicit/illicit; farther/further; economic/economical; credible/credulous/creditable; sensual/sensuous; healthy/healthful. The philosophical background is Immanuel Kant's Critique of Judgment (1790), which says that judgments of taste are disinterested, universal, purposive without a purpose, and necessary. Strategy for synonym-in-context questions: read the whole sentence, replace the word with each option, and check the sense; beware of options that match the popular misuse; use root clues (dis- plus interested, meaning 'not having an interest or stake'). Related roots: disinterest (noun) meaning impartiality; disinterestedness; altruistic as a close synonym in some contexts; objective, dispassionate, equitable, and neutral as synonyms. Antonyms include biased, partial, prejudiced, partisan, and self-serving. UPSC EPFO English questions also cover idioms, one-word substitutions, spelling, error spotting, fill in the blanks, para jumbles, and comprehension, so building a list of confusables is high value.

question: The hundred-year old college building was now in a derelict state
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a General English vocabulary question on the meaning of the word 'derelict'. As an adjective, 'derelict' means abandoned, deserted and in a poor condition because of neglect (for example, a derelict factory or a derelict ship). As a noun it can mean a person without home or property, or an abandoned vessel. The word comes from Latin 'derelictus', the past participle of 'derelinquere', meaning to forsake completely. The key idea is a combination of abandonment, neglect and decay. Elimination logic: (a) 'Preserved for historical value' implies active care, which is the opposite of neglect. (d) 'Retaining its original beauty' contradicts decay and the word 'now', which signals a change for the worse. (b) 'Unsafe for occupation' is a possible consequence of dereliction but is not the meaning of the word; a derelict building may be unsafe, but the word itself stresses neglect and ruin. Option (c) captures both the neglect and the resulting breakdown, so it is the best fit. In synonym-based questions, choose the option that matches the core meaning rather than a side effect.
explanations: Incorrect: Preservation means careful maintenance, which is the opposite of 'derelict', a word that implies abandonment and decay.
Incorrect: A derelict building may be unsafe, but this is a consequence and not the core meaning. The word focuses on neglect and disrepair, not on safety.
Correct: 'Derelict' means abandoned, neglected and falling into ruin, so 'neglected and broken down' matches it best.
Incorrect: Retaining original beauty contradicts the decline suggested by 'now in a derelict state' and the building's great age.
keyfact: Derelict = abandoned, neglected and falling into ruin; so 'neglected and broken down' is correct.
option_notes: 'Preserved for historical value' describes heritage conservation, in which old structures are protected and maintained because of their cultural or historical importance. In India, the ASI protects monuments under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958. The related adjectives are 'conserved', 'restored' and 'maintained'. It is the opposite of derelict, which implies abandonment and loss of upkeep.

'Unsafe for occupation' describes a structure that is hazardous to live in or use, for example a building declared 'dangerous' by a municipal authority. The related word is 'uninhabitable'. A derelict building may well be unsafe, but 'unsafe' describes risk, whereas 'derelict' describes neglect and abandonment. A building can also be unsafe without being derelict, for example because of a structural defect.

'Neglected and broken down' captures the meaning of 'derelict': abandoned, left without care and in ruin. Close synonyms are dilapidated, decrepit, ramshackle, run-down, tumbledown and abandoned. Antonyms include well-kept, maintained, restored and pristine. 'Dereliction of duty' is a related phrase meaning shameful neglect of responsibility, often used in service and military law.

'Retaining its original beauty' means keeping its first charm and appearance without deterioration. Related words are pristine, unspoiled, well-preserved and immaculate. It is the opposite of derelict, as the sentence says the building is now in a changed condition. Words like 'timeless' and 'ageless' are also used for old buildings that remain attractive.
related: Derelict (adj.): abandoned and in poor condition through neglect.
Dilapidated: in a state of disrepair, especially from age.
Dereliction of duty: wilful or negligent failure to perform one's duty.
Delinquent: failing in a duty or guilty of a minor offence.
Decrepit: worn out or weakened by age or long use.
Pristine: in its original, unspoiled condition (antonym of derelict).
Relinquish: to give up or let go, from the same Latin root as 'derelict'.
summary: The answer is (c) Neglected and broken down. 'Derelict' describes a building abandoned or left to decay through neglect, so the phrase 'now in a derelict state' for a hundred-year-old building means it has fallen into disrepair.
topic_notes: This question tests vocabulary, specifically the meaning of words in context, a staple of the General English section of the EPFO papers. Typical formats include synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitution, idioms and phrases, and words with similar spellings. For 'derelict' the central meaning is abandoned and in disrepair due to neglect. Its noun uses are an abandoned ship at sea or a vagrant. The Latin root 'relinquere' (to leave behind) also gives 'relinquish' and 'relic'. Synonyms to learn: dilapidated, decrepit, ruined, neglected, deserted, run-down, ramshackle. Antonyms: well-maintained, restored, cared-for, pristine. Phrases: 'dereliction of duty' (failure to perform a duty). Exam strategy: first understand the sentence's tone and any signal words such as 'now', which indicates a decline. Eliminate options that contradict that tone, then choose between the remaining options on the core meaning rather than on a consequence. Similar words that students often confuse: 'derelict' vs 'delinquent' (guilty of a minor offence or failing in duty), 'dilapidated' (in disrepair, especially from age) and 'decrepit' (worn out by age, applied to people or things). Practise building word families by root: 'liqu-' or 'linqu-' means leave, as in 'relinquish', 'delinquent' and 'derelict'. Reading newspaper editorials regularly helps build the context-based inference needed for these questions.

question: My serendipitous encounter with the man on the bus was to have a profound impact on my life
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Serendipitous is the adjective from 'serendipity', a word coined by Horace Walpole in 1754 in a letter, inspired by the Persian fairy tale 'The Three Princes of Serendip' (Serendip being an old name for Sri Lanka). The princes kept making fortunate discoveries by accident and sagacity. Serendipity means the occurrence of happy or beneficial events by chance. In the sentence, the encounter with a man on a bus was unplanned, yet it greatly influenced the speaker's life. The core idea is chance, so 'a chance event' fits best. Elimination: 'Fortunate' captures only the good outcome and not the accidental nature, and a word meaning 'fortunate' would be 'lucky' or 'auspicious', which is a partial and weaker match. 'Of historical significance' is unrelated, since the encounter was personal rather than historic. 'Sudden and abrupt' describes speed, not unplanned luck; an encounter could be sudden yet planned. Hence (d). Related words to remember: fortuitous (by chance), adventitious (accidental), fluke, happenstance, coincidental. Note that 'fortuitous' strictly means by chance, whereas 'fortunate' means lucky.
explanations: Incorrect: 'Fortunate' covers only the lucky outcome. It misses the essential element of accident or chance, so it is a weaker match than (d).
Incorrect: 'Of historical significance' has no link to the meaning of serendipitous. The sentence concerns a personal encounter, not a historic one.
Incorrect: 'Sudden and abrupt' refers to the speed of an event. Serendipity refers to an unplanned, chance discovery or meeting, not to suddenness.
Correct: Serendipitous means occurring by chance, usually with a happy result. 'A chance event' best conveys this unplanned meeting, as officially accepted.
keyfact: Serendipitous = happening by chance, usually with a happy result; the word was coined by Horace Walpole in 1754.
option_notes: Fortunate means favoured by luck or bringing good results. Synonyms are lucky, blessed, auspicious, providential. It differs from 'fortuitous', which means happening by chance without regard to whether the result is good. Its antonym is unfortunate or unlucky. UPSC often tests the contrast between fortunate and fortuitous in vocabulary and error-spotting questions, so memorise both words and their distinct nuances.

'Of historical significance' means important in history, worth recording or remembered by later generations. Related adjectives are historic (famous or important in history) and historical (belonging to the past or based on history). The 'historic' versus 'historical' distinction is a classic usage point. It has no relation to chance or luck, so it is wrong here.

'Sudden and abrupt' describes something happening quickly and unexpectedly, without warning or gradual build-up. Synonyms include swift, unexpected, precipitate, and hasty. 'Abrupt' can also describe curt speech or a sharp slope. This describes timing or manner rather than luck, so it does not capture serendipity, which stresses a happy accident.

'A chance event' means something that happens by accident, without planning or intention. Related words are fluke, coincidence, happenstance, fortuity, and accident. Serendipity is chance combined with a beneficial result. The word was coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, drawing on 'The Three Princes of Serendip'. It is the correct and official answer.
related: Serendipity was coined by Horace Walpole in 1754.
Serendip is an old name for Sri Lanka.
Fortuitous means happening by chance, not necessarily lucky.
Adventitious means accidental or coming from outside.
Providential means occurring at a fortunate time, as if by divine intervention.
Idiom 'out of the blue' means unexpectedly.
Idiom 'a blessing in disguise' means a good thing that seemed bad at first.
Antonyms of serendipitous: planned, deliberate, intentional.
summary: The answer is (d) A chance event. 'Serendipitous' describes something discovered or happening by accident, usually with a happy or beneficial result, so the closest meaning among the options is 'a chance event'.
topic_notes: This question tests vocabulary, specifically words describing chance and luck, a frequent theme in UPSC EPFO English sections. Serendipity was coined by Horace Walpole on 28 January 1754 in a letter to Horace Mann, based on the Persian tale 'The Three Princes of Serendip'. Serendip is an old Arabic name for Sri Lanka. Famous serendipitous discoveries include penicillin (Alexander Fleming, 1928), X-rays (Röntgen, 1895), the microwave oven (Percy Spencer), and Post-it notes. Key words in this family: fortuitous (happening by chance), adventitious (coming from outside, accidental), providential (timely, seen as divine intervention), propitious (favourable), auspicious (promising success), fluke (lucky accident), happenstance (coincidence), haphazard (lacking order or plan), random, and incidental. Common pitfalls: fortuitous is often wrongly used to mean lucky; strictly, it means by chance. Serendipitous implies a pleasant surprise, while fortuitous is neutral. Antonyms of serendipitous include deliberate, planned, intentional, premeditated, and calculated.
