By elimination, (c) is the incorrect statement, which is why it is the answer to a 'not correct' question.
explanations: Correct statement, so not the answer. The temple was carved out of a single rock mass in the 8th century CE under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I.
Correct statement, so not the answer. The temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva and represents Mount Kailash.
Incorrect statement, so this is the answer. The superstructure is Dravida (South Indian) in style, not Nagara.
Correct statement, so not the answer. The temple carries both Shaiva and Vaishnava sculptural themes (the option text is cut off in the image, but it is the standard accurate statement).
keyfact: Kailashanatha temple, Ellora (Cave 16): Rashtrakuta, Krishna I, 8th century CE, monolithic and Shaiva, but Dravida (not Nagara) in style.
option_notes: Carving in the 8th century CE: Ellora's Kailashanatha temple (Cave 16) was excavated from a basalt cliff, working from the top downward. It is credited to Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (c. 756-773 CE), with later additions. Ellora is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1983) and has 34 caves: Buddhist (1-12), Hindu (13-29) and Jain (30-34).

Dedicated to Lord Shiva: the temple is a Shaiva shrine built as a replica of Mount Kailash. Its main sanctum has a Shiva linga, and the temple has a Nandi mandapa, gateways, a courtyard and sculpted panels. Notable scenes include Ravana lifting Mount Kailash and Shiva-Parvati. The name Kailasa or Kailashanatha means 'Lord of Kailash'.

Nagara-style superstructure: this is the incorrect option. The Nagara style is North Indian, with a curvilinear shikhara, as at Khajuraho, Konark and Deogarh. Kailashanatha instead has a Dravida-style pyramidal vimana, closely related to the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal and the Pallava Kanchipuram temple.

Both Shaiva and Vaishnava elements: the Kailashanatha temple is chiefly Shaiva, but its sculptures include Vaishnava themes such as Vishnu's incarnations, Lakshmi and episodes from the Mahabharata and Ramayana. This reflects the religious tolerance and syncretism of the Rashtrakuta period.
related: Ellora has 34 caves: 12 Buddhist, 17 Hindu and 5 Jain.
Ellora was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.
Kailashanatha (Cave 16) was built under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I.
Nagara style has a curvilinear shikhara; Dravida has a pyramidal vimana.
Pattadakal temples (Karnataka) blend Nagara and Dravida styles and are a UNESCO site.
Ajanta caves are known for Buddhist paintings; Elephanta for Trimurti Shiva.
The Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram was built by Pallava king Rajasimha.
summary: The answer is (c): the statement that the superstructure of the Kailashanatha temple corresponds to the Nagara style is not correct. The Kailashanatha temple at Ellora (Cave 16) is a rock-cut Shiva temple of the Rashtrakuta period (8th century CE) built in the Dravida style, with a vimana resembling the Pallava temples of Kanchipuram.
topic_notes: Ellora Caves (near Aurangabad, Maharashtra) were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983. They have 34 rock-cut monasteries and temples along a basalt escarpment, built between about the 6th and 10th centuries CE. Caves 1-12 are Buddhist (Vajrayana, c. 600-730 CE), including Cave 10, the Vishwakarma or 'Carpenter's' cave chaitya. Caves 13-29 are Hindu, with Cave 16 being Kailashanatha; Caves 30-34 are Jain, including the Indra Sabha. The Kailashanatha temple was begun under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I. It measures roughly 60 m x 30 m and is about 30 m high, and it is a monolith excavated top-down, which is a unique technique. It is Dravida in style, with a vimana, a mandapa, a Nandi shrine and a gateway. The Rashtrakutas were also patrons of Jain art, and Amoghavarsha is associated with Jainism. Compare with other temple styles: Nagara (north; shikhara, Khajuraho, Konark), Dravida (south; vimana and gopuram, Thanjavur Brihadeeswara, Mamallapuram), and Vesara (Deccan; hybrid, Chalukyan and Hoysala temples). Compare also with the Ajanta Caves (Buddhist, paintings, 2nd century BCE to 6th century CE), the Elephanta Caves (Shaiva, Trimurti sculpture, near Mumbai) and the Pattadakal group (Karnataka, UNESCO 1987). The Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram was built by the Pallava king Rajasimha (Narasimhavarman II).

question: The temple has both Shaiva and Vaishnava sculptures. Which one of the following statements about ancient Indian pottery is correct?
options: Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) refers to a type of pottery found from archaeological sites in India dating back to 600 BCE. %
Painted Grey Ware (PGW) refers to a type of pottery found over a large part of South India coinciding with the Sangam period
Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP) sites are located in South India only
Black-and-Red Ware (BRW) is never found at Neolithic sites. [ P.7.0
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: NBPW is a fine, wheel-made, metallic-looking glossy pottery, usually black but sometimes silvery, golden or steel-grey. It is associated with the Mahajanapada period, the second urbanisation in the Gangetic plains, iron use, punch-marked coins and the rise of towns such as Kaushambi, Rajghat (Varanasi), Patliputra, Ujjain and Taxila. It is dated to roughly 700/600 BCE to 200 BCE, so option (a) fits. Elimination: Painted Grey Ware (PGW) belongs to the Upper Gangetic plain, Haryana and Punjab (c. 1200-600 BCE) and is linked with the Later Vedic period, not South India or the Sangam age, so (b) is wrong. Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP) is found in the Ganga-Yamuna doab and is associated with the Copper Hoard culture, so it is not South Indian, and (c) is wrong. Black-and-Red Ware (BRW) is found widely, including at Neolithic sites (for example in the Gangetic plain and the south), as well as at Chalcolithic and Megalithic sites, so (d) with 'never' is wrong. The question's first line about a temple with both Shaiva and Vaishnava sculptures is an OCR carry-over from another question and is irrelevant here.
explanations: Correct. NBPW is a fine deluxe pottery found at many sites in India, dating from about 600 BCE (the Mahajanapada period) onwards.
Wrong. PGW is found in the Ganga-Yamuna doab, Haryana, Punjab and western UP, c. 1200-600 BCE. It is not South Indian and does not coincide with the Sangam period.
Wrong. OCP sites are in the Upper Gangetic plain and the doab (Copper Hoard culture), so they are North Indian, not only South Indian.
Wrong. BRW occurs at Neolithic sites too (for example in Bihar and U.P. and in the south), so 'never' is false.
keyfact: NBPW (c. 700/600-200 BCE) is the deluxe pottery of the Mahajanapada and Mauryan period; PGW is Later Vedic and from the north.
option_notes: NBPW is a lustrous, fine, wheel-made ware with a glossy black surface, often called a luxury ware. It dates from about 700/600 to 200 BCE and is linked with the Mahajanapadas, the Mauryan period, iron use, punch-marked coins and urban centres. Key sites are Kaushambi, Patliputra, Rajghat, Ujjain and Taxila. It spread widely beyond the Ganga plains.

PGW is a fine grey pottery with black painted geometric patterns, c. 1200-600 BCE. It is found in Haryana, Punjab, western UP and Rajasthan at sites such as Hastinapur, Ahichchhatra, Bhagwanpura and Jakhera. It is associated with the Later Vedic period and with iron use. Examples are bowls and dishes, and it is not associated with South India or the Sangam age.

OCP is a thick, ochre-washed, wheel-made pottery of the Upper Gangetic plain. Dated c. 2000-1500 BCE, it is associated with the Copper Hoard culture. Sites include Atranjikhera, Bahadarabad and Saipai. It is linked in some theories with post-Harappan or Late Harappan people. The pottery is often poorly preserved, with an easily rubbed-off slip.

BRW has a black interior and rim with a red exterior, produced by inverted firing. It is found over a very wide area and a long time span, from the Chalcolithic (Ahar, Gilund) through the Neolithic to the Megalithic and Iron Age cultures of South India. It occurs at Neolithic sites such as Chirand and Senuwar and at Neolithic sites in the south.
related: PGW is associated with the Later Vedic period, c. 1200-600 BCE.
NBPW is linked with the Mahajanapadas, the second urbanisation and punch-marked coins.
OCP is associated with the Copper Hoard culture in the Ganga-Yamuna doab.
Black-and-Red Ware occurs from the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods to the Megalithic.
Arikamedu, a Roman trade site, was excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1945.
Malwa ware from Navdatoli is among the finest Chalcolithic wares.
Jorwe culture is a Chalcolithic culture of Maharashtra, c. 1400-700 BCE.
summary: The correct answer is (a). Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) is a fine, lustrous deluxe pottery found at archaeological sites across India, dating from about 700/600 BCE to around 200 BCE, and is linked with the Mahajanapada period and the second urbanisation.
topic_notes: Pottery is a key chronological marker in Indian archaeology. The typical sequence is: Neolithic hand-made pottery (Mehrgarh, Burzahom, Chirand); Harappan red pottery with black paintings, c. 2600-1900 BCE; Ochre Coloured Pottery (c. 2000-1500 BCE, doab); Black-and-Red Ware (Chalcolithic to Megalithic, widespread); Malwa ware (Navdatoli, c. 1700-1200 BCE, regarded as the best Chalcolithic ware in central India); Jorwe ware (Maharashtra, c. 1400-700 BCE); Painted Grey Ware (c. 1200-600 BCE, Later Vedic); Northern Black Polished Ware (c. 700/600-200 BCE, Mahajanapada to Mauryan); and Rouletted ware, Arretine ware and amphorae, which indicate Indo-Roman trade in the early centuries CE (Arikamedu, Tamil Nadu, was excavated by Wheeler in 1945). PGW sites are generally associated with iron use and with settlements mentioned in the Mahabharata, such as Hastinapur. NBPW is associated with urbanisation, punch-marked coins and the use of iron. Ahar-Banas culture (Rajasthan, c. 2100-1500 BCE) used black-and-red ware. Megalithic sites in the south (Brahmagiri, Adichanallur) also have BRW. Related archaeological terms include Copper Hoard culture, Rangpur, Lothal and Ahar. UPSC often asks matching questions on pottery types and their regions or periods, so remember the region, period and culture linked to each ware.

question: Which one of the following pairs is not correctly matched? (Ancient Text/Term) (Meaning)
options: Samarangana- : A_ scientific work Sutradhara on ancient Indian architecture
Harmika : A. style of temple architecture that originated under the Chola Kings
Vimana : A striking feature of the Dravidian style of temples
Kutagarashala_: A hut with a pointed roof where travelling mendicants halted
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: This question tests ancient Indian architectural terminology across Buddhist, Hindu and early texts. Harmika belongs to stupa architecture: the stupa has a base (medhi), hemispherical dome (anda), a square railing on top (harmika), a central mast (yashti) and umbrella (chhatra). It is seen at Sanchi (Stupa 1, Mauryan core, Shunga-Satavahana additions). It is not a Chola temple style. Chola temples belong to the Dravidian tradition, with vimana (the tower over the sanctum) and gopuram (gateway tower). Examples are the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur (c. 1010 CE, Rajaraja I), the Gangaikondacholapuram temple, and the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram, together the Great Living Chola Temples (UNESCO). Samarangana Sutradhara, attributed to the Paramara king Bhoja of Dhara (11th century), is a Sanskrit treatise on vastu and architecture. Kutagarashala, found in Buddhist texts, is a hut with a pointed (gabled) roof, such as the hall at Vaishali where the Buddha stayed and where wandering ascetics halted. Elimination: (a), (c) and (d) are textbook-correct, so (b) is the odd one.
explanations: Correct pairing: Samarangana Sutradhara is a Sanskrit work on architecture and town planning attributed to King Bhoja, so this is not the answer.
Incorrectly matched: Harmika is a part of a stupa, a square railing atop the dome, not a Chola-originated temple style. This is the answer.
Correct pairing: the vimana, the pyramidal tower over the sanctum, is the defining feature of Dravidian temples, so this is not the answer.
Correct pairing: Kutagarashala means a pointed-roof hut or hall used by wandering mendicants and associated with the Buddha at Vaishali, so this is not the answer.
keyfact: Harmika = railed box on top of a stupa's dome (not a Chola temple style); vimana = Dravidian sanctum tower.
option_notes: Samarangana Sutradhara is an 11th-century Sanskrit treatise attributed to the Paramara king Bhoja of Dhara (Malwa). It covers vastu shastra, town planning, house and temple construction, sculpture, and even machines (yantras). It is one of the main surviving texts on Indian architecture alongside the Mayamata, Manasara and Vishvakarma Vastushastra. Bhoja also founded Bhojpur and its famous Shiva temple.

Harmika is a square railed enclosure on top of the dome (anda) of a Buddhist stupa. A mast (yashti) rises from it carrying the chhatra (umbrella). It symbolises a heavenly abode of the gods and is a sacred relic enclosure. Sanchi Stupa 1 shows it clearly. It is not a temple style and did not originate under the Cholas.

Vimana is the tower over the garbhagriha (sanctum) in Dravidian temples, rising in storeys as a stepped pyramid. In the Chola Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur the vimana is about 60 m high and crowned by a single-stone shikhara. In Nagara temples the equivalent is the shikhara. Later Dravidian temples gave greater prominence to the gopurams (gateways).

Kutagarashala means a hall or hut with a pointed or gabled roof. In Buddhist literature, the Kutagarashala at Mahavana near Vaishali is where the Buddha stayed and preached. Such halls also sheltered wandering ascetics (paribbajakas). The term is linked to early Buddhist wooden architecture and the gabled form that influenced chaitya windows and rock-cut facades.
related: Harmika is the railed structure atop a stupa's dome, with the chhatra rising from it.
Samarangana Sutradhara is attributed to Paramara king Bhoja of Dhara.
Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur was built by Rajaraja I around 1010 CE and is a UNESCO site.
Great Living Chola Temples: Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram, Darasuram.
Vesara is a hybrid of Nagara and Dravidian styles, seen in Chalukya and Hoysala temples.
Konark Sun Temple was built by Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty.
Dashavatara temple at Deogarh is a Gupta-period temple.
Kutagarashala at Vaishali is linked with the Buddha's stay.
summary: The answer is (b). Harmika is not a temple style that originated under the Cholas; it is a square railed enclosure or balcony-like structure on top of a Buddhist stupa's dome, from which the chhatra (umbrella) rises. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
topic_notes: Ancient Indian architecture divides into Buddhist, Jain and Hindu traditions. Stupa architecture: medhi (base), anda (dome), harmika (railed box), yashti (mast), chhatra (umbrella), pradakshina patha (circumambulation path) and toranas (gateways). Famous stupas are Sanchi (Madhya Pradesh), Bharhut, Amaravati and Sarnath (Dhamekh). Chaitya is a prayer hall with a stupa, and vihara is a monastery, as at Karle, Ajanta and Ellora. Hindu temples developed in the Gupta period, with early examples at Deogarh (Dashavatara) and Bhitargaon (brick). Three major styles are Nagara (north India; shikhara, curvilinear tower), Dravidian (south; vimana, gopuram, mandapa, large tank) and Vesara (mixed, Deccan, associated with Chalukyas and Hoysalas). Pallava temples: Mahabalipuram rock-cut rathas and Shore Temple, and Kailasanatha at Kanchipuram. Chola temples: Brihadisvara (Thanjavur), Gangaikondacholapuram and Airavatesvara. Chalukyan sites: Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal. Hoysala temples have star-shaped plans at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura. Odisha's Nagara temples include Lingaraja, Jagannath and Konark Sun Temple (Narasimhadeva I). Khajuraho temples were built by the Chandellas. Texts on architecture are Vastu Shastra, Mayamata, Manasara, Samarangana Sutradhara (Bhoja), and Shilpa Shastras. Other terms are garbhagriha, mandapa, antarala, ardhamandapa, jagati, amalaka and kalasha. Mauryan pillars, such as Ashokan pillars with lion capitals, are a related area.

question: What is the time limit prescribed under the provisions of the Employees’ Compensation Act, 1923 from the date of reference within which the Commissioner is required to dispose of the matter relating to compensation and intimate the decision to the employee?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 (earlier the Workmen's Compensation Act, renamed by the 2009 Amendment) provides compensation to employees, or their dependants, for injury or death caused by accident arising out of and in the course of employment, and for prescribed occupational diseases. Disputes about the amount, the liability or the person entitled go to the Commissioner for Employees' Compensation, appointed under Section 20. The 2017 Amendment, effective 2017, added a time-bound disposal rule: the Commissioner must dispose of the matter within three months from the date of reference and intimate the decision to the employee. The 2017 changes also raised penalties for employers and required employers to inform employees of their rights in writing and electronically. Section 4 deals with the amount of compensation, Section 3 with employer's liability, Section 8 with distribution of compensation, and Section 10 with the notice and claim time of two years. Elimination logic: six months and one year are too long for a summary remedy, and two months is shorter than the statute allows. Only three months matches the amended text.
explanations: Incorrect: six months is not the period the Act prescribes for disposal by the Commissioner.
Incorrect: one year is far longer than the statutory limit, which is meant to give speedy relief.
Incorrect: two months does not match the Act; the prescribed period is three months.
Correct: the Commissioner must dispose of the matter within three months from the date of reference and intimate the decision to the employee.
keyfact: EC Act, 1923: Commissioner must dispose of the matter within three months from the date of reference and intimate the decision to the employee.
option_notes: Six months is a period often seen in labour law, for example limitation periods or time limits in other statutes, but it is not the Commissioner's disposal period under the EC Act. Under that Act, the claim itself must generally be made within two years of the accident or death, and the notice of accident has its own rules. Do not confuse these periods.

One year is not the disposal period under this Act. Some provisions use one-year periods in other contexts, such as limits on the Commissioner's power to condone delay in specific situations, but the disposal period after reference is three months. Treat one year as a distractor in this question.

Two months is a plausible-sounding distractor. Time limits of this length appear elsewhere, for example in the payment of compensation. Under Section 4A, compensation is payable from the date it falls due, and interest and penalty apply if the employer does not pay on time. It is not the Commissioner's disposal period.

Three months is the period fixed by the 2017 Amendment for the Commissioner to dispose of the matter from the date of reference and to intimate the decision to the employee. It reflects the purpose of the Act, which is to provide quick relief to injured employees and their dependants without long litigation.
related: The Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 was renamed the Employees' Compensation Act by the 2009 Amendment.
Section 20 provides for the appointment of Commissioners for Employees' Compensation.
Section 10 requires notice of the accident and a claim within two years.
Section 4 provides the amount of compensation, based on a percentage of monthly wages and a relevant factor.
Schedule III lists occupational diseases.
Section 30 provides for appeal to the High Court.
The ESI Act, 1948 provides employment injury benefit to insured persons, and ESI coverage excludes them from the EC Act where applicable.
summary: The answer is (d) Three months. Under the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923, as amended in 2017, the Commissioner must dispose of a compensation matter within three months from the date of reference and intimate the decision to the employee. The Act sets this time limit to make the remedy speedy.
topic_notes: The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 is a social-security and welfare statute that makes the employer liable to pay compensation for employment injury, death or occupational disease, without proof of fault. It was originally the Workmen's Compensation Act and was renamed by the Employees' Compensation (Amendment) Act, 2009. It extends to the whole of India. Compensation is payable under Section 3 when personal injury is caused by an accident arising out of and in the course of employment. Section 4 provides the amount of compensation, which depends on wages and a relevant factor based on age. Death and permanent total disablement are compensated by a percentage of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor. Schedule I lists injuries and the percentage of loss of earning capacity. Schedule II lists the categories of employees covered. Schedule III lists occupational diseases. Section 5 deals with the method of calculating wages. Section 8 deals with distribution of compensation, and a deposit for death must be made with the Commissioner. Section 10 requires notice and a claim within two years. Section 20 provides for the appointment of Commissioners. Section 22 deals with the procedure for claims. Section 30 provides for appeals to the High Court. Section 4A deals with the time and penalty for non-payment of compensation. Under the 2017 Amendment, the Commissioner must dispose of a matter within three months of the reference. The Amendment also provided for penalties on employers for default, along with intimation of rights to employees in writing and electronically. Related schemes include the ESI Act, 1948, which covers employment injury benefit for insured persons. In practice, the EC Act applies to employees outside the ESI coverage.

question: What is the minimum number of employees employed by an establishment functioning without the aid of power and is registered under the Cooperative Societies Act, 1912 that shall require it to come within the purview of the Employees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Section 1(3) of the EPF & MP Act, 1952 defines applicability. Clause (a) covers every establishment in a scheduled industry/class of establishments employing twenty or more persons. Clause (b) covers any other establishment employing twenty or more persons, or class of such establishments, notified by the Central Government. The first proviso to Section 1(3) allows the Central Government to apply the Act to a cooperative society employing fewer than fifty persons and working without the aid of power, subject to specified conditions. The proviso is therefore the source of the fifty threshold for cooperative societies working without power: such a society is covered only when it employs fifty or more persons. For cooperatives using power, the usual twenty-employee threshold applies. Section 1(5) provides that an establishment once covered continues to be covered even if the number of employees later falls below twenty. Elimination logic: 100, 120 and 150 are not thresholds anywhere in the Act's coverage provisions. The EPF Act has a standard threshold of 20 and a cooperative-without-power threshold of 50, so only (a) fits.
explanations: Correct: fifty is the threshold for cooperative societies working without the aid of power under the Act's applicability provision (Section 1(3)).
Incorrect: one hundred is not a coverage threshold in Section 1(3) of the EPF Act. 100 is relevant in other laws, such as the Industrial Disputes Act (Chapter VB).
Incorrect: one hundred twenty is not a threshold in the EPF Act.
Incorrect: one hundred fifty is not a threshold in the EPF Act's applicability provisions.
keyfact: Cooperative society working without power comes under the EPF Act at 50 employees; the general threshold is 20.
option_notes: Fifty: the minimum employee count at which a cooperative society working without power comes under the EPF Act. Establishments using power with 20 or more employees are covered in general. Once covered, an establishment stays covered under Section 1(5) even if its headcount later falls below the threshold. Coverage can also be voluntary by agreement under Section 1(4), where employer and majority of employees agree.

One hundred: not an EPF Act coverage number. It is more familiar from the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (Chapter VB layoff/retrenchment/closure permission applied to establishments with 100 or more workers, later raised to 300 under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020) and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, which applies to establishments with 100 or more workmen (earlier thresholds differ by state).

One hundred twenty: not a statutory threshold in the EPF Act or in the major labour laws. It is a distractor with no particular legal significance for EPF coverage. Students should remember only the key EPF numbers: 20 for general coverage, 50 for cooperative societies working without power, and 20 employees for establishments in notified classes.

One hundred fifty: not a statutory threshold in the EPF Act's applicability provisions. It is a distractor option. The real EPF thresholds are 20 (general) and 50 (cooperative societies without power). Higher employee numbers matter in other contexts, such as the Employees' State Insurance Act, which applies to establishments with 10 or more persons (20 in some states).
related: EPF Act, 1952 general coverage threshold: 20 or more employees.
Section 1(4) allows voluntary coverage by agreement between employer and majority of employees.
Section 1(5): once covered, always covered, even if headcount drops below 20.
EPF contribution: 12% of basic wages plus DA by employer and employee.
EPS 1995 is the pension scheme under the EPF Act; EDLI Scheme was introduced in 1976.
Wage ceiling for compulsory EPF coverage is Rs 15,000 per month.
Central Board of Trustees administers EPF; the Central Provident Fund Commissioner is its executive head.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 is intended to subsume the EPF Act, 1952.
summary: The answer is (a) Fifty. Under Section 1(3)(b) of the EPF & MP Act, 1952, the Act applies to a cooperative society registered under the Cooperative Societies Act, 1912 (or any other law for cooperative societies) that employs fifty or more persons and works without the aid of power. The Central Government's 1962 notification reduced this threshold from the earlier 50 persons for 'power' cases.
topic_notes: The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 provides for provident fund, pension and deposit-linked insurance for employees in factories and other establishments. It extends to the whole of India. Section 1(3) sets out applicability: it applies to every establishment that is a factory engaged in any industry specified in Schedule I and employing twenty or more persons, and to any other establishment employing twenty or more persons or class of such establishments that the Central Government notifies. The first proviso allows the Central Government to apply the Act to a cooperative society employing fewer than fifty persons and working without the aid of power. Section 1(4) permits voluntary coverage by agreement between employer and majority of employees. Section 1(5) says that an establishment, once covered, remains covered even if the number of employees falls below twenty. The Act creates three schemes: the Employees' Provident Fund Scheme, 1952; the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995; and the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976. The Central Board of Trustees (EPFO) administers them, headed by the Central Provident Fund Commissioner. The statutory contribution rate is 12% of basic wages plus dearness allowance and retaining allowance, for both employer and employee (10% in certain notified establishments). The wage ceiling for compulsory coverage is Rs 15,000 per month. Related areas UPSC may ask about: Section 7A (determination of dues), Section 14B (damages), Section 7I (Appellate Tribunal), the Social Security Code, 2020 (which subsumes the EPF Act once it is brought into force) and the coverage thresholds of the ESI Act.

question: Any question relating to disablement shall be determined by which one of the following authorities under the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948?
subject: Insurance
detail: Under the ESI Act, 1948, Chapter V-A, Section 54A deals with the determination of questions of disablement. It provides that any question as to the extent of disablement, whether the disablement is temporary or permanent, and the percentage loss of earning capacity shall be decided by a Medical Board. The Medical Board is constituted by the ESI Corporation and normally consists of medical practitioners appointed by it. If a person is aggrieved by the Medical Board's decision, they can appeal to the Medical Appeal Tribunal under Section 54A and Section 55 (as per the Act's provisions). Above the Tribunal, appeals on substantial questions of law lie to the High Court. Section 54A also gives the Medical Board the power to review its own decisions where there is a change in circumstances. The Insurance Medical Practitioner (IMP) is a first-line doctor who provides treatment and issues medical certificates for sickness benefit; he does not decide disablement questions. The Social Security Officer is an administrative officer of the Corporation (Section 17 related inspection and administration) and has no authority over medical disablement determinations. Elimination logic: first-instance decision on disablement means Medical Board; appeal means Medical Appeal Tribunal.
explanations: (a) Wrong: the Insurance Medical Practitioner treats insured persons and certifies sickness or temporary incapacity, but does not decide disablement questions under the Act.
(b) Wrong: the Social Security Officer is an administrative or inspecting officer of the ESIC and has no medical adjudicating role.
(c) Correct: Section 54A vests the Medical Board with determining the existence, nature, extent and duration of disablement, including loss of earning capacity.
(d) Wrong: the Medical Appeal Tribunal is an appellate body hearing appeals against Medical Board decisions, not the primary authority for determination.
keyfact: Disablement questions under the ESI Act are decided by the Medical Board (Section 54A); appeals go to the Medical Appeal Tribunal.
option_notes: The Insurance Medical Practitioner (IMP) is a registered medical practitioner appointed by the State Government or ESIC to give medical treatment to insured persons and families under the panel system. He issues medical certificates for sickness benefit and temporary disablement benefit, but final disablement assessment is outside his power. He is part of the medical benefit delivery framework, not an adjudicating authority.

The Social Security Officer is an officer of the ESI Corporation who performs administrative and inspection functions in regional or local offices, such as checking employer compliance, registration and contribution records. Officers of this rank are not medical adjudicators. The designation reflects the Act's shift in terminology from Inspector to Social Security Officer in the amended framework.

The Medical Board is a body constituted under the ESI Act to determine questions of disablement, including its extent, nature, duration and the percentage loss of earning capacity, which in turn decides entitlement to disablement benefit. Its decision is the first-instance authority and may be reviewed by the Board itself where circumstances change. Appeals against its decisions go to the Medical Appeal Tribunal.

The Medical Appeal Tribunal is an appellate body provided for in the ESI Act to hear appeals against the decisions of the Medical Board on disablement. It consists of a chairperson and members who are medical and legal experts as prescribed. Its decision is generally final on medical questions, and further appeal lies to the High Court only on a substantial question of law.
related: Section 54A of the ESI Act deals with determination of disablement questions by the Medical Board.
Appeals against the Medical Board decisions lie with the Medical Appeal Tribunal.
The Employees' Insurance Court is constituted under Section 74 of the ESI Act.
ESI wage ceiling for coverage is Rs 21,000 per month.
Employer contribution to ESI is 3.25 percent and employee contribution is 0.75 percent of wages.
Disablement benefit under ESI can be temporary or permanent.
The Standing Committee is the executive body of the ESI Corporation.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the ESI Act, 1948.
summary: The answer is (c) The Medical Board. Under Section 54A of the ESI Act, 1948, any question relating to the existence, extent, nature or duration of disablement is determined by a Medical Board constituted by the Corporation. The Medical Appeal Tribunal hears appeals against the Board's decision.
topic_notes: The Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 is a major social security statute for employees in factories and other establishments. It provides six main benefits: sickness benefit, maternity benefit, disablement benefit (temporary and permanent), dependants' benefit, medical benefit and funeral expenses. It is administered by the ESI Corporation, a body corporate whose members include representatives of employers, employees, the Central and State Governments, Parliament and the medical profession. The Standing Committee is its executive body, and the Medical Benefit Council advises on medical matters. The Union Minister of Labour and Employment is the Corporation's Chairperson. Adjudication machinery: disputes on contributions and benefits go to the Employees' Insurance Court under Section 74. The Employees' Insurance Court is the forum for most disputes, but questions of disablement are specially reserved for medical bodies: the Medical Board decides at first instance, and the Medical Appeal Tribunal hears appeals. Contributions are shared by employer and employee at prescribed rates, currently 3.25 percent from employer and 0.75 percent from employee of wages. Coverage applies to employees earning up to Rs 21,000 per month (Rs 25,000 for persons with disability). Temporary disablement benefit is payable at about 90 percent of wages from the first day, while permanent disablement benefit is also paid at about 90 percent of wages, adjusted by the percentage loss of earning capacity. Related Acts include the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 and the Code on Social Security, 2020, which subsumes the ESI Act once brought into force. Students should compare these adjudicatory bodies and their statutory sections.

question: What is the amount of compensation that is to be paid to an employee who is totally and permanently disabled as a result from injury under the provisions of the Employees’ Compensation Act, 1923? (Hints : Monthly wages drawn were ®22, 500 and relevant factor is 159-80)
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Section 4 and Schedule IV of the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 fix compensation for death and permanent total disablement. For permanent total disablement the formula is 60% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor, which depends on the employee's age at the last birthday before the accident. The factor is taken from Schedule IV. For death the percentage is 50%. The Act caps the monthly wages used in the computation. Under the notification of 2010 the ceiling is Rs 8,000 per month, and the 2009 amendment gave the Central Government power to revise it. The question's official answer implies a ceiling of Rs 15,000. Wages of Rs 22,500 therefore count only as Rs 15,000. The calculation is 15,000 x 60/100 = 9,000, and 9,000 x 159.80 = 14,38,200. Option (c) is the trap: it applies 60% to the full Rs 22,500 (13,500 x 159.80 = 21,57,300) and ignores the cap. Option (b) is 22,500 x 159.80 x 2/3, which is not the statutory formula, and is wrong. Option (d) is 50% of Rs 8,000 x 159.80 = 6,39,200, or an equally irrelevant figure, so it is also wrong. Check any figure against the wage ceiling and the percentage.
explanations: Correct: wages are capped at Rs 15,000, so 60% x 15,000 x 159.80 = Rs 14,38,200.
Incorrect: this is not obtained by any statutory formula. It is a distractor that uses an unsupported percentage on the uncapped wage.
Incorrect: this is 60% of the uncapped Rs 22,500 multiplied by 159.80. It ignores the wage ceiling.
Incorrect: this figure does not follow from the 60% formula with any wage ceiling used in the question. It is a distractor.
keyfact: Permanent total disablement compensation = 60% x capped monthly wages (Rs 15,000 here) x age factor = 9,000 x 159.80 = Rs 14,38,200.
option_notes: Rs 14,38,200 is the amount for permanent total disablement when monthly wages are capped at Rs 15,000: 9,000 x 159.80. Compensation under Section 4 is 60% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor. The factor depends on the age of the employee, and a younger employee gets a higher factor. Schedule IV lists the factors. The wage ceiling limits the wages counted, however high the actual pay. The Act also provides interest and penalty for delayed payment.

Rs 23,97,000 equals 22,500 x 159.80 x 2/3, which is 66.67% of uncapped wages. It is not a statutory percentage. The Act uses 60% for permanent total disablement and 50% for death. This option is a numerical distractor. Remember that compensation is calculated on capped wages, and that the Commissioner for Employees' Compensation decides disputes and awards compensation.

Rs 21,57,300 is 60% of the full Rs 22,500 multiplied by 159.80. It is the amount if there were no wage ceiling. Section 4 limits monthly wages to the notified ceiling, so this is wrong. Students often fall for this trap by using the actual wages. The Schedule IV factor for the injured person's age is applied after capping wages.

Rs 7,67,040 does not match the 60% formula on either Rs 22,500 or Rs 15,000. It is a distractor. The statutory minimum for permanent total disablement is Rs 1,40,000 and for death Rs 1,20,000. Compensation is never below these floors, whatever the age factor.
related: Permanent total disablement compensation is 60% of monthly wages x relevant factor.
Death compensation is 50% of monthly wages x relevant factor.
Minimum compensation: Rs 1,20,000 for death and Rs 1,40,000 for permanent total disablement.
Funeral expenses under the Act are Rs 5,000.
The Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 was renamed the Employees' Compensation Act in 2009.
The Commissioner for Employees' Compensation decides claims under Section 20.
Interest on delayed compensation is 12% per annum.
Schedule IV gives the relevant factors by age.
summary: The answer is (a) Rs 14,38,200. Under the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923, compensation for permanent total disability is 60% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor. Here that is 60% x 22,500 x 159.80 = Rs 21,57,300 on the uncapped wage, but the wage ceiling of Rs 15,000 applies, so 60% x 15,000 x 159.80 = Rs 14,38,200.
topic_notes: The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923, formerly the Workmen's Compensation Act, was renamed in 2009. It makes the employer liable to pay compensation for injury or death arising out of and in the course of employment, and for specified occupational diseases listed in Schedule III. It is a no-fault liability law. Section 3 deals with the employer's liability. Section 4 deals with the amount of compensation. Schedule I lists injuries deemed permanent total disablement (100% loss of earning capacity) and permanent partial disablement. Schedule II lists the persons treated as employees. Schedule IV gives the relevant factors by age. Death: 50% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor, subject to a minimum of Rs 1,20,000. Permanent total disablement: 60% of monthly wages multiplied by the factor, with a minimum of Rs 1,40,000. Temporary disablement: half-monthly payments of 25% of monthly wages, beginning from the 16th day after the injury, or from the 8th day in some cases. Permanent partial disablement: the percentage loss of earning capacity applied to the total-disablement amount. Funeral expenses are Rs 5,000. The Commissioner for Employees' Compensation, appointed under Section 20, decides claims, and appeals lie to the High Court on a substantial question of law. Notice of the accident must be given, and a claim must be made within two years. Interest is payable at 12% per annum on delayed compensation, and a penalty of up to 50% may be imposed. The wage ceiling was fixed at Rs 8,000 in 2010, and the ceiling used in this question is Rs 15,000 as per the official answer. Employer contributions to medical expenses are also part of the Act.

question: What is the minimum number of employees required to be working in an establishment, so that the employer, with the authorization of the majority of the employees of the establishment, may apply to the Central Government to authorize the employer to create a separate Provident Fund Account for the employees under the Employees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 is a central Act administered by the EPFO under the Ministry of Labour and Employment. Its general rule is that contributions of covered establishments go to the statutory Employees' Provident Fund. Section 17 allows exemption of an establishment or class of employees from the Scheme, if the benefits are no less favourable. Section 17(1)(a) covers exemption of establishments that maintain their own provident fund rules, subject to conditions. Section 17(2A) concerns exemption of employees. Where an employer wants a separate Provident Fund account, with the consent of the majority of employees, the threshold in this question is 100 employees, as the official key says. Exempted establishments must follow EPFO rules on investment pattern, audit, trust formation, and the same rate of contribution. Exempted trusts are monitored by the Regional PF Commissioner. For elimination, 300, 500 and 1000 are higher numbers that do not match the threshold in the question, so only 100 fits. Students should remember 100 as the key number in this context. It also appears in other labour laws, so avoid mixing thresholds: the EPF Act applies generally to establishments with 20 or more employees.
explanations: Correct: the official UPSC answer is 100 employees as the minimum for the employer, with majority authorization, to apply for a separate PF account.
Incorrect: 300 is not the threshold in the Act or the official answer for this question.
Incorrect: 500 is not the threshold; it is higher than the prescribed number.
Incorrect: 1000 is far above the prescribed minimum and is not the official answer.
keyfact: For a separate PF account application (with majority employee authorization), the official UPSC answer is 100 employees.
option_notes: One hundred: the threshold number of employees in an establishment from which the employer, with majority employee consent, may seek separate PF account treatment under the EPF & MP Act, 1952. Exempted establishments must provide benefits at least equal to the statutory scheme and are supervised by EPFO authorities. The figure is an important number to remember, and should not be confused with the 20-employee coverage threshold of the Act.

Three hundred: a distractor number. It is not the minimum for applying to create a separate provident fund account under the Act. Some labour laws use thresholds like 300 (for example, the Industrial Disputes Act's standing order and layoff-permission provisions use 100 and 300 in different contexts), so do not carry this figure over to the EPF Act.

Five hundred: a distractor number. It is not the EPF Act threshold for a separate PF account. Higher thresholds such as 500 appear in some other labour provisions, such as the Industrial Disputes Act's 'Works Committee' and similar rules in different contexts, but they do not apply to this question.

One thousand: a distractor number and the largest option. It is not the EPF Act threshold for separate PF account. Such large figures are sometimes used in welfare provisions of other statutes, but are not relevant to this EPF question.
related: EPF & MP Act, 1952 generally applies to establishments with 20 or more employees.
EPFO is headed by the Central Provident Fund Commissioner and is under the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
The EPS was introduced in 1995; EDLI in 1976.
Section 17 of the EPF Act provides for exemption of establishments.
Section 14B provides for damages for delayed payment of contributions.
Section 7A covers determination of moneys due from employers.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the EPF & MP Act, 1952.
The Central Board of Trustees (EPF) is a tripartite body.
summary: The answer is (a) One hundred. Under the EPF & MP Act, 1952 (Section 17 read with the exemption provisions and the Scheme), an employer of an establishment with 100 or more employees, backed by the majority of employees, can apply for separate treatment. The official answer is (a), and this note follows it.
topic_notes: The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 provides for the institution of provident funds, pension funds and deposit-linked insurance funds for employees in factories and other establishments. It is administered by the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), a statutory body under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, headed by the Central Provident Fund Commissioner. The Central Board of Trustees (EPF) is the apex body; it is tripartite, with representatives of government, employers and employees. Three schemes operate: the Employees' Provident Fund Scheme, 1952, the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 (EPS) and the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976 (EDLI). Coverage generally applies to establishments with 20 or more persons, with a wage ceiling for mandatory coverage of Rs 15,000 per month. The standard employee contribution is 12 percent of basic wages plus dearness allowance (and retaining allowance), and the employer matches it, of which 8.33 percent goes to EPS (with a government contribution of 1.16 percent). Section 17 deals with exemptions: an establishment may be exempted if its employees enjoy benefits no less favourable. Exempted establishments run their own trust-based provident funds, follow investment rules, and are subject to inspection and audit. Other angles UPSC could ask: Section 7A (determination of dues), Section 14B (damages for default), Section 7I (Appellate Tribunal), penalties in Section 14, the Nomination rules, the UAN and the Universal Account Number, the Employees' Pension Scheme minimum pension, and the Social Security Code, 2020, which subsumes this Act once brought into force.

ocr: Following are the Central Federations of Trade Unions of Workers formed in India : 13 Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC) All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) United Trade Union Congress (UTUC) Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU) 6. Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) Which one of the following is the correct sequence of their formation from the earliest to the latest? a. 1, 4,6, 5,3 (a) (b) 2,1, 54,625 (c) 1,2; 5,°4, 3, 6 1, 3, 2,.4, 5, 6 (a)
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Indian trade union movement began with the formation of AITUC in Bombay on 31 October 1920, with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first president and Joseph Baptista as vice-president. After Independence, political splits produced rival federations. INTUC was founded on 3 May 1947 and is linked to the Congress. UTUC was formed in 1949 by Leftist groups (RSP and others) that broke away from AITUC. BMS was established on 23 July 1955 by Dattopant Thengdi and is associated with the RSS/BJP ideology. CITU was formed in 1970 after the CPI split in 1964, when the CPI(M) faction left AITUC. SEWA was founded in 1972 in Ahmedabad by Ela Bhatt, and it grew out of the Textile Labour Association (TLA). Elimination: AITUC must come first, which rules out (c) and (d). Between (a) and (b), SEWA (1972) is the latest, since it comes after CITU (1970), so (b) is wrong. Only (a) fits the dates 1920, 1947, 1949, 1955, 1970, 1972.
explanations: Correct: it gives AITUC (1920), INTUC (1947), UTUC (1949), BMS (1955), CITU (1970), SEWA (1972) in correct order.
Wrong: it places SEWA third, before UTUC, BMS and CITU, although SEWA was formed in 1972, the latest of all.
Wrong: it starts with INTUC and places AITUC second, but AITUC (1920) predates INTUC (1947); it also puts CITU before UTUC.
Wrong: it begins with INTUC, places SEWA second, and has several incorrect positions, ignoring AITUC's 1920 founding as the earliest.
keyfact: Order of formation: AITUC 1920 → INTUC 1947 → UTUC 1949 → BMS 1955 → CITU 1970 → SEWA 1972.
option_notes: Sequence 2, 1, 4, 6, 5, 3: AITUC (1920), INTUC (1947), UTUC (1949), BMS (1955), CITU (1970), SEWA (1972). This follows the political evolution of Indian labour, from the first national body to splits along Congress, Communist, Leftist and Sangh Parivar lines, ending with SEWA, a union for informal women workers. It is the official answer.

Sequence 2, 1, 3, 4, 6, 5: it begins correctly with AITUC and INTUC, but places SEWA (1972) before UTUC (1949), BMS (1955) and CITU (1970). SEWA, founded by Ela Bhatt in Ahmedabad, is a union of self-employed women, registered in 1972, and later than the other central union organisations in this list.

Sequence 1, 2, 5, 4, 3, 6: it starts with INTUC (1947) and puts AITUC second, though AITUC was formed in 1920. It also puts CITU (1970) before UTUC (1949) and BMS last. INTUC was founded on 3 May 1947 and is Congress-affiliated. The sequence is wrong in almost every place.

Sequence 1, 3, 2, 4, 5, 6: it begins with INTUC (1947), then SEWA (1972) and then AITUC (1920), which is chronologically impossible. It also places BMS (1955) after CITU (1970). It shows confusion between the dates of SEWA, AITUC and the other central unions.
related: AITUC was founded on 31 October 1920 in Bombay; Lala Lajpat Rai was its first president.
INTUC was founded on 3 May 1947 and is linked to the Congress.
HMS (Hind Mazdoor Sabha) was founded in 1948 in Howrah by Socialists.
BMS was founded on 23 July 1955 by Dattopant Thengadi.
CITU was founded in 1970 after the CPI split; B. T. Ranadive was its first president.
SEWA was founded in 1972 by Ela Bhatt in Ahmedabad.
The Trade Unions Act, 1926 requires at least seven members to register a trade union.
The Textile Labour Association (1920) was founded by Gandhi, Anasuya Sarabhai and Shankarlal Banker.
statements: 1 — Correct in the sequence as the second formed: INTUC was founded in 1947. INTUC was established on 3 May 1947, shortly before Independence, under the Congress's guidance, with the Gandhian ideals of Textile Labour Association as inspiration. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was a key figure in its founding, and Gulzarilal Nanda later led it. It has traditionally been among the largest central unions by membership. It follows the principle of arbitration and conciliation over strikes, and believes in a nationalist, non-confrontational approach to labour relations.

2 — Correct as the first formed: AITUC was founded in 1920. AITUC was formed on 31 October 1920 in Bombay and was the first national trade union federation in India. Lala Lajpat Rai was its first president, and N. M. Joshi, Joseph Baptista and Dewan Chaman Lall were prominent early leaders. It was influenced by the formation of the ILO in 1919. It later came under Communist influence and is today associated with the CPI. It split several times (1929, 1931, 1947, 1949, 1970).

3 — Correct as the last formed: SEWA was founded in 1972. SEWA (Self-Employed Women's Association) was registered as a trade union in 1972 in Ahmedabad by Ela Bhatt, an offshoot of the Textile Labour Association. It organises women in the informal sector such as vendors, home-based workers and manual labourers. It runs cooperatives, a SEWA Bank (1974) and social security services. Ela Bhatt received the Ramon Magsaysay Award (1977) and the Padma Bhushan. It is a central trade union organisation recognised by the Government.

4 — Correct as the third formed: UTUC was founded in 1949. UTUC was formed in 1949 in Calcutta by Leftist groups, led mainly by the Revolutionary Socialist Party (RSP) and Forward Bloc elements, who left AITUC. It was meant as a united platform of radical-left unions. Later, a split occurred, creating UTUC (Lenin Sarani) in 1970 from the original UTUC. Its influence is concentrated in West Bengal and Kerala.

5 — Correct as the fifth formed: CITU was founded in 1970. CITU was formed in May 1970 at Calcutta, after the 1964 split in the CPI that created the CPI(M). It is affiliated with the CPI(M), and B. T. Ranadive was its first president. It is among the largest central trade unions in India. It is strong in West Bengal, Kerala and Tripura, and has a class-struggle approach, supporting strikes and mass mobilisation against labour-law changes.

6 — Correct as the fourth formed: BMS was founded in 1955. BMS was founded on 23 July 1955 in Bhopal by Dattopant Thengadi. It follows a nationalist philosophy of 'Bharatiya' thought, wanting to unite labour on the basis of national interests and industrialising the nation, labour-ising industry and nationalising labour. It is associated with the RSS family (Sangh Parivar). Since the early 2000s, it has been reported as the largest central trade union in terms of verified membership.
summary: The correct answer is (a) 2, 1, 4, 6, 5, 3. AITUC (1920) was the first central trade union federation, followed by INTUC (1947), UTUC (1949), BMS (1955), CITU (1970) and SEWA (1972).
topic_notes: Trade unionism in India began with early welfare associations such as the Bombay Mill Hands Association (1890, N. M. Lokhande) and grew with the Swadeshi movement and the Madras Labour Union (1918, B. P. Wadia). The Trade Unions Act, 1926 gave legal recognition and registration to unions, made registered unions a body corporate, and gave immunity from civil and criminal liability for legitimate activities. Seven or more members can form a union. AITUC (1920) was the first apex body; its early splits included the 1929 moderates (National Trade Union Federation) and the Red Trade Union Congress (1931). After 1947, INTUC (Congress), HMS (Hind Mazdoor Sabha, 1948, Socialists), UTUC (1949), BMS (1955), CITU (1970), and later NFITU, TUCC, SEWA (1972), LPF and NLO emerged. Central trade union organisations (CTUOs) are recognised by the Ministry of Labour on the basis of membership verification; the verification of 2013 (data of 2002) and later ones placed BMS first, followed by INTUC, AITUC, HMS and CITU. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 changed the framework for trade unions, with a 'sole negotiating union' provision (51% membership) and a negotiating council where none has 51%. Other angles to note are the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946, the ILO Conventions 87 and 98 (freedom of association and collective bargaining), which India has not ratified, and the Code on Wages and Social Security Code 2020. Remember also the Textile Labour Association (1920, Ahmedabad) of Gandhi, Anasuya Sarabhai and Shankarlal Banker, which followed the Gandhian model of arbitration.

question: Which one of the following core conventions adopted by the International Labour Organization (ILO) has not been ratified by India?
options: The Forced Labour Convention (No. 29) The Equal Remuneration
Convention (No. 100) The Freedom of Association and
Protection of the Right to Organize Convention (No. 87)
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The ILO's Fundamental (core) Conventions cover five categories of rights, which the 1998 Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work commits all members to respect whether or not they have ratified them. The categories are: freedom of association and collective bargaining (C87, C98), elimination of forced labour (C29, C105), abolition of child labour (C138, C182), non-discrimination (C100, C111), and since 2022 a safe and healthy working environment (C155, C187). India ratified C29 (Forced Labour) in 1954, C105 (Abolition of Forced Labour) in 2000, C100 (Equal Remuneration) in 1958, C111 (Discrimination) in 1960, C138 (Minimum Age) in 2017 and C182 (Worst Forms of Child Labour) in 2017. India has not ratified C87 and C98. The usual reason given is that ratification would conflict with restrictions on government servants, such as the Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, and with limits on their right to strike. Elimination logic: options (a), (b) and (d) are all ratified, which leaves (c). Article 19(1)(c) of the Constitution guarantees the right to form associations, but the government has still not ratified C87.
explanations: Incorrect: India ratified the Forced Labour Convention (C29) in 1954, so it is not the answer.
Incorrect: India ratified the Equal Remuneration Convention (C100) in 1958. It is also reflected in the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, now subsumed in the Code on Wages, 2019.
Correct: India has not ratified C87 (Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise, 1948). The government cites concerns about the rights of its own employees.
Incorrect: India ratified the Discrimination (Employment and Occupation) Convention (C111) in 1960, so it is not the answer.
keyfact: India has not ratified the core ILO conventions C87 (Freedom of Association) and C98 (Collective Bargaining); it has ratified C29, C100, C105, C111, C138 and C182.
option_notes: C29, adopted in 1930, requires suppression of forced or compulsory labour in all its forms, with limited exceptions such as compulsory military service and normal civic obligations. India ratified it in 1954. A 2014 Protocol supplements it on prevention, protection and remedies. India's domestic law includes the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, and Article 23 of the Constitution.

C100, adopted in 1951, establishes the principle of equal remuneration for men and women for work of equal value. India ratified it in 1958. Domestic implementation was through the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, which has now been subsumed into the Code on Wages, 2019. Article 39(d) of the Constitution (a Directive Principle) also provides for equal pay for equal work.

C87, adopted in 1948, guarantees workers and employers the right to establish and join organisations of their own choosing without prior authorisation. It is a core ILO convention and India has not ratified it, nor C98 (Right to Organise and Collective Bargaining, 1949). The reasons include restrictions on government employees' right to strike. Article 19(1)(c) of the Constitution protects the right to form associations, and the Trade Unions Act, 1926, governs unions.

C111, adopted in 1958, prohibits discrimination in employment and occupation on grounds such as race, colour, sex, religion, political opinion, national extraction and social origin. India ratified it in 1960. It is supported by constitutional provisions such as Articles 14, 15, 16 and 39, and by the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 and related labour laws.
related: India has ratified six of the eight original core ILO conventions; C87 and C98 remain unratified.
C98 (1949) covers the Right to Organise and Collective Bargaining; India has not ratified it either.
India ratified C138 (Minimum Age) and C182 (Worst Forms of Child Labour) in 2017.
In 2022 the ILO added a safe and healthy working environment to its fundamental principles (C155 and C187).
The ILO was established in 1919, is headquartered in Geneva, and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969.
India ratified C105 (Abolition of Forced Labour) in 2000.
Article 19(1)(c) guarantees the right to form associations or unions.
summary: The answer is (c): India has not ratified the Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise Convention, 1948 (No. 87). India has ratified C29, C100, C105, C111 and C138 and C182, but not C87 or C98, mainly because of restrictions on the associational rights of government employees.
topic_notes: The ILO was founded in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles, became a UN specialised agency in 1946, is headquartered in Geneva, and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969. It is unique for its tripartite structure of governments, employers and workers. India has been a founding member since 1919. The ILO adopts Conventions (binding on ratifying states) and Recommendations (non-binding). The eight fundamental conventions were: C29 Forced Labour (1930), C87 Freedom of Association (1948), C98 Right to Organise and Collective Bargaining (1949), C100 Equal Remuneration (1951), C105 Abolition of Forced Labour (1957), C111 Discrimination (1958), C138 Minimum Age (1973), and C182 Worst Forms of Child Labour (1999). In June 2022 the International Labour Conference added a safe and healthy working environment as the fifth fundamental principle, which brought in C155 (Occupational Safety and Health, 1981) and C187 (Promotional Framework for OSH, 2006), making ten core conventions. India has ratified six of the eight original core conventions, and the exceptions are C87 and C98. India has not yet ratified C155 or C187. India ratified C138 and C182 in June 2017. India has also ratified some governance conventions, such as C81 (Labour Inspection, in part), C144 (Tripartite Consultation) and C122 (Employment Policy). The ILO also publishes the World Employment and Social Outlook and the Global Wage Report. Its Director-General is Gilbert Houngbo (since 2022).

question: Suppose there are five trade unions, namely A, B, C, D and E functioning in an establishment currently employing 1100 workmen. The membership strength of each union is as follows : Union A : 100 Union B : 370 Union C : 110 Union D : 275 Union E : 80 Based on the strength of membership, which of the above unions can be registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926?
options: Unions A, B, C and D only
Unions B, C and D only
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 4(1) of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 provides that any seven or more members of a trade union may apply for registration. The 2001 amendment added a proviso: the application is valid only if the applicants are at least 10% or 100 of the workmen engaged or employed in the establishment or industry, whichever is less, and in no case fewer than 7. Apply it here: 10% of 1100 = 110, and 100 is less than 110, so the required strength is 100 workmen. Union A has exactly 100, which meets the requirement because the test is 'at least'. B (370), C (110) and D (275) clearly qualify. Union E has 80, which is below 100, so it cannot be registered. Elimination: (a) fails because E is ineligible; (c) wrongly drops A, which has exactly 100; (d) wrongly drops A and C. The trap is to use 10% (110) alone, which would exclude A. The lower-of-the-two rule is the key. Also note that the Registrar is appointed by the appropriate government under Section 3, and registered unions become bodies corporate under Section 13.
explanations: Wrong: Union E has only 80 members, below the 100 threshold (the lesser of 10% = 110 and 100), so it cannot be registered.
Correct: the threshold is the lesser of 10% of 1100 (110) or 100, i.e. 100. A (100), B (370), C (110) and D (275) meet it; E (80) does not.
Wrong: it excludes Union A, which has exactly 100 members and satisfies the 'at least 100' requirement.
Wrong: it excludes both A and C. Union C (110) meets even the 10% figure, and A meets the 100 figure, so both qualify.
keyfact: Registration of a trade union needs 7+ members and at least 10% or 100 of the workmen, whichever is less (Section 4, Trade Unions Act, 1926).
option_notes: All the unions: this would be correct only if the threshold were 80 or lower. The Act requires a minimum of 7 members and 10% or 100 of the workmen, whichever is less. Registration is voluntary, but it confers legal status as a body corporate with perpetual succession, a common seal, and the power to sue and be sued (Section 13). Unregistered unions do not enjoy these protections or the immunities in Sections 17 and 18.

Unions A, B, C and D only: this is the correct option. The qualifying threshold is 100 workmen, being less than 10% (110). It follows the 2001 amendment to Section 4 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926, which added the 10%-or-100 condition to prevent proliferation of tiny unions. Minimum 7 members always apply. The Registrar can refuse or cancel registration under Sections 8 and 10.

Unions B, C and D only: this results from wrongly treating 110 (10%) as the cut-off. It ignores the 'whichever is less' wording. Union A with exactly 100 members qualifies because the proviso uses the language 'ten per cent or one hundred of the workmen, whichever is less'. Students often fall into this trap, so always compute both figures and take the lower.

Unions B and D only: this would apply only if the threshold were above 110 but at most 275, for example 25% of the workforce (275). The Act does not require that. Union C (110) meets even the 10% figure exactly. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 proposes recognition as a negotiating union at 51% membership, which is a different concept from registration.
related: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927.
Minimum 7 members are needed to apply for registration of a trade union (Section 4).
The 2001 amendment added the 10% or 100 workmen, whichever is less, condition.
Section 13: a registered trade union is a body corporate with perpetual succession.
Section 17 gives immunity from criminal conspiracy; Section 18 from civil suits.
Section 22: at least half of the office-bearers must be actually engaged in the industry.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 merges the Trade Unions Act, the Industrial Disputes Act and the Standing Orders Act.
The Registrar of Trade Unions is appointed by the appropriate government (Section 3).
summary: The answer is (b): Unions A, B, C and D only. Under Section 4 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 (as amended in 2001), a union needs at least 7 members and a minimum of 10% of the workmen or 100 workmen, whichever is less, subject to a minimum of 7. Here 10% of 1100 is 110, so the threshold is 100 (the lower figure), and Unions A (100), B (370), C (110) and D (275) qualify, while E (80) does not.
topic_notes: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927 and legalised trade unions in India. It defines a trade union (Section 2(h)) as a combination formed for regulating relations between workmen and employers, between workmen and workmen, or between employers and employers. Registration is voluntary. Section 3 provides for the appointment of a Registrar of Trade Unions by the appropriate government. Section 4 governs the mode of registration: seven or more members may apply, and since the 2001 amendment the applicants must be at least 10% or 100 of the workmen, whichever is less, with a minimum of 7. Section 6 specifies the provisions required in the rules of a union. Section 8 covers registration, Section 10 cancellation of registration, and Section 11 appeals. Section 13 makes a registered union a body corporate. Sections 15 and 16 deal with objects on which funds may be spent and the political fund. Section 17 gives immunity from criminal conspiracy and Section 18 immunity from civil suits. Section 22 requires that at least half of the office-bearers be persons actually engaged in the industry, and outsiders are limited under the 2001 amendment (maximum of 1/3 of office bearers or 5, whichever is less). Section 28 requires annual returns. The Act is a Central law under the Concurrent List. The 2001 amendment also provided that a union of workers in unorganised sectors may include outsiders to a larger extent. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 will subsume the Act, along with the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. Related ideas include the sole negotiating union, the negotiating council, and recognition thresholds.

question: Registration of trade unions of workers under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 is
options: optional for workers working in non-public utility services
compulsory for workers working in public utility services [ate
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 (in force from 1 June 1927) provides a voluntary scheme of registration under Chapter II (Sections 3-13). Section 3 requires the appropriate Government to appoint a Registrar of Trade Unions. Section 4 allows any seven or more members of a trade union to apply for registration by subscribing their names to the rules; there is no provision penalising a union for staying unregistered. Registration confers benefits: a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal (Section 13), the capacity to sue and be sued, to hold property and enter contracts, immunity from criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B IPC for acts in furtherance of trade dispute (Section 17), and immunity from civil suits for certain acts (Section 18). Registered unions can also maintain a political fund (Section 16) and must follow rules on accounts, audit and returns. Elimination logic: since the Act contains no compulsion, (b) and (d) fail; (c) wrongly implies that registration is compulsory for other workers, and the Act makes no distinction between public utility and non-public utility services. The Act applies equally to all sectors. Article 19(1)(c) gives the fundamental right to form associations or unions, which supports the voluntary approach.
explanations: Correct: the Act makes registration voluntary; unregistered unions are lawful but lack the statutory privileges and legal personality.
Incorrect: no provision compels trade unions to register, and no penalty is attached to non-registration.
Incorrect: it implies registration is compulsory for other categories of workers, which the Act does not say. Registration is optional for all unions regardless of the nature of the service.

Incorrect: the Act does not make registration compulsory for public utility service workers; the public utility concept belongs to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, not to registration under the Trade Unions Act.
keyfact: Registration under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 is voluntary (optional) for every union, with seven members the minimum to apply; it brings corporate status and legal immunities.
option_notes: Optional registration is the position under the Trade Unions Act, 1926: workers can form a union freely under Article 19(1)(c), and registration under Section 4 is an option taken to gain legal status, corporate identity and immunities under Sections 13, 15, 17 and 18. Seven or more members must apply to the Registrar.

Compulsory registration is the opposite of the Indian position. Compulsory registration regimes would restrict freedom of association; India's law only incentivises registration through legal benefits, not mandates. Some other labour laws, such as the Contract Labour Act, require establishments to register, but this applies to establishments, not to trade unions.

Optional for non-public utility services only is a distractor. Public utility services are defined in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (First Schedule and Section 2(n)), such as railways, posts, water supply and electricity, where strike notice rules (Section 22) are stricter. They are irrelevant to union registration.

Compulsory for public utility workers is also a distractor. Though public utility workers face stricter notice requirements for strikes and lockouts under Section 22 of the ID Act, their unions are not compelled to register under the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
related: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927.
Section 4: a minimum of seven members is needed to apply for registration.
Section 13: a registered trade union is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal.
Section 17 gives immunity from criminal conspiracy; Section 18 gives immunity from civil suits.
The AITUC, founded in 1920, was India's first national trade union federation.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
Trade unions are in Entry 22 of the Concurrent List; Article 19(1)(c) guarantees the right to form unions.
Section 16 allows a registered union to maintain a separate political fund.
summary: The answer is (a) optional. Under the Trade Unions Act, 1926, registration of a trade union is voluntary; the Act does not compel any union to register, but only registered unions get legal status and statutory benefits.
topic_notes: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 was India's first law on trade unions, passed after the formation of the AITUC in 1920 and the Madras Labour Union (B.P. Wadia, 1918). It came into force on 1 June 1927 and has been amended several times (notably in 2001). Key provisions: a trade union is defined in Section 2(h) as a combination formed for regulating relations between workers and employers, or workers and workers, or employers and employers. Registration: Section 4 (application by at least seven members); the 2001 amendment requires a minimum of 10% of workmen or 100 workmen, whichever is less, subject to a minimum of seven, engaged in the establishment. Section 6 prescribes matters the rules must provide for. Section 8 deals with registration and Section 9 with certificates. Section 10 deals with cancellation. Section 13 makes a registered union a body corporate. Section 15 lists the objects on which general funds may be spent. Section 16 provides for a separate political fund. Section 17 gives criminal immunity and Section 18 civil immunity. Section 22 requires that not more than half of the office-bearers be outsiders (the 2001 amendment: not more than one-third or five, whichever is less), and Section 28 requires annual returns. The Registrar is appointed by the appropriate government. Related laws: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947; Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes the Trade Unions Act, the ID Act and the Standing Orders Act; it provides for recognition of a negotiating union (51% membership), and a negotiating council where no union has 51%. The Code is yet to be brought into force. Constitutional basis: Article 19(1)(c) and Entry 22 of the Concurrent List (trade unions; industrial and labour disputes).

question: The Right of workers to resort to strike is the
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Indian courts have repeatedly held that the right to strike is not a fundamental right. Article 19(1)(c) guarantees the right to form associations or unions, but it does not guarantee the right to strike, to be recognised, or to bargain collectively (All India Bank Employees' Association v. National Industrial Tribunal, 1962). In Kameshwar Prasad v. State of Bihar (1962) the Supreme Court held that there is no fundamental right to strike. In T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2003) it held that government employees have no fundamental, legal, moral or equitable right to strike. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 does not confer the right. It only regulates it through Section 22 (public utility services, notice required), Section 23 (general prohibition during conciliation and adjudication) and Sections 10(3) and 10A(4A) (prohibition once a reference is made). Section 2(q) defines a strike. Sections 24 and 26 govern illegal strikes and penalties, and Section 25 covers financial aid to them. The right therefore rests on common law and is a weapon of collective bargaining, subject to statutory limits. Elimination: (a) is rejected by the Supreme Court, (b) is wrong because the statute only restricts, and (d) is wrong because courts have denied any equitable right.
explanations: Wrong: the Supreme Court has held in many cases that the right to strike is not a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(c).
Wrong: the Industrial Disputes Act regulates and restricts strikes but does not grant the right, so it is not a statutory right.
Correct: the right to strike is treated as a common law right, a recognised form of collective bargaining that is subject to statutory regulation.
Wrong: in T.K. Rangarajan (2003) the Supreme Court said there is no equitable right to strike.
keyfact: The right to strike is a common law right, not a fundamental right (Art. 19(1)(c) does not cover it) and not conferred by statute; the ID Act, 1947 only regulates it.
option_notes: Fundamental rights are in Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12-35) and are enforceable under Article 32 and Article 226. Article 19(1)(c) protects the freedom to form associations and unions, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(4). The Supreme Court has held that this does not include a guaranteed right to strike, to collective bargaining or to recognition of a union. The Constitution (44th Amendment) removed the right to property from this list, but that is unrelated to strikes.

A statutory right is one created by an Act of the legislature. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 defines a strike in Section 2(q), but it only regulates it. Section 22 requires notice in public utility services, and Section 23 bars strikes during proceedings. It confers no positive right. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 retains the notice requirement and extends it to all industrial establishments, but it is not yet in force.

A common law right is one that comes from judge-made law, custom and precedent rather than a statute or the Constitution. The strike is a recognised weapon of workers in collective bargaining. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 gives immunity from civil and criminal liability for trade union activities in contemplation of a trade dispute. The right is conditional and can be restricted by statute, and it may not be used to defeat legitimate regulation.

An equitable right comes from the principles of equity developed by the English Court of Chancery, such as injunctions, specific performance and trusts, and was based on fairness. In India equity features in the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The Supreme Court in T.K. Rangarajan (2003) said employees have no equitable right to strike. Equity is therefore not the source of the right.
related: Strike is defined in Section 2(q) and lockout in Section 2(l) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
Section 22 of the ID Act requires strike notice in public utility services.
T.K. Rangarajan v. Govt of Tamil Nadu (2003): no fundamental, legal, moral or equitable right to strike.
Article 19(1)(c) gives the right to form unions, not the right to strike.
Industrial Relations Code, 2020 requires 14 days' notice for strikes in all industrial establishments.
Trade Unions Act, 1926 Sections 17 and 18 give immunity to registered unions in trade disputes.
