Section 24 of the ID Act deals with illegal strikes and lockouts, and Section 26 prescribes penalties.
ESMA, 1981 empowers the Centre to prohibit strikes in essential services.
summary: The official answer is (c) Common Law Right. The right to strike is not a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(c) and is not an absolute statutory right. It is recognised as a right in the nature of common law, i.e. a form of collective bargaining, and it is regulated and restricted by statute, mainly the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
topic_notes: The right to strike in India sits between the constitutional guarantee of association and statutory regulation of industrial conflict. Article 19(1)(c) protects forming unions, but the courts hold that strike and lockout are not fundamental rights. Key cases: All India Bank Employees' Association (1962), Kameshwar Prasad (1962), Radhey Shyam Sharma v. Post Master General (1965), Express Newspapers v. Union of India, Syndicate Bank v. Umesh Nayak (1994: wages for the strike period), Communist Party of India (M) v. Bharat Kumar (1997: bandh unconstitutional), T.K. Rangarajan (2003), and Harish Uppal v. Union of India (2002: lawyers cannot strike). The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947: Section 2(q) defines a strike as cessation of work by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in combination, or a concerted refusal to continue work. Section 2(l) defines a lockout. Section 22 requires 6 weeks' notice in public utility services, with strikes not allowed within 14 days of the notice, before the date in the notice, or during conciliation and 7 days after it ends. Section 23 contains the general prohibition. Section 24 defines illegal strikes. Section 26 sets penalties, and Section 25 penalises financial aid to illegal strikes. Section 10(3) and Section 10A(4A) allow prohibition once a reference is made. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 extends the 14-day notice requirement to all industrial establishments and treats mass casual leave by 50 percent or more of workers as a strike. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 gives immunity under Sections 17 and 18. ESMA (Essential Services Maintenance Act, 1981) lets the government ban strikes in essential services. Internationally, the ILO has no express convention on strike but supervisory bodies derive the right from Convention 87.

question:
PQ and RS are chords on a circle centred at O. Suppose A is the point of intersection of PQ and RS. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. If A and O coincide, then the four parts of the circle produced by the chords shall always have equal areas.
2. IfAand Odo not coincide, then two of the four parts of the circle produced by the chords shall always have equal areas. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Two chords PQ and RS intersecting at A divide the circle into four regions. Statement 1: if A = O, both chords pass through the centre and are therefore diameters. Diameters can intersect at any angle θ, so the four sectors have areas proportional to θ, 180°-θ, θ and 180°-θ. Opposite sectors are equal, but all four are equal only when the diameters are perpendicular (θ = 90°). 'Always' therefore fails. Statement 2: if A is not O, the regions are not sectors. Take a point A off-centre and draw two chords at arbitrary angles. The areas of the four regions depend on the distances and angles, so in general none of them is equal to another. Equality would hold only in special cases, such as one chord being a diameter and the other perpendicular to it. For example, if RS is a diameter and PQ is a chord perpendicular to it at A, then the regions are symmetric about RS, which gives two equal pairs. But a general oblique chord breaks this symmetry. The word 'always' is the trap. Eliminate (a), (b) and (c) by counterexample.
explanations: Wrong: Statement 1 is false because diameters at an arbitrary angle do not give four equal parts.
Wrong: Statement 2 is false because off-centre chords generally give four regions of unequal area, so equality is not 'always' guaranteed.
Wrong: Both statements fail the test of 'always', so they cannot both be correct.
Correct: Neither statement holds in general, and the official answer is (d).
keyfact: Chords through the centre give four equal parts only if they are perpendicular; 'always' statements in geometry usually fail by counterexample.
option_notes: Option (a) claims only statement 1 is correct. It would be true only for perpendicular diameters, which give four quadrants of πr²/4. Two diameters at angle θ give sectors θ, 180°-θ, θ and 180°-θ, so the four parts are equal only when θ = 90°. Since the statement says 'always', it fails.

Option (b) claims only statement 2 is correct. Chords meeting off-centre divide the circle into irregular regions. Equality of areas needs symmetry, as when a diameter is cut at right angles by a chord. For an arbitrary pair of chords the areas generally differ, so 'always' is false.

Option (c) claims both are correct. Both statements use 'always', and each has a simple counterexample: non-perpendicular diameters for statement 1 and oblique off-centre chords for statement 2. So (c) is wrong.

Option (d) says neither is correct, and it is the official answer. Each statement fails in the general case. Remember that UPSC often uses 'always' to turn a special case into a false universal claim. Counterexamples are the quickest way to eliminate such statements.
related: Intersecting chords theorem: PA·AQ = RA·AS.
A diameter divides a circle into two equal semicircles.
Two perpendicular diameters divide a circle into four equal quadrants.
Angle in a semicircle is 90°.
The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
Sector area = (θ/360°) × πr².
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: When A = O both chords are diameters, but unless they are perpendicular the four sectors are unequal; only opposite sectors are equal. Facts: a diameter is the longest chord and passes through the centre. It subtends 180° at the circumference and divides the circle into two semicircles of equal area. Sector area = (θ/360°) × πr². Two diameters make vertically opposite angles that are equal, so opposite sectors match. All four sectors are equal only at right angles, giving quadrants of πr²/4 each.

2 — Incorrect: When A ≠ O, no pair of regions is guaranteed to have equal area. A counterexample is two oblique chords through an off-centre point. Facts: the intersecting chords theorem says PA·AQ = RA·AS for chords meeting at an interior point A. That is a relation between lengths and not areas. Perpendicular distance from the centre to a chord is d = √(r² - (l/2)²). Equal areas arise only with symmetry, for example when one chord is a diameter and the other is perpendicular to it. In general the regions are unequal.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. If A coincides with O, both chords are diameters, but they can meet at any angle, so the four sectors need not be equal. If A is not the centre, no two of the four regions are guaranteed to have equal areas.
topic_notes: This question tests circle geometry and chords. A chord is a line segment joining two points on a circle, and the diameter is the longest chord and passes through the centre. Perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord. Equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and chords closer to the centre are longer. Intersecting chords theorem: if chords PQ and RS meet at an interior point A, then PA × AQ = RA × AS. If the point is outside the circle, the secant version is PA × QA = RA × SA, and the tangent-secant version is PT² = PA × PB. The angle between two intersecting chords equals half the sum of the arcs it and its vertical angle intercept. Angles in the same segment are equal, the angle in a semicircle is 90°, and the angle subtended at the centre is double that at the circumference. Area of the circle is πr², circumference 2πr, sector area (θ/360)πr², and arc length (θ/360)2πr. Segment area equals sector area minus triangle area. Areas of regions formed by chords are not equal unless there is symmetry. UPSC tests 'always' and 'never' statements, so quickly test with extreme or special cases: perpendicular diameters, parallel chords, or a chord near the edge. Related topics: cyclic quadrilaterals (opposite angles sum to 180°), tangents from an external point being equal, and the alternate segment theorem.

question:
P,Q, R, Sand T are five friends. The mean of weights of P, Q, R and S is 50 kg, whereas the mean of weights of Q, R, S and T is also 50 kg. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. The weight of T is 50 kg.
2. The weights of P and T are equal. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Statistics
detail: This is a basic averages problem. The mean of four people is 50, so their total weight is 200 kg. For the first group, P+Q+R+S = 200. For the second group, Q+R+S+T = 200. Subtracting the second equation from the first cancels the common terms Q, R and S, leaving P - T = 0, so P = T. That proves statement 2. Statement 1 claims T = 50 kg, but this needs Q+R+S = 150, which the data does not give. For example, P = T = 40 with Q+R+S = 160 satisfies both conditions, and so does P = T = 60 with Q+R+S = 140. Hence T can take many values and statement 1 is not necessarily true. The exam lesson is to distinguish what must be true from what can be true. Do not assume the common mean is also the value of the unshared members. Elimination: because statement 2 is certainly true, options (a) and (d) go; because statement 1 is not certain, (c) goes; this leaves (b). Always test with a counterexample for 'must be true' questions.
explanations: (a) is wrong: it says only statement 1 is correct, but statement 1 is not forced by the data and statement 2 is forced.
(b) is correct: the subtraction of the two sums gives P = T, so statement 2 is correct, while T's value is undetermined so statement 1 is not necessarily correct.
(c) is wrong: statement 1 cannot be established, since T may be any value as long as P = T and Q+R+S = 200 - T.
(d) is wrong: statement 2 is definitely correct, so 'neither' cannot be right.
keyfact: Equal means of two overlapping equal-sized groups mean the two non-shared members are equal (P = T), but their value stays undetermined.
option_notes: Option (a) 'Statement 1 only' would be right only if T = 50 were certain. That would need extra information such as Q+R+S = 150 or all five friends having equal weight. Note that statement 1 being true in a special case does not make it correct in general. UPSC options like this test whether you notice that a conclusion is possible but not necessary.

Option (b) 'Statement 2 only' is the correct choice. It reflects the logical deduction P = T from equal group means with three shared members. It is a typical pattern in averages questions: shared members cancel out when two sums are equated. The total of each group is 4 x 50 = 200 kg. The individual weights remain unknown but P and T are the same.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' would be correct only if the data forced T = 50 as well as P = T. That occurs if the mean of all five were also given as 50 or if Q+R+S were known to be 150. With the information given, the sum of Q, R and S can vary, so T is not fixed. Hence this option overstates what can be deduced.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' would hold if no relation could be drawn between P and T. In fact, the equal means of two overlapping groups give a definite relation, P = T. Choosing this option means missing the elimination of common terms. It is a trap for students who think that missing numbers mean nothing can be concluded.
related: Mean = Sum of observations / Number of observations.
If two equal-sized groups share all but one member and have equal means, the unshared members are equal.
Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean (empirical relation for moderately skewed data).
Average of the first n natural numbers = (n+1)/2.
Average speed for equal distances = 2ab/(a+b).
If every observation is increased by k, the mean increases by k.
Replacing a member changes the total by the difference of the two values, and the mean by that difference divided by n.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: T's weight is not determined. Only P = T follows; the common sum Q+R+S could be anything (e.g., 160 gives T = 40). The mean of a group of four does not fix the value of an individual member. Fact: Mean = Sum of observations / Number of observations, so a mean of 50 for four persons means a sum of 200. If the sum of the other three members is unknown, the fifth member's value cannot be found. Counterexamples are the best way to disprove a 'must be' claim in data sufficiency style questions. A mean only equals each member's value if all members are equal, which is not given here.

2 — Correct: Subtracting the two sum equations (P+Q+R+S = 200 and Q+R+S+T = 200) gives P = T. This holds for any values of Q, R and S. Fact: when two groups have the same size and the same mean and differ by only one member each, those two differing members must be equal. The same logic applies to a moving average: if the average of consecutive windows is unchanged, the entering and leaving values are equal. This is a standard shortcut in averages and sequence problems, and it works with any common mean. If the means were different, the difference between P and T would be 4 times the difference in means.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Since (P+Q+R+S)/4 = (Q+R+S+T)/4 = 50, subtracting gives P = T, but nothing fixes the individual value of T at 50 kg.
topic_notes: Averages (arithmetic mean) form a core part of the Quantitative Aptitude section of the EPFO papers. Mean = Sum / Number of items, so Sum = Mean x Number. Most problems become easy once you convert means into sums. Key techniques: (1) Equate sums of overlapping groups and cancel common members, as in this question. (2) When a member is replaced, the change in total equals the change in mean times the group size. (3) Weighted average = Sum of (weight x value) / Sum of weights, used when groups of different sizes are combined. (4) The average of the first n natural numbers is (n+1)/2; of the first n even numbers is n+1; of the first n odd numbers is n. (5) For consecutive numbers or an arithmetic progression, the mean equals the middle term (or the average of the first and last terms). (6) If every observation increases by k, the mean rises by k; if multiplied by k, the mean is multiplied by k. (7) Average speed over equal distances is the harmonic mean 2ab/(a+b), not the arithmetic mean. (8) Adding a new person to a group changes the average by (new value - old average)/(n+1). Logical reasoning aspects: a statement is 'correct' only if it must be true under every case consistent with the data, so test with counterexamples. UPSC may also ask the age or weight of a person after replacement, the effect on average when the oldest member leaves, or data sufficiency type statements. Related statistical measures include median (middle value), mode (most frequent value) and the relation Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean for moderately skewed data. Practice such problems by writing equations first, then subtracting or adding them.

ocr: P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W are sitting in a row facing North. P and S are neighbours; W is a neighbour of both Q and U; T is a neighbour of R and V. If there are four people between P and V, how many people are there between P and R? (a) 1 aun w (b) (c) (d)
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a linear arrangement puzzle with 8 people in a row. Turn each neighbour clue into a block. P and S are neighbours, so they form a 2-person block. W neighbours both Q and U, so W is in the middle of the 3-person block Q-W-U (or U-W-Q). T neighbours both R and V, so T is in the middle of the block R-T-V (or V-T-R). The blocks 2 + 3 + 3 fill all 8 seats. 'Four people between P and V' means their positions differ by 5. The pairs of positions that fit are (1,6), (2,7), (3,8) and their reverses. Test each one against the blocks. Whenever P and V sit in the middle seats, the leftover seats cannot hold a 3-person block together, so those cases fail. Only P at 1 and V at 6 works: P S Q W U V T R, with QWU in seats 3-5 and R at seat 8. The mirror case is R T V Q W U S P. In both cases P and R are at the two ends, so six people sit between them. The maximum possible gap in a row of 8 is 6, which confirms (d).
explanations: (a) 1 is wrong. P and R are at opposite ends of the row, so the gap cannot be this small.
(b) 3 is wrong. No valid arrangement gives only three people between P and R.
(c) 5 is wrong. Five between them would mean positions differ by 6, but the valid arrangement has them 7 seats apart, with 6 between.
(d) 6 is correct. The only valid layout is P S Q W U V T R (or its mirror image), with P and R at the extreme ends.
keyfact: Blocks PS, QWU and RTV with 'four between P and V' give P S Q W U V T R, so P and R are at opposite ends with 6 people between.
option_notes: Option (a) 1: this would put P and R almost adjacent. It is not possible here because the 3-person blocks QWU and RTV, plus the PS pair, force P and R to the ends. In seating puzzles, always test any offered gap against the block structure.

Option (b) 3: this would need P and R three seats apart, with a block in between. The constraint 'four between P and V' rules it out, because every arrangement that satisfies it and keeps the blocks intact puts P and R at the ends.
Option (c) 5: this is the near-miss distractor. Many students confuse 'four between P and V' (positions differ by 5) with the P-R gap. P and R are in fact 7 seats apart, so 6 people lie between them.

Option (d) 6: this is the maximum number of people that can sit between two people in a row of 8. It happens only when they occupy the two end seats. It is the official answer here: P is at one end and R at the other.
related: In a row of n people, the number of people between positions a and b is |a−b|−1.
Position from left + position from right = total people + 1.
'A is a neighbour of both B and C' means A sits between B and C.
In a row of 8, the maximum number of people between two persons is 6, when they sit at the two ends.
When people face North, their left is West and their right is East.
Facing South reverses left and right relative to a North-facing row.
Block method: merge neighbour clues into blocks, then check that the block sizes sum to the total seats.
summary: The answer is (d) 6. The arrangement must be P S Q W U V T R (or its mirror image), so P and R sit at opposite ends of the row with six people between them.
topic_notes: Linear seating arrangement is a staple of reasoning in UPSC EPFO and similar exams. The standard method is to translate every clue into a block or a relative position. 'A is a neighbour of both B and C' places A between B and C, giving a 3-block B-A-C or C-A-B. 'X and Y are neighbours' gives a 2-block. Then add up the block sizes against the total number of seats. Next convert the distance clue into positions: 'n people between' means positions differ by n+1. Test each possible pair of positions systematically and discard those where the remaining seats cannot fit a whole block. Facing North in a row means the person's left is the West side and the right is the East side, which matters for left/right questions. Related question types include circular arrangements (facing inside or outside), two-row arrangements, rank and position-from-end problems (position from left + position from right = total + 1), and floor or box puzzles. Shortcuts: mark the end seats first, use blocks to eliminate impossible placements, and check the maximum gap, which is total minus 2. In this puzzle the final arrangement is P S Q W U V T R, with an equally valid mirror image. Future questions may ask who sits at the third seat from the left, who sits in the middle, or how many people are between S and T. Practise by writing the arrangement as a strip of numbered boxes and filling it in.

question: The angles of elevation of the top of a tower from the top and bottom of a 10 metres tall building are 30° and 45° respectively. Approximately what is the height of the tower in metres from the top of the building (given that J3 = 1-73)?
subject: Computers
detail: This is a standard heights-and-distances problem with two angles of elevation taken from the same vertical line. Draw the building (10 m) and the tower on level ground, with d as the horizontal gap. From the building's bottom the angle is 45°, so tan45° = 1 and H = d. From the building's top the line of sight is horizontal, so the tower part above the building is H−10 and tan30° = 1/√3 = (H−10)/d. Substituting d = H gives H−10 = H/√3, so H(√3−1) = 10√3 and H = 10√3/(√3−1). Rationalising gives H = 10√3(√3+1)/2 = 5(3+√3) = 5(4.73) = 23.65 m. The question asks for the height from the top of the building, which is H−10 = 13.65 m. Equivalently, H−10 = d/√3 = 23.65/1.73 ≈ 13.67, which matches approximately. Elimination: 23.65 is not an option, which shows the question wants the part above the building. 10.65 and 15.41 do not fit the equations. 13.41 is close but comes from a slip in rounding. Key values: tan30° = 1/√3, tan45° = 1, tan60° = √3. The trap is giving the full tower height instead of the height above the building.
explanations: (a) 10.65 is wrong. It does not satisfy H−10 = H/√3. If the part above the building were 10.65, the tower would be 20.65 m and d/√3 would be about 11.9, which is inconsistent.
(b) 13.41 is wrong. It is close to the correct figure and looks like a rounding or arithmetic slip. The exact calculation gives 5(3+√3) − 10 = 5(1+√3) = 13.65 with √3 = 1.73.
(c) 13.65 is correct. H = 5(3+√3) = 23.65 m, and subtracting the building's 10 m gives 13.65 m, which equals 5(√3+1).

(d) 15.41 is wrong. It matches no consistent set of the given angles and heights, and the tower would then be 25.41 m, which gives a 45° angle from the bottom only if d = 25.41. The 30° condition then fails.
keyfact: H = d (45°) and H−10 = d/√3 (30°), so H = 5(3+√3) = 23.65 m and the height above the building is 13.65 m.
option_notes: 10.65 m: this is only a distractor, not a result of the problem. It would apply to a tower rising 10.65 m above a building. Its closeness to 10 is a trap for students who confuse the building height with the tower portion. The correct height above the building is 5(√3+1) = 13.65 m, with √3 = 1.73.

13.41 m: this is a near-miss distractor, close to 13.65. It arises from rounding errors, such as using a wrong value of √3 or mis-simplifying 10√3/(√3−1). Always rationalise: 10√3(√3+1)/2 = 5(3+√3). With √3 = 1.73 this gives 23.65 m in total and 13.65 m above the building.

13.65 m: this is the correct answer, the part of the tower above the building's top. It equals 5(√3+1). The total tower height is 5(3+√3) = 23.65 m and the horizontal distance is also 23.65 m, because tan45° = 1. The method uses two right triangles that share the same horizontal base d.

15.41 m: this is a distractor with no basis in the given data. It might arise from wrongly using tan60° or from adding rather than subtracting heights. If the tower portion above the building were 15.41 m, the total would be 25.41 m, and the 30° line of sight from the roof would not hold. The correct value is 13.65 m.
related: Angle of elevation is measured above the horizontal; angle of depression below it.
Angle of elevation of an object equals the angle of depression of the observer from that object.
If the angle at the foot is 45°, the tower's height equals its horizontal distance.
Height of a tower with angles 45° from the foot and 30° from the top of a building of height h: H = h√3/(√3−1) = 5(3+√3) for h = 10.
Rationalising: 1/(√3−1) = (√3+1)/2.
Height above the building = 5(√3+1) ≈ 13.65 m when the building is 10 m high.
summary: The answer is (c) 13.65 m. Let the tower height be H and its horizontal distance from the building be d. From the bottom, tan45° = 1 gives H = d. From the top, tan30° = (H−10)/d gives H−10 = d/√3. Solving, H ≈ 23.65 m, so the tower rises about 13.65 m above the building's top.
topic_notes: Heights and distances is a trigonometry application topic. The angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to the line of sight to an object above the observer's eye level. The angle of depression is measured downward from the horizontal to an object below it. The two are equal when measured on parallel horizontals (alternate angles). Standard values: sin30° = 1/2, cos30° = √3/2, tan30° = 1/√3; tan45° = 1; tan60° = √3. Use √2 = 1.41, √3 = 1.73 and √5 = 2.24 for approximations. General method: (1) draw a clear figure; (2) mark the right triangles; (3) write tanθ = height/base for each; (4) use the common quantity, here the horizontal distance d, to link the equations; (5) answer exactly what is asked (total height, part above a building, or the distance). Common types: two observation points on a line at the foot of a tower with angles θ1 and θ2; a tower on a hill or building, where the angles are taken from the top and the foot; a flagstaff on a tower; a ship or boat moving toward a lighthouse; and a kite or balloon with string length. For two angles 30° and 60° from points on a line, the distance between the points is 2/√3 times the height. When the angle at the foot is 45° and the angle at the roof is θ, the tower height is h·tanθ... use the relation H = d and H−h = d tanθ, giving H = h/(1−tanθ). Here H = 10/(1−1/√3) = 23.65. Typical errors are giving the whole height when the question asks for the part, mixing up angles of elevation and depression, and approximation slips. In EPFO papers, these questions are solved in under a minute by memorising the standard values and the rationalising step.

question: A multiple-choice question paper has 50 questions. Each question has got four options, namely A, B, C and D. Each correct answer carries 4 marks and each wrong answer carries —-1 mark. A candidate decides to tick in the pattern A,B GD, APB GD) ASBG, D, and so on starting from Question No. 1, till the end. If option (C) is the correct answer in each question, then what is the total score of the candidate?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: This is a pattern-and-marking-scheme problem. The candidate ticks A, B, C, D, A, B, C, D and so on from Question 1. The pattern repeats every 4 questions, and option C falls on questions 3, 7, 11, and so on, which is every 4th question starting at 3. Since 50 = 4×12 + 2, there are 12 complete cycles (48 questions) and 2 leftover questions (49 and 50), which get A and B. The leftover questions add no C, so the number of C ticks is 12. Because C is correct in every question, the candidate gets 12 correct answers. The remaining 50 − 12 = 38 answers are wrong. Marks are 12×4 = 48 for correct answers, minus 38×1 = 38 for wrong answers, so the total is 10. Elimination logic: 6, 8 and 12 come from miscounting. If you wrongly take 13 correct, you get 52 − 37 = 15, which is not an option. If you take 12 correct but forget the negative marking, you get 48. The check formula is score = 5×correct − total questions (for attempted questions), and 5×12 − 50 = 10. This formula works because every question is attempted.
explanations: (a) 6 is wrong. It would need 11.2 correct answers, which is impossible. 5×correct − 50 = 6 gives a non-integer, so it cannot arise.
(b) 8 is wrong. 5×correct − 50 = 8 gives 11.6 correct answers, which is not an integer, so it is not a valid score.
(c) 10 is correct. There are 12 correct answers (questions 3, 7, ..., 47) and 38 wrong answers. The score is 48 − 38 = 10.
(d) 12 is wrong. It would need 12.4 correct answers, which is not an integer. It is likely a trap from confusing the number of correct answers (12) with the score.
keyfact: Cycle A-B-C-D over 50 questions gives 12 correct (C) and 38 wrong: 48 − 38 = 10.
option_notes: 6 is not a possible score here. With all 50 questions attempted and +4/−1 marking, the score is 5×correct − 50, which can only be −50, −45, ..., 0, 5, 10, and so on, in steps of 5. Any score that is not a multiple of 5 is impossible. This divisibility check quickly rules out 6, 8 and 12. The same shortcut works in any 'all attempted' negative marking problem: score = (m + n)×correct − n×total, where m is the marks per correct answer and n is the penalty per wrong answer.

8 is not a possible score. Since every question is attempted, the score must be a multiple of 5 (offset by −50). That makes the possible scores 5k − 50, such as 0, 5, 10 and 15. Eight would need 11.6 correct answers. It is a distractor, perhaps from miscounting the cycle as 11 correct and then adjusting wrongly. In negative marking questions, always compute correct count first, then wrong count, then net marks.

10 is the correct score. Option C is ticked on every 4th question starting at question 3, giving 12 correct answers in 50 questions. The 38 others are wrong. Marks are 12×4 = 48 minus 38×1 = 38, so 10. The check formula is 5×12 − 50 = 10. This is the standard approach for periodic-pattern questions: divide the total by the cycle length, then examine the remainder positions.

12 is not a possible score. It is probably a distractor based on the 12 complete cycles and 12 correct answers. The actual score is 12×4 − 38 = 10, not 12. Candidates who confuse the count of correct answers with the score fall into this trap. A score of 12 would require 12.4 correct answers, which cannot happen because the score is always a multiple of 5 when all questions are attempted.
related: With +4/−1 marking and all 50 questions attempted, every possible score is a multiple of 5 (score = 5×correct − 50).
50 ÷ 4 = 12 remainder 2, so the first two options of the cycle (A and B) are ticked 13 times each, and C and D 12 times each.
If option A were correct throughout, the score would be 13×4 − 37 = 15.
Positions of C in the pattern are 3, 7, 11, ..., 47, an arithmetic progression with common difference 4.
Number of terms in an AP = (last − first)/d + 1 = (47 − 3)/4 + 1 = 12.
UPSC Prelims uses 1/3 negative marking for each wrong answer in GS and CSAT papers.
Net score formula: marks = m×correct − n×wrong.
summary: The answer is (c) 10. The candidate's ticks cycle A, B, C, D, so in 50 questions option C is ticked 12 times, giving 12 correct and 38 wrong answers. The score is 12×4 − 38×1 = 48 − 38 = 10.
topic_notes:
This question tests the quantitative aptitude topics of series and patterns, remainders, and negative marking. It is a common type in the APFC and EO/AO papers.

The method has four steps. First, find the cycle length, which is 4 here (A, B, C, D). Second, divide the total number of questions by the cycle length: 50 ÷ 4 gives quotient 12 and remainder 2. Third, count the target option in full cycles (12 × 1 = 12), then check whether the remainder positions (A, B) include it. They do not include C. Fourth, apply the marking scheme.

If the question asked for option A or B, the answer would change: A and B appear in the remainder, so they are ticked 13 times each, while C and D are ticked 12 times each. If A were correct for all questions, the candidate would have 13 correct and 37 wrong, scoring 52 − 37 = 15.

Useful formulas:
- Score = (m × correct) − (n × wrong).
- If all questions are attempted: Score = (m + n) × correct − n × total.
- With +4/−1 marking, scores are in steps of 5.
- For +x/−y marking where unattempted questions score 0, count the attempted questions separately.

Related angles UPSC could ask next:
- A different cycle length, such as a 3-option pattern or a pattern like A, A, B, C.
- Correct answers that follow a different pattern, such as every 3rd question.
- Finding how many questions must be correct to reach a cut-off score.
- Fractional negative marking (UPSC prelims uses 1/3 negative marking for each wrong answer).
- Minimum correct answers needed to score a certain total, using inequalities.

Exam tips: write the pattern for the first 8 questions to check the cycle, and use the divisibility check to eliminate options quickly.

question: The insurance claim received on account of machinery damaged completely by fire is
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: The classification of receipts and expenditures depends on their nature. A capital receipt arises from the sale or loss of a fixed asset, the raising of capital or loans, or the receipt of compensation for loss of a capital asset. It is non-recurring and does not appear in the Profit and Loss account as income. A revenue receipt arises from the normal course of business, such as sales, interest, commission or rent, and is recurring. Machinery is a fixed asset. When it is destroyed by fire, the insurance claim compensates for the loss of that asset, so it is a capital receipt. In accounting, the claim received is set against the book value of the machinery. Any excess over book value is a capital profit, and any shortfall is a capital loss. Under the Income-tax Act, compensation for a destroyed asset is treated under Section 45(1A) and Section 50 as a capital gain, or it adjusts the block of assets. If the claim were for destroyed stock-in-trade, it would be a revenue receipt. Options (c) and (d) are wrong because they describe payments (expenditures), not receipts. Option (b) is wrong because the receipt is not from operations.
explanations: Correct. The claim is compensation for a destroyed fixed asset (machinery). It is non-recurring and capital in nature, so it is a capital receipt.
Incorrect. A revenue receipt comes from normal business operations, such as sales or interest. Compensation for a destroyed fixed asset does not.
Incorrect. Capital expenditure is money spent to acquire or improve fixed assets. An insurance claim is money received, not spent.
Incorrect. Revenue expenditure is a day-to-day operating cost, such as wages or repairs. A claim is a receipt and not an expense.
keyfact: A claim for a fixed asset destroyed by fire is a capital receipt, while a claim for destroyed stock is a revenue receipt.
option_notes: Capital receipt: money received that is not part of regular business income. Examples are capital contributed by owners, loans raised, proceeds from selling fixed assets, and compensation for loss of a fixed asset. It is non-recurring and shown in the Balance Sheet, not the Profit and Loss account. It either increases liabilities or reduces assets.

Revenue receipt: income from normal business activities, such as sales, interest received, rent, commission and dividends. It is recurring, credited to the Profit and Loss account, and taxable as business income. It does not change the capital structure or the fixed assets of the business.

Capital expenditure: spending that gives benefits over more than one accounting year. It covers buying or improving fixed assets, installation costs, legal costs of acquiring property and similar items. It is shown on the Balance Sheet as an asset and depreciated over time. An example is a machine purchase.

Revenue expenditure: spending incurred to run the business and to maintain earning capacity in the current year, such as wages, rent, repairs, depreciation and insurance premiums. It is charged to the Profit and Loss account in the year incurred and its benefit is exhausted within that year.
related: Insurance claim for destroyed fixed asset is a capital receipt; for destroyed stock it is a revenue receipt.
Capital receipts do not appear in the Profit and Loss account.
Loss of profit (consequential loss) policy claims are revenue receipts.
Insurance premium on business assets is revenue expenditure.
Profit on sale of fixed assets is a capital profit.
Deferred revenue expenditure is spread over several years, such as heavy advertising.
Ind AS 16 deals with property, plant and equipment.
summary: The answer is (a) capital receipt. Insurance compensation for a completely destroyed machine replaces a fixed (capital) asset, so the receipt is capital in nature and is not part of normal operating income.
topic_notes: Accounting classifies transactions into capital and revenue items. Capital items are long-term and non-recurring, and they affect the Balance Sheet. Revenue items are short-term and recurring, and they affect the Profit and Loss account. Capital expenditure includes purchase of land, buildings and machinery, installation and erection costs, and expenses that increase earning capacity, such as freight and carriage on a new machine. Revenue expenditure includes ordinary repairs, salaries, rent, depreciation and interest on loans. Deferred revenue expenditure is a heavy revenue spend whose benefit spreads over several years, such as heavy advertising. Capital receipts include share capital, debentures, loans and sale of fixed assets. Revenue receipts include sales and interest. For insurance claims, the nature of the claim follows the nature of the loss. A claim for a destroyed fixed asset is a capital receipt, and the claim is adjusted against the asset's book value, giving a profit or loss on the asset. A claim for destroyed stock, or for loss of profit under a consequential-loss policy, is a revenue receipt. Under the principle of indemnity, the insured cannot receive more than the actual loss. Other angles include capital profit versus revenue profit, the treatment of capital losses, and the Accounting Standard on property, plant and equipment, AS-10, and its Ind AS equivalent, Ind AS 16. A common trap is mixing up receipts with expenditures, so check first whether money came in or went out.

question: According to the Accounting Standard-1, which of the following are the fundamental accounting assumptions?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: AS-1, issued by the ICAI, deals with the disclosure of significant accounting policies. Paragraph 5 lists three fundamental accounting assumptions: Going Concern, Consistency and Accrual. If these are followed in financial statements, specific disclosure is not required. If any one is not followed, the fact must be disclosed. Going concern assumes the enterprise will continue in operation for the foreseeable future and will not be liquidated or curtailed materially. Consistency assumes accounting policies are applied the same way from period to period. Accrual means revenues and costs are recognised when earned or incurred, not when cash is received or paid, and are recorded in the periods to which they relate. AS-1 also says that prudence (conservatism), substance over form and materiality should govern the selection and application of accounting policies. Prudence is therefore a consideration, not a fundamental assumption. Money measurement and accounting period are accounting concepts or conventions in general theory, but AS-1 does not list them as fundamental assumptions. Elimination: options (b), (c) and (d) each include Conservatism, Money Measurement or Accounting Period, so they are wrong. Only (a) has all three correct.
explanations: Correct: Going Concern, Consistency and Accrual are the three fundamental accounting assumptions under AS-1.
Incorrect: Money Measurement and Conservatism are not listed as fundamental assumptions in AS-1. Prudence (conservatism) is a consideration for choosing policies.
Incorrect: Conservatism (prudence) is a consideration for selecting accounting policies, not a fundamental assumption. Accrual is missing from this option.
Incorrect: Accounting Period is not listed in AS-1 as a fundamental assumption. Consistency is missing from this option.
keyfact: AS-1 fundamental assumptions: Going Concern, Consistency, Accrual. Prudence, Substance over Form and Materiality are considerations, not assumptions.
option_notes: Going Concern, Consistency and Accrual are the three assumptions in para 5 of AS-1. Going concern presumes continued operation. Consistency means policies are applied uniformly across periods. Accrual means recognising items when earned or incurred, not when cash moves. If they are followed, no separate disclosure is needed. If not, the fact must be disclosed.

Money Measurement means only transactions that can be expressed in money are recorded. It is a basic accounting concept, not an AS-1 assumption. Conservatism or prudence means providing for all probable losses but not anticipating profits. AS-1 treats prudence as a consideration in selecting accounting policies, not as a fundamental assumption.

This option mixes two genuine assumptions, Going Concern and Consistency, with Conservatism. Conservatism or prudence is a guiding consideration in AS-1 along with substance over form and materiality. It requires caution under uncertainty, for example by valuing stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value. It is not a fundamental assumption.

Accounting Period, also called the periodicity concept, divides the enterprise's life into intervals, usually 12 months, for reporting. It is a standard accounting convention but not an AS-1 fundamental assumption. In India the financial year runs 1 April to 31 March. Going Concern and Accrual in this option are valid assumptions.
related: AS-1 is titled Disclosure of Accounting Policies and is issued by ICAI.
The three fundamental accounting assumptions are Going Concern, Consistency and Accrual.
The three considerations in selecting policies are Prudence, Substance over Form and Materiality.
AS-2 deals with Valuation of Inventories, valued at lower of cost and net realisable value.
AS-3 deals with Cash Flow Statements.
AS-10 deals with Property, Plant and Equipment, and AS-6 with Depreciation Accounting.
Section 133 of the Companies Act 2013 empowers the Central Government to notify accounting standards.
Ind AS are converged with IFRS and apply to specified classes of companies.
summary: The answer is (a): Going Concern, Consistency and Accrual. AS-1 (Disclosure of Accounting Policies) names exactly these three as the fundamental accounting assumptions. They are presumed to be followed unless a disclosure says otherwise.
topic_notes: AS-1 is Disclosure of Accounting Policies, issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), and became mandatory for periods beginning on or after 1 April 1993. It requires enterprises to disclose all significant accounting policies adopted in preparing and presenting financial statements. Fundamental accounting assumptions (para 5): Going Concern, Consistency and Accrual. Their acceptance is assumed. Disclosure is needed only if one is not followed. Considerations in selecting and applying policies (para 6): Prudence, Substance over Form and Materiality. Prudence means provision should be made for all known liabilities and losses even if the amount cannot be determined with certainty. Substance over form means transactions are accounted for by their economic reality, not their legal form. Materiality means financial statements should disclose all items material enough to affect evaluations or decisions. Other points: changes in accounting policy that have a material effect must be disclosed with the amount, to the extent ascertainable. If the amount is not ascertainable, this should be stated. Policies are disclosed in one place, usually as the first note to the accounts. Related concepts that UPSC may test: business entity, money measurement, dual aspect, cost concept, matching concept, realisation, accounting period, full disclosure, conservatism. The Companies Act 2013 requires financial statements to comply with accounting standards notified under Section 133. Ind AS, converged with IFRS, apply to specified companies. The Conceptual Framework under Ind AS names accrual basis and going concern as underlying assumptions.

question: Which of the following errors is not detected by Trial Balance?
options: A credit purchase of ¥ 1, 000 from Mr. Singh is credited wrongly to the account of Mr. Akash
A credit purchase of ¥ 20, 000 from Mr. Sandhu is recorded in the day book as ¥ 2, 000
Conversion of a temporary shed into a permanent building is recorded as repairs and maintenance expense
Error in posting from the book of subsidiary record to the ledger 17 BNYR-B-GNS/75A
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: A Trial Balance is a statement of all ledger debit and credit balances, prepared to check arithmetical accuracy under the double-entry system. It proves only that total debits equal total credits. Errors that do not affect the agreement are not revealed: errors of omission (a transaction entirely omitted), commission (a wrong account of the same type, e.g. Singh credited to Akash), principle (capital treated as revenue, e.g. a shed converted into a building booked as repairs), compensating errors, and original-entry errors (a wrong amount in the day book, posted equally on both sides). Errors that do affect it include one-sided posting, wrong totalling, wrong balancing, and a posting made on the wrong side. Strictly, options (a), (b) and (c) are all undetectable, so the question is flawed. UPSC's key picks (d), probably reading a posting error from a subsidiary book as a broad category that can include compensating errors or a posting made to the wrong account. For revision, remember the official key, but also remember the standard rule: errors of commission, principle, omission and original entry, and compensating errors, are not detected.
explanations: Wrong: Credit purchase from Singh credited to Akash is an error of commission. The credit total is unchanged, so the Trial Balance still agrees and does not detect it.
Wrong: Recording ¥20,000 as ¥2,000 in the day book is an error of original entry. Both the debit and credit sides carry the same wrong amount, so the Trial Balance agrees and does not detect it.
Wrong: Treating capital expenditure as revenue expenditure is an error of principle. Debits and credits remain equal, so the Trial Balance does not detect it.

Correct (official key): The UPSC key treats an error in posting from a subsidiary book to the ledger as the item not detected by the Trial Balance. Note that this is contestable, since a one-sided posting would normally show up as a disagreement.
keyfact: A Trial Balance proves only that debits equal credits, so errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry and compensating errors remain hidden; the official key here is (d).
option_notes: Error of commission: a transaction is recorded in the correct books and for the correct amount, but in the wrong account of the same class, such as a personal account. It does not affect the Trial Balance. It is corrected by a rectifying journal entry, with the wrong party debited or credited and the right party then adjusted.

Error of original entry: the wrong amount is entered in the journal or subsidiary book (here the purchase day book). The wrong figure is then posted to both sides of the ledger, so the Trial Balance agrees. It is found only by checking against source documents such as the invoice.

Error of principle: capital and revenue items are confused, for example capital expenditure booked as revenue expenditure. Here, converting a shed into a permanent building is capital expenditure but is booked as repairs. The double entry is complete, so the Trial Balance agrees, but profit is understated and assets are understated.

Posting error from a subsidiary book to the ledger: the amount is posted to the wrong account, the wrong side, or not at all. A one-sided error normally makes the Trial Balance disagree and is found through a suspense account. The official key marks this as the answer.
related: A Trial Balance checks only arithmetical accuracy, not the correctness of accounting.
The difference in a Trial Balance is temporarily put in a Suspense Account.
Errors of principle involve confusion between capital and revenue items.
Compensating errors offset one another, so the Trial Balance agrees.
A one-sided posting is disclosed by the Trial Balance.
Errors of omission and commission do not affect the Trial Balance.
summary: The official answer is (d). Per the UPSC key, the question treats an error in posting from a subsidiary book to the ledger as the one a Trial Balance does not detect. Note, though, that a one-sided posting error would normally disturb the Trial Balance, so this is a debatable item. Options (a), (b) and (c) are classic errors that a Trial Balance does not reveal.
topic_notes:
The Trial Balance is prepared at the end of an accounting period from ledger balances. Its objective is to check arithmetical accuracy, and it also helps in preparing final accounts. It rests on the double-entry principle that every debit has an equal credit. Agreement of the Trial Balance is not conclusive proof of accuracy.

Errors not disclosed by a Trial Balance:
1. Errors of omission: a transaction is completely omitted from the books.
2. Errors of commission: the entry goes to the wrong account of the same nature.
3. Errors of principle: capital and revenue are confused.
4. Compensating errors: errors on opposite sides cancel each other out.
5. Errors of original entry: the wrong amount appears in the subsidiary book.
6. Complete reversal of an entry: the debit and credit accounts are swapped.

Errors disclosed by a Trial Balance:
1. A one-sided posting.
2. Wrong totalling of ledger accounts or subsidiary books.
3. Wrong balancing of accounts.
4. Posting an amount to the wrong side.
5. Posting a different amount on each side.

If the Trial Balance does not tally, the difference is temporarily placed in a Suspense Account until the errors are found. Errors are rectified by journal entries. Related topics include the subsidiary books (cash book, purchases book, sales book, returns books), the ledger, the capital versus revenue distinction, and bank reconciliation.

question: Which one of the following statements is correct? Capital reserves are normally
options: created out of free or distributable profits. Dividend equalization reserve is an
example of general reserve. General reserve can be used only
for some specific purposes. Provision’ is a charge against
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The question tests the distinction between reserves and provisions in company accounts. A provision (AS 29 / Ind AS 37 concept; Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013) is created for a known liability or loss whose amount is uncertain, or for a decline in asset value (for example depreciation, provision for doubtful debts, provision for tax). It is a charge against profit: it is debited to the P&L Account as an expense, so it reduces the profit available for distribution and must be made whether or not the business earns a profit. A reserve is an appropriation of profit, creating no expense, and is made only if profits exist. Reserves are of two types. Revenue reserves (general reserve, dividend equalisation reserve) come from normal business profits and are distributable. Capital reserves come from capital profits (profit on sale of fixed assets, profit on revaluation, premium on forfeiture of shares, profit prior to incorporation) and are not normally distributable as dividend. Elimination: (a) is wrong because capital reserves arise from non-distributable capital profits. (b) is wrong because the dividend equalisation reserve is a specific reserve, not a general one. (c) is wrong because a general reserve is free and can be used for any purpose. This leaves (d).
explanations: Incorrect: capital reserves are created out of capital profits, which are not free or distributable as dividend. They can be used only for purposes such as writing off capital losses or issuing bonus shares.
Incorrect: dividend equalisation reserve is a specific reserve, created to maintain a stable dividend rate in lean years. It is not a type of general reserve, which has no specific purpose.
Incorrect: general reserve is a free reserve with no specific purpose, so it can be used for any purpose, such as dividends, expansion, or meeting contingencies.
Correct: a provision is charged to the P&L Account as an expense, which reduces profit. It is a charge against profit, whereas a reserve is an appropriation of profit.
keyfact: Provision = charge against profit (compulsory, before profit); Reserve = appropriation of profit (optional, after profit).
option_notes: Capital reserves arise from capital profits such as profit on sale of fixed assets, revaluation gains, profit on redemption of debentures, share premium and profit prior to incorporation. They are not available for dividend. Permitted uses include issuing fully paid bonus shares (the share premium account is also used for this), writing off preliminary expenses, and absorbing capital losses. They are shown under Reserves and Surplus on the balance sheet.

This is a revenue reserve created to maintain a stable dividend rate and to pay dividends in years of low profit. It is created out of divisible profits and is a specific reserve, in contrast to a general reserve. It is shown under Reserves and Surplus and is used for equalising dividends over time. It is not a provision and not a capital reserve.

A general reserve is a free revenue reserve, created by transferring part of profits to strengthen the financial position or to meet unforeseen needs. It has no specific purpose. Under the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules, transfer to reserves before declaring a dividend is no longer compulsory. It can be used for dividends, bonus shares, expansion, or contingencies.

A provision is an amount written off or retained to provide for depreciation, renewal or diminution in asset value, or for a known liability whose amount cannot be determined with substantial accuracy. Examples are provision for doubtful debts, provision for tax, and provision for depreciation. It is a charge against profit, debited to the P&L Account, and it is mandatory regardless of profit. AS 29 / Ind AS 37 govern it.
related: Provision is a charge against profit; reserve is an appropriation of profit.
Capital reserves are not available for distribution as dividend.
Securities premium is used for bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, and similar purposes under Section 52.
Capital Redemption Reserve is created on redemption of preference shares out of profits.
Dividend equalisation reserve is a specific revenue reserve.
AS 29 / Ind AS 37 deal with provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets.
Secret reserves are not disclosed on the balance sheet.
summary: The correct answer is (d): a provision is a charge against profit. It is an amount set aside out of profit to meet a known liability or diminution in asset value whose amount cannot be determined with substantial accuracy, and it is debited to the Profit & Loss Account before arriving at net profit.
topic_notes: Reserves versus provisions is a standard topic in company accounts. A reserve is an appropriation of profit, created after profit is ascertained. It strengthens the financial position and is optional (except statutory reserves). It can be used to pay dividends, subject to the type of reserve. A provision is a charge against profit, created before profit is ascertained. It is compulsory and cannot be used to pay dividends. Classification of reserves: (1) Revenue reserves come from operating profits; they include general reserve, dividend equalisation reserve, investment fluctuation reserve and workmen's compensation fund (when it is a reserve). (2) Capital reserves come from capital profits; they include profit on sale of fixed assets, revaluation reserve, share premium (technically a securities premium reserve with restricted uses under Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013) and capital redemption reserve (CRR). (3) Specific reserves are meant for a particular purpose, such as the debenture redemption reserve, sinking fund, and dividend equalisation reserve. (4) Secret reserves are not disclosed on the balance sheet, through undervaluing assets or overvaluing liabilities. (5) Free reserves are those available for distribution as dividend. Provisions include provision for depreciation, bad and doubtful debts, taxation, and discount on debtors. Contingent liabilities are not provided for but disclosed in notes. Provisions for known liabilities are recognised when there is a present obligation, a probable outflow, and a reliable estimate (Ind AS 37). Also remember that a Reserve Fund is represented by earmarked investments while a Reserve is not necessarily so. Schedule III Division I covers the format of a company's balance sheet, with Reserves and Surplus under Shareholders' Funds.

question: Which one of the following is not an error of commission? Overcasting of sales book
options: credited to his account Wrong balancing of machinery
account Cash sales not recorded in cash
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Accounting errors are classified as errors of omission (complete or partial), commission, principle, and compensating errors. An error of omission occurs when a transaction is not recorded at all in the books (complete omission) or recorded only on one side (partial omission). An error of commission occurs when a transaction is recorded but wrongly: wrong posting to the wrong account, wrong amount, wrong totalling (overcasting or undercasting), wrong balancing, or wrong carrying forward. Here, overcasting of the sales book is a totalling mistake, so it is commission. Credit sales to Ramesh credited to his account is a posting on the wrong side of the correct account, so it is commission (it is not a principle error because the nature of the account is correctly identified). Wrong balancing of the machinery account is a balancing mistake, so it is commission. Cash sales not recorded in the cash book is a transaction never entered, so it is omission. Elimination: check whether the transaction was recorded; if yes with a mistake, it is commission. Errors of commission may affect the trial balance, whereas a complete omission does not.
explanations: Wrong: crediting Ramesh's account for a credit sale instead of debiting it is a wrong-side posting, a classic error of commission.
Wrong: wrong balancing of the machinery account is an error of commission, since the transaction was recorded but the balance was computed incorrectly.
Wrong as a choice: overcasting of the sales book is a totalling error, which is an error of commission (this option's content corresponds to the question's stem item).
Correct: cash sales not recorded at all in the cash book is an error of complete omission, so it is not an error of commission.
keyfact: Recorded wrongly = commission; not recorded at all = omission.
option_notes: Credit sales to Ramesh credited to his account: the personal account should have been debited as he is a debtor. Posting to the wrong side is a commission error. It causes the trial balance to disagree by twice the amount, and is rectified through a suspense account or a direct rectifying entry.

Wrong balancing of machinery account: balancing means finding the difference of the two sides and carrying it forward. A mistake here is an error of commission. It affects the trial balance and the final accounts, and is corrected through a rectifying entry or suspense account.

Overcasting of the sales book: overcasting means the total is added up more than it should be, and undercasting means less. Both are errors of commission, and they affect the sales account and the trial balance. Rectification is by a journal entry to reduce or increase sales with the corresponding account.

Cash sales not recorded in the cash book: this is a complete omission, because neither the debit nor the credit was entered. It does not affect the trial balance agreement, so it is not revealed by the trial balance. It is only corrected once discovered, by passing the omitted entry.
related: Complete omission does not affect the trial balance agreement.
Wrong posting to the wrong account is an error of commission.
Treating capital expenditure as revenue expenditure is an error of principle.
Compensating errors cancel each other out and the trial balance still agrees.
One-sided errors are rectified through a suspense account.
Overcasting means total more than actual; undercasting means total less than actual.
summary: The answer is (d): non-recording of cash sales in the cash book is an error of omission, not commission. Errors of commission arise from wrong posting, wrong totalling, wrong balancing or wrong carrying forward of transactions that were actually recorded.
topic_notes: Errors in accounting are classified into four groups. (1) Errors of omission: complete omission means the transaction is totally missed, so the trial balance still agrees; partial omission means only one aspect is recorded, so the trial balance will not agree. (2) Errors of commission: wrong posting, wrong totalling (overcasting or undercasting), wrong balancing, wrong carrying forward, wrong amount recorded, or posting to the wrong subsidiary book. These may or may not affect the trial balance. (3) Errors of principle: violating accounting principles, for example treating capital expenditure as revenue expenditure (such as repairs of a new machine charged to the profit and loss account), or revenue receipts as capital receipts. The trial balance agrees. (4) Compensating errors: errors that cancel each other, such as an overcast of 1,000 in one account and an undercast of 1,000 in another. The trial balance agrees. One-sided errors are generally disclosed by the trial balance and are rectified through a suspense account, which is closed once the errors are found. Two-sided errors do not affect the trial balance. Rectification can occur before or after closing the books. If it happens in the same year, the rectification is direct; if in the next year, adjustments through the profit and loss adjustment account are needed for items affecting profit. Other angles asked in exams: the effect of errors on profit, which errors are revealed by the trial balance, and which errors need the suspense account.

question: Which of the following operators connects a structure variable and its element?
subject: General Science
detail: In C, a structure is a user-defined data type that groups variables of different types under one name. Each variable inside it is called a member (element). To reach a member through a structure variable, C uses the member selection operator, also called the dot operator, written as structvar.member. If you hold a pointer to a structure, you use the arrow operator (->) instead, so ptr->member is the same as (*ptr).member. The dot operator has the highest precedence level in C, along with (), [] and ->, and it associates left to right. Example: struct student { int roll; float marks; }; struct student s1; s1.roll = 10; Here s1 is the structure variable and roll is its element. Elimination: plus (+), minus (-) and multiply (*) are arithmetic operators used for addition, subtraction and multiplication (or pointer dereference for unary *). None of them selects a member. The option '[' (square bracket) is the subscript operator used for arrays, not for structures. Hence only the dot operator fits.
explanations: Correct. The dot (member access) operator joins a structure variable to its member, e.g. s1.roll.
Wrong. The minus operator performs subtraction (or unary negation) and has no role in accessing structure members.
Wrong. The multiply operator performs multiplication; unary * dereferences a pointer. It does not select a structure element directly.
Wrong. The '[' (subscript) operator indexes array elements, not structure members. Note the plus operator in the OCR'd text is also an arithmetic operator and likewise incorrect.
keyfact: Structure variable to member: dot operator (s.member); pointer to structure: arrow operator (p->member).
option_notes: The dot operator (.) is the direct member selection operator in C and C++. It accesses a member of a structure or union through the variable name, as in emp.salary. It has top precedence (level 1) with (), [] and ->, and associates left to right. For pointers to structures, the arrow operator -> is used instead.

The minus operator (-) is an arithmetic operator. In binary form it subtracts one operand from another, and in unary form it negates a value. It also appears in pointer arithmetic and in the decrement operator --. It has no role in structure member access.

The multiply operator (*) is a binary arithmetic operator for multiplication. As a unary operator it is the indirection (dereference) operator, giving the value at a pointer's address. It also appears in pointer declarations. It does not connect a structure variable to its member directly, although (*p).member uses it with the dot.

The '[' symbol is the start of the array subscript operator [ ]. It is used to access array elements by index, as in a[3], and is equivalent to *(a+3). It has the same precedence level as the dot operator but is meant for arrays, not structure members.
related: Dot (.) operator accesses a structure member via a variable; arrow (->) via a pointer.
The dot operator has the highest precedence in C, along with (), [] and ->.
A union shares one memory location among all its members.
The keyword struct is used to define a structure in C.
sizeof returns the memory size of a structure, including padding.
Self-referential structures are the basis of linked lists and trees.
Scope resolution operator (::) is used in C++ to access class members and global names.
summary: The answer is (a) the dot operator. In C/C++, the dot (member selection) operator '.' links a structure variable to its member, as in student.roll. The other operators listed are arithmetic operators and cannot access structure members.
topic_notes: Structures in C are user-defined derived data types declared with the keyword struct. They let you bundle related data of different types, such as int, float and char arrays, into one unit. Members are accessed by the dot operator on a structure variable, or by the arrow operator -> on a pointer to a structure. Memory for a structure is allocated for all members separately, in declaration order, with possible padding for alignment, and sizeof gives the total size. Contrast this with a union, declared with the keyword union, where all members share the same memory location and the size equals that of the largest member. Structures can be nested, so you chain the dot operator, as in a.b.c. They can contain arrays, be passed to functions by value or by pointer, and can be returned from functions. Arrays of structures are also allowed. Structure members cannot be initialised inside the declaration in C, but can be initialised at the time of variable definition using braces. Self-referential structures hold a pointer to the same structure type and form the basis of linked lists and trees. Typedef is often used to simplify the structure name. Operator precedence: (), [], ., -> have the highest priority, followed by unary operators, then arithmetic, relational, logical and assignment operators. Other operators UPSC may ask about include sizeof, the comma operator, the conditional (ternary) operator ?:, the address-of operator & and the indirection operator *. Bit fields allow members to occupy a specified number of bits within a structure.

question: Which of the following is not a top-down language?
subject: Computers
detail: Programming design approaches are classified as top-down or bottom-up. In the top-down approach, the main problem is broken into smaller sub-problems or functions, which are refined step by step. The main() function (or main program) controls calls to subroutines. This is typical of procedural or structured languages such as FORTRAN (1957, John Backus, IBM), C (1972, Dennis Ritchie, Bell Labs) and Pascal (1970, Niklaus Wirth). Emphasis is on procedures and the sequence of actions, and data is often global and shared. In the bottom-up approach, small reusable components (classes and objects) are designed first and then combined into larger systems. Object-oriented languages like Java (James Gosling, Sun Microsystems, 1995), C++, Smalltalk and Python (in OOP style) follow it. Core OOP features are encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction. Elimination logic: identify the three classical procedural languages (C, FORTRAN, Pascal), and the remaining one, Java, is the OOP language, so it is the one that is not top-down. Note that C++ is a hybrid, but Java is almost purely object-oriented, since all code lives inside classes, though it has primitive types.
explanations: Wrong: C is a procedural, structured language that uses top-down decomposition into functions, so it is a top-down language and cannot be the answer.
Wrong: FORTRAN is one of the earliest procedural languages and uses top-down design with subroutines and functions, so it is top-down.
Correct: JAVA is object-oriented and follows the bottom-up approach, building from classes and objects, so it is not a top-down language.
Wrong: Pascal was designed by Niklaus Wirth to teach structured, top-down programming, so it is a top-down language.
keyfact: Java is object-oriented (bottom-up); C, FORTRAN and Pascal are procedural (top-down).
option_notes: C is a general-purpose procedural language developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs around 1972, used to rewrite UNIX. It is a middle-level language, with pointers, structured control flow, functions and efficient low-level access. It is the ancestor of C++, Java and C#. Programs are built from functions called from main(), which is the top-down style.

FORTRAN (FORmula TRANslation) was developed by John Backus's team at IBM, released in 1957. It is the first widely used high-level language, designed for scientific and numerical computing. It is procedural, with subroutines and functions, and is still used in supercomputing and weather modelling. Its program structure is top-down.

JAVA was created by James Gosling and colleagues at Sun Microsystems (initially called Oak), released in 1995 and now owned by Oracle. It is a class-based, object-oriented language with the slogan 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' via the Java Virtual Machine and bytecode. It has automatic garbage collection and no explicit pointers. It follows the bottom-up approach.

Pascal was designed by Swiss computer scientist Niklaus Wirth in 1970 and named after Blaise Pascal. It was built to encourage structured programming and good teaching practice. It is a procedural language with strong typing, and its descendants include Object Pascal and Delphi. It follows top-down design with procedures and functions.
related: Top-down approach is used in procedural or structured programming; bottom-up approach in object-oriented programming.
Java was developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems in 1995.
C was developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in 1972.
Pascal was designed by Niklaus Wirth in 1970.
FORTRAN (1957) was the first widely used high-level language.
The four pillars of OOP are abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
Java source code is compiled into bytecode that runs on the JVM.
C++ is a hybrid language supporting both procedural and object-oriented styles.
summary: The answer is (c) JAVA. C, FORTRAN and Pascal are procedural languages that follow the top-down (structured, procedural decomposition) approach, while Java is an object-oriented language that follows the bottom-up approach, building programs from classes and objects.
topic_notes: Program design approaches: Top-down design starts with the overall problem and decomposes it into modules or functions (stepwise refinement). It is used in procedural or structured programming. Its advantages are clear control flow, easier planning and easier debugging, while its weakness is limited code reuse and global data being exposed. Bottom-up design starts with basic reusable components, which are integrated into a larger system. It is used in object-oriented programming. Its advantages are reusability, data hiding, modularity and easy maintenance. Language classification: Procedural languages include C, FORTRAN, Pascal, COBOL and BASIC. Object-oriented languages include Java, C++, C#, Smalltalk, Eiffel and Python. Scripting languages include JavaScript, PHP and Perl. Functional languages include Haskell and Lisp. Pure OOP languages are Smalltalk and Eiffel. C++ is a hybrid, and Java is nearly pure OOP. Four pillars of OOP: abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. Other points: low-level languages (machine language, assembly) versus high-level languages; translators are compilers (whole program), interpreters (line by line) and assemblers (assembly to machine code). Java compiles to bytecode, which runs on the JVM. Generations: 1GL is machine language, 2GL is assembly, 3GL is high-level (C, Java), 4GL is SQL and report generators, and 5GL is AI and logic languages (Prolog). Typical future questions ask which language is object-oriented, who developed which language, or which is a compiled versus interpreted language.

question: Which one of the following attributes is required for internal linking in HTML?
subject: Computers
detail:
Internal linking (also called bookmark or fragment linking) lets a user jump to a specific location within the same web page, or to a particular section of another page. It is done in two steps. First, create the target (bookmark/anchor) using the anchor tag with the name attribute: Top. Second, create the link to it with the href attribute starting with a hash (#): Go to top. For a section on another page the syntax is . In HTML5 the name attribute on is deprecated and the id attribute on any element is preferred (

), but the href="#id" mechanism stays the same. The exam follows the classical textbook approach, so Name is the required attribute. Elimination: Align is a presentation attribute for alignment (deprecated in HTML5, replaced by CSS). Body is a tag, not an attribute, defining the visible page content. Link is an attribute of the tag in old HTML (sets unvisited link colour) and the element joins external resources such as CSS; neither creates internal links.
explanations: Correct: the name attribute of the anchor tag defines the bookmark target, which href="#name" then links to within the page.
Wrong: align only sets alignment of elements such as text, images or tables; it has nothing to do with linking, and it is deprecated in HTML5.
Wrong: body is an HTML tag that holds the page's visible content, not an attribute used for linking.
Wrong: link is an old attribute of <body> that sets the colour of unvisited links (and <link> is a separate tag for external resources such as stylesheets); it does not create internal links.
keyfact: Internal (bookmark) linking in HTML: define the target with <a name="x"> (or id) and link to it with <a href="#x">.
option_notes: Name: an attribute of the <a> (anchor) tag that gives a name to a location in a document so it can be a link target, e.g. <a name="sec1">. It is deprecated in HTML5, where id is used instead. It is also used as an attribute in form elements (input, select) to identify fields in submitted data, and in <meta> tags.

Align: a legacy attribute that specified horizontal alignment (left, right, center, justify) of elements like

,

Body: the <body> tag, which encloses all visible content of an HTML document (text, images, links, tables) and comes after <head> inside <html>. It is a tag/element, not an attribute. Its old attributes included bgcolor, text, link, alink and vlink, now replaced by CSS.

Link: in older HTML, an attribute of <body> (link="blue") that set the colour of unvisited hyperlinks; companions are vlink (visited) and alink (active). Separately, the <link> element in <head> connects external resources such as CSS files (rel="stylesheet"). It does not create bookmarks.
related: Anchor tag <a> with href attribute creates hyperlinks.
Bookmark link syntax: <a href="#section1"> pointing to <a name="section1"> or id="section1".
HTML5 prefers the id attribute over name for anchor targets.
target="_blank" opens a link in a new tab or window.
<link> element in <head> attaches external CSS files.
HTML was created by Tim Berners-Lee.

summary: The answer is (a) Name. Internal linking in HTML (jumping to a specific spot within the same page) uses a named anchor, created with <a name="section1"> (or, in modern HTML5, id), and referenced via <a href="#section1">.
topic_notes:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard markup language for web pages, created by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN around 1989-91; it is maintained today by WHATWG, with W3C earlier issuing versions (HTML 4.01 in 1999, HTML5 recommended in 2014). Hyperlinks are created with the anchor tag , whose href attribute holds the destination URL. Types of links: external links (absolute URL to another site), internal links to other pages of the same site (relative URL), and bookmark/fragment links within a page (#id). To make an internal bookmark, define the target with name or id and refer to it with href="#target". The target attribute controls where the link opens (_blank new tab, _self same window, _parent, _top). The title attribute shows tooltip text, and mailto: in href opens an email client. question: Which one of the following types of operating systems is designed to respond to an event within a predetermined time?
subject: Computers
detail: An RTOS is built around deterministic scheduling: the time between an event (interrupt or input) and the system's response is bounded and predictable. Correctness depends on both the result and the time at which it is produced. There are two types. Hard real-time systems treat a missed deadline as a total failure (airbag controllers, pacemakers, flight control, industrial robots, missile guidance). Soft real-time systems tolerate occasional missed deadlines with only degraded quality (video streaming, online gaming, multimedia playback). Key features include priority-based pre-emptive scheduling, minimal interrupt latency, fast context switching, small kernel size and predictable memory management. Examples are VxWorks, QNX, FreeRTOS, RTLinux and µC/OS. Elimination logic: Embedded describes where the OS runs (inside a dedicated device), not a timing guarantee. Multiuser describes allowing several users to access the system concurrently (Unix, Linux, Windows Server). Synchronized is not a standard OS category; synchronization is a process-coordination concept (semaphores, mutexes). Only 'Real time' directly means a response within a fixed time.
explanations: (a) Wrong: an embedded OS runs inside a dedicated device with limited resources; it may or may not be real-time, and the term does not itself imply a guaranteed response time.
(b) Correct: a real-time OS guarantees a response to an event within a predetermined deadline, which is exactly what the question describes.
(c) Wrong: a multiuser OS lets multiple users use the system simultaneously via time-sharing; it has no guaranteed deadlines.
(d) Wrong: 'Synchronized' is not a recognised OS type; synchronization refers to coordinating processes or threads to avoid race conditions.
keyfact: Real-Time OS = guaranteed response to an event within a predetermined deadline (hard or soft); e.g., VxWorks, QNX, FreeRTOS.
option_notes: Embedded OS: a specialised OS built into devices such as washing machines, ATMs, routers, smart TVs, cars and medical devices. It is compact, resource-efficient and dedicated to specific tasks. Examples include Embedded Linux, Windows IoT, and Android Things.
