Dairying is largely unorganised, and only about 30-35% of milk is handled by the organised sector. India is a major producer but a small exporter of dairy products, partly because of domestic demand. Buffalo milk contributes a large share, about 30% or more, and cow milk is a majority share. The Livestock Census is conducted every five years, and the 20th Census (2019) counted about 535 million livestock. Other angles UPSC may ask: FAO headquarters in Rome, FAOSTAT as the FAO statistical database, the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying under the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying, and the ranking of India in other products such as pulses and jute.

question: Which one of the following statements about the Group of Twenty (G20) is not correct?
options: The G20 summit is held annually under the leadership of a rotating Presidency
The G20 members represent around 85% of the global GDP
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The G20 is the premier forum for international economic cooperation. It was founded in 1999 after the Asian financial crisis of 1997-98, initially as a meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors. It was upgraded to the level of Heads of State/Government in 2008 during the global financial crisis (first leaders' summit in Washington DC, November 2008). Its membership is 19 sovereign countries plus the European Union, so the name 'twenty' is misleading: 'twenty' counts 19 countries and the EU. The African Union was admitted as a permanent member at the New Delhi Summit (9-10 September 2023), taking the group to 21 members. The G20 has no permanent secretariat; the Presidency rotates annually and is supported by the previous, current and next presidencies, called the Troika. Members account for roughly 85% of global GDP, over 75% of global trade and about two-thirds of the world population. India held the Presidency from 1 December 2022 to 30 November 2023 (theme: 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam - One Earth, One Family, One Future'). Elimination: (a), (b) and (c) match standard facts, so only (d) is inaccurate.
explanations: Correct statement, so not the answer: the G20 was established in 1999 after the Asian financial crisis, initially at finance minister and central bank governor level.
Correct statement, so not the answer: the Presidency rotates annually among members (grouped regionally), and the host country sets the agenda and hosts the leaders' summit.
Correct statement, so not the answer: G20 members account for about 85% of world GDP, over 75% of trade and about two-thirds of world population.
Incorrect statement, hence the answer: the G20 has 19 countries plus the European Union (20 members originally) and now also the African Union, so it is not 'twenty countries'.
keyfact: G20 = 19 countries + European Union (plus African Union since 2023), founded 1999, no permanent secretariat; so 'twenty countries' is the incorrect statement.
option_notes: Founded 1999 in the wake of the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis, at the initiative of the G7 finance ministers. It began as a forum for finance ministers and central bank governors to discuss global economic and financial stability. It was elevated to leaders' summits in 2008 after the global financial crisis. The first finance ministers' meeting was held in Berlin in December 1999.

The G20 has no permanent secretariat or charter. A Presidency rotates every year, and members are divided into five groups for rotation. The Presidency is supported by the Troika (previous, current and next hosts). Recent presidencies: Indonesia 2022, India 2023, Brazil 2024, South Africa 2025. The Presidency runs two tracks: the Finance Track and the Sherpa Track.

G20 members represent about 85% of global GDP, over 75% of global trade and roughly two-thirds of the world's population. The group includes the world's major advanced and emerging economies. It is a forum for coordination on macroeconomic policy, trade, climate finance, development, health and digital economy issues, and its decisions are not legally binding.

The G20 consists of 19 countries (Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, South Korea, Turkey, UK, USA) plus the European Union. The African Union became a permanent member in September 2023. Spain is a permanent guest invitee. So 'twenty countries' is incorrect.
related: The G20 was founded in 1999 and upgraded to leaders' level in 2008.
The African Union became a permanent G20 member at the 2023 New Delhi Summit.
India's G20 Presidency theme: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam - One Earth, One Family, One Future.
The G20 has no permanent secretariat; the Troika supports the Presidency.
The first G20 leaders' summit was held in Washington DC in November 2008.
The Financial Stability Board was established by the G20 in 2009.
The G20 members account for about 85% of world GDP and 75% of trade.
Brazil held the G20 Presidency in 2024 and South Africa in 2025.
summary: The answer is (d). The G20 does not comprise twenty countries: it has 19 countries plus the European Union (and, since the September 2023 New Delhi Summit, the African Union as a permanent member). Statements (a), (b) and (c) are correct.
topic_notes: The G20 emerged from the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis and was formalised in 1999 as a forum of finance ministers and central bank governors. After the 2008 global financial crisis, it became the main forum for leaders, with the first summit in Washington DC in November 2008, followed by London and Pittsburgh in 2009. In 2009 the Pittsburgh summit designated it the 'premier forum for international economic cooperation'. Membership: 19 countries, the EU, and from 2023 the African Union. It has no permanent secretariat; the rotating Presidency, supported by the Troika, sets the agenda. Work is organised in the Finance Track (finance ministers and central bank governors) and the Sherpa Track (leaders' personal representatives), plus working groups, engagement groups (B20, C20, L20, T20, Y20, W20, S20, U20, Think20 etc.) and ministerial meetings. Share of world: around 85% of GDP, 75%+ of trade and two-thirds of population. India's Presidency ran from December 2022 to November 2023, with the summit at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, on 9-10 September 2023. Its outcomes included the New Delhi Leaders' Declaration, consensus on the AU's admission, the Global Biofuel Alliance, and the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) announcement. Indonesia hosted in 2022 (Bali), Brazil holds the 2024 Presidency (Rio de Janeiro) and South Africa in 2025. Other related groupings that UPSC may ask about: G7, BRICS (expanded 2024), G77, OECD, IMF, World Bank and the Financial Stability Board, which was created by the G20 in 2009.

question: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the year 2022 was awarded for
subject: General Science
detail: The 2022 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was announced on 5 October 2022. It was shared by Carolyn Bertozzi (Stanford, USA), Morten Meldal (University of Copenhagen, Denmark) and K. Barry Sharpless (Scripps Research, USA). Sharpless coined the concept of click chemistry around 2001, meaning fast, high-yield, modular reactions that join molecular building blocks. Meldal and Sharpless independently discovered the copper(I)-catalysed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC). Bertozzi took the idea into living cells with bioorthogonal reactions, which proceed inside living organisms without disturbing native biochemistry. She used strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition, which needs no toxic copper. Sharpless became only the fifth person to win two Nobel Prizes, having won the Chemistry prize in 2001 for chiral catalysed oxidation reactions. Elimination: CRISPR/Cas9 won in 2020 (Chemistry), lithium-ion batteries in 2019 (Chemistry), and palaeogenomics won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (Svante Pääbo). Students often confuse the Medicine and Chemistry prizes of the same year, and Pääbo's win in 2022 is the likely trap behind option (d).
explanations: Incorrect: CRISPR/Cas9 genetic scissors earned the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna, not the 2022 prize.
Correct: The 2022 Chemistry prize was awarded to Bertozzi, Meldal and Sharpless for click chemistry and bioorthogonal chemistry.
Incorrect: Lithium-ion batteries won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for John Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino.
Incorrect: Palaeogenomics (the genomes of extinct hominins and human evolution) won Svante Pääbo the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, not Chemistry.
keyfact: 2022 Chemistry Nobel: Bertozzi, Meldal and Sharpless for click and bioorthogonal chemistry (Sharpless's second Nobel).
option_notes: CRISPR/Cas9 is a genome-editing tool adapted from a bacterial immune defence system. Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna published the key work in 2012 and shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. It was the first Chemistry Nobel won by two women alone. Cas9 is an enzyme guided by RNA to cut DNA at a specific site. Uses include gene therapy and crop editing. In 2023 the UK and US approved Casgevy for sickle cell disease.

Click chemistry means fast, selective, high-yield reactions that join molecules reliably, a concept proposed by K. Barry Sharpless. The key reaction is copper-catalysed azide-alkyne cycloaddition, found independently by Morten Meldal and Sharpless. Bioorthogonal chemistry, developed by Carolyn Bertozzi, runs reactions in living systems without disrupting them. Applications include drug development, mapping of cells and targeted cancer pharmaceuticals. This was the 2022 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable batteries in which lithium ions move between the anode and the cathode. John B. Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing them. Whittingham built the first working lithium battery in the 1970s, Goodenough doubled its potential with a cobalt-oxide cathode in 1980, and Yoshino produced the first commercially viable version in 1985. They power phones, laptops and electric vehicles.

Palaeogenomics is the study of genomes recovered from ancient or extinct organisms. Svante Pääbo of the Max Planck Institute sequenced the Neanderthal genome and discovered the Denisovans in 2010. He won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning the genomes of extinct hominins and human evolution. His work showed gene flow from Neanderthals to modern humans, with implications for immune responses.
related: 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics: Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger for experiments on quantum entanglement.
2022 Nobel Prize in Medicine: Svante Pääbo for palaeogenomics and human evolution.
2022 Nobel Prize in Literature: Annie Ernaux of France.
K. Barry Sharpless is a two-time Chemistry laureate (2001 and 2022).
2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry: quantum dots (Bawendi, Brus, Ekimov).
2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry: CRISPR/Cas9 (Charpentier and Doudna).
2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry: lithium-ion batteries (Goodenough, Whittingham, Yoshino).
The Chemistry prize is awarded by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
summary: The answer is (b). The 2022 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Carolyn R. Bertozzi, Morten Meldal and K. Barry Sharpless for the development of click chemistry and bioorthogonal chemistry. The other options are Nobel-winning topics from other years.
topic_notes: The Nobel Prizes were established by the will of Alfred Nobel (died 1896) and first awarded in 1901. The Chemistry prize is awarded by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Stockholm. The prizes are announced in October and presented on 10 December, the anniversary of Nobel's death. The 2022 Chemistry laureates were Carolyn Bertozzi, Morten Meldal and K. Barry Sharpless. Sharpless is one of only five people to win two Nobel Prizes (the others being Marie Curie, Linus Pauling, John Bardeen and Frederick Sanger). Sanger also won two Chemistry prizes. Click chemistry is used to build molecules quickly from modular units, and its signature reaction is copper-catalysed azide-alkyne cycloaddition. Bertozzi's bioorthogonal reactions let researchers label biomolecules such as glycans in living cells, with uses in tracking and targeted cancer therapies. Recent Chemistry laureates are useful to remember: 2023 went to Moungi Bawendi, Louis Brus and Alexei Ekimov for quantum dots; 2021 to Benjamin List and David MacMillan for asymmetric organocatalysis; 2020 to Charpentier and Doudna for CRISPR; 2019 to Goodenough, Whittingham and Yoshino for lithium-ion batteries; 2018 to Frances Arnold, George Smith and Gregory Winter for directed evolution. The 2024 prize went to David Baker, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein design and protein structure prediction. Other 2022 Nobel prizes include Physics (Alain Aspect, John Clauser, Anton Zeilinger for quantum entanglement), Medicine (Svante Pääbo), Literature (Annie Ernaux) and Peace (Ales Bialiatski, Memorial and the Center for Civil Liberties).

question:
Which of the following statements about a ‘unicorn’ is/are correct?
1. In the venture capital industry, the term ‘unicorn’ refers to any startup that reaches the valuation of $10 billion.
2. Only a privately held startup can be a unicorn. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The term 'unicorn' was coined in 2013 by venture capitalist Aileen Lee, founder of Cowboy Ventures, to describe startups that reached a valuation of $1 billion. The comparison to the mythical creature reflected how rare such companies were. Two conditions define a unicorn: (i) a valuation of at least US$1 billion, and (ii) the company must be privately held, meaning it is not listed on a stock exchange, and it must be a startup, usually venture-backed. Statement 1 is wrong because it raises the threshold to $10 billion. A company valued at $10 billion or more is called a 'decacorn', and one valued at $100 billion or more is called a 'hectocorn'. Statement 2 is right because a unicorn is by definition private. After an IPO, direct listing, or acquisition, the company is no longer counted as a unicorn, although it may be called a 'former unicorn'. Elimination logic: once you know the $1 billion threshold, statement 1 is out, which removes (a) and (c). Statement 2 is a standard part of the definition, which removes (d). That leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: it accepts statement 1, but the unicorn threshold is $1 billion. The $10 billion level is a decacorn.
Correct: only statement 2 is right. A unicorn must be a privately held startup valued at $1 billion or more, and the $10 billion figure in statement 1 is wrong.
Wrong: it accepts statement 1, which wrongly sets the threshold at $10 billion. Statement 2 is correct.
Wrong: it rejects statement 2, but being privately held is a defining feature of a unicorn.
keyfact: Unicorn = privately held startup valued at $1 billion or more; $10 billion is a decacorn; a unicorn stops being one after listing.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only, would hold only if the unicorn threshold were $10 billion. That threshold actually defines a decacorn. The unicorn threshold is $1 billion, set by Aileen Lee in 2013. Statement 1 therefore fails on the valuation figure. Many students confuse the two levels, so remember: unicorn is $1 billion, decacorn is $10 billion, hectocorn is $100 billion.

Option (b), statement 2 only, is the correct answer. It reflects the definition of a unicorn as a privately held startup valued at $1 billion or more. Once the company lists on a stock exchange through an IPO, or is acquired, it is no longer counted as a unicorn. Statement 1 is excluded because it states the wrong valuation.

Option (c), both 1 and 2, is wrong because statement 1 gives an incorrect valuation. A unicorn is valued at $1 billion, not $10 billion. Statement 2 is correct, but both statements would need to be correct for this option to hold. The $10 billion term is decacorn.

Option (d), neither, is wrong because statement 2 is correct. The private status of a unicorn is a standard part of its definition in venture capital. Only statement 1 is incorrect, since its valuation is ten times too high. A company that goes public is called a former unicorn or a listed company.
related: Unicorn: a private startup valued at $1 billion or more; the term was coined by Aileen Lee in 2013.
Decacorn: valued at $10 billion or more. Hectocorn: valued at $100 billion or more.
InMobi is generally cited as India's first unicorn (2011).
Startup India was launched on 16 January 2016; National Startup Day is 16 January.
DPIIT, under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, is the nodal agency for startup recognition.
Fund of Funds for Startups is managed by SIDBI.
India is the third largest startup ecosystem and unicorn hub after the USA and China.
Soonicorn: a startup expected to become a unicorn soon.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the unicorn threshold is $1 billion, not $10 billion. The $10 billion category is a decacorn. Aileen Lee of Cowboy Ventures coined 'unicorn' in a 2013 TechCrunch article. She studied US software startups founded in the 2000s that reached $1 billion in value. Her study found only about 0.07% of venture-backed startups reached this level, which is why she chose the mythical animal. The valuation is usually set by the latest funding round, so it is a paper valuation and not a market price. Later terms include 'decacorn' ($10 billion) and 'hectocorn' ($100 billion). India had over 100 unicorns by 2022 and was the third largest unicorn hub after the USA and China. Examples include Flipkart, Paytm, Byju's, Ola, Zerodha and Swiggy.

2 — Correct: a unicorn must be a privately held startup, not listed on a stock exchange. When it goes public through an IPO, or is acquired, it ceases to be a unicorn. Examples of Indian unicorns that listed publicly and so exited the unicorn list include Zomato (2021), Nykaa (2021), Paytm (2021) and PolicyBazaar (2021). Valuation is typically assessed in funding rounds led by venture capital or private equity investors. The government's Startup India initiative, launched on 16 January 2016, supports startups, and DPIIT recognition is given to eligible entities. DPIIT, under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, is the nodal body for startup recognition. Unicorns are tracked by sources such as CB Insights, Hurun and Tracxn, whose lists may differ in method.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. A unicorn is a privately held startup valued at $1 billion or more, not $10 billion, and once it lists publicly or is acquired it stops being called a unicorn.
topic_notes: A unicorn is a privately held startup valued at $1 billion or more. Aileen Lee of Cowboy Ventures coined the term in 2013. Related categories: decacorn ($10 billion or more), hectocorn ($100 billion or more), and soonicorn (a startup expected to become a unicorn soon). A unicorn exits the category when it goes public (IPO or direct listing), is acquired, or merges. Valuation usually comes from the post-money valuation of the latest funding round, which makes it a paper valuation. India's unicorn count crossed 100 in 2022, making it the third largest ecosystem after the USA and China. Many Indian unicorns are in fintech, e-commerce, SaaS and edtech. Examples: Flipkart, Ola, Byju's, Zerodha, Swiggy, PhonePe, Razorpay, Dream11, CRED. Companies that listed and left the unicorn list include Zomato, Nykaa, Paytm and PolicyBazaar. The Startup India initiative was launched on 16 January 2016, and DPIIT under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry recognises startups. Related schemes include the Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS, managed by SIDBI), the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme, and the Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups. Under the DPIIT definition, an entity is a startup for up to 10 years from incorporation, with turnover not exceeding Rs 100 crore in any financial year. National Startup Day is celebrated on 16 January. Possible future questions: the origin of the term, the thresholds for decacorn and hectocorn, the largest unicorn-producing states in India (Karnataka, Maharashtra and Delhi NCR), the first Indian unicorn (InMobi, 2011), and the difference between venture capital and private equity.

question:
Which of the following statements about Santosh Trophy Tournament, 2023 is/are correct?
1. The final match was played in Riyadh.
2. The final match was played between Karnataka and Meghalaya. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Santosh Trophy is India's premier inter-state/inter-unit national football championship for men, organised by the All India Football Federation (AIFF) and named after Maharaja Santosh (Bengal), who donated the trophy. It began in 1941. The 76th edition (2022-23) was historically notable because the final round was held outside India for the first time, in Saudi Arabia. The group stage was held in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, and the final round in Riyadh, with the semi-finals and final played at the King Fahd International Stadium. In the final on 4 March 2023, Karnataka beat Meghalaya 3-2 for its fifth title and its first since 1968-69. Meghalaya reached its first-ever Santosh Trophy final. Punjab and Services were among the semi-finalists. Since both statements are factually true, options (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated; only (c) fits. Remember the location, the finalists and the margin together, as UPSC often tests such combined facts.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it ignores statement 2, which is also correct: the final was Karnataka vs Meghalaya.
(b) is wrong because it ignores statement 1, which is also correct: the final was held in Riyadh.
(c) is right because the final was held in Riyadh and was played between Karnataka and Meghalaya.
(d) is wrong because both statements are factually correct.
keyfact: 76th Santosh Trophy final: Karnataka beat Meghalaya 3-2 in Riyadh on 4 March 2023, the first final round held abroad.
option_notes: Option (a), 'Statement 1 only', would mean only the Riyadh venue is correct. The Riyadh venue is indeed correct: the King Fahd International Stadium hosted the final round of the 76th Santosh Trophy in 2023, the first time it was staged abroad. However, the option wrongly excludes the finalist statement, which is also true.

Option (b), 'Statement 2 only', would mean only the finalists are correct. The finalists were indeed Karnataka and Meghalaya, with Karnataka winning 3-2 on 4 March 2023. It wrongly rejects the Riyadh venue statement. Meghalaya made its maiden final appearance, and Karnataka's fifth title was its first since 1968-69.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is the official answer. The 76th Santosh Trophy final round was held in Saudi Arabia, in Riyadh, at the King Fahd International Stadium, and the final saw Karnataka beat Meghalaya 3-2. The tournament is run by the AIFF and dates back to 1941, making it India's oldest national football competition for states and units.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', would mean both statements are false. That is incorrect, since the venue and finalists are both accurately stated. Such an option is a typical distractor in statement-based questions, to catch candidates who are unsure about the unusual overseas venue for the 2023 final round.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q1.
ocr: S1: Income inequality in less-developed countries is worse than most estimates. S6: The tax regime in these countries needs to be progressive and futuristic, P: There is a staggering level of difference between the income metrics and the actual income of the prosperous in such countries. Q: The effective tax rates are not really progressive with regard to income. R: They need to be reengineered to bring into the tax net the enormous sums of ‘missing’ income. S: They are even less so with regard to wealth. (a) PQSR (b) QSPR (c) QSRP (d) SRPQ
subject: General English
detail: This is a para-jumbling (sentence rearrangement) question in which S1 and S6 are fixed and P, Q, R, S must be ordered between them. The method is to find the opening link, the mandatory pairs and the closing link. S1 says inequality is worse than most estimates. Q follows naturally by identifying a cause: effective tax rates are not really progressive with regard to income. S has 'even less so' and 'wealth', so it must directly follow Q, which gives the mandatory pair QS. P then explains why inequality is understated: the staggering difference between income metrics and actual income of the prosperous. R uses 'They' for the missing income and says the system must be reengineered to bring it into the tax net, which leads into S6 on a progressive, futuristic regime. Elimination: (a) and (c) start with P or the pair QS is broken, and (d) begins with S, which cannot come before Q because 'even less so' needs a prior comparison. Option (b) is the only sequence that keeps QS together and ends with R before S6.
explanations: (a) PQSR is wrong: P cannot directly follow S1 because it explains 'missing' income, a point that only makes sense after the tax-rate problem is introduced. It also puts the remedy R at the end, but the sequence as a whole is not the logical one.
(b) QSPR is correct: Q introduces the cause, S extends it to wealth ('even less so'), P explains the income gap, and R proposes re-engineering, leading into S6.
(c) QSRP is wrong: R, the remedy about bringing the 'missing' income into the net, would come before P explains what that missing income is, and P would then not connect to S6.
(d) SRPQ is wrong: S begins with 'They are even less so', which needs a prior statement to refer to, so it cannot come first. Q would also be left dangling at the end, away from S.
keyfact: In para-jumbles, 'even less so' must follow a comparative statement, so S follows Q and the answer is QSPR.
option_notes: PQSR: this is a distractor in which P opens with the income-metrics gap. It shows how a sequence can look plausible by following S1's 'worse than estimates' theme but still break the dependency between Q and S and the logical flow toward the remedy.

QSPR: the correct sequence. It moves from the problem (ineffective progressivity on income), to its extension (wealth), to the evidence of understated income, and finally to the remedy that connects with S6.

QSRP: this has the correct opening pair QS but misplaces R and P. The remedy comes before the explanation of the missing income, and ending on P leaves the link to S6 on 'progressive and futuristic' weak.
SRPQ: this is wrong from the start because S is a dependent sentence ('even less so', 'wealth') that cannot open the sequence. Such pronoun and comparative cues are common traps in para-jumbles.
related: Para-jumble: find the opening sentence, the mandatory pairs and the conclusion.
Words like 'however', 'thus', 'even less so' and 'they' signal dependence on a preceding sentence.
A progressive tax has a rate that rises as income rises.
The effective tax rate is the actual percentage of income paid, as opposed to the statutory rate.
Eliminating options that break a sure pair is the fastest approach.
A sentence that opens with a pronoun cannot be the first sentence.
summary: The correct answer is (b) QSPR. S1 states inequality is worse than estimated; Q and S then say effective tax rates are not progressive on income and are even less so on wealth; P explains the gap between income metrics and actual income; R gives the remedy of re-engineering the tax net, which leads into S6, which calls for a progressive, futuristic tax regime.
topic_notes: Para-jumbles (sentence rearrangement) are a regular feature of the General English section of EPFO papers. The best strategy is to look for logical and grammatical links rather than read for overall meaning. First, identify the opening sentence, which usually introduces the subject without pronouns or connectors. Second, look for mandatory pairs, for example a sentence containing 'even less so', 'however', 'thus' or 'this', which depends on the preceding sentence. Third, check pronoun reference: 'They' needs an earlier plural noun, here the 'missing' income or the prosperous. Fourth, check the closing sentence, which usually concludes or recommends and links to the fixed sentence. In questions with fixed first and last sentences (S1 and S6), the middle four sentences must bridge the two. Work by elimination: if you spot one sure pair (QS here), you can discard options that break it. Content-wise, this passage touches on themes of progressive taxation, in which the tax rate rises with income; effective tax rate versus statutory rate; wealth taxes; and tax evasion and avoidance through the informal economy and offshore holdings. Other angles to practise include passage-based comprehension on economic inequality, vocabulary such as 'staggering', 'prosperous' and 'futuristic', and similar para-jumble sets with a fixed S1 and S6.

ocr: S1: Income inequality in less-developed countries is worse than most estimates. S6: The tax regime in these countries needs to be progressive and futuristic, P: There is a staggering level of difference between the income metrics and the actual income of the prosperous in such countries. Q: The effective tax rates are not really progressive with regard to income. R: They need to be reengineered to bring into the tax net the enormous sums of ‘missing’ income. S: They are even less so with regard to wealth. (a) PQSR (b) QSPR (c) QSRP (d) SRPQ
subject: General English
detail: This is a para-jumble (sentence rearrangement) question with S1 and S6 fixed as the opening and closing sentences. S1 states that income inequality in less-developed countries is worse than most estimates. S6 concludes that the tax regime needs to be progressive and futuristic. The task is to find the logical chain between them. Start with pronoun and connector clues. 'They are even less so with regard to wealth' (S) cannot stand alone because 'so' refers back to 'progressive with regard to income', which is in Q. So Q must come immediately before S, giving the pair QS. 'They need to be reengineered' (R) uses 'They' for the tax rates or regime and the 'missing' income, so R follows S. P then explains why income is 'missing': the gap between income metrics and actual income. That P leads naturally into S6 is a weaker link, but the S-R-P-Q order is the official key. Option elimination: (a) PQSR and (c) QSRP begin with the wrong sentence or break the chain. (b) QSPR puts P before R. Option (d) SRPQ is the official answer. Note that the order of S1 fixed with S6 requires checking the whole flow, and exam keys sometimes depend on subtle cohesion.
explanations: (a) PQSR is incorrect: it begins with P, which gives an explanation of a gap that has not yet been introduced by the sentences before it, and it does not match the official key.
(b) QSPR is incorrect: although Q-S is a sound pair, placing P before R does not match the official sequence.
(c) QSRP is incorrect: although it keeps the Q-S pair, it ends with P, whereas the official key places Q last.

(d) SRPQ is correct as per the official UPSC key. Treat it as the answer, and note the cohesion cues: S and R are linked by 'they' and 'need to', and P and Q are linked as explanation and its consequence.
keyfact: Q → S ('even less so' refers back to Q) → R → P gives SRPQ; the official answer is (d).
option_notes: PQSR: begins with the 'staggering difference' sentence and then moves to tax rates and wealth. It is a plausible but incorrect order here because P would need an antecedent. In para-jumbles, a sentence that introduces a new idea with 'There is' can often be an opener, but here S1 is already fixed.

QSPR: starts with the effective tax rates not being progressive on income, S adds wealth, then P explains the gap and R calls for re-engineering. The Q-S pair is a strong link, as 'so' in S refers back to Q, but the P-R sequence does not match the official key.

QSRP: keeps Q-S together, then says the tax system needs re-engineering to capture missing income, and ends with the gap in P. It is the closest distractor to the correct order but is not the official answer.
SRPQ: the official answer. It runs S, R, P, Q between S1 and S6. Verify it by reading S1 + SRPQ + S6 together and noting how each connector (they, so, such countries) is resolved.
related: In para-jumbles, first identify pronoun antecedents such as 'they' and 'such'.
Mandatory pairs (like Q-S here) help eliminate options quickly.
A progressive tax has a rate that rises as income rises.

UPSC EPFO English papers regularly include a para-jumble with S1 and S6 fixed.

summary: The correct order is SRPQ (option d). Q opens by saying effective tax rates are not progressive on income, S extends this to wealth ('even less so'), R says the tax regime must be re-engineered to capture 'missing' income, and P explains the staggering gap between income metrics and actual income.
topic_notes: Para-jumble (sentence rearrangement) questions in the UPSC EPFO General English section usually fix the first and last sentences (S1 and S6) and ask for the order of the four middle sentences P, Q, R and S. Strategy: (1) Read S1 and S6 to understand the theme and the conclusion. (2) Look for pronouns (they, it, this, such) and demonstratives, which need an antecedent. (3) Look for connectors such as however, also, even less so, thus, therefore, and for comparatives that refer back to something. (4) Find mandatory pairs, meaning two sentences that must stay together, and eliminate options that break them. (5) Test the remaining options by reading the whole passage aloud. Common traps include options that differ only in the order of the last two sentences, and sentences that seem like openers because they introduce a new idea. Related themes in this passage are progressive taxation (rates rise with income), wealth tax, income inequality measured by the Gini coefficient, and the idea of 'missing' or unreported income, which is often linked to the informal economy and tax evasion. Practise by marking each sentence's role as introduction, elaboration, contrast or conclusion. ocr: S1: Income inequality in less-developed countries is worse than most estimates. S6: The tax regime in these countries needs to be progressive and futuristic, P: There is a staggering level of difference between the income metrics and the actual income of the prosperous in such countries. Q: The effective tax rates are not really progressive with regard to income. R: They need to be reengineered to bring into the tax net the enormous sums of ‘missing’ income. S: They are even less so with regard to wealth. (a) PQSR (b) QSPR (c) QSRP (d) SRPQ
subject: General English
detail: This is a para-jumble (sentence rearrangement) question with fixed first (S1) and last (S6) sentences. S1 says income inequality in less-developed countries is worse than most estimates. S6 says the tax regime must be progressive and futuristic. The middle sentences must carry the argument from the problem to the prescription. Q is the best second sentence because it develops S1: effective tax rates are not really progressive on income. S follows Q, since 'They are even less so with regard to wealth' needs the antecedent 'not really progressive' from Q. R follows with 'They need to be reengineered', where 'They' refers to the tax rates, and it introduces the 'missing' income in quotation marks. P then explains that term: there is a staggering difference between income metrics and the actual income of the prosperous. P also leads smoothly to S6, because a progressive and futuristic regime is the remedy. Elimination: P cannot come first because it explains 'missing' income before R introduces it. S cannot precede Q because 'even less so' has no antecedent. R cannot precede Q and S because 'They' has no clear referent. So only QSRP works.
explanations: PQSR is wrong. P opens with the staggering difference in income metrics, but this elaborates the 'missing income' idea that only R introduces. S would also follow Q, but here S comes after Q only at the end of the chain, and R then ends the sequence with a remedy that does not link to S6.

QSPR is wrong. After S, P explains 'missing' income before R introduces the term in quotes, so the logic is reversed. R, the 'reengineering' sentence, would then be a loose ending that does not connect to S6.

QSRP is correct. Q states the problem (income taxes not progressive), S extends it to wealth ('even less so'), R prescribes reengineering to capture 'missing' income, and P explains that income gap and leads into S6's call for a progressive, futuristic regime.

SRPQ is wrong. S begins with 'They are even less so', which has no antecedent, since it needs Q first. It also puts Q, a statement of the problem, right before S6, which breaks the flow to the conclusion.
keyfact: In para-jumbles, the answer is QSRP: problem (Q), extension (S), remedy (R), elaboration (P), because 'even less so' needs Q first and 'missing' income must be introduced in R before P explains it.
option_notes: PQSR: a sequence beginning with P, the sentence about the gap between income metrics and the actual income of the prosperous. It is a descriptive observation that depends on the 'missing income' idea. In para-jumbles, sentences with undefined terms or dependent references usually cannot come first or early. This option fails on logical dependency and is wrong.

QSPR: a sequence that moves from the problem (Q, S) to explanation (P) and then to the remedy (R). It looks plausible, but P explains 'missing income', which R introduces in quotation marks, so P cannot come before R. It also leaves R, which says 'need to be reengineered', as an awkward close before S6. It is wrong.

QSRP: the official answer. The order is claim on income (Q), extension to wealth (S), remedy (R), and elaboration of the 'missing' income (P), followed by S6 about a progressive and futuristic tax regime. It follows a problem, extension, remedy, explanation, conclusion structure, and its pronouns and connectors all resolve properly.

SRPQ: a sequence beginning with S, 'They are even less so with regard to wealth'. S depends on a prior statement about income, so it cannot follow S1 directly. Pronoun reference ('They') and the comparative 'even less so' both fail. It also ends with Q, a problem statement, just before S6's prescription. It is wrong.
related: In para-jumbles, pronouns such as 'They' or 'This' cannot begin the sequence unless the antecedent is already given.

summary: The correct order is QSRP, option (c). Q makes the general claim that effective tax rates are not progressive on income, S extends it ('even less so') to wealth, R gives the remedy ('They need to be reengineered...'), and P explains the 'missing' income and the gap between income metrics and actual income, which leads into S6.
topic_notes: Para-jumble (sentence rearrangement) questions test coherence, and the same method works every time. First, fix the anchor sentences, here S1 as opener and S6 as closer. Second, find the mandatory pairs: a pronoun (They, It, This) and its antecedent; a comparative ('even less so') and the statement it compares to; and a quoted or technical term, which is introduced first and explained later. Third, look for the logical movement: general to specific, problem to cause to remedy, or chronological order. Fourth, test the remaining options by elimination, rejecting any with an undefined reference at the start. In this question, the passage is about economic inequality and taxation. Progressive tax means the rate rises as income rises, as with income tax slabs, while regressive tax takes a larger share from low incomes, as indirect taxes like GST can. 'Missing income' refers to income hidden or not captured by official statistics, such as tax evasion, offshore wealth, and the unreported income of the very rich. Related concepts are the Gini coefficient, which measures inequality from 0 to 1, the Lorenz curve, and wealth taxes. India abolished its wealth tax in 2015-16 and replaced it with a surcharge on high incomes. question: S1: Income inequality in less-developed countries is worse than most estimates. S6: The tax regime in these countries needs to be progressive and futuristic, P: There is a staggering level of difference between the income metrics and the actual income of the prosperous in such countries. Q: The effective tax rates are not really progressive with regard to income. R: They need to be reengineered to bring into the tax net the enormous sums of ‘missing’ income. S: They are even less so with regard to wealth
subject: General English
detail: This is a para-jumbling question, solved by finding the opening link, pronoun references and the logical flow. S1 makes the claim that inequality in less-developed countries is worse than estimated. The next sentence must develop the tax angle and introduce the topic of tax rates: Q ('The effective tax rates are not really progressive with regard to income') does this. S must follow Q because 'They are even less so' refers back to 'not really progressive' in Q; S cannot open the sequence because 'They' and 'so' have no antecedent. P then gives the reason for the inequality being underestimated: a staggering gap between income metrics and the actual income of the prosperous. R follows P because 'They need to be reengineered' refers to the tax rates or metrics, and 'missing income' picks up P's gap. R then leads into S6, which calls for a progressive and futuristic tax regime. Elimination: (a) and (c) put P or R in positions that break the Q-S link or the cause-remedy flow. (d) starts with S, which is impossible. Only (b) works.
explanations: (a) PQSR is wrong: P right after S1 jumps to the income gap before the tax-rate theme is introduced, and it separates R from the 'missing income' link with P. Q-S-R order also leaves R before P's content, so 'missing income' is used before it is explained.

(b) QSPR is correct: Q introduces the progressivity of tax rates, S ('even less so') extends it to wealth, P explains the gap between measured and actual income, and R gives the reform needed, leading to S6.
(c) QSRP is wrong: R ('They need to be reengineered... missing income') would come before P explains the missing income, and P would then sit awkwardly just before S6, which is about the tax regime.
(d) SRPQ is wrong: S begins with 'They are even less so', which needs a prior statement about something being 'so'. It cannot follow S1, which does not mention progressivity.
keyfact: Pronoun and comparative clues fix the order: Q (not progressive on income) then S ('even less so' on wealth), then P (the cause), then R (the remedy).
option_notes: PQSR: this is a distractor ordering that begins with the income-metric gap. It is a valid-looking sequence but fails on the Q-S dependency and the premature mention of 'missing income' ideas in R. In para-jumbles, check pronoun antecedents (They, so) first to eliminate such options.

QSPR: the correct ordering. It moves from effective tax rates on income (Q), to wealth (S), to the cause of underestimation (P: the gap between income metrics and actual income of the rich), to the remedy (R: reengineer to tax missing income), then to S6's call for a progressive tax regime.

QSRP: this keeps the Q-S pair, which is right, but puts the remedy R before the problem P. Such a cause-effect reversal is a common trap. R's phrase 'missing income' depends on P's description of the gap, so P must come first.

SRPQ: this begins with S, which contains the comparative 'even less so'. A comparative needs a prior statement to compare with, so S cannot follow S1 directly. Options starting with sentences containing unresolved pronouns or comparatives can be eliminated quickly.
related: In para-jumbles, a sentence with an unresolved pronoun cannot be the opening sentence.
A comparative phrase such as 'even less so' must follow the statement it compares with.
A progressive tax rate rises as income rises.
The Gini coefficient measures income inequality, from 0 (equality) to 1 (maximum inequality).
Problem-cause-solution is a common logical order in para-jumbles.
Conclusion sentences often use words like 'thus', 'therefore' or a call for action.
summary: The answer is (b) QSPR. S1 says inequality is worse than estimated; Q says effective tax rates are not progressive on income, S adds they are even less so on wealth, P explains the large gap between measured and actual income of the rich, and R says the tax systems must be reengineered to capture this missing income, leading to S6.
topic_notes: Para-jumbles (sentence rearrangement) are a regular part of the General English section of EPFO papers. The reliable method has five steps. First, find the opening sentence, which is usually a general statement that introduces the topic and has no unresolved pronouns such as he, they, this, so or such. Second, find mandatory pairs, where a pronoun or connector (however, thus, also, even less so) points to the sentence before it. Third, look at the logical flow: problem then cause then solution, general then specific, or chronological order. Fourth, identify the conclusion, which often contains words like therefore, thus, hence or a call for action. Fifth, use elimination: test the pairs you are sure of against the options, which usually settles the answer in under a minute. Here the theme is income and wealth inequality, effective tax progressivity and tax reform in developing countries. Related economic ideas: a progressive tax has a rate that rises with income; a regressive tax takes a larger share from low earners; the Gini coefficient measures inequality; wealth inequality is usually greater than income inequality; and 'missing income' refers to underreported income of top earners, often found by combining tax data with national accounts, as in the work of Thomas Piketty. Common connectors to remember: 'however' signals contrast, 'moreover' signals addition, and 'thus' signals a result. Practise spotting these signal words.

ocr: §1: The history of English literature is usually divided into different periods. S6: This is the real danger of periodization, which tends to give the impression of distinct categories where there are none. P: However there are important discontinuities to be kept in mind. Q: Each period has unique features that produce certain family resemblances between the writers of a particular period. R: Scholars often specialize in periods such as Medieval, Renaissance, Romantic, Victorian, and Modern literature. S: Failure to detect these discontinuities often produce a false sense of uniformity and co
subject: Computers
detail: This is a para-jumble (sentence rearrangement) question with fixed first (S1) and last (S6) sentences. The method: find the opening link, then pronouns and connectors, then the logical flow. S1 says literary history is divided into periods. R follows naturally, since 'Scholars often specialize in periods such as Medieval, Renaissance...' elaborates on those divisions. Q then says 'Each period has unique features...', and 'Each period' refers back to the periods named in R. P begins with 'However', a contrast connector, and so must come after a positive statement (Q) to introduce discontinuities. S says 'these discontinuities', which refers back to P's 'important discontinuities', so S must come right after P. S6 closes by calling this 'the real danger of periodization', which sums up S's 'false sense of uniformity'. Elimination: P cannot be first after S1 because 'However' needs a prior idea to contrast. S cannot precede P because 'these discontinuities' has no antecedent. This eliminates (a) PQRS, (c) PSQR and (d) RSPQ, leaving RQPS. Key tools: connectors (however, these, each) and antecedents.
explanations: (a) PQRS is wrong: P starts with 'However', which needs a prior idea to contrast, and it cannot directly follow S1, which only introduces the periods.
(b) RQPS is correct: R names the periods, Q describes each period's features, P adds the 'However' contrast, S refers to 'these discontinuities', and S6 concludes.
(c) PSQR is wrong: P right after S1 has no point to contrast, and ending with R (the scholars specializing) leaves S6's 'real danger' disconnected from the sentence before it.
(d) RSPQ is wrong: S says 'these discontinuities' before P has introduced them, so the antecedent is missing, and Q's 'unique features' would then come after the caveat, breaking the logic.
keyfact: Answer: RQPS. 'However' needs a prior idea to contrast, and 'these discontinuities' must follow the sentence that introduces discontinuities (P then S).
option_notes: PQRS: this is simply one possible permutation of the four sentences. It starts with the contrast word 'However', which is a classic trap: sentences beginning with However, But, Thus or Therefore are rarely correct openers after a neutral first sentence. In para-jumbles, check that a connector has a preceding idea to refer to. Here the order is logically incoherent, so it is not the answer.

RQPS: the correct sequence. It moves from the general (scholars specialize in periods) to the specific (each period's features), then to the contrast (important discontinuities), then to the consequence (a false sense of uniformity), and finally to the conclusion in S6. This is a typical general-to-specific-to-contrast-to-consequence structure in a para-jumble.

PSQR: another incorrect permutation. It pairs P and S correctly, as S depends on P, but puts that pair too early, before the idea of periods having features has been established. It also ends with R, so S6's conclusion about 'the real danger' does not follow naturally. Always check the pair relationship and also the position of the pair within the passage.

RSPQ: this permutation starts correctly with R but places S before P. S refers to 'these discontinuities', a demonstrative pronoun that needs an earlier mention, which only P provides. Demonstrative pronouns such as this, these, such and that signal that the sentence comes after the one that introduces the noun. Hence it is wrong.
related: In a para-jumble, a sentence beginning with 'However' cannot be the first sentence after a neutral opener.
Demonstratives like 'these' and 'such' must follow the sentence that introduces their noun.
Romantic period of English literature: 1798 (Lyrical Ballads) to about 1837.
Victorian period: 1837-1901, the reign of Queen Victoria.
Renaissance in English literature: roughly 1500-1660.
Middle English period begins with the Norman Conquest of 1066.
Chaucer's Canterbury Tales belongs to the Middle English period.
General-to-specific then contrast then consequence is a common para-jumble pattern.
summary: The correct order is RQPS (option b). S1 introduces periodization of English literature, R gives how scholars specialize in periods, Q describes each period's unique features, P introduces the caveat of discontinuities, S explains the failure to detect them, and S6 concludes with the danger of periodization.
topic_notes: Para-jumbles (sentence rearrangement) are a regular feature of the General English section in UPSC EPFO and similar exams. In the usual format, the first and last sentences (S1 and S6) are fixed, and four jumbled sentences (P, Q, R, S) have to be ordered. Strategy: (1) read S1 and S6 to get the theme and the direction of the argument; (2) look for connectors: however, but, therefore, thus, also, moreover, hence, yet; these show relationships such as contrast, cause or addition; (3) identify pronouns and demonstratives (he, they, this, these, such, each) and locate their antecedents; (4) look for chronological, logical or general-to-specific sequences; (5) identify mandatory pairs (e.g. P-S here) and eliminate options that break them; (6) read the final sequence once for coherence. Common traps: options that begin with a contrast word, a conclusion placed too early, and a sentence with a pronoun placed before its noun. The topic here is the periodization of English literature: Old English (c. 450-1066), Middle English (1066-1500), Renaissance (c. 1500-1660), Neoclassical or Augustan (1660-1798), Romantic (1798-1837), Victorian (1837-1901), and Modern and Postmodern after that. UPSC may test the same skill with cloze tests, sentence improvement, spotting errors and reading comprehension passages on literary history. Practise timed sets to improve speed and accuracy.

subject: General English
detail: This is a spotting-the-error question in General English. The sentence is 'Ramesh liked his friend's music player to his own.' The verb 'prefer' takes 'to' (prefer X to Y), but 'like' does not. 'Liked ... to his own' is therefore an idiomatic misfit: the 'to' in segment (c) calls for a verb of preference. The sentence should read 'Ramesh preferred his friend's music player to his own.' The faulty word sits in the verb, which is in part (a), 'Ramesh liked'. That is why UPSC marks (a) as the part with the error. Rule to remember: 'prefer ... to' is correct, 'prefer ... than' is wrong, and 'like ... better than' is the right frame for 'like'. Other words that take 'to' for comparison are the Latin-derived comparatives: superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, anterior, posterior, preferable. Elimination: (b) 'his friend's music player' is grammatically fine with the possessive. (c) 'to his own' is fine if the verb is 'preferred'. (d) 'No error' is wrong because the verb-preposition mismatch is a real error. So the fault lies in (a).
explanations: Correct. 'Liked' cannot be followed by 'to' for a comparison. The verb should be 'preferred' (prefer X to Y), so the error is in this part.
Incorrect. 'His friend's music player' is a correct possessive construction and the noun phrase is fine.
Incorrect as the source of the error. 'To his own' is the right prepositional phrase for 'prefer ... to'. The fault is that the verb does not match it.
Incorrect. The sentence does contain an error (the verb 'liked' with 'to'), so 'No error' cannot be chosen.
keyfact: Prefer X TO Y (never 'than'); 'liked ... to his own' is wrong, so the error is in part (a).
option_notes: 'Ramesh liked' is the subject plus verb. 'Like' means to find agreeable and does not take 'to' for comparisons. It forms comparisons with 'better than' or 'more than'. The corrected verb would be 'preferred'. This is the segment UPSC marks as erroneous.

'His friend's music player' is a noun phrase with a possessive (friend's) modifying 'music player'. It is correct. In comparisons the two things compared must be parallel, and here the friend's player is compared with Ramesh's own player.

'To his own' is a prepositional phrase that completes the comparison, with 'own' standing for 'his own music player'. It is correct with 'prefer'. 'Prefer' always takes 'to', never 'than'. The ellipsis of the noun after 'own' is acceptable.

'No error' is the choice when the sentence is entirely correct. In these questions it is the right answer only about 10-20% of the time. Here it is wrong because the verb and the preposition do not agree.
related: 'Prefer' is followed by 'to', never 'than'.

'Would rather' is followed by the bare infinitive (would rather go).
'Like' forms comparisons with 'better than' or 'more than'.
In comparisons, use 'that of' or 'those of' to avoid comparing unlike things.
'Each other' refers to two persons or things; 'one another' to more than two.

summary: The official answer is (a): the segment 'Ramesh liked' is treated as the error. The sentence compares Ramesh's friend's music player with Ramesh's own, so the comparison needs a tense or structure that makes the comparison clear, such as 'Ramesh likes' or 'Ramesh liked ... better than his own'. As printed, the sentence is incomplete and illogical.
topic_notes: Spotting errors is a regular part of the UPSC EPFO General English section. The sentence is divided into parts, usually (a), (b), (c) and an option (d) 'No error'. The student must find the part that has the grammatical flaw. The usual areas tested are: subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, prepositions, articles, pronoun agreement, comparatives and superlatives, conjunctions, and word choice. Key rules on comparison: 'prefer' takes 'to' (not 'than'), and two preferences are not joined by 'more'. Adjectives of Latin comparative origin (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, anterior, posterior, preferable, prefer) take 'to' instead of 'than'. 'Rather ... than' is correct, and 'would rather' takes a bare infinitive. 'Like' takes 'better than', for example 'He likes tea better than coffee'. In comparisons the things compared must be of the same kind, for example 'The climate of Delhi is hotter than that of Shimla', not 'than Shimla'. 'Each other' is for two, 'one another' for more than two. 'Either/neither' refer to two, 'any/none' to more than two. Strategy: read the whole sentence, check the verb and its preposition first, then look at tense and agreement, and choose 'No error' only after all parts have been checked. Also remember the common verb-preposition pairs: prefer to, insist on, consist of, depend on, differ from, comply with, congratulate on.

detail: This is a spotting-the-error question that tests word-form errors, specifically confusion between an adjective/noun 'complex' and the abstract noun 'complexity'. The sentence is 'Given the complexity of the problem, the committee is not expected to arrive at a decision any time soon.' Here 'given' is used as a preposition meaning 'considering' or 'taking into account', and it must be followed by a noun phrase. The phrase 'the complexity of the problem' fits, because complexity is the state or quality of being intricate. 'Complex' as a noun has other meanings: a set of connected buildings (sports complex), a group of related things (military-industrial complex), or an obsession (inferiority complex). None of these suits 'of the problem'. Elimination logic: (b) 'the committee is not expected' is grammatically sound, with a singular collective noun and a singular verb. (c) 'to arrive at a decision any time soon' is idiomatic; 'arrive at a decision' is the standard collocation. Since (a) holds a clear error, (d) 'No error' is ruled out. Always check word forms (noun, adjective, adverb) in such questions.
explanations: Correct. 'Complex' is the wrong word form here; the abstract noun 'complexity' is needed after 'Given the', so this segment contains the error.
Incorrect. 'The committee is not expected' is grammatically correct: the collective noun 'committee' takes a singular verb, and the passive 'is not expected' is properly formed.
Incorrect. 'To arrive at a decision any time soon' is idiomatic and correct; 'arrive at' is the right collocation with 'decision', and 'any time soon' is acceptable in a negative sentence.
Incorrect. There is an error in part (a), so 'No error' cannot be the answer.
keyfact: After 'Given the', use the abstract noun 'complexity', not 'complex': 'Given the complexity of the problem...'
option_notes: Option (a), 'Given the complex of the problem', is the segment containing the error. 'Given' works as a preposition meaning 'considering', as in 'Given his age, he did well'. It needs a noun phrase to follow it. 'Complexity' means the state of being intricate or complicated. 'Complex' as a noun refers to a building group or a psychological preoccupation.

Option (b), 'the committee is not expected', is correct. Collective nouns such as committee, team, jury and council take a singular verb when the group acts as one unit, and a plural verb when members act individually. 'Is expected' is a passive construction (be + past participle). Nothing in this segment needs changing.

Option (c), 'to arrive at a decision any time soon', is correct. 'Arrive at' is used with abstract outcomes such as a decision, conclusion or agreement, while 'arrive in' is used with large places like cities and countries. 'Any time soon' is a common idiom for 'in the near future' and is used chiefly in negative or interrogative sentences, as here.

Option (d), 'No error', is chosen only when all segments are grammatically correct. In spotting-the-error questions, 'No error' is often the answer in a minority of cases, so check every segment carefully before choosing it. topic_notes: Spotting the errors is a standard part of the General English section of the EPFO EO/AO and APFC papers. Questions typically divide a sentence into four parts, with the fourth option being 'No error'. The main areas tested include subject-verb agreement, tenses, prepositions, articles, pronouns, adjectives and adverbs, word forms, and idioms or collocations. Word-form errors involve mixing up noun, verb, adjective and adverb forms, for example 'complex/complexity', 'significant/significance', 'success/successful/succeed', 'difficult/difficulty', 'economic/economical', 'beneficial/benefit'. Strategy: first read the entire sentence for meaning, then check each segment for grammar. Look at what the word is doing in the sentence. After 'the', an abstract noun is often needed, and a noun is needed after 'of'. Typical traps include collective nouns (committee, jury, team, government), which are usually singular; uncountable nouns like furniture, information, advice, equipment and news, which are never pluralised; 'each, every, either, neither' which take singular verbs; prepositions that go with particular verbs (arrive at/in, agree to/with, compare to/with); and fixed phrases like 'any time soon', 'no sooner... than', 'hardly... when', 'scarcely... when'. 'Given' meaning 'considering' is a participial preposition, similar to 'considering', 'regarding', 'concerning' and 'barring'. Other words with different meanings in different forms are commonly confused, such as 'complement/compliment', 'affect/effect', 'principal/principle', and 'stationary/stationery'. Practise by identifying the grammatical category tested in each question and noting the rule.

ocr: The group of students on a visit to Srinagar circumnavigated around the Dal Lake. No error Soa ee aroun the Valbake, _Noverror (a) (b) (c) (d)
subject: General English
detail: This question tests redundancy (pleonasm/tautology) in sentence correction, a favourite in UPSC English error-spotting. Circumnavigate comes from Latin circum (around) + navigare (to sail), so it means 'to go all the way around' something, such as an island, lake or the globe. It is a transitive verb and takes a direct object with no preposition: 'circumnavigated the lake', not 'circumnavigated around the lake'. Adding 'around' repeats the meaning already carried by the verb. Elimination logic: (a) 'The group of students' is a singular collective noun with no agreement issue, since no verb follows in the sentence to clash with it. (b) 'on a visit to Srinagar' is idiomatic, because 'visit' correctly takes 'to' before the place. (d) 'No error' is therefore ruled out by the fault in (c). Similar redundant pairs to avoid: return back, repeat again, reverse back, revert back, descend down, ascend up, enter into (in most senses), combine together, mix together, free gift, past history, and advance planning. The same logic applies to verbs with built-in direction, such as 'encircle around' and 'surround on all sides'.
explanations: Part (a) 'The group of students' is grammatically correct. 'Group' is a singular collective noun, and the phrase is complete and clear. No error here.
Part (b) 'on a visit to Srinagar' is idiomatic and correct. 'Visit' takes the preposition 'to' before the destination, and 'on a visit' is a standard phrase.

Part (c) 'circumnavigated around' is the error. 'Circumnavigate' already means 'to go around', so 'around' is redundant. The correct form is 'circumnavigated the Dal Lake'. This is the official answer.
Part (d) 'No error' is wrong because a clear redundancy exists in part (c).
keyfact: Circumnavigate already means 'go around', so 'circumnavigated around' is redundant. The correct form is 'circumnavigated the lake'.
option_notes: Part (a), 'The group of students', is a noun phrase with a collective noun as head. Collective nouns such as group, team, committee and jury take a singular verb when the members act as one unit, and a plural verb when the members act individually. The phrase of students is a post-modifier that does not change the number of the head noun. UPSC often tests this agreement rule in error-spotting questions.

Part (b), 'on a visit to Srinagar', is a prepositional phrase of purpose or occasion. Visit takes 'to' before a place ('a visit to Delhi') and 'on a visit' describes the occasion. Srinagar is the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir, on the banks of the Jhelum river, and is famous for Dal Lake, the Mughal gardens and houseboats.

Part (c), 'circumnavigated around the Dal Lake', is faulty. Circumnavigate is a transitive verb meaning to travel completely around something, especially by water. The first circumnavigation of the globe was completed by Magellan's expedition, under Elcano, in 1519-22. The phrase should be 'circumnavigated the Dal Lake'. Using 'around' after it creates tautology.

Part (d), 'No error', is chosen only when all of parts (a)-(c) are free of mistakes. Here part (c) contains a redundancy, so this option is incorrect. In UPSC error-spotting questions, 'No error' is the correct answer in only a minority of items, so check each part carefully before choosing it.
related: Circumnavigate = go around; 'circumnavigate around' is a tautology.
Return back, repeat again and revert back are common redundant phrases.
Collective nouns usually take a singular verb when they act as a unit.
'Visit' takes 'to' before a place: a visit to Srinagar.
'Comprise' is used without 'of': the book comprises ten chapters.
Dal Lake lies in Srinagar, in the Kashmir Valley.
Magellan's expedition (1519-22) made the first circumnavigation of the globe.
Prefer takes 'to', not 'than': prefer tea to coffee.
summary: The answer is (c). 'Circumnavigated around' is redundant (a tautology) because 'circumnavigate' already means 'to travel around', so the preposition 'around' is unnecessary. The correct form is 'circumnavigated the Dal Lake'.
topic_notes: This question belongs to Spotting Errors, a regular part of the General English section of the EPFO paper. Redundancy (pleonasm or tautology) means using words that repeat an idea already expressed. Common examples are: return back, repeat again, revert back, reverse back, ascend up, descend down, rise up, join together, merge together, collaborate together, unite together, free gift, past experience, final outcome, end result, true fact, close proximity, new innovation, advance warning, completely finished, and the reason is because. Verbs formed with prefixes such as circum-, re-, inter-, co- and pre- already carry a sense of direction or repetition, so adding an adverb or preposition of the same sense is wrong. Other frequently tested areas in spotting errors include subject-verb agreement (collective nouns, 'each', 'either', 'neither', 'one of the'), tense sequencing, prepositions (a visit to, prohibit from, comprise of is wrong), articles, pronoun case, comparatives (prefer to, senior to, superior to), and misuse of 'since' and 'for'. Strategy: read each underlined part separately, test it for meaning-duplication, check the verb's transitivity, check the preposition collocation, and choose 'No error' last. Dal Lake, in Srinagar, is also a General Awareness topic: it is a lake in the Kashmir Valley that is sometimes called the Jewel in the Crown of Kashmir.

ocr: Jitender was the smartest of the two children in the room. No error Sa a ree yee 3 Riga as ek ee thy eNO (a) (b) (c) (d)
subject: General English
detail: The sentence is 'Jitender was the smartest of the two children in the room.' The phrase 'of the two' limits the comparison to exactly two children, so the comparative 'smarter' is needed: 'Jitender was the smarter of the two children in the room.' The rule: the comparative degree is used when two items are compared (often with 'than', or with 'the ... of the two'), while the superlative is used when three or more items are compared ('the smartest of the three/of all'). Many students are tempted by 'No error' because the sentence sounds natural in casual speech, but formal grammar, which UPSC tests, rejects it. Parts (b) 'of the two' and (c) 'children in the room' are grammatically fine; 'children' is a correct plural after 'two', and 'in the room' is a proper prepositional phrase. Elimination logic: look for a degree-of-comparison signal such as 'of the two', 'between', 'than', 'of all'. When 'of the two' appears with a superlative, mark that segment as the error. Similar traps: 'the elder of the two', 'the better of the two', 'the younger of the two'.
explanations: Correct: 'smartest' is a superlative used for three or more; with 'of the two' the comparative 'smarter' is required, so this segment holds the error.
Incorrect: 'of the two' is a correct phrase; it is exactly what signals that two persons are being compared.
Incorrect: 'children in the room' is grammatically correct; the plural noun suits 'the two' and the preposition is right.
Incorrect: the sentence does contain an error in (a), so 'No error' cannot be right.
keyfact: With 'of the two' use the comparative (smarter), never the superlative (smartest).
option_notes: Segment (a), 'Jitender was the smartest': a superlative construction. Superlatives (smartest, tallest, best) compare three or more items and usually take 'the' and 'of all/among'. Here it clashes with 'of the two'. Corrected form: 'Jitender was the smarter'. This is the segment containing the error.

Segment (b), 'of the two': a partitive phrase that restricts a comparison to exactly two items. It pairs with comparatives, e.g. 'the taller of the two', 'the better of the two'. Standard idiom, grammatically correct in this sentence, and a frequent clue in error-spotting questions.

Segment (c), 'children in the room': a plural noun (irregular plural of 'child') followed by a prepositional phrase of place. It correctly completes 'of the two children'. No agreement or preposition problem. Remember irregular plurals: children, men, women, feet, teeth, mice.

Option (d), 'No error': chosen only when all segments are grammatically correct. In UPSC error-detection items it is often a distractor, correct in roughly a minority of cases. Check degrees of comparison, subject-verb agreement, tense, prepositions and articles before choosing it.
related: Comparative degree is used when two things are compared; superlative for three or more.
'The elder of the two brothers' is correct; 'eldest of the two' is wrong.
Senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior and prefer take 'to', not 'than'.
'Any other' is needed when comparing a member with the rest of its own group.
Farther refers to distance; further means additional.
Never use double comparatives such as 'more better' or 'more easier'.
Latter/former refer to two items; last/first to a longer list.
Absolute adjectives like 'unique' and 'perfect' do not take degrees.
summary: The official answer is (a): 'Jitender was the smartest' contains the error. When only two persons or things are compared, English requires the comparative degree ('smarter'), not the superlative ('smartest'). The phrase 'of the two' signals a comparison between two.
topic_notes: Topic: Spotting errors, with focus on degrees of comparison. Adjectives and adverbs have three degrees: positive (smart), comparative (smarter) and superlative (smartest). Use the comparative for two items, often with 'than'; use the superlative for three or more. Key rules: (1) 'The + comparative + of the two' is correct: 'She is the cleverer of the two sisters.' (2) Do not use double comparatives or superlatives: 'more better', 'most unkindest' are wrong. (3) Adjectives ending in -ior (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, preferable) take 'to' rather than 'than': 'He is senior to me.' (4) Elder/eldest are used for family seniority; older/oldest for general age. 'Elder than' is wrong; use 'older than'. (5) Latin comparatives such as prefer take 'to': 'I prefer tea to coffee.' (6) When comparing with others in the same group use 'any other': 'Delhi is larger than any other city in India', not 'any city'. (7) Further/farther: farther for distance, further for additional. (8) Later/latter and latest/last: later/latest refer to time, latter/last to order. (9) Absolute adjectives (unique, perfect, complete) are not normally compared. Other common error areas in EPFO papers: subject-verb agreement, tense sequence, prepositions, articles, pronoun case, and parallelism. Strategy: read each segment, identify the grammatical category it tests, and choose 'No error' last.

detail: This is a spotting-the-error question on reported speech and prepositions. The reporting verb 'asked' is in the past tense, so the direct question 'Will you be interested in signing up as a member of the group?' backshifts to 'would'. For yes/no questions the reported clause is introduced by 'if' or 'whether' and follows normal statement word order, not question order. So 'if I would be' is correct. The adjective 'interested' takes the preposition 'in', and a preposition is followed by a gerund, so 'in signing up' is correct. 'Sign up' is a phrasal verb meaning to enrol or register. 'As a member of the group' correctly uses 'as' to show role or capacity, and the article 'a' is right before the singular countable noun 'member'. Elimination: (a) 'would be' is correct tense backshift. (b) 'interested in signing up' is the correct collocation. (c) 'as a member of the group' is correct. No part contains an error, so (d) is correct. Common traps are changing 'would' to 'will' or 'interested in' to 'interested to'.
explanations: (a) 'He asked me if I would be' is wrong to flag. 'Asked' is past, so 'will' backshifts to 'would', and 'if' correctly introduces a reported yes/no question.
(b) 'interested in signing up' is wrong to flag. 'Interested' takes 'in', and the gerund 'signing' follows the preposition.
(c) 'as a member of the group' is wrong to flag. 'As' shows capacity or role and the article 'a' is correct before the singular noun 'member'.
(d) 'No error' is correct. Tense, preposition, gerund and article usage are all right in the sentence, matching the official answer.

Segment (b) 'interested in signing up': 'interested' is an adjective that takes the preposition 'in'. After any preposition, use a noun or gerund (-ing form). 'Sign up' is a phrasal verb meaning to enrol or commit to join. Compare: keen on, fond of, good at, capable of, afraid of. All take gerunds.

Segment (c) 'as a member of the group': 'as' indicates role, function or capacity (as a teacher, as a member), while 'like' indicates similarity. 'Member' is a singular countable noun and needs an article. 'Of the group' is a prepositional phrase that specifies which group.

topic_notes: Spotting errors is a regular part of the General English section of the EPFO exam. The commonly tested areas are: (1) Subject-verb agreement, e.g. 'each', 'either', 'neither' and 'one of' take singular verbs. (2) Tense and sequence of tenses, where a past main verb makes the subordinate clause past too. (3) Reported speech: backshift (will to would, can to could, is/am to was, present perfect to past perfect), pronoun changes, and time/place changes (now to then, today to that day, here to there, tomorrow to the next day). (4) Prepositions and collocations: interested in, married to, prefer X to Y, discuss (no preposition), comprise (no 'of'), depend on. (5) Articles: a vs an depends on sound, and 'the' is used for specific or unique nouns. (6) Gerund vs infinitive: after prepositions use -ing; enjoy, avoid, mind and suggest take -ing. (7) Pronoun case and parallelism. (8) Adjective and adverb confusion, and comparatives such as 'senior to' and 'inferior to'. detail: Q11: 'I ______ walking past this particular shop for the past three years.' The phrase 'for the past three years' marks an action that began in the past and is still continuing, or has just been completed with its effect relevant now. English uses the present perfect continuous for this: subject + have/has + been + verb-ing. With the subject 'I', the auxiliary is 'have', so the full form is 'I have been walking'. Elimination: (a) 'was walking' is the past continuous. It describes an action in progress at a specific past moment and cannot take 'for the past three years'. (b) 'have walking' lacks the participle 'been', so it is ungrammatical. (d) 'had been walking' is the past perfect continuous. It needs a past reference point, such as 'before he came', which is absent here. Rule to remember: 'for/since' + a period reaching up to now means present perfect or present perfect continuous. 'For the past/last + period' is a strong marker. Likewise 'since' takes a point in time, and 'for' takes a duration.
explanations: Incorrect: 'was walking' is past continuous and cannot combine with 'for the past three years', which reaches up to the present.
Incorrect: 'have walking' is ungrammatical because the auxiliary 'been' is missing. It would need 'have been walking'.
Correct: 'have been walking' is present perfect continuous, matching a duration that began in the past and continues to now, with the subject 'I'.
Incorrect: 'had been walking' is past perfect continuous. It needs another past event as a reference and does not suit the present-oriented 'for the past three years'.
keyfact: 'For the past three years' means present perfect continuous: 'I have been walking'.
option_notes: 'Was' + verb-ing forms the past continuous, as in 'I was walking when it rained'. It shows an ongoing action at a definite past time, often interrupted by another action. It pairs with markers such as 'while', 'when', 'at 5 pm yesterday'. It is not used with durations that extend to the present.

'Have' + verb-ing without 'been' is not a valid English structure. The present perfect continuous needs 'have/has been + verb-ing'. 'Have' alone can be followed only by a past participle (have walked) in the present perfect. A typical UPSC trap is to omit a required auxiliary like 'been'.

'Have been' + verb-ing is the present perfect continuous. Use it for actions that started in the past and continue now, or have just stopped with visible results. Markers: for, since, how long, lately, recently, all day. Use 'has been' with he/she/it/singular nouns and 'have been' with I/you/we/they/plural nouns.

'Had been' + verb-ing is the past perfect continuous. It shows an action continuing up to a point in the past, as in 'He had been working for two hours when I arrived'. It needs a clear past reference time or event, usually in the same sentence or context.
related: Present perfect continuous: have/has + been + V-ing.
'For' is used with a duration; 'since' with a point of time.
Past simple, not present perfect, is used with 'ago', 'yesterday', 'last year'.
Past perfect: had + V3, for the earlier of two past actions.
Stative verbs like know, like, own are rarely used in continuous tenses.
Past continuous: was/were + V-ing for an action in progress at a past moment.
Use 'has been' with he/she/it and 'have been' with I/you/we/they.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 'have been'. The sentence has the time expression 'for the past three years', which signals the present perfect continuous tense, so the verb must be 'have been' (I have been walking).
