topic_notes: Topic: Tenses, especially the perfect and continuous aspects, which are a staple of the EPFO General English section (fill in the blanks, error spotting). Present perfect (have/has + V3) shows past actions with present relevance or unfinished time: 'I have lived here for five years'. Present perfect continuous (have/has been + V-ing) stresses duration or continuity: 'She has been studying since morning'. Past perfect (had + V3) shows the earlier of two past actions. Past perfect continuous (had been + V-ing) shows a duration before a past point. Key signals: 'since' + point of time (since 2010, since Monday), 'for' + period (for three years), 'for the past/last' + period suggests the perfect form, 'yesterday/ago/last year/in 1990' needs the simple past and never the present perfect, 'already/yet/just/ever/never' go with the present perfect. Stative verbs (know, like, believe, own, belong) normally avoid continuous forms, so use 'I have known him for years', not 'have been knowing'. Subject-verb agreement decides has/have. Other angles UPSC asks: sequence of tenses in reported speech, conditionals, and the use of 'since' versus 'for'. The same paper's Q12, 'may be a doubt vs may be doubted', tests the passive voice with modals. Practice: identify the time marker first, then decide the aspect, then check subject agreement.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q12.
ocr: He asked me if I would be interested in signing up as a member of the group. No error ee a member of thegroup. No error (a) (b) (c) (d) Directions : In the following five items, each sentence has a blank space and four options have been given after the sentence. Select the most appropriate option for the blank space and indicate your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly. co Bm | walking past this particular shop for the past three years. (a) was (b) have (c) have been (d) had been 42. All effects can be connected with immediate causes, but it whether they provide the whole explanation. (a)
subject: General English
detail: Q12 tests modal verbs and voice in a concessive sentence. The structure is 'All effects can be connected with immediate causes, but it ____ whether they provide the whole explanation.' The 'but' marks a contrast. Immediate causes can be linked to effects, but it remains open to question whether they explain everything. 'May be doubted' fits this: 'may' expresses possibility or tentative opinion, and the passive 'be doubted' takes the dummy subject 'it' followed by a 'whether' clause. This matches the idiom 'it may be doubted whether...', a formal construction meaning 'one may question whether...'. Elimination: (a) 'is doubted' is a flat present passive that asserts doubt as a settled fact. It is grammatical but lacks the hedging that matches 'can be connected' in the first clause. (b) 'is a doubt' is unidiomatic with a 'whether' clause. (c) 'may be a doubt' is ungrammatical here, since 'it may be a doubt whether' is not standard usage. (d) is the official answer. Revision tip: 'doubt' as a verb takes 'whether' in affirmative sentences and 'that' in negative ones, as in 'I do not doubt that...'. The modal 'may' adds a tone of formal hedging.
explanations: (a) 'is doubted' is a plain present passive that states doubt as a fact. It loses the modal hedging that the sentence's contrast with 'can be connected' requires, so UPSC does not treat it as the most appropriate option.
(b) 'is a doubt' makes 'doubt' a noun. The construction 'it is a doubt whether' is not idiomatic in standard English, which would prefer 'it is doubtful whether'. This option is therefore wrong.
(c) 'may be a doubt' combines the modal with a noun complement. It is awkward and non-idiomatic before 'whether they provide the whole explanation', so it is incorrect.

(d) 'may be doubted' is correct. It gives modal possibility plus a passive verb, with the dummy subject 'it' followed by a 'whether' clause. This is the standard formal idiom 'it may be doubted whether...', and it is the official answer.
keyfact: 'It may be doubted whether...' is the correct formal idiom, a modal passive with dummy 'it'.
option_notes: 'Is doubted' is the simple present passive, made from is/am/are plus the past participle. It is used when the doubt is a stated fact, for example 'His claim is doubted by many experts'. It does not carry the possibility or hedging that a modal verb adds.

'Is a doubt' uses 'doubt' as a noun after the linking verb 'is'. Nouns of this kind usually take 'that' or 'about', as in 'There is a doubt that...'. The adjective form 'doubtful' is what normally goes with 'whether', as in 'It is doubtful whether he will come'. Therefore this is a poor choice.

'May be a doubt' combines the modal 'may' with a noun complement. It can appear in sentences such as 'There may be a doubt about his honesty', which uses 'there', not 'it'. Before a 'whether' clause it sounds unnatural and is not standard.

'May be doubted' is a modal passive, made from modal plus be plus the past participle. 'May' expresses possibility, and the passive removes the doer. It is used in formal and academic writing, for example 'It may be argued that...' and 'It may be doubted whether...'.
related: Present perfect continuous is used with 'for' or 'since' for actions that began in the past and continue now.
Modal passive pattern: modal + be + past participle.
'Doubt' takes 'whether' in affirmative sentences and 'that' in negative sentences.
Reported speech: 'will' becomes 'would' after a past reporting verb.
'It may be argued that...' is a standard formal hedging idiom.
'Doubtful' is an adjective that can be followed by 'whether'.
'Can' expresses ability, while 'may' expresses possibility or permission.
Q10 with 'would be interested in signing up' has no error because the tense agrees with 'asked'.
summary: The answer is (d) 'may be doubted'. The sentence 'All effects can be connected with immediate causes, but it ____ whether they provide the whole explanation' needs a modal verb of possibility plus a passive verb, because the doubt is about the explanation and is not being asserted as a fact.
topic_notes: This question belongs to the sentence completion and error-spotting areas of General English, which come up in every UPSC EPFO paper. The key skills are: (1) Modal verbs. 'Can' shows ability or general possibility, 'may' shows permission or likelihood, 'might' is a weaker possibility, 'must' is necessity or strong deduction, and 'should' and 'ought to' show advice. Modal passives follow the pattern modal + be + V3, as in 'may be doubted' and 'can be connected'. (2) Dummy 'it' constructions such as 'It may be argued that...', 'It is said that...', and 'It is doubtful whether...'. (3) 'Whether' versus 'that'. 'Whether' introduces indirect yes/no questions and uncertainty, while 'that' introduces statements of fact. (4) Tense and aspect with duration. In Q11 on the same page, 'for the past three years' needs the present perfect continuous, so 'I have been walking' is correct. (5) Subjunctive and reported speech. In Q10, 'He asked me if I would be interested' is correct because 'would' agrees with the past reporting verb, so the answer there is 'No error'. Exam strategy: first identify the grammatical slot (verb, modal, voice), then check for idiomatic collocation, then eliminate options that are ungrammatical or change the meaning. Other angles UPSC may test are active and passive voice conversion, concord (subject-verb agreement), prepositions after verbs, conditional sentences, and parallelism.

question: Abird is better than two in the bush
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a fill-in-the-blank question on proverbs and idioms in the General English section. The OCR'd stem 'Abird' is read as 'A bird', and the 'inhand' in option (a) as 'in hand'. The proverb is 'A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush', also commonly given as 'A bird in hand is better than two in the bush'. Its sense is that it is wiser to keep what you already have than to risk it for something bigger that you may never get. It is among the oldest English proverbs and has been traced to medieval sources, and similar forms exist in Latin and in other European languages. For elimination, 'to hand' means within reach or available, so it does not fit the fixed phrase. 'Handy' is an adjective meaning convenient or useful and cannot follow 'bird' in this structure. 'In one's hands' means in one's control or charge and breaks the fixed proverb. Idiom questions are answered by recalling the exact fixed wording, because the proverb does not allow substitutions. Related proverbs include 'Look before you leap', 'Don't count your chickens before they hatch' and 'Make hay while the sun shines'.
explanations: Correct: 'in hand' completes the fixed proverb 'A bird in hand is better than two in the bush', so it matches the official answer.
Incorrect: 'to hand' means close by or readily available. It is a different idiom and is not part of this proverb.
Incorrect: 'handy' is an adjective meaning useful or convenient. It does not fit grammatically or idiomatically after 'bird'.
Incorrect: 'in one's hands' means under someone's control or responsibility. The proverb uses the fixed phrase 'in hand' (or 'in the hand'), so this is wrong.
keyfact: A bird in hand is worth two in the bush: a certain gain beats an uncertain bigger one.
option_notes: 'In hand' means in one's possession or under control, as in 'cash in hand' or 'the situation is in hand'. It is the phrase used in the proverb 'A bird in hand is worth two in the bush', which urges valuing a certain gain over an uncertain larger one.
'To hand' means within easy reach or immediately available, as in 'I have the documents to hand'. It is a separate idiom, common in formal and business English, and not part of the bird proverb.
'Handy' is an adjective meaning convenient, useful, or skilled with the hands, as in 'a handy tool' or 'handy around the house'. It is not an idiom of possession and cannot complete the proverb.
'In one's hands' means in someone's care, control or responsibility, as in 'the matter is in your hands'. It is a different expression from the proverb's fixed 'in hand' form.
related: Proverb: 'A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush' means a sure thing is better than a possible bigger gain.
'Out of hand' means beyond control.
'Hand in glove' means working in very close association, often for a bad purpose.
'To live hand to mouth' means to survive with barely enough money.
'Don't count your chickens before they hatch' means do not rely on uncertain future gains.
'A stitch in time saves nine' advises prompt action to prevent bigger trouble.
'Make hay while the sun shines' means use an opportunity while it lasts.
summary: The answer is (a) 'in hand'. The English proverb is 'A bird in hand is better than two in the bush', meaning a sure, present gain is better than a larger but uncertain one.
topic_notes: Idioms and proverbs are a regular feature of the EPFO General English section, usually in fill-in-the-blank, meaning-matching or error-spotting form. A proverb is a short, traditional saying that gives general advice or a truth, and its wording is fixed. An idiom is a phrase whose meaning cannot be worked out from the individual words. The proverb in this question teaches the value of certainty over speculation and is one of the oldest in English, with similar versions in Latin and other languages. A practical approach is to learn proverbs together with their meanings and to remember the exact preposition or article in each, because options often differ by a single word, as they do here. Common proverbs to revise are: 'A stitch in time saves nine' (act promptly), 'All that glitters is not gold' (appearances deceive), 'Too many cooks spoil the broth' (too many people on a task ruin it), 'Barking dogs seldom bite' (loud threats are seldom carried out), 'Birds of a feather flock together' (similar people stay together), 'Strike while the iron is hot' (act at the right moment), and 'Honesty is the best policy'. Hand-related idioms are also frequently asked: 'at hand' (near), 'on hand' (available), 'in hand' (under control), 'out of hand' (uncontrolled), 'hand in glove' (very close partners) and 'hand to mouth' (barely surviving). In the exam, first check the meaning, then check the grammar, and then eliminate options that change the fixed form.

question: Human history is ample proof that human ambition no limits
subject: Social Security
detail: This is a fill-in-the-blank question testing verb collocation and idiom. The full sentence reads: 'Human history is ample proof that human ambition knows no limits.' The idiom 'know no bounds / know no limits' is a standard English expression meaning something is unlimited or without restraint. Here the verb 'knows' is used figuratively, as if ambition were a person unaware of any boundary. The subject 'ambition' is singular, so the verb takes the singular '-s' form. Also note that 'no' already carries the negation, so the verb must be positive in form. Elimination: 'keeps no limits' is not a recognised collocation; one 'keeps within limits' or 'keeps a limit', but 'keeps no limits' is awkward and does not convey that ambition is boundless. 'Crosses no limits' would imply ambition never exceeds limits, which reverses the meaning intended by 'ample proof' from history. 'Marks no limits' is meaningless here because ambition does not mark boundaries. For such questions, first identify the idiom, then check subject-verb agreement and the logical meaning of the sentence.
explanations: Correct: 'knows no limits' is the standard idiom meaning unlimited or boundless, and it fits the sentence and its singular subject.
Incorrect: 'keeps no limits' is not an accepted collocation and does not express that ambition is boundless.
Incorrect: 'crosses no limits' would mean ambition never exceeds limits, which contradicts the sense that history shows unbounded ambition.
Incorrect: 'marks no limits' is unidiomatic and illogical, since ambition does not mark boundaries.
keyfact: 'Knows no limits' (like 'knows no bounds') is the idiom for something boundless.
option_notes: 'Knows' is the third-person singular of 'know'. In idiom, 'know no bounds/limits/end' means to be without restriction, as in 'her generosity knows no bounds'. It personifies the abstract noun and is common in formal and literary English.

'Keeps' means to retain, continue, or hold. It forms phrases like 'keeps within limits', 'keeps a promise' or 'keeps going'. 'Keeps no limits' is not an established idiom and sounds awkward, so it is wrong here.

'Crosses' means to go over or pass beyond something. It forms phrases such as 'crosses the line' or 'crosses all limits'. With 'no' it would say ambition never goes past limits, which is the opposite of the intended meaning.

'Marks' means to put a visible sign on something, to celebrate or note an event, or to grade work. 'Marks no limits' does not form a meaningful idiom, because ambition does not set or indicate limits.
related: Idiom: 'know no bounds' means to be without limit.
'Ambition' is a strong desire to achieve something; synonyms include aspiration and drive.
'Off limits' means forbidden or restricted.
'The sky is the limit' means there is no limit to what can be achieved.
'Cross the line' means to go beyond acceptable behaviour.
A singular subject like 'ambition' takes a singular verb ('knows').
Collocation means words that habitually occur together.
summary: The answer is (a) 'knows'. The sentence needs a verb that forms the idiom 'knows no limits', meaning there is no boundary to human ambition. The other options do not fit the sentence idiomatically or logically.
topic_notes: This question belongs to vocabulary and idioms in the General English section of the EPFO exam, in the form of sentence completion or fill-in-the-blanks. These questions test collocations (words that naturally go together), idioms, and grammar such as subject-verb agreement. The approach is to read the full sentence, identify the clue words (here 'ample proof' and 'no limits'), predict the missing word before looking at the options, and then test each option for meaning and fit. Useful related idioms with 'know': 'know no bounds', 'know no fear', 'know the ropes', 'know which way the wind blows'. Related collocations with 'limits': 'push the limits', 'exceed the limits', 'set limits', 'within limits', 'off limits', 'the sky is the limit'. Similar patterns UPSC may ask: 'knows no bounds', 'knows no end', 'knows no boundaries'. Other angles include preposition fill-ins, synonyms and antonyms of 'ambition' (aspiration, drive, zeal versus apathy, indifference), and one-word substitutions. Remember that a singular abstract noun takes a singular verb, and that double negatives such as 'does not know no limits' are incorrect in standard English. For revision, build a list of 30 to 40 common idioms and collocations, and practise by covering the options and guessing the word first.

ocr: Good history presents several perspectives on a period but these divergent views must into an integrated whole. (a) be made (b) be fused (c) fit (d) be balanced Directions : Read the following passage carefully and answer the five questions that follow by selecting your answers based solely on the content of the passage and opinion of the author only. The world's life-supporting resources are being depleted at a faster rate than ever before! We have to change our practices and those of the world as a whole towards a more sustainable future. To give us an idea about the dimensions of change, th
subject: General English
detail: This is a vocabulary-in-context and phrasal-collocation question from General English. The blank is followed by 'into an integrated whole', so the verb must express combining separate things into a single unit. 'Fuse into' means to blend or join so that distinct parts become one, which matches 'divergent views' becoming 'an integrated whole'. Elimination: (a) 'be made into' is grammatically possible, but it is vague and does not convey merging. It would need an object such as 'made into a whole', and it lacks the sense of blending distinct views. (c) 'fit' is intransitive here and idiomatically takes 'fit into' or 'fit together', but 'must fit into an integrated whole' does not say the views are merged and the sense is weaker; 'fit' also would not take the passive 'be fit'. (d) 'be balanced' pairs with 'against' or 'with', not 'into', and balancing keeps views separate rather than integrating them. Tip: in such questions check the preposition after the blank (fuse into, merge into, blend into, melt into) and test the meaning of 'integrated whole'.
explanations: Incorrect: 'be made into an integrated whole' is grammatically possible but vague. It does not express blending of divergent views and is weaker than the precise idiom 'fused into'.
Correct: 'be fused into an integrated whole' means merged so that separate views become one unified account. It matches both the preposition 'into' and the meaning of integration.
Incorrect: 'fit' does not work in the passive 'be fit', and 'fit into' implies placing something in a slot rather than merging views into a whole.
Incorrect: 'be balanced into' is not an idiom. Balancing weighs views against each other and keeps them separate rather than integrating them.
keyfact: Divergent views are 'fused into' an integrated whole: fuse means to blend separate things into one.
option_notes: 'Be made' is the passive of 'make'. 'Make into' means to transform something into another form, as in 'grapes are made into wine'. It is a general transformation verb with no specific sense of merging. It can follow a noun object with 'into', but it lacks the precision needed for combining several viewpoints. In exam questions it is often a plausible but weaker distractor.

'Fuse' means to join or blend two or more things to form a single entity, originally by melting together (Latin fusus, 'poured'). Common usage: 'fuse into', 'fuse with', 'fuse together'. A 'fusion' is such a blend, as in fusion music or cuisine. Related words: merge, amalgamate, coalesce, integrate, meld. It suits the idea of separate views becoming one whole.

'Fit' as a verb means to be the right size or shape, or to install or adapt something. Common phrases: 'fit in', 'fit into', 'fit together', 'fit with'. Its past participle is 'fitted', and 'be fit' as a passive is not standard. It suggests suitability or placement rather than blending, so it is a poor contextual match.

'Balance' means to keep in equilibrium or to weigh one thing against another. It usually takes 'against', 'with' or 'between': 'balance work against rest'. The phrase 'balanced view' means a fair view considering all sides. It does not take 'into' to mean a merged result, so it fails on both idiom and meaning.
related: Agenda 2030 was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2015 with 17 Sustainable Development Goals.
SDG 4 aims at inclusive and equitable quality education for all.
'Fuse into' and 'merge into' signify becoming one; 'balance against' signifies weighing.
'Synthesis' means combining separate elements into a coherent whole.
Collocation: blend with, merge with, integrate into, convert into.
The Brundtland Report (1987) defined sustainable development.
In comprehension questions, answer only from the passage as the directions say.
summary: The answer is (b) 'be fused'. The sentence says divergent perspectives must be merged 'into an integrated whole', and 'fuse into' is the standard idiom for blending separate elements into one unified entity.
topic_notes: This question tests contextual vocabulary and idiomatic usage, a recurring feature of the EPFO General English section. Typical question types are fill in the blanks, synonyms and antonyms, idioms and phrases, error spotting, sentence rearrangement, reading comprehension and cloze tests. For fill-in-the-blank questions, follow a fixed routine: first read the whole sentence for meaning and tone, then check the grammar (tense, voice, number), then look at the words around the blank, especially prepositions, and finally eliminate options that are wrong in either meaning or collocation. Collocation means words that naturally go together, such as fuse into, blend with, merge with, integrate into, divide into, convert into. Useful word families: merge, amalgamate, coalesce, unify, consolidate and synthesise (to combine into a coherent whole). Opposites: separate, divide, fragment, disperse, polarise. In the passage that follows, the theme is education for sustainable development, Agenda 2030 and global citizenship. Reading comprehension items in the same set can ask about the author's view that education should widen one's worldview, make one question 'unsustainability' and build competencies for global challenges. Answer only from the passage and avoid outside knowledge. Practise by noting prepositions with verbs, and revise one-word substitutions, phrasal verbs and commonly confused words. Time management matters: aim for under 30 seconds per vocabulary question so more time remains for passages.

ocr: Which one of the following areas holds a common key position in United Nations ‘Agenda 2030’ ? (a) Environment Gender (b) Globalization (c) (d) Education
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development was adopted by all 193 UN member states at the UN General Assembly on 25 September 2015 (Resolution A/RES/70/1, 'Transforming our World'), and came into effect on 1 January 2016. It has 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and 169 targets, built on the 5 Ps: People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership. It succeeded the Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015), which had 8 goals. SDG 4 is 'Quality Education': inclusive and equitable quality education and lifelong learning opportunities for all. Education is treated as both a goal in itself and an enabler of poverty reduction, health, gender equality, decent work and sustainable consumption. The question, taken from the official paper, treats education as the area holding a common key position. Elimination logic: Environment (SDGs 13, 14, 15), Gender (SDG 5) and Globalization are also present or related, but UPSC's official key picks education as the common key area. Globalization is not an SDG theme at all. Note that the Agenda has SDG 5 on gender and SDGs 6, 7, 12, 13, 14 and 15 on environment, so these are goal-specific rather than the common cross-cutting key pillar here.
explanations: (a) Wrong per the official key: environment is covered by specific goals (SDG 6, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15), but it is not the option UPSC treats as the common key position.
(b) Wrong per the official key: gender is covered by SDG 5 (Gender Equality) and mainstreamed in other goals, but it is not the option the key accepts.
(c) Wrong: globalization is not an SDG or a thematic pillar of Agenda 2030; the Agenda speaks of global partnership (SDG 17), not globalization.
(d) Correct: education (SDG 4, Quality Education) is the area the official answer identifies, and it is central across the Agenda as an enabler of the other goals.
keyfact: Agenda 2030 (adopted 25 Sept 2015): 17 SDGs, 169 targets; SDG 4 Quality Education is the official answer as the common key area.
option_notes: Environment: environmental sustainability is one of the three dimensions of sustainable development (economic, social, environmental). Related SDGs are 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), 13 (Climate Action), 14 (Life Below Water) and 15 (Life on Land). The Paris Agreement (2015) and UNEP are related. UNEP was founded in 1972 after the Stockholm Conference and is headquartered in Nairobi.

Gender: SDG 5 aims to achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls. Targets include ending discrimination and violence, recognising unpaid care work, and ensuring women's participation in leadership. UN Women was created in 2010 and is headquartered in New York. India's related measures include Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015) and the Women's Reservation Act, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam).

Globalization: the growing integration of economies, cultures and populations through trade, investment, technology and migration. Institutions linked to it include the WTO (est. 1995, Geneva), IMF and World Bank (Bretton Woods, 1944). It is not an SDG. Agenda 2030 refers to global partnership under SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals), covering finance, technology, trade and capacity building.

Education: SDG 4 is Quality Education, with 10 targets covering free primary and secondary schooling, early childhood development, technical and vocational skills, tertiary access, and eliminating gender disparity. UNESCO leads the Education 2030 Framework for Action (Incheon Declaration, 2015). India's linked measures are the Right to Education Act 2009 (Article 21A, 86th Amendment 2002) and the National Education Policy 2020.
related: Agenda 2030 was adopted on 25 September 2015 and has 17 SDGs and 169 targets.
SDG 4 is Quality Education; SDG 5 is Gender Equality; SDG 13 is Climate Action.
The MDGs (2000-2015) had 8 goals and preceded the SDGs.
NITI Aayog is India's nodal body for the SDGs and publishes the SDG India Index.
The High-Level Political Forum (HLPF) reviews SDG progress globally.
Article 21A (RTE) was inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment, 2002.
SDG 17 is Partnerships for the Goals.
The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction runs 2015-2030.
summary: The official answer is (d) Education. In UN 'Agenda 2030' (the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development), education is a common key area that is stressed across the framework: it is a stand-alone goal (SDG 4) and also underpins many other goals.
topic_notes: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development was adopted on 25 September 2015 at the UN Sustainable Development Summit in New York and took effect on 1 January 2016, with a 15-year timeline to 2030. It has 17 SDGs and 169 targets, and 231 unique indicators for monitoring. It replaced the MDGs (8 goals, 2000-2015). The SDGs are universal, apply to all countries (not only developing), and are integrated and indivisible. The 5 Ps are People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership. The 17 goals are: 1 No Poverty; 2 Zero Hunger; 3 Good Health and Well-being; 4 Quality Education; 5 Gender Equality; 6 Clean Water and Sanitation; 7 Affordable and Clean Energy; 8 Decent Work and Economic Growth; 9 Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure; 10 Reduced Inequalities; 11 Sustainable Cities and Communities; 12 Responsible Consumption and Production; 13 Climate Action; 14 Life Below Water; 15 Life on Land; 16 Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions; 17 Partnerships for the Goals. Monitoring happens through the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF) under ECOSOC, with Voluntary National Reviews (VNRs). In India, NITI Aayog is the nodal institution and publishes the SDG India Index (first released in 2018); the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) develops the National Indicator Framework. Kerala has often topped the SDG India Index. The UN's Sustainable Development Solutions Network publishes the annual Sustainable Development Report, with Finland usually ranking first and India around 100th. The Rio+20 conference (2012) launched the SDG process. Other angles: the Addis Ababa Action Agenda (financing, 2015), the Paris Agreement (2015) and the Sendai Framework (2015-2030), and the Brundtland Report 'Our Common Future' (1987), which defined sustainable development.

ocr: What is the role of Education in sustainable development ? Education will develop multiple competencies for sustainable development among people all (a) over the world Education will provide books to read on sustainable development (b) Education will increase the global capital (c) Education will reduce interdependence of the people (d)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Education is regarded as both a goal (SDG 4: inclusive and equitable quality education) and an enabler of all 17 SDGs. Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) empowers learners to make informed decisions and take responsible actions for environmental integrity, economic viability and a just society for present and future generations. UNESCO leads ESD, which was the focus of the UN Decade of ESD (2005-2014), then the Global Action Programme (2015-2019) and now 'ESD for 2030'. Target 4.7 says that by 2030 all learners should acquire the knowledge and skills needed to promote sustainable development, including through ESD, sustainable lifestyles, human rights, gender equality, a culture of peace and non-violence, global citizenship and appreciation of cultural diversity. ESD builds key competencies such as systems thinking, anticipatory, normative, strategic, collaborative, critical thinking, self-awareness and integrated problem-solving. India's NEP 2020 also stresses ESD. Elimination: (b) is far too narrow, since education is not just supplying books. (c) 'global capital' is a vague, meaningless economic claim. (d) is the opposite of the truth, because education promotes global citizenship and cooperation, so it increases awareness of interdependence rather than reducing it.
explanations: Correct. Education develops multiple competencies (knowledge, skills, values, attitudes) needed for sustainable development among people everywhere, in line with SDG 4.7 and ESD.
Wrong. Providing books is only a minor input and does not describe education's role in sustainable development, which is about transforming learners' competencies and behaviour.
Wrong. 'Global capital' is not a concept linked to the role of education. Human capital formation is the nearer idea, but this option does not state it.
Wrong. Education fosters global citizenship and understanding of interdependence among peoples. It does not reduce interdependence.
keyfact: Education builds multiple competencies for sustainable development worldwide (SDG 4.7, ESD, UNESCO lead agency).
option_notes: Developing multiple competencies is the core aim of ESD. UNESCO's key competencies include systems thinking, anticipatory, normative, strategic, collaborative and critical thinking, self-awareness and integrated problem-solving. The goal is for learners everywhere to act for a sustainable future. It links to SDG 4.7, UNESCO's ESD for 2030 framework and India's NEP 2020, which emphasises values, life skills and environmental awareness.

Provision of books and learning materials is part of the educational infrastructure under SDG 4.a and 4.c (facilities, qualified teachers). Textbooks matter, but they are only a tool. ESD is about pedagogy, participatory learning and action. Related Indian schemes include Samagra Shiksha, the PM e-Vidya and DIKSHA platforms and the National Book Trust, which publishes books.

'Global capital' is not an established concept in the sustainability and education discourse. Related ideas include human capital (education and skills raising productivity), natural capital and social capital. The World Bank's Human Capital Index (2018) measures how education and health contribute to future productivity. India's HCI score was about 0.49 in 2020.

Interdependence among peoples, economies and ecosystems is a basic premise of sustainable development, and the 1987 Brundtland Report 'Our Common Future' stressed shared global responsibility. Education is meant to build global citizenship (GCED, SDG 4.7), not reduce interdependence. This option misstates the relationship, which makes it a typical UPSC distractor.
related: SDG 4 is quality education; Target 4.7 specifically covers ESD and global citizenship.
UNESCO is the lead UN agency for Education for Sustainable Development.
The Brundtland Report (1987) gave the classic definition of sustainable development.
Agenda 21 (Rio 1992), Chapter 36, deals with education and public awareness.
The 2030 Agenda has 17 SDGs and 169 targets, adopted in 2015.
The UN Decade of ESD ran from 2005 to 2014.
NEP 2020 aligns India's education with SDG 4 and aims for universal access by 2030.
Article 21A (RTE) guarantees free and compulsory education for ages 6-14.
summary: The answer is (a). Education builds knowledge, skills, values and attitudes (multiple competencies) that enable people everywhere to contribute to sustainable development. This is the central idea of Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) and SDG 4, especially Target 4.7.
topic_notes: Sustainable development was defined in the 1987 Brundtland Commission report 'Our Common Future' as development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Key milestones: Stockholm Conference 1972; Rio Earth Summit 1992 with Agenda 21 (Chapter 36 on education, training and public awareness); Millennium Development Goals 2000-2015; Rio+20 in 2012; and the 2030 Agenda with 17 SDGs and 169 targets, adopted in September 2015 and effective from 1 January 2016. SDG 4 is 'Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all'. It has 10 targets: 4.1 to 4.7 are outcome targets, and 4.a, 4.b and 4.c are means of implementation. Target 4.7 covers ESD and Global Citizenship Education (GCED). UNESCO is the lead agency. The UN Decade of ESD ran 2005-2014; the Global Action Programme on ESD ran 2015-2019; 'ESD for 2030' was launched in 2020. The Berlin Declaration on ESD was adopted in 2021. The Incheon Declaration (2015) set the Education 2030 framework. In India, NEP 2020 aligns with SDG 4 and aims at universal school education and 100% GER by 2030. The Right to Education Act 2009 under Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education for ages 6-14. NITI Aayog publishes the SDG India Index. Mission LiFE (2022) promotes sustainable lifestyles. Article 51A(g) makes protecting the environment a fundamental duty. The Education 2030 Steering Committee oversees SDG 4 globally. UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring (GEM) Report tracks progress. Other topics UPSC may ask: the pillars of sustainability (economic, social, environmental), the Paris Agreement 2015, and Agenda 21.

question: We live in a highly interconnected and interdependent world’. What does this phrase mean in the passage ?
options: We are now more connected and dependent upon each other for our survival
The means of transport have become faster
We have become dependent on other countries
subject: General English
detail: This is a vocabulary-in-context question from a reading comprehension passage. The passage itself is not reproduced in the OCR, so the answer rests on the meaning of the two words and on the official key. 'Interconnected' means linked together, so that what happens in one place affects another. 'Interdependent' means mutually dependent: A depends on B and B depends on A. Together they describe a reciprocal relationship among all members of the world community, covering economies, environment, health, security and technology. Option (a) captures this by saying 'more connected' and 'dependent upon each other'. Elimination logic: (b) names only one cause of connectivity, faster transport, and does not explain the phrase. (c) is one-sided, because it says we depend on other countries, whereas 'interdependent' implies mutual reliance, and it also narrows the scope to nations only. (d) states a consequence or a challenge, and the phrase itself does not say challenges are being faced. For such questions, pick the option that paraphrases the phrase most completely and neutrally, and avoid options that add an opinion, a narrower scope or a cause.
explanations: Correct: it restates both parts of the phrase, 'connected' for interconnected and 'dependent upon each other' for interdependent, and it covers the whole world, not one aspect.
Wrong: faster transport may be one reason for greater connectivity, but it is not the meaning of the phrase. It is too narrow and confuses a cause with the meaning.
Wrong: it is one-directional and limited to countries. Interdependence is mutual and includes people, communities, economies and ecosystems, not only states.
Wrong: facing challenges from globalization is an evaluative consequence. The phrase only describes a state of mutual connection and does not say it is a threat.
keyfact: Interconnected = linked with each other; interdependent = mutually reliant, so the phrase means we are more connected and depend on each other.
option_notes: Mutual connectedness and dependence: this is the standard meaning of interdependence. Examples are global supply chains, climate change, pandemics such as COVID-19, and financial contagion such as the 2008 crisis. Interdependence means that actions in one place have effects elsewhere, so cooperation is needed for survival and prosperity. The term is widely used in international relations, for example in the work of Keohane and Nye on 'complex interdependence'.

Faster means of transport, such as jet aviation, container shipping and high-speed rail, have shrunk effective distances and boosted trade and travel. They are an enabler of globalization, not its definition. Containerisation from the 1950s onward cut shipping costs sharply. In an exam this would be a cause or an example, not the meaning of the phrase.

Dependence on other countries is a one-way idea, for example India's import dependence on crude oil or on electronics. It describes asymmetric dependence. Interdependence is reciprocal, as when exporters and importers need each other. It is also narrower, since it leaves out non-state links such as people, businesses and the environment.

Globalization is the growing integration of economies, cultures and societies through trade, investment, technology and migration. It accelerated after the 1990s, and in India after the 1991 reforms (LPG: liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation). Its challenges include inequality, job displacement, cultural homogenisation, and vulnerability to external shocks. This option is a consequence, not the meaning of the phrase.
related: Interdependence means mutual dependence; dependence alone is one-directional.
'Global village' was popularised by Marshall McLuhan.
India's LPG reforms began in 1991.
Prefix 'inter-' means between or among, as in interconnected and interstate.
In RC questions, choose the option that paraphrases the phrase fully and neutrally.
Keohane and Nye developed the theory of 'complex interdependence'.
summary: The answer is (a). 'Interconnected and interdependent' means that people, societies and nations are linked with one another and rely on each other, so each one's wellbeing and survival are tied to the others. The phrase describes mutual dependence in general, not one specific aspect such as transport, dependence of one country, or the challenges of globalization.
topic_notes: Reading comprehension and vocabulary questions in the UPSC EPFO paper test whether a candidate can grasp the meaning of a phrase from its context, not whether they can recall facts. The first step is to break the phrase into its parts: the prefix 'inter-' means between or among, so 'interconnected' means linked with one another, and 'interdependent' means dependent on one another. The second step is to pick the option that paraphrases the whole phrase without adding anything. Common traps are: an option that names only a cause, such as transport or technology; an option that is one-sided, such as 'dependent on other countries'; an option that gives a judgement or consequence, such as 'facing challenges'; and an option that narrows the scope to nations when the phrase covers people, societies and systems. Related vocabulary includes interdependence, globalization, global village (Marshall McLuhan, 1960s), supply chain, and economic integration. Interdependence is often illustrated by climate change, pandemics, financial crises, and trade networks. Related ideas that may appear in the same passage include cooperation, global governance (UN, WTO, WHO, IMF), sustainable development, and shared responsibility. Strategy: read the sentences before and after the phrase, look for the author's tone, avoid extreme words such as 'only' and 'always', and check each option for scope and direction. Similar question types include synonyms and antonyms, the tone of the passage, the central idea, and an inference from a line.

ocr: ‘The world's life-supporting resources are being depleted at a faster rate than ever before!’ What does this phrase mean in the passage ? Today we are facing an acute shortage of food products (a) Medical health systems are deteriorating at a fast pace (b) The natural resources necessary to sustain life are reducing drastically (c) Human life is becoming more dependent on the support of technology (d)
subject: General English
detail: This is a vocabulary-in-context question from a reading comprehension passage on environment and resource use. The key terms are 'life-supporting resources' and 'depleted'. 'Life-supporting' describes whatever sustains life on Earth: clean air, fresh water, fertile soil, forests, oceans, biodiversity and energy sources. 'Depleted' means used up, exhausted or greatly reduced, and 'at a faster rate than ever before' stresses acceleration. Together they describe natural resources shrinking drastically, which is option (c). Elimination: (a) narrows the phrase to food products only and speaks of an 'acute shortage', which is a much narrower claim than the phrase makes. (b) shifts to medical health systems, which are man-made institutions rather than resources that sustain life. (d) reverses the idea by talking about dependence on technology, whereas the phrase concerns loss of resources. In such questions, choose the option that paraphrases both the scope (general, natural resources) and the direction (decline) of the sentence, and reject options that are too narrow, off-topic or opposite. Related concepts include overexploitation, the carrying capacity of Earth, Earth Overshoot Day, and sustainable development.
explanations: Wrong: food is only one of the life-supporting resources, and the sentence does not say there is an acute food shortage. This option is too narrow and over-specific.
Wrong: medical health systems are human-made institutions, not natural life-supporting resources. The sentence says nothing about healthcare.
Right: 'life-supporting resources' means natural resources such as air, water, soil and forests, and 'depleted at a faster rate' means they are reducing drastically. This is the official answer.
Wrong: the sentence is about the loss of resources, not about humans depending more on technology. This option introduces an unrelated idea.
keyfact: 'Life-supporting resources depleted' = natural resources necessary to sustain life are reducing drastically (option c).
option_notes: Food shortage: refers to inadequate availability of food, linked to food security. India's National Food Security Act, 2013 gives subsidised grain to about two-thirds of the population. The FAO and the Global Hunger Index track hunger. Food is one of several life-supporting resources, so it does not capture the full phrase here.

Health systems: the network of hospitals, personnel, financing and policy that delivers healthcare. India's Ayushman Bharat (2018) includes PM-JAY and Health and Wellness Centres. The WHO assesses health systems. Health systems are man-made institutions, so they are not 'life-supporting resources' in the natural sense.

Natural resources: materials from nature that sustain life and economies, such as air, water, soil, forests, minerals and biodiversity. They are classed as renewable (water, forests) or non-renewable (coal, oil). Overuse causes depletion. Concepts such as sustainable development (Brundtland Report, 1987) and Earth Overshoot Day address this problem.

Technological dependence: the growing reliance of society on digital and technological tools in daily life, covering AI, automation and the internet. India's Digital India programme started in 2015. This is a social trend and not a measure of resource depletion, so it does not match the sentence.
related: Depleted means used up or greatly reduced; antonym: replenished.
Brundtland Report (1987) defined sustainable development.
Earth Overshoot Day marks when yearly resource use exceeds Earth's regeneration.
National Green Tribunal was established in 2010.
Environment (Protection) Act was enacted in 1986.
Coal and petroleum are non-renewable resources; water and forests are renewable.
SDG 12 deals with responsible consumption and production.
Rio Earth Summit took place in 1992.
summary: The answer is (c). The phrase 'life-supporting resources are being depleted at a faster rate than ever before' means that natural resources needed to sustain life (air, water, soil, forests, biodiversity, minerals) are shrinking drastically. 'Life-supporting' points to natural systems, and 'depleted' means used up or reduced.
topic_notes: Topic: vocabulary and inference in reading comprehension, with an environmental theme. Approach: first find the literal meaning of the key words, then match the option that preserves both scope and direction. 'Life-supporting' refers to systems that sustain life, such as the atmosphere, hydrosphere, soils and biosphere. 'Depleted' means exhausted or reduced, and its synonyms include drained, exhausted and diminished, while antonyms include replenished and augmented. Environmental background useful for context: natural resources are renewable or non-renewable. The Brundtland Commission (1987) defined sustainable development as meeting present needs without compromising future generations. Earth Overshoot Day marks when humanity's demand exceeds what the Earth can regenerate in a year, and it now falls in roughly late July to early August. The UN Sustainable Development Goals (2015) include SDG 12, responsible consumption and production, SDG 13, climate action, and SDG 15, life on land. Key events are the Stockholm Conference (1972), the Rio Earth Summit (1992), the Paris Agreement (2015) and COP meetings. In India, relevant bodies and laws include the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, the National Green Tribunal (2010) and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. Typical exam traps: options that are too narrow (only food), off-topic (health, technology), or reversed in meaning. Tips: read the sentence in context, avoid options that bring in outside ideas, and prefer the broader paraphrase when the phrase is general.

question: There is an increasing recognition of the importance of global citizenship’ because : People want to travel more and live in different parts of the world
options: It will unite people from all over the world to face the challenges of the 21% century
People believe that there is a future in foreign countries
People will cooperate with each other to save themselves from natural disasters
subject: Computers
detail: Global citizenship is the idea that individuals belong to a broader world community beyond their nation-state and share responsibility for its welfare. Its importance is growing because the main challenges of the 21st century are transnational: climate change, pandemics (COVID-19), terrorism, cyber threats, migration, inequality and financial instability. No single country can solve these alone, so a sense of common humanity and cooperation becomes necessary. UNESCO promotes Global Citizenship Education (GCED), and UN Sustainable Development Goal 4.7 explicitly calls for education for sustainable development and global citizenship. The Preamble-style ideals of 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' echo the same view in the Indian tradition. Elimination logic: the options about wanting to travel, believing in a future abroad, or cooperating only to survive natural disasters are narrow, self-interested or limited in scope. They describe personal motives or a single type of problem, not the broad, value-based reason for global citizenship. The option about uniting people to face 21st-century challenges is comprehensive and matches the concept, hence it is the answer.
explanations: The key marks (b) correct. In the official numbering, (b) is the option that global citizenship will unite people worldwide to face the challenges of the 21st century. This is the broad, principled reason behind the concept.

The option about people wanting to travel more and live in different parts of the world is a personal lifestyle motive. Mobility alone does not explain the recognition of global citizenship as a value.
The claim that people believe there is a future in foreign countries is about migration for opportunity. It is narrow and self-interested, and not the reason the idea is gaining importance.

The option about cooperating to save themselves from natural disasters covers only one type of challenge and frames cooperation as self-preservation. It is too limited compared with the full range of global challenges.
keyfact: Global citizenship is valued because shared 21st-century challenges like climate change and pandemics need united global action (SDG 4.7, UNESCO GCED).
option_notes: Option (a) as printed, 'People want to travel more and live in different parts of the world', reflects globalisation-driven mobility: cheaper transport, work and study abroad, and diaspora growth. India has one of the world's largest diasporas, about 18 million emigrants per UN data. Mobility makes people aware of global links, but it is not the principled basis of global citizenship.

Option (b) is the official answer: that global citizenship will unite people from all over the world to face 21st-century challenges. These challenges include climate change (Paris Agreement 2015), pandemics, terrorism, and inequality. UN SDGs (2015, Agenda 2030) rest on shared global responsibility, and UNESCO's GCED builds the required values and skills.

Option (c), 'People believe that there is a future in foreign countries', refers to brain drain and economic migration. Skilled workers move to countries such as the USA, UK, Canada and Gulf states for better prospects. This is a push-pull migration factor and not a defining reason for global citizenship, which concerns shared values and responsibilities.

Option (d), 'People will cooperate with each other to save themselves from natural disasters', relates to disaster cooperation such as the Sendai Framework (2015-2030) for Disaster Risk Reduction, and India's own NDMA (2005 Act). Such cooperation is valuable, but it covers one type of challenge and is not the full rationale for global citizenship.
related: SDG 4.7 covers education for sustainable development and global citizenship.
UNESCO promotes Global Citizenship Education (GCED).
India's G20 2023 theme: One Earth, One Family, One Future (Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam).
Article 51 DPSP promotes international peace and security.
Agenda 2030 with 17 SDGs was adopted in September 2015.
Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction covers 2015-2030.
The Paris Agreement on climate change was adopted in 2015.
summary: The official answer is (b). The question is OCR-jumbled: the option labelled (b) in the official key is the one stating that global citizenship will unite people from all over the world to face the challenges of the 21st century. Global citizenship is valued because shared global problems need collective, cross-border responses.
topic_notes: Global citizenship means identifying with humanity as a whole, with rights and duties that go beyond national borders. Key drivers are globalisation, digital connectivity, and shared global risks. UNESCO defines Global Citizenship Education (GCED) as fostering knowledge, skills, values and attitudes for a more inclusive, just and peaceful world. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon launched the Global Education First Initiative in 2012, with global citizenship as a priority. SDG 4, target 4.7 (Agenda 2030, adopted September 2015) covers education for sustainable development, human rights, gender equality, a culture of peace and non-violence, global citizenship and appreciation of cultural diversity. Related global frameworks: the UN Charter (1945), Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), Paris Agreement (2015), Sendai Framework (2015), and the WHO's role in pandemics. In India, the idea links to the ancient ideal 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' (the world is one family), which was also the theme of India's G20 presidency in 2023 ('One Earth, One Family, One Future'). The Constitution's Article 51 (Directive Principle) directs the State to promote international peace and security, respect international law, and encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration. Fundamental Duties under Article 51A promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood. NEP 2020 also stresses values of global citizenship in education. Critics argue that global citizenship can clash with national identity and may be unevenly accessible. Likely UPSC angles: UNESCO programmes, SDG targets, G20 themes, and Directive Principles on international relations.

question: Which one of the following was not provided 24 in the Regulating Act of 1773 ? *
options: It made the Presidency of Bengal supreme over those of Bombay and Madras in matters relating to war and peace
The tenure of the Governor-General and his Councillors was fixed as five years
The Supreme Court of Justice was 25. established at Calcutta
The Governor-General-in-Council was authorized to appoint successors to Bombay and Madras Presidencies
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The Regulating Act of 1773 (Act of 1773, passed by Lord North's government) was the first parliamentary step to control the East India Company's affairs after the financial crisis and the misrule seen after Plassey and Buxar. It designated the Governor of Bengal as Governor-General of Fort William, with a Council of four members, and the Governor-General had a casting vote. Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General, and the Councillors named were Clavering, Monson, Barwell and Philip Francis. The tenure of the Governor-General and Councillors was fixed at five years, and they could be removed only by the Crown on the Directors' representation. Bombay and Madras were made subordinate to Bengal in war, peace and diplomacy, except in emergencies or with prior Directors' orders. A Supreme Court was set up at Calcutta with a Chief Justice and three puisne judges; Sir Elijah Impey was the first Chief Justice. Company servants were barred from private trade and from accepting gifts. Directors had to report revenue, civil and military matters to the British government. Elimination: (a), (b) and (c) are real provisions. Only (d) invents a power of appointment that the Act did not give, since the Directors appointed the Presidency governors.
explanations: Incorrect choice for 'not provided': this was provided. Bengal was made supreme over Bombay and Madras in war and peace matters.
Incorrect choice for 'not provided': this was provided. The Governor-General and Councillors had a five-year term, removable only by the Crown.
Incorrect choice for 'not provided': this was provided. The Supreme Court was established at Calcutta under the Act, and it began functioning in 1774.
Correct choice: the Act gave no such power. Governors of Bombay and Madras were appointed by the Court of Directors, so this was not provided.
keyfact: Regulating Act 1773: Governor-General of Bengal with a four-member Council, five-year term, Supreme Court at Calcutta, Bengal supreme in war and peace; the Governor-General had no power to appoint Bombay or Madras governors.
option_notes: Bengal's supremacy: Section of the 1773 Act made the Governor-General-in-Council of Fort William superior over Bombay and Madras in matters of war and peace. Presidencies could not declare war or make treaties without his prior consent, except in emergencies or on direct Directors' orders. It was a first attempt at centralisation, though the control was weak and often ineffective in practice.

Tenure: the Act fixed a five-year term for the Governor-General (Warren Hastings) and four Councillors (Clavering, Monson, Barwell, Francis). They were removable only by the Crown on the Directors' representation. The Governor-General had a casting vote, but decisions were by majority, which caused friction between Hastings and the Council majority.

Supreme Court at Calcutta: established under the Act with a Chief Justice and three puisne judges, with Sir Elijah Impey as first Chief Justice. It began in 1774 and had jurisdiction over British subjects and Company servants in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Its conflict with the Council led to the Act of Settlement 1781 clarifying jurisdiction.

Appointment of successors: not a power of the Governor-General-in-Council. The Court of Directors appointed Presidency governors, and the Crown had removal rights over the top officers. The Pitt's India Act 1784 and later Acts shifted more control to the Crown but did not give this power as the option states.
related: The Regulating Act of 1773 made Warren Hastings the first Governor-General of Bengal.
Sir Elijah Impey was the first Chief Justice of the Calcutta Supreme Court.
The Pitt's India Act 1784 set up the Board of Control for political affairs.
The Charter Act 1833 made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India; Bentinck was the first.
The Amending Act of 1781 clarified the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.
The Governor-General's Council under the 1773 Act had four members with a five-year tenure.
The Government of India Act 1858 ended Company rule and transferred power to the Crown.
summary: The answer is (d). The Regulating Act of 1773 did not authorise the Governor-General-in-Council to appoint successors to the Bombay and Madras Presidencies. Governors of those Presidencies were appointed by the Company's Court of Directors, and the Act only made them subordinate to Bengal in matters of war and peace.
topic_notes: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first step by the British Parliament to regulate the East India Company, following the Company's near bankruptcy and its request for a loan of about 1 million pounds. Lord North's government introduced it. Main provisions: the Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Fort William; a four-member Council was created with a casting vote for the Governor-General; Bombay and Madras were subordinated to Bengal in war and peace; the Supreme Court was established at Calcutta in 1774; Company servants were forbidden from private trade and from taking presents; the Directors' term was set at four years, with one-fourth retiring each year; the qualification for voting in the Court of Proprietors was raised to 1,000 pounds; the Company had to submit revenue and civil and military correspondence to the Crown. Weaknesses: the Governor-General was often outvoted, the Supreme Court's jurisdiction overlapped with the Council, and control over the Presidencies was weak. Later changes: Amending Act 1781 (Act of Settlement) clarified jurisdiction; Pitt's India Act 1784 created the Board of Control and a dual system; Charter Acts of 1793, 1813, 1833 and 1853 progressively reduced the Company's powers; the Government of India Act 1858 transferred rule to the Crown. Under the Charter Act 1833 the Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India, with Bentinck as the first. The Regulating Act is also called the first constitutional milestone because it introduced parliamentary control over the Company's administration.

question: Which one of the following statements about the Government of India Act of 1935 is not correct ?
options: It was an outcome of the Round Table Conferences
It provided for the establishment of an All India Federation
It retained the authority of the Secretary of State over the Government of India
It introduced the provision of Provincial Autonomy
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: The Government of India Act, 1935 was the longest constitutional document passed by the British Parliament for India up to then. It followed the three Round Table Conferences (1930-32), the Simon Commission Report (1930), the White Paper (1933) and the Joint Select Committee under Lord Linlithgow. Its main features were: an All India Federation of British Indian provinces and princely states (never realised because the princes did not accede); abolition of dyarchy in provinces and introduction of Provincial Autonomy; introduction of dyarchy at the Centre; bicameral legislatures in six provinces; separate electorates extended to depressed classes, women and labour; a Federal Court (1937); the Reserve Bank of India; and Federal, Provincial and Joint Public Service Commissions. It abolished the Council of India, which had advised the Secretary of State since 1858, and the Secretary of State was left with only an advisory team. The question asks for the INCORRECT statement. Since (a), (b) and (d) are plainly true, (c) is the one that is not correct. Note that the Secretary of State's powers were curtailed in provincial matters, though the Governor-General retained special powers.
explanations: Incorrect choice for this question: the statement is true, since the Act came out of the Round Table Conferences, the White Paper and the Joint Select Committee.
Incorrect choice: the statement is true, as the Act provided for an All India Federation of provinces and princely states, though it never came into operation.

Correct choice: the statement is not correct, because the Act abolished the India Council and cut down the Secretary of State's control, particularly over the provinces, instead of retaining his authority as it stood.
Incorrect choice: the statement is true, as the Act abolished provincial dyarchy and introduced Provincial Autonomy, which took effect in 1937.
keyfact: The 1935 Act abolished the Council of India and introduced Provincial Autonomy; the proposed All India Federation never came into being.
option_notes: The Round Table Conferences were held in London in 1930, 1930-31 and 1932 to discuss constitutional reform after the Simon Commission. Congress boycotted the first, Gandhi attended the second after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, and the third was thinly attended. The Communal Award (1932) and the Poona Pact followed. Their discussions led to the White Paper of 1933 and then the 1935 Act.

The proposed All India Federation was to unite British Indian provinces and princely states under a Federal Legislature with two houses. It required accession by states representing at least half of the states' population and seats in the Council of State. The princes did not agree, so the federal part never came into force and the Centre continued under the 1919 arrangements.

Before 1935 the Secretary of State for India, a British Cabinet minister, controlled Indian administration, assisted by the Council of India created in 1858. The 1935 Act abolished the Council, replacing it with a body of advisers. His power over provincial governments was reduced, but the Governor-General and Governors retained special responsibilities and discretionary powers.

Provincial Autonomy meant that provinces became autonomous units with a responsible ministry answerable to the legislature, and dyarchy in the provinces was abolished. Elections were held in 1937 in eleven provinces. Congress formed ministries in most of them. Governors still had special powers, and the Provincial Legislative Lists were separate from those of the Centre.
related: The 1935 Act abolished the Council of India, set up in 1858.
Provincial elections under the 1935 Act were held in 1937; Congress won 8 of 11 provinces.
The Federal Court was established in 1937 at Delhi; the first Chief Justice was Sir Maurice Gwyer.
The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy in provinces; the 1935 Act ended it there and brought it to the Centre (never implemented).
The Act separated Burma from India in 1937.
The Reserve Bank of India was established in 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934.
The Federation never came into effect because the princely states did not accede.
The Constitution of India drew its federal scheme and Governor's office from the 1935 Act.
summary: The answer is (c). The Government of India Act, 1935 did not retain the Secretary of State's authority over the Government of India in the old form; it abolished the India Council and reduced the Secretary of State's control, especially over the provinces, which gained autonomy. The other three statements are correct.
topic_notes: The Government of India Act, 1935 was passed in August 1935 and was largely the basis of the Constitution of India, which borrowed its federal scheme, Governor's office, Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions and administrative details. It had 321 sections and 10 schedules. Background: the Simon Commission (1927-30, all-white), the Nehru Report (1928), Jinnah's 14 points, the three Round Table Conferences, the Communal Award (1932), the Poona Pact (1932) and the White Paper (1933). Key features: a three-fold division of powers into Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists, with residuary powers given to the Governor-General; dyarchy at the Centre for reserved subjects such as defence and external affairs; bicameralism in Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam and the United Provinces; the separation of Burma from India (1937) and the creation of Sind and Orissa as provinces; an increase in the franchise to about 10 percent of the population; the Federal Court at Delhi (1937); the Reserve Bank of India (1935 onward, begun in 1935 and commencing in 1935 as an institution); and the Federal Railway Authority. Criticism: Nehru called it a charter of slavery, and Jinnah called it thoroughly rotten. It remained in force until 1947, after which the Indian Independence Act 1947 amended it for use as an interim constitution. Other angles: the Government of India Acts of 1858, 1909 (Morley-Minto), 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford, dyarchy in provinces) and the Cabinet Mission 1946.

question:
Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the code given below the Lists: 26. List I List II (Congress (President) Session) A. Lahore Session,
1. Madan Mohan 1909 Malaviya B. Calcutta Session,
2. Raghunath 1911 Narasinha Mudholkar C. Bankipore
3. Bishan Narayan 27. Session, 1912 Dar D. Madras Session,
4. Bhupendra Nath 1914 Bose Code: A B Cc D
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The OCR-garbled question pairs each Congress session and year with its president. Read cleanly, List I is A. Lahore 1909, B. Calcutta 1911, C. Bankipore 1912, D. Madras 1914. List II is 1. Madan Mohan Malaviya, 2. Raghunath Narasinha Mudholkar, 3. Bishan Narayan Dar, 4. Bhupendra Nath Bose. These sessions fall in the period after the Surat split of 1907, when the Moderates controlled the Congress and the Morley-Minto reforms (1909) shaped politics. The Lahore session of 1909 is easily confused with the famous Lahore session of 1929, which Jawaharlal Nehru presided over and which declared Purna Swaraj. The 1911 Calcutta session is remembered because 'Jana Gana Mana' was first sung there. Bankipore (Patna) in 1912 was the first session held in Bihar. The 1914 Madras session was presided over by Bhupendra Nath Bose, a Bengal Moderate. For elimination, Malaviya at Lahore 1909 is certain. That removes (c) and (d), which give A as 4. Dar at Calcutta 1911 is well known, which removes (b) and leaves (a).
explanations: Correct. A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4 is exactly the historical sequence of presidents: Malaviya 1909, Dar 1911, Mudholkar 1912, Bose 1914.
Wrong. It makes Dar the president of 1912 and Mudholkar of 1911, swapping B and C. Dar presided at Calcutta 1911 and Mudholkar at Bankipore 1912.
Wrong. It gives Lahore 1909 to Bose and Madras 1914 to Malaviya. Malaviya presided in 1909 and Bose in 1914.
Wrong. It also swaps A and D, and in addition swaps B and C.
keyfact: Lahore 1909 – Malaviya; Calcutta 1911 – B. N. Dar; Bankipore 1912 – R. N. Mudholkar; Madras 1914 – Bhupendra Nath Bose (answer a).
option_notes: Option (a) pairs Lahore 1909 with Malaviya, Calcutta 1911 with Dar, Bankipore 1912 with Mudholkar and Madras 1914 with Bose. These were all Moderate-era sessions after the Surat split of 1907. They fall between the Allahabad session of 1910 under Sir William Wedderburn and the Karachi session of 1913 under Syed Mohammad Bahadur. This is the correct matching.

Option (b) pairs Lahore with Malaviya and Madras with Bose, which is right, but it swaps Calcutta and Bankipore. It would give Mudholkar to Calcutta 1911 and Dar to Bankipore 1912. Remember that Calcutta 1911 is the session where Jana Gana Mana was first sung, under Bishan Narayan Dar.

Option (c) gives Lahore 1909 to Bhupendra Nath Bose and Madras 1914 to Malaviya. Bose presided in 1914 at Madras. Malaviya presided in 1909, 1918 (Delhi), 1932 and 1933. This option also swaps Calcutta and Bankipore.

Option (d) wrongly gives Lahore 1909 to Bose and Madras 1914 to Malaviya, and it gets Calcutta and Bankipore right only in the wrong order. Its pairing of Calcutta with Dar and Bankipore with Mudholkar is wrong in the same way as (c) once the shifted letters are considered. It is a mirror-image distractor.
related: Jana Gana Mana was first sung at the Calcutta Congress session on 27 December 1911.
Lahore 1929 under Jawaharlal Nehru declared Purna Swaraj, and Independence Day was observed on 26 January 1930.
Malaviya was Congress president four times: 1909, 1918, 1932 and 1933.
The Surat split of 1907 divided the Congress into Moderates and Extremists.
W. C. Bonnerjee was the first Congress president, in 1885 at Bombay.
Annie Besant was the first woman Congress president, in 1917 at Calcutta.
The Lucknow session of 1916 under A. C. Majumdar reunited the Congress and saw the Lucknow Pact with the Muslim League.
Bankipore, near Patna, hosted the 1912 session, the first in Bihar.
statements: A — Correct: Lahore 1909 matches 1 (Madan Mohan Malaviya). Malaviya presided over the 1909 Lahore session, his first term as Congress president. He was president four times in all (1909, 1918, 1932, 1933). He founded Banaras Hindu University in 1916 and was awarded the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 2014. He also led the Hindu Mahasabha and edited papers such as Hindustan and The Leader. The 1909 session came after the Morley-Minto Reforms and the Surat split, and it welcomed the reforms with reservations. Do not confuse it with Lahore 1929 under Nehru.

B — Correct: Calcutta 1911 matches 3 (Bishan Narayan Dar). Dar was a Kashmiri Pandit lawyer from Lucknow and a Moderate. At this session 'Jana Gana Mana' by Rabindranath Tagore was first sung on 27 December 1911. The session met after the Delhi Durbar announced the annulment of the Partition of Bengal and the shifting of the capital to Delhi. The Congress welcomed the annulment and thanked the Crown. Dar later served in the Imperial Legislative Council.

C — Correct: Bankipore 1912 matches 2 (Raghunath Narasinha Mudholkar). Mudholkar was a Maharashtrian lawyer and Moderate from Amravati, and a member of the Imperial Legislative Council. The Bankipore session, near Patna, was the first held in Bihar. It followed the creation of the new province of Bihar and Orissa in 1912, after Bengal was reorganised. Mudholkar also served on the Indian Public Services Commission and was later associated with Berar politics.

D — Correct: Madras 1914 matches 4 (Bhupendra Nath Bose). Bose was a Bengal lawyer and Moderate who was a member of the Imperial Legislative Council and the Council of the Secretary of State for India. The Madras session of December 1914 met just after World War I broke out and expressed loyalty to the Empire. It also debated issues of Indians in the colonies and the Council of India. Annie Besant was based at Adyar, Madras, at this time.
summary: The correct answer is (a): A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4. Malaviya presided at Lahore in 1909, Bishan Narayan Dar at Calcutta in 1911, R. N. Mudholkar at Bankipore in 1912 and Bhupendra Nath Bose at Madras in 1914.
topic_notes: The early Congress presidents are a staple of UPSC and EPFO history questions. The first session was at Bombay in 1885 under W. C. Bonnerjee. Dadabhai Naoroji presided in 1886 (Calcutta), 1893 (Lahore) and 1906 (Calcutta, where swaraj was declared as the goal). The Surat split of 1907 came under Rash Behari Ghosh, with the Extremists led by Tilak, Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal on one side and the Moderates on the other. After it, Moderates held the Congress until the Lucknow session of 1916 (A. C. Majumdar), where the two wings reunited and the Congress-League Pact was signed. Key presidents: Badruddin Tyabji 1887, the first Muslim president; George Yule 1888, the first English president; Annie Besant 1917, the first woman president; Sarojini Naidu 1925, the first Indian woman president; Motilal Nehru at Amritsar 1919; Lala Lajpat Rai at the 1920 special Calcutta session; C. R. Das at Gaya 1922; Gandhi at Belgaum 1924, his only term; Jawaharlal Nehru at Lahore 1929; Vallabhbhai Patel at Karachi 1931; Subhas Chandra Bose at Haripura 1938 and Tripuri 1939; Maulana Azad at Ramgarh 1940; J. B. Kripalani in 1947; Pattabhi Sitaramayya in 1948. Madan Mohan Malaviya was the only person besides Nehru and Azad to hold the post more than once among the key names. The sessions of 1909 to 1914 were dominated by Moderates and reacted to the Morley-Minto Reforms, the annulment of the Partition of Bengal (1911), the move of the capital to Delhi, and World War I.

ocr: Who among the following started the Bhonsala Military School at Nashik ? (a) V.D. Savarkar (b) MLR. Jayakar (c) N.C. Kelkar (d) B.S. Moonje Arrange the following events associated with Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya in chronological order, starting with the earliest : 1. Founding of the Banaras Hindu University 2. Formation of the Congress Nationalist Party 8. Founding of the English newspaper “The Leader’ 4. Founding of the Hindu Boarding House at Allahabad
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: The Bhonsala Military School, Nashik, was set up in 1937 by Dr. B.S. Moonje (1872-1948) under the Central Hindu Military Education Society (founded 1935). It was named after the Bhonsle dynasty of Shivaji and aimed to give Hindu youth military training and to prepare them for the army and for national service. Moonje was a doctor from the Central Provinces and an early follower of Tilak in the Congress. He later became a leading Hindu Mahasabha figure and served as its president. He was also a mentor of K.B. Hedgewar, founder of the RSS (1925). In 1931 he visited Italy, met Mussolini and studied Fascist youth organisations such as the Balilla. These visits influenced his plan for a military school. He also attended the Round Table Conference (1930-31). Elimination logic: Savarkar is linked with Abhinav Bharat, Hindutva and Ratnagiri, Jayakar with Liberal and Swarajist politics and mediation, and Kelkar with Tilak's Kesari and the Responsivist wing. Moonje is the only one tied to military education and to the Nashik school.
explanations: Incorrect. V.D. Savarkar was a revolutionary and ideologue who led Abhinav Bharat, wrote 'Hindutva', and headed the Hindu Mahasabha from 1937 to 1943. He did not found the Bhonsala school.
Incorrect. M.R. Jayakar was a lawyer and Liberal and Swarajist leader known for mediating the Gandhi-Irwin talks (with Sapru) and the Poona Pact. He was not the founder of the Nashik school.
Incorrect. N.C. Kelkar was Tilak's close associate, editor of Kesari and Tilak's biographer, and a Responsivist leader. He had no role in founding the Bhonsala school.
Correct. B.S. Moonje founded the Bhonsala Military School in Nashik in 1937 through the Central Hindu Military Education Society. This matches the official answer.
keyfact: Bhonsala Military School, Nashik (1937) was founded by Dr. B.S. Moonje; Malaviya order: Boarding House 1904, The Leader 1909, BHU 1916, Nationalist Party 1934.
option_notes: V.D. Savarkar (1883-1966) founded Mitra Mela and Abhinav Bharat, was tried in the Nasik conspiracy case (1910), and was transported to the Cellular Jail. He wrote 'The Indian War of Independence 1857' and 'Essentials of Hindutva' (1923). He was Hindu Mahasabha president from 1937 to 1943 and was tried in the Gandhi murder case (1948) but acquitted.

M.R. Jayakar (1873-1959) was a Bombay barrister who joined the Swaraj Party and later turned Liberal. He took part in the Round Table Conferences, mediated with Sapru between Gandhi and Irwin in 1931, and helped settle the Poona Pact in 1932. He was a Federal Court judge from 1937 and the first Vice-Chancellor of Pune University.

N.C. (Narasimha Chintaman) Kelkar (1872-1947) was a Tilak loyalist, editor of Kesari and Mahratta, and author of Tilak's biography. In the 1920s he led the Responsivist wing of the Swarajists with Jayakar and Moonje. He was a member of the Central Legislative Assembly and was active in the Hindu Mahasabha.

B.S. Moonje (1872-1948) was a doctor from Nagpur and a Tilakite Congressman. He was Hindu Mahasabha president and Hedgewar's mentor. He met Mussolini in 1931 and founded the Central Hindu Military Education Society (1935) and the Bhonsala Military School (1937). He opposed the Poona Pact and was an official Hindu Mahasabha delegate to the Second Round Table Conference.
related: Bhonsala Military School, Nashik was founded in 1937 by B.S. Moonje.
The Central Hindu Military Education Society was founded in 1935.
Moonje met Mussolini in Italy in 1931 and studied Fascist youth organisations.
K.B. Hedgewar founded the RSS in 1925 at Nagpur; Moonje was his mentor.
