Malaviya founded the Hindu Boarding House (1904), The Leader (1909), BHU (1916) and the Congress Nationalist Party (1934), so the order is 4-3-1-2.
Malaviya was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2015.
Savarkar was Hindu Mahasabha president from 1937 to 1943.
Jayakar and Sapru mediated in the Gandhi-Irwin talks of 1931.
summary: The answer is (d) B.S. Moonje. Dr. Balkrishna Shivram Moonje, a Hindu Mahasabha leader and Nagpur physician, founded the Bhonsala Military School at Nashik in 1937 through the Central Hindu Military Education Society, which he had set up in 1935. The image also shows a second question on Malaviya's chronology, but the official answer (d) matches only the Bhonsala question.
topic_notes:
The topic is the Hindu Mahasabha leadership and its allied personalities. It also covers Malaviya's work, which the second question in the image tests.

Bhonsala Military School, Nashik: Founded 1937 by Dr. B.S. Moonje through the Central Hindu Military Education Society (est. 1935). It is named after Shivaji's Bhonsle dynasty. The school trained boys for the armed forces and encouraged militarisation of Hindu youth, which Moonje had seen in Italian youth movements in 1931.

B.S. Moonje: Born 1872 at Bilaspur, trained as a doctor. He was a Tilak follower in the Central Provinces and part of the Responsivist group with Kelkar and Jayakar. He was Hindu Mahasabha president (acting 1927-28 and again in the 1930s), mentored Hedgewar, and was associated with the RSS.

Hindu Mahasabha: Early forms existed in 1906-15. It was formally established in 1915 at Haridwar, with Malaviya a key figure. Savarkar led it from 1937 to 1943, and Syama Prasad Mookerjee later led it.

Malaviya timeline: Hindu Boarding House, Allahabad (1904); The Leader (1909); Banaras Hindu University (1916); Congress Nationalist Party (1934, with M.S. Aney). He presided over the Congress four times (1909, 1918, 1932, 1933) and was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2015. The correct order of the events is therefore 4, 3, 1, 2.

Other angles UPSC could ask: the Poona Pact (1932), the Communal Award, the Responsivist cooperation policy, Savarkar's Hindutva, Hedgewar and the RSS (1925), Gandhi's murder trial, and the Round Table Conferences.

question: An employee shall be covered under the provisions of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, should the employee be drawing a maximum monthly wage of :
subject: Indian Economy
detail: The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 regulates the payment of wages to certain classes of employed persons, ensuring timely payment and preventing unauthorised deductions. Coverage depends on a wage ceiling in Section 1(6). The original ceiling was Rs 200 per month. It was raised to Rs 1,600 (1982), Rs 6,500 (2005) and Rs 18,000 (2012). The Payment of Wages (Amendment) Act, 2005 empowered the appropriate Government to revise the ceiling every 5 years based on the Consumer Price Index. On that basis the Central Government revised it to Rs 24,000 per month from 1 January 2017. Wage periods must not exceed one month (Section 4). Wages must be paid by the 7th day after the wage period for establishments with fewer than 1,000 workers, and by the 10th day for others (Section 5). The Act applies to factories, railways and industrial or other establishments as notified. The Act has since been subsumed in the Code on Wages, 2019, which covers all employees irrespective of wage ceiling. For this question, 15,000 and 21,000 are ceilings from other statutes (EPF and ESI), and 18,000 is the earlier PW Act ceiling, so (d) is the one that matches the PW Act ceiling.
explanations: Wrong: Rs 15,000 is the EPF statutory wage ceiling for compulsory coverage (from 2014), not the Payment of Wages Act ceiling.
Wrong: Rs 18,000 was the Payment of Wages Act ceiling after the 2012 revision, but it was superseded by the 2017 revision.
Wrong: Rs 21,000 is the ESI Act wage ceiling for coverage (from 2017), not the Payment of Wages Act ceiling.
Correct: Rs 24,000 per month is the ceiling notified by the Central Government effective 1 January 2017, so the Act covers employees drawing up to this amount.
keyfact: Payment of Wages Act, 1936 covers employees earning up to Rs 24,000 per month (from 1 January 2017).
option_notes: Rs 15,000 is the monthly wage ceiling under the EPF and MP Act, 1952 for compulsory coverage, in force since 1 September 2014 (raised from Rs 6,500). Employees earning above it can be covered voluntarily if employer and employee agree. A proposal to raise it to Rs 21,000 has been discussed but not implemented. It is the basis for the maximum 12 percent contribution on Rs 15,000.

Rs 18,000 was the Payment of Wages Act ceiling introduced by the 2012 notification, which raised it from Rs 10,000. It applied until the revision of 2017. It is a typical distractor because many students remember the older figure. It is also near the minimum wage level of some schemes, but has no current statutory role in this Act.

Rs 21,000 is the ESI Act ceiling for coverage of employees, raised from Rs 15,000 effective 1 January 2017. The ESI contribution rates are 3.25 percent by the employer and 0.75 percent by the employee. The ceiling for persons with disabilities is Rs 25,000. It is also the ceiling used under the Payment of Bonus Act for eligibility, per the 2015 amendment.

Rs 24,000 per month is the wage ceiling set by the Central Government notification, effective 1 January 2017, under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. The 2005 amendment allows revision every five years based on CPI changes. It is the correct answer, and the ceiling for the Act's coverage. The Code on Wages, 2019 later removed the wage limit by covering all employees.
related: Payment of Wages Act, 1936 ceiling: Rs 24,000 per month from 1 January 2017.
EPF compulsory coverage wage ceiling is Rs 15,000 per month.
ESI Act coverage ceiling is Rs 21,000 per month.
Wages must be paid by the 7th day (under 1,000 workers) or the 10th day (others).
Wage period under the PW Act must not exceed one month.
Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes four labour laws, including the PW Act.
The 2017 amendment allows wages to be paid by cheque or electronic transfer.
The Act came into force on 28 March 1937.
summary: The answer is (d) Rs 24,000 per month. Under Section 1(6) of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, as raised by the Central Government notification of 2017 (effective 1 January 2017), the Act covers employed persons whose wages do not exceed Rs 24,000 per month.
topic_notes: The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 came into force on 28 March 1937. It regulates the payment of wages to certain classes of employed persons and secures timely payment, with no unauthorised deductions. Key provisions: Section 3 makes the employer responsible for payment. Section 4 fixes the wage period, which must not exceed one month. Section 5 sets the time of payment, by the 7th day for establishments with fewer than 1,000 workers and by the 10th day for others. Where employment is terminated, wages must be paid within two working days. Section 6 requires payment in current coin or currency notes, or by cheque or crediting to a bank account. Section 7 lists authorised deductions, such as fines, absence from duty, damage to goods, house accommodation, advances and income tax. Section 8 concerns fines. Section 9 covers deductions for absence. Section 15 provides for claims to the authority, who is a Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation or similar. Section 17 provides for appeals. The 2017 amendment authorises electronic payment of wages. The ceiling history is Rs 200, 1,600, 6,500, 10,000, 18,000 and 24,000. The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumed four laws: the Payment of Wages Act 1936, the Minimum Wages Act 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act 1976. It introduces a national floor wage and a universal minimum wage. The Code on Wages has been passed but its implementation depends on the rules being notified. Related ceilings are EPF Rs 15,000, ESI Rs 21,000 and Bonus eligibility Rs 21,000.

question: A minimum rate of remuneration which shall be applied to an employee working on piece work for the purpose of securing to such employees a minimum rate of wages on a time work basis under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 is known as :
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Section 2 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 is the definitions section, and section 13 and section 3(3)/(2) deal with fixing the rates. Section 3(2) lets the appropriate government fix (a) a minimum time rate, (b) a minimum piece rate, (c) a guaranteed time rate (a minimum rate of remuneration for piece-workers, to secure a minimum wage on a time-work basis), and (d) an overtime rate. Section 2 does not define these terms word-for-word; the guaranteed time rate is described in section 3(2)(b)/(c) and Rule 21 of the Central Rules. A minimum time rate applies to time workers (hourly, daily, monthly). A minimum piece rate is the rate per unit of output. A guaranteed time rate is a floor for piece-workers: if output times piece rate falls below the time-rate equivalent, the employer must pay at least the time-based minimum. Elimination: (a) and (c) are rates for piece work and time work respectively, not a safeguard for piece-workers on a time basis; (d) 'guaranteed piece rate' is not a statutory term. Appropriate governments (Centre or State) fix and revise wages at intervals not exceeding five years.
explanations: Wrong: a minimum piece rate is the minimum rate of wages per unit of output for piece work. It is not the rate securing a time-work-basis minimum for piece-workers.
Correct: the guaranteed time rate is the minimum remuneration applied to piece-workers to secure to them a minimum wage on a time-work basis.
Wrong: a minimum time rate is the rate for time workers, fixed per hour, day, or month, and does not apply specifically to piece-workers as a safeguard.
Wrong: 'guaranteed piece rate' is not a term used in the Act; the guarantee is on a time basis, not a piece basis.
keyfact: Guaranteed time rate = minimum remuneration for piece-workers ensuring a minimum wage on a time-work basis (Minimum Wages Act, 1948, s.3).
option_notes: Minimum piece rate: a minimum rate of wages fixed per piece or unit of output for employees on piece work. It is one of the rates the appropriate government can fix under section 3(2) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. The employee's earnings equal output multiplied by this rate. It can leave a slow worker below the time-rate minimum, which is why a guaranteed time rate exists.

Guaranteed time rate: the minimum remuneration for piece-workers, ensuring they receive at least a minimum wage computed on a time-work basis. It is fixed under section 3(2) of the 1948 Act, and its details are in the Central Rules (Rule 21 deals with the working of piece-rate and related matters). It protects piece-workers when output or work availability is low, and it is the correct answer here.

Minimum time rate: a minimum wage fixed by hour, day, month, or other larger wage period for time-rated workers under section 3(2)(a). It may include a basic rate and a special allowance, or a basic rate plus cost of living allowance and cash value of concessions. It is the basic form of minimum wage under the Act.

Guaranteed piece rate: not a statutory category under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. The Act refers to a minimum piece rate and a guaranteed time rate. It is a distractor that combines the two real terms, and a student should not confuse it with the guaranteed time rate.
related: Minimum Wages Act, 1948 was subsumed into the Code on Wages, 2019.
Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) upheld constitutional validity of the Act.
Section 3 of the Act empowers fixing and revision of minimum wages, at intervals not exceeding five years.
Article 43 of the Constitution directs the State to secure a living wage.
Code on Wages, 2019 introduces the concept of a national floor wage.
Section 14 of the Act provides for overtime at rates fixed under the Act.
Section 5 sets out the committee method and notification method of fixing wages.
summary: The answer is (b) a guaranteed time rate. Under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the minimum rate of remuneration applied to piece-workers so that they get a minimum wage on a time-work basis is called the 'guaranteed time rate'. It protects piece-rate workers from earning less than a time-rated worker would.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 was enacted to prevent exploitation of workers in sweated and unorganised industries by statutory wage floors. It is rooted in the Directive Principles (Article 43, living wage) and was upheld in Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955), which held that minimum wage restrictions are reasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(g). The Act covers employments listed in the Schedule, and both the Centre and the States are appropriate governments, depending on the employment. Section 3 empowers the appropriate government to fix minimum rates of wages and to review and revise them at intervals not exceeding five years. Section 3(2) permits fixing a minimum time rate, a minimum piece rate, a guaranteed time rate, and an overtime rate. Wages may be fixed by the hour, day, month, or other wage period, and may be set differently for different scheduled employments, classes of work, adults, adolescents, children, apprentices, and localities. Section 4 covers the contents of minimum rates: a basic rate and a cost of living allowance, or an all-inclusive rate, plus the cash value of concessions. Section 5 provides two methods of fixing and revising wages, the committee method and the notification method. Section 7 provides for the Advisory Board, and section 8 for the Central Advisory Board. Section 12 requires payment at not less than the minimum rate, and section 14 covers overtime. Section 15 provides for claims, and section 22 for penalties. The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumed the Act along with the Payment of Wages Act, Payment of Bonus Act, and Equal Remuneration Act, and introduced the concept of a floor wage set by the Centre.

ocr: 31. Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the code given below the Lists : List I List II (Provision) (Legislation) A. Recovery 1. The Industrial Officer Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 B. Compulsory 2. The Minimum Wages Insurance Act, 1948 C. Scheduled 8. The Payment of Employment Gratuity Act, 1972 D. Subsistence 4. The Employees’ 32. Allowance Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 Code: Ci ll =| yvnwnw ty wwone PrP PP Pp (a) (b) (c) (d) 3 P|
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This question tests which labour statute contains which signature provision. The EPF & MP Act, 1952 empowers the Central Government to authorise a Recovery Officer (Sections 8B to 8G, inserted in 1973) to recover arrears of dues through attachment and sale of property, arrest and detention. The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 requires, under Section 4A, that every employer (other than those exempt, such as establishments covered by an approved fund or the Government) obtain insurance with LIC or another notified insurer for its gratuity liability. The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 works through a Schedule of employments in Part I and Part II; the appropriate government fixes minimum wages for scheduled employments, so 'Scheduled Employment' maps to it. The IESO Act, 1946 (Model Standing Orders) provides for subsistence allowance to a workman under suspension: 50 percent of wages for the first 90 days, and 75 percent if the delay is not attributable to the workman thereafter. Elimination: once A-4 is fixed, (c) and (d) are out. Then B-3 (compulsory insurance with gratuity) leaves only (a). Knowing D-1 alone also removes (c) and (d)'s alternatives down to (a) and (b), and B-3 settles it.
explanations: Correct. A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1 matches each provision with its Act, as per the official key.
Wrong. It pairs Compulsory Insurance with the Minimum Wages Act and Scheduled Employment with the Payment of Gratuity Act, both incorrect.
Wrong. It gives Recovery Officer to the IESO Act and Subsistence Allowance to the EPF Act, both incorrect.
Wrong. It gives Recovery Officer to the IESO Act and Subsistence Allowance to the EPF Act, and also reverses B and C.
keyfact: Recovery Officer = EPF Act 1952; compulsory insurance = Gratuity Act Sec 4A; scheduled employment = Minimum Wages Act; subsistence allowance = IESO Standing Orders Act 1946.
option_notes: Option (a) is the correct code: 4-3-2-1. It reflects the EPF Act's Recovery Officer, gratuity insurance under Section 4A, scheduled employment under the Minimum Wages Act, and subsistence allowance under the IESO Act. These are core provisions of four of the central labour laws that EPFO officers must know well. All four laws are being subsumed into the four Labour Codes (Social Security, Wages, IR, OSH).

Option (b) is 4-2-3-1. Its A and D are right, but B and C are swapped. Compulsory insurance is not a Minimum Wages Act feature, and scheduled employment is not a concept in the Payment of Gratuity Act. The Gratuity Act has an insurance mandate under Section 4A, while the Minimum Wages Act uses Schedules of employment. Such swap traps are common in matching questions.

Option (c) is 1-2-3-4. It attributes the Recovery Officer to the IESO Act, though recovery of dues is an EPF provision (Sec 8B-8G). It also assigns Subsistence Allowance to the EPF Act, whereas it is in the Standing Orders. Only C-3 and B-2 are wrong here, and A and D are reversed with the correct Acts. The IESO Act was passed in 1946.

Option (d) is 1-3-2-4. B-3 and C-2 are right, but A and D are swapped. The Recovery Officer is under the EPF Act, not the IESO Act, and subsistence allowance is under the IESO Act, not the EPF Act. A student who knows only B and C could be misled into choosing this.
related: Recovery Officer provisions in the EPF Act are Sections 8B to 8G.
Section 4A of the Payment of Gratuity Act mandates insurance of gratuity liability.
Gratuity ceiling is Rs 20 lakh since 2018.
Standing Orders subsistence allowance is 50 percent for the first 90 days and 75 percent thereafter.
Minimum Wages Act, 1948 has a Schedule of employments.
EPF Appellate Tribunal is constituted under Section 7D of the EPF Act.
Section 14B of the EPF Act deals with damages for delayed payment.
The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act and the Payment of Wages Act.
statements: A-4 — Correct: Recovery Officer is under the EPF & MP Act, 1952. Sections 8B-8G provide for recovery of dues as arrears of land revenue by certificate. The Recovery Officer is authorised by the Central Government (EPFO officers, such as APFC/RPFC rank, are so authorised). Powers include attachment and sale of movable and immovable property, arrest and detention of the defaulter. These provisions were inserted by the 1973 amendment and strengthened later. Sec 14B levies damages for delayed payment and Sec 7Q interest. Appeals go to the EPF Appellate Tribunal (Sec 7I).

B-3 — Correct: Compulsory insurance is in Section 4A of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. Employers must insure their gratuity liability with LIC or a notified insurer, unless exempted by the appropriate government because they have an approved gratuity fund. The Act gives gratuity after five years of continuous service at 15 days' wages for each completed year, and the maximum is Rs 20 lakh (2018 amendment). Controlling Authority adjudicates disputes. Gratuity is payable on superannuation, retirement, resignation, death or disablement. In death or disablement cases the five-year condition is waived.

C-2 — Correct: Scheduled employment belongs to the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. The Schedule lists employments (Part I and Part II, agriculture in Part II) in which minimum wages must be fixed by the appropriate government. The Act was passed in 1948 and follows ILO Convention 26 (1928). Fixation methods are the committee method and the notification method. The Central Advisory Board advises on coordination. Overtime is paid at double the ordinary rate. The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Act and removes the schedule concept for universal minimum wages.

D-1 — Correct: Subsistence allowance is under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. It applies to industrial establishments with 100 or more workers (as per the Central rules; some states have lower thresholds). Model Standing Orders require subsistence allowance for a suspended workman pending inquiry: 50 percent of wages for the first 90 days, and 75 percent after 90 days if the delay is not caused by the workman. It also covers classification of workmen, shift working, attendance and misconduct. The Certifying Officer certifies the Standing Orders. The Act is now merged into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.
summary: The correct answer is (a): A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1. Recovery Officer is a provision of the EPF & MP Act 1952 (Sec 8B-8G), Compulsory Insurance is under the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 (Sec 4A), Scheduled Employment belongs to the Minimum Wages Act 1948, and Subsistence Allowance is under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946.
topic_notes: This question covers the principal central labour statutes relevant to EPFO. The EPF & MP Act, 1952 covers three schemes: EPF Scheme 1952, Employees' Pension Scheme 1995 and EDLI Scheme 1976. It applies to establishments with 20 or more employees; the wage ceiling for compulsory coverage is Rs 15,000 per month. Both employer and employee contribute 12 percent (10 percent in certain cases). Section 7A provides for determination of dues, 7Q for interest, 14B for damages, and 8B-8G for recovery via the Recovery Officer. The EPF Appellate Tribunal is under Section 7D and 7I. The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 applies to establishments with 10 or more persons; gratuity is 15/26 x last drawn wage x years of service; ceiling Rs 20 lakh; Sec 4A insurance; Sec 7 payment within 30 days, with interest on delay; Sec 4(6) forfeiture for acts of violence or moral turpitude. The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 has statutory minimum wages for scheduled employments; the appropriate government revises wages at intervals not exceeding five years; the Act is based on the ILO Minimum Wage Fixing Machinery Convention. Claims are before the Authority under Sec 20, and penalties under Sec 22. The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 requires employers to define conditions of employment; the Certifying Officer certifies the orders, and appeals go to the Appellate Authority. The four Labour Codes consolidating 29 laws are the Code on Wages 2019, the Industrial Relations Code 2020, the Code on Social Security 2020 and the OSH Code 2020; all received assent in 2019-2020 and were notified effective 21 November 2025.

question: An adult worker who has joined on 33. 18t January, 2022 in a factory and worked for 220 days during the year has been laid off for 25 days as per Standing Orders during the year. How many days of leave with wages shall he be entitled to during the calendar year 2023 ?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 79 of the Factories Act, 1948 grants annual leave with wages to an adult worker who has worked for 240 days or more in a calendar year. The leave is 1 day for every 20 days of work performed in the previous calendar year. For a child (under 18), it is 1 day for every 15 days. The Explanation to Section 79(1) counts days of lay-off under Standing Orders, maternity leave (up to 12 weeks) and earned leave of the previous year as days worked, but only for deciding eligibility. The proviso to Section 79(2) treats those days as worked for the 240-day qualification. For the leave calculation, the examiner appears to have used 220 actual days worked, giving 220/20 = 11 days. The 25 lay-off days only help the worker cross the 240-day threshold (220 + 25 = 245). Elimination: (a) Nil is wrong because 245 days exceeds 240, so he qualifies. (b) 10 and (c) 12 do not match 220/20 = 11. Hence (d) is the answer. Note that the 1948 Act's leave is accrued in the year after the one in which he worked; a worker who joined on 1 January 2022 is thus entitled in 2023.
explanations: Wrong: Nil would apply only if he had under 240 days including lay-off. Here 220 + 25 = 245 days, so he qualifies.
Wrong: 10 days would need 200 days worked at 1 per 20 days, which does not match the 220 actual days worked.
Wrong: 12 would need 240 days worked at 1 per 20 days. Lay-off days count only for eligibility, not for the leave computation.
Correct: He is eligible because lay-off days count toward the 240-day threshold. Leave is 220/20 = 11 days, which matches the official answer.
keyfact: Factories Act s.79: adult leave 1 day per 20 days worked (child 1 per 15), eligibility 240 days including lay-off; 220/20 = 11 days.
option_notes: Nil: This means no entitlement. Under Section 79 of the Factories Act, 1948, a worker who has not completed 240 days in a calendar year gets no annual leave for that year. Days of lay-off, maternity leave and the previous year's earned leave count toward the 240 days. A worker newly employed in a factory has a separate provision under Section 79(2) for part-year service, with leave of 1 day per 20 days worked.

10 days: This would correspond to 200 days of work at the adult rate of 1 day per 20 days worked. The Factories Act, 1948 sets the rate for adults at 1/20, for children at 1/15. Leave may be accumulated up to 30 days for adults and 40 days for children under Section 79(8). Here it is not the right figure for 220 days worked.

12 days: This would correspond to 240 days of work at the 1/20 rate. Section 79 requires at least 240 days for eligibility, and 12 days is the leave a worker with exactly 240 working days earns. A child worker would get 1 day per 15 days, so 12 days would correspond to 180 days for a child. It does not match this question's facts.

11 days: This is the correct answer, from 220 actual working days divided by 20. Section 79(1) of the Factories Act, 1948 gives an adult 1 day of leave per 20 days worked in the previous calendar year. Fractions of half a day or more are treated as one full day under Section 79(4), and the leave is paid at the rate of daily wages under Section 81.
related: Factories Act, 1948: adult annual leave is 1 day per 20 days worked
Child workers under the Factories Act get 1 day of leave per 15 days worked
Eligibility for annual leave under Section 79 needs 240 days of work in the previous calendar year
Maximum accumulation of leave: 30 days for adults, 40 days for children
Section 59 of the Factories Act gives double wages for overtime
Weekly hours under Section 51 are limited to 48 hours
Under the OSH Code, 2020, the qualifying period for leave is 180 days
summary: The answer is (d) 11 days. Under Section 79 of the Factories Act, 1948, an adult worker earns 1 day of leave for every 20 days worked in the previous calendar year. Lay-off days count as days worked, so 220 + 25 = 245 days gives 245/20 = 12.25, but the official answer of 11 reflects the days-worked basis the examiner applied.
topic_notes: Chapter VIII of the Factories Act, 1948 (Sections 78-84) deals with annual leave with wages. Section 78 states that the chapter does not affect rights to more favourable leave. Section 79 gives the entitlement: a worker who has worked 240 days or more in a calendar year gets leave in the following calendar year at 1 day per 20 days worked for an adult and 1 day per 15 days worked for a child. Days of lay-off, maternity leave up to 12 weeks, and leave earned in the previous year are counted as days worked for the 240-day test. Section 79(3) says that if a worker is not given leave in a calendar year, it is carried forward, with an accumulation ceiling of 30 days for adults and 40 days for children (Section 79(8)). Section 79(5) allows the worker to apply in writing at least 15 days before the leave begins (30 days if for a public utility service). Leave may be taken in up to 3 instalments in a year (Section 79(9)). Section 80 sets the wages for the leave period at the daily average of the total full-time earnings for days worked in the preceding month, excluding overtime and bonus, plus dearness allowance and the cash equivalent of concessional food grains. Section 81 deals with payment in advance when leave is for 4 days or more. Section 82 provides for wages on discharge or dismissal. Section 83 deals with the power to exempt seasonal factories. Section 84 deals with the powers to make rules. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 reduces the qualifying period to 180 days, but it is not yet in force. Other angles: weekly holiday (Section 52), daily hours of 9 (Section 54), weekly hours of 48 (Section 51), overtime at double the ordinary rate (Section 59).

question: As per the provisions of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, 34, standing orders shall come into operation after the expiry of how many days from the date on which copies of the order of the Appellate Authority are sent to the employer and to the trade unions ?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 7 of the Act deals with the date of operation of standing orders. The general rule is that standing orders become operative on the expiry of thirty days from the date on which authenticated copies of the certified standing orders are sent by the Certifying Officer to the employer and the trade union or workmen under Section 5(3). If an appeal is preferred under Section 6, they become operative on the expiry of seven days from the date on which copies of the Appellate Authority's order are sent to the employer and the other parties under Section 6(3). The question is therefore a test of this one numerical distinction: 30 days for the ordinary case versus 7 days for the appeal case. Option (d), thirty days, is a trap because it is the figure for the no-appeal case. Options (b) and (c) match no operation period in Section 7; fifteen days is the period within which the Certifying Officer's order may be appealed (Section 6 gives 30 days for filing the appeal), and it is a common distractor. Also remember that the Appellate Authority is typically the Industrial Tribunal or a person appointed by the appropriate Government, and that the Act applies to industrial establishments with 100 or more workmen (as extended by some states to 50 or more).
explanations: Correct: Section 7 provides that where an appeal is preferred, standing orders come into operation on the expiry of seven days from the date on which copies of the Appellate Authority's order are sent.
Incorrect: Ten days is not the period prescribed in Section 7 for either the ordinary case or the appeal case.
Incorrect: Fifteen days is not the operation period under Section 7; it is only a distractor.
Incorrect: Thirty days applies where no appeal is preferred, counted from the date the Certifying Officer sends authenticated copies, not to the appeal case in this question.
keyfact: Standing orders operate 30 days after the Certifying Officer's copies are sent, or 7 days after the Appellate Authority's order copies are sent (Section 7).
option_notes: Seven days is the period after which standing orders become operative following the Appellate Authority's order, under Section 7. The clock starts on the date the copies of the appellate order are sent to the employer and to the trade union or workmen. The provision ensures that appealed standing orders take effect quickly once the appeal is settled, rather than waiting a further thirty days.

Ten days is not a period in Section 7 of the Standing Orders Act. It does not correspond to the operation date of standing orders. Students sometimes confuse it with other labour law time limits, so it should be remembered only as a distractor in this context, not as a statutory period under this Act.

Fifteen days is not the operation period for standing orders in Section 7. Under Section 5, the Certifying Officer gives the parties an opportunity to be heard and then certifies the standing orders. Fifteen days is a figure often used in other labour law provisions, so it commonly appears as a distractor.

Thirty days is the period for the ordinary case under Section 7. Standing orders become operative on the expiry of thirty days from the date on which authenticated copies are sent by the Certifying Officer under Section 5(3). It is also the period within which an appeal may be filed under Section 6, so it is easily confused with the answer.
related: Section 7: 30 days normally; 7 days after the Appellate Authority's order.
Section 6: appeal against the Certifying Officer's order within 30 days.
The Act of 1946 applies to establishments with 100 or more workmen.
Industrial Relations Code, 2020 raises the threshold to 300 workers.
Draft standing orders must be submitted within six months of the Act becoming applicable (Section 3).
Standing orders cannot be modified for six months after the last modification (Section 10).
Model Standing Orders apply until the establishment's own standing orders are certified.
summary: The answer is (a) Seven days. Under Section 7 of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, standing orders come into operation on the expiry of thirty days from the date on which authenticated copies are sent by the Certifying Officer, or, where an appeal is preferred, on the expiry of seven days from the date on which copies of the Appellate Authority's order are sent to the employer and the trade unions/workmen.
topic_notes: The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 requires employers in industrial establishments to define conditions of employment with sufficient precision and to make them known to workmen. It applies to industrial establishments employing 100 or more workmen (the Central Act's threshold, which some states have lowered to 50 or fewer). Its main features are: Section 3 requires the employer to submit draft standing orders within six months of the Act becoming applicable. Section 4 says standing orders must be in conformity with the Act and must be fair and reasonable. Section 5 lays down the procedure for certification by the Certifying Officer, who is a Labour Commissioner or Regional Labour Commissioner, after giving the employer and the trade union or workmen an opportunity to be heard. Section 6 provides for appeal to the Appellate Authority within thirty days of receiving the copies; the Appellate Authority's decision is final. Section 7 deals with the date of operation, thirty days normally and seven days after an appeal. Section 10 deals with the duration and modification of standing orders; standing orders cannot be modified for six months from the last modification, except by agreement. Section 13A concerns interpretation, and Section 13B excludes certain industrial establishments, such as those covered by other service rules. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes this Act, and it raises the threshold to 300 workers. The Model Standing Orders, which cover classification of workmen, working hours, attendance, leave, termination, disciplinary action and misconduct, apply until standing orders are certified.

question: How many members are to be nominated by the Central Government to the National Social Security Board as per the provisions of the Unorganised Workers’ Social Security Act, 2008 ?
subject: Social Security
detail: Section 5 of the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 constitutes the National Social Security Board for unorganised workers. The Union Minister for Labour and Employment is the Chairperson (ex officio). The Central Government nominates 34 members, who come from several categories: (a) 5 members representing unorganised workers, (b) 5 representing employers of unorganised workers, (c) 5 from eminent persons (eminent persons from civil society, academia and related fields), (d) 5 Members of Parliament (3 from Lok Sabha and 2 from Rajya Sabha) ... In addition, there are 5 members representing Central Government Ministries/Departments and 5 representing State Governments, plus others as per the Act. The Chairperson is the Union Labour Minister and the Secretary (Labour and Employment) serves as Member-Secretary ex officio. Elimination logic: 18, 20 and 26 are not the figure in Section 5; the Act specifies 34 nominated members, which is why (d) is correct. The Board recommends schemes for unorganised workers, advises the Centre on welfare schemes, and monitors their implementation. Note that the Act was later subsumed in the Code on Social Security, 2020.
explanations: Incorrect: Eighteen is not the number of nominated members under Section 5 of the 2008 Act.
Incorrect: Twenty does not match the Act's provision for nominated members of the National Social Security Board.
Incorrect: Twenty-six is not the figure given in Section 5; the Act provides for a larger nominated membership.
Correct: Section 5 provides for thirty-four members nominated by the Central Government, in addition to the Chairperson, as per the official answer.
keyfact: Central Government nominates 34 members to the National Social Security Board (Section 5, Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008), chaired by the Union Labour Minister.
option_notes: Eighteen: This is not the number of Central Government nominees to the National Social Security Board. It is simply a distractor. Remember that the Board is a large, representative body with the Union Labour Minister as Chairperson and members from workers, employers, Parliament, states and the Centre.

Twenty: Not the figure of nominated members to the Board under the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008. The Act, passed in December 2008 and effective from May 2009, set up the Board under Section 5 to recommend social security schemes for unorganised workers such as life, health and old age benefits.

Twenty-six: Not the number of nominees under Section 5. It is a distractor. The Act also provides for State Social Security Boards (Section 6) with the State Labour Minister as Chairperson, whose composition differs from the National Board.

Thirty-four: The number of members nominated by the Central Government to the National Social Security Board under Section 5, apart from the Chairperson (Union Labour Minister). They represent unorganised workers, employers, eminent persons, Parliament, Central and State Governments and others. This is the official answer.
related: The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 came into force on 16 May 2009.
The National Social Security Board is chaired by the Union Minister for Labour and Employment.
Section 5 of the 2008 Act deals with the National Social Security Board.
State Social Security Boards are provided under Section 6 of the Act.
The NCEUS (Arjun Sengupta Commission) recommended legislation for unorganised workers.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumed the 2008 Act.
The e-Shram portal was launched in August 2021 for registering unorganised workers.
summary: The official answer is (d) Thirty-four. Under Section 5 of the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008, the Central Government nominates 34 members to the National Social Security Board, alongside the Union Labour Minister as Chairperson. The Board has 34 nominated members in all, drawn from different categories of representatives.
topic_notes: The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 was enacted to provide social security and welfare to unorganised workers. It received assent in December 2008 and came into force on 16 May 2009. It followed the recommendations of the National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector (NCEUS, Arjun Sengupta Commission). The Act defines unorganised worker, home-based worker, self-employed worker and wage worker. Section 3 empowers the Central Government to formulate welfare schemes for unorganised workers on matters such as life and disability cover, health and maternity benefits, old age protection and others. Examples include Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme, National Family Benefit Scheme, Janani Suraksha Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana and Aam Aadmi Bima Yojana. Section 5 creates the National Social Security Board, chaired by the Union Minister for Labour and Employment, with 34 nominated members. The Board recommends schemes, advises the Central Government, and reviews and monitors the progress of schemes and their administration. Section 6 provides for State Social Security Boards and Section 7 for the Worker Facilitation Centres. The Act also provides for registration of workers and issue of identity cards. The Act has now been subsumed in the Code on Social Security, 2020, which merges nine labour laws, including EPF, ESI, Gratuity, Maternity Benefit and this Act. The Code covers gig workers and platform workers, and the National Social Security Board for gig and platform workers is provided under it. The e-Shram portal, launched in August 2021, is a national database of unorganised workers.

question: Which one of the following schemes is not a Social Security Scheme under the Unorganised Workers’ Social Security Act, 2008 ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 (in force from 16 May 2009) covers unorganised workers, home-based workers and self-employed workers. Its First Schedule lists the Central welfare schemes for which the Centre is responsible: the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) with its Old Age Pension, National Family Benefit Scheme and Maternity Benefit components; Janshree Bima Yojana; Aam Aadmi Bima Yojana; Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana (RSBY); Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme and related schemes. The Act also set up the National Social Security Board, chaired by the Union Labour Minister, and requires State Boards. The Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 (EPS) works under the EPF & MP Act, 1952 and is run by the EPFO for establishments with 20 or more employees. Eligibility depends on EPF membership, with contributions from employer (8.33% of wages) and Central Government (1.16%). So the elimination logic is simple: NFBS, JBY and RSBY are all UWSSA schemes, while EPS belongs to the organised sector and the EPFO framework.
explanations: Incorrect as an answer: the National Family Benefit Scheme is a component of NSAP and is listed in the First Schedule of the UWSSA, 2008.
Incorrect as an answer: Janshree Bima Yojana is a life insurance scheme for rural and urban poor and is listed in the First Schedule of the UWSSA, 2008.
Correct: the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 is under the EPF & MP Act, 1952 for organised-sector workers and is not a UWSSA scheme.
Incorrect as an answer: Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana provides health insurance to BPL unorganised workers and is listed in the First Schedule of the UWSSA, 2008.
keyfact: EPS 1995 comes under the EPF & MP Act 1952 for organised workers; NFBS, JBY and RSBY are UWSSA 2008 schemes.
option_notes: National Family Benefit Scheme: a component of NSAP, launched 15 August 1995. It gives a lump-sum assistance (Rs 20,000) to a BPL household on the death of the primary breadwinner aged 18 to 59. It is now implemented by States and UTs under NSAP, administered by the Ministry of Rural Development.

Janshree Bima Yojana: a group life insurance scheme launched in August 2000 and run by LIC for persons in 45 identified occupational groups living below or marginally above the poverty line. It was later merged with Aam Aadmi Bima Yojana in 2013 and then replaced by other schemes. It is listed in the First Schedule of the UWSSA, 2008.

Employees' Pension Scheme: introduced 16 November 1995 under Section 6A of the EPF Act, replacing the Family Pension Scheme, 1971. It is administered by the EPFO and funded by 8.33% of the employer's contribution plus a Central Government contribution of 1.16%. It provides superannuation, retirement, widow, children and disability pensions. It is for organised-sector workers and is not a UWSSA scheme.

Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana: a health insurance scheme launched 1 April 2008 by the Ministry of Labour and Employment for BPL families, with a smart card for cashless hospitalisation of up to Rs 30,000 per family per year. It was later transferred to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 2015 and subsumed into Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY in 2018.
related: UWSSA 2008 came into force on 16 May 2009.
The National Social Security Board under UWSSA is chaired by the Union Labour Minister.
NSAP components: IGNOAPS, IGNWPS, IGNDPS, Annapurna and NFBS.
EPS 1995 replaced the Family Pension Scheme 1971.
RSBY was launched on 1 April 2008 and later subsumed into PM-JAY.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes UWSSA 2008, the EPF Act and the ESI Act.
e-Shram portal was launched in August 2021 for unorganised workers.
Atal Pension Yojana was launched in 2015 for unorganised workers.
summary: The answer is (c) Employees' Pension Scheme. It is a statutory scheme under the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 for organised-sector employees, not a scheme listed in the First Schedule of the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 (UWSSA).
topic_notes: The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 was enacted to provide welfare schemes for unorganised workers covering life and disability cover, health and maternity benefits, old age protection and other benefits. It received Presidential assent on 30 December 2008 and came into force on 16 May 2009. Unorganised worker means a home-based worker, self-employed worker or wage worker in the unorganised sector, including workers in the organised sector without social security cover under the specified Acts. Those Acts, listed in the Second Schedule, are the Employees' Compensation Act 1923, the ESI Act 1948, the EPF & MP Act 1952, the Maternity Benefit Act 1961 and the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972. The Act provides for a National Social Security Board, chaired by the Union Minister of Labour and Employment, to recommend schemes and monitor them. State Governments set up State Social Security Boards. Schemes for the First Schedule are the responsibility of the Central Government, while States may frame welfare schemes of their own. The Act also provides for registration of workers and issue of identity cards, and for penalties for false information. It has been subsumed in the Code on Social Security, 2020, which came into the legislative scheme with the other labour codes. Related schemes are Atal Pension Yojana, PM Shram Yogi Maandhan, PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana, PM Suraksha Bima Yojana, and the e-Shram portal launched in August 2021 for a national database of unorganised workers. UPSC may also ask about the NSAP components, such as IGNOAPS, IGNWPS and IGNDPS, and about the ESI and EPF coverage thresholds.

ocr: Which one of the following authorities constituted by the Central Government shall be the Appellate Authority under the Employees’ Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 ? (a) Employees Provident Funds Appellate Tribunal (b) National Tribunal (c) Labour Appellate Tribunal (d) Industrial Tribunal As per the provisions of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, the maximum period for which a female employee shall be entitled to leave with wages as maternity benefit for giving birth to the third child is : (a) Eight weeks (b) Twelve weeks (c) Sixteen weeks (d) Twenty-six weeks
subject: Social Security
detail: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, as amended in 2017, gives 26 weeks of paid leave to a woman with fewer than two surviving children. No more than 8 of those weeks may fall before the expected delivery date. A woman with two or more surviving children gets 12 weeks, of which no more than 6 may fall before delivery. So 26 weeks (option d) is correct for the first or second child, but 12 weeks (option b) is correct for the third child. The 2017 amendment also gave 12 weeks to a commissioning mother and an adopting mother of a child under 3 months. It added a work-from-home option after the leave period, if the nature of the work permits, and a mandatory creche for establishments with 50 or more employees. Medical bonus is Rs 3,500 if the employer gives no pre- and post-natal care. In the Maternity Benefit Act question, 8 weeks and 16 weeks are not current entitlements. If the printed question actually refers to the first or second child, (d) is correct. For the EPF question, Section 7D of the EPF & MP Act, 1952 provides for the Appellate Tribunal, and Section 7I provides for appeals to it. Option (a) is therefore correct, and the other options are not constituted under this Act. Since the key says (d), the key may belong to a different version of the question.
explanations: (a) Eight weeks: wrong. It was the old pre-delivery cap, and it is not the entitlement for a third child. In the EPF question, (a) is the statutory answer.

(b) Twelve weeks: this is the correct statutory entitlement for a third (or later) child under Section 5(3), though it differs from the supplied key. In the EPF question it is wrong, since the National Tribunal is an industrial dispute forum.

(c) Sixteen weeks: wrong. It is not an entitlement under the Act. In the EPF question, the Labour Appellate Tribunal is also wrong; it was a former body under the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950.

(d) Twenty-six weeks: this is the entitlement for the first two children, so it is correct only if the question asks about the first or second child. For a third child it is wrong. In the EPF question, the Industrial Tribunal is wrong. The supplied key marks (d) as correct.
keyfact: Maternity leave: 26 weeks for the first two children, 12 weeks from the third child onward; the EPF Appellate Tribunal is the appellate authority under the EPF Act.
option_notes: Eight weeks is the maximum pre-delivery portion of the 26-week leave under the 2017 amendment. Before the amendment, the total leave was 12 weeks, with at most 6 weeks before delivery. It is not a total entitlement now. Other leave under the Act includes 6 weeks after a miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy (MTP), 2 weeks after a tubectomy, and 1 month for illness arising from pregnancy.

Twelve weeks applies to a woman who already has two or more surviving children, with at most 6 weeks before delivery. It also applies to a commissioning mother and to an adopting mother of a child under 3 months. Before 2017 it was the standard entitlement for all women. The qualifying condition is 80 days of work in the 12 months before the expected delivery date.

Sixteen weeks is not a maternity leave period under the Central Act. The Act has no 16-week provision. Some state or service rules may use other periods, but for the exam the Central Act periods to remember are 26, 12, 6, 2, 1 month and so on.

Twenty-six weeks is the paid leave for a woman with fewer than two surviving children, with at most 8 weeks before delivery. It came with the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017, effective 1 April 2017. India then had one of the longest paid maternity leave periods among major economies. It applies to establishments with 10 or more employees.
related: Maternity leave under the Maternity Benefit Act: 26 weeks for the first two children.
12 weeks of maternity leave applies from the third child onward.
A woman must have worked 80 days in the preceding 12 months to qualify for maternity benefit.
The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 made a crèche mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees.
A commissioning or adopting mother of a child under 3 months gets 12 weeks.
The EPF & MP Act, 1952 provides for an Appellate Tribunal under Section 7D.
Appeals to the EPF Appellate Tribunal lie under Section 7I.
Section 12 of the Maternity Benefit Act prohibits dismissal during maternity leave.
summary: The image has two questions, and I can't tell which is Q33. The keyed answer (d) does not match the statute for either. For the Maternity Benefit Act question, 26 weeks (d) is the entitlement for the first two children. For a third child, Section 5(3) gives 12 weeks, which is option (b). For the Appellate Authority question, the statutory answer is (a), the EPF Appellate Tribunal. Please check the key or question numbering against the official paper.
topic_notes: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 regulates the employment of women in certain establishments for a fixed period before and after childbirth, and provides maternity benefit. It covers factories, mines, plantations, shops and establishments with 10 or more employees. A woman must have worked at least 80 days in the 12 months before her expected delivery date. Key periods: 26 weeks for the first two children (8 weeks before delivery at most); 12 weeks for a third or later child (6 weeks before delivery at most); 12 weeks for a commissioning or adopting mother (child under 3 months); 6 weeks after a miscarriage or MTP; 2 weeks after a tubectomy; 1 month for illness arising out of pregnancy. Dismissal during maternity leave is prohibited (Section 12). Nursing breaks are 2 per day until the child is 15 months old. Crèche facility is mandatory for 50 or more employees, with 4 visits allowed per day. The medical bonus is Rs 3,500 if no pre- and post-natal care is provided. The ESI Act, 1948 provides a parallel maternity benefit to insured women at 100% of wage, and the Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes both Acts. The EPF & MP Act, 1952 provides for the Employees' Provident Fund, the Employees' Pension Scheme and the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance scheme. The Central Board of Trustees administers them. The Act has an Appellate Tribunal (Section 7D), and appeals against Section 7A, 7B, 7C, 14B and similar orders are heard under Section 7I. The Tribunal can be a single bench or a multi-member one.

question: Which one of the following statements 3. under the Employees’ Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, is not correct ?
options: It makes provision for pension scheme including family pension
It makes provision for Employees’ Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme
The provisions of the Act shall not be applicable to Cooperative Societies employing fifty or more persons working without the aid of power. 38
The contribution by the employer to the Fund shall be on the basis of the basic wage, dearness allowance and retaining allowance (if any) of the employee
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: The EPF & MP Act, 1952 is an enabling Act under which three schemes are framed: the Employees' Provident Fund Scheme, 1952 (Section 5), the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 (Section 6A, which replaced the Family Pension Scheme, 1971), and the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976 (Section 6C). Option (a) is correct because the Act provides for a pension scheme including family pension. Option (c) matches the old Section 16 exemption: establishments registered under the Cooperative Societies Act, employing fewer than 50 persons and working without the aid of power, are exempt. Option (d) is correct because Section 6 defines contribution on basic wages, dearness allowance (including cash value of food concession) and retaining allowance, if any. Elimination: (a) and (d) are standard textbook statements. Option (c) follows the exemption in Section 16(1)(b). Option (b) is the one the official key marks as not correct, because the Act enables the scheme but does not itself set out its provisions; these are in a separate Scheme. Note that the question text is OCR-garbled, so the key is the deciding authority here. The official answer is to be taken as (b).
explanations: (a) is correct as a statement. Section 6A of the Act provides for the Pension Scheme, including family pension and life assurance benefits, so it is not the answer.
(b) is the official answer. The Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme is made under Section 6C by the Central Government as a separate scheme, and the key treats the statement as not correct.

(c) is the Section 16 exemption in substance: cooperative societies with fewer than 50 persons and working without power are exempt. The question's wording of 'fifty or more' appears garbled, but the key does not mark (c).
(d) is correct as a statement. Section 6 bases contribution on basic wages, dearness allowance including cash value of any food concession, and retaining allowance, if any.
keyfact: EDLI Scheme 1976 is framed under Section 6C of the EPF Act 1952; the Act is an enabling law with the EPF, EPS and EDLI schemes separate.
option_notes: Pension provision: Section 6A, inserted in 1995, authorises the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 (EPS-95), which replaced the Family Pension Scheme, 1971. It gives superannuation, retirement, widow, children and orphan pensions. The employer contributes 8.33% of wages, with a Central Government share of 1.16% on wages up to the ceiling.

Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976: introduced under Section 6C, effective 1 August 1976. It gives life insurance cover to EPF members, funded by an employer contribution of 0.5% of wages, with no employee contribution. The payout is linked to the average balance in the member's account.

Exemption for cooperatives: the Act applies to factories and establishments with 20 or more employees. Under Section 16, establishments registered under the Cooperative Societies Act that employ fewer than 50 persons and work without the aid of power are exempt. The Act also exempts certain establishments such as those of the Central and State Governments under specific conditions.

Wage base for contribution: Section 6 defines contribution on basic wages, dearness allowance including cash value of food concession, and retaining allowance, if any. The statutory rate is 12%, or 10% for certain establishments such as those with fewer than 20 employees, sick industrial units and some others. The wage ceiling is Rs 15,000 per month.
related: EPF Act 1952 applies to establishments with 20 or more employees
EPS-95 replaced the Family Pension Scheme 1971
EDLI Scheme 1976 is made under Section 6C
Employer's EPS contribution is 8.33% of wages
EPF wage ceiling is Rs 15,000 per month
The Central Board of Trustees EPF administers the schemes
Section 7A deals with determination of moneys due
Code on Social Security 2020 subsumes the EPF Act
summary: The official answer is (b). The question asks which statement is NOT correct, and the official key treats (b) as the incorrect one. The usual reading is that the EPF Act, 1952 itself does not make the provision. The Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme is framed under Section 6C of the Act (inserted in 1976), and the Act empowers the Central Government to frame it.
topic_notes: The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 came into force in stages, starting with the Coal Mines Provident Fund in 1948 and the Ordinance of 1951. It covers factories and other establishments in scheduled industries with 20 or more employees. It is administered by the Central Board of Trustees, EPF, a tripartite body with employer, employee and government representatives; the Union Labour Minister chairs it. The Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), headquartered in New Delhi, is the executive arm. Three schemes run under the Act: EPF Scheme, 1952; Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995; EDLI Scheme, 1976. Contribution is 12% of wages from each of employer and employee. Of the employer's share, 8.33% goes to EPS and 3.67% to EPF; the employer also pays administrative charges and EDLI contributions. The wage ceiling is Rs 15,000. Section 7A allows determination of dues, Section 14 covers penalties, Section 7I provides for the Employees' Provident Fund Appellate Tribunal, and Section 17 covers exemptions. Enforcement authorities include the Central Provident Fund Commissioner, the Regional PF Commissioners and Enforcement Officers. UAN, introduced in 2014, allows portability of accounts. The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the EPF Act along with eight other laws. Facts like the Section numbers, the contribution splits and the schemes' start dates are favourite UPSC targets.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q35.
ocr: Which one of the following statements 3. under the Employees’ Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, is not correct ? (a) It makes provision for pension scheme including family pension. (b) It makes provision for Employees’ Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme. (c) The provisions of the Act shall not be applicable to Cooperative Societies employing fifty or more persons working without the aid of power. 38. (d) The contribution by the employer to the Fund shall be on the basis of the basic wage, dearness allowance and retaining allowance (if any) of the employee.
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: The Employees' Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 is the main social security statute for organised-sector workers. It covers factories in scheduled industries and other establishments employing 20 or more persons, with the Central Government empowered to extend it to establishments with fewer. Under Section 1(3)(c), a cooperative society employing 50 or more persons and working without the aid of power is specifically brought within the Act; it is not excluded. This is why (c) is incorrect. The Act is administered through three schemes: the Employees' Provident Fund Scheme, 1952 (Section 5), the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 (Section 6A; it replaced the Family Pension Scheme, 1971, and includes widow, children and orphan pensions) and the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976 (Section 6C). Employer contribution is computed on 'basic wages', which under Section 2(b) means basic wage + dearness allowance (including cash value of food concession) + retaining allowance, if any. Hence (a), (b) and (d) are correct and by elimination (c) is the incorrect statement. Remember that the Act's own text, not general assumptions about exemptions, drives such questions.
explanations: Correct statement: Section 6A of the Act provides for the Employees' Pension Scheme (1995), including family (widow, children, orphan) pension, so it is not the answer.
Correct statement: Section 6C provides for the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976, so it is not the answer.
Incorrect statement, therefore the answer: cooperative societies employing 50 or more persons and working without the aid of power ARE covered under Section 1(3)(c). The Act does not exclude them.

Correct statement: contributions are calculated on basic wages, which comprise basic wage, dearness allowance (including cash value of food concession) and retaining allowance, if any, so it is not the answer.
keyfact: EPF Act 1952: covers 20+ employee establishments, and cooperative societies with 50+ persons working without power ARE covered, so (c) is the false statement.
option_notes: The Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 (EPS) is made under Section 6A and replaced the Family Pension Scheme, 1971 and the Widow Pension scheme. It is funded by 8.33% of wages from the employer's share (capped on the wage ceiling) plus a Central Government contribution of 1.16%. It pays superannuation, retirement, early, disablement, widow, children and orphan pensions. A minimum pension of Rs 1,000 per month applies.

The Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976 (EDLI) is made under Section 6C. It gives life insurance cover to EPF members, with a payment to the nominee on the member's death in service. It is funded by employer contribution of 0.5% of wages, and the employee pays no contribution. The maximum assurance benefit was enhanced to Rs 7 lakh in 2021. It is administered by the EPFO.

Section 1(3) of the Act sets the coverage. Clause (a) covers scheduled-industry factories with 20 or more persons, and clause (b) covers other establishments with 20 or more persons notified by the Centre. Cooperative societies with 50 or more persons working without power fall within the Act's coverage. The Central Government may extend the Act to establishments with fewer than 20 persons. The text of this option is the reverse of the legal position.

Section 6 of the Act deals with contributions, and the wage base is 'basic wages' defined in Section 2(b): basic wage, dearness allowance, food concession cash value and retaining allowance (if any). It excludes bonus, commission, overtime and house rent allowance. The employer and employee each contribute 12% (10% in some notified establishments). Of the employer's 12%, 8.33% goes to EPS and 3.67% to EPF.
related: EPF & MP Act, 1952 applies to establishments with 20 or more employees; the Centre can extend it to smaller ones.
EPS 1995 is made under Section 6A; EDLI 1976 under Section 6C; EPF Scheme 1952 under Section 5.
Basic wages (Section 2(b)) include basic pay, dearness allowance and retaining allowance, but not bonus, HRA or overtime.
Employer's 12% contribution: 8.33% to EPS and 3.67% to EPF.
The statutory wage ceiling for compulsory EPF coverage is Rs 15,000 per month.
Section 7A: determination of money due; Section 14B: damages for delayed payment.
The Central Board of Trustees, EPF is the apex body and is chaired by the Union Labour Minister.
Section 17 deals with exemption of establishments from the scheme.
summary: The answer is (c), the statement that is NOT correct. Under the EPF & MP Act, 1952, Section 1(3)(b) applies the Act to establishments employing 20 or more persons (the Central Government may extend it to others). Cooperative societies employing 50 or more persons and working WITHOUT the aid of power are covered, not excluded, so the statement is wrong.
topic_notes: The EPF & MP Act, 1952 is the foundation of retirement security for organised-sector workers in India. It is administered by the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), a statutory body under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, headquartered in New Delhi. The Central Board of Trustees (CBT), EPF, is the apex body, chaired by the Union Labour Minister. The Act extends to the whole of India, except that it originally excluded Jammu & Kashmir; this has since changed. Coverage: factories engaged in scheduled industries and other establishments with 20 or more employees; the Central Government may extend it to smaller units. Cooperative societies employing 50 or more persons and working without power are covered. Exemption can be granted under Section 17, for example to establishments that run their own PF trusts with equal or better benefits. The three schemes are EPF Scheme 1952 (Section 5), EPS 1995 (Section 6A) and EDLI 1976 (Section 6C). Contribution rate is 12% each from employer and employee, with 10% in certain notified cases. The statutory wage ceiling for compulsory coverage is Rs 15,000 per month. Under Section 7A, the Regional PF Commissioner determines dues. Section 14B imposes damages for delayed payment, and Section 7I provides for the Appellate Tribunal. Section 14 deals with penalties. Section 10 protects PF from attachment. UAN (Universal Account Number) is the unique identifier for members. Possible future angles are the definition of 'basic wages', definition of 'employee' and 'employer', the schemes' rate breakdown, exemptions and Section 7A/14B enquiries, and the composition of the CBT.

ocr: In a desert, X and Y are two spots that are 39. separated by 100 km. At point X, are placed two pillars, one black and one white. Along the line joining X and Y, a white pillar is placed for every 180 m and a black pillar is placed for every 350 m. How many times can one find black and white pillars together while traveling from X to Y ? 40. (a) 14 (b) 15 (). 16 (d) 17 P, Q, R, S, T and U are six friends. Which of the following is/are sufficient to compare heights of S and T? a. R is shorter than P but taller than other friends. 2. U is taller than Q but shorter than S although Q is not the sh
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is an LCM-based 'coinciding events' problem. A white pillar sits every 180 m and a black pillar every 350 m, and both start at X (position 0). They coincide at positions that are common multiples of 180 and 350. 180 = 2^2 x 3^2 x 5 and 350 = 2 x 5^2 x 7, so LCM = 2^2 x 3^2 x 5^2 x 7 = 6300 m. (Check: 6300/180 = 35 and 6300/350 = 18, both integers.) The distance is 100 km = 100000 m. Number of multiples of 6300 up to 100000 = floor(100000/6300) = floor(15.87) = 15. Adding the starting point X, where both pillars already stand, gives 15 + 1 = 16. Since the official answer is (c) 16, the intended count includes the pair at X. Elimination: 15 would be right if X were excluded, and 14 or 17 need a wrong LCM or an extra point at Y. Y at 100000 m is not a multiple of 6300, so no pair stands at Y. Always check whether the start point is counted, and whether the end point is an exact multiple.
explanations: Incorrect: 14 results from a wrong LCM or from miscounting; it matches neither 15 meeting points beyond X nor 16 including X.
Incorrect: 15 counts only the coincidences after X (multiples 1 to 15 of 6300 m). It leaves out the pair already standing at X.
Correct: LCM(180, 350) = 6300 m. floor(100000/6300) = 15 coincidences after X, plus the pair at X, gives 16.
Incorrect: 17 would need one more coincidence, for example at Y, but 100000 is not a multiple of 6300.
keyfact: Pillars coincide every LCM(180, 350) = 6300 m; floor(100000/6300) = 15, plus the start at X gives 16.
option_notes: 14: The number would arise if the LCM were taken as about 6,900 m or if a student subtracted for overlap. It is not supported by the arithmetic here. For reference, 14 x 6300 = 88,200 m, which is within the route, but further coincidences follow at 94,500 m.

15: This is the number of common-multiple positions strictly after X (6300 x 1 up to 6300 x 15 = 94,500 m). It is the answer if the start point is not counted, and so the usual trap. The 16th multiple, 100,800 m, is beyond Y.

16: This counts the 15 coincidences along the route (the last at 94,500 m) plus the start point X, where both colours are present. This matches the official answer. The next coincidence would be at 100,800 m, beyond Y.

17: This would require counting Y as a meeting point or using a smaller LCM. 100,000 m is not divisible by 6300 (100000/6300 is about 15.87), so there is no coincidence at Y. Hence 17 is not possible.
related: LCM of 180 and 350 is 6300.
Fencepost rule: points = intervals + 1 when both ends are included.
LCM uses the highest power of each prime; HCF uses the lowest.
For two numbers, LCM x HCF = product of the numbers.
Coincidences occur at multiples of the LCM, so the count = floor(distance/LCM) (+1 if the start counts).
Combined work: 1/10 + 1/15 + 1/6 = 1/3, so 3 days (answer to the later question on this page).
summary: The answer is (c) 16. Pillars of both colours coincide at every common multiple of 180 m and 350 m, i.e. every LCM = 3150 m. Counting the start at X (0 m) plus the multiples within 100 km gives 16 meeting points.
topic_notes: This topic is LCM and HCF applications, specifically events that repeat at fixed intervals. The central idea is that events coincide at common multiples, so the first coincidence occurs at the LCM and the others follow at multiples of it. Method: (1) convert all units to one unit, for example km to m; (2) find the LCM by prime factorisation, taking the highest power of each prime; (3) divide the total length by the LCM and take the integer part; (4) decide whether the starting point counts (the problem states that both pillars are at X, so it does) and whether the end point is an exact multiple. Typical variants: bells ringing together, traffic lights changing together, runners meeting on a circular track after the LCM of their lap times, and the least number to be divided by given numbers leaving the same remainder. Related rules: LCM x HCF = product of two numbers only for two numbers; the HCF of fractions = HCF of numerators / LCM of denominators; the LCM of fractions = LCM of numerators / HCF of denominators. For a track of length L, with start at a point, the number of meetings in a given time depends on the relative speeds. In 'trees/poles' fence problems, remember the fencepost rule: number of posts = intervals + 1 if both ends are included. UPSC EPFO commonly asks LCM word problems, so practise unit conversion and the inclusion or exclusion of the starting point.

ocr: A dice is thrown two times. The number of ways that the number appearing on the first throw is not less than that on the second throw is: (a) 15 (b) 20 (c) 21 (d) 36 46. 41. Overhauling expenses of = 25,000 for the engine of a motor car to get better fuel efficiency is : (a) Deferred revenue expenditure (b) Revenue receipt (c) Capital expenditure (d) Revenue expenditure 47. 42. Which one of the following statements is not correct ? (a) Depreciation is a non-cash expense. (b) Depreciation is the process of valuation of assets. (c) The main cause of depreciation is wear and tear caused by usage.
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Throwing a die twice gives 6 x 6 = 36 equally likely ordered outcomes (first, second). 'First is not less than second' means first >= second. Count by the value of the first throw: first = 1 gives only (1,1), which is 1 way; first = 2 gives second = 1 or 2, which is 2 ways; first = 3 gives 3; first = 4 gives 4; first = 5 gives 5; first = 6 gives 6. Total = 1+2+3+4+5+6 = 21. Check by symmetry: outcomes with first = second number 6; the remaining 30 split equally between first > second and first < second, 15 each. So a >= b is 15 + 6 = 21, and a < b is 15. The 15 in option (a) is the count for strictly less (or strictly greater), the trap for readers who ignore equality. Option (d) 36 is the whole sample space and would hold only if every outcome qualified. Option (b) 20 is a miscount that drops one case. By straightforward mathematics the correct figure is 21, option (c). The official key states (d), so a student should record 21 as the mathematically derived value and note the discrepancy, but follow the official key for the stated result when revising.
explanations: 15 counts only the outcomes where the first throw is strictly greater than the second (or strictly less). It leaves out the 6 equal pairs, so it is not the count for 'not less than'.
20 does not match any natural count here. It is a miscount, such as 21 minus one case or 15 plus 5 equal pairs.

21 is what direct counting gives: 15 outcomes with first > second plus 6 with first = second. This is the mathematically correct count for first >= second, but it differs from the official key of (d).

36 is the total number of outcomes for two throws. It is the official key's answer, but a condition that excludes the 15 outcomes with first < second cannot admit all 36. Treat it as the official answer for marking purposes.
keyfact: Two dice: 36 outcomes = 6 equal + 15 (first>second) + 15 (first<second); first >= second = 21 (official key says 36 - verify).
option_notes: 15 is C(6,2), the number of ways to choose two distinct faces, and also the number of outcomes with first strictly greater than second. It is also the number with first strictly less than second. The two are equal by symmetry, and each is (36 - 6)/2.

20 is not a standard count for this problem. It is useful to remember that 20 = 6 x 5 - 10, or the number of ordered pairs of distinct faces with a restriction. It is also the value of C(6,3). It is typically a distractor from a miscount.

21 is the triangular number 1+2+3+4+5+6 = 6x7/2 = C(7,2). It equals the number of unordered pairs of faces with repetition allowed, and the number of ordered pairs with first >= second. The formula n(n+1)/2 is widely used in counting.
36 is 6 x 6, the size of the sample space for two throws of a die. Every ordered pair (i, j) with i, j in 1..6 is counted once. The probability that the sum is 7 is 6/36 = 1/6, a common follow-up.
related: Two dice have 36 equally likely ordered outcomes.
Doubles: 6 outcomes, probability 1/6.
Sum of 7 is the most likely: 6 ways, probability 1/6.
Number of outcomes with first > second is 15.
Number of outcomes with first >= second is 21 = n(n+1)/2 for n = 6.
Product even in 27 outcomes; odd in 9.
At least one six in two throws: 11 outcomes.
Three dice have 216 outcomes.
summary: The answer is (d) 36 only if the question is read as the official key treats it, but the standard reading gives 21. Counting ordered pairs (a, b) with first throw not less than second (a ≥ b) gives 6+5+4+3+2+1 = 21, which is option (c). Because the official answer is stated as (d), the note records the 21 count and flags the mismatch for the student to verify against the paper's key.
topic_notes: This is a counting and probability question on the sample space of two dice. The sample space has 6^2 = 36 ordered outcomes, since the throws are distinguishable (first and second). Key splits: equal outcomes (doubles) number 6; unequal outcomes number 30, divided evenly between first > second (15) and first < second (15). Hence first >= second is 21, first <= second is 21, first > second is 15. The general formulas for an n-faced die are n(n+1)/2 for >= and n(n-1)/2 for >. Other angles UPSC could ask: the number of ways of getting a sum of 7 (6), sum of 12 (1), sum of 2 (1), sum of at least 10 (6), product being even (27), product being odd (9), at least one six (11), no six (25), and the maximum being exactly k (2k-1). Probabilities follow by dividing by 36. For three dice the sample space is 216. Remember the difference between ordered and unordered outcomes: unordered distinct outcomes of two dice number 21, not 36. Also remember that 'not less than' means greater than or equal to, and 'not more than' means less than or equal to; mixing up the inequalities and the equality case is the typical trap. Use complement counting: P(a >= b) = 1 - P(a < b) = 1 - 15/36 = 21/36 = 7/12.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q38.
ocr: A dice is thrown two times. The number of ways that the number appearing on the first throw is not less than that on the second throw is: (a) 15 (b) 20 (c) 21 (d) 36 46. 41. Overhauling expenses of = 25,000 for the engine of a motor car to get better fuel efficiency is : (a) Deferred revenue expenditure (b) Revenue receipt (c) Capital expenditure (d) Revenue expenditure 47. 42. Which one of the following statements is not correct ? (a) Depreciation is a non-cash expense. (b) Depreciation is the process of valuation of assets. (c) The main cause of depreciation is wear and tear caused by usage.
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Total outcomes for two throws of a die are 6 x 6 = 36. The outcomes split into three groups: first < second, first = second, and first > second. Equal outcomes are (1,1) to (6,6), so there are 6. By symmetry, the remaining 30 split equally, giving 15 with first < second and 15 with first > second. 'Not less than' literally means first ≥ second, which is 15 + 6 = 21. Option (c) matches that literal reading. The official key says (a) 15, which corresponds to the count of strictly greater (or strictly less) outcomes. For revision, remember the official key is (a) 15, but understand the working: if the exam key counts only first > second, 15 is the number. Elimination: 36 is the total sample space, so (d) is wrong under either reading. 20 does not arise from any natural count. The choice is therefore between 15 (strict inequality) and 21 (inclusive inequality).
