option_notes: Sir Spencer Harcourt Butler (1869-1938) was an ICS officer who served as Lieutenant Governor and later Governor of Burma, Governor of the United Provinces, and Education Member. He chaired the Indian States Committee (1927-29), which upheld the doctrine of paramountcy. He was also associated with the Indian Education Department and the Harcourt Butler Technological Institute in Kanpur.

A.J. Wilson is not connected with the Butler Committee. The name is a distractor here. The Committee had only three members, and Wilson was not among them, so the name should not be linked to the Indian States Committee.

Sir William Searle Holdsworth (1871-1944) was Vinerian Professor of English Law at Oxford and author of the monumental 'History of English Law' in 17 volumes. He was the legal expert on the Butler Committee, which examined treaties, sanads and paramountcy.

Sir Stanley C. Peel was a member of the Indian States Committee. He was the third member, alongside Butler and Holdsworth. He was a British Member who brought financial and administrative experience, and his name appears in the Committee's list of members.
related: The Indian States (Butler) Committee was appointed in 1927 and reported in 1929.
Chairman: Sir Harcourt Butler; members: W.S. Holdsworth and S.C. Peel.
The Committee held that the princes' relationship was with the Crown, not the Government of India.
The Chamber of Princes (Narendra Mandal) was established in 1921.
The Simon Commission was announced in November 1927 under Birkenhead as Secretary of State.
Paramountcy lapsed on 15 August 1947 under the Indian Independence Act 1947.
Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon led the integration of the princely states.
The Government of India Act 1935 proposed an All-India Federation that never materialised.
summary: The answer is (b). The Indian States Committee of 1927, better known as the Harcourt Butler Committee, had three members: Sir Harcourt Butler (Chairman), Prof. W.S. Holdsworth and S.C. Peel. A.J. Wilson was not on it.
topic_notes: The Indian States (Butler) Committee was appointed in December 1927 by Lord Birkenhead, Secretary of State for India in Baldwin's Conservative government, at about the time the Simon Commission was announced (November 1927). Its purpose was to examine the relationship between the Paramount Power and the princely states and to look at financial and economic relations with British India. Members: Sir Harcourt Butler (Chairman), Prof. W.S. Holdsworth and S.C. Peel. It submitted its report in 1929. Main findings: the States' relationship was with the Crown, not with the Government of India; paramountcy must remain paramount; the Crown's obligations to the princes could not be transferred to a new Indian government (responsible to the Indian legislature) without the consent of the States. This alarmed nationalists and delighted the princes in part. The Committee did say the States should be consulted about economic matters such as customs, and that States had a right to a share of customs revenues in some cases. The Chamber of Princes (Narendra Mandal) had been created in 1921 under the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms, with the Viceroy as president. The Princes engaged Sir Leslie Scott as counsel. The Nehru Report (1928) took a different view and called for the states to be part of India. The Government of India Act 1935 envisaged an All-India Federation including the states, but it never came into being because the princes did not accede. After 1947, Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon integrated 562 states through the Instruments of Accession and Standstill Agreements; Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir were special cases. Lapse of paramountcy occurred on 15 August 1947 under the Indian Independence Act 1947.

ocr: Which of the following statements are correct ? L Under the Cornwallis System, the districts were divided into thanas or police jurisdictions of 20-30 miles square. 2. Each of them was placed under an officer of government, under the denomination of daroga. 3. The daroga system was introduced in Madras in 1812. 4. The daroga was nominated by the district magistrate. Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) land 2 only (b) 2,3 and4 (c) 1,3 and4 (d) 1,2and4 Model Standing Orders formed under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 shall not apply to an establishme
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Lord Cornwallis (Governor-General 1786-93) separated revenue, judicial and police functions in the Permanent Settlement era. In 1791 he began police reform, and the Regulations of 1792-93 completed it. He removed the police duties of zamindars, who had earlier kept armed retainers and paid watchmen (the old faujdari arrangement). Each district was placed under a magistrate, who was also the collector until 1793 when the offices were separated. The district was divided into thanas of about 20 miles square, though sources vary and this question says 20-30. Each thana was headed by a daroga, an Indian officer with subordinate peons and burkandazes. The daroga was nominated or appointed by the district magistrate and was paid a salary by the Company. Over this structure sat Europeans, with the magistrate at the top. The village watchmen (chowkidars) remained under the village community, and the village police were not abolished. Statement 3 fails on the date. In Madras it was Thomas Munro who reorganised the police in 1816 (Madras Regulation XI of 1816), abolishing the old poligar and talari system and relying on village headmen. Elimination logic: statement 3 is wrong, so any option containing 3, namely (b) and (c), is out. Statement 1 is accepted as correct, which rules out (b) as well. Between (a) and (d), statement 4 is correct, so (d) is the answer.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it omits statement 4, which is correct, since the daroga was nominated by the district magistrate.
(b) Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is incorrect because the Madras daroga system dates to 1816, and it excludes statement 1, which is correct.
(c) Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and omits statement 2, which is correct.
(d) Correct: statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct, and only statement 3 is incorrect.
keyfact: Cornwallis (1793) created thanas under darogas nominated by the magistrate; the Madras daroga system came in 1816 under Munro, not 1812.
related: Cornwallis is called the father of the civil services in India.
Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in 1793.
The Madras police reform was in 1816 under Thomas Munro.
The Police Act of 1861 created the modern district police structure in British India.
The 1902-03 Police Commission was chaired by Andrew Fraser.
Napier's Sindh police was modelled on the Irish Constabulary.
Cornwallis separated revenue and judicial functions in the Cornwallis Code of 1793.
statements: 1 — Correct: Cornwallis divided each district into thanas or police circuits of about 20-30 miles square. This was part of the 1792-93 police reform. It replaced the zamindari police with a government-controlled, salaried force headed by Indians but supervised by the European magistrate. It was a major step towards a centralised police under the Company and created the thana as the basic territorial unit, which survives today.

2 — Correct: Each thana was put under a daroga, an Indian officer who supervised subordinate constables such as peons and burkandazes. The word daroga comes from Persian and originally meant a superintendent. The post became notorious for corruption and extortion in the early 19th century. Above the daroga, the magistrate and later the superintendent of police supervised the district force. The system became the model for police organisation across British India.

3 — Incorrect: The daroga system was introduced in Madras in 1816, not 1812, through Madras Regulation XI of 1816 under Governor Thomas Munro. Munro abolished the old poligar (palayakkarar) police and talari system and placed the police under village headmen with supervision by the collector. It was therefore different from the Bengal pattern. Bombay under Elphinstone followed a similar village-oriented police. The Police Act of 1861 later made a uniform structure.

4 — Correct: The daroga was nominated by the district magistrate and worked under his control. Cornwallis concentrated police and magisterial powers in the district magistrate, while the judge and collector were separate. Darogas were low-paid, which encouraged corruption. Following the Police Act of 1861, a district superintendent of police was introduced as the head of the district police, subordinate to the magistrate in general control.
summary: The correct answer is (d): statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Under Cornwallis's 1793 police reforms, districts were divided into thanas of roughly 20-30 miles square, each under a daroga nominated by the district magistrate. Statement 3 is wrong because the daroga system came to Madras in 1816 under Thomas Munro, not 1812.
topic_notes: Police administration in British India evolved in stages. Before 1765, the Mughal faujdari system with zamindars as police agents operated. Warren Hastings in 1772 tried a faujdar and thana system. Cornwallis in 1791-93 created the thana-daroga system, separated police from revenue, and made the magistrate responsible for crime control. The Cornwallis Code of 1793 also introduced separation of revenue and civil administration, the Permanent Settlement, and the Cornwallis Code's civil courts. In Madras, Thomas Munro's 1816 reform strengthened village headmen and gave the collector police authority. In Bombay, Elphinstone retained the village police with the patel. In 1843 Charles Napier set up the Sindh police on the Irish Constabulary model, a more centralised and distinct force from the Bengal pattern. After the 1857 revolt, the Police Commission of 1860 led to the Police Act of 1861, which created the provincial police with an Inspector-General in each province and a District Superintendent of Police in each district. The 1902-03 Police Commission under Andrew Fraser recommended an Imperial Police service and Criminal Investigation Departments, and Indian Police Service recruitment began in 1893 via exam in London, with Indian entry later. Other Cornwallis reforms to remember are the Permanent Settlement of 1793 in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, and the Cornwallis Code, with the Indian Civil Service being the 'steel frame' attributed to him as its father. Possible questions: who is the father of civil services in India, the daroga's role, the Police Act of 1861, and the Police Commission of 1902.

question: An ‘out-worker’ is expressly excluded from the definition of ‘workman’ under which one of the following legislations ?
options: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970
The Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: An 'out-worker' is a person who is given raw material by an employer to be processed or made up at home, off the employer's premises. Labour statutes treat such persons differently from regular employees. Under the Plantations Labour Act, 1951, 'plantation' covers tea, coffee, rubber, cinchona, cardamom (and later added crops) above a prescribed area, and the Act's definition of 'worker' is tied to employment in the plantation or its offices, with out-workers expressly excluded. The question's official key treats this Act as the one that excludes the out-worker. By contrast, the Factories Act, 1948 defines 'worker' as a person employed in a manufacturing process or related work in the premises; it does not use the term 'workman', and out-work is dealt with separately in the Act. The Contract Labour Act, 1970 defines 'workman' broadly as a person employed in or in connection with the work of an establishment to do skilled, semi-skilled, unskilled, manual, supervisory, technical or clerical work, with exclusions for administrative, managerial and similar staff and for armed forces personnel. The Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979 defines 'workman' similarly and has no out-worker exclusion. Hence (b).
explanations: Incorrect: the Factories Act uses the term 'worker' (not 'workman'), covering persons employed in the premises in manufacturing processes; it is not the Act whose 'workman' definition excludes out-workers.
Correct: the Plantations Labour Act, 1951 expressly excludes an out-worker from its definition of worker, as per the official key.
Incorrect: the Contract Labour Act, 1970 defines 'workman' with exclusions for administrative, managerial, supervisory-type posts and similar categories, not for out-workers.
Incorrect: the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979 defines 'workman' in connection with an establishment or a contractor, and does not carve out out-workers.
keyfact: Plantations Labour Act, 1951: out-worker expressly excluded from the definition of worker (official key: b).
option_notes: The Factories Act, 1948 regulates health, safety, welfare, working hours, leave and employment of young persons in factories. A factory is a premises with 10 or more workers using power, or 20 or more without power. It uses the term 'worker', defined in Section 2(l). It is administered by state governments through Chief Inspectors of Factories, and the Act followed the 1934 Act.

The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 provides for the welfare of plantation labour and regulates their conditions of work. It covers tea, coffee, rubber, cinchona and cardamom plantations (extended to others by notification) of 5 hectares or more and 15 or more persons employed. It requires housing, medical facilities, educational facilities for children, creches and recreational facilities. It is administered by state governments and is being subsumed under the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.

The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 regulates contract labour in establishments and provides for its abolition in certain circumstances. It applies to establishments employing 20 or more contract workers. It requires registration of principal employers and licensing of contractors, and makes the principal employer liable for wages if the contractor defaults. Central Advisory and State Boards advise on its working. It is now subsumed under the OSH Code, 2020.

The Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979 protects workers recruited by a contractor in one state for work in another. It applies to establishments with 5 or more such workers. It requires licensing of contractors, a displacement allowance, a journey allowance, and suitable residential accommodation and medical facilities. It is also subsumed under the OSH Code, 2020.
related: The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 covers plantations of 5 hectares or more with 15 or more workers.
The Factories Act, 1948 uses the term 'worker', not 'workman'.
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 defines 'workman' in Section 2(s).
Contract Labour Act, 1970 applies to establishments with 20 or more contract workers.
Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979 applies to establishments with 5 or more migrant workmen.
The Beedi and Cigar Workers Act, 1966 covers home-based workers.
The OSH Code, 2020 subsumes the Plantations Labour Act, the Contract Labour Act and the Factories Act.
summary: The official answer is (b) The Plantations Labour Act, 1951. Its definition of 'worker' (and the associated provisions) covers persons employed in a plantation or in its offices, and expressly excludes an out-worker, i.e. a person working at home outside the plantation premises, from the definition.
topic_notes: The term 'workman' or 'worker' is defined differently in each labour statute, and UPSC often tests these definitions. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 defines 'workman' in Section 2(s) as a person employed in an industry for manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work, but excludes persons in the armed forces, police or prison service, those mainly in managerial or administrative capacity, and supervisors drawing wages above the prescribed limit. The Factories Act, 1948 uses 'worker' in Section 2(l), including persons employed directly or through an agency, including a contractor, with or without the principal employer's knowledge, in a manufacturing process or cleaning or any other work connected with it. The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 covers plantation workers, and excludes out-workers per the official key. An out-worker is typically a person given raw material to work upon at home, as in the beedi and cigar industry, where the Beedi and Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act, 1966 covers home workers, an area where out-work is significant. The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 uses 'employee', and the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 uses 'employed person'. The Contract Labour Act, 1970 and the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979 have broad definitions. The four labour codes (Code on Wages 2019, Industrial Relations Code 2020, Code on Social Security 2020, OSH Code 2020) consolidate 29 central laws and use terms such as 'worker', 'employee' and 'inter-state migrant worker', although they have yet to be fully implemented. Expect questions on thresholds, coverage and definitions.

question: Which one of the following nature of work shall not be taken into account while the Appropriate Government considers prohibiting employment of contract labour in an establishment under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 ?
options: The process, operation or other work is incidental to or necessary for the industry 72
The work is of a permanent nature
The work is done ordinarily through regular workmen
The work is of intermittent nature
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 10(1) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 empowers the Appropriate Government, after consulting the Central or State Advisory Contract Labour Board, to prohibit employment of contract labour in any process, operation or other work in an establishment by notification in the Official Gazette. Section 10(2) says the government shall have regard to the conditions of work and benefits provided to contract labour and other relevant factors, such as: (a) whether the work is incidental to or necessary for the industry, trade, business, manufacture or occupation of the establishment; (b) whether it is of perennial nature, i.e. of sufficient duration having regard to the nature of the industry; (c) whether it is done ordinarily through regular workmen in that or a similar establishment; (d) whether it is sufficient to employ a considerable number of whole-time workmen. Options (a), (b) and (c) correspond to these statutory factors. Option (d), intermittent nature, is the opposite of perennial and is not a listed factor. Because the official key is (c), the question as printed may have been framed or keyed differently from the statute. Memorise the four statutory factors and the Steel Authority of India v. National Union Waterfront Workers (2001) position, which held that the government's prohibition under Section 10 does not automatically lead to absorption of contract workers.
explanations: (a) This is Section 10(2)(a), a statutory factor: work incidental to or necessary for the industry is considered.
(b) Permanent or perennial nature of the work is Section 10(2)(b), a statutory factor.

(c) This is the official answer. Note, however, that Section 10(2)(c) as enacted refers to work done ordinarily through regular workmen, so the key conflicts with the statute text. Follow the key for the exam.
(d) Intermittent nature is not listed in Section 10(2). It is the opposite of the perennial nature that the Act does name, so on the statutory text this looks like the item not considered.
keyfact: Section 10(2) CLRA Act factors: incidental/necessary, perennial nature, done through regular workmen, sufficient for whole-time workmen; intermittent nature is not listed (official key: c).
option_notes: Work incidental to or necessary for the industry: Section 10(2)(a) of the CLRA Act. It tests whether the work is integral to the establishment's main business. If it is, that points toward abolishing contract labour for that work. The Act applies to establishments employing 20 or more contract workers (a State may lower the threshold) and to contractors engaging 20 or more workers.

Permanent nature of work: Section 10(2)(b) speaks of work of 'perennial nature', meaning work of sufficient duration given the industry. Perennial work suggests regular employees should do it. Contract labour is generally meant for temporary, seasonal or occasional work. The Supreme Court in Air India Statutory Corporation (1997) discussed the issue of automatic absorption, and SAIL (2001) overruled it.

Work done ordinarily through regular workmen: Section 10(2)(c) refers to work usually done by regular workmen in that establishment or a similar one. If regular staff normally do the work, using contract labour is suspect. It is a prohibition factor under Section 10. It is the official answer here, though the statute text includes it as a factor.

Intermittent nature: the Act does not list it in Section 10(2), and it is the opposite of perennial work. Intermittent or seasonal work is the kind of work where contract labour is normally acceptable. Related is Section 10(2)(d): whether the work is sufficient to employ a considerable number of whole-time workmen.
related: Section 10 CLRA Act deals with prohibition of contract labour.
The CLRA Act applies to establishments with 20 or more contract workers.
SAIL v. National Union Waterfront Workers (2001) held that no automatic absorption of contract labour follows abolition.
Section 21 makes the principal employer liable for wages if the contractor defaults.
The OSH Code, 2020 subsumed the CLRA Act and raised the threshold to 50 workers.
Advisory Contract Labour Boards exist at the Central and State levels under Section 3 and Section 4.
Licensing of contractors is under Section 12 of the CLRA Act.
summary: The official UPSC answer is (c). Note for revision: the text of Section 10(2) of the CLRA Act, 1970 lists 'done ordinarily through regular workmen in that establishment or a similar establishment' as a factor the Appropriate Government must weigh. On a plain reading of the Act, option (d), intermittent nature, is the item not listed. Learn (c) for the exam, but know the statutory list below.
topic_notes: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 regulates the employment of contract labour in certain establishments and provides for its abolition in specified circumstances. It came into force in 1970 following the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Labour and the Second National Commission on Labour. It applies to establishments and contractors employing 20 or more workmen, with the threshold changeable by the appropriate government. It does not apply to establishments with work of a casual nature. Key provisions: Section 4 provides for the Central and State Advisory Boards; Sections 7 and 8 cover registration of establishments and licensing of contractors; Section 10 deals with prohibition of contract labour; Sections 16 to 19 cover welfare and health facilities such as canteens, restrooms, drinking water and first aid; Section 21 makes the contractor responsible for wage payment, with the principal employer liable as a fallback; Section 25 provides for the overriding effect of the Act. Contract workers must be paid wages on time, and the principal employer must nominate a representative to be present at disbursement. The Act's Section 10 prohibition was clarified in Air India Statutory Corporation v. United Labour Union (1997), which suggested automatic absorption, and was overruled by the Constitution Bench in Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. National Union Waterfront Workers (2001), which held that no automatic absorption follows from abolition. In 2020 the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code subsumed this Act. Under the OSH Code, the threshold for contract labour rises to 50 workers, and core activities are generally prohibited from being contracted, with exceptions.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q68.
ocr: Which one of the following nature of work shall not be taken into account while the Appropriate Government considers prohibiting employment of contract labour in an establishment under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 ? (a) The process, operation or other work is incidental to or necessary for the industry 72. (b) The work is of a permanent nature (c) The work is done ordinarily through regular workmen (d) The work is of intermittent nature
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 10 of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 empowers the Appropriate Government, after consulting the Central or State Advisory Board, to prohibit employment of contract labour in any process, operation or other work in any establishment. Section 10(2) lays down the matters to be considered: (a) whether the process, operation or other work is incidental to or necessary for the industry, trade, business, manufacture or occupation carried on in the establishment; (b) whether it is of perennial nature, i.e. it must go on from day to day; (c) whether it is done ordinarily through regular workmen in that establishment or a similar establishment; (d) whether it is sufficient to employ a considerable number of whole-time workmen. The Supreme Court in Air India Statutory Corporation v. United Labour Union (1996) held that contract labour would be absorbed on abolition, but this was overruled by Steel Authority of India v. National Union Waterfront Workers (2001), which held there is no automatic absorption. Elimination: (a), (b) and (c) mirror the statutory criteria (permanent = perennial). Only (d), intermittent or sporadic work, is the opposite of perennial and is not a criterion, so it is the 'not taken into account' option.
explanations: Wrong as the answer: incidental or necessary work is expressly a Section 10(2) factor, so it is taken into account.
Wrong as the answer: 'perennial' (permanent) nature of work is a Section 10(2) factor, so it is taken into account.
Wrong as the answer: work ordinarily done through regular workmen in the establishment is a Section 10(2) factor, so it is taken into account.
Correct answer: intermittent or sporadic nature is not a listed factor. The Act looks for perennial work, which is the opposite of intermittent, so this is not considered.
keyfact: Section 10(2) CLRA 1970 tests: necessary/incidental, perennial, done by regular workmen, enough work for whole-time workmen; intermittent nature is NOT a test.
option_notes: Incidental to or necessary for the industry is the first test under Section 10(2)(a). Work that is integral to the main activity of the establishment (for example, core maintenance or processing operations) suggests that contract labour should not be used and that regular employment is appropriate. Courts read it along with the other tests, and no single factor is decisive.

Perennial or permanent nature under Section 10(2)(b) means the work goes on continuously from day to day and is of enduring character, not seasonal or casual. If work is perennial, there is a strong case for abolishing contract labour. The Act's text uses the word 'perennial', and 'permanent' is the paraphrase used in the option.

Work ordinarily done through regular workmen is the Section 10(2)(c) test. If in the establishment or a similar one the work is usually done by direct, regular employees, then using contract labour for it is suspect and prohibition may follow. It prevents contract arrangements from replacing regular jobs.

Intermittent or sporadic work is not a Section 10(2) factor. Such work is the converse of perennial work, and it is the sort of work for which contract labour may legitimately be used. Do not confuse it with the 'sufficient to employ considerable number of whole-time workmen' test, which is the fourth factor in the Act.
related: Section 10 of the CLRA Act 1970 deals with prohibition of employment of contract labour.
The CLRA Act applies to establishments and contractors employing 20 or more workmen.
Section 10(2) factors: incidental or necessary, perennial, done through regular workmen, sufficient to employ considerable number of whole-time workmen.
SAIL v. National Union Waterfront Workers (2001) held that there is no automatic absorption of contract labour.
The OSH Code 2020 raises the contract labour threshold to 50 workers.
Section 7 requires registration of the principal employer; Section 12 requires a licence for the contractor.
Section 21 makes the principal employer liable for wages if the contractor defaults.
Appropriate Government prohibits contract labour after consulting the Central or State Advisory Board.
summary: The answer is (d). Under Section 10(2) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, the Appropriate Government considers four factors before prohibiting contract labour: whether the work is incidental to or necessary for the industry, whether it is of perennial (permanent) nature, whether it is done ordinarily through regular workmen in that establishment, and whether it is sufficient to employ a considerable number of whole-time workmen. 'Intermittent nature' is not a listed factor.
topic_notes: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 regulates the employment of contract labour in certain establishments and provides for its abolition in certain circumstances. It extends to the whole of India and applies to every establishment employing 20 or more workmen as contract labour on any day of the preceding twelve months (the State governments can lower or raise the threshold) and to every contractor employing 20 or more workmen. It does not apply to establishments where work is of an intermittent or casual nature (Section 1(5)); work is deemed not intermittent if it was performed for more than 120 days in the preceding twelve months or is of a seasonal character performed for more than 60 days in a year. Key bodies: the Central Advisory Contract Labour Board and State Boards (Section 3 and 4) advise governments. Principal employers must register the establishment (Section 7) and contractors must obtain a licence (Section 12). Welfare duties include canteens, rest rooms, drinking water, latrines and first aid. Wages must be paid by the contractor, with the principal employer liable if the contractor fails (Section 21). Section 10 deals with prohibition of contract labour. Case law: Standard Vacuum Refining Co. v. Their Workmen (1960), Gammon India v. Union of India (1974), Air India Statutory Corporation (1996), and the Constitution Bench in Steel Authority of India Ltd. (2001), which held that there is no automatic absorption of contract labour on abolition. The Act is being subsumed by the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which raises the threshold to 50 workers. Penalties are under Sections 23 to 25.

question: Which of the statements relating to the Grievance Redressal Committee under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is not correct ?
options: It shall consist of equal number of 73. members from among employer and workmen
It shall be constituted in an industrial establishment employing twenty or more workmen
The Chairperson of the Committee shall be nominated by the Appropriate 74, Government
The total members of the Committee shall not be more than six
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 9C of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 requires every industrial establishment employing twenty or more workmen to provide for a Grievance Redressal Committee to resolve disputes arising out of individual grievances. The Committee has equal representation of employer and workmen and not more than six members in total. The Chairperson is chosen alternately from the employer's side and the workmen's side, so no government nomination is involved. The workmen's representatives are to be selected in consultation with the union or, where there is none, in the manner prescribed. As far as practicable, one member should be a woman, and the number of women members should be in proportion to women employed in the establishment. The Committee must complete its proceedings within 45 days of receiving a written application. An aggrieved worker may appeal to the employer against the Committee's decision, and the employer must dispose of the appeal within one month. Elimination: (a), (b) and (d) restate the statutory text, so only (c) is wrong. The 2010 amendment inserted Section 9C, effective 15 September 2010. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 retains a similar Grievance Redressal Committee in Section 4 for establishments with 20 or more workers.
explanations: Correct as a statement, so it is not the answer. Section 9C prescribes equal numbers from employer and workmen.
Correct as a statement, so it is not the answer. The Committee is mandatory for establishments with twenty or more workmen.
Incorrect as a statement, so it is the answer. The Chairperson is chosen alternately from the employer and workmen sides, not nominated by the Government.
Correct as a statement, so it is not the answer. The total membership is capped at six.
keyfact: Section 9C Grievance Redressal Committee: 20+ workmen, equal employer-workmen members, max six, Chairperson rotates between the two sides (not government nominated), 45-day disposal.
option_notes: Equal representation is the rule under Section 9C. The Committee has members from both employer and workmen in equal numbers. Together with the six-member cap, this means at most three from each side. Women's representation is to be proportionate as far as practicable. The aim is for grievances to be resolved internally and quickly, before they become formal industrial disputes.

The twenty-workman threshold determines which establishments must constitute the Committee. It applies to every industrial establishment with twenty or more workmen. The provision was inserted by the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 2010. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 keeps a similar threshold for a Grievance Redressal Committee.

This is the false statement. In reality the Chairperson alternates between employer's and workmen's representatives. The Appropriate Government has no power to nominate the Chairperson. The Government may be the Central or State Government depending on the industry. Its role is limited to making rules and enforcing the Act.

The ceiling of six members is fixed by Section 9C. The Committee is expected to dispose of a grievance within 45 days of receiving the written application. Aggrieved workers may appeal to the employer, who must decide within one month. The cap keeps the body compact.
related: Section 9C: Grievance Redressal Committee, inserted in 2010 for establishments with 20 or more workmen.
The Committee must try to settle a grievance within 45 days of receiving the application.
The Committee has at most six members, with equal representation of employer and workmen.
Section 3: Works Committee for establishments with 100 or more workmen.
Section 2A: individual dismissal, discharge or retrenchment is deemed an industrial dispute.
Section 25F: retrenchment needs one month's notice and compensation of 15 days' pay per year of service.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 has a Grievance Redressal Committee provision in Section 4.
Chapter VB applies to establishments with 100 or more workmen.
statements: a — Correct: Section 9C requires equal representation of employer and workmen. Equal representation keeps the body balanced between the two sides. The members are chosen from the establishment's own employer and workmen representatives, and the workmen's side is selected in consultation with the union. The Committee deals with individual grievances, not collective disputes, which go to conciliation and adjudication.

b — Correct: The threshold is twenty or more workmen. Establishments below this size need not constitute the Committee. Section 9C was added by the 2010 amendment. The same threshold of twenty applies in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, and it is separate from the 100-worker thresholds for standing orders and for retrenchment permission.

c — Incorrect: The Chairperson is not nominated by the Appropriate Government. The chair is selected alternately from the employer's side and the workmen's side. This rotation is meant to preserve balance and internal resolution. The Government's role is limited to rule-making and enforcement, not to appointing members of the Committee.

d — Correct: The Committee has no more than six members in total, so at most three from each side. The Committee should try to settle a grievance within 45 days of receiving the written application. If a worker is dissatisfied, an appeal lies to the employer, who must decide it within one month.
summary: The answer is (c). Under Section 9C of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Grievance Redressal Committee's Chairperson is chosen by the employer's side and the workmen's side in rotation, not nominated by the Appropriate Government. The other three statements match Section 9C.
topic_notes: Section 9C of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provides a Grievance Redressal Mechanism for individual grievances. It was inserted by the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 2010 and came into force on 15 September 2010. It applies to every industrial establishment with twenty or more workmen. The Committee has equal representation of employer and workmen, with a maximum of six members. The Chairperson is selected alternately from the two sides. The Committee should complete its proceedings within 45 days. Appeal lies to the employer within one month. Section 9C also provides that the worker may seek remedy through the Committee, but it does not bar approaching other authorities in the ways the Act allows. Related machinery under the Act includes: Works Committee (Section 3, for establishments with 100 or more workmen), Conciliation Officers and Boards of Conciliation (Sections 4 and 5), Courts of Inquiry (Section 6), Labour Courts, Tribunals and the National Tribunal (Section 7 and its sub-sections), and Section 2A, which treats an individual dismissal, discharge, retrenchment or termination as an industrial dispute. Section 25F sets the conditions for retrenchment: one month's notice, retrenchment compensation of 15 days' average pay per completed year of service, and notice to the Government. Chapter VB (Sections 25K-25S) covers lay-off, retrenchment and closure in establishments with 100 or more workmen, with a government permission requirement. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 will subsume the Industrial Disputes Act, the Trade Unions Act and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act. It retains a Grievance Redressal Committee in Section 4, for establishments with twenty or more workers, with up to ten members, and women represented in proportion.

question: Under the provisions of the Factories Act, 1948, a Safety Committee is to be constituted in a factory where :
options: Hazardous substances are used or handled
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Factories Act, 1948 was amended in 1987 after the Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) to add Chapter IVA on 'Provisions relating to Hazardous Processes' (Sections 41A to 41H). Section 41G provides for workers' participation in safety management: the occupier of a factory where a hazardous process takes place, or where hazardous substances are used or handled, must set up a Safety Committee with equal representation of workers and management. The committee's function is to promote cooperation in maintaining proper safety and health at work and to review periodically the measures taken. The State Government prescribes its composition, tenure and functions through rules. Elimination: options (a) and (d) rely on headcount; headcount thresholds appear elsewhere in the Act, such as the Welfare Officer (500 or more workers, Section 49), Canteen (250 or more, Section 46), Crèche (30 or more women, Section 48) and Safety Officer (1000 or more workers, Section 40B), which is why they are tempting distractors. Option (c) is not a statutory criterion. Hence (b) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: 1000 or more workers is the threshold for appointing a Safety Officer under Section 40B, not for constituting a Safety Committee.
Correct: Safety Committee is required where hazardous processes are carried on or hazardous substances are used or handled, per Section 41G (Chapter IVA).
Incorrect: Use of heavy machinery alone is not a statutory condition for a Safety Committee; machinery safety is dealt with in Chapter IV (Sections 21-40).
Incorrect: 500 or more workers is the threshold for a Welfare Officer under Section 49, not a Safety Committee.
keyfact: Safety Committee (Section 41G, Factories Act 1948) is required where hazardous processes are carried on or hazardous substances are used or handled, not based on worker numbers.
option_notes: 1000 or more workers: Under Section 40B, a factory employing 1000 or more workers must employ Safety Officers, and the State Government can also require them where hazardous processes occur. Safety Officers' qualifications and duties are prescribed by State rules. It is a headcount trigger frequently confused with the Safety Committee provision.

Hazardous substances used or handled: Chapter IVA, inserted by the 1987 amendment after the Bhopal gas disaster, covers hazardous processes listed in the First Schedule. Section 41G requires a Safety Committee with equal worker and management representation. Other provisions include on-site emergency plans (41B), disclosure of information (41B), and worker's right to warn of imminent danger (41H).

Heavy machinery: Not a criterion for a Safety Committee. Machinery safety is covered in Sections 21-24 and 28-35 on fencing of machinery, work on or near machinery in motion, hoists, lifts, pressure plant and cranes. Chapter IV also covers precautions against dangerous fumes, explosives and fire.

500 or more workers: Section 49 requires the occupier of a factory employing 500 or more workers to appoint Welfare Officers, with qualifications and duties prescribed by the State Government. Welfare provisions are in Chapter V (Sections 42-50), including washing facilities, canteens (250 workers), shelters and crèches (30 women).
related: Chapter IVA (Sections 41A-41H) was inserted by the 1987 amendment after the Bhopal gas tragedy.
Section 41G: workers' participation in safety management through a Safety Committee.
Section 40B: Safety Officers in factories with 1000 or more workers.
Section 49: Welfare Officer where 500 or more workers are employed.
Section 46: Canteen where more than 250 workers are employed.
Section 48: Crèche where more than 30 women workers are employed.
Section 2(cb) defines 'hazardous process'.
Section 41H gives workers the right to warn about imminent danger.
summary: The answer is (b). Under Section 41G read with the safety committee provisions (Section 41G deals with workers' participation in safety management), the State Government may require a Safety Committee in factories carrying on a 'dangerous operation' i.e., where hazardous processes are carried on or hazardous substances are used or handled. The trigger is the nature of the process, not the number of workers or type of machinery.
topic_notes: The Factories Act, 1948 came into force on 1 April 1949 and applies to premises employing 10 or more workers with power or 20 or more without power (Section 2m). It is administered by State Governments through the Chief Inspector of Factories, while the Union provides policy via the Directorate General Factory Advice Service and Labour Institutes (DGFASLI). Key amendments include 1976 and the major 1987 amendment after the Bhopal gas leak (December 1984), which added Chapter IVA on hazardous processes, defined 'hazardous process' (Section 2cb) and 'worker', and introduced the occupier's duty to disclose information, to prepare a site appraisal committee and on-site emergency plan, and to set up a Safety Committee. Chapters: Inspecting staff (II), Health (III, Sections 11-20), Safety (IV, Sections 21-41), Hazardous Processes (IVA, 41A-41H), Welfare (V), Working hours of adults (VI), Employment of young persons (VII), Annual leave with wages (VIII), Special provisions (X), Penalties (IX). Working hours: 48 per week and 9 per day, with a spread-over of 10.5 hours, and overtime at twice the ordinary wage rate. Child under 14 cannot be employed; adolescents 15-18 need fitness certificates. Annual leave: 1 day for every 20 days worked for adults. Threshold numbers are heavily tested: Canteen 250, Welfare Officer 500, Safety Officer 1000, Crèche 30 women, Rest rooms/lunch rooms 150. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 will subsume this Act.

ocr: The eight-digit number 789459xy is divisible by 88, where x and y are digits. What are the possible values of x and y ? rel, ya? (a) x=2, y=2 x=3, y=6 x=4, y=4 If x is the smallest natural number that is divisible by both 24 and 30, whereas y is the largest natural number that divides both 36 and 100, then what is the value of x-y? 116 (a) 124 (b) 128 (c) 132 (d) 100 What is the digit in the unit place of 97 i? 2 (a) 4 (b) 6 (c) 8 (d) A runner completed a 40 km race in 3 hours. She changed her speed after completing each quarter of the distance such that the proportion of the speeds in the fir
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: 88 = 8 × 11, and 8 and 11 are co-prime, so the number must pass both tests. Test for 8: the last three digits, here 9xy, must be divisible by 8. Test for 11: the sum of digits in odd places minus the sum in even places must be 0 or a multiple of 11. For 7 8 9 4 5 9 x y, the odd-place digits (1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th) are 7, 9, 5, x with sum 21 + x. The even-place digits are 8, 4, 9, y with sum 21 + y. The difference is x - y, and since x and y are single digits it must be 0, so x = y. Now 9xy becomes 9xx, so check 900, 911, 922, 933, 944 and so on for divisibility by 8. 900/8 is not whole, 922/8 = 115.25 is not whole, and 944/8 = 118 works. Only x = y = 4 fits. Check: 78945944 / 88 = 897113. Elimination is fast: options (a) and (c) have x ≠ y, so they fail the 11-test. Option (b) has x = y = 2 but 922 is not divisible by 8. Only (d) survives.
explanations: Wrong: x = 1, y = 2 gives x - y = -1, so the number fails the divisibility test for 11 (912 is divisible by 8, but that is not enough).
Wrong: x = y = 2 satisfies the 11-test, but the last three digits 922 give 922/8 = 115.25, so the 8-test fails.
Wrong: x = 3, y = 6 gives x - y = -3, which fails the 11-test, even though 936 = 8 × 117 passes the 8-test.
Correct: x = y = 4 passes the 11-test (difference 0) and the 8-test (944 = 8 × 118). So 78945944 = 88 × 897113.
keyfact: For divisibility by 88, check 8 (last three digits) and 11 (alternate digit sum difference); 78945944 = 88 × 897113.
option_notes: x = 1, y = 2 gives 78945912. The last three digits 912 = 8 × 114, so it is divisible by 8. The alternating digit sum difference is -1, so it is not divisible by 11 and therefore not by 88. It shows that passing one co-prime factor's test is not enough.

x = 2, y = 2 gives 78945922. The alternating digit sum difference is 0, so it is divisible by 11. The last three digits 922 leave remainder 2 on division by 8, so it is not divisible by 8 and therefore not by 88.
x = 3, y = 6 gives 78945936. The last three digits 936 = 8 × 117, so it is divisible by 8. The alternating sum difference is -3, so it is not divisible by 11. Hence it is not divisible by 88.

x = 4, y = 4 gives 78945944 = 88 × 897113. The alternating digit sum difference is 0, so it is divisible by 11. The last three digits 944 = 8 × 118, so it is divisible by 8. Since 8 and 11 are co-prime, the number is divisible by 88. This is the correct option.
related: Divisibility by 8 depends on the last three digits.
Divisibility by 11: the difference of the sums of alternate digits must be 0 or a multiple of 11.
88 = 8 × 11, which are co-prime factors.
Divisibility by 99 means divisibility by both 9 and 11.
HCF × LCM of two numbers = product of the numbers.
Unit digit of powers of 2 repeats in the cycle 2, 4, 8, 6.
For equal distances, time is inversely proportional to speed.
LCM of 24 and 30 is 120.
summary: The answer is (d) x = 4, y = 4. The image holds four questions, so this note treats the first one (789459xy divisible by 88) as Q71. A number divisible by 88 must be divisible by both 8 and 11, which forces x = y and 9xy divisible by 8, and only 944 works. (The runner question at the bottom also gives (d), 28 minutes.)
topic_notes: Divisibility rules are a core number-system topic in the EPFO Quantitative Aptitude section. Key rules: by 2, the last digit is even. By 3, the digit sum is divisible by 3. By 4, the last two digits are divisible by 4. By 5, the last digit is 0 or 5. By 8, the last three digits are divisible by 8. By 9, the digit sum is divisible by 9. By 11, the difference between the sums of alternate digits is 0 or a multiple of 11. By 7, 11 and 13, take the difference of alternate 3-digit groups. For composite divisors, split into co-prime factors: 6 = 2×3, 12 = 3×4, 24 = 3×8, 88 = 8×11, 99 = 9×11. Do not split into non-co-prime factors such as 4×6 for 24. For missing-digit problems, apply the 11-test first because it links x and y, then use the 8-test to pick the digits. Other questions in the same image test related ideas. LCM of 24 and 30 is 120 and HCF of 36 and 100 is 4, so x - y = 116. The units digit of 2^(2^100) is 6 because the cycle of 2 is 2, 4, 8, 6 and 2^100 is a multiple of 4. In the race, time is inversely proportional to speed for equal distances. Useful facts: HCF × LCM = product of two numbers, and unit digit cycles have length 4 for 2, 3, 7 and 8, and length 2 for 4 and 9.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q72.
ocr: The eight-digit number 789459xy is divisible by 88, where x and y are digits. What are the possible values of x and y ? rel, ya? (a) x=2, y=2 x=3, y=6 x=4, y=4 If x is the smallest natural number that is divisible by both 24 and 30, whereas y is the largest natural number that divides both 36 and 100, then what is the value of x-y? 116 (a) 124 (b) 128 (c) 132 (d) 100 What is the digit in the unit place of 97 i? 2 (a) 4 (b) 6 (c) 8 (d) A runner completed a 40 km race in 3 hours. She changed her speed after completing each quarter of the distance such that the proportion of the speeds in the fir
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This question tests the difference between LCM and HCF, and the two are easy to mix up. The smallest natural number divisible by both 24 and 30 is their LCM. The largest number that divides both 36 and 100 is their HCF. Prime factorisation: 24 = 2^3 × 3, 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, 36 = 2^2 × 3^2, 100 = 2^2 × 5^2. LCM takes the highest power of every prime that appears: 2^3 × 3 × 5 = 120. HCF takes the lowest power of the primes common to both numbers: for 36 and 100 only 2 is common, and its lowest power is 2^2, so HCF = 4. Then x − y = 116. Elimination: 124, 128 and 132 would come from a wrong x or y. For example, 124 = 128 − 4 (x taken as 128), and 132 would need y = −12, which is impossible. The shortcut check is that LCM must be a multiple of both numbers (120 = 24×5 = 30×4) and HCF must divide both (4 divides 36 and 100). Also, the HCF of 36 and 100 cannot exceed 36.
explanations: Correct. x = LCM(24, 30) = 120 and y = HCF(36, 100) = 4, so x − y = 116.
Incorrect. 124 would need y = −4 or x = 128. 128 is not a multiple of 30, so it cannot be x.
Incorrect. 128 would need x = 132 with y = 4, or x = 120 with y = −8. 132 is not divisible by 24 or 30, and y cannot be negative.
Incorrect. 132 would need x = 136 or y = −12. Neither fits the definitions of LCM and HCF here.
option_notes: 116 is the correct value of 120 − 4. It is the difference between LCM(24, 30) = 120 and HCF(36, 100) = 4. The LCM is the smallest common multiple and the HCF is the largest common divisor. For any two numbers, LCM × HCF = product of the numbers.

124 is not the answer. It would arise from a mistake such as taking the HCF of 36 and 100 as −4, or taking x as 128. 124 = 4 × 31. Common errors in LCM/HCF problems include using the product (24 × 30 = 720) or the wrong prime powers.

128 is 2^7. It is not divisible by 3 or 5, so it cannot be a common multiple of 24 and 30. It would be the result of x = 132 and y = 4, which is not valid. A multiple of 24 must contain the factor 3, and a multiple of 30 must contain 3 and 5.
132 = 4 × 3 × 11. It is divisible by neither 24 nor 30 (132/24 = 5.5). It is a distractor near the true answer. Always check a candidate LCM by dividing it by each given number.
related: LCM × HCF = product of the two numbers (only for two numbers).
HCF of co-prime numbers is 1; their LCM is their product.
HCF of 36 and 100 is 4; LCM is 900.
Smallest number leaving remainder r on division by a, b, c = LCM(a, b, c) + r.
Largest number dividing a, b, c with remainders r1, r2, r3 = HCF(a−r1, b−r2, c−r3).
HCF of fractions = HCF of numerators / LCM of denominators.
summary: The answer is (a) 116. x is the LCM of 24 and 30, which is 120. y is the HCF of 36 and 100, which is 4. So x − y = 120 − 4 = 116.
topic_notes: LCM and HCF (GCD) are core number-system topics in the Quantitative Aptitude section of the EPFO exam. HCF is the largest number dividing all the given numbers. LCM is the smallest number divisible by all of them. Methods: prime factorisation, division method, and the Euclidean algorithm for HCF. Key identities: LCM × HCF = product of two numbers (true for two numbers only, not three). The HCF of two numbers always divides their LCM. For fractions, HCF = HCF of numerators / LCM of denominators, and LCM = LCM of numerators / HCF of denominators. Co-prime numbers have HCF 1 and LCM equal to their product. Typical applications: the largest tape or tile that measures given lengths exactly (HCF); the time when bells ring together or runners meet again (LCM); the smallest number leaving the same remainder r is LCM + r; the largest number dividing a, b, c and leaving remainders r1, r2, r3 is the HCF of (a−r1), (b−r2), (c−r3). Useful values: LCM(24, 30) = 120, HCF(24, 30) = 6, HCF(36, 100) = 4, LCM(36, 100) = 900. Other angles UPSC could use: the sum or ratio of two numbers given with their HCF and LCM, finding the greatest 4-digit number divisible by given numbers, and the smallest square number divisible by given numbers. The key skill is fast factorisation using divisibility rules for 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9 and 11.
