Tertiary: services that support production and consumption, including trade, transport, communication, banking, insurance, administration, health, education, tourism and entertainment. Quaternary: knowledge-based activities involving collection, production and dissemination of information, including R&D, IT, consulting, and high-end education and finance. Quinary: the highest level of decision-making in government, corporations, science, and media, covering policy making and top management. Another classification is red-collar, white-collar, grey-collar, gold-collar and pink-collar workers in geography texts: gold-collar covers top professionals in knowledge and R&D, while white-collar covers office and clerical work. For India: agriculture's share of GVA is about 17-18%, industry about 27-28% and services about 53-55%. Services dominate GDP but agriculture still employs about 42-46% of the workforce (PLFS). Key services include IT-BPM, tourism, telecom, financial services and trade. India's services exports are a major strength, with software exports leading. Related concepts include Kuznets's structural transformation and the Lewis dual-sector model, and the shift of economies from primary to tertiary is a common UPSC theme. Also note that UPSC may ask which activity falls under which sector, for example banking, teaching, or data processing, so memorise representative examples for every sector.

question:
Which of the following statements about the National Skill Development Corporation is/are not correct ?
1. It is a not-for-profit Public Limited Company set up by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship. 2, It promotes skill development by catalysing the creation of only large, quality and non-profit vocational institutions. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC) was set up in 2008-09 as a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) company under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013), a not-for-profit public limited company. The Government of India, through the Ministry of Finance at inception and now the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE, created November 2014), holds 49% equity, while private sector holds 51%. Its mandate is to catalyse skill development by funding and enabling the creation of large, quality and for-profit vocational institutions, and to provide funding to companies, enterprises and organisations that provide skill training. It also develops initiatives to improve the quality of training through Sector Skill Councils (SSCs). The question asks for statements that are NOT correct. Statement 1 matches NSDC's standard description. Statement 2 is wrong because of the word 'only' and the phrase 'non-profit': NSDC explicitly supports for-profit institutions too, and its work is not limited to large institutions. Hence only statement 2 is incorrect, giving option (b).
explanations: Option (a) is wrong because statement 1 is correct as per the official description; NSDC is a not-for-profit public limited company under MSDE's ambit, so it is not a 'not correct' statement.
Option (b) is right because only statement 2 is not correct: NSDC supports for-profit as well as quality vocational institutions, and the word 'only non-profit' is false.
Option (c) is wrong because it would require statement 1 to be incorrect too, but statement 1 is considered correct.
Option (d) is wrong because it says both statements are correct, but statement 2 is incorrect due to 'only' and 'non-profit'.
keyfact: NSDC (2008) is a not-for-profit PPP company (49% govt, 51% private) that funds quality for-profit vocational institutions too; 'only non-profit' is wrong.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: this would mean only statement 1 is incorrect. Statement 1 describes NSDC as a not-for-profit public limited company, set up in 2008 under the Companies Act. It has government 49% and private sector 51% equity. It is now under MSDE, formed in November 2014 as a separate ministry, so the statement matches the usual description of NSDC.

Option (b) 2 only: this is the official answer, meaning only statement 2 is not correct. NSDC funds and catalyses quality vocational institutions, including for-profit ones, through loans, equity and grants. It also fosters Sector Skill Councils and works on quality assurance. Its work covers a range of institution sizes and types, so 'only large, non-profit' is wrong.

Option (c) Both 1 and 2: this would mean both statements are not correct. It is wrong because NSDC is indeed a not-for-profit company set up as a PPP. NSDC was incorporated on 31 July 2008 with the aim of promoting skill development through private sector participation, and it runs several flagship skilling schemes for MSDE.

Option (d) Neither 1 nor 2: this would mean both statements are correct. It is wrong because statement 2 misrepresents NSDC's mandate by restricting it to non-profit and only large institutions. NSDC explicitly funds for-profit private training providers, and it supports institutions of varied scale, as part of its PPP skill-building model.
related: NSDC was incorporated in 2008 as a PPP with 49% government and 51% private equity.
MSDE was formed in November 2014; the first minister was Rajiv Pratap Rudy.
Skill India Mission was launched on 15 July 2015, World Youth Skills Day.
PMKVY is the flagship short-term skill training scheme implemented by NSDC.
NCVET (2018) regulates awarding bodies and assessment agencies in vocational education.
Sector Skill Councils are industry-led bodies that set National Occupational Standards.
NSQF has 10 levels of qualifications.
National Policy on Skill Development and Entrepreneurship was released in 2015.
statements: 1 — Correct (so not part of the answer): NSDC is described as a not-for-profit public limited company set up under the ministry responsible for skill development. NSDC was incorporated on 31 July 2008 as a PPP under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956, with an initial government equity of 49% and private 51%. The Finance Ministry originally set it up; it now works under MSDE. It implements Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana components, runs Skill India, and its subsidiary is NSDC International. Profits, if any, are reinvested in skilling rather than distributed.

2 — Incorrect: NSDC catalyses creation of large, quality and for-profit vocational institutions, not 'only' non-profit ones. It provides viability gap funding, loans and equity to private training providers, enterprises and start-ups in skilling. It also sets up and supports Sector Skill Councils (around 36-40 SSCs) led by industry, which define National Occupational Standards. It was designed to contribute about 30% of the 150 million target of skilling under the 11th Plan era vision, and aims to fill the skill gap through private sector participation, so exclusivity to non-profit bodies contradicts its model.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. Statement 2 is not correct because NSDC promotes skill development by catalysing the creation of large, quality and for-profit vocational institutions, not 'only' non-profit ones. Statement 1 is broadly correct as per the official framing, so it is not among the 'not correct' statements.
topic_notes: NSDC is the central pillar of India's PPP approach to skilling. It was set up in 2008-09 as a not-for-profit company (Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956; now Section 8 of the 2013 Act), with 49% government and 51% private equity. The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) was created in November 2014 and NSDC now operates under it. NSDC's mandate includes funding vocational training institutions, enterprises and training providers, creating Sector Skill Councils (SSCs) that are industry-led and develop National Occupational Standards and qualification packs, and ensuring quality through assessment and certification. It implements the Skill India Mission launched 15 July 2015 (World Youth Skills Day), and is the key implementing agency for the short-term training component of Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) launched 2015. The National Skill Development Mission was approved in 2015, and the National Policy for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship was issued in 2015, replacing the 2009 policy. The National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF) organises qualifications in levels 1 to 10. The National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET) was formed in 2018 to regulate awarding bodies, replacing NCVT and NSDA functions. Other bodies include the Directorate General of Training (DGT), which runs ITIs, the National Skill Development Agency (NSDA), and schemes like Skill Hub Initiative, SANKALP, STRIVE, and Jan Shikshan Sansthan. NSDC International promotes overseas skilling opportunities. Future questions may ask about the date of founding, equity pattern, SSC examples, and Skill India schemes.

question:
Which of the following statements with reference to the Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana (AVYAY) is/are correct ?
1. Fulfil basic needs of destitute elderly citizens
2. Build and strengthen intergenerational relationships through Regional Resource and Training Centres
3. Provide guaranteed monthly pension to elderly citizens 4, Establish Atal Incubation centres for elderly citizens Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana (AVYAY) is a Central Sector umbrella scheme of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (Department of Social Justice and Empowerment), running from 2021-22 to 2025-26. It brings together earlier schemes for senior citizens, notably the Integrated Programme for Older Persons (IPOP), and is guided by the National Policy for Older Persons 1999 and the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007. Its components include Senior Citizen Homes and Day Care Centres, Mobile Medicare Units, Helpline (Elderline 14567), the Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana (assisted living devices for BPL seniors), the Senior Citizens Welfare Fund, Regional Resource and Training Centres (RRTCs), the Vayo Abhinandan Awards, and the SAGE (Seniorcare Ageing Growth Engine) initiative for startups. Elimination logic: statement 3 is wrong because pensions come from schemes such as the National Social Assistance Programme (IGNOAPS) of the Ministry of Rural Development and from the EPS, not from AVYAY. Statement 4 is wrong because the 'Atal Incubation Centres' belong to Atal Innovation Mission (NITI Aayog). AVYAY's startup support is through SAGE. Dropping 3 and 4 leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 4, which is incorrect because Atal Incubation Centres belong to Atal Innovation Mission, not AVYAY.
Wrong: statements 3 and 4 are both incorrect, since AVYAY gives no guaranteed pension and has no Atal Incubation Centres.
Correct: only statements 1 (basic needs of destitute elderly) and 2 (intergenerational bonding including RRTCs) are true of AVYAY.
Wrong: statement 2 is also correct, so 1 alone is incomplete.
keyfact: AVYAY (MoSJE umbrella scheme for senior citizens) covers care for the destitute elderly and intergenerational bonding, but no guaranteed pension and no Atal Incubation Centres (AIM, NITI Aayog).
option_notes: 1, 2 and 4: this combination fails because of statement 4. Atal Incubation Centres (AICs) fall under the Atal Innovation Mission of NITI Aayog, launched in 2016 to promote innovation and entrepreneurship. Under AIM there are also Atal Tinkering Labs in schools and Atal Community Innovation Centres. AICs give incubation facilities to startups in institutions. SAGE, a different scheme, supports elderly-care startups.

3 and 4 only: both statements are wrong. A guaranteed pension is not part of AVYAY. Elderly pensions come from IGNOAPS under NSAP, from EPS-95 for EPFO members, and from the contributory Atal Pension Yojana (2015) run by PFRDA. AICs belong to NITI Aayog's AIM. This option contains nothing that is actually part of AVYAY.

1 and 2 only: the correct answer. AVYAY is the umbrella Central Sector scheme of MoSJE for senior citizens (2021-22 to 2025-26). It merged the IPOP and other schemes, funding senior citizen homes, day care centres, helplines and RRTCs. It also supports Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana, SAGE and the Vayo Abhinandan Awards. Intergenerational bonding is one of its stated objectives.

1 only: this is incomplete. Statement 1 is true, since AVYAY covers basic needs of destitute elderly, but statement 2 is also true because intergenerational bonding is an objective supported through RRTCs and awareness activities. Selecting only 1 would miss that. AVYAY covers many more components, including health, awareness and training.
related: AVYAY is a Central Sector umbrella scheme of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.
Elderline (National Helpline for Senior Citizens) number is 14567.
SAGE stands for Seniorcare Ageing Growth Engine, which supports startups in elderly care.
Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana gives physical aids to BPL senior citizens, funded from the Senior Citizens' Welfare Fund.
Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act is of 2007.
Atal Incubation Centres come under Atal Innovation Mission, NITI Aayog.
Atal Pension Yojana is administered by PFRDA and was launched in 2015.
International Day of Older Persons is observed on 1 October.
statements: 1 — Correct: AVYAY's objectives include providing food, shelter, care and medical support to destitute senior citizens through Senior Citizen Homes and Day Care Centres. Facts: these homes are run by NGOs, Panchayati Raj Institutions and other agencies with grants-in-aid. The scheme targets people aged 60+, and priority goes to those who are indigent or without family support. The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007 backs the legal side, and Elderline 14567 gives guidance. The aim is dignity, health and active ageing.

2 — Correct: AVYAY aims to build and strengthen intergenerational bonds, and RRTCs are among the components for this. Facts: Regional Resource and Training Centres are set up to train caregivers and to support research and awareness on ageing. Other activities cover sensitisation of children and youth and awareness campaigns. The Vayo Abhinandan Awards recognise outstanding work for seniors, and the National Action Plan for Senior Citizens (NAPSrC) is also part of this framework.

3 — Incorrect: AVYAY does not guarantee a monthly pension. Pensions for the elderly come from schemes like IGNOAPS (under the NSAP, Ministry of Rural Development), which gives support to BPL persons aged 60+, and from EPS-95 for EPFO members. Facts: the Central assistance under IGNOAPS is ₹200 a month for ages 60-79 and ₹500 for 80+, topped up by states. PM-SYM and the Atal Pension Yojana (PFRDA, launched 2015) are separate contributory pension schemes.

4 — Incorrect: Atal Incubation Centres (AICs) are an Atal Innovation Mission (NITI Aayog) initiative that supports startups, and have nothing to do with AVYAY. Facts: AIM was launched in 2016, with Atal Tinkering Labs in schools, AICs in institutions, and Atal Community Innovation Centres. The elderly-specific startup effort is SAGE, launched in 2021 by the Ministry of Social Justice, which backs startups with products and services for seniors.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 2 only. AVYAY is an umbrella scheme of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment for senior citizens. It covers basic needs of destitute elderly people and builds intergenerational bonds, and it does not provide a guaranteed pension or Atal Incubation centres.
topic_notes: AVYAY is the umbrella scheme of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment for senior citizens (60+), effective 2021-22 to 2025-26, and it consolidates IPOP and other earlier schemes. Its main components are: (1) Senior Citizen Homes, Day Care Centres and Continuing Care Homes; (2) Mobile Medicare Units; (3) Elderline, the National Helpline 14567; (4) Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana, which supplies aids and assisted living devices to BPL senior citizens, funded from the Senior Citizens' Welfare Fund; (5) Regional Resource and Training Centres, and awareness and sensitisation; (6) Vayo Abhinandan Awards, given on 1 October, the International Day of Older Persons; (7) SAGE (Seniorcare Ageing Growth Engine), a portal and startup-funding initiative launched in 2021. Legal and policy framework: National Policy on Older Persons 1999; Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007, under which Maintenance Tribunals can order maintenance of up to ₹10,000 per month (this cap was removed by the 2019 Amendment Bill proposal, which lapsed); Article 41 (DPSP on public assistance in old age); and Entry 24 of the Concurrent List (welfare of labour) and Entry 9 of the State List (relief of the disabled and unemployable). Pension and income support: IGNOAPS under NSAP, Atal Pension Yojana (2015), PM Shram Yogi Maan-dhan, Pradhan Mantri Vaya Vandana Yojana (LIC, for ages 60+), and EPS-95 under EPFO. Health: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE), and the Senior Citizen Savings Scheme. Atal brand schemes to distinguish: Atal Pension Yojana (PFRDA), Atal Innovation Mission (NITI Aayog), Atal Bhujal Yojana (water), Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT), and Atal Bimit Vyakti Kalyan Yojana (ESIC unemployment relief).

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I: In India, Central Government determines the inflation target, in consultation with Reserve Bank of India, in terms of Consumer Price Index once in five years.
Statement II : At present, the Monetary Policy framework in India is operated by Central Government. Which of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?
options: Both statement I and statement II are correct and statement II is the correct explanation for statement I
Both statement I and statement II are correct and statement II is not the correct explanation for statement I
Statement I is correct but statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct 114,
subject: Computers
detail: India adopted Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) through the Finance Act 2016, which amended the RBI Act, 1934. Section 45ZA empowers the Central Government, in consultation with the RBI, to determine the inflation target in terms of the CPI (Combined) once every five years and notify it in the Official Gazette. The target since 2016 is 4% with a tolerance band of +/-2% (upper limit 6%, lower limit 2%). It was retained in March 2021 for 2021-26 and again for the next period. Section 45ZB created the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC): three RBI members (Governor as ex-officio Chairperson, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one officer nominated by the Central Board) and three external members appointed by the Centre for four years, not eligible for reappointment. Decisions are by majority vote, and the Governor has a casting vote in a tie. The MPC, not the Government, fixes the policy repo rate to meet the target. The RBI fails if inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, and it must then report to the Government. Statement II is wrong because the RBI operates monetary policy, while the Government only sets the target. Since II is false, options (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated.
explanations: Wrong: although Statement I is correct, Statement II is false, so it cannot be a correct explanation.
Wrong: Statement II is not correct at all, so the question of it being a correct or incorrect explanation does not arise.
Right: Statement I is correct as the Centre notifies the target every five years in consultation with the RBI; Statement II is incorrect as the RBI/MPC runs monetary policy.
Wrong: it reverses the truth values, since Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.
keyfact: The Centre notifies the CPI inflation target (4% +/-2%) every five years in consultation with the RBI, but the RBI's six-member MPC operates monetary policy.
option_notes: Option (a) would require both statements true with II explaining I. It is false because the Government does not operate monetary policy. It resembles a common assumption that the body setting the target also implements policy. In reality, the Centre sets the goal, which is the target, while the RBI chooses the instruments, mainly the repo rate, to achieve it.

Option (b) says both statements are correct but unconnected. It fails because Statement II is wrong. Such an option is typical UPSC design to test whether students can separate the target-setting role of the Government from the operational role of the RBI under flexible inflation targeting.

Option (c) is the official answer: Statement I is correct as per Section 45ZA of the RBI Act, and Statement II is incorrect. The RBI's MPC operates monetary policy and the Central Government only notifies the target. India's target is 4% CPI inflation with a band of 2% to 6%, with a five-year review cycle.

Option (d) claims Statement I is incorrect and II correct, which is the exact reverse of the facts. Statement I accurately reflects Section 45ZA, and Statement II wrongly gives the Government operational control of monetary policy, which belongs to the RBI-led MPC.
related: Section 45ZA of the RBI Act sets the inflation target, notified by the Centre every five years.
Inflation target: 4% CPI with a tolerance band of +/-2% (2% to 6%).
MPC has 6 members: 3 from the RBI and 3 external, appointed by the Centre for 4 years.
The Governor is the MPC Chairperson and has a casting vote in a tie.
Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended inflation targeting using CPI.
Failure to meet the target means 3 consecutive quarters outside the band.
CPI-Combined (base 2012) is compiled by NSO, MoSPI; WPI is compiled by DPIIT.
MPC was constituted on 27 September 2016.
statements: 1 — Correct: Section 45ZA of the RBI Act, 1934 lets the Centre, in consultation with the RBI, set the CPI-based inflation target once every five years. The framework came from the Finance Act 2016, following the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommendation and the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement of February 2015. The target was 4% with a +/-2% band, retained for 2021-26 and again afterwards. The index used is CPI-Combined, compiled by NSO (MoSPI), with base year 2012 at present. If the target is missed for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must explain the reasons and remedial action to the Government.

2 — Incorrect: Monetary policy is operated by the RBI, through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee under Section 45ZB, established on 27 September 2016. The Governor is Chairperson, and the committee includes the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer, and three external members appointed by the Centre on the recommendation of a search committee under the Cabinet Secretary. External members serve four years without reappointment. The MPC meets at least four times a year, with quorum of four, and its decisions are binding on the RBI. Before 2016 the Governor decided with an advisory committee. Fiscal policy, in contrast, is operated by the Government.
summary: The answer is (c). Statement I is correct: under the RBI Act, 1934 (Section 45ZA, inserted in 2016), the Central Government, in consultation with the RBI, notifies the CPI-based inflation target once every five years. Statement II is incorrect: the monetary policy framework is operated by the RBI through the Monetary Policy Committee, not by the Central Government.
topic_notes: Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) is India's monetary policy framework. Its roots are the Expert Committee to Revise and Strengthen the Monetary Policy Framework (Urjit Patel Committee, January 2014), which recommended CPI as the nominal anchor and a 4% target with a +/-2% band. The Monetary Policy Framework Agreement between the Government and the RBI was signed in February 2015. The Finance Act 2016 amended the RBI Act, 1934, adding Chapter IIIF (Sections 45Z to 45ZO). Section 45ZA covers the inflation target, set by the Centre in consultation with the RBI once every five years. Section 45ZB covers the six-member MPC. Section 45ZC covers the MPC's meetings, voting and tie-breaking. Section 45ZN defines failure to meet the target (average inflation above the upper tolerance level or below the lower level for three consecutive quarters), after which the RBI must send a report to the Government on the reasons, remedial actions and the estimated time to return to target. The MPC must meet at least four times a year, with quorum of four members, and the minutes are published 14 days after each meeting. The main tool is the policy repo rate, supported by the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) rate, the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), open market operations, and the Liquidity Adjustment Facility corridor. Inflation is measured by CPI-Combined (base 2012=100), released by the NSO under MoSPI. WPI, by contrast, is released by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, and is not used for targeting. Earlier frameworks were multiple indicators (1998-2011) and monetary targeting (1985-1998). The Government can suspend the target only if failure persists, with parliamentary reporting involved.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I: In India, the RTGS and NEFT payment systems are owned and operated by National Payment Corporation of India.
Statement II : National Payment Corporation of India is an entity promoted by banks. Which of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?
options: Both statement I and statement II are correct and statement II is the correct explanation for statement I
Both statement I and statement II are correct and statement II is not the correct explanation for statement I
Statement I is correct but statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct A)
subject: Computers
detail: RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) and NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer) are the RBI's own large-value and retail electronic fund transfer systems. The RBI operates them under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. NEFT began in November 2005 and RTGS in March 2004. Both now run 24x7 (RTGS since December 2020, NEFT since December 2019). In 2019 the RBI also removed charges on RTGS and NEFT transactions for savings account holders. NPCI was incorporated in 2008 as a not-for-profit Section 25 company (now Section 8 under the Companies Act, 2013). It was set up by the RBI and IBA, and ten core promoter banks initially held its shares: SBI, PNB, Canara Bank, Bank of Baroda, Union Bank of India, Bank of India, ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, Citibank and HSBC. NPCI operates retail systems such as UPI, IMPS, NACH, RuPay, BHIM, NETC (FASTag), Bharat BillPay and AePS. Elimination: Statement I is false, so (a), (b) and (c), which all treat I as correct, are ruled out. This leaves (d). Remember the split: the RBI runs RTGS/NEFT, and NPCI runs UPI/IMPS/RuPay.
explanations: Wrong: this option treats Statement I as correct, but RTGS and NEFT are owned and operated by the RBI, not NPCI.
Wrong: Statement I is incorrect, so this option fails even though Statement II is correct.
Wrong: this reverses the truth. Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.
Correct: Statement I is incorrect because the RBI owns and operates RTGS and NEFT. Statement II is correct because NPCI was promoted by banks, with RBI and IBA guidance.
keyfact: RTGS and NEFT belong to the RBI; UPI, IMPS and RuPay belong to NPCI, which is a bank-promoted not-for-profit company.
option_notes: Option (a) says both statements are correct and II explains I. It is wrong here because RTGS and NEFT sit with the RBI. Such explanation-type options are always a trap when one statement fails. NPCI is a bank-promoted not-for-profit company that runs retail systems like UPI and IMPS, but it does not operate RTGS or NEFT. Remember that RBI is the central bank and the regulator and operator of the payment system under the PSS Act 2007.

Option (b) says both statements are correct but II does not explain I. It is wrong because Statement I is false. RTGS handles large-value transfers (minimum Rs 2 lakh) and NEFT handles retail transfers. Both are RBI-run and settle in RBI books. NPCI's retail systems are separate, and the two sets of systems should not be confused. NPCI was incorporated in 2008, and it is owned by banks.

Option (c) says Statement I is correct and II is incorrect. It is the exact opposite of the truth. NPCI is indeed promoted by banks, and it does not run RTGS or NEFT. Its shareholding started with ten core banks, and it was later broadened to include more banks, payment banks and small finance banks. RBI Governor-level guidance and IBA support shaped its creation, so Statement II holds.

Option (d) says Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct. This is the official answer. RTGS and NEFT are RBI systems, and NPCI is a bank-promoted umbrella entity for retail payments. NPCI operates UPI, IMPS, RuPay, NACH, AePS, BHIM, FASTag and Bharat BillPay. It was set up in 2008 as a Section 25 company, and it is a not-for-profit organisation.
related: RTGS minimum amount is Rs 2 lakh with no maximum limit.
NEFT has no minimum or maximum limit and runs 24x7 since December 2019.
NPCI was incorporated in 2008 as a not-for-profit company, headquartered in Mumbai.
UPI was launched by NPCI in April 2016.
RuPay is NPCI's domestic card payment network.
IMPS is an NPCI product for instant interbank mobile transfers.
The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 regulates payment systems in India, with the RBI as the authority.
NPCI took over the National Financial Switch (ATM network) from IDRBT in 2009.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: RTGS and NEFT are owned and operated by the RBI, not by NPCI. RTGS is the real-time gross settlement system for large-value transfers, with a minimum of Rs 2 lakh. NEFT is a deferred net settlement system with no minimum or maximum limit. RTGS started on 26 March 2004 and NEFT in November 2005. Both are authorised under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, and RBI is the regulator and operator. Since December 2020, both run 24x7x365. Settlement happens through accounts held with the RBI. NPCI's role is limited to retail systems such as UPI, IMPS, NACH and RuPay.

2 — Correct: NPCI is an umbrella organisation for retail payment and settlement systems in India. It was set up with guidance from the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. It was incorporated in December 2008 as a Section 25 not-for-profit company, and its registered office is in Mumbai. Ten banks were the original core promoters, and the shareholding was later widened to many more banks. Its products include UPI (2016), IMPS, RuPay cards, NACH, AePS, BHIM and NETC FASTag. NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL) is its overseas arm.
summary: The answer is (d). Statement I is incorrect because RTGS and NEFT are owned and operated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), not NPCI. Statement II is correct because NPCI is an umbrella organisation for retail payments that was promoted by banks, with RBI and the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) guiding its creation.
topic_notes: India's payment system architecture has the RBI at the centre. The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 gives the RBI the power to regulate and supervise payment systems, and a Board for Regulation and Supervision of Payment and Settlement Systems (BPSS) oversees this. RTGS is for large-value transfers (minimum Rs 2 lakh, no upper cap) and settles in real time on a gross basis. NEFT works in half-hourly batches with deferred net settlement and has no limits. Both operate 24x7. The RBI also runs the Centralised Payment Systems and the Cheque Truncation System. NPCI handles retail payments. Its main products: IMPS (2010, instant 24x7 mobile transfers), RuPay (domestic card network, 2012), NACH (bulk payments like salaries and subsidies), UPI (April 2016, real-time mobile payments through a Virtual Payment Address), AePS (Aadhaar-enabled payments), BHIM app (December 2016), NETC FASTag (electronic toll collection), Bharat BillPay (BBPS) and the e-RUPI voucher. NPCI is also the operator for CTS in some respects and for the National Financial Switch (NFS) for ATMs, which it took over from IDRBT in 2009. Other angles: Pre-paid Payment Instruments (PPIs), Payment Banks, the Payments Infrastructure Development Fund, the Digital Payments Index, UPI Lite, UPI 123PAY for feature phones, and cross-border UPI links with Singapore (PayNow), Bhutan, Nepal and UAE. Central Bank Digital Currency (e-rupee) pilots started in late 2022, and the RBI Ombudsman Scheme and Digital Payments Ombudsman deal with grievances.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I: A very strong US Dollar squeezes global credit.
Statement II : Many countries and companies outside America borrow in Dollars. Which of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?
options: Both statement I and statement II are correct and statement II is the correct explanation for statement I
Both statement I and statement II are correct and statement II is not the correct explanation for statement I
Statement I is correct but statement IT is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct
subject: Computers
detail: The US dollar is the world's dominant funding and invoicing currency. Borrowers outside the US, such as emerging-market governments, banks and corporates, raise large amounts through dollar bonds, ECBs (external commercial borrowings) and trade credit. Their revenues are often in local currency, so a strong dollar means they need more rupees, reais or lira to service the same dollar debt. This raises default and rollover risk. Lenders become cautious, spreads widen and fresh dollar lending falls, which is the 'squeeze' on global credit. A strong dollar also usually coincides with Fed rate hikes, which raise the cost of dollar funding, and with capital outflows from emerging markets. The BIS and IMF describe this as the 'dollar channel' or 'risk-taking channel' of exchange rates: a stronger dollar tightens global financial conditions and weakens cross-border lending and trade. Elimination logic: Statement I is an established economic observation, so (d) is out. Statement II is factually true, and it is the mechanism behind Statement I, so (b) and (c) are wrong. Only (a) fits.
explanations: Correct. Both statements are true, and dollar borrowing by non-US entities (II) is the mechanism by which a strong dollar squeezes credit (I).
Wrong. It accepts that both statements are true but denies the causal link. In fact II explains I.
Wrong. Statement II is true, since many foreign borrowers do use dollars.
Wrong. Statement I is true, as a strong dollar tightens global credit conditions.
keyfact: A strong dollar raises the local cost of servicing dollar debt for non-US borrowers, which tightens global credit.
option_notes: Both statements correct with II as the explanation: this is the standard assertion-reason format. Here the link is the dollar-debt channel. A stronger dollar raises the local-currency cost of servicing dollar debt, which reduces credit supply and increases defaults. It is the official answer. Related facts: the IMF and BIS call it the 'dollar channel', and the effect is strongest on emerging markets with large unhedged foreign-currency liabilities.

Both correct but II not the explanation: this would apply if the statements were true but unrelated. It is the usual trap option in assertion-reason questions. Here it fails because dollar-denominated borrowing is exactly why a rising dollar affects credit. The standard test is to ask whether the second statement answers 'why' the first is true.

Statement I correct, II incorrect: this would need the claim that few outside the US borrow in dollars. That is false. Dollar debt outside the US exceeds $12 trillion by BIS estimates, and offshore dollar funding markets, such as the eurodollar market that began in the 1950s, are huge.

Statement I incorrect, II correct: this would mean a strong dollar does not squeeze credit. In practice it does, through higher debt burdens, capital outflows and tighter financial conditions. Evidence includes the 2013 taper tantrum, the 2015 emerging-market stress and 2022, when dollar strength led to widespread currency depreciation, including the rupee's fall past 80 per dollar.
related: DXY measures the dollar against a basket of six currencies, with the euro having the largest weight.
The US dollar accounts for about 58% of global official reserves (IMF COFER).
The 2013 taper tantrum hit India among the 'Fragile Five' economies.
ECBs are foreign-currency loans raised by Indian entities and regulated by RBI and FEMA.
Masala bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued abroad, which shifts the currency risk to investors.
The RBI introduced a rupee international trade settlement mechanism in July 2022.
The Triffin dilemma describes the conflict facing a country that issues the global reserve currency.
The BIS is the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, which publishes the Triennial Central Bank Survey.
statements: 1 — Correct: A very strong dollar raises debt-servicing costs for dollar borrowers abroad and makes lenders risk-averse, so credit tightens globally. Facts: the dollar is on one side of about 88% of forex trades (BIS Triennial Survey) and accounts for roughly 58–60% of global reserves (IMF COFER). The DXY index measures the dollar against a basket of six currencies, with the euro the largest weight. Dollar surges have followed Fed tightening, for example 1980s, 2014–15 and 2022. Such episodes have caused emerging-market stress, such as the 2013 taper tantrum, and have forced central banks to intervene to defend their currencies.

2 — Correct: Many non-US governments, banks and companies borrow in dollars, and this is the reason a strong dollar hurts them. Facts: BIS data show non-bank borrowers outside the US owe well over $12 trillion in dollar debt. The reasons are deeper and cheaper dollar markets, the dollar's use as a reserve and invoicing currency, and investors' preference for dollar bonds. The risk is currency mismatch, where assets and revenues are in local currency but liabilities are in dollars. India's ECBs, FCCBs and Masala bonds (rupee-denominated overseas bonds, introduced 2014) relate to this. RBI hedging norms and ECB limits reduce the exposure.
summary: The answer is (a). Both statements are correct, and Statement II explains Statement I. Many non-US governments and firms hold dollar-denominated debt, so when the dollar strengthens, repaying it costs more in local currency, and this tightens global credit conditions.
topic_notes: The dollar's global role rests on three pillars: reserve currency, invoicing and trade currency, and funding currency. It makes up about 58% of global official reserves, and about 88% of forex transactions involve it (BIS 2022). Bretton Woods (1944) established dollar centrality, and after the 1971 Nixon shock the dollar stayed dominant even as the gold link ended. The DXY index tracks the dollar against the euro, yen, pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona and Swiss franc. The key transmission channels of a strong dollar are: (1) higher debt-servicing cost for dollar borrowers, (2) capital outflows from emerging markets as US yields rise, (3) tighter bank balance sheets and reduced cross-border lending, (4) imported inflation for countries that import oil and commodities priced in dollars, and (5) pressure on foreign-exchange reserves. The 2013 taper tantrum showed how Fed signals hit the rupee, which was one of the 'Fragile Five' currencies. For India, the effects show up in the current account deficit, RBI forex intervention, ECB and FPI flows, and the cost of oil imports. Related policy tools include forex reserves, swap lines, hedging norms for ECBs, and efforts toward rupee trade settlement (July 2022 RBI mechanism, with rupee vostro accounts). De-dollarisation talk, including BRICS payment initiatives, remains limited in practice. Likely future angles include DXY, the impact on gold prices, Fed rate decisions, and the Triffin dilemma.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I: The Government of India mandates the packaging of 100% sugar and food grains in diversified jute bags.
Statement II : The Government of India enacted the Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act, 1987. Which of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?
options: Both statement I and statement II are correct and statement II is the correct explanation for statement I
Both statement I and statement II are correct and statement II is not the correct explanation for statement I
Statement I is correct but statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct
subject: Computers
detail: The Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act, 1987 (JPMA) was enacted to protect jute farmers, workers and the jute industry by making jute packaging compulsory for specified commodities. Its operation is through orders issued by the Ministry of Textiles under Section 3, called reservation norms, which specify the commodities and the percentage that must be packed in jute. These norms are revised periodically, generally for each jute year (July-June), with Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) approval. Historically, foodgrains were reserved at 100% and sugar at 100%, but the sugar reservation was relaxed. Under recent norms, 100% of foodgrains and 20% of sugar are reserved for packing in jute, and 20% of the sugar reservation is to be met through diversified jute bags. So the claim that 100% of sugar and food grains must be in diversified jute bags is wrong on two counts: sugar is not 100%, and the mandate is for jute packaging, not diversified jute bags. Elimination: since the Act is real, options (c) and the 'both correct' options (a) and (b) fall away, leaving (d). The JPMA is administered by the Jute Commissioner's office in Kolkata.
explanations: Wrong: Statement I is incorrect, since the 100% mandate does not apply to both sugar and food grains and is not limited to diversified jute bags, so this option fails even before assessing the explanation.
Wrong: Statement I is not correct because sugar's reservation is only 20%, so the option claiming both statements are correct is untenable.
Wrong: It says Statement II is incorrect, but the 1987 Act does exist and is correctly described.
Correct: Statement I is factually wrong on the 100% claim for sugar and the diversified jute bags framing, while Statement II correctly names the 1987 Act.
keyfact: JPMA 1987 makes jute packaging compulsory, but reservation is 100% for foodgrains and only 20% for sugar, so the '100% sugar and food grains in diversified jute bags' claim is wrong.
option_notes: Both correct with II explaining I: this is the standard assertion-reason format in which statement II would be the reason for statement I. It is not applicable here because Statement I is factually wrong. The JPMA 1987 is the legal basis of reservation norms, but the norms themselves vary by commodity: foodgrains 100%, sugar 20%. Reservations are revised annually through CCEA approval and issued as orders under Section 3 of the Act by the Ministry of Textiles.

Both correct but II does not explain I: this is the second assertion-reason pattern, in which both statements are true but unrelated causally. It fails here since Statement I is false. Remember that UPSC often uses this pattern, so check each statement independently before judging the relation between them. The jute sector supports about 4 lakh workers and around 40 lakh farm families, concentrated in West Bengal.

Statement I correct, II incorrect: this would require the 100% claim to be right and the Act not to exist. In reality the reverse holds. The Act is genuine (1987), while the blanket 100% claim for sugar and foodgrains in diversified jute bags is not. Diversified jute products are promoted by the National Jute Board under the Ministry of Textiles, established under the National Jute Board Act, 2008, headquartered in Kolkata.

Statement I incorrect, II correct: this is the official answer. The JPMA 1987 is real and mandates jute packaging for specified commodities, but the actual reservation norms are 100% for foodgrains and a lower share, 20%, for sugar, with a portion of it linked to diversified jute bags. The Act's norms are reviewed every jute year to balance mill capacity, raw jute production, and user needs.
related: JPMA 1987 is administered through the Ministry of Textiles and the Jute Commissioner's office, Kolkata.
Current norms reserve 100% of foodgrains and 20% of sugar for jute packaging.
Jute Corporation of India (est. 1971) is the price support agency for raw jute.
National Jute Board was set up under the National Jute Board Act, 2008.
Jute-ICARE improves quality and retting of raw jute.
The jute year runs from July to June.
West Bengal is the largest producer of raw jute in India.
Raw jute MSP is fixed on the recommendation of the CACP.
statements: I — Incorrect: The mandate is not 100% for both commodities. Foodgrains have 100% reservation, but sugar has only 20% reservation, and the mandate applies to jute packaging in general rather than to diversified jute bags alone. Reservation norms are issued under the JPMA 1987 by the Ministry of Textiles after CCEA approval, usually for each jute year running July to June. They aim to ensure demand for raw jute and support lakhs of farm families and mill workers, mainly in West Bengal, Bihar, Assam and Odisha. Diversified jute products (DJPs) include bags, handicrafts, decor items, and are promoted separately through schemes and the National Jute Board.

II — Correct: The Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act, 1987 was enacted by Parliament to make jute packaging compulsory for certain commodities and thereby sustain demand for raw jute and jute goods. It empowers the Central Government to specify commodities and the extent of mandatory packaging in jute materials, and to issue directions to producers, suppliers and users. It has been in force since 1987, and reservation orders under it are revised regularly. The Jute Commissioner, based in Kolkata, administers it, while the Jute Corporation of India handles MSP-linked raw jute procurement.
summary: The answer is (d). Statement II is correct because the Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act, 1987 exists. Statement I is incorrect because the government does not mandate 100% jute packaging for sugar and food grains; the mandated share is lower and has changed over time through reservation norms.
topic_notes: India is the world's largest producer of raw jute, followed by Bangladesh, and jute is called the Golden Fibre. The jute year runs from July to June. Major producing states are West Bengal (the largest share), Bihar and Assam, with Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Meghalaya contributing smaller amounts. The industry supports roughly 4 lakh workers and about 40 lakh farm families. The Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act, 1987 protects demand by reserving packaging in jute for commodities. Reservation norms are notified by the Ministry of Textiles, with CCEA approval, and are typically reviewed each jute year. In recent norms, 100% of foodgrains and 20% of sugar are reserved for jute packaging. The Jute Commissioner's Office in Kolkata is the regulatory body, while the Jute Corporation of India (JCI), established in 1971, acts as the price support agency, buying raw jute at MSP set on the CACP's recommendation. The National Jute Board (under the National Jute Board Act, 2008, replacing the National Centre for Jute Diversification) promotes jute and diversified products. The Jute Manufactures Development Council existed earlier. Other initiatives include Jute-ICARE (Improved Cultivation and Advanced Retting Exercise) to improve fibre quality and farmer income, the Jute Technology Mission (2006) and the National Jute Policy 2005. The Jute Manufactures Cess Act 1983 imposes a cess on jute manufactures. Raw jute MSP is announced annually. Anti-dumping duty has been imposed on jute products from Bangladesh and Nepal to protect domestic mills. Possible UPSC angles include the percentage norms, the nodal ministry, the administering institutions, and the MSP mechanism.

question: Recently which one among the following} 11g, committed up to $ 25 billion for the next five years to fund India’s infrastructure creation under the Prime Minister Gati Shakti initiative as well as social development and climate action, thus aiding India’s aspirations for green growth ?
subject: Indian Economy
detail: The ADB, headquartered in Manila, was founded in 1966 and India is a founding member and among its largest borrowers. Its Country Partnership Strategy for India (2023-2027) was backed by a pledge of up to $25 billion, announced at the time of the ADB Annual Meeting in Incheon, South Korea (May 2023), by ADB President Masatsugu Asakawa. The money is aimed at the PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan (launched October 2021) for multimodal connectivity, urban and transport infrastructure, energy transition, social sectors and climate resilience. Elimination: the New Development Bank (BRICS bank, Shanghai, 2015) lends mainly through sovereign projects and does not frame such a five-year country envelope. The World Bank and IFC have separate India programmes, with the World Bank's Country Partnership Framework and IFC private-sector investments, but the specific $25 billion, five-year Gati Shakti-linked pledge is associated with ADB. The key cue is 'Gati Shakti plus climate action plus social development', which matches ADB's country strategy language.
explanations: Correct. ADB committed up to $25 billion over five years to India, covering Gati Shakti infrastructure, social development and climate action.
Wrong. IFC is the World Bank Group's private-sector arm; its India commitments are investments in private firms, not this sovereign five-year pledge.
Wrong. The NDB is the BRICS bank (2015, Shanghai); it has funded Indian projects but did not make this announcement.
Wrong. The World Bank has its own India Country Partnership Framework and loans, but this $25 billion figure is not its commitment.
keyfact: ADB pledged up to $25 billion over five years to India for Gati Shakti infrastructure, social development and climate action.
option_notes: The Asian Development Bank was established in 1966 and is headquartered in Manila, Philippines. It has 68 members, and Japan and the USA are the largest shareholders. Its presidents have always been Japanese; Masatsugu Asakawa has led it since 2020. India is a founding member and a major borrower, with funding for transport, energy, urban development and social sectors.

The International Finance Corporation was founded in 1956 and is headquartered in Washington DC. It is a member of the World Bank Group and the largest global development institution focused on the private sector in developing countries. It provides loans, equity and advisory services, and mobilises private capital. India is a member and a major IFC client.

The New Development Bank, also called the BRICS Bank, was agreed in 2014 at Fortaleza and began operations in 2015, headquartered in Shanghai. Its founding members are Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. Its first president was K. V. Kamath of India. It finances infrastructure and sustainable development projects, and later admitted Bangladesh, UAE and Egypt; Dilma Rousseff became president in 2023.

The World Bank, formed in 1944 at Bretton Woods and headquartered in Washington DC, comprises the IBRD and IDA. India is a founding member of the IBRD and a major borrower. The Bank publishes reports such as Ease of Doing Business (discontinued 2021) and the World Development Report. It is led by a president, traditionally American; Ajay Banga took office in June 2023.
related: ADB was founded in 1966 and is headquartered in Manila.
PM Gati Shakti was launched on 13 October 2021.
NDB (BRICS Bank) is headquartered in Shanghai and began in 2015.
AIIB is headquartered in Beijing and began operations in 2016.
IFC belongs to the World Bank Group and funds the private sector.
National Logistics Policy was launched on 17 September 2022.
ADB's 2023 Annual Meeting was held in Incheon, South Korea.
Ajay Banga became World Bank president in June 2023.
summary: The answer is (a) Asian Development Bank. In 2022-23 the ADB announced a commitment of up to $25 billion over five years (2023-2027) for India's infrastructure under PM Gati Shakti, social development and climate action, supporting green growth.
topic_notes: PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan was launched on 13 October 2021 as a digital platform for integrated planning and coordinated implementation of infrastructure projects. It brings together 16 ministries initially, including Railways and Roadways, and is meant to cut logistics costs and improve multimodal connectivity. It rests on seven engines: railways, roads, ports, waterways, airports, mass transport and logistics infrastructure. It is overseen by an Empowered Group of Secretaries, a Network Planning Group and a Technical Support Unit. The related National Logistics Policy was launched in September 2022, and the Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP) followed. Multilateral financiers active in India include ADB (Manila), World Bank (Washington DC), NDB (Shanghai), the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB, Beijing, operational since 2016, India the second-largest shareholder after China), and IFC. ADB's India programme focuses on transport corridors, urban services, power, water, skills and climate finance; it also supports the Delhi-Meerut Regional Rapid Transit System. UPSC often asks about headquarters, founding years, presidents and membership of these banks, and about the purpose and ministries linked to Gati Shakti. Also note the International Solar Alliance (HQ Gurugram), and green growth as a Union Budget 2023-24 priority under Saptarishi.

question:
Large Language Models’, sometimes described in news, can be used in which of the following ?
1. Creation of reimagined search engines
2. Health care
8. Software development 4, Translating a language Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Computers
detail: A Large Language Model is a deep-learning model, usually built on the Transformer architecture (Google, 2017, 'Attention Is All You Need'). It is trained on huge text corpora to predict the next token, and this gives it the ability to understand and generate human-like text. Examples are OpenAI's GPT series (ChatGPT), Google's PaLM/Gemini (Bard), Meta's LLaMA, Anthropic's Claude and Microsoft's Copilot, which is integrated with Bing. Applications include conversational search (Bing Chat, Google's generative search), clinical documentation, medical question-answering and patient communication, code generation and debugging (GitHub Copilot, Codex), machine translation (including Indian-language efforts such as Bhashini), summarisation, chatbots, content creation and education. Elimination logic: the question uses 'which of the following', and all four uses are well documented. Statement 3 was OCR-garbled as '8' and statement 4 was merged into the same line, but both are valid. Options (a), (b) and (c) each drop at least one valid use, so only (d) is correct. Risks to remember are hallucination, bias, privacy, copyright and deepfakes, which is why governance of AI is a recurring current-affairs theme.
explanations: Wrong: it lists only statements 1 and 3, and leaves out health care and translation, which are both valid uses of LLMs.
Wrong: it leaves out software development, and LLM-based code generation such as GitHub Copilot is a major use case.
Wrong: it leaves out search engines, and LLMs are central to reimagined search such as Bing Chat and Google's generative search.
Correct: all four applications (search, health care, software development and translation) are established uses of LLMs, matching the official answer.
keyfact: LLMs are Transformer-based generative models used for search, health care, coding and translation; all four listed uses are valid, so the answer is (d).
option_notes: Options 1 and 3 only means search engines and software development. Both are real LLM uses, for example Bing with GPT-4 and GitHub Copilot, but the option is incomplete. LLMs are general-purpose language models based on Transformers, which means their uses extend beyond these two to health care and translation.

Options 1, 2 and 4 only means search, health care and translation. Each is a real use, for example Bing Chat, Med-PaLM and Bhashini-style translation. The option wrongly excludes coding, one of the most mature LLM applications, seen in Codex, Copilot and Code Llama.

Options 2, 3 and 4 only means health care, software development and translation. They are valid uses, but the option wrongly excludes search. Conversational search was a headline development of 2023, with Microsoft Bing integrating GPT-4 and Google responding with Bard.

Options 1, 2, 3 and 4 is the correct answer. It reflects the general-purpose nature of LLMs, which can read, summarise, generate, translate and reason over text and code. Other uses include chatbots, education, legal drafting, customer service and content creation. Governance concerns are bias, hallucination, privacy and copyright.
related: Transformer architecture was introduced by Google researchers in 2017.
ChatGPT, built on GPT-3.5, was launched by OpenAI on 30 November 2022.
Bhashini is India's National Language Translation Mission for Indian-language AI translation.
Hallucination means an AI model generates confident but false output.
The UK hosted the first global AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park in November 2023.
GitHub Copilot is an AI coding assistant developed by GitHub and OpenAI.
The EU AI Act is the first comprehensive AI regulation, with a risk-based approach.
The IndiaAI Mission was approved by the Union Cabinet in March 2024.
statements: 1 — Correct: LLMs power reimagined, conversational search engines. Facts: Microsoft integrated GPT-4 into Bing in February 2023, and Google launched Bard (later Gemini) and generative search experiences. Instead of a list of links, these systems give a synthesised, conversational answer with citations. Perplexity AI is another example. Concerns include hallucinated answers, source attribution and the effect on publishers' traffic and copyright.

2 — Correct: LLMs are used in health care. Facts: uses include summarising clinical notes, drafting discharge summaries, answering patient queries, assisting diagnosis, supporting drug discovery and medical education. Examples are Google's Med-PaLM and Med-PaLM 2, which were tested on US medical licensing exam style questions. Risks are hallucination, patient-data privacy and liability, so human clinician oversight is required. India's DPDP Act 2023 governs the handling of personal data.

3 — Correct: LLMs are used in software development. Facts: they generate, complete, explain, test and debug code from natural-language prompts. Examples are GitHub Copilot (built on OpenAI Codex, 2021), Amazon CodeWhisperer, Google's Codey and Meta's Code Llama. They speed up programming and are used for code translation between languages. Risks include insecure code, licensing and copyright issues, and over-reliance. The item was garbled as '8' in OCR.

4 — Correct: LLMs are used for translating languages. Facts: Transformer models first transformed machine translation, as in Google Translate's neural system. Modern LLMs translate across many languages, including low-resource ones. In India, the Bhashini mission (National Language Translation Mission) uses AI for translation among Indian languages, and the Supreme Court's SUVAS tool translates judgments. Limitations are nuance, dialects and cultural context.
summary: The answer is (d): 1, 2, 3 and 4. Large Language Models (LLMs) are general-purpose language systems used in reimagined search engines, health care, software development and language translation, so all four statements are correct.
topic_notes: Large Language Models are AI systems based on the Transformer architecture, introduced by Google researchers in 2017. They are pre-trained on massive text datasets using self-supervised learning and then fine-tuned, often with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Key terms are token, parameters, prompt, context window, fine-tuning, hallucination, and generative AI versus discriminative AI. Major models: GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (OpenAI; ChatGPT launched 30 November 2022), PaLM, Bard and Gemini (Google), LLaMA (Meta), Claude (Anthropic), and Copilot (Microsoft). India-related items: Bhashini (National Language Translation Mission), the IndiaAI Mission (approved March 2024), BharatGPT efforts, and the SUVAS and SUPACE tools in the judiciary. Risks and governance: hallucination, bias, deepfakes, misinformation, data privacy, copyright disputes, energy use and job displacement. Global responses include the EU AI Act, the Bletchley Park AI Safety Summit (November 2023, UK), the US Executive Order on AI (October 2023) and the Global Partnership on AI (GPAI), for which India was the chair in 2024. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and the IT Rules are relevant for deepfakes. Related ideas UPSC may ask are generative AI, machine learning, neural networks, natural language processing, chatbots, AGI and the Turing test. Applications beyond this question include education, agriculture advisory, legal research, customer service and governance, such as AI-based grievance handling.

Scope 1 : Emissions as a result of emissions employee commuting, business travel and waste produced 2. Scope 2 : Emissions as a result of 120. emissions purchase of _ electricity, steam, heating and cooling for own use 3. Scope 3 : Emissions from fuels emissions consumed by company vehicles, owned and leased Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched ? (a) land2 (b) 2only (c) land3 (d) 3only ‘Quantified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax’ is generally talked about in the con
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol Corporate Standard, developed by the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD), divides corporate emissions into three scopes. Scope 1 covers direct emissions from sources the company owns or controls: fuel burnt in boilers and furnaces, company-owned or leased vehicles, and process emissions and fugitive leaks. Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from generating purchased energy (electricity, steam, heating, cooling) that the company consumes. Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions in the value chain, both upstream and downstream: purchased goods, employee commuting, business travel, waste generated, transport and distribution, use of sold products and investments. Scope 3 is usually the largest share of a company's footprint and the hardest to measure. Elimination logic: pair 1 gives Scope 3 examples (commuting, travel, waste) under Scope 1, so it is wrong. Pair 3 gives a Scope 1 example (company vehicles) under Scope 3, so it is wrong. Pair 2 is textbook Scope 2. Only 2 is correct, which is option (b). The key trick is that the examples in pairs 1 and 3 are interchanged.
explanations: Wrong. It includes pair 1, which is incorrect because commuting, travel and waste are Scope 3 emissions, not Scope 1.
Correct. Only pair 2 matches, since Scope 2 means indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heating and cooling.
Wrong. Pair 1 and pair 3 both have mismatched examples, so neither can be counted as correct.
Wrong. Pair 3 is incorrect because company vehicles' fuel is a Scope 1 emission, and pair 2 is also correct, so '3 only' fails.
keyfact: Scope 1 = direct (own fuel, company vehicles); Scope 2 = purchased electricity, steam, heat and cooling; Scope 3 = all other value-chain emissions (commuting, travel, waste).
option_notes: Options 'Scope 1 and 2' would be correct only if the examples were properly matched. Scope 1 means direct emissions from owned or controlled sources, such as boilers, furnaces and company vehicles. Scope 2 means indirect emissions from purchased energy. Here, pair 1 gives a Scope 3 example under Scope 1, which is why the option fails. The GHG Protocol is the world's most widely used standard, developed by the WRI and the WBCSD, and was first published in 2001 with a revised edition in 2004.

The option 'Scope 2 only' is the correct choice. Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from the generation of purchased electricity, steam, heating and cooling consumed by the reporting company. It is reported using both location-based and market-based methods under the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance of 2015. Companies reduce Scope 2 through energy efficiency, on-site renewables, renewable power purchase agreements and renewable energy certificates. It is often the second-largest emissions category for many companies.

The option 'Scope 1 and 3' fails because it counts pair 1 and pair 3, which are swapped. Scope 1 covers direct emissions and Scope 3 covers all other indirect value-chain emissions. Scope 3 has 15 categories under the 2011 Corporate Value Chain Standard, and is often the largest portion of a company's footprint. The SBTi (Science Based Targets initiative) requires Scope 3 targets if they exceed 40% of total emissions. Scope 3 is the hardest to measure because it depends on supplier and customer data.

The option 'Scope 3 only' fails because it relies on pair 3, which describes company vehicle fuel, a direct Scope 1 emission. Scope 3 covers upstream and downstream emissions not owned or controlled by the company, such as supplier production, employee commuting, business travel, waste disposal, product use and investments. Under the SEBI Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) framework in India, Scope 1 and 2 are reported under the Core indicators, while Scope 3 is a leadership indicator.
related: The GHG Protocol was developed by WRI and WBCSD; the Corporate Standard first appeared in 2001.
Scope 3 has 15 categories, 8 upstream and 7 downstream.
Scope 2 is reported using both location-based and market-based methods.
SEBI's BRSR is mandatory for the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation.
India's net-zero target year is 2070; its 2030 NDC aims for 45% lower emissions intensity of GDP versus 2005.
The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, 2023 was notified under the Energy Conservation Act, with BEE as administrator.
The EU CBAM puts a carbon price on imports of products such as steel, cement, aluminium and fertilisers.
The second question on the page, 'Quantified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax', relates to the Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) Rules, the OECD Pillar Two.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Commuting, business travel and waste are Scope 3 examples, not Scope 1. Scope 1 means direct emissions from sources the company owns or controls. These include on-site fuel combustion in boilers and furnaces, company-owned vehicles, process emissions from manufacturing such as cement or chemicals, and fugitive emissions such as refrigerant or methane leaks. They are the easiest to measure and are under the company's direct control. Under the GHG Protocol they must be reported by any company following the Corporate Standard. They are reported in tonnes of CO2-equivalent, covering the seven Kyoto gases including CO2, CH4, N2O and HFCs.

2 — Correct: Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heating and cooling consumed by the company. The emissions physically occur at the power plant or utility, but are counted in the buyer's inventory because the buyer's demand causes them. The GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance (2015) requires dual reporting: a location-based method, using average grid emission factors, and a market-based method, using contractual instruments such as renewable energy certificates and power purchase agreements. Shifting to renewable power is the main way to cut Scope 2. RE100 is a global initiative of companies committed to 100% renewable electricity.

3 — Incorrect: Fuel consumed by company-owned or leased vehicles is a Scope 1 example, not Scope 3. Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions across the value chain. The GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard, published in 2011, defines 15 categories, 8 upstream and 7 downstream. They include purchased goods and services, capital goods, fuel- and energy-related activities, transportation, waste generated in operations, business travel, employee commuting, use of sold products, end-of-life treatment and investments. Scope 3 is often over 70% of a company's footprint. Reporting is voluntary under the GHG Protocol, but disclosure rules such as the EU CSRD and the ISSB's IFRS S2 increasingly require it.
summary: The answer is (b): only pair 2 is correctly matched. Scope 2 emissions are indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heating and cooling for own use. The examples given for Scope 1 and Scope 3 are swapped, so pairs 1 and 3 are wrong.
topic_notes:
Corporate carbon accounting follows the GHG Protocol, a partnership of the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD). Its Corporate Standard was first published in 2001, with a revised edition in 2004. It covers the seven Kyoto gases: CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs, SF6 and NF3 (NF3 added from the Doha Amendment period). Emissions are expressed in CO2-equivalent using global warming potentials (GWP).

Scope 1 covers direct emissions from owned or controlled sources: stationary combustion, mobile combustion in company vehicles, process emissions and fugitive emissions. Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heat and cooling, reported by location-based and market-based methods. Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions across the value chain in 15 categories, 8 upstream and 7 downstream, under the 2011 Value Chain Standard.

These concepts are connected to the wider framework of climate disclosure. The Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) set the disclosure structure, and the ISSB's IFRS S2 now carries it forward. India's SEBI requires the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation to file the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR), with BRSR Core including assured metrics on greenhouse gas intensity. The SBTi validates corporate net-zero targets aligned with 1.5°C. The Indian Carbon Market is being developed under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022 and the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, 2023, with the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) as the administrator. The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) taxes embedded emissions in imports, and covers direct emissions and some indirect emissions. India's NDC targets 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP by 2030 from 2005 levels, and net zero by 2070.

Future questions could ask about the definitions of each scope, carbon credits, BRSR, net zero, CBAM, or the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme.

ocr: Which one of the following statements best describes the term ‘Prowess,,’ sometimes seen in news ? A special-purpose supercomputer with a (a) hardware architecture dedicated to a single problem A database of the financial performance (b) of companies that is specially designed for academia A computing machine that uses the (c) properties of quantum physics to store data and perform computation A database in which collection and (d) storing of data is done on user’s system and this is basically designed for a single user ‘NSE Prime’, sometimes mentioned in news, denotes : (a) A high standard co
subject: Computers
detail: NSE Prime is an initiative of the National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) that aims to promote better corporate governance among listed companies. Companies that choose to follow governance norms stricter than the statutory minimum (such as SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements, and earlier Clause 49 of the Listing Agreement) are recognised under the framework. These norms cover the board's composition and independence, the role of audit committees, transparency of disclosures, treatment of minority shareholders, related-party transactions and risk management. The idea is that investors can identify well-governed firms more easily, and that companies gain reputational and cost-of-capital benefits. A related index, the Prime Index, tracks such companies. Governance reforms matter in India because of scandals like Satyam (2009) and the Kotak Committee (2017) recommendations. Elimination: sovereign green bonds are issued by the government (first issuance in January 2023), not by NSE, so (b) is wrong. Tax holidays for start-ups come under Startup India and the Income Tax Act, section 80-IAC, not from a stock exchange, so (c) is wrong. NBFC privileges are set by the RBI through its scale-based regulation, so (d) is wrong. Only (a) fits an exchange-led governance initiative.
explanations: Correct. NSE Prime is a corporate governance initiative of the NSE, under which listed companies adopt high governance standards.
Incorrect. Sovereign Green Bonds are issued by the Government of India through the RBI (first tranche in January 2023). They have no link with NSE Prime, which is not a debt instrument.
Incorrect. Tax concessions and tax holidays for start-ups come from DPIIT's Startup India scheme and the Income Tax Act. A stock exchange cannot grant tax benefits.

Incorrect. NBFC categories and any privileges are regulated by the RBI, for example under the scale-based regulation framework (Upper, Middle, Base, Top layers). NSE Prime has nothing to do with them.
keyfact: NSE Prime = a National Stock Exchange corporate governance initiative (with a Prime Index) for companies following high governance standards.
option_notes: A corporate governance initiative is a voluntary or mandatory set of practices on board independence, audit committees, disclosure, shareholder rights and ethics. In India the main legal sources are the Companies Act 2013 and SEBI's LODR Regulations 2015. Earlier Clause 49 (1999-2000) was the key listing norm. The Kotak Committee (2017) and the Narayana Murthy Committee (2003) shaped the reforms. NSE Prime is of this type.

Sovereign Green Bonds are government securities whose proceeds fund climate-friendly, green public projects. India's SGB framework was approved in the Union Budget 2022-23. The first auctions took place in January and February 2023, raising about Rs 8,000 crore. They are tenors of 5 and 10 years, and proceeds are tracked by a Green Finance Working Committee under the Ministry of Finance. They are not an NSE product.

Tax holidays for start-ups are offered under the Startup India initiative (launched January 2016). Eligible DPIIT-recognised start-ups can claim a 3-year tax holiday out of the first 10 years under Section 80-IAC of the Income Tax Act. Related measures include the Fund of Funds for Startups (Rs 10,000 crore, managed by SIDBI) and exemption under Section 56 (angel tax) for recognised start-ups, which was later abolished in Budget 2024.

Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) are regulated by the RBI under the RBI Act 1934 (Chapter III-B). Since October 2022 the RBI uses scale-based regulation with four layers: Base, Middle, Upper and Top. Categories include NBFC-ICC, MFI, Factoring, Infrastructure Finance Companies and Systemically Important Core Investment Companies. Privileges and obligations vary by layer and are set by the RBI, not by the stock exchange.
related: SEBI was set up in 1988 and given statutory status by the SEBI Act 1992.
Clause 49 of the Listing Agreement came after the Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee (1999).
The Kotak Committee (2017) on corporate governance was set up by SEBI.
NFRA (National Financial Reporting Authority) was constituted in 2018 under the Companies Act 2013.
BRSR is mandatory for the top 1000 listed companies by market capitalisation.
Section 135 of the Companies Act 2013 governs CSR spending of 2% of average net profit.
India's first Sovereign Green Bond auction was held in January 2023.
NSE started operations in 1994 and its flagship index is Nifty 50.
summary: The question being explained is Q118, 'NSE Prime', and the official answer (a) is correct: NSE Prime is a high-standard corporate governance initiative of the National Stock Exchange. It is a framework (with a Prime Index) for listed companies that voluntarily adopt governance norms stricter than the minimum required by SEBI's listing rules.
topic_notes: Corporate governance is the system of rules, practices and processes by which companies are directed and controlled. In India, the framework has evolved through several steps. The CII Code (1998, Desirable Corporate Governance) was the first voluntary code. SEBI introduced Clause 49 in the Listing Agreement in 2000 after the Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee (1999). The Naresh Chandra Committee (2002) dealt with audit and auditors' independence. The Narayana Murthy Committee (2003) strengthened Clause 49. The Companies Act 2013 brought in independent directors, a mandatory woman director, audit committees, CSR (Section 135, 2% of average net profit for firms above the thresholds), vigilance mechanisms, and related party transaction rules. SEBI's LODR Regulations 2015 consolidated listing norms. The Uday Kotak Committee (2017) recommended a minimum of six directors for top listed companies, separation of the Chairman and MD roles, and more disclosure. Governance failures such as Satyam (2009), Kingfisher, IL&FS (2018) and Yes Bank led to reforms. The NSE and BSE are the main stock exchanges. The NSE was incorporated in 1992, started operations in 1994, and is based in Mumbai; its main index is the Nifty 50. NSE has various index and governance initiatives, including the Prime Index. Other angles UPSC could ask: the role of SEBI (established 1988, statutory since 1992), the Stewardship Code (2020), the ESG disclosure norm Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) mandatory for the top 1000 listed companies, Sovereign Green Bonds, SEBI's Takeover Code, and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' institutions like NFRA (2018), IEPF and IICA.
