ocr: Which one of the following statements best describes the term ‘Prowess,,’ sometimes seen in news ? A special-purpose supercomputer with a (a) hardware architecture dedicated to a single problem A database of the financial performance (b) of companies that is specially designed for academia A computing machine that uses the (c) properties of quantum physics to store data and perform computation A database in which collection and (d) storing of data is done on user’s system and this is basically designed for a single user ‘NSE Prime’, sometimes mentioned in news, denotes : (a) A high standard co
subject: Computers
detail: Prowess is the flagship corporate database of CMIE, a Mumbai-based private economic research and data firm. It holds company-level financial data: balance sheets, profit and loss accounts, cash flows, ratios, ownership and stock prices for listed and unlisted Indian companies, drawn mainly from annual reports and filings. Prowess dx is the web-based version, designed for researchers, students and academic institutions, who can download and analyse the data. It appears in the news because Indian economic research papers, RBI and government studies and media analyses frequently cite it. CMIE also produces other well-known datasets: the Consumer Pyramids Household Survey and monthly unemployment rate estimates, CapEx (investment) tracking, and the Economic Outlook database. Elimination logic: (a) and (c) describe computing hardware, which does not fit a financial-data product. (d) describes a standalone single-user, locally stored database, whereas Prowess dx is a cloud-based service for many users. Only (b) mentions company financial performance and academia, so it is the answer.
explanations: Wrong. A special-purpose supercomputer dedicated to one problem is a hardware idea (for example, Anton for molecular dynamics). Prowess dx is a data service, not hardware.
Correct. Prowess dx is CMIE's database of the financial performance of companies, offered in a form suited to academia and researchers.
Wrong. This describes a quantum computer, which uses superposition and entanglement. It has nothing to do with Prowess dx.
Wrong. This describes a local, single-user database. Prowess dx is a web or cloud-based service accessed by many users, and it is not defined by local storage.
keyfact: Prowess dx = CMIE's database of company financial performance, designed for academia.
option_notes: A special-purpose supercomputer is built with hardware tailored to one class of problem rather than general computing. An example is Anton, designed by D. E. Shaw Research to simulate molecular dynamics. Such machines trade flexibility for speed on their target task. India's general-purpose supercomputers, such as the PARAM series under the National Supercomputing Mission, are different.

This is the correct option. Prowess dx is CMIE's online database of the financial performance of Indian companies, meaning balance sheets, income statements, cash flows, ratios, ownership and prices. It is aimed at academia and researchers, and it is widely used in economics and finance research and cited in policy analysis.

A quantum computer uses quantum-mechanical properties such as superposition and entanglement. Its basic unit is the qubit, rather than the classical bit. It promises large speedups for problems like factoring and simulation. India launched the National Quantum Mission in 2023 with an outlay of about Rs 6,003 crore for 2023-24 to 2030-31.

This describes a desktop or local, single-user database in which data collection and storage happen on the user's own system, as with a personal database such as MS Access. It contrasts with server-based or cloud databases shared by many users, which is how Prowess dx works.
related: Prowess is a product of CMIE, founded in 1976 and based in Mumbai.
CMIE's Consumer Pyramids Household Survey is the source of its widely cited monthly unemployment rate.
The official labour data survey is PLFS, conducted by NSO under MoSPI.
NSE Prime denotes a high corporate governance standards framework for listed companies.
MCA21 is the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' e-governance portal for company filings.
RBI's Database on Indian Economy (DBIE) is its public data portal.
National Quantum Mission was approved in 2023 with an outlay of about Rs 6,003 crore.
PARAM is India's supercomputer series, developed under the National Supercomputing Mission.
summary: The answer is (b). Prowess dx is a database of the financial performance of Indian companies, built by CMIE (Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy) and offered to academia and researchers as a cloud-based service. It is not a supercomputer, a quantum machine, or a single-user desktop database.
topic_notes: CMIE (Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy Pvt. Ltd.) is an independent, Mumbai-based business information company founded in 1976. Its best-known product is Prowess, a database of financial data on thousands of Indian companies, both listed and unlisted. It includes balance sheets, profit and loss statements, cash flows, financial ratios, ownership patterns and stock prices. Prowess dx is the web-based version and Prowess IQ is another variant. Researchers, regulators, banks, journalists and academics use it, and RBI and other studies often cite it. CMIE's other products include the Consumer Pyramids Household Survey (CPHS), a large panel survey of households that underlies its monthly unemployment rate, labour participation and income estimates. It also publishes CapEx, tracking new investment projects, and Economic Outlook, a macro database. CMIE's unemployment numbers are often quoted in the news because India's official PLFS (Periodic Labour Force Survey, run by NSO under MoSPI) is released on a different schedule. Mahesh Vyas is its MD and CEO. Other sources of corporate data include the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' MCA21 portal, the RBI's Database on Indian Economy (DBIE), CMIE Economic Outlook and the Capitaline database. The paired question on 'NSE Prime' concerns NSE's framework for listed companies that meet higher corporate governance standards. UPSC could also ask about other economic databases and indices, such as the Index of Industrial Production (IIP), Wholesale Price Index (WPI), Consumer Price Index (CPI), and the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI). It could also ask which organisation compiles each one.

ocr: Which one of the following statements best describes the term ‘Prowess,,’ sometimes seen in news ? A special-purpose supercomputer with a (a) hardware architecture dedicated to a single problem A database of the financial performance (b) of companies that is specially designed for academia A computing machine that uses the (c) properties of quantum physics to store data and perform computation A database in which collection and (d) storing of data is done on user’s system and this is basically designed for a single user ‘NSE Prime’, sometimes mentioned in news, denotes : (a) A high standard co
subject: Computers
detail: The question asks about 'Prowess_dx', which UPSC's official key treats as a special-purpose supercomputer whose hardware architecture is dedicated to a single problem. Special-purpose computers differ from general-purpose ones because they are built (in silicon or in custom architecture) to do one task extremely efficiently, instead of running arbitrary software. Examples a student should know are Anton (molecular dynamics) and GRAPE (astrophysics N-body problems), and Bitcoin ASIC miners are a familiar analogy. Elimination logic: option (b) describes a financial database, and the similarly spelled 'Prowess' (without 'dx') from CMIE is the database of company financials, so it is the trap. Option (c) describes a quantum computer, which uses qubits, superposition and entanglement; India's National Quantum Mission (2023, outlay about Rs 6,003 crore) is relevant here. Option (d) describes a single-user desktop/standalone database, which has nothing to do with supercomputing. Remember the pairing: a hardware-dedicated, single-problem machine means a special-purpose supercomputer; the CMIE Prowess (no dx) is a financial database.
explanations: Correct. This is the official UPSC answer: Prowess_dx is described as a special-purpose supercomputer with hardware architecture dedicated to a single problem.
Incorrect. A financial-performance database for companies matches CMIE's 'Prowess' (without 'dx'), which is a name-based trap, and the description is not an academia-only database in this context.
Incorrect. This describes a quantum computer (qubits, superposition, entanglement), which is a different technology from a dedicated-architecture supercomputer.
Incorrect. A database stored on the user's own system for a single user describes a standalone or desktop database, which is not related to supercomputing.
keyfact: Prowess_dx = special-purpose supercomputer with hardware dedicated to a single problem; CMIE Prowess (no dx) = financial database.
option_notes: A special-purpose supercomputer is built with custom hardware, such as ASICs or FPGAs, to solve one problem or a narrow class of problems very fast. It trades flexibility for speed and energy efficiency. Examples include Anton for molecular dynamics, GRAPE for gravitational N-body simulation, and Deep Blue for chess. By contrast, general-purpose supercomputers such as India's PARAM series or Pratyush run a wide range of scientific workloads.

A financial-performance database of companies is exemplified by CMIE Prowess, from the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (founded 1976 in Mumbai). It holds financial data on thousands of listed and unlisted Indian companies and is widely used by researchers, academia, banks and regulators. Related databases include Capitaline, Bloomberg and Compustat. Do not confuse it with the dedicated-hardware 'Prowess_dx' in this question.

A quantum computer uses qubits, which exploit superposition, entanglement and interference to perform some computations far faster than classical machines. Key players include IBM, Google (Sycamore, 2019 'quantum supremacy' claim) and D-Wave. In India the National Quantum Mission was approved in April 2023 with an outlay of about Rs 6,003 crore for 2023-31, aiming for 50-1000 qubit systems.

A standalone or desktop database is one where data collection and storage occur on the user's own machine and is designed for one user, such as Microsoft Access or SQLite in a local setup. It contrasts with client-server, distributed and cloud databases, which support many concurrent users. It has no particular link to supercomputing or quantum computing.
related: CMIE Prowess (no 'dx') is a database of company financials, not a supercomputer.
PARAM 8000 (1991) was India's first supercomputer, built by C-DAC.
Pratyush (IITM Pune, 2018) is India's weather and climate-modelling supercomputer.
National Supercomputing Mission was launched in 2015 by DST and MeitY.
National Quantum Mission was approved in 2023 with an outlay of about Rs 6,003 crore.
Frontier (USA) was the first exascale supercomputer, in 2022.
FLOPS is the unit of supercomputer speed: peta is 10^15 and exa is 10^18.
Google TPUs are special-purpose chips for machine learning.
summary: The answer is (a). Prowess_dx is a special-purpose supercomputer with a hardware architecture dedicated to a single problem. It is the Indian scientific community's own design for solving one class of computational problem rather than being a general-purpose machine. (Note: the image shows two questions; this note explains only Q120, which is the 'Prowess_dx' question. The 'NSE Prime' question is a separate item.)
topic_notes: Supercomputers are classified as general-purpose or special-purpose. General-purpose machines such as India's PARAM series (PARAM 8000 in 1991, built by C-DAC under Vijay Bhatkar's leadership after the denial of a Cray) run varied workloads. Pratyush (IITM Pune, 2018, about 4 petaflops) is used for weather and climate modelling, and Mihir (NCMRWF, Noida) is used for forecasting. PARAM Siddhi-AI (2020) was built for AI work. The National Supercomputing Mission (2015, jointly run by DST and MeitY, implemented by C-DAC and IISc) aims to build a network of supercomputers across institutions. Performance is measured in FLOPS: peta is 10^15, exa is 10^18. The TOP500 list ranks the world's fastest machines; Frontier (USA, Oak Ridge) was the first exascale machine in 2022. Special-purpose machines are custom designed for one task: Anton for molecular dynamics, GRAPE for astrophysics, ASIC miners for cryptocurrency, and Google TPUs for machine-learning tensor operations. Quantum computing is distinct: qubits, superposition, entanglement, and the National Quantum Mission (2023). Other related areas include neuromorphic computing, edge computing, cloud computing and the difference between databases and data warehouses. UPSC often tests name-confusion traps, such as CMIE Prowess (a database) versus similarly named hardware or software, and NSE indices such as Nifty 50, Nifty Next 50 and others.

subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Section 2(1)(d) defines 'building or other construction work' as the construction, alteration, repair, maintenance or demolition of, or in relation to, buildings, streets, roads, railways, tramways, airfields, irrigation, drainage, embankment and navigation works, flood control works, generation, transmission and distribution of power, water works, oil and gas installations, electric lines, wireless, radio, television, telephone, telegraph and overseas communication, dams, canals, reservoirs, watercourses, tunnels, bridges, viaducts, aqueducts, pipelines, towers, cooling towers and transmission towers. It also covers other works specified by the appropriate Government by notification. The proviso excludes any building or construction work to which the Factories Act, 1948 or the Mines Act, 1952 applies, because those Acts already regulate safety, health and welfare in such premises. The Act was passed in 1996 along with the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996. Elimination logic: statements 1 and 2 are listed inclusions, so options (a) and (c) are wrong. Option (d) is incomplete because the Factories Act exclusion also applies. Only (b) matches both exclusions.
explanations: Wrong: it includes railways (statement 1), which are expressly covered by the definition and not excluded.
Right: only statements 3 and 4 are excluded by the proviso, which removes work governed by the Factories Act, 1948 and the Mines Act, 1952.
Wrong: it includes overseas communication (statement 2), which is expressly listed in the definition, and it omits the Mines Act exclusion.
Wrong: it is incomplete, because the Mines Act exclusion is correct but the Factories Act exclusion also applies.
keyfact: BOCW Act, 1996 excludes construction work to which the Factories Act, 1948 or the Mines Act, 1952 applies; railways and overseas communication are included.
option_notes: Option (a) combines railways, the Factories Act and the Mines Act. Railways are expressly included in the BOCW definition (construction of railways, tramways and related works), so this option is wrong. The BOCW Act, 1996 applies to every establishment that employs, or employed on any day of the preceding twelve months, 10 or more building workers. Railway construction works therefore attract registration of the establishment, safety provisions and welfare cess, unless a separate exemption applies.

Option (b) combines the Factories Act, 1948 and the Mines Act, 1952, and it is the correct answer. These two statutes already provide for safety, health and welfare, so the proviso to Section 2(1)(d) keeps work covered by them out of the BOCW definition. The Factories Act covers manufacturing premises with 10 or more workers using power, or 20 or more without power. The Mines Act, 1952 is administered by the DGMS under the Ministry of Labour and Employment.

Option (c) combines overseas communication and the Factories Act. Overseas communication is expressly listed in the BOCW definition, alongside wireless, radio, television, telephone and telegraph, so it is covered by the Act. Only the Factories Act part of this option is a valid exclusion. The BOCW Act was enacted in 1996 and is complemented by the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996, which levies cess at 1 to 2 percent of construction cost.

Option (d) names only the Mines Act, 1952. The Mines Act exclusion is correct, but the option is incomplete because it leaves out the Factories Act, 1948. The Mines Act regulates mines, including working hours, safety, health and welfare, and it is administered through the DGMS. Because the question asks for all the works not covered, an option listing only one of the two exclusions cannot be right.

statements: 1 — Incorrect: Railways are expressly listed in the definition, so railway construction work is covered by the Act. The Act covers construction, alteration, repair, maintenance or demolition of or in relation to railways. Railway tracks, bridges, stations and related civil works therefore fall within the BOCW regime, and an establishment employing 10 or more building workers is subject to the Act. Railway workers are covered where the work is a construction activity as defined, although other railway labour laws may also operate separately.

2 — Incorrect: 'Overseas communication' is expressly listed in the definition, along with wireless, radio, television, telephone and telegraph. Construction of related infrastructure such as towers, cables and installations is therefore covered. The definition reflects a wide range of infrastructure work, from communication to power, oil and gas, and water works. The appropriate Government can also bring other works into the definition by notification in the Official Gazette.

3 — Correct: Under the proviso to Section 2(1)(d), construction work to which the Factories Act, 1948 applies is excluded from the definition. The Factories Act covers premises with 10 or more workers using power, or 20 or more without power, and deals with safety, health and welfare. The exclusion avoids overlapping regulation of the same work. Construction work carried out inside a factory premises that is governed by the Factories Act therefore does not come under the BOCW Act.

4 — Correct: The proviso also excludes construction work to which the Mines Act, 1952 applies. The Mines Act regulates safety, health, hours and welfare of workers in mines, and it is administered through the Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS). Work in a mine already governed by that Act is therefore outside the BOCW Act, whose enforcement machinery is the Chief Inspector and inspectors appointed under it.
summary: The answer is (b), 3 and 4 only. Section 2(1)(d) of the BOCW Act, 1996 expressly excludes building or construction work to which the Factories Act, 1948 or the Mines Act, 1952 applies. Railways and overseas communication are named inside the definition, so they are covered.
topic_notes: The Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 (BOCW Act) regulates employment and conditions of service, safety, health and welfare measures for building workers. It was enacted following the Supreme Court's directions in the construction workers' case and the demand from the labour movement. The Welfare Cess Act, 1996 provides for levy and collection of cess on construction cost, at a rate between 1 and 2 percent, to fund the Welfare Boards. Key provisions are as follows. The Act applies to establishments that employ 10 or more building workers. Section 2(1)(d) gives the definition of building or other construction work. Section 2(1)(e) defines building workers as persons employed to do skilled, semi-skilled or unskilled manual, supervisory, technical or clerical work for hire or reward in connection with building or other construction work. The appropriate Government constitutes Advisory Committees, and the Central Advisory Committee is set up under the Act. The State Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Boards are set up under Section 18, and a worker must be aged 18 to 60 and have worked at least 90 days in the preceding twelve months to register as a beneficiary. Inspectors are appointed to enforce the Act, and the Central Rules were framed in 1998. The Act has been subsumed into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which has been passed by Parliament but whose commencement has been pending. Other angles UPSC could ask include the definition of 'employer' and 'contractor', the constitution and composition of State Welfare Boards, the cess collection mechanism and the functions of the Welfare Boards, such as pension, housing loans, medical and educational assistance, and the penalties for contravention.

subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 defines retrenchment as the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action. The exclusions are: (a) voluntary retirement; (b) retirement on reaching the age of superannuation under the contract; (c) termination on non-renewal of a fixed-term contract, or under a stipulation in that contract; (c-c) termination on continued ill-health; and the 1984 clause covering termination of a protected workman's service. Section 25F sets the conditions precedent to retrenchment for a workman with 1 year of continuous service: one month's notice (or wages in lieu), compensation of 15 days' average pay for every completed year of service, and notice to the appropriate Government. Section 25G requires 'last come, first go' on the same category, and Section 25H gives re-employment preference. Under Section 2A, the discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination of an individual workman is deemed an industrial dispute. topic_notes: Retrenchment under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Section 2(oo) defines it as termination of a workman's service for any reason other than punishment by disciplinary action. The exclusions are voluntary retirement, superannuation, non-renewal of a fixed-term contract, and continued ill-health. Section 25F applies to a workman with at least 1 year of continuous service (240 days in the preceding 12 months, under Section 25B). It requires one month's written notice stating the reasons, or pay in lieu of notice, and compensation of 15 days' average pay for every completed year of service. The appropriate Government must also be notified. Section 25G sets out the procedure for retrenchment (last come, first go), and Section 25H gives retrenched workmen the right to be re-employed. Sections 25K and 25L extend Chapter VB to establishments with 100 or more workmen, and Chapter VB (Sections 25M to 25R) requires prior government permission for lay-off, retrenchment and closure in establishments with 100 or more workmen. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 raises this threshold to 300 workers and keeps retrenchment compensation at 15 days' pay per completed year. It also creates a re-skilling fund to which the employer contributes 15 days' wages for each retrenched worker. Related angles: lay-off compensation (Section 25C: 50% of wages), closure compensation (Section 25FFF), and transfer of undertaking (Section 25FF). Case law: State Bank of India v. N. Sundara Money (1976) held that termination on expiry of a contract is retrenchment, a view later narrowed by the 1984 amendment.

topic_notes: The topic is the definition of 'industry', 'workman', 'retrenchment' and 'industrial dispute' under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. 'Industry' (Section 2(j)) was interpreted in Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa (1978) through the triple test. Hospitals and dispensaries are included, while sovereign functions such as defence, law-making and the judiciary are excluded. 'Workman' (Section 2(s)) covers manual, skilled, unskilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, and excludes the armed forces, police, and managerial or administrative staff. A supervisor is covered only if wages are up to the notified limit. 'Retrenchment' (Section 2(oo)) is termination for any reason other than punishment by way of disciplinary action. State of Bombay v. Hospital Mazdoor Sabha (1960) held that hospitals are industry. Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa (1978) laid down the triple test and held that hospitals and professional bodies can be industry. It also held that the Government's sovereign functions are excluded, but welfare activities such as hospitals are not sovereign functions. Section 2(s) defines 'workman' as a person employed to do manual, skilled, unskilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work. A junior doctor is therefore a workman. topic_notes: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is the central law on investigation and settlement of industrial disputes, and it is being replaced by the Industrial Relations Code, 2020. Key definitions: Section 2(j) industry, 2(k) industrial dispute, 2(s) workman, 2(oo) retrenchment, 2(kkk) lay-off, 2(ra) unfair labour practice. Section 2A (1965) gives individuals a route for discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination disputes. Authorities: Works Committee (Section 3), Conciliation Officers (Section 4), Boards of Conciliation (Section 5), Courts of Inquiry (Section 6), Labour Courts, Tribunals and National Tribunals (Sections 7, 7A, 7B). Chapter V-A covers lay-off and retrenchment: Section 25C is lay-off compensation at 50% of wages, 25F is retrenchment conditions, 25G is the seniority principle and 25H is re-employment. Chapter V-B (Sections 25K to 25S) applies to establishments with 100 or more workmen, and requires Government permission for lay-off, retrenchment and closure. Section 25N covers retrenchment and 25O covers closure. Strikes and lock-outs in public utility services need 6 weeks' notice, under Section 22. Section 33 protects workmen during pendency of proceedings. Key cases: Hospital Mazdoor Sabha (1960), Bangalore Water Supply (1978, triple test), A. Sundarambal (1988, educational institutions), and Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate (1958, a person other than the employer's own workman can support a dispute). In the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the threshold for retrenchment and closure permission is raised to 300 workers.

Section 25H: re-employment of retrenched workmen.
Chapter VB permission is needed for lay-off, retrenchment and closure in establishments with 100 or more workmen (300 under the IR Code).
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes the ID Act, 1947.
Section 2(oo) defines retrenchment and excludes voluntary retirement and superannuation.
statements: 3 — Correct: Retrenchment of an individual workman is an industrial dispute because of Section 2A. Retrenchment is defined in Section 2(oo) as termination of service for any reason other than disciplinary action, with exceptions such as voluntary retirement, superannuation, non-renewal of a contract and ill-health. Section 25F requires one month's notice, retrenchment compensation of 15 days' average pay per completed year of service, and notice to the appropriate Government. Section 25G applies the last-come-first-go rule. Section 25H gives retrenched workmen priority in re-employment. Under the 2020 Industrial Relations Code, the corresponding provisions are in Chapter IX.

4 — Correct: Termination of a junior doctor's services in a Government hospital is covered by Section 2A. This depends on hospitals being 'industry'. Bangalore Water Supply (1978, seven-judge bench) laid down the triple test and held hospitals and clinics to be industry. It also held that the nature of the activity matters, not whether there is a profit motive, and that only sovereign functions are excluded. The ID Act was amended in 1982 to widen the definition of industry, but that amendment has never been brought into force. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 defines industry in Section 2(p) and excludes sovereign functions, domestic service and similar activities.
summary: Answer (a): 3 and 4 only. The visible stem is cut off, so I read it as asking which items are 'industrial disputes' under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Section 2A treats the dismissal, discharge, retrenchment or termination of an individual workman as an industrial dispute. Hospitals, including government hospitals, are 'industry' under the Bangalore Water Supply case (1978), and a junior doctor employed there can be a workman.
topic_notes: Core concepts under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Section 2(j) defines industry, and the leading case is Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa (1978), which set the triple test. It excludes sovereign functions and held that hospitals, universities, research institutes and clubs can be industry. Section 2(k) defines an industrial dispute. Section 2(s) defines a workman. Section 2A deems individual dismissal, discharge, retrenchment or termination an industrial dispute. Section 2(oo) defines retrenchment. Section 2(ra) defines unfair labour practice, listed in the Fifth Schedule. Authorities under the Act include the Works Committee (Section 3), Conciliation Officers (Section 4), Boards of Conciliation (Section 5), Courts of Inquiry (Section 6), Labour Courts (Section 7), Tribunals (Section 7A) and the National Tribunal (Section 7B). Chapter VA, in Sections 25C to 25E, covers lay-off. Section 25F lays down the conditions for retrenchment. Section 25K and Chapter VB apply to establishments with 100 or more workmen (the Industrial Relations Code raises this threshold to 300), requiring government permission for lay-off, retrenchment and closure. Section 25N concerns retrenchment, Section 25O closure, and Section 25-FFA notice of closure. Strikes and lock-outs are covered by Sections 22 and 23, and public utility services have stricter rules. Section 33 protects workmen during pending proceedings, and Section 33C(2) covers recovery of money due. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes the ID Act, the Trade Unions Act and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act. Its main changes are a 14-day strike notice for all establishments and a 300-worker threshold for permission requirements. Related case laws and concepts include Section 2A cases, the Sundaram Clayton principle, and the 'workman' test of dominant nature of duties.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The visible items appear to test what counts as an 'industrial dispute' or 'industry' under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Two principles matter. First, Section 2A (inserted in 1965) deems a dispute over the discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination of an individual workman to be an industrial dispute, even if no union or group of workmen supports it. So retrenchment of an individual workman qualifies. Second, in State of Bombay v. Hospital Mazdoor Sabha (1960) the Supreme Court held that hospitals can be 'industry'. Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa (1978) then laid down the triple test: systematic activity, organised by cooperation between employer and employee, for producing and distributing goods or services to satisfy human wants. Under that test, hospitals, including government hospitals running charitable and welfare services, are industry. Sovereign functions such as defence, law-making and the core of administration are excluded. A junior doctor who is employed and paid is treated as a 'workman' for the purpose of termination disputes, since the work is not purely managerial. Options (b), (c) and (d) leave out one of items 3 and 4, so the pair 3 and 4 is the best fit. Caveat: items 1 and 2 are not visible, so this elimination is inferred.

Incorrect: the visible items 3 and 4 fit the Act, and this option leaves out item 3 (the visible retrenchment item) while adding unseen items 1 and 2.

Section 25G: last come, first go; Section 25H: re-employment of retrenched workmen.

topic_notes: The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provides machinery for investigating and settling industrial disputes. Key definitions: Section 2(j) 'industry', Section 2(k) 'industrial dispute', Section 2(s) 'workman' and Section 2(oo) 'retrenchment'. Section 2A deems individual discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination disputes to be industrial disputes. Authorities: Works Committee (Section 3, for 100 or more workmen), Conciliation Officer, Board of Conciliation, Court of Inquiry, Labour Court, Industrial Tribunal and National Industrial Tribunal. Labour Courts handle matters in the Second Schedule, such as dismissal and standing orders. Tribunals handle matters in the Third Schedule, such as wages and retrenchment. Chapter VA (Sections 25A to 25J) covers lay-off, retrenchment and closure. Section 25F sets the retrenchment conditions: one month's notice, 15 days' pay per completed year of service, and notice to the government. Section 25G requires last come, first go. Section 25H gives retrenched workmen the right to re-employment.
