Landmark cases: Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa (1978) gave the triple test for industry; Hospital Mazdoor Sabha (1960) held that hospitals can be industry; Safdarjung Hospital v. Kuldip Singh Sethi (1970) held that a government hospital's work is not an industry in certain situations. Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Industrial Disputes Act has been merged into a new code, which has been enacted but whose implementation depends on notification.

question:
Which of the following do not fall within the 41, scope of powers of the Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal under Section 11A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 ? iE. Discharge
2. Dismissal
3. Reduction in rank 4, Suspension Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 11A was inserted by the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1971, with effect from 15 December 1971. It was meant to overcome the earlier position under the Indian Iron & Steel Co. v. Workmen (1958) line of cases, under which tribunals could interfere with management's punishment only in limited situations such as mala fides, victimisation or unfair labour practice. Under Section 11A, where an industrial dispute about the discharge or dismissal of a workman is referred for adjudication and the Labour Court or Tribunal finds the punishment unjustified, it may set aside the order and direct reinstatement on terms it thinks fit. It may also substitute a lesser punishment. It may re-appraise the evidence, and it may also decide on the quantum of punishment. It does not cover other disciplinary actions such as demotion (reduction in rank), suspension, withholding of increments, censure or fine. Those can be examined only under the general principles of Section 10 and on grounds like victimisation, unfair labour practice or mala fides. Since the question asks which do NOT fall within scope, the answer is reduction in rank and suspension. That gives option (d).
explanations: Wrong. Discharge and dismissal are exactly the two actions that Section 11A covers, so they do not fall in the 'do not fall' category.
Wrong. Discharge alone is a covered matter, and the dismissed workman is covered as well. Options naming only 1 miss items 3 and 4, which are the ones outside scope.
Wrong, though only partly. Reduction in rank is outside Section 11A, but suspension (4) is also outside it, so '3 only' is incomplete.
Correct. Section 11A is confined to discharge and dismissal. Reduction in rank (3) and suspension (4) are not covered, so 3 and 4 only is the answer.
keyfact: Section 11A (ID Act, 1971 amendment) gives tribunals power to interfere only in discharge or dismissal, not in suspension or reduction in rank.
option_notes: Discharge and dismissal are the two actions covered by Section 11A. Discharge is termination without a punitive finding; dismissal is termination as punishment for misconduct. The tribunal can set aside the order, direct reinstatement with or without back wages, or impose a lesser punishment. The Section was added in 1971. It applies to workmen as defined in Section 2(s), and the dispute must be referred for adjudication. This option lists items that ARE covered.

Discharge on its own is one of the two covered actions. Discharge includes termination for reasons such as continued ill health or unsatisfactory work. If the discharge is found unjustified, the tribunal may order reinstatement. It differs from retrenchment under Section 2(oo) and from termination on closure under Sections 25FFF and 25FFA. This option leaves out items outside scope.

Reduction in rank (demotion) is a punishment that lowers a workman's grade or post. It is not covered by Section 11A. It is regulated by certified Standing Orders or service rules, and tribunals can interfere only on limited grounds like victimisation, mala fides or unfair labour practice. It is half of the correct set, but this option omits suspension.

Reduction in rank and suspension are both outside Section 11A. Suspension is a temporary removal from duty, either pending an inquiry or as punishment, and the employment relationship continues. The workman gets a subsistence allowance under the Standing Orders (generally 50 percent of wages for the first 90 days). Section 11A power relates only to termination of service, namely discharge or dismissal. This is the correct option.
related: Section 11A was inserted in 1971 and is effective from 15 December 1971.
It covers only discharge or dismissal of workmen.
Section 2A makes an individual dismissal dispute an industrial dispute.
Section 17B provides full wages to a workman during pendency of the employer's challenge in High Court or Supreme Court.
Section 33 bars changes in service conditions during pendency of proceedings without permission.
Section 25F lays down conditions for valid retrenchment: one month's notice, compensation of 15 days' pay per year of service.
In the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the corresponding section is 53.
Standing Orders under the 1946 Act govern suspension and demotion.
statements: 1 — Correct (it falls within Section 11A, so it is not the answer to a 'does not fall' question): Section 11A expressly mentions 'discharge'. Discharge is termination of service by the employer, for example for incapacity or after a non-punitive inquiry. The Labour Court or Tribunal can set it aside if it is not justified. It can direct reinstatement, with or without back wages or other terms, or award a lesser punishment. Section 2(oo) defines retrenchment separately, and Section 25F governs retrenchment compensation. Section 11A applies when the dispute has been referred or is pending adjudication.

2 — Correct (it falls within Section 11A, so it is not the answer): 'Dismissal' is expressly covered. Dismissal is termination as a punishment for misconduct, usually after a domestic inquiry. The tribunal may examine whether the punishment is proportionate. It may re-appraise the evidence and may substitute a lesser punishment. The Supreme Court in Workmen of Firestone Tyre v. Management (1973) and Gujarat Steel Tubes v. Mazdoor Sabha (1980) explained the wide power. The power is to be exercised judicially, and the tribunal must give reasons for interfering.

3 — Incorrect as a statement of scope, so it IS part of the answer: Reduction in rank (demotion) is not mentioned in Section 11A. A tribunal cannot use Section 11A to review a demotion. It can interfere only on general grounds such as victimisation, unfair labour practice, mala fides, or violation of natural justice or standing orders. Demotion is a punishment short of removal from service. It is typically governed by the certified Standing Orders under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, or by service rules.

4 — Incorrect as a statement of scope, so it IS part of the answer: Suspension, whether pending inquiry or punitive, is outside Section 11A because the workman's service continues. Suspension pending inquiry is not a punishment. The subsistence allowance is governed by Standing Orders and by Section 10A of the Standing Orders Act, 1946 (Central Rules). The Supreme Court has held that suspension can be challenged only on limited grounds such as mala fides or unreasonable delay. It is not covered by the Section 11A power to substitute lesser punishment.
summary: The answer is (d), 3 and 4 only. Section 11A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 empowers Labour Courts, Tribunals and National Tribunals to give relief only in cases of discharge or dismissal of a workman. Reduction in rank and suspension fall outside it.
topic_notes: Section 11A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is titled 'Powers of Labour Courts, Tribunals and National Tribunals to give appropriate relief in case of discharge or dismissal of workmen'. It was inserted by Act 45 of 1971, in force from 15 December 1971. Before it, tribunals had limited power over the quantum of punishment after a valid domestic inquiry. Under the Section, the Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal, if satisfied that the discharge or dismissal was not justified, may set aside the order and direct reinstatement on terms it thinks fit, or give any other relief including a lesser punishment. The Section includes a proviso that the tribunal must rely on the material already on record and need not take fresh evidence. This links to the Supreme Court's rulings in Workmen of Firestone Tyre (1973), Gujarat Steel Tubes (1980) and Ramakant Misra v. State of UP. The Section applies to workmen as defined in Section 2(s). Related provisions are Section 2A (individual dispute deemed an industrial dispute for discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination), Section 10 (reference), Section 11 (procedure and powers), Section 33 (conditions of service during pendency of proceedings), Section 33A, Section 25F (retrenchment conditions) and Section 25G (retrenchment procedure). Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 the equivalent provision is Section 53, which retains the relief in cases of discharge or dismissal. Other possible angles are the bodies themselves, the 2A power to approach the Conciliation Officer, Section 17B (wages during pendency of proceedings in higher courts), and the difference between discharge, dismissal, retrenchment and termination.

question: Which one among the following legal propositions was not laid down by the Supreme Court in State of Bombay v. KP. Krishnan, AIR 1960 SC 1223 with 49, reference to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947?
options: Power of Government under Section 10(1) is administrative in nature
Power of Government under Section 10(1) is wide and absolute
Second proviso to Section 10(1) gives no discretion to the Government in the matter of making reference to the Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal
Section 12(5) gives power to the appropriate Government to make reference of an industrial dispute independent of Section 10(1) to the Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: K.P. Krishnan (AIR 1960 SC 1223) is the leading case on the government's power to refer disputes under Section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Court held that the function under Section 10(1) is administrative, not judicial or quasi-judicial. The government may therefore consider expediency and the merits of the dispute when deciding whether to refer it. The power is wide, but it is not wholly unreviewable. If the government refuses a reference on irrelevant or extraneous grounds, the High Court can issue a writ of mandamus under Article 226, but it cannot compel a particular decision on the merits. The Court also read Section 12(5) together with Section 10(1). After a conciliation failure report, the government decides whether to refer, and any reference is made under Section 10(1). Section 12(5) therefore creates no separate, independent source of power, which is why option (d) is the proposition that was not laid down. The second proviso to Section 10(1), as it stood then, was treated as mandatory: where the proviso applies, the government has no discretion. Options (a), (b) and (c) therefore broadly reflect the judgment, and (d) is the odd one out.
explanations: Incorrect choice: the Court did hold the Section 10(1) power to be administrative in nature, so this proposition was laid down.

Incorrect choice: the Court described the discretion as wide, though reviewable if exercised on irrelevant grounds. The option is loosely worded, but it broadly reflects the discretionary character the Court recognised.
Incorrect choice: the Court treated the second proviso as mandatory, so the government has no discretion where it applies. This proposition was laid down.

Correct choice: the Court held that Section 12(5) does not confer an independent reference power. Any reference is made under Section 10(1), and the government retains discretion, so this was not laid down.
keyfact: K.P. Krishnan (1960): the Section 10(1) power is administrative, and Section 12(5) gives no independent reference power.
option_notes: Administrative function: the government acts as an executive authority in deciding whether to refer a dispute, not as an adjudicator. It does not decide the rights of the parties. Its decision is therefore not a quasi-judicial order. It can still be tested for mala fides or irrelevant considerations through a writ.

Wide discretion: the government may weigh expediency, industrial peace and the merits of the dispute before referring it. The discretion is not wholly unreviewable. A refusal based on irrelevant grounds can be challenged, and later cases such as Bombay Union of Journalists reaffirmed this.

The second proviso to Section 10(1) makes a reference mandatory in the situation it covers, notably in relation to public utility services and notice of strike or lockout. In that situation the government has no discretion to refuse. It is the exception to the general discretionary rule.

Section 12(5) deals with the government's action on the conciliation officer's report. If it finds no case for reference, it records its reasons and communicates them to the parties. If it does refer, the reference is made under Section 10(1). The provision is not a separate source of reference power.
related: K.P. Krishnan (1960): Section 10(1) power is administrative, not judicial.
Bombay Union of Journalists (1964): the government cannot decide the merits of a dispute when deciding on a reference.
A government order refusing reference can be challenged by writ under Article 226.
Section 12(5) requires the government to record and communicate its reasons for not referring a dispute.
Section 2A treats individual dismissals and discharges as industrial disputes.
Section 10A provides for voluntary arbitration.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
summary: The answer is (d). In State of Bombay v. K.P. Krishnan (1960), the Supreme Court held that Section 12(5) gives no reference power independent of Section 10(1). A reference after a failed conciliation is made under Section 10(1), and the government keeps its discretion.
topic_notes: Reference of industrial disputes under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is governed mainly by Section 10, with Sections 12 and 13 covering conciliation. Section 10(1) lets the appropriate government refer a dispute to a Board, Court, Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal. The Supreme Court's key rulings: State of Bombay v. K.P. Krishnan (1960) held the power to be administrative and the government's decision to be reviewable only on limited grounds. Other cases: Bombay Union of Journalists v. State of Bombay (1964) held that the government cannot adjudicate the merits of a dispute when deciding on a reference. Shambhu Nath Goyal v. Bank of Baroda (1978) held that the government's order of reference is not a judicial act. Sharad Kumar v. Government of NCT of Delhi (2002) held that the government should not reject a reference on a matter that only the adjudicator can decide. Ram Avtar Sharma v. State of Haryana (1985) held that the government may examine only a prima facie case and cannot decide the merits. Related provisions: Section 2A (individual dispute deemed an industrial dispute), Section 10(2) (reference on application of parties), Section 10(5) (National Tribunal), Section 10A (voluntary arbitration), Section 12(3) (failure report), Section 12(5) (government's decision after the report), Section 22 (notice for strike in public utility services), and Section 23 (general prohibition of strikes). The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 replaces the Act and, once in force, will restructure the reference system.

question: In Life Insurance Corporation of India v.| 13. D.J. Bahadur, AIR 1980 SC 2181, the Supreme Court held that once a notice of termination of settlement has been given under Section 19 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and period of two months has expired, the parties to the settlement shall :
options: not be bound by terms of the said settlement after the expiry of two months after notice, even if it results in a vacuum
continue to be bound by the said settlement until it is replaced by a new settlement or an award
be free to raise an industrial dispute on the subject matter of the settlement
_ be free to resort to voluntary arbitration on the subject matter of the settlement
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 19(2) provides that a settlement remains binding for the agreed period, and if none is agreed, for six months and thereafter until two months have elapsed from the date a party gives written notice of its intention to terminate. Section 19(6) deals with an award: it remains in operation for a period of one year, and continues to be binding after that until a notice of termination is given and 2 months expire (similarly s.19(6) for awards). In D.J. Bahadur, a case about LIC's Class III and IV employees' bonus settlement and the Life Insurance Corporation (Modification of Settlement) Act, 1976, the Court held that the settlement continues to bind the parties after the notice period until a fresh settlement or award replaces it. The reasoning is that industrial peace requires avoiding a vacuum in service conditions, which would invite chaos. The Court also noted that s.19(6) is not a rule of automatic extinction; it only lets parties raise a dispute and seek a new regime. Elimination: (a) states the vacuum view that the Court rejected. (c) and (d) are partly true as to raising a dispute or arbitrating, but they do not state the holding, which is that the old terms continue to bind.
explanations: Wrong: the Court rejected the idea that the settlement ends with a vacuum after two months; it remains binding.
Correct: the settlement continues to bind the parties until a new settlement or award replaces it, as laid down in D.J. Bahadur.

Wrong as the holding: although a dispute may be raised after notice, the question asks about the binding effect, which continues. Freedom to raise a dispute does not free the parties from the existing terms.
Wrong as the holding: voluntary arbitration may be chosen to settle the dispute, but the old terms remain binding in the meantime.
keyfact: D.J. Bahadur (1980): after notice under s.19 and expiry of two months, the settlement continues to bind the parties until a new settlement or award replaces it.
option_notes: This is the vacuum theory: a settlement ends automatically after the notice period. The Supreme Court did not accept it, because it would leave service conditions undefined and disturb industrial peace. It appears as a distractor in questions on s.19.

This is the correct position in D.J. Bahadur: a settlement or award that has been given notice of termination under s.19 continues to be binding after the two months, until it is replaced by a new settlement or award. This protects employees and employers from a gap in the terms of employment and preserves the status quo.

Under the ID Act a party can raise an industrial dispute for a fresh settlement after giving notice of termination, and the appropriate government may refer it for adjudication under s.10. This is a procedural right and does not end the binding effect of the earlier settlement.

Section 10A of the ID Act provides for voluntary reference of disputes to arbitration by written agreement before a dispute is referred to a Labour Court or Tribunal. It is available for any industrial dispute, but it does not release the parties from the existing settlement.
related: Section 18(1) ID Act: a bipartite settlement outside conciliation binds only the parties to the agreement.
Section 18(3): a conciliation settlement or award binds all parties, successors and workmen.
Section 19(2): a settlement with no stated period binds for six months and then until two months after notice of termination.
Section 19(3): an award operates for one year, extendable by the government up to three years.
Section 10A: voluntary reference of industrial disputes to arbitration.
Section 2(p): defines a settlement, which must be in writing and signed by the parties.
D.J. Bahadur (1980) also held that LIC is bound by the ID Act and that the Parliament's 1976 modification Act was valid.
summary: The answer is (b). In LIC of India v. D.J. Bahadur (AIR 1980 SC 2181), the Supreme Court held that a settlement terminated by notice under Section 19(6) ID Act does not simply lapse when the notice period of two months ends. The parties remain bound by its terms until a new settlement or award replaces it.
topic_notes: Section 18 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 deals with the persons on whom settlements and awards are binding. A settlement arrived at by agreement between the employer and workmen otherwise than in the course of conciliation proceedings binds only the parties to the agreement. A settlement arrived at in the course of conciliation proceedings (a settlement under s.12(3)) binds all parties to the dispute, including successor employers and all persons employed in the establishment at the time of the dispute and thereafter. Section 2(p) defines settlement, and it must be in writing and signed by the parties; a copy must be sent to the appropriate government and the conciliation officer. Section 19 deals with the period of operation of settlements and awards. Under s.19(2), a settlement is binding for the period agreed in the settlement, or for six months where no period is agreed, and it continues to be binding after that until two months have expired from notice of termination. Under s.19(3), an award remains in operation for one year, and the government may reduce or extend the period up to a total of three years. Under s.19(6), an award continues to be binding after the period of operation until it is superseded by another award. Section 19(7) provides that no notice given under s.19(6) has effect unless it is given by a party representing the majority of persons bound by the award. Related cases include Associated Cement Co. and Bharat Sugar Mills on binding effect of settlements.

question: A strike in a non-public utility service is not illegal under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 if it is declared or commenced during the pendency of :
options: arbitration proceedings before an arbitrator where notification under Sub-Section 3A of Section 10A has been issued by the appropriate Government
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Sections 22 and 23 form the statutory scheme on strikes. Section 22 covers public utility services. It requires a 6-week notice, forbids a strike within 14 days of giving notice, and forbids a strike before the date stated in the notice. It also bars strikes while conciliation proceedings before a conciliation officer are pending, and for 7 days after they conclude. Section 23 is the general prohibition and applies to any industrial establishment. Under it a strike is prohibited: (a) during pendency of conciliation proceedings before a Board and 7 days after conclusion; (b) during pendency of proceedings before a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal and 2 months after conclusion; (bb) during pendency of arbitration proceedings before an arbitrator where a Section 10A(3A) notification has been issued, and 2 months after; and (c) during any period when a settlement or award is in operation, in respect of matters covered by it. The question asks about a non-public utility service, so only Section 23 applies. Options (b), (c) and (d) are each expressly listed in Section 23 and are therefore illegal. Pendency before a conciliation officer is covered only by Section 22 (public utility), so option (a) is the one that is not illegal. Section 24 then defines illegal strikes as those in contravention of Sections 22 or 23.
explanations: Correct. Section 23 does not list conciliation before a conciliation officer. That bar is in Section 22(1)(c) and applies only to public utility services. In a non-public utility, a strike during such conciliation is not illegal.
Incorrect. Section 23(b) prohibits strikes during pendency of proceedings before a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal, and for 2 months after they conclude. A strike then is illegal.
Incorrect. Section 23(bb) prohibits strikes during arbitration proceedings under Section 10A where the Section 10A(3A) notification has been issued, and for 2 months after. A strike then is illegal.
Incorrect. Section 23(a) prohibits strikes during pendency of conciliation proceedings before a Board, and for 7 days after the conclusion. A strike then is illegal.
keyfact: Conciliation before a conciliation officer bars strikes only in public utility services (S.22); S.23 covers Board, Labour Court/Tribunal and S.10A(3A) arbitration, not the officer.
option_notes: Conciliation before a conciliation officer is under Section 12. The officer must try to settle the dispute and submit a failure or settlement report within 14 days. In public utility services, Section 22 bars strikes during its pendency and 7 days after. Section 23 does not cover it, so non-public utility strikes are not barred on this ground. Section 20 says the proceedings begin when notice of strike or lockout is received, and end when the report is received by the government.

A Labour Court is constituted under Section 7 and handles matters in the Second Schedule, such as the propriety of discharge or dismissal, and the interpretation of standing orders. It is presided over by a person who is or has been a High Court judge, a District or Additional District Judge, or a judicial officer of 7 years' standing. Section 23(b) bars strikes during its proceedings and for 2 months after the proceedings conclude.

Section 10A allows voluntary reference of a dispute to arbitration by written agreement before the dispute is referred to a Labour Court or Tribunal. It was inserted in 1956. The 1984 amendment added Section 10A(3A), under which the government publishes the arbitration agreement in the Official Gazette within 1 month. This notification triggers the Section 23(bb) bar on strikes, which also lasts 2 months after the arbitration ends.

A Board of Conciliation is constituted under Section 5 for a particular dispute. It has a chairman who is independent, and 2 or 4 other members who represent the parties equally. It is used more rarely than a conciliation officer. Its report is due within 2 months. Section 23(a) bars strikes and lockouts during its proceedings and for 7 days after they conclude. Section 22 also bars strikes in public utility services in the same circumstances.
related: Section 22 applies to public utility services; Section 23 applies to all industrial establishments.
Section 22 requires a strike notice of 6 weeks, with a strike barred within 14 days of giving notice.
Section 2(q) defines a strike; Section 2(l) defines a lockout.
Section 24 declares strikes in contravention of Sections 22 or 23 illegal.
Section 10A(3A) was inserted by the 1984 amendment.
Section 25 bars financial aid to an illegal strike; Section 26 sets out the penalties.
Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, strike notice of 14 days applies to all establishments.
Section 10(3) lets the government prohibit a continuing strike once a dispute is referred.
summary: The answer is (a). Section 23 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 bars strikes in non-public utility establishments only during specified proceedings: before a Board, Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal, or arbitrator (with a Section 10A(3A) notification), and while a settlement or award is in operation. Conciliation proceedings before a conciliation officer are not on that list, so a strike then is not illegal under Section 23. It would be illegal only in a public utility service, under Section 22.
topic_notes:
Chapter V of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 deals with strikes and lockouts. Section 2(q) defines a strike as a cessation of work by a body of persons employed in an industry acting in combination. It also covers a concerted refusal, or a refusal under a common understanding, to continue work. Section 2(l) defines a lockout as the temporary closing of a place of employment, the suspension of work, or a refusal by the employer to continue employing workmen.

Section 22 applies only to public utility services. It requires a notice 6 weeks before the strike, and the strike cannot take place within 14 days of giving the notice. It also bars a strike before the date given in the notice, during the pendency of conciliation proceedings and 7 days after, and during the 7 days after conclusion of proceedings before a Board. A strike is also barred for 6 months after conclusion of proceedings before a Tribunal, Labour Court or National Tribunal, and during arbitration under Section 10A. This applies to a lockout in the same way. Section 22(1) additionally bars a strike during any period in which a settlement or award is in operation.

Section 23 is the general prohibition and applies to all industrial establishments. It prohibits strikes and lockouts during: Board proceedings and 7 days after; Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal proceedings and 2 months after; arbitration under Section 10A(3A) and 2 months after; and any period in which a settlement or award is in operation on the matters covered.

Section 24 declares a strike or lockout illegal if it is commenced or continued in contravention of Sections 22 or 23. A continuing strike is also illegal if it was begun in contravention of the Act. Strikes in connection with an illegal strike are also illegal. Section 25 prohibits financial aid to illegal strikes. Section 26 provides penalties, and Section 27 penalises instigation. Section 10(3) lets the government prohibit a continuing strike or lockout once a dispute is referred to adjudication.

The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 replaces the Act. It extends the notice requirement of 14 days to all industrial establishments, and treats a mass casual leave of 50 percent or more as a strike.

question: Under Section 17B of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, during the pendency of proceedings relating to dismissal, discharge or retrenchment before a Constitutional Court, the employer is not liable to pay full wages to a workman if award directing reinstatement of workman is passed by :
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 17B (inserted in 1984) gives interim relief to a workman whose reinstatement award is challenged in higher courts. Where a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal directs reinstatement and the employer files proceedings in the High Court (Article 226/227) or the Supreme Court (Article 136), the employer must pay full wages last drawn, including any maintenance allowance, for the whole period those proceedings are pending. The wages are payable even if the High Court or Supreme Court has stayed the award. Two conditions apply: the workman must not have been employed in any establishment during that time, and he must file an affidavit to that effect. Payment continues until the proceedings end. If the employer wins, the wages already paid are generally not recoverable. The section names only the three industrial adjudicating authorities under Section 7, 7A and 7B. Civil Courts do not decide industrial disputes under the Act, and their jurisdiction is largely ousted for rights created by the Act. Hence (a), (c) and (d) attract Section 17B, while (b) does not. The question's wording is a negative one, so the correct option is the one outside the section.
explanations: Incorrect option: a Labour Court (Section 7) is named in Section 17B, so the employer must pay full wages when it directs reinstatement and the award is challenged.
Correct option: a Civil Court is not an authority under the Act and is not named in Section 17B. Its order is outside the section, so the employer has no Section 17B liability.
Incorrect option: an Industrial Tribunal (Section 7A) is named in Section 17B, so full wages are payable during the pendency of higher-court proceedings.
Incorrect option: a National Tribunal (Section 7B) is named in Section 17B, so full wages are payable during the pendency of higher-court proceedings.
keyfact: Section 17B covers only Labour Court, Industrial Tribunal and National Tribunal reinstatement awards, not Civil Court orders.
option_notes: Labour Court is constituted by the appropriate Government under Section 7. It is headed by a single presiding officer who is, or has been, a High Court or District Judge, or who has held judicial office for at least 7 years. It adjudicates matters in the Second Schedule, such as the propriety of dismissal, discharge, retrenchment, and the legality of strikes or lockouts. Its awards are challenged by writ in the High Court.

Civil Court is the ordinary court of civil jurisdiction under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. It is not an industrial adjudicating authority. Where the Industrial Disputes Act creates a right or remedy, such as Section 25F retrenchment compensation or Section 33C recovery, the Civil Court's jurisdiction is barred. Its orders are not covered by Section 17B or Section 11A.

Industrial Tribunal is constituted by the appropriate Government under Section 7A. It is headed by a person qualified as a High Court Judge or a District Judge. It adjudicates Second and Third Schedule matters, including wages, bonus, hours of work, and retrenchment of workmen. Its awards are published under Section 17 and become enforceable under Section 17A. Section 17B applies to reinstatement awards it passes.

National Tribunal is constituted by the Central Government under Section 7B for disputes of national importance, or those affecting industrial establishments in more than one State. It is headed by a sitting or former High Court Judge. Assessors may be appointed to assist it. Its awards are published under Section 17. Section 17B covers reinstatement awards it passes when they are challenged in the High Court or Supreme Court.
related: Section 17B was inserted in 1984 and gives full last-drawn wages during higher-court proceedings.
Section 17B requires the workman's affidavit that he has not been employed elsewhere.
Section 11A empowers adjudicators to modify punishment in discharge and dismissal cases.
Section 25F requires one month's notice and 15 days' average pay per year of service for retrenchment.
Section 7 covers Labour Courts, 7A covers Industrial Tribunals, and 7B covers National Tribunals.
Section 33C deals with recovery of money due from an employer.
Section 10 deals with referral of disputes to adjudicators.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
summary: The answer is (b) Civil Court. Section 17B applies only to an award of reinstatement by a Labour Court, Industrial Tribunal or National Tribunal that the employer challenges in the High Court or Supreme Court. A Civil Court is not an adjudicating authority under the Industrial Disputes Act, so the section does not cover its orders.
topic_notes: Section 17B was inserted by the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1984 (effective 1984) and is titled 'Payment of full wages to workman pending proceedings in higher courts'. Its purpose is to prevent hardship to a reinstated workman while the employer litigates for years. Key elements: (1) the award must direct reinstatement; (2) it must be passed by a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal; (3) the employer must have challenged it in the High Court or Supreme Court; (4) wages are the full wages last drawn, plus any maintenance allowance that has become payable; (5) the workman must not have been employed in any establishment during that period, shown by an affidavit; (6) payment runs for the whole pendency, even if the award is stayed. The Supreme Court has held that the wages need not be refunded even if the employer later succeeds. Related provisions: Section 11A gives the adjudicator power to set aside the punishment and order reinstatement or lesser punishment. Section 25F sets conditions for valid retrenchment: one month's notice or pay in lieu, and compensation of 15 days' average pay per completed year. Section 33 bars changes in service conditions during pendency of proceedings. Section 33A gives a remedy for contravention of Section 33. Section 33C covers recovery of money due. Section 17A covers the commencement of awards, and Section 17 covers their publication. Section 10 deals with referral of disputes by the appropriate Government. Section 2(s) defines 'workman' and Section 2(k) defines 'industrial dispute'. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 has replaced the 1947 Act, but the corresponding questions still draw on the 1947 provisions.

question: Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, who among the following is a ‘protected workman’ ?
options: Member of the executive or office bearer of a trade union
A workman recognized as protected workman by the employer
A person employed in an industry recognized as protected workman by the employer
Member of the executive or office bearer of a registered trade union connected with the establishment, who is recognized as protected workman by the employer
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 33 of the ID Act bars the employer from altering service conditions or punishing workmen during the pendency of conciliation or adjudication proceedings, except in limited ways. Section 33(1) covers matters connected with the dispute: the employer needs the express written permission of the authority. Section 33(2) covers matters not connected with the dispute: the employer may act in accordance with standing orders, but for discharge or dismissal he must give one month's wages and apply for approval. Section 33(3) gives additional protection to 'protected workmen': even for misconduct not connected with the dispute, no discharge, dismissal or punitive action is allowed without express permission of the authority concerned. A protected workman is an office-bearer of a REGISTERED trade union connected with the establishment, recognised under rules framed by the appropriate government. The number is limited: 1 percent of the workforce, subject to a minimum of 5 and a maximum of 100 (Industrial Disputes (Central) Rules, 1957, Rule 61). The union must send a list every year, and the employer recognises the persons within 15 days. Elimination: (a) omits registration and recognition, (b) omits the union office-bearer condition, (c) is about industry, not union office.
explanations: Incorrect: being an executive member or office-bearer is necessary but not enough. The union must be registered and connected with the establishment, and the workman must be recognised as protected.
Incorrect: employer recognition alone does not make a workman protected. He must be an office-bearer of a registered union, and the recognition follows the statutory rules.
Incorrect: employment in an industry says nothing about the union office requirement, and the employer cannot arbitrarily designate anyone as protected.
Correct: it matches the Explanation to Section 33(3), which requires an office-bearer of a registered trade union connected with the establishment, recognised as protected under the rules.
keyfact: Protected workman = office-bearer of a registered trade union connected with the establishment, recognised under the rules (ID Act Section 33(3)); capped at 1 percent of the workforce, minimum 5, maximum 100.
option_notes: Executive member or office-bearer of a trade union: a union is an association of workers or employers formed under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 for regulating relations. Office-bearers lead the union. Only office-bearers of a registered union connected with the establishment qualify as protected workmen, and only if recognised.

Workman recognised by the employer: 'workman' is defined in Section 2(s) of the ID Act, covering manual, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, but excluding the armed forces, police, and managerial or higher-paid supervisory staff. Recognition alone does not create protected status.

Person employed in an industry: 'industry' is defined in Section 2(j) and interpreted through the Bangalore Water Supply case (1978) triple test. Being employed in an industry makes a person a potential workman, not a protected workman.

Registered trade union office-bearer recognised as protected: this is the statutory definition in Section 33(3). The number is capped at 1 percent of the workforce, with a minimum of 5 and a maximum of 100. The union submits the list annually, and the employer must recognise the persons within 15 days.
related: Section 33(3) of the ID Act deals with protected workmen.
The number of protected workmen is 1 percent of the workforce, with a minimum of 5 and a maximum of 100.
Rule 61 of the Industrial Disputes (Central) Rules, 1957 governs recognition of protected workmen.
Section 33A gives a workman the right to complain to the authority about a Section 33 contravention.
Section 2(s) defines workman, and Section 2(j) defines industry.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 replaces the ID Act, the Trade Unions Act, and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act.
The trade union must be registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 for its office-bearers to be protected.
summary: The answer is (d). Under Section 33(3) read with the Explanation of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, a 'protected workman' is a workman who is a member of the executive or other office-bearer of a registered trade union connected with the establishment and who is recognised as such in accordance with the rules made in this behalf. Such a workman cannot be discharged, dismissed or have service conditions altered to his prejudice during a pending proceeding without the express written permission of the authority before which the proceeding is pending.
topic_notes: Section 33 of the ID Act, 1947 provides the 'conditions of service to remain unchanged during pendency of proceedings'. It applies during pending conciliation (before a conciliation officer or Board) and during adjudication or arbitration (before a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal). Section 33(1): for matters connected with the dispute, the employer cannot alter conditions to the prejudice of workmen or discharge or punish them for misconduct without the express written permission of the authority. Section 33(2): for matters not connected with the dispute, the employer may act per standing orders, but a discharge or dismissal requires paying one month's wages and applying for approval, and the action is not valid unless approved. Section 33(3): protected workmen get the highest protection, with prior permission needed for any action. Section 33A gives the workman a remedy by complaint to the authority if the employer contravenes Section 33. Section 33C covers recovery of money due. Protected workmen rules: Rule 61 of the Industrial Disputes (Central) Rules, 1957. The number is 1 percent of the workforce, with a minimum of 5 and a maximum of 100. Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 the equivalent provision is Section 126 on conditions of service during pendency of proceedings, with protected workmen provisions carried over. Other angles: strike and lockout (Sections 22-24), lay-off (Section 2(kkk)), retrenchment (Section 2(oo)), Chapter VA, and Sections 25F-25H.

question: Who among the following category of|17. employees are not entitled to form trade unions and get the same registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 ?
options: Supervisory staff drawing salary of = 35, 000 per month in the Ministry of Railways 18
Clerical staff employed in the district courts in Delhi
Peons employed in the Ministry of Civil Aviation
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 provides for registration of combinations of workmen or employers formed mainly to regulate relations between workmen and employers. Registration needs at least seven members (Section 4), and the Act has no wage ceiling. Under Article 19(1)(c) the right to form associations is a fundamental right, but it is not absolute: reasonable restrictions apply, and there is no fundamental right to strike. Industry is read broadly after Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa (1978), which excludes only sovereign functions such as legislation, the judiciary, defence and the police. Judicial administration is a core sovereign function, and court staff are governed by service rules of the High Court or state government, so they have no industrial employer-workman relationship. Railways is a classic industry, and railway staff form unions (AIRF, NFIR) and are recognised under Railway rules. Government teachers and Central Secretariat employees are generally treated as service associations under the Central Civil Services (Recognition of Service Associations) Rules, 1993, and the Trade Unions Act may be used. Armed forces, police and the like are restricted by Article 33. On elimination, (b) is railway staff, a classic industrial setting. (a) and (d) are ordinary government employees who form associations, and (c) is the sovereign judicial function. This is a contestable question, so verify against the Act's text.
explanations: (a) Not the best answer. Government school teachers commonly form teachers' associations or unions, and registration under the Trade Unions Act is not barred.
(b) Incorrect. Railways is an industry and its supervisory staff have recognised unions and federations. The Act has no wage ceiling for membership.

(c) Correct. District court staff serve the sovereign judicial function, so there is no industry or employer-workman relationship of the kind the Act addresses. They are governed by judicial service rules.
(d) Incorrect. Peons in a central ministry can form service associations under the CCS Recognition of Service Associations Rules, 1993, and are not barred from unions.
keyfact: Sovereign functions, such as the judiciary, are not 'industry', so court staff fall outside ordinary trade-union registration under the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
option_notes: Government school teachers are public employees, usually governed by state education service rules. Teachers are generally not 'workmen' under the Industrial Disputes Act (Miss A. Sundarambal v. Government of Goa, 1988), but they form teachers' associations and unions, and the right to associate under Article 19(1)(c) applies. Strike rights are not recognised.

Supervisory staff in Railways work in a departmental undertaking that is treated as an industry. Railway employees are organised under AIRF and NFIR, with recognition by the Railway Board. Supervisors may fall outside 'workman' under the Industrial Disputes Act if they earn above the threshold or are mainly supervisory, but they can still join associations.

District court clerical staff are in the subordinate judiciary establishment and are governed by state or High Court service rules. The judiciary is a sovereign function and not an 'industry' under Bangalore Water Supply (1978). Their service conditions are regulated under the Constitution (Articles 229 and 235) and by service rules, not by an industrial employer-workman relationship.

Peons in a central ministry are Group D (now MTS) employees of the Central Government. Their associations are governed by the CCS (Recognition of Service Associations) Rules, 1993, and the Joint Consultative Machinery works through the National Council (JCM). They are not engaged in an industry, but they can form associations.
related: Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927.
Minimum 7 members are needed to register a trade union (Section 4).
Bangalore Water Supply case (1978) gave the triple test for 'industry' and excluded sovereign functions.
Article 19(1)(c) guarantees the right to form associations or unions.
Strike is not a fundamental right (T.K. Rangarajan, 2003).
Article 33 allows Parliament to restrict association rights for armed forces and police.
Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
CCS (Recognition of Service Associations) Rules, 1993 govern central employee associations.
summary: The best answer is (c), clerical staff in the district courts in Delhi. This rests on my own reasoning, as no official key is available. Court staff discharge the sovereign judicial function of the State and are not employed in an 'industry', so they are not ordinary workmen for forming and registering unions under the Trade Unions Act, 1926. The other groups work in settings that are industrial, quasi-industrial, or covered by ordinary association rights.
topic_notes: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927 and was the first law recognising trade unions in India. It provides for voluntary registration, legal status as a body corporate, and immunity from criminal conspiracy (Section 17) and civil suits (Section 18). Seven or more members can apply for registration (Section 4), and at least half of the office-bearers must be actually engaged in the industry (the 2001 amendment allows up to one-third or five outsiders, whichever is less). Registered unions must submit annual returns and may keep a political fund (Section 16). The Registrar is appointed by the appropriate government. The 2001 amendment also required that a union with 100 or 10% of workmen, whichever is less, and not less than seven, can be registered. Union rights under the Act are now consolidated in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which has received presidential assent and awaits notification of effective dates. The Code introduces a negotiating union (51% rule) and recognition of a sole negotiating union. Article 19(1)(c) gives the right to form associations or unions, with reasonable restrictions on grounds of public order or sovereignty. Article 33 lets Parliament restrict these rights for armed forces and police. Strike is not a fundamental right (T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu, 2003). Key case: Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa (1978) gave the triple test on industry. The CCS (Recognition of Service Associations) Rules, 1993 govern central government employee associations. Related: Section 2(h) defines trade union, Section 8 covers registration certificate, Section 10 cancellation of registration.

question: Not less than how many of the total number of the office-bearers of every registered trade union in an unorganized sector shall be persons actually engaged or employed in an industry with which the trade union is 19. connected ?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 22 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 deals with the proportion of office-bearers to be connected with the industry. The Trade Unions (Amendment) Act, 2001 rewrote it to allow outsiders (non-workers such as lawyers, leaders and social workers) as office-bearers, but only within limits. For a union in an organised sector, which means establishments covered by the Act, not more than one-third of the office-bearers, or five, whichever is less, may be outsiders. The rest must be employed in the industry. For a union in an unorganised sector, not less than one-half of the total office-bearers must be persons actually engaged or employed in the industry, so up to half may be outsiders. Section 21A disqualifies persons from office-bearer positions, for example those under 18 or convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude. Section 4 requires at least 7 members to register a union, and the 2001 amendment added that at least 10% of workmen or 100 workmen, whichever is less, must be members, with a minimum of 7. Elimination: one-third is the organised-sector outsider ceiling, a different rule. One-fifth and one-fourth appear nowhere in the Section 22 rule.
explanations: Incorrect: one-fifth is not a figure used in Section 22 for office-bearer composition.
Incorrect: one-fourth is not the prescribed proportion under Section 22.
Incorrect: one-third is the maximum share of outsiders (or five, whichever is less) allowed in organised-sector unions. It is not the minimum share of insiders in unorganised-sector unions.
Correct: Section 22(2) requires not less than one-half of the office-bearers of an unorganised-sector union to be actually engaged or employed in the connected industry.
keyfact: Unorganised sector union: at least one-half of the office-bearers must be from the industry (Sec 22, Trade Unions Act 1926).
option_notes: One-fifth is not a statutory proportion for trade union office-bearers. In labour law, fractions of this kind appear elsewhere, for example in quorum and representation rules. Under the Trade Unions Act, the key ratios are one-half for unorganised-sector insiders and one-third for organised-sector outsiders. Do not confuse these with one-fifth.

One-fourth is not the prescribed ratio in Section 22. It is a distractor. Remember that Section 22 uses one-half for unorganised-sector unions, and for organised-sector unions it caps outsiders at one-third of office-bearers or five, whichever is less. The 2001 amendment introduced these figures.

One-third is the ceiling on outsiders, meaning office-bearers not connected with the industry, in a registered union of the organised sector. The limit is one-third of the total office-bearers or five persons, whichever is less. The 2001 amendment introduced this. Students often mistake it for the unorganised-sector rule.

One-half is the correct figure. Not less than half of the office-bearers of a registered union in an unorganised sector must be actually engaged or employed in the connected industry. Under the 2001 amendment of the Trade Unions Act, 1926, up to half may therefore be outsiders such as advocates or social workers. The Act is administered by the Registrar of Trade Unions at the state level.
related: Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927.
Minimum 7 members are needed to apply for registration of a trade union.
Organised sector: outsiders are limited to one-third of office-bearers or five, whichever is less.
Unorganised sector: at least one-half of office-bearers must be from the industry.
Section 13 makes a registered trade union a body corporate.
Section 16 permits a separate political fund.
Section 21A disqualifies certain persons from being office-bearers.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
summary: The answer is (d) one-half. Under Section 22 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926, as amended in 2001, at least one-half of the office-bearers of a registered trade union in an unorganised sector must be persons actually engaged or employed in the industry the union is connected with.
topic_notes: The Trade Unions Act, 1926 came into force on 1 June 1927. It provides for registration of trade unions and gives registered unions legal status as a body corporate (Section 13), with perpetual succession and a common seal. Section 15 lists the objects on which funds may be spent. Section 16 permits a separate political fund, which members may opt out of contributing to. Section 17 gives immunity from criminal conspiracy for acts furthering trade union objects. Section 18 gives immunity from civil suits for acts done in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute. Registration is done by the Registrar appointed by the appropriate government, and an application needs at least 7 members. Under the 2001 amendment, the application must also have the support of at least 10% of workmen or 100 workmen, whichever is less, subject to a minimum of 7. Section 22 covers the proportion of office-bearers, Section 21A the disqualification of office-bearers, and Section 28 the annual returns. Section 9A restricts the membership of ordinary members to those engaged in the industry. Section 6 lists the provisions that must be in the rules of the union. The 2001 amendment also added Section 22 limits on outsiders, and Section 9A. Related labour codes: the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 will subsume the Trade Unions Act, the Industrial Disputes Act and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act. In it, the Code retains the outsider-limits approach and adds provisions on recognition of a sole negotiating union. Trade union recognition is not mandatory in the old Act. Central trade union organisations include INTUC, AITUC, HMS, CITU and BMS.

question: &’ and ‘Y’ are two registered trade unions of workers in MB Cotton Mills. ‘X’ and ‘Y have membership of 150 and 120, respectively. Both the trade unions want to amalgamate as one trade union — ‘XY’. In ‘X’, 110 members cast their votes and in ‘Y’, 70 members cast their votes to decide for or against the amalgamation. What is the minimum of the votes recorded, that is required to decide in favour of amalgamation ?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 24 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 governs amalgamation of registered trade unions. Two or more registered unions may amalgamate, with or without dissolution or division of funds, provided two conditions are met. First, the votes of at least one-half of the members of each union entitled to vote must be recorded. Second, at least 60% of the votes recorded in respect of each union must be in favour of the proposal. Here, X has 150 members, so half is 75, and 110 voted, which satisfies the condition. Y has 120 members, so half is 60, and 70 voted, which also satisfies it. Votes recorded are 110 + 70 = 180. Sixty percent of 180 is 108, so 108 is the minimum number of favourable votes needed. Per union, X needs 66 (60% of 110) and Y needs 42 (60% of 70), and 66 + 42 = 108. Elimination: 90 is only 50% of the votes recorded. 100 is an arbitrary figure. 135 is not a 60% figure at all, being 90% of X's membership, or half of the combined membership of 270. Notice must also be given to the Registrar, and the amalgamation takes effect on registration under Section 25.
explanations: Incorrect: 90 is exactly 50% of the 180 votes recorded, but the Act requires at least 60%.
Incorrect: 100 corresponds to no statutory threshold; it is about 55.6% of the votes recorded, below 60%.
Correct: 60% of the 180 votes recorded (110 + 70) is 108. It equals 66 for X plus 42 for Y, and the half-membership quorum is satisfied by both unions.
Incorrect: 135 is neither 60% of the votes recorded nor related to the quorum. It is 90% of X's membership, or half of the combined membership of 270.
keyfact: Under Section 24 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926, amalgamation needs at least half of each union's members voting and 60% of votes recorded in favour; here 60% of 180 = 108.
option_notes: 90: This is half of the 180 votes recorded. It resembles the quorum rule in Section 24, which asks for at least half of the members of each union to vote, but that rule concerns turnout, not the share in favour. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 (Section 24) fixes the favourable share at 60% of votes recorded. Under a simple-majority rule 90 would be only the bare threshold, and that is not the law for amalgamation.

100: This is not a statutory figure in the Trade Unions Act. It is about 55.6% of the votes recorded, which is below 60%. It is a distractor. The real thresholds under Section 24 are a quorum of half of the members of each union and 60% of recorded votes in favour. The Act does not use fixed absolute numbers for amalgamation.

108: This is 60% of 180 votes recorded, the correct minimum. Section 24 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 lays down two conditions: at least half of the members of each union must vote, and at least 60% of the votes recorded must be in favour. Per union, X needs 66 and Y needs 42. Notice of the amalgamation must then be sent to the Registrar, and the amalgamation takes effect from registration under Section 25.

135: This is not a threshold under the Act. It equals half of the combined membership (150 + 120 = 270) and also 90% of X's membership. Mine: mines are regulated by the Central Government under the Mines Act, 1952 and the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. Under the Standing Orders Act, a mine has the Central Government as appropriate government.

topic_notes: The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 requires employers of industrial establishments to define conditions of employment formally and make them known to workmen. It applies to industrial establishments employing 100 or more workmen (the Central Act's threshold; many States have lowered it, for example to 50). Standing orders cover classification of workmen, shift working, attendance, holidays, termination of employment, suspension or dismissal for misconduct, and grievance redress. The employer submits draft standing orders to the Certifying Officer, who is an officer such as the Labour Commissioner or Regional Labour Commissioner. Objections are heard from the workmen's trade union, and the certifying officer then certifies them. Appeals go to the Appellate Authority, whose decision is final. Standing orders come into force 30 days after authentication, and modification needs at least six months between modifications. The Act binds all employers in establishments covered, and it requires standing orders to be prominently displayed in English and the language understood by majority of workmen. Section 2(a) defines appropriate government: Central for establishments under Central Government control, railways, major ports, mines, oil-fields; State otherwise. Subsistence allowance during suspension: 50% of wages for the first 90 days and 75% thereafter, if delay is not attributable to the workman. The Act has been subsumed in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which raises the threshold to 300 workers and, as of the latest status, is awaiting full implementation through rules.

United Labour Union (1996) held that contract labour is automatically absorbed on abolition, but this was overruled by the Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. National Union Waterfront Workers (2001) Constitution Bench, which held there is no automatic absorption. The Act is being subsumed into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, where the contract labour threshold is raised to 50 workers. Related laws: Industrial Disputes Act 1947, Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979, Factories Act 1948.

topic_notes: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 regulates employment of contract labour in establishments and provides for its abolition in certain circumstances. It applies to establishments employing 20 or more workmen as contract labour (50 under the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020) and to contractors engaging 20 or more workmen. subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 10(1) of the CLRA Act, 1970 empowers the appropriate Government, after consulting the Central or State Advisory Board, to prohibit by notification the employment of contract labour in any process, operation or other work in any establishment. Section 10(2) lays down the factors it must take into account: (a) whether the process, operation or other work is incidental to, or necessary for, the industry, trade, business, manufacture or occupation carried on in the establishment; (b) whether it is of perennial nature, i.e. of sufficient duration having regard to the nature of the industry; (c) whether it is done ordinarily through regular workmen in that establishment or an establishment similar thereto; and (d) whether it is sufficient to employ a considerable number of whole-time workmen. All three statements reproduce these clauses almost verbatim, so none can be eliminated. Since statements 1, 2 and 3 are each correct, options (a), (b) and (c), which each drop one, are wrong. The key judicial landmark is Air India Statutory Corporation v. United Labour Union (1996), which held that abolition led to automatic absorption, but this was overruled by the Constitution Bench in SAIL v. National Union Waterfront Workers (2001), which held there is no automatic absorption. Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. National Union Waterfront Workers (2001) is therefore the key case.

statements: 1 — Correct: This is Section 10(2)(a) of the CLRA Act. The work must be incidental to or necessary for the establishment's main business. Section 10 gives the appropriate Government the power to prohibit contract labour after consulting the Advisory Board (Central or State). The Act applies to establishments employing 20 or more workmen as contract labour, and to contractors who employ 20 or more workmen. The Act was passed in 1970 and came into force in 1971. The Central Government is the appropriate Government for establishments such as railways, mines, major ports, and banks.

2 — Correct: This is Section 10(2)(c). It asks whether the work is ordinarily done through regular workmen in that establishment or in a similar establishment. If regular employees usually do such work, the use of contract labour is suspect. This factor tests whether contract labour is being used as a substitute for permanent employees. The Supreme Court in Vegoils (P) Ltd. v. Workmen (1971) laid down tests for the genuineness of a contract. The Act regulates contractors through licensing under Section 12 and registration of principal employers under Section 7.

3 — Correct: This is Section 10(2)(b). Perennial work is work of sufficient duration having regard to the nature of the industry, trade, business, manufacture or occupation. Permanent, continuing work should ordinarily be done by regular workmen. The Explanation to Section 10 says that if a question arises whether any process or operation is of a perennial nature, the appropriate Government's decision is final. The fourth factor in Section 10(2)(d) is whether the work is sufficient to employ a considerable number of whole-time workmen.

topic_notes: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 regulates the employment of contract labour in certain establishments and provides for its abolition in certain circumstances. It does not apply to establishments where the work is of an intermittent or casual nature. Principal employers must register their establishments under Section 7, and contractors must obtain a licence under Section 12. Welfare provisions include canteens (Section 16), rest rooms (Section 17), drinking water and latrines (Section 18), and first-aid facilities (Section 19). The principal employer is liable to pay wages if the contractor fails (Section 21). Advisory Boards are set up under Sections 3 and 4. Prohibition of contract labour is covered in Section 10. subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Chapter V of the CLRA Act, 1970 is titled 'Welfare and Health of Contract Labour'. Section 16 requires canteens where the contract employs 100 or more workers and is expected to last over 6 months. Section 17 requires rest-rooms or other suitable alternative accommodation where workers must halt at night. Section 18 requires sufficient supply of wholesome drinking water, latrines and urinals, and washing facilities. Section 19 requires first-aid facilities. Section 20 makes the principal employer liable to provide these amenities if the contractor fails, and recover the cost from the contractor. Section 21 makes the contractor responsible for paying wages, with the principal employer's representative present at disbursement. Creche facilities appear in other labour laws: Factories Act 1948 (Sec 48, 30+ women), Plantations Labour Act, Mines Act, Building and Other Construction Workers Act and the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act. They are not in the CLRA Act. Elimination: canteens, rest-rooms and first-aid are all expressly in the Act, leaving creche as the answer.

Wrong: canteens are provided under Section 16 for contracts with 100 or more workers lasting over 6 months.
Wrong: rest-rooms are provided under Section 17 for workers who halt at night.

option_notes: Creche: a facility for the children of working women, mandated by the Factories Act Sec 48 (30+ women), the Mines Act, the Plantations Labour Act, the BOCW Act and the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 (50+ employees). It is not in the CLRA Act 1970. The Code on Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions 2020 also deals with creches.

Canteens: Section 16 of the CLRA Act. The appropriate Government's rules can require canteens where the contract employs 100 or more workers and is likely to last over 6 months. The contractor must provide and maintain them, and if he fails, the principal employer is liable under Section 20.

Restrooms: Section 17 of the CLRA Act. The contractor must provide suitable rest-rooms or alternative accommodation to workers who must halt at night in connection with their work. The accommodation must be clean, well ventilated and have water and light. Under Section 20 the principal employer must provide it if the contractor fails.

First-aid facilities: Section 19 of the CLRA Act. First-aid boxes with prescribed contents must be readily accessible during working hours at every place where contract labour is employed. The contractor is primarily responsible, and the principal employer becomes liable on default under Section 20.

topic_notes: The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 regulates contract labour in establishments employing 20 or more workmen (the Code on Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions 2020 raises the threshold to 50) and provides for abolition in certain circumstances. It applies to contractors who employ 20 or more workmen. Central and State Advisory Boards (Sections 3 and 4) advise the governments. Establishments and contractors must register (Sections 7 and 12), and the contractor must hold a licence. Section 10 empowers the appropriate Government to prohibit contract labour in a process, operation or work after consulting the Advisory Board. The tests are whether the work is incidental or necessary, perennial, done through contractors in the industry, and sufficient to employ a considerable number of whole-time workmen. Welfare provisions are in Sections 16-19, and the principal employer's liability for amenities is in Section 20. Section 21 makes the contractor responsible for wage payment. If the contractor defaults, the principal employer must pay and may recover the amount from the contractor. Penalties are in Sections 23-25. The key cases are Standard Vacuum Refining (1960), Air India Statutory Corporation v United Labour Union (1996), Steel Authority of India v National Union Waterfront Workers (2001) and Balwant Rai Saluja (2014). SAIL overruled Air India's automatic absorption doctrine, so a Section 10 abolition does not automatically make contract workers employees of the principal employer. The Code on Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions 2020 subsumes this Act.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Section 14 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 deals with Inspectors. Section 14(1): the appropriate Government may appoint Inspectors for the purposes of the Act. Section 14(1)(a) says the appropriate Government may appoint Inspectors of Factories as Inspectors for all factories; Section 14(1)(b) says it may appoint Inspectors for the purposes of the Act in respect of all persons employed upon a railway (otherwise than in a factory), the Central Government may appoint any officer of the railway administration or any Inspector of railway; and 14(1)(c) (as per the Act) for persons employed in air transport services, mines, oil fields. Sub-clause (d) of the Section lets the appropriate Government appoint other persons by notification in the Official Gazette. Under Section 14(2), every Inspector is deemed a public servant within the meaning of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Hence option (a), which says Inspectors are NOT public servants, is the false statement. explanations: Wrong as a true statement: Section 14(2) says every Inspector appointed is deemed a public servant under IPC 1860, so saying they are not public servants is false. This is therefore the incorrect statement the question asks for.
Correct statement: under Section 14(1)(a), Inspectors of Factories appointed under the Factories Act, 1948 are Inspectors for the Act's purposes.
Matches the Act's provision that Government may appoint Inspectors for persons employed on railways (other than in factories); treated as a true statement.
Correct: Section 14(1)(d) allows appointment of other persons by Gazette notification.
keyfact: Under Section 14(2) of the Payment of Wages Act 1936, Inspectors are public servants under IPC, so statement (a) is false.
option_notes: Option (a) concerns the status of Inspectors under Section 14(2): they are deemed 'public servants' under Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (now Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 2(28)). This gives them legal protection and attracts obstruction offences. The option denies this, so it is false.

Option (b) concerns Factory Inspectors under the Factories Act, 1948 (Section 8), who are appointed by the State Government. Under the Payment of Wages Act they function as Inspectors for factories. It reflects Section 14(1)(a).

Option (c) concerns Government's power to appoint Inspectors for persons employed upon railways (other than in factories) and for other classes such as mines, air transport and oil fields. The Central Government is the appropriate Government for railways, mines and air transport.

Option (d) concerns the residual power under Section 14(1)(d): the appropriate Government may appoint, by Gazette notification, other persons as Inspectors for the Act's purposes in respect of all persons employed to whom the Act applies.

Hence (c) is the incorrect statement here.
topic_notes: Payment of Wages Act, 1936 regulates payment of wages to employees drawing up to a prescribed wage ceiling (Rs 24,000 per month after 2017 amendment) in factories, railways and other establishments. Key points: Section 3 – responsibility for payment of wages lies with employer; Section 4 – fixation of wage periods (not exceeding one month); Section 5 – time of payment (before 7th day for under 1000 employees, 10th day otherwise); Section 7 – permitted deductions; Section 8 – fines; Section 9 – deductions for absence; Section 14 – Inspectors; Section 15 – claims arising out of deductions or delay (authority appointed under Section 15, with a Labour Court or Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation); Section 17 – appeal; Section 20 – penalty. The Act has been subsumed in the Code on Wages, 2019, which subsumes four Acts: Payment of Wages Act 1936, Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Bonus Act 1965 and Equal Remuneration Act 1976. The Code was passed in August 2019. Under the Code, inspector cum facilitator replaces Inspector.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 regulates the payment of wages to employed persons earning up to the notified wage ceiling, which is now Rs 24,000 per month. It ensures timely payment and controls unauthorised deductions and fines. The Act is organised by subject. Sections 3-6 cover the responsibility for payment, wage-periods, the time of payment and the mode of payment. Sections 7-13 deal with deductions and fines. Section 14 provides for Inspectors. Sections 15-18 cover claims, appeals and the powers of the authorities. Section 20 provides penalties. Section 22 bars civil suits for matters the authority can decide. Section 25A deals with payment of undisbursed wages when an employed person dies. Section 26 is the power to make rules; it was amended in 2005 so that the 'appropriate Government' (Central or State) may make rules, for example on procedure, registers and forms. Elimination: 25A concerns payment of a deceased employee's unpaid wages, 22 bars suits, and 16 concerns a single application for claims from an unpaid group. None of these gives rule-making power, so only 26(1) fits.
explanations: Correct. Section 26(1) of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 gives the appropriate Government the power to make rules.
Incorrect. Section 25A deals with payment of undisbursed wages to a nominee or to the prescribed authority when an employed person dies. It is not a rule-making section.
Incorrect. Section 22 is the bar of suits. A civil court cannot entertain a suit for wages or deductions that fall within the authority's jurisdiction under section 15.
Incorrect. Section 16 concerns a single application for claims arising out of unpaid groups, which is procedural for claims and not rule-making.
keyfact: Rule-making power under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is in Section 26(1).
option_notes: Section 26 is titled 'Power to make rules'. Under sub-section (1) the appropriate Government (Central or State, as applicable) may make rules by notification in the Official Gazette to regulate the procedure of authorities and courts, prescribe registers, records, forms, and the duties of Inspectors. Sub-section (2) deals with rules made by the Central Government. Rules are also subject to prior publication. The Act applies to employed persons whose wages do not exceed the notified ceiling.

Section 25A deals with payment of undisbursed wages in case of the death of an employed person. Wages due to a deceased worker are paid to the person nominated by him under the Act. If there is no nominee, or the amount cannot be paid to the nominee, the employer deposits it with the prescribed authority. The employer is then discharged from his liability to pay those wages.

Section 22 is the bar of suits. A civil court cannot entertain a suit for recovery of wages or of deductions when the claim could have been brought under section 15, or when the matter has been decided under the Act. Section 22A gives protection to persons acting in good faith under the Act. These provisions keep wage disputes in the special authority's jurisdiction.

Section 16 deals with a single application in respect of claims from unpaid groups. Where several employed persons of the same unpaid group have claims, one application can be made for them together, which avoids multiplicity of proceedings. It supports the claims machinery under sections 15-17 and does not confer any rule-making power on the Government.
related: Payment of Wages Act, 1936 section 26 gives the rule-making power.
Section 25A deals with undisbursed wages on the death of an employed person.
Section 15 provides the claims machinery for wrongful deduction and delayed wages.
