summary: The answer is (a) Section 26(1). Section 26 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is the rule-making provision, and sub-section (1) empowers the appropriate Government to make rules to carry out the Act's purposes. The other sections deal with different subjects.
topic_notes: The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 came into force on 28 March 1937 and was originally intended for factories and railways, with extension to other establishments by State Governments. It regulates the payment of wages and prevents arbitrary deductions and fines. The wage ceiling was raised to Rs 24,000 per month in 2017. Key provisions: wages are paid in current coin or currency notes, or by cheque or crediting to a bank account with the worker's written authority. Wage-period cannot exceed one month. For establishments with fewer than 1,000 employed persons, wages are paid before the 7th day after the wage-period ends; for others, before the 10th day. Deductions are permitted only if authorised under the Act (fines, absence from duty, damage or loss, house accommodation, advances, taxes and so on). Section 7(2) places a cap on total deductions of 50 percent, or 75 percent where cooperative society payments are included. Claims for wrongful deductions or delay are heard under section 15 by an authority such as a Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation or a Labour Court judge. Appeals lie under section 17. Penalties are under section 20. The Act is now subsumed into the Code on Wages, 2019, which also subsumes the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. Under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, section 3 deals with fixing and revising minimum wages, and different rates can be fixed for different scheduled employments, classes of work, adults, adolescents, children and apprentices, and localities.

question: Under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, which one of the following is not a ground on which deductions can be made from wages payable ?
options: House accommodation supplied by the employer or any Government authority or any housing board set up under any law in force
Bonus paid under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965
Damage to, or loss of, goods which are expressly entrusted to the employed person for custody
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 7 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 says wages must be paid to the employed person without deduction, except those authorised by the Act. Section 7(2) exhaustively lists the permitted deductions: (a) fines; (b) deductions for absence from duty; (c) deductions for damage to or loss of goods expressly entrusted to the employed person for custody, or for loss of money for which he is required to account, where the damage or loss is directly attributable to his neglect or default; (d) deductions for house accommodation supplied by the employer; (e) deductions for amenities and services supplied by the employer; (f) recovery of advances and adjustment of overpayments; (g) income tax; (h) deductions required by court or other competent authority orders; (i) deductions for subscriptions to and repayment of advances from provident fund; (j) deductions for payments to co-operative societies and insurance schemes such as LIC; (k) deductions made with the employee's written authorisation for fidelity guarantee; (l) other permitted deductions. Options (a), (b) and (d) match listed grounds. Bonus is not a deduction ground, so (c) is the answer by elimination. The Act applies to employees drawing wages up to Rs 24,000 per month (the threshold was revised in 2017).
explanations: Incorrect as the answer: house accommodation supplied by the employer, the Government or a housing board is a permitted deduction under Section 7(2)(d), subject to Section 11 conditions.

Incorrect as the answer: deduction for absence from duty is permitted under Section 9. It is limited to the proportion of wages for the period of absence, though in some cases the deduction may exceed that proportion.

Correct answer: bonus under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 is a payment to the employee, not a ground for deduction under Section 7(2). Under the Bonus Act, set-off of customary bonus or interim bonus is a different matter.

Incorrect as the answer: Section 7(2)(c) and Section 10 permit deductions for damage to or loss of goods expressly entrusted for custody, if directly attributable to the employee's neglect or default.
keyfact: Bonus is not a ground for deduction under Section 7(2) of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936.
option_notes: House accommodation: Section 7(2)(d) allows deduction for house accommodation supplied by the employer, the Government or a housing board, and Section 7(2)(e) covers other amenities and services supplied. Section 11 limits these deductions to the value of the amenity supplied, and the employee must have accepted it. They are not allowed for amenities a law requires the employer to provide.

Absence from duty: Section 9 permits deductions for absence. The deduction can only be made for the period of absence, and the amount cannot exceed the wages for that period. Where ten or more workers are absent without due notice and without reasonable cause, the deduction may include up to 8 days' wages in lieu of notice. The employee must be absent from the place where he is required to work.

Bonus under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965: This Act requires establishments with 20 or more employees to pay a minimum bonus of 8.33% and a maximum of 20% of salary. Eligibility covers employees earning up to Rs 21,000 per month, with the calculation ceiling at Rs 7,000 or the minimum wage. It is a payment to the employee, not a deduction ground under the Payment of Wages Act.

Damage or loss of goods: Section 9 and Section 10 govern deductions for damage or loss. The employee must be given a chance to show cause, and the deduction cannot exceed the value of the damage or loss. The goods must have been expressly entrusted to the employee for custody. A deduction can be made only if the damage or loss is directly attributable to the employee's neglect or default.
related: Section 7 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 lists the authorised deductions.

Wage period cannot exceed one month (Section 4).

Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes four wage-related Acts.
Bonus Act, 1965 provides a minimum bonus of 8.33% and a maximum of 20%.
Section 15 allows claims for delayed payment or unlawful deductions.
summary: The answer is (c). Section 7(2) of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 lists the only permitted deductions, and bonus paid under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 is not one of them. Bonus is an amount payable to the employee, not a ground for deducting from wages.
topic_notes: The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 regulates payment of wages to certain classes of employed persons, mainly in factories, railways and industrial establishments. It ensures timely payment and prevents unauthorised deductions. Wages must be paid within 7 days of the wage period for establishments with fewer than 1,000 workers, and within 10 days for others. Where employment is terminated, wages are paid within 2 working days. Wages are paid in cash or by cheque or crediting to the bank account. Section 4 fixes the wage period, which cannot exceed one month. Section 7 lists the permitted deductions. Section 8 governs fines, and fines cannot exceed 3% of wages for the wage period. No fine can be imposed on a person under 15 years. Section 15 provides for claims arising out of deductions or delay in payment. Authorities under this Act include the Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation and the Presiding Officer of the Labour Court. Section 17 governs appeals. The Act was amended in 2005 and 2017. The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. Under the Code, the wage definition includes basic pay, dearness allowance and retaining allowance, and excludes bonus, among other items. Under the Code, if excluded payments exceed 50% of total remuneration, the excess is added to wages.

question: Which one of the following statements with regard to ‘Inspectors’ under Section 14 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, is not correct?
options: Inspectors appointed under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 are not ‘public servants’ as defined under the Indian Penal Code, 1860
An Inspector of Factories appointed 31. under the Factories Act, 1948 shall be an inspector for the purposes of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936

The appropriate Government may appoint Inspectors for the purposes of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 in respect of all persons employed upon a railway (otherwise than in a factory) to whom the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 applies
The appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint such other persons as it thinks fit to be Inspectors for the purposes of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 14 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 deals with Inspectors. Section 14(1) says that (a) an Inspector of Factories appointed under section 8 of the Factories Act, 1948 is an Inspector for the purposes of the Act in respect of all persons employed in factories; (b) the appropriate Government may appoint other persons as Inspectors by notification in the Official Gazette; and (c) the appropriate Government may appoint Inspectors for all persons employed upon a railway (otherwise than in a factory), or in an industrial or other establishment, to which the Act applies. The proviso under (b) allows the Government to appoint Inspectors for different areas. Section 14(2) says every Inspector appointed is deemed a public servant within the meaning of the Indian Penal Code (now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023). Section 14(3) lets the appropriate Government, by general or special order, specify the Inspector's powers and also the local limits of jurisdiction. Section 14(4) is a general power to prescribe duties. Under Section 14(1), Inspectors may enter and inspect premises, examine persons, seize or copy registers, and take evidence. Elimination logic: only (a) contradicts the statute, since the Inspector is deemed a public servant. Note that the 'Inspector' is replaced by 'Inspector-cum-Facilitator' in the Code on Wages, 2019.
explanations: Not correct. Section 14(2) deems every Inspector appointed under the Act to be a public servant within the meaning of the IPC, so this option states the opposite of the law.
Correct. Section 14(1)(a) makes an Inspector of Factories under the Factories Act, 1948 an Inspector under the Payment of Wages Act for factories, so this statement is accurate.
Correct. Section 14(1)(b) allows the appropriate Government to appoint Inspectors for persons employed on a railway (other than in a factory), so this statement is accurate.
Correct. The Government may appoint other persons as Inspectors by notification in the Official Gazette, so this statement is accurate.
keyfact: Under Section 14(2) of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, every Inspector is deemed a public servant under the IPC.
option_notes: This option claims Inspectors are not public servants, which is wrong. Section 14(2) deems them public servants under Section 21 of the IPC (now Section 2(28) of the BNS, 2023). The status brings protection and accountability: obstruction of an Inspector is punishable, and prosecution of them needs sanction in the usual way. It is the wrong statement and so the correct answer.

Inspectors of Factories are appointed under Section 8 of the Factories Act, 1948 by the State Government to enforce factory law. Under Section 14(1)(a) of the Payment of Wages Act they are automatically Inspectors for the purposes of that Act within factories. No separate appointment is needed. This reflects the overlap of labour law enforcement machinery.

The Payment of Wages Act applies to persons employed in factories, on railways, in industrial establishments, and in other classes notified by the Government. For railway employees not in factories, the appropriate Government (often the Central Government) can appoint Inspectors. Railways are a central subject, so the Central Government is the appropriate Government there. This is a correct statement.

Section 14(1)(b) permits the appropriate Government to appoint any other persons as it thinks fit, by Official Gazette notification, to be Inspectors for the Act. It may also limit them to particular local areas. This gives flexibility in enforcement. The statement is correct.
related: Section 14(2) of the Payment of Wages Act deems Inspectors public servants under the IPC.
Section 15 deals with claims arising out of deductions from wages or delay in payment.
Section 5 requires wages to be paid by the 7th day (under 1,000 workers) or the 10th day otherwise.
Section 7 lists authorised deductions; Section 8 deals with fines.
The wage ceiling for coverage under the Act was raised to Rs 24,000 per month in 2017.
The Code on Wages, 2019 replaces the Act with 'Inspector-cum-Facilitator'.
The claim application under Section 15 must generally be filed within 12 months.
summary: The answer is (a). Section 14(2) of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 says every Inspector appointed under the Act is deemed a 'public servant' within the meaning of the Indian Penal Code, so the claim that they are not public servants is incorrect. Options (b), (c) and (d) correctly reflect Section 14(1).
topic_notes: The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 regulates the payment of wages to certain classes of employed persons, ensuring timely payment and preventing unauthorised deductions. It applies to persons employed in factories, railways, and industrial or other establishments, with wages up to a ceiling (currently Rs 24,000 per month, revised in 2017). It covers wage periods (not more than one month, Section 4), the time of payment (7th day for establishments with fewer than 1,000 employees, 10th day for others, Section 5), authorised deductions (Section 7: fines, absence from duty, damage or loss, house accommodation, etc.), and the limit on total deductions (75 per cent of wages in cash for societies, otherwise 50 per cent, Section 7(3)). Section 15 provides claims for wrongly deducted or delayed wages before the authority appointed under it (a Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation, a Labour Court judge or similar). The claim must be filed within 12 months. Section 17 provides an appeal, and in some cases only when the amount exceeds Rs 300 for deductions. Section 20 prescribes penalties. Section 22 bars civil suits in respect of matters it covers. The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes this Act, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. It introduces the 'Inspector-cum-Facilitator' and a floor wage. Related enforcement officers include Inspectors of Factories, Labour Enforcement Officers, and Assistant Labour Commissioners (Central).

subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 3 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 empowers the appropriate Government (Centre or State) to fix and revise minimum rates of wages for scheduled employments. Section 3(3) says that, in fixing or revising, different minimum rates may be fixed for: (a) different scheduled employments; (b) different classes of work in the same scheduled employment; (c) adults, adolescents, children and apprentices; and (d) different localities. The rates may be fixed by the hour, day, month or any larger wage period. Sex is deliberately absent from this list. This is consistent with Article 39(d) of the Constitution (equal pay for equal work), Article 15 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, which is now subsumed in the Code on Wages, 2019. The Code on Wages likewise bars discrimination on the ground of gender in wages. Elimination: localities, age and category groups, and different employments are all expressly permitted, so (a), (b) and (d) are ruled out. Only (c), gender-based differentiation, is not permitted, so it is the answer to the 'cannot' question.
explanations: Wrong. Different localities are expressly allowed under Section 3(3)(b)(iv) in the Act, since living costs vary by area, so rates can differ by locality.
Wrong. Section 3(3) expressly allows different rates for adults, adolescents, children and apprentices, so this can be done.

Correct. Section 3(3) does not list sex as a ground for differentiation. Differential minimum wages for men and women would conflict with the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 and Article 39(d), so this is what cannot be done.
Wrong. Different rates for different scheduled employments (and for different classes of work within one) are expressly allowed, so this can be done.
keyfact: Under Section 3(3) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, different rates are allowed by employment, class of work, age group and locality, but not by sex.
option_notes: Locality-wise rates: because the cost of living differs, State Governments commonly divide areas into zones (A, B, C or by municipal and rural area) and fix different minimum wages for each. The Central Government does the same for central-sphere employments, with area-wise rates, and also announces a National Floor Level Minimum Wage, which is not statutory but is an advisory floor. Locality-based differentiation is permitted by Section 3(3).

Age and category differentiation: the Act recognises adults, adolescents (14-18 years), children (below 14) and apprentices as different classes. Different minimum rates may be fixed for them under Section 3(3). The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, as amended in 2016, now prohibits child employment below 14 and hazardous work for adolescents, but the wage-fixing provision remains in the Act.

Male and female workers: the law forbids discrimination in remuneration on the ground of sex. The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 requires equal pay for the same or similar work, and Article 39(d) is a Directive Principle on equal pay for equal work. The Code on Wages, 2019 continues this ban on gender discrimination. The Minimum Wages Act does not give power to fix separate rates by sex.

Different scheduled employments: the Act has a Schedule listing employments (Part I and Part II, covering agriculture and others) for which minimum wages are fixed. Rates can differ between them and between classes of work within one employment, such as skilled, semi-skilled, unskilled and clerical. Governments add employments to the Schedule after due procedure, so differences by employment are fully permitted.
related: Minimum Wages Act, 1948 Section 3(3) permits rates differing by employment, class of work, age category and locality, not sex.
Minimum wages must be revised at intervals not exceeding five years.
Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) upheld the validity of the Minimum Wages Act.
Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 prohibits gender discrimination in pay and recruitment.
Code on Wages, 2019 subsumed four wage laws including the Minimum Wages Act.
Article 39(d) of the Constitution lays down equal pay for equal work for men and women.
Minimum wage components under Section 4 are a basic rate plus cost-of-living allowance, or an all-inclusive rate.
Central Advisory Board under Section 8 advises on minimum wage matters.
summary: The answer is (c). Section 3(3) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 lets the appropriate Government fix different minimum rates for different scheduled employments, for different classes of work in the same employment, for adults, adolescents, children and apprentices, and for different localities. Sex is not a permitted ground, so male and female workers cannot be given different minimum rates.
topic_notes:
The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 was enacted to prevent exploitation of workers in sweated and unorganised industries by statutorily fixing minimum wage rates. Its constitutional basis includes Article 43 (living wage) and Article 23 (forced labour), and Article 39(d) on equal pay. Its upholding in Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) established that minimum wage restrictions are reasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(g).

Key provisions: Section 3 covers fixing and revising of minimum rates, and rates must be revised at intervals not exceeding five years. Section 4 covers the components of the minimum wage: a basic rate with or without a cost-of-living allowance, or a basic rate plus a special allowance adjusted to the cost-of-living index, or an all-inclusive rate. Section 5 sets the procedure, using either the committee method or the notification method. Section 7 provides for Advisory Boards, and Section 8 for the Central Advisory Board. Section 9 covers Committees. Section 12 requires payment of the minimum rate. Section 13 covers fixing of hours of work, and Section 14 covers overtime. Section 17 covers claims, and Section 20 covers penalties and the authority for claims. Section 22 covers offences by employers, and Section 22A the general penalty. Section 26 gives exemption powers. The 'appropriate Government' is the Centre for railways, mines, oilfields, major ports and central-sphere undertakings, and the State for the rest.

Related: the Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act, the Payment of Wages Act, the Payment of Bonus Act and the Equal Remuneration Act. It introduces a floor wage set by the Centre, which State minimum wages may not go below. In the Code on Wages, 2019 the term 'minimum wages' is retained, and revision is at intervals not exceeding five years. The Code was passed in August 2019 and the Central rules were notified in draft. A very common UPSC angle is to ask which grounds are permitted for wage differentiation and which are barred.

question: Which one of the following statements with 35. respect to the payment of ‘wages in kind’ under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 is not correct ?
options: Where it has been the custom to pay wages wholly or partly in kind, the appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, authorize the payment of minimum 36. wages either wholly or partly in kind

If the appropriate Government is of the opinion that provision should be made for the supply of essential commodities at concessional rates, it may, by notification in the Official Gazette, authorize the provision of such supplies at concessional rates
The cash value of wages in kind and of concessions in respect of supplies of essential commodities shall be estimated in the manner prescribed by the Act
Minimum wages may be payable either in kind or in the form of an ‘essential commodity which can be made convertible on pro rata basis
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 11 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 deals with payment of minimum wages in cash. Sub-section (1) says minimum wages shall be paid in cash. Sub-section (2) says that where it has been the custom to pay wages wholly or partly in kind, the appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, authorise payment wholly or partly in kind. Sub-section (3) says that if the appropriate Government considers it necessary that essential commodities be supplied at concessional rates, it may authorise such supply by notification. Sub-section (4) says the cash value of wages in kind and of concessions on essential commodities shall be estimated in the prescribed manner. Options (a), (b) and (c) track sub-sections (2), (3) and (4) closely. Option (d) invents a rule: it treats wages in kind as freely payable in an essential commodity convertible pro rata, which the Act does not provide. The default is cash, and kind payment is an exception that needs a notification and a custom. So (d) is the statement that is not correct. Also remember that the Section 11 arrangement is carried into the Code on Wages, 2019, which has not yet replaced the Act in practice. Under the Code, Section 17 requires payment in cash, cheque or electronic credit.
explanations: Correct statement, so not the answer. It restates Section 11(2): the custom of payment in kind plus a Gazette notification permits wholly or partly kind payment.
Correct statement, so not the answer. It reflects Section 11(3): the Government may authorise supply of essential commodities at concessional rates by notification.
Correct statement, so not the answer. Section 11(4) requires the cash value of kind wages and concessions to be estimated in the prescribed manner.

Incorrect statement, so this is the answer. The Act makes cash the rule, and kind payment is allowed only under a notification where custom exists. There is no provision for commodity payment convertible pro rata.
keyfact: Under Section 11 of the Minimum Wages Act, wages are paid in cash, with kind payment allowed only by notification where custom exists.
option_notes: Authorisation of wages in kind: Section 11(2) lets the appropriate Government (Central or State, depending on the scheduled employment) permit this by Gazette notification. The condition is an existing custom of paying wholly or partly in kind. It is an exception to the cash rule in Section 11(1) and is relevant mainly in agriculture and plantations.

Concessional supply of essential commodities: Section 11(3) lets the appropriate Government authorise this by notification. Its purpose is the welfare of workers, especially where market prices are high or supplies scarce. The value of the concession is counted in the wages, and the estimation method is as prescribed.

Cash value estimation: Section 11(4) provides that the cash value of kind wages and concessions is estimated as prescribed. The Minimum Wages (Central) Rules, 1950 set out the method. This ensures that kind payments still meet the notified minimum wage rate in monetary terms.

This option is a distractor with no basis in the Act. Section 11(1) fixes the default of payment in cash. The Act has no concept of a pro rata convertible essential commodity as a form of wages. Kind payment is an exception only through notification under Section 11(2) and 11(3).
related: Section 11(1): minimum wages are to be paid in cash.
Section 11(2): payment in kind needs a custom and a Gazette notification.
Section 12: employer must pay not less than minimum rates.
Section 14: overtime is paid at twice the normal rate.
Section 3: minimum wage rates are to be reviewed at intervals not exceeding five years.
The Code on Wages, 2019 introduced a floor wage under Section 9.
Article 43 (DPSP) promotes a living wage for workers.
Bijay Cotton Mills (1955) upheld the Act's validity.
summary: The answer is (d). Under Section 11 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, minimum wages are normally paid in cash. Payment in kind is allowed only by government authorisation, and nothing in the Act lets wages be paid as an 'essential commodity' convertible on a pro rata basis.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948. It empowers the appropriate Government to fix minimum wage rates for scheduled employments. It rests on Article 43 (living wage) of the Directive Principles. Its constitutional validity was upheld in Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955). Section 3 covers fixation and revision of rates, and revision is to occur at intervals not exceeding five years. Section 4 covers the contents of minimum wages: a basic rate and a special allowance (cost of living allowance), or an all-inclusive rate. Section 5 sets out the procedure for fixing wages, by committees or by notification of proposals. Section 7 provides for the Advisory Board, and Section 8 for the Central Advisory Board. Section 11 deals with payment in cash or kind. Section 12 requires payment of not less than the minimum rates. Section 13 covers fixing of hours of work, Section 14 overtime (at double the rate in the Act), Section 15 claims and Section 17 the claims authority. Section 18 covers maintenance of registers and records, Section 19 inspectors and Section 20 penalties. Fixation methods are the committee method and the notification method. Wage fixation criteria draw on the 15th ILC (1957) norms and the Reptakos Brett judgment (1992). The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Wages Act, Payment of Bonus Act and Equal Remuneration Act. The Code introduces a statutory floor wage under Section 9.

question: Which one of the following statements is not 37, correct with regard to fixing the number of hours for a normal working day under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 ?
options: Fixation of the number of hours of work which shall constitute a normal working day, inclusive of one or more specified intervals
Provision for a day of rest in every period of seven days for all employees or any specified class of employees
Provision for grant of payment for work on a day of rest at a rate which is not less than the overtime rate
Fixation of the number of hours of work which shall not exceed eight hours a day inclusive of one or more _ specified intervals
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Section 13 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 deals with the 'Hours of work'. For any scheduled employment, the appropriate government (Centre or State) may: (a) fix the number of hours of work that constitute a normal working day, inclusive of one or more specified intervals; (b) provide for a day of rest in every period of seven days for all employees or any specified class of them, along with remuneration for those rest days; and (c) provide for payment for work on a day of rest at a rate not less than the overtime rate. Section 14 then deals with overtime. An employee who works more than the normal working day, or on a rest day, is entitled to wages at the overtime rate fixed under the law of the appropriate government. The Act itself gives no fixed daily-hours figure. The actual numbers come from rules, for example the Minimum Wages (Central) Rules, 1950, and from State rules. Option (d) inserts a statutory 'not exceed eight hours' limit that the Section does not contain. That limit looks more like the Factories Act or Shops and Establishments laws. It is therefore the incorrect statement, which is what the question asks for.
explanations: Incorrect choice for 'not correct': this matches Section 13(1)(a), which allows fixing hours of a normal working day inclusive of one or more specified intervals.

Incorrect choice for 'not correct': this matches Section 13(1)(b), which provides for a weekly day of rest for all employees or a specified class. The Section also provides for remuneration on those days.
Incorrect choice for 'not correct': this matches Section 13(1)(c), which provides for payment for work on a rest day at a rate not less than the overtime rate.
Correct answer: Section 13 contains no statutory cap of eight hours a day. It only empowers the appropriate government to fix the hours, so the stated eight-hour limit is not in the Act.
keyfact: Section 13 Minimum Wages Act: the government fixes the hours of a normal working day, but the Act has no fixed eight-hour cap.
option_notes: Section 13(1)(a) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. The appropriate government may fix the number of hours that make up a normal working day, inclusive of one or more specified intervals. The Act sets no number itself. The hours are fixed through rules and notifications, for example the Central Rules, 1950 for the Central sphere. This power applies only to scheduled employments.

Section 13(1)(b). It provides for a day of rest in every period of seven days, allowed to all employees or to any specified class of employees. The provision also covers payment of remuneration for such rest days. This is the weekly-off concept in minimum wage law and is a standard exam point.

Section 13(1)(c). Work done on a rest day is paid at a rate not less than the overtime rate. Section 14 separately governs overtime. Overtime is paid at the rate fixed under the law of the appropriate government, commonly double the ordinary rate. Rest-day work therefore attracts a premium.

This is not found in the Act. The Minimum Wages Act does not fix an eight-hour ceiling. It only empowers the government to fix the hours of a normal working day. Hour limits such as 9 hours a day and 48 hours a week appear in the Factories Act, 1948, and in the rules and State laws. It is the incorrect statement in this question.
related: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948.
Section 13 covers hours of work and the weekly day of rest; Section 14 covers overtime.
Minimum wage revision interval is not more than five years.
The Supreme Court upheld the Act's validity in Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955).
The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.
The Act has its constitutional basis in Article 43, the Directive Principle on a living wage.
Under Section 7, the Advisory Board is constituted to advise on fixing and revising wages.
Under Section 22, a breach of the Act attracts penalties.
summary: The answer is (d). Section 13 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 lets the appropriate government fix the hours of a normal working day, inclusive of specified intervals, but it does not set an eight-hour ceiling. Options (a), (b) and (c) closely track the wording of Section 13(1).
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948. It empowers the appropriate government to fix minimum rates of wages for scheduled employments. Its constitutional basis is the Directive Principle in Article 43 (living wage). The Supreme Court upheld the Act's validity in Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955), holding that the restriction on freedom of contract is a reasonable restriction under Article 19(1)(g). Key provisions: Section 3 deals with fixing minimum wage rates; Section 4 sets out what the minimum wage consists of, including a basic rate and a cost of living allowance; Section 5 gives the procedure for fixing and revising wages; Section 7 provides for the Advisory Board; Section 8 provides for the Central Advisory Board; Section 12 requires payment of the minimum wage; Section 13 covers hours of work and the weekly day of rest; Section 14 covers overtime; Section 18 covers records and registers; Section 20 covers claims; Section 22 covers penalties; Section 22A covers a general provision for punishing offences. Minimum wages are revised under Section 3(1)(b), at intervals not exceeding five years. The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes this Act along with the Payment of Wages Act, the Payment of Bonus Act and the Equal Remuneration Act. It introduces a statutory floor wage and an Advisory Board. Related angles UPSC could ask: the Act's coverage of scheduled employments, the committee-based and notification-based methods of fixing wages, the National Floor Level Minimum Wage, the Code on Wages, and comparisons with the Factories Act limits on working hours.

question: The appropriate Government, under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, may not fix :
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 3(2) lists the kinds of rates the appropriate Government may fix: (a) a minimum time rate (minimum rate of wages for time work); (b) a minimum piece rate (for piece work); (c) a guaranteed time rate, which is a minimum rate of remuneration for piece-workers so that they earn at least the time-work minimum; and (d) an overtime rate, which is a minimum rate, time or piece, applying in place of the normal rate for overtime work. The Act speaks of an 'overtime rate', and the word 'guaranteed' is attached only to the time rate. Option (d) therefore invents a rate the Act does not provide, while (a), (b) and (c) are all expressly covered by Section 3(2). The elimination logic is to check each option against the four clauses of Section 3(2). Only (d) fails to match any of them. Overtime itself is dealt with in Section 14, which requires payment at the overtime rate fixed. Section 13 deals with hours of work.
explanations: Wrong option: a minimum time rate is expressly fixable under Section 3(2)(a)(i), as a minimum rate of wages for time work, so the Government may fix it.
Wrong option: a minimum piece rate is fixable under Section 3(2)(a)(ii), so the Government may fix it.
Wrong option: the guaranteed time rate is fixable under Section 3(2)(b), as a minimum rate of remuneration for piece-workers to secure the time-work minimum, so the Government may fix it.
Correct answer: the Act provides for an 'overtime rate' under Section 3(2)(c), not a 'guaranteed overtime rate'. The Government is not empowered to fix a rate by this name.
keyfact: Section 3(2) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 provides for time, piece, guaranteed time and overtime rates; there is no 'guaranteed overtime rate'.
option_notes: Minimum time rate: the minimum wage for time work, which may be fixed per hour, day, month or another longer wage period (Sec 3(3)). It may consist of a basic rate plus a cost of living allowance, or the cash value of concessions (Sec 4). It is the standard minimum wage for workers paid by time.

Minimum piece rate: the minimum wage for work paid by the unit of output (piece work). It is fixed by the appropriate Government under Section 3(2)(a). It ensures that piece-workers are paid a statutory floor per piece produced.

Guaranteed time rate: the minimum rate of remuneration for piece-workers, fixed so that they secure the minimum rate of wages on a time-work basis. It protects piece-workers whose output is low, so that their earnings never fall below the time-rate minimum. Section 3(2)(b).

Guaranteed overtime rate: this is not a statutory term under the Act. The Act provides only an 'overtime rate', a minimum rate (time or piece) applying in substitution for the normal rate to overtime work. Section 14 requires payment at that rate, generally at double the ordinary rate where applicable.
related: Section 3(2) lists the types of minimum rates: time, piece, guaranteed time and overtime.
The Minimum Wages Act came into force on 15 March 1948.
Section 10 requires minimum wages to be reviewed at intervals not exceeding five years.
The Central Advisory Board is constituted under Section 8 of the Act.
Section 22 provides penalties for offences under the Act.
Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) upheld the constitutional validity of the Act.
The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 and introduces a floor wage.
Section 14 deals with overtime wages for work beyond normal working hours.
summary: The correct answer is (d). Section 3(2) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 lets the appropriate Government fix a minimum time rate, a minimum piece rate, a guaranteed time rate and an overtime rate. 'Guaranteed overtime rate' is not a category in the Act.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948. It is based on the ILO Minimum Wage-Fixing Machinery Convention, 1928 (No. 26), and it empowers the appropriate Government to fix minimum wages for scheduled employments. The appropriate Government is the Central Government for scheduled employments under it, such as railways, mines and oilfields, and the State Government for other employments. Section 3 deals with fixation of minimum rates. Section 3(1) requires fixing for the scheduled employments and allows extension to others. Section 3(2) lists the rate types discussed above. Section 3(3) covers the wage periods: hour, day, month or another longer period. Section 4 describes the composition of minimum wages: a basic rate with or without a cost of living allowance, or an all-inclusive rate. Section 5 sets out the procedure for fixing and revising wages, either by committees or by notifying proposals. Section 7 covers advisory committees, Section 8 the Central Advisory Board, and Section 9 the Central and State Advisory Boards. Section 10 provides for review at intervals not exceeding five years. Section 12 requires payment of at least the minimum rate. Section 13 covers hours of work and the weekly day of rest. Section 14 deals with overtime. Section 18 covers maintenance of registers. Section 20 provides for claims, and Section 22 for penalties. Constitutional links: Article 43, a Directive Principle, on a living wage. The Supreme Court in Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer upheld the Act's validity, and in Unichoy v. State of Kerala held that the capacity of the employer to pay is irrelevant. The Act is being subsumed into the Code on Wages, 2019, which introduces a national floor wage.

question: Under Section 16 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, where an employee does two or more classes of work for each of which a different minimum rate of wage applies, he shall be paid :
options: rate of wage whichever is higher
rate of wage as may be prescribed by the appropriate Government
rate of wages as fixed by the employer under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946
rate of wages in respect of the time respectively occupied in each such class of work, wages at not less than the minimum rate in force in respect of each such class
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 16 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 deals with employees who do two or more classes of work. Where an employee does two or more classes of work, each of which has a different minimum rate of wages, the employer must pay him for the time he spends on each class at not less than the minimum rate in force for that class. The wage is therefore apportioned by time. It is neither the highest rate for the whole period nor a rate that the employer or the Government fixes separately. Related sections to remember: Section 3 covers fixing of minimum rates of wages, Section 4 the contents of the minimum wage (basic rate plus cost-of-living allowance), Section 13 the fixing of hours of work, Section 14 overtime, Section 15 wages of an employee who works less than a normal working day, Section 17 wages for piece-work, Section 18 the maintenance of registers and records, Section 20 claims, and Section 22 offences. Elimination logic: (a) is wrong because the Act does not give the higher rate for all the time. (b) is wrong because the Government prescribes the minimum rates under Section 3, not the rate for mixed work under Section 16. (c) is wrong because the Standing Orders Act has no role in this provision. Option (d) closely follows the statutory wording.
explanations: Incorrect: Section 16 does not give the higher rate for the entire period; each class of work is paid at its own rate for the time spent on it.
Incorrect: The appropriate Government fixes minimum rates under Section 3, but Section 16 itself lays down the time-proportionate method for mixed work.
Incorrect: Rates fixed by the employer under Standing Orders cannot override statutory minimum rates, and Section 16 does not refer to them.
Correct: This matches Section 16, which requires payment for the time occupied in each class of work at not less than the minimum rate in force for that class.
keyfact: Section 16 Minimum Wages Act: for mixed classes of work, pay each class's minimum rate for the time spent on it.
option_notes: Paying the higher rate for all work is a plausible-sounding rule, but it does not appear in the Act. Section 16 uses time-based apportionment instead. A higher rate applies only to the time actually spent on the higher-rated class. Do not confuse this with overtime under Section 14, which is paid at double the ordinary rate, or at the rate the appropriate Government prescribes if that is higher.

Under Section 3, the appropriate Government (Central or State, depending on the scheduled employment) fixes minimum time rates, piece rates, overtime rates and so on. The Government can fix wage periods and revise rates at intervals not exceeding five years. Section 16 is a self-operating rule and needs no separate prescription of rates for mixed work.

The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 requires employers of industrial establishments to define conditions of service in certified standing orders. It applies to establishments with 100 or more workers (the threshold varies by state). It has no bearing on minimum wage rates. It has since been subsumed into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which is not yet fully in force.

This is the correct option. It reflects the apportionment principle of Section 16. Wages are computed separately for the time occupied in each class of work, each at not less than the minimum rate in force for that class. It protects workers who are moved between jobs of different skill or rate, and a shortfall can be recovered by a claim under Section 20.
related: Section 3 of the Minimum Wages Act covers fixing of minimum rates of wages.
Section 14 deals with overtime, paid at the rate the appropriate Government prescribes, or double the ordinary rate.
Section 17 covers wages for piece-work.
Section 20 covers claims, which must be filed within 6 months.
Minimum wages must be revised at intervals not exceeding 5 years.
The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.
The Central Advisory Board is constituted under Section 8.
Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) upheld the Act's validity.
summary: The answer is (d). Under Section 16 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, an employee who does two or more classes of work, each with a different minimum rate, must be paid for the time spent on each class at not less than the minimum rate in force for that class.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948. It is a welfare law rooted in Directive Principles (Article 43, living wage). It empowers the appropriate Government to fix minimum wages for scheduled employments. Its constitutional validity was upheld in Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955). Key provisions: Section 3 (fixing minimum wages), Section 4 (minimum rate of wages), Section 5 (procedure for fixing and revising), Section 7 (Advisory Board), Section 8 (Central Advisory Board), Section 9 (composition of committees), Section 10 (notification of rates), Section 12 (payment of minimum rates), Section 13 (hours of work), Section 14 (overtime), Section 15 (employees working less than a normal day), Section 16 (two or more classes of work), Section 17 (piece-work), Section 18 (registers), Section 19 (inspectors), Section 20 (claims authority), Section 21 (single application for claims), Section 22 (penalties), and Section 22A (general penalty). Section 22 punishes failure to pay minimum wages with imprisonment up to 6 months or a fine up to Rs 500, or both. Revisions are to occur at intervals of not more than 5 years. Under Section 20, claims must be filed within 6 months of the date the minimum wages became payable, or 6 months from when the employment ceased. The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes this Act along with the Payment of Wages Act, the Payment of Bonus Act and the Equal Remuneration Act. It introduces a statutory floor wage and universal minimum wage coverage. Likely future questions concern the sections above, the Advisory Board composition, the time limits for claims, the penalties, and the provisions of the Code on Wages.

question: Under which one of the following situations will the employer be exempted from criminal liability for non-payment of wages under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 ?
options: That he has contravened Section 11 of the Act and paid wages in kind for articles which are essential commodities
That he has contravened the provision of Section 3(2) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948
That he has contravened the provisions of Section 3(3) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948
That another person has committed the offence without his knowledge, consent or connivance
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 makes non-payment of minimum wages an offence under Section 22 (penalty: imprisonment up to six months or fine up to Rs 500, or both, for paying less than the minimum rate or contravening other provisions). Section 22A is a general penalty for other offences (fine up to Rs 500). Section 22C deals with offences by companies: every person in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business is deemed guilty, but he escapes liability if he proves the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent it. The 'without knowledge, consent or connivance' defence is the statutory exemption. Section 22B has a time-bound cognizance limit (six months from the date the offence comes to the inspector's knowledge). Section 3 empowers the appropriate government to fix minimum wages: 3(2) concerns review and revision of wages at intervals not exceeding five years, and 3(3) allows different minimum rates for different scheduled employments, classes of work, adults, adolescents, children, apprentices, localities. Section 11 covers payment of minimum wages in cash, with permitted payment in kind by government authorisation. These are duty provisions, not shields. Hence options (a), (b) and (c) are just contraventions and carry liability, while only (d) is a defence.
explanations: Wrong: contravening Section 11 by paying in kind is itself a breach; paying in kind for essential commodities is only valid if authorised by the government, so it is not an exemption from liability.
Wrong: Section 3(2) concerns the fixing and review of minimum wages; contravening it does not exempt the employer from liability.
Wrong: Section 3(3) concerns differential rates and fixation by class, area and category; contravention is not a ground for exemption.

Correct: the Act's offences-by-companies and responsibility provisions exempt a person who proves the offence was committed by another without his knowledge, consent or connivance and that he exercised due diligence.
keyfact: An employer escapes liability only if the offence was committed by another without his knowledge, consent or connivance; contravening Sections 3 or 11 is no defence.
option_notes: Section 11 provides that minimum wages shall be paid in cash. The appropriate government may authorise payment wholly or partly in kind where custom exists, and may authorise supply of essential commodities at concession rates. Payment in kind outside these conditions is a contravention and is penalised, so it is not a defence.

Section 3(2) provides that the appropriate government shall review at intervals not exceeding five years the minimum rates fixed and revise them if necessary. It is a statutory duty of the government in fixing wages, not an employer exemption. Section 3(1) requires fixing wages for scheduled employments.

Section 3(3) allows the appropriate government to fix minimum wages differently for different scheduled employments, classes of work (adults, adolescents, children, apprentices), different localities, and wage periods (hour, day, month). It is a government power, and breach by an employer is not an exemption from liability.

This is the defence recognised for persons in charge of a business: if another person committed the offence without the knowledge, consent or connivance of the employer, and the employer exercised due diligence, he is not criminally liable. This follows the general principle of mens rea and vicarious liability in labour legislation, and appears in the offences-by-companies provisions.
related: Minimum Wages Act, 1948 flows from Article 43 of the Constitution.
Bijay Cotton Mills v State of Ajmer (1955) upheld the Act's constitutionality.
Section 3(2) requires review of minimum wages at intervals not exceeding five years.
Section 11 provides that minimum wages be paid in cash, with limited exceptions.
Section 22 provides imprisonment up to six months or fine up to Rs 500.
The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.
The Act has two methods for fixing wages: the committee and notification methods.
summary: The answer is (d). Under Section 22A and Section 22C of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, an employer who is the 'occupier' or the person responsible is not criminally liable if the offence was committed by another person without his knowledge, consent or connivance and he exercised due diligence. Contravening Sections 3(2), 3(3) or 11 does not give any exemption.
topic_notes: The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 came into force on 15 March 1948 and applies to scheduled employments. It rests on Article 43 (living wage) of the Directive Principles. The Supreme Court upheld its constitutionality in Bijay Cotton Mills v State of Ajmer (1955). Under Section 3 the appropriate government fixes minimum wages; the central government is appropriate for employments under it, railways, mines, oil fields and major ports, and the state government for others. Section 4 deals with the components of minimum wages: a basic rate and special allowance, or a basic rate with cost-of-living allowance, or an all-inclusive rate. Section 5 sets out two methods of fixing and revising wages: the committee method and the notification method. Section 7 provides for the Advisory Board, Section 8 for the Central Advisory Board, and Section 9 for the composition of committees (equal representatives of employers and employees, plus independent persons, one of whom is chairman). Section 12 mandates payment of minimum rates, Section 13 covers working hours, Section 14 overtime, Section 17 claims, Section 18 maintains registers, and Section 19 deals with inspectors and claims. Section 20 provides for claims by authority. Section 22 provides penalties, and Section 22A general penalty. The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes this Act, the Payment of Wages Act, the Payment of Bonus Act and the Equal Remuneration Act. Under the Code, the floor wage concept is introduced under Section 9, and the Code applies to all employments.

question: Under Section 3(3) of the Minimum Wages a Act, 1948, wages may not be fixed in which one of the following wage periods ?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 3 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 empowers the appropriate government (Central or State) to fix minimum rates of wages for scheduled employments. Section 3(3) lays down how the rates are fixed. Clause (a) allows different rates for different scheduled employments, different classes of work in the same employment, adults, adolescents, children and apprentices, and different localities. Clause (b) allows the rates to be fixed by any one or more of these wage-periods: (i) by the hour, (ii) by the day, (iii) by the month, or (iv) by such other larger wage-period as may be prescribed. The Act also says that where rates are fixed by the day or month, the manner of calculating wages for a month or day may be indicated. The statutory list therefore does not contain 'week'. A week is shorter than a month, so it is not a 'larger' period either. Elimination: hour, day and month are named in the section, so (a), (b) and (d) are permitted. Only (c) is not named. Related provisions: Section 4 (contents of minimum wage, including cost of living allowance), Section 5 (procedure for fixing wages), Section 12 (payment of minimum rate), Section 13 (hours of work), Section 14 (overtime).
explanations: Wrong: 'by the hour' is expressly listed in Section 3(3)(b)(i), so wages may be fixed hourly.
Wrong: 'by the day' is expressly listed in Section 3(3)(b)(ii), so daily rates are permitted.
Correct: 'by the week' does not appear in Section 3(3)(b). The permitted periods are hour, day, month, or a larger prescribed period, so a weekly wage-period is not provided for.
Wrong: 'by the month' is expressly listed in Section 3(3)(b)(iii), so monthly rates are permitted.
keyfact: Section 3(3)(b), Minimum Wages Act 1948: wages are fixed by the hour, day, month or a larger prescribed period, and a week is not listed.
option_notes: Hourly wage period: Section 3(3)(b)(i) permits the appropriate government to fix minimum wages per hour. It suits casual, part-time or piece-type work. Hourly rates must still meet the minimum wage, and work beyond the normal working day attracts overtime under Section 14 at not less than double the ordinary rate. The hourly rate is often derived from the daily rate divided by the normal working hours.

Daily wage period: Section 3(3)(b)(ii) permits fixing the minimum wage by the day. It is the most common basis for minimum wage notifications, especially for unskilled agricultural and construction workers. Under Section 13, the normal working day is generally fixed at 9 hours with a weekly day of rest. The Central Government notifies daily floor wages by area (A, B, C) for central-sphere employments.

Weekly wage period: this is not mentioned in Section 3(3)(b). A week is shorter than a month, so it cannot be a 'larger wage-period' prescribed by rules either. Weekly payment of wages is a practice, and under the Payment of Wages Act wage-period cannot exceed one month. Minimum wage fixation, however, is by hour, day, month or a larger prescribed period.

Monthly wage period: Section 3(3)(b)(iii) permits fixing the minimum wage by the month. Many State notifications for skilled, clerical and shop or establishment staff state monthly rates. The Act allows the government to specify how the daily rate is computed from the monthly rate and vice versa. Larger periods than a month can be fixed only if prescribed by rules.
related: Section 3 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 deals with fixation of minimum rates of wages.
Permitted wage periods: hour, day, month, or a larger prescribed period.
Section 4 includes the cost of living allowance in minimum wages.
Section 13 fixes working hours and a weekly day of rest.
Section 14 provides overtime at double the ordinary rate.
Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) upheld the Act's constitutionality.
The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.
Revision of minimum wages must be done at intervals not exceeding five years.
summary: The answer is (c) by the week. Section 3(3)(b) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 allows minimum wage rates to be fixed by the hour, by the day, by the month, or by a larger wage-period prescribed by rules. A week is not listed.
topic_notes:
The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 is a central labour law enacted to prevent exploitation of workers in sweated industries. It rests on the Directive Principle in Article 43 (living wage) and was upheld in Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955), which held that the restriction on freedom of contract is reasonable. The Act came into force on 15 March 1948. It applies to employments listed in the Schedule (Part I and Part II, with Part II covering agriculture). The appropriate government may add employments to the Schedule. Employers with 1,000 or more workers in an employment can be covered under the Act.

Key sections:
- Section 3: fixing of minimum rates (hour, day, month or larger prescribed period).
- Section 4: contents of minimum rates, including the basic rate, cost of living allowance and cash value of concessions.
- Section 5: procedure for fixing and revising wages (committee method or notification method).
- Section 7: Advisory Board.
- Section 8: Central Advisory Board.
- Section 9: Composition of Committees.
- Section 12: payment of not less than the minimum rate.
- Section 13: working hours.
- Section 14: overtime.
- Section 20: claims authority.
- Section 22: penalties.

Wages are revised at intervals not exceeding five years. The Central Advisory Board is tripartite with an independent chairman. The National Floor Level Minimum Wage is a non-statutory recommendation.

The Code on Wages, 2019 subsumes this Act along with the Payment of Wages Act, the Payment of Bonus Act and the Equal Remuneration Act. It introduces a statutory floor wage and universal minimum wage coverage. It also provides for fixing minimum wages by time, piece or other rates.

question: For the purposes of the Building and Other Construction Workers’ (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996, there shall be levied and collected a Cess at such rate of the cost of construction incurred by an employer not exceeding :
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The question mixes the BOCW (RE&CS) Act, 1996 with its companion law, the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996. Section 3 of the Cess Act says the cess is levied at a rate not less than 1 percent and not more than 2 percent of the cost of construction incurred by an employer. The Central Government, by notification dated 26 September 1996, fixed the rate at 1 percent, and it remains 1 percent today. The cess is collected by the local authority or the State Government, and in the case of Central Government or public sector undertaking projects, it is deducted at source from the bills. It is paid into the State Welfare Board's fund and funds the welfare of construction workers. The Cess Act does not apply to the cost of land and compensation. Elimination: the statutory ceiling is 2 percent, so 4 percent and 6 percent are impossible. Both 1 percent and 2 percent appear in the statute's range. Because the question has no 'not less than' wording, and because the notified and actual rate is 1 percent, option (d) is the one that best matches the commonly examined fact. Note there is some ambiguity: strictly the statutory ceiling is 2 percent, so students should read the wording carefully. The notified rate is 1 percent.
explanations: Incorrect: 4 percent exceeds the statutory ceiling of 2 percent in Section 3 of the Cess Act.
Incorrect: 6 percent is well above the maximum permitted rate.

Incorrect as the chosen answer: 2 percent is the upper statutory limit but not the notified rate; the notified rate is 1 percent. If a question asks for the maximum permitted under the Act, 2 percent would be correct.
Correct: the Central Government notified the cess at 1 percent of the cost of construction in 1996, and this is the rate levied and collected.
keyfact: Construction workers' cess: range 1 to 2 percent under the Cess Act 1996, notified at 1 percent of the cost of construction.
option_notes: Four percent: not a rate under the Act. The Cess Act, 1996 allows a range of 1 to 2 percent. Four percent is a distractor and has no link to the building workers' cess scheme.
Six percent: not found in the Act. It has no relation to the cess; it is a distractor. Cess rates for construction workers have never been above 2 percent in law.

Two percent: the upper limit of the cess range under Section 3 of the Cess Act, 1996 (not less than 1 percent, not more than 2 percent). It has never been notified at this level; it would take an amending notification by the Central Government.

One percent: the notified rate of cess on the cost of construction, effective from 3 November 1996 under the Cess Act, 1996. It is collected by the State Governments, local authorities and by deduction at source on government projects, and is credited to the State Building Workers' Welfare Boards.
related: The Cess Act, 1996 permits a cess of 1 to 2 percent of the cost of construction.
The notified cess rate is 1 percent, effective from 3 November 1996.
The BOCW Act, 1996 applies to establishments employing 10 or more workers.
Beneficiary eligibility is age 18 to 60 and 90 days of work in the past 12 months.
State Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Boards receive the cess proceeds.
The BOCW Central Rules were framed in 1998.
The OSH Code, 2020 subsumes the BOCW Act.
summary: The answer is (d) one percent. Under the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996, Section 3 allows a cess on the cost of construction incurred by an employer at a rate not exceeding 2 percent, but the question's options and the notified rate point to 1 percent. The Central Government notified the cess at 1 percent of the cost of construction in September 1996.
topic_notes: Two linked laws were enacted in 1996 for construction workers: the BOCW (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 and the BOCW Welfare Cess Act, 1996. The first regulates safety, health, hours of work and welfare for workers in building and other construction work. It applies to every establishment employing 10 or more workers in building or other construction work. The Act provides for Central and State Advisory Committees, and for State Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Boards, which register beneficiaries aged 18 to 60 who have worked at least 90 days in the preceding 12 months. The Cess Act enables a levy on the cost of construction incurred by employers, at a rate not less than 1 percent and not more than 2 percent. The notified rate is 1 percent. Cess is collected by the designated officer and deposited with the State Welfare Boards. Welfare schemes include pensions, accident and medical benefits, maternity benefits, education support for children and housing assistance. The Rules for the Act are the BOCW Central Rules, 1998. The Central Advisory Committee is set up under Section 3 of the Regulation Act. Both Acts are under the Ministry of Labour and Employment and are to be subsumed into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. Cess is not levied on the cost of the land or on compensation. Cess collections are very large, but utilisation has repeatedly been criticised by the Supreme Court in Writ Petition (Civil) 318 of 2006 in National Campaign Committee for Central Legislation on Construction Labour vs Union of India.

ocr: Who can exempt any employer or class of employers in a State from the payment of Cess payable under the Building and Other Construction Workers’ Welfare Cess Act, 1996, where such Cess is already levied and payable under any corresponding law in force in the State ? (a) President of India (b) Government of the State (c) Central Government (d) State Government After the receipt of any appeal under Section 11(1) under the Building and Other Construction Workers’ Welfare Cess Act, 1996, the appellate authority shall dispose of the appeal within : (a) sixty days. (b) ninety days. (c) one hundred a
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996 was enacted alongside the BOCW (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996. It lets the appropriate Government levy a cess at a rate of not less than 1% and not more than 2% of the cost of construction incurred by an employer. The current notified rate is 1%. Section 10 deals with exemption: the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, exempt any employer or class of employers in the State from payment of cess where such cess is already levied and payable under any corresponding law in force in the State. The reason is to avoid double taxation of the same construction activity. Section 3 is the levy and collection provision. Section 4 covers the cess on cost of construction by the employer, Section 5 the power to exempt for small constructions, and Section 11 the appeals provision. Elimination: the President and the Central Government are not the exempting authority in this section, and option (b), Government of the State, is a loose rewording of the statutory term 'State Government'. The Act uses the defined term 'State Government', so (d) is the best answer. Note that the Act's definition of 'appropriate Government' differs from this section.
explanations: Wrong: The President of India has no role in exempting employers from this cess under the Act.
Wrong in form: 'Government of the State' is a loose phrasing, whereas the Act uses the term 'State Government'. Both refer to the same authority in substance, but (d) matches the statutory term.
Wrong: The Central Government levies and collects the cess for central-sphere establishments but does not exempt State-law cess cases under Section 10.
Correct: Section 10 empowers the State Government to exempt employers where cess is already payable under a corresponding State law.
keyfact: Section 10 of the BOCW Cess Act, 1996: the State Government may exempt employers where cess is already payable under a corresponding State law.
option_notes: The President of India is the constitutional head of the Union executive under Article 52 and 53. The President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74). The President is not the notified authority for cess exemption under the 1996 Cess Act, which assigns powers to the appropriate Government and the State Government.

'Government of the State' is the executive of a State, headed by the Governor under Article 153 with a Council of Ministers under Article 163. In labour law drafting, the statute's term 'State Government' is defined through the General Clauses Act, 1897, and refers to the Governor in a State. This option is the same body but not the statutory wording.

The Central Government is the Union executive and is the appropriate Government for establishments such as those of the Central sphere, railways, mines, major ports and similar. It sets the cess rules and administers the cess for those establishments. Under Section 10, however, the power to exempt where a State cess already exists rests with the State Government.

The State Government is the appropriate Government for most construction establishments within the State. It notifies exemptions under Section 10, frames rules and sets up the State Welfare Board. It collects cess through designated officers and credits it to the State Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Board, which uses it for worker welfare.
related: The Cess Act, 1996 levies cess at 1% to 2% of the cost of construction.
The notified rate of cess is 1% of the cost of construction.
Cess proceeds go to the State Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Boards.
Section 10 lets the State Government exempt employers where a corresponding State cess already applies.
Section 11 provides for appeals against assessment orders.
BOCW Act and Cess Act both came into force on 19 March 1996.
The BOCW Acts are subsumed in the OSH&WC Code, 2020.
summary: The answer is (d) State Government. Under Section 10 of the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996, the State Government may exempt any employer or class of employers from paying cess where cess is already levied and payable under a corresponding State law.
topic_notes: The Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996 was enacted to provide resources for the welfare boards set up under the BOCW Act, 1996. Both Acts came into force on 19 March 1996. The cess is levied at a rate between 1% and 2% of the cost of construction, and the Central Government notified 1%. The cess is payable by the employer. Collection is by the local authority or officers designated by the appropriate Government. Proceeds go to the State Welfare Boards. Key provisions include the following. Section 3 is the levy and collection of the cess. Section 4 deals with the time and manner of payment. Section 5 concerns the power to exempt. Section 8 requires the Government to deposit collected sums with the Board. Section 10 deals with exemption where a corresponding State cess exists. Section 11 is the appeal provision: an appeal lies against an assessment order to the prescribed appellate authority within the prescribed time. Section 12 covers penalty for non-payment. The Act also has provisions on interest, penalties, and offences by companies. The Welfare Boards provide benefits such as pension, medical assistance, education and housing assistance for registered workers. Related angles: the Supreme Court in the case of National Campaign Committee for Central Legislation on Construction Labour v. Union of India directed utilisation of cess funds. The BOCW Acts were subsumed in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.

ocr: Whoever, being liable to pay Cess under the Building and Other Construction Workers’ Welfare Cess Act, 1996, wilfully evades or attempts to evade the payment of such Cess shall be punishable with : (a) imprisonment which may extend to one month or with fine or both. (b) imprisonment which may extend to six months or with fine or both. (c) imprisonment which may extend to one year or with fine up to maximum = 2,000 or both. (d) imprisonment which may extend to one year or with fine up to maximum = 1,000 or both. ‘A’, while travelling in a State Transport Corporation bus from his residence to th
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996 works together with the BOCW (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996. It lets the government levy and collect a cess on the cost of construction at a rate between 1% and 2% (notified at 1%). The proceeds go to the State Welfare Boards for workers' welfare. The Act has an offence-and-penalty provision for evasion. A person liable to pay the cess who wilfully evades or attempts to evade payment is punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or with fine up to Rs 2,000, or with both. Other provisions in the Act and its Rules cover assessment, collection by the employer or local authority, appeals, and penalty for non-payment. Elimination logic: one month and six months are too short and do not match the Act. Both (c) and (d) say one year, so the only difference is the fine amount. The statutory figure is Rs 2,000, so (c) is right and (d) is wrong. Remember the three elements: imprisonment up to one year, fine up to Rs 2,000, or both.
explanations: (a) Wrong: one month imprisonment is not what the Act prescribes. The Act provides up to one year.
(b) Wrong: six months is not the statutory maximum for this offence. The maximum is one year.
(c) Correct: imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to Rs 2,000, or both, as the Act provides for wilful evasion of cess.
(d) Wrong: the term of one year is right, but the fine is Rs 2,000, not Rs 1,000.
keyfact: Cess evasion under the 1996 Cess Act: imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine up to Rs 2,000, or both.
option_notes: One month imprisonment is a short penalty term. It is a common distractor in labour-law penalty questions. Statutes often use different terms for different offences, such as non-furnishing of returns, obstruction of officers, or false statements. For wilful evasion of the cess, the Act sets a longer term of up to one year.

Six months imprisonment is a typical penalty in many labour laws, for example for contravention of certain provisions of the BOCW Act and other welfare statutes. It is not the figure for cess evasion under the Cess Act. Do not confuse the penalty for contravention of the BOCW Act with the penalty for cess evasion.

The statutory penalty for wilful evasion of cess is imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to Rs 2,000, or both. The Act is a central law of 1996 that provides funds for the welfare of construction workers through State Welfare Boards. Cess is levied at up to 2% of construction cost (notified at 1%) on the employer or builder.

This option correctly states imprisonment up to one year but gives the fine as Rs 1,000. It is a numeric distractor. UPSC often alters monetary amounts to test precise recall. The actual maximum fine for cess evasion is Rs 2,000.
related: Cess under the BOCW Cess Act: not less than 1% and not more than 2% of construction cost.
Cess Act and BOCW Act were both enacted in 1996.
Penalty for cess evasion: imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine up to Rs 2,000, or both.
State Welfare Boards use the cess funds for worker welfare.
BOCW Act applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers.
Registration as a beneficiary requires age 18 to 60 and 90 days of work in the past year.
The BOCW laws are subsumed in the OSH Code, 2020.
