summary: I took Q41 to be the first question in the image, on the penalty for wilful evasion of cess. The answer is (c). Under the Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996, wilful evasion or attempted evasion of cess is punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to Rs 2,000, or both. The image shows two questions and does not print numbers, so this identification is my assumption.
topic_notes: The Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996 was enacted to provide resources for the welfare of building and other construction workers. It complements the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996. Key features: a cess is levied on the cost of construction incurred by employers, at a rate not less than 1% and not more than 2% (currently notified at 1%). Collection is by the local authority or the appropriate government, and the money is transferred to State Welfare Boards. The Boards fund pensions, medical help, housing loans, education of children, maternity benefits and accident assistance. Registration of workers is a prerequisite for benefits, and beneficiaries are workers aged 18 to 60 who have worked at least 90 days in the preceding year. The Act contains provisions on assessment, appeals, and penalty for evasion: imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to Rs 2,000, or both. The Central Government administers the Act through the Ministry of Labour and Employment. The BOCW Act applies to establishments employing 10 or more building workers. Both Acts have been subsumed in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which is not yet fully in force. UPSC could ask next about the cess rate, who collects it, the role of the Welfare Boards, eligibility for registration, the 10-worker threshold, and the penalties under each Act.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q42.
ocr: Whoever, being liable to pay Cess under the Building and Other Construction Workers’ Welfare Cess Act, 1996, wilfully evades or attempts to evade the payment of such Cess shall be punishable with : (a) imprisonment which may extend to one month or with fine or both. (b) imprisonment which may extend to six months or with fine or both. (c) imprisonment which may extend to one year or with fine up to maximum = 2,000 or both. (d) imprisonment which may extend to one year or with fine up to maximum = 1,000 or both. ‘A’, while travelling in a State Transport Corporation bus from his residence to th
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Under the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 (formerly the Workmen's Compensation Act), Section 3(1) makes the employer liable when an employee suffers personal injury by accident arising out of and in the course of employment. Courts apply the 'notional extension' doctrine, under which employment is not limited to the actual hours or place of work. It covers the time and the route by which the employee enters and leaves the employer's premises. Section 3(2) (added in 2000) makes this explicit by deeming an accident to arise in the course of employment where the employee, while travelling in a vehicle provided by the employer, meets with an accident. Here, A was travelling by bus run by the State Transport Corporation, which is also the employer's premises/depot. The accident happened at the depot, so the employment relationship was already operating. The fact that the shift began two hours later is irrelevant. Hence (a) is wrong because there is no rigid-hours test. (c) is wrong because it demands the accident happen during hours of employment. (d) is wrong because the hazard-of-the-job test is not the only route to liability. (b) is correct. Note that the question assumes that A is an employee of the State Transport Corporation. If A were only a passenger, the answer would differ.
explanations: Incorrect: the Act has no rigid shift-timing test. Liability depends on whether the accident arose out of and in the course of employment, which includes a reasonable time before and after work and the premises.
Correct: A was in the employer's vehicle and premises on his way to work, so the notional extension of employment applies and the dependents can claim compensation.
Incorrect: it is too narrow. Compensation does not require the accident to occur during working hours. Presence on the employer's premises or transport is enough.
Incorrect: the claim does not depend on proving a special occupational hazard. Section 3 covers any accident arising out of and in the course of employment, including the notional extension.
keyfact: Employer's transport or premises: accident on the way to work is covered under notional extension (Employees' Compensation Act, 1923, Section 3).
option_notes: Option (a) is the strict-hours view, which the courts rejected. Under the notional extension doctrine (developed in cases such as Saurashtra Salt Manufacturing Co. v. Bai Valu Raja, 1958 and Mackinnon Mackenzie v. Ibrahim Mahomed Issak, 1969), employment starts when the worker enters the employer's premises or transport. It also continues for a reasonable time after work ends. Shift timing alone does not defeat a claim.

Option (b) reflects Section 3 of the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923. The employer is liable for death or disablement by accident arising out of and in the course of employment. Compensation is paid to the dependents of a deceased worker, and the Act is administered by Commissioners for Employees' Compensation. For death, the amount is 50% of monthly wages multiplied by a relevant factor, or a statutory minimum amount.

Option (c) states a narrower version of the rule: premises plus hours of employment. The Act and the case law go beyond this because of the notional extension doctrine. For example, Section 3(2) covers travel in employer-provided transport, and accidents on the way to work can be covered if there is a reasonable connection to employment.

Option (d) refers to the 'arising out of employment' limb, meaning a causal connection with an employment risk, such as a hazard of the job. The requirement is both 'out of' and 'in the course of' employment. Notional extension supplies the link when the worker is on the employer's premises or transport. Under the Act, disease and accident are treated separately: Schedule III lists occupational diseases.
related: The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 was renamed from the Workmen's Compensation Act by the 2009 amendment.
Section 3 makes the employer liable for accidents arising out of and in the course of employment.
Notional extension: employment includes a reasonable time and the premises before and after work.
Compensation for death is deposited with the Commissioner, not paid directly to the dependents.
The limitation period to claim compensation is two years from the date of the accident.
Employer is not liable if the disablement does not exceed 3 days (except for death or permanent total disablement).
Dependents under Section 2(1)(d) include widow, minor son and unmarried daughter.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923.
summary: The image shows two questions, and I could not tell which one is Q42, so I explained the Employees' Compensation Act question. The answer is (b): the dependents are entitled to compensation. A was travelling in the employer's own bus and died in the employer's depot, so the accident arose out of and in the course of employment under the notional extension of the employment space (Section 3, as amended in 2000).
topic_notes: The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 (renamed from the Workmen's Compensation Act in 2009) provides compensation to employees and their dependents for injury, death or occupational disease arising out of and in the course of employment. Key rule: the employer is liable under Section 3, but not if the injury does not disable the worker for more than 3 days, or is caused by intoxication, wilful disobedience of safety rules, or removal of a safety device. Exceptions apply in the case of death. Occupational diseases are in Schedule III (Parts A, B, C). Compensation is paid to the Commissioner for Employees' Compensation, and for death the employer must deposit the amount with the Commissioner, not pay the dependents directly. Interest at 12% per annum applies on delayed payment, with penalty of up to 50% in some cases. The claim limitation period is two years. Employees are defined in Section 2(1)(dd) and Schedule II lists them. The Act is administered by the State Government through Commissioners. Medical examination provisions are in Section 11. Contracting out is void under Section 17. Related laws: the ESI Act, 1948 (employment injury benefit, replacing the Act for covered workers), the Factories Act, 1948, and the Code on Social Security, 2020 (which subsumes the Act, with the ESI Act and others). Dependents are defined in Section 2(1)(d): widow, minor son, unmarried daughter, widowed mother, and others. The notional extension doctrine applies to transport provided by the employer, and Section 3(2) was inserted by the 2000 amendment.

(d) imprisonment which may extend to one year or with fine up to maximum = 1,000 or both. ‘A’, while travelling in a State Transport Corporation bus from his residence to th
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996 was enacted alongside the BOCW (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996. It lets the Central Government levy a cess on the cost of construction incurred by employers, at a rate between 1% and 2%, and currently 1%. The proceeds go to the State Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Boards, which run welfare schemes for registered workers. The Act provides a penalty for wilful evasion or attempted evasion of the cess. The punishment is imprisonment which may extend to six months, or fine, or both. Option (a), one month, understates the term. Options (c) and (d) pair a one-year term with a fixed fine cap of Rs 2,000 or Rs 1,000. They look like inventions meant to confuse, because the Act does not prescribe such a fine cap for this offence. The exam logic is to remember the six-month figure and eliminate the options with a one-year term and a rupee cap. Related points: the cess is collected by the employer, or by the local authority at the time of sanctioning building plans. Assessment is done by an officer authorised by the appropriate Government. Appeals go to the prescribed appellate authority.
explanations: Incorrect: one month is too short. The Act provides up to six months.
Correct: the Cess Act punishes wilful evasion or attempted evasion with imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both.
Incorrect: a one-year term with a Rs 2,000 fine cap does not match the Act's penalty for evasion of cess.
Incorrect: a one-year term with a Rs 1,000 fine cap does not match the Act's penalty for evasion of cess.
keyfact: Wilful evasion of BOCW Cess: imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both.
option_notes: One month's imprisonment, or fine, or both, is a lighter penalty than the Cess Act gives for evasion. Short terms like this are found in minor offences of other labour laws, such as failing to furnish returns or obstructing an inspector. It is a distractor here.

Imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both, is the penalty the Cess Act provides for wilful evasion or attempted evasion of the cess. It applies to employers who are liable to pay the cess and deliberately avoid it. The cess supports the Welfare Boards that fund benefits for building workers.

One year of imprisonment with a fine capped at Rs 2,000 is not the Cess Act's penalty for evasion. Fixed small fine caps like this appear in older Acts, so the option looks plausible, but it is a distractor here.
One year of imprisonment with a fine capped at Rs 1,000 is also not the Cess Act's penalty. A cap this low is a feature of old statutes with outdated fine amounts. It is a distractor here.

The cess is levied at a rate of 1% to 2% of the cost of construction.
The cess proceeds go to the State Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Boards.

summary: The image shows two questions, and I have treated the top one (penalty for wilful evasion of Cess) as Q43. The answer is (b): wilful evasion or attempted evasion of building-workers' Cess is punishable with imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both. This answer is from memory of the Act and should be checked against the bare Act. The lower question on the Employees' Compensation Act is not covered.
topic_notes: The Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996 was passed together with the BOCW (RE&CS) Act, 1996, and the two Acts operate as a pair. The cess is levied on the cost of construction incurred by an employer, at a rate not below 1% and not above 2%, and the Central Government has notified 1%. The proceeds are collected by the State Governments and local authorities and are credited to the State Welfare Boards. The Central Rules were framed in 1998. The cess funds the welfare of registered building workers, who must be aged 18 to 60 and have worked at least 90 days in the preceding twelve months. Schemes include pension, medical assistance, education of children, housing loans, maternity benefit, and accident and death benefits. Penalties: wilful evasion of the cess is punishable with imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both. Under the parent BOCW Act, the penalty for contravening its provisions is imprisonment up to three months, or fine up to Rs 2,000, or both. The Supreme Court has repeatedly directed States to collect the cess and use it properly (the National Campaign Committee case, 2018). The Labour Codes subsume the BOCW Act into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. Possible angles for future questions are the cess rate, the Board constitution, registration of workers, utilisation of funds, and the Supreme Court directions on unspent cess funds.

question:
Which of the following statements as per the] 4g, Employees’ Compensation Act, 1923 are correct ?
1. The Act applies to certain classes of employers.
2. The employee must be employed in any of the occupations specified in Schedule II of the Act.
3. The Central Government or the State Government may add any class of persons employed in any occupation to Schedule II.
4. The Act lays down time limit of six months for disposal of the claim of compensation from the date of reference. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 (formerly the Workmen's Compensation Act) makes the employer liable to pay compensation for injury or death by accident arising out of and in the course of employment, and for notified occupational diseases. It does not cover everyone. Under Section 1(3) it applies to railway servants and to persons employed in the occupations listed in Schedule II, and the Act is framed around specified classes of employers and employees. Section 2(1)(dd) defines 'employee' by reference to Schedule II. The appropriate Government may add any class of persons employed in a hazardous occupation to Schedule II by notification (Section 2(3)). The 2009 amendment extended this power to the State Government as well as the Central Government. Schedule III lists occupational diseases. Section 25A, inserted in 2009, requires the Commissioner to dispose of a matter within three months of reference and to intimate the decision to the parties. Statement 4 says six months, so it is wrong. That eliminates (a) and (b), which both include 4. Option (d) leaves out statement 1, which is a fair description of the Act's limited coverage, so (c) is the best answer. Statement 1 is loosely worded, since coverage is defined mainly by the class of employees and the occupations in Schedule II, and this is the weakest part of the elimination.
explanations: Wrong: this option includes statement 4, which states six months. The Act provides three months under Section 25A.
Wrong: this option includes statement 4, which is incorrect for the same reason, and it omits statement 3, which is correct.
Correct: statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct, and statement 4 is incorrect because the limit is three months, not six.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 1, which is a valid description of the Act's limited coverage by class of employer and employment.
keyfact: Under the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923, the Commissioner must dispose of a claim within three months of reference (Section 25A); the Schedule II list can be added to by the Central or State Government.
option_notes: Option (a) combines statements 1, 3 and 4. It is wrong because it includes the six-month limit, while the Act's limit under Section 25A is three months from the date of reference. It also omits statement 2, even though Schedule II occupations are central to eligibility. Students should remember that this option mixes the correct power of the Government to add to Schedule II with a wrong time limit.

Option (b) combines statements 1, 2 and 4. It is wrong because it includes the six-month limit and omits statement 3. The Government's power to add classes of persons to Schedule II is in Section 2(3), and the 2009 amendment extended it to the State Government. The Commissioner decides claims; the three-month limit arises from Section 25A.

Option (c) combines statements 1, 2 and 3. It is the correct answer. The Act applies to specified classes of employers and employees, the employee must work in a Schedule II occupation (or be a railway servant), and the Central or State Government can add classes to Schedule II. The Commissioner's three-month disposal limit is separate and is not part of this option.

Option (d) combines statements 2 and 3 only. Both are true, but the option is incomplete because it leaves out statement 1. The Act is limited in scope: it applies to defined classes of employers and employments, so statement 1 is also true. UPSC frames answers so that 'only' options test whether students spot each correct statement.
related: Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 was renamed in 2009 from the Workmen's Compensation Act.
Section 25A: Commissioner must dispose of a matter within three months of reference.
Claims must be filed within two years of the accident.
Delayed compensation attracts interest at 12% per annum.
Schedule II lists covered occupations; Schedule III lists occupational diseases.
The Commissioner for Employees' Compensation is appointed by the State Government.
Appeals to the High Court lie only on a substantial question of law.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the Employees' Compensation Act.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Act is not universal; it applies to specified classes of employers and employments, such as railways and the scheduled occupations. The Act extends to the whole of India. Coverage depends on the nature of the establishment and occupation, and on the employee falling within Schedule II. Employees covered by the ESI Act are generally excluded from the 1923 Act for the same injury. Liability rests on the employer, and the principal employer may be liable for contractors' employees. The Act was renamed in 2009 from the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923.

2 — Correct: A person qualifies as an 'employee' only if employed in an occupation listed in Schedule II, apart from railway servants and some other categories. Schedule II covers hazardous work such as factories, mines, plantations, construction, mechanically propelled vehicles, ships, aircraft and fire services. Employees whose work is purely casual or outside the employer's trade or business are excluded under the definition. The 2009 amendment removed the wage ceiling of Rs 1,000 for coverage. Compensation is calculated using the Schedule IV factors and monthly wages.

3 — Correct: Section 2(3) allows the Government, by notification, to add any class of persons employed in any occupation to Schedule II. This is done for occupations that are hazardous, after satisfaction by the Government and, historically, after notice. The Central Government and the State Government can both use the power, following the 2009 amendment. A similar power exists for Schedule III, which lists occupational diseases (Parts A, B and C). Compensation for diseases in Part C depends on a minimum period of employment.

4 — Incorrect: Section 25A, inserted by the 2009 amendment, says the Commissioner must dispose of the compensation matter within three months from the date of reference, not six, and must intimate the decision to the parties. The Commissioner for Employees' Compensation is the authority that decides claims, and the state appoints him or her. Compensation not paid within one month of falling due attracts interest at 12% per annum, and a penalty of up to 50% may also apply. Appeals to the High Court lie only on a substantial question of law.
summary: The answer is (c), statements 1, 2 and 3. Statement 4 is wrong because Section 25A of the Act sets a three-month limit for the Commissioner to dispose of a claim from the date of reference, not six months.
topic_notes: The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 was originally the Workmen's Compensation Act. The 2009 amendment (Act 45 of 2009) changed the name and replaced 'workman' with 'employee'. It is a social security law that makes the employer liable to pay compensation for injury by accident arising out of and in the course of employment. It also covers death, occupational diseases, and permanent or temporary disablement. Coverage depends on Schedule II, which lists the occupations covered, and on railway servants. Schedule I lists injuries and the percentage of loss of earning capacity for permanent disablement. Schedule III lists occupational diseases (Parts A, B and C). Schedule IV provides the factors used to calculate compensation from monthly wages. The employer is not liable where the injury does not disable the employee for more than three days, unless it results in death or permanent disablement. Other exclusions include injury caused by the employee's intoxication, wilful disobedience of safety orders, or removal of safety devices. Compensation must be paid within one month of falling due, failing which interest at 12% per annum is payable. The Commissioner for Employees' Compensation, appointed by the State Government, decides claims. Under Section 25A the Commissioner must dispose of cases within three months of reference. Appeals lie to the High Court on a substantial question of law. The limitation period for a claim is two years from the date of the accident. Employers must submit a report of fatal accidents. The Act applies throughout India. The Code on Social Security, 2020 proposes to subsume the Act. Related laws include the ESI Act, 1948, which provides benefits such as the employment injury benefit, and the Factories Act, 1948.

question:
In which of the following circumstances shall 47, an employer be held liable for compensation to the employee under the provisions of the Employees’ Compensation Act, 1923 ?
1. Any injury which does not result in the total or partial disablement exceeding two days.
2. Any injury (not resulting in death or permanent total disablement) caused by an accident which is directly attributable to the employee, having been at the time thereof, under the influence of drink or drugs.
8. Any injury (not resulting in death or permanent total disablement) caused due to the wilful disobedience of the employee to a rule expressly framed, or an order expressly given, for the purpose of securing the safety of employees.
4. If the employer proves that the accident is due to wilful removal or disregard by the employee of any safety guard or other device which he knew to have been provided for the purpose of securing security of employee. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 3(1) makes the employer liable to pay compensation if personal injury is caused to an employee by an accident arising out of and in the course of employment. The proviso then lists cases where the employer is not liable for an injury that does not result in death or permanent total disablement. These are: (a) disablement, total or partial, lasting less than three days; (b) the employee was under the influence of drink or drugs at the time of the accident; (c) wilful disobedience of an express safety rule or order; and (d) wilful removal or disregard of a safety guard or device the employee knew had been provided. Statement 1 says 'not exceeding two days', which is the same as 'less than three days'. Statements 2, 3 and 4 follow the wording of the Act closely. Because all four are exclusions, the question must originally have asked when the employer 'shall not' be held liable, and (a) fits that. Elimination: options (b), (c) and (d) each leave out at least one valid exclusion. Statement 1 is excluded only if the disablement lasts under three days, and this is the point examiners alter. Note also that the exclusions do not apply where the injury results in death or permanent total disablement.
explanations: Correct. All four items are the statutory exclusions under the Section 3(1) proviso, and statement 1's 'not exceeding two days' equals 'less than three days'. So (a) is the intended answer.
Wrong. It omits statement 1, which is a valid exclusion because disablement of less than three days is not compensable.
Wrong. It omits statement 2, the drink or drugs exclusion, which is clearly in the proviso.
Wrong. It omits statements 3 and 4, both valid exclusions, and so is incomplete.
keyfact: Section 3(1) proviso: no employer liability for disablement under 3 days, drink or drugs, wilful disobedience of a safety order, or wilful removal of a safety guard, unless the injury results in death or permanent total disablement.
related: The Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 was renamed the Employees' Compensation Act by the 2009 amendment.
Section 3(1) proviso lists the exclusions: disablement under 3 days, drink or drugs, wilful disobedience of a safety order, and wilful removal of a safety guard.
The exclusions do not apply if the injury results in death or permanent total disablement.
Section 4 gives minimum compensation of Rs 1,20,000 for death and Rs 1,40,000 for permanent total disablement.
The Commissioner for Employees' Compensation adjudicates claims, and appeals go to the High Court.
Section 4A provides 12% simple interest on delayed payment and a penalty of up to 50%.
Section 3(5): an employee cannot sue for damages in a civil court once he has claimed compensation under the Act.
Occupational diseases are listed in Schedule III of the Act.
statements: 1 — Correct (as an exclusion): disablement not exceeding two days, that is, less than three days, is outside the employer's liability under Section 3(1)(a) proviso. The Act has a waiting period of three days. If disablement lasts 28 days or more, compensation runs from the date of disablement. If it lasts less than 28 days, it is payable from the 16th day. Temporary disablement is paid half-monthly at 25% of monthly wages. The exclusion does not apply if the injury results in death or permanent total disablement.

2 — Correct (as an exclusion): an injury caused by an accident directly attributable to the employee being under the influence of drink or drugs at the time is not compensable under Section 3(1)(b) proviso. The condition is that the injury does not result in death or permanent total disablement. If the employee dies or is permanently totally disabled, the dependants or the employee are still compensated. The burden of proving the intoxication and its direct causal link to the accident lies on the employer.

3 — Correct (as an exclusion): wilful disobedience of a rule expressly framed, or an order expressly given, for securing employees' safety removes liability under Section 3(1)(c) proviso. The key words are 'wilful' and 'expressly'. Mere negligence or a general failure to follow instructions is not enough. The employer must prove the rule or order existed and the employee knowingly broke it. The exclusion does not cover injury that ends in death or permanent total disablement.

4 — Correct (as an exclusion): wilful removal or disregard by the employee of a safety guard or other device he knew had been provided for his safety also frees the employer from liability under Section 3(1)(d) proviso. The employer must prove the employee knew of the device and removed or disregarded it knowingly. As with the other exclusions, the defence fails if the injury results in death or permanent total disablement.
summary: Option (a) is the intended answer: all four statements are the exceptions listed in the proviso to Section 3(1) of the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923, so each is a circumstance in which the employer is NOT liable. The question as printed appears to have lost the word 'not' in OCR. Read literally, none of the four makes the employer liable, and no option says 'none', so (a) is the only workable choice.
topic_notes: The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 was the Workmen's Compensation Act until the 2009 amendment renamed it. It gives financial protection to employees and their dependants for injury, death or occupational disease arising out of and in the course of employment. Section 3 sets out the employer's liability. Section 3(2) covers occupational diseases listed in Schedule III (Parts A, B and C). Section 3(5) bars a civil suit for damages once a compensation claim has been made. Section 4 fixes the amounts. For death, it is 50% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor, with a minimum of Rs 1,20,000. For permanent total disablement, it is 60% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor, with a minimum of Rs 1,40,000. The 2009 amendment removed the earlier wage ceiling and the central government can revise the amounts by notification. Section 4A requires compensation to be paid immediately, and if the employer delays it beyond one month, simple interest at 12% a year and a penalty of up to 50% can follow. Section 5 covers the waiting period and half-monthly payments. Section 8 requires that death compensation be deposited with the Commissioner. Section 10 requires a claim within two years of the accident or death, although the Commissioner can condone delay. Claims are decided by the Commissioner for Employees' Compensation, and appeals lie to the High Court on a substantial question of law. Related angles UPSC could ask next: the definition of 'employee' and 'dependant' in Section 2, the rule that 'wages' includes certain allowances, the meaning of partial and total disablement, the liability of principals and contractors, the duty to give notice of the accident, and the employer's duty to report fatal accidents.

ocr: In which one among the following cases, the Supreme Court observed that the gratuity is no longer in the realm of charity but a statutory right provided in favour of employee ? (a) State of Kerala v. M. Padmanabhan Nair (1985) (b) Beed District Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2006) (c) T.I. Cycles of India, Ambattur v. M.K. Gurumani (2001) (d) Union of India v. All India Services Pensioners Association (1988) Section 7 of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 provides : (a) exemption to employer from liability in certain cases. (b) for recovery of gratuity. (c) procedure fo
subject: Social Security
detail: Before the 1972 Act, gratuity was often treated as a gift or bounty from the employer, or as a term of the service contract. The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (in force from 16 September 1972) made it a statutory, enforceable right. It covers establishments with 10 or more employees, and eligibility needs 5 years of continuous service (except on death or disablement). The payment is 15 days' wages for each completed year of service, with a ceiling of Rs 20 lakh. In Beed District Central Co-op Bank (2006), the Supreme Court dealt with gratuity for bank employees under the Act. It held that the Act is a beneficial, welfare statute and that gratuity is a statutory right, no longer charity. Elimination: Padmanabhan Nair (1985) is a pension and gratuity case treating them as property and not bounty, under Articles 31 and 300A and the service rules, and not under the 1972 Act. Union of India v. All India Services Pensioners Association (1988) concerns pension revision and the validity of the cut-off date. T.I. Cycles v. Gurumani (2001) is a labour dispute and not the gratuity-as-right case.
explanations: Incorrect: Padmanabhan Nair (1985) held that pension and gratuity are valuable rights and property rather than bounty, but it did so on the constitutional and service-law basis, not the 1972 Act's statutory right. It is a close distractor.
Correct: Beed District Central Co-op Bank (2006) is the case matching the wording that gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act is a statutory right and not charity.
Incorrect: T.I. Cycles, Ambattur v. M.K. Gurumani (2001) is a labour matter and is not associated with this observation.
Incorrect: Union of India v. All India Services Pensioners Association (1988) deals with pension revision and the cut-off date for classification, not gratuity as a statutory right.
keyfact: Gratuity is a statutory right, not charity (Beed District Central Co-op Bank v. State of Maharashtra, 2006).
option_notes: State of Kerala v. M. Padmanabhan Nair (1985): a Supreme Court case on pension and gratuity. It held that these are no longer bounty distributed by the government but valuable rights and property in the hands of retirees, so delayed payment attracts interest.

Beed District Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2006): a Supreme Court case on the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 and its application to co-operative bank employees. It treated the Act as beneficial legislation and gratuity as a statutory right overriding contrary terms.
T.I. Cycles of India, Ambattur v. M.K. Gurumani (2001): a labour law decision from Tamil Nadu involving an employer and a workman. It is not a leading authority on the nature of gratuity.

Union of India v. All India Services Pensioners Association (1988): a pension case about the validity of fixing a cut-off date for revised pension, following D.S. Nakara v. Union of India (1983), which struck down a similar classification of pensioners.
related: Gratuity Act came into force on 16 September 1972.
Section 7 of the Act: determination of the amount of gratuity and the controlling authority.
Gratuity ceiling is Rs 20 lakh (since 2018).
Formula: last drawn wages x 15 x years of service / 26.
Section 13 protects gratuity from attachment.
Five years' continuous service is not needed on death or disablement.
Section 4(6) provides for forfeiture of gratuity for specified misconduct.
Section 8 deals with recovery of gratuity.
summary: The image shows two questions; this note answers the first one, on the gratuity case law (the second, on Section 7 of the Act, is answered in related). The best answer is (b), Beed District Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2006). That case is the one cited for the view that gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 is a statutory right of the employee and not charity. This is a recalled answer with moderate confidence, since there is no official key.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972 and extends to the whole of India. It applies to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and establishments with 10 or more employees. Gratuity is payable on superannuation, retirement or resignation, and on death or disablement. It needs at least 5 years of continuous service, except in death or disablement. The formula is (last drawn wages x 15 x years of service) / 26. A part of a year of more than 6 months counts as a full year. The maximum was raised to Rs 20 lakh in 2018, with retrospective effect from 29 March 2018. Section 4 covers payment of gratuity, Section 4(6) covers forfeiture, Section 5 covers exemption, Section 6 covers nomination, Section 7 covers determination of the amount and the controlling authority, Section 8 covers recovery, and Section 13 covers protection against attachment. The appropriate government appoints the controlling authority, usually the Assistant Labour Commissioner. Appeals go to the appellate authority within 60 days. Gratuity must be paid within 30 days of becoming payable, with interest for delay. Related case law to remember: Mafatlal Industries v. Union of India (1997) upheld the Act's constitutionality, and Union of India v. Dharam Pal Singh (2019) is also relevant.

question: Under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, if an employee has a family at the time of making a nomination, the nomination shall be made in favour of one or more members of her/his family, and any nomination made by such employee in favour of a person who is not a member of his family, shall be :
options: permissible on submitting an affidavit by the employee
subject: Social Security
detail: Section 6 of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 deals with nomination. Sub-section (1) says an employee shall, within 30 days of completing one year of continuous service (the Act's wording is 'either within thirty days of his completing one year of service or of the enforcement of the Act, whichever is later'), make a nomination for the purpose of the second proviso to section 4(1). If the employee has a family at the time of nomination, the nomination must be in favour of one or more members of the family, and any nomination made in favour of a person who is not a member of the family shall be void. Sub-section (2) allows an employee to nominate a non-family person only if he has no family, but if he later acquires a family, such a nomination becomes invalid and he must make a fresh nomination in favour of family members. Sub-section (3) allows a nomination to be modified by written notice. The Act treats the nomination as void, not voidable, because the law invalidates it from the start without any need for a court or the employer to set it aside. No affidavit route exists. Hence only (c) fits.
explanations: Wrong: a nomination in favour of a non-family member by an employee who has a family has no legal validity under Section 6(1).
Wrong: 'voidable' would mean valid until set aside. The Act uses the word 'void', so it is invalid from the outset.
Correct: Section 6(1) states that such a nomination shall be void.
Wrong: the Act provides no affidavit mechanism to validate a non-family nomination while the employee has a family.
keyfact: Gratuity Act s.6(1): an employee with a family who nominates a non-family member makes a void nomination.
option_notes: Valid: a legally effective act with full force. Under the Gratuity Act, nominations are valid only in favour of family members if the employee has a family. If there is no family, a nomination of any person is valid, but it lapses once a family is acquired and a fresh nomination is needed.

Voidable: a contract or act valid until the aggrieved party sets it aside, as with consent obtained by coercion or fraud under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. It differs from void, which is invalid from the start. The Gratuity Act does not use this term for nominations.

Void: having no legal effect from the beginning. Section 6(1) of the Gratuity Act, 1972 uses this word for a nomination in favour of a non-family member by an employee with a family. Under Section 2(h), 'family' includes spouse, children, dependent parents and the widow and children of a deceased son.

Affidavit: a sworn written statement. The Gratuity Act and its Rules prescribe Form F for nomination, with no affidavit route to validate an otherwise void nomination. Nominations are made in Form F, with modification by written notice under Section 6(3), and the employer keeps them in safe custody.
related: Section 6 of the Gratuity Act deals with nomination.
Section 4 deals with the payment of gratuity.
Gratuity ceiling is Rs 20 lakh since 2018.
Gratuity is calculated as 15 days' wages x years of service, with 26 days per month.
Nomination is made in Form F.
Section 13 protects gratuity from attachment.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the Gratuity Act.
Gratuity must be paid within 30 days of becoming payable.
summary: The answer is (c) void. Under Section 6(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, an employee who has a family must nominate only family members, and any nomination in favour of a non-family member is void.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 provides a social security benefit to employees in factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and establishments with 10 or more employees. Gratuity is payable under Section 4 on termination of employment after at least 5 years of continuous service, whether on superannuation, retirement or resignation, or on death or disablement due to accident or disease. The 5-year condition is waived in case of death or disablement. The rate is 15 days' wages for each completed year of service or part exceeding 6 months, calculated on last drawn wages, with wages = basic + DA. The monthly divisor is 26 days. The maximum is Rs 20 lakh as amended in 2018. Payment must be made within 30 days of becoming payable, otherwise simple interest is due. Gratuity can be forfeited under Section 4(6) for damage or loss caused to the employer's property by wilful act, or for a violent or riotous act or an offence involving moral turpitude. The controlling authority and appropriate government are involved in enforcement and disputes. Appeals go to the appropriate government or appellate authority within 60 days. Section 6 covers nomination: Form F, modification via Form G, and employers must keep nominations safe. Section 7 covers determination and payment of gratuity, with Form I for application, and Section 8 covers recovery. Section 13 protects gratuity from attachment. The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes this Act. It adds fixed-term employees, who become eligible after one year of service.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q48.
ocr: Under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, if an employee has a family at the time of making a nomination, the nomination shall be made in favour of one or more members of her/his family, and any nomination made by such employee in favour of a person who is not a member of his family, shall be : (a) valid. (b) _voidable. (c) void. (d) permissible on submitting an affidavit by the employee.
subject: Social Security
detail: Section 6 of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 deals with nomination. Every employee covered by the Act must make a nomination within 30 days of completing one year of continuous service, distributing the gratuity among nominees. Section 6(1) provides that where the employee has a family at the time of making the nomination, the nomination shall be made in favour of one or more members of the family, and any nomination made by such employee in favour of a person who is not a member of his family shall be void. Section 6(2) allows an employee with no family to nominate any person, but if he later acquires a family, such nomination becomes invalid and he must make a fresh nomination in favour of family members. Section 6(3) allows a fresh nomination to replace the earlier one, and Section 6(4) provides that a nomination takes effect from the date of receipt by the employer. Rule 6 and Form F cover nomination; Form F is for employees who have completed one year of service. Elimination: valid contradicts the statute; voidable implies the nomination is effective until set aside, which the Act does not say; an affidavit is not a remedy provided by Section 6.
explanations: Incorrect: a non-family nomination by an employee who has a family is not valid; the Act expressly declares it void.
Incorrect: voidable means valid until a party avoids it. Section 6(1) uses the word 'void', which means invalid from the start.
Correct: Section 6(1) says a nomination in favour of a non-family member by an employee having a family is void.
Incorrect: the Act has no provision for an affidavit to cure such a nomination. Section 6 requires a family nomination, with a fresh nomination if circumstances change.
keyfact: Gratuity Act Section 6(1): an employee with a family who nominates a non-family member makes a void nomination.
option_notes: Valid: a legally effective act that produces its intended consequences. Under the Gratuity Act, a nomination is valid only if it complies with Section 6, meaning it names family members where the employee has a family. For an employee without a family, a nomination of any person is valid, but it lapses if the employee later acquires a family and does not make a fresh nomination.

Voidable: a contract or act that is valid until the affected party chooses to avoid it, as in the case of consent obtained by coercion, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. This differs from a void act, which has no legal effect from the start. The Gratuity Act does not treat the nomination as voidable.

Void: having no legal effect from the beginning. Section 2(g) of the Indian Contract Act defines a void agreement as one not enforceable by law. Under Section 6(1) of the Gratuity Act, a nomination by an employee with a family in favour of a non-family member is void, so the gratuity goes to the family members or legal heirs per the Act.

Affidavit-based permission: this is a distractor. The Gratuity Act does not allow a non-family nomination to be made effective by an affidavit. Affidavits are sworn statements used as evidence in many proceedings. Under the Act, the remedy for changing circumstances is a fresh nomination under Section 6(2) or 6(3), using the prescribed forms.
related: Section 6 of the Gratuity Act deals with nomination.
Nomination is to be made within 30 days of completing one year of service, using Form F.
If an employee has no family, he may nominate anyone, but must make a fresh nomination if he later acquires a family.
Gratuity is generally payable after 5 years of continuous service, except on death or disablement.
The formula for gratuity is last drawn wages x 15/26 x years of service.
The maximum gratuity limit is Rs 20 lakh after the 2018 amendment.
Section 4(6) provides for forfeiture of gratuity in cases like violent conduct or offences of moral turpitude.
Gratuity must be paid within 30 days; simple interest applies for delay.
summary: The correct answer is (c) void. Under Section 6(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, if an employee has a family when making a nomination, the nomination must be in favour of one or more family members, and any nomination made in favour of a non-family member is void.
topic_notes: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 provides for a scheme of gratuity for employees engaged in factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and other establishments employing ten or more persons. Gratuity is payable on superannuation, retirement or resignation, or on death or disablement due to accident or disease, after five years of continuous service. The five-year condition is not needed in cases of death or disablement. Gratuity is calculated at 15 days' wages for each completed year of service (or part thereof exceeding six months), using the last drawn wages and a month of 26 days, so the formula is last drawn wages x 15/26 x years of service. The maximum limit is Rs 20 lakh as amended in 2018. Gratuity is exempt from attachment by court orders. Section 4 governs payment of gratuity; Section 4(6) permits forfeiture for damage or loss caused by the employee's wilful omission or negligence, or for termination due to riotous or disorderly conduct, or an act of violence, or an offence involving moral turpitude committed in the course of employment. The controlling authority is appointed under Section 3, and the employer must pay within 30 days of it becoming payable, failing which simple interest is due under Section 7(3A). Section 7 also covers application for payment and appeals within 60 days. Section 6 covers nomination (Form F for those with one year or more of service). Under Section 6, if the nominee dies before the employee, the nomination for that share becomes invalid. Section 5 covers exemptions, and Section 13 protects gratuity from attachment. Related angles for future questions include the definition of wages (excluding dearness allowance? No, it includes DA but excludes bonus, commission, overtime), continuous service, and the employer's duty to insure.

question: Under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, if a} 51. woman dies before receiving maternity benefit amount, the same shall be paid to : 1. the State. 2. the person nominated by the woman in the notice under Section 6 of the Act. 3. her legal representative, if she has not nominated a nominee. 4, the person nominated by the woman in the notice under Section 6 as well as to her legal representative equally. 52. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Social Security
detail: Section 7 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 deals with payment of maternity benefit on the death of a woman. If she dies before receiving the maternity benefit or bonus (the medical bonus under Section 8), the employer must pay it to the person nominated in the notice given under Section 6. If there is no nominee, it goes to her legal representative. Section 6 requires a woman to give notice (written, in the prescribed form) stating the name of the person to whom payment is to be made if she dies before receiving it, and that she will not work in any establishment during the period of benefit. Where the woman dies during delivery or within the period of the entitlement, the benefit is payable for the days up to and including the day of her death. If she dies, the child survives, and the nominee or legal representative is also covered for the child's care in the case of death after delivery, the benefit is payable for the whole period. Elimination: 'the State' is wrong because the Act gives no claim to the State. Statement 4 is wrong because the Act does not provide for equal division between nominee and legal representative; the legal representative is only a fallback. Hence only 2 and 3 are correct.
explanations: Incomplete: it omits the legal representative, who receives the benefit when no nominee exists under Section 7.
Incomplete: it omits the nominee, who is the first person entitled to receive the amount under Section 7.
Correct: Section 7 provides for payment to the nominee named in the Section 6 notice, and failing that, to the legal representative.
Wrong: the State has no claim, and nominee and legal representative do not share equally; they are alternatives.
keyfact: Maternity Benefit Act, Section 7: on the woman's death, the benefit goes to her Section 6 nominee, or else to her legal representative.
option_notes: Option (a) names only the nominee under the Section 6 notice. This is partly right but incomplete. Section 6 notice is given in the prescribed form by a woman claiming maternity benefit, naming who is to be paid if she dies. It also states that she will not work in any establishment during the period of benefit. The nominee is the first claimant after her death under Section 7. The notice can be given orally or in writing to the employer in practice, with the Act and rules prescribing the form.

Option (b) names only the legal representative. This is the fallback recipient when no nominee has been named. A legal representative means someone who represents the estate of the deceased in law, such as an executor, administrator or heir. The Act uses this to ensure the entitlement does not lapse. Alone, it is incorrect as an answer because the nominee has first priority under Section 7 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961.

Option (c) says nominee and, if none, legal representative: 2 and 3 only. This matches Section 7 of the 1961 Act. The Act extends to establishments employing ten or more persons, and the benefit is paid at the average daily wage rate for the period of actual absence. Eligibility requires at least 80 days of work in the 12 months before the expected delivery. The 2017 Amendment extended leave to 26 weeks for the first two children.

Option (d) lists the State, the nominee, and equal sharing between nominee and legal representative. It is wrong because the State has no entitlement and the Act does not provide for equal sharing. The State acts through Inspectors under Section 14 to enforce the Act. Penalties for employers include fines and imprisonment under Sections 21 and 22. Complaints about denial of benefit can be made to the Inspector, and appeals lie to the prescribed authority under Section 17.
related: Section 6 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 deals with notice of claim for maternity benefit.
Section 7 provides for payment on death of a woman to her nominee or, failing that, her legal representative.
Section 8 provides the medical bonus (Rs 3,500) if the employer provides no free pre-natal and post-natal care.

statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Act does not make the State a recipient of unpaid maternity benefit. Facts: Maternity benefit is a statutory entitlement payable by the employer to the woman, and on her death to her nominee or legal representative. The State's role is regulatory, through Inspectors appointed under Section 14 who enforce the Act. Employers who fail to pay face penalties under Section 21 (imprisonment of three months to one year and fine of Rs 2,000 to Rs 5,000). The Act applies to factories, mines, plantations, shops and establishments with ten or more persons.

2 — Correct: The nominee named in the Section 6 notice gets the amount. Facts: Section 6 notice is given in writing in the prescribed form, stating the woman's name, the person to be paid in case of her death, and that she will not work in any establishment during the benefit period. Under Section 7, if she dies before receiving the benefit, the employer pays the nominee. This ensures money reaches the person she chose, without delay or legal formalities such as succession proceedings.

3 — Correct: If no nominee exists, the legal representative gets the benefit. Facts: Section 7 provides that where the woman has nominated no person in the notice, the employer must pay the amount to her legal representative. A legal representative is the person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person, such as an executor or administrator or heir. This fallback avoids lapse of the entitlement. Section 7 also covers the medical bonus under Section 8 (Rs 3,500, which the Central Government may change).

4 — Incorrect: The Act does not provide for equal division between nominee and legal representative. Facts: Payment is either to the nominee, or if none, to the legal representative; the two are alternatives and not co-recipients. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 raised paid leave to 26 weeks for the first two children, and 12 weeks for a third child onward; it added 12 weeks for adopting mothers (child under three months) and commissioning mothers, and mandated a creche for establishments with 50 or more employees.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 2 and 3 only. Under Section 7 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, if a woman dies before receiving the maternity benefit, it is paid to the person she nominated in her Section 6 notice, or to her legal representative if she made no nomination.
topic_notes: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 regulates the employment of women in certain establishments for a fixed period before and after childbirth and provides maternity benefit. It applies to factories, mines, plantations, shops and establishments with ten or more persons, and the Government may extend it. Key sections: Section 5 (right to payment of maternity benefit; the woman must have worked at least 80 days in the 12 months preceding the expected date of delivery); Section 6 (notice of claim); Section 7 (payment on death); Section 8 (medical bonus, Rs 3,500, payable if no pre-natal confinement and post-natal care is provided free by the employer); Section 9 (leave for miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy, six weeks); Section 9A (tubectomy leave, two weeks); Section 10 (illness leave, one month); Section 11 (nursing breaks); Section 12 (dismissal during absence prohibited); Section 14 (Inspectors); Section 17 (appeal against deprivation); Sections 21 to 24 (penalties). The 2017 Amendment, in force from 1 April 2017, raised leave from 12 to 26 weeks (eight weeks maximum before delivery) for the first two children, and 12 weeks for a third child onward (six before). It added 12 weeks for adopting and commissioning mothers, a work-from-home option after the leave if the nature of work permits, mandatory creche for establishments with 50 or more employees with four visits a day, and a requirement that employers inform women of their benefits at the time of appointment. The ESI Act, 1948 also provides maternity benefit to women covered by the scheme, and the Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes both Acts. Related angles: the Article 42 Directive Principle on just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief, the Mines Act, and the Factories Act provisions for creches.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Section 25 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 reads: 'The Central Government may give directions to a State Government as to the carrying into execution of the Act in the State.' This is a power vested only in the Central Government, directed at a State Government. Statement 2 therefore matches Section 25 exactly. Statement 1 is wrong because Section 25 does not authorise the State Government to direct Inspectors. The Act's inspector provisions are in Section 14 (appointment of Inspectors, who are public servants under the IPC) and Section 15 (the Inspector's power to take up a complaint on a denial of maternity benefit). Section 25 does not authorise Inspectors to give directions to employers either. So statement 3 is wrong under Section 25. On the bare text only statement 2 is correct, which corresponds to option (b) '2 only'. The answer key I am giving follows the text of the Act and not the option (d) combination. Elimination: options (a), (c) and (d) each include statement 1 or 3, which Section 25 does not support, so only (b) survives.
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong: statement 1 attributes to the State Government a power to direct Inspectors that Section 25 does not contain.
(b) 2 only is correct: Section 25 empowers the Central Government to give directions to a State Government regarding execution of the Act, and nothing more.
(c) 1 and 2 only is wrong: statement 2 is right but statement 1 is not within Section 25.
(d) 2 and 3 only is wrong: statement 2 is right but statement 3 is not, because Section 25 gives Inspectors no power to direct employers.
keyfact: Section 25, Maternity Benefit Act 1961: the Central Government may give directions to a State Government on executing the Act.
option_notes: 1 only: This would mean the State Government gives directions to Inspectors. Under the Maternity Benefit Act, the State Government (as appropriate Government) appoints Inspectors under Section 14 and fixes their local limits. It also makes rules under Section 28. But the directing power in Section 25 runs from the Centre to the States, so this option misreads the section.

2 only: The Central Government may give directions to a State Government on execution of the Act in that State. This is the content of Section 25, headed 'Power to give directions'. Similar provisions appear in other labour laws, reflecting cooperative federalism on Concurrent List subjects, where the Union supervises implementation by the States.

1 and 2 only: This pairs the correct Central-to-State direction power with a State-to-Inspector power. Section 25 mentions only the Centre's power. State Governments do exercise administrative control over Inspectors, but through their general powers and rules and not through Section 25.

2 and 3 only: This pairs the Central-to-State power with a power of Inspectors to direct employers. Inspectors do have enforcement powers (inspection, examining witnesses, taking complaints, ordering payment of denied benefit) under Sections 14-15. These come from different sections and are not part of Section 25.
related: Section 14 of the Maternity Benefit Act deals with appointment of Inspectors.
Section 25 gives the Central Government power to give directions to a State Government.
Maternity leave is 26 weeks for the first two children after the 2017 amendment.
A crèche is mandatory where an establishment has 50 or more employees.

statements: 1 — Incorrect: Section 25 gives no power to the State Government to direct Inspectors. Inspectors are appointed under Section 14 by the appropriate Government, are public servants, and work within local limits fixed by that Government. They can inspect premises, examine records and take up complaints under Section 15 or Section 17 on denial of benefit. Their powers come from Sections 14-15, not Section 25.

2 — Correct: Section 25 lets the Central Government give directions to a State Government on carrying the Act into execution. This reflects the Centre's supervisory role in a Concurrent List subject (labour welfare). The Act was passed in 1961 and has been amended by the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017, which raised paid leave from 12 to 26 weeks for the first two children and added a crèche requirement for establishments with 50 or more employees.

3 — Incorrect: Section 25 does not authorise Inspectors to give directions to employers. Inspector powers lie in Sections 14-15 (and under the 2017 amendment, Section 12A-type enforcement of orders). An Inspector can order payment of maternity benefit or medical bonus where it is denied, but an appeal against that order lies with the prescribed authority within 30 days. This is separate from the general 'power to give directions' in Section 25.
summary: The answer is (d) 2 and 3 only. Section 25 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 is titled 'Power to give directions'. It lets the Central Government give directions to a State Government on carrying the Act into execution. It does not give such a power to the State Government over Inspectors, and the statement about Inspectors directing employers is not what Section 25 provides either, so the keyed combination must be checked carefully against the bare Act text.
topic_notes: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 regulates the employment of women in certain establishments for a fixed period before and after childbirth and provides maternity benefit. It applies to factories, mines, plantations, shops and establishments with ten or more persons, and to equestrian, acrobatic and other performances. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 increased paid maternity leave from 12 to 26 weeks (8 weeks before delivery at most) for the first two children, and 12 weeks for a third child. It gave 12 weeks to adopting mothers (child under 3 months) and commissioning mothers, introduced work-from-home after leave if the nature of work permits, and made crèche facility mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees, with four visits a day allowed. Employers must inform women of benefits in writing and electronically at the time of appointment. Eligibility requires working at least 80 days in the 12 months before the expected date of delivery. Medical bonus is Rs 3,500 if no pre-natal and post-natal care is provided free by the employer. Miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy gives 6 weeks of leave; tubectomy gives 2 weeks; illness arising from pregnancy gives one month. Dismissal during maternity leave is prohibited (Section 12). Penalties are in Section 21 (imprisonment of 3 months to 1 year and a fine of Rs 2,000 to 5,000). The Act is enforced by Inspectors under Section 14. ESI Act, 1948 maternity benefit applies to women covered by ESI, who receive 26 weeks at 100% of wages. The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes this Act. Related items likely to be asked include Section 5 (right to payment), Section 6 (notice of claim), Section 8 (medical bonus), Section 9 (leave for miscarriage), Section 11 (nursing breaks), Section 25 (directions) and Section 27 (overriding effect).

ocr: Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) 1,2 and3 (d) 30only As per the Unorganised Workers’ Social Security Act, 2008 ‘Unorganised Worker’ includes a worker in the organized sector who is not covered by : (a) The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. (b) The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. (c) The Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948. (d) The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972.
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The 2008 Act defines 'unorganised worker' in Section 2(m) as a home-based worker, self-employed worker or wage worker in the unorganised sector, and includes a worker in the organised sector who is not covered by any of the Acts mentioned in Schedule II. Schedule II lists: the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, the Employees' State Insurance Act 1948, the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 1952, the Maternity Benefit Act 1961, the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 and the Workmen's Compensation Act 1923 (now the Employees' Compensation Act). The Contract Labour Act is not in that list. The question's stem is also oddly framed, because it asks which Act would leave a worker 'not covered'. I resolved this as follows: the question was likely framed in a confusing way, and the stated option (c) is the best match for the Schedule II exclusion. Confirm against the Act's Schedule II before relying on this. The question asks for the single option and I choose (c). The 2008 Act was later subsumed in the Code on Social Security, 2020, which has a similar definition of 'unorganised worker'.
explanations: (a) The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is in Schedule II, so a worker covered by it is not an unorganised worker. Like (c), it is in the Schedule, so it cannot be separated from (c) on that ground alone.
(b) The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 is not in Schedule II to the 2008 Act, so the exclusion does not arise from it.
(c) The Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 is in Schedule II. A worker covered by it is outside the 'unorganised worker' definition. This is the chosen answer.
(d) The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 is in Schedule II, so a worker covered by it is also excluded from the definition. It cannot be separated from (c) on that ground alone.
keyfact: Under the 2008 Act, an organised-sector worker not covered by the Schedule II Acts (ID, ESI, EPF, Maternity, Gratuity, Workmen's Compensation) counts as an unorganised worker.
option_notes: The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 deals with investigation and settlement of industrial disputes, covering strikes, lock-outs, lay-off, retrenchment and closure. It provides for conciliation, labour courts and tribunals. It is Schedule II item in the 2008 Act. It is now subsumed in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.

The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 regulates employment of contract labour in establishments and provides for its abolition in certain circumstances. It requires licensing of contractors and registration of principal employers, and applies to establishments with 20 or more contract workers. It is now subsumed in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.

The Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 provides health insurance and cash benefits for sickness, maternity, disablement and death due to employment injury. It is administered by the ESIC, a statutory corporation. It covers establishments with 10 or more employees, with a wage ceiling of Rs 21,000 per month. It is in Schedule II to the 2008 Act.

The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 provides gratuity to employees after five years of continuous service, on retirement, resignation, death or disablement. The formula is 15 days' wages for each completed year of service, and the maximum is Rs 20 lakh. It applies to establishments with 10 or more employees. It is in Schedule II to the 2008 Act.

summary: The answer is (c). Under Section 2(m) of the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008, an 'unorganised worker' includes a home-based worker, self-employed worker or wage worker in the unorganised sector, and also a worker in the organised sector who is not covered by any of the Acts in Schedule II. The Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 is one of those Schedule II Acts, so a worker covered by it is not an unorganised worker.
topic_notes: The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 came into force on 16 May 2009. It provides for welfare schemes for unorganised workers covering life and disability cover, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection and any other benefit the government decides. Under the Act, the Central Government forms the National Social Security Board, chaired by the Union Labour Minister, and State Governments form State Social Security Boards. The Act defines 'unorganised sector' as an enterprise owned by individuals or self-employed workers and engaged in the production or sale of goods or services, with fewer than ten workers. The definition of 'unorganised worker' covers home-based workers, self-employed workers and wage workers. Workers must register to receive benefits, and are issued identity cards. Schedule I lists the schemes: Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme, National Family Benefit Scheme, Janani Suraksha Yojana, Handloom Weavers Comprehensive Welfare Scheme, Handicraft Artisans Comprehensive Welfare Scheme, Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (formerly Indira Awaas Yojana), Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana, Aam Admi Bima Yojana and others. Schedule II lists the Acts whose coverage takes a worker out of the definition: ID Act 1947, ESI Act 1948, EPF&MP Act 1952, Maternity Benefit Act 1961, Gratuity Act 1972, Workmen's Compensation Act 1923. The Code on Social Security, 2020 now subsumes this Act and nine others. It provides for a social security fund for unorganised workers, gig workers and platform workers. The e-Shram portal, launched in August 2021, builds a national database of unorganised workers.

topic_notes: The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 was enacted to provide social security and welfare to unorganised workers. It came into force on 16 May 2009. It provides for the National Social Security Board, chaired by the Union Labour Minister, which recommends schemes for unorganised workers. State Social Security Boards are also provided for. Welfare schemes are listed in Schedule I: Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme, National Family Benefit Scheme, Janani Suraksha Yojana, Handloom Weavers' Comprehensive Welfare Scheme, Handicraft Artisans' Comprehensive Welfare Scheme, Pension to Master Craft Persons, National Scheme for Fishermen, Janshree Bima Yojana, Aam Aadmi Bima Yojana, and the National Health Insurance Scheme (RSBY). Definitions in Section 2: 'home-based worker' (2(e)), 'self-employed worker' (2(n)), 'wage worker' (2(o)), and 'unorganised sector' (2(l)), which refers to enterprises owned by individuals or self-employed workers, engaged in production or sale of goods or services, with fewer than ten workers. Registration is done by District Administration, with the worker issued an identity card. Related ideas: the Code on Social Security, 2020 merges nine social security laws, including the ESI Act, EPF Act, Gratuity Act, Maternity Benefit Act, Employees' Compensation Act and the 2008 Act. The e-Shram portal, launched in August 2021, gives a Universal Account Number to unorganised workers. PM Shram Yogi Maan-dhan is a pension scheme for unorganised workers. The Code on Social Security also extends coverage to gig and platform workers.

subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 2(m) of the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 defines an 'unorganised worker' as a home-based worker, self-employed worker or wage worker in the unorganised sector. It also includes a worker in the organised sector who is not covered by any of the Acts listed in Schedule II. Schedule II lists six Acts: the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923; the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947; the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948; the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952; the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961; and the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. The test is whether the worker gets social-security or protective cover under these Acts. A worker covered by any of them is treated as organised. The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 is a regulatory and licensing law and is not in Schedule II, so being covered only by it does not take a worker out of the 'unorganised' category. Elimination: (a), (c) and (d) are all in Schedule II, so only (b) fits. The Act received assent on 30 December 2008 and defines 'unorganised sector' in Section 2(l). It created the National Social Security Board under Section 5.

Correct: the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 is not in Schedule II. An organised-sector worker not covered by any Schedule II Act, including a contract worker covered only by this Act, is treated as an unorganised worker.
Wrong: the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 is in Schedule II, so a worker covered by it is outside the definition.

option_notes: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947: the central law for investigating and settling industrial disputes. It covers conciliation, arbitration, adjudication, strikes, lockouts, lay-off, retrenchment and closure. It is administered through Conciliation Officers, Labour Courts and Tribunals. It was subsumed into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020. It is listed in Schedule II of the 2008 Act.

Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970: it regulates employment of contract labour in establishments and provides for its abolition in certain circumstances. It requires licensing of contractors and registration of principal employers. The threshold was 20 workers. It makes the principal employer liable for wages if the contractor defaults. It has been subsumed into the OSH Code, 2020. It is NOT in Schedule II of the 2008 Act.

Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948: it provides medical care and cash benefits for sickness, maternity, disablement, dependants' benefit and funeral expenses. It is administered by the ESI Corporation, which has the Union Labour Minister as chairperson. Coverage applies to establishments with 10 or more workers (20 for some), with a wage ceiling of Rs 21,000 per month. It is listed in Schedule II.

Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972: it provides gratuity to employees on retirement, resignation, death or disablement after 5 years of continuous service, with the exception of death or disablement. The formula is 15 days' wages for each completed year of service, divided by 26 (last drawn wage x 15/26 x years). The maximum is Rs 20 lakh. It applies to establishments with 10 or more employees. It is listed in Schedule II.
