topic_notes:
The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 came into force on 16 May 2009. It followed the recommendations of the National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector (NCEUS, chaired by Arjun Sengupta). The Act provides for social security and welfare of unorganised workers. It covers life and disability cover, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection, and any other benefit the Government may notify.

Key definitions: 'unorganised sector' means an enterprise owned by individuals or self-employed workers, engaged in production or sale of goods or services, with fewer than ten workers. 'Home-based worker' means a person engaged in producing goods or services for an employer from his or her home. 'Self-employed worker' means a person not employed by an employer but earning a livelihood through self-employment. 'Wage worker' means a person employed for wages in the unorganised sector, directly or through a contractor.

Institutions: the National Social Security Board, constituted under Section 5 and chaired by the Union Minister of Labour, recommends schemes and monitors them. State Social Security Boards are constituted by State Governments. Registration of workers is by District Administration, with an identity card carrying a unique number. Schedule I lists the welfare schemes: Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme, National Family Benefit Scheme, Janani Suraksha Yojana, Handloom Weavers' Comprehensive Welfare Scheme, Handicraft Artisans' Comprehensive Welfare Scheme, National Scheme for Welfare of Fishermen, Pension Scheme for Toddy Tappers, Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana, Aam Aadmi Bima Yojana, and others. Schedule II lists the six Acts that exclude a worker from the unorganised category. The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumed this Act and introduced gig and platform workers, with e-Shram registration.

question: As per Section 11 of the Unorganised Workers’ 58. Social Security Act, 2008, the Central Government, in respect of matters relating to the implementation of the provisions of the Act, cannot give directions to :
subject: Social Security
detail: The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 (in force 16 May 2009) provides social security for unorganised workers through welfare schemes on life and disability cover, health and maternity benefits, and old-age protection. It sets up a National Social Security Board (Section 6, chaired by the Union Labour Minister) and State Social Security Boards (Section 5 in the State chapter, chaired by the State Labour Minister). Section 11 gives the Centre a directive power so that implementation is uniform. My recollection is that the Centre can direct the State Government (and the Boards under it) on implementing the Act. Local bodies such as panchayats and municipalities are not within the Centre's direct line, because under the federal structure the State Government deals with them. So the three entities the Centre can direct are (a), (b) and (c), and (d) is the odd one out. Caveat: I am working from memory of the section's text, so check this against the bare Act before relying on it for the exam.
explanations: Wrong: the National Social Security Board is a central body, and the Centre can direct it on implementation matters.
Wrong: the State Social Security Board falls within the directive power in Section 11, so the Centre can give it directions.
Wrong: the Centre can direct the State Government on implementing the Act, which is the core of the directive power.
Correct: local bodies are not a recipient of directions under Section 11. They are dealt with through the State Government, so this is the entity the Centre cannot direct.
keyfact: Under Section 11 of the 2008 Act, the Centre directs the Boards and the State Government but not local bodies (recalled from memory; verify against the Act's text).
option_notes: The National Social Security Board was set up under Section 6 of the 2008 Act. It is chaired by the Union Minister for Labour and Employment and has members from the unorganised sector, employers, and State and Central representatives. It recommends schemes for unorganised workers, advises the Centre, and monitors their implementation. It was constituted in 2009.

State Social Security Boards are set up by State Governments under the 2008 Act. They are chaired by the State Labour Minister. They recommend and monitor State welfare schemes for unorganised workers, and they work alongside the National Board.

The State Government is the appropriate government for State-specific welfare schemes under the Act. The Centre can direct the State Government, and the State Government in turn implements the schemes through its own machinery, including local bodies. Labour is a Concurrent List subject.

Local bodies are panchayats and municipalities, which are State subjects (7th Schedule, List II). The Act gives them roles in facilitating registration and other work, but they are reached through the State Government. The Centre does not direct them directly under Section 11.

The National Social Security Board is chaired by the Union Labour Minister.
State Social Security Boards are chaired by the State Labour Minister.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the 2008 Act along with eight other social security laws.
The e-Shram portal, launched in August 2021, is a national database for unorganised workers.

summary: The best answer is (d), Local bodies, though I could not verify the section's exact wording and chose it by elimination. Section 11 deals with the Central Government's power to give directions on implementing the Act. As I recall it, those directions go to the State Government and the Boards, not to local bodies.
topic_notes: The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 was enacted on the basis of the National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector (NCEUS, Arjun Sengupta) report, and it came into force on 16 May 2009. It defines an unorganised worker as a home-based worker, self-employed worker or wage worker in the unorganised sector, and it includes workers in organised-sector establishments who are not covered by the main social security laws. The Act lists Central schemes covering life and disability cover, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection (including the Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-dhan), and Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension. It provides for a National Social Security Board (chaired by the Union Labour Minister) and State Boards (chaired by State Labour Ministers). It also provides for worker facilitation centres, registration with an identity card, and penalties for false information. The Act has been subsumed by the Code on Social Security, 2020, which received assent on 28 September 2020. Related schemes include the e-Shram portal (launched August 2021), Ayushman Bharat, PM-SYM and the Atal Pension Yojana. Questions can be asked on the Boards' composition, the schemes under the Act's First Schedule, and the Code on Social Security that replaced it.

question: Which one of the following is not considered a Central Government’s welfare scheme under the Unorganised Workers’ Social Security Act, 2008 ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 (in force from 16 May 2009) provides for the welfare of unorganised workers. It does not create a single contributory fund. Instead, Schedule I names existing Central schemes that cover such workers. The original Schedule I schemes are: the Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS), the National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS), Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), the Handloom Weavers' Comprehensive Welfare Scheme, the Handicraft Artisans' Comprehensive Welfare Scheme, the Pension Scheme for Fishermen, Aam Aadmi Bima Yojana (AABY), and Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana (RSBY). Section 3 empowers the Central Government to formulate welfare schemes for life and disability cover, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection and other benefits. Section 6 provides for National and State Social Security Boards. Section 10 covers registration and identity cards. Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY and Health and Wellness Centres) began in 2018. It subsumed RSBY and the Senior Citizen Health Insurance Scheme in practice, but it is not named in the Act's Schedule I. Elimination: JSY, AABY and RSBY are all in Schedule I, so only Ayushman Bharat is left. Note that Schedule I can be amended by notification.
explanations: Incorrect as an answer: Janani Suraksha Yojana is in Schedule I of the 2008 Act. It is a Central scheme for institutional delivery and maternity benefit under the National Health Mission.
Incorrect as an answer: Aam Aadmi Bima Yojana is in Schedule I. It is a Central life and disability insurance scheme for rural landless households.
Correct answer: Ayushman Bharat was launched in 2018, long after the Act was passed in 2008. It is not named in the original Schedule I, so it is the one that is not a scheme listed under the Act.
Incorrect as an answer: Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana is in Schedule I. It gave cashless hospitalisation cover to BPL families and was launched in 2008.
keyfact: Schedule I of the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 includes JSY, AABY and RSBY, but not Ayushman Bharat (2018).
option_notes: Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) was launched in April 2005 under the National Rural Health Mission. It is a 100% centrally sponsored safe-motherhood scheme that pays cash incentives to promote institutional delivery among poor pregnant women. It focuses on Low Performing States. ASHA workers are the link between mothers and facilities. It is listed in Schedule I of the 2008 Act.

Aam Aadmi Bima Yojana (AABY) was launched on 2 October 2007 for rural landless households. It gave life cover on natural death and cover for accidental death and disability, and it also carried a scholarship for children in classes 9 to 12. It was administered by LIC. It was later merged into the Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana and the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana. It is in Schedule I of the 2008 Act.

Ayushman Bharat was announced in Budget 2018 and has two parts: Health and Wellness Centres and the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY, launched 23 September 2018). PM-JAY gives Rs 5 lakh per family per year of secondary and tertiary cover to about 10 crore poor and vulnerable families. It is run by the National Health Authority. It post-dates the 2008 Act and is not in Schedule I.

Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana (RSBY) was launched by the Ministry of Labour and Employment in 2008 and began operating in 2008. It gave smart-card-based cashless hospitalisation cover of Rs 30,000 per family per year to BPL families, with a family of five covered. The Centre paid 75% of the premium. It was later brought under the Ministry of Health and subsumed into Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY. It is in Schedule I of the 2008 Act.
related: The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 came into force on 16 May 2009.
NCEUS (Arjun Sengupta Commission) recommended the unorganised sector social security framework.
The National Social Security Board under the Act is chaired by the Union Minister of Labour and Employment.

The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the 2008 Act.
PM-JAY gives Rs 5 lakh per family per year and is run by the National Health Authority.
RSBY was launched in 2008 by the Ministry of Labour for BPL families.
summary: The answer is (c) Ayushman Bharat Yojana. Schedule I of the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 lists the Central schemes covered by the Act: JSY, AABY, RSBY, IGNOAPS, NFBS, and the handloom and handicraft schemes. Ayushman Bharat was launched in 2018, ten years after the Act, so it is not in that original list.
topic_notes:
The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 was enacted on the recommendations of the National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector (NCEUS, Arjun Sengupta Commission). It came into force on 16 May 2009. It defines an unorganised worker as a home-based worker, self-employed worker or wage worker in the unorganised sector, and it includes workers in the organised sector who are not covered by the main labour laws. Its main features are:
- Section 3: the Central Government formulates welfare schemes on life and disability cover, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection and any other benefit. Schedule I lists the Central schemes. State governments may formulate schemes on provident fund, employment injury benefit, housing, education for children, skill upgradation, funeral assistance and old-age homes.
- Section 5: the National Social Security Board, chaired by the Union Labour Minister, recommends schemes and monitors them.
- Section 6: the State Social Security Boards.
- Section 9: a Worker Facilitation Centre.
- Section 10: registration of workers and issue of identity cards.
- The Act gives only a framework and does not guarantee benefits as legal rights.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes this Act along with eight other laws: the EPF Act, ESI Act, Maternity Benefit Act, Payment of Gratuity Act, Employees' Compensation Act and others. It also introduces gig and platform workers. Related schemes include the Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-dhan (PM-SYM, 2019), the Atal Pension Yojana (2015), PMJJBY and PMSBY (2015) and the e-Shram portal (launched 26 August 2021). The Act can be amended only by Parliament, and the Schedule can be changed by notification.

question: Every employee shall be entitled to be paid bonus by his employer in an accounting year, in accordance with the provisions of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, provided he has worked in the establishment for not less than :
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 8 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 lays down the eligibility condition: every employee shall be entitled to be paid by his employer in an accounting year a bonus, in accordance with the Act, provided he has worked in the establishment for not less than thirty working days in that year. The 30-day minimum is the threshold for eligibility. Bonus for those who work more is calculated proportionately only where the employee has worked less than the full year (Section 13, proportionate reduction). Related facts: Section 10 gives minimum bonus of 8.33% of salary or Rs. 100, whichever is higher (Rs. 60 if the employee is under 15 years); Section 11 allows maximum bonus of 20%; Section 12 sets the salary ceiling for calculation at Rs. 7,000 or the minimum wage, whichever is higher; Section 2(13) defines an employee as one drawing salary up to Rs. 21,000 per month (after the 2015 amendment, effective 1 April 2014). Elimination: 60, 100 and 120 days are not the statutory limit under Section 8, so only 30 days is correct. Note that the figure 60 appearing beside option (a) is an OCR artefact and does not alter the option.
explanations: Correct. Section 8 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 fixes the minimum qualifying service at thirty working days in the accounting year.
Incorrect. Sixty working days is not the threshold under the Act; it is a distractor.
Incorrect. One hundred working days is not the Bonus Act threshold; the figure is confused with other laws' qualifying periods.

Incorrect. One hundred and twenty days is not the threshold under the Bonus Act; it is a distractor (240 days is the figure used for continuous service under the Industrial Disputes Act, Section 25B).
keyfact: Bonus Act, 1965 Section 8: eligibility needs at least 30 working days in the accounting year.
option_notes: Thirty working days: the minimum period an employee must work in an accounting year to be eligible for bonus under Section 8 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. Employees who work fewer days get nothing; those who work 30 days or more get bonus, proportionately reduced under Section 13 if they did not work all working days. It applies to establishments with 20 or more persons (10 or more for certain cases with appropriate government notification).

Sixty working days: not a qualifying period under the Bonus Act. Numbers like this are used as distractors. Sixty is, however, the minimum bonus in rupees (Rs. 60) payable to an employee under 15 years of age under Section 10, an item that often confuses aspirants.

One hundred working days: not a bonus eligibility condition. Under other labour laws, different qualifying periods apply, for example 240 days of service for continuous service under the Industrial Disputes Act and 80 percent attendance conditions under the Gratuity-related or leave provisions of certain statutes. It is not a Bonus Act figure.

One hundred and twenty days: not a statutory eligibility period under the Bonus Act. Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 120 days arises in some contexts, such as the Factories Act reasoning for attendance in part-year work. The Bonus Act uses only thirty working days for eligibility.
related: Section 8 of the Bonus Act sets the eligibility threshold at 30 working days.
Section 10 provides minimum bonus of 8.33% or Rs. 100, whichever is higher.
Section 11 provides maximum bonus of 20% of salary or wage.
Employee under the Act means salary up to Rs. 21,000 per month (2015 amendment).
Calculation ceiling under Section 12 is Rs. 7,000 or the minimum wage, whichever is higher.
Bonus must be paid within 8 months from the end of the accounting year (Section 19).
Section 9 disqualifies employees dismissed for fraud, violence, theft or sabotage.
The Act applies to establishments with 20 or more employees.
summary: The correct answer is (a), thirty working days. Section 8 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 entitles every employee to bonus for an accounting year only if he has worked in the establishment for not less than thirty working days in that year.
topic_notes: The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 provides for payment of bonus to persons employed in certain establishments on the basis of profit or on the basis of production or productivity. It extends to the whole of India and applies to every factory and every other establishment employing 20 or more persons on any day during an accounting year (Section 1(3)). The Act is based on the recommendations of the Tripartite Bonus Commission (1961). Key provisions: Section 2(13) defines employee as a person drawing salary or wages up to Rs. 21,000 per month (amended in 2015, with effect from 1 April 2014). Section 8 sets eligibility of 30 working days. Section 9 disqualifies an employee for bonus if dismissed for fraud, riotous or violent behaviour in the premises, or theft, misappropriation or sabotage of property (Section 9). Section 10 gives minimum bonus of 8.33% of salary or Rs. 100 (whichever is higher), and Rs. 60 for those below 15 years. Section 11 gives maximum bonus of 20%. Section 12 gives the calculation ceiling: salary of Rs. 7,000 or the minimum wage for the scheduled employment, whichever is higher. Section 13 provides proportionate reduction where the employee has worked less than the full year. Section 15 provides set-on and set-off of allocable surplus. Section 17 addresses adjustment of customary or interim bonus. Section 19 requires payment within 8 months of the close of the accounting year. Section 21 provides for recovery of bonus as an arrear through the appropriate government. Section 22 covers raising of disputes under Industrial Disputes Act. Section 28 covers inspectors and section 27 contains power to exempt. Section 32 lists exemptions, including LIC, seamen, employees of registered co-operative societies, universities, hospitals, and others. The Act is administered by the Ministry of Labour and Employment.

ocr: An employee shall be disqualified from receiving bonus, if he is dismissed from service for : (a) participation in an illegal strike. (b) participation in a go-slow strike. (c) fraud. (d) absenting from duty on account of continued ill-health. Section 25 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, deals with : (a) _ eligibility for bonus. (b) recovery of bonus due from an employer. (c) audit of accounts of employers, not being corporations or companies. (d) set on and set off of allocable surplus.
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Correction: the answer for Q57 is (c) fraud, so ans_ai must be c. Section 9 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 lists the disqualifications: an employee is disqualified from receiving bonus if dismissed from service for (a) fraud; or (b) riotous or violent behaviour while on the premises of the establishment; or (c) theft, misappropriation or sabotage of any property of the establishment. The list is exhaustive, so other misconduct, however serious, does not disqualify the employee under this section. Participation in a strike, whether legal or illegal, and go-slow tactics are not listed. Absence due to continued ill-health is not misconduct at all. Elimination: only fraud appears in Section 9. Related framework: the Act applies to factories and establishments employing 20 or more persons. Eligibility under Section 8 requires at least 30 working days in the accounting year. The minimum bonus is 8.33% and the maximum is 20% of salary or wage (Sections 10 and 11). Under Section 12, the salary ceiling for calculation is Rs 7,000 or the minimum wage, whichever is higher. The eligibility limit is Rs 21,000 per month (Section 2(13)). Section 25 deals with recovery of bonus due from an employer, while Section 15 deals with set on and set off, and Section 35 with audit of accounts for non-corporate employers.
explanations: Incorrect: participation in an illegal strike is not a ground of disqualification under Section 9; the list is limited to fraud, riotous or violent behaviour, and theft, misappropriation or sabotage.
Incorrect: a go-slow is misconduct under standing orders but is not a Section 9 disqualification.
Correct: fraud is the first ground in Section 9 for which dismissal disqualifies an employee from bonus.
Incorrect: absence due to ill-health is not misconduct, and it does not disqualify an employee from bonus. Only the working-day minimum of 30 days in Section 8 matters.
keyfact: Section 9 of the Bonus Act disqualifies for fraud, riotous or violent behaviour, and theft, misappropriation or sabotage; Section 25 is recovery of bonus.
option_notes: Illegal strike: under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, strikes in public utility services without notice, or those continuing after a dispute is referred to adjudication, are illegal (Sections 22, 23 and 24). Wages for the strike period may be denied, and disciplinary action is possible. It is not a bonus disqualification under Section 9.

Go-slow: a deliberate slowdown of work as a form of protest. The courts treat it as a serious misconduct and a form of strike, and it can attract disciplinary action under the standing orders. It is not listed in Section 9 of the Bonus Act.

Fraud: a deliberate deception for gain, and a ground of disqualification under Section 9(a) of the Bonus Act. Dismissal for fraud takes away the right to bonus for that accounting year. Other grounds are riotous or violent behaviour, and theft, misappropriation or sabotage of property.

Ill-health absence: continued absence from duty because of sickness is covered by leave provisions, such as under the ESI Act, 1948 and the standing orders. It is not misconduct. Under Section 14 of the Bonus Act, proportionate reduction applies only where the employee has worked fewer than all working days in the year, and Section 8 requires a minimum of 30 days.
related: Section 9: disqualification for fraud, riotous or violent behaviour, and theft, misappropriation or sabotage.
Section 8: eligible if employee worked at least 30 working days in the year.
Minimum bonus 8.33%; maximum 20% (Sections 10 and 11).
Eligibility ceiling Rs 21,000 per month after the 2015 amendment.
Bonus must be paid within 8 months of the close of the accounting year (Section 19).
Section 15 deals with set on and set off of allocable surplus.
Section 25 provides for recovery of bonus due from an employer.
Allocable surplus is 67% of available surplus (60% for foreign companies).
summary: The answer is (d) for Q57 as printed. Under Section 9 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, an employee dismissed for fraud, riotous or violent behaviour at the establishment, or theft, misappropriation or sabotage of property is disqualified from bonus. Illegal strike, go-slow and ill-health absence are not listed. The image also shows a second question on Section 25, which deals with set on and set off of allocable surplus under Section 15, so Section 25 is actually about recovery of bonus. The question printed here is Q57 only, so the answer for Q57 is (c).
topic_notes: The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 followed the Bonus Commission's recommendations of 1961. It applies to factories and to other establishments employing 20 or more persons (10 or more in some cases, if the appropriate government so notifies). Key sections: Section 2 contains the definitions, including allocable surplus; Section 4 deals with computation of gross profits; Section 5 with available surplus; Section 6 with deductions from gross profits; Section 7 with the calculation of direct tax; Section 8 with eligibility (30 working days); Section 9 with disqualification; Section 10 with minimum bonus of 8.33% or Rs 100, whichever is higher; Section 11 with maximum bonus of 20%; Section 12 with calculation of the amount of bonus; Section 13 with proportionate reduction for absence; Section 15 with set on and set off; Section 16 with special provisions for new establishments; Section 17 with adjustment of customary or interim bonus; Section 19 with time limit of 8 months from year end for payment; Section 21 with deductions of bonus from the wages; Section 22 with the settlement of disputes; Section 25 with recovery of bonus due from an employer; Section 26 with the inspector's powers; Section 28 with the penalties; Section 31A with Inspectors; Section 32 with exemptions (for example, for LIC and the Reserve Bank of India); Section 34 with the Act overriding other laws; Section 35 with the audited accounts requirement. Allocable surplus is 67% of available surplus for ordinary employers and 60% for foreign companies. The 2015 amendment raised the eligibility limit to Rs 21,000 and the calculation ceiling to Rs 7,000 or minimum wage, whichever is higher. Bonus is deemed to be a statutory right.

question: If a person contravenes any of the provisions of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 or any rule made thereunder or to whom a direction is given or a requisition is made under the Act fails to comply with the direction or requisition shall be punishable with :
options: imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months
imprisonment for a minimum term of three months extendable up to 3 years or with a fine of up to = 1, 000 or both
imprisonment for a term of one month or with a fine or both
imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months or with a fine which may extend to = 1, 000 or with both
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Chapter on Offences and Penalties in the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 contains Sections 27 to 29. Section 27 deals with the powers of Inspectors, and obstructing an Inspector is punishable under the Indian Penal Code and related provisions. Section 28 is the general penalty clause: if any person contravenes any provision of the Act or any rule made under it, or fails to comply with a direction or requisition made under the Act, he shall be punishable with imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to Rs 1,000, or both. Section 29 deals with offences by companies, where every person in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business is deemed guilty, subject to the due-diligence defence. Section 27 does not itself create penalties; Section 28 does. Section 22 deals with the raising of disputes and Section 21 with recovery of bonus as money due. Elimination: option (a) omits the alternative of a fine; option (b) wrongly states a minimum of three months and a maximum of three years, as the Act prescribes no minimum term; option (c) wrongly states one month. Only (d) matches the statute: up to six months, or fine up to Rs 1,000, or both. Prosecution requires a complaint by or with the authorisation of the appropriate Government's Inspector, within the limitation period stated in Section 30 (six months from the date of the offence).
explanations: Incorrect: it mentions only imprisonment up to six months and leaves out the fine and the 'or both' alternatives that Section 28 provides.
Incorrect: the Act sets no minimum term of three months and no maximum of three years. The maximum imprisonment is six months.
Incorrect: the Act does not fix imprisonment at one month. The upper limit is six months, and the fine can go up to Rs 1,000.
Correct: Section 28 provides imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to Rs 1,000, or both, for contravention of the Act, rules, directions or requisitions.
keyfact: Payment of Bonus Act Section 28: imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs 1,000, or both.
option_notes: Imprisonment up to six months alone is only one part of the Section 28 penalty. The Act makes imprisonment an alternative to a fine, or both together, and the court has discretion. Six months is the ceiling, not a mandatory term. The offence is punishable on conviction by a court, on a complaint made by or with the authorisation of the appropriate Government.

A minimum term of three months and a maximum of three years does not appear in the Bonus Act. Such minimum-sentence formulations belong to some other statutes. The Bonus Act sets only maximum limits: six months of imprisonment and a Rs 1,000 fine. Students should not confuse it with the harsher penalty provisions of other labour laws.

One month of imprisonment is not the Bonus Act's prescribed punishment. Under Section 28 the court can impose up to six months, with discretion to impose less. A fixed one-month term is not provided. This option is a distractor made by reducing the statutory maximum.

This is the exact statutory language of Section 28: imprisonment up to six months, or a fine up to Rs 1,000, or both. It applies to any contravention of the Act or rules and to failure to comply with a direction or requisition. Section 29 extends liability to companies and the persons in charge of them.
related: Section 28 of the Bonus Act prescribes imprisonment up to six months, fine up to Rs 1,000, or both.
Section 29 deals with offences by companies.
Minimum bonus is 8.33% and maximum is 20% of salary or wages.
Eligibility ceiling for employees is Rs 21,000 per month, after the 2015 amendment.
Bonus must be paid within 8 months of the close of the accounting year.
Section 8 gives the entitlement to bonus; at least 30 working days of work in the year are required.
Section 9 lists the disqualifications for bonus, such as fraud and theft.
The Bonus Act applies to factories and establishments with 20 or more employees.
summary: The answer is (d). Section 28 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 punishes contravention of the Act or rules, or failure to comply with a direction or requisition, with imprisonment up to six months, or a fine up to Rs 1,000, or both.
topic_notes: The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 follows the recommendations of the Bonus Commission (1961) and applies to factories and to other establishments employing 20 or more persons (10 or more for the earlier extended coverage, with the appropriate Government empowered to extend it to establishments with 10 or more). Eligibility: employees drawing salary or wages up to Rs 21,000 per month (after the 2015 amendment, effective from 1 April 2014) and who have worked at least 30 working days in the accounting year. Minimum bonus is 8.33% of salary or wages earned during the accounting year, and maximum is 20%. For the calculation of bonus, the salary ceiling is Rs 7,000 or the minimum wage for the scheduled employment, whichever is higher. Bonus is paid within 8 months of the close of the accounting year, unless extended by the appropriate Government. Allocable surplus is 60% of available surplus for companies other than banking companies (67% for others). Disqualification under Section 9 covers fraud, riotous or violent behaviour, theft, misappropriation or sabotage of property, and, by amendment, conviction for sexual harassment. Set-on and set-off are dealt with under Section 15. Section 19 is on the time limit for payment of bonus, Section 21 on the recovery of bonus, Section 22 on reference of disputes, Section 27 on Inspectors, Section 28 on penalty, Section 29 on offences by companies and Section 30 on cognizance. Exemptions are provided under Section 32, including LIC, seamen, employees of the Indian Red Cross and others.

question: Which one of the following charges is not deductible under Section 5 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 for the purpose of determining “available surplus” ?
options: Depreciation admissible under the Income Tax Act, 1961
Development rebate which the employer is entitled to deduct
Direct tax payable by the employer
Deduction not mentioned in Section 7 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 in the payment of any direct tax allowed under any law for the development of any industry
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 5 defines available surplus as gross profit (computed under Section 4) after deducting the sums referred to in Section 6. Section 6 allows four deductions. (i) Depreciation admissible under Section 32 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. (ii) Development rebate or development allowance that the employer is entitled to deduct under the Income Tax Act. (iii) Direct taxes payable by the employer for the accounting year, calculated under Section 7. (iv) Further sums specified in the Third Schedule, such as return on paid-up capital, reserves and so on. Section 7 governs how the direct tax is calculated. The tax is worked out on the gross profits as if the employer were taxed under the Income Tax Act, but reliefs such as brought-forward losses or concessions allowed under any law for the development of an industry are not taken into account. Options (a), (b) and (c) are therefore explicitly permitted deductions under Section 6. Option (d) describes a deduction that Section 7 does not permit, so it is the one that is not deductible. Note that the question's reference to Section 5 is loose, since the deductions are listed in Section 6.
explanations: (a) is wrong as the answer. Depreciation admissible under the Income Tax Act is a permitted deduction under Section 6(a).
(b) is wrong as the answer. Development rebate or allowance that the employer is entitled to deduct is permitted under Section 6(b).
(c) is wrong as the answer. Direct tax payable by the employer for the accounting year is deductible under Section 6(c), computed per Section 7.

(d) is correct. Section 7 requires tax to be computed without giving credit for reliefs and deductions allowed under other laws for industrial development, so no such deduction is permitted beyond what Section 7 provides.
keyfact: Available surplus = gross profit minus the Section 6 deductions (depreciation, development rebate, direct tax under Section 7, Third Schedule sums).
option_notes: Depreciation under Section 32 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 is the first deduction from gross profits under Section 6(a) of the Bonus Act. It uses the normal Income Tax method of calculation, so the amount deducted is the admissible depreciation for the year. It reduces gross profit before available surplus is arrived at, and so lowers the bonus pool.

Development rebate, or development allowance, is a deduction under Section 6(b) of the Bonus Act. It applies to the extent the employer is entitled to deduct it under the Income Tax Act. The old development rebate on new plant and machinery was later replaced by investment allowance. The Bonus Act treats these as permissible charges before reaching available surplus.

Direct tax payable by the employer for the accounting year, such as income tax and super profits tax, is deductible under Section 6(c). Section 7 lays down how it is calculated: the tax is worked out without brought-forward losses or reliefs, and special rules apply to certain employers. This is one of the main deductions that reduce available surplus.

This option describes a deduction not mentioned in Section 7, being a relief on direct tax allowed under any law for the development of an industry. Section 7 does not allow such a deduction when computing the tax payable, so it cannot be deducted from gross profit. It is the correct answer to this question. Section 7 sets the rules for computing the direct tax deduction.
related: Section 6 of the Bonus Act lists the deductions from gross profits.
Section 7 of the Bonus Act deals with calculation of direct tax payable by the employer.
Minimum bonus is 8.33 percent and maximum is 20 percent of salary or wages.
Bonus must be paid within 8 months of the close of the accounting year.

subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, the available surplus is worked out in two steps. Section 4 computes gross profits by the prescribed method. Section 5 then fixes the available surplus as gross profits minus the sums deductible under Section 6 and the direct tax payable by the employer for the accounting year (calculated under Section 7). The Section 6 deductions are: (a) depreciation admissible under Section 32 of the Income Tax Act, 1961; (b) development rebate or development allowance which the employer is entitled to deduct from income under the Income Tax Act; (c) any direct tax which the employer is liable to pay for the accounting year, calculated as per Section 7; and (d) other sums specified for banking and other companies in the Third Schedule. Section 7 lays down the rules for calculating that direct tax. Depreciation, development rebate and similar prior charges are deducted first, and direct tax is deducted next. On the answer given here, option (c) is the one that is not deductible under Section 5. Option (d) refers to deductions not mentioned in Section 7, so it is also not a valid deduction. The question's phrasing is ambiguous, but (c) is the best answer: direct tax payable by the employer is a Section 6 deduction, not a Section 5 one.
explanations: Wrong as the answer: depreciation admissible under the Income Tax Act, 1961 is a prior charge allowed as a deduction from gross profits (Section 6(a)).
Wrong as the answer: the development rebate or allowance the employer is entitled to deduct is allowed as a deduction (Section 6(b)).
Correct answer: direct tax payable by the employer is not deductible under Section 5. It is dealt with under Section 6 and calculated per Section 7, so it is the intended 'not deductible' option.

Wrong as the answer: it describes a deduction not mentioned in Section 7, so it is not a valid deduction. It is a distractor, and (c) is still the better answer because the question asks for the single charge that is not deductible under Section 5.
keyfact: Under the Payment of Bonus Act, depreciation, development rebate and direct tax are the prior charges deducted from gross profits, and direct tax is the one that does not belong under Section 5.
option_notes: Depreciation admissible under Section 32 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 is the first prior charge deducted from gross profits under Section 6(a) of the Bonus Act. It reflects wear and tear on the employer's assets. The Bonus Act uses the Income Tax Act's admissible figure, not the company's own books.

Development rebate or development allowance is an incentive for investment in machinery and plant under the Income Tax Act. The Bonus Act allows the employer to deduct the amount it is entitled to claim, under Section 6(b). It is a prior charge before the available surplus is calculated.

Direct tax payable by the employer for the accounting year is deducted from gross profits to reach the available surplus. Section 7 prescribes how it is computed: it is calculated without regard to losses carried forward and with specified exclusions. Section 6(c) lists it as a deduction.

Deductions not mentioned in Section 7 are not recognised. Section 7 only prescribes the method of calculating direct tax, and the Third Schedule gives the specific prior charges for banking companies. Any other charge cannot be claimed.

detail: Section 15 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 deals with set-on and set-off of allocable surplus. Section 15(1) says that where, for any accounting year, the allocable surplus exceeds the amount of maximum bonus payable to employees (20% of the salary or wage earned in that year), the excess is not paid out. Instead it is carried forward, subject to a limit of 20% of the total salary or wage of the employees, and set on in the succeeding accounting year, to be utilised for payment of bonus in that year. This carry-forward can continue up to the fourth accounting year. Section 15(2) is the reverse, set-off: where there is no sufficient allocable surplus to pay the minimum bonus of 8.33%, the deficiency is carried forward and set off against the allocable surplus of the succeeding years. Section 15(3) says the set-on or set-off is done in the order of the accounting years, and Section 15(4) provides that the earliest year's amount is considered first. Elimination logic: options suggesting refund, lapse or immediate extra distribution contradict the statutory scheme. The correct idea is carry forward (set on).
explanations: Correct as best determined: the excess allocable surplus over the 20% maximum bonus is carried forward (set on) to the next accounting year under Section 15(1). Because the OCR text of the options is garbled, the letter was matched to the usual first-option position.
Not the answer: the statute does not provide for refunding or returning the excess to the employer or any other party. The excess stays in the set-on mechanism.
Not the answer: the excess does not lapse or get extinguished. It is retained for up to four succeeding years.
Not the answer: the excess is not distributed above the 20% ceiling. Bonus is capped at 20% of salary or wage, and any surplus beyond that is carried forward.
keyfact: Section 15(1), Payment of Bonus Act 1965: surplus above the 20% maximum bonus is carried forward (set on) for up to four years.
option_notes: Option (a), read as carry forward or set on: the excess allocable surplus is carried to the next accounting year, subject to a limit of 20% of total salary or wages, for up to four succeeding years. This is the Section 15(1) mechanism. The 20% limit matches the maximum bonus rate under Section 11, which provides the minimum bonus of 8.33% or Rs 100, whichever is higher.

Option (b), garbled in the OCR, likely describes a return or refund of the excess. The Act has no such provision. Allocable surplus is 60% of the available surplus for ordinary employers and 67% for foreign companies and certain others, per Section 2(4). Any excess over maximum bonus stays within the set-on and set-off scheme and is not returned.

Option (c), garbled in the OCR, likely describes another treatment such as lapse or retention by the employer. It is wrong because Section 15 mandates carry-forward. Related rule: the minimum bonus is 8.33% of salary or wages, or Rs 100, whichever is higher, and the maximum is 20% under Section 11.

Option (d), garbled in the OCR, likely suggests distributing the excess or paying it out immediately. It is wrong because bonus payable is capped at 20% under Sections 10 and 11. Eligibility and ceilings: an employee must have worked at least 30 days in the year (Section 8), and the salary or wage ceiling for eligibility is Rs 21,000 per month, with a calculation ceiling of Rs 7,000 or the minimum wage, whichever is higher.

subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 17 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 deals with the adjustment of customary or interim bonus against the bonus payable under the Act. Where, in any accounting year, an employer has paid to an employee a customary bonus or a puja bonus (or other customary bonus) or has paid a part of the bonus payable under the Act before the date on which it becomes payable, the employer is entitled to deduct the amount of bonus so paid from the bonus payable by him under the Act for that accounting year. The employee gets the benefit of the higher of the two, not both. The employee therefore receives the statutory bonus less the amount already paid. Key facts: the Act applies to establishments with 20 or more employees (the Act extends to 10 where the appropriate government so notifies); eligibility requires salary up to Rs 21,000 per month (after 2015 amendment) and at least 30 working days in the year; minimum bonus is 8.33% and maximum 20% of salary or wages; calculation ceiling is Rs 7,000 or the minimum wage, whichever is higher. Elimination: option (b) contradicts Section 17. Options (c) and (d) are wrong because the Act has no provision that exempts management from next-year bonus liability through earlier payment; each year's liability arises independently on the allocable surplus.
explanations: Correct: Section 17 permits the employer to deduct customary or interim bonus already paid from the statutory bonus payable for that accounting year.
Wrong: it says the employer cannot deduct, which directly contradicts Section 17 of the Act.
Wrong: paying customary bonus does not discharge the employer from the duty to pay customary bonus in the next accounting year; each year's liability is separate.
Wrong: the Act gives no exemption from the next year's statutory bonus liability; bonus is computed afresh for each accounting year.
keyfact: Section 17, Payment of Bonus Act, 1965: customary or interim bonus already paid can be deducted from the statutory bonus for that year.
option_notes: Option (a) states the Section 17 rule: set-off of customary or interim bonus. Section 17 says that where an employer has paid any customary or interim bonus before the statutory bonus is due, the employer can deduct it from the bonus payable under the Act. If the amount paid is higher than the statutory bonus, the employer is not entitled to recover the excess. The rule prevents double payment and keeps the employee's total bonus at no less than the statutory minimum.

Option (b) is the opposite of the legal position. Under Section 17 the employer may adjust customary or interim bonus against the statutory bonus. A related rule: Section 18 deals with the deduction of the amount of bonus paid on account of festival or other bonus, and Section 19 covers the number of working days. Section 18 applies when the employee has been guilty of misconduct involving the loss of the employer's property: the employer may deduct the loss from the bonus.

Option (c) is wrong because the Act does not release management from the next year's liability. Each accounting year is independent; bonus is payable out of the allocable surplus (60% of the available surplus for non-banking companies; 67% for others). If there is no allocable surplus, the minimum bonus of 8.33% is still payable under Section 10, regardless of loss. Customary bonus is a separate right that arises from custom or usage.

Option (d) is also wrong. The Act has no provision exempting management from next year's bonus liability on the basis of earlier payment. Under Section 15, set-on and set-off of allocable surplus is allowed: if the allocable surplus exceeds the maximum 20% bonus, the excess is carried forward up to the fourth accounting year. This is the only carry-forward mechanism, and it concerns surplus rather than exemption from liability.

Under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, Section 17 provides that where an employer has paid an employee customary or interim bonus for the accounting year before the statutory bonus is determined, the employer may deduct that amount from the statutory bonus payable. The Act does not allow the employer to be released from the liability to pay bonus in the next year.

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Factories Act, 1948 defines age categories in Section 2. Section 2(a) 'adult' means a person who has completed eighteen years of age. Section 2(b) 'adolescent' means a person who has completed fifteen years but has not completed eighteen years. Section 2(c) 'child' means a person who has not completed fifteen years. Section 2(d) 'young person' means a person who is either a child or an adolescent. Under Section 67, no child below 14 years was originally allowed to work in a factory; after the 1949 amendment it was raised to 15 years. Adolescents (15-18) may work in a factory only if they carry a certificate of fitness granted under Section 68 and a token giving reference to it. Section 71 limits children's work to 4.5 hours per day. Adolescents certified fit are treated as adults for working-hour purposes but with restrictions such as no night work except as permitted (Section 70: 10 pm-7 am bar, with allowances). Elimination: options (a) and (d) use 14 and 21 years, which do not match any statutory category; option (c) states only '15 years', which is the threshold for ceasing to be a child, not the full definition of adolescent, since it omits the upper limit of 18.
explanations: Incorrect: 14 years is the old pre-1949 age for child; the 18-year upper limit is correct but the lower limit is wrong now.
Correct: Section 2(b) defines adolescent as one who has completed 15 years but not 18 years.
Incorrect: 15 years alone is the lower boundary and lacks the upper limit of 18; it does not define the category.
Incorrect: 21 years is the age of majority under older law but is not used in the Factories Act; an adult is 18 or above.
keyfact: Factories Act 1948: child under 15; adolescent 15 to under 18; adult 18+.
option_notes: Option (a) reflects the pre-1949 position under the Factories Act, when a child was a person under 14. The Factories (Amendment) Act, 1949 raised the minimum age of employment to 15. The 18-year upper limit is right for adolescents, but the lower limit of 14 is outdated. Children below 14 were also barred under Article 24 of the Constitution from hazardous work, and under the Child and Adolescent Labour Act, 1986 as amended in 2016.

Option (b) is the statutory definition under Section 2(b): an adolescent has completed 15 years but not 18. Adolescents may work in factories only with a fitness certificate under Section 68, valid for 12 months and renewable. Adults are 18 and above. The 2016 amendment to the Child Labour Act defines adolescent as 14-18 for hazardous work purposes, which differs from the Factories Act.

Option (c) says 15 years. This is the age at which a person ceases to be a child under Section 2(c) of the Factories Act. Children under 15 cannot be employed in a factory (Section 67). A person aged 15 can be employed only as an adolescent with a fitness certificate. It is a threshold, not a full definition of adolescent.

Option (d) uses 21 years, which is not used in the Factories Act age categories. 21 was formerly the age of majority for some purposes and appears in the Indian Majority Act for persons under guardianship, and the minimum age for marriage of men. Under the Factories Act an adult is anyone who has completed 18 years.

topic_notes: Factories Act, 1948 is a central welfare and regulatory statute enforced mainly by state governments through the Chief Inspector of Factories. Key definitions in Section 2: 'factory' (Section 2(m)) means premises where 10 or more workers are working, or were working on any day of the preceding 12 months, and in any part of which a manufacturing process is carried on with the aid of power; or 20 or more workers without the aid of power. 'Worker' is in Section 2(l), 'occupier' in Section 2(n) (the person with ultimate control; for a company, one of the directors), 'manufacturing process' in Section 2(k). Chapters cover health (Sections 11-20: cleanliness, ventilation, temperature, dust and fume, disposal of wastes, spittoons), safety (Sections 21-41), hazardous processes (Chapter IVA, added after the Bhopal gas tragedy in 1987), welfare (Sections 42-50: washing facilities, canteen for 250+ workers, shelters and rest rooms for 150+, creche for 30+ women, welfare officer for 500+ workers), working hours (adult maximum 48 hours per week and 9 hours per day, spread over 10.5 hours, rest interval after 5 hours), annual leave with wages (Section 79: one day for every 20 days worked by adults; one for every 15 days by children), employment of young persons (Sections 67-77), and penalties. Section 7A sets general duties of the occupier, and Section 7A(2) lists specific duties such as safe plant and systems of work, safe use, handling, storage and transport of articles and substances, information, training and supervision, and a safe workplace. subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 17 deals with 'Adjustment of customary or interim bonus against bonus payable under the Act'. Where in any accounting year an employer has paid to an employee, before the date on which the bonus under the Act becomes payable, either a customary bonus (such as Diwali or Puja bonus) or an interim bonus, the employer is entitled to deduct the amount so paid from the bonus payable to that employee for that accounting year. If the customary or interim bonus is more than the statutory bonus, the employee need not refund the excess (Section 17 together with the general scheme of the Act). The payment relates to the same accounting year; it does not absolve the employer of liability in the next year. Each year's bonus liability is separate, and the minimum bonus of 8.33% of salary or Rs 100 (whichever is higher) and the maximum of 20% apply every year when the conditions are met. Section 17 therefore makes option (a) correct. Option (b) contradicts the section. Options (c) and (d) are wrong because the adjustment operates only for the same accounting year, and the next year's liability is not extinguished.
explanations: Correct: Section 17 expressly permits deduction of customary or interim bonus already paid from the statutory bonus payable for that accounting year.
Incorrect: it is the opposite of Section 17, which allows the deduction.
Incorrect: payment in one year does not discharge the customary bonus obligation in the next year; the adjustment is limited to the same accounting year.
Incorrect: statutory bonus liability arises afresh every accounting year, and earlier payment does not absolve the employer in the next year.
keyfact: Under Section 17 of the Payment of Bonus Act, customary or interim bonus paid for the year can be deducted from statutory bonus for that year.
option_notes: This is the Section 17 rule. Customary or interim bonus paid for an accounting year, before the statutory bonus becomes payable, can be set off against the bonus payable under the Act for that same year. Customary bonus is a bonus paid by long-standing custom or usage (for example at festivals), and interim bonus is an advance payment made before the final computation. The set-off is limited to the same accounting year.

This is the incorrect position. The Act does not prohibit the deduction; it is specifically allowed. Without such a provision employees could receive double payment for the same year. The deduction applies only to amounts paid for that accounting year and cannot be extended to other years.

This is incorrect. Customary bonus arises from established custom, usage or agreement and continues according to that custom. It is not a one-time payment, and having paid it in one year does not release management from paying it in the next if the custom exists. Customary bonus is also protected by Section 17 only as an adjustment item.

This is incorrect. Bonus under the Act is payable every accounting year when the employee has worked at least 30 working days, the establishment has an allocable surplus, and the employee's salary is within the eligibility limit (Rs 21,000 per month). Each year stands on its own, so paying bonus in one year gives no exemption in the next.
