Eligible employees are those drawing salary or wages up to Rs 21,000 per month (after the 2015 amendment, effective from 1 April 2014) and who have worked at least 30 working days in the year. Bonus is payable within 8 months of the close of the accounting year (Section 19), unless extended by the appropriate government. The minimum bonus is 8.33% of salary or Rs 100, whichever is higher (Section 10), and the maximum is 20% (Section 11), computed on salary subject to a ceiling of Rs 7,000 per month or the minimum wage for the scheduled employment, whichever is higher (Section 12). Allocable surplus is 60% of available surplus (67% for foreign companies or those which are not Indian public companies) under Section 2(4). Set-on and set-off of allocable surplus is covered by Section 15. Section 8 provides for disqualification from bonus (fraud, riotous or violent behaviour, theft or misappropriation, sabotage), and 2015 amendment includes conviction for sexual harassment. Section 17 provides for adjustment of customary or interim bonus. Section 18 deals with deduction of festival bonus or other customary bonus given for the same year, and also with the deduction of the amount of loss caused by misconduct. Section 21 deals with recovery of bonus as a money due from the employer. Section 22 provides for the claim to be made by the employee within one year. Inspectors are appointed under Section 27. The Act is part of the Code on Wages, 2019 (the bonus provisions are in Chapter V).

question: Under the Factories Act, 1948, a person is an ‘adolescent’ on attaining the age of :
options: 14 years but has not completed 18 years of age
15 years but has not completed 18 years of age
14 years but has not completed 21 years of age
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 2 of the Factories Act, 1948 defines the age categories of workers. Section 2(c) defines 'child' as a person who has not completed his fifteenth year of age. Section 2(b) defines 'adolescent' as a person who has completed his fifteenth year but has not completed his eighteenth year. Section 2(a) defines 'adult' as a person who has completed his eighteenth year. The 1948 Act originally set the child limit at 14 years; the Factories (Amendment) Act, 1954 raised it to 15 years, aligning with the Children (Pledging of Labour) Act and ILO standards. Section 67 prohibits employment of a child below 14 years in any factory; this is the operative prohibition (the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 as amended in 2016 defines 'child' as under 14 and 'adolescent' as 14 to 18, which is a different statute and a common trap). Adolescents (15-18) may work only if they hold a certificate of fitness (Section 68) and carry a token (Section 69), and their working hours are limited to 4.5 hours a day; night work is generally restricted (Section 70). Elimination: options (a) and (d) use 14, the 1986 Act's threshold, and (d) uses 21, which is the old majority age. Option (c) omits the upper limit.
explanations: Incorrect: 14 years as the lower limit belongs to the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (as amended 2016), not the Factories Act, which uses 15.
Correct: Section 2(b) of the Factories Act, 1948 defines an adolescent as one who has completed 15 years but not 18 years.
Incorrect: It gives only the lower age and no upper limit; a person who completes 18 years becomes an adult.
Incorrect: Both the lower limit of 14 and the upper limit of 21 are wrong; 21 is not a threshold in the Act, and 18 marks adulthood.
keyfact: Factories Act 1948: child under 15; adolescent 15 to under 18; adult 18 and above.
option_notes: 14 to 18 years is the definition of 'adolescent' under the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 as amended in 2016. The amendment banned employment of children below 14 in all occupations, and banned adolescents (14-18) from hazardous occupations and processes. It is distinct from the Factories Act's definitions, which are 15 and 18. Violations attract imprisonment and fines.

15 to 18 years is the Factories Act, 1948 definition of an adolescent in Section 2(b). Adolescents need a certificate of fitness from a certifying surgeon (Section 68) and must carry a token giving the reference to that certificate (Section 69). They can work in a factory only if they meet these conditions, and their daily work is restricted to 4.5 hours with restrictions on night work (10 pm to 6 am, with limited exceptions).

Fifteen years is the threshold in the Factories Act that separates a 'child' (under 15) from an adolescent (15 or above). The 1954 amendment raised the child age from 14 to 15. However, Section 67 prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories. Children aged 14-15 may be employed only for limited hours (4.5 per day) and not at night, under conditions in Sections 71-72.

The 14-to-21 range does not correspond to any definition in the Factories Act. Twenty-one was the age of majority under older laws, and the Indian Majority Act, 1875 set majority at 18 (21 where a guardian is appointed). Under the Factories Act an adult is a person who has completed 18 years, and the Act has no category stretching to 21.
related: Factories Act, 1948: 'child' means a person who has not completed 15 years.
Adult under the Factories Act is a person who has completed 18 years.
Section 68 requires a certificate of fitness for adolescents; Section 69 requires a token.
Section 67 prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories.
Adolescents and children work at most 4.5 hours per day.
Article 24 bans child employment under 14 in hazardous work.
The 1986 child labour Act was amended in 2016 to define adolescent as 14-18.
Factories Act 1948 came into force on 1 April 1949.
summary: The correct answer is (b). Under Section 2(b) of the Factories Act, 1948 (as amended in 1954), an 'adolescent' is a person who has completed 15 years of age but has not completed 18 years. The Act defines 'child' as a person who has not completed 15 years, and 'adult' as one who has completed 18 years.
topic_notes: The Factories Act, 1948 came into force on 1 April 1949 and replaced the Factories Act, 1934. It applies to the whole of India and covers manufacturing premises employing 10 or more workers with power, or 20 or more without power (Section 2(m)). Key definitions in Section 2: adult (18 or over), adolescent (15 to under 18), child (under 15), worker (Section 2(l)), occupier (Section 2(n)), manufacturing process (Section 2(k)). Chapters cover health (Sections 11-20), safety (Sections 21-41), hazardous processes (Chapter IV-A, added in 1987 after the Bhopal gas tragedy), welfare (Sections 42-50), working hours of adults (Sections 51-66: 48 hours a week, 9 hours a day, spread-over of 10.5 hours, an interval after 5 hours), employment of young persons (Sections 67-77), annual leave with wages (Sections 78-84), and penalties (Sections 92-106). Section 66 deals with women, who may work 6 am to 7 pm, with night work allowed under state conditions. Child labour: Section 67 bars children under 14 from factories; adolescents need a fitness certificate; Section 71 limits child working hours to 4.5 per day. The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 was amended in 2016. Article 24 of the Constitution prohibits employment of children under 14 in factories, mines, or hazardous employment; Article 21A provides free and compulsory education for ages 6-14. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 will subsume the Factories Act when brought into force, and it keeps the 18-year adult limit and a minimum age for hazardous work.

ocr: Under the Factories Act, 1948, ‘factory’ means any premises whereon : L, ten or more workers are/were working on any day of the preceding 12 months, in any premise where manufacturing process is being carried on with the aid of power. 2. twenty or more workers are/were working on any day of the preceding 12 months, in any premise where manufacturing process is being carried on without the aid of power. Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) Both1and2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 Which among the following is/are general duty/duties of an ‘occupier’ under Section 7
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Chapter III (Sections 11-20) of the Factories Act, 1948 covers Health. It deals with: cleanliness (Sec 11), disposal of wastes and effluents (12), ventilation and temperature (13), dust and fume (14), artificial humidification (15), overcrowding (16), lighting (17), drinking water (18), latrines and urinals (19) and spittoons (20). Sec 13 requires a temperature that secures reasonable comfort to workers and prevents injury to health, so option (c) is covered. Sec 19 requires sufficient latrines and urinals, kept clean and sanitary, with a sweeper whose primary duty is to keep latrines, urinals and washing places clean, so option (b) is covered. Sec 20 requires spittoons in convenient places, maintained in a clean and hygienic condition, so option (a) is covered. Welfare is a separate chapter (Chapter V, Sections 42-50). It covers washing facilities, storing and drying clothing, sitting facilities, first aid, canteens (more than 250 workers), shelters/rest rooms/lunch rooms (more than 150 workers), creches (more than 30 women) and welfare officers (500 or more workers). Overnight accommodation appears in neither chapter, so (d) is the 'not covered' item. It is a distractor built from the 500-worker welfare officer threshold.
explanations: Wrong as the answer: Sec 20 requires spittoons in convenient places, maintained in a clean and hygienic condition, so this is covered under Health.
Wrong as the answer: Sec 19 requires a sweeper whose primary duty is to keep latrines, urinals and washing places clean, so this is covered under Health.
Wrong as the answer: Sec 13 requires adequate ventilation and a temperature that secures reasonable comfort to workers, so this is covered under Health.
Correct: the Act has no provision for overnight accommodation. The 500-worker figure relates to Welfare Officers (Sec 49), and Chapter III does not mention accommodation.
keyfact: Factories Act Health = Secs 11-20 (cleanliness, ventilation, temperature, lighting, water, latrines, spittoons); no overnight accommodation provision, and the 500-worker threshold is for Welfare Officers.
option_notes: Spittoons (Sec 20): spittoons must be provided in convenient places and maintained in a clean and hygienic condition. The State Government may make rules on their number and placement. Spitting except in spittoons is prohibited, and a notice to that effect must be displayed. Contravention is punishable with a fine of up to Rs 5. This provision is part of the Health chapter.

Latrines and urinals (Sec 19): sufficient, separate latrines and urinals must be provided for male and female workers. They must be conveniently situated and accessible, and kept clean and sanitary. Sweepers must be employed to keep latrines, urinals and washing places clean. Sufficient washing places are also provided for. This is part of the Health chapter, and State rules prescribe the scales.

Temperature (Sec 13): every factory must maintain a temperature that secures to workers reasonable conditions of comfort and prevents injury to health. Walls and roofs must be of heat-resisting material, and the temperature can be reduced by whitewashing, spraying or screens. Sec 13 also requires adequate ventilation. The State Government prescribes standards, and this is part of the Health chapter.

Overnight accommodation is not a Health provision, and the Act contains no such obligation. The 500-worker threshold is associated with Welfare Officers (Sec 49). Welfare facilities under Chapter V include washing facilities, first aid, canteens, shelters or rest rooms, creches, and welfare officers. Housing is treated under the Plantations Labour Act and mining laws, not the Factories Act.
related: Sec 11 deals with cleanliness and Sec 12 with disposal of wastes and effluents.
Sec 18 deals with drinking water, and cool water is mandatory in hot weather.
Canteens (Sec 46) are required where more than 250 workers are employed.
Creches (Sec 48) are required where more than 30 women are employed.
Welfare Officers (Sec 49) are required where 500 or more workers are employed.
Shelters, rest rooms and lunch rooms (Sec 47) are required where more than 150 workers are employed.
Sec 7A lists the general duties of the occupier.
Weekly working hours for adults are 48, and daily hours are 9.
summary: The answer is (d). Overnight accommodation is not a 'Health' provision under Chapter III of the Factories Act, 1948, and no provision requires it for factories employing more than 500 workers. The 500-worker threshold applies to the appointment of Welfare Officers (Sec 49). Note: the image shows three questions, and I have assumed Q66 is the third one, on 'Health'.
topic_notes: The Factories Act, 1948 came into force on 1 April 1949. It extends to the whole of India, and its main objects are the health, safety, welfare, working hours and leave of factory workers. Definitions in Sec 2: 'factory' means premises where 10 or more workers are working on any day of the preceding 12 months and a manufacturing process is carried on with the aid of power, or 20 or more workers where it is carried on without power. The Act excludes mines and mobile units of the armed forces, railway running sheds, and hotels, restaurants and eating places. The 'occupier' is the person with ultimate control over the affairs of the factory. For a company, one of the directors must be the occupier. Sec 7A lists the occupier's general duties: health, safety and welfare of all workers while at work, safe plant and systems of work, safe use, handling, storage and transport of articles and substances, information, instruction, training and supervision, safe places of work and access, and a safe working environment. Sec 7B sets out the general duties of manufacturers. Chapter III covers Health (Secs 11-20). Chapter IV covers Safety (Secs 21-41), including fencing of machinery, work on or near machinery in motion, hoists and lifts, pressure plant, precautions against dangerous fumes, and fire precautions. Sec 41A deals with Site Appraisal Committees, and Secs 41B-41H cover hazardous processes. Chapter V covers Welfare (Secs 42-50). Chapter VI covers working hours of adults (Secs 51-66): 48 hours per week, 9 hours per day, and a spread-over of 10.5 hours. Chapter VII covers employment of young persons, and Chapter VIII covers annual leave with wages. Penalties are in Chapter X.

question:
Which of the following provisions regarding 69 ‘fencing of machinery’ is/are provided by the] ~ Factories Act, 1948 ?
1. Every moving part, whether prime mover or fly wheel connected to the prime mover, shall be securely fenced. 2. _Headrace and tailrace of every water wheel and water turbine shall be securely fenced.
3. Lubricated belts of machinery shall be compulsorily fenced.
4. Any part of a stock-bar which projects beyond the head stock of a lathe shall be compulsorily fenced. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Indian Economy
detail: Section 21 (Fencing of machinery) is the key provision on machine safety. It has two tiers. The first tier is absolute: certain items must always be securely fenced. These are (i) every moving part of a prime mover and every flywheel connected to a prime mover, whether or not they are in the engine house; (ii) the headrace and tailrace of every water-wheel and water turbine; and (iii) any part of a stock-bar which projects beyond the head stock of a lathe. The second tier is conditional: unless they are in a position or of a construction that is safe to every person employed in the factory, every part of an electric generator, motor or rotary converter, every part of transmission machinery, and every dangerous part of any other machinery must be fenced. Fencing must conform to the standards in the State Rules and must be kept in position while the parts are in motion or in use. There is no provision making lubricated belts compulsorily fenced; belts are covered only under the general transmission-machinery clause. Related sections: Section 22 (work on or near machinery in motion), Section 23 (employment of young persons on dangerous machines), Section 24 (striking gear and devices for cutting off power), Section 25 (self-acting machines) and Section 26 (casing of new machinery). So statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct and 3 is not, giving option (d).
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statements 1 and 4, which are also stated in Section 21 of the Act.
Wrong: it includes statement 4 but omits statement 2, and statement 1 is also correct, so it is incomplete.
Wrong: statement 3 on lubricated belts is not in the Act, so this option is incorrect even though statement 2 is correct.
Correct: statements 1, 2 and 4 are each in Section 21(1), while statement 3 has no basis in the Act.
keyfact: Section 21 absolutely requires fencing of prime mover parts, flywheels, headrace and tailrace of water-wheels and turbines, and projecting lathe stock-bars; lubricated belts are not listed.
option_notes: Statement 2 alone is the headrace and tailrace rule. The headrace is the channel taking water to a water-wheel or turbine, and the tailrace carries it away. It is one of the absolute fencing requirements under Section 21(1)(ii), alongside prime movers, flywheels and lathe stock-bars. Alone it is incomplete, because the other first-tier items are also required.

Statements 1 and 4 cover the prime mover/flywheel rule and the projecting lathe stock-bar rule. Both are absolute fencing duties under Section 21(1)(i) and (iii). The option is incomplete because it omits the headrace and tailrace rule in Section 21(1)(ii), which is also correct.

Statements 2 and 3 combine the valid headrace and tailrace rule with the invalid lubricated-belt claim. Belts fall under transmission machinery, which is fenced only unless safe by position or construction. The lubrication rules lie elsewhere, in Section 22 and the State Rules. The option fails because it adds a wrong item and omits two correct ones.

Statements 1, 2 and 4 together make up the full first-tier list of Section 21(1)(i)-(iii): prime mover and flywheel parts, headrace and tailrace of water-wheels and turbines, and a projecting lathe stock-bar. These must always be fenced. The second tier covers generators, motors, transmission machinery and other dangerous parts, which are fenced unless safe by position or construction.
related: Section 21 of the Factories Act, 1948 deals with fencing of machinery.
Section 22 restricts work on or near machinery in motion; only trained adult males may examine it.
Section 23 bars employment of young persons on dangerous machines unless trained and supervised.
Section 24 provides striking gear and devices for cutting off power.
Section 40B provides for Safety Officers where 1,000 or more workers are employed.
Section 41A provides for Site Appraisal Committees; 41B covers hazardous processes.
Section 36A deals with portable electric light, and Section 37 with explosive or inflammable dust or gas.
Section 92 is the general penalty provision of the Factories Act.
statements: 1 — Correct: Section 21(1)(i) requires every moving part of a prime mover and every flywheel connected to a prime mover to be securely fenced, whether or not it is in the engine house. A prime mover is an engine, motor or other appliance that generates or provides power. This is an absolute duty, not subject to the 'safe by position' exemption. The section is enforced by Inspectors, and breach is punishable under Section 92.

2 — Correct: Section 21(1)(ii) requires the headrace and tailrace of every water-wheel and water turbine to be securely fenced. The headrace is the channel bringing water to the wheel or turbine, and the tailrace carries it away. Fencing prevents workers falling in or being swept into the flow. This item is part of the first tier of absolute fencing, along with prime movers and flywheels.

3 — Incorrect: No clause of Section 21 makes lubricated belts compulsorily fenced. Belts and pulleys are transmission machinery, which Section 21(1)(iv)(b) requires to be fenced only unless they are in a safe position or construction. Lubrication is addressed in the State Rules and in Section 22, which restricts lubricating or adjusting machinery in motion to specially trained adult male workers wearing tight-fitting clothing. Do not confuse fencing with lubrication safety.

4 — Correct: Section 21(1)(iii) requires any part of a stock-bar which projects beyond the head stock of a lathe to be securely fenced. A stock-bar is a long bar of material fed through the hollow spindle of the lathe. The projecting length can whip around when rotating at speed and cause serious injury. This is one of the three absolute items in Section 21(1), alongside prime movers and water-wheel races.
summary: The answer is (d), statements 1, 2 and 4. Section 21 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires moving parts of prime movers, flywheels, headrace and tailrace of water wheels and turbines, and projecting stock-bars of lathes to be securely fenced. Statement 3 on lubricated belts is not a Section 21 requirement.
topic_notes: Chapter IV of the Factories Act, 1948 (Sections 21-41) deals with Safety. Section 21 covers fencing of machinery. Its first tier is absolute: moving parts of a prime mover and flywheels connected to it, the headrace and tailrace of water-wheels and turbines, and projecting stock-bars of lathes. Its second tier is conditional on the part not being safe by position or construction: electric generators, motors and rotary converters, transmission machinery, and other dangerous machinery parts. The Section also lets the State Government prescribe further safeguards. Section 22 restricts work on or near machinery in motion; examination and lubrication are done only by specially trained adult male workers wearing tight-fitting clothing, and women and young persons may not clean, lubricate or adjust moving machinery. Section 23 prohibits young persons from working at dangerous machines unless properly instructed, trained and supervised. Section 24 provides striking gear and devices for cutting off power. Section 25 covers self-acting machines, requiring a clear space of 45 cm (18 inches) from fixed structures. Section 26 requires casing of new machinery, such as set screws, bolts and gearing. Section 27 prohibits employing women and children near cotton openers. Section 28 covers hoists and lifts, Section 29 lifting machines, chains, ropes and lifting tackle, Section 30 revolving machinery (maximum safe working speed), Section 31 pressure plant, Section 32 floors, stairs and means of access, Section 33 pits, sumps and openings in floors, Section 34 excessive weights (limits set by State Governments), Section 35 protection of eyes, Section 36 precautions against dangerous fumes, Section 36A portable electric light, Section 37 explosive or inflammable dust, gas, Section 38 precautions in case of fire, Section 39 power to require specifications of defective parts, Section 40 safety of buildings and machinery, Section 40A maintenance of buildings, Section 40B safety officers (for factories with 1,000 or more workers or hazardous processes). Section 41 covers the power to make rules. Penalties are in Section 92, with enhanced penalties for contravention causing death or serious injury.

question:
Which of the following provisions, relating to 79the measures to be taken to prevent explosion in a factory engaged in a manufacturing process which produces dust, gas, fumes, etc. and is likely to explode on ignition, is/are provided in the Factories Act, 1948 ?
1. Effective enclosure of plant and machinery used in the process
2. Ensure accumulation of the dust at one corner
3. Exclusion or effective enclosure of all possible sources of ignition
4. Ensure that the gas is not foul smelling Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Indian Economy
detail: Section 37 deals with 'Explosive or inflammable dust, gas, etc.' Where a manufacturing process produces dust, gas, fume or vapour of such character and to such extent as to be likely to explode on ignition, the occupier must take all practicable measures to prevent an explosion. First, effective enclosure of the plant or machinery used in the process broadly. Second, removal or prevention of the accumulation of such dust, gas, fume or vapour (not accumulation in a corner; the aim is to prevent build-up). Third, if the dust etc. is likely to be enclosed, the enclosure must have effective explosion-venting arrangements. Fourth, exclusion or effective enclosure of all possible sources of ignition. Section 37(2) covers plant that is subject to internal pressure of explosion, and 37(3) deals with the pressure-relief arrangements. 37(4) lets the Chief Inspector order measures, and the plant must be built to withstand the pressure. Elimination: statement 2 reverses the rule, since the Act requires prevention of accumulation, so it is wrong. Statement 4 is irrelevant to explosion safety and is not in the Act. This leaves 1 and 3 only.
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is correct, but the option omits statement 3, which is also in Section 37.
Wrong: statement 2 is not a provision of the Act; the Act requires preventing accumulation, not collecting dust in a corner.
Correct: statements 1 and 3 appear in Section 37 (enclosure of plant and exclusion or enclosure of ignition sources).
Wrong: statements 2 and 4 are not provisions of the Act, so this combination fails.
keyfact: Section 37 requires enclosure of plant, prevention of accumulation, venting, and exclusion of ignition sources, not accumulating dust in a corner.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: statement 1 is true (Section 37(1)(a)), but the option is incomplete. Section 37 also requires the exclusion or enclosure of ignition sources, venting arrangements and prevention of accumulation of dust, gas, fume or vapour. UPSC often uses incomplete-but-true options as distractors, so check all statements.

Option (b) 1 and 2 only: this pairs a true statement with a false one. The Act asks for prevention or removal of accumulation, not gathering it in a corner. Dust accumulation is itself the hazard, which is why housekeeping and exhaust systems are required in dust-prone industries such as flour mills, textiles and coal.

Option (c) 1 and 3 only: this is the correct option. It reflects Section 37(1)(a) and (c). Section 37 also contains Section 37(2) on plant subject to explosion pressure, Section 37(3) on pressure-relief arrangements, and Section 37(4) on Chief Inspector's powers.

Option (d) 2, 3 and 4: this contains two invalid statements, 2 and 4. Statement 3 alone is valid. The option is a distractor combining a true item with fabricated ones. Smell of gas is irrelevant to the statutory explosion-prevention duty.
related: Section 37 of the Factories Act is on explosive or inflammable dust, gas, etc.
Section 36 deals with dangerous fumes and confined spaces; portable lights in them are limited to 24 volts.
Section 38 deals with fire precautions and means of escape.
Section 31 deals with pressure plant.
Section 40B provides for safety officers.
Chapter IVA (Sections 41A-41H) covers hazardous processes, inserted in 1987 after Bhopal.
Section 7A lists the general duties of the occupier.
Section 2(k) defines manufacturing process.
statements: 1 — Correct: Section 37(1)(a) requires effective enclosure of the plant or machinery used in the process. Section 37 is titled 'Explosive or inflammable dust, gas, etc.' and applies to any manufacturing process producing dust, gas, fume or vapour likely to explode on ignition. The occupier must take all practicable measures, including enclosure, preventing accumulation, venting arrangements and ignition-source control. Chapter IV (Sections 21-41) covers the safety provisions of the Act, and Section 37 is a key provision there.

2 — Incorrect: The Act requires the removal or prevention of accumulation of dust, gas, fume or vapour, not its accumulation in one corner. Section 37(1)(b) states this. Dust accumulation is a primary explosion hazard because it can form explosive clouds when disturbed. Practical measures include exhaust ventilation, regular cleaning and dust collection. The statement inverts the legal requirement, so it is wrong.

3 — Correct: Section 37(1)(c) requires the exclusion or effective enclosure of all possible sources of ignition. Examples include sparks, naked flames, hot surfaces and static electricity. Flameproof electrical fittings, spark-free tools and earthing or bonding are typical measures. This is a core preventive duty of the occupier under Chapter IV on safety.

4 — Incorrect: Nothing in Section 37 or elsewhere requires that gas be non-foul-smelling. The Act is concerned with explosion risk, not odour. Odour may matter for leak detection, such as mercaptan added to LPG, but it is not a statutory explosion-prevention measure here. Related provisions on dangerous fumes are in Section 36 (precautions against dangerous fumes in confined spaces).
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Section 37 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires effective enclosure of the plant or machinery used in the process and exclusion or effective enclosure of all possible sources of ignition. It does not require dust to be accumulated at one corner or gas to be non-foul-smelling.
topic_notes: Chapter IV of the Factories Act, 1948 (Sections 21-41) covers Safety. Key sections: 21 fencing of machinery; 22 work on or near machinery in motion; 23 employment of young persons on dangerous machines; 24 striking gear and devices for cutting off power; 25 self-acting machines; 26 casing of new machinery; 27 prohibition of women and children near cotton openers; 28 hoists and lifts; 29 lifting machines, chains, ropes; 30 revolving machinery; 31 pressure plant; 32 floors, stairs and means of access; 33 pits, sumps, openings in floors; 34 excessive weights; 35 protection of eyes; 36 precautions against dangerous fumes; 36A portable electric light; 37 explosive or inflammable dust, gas; 38 precautions in case of fire; 39 power to require specifications of defective parts; 40 safety of buildings and machinery; 40A maintenance of buildings; 40B safety officers; 41 and 41A-41H cover hazardous processes (Chapter IVA, added after the Bhopal gas tragedy 1984 by the 1987 amendment). Section 36 covers confined spaces, requiring manholes of specified size and the use of 24 V lamps. Section 38 requires means of escape and fire-warning, and doors opening outward and not locked. Section 40B requires safety officers where 1,000 or more workers are employed or where hazardous processes are involved. Other related provisions: Section 2(k) defines manufacturing process, Section 2(cb) hazardous process, Section 7A general duties of occupier. Chapter IVA includes site appraisal committees, on-site emergency plans and the right of workers to warn of imminent danger (Section 41H).

ocr: Which one of the following statements relating to the Factories Act, 1948 is not correct ? Creche should be provided in a factory (a) employing ordinarily more than thirty women. Creche can be used by all children. (b) Every factory employing ordinarily five (c) hundred or more workers should employ prescribed number of welfare officers. Adult means a _ person who has (d) completed 18 years of age. X, who is an ‘occupier’ of a factory Mr. employing 20 workers, asked the employees to work from 9:00 am to 6:30 pm with a half-an-hour break in between. The workers are given Sunday as weekly holida
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 48 requires a creche (a room or rooms for children under six years of age) in every factory where more than thirty women workers are ordinarily employed. It must be adequately lighted and ventilated, kept clean, and run by women trained in child care. The State Government may make rules on its location, standards and facilities such as washing and changing clothes. Section 49 requires a factory ordinarily employing 500 or more workers to employ welfare officers, and the State Government prescribes their number, qualifications and conditions of service. Section 2(a) defines an adult as a person who has completed 18 years of age. Section 2(c) defines a child as a person who has not completed 15 years, and Section 2(b) defines an adolescent as a person who has completed 15 but not 18 years. The question asks for the INCORRECT statement. Statements (a), (c) and (d) match the Act, and (b) is wrong because the creche is restricted to young children (under six) of women workers, not all children. The words 'all children' are the trap.
explanations: Correct statement, so not the answer. Section 48 requires a creche where more than thirty women are ordinarily employed.
Incorrect statement, so this is the answer. The creche is for children below six years of the women workers, not for all children.
Correct statement, so not the answer. Section 49 requires welfare officers in factories ordinarily employing 500 or more workers.
Correct statement, so not the answer. Section 2(a) defines an adult as a person who has completed 18 years.
keyfact: Factories Act creche (Sec 48): more than 30 women workers, for children below 6 years of women workers only.
option_notes: Section 48 (creche): it applies where more than thirty women workers are ordinarily employed. The creche must be adequately lighted, ventilated and kept clean, and run by women trained in child care. It is for children under six. The State Government makes rules on location and standards. The threshold is 'more than thirty', not 'thirty or more'.

Creche use is limited to children under six years of the women employees, not all children. This is the false statement. Many students confuse the age limit of a creche (below 6) with the definition of a child in Section 2(c) (below 15). The creche is a welfare measure for working mothers.

Section 49 (welfare officers): factories ordinarily employing 500 or more workers must employ welfare officers. The State Government prescribes their number, qualifications, duties and conditions of service. Section 49 also requires canteens, shelters and similar welfare facilities to be provided. Other thresholds to remember: canteen at 250 workers (Sec 46), and rest rooms or shelters at 150 workers (Sec 47).

Section 2(a): an adult is a person who has completed 18 years of age. An adolescent is 15 to 18 years (Sec 2(b)), and a child is under 15 (Sec 2(c)). Children below 14 cannot be employed in a factory (Sec 67). Adolescents need a fitness certificate to work as adults.

topic_notes: The Factories Act, 1948 came into force on 1 April 1949 and applies to premises employing 10 or more workers with power, or 20 or more without power. Chapters cover inspecting staff, health, safety, hazardous processes, welfare, working hours of adults, employment of young persons, annual leave with wages, and penalties. Key definitions: 'worker' (Sec 2(l)), 'occupier' (Sec 2(n)), who has ultimate control over the factory affairs, and 'manufacturing process' (Sec 2(k)). Health (Secs 11-20): cleanliness, ventilation and temperature, overcrowding, drinking water, latrines, spittoons. Safety (Secs 21-41): fencing of machinery, work on or near machinery, hoists and lifts, pressure plants. Welfare (Secs 42-50): washing facilities, first aid (one box per 150 workers), canteen (250 workers), shelters or rest rooms and lunch rooms (150 workers), creche (more than 30 women), welfare officers (500 workers). Working hours: 48 hours a week and 9 hours a day (Secs 51-54), with an interval of rest after 5 hours (Sec 55), and spread-over not exceeding 10.5 hours (Sec 56). Overtime is paid at twice the ordinary rate (Sec 59). A weekly holiday applies (Sec 52). Women are not allowed to work between 7 pm and 6 am, subject to State exemptions (Sec 66). Young persons: children below 14 are prohibited from work (Sec 67), and adolescents need a fitness certificate. Annual leave with wages is 1 day for every 20 days worked by adults (Sec 79). Safety committees and the inspector's powers were strengthened after the Bhopal gas tragedy through the 1987 amendment.

detail: The Factories Act, 1948 applies to premises with 10 or more workers if power is used, or 20 or more workers if power is not used, so a 20-worker factory is covered where it does not use power. Here the day runs 9:00 am to 6:30 pm, which is 9.5 hours. Less a 0.5-hour break, that is 9 hours of work. Section 54 caps adult work at 9 hours a day, so a 9-hour day is just permissible. Section 55 requires a rest interval of at least half an hour after at most 5 hours of work, and Section 56 limits the spread-over to 10.5 hours. Section 51 caps weekly hours at 48, and 6 days of 9 hours is 54, so the weekly cap is breached unless the days are shortened or overtime rules apply. Sunday as the weekly holiday satisfies Section 52. Relaxations are available with the Chief Inspector's permission, as under Section 54's proviso, and overtime is governed by Section 59. Elimination: (a) ignores the weekly limit. (b) is wrong because extra incentive cannot override statutory limits. (d) is wrong because the hours rules are not gender-specific, and women are in fact more restricted. So (c) is the only option that links the permission to the Section 51 limit.
explanations: Incorrect: an unconditional 'Yes' ignores the 48-hour weekly cap of Section 51. Six 9-hour days make 54 hours.
Incorrect: a statutory limit on working hours cannot be waived by paying an incentive. Only overtime under Section 59, with extra wages, is permitted.
Correct: the schedule is workable only within Section 51's limit, and with the Chief Inspector's approval or exemption in specified situations such as the Section 54 proviso or Section 64.
Incorrect: the hours limits apply to all adult workers. Women face extra restrictions, such as day-time work only under Section 66, not a special permission for men.
keyfact: Factories Act: 9 hours a day (S.54), 48 hours a week (S.51), 5 hours before a half-hour rest (S.55), spread-over 10.5 hours (S.56).
option_notes: Option (a) is an unconditional yes. Under the Act, adult workers may work at most 48 hours a week (Section 51), 9 hours a day (Section 54), with a rest interval after 5 hours (Section 55) and a spread-over of 10.5 hours (Section 56). A weekly holiday is required by Section 52. A schedule is lawful only if it meets all of these together, so an unconditional yes is not safe.

Option (b) makes permission depend on an incentive. Overtime is governed by Section 59. Workers get double the ordinary rate of wages for work beyond 9 hours a day or 48 hours a week. The overtime is limited by state rules, and the wages are statutory, not a voluntary incentive. Incentive pay does not legalise extra hours.

Option (c) is the Act's mechanism of limits plus relaxations. Section 51 gives the 48-hour week. Section 54 gives the 9-hour day, and the Chief Inspector can allow exemptions in specified circumstances. Section 64 allows exemption for supervisory staff, and Section 65 gives power to exempt for urgent repairs and similar cases. Compensatory holidays are covered by Section 53.

Option (d) is incorrect because working hours are not restricted to males. Women's work in factories is regulated by Section 66: generally only 6 am to 7 pm, with other hours allowed by state government exemption, plus provisions on dangerous operations and creches. The rules on hours apply to adult workers of either sex.

topic_notes: The Factories Act, 1948 came into force on 1 April 1949 and is administered by state governments through the Chief Inspector of Factories. A 'factory' is premises with 10 or more workers using power, or 20 or more workers without power, where a manufacturing process is carried on. The occupier is the person with ultimate control of the factory affairs. Adult means a person who has completed 18 years, and an adolescent is 15 to 18. Key hour rules are: 48 hours a week (S.51); weekly holiday (S.52); compensatory holidays (S.53); 9 hours a day (S.54); rest interval of half an hour after 5 hours (S.55); spread-over of 10.5 hours (S.56); overtime at double the ordinary rate (S.59); no double employment (S.60); and notice of periods of work (S.61). detail: Section 46 of the Factories Act, 1948 deals with canteens. It empowers the State Government to make rules requiring the occupier of a factory wherein more than 250 workers are ordinarily employed to provide and maintain a canteen or canteens for the use of workers. The rules may cover the date by which the canteen is to be provided, standards of construction, accommodation, furniture and equipment, the foodstuffs to be served and charges, the constitution of a managing committee representing the workers, and the delegation of the Chief Inspector's power to approve the food and prices. Compare the other welfare thresholds that students often confuse: shelters, rest rooms and lunch rooms (Section 47) are required where more than 150 workers are ordinarily employed; creches (Section 48) where more than 30 women workers are employed; a welfare officer (Section 49) where 500 or more workers are employed. Because the canteen threshold is 'more than 250', options 100, 200 and 300 are incorrect. 100 is not a threshold in the welfare chapter. 200 and 300 are distractors. Chapter V (Sections 42-50) covers Welfare.

detail: Q74 asks which was the first federation (parishangh) of trade unions in India. The All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) was formed on 31 October 1920 in Bombay. Lala Lajpat Rai was its first President and Joseph Baptista its first Vice-President; Dewan Chaman Lall was a prominent early leader, and N. M. Joshi was a founding General Secretary. It was formed partly to nominate Indian workers' delegates to the ILO's International Labour Conference, after the ILO was established in 1919. Earlier bodies such as the Madras Labour Union (1918, B. P. Wadia) were unions, not national federations. The Textile Labour Association (Ahmedabad, 1920, Gandhi-inspired) is a single-industry union. INTUC (1947) was the Congress-affiliated federation after independence, and Hind Mazdoor Sabha (1948) was set up by socialists. Elimination: any body formed after 1920 or a local union cannot be the first national federation, so (c) is correct.

option_notes: Textile Labour Association (TLA), Ahmedabad: founded in 1920 on Gandhi's inspiration, with Anasuya Sarabhai and Shankarlal Banker prominent. It followed the 1918 Ahmedabad mill strike and Gandhi's arbitration and fast. It is based on Gandhian principles of arbitration and non-violence, and is a single-industry union rather than a national federation. It later affiliated with INTUC.

Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC): established on 3 May 1947 and is the labour wing of the Indian National Congress. It was formed under the guidance of Sardar Patel and others. It follows Gandhian ideas of arbitration and cooperation between labour and capital. It is among the largest central trade unions in India by verified membership and has been recognised in tripartite forums such as the Indian Labour Conference.

All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC): the oldest central trade union organisation in India, founded 31 October 1920 in Bombay. Lala Lajpat Rai was the first President, and Dewan Chaman Lall was an early leader. It later came under communist influence and is now linked to the Communist Party of India. It split several times, in 1929 and 1931, and again in 1947 and later.

Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS): formed in December 1948 in Howrah by socialists, Forward Bloc members and others who rejected both Congress-controlled INTUC and communist-leaning AITUC. It was historically associated with the Praja Socialist Party and later Janata groups. It is an independent central trade union and is not affiliated with any political party.
