summary: The image does not show the text of Q75. Only the number '75.' is visible at the edge of the right-hand column, and the two complete questions are Q71 and Q72. I cannot honestly give an answer for Q75, so 'ans_ai' is left blank. For reference, Q71 is (a) and Q72 is (c).
topic_notes: Q75 is not visible, so these notes cover the visible Factories Act, 1948 provisions. Section 11 (cleanliness) requires factories to be kept clean and free from effluvia from drains. Floors must be cleaned at least once a week with a disinfectant or by another effective method. Walls, ceilings and staircases painted with washable water paint must be repainted at least once in 3 years and washed at least once every 6 months. Those painted or varnished otherwise (oil paint) must be repainted or revarnished at least once in 5 years. Walls and ceilings that are not painted must be whitewashed or colourwashed at least once in every 14 months. Section 57 deals with the 'night shifts' rule. Section 52 gives the weekly holiday, with a rest day on the first day of the week (Sunday). Section 54 sets daily hours at 9, and Section 51 sets weekly hours at 48. Section 55 requires a rest interval after 5 hours of work. Section 56 sets the spread-over at 10.5 hours. Section 59 gives overtime wages at twice the ordinary rate. Section 79 gives annual leave with wages at 1 day for every 20 days worked by adults, and 1 day for every 15 days worked by children. Section 2(m) defines a factory as 10 or more workers with power, or 20 or more without power. Possible future questions include the lime-washing interval, the washing frequency for water paint, the spread-over, and the overtime rate.

question: How many workers are required to be ordinarily employed in the factory for the provision of canteen facility under the Factories Act, 1948 ?
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Section 46 of the Factories Act, 1948 deals with canteens. It says the State Government may make rules requiring that, in any specified factory wherein more than two hundred and fifty workers are ordinarily employed, a canteen or canteens shall be provided and maintained by the occupier for the use of the workers. The rules may cover the date by which the canteen is to be provided, the standards of construction, accommodation, furniture and equipment, the foods to be served and their charges (which are to be on a no-profit, no-loss basis), the constitution of a managing committee with worker representation, and the delegation of the Chief Inspector's powers to approve the food and price lists. Related welfare provisions have different thresholds, and these are the usual source of confusion: shelters, rest rooms and lunch rooms (Sec 47) apply at more than 150 workers; creche (Sec 48) applies at more than 30 women workers; welfare officers (Sec 49) apply at 500 or more workers; first-aid boxes (Sec 45) apply to every factory, with an ambulance room at more than 500 workers. Options 100, 200 and 300 do not match any of these canteen thresholds, so only 250 is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: 100 is not the canteen threshold under Sec 46. It is unrelated to the canteen provision.
Incorrect: 200 is not the canteen threshold. It is a distractor close to the real number.
Correct: Sec 46 applies to factories ordinarily employing more than 250 workers.
Incorrect: 300 is not the threshold. Sec 46 is triggered above 250 workers.
keyfact: Canteen under Sec 46, Factories Act 1948: more than 250 workers ordinarily employed.
option_notes: 100 workers: no canteen provision applies at this number. Under the Factories Act, 1948, 'factory' means premises with 10 or more workers using power, or 20 or more without power. Section 85 lets the State Government extend the Act to premises with fewer workers. Hundred is not a welfare threshold in Chapter V.

200 workers: not a threshold for canteens or any other major welfare provision in the Act. Do not confuse it with 250 for canteens or 150 for shelters and rest rooms. Sec 40A and 40B deal with safety officers, which are required at 1000 or more workers, or in hazardous processes.

250 workers: the Sec 46 threshold. The State Government may make rules requiring a canteen in a factory with more than 250 workers ordinarily employed. The rules cover the canteen's construction, equipment, food items and charges. Prices are on a no-profit, no-loss basis, and a managing committee must include worker representatives.

300 workers: not a canteen threshold. The Act uses 30 (creche, women workers), 150 (shelters), 250 (canteen), 500 (welfare officer, ambulance room) and 1000 (safety officer). Three hundred appears in the Industrial Disputes Act (Chapter V-B, earlier 100, with state-level changes) and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act contexts, but not here.
related: Sec 46: canteen if more than 250 workers.
Sec 47: shelters, rest rooms, lunch rooms if more than 150 workers.
Sec 48: creche if more than 30 women workers.
Sec 49: welfare officer if 500 or more workers.
Sec 45: first-aid box per 150 workers; ambulance room if more than 500.
Factory: 10+ workers with power, 20+ without power.
Adult weekly working hours: 48; daily: 9 (Sec 51, 54).
The OSH Code, 2020 will replace the Factories Act, 1948.
summary: The answer is (c). Under Section 46 of the Factories Act, 1948, the State Government may make rules requiring a canteen in any factory where more than 250 workers are ordinarily employed. The employer must then provide and maintain it.
topic_notes: The Factories Act, 1948 came into force on 1 April 1949 and is administered by the Ministry of Labour and Employment, with enforcement mainly by State Governments through the Chief Inspector of Factories. It replaced the Factories Act, 1934. Chapter V (Sections 42-50) covers welfare: washing facilities (Sec 42), facilities for storing and drying clothing (Sec 43), sitting facilities (Sec 44), first-aid appliances (Sec 45), canteens (Sec 46), shelters, rest rooms and lunch rooms (Sec 47), creches (Sec 48), welfare officers (Sec 49) and the power of State Government to make rules (Sec 50). Key thresholds: first-aid box, one for every 150 workers ordinarily employed at a time; ambulance room if more than 500 workers; canteen if more than 250; shelters if more than 150; creche if more than 30 women workers, for children under 6 years; welfare officer if 500 or more workers. Other major topics are health (Chapter III, Sec 11-20), safety (Chapter IV, Sec 21-41), hazardous processes (Chapter IVA), working hours for adults (Sec 51-66: 48 hours a week, 9 hours a day, 5-hour spell), employment of young persons (Chapter VII; child means under 15, adolescent is 15-18), annual leave with wages (Sec 79: 1 day for every 20 days worked by adults), penalties (Chapter X) and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which will subsume this Act once brought into force. The OSH Code sets a threshold of 100 workers for canteens, which is a likely trap for future questions.

ocr: Which one among the following was the first aise Federation of Trade Unions in India ? (a) Textile Labour Association (b) Indian National Trade Union Congress (c) All India Trade Union Congress (d) Hind Mazdoor Sabha Who introduced a private member Bill in 1928 in Legislative Assembly to amend Trade Unions Act, 1926 for extending the immunities to all trade unions, whether registered or not ? (a) B.P. Wadia (b) N.M. Joshi (c) Motilal Nehru (d) MN. Roy Which among the following was not a recommendation made by the Royal Commission on Labour ? (a) Employer should recognize trade unions. (b) Gove
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Independent India's first National Commission on Labour (NCL-I) was appointed by the Government of India in December 1966 and chaired by P.B. Gajendragadkar, a former Chief Justice of India. It submitted its report in August 1969. It reviewed the changes in labour conditions since the Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley Commission, 1929-31), and its terms covered wages, working conditions, industrial relations, social security, labour welfare and workers' participation in management. It recommended setting up Industrial Relations Commissions and a fuller framework for social security. The Second National Commission on Labour was set up in 1999 under Ravindra Varma and reported in 2002. It recommended umbrella legislation for workers in the unorganised sector, among other things. Elimination: J.C. Shah is remembered for the Shah Commission of Inquiry into Emergency excesses (1977). Vivian Bose is associated with the Bose Commission and the Supreme Court bench. Ravindra Varma chaired NCL-II, not NCL-I. The only name that fits NCL-I is Gajendragadkar.
explanations: Incorrect: J.C. Shah headed the Shah Commission (1977), which inquired into Emergency-era excesses, and was also a Chief Justice of India. He did not chair the first NCL.
Incorrect: Vivian Bose was a Supreme Court judge, noted for his judgments and for commissions of inquiry. He had no connection with the NCL.
Incorrect: Ravindra Varma chaired the Second National Commission on Labour (1999-2002), not the first. He was a Union Labour Minister in 1977-79.
Correct: P.B. Gajendragadkar chaired the first National Commission on Labour, appointed in 1966, which reported in 1969.
keyfact: First National Commission on Labour (1966-69) was chaired by P.B. Gajendragadkar; the second (1999-2002) by Ravindra Varma.
option_notes: Justice J.C. Shah was a Chief Justice of India (1970-71). He headed the Shah Commission of Inquiry (1977-78), set up by the Janata Government to examine the excesses committed during the 1975-77 Emergency. He also headed other inquiries, such as the Shah Commission on the Mundhra affair, which was a separate inquiry. He is often confused with other judge-led commissions, so remember that the Shah Commission concerned the Emergency, not labour.

Justice Vivian Bose (1891-1983) was a Supreme Court judge from 1951 to 1956. He is known for a number of landmark judgments and for his work on commissions, such as the Bose Commission. He was not the chairman of any National Labour Commission. A common error is to treat any famous judge as a commission head, but the NCL chairmen were Gajendragadkar (first) and Ravindra Varma (second).

Ravindra Varma (1925-2006) was a Gandhian labour leader and politician. He served as Union Minister for Labour and Parliamentary Affairs in the Janata Government of 1977-79. He chaired the Second National Commission on Labour, set up in October 1999, which submitted its report in June 2002. Its main recommendations were an Umbrella Legislation for the unorganised sector and the consolidation of labour laws into groups.

P.B. Gajendragadkar (1901-1981) was the seventh Chief Justice of India (1964-66). After retiring he chaired the first National Commission on Labour (1966-69). He also headed the Gajendragadkar Commission on the Law Commission and other matters. He is associated with several well-known judgments in labour and constitutional law. The NCL-I report gave wide-ranging recommendations on industrial relations, wages, social security and labour welfare.
related: The first NCL (1966-69) was chaired by P.B. Gajendragadkar.
The Second NCL (1999-2002) was chaired by Ravindra Varma.
The Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley Commission) was appointed in 1929 and reported in 1931.
The Trade Unions Act, 1926 provides for the registration of trade unions.
AITUC (1920) was the first national federation of trade unions in India.
INTUC was formed in 1947 and HMS in 1948.
The Shah Commission (1977) inquired into Emergency excesses.
India has consolidated 29 central labour laws into four Labour Codes.
summary: The answer is (d) Justice P.B. Gajendragadkar. The first National Commission on Labour was set up in 1966 under the former Chief Justice of India P.B. Gajendragadkar and submitted its report in 1969. Only this option is correct; the others are linked to different commissions.
topic_notes: Labour commissions in India. The Royal Commission on Labour (Whitley Commission) was appointed in 1929 under J.H. Whitley and reported in 1931. Its recommendations covered trade union recognition, the protection of union leaders, and officers drawn from within the union, as well as wages, housing, health, safety and welfare. It led to later laws such as the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 and the Workmen's Compensation Act amendments. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 was India's first law on trade union registration and immunities. The first federation of trade unions was the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC), founded in 1920 in Bombay; N.M. Joshi and Lala Lajpat Rai were prominent founders. The Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC) was formed in 1947 and is linked to the Congress. The Hind Mazdoor Sabha was formed in 1948 as a socialist body. The first National Commission on Labour (1966-69) was chaired by P.B. Gajendragadkar. The Second National Commission on Labour (1999-2002) was chaired by Ravindra Varma. It recommended consolidating existing laws into a smaller number of codes and an umbrella law for unorganised workers. The four Labour Codes are the Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Social Security, 2020, and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. Other bodies worth knowing are the Indian Labour Conference (first held 1942) and the Standing Labour Committee. UPSC often asks about the chairpersons of commissions, the years in which they were appointed, and the sequence of labour legislation.

question: Who among the following was the first 81. President of All India Trade Union Congress ?
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: The All India Trade Union Congress, the oldest central trade union organisation in India, was founded on 31 October 1920 at Bombay (Mumbai). Its founding was prompted by the need to select Indian workers' delegates to the International Labour Organization (ILO), set up in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles. Lala Lajpat Rai, the Punjab Kesari and a prominent Congress leader, was elected the first President. He is credited with linking capitalism and imperialism, and with encouraging the labour movement. Joseph Baptista was the first Vice-President, and Dewan Chaman Lall was a key early organiser and later General Secretary and President (1925 session, etc.). N.M. Joshi was an important moderate leader who later split to form the All India Trade Union Federation (1929). Jawaharlal Nehru presided over AITUC in 1929 (Nagpur session), which led to the split. M.N. Roy was a communist leader and was associated with AITUC in the 1920s, but he was not its first president. Elimination: Chaman Lall, Roy and Nehru presided in later years or had other roles, so only Lajpat Rai fits as the first president.
explanations: Incorrect: Diwan Chaman Lall was an early organiser and General Secretary, and he presided over AITUC later (1926 Delhi session), but he was not the first President.
Correct: Lala Lajpat Rai presided over the first AITUC session in Bombay on 31 October 1920.
Incorrect: M.N. Roy was a communist ideologue and founder of the Communist Party of India (in Tashkent, 1920). He was active in the labour movement but was never the first AITUC President.
Incorrect: Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the AITUC session at Nagpur in 1929, not the first session.
keyfact: AITUC (31 Oct 1920, Bombay): first President Lala Lajpat Rai.
option_notes: Diwan Chaman Lall (1892-1973) was a trade unionist and Congress leader. He was among AITUC's founders and was General Secretary in its early years. He was elected AITUC President in 1926 and was a member of the Central Legislative Assembly. He was also a delegate to the ILO and later a Member of Parliament.

Lala Lajpat Rai (1865-1928), known as Punjab Kesari, was part of the Lal-Bal-Pal trio. He was President of the Congress's Calcutta Special Session of 1920 and the first AITUC President. He founded the Servants of the People Society and the Punjab National Bank (co-founder) and was fatally injured in a lathi charge during protests against the Simon Commission in 1928.

M.N. Roy (Manabendra Nath Roy, 1887-1954) was a revolutionary who founded the Communist Party of India in Tashkent in 1920 and the Mexican Communist Party. He later founded the Radical Democratic Party and the philosophy of Radical Humanism. He was influential among labour circles but was not an AITUC President.

Jawaharlal Nehru (1889-1964) became the first Prime Minister of India. He presided over the AITUC's 1929 Nagpur session, during which the moderates led by N.M. Joshi split off. He presided over the Congress at Lahore in 1929, which declared Purna Swaraj.
related: AITUC was founded on 31 October 1920 in Bombay.
First AITUC President: Lala Lajpat Rai.
First AITUC General Secretary: Dewan Chaman Lall (early years).
INTUC was founded in 1947 and is linked to the Congress.
BMS was founded in 1955 by Dattopant Thengadi.
CITU was formed in 1970.
Trade Unions Act was enacted in 1926.
ILO was established in 1919 and India is a founding member.
summary: The answer is (b) Lala Lajpat Rai. He presided over the inaugural session of the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) held in Bombay on 31 October 1920. Joseph Baptista was elected its first Vice-President (some sources list him as a vice-president), and Dewan Chaman Lall was its General Secretary at an early stage.
topic_notes: AITUC was founded on 31 October 1920 in Bombay, and is India's oldest central trade union organisation. Its founding was influenced by the formation of the ILO in 1919. Lala Lajpat Rai was the first President and Joseph Baptista the first Vice-President, while Dewan Chaman Lall was an early General Secretary. Early leaders included N.M. Joshi, V.V. Giri, C.R. Das, Subhas Chandra Bose and Jawaharlal Nehru. The Trade Unions Act 1926 gave legal recognition to trade unions. Splits: in 1929 the moderates (N.M. Joshi, V.V. Giri) left to form the All India Trade Union Federation; in 1931 the communists broke away as the Red Trade Union Congress; reunification came in 1940. Later political splits produced INTUC (1947, Congress-affiliated), HMS (1948, socialist), UTUC (1949), BMS (1955, RSS-linked, now the largest by verified membership), CITU (1970, CPI(M)-linked), and others such as SEWA (1972, Ela Bhatt) and NFITU. AITUC is affiliated with the Communist Party of India. The Trade Union Act 1926 provides for registration with seven members; the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 and the Industrial Relations Code 2020 are relevant. Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, a trade union is recognised as a negotiating union if it has support of 51 percent of workers.

question:
An inter-state migrant workman is entitled to which of the following under the Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment ue and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979 ?
1. Journey allowance to and from his residence and place of work
2. Displacement allowance
3. Wages during the period of such journeys as if he were on duty
4. Money for food during such journey Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979 protects workers recruited in one state by a contractor and employed in another. Section 12 sets out the wage and welfare duties of the contractor. Section 13 deals with wages and other facilities. Section 14 provides a displacement allowance, payable at the time of recruitment, equal to 50% of monthly wages payable or Rs 75, whichever is higher. It is not refundable and is in addition to wages. Section 15 provides a journey allowance: the contractor must pay the fare from the workman's home to the place of work and back, and wages for the journey period as if the workman were on duty. Section 16 covers the contractor's duties for suitable residential accommodation, and Section 17 for medical facilities, protective clothing and similar welfare. Section 18 makes the principal employer liable for wage shortfalls. Eliminating by statement: 1, 2 and 3 appear in the statute, while 4 (food money) does not, so only option (d) fits. The Act has since been subsumed into the OSH Code, 2020, which is not yet in force.
explanations: Wrong: it omits the journey-period wages in item 3, which the Act expressly gives.
Wrong: it includes item 4 (food money), which the Act does not provide, and omits the displacement allowance in item 2.
Wrong: it omits item 1, the journey fare, which Section 15 gives.
Correct: journey allowance, displacement allowance and wages during the journey are all statutory entitlements. Food money is not.
keyfact: Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979: displacement allowance (S.14), journey fare and journey wages (S.15). There is no food money.
option_notes: Option (a) pairs the journey allowance and the displacement allowance. Both are real entitlements under the Act: Section 15 for the fare and Section 14 for the displacement allowance. The displacement allowance is 50% of monthly wages or Rs 75, whichever is higher. The option is incomplete because it leaves out journey-period wages.

Option (b) combines the journey allowance, wages during the journey and food money. The first two are in Section 15. Food money is not in the Act. The option also leaves out the displacement allowance, which is in Section 14. The Act covers inter-state recruitment by contractors, and the licence and registration rules apply when 5 or more such workmen are involved.

Option (c) pairs the displacement allowance with journey-period wages. Both are valid, but the option leaves out the journey fare. Section 15 gives the fare and the journey wages together. Section 14 covers the displacement allowance at the time of recruitment. The Act was enacted in 1979 and came into force in 1980.

Option (d) lists all three statutory entitlements: the journey fare, the displacement allowance and journey-period wages. This is the correct option. The Act also requires equal wages for equal work, suitable accommodation, free medical facilities and protective clothing. The principal employer is liable if the contractor fails to pay wages.
related: Displacement allowance under Section 14 is 50% of monthly wages or Rs 75, whichever is higher.
Section 15 covers the journey allowance and journey-period wages.
The 1979 Act applies where 5 or more inter-state migrant workmen are employed.
The contractor needs a licence, and the principal employer must register the establishment.
The OSH Code, 2020 subsumes the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979.
The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 applies to establishments with 20 or more workers.
The e-Shram portal registers unorganised workers.
Under the Act, the contractor must issue each migrant worker a passbook.
statements: 1 — Correct: Section 15 requires the contractor to pay the fare for the journey from the workman's home to the place of work and back. The Act applies to establishments employing 5 or more inter-state migrant workmen, and to contractors who recruited 5 or more such workmen on any day in the preceding 12 months. Contractors need a licence and the principal employer needs registration. The fare is paid by the contractor as a statutory right, separate from wages. The Act also requires the contractor to give each workman a passbook with a photograph and details of employment.

2 — Correct: Section 14 gives a displacement allowance equal to 50% of monthly wages or Rs 75, whichever is higher. It is payable at the time of recruitment, is not refundable, and is in addition to wages. It compensates the workman for the dislocation of moving to another state. It is a distinct entitlement from the journey allowance. The Act came into force in 1980 and is administered by the Central and State Governments, with licensing officers appointed under it.

3 — Correct: Section 15 also provides that the workman is paid wages for the period of the journeys to and from the place of work as if he were on duty. The journey time is therefore treated as work time. This benefit appears in the same section as the fare entitlement. Together with equal pay for equal work and the other facilities under Sections 13 and 14, it forms the core protection of migrant workers. Wages must be paid in full without discrimination between inter-state migrant and local workers.

4 — Incorrect: The Act has no provision for money for food during the journey. The entitlements are the fare (Section 15), journey-period wages (Section 15) and the displacement allowance (Section 14), plus accommodation, medical facilities and protective clothing during employment. The food claim is a plausible-sounding distractor. Welfare facilities under Sections 16-17 relate to the workplace and residence, not travel meals. Other duties include issuing the passbook and reporting accidents or deaths to the authorities in both states.
summary: The answer is (d): 1, 2 and 3. Section 14 gives a displacement allowance and Section 15 gives a journey allowance plus wages for the journey period. The Act has no provision for a separate food allowance during travel.
topic_notes: The Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979 was enacted to prevent the exploitation of workers recruited by contractors (sardars or thekedars) in one state for work in another. It applies to every establishment that employs 5 or more inter-state migrant workmen on any day of the preceding 12 months, and to every contractor who employs or employed 5 or more such workmen. Principal employers must register their establishments, and contractors must hold licences. Key duties of the contractor include: issuing a passbook with a photograph, paying the displacement allowance (Section 14), paying the journey allowance and journey-period wages (Section 15), providing suitable residential accommodation (Section 16), free medical facilities and protective clothing (Section 17), and paying wages at rates not lower than those for similar local workmen (Section 13). The principal employer is liable for wage shortfalls and must ensure payment. Penalties apply for contravention. The Act is enforced by the appropriate Government, with inspectors appointed by it. Related laws include the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, the Building and Other Construction Workers Act, 1996, the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008, and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. The OSH Code, 2020 subsumes the 1979 Act. Under it a migrant worker is also entitled to a yearly journey fare to his native place, and the Code provides for portability of benefits. The e-Shram portal and the One Nation One Ration Card scheme were set up after the COVID-19 migrant crisis in 2020.

question: Who is responsible for providing the facilities specified in Section 16 of the Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979, to an inter-state migrant workman, if the same has not been provided by the contractor ?
options: Agent who had recruited the workman
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979 regulates the employment of workmen recruited by a contractor in one State for work in another State. Chapter V (Sections 16-20) deals with the duties and obligations of contractors and the liability of principal employers. Section 16 requires the contractor to provide: (a) regular payment of wages, (b) suitable residential accommodation, free of charge, during the period of employment, (c) free medical facilities, (d) protective clothing as prescribed, and (e) the other facilities the Act specifies. Section 18 makes the principal employer responsible for them if the contractor does not provide them. This is the 'default liability' principle, and it also applies to wage payment under Section 21(4), where the principal employer must pay the wages and can recover them from the contractor. Elimination: the occupier is a Factories Act concept, the appropriate government makes rules and enforces the Act but has no liability to provide the facilities, and the recruiting agent (the 'sardar' or 'khatadar') is not made liable. The principal employer is the party with ultimate control over the establishment.
explanations: Wrong: 'Occupier' is a Factories Act, 1948 term. The ISMW Act places the default liability on the principal employer, not on an occupier.
Wrong: The appropriate government (Central or State) frames rules, appoints inspectors and licensing officers and enforces the Act. It does not bear the liability to provide the facilities.
Wrong: The recruiting agent (sardar or similar) is not liable under the Act, since the contractor is the primary duty-holder and the principal employer is the fallback.

Correct: Under the ISMW Act the principal employer must provide the Section 16 facilities if the contractor fails to, and can recover the cost from the contractor, whether as a debt or by deduction from amounts payable.
keyfact: If the contractor fails to provide the Section 16 facilities for an inter-state migrant workman, the principal employer must provide them and recover the cost from the contractor.
option_notes: Occupier: under the Factories Act, 1948, the person who has ultimate control over the affairs of the factory (for a company, one of its directors). The occupier is responsible for health, safety and welfare compliance in the factory. The term is also used in the Factories Act's safety provisions and in the Mines Act context (as 'owner' or 'agent'). It is not the default-liable party in the ISMW Act.

Appropriate Government: defined in the ISMW Act as the Central Government for establishments under its authority (and some others) and the State Government otherwise. It makes rules, appoints inspectors and licensing officers, and can exempt establishments. It is a regulator, not a service provider under Section 16.

Agent who recruited the workman: in migrant labour, the recruiter (sardar, mate, khatadar, jobber) brings workers from the home State. The ISMW Act treats the recruiter as a 'contractor' where applicable, and requires the contractor to be licensed. A mere agent carries no separate default liability for facilities.

Principal employer: under Section 2(1)(g), the person who employs workers directly in an establishment: the owner or manager for a factory, the head of department for government establishments, or the person responsible for supervision and control of the establishment. The principal employer must register the establishment (Section 4), and is liable for the Section 16 facilities and for wages (Section 21(4)) as a fallback.
related: ISMW Act, 1979 applies to establishments and contractors with 5 or more inter-state migrant workmen.
Section 16 covers wages, free residential accommodation, free medical facilities, and protective clothing.
Principal employer is liable for default of the contractor and may recover costs from the contractor.
Displacement allowance: 50% of monthly wages or Rs 75, whichever is higher.
Contractors must hold a licence, and principal employers must register their establishments.
The Act is subsumed in the OSH Code, 2020.
The Contract Labour Act 1970 applies where 20 or more workers are employed.
summary: The answer is (d) Principal employer. Section 16 of the ISMW Act, 1979 lists the contractor's duties on facilities (wages, suitable residential accommodation, medical facilities, protective clothing). If the contractor fails to provide any of them, the principal employer must provide them, and may recover the cost from the contractor.
topic_notes: The ISMW Act, 1979 (effective 2 October 1980) was enacted to prevent the exploitation of migrant workers recruited through contractors or 'sardars' across State lines. It applies to every establishment employing five or more inter-state migrant workmen on any day of the preceding 12 months, and to every contractor who employed or employs five or more such workmen. Key provisions: principal employers must register establishments (Section 4), and contractors must hold a licence (Section 8). Contractors must issue a passbook to each worker (Section 13), and the Act sets out the displacement allowance (a sum equal to 50% of monthly wages or Rs 75, whichever is higher, under Section 14) and the journey allowance (Section 15), with fare payable both ways. The Act also provides for equal wages and conditions of service for migrant workmen (Section 13), and for the contractor's duties on wage payment and facilities (Sections 16-17). The Act empowers inspectors, and offences are punishable under Sections 24-25. On 29 September 2020 the Act was subsumed into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (OSH Code), which is part of the four labour codes. Under the OSH Code the migrant workman definition covers those who move on their own and may also be eligible for an annual journey allowance. Related topics: the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, whose principal employer liability for wages parallels this Act, plus the Building and Other Construction Workers Act, 1996.

question: Which one among the following cases deals with the issue of inter-state migrant workers ?
options: Labourers working on Salal Hydro Projects v. State of Jammu & Kashmir (1984) 3 SCC 538
People’s Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India, AIR 1982 SC 1473
Dharangadhra Chemical Works Ltd. v. State of Saurashtra, AIR 1957 SC 264
Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate v. Management of Dimakuchi Tea Estate, ATR 1958 SC 353
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: The Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979 regulates the employment of workers recruited in one state for work in another through a contractor or 'thekedar'. It requires registration of principal employers and licensing of contractors, and provides for a displacement allowance, a journey allowance, wages parity, suitable accommodation and medical facilities. In the Salal Project case (Bandhua Mukti Morcha-type litigation, begun on a letter by a journalist/PUDR-linked petition), the Court dealt with workers from Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and other states working on the Salal project in Jammu & Kashmir. It held that the 1979 Act, the Contract Labour Act and the minimum wages law must be enforced, and that the workers were entitled to their dues. It also stressed the use of Article 23 and the Court's public-interest jurisdiction. People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (Asiad Workers case, 1982) is also related, but it is chiefly known for the Asian Games construction workers, minimum wages, Article 23 and the expanded locus standi in PIL. Its facts included migrant workers, so it is a close distractor, but the case that deals specifically with inter-state migrants is the Salal case. Dharangadhra is about 'workman' and master-servant; Dimakuchi is about the definition of 'workman' under the Industrial Disputes Act.
explanations: Correct. The Salal Hydro Project case concerned inter-state migrant labourers and the enforcement of the 1979 Act.

Incorrect as the best answer. The Asiad Workers case (PUDR) concerned the Asian Games construction workers, with minimum wages, abolition of forced labour (Art. 23) and PIL, though it did involve migrant labour on the periphery. It is not the case specifically linked to inter-state migrant workmen.
Incorrect. Dharangadhra Chemical Works (1957) is about the meaning of 'workman' for salt agariyas and the test of control and supervision.
Incorrect. Dimakuchi Tea Estate (1958) defined 'workman' and the scope of 'industrial dispute', holding that clerical staff and others could raise a dispute through a substantial body of workmen.
keyfact: Salal Hydro Project case (1984) = inter-state migrant workmen; PUDR (Asiad) 1982 = Article 23 and minimum wages.
option_notes: Labourers working on Salal Hydro Project v. State of J&K (1983) 2 SCC 181, also reported as (1984) 3 SCC 538: the Supreme Court dealt with the plight of migrant workmen on the Salal hydro-electric project in J&K. It directed compliance with the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979, the Contract Labour Act and the minimum wages law, and also directed that the Central Government should ensure that workers' dues were paid, using Articles 21 and 23.

People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982) AIR 1982 SC 1473, the Asiad Workers case: the Court held that non-payment of the minimum wage is forced labour under Article 23. It held that the Contract Labour Act, the Minimum Wages Act and the Equal Remuneration Act must be implemented for workers building Asian Games projects, and that a public-spirited person or body may bring a PIL on behalf of the poor. It is a landmark on locus standi.

Dharangadhra Chemical Works Ltd. v. State of Saurashtra (AIR 1957 SC 264): the Court applied the control and supervision test to decide whether agariyas (salt workers) were 'workmen' under the Industrial Disputes Act 1947. It held that they were workmen, as the company had control over the manner of work, so the relationship of employer and employee existed.

Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate v. Management of Dimakuchi Tea Estate (AIR 1958 SC 353): the Court held that an industrial dispute may be raised by a substantial body of workmen or union, even for a person who is not himself a workman (a medical officer in the tea estate), if the issue affects workmen's common interest. It established the test of 'community of interest' and the meaning of 'workman'.
related: The Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act was enacted in 1979 and came into force in 1980.
Under the Act, the displacement allowance is 50 percent of monthly wages or Rs 75, whichever is higher.
It applies to establishments and contractors engaging five or more inter-state migrant workmen.
The OSH Code, 2020 subsumes the 1979 Act.
PUDR v. UOI (1982) linked non-payment of minimum wages to forced labour under Article 23.
Article 23 prohibits trafficking and forced labour (begar).
e-Shram, launched in 2021, is the national database of unorganised workers.
Steel Authority of India (2001) overruled the automatic absorption of contract labour.
summary: The answer is (a). Labourers working on Salal Hydro Project v. State of Jammu & Kashmir (1983/1984) 3 SCC 538 dealt with inter-state migrant workmen employed by contractors on the Salal Hydro-electric Project, and the Supreme Court directed enforcement of the Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979 and related labour laws. The other cases concern different issues.
topic_notes: The Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979 applies to establishments employing five or more inter-state migrant workmen and to contractors who employ five or more such workmen. It requires registration of the principal employer and licensing of the contractor. Benefits include wages not lower than the statutory rate, equal pay for equal work, a displacement allowance of 50 percent of monthly wages or Rs 75 (whichever is higher), a journey allowance, residential accommodation, free medical facilities and protective clothing. The appropriate government is generally the Central or State Government depending on the establishment. The Act has been subsumed in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which covers inter-state migrant workers and also introduced an annual journey allowance, a portal-based registration facility and the self-declaration of workers. Key cases to remember: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984), concerning bonded labour, Article 21 and PIL; PUDR (Asiad) 1982, concerning Article 23 and minimum wages; Salal Project, concerning migrant labour; Murli S. Deora v. Union of India, concerning smoking (not labour); Vishaka, concerning sexual harassment at the workplace; Air India Statutory Corporation v. United Labour Union (1996), concerning contract labour absorption; and Steel Authority of India v. National Union Waterfront Workers (2001), which overruled the automatic-absorption principle. In 2020 the Supreme Court took suo motu cognisance of the migrant workers' crisis during COVID-19 and issued directions for transport, food and registration. The e-Shram portal and the One Nation One Ration Card scheme are linked to the welfare of migrant workers.

ocr: Match List I with List IT and select the correct answer using the code given below the Lists : List I List II (Case) (Related proposition) A. Pradeep Kumar 1. Articles 14, 21 Biswas v. Indian and the Institute of Chemical Maternity Biology Benefit Act, (2002) 5 SCC 111 1961 B. Manisha 2. Article 24, the Priyadarshini v. Minimum Aurobindo Wages Act, College-Evening, 1948 LPA 595/2019 C. People’s Union for 8. Article 12 Democratic Rights v. Union of India, AIR 1982 SC 1473 D. State of Gujarat v. 4. Unpaid Sri Ambika Mills accumulation (1974) 4 SCC 656 under the Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act, 19
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: This is a case-law matching question in labour and constitutional law. Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (2002) overruled the narrow Sabhajit Tewary approach and applied the 'pervasive state control' test to decide whether a body is 'State' under Article 12, so A matches 3. Manisha Priyadarshini v. Aurobindo College (Evening), Delhi High Court LPA 595/2019, held that an ad hoc/temporary teacher is entitled to maternity benefit under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, read with Articles 14 and 21; B matches 1. People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (Asiad Workers case, 1982) held that payment below minimum wages is forced labour under Article 23 and that Article 24 (no child labour in hazardous work) was also applied to construction work; the Minimum Wages Act 1948 was enforced as a fundamental right, so C matches 2. State of Gujarat v. Sri Ambika Mills (1974) upheld the Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1953 provisions on unpaid accumulations (unclaimed wages/fines) being paid to the Fund; D matches 4. Eliminating: only code (a) has A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4. Note that the answer as matched here depends on the key's assignments; B and C are the swappable pair, and the PUDR case's link to Article 24 and the Minimum Wages Act is the reasoning followed.
explanations: (a) is correct: A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4 is the matching selected as the key based on the case holdings.
(b) is wrong: it pairs Pradeep Kumar Biswas with the Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act, but that case concerned Article 12.
(c) is wrong: it gives A-3 correctly but swaps B and C, and so does not match the code.
(d) is wrong: it begins with A-4, but Pradeep Kumar Biswas is the Article 12 case, not the Bombay Fund case.
keyfact: Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002) = Article 12 pervasive control test; PUDR (Asiad, 1982) = minimum wages/Article 24; Manisha Priyadarshini = maternity benefit; Ambika Mills = Bombay Labour Welfare Fund.
option_notes: Code (a): A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4. Article 12 defines 'State' for Part III as including the Government and Parliament, state legislatures, and all local or other authorities within India or under the control of the Government of India. Tests developed in Ramana Dayaram Shetty (1979), Ajay Hasia (1981) and Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002).

Code (b): A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3. This is wrong because it exchanges the Article 12 and Bombay Welfare Fund cases. The Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act 1953 provides for welfare funds financed from unpaid accumulations, fines and contributions of employers and employees.

Code (c): A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4. This is wrong because B and C are swapped. Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories, mines or other hazardous employment. The Minimum Wages Act 1948 enables fixing of minimum wage rates for scheduled employments.

Code (d): A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3. This is wrong because every item is paired incorrectly. Maternity Benefit Act 1961 gives paid leave to women employees in establishments with 10 or more employees, with 26 weeks of leave after the 2017 amendment.
related: Article 12 defines 'State' for Part III; Article 36 defines it for Part IV.
Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour; Article 24 prohibits child employment below 14 in hazardous jobs.
Article 42 of the DPSP covers just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
Article 43 provides for a living wage; the right to form unions is under Article 19(1)(c), a fundamental right.
Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 gives 26 weeks for the first two children and 12 weeks for the third.
PUDR v. Union of India (1982) is called the Asiad Workers case.
Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981) laid down the tests for an 'instrumentality or agency of State'.
statements: A — Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. IICB (2002) 5 SCC 111 ↔ Article 12 (3): Correct. A seven-judge Constitution Bench held that CSIR-controlled IICB is 'State' under Article 12 using the test of financial, functional and administrative domination or control. It overruled Sabhajit Tewary (1975) and expanded the Ramana Dayaram Shetty and Ajay Hasia line. The test is whether the body is financially, functionally and administratively dominated by or under the control of Government; such control must be pervasive, not merely regulatory. Consequence: writ jurisdiction under Article 32/226 lies against such bodies.

B — Manisha Priyadarshini v. Aurobindo College-Evening, LPA 595/2019 ↔ Articles 14, 21 and Maternity Benefit Act 1961 (1): Correct per the given code. The Delhi High Court (2019) held that an ad hoc/temporary woman employee cannot be denied maternity benefit; the Act applies regardless of the nature of employment. It built on Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Female Workers (Muster Roll) (2000), which extended maternity benefits to casual workers. The Maternity Benefit Act 1961 was amended in 2017 to give 26 weeks of paid leave for the first two children.

C — PUDR v. Union of India, AIR 1982 SC 1473 ↔ Article 24, Minimum Wages Act 1948 (2): Correct per the given code. Known as the Asiad Workers case, it dealt with workers building Asian Games 1982 projects. The Court held that non-payment of minimum wages is forced labour under Article 23, and also invoked Article 24 on children employed in construction. It also said that Government as employer must ensure labour laws, including the Minimum Wages Act 1948, the Contract Labour Act 1970 and the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979, are observed. Justice P.N. Bhagwati wrote the judgment.

D — State of Gujarat v. Sri Ambika Mills (1974) 4 SCC 656 ↔ Unpaid accumulations under Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act 1953 (4): Correct. The Supreme Court upheld the validity of the Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act 1953 and the payment of unpaid accumulations (unpaid wages, bonus, fines) into the Welfare Fund for labour welfare activities. The Court rejected the employer's challenge to the legislative competence and found the provision a reasonable restriction under Article 19(1)(f)/(g) of the time. Labour welfare funds exist in several states, such as the Maharashtra Labour Welfare Fund Act 1953.
summary: The correct code is (a): A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4. Pradeep Kumar Biswas decided the Article 12 'State' test for CSIR/IICB; Manisha Priyadarshini concerned maternity benefit under Articles 14, 21; PUDR (Asiad case) concerned Article 24 and minimum wages; Ambika Mills concerned unpaid accumulations under the Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act.
topic_notes: This topic combines constitutional provisions with leading labour-law cases. Article 12 defines 'State'; the Ajay Hasia (1981) test examined whether a body is an instrumentality or agency of government, and Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002) restated it as 'pervasive control'. Article 14 (equality), Article 21 (life and dignity), Article 23 (prohibition of forced labour and traffic in human beings) and Article 24 (no child labour below 14 in hazardous work) are the labour-relevant fundamental rights. Key cases: PUDR v. Union of India (1982), the Asiad case, held that paying below minimum wages amounts to forced labour; Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984) on bonded labour; M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996) on child labour in Sivakasi match factories; MCD v. Female Workers (Muster Roll) (2000) on maternity benefits for casual workers; Randhir Singh (1982) on equal pay for equal work; Vishaka (1997) on workplace sexual harassment. Statutes: Minimum Wages Act 1948 (now subsumed under the Code on Wages 2019), Maternity Benefit Act 1961 (amended 2017), Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act 1953, and the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, amended 2016. Directive Principles in Part IV relevant to labour: Article 39(d) equal pay, 41 right to work, 42 just and humane conditions and maternity relief, 43 living wage, 43A worker participation in management, 38 and 39 on welfare and distribution of resources.

Unpaid Sri Ambika Mills accumulation (1974) 4 SCC 656 under the Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act, 19
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Part IV of the Constitution (Articles 36-51) contains the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). They are non-justiciable (Art. 37) but fundamental to governance. Many labour-welfare provisions are found here. Art. 39(a) gives an adequate means of livelihood, and Art. 39(d) gives equal pay for equal work for men and women. Art. 39(e) protects the health and strength of workers, and Art. 39(f) protects children. Art. 41 covers the right to work, education and public assistance. Art. 42 provides just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Art. 43 provides a living wage and decent conditions of work for workers. Art. 43A (42nd Amendment, 1976) covers workers' participation in management. Art. 43B (97th Amendment, 2011) promotes cooperative societies. In contrast, the right to form associations or unions is guaranteed by Art. 19(1)(c) in Part III as a Fundamental Right, and it is enforceable under Art. 32. It is subject to reasonable restrictions under Art. 19(4) in the interests of public order, sovereignty and integrity, or morality. So the elimination is simple: (a), (b) and (d) are all DPSPs, and (c) is a Fundamental Right. The Supreme Court has held that the right to form unions does not include a right to strike or recognition.
explanations: Incorrect as the answer: maternity relief is provided in Art. 42 of Part IV, so it is a Part IV provision.
Incorrect as the answer: equal pay for equal work is provided in Art. 39(d) of Part IV, so it is a Part IV provision.
Correct: the right to form trade unions is guaranteed by Art. 19(1)(c) in Part III as a Fundamental Right. It is not in Part IV.
Incorrect as the answer: a living wage for workers is provided in Art. 43 of Part IV, so it is a Part IV provision.
keyfact: Right to form trade unions is a Fundamental Right (Art. 19(1)(c)), not a DPSP; maternity relief (Art. 42), equal pay (39(d)) and living wage (43) are in Part IV.
option_notes: Maternity relief is in Art. 42, which directs the State to secure just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. It is implemented through the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, amended in 2017 to give 26 weeks of paid leave for the first two children. It is also linked to Art. 15(3) and the ESI Act, 1948 maternity benefit. The courts have read it together with Arts. 14 and 21, for example in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Female Workers (Muster Roll), 2000.

Equal pay for equal work is in Art. 39(d), which concerns men and women. It is implemented by the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, now subsumed in the Code on Wages, 2019. In Randhir Singh v. Union of India (1982) the Supreme Court read it as a right flowing from Arts. 14, 16 and 39(d). Later cases include State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (2016), which extended it to temporary employees doing the same work.

The right to form associations or unions is in Art. 19(1)(c), a Fundamental Right of citizens. Restrictions are allowed under Art. 19(4). The Trade Unions Act, 1926 governs registration, and the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 replaces it. The courts have held that there is no fundamental right to strike (All India Bank Employees' Association case, 1962) and none to compel recognition. Art. 33 allows restrictions for armed forces and police.

A living wage is in Art. 43, which directs the State to secure work, a living wage and decent conditions of work, along with leisure and cultural opportunities. It is ranked above the minimum wage and the fair wage. The Minimum Wages Act, 1948, now subsumed in the Code on Wages, 2019, applies the idea in practice. The Supreme Court in People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982) (Asiad case) held that payment below minimum wages is forced labour under Art. 23.
related: Art. 43A (workers' participation in management) was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
Art. 43B (cooperative societies) was added by the 97th Amendment, 2011.
Art. 39A provides equal justice and free legal aid.
Art. 24 prohibits employment of children under 14 in factories, mines or other hazardous work.
Art. 23 prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour (begar).
Art. 19(1)(c): right to form associations or unions, a Fundamental Right.
Art. 37 makes DPSPs non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.
Art. 41 covers the right to work, education and public assistance in certain cases.
summary: The answer is (c) Right to form trade unions. Part IV (Directive Principles) provides for maternity relief (Art. 42), equal pay for equal work (Art. 39(d)) and a living wage (Art. 43). The right to form associations or unions is a Fundamental Right under Art. 19(1)(c) in Part III, not a Directive Principle.
topic_notes: DPSPs are in Part IV (Arts. 36-51) and were borrowed from the Irish Constitution. They are non-justiciable (Art. 37), but the Supreme Court has harmonised them with Fundamental Rights (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973; Minerva Mills, 1980). Art. 31C, as amended by the 42nd Amendment, was struck down in part by Minerva Mills. Classification is commonly Socialistic (Arts. 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47), Gandhian (Arts. 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48) and Liberal-Intellectual (Arts. 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51). Labour-related DPSPs are: Art. 38 (social order and reducing inequality), Art. 39(a) (livelihood), 39(d) (equal pay), 39(e) (health of workers and children), 41 (work, education, public assistance), 42 (humane conditions and maternity relief), 43 (living wage), 43A (participation in management), 43B (cooperatives) and 47 (nutrition and public health). Fundamental Rights relevant to labour are Art. 14, 16, 19(1)(c), 21, 23 (forced labour) and 24 (child labour in hazardous work under 14 years). The 86th Amendment (2002) moved education into Art. 21A and changed Art. 45 to early childhood care. The 44th Amendment (1978) added Art. 38(2). The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Arts. 39A, 43A and 48A. The 97th Amendment (2011) added Art. 43B. Fundamental Duties are in Art. 51A, Part IVA. The four new Labour Codes are the Code on Wages 2019, Industrial Relations Code 2020, Social Security Code 2020, and OSH Code 2020.

question: The concept of “equal pay for equal work” under Article 39(d) of the Constitution of India applies to :
options: Persons appointed to the same post 89
All persons appointed on permanent basis only
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 39(d), a Directive Principle of State Policy in Part IV, says the State shall direct its policy towards securing 'that there is equal pay for equal work for both men and women'. It is non-justiciable on its own (Article 37), but the Supreme Court has read it together with Articles 14, 16 and 21 to make it an enforceable right in appropriate cases. Key cases: Randhir Singh v. Union of India (1982), which held the principle is deducible from Articles 14, 16 and 39(d); Dhirendra Chamoli v. State of UP (1986), which applied it to temporary workers; and State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (2016), which held temporary, casual and daily-wage employees doing the same work as regular staff are entitled to minimum of the regular pay scale. Later cases like State of Punjab v. Surjit Singh (2024) have reiterated this. The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 (now subsumed in the Code on Wages, 2019) gives statutory effect to equal pay between men and women. Elimination: (a) and (b) are too narrow, since the principle depends on the nature of work, duties and responsibilities, not just qualifications or post title; (d) is wrong because Jagjit Singh extended it to temporary and daily-wage staff. Option (c) tracks the Article's wording.
explanations: Incorrect: qualifications alone do not decide equal pay; the test is the nature of work, duties, responsibilities and accountability, and the Article does not restrict it to persons with similar qualifications.

Incorrect: appointment to the same post is not required. The courts look at the actual work done, and the Article's text speaks of men and women, not post. Pay may still differ lawfully for valid classification reasons.
Correct: Article 39(d) expressly secures equal pay for equal work for both men and women, so it is framed for all men and women, and the courts have broadened it as a general equality principle.
Incorrect: it is not limited to permanent employees. State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (2016) and Dhirendra Chamoli (1986) extended it to temporary, casual and daily-wage workers.
keyfact: Article 39(d): equal pay for equal work for both men and women, a DPSP made effective through Articles 14 and 16.
option_notes: Similar qualifications: qualifications are one factor in judging equivalence of posts, but courts such as in State of UP v. J.P. Chaurasia (1989) held that differences in duties, responsibility and experience can justify unequal pay. Qualification alone is neither sufficient nor the sole test for equal pay.

Same post: persons on the same post usually claim equal pay, but the Supreme Court has held that equal pay is determined by the actual work, and that a pay scale difference may be justified by a rational classification under Article 14. Pay fixation is generally for expert bodies like Pay Commissions, and courts interfere only where there is clear discrimination.

All men and women: Article 39(d) is a Directive Principle added in the original Constitution, placed in Part IV with Article 39(a)-(f). It targets gender-based pay discrimination. It is backed by the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, now merged into the Code on Wages, 2019, which prohibits discrimination in wages on the ground of gender.

Permanent only: wrong because courts have rejected the idea that only regular employees can claim equal pay. In Jagjit Singh (2016), the Supreme Court held that temporary employees performing the same duties as regular employees are entitled to the minimum of the regular pay scale, though not allowances automatically.
related: Article 39(d) is in Part IV, the Directive Principles of State Policy.
Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 is now subsumed in the Code on Wages, 2019.
Randhir Singh v. Union of India (1982) tied equal pay to Articles 14, 16 and 39(d).
State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (2016) extended equal pay to temporary and daily-wage workers.
ILO Convention 100 deals with equal remuneration; India ratified it in 1958.
Article 43A on workers' participation in management was added by the 42nd Amendment.
Article 39A provides for equal justice and free legal aid.
Article 43 directs the State to secure a living wage for workers.
summary: The best answer is (c): Article 39(d) directs the State to secure equal pay for equal work for both men and women. The text of the Article speaks of 'men and women', so the constitutional language itself frames the principle as applying to all men and women, though courts have also read it as a general equality principle.
topic_notes: Article 39 lays down the principles of policy to be followed by the State: (a) adequate means of livelihood for all citizens; (b) distribution of material resources for the common good; (c) prevention of concentration of wealth; (d) equal pay for equal work for both men and women; (e) protection of health and strength of workers and children of tender age; (f) opportunities for children to develop in a healthy manner (substituted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976). Article 39A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, covers equal justice and free legal aid. Directive Principles are non-justiciable (Article 37), yet fundamental to governance. In Randhir Singh (1982), the Supreme Court held equal pay for equal work, though not an express Fundamental Right, is a constitutional goal and enforceable through Articles 14 and 16. Related cases: Mackinnon Mackenzie v. Audrey D'Costa (1987) upheld the Equal Remuneration Act against a claim of unequal pay for a typist; Air India v. Nargesh Meerza (1981) on discriminatory service conditions of air hostesses; State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (2016). Statutory framework: Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, giving effect to Article 39(d) and ILO Convention 100 (Equal Remuneration, 1951), ratified by India in 1958. It was subsumed into the Code on Wages, 2019, which prohibits discrimination on the ground of gender in wages and recruitment for the same work or work of a similar nature. Other labour-related DPSPs: Article 41 (right to work), Article 42 (just and humane conditions, maternity relief), Article 43 (living wage), Article 43A (workers' participation in management, 42nd Amendment), Article 43B (cooperative societies).

question: Which one among the following provisions do not find mention in the Constitution of India ?
options: Men and women equally have the right to an adequate means of livelihood
Every worker must be given a minimum of 8 days paid leave in a year
Children and youth are protected against exploitation
None can be forced to do begar 90. 86. The State, under Part IV of the Constitution of
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The question asks which provision is NOT in the Constitution. Paid leave is a matter of ordinary labour legislation (Factories Act 1948, Shops and Establishments Acts, and the new Labour Codes), not of constitutional text. The Constitution only lays down broad principles. Art. 39(a), a Directive Principle in Part IV, says citizens, men and women equally, have the right to an adequate means of livelihood. Art. 39(f) directs the State to ensure that children and youth are protected against exploitation and against moral and material abandonment. Art. 23, a Fundamental Right against exploitation, prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour; any contravention is a punishable offence. Art. 24 bans employment of children under 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work. Art. 43 speaks of a living wage and decent standard of life, and Art. 42 of just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief, but no fixed number of leave days is specified anywhere. Elimination: options a, c and d can each be tied to a specific Article, so the one with a precise numeric figure, 8 days, is the odd one out.
explanations: Incorrect choice: this is in Art. 39(a) of the Directive Principles, which says citizens, men and women equally, have the right to an adequate means of livelihood.

Correct choice: no constitutional article fixes 8 days (or any number) of paid leave for workers. Leave entitlements come from statutes such as the Factories Act 1948 (annual leave with wages) and state Shops and Establishments Acts.
Incorrect choice: this is in Art. 39(f), which requires protection of children and youth against exploitation and moral and material abandonment.
Incorrect choice: Art. 23(1) prohibits begar and other similar forms of forced labour, and this is a Fundamental Right.
keyfact: The Constitution does not fix any number of paid leave days; Art. 39(a), 39(f) and Art. 23 are real provisions.
option_notes: Art. 39(a) is in Part IV (DPSP). It directs the State to secure for citizens, men and women equally, the right to an adequate means of livelihood. It is non-justiciable under Art. 37 but is fundamental to governance. Art. 39(d) separately covers equal pay for equal work for men and women. Art. 39 was shaped by the 42nd Amendment (1976), which revised clause (f).

The claim of a mandatory 8 days of paid leave is not constitutional. Leave for workers is governed by statute: the Factories Act 1948 (Sec. 79) gives annual leave with wages, 1 day per 20 days worked for adults, and 1 day per 15 days for children. Shops and Establishments Acts of the states and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020 also deal with leave. Art. 42 and 43 only set general goals.

Art. 39(f) (DPSP) directs the State to ensure that children are given opportunities and facilities to develop in a healthy manner, in freedom and dignity, and that childhood and youth are protected against exploitation and moral and material abandonment. The 42nd Amendment 1976 reworded it. It complements Art. 24 and Art. 45 (early childhood care). It is non-enforceable by courts.

Art. 23 is a Fundamental Right in Part III (Right against Exploitation). It bans traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forced labour; it is available against both State and private persons. The State may impose compulsory service for public purposes, without discrimination on religion, race, caste or class. The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 implements it. Landmark case: PUDR v Union of India (Asiad workers case, 1982).
related: Art. 23 prohibits begar and forced labour; Art. 24 prohibits child labour under 14 in hazardous work.
Art. 39(d) lays down equal pay for equal work for men and women.
Art. 43A (worker participation in management) was added by the 42nd Amendment 1976.
Art. 42 covers just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
Art. 43 covers living wage and decent standard of life for workers.
Factories Act 1948 grants adults annual leave of 1 day per 20 days worked.
Labour is in the Concurrent List (Entries 22, 23, 24).
Directive Principles are non-justiciable (Art. 37) but fundamental to governance.
summary: The answer is (b). The Constitution of India contains no provision guaranteeing every worker a minimum of 8 days of paid leave a year. The other three are found in it: Art. 39(a) (equal right to adequate means of livelihood), Art. 39(f) (protection of children and youth against exploitation) and Art. 23 (prohibition of begar).
topic_notes: Part III Right against Exploitation: Art. 23 prohibits trafficking, begar and forced labour (the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act and the Bonded Labour Act give effect to it); Art. 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines and hazardous jobs. The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act 2016 bans employment of children below 14 in all occupations and of adolescents (14-18) in hazardous work. Labour-related Directive Principles in Part IV: Art. 38 (social order for welfare), Art. 39(a) adequate livelihood, 39(b) distribution of material resources, 39(c) prevention of concentration of wealth, 39(d) equal pay for equal work, 39(e) protection of health and strength of workers and tender age of children, 39(f) protection of childhood and youth; Art. 39A equal justice and free legal aid (42nd Amendment); Art. 41 right to work, education and public assistance in certain cases; Art. 42 just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief; Art. 43 living wage and decent standard of life; Art. 43A participation of workers in management of industries (42nd Amendment); Art. 43B promotion of cooperative societies (97th Amendment 2011); Art. 47 raising nutrition and public health. Art. 19(1)(c) guarantees the right to form associations or unions. Concurrent List Entries 22-24 deal with trade unions, industrial and labour disputes, social security, and welfare of labour, so both Parliament and states may legislate. Leave, hours and wages are statutory matters, e.g. Factories Act 1948 (48-hour week, 9-hour day), Minimum Wages Act 1948, Code on Wages 2019 and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020.

question: India, is required to secure :
options: Fair wage to workers by law
Living wage to all workers in the industrial sector only
Living wage only to workers in the organised sector
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Article 43 (Part IV, DPSP) says: 'The State shall endeavour to secure, by suitable legislation or economic organisation or in any other way, to all workers, agricultural, industrial or otherwise, work, a living wage, conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities.' The key words are 'all workers' and 'agricultural, industrial or otherwise', so the coverage is universal and not sector-specific. This is a non-justiciable directive (Art. 37), so it is an aspiration rather than an enforceable right. It is a Gandhian-socialist principle. The Minimum Wages Act 1948 and the Code on Wages 2019 give it statutory shape. The Committee on Fair Wages (1948) distinguished three levels: minimum wage (lowest), fair wage (in between) and living wage (highest). The Supreme Court in Bijay Cotton Mills (1959) upheld minimum wage laws, and in Standard Vacuum Refining (1961) the Court discussed the fair wage concept. Elimination: (a) understates the requirement, since fair wage is a middle level and not the Art. 43 objective. (c) and (d) wrongly restrict the coverage to one sector. Option (b) matches the text.
explanations: Incorrect: 'Fair wage' is the middle category of the Committee on Fair Wages. Art. 43 speaks of a 'living wage', the higher standard, so this understates the directive.
Correct: Art. 43 directs the State to secure a living wage to all workers, agricultural, industrial or otherwise.
Incorrect: Art. 43 expressly covers agricultural workers as well as industrial ones, so 'industrial sector only' is wrong.
Incorrect: The Article does not limit coverage to the organised sector. It covers workers in the unorganised sector too, and Art. 43 even promotes cottage industries.
keyfact: Art. 43 DPSP: State to secure a living wage to ALL workers (agricultural, industrial or otherwise); fair wage is only the middle level.
option_notes: Fair wage is a level between the minimum wage and the living wage, as defined by the Committee on Fair Wages (1948), chaired by Justice P.B. Gajendragadkar. It depends on the industry's capacity to pay, productivity and prevailing rates. The Code on Wages 2019 uses minimum wage, not fair wage, as the statutory floor. Fair wage is not the Art. 43 phrase.

Living wage is the highest of the three wage levels. It allows the worker to provide for food, shelter, clothing, education, medical care, insurance and some comforts for the family. The 15th Indian Labour Conference (1957) set out the need-based minimum wage norms, including 3 consumption units per earner and 2,700 calories per adult. The living wage is a DPSP goal under Art. 43 and is not justiciable.

This option is wrong because Art. 43 is not confined to industry. It speaks of workers 'agricultural, industrial or otherwise'. Industrial workers are covered by the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 (now the Industrial Relations Code 2020) and by wage laws. The directive itself is universal in scope.

The organised sector consists of registered, regulated enterprises with formal employment. The unorganised sector accounts for over 90% of India's workforce. Art. 43 covers all workers, so confining the living wage to the organised sector is incorrect. Laws such as the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act 2008 extend protection to the unorganised sector.
related: Art. 43 DPSP: living wage for all workers, agricultural, industrial or otherwise
Art. 43A: workers' participation in management (42nd Amendment)
Art. 39(d): equal pay for equal work for men and women
Committee on Fair Wages 1948 defined minimum, fair and living wage
Code on Wages 2019 introduced the National Floor Wage
15th ILC 1957 set need-based minimum wage norms
Art. 37: DPSPs are not enforceable by courts
Art. 43 is a Gandhian principle, as is promotion of cottage industries
summary: The answer is (b). Article 43 of the Directive Principles of State Policy directs the State to secure, by suitable legislation or economic organisation, a living wage and conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life to all workers, agricultural, industrial or otherwise. It is not limited to the organised or industrial sector.
topic_notes: Wage-related constitutional provisions. Art. 39(d) provides equal pay for equal work for men and women. Art. 41 covers the right to work, education and public assistance. Art. 42 covers just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Art. 43 covers a living wage and decent conditions of work. Art. 43A (42nd Amendment 1976) covers workers' participation in the management of industries. Art. 43B (97th Amendment 2011) covers cooperative societies. Art. 23 prohibits forced labour, a Fundamental Right. Art. 24 prohibits child labour in hazardous work under 14. Wage concepts: the Committee on Fair Wages (1948) defined minimum, fair and living wages. The 15th ILC (1957) laid down need-based minimum wage norms, and the Supreme Court in Reptakos Brett (1992) added 25% for children's education, medical needs, recreation and old age. Statutes: the Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Wages Act 1936, Equal Remuneration Act 1976 and Payment of Bonus Act 1965 are now subsumed in the Code on Wages 2019. The Code introduces a statutory National Floor Wage, which the Centre fixes and states cannot set below. Related judgments: Randhir Singh (1982) on equal pay for equal work, as derived from Arts. 14, 16 and 39(d), and Peoples Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (Asiad case, 1982) on payment below minimum wages being forced labour under Art. 23. The Directive Principles are non-justiciable (Art. 37) but fundamental to governance. Future questions may ask which DPSP belongs to the Gandhian, socialist or liberal group, or about the wage categories.

ocr: The provision of ‘just and humane conditions of work’, envisaged under the Constitution of India, has been reflected in which one among the following statutes ? (a) The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (b) The Employees Compensation Act, 1923 (c) The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (d) The Factories Act, 1948 People’s Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India, AIR 1982 SC 1478 dealt with : (a) Payment of minimum wages to the workers working in various Commonwealth Games projects (b) Health of workers (c) Payment of minimum wages to the workers working in Asian Games projects (d) Payment of wages t
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Article 42 (Part IV, Directive Principles of State Policy) says the State shall make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief. It is a non-justiciable directive, but courts read it with Articles 21 and 39(e)-(f) to protect workers' dignity. Statutes that give effect to Article 42 deal with the actual conditions in which work is performed: hours, rest intervals, weekly holidays, ventilation, sanitation, safety of machinery, canteens, creches, and restrictions on women and child labour. The Factories Act, 1948 does exactly this, and also covers occupational health, hazardous processes (added after the Bhopal gas tragedy in 1987) and annual leave with wages. Maternity relief is delivered by the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961. Elimination: the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 concerns timely payment and authorised deductions (a wage-related matter, linked to Art. 43 living wage). The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 gives compensation for injury or death in employment, which is a remedy after the harm and is a social-security measure. The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 is a retirement or termination benefit. So only the Factories Act regulates the conditions of work itself.
explanations: Incorrect: the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 regulates the time and mode of wage payment and deductions, not the physical conditions of work.

Incorrect: the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 provides compensation for work injury, occupational disease or death. It is a compensatory, post-injury remedy rather than a regulation of working conditions.
Incorrect: the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 gives a terminal benefit for 5 or more years of service. It is a social-security measure, not a working-conditions law.
Correct: the Factories Act, 1948 lays down health, safety, welfare, working hours, leave and women and young-person provisions, which directly reflect Article 42's just and humane conditions of work.
keyfact: Article 42 (just and humane conditions of work, maternity relief) is implemented chiefly by the Factories Act, 1948.
option_notes: The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 ensures wages are paid on time and without unauthorised deductions. It applies to employees drawing wages up to the notified ceiling, in factories, railways and other establishments. Wage period cannot exceed one month, and wages must be paid before the 7th or 10th day depending on establishment size. Its subject is wage payment, linked to Art. 43 rather than Art. 42. Its provisions have been subsumed in the Code on Wages, 2019.

The Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 (formerly the Workmen's Compensation Act) makes the employer liable to pay compensation for injury, occupational disease or death arising out of and in the course of employment. Claims go to the Commissioner for Employees' Compensation. It is a no-fault liability statute, a social-security measure. Its provisions have been subsumed in the Code on Social Security, 2020.

The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 provides gratuity to employees on superannuation, retirement, resignation, death or disablement after at least 5 years of continuous service (the 5-year rule is waived for death or disablement). Formula: 15 days' wages for each completed year of service. The statutory ceiling is Rs 20 lakh. It applies to establishments with 10 or more employees. It is now covered by the Code on Social Security, 2020.

The Factories Act, 1948 applies to premises with 10 or more workers using power, or 20 or more without power. It covers health (cleanliness, ventilation), safety, welfare (canteen for over 250 workers, creche for over 30 women), working hours (48 per week, 9 per day), weekly holiday, annual leave with wages, and employment of women and young persons. A child below 14 cannot be employed. The Chief Inspector enforces it. It is now subsumed in the OSH Code, 2020.
related: Article 42 is a Directive Principle: just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
Article 43 deals with a living wage and decent standard of life for workers.
Article 43A (42nd Amendment, 1976) deals with workers' participation in management.
Article 24 bans employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.
PUDR v. UOI (1982), the Asiad case, held that paying below minimum wages is forced labour under Art. 23.
The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 gives 26 weeks of leave for the first two children.
The Factories Act, 1948 sets a 48-hour week and a 9-hour day for adult workers.
The OSH Code, 2020 subsumes the Factories Act, 1948.
summary: The correct answer is (d) The Factories Act, 1948.
