Article 42 of the Constitution (a Directive Principle) directs the State to make provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Among the listed statutes, the Factories Act, 1948 is the one that regulates working conditions: health, safety, welfare, working hours, leave and employment of women and young persons.
topic_notes: Article 42 (DPSP) provides for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Related labour directives: Art. 39(a) adequate means of livelihood, 39(d) equal pay for equal work, 39(e) protection of workers' health and strength and of children from abuse, 39(f) healthy development of children, Art. 41 right to work, education and public assistance, Art. 43 living wage and decent standard of life, Art. 43A participation of workers in management of industry (added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976), and Art. 24 prohibition of child labour in factories and mines below 14, a Fundamental Right. The Factories Act, 1948 is the central workplace-conditions law, with a working week of 48 hours, a day of 9 hours, spread-over of 10.5 hours and overtime at double rate. The Act defines occupier, manufacturing process and worker, and imposes duties on occupiers. Hazardous-process provisions were added in 1987 after the Bhopal gas tragedy. The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 gives 26 weeks of paid leave (after the 2017 amendment) for the first two children. Supreme Court cases: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982, Asiad workers case) held that non-payment of minimum wages is forced labour under Art. 23; Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984) on bonded labour; Vishaka (1997) on workplace sexual harassment. The four Labour Codes (Wages 2019, Industrial Relations 2020, Social Security 2020, OSH and Working Conditions 2020) subsume 29 central laws, including the Factories Act, and were brought into force on 21 November 2025.

question: Which one among the following cases does not pertain to Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution of India ?
options: Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa, AIR 1978 SC 548
Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India, AIR 1984 SC 802
M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu, ATR 1997 SC 699
People’s Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India, AIR 1982 SC 1473
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other forms of forced labour; it is available against private individuals as well as the State. Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines or any hazardous employment. PUDR v. Union of India (Asiad Workers case, 1982) held that payment below minimum wages amounts to forced labour under Art. 23 and that 'force' includes economic compulsion. Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984) dealt with bonded labour in stone quarries, held that the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 must be enforced, and read Art. 21 with Art. 23 to give a right to live with dignity. M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996/1997) concerned children in the Sivakasi match and fireworks factories; the Court directed a welfare fund with Rs 20,000 compensation per child, relying on Art. 24. Rajappa (1978, 7-judge bench, Krishna Iyer J.) laid down the 'triple test' for industry: systematic activity, cooperation between employer and employee, and production/distribution of goods or services to satisfy human wants. It is an industrial law case, so it is the odd one out.
explanations: Correct choice: Rajappa concerns the definition of 'industry' under Sec. 2(j) of the ID Act, not Arts. 23 or 24.
Incorrect choice: Bandhua Mukti Morcha is a bonded labour case decided under Arts. 21 and 23.
Incorrect choice: M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu deals with child labour in hazardous employment (Art. 24).
Incorrect choice: PUDR (Asiad case) is a leading Art. 23 case on forced labour and minimum wages.
keyfact: Rajappa (1978) is about the definition of 'industry' under the ID Act, not Arts. 23/24.
option_notes: Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa (1978): a 7-judge bench judgment by Krishna Iyer J. It laid down the triple test for 'industry' under Sec. 2(j) of the ID Act, 1947. It brought hospitals, educational institutions, clubs and professions within the ambit of industry, subject to certain exceptions. It was doubted in later cases, and the 2005 reference to a larger bench remains pending. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 redefines industry.

Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984): a PIL by a group working for the release of bonded labourers in stone quarries near Faridabad. The Court, through Bhagwati J., held that Art. 21 includes the right to live with human dignity. It required identification, release and rehabilitation of bonded labourers under the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976. It also affirmed that Art. 23 applies against private persons as well as the State.

M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996): the case concerned child labour in the Sivakasi match and fireworks industry. The Court held that children cannot be employed in hazardous processes. It directed offending employers to pay Rs 20,000 per child into a fund, with a job for an adult family member or Rs 5,000 from the government. It also directed that children be given education, and relied on Art. 24 and the Directive Principles.

People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982), the Asiad Workers case: the construction workers for the Asian Games were paid below minimum wages. Bhagwati J. held that this is forced labour under Art. 23, because 'force' includes economic circumstances. The Court held that the Minimum Wages Act, the Contract Labour Act and the Equal Remuneration Act were being violated, and said that Art. 23 applies against private persons as well.
related: Art. 23 is enforceable against both the State and private persons.
Art. 24 bans child employment below 14 years in hazardous occupations.
Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act was passed in 1976.
Rajappa applied the triple test for 'industry' under Sec. 2(j) of the ID Act.
PUDR (Asiad case, 1982) held that payment below minimum wages is forced labour.
Sanjit Roy (1983) held that famine relief work paid below minimum wage violates Art. 23.
The Child Labour Amendment Act 2016 prohibits adolescents (14-18) from hazardous work.
Art. 21A provides free education for ages 6-14.
summary: The answer is (a). Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa (1978) is the landmark case defining 'industry' under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and has nothing to do with Articles 23 (prohibition of forced labour/trafficking) or 24 (prohibition of child labour in hazardous employment). The other three cases are classic Article 23/24 precedents.
topic_notes: Articles 23 and 24 fall under the Right against Exploitation (Part III, Arts. 23-24). Art. 23(1) bans traffic in human beings, begar and similar forced labour, and makes contravention a punishable offence. Art. 23(2) permits the State to impose compulsory service for public purposes, without discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste or class. Art. 23 is enforceable against private individuals too. The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, and the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 implement it. Art. 24 bans employment of children below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work. The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, as amended in 2016, bans employment of children below 14 in all occupations, with exceptions for family enterprises and audio-visual entertainment, and prohibits adolescents (14-18) from hazardous work. Art. 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) gives free and compulsory education for ages 6-14. Related cases: Sanjit Roy v. State of Rajasthan (1983), where wages below the minimum for famine relief work were held to be forced labour; Deena v. Union of India (1983), on labour in jail; Neerja Chaudhary v. State of M.P. (1984), on rehabilitation of bonded labourers; and Bachpan Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2011), on child trafficking in circuses. The Industrial Disputes Act case law includes Rajappa (industry), Hussainbhai v. Alath Factory (1978, on the employer-employee relationship), and Workmen of Nilgiri Cooperative v. State of TN. For exams, note the contrast between Art. 24 (children) and Art. 21A (education), and between the Art. 23 and Art. 35 provisions.

question: Which one among the following cases was filed as a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India which pertained to the occupational health hazards and diseases to the workmen employed in asbestos industries ?
options: A. Sundarambal v. Government of Goa, Daman and Diu, AIR 1988 SC 1700
Consumer Education and Research Centre v. Union of India, AIR 1995 SC 922
Rohtas Industries Staff Union v. State of Bihar, AIR 1963 Pat 170
Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate v. Management of Dimakuchi Tea Estate, ATR 1958 SC 353
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: In CERC v. Union of India (1995) 3 SCC 42, the Consumer Education and Research Centre, Ahmedabad, filed a writ petition under Article 32 on behalf of workers in asbestos industries who suffered from asbestosis and other occupational diseases. A bench led by Justice K. Ramaswamy held that the right to health, medical aid and a safe working environment is part of the right to life under Article 21. It read Articles 39(e), 41, 42 and 43 and the Preamble together with Article 21. The Court issued guidelines: health records of workers to be maintained for the period of employment and 40 years after retirement or beyond; periodic medical examinations by ESI-recognised or similar institutions; ESI coverage for all such workers irrespective of wage limits; compensation of Rs 1 lakh for affected workers; and the Factories Act 1948 and ESI Act 1948 to be honoured strictly. Elimination: Sundarambal concerns the Goa Daman and Diu Labour Laws and the Payment of Bonus Act; Rohtas Industries is a Patna High Court case, so it cannot be an Article 32 petition; Dimakuchi Tea Estate concerns the definition of workman and the meaning of an industrial dispute.
explanations: Incorrect: A. Sundarambal v. Government of Goa, Daman and Diu (AIR 1988 SC 1700) dealt with the Payment of Bonus Act and the Goa, Daman and Diu legal framework, not asbestos hazards.
Correct: CERC v. Union of India (AIR 1995 SC 922) was an Article 32 PIL on asbestosis and occupational health hazards among asbestos workers. It held that the right to health is part of Article 21.

Incorrect: Rohtas Industries Staff Union v. State of Bihar (AIR 1963 Pat 170) is a Patna High Court decision. An Article 32 petition lies only in the Supreme Court, and the case did not concern asbestos.

Incorrect: Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate v. Management (AIR 1958 SC 353) is the leading case on who is a workman and on when a dispute raised by non-workmen becomes an industrial dispute. It is not about asbestos.
keyfact: CERC v. Union of India (1995): asbestos workers, Article 32 PIL, right to health is part of Article 21.
option_notes: A. Sundarambal v. Government of Goa, Daman and Diu (AIR 1988 SC 1700): a Supreme Court labour law case on the Payment of Bonus Act and its application in the Union Territory. The Court examined the statutory entitlement to bonus and the position of the employee. It is not a health or Article 21 case.

Consumer Education and Research Centre v. Union of India (1995): a landmark PIL under Article 32 on asbestos workers. The Court declared the right to health and medical care a fundamental right under Article 21 and issued detailed guidelines on medical records, ESI coverage and compensation. It is widely cited for workers' health and safety.

Rohtas Industries Staff Union v. State of Bihar (AIR 1963 Pat 170): a Patna High Court case on the Industrial Disputes Act and the State's power of reference. High Courts hear writs under Article 226, not Article 32, so this case cannot be the answer.

Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate v. Management (AIR 1958 SC 353): the Supreme Court held that a dispute can be an industrial dispute only if the persons for whom it is raised have a substantial interest in it and are workmen. It also dealt with the status of a medical officer or other employees. It is a key case on the definition of workman.
related: Article 32 is the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights.
Article 226 gives High Courts wider writ jurisdiction than Article 32.
CERC (1995) held the right to health to be part of Article 21.
Compensation of Rs 1 lakh was awarded to the affected asbestos workers in CERC.
Section 89 of the Factories Act deals with notice of certain diseases.
Schedule III of the Employees' Compensation Act lists occupational diseases.
Vishaka (1997) laid down guidelines on sexual harassment at the workplace.
The OSH Code 2020 subsumes the Factories Act 1948.
summary: The answer is (b). Consumer Education and Research Centre (CERC) v. Union of India, AIR 1995 SC 922, was a PIL filed under Article 32 about occupational health hazards and asbestosis among workers in asbestos industries. The Supreme Court held the right to health and medical care to be a fundamental right under Article 21.
topic_notes: Right to health and occupational safety in Indian jurisprudence. CERC v. Union of India (1995) is the leading case. The Court read Article 21 with Articles 39(e), 41, 42 and 43 and held that the right to health and medical care is a fundamental right of workers, in service and after retirement. Guidelines covered mandatory health records, periodic examination, ESI coverage and compensation. Related cases: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984) on bonded labour and Article 21; Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) on sexual harassment at the workplace; M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Shriram gas leak, 1986) on absolute liability; Bhopal Gas Leak case (Union Carbide); Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (consolidating 13 labour laws including the Factories Act); Factories Act 1948 (chapter on health, safety, welfare; notifiable diseases under Section 89); Employees' State Insurance Act 1948 (benefits for occupational disease); Employees' Compensation Act 1923 (Schedule III lists occupational diseases). Article 32 is the right to constitutional remedies and Dr Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution. The Supreme Court can issue writs only for enforcement of fundamental rights, while High Courts under Article 226 can do so for any other legal purpose as well.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q90.
ocr: Which one among the following cases was filed as a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India which pertained to the occupational health hazards and diseases to the workmen employed in asbestos industries ? (a) A. Sundarambal v. Government of Goa, Daman and Diu, AIR 1988 SC 1700 (b) Consumer Education and Research Centre v. Union of India, AIR 1995 SC 922 (c) Rohtas Industries Staff Union v. State of Bihar, AIR 1963 Pat 170 (d) Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate v. Management of Dimakuchi Tea Estate, ATR 1958 SC 353
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: In Consumer Education and Research Centre (CERC) v. Union of India (1995), a consumer body filed a public interest writ petition under Article 32 about the occupational diseases, especially asbestosis, suffered by workmen in asbestos industries. Justice K. Ramaswamy's bench held that the right to health and medical care to protect a worker's health and vigour during service and after retirement is a fundamental right under Article 21, read with Articles 39(e), 41, 43 and 48A and the Preamble. The Court issued guidelines: health surveillance of workers for the period of employment and for 40 years after retirement or cessation of service; recording of health details by the Factories Inspectorate/ESI; compensation of at least Rs 1 lakh to affected workers; and ESI coverage for all workers irrespective of wage ceiling. Elimination: Sundarambal concerned the Goa, Daman and Diu Agricultural Tenancy Act (a different issue). Rohtas Industries Staff Union was a Patna HC case on Article 226 and industrial awards. Dimakuchi Tea Estate (1958) concerned who is a 'workman' and the standing of a union to raise an industrial dispute for non-employees, and was not a health case.
explanations: Incorrect: A. Sundarambal v. Govt of Goa (1988) was about the Goa, Daman and Diu Agricultural Tenancy Act, and is not an asbestos or occupational health case.
Correct: CERC v. Union of India (1995) was an Article 32 PIL on asbestosis and occupational health hazards, and it declared the right to health a fundamental right under Article 21.
Incorrect: Rohtas Industries Staff Union v. State of Bihar (1963 Pat) was a Patna High Court case on industrial adjudication, so it was not an Article 32 petition and not about asbestos.
Incorrect: Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate (1958) is the leading case on 'industrial dispute' and the definition of 'workman', not on occupational hazards.
keyfact: CERC v. Union of India (1995): an Article 32 PIL on asbestos workers that made the right to health a part of Article 21.
option_notes: A. Sundarambal v. Government of Goa, Daman and Diu (AIR 1988 SC 1700) is a Supreme Court case on the Goa, Daman and Diu Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1964, concerning tenancy rights and agricultural land. It is a land and tenancy matter, not a labour or health case, so it is not linked to asbestos or Article 32 health claims.

Consumer Education and Research Centre v. Union of India (AIR 1995 SC 922; (1995) 3 SCC 42) is a PIL by a consumer organisation of Ahmedabad concerning asbestos workers. The Court held the right to health and medical aid to be a fundamental right under Article 21 and gave binding directions on worker health records, compensation and ESI coverage. It is a landmark case on workers' health.

Rohtas Industries Staff Union v. State of Bihar (AIR 1963 Pat 170) is a Patna High Court decision on industrial disputes and the powers of the State government under the Industrial Disputes Act. Because it is a High Court case, it falls under Article 226, not Article 32, and has no link to asbestos.

Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate v. Management of Dimakuchi Tea Estate (AIR 1958 SC 353) is a leading Supreme Court case on the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. It held that a dispute becomes an 'industrial dispute' only if supported by a union or substantial body of workmen with a direct and substantial interest in the matter, and it also dealt with who counts as a 'workman'.
related: Article 32 is the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution (Dr B.R. Ambedkar).
CERC v. UOI (1995): the right to health is part of Article 21.
The CERC guidelines require health records of asbestos workers to be maintained for 40 years after retirement or cessation of service.
M.C. Mehta (oleum gas leak, 1986) laid down the principle of absolute liability.
Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984) dealt with bonded labour and human dignity under Article 21.
Vishaka (1997) laid down guidelines on sexual harassment at the workplace.
Article 39(e) of the DPSP protects the health and strength of workers.
Asbestosis is a notified occupational disease under the Factories Act, 1948.
summary: The correct answer is (b) Consumer Education and Research Centre v. Union of India, AIR 1995 SC 922. It was a PIL writ petition under Article 32 on occupational health hazards and asbestosis among workers in asbestos industries, in which the Supreme Court held the right to health and medical care to be a fundamental right under Article 21.
topic_notes: Article 32 gives the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights, and Dr Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. Article 226 gives High Courts wider writ powers, extending to any other purpose as well. The Supreme Court has used Article 21 to build a body of workers' rights: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984), which dealt with bonded labour and held that the right to live with human dignity includes protection of workers' health and strength; Francis Coralie Mullin (1981); and Olga Tellis (1985) on livelihood. CERC (1995) specifically established the right to health and medical care as a fundamental right, with guidelines for 'occupational diseases' such as asbestosis. Related health and safety cases include Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) on sexual harassment at the workplace, M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (oleum gas leak, 1986), which created the absolute liability principle, and the Bhopal gas disaster litigation. Statutory links are the Factories Act, 1948 (health, safety and welfare chapters, including notifiable diseases and a Section 41 schedule), the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948, the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 (occupational diseases listed in Schedule III), and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. Directive Principles relevant here: Article 39(e) (health of workers), 41, 42 (just and humane conditions of work), 43 (living wage) and 47 (public health). Asbestos-related disease is asbestosis, a lung fibrosis, with a risk of mesothelioma.

question: Which one among the following cases is|95. referred as the ‘Sivakasi fire cracker case’ ?
options: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, AIR 1988 SC 1037
M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu, ATR 1983 SC 1055
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, AIR 1987 SC 1086
M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu, AIR 1997 SC 699
subject: Current Affairs
detail: In M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996 6 SCC 756; AIR 1997 SC 699), a PIL under Article 32 about child labour in the match and fireworks factories of Sivakasi, Justice K. Ramaswamy and Justice Hansaria applied Articles 24, 39(e)-(f), 45 and 21 and the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986. The Court held that children cannot be employed in hazardous work such as fireworks manufacture. It directed that offending employers pay compensation of Rs 20,000 per child to a Child Labour Rehabilitation-cum-Welfare Fund, and that the State provide alternative employment to an adult member of the child's family or contribute Rs 5,000 per child. It also directed that education be provided and that non-hazardous employment be limited to 4-6 hours a day. Elimination: the other M.C. Mehta cases concern different subjects. The 1987 Union of India case is the Oleum gas leak case (absolute liability), the 1988 case is the Ganga pollution (tanneries) case, and the 1983 State of Tamil Nadu citation is a distractor. Remember the case name with the child-labour theme and the State of Tamil Nadu.
explanations: Wrong: AIR 1988 SC 1037 is M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, the Ganga pollution (Kanpur tanneries) case, which is about environmental protection and not child labour.
Wrong: this citation, with the 1983 year and the 'ATR' OCR error, is a distractor. The Sivakasi case was decided in 1996 and reported in 1997, not 1983.
Wrong: AIR 1987 SC 1086 is M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum gas leak case), which laid down the principle of absolute liability for hazardous industries.
Correct: AIR 1997 SC 699, M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu, is the Sivakasi fire cracker case on child labour in hazardous industries.
keyfact: Sivakasi fire cracker (child labour) case = M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu, AIR 1997 SC 699.
option_notes: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1988), the Ganga pollution case on tanneries at Kanpur. The Court ordered tanneries to set up effluent treatment plants and held that the Court could act under Article 32 and the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974. It is part of the Mehta environmental PIL series that developed the public trust and polluter pays principles.

This citation, with the year 1983, is a distractor. M.C. Mehta litigation began in the early 1980s, but the Tamil Nadu child-labour case was decided in 1996. In 1983 the Court dealt with other Mehta petitions, such as pollution and the Taj Mahal matters in later years. Always check the year against the subject.

M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), the Oleum gas leak case (Shriram Foods and Fertilizer). Arising from a gas leak in Delhi, the Court under Chief Justice P.N. Bhagwati laid down the rule of absolute liability, departing from Rylands v. Fletcher. It also held that Article 21 compensation applies against enterprises engaged in hazardous activities and that Article 32 allows new remedies.

M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996; AIR 1997 SC 699), the Sivakasi child labour case. It held that children cannot work in hazardous industries such as match and fireworks factories. It ordered compensation of Rs 20,000 per child to a welfare fund, alternative jobs for adults, and education for the children. It relied on Articles 24, 39, 45 and 21 and the Child Labour Act 1986.
related: Oleum gas leak case: absolute liability (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India 1987).
Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in hazardous work.
Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act 2016 bans work for children under 14 in all occupations.
Sivakasi case: Rs 20,000 per child compensation to the welfare fund.
Article 21A (86th Amendment 2002) gives free education for ages 6-14.
Asiad workers case: PUDR v. Union of India 1982 on Article 23 and minimum wages.
Bandhua Mukti Morcha 1984 is the leading bonded labour PIL.
Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976.
summary: The answer is (d). The 'Sivakasi fire cracker case' is M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu, AIR 1997 SC 699, in which the Supreme Court held that children cannot be employed in hazardous work such as match and fireworks manufacture at Sivakasi, and issued directions for their welfare.
topic_notes: M.C. Mehta is a public interest lawyer whose PIL cases shaped Indian environmental and labour law. Key cases: (1) Oleum gas leak 1986/87: absolute liability and Article 21. (2) Ganga pollution cases 1987-88: tanneries and effluent treatment. (3) Taj Mahal case 1996-97: industries around Agra moved or shifted to natural gas, and the Taj Trapezium Zone was set up. (4) Delhi vehicular pollution: CNG for public transport. (5) Sivakasi child labour case 1996: compensation fund and rehabilitation. Child labour law: Article 24 bars employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and other hazardous work; Article 39(e)-(f) and Article 45 (now Article 21A, the right to education added by the 86th Amendment 2002) are related. The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 was amended in 2016 and now prohibits employment of children below 14 in all occupations, with adolescents (14-18) barred from hazardous work. Related cases: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (Asiad workers, 1982), on Article 23, forced labour and minimum wages; Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984), on bonded labour; Labourers working on Salal Hydroelectric Project v. State of J&K; and Gaurav Jain v. Union of India (1997), on the children of sex workers. Also note the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 and the National Child Labour Project scheme, which runs special schools for rescued children. UPSC often asks the doctrine that each case established, so pair the case name with its principle.

question: Which one among the following provisions of the Constitution of India enables the State to impose compulsory service for public purpose ?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Articles 23 and 24 form the Right against Exploitation (Part III, Fundamental Rights). Article 23(1) prohibits traffic in human beings, begar (forced labour without payment) and other similar forms of forced labour, and makes contravention a punishable offence. Article 23(2) is the exception: nothing in the Article prevents the State from imposing compulsory service for public purposes, and in doing so the State shall not discriminate on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class or any of them. Examples are compulsory military service (conscription), national service, and jury duty. Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines or other hazardous employment. Article 25(1) concerns freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion, subject to public order, morality and health. Key cases are PUDR v. Union of India (1982, Asiad workers; payment below minimum wage is forced labour) and Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984, bonded labour). Elimination: only 23(2) deals with State-imposed compulsory service, so (d) is correct. Article 23 is available to citizens and non-citizens alike, and against private individuals as well as the State.
explanations: Wrong: Article 25(1) guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion; it has nothing to do with compulsory service.
Wrong: Article 24 prohibits child labour (below 14 years) in factories, mines and hazardous work; it is not about State compulsory service.
Wrong: Article 23(1) is the prohibition itself, covering traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour. It does not enable the State to impose compulsory service.
Correct: Article 23(2) permits the State to impose compulsory service for public purposes, with no discrimination only on grounds of religion, race, caste or class.
keyfact: Article 23(1) bans begar and forced labour; Article 23(2) lets the State impose compulsory service for public purposes without discrimination on religion, race, caste or class.
option_notes: Article 25(1): Every person is equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion. It is subject to public order, morality, health and other Fundamental Rights. Article 25(2) allows the State to regulate economic, financial, political or secular activity associated with religion and to provide for social welfare and reform. The Explanation includes the wearing of kirpans by Sikhs. It is part of the Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28).

Article 24: Prohibits employment of children below 14 years in any factory, mine or other hazardous employment. It is part of the Right against Exploitation. It is operationalised through the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, amended in 2016 to ban employment of children below 14 in all occupations and to regulate adolescents (14-18) in hazardous work. The 86th Amendment (2002) added Article 21A on free education for ages 6-14. M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996) is a key case.

Article 23(1): Prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour, and declares any contravention an offence punishable by law. It is enforceable against both the State and private individuals. Begar means compulsory work without payment. Parliament made the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956 under Article 35. The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 also gives it effect. PUDR v. Union of India (1982) held that forced labour includes paying less than minimum wage.

Article 23(2): Nothing in Article 23 prevents the State from imposing compulsory service for public purposes. In imposing it, the State shall not make any discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class or any of them. Examples are conscription, national service and social service as a condition of education or a degree. Dulal Samanta v. Union (1958) concerned compulsory service in this context. It is an exception to the Article 23(1) prohibition.
related: Article 23 is available to citizens and non-citizens, and against the State and private persons.
Article 24 bans child employment below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.
PUDR v. Union of India (1982) is the Asiad case: payment below minimum wage amounts to forced labour.
Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 gives effect to Article 23.
Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) gives free and compulsory education for ages 6-14.
Right against Exploitation comprises Articles 23 and 24.
Article 25 begins the Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28).
Article 35 empowers Parliament to make laws on offences under Article 23.
summary: The answer is (d) Article 23(2). Article 23(1) prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour, but Article 23(2) expressly allows the State to impose compulsory service for public purposes, provided it makes no discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class.
topic_notes: Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24) is part of Part III of the Constitution. Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other forms of forced labour. 'Traffic in human beings' covers trade in men, women and children for immoral or other purposes, including prostitution and slavery. Begar is forced labour without remuneration. The Supreme Court in PUDR v. Union of India (1982) held that 'forced labour' includes labour paid less than minimum wages, and that the Article covers non-payment, economic compulsion and hunger-driven work. Article 23 is enforceable against private individuals as well as the State, and is available to both citizens and non-citizens. Article 23(2) is the exception: the State may impose compulsory service for public purposes, without discrimination only on grounds of religion, race, caste or class. Article 24 prohibits employment of children under 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work. Related laws: Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976; Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act 2016; Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956; Minimum Wages Act; Equal Remuneration Act 1976 (now subsumed in the Code on Wages 2019). Landmark cases: Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984), M.C. Mehta (1996), Sanjit Roy v. State of Rajasthan (1983; famine relief work below minimum wage is forced labour), Deena v. Union of India (1983; labour in jails). Other angles UPSC may ask: Article 21A (free education for ages 6-14), Directive Principles in Articles 39(e), 39(f), 41 and 45, and Article 35 (Parliament's power to legislate on offences under Article 23).

question: Which one among the following propositions was laid down by the Supreme Court in Randhir Singh v. Union of India, ATR 1982 SC 879 ?
options: Right to assemble peacefully and without arms
Responsibility of the State to provide free legal aid
Participation of workers in management of industries
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Randhir Singh was a Delhi Police driver-constable who claimed the same pay as drivers in other departments of the Delhi Administration. Justice P.N. Bhagwati's bench held that the principle of equal pay for equal work, though not expressly declared a fundamental right, is a constitutional goal. It must be read into the equality guarantees of Articles 14 and 16, together with the Directive Principle in Article 39(d), which directs the State to secure equal pay for equal work for both men and women. The Court held that when persons doing the same work are paid differently without a rational classification, Articles 14 and 16 are violated. The principle was later applied in Dhirendra Chamoli v. State of UP (1986), where casual workers doing the same work as regular employees were held entitled to the same pay. It was also applied in Bhagwan Dass (1987) and in the Mackinnon Mackenzie case (1987) on equal remuneration for women. The principle was qualified in State of Haryana v. Jasmer Singh (1996) and in Supreme Court judgments of the 2010s, which said that differences in duties, responsibility and qualifications can justify differences in pay. Option (a) concerns Article 19(1)(b), option (c) concerns Article 39A with Hussainara Khatoon and M.H. Hoskot, and option (d) concerns Article 43A, so all three are different matters.
explanations: Wrong: the right to assemble peacefully and without arms is Article 19(1)(b), not the subject of Randhir Singh.
Correct: Randhir Singh laid down that equal pay for equal work is enforceable through Articles 14, 16 and 39(d).
Wrong: free legal aid as a State duty was developed in Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979) and M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra (1978), with Article 39A as the basis.
Wrong: workers' participation in management is Article 43A, added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, and is not the subject of this case.
keyfact: Randhir Singh v. UOI (1982): equal pay for equal work is a constitutional goal under Articles 14, 16 and 39(d), enforceable via Article 32.
option_notes: Article 19(1)(b) gives citizens the right to assemble peacefully and without arms. It is subject to reasonable restrictions on grounds of public order and sovereignty and integrity of India under Article 19(3). Section 144 CrPC (now BNSS Section 163) and police permission rules for meetings are linked to this. Related cases include Ramlila Maidan (2012) and Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (2018) on protest sites at Jantar Mantar. The right is available only to citizens and can be suspended during a National Emergency under Article 358.

Equal pay for equal work comes from Article 39(d), a Directive Principle, and is read with Articles 14 and 16. It was recognised in Randhir Singh (1982). The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 is now subsumed in the Code on Wages, 2019. Later cases include Dhirendra Chamoli (1986) and State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (2016), which gave temporary employees minimum of regular pay scale for the same work. Courts accept that pay differences based on qualifications and responsibilities can be valid.

Free legal aid is provided under Article 39A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. It requires the State to secure equal justice and provide free legal aid. Hussainara Khatoon (1979) and M.H. Hoskot (1978) held it part of the Article 21 guarantee of a fair procedure. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 created NALSA, which came into operation in 1995. Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer were the key judges behind this development.

Article 43A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, directs the State to take steps to secure workers' participation in the management of undertakings and industrial establishments. It is a Directive Principle and is not enforceable in court. Related provisions include the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which provides for works committees, and the Participation of Workers in Management Bill, 1990, which was introduced but not enacted. The Ministry of Labour has also promoted joint management councils and bipartite forums.
related: Article 39(d) says equal pay for equal work for both men and women.
Randhir Singh (1982) was decided by a bench led by Justice P.N. Bhagwati.
Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 is now part of the Code on Wages, 2019.
Dhirendra Chamoli v. State of UP (1986) extended equal pay to casual workers.
State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (2016) applied equal pay to temporary employees.
Article 43A (workers' participation in management) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment.
Article 39A (free legal aid) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
Article 32 gives the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
summary: The answer is (b) Equal pay for equal work. In Randhir Singh v. Union of India (AIR 1982 SC 879), the Supreme Court held that although 'equal pay for equal work' is not an express fundamental right, it is a constitutional goal derived from Articles 14, 16 and 39(d), and it can be enforced through Article 32.
topic_notes: Randhir Singh v. Union of India (1982) is a landmark service law and labour jurisprudence case. The petitioner was a driver-constable in Delhi Police and claimed equal pay with drivers in other Delhi Administration departments. The Supreme Court, speaking through Justice P.N. Bhagwati, held that equal pay for equal work is not expressly a fundamental right but is a constitutional goal. It is deduced from the Preamble, Articles 14, 16 and 39(d), and it can be enforced through Article 32 when unequal scales are given to equals without a rational basis. The case shows how the Court read Directive Principles into Fundamental Rights to give them practical effect. Follow-up cases: Dhirendra Chamoli v. State of UP (1986), which held that casual workers doing the same work as permanent ones are entitled to the same pay; Surinder Singh v. Engineer-in-Chief, CPWD (1986); and Mackinnon Mackenzie v. Audrey D'Costa (1987), which applied the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. Limits were set in State of Haryana v. Jasmer Singh (1996) and Union of India v. Dineshan K.K. (2008), which said the principle depends on the nature of work and cannot be applied mechanically. State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (2016) restored a wider application for temporary workers. Statutory framework: the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, now merged into the Code on Wages, 2019, which prohibits discrimination in wages on the basis of gender. Related constitutional provisions: Article 39(a) (adequate means of livelihood), Article 41 (right to work), Article 43 (living wage) and Article 43A (workers' participation in management). The Pay Commissions are the usual body for deciding pay scales in government service.

question: Which of the following legislations is related to Article 23(1) of the Constitution of India ? 96
options: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986
subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Article 23 falls under the Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24) in Part III of the Constitution. Article 23(1) prohibits traffic in human beings, begar (unpaid compulsory labour) and other similar forms of forced labour, and makes any contravention an offence punishable by law. Article 23(2) permits the State to impose compulsory service for public purposes, such as national service, but without discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste or class. Article 23 is available against private individuals as well as the State. In PUDR v. Union of India (1982, Asiad case) the Supreme Court held that paying less than minimum wages amounts to forced labour. In Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984) the Court directed the identification and rehabilitation of bonded labourers. The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 implemented Article 23 by abolishing bonded labour and extinguishing debts arising from it. Elimination: the Child Labour Act, 1986 relates to Article 24 (no child under 14 in hazardous work). The Factories Act, 1948 and the Mines Act, 1952 are general labour welfare and safety laws, with links to Directive Principles such as Articles 39 and 42, not to Article 23.
explanations: Correct: the 1976 Act abolishes bonded labour, a form of forced labour covered by Article 23(1).
Wrong: the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 gives effect to Article 24, the prohibition of employment of children in hazardous work.
Wrong: the Factories Act, 1948 regulates health, safety, working hours and welfare in factories. It is not an enactment of Article 23.
Wrong: the Mines Act, 1952 regulates safety, health and working conditions in mines. It is not tied to Article 23.
keyfact: Article 23(1) bans trafficking, begar and forced labour, and the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 implements it.
option_notes: The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 came into force on 25 October 1975 through an Ordinance, which the Act later replaced. It abolished the bonded labour system, freed bonded labourers and cancelled their debts. District Magistrates and Vigilance Committees implement it. Offences are punishable with up to 3 years of imprisonment and a fine. A Central Sector Scheme for rehabilitation of bonded labourers has been in operation since 1978 and was revised in 2016, with rehabilitation assistance of Rs 1 lakh to Rs 3 lakh per person.

The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 banned the employment of children below 14 in hazardous occupations and processes and regulated conditions of work in others. It was amended in 2016 to prohibit employment of children below 14 in all occupations, with an exception for family enterprises and the audio-visual entertainment industry. It also banned adolescents (14-18) from hazardous work. It relates to Article 24 and to Article 21A, the right to education.

The Factories Act, 1948 applies to premises with 10 or more workers using power, or 20 or more without power. It lays down provisions on health, safety, welfare, working hours (48 hours per week, 9 hours per day), the employment of young persons and annual leave with wages. It is administered by state governments through Factory Inspectors, and it is being subsumed in the OSH Code, 2020.

The Mines Act, 1952 regulates the working conditions, safety, health and welfare of mine workers. It sets weekly hours (48 above ground, 8 hours per day underground) and bars employment of persons below 18 in mines. It is administered by the Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS) under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, and it is also being subsumed in the OSH Code, 2020.
related: Article 23: prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour; Article 24: prohibition of child labour below 14 in hazardous work.
Article 23(2) allows compulsory service for public purposes.
PUDR v. Union of India (1982): non-payment of minimum wages is forced labour.
Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 implements Article 23 against trafficking.
Bonded labour rehabilitation scheme was revised in 2016.
Article 21A: free and compulsory education for ages 6-14 (86th Amendment, 2002).
The Child Labour Act was amended in 2016 to ban employment of children below 14 in all occupations.
Articles 23 and 24 together form the Right against Exploitation.
summary: The answer is (a), the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976. Article 23(1) prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour, and the 1976 Act was enacted specifically to abolish bonded labour, which is a form of forced labour.
topic_notes: Articles 23 and 24 together form the Right against Exploitation. Article 23(1) prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour. 'Traffic in human beings' includes trade in women and children, and is implemented through the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956. Article 23 protects against private individuals as well as the State. Exception in Article 23(2): the State may impose compulsory service for public purposes, but without discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste or class. Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines or other hazardous work. Key cases: PUDR v. Union of India (1982), which held that non-payment of minimum wages is forced labour; Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984); and M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996) on child labour in the Sivakasi matchstick and fireworks industry. Related laws: the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976; the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956; the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 as amended in 2016; the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009; and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, now subsumed in the Code on Wages. The 86th Amendment added Article 21A. Directive Principles Articles 39(e) and 39(f), 41, 42 and 43 are related. Section 370 IPC, and now the BNS provisions on trafficking, also apply. Note that these rights are enforceable by the Supreme Court under Article 32.

ocr: Which one of the following statements is not correct with regard to the decision of the Supreme Court in Employees Provident Fund Organisation v. Sunil Kumar, SLP (C) Nos. 8658-8659/2019 ? (a) All employees who had retired prior to 18* September, 2014 were entitled to the benefit of the decision in the above case. (b) The employees were entitled to the benefit of the above decision if they had retired prior to 18* September, 2014 after exercising option provided in para 11(3) of the pre-amended Employees’ Pension Scheme, 1995 as amended by the Central Government. (c) The directions issued in R
subject: Social Security
detail: The question rests on the Supreme Court's judgment of 4 November 2022 in Employees' Provident Fund Organisation v. Sunil Kumar B. (SLP (C) 8658-8659/2019). A three-judge bench (U.U. Lalit CJI, Ajay Rastogi and Aniruddha Bose JJ) was settling a conflict among High Court decisions (Kerala, Rajasthan, Delhi) on the 2014 amendment to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995. The bench upheld the 2014 amendment, which introduced a Rs 15,000 wage ceiling and a 60-month averaging period for pensionable salary, but struck down the requirement of an additional 1.16% contribution from wages above the ceiling. The Court held the Kerala, Delhi and Rajasthan High Court judgments invalid to the extent they conflicted. Under the pre-amended para 11(3), members could opt for pension on higher wages with the employer's joint consent, and this option was open to those who had retired before 1 September 2014 if they had exercised it. The Court granted relief to those who had exercised the option but were denied it because of the cut-off date. It gave a further 4 months for members to exercise the option. Elimination: (b), (c) and (d) match the judgment, so (a), which says 'all' retirees are covered, is the statement that is not correct.
explanations: Incorrect statement, so this is the answer. The benefit was not extended to all pre-September 2014 retirees. It went only to those who had exercised the para 11(3) option, or who were denied it because of the cut-off date.
Correct. Those who retired before 1 September 2014 after exercising the para 11(3) option under the pre-amended scheme were held entitled to the benefit.
Correct. The Court directed that the directions in R.C. Gupta v. Regional PF Commissioner (2018) 14 SCC 809 be complied with.

This option is cut off in the question. It most likely records the Court's holding that the 1.16% additional-contribution proviso was ultra vires, which fits the judgment. So it is a correct statement, not the answer.
keyfact: EPFO v. Sunil Kumar (4 Nov 2022): 2014 EPS amendment upheld, 1.16% additional contribution proviso struck down, and relief only for those who exercised the para 11(3) option.
option_notes: Option (a) is the claim that every employee retired before 1 Sept 2014 gets the benefit. The cut-off date of 1 September 2014 was when the EPS amendment (notification of 22 Aug 2014) took effect. The Court did not extend relief blanket-wise. It required the para 11(3) option to have been exercised, so this is a wrong claim.

Option (b) restates the actual holding. Para 11(3) of the pre-amended EPS 1995 allowed members to contribute on salary above the Rs 5,000/6,500 ceiling, with the employer's consent, and so get pension on higher wages. Exercising this option before retirement is the condition for relief. It is a correct statement.

Option (c) refers to R.C. Gupta v. Regional PF Commissioner, Employees Provident Fund Organisation (2016), reported at (2018) 14 SCC 809. It held that employees were not barred from seeking pension on actual higher salary and that no cut-off was needed. The Sunil Kumar bench held its directions were to be complied with. It is a correct statement.

Option (d) is truncated in the image. It begins 'The Supreme Court held as ultra vires...'. In the judgment, the Court held the proviso to para 11(3), which required an additional 1.16% contribution from wages above Rs 15,000, to be ultra vires. This would be a correct statement.
related: EPS 1995 came into force on 16 November 1995.
The 2014 EPS amendment took effect from 1 September 2014.
The wage ceiling under EPS was raised from Rs 6,500 to Rs 15,000.
The Sunil Kumar judgment was delivered on 4 November 2022.
The pension averaging period was changed from 12 months to 60 months.
The 1.16% additional contribution proviso was held ultra vires.
R.C. Gupta v. Regional PF Commissioner is reported at (2018) 14 SCC 809.
The EPF & MP Act was enacted in 1952.
summary: The answer is (a). In EPFO v. Sunil Kumar (4 Nov 2022), the Supreme Court upheld the 2014 Employees' Pension Scheme amendment and struck down the cut-off date for the unamended scheme. It gave a limited benefit to those who had exercised the para 11(3) option before retirement. It did not give relief to all employees who retired before 1 September 2014, so statement (a) is incorrect.
topic_notes: Employees' Pension Scheme 1995 (EPS) was introduced under para 3 of the EPF Scheme, 1952, via Section 6A of the EPF & MP Act 1952. It replaced the Family Pension Scheme 1971. Employers contribute 8.33% of wages to EPS, and the Central Government contributes 1.16% (later 1.16% of wages up to the ceiling). Before the 2014 amendment, the wage ceiling was Rs 6,500 per month, and the pension was calculated on the average of the last 12 months' salary. Para 11(3) of the pre-amended scheme allowed higher-wage contributions with joint request and consent of employer. The 2014 amendment, effective 1 Sept 2014, raised the ceiling to Rs 15,000 and increased the averaging period to 60 months. The amendment also brought in a requirement that members with wages above Rs 15,000 contribute an additional 1.16% of wages above that limit. This was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2022. Earlier, the Kerala High Court in 2018 had set aside the 2014 amendment, and the Supreme Court dismissed the EPFO's SLP, which led to this review. EPFO issued implementing circulars in 2022-23 for exercising the option, with a deadline extended to 26 June 2023. Related ideas include the EPF contribution rate (12% each from employer and employee), the EDLI Scheme 1976, and the EPF Appellate Tribunal. UPSC could ask who heads the EPFO Central Board of Trustees (the Union Labour Minister) and what the statutory basis for EPFO is (the EPF & MP Act 1952).

subject: Industrial Relations & Labour Laws
detail: Legislative competence is distributed by Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule. Parliament has exclusive power over List I (Union List). States have exclusive power over List II (State List). Both can legislate on List III (Concurrent List), with Parliament's law prevailing under Article 254 in case of conflict. Labour matters are mostly Concurrent: Entry 22 (Trade unions; industrial and labour disputes), Entry 23 (Social security and social insurance; employment and unemployment), Entry 24 (Welfare of labour including conditions of work, provident funds, employers' liability, workmen's compensation, invalidity and old age pensions and maternity benefits), and Entry 20 (Economic and social planning). Mines are the exception: Entry 55 of the Union List covers regulation of labour and safety in mines and oilfields, so only Parliament can legislate (e.g., the Mines Act, 1952). Elimination: (a) Trade Union is Concurrent Entry 22, so States can legislate. (b) Labour welfare is Entry 24, Concurrent. (d) Social insurance is Entry 23, Concurrent. Only (c) is exclusively a Union subject. The Employees' Provident Fund case in the stem is a context passage and not needed to answer.
explanations: Incorrect: Trade unions are in Concurrent List Entry 22, so States can make laws on them (e.g., State amendments to the Trade Unions Act, 1926).
Incorrect: Welfare of labour, including conditions of work, provident funds and similar matters, is Concurrent List Entry 24, so States can legislate.
Correct: Regulation of labour and safety in mines and oilfields is Union List Entry 55, so only Parliament can legislate; States cannot.
Incorrect: Social security and social insurance is Concurrent List Entry 23, so States can legislate.
keyfact: Labour and safety in mines and oilfields is Union List Entry 55, so States cannot legislate on it, whereas trade unions, labour welfare and social insurance are Concurrent.
option_notes: Trade Union: Concurrent List Entry 22 covers trade unions and industrial and labour disputes. The central Trade Unions Act, 1926 governs registration and the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 governs disputes. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumes these. States may add amendments, with Presidential assent if they conflict with a central law (Art. 254(2)). Freedom to form unions is a fundamental right under Art. 19(1)(c).

Labour Welfare: Concurrent List Entry 24 covers welfare of labour, including conditions of work, provident funds, employers' liability, workmen's compensation, invalidity and old age pensions and maternity benefits. Several States have Labour Welfare Fund Acts, and central laws such as the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 and the EPF & MP Act, 1952 also operate. The Directive Principles in Arts. 42 and 43 support this.

Regulation of labour in mines: Union List Entry 55 covers regulation of labour and safety in mines and oilfields. Entry 54 covers regulation of mines and mineral development to the extent declared expedient by Parliament. Key laws are the Mines Act, 1952, the Coal Mines Provident Fund Act, 1948 and the Mines Rules. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 now covers mines, and the DGMS enforces mine safety.

Social insurance: Concurrent List Entry 23 covers social security and social insurance, and employment and unemployment. Central laws include the ESI Act, 1948, the EPF & MP Act, 1952, the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 and the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. The Code on Social Security, 2020 consolidates nine such laws. Parliament and States can both legislate.

Entry 23 Concurrent List: social security and social insurance, employment and unemployment.
Entry 24 Concurrent List: welfare of labour, provident funds, pensions, maternity benefits.

Art. 254 resolves repugnancy between Union and State laws on Concurrent subjects.
Labour Codes, 2019-2020, consolidate 29 central labour laws into four codes.

summary: The answer is (a) Trade Union. Under the Seventh Schedule, 'Trade unions; industrial and labour disputes' is Entry 22 of the Concurrent List, so State Legislatures can make law on it. The question asks which subject States cannot legislate on, and the key is the Union List: 'Regulation of labour and safety in mines and oilfields' is Entry 55 of the Union List (List I). Therefore the correct option is (c) Regulation of labour in mines, so ans_ai is (c).
topic_notes:
Article 246 divides legislative powers into three lists: Union (List I, now 100 entries), State (List II, 61 entries) and Concurrent (List III, 52 entries). Residuary powers lie with Parliament (Art. 248, Entry 97 of List I). Parliament can legislate on State subjects in special cases: Art. 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds in the national interest), Art. 250 (Emergency), Art. 252 (consent of States) and Art. 253 (international agreements). On Concurrent subjects, Art. 254 provides central law prevails over conflicting State law, unless the State law was reserved for and received Presidential assent.

Labour entries: Concurrent List has 22 (trade unions, industrial and labour disputes), 23 (social security and insurance, employment and unemployment), 24 (labour welfare), and 20A-type planning entries. Union List has 55 (labour and safety in mines and oilfields), 61 (industrial disputes concerning Union employees), 65 (Union agencies for vocational and professional training), 80-81 (inter-State migration, quarantine), and 24 (shipping and navigation on inland waterways for mechanically propelled vessels) and dock labour issues via ports (Entries 27, 52 and 56 on regulated industries and inter-State rivers). Entry 24 of List I covers inland waterways; Entries 30 and 31 cover other transport.

The Four Labour Codes passed in 2019-2020: Code on Wages 2019, Industrial Relations Code 2020, Code on Social Security 2020, and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020. They subsume 29 central laws. The EPF case in the stem concerns the court's rulings on the scope of delegated legislation (ultra vires), where rules cannot exceed the parent Act.

question: Under the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948, any arrears of amount due from a factory or an establishment may be recovered, from the principal or immediate employer by 102. distraint and sale of its or his movable property in the manner laid down in :
options: Second Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961
Third Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961
Fourth Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961
First Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Chapter on recovery of contributions in the ESI Act, 1948 contains Sections 45B to 45J. Section 45B lets the Corporation recover contributions in arrears as arrears of land revenue. Section 45C empowers the Recovery Officer to recover arrears by (a) attachment and sale of movable or immovable property, (b) arrest of the employer and detention in prison, (c) attachment of the establishment. Section 45C-45D-45E prescribe the procedure, issuing of a certificate by the Corporation's authorised officer to the Recovery Officer, and Recovery Officer's powers. The Income Tax Act, 1961 Second Schedule contains the procedure for recovery of tax (attachment and sale, with Rules 1-69 or so), and the ESI Act borrows this procedure with the necessary modifications. The Third Schedule of the IT Act was about recovery rules for tax before reorganisation (omitted/earlier procedure for recovery of tax by distress, now largely repealed), and the Fourth Schedule deals with recognised provident funds (Part A: recognised PF rules), while the First Schedule dealt with insurance business profits computation. Elimination: only the Second Schedule concerns the recovery procedure for attachment and sale, so options b, c and d fail.
explanations: Correct. The Second Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961 sets out the procedure for recovery of tax, including distraint/attachment and sale of movable property, which the ESI Act adopts for arrears.
Incorrect. The Third Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961 is not the recovery procedure; it related to tax recovery by distress and sale under old rules and is not the one referred to in the ESI Act.
Incorrect. The Fourth Schedule deals with the rules for recognised provident funds, a different subject from recovery of arrears.
Incorrect. The First Schedule relates to computation of profits and gains of insurance business, not to distraint and sale.
keyfact: ESI arrears recovery by distraint and sale of movables follows the Second Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
option_notes: The Second Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961 contains the procedure for recovery of tax: attachment and sale of movable and immovable property, arrest and detention, and Recovery Officer powers. The ESI Act, EPF Act and other laws borrow it for recovering dues. It is the standard reference for 'recovery as arrears of tax'.

The Third Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961 contained the earlier recovery procedure for tax, by distress and sale of movables, and is not the procedure referenced in the ESI Act. Students often confuse it with the Second Schedule, which is the actual recovery procedure schedule.

The Fourth Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961 contains the rules for recognised provident funds, covering the conditions for recognition, contributions and withdrawals. It is relevant to PF taxation (employee exemptions) and not to ESI recovery of arrears.

The First Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961 relates to the computation of profits and gains of insurance business (rules for life insurance and other insurance profits). It is unrelated to the recovery of arrears under the ESI Act.
related: Section 45A of the ESI Act: assessment of contributions where returns not filed
Section 45B: arrears recoverable as arrears of land revenue
Section 45C: recovery by Recovery Officer, including attachment and sale of property and arrest
Section 85B: damages for default in payment of contributions
Section 75: Employees' Insurance Court has jurisdiction
Income Tax Act, 1961 Second Schedule: procedure for recovery of tax
EPF Act Section 8: recovery of money due as arrears of land revenue
EPF Act Section 14B: damages for delay in payment
summary: The correct answer is (a): the Second Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 1961. Section 45C of the ESI Act, 1948 lets arrears due from a factory or establishment be recovered as arrears of land revenue, and Section 45C(a)-(b) read with 45D and 45E applies the Income Tax recovery procedure, including attachment and sale of movable property as laid down in the Second Schedule.
topic_notes: Recovery of dues under the ESI Act, 1948 is found in Sections 45B to 45J. Section 45A deals with determination of contributions in certain cases where the employer does not submit returns, and allows the Corporation to determine contributions on the basis of information available, after giving the employer a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Section 45B states that contributions in arrears may be recovered as arrears of land revenue. Section 45C empowers recovery from the principal or immediate employer by attachment and sale of movable or immovable property as per Income Tax Act's Second Schedule, by arrest and detention, and by attachment of the establishment. Section 45D provides that the Recovery Officer can recover on a certificate issued by an authorised officer of the Corporation. Sections 45E to 45I deal with the validity of certificate and amendments, stay or amendment of proceedings, other modes of recovery, application of certain provisions of the Income Tax Act, and the power to take action on the certificate. Section 45J allows the Recovery Officer to use Income Tax Act's Second and Third Schedule provisions on the basis of certificate. Section 85 is the penal provision for offences by employers, and Section 85B provides for damages for default in payment of contributions, up to the amount of arrears, as determined by the Corporation (with rates set by the Central Government). Section 75 covers the Employees' Insurance Court and Section 77 the claims to be submitted to it. Related ideas include the EPF Act's Section 8 (recovery of money as arrears of land revenue), Section 14B (damages) and 7A (determination of dues), which UPSC often compares with the ESI provisions.

question: Which one of the following is not a benefit under the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 ?
options: Funeral expenses 103. 100. Consider the following statements with reference to the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 :
subject: Social Security
detail: The Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 is a social security law for employees in factories and establishments covered under it. It is administered by the ESI Corporation (ESIC). Benefits under Chapter V (Sections 46 onwards) are: (1) Sickness benefit (SB), paid in cash during certified sickness, at about 70% of average daily wages (the standard rate), for up to 91 days in any two consecutive benefit periods; extended sickness benefit (ESB) is paid for specified long-term diseases at about 80% of wages; (2) Maternity benefit (MB), at 100% of wages, for 26 weeks under the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017; (3) Disablement benefit, temporary (TDB) and permanent (PDB), at about 90% of wages; (4) Dependants' benefit, paid to dependants of an insured person who dies of an employment injury; (5) Medical benefit, which is full medical care for the insured person and family from day one; (6) Funeral expenses, a lump sum paid to the eldest surviving member of the family or the person who performs the last rites (Rs 15,000 at present). Other ESIC measures, such as the unemployment allowance under the Rajiv Gandhi Shramik Kalyan Yojana and the Atal Bimit Vyakti Kalyan Yojana, are schemes, not statutory benefits. Elimination: options a, b and d are statutory benefits, so c is the one that is not.
explanations: Sickness benefit is a statutory cash benefit under Section 46(1)(a) of the ESI Act, so it is a benefit and not the answer.
Maternity benefit is a statutory benefit under Section 46(1)(b), paid for 26 weeks at full wages, so it is not the answer.
The ESI Act contains no child education benefit. Education-related assistance exists only under other welfare schemes, not as an ESI benefit. This is the correct answer.
Funeral expenses are a statutory benefit under Section 46(1)(e), paid on the death of an insured person (currently Rs 15,000), so it is not the answer.
keyfact: ESI benefits: sickness, maternity, disablement, dependants', medical and funeral expenses; no child education benefit.
option_notes: Sickness benefit is a periodic cash payment to an insured person who is certified sick and cannot work. It is paid at about 70% of average daily wages for up to 91 days in a year. Extended sickness benefit, at about 80% of wages, is available for specified long-term diseases for up to 2 years. A minimum contribution period is required.

Maternity benefit is paid to an insured woman for confinement, at 100% of wages for 26 weeks (12 weeks may be taken before delivery). It is 12 weeks for a third child or more, and 12 weeks for adoption or commissioning mothers. It was extended from 12 to 26 weeks by the 2017 amendment. Medical bonus is also payable.

Child education benefit is not a statutory benefit under the ESI Act, 1948. The Act's benefits are sickness, maternity, disablement, dependants', medical and funeral expenses. Education-related support belongs to other welfare schemes, such as those under labour welfare funds. ESIC has some skill and education schemes for dependants, but they are separate from the Act.

Funeral expenses are a lump sum paid on the death of an insured person, to the eldest surviving member of the family or the person who actually incurs the expense. The amount was raised to Rs 15,000. It is payable from the first day of employment, with no minimum contribution period.
related: ESI Act enacted in 1948; first implemented at Kanpur and Delhi on 24 Feb 1952.
Current ESI contribution: employer 3.25%, employee 0.75%.
Wage ceiling for ESI coverage is Rs 21,000 per month.
Maternity benefit is 26 weeks under the 2017 amendment.
Funeral expenses under ESI are Rs 15,000.
Employees' Insurance Court is under Section 74.
Sickness benefit is about 70% of wages for up to 91 days.
The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes the ESI Act.
summary: The answer is (c) Child education benefit. The ESI Act, 1948 provides sickness, maternity, disablement, dependants' and medical benefits, plus funeral expenses, but it has no child education benefit.
topic_notes: The ESI Act, 1948 was the first major social security legislation in independent India. It is based on the Beveridge-influenced ideas of Prof. B.P. Adarkar's report. The Act is administered by the ESI Corporation, a body corporate with the Union Labour Minister as chairman. It has a Standing Committee and a Medical Benefit Council. The scheme applies to non-seasonal factories using power with 10 or more persons, and to shops, hotels, restaurants, cinemas, road transport, newspaper establishments, and private medical and educational institutions with 10 or more employees (20 in some states). Coverage extends to employees earning up to Rs 21,000 per month (Rs 25,000 for persons with disability). Contribution rates since July 2019 are employer 3.25% and employee 0.75% of wages, 4% in total. Employees earning up to Rs 176 per day are exempt from paying their contribution. The Act contains the following benefits: sickness, maternity, disablement (temporary and permanent), dependants', medical and funeral expenses. Disputes are decided by the Employees' Insurance Court under Section 74. The state shares 1/8 of medical benefit costs. The Act provides for an Insurance Medical Officer. Other aspects are the ESI Fund, the ESIC pension-like dependants' benefit, and the Code on Social Security, 2020, which will subsume the Act.
