Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) lonly (b) land 2 only (c) 3only (d) 1,2and3 Alice tells Bob, “I will not come to meet you tomorrow if it rains.” Bob replies, “If it rains tomorrow, I will come to meet you at your place.” On the basis of the discussion of Alice and Bob, which of the following statements is/are true ? a If it rains tomorrow, Alice and Bob will meet. 28 If it does not
subject: Computers
detail: This is a conditional-reasoning (logical deduction) question. Treat each speaker's words as an 'If P then Q' promise. Alice says: If rain, then Alice does not go to Bob. Bob says: If rain, then Bob goes to Alice's place. Under the rain condition, Alice stays home and Bob travels to her, so they meet at Alice's place. Statement 1 is therefore a valid deduction. For statement 2, the no-rain case, neither speaker made any commitment. The rule is that the truth of 'If P then Q' tells us nothing about what happens when P is false. Concluding that they will meet when it does not rain is the fallacy of denying the antecedent (inverse error). Alice's words may suggest she would come, but that is a conversational implicature, not a logical consequence, and nothing is said about Bob at all. Elimination: (b) and (c) include statement 2, which is not deducible. (d) denies statement 1, which is clearly derivable. Hence (a). In UPSC reasoning questions, accept only what follows necessarily from the given statements and do not add outside assumptions.
explanations: Correct. Statement 1 follows necessarily from the two promises, since Bob goes to Alice's place and Alice does not need to travel. Statement 2 is not deducible, so 1 only is right.
Wrong. It claims that only statement 2 is true, but statement 2 cannot be deduced and statement 1 is valid.
Wrong. It includes statement 2, which is not supported by anything in the dialogue, because no commitment was made for the no-rain case.
Wrong. It denies statement 1, but if it rains Bob will go to Alice's place and they will meet.
keyfact: 'If P then Q' says nothing about what happens when P is false, so do not infer the no-rain outcome from the rain promises.
related: 'If P then Q' is false only when P is true and Q is false.
The contrapositive of 'If P then Q' is 'If not Q then not P', and it is logically equivalent.
Converse (Q→P) and inverse (~P→~Q) are not equivalent to the original statement.
Denying the antecedent is a fallacy.
Modus ponens: P→Q and P, therefore Q.
Modus tollens: P→Q and ~Q, therefore ~P.
'P only if Q' is written as P→Q.
'Unless P, Q' means 'If not P, then Q'.
statements: 1 — Correct: In the rain case, Alice's promise is that she will not go to Bob, and Bob's promise is that he will go to Alice's place. The two promises are compatible and together guarantee a meeting at Alice's place. Facts: this is a conditional proposition (If P then Q), made up of an antecedent (the condition) and a consequent (the result). Using modus ponens, if P is true then Q must follow. Here P is 'it rains', and the consequents are 'Alice stays away from Bob's place' and 'Bob goes to Alice's place'. The meeting happens because the two consequents are about different locations, so there is no conflict between them.

2 — Incorrect: Neither speaker gave any commitment for the no-rain case. Alice only said what she would do if it rains. Facts: from 'If P then Q' you cannot infer 'If not P then not Q' (inverse) or 'If Q then P' (converse). Only the contrapositive, 'If not Q then not P', is logically equivalent to the original. Concluding that they will meet when it does not rain is the fallacy of denying the antecedent. For a valid conclusion, the statements would need to be biconditional ('if and only if'), and that was not stated. The result is 'cannot be determined', not 'false'.
summary: The answer is (a), statement 1 only. If it rains, Alice will not come to Bob, but Bob has promised to go to Alice's place, so they meet there. Neither person has said anything about what happens if it does not rain, so statement 2 cannot be deduced.
topic_notes: This question tests conditional (hypothetical) propositions in logical reasoning, a regular topic in the Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning section. A conditional statement has the form 'If P, then Q'. P is the antecedent (sufficient condition) and Q is the consequent (necessary condition). Valid forms: Modus ponens (P→Q, P, therefore Q) and Modus tollens (P→Q, not Q, therefore not P). The contrapositive (not Q → not P) is equivalent to the original. Invalid forms: the converse (Q→P) and the inverse (not P → not Q). Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are the two classic fallacies. Related phrases: 'only if' introduces the necessary condition (P only if Q means P→Q), while 'unless' means 'if not'. A biconditional ('if and only if') makes both directions valid. Negation of 'If P then Q' is 'P and not Q'. Typical UPSC strategies: first symbolise each statement, then test each conclusion using only valid inference rules, and mark a conclusion as not deducible if it relies on an assumed converse or inverse. Also watch for everyday language: people often use 'if' to mean 'if and only if', but in exam logic you must not assume this unless it is stated. Other angles: Venn diagram syllogisms, truth tables for implication (false only when P is true and Q is false), and 'which of the following must be true' versus 'could be true' questions.

ocr: Which of the following statements is/are necessary and sufficient for a _ positive real number x to satisfy the inequality : <oe <3? a 1 ges) 2s Ff x2 2. x ss 3+ V5 Z (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 Mr. Deen Dayal donates = x to the i-th person he meets after he has donated = y to the (i — 1)-th person where x is the largest integer smaller than or equal to 7 He stops after donating © 1 to the last person. If he had = 100 left after donating = 100 to a person, how much money (in =) will he have at last ? (a) 0 a (C) Fae (d) 3
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The solution set of x + 1/x ≤ 3 for x>0 comes from multiplying by x: x² − 3x + 1 ≤ 0. The roots are (3±√5)/2, so the set is the closed interval [(3−√5)/2, (3+√5)/2]. 'Necessary and sufficient' means the statement must define exactly this set, so the statement and the inequality must be equivalent. Key identity: (x+1/x)² = x² + 1/x² + 2. For x>0, x+1/x is positive (and ≥2 by AM-GM). Therefore x²+1/x² ≤ 7 gives (x+1/x)² ≤ 9, so x+1/x ≤ 3, and the steps reverse, so the two are equivalent. Statement 2 only caps x at (3+√5)/2 ≈ 2.618. Small values such as x = 0.1 satisfy it, but 0.1 + 10 = 10.1 > 3, so it is not sufficient. It is necessary, because every solution satisfies it. Elimination: statement 1 is exactly equivalent, so (a) is correct. Statement 2 is not sufficient, which rules out (b), (c) and (d).
explanations: Correct. Statement 1 is exactly equivalent to x+1/x ≤ 3 for positive x, so it is necessary and sufficient, and statement 2 is not.
Wrong. Statement 2 gives only the upper bound, so x = 0.1 satisfies it but violates x+1/x ≤ 3. It is necessary but not sufficient.
Wrong. Statement 2 fails to be sufficient, so 'both' cannot be the answer.
Wrong. Statement 1 is necessary and sufficient, so 'neither' is false.
keyfact: For x>0: x²+1/x² ≤ 7 ⇔ (x+1/x)² ≤ 9 ⇔ x+1/x ≤ 3, so statement 1 alone is necessary and sufficient.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: the statement x²+1/x² ≤ 7 is a squared form of the original inequality. Squaring preserves equivalence only when both sides are non-negative, which holds here because x>0 makes x+1/x>0. Related identity: x²+1/x² = (x+1/x)²−2. This is the correct choice.

Option (b), 2 only: x ≤ (3+√5)/2 is the upper root of x²−3x+1=0, about 2.618, which equals φ², the square of the golden ratio. It is a necessary condition but ignores the lower bound (3−√5)/2 ≈ 0.382, so it is not sufficient. It is wrong.

Option (c), 1 and 2 both: this would require both statements to be individually necessary and sufficient, or jointly so. Statement 1 already defines the exact set, and statement 2 is merely implied by it. A weaker implied condition does not make the pair correct. Combining a necessary-and-sufficient condition with a merely necessary one adds nothing. It is wrong.

Option (d), neither: this would hold only if no statement were equivalent to the inequality. Statement 1 is equivalent, so (d) is wrong. Remember the distinction: necessary means the inequality implies the statement, and sufficient means the statement implies the inequality.
related: For x>0, x+1/x ≥ 2, with equality at x=1.
If x+1/x = 3, then x²+1/x² = 7 and x³+1/x³ = 18.
Roots of x²−3x+1=0 are (3±√5)/2, and their product is 1.
(3+√5)/2 = φ² where φ = (1+√5)/2 is the golden ratio.
Minimum of x+a/x for x>0 is 2√a, at x=√a.
Squaring an inequality preserves it only when both sides are non-negative.
statements: 1 — Correct: x²+1/x² ≤ 7 is equivalent to (x+1/x)² ≤ 9, and since x+1/x>0 this means x+1/x ≤ 3. It is both necessary and sufficient. Facts: the identity (x+1/x)² = x²+1/x²+2 and its twin (x−1/x)² = x²+1/x²−2 are standard. For positive x, x+1/x ≥ 2 with equality at x=1 (AM-GM). If x+1/x = k, then x²+1/x² = k²−2, and x³+1/x³ = k³−3k. At k=3 this gives x²+1/x² = 7 and x³+1/x³ = 18. These are frequent exam tools.

2 — Incorrect: x ≤ (3+√5)/2 is only the upper end of the solution interval [(3−√5)/2, (3+√5)/2]. It is necessary but not sufficient, because small positive x such as 0.1 satisfies it but fails the inequality. Facts: (3±√5)/2 are the roots of x²−3x+1=0. They are reciprocals of each other (product 1). The upper root is φ² ≈ 2.618, where φ is the golden ratio (1+√5)/2 ≈ 1.618, and the lower root is 1/φ² ≈ 0.382. Always check that a bound is two-sided before calling it sufficient.
summary: The answer is (a): statement 1 alone is necessary and sufficient. For positive x, (x+1/x)² = x²+1/x²+2, so x²+1/x² ≤ 7 is the same as (x+1/x)² ≤ 9, which is the same as x+1/x ≤ 3. Statement 2 gives only the upper bound of the solution interval, so it is necessary but not sufficient.
topic_notes: Topic: inequalities and algebraic identities involving x + 1/x, a favourite area in the UPSC EPFO Quantitative Aptitude section. Core facts: (1) AM-GM: for x>0, x+1/x ≥ 2, with equality only at x=1. For x<0, x+1/x ≤ −2. (2) Identities: (x+1/x)² = x²+1/x²+2; (x−1/x)² = x²+1/x²−2; x³+1/x³ = (x+1/x)³ − 3(x+1/x). (3) If x+1/x = 3, then x²+1/x² = 7, x³+1/x³ = 18, and x⁴+1/x⁴ = 47. (4) Solving x+1/x ≤ k with k>2 for x>0: x²−kx+1 ≤ 0, so x lies between the roots (k±√(k²−4))/2, which are reciprocals of each other. For k=3 the roots are (3±√5)/2 ≈ 2.618 and 0.382. (5) The inequality is symmetric under x → 1/x, so the solution interval maps onto itself. (6) Logic of conditions: A is necessary for B if B implies A. A is sufficient if A implies B. 'Necessary and sufficient' means equivalent, so the solution sets must be identical. Test with a counterexample inside A but outside B. Other angles UPSC may ask: x+1/x ≥ k forms, where the solution is the union of two outer intervals; conditions on x−1/x; minimum values of expressions like x+4/x (equal to 4 at x=2); and sets defined by |x−1/x|. Always check the sign of x before squaring, and whether squaring preserves the direction of the inequality.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q102.
ocr: Which of the following statements is/are necessary and sufficient for a _ positive real number x to satisfy the inequality : <oe <3? a 1 ges) 2s Ff x2 2. x ss 3+ V5 Z (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 Mr. Deen Dayal donates = x to the i-th person he meets after he has donated = y to the (i — 1)-th person where x is the largest integer smaller than or equal to 7 He stops after donating © 1 to the last person. If he had = 100 left after donating = 100 to a person, how much money (in =) will he have at last ? (a) 0 a (C) Fae (d) 3
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a repeated-halving problem with the floor function. If a person receives ₹y, the next person receives floor(y/2), the greatest integer not exceeding y/2. Starting at the ₹100 donation, the sequence is 100 → 50 → 25 → floor(12.5)=12 → 6 → 3 → floor(1.5)=1. He stops after giving ₹1 to the last person. The question says he had ₹100 left right after giving ₹100, so the remaining gifts must come out of that ₹100. Those gifts are 50+25+12+6+3+1 = 97, which leaves 100−97 = ₹3. Method: (1) list the sequence carefully, applying the floor at each odd number (25→12, 3→1); (2) add only the gifts after the ₹100 one; (3) subtract from the balance. Common traps are including the ₹100 gift again, which would give a negative balance, rounding 12.5 up to 13, which gives a different total, and stopping the chain at 3 instead of continuing to 1. Elimination: 97 is the total of later gifts, so the leftover cannot be 0, 1 or 2 unless a rounding error is made. Checking the sum twice is worthwhile.
explanations: (a) 0 is wrong. It would need the later gifts to total ₹100, which happens only if 12.5 is wrongly rounded up and extra gifts are added. The correct total is 97.
(b) 1 is wrong. It would result if the last gift of ₹1 were mistaken for the amount left, or if the total were taken as 99. The correct leftover is 100−97 = 3.
(c) 2 is wrong. It would need the later gifts to sum to 98, which does not match the floor sequence 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1.
(d) 3 is correct. The gifts after ₹100 are 50+25+12+6+3+1 = 97, and 100−97 = ₹3 remains at the end.
keyfact: Halving with floor from 100 gives 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1 (sum 97), so 100−97 = ₹3 is left.
option_notes: Option (a), ₹0, would mean he gives away exactly the money he had left. Here the later gifts total only 97, so some money remains. Zero-balance outcomes are typical distractors in such sequence problems. Always compute the total of the series explicitly instead of assuming the money is exhausted. The stopping rule (stop after giving ₹1) fixes the sequence length and does not force the balance to zero.

Option (b), ₹1, is the value of the last gift, not the leftover. Such options exploit confusion between the final donation and the final balance. The last term of the floor-halving chain from 100 is 1 (since floor(3/2)=1), and the chain ends there by the problem's rule. The leftover is the starting balance minus all gifts after the ₹100 gift.

Option (c), ₹2, would come from a slightly wrong sum, for example using 13 instead of 12 for floor(25/2)'s neighbour or miscounting a term. Floor of 25/2 is 12, not 13, and floor of 3/2 is 1. Remember that floor means rounding down, so 12.5 becomes 12 and 1.5 becomes 1. Using ordinary rounding would change the total and the answer.

Option (d), ₹3, is correct. The gift sequence after ₹100 is 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1, which sums to 97. Starting with ₹100 in hand, the final balance is 100−97 = 3. A useful check is that each gift is the floor of half the previous one, and the chain stops at ₹1, as the problem states.
related: floor(n/2) chain from n ends in 0 after as many steps as n has binary digits
Sum of floor(n/2^k), k≥1, equals n minus the number of 1s in binary n
100 in binary is 1100100, which has three 1s
floor(12.5)=12 and floor(1.5)=1
For x>0, x+1/x≥2 with equality at x=1
x+1/x ≤ 3 holds for x between (3−√5)/2 and (3+√5)/2
Greatest integer function is also called the floor function, written ⌊x⌋
summary: The answer is (d) 3. The donations form the sequence 100, 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1, and the 100 left after the ₹100 gift must cover everything after it. The later gifts total 97, so ₹3 remains. (The image shows two questions; I have taken Q102 to be the second one, the Deen Dayal donation problem.)
topic_notes: This question tests sequences with the floor (greatest integer) function, a recurring theme in the UPSC EPFO Quantitative Aptitude section. Key ideas: floor(n/2) for even n is n/2, and for odd n it is (n−1)/2. Starting from 100 the chain is 100, 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1, 0. This is related to binary representation: repeatedly halving with the floor counts the bits of the number, since 100 has 7 binary digits (1100100), which matches the 7 terms before 0. The sum of floor(n/2^k) for k≥1 equals n minus the number of 1s in the binary form of n (Legendre's formula for the exponent of 2 in n!). Check: 100 has three 1s in binary, so the sum of 50+25+12+6+3+1 = 97 = 100−3. This gives a fast shortcut: the leftover is exactly the number of 1s in binary, which is 3. Other angles UPSC could ask: different starting amounts (for example start at 64 or 99), asking for the number of persons, the total donated, or the amount after a fixed number of donations. Also practise inequalities: for positive x, x+1/x≥2 by AM-GM, with equality at x=1, and x²+1/x²=(x+1/x)²−2. For the paired first question, x+1/x≤3 gives (3−√5)/2≤x≤(3+√5)/2, so the upper bound alone is not sufficient. Practise with number-series shortcuts, binary conversion, and careful handling of floors.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q103.
ocr: Which of the following statements is/are necessary and sufficient for a _ positive real number x to satisfy the inequality : <oe <3? a 1 ges) 2s Ff x2 2. x ss 3+ V5 Z (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 Mr. Deen Dayal donates = x to the i-th person he meets after he has donated = y to the (i — 1)-th person where x is the largest integer smaller than or equal to 7 He stops after donating © 1 to the last person. If he had = 100 left after donating = 100 to a person, how much money (in =) will he have at last ? (a) 0 a (C) Fae (d) 3
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Solve x + 1/x ≤ 3 for x > 0. Multiplying by x gives x² − 3x + 1 ≤ 0. The roots are (3 ± √5)/2, so the solution set is the closed interval [(3 − √5)/2, (3 + √5)/2]. Note that (3 − √5)/2 is approximately 0.382 and (3 + √5)/2 is approximately 2.618, and the two are reciprocals of each other because their product is 1. 'Necessary and sufficient' means a statement must define exactly this set, with no more and no less. Statement 1: since x > 0, x + 1/x is positive, so squaring is reversible. x² + 1/x² = (x + 1/x)² − 2 ≤ 7 gives (x + 1/x)² ≤ 9, so x + 1/x ≤ 3 (the value cannot be negative). The two conditions are therefore identical. Statement 2: x ≤ 2.618 also admits x = 0.1, for which x + 1/x = 10.1 > 3. So it is necessary (every solution satisfies it) but not sufficient. The elimination logic is that statement 1 is an equivalence, statement 2 is only a one-way implication, and the answer is (a). Always check whether a condition cuts off both ends of the interval.
explanations: Correct. Statement 1 is equivalent to x + 1/x ≤ 3 for positive x, so it is necessary and sufficient. Statement 2 is not sufficient.
Incorrect. Statement 2 alone allows x values below (3 − √5)/2, which violate the inequality, so it is not sufficient.
Incorrect. Statement 2 fails the sufficiency test, so 'both 1 and 2' cannot be the answer.
Incorrect. Statement 1 is exactly equivalent to the given inequality, so 'neither' is false.
keyfact: For x > 0: x + 1/x ≤ 3 ⇔ x² + 1/x² ≤ 7, with solution interval [(3 − √5)/2, (3 + √5)/2].
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', means statement 1 alone is necessary and sufficient. It is true here because squaring a positive quantity preserves the inequality. The identity x² + 1/x² = (x + 1/x)² − 2 is a standard tool for such problems. The same trick converts the sum of cubes: x³ + 1/x³ = (x + 1/x)³ − 3(x + 1/x). Keep both identities ready for the exam.

Option (b), '2 only', would mean the upper bound x ≤ (3 + √5)/2 alone characterises the solution. It does not, because the lower bound (3 − √5)/2 is also needed. The interval is bounded on both sides since x + 1/x tends to infinity as x tends to 0 or to infinity. The minimum of x + 1/x for x > 0 is 2 at x = 1, by AM–GM.

Option (c), 'both 1 and 2', would require statement 2 to be sufficient too. It is not, since it permits small x such as 0.1. For both statements to hold together, the combined condition would give the interval up to 2.618 intersected with statement 1, which is just statement 1 itself. So 'both' is not needed, and statement 2 on its own does not work.

Option (d), 'neither 1 nor 2', would be correct only if statement 1 failed to be equivalent. It is equivalent because x > 0 makes x + 1/x positive, so squaring the bound 3 loses no information. The negative branch, x + 1/x ≥ −3, would matter only for negative x, which the question excludes.
related: For x > 0, x + 1/x ≥ 2, with equality at x = 1.
If x + 1/x = 3, then x² + 1/x² = 7.
If x + 1/x = 3, then x³ + 1/x³ = 18.
Roots of x² − 3x + 1 = 0 are (3 ± √5)/2, which are reciprocals of each other.
(3 + √5)/2 equals the square of the golden ratio φ ≈ 1.618.
Squaring an inequality preserves it only if both sides are non-negative.
If 'A is necessary and sufficient for B', then A ⇔ B.
Same page, donation question: sequence 100, 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1 leaves 3 rupees (option d).
statements: 1 — Correct: for x > 0, x² + 1/x² ≤ 7 ⇔ (x + 1/x)² ≤ 9 ⇔ x + 1/x ≤ 3, so it is exactly equivalent to the given inequality. Useful identities: (x + 1/x)² = x² + 1/x² + 2, and (x − 1/x)² = x² + 1/x² − 2. By AM–GM, x + 1/x ≥ 2 for every positive x, with equality only at x = 1. So x + 1/x ≤ 3 has solutions only in the interval around 1, namely [(3 − √5)/2, (3 + √5)/2]. The square-root step is valid only because x + 1/x is positive. If x could be negative, squaring would not be reversible.

2 — Incorrect: x ≤ (3 + √5)/2 ≈ 2.618 is only the upper bound of the solution interval. It is necessary but not sufficient, because small positive x (for example 0.1) satisfies it yet gives x + 1/x = 10.1 > 3. The lower bound (3 − √5)/2 ≈ 0.382 is missing. The two endpoints are reciprocals of each other, with product 1 and sum 3. They are related to the golden ratio, since (3 + √5)/2 = φ² where φ = (1 + √5)/2 ≈ 1.618. The solution set of such quadratic inequalities is always bounded by both roots.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is necessary and sufficient. For positive x, x² + 1/x² = (x + 1/x)² − 2, so x² + 1/x² ≤ 7 is equivalent to (x + 1/x)² ≤ 9, which is equivalent to x + 1/x ≤ 3. Statement 2 gives only the upper end of the solution interval, so it is necessary but not sufficient. (The image also shows a second question, the Deen Dayal donation puzzle, which is not explained here. Its answer works out to 3, option (d).)
topic_notes: This is a question on inequalities and algebraic identities involving reciprocals. Key facts: (1) AM–GM: for positive a, b, (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab). For x > 0, x + 1/x ≥ 2, with equality at x = 1. (2) Identities: (x + 1/x)² = x² + 1/x² + 2, and x³ + 1/x³ = (x + 1/x)³ − 3(x + 1/x). (3) A quadratic inequality ax² + bx + c ≤ 0 with a > 0 holds between the roots. Here the roots of x² − 3x + 1 = 0 are (3 ± √5)/2, with sum 3 and product 1. (4) Necessary versus sufficient: A is necessary for B if B implies A. A is sufficient for B if A implies B. 'Necessary and sufficient' means the two are equivalent. (5) Squaring an inequality is reversible only when both sides are non-negative. Other angles UPSC may ask: find the value of x² + 1/x² given x + 1/x = 3, which is 7. Find x³ + 1/x³ given x + 1/x = 3, which is 27 − 9 = 18. Find the minimum of x + 1/x, which is 2. Find the range of x satisfying x + 1/x ≥ 5/2, which is x ≤ 1/2 or x ≥ 2. Solve for x given x − 1/x = k. The same method applies to modulus and rational inequalities. The 'DeenDayal donation' question printed on the same page is a floor-halving sequence: 100, 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1.

ocr: A plant grows 20% of its height every year. | 107. After how many years will it grow at least twice of its present height for the first time ? (a) 3 (b) 4 @rerb @276
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Compound growth: height after n years = H × (1.2)^n. Compute: 1.2^1 = 1.2; 1.2^2 = 1.44; 1.2^3 = 1.728; 1.2^4 = 2.0736; 1.2^5 = 2.48832. The condition is height ≥ 2H. After 3 years the height is 1.728H, which is less than 2H. After 4 years the height is 2.0736H, which is at least 2H. So the first time the plant is at least twice its present height is after 4 years, and the correct option is (b) 4. Note that if growth were simple (non-compounding) at 20% of the ORIGINAL height each year, it would need 5 years to double (1 + 0.2n = 2 gives n = 5). The phrase 'grows 20% of its height every year' means 20% of the current height, so it is compounding. Rule of 72 check: doubling at 20% takes about 72/20 = 3.6 years, so the first whole year is 4. Elimination: 3 years gives 1.728, too low; 5 and 6 are not the first time.
explanations: Wrong: after 3 years the height is 1.728 times the original, which is below 2 times.
Correct: after 4 years the height is 1.2^4 = 2.0736 times the original, which is at least 2 times, and 3 years was not enough. So 4 is the first year.
Wrong: 5 years is what simple (non-compounded) growth would need, and under compounding the plant has already doubled by year 4, so 5 is not the first time.
Wrong: 6 years is far more than needed; 1.2^6 is about 2.986, and the plant had already doubled earlier.
option_notes: 3 years: under 20% compound growth the height is 1.728 times the present, which is about 72.8% growth. It is a common trap because 3 × 20% = 60% is wrongly thought close to doubling. Compound growth formula: A = P(1 + r/100)^n.

4 years: 1.2^4 = 2.0736, so growth is about 107.4%. This is the first whole year in which the height reaches at least double. Rule of 72 estimates doubling time of about 3.6 years at 20%, which rounds up to 4 whole years.
5 years: 1.2^5 = 2.48832, so about 148.8% growth. Under simple growth of 20% of the original height per year, 5 years gives exactly double. This is the distractor for students who ignore compounding.
6 years: 1.2^6 = 2.985984, nearly triple the height. It is a valid 'at least twice' point but not the first time. Questions often include later years as distractors for 'first time' wording.
related: Compound growth: A = P(1 + r/100)^n.
Rule of 72: doubling time is about 72 divided by rate percent.
CI − SI for 2 years = P(r/100)^2.
Two successive changes of a% and b%: net = a + b + ab/100.
Simple interest doubling time at r% is 100/r years.
summary: The answer is (c) 5. Growth of 20% per year compounds, so the height after n years is 1.2^n times the present height. The first n for which 1.2^n ≥ 2 is n = 4 only if 1.2^4 ≥ 2, which it is not (2.0736 is reached at n = 4)... see detail for the exact check.
topic_notes: This is a compound growth question, a staple of the Quantitative Aptitude section. The formula is Final = Initial × (1 + r/100)^n for growth, and Initial × (1 − r/100)^n for decay. Compound interest is the same idea: amount A = P(1 + r/100)^n, and CI = A − P. Simple interest is linear: SI = PRT/100. Key powers of 1.2 to memorise: 1.44, 1.728, 2.0736, 2.48832, 2.985984. Powers of 1.1: 1.21, 1.331, 1.4641, 1.61051. Powers of 1.25: 1.5625, 1.953, 2.441. Rule of 72: doubling time in years is about 72 divided by the percentage rate; exact doubling time is ln2/ln(1+r). For 10% it is about 7.27 years, for 20% about 3.80 years (ln2/ln1.2 = 0.6931/0.1823), so the first whole year is 4. Related question types: population growth, depreciation of machines, bacteria doubling, successive percentage change (net change = a + b + ab/100), and difference between CI and SI for 2 years = P(r/100)^2. Always check the wording: 'at least' means ≥, and 'first time' needs the smallest whole n that satisfies it. Test each n by successive multiplication rather than guessing, and watch whether growth applies to the original or the current value.

ocr: A packet of chewing gum costs = 5 and along 108. with each packet you receive two coupons. Using nine such coupons, you can buy a packet of chewing gum of the same type along with two coupons in it. If you have = 1,000, and you buy maximum number of chewing gum packets, how many coupons will you have unspent ? 109. (a) 0 (b) 4 (ce). 6. (dd) 8 Directions : Consider the following for the next three (03) items that follow : Expenses of a company on five different heads, 110. namely, raw material, advertisement, transportation, infrastructure and salary to the employees are denoted by u, v, x, y a
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: This is a recycling (exchange-offer) problem. Step 1: Rs 1,000 / Rs 5 = 200 packets, and 200 x 2 = 400 coupons. Step 2: every exchange uses 9 coupons and returns 2 coupons with the new packet, so the net loss is 7 coupons per extra packet. Step 3: an exchange is possible only while the coupons in hand are at least 9. Before the k-th exchange we hold 400 - 7(k-1) coupons, and we need 400 - 7(k-1) >= 9, so 7(k-1) <= 391 and k-1 <= 55. So the largest k is 56. After 56 exchanges: 400 - 7 x 56 = 400 - 392 = 8 coupons. Check by totals: packets = 200 + 56 = 256, coupons ever earned = 256 x 2 = 512, coupons spent = 56 x 9 = 504, and 512 - 504 = 8. Since 8 < 9, no further packet can be bought. Elimination: 0, 4 and 6 would need more than 56 exchanges, which is impossible because the coupon count falls below 9 first. Remember the shortcut: unspent = start - (net loss x number of exchanges), where the number of exchanges is found from the threshold. The same method works for bottle-cap and wrapper problems.
explanations: (a) 0 is wrong. After the last possible exchange 8 coupons remain, and there is no way to spend all of them because 9 are needed per packet.
(b) 4 is wrong. It would need 56.57 exchanges' worth of loss (396/7), which is not an integer and is not what happens. The correct count of 56 exchanges leaves 8, not 4.
(c) 6 is wrong. It would need 394/7 exchanges, which is not an integer. Counting exchanges properly gives 8 left.
(d) 8 is correct. 400 coupons - 56 x 7 = 8, and 8 < 9 so no further exchange is possible.
keyfact: Exchange puzzles: net loss per exchange = needed - returned (9 - 2 = 7); 400 coupons give 56 exchanges and 8 are left.
option_notes: Option (a) 0 would mean every coupon was used. That would happen only if the final exchange used exactly the coupons left, but here the net 7-per-exchange pattern leaves a remainder, because 400 mod 7 = 1 and the end condition (below 9) stops the process at 8. Zero leftover occurs in problems whose last exchange has no returned coupons.

Option (b) 4 would be the leftover if the coupon count were 396 - 7k with a different start, for example 4 = 400 - 396 with 396 not divisible by 7. It is a distractor from counting exchanges wrongly (for example, using 400/9 = 44 exchanges and ignoring the 2 coupons returned each time).

Option (c) 6 is a distractor. It could come from ignoring the returned coupons partly, or from miscounting an exchange. In recycling problems always add back the returned coupons after every exchange and stop only when the stock is below the exchange rate.

Option (d) 8 is the correct leftover. It equals the remainder after the process stops when coupons fall below 9. Note that 8 is the largest possible leftover, since any stock of 9 or more allows another exchange, and the same reasoning works for any rate-exchange problem.
related: Net coupon loss per exchange here = 9 - 2 = 7.
Rs 1,000 / Rs 5 = 200 packets, giving 400 coupons.
Total packets after recycling = 256, total coupons earned = 512.
Exchange continues only while coupons >= 9, so the maximum leftover is 8.
Pie chart: all central angles total 360 degrees.
In the paired pie chart, z (salary) = 360 - (30+45+60+90) = 135 degrees.
Sector share = angle / 360 x 100 percent.
summary: The answer is (d) 8. Rs 1,000 buys 200 packets, which give 400 coupons. Each exchange of 9 coupons returns 2 coupons, so it costs a net 7 coupons. After 56 exchanges, 8 coupons are left, which is too few for another packet.
topic_notes: Topic: Quantitative Aptitude, arithmetic word problems on exchange and recycling offers (coupons, empty bottles, wrappers). Standard method: (1) find the initial number of items bought with the money; (2) find the initial tokens; (3) find the net token loss per exchange = tokens needed - tokens returned; (4) the exchange continues while the stock is at least the tokens needed; (5) the number of exchanges is floor((initial - needed)/net loss) + 1; (6) leftover = initial - net loss x exchanges. Check by the total-earned minus total-spent method. Related variants: borrowing an empty bottle to complete an exchange (the borrowed one is returned after drinking, which changes the final count); 'free item with each purchase' offers; maximum items for a given money including the free items. Common errors: dividing 400 by 9 directly (ignoring the returned coupons), forgetting the second step of the new coupons, and stopping early or late at the threshold. Related UPSC EPFO quantitative topics: percentages, profit and loss, ratio and proportion, time and work, simple and compound interest, averages, number system and remainders, and data interpretation with pie charts, which is the next set of questions in this paper (angles of a pie chart sum to 360 degrees, and a central angle of x degrees represents x/360 of the total). In the pie-chart passage, u, v, x, y have 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees, so z = 360 - 225 = 135 degrees.

question: If the company spent = 55-4 crore on raw material, how much did it spend on 111. infrastructure ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a data-interpretation question. The original paper gave a pie chart, bar graph or table showing how a company's total expenditure was split among heads such as raw material, infrastructure, salaries, and so on. The question asks for the infrastructure spend when raw material spend is given as about 55.4 crore (the OCR text reads '55-4', where the hyphen stands for a decimal point). The method is: (1) read the percentage or ratio share for raw material and for infrastructure from the chart; (2) infrastructure spend = raw material spend x (infrastructure share / raw material share); (3) check the arithmetic and match it to an option. Without the chart, the two shares are unknown, so the ratio cannot be computed. The options (114.5, 115.6, 166.2, 118.0 crore) are also garbled by OCR, with symbols replacing the rupee sign. Option (c) 166.2 is far from the others, so it may be a distractor, but this is only a guess. For revision, treat this as a method note and consult the original paper's chart before relying on any option.
explanations: Option (a) 114.5 crore: cannot be verified without the chart, so it is not confirmed as correct or incorrect.
Option (b) 115.6 crore: cannot be verified without the chart, so it is not confirmed as correct or incorrect. It is chosen only as a placeholder guess.
Option (c) 166.2 crore: it is an outlier compared with the other three options, which cluster near 115 crore. This hints that it is a distractor, but it is not verifiable.
Option (d) 118.0 crore: cannot be verified without the chart, so it is not confirmed as correct or incorrect.
keyfact: Question is incomplete (chart missing); infrastructure spend = raw material spend x (infrastructure % / raw material %).
option_notes: 114.5 crore: one of the numeric answer choices. It has no meaning on its own outside the missing chart. In data interpretation, always compute the answer from the given shares before matching the option.
115.6 crore: one of the numeric answer choices. It lies close to the 114.5 and 118.0 options, which is typical of UPSC's near-value distractors. Careful calculation is needed to separate such values.

166.2 crore: one of the numeric answer choices. It is much larger than the others and would imply an infrastructure share well above the raw material share. Check the proportions before accepting such a value.
118.0 crore: one of the numeric answer choices. Like the others, it can only be validated using the ratio of infrastructure to raw material expenditure from the chart.
related: Pie chart central angle = (share % / 100) x 360 degrees.
Amount of head B = amount of head A x (B% / A%).
1 crore = 100 lakh = 10 million.
Percentage change = (change / original) x 100.
Ratio questions: first convert all quantities to the same unit.

question: The number of pair of values of (x, y) for x<y, where x, y are natural numbers, such that xy = 14(x + y) are:
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The method is Simon's Favourite Factoring Trick. Start with xy = 14x + 14y, so xy - 14x - 14y = 0. Add 196 to both sides to get (x-14)(y-14) = 196 = 2^2 × 7^2. The number of positive divisors is (2+1)(2+1) = 9, namely 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28, 49, 98 and 196. Pair them as (1,196), (2,98), (4,49), (7,28), (14,14). The pair (14,14) gives x = y = 28, which is excluded because the question requires x<y. The other four pairs give (15,210), (16,112), (18,63) and (21,42). Negative factor pairs need both x and y below 14. Then each of (x-14) and (y-14) lies between -13 and -1, so the product is at most 169, which is less than 196. So no negative pairs work. Check: 21×42 = 882 and 14×63 = 882, which matches. The count is therefore 4. Option (d) 6 would wrongly count extra or negative cases, and the garbled options (a) and (c) cannot be read, but 4 is the verified count.

(b) Correct. (x-14)(y-14) = 196 has 4 factor pairs with x<y, giving (15,210), (16,112), (18,63) and (21,42).
(c) The option text is garbled in the OCR and unreadable. It does not match the verified count of 4.
(d) Incorrect. 6 is not the number of solutions. The 9 divisors of 196 give only 4 unordered pairs with x<y, since (14,14) is excluded and negative pairs are impossible.

For reference, the correct count is 4, found from the factor pairs of 196 = 2^2 × 7^2. The number 196 has 9 positive divisors, which give 4 unordered pairs with x<y and one equal pair (14,14), which is excluded.

Option (b), 4, is the correct count. The four solutions are (15,210), (16,112), (18,63) and (21,42). They come from the factor pairs (1,196), (2,98), (4,49) and (7,28) of 196, added to 14 on each side. A general rule is that xy = k(x+y) becomes (x-k)(y-k) = k^2. The number of solutions with x<y is (d(k^2) - 1)/2, where d is the divisor count. Here d(196) = 9, so (9-1)/2 = 4.

Option (c) is garbled by OCR (it reads 'a)') and has no usable value. It cannot be identified, and the correct count is 4. The factor pairs of 196 with x<y give exactly four solutions, so any other number is wrong. Remember that (14,14) gives x = y = 28, which does not satisfy x<y.

Option (d), 6, is incorrect. A student might reach it by counting some negative or ordered pairs, but negative factors are impossible because x and y would have to be less than 14, which gives a product of at most 169 and not 196. Ordered pairs would give 9 (or 8 excluding x=y), not 6. The correct count with x<y is 4.

It is rewritten as (x-k)(y-k) = k^2, so the solutions correspond to divisor pairs of k^2. For k = 14, k^2 = 196 = 2^2 × 7^2. The divisor count of a number with prime factorisation p^a q^b is (a+1)(b+1), so d(196) = 9. The number of unordered solutions with x<y is (9-1)/2 = 4. Japan hosted him at the G7 but did not confer its top honour, the Order of the Chrysanthemum. The remaining possibility, Fiji, matches the record. Later honours in 2023 were Egypt's Order of the Nile (June) and France's Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour (July). By then Modi had received more than a dozen foreign state honours.
explanations: Incorrect: Australia hosted Modi in Sydney on 23-24 May 2023, but it did not confer any honour on him. The Order of Australia was not given.
Correct: Fiji conferred the Companion of the Order of Fiji, its highest civilian honour, on Modi on 22 May 2023. PM Rabuka presented it.
Incorrect: New Zealand was not on Modi's May 2023 itinerary, and it conferred no honour on him. Its highest honour is the Order of New Zealand.
Incorrect: Japan hosted Modi at the G7 Hiroshima summit but did not confer its highest honour on him. That honour is the Order of the Chrysanthemum.
keyfact: May 2023: Fiji gave Modi the Companion of the Order of Fiji; PNG gave the Order of Logohu; Palau gave the Ebakl Award.
option_notes: Australia: a Commonwealth country whose highest civilian honour is the Companion of the Order of Australia (AC), part of the Order of Australia created in 1975. Modi visited Sydney on 23-24 May 2023 for a community event at Qudos Bank Arena and bilateral talks with PM Anthony Albanese. The Quad leaders' summit planned there was cancelled. India and Australia are a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (2020), and the ECTA trade pact took effect in December 2022.

Fiji: a Pacific island nation and Commonwealth member whose capital is Suva. Its highest honour is the Companion of the Order of Fiji (CF), within the Order of Fiji established in 1995. PM Sitiveni Rabuka conferred it on Modi on 22 May 2023. Fiji is part of FIPIC (Forum for India-Pacific Islands Cooperation), launched in 2014 in Suva. Hindi is an official language of Fiji, where there is a large Indo-Fijian population.

New Zealand: its highest honour is the Order of New Zealand (ONZ), established in 1987, with a membership limit of 20 living ordinary members. Modi did not visit New Zealand in May 2023. India-NZ relations cover trade, education, dairy and Commonwealth ties. A free trade agreement has been under negotiation for years. NZ is not a Quad member.

Japan: its highest honour is the Supreme Order of the Chrysanthemum, with the Order of the Rising Sun below it. Modi attended the G7 Hiroshima summit on 19-21 May 2023 as an invited guest and met PM Fumio Kishida and Ukraine's Zelensky. Japan is a Quad member and has a Special Strategic and Global Partnership with India. The Japanese honour Modi had earlier received was not a state order of this rank. Japan's Order of the Chrysanthemum is rarely given to Indians.
related: Fiji's highest honour: Companion of the Order of Fiji (conferred on Modi, 22 May 2023).
Papua New Guinea's honour to Modi: Grand Companion of the Order of Logohu.
Palau's honour to Modi: Ebakl Award (May 2023).
FIPIC was launched in 2014 in Suva, Fiji; the 3rd summit was in Port Moresby in 2023.
Egypt's Order of the Nile was conferred on Modi in June 2023.
France's Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour was conferred on Modi in July 2023.
Japan's highest honour: Supreme Order of the Chrysanthemum.
Australia's top honour: Companion of the Order of Australia (AC).
summary: The answer is (b) Fiji. During his Pacific tour on 22 May 2023, Fiji's PM Sitiveni Rabuka conferred the Companion of the Order of Fiji on PM Narendra Modi. This is Fiji's highest civilian honour.
topic_notes: Modi's 19-24 May 2023 tour covered three countries. In Japan he attended the G7 Hiroshima summit as an outreach guest, with the Quad summit planned for Sydney being cancelled. In Papua New Guinea he co-hosted the 3rd FIPIC summit with PM James Marape in Port Moresby on 22 May. PNG gave him the Grand Companion of the Order of Logohu, and Fiji's PM Rabuka gave him the Companion of the Order of Fiji. Palau's President Surangel Whipps Jr. conferred the Ebakl Award. In Australia he met PM Albanese in Sydney and addressed the Indian diaspora. FIPIC was launched in Suva in November 2014 and covers 14 Pacific Island countries. Other foreign honours for Modi: Saudi Arabia's King Abdulaziz Sash (2016), Afghanistan's Amir Amanullah Khan Award (2016), Palestine's Grand Collar (2018), UAE's Order of Zayed (2019), Russia's Order of St Andrew (2019), Maldives' Nishan Izzuddeen (2019), Bahrain's King Hamad Order of the Renaissance (2019), USA's Legion of Merit (2020), Bhutan's Order of the Druk Gyalpo (2024), and Egypt's Order of the Nile (June 2023). France's Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour came in July 2023. Fiji's honour is often described as a rare award for non-Fijians. Questions often combine the visit with the honour, so memorise country-honour pairs. Also know the highest civilian honour of India (Bharat Ratna) and the Pacific region basics such as the Pacific Islands Forum.

question: Which Indian sportsperson won gold for India in the Archery World Cup held in Shanghai in the year 2023 ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The 2023 Hyundai Archery World Cup had four stages and a final: Stage 1 in Antalya (Turkey), Stage 2 in Shanghai (China, April 2023), Stage 3 in Medellin (Colombia), Stage 4 in Paris (France), and the Final in Hermosillo (Mexico). In Shanghai, India's compound archers did very well. Abhishek Verma, the Arjuna Award winner from Haryana, took the men's compound individual gold. Prathamesh Jawkar and Ojas Deotale were the other prominent Indian compound men in the 2023 season, and they won medals in the team and individual events across various stages. Atanu Das is a recurve archer (husband of Deepika Kumari) and is not a compound specialist. Neeraj Chauhan is a distractor and is not a known World Cup gold medallist. Elimination: the individual medallist from Shanghai was a compound archer with a long World Cup record, which points to Verma. Treat this as a memory-based answer and cross-check it against the World Archery records if you can.
explanations: Correct: Abhishek Verma won the men's compound individual gold at the Shanghai World Cup Stage 2 in 2023.
Incorrect: Atanu Das is a recurve archer. He was not the Shanghai 2023 gold medallist.
Incorrect: Prathamesh Jawkar is a compound archer who won medals in the 2023 season, but he is not the person credited with the Shanghai individual gold.
Incorrect: Neeraj Chauhan is not associated with a World Cup gold in Shanghai 2023.
keyfact: Abhishek Verma won men's compound individual gold at Archery World Cup Stage 2, Shanghai 2023.
option_notes: Abhishek Verma is a compound archer from Haryana and an Arjuna Awardee (2021). He won Asian Games 2023 team gold and individual medals, and multiple World Cup medals. He is a regular in India's compound team alongside Ojas Deotale and Prathamesh Jawkar.

Atanu Das is a recurve archer from West Bengal who competed at the Olympics (2012, 2016, 2020). He is married to Deepika Kumari. He has won World Cup team medals and an Asian Games medal. He is a recurve specialist, not compound.

Prathamesh Jawkar is a compound archer from Maharashtra. He was part of India's compound men's team that won medals in the 2023 World Cup season and the Asian Games. He is among the rising stars of Indian compound archery.
Neeraj Chauhan is an Indian archer and Arjuna-related recognition is not tied to him for a Shanghai World Cup gold. He is mainly a distractor option in this question.
related: World Archery HQ is in Lausanne, Switzerland.
2023 Archery World Cup Final was held in Hermosillo, Mexico.
Aditi Swami won the individual compound title at the 2023 World Championships in Berlin.
Deepika Kumari and Atanu Das are recurve archers.
Jyothi Surekha Vennam is a leading Indian compound archer.
Compound archery is not an Olympic event.
summary: The answer is (a) Abhishek Verma. He won the men's compound individual gold at the 2023 Archery World Cup Stage 2 in Shanghai, which is my recollection from memory and I could not check it against a source. The Indian compound team also had a strong run there.
topic_notes: The Archery World Cup is organised by World Archery, the international federation (founded 1931, headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland). Events: recurve and compound, individual, team and mixed team, for men and women. The season has several stages and a final. The 2023 season stages were Antalya, Shanghai, Medellin and Paris, with the Final in Hermosillo, Mexico. India has strong compound archers, including Jyothi Surekha Vennam, Aditi Swami, Parneet Kaur, Abhishek Verma, Ojas Deotale and Prathamesh Jawkar. India's recurve stars include Deepika Kumari, Atanu Das, Dhiraj Bommadevara and Ankita Bhakat. At the 2023 World Championships in Berlin, India's women compound team won gold, and Aditi Swami became the youngest individual compound world champion. At the Asian Games 2022, held in Hangzhou in 2023, Indian compound archers won several golds. The Archery Association of India is the national body, and the sport has been included in the Olympics since 1972 (reintroduced). Compound archery is not an Olympic event but is in the Asian Games and World Games, and it is on the programme for the 2028 Los Angeles Paralympics.

question: What was the name of the search and rescue operation carried out by NDRF in the aftermath of the earthquake in Turkey in February 2023 ?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: On 6 February 2023 a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck south-eastern Turkey (Kahramanmaras region, near the Syrian border), followed by a strong aftershock. It killed over 50,000 people across Turkey and Syria. India responded within hours under the name Operation Dost ('friend'). Teams from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) flew out in IAF C-17 Globemaster aircraft with sniffer dogs, drilling and cutting equipment, and medical supplies. Indian Army field hospitals were set up at Iskenderun in Hatay province, and relief went to Syria as well. NDRF teams from Ghaziabad and Kolkata battalions were involved, and the NDRF was created under the Disaster Management Act, 2005. Elimination: Operation Sahayata and Operation Himmat are not linked to Turkey; Himmat is associated with other relief contexts. Operation Sahyog is the name for India's assistance to Haiti after its 2010 earthquake, and Operation Sahayata was used for Nepal-related contexts, so these are distractors. Remember Dost = Turkey and Syria 2023.
explanations: Incorrect: Operation Sahayata is not the name of the Turkey earthquake mission. It is a distractor.
Incorrect: Operation Sahyog is associated with earlier relief missions, such as Haiti in 2010, and not with Turkey 2023.
Correct: Operation Dost was India's rescue and relief mission to Turkey and Syria after the 6 February 2023 earthquake, with NDRF teams, Army medical units and relief supplies.
Incorrect: Operation Himmat is not the Turkey earthquake operation.
keyfact: Operation Dost = India's NDRF and Army relief to Turkey and Syria after the 6 February 2023 earthquake.
option_notes: Operation Sahayata: the name is generic and means 'assistance'. It is not the operation for the 2023 Turkey quake. Indian operations are typically named for the mission, such as Dost, Ganga, Kaveri or Ajay. Do not confuse it with the Turkey mission.

Operation Sahyog: a name used for Indian humanitarian aid, notably the Indian Navy and Coast Guard relief to Haiti after the January 2010 earthquake. It also appears in Indian Coast Guard cooperation contexts. It is not the 2023 Turkey operation.

Operation Dost: India's humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operation launched in February 2023 for earthquake-hit Turkey and Syria. It involved NDRF search and rescue teams (about 100 personnel with dogs), Army field hospital, medicines and equipment sent by IAF C-17 aircraft. Dost means friend.
Operation Himmat: a name associated with other Indian relief or defence contexts, not the Turkey earthquake mission. Himmat means courage. It is not the operation for Turkey in 2023.
related: Operation Dost: India's aid to Turkey and Syria, February 2023.
Operation Kaveri: evacuation of Indians from Sudan, April 2023.
Operation Ganga: evacuation of Indians from Ukraine, 2022.
Operation Ajay: evacuation from Israel, October 2023.
NDRF was constituted under the Disaster Management Act, 2005.
Operation Maitri: Indian relief for the 2015 Nepal earthquake.
Operation Brahma: India's relief for Myanmar after the March 2025 earthquake.
summary: The answer is (c) Operation Dost. India launched Operation Dost after the 6 February 2023 Turkey-Syria earthquakes, sending NDRF search and rescue teams, medical teams and relief material to Turkey and Syria.
topic_notes: The Turkey-Syria earthquake of 6 February 2023 had a magnitude of 7.8 with its epicentre near Gaziantep and Kahramanmaras in Turkey, along the East Anatolian Fault. Deaths exceeded 50,000. India sent aid to both countries under Operation Dost, with NDRF teams, specially trained dog squads, the Army's medical corps with a 30-bed hospital at Iskenderun, and relief material to Syria through Damascus. Turkey's ambassador thanked India, and the phrase 'Dost' was used for friendship. The National Disaster Response Force was constituted under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, with its headquarters in New Delhi and 16 battalions drawn from BSF, CRPF, CISF, ITBP and SSB. Its first operation abroad was in Nepal (Operation Maitri 2015 was the Army's rescue effort). Other Indian operations: Operation Ganga (Ukraine evacuation 2022), Operation Devi Shakti (Afghanistan 2021), Operation Kaveri (Sudan 2023), Operation Ajay (Israel 2023), Operation Brahma (Myanmar earthquake 2025), Operation Raahat (Yemen 2015), Operation Sankat Mochan (South Sudan 2016), Operation Vande Bharat Mission (COVID evacuation), Operation Samudra Setu (COVID). Operation Sadbhav was relief for Sri Lanka, Laos, Vietnam and Myanmar in 2024 after Cyclone Yagi (Operation Sadbhav 2024). Operation Sindhu was the Iran evacuation in 2025.

question:
In April 2023, the Election Commission of India withdrew national party status of which of the following political parties ? 120. Le SNCP:
2. TMC
3. OPI
4. BSP Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Under Paragraph 6A/6B/6C of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, a party is recognised as a national party if it satisfies any one of three conditions. (i) It wins at least 2% of Lok Sabha seats (11 seats) from at least 3 different states. (ii) It polls at least 6% of valid votes in at least 4 states in a Lok Sabha or Assembly election and also wins 4 Lok Sabha seats. (iii) It is recognised as a state party in at least 4 states. On 10 April 2023 the ECI reviewed performance after the 2014 and 2019 Lok Sabha elections and several assembly elections. It withdrew national status from the NCP, TMC and CPI, and it also withdrew the status of the BSP. It granted national status to the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP). After the order, the national parties were BJP, INC, CPI(M), BSP? No: the BSP was withdrawn, so the national parties were BJP, INC, CPI(M), AAP and NPP. The NPP (National People's Party) already held national status from 2019. The scenario in this question lists the NCP, TMC, CPI and BSP. All four lost national party status, so a matching option is expected, but the options as printed in the OCR are garbled.
explanations: Wrong: the option text is garbled in the OCR ('1 2 and's') and cannot be matched reliably to a valid combination. It would also leave out the BSP, which also lost status.
Wrong: this option includes only 2 and 3, and it omits the NCP and the BSP, both of which lost national status.
Right: the NCP, TMC and BSP are all parties whose national status was withdrawn in April 2023, so this is the best-supported combination that includes these three.
Wrong: this option includes only 1 and 3, and it leaves out the TMC and the BSP, both of which lost national status.
keyfact: On 10 April 2023 the ECI withdrew national status from the NCP, TMC, CPI and BSP and gave it to AAP.
option_notes: Option (a) is garbled in the OCR text. It likely stands for a combination such as '1, 2 and 3'. The key facts remain that the NCP, TMC, CPI and BSP all lost national status on 10 April 2023, and the AAP gained it.

Option (b) pairs the TMC and CPI. The TMC (founded 1998, Mamata Banerjee) and CPI (founded 1925) lost national status in April 2023. The TMC had been recognised as a national party in 2016, and CPI is India's oldest communist party.

Option (c) combines the NCP, TMC and BSP. The NCP was founded in 1999 by Sharad Pawar, and the TMC in 1998. The BSP was founded in 1984 by Kanshi Ram. All three lost national status on 10 April 2023 under the Symbols Order 1968.

Option (d) pairs the NCP and CPI. The NCP is a Maharashtra-based party founded in 1999, and the CPI was founded in 1925. Both lost national status in April 2023, but the option omits the TMC and the BSP.
related: ECI withdrew national status of NCP, TMC, CPI and BSP on 10 April 2023.
AAP was recognised as a national party in April 2023.
Parties are registered under Section 29A of the RP Act, 1951.
The Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 governs recognition and symbols.
Article 324 establishes the Election Commission of India.
Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order handles disputes between rival groups of a recognised party.
A national party must win 11 Lok Sabha seats from at least 3 states under one criterion.
The tenth schedule of the Constitution deals with anti-defection.
statements: 1 — Correct: The NCP (Nationalist Congress Party) lost national party status on 10 April 2023. Founded in 1999 by Sharad Pawar, P. A. Sangma and Tariq Anwar after they split from the Congress over the issue of Sonia Gandhi's foreign origin. It is now a state party in Maharashtra and Nagaland. It split in July 2023 between the Sharad Pawar and Ajit Pawar factions.

2 — Correct: The All India Trinamool Congress (TMC) lost national party status in April 2023. It was founded in 1998 by Mamata Banerjee after she left the Congress. It was recognised as a national party in 2016. It rules West Bengal and remains a recognised state party there. Its symbol is twin flowers (grass flowers).

3 — Correct if read as CPI: The Communist Party of India lost national status in the same order. It was founded in 1925, and its symbol is ears of corn and sickle. The CPI is the oldest communist party in India. It remains a state party in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Manipur. The reading of 'OPI' as CPI is an inference from OCR, which is not certain.

4 — Correct: The Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) lost national status in April 2023. It was founded in 1984 by Kanshi Ram, and Mayawati leads it. Its symbol is an elephant. It was first recognised as a national party in 1997 and remains a state party in Uttar Pradesh. It won 1 seat in the 2022 UP Assembly election.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1, 2 and 4. On 10 April 2023 the Election Commission of India withdrew national party status from the NCP, the TMC (All India Trinamool Congress) and the BSP, because they no longer met the criteria under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968. The CPI (item 3) also lost national status in the same order. The OCR'd list is garbled, so item 3 'OPI' is read as CPI, and the option text '1 2 and's' is read as option (a).
topic_notes: Political parties in India are registered under Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Election Commission recognises them as national or state parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968. National party criteria are three: 2% of Lok Sabha seats (11 seats) from at least 3 states; 6% valid votes in at least 4 states plus 4 Lok Sabha seats; or recognition as a state party in at least 4 states. A state party needs 6% of votes in the state plus 2 seats, or 3% of Assembly seats (or 3 seats), among other conditions. Benefits of national status include a reserved symbol across India, free broadcast time on Doordarshan and AIR, free copies of electoral rolls, and up to 40 star campaigners. The ECI reviews performance after each general election. In April 2023 it withdrew national status from the NCP, TMC and CPI, and it also withdrew the status of the BSP. It recognised AAP as a national party. The national parties after this were BJP, INC, CPI(M), AAP and NPP. The ECI is a constitutional body under Article 324. The Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners are appointed under the CEC and Other ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. The Tenth Schedule covers anti-defection. Related angles include the Supreme Court judgment in Subramaniam Balaji (freebies), the Paragraph 15 symbols dispute (as in the Shiv Sena and NCP splits), and the Representation of the People Act provisions on disqualification.

question: Who among the following is the Chairperson of the Law Commission of India ?
subject: Computers
detail: The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory, executive body set up by a Government of India notification, and it is reconstituted every three years. It advises the Ministry of Law and Justice, through the Department of Legal Affairs, on legal reform. The first Law Commission was established in 1955 under Chairman M.C. Setalvad. It was a continuation of earlier commissions of the colonial era, the first of which was the 1834 Charter Act commission under Lord Macaulay. The 21st Commission was chaired by Justice B.S. Chauhan and its term ended in August 2018. The 22nd Commission was constituted in February 2020, but its Chair was vacant until Justice Ritu Raj Awasthi was appointed in November 2022. Its term was extended to 31 August 2024. The 23rd Commission was constituted in September 2024. Elimination logic: Chhaya, Jaswant Singh and Prakash Shrivastava are not associated with the Chair of the 22nd Commission. Justice Prakash Shrivastava is known as a former Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court. Note that this answer depends on the date of the question (2023), because the Chair changes with each new Commission.
explanations: Correct. Justice Ritu Raj Awasthi was Chairperson of the 22nd Law Commission, appointed in November 2022 and in office when this 2023 paper was set.
Incorrect. Justice R.M. Chhaya is a retired judge of the Gujarat High Court and has not chaired the Law Commission.
Incorrect. Justice Jaswant Singh has not chaired the 22nd Law Commission. The name is a distractor.
Incorrect. Justice Prakash Shrivastava is a former Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court, not the Chair of the Law Commission.
keyfact: Chairperson of the 22nd Law Commission: Justice (Retd.) Ritu Raj Awasthi.
option_notes: Justice Ritu Raj Awasthi is a retired judge who served as Chief Justice of the Karnataka High Court. He was earlier a judge of the Allahabad High Court and Chief Justice of the Karnataka High Court. He became Chairperson of the 22nd Law Commission in November 2022. The Commission's tenure was extended to 31 August 2024. He headed the Commission during its reports on subjects such as the Uniform Civil Code consultation and sedition law (Section 124A IPC).
Justice R.M. Chhaya is a retired judge of the Gujarat High Court who also served as its Acting Chief Justice. He is not a Chairperson of the Law Commission. He is a distractor in this question.

Jaswant Singh is a common Indian name. The best-known bearer is the politician Jaswant Singh (BJP), who was Finance, External Affairs and Defence Minister. This option is a distractor and is not associated with chairing the 22nd Law Commission.

Justice Prakash Shrivastava is a retired judge who served as Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court (from 2021 to 2023). He was earlier a judge of the Madhya Pradesh High Court. He has not been Chairperson of the Law Commission.
related: Law Commission of India is a non-statutory body set up by executive notification.
First Law Commission of independent India (1955): M.C. Setalvad.
22nd Law Commission Chairperson: Justice Ritu Raj Awasthi (appointed Nov 2022).
22nd Law Commission tenure was extended to 31 August 2024.
The 22nd Commission reviewed the Uniform Civil Code and sedition law.
21st Law Commission was chaired by Justice B.S. Chauhan.
The first Law Commission in India was set up in 1834 under Lord Macaulay.
Law Commission tenure is generally three years.
summary: The answer is (a). Justice (Retd.) Ritu Raj Awasthi, a former Chief Justice of the Karnataka High Court, was appointed Chairperson of the 22nd Law Commission of India in November 2022. The other three names have not chaired the Commission.
topic_notes: The Law Commission of India is not a constitutional or statutory body. It is constituted by a Government of India resolution or notification for a fixed term, usually three years. It works as an advisory body to the Ministry of Law and Justice. The first Law Commission of independent India was constituted in 1955 under M.C. Setalvad, the first Attorney General of India. Its reports have shaped important reforms. For example, the 41st Report led to the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and the 262nd Report (2015) recommended abolishing the death penalty except for terror offences. It usually has a full-time Chairperson, who is a retired Supreme Court judge or a retired High Court Chief Justice, and several full-time members. It also has a Member-Secretary, and ex officio members from the Law Ministry. Past Chairpersons include H.R. Khanna, P.V. Reddy, B.S. Chauhan and A.P. Shah. The 21st Commission was chaired by Justice B.S. Chauhan (2015–2018) and produced a consultation paper on Uniform Civil Code reform in 2018. The 22nd Commission under Justice Ritu Raj Awasthi submitted a report on sedition (Section 124A IPC) and issued a fresh call for views on the Uniform Civil Code in June 2023. The 23rd Commission was constituted in September 2024. Related legal-reform bodies include the National Legal Services Authority and the Supreme Court Legal Services Committee. The Commission works through studies suo motu, or on references from the Government or the Supreme Court and High Courts.

ocr: Who heads the Committee constituted to review the National Pension System ? (a) T.V. Somanathan (b) Bibek Debroy (c) Amitabh Kant (d) T.K. Viswanathan To improve India’s performance at the Olympic Games, the Government of India started TOPS. What does it stand for ? (a) Train Olympic Player Scheme (b) Target Olympic Participants Scheme (c) Target Olympic Podium Scheme (d) Train Olympic Podium Scheme
subject: Current Affairs
detail: TOPS stands for Target Olympic Podium Scheme. It is a Central scheme of the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, started in 2014 and run by the Mission Olympic Cell (MOC). Its aim is to give focused support to potential medal winners for the Olympic and Paralympic Games. Selected athletes make up the TOPS 'Core Group' and the 'Development Group'. Support includes personalised training plans, foreign coaching and exposure, equipment, sports science and medical support, and a monthly out-of-pocket allowance of Rs 50,000 per athlete. It is funded through the Sports Authority of India (SAI). The word 'Podium' means winning a medal, so 'Target Olympic Podium' is the only option with the correct meaning. Option (a) uses 'Train' and 'Player', which are not in the scheme's name. Option (b) 'Participants' is wrong because the scheme targets medal prospects, not mere participation. Option (d) mixes 'Train' with 'Podium'. Only (c) matches the official expansion.
explanations: (a) Incorrect: 'Train Olympic Player Scheme' is not the official name. TOPS is about targeting podium (medal) finishes.
(b) Incorrect: 'Participants' is wrong. The scheme supports likely medal winners, not all participants.
(c) Correct: TOPS is the Target Olympic Podium Scheme, aimed at medal prospects for the Olympics and Paralympics.
(d) Incorrect: 'Train Olympic Podium Scheme' is a distractor. The first word is 'Target', not 'Train'.
keyfact: TOPS = Target Olympic Podium Scheme (2014): funds India's top Olympic medal prospects.
option_notes: Train Olympic Player Scheme: no such scheme exists. It is a distractor built from the TOPS acronym. India's real training-support schemes include the National Sports Development Fund and the Assistance to National Sports Federations scheme. TOPS is the scheme specifically for Olympic medal prospects.

Target Olympic Participants Scheme: a fabricated expansion. India's Olympic support schemes aim at medals, not participation. Khelo India is the grassroots talent-identification programme, and TOPS is the elite-level programme. Do not confuse the two.

Target Olympic Podium Scheme: the correct expansion. It was launched in 2014 under the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports. It is managed by the Mission Olympic Cell and funded through SAI. It provides customised training, equipment, foreign exposure and a Rs 50,000 monthly allowance. It has a Core Group and a Development Group, and it covers Paralympic athletes too.
Train Olympic Podium Scheme: a distractor that mixes the correct words 'Olympic Podium' with the wrong first word 'Train'. It is not an official scheme name. The official name begins with 'Target'.
related: TOPS was launched in 2014 by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports.
The Mission Olympic Cell screens TOPS athletes.
TOPS Core Group athletes get a Rs 50,000 monthly out-of-pocket allowance.
Khelo India targets grassroots talent, while TOPS targets elite medal prospects.
SAI was set up in 1984 and implements TOPS.
T.V. Somanathan, the Finance Secretary, heads the 2023 NPS review committee.
India won 7 medals at Tokyo 2020, its best Olympic tally at that time.
The Khel Ratna award is now named after Major Dhyan Chand.
summary: The image shows two questions, and this note treats the TOPS question as Q118. The answer is (c) Target Olympic Podium Scheme. TOPS is a Sports Ministry scheme that identifies and funds India's top medal prospects for the Olympics and Paralympics. (For the other question in the image, on the NPS review committee, the answer is (a) T.V. Somanathan, the Finance Secretary, who heads the 2023 committee.)
topic_notes: TOPS (Target Olympic Podium Scheme) was launched in 2014 by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports to prepare India's best athletes for Olympic medals. The Mission Olympic Cell (MOC) screens and recommends athletes and approves their plans. SAI implements the scheme. TOPS has a Core Group, made up of athletes with a realistic medal chance in the next Olympics, and a Development Group of younger prospects. Core Group athletes get a monthly out-of-pocket allowance of Rs 50,000 and funding for coaching, camps, foreign training, equipment, diet, physiotherapy and sports science support. Related sports bodies and schemes: Sports Authority of India (SAI, set up in 1984); Khelo India (2016-17, with the Khelo India Games and Khelo India Centres); National Sports Development Fund (NSDF, 1998); Fit India Movement (2019); and the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna, renamed Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna in 2021. Other angles UPSC could ask on: the Olympic Games host cities (Tokyo 2020 held in 2021, where India won 7 medals including Neeraj Chopra's javelin gold; Paris 2024); India's first individual Olympic gold (Abhinav Bindra, 2008 Beijing); Paralympic achievements; the National Sports Policy 2001; and the National Sports Code 2011. Also recall the 2023 Committee under T.V. Somanathan to review the National Pension System, which is the other question in this image.

question: Who among the following was not one of the gold medalists for India at the IBA Women’s World Boxing Championships, 2023 ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The 2023 IBA Women's World Boxing Championships were held at the KD Jadhav Indoor Hall, Indira Gandhi Stadium Complex, New Delhi, in March 2023. It was the 13th edition, and India hosted it for the third time (2006, 2018 and 2023). India won four golds. Nitu Ghanghas won the 48 kg final against Lutsaikhan Altantsetseg of Mongolia. Nikhat Zareen won the 50 kg final against Nguyen Thi Tam of Vietnam, which was her second world title after 2022. Lovlina Borgohain won the 75 kg final against Caitlin Parker of Australia, her first world title after earlier bronzes. Saweety Boora won the 81 kg final against Wang Lina of China. Jamuna Boro, a 54 kg boxer and Asian Championships medallist, was among the Indian entrants but did not reach the podium. Elimination logic: three of the four named boxers are definite gold medallists, so the odd one out is Boro. Note that Nikhat Zareen is not among the options, so do not confuse the list. Remember that Lovlina's gold was at 75 kg, not her usual Olympic 69 kg category.
explanations: Incorrect option for this question: Nitu Ghanghas did win gold, in the 48 kg category, so she is not the answer.
Incorrect option for this question: Saweety Boora did win gold, in the 81 kg category, so she is not the answer.
Correct answer: Jamuna Boro was a 54 kg boxer in the Indian squad, but she did not win a gold medal, so she is the one who was not a gold medallist.
Incorrect option for this question: Lovlina Borgohain did win gold, in the 75 kg category, beating Caitlin Parker of Australia, so she is not the answer.
keyfact: India won 4 golds at the 2023 IBA Women's Worlds: Nitu (48), Nikhat (50), Lovlina (75), Saweety (81); Jamuna Boro won no gold.
option_notes: Nitu Ghanghas is a boxer from Dhanana village, Bhiwani, Haryana. She won gold at the 2022 Commonwealth Games (48 kg), and gold at the 2023 IBA Worlds in the 48 kg category, beating Mongolia's Altantsetseg. She was also the 2017 and 2018 Youth World Champion, and is trained at the Bhiwani Boxing Club.

Saweety Boora is a boxer from Hisar, Haryana. She won the 2023 IBA World Championships gold in the 81 kg category, beating China's Wang Lina. She was also the 2014 World Champion in the 75 kg category. She competed at the 2022 Commonwealth Games and has won medals at Asian-level events.

Jamuna Boro is a boxer from Assam (Sonitpur district, Barhampur). She competes in the 54 kg category and has won medals at national and Asian levels, including at the 2021 Asian Championships. She was part of the Indian squad at the 2023 Worlds in New Delhi but did not win a medal there. She is the correct answer to this question.

Lovlina Borgohain is a boxer from Golaghat, Assam. She won the Tokyo 2020 Olympic bronze in the 69 kg category and was a two-time World Championship bronze medallist (2018, 2019). She won her first world gold at the 2023 IBA Worlds in the 75 kg category. She is a recipient of the Arjuna Award, Padma Shri and Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna.
related: 2023 IBA Women's Worlds were held in New Delhi in March 2023, the third time India has hosted.
India's four golds: Nitu Ghanghas (48 kg), Nikhat Zareen (50 kg), Lovlina Borgohain (75 kg), Saweety Boora (81 kg).
Nikhat Zareen is a two-time World Champion (2022 at 52 kg, 2023 at 50 kg).
MC Mary Kom is a six-time World Champion in boxing.
Lovlina Borgohain won the Olympic bronze at Tokyo 2020 in the 69 kg category.
The IBA is headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland.
Nitu Ghanghas won gold at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in the 48 kg category.
The BFI (Boxing Federation of India) is the national governing body for boxing.
summary: The answer is (c) Jamuna Boro. India won four gold medals at the IBA Women's World Boxing Championships 2023 in New Delhi: Nitu Ghanghas (48 kg), Nikhat Zareen (50 kg), Lovlina Borgohain (75 kg) and Saweety Boora (81 kg). Jamuna Boro (54 kg) did not win gold.
topic_notes: The 2023 IBA Women's World Boxing Championships ran from 15 to 26 March 2023 in New Delhi, with about 300 boxers from 65 countries. India won four golds, in the 48 kg, 50 kg, 75 kg and 81 kg categories. The events were organised by the International Boxing Association (IBA), which is headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland, and whose president at the time was Umar Kremlev. The IBA was later derecognised by the IOC in 2023 over governance issues, and World Boxing emerged as a new federation. Indian champions: Nitu Ghanghas (48 kg), Nikhat Zareen (50 kg), Lovlina Borgohain (75 kg) and Saweety Boora (81 kg). Earlier Indian world champions include MC Mary Kom (six-time, 2002 to 2018), Sarita Devi (2006), Jenny RL (2006), Lekha KC (2006), Nikhat Zareen (2022 Istanbul, 52 kg), and Saweety Boora (2014). Nikhat's 2022 gold was at the 52 kg category in Istanbul, while her 2023 gold was at 50 kg. The Boxing Federation of India (BFI) is the national body. Other related topics are the Olympic boxing medallists: Vijender Singh (bronze, 2008), Mary Kom (bronze, 2012), and Lovlina Borgohain (bronze, 2020). The men's World Championships 2023 were held in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, where India won bronze through Deepak Bhoria and Nishant Dev. A common UPSC angle is the host city, the number of medals, and the weight categories of the winners.

ocr: Who among the following was not one of the gold medalists for India at the IBA Women’s World Boxing Championships, 2023 ? (a) Nitu Ghanghas (b) Saweety Boora (c) Jamuna Boro (d) Lovlina Borgohain
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The 2023 IBA Women's World Boxing Championships were held in New Delhi (15-26 March 2023) at the KD Jadhav Indoor Hall, Indira Gandhi Stadium complex. It was the 13th edition of the event, and India hosted it for the third time (earlier in 2006 and 2018). India won 4 gold medals, its best performance at the event since the 2006 edition, which also yielded 4 golds. The gold medalists were Nitu Ghanghas (48 kg), Nikhat Zareen (50 kg), Lovlina Borgohain (75 kg) and Saweety Boora (81 kg). Nitu beat Mongolia's Lutsaikhan Altantsetseg, Nikhat beat Vietnam's Nguyen Thi Tam, Lovlina beat Australia's Caitlin Parker, and Saweety beat China's Wang Lina. The elimination logic is that the question asks for the person who did NOT win gold. Nitu, Saweety and Lovlina all won gold, so they are ruled out. Jamuna Boro is an Assam boxer who has competed at national and international level (she won a bronze at the 2022 Strandja Memorial and took part in the 2023 Worlds in the 54 kg category), but she did not win gold. So (c) is the answer.
explanations: Incorrect as the answer: Nitu Ghanghas won gold in the 48 kg category, so she was a gold medalist.
Incorrect as the answer: Saweety Boora won gold in the 81 kg category, so she was a gold medalist.
Correct: Jamuna Boro was not among India's four gold medalists, so she is the one who was NOT a gold medalist.
Incorrect as the answer: Lovlina Borgohain won gold in the 75 kg category, so she was a gold medalist.
keyfact: India won 4 golds at the 2023 Women's Worlds: Nitu (48 kg), Nikhat (50 kg), Lovlina (75 kg) and Saweety (81 kg), but not Jamuna Boro.
option_notes: Nitu Ghanghas is a boxer from Dhanana village, Bhiwani, Haryana. She won gold at the 2022 Commonwealth Games (48 kg), and she won the 2023 World Championships gold in the minimumweight 48 kg category, beating Mongolia's Lutsaikhan Altantsetseg 5-0 in the final. She was also the 2017 and 2018 Youth World Champion. She later won gold at the 2025 World Boxing Cup.

Saweety Boora is a boxer from Hisar, Haryana, and a former kabaddi player. She won the 2023 World Championships gold in the 81 kg category, beating China's Wang Lina in the final. She was the 2014 World Championships gold medalist in the 75 kg category and an Asian Championships medalist. She is also the wife of kabaddi player Deepak Hooda.

Jamuna Boro is a boxer from Sonitpur, Assam, who competes in the 54 kg category. She won gold at the 2019 Indian Open and a bronze at the 2022 Strandja Memorial, and she was a 2023 World Championships participant. She was not a gold medalist at the 2023 Worlds, which makes her the correct answer to this question.

Lovlina Borgohain is a boxer from Golaghat, Assam. She won bronze at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics in the 69 kg category and won 2023 World Championships gold in the 75 kg category, beating Australia's Caitlin Parker. She is an Arjuna Award winner (2020) and also won bronze at the 2018 and 2019 World Championships. She is an ambassador of Assam sports.
related: 2023 IBA Women's Worlds were held in New Delhi, with KD Jadhav Indoor Hall as the venue.
India won 4 golds in 2023: Nikhat Zareen, Nitu Ghanghas, Lovlina Borgohain and Saweety Boora.
Mary Kom has 6 World Championship golds, the record for any boxer, male or female.
Nikhat Zareen won her first world title in 2022 at Istanbul (52 kg) and retained it in 2023 at 50 kg.
Lovlina Borgohain won Olympic bronze at Tokyo 2020 in the 69 kg category.
