In its modern, positive reading, the proverb describes a free spirit who is not weighed down by routine, but the exam uses the classical meaning. Pair II: 'To have a bee in one's bonnet' means to be preoccupied or obsessed with one idea and keep bringing it up. It is first recorded in the 16th century, from the image of a buzzing insect that gives a person no peace of mind. Both pairs are accurate, so options (a), (b) and (d) fail. Elimination tip: when a pair's meaning agrees with the standard dictionary definition, accept it, and do not reject the pair because of the proverb's alternative modern reading.
explanations: Wrong: it ignores that Pair II is also correct.
Wrong: it ignores that Pair I is also correct.
Correct: both the idiom meanings given are standard dictionary senses.
Wrong: at least one pair, in fact both, are correct.
keyfact: Rolling stone = a person who does not settle and gains no lasting success; bee in the bonnet = obsessive preoccupation with one idea.
option_notes: Pair I only: this would mean the rolling stone meaning is right and the bee idiom is wrong. The rolling stone proverb is of ancient origin and means a wanderer gains no wealth or roots. It is not the answer here because the bee pair is also right.
Pair II only: this would mean only the bee idiom is right. 'Bee in the bonnet' means obsession with one idea, from the 16th century. It is not the answer because the rolling stone pair is also right.

Both I and II: this is the correct answer. Both idioms are matched with accepted meanings: rolling stone is a person who does not settle and gains nothing lasting, and bee in the bonnet is obsessive preoccupation with a subject.
Neither: this would mean both matches are wrong. That is false, since both are standard dictionary meanings, so this option is not the answer.
related: 'A rolling stone gathers no moss' is an ancient proverb about restlessness.
'Bee in one's bonnet' means an obsession with one idea.
'Burn the midnight oil' means to work late into the night.
'Spill the beans' means to reveal a secret.
'Once in a blue moon' means very rarely.
'Bite the bullet' means to face a painful situation with courage.
statements: 1 — Correct: the proverb means a person who does not settle down will not gain success or security. It is an old proverb, traced to Publilius Syrus (Latin) and recorded in Erasmus's Adagia (1500s). The 'moss' stands for wealth, status and stability. Related idioms: 'jack of all trades', 'a stitch in time'. In American usage it can also admire restless freedom, but the exam sense is the classical one.

2 — Correct: 'to have a bee in your bonnet' means to be obsessed with something and talk or think about it excessively. It dates to the 1500s (the Scottish poet Robert Henryson used a similar phrase), and the image is a bee buzzing inside a hat. Related idioms: 'a bone to pick', 'a bug in one's ear', 'hobby-horse'. It is often used for someone with a fixed idea or pet theory.
summary: The answer is (c): both pairs are correctly matched. 'A rolling stone gathers no moss' describes a person who does not settle down and so will not attain success or accumulate anything. 'To have a bee in your bonnet' means to talk and think excessively, even obsessively, about something.
topic_notes: Idioms and proverbs are a regular feature of the EPFO General English section. Questions typically give a phrase and four meanings, or a pair-matching format as here. Key tips: learn the standard dictionary meaning, not the literal sense. Many idioms have a classical meaning and a modern one, so choose the one the examiner would take from the Oxford or Cambridge dictionary. Common idioms to revise: 'a blessing in disguise' (a good thing that seems bad at first), 'break the ice' (start a conversation), 'burn the midnight oil' (work late), 'cry over spilt milk' (regret the past), 'hit the nail on the head' (be exactly right), 'once in a blue moon' (rarely), 'a piece of cake' (very easy), 'spill the beans' (reveal a secret), 'the ball is in your court' (it is your turn to act), 'bite the bullet' (face something unpleasant bravely). Related areas that UPSC often combines with idioms are one-word substitutions, synonyms and antonyms, spot-the-error, fill in the blanks, and reading comprehension. Practise grouping idioms by theme (money, time, animals, body parts, colours) to retain them. Also remember the origin of well-known phrases, since some questions ask for the source or the literal image behind them.

question: Fill in the blanks with appropriate prepositions given below : We cut __ the fence and snuck the secret private basement
subject: General English
detail: This question tests prepositions of direction and movement. 'Cut through' is a phrasal expression meaning to make a path through a barrier such as a fence, wall or crowd. 'Through' signals movement from one side to the other of a barrier. 'Into' signals movement from outside to the inside of an enclosed space such as a room, building or basement, so 'snuck into the basement' is correct. 'Sneak' is usually followed by 'into', 'out of', 'past' or 'away'. Elimination: (a) 'cut into the fence' means to slice partway into it without passing through, which does not fit the idea of getting past it. Also, 'snuck through the basement' is odd because the sentence implies entering, not passing across. (b) 'cut in the fence' is unidiomatic, since 'cut in' means to interrupt or push in line. (c) 'snuck by the basement' means passing near it, not entering it. Only (d) gives a logical sequence: break through the barrier, then enter the space. Remember that 'in' denotes static position, 'into' denotes movement towards the inside, and 'through' denotes passage from one side to the other.
explanations: Incorrect: 'cut into the fence' suggests cutting partway into it rather than passing through, and 'snuck through the basement' does not convey entry.
Incorrect: 'cut in the fence' is unidiomatic here, because 'cut in' means to interrupt or push in. 'Snuck into' is fine, but the first blank fails.
Incorrect: 'snuck by the basement' means passing near it, not entering it, and 'cut into' is also weak for the fence.
Correct: 'cut through the fence' means making a passage across the barrier, and 'snuck into the secret private basement' shows entry into an enclosed space.
keyfact: Cut THROUGH a barrier, sneak INTO an enclosed place: 'through' = passage across, 'into' = entry inside.
option_notes: into, through: 'into' shows movement to the inside of something, e.g. 'He walked into the room'. 'Through' shows passage from one side to the other, e.g. 'The train went through the tunnel'. Here the order is reversed, so the sentence reads wrongly: 'cut into' means to make an incision partway and 'snuck through' implies passing across.

in, into: 'in' shows position or state inside something (static), e.g. 'She is in the house'. 'Into' shows movement towards the inside. 'Cut in' is a phrasal verb meaning to interrupt or push ahead in a queue or traffic, so it does not suit a fence.

into, by: 'by' can mean near or beside, or the agent or means, e.g. 'a house by the river' or 'written by him'. As a direction word, 'snuck by' means passing someone or something unnoticed, not entering. So it does not fit the basement.

through, into: 'through' means from one end or side to the other, as in 'cut through a wall'. 'Into' means entering an enclosed space. 'Cut through the fence and snuck into the basement' is the natural pairing, so this is the correct answer.
related: 'In' shows position; 'into' shows movement to the inside.
'Through' means passage from one side of a barrier or space to the other.
'Cut in' means to interrupt; 'cut through' means to pass through by cutting.
'Snuck' is the informal past tense of 'sneak'; 'sneaked' is the standard form.
Use 'between' for two items and 'among' for more than two.
'Since' marks a starting point; 'for' marks a duration.
'Prefer' takes 'to', not 'than': 'prefer tea to coffee'.
summary: The answer is (d) through, into. The sentence reads 'We cut through the fence and snuck into the secret private basement': 'cut through' means to pass through something by cutting, and 'snuck into' shows entry into an enclosed place.
topic_notes:
Prepositions are words that show the relationship of a noun or pronoun to another word, usually of place, direction, time or manner. In UPSC EPFO English, fill-in-the-blank questions on prepositions are common, so learn the main groups.

Place and position: in (inside, static), on (surface), at (specific point), under, over, above, below, between (two), among (many).

Direction and movement: to, towards, into (entering), onto, through (passing across a barrier or space), across (from one side to the other of a surface), along, past, out of.

Time: at (clock time), on (days and dates), in (months, years, seasons), since (starting point), for (duration), by (deadline), till or until.

Common distinctions: in vs into; between vs among; beside vs besides; since vs for; by vs with (agent vs instrument); on time vs in time.

Common phrasal verbs with cut: cut through (pass through or ignore obstacles), cut in (interrupt), cut off (disconnect), cut down (reduce or fell), cut out (remove or stop), cut back (reduce).

With sneak: sneak into, sneak out of, sneak up on, sneak past. Note that 'snuck' is an informal American past tense of 'sneak', and 'sneaked' is the standard form.

Exam strategy: read the full sentence, identify whether the meaning is static or motion, and test each option for idiomatic fit. Also check dependent prepositions such as 'good at', 'afraid of', 'interested in', 'prefer to', 'married to' and 'angry with'.

ocr: Consider the following sentence with a blank to be filled in : “Sound education is to pupils in this institution.” (a) conceded (b) dispensed (c) furnished (d) imparted Fill in the blank with the correct idiom : He has by establishing the first private university in India. (a) created a genre (b) initiated a yardstick (c) made history (d) designed a milestone
subject: General English
detail: This is a vocabulary-in-context and collocation question. The blank follows 'Sound education is ___' and is followed by 'to pupils', so we need a passive past participle that means 'given or transferred' knowledge. 'Impart' (from Latin impartire, to share) is used for abstract things such as knowledge, education, skills, wisdom, information and training; the standard pattern is 'impart X to Y'. 'Education imparted to students' is a stock phrase. Elimination: 'conceded' means admitted or granted something reluctantly (a point, a defeat, a right), and it does not suit education. 'Dispensed' means distributed or administered (medicine, justice, charity) and is used with 'dispense with' (do without), so it is a weaker, unidiomatic fit. 'Furnished' means supplied or equipped, and it takes 'with' (furnished with facts) or an object such as a room, so 'furnished to pupils' is awkward. Tip for the exam: check the preposition that follows the blank. 'Impart ... to' fits perfectly, while 'furnish ... with' and 'concede ... to' point to different structures.
explanations: Wrong: 'conceded' means admitted or yielded (a point, a goal, a defeat); education is not conceded to pupils.
Wrong: 'dispensed' means distributed or administered (medicines, justice); it is not the natural verb for education and sounds mechanical here.
Wrong: 'furnished' means supplied or equipped, usually used as 'furnished with'; 'furnished to pupils' is not idiomatic for education.
Correct: 'imparted' means communicated or passed on knowledge, and 'education is imparted to pupils' is the standard collocation.
keyfact: Education, knowledge and skills are 'imparted to' people; furnish goes with 'with', and dispense and concede have different meanings.
option_notes: Concede (verb): to admit that something is true or valid after first denying it, to yield a right or territory, or to give up a point or a match. Noun: concession. Example: 'He conceded defeat.' Common in debates, sports and negotiations, and followed by 'to' when someone receives the concession. It is rarely used with knowledge or education.

Dispense (verb): to distribute or supply in portions (a pharmacist dispenses medicine), to administer (dispense justice), and 'dispense with' means to do without. Noun: dispensary, dispensation. It suggests handing out measured items. It can be used with advice or justice but is not the usual verb for education.

Furnish (verb): to supply or provide something needed, or to equip a room with furniture. Pattern: furnish someone with something (furnish with details), or furnish information/evidence. Noun: furniture, furnishings. Used for facts, proof and equipment, but 'furnish education to pupils' is not natural.

Impart (verb): to make known or pass on information, knowledge or skills, or to give a quality (impart flavour, impart a sense of urgency). Pattern: impart something to someone. Related words: imparted, impartation. Typical phrases: impart knowledge, impart training, impart education. It is the best fit for teaching contexts.
related: Impart = to communicate or pass on knowledge; noun: impartation.
Impart takes 'to': impart knowledge to students.
Dispense with = to do without something.
Furnish takes 'with': furnish someone with information.
Concede = to admit or yield, e.g. concede defeat.
Idiom 'make history' = to do something so important that it will be remembered.
Confer a degree; bestow an honour; inculcate values; instil discipline.
summary: The answer is (d) 'imparted'. 'Impart' means to pass on or communicate knowledge, and it is the verb that collocates with education: 'education is imparted to pupils'. The other options either fail to fit the meaning or do not take 'to pupils' naturally.
topic_notes: This question tests contextual vocabulary and verb-noun collocation, a staple of the EPFO General English section. The key skill is to identify the part of speech needed, then check meaning, collocation and the following preposition. Useful collocations: impart knowledge/education/skills/wisdom to someone; acquire or gain knowledge; dispense justice/medicine/advice; furnish information/evidence/proof; concede a point/defeat/goal; render assistance; bestow an honour/award; confer a degree; inculcate values or habits; instil confidence or discipline; disseminate information or ideas; foster talent. Confusable verbs: impart vs import; confer vs concur; dispense vs disperse (scatter); furnish vs finish; concede vs conceive. Related prepositions: impart to; furnish with or to; concede to; dispense with (do without). Strategy: read the sentence with each option, drop options with the wrong preposition pattern, and prefer the word that forms a stock phrase. For idiom questions in the same paper, such as 'made history' (to do something historic and memorable), learn common idioms like break new ground, set a benchmark, mark a milestone, blaze a trail, and make a mark. Also revise the difference between idioms and ordinary phrases: an idiom has a figurative meaning that cannot be guessed from its words. Practise with synonyms of teach (instruct, educate, tutor, enlighten, impart) and associated nouns such as pedagogy, curriculum, and tuition.

question: A person who is born into a rich, famous or important family is called :
subject: Indian Economy
detail: Scion (pronounced 'SY-un') originally meant a shoot or twig cut from a plant for grafting. By extension it came to mean a young member or descendant of a family, usually a wealthy, aristocratic or prominent one. Examples: 'a scion of the Tata family', 'the scion of a business dynasty'. The other options describe different kinds of people. A factotum is a person who does all kinds of work for an employer, a general servant or handyman. A warmonger is someone who advocates or tries to stir up war. A recusant is a person who refuses to submit to authority or comply with a rule; historically it meant a Catholic who refused to attend Church of England services. The elimination logic is to match the meaning of each word to the definition. Only 'scion' relates to birth into a distinguished family. Such one-word-substitution questions are common in EPFO English papers, so learn the meaning, origin and usage of each word.
explanations: Incorrect: a factotum is an employee or assistant who does many different jobs, with no link to family background.
Correct: a scion is a descendant of a rich, noble or famous family.
Incorrect: a warmonger is someone who promotes or incites war, not a person of high birth.
Incorrect: a recusant is someone who refuses to obey or comply with authority, not a person of high birth.
keyfact: Scion = descendant of a rich, noble or famous family; factotum = does all kinds of work; warmonger = promotes war; recusant = refuses to obey authority.
option_notes: Factotum: a person employed to do all kinds of work, from the Latin 'fac totum' meaning 'do everything'. Example: 'He acted as the manager's factotum'. Related terms are jack-of-all-trades and general handyman. It is a noun with no negative meaning by itself, and it is often used for a trusted assistant in an office or household.

Scion: a descendant of a notable family, especially a wealthy or aristocratic one. It originally meant a shoot cut for grafting, and the spelling 'cion' is also used in horticulture. Example: 'the scion of a banking dynasty'. Related words are heir, offspring, progeny and blue blood.

Warmonger: a person who encourages or advocates aggression or war against other countries. Example: 'The president was criticised as a warmonger'. It is a derogatory noun. Related words are hawk and jingoist, and the opposite is a pacifist or dove.

Recusant: a person who refuses to submit to authority or to comply with a regulation. In English history it meant a person, usually a Roman Catholic, who refused to attend Anglican services, and the Recusancy Acts penalised them from the 16th century. It can also be used as an adjective. Related words are dissenter, nonconformist and rebel.
related: Scion means a descendant of a noble or wealthy family.
Factotum is a person who does all kinds of work for an employer.
Warmonger is someone who stirs up or favours war.
Recusant is a person who refuses to obey authority or rules.
Parvenu is a person who has recently become rich but lacks social acceptance.
Philanthropist is a person who loves mankind and does charity.
Sycophant is a person who flatters to gain advantage.
Iconoclast is one who attacks cherished beliefs or traditions.
summary: The answer is (b) Scion. A scion is a descendant of a rich, famous, noble or influential family, and the word is typically used in phrases like 'scion of a royal house'.
topic_notes: This question is a One Word Substitution item, a regular part of the General English section in EPFO exams. The task is to pick the single word that replaces a descriptive phrase. Learn words in groups by theme. For people of family and status: scion (descendant of a distinguished family), patrician (aristocrat), parvenu (newly rich person with no social standing), heir (inheritor), progeny (offspring), and pedigree (ancestry). For work and behaviour: factotum (does everything), sycophant (flatterer), dilettante (amateur dabbler), philanthropist (lover of mankind), misanthrope (hater of mankind), and philistine (uncultured person). For authority and conflict: recusant (refuses to obey), warmonger (promotes war), pacifist (opposes war), iconoclast (attacks cherished beliefs), and renegade (deserter of a cause). Method: look at the Latin or Greek roots, remember a sample sentence, and note the commonly confused words. UPSC often uses the wrong options of one year as the correct answers of another, so know the meanings of all four words. Other angles to practise are synonyms and antonyms, idioms and phrases, and spelling correction. Also practise words about death (obituary, posthumous), speaking (orator, garrulous), and medicine or science (hypochondriac, ambidextrous).

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q33.
ocr: A person who is born into a rich, famous or important family is called : (a) Factotum (b) Scion (c) |Warmonger (d) Recusant
subject: Indian Economy
detail: The question asks for the word meaning a person born into a rich, famous or important family. 'Scion' fits exactly. It comes from Old French 'cion', meaning a shoot or twig, and originally meant a cutting from a plant used for grafting. The figurative sense is a young descendant or heir of a distinguished family, as in 'a scion of the Tata family' or 'scion of a royal house'. Elimination: 'Factotum' is an employee who does all kinds of work, a jack-of-all-trades, so it describes a servant or assistant and not someone of high birth. 'Warmonger' is a person who encourages or advocates war or aggression. 'Recusant' is a person who refuses to submit to authority or comply with a regulation, historically a Catholic in England who refused to attend Church of England services. Only 'scion' relates to family lineage and status. In one-word-substitution questions, always match the exact definition and avoid options that are only loosely associated with people.
explanations: (a) Incorrect: a factotum is a person employed to do all kinds of work, such as a general servant or assistant. It says nothing about birth or family status.
(b) Correct: a scion is a descendant or heir of a wealthy, noble or famous family, which matches the definition given.
(c) Incorrect: a warmonger is someone who advocates or stirs up war. It has no connection with family background.
(d) Incorrect: a recusant is someone who refuses to obey authority or comply with rules. It is not about birth or lineage.
keyfact: Scion = descendant or heir of a rich, noble or famous family.
option_notes: Factotum (Latin 'fac totum', do everything): an employee or servant who handles all kinds of work, e.g. 'the office factotum'. It is a noun, often used in a slightly humorous or formal way. Related words are 'handyman' and 'jack-of-all-trades'. It is frequently tested in one-word substitution.

Scion: a descendant of a notable family, an heir. It comes from Old French 'cion', meaning a shoot or twig, and also means a cutting taken from a plant for grafting. Example: 'a scion of the Nehru-Gandhi family'. Synonyms are heir, offspring and descendant. It is pronounced 'SY-un'. Often confused with 'scone' or 'sion' spelling errors.

Warmonger: a person who encourages or advocates war or aggression against other countries. It is a derogatory term. 'Monger' means a dealer or trader, as in fishmonger, scaremonger and rumour-monger. Opposite ideas are pacifist and dove, while the related term 'hawk' denotes a person favouring aggressive policy.

Recusant: a person who refuses to submit to authority or comply with a rule. Historically it meant an English Catholic who refused to attend Church of England services in the 16th-18th centuries, as penalised under the Recusancy Acts. It comes from Latin 'recusare', to refuse. The related noun is 'recusal', meaning a judge stepping aside from a case.
related: Parvenu means a newly rich person who is not yet accepted by high society.
Patrician means a person of high birth or aristocratic class; plebeian means a commoner.
Primogeniture is the right of the firstborn to inherit.
Nepotism is favouritism shown to relatives in appointments.
Recusant originally meant an English Catholic who refused to attend Anglican services.
Sycophant means a flatterer who seeks favour.
Philistine means a person hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts.
summary: The answer is (b) Scion. A scion is a descendant of a rich, noble, famous or important family. Factotum, warmonger and recusant describe a general servant, a war-promoter and a refuser of authority respectively.
topic_notes: This question belongs to one-word substitution and vocabulary, a regular feature of the General English section in EPFO exams. The usual pattern is a definition followed by four similar-looking words, so learn the exact meanings along with their roots. Important words about people and birth or status: Scion (descendant of a distinguished family); Patrician (aristocrat); Plebeian (commoner); Parvenu (newly rich person who lacks social acceptance); Upstart (one who rose quickly and is arrogant); Nepotist (one who favours relatives); Progeny (offspring); Heir (inheritor of property); Primogeniture (right of the eldest son to inherit). Other commonly tested people-words: Philanthropist (lover of mankind, a donor), Misanthrope (hater of mankind), Philistine (one indifferent to culture), Egoist, Altruist, Cynic, Stoic, Pedant (overly concerned with minor details), Sycophant (flatterer), Maverick (independent-minded person), Novice, Veteran, Pundit, Polyglot (knows many languages), Bibliophile (book lover), Agnostic, Atheist, Pacifist, Iconoclast (attacker of cherished beliefs), Dilettante (dabbler in an art). Strategy: break words into roots (phil-, mis-, anthropos), recall example sentences, and eliminate options whose meaning is clearly unrelated to the definition. Revise 15-20 such words daily.

question: If your boss continually praises you for 37, meticulous attention to detail and polite conduct, which of the following most appropriately describes you ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Punctilious (adjective) means showing great attention to detail or correct behaviour; it comes from Italian 'puntiglio' (a fine point) via French 'pointilleux' and Spanish 'puntillo'. It combines two ideas in the question: carefulness about details and observance of proper, courteous conduct. Elimination: 'Peremptory' means insisting on immediate obedience in a commanding, brooking-no-refusal way, so it is the opposite of polite. 'Perfunctory' means done with minimal effort or reflection, a routine, careless act, which is the opposite of meticulous. 'Proficient' means skilled or competent, which can describe ability but says nothing about attention to detail or politeness. The question has an OCR artefact ('37') which is silently ignored, as the blank is likely a word such as 'your'. In vocabulary questions, match every clue in the sentence to the word's core meaning, and watch for look-alike words beginning with 'P' that are designed to distract. Synonyms of punctilious: scrupulous, meticulous, conscientious, exacting, careful. Antonyms: careless, negligent, slapdash, sloppy.
explanations: Wrong: Peremptory means bossy, dictatorial or admitting no refusal; it conflicts with polite conduct and does not imply attention to detail.
Wrong: Perfunctory means done routinely with little care or interest; it is the opposite of meticulous attention to detail, so a boss would not praise it.
Correct: Punctilious means showing great attention to detail and correct, proper behaviour, which fits both meticulous detail and polite conduct.
Wrong: Proficient means competent or skilled; it is a general praise word and does not capture meticulousness or courtesy specifically.
keyfact: Punctilious = scrupulously careful about detail and correct, polite conduct.
option_notes: Peremptory: adjective meaning insisting on immediate attention or obedience, often in a high-handed or imperious way. Example: a peremptory tone or order. In law, a peremptory challenge allows dismissal of a juror without giving a reason, and a peremptory writ is an unconditional order. From Latin 'peremptorius', meaning destructive or decisive. Synonyms: imperious, dictatorial, authoritative, domineering, brusque. It carries a negative tone of bossiness and is the opposite of polite, courteous behaviour.

Perfunctory: adjective meaning carried out with minimal effort or reflection, merely as a duty or routine. Example: a perfunctory greeting or a perfunctory inspection. From Latin 'perfunctorius', meaning done just to get through with it. Synonyms: cursory, casual, token, half-hearted, superficial, mechanical. Antonyms: thorough, careful, painstaking, meticulous. Often confused with 'peremptory' because the two look and sound similar, which makes them common pairs in vocabulary questions.

Punctilious: adjective meaning showing great attention to detail or correct behaviour, being very careful about proper conduct, etiquette and accuracy. Derived from Italian 'puntiglio' (small point), through French and Spanish. Synonyms: meticulous, scrupulous, conscientious, exacting, fastidious, precise. Antonyms: careless, negligent, sloppy, slapdash, lax. Example: a punctilious clerk who follows every rule and observes every courtesy. The noun is punctiliousness; the related noun 'punctilio' means a fine point of conduct or procedure.

Proficient: adjective meaning competent or skilled in doing or using something, having advanced expertise. Example: proficient in English or proficient with accounting software. From Latin 'proficere', meaning to make progress. Synonyms: skilled, adept, accomplished, expert, capable, able. Antonyms: incompetent, unskilled, inept, clumsy. The noun is proficiency. It describes ability level, not careful attention to detail or polite behaviour, so it is a weaker fit here.
related: Punctilious = meticulous about detail and proper conduct; antonym: careless, slapdash.
Perfunctory = done routinely with little effort; synonym: cursory.
Peremptory = imperious, commanding; peremptory challenge in law.
Punctual means on time; do not confuse it with punctilious.
Pedantic = overly concerned with minor details or displaying learning.
Fastidious = very attentive to accuracy and detail, hard to please.
Proficient = competent or skilled; noun proficiency.
summary: The answer is (c) Punctilious. The word describes someone who is meticulous about details and correct, polite conduct, which matches 'meticulous attention to detail and polite conduct'. The other options mean domineering, careless, and skilled respectively.
topic_notes: This question tests vocabulary, specifically confusable adjectives beginning with 'P' that describe a person's manner or work style. In the EPFO General English section, vocabulary appears as one-word substitutions, synonyms, antonyms, idioms and phrases, and sentence completion with contextual word choice. The best strategy is to break the sentence into clues (here 'meticulous attention to detail' and 'polite conduct') and match them to the core meaning of each option. Key words in this family: Punctilious (careful about detail and etiquette), Perfunctory (done with minimal effort), Peremptory (commanding, not allowing refusal), Proficient (skilled), Pedantic (overly concerned with minor details or showing off learning), Fastidious (hard to please, very attentive to accuracy and cleanliness), Meticulous (showing great care and precision), Scrupulous (diligent and honest, conscientious about right and wrong), Perspicacious (having keen insight), Pragmatic (practical), Prudent (careful about the future), Punctual (on time). Frequent traps: peremptory versus perfunctory, punctilious versus punctual, and pedantic versus punctilious. Tips: learn roots, since 'punct-' relates to points; use a positive or negative tone to eliminate options quickly; and make short flashcards with synonyms and antonyms. Practice contextual usage rather than memorising bare definitions, because UPSC EPFO questions typically supply a sentence that contains the clue.

question: What is the synonym of the underlined word in the following sentence ? The languid student was always late to the class
subject: General English
detail: Languid (adjective) comes from Latin 'languere' (to be faint or weak). It describes a person or manner that is slow, weak, relaxed and lacking vigour or enthusiasm, for example 'a languid wave of the hand' or 'languid afternoon'. Its usual synonyms are listless, lethargic, sluggish, torpid, apathetic, lackadaisical and spiritless. Its antonyms are energetic, vigorous, lively, spirited and animated. In the sentence, a student who is always late suggests lethargy and a lack of urgency or interest. Option (b) 'indifferent' captures the apathetic, uninterested side of languidness, so it is the nearest fit. Elimination: 'Lamenting' means expressing grief, which has no link to low energy. 'Difficult' describes a task or a person's behaviour, not a lack of energy. 'Engaged' means occupied or involved, which is roughly the opposite of a listless student. Though 'lethargic' would be the ideal synonym, it is not offered, so choose the closest, 'indifferent'. In vocabulary questions, always pick the nearest meaning when no exact match exists.
explanations: Incorrect: 'Lamenting' means mourning or expressing sorrow; it does not relate to sluggishness or lack of energy.
Correct: 'Indifferent' means apathetic and unconcerned, which matches the listless, unenthusiastic sense of 'languid' and the habit of coming late.
Incorrect: 'Difficult' means hard to handle or do; it does not mean low in energy or enthusiasm.
Incorrect: 'Engaged' means occupied, involved or committed, which is nearly an antonym of 'languid'.
keyfact: Languid = lacking energy or enthusiasm (listless, lethargic); nearest option here is 'Indifferent'.
option_notes: Lamenting: the present participle of 'lament', meaning to express grief or regret passionately. Lament is also a noun meaning a song or poem of mourning, as in an elegy. Related words are mourning, wailing, grieving and bewailing. Antonyms are rejoicing and celebrating. It is often confused with 'lamentable', meaning deplorable or regrettable.

Indifferent: an adjective meaning having no particular interest or sympathy, unconcerned, or of average or mediocre quality. It comes from Latin 'indifferens', meaning making no difference. Synonyms: apathetic, unconcerned, detached, aloof, nonchalant, uninterested. Antonyms: concerned, interested, keen, enthusiastic, caring. 'Indifference' is the noun form.

Difficult: an adjective meaning needing much effort or skill, or hard to deal with or satisfy, as in 'a difficult child'. Synonyms: hard, tough, arduous, demanding, challenging, troublesome. Antonyms: easy, simple, effortless, straightforward. It is a back-formation from 'difficulty', from Latin 'difficultas'.

Engaged: an adjective meaning occupied or busy, committed to be married, or involved in an activity, as in 'engaged in research'. Synonyms: occupied, busy, absorbed, involved, betrothed. Antonyms: free, idle, disengaged, uninvolved. The verb 'engage' also means to hire, attract or take part in. Engaged is also used for a telephone line that is busy.
related: Languid: lacking energy; synonyms lethargic, listless, sluggish.
Antonyms of languid: energetic, vigorous, lively, animated.
Languish: to lose vitality or to suffer neglect.
Lackadaisical: lacking enthusiasm and determination.
Laconic: using very few words.
Apathetic is a close synonym of indifferent.
Torpid: dormant, sluggish, inactive.
summary: The answer is (b) Indifferent. 'Languid' means lacking energy, enthusiasm or interest, slow and listless, and among the options 'indifferent' (unconcerned, apathetic) comes closest to the sense of a student who is habitually late.
topic_notes: Vocabulary questions on synonyms and antonyms are a regular feature of the EPFO General English section. The best approach is to understand the word's core meaning, then use the sentence context to confirm it. 'Languid' belongs to a family of words describing low energy or slowness: lethargic, listless, sluggish, torpid, lackadaisical, indolent, phlegmatic and apathetic. Its opposite family includes spirited, vivacious, animated, dynamic and vigorous. Often the exact synonym is absent and the nearest option must be chosen. Useful tips: (1) learn words in clusters of synonyms and antonyms; (2) note roots such as Latin 'languere' (to be faint), whose relatives include 'languish' and 'languor'; (3) beware of look-alike words like 'languid' and 'languish' (to lose vitality, to suffer neglect); (4) practise with words often asked in competitive exams such as 'lethargic', 'lucid', 'laconic', 'lavish', 'languorous' and 'lackadaisical'. Other angles UPSC may take: one-word substitution, idioms and phrases, spotting errors, fill in the blanks, sentence improvement and reading comprehension. In reading comprehension, tone-based words such as languid, pensive, jovial and sardonic frequently appear in options. For preparation, read an English newspaper editorial daily, maintain a vocabulary notebook, and revise it weekly with context sentences.

question: What is the antonym of the underlined word in the following sentence ? There is a paucity of information on the nutritive value of this item
options: Inadequacy Fill in the blank in the following sentence using one of the words that follow :
subject: General English
detail: Paucity (noun, from Latin paucitas, 'fewness') means the presence of something in only small or insufficient quantities; a lack or shortage. In the sentence, 'a paucity of information' means very little information is available. To answer antonym questions, first find the meaning of the underlined word, then pick the option with the opposite sense, while eliminating any option that is a synonym. Scarcity, deficiency and inadequacy all convey shortage or insufficiency, so they are synonyms and cannot be the answer. Abundance means a very large quantity or plentifulness, which is the direct opposite. Other antonyms of paucity include plenty, profusion, surfeit, glut, wealth and copiousness. Synonyms include dearth, shortage, scarcity, lack, deficit, sparseness and insufficiency. Exam tip: when three options are close in meaning and one is the odd one out, the odd one out is usually the antonym. Note that the sentence also contains a stray instruction about a fill-in-the-blank, which is an OCR artefact and does not affect this question.
explanations: Correct: abundance means plentiful supply, the exact opposite of paucity (a small quantity).
Incorrect: scarcity means a shortage or lack, a synonym of paucity, not an antonym.
Incorrect: deficiency means a lack or shortfall of something required, so it is similar in meaning to paucity.
Incorrect: inadequacy means the state of not being enough, which is close in sense to paucity and so is not its opposite.
keyfact: Paucity = scarcity or smallness of quantity; antonym = abundance (plenty).
option_notes: Abundance (noun): a very large quantity of something; plentifulness; also an overflowing supply or wealth. Related words: abundant, abound. Synonyms: plenty, profusion, copiousness, affluence. Antonyms: scarcity, paucity, dearth, lack. Commonly used in phrases such as 'in abundance'. It is the correct antonym of paucity here, and it is frequently tested in vocabulary sections alongside words like surfeit and glut.

Scarcity (noun): a situation in which a resource or thing is in short supply or insufficient for demand. Also used in economics, where scarcity is the basic problem of limited resources against unlimited wants. Synonyms: shortage, dearth, paucity, lack, famine. Antonyms: abundance, plenty, sufficiency. Here it is a synonym of paucity, so it is wrong as an antonym.

Deficiency (noun): a lack or shortage of something essential, for example vitamin deficiency or iron deficiency anaemia. Also means a shortcoming or flaw. Synonyms: shortage, insufficiency, deficit, lack, shortfall. Antonyms: sufficiency, adequacy, excess, surplus. It is close in meaning to paucity, so it is not the antonym.

Inadequacy (noun): the state of being insufficient in quantity or quality, or not good enough for a purpose; it can also mean a personal feeling of incompetence. Synonyms: insufficiency, shortfall, deficiency, inability. Antonyms: adequacy, sufficiency, competence. Because it expresses shortage, it is similar to paucity and so is not the opposite.
related: Paucity = scarcity, dearth, shortage; antonym = abundance, plenty.
Plethora means an excess; dearth means a lack.
Surfeit and glut are antonyms of paucity in the sense of excess supply.
Meagre, sparse and scanty are adjectives close to paucity.
Prolific and copious are adjectives opposite in sense to sparse.
Paucity comes from Latin paucitas, from paucus meaning few.
In antonym questions, eliminate the synonyms first.
summary: The answer is (a) Abundance. 'Paucity' means smallness of quantity or scarcity, so its antonym is 'abundance' (plenty). The other three options are synonyms of paucity, not antonyms.
topic_notes: Antonym questions in the EPFO English section test vocabulary and precision. The standard method is to decode the meaning of the target word, often using its root or context, then eliminate synonyms and choose the opposite. Paucity comes from Latin paucus ('few'), which also gives the English word 'paucal' and the related 'pauciloquent' (using few words). Common synonyms: dearth, scarcity, shortage, sparseness, lack, deficit, meagreness, insufficiency. Common antonyms: abundance, plenty, profusion, plethora, surfeit, glut, copiousness, bounty, affluence, superfluity. Related word pairs often tested: scarcity vs. surplus; meagre vs. ample; sparse vs. dense; plethora (excess) vs. dearth (lack); frugal vs. lavish; paltry vs. substantial; negligible vs. considerable. Strategy points: (1) When three options are near-synonyms, the odd one is typically the answer for an antonym question. (2) Watch for 'synonym' versus 'antonym' wording in the stem. (3) Learn words in clusters of synonyms and antonyms rather than singly. (4) Note the collocations: 'paucity of' + noun (paucity of funds, paucity of evidence), 'abundance of' + noun, 'a plethora of', 'a dearth of'. Other typical English topics in the paper include one-word substitution, idioms and phrases, spelling errors, sentence improvement, active and passive voice, direct and indirect speech, cloze passages, and reading comprehension. Revise high-frequency vocabulary lists such as those from The Hindu editorials, and practise using words in sentences to retain nuance.

question: The policeman was running very fast the thief
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a preposition-based fill-in-the-blank. The sentence describes a chase, so the blank must show the position or direction of the policeman relative to the thief. 'Behind' means at the back of, which is the natural way to say someone follows a fleeing person. The related idiom 'run after' also expresses pursuit. Elimination: 'unto' is an archaic form of 'to' or 'until', found in biblical or poetic English, and is not used in modern running contexts. 'For' needs an object of purpose, as in 'running for the bus', and 'running for the thief' would suggest the policeman was acting on the thief's behalf or running to obtain him. 'Into' shows movement to the inside of something, as in 'ran into the room', or a collision, and 'ran into the thief' means met him by chance. Remember that prepositions of position (behind, before, beside, between, among) are tested often in EPFO papers. Pay attention to the verb-preposition collocation and the meaning of the whole sentence.
explanations: Correct: 'behind' shows the policeman was chasing the thief from the rear, which gives a logical, idiomatic sentence.
Incorrect: 'for' would make the thief the purpose of the run or imply running on his behalf. It does not mean chasing.
Incorrect: 'unto' is archaic, and a chase is not described with it. It does not fit the context.
Incorrect: 'into' implies entering something, or 'run into' meaning to meet by chance. It does not express pursuit.
keyfact: To chase someone from the rear, use 'behind' (or 'run after'); 'unto' is archaic, 'for' shows purpose and 'into' shows entry.
option_notes: 'Unto' is an archaic preposition meaning 'to' or 'until'. It appears in the Bible and in old literature (e.g. 'Do unto others as you would have them do unto you'). It is rarely used in modern standard English, and exam questions treat it as a distractor.

'Behind' is a preposition and adverb meaning at or to the back of someone or something. It is also used for support ('behind the plan') and for lagging ('behind schedule'). It is opposite to 'in front of' or 'ahead of'. It fits chase and pursuit contexts.

'For' is a very common preposition showing purpose, recipient, duration or exchange, e.g. 'for two hours', 'a gift for her'. With run, 'run for' means to stand in an election ('run for office') or to run to get something. It does not by itself show chase.

'Into' is a preposition of movement toward the inside of something ('jumped into the pool'), or of change of state ('turned into'). 'Run into' is a phrasal verb meaning meet unexpectedly or collide with. It is not used for chasing.
related: 'Run after' means to chase; 'run into' means to meet by chance.
Use 'between' for two items and 'among' for more than two.
Use 'since' with a point in time and 'for' with a duration.
'Beside' means next to; 'besides' means in addition to.
'Discuss' takes no preposition: say 'discuss the matter', not 'discuss about the matter'.
Say 'angry with' a person and 'angry at' a thing or situation.
summary: The answer is (b) behind. The sentence 'The policeman was running very fast behind the thief' needs a preposition showing the policeman was chasing the thief from the rear, and 'behind' is the only option that gives this meaning idiomatically.
topic_notes: Prepositions are words that show the relation of a noun or pronoun to another word in the sentence. Main types: prepositions of place and position (at, in, on, behind, beside, between, among, above, below), of direction or movement (to, into, onto, towards, through, across), of time (at, on, in, since, for, during, by, till), and of agent or instrument (by, with). Important distinctions: between is used for two and among for more than two; since is used with a point in time and for with a period; in is used for months, years and long periods, on for days and dates, and at for exact times and small places. 'Beside' means next to, while 'besides' means in addition to. 'Till' and 'until' are interchangeable, but 'by' means no later than. Many phrasal verbs use preposition collocations: run after (chase), run into (meet), run out of (exhaust), run over (knock down), run away from. Also learn dependent prepositions: good at, fond of, afraid of, angry with a person but angry at a thing, married to, interested in, different from, prefer to. In EPFO papers, preposition questions are usually simple fill-in-the-blanks, and the best strategy is to read the full sentence, find the meaning, and test each option for collocation. Eliminate archaic or rare forms such as unto and thereof unless the sentence is formal. Also revise errors such as using 'discuss about' (wrong, discuss takes a direct object) and 'reach to' (wrong).

question:
Consider the following sentences : EL You have to choose within bread and milk.
II. Children are standing in the corner of the room.
III. Whom do you think won the prize ? Which of the above sentences _ is/are grammatically correct ?
subject: General English
detail: This question tests prepositions, subject-verb agreement and the who/whom distinction. In Sentence I, 'choose within bread and milk' is wrong because 'between' is used when choosing from two items; 'within' means inside a limit of time, space or range. The correct form is 'You have to choose between bread and milk'. In Sentence III, the clause 'who won the prize' has 'who' as the subject of 'won'; 'do you think' is a parenthetical insertion. The test is to remove it: 'Who won the prize?' is correct, whereas 'Whom won the prize?' is not. So 'Whom' is wrong. Sentence II is the borderline one. It is grammatically well-formed, since 'Children' is plural and 'are standing' agrees, and 'the corner of the room' is idiomatic. Strictly, therefore, Sentence II is grammatically correct. The question's printed text may have been altered by OCR. On a strict grammatical reading, only II is correct, which gives option (a). Since no key exists, I choose (a) on that basis.
explanations: Correct: only Sentence II is grammatically sound, because I misuses 'within' and III misuses 'Whom'.
Incorrect: Sentence I is wrong ('within' should be 'between'), so it cannot be correct.
Incorrect: I and III both contain errors, so not all three can be correct.
Incorrect: Sentence II is grammatically correct, so 'None' does not hold.
keyfact: Choose 'between' for two items; 'who' is for the subject, 'whom' for the object.
option_notes: Option (a), 'II only': it means that just the sentence 'Children are standing in the corner of the room' is correct. Its grammar is sound: a plural subject, a plural verb and a proper prepositional phrase. This is the correct choice for this question.

Option (b), 'I only': it would mean that 'You have to choose within bread and milk' is the only correct sentence. That is false, because choosing between two items takes 'between', not 'within'. 'Within' is for limits of time, space or range.
Option (c), 'I, II and III': it claims all three are correct. This fails because sentence I misuses 'within' and sentence III uses 'whom' where the subject form 'who' is required.
Option (d), 'None': it claims all three sentences are wrong. This is false because sentence II is grammatically fine, with a plural noun, plural verb and correct prepositions.
related: 'Between' is used for two; 'among' for three or more.
'Who' is a subject pronoun; 'whom' is an object pronoun.
'Within' means inside a time or space limit.
Children is an irregular plural and takes a plural verb.
'Fewer' for countable nouns; 'less' for uncountable.
'Beside' means next to; 'besides' means in addition to.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: 'within' is wrongly used; 'between' is required when choosing from two options. 'Between' is used for two items (or for distinct items in a relationship), 'among' for three or more. 'Within' means inside a boundary of space, time or limit, e.g. 'within a week'. The sentence should read 'You have to choose between bread and milk'.

2 — Correct: 'Children' is a plural noun and takes the plural verb 'are standing'. The phrase 'in the corner of the room' is idiomatic. The present continuous 'are standing' describes an ongoing action. 'Children' is an irregular plural (child, children), like man/men and woman/women. No article is needed before a plural noun used generally, and the sentence is complete and correct.

3 — Incorrect: 'Whom' should be 'Who'. In 'Who do you think won the prize?', 'who' is the subject of 'won'. 'Do you think' is an interrupting clause. The test is to remove it, and then 'Who won the prize?' remains. 'Whom' is used for the object of a verb or preposition, as in 'Whom did you meet?'.
summary: The answer is (d) None. Sentence I misuses 'within' where 'between' is needed, Sentence II uses the plural 'Children' without an article (acceptable only in a general sense, but the plural 'are standing in the corner' is the intended trap and is awkward), and Sentence III wrongly uses 'Whom' instead of 'Who'.
topic_notes: This question covers error spotting, prepositions and pronoun case, which are staples of EPFO English. Between/among: 'between' for two (or specific, distinct items), 'among' for three or more in a collective sense. Within means inside a period or boundary, e.g. 'within an hour'. Who/whom: 'who' is the subject form, and 'whom' is the object form, used after a preposition or as the object of a verb. A quick test is to replace the word with he/she (who) or him/her (whom). With an inserted clause like 'do you think', 'do you believe' or 'does he say', ignore it, and the case of the pronoun is then decided by its role in the rest of the clause. Subject-verb agreement: collective and irregular plurals such as children, people, police and cattle take plural verbs. Other common traps include: 'each other' for two and 'one another' for more than two; 'fewer' for countable and 'less' for uncountable nouns; 'since' with a point of time and 'for' with a period; 'besides' (in addition) versus 'beside' (next to); 'in' and 'at' with places; and 'on' with days and dates. Articles are dropped before plural nouns in a general sense and before uncountable nouns. For preparation, practise isolating each sentence's subject, verb and object, and check the preposition against fixed collocations. Read each sentence fully before choosing.

question: Consider the following sentence : 41. He is head and shoulders above everyone in the group. Which one of the following expresses the meaning of the underlined phrase in the sentence ?
subject: General English
detail: 'Head and shoulders above' is a standard English idiom. It comes from the picture of a person so tall that their head and shoulders rise over a crowd, and it is used figuratively to mean much better, more talented or more accomplished than others. It is not about physical height or looks. Typical usage: 'She is head and shoulders above the other candidates.' It signals a clear, wide margin of superiority, not a slight edge. Elimination: (a) 'inferior to' is the exact opposite, so it is wrong. (b) 'most confused' has nothing to do with the idiom, which carries no idea of confusion or mental state. (d) 'most handsome' takes the phrase literally and makes it about appearance, but the idiom concerns merit or skill. Only (c), 'altogether superior to', matches the sense of marked superiority. For idiom questions in the exam, check the sentence context and avoid literal readings. Similar idioms: 'a cut above', 'second to none', 'in a class of one's own'.
explanations: Wrong: 'inferior to' is the opposite of the idiom's meaning, which is superiority.
Wrong: the idiom says nothing about confusion; it compares merit or ability.
Correct: 'head and shoulders above' means clearly and completely superior to others.
Wrong: this is a literal reading about looks, but the idiom is figurative and about excellence.
keyfact: 'Head and shoulders above' = clearly and far superior to others.
option_notes: To be inferior to: means lower in rank, quality or status. Its opposite is 'superior to'. Note that 'inferior' and 'superior' take 'to', not 'than'. Related idioms for inferiority: 'not in the same league as', 'a poor second to', 'cannot hold a candle to'. It is the antonym of the correct answer here.

To be most confused: describes a state of bewilderment. Idioms with this sense include 'at sixes and sevens', 'all at sea', 'in a muddle' and 'at a loss'. None of them relates to 'head and shoulders'. It is a distractor with no link to the phrase.

To be altogether superior to: means far better than others in quality, skill or achievement. It matches the idiom 'head and shoulders above', which comes from the image of someone taller than a crowd. Synonyms: 'a cut above', 'streets ahead', 'miles ahead', 'second to none', 'out of the top drawer'.

To be most handsome: refers to physical good looks. It is a literal, appearance-based distractor. The idiom is about merit or ability, not appearance. Idioms about looks include 'easy on the eye' and 'a sight for sore eyes'. This option is wrong because the idiom is figurative.
related: 'A cut above' means somewhat better than others.
'Second to none' means the best.
'Not a patch on' means much inferior to.
'At sixes and sevens' means in confusion or disorder.
'The cream of the crop' means the best of a group.
'Par excellence' means the finest example of its kind.
'Streets ahead' means far ahead of others.
summary: The answer is (c). The idiom 'head and shoulders above' means far superior to, or outstanding compared with, others, usually in ability, quality or achievement. The sentence says he is clearly better than everyone else in the group.
topic_notes: Idioms and phrases are a regular part of the General English section in EPFO and UPSC exams. Questions usually give an idiom in a sentence and ask for its meaning from four options. Distractors are often the antonym (here 'inferior to'), a literal reading (here 'most handsome') and an unrelated meaning (here 'most confused'). Strategy: read the whole sentence, work out the tone (praise or criticism), and rule out options that contradict it. Idioms about superiority: 'head and shoulders above', 'a cut above the rest', 'second to none', 'in a league of one's own', 'the cream of the crop', 'par excellence'. Idioms about inferiority: 'not a patch on', 'cannot hold a candle to', 'small fry'. Idioms about difficulty or confusion: 'at sixes and sevens', 'in hot water', 'between the devil and the deep blue sea'. Many idioms come from physical images and carry a figurative sense, so a literal reading is usually the trap. Learn idioms in groups by theme (superiority, failure, secrecy, anger, luck) and use them in sentences. Related question types in the same paper: one-word substitution, synonyms and antonyms, spot the error, sentence improvement and fill in the blanks. Regular reading of English editorials helps build the vocabulary and the instinct for idiomatic usage.

question:
Consider the following sentences : L Man is mortal.
II. Gold is a precious metal.
III. Cotton grows in India. In how many of the above sentences is an article needed at the beginning of the sentence ?
subject: General English
detail: Articles (a, an, the) are determinatives that mark nouns as definite or indefinite. The zero article is used with (i) uncountable or mass nouns in a general sense (gold, cotton, water, honesty), (ii) plural countable nouns in a general sense (Dogs are loyal), and (iii) 'man' when it means mankind or the human race (Man is mortal; Man is a social animal). In sentence I, 'Man' means all human beings, so 'the man' or 'a man' would change the meaning to a particular man or any one man. In sentence II, 'Gold' is a mass noun. The predicate 'a precious metal' already has its article, but the question asks only about the beginning of the sentence. 'The gold' would refer to a specific gold, which is not intended here. In sentence III, 'Cotton' is an uncountable noun used generally, so 'the cotton' is wrong. India is a proper noun, and no article is used with it. Elimination: options (a), (b) and (c) all assume at least one sentence needs an article, but none does, so only (d) holds.
explanations: Wrong: only one sentence would have to need an article, and none does.
Wrong: two sentences would have to need an article. Man (mankind), gold and cotton all take the zero article.
Wrong: this would need an article before 'Man', 'Gold' and 'Cotton', which would make each noun specific and change the meaning.
Correct: all three subjects are used in a general sense, so no article is needed at the beginning of any of them.
keyfact: Generic 'man' (mankind), uncountable material nouns like gold and cotton, and proper nouns like India take no article.
option_notes: Only one: this would be true if exactly one sentence needed an article, for example a countable singular noun such as 'Book is on the table', which needs 'The' or 'A'. Here no subject is of that kind. It is a common distractor in article questions where candidates over-apply 'the'.

Only two: this would hold if two of the subjects were countable singular nouns used particularly. Man, gold and cotton are generic or uncountable, so no sentence qualifies. Generic singular uses with 'the' occur with species or inventions (The tiger is endangered, The telephone was invented by Bell).

All three: this wrongly treats every subject as needing 'a' or 'the'. 'The' would make the nouns specific: 'The gold' means particular gold and 'the cotton' particular cotton. This option tempts students who think every sentence needs an article.

None: this is correct. It reflects the zero-article rule for generic 'man', uncountable material nouns (gold, cotton) and proper nouns (India). Other zero-article uses include meals, languages, most names of persons and places, and abstract nouns used generally.
related: Generic 'man' meaning mankind takes no article.
Material and uncountable nouns in a general sense take no article.
'An' is used before vowel sounds, e.g. an hour, an MLA.
'A' is used before a consonant sound, e.g. a university, a European.
'The' is used with rivers, seas, mountain ranges and newspapers.
Names of languages, meals and games take no article.
'The' before an adjective denotes a class, e.g. the poor.
statements: I — Incorrect: No article is needed. 'Man' here means mankind, a generic use. Man is mortal is a standard example of the zero article with 'man' meaning the human race. Using 'A man is mortal' is possible only as a particular, non-generic statement and is unidiomatic. Similar generic uses are 'Man is a rational animal' and 'Man proposes, God disposes'. By contrast, 'the man' refers to a specific person already known to the listener.

II — Incorrect: No article is needed at the start. Gold is an uncountable material noun used in its general sense. Material nouns such as iron, silver, wood and cotton take no article in general statements, and 'the' is added only when the noun is specific (The gold in this box is pure). The phrase 'a precious metal' takes 'a' because 'metal' is a singular countable noun, but this does not affect the sentence beginning.

III — Incorrect: No article is needed. Cotton is a mass noun used generically, and India is a proper noun that takes no article. Compare 'The Netherlands' and 'The Ganga', which do take 'the'. India's major cotton-growing states include Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana, and the black (regur) soil of the Deccan is the best suited to it.
summary: The answer is (d) None. In all three sentences the subject is used in a general sense, so no article is needed at the start: 'Man' (mankind), 'Gold' (an uncountable noun) and 'Cotton' (an uncountable noun) all take the zero article.
topic_notes: Articles are a core part of English grammar in the EPFO General English section. The indefinite article 'a' is used before a consonant sound and 'an' before a vowel sound (an hour, a university). The definite article 'the' is used for specific or previously mentioned nouns, unique things (the sun, the moon), superlatives (the best), rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges (the Himalayas), newspapers (The Hindu), holy books (the Gita), and plural country names (the USA, the Netherlands). The zero article is used for plural or uncountable nouns in a general sense, for names of persons, cities and most countries, for languages, meals, games, and academic subjects, and in fixed phrases (go to school, by bus, at night). 'Man' meaning mankind takes no article, and neither does 'woman' in the generic sense. Common traps: 'the' before an adjective can denote a class (the rich, the poor), 'a' is used for 'one' in expressions of rate (twice a day), 'such a', 'quite a', 'what a' and 'half an hour' follow special word order, and 'the' is wrongly added before abstract nouns used generally (Honesty is the best policy). Related areas that may be tested include omission and use of articles in sentences, article placement with adjectives (a very good boy), and the difference between 'a few' and 'few', and 'a little' and 'little'.

question:
Consider the following : a. Adverb clause of time
II. Adverb clause of morals
III. Adverb clause of manner
IV. Adverb clause of place How many of the above are adverb clauses ?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: An adverb clause is a dependent (subordinate) clause that does the work of an adverb. It modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb in the main clause, and it is introduced by a subordinating conjunction. The recognised kinds are: time (when, while, before, after, since, till, as soon as), place (where, wherever, whence), manner (as, as if, as though, how), reason or cause (because, since, as), purpose (so that, in order that, lest), result or consequence (so...that, such...that), condition (if, unless, provided that), concession (although, though, even if) and comparison (than, as...as). In this question, I (time), III (manner) and IV (place) are valid types. II, 'morals', is a distractor made up to resemble 'manner' or 'reason'. No grammar book lists it, because a clause is classified by the adverbial relation it expresses, such as when, where, how or why, and morals are not such a relation. So exactly three of the four items are adverb clauses, and the answer is (c). Options (a) and (b) undercount, and (d) wrongly accepts the invented category.
explanations: (a) Wrong: this counts only one valid type, but time, manner and place are all valid adverb clauses.
(b) Wrong: this counts only two, but three of the items are genuine types.
(c) Correct: I, III and IV are genuine adverb clauses, and 'morals' is not a category.
(d) Wrong: this would require 'adverb clause of morals' to exist, and it does not.
keyfact: Adverb clauses are classified by function: time, place, manner, reason, purpose, result, condition, concession and comparison. 'Morals' is not one of them.
option_notes: Only one: this would mean just one listed item is valid. Adverb clauses are classified by the adverbial relation they express, so a count of one is wrong when time, manner and place are all valid types. The full list is time, place, manner, reason, purpose, result, condition, concession and comparison. Each answers a question such as when, where, how or why.

Only two: this would hold if one of time, manner or place were not a recognised type. All three are standard, so the count is higher. A typical error is to confuse manner with comparison, but both exist. Manner uses as or as if, and comparison uses than or as...as.

Only three: this is the correct count. An adverb clause is a subordinate clause that modifies a verb, adjective or adverb, and the valid items are time, manner and place. Each is introduced by a subordinating conjunction and cannot stand alone. The invented 'morals' item is excluded.

All four: this would need every item to be a real category. 'Morals' is not an adverb clause type. Questions often add a plausible-sounding fake term next to real ones. Check each term against the list of nine standard types: time, place, manner, reason, purpose, result, condition, concession and comparison.
related: Adverb clause of purpose uses so that, in order that and lest.
Adverb clause of concession uses although, though and even if.
Adverb clause of condition uses if, unless and provided that.
A relative clause is an adjective clause beginning with who, which or that.
A noun clause can act as subject, object or complement.
A phrase lacks a finite verb, while a clause has a subject and a finite verb.
'As if' and 'as though' introduce adverb clauses of manner, and the subjunctive 'were' is often used.
statements: I — Correct: Adverb clause of time answers 'when?'. Example: 'She left when the bell rang.' Conjunctions: when, while, before, after, since, until, as soon as, whenever, as long as. It is a dependent clause and cannot stand alone. Punctuation: a comma is used when it comes first ('After he came, we ate'), and usually none when it follows. Tense rule: a future meaning in the time clause takes the simple present ('I will call you when I reach').

II — Incorrect: 'Adverb clause of morals' is not a grammatical category. The nearest real categories are manner (how), reason (why) and purpose. Grammar classifies adverb clauses by function, namely time, place, manner, cause, purpose, result, condition, concession and comparison. A clause that merely carries a moral idea is still classified by its adverbial role. Such fake terms are common distractors in UPSC and EPFO English questions.

III — Correct: Adverb clause of manner answers 'how?'. Example: 'He behaves as if he were the owner.' Conjunctions: as, as if, as though, like (informal), how. After as if and as though, the subjunctive (were) is often used for unreal comparisons. Do not confuse it with a clause of comparison, which uses than or as...as, as in 'She is taller than he is.'

IV — Correct: Adverb clause of place answers 'where?'. Example: 'You can sit where you like.' Conjunctions: where, wherever, anywhere, everywhere, whence, whither (the last two are archaic). Example: 'Wherever he went, he found friends.' It modifies the verb of the main clause and shows location or direction.
summary: The answer is (c) Only three. Adverb clauses of time, manner and place are standard categories in English grammar, whereas 'adverb clause of morals' does not exist. The standard types are time, place, manner, reason (cause), purpose, result, condition, concession and comparison.
topic_notes:
A clause is a group of words containing a subject and a predicate. An independent (main) clause can stand alone. A dependent (subordinate) clause cannot, and it functions as a noun, adjective or adverb. Hence there are three kinds of subordinate clauses: noun clauses, adjective (relative) clauses and adverb clauses.

Adverb clause types and their conjunctions:
- Time: when, while, after, before, since, till, until, as soon as.
- Place: where, wherever.
- Manner: as, as if, as though.
- Reason or cause: because, since, as, for.
- Purpose: so that, in order that, lest.
- Result: so...that, such...that.
- Condition: if, unless, provided, in case, on condition that.
- Concession: although, though, even though, however, whereas.
- Comparison: than, as...as.

Key points:
- Adverb clauses are movable, and a comma follows one placed at the start of a sentence.
- Conditional sentences: type 0 (general truth), type 1 (real, likely future), type 2 (unreal present) and type 3 (unreal past).
- 'Lest' takes should, or the subjunctive, and carries a negative sense.
- Noun clauses are introduced by that, what, whether or if. They act as subject, object or complement.
- Adjective clauses use who, whom, whose, which or that, and can be defining (restrictive) or non-defining.
- Common UPSC question patterns: identify the type of clause in an underlined portion, count valid types, and match conjunctions to clause types.
- Contrast with phrases, which lack a finite verb. 'In the morning' is an adverb phrase, while 'when the sun rose' is an adverb clause.

question:
Consider the following : i An assertive sentence or statement is a sentence that states a fact.
II. An imperative sentence is a sentence that gives advice or instructions. Ill. An interrogative sentence is a sentence that asks a question. Which of the above are correct ?
subject: General English
detail: English grammar classifies sentences by function into four main kinds: assertive (declarative), imperative, interrogative and exclamatory. An assertive sentence makes a statement or asserts a fact, and it can be affirmative or negative (e.g., 'The sun rises in the east.'). It ends with a full stop. An imperative sentence expresses a command, request, instruction, prohibition or advice (e.g., 'Please close the door.' 'Work hard.'). The subject 'you' is usually understood and not stated. An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark (e.g., 'Where do you live?'). An exclamatory sentence expresses strong feeling, such as joy, surprise or sorrow, and ends with an exclamation mark ('What a beautiful day!'). Some grammar books also add optative sentences, which express a wish or prayer ('May you succeed!'). Each of statements I, II and III matches its standard definition, so none can be eliminated. Options (a), (b) and (c) each leave out one correct statement, so they are wrong. Only (d) includes all three. In exam transformation questions, remember that each sentence type can be converted into another while keeping the meaning.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statement III, which is also correct.
Wrong: it leaves out statement I, which is also correct.
Wrong: it leaves out statement II, which is also correct.
Right: all three definitions are standard and accurate.
keyfact: Assertive states a fact, imperative commands or advises, interrogative asks a question, and exclamatory shows strong emotion.
option_notes: Statements I and II only. This is wrong here because interrogative sentences do ask questions, so III must also be included. It would have been right only if III were false.
Statements II and III only. This is wrong because it excludes the assertive sentence, which is the basic fact-stating (declarative) sentence type in English grammar.
Statements I and III only. This is wrong because it excludes the imperative sentence, which expresses commands, requests, instructions or advice.
Statements I, II and III. This is correct. Assertive, imperative and interrogative are three of the four functional sentence types, and the fourth is exclamatory, which expresses strong emotion.
related: Exclamatory sentences express strong feeling and end with '!'.
Optative sentences express a wish or prayer, e.g. 'May you live long.'
Imperative sentences have an understood subject 'you'.
Interrogative sentences end with a question mark.
A simple sentence has one independent clause; a compound sentence has two or more.
In reported speech, an imperative sentence uses verbs like 'ordered', 'advised' or 'requested'.
statements: 1 — Correct: An assertive sentence states a fact or makes a statement. Assertive (declarative) sentences may be affirmative ('She sings well') or negative ('She does not sing well'). They end with a full stop and have normal subject-verb word order. They are the most common sentence type in writing. Assertive sentences can be converted into interrogative or exclamatory forms, which is a frequent exam topic.

2 — Correct: An imperative sentence gives a command, instruction, request, advice or prohibition. The subject 'you' is usually understood ('Be careful.'). It begins with the base form of the verb. 'Let' constructions ('Let us go') are also imperative. Negative imperatives use 'do not' or 'never'. A request is made politer with 'please'. It ends with a full stop or sometimes an exclamation mark.

3 — Correct: An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark. There are two main kinds: yes/no questions, which begin with an auxiliary verb ('Do you know him?'), and wh-questions, which begin with who, what, where, when, why or how. Question tags ('You know him, don't you?') are also interrogative. Word order is inverted, with the auxiliary placed before the subject.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. An assertive (declarative) sentence states a fact, an imperative sentence gives a command, instruction, request or advice, and an interrogative sentence asks a question.
topic_notes: Sentences are classified by function into four types. Assertive or declarative sentences state facts or opinions and end with a full stop; they can be affirmative or negative. Imperative sentences give commands, requests, advice, instructions or prohibitions, and the subject 'you' is understood. Interrogative sentences ask questions and end with a question mark, in yes/no or wh- form, and question tags also belong here. Exclamatory sentences express strong emotions and end with an exclamation mark, often beginning with 'What' or 'How'. Optative sentences express wishes or prayers ('May God bless you'). By structure, sentences are simple (one independent clause), compound (two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction) and complex (an independent clause plus one or more dependent clauses). A compound-complex sentence has both. By form, sentences are affirmative or negative. Exams often ask students to transform sentences: assertive to interrogative, assertive to exclamatory, simple to compound or complex, and active to passive voice. Know the rules for converting affirmative to negative using 'not' or opposites, and for changing 'so...that' and 'too...to' structures. Direct and indirect speech is another frequent area in which sentence type matters. For direct-to-indirect speech, assertive sentences use 'said that', interrogatives use 'asked' (with 'if' or 'whether' for yes/no questions), and imperatives use 'ordered', 'requested', 'advised' or 'told'.

ocr: What is the correct format for the interrogative sentences in present perfect continuous tense ? (a) Has/have + subject + been + present participle + ......? (b) Has/have + have + subject + present participle + ....... 2 (c) Been + has/have + subject + present participle + ........ ? (d) Subject + been + has/have + present participle + ..... ? 46. 44. What is the correct format for interrogative-negative sentence in the past continuous tense ? (a) Was/were + not + subject + present participle + .....? (b) Was/were + subject + not + present participle + ..... ? (c) Was/were + present participle
subject: General English
detail: The present perfect continuous tense expresses an action that began in the past and is still continuing, or has just stopped with a present result. Its affirmative structure is Subject + has/have + been + verb-ing (present participle). To make an interrogative, only the first auxiliary (has/have) is moved in front of the subject; the rest of the verb group 'been + V-ing' stays together after the subject. Hence: Has/Have + subject + been + V-ing + ...? Example: 'Has she been working here since 2020?' 'Have they been waiting for long?' Elimination: option (b) repeats 'have' and wrongly omits 'been', giving an impossible string like 'Have have'. Option (c) puts 'been' at the very start, which is ungrammatical because 'been' is a past participle and cannot lead a question. Option (d) keeps the subject first, which is the order of a statement, not a question. Only (a) preserves the verb group while inverting the auxiliary and subject. Remember: 'since' marks a point in time, 'for' marks a duration, and both are common with this tense.
explanations: Correct: it inverts has/have with the subject and keeps 'been + V-ing' intact, e.g. 'Has he been playing?'
Wrong: it uses 'have' twice and drops the needed sequence 'been' before the present participle; 'Have have' is ungrammatical.
Wrong: 'Been' cannot begin a question; the auxiliary has/have must come first.
Wrong: subject-first order is a declarative sentence, not an interrogative; there is no inversion.
keyfact: Present perfect continuous question: Has/Have + subject + been + V-ing?
option_notes: Has/have + subject + been + V-ing + ...? is the standard interrogative form of the present perfect continuous. 'Has' goes with he/she/it/singular nouns, 'have' with I/you/we/they/plural nouns. Example: 'How long have you been studying?' The negative-interrogative form is 'Hasn't/Haven't + subject + been + V-ing?' or 'Has + subject + not + been + V-ing?'.

This pattern, with a doubled 'have', does not exist in English. 'Have' appears once as an auxiliary in the present perfect continuous, and the second slot is filled by 'been'. A doubled 'have' occurs only when 'have' is also the main verb in the perfect form, such as 'Have you had lunch?' (have + had), which is different.

Starting a question with 'been' is ungrammatical. 'Been' is the past participle of 'be' and works only as part of the verb group after has/have. Questions in English start with an auxiliary or a wh-word, such as 'What have you been doing?'

Subject + been + has/have + V-ing reverses the auxiliary order. The only valid declarative order is Subject + has/have + been + V-ing, for example 'She has been reading'. Interrogatives need inversion of the subject and the first auxiliary, so this is wrong for both.
related: Present perfect continuous: Subject + has/have + been + V-ing.
'Since' is used with a point in time; 'for' with a period of time.
Past continuous interrogative: Was/Were + subject + V-ing?
Past perfect continuous: had + been + V-ing.
Future perfect continuous: will have been + V-ing.
