topic_notes: Article 170 fixes the composition of State Legislative Assemblies: not more than 500 and not less than 60 members, directly elected from territorial constituencies. Parliament may relax the minimum for small States: Sikkim 32, Goa 40, Mizoram 40 are below 60. Among Union Territories with Legislatures, Delhi has 70 and Puducherry has 30 elected members (plus 3 nominated), and Jammu and Kashmir has 90 elected members. Largest Assembly: Uttar Pradesh with 403 seats. Next: West Bengal 294, Maharashtra 288, Bihar 243. Smallest: Sikkim (32), then Puducherry (30, a UT). Legislative Councils (Article 171) may have up to one-third of the Assembly strength and a minimum of 40 members; six States currently have them: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh. Article 333 provides for nomination of one Anglo-Indian member by the Governor; this was removed by the 104th Amendment in 2019. Article 332 provides reserved seats for SC and ST. The 104th Amendment also ended SC/ST reservation extension issues, extended to 2030. Delimitation is done by the Delimitation Commission, and the freeze on seat numbers was extended by the 84th Amendment until the first Census after 2026. Other points: North-East States Manipur, Nagaland, Tripura each have 60 seats, Assam has 126, Mizoram 40.

question:
With reference to Government of India, consider the following Departments : £ Department of Defence Research and Development
II. Department of Justice Ill. Department of Atomic Energy
IV. Department of Space Which of the above are Independent Departments, not forming part of any Ministry ?
subject: Computers
detail: Under the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, the work of the Government is divided among Ministries and Departments. Usually a Department is a wing of a Ministry, headed by a Secretary, and is subordinate to the Minister. A few Departments are not part of any Ministry and function as independent departments. The Department of Atomic Energy (created 1954, after the Atomic Energy Commission of 1948) and the Department of Space (created 1972 with the Space Commission; ISRO functions under it) are the standard examples. Both are directly under the Prime Minister and are headed by a Secretary. The Department of Defence Research and Development (DRDO, est. 1958) is one of the departments of the Ministry of Defence, along with Defence, Defence Production, Military Affairs and Ex-Servicemen Welfare. The Department of Justice, with the Department of Legal Affairs and the Legislative Department, is under the Ministry of Law and Justice. Elimination: I and II are each housed in a Ministry, so any option containing either is wrong. That leaves III and IV only.
explanations: Wrong: it includes I (DRDO's department, under the Ministry of Defence) and II (Department of Justice, under the Ministry of Law and Justice); neither is independent.
Wrong: it includes II, which is under the Ministry of Law and Justice, and it omits IV, which is independent.
Right: the Department of Atomic Energy (III) and the Department of Space (IV) are independent departments under the Prime Minister.
Wrong: it includes I, the Department of Defence R&D, which is part of the Ministry of Defence.
keyfact: Only the Departments of Atomic Energy and Space are independent departments, both under the Prime Minister; DRDO's department and the Department of Justice sit in Ministries.
option_notes: I, II and IV: this mixes two departments that sit inside Ministries (Defence R&D and Justice) with Space. The Department of Defence R&D is under the Ministry of Defence and the Department of Justice is under the Ministry of Law and Justice, so the combination is wrong. Only Space is independent. Remember that the independence test is whether a Department has its own Minister or Prime Minister and no parent Ministry.

II and III only: pairs the Department of Justice, a wing of the Ministry of Law and Justice, with the independent Department of Atomic Energy. Justice handles the judiciary's administrative matters, including judges' appointments and court infrastructure. It is not independent, and this option wrongly omits Space.

III and IV only: the Departments of Atomic Energy and Space are the two independent departments under the Prime Minister. DAE dates from 1954 and Space from 1972. Both are scientific and strategic, and each has a high-level Commission (Atomic Energy Commission, Space Commission) whose chairman is the Secretary of the Department. This is the correct option.

I, III and IV: adds the Department of Defence R&D to the two independent departments. DRDO's department was set up in 1958 and is one of the Ministry of Defence's five departments. Its Secretary reports through the Defence Ministry, with the Raksha Mantri as Minister, so it is not independent and the option is wrong.
related: Department of Atomic Energy was created in 1954; Atomic Energy Commission in 1948 (Homi Bhabha first chairman).
Department of Space was created in 1972; ISRO was formed in 1969.
DRDO was formed in 1958; the Department of Defence R&D is under the Ministry of Defence.
The Department of Justice is under the Ministry of Law and Justice, with Legal Affairs and Legislative.
The Prime Minister heads DAE, the Department of Space and the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.
IN-SPACe (2020) is the single-window regulator and promoter for private space activities.
The Ministry of Defence has five departments, including Military Affairs, headed by the CDS.
Rules of Business flow from Article 77(3), with the Allocation of Business Rules, 1961.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Department of Defence R&D is part of the Ministry of Defence. It is headed by a Secretary who is also Chairman of DRDO, and it advises the Defence Minister through the Scientific Adviser. DRDO was formed in 1958 by merging the Technical Development Establishment and the Defence Science Organisation. It has about 50 laboratories, and its mission areas include missiles (the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme under A.P.J. Abdul Kalam), aeronautics, naval systems and armaments. The Ministry of Defence has five departments: Defence, Defence Production, Defence R&D, Ex-Servicemen Welfare and Military Affairs.

2 — Incorrect: The Department of Justice is under the Ministry of Law and Justice, along with the Department of Legal Affairs and the Legislative Department. It deals with the appointment, resignation and removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges, the National Judicial Data Grid, e-Courts, and the infrastructure of subordinate courts. It also administers Fast Track Courts and access-to-justice schemes such as Tele-Law. It has a Secretary (Justice). The Department of Legal Affairs is the oldest, while the Legislative Department drafts Central legislation.

3 — Correct: The Department of Atomic Energy was set up in 1954 by Presidential order and works directly under the Prime Minister, who is its Minister in charge. The Atomic Energy Commission was formed in 1948 under Homi J. Bhabha. DAE units include BARC, IGCAR, RRCAT, VECC, NPCIL, BHAVINI, IREL, ECIL and UCIL. The Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (1983) provide the legal and regulatory framework. India's three-stage nuclear programme is its main long-term strategy.

4 — Correct: The Department of Space was set up in 1972, along with the Space Commission, and is under the Prime Minister's charge. ISRO (formed 1969, replacing INCOSPAR of 1962) is its main agency. Other bodies are Antrix Corporation, NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), IN-SPACe (the 2020 regulator and promoter for private players), PRL and NARL. Its major missions include Chandrayaan, Mangalyaan (MOM) and Aditya-L1. The Department's headquarters are in Bengaluru. Its Secretary is also ISRO Chairman.
summary: The answer is (c): III and IV only. The Department of Atomic Energy and the Department of Space are independent departments, each under the Prime Minister's charge and not part of any ministry. The Department of Defence R&D sits within the Ministry of Defence, and the Department of Justice sits within the Ministry of Law and Justice.
topic_notes: Structure of the Union executive: Article 77 provides for conduct of Government business and Article 53 vests executive power in the President. The Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961 and the Transaction of Business Rules, 1961 allocate subjects among Ministries and Departments. A Ministry is the principal unit and is headed by a Cabinet Minister, who is assisted by Ministers of State. Its administrative head is a Secretary. A Ministry may have several Departments, each headed by a Secretary, plus attached offices (executive arms) and subordinate offices. Statutory and autonomous bodies are also attached to Ministries. Independent departments have no parent Ministry and are under the Prime Minister. The classic examples are the Department of Atomic Energy and the Department of Space. Note that the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, which is also under the PM, is a Ministry and not an independent department. The Prime Minister also holds charge of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, the Department of Atomic Energy, the Department of Space, and policy matters not allocated to any other Minister. Other related facts: the Cabinet Secretariat is under the Prime Minister and the Cabinet Secretary heads the civil services. The Ministry of Finance has Departments of Economic Affairs, Expenditure, Revenue, Financial Services, DIPAM and Public Enterprises. The Ministry of Defence has five Departments, including Defence R&D. The Ministry of Law and Justice has the Departments of Legal Affairs, Legislative, and Justice. The Department of Atomic Energy was established in August 1954, and the Department of Space in June 1972. Likely angles for the next paper include the Atomic Energy Commission, Space Commission, ISRO, IN-SPACe, and which Ministry houses which Department.

question: Consider the following statements : 61. IL Solicitor General of India is a Constitutional post. Il. Solicitor General of India assists Attorney General of India. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: General Science
detail: Article 76 provides for the Attorney General of India (AG), who is appointed by the President and must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge. The AG is the highest law officer of the country and holds office during the President's pleasure. Articles 76 and 88 give the AG the right to speak in Parliament without voting. The Constitution does not mention the Solicitor General (SG) or the Additional Solicitors General. These posts are created by executive or statutory arrangements: the Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1987, and the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) appoints them. The SG is the second-highest law officer and assists the AG in official legal duties. The SG is in turn assisted by Additional Solicitors General. Elimination: Statement I fails because the post is not constitutional, so options (a) and (c) are out. Statement II is correct, so (d) is out. That leaves (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement I is false: the Solicitor General is not a constitutional post.
(b) is correct because only Statement II is true: the SG assists the AG, and the post is not constitutional.
(c) is wrong because it accepts Statement I, which is false.
(d) is wrong because it rejects Statement II, which is true.
keyfact: Only the Attorney General is a constitutional law officer (Art. 76); the Solicitor General is non-constitutional and assists the AG.
option_notes: Option (a) would make only Statement I correct. It is wrong, since only the Attorney General (Art. 76) is a constitutional law officer. The SG's post exists by government rules and ACC appointment, not by constitutional text.

Option (b), only Statement II, is correct. The SG is the second law officer, below the Attorney General and above the Additional Solicitors General. The SG assists the AG in the Supreme Court and other courts, and the post is not mentioned in the Constitution.

Option (c) would make both statements correct. It fails because Statement I is false. Constitutional posts include the AG (Art. 76), the CAG (Art. 148) and the Advocate General of a State (Art. 165). The SG is not among them.

Option (d) would make both statements incorrect. It fails because the SG does assist the AG. The Law Officers Rules 1987 describe how law officers assist the Government, and the SG works with the AG in major litigation.
related: Article 76 provides for the Attorney General of India.
Article 165 provides for the Advocate General of a State.
The AG can speak in Parliament but cannot vote (Art. 88).
The SG and Additional SGs are not constitutional posts.
The AG's tenure is not fixed and he holds office during the President's pleasure.
The AG must be qualified to be appointed a Supreme Court judge.
Tushar Mehta has been the Solicitor General since 2018.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Constitution does not mention the Solicitor General. Only the Attorney General is covered, under Article 76. The SG's post is non-constitutional and non-statutory in the strict sense, being created by executive arrangement and governed by the Law Officers Rules 1987. The SG is appointed by the ACC, and the term is usually tied to the government's tenure. The SG ranks second in the legal hierarchy and appears for the Union in the Supreme Court and High Courts. Additional Solicitors General (currently several) also hold non-constitutional posts. Famous SGs include Soli Sorabjee (as AG), Tushar Mehta (SG since 2018) and Ranjit Kumar.

2 — Correct: The SG assists the Attorney General and acts as the second law officer of the Government of India. The SG advises the Union Government on legal matters and represents it in important cases, especially before the Supreme Court. The AG, in turn, gives legal advice to the Government on matters referred by the President. Both are part of the Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law and Justice. The SG may appear in the AG's absence. Additional Solicitors General then assist the SG and AG. Tushar Mehta became SG in 2018 and has been repeatedly extended. The AG as of 2022 is R. Venkataramani.
summary: The answer is (b): only Statement II is correct. The Solicitor General of India assists the Attorney General, but the post is statutory/non-constitutional, since Article 76 mentions only the Attorney General.
topic_notes: Law officers of the Union: The Attorney General is covered by Article 76. He is appointed by the President, must be eligible to be a Supreme Court judge, and holds office during the President's pleasure. His remuneration is determined by the President, since the Constitution fixes none. He advises the Government on legal matters referred to him, performs duties assigned by the President, and discharges the functions conferred by the Constitution or any other law. He has the right of audience in all courts in India and the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament and their committees without the right to vote (Art. 88). He enjoys all the privileges of an MP. He is not a government servant and is not debarred from private legal practice, though he cannot advise against the Union Government. The Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General are not constitutional posts and assist the AG. Similar State-level post: the Advocate General under Article 165, appointed by the Governor, who must be qualified to be a High Court judge. Other constitutional posts to remember: CAG (Art. 148), Election Commission (Art. 324), Finance Commission (Art. 280), UPSC (Art. 315). Non-constitutional or statutory bodies: NITI Aayog (executive), NHRC (statutory), CVC (statutory since 2003), Lokpal (statutory). Questions often compare the AG's removal procedure, which is not specified in the Constitution, with the removal of a judge.

question: Which one of the following is an objective of Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana ?
options: Extending the coverage of quality generic medicines to the people
Supplying quality medicines to rural people free of cost
Establishing special health centres in inaccessible areas and to maintain gg steady supply of medicines there
Supplying medicines freely to migrant workers in unorganized sector
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP) is run by the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. The Bureau of Pharma PSUs of India (BPPI) implements it. It began in 2008 as the Jan Aushadhi Campaign and was relaunched as PMJAY in 2015. It was renamed PMBJP in 2016. Its core objective is to bring down the out-of-pocket health expenditure of citizens by providing quality generic medicines at prices much lower than branded ones, often 50 to 90 percent cheaper. It also creates awareness that generics are equal in quality and efficacy to branded drugs. Further goals are to generate employment through Kendra owners and to extend coverage across all districts. The medicines are sold, not given free, and the scheme is not confined to rural people, special health centres or migrant workers. Option (a) is therefore the only one that matches the scheme's stated objective. Options (b) and (d) fail because of the word 'free'. Option (c) describes health infrastructure schemes such as health and wellness centres, not a medicine retail scheme. The Kendras are run by individuals, NGOs, trusts, societies and others, with a financial incentive from the government. Quality is ensured through testing at NABL-accredited labs.
explanations: Correct: extending the coverage of quality generic medicines at affordable prices to all, especially the poor, is the stated objective of PMBJP.
Incorrect: the medicines are sold at low prices, not supplied free, and the scheme is not limited to rural people.
Incorrect: PMBJP does not establish special health centres in inaccessible areas. It opens generic medicine outlets (Janaushadhi Kendras).
Incorrect: medicines are not supplied free, and the scheme is not targeted only at migrant workers in the unorganised sector.
keyfact: PMBJP = affordable quality generic medicines for all through Janaushadhi Kendras, implemented by BPPI under the Department of Pharmaceuticals; not free supply.
option_notes: Generic medicines have the same active ingredient, dosage, strength and efficacy as branded drugs but cost much less because they carry no brand marketing costs. PMBJP supplies them through Janaushadhi Kendras and tests them at NABL-accredited labs. The aim is to cut households' out-of-pocket health spending and make quality medicines available to all sections of society.

Free supply of medicines is not a PMBJP feature. Free drugs are given under other programmes, such as the Free Drugs Service Initiative under the National Health Mission, which covers public health facilities. PMBJP works on a retail model with low prices and is open to all, not only rural people.

Special health centres in inaccessible areas relate to the National Health Mission, Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres (now Ayushman Arogya Mandirs) and similar infrastructure efforts. They provide primary care and are not the same as PMBJP's generic medicine outlets.

Migrant workers in the unorganised sector are covered by social security measures such as the e-Shram portal, Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY and the One Nation One Ration Card. PMBJP is open to everyone, does not target migrant workers, and sells medicines at low cost rather than giving them out free.
related: PMBJP is implemented by the Bureau of Pharma PSUs of India (BPPI).
It is under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers.
PMBJP was renamed from Jan Aushadhi Yojana in 2016.
Janaushadhi Diwas is observed on 7 March.
Janaushadhi medicines are priced at least 50 percent below market rates.
The Janaushadhi Sugam app locates Kendras and compares prices.
The Free Drugs Service Initiative is under the National Health Mission.
summary: The answer is (a). PMBJP aims to make quality generic medicines available at affordable prices to everyone, especially the poor and disadvantaged, through dedicated Janaushadhi Kendras. The medicines are sold at low prices, not given free.
topic_notes: PMBJP is a flagship scheme of the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. It began in 2008 as the Jan Aushadhi Campaign, was relaunched in 2015 as the Pradhan Mantri Jan Aushadhi Yojana, and was renamed PMBJP in November 2016. The Bureau of Pharma PSUs of India (BPPI), set up in 2008 under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, is the implementing agency. Janaushadhi Kendras can be opened by individuals, NGOs, trusts, charitable institutions, self-help groups and others, with government incentives and support. Special incentives apply for women entrepreneurs, SC/ST applicants, and those in the Northeast, island and hilly areas. The product basket includes over 1,800 medicines and about 285 surgical and consumables items, and the number of Kendras has crossed 10,000. Medicines are priced at least 50 percent lower than market prices, and in many cases 80 to 90 percent lower. Quality is ensured through testing at NABL-accredited labs. Janaushadhi Diwas is observed on 7 March every year. The scheme also supports employment generation and the Janaushadhi Sugam mobile app helps users find Kendras and compare prices. Related health schemes UPSC may ask about include Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, the National Health Mission, the Free Drugs Service Initiative, Mission Indradhanush and the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana. Key point: the scheme sells generics cheaply and does not give them free.

question: With reference to Government of India, the Department of Border Management is under :
options: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has several departments: Department of Internal Security, Department of Home, Department of Jammu and Kashmir Affairs, Department of Border Management, Department of States, and Department of Official Language. The Department of Border Management was created in January 2004 to give focused attention to the management of international borders, including the coastal borders. It handles the creation of border infrastructure such as Integrated Check Posts (ICPs), border fencing, floodlighting and border roads. It also runs the Border Area Development Programme (BADP), which began in the 1986-87 period as a Western Region scheme and was later extended to all land borders. The Border Security Force, Indo-Tibetan Border Police, Sashastra Seema Bal and Assam Rifles are manned by the MHA's Central Armed Police Forces. The Land Ports Authority of India (LPAI, set up in 2012 under the LPAI Act 2010) works under this department. Elimination: Defence handles the armed forces. External Affairs handles diplomacy and boundary negotiations. Road Transport handles highways, although the Border Roads Organisation is under Defence.
explanations: (a) Incorrect: The Ministry of Defence has the Departments of Defence, Military Affairs, Defence Production, Defence Research and Development, and Ex-Servicemen Welfare. It has no Department of Border Management.
(b) Incorrect: The Ministry of External Affairs handles foreign relations and diplomatic negotiations on boundaries, but border management is not a department under it.
(c) Correct: The Department of Border Management is a department of the Ministry of Home Affairs, created in 2004.
(d) Incorrect: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways deals with national highways and transport policy. Border roads are handled by the BRO under Defence, and border infrastructure by the MHA.
keyfact: Department of Border Management (2004) is part of the Ministry of Home Affairs.
option_notes: Ministry of Defence: Headed by the Raksha Mantri, it has four departments, namely Defence, Military Affairs (created 2019, headed by the Chief of Defence Staff), Defence Production, and Defence Research & Development, as well as Ex-Servicemen Welfare. It oversees the Army, Navy, Air Force and the Border Roads Organisation (BRO).

Ministry of External Affairs: Headed by the External Affairs Minister, it conducts India's foreign policy, diplomatic missions, passports and consular services, and treaty negotiations. It negotiates boundary settlements with neighbours, but does not run border management or border force operations. The Indian Foreign Service staffs it.

Ministry of Home Affairs: It is responsible for internal security, centre-state relations, border management, disaster management, and the Central Armed Police Forces. Its departments include Internal Security, Home, J&K Affairs, Border Management, States, and Official Language. The Home Minister heads it, and Amit Shah has held the post since 2019.

Ministry of Road Transport and Highways: It formulates policy for road transport and national highways and oversees the NHAI, set up in 1988 and operational from 1995. It administers the Motor Vehicles Act 1988. It is not involved in border management, though it may build strategic roads in coordination with others.
related: Department of Border Management was created in January 2004 in the MHA.
Land Ports Authority of India was set up in 2012 under the MHA.
BSF guards the borders with Pakistan and Bangladesh.
ITBP guards the India-China border; SSB guards the Nepal and Bhutan borders.
Assam Rifles guards the India-Myanmar border and is under MHA administrative control.
Border Roads Organisation was set up in 1960 and is under the Ministry of Defence.
Vibrant Villages Programme was announced in 2023 for northern border villages.
Indian Coast Guard works under the Ministry of Defence.
summary: The correct answer is (c) Ministry of Home Affairs. The Department of Border Management is one of the departments of the MHA. It deals with the management of international borders, border infrastructure and the Border Area Development Programme.
topic_notes: Border management in India is led by the Ministry of Home Affairs, which has had a dedicated Department of Border Management since January 2004, following the Group of Ministers' recommendations after the Kargil Review Committee (1999). The department handles the land borders with Pakistan, Bangladesh, China, Nepal, Bhutan and Myanmar, and the coastal borders. India's land border is about 15,106 km long, and the coastline is about 7,516 km including islands. Border-guarding forces include the BSF (Pakistan and Bangladesh borders), ITBP (China border), SSB (Nepal and Bhutan borders), and Assam Rifles (Myanmar border). The Assam Rifles is administratively under the MHA but operationally under the Army. The Indian Coast Guard works under the Ministry of Defence. The Border Area Development Programme (BADP) provides funds for infrastructure and welfare in border villages. The Comprehensive Integrated Border Management System (CIBMS) uses sensors and surveillance technology to create smart fencing. The Vibrant Villages Programme (2023) targets villages along the northern border. The Land Ports Authority of India, set up in 2012, manages Integrated Check Posts such as Attari, Petrapole and Moreh. The Border Roads Organisation, established in 1960, is under the Ministry of Defence. The Free Movement Regime with Myanmar was ended by the government in 2024 with a plan for fencing.

question: The President of India has discretionary power in:
options: the imposition of President’s rule in a State
withholding assent to the Money Bill
the appointment of the Prime Minister
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Under Article 74 the President must act on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made this advice binding, and the 44th Amendment (1978) allowed the President to send it back once for reconsideration, but the advice given after reconsideration is binding. Situational (discretionary) powers are not written in the Constitution but are recognised by convention. They include: appointing the PM when no party has a clear majority or when a PM dies suddenly without a clear successor; dismissing the Council of Ministers when it cannot prove its majority in the Lok Sabha; dissolving the Lok Sabha if the ministry has lost its majority; returning a non-money bill (suspensive veto); and the pocket veto, since no time limit is fixed for assent. Option (a) is wrong because President's rule under Article 356 is imposed on the Governor's report or otherwise, but in practice on Cabinet advice. Option (b) is wrong because a Money Bill is introduced on the President's recommendation, so assent cannot be withheld in practice. Option (c) is wrong because the Proclamation of Emergency under Article 352 needs the Cabinet's written advice (44th Amendment).
explanations: (a) Wrong. Article 356 is exercised on the Union Cabinet's advice, even though a Governor's report is the usual trigger. It is not a personal discretion of the President.
(b) Wrong. A Money Bill can be introduced only on the President's recommendation, so he cannot withhold assent in practice. He may in theory, but by convention he never does so.
(c) Wrong. Under Article 352, as amended by the 44th Amendment, the President can proclaim an Emergency only on the written advice of the Union Cabinet.
(d) Correct. When no party or coalition has a clear majority in the Lok Sabha, the President uses personal discretion to choose the PM, as in 1979, 1989, 1991, 1996 and 1998.
keyfact: The President's real discretion is mainly in appointing the PM in a hung Lok Sabha; otherwise Article 74 makes Cabinet advice binding.
option_notes: President's rule (Article 356) applies when a State's constitutional machinery fails. It needs parliamentary approval within 2 months and lasts 6 months at a time, up to a maximum of 3 years with conditions. S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) made the proclamation subject to judicial review. Article 365 covers failure to comply with Union directions.

A Money Bill is defined in Article 110. It is introduced only in the Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation. The Rajya Sabha may only recommend changes within 14 days. The Speaker certifies a Money Bill. The President may give assent or withhold it, but cannot return it for reconsideration.

Article 352 provides for National Emergency on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion. The 44th Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion', and requires written Cabinet advice. Parliament must approve within 1 month, by a special majority. Emergencies were declared in 1962, 1971 and 1975.

Article 75(1) says the PM is appointed by the President. By convention, the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha is appointed. The PM need not be a member of Parliament at the time of appointment but must become one within 6 months (Article 75(5)). Discretion arises in hung-house situations.
related: Article 74: the Council of Ministers' advice is binding on the President (42nd Amendment).
The 44th Amendment lets the President return advice for reconsideration once.
Article 75(5): a non-member minister must get elected to Parliament within 6 months.
Article 61 provides for impeachment of the President, needing two-thirds of the total membership of each House.
Article 111: the President's assent to bills; the pocket veto has no time limit.
Zail Singh used the pocket veto on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill in 1986.
S.R. Bommai (1994): President's rule is judicially reviewable.
Article 123: the President's ordinance-making power.
summary: The answer is (d). The President can use real discretion in appointing the Prime Minister when no party or coalition has a clear majority in the Lok Sabha. In the other three matters the President is bound by Union Cabinet advice or by convention, or acts on the Governor's report (President's rule).
topic_notes: The President of India is the nominal executive head under Articles 52 to 62. Article 74(1) provides for a Council of Ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise the President. The 42nd Amendment made the advice binding. The 44th Amendment (Article 74(1) proviso) allows the President to ask the Council to reconsider its advice once. Courts cannot inquire into what advice was given (Article 74(2)). Vetoes: the absolute veto is withholding assent (used in the PEPSU Appropriation Bill 1954 and the Indian Post Office Bill 1986 under Zail Singh as a pocket veto); the suspensive veto applies to ordinary bills, which the legislature can repass; and the pocket veto means taking no action. The President has no veto over constitutional amendment bills, since the 24th Amendment made assent obligatory. The President has a suspensive veto on state bills reserved by Governors under Article 201. The President can promulgate ordinances (Article 123) when Parliament is not in session, and these must be approved within 6 weeks of reassembly. Pardoning powers are under Article 72. Discretionary or situational powers are: appointing the PM in a hung Parliament; dismissing a ministry that has lost confidence but refuses to resign; dissolving the Lok Sabha; returning bills; and the pocket veto. Impeachment (Article 61) needs a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each House. Election is by an electoral college under Article 54, with proportional representation by single transferable vote (Article 55). Qualifications: citizen, at least 35 years old, and eligible to be a Lok Sabha member.

ocr: With reference to the history of India, which of the following statements is/are correct ? Independence Day was observed all over ie, India on 26" January, 1930. The Indian Independence Act, 1947 was IL. passed in the British Parliament. Select the answer using the code given below : Tonly (a) TI only (b) Both I and II (c) Neither I nor II (d)
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Both statements are historically accurate. At the Lahore session of the Indian National Congress (December 1929), presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru on the banks of the Ravi, the goal of Purna Swaraj (complete independence) was adopted and the tricolour was hoisted. The Congress Working Committee asked the country to observe 26 January 1930 as Independence Day (Purna Swaraj Day), and public meetings across India took the pledge of independence. This date was later chosen for the commencement of the Constitution in 1950, which is why we celebrate Republic Day on 26 January. The Indian Independence Act, 1947 was based on the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947. It was introduced in the House of Commons in July 1947, passed by the British Parliament, and received royal assent on 18 July 1947. It created two dominions, India and Pakistan, from 15 August 1947, ended British paramountcy over princely states, and abolished the office of Secretary of State for India. Since both statements are correct, options (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated.
explanations: Wrong: Statement I is correct but Statement II is also correct, so 'I only' is incomplete.
Wrong: Statement II is correct but Statement I is also correct, so 'II only' is incomplete.
Correct: both statements are factually accurate. 26 January 1930 was Purna Swaraj Day and the Independence Act of 1947 was passed by the British Parliament.
Wrong: neither-option would require both statements to be false, but both are true.
keyfact: 26 Jan 1930 = Purna Swaraj Day (after Lahore Congress 1929); Indian Independence Act 1947 = British Parliament statute, royal assent 18 July 1947.
option_notes: Option (a) 'I only' would hold if only the 26 January 1930 observance were correct. That event was Purna Swaraj Day, declared after the Lahore Congress of 1929 under Nehru. The Congress pledged complete independence and observed the day annually until 1947. The date was later chosen for the Constitution's commencement on 26 January 1950, making it Republic Day. It was not the actual date of independence, which was 15 August 1947.

Option (b) 'II only' would apply if only the Act's passage by the British Parliament were true. The Indian Independence Act, 1947 received royal assent on 18 July 1947 and created India and Pakistan as dominions from 15 August 1947. It ended paramountcy over princely states, abolished the Secretary of State for India's post, and empowered the Constituent Assemblies as legislatures. It followed the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947.

Option (c) 'Both I and II' is the correct choice. It combines two key events: the Purna Swaraj Day pledge of 26 January 1930, following the Lahore Congress resolution of December 1929, and the Indian Independence Act 1947, passed by the British Parliament in July 1947 to end British rule and create two dominions. Both are staple UPSC facts of the freedom struggle and the constitutional history of India.

Option (d) 'Neither I nor II' would be right only if both statements were false. Common traps are confusing the 1930 Independence Day with the actual independence date of 15 August 1947, or thinking the Act was passed by the Constituent Assembly of India. In reality, the Act was a British parliamentary statute, and the 1930 observance was a nationwide Congress-led pledge for Purna Swaraj.
related: Lahore Congress, December 1929, was presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru and adopted the Purna Swaraj resolution.
The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, honouring the 1930 Purna Swaraj Day.
The Indian Independence Act 1947 received royal assent on 18 July 1947.
The Mountbatten Plan was announced on 3 June 1947, also called the 3 June Plan.
The Act abolished the post of Secretary of State for India and ended paramountcy over princely states.
The Radcliffe Commission demarcated the India-Pakistan boundary in 1947.
The Dandi March began on 12 March 1930, launching the Civil Disobedience Movement.
The Constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949.
statements: I — Correct: The Congress asked the nation to observe 26 January 1930 as Independence Day, and it was observed widely across India. Background: after the Lahore Congress (December 1929, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru), the Purna Swaraj resolution was passed on 19 December 1929 and the tricolour was hoisted on the Ravi banks on 31 December 1929. The Working Committee fixed 26 January 1930 for the pledge, and meetings were held in villages and towns. It was observed annually until 1947. The Constitution was later brought into force on 26 January 1950 to honour this date, and Republic Day is celebrated on it. The Civil Disobedience Movement (Dandi March, 12 March 1930) followed soon after.

II — Correct: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 was an Act of the British Parliament. It was passed on the basis of the Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947) and received royal assent on 18 July 1947. It provided for the partition of British India into two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, effective 15 August 1947, ended the British Crown's suzerainty over princely states, which could accede to either dominion, and abolished the post of Secretary of State for India. It gave the Constituent Assemblies the powers of legislature for their dominions and made the Governor-General a constitutional head. Lord Mountbatten was the first Governor-General of independent India. The Act stayed in force until the Constitution commenced on 26 January 1950.
summary: The correct answer is (c) Both I and II. Independence Day (Purna Swaraj Day) was observed all over India on 26 January 1930 following the Lahore Congress resolution, and the Indian Independence Act, 1947 was passed by the British Parliament.
topic_notes:
Purna Swaraj: The Madras Congress (1927) first declared complete independence as the goal, but the Nehru Report (1928) sought dominion status. The Calcutta Congress (1928) gave the British a one-year ultimatum for dominion status. When Lord Irwin's declaration (Oct 1929) was non-committal, the Lahore Congress (Dec 1929) under Jawaharlal Nehru declared Purna Swaraj as the goal, authorised the Civil Disobedience Movement, and the tricolour was hoisted on 31 December 1929. 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day. Civil Disobedience began with the Dandi March on 12 March 1930. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact came in March 1931.

Transfer of power: The Cripps Mission (1942), the Quit India Movement (August 1942), the Cabinet Mission (1946), the Interim Government (September 1946), the Attlee Declaration (20 February 1947: British to leave by June 1948), and the Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947) are the key steps. The Indian Independence Bill was introduced in the House of Commons on 4 July 1947, and the Act received royal assent on 18 July 1947. Provisions: partition into India and Pakistan from 15 August 1947; Governor-General for each dominion; Constituent Assemblies act as legislatures; the Government of India Act 1935 to govern until new constitutions, with adaptations; lapse of paramountcy; Radcliffe Commission for boundaries. Later events: the Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, and it came into force on 26 January 1950. The Constitution (First) and the integration of princely states under Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon are also related angles.

question:
Which of the following are partner countries in the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework for Prosperity (IPEF) ? 16 Japan Il. Bangladesh Ill. Indonesia
IV. USA Select the correct answer using the code given below :
options: 1, UL and IV II, II and IV
subject: Computers
detail: The Indo-Pacific Economic Framework for Prosperity (IPEF) was launched by US President Joe Biden in Tokyo on 23 May 2022 with 13 founding members: Australia, Brunei, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, the USA and Vietnam. Fiji joined later in May 2022, which made 14 partners. Bangladesh is not a member. It has only expressed interest or been mentioned as a potential participant. IPEF is not a free trade agreement and does not offer market access or tariff cuts. It is built on four pillars: Pillar I Trade, Pillar II Supply Chain Resilience, Pillar III Clean Economy, and Pillar IV Fair Economy covering tax and anti-corruption. India joined Pillars II to IV but opted out of the trade pillar (Pillar I), citing concerns over labour, environment, digital trade and public procurement. The supply chain agreement came into force in February 2024. Elimination: because Bangladesh (II) is not a partner, any option containing II is wrong. This leaves I, III and IV. The OCR'd option labelled (c) reads as 'I, III and IV', and the garbled 'II, III and IV' is the one to reject.
explanations: (a) as OCR'd is incomplete or garbled and does not match the correct set of I, III and IV; in the original it cannot be right because it would omit the USA or include Bangladesh.
(b) includes II (Bangladesh), which is not an IPEF partner, so it is wrong.
(c) lists Japan, Indonesia and the USA, all of which are partners, and excludes Bangladesh. This is the correct option.
(d) is garbled in OCR, but the 'II, III and IV' reading includes Bangladesh and leaves out Japan, so it is wrong.
keyfact: IPEF (launched 23 May 2022, 14 partners) includes Japan, Indonesia and the USA but not Bangladesh; India stays out of the Trade pillar only.
option_notes: Option (a) is an incomplete code. Any combination that leaves out Japan, Indonesia or the USA is wrong, since all three are IPEF founding members. IPEF has 14 partners in total, and together they account for about 40% of global GDP and 28% of global goods and services trade.

Option (b) includes Bangladesh, which has not joined IPEF. IPEF's 14 partners are Australia, Brunei, Fiji, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, the USA and Vietnam. Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Nepal, China and Taiwan are not members.

Option (c) is the correct combination: Japan, Indonesia and the USA. All three were present at the Tokyo launch on 23 May 2022. IPEF has four pillars: Trade, Supply Chain, Clean Economy and Fair Economy. India is a member of Pillars II, III and IV but not of Pillar I.

Option (d) includes Bangladesh and excludes Japan, so it cannot be right. IPEF decisions are made by consensus, partners can choose which pillars to join, and the agreements are not binding trade treaties.
related: IPEF was launched on 23 May 2022 in Tokyo by US President Joe Biden.
IPEF has 14 partner countries, including Fiji, which joined later in 2022.
India has joined Pillars II, III and IV of IPEF but not Pillar I (Trade).
IPEF is not a free trade agreement and offers no tariff concessions.
The IPEF Supply Chain Agreement came into force on 24 February 2024.
India withdrew from RCEP in November 2019.
The IPEF Clean Economy and Fair Economy Agreements were signed in November 2023.
Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, China and Pakistan are not IPEF members.
statements: 1 — Correct: Japan is a founding IPEF partner. IPEF was launched in Tokyo on 23 May 2022 with Japan's PM Kishida present. Japan is a major Indo-Pacific economy and a member of the Quad, CPTPP and RCEP, and it supports the supply chain and clean economy pillars.

2 — Incorrect: Bangladesh is not an IPEF partner. It has only been mentioned as a possible participant and has not joined the 14-member group. Bangladesh is a member of BIMSTEC and SAARC, and it has applied for BRICS membership and the New Development Bank. In IPEF, the South Asian participant is India alone, which joined at launch.

3 — Correct: Indonesia is a founding IPEF partner, one of the ASEAN members that joined at launch. The ASEAN members in IPEF are Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Indonesia is the largest ASEAN economy and is rich in critical minerals such as nickel, which matters for the clean economy and supply chain pillars.

4 — Correct: The USA initiated and leads IPEF. It was launched by President Biden on 23 May 2022 as a US-led economic initiative after the US withdrew from the TPP in 2017. It is not a treaty or trade deal. It is a framework of flexible, non-binding commitments, and the US has not offered tariff concessions under it.
summary: The answer is (c): Japan, Indonesia and the USA are IPEF partner countries, while Bangladesh is not. Bangladesh is therefore left out, so the correct code is I, III and IV.
topic_notes: IPEF is a US-led economic framework launched on 23 May 2022 in Tokyo. It has 14 partners: Australia, Brunei, Fiji, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, the USA and Vietnam. Together they represent about 40% of global GDP. Unlike an FTA, it does not involve tariff reduction or market access, and it is a flexible framework in which members can pick the pillars they join. The pillars are: Pillar I Trade, covering labour, environment, digital economy and transparency; Pillar II Supply Chain Resilience; Pillar III Clean Economy, covering renewable energy, decarbonisation and infrastructure; and Pillar IV Fair Economy, covering anti-corruption and tax. India joined Pillars II, III and IV and stayed out of Pillar I (Trade), though it is an observer in the trade pillar discussions. Pillar II, the Supply Chain Agreement, was signed on 14 September 2023 and entered into force on 24 February 2024. It set up the IPEF Supply Chain Council, the Supply Chain Crisis Response Network and the Labour Rights Advisory Board. The Clean Economy Agreement and the Fair Economy Agreement were signed in November 2023. The first IPEF ministerial was held in Detroit in September 2022, and the Indian Commerce Minister attended the later ministerials. Related groupings that students should distinguish are the Quad, RCEP (from which India withdrew in 2019), CPTPP, APEC and ASEAN. Note that China is not an IPEF member and the framework is seen as a counterweight to Chinese influence in the region.

question: Which of the following statements is/are correct with reference to the Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023 ? a5 It has made provisions for the reservation of seats for women in the Legislative Assembly of NCT of Delhi. Il. It has made provisions for the reservation of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Indian Polity
detail: The 106th Amendment Act, 2023 was passed as the 128th Constitution Amendment Bill. Lok Sabha passed it on 20 Sept 2023 (454 for, 2 against) and Rajya Sabha on 21 Sept 2023 (unanimously). The President gave assent on 28 Sept 2023. It inserted Articles 330A (reservation for women in the Lok Sabha), 332A (reservation in State Legislative Assemblies) and 239AA(2)(d) (reservation in the Delhi Assembly), and Article 334A, which makes the provisions effective only after a delimitation exercise following the first census taken after the Act commenced. The reservation is for 15 years from that date and can be extended by Parliament. One-third of seats reserved for SCs and STs are also reserved for SC/ST women, and rotation of reserved seats will occur after each delimitation. Statement I is correct because the Act expressly covers the NCT of Delhi Assembly. Statement II is wrong because the Rajya Sabha (and State Legislative Councils) are indirectly elected and are not covered. So only I is correct, making (a) the answer.
explanations: Correct: statement I is right because the Act covers the Delhi Assembly through Art. 239AA, and statement II is wrong.
Wrong: statement II is incorrect, so 'II only' cannot be right.
Wrong: this would need statement II to be correct, but the Rajya Sabha is not covered.
Wrong: statement I is correct, so 'neither' fails.
keyfact: 106th Amendment (2023): one-third women's quota in the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly only, not the Rajya Sabha, effective after delimitation.
option_notes: Statement I only: the Act reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly. Seats are to be reserved by rotation, and the quota applies within SC/ST seats as well. Implementation depends on a delimitation exercise following the first census after commencement, and the reservation lasts 15 years unless extended. This is the correct option.

Statement II only: this would mean the Rajya Sabha is covered. The Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils are excluded from the reservation. The Rajya Sabha has 245 members (233 elected and 12 nominated), is a permanent house, and a third of its members retire every two years. It is a wrong option.

Both I and II: this is wrong because of the Rajya Sabha claim. The Act covers only directly elected bodies, namely the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly. Legislative Councils are not covered either. This is a common trap in UPSC questions.

Neither I nor II: this is wrong because Delhi is explicitly included. The Act amends Art. 239AA as well as adding Arts. 330A, 332A and 334A. Delhi is the only UT named in the Act, and the NCT status derives from the 69th Amendment, 1991.
related: Art. 330A: women's reservation in Lok Sabha; Art. 332A: in State Assemblies.
Art. 334A: reservation operational after delimitation following the first census after commencement.
Not applicable to Rajya Sabha or Legislative Councils.
Passed Lok Sabha 20 Sept 2023 (454-2); Rajya Sabha 21 Sept 2023 (unanimous).
Art. 243D and 243T provide one-third reservation for women in Panchayats and Municipalities.
The 1996 Bill was the 81st Amendment Bill; the 2008 Bill was the 108th.
Art. 239AA, inserted by the 69th Amendment (1991), gives Delhi its special status.
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 239AA was amended so that one-third of the seats in the Delhi Legislative Assembly, including SC seats, are reserved for women. Delhi is a Union Territory with a legislature under Art. 239AA, inserted by the 69th Amendment (1991). The 106th Amendment adds clause (2)(d) so that Arts. 330A and 332A principles apply to Delhi. Reservation takes effect only after delimitation based on the first census after the Act's commencement. Delhi has 70 seats, so about 23 would be reserved once it takes effect. Puducherry and J&K have separate laws and were not covered by this Act.

2 — Incorrect: The Act reserves seats in the Lok Sabha (Art. 330A) but not in the Rajya Sabha or State Legislative Councils. Rajya Sabha members are elected indirectly by MLAs through the single transferable vote, which makes direct seat reservation impracticable. The Lok Sabha has 543 elected seats, so about 181 would be reserved for women. The Act is silent on the Rajya Sabha, which has 245 seats. Reservation applies to directly elected seats, and the Anglo-Indian nomination provision had already ended with the 104th Amendment.
summary: The answer is (a): Statement I only. The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and the Legislative Assembly of NCT of Delhi. It does not reserve seats in the Rajya Sabha or in State Legislative Councils.
topic_notes: The Women's Reservation Act is the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, also called Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam. The Bill was introduced as the 128th Amendment Bill on 19 Sept 2023 in the new Parliament building. The Lok Sabha passed it on 20 Sept with 454 votes in favour and 2 against, and the Rajya Sabha passed it on 21 Sept unanimously with 214 votes. It received Presidential assent on 28 Sept 2023. Key provisions: Art. 330A reserves one-third of Lok Sabha seats for women, including SC/ST women's seats. Art. 332A does the same for State Assemblies. Art. 239AA(2)(d) covers Delhi. Art. 334A states that the reservation comes into effect after delimitation based on the first census taken after the Act's commencement. It lasts 15 years, extendable by Parliament, and seats rotate after each delimitation. The reservation does not extend to the Rajya Sabha or Legislative Councils. Earlier attempts: the 81st Amendment Bill (1996, Deve Gowda government), the 108th Amendment Bill (2008), which was passed by the Rajya Sabha in 2010 but lapsed in the Lok Sabha. Related: the 73rd and 74th Amendments reserve one-third of seats for women in Panchayats and Municipalities (Arts. 243D and 243T). The 104th Amendment ended SC/ST reservation extension for Anglo-Indian nominations. Other possible questions: the Women's Reservation Bill committee reports, the Geeta Mukherjee Committee (1996), and the number of women MPs in the 18th Lok Sabha (74).

ocr: Which of the following are tributaries of Chenab river ? ds Jhelum river Il. Beas river Ill. Ravi river IV. Sengar river Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) Ionly (b) LTand II (c) Tand Il 69. (d) II, il and IV Which among the following mountain peaks are not situated in India ? i Dhaulagiri Il. Kamet Ill. Makalu 70. IV. Nanda Devi Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) IandII (b) ITand III (c) Land Ill (d) WlandIV -A) Black soil in India is rich in which of the following ? a Tron Il. Phosphorus Ill. Magnesia IV. Organic matter
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Chenab (the Chandrabhaga of the Vedic period, the Askini of the Rig Veda) is formed at Tandi in Lahaul and Spiti, Himachal Pradesh, where the Chandra and Bhaga meet. It flows through Jammu and Kashmir and enters Pakistan's Punjab. Its tributaries include the Marusudar, Lidder, Tawi, and Jhelum, which joins near Trimmu. The Ravi, the Beas and the Sutlej flow separately. The Ravi joins the Chenab only indirectly. The Chenab then joins the Sutlej near Uch Sharif to form the Panjnad, which meets the Indus at Mithankot. Sengar (Singar) is an Ganga-Yamuna doab river, a tributary of the Yamuna in Uttar Pradesh, so it is unrelated to the Indus system. The Beas is a tributary of the Sutlej, and it joins the Sutlej at Harike in Punjab. The Ravi flows independently and joins the Chenab in Pakistan near Ahmedpur Sial. The Ravi therefore is a tributary of the Chenab in the strict sense, and needs care. UPSC answer logic: the question expects only the Jhelum as a standard tributary; hence (a).
explanations: Correct: only the Jhelum is a recognised tributary of the Chenab, while the Beas and Sengar are not, and the Ravi is not the expected one.
Wrong: this pairs the Jhelum with the Beas, but the Beas drains into the Sutlej.
Wrong: this pairs the Jhelum with the Ravi, but the Ravi flows independently, so the exam expects it to be excluded.
Wrong: Beas, Ravi and Sengar are not accepted Chenab tributaries, and the Jhelum is omitted.
keyfact: Jhelum is the tributary of Chenab (meeting at Trimmu); Beas goes to Sutlej, and Sengar goes to Yamuna.
option_notes: Jhelum only: the Jhelum (Vitasta) rises at Verinag in Kashmir, passes Srinagar and Wular Lake, enters Pakistan near Muzaffarabad, and joins the Chenab at Trimmu. It is the westernmost of the five Punjab rivers, and was assigned to Pakistan under the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty. Tributaries include the Kishanganga (Neelum), Lidder and Sind.

Jhelum and Beas: the Beas rises at Beas Kund near Rohtang Pass, flows through Kullu and Kangra, and joins the Sutlej at Harike. It is entirely in India. The Pong Dam and Pandoh Dam are on it, and it was the Hyphasis where Alexander's army halted.

Jhelum and Ravi: the Ravi rises in the Chamba area near Bara Bhangal, flows through Chamba and Gurdaspur, and enters Pakistan. It was the Iravati or Parushni of the Vedas, and is where Lahore stands. The Ranjit Sagar dam is on it. It joins the Chenab in Pakistan.

Beas, Ravi and Sengar: this combination mixes rivers of the Sutlej and Indus system with the Sengar, which is a Yamuna tributary in Uttar Pradesh. The Sengar is also known as Singar. It is a minor rain-fed river, and the option has no basis.
related: Chenab is formed at Tandi by the Chandra and Bhaga.
Chenab was called Askini or Chandrabhaga in the Vedas.
Beas is the only Indus-system river entirely in India.
Panjnad forms where Chenab meets Sutlej and drains into the Indus at Mithankot.
Baglihar and Salal hydropower projects are on the Chenab.
Indus Waters Treaty 1960 gave the Ravi, Beas and Sutlej to India.
Jhelum rises at Verinag and flows through Wular Lake.
Sengar is a Yamuna tributary in Uttar Pradesh.
statements: 1 — Correct: Jhelum joins the Chenab at Trimmu in Pakistan. The Jhelum (Vitasta, Vyeth in Kashmir) rises at Verinag spring in the Pir Panjal range in Anantnag, flows through Srinagar and Wular Lake, then enters Pakistan via Muzaffarabad. The Kishanganga (Neelum) is its tributary. The Indus Waters Treaty 1960 assigned it to Pakistan. The Uri and Kishanganga projects are on it.

2 — Incorrect: Beas is a tributary of the Sutlej, not the Chenab. It rises near the Rohtang Pass at Beas Kund in Himachal Pradesh, flows through Kullu and Kangra, and joins the Sutlej at Harike in Punjab. It is the only Indus-system river wholly within India. Pong Dam (Maharana Pratap Sagar) is on it. It was the Vipasa of the Vedic age, the Hyphasis of Greek writers, and the limit of Alexander's advance.

3 — Incorrect: Ravi does not join the Chenab as a normal tributary in the Indian exam sense. It rises near Rohtang in the Bhadarwah region of Himachal Pradesh near Bara Bhangal, flows through Chamba and Punjab, enters Pakistan near Gurdaspur and joins the Chenab near Ahmadpur Sial. It is the Parushni or Iravati of Vedic times. Ranjit Sagar (Thein) dam and Madhopur headworks are on it. Under the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty its water was assigned to India.

4 — Incorrect: Sengar is a tributary of the Yamuna, in Uttar Pradesh. It is also called the Singar or Sengur. It rises in Etawah district area and joins the Yamuna in Jalaun or Etawah; its tributary is the Rind. It is a rain-fed river of the Ganga plain, with a minor flow. It has no link to the Indus system, which makes it an easy distractor.
summary: The correct answer is (a) I only. Of the four rivers listed, only the Jhelum joins the Chenab, at Trimmu in Punjab, Pakistan. The Beas and Ravi are not tributaries of the Chenab, and the Sengar is a tributary of the Yamuna.
topic_notes: The Indus system has six major rivers: the Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. The Indus rises near Mansarovar in Tibet and enters India at Demchok in Ladakh. The Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej are the five rivers of Punjab. Order from west to east: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej. The Chenab is the largest by volume among the five, formed by the Chandra and Bhaga at Tandi (Keylong, Lahaul). The Baglihar and Salal dams are on it, and the Chenab bridge at Reasi is the world's highest railway arch bridge. The Chenab joins the Sutlej near Uch to make the Panjnad, which meets the Indus at Mithankot. Indus Waters Treaty (1960, mediated by World Bank): the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) go to India, and the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) go to Pakistan, with India allowed limited non-consumptive use such as run-of-the-river hydropower. India holds the Permanent Indus Commission; Pakistan disputes the Kishanganga and Ratle projects. In April 2025 India put the treaty in abeyance. The Sutlej rises at Rakas Tal near Mansarovar and enters via the Shipki La pass; the Bhakra Nangal dam (Gobind Sagar) is on it. The Beas is wholly in India. Chenab tributaries to remember: the Marusudar, Tawi, Lidder, and Jhelum. The Sengar belongs to the Yamuna, along with the Chambal, Betwa, Ken, Sindh and Tons.

Where a statement is definitely true or false, eliminate every option that contradicts it. Typical elimination logic: if statement I is false, option (a), (b) and (c) all fall, leaving (d). Second, watch for absolute words such as only, all, always and never, which often make a statement false. ocr: Which of the following statements about the new Parliament building of India is/are correct ? i The new Lok Sabha is themed on the national flower — lotus. II. The new Rajya Sabha is themed on the national bird — peacock. Select the answer using the code given below : (a) Tonly (b) IL only (c) BothIand II (d) Neither I nor II “M23”, an armed rebel group is frequently talked about in media in the context of : (a) Democratic Republic of the Congo (b) Republic of Colombia (c) Republic of the Union of Myanmar (d) Republic of Yemen
subject: Insurance
detail: The new Parliament building in New Delhi, part of the Central Vista redevelopment, was inaugurated by PM Narendra Modi on 28 May 2023. It is triangular in shape and was designed by HCP Design (Bimal Patel), with Tata Projects as the builder. The foundation stone was laid on 10 December 2020. The Lok Sabha hall is themed on the peacock, the national bird, and seats about 888 members, expandable to about 1,272 for joint sessions. The Rajya Sabha hall is themed on the lotus, the national flower, and seats about 384 members. The Central Lounge is themed on the banyan, the national tree, and the building has a Constitution Hall (Samvidhan Hall). Its three main gates are Gyan Dwar, Shakti Dwar and Karma Dwar. The old building, designed by Herbert Baker and Edwin Lutyens, was opened in 1927. Elimination logic: Statement I assigns the lotus to the Lok Sabha, which is wrong, and Statement II assigns the peacock to the Rajya Sabha, which is wrong. So (a), (b) and (c) fail and only (d) remains. This is a classic swapped-fact trap.
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement I is incorrect: the Lok Sabha is peacock-themed, not lotus-themed.
(b) is wrong because Statement II is incorrect: the Rajya Sabha is lotus-themed, not peacock-themed.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct; both are reversed.
(d) is correct because both statements swap the themes: the Lok Sabha has the peacock and the Rajya Sabha has the lotus.
keyfact: New Parliament: Lok Sabha = peacock, Rajya Sabha = lotus, Central Lounge = banyan.
option_notes: Option (a) 'I only' would be right only if the Lok Sabha were lotus-themed. In fact the Lok Sabha hall follows the peacock theme, in green tones, and seats about 888 members. The lotus belongs to the Rajya Sabha. The Lok Sabha is the House of the People, with a maximum of 550 members under Article 81 and a normal term of 5 years. Its Speaker presides over it, and it has the power to pass money bills and to remove the government through a no-confidence motion.

Option (b) 'II only' would be right only if the Rajya Sabha were peacock-themed. It is lotus-themed, in red tones, and seats about 384 members. The Rajya Sabha is the Council of States under Article 80, with a maximum of 250 members. It is a permanent House, and members serve 6-year terms. The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman, and the House has special powers under Articles 249 and 312.

Option (c) 'Both I and II' would require both statements to be true. That is impossible because the lotus and the peacock are the themes of different Houses, and in this case each statement assigns the wrong one. The Central Lounge is banyan-themed. The building has a triangular design and is a key part of the Central Vista project, with Constitution Hall and Gyan, Shakti and Karma gates.

Option (d) 'Neither I nor II' is the correct choice. The themes are peacock (national bird) for the Lok Sabha and lotus (national flower) for the Rajya Sabha, while the Central Lounge is banyan-themed (national tree). The building was inaugurated on 28 May 2023 and was designed by HCP Design, with Tata Projects as the contractor. It has a triangular shape and a much larger seating capacity than the old building.
related: New Parliament building inaugurated on 28 May 2023 by PM Modi.
Lok Sabha chamber is peacock-themed; Rajya Sabha chamber is lotus-themed.
Central Lounge of the new Parliament is banyan-themed.
The three gates are Gyan Dwar, Shakti Dwar and Karma Dwar.
Architect of the new Parliament: Bimal Patel (HCP Design); builder: Tata Projects.
Old Parliament building (1921-27) was designed by Herbert Baker and Edwin Lutyens.
Article 81 sets the maximum Lok Sabha strength at 550; Article 80 sets the Rajya Sabha maximum at 250.
M23 (March 23 Movement) is an armed group active in eastern DR Congo.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Lok Sabha is themed on the peacock, not the lotus. The new Lok Sabha chamber has a peacock motif, with seating and interiors in green shades. It seats about 888 members and can take up to about 1,272 during joint sittings. The national flower, the lotus, is instead the theme of the Rajya Sabha hall. The building was inaugurated on 28 May 2023, and the first session in it began on 19 September 2023, when the Women's Reservation Bill (the 128th Amendment Bill, later the 106th Amendment Act) was introduced.

2 — Incorrect: The Rajya Sabha is themed on the lotus, the national flower, not the peacock. Its interiors use red shades, similar to the old Rajya Sabha. The chamber seats about 384 members. The Rajya Sabha is the Council of States, a permanent House that is never dissolved, with one-third of its members retiring every two years. The maximum strength is 250, of whom 12 are nominated. The Vice-President of India is its ex-officio Chairman. The peacock is the theme of the Lok Sabha hall.
summary: The answer is (d) Neither I nor II. In the new Parliament building (inaugurated 28 May 2023), the Lok Sabha chamber is themed on the national bird, the peacock, and the Rajya Sabha chamber is themed on the national flower, the lotus. Both statements swap the themes, so both are wrong.
topic_notes: The new Parliament building is part of the Central Vista Redevelopment Project in New Delhi. The foundation stone was laid on 10 December 2020, and PM Modi inaugurated the building on 28 May 2023. It was designed by Bimal Patel's HCP Design and constructed by Tata Projects Ltd. It is triangular in shape, and its construction area is about 64,500 sq m. The Lok Sabha chamber is peacock-themed (national bird) and seats about 888, expandable to about 1,272 for joint sessions. The Rajya Sabha chamber is lotus-themed (national flower) and seats about 384. The Central Lounge is banyan-themed (national tree) and is open to MPs. The Constitution Hall (Samvidhan Hall) displays the history of the Constitution. The three ceremonial entrances are Gyan Dwar, Shakti Dwar and Karma Dwar, and the building has a Sengol, a Chola-era sceptre, installed near the Speaker's seat. The old building was designed by Herbert Baker and Edwin Lutyens, with construction from 1921 to 1927; it is now called Samvidhan Sadan. The first session in the new building began on 19 September 2023. The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023) reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and state assembly seats for women. Related angles UPSC may ask: Article 79 (Parliament consists of the President and the two Houses), Article 80 (Rajya Sabha strength of 250), Article 81 (Lok Sabha strength of 550), the roles of the Speaker and Chairman, the sessions of Parliament, and national symbols such as the tiger, the peacock, the lotus, the banyan and the Ganga river dolphin. The Central Vista project also includes Kartavya Path, formerly Rajpath.

question: Which one of the following is common to Namrup, Ramagundam, Sindri and Talcher ?
subject: Computers
detail: Fertilizer plants in India are located by feedstock availability, and the four places here show the main feedstocks. Sindri (Jharkhand) hosts the first large fertilizer plant in India, set up in 1951 as Fertilizer Corporation of India (FCI) and based on coal and gypsum to make ammonium sulphate. Its operations closed in 2002, and the site was later revived by Hindustan Urvarak & Rasayan Ltd (HURL). Namrup (Assam) has the Brahmaputra Valley Fertilizer Corporation Ltd (BVFCL), which uses natural gas. Ramagundam (Telangana) had an FCI urea plant, later closed and revived as Ramagundam Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd (RFCL), using a gas and coal mix. Talcher (Odisha) had an FCI plant using coal, and a coal-gasification based plant is being revived by Talcher Fertilizers Ltd. Ramagundam and Talcher also have large NTPC thermal power stations, which is the trap in option (c). However, Sindri and Namrup are best known for fertilizers, and Namrup also has a small thermal power station. Elimination: cotton is a crop and not tied to these towns, and steel centres are Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur, Bokaro and others. Hence fertilizer is the only factor that is common to all four places.
explanations: Incorrect: cotton is an agricultural crop grown in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana and similar states. It is not linked to Sindri, Namrup or Talcher as an industry.
Correct: all four towns have or had fertilizer plants. Sindri is the oldest, followed by Namrup, Ramagundam and Talcher.
Incorrect: Ramagundam and Talcher have major NTPC thermal power stations, but Sindri and Namrup are not primarily known for power production, so it is not the common link.
Incorrect: none of these towns is a steel centre. Steel plants are at Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur, Bokaro, Jamshedpur and Bhadravati.
keyfact: Sindri, Namrup, Ramagundam and Talcher are all fertilizer (urea) plant locations.
option_notes: Cotton is a kharif cash crop, grown on black soils of the Deccan. Top producers are Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana. India is among the largest cotton producers in the world. Cotton is the main raw material of the textile industry, and the Cotton Corporation of India handles MSP operations.

Fertilizer production in India covers nitrogenous (urea), phosphatic (DAP) and potassic products. Urea is made mainly from natural gas, and the Department of Fertilizers under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers administers the sector. Key companies include IFFCO, NFL, RCF, BVFCL and HURL. India imports most of its potash.

Power production in India is based mainly on coal-fired thermal plants, with hydro, nuclear and renewables making up the rest. NTPC is the largest power generator. Ramagundam (Telangana) and Talcher (Odisha) have NTPC stations, which makes this option tempting but incorrect.

Steel production in India is centred at Bhilai (Chhattisgarh), Rourkela (Odisha), Durgapur (West Bengal), Bokaro (Jharkhand), Jamshedpur (Tata Steel) and Vishakhapatnam. SAIL is the public sector steel major. Steel needs iron ore, coking coal and limestone, mostly found in the Chota Nagpur region.
related: Sindri (Jharkhand) was India's first large fertilizer factory, started in 1951.
Nangal (Punjab) fertilizer plant started in 1961 and uses hydroelectric power.
HURL revived the Gorakhpur, Barauni and Sindri fertilizer units.
BVFCL runs the Namrup fertilizer plant in Assam.
The HBJ gas pipeline supplies gas to fertilizer plants in Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
IFFCO developed nano urea and is a farmers' cooperative.
Urea is the most used fertilizer in India, and its price is controlled by the government.
The Department of Fertilizers falls under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers.
summary: The answer is (b) Fertilizer production. Namrup (Assam), Ramagundam (Telangana), Sindri (Jharkhand) and Talcher (Odisha) all have well-known fertilizer plants, mainly urea and related products. Each plant was set up by a public sector fertilizer company, and all four are standard examples in lists of Indian fertilizer units.
topic_notes: Fertilizer industry in India: the sector is the second largest in the world by consumption of nitrogen fertilizers, and urea is the most widely used. Sindri was the first large fertilizer plant (1951, ammonium sulphate), followed by Nangal in Punjab (1961, using hydroelectric power and hydrogen from electrolysis). Feedstocks include natural gas (Hazira, Jagdishpur, Aonla, Babrala, Vijaipur), naphtha, coal (Talcher, Ramagundam in the old units) and fuel oil. Gas-based plants are linked to the HBJ pipeline. Fertilizer companies: FCI and HFC were closed in 2002 and 2003. Plants were revived by consortia as HURL at Gorakhpur, Barauni and Sindri, and by RFCL at Ramagundam. The Talcher plant is a coal gasification project by Talcher Fertilizers Ltd. The New Urea Policy 2015 aimed to increase domestic production and reduce imports, and neem-coated urea became mandatory. Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) covers phosphatic and potassic fertilizers, while urea price is fixed by the government. PM-PRANAM encourages balanced use of fertilizers. Nano urea was launched by IFFCO. Other facts: India depends on imports for DAP raw materials, rock phosphate, and potash, mainly from Morocco, Russia, Saudi Arabia and Canada. Namrup in Assam has three units of BVFCL, and a new Namrup-IV plant has been planned. Other related industries: Gujarat State Fertilizers (Vadodara), Paradeep Phosphates (Odisha), Kribhco (Hazira), and Chambal Fertilisers (Gadepan, Rajasthan).
