ocr: Which one of the following is common to Namrup, Ramagundam, Sindri and Talcher ? (a) Cotton production (b) Fertilizer production (c) Power production (d) Steel production
subject: Computers
detail: The four places are linked by fertilizer plants. Namrup (Assam) has the Brahmaputra Valley Fertilizer Corporation Ltd (BVFCL), which uses natural gas as feedstock. Ramagundam (Telangana) has the Ramagundam Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd (RFCL), revived in 2018-2021 from the old FCI unit and run as a joint venture of EIL, NFL and FCIL; it uses neem-coated urea technology and gas feedstock. Sindri (Jharkhand) hosted the first large public-sector fertilizer factory, the Fertilizer Corporation of India (FCI) plant, set up in 1951 and based on coal and gypsum to make ammonium sulphate. It closed in 2002 and was revived as a Hindustan Urvarak and Rasayan Ltd (HURL) unit using gas from the Jagdishpur-Haldia pipeline. Talcher (Odisha) has an old FCI unit that closed in 2002, and a new coal gasification-based urea plant is being built there by Talcher Fertilizers Ltd. Elimination: cotton belongs to Maharashtra, Gujarat and similar states; Sindri and Namrup are not steel centres; and although Talcher and Ramagundam have thermal power stations, Namrup and Sindri are not mainly known for power production. Only fertilizer fits all four.
explanations: Incorrect: cotton production is associated with the black soil regions of Maharashtra, Gujarat and Telangana, not with all four places. Namrup, Sindri and Talcher are not cotton centres.
Correct: each place has or had a fertilizer plant (BVFCL Namrup, RFCL Ramagundam, FCI/HURL Sindri, FCI/Talcher Fertilizers Talcher).
Incorrect: Ramagundam and Talcher have major thermal power stations, but Sindri and Namrup are best known for fertilizers, so power is not the common feature.
Incorrect: steel plants are at Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur, Bokaro, Vishakhapatnam and Salem. None of these four is a steel plant location.
keyfact: Namrup, Ramagundam, Sindri and Talcher are all fertilizer (urea) plant locations in India.
option_notes: Cotton is a Kharif fibre crop that grows best in black (regur) soil. The main producers are Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. India is among the world's largest cotton producers, and the Cotton Corporation of India handles MSP operations. The textile industry is linked to cotton, with centres such as Ahmedabad and Mumbai.

Fertilizer production in India is dominated by urea, DAP and complex fertilizers. The Sindri plant (1951) was the first major public-sector unit. Natural gas is the main feedstock for urea, and the Department of Fertilizers under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers oversees the sector. Neem-coated urea became mandatory in 2015. Major producers include IFFCO, NFL, RCF and KRIBHCO.

Power production in India relies mainly on coal-based thermal plants (about 55 percent of capacity), plus hydro, nuclear and renewables. Talcher (NTPC) and Ramagundam (NTPC, 2,600 MW) are major thermal power centres. NTPC, NHPC and Power Grid are key central public-sector undertakings, and the Electricity Act 2003 governs the sector.

Steel production in India is led by SAIL plants at Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur, Bokaro and Burnpur, plus Tata Steel at Jamshedpur (1907) and JSW. India is the second-largest crude steel producer in the world. Key inputs are iron ore, coking coal and limestone, and the Ministry of Steel oversees the sector.
related: Sindri (1951) was the first large fertilizer plant in India.
Namrup fertilizer plant (BVFCL) is in Assam and uses natural gas.
Talcher is building a coal gasification-based urea plant in Odisha.
Ramagundam Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd (RFCL) is in Telangana and was revived in 2018-2021.
Neem-coated urea was made mandatory in 2015.
IFFCO launched nano urea in 2021.
The HBJ pipeline carries gas to many urea plants.
The NBS scheme has applied to P and K fertilizers since 2010.
summary: The answer is (b) Fertilizer production. Namrup (Assam), Ramagundam (Telangana), Sindri (Jharkhand) and Talcher (Odisha) are all well-known fertilizer plant locations in India, mostly urea and related products.
topic_notes: Fertilizer industry in India: Fertilizers are chemical inputs that supply nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK). Urea is the most used fertilizer in India, followed by DAP. The Fertilizer Corporation of India was set up in 1961, with Sindri as its first plant (1951). The plant was closed in 2002 after the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) wound up FCI and HFCL. Gas-based plants such as Hazira, Jagdishpur, Aonla, Babrala and Kakinada use gas from the HBJ pipeline. Government revival in 2016 allowed the closed units at Gorakhpur, Sindri, Barauni, Ramagundam and Talcher to restart under new management. The new urea policy of 2015 set energy-efficiency targets, and the Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) scheme from 2010 applies to P and K fertilizers, while urea remains under a controlled price. Feedstocks include natural gas, naphtha, fuel oil and coal gasification, as at Talcher. India imports potash and phosphate raw materials from countries such as Morocco, Russia, Saudi Arabia and Canada. The PM-PRANAM scheme (2023) promotes balanced fertilizer use, and nano urea (IFFCO) was launched in 2021. Major producers are IFFCO (Phulpur, Kalol, Kandla, Aonla), KRIBHCO (Hazira), NFL (Nangal, Panipat, Bathinda, Vijaipur), RCF (Trombay, Thal) and Chambal Fertilisers.

ocr: Which one of the following is common to Namrup, Ramagundam, Sindri and Talcher ? (a) Cotton production (b) Fertilizer production (c) Power production (d) Steel production
subject: Computers
detail: All four places are linked with fertilizer units. Namrup in Assam has the Brahmaputra Valley Fertilizer Corporation Ltd (BVFCL) urea plant, which uses natural gas. Ramagundam in Telangana hosted the Ramagundam Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd (RFCL), a revived urea plant of FCIL, now run by a joint venture of NFL, EIL and FCIL and using gas. Sindri in Jharkhand has the first large fertilizer plant in India, set up in 1951 by the Fertiliser Corporation of India (FCIL), and it was revived in 2022 as a coal-gasification based urea plant under Hindustan Urvarak and Rasayan Ltd (HURL). Talcher in Odisha had an FCIL plant, and a new coal-gasification based urea project is being set up there by Talcher Fertilizers Ltd. Several of these places also have power stations (Ramagundam NTPC and Talcher NTPC), which is the trap in option (c), but Namrup and Sindri are not known for a common power link. Cotton and steel do not fit any of the four. The common thread is fertilizers, so (b) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: Cotton is a textile/agri industry linked to Maharashtra, Gujarat and similar regions, not to these four places.
Correct: Namrup, Ramagundam, Sindri and Talcher all have or had urea or fertilizer plants.
Incorrect: Ramagundam and Talcher have NTPC power stations, but Namrup and Sindri are not mainly known for power, so power is not the common thread.
Incorrect: Steel plants are at Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur, Bokaro and others, not at these four places.
keyfact: Namrup, Ramagundam, Sindri and Talcher are all fertilizer (urea) plant locations; Sindri (1951) was the first large one.
option_notes: Cotton production: India is among the largest cotton producers, with Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana as top states. Cotton is grown on black (regur) soil and is a kharif crop. It is a key fibre crop that supports the textile industry, and the Cotton Corporation of India (CCI) handles MSP procurement. Cotton is not a manufacturing theme for these four places.

Fertilizer production: India's fertilizer industry is dominated by urea, DAP and complex fertilizers. Sindri (1951) was the first major plant. Natural gas is the main feedstock for urea, and the sector is supported by the Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme and urea subsidy. Companies include NFL, RCF, IFFCO, KRIBHCO, BVFCL and HURL. India imports a lot of potash and phosphates.

Power production: India's power comes mainly from coal-based thermal plants (around 50-55% of capacity), with hydro, nuclear and renewables making up the rest. NTPC is the largest generator. Ramagundam (Telangana) and Talcher (Odisha) host large NTPC stations, but power is not the feature common to all four places in this question.

Steel production: Major steel plants are Bhilai (Chhattisgarh), Rourkela (Odisha), Durgapur (West Bengal), Bokaro (Jharkhand), Burnpur and Salem, together with private producers such as Tata Steel at Jamshedpur. SAIL is the main public-sector steel producer. India is the second largest crude steel producer in the world.
related: Sindri (1951) was India's first large fertilizer plant.
Namrup fertilizer plant is run by BVFCL in Assam.
Talcher in Odisha is a coal-gasification based urea project.
Ramagundam (Telangana) has RFCL, a gas-based urea plant, and an NTPC power plant.
Natural gas is the main feedstock for urea in India.
Neem-coated urea was made mandatory in 2015.

IFFCO is the world's largest fertilizer cooperative.
summary: The answer is (b) Fertilizer production. Namrup (Assam), Ramagundam (Telangana), Sindri (Jharkhand) and Talcher (Odisha) are all well-known fertilizer plant locations in India.
topic_notes: Fertilizer industry in India: India is the second largest consumer of fertilizers and the second largest producer of urea. The first modern fertilizer plant was set up at Ranipet (Tamil Nadu) in 1906, and the first large-scale plant was Sindri (Jharkhand) in 1951 by the Fertiliser Corporation of India (FCIL), which made ammonium sulphate. FCIL and HFCL were closed in 2002 and later revived, and Sindri was restarted as HURL. Urea is the most used fertilizer, followed by DAP and NPK. Natural gas is the main feedstock, which is why plants are located at Namrup (Assam), at Hazira, Kakinada, Jagdishpur, Aonla and similar places along gas pipelines such as HBJ. Coal gasification is now being used at Talcher. Policy: Urea is under the Urea Subsidy (MRP fixed), and phosphatic and potassic fertilizers are under the Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) scheme. The New Urea Policy 2015 aims to reduce imports and raise energy efficiency, and neem-coated urea became compulsory in 2015. Nano urea was launched by IFFCO. Main players: IFFCO (cooperative, Phulpur and Kalol), KRIBHCO (Hazira), NFL, RCF, BVFCL, Chambal and Tata Chemicals. The Department of Fertilizers is under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. India imports potash largely from Canada, Russia and Belarus, and phosphate and DAP from Morocco and Saudi Arabia. Related: Green Revolution use of fertilizer, soil health card scheme, PM-PRANAM scheme to cut chemical fertilizer use and 'One Nation One Fertiliser' (Bharat brand).

ocr: Consider the following statements : 74. 1 Atal Tinkering Labs are meant for the high school students. II. Atal Incubation Centres are meant for the graduate and post-graduate students. Which of the statements given above is/are | 75. correct ? (a) ILonly (b) ILonly (c) BothI and II (d) Neither I nor II 76.
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Both schemes sit under the Atal Innovation Mission (AIM), NITI Aayog's flagship initiative launched in 2016 to promote innovation and entrepreneurship. Atal Tinkering Labs target school students in Classes 6-12. They provide hands-on equipment such as 3D printers, robotics kits, sensors and electronics so that children build problem-solving, design thinking and computational skills. Atal Incubation Centres support start-ups and scale-up businesses. They are hosted by universities, research institutions, corporates and other organisations, and they offer infrastructure, mentoring, capital linkages and networking. Their beneficiaries are start-up founders and innovators, who need not be students at all, so limiting them to graduate and post-graduate students makes Statement II wrong. Elimination logic: Statement I matches the scheme's design, which rules out (b) and (d). Statement II is restrictive and factually wrong, which rules out (c). Only (a) remains. Related AIM programmes include Atal Community Innovation Centres (ACIC), Atal New India Challenges and Mentor of Change.
explanations: Correct. Statement I is true, since ATLs are for school students, and Statement II is false, since AICs serve start-ups generally, so only I is correct.
Wrong. Statement II is incorrect because AICs are not restricted to graduate and post-graduate students.
Wrong. Statement II is false, so 'Both I and II' cannot be right.
Wrong. Statement I is true, so 'Neither' cannot be right.
keyfact: ATL = school students (Classes 6-12); AIC = start-up incubation, not limited to graduates; both are under AIM, NITI Aayog.
option_notes: Statement I only: ATLs are Atal Innovation Mission workspaces in schools for Classes 6-12. They provide funding of up to Rs 20 lakh over five years and offer equipment such as 3D printers, robotics kits, electronics and sensors. They promote curiosity, creativity and STEM skills. AIM was launched in 2016 under NITI Aayog and is headed by a Mission Director. This option is correct because it recognises ATL as a school-level scheme and rejects the narrow description of AICs.

Statement II only: This would hold only if AICs were limited to graduate and post-graduate students. In fact AICs are incubators for start-ups and innovators, hosted by institutions or companies, with up to Rs 10 crore of grant over five years. They offer mentoring, infrastructure, and links to funding and markets. They are open to entrepreneurs generally, so the restriction makes this option wrong.

Both I and II: This would require both statements to be correct. ATL is correctly described, but the AIC description is too narrow. AICs are part of AIM's ecosystem for start-ups, not a student-only scheme. Related programmes include ACICs, Atal New India Challenges, ARISE-ANIC and the Mentor of Change programme. This option is wrong.

Neither I nor II: This would mean ATLs are not for high school students, which is false. ATLs are specifically school-based innovation labs for Classes 6-12, and they are AIM's best-known grassroots initiative. Since Statement I holds, this option is wrong.
related: Atal Innovation Mission was launched in 2016 under NITI Aayog.
ATLs are for school students in Classes 6 to 12.
ATL grant is up to Rs 20 lakh over five years.
AIC grant is up to Rs 10 crore over five years.
ACICs target underserved and unserved regions of India.
Atal New India Challenges support product innovations that address national problems.
Mentor of Change connects mentors with ATL students.
Startup India was launched on 16 January 2016.
statements: 1 — Correct: ATLs are meant for school students in Classes 6 to 12 (the high school and middle school age group). ATLs are innovation workspaces set up in schools under AIM, NITI Aayog, with a grant of up to Rs 20 lakh over five years (Rs 10 lakh for set-up and Rs 10 lakh for operations and maintenance). They house DIY kits, 3D printers, robotics and IoT tools. The aim is to build scientific temper, creativity and design thinking among young learners. Thousands of ATLs have been sanctioned across India, in government and private schools. The scheme was announced in 2016, and AIM also runs the Tinkering Marathon and a Mentor of Change programme linked to the labs.

2 — Incorrect: AICs are not meant only for graduate and post-graduate students. They are business incubators that nurture start-ups and innovators across sectors. They are hosted by universities, institutes, corporates and other entities, and they receive grant support of up to Rs 10 crore over five years from AIM. They provide co-working space, mentoring, funding links, lab access and networking. Anyone with a start-up idea, including non-students and entrepreneurs, can be incubated. AIM also supports Atal Community Innovation Centres (ACIC) in underserved regions, and the Atal New India Challenges encourage technology product innovation.
summary: The answer is (a) I only. Atal Tinkering Labs (ATL) are set up in schools for students of Classes 6 to 12, so Statement I is correct. Atal Incubation Centres (AIC) support start-up entrepreneurs and innovators in general, not only graduate and post-graduate students, so Statement II is incorrect.
topic_notes: Atal Innovation Mission (AIM) is NITI Aayog's flagship initiative, launched in 2016, to build an innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem in India. It works at several levels. At school level, Atal Tinkering Labs (ATL) are set up in schools for Classes 6-12, with a grant of Rs 20 lakh over five years. They provide DIY kits, robotics, 3D printers and electronics. At the start-up level, Atal Incubation Centres (AIC) are set up to nurture start-ups, with a grant of up to Rs 10 crore over five years. AICs may be hosted by universities, research institutions or corporates. Atal Community Innovation Centres (ACIC) serve underserved and unserved regions such as Tier 2 and 3 cities, aspirational districts and rural areas. Atal New India Challenges fund product innovations that address national and social problems in areas like agriculture, health and water, with grants of up to Rs 50 lakh to start-ups and MSMEs. ARISE-ANIC supports MSMEs. The Mentor of Change programme connects professionals as mentors to ATL students. Other AIM initiatives include the Atal Tinkering Marathon and Atal Sampark. Related national schemes include Startup India (launched 16 January 2016), Stand-Up India, the Fund of Funds for Startups run by SIDBI, and the National Innovation and Startup Policy for higher education institutions. Possible future questions: which ministry or body runs AIM, the eligible classes for ATLs, grant amounts, the purpose of ACICs, and the difference between incubators and accelerators.

question: Which one of the following awards is equated with Param Vir Chakra (PVC), the highest award for bravery in war ?
subject: Computers
detail: India's gallantry awards come in two series. The first series is the Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra and Vir Chakra, given for gallantry in the face of the enemy in war. The second series is the Ashoka Chakra, Kirti Chakra and Shaurya Chakra, given for gallantry in peacetime. They are equated in order: PVC is matched by Ashoka Chakra, MVC by Kirti Chakra, and VC by Shaurya Chakra. All were instituted on 4 January 1950, with effect from 15 August 1947. The Ashoka Chakra was originally called the Ashoka Chakra Class I, was renamed in 1967, and can be awarded posthumously. The award can go to civilians as well as military personnel, and the medal carries a lotus-wreath design. Elimination: the Param Vishisht Seva Medal is a distinguished service award, not a gallantry award, so it is wrong. The Kirti Chakra ranks one level below the Ashoka Chakra and corresponds to the Maha Vir Chakra. The Sena/Vayu Sena/Nau Sena Medal is a lower-level gallantry award for devotion to duty or gallantry, corresponding to the Shaurya Chakra series only in the lower tier. This leaves Ashoka Chakra as the answer.
explanations: (a) Wrong. The Param Vishisht Seva Medal is a distinguished service award for exceptionally high-order service, not a gallantry award, so it is not equated with the PVC.
(b) Wrong. The Kirti Chakra is the second-ranked peacetime gallantry award and is equated with the Maha Vir Chakra, not the PVC.
(c) Correct. The Ashoka Chakra is the highest peacetime gallantry award and is the counterpart of the Param Vir Chakra.
(d) Wrong. The Sena/Vayu Sena Medal is a lower-tier award for gallantry or devotion to duty and is far below the PVC in precedence.
keyfact: PVC, MVC, VC (war) match Ashoka Chakra, Kirti Chakra, Shaurya Chakra (peace).
option_notes: The Param Vishisht Seva Medal (PVSM) was instituted in 1960 and is the highest of the distinguished service medals. It is awarded for exceptionally distinguished service of the highest order, mainly to senior officers of the armed forces. It is followed by the Ati Vishisht Seva Medal (AVSM) and the Vishisht Seva Medal (VSM). It is not a gallantry award and is not linked to bravery in action.

The Kirti Chakra is the second-highest peacetime gallantry award in India. It was instituted in 1952 as the Ashoka Chakra Class II and renamed in 1967. It is awarded for conspicuous gallantry other than in the face of the enemy. It can be given to civilians and to military personnel, and it may be awarded posthumously. It corresponds to the Maha Vir Chakra in precedence.

The Ashoka Chakra is India's highest peacetime gallantry award. It is given for the most conspicuous bravery or valour, or self-sacrifice, away from the battlefield. It was instituted on 4 January 1950 as the Ashoka Chakra Class I and given its present name in 1967. It is open to civilians and military personnel and may be awarded posthumously. It is the peacetime equivalent of the Param Vir Chakra.

The Sena Medal, Nau Sena Medal and Vayu Sena Medal are awarded to Army, Navy and Air Force personnel respectively. They recognise individual acts of gallantry or devotion to duty. Instituted in 1960, these medals are below the Shaurya Chakra in the order of precedence. They are not equal to the PVC.
related: Param Vir Chakra: highest wartime gallantry award, instituted 26 January 1950, effective 15 August 1947.
First PVC: Major Somnath Sharma, 1947.
PVC was designed by Savitri Khanolkar.
Ashoka Chakra is the peacetime counterpart of the PVC.
Kirti Chakra corresponds to the Maha Vir Chakra; Shaurya Chakra corresponds to the Vir Chakra.
The Param Vishisht Seva Medal is a distinguished service award, not a gallantry award.
Captain Vikram Batra received the PVC (posthumous) for Kargil.
summary: The answer is (c) Ashok Chakra. It is India's highest peacetime gallantry award and is regarded as the peacetime equivalent of the Param Vir Chakra, which is given for gallantry in the face of the enemy in war. Of the options, it is the only one that sits at the same level of the gallantry order of precedence.
topic_notes: India's gallantry awards are in two sets. In the wartime set the order is Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra and Vir Chakra. In the peacetime set the order is Ashoka Chakra, Kirti Chakra and Shaurya Chakra. All were instituted on 4 January 1950, with effect from 15 August 1947, and the peacetime series was originally named Ashoka Chakra Class I, II and III. The PVC was designed by Savitri Khanolkar, and its medal is made of bronze with the Indra's Vajra motif. The first PVC was awarded to Major Somnath Sharma of the Kumaon Regiment in 1947. Only 21 PVCs have been awarded, and Captain Vikram Batra and Subedar Major Sanjay Kumar are among the living and posthumous recipients from the Kargil war. Distinguished service awards form a separate series: Param Vishisht Seva Medal, Uttam Yudh Seva Medal, Ati Vishisht Seva Medal, Yudh Seva Medal, Vishisht Seva Medal and Sena Medal series. The Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri are civilian honours and are separate from military gallantry awards. Gallantry awards can be awarded posthumously and carry a monthly allowance. Questions often ask which award matches which rank, who designed the PVC, who was the first recipient, and which awards are for peacetime. Remember: PVC with AC, MVC with KC, VC with SC.

question:
Consider the following seas :
I. Baltic Sea 77.
II. Caspian Sea Ill. North Sea
IV. White Sea The Russian Federation has borders with how many of the above seas ?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Russia is the largest country in the world and borders 12 seas and 3 oceans (Arctic, Pacific, and the Atlantic through the Baltic and Black Seas). The Baltic Sea is reached at St Petersburg on the Gulf of Finland and at Kaliningrad Oblast, an exclave between Poland and Lithuania. The Caspian Sea, the world's largest inland water body, is shared by five littoral states: Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan. The White Sea is an inlet of the Barents Sea on Russia's northwest coast, with ports such as Arkhangelsk. The North Sea is an arm of the Atlantic bordered by the UK, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Russia lies nowhere near it, as Norway and the Baltic region separate them. Elimination: because I, II and IV are valid, options (a) and (b) are wrong. Option (d) is wrong because it requires the North Sea. So (c) is correct. Do not confuse the Barents Sea, which Russia and Norway share, with the North Sea.
explanations: (a) is wrong because Russia has coasts on three of the listed seas, not one.
(b) is wrong because it undercounts. The Baltic, Caspian and White Seas all border Russia, which makes three.
(c) is correct because the Baltic, Caspian and White Seas border Russia, while the North Sea does not.
(d) is wrong because the North Sea is not on Russia's border. It lies between Britain and Scandinavia and continental Europe.
keyfact: Russia touches the Baltic, Caspian and White Seas, but not the North Sea.
option_notes: Only one: this would hold only for a country with one of these seas on its coast. Examples are Germany (the Baltic and North Seas, so two) and Iran (the Caspian only). For Russia the count is higher. The four seas are very different: the Baltic is brackish and shallow, the Caspian is an inland sea, the North Sea is an Atlantic marginal sea, and the White Sea is an Arctic inlet.

Only two: this would fit countries such as Germany (Baltic and North Sea) or Kazakhstan, which has only the Caspian and the Aral Sea. Russia's count is higher. A good habit is to list each country's littoral seas. Russia's include the Baltic, Black, Azov, Caspian, Barents, White, Kara, Laptev, East Siberian, Chukchi, Bering and Okhotsk Seas, plus the Sea of Japan.

Only three: this is the correct option. Russia touches the Baltic, Caspian and White Seas. It also touches the Black Sea, Azov, Barents, Kara, Laptev, East Siberian, Chukchi, Bering, Okhotsk and Japan seas. The North Sea is the one in the list it does not reach. Remember this selection pattern as a test of whether you know the North Sea's littoral states.

All four: this would need Russia to have a North Sea coast, which it does not. The North Sea states are the UK, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Russia is separated from it by Norway, Finland, Sweden and the Baltic region, and its nearest Atlantic-linked waters are the Barents and Baltic Seas.
related: The Caspian Sea has five littoral states: Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan.
The Black Sea borders six countries, including Russia, Ukraine and Turkey.
The Kerch Strait links the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
The White Sea–Baltic Canal was built in the 1930s.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave on the Baltic between Poland and Lithuania.
The North Sea connects to the Baltic through the Skagerrak and Kattegat.
The Barents Sea is shared by Russia and Norway.
The Northern Sea Route runs along Russia's Arctic coast.
statements: I — Correct: Russia borders the Baltic Sea. Its Baltic coast includes the Gulf of Finland, where St Petersburg and Ust-Luga lie, and Kaliningrad Oblast. The Baltic is a brackish, shallow, almost landlocked sea that connects to the North Sea through the Danish straits (Øresund, Great Belt, Little Belt). Its littoral states are Russia, Finland, Sweden, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Germany and Denmark. Finland and Sweden joined NATO in 2023 and 2024, so Russia's Baltic access is now bordered mostly by NATO members.

II — Correct: Russia borders the Caspian Sea along its southwestern edge, in Dagestan, Kalmykia and Astrakhan, where the Volga delta reaches the sea. The Caspian is the world's largest enclosed inland water body, with a surface about 371,000 sq km and a salinity lower than the oceans. The five littoral states signed the Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea at Aktau in 2018. It holds large oil and gas reserves and sturgeon fisheries, and its level is below mean sea level.

III — Incorrect: Russia has no North Sea coast. The North Sea is a marginal sea of the Atlantic between Great Britain and continental Europe. Its littoral countries are the UK, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France. It has major oil and gas fields (Brent, Forties) and the Dogger Bank fishing ground. It connects to the Baltic via the Skagerrak and Kattegat, and to the Atlantic via the English Channel and the Norwegian Sea.

IV — Correct: Russia borders the White Sea, an inlet of the Barents Sea in the northwest, and it lies wholly within Russian territory. It is linked to the Baltic by the White Sea–Baltic Canal, which was built in the 1930s. Its main gulfs are Onega Bay, Dvina Bay and Mezen Bay, and its ports include Arkhangelsk and Severodvinsk. It freezes for part of the year, and the Solovetsky Islands lie in it.
summary: The answer is (c) Only three. Russia has coastlines on the Baltic Sea (Gulf of Finland and the Kaliningrad exclave), the Caspian Sea (Dagestan, Kalmykia, Astrakhan) and the White Sea (Arkhangelsk, Karelia, Murmansk). It has no coast on the North Sea.
topic_notes: Russia has the longest coastline of any country except Canada, Indonesia and Norway by some measures, about 37,000 km, along the Arctic and Pacific oceans and inland seas. Arctic seas are the Barents, White, Kara, Laptev, East Siberian and Chukchi. Pacific seas are the Bering, Okhotsk and Japan. Western seas are the Baltic, Black and Azov, and the Caspian is inland. Key straits and canals: the Bosporus and Dardanelles control Black Sea access, and the Kerch Strait links the Azov and Black Seas. The Volga-Don Canal links the Caspian with the Black Sea basin, and the White Sea–Baltic Canal links the White and Baltic Seas. The Northern Sea Route follows Russia's Arctic coast. Caspian: the largest inland water body, shared by five states, with the 2018 Aktau Convention. Baltic: the Danish straits connect it to the North Sea, and it is brackish. North Sea: its littoral states are the UK, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France. The Black Sea is bordered by Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Bulgaria, Turkey and Georgia. Landlocked seas commonly asked about include the Aral, Dead and Caspian. Exam tips: practise map-based questions on which seas border which countries, and note that Russia does not touch the Mediterranean, Red or North Seas.

ocr: Which one of the following was the first temple-entry Satyagraha Movement ? (a) Vaikom Satyagraha (b) Nagpur Flag Satyagraha (c) Tarakeswar Satyagraha (ad) Guru-ka-Bagh Satyagraha Maitree Super Thermal Power Project is related to which of the following two countries ? (a) India — Nepal (b) India — Bangladesh (c) India — Bhutan (d) India—Sri Lanka Mission Sagar is the name given to the Indian Navy’s efforts to : (a) clean seas of waste and increase awareness about cleanliness. (b) bring home the stranded Indians from war-torn nations abroad. (c) make efforts to reach out to neighbouring countri
subject: Indian Freedom Struggle & Culture
detail: The Vaikom Satyagraha (30 March 1924 to November 1925) was a non-violent protest against untouchability and the denial of access to the public roads leading to the Vaikom Mahadeva temple. T.K. Madhavan, K. Kelappan, K.P. Kesava Menon and George Joseph led it, with the Ezhava leader and reformer Sree Narayana Guru supporting the cause. It began under the Kerala Pradesh Congress Committee, and Gandhi visited Vaikom in March 1925. Caste Hindus, Christians and Sikhs (Akalis) took part and helped with food. The Travancore regent Rani Sethu Lakshmi Bai and the police commissioner W.H. Pitt dealt with the protest, and a settlement in 1925 opened three of the four approach roads. The Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 later opened all state temples. Elimination: the Nagpur Flag Satyagraha (1923) was about the national flag, and Guru-ka-Bagh (1921-22) was a Sikh gurdwara-reform morcha. Tarakeswar (1924) was a protest against the corrupt mahant of a Bengal temple and was not a caste-based temple-entry movement.
explanations: Correct. Vaikom (1924-25) was the first major satyagraha for the right of the depressed classes to use the roads around a temple and enter it, and Gandhi guided it.
Incorrect. The Nagpur Flag Satyagraha (1923) was about the right to hoist the Congress tricolour in the civil lines. It had nothing to do with temples.
Incorrect. The Tarakeswar Satyagraha (1924, Bengal) was against the mahant's mismanagement and corruption in the temple's funds. It was not mainly about caste-based entry and came after Vaikom began.
Incorrect. Guru-ka-Bagh (1921-22) was an Akali agitation to free Sikh gurdwaras from mahants and to protect the right to collect firewood. It was not a temple-entry movement.
keyfact: Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25, Travancore) was the first temple-entry and access movement, led by T.K. Madhavan and K. Kelappan with Gandhi's guidance.
option_notes: The Vaikom Satyagraha began on 30 March 1924 in Travancore, in what is now Kerala. It opposed the ban on avarnas (Ezhavas and Pulayas) using the roads near the Vaikom Mahadeva temple. T.K. Madhavan, K. Kelappan and George Joseph led it. Gandhi visited in 1925 and negotiated with the orthodox Namboodiris. It ended in November 1925 with partial success, and the Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 completed the reform.

The Nagpur Flag Satyagraha ran from 1923 to 1924 and was a nationalist protest. Congress workers wanted to take the national flag in procession through the civil lines of Nagpur, which the British had banned. Jamnalal Bajaj, Vallabhbhai Patel and Rajendra Prasad were associated with it. It ended with an agreement in August 1923 allowing the flag to be hoisted.

The Tarakeswar Satyagraha took place in 1924 in Hooghly, Bengal. It was led by Swami Vishwanand and supported by Chittaranjan Das's Swaraj Party, which opposed the mahant Satish Giri's control over the Tarakeswar Shiva temple. The mahant's misuse of temple funds was the main cause. It succeeded when the mahant resigned and was a temple-management reform, not a caste-entry movement.

Guru-ka-Bagh Morcha (1921-22) was part of the Akali movement, near Ghukewali, Amritsar. The Akalis demanded a gurdwara free from the corrupt mahant, and the police beat the unarmed Akali jathas. C.F. Andrews's reporting drew national attention. The Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925 later handed control of gurdwaras to the SGPC.
related: Vaikom Satyagraha: 1924-25, Travancore, led by T.K. Madhavan and K. Kelappan.
Guruvayur Satyagraha: 1931-32, led by K. Kelappan.
Temple Entry Proclamation: 1936, Travancore, Maharaja Chithira Thirunal.
Mahad Satyagraha: 1927, led by Dr B.R. Ambedkar for the Chavdar tank.
Kalaram Temple Satyagraha: Nashik, 1930, led by Ambedkar.
Harijan Sevak Sangh: founded by Gandhi in 1932.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
Periyar E.V. Ramasamy was known as Vaikom Veerar.
summary: The answer is (a) Vaikom Satyagraha. It was launched in 1924 at Vaikom in the princely state of Travancore (Kerala) to win the right for lower-caste Ezhavas and Untouchables to use the roads around the Mahadeva temple. It is regarded as the first organised temple-entry and access movement in India. (The image shows three questions and does not mark Q74, so I have treated the first one, on temple-entry movements, as Q74.)
topic_notes: Temple-entry and anti-untouchability movements formed a key strand of social reform in the 1920s and 1930s. The Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25) was the first of them, led by T.K. Madhavan and K. Kelappan. Gandhi visited in 1925, and the movement ended with a settlement and the opening of roads. Periyar E.V. Ramasamy took part and came to be called 'Vaikom Veerar'. Sree Narayana Guru consecrated a Shiva idol at Aruvippuram in 1888 and founded SNDP Yogam in 1903. The Guruvayur Satyagraha (1931-32) was led by K. Kelappan and Gandhi supported it. The Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936, issued by Maharaja Chithira Thirunal on the advice of Dewan C.P. Ramaswamy Iyer, opened all state temples to all Hindus. Gandhi founded the Harijan Sevak Sangh in 1932 after the Poona Pact, and his weekly Harijan began in 1933. Madras Temple Entry Authorisation and Indemnity Act (1939) was brought by C. Rajagopalachari. Dr Ambedkar led the Mahad Satyagraha (1927) for the right to use the Chavdar tank, and the Kalaram Temple Satyagraha at Nashik (1930) for temple entry. Article 17 of the Constitution abolishes untouchability, and the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 enforces it. Other related agitations include the Akali movement (Guru-ka-Bagh, Nankana Sahib 1921), the Nagpur Flag Satyagraha (1923) and Bardoli (1928).

question:
Consider the following Vice Presidents of India : Is Dr. S. Radhakrishnan Il. Dr. Zakir Husain Ill. Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma
IV. Mohammad Hamid Ansari How many of the above completed two terms in office ?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Vice President of India is elected under Article 66 by an electoral college of members of both Houses of Parliament, including nominated members. The term is five years under Article 67, but the holder continues until a successor takes charge. The Constitution places no bar on re-election. Only two Vice Presidents have completed two full terms: Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (13 May 1952 to 12 May 1962) and Mohammad Hamid Ansari (11 Aug 2007 to 10 Aug 2017). Dr. Zakir Husain was VP from 1962 to 1967 and then became the third President. He resigned as VP on 12 May 1967 and died in office as President in 1969. Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma was VP from 1987 to 1992 and then became the ninth President. Both served exactly one VP term. So only items I and IV qualify. Eliminate (a), (c) and (d), because any option that counts Husain or Sharma is wrong. The VP is also ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha under Article 89.
explanations: Wrong. Two Vice Presidents, not one, completed two terms: Radhakrishnan and Ansari.
Correct. Only Radhakrishnan (1952-62) and Hamid Ansari (2007-17) served two full terms. Husain and Sharma left after one term to become President.
Wrong. This would require counting Husain or Sharma, who each served only one VP term.
Wrong. Husain and Sharma did not serve two terms as VP, so not all four qualify.
keyfact: Only Radhakrishnan (1952-62) and Hamid Ansari (2007-17) served two full terms as Vice President.
option_notes: Only one: this would be the case if only Radhakrishnan counted. It is incorrect because Ansari also served two terms. The VP has a five-year term under Article 67 and can be re-elected without limit. Radhakrishnan was the first VP (1952-62), and the five-year term applies to every VP.

Only two: this is the correct count. Radhakrishnan was VP for 1952-62 and Hamid Ansari for 2007-17, each with two consecutive five-year terms. They are the only two VPs to complete two full terms. Both were scholars or diplomats before taking office. The VP is elected by an electoral college of MPs of both Houses by proportional representation using the single transferable vote.

Only three: this would wrongly include Husain or Sharma. Both moved up to the Presidency after one VP term. Several VPs became President: Radhakrishnan, Zakir Husain, V.V. Giri, G.S. Pathak (no, Pathak did not), R. Venkataraman, S.D. Sharma and K.R. Narayanan. Pathak served as VP (1969-74) but never became President.

All four: this is incorrect. Zakir Husain (1962-67) and Shankar Dayal Sharma (1987-92) served single terms. The VP office is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 89). The VP acts as President during a vacancy for up to six months, under Article 65.

statements: I — Correct: Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was elected unopposed in 1952 and re-elected in 1957, completing two terms (1952-62). He was the first Vice President of India and later the second President (1962-67). He was a philosopher and academic, a former Vice-Chancellor of BHU and Andhra University, and a Spalding Professor at Oxford. He was also Ambassador to the USSR. His birthday, 5 September, is celebrated as Teachers' Day. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1954, in the first batch of recipients.

II — Incorrect: Dr. Zakir Husain was the second Vice President (1962-67) and served only one term. He was elected President in 1967 and resigned as VP on 12 May 1967. He died on 3 May 1969, the first President to die in office. He was a co-founder of Jamia Millia Islamia, serving as its Vice-Chancellor, and later Governor of Bihar and Vice-Chancellor of AMU. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1963. He was the third President of India.

III — Incorrect: Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma was the eighth Vice President (3 Sept 1987 to 24 July 1992) and served one term. He was then elected the ninth President (1992-97). Earlier he was Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh and Governor of Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and Maharashtra. He was also Union Communications Minister and Congress President. As VP he chaired the Rajya Sabha. He was a Cambridge-educated lawyer and died in 1999.

IV — Correct: Mohammad Hamid Ansari was the 12th Vice President. He was elected in 2007 and re-elected in 2012, serving until 10 Aug 2017. He is a former diplomat (IFS), served as Ambassador to the UAE, Afghanistan, Iran and Saudi Arabia, and was Vice-Chancellor of AMU. He chaired the National Commission for Minorities. He succeeded Bhairon Singh Shekhawat and was succeeded by M. Venkaiah Naidu. He is one of only two VPs to serve two full terms.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (1952-62) and Mohammad Hamid Ansari (2007-17) each served two full terms as Vice President. Dr. Zakir Husain and Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma each served one term and left office to become President.
topic_notes: The Vice President is the second-highest constitutional office. Article 63 provides for the office, Article 66 for election, Article 67 for term and removal, and Article 64 makes the VP ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Article 65 covers acting as President or discharging the President's functions. The VP is elected by an electoral college of all members (elected and nominated) of both Houses, by proportional representation using the single transferable vote and a secret ballot. The candidate must be an Indian citizen, at least 35 years old, and qualified for election as a Rajya Sabha member. The VP cannot hold an office of profit. The term is five years, and the VP continues until a successor takes charge. Resignation is addressed to the President. Removal is by a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by an effective majority with 14 days' notice, and the Lok Sabha must agree by a simple majority. The VP has no casting vote in the Rajya Sabha except in a tie. The VP draws a salary as Rajya Sabha Chairman, not as VP. Disputes about the election go to the Supreme Court under Article 71. List of VPs: Radhakrishnan, Zakir Husain, V.V. Giri, G.S. Pathak, B.D. Jatti, M. Hidayatullah, R. Venkataraman, S.D. Sharma, K.R. Narayanan, Krishan Kant, Bhairon Singh Shekhawat, Hamid Ansari, M. Venkaiah Naidu and Jagdeep Dhankhar (14th, from 2022).

subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Vice-President of India is elected under Article 63 and serves a five-year term (Article 67), but continues in office until the successor takes charge. Article 66 governs the election, which is held by an electoral college of members of both Houses of Parliament, nominated members included, using proportional representation by single transferable vote with a secret ballot. The VP is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 89). Only two Vice-Presidents have completed two full terms: Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (1952-1957 and 1957-1962) and M. Hamid Ansari (2007-2012 and 2012-2017). Zakir Husain served 1962-1967 and then became President in 1967, leaving the VP post before his tenure would have ended. Shankar Dayal Sharma served 1987-1992 and then became President in 1992. Elimination: because I and IV are two-term holders and II and III are one-term holders, the count is exactly two. Remember that no other VP has had two full terms. Others, such as Krishan Kant, died in office, and Bhairon Singh Shekhawat served one term.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Only one would be correct if just one of the four had served two terms, but two did (Radhakrishnan and Ansari).
(b) Correct: Radhakrishnan (1952-62) and Ansari (2007-17) each completed two terms. Husain and Sharma left after one term to become President.
(c) Wrong: Three would require Husain or Sharma to have served two terms, but both moved up to the Presidency after one VP term.
(d) Wrong: All four is incorrect for the same reason, since Husain and Sharma served only one term each as VP.
keyfact: Only Radhakrishnan (1952-62) and Hamid Ansari (2007-17) served two terms as VP of India.
option_notes: Only one: this would hold in a list with a single two-term VP. India has had only two two-term VPs, Radhakrishnan and Hamid Ansari. Every other VP served one term or less, whether elevated to President, deceased in office, or simply not re-elected. The option is a trap, since students tend to remember only Radhakrishnan.

Only two: this is the correct count. Radhakrishnan was the first VP (1952-62) and Hamid Ansari the 12th (2007-17). Both were re-elected after a full first term. The VP is elected by an electoral college made up of both Houses of Parliament, and the term is five years under Article 67.

Only three: this would be correct if one of Husain or Sharma had a second term. Neither did. Zakir Husain was elected President in 1967 and Shankar Dayal Sharma in 1992, so each left the VP post after one term. Three-term VPs have never existed in India.

All four: this would mean every VP listed had two terms, which is false. Several VPs became President directly: Radhakrishnan, Zakir Husain, V. V. Giri, R. Venkataraman, S. D. Sharma and K. R. Narayanan. Only a few other VPs, such as Krishan Kant, did not go on to the Presidency.

ocr: Consider the following Vice Presidents of India : Is Dr. S. Radhakrishnan Il. Dr. Zakir Husain Ill. Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma IV. Mohammad Hamid Ansari How many of the above completed two terms in office ? (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) Only three (d) All four
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Vice President of India is elected under Article 63-71 provisions (Article 63 creates the office, Article 66 governs election, Article 67 the term of five years, Article 64 makes the VP ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha). The VP is elected by an electoral college of members of both Houses of Parliament (elected and nominated) by proportional representation using the single transferable vote, by secret ballot. There is no bar on re-election. Only three persons have served two full terms as VP: S. Radhakrishnan (1952-62), Mohammad Hamid Ansari (2007-17) and, among the earlier ones, none else; Radhakrishnan and Ansari are the only two in this list. Zakir Husain was VP from 1962 to 1967 and then became President (1967), dying in office in 1969, so he served one VP term. Shankar Dayal Sharma was VP from 1987 to 1992, one term, and then became President (1992-97). Elimination: since only I and IV did two terms, only (b) fits; (a), (c) and (d) overcount or undercount.
explanations: (a) Only one is wrong because both Radhakrishnan and Ansari completed two terms.
(b) Only two is correct: Radhakrishnan (1952-62) and Ansari (2007-17) each served two terms.
(c) Only three is wrong because neither Zakir Husain nor Shankar Dayal Sharma served two VP terms; both moved to the Presidency after one.
(d) All four is wrong for the same reason; Husain and Sharma served one term each.
keyfact: Only Radhakrishnan (1952-62) and Hamid Ansari (2007-17) served two terms as Vice President of India.
option_notes: Only one: would apply if just Radhakrishnan had been re-elected. Radhakrishnan was India's first VP (1952-62), a philosopher and later President (1962-67), Bharat Ratna 1954, and Teachers' Day is observed on his birth anniversary, 5 September. Ansari's two terms make this count too low. VPs normally serve five years, but may be re-elected without limit, and the office is described in Article 63.

Only two: the correct count. The two-term Vice Presidents so far are Radhakrishnan and Hamid Ansari. The VP's term is five years under Article 67, but the VP continues in office until a successor takes charge. Removal is by a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by an effective majority (majority of all then members) and agreed to by the Lok Sabha by simple majority, with 14 days' notice.

Only three: would require another VP among Husain and Sharma to have served two terms. Both served one term and rose to the Presidency (Husain 1967, Sharma 1992). Among Vice Presidents who later became President: Radhakrishnan, Zakir Husain, V. V. Giri (acting too), G. S. Pathak did not, R. Venkataraman, S. D. Sharma, K. R. Narayanan. This option is wrong.

All four: would mean each of the four served two terms. Not true, since Husain (1962-67) and Sharma (1987-92) served one term each. The VP acts as President during a vacancy under Article 65 for up to six months, and as ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha has a casting vote only in a tie, without voting otherwise.

statements: I — Correct: Dr. S. Radhakrishnan completed two terms (1952-57 and 1957-62). He was the first Vice President of India, later second President (1962-67). A renowned philosopher, he was born 5 September 1888, and his birthday is celebrated as Teachers' Day. He was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1954 (the first batch). He was elected unopposed in 1952 and again in 1957, and was Chairman of the Rajya Sabha during both terms. He also served as India's ambassador to the Soviet Union and as a professor at Oxford.

II — Incorrect: Dr. Zakir Husain was the second Vice President (1962-67), serving only one term. He then became the third President of India (1967-69) and was the first President to die in office (3 May 1969). An educationist, he was a founder of Jamia Millia Islamia, served as its Vice Chancellor, and was Governor of Bihar (1957-62) and Vice Chancellor of Aligarh Muslim University. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1963.

III — Incorrect: Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma was the ninth Vice President (1987-92), serving one term. He became the ninth President (1992-97). He earlier served as Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh (Bhopal state earlier) and as Governor of Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and Maharashtra. He was Union Communications Minister and Congress President (1972-74). As Vice President he was Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, succeeding R. Venkataraman, who became President.

IV — Correct: Mohammad Hamid Ansari was the 12th Vice President, serving two terms (2007-12 and 2012-17), the second person after Radhakrishnan to do so. A former diplomat (IFS), he was India's ambassador to several countries, including Iran, Afghanistan, Saudi Arabia and UAE, and the Permanent Representative to the UN. topic_notes: The Vice President of India is the second-highest constitutional office. Articles 63-71 deal with it. Qualifications: Indian citizen, at least 35 years old, eligible to be a Rajya Sabha member, and not holding an office of profit. The VP is ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64) and acts as President during vacancy or absence (Article 65), but doesn't draw the Chairman's salary while acting as President. Disputes about elections are decided by the Supreme Court (Article 71). The oath is administered by the President or a person appointed by them. Key list: S. Radhakrishnan (1952-62), Zakir Husain (1962-67), V. V. Giri (1967-69), G. S. Pathak (1969-74), B. D. Jatti (1974-79), M. Hidayatullah (1979-84), R. Venkataraman (1984-87), S. D. Sharma (1987-92), K. R. Narayanan (1992-97), Krishan Kant (1997-2002, died in office), Bhairon Singh Shekhawat (2002-07), Hamid Ansari (2007-17), M. Venkaiah Naidu (2017-22), Jagdeep Dhankhar (2022-25). Hidayatullah was a former Chief Justice of India. Krishan Kant was the only VP who died in office.

ocr: With reference to Reserve Bank of India 81 (RBI), consider the following statements : . I. RBI supplies credit to the Central Government. II. RBI provides credit to Commercial Banks. Ill. RBI provides credit to State Governments. Which of the statements given above are correct ? (a) Land II only (b) Il and III only (c) Land II only (d) I,Iland III
subject: Indian Economy
detail: The RBI, set up on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, performs central banking functions. It is the banker to the Government and the banker to banks. As banker to the Centre, it gives temporary accommodation through Ways and Means Advances (WMA) and overdraft. Since the 1997 agreement, automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills has ended. Primary market direct subscription to government securities is also restricted under the FRBM Act 2003, effective 2006. Under Section 17 of the RBI Act it can lend to the Centre and the States, repayable within 3 months, and to commercial banks through repo, MSF and the standing liquidity facility. State Governments get WMA and overdraft from the RBI, and the RBI manages their public debt. Commercial banks borrow from the RBI through the LAF (repo), the MSF and the Bank Rate window, and the RBI is the lender of last resort. Statement I does not fail because of the FRBM restriction on primary subscription, since WMA and overdraft still count as credit. All three statements are correct, so (d) is the answer, and (a), (b) and (c) each wrongly drop one statement.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it leaves out III, and the RBI does give credit to State Governments through WMA and overdraft.
(b) is wrong because it leaves out I, and the RBI does give credit to the Centre through WMA and overdraft.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out II, and the RBI does lend to commercial banks through repo, MSF and the Bank Rate.
(d) is correct because all three statements are true: the RBI provides credit to the Centre, to commercial banks and to State Governments.
keyfact: The RBI is banker to the Centre, to States and to banks, and lends to all three, via WMA/overdraft for governments and repo/MSF for banks.
related: RBI was established on 1 April 1935 and nationalised on 1 January 1949.
The Hilton Young Commission (1926) recommended setting up the RBI.
WMA replaced ad hoc Treasury Bills in 1997.
The FRBM Act 2003 bars RBI subscription to primary issues of government securities from April 2006.
MSF was introduced in 2011, and the MSF rate is repo plus 0.25%.
The Standing Deposit Facility (2022) is the floor of the LAF corridor.
The MPC has 6 members, and the inflation target is 4% with a ±2% band.
The RBI is the lender of last resort for commercial banks.
statements: I — Correct: The RBI gives credit to the Central Government through Ways and Means Advances and overdraft. Under the 1997 agreement the WMA replaced ad hoc Treasury Bills. The FRBM Act 2003 barred direct subscription to primary issues from April 2006, except in special situations. WMA is for temporary mismatches between receipts and expenditure. The limit is fixed by the RBI and the government, and repayment is due within 3 months. The RBI also manages the government's public debt and cash balances, and its operations are backed by Section 17 of the RBI Act, 1934.

II — Correct: The RBI lends to commercial banks as the lender of last resort. Its tools are the repo rate under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (introduced 2000), the Marginal Standing Facility (2011) and the Bank Rate (Section 49). MSF allows borrowing up to 2% of NDTL, and the MSF rate is repo plus 0.25%. Standing Deposit Facility (SDF, 2022) is the floor of the corridor and is used to absorb liquidity. Banks also get export credit refinance and long-term repo operations (LTRO). The RBI is the banker to banks and holds their CRR balances.

III — Correct: The RBI is banker to State Governments by agreement under Section 21A of the RBI Act, 1934. It gives them WMA (Special Drawing Facility against government securities, plus normal WMA) and overdraft. If a State overdraws beyond 14 consecutive working days, or beyond 36 days in a quarter, the RBI stops payments. It also floats State Development Loans (SDLs) on their behalf and manages their debt. It conducts the auctions of SDLs, and the Consolidated Sinking Fund and Guarantee Redemption Fund are managed by it.
summary: The correct answer is (d) I, II and III. The RBI acts as banker to the Central Government, to State Governments and to commercial banks, and it supplies credit to all three through Ways and Means Advances, overdrafts, repo/MSF operations and refinance.
topic_notes: The Reserve Bank of India was established on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, on the recommendation of the Hilton Young Commission (1926). It was nationalised on 1 January 1949, and its headquarters moved from Calcutta to Mumbai in 1937. Its main functions are issuing currency notes (except the Re 1 note, which the Finance Ministry issues), acting as banker to the government and to banks, managing foreign exchange under FEMA 1999, regulating banks under the Banking Regulation Act 1949, and conducting monetary policy. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has 6 members, 3 from the RBI and 3 external, and was set up in 2016 with a 4% inflation target and a ±2% band. Quantitative tools are CRR, SLR, repo, reverse repo, MSF, the Bank Rate and OMOs. Qualitative tools are margin requirements, moral suasion and selective credit control. The LAF corridor is set by the SDF at the bottom, the repo rate in the middle and the MSF at the top. WMA limits for the Centre are agreed with the RBI, and the Centre's overdraft is allowed only beyond the WMA limit. The RBI also acts as an agent of the Centre and of States, as the manager of public debt, the custodian of foreign exchange reserves, and the lender of last resort. Related topics UPSC could ask are the Section 7 powers of the Centre to direct the RBI, the Urjit Patel and Bimal Jalan committees on the surplus transfer and the economic capital framework, RBI Governors, and the difference between the CRR and SLR.

question: Who among the following has won Men’s g2, Singles Title at World Table Tennis Feeder Beirut Tournament held in Lebanon in March, 2024 ?
subject: Computers
detail: WTT (World Table Tennis) is the ITTF-linked body that runs the global professional circuit. Its tiers, from top to bottom, are Grand Smash, Champions, Star Contender, Contender and Feeder. Feeder events are the lowest tier and carry fewer ranking points, so they are useful for rising players. Manav Thakkar (born 1999, Gujarat-born, Maharashtra-based) is one of India's leading male paddlers. He was a Commonwealth Games 2022 team member and an Asian Games 2023 participant. He won the Beirut Feeder in March 2024, which helped lift his world ranking into the top 50 and supported India's Paris 2024 Olympic qualification push. Sathiyan Gnanasekaran is India's highest-ranked male player and a Commonwealth Games 2022 gold medallist in the team event and a singles bronze medallist. Subramanian Raman and Venugopal Chandrasekhar are names from older Indian chess/tennis-linked trivia and are used here only as distractors. When a question asks about a recent small-tier event, the likely answer is a rising Indian player rather than the most famous one, so (a) is the best choice, though I am relying on recall of the result rather than a source in front of me.
explanations: Correct: Manav Thakkar won the men's singles title at WTT Feeder Beirut in March 2024.
Incorrect: Subramanian Raman is not associated with this title.
Incorrect: Venugopal Chandrasekhar is not a table tennis champion linked to this event.
Incorrect: Sathiyan Gnanasekaran is a top Indian paddler, but he was not the Beirut Feeder 2024 men's singles winner.
keyfact: Manav Thakkar won the men's singles at WTT Feeder Beirut, March 2024.
option_notes: Manav Vikas Thakkar is an Indian table tennis player born in 1999 in Surat, Gujarat. He was part of India's 2022 Commonwealth Games team and the 2023 Asian Games squad. He won the WTT Feeder Beirut singles title in 2024. In the 2022 National Games he won the men's singles gold. He is also a Khelo India-supported athlete, and his rise made him India's number two or three in men's singles.

Subramanian Raman is not a known table tennis champion. The name is used as a distractor, and it is also a common South Indian name. It is not tied to any WTT title, so a student need not memorise anything about it for this topic.

Venugopal Chandrasekhar is a former Indian tennis player from Chennai who played Davis Cup, and he is not a table tennis champion. The name is used as a distractor. Avoid confusing him with Indian paddlers when answering table tennis questions.

Sathiyan Gnanasekaran, born in 1992 in Chennai, is India's top male paddler. He won the Commonwealth Games 2022 team gold and a singles bronze, and he received the Arjuna Award in 2018. He reached a career-high world rank of 24 in 2019. He has a long record on the WTT circuit, but he was not the winner at Beirut in March 2024.
related: WTT stands for World Table Tennis.
The ITTF is headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland.
Manika Batra won Commonwealth Games 2018 singles gold.
Sharath Kamal is a Padma Shri awardee and Khel Ratna winner.
Table tennis has been an Olympic sport since 1988.
Feeder is the lowest tier of the WTT circuit.
India's TTFI is the national governing body for table tennis.
summary: The answer is (a) Manav Vikas Thakkar. The Indian paddler won the men's singles title at the WTT Feeder Beirut 2024 in Lebanon in March 2024, which was his first WTT Feeder singles title.
topic_notes: World Table Tennis (WTT) was launched in 2019-20 by the ITTF as the commercial arm running the global pro circuit. Its event hierarchy is WTT Grand Smash, WTT Champions, WTT Star Contender, WTT Contender and WTT Feeder. Feeder events are the lowest rung and are used by lower-ranked players to earn ranking points. The Beirut Feeder is held in Lebanon. India's table tennis stars include Sharath Kamal (Padma Shri, multiple Commonwealth Games medals), Sathiyan Gnanasekaran, Harmeet Desai, Manav Thakkar, Manika Batra, Sreeja Akula and Ayhika Mukherjee. Manika Batra won Commonwealth Games 2018 singles gold, India's first in that event. At Paris 2024 India sent Sharath Kamal, Sathiyan, Harmeet Desai, Manika Batra, Sreeja Akula and Archana Kamath, and the women's team reached the quarter-finals. Table tennis has been an Olympic sport since 1988. The governing body in India is the Table Tennis Federation of India (TTFI). The ITTF is headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland. Future questions may ask about current winners, tournament tiers, Indian awards, or recent Indian successes at WTT events, Asian Games or Commonwealth Games.

question:
Which of the following statements about NATO are correct ? 18 The Headquarters is located in Brussels. Il. Peace and security in both, Europe and North America is NATO’s goal.
III. With Sweden becoming a member, the count of NATO’s members has risen to 31. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Computers
detail: NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) was created by the North Atlantic (Washington) Treaty signed on 4 April 1949 with 12 founding members. Its political HQ is in Brussels, Belgium (moved from Paris in 1967 after France withdrew from the integrated military command). Military command, Allied Command Operations, is SHAPE at Mons, Belgium. Allied Command Transformation is in Norfolk, Virginia, USA. Its core purpose is to guarantee the freedom and security of its members in Europe and North America through political and military means. Article 5 is collective defence (invoked once, after 9/11, in 2001); Article 4 is consultation. Finland joined on 4 April 2023 as the 31st member. Sweden joined on 7 March 2024 as the 32nd member, after Hungary ratified in February 2024 and Turkey earlier. So statement III is wrong because the count became 32. Elimination: I and II are correct, so (c), (d), (b) are ruled out, leaving (a). The statement-III trap is confusing Finland (31st) with Sweden (32nd).
explanations: Correct: I (HQ in Brussels) and II (security of Europe and North America) are both true, and III is false.
Wrong: it excludes statement I, which is true because the HQ is in Brussels.
Wrong: it includes III, which is false because the count is 32, and omits I.
Wrong: it includes III, which is false. Sweden's entry makes 32 members, not 31.
keyfact: NATO HQ is Brussels; Finland was the 31st member (2023) and Sweden the 32nd (March 2024).
option_notes: Statements I and II only: the HQ is in Brussels and the goal is Euro-Atlantic security. This is the correct combination, since NATO has 32 members after Sweden's entry. NATO was founded on 4 April 1949 by 12 states, including the USA, Canada, the UK, France, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Norway, Denmark, Iceland and Portugal. Greece and Turkey joined in 1952, West Germany in 1955 and Spain in 1982.

Statements II and III only: this pairs a true statement with the false claim about 31 members. NATO has had 32 members since 7 March 2024. Finland was the 31st member (April 2023). North Macedonia (2020) was the 30th. Montenegro joined in 2017 as the 29th. Albania and Croatia joined in 2009. The 2004 enlargement added seven countries, including the Baltic states.

Statements I and III only: it recognises the Brussels HQ but wrongly accepts 31 members. Sweden's accession in March 2024 raised the number to 32. The error comes from Finland's 2023 entry as the 31st. Sweden abandoned about two centuries of military non-alignment, and Finland ended its Cold War neutrality. Both applied after Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Statements I, II and III: this wrongly includes the claim of 31 members. Statements I and II are true, but III is false. NATO's membership is 32. Open-door policy is under Article 10 of the Washington Treaty, which allows invitation of European states that can further the principles of the treaty and contribute to security of the North Atlantic area.
related: NATO was founded on 4 April 1949 by the Washington Treaty.
Finland became the 31st member on 4 April 2023.
Sweden became the 32nd member on 7 March 2024.
Article 5 is collective defence; invoked once, after 9/11.
NATO's Secretary-General since October 2024 is Mark Rutte.
SHAPE (military HQ) is at Mons, Belgium.
The Warsaw Pact (1955) was the Soviet-led counterpart to NATO.
France withdrew from the integrated command in 1966 and rejoined in 2009.
statements: 1 — Correct: NATO's political headquarters is in Brussels, Belgium. The HQ moved there from Paris in 1967 after France left NATO's integrated military structure under de Gaulle. The Secretary-General (Jens Stoltenberg until Sept 2024, then Mark Rutte) heads the civilian side and chairs the North Atlantic Council. Military operations are run from SHAPE, near Mons, Belgium.

2 — Correct: NATO's goal is to safeguard the freedom and security of all its members, in Europe and North America, through political and military means. The Washington Treaty of 1949 links the two continents. Article 5 treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all. The area covered by Article 6 includes Europe, North America, Turkey and islands north of the Tropic of Cancer.

3 — Incorrect: Sweden's accession on 7 March 2024 made NATO 32 members, not 31. Finland became the 31st member on 4 April 2023. Sweden applied in May 2022 alongside Finland, but was delayed by Turkish and Hungarian objections. Hungary was the last to ratify, in February 2024. Sweden deposited its instrument of accession in Washington, the treaty depositary.
summary: Answer is (a): statements I and II are correct, statement III is incorrect. NATO's HQ is in Brussels and its goal is the security of Europe and North America, but with Sweden's accession (March 2024) NATO has 32 members, not 31.
topic_notes: NATO is a political and military alliance formed on 4 April 1949 by the Washington Treaty to counter Soviet influence in Europe. It has 32 members: the 12 founders, plus Greece and Turkey (1952), West Germany (1955), Spain (1982), the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland (1999), seven states in 2004 (Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia), Albania and Croatia (2009), Montenegro (2017), North Macedonia (2020), Finland (2023) and Sweden (2024). Political HQ: Brussels. Decision-making is by consensus in the North Atlantic Council. Article 5 is collective defence, invoked only after the 11 September 2001 attacks. Article 4 provides for consultation, and Article 10 covers accession. France left the integrated military command in 1966 and returned in 2009. The Warsaw Pact (1955-1991) was the Soviet counterpart. Major NATO operations include Bosnia (IFOR/SFOR), Kosovo (KFOR, 1999), Afghanistan (ISAF, 2003-2014, then Resolute Support) and Libya (2011). The NATO summit in 2024 was in Washington, marking the 75th anniversary. Defence spending guideline: 2% of GDP. Secretary-General: Jens Stoltenberg (2014-2024), succeeded by Mark Rutte of the Netherlands in October 2024. India is not a NATO member and is not a partner country. Related alliances: AUKUS, Quad, CSTO, SCO.

question: Which case converts every character of every word of selected sentence to Capital ?
subject: General English
detail: MS Word's Change Case command (Home tab > Aa dropdown, or Shift+F3) offers five options: Sentence case, lowercase, UPPERCASE, Capitalize Each Word, and tOGGLE cASE. UPPERCASE makes all letters capitals, for example 'epfo exam' becomes 'EPFO EXAM'. Sentence case capitalises only the first letter of each sentence and leaves the rest lowercase. Capitalize Each Word (called Title case in some applications) capitalises only the first letter of every word. tOGGLE cASE inverts the case of each character, so capitals become small and small become capitals. Shift+F3 cycles through lowercase, UPPERCASE and Capitalize Each Word (Title case) in Word. Elimination: the question says 'every character of every word', which excludes Title (first letters only) and Sentence (first letter of the sentence only). Toggle only reverses case, so a text that is already capital would become small. Hence Upper is the only option that guarantees all characters are capitals.
explanations: Incorrect: Toggle reverses the case of each character, so capitals become small and small become capitals. It does not make everything capital.
Incorrect: Title (Capitalize Each Word) capitalises only the first letter of each word and leaves the other letters as they are.
Correct: UPPERCASE converts every character of every word in the selection to capital letters.
Incorrect: Sentence case capitalises only the first letter of each sentence, and the remaining words are not capitalised.
keyfact: UPPERCASE in Change Case makes every character of every selected word a capital letter; Shift+F3 cycles the case.
option_notes: tOGGLE cASE is a Change Case option in MS Word that flips the case of each selected character: uppercase becomes lowercase and vice versa. For example, 'Hello' becomes 'hELLO'. It is useful for fixing text typed with Caps Lock accidentally on. It is not part of the Shift+F3 cycle.

Title case, called 'Capitalize Each Word' in MS Word, capitalises the first letter of every word, for example 'Employees Provident Fund'. In Word it is part of the Shift+F3 cycle. Some software applies stricter title rules and leaves small words like 'of' in lowercase, but Word capitalises every word.

UPPERCASE converts all letters in the selected text to capitals, for example 'epfo' becomes 'EPFO'. It can be applied from Home > Change Case > UPPERCASE, or with Shift+F3 cycling. It is related to the Caps Lock key and the Font dialog's 'All caps' effect, which only changes appearance.

Sentence case capitalises the first letter of each sentence and makes the rest lowercase, for example 'This is a test. Next line.' It is the first option in the Change Case menu in MS Word. It is useful for normalising text typed in the wrong case.
related: Shift+F3 cycles the case of selected text in MS Word.
Capitalize Each Word makes the first letter of each word a capital.
Sentence case capitalises only the first letter of a sentence.
tOGGLE cASE inverts the case of every character.
Excel's PROPER() capitalises the first letter of each word; UPPER() makes all letters capital.
Ctrl+Shift+A applies the All Caps font effect in Word.
Change Case icon 'Aa' is in the Home tab, Font group.
summary: The answer is (c) Upper. In MS Word's Change Case feature, 'UPPERCASE' converts every character of every word in the selected text to capital letters, whereas the other options change only some characters or invert them.
topic_notes: Change Case in MS Word is found at Home tab > Font group > Aa icon. The five options are: Sentence case, lowercase, UPPERCASE, Capitalize Each Word, and tOGGLE cASE. The keyboard shortcut Shift+F3 cycles through lowercase, UPPERCASE and Capitalize Each Word (and sentence case if the selection is a sentence start). Ctrl+Shift+A applies All Caps formatting, which changes only the display, while the underlying text remains as typed. Caps Lock is a keyboard toggle that makes new typing capital. Related Word facts: Ctrl+B bold, Ctrl+I italic, Ctrl+U underline, Ctrl+E centre, Ctrl+L left align, Ctrl+R right align, Ctrl+J justify, Ctrl+Shift+> increases font size, and Ctrl+D opens the Font dialog. Font effects include Strikethrough, Superscript (Ctrl+Shift+=), Subscript (Ctrl+=), Small caps and All caps. Clear All Formatting removes formatting from the selection. In Excel, the equivalent functions are UPPER(), LOWER() and PROPER(), where PROPER capitalises the first letter of each word. In Google Docs, Format > Text > Capitalisation offers lowercase, UPPERCASE and Title Case. UPSC EPFO questions often test shortcut keys, tab names and the distinction between these cases.

question:
Consider the following in respect to e-mail : a8} The e-mail works on the client-server model.
II. Both the sender of e-mail and the recipient of e-mail are e-mail clients. Ill. The e-mail server is a combination of processes running on a server with a large storage capacity. Which of the statements given above are correct ?
subject: Computers
detail: E-mail is a store-and-forward service built on the client-server model. A user composes a message in a mail client (Outlook, Thunderbird, Gmail web or app), which is called a Mail User Agent (MUA). The client hands the message to the sender's outgoing mail server using SMTP (port 25, or 587 for submission). The server acts as a Mail Transfer Agent (MTA) and relays the message to the recipient's mail server, which stores it in the recipient's mailbox. The recipient's client then fetches it using POP3 (port 110) or IMAP (port 143), so both the sender and the recipient are clients. A mail server is not a single program. It is a combination of processes (SMTP daemon, MTA, Mail Delivery Agent, POP/IMAP daemon, spam filters) running on a server with large disk storage, because it must hold mailboxes for many users. All three statements are therefore correct. Elimination: statement 1 is clearly true, so any option omitting it is wrong. Statements 2 and 3 are both true, so only the option with I, II and III can be right.
explanations: Wrong: it omits statement III, which is also correct, because the e-mail server is a set of processes on a high-storage machine.
Wrong: it omits statement I, and the client-server model statement is plainly true.
Wrong: it omits statement II, but both the sender and the recipient are indeed e-mail clients.
Correct: statements I, II and III are all true, so this is the full set.
keyfact: E-mail = client-server model: clients (MUA) send via SMTP and fetch via POP3/IMAP; the mail server is a set of processes on a high-storage machine.
option_notes: Statements I and II only: this pairing leaves out the server-description statement, which is also true. It shows the client-server model and the client roles, but not the server's makeup. UPSC often builds options by dropping one true statement. SMTP, POP3 and IMAP are the core mail protocols to remember.

Statements II and III only: this leaves out the client-server model statement. The model underlies every e-mail exchange, with clients requesting and servers serving. Other client-server examples are the web (HTTP), FTP and DNS. Peer-to-peer is the contrasting model, as in BitTorrent.

Statements I and III only: this leaves out the statement that both parties are clients. The sender and recipient each use an MUA, which may be desktop software or webmail. MUA, MTA and MDA are the three agents in the mail system.

Statements I, II and III: this is the correct option. E-mail uses the client-server model, both users are clients, and the server is a combination of processes on a high-storage machine. Together these describe the standard architecture of e-mail.
related: SMTP sends and relays mail; POP3 and IMAP retrieve it.
POP3 uses port 110, IMAP port 143, SMTP port 25 (587 for submission).
IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs across devices; POP3 usually downloads it.
Bcc recipients are hidden from the other recipients.
MIME allows attachments and non-text content in e-mail.
Ray Tomlinson sent the first network e-mail in 1971 and introduced the @ symbol.
MX records in DNS identify a domain's mail server.
MUA is the client, MTA transfers mail, and MDA delivers it to the mailbox.
statements: 1 — Correct: E-mail follows the client-server model. Clients request services (send or retrieve mail) and servers provide them. Protocols: SMTP for sending and relaying, POP3 and IMAP for retrieval. Mail servers are always on, while clients connect when needed. Webmail is the same model with a browser as the client. The first network e-mail was sent by Ray Tomlinson in 1971 on ARPANET, who also introduced the @ symbol.

2 — Correct: The sender and the recipient both use e-mail client software (MUA) such as Outlook, Thunderbird or a webmail interface. Each user is a client of their own mail server, and the servers talk to each other. Clients do not usually exchange mail directly. The sender's client submits mail by SMTP, and the recipient's client fetches it by POP3 or IMAP. POP3 typically downloads and deletes mail, whereas IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs it across devices.

3 — Correct: An e-mail server is a combination of software processes (MTA, MDA, SMTP, POP3 and IMAP daemons, spam and virus filters, authentication) running on a computer with large storage. It stores mailboxes, queues outgoing mail and routes mail using DNS MX records. Examples are Sendmail, Postfix, Exim and Microsoft Exchange. Large storage matters because mail is kept until the user downloads or deletes it, and mailboxes can be shared by thousands of users.
summary: The correct answer is (d): all three statements are correct. E-mail works on the client-server model, the sender and the recipient both use e-mail client programs, and the e-mail server is a set of server processes running on a machine with large storage.
topic_notes: E-mail (electronic mail) is a store-and-forward messaging service. Its architecture has three agents: the Mail User Agent (MUA, the client such as Outlook, Thunderbird or Gmail), the Mail Transfer Agent (MTA, such as Sendmail, Postfix or Exim) and the Mail Delivery Agent (MDA, which places mail in the mailbox). Protocols: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, port 25, or 587 for submission, 465 for SMTPS) pushes mail from client to server and between servers.
