3. Among the members of the community the local doctor was the one who was most respected. Select the answer using the codes given below :
options: 1, 2 and 3 Raj’s apartment was three floors underneath the Subramanian residence. There was little space below the tin roof and the scaffolding for the squirrel to hide in. Inside the box was the secret he had been searching for all his life
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The stem was lost in OCR. The three sentences all turn on the choice between amid/amidst and among/amongst, so the question most likely asks which sentences use the preposition correctly. Amid(st) means 'in the middle of' and normally takes an uncountable noun or an abstract situation, such as amid confusion, amid cheers or amid the noise. Among(st) means 'in a group of' and takes plural, countable nouns or people, such as among friends or among the members. Amongst is a British variant of among, and both are acceptable. Sentence 1 uses 'amidst the scuffle and resultant confusion', a situation, so it is correct. Sentence 2 uses 'amongst those assembled', a group of people, so it is correct. In sentence 2 the numeral '20.' is a stray line number from the OCR. Sentence 3 uses 'Among the members of the community', a countable group, so it is correct. The 'most respected' superlative is also correct because it compares one person with many. Since all three are correct, only option (d) fits. The extra lines in the prompt (underneath, below, inside) are separate sentences that do not affect this answer.
explanations: (a) is wrong because sentence 3 is also correct, so '1 and 2 only' leaves out a correct sentence.
(b) is wrong because sentence 1 is also correct. 'Amidst' is rightly used with 'scuffle and confusion'.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out sentence 2, where 'amongst those assembled' is correct.
(d) is right because all three sentences use their prepositions and agreement correctly.
keyfact: Amid(st) goes with abstract or mass nouns, and among(st) goes with countable groups.
option_notes: Option (a) '1 and 2 only' would mean sentence 3 is flawed. It is not, because 'among the members of the community' is the standard usage and the superlative 'most respected' is formed correctly.
Option (b) '2 and 3 only' would mean sentence 1 is flawed. It is not, because 'amidst' is acceptable before an abstract noun phrase such as 'scuffle and the resultant confusion'.
Option (c) '1 and 3 only' would mean sentence 2 is flawed. It is not, because 'amongst' is a valid variant of 'among' and refers correctly to a group of people.
Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is correct because all three sentences use their prepositions properly.
related: Amid(st) takes mass or abstract nouns; among(st) takes countable plural nouns.
Between is for two items or distinct relationships; among is for a general group.
Beside means next to; besides means in addition to.
'Not a single person' takes a singular verb.
Superlatives take 'the': the most respected.
Amongst, whilst and amidst are British variants and are acceptable.
Underneath and beneath imply contact or cover; below only implies a lower position.
statements: 1 — Correct: 'Amidst' suits the abstract situation 'scuffle and confusion'. Amid or amidst means in the middle of, and it is used with uncountable or abstract nouns or surroundings (amid the chaos, amidst rejoicing). 'Amidst' is the older, literary variant of 'amid'. 'Slip away' means to leave unnoticed, and the sentence is grammatically sound.

2 — Correct: 'Amongst those assembled' refers to a countable group of people, so among or amongst is right. 'Not a single person' takes a singular verb ('was'), and 'who was willing' agrees with it. Among and amongst mean the same thing, and amongst is more common in British English. Among is used for three or more items in a group, while between is used for two or for distinct pairs.

3 — Correct: 'Among the members of the community' correctly uses among with a plural, countable group. 'The one who was most respected' is a proper superlative construction, because a superlative compares one item with several. The definite article 'the local doctor' is also correct. Among is used for a general group and between for specific one-to-one relations.
summary: The answer is (d) 1, 2 and 3. Each sentence uses 'amidst' or 'among(st)' correctly: 'amidst' goes with a mass or abstract situation (scuffle, confusion), and 'among(st)' goes with a countable group (those assembled, members of the community). The OCR dropped the question's instruction line, so I have assumed it asks which sentences are correct in their use of these prepositions.
topic_notes: This question tests prepositions and word usage, especially amid/amidst versus among/amongst versus between. Amid(st) means in the middle of and takes an uncountable, abstract or mass noun (amid the noise, amidst uncertainty). Among(st) means in a group and takes countable plural nouns (among the students). Between is used for two items, or for relationships between distinct individuals even when there are more than two (a treaty between three nations). Amongst, whilst and amidst are British variants of among, while and amid, and both forms are correct. Related areas UPSC EPFO commonly tests are: (1) prepositions of time and place (in, on, at; since and for); (2) prepositions after verbs and adjectives (angry with someone, angry at something; good at, fond of, afraid of); (3) beside versus besides (beside means next to, besides means in addition to); (4) underneath, below and beneath (beneath and underneath imply contact or cover, while below only implies a lower position); (5) superlatives and comparatives (the most respected, with 'the' before the superlative); (6) subject-verb agreement with 'not a single person', 'each' and 'every', which take singular verbs. In sentence-correction items, check for mismatches between the noun's countability and the preposition, then check agreement and tense. Elimination works well when the choice is between combinations such as '1 and 2 only' and '1, 2 and 3', so check each sentence separately and find which are actually faulty.

statements: 1 — Correct: 'takes after' means resembles a relative in appearance or character. Examples: she takes after her mother. It is a separable-free, inseparable phrasal verb (take after + person) and cannot be split. It is not used for imitation by choice, which is 'model oneself on'. It is the standard idiom in family-resemblance contexts and is commonly tested in phrasal verb questions.

2 — Correct (acceptable): 'take in' means to accept or admit, as in taking in more work or lodgers. Other senses are to deceive (He was taken in by the con man), to understand (She took in the lecture), to reduce a garment's size, and to visit or include (take in the sights). Strictly, 'take on' is the usual phrase for responsibility, but 'take in' is tolerated in the sense of accepting.

3 — Incorrect: 'take out' means to remove, extract, withdraw money, or escort someone on a date, and in slang to kill or destroy. It does not mean to address a matter. The right phrase would be 'take up the matter', meaning to begin to deal with or consider it. Compare 'take up' (start a hobby, occupy space or time, accept an offer), which is often confused with take out and take on.

topic_notes: Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle (preposition or adverb) to create a meaning different from the verb alone. UPSC EPFO regularly tests them in fill-in, replacement and usage questions. Types: transitive or intransitive, and separable (take the offer up) or inseparable (take after her). Key 'take' phrasal verbs: take after (resemble), take in (deceive, absorb, accept, shelter), take on (accept responsibility, hire, confront), take up (begin a hobby, deal with a matter), take off (remove, leave the ground, imitate, become successful), take over (assume control), take to (develop a liking), take down (write down, dismantle), take apart (dismantle), take back (retract), take out (remove, obtain a service or loan, date someone). Key 'put' phrasal verbs from the other block: put in (enter port, submit, spend time), put out (publish or extinguish), put off (postpone or discourage), put up (accommodate, erect), put up with (tolerate), put down (suppress, insult, write), put through (connect call), put away (store). Tips: watch for particles that change meaning completely, check whether a phrase is separable, and look for the nearest standard idiom such as 'take on' versus 'take in' for responsibility. Other likely angles: replacing a verb with a phrasal verb, spotting the wrongly used particle, and idioms and one-word substitutions.
