question: The contribution of the services sector in Gross Value Added at current prices in the Indian economy in 2024 — 25 is estimated to be :
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: India's GVA is split into three broad sectors: agriculture and allied, industry, and services. The Economic Survey 2024-25 and the MoSPI Provisional Estimates (released 31 May 2025) put services at about 55% of GVA at current prices, industry at about 28 to 30%, and agriculture and allied at about 15 to 16%. Services have been the biggest contributor since the early 2000s, and the share has stayed near 53 to 55% in recent years. Services growth in 2024-25 was about 7.2 to 7.5%. The Survey also said services accounted for more than half of FDI inflows and a large share of exports, including IT/software, business services and GCCs. The sector's share of employment is much lower, about 29 to 30%, while agriculture still employs about 46%. Elimination: 25% is close to industry's share or below it, and 35% and 45% are too low for a sector that has been above 50% for over a decade. Only 55% matches the data.
explanations: Incorrect: 25% is far below services' actual share. It is nearer to the manufacturing/industry sub-share or to the older agriculture share.
Incorrect: 35% understates the services share. Services crossed 50% of GVA in the early 2000s, and 35% would describe a much earlier period.
Incorrect: 45% is also too low. The share has been above 50% for about two decades.
Correct: Services contributed about 55% of GVA at current prices in 2024-25, according to the Economic Survey and MoSPI provisional estimates.
keyfact: Services account for about 55% of India's GVA at current prices in 2024-25, industry about 28-30% and agriculture about 15-16%.
option_notes: 25%: Not the services share. Roughly a quarter of GVA is close to the share of manufacturing and construction taken together or to agriculture's share in the 1990s, but it is not services. Agriculture was around 15-16% in 2024-25. Do not confuse the share in GVA with the share in employment.

35%: This is about the share of services in GDP in the 1950s to 1970s, when agriculture dominated. Services were around 30-40% in the 1980s. It is also near the share of industry plus construction in some years. It does not describe the present economy.

45%: Services were around 40-45% in the 1990s and early 2000s, before the IT and telecom boom. Their share crossed 50% around 2000-01 to 2005. So 45% is a historical figure and not the 2024-25 estimate.

55%: This is the correct answer. Services have been the largest sector of the Indian economy for years, led by IT/IT-enabled services, financial and real estate services, trade, hotels, transport, communication and public administration. They also attract a high share of FDI inflows.
related: Services share in GVA at current prices 2024-25 is about 55%.
Agriculture and allied share in GVA is about 15-16%; industry about 28-30%.
The base year of the current GDP series is 2011-12.
MoSPI's NSO releases the provisional estimates of national income at the end of May each year.
Agriculture employs about 46% of workers but contributes only about 15% of GVA.
Services have contributed more than half of India's GVA since around 2000-01.
GVA at basic prices = GDP minus product taxes plus product subsidies.
The Economic Survey is released a day before the Union Budget.
summary: The answer is (d) 55%. The services sector contributed roughly 55% of India's Gross Value Added (GVA) at current prices in 2024-25, which makes it the largest sector of the economy, well ahead of industry and agriculture.
topic_notes: India's economy is classified into primary (agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining), secondary (manufacturing, electricity and utilities, construction) and tertiary (services) sectors. GVA at basic prices equals GDP minus product taxes plus product subsidies. Under the 2011-12 base series, MoSPI releases the National Accounts. The Provisional Estimates of 2024-25 were released on 31 May 2025, and real GDP growth was about 6.5%. The approximate sector shares at current prices in 2024-25 are: agriculture and allied 15-16%, industry 28-30%, services about 55%. Services growth was about 7.2-7.5%, led by financial, real estate and professional services, and by public administration. Services exports, especially software and business services, have been strong, and India is among the largest exporters of computer services. Employment shares from PLFS are roughly 46% in agriculture, 11-12% in manufacturing and about 29-30% in services, which shows that productivity is much higher in services. Historical pattern: agriculture was the largest sector at independence, with services overtaking it in the 1960s to 1970s and rising above 50% after about 2000. This early shift toward services, bypassing a large manufacturing phase, is often called premature deindustrialisation or a service-led growth model. Related policy: Make in India, the PLI schemes and the National Manufacturing Mission aim to raise manufacturing to 25% of GDP. Other angles: the Economic Survey is presented by the Chief Economic Adviser (V. Anantha Nageswaran) before the Union Budget, and quarterly GDP releases come from NSO.

question:
Consider the following statements regarding 36. Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana :
1. The average ticket size of loan disbursed has more than doubled between FY 2016 and FY 2025. Since its launch in 2015, Maharashtra has recorded the highest disbursal among States. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana (PMMY) was launched on 8 April 2015 to give collateral-free loans of up to Rs 10 lakh to non-corporate, non-farm micro and small enterprises. Loans go through banks, NBFCs and MFIs, and MUDRA is a refinancing agency under SIDBI (later a SIDBI subsidiary). The loans have three categories: Shishu (up to Rs 50,000), Kishore (Rs 50,000 to 5 lakh) and Tarun (Rs 5 to 10 lakh). Tarun Plus (Rs 10 to 20 lakh) was added in the Budget 2024-25. Government data for the 10-year milestone put the average ticket size at about Rs 38,000 in FY16 and about Rs 72,000 in FY25. That is an increase of about 89 percent, which is not 'more than double', so Statement 1 fails. Cumulative disbursal by State is led by Uttar Pradesh, with Tamil Nadu, Bihar, Karnataka and Maharashtra following in the top group. Maharashtra is not first, so Statement 2 fails too. In 'more than doubled' type statements, always compute the ratio. 72/38 is about 1.9, which is less than 2.
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement 1 is incorrect. The ticket size rose about 1.9 times, which is less than double.
(b) is wrong because Statement 2 is incorrect. Maharashtra is not first in cumulative disbursal; UP, Tamil Nadu and Bihar lead.
(c) is wrong because neither statement holds.
(d) is correct because both statements are factually incorrect.
keyfact: PMMY ticket size rose about 1.9x (Rs 38k to Rs 72k, FY16 to FY25), not more than double, and Maharashtra is not the top State.
option_notes: Option (a), Statement 1 only: this would require the ticket size to have more than doubled. The real figures are about Rs 38,000 to Rs 72,000, an increase of about 89 percent. PMMY was launched on 8 April 2015 and provides collateral-free loans to micro-enterprises. The loans have no collateral requirement and are under the Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units (CGFMU). Its categories are Shishu, Kishore, Tarun and Tarun Plus.

Option (b), Statement 2 only: this would make Maharashtra the top State by cumulative disbursal. In fact Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Bihar are ahead of it. Maharashtra is a large economy but has fewer micro-loan accounts than these States. Per-capita and absolute disbursal rankings differ, and Karnataka, West Bengal and Maharashtra feature in the top ten.

Option (c), Both 1 and 2: this would need both claims to be true. Neither is. It is the typical trap option in statement questions where one claim looks plausible, such as 'doubled' for 38k to 72k and 'Maharashtra' as the biggest economy. Always verify exact figures.

Option (d), Neither 1 nor 2: this is the correct option. The ticket size grew about 1.9 times, which is not more than double. Maharashtra is not the leading State. PMMY covers non-farm income-generating activities such as manufacturing, trading and services, and also allied agricultural activities. MUDRA Ltd is a SIDBI subsidiary and refinances lending institutions.
related: PMMY launched 8 April 2015; collateral-free loans up to Rs 10 lakh.
Categories: Shishu (up to 50k), Kishore (50k to 5 lakh), Tarun (5 to 10 lakh), Tarun Plus (10 to 20 lakh).
MUDRA Ltd is a subsidiary of SIDBI.
Average ticket size: about Rs 38,000 (FY16) to about Rs 72,000 (FY25).
Women make up roughly two-thirds of PMMY borrower accounts.
Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units (CGFMU) covers MUDRA loans.
Stand-Up India (2016) gives Rs 10 lakh to 1 crore loans to SC/ST/women entrepreneurs.
Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Bihar are among the top States by cumulative PMMY disbursal.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The average ticket size went from about Rs 38,000 (FY16) to about Rs 72,000 (FY25), a rise of about 1.9 times, which is not more than double. PMMY started on 8 April 2015. FY16 saw roughly 3.5 crore loans worth about Rs 1.37 lakh crore. Cumulatively, over 50 crore loans worth more than Rs 32 lakh crore were sanctioned in ten years. Shishu loans form the bulk of accounts, while Kishore and Tarun account for a growing share of the amount. The rising average ticket size shows a shift toward larger loans. Tarun Plus (Rs 10 to 20 lakh) was introduced in 2024 for borrowers who repaid earlier Tarun loans.

2 — Incorrect: Maharashtra is not the State with the highest cumulative PMMY disbursal. Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Bihar are the front-runners, with Karnataka and Maharashtra among the top five or six. Large populations and many micro-enterprises explain the lead of UP and Tamil Nadu. Women borrowers account for roughly two-thirds or more of the accounts. SC/ST/OBC borrowers are a large share of accounts. Loans carry no processing fee for Shishu, and MUDRA cards (RuPay debit cards) are issued for working-capital limits.
summary: The answer is (d), neither statement is correct. The average MUDRA ticket size rose from about Rs 38,000 in FY2016 to about Rs 72,000 in FY2025, which is roughly 1.9 times and falls just short of doubling. Maharashtra is not the top State by cumulative disbursal; Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Bihar lead.
topic_notes: PMMY was launched on 8 April 2015. It offers collateral-free loans up to Rs 10 lakh for non-corporate, non-farm small and micro enterprises, and allied agricultural activities such as poultry and dairy are included. Loans come from Scheduled Commercial Banks, RRBs, Small Finance Banks, cooperative banks, MFIs and NBFCs. MUDRA (Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency) was set up as a SIDBI subsidiary and was announced in Budget 2015-16. Product categories: Shishu (up to Rs 50,000), Kishore (Rs 50,000 to 5 lakh), Tarun (Rs 5 to 10 lakh) and Tarun Plus (Rs 10 to 20 lakh, from Budget 2024-25). MUDRA loans are covered by the Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units (CGFMU), managed by NCGTC. Borrowers also receive RuPay MUDRA cards for working capital. Shishu loans make up the large majority of accounts. Women are the majority of borrowers (about 68 percent of accounts) and a large share of borrowers are from SC/ST/OBC groups. Over ten years, more than 50 crore loans worth over Rs 30 lakh crore have been sanctioned. Average ticket size rose from about Rs 38,000 in FY16 to about Rs 72,000 in FY25. Related schemes: Stand-Up India (Rs 10 lakh to 1 crore for SC/ST/women greenfield enterprises, 2016), PM SVANidhi (street vendors), PMEGP (KVIC subsidy scheme), CGTMSE (credit guarantee for MSMEs), and the Udyam registration portal. UPSC may ask about the launching date, categories, the refinancing agency, the ceiling on loans, beneficiary profile and State-wise leaders.

question: Consider the following statements : NISHTHA is an_ integrated teacher LK training programme that has been extended to cover teachers at all stages of school education. PM POSHAN covers only those school children who are studying in classes I-VI in Government and Government-aided schools. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? #
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: NISHTHA was launched by the Department of School Education and Literacy, Ministry of Education, in 2019 under Samagra Shiksha as the world's largest teacher training programme. It began with elementary teachers (NISHTHA 1.0, classes I-VIII), then expanded to NISHTHA 2.0 (secondary stage), NISHTHA 3.0 (foundational stage, FLN), and NISHTHA 4.0 (preschool/ECCE). It is therefore an integrated programme now covering teachers at all stages: preschool, foundational, preparatory, middle and secondary. Training is delivered via NCERT, with DIKSHA as the digital platform. PM POSHAN (formerly Mid-Day Meal Scheme, renamed in September 2021) is a centrally sponsored scheme that covers children in Classes I-VIII in Government, Government-aided, and local body schools, and since 2021-22 also Bal Vatika (pre-primary) in government and aided primary schools. The statement limiting coverage to classes I-VI is a factual distortion: the upper limit is class VIII. Elimination: since Statement 2 is wrong, options (b) and (c) fall; Statement 1 is right, so (d) falls, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: Statement 1 is true as NISHTHA covers teachers at all stages, and Statement 2 is false because PM POSHAN covers classes I-VIII, so only Statement 1 is correct.
Wrong: Statement 2 is incorrect because the scheme is not limited to classes I-VI; it covers I-VIII and Bal Vatika.
Wrong: Statement 2 fails, so 'both' cannot be correct.
Wrong: Statement 1 is true, so 'neither' cannot be correct.
keyfact: NISHTHA covers teachers of all school stages; PM POSHAN covers classes I-VIII plus Bal Vatika, not just I-VI.
option_notes: Statement 1 only: the correct choice here. NISHTHA, launched in 2019 under Samagra Shiksha, is the National Initiative for School Heads' and Teachers' Holistic Advancement, run by NCERT. It began with elementary teachers and was extended through versions 2.0 (secondary), 3.0 (foundational literacy and numeracy) and 4.0 (preschool/ECCE). Training is delivered via DIKSHA and state-level resource persons, aligned to NEP 2020 and competency-based learning goals.

Statement 2 only: would be correct only if PM POSHAN were limited to classes I-VI, which it is not. PM POSHAN, which replaced the Mid Day Meal Scheme in 2021, covers classes I-VIII and Bal Vatika in government, aided and local body schools. It is a centrally sponsored scheme for 2021-22 to 2025-26, with an outlay of about Rs 1.3 lakh crore, and aims to improve nutrition and enrolment.

Both 1 and 2: wrong, since Statement 2 misstates the class coverage. This option would imply that PM POSHAN is limited to classes I-VI. In fact the scheme covers about 11.8 crore children across classes I-VIII and pre-primary in participating schools. NISHTHA being all-stage is accurate, but the combination fails because of Statement 2.

Neither 1 nor 2: wrong because NISHTHA does cover teachers at all stages of school education following its extensions. It is a flagship teacher training programme of the Ministry of Education that has expanded beyond elementary level. Choosing this option would deny the well-documented extension to preschool, foundational and secondary stages.
related: NISHTHA was launched in 2019 by the Ministry of Education and implemented by NCERT.
PM POSHAN replaced the Mid Day Meal Scheme in September 2021.
PM POSHAN covers classes I-VIII and Bal Vatika in government and aided schools.
Samagra Shiksha subsumed SSA, RMSA and Teacher Education in 2018.
NIPUN Bharat Mission targets foundational literacy and numeracy by Grade 3.
Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment (2002), gives the right to education for ages 6-14.
PM SHRI scheme aims to develop over 14,500 schools as NEP 2020 exemplars.
statements: 1 — Correct: NISHTHA has been extended from elementary to foundational, preschool and secondary stages, so it now covers teachers at all stages of school education. NISHTHA was launched in 2019 by the Ministry of Education under Samagra Shiksha, run by NCERT with state SCERTs and key resource persons. It is a capacity-building programme for teachers and school heads. NISHTHA 2.0 covers secondary teachers, NISHTHA 3.0 covers FLN (foundational literacy and numeracy), and NISHTHA 4.0 covers preschool/ECCE. Training is available through the DIKSHA platform, aligned to NEP 2020 and learning outcomes.

2 — Incorrect: PM POSHAN covers children in classes I-VIII, not only I-VI, and was also extended to Bal Vatika (pre-primary) in government and aided primary schools. It was approved in September 2021 for 2021-22 to 2025-26, replacing the National Programme of Mid Day Meal in Schools (1995 origin). It is centrally sponsored, with cost shared between Centre and states (60:40 generally; 90:10 for NE and Himalayan states). It covers government, government-aided and local body schools, and madrasas/maktabs supported under Samagra Shiksha. Food-grain norms are 100 g per child for primary and 150 g for upper primary. Tithi Bhojan and school nutrition gardens are features.
summary: The answer is (a): only Statement 1 is correct. NISHTHA (National Initiative for School Heads' and Teachers' Holistic Advancement) has been extended from elementary to secondary, foundational and preschool stages, so it covers teachers at all stages of school education. PM POSHAN covers classes I-VIII (and Bal Vatika/pre-primary in later extension), not just I-VI, so Statement 2 is wrong.
topic_notes: School education schemes are a recurring area in UPSC papers. Samagra Shiksha (2018) is an integrated scheme subsuming Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan and Teacher Education, covering preschool to class XII. NISHTHA (2019) is its teacher training arm, executed by NCERT; NISHTHA 1.0 covered elementary teachers, 2.0 secondary, 3.0 foundational, 4.0 preschool/ECCE. DIKSHA is the national digital platform for school education, and the NIPUN Bharat Mission (2021) targets foundational literacy and numeracy by Grade 3 by 2026-27. PM POSHAN, approved September 2021, renamed the Mid Day Meal Scheme, which began in 1995 as a national programme of nutritional support to primary education and was extended to upper primary in 2008. The Supreme Court in the PUCL v. Union of India case (2001) made cooked mid-day meals a legal entitlement. The National Food Security Act 2013 also gives a legal basis. Coverage includes classes I-VIII and Bal Vatika; supplementary nutrition for children in aspirational districts with high anaemia is also included. Other angles: PM SHRI Schools (2022) aims to develop over 14,500 model schools showcasing NEP 2020; PARAKH is the national assessment centre; Vidyanjali encourages volunteers; and PM eVidya integrates digital learning. NEP 2020 introduced a 5+3+3+4 structure, a target of 100% GER in school education by 2030 and 6% GDP public spending on education. RTE Act 2009 (Article 21A) covers ages 6-14 and mandates 25% reservation for disadvantaged groups in private schools.

question: Consider the following statements : India’s bio-economy contributes about i 4-25 % to the GDP in India. BioE3 promotes regenerative bio-manufacturing and supports a circular bio-economy aligned with India’s net-zero goals. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: India's bio-economy grew from about USD 10 billion in 2014 to about USD 130 billion in 2022 and about USD 165.7 billion in 2024. That is roughly 4.25% of GDP, and the target is USD 300 billion by 2030. The OCR'd statement reads 'about 4-25 %', which is most likely a garbled '4.25%'. Read as a range of 4 to 25%, it is plainly false. Read as 4.25%, it would be correct, which creates ambiguity. However, the question was likely framed to test the figure. Since the printed text is 4-25%, the intended trap is the wrong range, so statement 1 is treated as incorrect. Statement 2 is correct: the BioE3 Policy, led by the Department of Biotechnology, covers six thematic sectors: bio-based chemicals and enzymes, functional foods and smart proteins, precision biotherapeutics, climate-resilient agriculture, carbon capture and utilisation, and marine and space research. It also sets up Biomanufacturing Hubs, Bio-AI Hubs and Biofoundries, and it supports 'Lifestyle for Environment' and the circular bio-economy. Elimination: since statement 2 is certainly correct, options (a) and (d) go. The only choice left is between (b) and (c), decided by the figure in statement 1.
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 gives the share as 4-25% of GDP, but the actual share is about 4.25%. Statement 2 is also correct, so '1 only' is not right either.
Correct: statement 2 matches the BioE3 Policy's aims. Statement 1, as printed, gives an incorrect range for the bio-economy's share of GDP.
Wrong: this would need statement 1 to be correct, but the 4-25% range is wrong. The real figure is about 4.25%.
Wrong: statement 2 on BioE3 is correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: BioE3 (Aug 2024, DBT) backs regenerative bio-manufacturing and a circular bio-economy for Net Zero 2070; India's bio-economy is ~4.25% of GDP.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: it would hold only if the bio-economy share claim were right and BioE3 did not support a circular bio-economy. India's bio-economy is about 4.25% of GDP (about USD 165.7 billion in 2024), with a target of USD 300 billion by 2030. It is not 4-25%, so this option is wrong.

Option (b) 2 only: it fits the facts. BioE3 was approved by the Cabinet in August 2024. It promotes regenerative bio-manufacturing and a circular bio-economy aligned with Net Zero 2070. It is run by DBT, and it provides for bio-manufacturing hubs, Bio-AI hubs and biofoundries, plus skilling for biotech jobs.

Option (c) Both 1 and 2: it would be right only if the GDP figure were exactly right. The printed range of 4-25% is wrong, because the actual share is about 4.25%. Statement 2 holds true. The sector's growth was from about USD 10 billion (2014) to about USD 165.7 billion (2024).

Option (d) Neither 1 nor 2: it is wrong because statement 2 is true. BioE3 explicitly focuses on regenerative bio-manufacturing, a circular bio-economy, and climate-friendly biotech solutions that support India's Net Zero 2070 commitment, announced at COP26 in 2021.
related: BioE3 Policy was approved by the Union Cabinet in August 2024.
The nodal department for BioE3 is the Department of Biotechnology (DBT).
India's bio-economy is about 4.25% of GDP, with a target of USD 300 billion by 2030.
India's Net Zero target year is 2070, announced at COP26 in Glasgow.
BIRAC was established in 2012 to support biotech startups.
BioRIDE is the umbrella scheme of DBT for research, innovation and entrepreneurship.
GEAC under the Environment Ministry regulates GM organisms.
Mission LiFE was launched in 2022 to promote sustainable lifestyles.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: As printed, 4-25% overstates the range; the actual share is about 4.25% of GDP. India's bio-economy was about USD 165.7 billion in 2024, up from about USD 10 billion in 2014, with a target of USD 300 billion by 2030. The sector includes biopharma, bioindustrial, bioagri and bio-IT/research. India has over 8,500 biotech startups, and it ranks among the top 12 biotech destinations globally. Note that the OCR may have garbled 4.25, so check the exact figure when revising.

2 — Correct: BioE3 stands for Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment. The Union Cabinet approved it on 24 August 2024 and the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) runs it. It promotes regenerative bio-manufacturing, bio-based products, and a circular bio-economy, in line with the Net Zero 2070 goal and the LiFE mission. It sets up Bio-manufacturing Hubs, Bio-AI Hubs and Biofoundries. It covers six thematic sectors, including climate-resilient agriculture and carbon capture.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The BioE3 (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment) Policy, approved by the Union Cabinet in August 2024, promotes regenerative bio-manufacturing and a circular bio-economy aligned with Net Zero goals. India's bio-economy is only about 4.25% of GDP (about USD 165.7 billion in 2024), not 4-25%, so statement 1 as printed is wrong.
topic_notes: India's bio-economy has grown rapidly. It was about USD 10 billion in 2014, about USD 130 billion in 2022 and about USD 165.7 billion in 2024, which is around 4.25% of GDP. The target is USD 300 billion by 2030. The Department of Biotechnology (DBT) under the Ministry of Science and Technology is the nodal agency. The BioE3 Policy (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment) was approved by the Union Cabinet on 24 August 2024. It promotes high-performance bio-manufacturing and aligns with the circular bio-economy, LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) and Net Zero 2070. Its six thematic sectors are: bio-based chemicals and enzymes; functional foods and smart proteins; precision biotherapeutics; climate-resilient agriculture; carbon capture and its utilisation; and futuristic marine and space research. It sets up Bio-manufacturing Hubs, Bio-AI Hubs and Biofoundries, and it encourages regenerative bioeconomy models. Other related items: BIRAC (Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council), set up in 2012 as a Section 8 company, supports startups. The National Biotechnology Development Strategy 2021-25 is the earlier strategy. The Biotech-KISAN scheme supports farmers. Genome India Project sequenced 10,000 genomes. BioRIDE is the umbrella scheme for biotech research, innovation and entrepreneurship development. Also note the Biosafety framework run by the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) under the Environment Ministry. India hosts the world's largest vaccine manufacturing capacity and is called the 'pharmacy of the world'.

question:
Which of the following Development Financial Institutions were set up in India between 1950s and 1960s ?
1. Industrial Finance Corporation of India (FCI)
2. Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India (ICICI)
3. Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI)
4. National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NaBFID) Select the answer using the codes given below :
options: 1, 2,3 and 4 Core inflation includes which of the following ? 1. Food prices 2. Energy prices
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Development Financial Institutions (DFIs) provide long-term finance for industry and infrastructure. India's DFI architecture began with the Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI), established in 1948 under the IFC Act 1948 as the first DFI. The Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India (ICICI) was set up in 1955 with World Bank support as a private-sector initiative. The Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) was established in 1964 as a subsidiary of the RBI and became the apex DFI; it was delinked from the RBI in 1976. Later came SIDBI (1990), NABARD (1982), EXIM Bank (1982) and others. After the 1990s reforms, ICICI merged with ICICI Bank (2002) and IDBI with IDBI Bank (2004), as universal banking replaced the DFI model. NaBFID was created by the NaBFID Act, 2021 to finance infrastructure, so it falls in the 2020s. Elimination: NaBFID is clearly modern, so options (b) and (d) are out. Option (c) omits IFCI, which is certainly a DFI from the early post-independence period. Hence (a) is the best choice, with the caveat that IFCI dates to 1948, just before the 1950s.
explanations: Correct: it includes IFCI, ICICI and IDBI, the early DFIs, and excludes the 2021 NaBFID.
Wrong: it includes NaBFID, which was set up in 2021, and it omits ICICI and IDBI.
Wrong: ICICI and IDBI are right, but dropping IFCI, the earliest DFI, makes it incomplete.
Wrong: NaBFID is a 2021 institution, so all four cannot be correct.
keyfact: IFCI 1948, ICICI 1955, IDBI 1964 are the early DFIs; NaBFID dates from 2021.
option_notes: IFCI (1948), ICICI (1955) and IDBI (1964) were the three early DFIs. IFCI was the first, ICICI was the first private-sector DFI backed by the World Bank, and IDBI was the apex DFI. All three have since changed their role: IFCI is a government-owned NBFC, while ICICI and IDBI became banks.

IFCI and NaBFID: IFCI was set up in 1948 and NaBFID in 2021. The pairing mixes two different eras. NaBFID is a new infrastructure-focused DFI with a statutory framework under the 2021 Act, and it can raise funds in India and abroad, and is supervised by RBI.

ICICI and IDBI: both were set up in the 1950s-60s (1955 and 1964). ICICI was a private-sector DFI, while IDBI was set up by the government under the RBI. This pair omits IFCI, which is also an early DFI, so the option is incomplete.

All four would include NaBFID, but it was set up in 2021. NaBFID has an authorised capital of Rs 1 lakh crore, and the government owns 100% initially, aiming to reduce its stake to 26% later. It builds a pipeline of infrastructure projects under the National Infrastructure Pipeline.
related: IFCI (1948) was India's first DFI.
ICICI was set up in 1955 with World Bank support.
IDBI was set up in 1964 as an RBI subsidiary and delinked in 1976.
NaBFID was set up under the NaBFID Act 2021.
SIDBI was set up in 1990 as an IDBI subsidiary.
NABARD was set up in 1982 on the Shivaraman Committee's recommendation.
ICICI merged with ICICI Bank in 2002.
IDBI Bank became a bank in 2004; LIC took a controlling stake in 2019.
statements: 1 — Correct (approximately): IFCI was established in 1948, the first DFI, just before the 1950s, but it is counted in the early post-independence DFI set. IFCI was set up under the IFC Act 1948 to give medium and long-term credit to industry. It was converted into a public limited company in 1993. It later faced financial stress, and the government has held a majority stake. It was classified under RBI's prompt corrective action framework and its lending was restricted.

2 — Correct: ICICI was set up in 1955 as a joint-venture DFI with support from the World Bank, the Government of India and Indian and foreign investors. It provided project finance to private industry. It was promoted by figures such as A. Ramaswami Mudaliar and others. It became a universal bank when it merged with its subsidiary ICICI Bank in 2002, the first such big reverse merger in Indian banking.

3 — Correct: IDBI was established in 1964 under the IDBI Act 1964 as a wholly owned RBI subsidiary and served as the apex term-lending institution coordinating other DFIs. In 1976 ownership passed to the Government of India. It became IDBI Bank Ltd in 2004. LIC acquired a controlling stake in 2019, and IDBI was categorised as a private sector bank by RBI for regulatory purposes. A strategic sale was under way.

4 — Incorrect: NaBFID was set up by the NaBFID Act, 2021 as a DFI to fund infrastructure, with an initial capital of Rs 20,000 crore. It is regulated by the RBI as an All India Financial Institution. It was announced in the Union Budget 2021-22, and was set up in 2021, not in the 1950s or 1960s. Its Chair was initially K.V. Kamath.
summary: The answer is (a): IFCI (1948), ICICI (1955) and IDBI (1964) are the DFIs listed here, but the question's 'between 1950s and 1960s' wording is loose. NaBFID was set up only in 2021, so statement 4 is wrong. Note that IFCI was set up in 1948 (a strict reading would exclude it), but among the given options (a) is the only one that excludes NaBFID and includes ICICI and IDBI. (The question text also has an unrelated fragment on core inflation appended, which is not part of this question.)
topic_notes: Development Financial Institutions are specialised institutions that provide long-term finance for industry, agriculture and infrastructure where commercial banks lack the appetite. India's DFI network developed after independence in tiers. All-India institutions: IFCI (1948), ICICI (1955), IDBI (1964), IDBI as apex, UTI (1964), IRBI (1971, later IIBI), SIDBI (1990). Specialised: EXIM Bank (1982), NABARD (1982), NHB (1988), TFCI (1989), PFC (1986), IREDA (1987), IIFCL (2006). State-level: SFCs under the SFC Act 1951 and SIDCs. After 1991 liberalisation, the Narasimham Committee and the Khan Working Group (1997) recommended moving to universal banking; DFIs became banks (ICICI Bank 2002, IDBI Bank 2004). IDBI was delinked from RBI in 1976, and the RBI's ownership of NABARD was transferred to the government in 2000s. NaBFID, established in 2021, revives the DFI model for infrastructure under the NaBFID Act 2021, with the government providing Rs 20,000 crore equity and a target of Rs 3 lakh crore lending by 2024-25. The Union Budget 2021-22 announced it. Related topics for the exam are AIFIs recognised by RBI (NABARD, NHB, EXIM, SIDBI, NaBFID), the role of the World Bank in funding early DFIs, and the difference between DFIs and commercial banks. Also remember the Industrial Policy Resolution 1948 and 1956, the Five Year Plans' industrial finance emphasis, and the Narasimham Committee on financial sector reforms.

question:
Which of the following statéments are'correct? 41.
1. The Chief Justice of India is the highest Administrative Officer of the Supreme Court of India. 29 Wile administrative powers for determining the work structure of the Supreme Court and its Registry are exclusively vested in the Chief Justice of India.
3. A person who has been a Judge of the Supreme Court of India can practice after retirement only in the Supreme Court of India and not in any other court within India.
4. A designated Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of India is not entitled to appear in the Supreme Court of India without an Advocate-on-Record. Select the answer using the codes given below :
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 124(7) says no person who has held office as a Supreme Court judge shall plead or act in any court or before any authority within the territory of India. Statement 3 wrongly says the bar covers only the Supreme Court, so options (b) and (c) are eliminated. Article 146 gives the CJI (or a judge he nominates) the power to appoint officers and servants of the Court. He also frames their service conditions, subject to the President's approval where rules are concerned. The CJI is also Master of the Roster and controls the Registry's functioning, so statement 2 is accepted. Under Order IV of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013, a Senior Advocate cannot appear in the Supreme Court without an Advocate-on-Record, and cannot draft pleadings or accept briefs directly. So statement 4 is correct. Statement 1 is commonly stated as true, since the CJI is the head of the Court's administration. Strictly, though, the Constitution does not use the phrase 'highest Administrative Officer'. Since 2 and 4 are well supported and the options only allow 1 and 2 or 2 and 4, I chose (d). Statement 1 is the weak link, and the correct set by strict facts would arguably be 1, 2 and 4, which no option offers.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 only would require statement 4 to be false, but Order IV of the Supreme Court Rules bars a Senior Advocate from appearing without an AOR, so this is less likely to be the setter's key.
(b) Wrong because statement 3 is false: Article 124(7) bars retired Supreme Court judges from practising in any court or before any authority in India, not only the Supreme Court.
(c) Wrong because statement 3 is false, even though statement 4 is true.

(d) Chosen: statements 2 and 4 are well supported, and statement 3 is false. It treats statement 1, with its non-constitutional wording, as the doubtful one, though this is a judgement call without an official key.
keyfact: Article 124(7): a retired Supreme Court judge cannot practise in any court or authority in India, and Senior Advocates need an AOR in the Supreme Court.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2 both concern the CJI's administrative role. The CJI heads the Supreme Court's administration, is Master of the Roster, and appoints Registry staff under Article 146. This pairing leaves out the Senior Advocate/AOR rule, which is a genuine rule in Order IV of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013.

Statements 1, 2 and 3 together include the false claim that the post-retirement bar applies only in the Supreme Court. Article 124(7) covers all courts and authorities in India. The article applies to retired Supreme Court judges only. Retired High Court judges are governed by Article 220.

Statements 3 and 4 together combine one false and one true statement. Statement 3 is wrong because Article 124(7) bars practice anywhere in India. Statement 4 is right because Senior Advocates need an AOR to appear in the Supreme Court.

Statements 2 and 4 together cover the CJI's power over the Registry (Article 146) and the Senior Advocate/AOR rule. Under that rule a Senior Advocate must appear with an Advocate-on-Record in the Supreme Court. It is the best-supported option, though it assumes statement 1 is treated as not correct.
related: Article 124(7): retired Supreme Court judges cannot practise in any court or authority in India.
Article 220: restriction on practice after retirement for High Court judges.
Article 146: appointment of Supreme Court staff by the CJI.
Section 16 of the Advocates Act, 1961 provides for Senior Advocate designation.
Senior Advocates cannot appear in the Supreme Court without an Advocate-on-Record.
CJI is the Master of the Roster.
Supreme Court strength: 34 judges including the CJI.
Retirement age of Supreme Court judges: 65 years.
statements: 1 — Doubtful/Likely treated as Incorrect by the setter: the CJI is the administrative head of the Court, but the Constitution has no phrase 'highest Administrative Officer'. The CJI is head of the Supreme Court. Under Article 146 he appoints the officers and servants of the Court, and he is Master of the Roster, allocating benches and cases. The Registrar General and Secretary General handle day-to-day administration under his control. His administrative authority is recognised in Asok Pande v. Supreme Court of India (2018) and in the Supreme Court Rules, 2013.

2 — Correct: Article 146 gives the CJI power over appointments and the structure of the Registry. Appointments of officers and servants are made by the CJI or a judge or officer he directs. Service conditions are fixed by rules made by the CJI, with the President's approval for rules on salaries, allowances, leave and pensions. The Court's administrative expenses are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 146(3)). The CJI also constitutes benches and sets the work allocation through the roster, which is why he is called Master of the Roster.

3 — Incorrect: Article 124(7) bars a retired Supreme Court judge from pleading or acting in any court or before any authority within India. The bar is therefore not limited to the Supreme Court. High Court judges are treated differently, under Article 220: a retired permanent High Court judge cannot practise in the Supreme Court or in any High Court except the High Courts in which he never served as a judge. The Constitution Bench in the Second Judges Case referred to these provisions.

4 — Correct: Order IV of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013 (and earlier rules) bars a Senior Advocate from appearing without an Advocate-on-Record. A Senior Advocate cannot file pleadings or accept briefs directly, and must be instructed by an AOR. Senior designation is under Section 16 of the Advocates Act, 1961, and the process was laid down in Indira Jaising v. Supreme Court (2017, revised 2023). Only advocates who pass the AOR exam can file matters in the Supreme Court.
summary: Best answer is (d), 2 and 4 only, though this is a judgement call because the paper has no official key. Statement 3 is clearly wrong: Article 124(7) bars a retired Supreme Court judge from practising in any court or before any authority in India. Statements 2 and 4 are sound, which leaves statement 1 as the doubtful one.
topic_notes: Supreme Court administration and bar rules. Article 124 deals with the establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court. Article 124(7) bars a retired Supreme Court judge from pleading or acting in any court or before any authority within India. Article 220 restricts retired permanent High Court judges from practising in the Supreme Court and in any High Court except those in which they never served. Article 146 covers officers and servants of the Supreme Court and its expenses. Appointments are made by the CJI, or a judge or officer he directs. Service-condition rules are made by the CJI and need the President's approval where they relate to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions. Administrative expenses are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India. The CJI is Master of the Roster, a position confirmed in Shanti Bhushan v. Supreme Court (2018) and Asok Pande (2018). The Supreme Court Rules, 2013 govern practice and procedure. Under Order IV, only Advocates-on-Record can file pleadings, and a Senior Advocate must be assisted by an AOR. Section 16 of the Advocates Act, 1961 provides for designation of Senior Advocates, which was reworked in Indira Jaising v. Supreme Court (2017) and refined in 2023. Section 30 gives advocates the right to practise throughout India. Other points to revise are the Supreme Court judges' retirement age of 65 and the 34-judge strength fixed by the 2019 amendment. Also revise Article 128 on ad hoc and retired judges and Article 130 on the seat of the Court. Possible future angles are the AOR examination, the Collegium system and the removal procedure under Article 124(4).

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Supreme Court of India and High Courts have exclusive original jurisdiction in disputes amongst two or more States.
2. Only the Supreme Court of India, High Courts and District Courts have the power to issue Writs.
3. Chief Minister of a State has absolutely no role in the entire appointment process of a High Court Judge.
4. Local customs and conventions which do not contradict a Statute or the Constitution are recognised and taken into account by Courts while administering justice in certain spheres. How many of the above statements is/are correct ?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Statement 1 is wrong because Article 131 gives the Supreme Court alone exclusive original jurisdiction in disputes between the Centre and States, or between States. High Courts have no such jurisdiction. Statement 2 is wrong because writs are issued under Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Courts). District Courts have no writ power. Statement 3 is wrong because, under the Memorandum of Procedure, the proposal for a High Court judge is initiated by the Chief Justice of the High Court. The Governor and Chief Minister are then consulted, and the Chief Minister advises the Governor on the matter. The collegium and the Union Law Ministry follow, and the President finally appoints under Article 217. So the claim of 'absolutely no role' is false. Statement 4 is correct because custom is a recognised source of law. Courts apply valid customs in personal law, such as Hindu law customs, and in tribal areas, provided they are ancient, certain, reasonable and not contrary to statute or the Constitution. Only one statement is correct, so the answer is (a).
explanations: (a) One is correct: only statement 4 holds. The other three fail on Article 131, Articles 32 and 226, and Article 217 respectively.
(b) Two is wrong: no second statement is correct, since statements 1, 2 and 3 are all false.
(c) Three is wrong: three statements would have to be correct, but only one is.
(d) Four is wrong: statements 1, 2 and 3 each contain an error.
keyfact: Article 131 (inter-State disputes) is exclusive to the Supreme Court. Writs come only from the SC (Art 32) and High Courts (Art 226). The CM advises the Governor on High Court judge appointments.
option_notes: One: the correct count. Only statement 4 (valid custom recognised by courts) is true. Statements 1, 2 and 3 fail because of Article 131 (SC exclusive), Articles 32 and 226 (writs) and Article 217 (consultative process).

Two: would require another correct statement. Examiners often make a statement look plausible by adding 'High Courts' or 'District Courts', or by using 'absolutely' or 'only'. Words like these usually signal a false statement.

Three: would require three correct statements. A student who accepted that High Courts share Article 131 jurisdiction, or that the Chief Minister has no role, might choose this. Both claims are wrong.
Four: would mean every statement is correct. This is unlikely given the absolute wording in statements 2 and 3 and the exclusive jurisdiction in statement 1.
related: Article 131: exclusive original jurisdiction of the SC in Centre-State and inter-State disputes.
Article 32 is called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution by Dr. Ambedkar.
Article 226 writ power is wider than Article 32 because it also covers ordinary legal rights.
Article 217 governs appointment of High Court judges; Article 124 governs SC judges.
Article 262 provides for adjudication of inter-State river water disputes.
Article 13(3)(a) includes custom or usage in the definition of law.
The Second Judges Case (1993) established the collegium and gave primacy to the CJI.
The NJAC was struck down in 2015 in the Fourth Judges Case.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Only the Supreme Court has exclusive original jurisdiction under Article 131. Article 131 covers disputes between the Centre and one or more States, between the Centre and States on one side and other States on the other, and between two or more States. The dispute must involve a legal right, not a political question. Article 131 does not cover treaty matters, inter-State water disputes (Article 262) or Finance Commission matters. High Courts have original jurisdiction only in limited areas, such as writs, admiralty, company and testamentary matters, and in Chartered High Courts.

2 — Incorrect: Only the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226) can issue writs. The five writs are habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right, while Article 226 is wider because it covers 'any other purpose' as well. Parliament may empower other courts to issue writs under Article 32(3), but it has not done so. District Courts cannot issue writs. Tribunals under Article 323A and 323B are also not general writ courts.

3 — Incorrect: The Chief Minister does have a role. Under Article 217, a High Court judge is appointed by the President after consultation with the CJI, the Governor and the Chief Justice of the High Court. The Memorandum of Procedure has the High Court collegium recommend names. The Governor, acting on the Chief Minister's advice, then conveys the State's views. The Union Law Ministry processes the file and the Supreme Court collegium finalises the names. The 1993 Second Judges Case and the 1998 Third Judges Case set up the collegium. The NJAC (99th Amendment) was struck down in 2015.

4 — Correct: Custom is a recognised source of law in India. Courts enforce a custom if it is ancient, continuous, certain, reasonable and not opposed to statute, public policy or the Constitution. Customs are applied mainly in personal law, such as Hindu marriage and succession and tribal laws. Article 13(3)(a) includes 'custom or usage' within the definition of 'law'. Article 244 and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules protect tribal customary practices. Article 371A protects Naga customary law.
summary: Only statement 4 is correct, so the answer is (a) One. Original jurisdiction in inter-State disputes belongs exclusively to the Supreme Court, only the SC and High Courts can issue writs, and the Chief Minister does have a role in High Court judge appointments.
topic_notes: Judiciary and jurisdiction in India. The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction (Article 131), writ jurisdiction (Article 32), appellate jurisdiction (Articles 132-136), advisory jurisdiction (Article 143) and review (Article 137). Article 139A allows transfer of cases. Article 129 makes the SC a court of record. High Courts have writ jurisdiction under Article 226, supervisory jurisdiction over subordinate courts under Article 227 and appointment under Article 217. Article 124 deals with SC judges. The collegium system arose from the Three Judges Cases: S.P. Gupta (1981), Second Judges (1993) and Third Judges (1998). The NJAC Act 2014 and the 99th Amendment were struck down in 2015. SC judges retire at 65 and High Court judges at 62. Article 222 deals with transfer of High Court judges. Article 233 deals with appointment of district judges by the Governor in consultation with the High Court. Article 235 gives High Courts control over subordinate courts. Article 215 makes High Courts courts of record. Sources of law include the Constitution, statutes, precedents (Article 141), custom and personal law. Article 13 defines 'law' to include custom or usage. Other topics: PIL, Lok Adalats under the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987, Article 39A on free legal aid, tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B, and Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008.

question:
Consider thé ‘following statements about Electronic Voting Machine (EVM) in India :
1. The first use of EVMs in a Lok Sabha election was in the year 2004, when EVMs were deployed nationwide.
2. Votes are recorded in Control Units and VVPATSs at exactly the same time.
3. Two PSUs, namely Bharat Electronics Ltd., and Electronics Corporation of India Ltd. have been engaged by the Election Commission of India to design and manufacture the EVMs. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: General Science
detail: EVMs were developed by the Election Commission with two PSUs: Bharat Electronics Ltd (BEL), Bangalore, and Electronics Corporation of India Ltd (ECIL), Hyderabad. They were first used experimentally in the Parur assembly constituency of Kerala in 1982 (for 50 polling stations). Section 61A was inserted into the Representation of the People Act, 1951 in 1989 and legalised their use, and the amendment came into force in 1989-90. EVMs were used on an experimental basis in 1998 assembly polls in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Delhi. They were used in Goa's assembly election in 1999 in full. They were used in all constituencies in the 2004 Lok Sabha election, which was the first time they covered the entire country. In 2004 EVMs were used in all 543 constituencies, but the 1999 Lok Sabha polls had used them in 46 constituencies, so statement 1's claim of first use in 2004 is wrong. VVPAT was introduced to give a paper slip for the voter to verify; it was first used in Noksen (Nagaland) bye-election in 2013. The EVM has a Ballot Unit, Control Unit and, with VVPAT, a printer unit. The vote is recorded in the Control Unit when the voter presses the button, and the VVPAT prints a slip that is visible for seven seconds before it drops, so the two are not exactly simultaneous. Hence only 3 is correct.
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because EVMs were used in a Lok Sabha election before 2004 (1999, in 46 seats), and statement 2 is also incorrect.
Wrong: statement 2 is incorrect, since recording in the Control Unit and printing by the VVPAT are sequential steps and not exactly simultaneous.
Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect, so the combination including it fails even though statement 3 is correct.
Correct: only statement 3 is true; BEL and ECIL manufacture the EVMs under the ECI's direction.
keyfact: EVMs are made by BEL (Bangalore) and ECIL (Hyderabad); first used in Parur, Kerala 1982, and nationwide in the 2004 Lok Sabha polls.
option_notes: Option (a) combines statements 1 and 2, both false. It relies on the common idea that 2004 was the first Lok Sabha use of EVMs, but the 1999 Lok Sabha polls used them in 46 constituencies. Statement 2 wrongly treats the Control Unit and VVPAT as recording at exactly the same instant, which is not the way the process works.

Option (b) combines statements 2 and 3. Statement 3 is true, but statement 2 is false because the vote is registered in the Control Unit and the VVPAT slip is printed after that and displayed for seven seconds. The VVPAT is an independent verification system that was first used in Noksen in 2013 and fully rolled out in 2019.

Option (c) combines statements 1 and 3. Statement 3 is true, but statement 1 is false because EVMs were used in a Lok Sabha election before 2004. Their nationwide, all-constituency deployment in a Lok Sabha election did happen in 2004, which makes this a plausible trap, but the claim of first use is wrong.

Option (d), statement 3 only, is correct. BEL (Bangalore) and ECIL (Hyderabad) are the two public sector undertakings that design and make the EVMs for the ECI. BEL is under the Ministry of Defence and ECIL is under the Department of Atomic Energy. Both work with the ECI's Technical Expert Committee, which includes experts from IIT and other institutes.
related: EVM first used in Parur (Kerala) in 1982
Section 61A of the RP Act 1951 permits voting machines
VVPAT first used in Noksen (Nagaland) in 2013
VVPAT slip is visible for 7 seconds
EVMs are made by BEL and ECIL
NOTA was introduced in 2013 after the PUCL case
All Lok Sabha constituencies used EVMs in 2004
statements: 1 — Incorrect: EVMs were used in 46 Lok Sabha constituencies in 1999 and in all constituencies in 2004, so 2004 was not the first use. Facts: EVMs were first tried in Parur, Kerala (1982). Section 61A of RP Act 1951 (inserted in 1989) gave legal sanction. Experimental use in 1998 state polls in MP, Rajasthan and Delhi. Goa 1999 was the first state fully on EVMs. 2004 was the first Lok Sabha election with EVMs across all 543 seats. Since 2000 they have been used in all state elections.

2 — Incorrect: The vote is recorded in the Control Unit when the voter presses the ballot unit button, and the VVPAT then prints a slip, which is displayed for about 7 seconds through a transparent window before it falls into a sealed box. The processes are sequential, not simultaneous. VVPAT was first used in Noksen, Nagaland in 2013 and was fully implemented in all constituencies in 2019. In 2019 the Supreme Court directed matching of VVPAT slips from five randomly chosen polling stations per assembly segment.

3 — Correct: The ECI's Technical Expert Committee oversees design and manufacture, which is done by two PSUs, BEL (Bangalore, Karnataka) and ECIL (Hyderabad, Telangana). Both are under the central government. M3 EVMs are the latest generation (since 2013), with tamper-detection features. EVMs are standalone machines that are not networked, use a one-time programmable microcontroller, and run on batteries. A control unit can handle up to 2,000 votes and a ballot unit supports 16 candidates (up to 24 ballot units linked for 384 candidates in M3).
summary: Only statement 3 is correct, so the answer is (d). BEL (Bangalore) and ECIL (Hyderabad) are the two PSUs that make EVMs for the ECI. EVMs were first used nationwide in the 2004 Lok Sabha elections, but that was not their first use in a Lok Sabha election, and votes are not recorded in the Control Unit and the VVPAT at exactly the same time.
topic_notes: EVMs in India were conceived in the late 1970s. The ECI mooted the idea in 1977, and ECIL developed a prototype in 1979, which was demonstrated to political parties in 1980. The first field use was in 1982 in the Parur assembly constituency (North Paravur) in Kerala. The Supreme Court struck down that use because the law did not allow it, and Parliament then inserted Section 61A in the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (in 1988, effective 15 March 1989). Experimental use occurred in 1998, and in 1999 EVMs were used in 46 Lok Sabha seats and in Goa. In 2001 the Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Puducherry and West Bengal assembly elections used EVMs fully, and in 2004 the Lok Sabha election was fully on EVMs. An EVM has three parts: the Control Unit (kept with the presiding officer), the Ballot Unit (inside the voting compartment) and the connecting cable. The VVPAT was added after an amendment to the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961 in 2013. The Supreme Court in Subramanian Swamy v. ECI (2013) directed the ECI to introduce VVPAT. Another judgment in 2019 required five random polling stations per assembly segment to have VVPAT verification, and a 2024 judgment rejected the demand to return to ballot papers or to count all VVPAT slips, while allowing checking of the burnt memory of microcontrollers on request by candidates who finish second and third. M3 EVMs allow up to 24 ballot units (384 candidates including NOTA). NOTA was introduced in 2013 following PUCL v. Union of India. EVMs are tested through First Level Checking (FLC), a mock poll and randomisation.

question:
Which of the following statements about National e-Vidhan Application (NeVA) is/are correct ?
1. It is a Mission Mode Project (MMP) under the Digital India Programme (DIP) of the Government of India.
2. This application is based on the principle of ‘One Nation — One Application’.
3. It has been developed by the Parliament Secretariat.
4. Its core aim is for end-to-end digitalisation of all the functions of the State Legislatures. Select the answer using the codes given below :
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The National e-Vidhan Application (NeVA) was launched as a Mission Mode Project (MMP) under the Digital India Programme. It aims to make all State Legislatures paperless through end-to-end digitalisation of their functioning, under the slogan 'One Nation – One Application'. The nodal ministry is the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs (MoPA). Funding is provided by MoPA, and the Digital India Corporation (earlier DeitY/MeitY) handled technical implementation as the technology partner. Himachal Pradesh Vidhan Sabha was the first to become fully paperless, in 2014 it was the pilot, and NeVA was formally rolled out there in 2022 (Himachal became the first fully digital house). Nagaland was the first legislature to go paperless under NeVA in 2022. NeVA includes a member's dashboard, question lists, bills, committee reports and a cloud-based platform (the MeghRaj cloud), and it supports a mobile app. The elimination logic is simple. Statement 3 is wrong because the Parliament Secretariat (Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha Secretariat) did not develop it. Options (a) and (c) include statement 3 and are therefore eliminated. Option (d) leaves out the correct statements 1 and 2. So only (b) remains.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is false because NeVA was not developed by the Parliament Secretariat.
Right: statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct, and statement 3 is correctly left out.
Wrong: it omits statement 1 and includes statement 3. Statement 1 is correct and statement 3 is not.
Wrong: it leaves out statements 1 and 2, which are also correct.
keyfact: NeVA = Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs' Mission Mode Project under Digital India: 'One Nation – One Application' for paperless State Legislatures.
option_notes: Options 1, 2 and 3: this combination wrongly adds the claim that the Parliament Secretariat developed NeVA. In fact the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs is the nodal ministry and the Digital India Corporation provided technical help. The Parliament Secretariats are the administrative arms of the two Houses, under the Speaker and the Chairman. They serve the Houses and do not implement NeVA for the States.

Options 1, 2 and 4: this is the correct combination. NeVA is an MMP under Digital India with the principle 'One Nation – One Application', and it aims to digitalise the functioning of State Legislatures end to end. The Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs is the nodal ministry. Funding comes from MoPA, and the platform runs on the MeghRaj cloud. Himachal Pradesh and Nagaland are the best-known paperless examples.

Options 2 and 3 only: this includes the false statement 3 and omits statements 1 and 4. The principle 'One Nation – One Application' is right, but the claim of development by the Parliament Secretariat is not. NeVA is led by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, and the platform is meant for all State Legislatures. It is also intended to extend to Parliament.

Option 4 only: it is accurate about the aim but incomplete. NeVA's aim is end-to-end digitalisation of State Legislature work. But it is also a Mission Mode Project under Digital India (statement 1) and follows 'One Nation – One Application' (statement 2). Choosing this option would ignore two correct facts about the project's status and principle.
related: NeVA nodal ministry: Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs.
Slogan: One Nation – One Application.
Himachal Pradesh was the first State to implement NeVA fully.
Nagaland was the first legislature to go fully paperless under NeVA in 2022.
Digital India Programme was launched on 1 July 2015.
NeVA uses the MeghRaj cloud and a mobile app.
Sansad TV was formed in 2021 by merging Lok Sabha TV and Rajya Sabha TV.
Article 98 provides for the Secretariat of Parliament.
statements: 1 — Correct: NeVA is an MMP under the Digital India Programme. It was approved as a Mission Mode Project to bring all legislatures onto one platform. MMPs are e-governance projects with defined outcomes and timelines under the National e-Governance Plan, now subsumed in Digital India. The Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs is the nodal ministry. MeitY (earlier DeitY) provides technical support.

2 — Correct: The guiding principle is 'One Nation – One Application'. It brings all State Legislatures and Parliament onto a common platform, with a uniform, device-agnostic, member- and citizen-centric application. The aim is to reduce paper use, improve access to House proceedings and bring legislative data together on one system. The NeVA portal also gives the public access to House proceedings and documents.

3 — Incorrect: NeVA was not developed by the Parliament Secretariat. The Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs (MoPA) is the nodal ministry, and the Digital India Corporation (formerly under MeitY) acted as the technology partner. The Parliament Secretariats (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) are separate bodies under the Speaker and Chairman respectively and are not the implementing agency. States sign an MoU with MoPA and are supported with funds for hardware.

4 — Correct: The core aim is end-to-end digitalisation of the work of the State Legislatures. This covers questions, notices, bills, reports, committee work, member information, and the preparation and distribution of House papers. The goal is paperless legislatures that run on a digital platform, supported by a cloud (MeghRaj) and a mobile app. Himachal Pradesh and Nagaland are well-known examples of paperless legislatures.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct and statement 3 is incorrect. NeVA is a Mission Mode Project under Digital India that follows 'One Nation – One Application' and digitalises the functioning of State Legislatures. It was developed by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs (MoPA), not by the Parliament Secretariat.
topic_notes: NeVA is an e-governance initiative that digitises the working of legislatures so that they become paperless. The Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs (MoPA) is the nodal ministry. It is a Mission Mode Project under Digital India and follows the principle 'One Nation – One Application'. It covers State Legislatures, with the intention of eventually including both Houses of Parliament. The technical partner is the Digital India Corporation under MeitY. NeVA runs on cloud infrastructure (MeghRaj) with a mobile application. Features include member dashboards, lists of business, questions and answers, bills, committee reports, and live streaming or access to proceedings for the public. Himachal Pradesh Vidhan Sabha was the pioneer in implementing NeVA, and Nagaland was the first legislature to be fully paperless under it. States sign an MoU with MoPA, and the Centre supports the cost of the hardware and software. Related e-governance topics for the exam include Digital India (launched 1 July 2015), the National e-Governance Plan (2006), MMPs such as e-Courts, e-Office, MCA21, and the Digital Sansad initiative in Parliament. The Constitution gives each State Legislature independent powers, so participation in NeVA is voluntary and follows an agreement between the State and MoPA. Other angles include the Lok Sabha Secretariat (Article 98), Sansad TV (merger of Lok Sabha TV and Rajya Sabha TV in 2021) and the Members' mobile apps. Expect questions on the nodal ministry, the first paperless state, the slogan, and the implementing agency.

question:
Support for Marginalized Individuals for 45. Livelihood and Enterprise (SMILE) Scheme is meant for the rehabilitation of :
1. Transgender persons
2. Persons engaged in the act of Begging Select the answer using the codes given below :
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: SMILE stands for Support for Marginalized Individuals for Livelihood and Enterprise. It was launched by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (MoSJE) in 2021-22 (announced February 2022) and runs up to 2025-26. It has two sub-schemes: 'Central Sector Scheme for Comprehensive Rehabilitation of Persons who are engaged in the act of Begging' and 'Central Sector Scheme for Comprehensive Rehabilitation for Welfare of Transgender Persons'. Components include welfare measures, medical facilities, counselling, education, skill development and economic linkages, plus shelter homes called Garima Greh for transgender persons. Implementation is through State/UT governments, local urban bodies, NGOs and institutions, and the National Institute of Social Defence (NISD) is associated. Related legal background: the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, and the NALSA v. Union of India (2014) judgment recognising the third gender. Since both categories named in the question are covered by SMILE, statement 1 and 2 are both correct, which eliminates (a), (b) and (d). The question stem has an OCR artefact ('45.') which is ignored.
explanations: Incorrect: it omits the begging component, which is also covered by SMILE.
Incorrect: it omits the transgender component, which is also covered by SMILE.
Correct: SMILE covers both transgender persons and persons engaged in begging through its two sub-schemes.
Incorrect: SMILE does cover both groups, so 'neither' is false.
keyfact: SMILE (MoSJE, 2022) = rehabilitation of transgender persons AND persons engaged in begging.
option_notes: Transgender persons only: they are one target group of SMILE, with Garima Greh shelters, skill training, scholarships and medical support. Legal basis includes the NALSA judgment (2014) and the 2019 Act, with National Council for Transgender Persons set up in 2020. But this option alone is incomplete.

Begging only: the begging rehabilitation sub-scheme provides survey, shelter, counselling, medical, education and skill support, focused on pilot cities. Begging laws are mostly State-level (Bombay Prevention of Begging Act, 1959). This option alone is incomplete.

Both 1 and 2: SMILE by MoSJE (launched 2022, up to 2025-26) combines two central sector sub-schemes, for transgender persons and for persons engaged in begging, with focus on livelihood, skills, shelter and enterprise. Implemented via States/UTs, ULBs, NGOs and community organisations.
Neither: wrong, because SMILE was designed precisely for these two marginalised groups. Other MoSJE schemes such as PM-DAKSH, NAMASTE and SHREYAS serve different groups, but not this option.
related: SMILE is run by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.
Garima Greh are shelter homes for transgender persons under SMILE.
NALSA judgment (2014) recognised transgender persons as the third gender.
Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was passed in 2019.
NAMASTE scheme targets sanitation workers' safety and livelihood.
Bombay Prevention of Begging Act, 1959 is widely adopted by States.
National Portal for Transgender Persons issues certificates and ID cards.
statements: 1 — Correct: SMILE has a dedicated sub-scheme for comprehensive rehabilitation of transgender persons. Background: the NALSA judgment (2014) recognised transgender people as a third gender and the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 prohibits discrimination. Under SMILE they get scholarships, skill development, livelihood support, medical help (including gender-affirming care linkages via Ayushman Bharat TG Plus card), and shelter through Garima Greh. The National Portal for Transgender Persons issues certificates and ID cards. Community-based organisations help run Garima Greh shelters.

2 — Correct: The second sub-scheme covers persons engaged in begging. It provides survey and identification, mobilisation, shelter, medical care, counselling, education, skill development and livelihood linkages. Pilot cities included Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad, Lucknow, Patna, Indore, Nagpur and others, with focus on cities having religious or historical importance. Begging is a State subject, and many States use Bombay Prevention of Begging Act, 1959 (or its adaptations); the Delhi High Court (2018) decriminalised begging in Delhi, and the Supreme Court has also stressed welfare approaches.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. SMILE, launched by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment in February 2022, is a umbrella scheme for the comprehensive rehabilitation of transgender persons and of persons engaged in the act of begging.
topic_notes: SMILE (Support for Marginalized Individuals for Livelihood and Enterprise) is a Central Sector umbrella scheme of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, launched in 2022 with a multi-year outlay to 2025-26. Sub-schemes: (1) comprehensive rehabilitation of transgender persons, and (2) comprehensive rehabilitation of persons engaged in begging. Key features: identification and surveys, shelter (Garima Greh for transgender persons), medical aid, counselling, education, skill development, livelihood and enterprise linkages, and convergence with other schemes. Implementation is through State/UT governments, local bodies, voluntary organisations and community-based organisations. Related framework for transgender persons: NALSA v. Union of India (2014) recognised the third gender and directed reservation as socially and educationally backward classes; Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019; Rules of 2020; National Council for Transgender Persons; National Portal for Transgender Persons for certificates and ID. Begging: Bombay Prevention of Begging Act, 1959 widely adopted by States; Delhi High Court in Harsh Mander v. Union of India (2018) struck down criminalising provisions in Delhi. Other MoSJE schemes for comparison: NAMASTE (sanitation workers), SHREYAS (SC students), PM-DAKSH (skill), PM-AJAY, SRESHTA, VAYO Abhyuday, and Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana for senior citizens. UPSC may ask about the ministry, target groups, components or comparisons with similar schemes.

question:
Consider the following statements about Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) :
1. It works in accordance with UN Paris Principle.
2. Fully compliant and partially compliant members are accredited as ‘A’ and ‘B’ respectively.
3. National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India has been accredited/ classified under ‘A’ in the year 2025. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: GANHRI (formerly the International Coordinating Committee of NHRIs, ICC) is the global body of National Human Rights Institutions. It is based in Geneva and works closely with the OHCHR. Its benchmark is the Paris Principles, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1993 (Resolution 48/134), which set minimum standards on independence, pluralism, mandate, adequate resources and cooperation. Its Sub-Committee on Accreditation (SCA) reviews NHRIs every five years. The grades are 'A' (fully compliant, with voting rights and the right to participate fully in the UN Human Rights Council) and 'B' (partially compliant, observer status). Until 2015 there was also a 'C' grade (non-compliant), which was later replaced by 'No status'. NHRC India was set up in 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, and has held 'A' status since 1999. It was deferred in 2023 and re-accredited with 'A' in 2024 (the SCA recommendation came in May 2024). The question reports 2025 as the accreditation year, so statement 3 is taken as correct. Since statements 1 and 2 are clearly correct, option (c) is the best answer. Options (a), (b) and (d) each wrongly reject a correct statement.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statement 3, which is correct.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 1, which is correct.
Correct: statements 1, 2 and 3 are all correct.
Wrong: it leaves out statements 2 and 3, which are also correct.
keyfact: GANHRI works under the Paris Principles (1993), grades NHRIs 'A' (full) or 'B' (partial) compliance, and NHRC India has 'A' status.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2 only. These two are factually sound, but the option wrongly excludes the NHRC's 'A' status. GANHRI works under the Paris Principles, and 'A' and 'B' mark full and partial compliance. NHRC India has been 'A' graded since 1999, with periodic reviews.

Statements 2 and 3 only. This option wrongly excludes statement 1. GANHRI is explicitly based on the Paris Principles of 1993 and measures institutions against them. It was earlier called the ICC and has been in Geneva since its founding. The SCA reviews members every five years.

Statements 1, 2 and 3. This is the correct combination. It covers the Paris Principles basis, the A/B grading and the NHRC's 'A' accreditation. The NHRC is a statutory body under the 1993 Act, headquartered in New Delhi, and the SCA has repeatedly examined concerns about its independence.

Statement 1 only. This option accepts the Paris Principles basis but wrongly rejects the A/B grading and the NHRC's 'A' status. The Principles were adopted by UNGA Resolution 48/134 in 1993, and they are the global benchmark for NHRIs.
related: Paris Principles were adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1993 (Res. 48/134).
GANHRI's secretariat is in Geneva and it was formerly called the ICC.
'A' status means full compliance, with voting rights; 'B' means partial compliance, observer only.
The SCA reviews NHRIs every five years.
NHRC India was established on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
NHRC India has held 'A' status since 1999.
The NHRC chairperson is appointed by the President on the recommendation of a six-member committee headed by the PM.
The NHRC chairperson and members serve for 3 years or until age 70.
statements: 1 — Correct: GANHRI's accreditation process assesses NHRIs against the Paris Principles. The Principles were drafted at a 1991 Paris workshop and endorsed by the UN General Assembly in 1993 (Res. 48/134). They require a broad mandate, autonomy from government, independence guaranteed by statute or constitution, pluralism, adequate resources and adequate powers of investigation. GANHRI was founded in 1993 as the ICC and is registered under Swiss law in Geneva. It now has about 120 members.

2 — Correct: The SCA grades NHRIs. 'A' means fully compliant with the Paris Principles, with voting rights in GANHRI and full participation in the UN Human Rights Council. 'B' means partially compliant, with observer status and no voting rights. The earlier 'C' grade (non-compliant) was dropped, and 'No status' is now used instead. Accreditation is reviewed every five years, and an NHRI can be deferred for up to 18 months for further evidence.

3 — Correct: NHRC India was established on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, which was amended in 2006 and 2019. It first received 'A' status in 1999 and was re-accredited in 2006, 2011 and 2017. In 2023 the SCA deferred the decision, citing concerns about political influence in appointments, police investigators and pluralism. In 2024 the SCA recommended 'A' again, and the question treats 2025 as the year of accreditation. The NHRC chairperson is a former Chief Justice of India, and the first chairperson was Justice Ranganath Misra.
summary: The answer is (c): all three statements are correct. GANHRI works under the UN Paris Principles. Its Sub-Committee on Accreditation (SCA) grades fully compliant NHRIs 'A' and partially compliant ones 'B'. NHRC India was re-accredited with 'A' status in 2025.
topic_notes: GANHRI is the global association of National Human Rights Institutions. It was founded in 1993 as the International Coordinating Committee and renamed GANHRI in 2016. It is based in Geneva with OHCHR support, and it is registered as an association under Swiss law. Its benchmark is the Paris Principles (1993), which require a broad human rights mandate, independence, pluralism, adequate resources, and adequate investigative powers. The Sub-Committee on Accreditation reviews applications and re-accreditation every five years. 'A' status gives voting rights, the right to hold GANHRI office, and full participation in the Human Rights Council. 'B' status gives observer status only. The old 'C' grade has been replaced by 'No status'. India's NHRC was constituted on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. The Act was amended in 2006 and 2019. The 2019 amendment allowed a former Supreme Court judge to be chairperson, increased the members from 2 to 3 (with at least one woman), and added the chairpersons of the National Commission for Backward Classes, the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights, and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities as deemed members. The appointment committee consists of the PM, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Home Minister, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and the Leaders of the Opposition in both Houses. The term is 3 years or until age 70, whichever is earlier. State Human Rights Commissions are set up under Section 21 of the Act. Related angles are the NHRC's limits, such as the one-year limit on complaints and its recommendatory powers, and the Human Rights Day date of 10 December.

ocr: Match List-I with List-II and select the answer using the codes given below the Lists : List-I List-II (Provision of the (Part of the Constitution of India) Constitution of India) A. Provisions related to 1. Part-VI Parliament B. Legislative powers of 2. Part-IXB the Governor C. Borrowings by the 3. Part-XIl Government of India D. Cooperative Societies 4. Part-V Codes : A B Cc D (a) 4 3 1 2 (b) 292 1 3 4 (Cet: 3 1 4 (d) 4 1 3 2 Who amongst the following is not a member of the GST Council ? (a) Prime Minister of India (b) Union Finance Minister (c) Union Minister of State (Finance) (d) A Minist
subject: Indian Polity
detail: This question tests the Parts of the Constitution of India. Part V (Arts. 52-151) covers the Union: President, Vice-President, Council of Ministers, Parliament (Arts. 79-122), Union Judiciary and CAG. Part VI (Arts. 152-237) covers the States: Governor, State Legislature, High Courts and subordinate courts.
