The Governor's legislative powers, including the ordinance-making power under Art. 213, sit in Part VI. Part XII (Arts. 264-300A) covers Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits. Borrowing by the Government of India is in Art. 292, and borrowing by States is in Art. 293. Part IX B (Arts. 243ZH-243ZT) covers Cooperative Societies, inserted by the 97th Amendment Act, 2011. Elimination logic: Parliament is the Union, so A=4. This leaves only (a) and (d). In (a), B=3 would put the Governor's powers in Part XII, which is wrong. So B=1 and the answer is (d). C=3 and D=2 confirm it.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it matches B with 3, which would put the Governor's legislative powers in Part XII. These are in Part VI.
(b) is wrong because it matches A with 2, which would put Parliament in Part IX B. Parliament is in Part V.
(c) is wrong because it matches A with 2 and B with 3, and both matches are incorrect.
(d) is correct. It gives A-4 (Part V), B-1 (Part VI), C-3 (Part XII) and D-2 (Part IX B).
keyfact: Parliament = Part V; Governor = Part VI; Union borrowing (Art. 292) = Part XII; Cooperatives = Part IX B (Arts. 243ZH-243ZT) — code (d) 4-1-3-2.
option_notes: Code (a) is 4-3-1-2. It gets A and D right but swaps B and C. Part XII is on Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits (Arts. 264-300A). Part VI is on the States (Arts. 152-237). Borrowing by the Union is in Art. 292, which is in Part XII. The Governor's powers are in Part VI. A student must keep these two Parts distinct, since both deal with governance and money.

Code (b) is 2-1-3-4. It places Parliament in Part IX B and Cooperative Societies in Part V, which swaps A and D. Part V is the Union and Part IX B is Cooperative Societies. Part IX is Panchayats (Arts. 243-243O), Part IX A is Municipalities (Arts. 243P-243ZG), and Part IX B is Cooperative Societies (Arts. 243ZH-243ZT). Part IX B was added by the 97th Amendment in 2011. Only B and C are correct here.

Code (c) is 2-3-1-4. Every pair in this code is wrong. It is the full reversal of the correct matching. The correct pairs are Parliament in Part V, Governor in Part VI, Borrowing in Part XII and Cooperatives in Part IX B. Part V covers Arts. 52-151, Part VI covers Arts. 152-237, and Part XII covers Arts. 264-300A. Keeping the Article ranges in mind helps avoid such mix-ups.

Code (d) is 4-1-3-2, the correct code. Part V is the Union (Arts. 52-151) and includes Parliament. Part VI is the States (Arts. 152-237) and includes the Governor. Part XII is Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits (Arts. 264-300A) and includes borrowing under Art. 292. Part IX B (Arts. 243ZH-243ZT) is Cooperative Societies, added by the 97th Amendment in 2011.
related: Part IX covers Panchayats (73rd Amendment, 1992) and Part IX A covers Municipalities (74th Amendment).
Art. 213 gives the Governor the power to promulgate ordinances when the Legislature is not in session.
Art. 292 deals with Union borrowing and Art. 293 deals with State borrowing.
Art. 279A (101st Amendment, 2016) created the GST Council.
The 97th Amendment (2011) inserted Part IX B and Art. 43B.
Art. 280 provides for the Finance Commission, which is constituted every five years.
Part XIV A (Tribunals) was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.
Part XII covers Arts. 264-300A.
statements: A — Correct match with 4: Provisions related to Parliament are in Part V. Part V (Arts. 52-151) is titled 'The Union'. It covers the President, Vice-President, Council of Ministers, Attorney General, Parliament (Arts. 79-122), the Supreme Court (Arts. 124-147) and the CAG (Art. 148). Chapter II of Part V deals with Parliament: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, officers, procedure, powers and privileges.

B — Correct match with 1: The Governor's legislative powers are in Part VI. Part VI (Arts. 152-237) deals with the States. The Governor's legislative powers include summoning, proroguing and dissolving the Assembly, nominating members, reserving Bills for the President (Art. 200) and promulgating ordinances (Art. 213). Part VI does not apply to Jammu & Kashmir in its earlier form. The Governor is appointed by the President under Art. 155.

C — Correct match with 3: Borrowings by the Government of India are in Part XII. Part XII covers Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits. Art. 292 empowers the Union to borrow on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, within limits set by Parliament. Art. 293 governs borrowing by States, which needs Union consent if a loan to the State is outstanding. Art. 266 deals with the Consolidated Fund and Public Account.

D — Correct match with 2: Cooperative Societies are in Part IX B. The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011 inserted Part IX B (Arts. 243ZH-243ZT) and made the right to form cooperative societies a Fundamental Right under Art. 19(1)(c). It also added the DPSP Art. 43B. Part IX B provides for the incorporation, board of directors, elections and audit of cooperatives. In 2021, the Supreme Court struck down the Part IX B provisions on State cooperatives, holding that cooperative societies are a State subject, but upheld them for multi-State cooperative societies.
summary: The image shows two questions; this note covers the first, the matching question (Q45). The correct code is (d) 4-1-3-2. Provisions related to Parliament are in Part V, the Governor's legislative powers are in Part VI, borrowing by the Government of India is in Part XII, and Cooperative Societies are in Part IX B.
topic_notes: The Constitution had 22 Parts originally and now has 25, because Parts IV A, IX A, IX B, XIV A and XVI were added, while Part VII was repealed. Key Parts: Part I Union and its Territory (Arts. 1-4); Part II Citizenship (5-11); Part III Fundamental Rights (12-35); Part IV DPSP (36-51); Part IV A Fundamental Duties (51A); Part V Union (52-151); Part VI States (152-237); Part VIII Union Territories (239-242); Part IX Panchayats (243-243O); Part IX A Municipalities (243P-243ZG); Part IX B Cooperative Societies (243ZH-243ZT); Part X Scheduled and Tribal Areas (244-244A); Part XI Centre-State Relations (245-263); Part XII Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits (264-300A); Part XIII Trade and Commerce (301-307); Part XIV Services (308-323); Part XIV A Tribunals (323A-323B); Part XV Elections (324-329A); Part XVI Special Provisions for Certain Classes (330-342); Part XVII Official Language (343-351); Part XVIII Emergency (352-360); Part XIX Miscellaneous (361-367); Part XX Amendment (368); Part XXI Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions (369-392); Part XXII Short title, commencement, etc. (393-395). Related financial provisions: Art. 265 (no tax without law), Art. 266 (Consolidated Fund and Public Account), Art. 267 (Contingency Fund), Art. 268-293 (distribution of revenues), Art. 280 (Finance Commission), Art. 300A (right to property). Part VII (States in Part B) was repealed by the 7th Amendment in 1956. The GST Council is under Art. 279A, inserted by the 101st Amendment, 2016, and sits in Part XII.

ocr: The Chief Information Commissioner and Fe other Information Commissioners are appointed by the President of India on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Chief Justice of India. While the Chief Information Commissioner is not eligible for reappointment after completion of the term of five years, other Information Commissioners are eligible _ for reappointment. Select the answer using the codes given below : 1 only (a) 2 only (b) Both 1 and 2 () 50. Neither 1 nor 2 (d)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Right to Information Act, 2005 sets up the Central Information Commission (CIC) as a statutory body. Section 12 provides that the CIC consists of the Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners. They are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee made up of the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha (or the leader of the single largest opposition group) and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM. The Chief Justice of India has no role, which makes Statement 1 wrong. Originally, Section 13 fixed the term at five years or until age 65, whichever is earlier, with no reappointment. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 removed the fixed term and left tenure and salary to be prescribed by the Central Government. The 2023 Rules prescribe a three-year term. An Information Commissioner may become CIC but cannot serve more than the total tenure, and the CIC is not reappointed. Statement 2 is wrong because the original Act barred reappointment for all Commissioners, and even now there is no distinction in which only ICs are reappointable. Both statements fail, so (d) is correct.
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement 1 is false: the committee is headed by the Prime Minister, not the Chief Justice of India.
(b) is wrong because Statement 2 is false: the Act does not allow reappointment of ICs, and it does not distinguish them from the CIC on this point.
(c) is wrong because both statements are incorrect.
(d) is correct because both statements are factually wrong.
keyfact: CIC/ICs are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Prime Minister (not the CJI), and original Section 13 barred reappointment.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this would require the CJI to head the selection committee. In reality the PM chairs it. The CJI sits on committees for other bodies, such as the Lokpal selection committee, where the CJI or a nominated Supreme Court judge is a member. The CJI is also not a member of the CIC selection panel, whereas the Leader of Opposition is. This statement mixes up the CIC with other appointments.

Option (b), 2 only: this would mean ICs can be reappointed while the CIC cannot. Section 13 of the original RTI Act barred reappointment for both. An IC can be promoted to CIC, but the total tenure remains capped. After the 2019 Amendment, the tenure is fixed by Central Government rules at three years rather than by the statute.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: this would need both claims to be true. Neither holds. It is a trap for students who confuse the CIC with constitutional bodies such as the Election Commission or the Supreme Court, where the CJI plays a prominent role in some appointments and tenure is fixed differently.

Option (d), neither 1 nor 2: this is correct. The CIC and ICs are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee headed by the PM. They are not eligible for reappointment. Know that the State Information Commissions follow a similar structure, with the Chief Minister heading the committee and the Governor appointing.
related: RTI Act 2005 came into force on 12 October 2005 and is observed with RTI Day on 12 October.
CIC and ICs are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee led by the PM.
The CIC selection committee includes the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha.
RTI Amendment Act 2019 let the Centre decide tenure, salary and conditions of service.
Response time under RTI is 30 days, or 48 hours in matters of life and liberty.
Penalty on a PIO is Rs 250 per day, capped at Rs 25,000.
First Chief Information Commissioner was Wajahat Habibullah.
Section 24 exempts Second Schedule organisations like IB and RAW, except on corruption and human rights violations.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The selection committee is headed by the Prime Minister, not the Chief Justice of India. Facts: Section 12(3) of the RTI Act 2005 sets up the committee of the PM, the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM. The President makes the appointment on its recommendation. Appointees must be persons of eminence in public life with wide knowledge and experience in law, science and technology, social service, management, journalism, mass media or administration and governance. They cannot be MPs, MLAs, hold an office of profit, or be connected with a political party or business. The CIC is headquartered in New Delhi. The Chief Justice leads committees for bodies like the Lokpal's search panel members, not for the CIC.

2 — Incorrect: Under Section 13 of the original Act, neither the CIC nor Information Commissioners were eligible for reappointment. Facts: The original term was five years or age 65, whichever was earlier. An Information Commissioner could be elevated to CIC, but the combined tenure could not exceed five years. The RTI Amendment Act 2019 changed the term to one prescribed by the Central Government, and the 2019 Rules set three years. The Amendment also made the salary, allowances and service conditions of Commissioners equal to those of Election Commissioners no longer applicable; the Centre now prescribes them. The Amendment was criticised for weakening the independence of the Commission. Removal is by the President on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity after a Supreme Court inquiry.
summary: The answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2. Under the RTI Act 2005 (Section 12), the CIC and Information Commissioners are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Prime Minister, not the Chief Justice. Also, under Section 13, neither the CIC nor the ICs are eligible for reappointment.
topic_notes: The Right to Information Act, 2005 came into force on 12 October 2005. It lets citizens request information from public authorities. Section 12 creates the Central Information Commission, and Section 15 creates State Information Commissions. The CIC has the Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners. The selection committee has the PM as chair, the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM. For States, the committee has the Chief Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Assembly and a Cabinet Minister nominated by the CM, and the Governor appoints. Eligibility requires eminence in public life and wide knowledge in fields like law, science, social service, management, journalism and administration. They cannot be MPs or MLAs, hold other offices of profit, or have political party or business links. Original tenure was five years or 65 years of age, with no reappointment, and salary equal to Chief Election Commissioner for the CIC and Election Commissioner for ICs. The 2019 Amendment gave the Centre power to set tenure and pay, and the 2019 Rules fixed three years. Removal is by the President for proved misbehaviour or incapacity after the Supreme Court inquiry, or without inquiry on grounds such as insolvency, conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude, or infirmity. The Commission can receive complaints, order disclosure, and impose penalties of Rs 250 per day up to Rs 25,000 on defaulting Public Information Officers. Appeals go first to the First Appellate Authority, then to the Commission. Exemptions are in Section 8, and Section 24 exempts intelligence and security organisations in the Second Schedule, though they must disclose information about corruption and human rights violations. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 amended Section 8(1)(j). Time limit for response is 30 days, or 48 hours for life and liberty matters. The first CIC was Wajahat Habibullah. Know also the Section 4 proactive disclosure duty.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q47.
ocr: The Chief Information Commissioner and Fe other Information Commissioners are appointed by the President of India on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Chief Justice of India. While the Chief Information Commissioner is not eligible for reappointment after completion of the term of five years, other Information Commissioners are eligible _ for reappointment. Select the answer using the codes given below : 1 only (a) 2 only (b) Both 1 and 2 () 50. Neither 1 nor 2 (d)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Right to Information Act, 2005 sets up the Central Information Commission (CIC). Section 12 provides that the CIC consists of the Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners, appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee consisting of the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister. The Chief Justice of India is not on this committee, so Statement 1 fails. Originally, Section 13 fixed the term at five years or age 65, whichever is earlier, with no reappointment for either the CIC or Information Commissioners; an Information Commissioner could, however, be appointed as CIC, but the total tenure including both posts could not exceed five years. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed this: the term is now as prescribed by the Central Government, and salaries, allowances and service conditions are likewise prescribed by the Centre. Statement 2 is wrong because the Act (as originally framed and in the amended form) does not give the Information Commissioners eligibility for reappointment. Both statements are wrong, so (d) is correct.
explanations: (a) is wrong: Statement 1 is false because the selection committee is chaired by the Prime Minister, not the CJI.
(b) is wrong: Statement 2 is false because neither the CIC nor the Information Commissioners are eligible for reappointment.
(c) is wrong: Both statements are incorrect, so they cannot both be true.
(d) is correct: Statement 1 is incorrect on the committee head and Statement 2 is incorrect on reappointment eligibility.
keyfact: CIC/IC selection committee is headed by the PM (with the LoP and a Union Cabinet Minister), not the CJI, and the CIC and ICs are not eligible for reappointment.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only, would be correct only if the CJI headed the committee, which is not so. The CJI features in the selection committees for other bodies. The CBI Director committee includes the PM, the LoP and the CJI or a Supreme Court Judge nominated by the CJI. The Lokpal selection committee includes the PM, the Lok Sabha Speaker, the LoP, the CJI or a Supreme Court Judge nominated by the CJI, and an eminent jurist. The CIC committee has no judicial member.

Option (b), 2 only, would require the CIC to be ineligible for reappointment but the Information Commissioners to be eligible. The Act does not make this distinction. The only special provision is that an Information Commissioner may be appointed CIC, but the total term must not exceed five years under the original Act. Compare this with the Election Commission, where the CEC and ECs have a 6-year term or age 65 limit.

Option (c), Both 1 and 2, is wrong since both statements fail. The correct position is that the PM heads the committee and no reappointment is allowed. The RTI Act 2005 came into force on 12 October 2005, replacing the Freedom of Information Act 2002. It applies to all of India except Jammu and Kashmir originally, a restriction removed after the 2019 reorganisation. The CIC has appellate and complaint-handling powers under Sections 18 and 19.

Option (d), Neither 1 nor 2, is the correct choice. The committee is headed by the PM and includes the LoP and a Union Cabinet Minister. Neither the CIC nor the Information Commissioners can be reappointed. The 2019 Amendment shifted the term and salary from statutory fixity to the Central Government's prescription, which critics said weakened the Commission's independence. The Commission can impose penalties up to Rs 25,000 on defaulting Public Information Officers.
related: RTI Act 2005 came into force fully on 12 October 2005.
The Central Information Commission is a statutory body, not constitutional.
CIC selection committee: PM (Chair), Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM.
State Information Commissioners are appointed by the Governor on the recommendation of a committee headed by the CM.
The RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 let the Centre prescribe the term and salaries of Information Commissioners.
Section 4 of the RTI Act deals with proactive disclosure by public authorities.
Section 8 lists exemptions from disclosure; Section 24 exempts certain security and intelligence organisations.
The RTI application fee at the central level is Rs 10; the normal reply time is 30 days.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The selection committee is headed by the Prime Minister, not the Chief Justice of India. The CJI is a member of committees for the CBI Director, Lokpal and similar appointments, but not for the CIC. Facts: The committee under Section 12(3) comprises the PM (Chair), the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha (or the leader of the single largest opposition party if there is no recognised LoP), and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM. The President formally appoints. Candidates must be persons of eminence in public life with wide knowledge and experience in law, science and technology, social service, management, journalism, mass media, or administration and governance. They cannot be MPs, MLAs, hold any office of profit, or be connected with a political party or business. The same pattern applies to State Information Commissions, where the committee is headed by the Chief Minister.

2 — Incorrect: Neither the CIC nor the Information Commissioners are eligible for reappointment under Section 13. The only route is that an Information Commissioner may be elevated to CIC, but the total tenure cannot exceed five years in the original provision. Facts: The original Act fixed the term at five years or age 65, whichever is earlier. The 2019 Amendment made the term as prescribed by the Central Government, and the 2019 Rules prescribed three years. The status and salary of the CIC were originally equal to the Chief Election Commissioner, and Information Commissioners to Election Commissioners; the 2019 Amendment removed this parity. Removal is by the President on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity after a Supreme Court inquiry, or for insolvency, conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude, and similar grounds. The CIC was set up in October 2005 and is headquartered in New Delhi.
summary: The answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2. Under the RTI Act 2005 (Section 12), the CIC and Information Commissioners are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Prime Minister, not the Chief Justice of India. Under Section 13, the CIC and Information Commissioners hold office for the term prescribed by the Central Government (not exceeding five years) or until age 65, and neither is eligible for reappointment.
topic_notes: The Right to Information Act, 2005 gives citizens the right to access information held by public authorities. It was passed by Parliament in June 2005 and came into force on 12 October 2005. It replaced the Freedom of Information Act, 2002. The movement for RTI began with the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS) in Rajasthan under Aruna Roy. The Supreme Court had earlier read the right into Article 19(1)(a) (State of UP v Raj Narain, 1975). The RTI Act establishes a two-tier machinery: Public Information Officers (PIOs) and First Appellate Authorities in each public authority, then the Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions for second appeals and complaints. Time limits: 30 days for a normal reply, 48 hours for matters concerning life and liberty, and 45 days where third-party information from the Union is involved. The application fee is Rs 10. Section 8 lists exemptions, such as threats to sovereignty, security, and cabinet papers, and Section 24 exempts certain intelligence and security organisations in Schedule II, with a proviso for corruption and human rights violations. Section 4 requires proactive disclosure. Section 8(2) provides a public-interest override. The CIC consists of the CIC and up to 10 Information Commissioners, appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee of the PM, the LoP, and a Union Cabinet Minister. State Information Commissions are appointed by the Governor on the recommendation of a committee headed by the CM, with the LoP in the Assembly and a Cabinet Minister nominated by the CM. The 2019 Amendment altered the terms, salaries and service conditions, making them as prescribed by the Central Government. The Supreme Court in Anjali Bhardwaj v Union of India (2019) stressed timely appointments. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 amended Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act, drawing criticism.

question: Consider the following statements with reference to the Constitution of India : The Parliament can make laws on matters Ts enumerated in the Union List and/or the Concurrent List. The Parliament can make laws on any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or the State List. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Article 246 divides legislative powers among three lists in the Seventh Schedule. Parliament has exclusive power over the Union List (Art. 246(1)). Parliament and State Legislatures both have power over the Concurrent List (Art. 246(2)), but if the two conflict, the Union law prevails under Art. 254, unless a State law on a Concurrent subject has received Presidential assent. State Legislatures have exclusive power over the State List (Art. 246(3)), subject to Parliament's overriding powers. Residuary powers rest with Parliament under Art. 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List. This includes the power to impose taxes not mentioned in any list. This differs from the USA and Australia, where residuary powers lie with the states, and it follows the Canadian model. Parliament can also legislate on State List subjects in special cases: Art. 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution in the national interest), Art. 250 (Emergency), Art. 252 (consent of States), Art. 253 (international agreements) and Art. 356. Statement 1 is correct because Parliament can legislate on both the Union and Concurrent Lists. Statement 2 is correct because anything outside the Concurrent and State Lists is residuary and falls to Parliament. So (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated.
explanations: (a) is wrong: statement 1 is correct, but statement 2 is also correct, so 'only 1' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong: statement 2 is correct, but statement 1 is also correct.
(c) is right: Parliament legislates on the Union and Concurrent Lists, and it also holds residuary power over matters outside the Concurrent and State Lists.
(d) is wrong: both statements are correct.
keyfact: Art. 246 gives Parliament the Union and Concurrent Lists, and Art. 248 plus Entry 97 give it residuary power (Canadian model).
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: Parliament's power over the Union and Concurrent Lists comes from Art. 246. The Union List has 98 entries and is exclusive to Parliament. The Concurrent List has 52 entries and is shared with the States. Under Art. 254, a Union law prevails over a State law on a Concurrent subject unless the State law has Presidential assent.

Option (b), statement 2 only: Residuary power is the power to legislate on matters not listed in the Concurrent or State List. It lies with Parliament under Art. 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List. The model is Canadian. It includes the power to impose taxes not mentioned in any list. Courts decide whether a matter is residuary.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: This is the correct answer. Parliament has exclusive power over the Union List and concurrent power over the Concurrent List, and it holds residuary powers. Parliament can also legislate on State List subjects in special situations under Arts. 249, 250, 252 and 253.

Option (d), neither: This would imply Parliament lacks power over the Union and Concurrent Lists and residuary subjects, which contradicts Arts. 246 and 248. It is wrong. The Constitution is quasi-federal, with a Union bias in the distribution of legislative powers.
related: Art. 246 distributes legislative powers via the Seventh Schedule.
Residuary power is in Art. 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved five subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List.
Art. 249 lets Parliament legislate on a State List subject by a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by a two-thirds majority.
Art. 254 deals with repugnancy between Union and State laws on Concurrent subjects.
Art. 246A (101st Amendment) is the GST provision.
Art. 253 lets Parliament legislate to implement international treaties.
The residuary power follows the Canadian model.
statements: 1 — Correct: Art. 246 gives Parliament exclusive power over the Union List and concurrent power over the Concurrent List. The Union List has 98 entries, originally 97, and covers defence, foreign affairs, banking, railways and currency. The Concurrent List has 52 entries, originally 47, and covers criminal law, marriage, education, forests and trade unions. Education, forests, weights and measures, and protection of wild animals and birds were moved there by the 42nd Amendment (1976). On Concurrent subjects, Union law prevails in a conflict (Art. 254), except where a State law has received Presidential assent.

2 — Correct: Art. 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List give Parliament residuary power over any matter not in the Concurrent or State List, including taxes not mentioned there. This follows the Canadian model, whereas the USA and Australia leave residuary powers with the states. The Sarkaria Commission recommended that residuary power be kept with Parliament, though taxation should go to the Union. The courts decide whether a subject is residuary, using doctrines such as pith and substance and colourable legislation. GST was introduced through the 101st Amendment (2016), which added Art. 246A.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. Parliament legislates on Union List and Concurrent List subjects (Art. 246), and it holds residuary power over any matter not in the Concurrent or State List (Art. 248 read with Entry 97 of the Union List).
topic_notes: Part XI (Arts. 245-255) deals with Centre-State legislative relations. Art. 245 sets out the territorial extent of laws: Parliament can make laws for the whole or any part of India, and a State can make laws for its own territory. Art. 246 provides for the Seventh Schedule's three lists, Union (98 entries), State (59 entries in practice, as some were deleted) and Concurrent (52 entries), and gives the Union List priority over the State and Concurrent Lists. Art. 246A (101st Amendment) gives Parliament and States concurrent power on GST. Art. 248 gives residuary powers to Parliament. Parliament can legislate on State subjects in these cases: Art. 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution passed by two-thirds of members present and voting, valid for one year and extendable), Art. 250 (during a National Emergency), Art. 251 (resolving inconsistency between Union and State laws), Art. 252 (two or more States consent), Art. 253 (treaties and international agreements), and Art. 356 (President's Rule). The Governor can reserve a State bill for the President (Art. 200), and the Centre can give directions to States (Arts. 256-257). Related doctrines are pith and substance, territorial nexus, colourable legislation, harmonious construction and repugnancy. Commissions to remember: Sarkaria (1983), Punchhi (2007) and the Rajamannar Committee (1969). Important cases include State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963), the S.R. Bommai case (1994) and the Kesavananda Bharati case, which treated federalism as part of the basic structure.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. Only the Supreme Court of India is vested with the power to punish for contempt of itself.
2. Both the Supreme Court of India and High Courts have advisory jurisdiction. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Indian Polity
detail: Statement 1 is wrong because Article 129 makes the Supreme Court a court of record with power to punish for contempt of itself, and Article 215 gives every High Court the same power for itself. The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 defines civil and criminal contempt and sets the punishment: simple imprisonment up to six months, a fine up to Rs 2,000, or both. The 1971 Act also recognises the High Courts' power. Section 12 and Article 142 also matter here. Statement 2 is wrong because advisory jurisdiction rests only with the Supreme Court. Under Article 143 the President may refer a question of law or fact of public importance, or a pre-Constitution treaty or similar matter, to the Court. In the first case the Court may give or decline to give its opinion. In the second it must give its opinion. The opinion is not binding on the President and is not a judgment under Article 141. High Courts have original, appellate, writ (Article 226), and supervisory (Article 227) jurisdiction, but no advisory jurisdiction. Both statements are wrong, so (d) is correct.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect. High Courts also punish for their own contempt under Article 215.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is incorrect. Advisory jurisdiction belongs only to the Supreme Court, under Article 143.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct.
(d) is correct. Statement 1 ignores Article 215, and statement 2 wrongly extends advisory jurisdiction to High Courts.
keyfact: Contempt power: Supreme Court (Art. 129) and High Courts (Art. 215). Advisory jurisdiction: Supreme Court only (Art. 143).
option_notes: Option (a) would make statement 1 alone correct, which would mean only the Supreme Court can punish for contempt. In fact, Article 129 covers the Supreme Court and Article 215 covers High Courts. Both are courts of record. The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 governs the procedure. Subordinate courts have no power to punish for contempt themselves and refer such matters to the High Court under Section 10.

Option (b) would make statement 2 alone correct, which would mean both courts have advisory jurisdiction. This is wrong. The Supreme Court alone has it, under Article 143, on a reference from the President. The opinion is not binding. High Courts have original, appellate, writ and supervisory jurisdiction but no advisory jurisdiction. Governors cannot refer questions to High Courts for opinion.

Option (c) would mean both statements are correct. Neither is. Contempt power exists for both the Supreme Court and High Courts. Advisory jurisdiction belongs only to the Supreme Court. Students should remember the pairing: Articles 129 and 215 for contempt, and Article 143 for advisory jurisdiction.

Option (d) is the correct answer. It reflects two facts. First, both the Supreme Court and the High Courts are courts of record with contempt powers (Articles 129 and 215). Second, only the Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction, and that jurisdiction is exercised on a Presidential reference under Article 143.
related: Article 129: the Supreme Court is a court of record.
Article 215: High Courts are courts of record.
Article 143: the President's power to consult the Supreme Court.
Advisory opinions are not binding on the President.
Contempt of Courts Act, 1971: maximum punishment is six months' imprisonment, a Rs 2,000 fine, or both.
Article 32 gives the Supreme Court writ jurisdiction. Article 226 gives High Courts a wider one.
Article 131 gives the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction in Centre-state disputes.
The Court declined the Ayodhya reference in 1993 (Ismail Faruqui).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: High Courts also have the power to punish for contempt of themselves under Article 215, so the power is not limited to the Supreme Court. Article 129 gives the Supreme Court this power as a court of record. Article 215 gives the same status and power to every High Court. The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 divides contempt into civil (wilful disobedience of a court order) and criminal (scandalising or lowering the authority of a court, prejudicing judicial proceedings, or obstructing justice). The maximum punishment is six months' simple imprisonment, a Rs 2,000 fine, or both. The 2006 amendment added truth as a defence if it is in public interest and bona fide. Under Section 15, the Advocate General's consent is needed for others to start proceedings in a High Court. In the Supreme Court, the Attorney General's consent is needed.

2 — Incorrect: Only the Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction, under Article 143. The President may refer a question of law or fact of public importance. Article 143(2) covers disputes arising from pre-Constitution treaties, agreements and similar instruments, where the Court must give its opinion. Under Article 143(1) the Court may decline. The advisory opinion is not binding and is not law under Article 141. Examples: the Berubari Union case (1960), the Kerala Education Bill (1958), the Presidential Reference on the Ram Janmabhoomi issue (1993, declined by the Court), the Cauvery tribunal reference (1992), and the Presidential Reference on Governors' assent to Bills (2025). High Courts have no such jurisdiction.
summary: The answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2. Both the Supreme Court and the High Courts are courts of record that can punish for contempt, and only the Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction, under Article 143.
topic_notes: The Supreme Court's jurisdictions are original (Article 131, Centre-state and inter-state disputes), writ (Article 32), appellate (Articles 132-136), advisory (Article 143), review (Article 137), and the power to do complete justice (Article 142). It is a court of record under Article 129, which means its judgments are preserved as precedent and it can punish for contempt. Article 141 makes its law binding on all courts in India. High Courts: Article 215 makes them courts of record. Article 226 gives writ jurisdiction, wider than Article 32 because it covers 'any other purpose'. Article 227 gives superintendence over subordinate courts. The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 defines civil and criminal contempt. Punishment is up to six months' simple imprisonment, a Rs 2,000 fine, or both. Truth became a defence under the 2006 amendment. Article 19(2) lists contempt of court as a ground for reasonable restrictions on free speech. Advisory jurisdiction has two parts. Article 143(1) is discretionary, so the Court may decline. Article 143(2) is mandatory and concerns disputes from pre-Constitution treaties. Notable references include Delhi Laws Act (1951), Berubari (1960), Kerala Education Bill (1958), and Special Courts Bill (1978). The Court declined to answer the Ayodhya reference in 1993. Other angles: Article 144 (all authorities act in aid of the Supreme Court), Article 145 (rules of Court), Article 124 (judges' appointment), and Article 147 (interpretation of the Constitution).

question:
Which of the following subjects/provisions fall(s) under the Directive Principles of State Policy of the Constitution of India ?
1. Uniform Civil Code for all persons living in India
2. Provision for early childhood care and education to children up to the age of 14 years
3. Promotion of international peace and security Select the answer using the codes given below :
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Part IV of the Constitution (Articles 36-51) contains the Directive Principles of State Policy. They are non-justiciable (Art. 37) but fundamental to governance. They were borrowed from the Irish Constitution. Article 44 directs the State to secure a Uniform Civil Code for citizens throughout the territory of India. Article 45 originally dealt with free and compulsory education up to age 14. The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Art. 21A (right to education for ages 6-14 as a Fundamental Right) and changed Art. 45 to require early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years. Art. 51A(k) added a Fundamental Duty on parents to provide education for children aged 6-14. The question's phrasing 'up to the age of 14' is loose, but the subject, early childhood care and education, is within Art. 45. A student may suspect this item is a trap, but it is a DPSP subject. Article 51 covers international peace and security: it promotes peace, just and honourable relations between nations, respect for international law and treaty obligations, and settlement of disputes by arbitration. Because all three items are in Part IV, option (a) is correct.
explanations: Correct: all three items are in Part IV, namely Art. 44, Art. 45 and Art. 51.
Wrong: it excludes item 1, the UCC, which is Art. 44 and a DPSP.
Wrong: it excludes item 1, although the UCC is a DPSP. Item 3 is also correct, so this option is incomplete.
Wrong: it excludes items 1 and 2, which are both in Part IV.
keyfact: Art. 44 = UCC, Art. 45 = early childhood care (until age 6), Art. 51 = international peace; all are DPSPs.
option_notes: Option (a) 1, 2 and 3: all are DPSPs, under Arts. 44, 45 and 51. Part IV (Arts. 36-51) is non-justiciable but fundamental to governance. It was influenced by the Irish Constitution, and the Directives are often grouped as Socialistic, Gandhian and Liberal-Intellectual. Art. 51 deals with international peace, Art. 44 with the UCC, and Art. 45 with early childhood care.

Option (b) 2 and 3 only: both items are valid DPSPs, but the option wrongly omits the UCC. Art. 45 covers early childhood care and education until six years, after the 86th Amendment 2002. Art. 51 covers international peace and security, respect for international law and arbitration. Both are in Part IV, but the option is incomplete.

Option (c) 1 only: the UCC under Art. 44 is a Liberal-Intellectual principle. It directs the State to secure a uniform civil code across India. Cases: Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal and John Vallamattom. Goa has a common civil code from the Portuguese era, and Uttarakhand passed a UCC law in 2024. The option wrongly excludes Arts. 45 and 51.

Option (d) 3 only: Art. 51 promotes international peace and security. It also covers just and honourable relations between nations, respect for international law and treaty obligations, and arbitration of disputes. It is the only DPSP on foreign policy. The option wrongly excludes the UCC and early childhood care.
related: Part IV spans Articles 36 to 51.
DPSPs were borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
The 86th Amendment 2002 inserted Art. 21A and revised Art. 45.
The 42nd Amendment added Arts. 39A, 43A and 48A.
The 97th Amendment 2011 added Art. 43B on cooperative societies.
Art. 48A protects the environment and wildlife.
Art. 50 separates the judiciary from the executive.
Minerva Mills (1980) held that harmony between FRs and DPSPs is a basic feature.
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 44 directs the State to secure a Uniform Civil Code. Article 44 is in Part IV. It aims at national integration and gender justice by replacing personal laws with a common code. Related cases: Shah Bano (1985), Sarla Mudgal (1995), and Shayara Bano (2017) on triple talaq. Goa is often cited as having a uniform civil code. Uttarakhand enacted a UCC law in 2024. It is not enforceable by courts.

2 — Correct: Article 45, as amended by the 86th Amendment Act 2002, directs the State to provide early childhood care and education to all children until they complete six years. Before 2002, Art. 45 covered free and compulsory education to age 14. Art. 21A now makes education a Fundamental Right for ages 6-14, backed by the RTE Act 2009, in force from 1 April 2010. The question's age-14 wording is imprecise, but the subject falls within Art. 45.

3 — Correct: Article 51 lists the directive on promoting international peace and security. The State shall endeavour to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration. It guides India's foreign policy, including non-alignment and Panchsheel. It is in Part IV and is non-justiciable.
summary: The answer is (a): all three items are in the Directive Principles of State Policy. Article 44 covers the Uniform Civil Code, Article 45 covers early childhood care and education, and Article 51 covers the promotion of international peace and security.
topic_notes: Part IV of the Constitution (Articles 36-51) contains the DPSPs, borrowed from the Irish Constitution. Art. 36 defines 'State' and Art. 37 makes them non-justiciable but fundamental in governance. Classification: Socialistic (Arts. 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47), Gandhian (Arts. 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48), and Liberal-Intellectual (Arts. 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51). Key articles: Art. 38 secures a social order and reduces inequalities. Art. 39 sets out principles of policy, including equal pay for equal work. Art. 39A provides equal justice and free legal aid. Art. 40 covers village panchayats. Art. 41 covers the right to work and education. Art. 42 covers just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Art. 43 covers a living wage. Art. 43A covers workers' participation in management (42nd Amendment). Art. 43B covers cooperative societies (97th Amendment). Art. 44 is the UCC. Art. 45 is early childhood care. Art. 46 covers SC/ST and weaker sections. Art. 47 covers nutrition and public health. Art. 48 covers agriculture and animal husbandry, including cow protection. Art. 48A covers environment protection. Art. 49 covers monuments. Art. 50 separates the judiciary from the executive. Art. 51 covers international peace. The 42nd Amendment 1976 added Arts. 39A, 43A and 48A. The 44th Amendment 1978 added Art. 38(2). Cases: Champakam Dorairajan, Kesavananda Bharati, Minerva Mills (balance between FRs and DPSPs), and the Unni Krishnan education case. Art. 31C gives DPSPs priority over Arts. 14 and 19 in certain cases. Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA, Art. 51A.

question: Which one among the following correctly stands 55, for the acronym AWACS ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: AWACS stands for Airborne Warning and Control System. It is a mobile, long-range radar surveillance and command-and-control system carried on an aircraft, typically with a rotating radar dome (rotodome) mounted above the fuselage. It gives early warning of hostile aircraft, missiles and ships, and it lets controllers on board direct friendly fighters, tankers and strike aircraft. The best-known platform is the US Boeing E-3 Sentry, which is based on the Boeing 707. NATO also operates E-3 aircraft. Russia uses the A-50 Mainstay, based on the Ilyushin Il-76. India operates the Phalcon-based IAF AWACS on the Il-76 (supplied by Israel and Russia), and the indigenous Netra AEW&C built by DRDO on the Embraer ERJ-145. Elimination: option (a) swaps in 'Advanced' and 'Critical Scanning', which are not part of the term. Option (b) contains 'Arial' (a misspelling of 'Aerial') and 'Case Study', which makes no sense in a military context. Option (c) has the right first word 'Airborne' but 'Warfare and Critical Solutions' is invented. Only (d) matches the standard expansion, and the term 'Warning and Control' describes the system's function.
explanations: Wrong: 'Advanced Warning and Critical Scanning' is not the accepted expansion; the A stands for Airborne and the C for Control.
Wrong: 'Arial Warfare and Case Study' is nonsensical, and 'Arial' is a misspelling. AWACS is a radar surveillance system, not a study.
Wrong: 'Airborne Warfare and Critical Solutions' gets only the first word right; W is Warning and C is Control.
Correct: Airborne Warning and Control System is the standard expansion of AWACS.
keyfact: AWACS = Airborne Warning and Control System, a radar-equipped command aircraft such as the E-3 Sentry or India's Phalcon on the Il-76.
option_notes: Advanced Warning and Critical Scanning is not a real defence term. It is a distractor built from the same initials. Real early-warning systems include AEW&C (Airborne Early Warning and Control) and ground-based radar networks, and none of them use this phrase.

'Arial Warfare and Case Study' is an invented phrase. 'Arial' is a typeface, and the correct word would be 'Aerial'. Aerial warfare means combat conducted by aircraft. A case study is an academic method, so the phrase has no military meaning.

Airborne Warfare and Critical Solutions is invented. Airborne warfare does exist as a concept: it means troops and equipment delivered by air, as with paratroopers and airborne divisions. It is unrelated to the radar-based AWACS.

Airborne Warning and Control System is a radar and command platform on an aircraft. The US E-3 Sentry (Boeing 707 based) is the classic example. India's IAF operates Phalcon AWACS on the Il-76, and DRDO's Netra AEW&C is on the Embraer ERJ-145. Its main roles are surveillance, early warning, and directing air battles.
related: AWACS = Airborne Warning and Control System
US AWACS platform: Boeing E-3 Sentry (based on the Boeing 707)
India's Phalcon AWACS is mounted on the Ilyushin Il-76
DRDO's Netra is an indigenous AEW&C on the Embraer ERJ-145
CABS, Bengaluru, develops airborne early warning systems
AEW&C = Airborne Early Warning and Control
Russia's AWACS-type aircraft is the A-50 Mainstay
summary: The correct answer is (d) Airborne Warning and Control System. AWACS is an airborne radar-picket platform that detects aircraft and ships at long range and directs friendly aircraft in battle.
topic_notes: AWACS belongs to the wider family of Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) platforms. These aircraft carry powerful look-down radar that can detect low-flying targets far beyond the range of ground radar, because they fly at altitude and are not limited by terrain. They also act as flying command posts, so they pass tracking data to fighters and ground commanders. The US E-3 Sentry entered service in 1977. NATO operates its own E-3A fleet. Russia's A-50 is based on the Il-76. China fields the KJ-2000 and KJ-500. Israel's Phalcon radar was fitted by IAI on Il-76 aircraft supplied to India, and the first Indian AWACS arrived in 2009. India's DRDO developed Netra, an indigenous AEW&C on the Embraer ERJ-145, using an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar. The Centre for Airborne Systems (CABS) in Bengaluru leads this work. A larger programme called AEW&C Mk-II is based on the Airbus A321. Other acronyms to know: AWACS, AEW&C, ISTAR (Intelligence, Surveillance, Target Acquisition and Reconnaissance), UAV, SAM, BVR, MRFA, LCA, DRDO, HAL. Typical exam angles include expansions of defence acronyms, which country made a platform, and which Indian organisation developed it.

question: As a countermeasure to drone swarm attack, an effective way is to use electromagnetic (EM) drone jamming to disrupt the GPS and communication system of the drones. Which one among the following is the correct frequency range used for EM drone jamming ?
subject: Statistics
detail: Most commercial and military drones depend on two radio links: a command-and-control/telemetry link and satellite navigation (GPS/GNSS) for positioning. The control links commonly use the 433 MHz, 900 MHz, 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz ISM bands, while GPS L1 is 1575.42 MHz and L2 is 1227.60 MHz. These lie in the UHF to microwave part of the spectrum (roughly 300 MHz to 300 GHz). A jammer transmits higher-power noise on the same frequencies, so the drone's receiver cannot decode the real signal. The drone then loses control and either hovers, lands, returns home or drifts. Against a swarm, wide-beam or directional jammers can affect many drones at once, and the swarm's inter-drone mesh links can be disrupted too. By contrast, visible, infrared and far-infrared radiation are optical or thermal bands. They are used for cameras, thermal imaging, lidar or laser dazzlers, and they are not the bands used for radio communication or GPS. They are therefore not 'EM jamming' frequencies for disrupting GPS. Eliminating (a), (c) and (d) leaves (b). The stray '56' in the option is an OCR artefact.
explanations: Incorrect: far-infrared is thermal radiation, used for heat sensing, and it carries no drone control or GPS signals.
Correct: drone control links and GPS operate in the radio/microwave range (about 1-6 GHz), and jammers target these bands.
Incorrect: visible light is used for cameras and optical sensing, not for radio links or GPS. Bright light or lasers can only dazzle optical sensors.
Incorrect: infrared is used for IR sensors and thermal cameras, and for short-range remote controls. It is not the band for drone GPS or control links.
keyfact: Drone GPS and control links use radio/microwave bands (about 1-6 GHz), so EM jammers use microwave frequencies.
option_notes: Far-infrared covers wavelengths of roughly 15 µm to 1 mm (about 0.3-20 THz). It is emitted by warm bodies and used in thermal imaging, heating and astronomy. It is not used in satellite navigation or drone radio links.

Microwaves have frequencies of about 300 MHz to 300 GHz and wavelengths from 1 m to 1 mm. They are used in radar, satellite links, Wi-Fi (2.4/5 GHz), GPS (L-band) and mobile networks. Drone control and GNSS signals sit in these bands, and microwave ovens run at 2.45 GHz.

Visible light spans about 400-700 nm (roughly 430-750 THz). Human eyes and ordinary cameras detect it. Drones use it for imaging and optical navigation. Lasers or dazzlers can blind cameras, but they do not jam radio links.

Infrared runs from 700 nm to 1 mm, divided into near, mid and far IR. It is used for night vision, thermal sensors, remote controls and fibre-optic communication. Infrared sensors can detect drones, but IR is not used to jam GPS or radio control.
related: GPS L1 frequency is 1575.42 MHz; NavIC uses L5 and S bands.
Jamming blocks signals with noise; spoofing sends fake GPS signals.
DRDO developed an anti-drone system with a laser directed-energy weapon and a jammer.
High-power microwave weapons can disable many drones at once.
Microwave band covers about 300 MHz-300 GHz.
Drone control commonly uses the 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz ISM bands.
Bhargavastra is an Indian micro-missile counter-swarm system.
Akashteer is the Indian Army's automated air defence control and reporting system.
summary: The answer is (b), microwave frequency. Drone control links and GPS/GNSS signals operate in the radio and microwave bands (about 1.1-1.6 GHz for GPS, 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz for control and video links), so EM jammers transmit noise in these bands to disrupt them.
topic_notes: Counter-drone (C-UAS) systems follow a detect, track, identify and neutralise sequence. Detection uses radar, RF sensors, electro-optical/infrared cameras and acoustic sensors. Neutralisation falls into soft-kill and hard-kill methods. Soft-kill methods include RF jamming of control links, GNSS jamming and spoofing (broadcasting false GPS signals), and cyber takeover. Hard-kill methods include guns, missiles, nets, interceptor drones, and directed-energy weapons such as high-power lasers and high-power microwave (HPM) systems. HPM can fry electronics and so can disable whole swarms. Key frequencies: GPS L1 1575.42 MHz, L2 1227.60 MHz, L5 1176.45 MHz. India's NavIC (IRNSS) uses L5 and S-band (2492.028 MHz). Drone control bands are 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz, plus 433 MHz and 915 MHz for long-range control. Jamming overwhelms the receiver with noise, while spoofing deceives it. A drone swarm is a group of autonomous drones coordinating through mesh networking and AI. Indian systems: DRDO's Anti-Drone System (laser DEW plus jammer, used at the 2021 Independence Day event and for VVIP security), Bhargavastra (a micro-missile counter-swarm system tested in 2025), the D4 anti-drone system from DRDO and BEL, and Akashteer for air defence control. After the Jammu air base drone attack of June 2021, the Drone Rules 2021 were issued, with liberalised Drone Rules 2021 replacing the 2021 draft. The Digital Sky platform manages drone permissions.

question: Which one among the following is the correct method employed by GPS to find the location of a target ?
options: Trilateration method, which measures lengths of sides of triangle with target location as one of the heads of the triangle ST:
Dilation method, which measures distance of target location from two already known landmarks
Measurement of the distance of target from the designated geostationary satellite
Measurement of the distance of target from the designated polar satellite
subject: Computers
detail: GPS (Global Positioning System) is a satellite navigation system run by the US Space Force, with a constellation of about 31 operational satellites in Medium Earth Orbit at roughly 20,200 km, orbital period about 12 hours, in 6 orbital planes inclined at 55 degrees. Each satellite broadcasts its position and the precise time from an atomic clock. The receiver calculates the signal travel time and multiplies by the speed of light to get the distance (pseudorange). Knowing the distance from one satellite puts the receiver on a sphere; two spheres give a circle; three give two points, one of which is usually absurd; the fourth satellite is needed to correct the receiver's cheap clock error, so there are four unknowns: x, y, z and time. This distance-based method is trilateration, not triangulation, which uses angles. Elimination: (b) 'dilation' is not a positioning method and GPS does not use ground landmarks; (c) a single geostationary satellite cannot fix a location, and GPS satellites are not geostationary; (d) polar satellites are not used for GPS, and one satellite's distance alone is insufficient.
explanations: Correct. GPS uses trilateration: distances to multiple satellites define spheres whose intersection gives the receiver's position, so the target is a vertex of the triangles whose sides are measured.
Wrong. 'Dilation' is not a positioning technique, and GPS relies on satellites with known positions, not on two ground landmarks.
Wrong. GPS satellites are in MEO, not geostationary orbit, and distance from a single satellite cannot fix a location.
Wrong. GPS does not use a single polar satellite; its satellites are in inclined MEO orbits, and one distance gives only a sphere of possible positions.
keyfact: GPS = trilateration: distances from at least 4 MEO satellites give position and time; it is not angle-based triangulation.
option_notes: Trilateration finds a position from measured distances to known points, unlike triangulation, which uses measured angles. GPS uses spheres centred on satellites. Three satellites are enough for a 2D fix, and four are needed for 3D position plus receiver clock bias. The method is also used in other GNSS systems, such as GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou and NavIC.

'Dilation' is a distractor: in geometry it means scaling a figure, and in image processing it means expanding boundaries. It is not a navigation method. Position fixing from two known landmarks resembles classical bearing or resection surveying and is not what GPS does.

Geostationary satellites orbit at about 35,786 km above the equator with a 24-hour period and appear fixed over one point. Examples are INSAT/GSAT communication satellites and the GAGAN augmentation payloads. GPS itself uses MEO satellites. India's NavIC uses a mix of 3 GEO and 4 GSO (inclined geosynchronous) satellites.

Polar satellites are in low Earth orbit at roughly 600-900 km, passing near the poles in sun-synchronous orbit. They are used for remote sensing and weather (IRS, Cartosat, and launches by PSLV). They are not used for GPS positioning, which needs multiple simultaneously visible satellites.
related: Trilateration uses distances; triangulation uses angles.
GPS needs at least 4 satellites for a 3D fix plus time correction.
GPS satellites orbit at about 20,200 km in MEO with a period of about 12 hours.
NavIC, India's regional system, is operated by ISRO and has 7 satellites.
GAGAN is India's satellite-based augmentation system for aviation, built by AAI and ISRO.
Selective Availability for GPS was discontinued in May 2000.
GPS is owned by the US government and operated by the US Space Force.
summary: The answer is (a). GPS uses trilateration: the receiver measures its distance from several satellites (at least 4 for a full 3D fix plus clock correction) and finds the one point consistent with all those distances. It works with the lengths of the sides of triangles whose one vertex is the receiver.
topic_notes: GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite Systems) covers GPS (USA, fully operational in 1995, with the first satellite launched in 1978), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU), BeiDou (China) and regional systems such as NavIC (India) and QZSS (Japan). GPS has three segments: space (satellites), control (ground monitoring stations and master control) and user (receivers). Satellites carry atomic clocks (caesium and rubidium) and transmit on L1 (1575.42 MHz), L2 (1227.60 MHz) and L5 frequencies. Relativistic effects (special and general relativity) must be corrected for accuracy: the net effect is satellite clocks running about 38 microseconds per day faster. Civilian accuracy is about 3-5 m, and it can be improved to centimetres with differential GPS or RTK. Selective Availability, the deliberate degradation of civilian signals, was switched off in May 2000. India's NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation, formerly IRNSS) is operated by ISRO and provides about 20 m accuracy over India and up to 1500 km beyond its borders. GAGAN (GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation) is the ISRO-AAI satellite-based augmentation system for aviation. Applications include navigation, surveying, disaster management, precision agriculture, timing for banks and power grids, and mapping. Signals can be affected by ionospheric delay, multipath and urban canyons.

question: Which one among the following is the correct 58. nature of the substance filling up the pleural cavity, the space between the lungs and the chest ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The lungs are enclosed by a double-layered membrane called the pleura. The inner layer (visceral pleura) adheres to the lung surface and the outer layer (parietal pleura) lines the thoracic wall and diaphragm. Between them lies the pleural cavity, which holds about 5-15 ml of watery serous fluid secreted by the pleural membranes. This fluid has two main functions: it reduces friction as the lungs expand and recoil, and its surface tension keeps the two layers close together, so the lungs follow the movement of the chest wall. The pressure inside the cavity (intrapleural pressure) is normally slightly below atmospheric pressure, about -4 mmHg at rest. Air in the cavity is abnormal and causes pneumothorax, which can collapse the lung. Excess fluid causes pleural effusion, and inflammation of the pleura is pleurisy. Elimination: dry or humid air (b, c) would mean pneumothorax, a disease state. Fatty muscle (d) is wrong because the cavity is a space containing fluid, not tissue. Hence the answer is (a).
explanations: Correct: the pleural cavity contains a thin film of serous pleural fluid that lubricates the pleural surfaces.
Wrong: air in the pleural cavity is abnormal (pneumothorax) and can cause lung collapse. Dry air is not its normal content.
Wrong: humid air is found in the airways and alveoli, not the pleural cavity. Air in the cavity would be pathological.
Wrong: the pleural cavity is a potential space, not filled with muscle or fat. Muscles such as the diaphragm and intercostals lie outside it.
keyfact: The pleural cavity is filled with a thin film of serous (lubricating) pleural fluid, not air.
option_notes: Liquid: the pleural cavity holds about 5-15 ml of serous fluid, secreted by the pleura. It is a watery, lubricating fluid with some protein. It reduces friction and holds the lung to the chest wall by surface tension. Excess fluid is pleural effusion, and infected fluid is empyema.

Dry air: not found in the pleural cavity under normal conditions. Air entering the cavity, through chest injury or lung rupture, causes pneumothorax. Intrapleural pressure rises to atmospheric and the lung collapses. Treatment is a chest tube. Dry air is also not what the airways carry, since inhaled air is humidified in the respiratory tract.

Humid air: inspired air is warmed and humidified in the nose and trachea, so humid air is found in the respiratory passages and alveoli. Alveolar air is saturated with water vapour. It does not occupy the pleural cavity, so this option confuses the airways with the pleural space.

Fatty muscle: this is not a substance filling the pleural cavity. Muscles related to breathing are the diaphragm and the external and internal intercostals. Fat is found in the extrapleural tissue outside the parietal pleura. The pleural cavity itself is only a potential space with a fluid film.
related: Pleura is a double-layered membrane around each lung.
Pleural fluid is serous and about 5-15 ml in volume.
Air in the pleural cavity is called pneumothorax.
Excess pleural fluid is pleural effusion; inflammation is pleurisy.
The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two.
Surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells.
The respiratory centre lies in the medulla oblongata.
summary: The correct answer is (a) Liquid. The pleural cavity is a thin space between the visceral and parietal pleura filled with a small amount of serous (pleural) fluid. This fluid lubricates the lungs and lets them move smoothly during breathing.
topic_notes: The respiratory system includes the nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli. The lungs are protected by the rib cage, and each lung is covered by a double pleural membrane. The visceral pleura covers the lung and the parietal pleura lines the chest wall. The space between them, the pleural cavity, contains a thin layer of pleural fluid, which lubricates and creates cohesion. The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two lobes, with a cardiac notch for the heart. Breathing mechanics: during inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostals lift the ribs, so thoracic volume increases and the pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric, drawing air in. Expiration is largely passive. Intrapleural pressure stays below atmospheric pressure, which keeps the lungs inflated. Disorders: pneumothorax (air in the pleural cavity), hydrothorax or pleural effusion (excess fluid), hemothorax (blood), pleurisy (inflammation of the pleura), and empyema (pus). Other points: surfactant, produced by type II alveolar cells, reduces surface tension in alveoli, and its lack causes infant respiratory distress syndrome. The respiratory centre is in the medulla oblongata and pons. Normal tidal volume is about 500 ml, vital capacity about 3.5-4.5 L, and residual volume about 1100-1200 ml. Gas exchange occurs by simple diffusion across the alveolar membrane. Oxygen is carried mainly as oxyhaemoglobin and carbon dioxide mostly as bicarbonate. Related diseases that UPSC may test include asthma, emphysema, pneumonia, tuberculosis and silicosis.

question: Which one among the following statements with regard to fatty acids is correct ? Most fatty acids have carboxyl group at
options: one end and methyl group at the other end. Saturated fatty acids carry even number of
double bonds between carbon atoms. Saturated fatty acids carry odd number of
double bonds between carbon atoms. Monounsaturated fatty acids carry as
many hydrogen atoms as they can
subject: General Science
detail: A fatty acid is a long hydrocarbon chain with a terminal carboxylic acid group. The carboxyl end is the hydrophilic head; the opposite end is a methyl group, called the omega (n) end. Natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons (commonly 12 to 24) because they are built from 2-carbon acetyl-CoA units. Saturated fatty acids (palmitic C16:0, stearic C18:0) have only single C-C bonds, so every carbon carries the maximum number of hydrogens; they are generally solid at room temperature (animal fats, butter, ghee, coconut and palm oil). Monounsaturated fatty acids (oleic acid C18:1, in olive and groundnut oil) have exactly one double bond. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (linoleic, alpha-linolenic, EPA, DHA) have two or more double bonds; linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids are essential and must come from the diet. Elimination: (b) and (c) fail because saturated acids have zero double bonds, and zero is neither an odd count nor a non-trivial even count of double bonds. (d) describes saturated acids, not monounsaturated ones, which have two fewer hydrogens because of the double bond. That leaves (a).
explanations: Correct. Most fatty acids are unbranched chains with -COOH at one end and -CH3 at the other.
Incorrect. Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds at all. Zero is technically even, but the option implies they carry double bonds, and the statement is not a valid description of saturation.
Incorrect. Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds, so they cannot carry an odd number of them.
Incorrect. Monounsaturated fatty acids have one double bond and so are not fully loaded with hydrogen. Holding as many hydrogens as possible describes saturated fatty acids.
keyfact: Fatty acid = carboxyl (-COOH) head at one end and methyl (-CH3) tail at the other; saturated = no double bonds, maximum hydrogen.
option_notes: Structure of a typical fatty acid: a carboxyl head (hydrophilic) and a hydrocarbon tail ending in a methyl group (the omega end). Chains are mostly unbranched with an even number of carbons (12-24). They are the building blocks of triglycerides, phospholipids and cholesterol esters, and they supply 9 kcal per gram.

Saturated fatty acids contain only single C-C bonds, so the chain is saturated with hydrogen. Examples: palmitic (C16), stearic (C18), lauric and myristic acids. They are solid at room temperature, found in butter, ghee, lard, coconut and palm oil. A high intake raises LDL cholesterol and the risk of heart disease.

This describes no real class of fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids have zero double bonds. Unsaturated fatty acids may have one (mono) or several (poly) double bonds, mostly in cis form in nature. Trans fats, formed by partial hydrogenation, contain trans double bonds and are harmful.

Monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA) have exactly one double bond, so they have two fewer hydrogens than the corresponding saturated acid. Oleic acid (C18:1, omega-9) is the main example, found in olive oil, groundnut oil, mustard oil and avocado. They are liquid at room temperature and considered heart-healthy.
related: Essential fatty acids: linoleic (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic (omega-3).
Fats give 9 kcal/g; carbohydrates and proteins give 4 kcal/g.
Oleic acid is a monounsaturated C18:1 omega-9 fatty acid.
Hydrogenation of oils produces trans fats, which raise LDL.
Natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbon atoms.
FSSAI caps industrial trans fat at 2% of oils and fats.
Iodine value measures the degree of unsaturation of a fat.
summary: The correct answer is (a). Most fatty acids are straight-chain molecules with a carboxyl (-COOH) group at one end and a methyl (-CH3) group at the other. The other options misdescribe saturation: saturated fatty acids have no double bonds, and it is saturated (not monounsaturated) fatty acids that hold as many hydrogen atoms as possible.
topic_notes: Lipids are a group of biomolecules insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents. Fatty acids are their basic units. Classes: simple lipids (fats and oils, which are triglycerides, and waxes), compound lipids (phospholipids, glycolipids, lipoproteins) and derived lipids (steroids such as cholesterol). Saturation: saturated acids have no double bonds; MUFA have one; PUFA have two or more. Essential fatty acids are linoleic (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic (omega-3), which the human body cannot synthesise. Omega-3 sources: fish oil, flaxseed, walnuts. Fats supply 9 kcal/g, against 4 kcal/g for carbohydrates and proteins. Fats are stored in adipose tissue, insulate the body, protect organs and carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Hydrogenation converts vegetable oils to solid fats (vanaspati) and creates trans fats, which raise LDL and lower HDL. FSSAI has limited trans fat to 2% of total oil/fat in foods and aims to eliminate industrially produced trans fats. Rancidity is the oxidation of fats. Saponification value measures the average chain length, and iodine value measures unsaturation. Cholesterol is carried by LDL (bad) and HDL (good). WHO recommends that saturated fat be below 10% of energy intake and trans fat below 1%. Related nutrition topics: the RDA for fat, the role of vitamins, and the fact that unsaturated oils are liquid because of cis kinks in the chain.

ocr: Which one among the following are the primary reactants of photochemical smog ? Sulphur Hexafluoride and Soot (a) Carbon Monoxide and Ozone (b) Nitric Oxide and Unburnt Hydrocarbons (c) Peroxy Radicals and Sub-oxides (d)
subject: General Science
detail: Photochemical smog (Los Angeles type, or oxidising smog) occurs in warm, dry, sunny weather with heavy vehicular traffic. Its primary pollutants (those emitted directly) are nitric oxide (NO) and unburnt hydrocarbons/VOCs. NO is oxidised to NO2, and sunlight splits NO2 into NO and atomic oxygen. The atomic oxygen combines with O2 to form ozone (O3). Ozone reacts with hydrocarbons to form formaldehyde, acrolein and peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), along with peroxy radicals. These products, not the starting materials, are the secondary pollutants and are eye irritants that damage lungs and plants and crack rubber. Classical or London smog is different: it is reducing smog, cold and humid, with SO2 and particulates (smoke plus fog). To eliminate options, ask which substances are emitted directly and which are formed in the atmosphere. Ozone, peroxy radicals and PAN are secondary. Sulphur hexafluoride is a greenhouse gas with no role in smog. Soot is particulate matter. Carbon monoxide is a primary pollutant but is not the key smog reactant. Catalytic converters, which reduce NOx and hydrocarbons, help control photochemical smog.
explanations: Wrong: SF6 is a potent, long-lived greenhouse gas, and soot is black carbon particulate matter. Neither is the key reactant pair in photochemical smog.
Wrong: Ozone is a secondary pollutant formed in the smog reactions, so it is not a primary reactant. CO is a primary pollutant but does not drive the smog chemistry.
Correct: NO (from NOx) and unburnt hydrocarbons/VOCs from vehicle exhaust react in sunlight to form O3, PAN and aldehydes.
Wrong: Peroxy radicals are reactive intermediates formed during the reactions. 'Sub-oxides' is not a recognised smog reactant.
keyfact: Photochemical smog = NOx + unburnt hydrocarbons + sunlight → ozone, PAN and aldehydes (secondary pollutants).
option_notes: Sulphur hexafluoride (SF6) is a colourless, odourless, non-toxic gas used as an electrical insulator in switchgear. It has a very high global warming potential (about 23,500 times CO2 over 100 years) and a very long atmospheric life. It is listed under the Kyoto Protocol basket of gases. Soot is black carbon from incomplete combustion; it is a particulate pollutant (PM) that absorbs sunlight and warms the atmosphere.

Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless toxic gas from incomplete combustion. It binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport. Ozone is a triatomic oxygen molecule. In the stratosphere it shields against UV-B, while in the troposphere it is a harmful secondary pollutant and a component of smog. Ground-level ozone is formed from NOx and VOCs in sunlight.

Nitric oxide (NO) is formed at high combustion temperatures in engines from N2 and O2 and is quickly oxidised to NO2. Unburnt hydrocarbons (VOCs) come from incomplete fuel combustion, evaporation of fuel and solvents. Together they are the precursors of photochemical smog. NO2 is a brown, irritant gas that absorbs sunlight and starts the smog photochemistry. Both are controlled by catalytic converters and BS-VI norms.

Peroxy radicals (RO2) are reactive intermediates formed when hydrocarbons are oxidised by OH radicals or O3. They convert NO to NO2, which causes ozone build-up, and they also help form PAN. They are secondary or intermediate species, not primary emissions. 'Sub-oxides' (such as C3O2) are unusual oxides with a low oxygen content and play no role in smog.
related: Photochemical smog is also called Los Angeles smog or oxidising smog.
PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate) is a powerful eye irritant and a secondary pollutant in smog.
London smog is reducing smog caused by SO2 and smoke in cold, humid conditions.
Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant, not emitted directly.
Catalytic converters reduce NOx, CO and hydrocarbons in vehicle exhaust.
The National Clean Air Programme was launched in 2019.
India's National AQI was launched in 2014 with six categories.
summary: The answer is (c) Nitric Oxide and Unburnt Hydrocarbons. Photochemical smog forms when sunlight drives reactions between nitrogen oxides (NO, NO2) and volatile organic compounds (unburnt hydrocarbons) emitted mainly by vehicles. These primary pollutants then produce secondary pollutants such as ozone, PAN and aldehydes.
topic_notes: Smog is a combination of smoke and fog, and there are two types. Classical (London) smog is reducing smog: it forms in cold, humid conditions from coal smoke, SO2 and particulates, and was notorious in the London smog of 1952. Photochemical (Los Angeles) smog is oxidising: it forms in warm, dry, sunny weather from NOx and VOCs. Key reactions: NO2 + sunlight → NO + O; O + O2 → O3; NO + O3 → NO2 + O2. Ozone and VOCs then give PAN, formaldehyde and acrolein. Effects: eye and lung irritation, asthma, plant damage (leaf bleaching), rubber cracking and reduced visibility. Peak concentrations occur around midday. Control: catalytic converters, cleaner fuels (BS-VI), CNG, vehicle emission norms and VOC controls. Related ideas: primary pollutants (CO, NOx, SO2, SPM) versus secondary pollutants (O3, PAN, acid rain components). Tropospheric ozone is a pollutant while stratospheric ozone is protective. In India, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the National Clean Air Programme (2019) and the National Air Quality Index (2014) are relevant. The AQI has six categories, from Good to Severe. Delhi's winter smog is mostly a particulate and fog problem aggravated by stubble burning, though it also has photochemical aspects. The Montreal Protocol (1987) concerns ozone-depleting substances, and the Kigali Amendment concerns HFCs.

ocr: Which one among the following is known as Carbolic acid ? Phenol (a) (b) Alcohol (c) Ether (d) Acetone
subject: Insurance
detail: Phenol, C6H5OH, is an aromatic compound in which an -OH group is bonded directly to an sp2 carbon of a benzene ring. It was first isolated from coal tar by Friedlieb Runge in 1834 and was called 'carbolic acid' (carbolic oil). It is a colourless crystalline solid that turns pink on exposure to air and light because of oxidation. It is mildly acidic (pKa about 10) because the phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance. It is more acidic than alcohols but weaker than carboxylic acids and carbonic acid, so it does not liberate CO2 from sodium bicarbonate. Joseph Lister used dilute carbolic acid as an antiseptic in surgery in 1867. A dilute solution of phenol is the antiseptic and disinfectant found in Dettol-type products (though Dettol's main ingredient is chloroxylenol). Phenol is used to make Bakelite (phenol-formaldehyde), aspirin, dyes, nylon-6 intermediates and picric acid. Elimination: alcohols have the -OH on an alkyl carbon, ethers have a C-O-C linkage, and acetone is a ketone, so none of these is carbolic acid.
