summary: The answer is (a) Error of principle. Treating the purchase of an asset (capital expenditure) as an expense (revenue expenditure) violates a basic accounting principle, the distinction between capital and revenue items, so it is an error of principle.
topic_notes: Errors in accounting are mistakes in recording, classifying or summarising transactions. They are broadly divided into: (1) Errors of omission, either complete or partial; (2) Errors of commission, such as wrong posting, wrong casting, wrong balancing or wrong carry forward; (3) Errors of principle, where capital and revenue items are confused or the accounting treatment is wrong; (4) Compensating errors, which offset each other. Errors that do not affect the trial balance are complete omission, errors of principle, compensating errors, and posting to a wrong account of the same nature. Errors that affect the trial balance include one-sided posting, wrong totalling, wrong balancing and posting a wrong amount on one side only. Rectification: errors affecting the trial balance and not yet closed are corrected by adjusting the accounts, using the Suspense Account when the trial balance does not agree. Once the Suspense Account is cleared, the books balance. Related concepts: capital expenditure gives benefits over several years and is shown in the balance sheet, while revenue expenditure is consumed in the current year and is charged to the profit and loss account. Deferred revenue expenditure is spread over several years. Capital receipts and revenue receipts are classified in the same way. The trial balance is only arithmetical proof of accuracy and not conclusive proof. Errors of principle also include treating the drawings of the proprietor as a business expense and treating a credit sale as a cash sale (the latter is more often an error of commission). Typical exam angles: identifying an error type from an example, whether the trial balance is affected, and the rectification entry.

question: In accounting context, which one of the 104. following statements is correct ?
options: Reserve created is a charge against profits
Capital reserves are normally created out of distributable profits
General reserve can be used only for some specific purposes
Provision’ is a charge against profit
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The key distinction is between a provision and a reserve. A provision is a charge against profit: it is debited to the P&L Account as an expense (for example provision for doubtful debts, depreciation, or provision for taxation) and is created whether or not the business earns a profit. It reduces profit. It is meant for a known liability or a likely loss whose exact amount is uncertain (AS 29 / Ind AS 37 govern provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets). A reserve is an appropriation of profit, shown in the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account or in the statement of changes in equity. It is created only when there are profits and strengthens the financial position. Reserves are of two types. Revenue reserves, such as the general reserve, come from distributable operating profits and can be used for any purpose, including dividends. Capital reserves come from capital profits (profit on sale of fixed assets, premium on shares, profit on revaluation or forfeiture of shares) and are not normally distributable as dividends. Elimination: (a) is wrong because a reserve is an appropriation, not a charge. (b) is wrong because capital reserves arise from capital profits. (c) is wrong because a general reserve is free and has no specific purpose.
explanations: Incorrect. Creating a reserve is an appropriation of profit, made after the profit has been determined. A charge is an expense deducted to arrive at profit.
Incorrect. Capital reserves arise out of capital profits such as share premium, profit on sale of fixed assets or profit on revaluation. They are not created from distributable (revenue) profits.

Incorrect. A general reserve is a free reserve created for no specific purpose. It can be used for dividends, bonus shares, expansion and meeting contingencies. Specific reserves are the ones with a designated purpose.
Correct. A provision is debited to the P&L Account as a charge against profit. It must be made irrespective of whether there is a profit, and it covers a known liability or loss of uncertain amount.
keyfact: Provision = charge against profit (made even in a loss); Reserve = appropriation of profit (only when profit exists).
option_notes: Reserve: a portion of profit retained in the business and not distributed. It is created by appropriation after profit is determined, for example general reserve, dividend equalisation reserve or capital redemption reserve. It increases owners' funds and is shown under Reserves and Surplus. The claim that it is a charge against profit is wrong. Charges include expenses and provisions.

Capital reserve: created from capital profits, such as profit on sale of fixed assets, share premium (subject to Section 52), profit on revaluation, profit on forfeiture of shares and profit before incorporation. It is generally not available for dividend distribution. It can be used for issuing bonus shares or writing off capital losses and preliminary expenses. It is not created from distributable revenue profits.

General reserve: a revenue reserve created by transferring part of profit to it, voluntarily and not for any specific purpose. It strengthens the financial position and can be used freely for dividends, bonus shares, expansion or contingencies. Under the Companies Act there is no compulsory transfer, though earlier dividend rules linked transfers to dividend rates. It is called a free reserve.

Provision: an amount set aside to meet a known liability or an expected loss whose amount cannot be determined accurately, for example provision for bad debts, depreciation, taxation or discount on debtors. It is a charge against profit, debited to the P&L Account. It must be created even if there is a loss. AS 29 or Ind AS 37 governs recognition. It is shown as a liability or deducted from the related asset.
related: Provision is a charge against profit; reserve is an appropriation of profit.
Capital reserve arises from capital profits and is not available for dividends.
General reserve is a free revenue reserve with no specific purpose.
Securities premium use is governed by Section 52 of the Companies Act 2013.
Ind AS 37 deals with provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets.
Secret reserves are created by undervaluing assets or overvaluing liabilities.
A provision must be made even if the business incurs a loss; a reserve needs profit.
summary: The correct option is (d). A provision is an amount set aside out of profits to meet a known liability or an anticipated loss whose amount cannot be determined with substantial accuracy, and it is charged to the Profit & Loss Account before arriving at net profit. A reserve, by contrast, is an appropriation of profit.
topic_notes:
Provisions versus reserves is a favourite accounting topic. A provision is a charge against profit (an expense) and is debited to the P&L Account. It is mandatory under the prudence concept. Examples: depreciation, provision for doubtful debts, provision for taxation, provision for repairs and renewals. A provision is shown on the liabilities side or deducted from the related asset, and it cannot be used to pay dividends. A reserve is an appropriation of profit. It is created only if profits exist, is shown in the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account, and forms part of shareholders' funds.

Types of reserves:
- Revenue reserves come from normal trading profits. Examples are general reserve, dividend equalisation fund and investment fluctuation reserve. These are distributable.
- Capital reserves come from capital profits. They are not distributable as dividends, though they can be used for bonus shares.
- Specific reserves are created for a designated purpose, such as a debenture redemption reserve (DRR) or workmen's compensation reserve.
- Secret reserves are hidden, created by undervaluing assets or overvaluing liabilities.
- Free reserves are those available for dividend distribution, and they exclude capital reserves and revaluation reserve.

Other angles for the exam: a contingent liability is only disclosed in notes and no provision is made unless the outflow is probable and can be estimated (Ind AS 37). A sinking fund is a reserve backed by earmarked investments. A reserve fund is a reserve backed by specific investments outside the business. A capital redemption reserve is created out of profits when preference shares are redeemed. Securities premium is applied under Section 52 of the Companies Act 2013. Provisions affect profit, while reserves do not.

question: Which one of the following statements is correct ?
options: Agreement of trial balance is a conclusive proof of the accuracy. 105
Suspense account opened in a trial balance is a permanent account
At the end of the accounting year, all the nominal accounts of the ledger book are balanced
A ledger is known as the principal book of accounts
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: The ledger is the principal book of accounts. Transactions are first recorded in the journal and subsidiary books (cash book, purchase book, sales book and returns books), which are books of original entry. They are then posted to ledger accounts, which makes the ledger the book of final entry. Accounts in the ledger are classified as personal, real and nominal. Personal and real accounts are permanent (they carry balances forward). Nominal accounts (income and expenses) are temporary: they are closed by transfer to the Trading and Profit & Loss Account at year end, not merely balanced and carried forward. The trial balance is a statement of ledger balances that checks only arithmetical accuracy of double entry. It is not conclusive proof of accuracy because errors of omission, commission, principle, compensating errors and original errors do not affect it. A suspense account is opened only temporarily to make the trial balance agree when a difference is found. It is cleared once the errors are located and rectified, so it is not a permanent account. Elimination: (a) is wrong because of the limits of the trial balance, (b) because a suspense account is temporary, and (c) because nominal accounts are closed, not balanced. Only (d) remains.
explanations: Incorrect: agreement of the trial balance shows only arithmetical accuracy. Errors of omission, commission, principle and compensating errors remain undetected, so it is not conclusive proof.
Incorrect: a suspense account is a temporary account opened to balance the trial balance. It is closed once the errors are found and rectified.
Incorrect: at year end nominal accounts are closed by transfer to the Trading and P&L Account. Balancing and carrying forward applies to personal and real accounts.
Correct: the ledger is the principal book of accounts, or book of final entry, in which all transactions are classified account-wise.
keyfact: Ledger = principal book of accounts (book of final entry); the trial balance proves only arithmetical accuracy.
option_notes: Trial balance: a statement of debit and credit balances of all ledger accounts on a given date. It checks the arithmetical accuracy of double-entry bookkeeping. It does not detect errors of omission, commission, principle or compensating errors. It is therefore prima facie but not conclusive evidence of accuracy. It is prepared before the final accounts.

Suspense account: a temporary account into which the difference in the trial balance is placed so the totals agree. The difference arises from errors. It is eliminated when the errors are located and corrected through rectifying entries. Any balance remaining at the balance sheet date is shown as a temporary item.

Nominal accounts record expenses, losses, incomes and gains, for example rent, salaries and commission. The rule is to debit expenses and losses and credit incomes and gains. At year end their balances are transferred to the Trading and Profit & Loss Account. They are temporary accounts and start afresh each year.

Ledger: the principal book of accounts and the book of final entry. It contains all accounts (personal, real and nominal) to which journal and subsidiary book entries are posted. It is balanced periodically, and its balances are used to prepare the trial balance and then the final accounts.
related: Ledger is the book of final entry; journal is the book of original entry.
Trial balance checks arithmetical accuracy only, not the correctness of the accounts.
Errors of principle and compensating errors do not affect the trial balance.
Suspense account is a temporary account for the trial balance difference.
Nominal accounts are closed to the P&L Account at year end.
Cash book serves as both a journal and a ledger.
Real and personal accounts are permanent and carried forward.
summary: The correct answer is (d): the ledger is known as the principal book of accounts (book of final entry) because every transaction recorded in the journal or subsidiary books is finally posted to it. The other options misstate the limits of the trial balance, the nature of a suspense account, and the treatment of nominal accounts.
topic_notes: Accounting cycle: transaction, journal or subsidiary books, ledger posting, trial balance, adjustments, final accounts (Trading, P&L, Balance Sheet). Books of original entry: journal and subsidiary books (cash, purchases, sales, purchase returns, sales returns, bills receivable and payable). The ledger is the book of final entry. Classification of accounts: personal (natural, artificial, representative), real (tangible and intangible) and nominal. Golden rules: Personal: debit the receiver, credit the giver. Real: debit what comes in, credit what goes out. Nominal: debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains. Permanent (real) accounts are carried forward, while nominal accounts are closed at year end. Trial balance: it can be prepared by the total method, the balance method or the total-cum-balance method. Errors not revealed by it: omission, commission (wrong account but same side), principle, compensating and original-entry errors. Errors revealed by it: wrong totalling, one-sided posting, wrong balancing, and posting of the wrong amount on one side. Suspense account: opened for trial balance differences, and also when the nature of a receipt is unclear. Rectification: errors affecting the trial balance are rectified using the suspense account. Other points: the cash book is both a journal and a ledger, and is therefore called a book of both original and final entry. Contra entries appear on both sides of the cash book. Ledger accounts are balanced, and the trial balance is the starting point for the final accounts. UPSC can also ask about the dual aspect concept, the accrual basis, and the matching and going concern concepts.

ocr: Which one of the following statements is not correct ? (a) Capital account has a debit balance. (b) Discount column of cash book records cash discount. (c) Under traditional approach, rent outstanding is a personal account. (d) Cash sales are not recorded in the sales day book. 106. 103. Which one of the following is correct ? (a) Operating profit = Net profit — Non-operating expenses — Non-operating incomes (b) Operating profit = Net profit + Non-operating expenses + Non-operating incomes (c) Operating profit = Net profit + Non-operating expenses — Non-operating incomes (d) Operating profit =
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Under the traditional (British) approach, accounts are classified as Personal, Real and Nominal. Personal accounts relate to persons (natural, artificial or representative). Real accounts relate to assets and properties. Nominal accounts relate to expenses, losses, incomes and gains. Golden rules are: Personal - debit the receiver, credit the giver; Real - debit what comes in, credit what goes out; Nominal - debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains. Outstanding rent is an expense that has accrued but is not paid. It is a liability, but in the traditional classification, outstanding expenses are treated as representative personal accounts in some textbooks. The commonly accepted view in many Indian textbooks, however, is that outstanding rent is a representative personal account, and so the intended 'not correct' choice needs checking. Check the others: (a) Capital account has a credit balance, so the statement that it has a debit balance is wrong. Hence (a) is the incorrect statement and the real answer is (a).
explanations: Capital account normally has a CREDIT balance because capital is a liability of the business to the owner. Saying it has a debit balance is wrong (except when drawings or losses exceed capital). So this is the incorrect statement.
The discount column of the three-column cash book records cash discount allowed (debit side) and received (credit side). Correct.
Under the traditional approach, outstanding expenses such as outstanding rent are treated as representative personal accounts (the landlord is represented). Correct.
Cash sales are recorded in the cash book, not in the sales day book, which records only credit sales of goods. Correct.
keyfact: Capital account has a credit balance; the claim that it has a debit balance is the incorrect statement.
option_notes: Capital account records the owner's investment in the business. It has a credit balance, is a personal account, and is increased by profits and further capital, and reduced by drawings and losses. Under the accounting equation, Capital = Assets - Liabilities. A debit balance in capital is abnormal.

The discount column in a three-column cash book has the discount allowed on the debit side and the discount received on the credit side. Cash discount is given for prompt payment. It is a nominal account item. Discount columns are totalled and posted at the period end, not individually.

Representative personal accounts represent a group of persons, such as outstanding rent, prepaid insurance, outstanding salaries and capital. Under the traditional approach, rules for personal accounts apply to them. They are adjustments made at the period end under the accrual concept.

The sales day book (sales journal) records only credit sales of goods in which the business deals. Cash sales go to the cash book and credit sales of assets go to the journal proper. Entries are posted to the customers' ledger accounts and the total to the sales account.
related: Capital account has a credit balance.
Cash sales are recorded in the cash book, not the sales day book.
Three-column cash book: cash, bank and discount.
Outstanding expenses are representative personal accounts.
Operating profit = Net profit + non-operating expenses - non-operating incomes.
Drawings account has a debit balance.
summary: The answer is (c). Under the traditional approach, outstanding rent is a personal account (it is a liability, which is not a personal account in the sense of a person). It is a nominal account because rent is an expense. Statement (c) is therefore the incorrect one.
topic_notes: Accounting classification and books of original entry. Traditional approach: Personal (natural, artificial, representative), Real (tangible and intangible), Nominal. Modern approach: Assets, Liabilities, Capital, Revenue, Expenses. Rules of debit and credit: Assets and expenses are debited when they increase, while liabilities, capital and incomes are credited when they increase. Subsidiary books: Purchase book (credit purchases of goods), Sales book (credit sales of goods), Purchase returns book, Sales returns book, Bills receivable and payable books, Cash book, and Journal proper. Cash book types: single-column, double-column (cash and discount or cash and bank), three-column (cash, bank, discount) and petty cash book (imprest system). Contra entries appear on both sides of the cash book. Normal balances: Capital, liabilities and income - credit; assets, drawings and expenses - debit. Trial balance checks arithmetical accuracy only. Errors of omission, commission, principle and compensating errors do not disturb the trial balance in some cases. Related: operating profit = net profit + non-operating expenses - non-operating incomes (Q103 answer is (c)).

question: Which one of the following costs is generally not included in computing the cost of inventory ?
options: Storage cost assuming a special storage is required as part of production process
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: Inventory valuation is governed by AS-2 (Valuation of Inventories) and Ind AS 2. Cost of inventories comprises: (i) costs of purchase (purchase price, import duties and non-recoverable taxes, freight inward, handling, less trade discounts, rebates and recoverable taxes like credit-eligible GST); (ii) costs of conversion (direct labour, and systematic allocation of fixed and variable production overheads); and (iii) other costs incurred in bringing inventories to their present location and condition. Excluded from cost are: abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour or other production costs; storage costs, unless necessary in the production process before a further production stage; administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing inventories to their present location and condition; and selling costs. Normal wastage is an inherent part of the production process, so it is absorbed into cost. Abnormal wastage is charged to the Profit and Loss account. Inventory is measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Elimination: (b) and (c) are included, (d) is an explicit exception allowing inclusion, leaving (a) as the cost generally excluded.
explanations: Correct: general administration overheads are not related to bringing inventory to its present location and condition, so they are expensed in the period and excluded from inventory cost.
Incorrect: all costs of purchase (price, duties, freight inward, non-recoverable taxes, less discounts) are part of inventory cost.
Incorrect: normal wastage is an unavoidable part of production and is included in cost; only abnormal wastage is excluded.
Incorrect: storage cost is normally excluded, but where storage is necessary in the production process before a further production stage, it is included in cost.
keyfact: Inventory cost = purchase + conversion + other costs to bring to present location and condition; admin overheads, selling costs, abnormal wastage and ordinary storage are excluded.
option_notes: Administration overheads are general office and management costs such as head office salaries, audit fees and general office rent. They are not linked to production or to bringing goods to their present condition. Under AS-2 / Ind AS 2 they are period costs charged to profit and loss. Only the portion clearly attributable to production, such as factory administration, may be allocated to conversion cost.

Costs of purchase include the purchase price, import duties, non-recoverable taxes, freight inward, handling and other directly attributable costs, less trade discounts, rebates and similar items. Duties and taxes later recoverable from tax authorities, such as GST input credit, are not included. These form the base of inventory cost under AS-2 and Ind AS 2.

Normal wastage is the loss expected under normal operating conditions, such as evaporation or cutting loss. Its cost is absorbed into the cost of good units produced. Abnormal wastage arises from inefficiency, accidents or unusual events, and is charged separately to the profit and loss account as a loss, not included in inventory cost.

Storage cost is generally excluded from inventory cost, being a period expense. The exception is storage necessary in the production process before a further production stage, for example maturing of wine, whisky or cheese, or seasoning of timber. In such cases it is capitalised into inventory cost under AS-2 and Ind AS 2.
related: AS-2 is the Indian accounting standard on valuation of inventories; Ind AS 2 is the converged version.
Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
LIFO is not permitted under AS-2 or Ind AS 2.
Abnormal wastage is expensed, not included in inventory cost.
Selling and distribution costs are excluded from inventory cost.
Fixed production overheads are allocated on the basis of normal capacity.
Ind AS 2 permits reversal of inventory write-down when NRV increases.
summary: The answer is (a) Administration overheads. Under AS-2 / Ind AS 2, inventory cost includes purchase cost, conversion cost and other costs incurred to bring inventory to its present location and condition. General administration overheads that do not contribute to bringing inventory to its present location and condition are excluded and treated as period expenses.
topic_notes: AS-2 (Valuation of Inventories), issued by ICAI, and its converged counterpart Ind AS 2 govern inventory accounting. Inventories are assets held for sale in the ordinary course of business, in the process of production for such sale, or as materials or supplies consumed in production or services. Measurement is at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV). NRV is the estimated selling price less estimated costs of completion and costs necessary to make the sale. Cost formulas: FIFO and weighted average are permitted; LIFO is not permitted under AS-2 or Ind AS 2. Specific identification is used for items that are not ordinarily interchangeable. Techniques for measuring cost include the standard cost method and the retail method, if results approximate actual cost. Fixed production overheads are allocated on the basis of normal capacity of the production facilities; unallocated overheads are expensed in the period. Variable overheads are allocated on the basis of actual use. Costs excluded: abnormal wastage, storage costs (except as above), administrative overheads unrelated to production, selling and distribution costs, and in Ind AS also foreign exchange differences are not included generally. Inventory is excluded from scope for work in progress under construction contracts (AS-7 / Ind AS 115), financial instruments, and biological assets. Other related angles: periodic vs perpetual inventory systems, effect of inventory errors on profit, the conservatism principle underlying lower of cost or NRV, and reversal of write-downs under Ind AS 2 when NRV recovers.

question: Which one of the following will be the adjustment journal entry if the rent received in advance is € 2, 000 ?
options: Debit profit and loss account and Credit rent account
Debit rent received account and Credit rent received in advance account
Debit rent received in advance account and Credit rent received account
Debit rent account and Credit profit and loss account
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Under the accrual (mercantile) system and the matching concept, only income that has been earned during the accounting year is credited to the Profit and Loss account. Rent received in advance is cash collected for a future period, so it is not income of the current year. At the year end an adjusting entry removes it from current income: debit Rent Received (the income account, so the debit reduces it) and credit Rent Received in Advance (a liability, also called unearned or deferred income). The rent received account is then transferred to P&L at the reduced figure. In the Balance Sheet, rent received in advance appears under current liabilities. In the next year the entry is reversed: Rent Received in Advance A/c Dr., To Rent Received A/c, so the income is recognised when earned. Elimination: (a) and (d) post directly to P&L and ignore the liability. (c) is the reverse entry, which would increase current income and wrongly cut the liability. Only (b) reduces current income and creates the liability. Remember the rule: debit what comes in (an expense or loss), credit what goes out (an income or gain). Here the income is being reduced, so it is debited.
explanations: Incorrect: it debits P&L and credits the rent account, which wrongly treats the item as income earned or rent receivable. It does not create the liability.
Correct: debiting Rent Received reduces current-year income by 2,000, and crediting Rent Received in Advance records the liability for the unearned amount.
Incorrect: this is the reversing entry passed at the start of the next year, not the year-end adjustment. Passing it now would increase income and remove a liability that does not yet exist.
Incorrect: debiting a rent account suggests an expense, and crediting P&L is not the way to adjust income received in advance. It does not recognise the liability.
keyfact: Rent received in advance: Rent Received A/c Dr. To Rent Received in Advance A/c, a current liability that is deducted from income.
option_notes: Debit P&L and credit Rent A/c is not a standard adjusting entry for advance rent. The closing entry for rent income is actually Rent Received A/c Dr. To P&L A/c, which is the opposite direction. Closing entries transfer nominal account balances to P&L at the year end, after adjustments have been made.

Rent Received A/c Dr. To Rent Received in Advance A/c is the correct year-end adjustment. Rent received in advance is unearned income. It is a current liability in the Balance Sheet, and it is deducted from rent received in the Profit and Loss account (or shown as a deduction on the income side).

Rent Received in Advance A/c Dr. To Rent Received A/c is the reversing entry made on the first day of the next accounting period. It transfers the earned portion into income. It follows the accrual principle that income is recognised when earned, not when cash is received.

Rent A/c Dr. To P&L A/c is not a valid adjustment. Rent paid is an expense, and its closing entry is P&L A/c Dr. To Rent A/c. Rent received is income, and its closing entry is Rent Received A/c Dr. To P&L A/c. This option mixes up the two and does not touch the liability.
related: Income received in advance is a current liability, also called unearned or deferred income.
Prepaid expenses and accrued income are current assets.
Outstanding expenses are current liabilities and are added to the relevant expense in P&L.
Accrued income entry: Accrued Income A/c Dr. To Income A/c.
The accrual (mercantile) system records income when earned and expenses when incurred.
The matching concept matches revenues of a period with the expenses of that same period.
Closing entry for rent received: Rent Received A/c Dr. To P&L A/c.
summary: The answer is (b). Rent received in advance is income that belongs to the next accounting period, so the rent received account is debited to reduce current-year income, and rent received in advance is credited as a liability. The entry is: Rent Received A/c Dr. 2,000 To Rent Received in Advance A/c 2,000.
topic_notes: Adjustment entries apply the accrual or mercantile system so that profit reflects the income and expenses of the period, not just cash flows. There are four main adjustments for accruals and prepayments. (1) Outstanding expense: Expense A/c Dr. To Outstanding Expense A/c. It is a liability, and it is added to the expense in P&L. (2) Prepaid expense: Prepaid Expense A/c Dr. To Expense A/c. It is an asset, and it is deducted from the expense. (3) Accrued income (income receivable): Accrued Income A/c Dr. To Income A/c. It is an asset, and it is added to the income. (4) Unearned or advance income: Income A/c Dr. To Income Received in Advance A/c. It is a liability, and it is deducted from the income. Other common adjustments are depreciation, bad debts, provision for doubtful debts, interest on capital, interest on drawings and closing stock. A trial balance is only a check on arithmetical accuracy of the ledger. The matching concept, the accrual concept and the revenue recognition principle all underlie these entries. Real accounts follow the rule 'debit what comes in, credit what goes out'. Personal accounts follow 'debit the receiver, credit the giver'. Nominal accounts follow 'debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains'. Be ready for questions on where each item appears in the final accounts (asset or liability side) and on the reversing entries passed in the next year.

ocr: In case of contract of insurance, the principle which states that it is the duty of the insured to take reasonable steps to minimize the loss or damage to the insured property is called : (a) Principle of Subrogation (b) Principle of Utmost Good Faith (c) Principle of Co-operation (d) Principle of Mitigation 111. 107. Which one of the following is mot a Contract of Indemnity ? (a) Contract of Fire Insurance (b) Contract of Life Insurance (c) Contract of Marine Insurance (d) Contract of Motor Insurance 112.
subject: Insurance
detail: The principle of mitigation (also called minimisation of loss) is a corollary of the principle of indemnity. When an insured event such as fire, collision or flooding occurs, the insured must act as if he were uninsured: call the fire brigade, save and protect salvage, move goods to safety, and avoid further damage. The insurer will not pay for loss that could reasonably have been avoided, although it does bear the reasonable expenses of mitigation (for example, sue and labour charges in marine insurance). The aim is to prevent moral hazard, where insurance makes the insured careless once cover is in place. Elimination: Subrogation is the insurer's right, after paying a claim, to step into the insured's shoes and recover from a third party who caused the loss. Utmost Good Faith (uberrimae fidei) requires full and honest disclosure of material facts at the time of proposal. Co-operation is not one of the standard classical principles of insurance. Only mitigation matches the duty to minimise loss after the event.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Subrogation is the insurer's right to recover from a third party after paying the claim, so it does not describe a duty of the insured to minimise loss.
(b) Wrong: Utmost Good Faith concerns honest, full disclosure of material facts before and at the time of the contract, not loss-minimising conduct after a loss.
(c) Wrong: 'Co-operation' is not a recognised classical principle of insurance, although insureds do have claim-related duties such as giving notice and assisting the insurer.
(d) Correct: The Principle of Mitigation obliges the insured to take reasonable steps to reduce loss or damage to the insured property once an insured event occurs.
keyfact: Mitigation = insured must act like a prudent uninsured owner to minimise loss; life insurance is not a contract of indemnity.
option_notes: Subrogation: after indemnifying the insured, the insurer acquires the insured's rights against third parties responsible for the loss. It applies only to contracts of indemnity (fire, marine, motor) and not to life insurance. The insurer can recover no more than it paid, and the insured must not impair these rights. It prevents the insured from profiting twice, once from the insurer and once from the wrongdoer.

Utmost Good Faith (uberrimae fidei): both parties must disclose all material facts honestly. It originates from Carter v Boehm (1766), Lord Mansfield. The insured must disclose material facts in the proposal form, and non-disclosure or misrepresentation makes the contract voidable. In India, Section 45 of the Insurance Act 1938 limits challenges to life policies after two years. It applies to all insurance contracts.

Co-operation is not a classical principle of insurance. The classical principles are utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity, contribution, subrogation, proximate cause and mitigation of loss. Co-operation in practice refers to the insured's duty to assist the insurer in investigating claims, give prompt notice and supply documents, which is a policy condition rather than a core principle.

Mitigation of loss: the insured must behave like a prudent uninsured person and minimise loss at the time of an insured event. The insurer is not liable for loss caused by the insured's failure to take reasonable steps, but it does pay the reasonable costs of mitigation. It operates within indemnity contracts and aims to curb moral hazard and carelessness.
related: Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity; it is a contingent contract.
Fire, marine and motor insurance are contracts of indemnity.
Subrogation applies only to indemnity contracts.
Carter v Boehm (1766) established utmost good faith.
Contribution applies when there is double insurance.
The doctrine of average applies in cases of underinsurance.
The Marine Insurance Act is of 1963.
Section 45 of the Insurance Act 1938 sets the two-year incontestability period for life policies.
summary: The correct answer is (d) Principle of Mitigation. Under a contract of insurance the insured must take all reasonable steps, as a prudent uninsured owner would, to minimise loss or damage when an insured peril occurs. Failure to do so can reduce or defeat the claim for the avoidable part of the loss.
topic_notes: Principles of insurance are core EPFO Insurance material. 1) Utmost good faith: Carter v Boehm 1766; applies to all insurance. 2) Insurable interest: financial stake in the subject matter. In life insurance it must exist at inception; in fire insurance it must exist at inception and at the time of loss; in marine insurance it must exist at the time of loss. 3) Indemnity: restores the insured to the pre-loss position and applies to property, marine, fire and motor, but not to life or personal accident, which are contingent or benefit contracts. 4) Contribution: when there is double insurance, insurers share the loss rateably. 5) Subrogation: the insurer takes over the insured's rights after payment. 6) Proximate cause: the dominant, effective cause of the loss decides liability, as in Pawsey v Scottish Union. 7) Mitigation: the duty to minimise loss. 8) Doctrine of average (underinsurance): the claim is reduced in proportion to the shortfall in cover. Related terms: moral hazard (dishonesty or carelessness induced by cover), morale hazard, salvage, abandonment (marine), sue and labour clause, and warranties. Regulators and laws: the Insurance Act 1938, IRDA Act 1999, Marine Insurance Act 1963, and the IRDAI as regulator. Life insurance is a contract of contingency, not indemnity, so principles such as contribution and subrogation do not apply to it. Be able to match each principle with its application and its case law.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q106.
ocr: In case of contract of insurance, the principle which states that it is the duty of the insured to take reasonable steps to minimize the loss or damage to the insured property is called : (a) Principle of Subrogation (b) Principle of Utmost Good Faith (c) Principle of Co-operation (d) Principle of Mitigation 111. 107. Which one of the following is mot a Contract of Indemnity ? (a) Contract of Fire Insurance (b) Contract of Life Insurance (c) Contract of Marine Insurance (d) Contract of Motor Insurance 112.
subject: Insurance
detail: The Principle of Mitigation (also called the duty to minimise loss) is a corollary of the principle of indemnity in general insurance, especially fire, marine and motor insurance. When an insured event such as a fire occurs, the insured must act as a prudent uninsured person would: call the fire brigade, protect salvage, and prevent further damage. Failure to do so can lead the insurer to reduce or reject the claim for the avoidable part of the loss. Reasonable expenses incurred in mitigation are generally recoverable from the insurer, often under the 'sue and labour' clause in marine insurance. This principle prevents moral hazard and carelessness. Elimination: Subrogation concerns the insurer stepping into the insured's shoes to recover from third parties after paying the claim. Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) requires full and true disclosure of material facts. 'Principle of Co-operation' is not one of the standard classical insurance principles. Hence only Mitigation matches the described duty.
explanations: Wrong: Subrogation gives the insurer the insured's rights against third parties after the claim is paid. It prevents the insured from profiting twice and is not about minimising loss.
Wrong: Utmost good faith concerns honest disclosure of material facts before and at the time of contract. It is not about conduct after a loss.
Wrong: Co-operation is not a recognised classical principle of insurance in this sense. It is a distractor, though insureds are expected to assist insurers in claims.
Correct: Mitigation is the duty of the insured to take reasonable steps to reduce loss or damage to the insured property when an insured event occurs.
keyfact: Mitigation = duty of the insured to minimise loss like a prudent uninsured; Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity (Q107 answer: b).
option_notes: Subrogation: after paying an indemnity claim, the insurer acquires the insured's rights and remedies against third parties who caused the loss. It applies only to contracts of indemnity, not life insurance. The insurer can recover only up to the amount it paid. It prevents unjust enrichment and holds wrongdoers liable. It is closely linked with contribution and the doctrine of indemnity.

Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei): both parties must disclose all material facts honestly, because the insurer relies on the proposer's information to assess risk. Concealment or misrepresentation makes the contract voidable at the insurer's option. In India, Section 45 of the Insurance Act 1938 limits challenging life policies after a set period (now three years). It applies at the pre-contract stage and throughout the contract.

Principle of Co-operation: not a standard classical principle of insurance. The classical principles are insurable interest, utmost good faith, indemnity, contribution, subrogation, proximate cause, and mitigation of loss. Policy conditions do require the insured to co-operate with insurers during claim investigation and surveys, but this is a policy condition rather than a named principle.

Mitigation of loss: the insured must act as a prudent uninsured would to minimise loss when an insured peril occurs, for example by calling the fire brigade or saving goods. The insurer is not liable for loss that reasonable care would have avoided. Mitigation costs are usually recoverable, and in marine insurance the 'sue and labour' clause covers them. It supports indemnity and curbs moral hazard.
related: Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity; it is a contract of assurance for a fixed sum.
Fire, marine, motor and burglary insurance are contracts of indemnity.
Subrogation allows the insurer to recover from third parties after paying a claim.
Contribution applies when the same risk is covered by more than one insurer.
Uberrimae fidei means utmost good faith.
The sue and labour clause in marine insurance covers mitigation expenses.
Moral hazard refers to dishonesty; morale hazard refers to carelessness.
Proximate cause means the dominant and effective cause of loss.
summary: The answer is (d) Principle of Mitigation. This principle obliges the insured to take all reasonable steps to minimise loss or damage to the insured property when an insured peril occurs, as a prudent uninsured owner would. The insured cannot become careless just because the property is covered.
topic_notes: Principles of insurance are a core Insurance-paper topic. The main principles are: (1) Insurable interest: a legal financial stake in the subject matter. In life insurance it must exist at inception; in fire insurance it must exist at the time of loss; in marine insurance it must exist at the time of loss. (2) Utmost good faith: full disclosure of material facts. (3) Indemnity: the insured is restored to the pre-loss position and cannot profit. It applies to fire, marine, motor and other general insurance, but not to life or personal accident insurance, which are contracts of assurance with fixed sums. (4) Contribution: where there are multiple policies on the same risk, insurers share the loss rateably. (5) Subrogation: the insurer takes over the insured's rights against third parties after paying. (6) Proximate cause: the dominant, effective cause of the loss determines liability. (7) Mitigation: the duty to minimise loss. (8) Causa proxima and warranties are also associated concepts. Related ideas include moral hazard (dishonesty) and morale hazard (carelessness), underinsurance and the average clause, salvage, abandonment, and sue and labour clauses. Key legislation: Insurance Act 1938, Life Insurance Corporation Act 1956, General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act 1972, and the IRDA Act 1999. The regulator is IRDAI. Typical exam angles include which insurance contracts are indemnity contracts, which principles apply to life insurance, and matching principles to definitions.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q107.
ocr: In case of contract of insurance, the principle which states that it is the duty of the insured to take reasonable steps to minimize the loss or damage to the insured property is called : (a) Principle of Subrogation (b) Principle of Utmost Good Faith (c) Principle of Co-operation (d) Principle of Mitigation 111. 107. Which one of the following is mot a Contract of Indemnity ? (a) Contract of Fire Insurance (b) Contract of Life Insurance (c) Contract of Marine Insurance (d) Contract of Motor Insurance 112.
subject: Insurance
detail: A contract of indemnity means the insurer promises to compensate the insured for the actual loss suffered, no more and no less, so the insured cannot profit from the loss. It applies to property, liability and pecuniary losses, which can be measured in money. Fire, marine and motor (own damage) insurance are therefore indemnity contracts. They carry the related principles of insurable interest at the time of loss, subrogation, contribution, average clause and mitigation of loss. Life insurance is different. The value of a human life cannot be measured in money, so the insurer pays the agreed sum assured on death or maturity, regardless of the actual financial loss. For this reason it is called a contract of assurance, or a contingent contract. Subrogation and contribution do not apply to it. Insurable interest is required only at inception. Personal accident and some health policies with fixed benefits are treated similarly. Elimination: (a), (c) and (d) all cover measurable property loss, so they are indemnity contracts. (b) is the exception, and the question asks which one is NOT an indemnity contract. The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 (Section 3) defines marine insurance expressly as a contract of indemnity.
explanations: Incorrect: fire insurance is a classic indemnity contract. The insurer pays the actual loss, subject to the sum insured, the average clause and so on.
Correct: life insurance is a contract of assurance, not indemnity. A fixed sum is payable on the contingency, and the loss of life cannot be measured in money.
Incorrect: marine insurance is a contract of indemnity under Section 3 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. Subrogation and contribution apply.
Incorrect: motor insurance covering own damage and third-party liability is based on indemnity. The insurer pays the actual loss, with depreciation and the IDV considered.
keyfact: Life insurance is a contract of assurance, not indemnity; fire, marine and motor insurance are indemnity contracts.
option_notes: Fire insurance covers loss or damage to property by fire and allied perils. It is an indemnity contract, and the insured must have insurable interest at the time of loss. Features include the average (underinsurance) clause, reinstatement, and subrogation. The Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy is the common product in India. The claim is limited to the actual loss or the sum insured, whichever is less.

Life insurance pays a fixed sum assured on death or maturity. It is a contract of assurance, not indemnity. Insurable interest is needed only at inception. The Life Insurance Corporation of India was formed in 1956 by nationalisation. The contract is based on utmost good faith, and the policy can be assigned. Subrogation and contribution do not apply, and the insurer cannot recover from third parties.

Marine insurance covers ships, cargo and freight against perils of the sea. Section 3 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 defines it as a contract of indemnity. Policies include voyage, time, mixed and floating policies. Insurable interest is needed at the time of loss. Valued policies, general and particular average, and abandonment are key concepts.

Motor insurance covers vehicles against damage and third-party liability. Third-party cover is compulsory under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The own-damage section is an indemnity contract based on the Insured Declared Value (IDV). The No Claim Bonus rewards claim-free years. Subrogation and contribution apply, and the insured must mitigate loss.
related: Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines the contract of indemnity.
Life insurance is a contract of assurance, not indemnity.
Subrogation is the insurer's right to step into the insured's position after paying the claim.
Contribution applies when the same risk is covered by more than one insurer.
The principle of mitigation requires the insured to act as a prudent uninsured person would.
Uberrimae fidei means utmost good faith.
The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 defines marine insurance as a contract of indemnity.
LIC was formed in 1956, and general insurance was nationalised in 1972.
summary: The answer is (b) Contract of Life Insurance. Life insurance is a contract of assurance, not indemnity, because a human life cannot be valued in money, so a fixed sum is paid on the event. Fire, marine and motor insurance are contracts of indemnity, where the insurer compensates only the actual loss.
topic_notes: Insurance contracts are based on certain fundamental principles. Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) requires full disclosure of material facts. Insurable interest means the insured has a financial stake in the subject matter. Indemnity means the insured is restored to the pre-loss position and no more. Subrogation lets the insurer step into the insured's shoes after paying a claim, to recover from third parties. Contribution applies when several insurers cover the same risk, and each shares the loss proportionately. Proximate cause means the loss must be caused by an insured peril. Mitigation (the duty to minimise loss) requires the insured to act as if uninsured. Loss minimisation is also called the principle of mitigation of loss. Contracts of indemnity cover fire, marine, motor, burglary, liability and fidelity insurance. Contracts of assurance or contingency cover life insurance, which pays a fixed sum, and often personal accident policies with fixed benefits. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 124 defines the contract of indemnity and Section 125 gives the rights of the indemnity-holder. Key legislation includes the Insurance Act, 1938, the LIC Act, 1956, the General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, the IRDA Act, 1999 and the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. Life insurance was nationalised in 1956 and general insurance in 1972. Related ideas include the average clause, reinstatement, double insurance, reinsurance, and the doctrine of waiver and estoppel. Exam angles: which principle applies to which insurance, which contracts are not indemnity, and the difference between subrogation and contribution.

question: Which one of the following statements about audit documentation is mot correct ? Audit documentation includes audit
options: programmes. Audit file and audit documentation are the
of significant matters. 113. Audit documentation may be recorded on
paper or electronic or any other media
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Under SA 230 (Audit Documentation), audit documentation is the record of audit procedures performed, relevant audit evidence obtained, and conclusions the auditor reached. It serves to provide sufficient and appropriate evidence of the basis for the auditor's report, and evidence that the audit was planned and performed in accordance with SAs and legal requirements. It may be on paper, electronic or other media. It includes audit programmes, analyses, issues memoranda, summaries of significant matters, check lists, confirmation letters, representation letters, and abstracts or copies of entity records. The audit file is defined as one or more folders or other storage media, in physical or electronic form, containing the records that comprise the audit documentation for a specific engagement. So the file is the container and the documentation is its content. The auditor must assemble the final file on a timely basis, ordinarily not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report. Retention is governed by SQC 1 (now SQM 1), ordinarily not less than seven years from the report date. Elimination: options (a), (c) and (d) restate SA 230 accurately. Option (b) wrongly equates the two terms.
explanations: (a) Correct statement: audit programmes are part of audit documentation, so it is not the answer.
(b) Incorrect statement: audit file and audit documentation are not the same. The file is the container and the documentation is its content, so this is the answer.
(c) Correct statement: summaries of significant matters are part of audit documentation, so it is not the answer.
(d) Correct statement: audit documentation may be on paper, electronic or other media, so it is not the answer.
keyfact: Audit file is the container; audit documentation is its content (SA 230), so the two are not the same.
option_notes: Audit programmes are a set of planned audit procedures, covering nature, timing and extent, for each area of the audit. They are prepared at the planning stage under SA 300 and form part of audit documentation. They act as instructions to the audit team and as a record of work done. They are updated as the audit progresses, and the person who signs off each step is recorded.

The audit file is one or more folders or other storage media, physical or electronic, that contain the records making up the audit documentation for a specific engagement. It is the container and not the same as the documentation. Assembly of the final file should be completed ordinarily within 60 days after the auditor's report date. After assembly, the auditor must not delete or discard documentation before the end of its retention period.

Summaries of significant matters, sometimes called completion memoranda, record significant matters arising during the audit, the conclusions reached on them, and significant professional judgments made. SA 230 treats them as part of audit documentation. They help the experienced auditor and the reviewer understand the key issues, and may be prepared in place of cross-referencing detailed working papers.

Audit documentation may be recorded on paper, electronic or other media, as SA 230 permits. Examples are working papers, scanned documents and audit software files. The integrity, accessibility and retrievability of the documentation must be preserved. If original documents are scanned, the auditor retains the scanned copies as per firm policy. Retention is ordinarily at least seven years from the report date.
related: SA 230 deals with audit documentation.
Final audit file assembly is ordinarily within 60 days of the auditor's report date.
Retention period is ordinarily not less than seven years from the report date.
The permanent audit file holds information of continuing relevance across years.
Audit working papers belong to the auditor.
SA 300 covers planning an audit, and the audit programme is prepared at the planning stage.
The ISA equivalent of SA 230 is ISA 230.
summary: The answer is (b). Audit documentation is the record of audit procedures performed, evidence obtained and conclusions reached, whereas the audit file is the physical or electronic folder holding that documentation. They are therefore related but not the same thing.
topic_notes: SA 230 (Audit Documentation) is the Standard on Auditing issued by ICAI and corresponds to ISA 230. Purposes of audit documentation: evidence of the basis for the auditor's conclusion, evidence that the audit was planned and performed per SAs, assistance to the engagement team in planning, performing and supervising, enabling review, accountability for work, retention of matters of continuing significance, and support for quality control and inspections. Form, content and extent depend on the nature of the engagement, the size and complexity of the entity, the audit methodology and the risks. The documentation must be sufficient for an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the audit to understand the nature, timing and extent of procedures performed, the results and evidence obtained, and significant matters and judgments. It should record the identifying characteristics of items tested, who performed and who reviewed the work and when. Departures from relevant requirements must be documented with reasons. The auditor should document discussions of significant matters with management and those charged with governance. If new information is added after the report date, the auditor documents who made and reviewed the changes, when, and the reasons. Ownership: audit working papers belong to the auditor, and confidentiality applies, though access may be given to others at the auditor's discretion. Related standards are SA 220 (quality control for an audit), SQM 1 (earlier SQC 1), SA 300 (planning), SA 315 (risk assessment) and SA 580 (written representations). The permanent audit file contains information of continuing relevance, such as the constitutional documents, and the current file covers the year's audit.

question: In the context of auditing, the primary objective of vouching is : To detect errors in financial statements
options: To verify the authenticity of transactions
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Vouching is the core of the audit of books of account. The auditor checks recorded transactions against supporting documents (vouchers, invoices, bank statements, contracts, board minutes) to establish that the transaction actually took place, was properly authorised, relates to the entity, is recorded in the correct amount, in the correct period and in the correct account. It is mainly a substantiation of the 'occurrence/existence', 'accuracy' and 'authorisation' assertions. It is not the same as verification, which covers the existence, ownership and valuation of assets and liabilities. Vouching mainly serves the audit of the Profit and Loss (revenue) side and the cash book, while verification serves the Balance Sheet. Detecting errors and fraud is a secondary result of vouching. Evaluating internal controls is done through tests of controls and internal control questionnaires, and assessing management performance falls under a management or performance audit. Note that the OCR garbled the stem. 'To detect errors in financial statements' appears to be the first option, which makes the options (a) to (d) shift by one. Treating the four options as errors, internal controls, authenticity and management performance, the authenticity option is the correct one. Because of this shift, the letter should be read against the option text, which is 'authenticity of transactions'.
explanations: (a) Evaluating internal controls is the purpose of control testing and the study of the internal control system. Vouching only uses documents to test transactions, so this is wrong.
(b) Correct as per the intended text: vouching verifies the authenticity of transactions, meaning that entries are supported by valid documentary evidence.
(c) Assessing management performance belongs to management or efficiency audit and is not the aim of vouching.
(d) The 'option' here is the stray number 114, an OCR artefact with no meaning, so it cannot be correct.
keyfact: Vouching = checking the documentary evidence behind entries to establish that transactions are genuine and authorised.
option_notes: Detecting errors in financial statements: the general aim of an audit, which is to express an opinion on whether the statements give a true and fair view. Detecting errors and fraud is a by-product of vouching, not its primary objective, and the audit also covers materiality and risk assessment under the Standards on Auditing (SA).

Evaluating internal controls: the auditor reviews the design and operation of controls using questionnaires, flowcharts and checklists. SA 315 and SA 330 govern risk assessment and responses. The strength of controls determines how much vouching and substantive testing the auditor does.

Verifying the authenticity of transactions: this is vouching, the inspection of documentary evidence supporting entries in the books of account. It checks occurrence, authorisation, amount, period and classification. It is done mainly for cash and revenue transactions, and often on a test basis.

Assessing management performance: this belongs to management audit or performance audit, which looks at economy, efficiency and effectiveness (the 3 Es), as done by the CAG for public bodies. It is separate from financial audit and from vouching.
related: Vouching is the backbone of the audit of the books of account.
Verification relates to assets and liabilities, whereas vouching relates to transactions.
SA 500 deals with audit evidence.
Section 143 of the Companies Act 2013 sets out the powers and duties of auditors.
The CAG's audit powers come under Articles 148-151.
Internal audit is covered by Section 138 of the Companies Act 2013.
Test checking is acceptable where internal controls are strong.
summary: The answer is (b): the primary objective of vouching is to verify the authenticity of transactions. Vouching means examining documentary evidence such as invoices, receipts and vouchers to confirm that each entry in the books is genuine, authorised and correctly recorded.
topic_notes: Vouching is the examination of documentary evidence (vouchers) supporting entries in the books of account. Its objectives are to confirm that the transaction is genuine, recorded in the books of the right entity, authorised by a competent person, correctly calculated and classified, and recorded in the right period. Typical vouchers are cash memos, invoices, receipts, debit and credit notes, bank statements, and minutes of meetings. Vouching is mostly for the cash book, purchases, sales, and expenses. Verification is different: it confirms the existence, ownership, valuation and encumbrance of assets and liabilities in the Balance Sheet. Related ideas are audit evidence (SA 500), audit sampling (SA 530), audit documentation (SA 230), and the audit assertions, which include occurrence, completeness, accuracy, cut-off and classification. Types of audit include statutory audit under the Companies Act 2013 (Section 143), internal audit (Section 138), cost audit, tax audit under Section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, and CAG audit under Articles 148-151 of the Constitution. Audit techniques include inspection, observation, inquiry, confirmation, recalculation, reperformance and analytical procedures. Vouching is also linked to routine checking, test checking, and the auditor's concern with the 'true and fair view'. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) issues the SAs, and the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) oversees audit quality.

ocr: Which one of the following is not the objective of verification in auditing ? (a) Checking the historical accuracy of accounts (b) Verification of the existence of the assets (c) Verification of the valuation of the assets (d) Verification of the authority of the acquisition of the assets Shri Jatin Goswami, a Padma Bhushan awardee in the year 2025, is an exponent of which one of the following dance forms ? (a) Bharatanatyam (b) — Sattriya (c) Kathakali (d) Kathak
subject: Accounting & Auditing
detail: Verification means confirming the truth, accuracy and proper presentation of assets and liabilities as shown in the Balance Sheet. It is a balance-sheet-oriented process. Vouching, by contrast, checks the transactions recorded in the books (the Profit and Loss and cash flows) against documentary evidence, and so tests the historical accuracy of entries. The main objectives of verification are: (1) existence of the asset on the balance sheet date; (2) ownership or title, so that the asset really belongs to the business; (3) correct valuation, following accounting standards such as AS-10 (PPE) and AS-2 (Inventories); (4) proper authority for acquisition, e.g. board resolutions and approvals; (5) absence of undisclosed charges or encumbrances; (6) proper disclosure and classification under Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013. Option (a) speaks of the historical accuracy of accounts. That is the realm of vouching and the general audit of books, so it is the 'not' answer. Options (b), (c) and (d) are all classic verification objectives. Remember: vouching deals with the Profit and Loss Account and transactions, verification with the Balance Sheet, and valuation is a part of verification.
explanations: Correct answer. Historical accuracy of accounts is checked by vouching and the audit of books. It is not a verification objective, so it is the exception asked for.
Incorrect as an answer. Existence of assets on the balance sheet date is a primary objective of verification, so it is not the exception.
Incorrect as an answer. Valuation of assets is a core part of verification, so it is not the exception.
Incorrect as an answer. Verifying the authority behind an asset's acquisition, such as board approval and sanction, is a recognised verification objective, so it is not the exception.
keyfact: Verification proves existence, ownership, valuation and authority of balance-sheet assets; historical accuracy of entries is the job of vouching.
option_notes: Historical accuracy of accounts: the aim of vouching and of examining the books of account. It involves checking the arithmetical accuracy of entries, their posting and their supporting vouchers. It is concerned with past transactions rather than with the closing balances of assets and liabilities. It is distinct from verification, which is balance-sheet focused. Audit of the books establishes that the Profit and Loss Account and the Balance Sheet are drawn from correct records.

Existence of assets: the auditor must confirm that the assets shown actually exist at the balance sheet date. Methods include physical inspection, confirmation from third parties, and examination of title documents. It guards against fictitious assets and overstatement. For inventory, the auditor attends the physical count (SA 501). It is one of the first objectives of verification, along with ownership and valuation.

Valuation of assets: verification checks that assets are valued on a proper, consistent basis. Fixed assets are shown at cost less depreciation (AS-10, AS-6). Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (AS-2). Investments follow AS-13. The auditor ensures there is no overvaluation or undervaluation, which would distort the true and fair view. The auditor may rely on expert valuers (SA 620).

Authority for acquisition: the auditor verifies that the acquisition of assets was properly authorised, for example by a board resolution, a general meeting where required, or the powers set out in the Memorandum and Articles. This confirms that the purchase was within the company's powers and was properly sanctioned. It is closely related to checking title or ownership and to vouching capital expenditure.
related: Vouching checks transactions against documents. Verification checks the assets and liabilities in the balance sheet.
Verification objectives include existence, ownership, valuation, authority and disclosure.
Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and NRV under AS-2.
SA 501 deals with the auditor's attendance at the physical inventory count.
SA 500 covers audit evidence and SA 505 external confirmations.
CARO 2020 requires reporting on the title deeds of immovable property.
Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes the format of the Balance Sheet.
Vouching is called the 'backbone of auditing'.
summary: The answer is (a). Verification in auditing is concerned with proving the existence, ownership/title, valuation, authority for acquisition and proper disclosure of assets and liabilities on the balance sheet date. Checking the historical accuracy of accounts is the objective of vouching and the audit of the books of account, not of verification.
topic_notes: Verification is the process of establishing the existence, ownership, valuation, and proper disclosure of assets and liabilities appearing in the Balance Sheet. Vouching is the examination of documentary evidence supporting entries in the books. Vouching is therefore transaction-based and mainly concerns the Profit and Loss Account and cash book, while verification is balance-sheet based. Key objectives of verification: existence, ownership/title, valuation, authority for acquisition, freedom from charges or encumbrances, proper classification and disclosure, and the absence of fictitious or overstated items. Important points: (1) Verification is a part of the auditor's duty to report a true and fair view. (2) The auditor can rely on a certificate from a competent person, such as a valuer or an expert, but remains responsible for the opinion. (3) Under Section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013, the auditor reports on the financial statements. (4) Related Standards on Auditing: SA 500 (Audit Evidence), SA 501 (Specific Considerations: inventory), SA 505 (External Confirmations), SA 620 (Using the Work of an Auditor's Expert), SA 230 (Documentation). (5) The Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 (CARO) requires reporting on the maintenance of fixed asset records, physical verification of PPE and inventory, and title deeds of immovable property. (6) Assets are verified in a typical order: fixed assets (land, buildings, plant), investments, inventory, receivables, and cash and bank. (7) Liabilities are verified for completeness, so that none is omitted. Other angles UPSC could ask: the difference between vouching and verification, the verification of particular items such as goodwill, patents and investments, and the techniques of audit evidence such as inspection, observation, inquiry, confirmation, recomputation and analytical procedures.

question: Two Indian Serviceman were posthumously conferred with the Dag Hammarskjéld medal in the year 2025 by which one of the following international organisations ?
options: Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE)
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: The Dag Hammarskjöld Medal was established by the UN General Assembly in 1997 and is named after the second UN Secretary-General, who died in a plane crash in 1961 while on a peace mission in Congo (Northern Rhodesia, now Zambia). It is awarded posthumously to peacekeepers (military, police, civilian) who die in the line of duty in UN peacekeeping operations. It is presented on 29 May each year, the International Day of UN Peacekeepers. India is among the largest historical troop-contributing countries, with about 180,000 personnel having served in more than 50 missions, and over 170 Indian peacekeepers have died, the highest number of any country. In 2025 the medal was conferred on Indian soldiers who died in UN missions, for example in UNIFIL (Lebanon) and UNDOF/MONUSCO, and was received by their families. Elimination: OSCE is a European security body, NORDEFCO is a Nordic military cooperation framework, and SIPRI is a Swedish research institute. None of them runs peacekeeping medals, and none is linked to Hammarskjöld's medal.
explanations: Correct: the medal is a UN honour for peacekeepers who died serving in UN operations, and Indian personnel were honoured on the International Day of UN Peacekeepers in 2025.
Wrong: the OSCE is a regional security organisation for Europe, Central Asia and North America. It is not linked to this medal, and India is not a member.
Wrong: NORDEFCO is a defence cooperation arrangement among Nordic states (Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden). It has no connection to Indian soldiers or UN medals.
Wrong: SIPRI is a Stockholm-based think tank on arms, conflict and disarmament, known for its yearbook and arms-transfer data. It does not award medals to soldiers.
keyfact: The Dag Hammarskjöld Medal is a UN award given posthumously to peacekeepers who died in service, and it is presented on 29 May.
option_notes: The UN was founded on 24 Oct 1945, has its headquarters in New York, and has 193 members. Its Department of Peace Operations manages peacekeeping, which began in 1948 with UNTSO. India is a founding member and a leading contributor of troops and police. The UN awards the Dag Hammarskjöld Medal and the UN Medal for service.

The OSCE was formed from the Helsinki Process (1975, CSCE) and renamed OSCE in 1995. It has 57 participating states, its secretariat is in Vienna, and it works on arms control, conflict prevention, human rights and election monitoring. It is the world's largest regional security organisation. India is not a member.

NORDEFCO was set up in 2009 and merged earlier Nordic defence arrangements. It brings together Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden for joint training, procurement and capability development. It is a cooperation framework rather than a military alliance, and it has no role in awarding peacekeeping medals.

SIPRI was founded in 1966 in Stockholm and is an independent institute for research on conflict, armaments, arms control and disarmament. It publishes the SIPRI Yearbook and databases on military expenditure and arms transfers, and it is often cited in questions on global arms imports, where India ranks among the top importers.
related: The Dag Hammarskjöld Medal was established by the UNGA in 1997 and is given posthumously.
The International Day of UN Peacekeepers is observed on 29 May.
Dag Hammarskjöld was UN Secretary-General from 1953 to 1961 and died in a 1961 air crash.
The UN Peacekeeping Forces won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988.
India's Centre for UN Peacekeeping (CUNPK) is in New Delhi and was set up in 2000.
India sent the first all-women formed police unit to UN mission UNMIL in Liberia in 2007.
UNTSO (1948) was the first UN peacekeeping mission.
India has lost more peacekeepers than any other country.
summary: The answer is (a) United Nations Organization. The Dag Hammarskjöld Medal is a UN honour awarded posthumously to military, police and civilian personnel who lost their lives serving under the UN flag in peacekeeping operations. Indian peacekeepers have received it regularly, including in 2025.
topic_notes: UN peacekeeping began in 1948 with UNTSO in the Middle East. The first armed mission was UNEF I in 1956. Peacekeeping is not mentioned in the UN Charter and is often called 'Chapter Six and a Half'. Its three basic principles are consent of the parties, impartiality, and non-use of force except in self-defence and defence of the mandate. Peacekeepers wear blue helmets or berets, and the 1988 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to UN Peacekeeping Forces. The International Day of UN Peacekeepers is 29 May. The Dag Hammarskjöld Medal was created by UNGA in 1997 and is given posthumously. Hammarskjöld served as Secretary-General from 1953 to 1961 and received the Nobel Peace Prize posthumously in 1961. India has taken part in missions in Korea (custodian force, 1950s), Congo, Cyprus, Lebanon (UNIFIL), Golan Heights (UNDOF), South Sudan (UNMISS), DR Congo (MONUSCO), Abyei (UNISFA) and Western Sahara. Indian women have served too, including the first all-women formed police unit in Liberia (2007). India is among the top contributors of uniformed personnel, and Indian peacekeepers have suffered the highest number of fatalities of any country. India also runs the Centre for UN Peacekeeping (CUNPK) in New Delhi, set up in 2000. Related angles are the UN Peacebuilding Commission (2005), the Security Council's role in mandating missions, and the Action for Peacekeeping (A4P) initiative launched in 2018.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. Space Exploration Technologies Corp. is commonly known as SpaceX.
2. ‘Falcon’ is a space vehicle developed by SpaceX whereas ‘Dragon’ is a space vehicle developed by ‘NASA’. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? i
subject: Quantitative Aptitude & Reasoning
detail: SpaceX was founded by Elon Musk in 2002 and is headquartered at Hawthorne, California, with launch operations at Starbase in Texas. Its Falcon family of rockets (Falcon 1, Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy) are launch vehicles, and Falcon 9 is partially reusable, with the first stage landing back for reuse. Dragon is a spacecraft launched on Falcon 9, with Cargo Dragon (Dragon 1 and Dragon 2) and Crew Dragon variants. Dragon became the first commercial spacecraft to dock with the ISS in 2012, after NASA's Commercial Orbital Transportation Services (COTS) and Commercial Crew Program funded and certified it. In May 2020, Crew Dragon Demo-2 carried NASA astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley, the first crewed orbital launch from US soil since 2011. NASA is a customer and partner, not the developer. Elimination logic: statement 1 is true, so options (b) and (d) go. Statement 2 wrongly assigns Dragon to NASA, so option (c) goes. Only (a) remains. Related: Starship is SpaceX's next-generation fully reusable super-heavy launch system, and Starlink is its satellite internet constellation.
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is true and statement 2 is false, so only statement 1 is correct.
Wrong: statement 2 is false, since Dragon was developed by SpaceX, not NASA.
Wrong: statement 1 is correct, but statement 2 is not, so 'both' fails.
Wrong: statement 1 is clearly correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: Both Falcon (rocket) and Dragon (capsule) are SpaceX products; NASA is only the customer and partner.
option_notes: Statement 1 only: the right answer. It reflects that SpaceX is the common name of Space Exploration Technologies Corp., a private US aerospace firm founded in 2002 by Elon Musk. It makes Falcon rockets, Dragon spacecraft and Starship, and runs the Starlink satellite internet service.

Statement 2 only: incorrect. It would require Dragon to be a NASA vehicle and statement 1 to be false. In fact Dragon is SpaceX's capsule, the first commercial spacecraft to reach the ISS (2012). NASA's own crew vehicle is Orion, used for the Artemis programme.

Both 1 and 2: incorrect. Statement 1 is true, but statement 2 is false because Dragon is not a NASA-developed vehicle. Falcon 9, which launches Dragon, is partially reusable, with boosters landing on drone ships or landing zones.

Neither 1 nor 2: incorrect, since SpaceX is indeed the common name of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. The company is based at Hawthorne, California, and operates Starbase in Texas for Starship development and testing.
related: SpaceX was founded in 2002 by Elon Musk
Falcon 9 is a partially reusable two-stage launch vehicle
Dragon was the first commercial spacecraft to dock with the ISS (2012)
